That put pressure on executives to\narticulate their mobile strategy as they marketed the stock to\npotential investors ahead of the IPO. While the candidates\u2019 names and faces change, the lawyers stay the same.  Attorney Michael Toner began his presidential-campaign legal career in 1996 working for Republican nominee  Bob Dole . He worked for  George W. Bush  in 2000. In 2008, his first client was former Tennessee Senator Fred Thompson before signing with party nominee  Arizona  Senator  John McCain .  Democrat Bob Bauer worked for former New Jersey Senator  Bill Bradley \u2019s presidential campaign in 2000, his law partner represented Massachusetts Senator  John Kerry  in 2004, and Bauer landed then-Senator Barack Obama of Illinois in 2008. Republican Ben Ginsberg cut his teeth in 1996 working for then-California Governor Pete Wilson\u2019s White House run before joining Bush in 2000 and 2004. Four years later, he landed a new client, former Massachusetts Governor Mitt Romney, and he\u2019s still representing him today.  At the presidential level, \u201cyou go to people who aren\u2019t going to learn on the job,\u201d said U.S. Court of Appeals Senior Judge Ralph K. Winter Jr., who taught election law at  Yale University  in Connecticut and is still an adjunct professor there.  The Fraternity  Or, as Toner put it, you go to the \u201cfraternity,\u201d a tight- knit pool of campaign finance and election-law specialists who spend much of their time in between presidential contests either helping to write new laws or blowing up the ones already on the books. Either outcome is good for business.  The five law firms specializing in presidential campaigns have been paid $50 million since 1999 by candidates, political parties and political action committees, according to the Center for Responsive Politics, a Washington-based research group that tracks campaign spending.  As candidates forgo taxpayer campaign financing, which imposes spending limits, and dedicate unlimited sums to their races, the rate of payment is accelerating.  The five firms\u2019 earnings from candidates, PACs, and party committees increased four times to more than $10 million through June 2012, up from $2.5 million for all of the 2000 campaign.  Presidential Fees  Obama and McCain spent $5.9 million between them on legal fees for the 2008 campaign, more than double the $2.5 million that Kerry and Bush spent four years earlier, Federal Election Commission records show. In the 2012 race, Bauer\u2019s firm,  Perkins Coie  LLP, is the Obama campaign\u2019s ninth biggest vendor, taking in $2 million through June 30, according to the center and Federal Election Commission reports.  With super-political action committees, organizations that can raise and spend unlimited amounts, now joining the mix, new clients are coming on board.  Bauer\u2019s firm is working for the two super-PACs trying to elect congressional Democrats, Majority PAC and House Majority PAC, which combined paid the firm $254,564 through June 30, FEC records show. Two super-PACs trying to elect  House Republicans , YG Action Fund and Congressional Leadership Fund, paid Toner\u2019s firm, Wiley Rein LLP, $165,492.  \u201cIt was lawyers who conceived of the creation of super- PACs,\u201d said Richard Hasen, a professor at the  University of California  School of Law in  Irvine . And they created them \u201cthrough the litigation.\u201d  Troubling Development  James Bopp, the attorney who filed the  Citizens United  v. the Federal Election Commission case that helped pave the way for super-PACs, said the laws have become so complicated that \u201cit\u2019s a high entry price\u201d to run for office -- a development he said is troubling. \u201cThe Founding Fathers didn\u2019t want people to have to hire high-priced Washington lawyers in order to engage in political activity,\u201d he said.  The contacts with wealthy donors and other candidates while representing the next president -- or his defeated challenger -- turns the attorneys into rainmakers.  \u201cPolitical activity and lobbying have just become another business,\u201d said attorney Jan Witold Baran, a legal veteran of the 1988  George H.W. Bush  presidential campaign, who last year convinced Toner to return to Wiley Rein.  Since 1998, Patton Boggs, where Ginsberg is a partner, has been paid $452.3 million by such lobbying clients as  Northrop Grumman Corp. (NOC) , Microsoft Corp. and Bristol-Myers Squibb Co., more than any other firm, according to the center.  More Clients  The political law practice at Bauer\u2019s firm, Perkins Coie, now lists 28 lawyers, including Marc Elias, counsel to Kerry in 2004 and unsuccessful 2008 candidate  Chris Dodd , according to its website. The firm has been paid $26.2 million since 2000 to provide legal advice for candidates and others involved in politics.  Since Toner became co-chairman with Baran of the election law and government ethics practice at Wiley Rein a year ago, the firm has earned $1.2 million for the 2012 races with Election Day still four months away. In 2000, it was paid $363,441.  \u201cYou can really get to know someone well,\u201d Toner said. \u201cIf a year later, they or their company needs legal work, you might be a natural person for them to turn to. Also from a marketing perspective, it\u2019s a highly visible endeavor.\u201d  Although the attorneys work exclusively on their side of the partisan divide, their thin ranks create deeper bonds.  \u2018Everyone Knows Everyone\u2019  \u201cI know everybody in this small circle,\u201d said Katie Biber, general counsel for Romney\u2019s presidential campaign in both 2008 and 2012 who was mentored and ushered into the inner- circle by Ginsberg. \u201cEveryone knows everyone. I\u2019ve worked with or against almost everybody who works in this business.\u201d  Baran and Bauer, who socialize outside of work with their families, were among the first practitioners in the field, meeting in 1981 when they argued a campaign finance case before the U.S. Supreme Court focused on the degree that the  National Republican Senatorial Committee  could help its candidates. Baran, arguing on behalf of the NRSC, won.  Republican election lawyers meet once a year for dinner in Washington. At Perkins Coie\u2019s annual retreat, held this year in May at Washington\u2019s Omni Shoreham Hotel, Bauer, who served as Obama\u2019s White House attorney, and Ginsberg, a Romney legal adviser, parried over the 2012 elections in front of 300 lawyers and their spouses.  Common Bonds  \u201cWorking on a presidential campaign is a unique and wonderful experience,\u201d Ginsberg said. \u201cThe people who have done that certainly share a common bond and language and an appreciation for the unique set of issues that you face.\u201d  There are also moments of mischief inside the club.  While representing Obama in the 2008 primary, Bauer was pitted against fellow Democratic legal heavyweight, Lyn Utrecht, who was counsel for  Hillary Clinton  and an alum of President  Bill Clinton \u2019s campaigns.  After Clinton supporters complained of being excluded from the Texas caucuses, Utrecht scheduled a media conference call to air those grievances. When Obama\u2019s campaign learned of it, Bauer dialed in and began refuting Utrecht\u2019s assertions as reporters took notes.  \u201cI crashed that call,\u201d Bauer said. \u201cIt was a brilliant idea that was put to me on the spur of the moment by the communications staff.\u201d Utrecht didn\u2019t return phone calls and e- mails seeking comment.  Odd Queries  Besides helping campaigns comply with election laws and crashing media conference calls, these attorneys field dozens of legal queries of all forms.  Toner researched whether special insurance riders are needed for a skydiver (yes, according to Toner), while Biber did a similar study for a moon bounce for the children of supporters attending the Iowa straw poll (yes, too, Biber said).  Trevor Potter , who was counsel to John McCain\u2019s 2008 presidential campaign and now advises comedian  Stephen Colbert \u2019s super-PAC, recalled his work for George H.W. Bush in 1988. Potter said he fielded a call from a Bush campaign staff member saying that the press plane, circling over Lake Michigan, had smoke in the cabin.  \u201cWhat do we do?\u201d Potter said he was asked. His response: \u201cI think we land.\u201d  The increased use of Web advertising is ratcheting up the speed in which the legal teams must review everything -- from the legal disclosures to the music played -- that a candidate airs publicly.  In prior cycles, campaign lawyers might review 60 national television ads during a campaign season. Now, they\u2019re asked to approve as many as 30 Web ads in a week.  With expanding workloads and profits, the political bar also is growing.  \u201cThere\u2019s now a real field called election law,\u201d said Joel Gora, who teaches that subject at Brooklyn Law School in New York. \u201cCertainly, 10 years ago there was nothing out there. Now it\u2019s a burgeoning kind of field. There is more law, and when there is more law, there\u2019s going to be more lawyers.\u201d  To contact the reporter on this story: Jonathan D. Salant in Washington at   jsalant@bloomberg.net . (GOOG)  and  Facebook Inc. (FB)  are\nholding discussions with the U.S. government to disclose more\ninformation about national-security requests, people with\nknowledge of the matter said.  The people asked not to be identified because the talks\naren\u2019t public. The negotiations follow Google\u2019s  open letter  to\nAttorney General Eric Holder and Federal Bureau of Investigation\nDirector  Robert Mueller  earlier this week, asking for more\nleeway to report aggregate numbers of data requests.  Facebook General Counsel Ted Ullyot wrote in a  blog post \nlate today that the social-networking service received\npermission to disclose some information about U.S. national\nsecurity-related orders, though it may release numbers only in\naggregate and as a range. He wrote that Facebook received\nbetween 9,000 and 10,000 requests for user data, affecting\n18,000 to 19,000 user accounts, in the second half of 2012.  Microsoft Corp. (MSFT)  and Facebook joined Google in asking for\ndisclosure permission, seeking to reassure customers that\nauthorities don\u2019t have unfettered access to users\u2019 personal\ndetails. While the companies have said they don\u2019t give the\ngovernment direct access to their systems, thousands of\ntechnology, finance and manufacturing businesses are swapping\nintelligence with U.S. national security agencies, four other\npeople familiar with the process said.  Chris Gaither , a spokesman for Google, and Andrew Ames, a\nspokesman for the  Justice Department , declined to comment.  AllThingsD reported the Web companies\u2019 negotiations with\nthe government earlier today.  PRISM Program  The role of private companies has come under scrutiny since\nEdward Snowden, a computer technician who did work for the\nNational Security Agency, disclosed this month that the agency\nis collecting millions of U.S. residents\u2019 telephone records and\nthe computer communications of foreigners from Google and other\nInternet companies under court order.  \u201cGoogle\u2019s numbers would clearly show that our compliance\nwith these requests falls far short of the claims being made,\u201d\n David Drummond , chief legal officer at Google, wrote on a blog\npost. \u201cGoogle has nothing to hide.\u201d  Secret Panel  The U.S. government program, code-named PRISM, traces its\nroots to warrantless domestic-surveillance efforts under former\nPresident  George W. Bush . According to slides provided by\nSnowden, PRISM gathers e-mails, videos and other private data of\nforeign surveillance targets through arrangements that vary by\ncompany, overseen by a secret panel of judges.  The technology companies said they hand over data to the\ngovernment only when compelled by law to do so. AOL Inc.,  Apple\nInc. (AAPL)  and Paltalk.com released statements saying they\u2019ve never\nheard of PRISM and don\u2019t give authorities access without a court\norder. Republicans will use their new majority in the House to\nbolster their campaign to extend Bush-era tax cuts for couples\nearning more than $250,000. They\u2019ll also side with companies\nsuch as  International Business Machines Corp .,  Microsoft Corp. ,\n Blackstone Group LP  and  Occidental Petroleum Corp. , which have\nlobbied against President  Barack Obama \u2019s proposals to increase\ntaxes on overseas profits.  \u201cRepublicans have pretty much staked their claim that\nthey\u2019re not going to raise taxes,\u201d said  John Feehery , who was\nan adviser to former House Speaker  Dennis Hastert , the last\nRepublican to hold that top post. \u201cRepublicans are much more\ncognizant and care more about the financial impact of these\ntaxes on jobs.\u201d  Midterm elections yesterday gave Republicans a majority in\nthe House of Representatives with a net gain of at least 60\nseats, their biggest increase since 1938. Republicans also\nscored a net gain of at least six seats in the Senate, though\nDemocrats retained control of that body. Analysts say the new\nmakeup improves the chances Congress will prevent any  Bush-era\ntax cuts  from expiring as scheduled at year\u2019s end. Businesses\nwill get powerful allies as they seek to forestall tax\nincreases sought by Obama to fund other priorities.  \u2018Pillaged by Congress\u2019  Businesses \u201care not going to be seen as a pool of funds\nto be pillaged by Congress anymore,\u201d said  Curtis Dubay , a\nsenior tax policy analyst at the Washington-based Heritage\nFoundation, a research organization that usually sides with\nRepublicans.  Still, even with the gains in the House, the Republicans\nwill need to reach compromises with Democrats to achieve\nanything of substance. The president has veto power and the\nDemocrats retain a majority in the Senate that allows them to\nprevent any measure from getting the 60 votes required to\novercome procedural hurdles.  Immediately at stake is the renewal of more than $5\ntrillion of tax cuts passed in 2001 and 2003 that expire Dec.\n31. These include lower income-tax rates and reduced rates on\nmost capital gains and dividends.  Permanent Cuts  Republicans want the cuts extended permanently for all\nAmericans; Obama and most Democrats favor extending them only\non the first $250,000 of a couple\u2019s income. The parties also\ndisagree on what to do about the estate tax, which was repealed\nfor one year for 2010. Failure by Congress to act would trigger\n$400 billion in scheduled tax increases this year and next.  \u201cWe\u2019re hoping the president puts the class warfare\nrhetoric aside, puts the redistribution ideology aside and\nworks for the better of the economy and sends a signal to the\nmarkets that we\u2019re going to prevent these tax increases,\u201d said\nWisconsin Representative  Paul Ryan , the Republican likely to\nchair the House Budget Committee in the next Congress. Ryan\nsaid Republicans would seek to retroactively renew the Bush-era\ntax cuts next year if no action is taken in 2010.  If Congress fails to act, income tax-rates are scheduled\nto increase across the board. The $1,000 per child tax credit\nwill be cut in half and other benefits for adoption, college\ntuition and child care will be reduced or lapse.  Capital Gains  In addition, incentives for small businesses to invest\nwill decrease and tax rates on most capital gains and dividends\nwill rise to 20 percent and as high as 39.6 percent from 15\npercent now. The federal tax on estates, which lapsed for 2010\nonly, is scheduled to return with a top 55 percent rate on\nestates of more than $1 million.  Most lawmakers in both parties favor retaining lower taxes\nfor joint filers earning less than $250,000. Republicans want\nto extend the cuts for everyone, while Democrats want to\nincrease the two top rates -- currently 33 percent and 35\npercent -- to 36 percent and 39.6 percent. Republicans also\nwant to keep the preferential tax rates on investments and a\nrepealed or lower estate tax.  The nonpartisan  Congressional Research Service  estimated\non Oct. 27 that it would cost the government $5 trillion in\nrevenue and interest costs on the  national debt  to extend the\nBush-era tax cuts for all income classes through 2020.  Lame-Duck Session  The interim period and the looming deadline for expiration\nof the Bush tax cuts will present Republicans with a dilemma:\nThey will need to decide whether it would be most beneficial to\nmake a deal during a so-called lame-duck session, before the\nnext Congress convenes and during which Democrats still have\nmajorities, or whether they would prefer to negotiate with\nObama on a reinstatement of the tax cuts on their own terms in\n2011, said former Texas Representative  Bill Archer .  \u201cIt\u2019s not going to be easy for them to cut what I would\nconsider to be a good deal with Democrats who\u2019ve got their nose\nout of joint because they\u2019re no longer in control and a\npresident who wants to show he\u2019s still president,\u201d said\nArcher, who became the first Republican to head the tax-writing\n Ways and Means Committee  in 40 years the last time Republicans\ntook control of the chamber from Democrats in 1995.  Still, even divided government may benefit businesses such\nas Armonk, New York-based  IBM  and Redmond, Washington-based\n Microsoft  by making it impossible for Obama to push ahead with\nproposals to boost taxes on U.S. companies\u2019 overseas income.\n Mike Fay , a spokesman for IBM, and  Mark Murray , a Microsoft\nspokesman, didn\u2019t respond to requests for comment.  Oil Companies  Gridlock may also stave off changes in tax policy sought\nby Obama that would cost oil companies such as  Occidental  tens\nof billions more a year by raising taxes on their non-U.S.\noperations.  Obama has advocated eliminating the so-called dual-\ncapacity tax credit, which allows companies to deduct a portion\nof foreign taxes paid when calculating U.S. taxes. The credit\nlowers a company\u2019s U.S. tax burden by not double-taxing foreign\nsources of revenue. In 2009, 39 percent of  Occidental \u2019s revenue\ncame from foreign sources, yet 64 percent of the company\u2019s\ntaxes due were to foreign governments. If the credit is\neliminated, companies will owe more taxes in the U.S.  \u201cThe punitive-type tax changes against the energy\nindustry will be much more difficult to pass with Republicans\nin charge of the House,\u201d said Gerald McPhee, senior vice\npresident of federal relations at Los Angeles-based  Occidental ,\nthe fourth-largest U.S. oil company by market value.  Carried Interest  The Republican victory may also give private-equity firms\nsuch as New York-based  Blackstone  some clout in their four-year\nfight to thwart efforts by congressional Democrats to raise\ntaxes on the incentive pay paid to executives known as carried\ninterest. That pay can currently qualify as capital gains, and\nbe taxed at a 15 percent rate, and Democrats say it should be\ntaxed at higher rates for wages, or as high as 39.6 percent.\nMost Republicans oppose the change.  Asked on Bloomberg Television on Oct. 30 whether a\nRepublican win would delay the tax, Blackstone\u2019s Chief\nExecutive Officer  Stephen Schwarzman  said he didn\u2019t know.  \u201cThere\u2019s a real need for revenue in the  budget  cycle,\u201d\nSchwarzman said. \u201cWhat gets through Congress, I can\u2019t\npredict.\u201d  Tax Holiday  Besides blocking prospective increases, businesses may\nfind the Republican sweep provides a ripe political environment\nfor getting through Congress some long-sought tax benefits.\nCompanies such as San Jose, California-based  Cisco Systems Inc. \nmay find new support for a temporary tax holiday on their\nforeign earnings that was rejected by the Senate in 2009.  Terry Anderson , a Cisco spokeswoman, didn\u2019t return a call seeking\ncomment.  Moreover, Obama and Republicans may cooperate on business\ntax incentives designed to stimulate the economy, said  Grover Norquist , president of Americans for Tax Reform, a Washington-\nbased group that advocates lower taxes.  That would benefit manufacturers including  General\nElectric Co. ,  Corning Inc. , and  Caterpillar Inc .  Anne Eisele , a\nspokeswoman for Fairfield, Connecticut-based GE, declined to\ncomment.  Daniel Collins , a spokesman for Corning, New York-based\nCorning, said, \u201cwe really haven\u2019t formed an opinion about what\nmay or may not happen.\u201d  Research Credit  Obama has proposed renewing, expanding and making\npermanent a tax credit for research and experimentation along\nwith a two-year period to allow companies a full deduction for\nequipment purchases that ordinarily would have to be\ndepreciated over as many as 20 years. Republicans and business\ngroups generally favor both policies, though they have objected\nto Obama\u2019s plan to offset the cost of those measures with tax\nincreases on U.S. companies\u2019 global profits.  \u201cIt would have a very big stimulative effect for new\ninvestment,\u201d and the president needs a growing economy before\nthe 2012 election, Norquist said. \u201cObama can hold his head up\nand say that was my idea.\u201d  Republicans and Obama also may find common ground on\nreducing the 35 percent top marginal corporate tax rate, the\nsecond-highest in developed countries, Norquist and Dubay said.\nDemocrats such as New York Representative  Charles Rangel , the\nformer head of the tax-writing Ways and Means Committee, and\nSenator  Ron Wyden  of Oregon have offered proposals to trim it.  Gridlock Losers  Gridlock may have a downside for companies, by blocking\nefforts to renew dozens of business-oriented tax breaks that\nexpired last January. The provisions, which are being pushed by\ncompanies including  Corning  and  GE , include a different version\nof the research credit and deferral of U.S. tax on profits from\nforeign lending that benefits global lenders including GE.  There\u2019s also a separate tax issue that requires lawmakers\u2019\nimmediate attention: making a deal before year-end to prevent\n30 million households from being subject to a $66 billion tax\nincrease under the alternative minimum tax. That parallel\nsystem, introduced in the 1960s to ensure the richest Americans\ndon\u2019t avoid taxation through the use of deductions, was never\nindexed for inflation and Congress has been forced to limit its\neffect by enacting a series of costly fixes. The latest such\nfix expired at the beginning of 2010. Republicans for the\nmost part are holding out for a full repeal. Some in both\nparties back a bipartisan proposal by Arizona Republican\nSenator  Jon Kyl  and Senator  Blanche Lincoln , an Arkansas\nDemocrat, to increase the exemption to $5 million and reduce\nthe rate to 35 percent. That compromise may be imperiled as\nLincoln lost her bid for re-election yesterday.  \u201cIt\u2019s much easier to see a compromise between the still-\nDemocratic House and the Senate on the Bush tax cuts,\u201d Stretch\nsaid. \u201cIt\u2019s harder to see compromise on estate taxes.\u201d  Dubay said he was less optimistic about the chances of all\nthe 2001 and 2003 tax cuts being extended while Democrats still\ncontrol Congress. \u201cI can\u2019t imagine that the last act of\nSpeaker  Nancy Pelosi  is to extend the Bush tax cuts,\u201d he said. (AAPL) , the maker of the iPhone\nand iPad, is seeking a patent on a technology that will make it\npossible to present street-level imaging in a mobile device.  Application  20130083055 , published in the database of the\nU.S. Patent and  Trademark Office  April 4, is for position-\ntracking subsystems and onboard sensors that enable a mobile\ndevice\u2019s virtual navigation of a location in panoramic imagery.  When the device is moved through space, translation data\ncan be used to move up or down a street, or even into a\ncommercial establishment, or navigate a turn at an intersection.  Cupertino, California-based Apple filed its patent\napplication in September 2011.  Google Seeks U.S. Probe of Patent Privateering Defended by Nokia  Google Inc. (GOOG) , joined by BlackBerry, urged U.S. regulators to\ninvestigate whether some competitors violate antitrust laws by\nhiring companies to file patent-infringement suits for them.  There\u2019s been a rise of so-called privateers, which obtain\npatents from technology companies and then file infringement\nlawsuits against the sellers\u2019 competitors, Google and BlackBerry\nsaid in an April 5 filing with the U.S. Federal Trade Commission\nand  Department of Justice . Internet service provider  EarthLink\nInc. (ELNK)  and  Red Hat Inc. (RHT) , the largest seller of Linux operating-\nsystem software, also joined the submission.  The filing was part of broader comments by the companies on\nso-called patent assertion entities, which obtain patents for\nthe sole purpose of extracting royalties. Such companies\n\u201cimpose an ever-rising tax on innovative industries,\u201d Google,\nowner of the most widely used search engine, said in the filing.  \u201cWe are also concerned with, and suggest that the agencies\nshould seriously examine, the outsourcing of patent enforcement\nby operating companies -- companies that develop technology and\nsell products -- to PAEs and the competitive implications of\nsuch activities,\u201d Google and  BlackBerry (BBRY)  wrote. \u201cSo-called\nprivateering amplifies the threat to innovation and competition\nalready posed by PAEs.\u201d  Nokia Oyj (NOK1V) , Microsoft Corp.,  BT Group Plc (BT\/A) \u2019s British Telecom\nand Alcatel-Lucent are among companies connected with these\nlicensing firms. Companies that would, in the past, assert their\npatents in lawsuits to protect their property now say they work\nwith privateers to make money from past research.  In a typical lawsuit, competing companies accuse each other\nof infringing patents and then reach a cross-licensing\nagreement, which lowers the amount of money that has to change\nhands. That type of resolution isn\u2019t possible when one side\ndoesn\u2019t make any products, and therefore doesn\u2019t have to fear a\nretaliatory lawsuit.  By transferring patents to such a firm, for a cut of any\nrevenue from a settlement or fees, a manufacturer can get a\nfinancial reward while insulating itself and its products from\ninfringement claims and limiting its legal costs, Google and\nBlackBerry said.  Google said assertion entities can increase the cost of\nlicensing because a portfolio can be split among multiple\nprivateers, each demanding a royalty. That\u2019s especially true\nwhen the larger company has patents that relate to technology\nused across the industry.  \u201cThese arrangements (and others) between operating\ncompanies and PAEs can, depending on the facts, transgress the\nantitrust laws,\u201d Google and BlackBerry wrote. (KCG)  in December, may consider an initial public offering and\nacquisitions as it expands, according to President Doug Cifu.  Virtu, which Cifu says accounts for more than 5 percent of\nU.S. equities volume, plans to add products and enter new\nmarkets as the firm diversifies its trading. It earned about\n$240 million before interest, taxes and other expenses last\nyear, according to a person familiar with the matter who\ndeclined to be named because the information is private. Cifu\nsaid an IPO could make sense under certain conditions and that\nacquisitions may accelerate expansion into new businesses.  The company, which traded only stocks listed in the U.S.\nwhen it started five years ago, now handles shares on six\ncontinents, along with  government bonds , foreign currencies,\ncontracts in energy and metals, and futures. Its profile rose\nlast year when it bid for Knight and again last month after\nChris Concannon, a partner at the New York-based firm, met with\nnew Securities and Exchange Commission Chairman Mary Jo White\nabout overseeing the agency\u2019s trading and markets division.  The firm would consider an IPO \u201cat the right time and in\nthe right market,\u201d Cifu said in an interview at Virtu\u2019s\nManhattan office. While the firm continues to build its market\nmaking, \u201cthe allure of M&A is that with a wave of the pen we\ncan get into a business and scale quickly,\u201d he said.  Profit Decline  Virtu is boosting its trading even as some rivals struggle.\nGetco LLC, which won the Knight bidding war, saw profit fall 90\npercent to $16.2 million last year, according to an April 15\nregulatory filing by Knight.  Interactive Brokers Group Inc. (IBKR)  is\ncommitting less capital to its market-making unit and may get\nout of the business if  profitability  doesn\u2019t improve, Chairman\nand Chief Executive Officer Thomas Peterffy said on a conference\ncall on April 16.  Trading firms have seen key sources of profits get squeezed\nas U.S. equities volume has  fallen  three years in a row and\nvolatility, as measured by the Chicago Board Options Exchange\nVolatility Index, or VIX, reached a six-year low in March.\nElectronic market making, in which firms earn money by buying at\nthe bid price and selling at the offer, depends on scale and\ntechnology to eke out tiny profits as the bid-ask spread across\nassets have shrunk over the last decade.  New Products  Virtu, which provides bids and offers on 205 venues around\nthe world in products from U.S. equities to silver and copper\nfutures, says its fastest growth is currently in  currency\ntrading  and providing liquidity to stocks in Asian markets\nincluding Japan and  Australia . It expects rapid growth in new\nproducts that will become available when over-the-counter\nderivatives start trading electronically under rules mandated by\nthe Dodd-Frank Act, Cifu and Concannon said.  \u201cDodd-Frank is the biggest IPO the financial markets have\never seen,\u201d Concannon said, referring to the 2010 legislation\npassed by Congress that mandated changes to the financial\nsector, including a requirement to process most swaps through a\nclearinghouse to cut counterparty risk. \u201cYou can\u2019t find a\nbetter time to be in the market as an electronic market maker.\u201d  The rules, part of an effort by regulators around the world\nto overhaul the $639 trillion derivatives market of privately\nnegotiated swaps, will boost price competition for derivatives\nand new futures, Concannon said. Virtu expects to buy and sell\n interest-rate swaps  and other products electronically on\nexchanges and so-called swap execution facilities, he said.  Market Access  Such regulations can benefit trading firms including Virtu\nbecause they establish rules everyone must follow and provide an\nentry to markets that previously were opaque and dominated by\nbanks, Sang Lee, managing partner at Boston-based research firm\nAite Group LLC, said in a phone interview. It also enables them\nto diversify their businesses, he said.  \u201cIt seems counterintuitive to some people, but it\u2019s\nactually true they like regulation, as long as it\u2019s not\nregulation that says, \u2018You can\u2019t trade in microseconds,\u2019\u201d Lee\nsaid. \u201cAs long as it\u2019s a set of rules that puts a framework\naround these markets, it\u2019s good for them.\u201d  Bloomberg LP, the parent of  Bloomberg News , sued the\nCommodity Futures Trading Commission last month, arguing that\nrules setting higher collateral standards for swaps than\ncomparable futures are arbitrary.  High-frequency trading continues to draw criticism and run\nthe risk of attracting regulation that could limit business by\nfirms such as Virtu. Hundreds of academic papers have been\nwritten and regulatory studies done seeking to gauge its impact\non trading, price discovery and competition for orders. High-\nfrequency trading relies on the automated and rapid placement of\norders, many of which are immediately canceled or updated, and\nencompasses strategies such as market making, statistical\narbitrage and momentum-based tactics.  Risk Management  Fighting the image of high-speed participants as firms that\nexacerbate volatility and trade only when it\u2019s in their interest\nhas been like pushing a rock up a hill, Cifu said. Virtu\nacquires positions by posting bids and offers and not by taking\nliquidity supplied by others, he said. It trades against bids\nand offers solely to manage risk.  \u201cWe don\u2019t try to convince the world that high-frequency\ntrading is good,\u201d Concannon said. \u201cWe simply explain that\nwe\u2019re a registered market maker with obligations around the\nworld.\u201d  Virtu also commits to providing liquidity for a certain\nnumber of shares or contracts and at certain bid-offer widths in\nbroker-run dark pools and private venues quoting foreign\ncurrencies, Concannon said. The market maker offers quotes in\nabout 30 U.S. dark pools, he said.  Controlling Shareholder  Concannon and Cifu run the firm\u2019s daily operations with\nVincent Viola, Virtu\u2019s controlling shareholder, chairman and\nchief executive officer. Viola, who was chairman of the  New York\nMercantile Exchange  from 2001 to 2004, cofounded the company in\n2008 with Cifu and Graham Free, its global head trader. Cifu,\nwho is also chief operating officer, previously was a partner\nand co-head of the private-equity group at law firm Paul, Weiss,\nRifkind, Wharton & Garrison LLP.  Concannon, a former executive vice president at exchange\noperator Nasdaq OMX Group Inc., met with the SEC\u2019s new chairman\nabout running the agency\u2019s division that regulates exchanges and\nsets policies for markets on April 10, White\u2019s first day on the\njob, according to people briefed on the discussions who spoke on\ncondition of anonymity because the meeting was private.  The lawyer and former exchange executive said he plans to\nstay at Virtu. He worked at the SEC in the mid-1990s and later\nheld several positions at Island ECN and Instinet Group Inc.\nbefore joining Nasdaq Stock Market in 2003 when it bought a\nbusiness owned by Instinet.  Silver Lake  Private-equity firm  Silver Lake  Partners LLC  invested  in\nVirtu in 2011 in connection with the market maker\u2019s acquisition\nof Madison Tyler Holdings LLC, which Viola and David Salomon, a\nformer arbitrage trader at Goldman Sachs Group Inc., cofounded\nin 2002. Virtu is profitable every day, according to Cifu.  \u201cAs a market-making firm that does not take a directional\nview of the market, we historically have not had trading days\nwhere we lose money across the firm,\u201d he said.  Virtu lost its all-cash bid for Knight to Getco\u2019s offer of\ncash and stock. Chicago-based Getco, one of six firms that\nrescued Knight from the brink of bankruptcy with a $400 cash\ninfusion in August, planned to retain the firm\u2019s public listing\nwhile Virtu intended to take it private and go public later, a\nperson familiar with the matter said in December.  An automated market-maker going public now would have to\nprove it has a \u201csustainable competitive advantage\u201d over rivals\nin a business anyone can enter, James Angel, a professor of\nfinance at  Georgetown University  in  Washington , said by phone.  \u2018Intense Competition\u2019  \u201cThe basic strategy is well known: buy at the bid and sell\nat the offer,\u201d Angel said. \u201cWhen a bunch of other people\nfigured out they could do the same thing, the result was intense\ncompetition. From a corporate-strategy perspective, the\nelectronic market-making business is hell on earth.\u201d  Virtu, which often accounts for more than 10 percent of\naverage daily  volume  in  Microsoft Corp. (MSFT) , usually makes less than\n$1,000 a day trading its shares, underscoring the shrinkage in\nbid-offer spreads and importance of managing its risk at every\nmoment, Cifu said. The company has millions of dollars in\npositions across asset classes globally at any point in time and\ncan lose thousands of dollars in a millisecond, he said.  Cifu declined to say how much Virtu spends annually on risk\nmanagement, technology and colocation services, in which its\ncomputers are placed near the trading engines of exchanges or\nother venues. Virtu has 130 employees and hires mainly\nindividuals with advanced degrees in computer science and\nprogramming, math, chemistry and physics. The\nTennessee company is also causing its business telephone number\nto be associated with the mark, according to the complaint.  American Cruise Lines says its studies indicate that by the\nend of December 2012, 15 percent of the Internet searches for\n\u201cGreat American Steamboat Co.\u201d continued to be directed to\nAmerican Queen\u2019s websites. The Connecticut company says it\u2019s\nharmed by these actions and that the public is confused and is\nlikely to assume falsely that an affiliation exists between the\ndisputed trademark and American Queen. American Queen didn\u2019t respond immediately to an e-mailed\nrequest for comment.  The case is American Cruise Lines Inc. v. HMS American\nQueen Steamboat Co. In the same case in 2012, also overseen by Payne, the court\nordered Kolon to quit manufacturing Heracron for 20 years. Kolon\nfiled an appeal and a federal appeals court granted a stay of\nthe order.  The criminal case is U.S.A. v. (AAPL) \nproduct to suffer a lack of attention? Probably not, but if it\nwere, it might be the recently revamped  MacBook Air .  Released at the same time as Lion, the new version of the\nOS X operating system, the Air at first glimpse is little\nchanged from the model that was introduced last year. But Apple\nhas made enough improvements, most of them under the hood, to\ncement its position as the most enjoyable laptop you can buy.  The Air comes in two models. The smaller, weighing in at\njust under 2.5 pounds, has an 11.6-inch screen and 2 gigabytes\nof memory. Starting at $999, it is the cheapest MacBook of any\nkind. The larger, weighing just under 3 pounds, has a 13.3-inch\ndisplay and 4 gigabytes; it starts at $1,299.  I\u2019ve been testing the 13.3-incher, which comes with a\ngorgeous 1,440-by-900 high-resolution screen. Like all the Airs,\nit uses chips rather than a hard drive to store data.  The chips take up little space, helping make possible the\nAir\u2019s lightness and thinness. And they contain no moving parts,\nmaking them more power-efficient and reliable than physical hard\ndrives, which can fail with sometimes disastrous consequences.\n(Though not for you, of course, because you always back up your\nstuff, right?)  No Waiting  Since there\u2019s no waiting around for a mechanical head to\nlocate your data on a spinning platter, the chips make the Air\nvery, very fast. From a cold start, it took me 28 seconds to get\nto the log-in screen on a hard-drive based MacBook Pro; the Air\ntook 15 seconds. Shutting down the Pro took six seconds, the Air\nthree seconds.  When Apple unveiled a redesigned Air last year, its brain,\n Intel Corp. (INTC) \u2019s Core 2 Duo microprocessor, was already antiquated.\nIt could bog down if you had too many tasks going at one time.  The new models remedy that by replacing the Core 2 Duo with\nIntel\u2019s newest-generation Core i5 processors, known as  \u201cSandy\nBridge.\u201d  Programs open quickly and there\u2019s little slowdown even\nif you\u2019ve got a lot of windows open. The zippier performance is\nparticularly evident if you\u2019re doing processor-intensive tasks\nlike editing videos.  As with all current MacBooks, you can\u2019t replace the Air\u2019s\nbattery, yet it delivers almost iPad-like performance. Apple\nsays the 13-inch model provides up to seven hours of use, but I\nwas actually able to do even better. (The smaller model claims\nup to five hours of battery life.)  Let There Be Backlight  That\u2019s especially good considering that the new Airs bring\nback the backlit keyboard that went missing with the 2010\nmodels. And speaking of keyboards, typing on the Air is a\nlargely comfortable experience, thanks to the generous expanses\nof brushed metal flanking a track pad more than big enough to\naccommodate all of Lion\u2019s gesture-based operations.  One area where the Air is a little too light, at least for\nthe moment, is in connectivity. While the new high-speed USB 3.0\nconnections are fast becoming commonplace, Apple sticks with the\nolder, slower 2.0 standard, and only provides two of them. It\u2019s\nbetting that a new kind of connection, called  Thunderbolt , will\nbe the wave of the future.  Problem is, there aren\u2019t a lot of accessories that support\nThunderbolt, and it isn\u2019t clear how widespread it will be beyond\nthe Apple universe. So far, the most impressive Thunderbolt\nperipheral out there is Apple\u2019s own $999, 27-inch  external\ndisplay , which does double-duty as monitor and docking station.\nIt\u2019s pretty awesome, but at least one more USB port on the\ncomputer, preferably of the 3.0 variety, would prove more\nuseful, at least in the short run.  Costly Gigs  The Air\u2019s other significant drawback is the cost per\ngigabyte of its solid-state storage. The base 11-inch model\nholds just 64 GB, as much as a high-end iPod Touch. The larger\nAir stores 128 GB. Doubling the capacity of each will set you\nback another $200 or $300, respectively.  Even so, the Air is a bargain compared to other ultra-thin-\nand-light laptops. For example, the Series 9 from Samsung\nElectronics Co., which runs  Microsoft Corp. (MSFT) \u2019s Windows operating\nsystem, costs $350 more than the comparable Apple. That price\nadvantage, coming on top of the MacBook Air\u2019s latest\nenhancements, reaffirms its position as the best laptop on the\nmarket.  ( Rich Jaroslovsky  is a Bloomberg News columnist. Shareholders meeting in Helsinki yesterday approved the disposal of the business that makes Lumia smartphones and Asha feature phones to the software giant, Nokia officials announced at the event. More than 99 percent voted in favor of the deal.  The sale lets Espoo, Finland-based Nokia concentrate on its network-equipment unit while freeing it from a shrinking business that struggled to gain ground against  Apple Inc.  and Samsung Electronics Co. The deal is the largest strategic change for Nokia since it stopped making rubber boots and tires and left businesses such as paper more than two decades ago.  \u201cContinuing our existing strategy would have resulted in great difficulties,\u201d Chairman  Risto Siilasmaa  told investors. \u201cWe have no doubt that this is the right decision.\u201d  Nokia agreed to sell the phone division in September, after failing to regain relevance in smartphones following Apple\u2019s iPhone introduction in 2007. Once the world\u2019s largest smartphone maker with a market share topping 50 percent, Nokia now ranks outside the top five with about 3 percent share.  Lumia\u2019s Struggle  Shares  of Nokia fell 0.7 percent to 5.78 euros at 10:31 a.m. in Helsinki. They have almost doubled since the deal was announced, bringing its market value to 21.6 billion euros. Microsoft dropped 1.2 percent to $36.74 in New York trading yesterday.  Nokia\u2019s  Stephen Elop , who joined as chief executive officer three years ago from Microsoft, scrapped the phonemaker\u2019s own operating system in favor of his former employer\u2019s Windows software. Elop, who now heads the device unit that will go to Microsoft, cut more than 21,000 jobs and shuttered production facilities in an attempt to make Nokia profitable.  Elop will get more than $25 million for completing the divestment and is a contender to be Microsoft\u2019s next CEO. Nokia and Microsoft expect to complete the deal in the first quarter.  While sales of Nokia\u2019s Lumia smartphones have steadily risen, climbing to 8.8 million devices last quarter, the device remains far behind Samsung and Apple, who sold more than 120 million smartphones in the period combined.  National Pride  Nokia introduced its first tablet and two smartphones with six-inch displays last month. The products will help Microsoft expand the Windows device lineup to better challenge Apple and Samsung\u2019s dominance of the tablet and smartphone markets.  Yesterday\u2019s meeting lasted for hours as shareholders voiced concerns over the future of Nokia, whose phones were a source of national pride in Finland and at one point were carried by 90 percent of Finns. After introducing its first handsets three decades ago, Nokia emerged as Finland\u2019s first major global corporation and symbolized the country\u2019s transformation into a technology-driven economy.  Some shareholders criticized Elop\u2019s reward as too large, while others pushed Siilasmaa to explain how Nokia ended up in a position leading to the sale. Many individual shareholders at the event supported the disposal.  \u201cI consider the sale as positive,\u201d Kari Nieminen, 49, a Finnish doctor and a shareholder, said in an interview. \u201cNokia is able to rid itself of the more unstable business and focus on growing the stable ones.\u201d  Networks Focus  Nokia lost its competitiveness in mobile phones before Elop\u2019s tenure, when the company was characterized by arrogance, Nieminen said. Nokia\u2019s  management  in recent years made several wrong choices, including not pushing forward with innovations the company made, said Veijo Laine, 66.  \u201cNow I\u2019m finally in the black,\u201d said Laine, who is retired. \u201cThe future looks good.\u201d  After the divestment, Nokia will make more than 90 percent of its  sales  from the networks business it fully took over from Siemens AG in August. Revenue at the unit, Nokia Solutions and Networks, fell 26 percent to 2.59 billion euros last quarter. The unit\u2019s operating profit, excluding some items, was 218 million euros.  \u201cNokia can now focus on its remaining business,\u201d said  Hannu Rauhala , an analyst at Pohjola Bank in Helsinki. \u201cMargins for the handset business will in the long term fall as they did in the laptop industry.\u201d  NSN chief  Rajeev Suri  has cut more than 20,000 jobs at the network unit to bring it back to profit. Nokia last month predicted improving profitability for NSN this quarter, helped by the job cuts and focus on more lucrative contracts.  Cash Proceeds  Nokia is looking for a new CEO and is working on a new strategy for a life after mobile phones. Besides networks, the company is keeping its mapping and location services business, called Here, and its technology development and licensing unit.  Among the options Nokia is considering is a tie-up with Alcatel-Lucent\u2019s wireless-equipment unit, a person familiar with the plan said in September. The deal would boost NSN\u2019s market share especially in the U.S., allowing it to better challenge larger Ericsson AB. Alcatel-Lucent shares have tripled this year and were  unchanged  at 2.90 euros in Paris yesterday.  Nokia\u2019s gross cash is set to expand to more than 14 billion euros, the highest on record, after it gets the proceeds from the sale to Microsoft. Either a special dividend or stock buyback is possible, activist investor  Daniel Loeb \u2019s Third Point LLC said last month as it disclosed a stake in the company. Embryonic Stem-Cell Patents Infringe EU Law, Top Court Says  The European Union\u2019s highest court said that stem-cell\nresearch involving human embryos can\u2019t be patented, in a ruling\nthat scientists called \u201cdevastating\u201d for medical research.  Inventions based on the use of human embryonic stem cells\nfor scientific research purposes can\u2019t be patented, the  European\nCourt  of Justice in Luxembourg said. The case was triggered when\nGreenpeace challenged a German patent awarded to Oliver\nBruestle, a professor and specialist in stem-cell research.  \u201cThis is an unbelievable setback for bio-medical research\nin the area of stem cells,\u201d Bruestle said in an interview after\nthe ruling. The EU court \u201ctook an extreme position on\nrestrictions in this area, which will have huge repercussions\nglobally, especially in the competition with the U.S. and  Asia ,\nand in scientific research.\u201d  Under an EU law from 1998, research methods that involve\nhuman embryos for industrial or commercial purposes can\u2019t be\npatented. A German court handling the dispute at the center of\nyesterday\u2019s case sought the EU tribunal\u2019s view on how to\ninterpret the phrase \u201cfor scientific research involving human\nembryos\u201d and to clarify the term \u201chuman embryo.\u201d  \u201cA process which involves removal of a stem cell from a\nhuman embryo at the blastocyst stage, entailing the destruction\nof that embryo, cannot be patented,\u201d the EU court said. The\nblastocyst stage is about five days after fertilization.  Greenpeace, which said it sued for \u201cethical reasons,\u201d\nargued the patent for a stem-cell research process developed by\nBruestle to treat neural diseases is invalid because it covers\ncells derived from human embryos. The Federal Court of Justice,\nGermany\u2019s highest civil court, last year asked the EU tribunal\nfor guidance on the case.  The court clarified that \u201conly use\u201d of human embryos\n\u201cfor therapeutic and diagnostic purposes which are applied to\nthe human embryo and are useful to it\u201d are patentable.  \u201cOne consequence is that the benefits of our research will\nbe reaped in America and Asia,\u201d said Austin Smith, a professor\nat the Wellcome Trust Centre for Stem Cell Research at the\nUniversity of Cambridge.  The ruling might actually allow scientists a \u201csigh of\nrelief,\u201d said Julian Hitchcock, a lawyer and  intellectual\nproperty  specialist in the London office of law firm Field\nFisher Waterhouse LLP.  Researchers \u201cwon\u2019t have to worry about inadvertently\ninfringing someone else\u2019s patent,\u201d Hitchcock said in a phone\ninterview. \u201cWhile the ruling restricts patentability of such\ninventions, it doesn\u2019t in any way restrict the use of embryonic\nstem cells.\u201d  While patent protection might not be available, European\nscientists can seek so-called data exclusivity, which protects\ndocumentation for as much as eight years and prevents the\nmarketing of competing products based on the same data for up to\n10 years, said Hitchcock. Copyright  Viacom Tells Court YouTube Deliberately Violated Copyrights  Viacom Inc. (VIA\/B)  told an appeals court that  Google Inc. (GOOG) \u2019s\nYouTube video-sharing website willfully violated copyrights by\nletting users post videos of television shows without\nauthorization.  Both sides made oral arguments yesterday before the U.S.\nCourt of Appeals in Manhattan. YouTube told the court it removed\ninfringing videos from the site when it was notified by\ncopyright owners.  Viacom sued YouTube in 2007, claiming the site\u2019s users were\nillegally uploading thousands of videos from Viacom as well as\nmovies from its Paramount Pictures studio. The New York-based\nentertainment company sought $1 billion in damages.  In the appeal, Viacom seeks to overturn a decision in\nGoogle\u2019s favor last year by a judge without a trial.  Viacom raised questions of fact \u201ca jury might find\nrelevant\u201d in its court papers, Circuit Judge Jose Cabranes told\na lawyer for Mountain View, California-based Google. The three-\njudge panel said it will announce a decision later.  U.S. District Judge Louis Stanton ruled last year that\nYouTube was protected from liability by the Digital Millennium\nCopyright Act because it removed the offending videos when told\nthey had been posted.  \u201cThere\u2019s no evidence of a single clip YouTube knew was\ninfringing that it failed to take down,\u201d Andrew Schapiro, a\nlawyer for YouTube, told the panel yesterday.  Viacom said YouTube was aware of the copyright violations\nwhen it displayed the videos without authorization.  The lower-court ruling, if not reversed, \u201cwill lead to\nmassive exploitation of copyrighted material on the Internet,\u201d\nPaul Smith, a lawyer for Viacom, said at yesterday\u2019s hearing.  More than 125 briefs supporting either Google or Viacom\nwere filed by parties such as the Associated Press,  Microsoft\nCorp. (MSFT) ,  the Songwriters Guild of America, singers Garth Brooks\nand Sting.  Google, operator of the world\u2019s biggest Internet search\nengine, bought YouTube in 2006 for $1.65 billion. It said in its\nbrief that Viacom was also interested in buying the site. After\nnegotiations over a content partnership broke down and Google\nmade its successful offer, Viacom sent the \u201ctakedown\u201d notices\nrequired by law when a content provider wants infringing\nmaterial removed from a site.  Viacom said YouTube offered it a partnership agreement\nvalued at $590 million before talks ended. Viacom also alleged\nthat YouTube refused to deploy filtering technology to identify\ninfringing videos unless Viacom agreed to be a financial\npartner.  The cases are Viacom International v. YouTube, 10-03270,\nand the Football Association v. YouTube, 10-03342, U.S. Court of\nAppeals for the Second Circuit (Manhattan).  Losing $13.5 Billion to Piracy Spurs Europe Law Reformers  Microsoft Corp. and  Adobe Systems Inc. (ADBE)  are among software\ncompanies that lost $13.5 billion to program pirates and\ncounterfeiters in Europe last year. Their message to lawmakers:\nLearn from the U.S. and punish the thieves.  As the European Union considers changes to its intellectual\nproperty rules, it needs to make sure that higher damage\npayments deter pirates, who often benefit because of\ninsufficient fines, said Warren Weertman, manager of legal\naffairs for the Washington-based  Business Software Alliance \ntrade group. Its members include Microsoft, Adobe,  Apple Inc. (AAPL) \nand  Siemens AG. (SIE)   In Europe, about 35 percent of software deployed on\npersonal computers was pirated every year since 2007, compared\nwith 20 percent in the U.S., according to a May study by BSA and\nresearcher IDC.  Last year, France lost $2.6 billion in pirated software,\nwhile Germany lost $2.1 billion, Italy $1.9 billion and the U.K.\n$1.8 billion. Across the EU, Bulgaria recorded the highest rate\nof software piracy in 2010 at 65 percent, while Luxembourg had\nthe lowest at 20 percent, according to BSA.  Globally, the value of pirated software rose 14 percent to\n$58.8 billion last year, almost double the total in 2003. In\n China , almost four out of five programs in use are pirated, and\n65 percent in Russia is stolen, according to BSA.  The European Commission, the 27-nation EU\u2019s executive arm,\nlast year published a report showing that some provisions of the\ncurrent law, which was introduced in 2004, need \u201cfurther\nclarification and have resulted in diverging interpretations at\nnational level,\u201d said Chantal Hughes, a spokeswoman for EU\nInternal Markets Commissioner Michel Barnier.  Software firms such as engineering and design software\ncompany  Autodesk Inc. (ADSK)  say they also suffer from so-called under\nlicensing, where clients only pay for some of the programs used.  In Germany, Europe\u2019s biggest economy, there are neither\nstatutory nor punitive damages but it is up to the discretion of\nthe court whether to fine, with no fixed amount, Weertman said.\nThe highest total settlement in an \u201cend-user case\u201d was 1.5\nmillion euros, he said. In the U.K.\u2019s criminal courts, the\nmaximum statutory fine is 10,000 pounds ($15,800) and punitive\ndamages aren\u2019t recognized, he said.  In the U.S., punitive damages are often awarded in piracy\ncases, with a statutory maximum rate per infringement of\n$150,000 if it is found to be willful, according to the BSA.  The low rate of piracy in Belgium, one of the EU countries\nwhere lump-sum or multiple damages are possible, backs up the\nsoftware companies\u2019 claim. About 25 percent of software deployed\non PCs in the country was pirated in 2010, below the EU average\nof 35 percent.  For more copyright news, click here. That case was transferred to Indianapolis federal court\nwhere it was unsealed yesterday.  The crime of economic espionage is punishable by as long as\n15 years imprisonment, and trade secret theft carries a term of\nup to 10 years, the Justice Department said.  The cases are U.S. v. Huang, 10cr102 and 11cr163, U.S.\nDistrict Court, Southern District of Indiana (Indianapolis). I then turned to a handful of disruptive experts to get their perspectives. Without further ado, the results: \n\n Established high-technology companies Winner:  Apple Runner-up:  Cisco Systems Other finalists:  Hewlett Packard, IBM, Microsoft, and Dell \n\n Apple was, probably not surprisingly, readers' most-nominated company. More than 800 readers individually named the Cupertino colossus, who drove disruption in music (iPod), mobile phone (iPhone), and retailing markets (branded company stores). As one of my experts said, \"Apple is the iconic company of the decade.\" \n\n A slight contrarian was  Clayton Christensen . He picked Cisco, noting, \"Everything that is done over the internet is enabled by them, and they are not done yet. Apple gets points for its historic efforts, but I really worry about its sustainability over the next few years.\" \n\n Established non high-technology companies Winner:  Wal-Mart Runner-up:  Verizon Other nominations:  Dow Corning, General Electric, Goldman Sachs, Ford  \n\n Dow Corning received the most nominations in this group by a wide margin. Of course, about 80 percent of those nominations came from the same Internet Protocol address, which  might  trace back to Dow Corning headquarters in Midland, Michigan. That's not to dismiss Dow Corning's excellent decade. The company's  low-cost Xiameter distribution model  is a case study example of how companies can create growth through business model innovation.  \n\n But Wal-Mart was the winner in this category. The company earned points for continuing to drive disruption in a range of different categories. As one of my experts (whose company is a Wal-Mart supplier) noted, \"The move from boots to suits has given them the ability to master change so they can keep disrupting.\" Ford could be an interesting one to watch over the next few years with its strategy of creating  small cars  that are built on global platforms. \n\n Emerging companies Winner:  Google Runner up:  Amazon Other Nominations:  eBay, Research in Motion, Facebook,  Netflix \n\n My own bias at the start of this contest was that Amazon deserved to take the crown as the overall Disruptor of the Decade. What impresses me so much about the company is the diversity of its disruptions. As Christensen told me, \"The thing about Amazon is, it isn't just retailing. It is what it is doing to publishing and Web services. I think it is very well positioned to be an integrated provider that makes cloud computing simple.\" \n\n Still, it's hard to argue with Google's disruptive success over the 2000s. \"Google has brought new consumption of information that was previously inaccessible to the masses,\" one expert commented. \"And, I think we've only seen the beginning as they try to own and integrate all of our information needs.\" \n\n Facebook is the newest company on the list. One of my experts said he expects Facebook to be acquired, but \"if it survives it would be this decade's disruptor.\" \n\n What's next? \nAs the 2010s begin, my guess is that the disruptive titans of the next decade are more likely than not to: \n Come from outside the United States.  100% of the shortlisted nominations were U.S.-based companies (though European and Asian companies received a number of nominations). That won't be true when we re-run the competition in 2020. \n Be in health care, education, or cleantech.  These three industries are screaming for disruptive innovation, and the innovators that deliver the disruptive goods are well positioned to create massive success stories. \n Originate from established companies.  Admittedly, some of the nominations in the \"established non high-technology\" company left a bit to be desired. But expect \"old line\" incumbents to increasingly figure out how to use disruptive innovation to their advantage. \n Thanks to everyone who participated in picking the Disruptor of the Decade!","path":".\/2008_2012_msft_bloomberg_news\/e-disruptors-of-the-decade.txt"},{"id":3026860,"title":"Microsoft Says Cash to Be Bigger Part of Worker Compensation","released_at":"<date>April 21 2011<\/date> <time>19:48:44<\/time>","content":"Microsoft Corp. Copyright  Righthaven\u2019s Lack of Standing to Sue Confirmed by Appeals Court  Righthaven, the organization attempting to enforce the\ncopyrights of Las Vegas-based Stephens Media Group, received no\nsupport for its position from a federal appeals court.  Ruling in two cases Las Vegas\u2019s Righthaven brought against\ntwo men who posted articles from Stephens\u2019 Las Vegas Review-Journal on their websites without authorization, the Ninth U.S.\nCircuit Court of Appeals said Righthaven had no standing to\npursue the cases.  The court noted that the agreement that purported to assign\nthe copyrights to Righthaven contained restrictions on how\nRighthaven could use those rights. A later agreement between\nRighthaven and Stephens after the cases had been filed didn\u2019t\ncure the problem, the court said, noting that \u201cin general,\njurisdiction is based on facts that exist at the time of\nfiling.\u201d  Under either the original or the amended agreement between\nRighthaven and Stephens, Righthaven lacked standing to sue for\ninfringement, the appeals court ruled, saying the lower court\nproperly granted motions to dismiss the case.  The appeals court then rejected lower court rulings with\nrespect to copyright law\u2019s \u201cfair use\u201d provisions. The court\nagreed with Righthaven and two content-owners\u2019 trade\norganizations that filed friend of the court briefs, the\n Association of American Publishers  and the  Recording Industry\nAssociation of America .  All had argued that if Righthaven lacked standing to pursue\nthe infringement actions, than the court had no power to address\nthe issue of fair use. The appeals court agreed, saying it was\n\u201cnot appropriate\u201d for it to address the issue or for the lower\ncourt\u2019s finding of fair use to stand.  Previously a federal court in  Nevada  had awarded\nRighthaven\u2019s assets to one of the defendants in the two\ninfringement cases. That court found at Wayne Hoehn hadn\u2019t\ninfringed the copyrights, and awarded him attorney fees.  In the wake of Righthaven\u2019s non-payment, Hoehn was given\nthe firm\u2019s assets, and a receiver was set up to enforce the\npayment.  That case was Righthaven LLC v. Hoehn, 11-cv-00050,\nU.S. District Court, District of Nevada (Las Vegas).  The appeals court cases are Righthaven LLC v. Wayne Hoehn,\n11-16751, and Righthaven LLC v. There were 54 percent\nfewer infections among those who used the gel more than 80\npercent of the time and a 28 percent reduction among those who\nused it least.  \n About 2.7 million people are newly infected with AIDS each\nyear, and new methods are needed to curb the epidemic that still\nravages countries in sub-Saharan Africa. Previous gels relied on\ndrugs that weren\u2019t specifically designed to target HIV, the\nvirus that causes AIDS. The new approach, in which medicines are\nused before sex to prevent infection, is also being tested with\nantiviral pills and rings inserted vaginally once a month,\neliminating the need to use the gel every time women have sex.  \n \u201cIt\u2019s a game-changing trial,\u201d said  Mitchell Warren ,\nexecutive director of the New York-based AIDS Vaccine Advocacy\nCoalition, a nonprofit group, in an interview. \u201cAt last, here\nis now proof of concept that we can use a microbicide against\nHIV. It\u2019s a transformative moment in prevention science.\u201d  \n Prevention Trials  \n Women who used the gel had the added benefit of being\nprotected from genital herpes, or HSV-2, a disease that\nincreases a person\u2019s susceptibility to HIV infection. Women who\nused the gel had a 51 percent reduction in new herpes\ninfections, said Salim Abdool Karim, the director of the Centre\nfor the AIDS Programme of Research in South Africa, or  Caprisa ,\nwhich coordinated the study.  \n Herpes, which causes open lesions in some patients, affects\nas much as 74 percent of some populations in developing\ncountries, according to the World Health Organization in Geneva.\nWomen who have herpes are twice as likely to acquire HIV, and\nblocking herpes will help the gel decrease AIDS infections over\ntime, Karim said.  \n The gel was developed by  Conrad , a nonprofit organization\nbased in Arlington, Virginia, and funded by the U.S. and South\nAfrican governments under royalty-free license from Foster City,\nCalifornia-based Gilead, the world\u2019s biggest maker of AIDS\nmedicines.  \n PrEP Theory  \n The experimental product is the first gel to employ a\nproven treatment to prevent infections, and may indicate the\nprospects for five other major trials of the pre-exposure\nprophylaxis, or PrEP, theory of HIV prevention. Researchers are\nalso testing Viread and Gilead\u2019s Truvada as a means of blocking\nthe virus in gay men, drug users and heterosexuals.  \n \u201cIt\u2019s a fantastic outcome and one that everyone should\nlook to as another step,\u201d  Howard Jaffe , chairman of the Gilead\nFoundation, which manages the company\u2019s relationship with\nConrad, said today in an interview. \u201cThe bigger line item for\nGilead is, what does this mean in terms of PrEP overall? One\ncan\u2019t help but come away from these results and feel even more\noptimism.\u201d  \n Gilead , which donated the active ingredient in the gel,\nwon\u2019t participate in the commercialization of the product in\ndeveloping nations. It\u2019s \u201can open question\u201d as to whether the\ncompany markets it in the U.S. and Europe, he said.  \n \u201cWe\u2019re not in the business of doing vaginal or rectal\ngels,\u201d Jaffe said. \u201cI\u2019ve always believed that it\u2019s easier to\npop a pill than it is to apply a gel.\u201d  \n Gilead\u2019s top three drugs, which all rely on Viread as a key\ningredient, are given to 85 percent of newly diagnosed AIDS\npatients in the U.S. Gilead  shares  rose 97 cents, or 3 percent,\nto $32.91 at 4 p.m. New York time in Nasdaq Stock Market\ncomposite trading.  \n Sexual Pleasure  \n Gels could be made more appealing by emphasizing their\nability to increase sexual pleasure, Karim said in a conference\ncall with reporters.  \n \u201cThe future is going to involve making this gel something\nthat is part of the sex act, that enhances sex even,\u201d said\nKarim. The gel in the trial \u201cis a simple cylindrical white\nplastic tube. There is no color, no design, nothing. Even Coke\nwould have gone bankrupt if they took this approach in marketing\ntheir product.\u201d  \n A product could be ready as early as 2013 if the results\nare confirmed by a second study known as Voice that is enrolling\npatients, said Warren, of the AIDS advocacy group.  \n Further Tests  \n \u201cAfter these results are confirmed in an ongoing and\nsimilar study supported by the National Institutes of Health in\nthe U.S. Department of Health and Human Services, as well as\nother studies, we will work with partners at the global and\ncountry levels to integrate this product into programs,\u201d said\nUSAID Administrator  Rajiv Shah  in a statement.  \n Conrad gave the rights to manufacture the gel to the\ngovernment of South Africa to get the product to women in the\ncountry most affected by the disease as quickly as possible,\nsaid  Henry Gabelnick , the nonprofit\u2019s executive director, in a\nstatement.  \n \u201cIt\u2019s not something that can happen overnight, but it\nshould be achievable that when you have a positive result it\u2019s\nless than three years before it\u2019s scaled up quite\nsubstantially,\u201d  Bill Gates , the co-founder of Microsoft Corp.\ntold reporters at the biennial  International AIDS Conference  in\nVienna today. His foundation helped fund the trial.  \n The WHO and the United Nations will meet with the South\nAfrican government next month to discuss how to speed plans for\nmore testing of the gel, said  Cate Hankins , the chief scientific\nofficer of UNAIDS, a UN agency. The Voice trial will take too\nlong to complete, and a quicker study may be developed using the\nsame patients from South Africa trial, she said.  \n \u2018First Time\u2019  \n \u201cIt\u2019s the first time we have something women can use,\u201d\nHankins said in an interview in Vienna. \u201cWhat\u2019s really\nimportant now is to move very, very quickly.\u201d  \n A study in pregnant women will be needed, Hankins said.\nWomen in the South African trial were taken off the gel if they\nbecame pregnant, though there were no signs of complications in\nthose pregnancies. No serious side effects were reported, and\nthere was no evidence of the virus developing resistance to\nViread, according to the study.  \n The results are scheduled to be presented tomorrow at the\nconference in Vienna.  \n In studies presented today,  Merck & Co. \u2019s Isentress tablets\nsuppressed HIV as successfully as older drugs by Abbott\nLaboratories and Gilead, and London-based  GlaxoSmithKline Plc\u2019s \nexperimental AIDS drug cut virus levels in patients for whom\nIsentress no longer worked. Research on medicines from Gilead,\nGlaxo and New Brunswick, New Jersey-based  Johnson & Johnson  will\nbe reported later this week.  \n To contact the reporters on this story:\n Tom Randall  in New York at \n trandall6@bloomberg.net ;\n Simeon Bennett  in Singapore at \n sbennett9@bloomberg.net   \n          \n          \n\n\n  \n     \n       \n     \n           \n                            \n                     \n                     Founder of Microsoft Corp.
