To contact the editor responsible for this story:\nNick Baker at   nbaker7@bloomberg.net .","path":".\/2008_2012_msft_bloomberg_news\/u-s-stocks-gain-as-dow-average-tops-11-000-on-fed-easing-bets.txt"},{"id":42123197,"title":"Apple Said to Be Exploring Switch From Intel for Mac","released_at":"<date>November 6 2012<\/date> <time>21:20:19<\/time>","content":"Apple Inc. (AAPL)  is exploring ways to replace  Intel Corp. (INTC)  processors in its Mac personal computers with a version of the chip technology it uses in the iPhone and iPad, according to people familiar with the company\u2019s research.  Apple engineers have grown confident that the chip designs used for its mobile devices will one day be powerful enough to run its desktops and laptops, said three people with knowledge of the work, who asked to remain anonymous because the plans are confidential. Apple began using Intel chips for Macs in 2005.  While Apple is now committed to Intel in computers and is unlikely to switch in the next few years, some engineers say a shift to its own designs is inevitable as the features of mobile devices and PCs become more similar, two people said. Any change would be a blow to Intel, the world\u2019s largest processor maker, which has already been hurt by a stagnating market for computers running  Microsoft Corp. (MSFT) \u2019s Windows software and its failure to gain a foothold in mobile gadgets. A move by Apple may lead others to follow suit.  \u201cApple is a trendsetter, and once they did their own chip many others may pursue a similar path,\u201d said  Sergis Mushell , an analyst at Gartner Inc. \u201cIf mobility is more important than functionality, then we will have a completely different environment than we are dealing with today.\u201d  As handheld devices increasingly function like PCs, the engineers working on this project within Apple envision machines that use a common chip design. If Apple Chief Executive Officer  Tim Cook  wants to offer the consumer of 2017 and beyond a seamless experience on laptops, phones, tablets and televisions, it will be easier to build if all the devices have a consistent underlying chip architecture, according to one of the people.  ARM Technology  Bill Evans , a spokesman for Cupertino, California-based Apple, declined to comment. Intel referred questions on Apple\u2019s plans to Apple.  Intel shares fell less than 1 percent to $21.73, while Apple was little changed at $582.85.  Apple announced the switch to Intel chips seven years ago because they ran faster and generated less heat than the products built by Motorola Inc. and International Business Machines Corp. that Apple had used. The Mac maker has in the past few years acquired chip companies, added engineers and created designs based on technology from  ARM Holdings Plc (ARM)  for its best-selling iPhone and iPad.  ARM, based in Cambridge,  England , licenses chip designs and the technology behind them to phone-chip companies such as  Qualcomm Inc. (QCOM)  ARM shares rose 2.1 percent to 709.50 pence in  London , after jumping as much as 5.8 percent.  \u2018Ambitious Plans\u2019  Semiconductor development was part of Apple\u2019s management overhaul announced Oct. 29. Chip research is being led by Bob Mansfield, whom Cook put in charge of a new group called Technologies. In the statement announcing the leadership changes, Apple said that its semiconductor teams have \u201cambitious plans for the future.\u201d  Mansfield has overseen Apple\u2019s investigations into other chip alternatives, though he didn\u2019t have authority over some of the computer scientists who specialize in writing the software that govern these chips, according to one person. These people formerly worked for software chief  Scott Forstall , who left the company in the management shakeup.  While Forstall was focused mostly on improving the mobile iOS operating system his group created, Mansfield has been more interested in melding iOS with the Mac to create a more uniform experience for all Apple devices, this person said. Craig Federighi, who now runs development of all of Apple\u2019s software, is also considered likely to push for this more integrated experience, the person said.  Thinner, Smaller  The shift is part of Apple\u2019s push to make products thinner and smaller without sacrificing performance. It is aiming to move computing tasks that now require separate parts into the central chip, said one person, who said this has long been an interest of Mansfield\u2019s. The MacBook Air, Apple\u2019s least power- hungry line of computers, would be easiest to transition to a new chip design, said Gartner\u2019s Mushell.  To make this switch, Apple could hire a contract manufacturer such as  Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co. (2330)  to build the Apple-designed component based on ARM\u2019s technology, similar to how  Samsung Electronics Co. (005930)  now builds the semiconductor inside the iPhone and iPad. Intel manufactures its own chips. Apple\u2019s $121.3 billion in cash and investments would give Cook the ability to tap new suppliers.  In addition, Cook has experience managing such a sweeping technological shift. When Apple made the switch to Intel, Apple co-founder  Steve Jobs  put Cook in charge, having him negotiate terms of the deal with Intel and organize the supply chain so the products were ready for release on time.  Past Lessons  To be sure, no final decision has been made and Apple may opt to continue working with Intel for years to come. For Apple, the risk of turning its back on Intel is a repeat of its situation in 2005, when it had to abandon the PowerPC chips -- made by Motorola and IBM -- it had used in its Mac line. At the time, its processors had fallen so far behind Intel\u2019s in performance that it decided to team up with the chipmaker. The first Mac models running Intel chips were unveiled in January 2006.  Now, as consumers and businesses increasingly turn to smartphones and tablets, mobile devices like Apple\u2019s are playing a leading role in component development. Smartphone shipments rose 62 percent last year, while sales of the iPad and other tablets more than doubled, according to market researcher IDC. By contrast, the PC industry grew just 1.7 percent.  The lackluster growth is hurting Intel. The  Santa Clara , California-based company recently reported its first sequential decline in third-quarter sales in two decades.  Intel\u2019s Challenge  While Intel so far has failed to parlay its more than 80 percent market share in PCs into a slice of the mobile-phone and tablet market, it has forced all of its rivals out of the PC- chip business except  Advanced Micro Devices Inc. (AMD)   Intel spent  $10.8 billion  on new plants and equipment last year and a further $8.4 billion on research and development, and says its manufacturing-process technology is more than a year ahead of other chipmakers\u2019. Only  South Korea \u2019s Samsung spends about as much on its facilities.  As the PC market evolves, Intel is increasingly designing its processors to work better while consuming less power, an effort to compete in the world of limited battery power and mobile devices. Its latest Clover Trail product is designed to fit into the thinnest tablets and laptops without requiring a fan to cool them.  Mobile Shift  Meantime, Apple\u2019s success in mobile computing has been central to the rise of ARM technology and its expansion into larger devices, such as tablets, that have challenged the role of larger computers running Intel chips. Apple engineers won a fight with Jobs to have the iPad built on phone chips --which use ARM technology -- rather than Intel\u2019s PC processors, according to Jobs biographer Walter Isaacson.  Apple\u2019s technologists have grown more concerned in recent years about Intel\u2019s ability to create lower-power chips. The computer maker has brought out thinner, lighter products such as the MacBook Air that have less room for the batteries needed to keep Intel\u2019s powerful chips running all day, according to three people familiar with the relationship.  The concerns came to a head in late 2011. Apple was working on thinner versions of its MacBook line, featuring its power- hungry high-resolution retina display, and Intel had failed to convince Apple executives it was serious about focusing on lower-power chips. Apple executives, including Mansfield, met repeatedly with their Intel counterparts to share their questions, and to tell the chipmaker it was examining ways to use its own chips in the Mac line, one of the people said.  Intel\u2019s Pledge  Intel helped allay some of Apple\u2019s most pressing concerns when it announced that it would develop chips that don\u2019t require as much power as existing chips, this person said. That pledge to prioritize power conservation led some within Apple to conclude the company has a few years before it would need to make any change, if it makes a switch at all, this person said.  And if Apple can\u2019t design ARM-based chips that are far more powerful than current models, the company would probably need to stay with Intel to satisfy Mac power users, who need lots of computing performance for tasks such as developing software or doing high-end graphics.  \u201cThis is a geek technical issue, but the ultimate question is could Apple keep up with what Intel is doing in terms of speed and graphics?\u201d said  Tim Bajarin , an analyst at Creative Strategies Inc. \u201cAt this moment, I\u2019m not sure.\u201d  Even so, Apple continues to explore moving in a new direction. The iPhone, iPad and Mac operating systems are increasingly sharing features. Yet the different chip technology makes it difficult to build features that work together seamlessly. For example, the thousands of applications for the iPhone and iPad and some of Apple\u2019s newest features, such as the Siri voice-command tool, don\u2019t work on Intel-based Macs. It made three months of log files from its\nsearch service available to all.  The company took many steps to preserve privacy, removing\npersonal information and randomizing ID numbers in the belief\nthat this would make it impossible to identify any of the more\nthan 650,000 customers who\u2019d used the service. But Internet\nhobbyists, professional researchers, and journalists were able\nto ferret out many of the users. No.\u20094417749, for example, was a\nGeorgia widow. Another user appeared to be planning a murder.  Today, the AOL Search Log Scandal is remembered as one of\nthe weirdest missteps in Internet history.  That took place an epoch ago, way back in 2006. Now anyone\nwith a few dollars and a knack for computers can rent some cloud\ncapacity and set up a stack of totally free technologies to deal\nwith enormous amounts of data. Managing this data is a key part\nof functioning as a large Internet company.  If you\u2019re the intelligence apparatus of a global\nsuperpower, and your job is to keep an eye on people who are\ncontemplating terrible acts, this data is incredibly valuable.\nYou\u2019re going to do what you can to get your hands on it. Once\nyou do, you can employ beautiful, supple pieces of software --\nsome with point-and-click interfaces and little icons -- to help\nyou understand what you\u2019re seeing. It\u2019s powerful stuff.  That\u2019s essentially what\u2019s been going on. From a series\nof leaks to the  Guardian newspaper  we\u2019ve learned that  Verizon\nCommunications Inc. (VZ)  turns over logs of all its calls -- the\nnumbers, locations, and other \u201cmetadata,\u201d but not audio from\ncalls themselves -- to the National Security Agency every day.  Discovering Prism  Thanks to a 29-year-old consultant for  Booz Allen Hamilton\nHolding Corp. (BAH)  named Edward Snowden, we also learned of a program\ncalled Prism. The details are uncertain: At first it seemed that\ncompanies such as  Google Inc. (GOOG) , Apple Inc.,  Facebook Inc. (FB) , and\nMicrosoft Corp. had given the NSA open access to all of their\nuser information. Now it seems that these companies are merely\nstreamlining the way that Foreign Intelligence Surveillance Act\nrequests work, setting up a secured drop-point service for the\nNSA to use.  Of course, this implies that there are so many requests\nthat a special expediting system is needed -\u2014 and since we don\u2019t\nknow how much data is being shared, nor which is domestic or\ninternational, the leak about the NSA program has become a\nglobal sensation.  Public debate about how to strike a balance between security\nand liberty in the age of global terrorism and big data is long\noverdue. And despite the insistence of the country\u2019s elected\nleaders that the NSA\u2019s activities pose no threat to law-abiding\ncitizens, we can\u2019t merely shrug off the details.  Total Absorption  The total absorption of our telecommunications system into\nthe national-security apparatus should give all of us pause. But\nit shouldn\u2019t be shocking. That\u2019s because the vast digital trove\nof secrets amassed by the government isn\u2019t a secret.  Amid all the fury over the Snowden leak, it\u2019s easy to forget\nthat when asked in a March\u00a012 hearing if the NSA collects \u201cany\ntype of data at all\u201d on millions of Americans, the director of\nNational Intelligence,  James Clapper , said, \u201cNo sir, not\nwittingly.\u201d Later, on NBC, Clapper offered this explanation:\n\u201cWhat I was thinking of is looking at the Dewey Decimal numbers\nof those books in the metaphorical library.\u201d Collecting data,\nhe said, \u201cwould mean taking the books off the shelf, opening it\nup, and reading it.\u201d  Human Card Catalog  In other words, the NSA is building a giant card catalog\nof human beings, many of whom are Americans. They\u2019re not\nactually collecting their conversations, or the people\nthemselves, but all the data about their conversations -\u2014 not\nthe data but the metadata.  It\u2019s entirely possible that Clapper believes he has drawn\na sensible ethical line here. Yet as that AOL case in 2006 made\nclear, metadata can be revealing. Search histories or call logs\nlike those the NSA ingests and presumably stores are hardly the\nsame as Dewey Decimal numbers. They\u2019re more like the index in\nthe back of a book. What the NSA seems to be doing is treating\nhundreds of millions of people like open books and indexing\nthem: Who are they, who do they know, where have they been, and\nso forth.  Data that\u2019s well-defined and cleanly organized can be\nconnected to whole other swaths of data. So once you build big\norganized indexes of human beings -- one of their search terms,\none of their phone calls, for example -- you can merge them into\none mega-index. And you can combine that mega-index with other\nmega-indexes.  Linking Power  There\u2019s enormous power in linking things. Google famously\ngot its start by judging the way one page connected to another\non the Web. Facebook has its \u201csocial graph\u201d of interconnected\npeople and organizations. Person A connects to person B, and by\ninference to all of person B\u2019s friends, too.  This capability is so powerful and compelling that it gets\nhard not to link things. That a midlevel external consultant\nsuch as Snowden could have access to so many poorly designed\nPowerPoint slides doesn\u2019t necessarily demonstrate that the NSA\nis bad at keeping secrets. It could imply that these programs\nare so typical inside the organization that they\u2019re almost taken\nfor granted. Perhaps people like Director Clapper really do\nbelieve, or have chosen to believe, that building a huge index\nto the invisible library of humanity is essentially a clerical\nact that doesn\u2019t fall under the same moral category as\nsurveillance. He might argue that a program like Prism doesn\u2019t\ninvolve digging up secrets so much as combining ways of seeing\nthe world.  Statistical Self  There\u2019s a weird side effect for the rest of us. We are not\njust ourselves anymore. Each one of us has a new, statistical\nself living in databases around the world. It\u2019s those selves,\nuniquely identified bundles of behavior, that marketers target\nand companies try to reach. These are remarkable, distributed\nportraits of what we read, what we eat, and where we sleep.  When it comes to our statistical selves, the difference\nbetween the NSA and private companies such as Facebook or Google\nor  Amazon.com Inc. (AMZN)  lies in what the government can do with the\ndata it collects. It\u2019s building that giant index so that, if it\nneeds to, it can actively cross the line between your\nstatistical self and your real, physical self. It\u2019s the\ndifference between \u201cwould you like to receive local coupons for\nbusinesses you love?\u201d and \u201cwhy is there a van in front of our\nhouse?\u201d  Less Snoopable  Do we have a choice? Not much of one, not yet. It\u2019s\npossible but very burdensome to encrypt all of your data and\nbecome less snoopable. Americans, according to polls, just don\u2019t\ncare that much about this sort of privacy. As long as the line\nbetween the statistical self and the real self isn\u2019t crossed,\nwhy worry? Full participation in modern culture, one could\nargue, requires us to continually leave these data trails, to\nbuild these other selves, all bound to be indexed inside the\nNSA\u2019s secret empire at Fort Meade,  Maryland .  Will that change, now that the extent of surveillance has\nbeen revealed? It\u2019s hard to imagine the president doing much,\nsince the executive branch has become an executive dashboard: a\nworld of online petitions and spreadsheets and briefings\nproduced from the very data under discussion. The legislature\ncould act, but no one ever went broke underestimating the\ntechnical savvy of the  U.S. Congress .  Requesting Files  There are, however, some basic questions an informed\ncitizenry can and should ask. Where is this data being\ncollected? Where does it come from? How long is it stored? Which\ndatabases are linked? And another one: Can I see? To its credit,\nthe NSA does allow you to request your own file and see the\ninformation it has on record. You can mail the request to Fort\nMeade, fax it, or e-mail it (with a special digital signature).\nIt takes a while to process; obviously the NSA would prefer not\nto share this information with you.  The irony is that the NSA is very likely the organization\nthat best understands the digital self-portraits we\u2019ve painted\nover the Internet years. Searching for terrorists, it\u2019s built an\nunbelievably large index of human events.  As the conversation unfolds, it\u2019s likely that the media\nwill focus on individuals: Edward Snowden and his motives, or\nthe terrorists caught out. But don\u2019t forget all of that data,\nall those captured moments. We deserve to know this database\u2019s\nshape and how it protects us.  As the weeks go on and people in power talk about needles,\nkeep your eye on the haystack.  (Paul Ford is a programmer and the creator of\nSavePublishing.com.) City planners are preparing a recommendation on raising\nheight limits for new buildings in South Lake Union, the former\nwarehouse district north of downtown where  Amazon.com Inc. (AMZN)  moved\nits headquarters. Vulcan Inc., Allen\u2019s Seattle-based investment\ncompany, is the main proponent of taller buildings in the area.  It would be the third time since 2005 that  Seattle  has\nraised the maximum height of buildings in and near downtown. The\npotential change, to be presented by June to the mayor, was\nspurred in part by a  forecast  that Seattle will gain as many as\n100,000 residents and 84,000 jobs by 2024. Mayor Mike McGinn\nwill make a recommendation to the city council, which is likely\nto reach a decision by the end of the year.  Vulcan\u2019s  real estate unit  owns about one-sixth of the land\nin South Lake Union, where it has added or is building 5 million\nsquare feet (465,000 square meters) of offices, stores,\nrestaurants, apartments and medical-research labs.  \u201cThere are many community benefits to building up,\u201d said\nAda M. The best solution for the city is a\nsmart approach to density that incorporates taller buildings\nwhere it makes sense.\u201d  \u2018Hottest Neighborhood\u2019  Vulcan wants new apartment towers near the lake shore. More\nstories will mean more residents, creating a  livelier\nneighborhood , generating  tax revenue  and allowing people who\nwork downtown to walk to their jobs or use public\ntransportation, which would reduce pollution, Healey said.  \u201cSouth Lake Union is the hottest neighborhood for retail\nin Seattle,\u201d said Jeremy Moller, a broker at JSH Properties\nInc. \u201cTraditional retail strongholds command higher rents and\nhave higher sales volumes, but no neighborhood has more buzz or\ninterest from retailers at this time.\u201d  A group called the  Lake Union Opportunity Alliance \nadvocates a step-down to the waterfront, with the tallest\nproperties farthest from the lake, home to Seattle\u2019s annual\nFourth of July fireworks display. The alliance doesn\u2019t oppose\ntaller buildings, as long as they aren\u2019t built adjacent to the\nwater, said Chris Gemmill, a spokesman for the group, made up\nmainly of residents and small-business owners in the area.  No \u2018Money Block\u2019  \u201cWe don\u2019t want a \u2018money block\u2019 of 300-foot towers at the\nlake, which could cause the rest of the area to stagnate\neconomically,\u201d Gemmill said in an interview. Mexico Joins Madrid Protocol International Trademark System  Mexico  has joined the Madrid Protocol for the International\nRegistration of Marks, the World  Intellectual Property \nOrganization said in a  statement .  The Madrid Protocol, established in 1989, offers a\ntrademark owner the possibility to have a trademark protected in\nseveral countries by simply filing one application directly with\nthe owner\u2019s national or regional trademark office.  An international mark registered under the protocol, is\nequivalent to an application or registration in each of the\nprotocol\u2019s member countries the applicant designates.  According to WIPO Director General Francis Gurry, Mexico is\nthe third Latin American country to join this system.  Other countries that joined the Madrid system this year are\n Philippines ,  Colombia  and  New Zealand .  WIPO is a United Nations agency responsible for the\ndevelopment and protection of an international intellectual\nproperty system. More Details  Now, as the company tries to find an alternative buyer,\naccording to its statement, Raina will probably face more\nquestions about his company\u2019s accounting and compliance\npractices. New details may emerge in court filings as he\nprepares to be questioned in two lawsuits that are headed to\ntrial.  Ebix plunged $8.72 to $11.00 yesterday in Nasdaq Stock\nMarket trading.  The SEC probe comes while the commission has begun to focus\non the type of gray areas that have been essential to Ebix\u2019s\nsuccess, namely the company\u2019s use of an accounting policy that\nallows it to report relatively high book earnings while\nminimizing taxable income.  Under Raina\u2019s leadership, no regulatory allegations have\nbeen filed against the company, and none of Ebix\u2019s four auditors\nduring the past decade has issued anything other than a clean\nopinion of its financials.  Questions Abound  Still, questions abound about the quality of Ebix\u2019s\nearnings, according to accounting experts such as Joseph Carcello, co-founder of the Corporate Governance Center at the\nUniversity of  Tennessee .  Carcello pointed to the company\u2019s use of four auditors over\nthe past decade, along with Ebix\u2019s reliance on earnings from\nforeign subsidiaries, which haven\u2019t been audited by its current\nfirm, Cherry Bekaert, according to securities filings.  \u201cYou have multiple auditor changes, the heavy percentage\nof operations overseas, the lack of filings overseas,\u201d said\nCarcello in a phone interview, prior to the termination of the\nGoldman Sachs deal. \u201cYou start putting it all together and,\nalthough we don\u2019t have evidence of anything fraudulent, what we\ndo have is a lot of questions.\u201d  Marc Cohodes, a short-seller who helped expose accounting\nfrauds at Lernout & Hauspie, Aremisoft and Computer Associates,\nquestioned the quality of Ebix\u2019s earnings and the motivations\nbehind the deal.  \u201cIn my experience uncovering and dealing with some of the\ngreat software frauds in the past, Ebix could rise to that\nlevel,\u201d Cohodes said.  Cohodes said he\u2019d \u201cnever seen a company being investigated\nor sued on so many fronts\u201d while it was a takeover target.  Sales Skills  From an early age, Raina\u2019s sales skills set him apart from\nhis peers. After graduating with an industrial engineering\ndegree from Thapar University in Punjab in 1990, he joined a\ncompany that distributed Dell Inc. computer products in  India .\nFirst in Mumbai, then in New Delhi, he became one of the\ncompany\u2019s top salesmen.  His next stops were Singapore and the U.S. There he was\nrecruited in 1997 to help turn around Delphi Information\nSystems, an also-ran in the business-to-business software\nindustry. Delphi\u2019s sales had dropped from $53 million to $28\nmillion over the previous two years.  As head of sales and marketing, Raina immersed himself in\nother parts of the company.  \u2019Very Aggressive\u2019  \u201cRobin was very aggressive, open to change and open to new\nbusiness models,\u201d said Bill Baumel, a board member at the time.\n\u201dHe was ready to be unleashed.\u201d  By 1999, Raina was pushing an entirely new platform for\nDelphi, a Web portal called Ebix. In September of that year, the\nboard named Raina, who had just turned 32, chief executive\nofficer of the publicly traded company.  Raina initially drew on the expertise of a board of\ndirectors who had deep experience in management, insurance and\ntechnology. Even as he learned from the directors, many of whom\nwere older, he clashed with them on a few issues, including\ncompensation, several of them said.  \u201dThere were a lot of battles,\u201d recalled Dennis Drislane,\nwho was recruited to the Ebix board in 2000. \u201dHe makes a\ndecision and acts. The old board wanted to see a five-year plan,\nor a one-year plan. That was not Robin.\u201d  When Raina talked about acquisitions, board member Doug\nChisholm would press him to project growth from acquisitions and\nexisting business in any given year. Raina balked.  \u2019Very Astute\u2019  \u201dHe had it all in his mind,\u201d said Chisholm, who had come\nto Ebix from Hewlett Packard Co. \u201dRobin was very astute at\nassessing distressed properties and assets, and making an offer\nto people who wanted out.\u201d  As early as 2002, after the turnaround had taken hold but\nbefore the company was flush with cash, Raina pushed the idea of\noutsourcing the company\u2019s software production to India. Several\ndirectors wanted to wait until the company\u2019s finances were\nstronger.  Raina dug in on the India initiative and set up shop\noutside of New Delhi. To showcase Ebix\u2019s new offices, Raina flew\nseveral directors to India for a meeting.  Drislane said his only issue with the subsidiary was a lack\nof transparency.  \u201cThat\u2019s where things got a little murky,\u201d he recalled.\n\u201dThere was a lot of stuff in India that we didn\u2019t have\nvisibility on.\u201d Still, he regarded the India project as a\nsuccess, he said. Jonathan Keehner, a spokesman for Ebix,\ndeclined to comment in a written statement.  Net Income  Through internal growth and acquisitions, Raina transformed\nEbix from a loss of $11 million on sales of $12 million in 2000\nto $4.3 million in net income on sales of $24 million in 2005.  He strengthened profit margins by running a lean operation,\nkeeping a tight grip on expenses and cutting staff at acquired\ncompanies. He also took newly acquired software assets and\ncombined them with operations in India and  Singapore , where Ebix\nbenefits from low tax rates  \u201dRobin was ahead of the curve,\u201d Drislane said of the\noutsourcing initiative. \u201dHe cut costs and increased\nproductivity, and he did it on his own. There were no\nconsultants, no partners. He can be arrogant and difficult to\ndeal with, but he is smart.\u201d  By 2006, Raina had replaced his old board with a new set of\ndirectors, four of whom are based in Europe.  \u201dThere were a lot of battles, and that was one reason he\nwanted a new board,\u201d Drislane said. When Chisholm\u2019s term\nexpired in 2004, he recalled, it was clear Raina didn\u2019t want him\nto stand for re-election. Baumel, Raina\u2019s biggest champion, said\nhe stepped down because of the time and travel required of an\nEbix director. Ebix spokesman Keehner declined to comment.  Foreign Subsidiaries  Along with the foreign representation on the board came\nthe addition of subsidiaries around the world, not just in\ncountries where Ebix did business. They included Sweden and\nMauritius, where holding companies were registered to serve as\nnodes in the company\u2019s complex web of financial transactions.  Even as Ebix\u2019s accounting issues have grown more complex,\nthe company has migrated toward smaller, less expensive auditing\nfirms in the U.S. KPMG LLP, which had been Delphi\u2019s auditor,\nreported potential shortcomings in Ebix\u2019s internal controls in\n2003.  In 2004, as part of a cost-cutting move, Ebix replaced the\nBig Four accounting firm with BDO LLP. BDO also identified\ndeficiencies \u201drelating to the company\u2019s internal control over\nfinancial reporting,\u201d according to a securities filing.  \u2019Inadequate Documentation\u2019  The deficiencies related \u201dto the lack of accounting\nknowledge and leadership in foreign locations, inadequate\ndocumentation for certain accounting transactions, insufficient\nanalysis and review of domestic account reconciliations, lack of\ndocumentation of development costs and related agreements, and\nthe lack of documentation to support the company\u2019s income tax\nprovisions and related accounts,\u201d according to a 2005\nsecurities filing.  Not a problem, Raina said. He and his chief financial\nofficer at the time, Richard Baum, reviewed the matter and\nconcluded that \u201dthe company\u2019s internal control over financial\nreporting is effective,\u201d according to the filing.  The willingness of the board\u2019 audit committee to allow\nRaina to ratify the company\u2019s internal controls is alarming,\nsaid Lynn Turner, former chief accountant of the SEC.  \u201dThis is not an accident waiting to happen -- it\u2019s an\naccident in motion,\u201d Turner said.  In April 2007, Ebix replaced BDO with an Atlanta-based\naccounting firm, Habif, Arogeti & Wynne.  Acquisition Spurt  During the next 20 months, Raina spent more than $90\nmillion to acquire five companies, including an Australian\nsoftware provider, lifting Ebix\u2019s revenue to $75 million. After\nthis buying spree, Habif, Arogeti & Wynne resigned as auditor in\nDecember 2008. The firm declined to immediately comment.  The timing of the resignation seems unusual, according to\nCarcello, since it occurred before the audit engagement was\ncompleted, and \u201din the teeth of the worst recession in many\nyears.\u201d  The new auditor, Cherry Bekaert, signed off on Ebix\u2019s\nfinancial statements for 2008.  In 2009 the buying spree continued, as Raina spent $62.5\nmillion on acquisitions, and Ebix\u2019s revenue grew to $97.7\nmillion. Even as Ebix increased in size, Raina maintained tight\ncontrol over accounting-related decisions, several former Ebix\nexecutives said.  Unusual Structure  Each month, Raina would meet with controller Sean Donaghy\nand Darren Joseph, corporate vice president of finance and human\nresources, to go over the company\u2019s revenue and determine how it\nshould be allocated, said two former executives, who asked not\nto be named. Absent from this group was Robert Kerris, the\ncompany\u2019s chief financial offer, who relied on the trio\u2019s\ndecisions when compiling the company\u2019s financial disclosures,\nsaid the former executives, who requested anonymity because the\nmatter wasn\u2019t public.  The structure is unusual, said Carcello.  \u201dWhenever you see a company where the CEO takes an active,\nongoing interest in how transactions are accounted for, that\u2019s a\nhuge red flag,\u201d he said. \u201cChief executives need to run the\nbusiness, they don\u2019t need to run the accounting.\u201d  Ebix spokesman Keehner didn\u2019t directly address Raina\u2019s role\nin reviewing the company\u2019s revenue allocation. He said in his\nstatement that \u201cThe CFO is an integral part of this process,\nand the primary contact with Cherry Bekaert.\u201d  \u201cThe members of the audit committee reviewed, and the\nchairman of the committee discussed with management and Cherry\nBekaert LLP\u201d financial information \u201ccontained in each\nquarterly and annual earnings release prior to the release of\nsuch information to the public,\u201d Keehner said.  More Revenues  As Ebix began to allocate more revenue to offshore\nsubsidiaries, Cherry Bekaert had to rely more on the company\u2019s\nforeign financial statements.  Several overseas subsidiaries have fallen behind in filing\naudited numbers. Ebix Singapore, which accounted for $25.2\nmillion of Ebix\u2019s $78 million in pretax income last year,\naccording to SEC filings, still hasn\u2019t filed locally audited\nfigures for 2011 or 2012.  Ebix India, which recorded $35.7 million of the company\u2019s\npretax income last year, hasn\u2019t filed audited figures for 2012.\nEIH Holdings, the company\u2019s Swedish subsidiary, is being\nliquidated by Swedish regulators for lack of timely filings.\nYet, according to SEC filings approved by Cherry Bekaert, the\nSwedish unit earned $7 million of the company\u2019s $78 million in\npre-tax income last year.  As for Ebix Asia Holdings Ltd., the company\u2019s subsidiary in\nMauritius, an island nation in Indian Ocean, the only filing\navailable online is a registration. No earnings or revenues have\nbeen attributed to the unit since its inception in 2008.  Even if Ebix finds an alternative buyer, some accounting\nissues will remain. As part of a lawsuit filed by a former\nexecutive in 2011, and scheduled to go to trial next year,\nallegations of accounting irregularities at the company have\nbeen made in court papers.  The complaint was filed in an Ohio federal court by the\nfounder of Peak Performance Solutions, which Ebix acquired in\n2009. Peak\u2019s founder, Steven Isaac, and two partners say that\nEbix owes them a $1.5 million \u201dearnout\u201d as part of the sale.  Different Calculations  Filings in the lawsuit allege that the company\u2019s controller\nand CFO provided different calculations of Peak\u2019s revenues in\nthe year after the acquisition. Peak\u2019s founders also reported\nthat an Ebix check sent to them bounced. Raina, in a 2011\ninterview, blamed the bounced checks on a mistake at Bank of\nAmerica Corp.  In a court filing earlier this month, Peak\u2019s lawyers\ndisclosed that Cherry Bekaert had notified Ebix in March 2010\nthat \u201dit had found significant deficiencies in internal\ncontrols and the company\u2019s accounting operations,\u201d including\nerrors in preliminary financial statements, schedules and\ndisclosures, insufficient analysis and lack of documentation to\nsupport revenue recognition.  Ebix spokesman Keehner said the accounting firm had\nnotified the company\u2019s audit committee of its findings. He\ndeclined further comment on the matter.  Two Subpoenas  SEC investigators, who have issued two subpoenas to Ebix,\naccording to the company\u2019s latest quarterly statement, have also\nexpressed interest in payouts that have been promised if\nacquired firms reach revenue targets, according to a person who\nhas discussed the issue with the agency.  Investigators are examining the possibility that Raina\u2019s\npreference for embedding an earnout in the acquisition price\ncould create a \u201dcookie jar\u201d that the company can later to use\nto boost income, according to the person, who requested\nanonymity because the matter is confidential.  For example, when Ebix announced the Peak acquisition in\n2009, it set aside $8 million for the purchase, which consisted\nof a $6.5 million cash payment, and an accrual of $1.5 million\nfrom Ebix\u2019s cash reserves to be paid out when Peak hit its\nrevenue targets over a 12-month period.  Microsoft Lawsuit  In 2011, after concluding that Peak failed to achieve those\ntargets -- a determination being contested by Peak in its\nlawsuit -- Ebix management reversed the $1.5 million accrual,\nwhich flowed directly to its bottom line. It didn\u2019t adjust the\ngoodwill associated with the original purchase downward. Thus,\nEbix was able to convert $1.5 million from its cash reserve in\n2009 into $1.5 million in net income for 2010.  The due diligence team at Goldman Sachs had an opportunity\nto review the claims made in the Peak lawsuit, as well as in a\nclass-action suit filed two years ago. The Microsoft suit,\nhowever, was filed after the announcement of the LBO.  Microsoft claimed Ebix breached its licensing contract and\nignored the company\u2019s demand for an audit to determine the\nextent of overuse, according to the complaint. Ebix said it was\nusing unlicensed copies of the company\u2019s software products while\nputting off Microsoft\u2019s attempt to conduct an independent audit,\naccording to the filing. Keehner declined to comment on the\nsuit.  Charity Work  Raina is eager to talk about his work in India and seems to\nrevel in the publicity. Through his charity, the Robin Raina\nFoundation, he has financed the construction of more than 1,700\nhomes for slum dwellers in New Delhi.  In various Indian television interviews, which Raina has\nposted to YouTube Inc.\u2019s website, he is referred to as\n\u201dSanta,\u201d the \u201dkindest millionaire,\u201d \u201dan angel for poor\npeople\u201d and an \u201dexample of patriotism.\u201d  Two years ago, in response to questions about Ebix\u2019s\naccounting practices, Raina passed along an e-mail account of a\ntour through New Delhi\u2019s slums with the family of one of his\nshareholders.  \u201dRobin was treated like a God,\u201d wrote Kathryn Lebovitz,\nwhose father, Steven Lebovitz of G&L Realty, owned Ebix stock.\n\u201dA group of at least 100 people followed us around chanting his\nname and waving and smiling at all of us.\u201d  In 2009, the foundation produced a documentary celebrating\nRaina\u2019s work with the underprivileged, called \u201dMere Apney,\u201d or\n\u201dMy own people.\u201d  \u2019Dilli\u2019  Two years later, the foundation financed another\ndocumentary, \u201cDilli,\u201d which celebrated Raina\u2019s work with the\nunderprivileged. It was shot and directed by Black Ticket Films.  At Ebix, Raina is less involved in day-to-day operations\nthan he was a decade ago, as evidenced by his focus on the\n\u2019Dilli\u2019 documentary. Raina\u2019s primary areas of interest are\nidentifying acquisition targets and cutting costs, according to\npeople who have worked for him.  Rolf Herter, an Ebix director, said in a statement provided\nby Keehner that \u201cRobin remains as committed to Ebix today as\nwhen he joined the company.\u201d  Last year, after former Delphi board member Larry Gerdes\nsold his own Atlanta-based company, he received a call from\nRaina. In the course of congratulating Gerdes, Raina broached\nthe idea of selling Ebix.  \u201dRobin didn\u2019t feel like the public markets were valuing\nhis company appropriately,\u201d Gerdes said. \u201dHe was frustrated\nwith managing a public entity.\u201d  Grown Weary  Raina had also grown weary of defending himself against\nshort-sellers, who have amassed a large negative position in the\nstock, said David Collins of Catalyst Global, who served as\nEbix\u2019s outside investor-relations spokesman from 2004 to 2006.  The Goldman Sachs deal would have given him a way out.  \u201dThe sale of company was Robin\u2019s only way to get his life\nback,\u201d Collins said in an interview prior to the announcement\nof the deal\u2019s demise. \u201dI can relate to a guy who\u2019s come to\nAmerica as a land of opportunity, and created huge wealth for\nanyone willing to invest in him, and he\u2019s publicly reviled and\nhis charitable activities are questioned in a purely personal\nway.\u201d  The shorts saw a dash to the exits.  \u201dWho\u2019s pregnant here?\u201d asked short-seller Cohodes, who\nhas clashed with Goldman Sachs in the past, before the deal was\nscrapped. \u201dWhat was the rush to do this deal? Why wouldn\u2019t\nanyone want the regulatory process, the legal process to work\nitself through?\u201d  Andrea Raphael, a spokeswoman for Goldman Sachs, said in an\ne-mailed statement that the bank \u201cdid comprehensive due\ndiligence over a period of months working closely with our\noutside advisors, but the DOJ investigation launched subsequent\nto our signing was a new fact.\u201d  Facebook  Raina communicates information about Ebix with shareholders\non conference calls following quarterly earnings statements, and\nat \u201cinvestor day\u201d meetings. As for his philanthropic efforts,\nhe uses his Facebook Inc. website account to expound on his\nbeliefs.  In a Facebook posting three years ago, Raina mused on the\nimportance of charity, and how his battle to eliminate poverty\nfrom the planet by 2050 helped him keep his business\naccomplishments in perspective.  \u201dAs I reflected more on what I saw and tried to think\nabout my own life, I realized that even though I had built a so-called \u2019successful business\u2019 it did not guarantee happiness to\nme irrespective of who I was or how much I had,\u201d he wrote. \u201dI\nthought I had built security, I thought I had built success. (GS) ,  Microsoft Corp. (MSFT)  and  Starbucks Corp. (SBUX)  is gathering steam to change policies in states that bar same-sex couples from tying the knot.  Two U.S.  Supreme Court   decisions  on June 26 heartened supporters of the cause while showing an increased willingness of business to back the effort. In one case, more than 200 companies signed a brief against a federal law that denied benefits to same-sex couples. Five years ago, only a handful had lobbied against  California \u2019s Proposition 8 ban on same-sex marriages, the target of the high court\u2019s other decision.  State legislators stand to feel the heat as more businesses speak out against laws in states including  Texas , Florida and Michigan that recognize only heterosexual marriage. While fewer than half the companies in the  Standard & Poor\u2019s 500 (SPX)  are based in states that allow gays to wed, most already have policies that ban discrimination based on sexual orientation.  \u201cCompanies do have the choice where they locate, where they set up shop,\u201d said Kellie McElhaney, founding faculty director of the Center for Responsible Business at the  University of California  Berkeley. Local policies on sexual orientation \u201cwill eventually become part of the choice process.\u201d  Goldman Sachs and  Expedia Inc. (EXPE)  are among businesses gearing up to support a federal bill to prevent workforce discrimination based on sexual orientation. Of Fortune 500 companies, 88 percent include orientation in their nondiscrimination policies and more than 60 percent offer domestic partner health benefits, according to the  Human Rights Campaign (014536D) .  Embracing Diversity  \u201cWe thrive as an organization because we embrace that diversity -- diversity of opinion, of orientation, of race,\u201d said Dara Khosrowshahi, Expedia\u2019s chief executive officer, in an e-mail response to questions. The online travel-booking service is based in Bellevue,  Washington .  Companies moved ahead on providing health benefits for same-sex couples and adopting nondiscrimination rules since the 1990s just as Congress went in the opposite direction to approve the federal government\u2019s rejection of gay marriage in the 1996  Defense of Marriage Act . Now, corporate America is pushing for uniform laws that protect against workplace discrimination, said Edith Hunt, Goldman Sachs\u2019s chief diversity officer.  \u201cNow you can be fired in some places just for being gay or lesbian, and that seems totally unacceptable to us,\u201d Hunt said in a Bloomberg Television interview last week. \u201cThe firm has long embraced a wide array of diversity activities and issues. There\u2019s really a very strong business case around it.\u201d  Austin Example  Kevin Johns, who heads the economic development office for the city of Austin, Texas, can attest to how a more liberal stance on social issues can help lure companies. Johns makes trips to California,  New York  and Chicago to tout Austin\u2019s support of domestic-partner benefits and tolerant attitude toward sexual orientation, even though it\u2019s the capital city of a state whose governor,  Rick Perry , is an outspoken conservative. Austin has reeled in investment from  Apple Inc. (AAPL) ,  EBay Inc. (EBAY)  and International Business Machines Corp.  \u201cWe\u2019re trying to attract the most creative, smartest people regardless of their orientation, color, sex or anything,\u201d Johns said. \u201cIt\u2019s been very successful here.\u201d  States that have authorized same-sex marriage have jumped to 13 from none at the beginning of 2004, and others, such as New Jersey, are debating legislation for approval. Of the states that bar gay unions, 29 have the prohibition written in their constitutions, including Texas and Michigan.  Microsoft, Starbucks  The federal law made it difficult to treat all employees equally, interfered with diversity efforts and caused \u201csignificant\u201d costs and administrative burdens, said  Brad Smith , Microsoft\u2019s general counsel and executive vice president for legal and corporate affairs, in a statement.  Starbucks, which has offered domestic partner benefits for more than two decades, is pleased with the court\u2019s decision, said Zack Hutson, a spokesman, in an interview.  \u201cEquality and inclusion are core values of our company,\u201d Hutson said.  The corporate support for same-sex couples, combined with the high acceptance among young people, could make it costly for states to buck the trend, said  Richard Florida , author of the best-selling book \u201cThe Rise of the Creative Class.\u201d Higher-paying jobs that require more education and creativity will gravitate toward those regions of the country that are more open and tolerant, he said.  \u2018Fractious Divide\u2019  \u201cI see this as a pretty fractious divide in our economy between the kind of places that get it and the places that don\u2019t,\u201d he said. \u201cPressure will mount in those communities, but people will also dig in their heels.\u201d  The movement has picked up speed because people look back on those who opposed civil rights for blacks during the 1960s and now want to be on the right side of history on this issue, Florida said.  \u201cI\u2019ve always looked at this as the current-day equivalent to the civil-rights movement,\u201d he said. \u201cThe gay and lesbian community is kind of the last frontier.\u201d  Companies had a more practical motive for wanting to strike down the Defense of Marriage Act, known as DOMA, said Paul Fronstin, a director at the  Employee Benefit Research Institute (0702926D) . The ruling lowers the tax bill on federal benefits for married couples for both employees and the company, and will streamline some accounting rules.  \u201cEmployers are getting a tax break that they weren\u2019t getting before,\u201d he said. \u201cCompanies like simplicity.\u201d  Creating Confusion  The decision has created confusion, he said. Companies aren\u2019t clear how to treat a same-sex couple that\u2019s legally married in one state and lives in another that doesn\u2019t recognize the union. Many are looking to the  Internal Revenue Service  to provide guidance, Fronstin said.  Time Warner Cable Inc. (TWC)  has had trouble answering employees\u2019 questions on the decision\u2019s impact, said Mark Imhoff, group vice president of human resources. Most types of benefits for workers won\u2019t change because the company already offers dependent health coverage and  life insurance  for same-sex partners, he said.  \u201cThe frustrating part for us is that there\u2019s still a lot of questions out there -- probably more questions than answers at this point,\u201d Imhoff said.  It\u2019s also unclear how DOMA\u2019s demise may affect companies such as  Exxon Mobil Corp. (XOM) , which doesn\u2019t extend benefits to same-sex unions based on how federal law defined marriage. \u201cIn the  United States , we have adopted the definition of spouse used in federal law, which has the effect of limiting coverage to heterosexual couples only,\u201d Exxon Mobil said in a May filing.  Alan Jeffers , a company spokesman, declined to comment.  Lobbying Effort  On the heels of the Supreme Court\u2019s decision, Deena Fidas, deputy director of the workplace project at the Human Rights Campaign, is focused on lobbying for the Employment Non-Discrimination Act, a bill to protect gay and transgender workers that was introduced in the Senate in April. Her group is about to celebrate the 100th company announcing support of the bill, she said.  \u201cThe remarkable fact that in 2013 you can still be fired for being gay in 29 states is so stunning and so unpalatable to most businesses that you will continue to see many more lend their name in support of legislation to fix those issues,\u201d Fidas said. Facebook\u2019s Trademark Case Against Faceporn Site Tossed by Court  Facebook Inc.\u2019s trademark infringement suit against the\noperators of the  Faceporn.no  website was dismissed May 21 by a\nfederal judge in  San Francisco .  U.S. District Judge Jeffrey S. White said his court didn\u2019t\nhave jurisdiction over Thomas Pedersen, the Norwegian operator\nof the adult-oriented social networking site. Facebook, which\nhas been in operation since 2004, had filed the suit in October\n2010, claiming it was harmed and its marks could be tarnished by\nthe public\u2019s potential confusion with the Norwegian site.  The company, based in Palo Alto,  California , which held its\ninitial public offering last week, said Faceporn\u2019s site imitated\nits pages, down to a logo that was \u201cstrikingly similar\u201d to\nFacebook\u2019s.  White said he followed the recommendations in a report by\nMagistrate Judge Nathanael M. Cousins. Cousins\u2019s report, filed\nwith the court in March, said Facebook had failed to establish\nthat Faceporn had sufficient contacts with California to justify\nthe court\u2019s jurisdiction.  Facebook was represented by Anne Harris Peck, Jeffrey\nThomas Norberg and Michael Graham Rhodes of Cooley LLP of San\nFrancisco. Pedersen, who was unrepresented by counsel, did not\nfile any court papers.  The case is  Facebook Inc. (FB) , v. Thomas Pedersen, 3:10-\ncv-04673-JSE, U.S. District Court, Northern District of\nCalifornia (San Francisco). Myhrvold\u2019s, Other Inventor Claims Properly Rejected, Court Says  A group of inventors including Nathan Myhrvold was told\nthat the U.S. Patent and  Trademark Office  properly refused to\npatent claims on two inventions related to oscillators.  Myhrvold, the former chief technology officer at Microsoft\nCorp., is now chief executive officer of Intellectual Ventures\nof Bellevue,  Washington . He characterized Intellectual Ventures\nas an \u201cinvention company,\u201d and periodically brings together a\nteam of inventors to brainstorm and come up with new ideas for\nwhich they then seek patents.  Several of the named inventors listed on the patent\napplication along with Myhrvold are members of Intellectual\nVentures\u2019 team of inventors, including Casey Tegreene, the\ncompany\u2019s chief patent counsel.  In its May 21 ruling, the  U.S. Court of Appeals  for the\nFederal Circuit, which hears appeals of determinations by the\npatent office, said the patent office was correct in rejecting\nall the claims in the patent application.  The Washington-based court noted that the Board of Patent\nAppeals and Interferences found that while the application\n\u201ccontains a well-written summary of college level optical\nphysics courses and included many of the basic equations and\nphysical parameters taught in any electrical or optical\nengineering curriculum,\u201d it failed to make a connection between\nthe theory and the technology the application covered in such a\nway that it would be possible to duplicate the invention.  Under patent law, this is called a lack of enablement. The\ncourt said that the two applications \u201cmerely describe the well-\nknown science of optical physics and suggest potential\napplications.\u201d This isn\u2019t enough information to make it\npossible for someone skilled in the technology to create either\nthe optical component described in one application or to perform\nthe method described in the other, the court said.  Manu J. Tejwani argued the case on behalf of Intellectual\nVentures. The government\u2019s argument was made by Raymond T. Chen,\nsolicitor for the patent office.  The case is In re Hillis, 11-01401, U.S. Court of Appeals\nfor the Federal Circuit (Washington).  For more patent news, click here. Lazard Ltd. (LAZ) ,  Evercore Partners Inc. (EVR)  and  Barclays Plc (BARC)  are\nbanking on a turf typically dominated by lawyers. While global\nmergers and acquisitions volume is down 27 percent so far this\nyear, patent deals have jumped in the past 12 months to $18.8\nbillion from $450 million the year before, according to\ncalculations based on data compiled by Bloomberg. The\ncompetition among Apple Inc.,  Google Inc. (GOOG) ,  Microsoft Corp. (MSFT)  and\n Facebook Inc. (FB)  to dominate the wireless market largely accounts\nfor the rise.  \u201cPatents have historically been a small, private and\nilliquid asset. Now you have money piling in from all kinds of\nsources,\u201d said Robert Heath, head of corporate development at\n RPX Corp. (RPXC) , a San Francisco-based firm that buys and licenses\npatents.  For technology companies patents have become a valuable\nasset to wield against competitors and to defend themselves\nagainst intellectual-property infringement lawsuits. Activist\ninvestors including  Carl Icahn  and hedge fund Starboard Value LP\nhave been riding the trend, urging companies such as Motorola\nMobility Holdings Inc. and AOL Inc. to extract value from their\npatents as well.  \u2018Niche Asset\u2019  Until recently, most Wall Street firms stayed on the\nsidelines in patent deals because they\u2019ve been \u201ctoo much of a\nniche asset,\u201d said Craig Opperman, partner and intellectual-\nproperty asset specialist at  law firm  DLA Piper LLP. \u201cLazard,\nEvercore and Barclays are the banks that I come across the\nmost\u201d in patent deals, said Opperman, based in  Palo Alto ,\n California .  Lazard\u2019s specialty is selling patents out of bankruptcy,\nhoned when it advised Nortel Networks Corp. on its restructuring\nafter it filed for Chapter 11 protection in 2009.  The Bermuda-based investment bank\u2019s strategy was to first\nsell Nortel\u2019s operating assets, making sure not to give away\neach asset\u2019s underlying patents, said David Descoteaux, a New\nYork-based restructuring banker at Lazard. Then it turned to\nselling Nortel\u2019s 6,000 patents that are part of the wireless\nindustry standards for devices, the so-called 4G high speed\ntechnology.  After 18 months of negotiations and an auction, Nortel sold\nthe patent portfolio last year to a group including  Apple Inc. (AAPL) ,\nMicrosoft and Research in Motion Ltd. for $4.5 billion --almost\nquintupling Google\u2019s initial offer of $900 million. The patents\nfetched a price higher than all of Nortel\u2019s other asset sales\ncombined.  Advising Google  \u201cBanks are contributing to make the patent market more\nliquid by attracting more potential buyers,\u201d said David Berten,\nfounder and partner of Global IP Law Group LLC, a Chicago-based\nlaw firm, which advised Nortel together with Lazard.  Lazard also advised Google last year when it agreed to buy\n100 percent of Motorola for $12.5 billion. The deal was largely\nmotivated by Google\u2019s desire for Motorola\u2019s patents, after it\nlost its chance for Nortel\u2019s. The sale came a month after Icahn\nurged Motorola to explore alternatives for its patents.  For Evercore, a New York-based banking boutique, patents\nwill represent as much as 20 percent of its technology business\nthis year, up from 5 percent a year ago, said Naveen Nataraj, a\ntechnology banker.  Nortel, AOL  Evercore advised AOL together with Goldman Sachs Group Inc.\nwhen it agreed on April 9 to sell to Microsoft its patent\nportfolio for about $1.05 billion, more than triple the $290\nmillion value patent-advisory firm M-Cam Inc. had estimated.\nStarboard, with a 5.2 percent stake, had been agitating for an\nauction of AOL\u2019s patent.  \u201cThe success of the Nortel and AOL patent sales has added\nto a growing awareness among large patent holders of the value\ntrapped in their portfolio of inventions,\u201d said Nataraj.  Unlike the boutique investment banks, London-based Barclays\nparlays its  balance sheet  to help patent-licensing companies\nraise equity and debt financing. It worked on six patent-related\ntransactions in 2011 compared with none in the two previous\nyears.  \u201cBig banks like Barclays can\u2019t ignore the trend because\ntoo much transaction volume is at stake,\u201d said Kirk Kaludis,\nwho runs its communications technology practice in  Menlo Park ,\nCalifornia.  Barclays was the lead underwriter on RPX\u2019s $160 million\ninitial public offering last year. Barclays also placed\nprivately this year $225 million worth of shares in Acacia\nResearch Corp., which develops, buys and licenses patented\ntechnologies.  Banker Flops  Bankers have had their flops. Last year, Evercore and\nBarclays advised InterDigital Inc., a mobile-phone technology\ndesigner with more than 19,500 patents, on attempts to find a\nbuyer. InterDigital called off the auction in January as bids\ncame in lower than expected, according to a person close to the\nsituation. Evercore alone advised InterDigital when it agreed to\nsell  Intel Corp . roughly 1,700 of the patents for $375 million,\nInterDigital said on June 18.  Lazard failed to sell 1,100 imaging patents owned by\nEastman Kodak Co. last year as the photography pioneer tried to\navoid bankruptcy. Lazard is again trying to sell the portfolio\nfor Kodak, which filed for  bankruptcy protection  in January.  Valuing a patent is as much art as science. It varies based\non such factors as the extent of its licensing, the strength of\nits validity and its expiration date, said Mike Lasinski,\nfounding partner of 284 Partners, a patents service firm based\nin  Ann Arbor ,  Michigan . Often litigation is the only way to\nassess a patent\u2019s value.  To reflect the longer time spent on a patent sale compared\nwith an average M&A deal, Lazard charges a success-based fee and\na monthly retainer, said Descoteaux. Evercore\u2019s fees are\nsuccess-based like those of a normal deal, said Nataraj.  \u201cIt\u2019s traditional M&A with a few important tweaks and some\nesoteric aspects,\u201d said Nataraj. (GOOG)  unfairly dominates the Internet search market. The\nconsumer agency  ended  the case today without bringing charges\nover the main issue -- whether Google favors its own products in\nsearch results and, consequently, stifles competition.  The  FTC  missed an opportunity to explore publicly one of\nthe paramount questions of our day: Is Google abusing its role\nas gatekeeper to the digital economy? Lawmakers, economists,\nother regulators and consumers should all be in on this\nimportant debate over whether Google is leveraging its\noverwhelming dominance of search into unassailable market power\nin other areas.  There is some  evidence  it is. When a consumer looks for\nflights on Google, the search engine first provides a short list\nof airfares offered by Google\u2019s advertisers. Next comes a\n\u201cGoogle flight search\u201d box listing the major carriers and their\nprices. Only after that do online travel services, including\nExpedia, Kayak and TripAdvisor, appear. They often provide less\nexpensive fares, yet require more time filtering through\nnumerous options.  As far as Google is concerned, it\u2019s making life easier for\nsearchers by listing its service first, and those wishing to use\nthe discounters are free to keep clicking.  Shopping Around  Price comparison websites are another example. Such\nservices, in existence since the 1990s, are highly dependent on\nGoogle, by far the dominant search engine in the U.S. and\n Europe , to bring potential customers to them. Google\u2019s own\nshopping service, Google Shopping, caught on slowly (it was\noriginally called \u201cGoogle Product Search\u201d) until Google began\ninserting its own price-comparison site near the top of Google\nsearch results, pushing down competitors\u2019 listings and thus\nreducing chances that a consumer would click on them.  Google claims not to be gaming its algorithms to favor its\nown services. Yet at a  Senate hearing  a year ago, Chairman  Eric Schmidt  said this: \u201cWe give preference in the context of our\nbest judgment as to the sum of what the person wants to do.\u201d  In other words, Google assumes that consumers who search\nfor TV prices or airfares don\u2019t want to be directed to yet\nanother search engine. As Google posted on its  blog  today, its\nso-called specialized search results \u201ccan save you the hassle by\nproviding direct answers to your questions\u201d before providing\nlinks to other sites. The strategy has worked: Google Shopping\nranks among the highest product sites, while traffic to rivals,\nincluding Nextag, Shopper.com and PriceGrabber, has plummeted.  Fair or unfair? The FTC, in considering that Internet\nsearch is free and that many alternatives are just a click away,\nvoted unanimously not to bring a search-bias case. Still, legal\nexperts are split over whether Google\u2019s practices violate\nantitrust statutes. Google may not have an obligation under\nexisting law to neutrally direct  Internet traffic , but that\ncould be because lawmakers never envisioned that one company\nwould emerge as a public utility of sorts for e-commerce.  The European Union\u2019s competition authority, meanwhile, is\nrunning a similar investigation and may soon accomplish what the\nFTC concluded it should not. Google committed to the EU last\nmonth that it would outline changes to the way it displays its\nown services in search results \u201cas compared to services of\ncompetitors.\u201d  Pushing Back  State attorneys general, consumer advocates and some\nlawmakers may push back against the FTC. Google\u2019s competitors,\nnotably  Microsoft Corp. (MSFT) , which hopes to use the same antitrust\nlaws that were used against it in the 1990s against its biggest\nrival now, are also likely to be livid.  The commission\u2019s job, however, is to safeguard consumers,\nnot corporate rivals. U.S. antitrust laws don\u2019t give\ntrustbusters the authority to protect competitors, as  European\nUnion law  does. Still, at the root of the case, on both sides of\nthe Atlantic, is the same vital issue: Is Google thwarting\ncompetition and thereby limiting consumer choice and reaping the\nbenefit? If so, it\u2019s up to the FTC to invoke relevant antitrust\nlaws and make it stop.  Ask yourself this simple question: Am I harmed when rival\nservices, whether for product comparisons, hotel bookings,\nairfares, restaurant reviews or maps, go out of business because\nthey can\u2019t compete with Google? We suspect the answer is yes. (DELL)  founder  Michael Dell  will only consider backing a buyout by  Blackstone Group LP (BX)  if the private-equity firm guarantees he can remain as chief executive officer, according to a person familiar with the discussions.  In several recent meetings in Austin,  Texas , with Chinh Chu and David Johnson -- the Blackstone executives overseeing the firm\u2019s bid -- Michael Dell said he would be more likely to support their proposal if he retained an influential role, a second person familiar with the talks said. Negotiations are ongoing and the two sides may not reach an understanding.  Michael Dell said on Feb. 5 that he agreed to take his company private in a $24.4 billion transaction with Silver Lake Management LLC. He\u2019s now using his 15.6 percent stake as leverage to preserve his leadership position as the company weighs competing offers from Blackstone and billionaire investor  Carl Icahn , said one of the people, who asked not to be named because the talks are private.  If another bid is superior and bars him from future involvement in the company, CEO Dell would cash in his shares and walk away, leaving the buyer to replace about $4.5 billion in financing he could have contributed, one person said.  Silver Lake  Blackstone had initially assumed Michael Dell wouldn\u2019t participate in a buyout with the firm, according to one of the people. Silver Lake, which until a few days ago perceived Michael Dell as hostile to Blackstone\u2019s proposal, now considers it possible that the CEO will drop out of their joint bid to back an alternative proposal, another person said. Michael Dell didn\u2019t inform Silver Lake of his recent meetings with Blackstone, one person said.  David Frink , a spokesman for Dell, couldn\u2019t be reached for comment. Peter Rose a spokesman for Blackstone, and  Charlotte  McCrum, a Silver Lake spokeswoman at Brunswick Group, declined to comment.  The offers from Blackstone and Icahn could end up being superior to the $13.65-a-share buyout planned by Michael Dell and Silver Lake, according to a statement last week from Dell. Silver Lake and Michael Dell\u2019s buyout proposal -- which requires approval from a majority of shareholders excluding the CEO -- has been criticized by the company\u2019s biggest outside investors as too low. Rival bidders had a deadline to put forth alternatives, and the company has said it\u2019s open to working with third parties on new proposals.  Original Bid  The challenges to the original bid, which came as Dell struggles to catch up with a new wave of nimbler competitors in mobile computing and business services, mean Michael Dell could lose control of the firm he founded in his Texas dorm room. His plan was to retool Dell as a maker of data-center gear and software for corporations -- without the scrutiny of public investors.  Blackstone\u2019s plan values Dell at more than $14.25 a share, while Icahn would pay $15 a share in cash for as much as 58.1 percent of the stock, Dell said March 25. Under both plans, some shares may continue to be publicly traded. Icahn\u2019s proposal wouldn\u2019t require Dell\u2019s involvement.  Blackstone\u2019s discussions with Michael Dell have been constructive, and the private-equity firm hasn\u2019t indicated that it wants to replace him, one person said. Blackstone had approached  Oracle Corp. (ORCL)  President Mark Hurd about running Dell, a person familiar with the matter told Bloomberg last month. Initial discussions included Southeastern, company executives, a special committee of the board, Silver Lake and their respective financial and legal advisers.  CEO Dell told his board that going private would be the best course of action because it would let him boost spending on acquisitions, sales staff and research and development, while investing in PCs and tablets and expanding Dell\u2019s reach in emerging countries, according to the  filing .  Undertaking those investments while trading on public markets would be \u201cpoorly received\u201d by investors since they would \u201cweaken earnings and cause greater volatility\u201d in the stock price, Dell told the board during a presentation in December.  Contentious Negotiations  The documents also lend insight into the sometimes contentious negotiations between Dell\u2019s representatives and private-equity firm Silver Lake, which came close to walking away from the deal in January, as well as a stalemate that wasn\u2019t resolved until Silver Lake upped its final offer by 5 cents a share at the eleventh hour -- ultimately boosting the bid 22 percent from $11.22 at the outset.  On July 17, Michael Dell met a representative of Silver Lake at the Fortune Brainstorm technology conference in Aspen,  Colorado , and they arranged to meet again in August.  In mid-August Dell told Alex Mandl, the company\u2019s lead independent director, that he was interested in possibly taking the company private and asked for information to study the feasibility of a leveraged buyout. The board was open to the idea. In late August, the company reported  revenue  of $14.5 billion, about $800 million less than the board had forecast in June and $300 million below a revised outlook.  Non-Binding Proposals  By the end of the month, the board had retained law firm Debevoise & Plimpton LLP and JPMorgan Chase & Co. as its advisers, and by early September, the company had entered into confidentiality agreements with Dell, Silver Lake and a second private equity firm identified only as \u201cSponsor A.\u201d That firm is KKR, according to a person with knowledge of the matter.  On Oct. 23, when Dell\u2019s  share price  closed at $9.35, Silver Lake and KKR submitted preliminary, non-binding proposals to acquire the company. Silver Lake bid $11.22-$12.16 a share for all stock excluding that of Michael Dell, whose collaboration was a condition of the offer. Sponsor A bid $12-$13 for all shares except Dell\u2019s and Southeastern\u2019s, and suggested an additional $500 million investment on Michael Dell\u2019s part.  On Nov. 15, Dell reported quarterly earnings that missed analysts\u2019 expectations and its own guidance again, causing its shares to fall about 7.3 percent to a three-year low of $8.86. By then, it had hired Goldman Sachs Group Inc. and Boston Consulting Group Inc. as advisers.  Revised Bids  Boston\u2019s research would later underscore the decline in Dell\u2019s business. The division that includes PCs would decline by as much as $10 billion in four years, Boston predicted. Acquisitions \u201chad yielded far lower returns\u201d than management had expected, the firm said.  Also in November, Silver Lake and Sponsor A submitted revised bids, and on Nov. 30, Dell expressed his enthusiasm for an LBO to the board, saying he could \u201csupply as much additional equity as might be needed for a transaction.\u201d  On Dec. 3, Goldman Sachs analysts wrote a report suggesting that Dell might be the target of an LBO, sending the company\u2019s shares up 4.4 percent to $10.06. That same day, Sponsor A withdrew from the process, later citing the uncertain market for personal computers and competitive pressures on Dell for its decision.  The following day, Silver Lake submitted a revised bid of $12.70 per share.  On Dec. 6, Michael Dell told the board he thought that his plans to invest in research, development and M&A, as well as expanding the company\u2019s sales staff and  emerging markets  operations, would be better undertaken as a private company than as a listed one.  \u2018Weaken Earnings\u2019  \u201cMr. Dell reiterated his belief that implementing such initiatives would require additional investments that could weaken earnings and cause greater volatility in the performance of the common stock,\u201d according to the filing.  On Dec. 10, the board told Silver Lake any bid would have to be significantly higher. At that point, Silver Lake said it would need to seek financing from  Microsoft Corp. (MSFT)  That month, TPG -- identified in the proxy only as Sponsor B -- also signed a confidentiality agreement with Dell, a person with knowledge of the matter said.  On Jan. 16, two days after Bloomberg News first reported that Dell was in buyout talks, Silver Lake submitted a bid of $12.90 per share, backed by commitments from Barclays Plc, Bank of America Corp., Royal Bank of  Canada  and Credit Suisse Group AG, as well as $2 billion from Microsoft.  General Electric  The board balked at the price, and said it would support a bid of $13.75 per share. Silver Lake responded that it could offer no more than $13.25, though it raised that to $13.50 later in January. Dell lowered the valuation of his rollover shares to $13.36 so that Silver Lake could raise its bid to $13.60.  On January 24, Dell advisers received calls from Blackstone, Southeastern and a so-called Strategic Party A expressing interest in all or part of the company. The unidentified party is General Electric Co., which sought Dell\u2019s financial services division, a person with knowledge of the matter said.  Silver Lake raised its bid to $13.65 per share on Feb. 4. After meeting throughout the day, Dell\u2019s board finalized the merger agreement, which included a go-shop period, and announced its plans the next morning.  Employment Agreement  During the go-shop process, Evercore Partners Inc. contacted 67 parties, including 19 potential strategic bidders, 18 financial sponsors and 30 others, including sovereign wealth funds. Four others expressed interest unsolicited. Altogether, 11 parties were open to a transaction, but only three -- Icahn, Blackstone and Strategic Party A -- submitted proposals by the end of the go-shop process on March 23. Two days later, the board said in a press release that it would support the merger agreement with Silver Lake while continuing negotiations with Blackstone and Icahn.  Michael Dell\u2019s employment agreement with the Silver Lake group entails a stock-option grant with an aggregate exercise price of $150 million. The company didn\u2019t give an estimate of the value of those options, which have a 10-year term. The company estimated last year that a 2011 10-year option grant to Dell was worth about one-third of the options\u2019 exercise price. The Silver Lake group may strike employment agreements with the company\u2019s other top executives and let them invest in the new company, according to the filing. Levin today labeled them \u201cghost companies.\u201d  The offshore entities of the Cupertino, California-based company have paid little or no tax in recent years, the congressional report said. If Apple brought that money back to the U.S., the company would owe $13.8 billion, according to the filings.  The panel\u2019s report is designed to be a \u201ccase study\u201d of how a company is able to pay an effective tax rate much lower than the 35 percent U.S. corporate rate, according to staff members on the subcommittee. (AAPL)  employees located at its California headquarters. All 33 ASI board meetings between May 2006 and March 2012 took place in Cupertino, the report found.  ASI buys Apple\u2019s finished products from a Chinese manufacturer, resells them at a higher price to Apple affiliates and retains the profits, the report said.  From 2009 to 2012, the ASI arrangement facilitated a shift of about $74 billion in global profits away from the U.S., the report said, and the entity paid little in taxes worldwide. The report said Apple benefits from part of the so-called \u201ccheck-the-box\u201d tax regulations. Those rules allow dividends, royalties and other fees of lower-tiered subsidiaries to avoid IRS scrutiny because they can be marked as \u201cdisregarded\u201d and no longer considered separate entities. The \u201cpassive income\u201d paid by the subsidiaries to a higher-tiered parent company effectively disappears, the report said.  $9 Billion  Using this method, Apple avoided paying $9 billion in U.S. taxes in 2012, the report found.
