Regan at \n mregan12@bloomberg.net","path":".\/2008_2012_msft_bloomberg_news\/asian-stocks-advance-as-won-climbs-aussie-drops.txt"},{"id":40742410,"title":"Apple Goes Into Debt to Make a Fortune","released_at":"<date>May 1 2013<\/date> <time>17:09:33<\/time>","content":"At first, it struck many people (including me) as passing strange that Apple Inc., which is sitting on a $145 billion cash stockpile, would partially finance a $100 billion reward for shareholders  by issuing  $17 billion in debt.  Apple's annual cash flow, moreover, is twice the size of the debt issue.  Turns out, $102 billion of that mountain of cash is sitting in overseas accounts. Apple doesn't want to pay the corporate tax bill that would come due if it brought the money home to pay dividends or to buy back its shares. Instead, it's selling $17 billion of corporate debt. That's how twisted the corporate-finance logic and corporate-tax system seem to have gotten in the U.S. A major company is taking on a huge amount of debt, interest payments on which will be tax-deductible, to reward its shareholders. Meanwhile, the company avoids repatriating overseas profits, which would have been taxable once they entered the U.S., depriving American taxpayers of much-needed revenue.  It all makes perfect sense if you're Apple Chief Executive Officer Tim Cook. First, the debt allows him to make good on his recent pledge to return $100 billion to shareholders through 2015. Cook is fighting the perception that Apple is hoarding cash because it can't figure out what to do with it -- and that its extraordinary pace of innovation is slowing down. The company's share price had plunged 44 percent in the last seven months to $390, from a high of $702 in September. The shares have since rebounded to about $443.  Apple had its first profit decline in a decade last quarter, in the face of competition in mobile devices from Samsung Electronics Co. Large shareholders, notably hedge fund manager David Einhorn, are demanding special payouts to reward their patience, and Cook hopes the $100 billion will silence them. It will cost him far less to borrow the money than to would to pay corporate taxes on repatriated funds.  Second, because Apple's balance sheet is so stellar, it can borrow at interest rates that are only slightly higher than what the U.S. Treasury pays, and barely above the rate at which banks say they can borrow from each other, as measured by the London interbank offered rate.  Bloomberg News reports that Apple's five-year notes pay 40 basis points, or 0.4 percentage point, more than similar-maturity Treasuries. Its 10-year securities are yielding 75 basis points more than Treasuries and its 30-year bonds are paying an extra 100 points. Third, at a time when the U.S. Federal Reserve is snapping up Treasuries and driving down interest rates, institutional investors and even sovereign governments must look elsewhere for extremely safe, high-yielding investments. The demand is driving down borrowing costs: Average yields on investment-grade debt worldwide dropped to a record-low 2.45 percent this week, from 3.37 percent a year ago, according to Bank of America Merrill Lynch's Global Corporate Index. Apple isn't the only company taking advantage of the situation. Microsoft Corp. last week issued $1.95 billion in debt. Microsoft  sold  10-year, 2.375 percent securities at a yield 70 basis points higher than Treasuries -- an even tighter spread than that on Apple's 10-year bonds.  So Apple's bond sale, its first since 1996, is being welcomed with open arms. It is the largest U.S. dollar-denominated corporate offering on record. (Roche Holding AG did a $16.5 billion deal in 2009.) My only question: Where do I go to get cheap money like that?  (Paula Dwyer is a member of the Bloomberg View editorial board. BlackBerry\u2019s sales have tumbled 44 percent since 2011. Investors are seeking yields of about 5.3 percent to take on the risk of offering loans to single-B rated firms this month, according to Standard &Poor\u2019s Capital IQ Leveraged Commentary and Data. The information again comes from former NSA contractor Edward Snowden, via the weekly magazine Der Spiegel. Merkel called U.S. President Barack Obama to ask if the spying allegation was true, and Obama replied that the U.S. government \"is not monitoring and will not monitor\" her communications, ostensibly declining to say whether it did so in the past. To Germans, staunch U.S. allies in Europe, U.S. spying on their popular chancellor would constitute a major breach of trust. It will probably prompt Germany to back a new European  data-protection  law that would, among other things, allow internet users to opt out of providing personal information to companies like Google. For U.S. internet giants, the law might mean an overhaul of their business models. They would pay a heavy price for cooperating with the U.S. government in its spying efforts revealed by Snowden. EU  summit  to agree new digital policy, push banking union According to the draft conclusions of the EU summit starting Oct. 24, European leaders will concentrate on adopting a common digital policy that includes investments in infrastructure and ICT training as well as moving toward a single digital and mobile services market. The data protection issue, forced onto the agenda by recent U.S. cyber-intelligence scandals, will be discussed. Two other areas of importance are the banking union and immigration. The leaders will seek to agree on a \"single resolution mechanism\" and euro area-wide deposit guarantee. On immigration, Italy and Spain will push for more EU aid to prevent disasters like two recent ones near the Italian island of Lampedusa, where hundreds of asylum seekers drowned when their overloaded boats foundered. Money is unlikely to be forthcoming, however. Perhaps the biggest factor affecting EU decisions now is Germany's desire to cut the cost of European solidarity without appearing uncooperative. Thus, on the banking union, Germany will insist that deposit guarantees and bailout funding only be available for the 130 large banks directly supervised by the European Central Bank. End of Spanish  recession  confirmed Spain's central bank confirmed that the fourth largest economy in the EU is out of a prolonged recession, posting 0.1 percent gross domestic product growth in the third quarter. This is psychologically important news for investors, who drove up the price of Spanish bonds after the announcement. It is also considered smart these days to invest in Spanish equities, even Microsoft co-founder Bill Gates having acquired a stake in the construction company FCC. Yet as the economy expanded, domestic demand in Spain shrank 0.3 percent quarter-on-quarter. Only exports are showing any real growth. It might not be wise to make a wholesale bet on Spanish stocks and bonds despite the formal signs of recovery. GlaxoSmithKline growth stalls on China  bribery  charges U.K.-based GlaxoSmithKline's quarterly results showed a 61 percent drop in pharmaceutical and vaccine sales in China, formerly a major growth area. Glaxo and other European companies are under investigation for bribery in China, some of their employees detained. As a result, doctors hesitate to prescribe Glaxo products, fearing they will be accused of being on the company's payroll. For the company as a whole, this is not a major disaster: China accounted for only 4 percent of its sales. Yet quarterly sales were flat at $10.6 billion, and profit fell 12 percent to $1.6 billion year-on-year. Emerging markets provide a powerful growth opportunity, but it does not pay to milk it too crudely, especially in a highly competitive industry like pharma. Glaxo's competitors such as Novartis and Roche, have reported healthy growth in China. French  prefer  interior minister to Hollande Francois Hollande may be the first French president since 1974 not in a position to run for a second term in office. A poll commissioned by Le Figaro Magazine said 80 percent of the French do not believe the Socialist leader would win against a center-right candidate in the 2017 election. His interior minister Manual Valls could, though: 54 percent of those polled believe so. In fact, 33 percent of those polled would like Valls to be the Socialist candidate for president in 2017, compared to only 9 percent for Hollande. Valls is known for his hardline stand on immigration, and his popularity reflects a shift to the right, even though Socialist Party supporters still prefer Hollande. It is still early days to talk about who might win the next election, but it's clear that France's indecisive leader has squandered his popularity in just two years in power. It will be an uphill battle for Hollande to regain it as he faces strong competition within his own party. (Leonid Bershidsky, an editor and novelist, is a Bloomberg View contributor. Regulators now agree with them.  The U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission exempted\nventure firms last week from a rule that requires private equity\nfunds and hedge funds to register with the regulator, saving\nthem millions in compliance fees and sparing their investments\nfrom a greater degree of scrutiny.  The ruling marked a victory for an industry that champions\nitself as having spent a half-century backing startups that\nlater emerged as technology stalwarts such as  Cisco Systems\nInc. (CSCO) ,  Microsoft Corp. (MSFT) ,  Google Inc. (GOOG)  and Facebook Inc. Too much\nregulation, the venture capital industry said, would harm its\nability to fund innovation and support job creation, while doing\nnothing to protect the country from another financial crisis.  \u201cThe venture industry is never going to create systemic\nrisk, so let\u2019s not screw up the golden goose that\u2019s producing so\nmany jobs and doing so much to stimulate the economy,\u201d said Bob Goodman, a partner at Bessemer Venture Partners in Larchmont,\n New York , and a director at the  National Venture Capital\nAssociation . \u201c Washington  has done the right thing.\u201d  Similar Structures  Venture capitalists, private equity firms and hedge funds\nare often grouped together because they are structured\nsimilarly. Partners in each get paid a management fee, which is\ntypically about 2 percent of a fund\u2019s assets, and a performance\nfee of 20 percent or more of profit from the investments.  Venture firms are different in that capital is used to fund\nnew companies and often enables startups to bolster their\nworkforce.  Hedge funds  invest in assets, including stocks, bonds\nand commodities. Private equity firms usually purchase all or\npart of existing companies, often using borrowed capital, with\nthe goal of eventually selling their stake for a profit.  Firms that borrow are considered a greater financial risk,\nbecause swings in the economy can hurt their ability to repay\nthe lenders. The credit crisis of 2008 was caused by individuals\nand corporations defaulting on loans.  In 2010, venture funds in the U.S. raised $12.3 billion,\ncompared with $85.1 billion for private equity funds and $22.6\nbillion for hedge funds, according to data cited by the SEC.\nVenture funds managed $176.7 billion in assets at the end of\nlast year, compared with $1.7 trillion at global hedge funds,\nthe agency said.  Disclosure Requirement  SEC commissioners voted 3-2 on June 22 to approve a Dodd-\nFrank Act measure calling for about 750 private fund advisers to\npublicly disclose data about their investors and employees,\nassets under management and potential conflicts of interest.  Venture firms are excluded from having to report, assuming\nthey commit at least 80 percent of their capital to traditional\nventure investments and don\u2019t borrow funds to finance deals. The\nrules only apply to new funds, while firms with less than $150\nmillion in assets under management are automatically exempted.  In a letter to the SEC lobbying for an exemption, the NVCA\ncited a 2009 study from research firm  IHS Global Insight , which\nsaid that venture-backed companies in 2008 accounted for 12.1\nmillion jobs, or 11 percent of private-sector employment, and\n$2.9 trillion in revenue in the U.S.  While the NVCA succeeded in keeping members from having to\nregister, exempt firms are required to file a minimal amount of\ninformation with the SEC, such as business activities and\ncontrolling individuals. The SEC has a one-year window to ask\nfor more information.  \u2018A Different Environment\u2019  \u201cThis puts the venture capital community on notice that we\nare playing in a different environment today than before the\nmeltdown,\u201d said  Mark Heesen , chairman of the Arlington,\nVirginia-based NVCA, which represents more than 400 U.S. venture\nfirms. \u201cThe government, like it or not, is going to be looking\nover your shoulder.\u201d  Firms with more than 20 percent of assets in nontraditional\nventure investments will have to report with the SEC. For\nexample, investments in startups purchased on secondary markets\n-- including exchanges like SharesPost Inc. -- would fall into\nthat category. Morgenthaler Partners, with $3 billion under\nmanagement, has separate funds dedicated to venture capital and\nprivate equity, and thus may have to disclose. Ching Wu, a\nspokeswoman at Morgenthaler, declined to comment.  Still, for the industry, the burden could have been\nheavier. Venture capitalists have estimated in interviews that\ncosts to their firms for full SEC reporting would have been\n$500,000 to $1 million a year. About 280 U.S. firms have more\nthan $150 million in assets, so an unfavorable ruling would have\ncost the industry at least $140 million a year.  \u2018Existential Threat\u2019  Beyond the costs, regulation would hinder venture firms\u2019\nability to operate because they would have to disclose data on\nearly investments when their competitive advantage is keeping\nthat information private, said Paul Maeder, chairman of the\nNVCA. When they pay off, like Google or Facebook, a\nmultimillion-dollar investment can produce a multibillion-dollar\nreturn.  \u201cWe viewed this as almost an existential threat to venture\ncapital,\u201d said Maeder, who is also a general partner at\nHighland Capital Partners in Lexington,  Massachusetts . \u201cIf all\nor the majority of venture capital firms were required to\nregister, it would change the character of what we do. We\u2019re\ninvesting in stuff that none of us can predict five years in\nadvance.\u201d  The ruling may provide further momentum for an industry\nrebounding from a decade-long slump, which saw the dot-com bust\nand global financial crisis put scores of startups out of\nbusiness.  Fundraising, IPOs  Fundraising rose 76 percent in the first quarter from a\nyear earlier to $7.1 billion, the NVCA said. Last month,\n LinkedIn Corp. (LNKD)  became the first U.S. social-media company to\nsell shares to the public, and is now valued at about $8.4\nbillion. Pandora Media Inc. held its initial public offering\nthis month, and Groupon Inc. filed its IPO prospectus.  One reason it\u2019s taken so long for companies to start going\npublic again is the regulations that were created after the dot-\ncom crash, said  Dixon Doll , a former chairman of the NVCA and\nco-founder of venture firm DCM in  Menlo Park ,  California . The\n Sarbanes-Oxley Act  of 2002 raised the legal and auditing fees\nassociated with being a public company in the U.S., making it\nprohibitive for smaller companies, he said.  \u201cThe last thing in the world the U.S. venture industry\nneeds is more layers of government,\u201d Doll said. To contact the editor responsible for this story:\nMichael Hytha at   mhytha@bloomberg.net .","path":".\/2008_2012_msft_bloomberg_news\/samsung-novartis-apple-liberty-media-intellectual-property.txt"},{"id":11426088,"title":"Biggest Overhaul of Patent System Since 1952 Passes Senate","released_at":"<date>September 9 2011<\/date> <time>15:50:54<\/time>","content":"The Senate passed an overhaul of the\nU.S. patent system that President  Barack Obama  has called\ncrucial to his administration\u2019s effort to boost job growth.  In an 89-9 vote yesterday, the Senate cleared a bill passed\nby the House in June that would fundamentally alter the way\npatents are reviewed and mark the biggest change to U.S. patent\nlaw since at least 1952. The measure, called the America Invents\nAct, now heads to the White House for Obama\u2019s signature.  The legislation, H.R. 1249, would let the U.S. Patent and\nTrademark Office set its own fees and exercise greater control\nover its budget, providing the agency with more funding to\naddress a backlog of almost 700,000  applications  awaiting first\nreview. Reducing the time it takes to give inventions legal\nprotection will speed new products to the market and spur\neconomic growth, according to the bill\u2019s supporters.  \u201cThe creativity that drives our economic engine has made\nAmerica the global leader in invention and innovation,\u201d Senator\n Patrick Leahy , a Vermont Democrat who sponsored the measure,\nsaid in a statement. \u201cThe America Invents Act will ensure that\ninventors large and small maintain the competitive edge that has\nput America at the pinnacle of global innovation.\u201d  The legislation, which culminates more than six years of\nnegotiations and lobbying, covers every step of the patent\nprocess, setting new procedures to review issued patents while\ncurtailing some litigation. It has the support of large\ncompanies including  Microsoft Corp. (MSFT) ,  International Business\nMachines Corp. (IBM)  and a group that represents  Johnson & Johnson (JNJ) ,\n Eli Lilly & Co. (LLY) ,  3M Co. (MMM)  and  General Electric Co. (GE)   \u2018Rational Patent System\u2019  \u201cThe America Invents Act, coupled with recent court\ndecisions that provide more clarity and confidence for\ninventors, puts our patent system in a much better position to\nspur innovation and economic growth in the 21st century,\u201d\nRobert Weber, IBM\u2019s general counsel, said in an e-mail. He\ncalled the measure a \u201cbipartisan, common-sense bill that will\nsignificantly improve the U.S. patent system.\u201d  The funding provision, which also would let the agency\nincrease fees paid by inventors and patent owners, is the\ncornerstone of the bill and has been a unifying issue even for\nthose who oppose other provisions. Since 1990, the agency says,\nmore than $800 million in fees have been diverted by lawmakers\nto non-patent purposes.  34-Month Wait  The patent office is funded entirely by user fees. The\nObama administration says the money is needed to hire more\nexaminers and improve agency computer systems to cut the current\n34-month wait for patent approval.  \u201cThis legislation should enable us to access all of our\nfees,\u201d David Kappos, director of the patent office, said in a\nstatement. \u201cHaving access to all of our fee collections will\nenable us to immediately start hiring new examiners, instituting\nnew patent acceleration tools, and aggressively modernizing our\nIT infrastructure.\u201d  The U.S. Chamber of Commerce,  Washington \u2019s largest business\nlobbying organization, supported passage, as did the  United\nSteelworkers . A group representing large technology companies\nincluding Google Inc.,  Apple Inc. (AAPL) , and  Intel Corp. (INTC)  also  backed \nthe measure.  \u201cBy promoting clearer, more certain and more consistent\n patent rights , this bipartisan legislation gives America\u2019s\ninventors the intellectual property guarantees they need to\nraise funds, invest in research and development and launch\ntechnologies that will help them expand and hire more workers,\u201d\nActing Commerce Secretary Rebecca Blank said in a statement.  Job Creation  Representative  Lamar Smith , the Texas Republican who\nsponsored the House version, said that once the president signs\nit into law, the measure \u201cwill be one of the most significant\njobs creation bills enacted by Congress this year.\u201d  Obama cited the bill\u2019s passage in his speech last night to\na joint session of Congress. \u201cYou passed reform that will speed\nup the outdated patent process, so that entrepreneurs can turn a\nnew idea into a new business as quickly as possible,\u201d he said.\n\u201cThat\u2019s the kind of action we need.\u201d  A group of technology companies that includes InterDigital\nInc. and  Tessera Technologies Inc. (TSRA)  had said the House-passed\nmeasure doesn\u2019t do enough to guarantee more funding for the\npatent office since the agency still has to get congressional\napproval to spend money it collects above its annual budget.  Coburn Criticism  \u201cHopefully, Congress will deliver on the funding the PTO\nneeds to administer its charge,\u201d Brad Ditty, general patent\ncounsel for InterDigital, said in an interview. \u201cOne of the\nthings we\u2019re concerned about is the PTO has a lot of difficult\nwork ahead of it, and without knowing what type of multiyear\nfunding situation they\u2019re in, it could be difficult for them to\nexecute some of the more aggressive steps they need to take.\u201d  Senator  Tom Coburn , an Oklahoma Republican who tried\nunsuccessfully to alter the bill to give the agency full control\nover the fees it collects, said language in the House bill was\ninadequate to keep Congress from diverting the funds.  Groups  representing  small businesses say the legislation\nwill benefit large companies over independent inventors, create\na rush to the patent office and establish onerous review\nprocedures that will weaken the power of patents to protect\ninventions.  \u201cThis legislation will irreversibly damage the ability of\nsmall-business owners and entrepreneurs to create, develop and\ncommercialize their innovations,\u201d said Todd McCracken,\npresident of the National Small Business Association, a\nWashington-based group that says it represents 150,000 small\nbusinesses nationwide. \u201cTo think this bill will have anything\nbut negative implications on job creation is absurd.\u201d  First to File  Under the bill, patents would be granted to the first\ninventor to file an application, ending an often time-consuming\nprocedure to determine who came up with an idea first and\nbringing the U.S. in line with patent laws in other countries.  All newly issued patents may be subject to a challenge from\nthird parties, a variation of a process used by the  European\nPatent Office . Third parties would be allowed to submit\ninformation for consideration during the application process.  The bill also would limit patents on tax-avoidance\nstrategies, though companies including  Intuit Inc. (INTU)  and  H&R Block\nInc. (HRB)  have said they would retain protections for their tax-\npreparation software.  Finance Patents  Banks including  Bank of America Corp. (BAC)  and  Citigroup Inc. (C) \nwould get new power to seek to cancel finance-related business\nmethod patents that they argue are of questionable validity.\nCompanies that own such patents, including DataTreasury Corp.\nand Trading Technologies International Inc., have accused the\nbanks of using their clout in Washington to avoid paying for\nusing someone else\u2019s inventions.  The trade group for generic-drug companies including Mylan\nInc. and Watson Pharmaceuticals Inc. opposes the bill because\nthere\u2019s a provision that lets patent owners retroactively\ncorrect errors that might otherwise lead a court to invalidate\nthe patents.  The Washington-based Generic Pharmaceutical Association\nalso objects to language in the bill that would ease deadlines\nfor seeking a patent-term extension granted to compensate\ndrugmakers for the time it takes to get regulatory approval.  The provision would provide a clear victory to  Medicines\nCo. (MDCO) , which won a court ruling that it was entitled to an\nextension even though it missed a deadline for an extension on\nthe main patent for its only drug, the anticoagulant Angiomax. Hunt","released_at":"<date>October 23 2011<\/date> <time>15:01:18<\/time>","content":"The anti- Wall Street  movement has\nconfounded Republicans, Democrats and analysts alike.  The take on the right is that Occupy Wall Street is the\nsame old riff-raff of leftist anarchists, unlike the grassroots\nconservative Tea Party; seen from the left, it\u2019s an authentic\nuprising against the huge income disparity in America and a call\nfor redistributing the wealth.  Actually, it is part of a combustible global protest that\ngoes beyond the professional rabble rousers. There is a focus on\n income inequality ; \u201cTax the Rich\u201d is a favorite slogan. The\nprotesters are diverse and seemingly directionless.  Income and wealth inequality in America have been growing\nfor decades with little public outcry. The catalyst for the\nmovement now is that during the worst financial crisis since the\nDepression, there is a perception that Wall Street and the\nwealthy were taken care of while average folks suffer. That\nisn\u2019t a fringe view.  Wall Street generally has flourished since the government\nrescue of 2008 and the big banks have posted record profit and\nbooming bonuses. Although Goldman Sachs Group Inc. reported a\nrare quarterly loss last week,  Lloyd Blankfein , its able\nchairman and chief executive officer, was paid $19 million for\nhis work last year, up 50 percent from the year before. JPMorgan\nChase & Co.\u2019s  Jamie Dimon  was awarded $23 million in\ncompensation. A prime target of the protesters in  New York  is\n John Paulson , the hedge fund billionaire who made a fortune\nbetting on the mortgage debacle, assisted by a sweetheart deal\nfrom his banker.  Taxpayer Resentment  In good times it\u2019s considered class warfare to rail against\nsuccessful leaders who\u2019ve added value. There have been few\ncomplaints about the wealth that accrued to Microsoft Corp.\u2019s\nBill Gates, Apple Inc.\u2019s Steve Jobs or Jack Welch of General\nElectric Co. When taxpayers directly facilitate that success and\nfirms then lavish massive payouts on executives, it would be\nna\u00efve not to expect public resentment.  One of the critics of the Wall Street demonstrations cited\na survey showing that three-quarters of the protesters favored\nhigher taxes on the rich. In major U.S. media polls -- by the\nWall Street Journal\/NBC News and Bloomberg News\/  Washington  Post\n-- two-thirds of the public agree.  American politicians are dancing around the issue. Two\nRepublican presidential candidates,  Ron Paul  and  Jon Huntsman ,\nsaid the anti-Wall Street protests have struck a responsive\nchord. The frontrunner,  Mitt Romney , initially blasted the anti-\nWall Street rallies as \u201cdangerous\u201d and \u201cclass warfare.\u201d\nWithin a week, he said he understood \u201chow these people feel.\u201d  \u2018Really Dumb Ideas\u2019  Newt Gingrich  said the protests were a \u201cnatural outcome of\na bad education system teaching them really dumb ideas.\u201d Then,\nin a debate at Dartmouth College two weeks ago, he was asked\nwhether anyone should have gone to jail for their role in the\ncrisis. His answer: not Wall Street executives, but Congressman\n Barney Frank  of Massachusetts and former Senator Chris Dodd of\nConnecticut.  Gingrich cited the mortgage Dodd obtained from Countrywide\nFinancial Corp., the failed mortgage-lending company. The former\nsenator may have gotten generous, though totally legal, terms;\n Angelo Mozilo , the chief executive officer of Countrywide, who\nGingrich didn\u2019t mention, had to settle a Securities and Exchange\nCommission suit alleging  securities fraud  for misleading\ninvestors even as he made $140 million through stock sales and\nwas driving his company into the ditch. It was the fact that\nMozilo and his ilk created devastation for so many people and\nwalked away free and rich that fuels so much of the populist\nsentiment.  Contributions to Democrats  The Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee recently\nurged its supporters to back the Occupy Wall Street protests.\nThis gave heartburn to the committee\u2019s fundraisers who rely\ndisproportionately on the financial community for donations.  President  Barack Obama , who has raised millions from Wall\nStreet, has sought to embrace the protesters, saying they are\n\u201cgiving voice to a more broad-based frustration with how our\nfinance sector works. The American people understand that not\neverybody\u2019s been following the rules.\u201d  Who sets the rules today? There are reasons Democrats\naren\u2019t entirely comfortable identifying with the anti-Wall\nStreet crowd.  For all the corporate griping about reregulation, the Obama\nadministration in 2009, led by White House economics aide  Larry Summers  and Treasury Secretary  Tim Geithner , eschewed a hard\nline on Wall Street and was soft on excessive  executive\ncompensation .  The other fear is that the Occupy Wall Street protests\ncould get out of hand, turn violent, creating a political\nbacklash. That occurred during the anti-Vietnam War protests a\ncouple of generations ago.  Tea Party  Echoes  There have been a few raucous or ugly scenes, and there are\nremnants of the radical left; anti-Semitic signs have been\nspotted.  It\u2019s instructive to look back at the Tea Party, circa 2009.\nThey disrupted congressional meetings, and their ranks included\nkooks, vestiges of the old John Birch Society, and racist\nsentiments surfaced.  Ultimately the movement got smarter and provided an\ninfusion of energy for Republican candidates in the 2010\nelections. After that success, the popularity of the Tea Party\nsteadily declined.  No one knows if the Occupy Wall Street movement will chart\na similar course. A visit to the protest\u2019s Washington\u2019s outpost,\nin McPherson Square, is illuminating. There are more than 100\ntents pitched and there are some characters who resemble\ndisciples of Che Guevara. On a small bookshelf, there\u2019s a copy\nof \u201cDas Kapital.\u201d That same bookshelf has a copy of David McCullough\u2019s biography of Harry Truman and of \u201cThe Gamble,\u201d a\nbook on the Iraq war by noted defense author Thomas Ricks.  \u2018Moment of Possibility\u2019  There are a few Ron Paul-supporting libertarians, and there\nare people like Hillary Lazar, an earnest 33-year-old anti-\npoverty worker. She says the crash and its aftermath\ncrystallized an American economic, social and political dilemma.  \u201cOur political system is beholden to powerful corporations\nand financial interests, and the current system of wealth and\nincome distribution is unimaginable,\u201d she says. Rather than\ndespair, Ms. Lazar insists, this is \u201ca moment of possibility.\u201d  When a cold Washington winter arrives, most of these tents\nare likely to fold up. Camp, the top Republican tax writer in the U.S. House of\nRepresentatives, says putting a rate of 15 percent on all\nforeign income from intellectual property rights and intangibles\nwould limit revenue erosion when Congress pursues broad  tax\nreform , Bloomberg BNA reported.  The incentive would be a deduction for income related to\nintangibles kept in the U.S.; the disincentive is an immediate\ninclusion for income related to such intangibles held abroad.\nCompanies would have less pressure to shift income to low-tax\nlocales because that income would be taxed at the same rate,\nwhether it is earned in the U.S. or  Bermuda , Camp said.  \u201cMoving intangibles to  tax havens  would have little or no\nappeal, since the income earned from those intangibles obviously\nwould be taxed at the same rate, regardless of location,\u201d said\nCamp, who is from  Michigan  and heads the  House Ways and Means\nCommittee .  These intangibles are part of the fight over offshore cash\nand taxes. U.S. companies are shifting more of their revenues\noverseas. The nation\u2019s 83 biggest companies increased their\nuntaxed offshore holdings by 14.4 percent to $1.46 trillion in\nthe past year, according to data compiled by Bloomberg.  Camp is working on the first major overhaul of the tax code\nsince 1986 and says he wants Congress to have something done by\nyear-end. A discussion draft Camp released in late 2011 included\nthis idea, referred to as \u201cOption C,\u201d as one of three choices to\ntry to avoid erosion of the tax base.  Effective Safeguard  Companies could get below a 15 percent effective rate by\nsubtracting any credits for foreign taxes paid on the same\nincome under Option C, Camp said at a hearing last week on tax\nhavens, base erosion and profit-shifting. Camp didn\u2019t discuss\nthe other two options at the hearing.  He said work on the matter with the Joint Committee on\nTaxation has led him to believe this plan is an effective\nsafeguard, and said it has also received the most business\ncommunity support among the discussion draft options.  The committee\u2019s ranking member, Michigan Democrat  Sander Levin , noted the recent Senate Permanent Subcommittee on\nInvestigations hearing on  Apple Inc. (AAPL) , which has an Irish entity\nthat has received tens of billions of dollars of income with no\ntax residence, and also complained that other major U.S.\ncorporations use legal  tax avoidance  techniques to shift income\noverseas, including  Microsoft Corp. (MSFT)  and  Google Inc. (GOOG)   \u201cThe challenge of ending massive tax avoidance must be at\nthe forefront of any tax reform effort worth its salt,\u201d Levin\nsaid.  Transition Rules  Option C won support from one of the hearing\u2019s witnesses,\nPaul Oosterhuis, a partner at Skadden, Arps, Slate, Meagher &\nFlom LLP. He said it would help neutralize where businesses\nlocate their factories and similar activities. Differentiation\nof products sold into foreign markets from products sold into\nthe U.S. market represents the top advantage, he said.  Transition rules may be needed for products sold back to\nthe U.S., similar to what Option C proposes for profits on\nintellectual property, he said.  For foreign products, most of which he said come from\nconsumer businesses, Oosterhuis said the country where the\nproducts are consumed has a large right to tax that income.  Sensible Distinction  For example, he pointed to recent complaints in the U.K.\nover inbound companies such as  Starbucks Corp. (SBUX)  and their income\nin the country. Option C recognizes that U.S. authorities have\nmuch less of a right to assert jurisdiction to collect revenue\nout of that income.  \u201cAnd I think that\u2019s a very sensible distinction over the\nlong run,\u201d Oosterhuis said.  University of Southern California law school professor\nEdward Kleinbard, another witness at the hearing, expressed\nconcerns about administering such a plan. He instead advocated a\ngenuine worldwide tax consolidation with a 25 percent corporate\ntax rate.  Kleinbard, who served as the Joint Committee on Taxation\u2019s\nchief of staff from 2007 to 2009, said multinational firms are\nable to operate within current rules to produce stateless income\nby engaging in large-scale base erosion and profit shifting. He\nsaid his option would offer more simplicity and prove more\ndifficult for tax gaming.  Trapped Cash  \u201cThis idea is less wacky than you might think,\u201d Kleinbard\nsaid. \u201cThe economic effects of worldwide consolidation are\nbasically the same as a territorial tax with a 25 percent\nworldwide minimum tax as an anti-abuse measure.\u201d  By contrast, he said current law or unprotected\nterritoriality heavily subsidizes foreign investment at the\nexpense of the  U.S. economy . Kleinbard conceded that whatever\ninternational taxation choices legislators make in overhauling\nthe code, a new system will lead to higher statutory taxes paid\nby multinational companies, either to the U.S. or abroad.  A growing number of executives at such firms back higher\nstatutory rates to free up \u201ctrapped\u201d cash, the liquid reserves\nthey cannot easily mobilize at present because of the current\ntax system, Oosterhuis said. He added that a corporate  tax rate \nlower than 25 percent would be preferable. (RIM) , the Ontario-based maker of the BlackBerry mobile messaging\ndevice, follow a pattern sadly familiar to technology-company\nwatchers and admirers of classical tragedy. Brave innovation and\nsuperb execution create a new market, which the upstart\ndominates. But ultimately the very scale of the new champion\u2019s\nsuccess drags it down.  No tech company, least of all RIM, can be unaware of this\ncycle. The main lesson is in plain sight: Technology firms must\nbe their own most formidable competitor. They must strive as\neagerly as their rivals to displace their own commanding\ntechnologies. If they don\u2019t, somebody else will.  The lesson may be clear, yet applying it is almost\nimpossibly hard. One reason is that the bigger the initial\nsuccess, the greater the reluctance to dismantle it. On Jan. 22,\nRIM proved the point. Its formerly class-leading, class-creating\nproducts have been failing in the new market for smartphones.\nConsumers and businesses are dumping their BlackBerrys for Apple\nInc.\u2019s iPhones or smartphones powered by Google Inc.\u2019s Android\noperating system. RIM\u2019s belated effort to market an iPad\ncompetitor was a costly and embarrassing flop.  Revenue (RI1)  and  profit  have slumped and investors have hammered\nthe share price. Earlier this week, RIM announced that its\nfounders and co-chief executive officers,  Jim Balsillie  and  Mike Lazaridis , were stepping down. But the new CEO, Thorsten Heins,\nis a company insider who promptly affirmed his commitment to the\nfounders\u2019 vision.  Future Disruption  What leads technology innovators astray is the idea that\nmarket dominance, once achieved by their own disruptive\ntechnologies, can be guarded from future disruption. This\ncomplacency is understandable because great innovators\nexperience their sector\u2019s barriers to entry firsthand. Economies\nof scale, the power of established networks, and the salience of\nindustrywide standards and platforms make it hard to break\nthrough. However, the force of a sufficiently powerful\ninnovation can overcome these barriers. And here\u2019s the point:\nthe next sufficiently powerful innovation is always on its way.  RIM created valuable proprietary technologies. The\nparticular way BlackBerrys connect to mobile networks was its\nmain strength because it allowed the devices to work more\nsecurely and corporate IT managers to exert the control they\ndesired. These benefits were overwhelmed, however, by the\namazing ease of use and range of applications offered by newer\nsmartphones.  RIM was too concerned about defending the technologies it\nhad created, and not concerned enough about giving users of its\ndevices the best possible experience -- a strategy that could\nhave meant surrendering its previous advantage.  Eastman Kodak Co., which filed for  bankruptcy  this month,\nis the classical instance of this syndrome. A paradigm-shifting\ninnovator -- in the 19th and 20th centuries, that is -- Kodak\nled the development of film-based photography, established\noverwhelming presence in its burgeoning new market, and for\ndecades reaped profit accordingly.  Sadly, Kodak can also fairly claim to have invented digital\nphotography, the technology that destroyed film. But with a\nnear-monopoly to protect, the company grew that business too\ntentatively. In a way, it wanted digital to fail. It rested on\nits laurels and the power of its brand.  Newcomers with less to lose arrived and swept its business\naway. Fujifilm Holdings Corp., its Japanese competitor, is one\nsuch rival. Less wedded to past success, it innovated across a\nwider range of technologies and embraced digital photography\nmore wholeheartedly. Fujifilm is still a successful business,\nwhereas Kodak is bust.  Defending Windows  Will Microsoft Corp. one day be another Kodak? It\u2019s\npossible. Microsoft still has a hugely profitable near-monopoly\nin its  Windows operating system  to defend, and has been an\nunimpressive innovator in technologies, including smartphones,\nwhich now threaten to challenge it. Compare that with Apple,\nwhich began its recent startling run with no similar grand\nsuccess to inhibit it. That, by the way, has now changed. Today,\nApple has its own platforms to defend and is no longer led by\none of history\u2019s most instinctively disruptive bosses.  Examples of wholesale corporate reinvention -- of\nshattering competition that works from the inside out -- are few\nand far between. In the technology sector, International\nBusiness Machines Corp. comes to mind. In its 100-year history,\nthe company has been a serial self-reinventor: from mechanical\ntabulating machines to computers, from  mainframe computers  to\npersonal computers, from computing machines to computing\nservices. Transitions as demanding as the one that leveled Kodak\nhave been taken in stride, not once but repeatedly.  Paradoxically, innovation for its own sake has not been the\nanimating spirit of IBM, one of the world\u2019s most innovative\ncompanies. Instead, it has been the desire to build and keep\nrelationships with customers. That is worth pondering.\nTechnologies come and go, but you always need customers. (GOOG) \u2019s\n$125 million settlement with publishers and authors, saying the\ndeal to create the world\u2019s biggest digital book library would be\nunfair to authors.  The expansive nature of the settlement, calling for\ncopyright owners to opt out or be automatically included,\n\u201cwould simply go too far,\u201d said U.S. Circuit Judge Denny Chin\nin  Manhattan , who was a district-court judge when the case first\ncame before him. He suggested the settlement would have a better\nchance at approval were it revised to cover only those who opt\ninto the agreement.  As written now, the settlement \u201cwould grant Google\nsignificant rights to exploit entire books, without permission\nof copyright owners,\u201d Chin wrote yesterday. It \u201cwould give\nGoogle a significant advantage over competitors, rewarding it\nfor engaging in wholesale copying of copyrighted works without\npermission, while releasing claims well beyond those presented\nin the case.\u201d  Google, based in  Mountain View ,  California , was sued in\n2005 by authors and publishers who said the company was\ninfringing their copyrights on a massive scale by digitizing\nbooks. The agreement includes a  Book Rights Registry  to\ncompensate copyright holders.  Amazon.com Inc. (AMZN) ,  Microsoft Corp. (MSFT)  and Yahoo! Inc., along\nwith the German and French governments, said the agreement would\ngive Google unfair control over digitized works and expand its\npower in the search engine market. Copyright Protection  The agreement focuses on out-of-print books still protected\nby U.S. copyright law. Google struck agreements with publishers\nto allow limited access to books that are still commercially\navailable, and the site has links to let consumers buy the books\nfrom various sources, including Amazon.com and Barnes & Noble. Pressing Issues  A  survey  by the Washington Post and the nonprofit Kaiser\nFamily Foundation found 10 percent of Americans identified\nHIV\/AIDS as the most urgent health problem facing the U.S.,\nbehind cancer, which was mentioned by more than a third,\nobesity, diabetes, heart disease, insurance and health costs. If Obama\u2019s current budget plan is enacted, the funding\nwill fall to $6.4 billion in fiscal 2013.  \u201cIt\u2019s ironic but Bush, I think, when it came to HIV\/AIDS,\nunderstood the public health issue better than Obama,\u201d said\nJessica Reinhart, a grassroots manager with the AIDS Healthcare\nFoundation, a Los Angeles-based group that provides AIDS\ntreatment. \u201cThe fact that Obama\u2019s going to cut funding for\nPepfar could possibly increase new infections.\u201d  Human immunodeficiency virus, or HIV, causes AIDS. A record 34.2 million people worldwide are living with\nHIV\/AIDS according to the  World Health Organization . Baucus\u2019s plan to restructure the international tax system\nwould lower the corporate rate by an unspecified amount, end a\nrule that has encouraged companies to accumulate about $2\ntrillion in earnings in their foreign subsidiaries and impose a\n20 percent tax on those stockpiled profits.  The proposal is the first of three drafts the Montana\nDemocrat plans to release this week. It will be followed by\nproposals on tax administration and capital-cost recovery.\nBaucus, who is retiring from Congress at the end of 2014, said\nhe wants to kick off discussions about revising the tax system.  \u201cIt\u2019s time to move; it\u2019s time to go,\u201d Baucus told\nreporters in his office in Washington, saying his tax plan would\nprove politically popular. \u201cYou can create your own destiny.\u201d  Whether he can succeed is far from clear. Efforts by Baucus\nand House Ways and Means Chairman  Dave Camp  to make the biggest\nchanges to the U.S. tax code since 1986 are stalled, partly\nbecause of a partisan dispute over whether the government should\ncollect more revenue as part of the changes. Camp is a Michigan\nRepublican.  Criticizing Plan  Corporate groups, including the  Business Roundtable , issued\nstatements within hours that criticized the Baucus plan.\nRoundtable President  John Engler , who represents chief\nexecutives of large companies, said the senator\u2019s approach would\nmake many U.S. companies less competitive.  Baucus\u2019s international tax plan is designed to be revenue\nneutral in the long run. He would reserve the one-time revenue\nof about $200 billion from the tax on accumulated earnings for\nan unspecified purpose.  The international system is one of the most technically\ncomplex areas of the U.S. tax code and potential changes are\nbeing watched closely by companies including  Pfizer Inc. (PFE)  and\n General Electric Co. (GE)  that have significant global businesses.  General agreement exists across party lines on moving to a\nsystem that lessens burdens on companies that face lower-taxed\nforeign competition while tightening rules on U.S. companies\u2019\ntax-avoidance tactics.  President  Barack Obama  said today that the differences\nbetween the parties on business taxation \u201cshould be\nbridgeable.\u201d Speaking at the Wall Street Journal CEO Council in\nWashington, he reiterated the administration\u2019s support for a\n\u201cmodest, clear\u201d global minimum tax without endorsing Baucus\u2019s\nversion of it.  Business Location  Each detail in Baucus\u2019s proposal affects companies in\ndifferent ways depending on how they have set up their\nbusinesses, where they operate and where they have located their\nintellectual property.  His plan will make it tougher for companies to claim\nprofits in low-tax countries, said Ed Kleinbard, a tax-law\nprofessor at the University of  Southern California .  \u201cThis is obviously bad news for tech firms and pharmas and\nothers that have effective tax rates in the single digits,\u201d\nsaid Kleinbard, a former chief of staff of the congressional\nJoint Committee on Taxation. \u201cIt\u2019s impossible that they will\nmaintain foreign effective tax rates in the single digits.\u201d  Federal Rate  Under current law, U.S. companies owe taxes at the full\nfederal rate of 35 percent on all income they earn around the\nworld. They receive tax credits for payments to foreign\ngovernments and can defer U.S. taxation until they repatriate\nthe money.  That system has encouraged companies to accumulate untaxed\nearnings in foreign subsidiaries. It also has created incentives\nfor companies to move intellectual property out of the U.S. and\ninto low-tax jurisdictions.  U.S. lawmakers such as Senator  Carl Levin , a Michigan\nDemocrat, have criticized maneuvers by companies including Apple\nInc. and  Microsoft Corp. (MSFT)  that have reduced their tax bills.  Many other countries, including the U.K. and Japan, have\nshifted to what\u2019s known as a territorial tax system in which\nU.S. companies would owe little or no taxes on their foreign\nincome.  The Let\u2019s Invest for Tomorrow America Coalition, which\nadvocates for a territorial system, said that Baucus\u2019s proposal\nwould take the country further from a pro-growth position.\nCoalition members include  Oracle Corp. (ORCL) ,  Johnson & Johnson (JNJ)  and\n Cisco Systems Inc. Baucus, in suggesting a hybrid between current law and a\nterritorial system, is proposing two options for his minimum\ntax. Baucus has said he hopes to lower the new tax rate to less\nthan 30 percent. If it were set at 28 percent, for example, the\nminimum tax would be set at 22.4 percent.  That rate would apply to a company\u2019s earnings in each\njurisdiction, so that companies operating in high-tax areas\nwould owe no incremental U.S. tax on their foreign earnings. A\ncompany operating in Ireland, by contrast, would effectively\nhave to pay the U.S. the difference between the Irish tax rate\nof 12.5 percent and 22.4 percent.  Narrowing Definition  The second option would set a lower minimum tax rate, 60\npercent of the U.S. rate, while narrowing the definition of\nincome eligible to only income from active business operations.\nOther income would be taxed at the full U.S. rate immediately.  The earnings that companies have accumulated under the\ncurrent system would be taxed at 20 percent over eight years,\nregardless of whether companies have the money in liquid form\nand regardless of whether they bring it back to the U.S.  That tax would generate more than $200 billion, and Baucus\nhasn\u2019t decided what to do with the revenue. A split Congress shunned\ncompromise on financial rules or fixes for the economy.  That made it all the more surprising to see President\nBarack Obama celebrating with top House Republicans at a Rose\nGarden ceremony last month. Together they lauded passage of a\nlaw making some of the biggest regulatory changes to U.S.\ncapital markets in decades.  While the Jumpstart Our Business Startups Act -- JOBS for\nshort -- was touted as a rare show of bipartisanship, it had\nmore to do with the growing political sway of emerging\ntechnology companies and Silicon Valley venture capitalists,\naccording to interviews with more than a dozen participants.  \u201cThis showed the next generation of entrepreneurs, start-\nups and investors have found their voice in Washington,\u201d said\nIsrael Klein, a lobbyist at the Podesta Group in Washington, who\nhelped lead the charge for the law on behalf of his client\nSecondMarket Inc., an exchange for shares of private companies.  The coalition argued that expensive and outdated rules were\nkeeping companies from going public and creating jobs. Obama\nagreed, backing the measure over the objections of his\nSecurities and Exchange Commission chairman and some Democrats\nwho said it would roll back investor protections dating to the\nGreat Depression and the Enron accounting scandal.  For Republicans, whose support allowed the White House to\nclaim political credit, the tradeoff was worth it. They saw the\nlaw as a major piece of deregulation that also fit with their\ncampaign to convince California technology executives to\ncontribute to Republicans as well as Democrats.  Capturing the Scene  Among those on hand at the April 5 bill-signing ceremony\nwere two leaders from the technology coalition. Steve Case, a\nfounder of America Online Inc. who now runs an investment fund,\nstood on the dais behind the president, his iPhone raised to\ncapture the scene. Kate Mitchell, a venture capitalist who\nhelped write proposals for the bill from her Northern California\nkitchen table, had a front-row seat in the audience.  Lawmakers who showed up included two House Republicans\nwho\u2019ve been among Obama\u2019s most persistent critics on financial\nmatters, Majority Leader  Eric Cantor  of Virginia and Financial\nServices Chairman Spencer Bachus of Alabama. Still, the event\nhad a Silicon Valley feel: Some guests \u201cchecked in\u201d via\nFoursquare while others marked their arrival with Twitter posts.  The JOBS act consolidates ideas that had been floated for\nyears without success on Capitol Hill.  Quadruple Shareholders  It speeds initial stock offerings of firms with less than\n$1 billion of annual revenue, removes restrictions on how Wall\nStreet analysts cover smaller companies, allows  hedge funds  to\nadvertise for investors and gives companies the ability to\n\u201ccrowd-fund\u201d by selling stock on the Internet. It also\nquadruples -- from 500 to 2,000 -- the number of shareholders a\ncompany can have before it must publicly disclose its finances.  Before it passed, the legislation was attacked by consumer\nadvocates as well as current and former SEC officials.  SEC Chairman  Mary Schapiro  asked that the bill be\n\u201cmodified to improve investor protections.\u201d Lynn Turner, a\nformer SEC chief accountant, suggested it be renamed \u201cthe\nbucket-shop and penny-stock fraud reauthorization act of 2012.\u201d\n Barbara Roper , of the Consumer Federation of America, said,\n\u201cit\u2019s frankly bewildering that the Democrats have been so\nwilling to buy into the traditional Republican argument.\u201d  \u2018Significant Failure\u2019  Arthur Levitt, who served as SEC chairman under President\nBill Clinton, said in an interview that the law \u201cis a\nsignificant failure\u201d of the Obama administration.  \u201cIf they truly believe in protecting the interests of the\nmiddle class and the small investor they should have never, ever\nsigned on to such a bill,\u201d said Levitt, who is a director of\nBloomberg LP, parent of Bloomberg News.  Critics of the law said their concerns center on its\nloosening of accounting and disclosure rules for emerging\ncompanies. Lack of such controls, they said, fed the penny-stock\ncraze in the mid-1980s and the dot-com bubble of the late 1990s.  Under the new rules, companies with $1 billion in revenue\nor less are exempt for five years from an audit of internal\nfinancial controls that was required by the 2002 Sarbanes-Oxley\naccounting reform law. That means investors have less of a\nchance to learn about the kind of weaknesses that led some dot-\ncoms to crash after going public, the critics say.  State regulators told Congress they worried that other\nchanges in the law -- permitting crowd-funding and lifting the\nban on hedge funds soliciting investors -- could leave\nunsophisticated share-buyers more vulnerable to fraud.  Proponents said the loosening wouldn\u2019t lead to more fraud.\nMost important, they said, the old rules were so costly and\ntime-consuming that strong young firms were foregoing expansion.  Campaign Cash  That message resonated in both parties, which are also keen\nto raise cash from the technology industry. Democrats hope to\nretain their edge while Republicans are looking to make inroads.  In 2008, employees at technology and Internet firms donated\n$9.3 million to Obama and just $1.6 million to Senator John McCain of Arizona, his Republican opponent, according to the\nCenter for Responsive Politics. In this election year, both the\npresident and Republican opponent Mitt Romney have been making\nfund-raising trips to northern California.  These firms, \u201care creating jobs and bringing cool\ntechnologies to the marketplace\u201d making them \u201cappeal to both\nsides of the aisle,\u201d said Klein, of the Podesta Group.  While the largest technology companies weren\u2019t the prime\nmovers behind the act,  Facebook Inc. (FB) \u2019s brush with some of the\nregulations helped propel the campaign. Lawmakers took notice in\nJanuary 2011 when  Goldman Sachs Group Inc. (GS) , which planned to\nsell $1.5 billion in private Facebook shares to U.S. investors,\ndropped the idea after saying that publicity about the offering\ncould violate SEC rules on marketing private securities.  Facebook Delay  Facebook, which went public May 18, had started the IPO\nprocess months earlier in part because it had been bumping up\nagainst the SEC\u2019s 500-shareholder limit for closely held firms.\nOne top executive told Cantor that the company wouldn\u2019t have\ngone public so soon if the new law had been in place, the\nmajority leader said in an interview.  Support from Silicon Valley wasn\u2019t the only reason the JOBS\nmeasure was approved. Another player was the Pennsylvania-based\nconvenience store chain Wawa Inc., a closely held firm that also\nwanted the shareholder limit increased. In addition, Wall Street\nlobbyists got involved at the eleventh hour.  Still, Case and Mitchell were instrumental. They began\nworking separately on the idea after Democrats lost control of\nthe House and the White House, smarting from being labeled anti-\nbusiness, moved to refocus on jobs by streamlining regulations\nand stoking entrepreneurship.  White House Councils  Case, whose Revolution LLC has backed start-ups including\nZipcar and LivingSocial, joined Obama\u2019s new Council on Jobs and\nCompetitiveness in early 2011. He also agreed to serve as\nchairman of the Startup America Partnership, an independent\ngroup that kicked off with a White House press conference.  Case was careful to keep contact with Republicans as well,\nadvising Cantor, the House majority leader, on proposals aimed\nat reducing rules and taxes on technology and start-up firms.  The competitiveness council, headed by  General Electric (GE)  Co.\nChief Executive Officer Jeffrey Immelt, gave recommendations to\nObama last year that called for removing some regulations\nimposed by Sarbanes-Oxley and rescinding other securities rules\nfor closely-held firms.  Case met with Cantor the next day. He said, \u201cWhy don\u2019t you\njust take what we\u2019re doing, since it already has the imprimatur\nof the White House behind it, and take it up?\u201d Cantor recalled\nin an interview.  Geithner Conference  Mitchell, co-founder of investing firm Scale Venture\nPartners in Foster City, California was at work on her own plan.  She began developing recommendations during a March 2011\nsmall-business conference convened by Treasury Secretary  Timothy Geithner . During a break, Mitchell and other Silicon Valley\nattendees grabbed an empty conference room. Among them were Greg Becker, CEO of Santa Clara, California-based Silicon Valley\nBank; Steven Bochner, a partner at the Wilson Sonsini Goodrich &\nRosati law firm in Palo Alto, California; and Carter Mack,\npresident of investment bank  JMP Group Inc. (JMP)  of  San Francisco .  The ad-hoc group decided to gather entrepreneurs, bankers,\naccountants, academics and investors to research possible\nchanges in federal policy. They also invited lobbyists for NYSE\nEuronext and the National Venture Capital Association to offer\nadvice. The 17-member committee ultimately called for a\n\u201cregulatory on-ramp\u201d to encourage start-ups to go public.\nAmong the proposals was the audit exemption later attacked by\nopponents of the bill.  Republican Outreach  In the House, Cantor was encouraging Republicans to\nstrengthen their ties to technology firms. He and his top policy\nadviser, Mike Ference, contacted venture capital and private\nequity funds in Silicon Valley, Boston, the research triangle in\nNorth Carolina and in Cantor\u2019s home state of Virginia. They\nasked the companies for ideas and support.  \u201cThis is critical to how we\u2019re going to regain the growth\nprospects in the economy,\u201d Cantor said.  Silicon Valley, a Democratic stronghold, has been a\nchallenge for Republicans because many of the industry\u2019s\nemployees don\u2019t align with the party\u2019s stand on social issues\nsuch as gay marriage and abortion, Representative Kevin\nMcCarthy, who represents a southern California district and is\nthe third-ranked House Republican, said in an interview.  Republicans saw the sluggish economy as offering an\nopportunity to make inroads, McCarthy said.  \u2018Ignore Us\u2019  \u201cWhen the times are good they ignore us,\u201d McCarthy said.\n\u201cWhen the times are bad, they come to us because they like what\nwe stand for.\u201d  Cantor, McCarthy and Republican Representative Paul Ryan of\nWisconsin worked as a trio to make Silicon Valley connections.\nIn September, they held an interactive town hall at Facebook\u2019s\nMenlo Park headquarters. Meetings with  Google Inc. (GOOG) ,  Apple Inc. (AAPL) \nand  Microsoft Corp. (MSFT)  dotted their calendars.  A joint campaign account set up by the three pulled in\n$248,000 exclusively from northern California, including $15,000\neach from Mary Meeker and Floyd Kvamme of Kleiner Perkins\nCaufield & Byers, a Silicon Valley venture capital firm, and\n$7,500 from Kurt Wheeler, managing director at Clarus Ventures\nLLC in San Francisco.  Matt Lira, head of digital communications for Cantor,\nnoticed a streaming Twitter feed mounted on a wall during a\nvisit to Quora Inc. in Palo Alto, California. Cantor soon had a\nsimilar screen installed in his Capitol Hill office.  Joint Session  Obama went public with his de-regulatory stance in a speech\nto a joint session of Congress Sept. 8. He announced that the\nadministration supported the removal of \u201cred tape\u201d for start-\nups and businesses trying to raise capital.  Case attended, sitting a row behind  Michelle Obama  as a\nguest of the White House.  \u201cI certainly recognized that the odds were long to get\nsomething actually turned into law, but at minimum we could\ncreate some momentum and visibility around the issue,\u201d Case\nsaid in an interview.  But within a month, the House\u2019s Republican-controlled\nFinancial Services panel began voting on bills. By the beginning\nof November, with little attention from the news media, the\nHouse had passed four separate measures that would later be\nconsolidated into the JOBS Act.  In the Senate, support had been gathering too, thanks in\npart to a decidedly low-tech business. Closely held Wawa, which\nruns more than 590 convenience stores in states including\nPennsylvania, Delaware and Virginia, was bumping up against the\n500-shareholder limit and wanted the ceiling raised.  Empty Room  Wawa found receptive ears on both sides of the aisle.\nSenator Pat Toomey, a Pennsylvania Republican, and Senator Tom Carper, a Delaware Democrat, agreed to take on the issue,\naccording to two congressional aides. Toomey\u2019s top banking aide,\nDina Ellis, began working with Jonah Crane, the legislative\ncounsel for Senator Charles Schumer, a  New York  Democrat, to\ndraft a bill modeled on the proposals from venture capitalist\nMitchell\u2019s IPO task force.  When Schumer and Toomey held a press conference Dec. 1 to\nunveil their legislation, the room was nearly empty. In the\nHouse, though, Cantor was paying attention and Obama was about\nto provide the momentum for a final push.  \u201cMost new jobs are created in start-ups and small\nbusinesses, so let\u2019s pass an agenda that helps them succeed,\u201d\nObama told lawmakers in his  State of the Union  address Jan. 25.\n\u201cTear down regulations that prevent aspiring entrepreneurs from\ngetting the financing to grow.\u201d  Shortly after, Cantor and Bachus, the financial services\ncommittee chairman, decided to take the bills the House had\nalready passed, add some language from the Senate proposal and\noffer it as one piece of legislation.  White House Backing  They tapped Representative Stephen Fincher, a freshman\nTennessee Republican who had introduced the Schumer-Toomey\nlegislation in the House, to serve as the face of the measure.\nRepresentative John Carney, a Delaware Democrat who also had\nheard from Wawa, was a co-sponsor.  For emphasis, the White House put out a statement strongly\nbacking the bill two days before the March 8 House vote. While\nsome Democrats publicly and privately expressed misgivings about\nthe loss of investor protections, Obama\u2019s support diluted the\nopposition. All but 23 Democrats voted in favor.  Next up was the Senate, where Democrats were still in\ncontrol and opponents to the measure were waking up. Schapiro,\nthe SEC chairman, sent a six-page letter to lawmakers March 13,\ncriticizing the House bill and raising the Enron collapse as the\nkind of fraud that existing rules were meant to prevent. SEC\nspokesman  John Nester  didn\u2019t respond to requests for comment.  Democratic Alternative  The letter was wielded by the bill\u2019s opponents, led by\nDemocrats Jack Reed of Rhode Island and Carl Levin of Michigan.\nThe senators wanted a chance to craft their own version of the\nHouse bill -- one with a higher level of investor protection,\nthey told Senate Majority Leader Harry Reid of Nevada, according\nto three people familiar with the conversations.  When the majority leader said no, Reed and Levin drafted an\nalternative bill anyway.  To beat back the opposition, the legislation\u2019s Silicon\nValley backers resorted to their own social media tools.\nAngelList, a platform that connects investors with start-ups,\ninitiated an online movement via Twitter asking supporters to\nsign a petition urging Reid and Senate Minority Leader Mitch McConnell of Kentucky to pass the House bill.  Within two days, more than 5,000 had signed, including Biz\nStone, co-founder of Twitter Inc., Max Levchin, co-founder of\nPayPal Inc., Justin Waldron, co-founder of  Zynga Inc. (ZNGA)  and Mitch Kapor, the founder of Lotus Development Corp.  \u201cWe clearly recognized there was an opening and it was\ntime to push hard,\u201d said Case, who also signed the petition.  Wall Street Lobby  The Senate defeated the Democrats\u2019 alternative bill. Reed\nmade one last attempt to slow the train, introducing an\namendment that would, in effect, have sent the bill to a House-\nSenate conference for more work.  For the first time, Wall Street lobbyists and major\nbusiness groups including the U.S. Chamber of Commerce got\ninvolved. Goldman Sachs and  JPMorgan Chase & Co. (JPM)  saw the\namendment, which would have required the SEC to use a broader\nmethod for counting shareholders in a fund, as a threat to much\nof their investment management work.  Lobbyists and lawyers from the banks flooded Senate offices\nwith calls and analysis papers, according to two aides with\nknowledge of the efforts who spoke on condition of anonymity\nbecause the talks were private.  Small Victory  The Reed amendment failed. Opponents did have one small\nvictory -- an amendment by Democratic Senators Michael Bennet of\nColorado and  Jeff Merkley  of Oregon, and Scott Brown, a\nMassachusetts Republican, to increase SEC oversight of Internet\ncrowd-funding.  On a sunny afternoon two weeks later, Obama signed the\nmeasure into law. One person was missing: Fincher, the Tennessee\ncongressman who had been listed as the bill\u2019s prime sponsor. He\nwas back home addressing his local chamber of commerce. The\nbipartisan spirit had already faded from his discussion as he\nspoke of Obama.  \u201cAnything that creates division is what he\u2019s using to\nwin,\u201d Fincher told his constituents. He didn\u2019t respond to\nrequests for comment.  In the aftermath of its initial success in Washington, the\ntechnology coalition is looking to get its way on other issues\nincluding visas for high-tech workers and an exemption from\ncapital gains taxes for investments in start-ups that are held\nfor at least five years.  \u201cThere was a real sense in the entrepreneurial community\nthat they had started a constructive dialogue with the\npolicymakers,\u201d Mitchell said.  -- Editors: Lawrence Roberts, Maura Reynolds  To contact the reporters on this story:\nPhil Mattingly in Washington at \n pmattingly@bloomberg.net ;\nRobert Schmidt in Washington at \n rschmidt5@bloomberg.net   To contact the editor responsible for this story:\nMaura Reynolds at \n mreynolds34@bloomberg.net","path":".\/2008_2012_msft_bloomberg_news\/startup-act-shows-silicon-valley-clout-growing-in-dc.txt"},{"id":46970759,"title":"World\u2019s Richest Worth $1 Trillion on Billionaire List","released_at":"<date>April 19 2012<\/date> <time>17:03:12<\/time>","content":"The 40 richest individuals on Earth\nlost a combined $6.2 billion yesterday as stocks dropped amid\ndisappointing U.S. earnings, according to the Bloomberg\nBillionaires Index, a daily ranking of the wealthiest people. Motorola Mobility Holdings Inc.  has dusted off its once-\ndominant Razr brand for a new addition to Verizon Wireless\u2019s\nDroid line of high-end smartphones. At the same time,  Nokia Oyj (NOK1V) \nis introducing the Lumia 800, the first fruit of its bet-the-\ncompany partnership with  Microsoft Corp. (MSFT)   Both phones are solid performers and so physically\ndistinctive that they won\u2019t be mistaken for any competitor.  I found Lumia the more intriguing of the two. Once the\nworld\u2019s largest smartphone maker, Nokia saw its fortunes implode\nwith the move to app-centric devices like  Apple. Inc. (AAPL) \u2019s iPhone\nand handsets running  Google Inc. The Lumia is currently being rolled out in the U.K.,\n Germany  and  France , among other markets. It\u2019s slated to show up\nin the U.S. in early 2012, although carriers and pricing haven\u2019t\nbeen announced. I used my unlocked review unit on  AT&T Inc. (T) \u2019s 3G\nnetwork.  Fast, Fluid  Fast and fluid, with a bright screen and decent battery\nlife, the Lumia turns out to be an ideal platform for the\nMicrosoft OS.  The Lumia\u2019s dimensions are similar to the iPhone 4, but the\nresemblance ends there. The 3.7-inch screen is ever so slightly\nraised and curved, giving the phone a sleek shape and look. The\npolycarbonate body makes it feel solid but not heavy.  The 8-megapixel camera includes a flash and features a Carl\nZeiss lens. I found it a bit disappointing after the Nokia N8,\nwhich was released last year and had one of the best phone\ncameras I\u2019ve ever used. Also (and somewhat ironically, since\nMicrosoft now owns  Skype ), the Lumia has no front-facing camera\nfor video chatting. That\u2019s one of its biggest shortcomings,\nalong with the hard-to-open and potentially breakable hatch\ncovering the micro-USB port on the top edge.  Fewer Apps  All Windows phones function at a disadvantage to Apple and\nAndroid devices in terms of the number of apps available. Nokia,\nthough, has brought over several apps from its previous\noperating system, including very good turn-by-turn navigation.\nThe Lumia augurs well for the future of the Microsoft platform -\n- and perhaps for Nokia as well.  Back in the day, the Razr was synonymous with thin. But\nthose phones are obese compared with the Droid Razr, which at\nits thinnest point measures just .28 of an inch. As with many\nhigh-end Motorolas these days, the Droid bulges at the top to\nhouse the camera as well as audio, video and power connectors.\nStill, the whole package, including a big, bright 4.3-inch\nscreen, weighs only 4.5 ounces, which is less than an iPhone 4S.  A phone that thin and light naturally raises concerns about\ndurability. In part to allay them, Motorola touts a layer of\nKevlar -- the same material used in bulletproof vests -- that\ncovers the back of the phone. While it certainly protects the\nRazr from scratches, it also makes it feel slippery. The image\nof ironclad security it\u2019s supposed to project was undermined on\nmy test model by an air bubble that prevented a taut fit.  Fastest Network  The Razr runs on  Verizon (VZ) \u2019s LTE network, the best and\nfastest in the U.S. (The phone, minus the \u201cDroid\u201d label, is\nalso being rolled out internationally.) The tradeoff is that, as\nwith other LTE phones I\u2019ve used, battery life isn\u2019t great.  While you can get through a day of normal use on a single\ncharge, heavy users may find themselves packing an extra\ncharger; as with the Lumia, the battery isn\u2019t user-replaceable.  Along with the phone itself -- which costs $300 on a two-\nyear contract -- Motorola and Verizon offer a host of expansion\noptions, including a slot for a microSD card (the phone comes\nwith 16 gigabytes of onboard storage and a 16-gigabyte card) and\nthe ability to use the phone as the brain of a laptop computer-\ndock add-on. The Motorola system uses a PC-like interface called\nWebtop, providing an adequate netbook substitute for lightweight\ntasks like Web surfing or tweaking documents.  In addition, Motorola -- which is in the process of being\nacquired by Google -- says the Razr will be upgradeable to run\n\u201cIce Cream Sandwich,\u201d the new version of Android just\nbeginning to show up on phones and tablets.  It all signifies a healthy dose of future-proofing. As with\nthe Nokia, the brands may evoke nostalgia but the products are\npointed in the right direction. To contact the editor responsible for this story:\n Tom Giles  at   tgiles5@bloomberg.net .","path":".\/2008_2012_msft_bloomberg_news\/yahoo-s-thompson-quits-amid-inquiry-levinsohn-is-interim-ceo.txt"},{"id":97593144,"title":"Searching for China's Steve Jobs","released_at":"<date>November 8 2013<\/date> <time>21:36:40<\/time>","content":"As Communist Party leaders begin a four-day  retreat  to decide where to take China's economy, they would be wise to think about Steve Jobs. Their country's economic well-bearing may be at risk if they don't.  It's true that China boasts what so many politicians around the globe surely dream about: growth of more 7 percent; armies of laborers who stomach low wages and sketchy work conditions; legions of foreign executives who value profits at the expense of environmental calamity; and the kind of monopoly on power that lets officials snap their fingers and do what they want.  Here's what China lacks: young citizens with a dream and a laptop getting ready to create the next game-changing company. In other words, the next Apple, Google, Rovio or Samsung.  Making the yuan a viable international currency, changing property rights and tweaking household-registration laws are all well and good. But nothing would redirect China's economy for the better like a surge of entrepreneurship. China may make just about everything people buy these days, including iPhones and iPads, but it creates almost nothing.  The good news is that China is taking steps in that direction. Details might get fleshed out at the party's conclave that starts tomorrow. Among the ideas are plans to support asset-backed lending and cut borrowing costs for smaller companies to boost job creation. This might help achieve Premier  Li Keqiang's  goal of cultivating small- and mid-size enterprises. That would accelerate a re-balancing away from state-owned export manufacturers and the pollution they produce.  The idea also is to reduce reliance on the shadow-banking system, which potentially poses systemic risks to the economy. Right now, the smaller companies that China needs to maintain employment growth are forced to turn to financiers who are little more than loan sharks in ties. That's a significant constraint on start-up enterprises.  Beijing also needs to think much bigger than just changing how businesses gain access to capital. An obvious problem is China's obsessive Internet censorship. How, exactly, do China's young tap into the global exchange of ideas if they are walled off from -- or only getting the abridged version -- of some of the biggest debates of our day? It's fascinating to see how China's most respected innovators, be they Jack Ma of Alibaba or Robin Li of  Baidu , try to wiggle away from this question in interviews. They, more than anyone, know that China's censorship is an economic millstone.  Just as important, China needs to create a stronger legal and regulatory environment. Why would someone invent, design or brand a product when intellectual-property rights are lacking and pirates make all the money?  Corruption is at the core of one of China's greatest paradoxes. Small companies generate about 60 percent of gross domestic product, 75 percent of the new jobs, half of all tax revenue and yet have almost no sway in Beijing. The real influence lies with the huge state-owned enterprises that enrich politicians and support the graft that ensure their dominance. To continue thriving, though, China needs a complete reversal of today's pecking order.  Unfortunately, China is reinforcing the status quo. Consider the acquisitions strategy of the state-owned business, which make deals designed to leapfrog over the years needed for organic growth. It\u2019s easier to buy a chunk of International Business Machines Corp. than to create new lines of business and products. Why fear Google, the thinking goes, when the chance may come to buy it someday?  Yet China needs more of the opposite. Officials in Beijing say stay tuned and refer skeptics to Shanghai's new enterprise zone.   That's fine, but until China figures out how to make room for innovation the odds will be against the emergence of a Chinese Steve Jobs. Apple wasn't always the iPod-making game changer, remember. There was a time when IBM, Microsoft, Nokia or Dell might have eclipsed it.  Jobs never could have changed the world the way he did had he lived and worked in China. China's leader should think about that when they gather to map out their country's economic future. (William Pesek is a Bloomberg View columnist. Gupta may also repeat it in his new role, said Guru Gowrappan, a technology veteran who worked with him at Yahoo and\nZynga.  \u201cI wouldn\u2019t be surprised if he does the same thing for\nTwitter,\u201d Gowrappan said in an interview.
