While the decision was unanimous,\nthe justices divided 5-4 in their reasoning, with the majority\ndeclining to bar all patents on methods of conducting business.  \n The justices voting in the majority said there needs to be\na flexible test for emerging technologies. The case drew record\ninterest for a business dispute before the highest U.S. court,\nwith  Microsoft Corp.  and  Morgan Stanley  among dozens of\ncompanies filing briefs. The fight split industries, dividing\ncompanies that rely on their own intellectual property from\nthose aiming to head off expensive infringement lawsuits.  \n The dispute involved Bernard L. Bilski and Rand A. Warsaw,\nfounders of a Pittsburgh company that sells customized consumer\nenergy products. The Supreme Court was reviewing a decision by\nthe U.S. Court of Appeals for the Federal Circuit against Bilski\nthat said methods can be patented only if they have some\nphysical component, through either a connection to a machine or\ntheir power to transform an item into a different state.  \n Writing for the Supreme Court, Justice  Anthony Kennedy  said\nthe federal circuit\u2019s standard was only a \u201cuseful and important\nclue\u201d and isn\u2019t the sole test that should be used in\ndetermining whether a process is eligible for a patent. He did\nsay business methods \u201craise special problems in terms of\nvagueness and suspect validity.\u201d  \n The decision leaves it up to the federal circuit, which\nspecializes in patent law, to create a more flexible test.  \n Companies that argued that the lower court standard was too\nrestrictive included  Bank of America Corp. ,  Medtronic Inc. ,\nNovartis Corp.,  Palm Inc.  and Accenture Plc. Small software,\nfinancial services and electronic commerce companies also backed\nbroad patent rights. Another supporter was Ananda Chakrabarty,\nthe scientist whose patent 4,259,444, was the subject of intense\ndebate about the patentability of bioengineered organisms.  \n Those urging restrictions on method patents included\nMicrosoft, Morgan Stanley,  Google Inc.  and  J.C. Penney Co.  The\nObama administration also advocated a high standard for granting\nmethod patents, as did Bloomberg LP, the New York-based parent\ncompany of Bloomberg News.  \n Patents can be granted for machines, articles of\nmanufacture, compositions of matter, and processes. Big Brother  Both models come with two gigabytes of memory standard. The\nsmaller one weighs in at 2.3 pounds (1 kilogram); Big Brother is\n2.9 pounds. There\u2019s a spacious keyboard and generously sized\ntrackpad that makes it easy to use even in tight spaces, such as\non an airline tray table.  The Air blurs the line between laptop and tablet computing:\nSome of its key features are borrowed directly from the  iPad .\nIts secret sauce is the hard disk -- or rather, the lack of one.\nWith the new models, Apple has eliminated mechanical drives from\nthe Air line in favor of the same sort of flash-memory chips it\nuses in the iPad, and the benefits ripple throughout the\nexperience of using the machine.  For one thing, the solid-state memory responds so quickly\nthat it makes the MacBook Air feel faster and more powerful than\nit really is. Both Airs are powered by  Intel Corp. \u2019s Core 2 Duo\nmicroprocessors, which -- while more potent than the Intel Atom\nchips found in many Microsoft Windows-based netbooks -- are\nstill previous-generation technology.  Instant On  In addition, the flash memory speeds boot-up time: A cold\nstart takes less than 15 seconds -- about as close to instant-on\nperformance as we\u2019re likely to see in anything this side of an\n Amazon  Kindle. (My Windows 7-powered  Toshiba  NB 305 netbook\ntakes two minutes, give or take.) Moreover, the combination of\nsolid-state memory and the Mac\u2019s power-management features means\nyou aren\u2019t as likely to turn it off in the first place, making\nthe experience of using it that much more iPad-like -- just lift\nthe lid and you\u2019re ready to go.  Using the computer for basic tasks, including word\nprocessing and surfing the Web over a Wi-Fi connection, I was\nable to easily exceed Apple\u2019s claims of five-hour battery life\nfor the smaller Air; the 13.3-inch model, which has a beefier\nbattery, promises seven hours of operation. Apple claims up to\n30 days of standby time for both models, and while I haven\u2019t had\nthe Air long enough to test that statement, my experience with\nthe device so far leads me to believe it.  Main Drawbacks  The principal compromises imposed by the Air are storage\nand the inconvenience of adding software or watching a movie.\nWhile flash-memory chips have come down in price, spending four\nfigures on a computer that doesn\u2019t store much more than a\ntypical smartphone may rub you the wrong way.  The other drawback -- the absence of a DVD slot -- isn\u2019t as\nbig a hindrance as you might think, and is growing less so by\nthe day. The MacBook Air\u2019s emergency recovery disk, for\ninstance, isn\u2019t a disk at all -- it\u2019s a USB thumb drive. (The\nAir now has two USB ports, one more than the previous model,\nthough not the new, high-speed 3.0 version.)  More and more video content is arriving online, via\nstreaming services like  Netflix  and Apple\u2019s own iTunes Store.\nAlso, Apple is promising to bring the iPhone\u2019s App Store concept\nto the Mac within the next three months, which will make it\neasier to download software directly onto the Air.  In the meantime, if you want to install, say,  Microsoft\nCorp. \u2019s new  Office 2011 for Mac  from a disk, you\u2019ll either have\nto bear the hassle of configuring an optical drive on some other\nnearby computer to allow the Air to borrow it, or pay $79 for\nApple\u2019s external read-write DVD drive.  Two years ago, Apple\u2019s Jobs dismissed the idea of making an\nultra-small Mac because \u201cwe don\u2019t know how to make a $500\ncomputer that\u2019s not a piece of junk.\u201d With its sleek looks,\nswift performance,  Nvidia Corp.  graphics processor and other\npremium features, the MacBook Air is most certainly not a piece\nof junk. Then again, it doesn\u2019t cost $500 either. Just don\u2019t let\nApple catch you calling it a netbook.  ( Rich Jaroslovsky  is a Bloomberg News columnist. The\nopinions expressed are his own.) (AAPL)   A jury found on Aug. 24 that Samsung Electronics Co. must pay Apple $1.05 billion for infringing six patents, including four covering the design of its mobile devices.  Courts tend to give greater credence to utility patents, which cover a product\u2019s underlying technology. This case was distinct for its emphasis on design patents, which reflect Jobs\u2019s focus on the stylized nature of Apple\u2019s devices. Of the 359 patents listing Jobs as co-inventor, 86 percent are the design variety, according to  MDB Capital Group LLC .  \u201cGiven the infringement of the design patents, which protects the non-functional appearance of the iPad and iPhone, Apple now has considerable power to keep knock-off phones off the market,\u201d said  Tim Holbrook , a professor at Emory University School of Law in Atlanta.  The shares of Cupertino, California-based Apple rose 1.9 percent to a record $675.68 at the close in  New York . The stock has gained 67 percent this year.  The ruling could prompt more technology companies to issue design patents and bring suits to protect them, said MDB CEO Christopher Marlett. It also deals a setback to  Google Inc. (GOOG) , maker of the Android mobile operating system running Samsung\u2019s phones.  In a court filing today, Apple sought a ban on eight models of Samsung\u2019s smartphones, including several of its Galaxy S devices.  \u2018Consumer Desires\u2019  \u201cBecause the use of an iPhone is so intuitive, competitors attempting to design around the patents will have a far more difficult time connecting with the needs and desires of consumers,\u201d Holbrook said. \u201cGoogle\u2019s Android system may suffer as a result.\u201d  Jobs, whose patents cover the final design of many Apple products, including docks, chargers and even the glass staircases found in many Apple stores, died in October 2011.  Courts have historically favored heavy-duty technology involving electronic circuitry or computing algorithms over the brand of innovation that has made Apple\u2019s products more appealing to use and look at. That was the case in the 1980s, when Apple failed to convince courts that  Microsoft Corp. (MSFT)  CEO  Bill Gates  had violated Apple\u2019s copyright on the look and feel of the Macintosh operating system in early versions of Windows.  \u201cSteve was furious when Bill Gates introduced Windows 1.0 as he thought Microsoft was ripping Apple off and he told Bill so,\u201d former Apple CEO  John Sculley  said via e-mail. \u201cThat\u2019s when Apple began its lawsuit, which went on for years and Apple eventually lost.\u201d  Design Matters  Jurors who sided with Apple in the case against Samsung were swayed by internal e-mails describing how Google asked Samsung to change the design of its products to look less like Apple\u2019s, Velvin Hogan, foreman of the panel, said in an Aug. 25 interview.  The trial showcased how, in the increasingly competitive market for consumer electronics, design is taking on a more central role. Apple rose above rivals in the nascent personal computing world of the 1970s in part because it was the first to package its device in an attractive enclosure with built-in display.  Jobs often spoke of his fascination with design. In a 1996  interview  with Robert Cringely, he described a 1979 visit to  Xerox Corp. (XRX) \u2019s Palo Alto Research Center. While there, Jobs was so taken with the graphical user interface of its prototype PC that he didn\u2019t even notice other technical breakthroughs, including the use of networking that linked more than 100 machines.  \u2018No Taste\u2019  Jobs made no bones about drawing on what he saw at PARC as inspiration for the Mac.  \u201cPicasso had a saying: good artists copy, great artists steal,\u201d Jobs said in the interview. \u201cAnd we have always been shameless about stealing great ideas.\u201d  He drove Apple engineers to build on the concepts, creating a user interface based on a desktop metaphor, such as moving files into folders, that largely defined the modern PC. Jobs hired graphic designer  Susan Kare  to create fun, easily- understandable icons, such as the trashcan used for deleting files.  Jobs often bemoaned his competitors\u2019 lack of attention to design, even as Apple benefited from it.  \u201cThe only problem with Microsoft is that they just have no taste,\u201d he said in the  interview  with Cringely. \u201cI don\u2019t mean that in a small way, I mean that in a big way -- in the sense that they don\u2019t think of original ideas, and they don\u2019t bring much culture into their products.\u201d  Pixar Patents  After his return to Apple in 1997, the company benefited all the more from Jobs\u2019s obsession with detail. When Apple introduced its transparent, blue iMac the following year, other PC makers began experimenting with colors other than beige or black.  Jobs was undeterred by Apple\u2019s legal defeat versus Microsoft, and he became adept at using intellectual property to achieve business goals. Microsoft and Pixar instead reached a licensing deal that gave Pixar\u2019s sales a much-needed boost.  Tara Walberg, an outside spokeswoman for Microsoft, declined to comment.  Apple has stepped up efforts to protect intellectual property, in part due to the rise of Google\u2019s competing Android operating system. Apple in recent years has offered engineers financial incentives for patent applications that increase with the number of filings, said one former Apple manager who requested anonymity because the information is not public.  Kristin Huguet, a spokeswoman for Apple, declined to comment.  By early 2011, Jobs had decided to use the legal system as aggressively as possible to protect Apple\u2019s intellectual property. He famously told his biographer, Walter Isaacson, that he would spend \u201cevery penny\u201d in Apple\u2019s coffers to combat Google\u2019s software.  \u201cI\u2019m going to destroy Android, because it\u2019s a stolen product,\u201d Jobs said. \u201cI\u2019m willing to go to thermonuclear war on this.\u201d  On Aug. 24, Jobs posthumously enlisted allies in that war in a nine-person jury in federal court in California. (AAPL)  to sell four million new iPhones last week, millions more\nusers will be affected by another release: iOS 5, the latest\nversion of the operating system that runs every iPhone, iPad and\niPod touch.  I\u2019ve been testing the software and a lot of its claimed 200\nnew features for a couple of weeks and find it generally\nimpressive. But unlike the iPhone 4S, with its breakthrough Siri\nvoice-based personal assistant, iOS 5 feels more catch-up than\nforge-ahead.  Many of the new features -- secure texting, tabbed Web\nbrowsing, pull-down notifications -- may already be familiar to\nusers of devices running  Google Inc. (GOOG) \u2019s Android software,\n Microsoft Corp. (MSFT) \u2019s Windows Phone 7 and  Research In Motion Ltd. (RIM) \u2019s\nBlackBerry. As usual, Apple\u2019s contribution is to polish the\nconcepts, making them seamless and painless.  That doesn\u2019t necessarily extend to setting up iOS 5, which\nwasn\u2019t as smooth as it should have been. When I updated my iPad\n2, my Mac continued to display a \u201cRestoring iPad apps\u201d message\nlong after the iPad itself was telling me that everything had\nalready been installed.  At the end of the process, I was presented on my Mac with\nan obscure, Windows-worthy error message. The new software\nfinally appeared on the iPad, more than an hour from when I\nstarted. After that, things got a lot better.  Demoting the Computer  The importance of iOS 5 is the way it reduces the personal\ncomputer\u2019s role as hub for all your digital devices, the vital\nmiddleman for transferring and synchronizing information. Now,\nit\u2019s just one more spoke on the wheel, while the hub becomes iOS\n5\u2019s new iCloud feature.  ICloud automatically stores your content and data on\nApple\u2019s remote servers, where they are accessible by all your\nenrolled devices. Take pictures with your iPhone and a new\nfeature called Photo Stream will automatically push them up to\nthe cloud, then down to your iPad, where they will pop up almost\nimmediately. Documents, apps, media and contacts work the same\nway.  The iCloud service is free and replaces Apple\u2019s paid,\nproblematic  MobileMe . You get five gigabytes of online storage\nfree, and can buy more; photos as well as content purchased from\nApple\u2019s iTunes Store and  App Store  don\u2019t count against your\nstorage limit.  Liberating  In my testing, iCloud generally performed well, and it was\nliberating to be cut loose from the computer. When I took a\nphoto I liked, I no longer had to e-mail it to myself or rush\nback to sync devices and ensure that I had a fail-safe copy.  About the only downer was the difficulty I had migrating my\nexisting MobileMe account to iCloud; even days after the launch\nof iOS 5, I continued to run into a \u201cplease try again later\u201d\nmessage, blaming the volume of requests. I didn\u2019t think MobileMe\nwas that popular.  Among the other new features of iOS 5, a couple stand out.\nOne is iMessage, which allows you to directly text other iOS 5\nusers. For those using an iPhone, the service is fully\nintegrated with the device\u2019s existing text app. And iMessages\ndon\u2019t count against any message limits in your wireless-phone\nplan. In addition, iPad and iPod touch users also can use those\ndevices to text iPhones and each other.  Integrated Tweeting  Then there\u2019s the Notification Center: Swipe your finger\ndown from the top of any screen, and a windowshade-like overlay\ndisplays your alerts and reminders. And  Twitter  users will\nappreciate the ability to tweet directly from within Safari as\nwell as the camera, photo, YouTube and map apps.  One thing I couldn\u2019t try was iTunes Match, which the\ncompany says will launch later this month. For $25 a year, Apple\nwill scan your entire music library, looking for tunes you might\nhave ripped yourself from a CD or downloaded from some source\nother than iTunes. If Apple has the same song, you\u2019ll get access\nto it on all your devices via iCloud; if not, it will upload\nyour copy of the tune and give you full access to it.  Though it isn\u2019t being billed this way, the service is\nessentially offering absolution -- at a nominal cost -- to\npeople who have illegally downloaded music. And they\u2019ll get\naccess to Apple\u2019s high-quality versions even if their originals\nwere of lower quality. It\u2019s a way to gain a benefit and assuage\na guilty conscience at the same time.  ( Rich Jaroslovsky  is a Bloomberg News columnist. The\nopinions expressed are his own.) But there\u2019s a new, easier way to access Google Now: on an iPhone.  A recent update to  Google (GOOG) \u2019s iOS search app introduced the free service to hundreds of millions of iPhones and iPads, providing competition for Apple\u2019s voice-based assistant, Siri. I tried Google Now on both an iPhone 5 and a third-generation iPad and found it very useful, though not as convenient or powerful as its Android counterpart.  Using Google Now for either  Apple (AAPL)  or Android devices first requires you to clear a psychological hurdle: How willing are you to share your life with Google?  Now is based on Google\u2019s analysis of your browsing history, mail, calendar and other online activities to predict the information you\u2019ll need before you actually need it.  There are extensive privacy controls that let you prohibit Google from, say, extracting information from your Gmail account about packages you\u2019re expecting. But the more information you restrict, the less useful Now becomes.  All In  To test the service, I decided to go all in, even moving entries from my  Microsoft (MSFT)  Outlook and Apple calendars to the Google version to give Now the fullest view of my life.  Accessing Now on an iOS device isn\u2019t as easy as in Android, where it\u2019s deeply integrated and can be summoned by a finger swipe. On the iPhone, by contrast, you first have to launch the Google search app. Google Now appears as a stack of cards on the bottom of the screen.  When I swiped the stack, the familiar sparse white page and multicolor logo gave way to a location-customized logo -- in my case featuring images of the Golden Gate Bridge and other  San Francisco  landmarks. Meanwhile, the cards expanded into individual windows, each presenting me with specific information that Now concluded I\u2019d like to know.  Based on my calendar, for instance, Now knew I had a meeting coming up at Google headquarters in Silicon Valley -- so a card provided a map, directions and current traffic conditions.  Owing to my search history and location, it knew of my devotion to the  San Francisco Giants , so it automatically displayed the previous night\u2019s score.  Scenic Spots  Other cards appeared and disappeared from the stack depending on where I was and what I was doing. In the coastal town of Half Moon Bay, where I hadn\u2019t been for months, a card suggested scenic photo spots, and at the Caltrain station in  Palo Alto  I got info about the next northbound train.  In an airport, it would have provided gate and departure-time for my flight; in a foreign country, translation and currency conversion.  Like Apple\u2019s Siri, you can use your voice to launch a search, though you can\u2019t tell it to create an alert or a reminder, or send an e-mail -- a significant limitation. And Google Now only works with Google services. Had I entered my meeting using Apple\u2019s iCloud instead of Google Calendar, I wouldn\u2019t have gotten the driving-direction card.  Glitches  I encountered other drawbacks and glitches as well. Asking for directions in the iPad version of Google Now launched the shrunken iPhone version of  Google Maps , a much less pleasant experience than the Web-based version, or even Apple\u2019s mapping app.  When I stood in San Francisco\u2019s Embarcadero Center and asked each assistant to \u201cfind a  Chipotle (CMG)  near me,\u201d Google\u2019s top choice was in Berkeley, 12 miles away. Siri pointed me to the one within two blocks.  Most maddening, while Google Now correctly deduced my home address, it flubbed my work location, targeting Bloomberg\u2019s Palo Alto office, where I usually work only one day a week, and resisting several efforts to override it with the correct San Francisco address.  On the other hand, I saw no evidence of an unusual power drain, a concern raised by some users.  Google says  the service uses cell-phone towers and Wi-Fi hotspots to calculate where you are, rather than your device\u2019s more precise but power-hungry global positioning system.  Are the privacy implications of Google Now too creepy to justify using it? I don\u2019t think so -- but that\u2019s something you\u2019ll have to decide for yourself, depending on how much you trust Google.  As the saying goes, if you\u2019re not paying for a tech product, the real product is probably you.  ( Rich Jaroslovsky  is a Bloomberg News columnist. The opinions expressed are his own.) Allegations of Deception  It\u2019s possible the FTC, which handles consumer-protection\nissues, could begin a probe examining allegations of deception\nby Google, expanding it into a broader antitrust investigation,\nLande said.  On March 30, Google agreed to settle FTC claims that it\nused deceptive tactics and violated its own privacy policies\nwhen it introduced the Buzz social-networking service last year.  Last month, Rosch said if the FTC opens an investigation\ninto the search industry and decides to bring a case, it could\nrely on powers it used to reach a settlement with  Intel Corp. (INTC) \nlast year.  In the Intel case, the FTC invoked Section 5 of the law\nthat established the agency in 1914 to challenge \u201cunfair or\ndeceptive\u201d practices, going beyond what is specifically banned\nby other federal antitrust statutes.  The use of Section 5 and FTC\u2019s ability to handle its cases\nthrough its own administrative processes rather than necessarily\ngoing to court, as the Justice Department must, would make it\neasier for the FTC to pursue Google, said  Herbert Hovenkamp , a\nprofessor at the University of Iowa College of Law. Look Back.","released_at":"<date>June 7 2013<\/date> <time>23:41:55<\/time>","content":"You might not love  Big Brother . But you must know he\u2019s part of your family.  He\u2019s been with us since J. Edgar Hoover created the modern U.S. surveillance state, with the invaluable help of the National Security Agency, at the dawn of the  Cold War . Every president since has embraced Big Brother, some closely. So has every Congress -- save one, almost 40 years ago.  President  Barack Obama  has said he welcomes a debate on the clash between national security and civil liberties. Fine, let\u2019s have one -- preferably in public, with witnesses under oath, starting with the NSA\u2019s director and  Google Inc. (GOOG) \u2019s \u201cdon\u2019t be evil\u201d executives. After this week\u2019s reports on the scope of the American intelligence dragnet, the Senate should revive the Church Committee, which exposed the NSA\u2019s spying on Americans in the months before the U.S. bicentennial in 1976.  The NSA is a military intelligence service dedicated to gathering and analyzing the telecommunications of foreign nations -- tapping their phones, breaking their diplomatic and military codes -- and securing our own. Created in 1952, it immediately began spying on Americans.  From day one, the NSA collected millions of messages from RCA, ITT and Western Union, the three great global telecommunications companies of the day. The program, Shamrock, ran under presidents from  Harry Truman  to  Gerald Ford . Its roots lay in FBI-Army counterespionage against the Soviets. If it caught a spy of great note, that fact remains unrecorded in the annals of American intelligence.  Snooping Expands  More ominously, the NSA, by request of the Central Intelligence Agency and the  Federal Bureau of Investigation , eavesdropped on Americans for a decade under Presidents  Lyndon Johnson  and  Richard Nixon . The CIA wanted to snoop on Americans suspected of \u201ccivil disorders, radical student or youth activities, racial militant activities, radical antiwar activities [and] related media activities.\u201d  Hoover and the FBI wanted all that and more: wiretaps of civil-rights and black-power advocates. This program, Minaret, created thousands of intelligence reports. NSA instructed its personnel to keep their fingerprints off the reporting.  The NSA and the CIA were created to collect foreign intelligence. When they chased foreign terrorists and spies, these programs were legal. But the CIA has no police powers; it cannot spy on Americans. When the FBI was involved -- and it was, at all levels, opening mail, tapping phones, breaking and entering without judicial warrants -- that was as illegal as it gets.  In 1973, after Hoover\u2019s death, the  Justice Department   caught  wind of Minaret. Who, me? the NSA said. It falsely contended that its spying on Americans was \u201can incidental and unintended act,\u201d a lie that didn\u2019t stand for long.  The same thing happened three months into the first Obama administration. After the passage of the new laws on government eavesdropping, the laws that stand today, the NSA was caught in the act of systemically \u201covercollecting\u201d the domestic communications of Americans in the spring of 2009. Oops, sorry, the NSA said. Never again.  Let\u2019s talk about the laws. After the Church Committee exposed the depths of illegal spying on Americans in 1975 and 1976, Congress created the Foreign Intelligence Surveillance Court. If the intelligence services wanted to open mail or tap a phone, they had to get a warrant from those federal judges, who meet in secret in a lead-lined chamber atop the Justice Department. They almost never say no.  This system served well -- until the government started bending the law, then breaking it.  Unimaginable Latitude  The NSA was in deep trouble in the years before the Sept. 11 attacks. Fiber-optic cables, encrypted e-mail and digital telephony put the agency behind the technological curve in its quest for global electronic eavesdropping.  After the attacks, President George W. Bush and Congress gave the NSA almost unimaginable latitude under the law to collect e-mail and telecommunications inside the U.S.  The NSA again quickly overstepped the Fourth Amendment\u2019s prohibition of unwarranted searches and seizures. The FBI director and the acting attorney general had to threaten to resign in March 2004 before Bush backed down and promised to put the NSA under the limits of the law.  So, after long struggle, Congress repeatedly rewrote the spying statutes. In 2008, late in the  Bush administration , it amended the law governing the Foreign Intelligence Surveillance Court. It added a provision allowing the NSA to obtain a \u201cprogrammatic\u201d search warrant. A programmatic warrant is not a probable-cause warrant. It allows the NSA to collect phone calls and e-mails with no requirement that the senders or recipients might be suspected terrorists or spies.  The NSA acknowledges it has violated the letter and spirit of that law once or twice or three times. Sorry about that.  Congress should be sorry too. A programmatic warrant sounds a little too much like a \u201cgeneral warrant\u201d -- a proximate cause of the American Revolution against the British.  The Prism program revealed this week by the  Guardian  and the Washington Post was one immediate result of the intelligence law revisions. They appear to allow the NSA access to  Microsoft Corp. (MSFT) ,  Yahoo! Inc. (YHOO) , Google,  Facebook Inc. (FB) , Skype Inc., YouTube,  AOL Inc. (AOL)  and  Apple Inc. (AAPL)  data. They also seem to allow dragnets of metadata from major American telecommunication companies, like Verizon -- including logs of calls within the  United States  -- without having to obtain individual warrants.  President Obama says this is perfectly legal, that the courts and Congress are on board, and that no Americans have been harmed. He may well be right. But, in the words of  Michael Kinsley , the scandal is not what is illegal -- it is what is legal.  We are surely in uncharted terrain when government spies and social-media giants collaborate in secret. We have to map this new world to keep our bearings as a democracy.  We know that information is power, secret information is power squared, and secret information that\u2019s eyes-only for the president is power cubed. That\u2019s why we have intelligence services.  Secret power can be a danger in a democracy. U.S. intelligence services have a history of operating at the edge of the law and beyond. But fewer judges, politicians and reporters today have the courage to check them than back in the days when the Church Committee let us see the skeletons in the closets of our spooks. That\u2019s why the laws governing intelligence need a public hearing.  (Tim Weiner, a former reporter for the  New York  Times, has won the Pulitzer Prize and the National Book Award for writing on national security. He is the author, most recently, of \u201c Enemies: A History of the FBI .\u201d)  To contact the writer of this article: Tim Weiner at tiwein@hotmail.com.  To contact the editor responsible for this article: Katy Roberts at  kroberts29@bloomberg.net .","path":".\/2008_2012_msft_bloomberg_news\/big-brother-is-watching-you-look-back-.txt"},{"id":76835450,"title":"New Nokia Is Good Phone at Great Price: Rich Jaroslovsky","released_at":"<date>April 4 2012<\/date> <time>03:01:52<\/time>","content":"When people buy smartphones, they\ndon\u2019t usually base their decision on how many cores the\nprocessor has or other arcane specs. They want to know how the\nphone looks and feels, how enjoyable it is to use, and how much\nit costs.  On those points, the  Nokia (NOK1V)  Lumia 900, which goes on sale\nthis weekend, measures up well. It\u2019s a very good phone and an\neven better value, delivering advanced features for $100 on a\ntwo-year contract, much less than competitive offerings.  A lot is riding on this phone\u2019s success. For Nokia and its\npartner Microsoft, it\u2019s a chance to become relevant in a\nmarketplace that has largely passed them by. For AT&T, it\u2019s an\nopportunity to attract users to its newest high-speed data\nnetwork and set itself apart now that its monopoly on  Apple (AAPL) \niPhone sales in the U.S. has expired.  The Lumia 900, which runs Microsoft\u2019s Windows Phone 7\noperating system, doesn\u2019t match the iPhone\u2019s ease of use or the\nvast ecosystems of apps and services that have grown up around\nboth it and phones running  Google (GOOG) \u2019s Android operating system.\nBut I found it more pleasurable than any of a half-dozen largely\nindistinguishable Android phones I\u2019ve recently checked out.  Extra Texture  The phone weighs 5.6 ounces, features a vivid 4.3-inch\nscreen and comes with 16 gigabytes of storage. You have your\nchoice of three colors and, curiously, two textures: The\npolycarbonate bodies of the blue and black models have a matte\nsurface similar to the smaller Lumia 800. The white version has\na glossy finish.  While the case of my blue test model proved impressively\nimpervious to smudges, the feel of the phone still took some\ngetting used to, due to the raised ridges around the screen\nwhere it\u2019s set into the case. My ears took a while to adjust.  I\u2019m a fan of Windows Phone 7, whose user-friendly interface\nfeatures large, colorful tiles that display continuously updated\ndata about people, messages and other things important to you.  One thing I\u2019m not a fan of, though, is turning on a new\ndevice and immediately having to delete a bunch of stuff I don\u2019t\nwant.  Junked Up  AT&T (T)  has junked up the home screen with proprietary apps\nfor, among other things, its  U-verse  television service and a\npaid navigation service. If you want Nokia\u2019s free navigation app\n-- and you do -- you\u2019ll have to download it yourself from the\n\u201cNokia collection\u201d listing on the Windows Phone online store.  Once you take care of the housekeeping, you\u2019ll find the\nLumia 900 a pleasure to use, thanks in part to a couple of\nimportant firsts.  It\u2019s the first Windows phone to run over AT&T\u2019s 4G LTE,\nfor \u201cLong-Term Evolution,\u201d network. If you\u2019re lucky enough to\nlive in one of the areas where it\u2019s been introduced, you\u2019ll find\nthat apps and data download far faster than on the older 3G\nnetwork (including the tweaked 3G service that AT&T confusingly\nmarkets as \u201c4G\u201d). But be sure to check on  coverage ; AT&T still\nlags behind rival  Verizon Wireless  in rolling out the new high-\nspeed service.  Facing Front  The other first, for a Nokia Windows phone, is the front-\nfacing camera. Using the Lumia 900 and a beta version of\n Microsoft (MSFT) \u2019s  Skype  app, I was able to easily video-chat over LTE\nwith an iPhone user.  I also liked the rear-facing camera, unusually nice for a\n$100 phone, with its Carl Zeiss optics and eight-megapixel\nsensor. Unlike some more expensive phones, which can shoot 1080p\nvideo, the Lumia is limited to 720p, but that\u2019s still good\nenough to be considered high-definition.  Battery life on the 900 is good, not great. In my tests, I\nwas able to get through a full day of normal use but found the\nbattery level dropped appreciably while the phone was in standby\nmode if I kept the power-hungry LTE service turned on.  The Nokia\u2019s performance was slightly better than my Droid\nCharge, which runs over  Verizon (VZ) \u2019s LTE network. On the other\nhand, the Charge has a replaceable battery; the Lumia\u2019s case,\nlike the iPhone\u2019s, is sealed.  Even at twice the price, the Lumia 900 would be a\ncreditable challenger to Android phones from the likes of\nSamsung,  Motorola Mobility (MMI)  and  HTC. (2498)  It may not be enough to\nrestore the mobile fortunes of Nokia and Microsoft, but for $100\nit\u2019s a premium product at a value price, and well worth\nconsidering. Hackers targeted Google, owner of the most popular search\nengine, 38 percent of the time as of Dec. 31, according to the\nreport to be released later this month by Barracuda Networks\nInc., a web security firm.  Mountain View , California-based\nGoogle accounted for 69 percent of the attacks in a sample\nconducted around June, the report says. A Barracuda  report  in\nJuly labeled Google \u201cking of malware.\u201d  Even as Google improved its security, the number of attacks\nincreased. In the December sample, Barracuda said it found 226\npieces of bad software a day, compared with 146 in June.\nMeanwhile, Google\u2019s competitors recorded an increase in malware-\nlaced search results: Cyber criminals placed 30 percent of their\nbad software on Yahoo! search results in December, up from 18\npercent in June. Bing accounted for 24 percent in December, up\nfrom 12 percent in June. And the targeting of Twitter rose to 8\npercent from 1 percent, the report says.  Google said it has ratcheted up efforts to identify and\nscrub attempts at so-called search poisoning, which allows\ncriminals to take control of computers to perpetuate cyber\nattacks, as well as large-scale banking and identity-theft\nswindles.  Faster Detection  \u201cWe have done a lot of work to detect these quickly and to\nwarn users,\u201d  Niels Provos , principal software engineer in\nGoogle\u2019s infrastructure security group, said in an interview.\nLast year, it took 10 hours to remove the bugs; now it takes an\nhour, he said. The cyber\nthieves\u2019 gambit to infect search results is harder to bypass.\nAmericans conducted 17.8 billion searches in November 2010, a 23\npercent increase from a year earlier, according to  ComScore\nInc. , a Reston Virginia-based market-research firm.  \u201cOne of the reasons this is so highly targeted is the\nvolume of searches is increasing rapidly,\u201d said Paul Judge,\nchief research officer of Campbell, California-based Barracuda.\n\u201cPeople have become lazy and dependent on\u201d Google and its\nrivals. SEC Enforcement Director  Robert Khuzami  said in November\nthat the unit filed 735 actions in fiscal 2011, \u201ca record-\nbreaking performance during a period of resource constraints.\u201d\nCiting the numbers, SEC Chairman  Mary Schapiro  told a Washington\nconference last week that the agency\u2019s changes \u201care already\nproducing record results.\u201d The SEC also noted the record\nnumbers in justifying its 2013 budget request to Congress.  Still, more than 230, or 31 percent, of the 735 matters\nweren\u2019t new. They were so-called follow-on administrative\nproceedings that institute penalties in cases that already had\nbeen brought, the examination by Bloomberg News shows.  Excluding those actions, such as barring people who\u2019ve\nalready been found guilty of fraud from working in the industry,\nthe SEC filed 499 original cases last year, fewer than the 520\nin 2009, the year before the reorganization. In 2009, 144, or 22\npercent, of the 664 total actions were follow-on proceedings.  The SEC has been under pressure for more than three years\nto show results, while struggling to get additional funding from\nCongress. Schapiro is scheduled to defend her budget request\ntomorrow before a House panel.  For more, click here. The announcement came a day after European Union regulators\n dropped  a similar probe into  AstraZeneca Plc (AZN) , the U.K.\u2019s second-\nbiggest drugmaker, and  Takeda Pharmaceutical Co. (4502) \u2019s Nycomed unit\nover possible collusion to keep cheaper copies of medicines off\nthe market. That case was brought to a halt because of a lack of\nevidence.  Antitrust regulators on both sides of the Atlantic are\nfocusing on how settlements between companies that make branded\nmedicines and generic-drug producers might harm consumers. Inc.  are fighting back against the  National Security Agency  by using harder-to-crack code to shield their networks and online customer data from unauthorized U.S. spying.  The companies, burned by disclosures they\u2019ve cooperated with U.S. surveillance programs, are protecting user e-mail and social-media posts with strengthened encryption that the U.S. government says won\u2019t be easily broken until 2030.  While the NSA may find ways around the barriers, the companies say they have to assure users their online connections are secure and data can\u2019t be grabbed when transmitted over fiber-optic networks or digitally stored.  Microsoft Corp.  is convinced it must \u201cinvest in protecting customers\u2019 information from a wide range of threats, which if the allegations are true, include governments,\u201d Matt Thomlinson, general manager of trustworthy computing, said in an e-mail. He didn\u2019t provide details.  Internet companies including Google, Yahoo, Facebook, Microsoft and Apple Inc. are trying to distance themselves from news reports that they gave the agency data on electronic communications of Americans and foreigners or have lax security.  While the companies are trying to prevent the NSA from gaining unauthorized access to their data, they say they comply with legal court orders compelling them to provide the government information.  The NSA has tapped fiber-optic cables abroad in order to siphon off data from Google and Yahoo, circumvented or cracked encryption, and covertly introduced weaknesses and back doors into coding, according to reports in the Washington Post, the New York Times and the U.K.\u2019s Guardian newspaper based on documents leaked by former NSA contractor  Edward Snowden .  Game On  Companies are fighting back primarily by using increasingly complex encryption, which scrambles data using a mathematical formula that can be decoded only with a special digital key. The idea is to protect sensitive information like e-mails, Internet searches and digital calls.  Google has accelerated efforts to encrypt information flowing between its data centers, doubled the length of its digital keys and implemented measures to detect fraudulent certificates for verifying the authenticity of websites, according to a statement from the Mountain View, California-based company.  Read more from the New World of Risk  Special Report : NSA spy programs have \u201cthe great potential for doing serious damage to the competitiveness\u201d of U.S. companies, Richard Salgado, Google\u2019s director of law enforcement and information security,  told a Senate subcommittee  Nov. 13.  \u201cIt\u2019s very important that the users of our services understand that we are stewards of their data, we hold it responsibly, we treat it with respect,\u201d Salgado said. \u201cWe\u2019ve already seen impacts on the businesses.\u201d  Government Threat  Google, Yahoo and Facebook generated $44.4 billion in advertising revenue so far in 2013 in part by mining users\u2019 private data, according to Bloomberg Industries.  An  Aug. 14 analysis  by  Forrester Research Inc.  analyst  James Staten  found the U.S. cloud computing industry could lose as much as $180 billion by 2016 due to the spying disclosures.  Yahoo will make encrypted connections standard by January for all its Mail users with 2048-bit digital keys, Sarah Meron, a spokeswoman for the Sunnyvale, California-based company, said in an e-mail.  Facebook, in addition to moving toward 2048-bit encryption keys, is accelerating a tactic known as \u201cperfect forward secrecy\u201d that prevents the NSA from deciphering the communications of users if it obtains a security code,  Jodi Seth , a company spokeswoman, said in an e-mail.  Slow Adoption  While Google has led the industry in adopting security practices, \u201cmany of its competitors have been slow to follow,\u201d Christopher Soghoian, principal technologist for the American Civil Liberties Union\u2019s speech, privacy and technology project, said in e-mail.  \u201cYahoo is waiting until 2014 to do what Google did in 2010,\u201d he said. \u201cThe National Security Agency is harvesting hundreds of millions of contact lists from personal e-mail and instant messaging accounts around the world, many of them belonging to Americans.\u201d  The National Institute of Standards and Technology has determined that known computing power won\u2019t be able to break 2048-bit encryption until at least 2030.  Agencies like the NSA use stronger encryption, said  Bruce Schneier , a fellow at the Berkman Center for Internet and Society at Harvard Law School.  Schneier recommends companies encrypt everything even though the NSA can often defeat it by, among other tactics, installing malicious software on computers to steal the security keys that unlock encryption codes.  Backdoor Grab  \u201cThe NSA has turned the Internet into a giant surveillance platform,\u201d Schneier, a computer security and privacy specialist, said in a phone interview.  The companies may not be moving fast enough in a cat-and-mouse game with the NSA, said  Kurt Opsahl , senior staff attorney for the San Francisco-based digital rights group Electronic Frontier Foundation.  \u201cThe NSA is one of the largest, most powerful, well-funded intelligence agencies in the world,\u201d Opsahl said in a phone interview. \u201cWhile the government has been misusing its legal authorities to require a set of data at the front door, the NSA has been sneaking in the back door to grab all the data.\u201d  The NSA collects \u201cthe communications of targets of foreign intelligence value, irrespective of the provider that carriers them,\u201d the agency said in an Oct. 31 statement.  \u2018Political Problem\u2019  The U.S. uses \u201cevery intelligence tool available\u201d to intercept electronic communications of suspected terrorists relying on \u201cthe very same social networking sites, encryption tools and other security features\u201d as innocent Americans, Director of National Intelligence  James Clapper  said in an Oct. 4 statement.  Encryption isn\u2019t foolproof. The NSA can use hacking attacks to obtain security keys or compel companies to hand them over with court orders, said Jonas Falck, chief executive officer and co-founder of  Halon Security  Inc., a network security company with U.S. headquarters in San Francisco.  Companies like Google also introduce security vulnerabilities when they decrypt data to analyze user trends for advertising purposes, Falck said in a phone interview. Google spokeswoman  Niki Fenwick  said the company declined to respond to this concern.  Companies have different levels of encryption, which mean electronic communications sent between them may not be protected from starting point to end point, Opsahl said.  Encrypting data can, at the least, make it harder for the NSA to gain unauthorized access to information, forcing the agency to pick targets or come out of the shadows and go before a court to obtain it legally, Opsahl said.  The other thing companies can do is lobby Congress to change the law to restrict what the NSA is able to do, according to Schneier.  \u201cThere is a technology component, but primarily this is a political problem,\u201d Schneier said. The agency\u2019s 11-member\nboard will meet Dec. 16 to decide whether to approve the cap-\nand-trade plan.  This month, voters in California rejected a ballot measure\nbacked by oil refineries that would have suspended the global-\nwarming law signed by Republican Governor  Arnold Schwarzenegger .  Oil refiners  Tesoro Corp .,  Valero Energy Corp . and Flint\nHills Resources LLC, a subsidiary of Koch Industries Inc.,\nhelped fund efforts to delay the law through a proposition on\nthe Nov. 2 ballot. The measure, which would have suspended the\nlaw until California\u2019s unemployment rate is cut by more than\nhalf, was defeated with 62 percent of voters opposed, according\nto state election records.  Gates, Brin, Doerr  Supporters of the global-warming law, including Microsoft\nCorp. founder  Bill Gates , Google Inc. co-founder  Sergey Brin  and\nventure capitalist  John Doerr , raised more than $30 million to\ncampaign against the ballot measure with radio, television and\nprint advertising.  The program will cover almost 400 million metric tons of\ncarbon dioxide from power plants, factories, refineries and the\ntailpipes of cars and trucks once fully phased in by 2015.\nThat\u2019s more than double the emissions covered by a carbon market\nfor power plants in the U.S. Northeast, called the Regional\nGreenhouse Gas Initiative, and almost one-fifth the current size\nof Europe\u2019s cap-and-trade program, according to data compiled by\nBloomberg.  State-Run Auctions  By 2015, refiners in California would probably have to buy\npermits in state-run auctions and would be able to pass on\nhigher costs to consumers, the air resources board said in a\nreport last month. Gasoline prices may increase 4 percent to 8\npercent if permits are priced from $15 to $30 each, the agency\nsaid in a report. If carbon allowance prices climbed to $75\neach, gasoline prices would be 19 percent higher in 2020.  Higher fuel prices \u201cmay induce some consumers to switch to\nsmaller vehicles that are both more fuel-efficient but less\nexpensive than the larger vehicles chosen without cap-and-\ntrade,\u201d according to the agency\u2019s economic analysis. Others may\nrespond by driving less, the agency found.  California will try to expand its carbon market by\npersuading other U.S. states and some Canadian provinces to set\nup similar cap-and-trade programs, which could be linked, the\nair resources board said in its report.  \u201cLower transaction costs and market efficiency are the\nbest tools for managing carbon risk,\u201d Brannen McElmurray,\ndirector of environmental commodities at NRG, said in a\nstatement.  Farms, Forests  California\u2019s cap-and-trade program would also let companies\nbuy a limited number of offsets, which are pollution cuts from\nunregulated sources such as farms, instead of state-issued\ncarbon allowances.  U.S. forests, farms that capture methane from livestock\nmanure and projects that destroy ozone-depleting industrial\ngases, such as hydrochlorofluorocarbons used in refrigeration,\nwould be the approved sources of carbon offsets at the beginning\nof the cap-and-trade program, the air resources board said last\nmonth.  Schwarzenegger announced partnerships yesterday with state\ngovernments in Brazil and Mexico to protect tropical rainforests\nthat store large volumes of carbon. The partnership aims to\ncreate an additional source of offsets -- saving tropical\nrainforests in developing countries -- that companies can use in\nCalifornia\u2019s carbon market, Schwarzenegger said in a  statement . (GOOG) \u2019s $12.4 billion purchase last year of mobile-phone pioneer Motorola Mobility Holdings partly for its trove of more than 17,000 patents is showing signs it wasn\u2019t much of a bargain.  A federal judge last week said  Microsoft Corp. (MSFT)  owes only pennies in royalties per sale of each Xbox video-gaming system and Windows operating system instead of the potential billions of dollars Google sought in a patent-infringement case. Four days earlier, the Google unit lost another patent case against  Apple Inc. (AAPL)   Google, owner of the most-used search engine and the Android operating system for wireless devices, estimated in regulatory  filings  that $5.5 billion of the purchase price for Motorola was for patents and developed technology. Chief Executive Officer  Larry Page  in August 2011 said Motorola\u2019s patent portfolio would \u201chelp protect Android from anticompetitive threats from Microsoft, Apple and other companies.\u201d  \u201cIt wasn\u2019t an irrational decision at the time but they\u2019ve gotten nothing but heartbreak for that money,\u201d said Rodney Sweetland, a patent lawyer with Duane Morris in  Washington  who has watched the legal disputes over smartphones. \u201cShould they have bought? Not at that price.\u201d  While the acquisition may have deterred  Apple (AAPL)  and Microsoft from filing new patent lawsuits against it, Mountain View, California-based Google hasn\u2019t won a decisive legal case with a big payoff -- such as a lucrative licensing deal. Motorola\u2019s patents also opened up the company to increased antitrust scrutiny, leaving Google to face legal battles in  Europe  and the U.S. with patents that may not be as valuable as investors thought.  \u2019Striking Out\u2019  Since Google acquired Motorola Mobility in May 2012, most of the company\u2019s efforts to limit sales of Microsoft\u2019s products in Europe have been averted, a U.S. judge in  Chicago  threw out claims Apple and Motorola Mobility lodged against each other, and a U.S. trade panel rejected claims against Apple over wireless technology.  \u201cThey just keep striking out when they have all this ammunition allegedly behind them,\u201d said  Will Stofega , a program manager at Framingham, Massachusetts-based researcher IDC. \u201cThey don\u2019t have any home runs to show for it.\u201d  U.S. District Judge James Robart in  Seattle  on April 25 released his decision that Google\u2019s Motorola unit isn\u2019t entitled to royalties of 2.25 percent of retail sales it sought for Xbox and Windows, which Microsoft estimated would cost it $4 billion. Instead, Robart put the value of patents for video-decoding and wireless technology at a few cents per unit, equal to about $1.8 million, according to Microsoft.  Long-term Investment  On April 22, the U.S. International Trade Commission in Washington invalidated Motorola Mobility\u2019s patent on a phone sensor in a case that could have limited Apple\u2019s ability to ship Chinese-made iPhones into the U.S.  \u201cWe acquired Motorola to level the playing field in patent attacks against Android and draw on Motorola\u2019s long history of innovation,\u201d said Matt Kallman, Google\u2019s spokesman, in an e- mail. \u201cIn just under a year they\u2019ve accomplished a lot, with impressive velocity and execution. The patents didn\u2019t fall into the hands of a Google rival, nor did Motorola Mobility become like Ericsson AB or  Nokia Oyj (NOK1V) , using litigation to try to recoup the billions they spent on wireless research.  Handset Help  When Google announced in August 2011 it was going to buy Motorola Mobility, it was being criticized by handset makers for not helping them fight off patent lawsuits over phones running on Android, the most popular operating system for mobile devices.  Google at the time had fewer than 1,000 of its own patents, most related to search. The company needed to bolster its negotiating position for a licensing deal that would protect all Android customers because in a typical patent dispute, competitors assess each other\u2019s patent holdings, with net licensing fees going to the company with stronger patents.  \u201cIt definitely has taken a lot of pressure off Android,\u201d said  Colin Sebastian , an analyst with Robert Baird & Co. \u201cThere was the appearance of multiple storm clouds in the patent litigation for Android until they closed this acquisition.\u201d  Apple, which contends that Android phones copied the look and features that made the iPhone so popular, brought cases against Motorola Mobility,  HTC Corp. (2498)  and  Samsung Electronics Co. (005930)  Microsoft, whose Windows operating system dominates on personal computers, likewise demanded royalties from companies that made products using Android.  Even as it fights in courts with Motorola Mobility, Microsoft has been landing patent agreements with manufacturers that use Android software, such as Samsung, HTC and  ZTE Corp. (000063)   Portfolio Value  Given the results of the litigation, \u201cthe perceived value of the portfolio is clearly less\u201d than what Google paid, said Erin-Michael Gill, managing director of MDB Capital Group LLC, a Santa Monica, California-based investment bank that specializes in patent issues.  The Motorola Mobility unit generated $4.14 billion in revenue last year, about 8 percent of Google\u2019s total sales, and had about $1.1 billion in losses, according to data compiled by  Bloomberg (GOOG) .  Page is streamlining the unit to bolster efforts in the smartphone and tablet market. The Motorola Home set-top box division was sold for about $2.35 billion, and more than 5,200 jobs are being cut. Stofega said investors are looking for new devices or innovations to come out of Motorola Mobility, perhaps at the  Google I\/O  2013 meeting in San Francisco next month.  Patent Sprees  \u201cMotorola has a great set of assets,\u201d Google Chief Financial Officer Patrick Pichette said at a conference in February. \u201cIt had a pipeline of products that were fine, but not really to the standards that Google would say is wow, innovative, transformative. (6758)   As the exporters prepare to announce first-quarter  earnings  this week, 14 of  Japan \u2019s 27 largest are projected to beat their own full-year operating profit forecasts by 5 percent or more, according to data compiled by Bloomberg. Net income may surge 75 percent from a year earlier among companies that sell abroad and 33 percent at domestic-oriented firms, UBS AG said this month.  Abe\u2019s drive to end 15 years of deflation in Japan through monetary easing and fiscal stimulus benefited manufacturers as the  yen  dropped 5 percent against the dollar last quarter and about 20 percent in the past 12 months, boosting earnings from overseas. Toyota, the world\u2019s largest carmaker, may exceed its fiscal-year net income target by 21 percent, according to the average of 23 analyst  estimates  compiled by Bloomberg.  \u201cAbe introduced a real bullet,\u201d said Ichiro Takamatsu, a  fund manager  in  Tokyo  at Bayview Asset Management Co. \u201cCompanies will report stronger numbers because of the weak yen.\u201d  Toyota, set to report earnings on Aug. 2, may say first-quarter net income rose 48 percent to 430 billion yen ($4.3 billion), according to the average of four analyst  estimates . Profit for the year ending March may jump 72 percent to 1.66 trillion yen, based on 23 projections.  Sony, Japan\u2019s biggest smartphone maker, may boost full-year profit 28 percent to 55 billion yen, according to the average of 16  analyst  estimates. The Tokyo-based company will report first-quarter earnings on Aug. 1. Sony shares, which have more than  doubled  this year, declined 3.6 percent to 2,057 yen. Japan\u2019s broader Topix index fell 3.3 percent. Companies such as Toyota, after stockpiling cash, could bolster Abe\u2019s stimulus efforts by increasing  capital investment , wages and dividends.  \u201cCompanies are of course happy to receive the windfall from a weaker yen and stronger exports, but extremely reluctant to spread this additional income,\u201d said  Martin Schulz , an economist at Fujitsu Research Institute in Tokyo. \u201cThey would rather keep that income and focus on investment, particularly overseas.\u201d  Weaker Yen  Analysts expect exporters including Toyota and Sony to beat their forecasts in part because the yen is trading at lower levels than the companies predicted. Sony targets 50 billion yen in full-year net income based on the same projected rates. Because of invaluable Internet technology, the world is\nat our fingertips. Vast quantities of data are available with a\ntap or a click.  It isn\u2019t news how much information is collected, shared or\nsold on the Internet. What is news is how much of that\ninformation might be about you.  Every time you go online, a host of invisible data\ncatchers, placed on your computer without your permission,\nfollow you as you browse, reporting your stops and actions to\nthird-party businesses unrelated to, and sometimes without the\nknowledge of, the owners of the sites you visit.  This behind-the-scenes data collection is different from\nthat done by websites you choose to visit. We know that those\nsites track our purchases and navigation on their sites, and use\nthe information to serve us better by remembering our address,\nsuggesting products we might enjoy and adjusting their offerings\nto meet our apparent interests. In this way, the Internet has\nallowed large companies to give us the personal service of a\nneighborhood butcher, who puts aside your son\u2019s favorite cut of\nmeat whenever he comes home from college.  We know less about the third-party data miners. They\ncompile profiles of our online behavior for their own use or to\nsell to other companies, primarily to target  Internet\nadvertising  to your particular interests. This marketing\nstrategy helps support the free Web content we all enjoy. But it\nalso raises serious privacy concerns, especially when the data\ninvolves your health, finances, children or whereabouts.  Consumer Choice  To the extent that this data is used to advertise a shirt,\na car, a vacation destination or a soft drink, we might view it\nas innocuous, even beneficial to the thriving Internet market\nthat has increased choice for consumers everywhere. And that\nwould be fine, if we knew that your tracked information stopped\nat the online ad company. But we don\u2019t. It might continue to\ntravel throughout an invisible lattice of online and offline\ncompanies, developing into a profile of you that anyone might\nbuy, including those making decisions about your career, your\ncredit, your health, your reputation.  Let\u2019s say you print out a fact sheet on alcoholism to help\nyour son with a project for health class; you know you are a\ndutiful parent, but a potential employer might see a boozy job\napplicant. You order a big box of your mother\u2019s favorite candy\nto take her when you go to visit; you know you are a thoughtful\ndaughter, but a health insurer could see a destined diabetic.\nYou buy the book \u201cThe Winner\u2019s Guide to Casino Gambling\u201d as a\nraffle prize for your church\u2019s Las Vegas Night; you know you are\na generous member of the community, but a loan officer might see\na risky gambler.  \u2018Do Not Track\u2019  At the Federal Trade Commission, we want you to have a\nchoice about what you make public and what you keep private.\nLast December, our staff proposed a \u201cDo Not Track\u201d mechanism\nthat would let you choose the information you share about your\nbrowsing behavior; your tracking preferences would travel with\nyou every time you went online. We envision a system you can\nfind and use easily, and one that all companies tracking you on\nthe Internet would need to respect or face serious consequences.  When we first proposed Do Not Track, many in the online\ncommunity complained that it would destroy the Internet\nadvertising business. But Do Not Track doesn\u2019t stop advertisers\nfrom collecting information about consumers. It does, however,\nrequire them to convince us that they will treat personal data\nwith care. And at the FTC, we are certain that the advertisers\nmarketing on the Web today are up to that task.  In fact, a number of leading online businesses, including\nMicrosoft, Mozilla and Apple, have responded by developing Do\nNot Track systems, and other companies may soon join them. A\ncoalition of advertising industry groups has redoubled efforts\nto establish Do Not Track architecture. And key Internet\nstandards-setting bodies are working on Do Not Track.  Congress Is Looking  With continued work, I am confident that industry will be\nable to devise a Do Not Track mechanism that is universal,\nsimple, persistent, effective and enforceable. Admittedly, this\nisn\u2019t easy -- from a technical or a business perspective -- and\nthe FTC is considering various alternatives.  During hearings in the past year, members of Congress have\ninquired about Do Not Track. And last month, Senator John D. Rockefeller IV, chairman of the U.S. Senate Committee on\nCommerce, Science and Transportation, introduced legislation\nthat would empower the FTC to establish an industry-run Do Not\nTrack mechanism through regulation; the FTC and state attorneys\ngeneral would enforce compliance. So Internet companies have a\nchoice: they can develop a voluntary system that gives consumers\ncontrol of their private data, or accept that Congress might\nmandate a system they don\u2019t like.  Ideally, the private sector would police itself. The FTC\ndoesn\u2019t want to set up roadblocks to the online freedom that has\nspawned everything from ingenious new technologies to democratic\nrevolutions. But we also don\u2019t want cyberspace to morph into a\nplace where you have to surrender your privacy. We call on the\ninnovators of the Internet to use their brain power to develop a\nDo Not Track system that protects every individual and not just\nthose with something to sell.  (Jon Leibowitz is chairman of the Federal Trade Commission.\nThe opinions expressed are his own.) Ever since the iPhone ushered in the era of ubiquitous mobile computing -- and especially since the release of the first iPad began a shift away from traditional personal computers -- the question has been whether and how Microsoft Office would adapt.  Here\u2019s the answer: Grudgingly, and not very well. Office Mobile, which slipped into Apple\u2019s  App Store  with little fanfare, turns out to be a stripped-down add-on that will leave both Office and Apple users wondering, \u201cIs that all there is?\u201d  Office Mobile is technically free. But it\u2019s useless unless you\u2019ve already paid at least $100 for a year of Office 365,  Microsoft (MSFT) \u2019s effort to convert its traditional shrink-wrapped, purchase-one-time-only software business into a pay-as-you-go subscription model. (By contrast, the version of Office Mobile included on devices running Microsoft\u2019s own Windows Phone software doesn\u2019t require an Office 365 subscription.)  That\u2019s just one of the limitations the company has imposed on its iOS app. Another is that it\u2019s intended only for the iPhone; there\u2019s no separate version designed to take advantage of the iPad\u2019s larger display.  Blown Up  Office Mobile will still run on an iPad; in fact, I\u2019m typing these words on one, using the docking-station keyboard Apple introduced when it unveiled the iPad three years ago. But it\u2019s just a blown-up view of the phone app. Microsoft says iPad users are better off using its online  Office Web Apps .  Office Mobile contains pocket versions of three of the Office desktop suite\u2019s core applications: Word, Excel and PowerPoint. There\u2019s no version of Outlook, the e-mail and calendar program, but I didn\u2019t find its absence to be a big deal, since the iPhone\u2019s built-in mail and calendar programs already work and play well with Microsoft.  To benefit from Office Mobile, you have to use Microsoft\u2019s free  SkyDrive  cloud-based service to store your Office documents; other popular storage options like  Dropbox  and  Google Drive  aren\u2019t supported.  When I logged into the app for the first time, all the SkyDrive documents I had previously created using Office 365 on my Windows PC were waiting for me. I could edit them, sort of, and create new ones, sort of.  Missing Pieces  This column, for instance, was started in the Mobile version of Word, and I also created a couple of Excel spreadsheets. But once I did, there was a whole lot I couldn\u2019t do with them.  I could enter text and formulas, make and review comments, and change the color and size of text. But I couldn\u2019t create or edit a macro, switch to a different font or even check my spelling.  PowerPoint is even more limited. There\u2019s no way to begin a presentation, or even to insert a new slide into an existing one. So if you have a last-minute brainstorm on the way to your meeting, you\u2019re out of luck.  Office Mobile did allow me to work on documents even when I wasn\u2019t connected to the Internet; my changes were saved on the phone until I got back online. But the syncing process with SkyDrive wasn\u2019t smooth. Instead of having my files upload automatically after I reconnected, I had to go back into the app and manually force it to sync.  SkyDrive-Saved  Even then, the app continued to display a \u201cCouldn\u2019t upload\u201d message and the document was saved to SkyDrive as a second copy rather than overwriting the original. Microsoft says it isn\u2019t sure what happened, but that the syncing should have been automatic and the new version should have overwritten the old one.  Microsoft\u2019s arms-length attitude toward iOS stands in stark contrast to arch-rival  Google (GOOG) , which devotes considerable resources to putting its most important software onto rival platforms. (The Google Now intelligent-assistant software, for instance, is more widely available on iOS devices than on Google\u2019s own Android operating system.)  Office Mobile\u2019s shortcomings mightn\u2019t be so obvious if there weren\u2019t so many higher-quality Office-compatible apps already available for iPads and iPhones. These include Apple\u2019s own iWork suite ($30) and Quickoffice Pro ($15 for iPhone, $20 for iPad), which Google bought last year. Still, none of them is the official, Microsoft-endorsed solution.  A lot of iOS users have wanted to get Microsoft Office onto their devices in the worst way. And that\u2019s just how they\u2019ve gotten it.  ( Rich Jaroslovsky  is a Bloomberg News columnist. The opinions expressed are his own.)  Muse highlights include  Jason Harper  on  cars  and Lance Esplund on  art . (WMT)  is the new gold.  The world\u2019s largest retailer is attracting investors who\nsee its shares as a safe haven amid a slowing global economy and\nvolatile  growth stocks . With U.S. same-store sales improving\nafter nine straight quarters of declines, investors are betting\nconsumers will continue seeking deals at Wal-Mart and have\ndriven the shares up 24 percent this year.  As a result, late last month Wal-Mart briefly became the\nworld\u2019s third most valuable company before slipping back into\nfourth place behind PetroChina Co. Wal-Mart fell 0.4 percent to\n$74.28 yesterday at the close in  New York .  Now some investors are asking how much higher the shares\ncan go. When consumers become more confident and middle-market\nretailers regain traction, investors may start looking\nelsewhere, according to  David Abella , a portfolio manager with\nRochdale Investment Management.  \u201cIn some sense, it is like gold,\u201d Abella said in a\ntelephone interview. \u201cIt\u2019s a safe bet in an economy like this.\nIf you start to see other retailers do well or consumers appear\nmore confident, then it is time to take gains and get out.\u201d  The economy is recovering more slowly than some investors\nexpected and some fear a renewed downturn, said Abella, who is\nbased in New York. While that is not the likely outcome, when\ninvestors get nervous, Wal-Mart  shares  go up, he said.  The Rochdale Dividend & Income Portfolio fund owns 57,000\nWal-Mart shares, making the holding the fund\u2019s fourth largest.\nAbella said he plans to hold the shares because Wal-Mart\u2019s\nperformance has been fundamentally sound and he expects the\neconomy to remain sluggish this year. If the stock rises, he may\nsell, he said.  Market Capitalization  Wal-Mart\u2019s market capitalization raced past  China Mobile\nLtd. (941)  in May, then passed  International Business Machines Corp. (IBM) \nin June and then slid ahead of  Microsoft Corp. (MSFT)  and PetroChina to\nthird before falling back to fourth behind Apple Inc. and Exxon\nMobil Corp. With a value of $251.3 billion, Wal-Mart is worth\nthe most since March 2004.  All of that happened after Wal-Mart said it would cooperate\nwith investigations by the U.S. Securities and Exchange\nCommission and  Department of Justice  into allegations that the\nretailer systematically bribed Mexican officials to open stores\nmore quickly.  The investigations became public in April. Investors seem\nto think that the bribery probe will not affect earnings in the\nnear term, Abella said.  More Upside  Wal-Mart\u2019s price-to-earnings ratio reached a peak of 16.8\nin 2008, said  Colin McGranahan , an analyst with New York-based\nresearch firm Sanford Bernstein & Co. The stock trades at 16.2\ntimes earnings now, implying there is a little more upside to\nthe shares, McGranahan said in a telephone interview.  The share performance partly reflects Wal-Mart\u2019s efforts to\nreclaim its role as a one-stop shopping destination by adding\nmerchandise, working to keep it in stock and lowering costs so\nit can offer deal-hungry customers lower prices.  Sales rose 8.5 percent in the first quarter to $113\nbillion. Net  income  rose 10 percent to $3.74 billion. U.S. same-\nstore sales rose 2.6 percent.  Even so, some investors are waiting to see more improvement\nbefore buying the shares, said  Brian Sozzi , an analyst with New\nYork research firm Decoding  Wall Street . Sozzi told clients to\nget out of the stock on July 30. He\u2019s waiting for the shares to\ndrop before recommending investors start buying again, he said\nin a telephone interview.  \u201cIf we get a sell-off, that could be interesting,\u201d Sozzi\nsaid.
