(SATS) \u2019s Sling Media, whose\ngadgets lets users watch live television shows on their mobile\ndevices, filed a U.S. trade complaint seeking to keep its\ncompetitors out of the burgeoning market.  Sling Media claims  Belkin International Inc. \u2019s @TV Plus and\n@TV Premium and  Monsoon Multimedia Inc. \u2019s Vulkano and HAVA\ndevices are using a technology it invented called place-shifting\ntechnology, which allows media stored on one device to be\naccessed on another. The company contends its rivals infringe\nsix patents.  The EchoStar unit makes the Slingbox, a device that lets\ncustomers get their pay-TV channels \u201cslung\u201d to laptops,\nsmartphones and tablet computers. The patented inventions are\nincorporated in the company\u2019s new Slingbox 350 and Slingbox 500,\nas well as  Dish Network Corp. (DISH) \u2019s Hopper With Sling set-top box.  \u201cSling Media has invested tens of millions of dollars in\nresearch and development,\u201d the company said in the complaint\nfiled with the U.S. International Trade Commission.  Rachel Jones-Pittier, a spokeswoman for Playa Vista,\nCalifornia-based Belkin, didn\u2019t immediately return a voice-mail\nmessage seeking comment. A phone message left with FortyThree\nPR, an agency that handles press inquiries for Monsoon according\nto the technology company\u2019s website, also wasn\u2019t immediately\nreturned.  The ITC complaint, filed March 12 in Washington, also\ntargets chips made by San Jose, California-based C2 Microsystems\nInc. for the Belkin and Monsoon products. The company couldn\u2019t\nimmediately be reached for comment.  The devices allow consumers to watch their favorite show\nwhen it airs without being tied to the television or waiting for\nit to become available on cable companies\u2019 on-demand services.\n Charlie Ergen , chairman of Englewood, Colorado-based EchoStar,\nbought Sling Media in 2007 and has used it as part of a strategy\nto push the satellite-technology company and Dish, which he also\nruns, into Internet and on-demand services.  Sling Media also filed a lawsuit against closely held\nBelkin and Monsoon in January over some of the same patents.\nThat case is pending.  In addition to its Vulkano devices, San Mateo, California-\nbased Monsoon makes circuit boards that are used in Belkin\nproducts, according to the complaint. Sling Media said the\nMonsoon and Belkin products are made in China.  The ITC is a quasi-judicial agency that investigates\nallegations of unfair trade practices, including patent\ninfringement, and has the power to block products from entering\nthe U.S. It typically completes investigations in 15 to 18\nmonths.  The case is In the Matter of Certain Electronic Devices\nHaving Placeshifting or Display Replication Functionality and\nProducts Containing Same, Complaint No. 2943, U.S. International\nTrade Commission (Washington).  Nintendo Told by Jury to Pay $30 Million in 3-D Patent Suit  Nintendo Co. (7974)  was ordered to pay $30.2 million to a former\n Sony Corp. (6758)  employee after a jury in New York found the company\u2019s\n3DS machine infringed his patent.  The handheld 3DS game and video player infringed a 3-D\ntechnology patent held by Seijiro Tomita, the Manhattan jury\nfound March 13, according to the office of U.S. District Judge\nJed Rakoff, who tried the case.  Tomita, who worked for Sony for almost 30 years before\nquitting in 2002, sued Nintendo in June 2011. That year\nNintendo, the world\u2019s biggest video-game console maker,\nintroduced the 3DS, which allows users to see 3-D images without\nspecial glasses. Nintendo said it will appeal.  \u201cWe believe we can win a ruling that our 3DS doesn\u2019t\ninfringe the patent,\u201d  Yasuhiro Minagawa , a spokesman for\nNintendo, said by phone.  In April 2012 Rakoff denied Nintendo motions for judgment\nwithout a trial on the grounds that Tomita couldn\u2019t prove either\nthat Nintendo infringed the patent or that it had willfully\ninfringed it.  \u201cA reasonable jury could find, based on clear and\nconvincing evidence, that Nintendo\u2019s defenses are so\nunpersuasive that an objectively high likelihood of infringement\nin fact exists,\u201d Rakoff said in a memo explaining his ruling.  Tomita said he met representatives of Nintendo in August\n2003 to demonstrate his technology, according to court papers. A\nmonth later, he was asked to create a sample for the company,\naccording to the filings. Tomita said he requested payment or a\nlicensing agreement and received no response. He said he had no\n\u201cdirect communications\u201d with Nintendo from September 2003\nuntil the suit was filed in 2011.  \u201cThe same employees who attended the demonstration helped\nto develop the 3DS, and a reasonable jury could find that they\nwould have understood the similarities between the 3DS and the\nprototype Mr. Tomita had shown them,\u201d Rakoff wrote.  Nintendo released its latest home console, the Wii U, last\nyear.  Tomita Technologies Ltd. is based in Yokohama, Japan.  The case is Tomita Technologies USA v. Nintendo Co., 1:11-\ncv-04256, U.S. District Court, Southern District of New York\n(Manhattan).  VirnetX Loses Patent Trial to Cisco Over Private Networks  VirnetX Holding Corp. (VHC)  lost a patent-infringement trial\nagainst  Cisco Systems Inc. (CSCO) , as a jury cleared the networking-\nequipment maker of allegations it infringed inventions related\nto virtual private networks.  A jury in Tyler,  Texas , said the company\u2019s patents weren\u2019t\ninfringed. VirnetX was seeking $258 million in damages.  The dispute is over virtual private networks, through which\na website owner can securely interact with a customer or an\nemployee can work at home and have protected access to a\ncompany\u2019s electronic files. Doug Cawley of  McKool Smith , a\nlawyer representing VirnetX, said Cisco used the technology to\nimprove security in its own networks.  VirnetX won a $368.2 million verdict against  Apple Inc. (AAPL)  in\nNovember over the same technology, including two of the same\npatents, before a different Tyler jury. In 2010, Zephyr Cove,\nNevada-based VirnetX reached a $200 million settlement with\nMicrosoft Corp. over the same inventions.  The case decided yesterday focused on Cisco routers,\nsoftware and phones that have virtual-private-networking\nfunctions including its Unified Communications Manager product,\nTelepresence or AnyConnect. Cisco, whose products handle traffic\nover the Internet, reported sales of $12.1 billion in the\nquarter ended Jan. 26.  VirnetX relies on patent licensing for its revenue. The\ncompany is testing its Gabriel Connection Technology to create\nsecure communications links, according to its annual report.  U.S. District Judge Leonard Davis, who is presiding over\nthe Apple and Cisco cases, on Feb. 26 upheld the jury verdict\nagainst Apple. Davis denied a VirnetX request for an order that\nwould have limited Apple\u2019s ability to provide virtual private\nnetworks on its products.  The case is VirnetX Inc. v. Cisco Systems Inc., 10-cv-\n00417, U.S. District Court, Eastern District of Texas (Tyler).  ISE Opts Out of CBOE Patent Trial in Favor of Appellate Path  International Securities Exchange LLC, an all-electronic\noptions trading market, opted out of a patent trial against\nChicago Board Options Exchange Inc. on the day its lawyers were\nto deliver opening statements to a jury.  U.S. District Judge Joan H. Lefkow, who was presiding over\nthe lawsuit in federal court in Chicago, issued a series of\nadverse pre-trial rulings that compelled ISE to \u201ccease pursuit\nof the case,\u201d it said in a statement yesterday.  The Deutsche Borse AG unit alleged the Chicago exchange\ninfringed an automated trading patent. CBOE, in a separately\nfiled case, asked Lefkow to find the ISE patent was invalid.  \u201cISE strongly believes in the merits of its case that CBOE\ncopied and continues to infringe ISE\u2019s patented trading\ntechnology,\u201d the New York-based company said. \u201cISE plans to\nimmediately file an appeal to the Federal Circuit to reverse\nthese rulings.\u201d  The trial, which was set to start on March 11 and delayed\nfor three days while Lefkow addressed the preliminary motions,\nwas one of at least three legal disputes between ISE and\nChicago-based  CBOE Holdings Inc. (CBOE) , operator of the biggest U.S.\noptions exchange.  Jurors were discharged yesterday without ever hearing\narguments or evidence in the trial Lefkow had told them on March\n11 would last until early April.  Jonathan Marshall of New York\u2019s Fish & Richardson PC, an\nattorney for the CBOE, said in a courtroom interview that\nlawyers for ISE asked the judge to enter a judgment of non-\ninfringement, freeing ISE to appeal.  ISE concluded the \u201cnet effect of the rulings would make it\nimpossible to make their case at trial,\u201d Marshall said.  In one ruling, made public on March 11, Lefkow had barred\nISE from presenting evidence of pre-suit damages to the jury,\nconcluding that the exchange had failed to comply with a federal\n\u201cmarking statute,\u201d requiring it to make public its patent\nclaim.  \u201cWe are gratified that this case has reached the correct\nresult,\u201d CBOE Chairman and Chief Executive Officer William J. Brodsky said in a statement.  The cases are Chicago Board Options Exchange Inc. v.\nInternational Securities Exchange LLC, 07-cv-00623, and\nInternational Securities Exchange LLC v. Chicago Board Options\nExchange Inc., 07-cv-04709, U.S. District Court, Northern\nDistrict of Illinois (Chicago).  For more patent news, click here. Copyright  Universal Loses Appeal Bid to Restore Veoh Copyright Suit  Copyright claims by  Universal Music Group  and other studios\nagainst the Internet video-site operator Veoh Networks Inc. were\nproperly dismissed, a federal appeals court ruled.  Veoh was protected from the claims by \u201csafe harbor\u201d\nprovisions of the Digital Millennium Copyright Act, which\nshields Internet service providers that unknowingly post\ncopyrighted material and remove it when alerted, a three-judge\npanel in  San Francisco  said yesterday.  The court previously ruled in favor of Veoh in 2011,\ngranting the studio\u2019s request for rehearing. It issued a new\nopinion yesterday. The lawsuit was filed in 2007 against Veoh\nand its backers. Most of Veoh\u2019s assets were acquired in 2010 by\n Qlipso Media Networks Ltd.   Universal Music  is a unit of Paris-based  Vivendi SA. (VIV)   Steven Marenberg, an attorney for Universal, didn\u2019t\nimmediately reply to a voice-mail message seeking comment about\nthe ruling.  The case is UMG Recordings Inc. v. Veoh Networks Inc., 10-\n0955902,  U.S. Court of Appeals  for the Ninth Circuit (San\nFrancisco).  Pirate Bay Founders\u2019 Infringement Appeal Rejected by Court  The European Court of  Human Rights  held that the conviction\nof two founders of the Pirate Bay file-sharing site for criminal\ncopyright infringement was justified. As vice president of leasing for  Brookfield Office Properties Inc. (BPO) , Cheikin is leading the push to remake lower  Manhattan \u2019s former World Financial Center into a destination for technology and media companies. Once home to the Merrill Lynch & Co., the brokerage firm known for its bull logo, the Hudson riverfront complex is now Brookfield Place  New York , and much more than the name is changing.  Brookfield is stripping away brass and marble trims and adding bicycle parking, free Wi-Fi in public spaces and electric-car charging stations. At Merrill\u2019s former headquarters, clear glass is replacing the imposing, dark-tinted facade built as a barrier to the public, Cheikin said.  \u201cWe\u2019re just trying to work out ways to make it more in line with how people want to work today,\u201d he said.  Downtown landlords with millions of square feet of empty space are transforming offices that were designed for the global financial elite to better appeal to New York\u2019s technology and media firms. They\u2019re pitching their properties as an alternative to the converted factories of midtown south, where a frenzy of demand has pushed up rents and driven  vacancies  to the lowest in the U.S. The image makeover is only part of the challenge as the area faces a glut of space from skyscrapers that are nearing completion at the  World Trade Center site .  Empty Space  Consolidating financial companies have left landlords with at least 6.3 million square feet (585,000 square meters) of space to fill, almost 7 percent of the  lower Manhattan  office market, according to data from brokerage Newmark Grubb Knight Frank. Another 2.4 million square feet remains unrented at two new trade center towers scheduled for completion by mid-2014. At Brookfield Place, vacancies loom on about a third of its 8 million square feet.  Across the street at 1 World Trade Center, the Durst Organization is preparing a marketing campaign to convince creative firms that they\u2019ll feel at home in the Western Hemisphere\u2019s tallest building. Almost half of the tower, scheduled to open next year, is available for lease.  Durst, equity partner with the  Port Authority  of New York and  New Jersey  on the 1,776-foot (541-meter) skyscraper, is targeting companies that are in \u201cphase-two growth, after the incubation startup stages,\u201d said Tara Stacom, the Cushman & Wakefield Inc. executive vice chairman who is working with the developers on the leasing effort.  New Construction  \u201cThere\u2019s something that the new construction can accommodate for all these tech users that the old construction can\u2019t, and that is growth,\u201d Stacom said. \u201cA lot of these tenants are one size today, and they\u2019re 200 times that size in less than a decade, and in some cases less than half a decade. We\u2019re only now going out to speak to this audience.\u201d  Tenants could agree to take a small space at first, then expand into larger offices in the tower, Stacom said. As rents soar in the older buildings of midtown south, available government  incentives  and the efficiencies of new real estate would make the trade center more cost-effective, even at an asking rent of $75 a square foot, among the highest for downtown, she said.  The tower\u2019s open, column-free space offers more flexibility and the developers are even ready to duplicate a look that\u2019s become popular with technology firms, leaving the ductwork exposed, Stacom said.  Space \u2018Mismatch\u2019  About 1.4 million square feet are unspoken for in the skyscraper, which is slated to open to tenants next year and will have Conde Nast Publications Inc. as its anchor tenant. Another 1 million square feet are available at  Silverstein Properties Inc .\u2019s 4 World Trade Center, to open before year-end.  There\u2019s \u201ca mismatch between the unprecedented amount of class A space currently available and the preferences of the tech sector for loft space in a neighborhood with a non-corporate vibe,\u201d according to tenant brokerage Studley Inc.  \u201cTech and creative-sector companies in Manhattan are indisputably growing by leaps and bounds,\u201d Steven Coutts, senior vice president for national research at New York-based Studley, said in a July 24 report. \u201cNevertheless, this sector still lacks the heft to fill the void\u201d left by contracting banks and other traditional office users, such as accounting and insurance companies.  Lowest Rents  Downtown Manhattan has the lowest rents and the highest office availability of the borough\u2019s three major submarkets. The availability rate -- empty space and offices due to become vacant within 12 months -- was almost 16 percent at the end of June, up from 10.8 percent a year earlier, data from CBRE Group Inc. show. Asking rents jumped 20 percent to an average of $47.13 a square foot, a reflection of landlords\u2019 expectations for the high-end space added to the market in the past year, according to Los Angeles-based CBRE.  Rents in midtown south -- including such neighborhoods as Chelsea, the Flatiron District and Soho -- averaged $63.44 a square foot and the availability rate was 10 percent.  Brookfield has about 2.7 million square feet of former Merrill offices to fill at its namesake complex.  Bank of America Corp. (BAC) , which took over the space when it bought Merrill in 2009, is keeping about 775,000 square feet and will stop paying rent on the rest in September when its leases expire.  Former Restaurant  At Merrill\u2019s former headquarters at 250 Vesey St., the vacant restaurant that once housed the Hudson River Club, where brokers dined on grouse and pheasant, has been removed. It\u2019s now an open area where anyone can gaze at the Statue of Liberty in the distance. The change is part of a $250 million makeover of the World Financial Center\u2019s retail space that will include an upscale food market and eateries that overlook the marina.  Another selling point, according to Cheikin, will be the completion in the next two years of a $3.94 billion transit hub designed by the Spanish architect  Santiago Calatrava . Brookfield is close to completing a 55-foot glass entryway supported by a pair of cyclone-shaped steel columns that will link Brookfield Place with the transportation center.  Across town on the  East River  waterfront,  SL Green Realty Corp. (SLG)  is marketing about 900,000 square feet at 180 Maiden Lane, a black-glass tower south of the  Brooklyn  Bridge. Most of that is space that  American International Group Inc. (AIG) , once the world\u2019s largest insurer, will vacate next year.  \u2018Communal\u2019 Amenities  SL Green, Manhattan\u2019s biggest office landlord, is spending $40 million on renovations that include making over the interior plaza, as well as AIG\u2019s cafeteria, auditorium and health club to transform them into \u201ccommunal-type amenities,\u201d said Steve Durels, director of leasing.  \u201cI want the cafeteria to look like it\u2019s a Starbucks, and I want the fitness center to look like it\u2019s a Soul Cycle,\u201d Durels said. \u201cAnd I want the auditorium to look like the presentation space you\u2019d find in a  W Hotel .\u201d  Most importantly, he said, the ground-floor atrium will work like an indoor park, with seating areas where people can get a coffee and work on their laptops. Half of the floor will be covered in artificial turf, where tenants could arrange a volleyball, badminton or bocce game.  Choosing Elsewhere  So far, downtown landlords\u2019 efforts to land creative firms have borne little fruit. Some of the industry\u2019s biggest names -- Yahoo! Inc., EBay Inc., LinkedIn Corp., Microsoft Corp. and Facebook Inc. -- have opted to go elsewhere. Yahoo took four floors in the century-old former New York Times headquarters in Midtown, while LinkedIn went to the 82-year-old Empire State Building. EBay chose a onetime department store on Sixth Avenue in Chelsea that dates back to the 1890s, when the corridor was known as Ladies\u2019 Mile.  Facebook went to the East Village, taking about 100,000 square feet in 770 Broadway, which was designed in 1905 by Daniel Burnham, the architect who conceived the Flatiron Building. The social-media company joins tenants including AOL Inc. and the  Huffington Post  in the 15-story property.  \u201cThose firms are all iconic,\u201d said Miles Rose, founder of  SiliconAlley.com , a Web-based community for New York\u2019s emerging technology industry. \u201cThe big, plain boxes don\u2019t work for either their corporate culture or their workers. Older, iconic buildings have character and they have presence.\u201d  Of the 50 largest Manhattan leases made by technology, media, information and fashion tenants in the past two years, only 10 were in buildings completed later than 1970, according to Compstak Inc., a New York-based provider of leasing data.  10gen Lease  When 10gen Inc., maker of MongoDB data-management software, sought to expand out of its Soho offices last year, \u201cdowntown wasn\u2019t exactly right for us,\u201d said Eliot Horowitz, co-founder and chief technology officer. \u201cWe wanted some place that was pretty wide-open and feeling kind of lofty. We sort of wanted a Soho feel, but with a lot more flexibility and a lot more space than you can actually get in Soho.\u201d  10Gen wound up taking about 32,000 square feet at the Times Building, he said. This month, it expanded its commitment to almost 50,000 square feet.  Some creative companies that have gone downtown have favored the market\u2019s older buildings. When HarperCollins Publishers Ltd. agreed to leave its longtime Midtown headquarters, it took 180,000 square feet at 195 Broadway, a colonnaded tower built in 1916 that was originally the American Telephone & Telegraph Co. building. WeWork, a company founded three years ago to provide shared  office space  to startups, took 120,500 square feet at 222 Broadway, a 27-story property completed in 1961 that once housed Merrill offices.  Brooklyn Projects  Brooklyn, across the East River from lower Manhattan, may emerge as competition for technology and media tenants. Developers have plans for about 630,000 square feet of offices at the former Domino Sugar plant on the Williamsburg neighborhood\u2019s waterfront. In an industrial district near the Brooklyn Bridge, 1.2 million square feet of buildings long-owned by the Jehovah\u2019s Witnesses are under contract to be sold to a partnership that may make much of the space into offices.  There are about 20 million square feet of warehouses along the western edge of Brooklyn and Queens, from Sunset Park to  Long Island City , that are ripe to be converted to support creative firms, according to Tucker Reed, president of the Downtown Brooklyn Partnership, an advocacy group for businesses in the area.  New York\u2019s Economic Development Corp. projects that fast-growing technology companies will need an additional 20 million square feet of space over the next 12 years, and they\u2019ll be seeking rents of less than $40 a square foot.  Brookfield Leases  Melissa Coley , a Brookfield spokeswoman, declined to say what rents it\u2019s seeking at Brookfield Place. The landlord last week said it had rented about 191,000 square feet combined to Bank of  Nova Scotia , Oppenheimer Funds Inc. and fitness-club chain Equinox Holdings Inc. Earlier this year, it landed GFK SE, a German retail-research firm, for 75,000 square feet at 200 Liberty St., formerly 1 World Financial Center. GFK is moving from an older building in Chelsea.  The World Trade Center site is poised to get its second large media tenant. GroupM, an advertising planning and placement firm owned by WPP Inc., is working on terms to lease 515,000 square feet at 3 World Trade Center, according to two people with knowledge of the talks.  The skyscraper, slated for completion in 2016, is being developed by  Larry Silverstein , who considered capping the tower at seven stories if he couldn\u2019t land an anchor tenant. If he goes ahead with building it to the full 80-story height, he\u2019ll have another 2 million square feet to fill.  The 70,000-square-foot spaces planned for 3 World Trade Center, called \u201ctrading floors\u201d on the developer\u2019s website, can be designed for \u201cany industry,\u201d according to Jeremy Moss, Silverstein\u2019s director of leasing. GroupM is planning to use some of the five base floors, according to the people.  Greg Taubin, a broker at Studley who represented 10gen, said certain technology tenants will be tempted by landlords\u2019 efforts, while others \u201cwon\u2019t go below 14th Street, period.\u201d  \u201cIt\u2019s very tenant-specific,\u201d he said. \u201cBut as midtown south continues to be tight for these types of tenants, certain buildings downtown will be the beneficiaries of this.\u201d  To contact the reporter on this story: David M. (GOOG) , owner of the world\u2019s largest search engine, rose the most since 2011 after reporting profit that topped analysts\u2019 estimates as advertisers boosted spending to reach consumers during the holiday season. Analysts had projected per-share earnings of $10.50, according to data compiled by Bloomberg. The adjusted figure excludes items such as taxes tied to stock-based compensation. Net income rose 6.7 percent to $2.89 billion, or $8.62 a share.  Google\u2019s earnings were boosted after retailers poured money into online advertising and extended the gift-buying season. Total U.S. e-commerce spending jumped 14 percent during the last two months of 2012 as retailers began promoting Web deals earlier, according to  ComScore  Inc. That\u2019s helping compensate as Google relies more on mobile advertising, which tends to be less lucrative than ads on traditional computers.  \u201cPeople were probably expecting something more on the downside, and results were pretty good,\u201d said  Benjamin Schachter , an analyst at Macquarie Securities USA Inc., who has a buy rating on the stock. \u201cThe transition to mobile is still a work in progress, but they are showing they can manage that process quite well.\u201d  The  shares  of  Mountain View , California-based Google rose 5.5 percent to $741.50 at the close in  New York , their biggest gain since October 2011.  Ad Costs  Rates for mobile ads can be about 55 percent less than for promotions on desktop machines, according to Covario Inc., an online marketing agency. Still, Google managed to tap the brakes on the pace of decline in the average amount advertisers paid each time a user clicks on a promotion. The so-called cost per click decreased 6 percent, following a 15 percent decline in the previous period. The total number of clicks advanced 24 percent, after a 33 percent increase in the third quarter.  \u201cIt\u2019s big, bad Google doing pretty well,\u201d said  Jordan Rohan , an analyst at Stifel Nicolaus & Co. in New York. \u201cGoogle continues to monetize its searches very well.\u201d  Revenue, excluding sales passed on to partner sites, rose 39 percent to $12.2 billion, compared with $12.4 billion projected by analysts. Sales from operations excluding the Motorola Home set-top box unit, which Google agreed to sell last month, increased 36 percent to $14.4 billion.  \u201cWe ended 2012 with a strong quarter,\u201d Chief Executive Officer  Larry Page  said yesterday on a conference call. \u201cI am incredibly optimistic about the opportunities we have as a technology company focused on user benefits.\u201d  Global Gains  Page, who refrained from joining an earnings call last year due to difficulties with his voice, spoke in quiet tones and a voice that sounded hoarse at times.  International markets represented 54 percent of sales, up a percentage point from a year earlier and in the third quarter. Google benefited from strength in Northern European markets,  Nikesh Arora , chief business officer, said during the call.  Google made a $12.4 billion purchase of smartphone-maker Motorola Mobility Holdings last year. In August, Google said it would cut 4,000 Motorola jobs and close about a third of its 90 facilities.  Arris Group Inc. (ARRS)  agreed to buy the Motorola Home unit for $2.35 billion in December.  With the cutbacks, Motorola now can focus on its handset business, which uses Google\u2019s Android operating system to run the smartphones. Still, the Motorola unit had a net operating loss of $353 million.  Android Push  \u201cWe do care about profitability, and that is our goal with every one of the areas where we invest,\u201d Patrick Pichette, chief financial officer, said during the call. \u201cWe\u2019ve made a ton of progress.\u201d  He said that Google\u2019s effort to bring faster network service to users in  Kansas City  is performing well. The company is considering expanding the service in the future, he said.  Android, which is provided for free to manufacturers, has become a key part of the company\u2019s push into mobile, giving Google access to user data around the world. Android snared 72 percent of the global smartphone market in the third quarter, according to Gartner Inc.  The company also has a leadership position in search, its core business. Google grabbed 67 percent of the market in the U.S. in December, according to  ComScore Inc. (SCOR)  That compares to 16 percent for  Microsoft Corp. (MSFT)  and 12 percent for Yahoo! Inc.  Despite its lead, Google could come under pressure from Facebook Inc., owner of the world\u2019s largest social-networking service. Last week, Facebook announced a new search tool that lets users discover people, photos, places and interests on the service.  When fully rolled out, the feature could give Web users an incentive to use Google less. Facebook also has a partnership with Microsoft\u2019s Bing search engine, which will deliver additional results from the Web when Graph Search doesn\u2019t deliver clear answers to queries. (GOOG) \u2019s bid to block imports of\n Microsoft Corp. (MSFT) \u2019s Xbox gaming system and  Apple Inc. (AAPL) \u2019s iPhone\nbased on patents owned by its Motorola Mobility unit may hurt\ncompetition, the U.S. Federal Trade Commission said.  Weighing in on cases before another U.S. agency, the\nInternational Trade Commission, the FTC said in filings\nyesterday that companies should be limited in their ability to\nwin orders blocking imports of competitors\u2019 products over the\nuse of patents built into industrywide standards.  Motorola Mobility is citing its standard-essential patents\nto persuade the ITC to stop imports of Apple and Microsoft\ndevices made in  Asia . The ITC is gathering comments on whether\nsuch an import ban would be in the public interest. An import ban on the iPhone would affect sales of a product\nthat generated $47 billion in sales last year, or 43 percent of\nApple\u2019s revenue. Microsoft\u2019s  entertainment division , which\nincludes sales of the Xbox, generated $8.9 billion in global\nsales in fiscal 2011, about 13 percent of Microsoft\u2019s revenue.  Patent Disputes  The FTC\u2019s position would limit the power of companies like\nMotorola Mobility, Samsung Electronics Co. and  InterDigital Inc. (IDCC) \nto use the international trade agency as a forum in patent\ndisputes. Each company has asserted patents that cover aspects\nof industry standards they helped establish.  Companies participating in standard-setting groups pledge\nto license patents that cover aspects of the standards on\n\u201creasonable and non-discriminatory\u201d terms. Such patents should\nbe treated differently than other patents, Leibowitz said.\nPatents convey the power to exclude others from using an\ninvention.  \u201cA royalty negotiation that occurs under threat of an\nexclusion order may be weighted heavily in favor of the patentee\nin a way that is in tension with the  RAND  commitment,\u201d the FTC\nwrote.  The result could be royalty rates that would lead to higher\nprices for consumers and less participation in standard-setting\ngroups, the agency said. It suggested the ITC refrain from\nimposing an import ban or delay imposition until both sides\nmediate in good faith.  Good-Faith Talks  Google, in filings with European and U.S. regulators in\nFebruary, said it wouldn\u2019t seek to block the use of standard-\nessential patents as long as good-faith licensing talks are\nunder way. Motorola Mobility said it \u201cwould welcome having\nApple and Microsoft join the more than 50 other companies\u201d who\nhave licensed the company\u2019s portfolio.  \u201cTo date, however, neither party has been willing to enter\ninto a cross-license on reasonable terms and thus we all find\nourselves in seemingly endless litigation,\u201d Motorola Mobility\nsaid in an e-mailed statement.  An ITC judge in April said Microsoft\u2019s Xbox infringes four\nMotorola Mobility patents, including three related to industry\nstandards covering Wi-Fi technology and video decoding. Another\njudge said Apple\u2019s iPhone and iPad tablet computer infringed a\npatent related to 3G technology.  \u2018Growing Chorus\u2019  \u201cThe FTC joins a growing chorus of regulators from around\nthe world who recognize the danger posed by companies who try to\nuse standard-essential patents to block the sale of products,\u201d\n David Howard , Microsoft\u2019s deputy general counsel, said in an e-\nmailed statement.  The European Union is investigating complaints by Microsoft\nand Apple that Motorola Mobility is unfairly using standard-\nessential patents to block competition. Samsung also is being\nprobed by the EU. Huawei Technologies Co. filed a complaint over\nroyalty demands by InterDigital over third-generation technology\non mobile phones.  There\u2019s no clear definition of fair and reasonable, said\nAndrew Updegrove, a lawyer with Gesmer Updegrove in  Boston  who\nadvises standards boards.  \u201cIf people knew what RAND meant, there\u2019d be a lot less to\nargue about,\u201d Updegrove said. \u201cWhat the big patent owners want\nto do is retain complete flexibility of negotiation.\u201d  The  Business Software Alliance , a trade group whose members\ninclude Apple and Microsoft, and computer maker  Hewlett-Packard\nCo. Android Challenge  Motorola Mobility filed its ITC case against Cupertino,\nCalifornia-based Apple after the iPhone maker challenged other\nmakers of phones running on Google\u2019s Android operating system.  The dispute over Xbox began after Microsoft approached\nMotorola Mobility and demanded patent royalties on smartphones\nthat run on Android. Motorola Mobility responded by claiming it\nwas entitled to royalties on the Xbox.  Motorola Mobility sent letters to Microsoft with what it\nsaid was a standard demand for a 2.25 percent royalty on the end\nprice of products that use the inventions, including the Xbox\nand Windows products. Microsoft contends that would add up to as\nmuch as $4 billion in annual royalties, a figure Motorola\nMobility disputes.  Microsoft, based in Redmond, Washington, filed a lawsuit\naccusing Motorola Mobility of breaching its contractual\nobligations.  Company Pledges  Apple and Microsoft have pledged that they wouldn\u2019t use\ntheir own standard-essential patents to block products.  \u201cWe think it\u2019s an abuse of the patent system to use an\nessential patent to block the import and sale of a competitor\u2019s\nproduct, and Apple has never used standards-essential patents in\nthat way,\u201d Apple said in February. Kristin Huguet, an Apple\nspokeswoman, said the company stood by that statement.  The ITC has more than a dozen pending cases involving\nsmartphones and tablet computers, and lawsuits have spanned four\ncontinents with Apple and Microsoft going against makers of\nAndroid devices. Most don\u2019t involve standard-essential patents.  The case against Microsoft is In the Matter of Gaming and\nEntertainment Consoles, 337-752 and the case against Apple is In\nthe Matter of Wireless Communication Devices, 337-745. Both are\nat the U.S. International Trade Commission (Washington). Since Robert Downey Jr. was told to \u201cHold This Cat\u201d back in August, HTC has gone on to have an historic quarter. That's not hyperbole, it really was historic.  In addition to the humdrum of unveiling, well, smartphones, HTC's also been toiling away at a few side projects.  Talks with Amazon.com  about doing a handset for the online retailer's Prime members progressed during the period, with both sides staying mum on the project. The phone maker is also looking at doing a  smartwatch , following on the heels of Samsung, Sony and Dick Tracy. HTC folks again chose to keep their lips sealed. Somewhat less sealed was HTC's treasure chest of intellectual property and trade secrets. After complaints from the company, Taiwan authorities searched the offices and homes of some employees before detaining two R&D executives on the suspicion of  leaking company secrets . Low-key co-founder and Chairwoman Cher Wang  came out of the shadows  as well, doubling her days at the office and taking over more logistical work from CEO Peter Chou (who remains the boss, she said more than once). In an address to staff, she outlined customer service and consumer experience as an area the company needs to work on, while in an interview with Bloomberg Television, she said \u201cHTC does have some problem of communication,\u201d in terms of marketing its product design and technology. Its PR situation didn't improve much either. Four months after HTC heralded her arrival, the \u201cnew\u201d head of global PR, corporate and internal communications Lorain Wong quietly  became the \u201cex\u201d head  of global PR, corporate and internal communications.  HTC's balance sheet does look set to improve after it unwound two of its biggest acquisitions of the past few years, selling off Saffron Digital and exiting from headphones maker  Beats . Meanwhile, Microsoft - the software company that got any kind of traction in mobile phones because HTC decided to devote much of its 16 years exclusively to their operating system - offered an olive branch (or perhaps a juicy carrot) soon after its long-awaited Nokia handset deal had other Windows handset makers annoyed. Microsoft basically  said to HTC : How about you load Windows Phone on your Android handsets, and heck, we might even cut the license fee to zero (or very close to)? None of that, though, is historic for HTC (although that last one is unusual for Microsoft), it's merely the ebb and flow of a modern tech company.  What's historic is that on Oct. 4, at a time and in a manner totally out of line with years of standard practice, HTC announced to the world its first loss on record.  We all know that losses happen in the corporate world. For some tech companies, losses seem to be the rule more than the exception.  To be fair, HTC still has more than $1.6 billion in cash (at the end of June) and minimal long-term debt, financial metrics that have been noticed by Jimmy Lai -- best known in Greater China as the founder of Next Media, and (not) known in the West as the man whose team created those Taiwanese Next Media Animation skits that have  satirized the likes of Tiger Woods , Brett Favre and Justin Bieber. Lai, according to spokesman Mark Simon, has seen value in HTC's stock (down about 50 percent this year) and quietly built a stake of about 2 percent as a purely financial investment over the past few months. Lai isn't planning to get involved in management, says Simon, a fact that hasn't stopped speculation of how a Next Media-HTC tie-up might look. In the smartphone business, though, history has shown that losses haven't tended to be followed by very happy tales. Motorola, Nokia and Blackberry are former handset titans whose earnings dipped below the waterline and have found, or are seeking, life preservers.  In the past few months, the rumors surrounding the future of HTC have poured forth.  M&A  seems to be the most likely escape route, with Lenovo and ZTE the names that get mentioned most. China Mobile, the world's largest mobile phone carrier, was also thrown into the mix as a possible suitor before HTC shot it down. M&A in Taiwan, however, is a giant hill to climb. Cross-border deals are rare and difficult to pull off, and hostile takeovers are unheard of.  Without the nod of Chairwoman Wang, who owns a significant minority, any deal is a non-starter. And Wang is adamantly withholding any such nod. Compliance Policy  Decades-Old Chemical Laws Must be Revised for Kids, Doctors Say  Environmental regulators should be able to demand more\nsafety data about toxic chemicals and halt sales if the products\nare suspected of harming children or pregnant women, the\n American Academy of Pediatrics  said.  The doctors group, based in Elk Grove Village, Illinois,\ncalled yesterday for an overhaul of a 1976 statute that requires\ncompanies to notify the U.S.  Environmental Protection Agency \nbefore manufacturing the products and to test them when concerns\narise. The group\u2019s policy statement is published in the journal\nPediatrics.  Chemical companies such as  Dow Chemical Co. (DOW) , based in\nMidland, Michigan, produce or import about 27 trillion pounds of\nproducts each year, the statement said. Children\u2019s smaller\nbodies take in proportionately more toxins that may be in air or\nwater than adults, and changes as they grow make them more\nvulnerable to chemical exposures, according to the academy.  The academy wants testing to include studies on\nreproductive and developmental toxicity as well as post-market\nsurveillance on the effects of a chemical. They also call for\nadditional federal research to evaluate the effects of child\nexposure to chemicals.  Congress didn\u2019t act when the EPA made six suggestions in\n2009 about modifying the Toxic Substances Control Act of 1976.  The EPA will lose $1.6 billion as part of a deal between\nPresident Barack Obama and congressional leaders to produce $38\nbillion in spending cuts for the rest of the 2011 fiscal year,\naccording to legislation made public April 12. Courts  Supreme Court Won\u2019t Expedite Review of U.S. Health-Care Law  The U.S. Supreme Court yesterday declined an opportunity to\nreview President Barack Obama\u2019s health-care overhaul, rejecting\nVirginia\u2019s bid to have its challenge to the law considered on an\nunusual fast-track basis.  Virginia, one of 28 states suing to invalidate the measure,\nurged the justices to schedule arguments without waiting for the\nfour appeals courts that are poised to consider the law. The\nstates say Congress overstepped its authority by requiring\nAmericans to either obtain insurance or pay a penalty.  The rebuff doesn\u2019t preclude the Supreme Court from hearing\nthe case later, perhaps even before the 2012 election. For the\ntime being, yesterday\u2019s action is a victory for the Obama\nadministration, which urged the justices not to grant Virginia\u2019s\nbid for a hearing.  The step sought by Virginia, known as certiorari before\njudgment, is one the court has taken only a handful of times.  The Obama administration argued that the health-care\ndispute doesn\u2019t rise to the level of urgency required for an\nexpedited hearing, in part because the disputed provision\ndoesn\u2019t take effect until 2014.  U.S. District Judge Henry Hudson ruled in December that\nCongress\u2019s authority over interstate commerce didn\u2019t give it the\npower to enact the insurance mandate. A federal appeals court\nbased in Richmond, Virginia, is scheduled to hear the Obama\nadministration\u2019s appeal of that ruling May 10 -- alongside an\nappeal of a different judge\u2019s decision upholding the law.  Another appeals court, based in Cincinnati, will consider\nthe issue June 1, and a third, based in Atlanta, will hear\narguments June 8 in a case involving the other 26 states\nchallenging the law. An appeals court in  Washington  will\nconsider the matter later this year.  The Supreme Court case is Virginia ex rel. Cuccinelli v.\nSebelius, 10-1014.  For more, click here. Fees  Lehman Fees Exceed $2 Billion Since 2008 Bankruptcy Filing  Lehman Brothers Holdings Inc., which is still liquidating\nafter exiting court protection last year, paid advisers and\nmanagers $153.8 million in December, putting total fees over the\n$2 billion mark in the more than four years since it filed for\nbankruptcy.  December\u2019s outlays included $84 million in incentives for a\nplan that will pay creditors an average of 18 cents on the\ndollar, according to a Jan. 31  filing  in  U.S. Bankruptcy Court \nin Manhattan. Restructuring firm Alvarez & Marsal LLC, which\nruns the defunct investment bank, has made almost $583 million\nso far, including incentive payments. Lead bankruptcy law firm\nWeil, Gotshal & Manges LLP has earned $454 million.  Lehman became the most expensive bankruptcy in U.S. history\nin April 2010, when it topped the record $757 million tab for\nenergy trader Enron Corp.\u2019s three-year liquidation, according to\nthe database of  Lynn LoPucki , a bankruptcy-law professor at the\n University of California ,  Los Angeles . Fees surpassed $1 billion\nafter 24 1\/2 months in bankruptcy in October 2010.  Enron\u2019s payback to general unsecured creditors was about 53\npercent, albeit with a long wait after it came out of bankruptcy\ncourt in 2004.  The high fees result from competition among bankruptcy\ncourts for big cases, LoPucki, author of \u201cCourting Failure: How\nCompetition for Big Cases Is Corrupting the Bankruptcy Courts\u201d\n(University of Michigan Press, 2005), said at the time. Judges\ndon\u2019t often challenge payments to lawyers who bring in big\ncases, because under current laws those lawyers are free to take\nfuture cases to competing courts that won\u2019t question the fees,\nhe said.  Lehman, once the world\u2019s fourth-biggest  investment bank ,\nfiled the biggest bankruptcy in U.S. history in September 2008\nwith  assets  of $639 billion. Creditors included  Goldman Sachs\nGroup Inc. (GS) ,  UBS AG (UBSN) , the New York Giants professional football\nteam and Abu Dhabi Investment Authority.  The case is In re Lehman Brothers Holdings Inc., 08-13555,\nU.S. Bankruptcy Court, Southern District of New York\n(Manhattan). The\nquestion is important because challenging an invention\u2019s\neligibility for a patent can be quicker and cheaper than\ncontesting a patent\u2019s validity on other grounds.  \u201cThe patent system has had a hard time figuring out what\npatents are valid when you are using a computer to make\nsomething easier,\u201d said  Lynn Pasahow , who represented\nAmazon.com Inc. in its 1999 lawsuit alleging Barnes & Noble Inc.\nviolated a patent for one-click shopping. \u201cThere\u2019s an idea out\nthere that it\u2019s like pornography, you know it when you see it,\nor when the Federal Circuit or Supreme Court rules on it.\u201d  The case before the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Federal\nCircuit in Washington has divided technology companies that have\nfiled legal arguments with the court.  Patent Growth  Google, Facebook Inc. and Red Hat Inc. say patent standards\nare too lax.  International Business Machines Corp.  warns that\nstringent rules could stifle innovation. Computer software was\nthe fastest-growing area of patents between 1980 and 2005,\naccording to a  report  this month by the Brookings Institution, a\nWashington research group.  While technology companies often use the derisive term\n\u201ctrolls\u201d for patent holders that don\u2019t make products, they\ndirect particular ire at owners of software patents who sue\ndozens, or even hundreds of companies claiming to have invented\naspects of widely used technologies like online shopping,\nInternet mapping or tracking delivery vehicles.  Of the more than 5,600 patent-infringement lawsuits filed\nin the U.S. last year, more than 12 percent were filed by just\n10 companies over software, according to Bloomberg Law data.  \u201cComing up with a product that\u2019s useful requires some\ndifficult and sophisticated programming -- that\u2019s the hard\npart,\u201d  Suzanne Michel , Google\u2019s senior patent counsel, said in\nan interview. \u201cYou\u2019ve got a system that\u2019s over-rewarding the\neasy stuff and blocking off the hard part of innovation.\u201d  Unclear Rules  In the past, the legal rules weren\u2019t clear enough for the\nU.S. Patent and Trademark Office to reject vague applications,\nsaid former PTO Director  David Kappos , who left his post Feb. 1\nand is now with the Cravath Swaine & Moore law firm. That\ndoesn\u2019t mean software patents aren\u2019t valuable, he said.  \u201cLook at Google -- who would be the first of us to throw a\nstone and say that wasn\u2019t a great idea?\u201d Kappos said. \u201cIf\nyou\u2019ve got a patent and sue 50 to 100 manufacturers all at once,\nwhat you\u2019re really saying is that your patent covers the\nproblem, not the particular solution.\u201d  The patents before the Federal Circuit concern a\ncomputerized method for using an intermediary to make sure\nbuyers and sellers meet their obligations in stock and currency\ntrading. Patent owner Alice Corp., an Australian company jointly\nowned by  National Australia Bank Ltd.  and Alice Ventures Pty,\nfiled infringement claims in 2007 against  CLS Bank\nInternational , which settles about $4.5 billion foreign-exchange\ntransactions daily.  2011 Ruling  A federal judge in Washington ruled in 2011 that the idea\nof using an intermediary to settle trades isn\u2019t eligible for a\npatent, and computerizing the notion didn\u2019t make it patentable.  In a 2-1 decision in July, the appeals court reversed that\ndecision, ruling that Alice\u2019s suit should proceed because the\npatents cover \u201cpractical applications of the invention\u201d and\nnot an abstract idea.  The Federal Circuit agreed to have all active judges on the\ncourt rehear the case tomorrow, with a  focus  on how to determine\nif a computer-implemented invention can be patented.  \u201cThere\u2019s been a push for the past decade or even longer,\nwith voices saying these shouldn\u2019t be patentable,\u201d said  Scott Doyle , a patent lawyer with Shearman & Sterling in Washington,\nwho successfully represented Daimler AG\u2019s Mercedes-Benz unit\nagainst claims it infringed a patent for a monitor to detect\nwhen a motorist is drowsy. \u201cThey are trying to figure out a\nworkable way to deal with these cases.\u201d  Long-Standing Practices  The Clearing House Association, a trade group representing\nthe largest commercial banks, said in a  filing  that too many\npatents simply add a computer to long-standing business\npractices.  \u201cSome software patents are dangerously broad and\ndangerously vague,\u201d said Julie Samuels, a staff lawyer with the\nElectronic Frontier Foundation in San Francisco. \u201cIf I had a\nmagic wand and could go to day one, software should not be\npatented at all. The harm software patents cause outweighs the\nbenefit.\u201d  In the appeals court\u2019s July ruling, Circuit Judge  Richard Linn  said that, unless it\u2019s \u201cmanifestly evident\u201d that patents\ncover abstract ideas ineligible for protection, they should be\nchallenged on other grounds, such as whether they\u2019re new or\nobvious variations of others\u2019 work.  Threshold Issue  A group that includes British Airways, Intuit Inc., Twitter\nInc., Yelp and SAP AG said the ruling may keep courts from\nquickly resolving cases about patents that wouldn\u2019t have been\nissued under current standards.  \u201cIt encouraged trial courts to delay deciding this\nthreshold issue of law, allowing innovation-harming patents to\nstand for months or years without any judicial scrutiny,\u201d the\ncompanies said in a Dec. 7  filing .  IBM, which has received the most U.S. patents for the past\n20 years, said in a Dec. 7  filing  that the \u201cvast majority of\ncomputer-implemented inventions are patent eligible\u201d and\ncreated technology that transformed society.  \u201cSoftware patents as a class are under attack and have\nbeen ever since the software industry began to rely on patent\nprotection as a rule rather than an exception,\u201d IBM said.  The Business Software Alliance, whose members include  Apple\nInc.  and  Microsoft Corp. , said the Alice patents shouldn\u2019t have\nbeen issued because they cover \u201can idea that has existed in\nnon-digital form for millennia.\u201d Still, the group said,\nsoftware inventions \u201cconstitute a growing and significant\nportion of both the U.S. economy and U.S. export market.\u201d  While the Federal Circuit will try to clarify the rules,\nit\u2019s unlikely to foreclose patenting of all software, said  Erika\nArner , a lawyer in Washington who represented a patent owner in\na 2010 Supreme Court case involving business method patents,\nwhich often overlap with software.  \u201cThe court is aware that the patent office has been\nissuing patents on software for 20 to 30 years, so there are\ntens of thousands of patents that represent settled property\nrights by inventors around the world,\u201d she said. Banks, brokers and insurance companies make up 16.8 percent of the  S&P 500 , almost double the level from 2009 and closing in on technology companies at 17.6 percent, according to data compiled by Bloomberg.  Bank of America Corp.  and Morgan Stanley are helping lead gains in the index this month after profits topped analyst estimates.  Intel Corp. (INTC)  and Microsoft Corp. are among the worst after earnings trailed forecasts.  For bulls, the change signals banks will lead the economy even after the  Federal Reserve  begins to reduce stimulus. Bears say S&P 500 profits would be down this quarter if not for banks. They note that the last time financials were the biggest industry was in 2008 and the consequences were disastrous.  \u201cThe fact that we are seeing banks perform reasonably well provides a certain sense of confidence in the underlying economy,\u201d Kevin Caron, a Florham Park, New Jersey-based market strategist at Stifel Nicolaus & Co., which oversees about $130 billion, said in a July 25 phone interview. \u201cWithout the financials working, it would be hard to imagine that all the rest would be working at all.\u201d  First Drop  Equities  snapped  a four-week rally as earnings from Netflix Inc. to Caterpillar Inc. trailed  forecasts  and Chinese manufacturing contracted more than estimated. The S&P 500 fell less than 0.1 percent to 1,691.65, after hitting a record 1,695.53 on July 22. The benchmark gauge for U.S. stocks is up 19 percent for the year, bringing the advance since the market bottomed in March 2009 to 150 percent.  The S&P 500 slipped 0.2 percent to 1,687.76 at 10:09 a.m.  New York  time today.  Earnings for companies in the S&P 500 are projected to climb 3.3 percent, led by a 27 percent increase in bank profits, based on more than 11,000 analyst projections compiled by Bloomberg. Without the financial industry, S&P 500 income would contract 1.2 percent.  Bank of America, Morgan Stanley and E*Trade Financial Corp. rose at least 13 percent and helped lead financial shares higher this month.  Broadcom Corp. (BRCM) , down 19 percent in July, and Microsoft, which has lost 8.5 percent, are  dragging  technology shares to the second-worst industry performance. Computer makers and software designers have reported  earnings  0.4 percent below analysts\u2019 estimates on average, data compiled by Bloomberg show.  Economic Growth  Banks were the largest U.S. industry during the  bull market  that began in 2002, when the S&P 500  more than doubled  and the economy expanded as much as 3.5 percent annually, according to data compiled by Bloomberg. In the late 1990s, financial firms grew to 18.8 percent of the index, coinciding with the biggest stock rally in history and more than 4 percent average annual growth in gross domestic product.  While both  JPMorgan Chase & Co. (JPM)  and  Microsoft (MSFT)  had about $21 billion in net income in 2012,  earnings  at the largest  U.S. bank  by assets were higher than the computer company last quarter as trading and  investment banking  picked up and demand for personal computers declined. The  banking industry  lost a record $14.65 a share during the fourth quarter of 2008 and took more than $2 trillion of credit-related losses and writedowns, after risky trading and home lending led to the credit crisis. You know those  baby sea turtles  that get eaten by birds and crabs on their way from the nest to the water? It's like that. Corporations have narrowed the focus of their R&D by pressing for clear, short-term wins; venture capitalists are too quick to get caught up in the latest, hottest thing; and even the vaunted crowdfunding option is pretty limited: It's great if you're an internet star, but try getting a crowd excited about an innovative idea in industrial machinery. It doesn't have to be this way. Effective means of boosting innovation already exist, but not enough companies are making use of them. Two in particular are corporate venture funds, which invest in start-ups outside companies' walls, and internal idea contests. I'll describe both, but first let's look at what's wrong with some of the traditional sources of innovation. Corporate R&D too often focuses on refining technologies that are already in use. You can see why: For decades in the U.S., billions were spent on big science, and the commercial returns were disappointing. But cutting back on research funding doesn't work either. In the 1990s, Eastman Kodak cut its R&D spending and focused on film, a technology that was clearly successful (you know where this is going); and in the 2000s, Nokia focused on maintaining its strong position in low-end phones (you know where this is going too \u2014 Kodak filed for bankruptcy, and Nokia, whose phone business is now being  bought by Microsoft , suffered from having missed the smartphone wave). Even in companies that are diligent about looking to the future, R&D has a tendency to be slow, rigid, and expensive. Independent venture capital is a vital force in funding start-ups, but VCs tend to have a narrow focus on certain industries and geographies. Their funding cycles are volatile, too \u2014 it's either feast or famine \u2014 and they expect returns within a few years. Crowdfunding has undeniable power, but rather than solve the problems of venture capital, it exaggerates them. The glamorous projects inevitably get the bulk of the funding, while more experimental, more complex, and more pedestrian projects lose out. If VC is \"unfair,\" crowdfunding is even more unfair. Corporate venture capital can avoid some of these problems. A corporate venture-capital fund can often do a better job than corporate R&D of exploring new territory, and at the same time, it can move more quickly, flexibly, and cheaply than traditional R&D. In the 1990s and 2000s, for example, several corporate-venture initiatives helped pharmaceutical companies catch up with rapid advances in bioscience that were threatening to undermine the value of their well-established expertise. And corporate venture funds, if well managed, can avoid the fickleness problem that plagues independent venture capital and crowdfunding.  Many large companies have been wary of corporate venturing, because they've seen such funds deployed ineffectively. And it's true that if companies aren't careful, their internal venture capitalists can become entangled in the agendas of various corporate stakeholders or demotivated by inadequate or poorly designed financial incentives. That's why it's important that venture funds' goals be aligned with corporate objectives, approvals for funding be streamlined, and compensation levels match those offered by independent venture groups. Companies that fail to provide adequate incentives face a steady stream of defections; after too many board meetings in which the corporate investor parks his Fiesta next to the independent venture capitalist's Ferrari, the temptation to go elsewhere becomes too great.  Contests are at the opposite end of the size and cost scales from venture funding, but they can be an effective complement to a corporate innovation program. Companies should consider offering rewards for people who solve internal problems or create new products. It's important to have a specific goal at the outset, and the rewards should be meaningful, but they don't always have to involve cash. Recognition is a powerful reward too.  These two very different approaches aren't the only ways to improve innovation, of course, but they're particularly cost-effective as well as powerful in tapping the best aspects of both venture capital and the traditional corporate R&D approach. They demonstrate that with experimentation and ingenuity, even the most intractable problems are  surmountable . They illustrate the range of programs that companies should be implementing to stimulate innovation and shepherd ideas toward marketable products.","path":".\/2008_2012_msft_bloomberg_news\/ow-corporate-venture-capital-helps-firms-explore-new-territory.txt"},{"id":60482668,"title":"Google Seen Passing Apple in Tablets as IPad Loses Ground","released_at":"<date>March 12 2013<\/date> <time>15:25:44<\/time>","content":"Google Inc. Slim\u2019s lead over the next-wealthiest man, Bill Gates, narrowed last week to about $4.8 billion -- the closest spread in almost a year. The Lebanese immigrant\u2019s son, who acquired Mexico\u2019s phone monopoly and turned it into a pan-Latin American powerhouse, lost almost a 10th of his net worth last month, winnowing his fortune to $71 billion, according to the  Bloomberg Billionaires Index .  The main culprit: Slim\u2019s holdings in  America Movil SAB (AMXL) , whose dominance in Latin America and especially its home country of Mexico is under fire, with lawmakers and regulators pushing for tighter controls. The shifting landscape in Latin America threatens to close the steady spigot of cash that enabled Slim to make bets in  Europe  last year.  \u201cThe challenge facing America Movil starts in Mexico because of the increasing resistance to its dominance,\u201d said Mark Mobius, executive chairman of Templeton  Emerging Markets  Group, which manages funds that include Slim\u2019s phone carrier. \u201cAs its competitors become much more viable, you\u2019re going to find America Movil in trouble in Mexico, not having the kind of earnings they\u2019ve had in the past.\u201d  Arturo Elias , a spokesman for Slim, declined to comment.  \u2018Most Disconcerting\u2019  Outside shareholders in America Movil are selling off the stock as their fears are realized -- that even Slim isn\u2019t immune as Latin America\u2019s days of dizzying growth come to an end. That\u2019s driven down the shares to an almost four-year low.  \u201cIf they can\u2019t hold up their margins, no one else really has a chance,\u201d said Christopher King, an analyst at Stifel Nicolaus & Co. in Baltimore. \u201cThey\u2019re going lower for everybody across the board. That is the most disconcerting thing.\u201d  King cut his recommendation on Mexico City-based America Movil to a neutral rating in October 2010 after recommending buying the shares for more than four years. It turned out to be a prescient move. The shares are down 25 percent since then, compared with a 25 percent gain for Mexico\u2019s benchmark IPC index.  Slim first became the world\u2019s richest person in 2007, according to data compiled by Bloomberg. To get there, he passed Gates, the founder of Microsoft Corp., and  Warren Buffett , the stock picker and takeover master behind Berkshire Hathaway Inc. Slim led Gates by as much as $14.5 billion as recently as January.  Wealth Giveaways  Gates and Buffett have pledged to give away most of their wealth before they die and have already placed billions of dollars in Gates\u2019s foundation, putting a dent in their fortunes. Buffett slid to fourth place last year behind Amancio Ortega, the Spaniard who founded the Zara clothing chain.  America Movil has long faced accusations from competitors and regulators that it wields monopoly power in Mexico, where it holds 70 percent of the wireless market and about 80 percent of landlines. While Slim has said the existence of competitors proves he doesn\u2019t have a monopoly, shareholders have clearly valued America Movil\u2019s dominance, said Pablo Vallejo, an analyst at Corporativo GBM SAB in  Mexico  City.  Monopoly Premium  \u201cThe market used to pay a premium for it to be in the dominant position in two of its operations, Mexico and Colombia,\u201d he said. \u201cAll the scenarios contemplated in the reform are bad news for America Movil.\u201d  A draft of a new telecommunications reform bill in Mexico stipulates that companies with at least 40 percent market share would be declared dominant and could be forced to rent parts of their network to rivals, the Reforma newspaper said last week. Regulators could also revoke operating licenses for monopolistic behavior, the paper said, citing the draft it obtained.  America Movil continues to have the largest, most robust telecommunications network in the region, an asset that generates almost $16 billion in cash a year and puts Slim in position to capitalize on growing demand for wireless Internet and pay-TV services.  Less Lucrative  The challenge is that neither of those services are as profitable as mobile-phone calls and landlines. America Movil and its competitors are offering smartphone discounts to get Internet-accessible devices in customers\u2019 hands, cutting into income. To lure satellite and cable television subscribers, the company must pay companies such as  Time Warner Inc. (TWX)  and Walt Disney Co. for programming. That\u2019s reducing margins.  Meanwhile, the stable old business of mobile-phone voice service is deteriorating. In Mexico,  Brazil  and Colombia --which together make up about 70 percent of America Movil\u2019s sales -- regulatory agencies have reduced the fees Slim\u2019s company can charge competitors to connect calls from their subscribers to its own users.  At the same time, the percentage of Latin America\u2019s population that already has a mobile phone has crept closer to 100 percent -- and even higher in countries such as Brazil and  Argentina , where people own multiple devices. America Movil\u2019s mobile-phone subscriber growth hasn\u2019t topped 15 percent since 2008 after regularly doing so in the previous decade.  Free Roaming  With little opportunity to pick up customers who are buying mobile phones for the first time, companies are scrambling to offer better deals on airtime and devices just to lure subscribers away from one another. America Movil, for instance, began last year offering plans with no extra charge for national roaming or long-distance calls.  All these trends converged in America Movil\u2019s fourth quarter, which produced profit that fell short of analysts\u2019 estimates. The margin of earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortization dropped 240 basis points, or 2.4 percentage points, to 31.1 percent, with the Mexican and Brazilian units dropping 260 basis points each.  Investors responded, reducing the stock price by one-tenth. The shares have continued to fall since, closing at 13.32 pesos on March 1, the most recent trading day, down 16 percent since the Feb. 12 report.  Worse still for shareholders, America Movil Chief Executive Officer Daniel Hajj, Slim\u2019s son-in-law, said there was no end in sight to the severe level of competition.  Under Pressure  \u201cThis quarter revealed a lot,\u201d said Vallejo of GBM. \u201cThe pressure in margins isn\u2019t going to go away as long as these markets remain highly competitive.\u201d  Then there\u2019s Europe. After spending more than 3 billion euros ($4 billion) last year to acquire a 28 percent stake in Royal KPN NV, America Movil has seen the former Dutch phone monopoly\u2019s shares fall 65 percent. It decided last month to spend an additional 900 million euros to help the flailing KPN shore up its finances. Shares of Telekom Austria AG, meanwhile, have dropped 36 percent since America Movil agreed to buy a 21 percent stake.  Slim has said he considers the stakes in European carriers as long-term investments. The  National Association of REITs  found that a portfolio 30\npercent invested in commercial property shares delivered a\nhigher return relative to one more heavily tilted toward\nprivate-equity funds, based on a study to be published today on\nthe group\u2019s website. Pension funds typically put less than 10\npercent of their real estate allocations into publicly traded\nREITs to protect against stock-market volatility.  The Washington-based real estate association, which\nrepresents about 200 companies, says that what it calls \u201cthe\nREIT third\u201d can help state and corporate pensions  narrow  a\nfunding shortfall that totals almost $1.5 trillion, according to\nthe Center for Retirement Research at  Boston College . A bigger\nREIT allocation, and a smaller one in private equity, would\noffer better diversification and more consistent returns, said\nBrad Case, NAREIT\u2019s vice president for research.  The trick is in the timing, he said.  \u201cThe public side is liquid, so therefore when investors\nstart to get concerned about the future of asset values, they\nsell their REIT stocks, whereas they can\u2019t get out of their\nprivate-equity real estate funds,\u201d he said in a telephone\ninterview. \u201cThat lag is what gives the institutional investor\nthe diversification benefit.\u201d  Three Fund Types  The NAREIT study analyzed 22 years of data encompassing\nboth the 2008 credit crisis and the savings and loan collapse of\nthe early 1990s. It examined REIT returns compared with the\nthree main types of real estate private equity: so-called core\nfunds, which buy properties with mostly cash; high-yield\n\u201copportunity\u201d funds, which can use as much as 70 percent\nborrowed money and aim to boost returns beyond 20 percent; and\n\u201cvalue-added\u201d funds, which exist between the two.  The study found that a portfolio consisting of 30 percent\nREITs, 49 percent in core private funds and 21 percent in high-\nyield funds averaged an 8.2 percent annual return from 1992 to\nthe third quarter of 2010. A portfolio with 9 percent REITs and\n20 percent in value-added funds returned 6.7 percent a year for\nthe same period. The NAREIT-preferred allocation also had a\nsuperior Sharpe Ratio, a measurement that seeks to balance\nvolatility with return expectations.  The private and public sides of real estate are contending\nfor slices of what NAREIT estimates is a half-trillion dollar\npie, or about 10 percent of the $5.3 trillion in pension\ninvestments.  Increasing Leverage  A portfolio 30 percent in REITs may add too much risk to\nthe investments, said Mark Roberts, global head of research at\nDallas-based Invesco Real Estate, an asset-management company\nwhose property-investment options includes private-equity funds.  \u201cWhen you\u2019re looking at that kind of composition of real\nestate, what investors need to be mindful of is that is starting\nto take the leverage level of their real estate portfolio\nupwards of 40 or 50 percent or more,\u201d he said in a telephone\ninterview. \u201cRelative to, say, an unlevered real estate market,\nthat amount of leverage will double the volatility of returns.\u201d  Invesco research shows that about 15 percent invested in\nREITs maximizes returns without increasing risk, Roberts said.  The largest, best-known real estate private-equity funds\nare run by investment banks including  Goldman Sachs Group Inc .\nand Morgan Stanley, as well as asset managers such as  Blackstone\nGroup LP , Starwood Capital Group LLC, and AREA Property Partners\nLP. Many of them made their reputations with high-yield\nopportunity funds that delivered annual returns of as much as 40\npercent in the late 1990s.  Credit-Crisis Losses  There were 414 high-yield funds last year, down from a 2009\npeak of 466, according to a March survey by Real Estate Alert, a\ntrade newsletter that covers commercial property investment.\nAfter losses brought on by the 2008 credit crisis, those funds\nreduced their equity-raising goals and yield targets, which\naveraged 16.9 percent last year, according to the survey.  The Bloomberg REIT Index, a measure of 117 commercial\nproperty stocks, fell 77 percent from its February 2007 peak to\nits March 2009 low as credit dried up and real estate values\nplummeted. It has since rebounded 176 percent.  Pension funds are \u201cclearly\u201d adding REITs to their\nportfolios, said Anatole Pevnev, a principal with Cleveland-\nbased  Townsend Group , the biggest real estate consultant to\npublic pension funds, advising on about $105 billion of property\nallocations. It\u2019s \u201ctough\u201d to give numbers, since many funds\nassign REITs to their public securities category, alongside\nstocks such as Microsoft Corp. and  Google Inc ., instead of\nlisting them as property investments, he said.  Investor Opportunity  \u201cAs REITs got hit hard, it did give an opportunity for\ninvestors to get into it,\u201d Pevnev said in a telephone interview\nlast month. \u201cThere was a massive blow to the financial system.\nThe ability of the REITs to recapitalize themselves went a long\nway to convincing investors that REITs are a viable long-term\ninvestment.\u201d  An October report by the Pension Real Estate Association\nfound that since 1994, the dawn of that decade\u2019s commercial real\nestate boom, private equity outperformed REITs when adjusted for\nrisk. REITs beat private funds by 1 percent per quarter in\nreturn percentage, though with more than three times the\nvolatility, according to the report.  \u201cNAREIT agrees that REITs are certainly more volatile, and\nthe fact of the matter is they\u2019ve also had a higher return\nhistorically than private equity real estate,\u201d said Greg\nMacKinnon, the association\u2019s research director. \u201cBut if you do\nthat risk-versus-return comparison, private real estate comes\nout on top. Really there\u2019s room for both in a portfolio.\u201d    Oregon \u2019s Pension  Katy Durant, a member of the  Oregon Investment Council  and\na retail property developer in  Portland , Oregon, said she\u2019s not\ninclined to push REITs at the expense of the private-equity\nfunds that have served her state pension funds well. Oregon\ninvests about 21 percent of its real estate allocation in REITs,\nand 39 percent in high-yield opportunity funds, including  John\nGrayken \u2019s Dallas-based Lone Star Funds, which has invested about\n$24 billion since its 1995 founding, according to its website.  What matters is which funds you choose, Durant said. Oregon\nhas invested in seven Lone Star funds starting in 1996 and, as\nof the third quarter, only one had a loss -- a 1.64 percent loss\nin the 2005 fund, according to the state treasury website.\nReturns aren\u2019t given for the two most recent funds, both from\n2008, because it\u2019s too early for the figures to be meaningful,\nsaid James Sinks, spokesman for the treasury. Returns on the\nearlier funds ranged from 7.4 percent to 32 percent.  \u201cI would like to think that Oregon, by virtue of how long\nwe\u2019ve been playing private-equity and real estate partnerships,\nthey can pick from the cream of the crop,\u201d Durant said. \u201cI\nwould hate to have lowered our allocation to  Lone Star  and been\nin a bucket of REITs the entire time.\u201d  To contact the reporter on this story:\nDavid M. Yet Apple and Cisco aren't the biggest hoarders of overseas cash. According to  Bloomberg Rankings , which looked at the regulatory filings of the 70 companies in the S&P 500 Information Technology Index and the five in the S&P 500 Internet & Catalog Retail Index, the distinction belongs to Microsoft and IBM.  Microsoft had $76.4 billion and IBM had $44.4 billion in foreign profits on their books in 2012 that were untaxed by the U.S., according to the documents. Microsoft responded to a request for comment by pointing to congressional testimony from September, when Bill Sample, corporate vice president for worldwide tax at Microsoft, said that U.S. taxes on foreign earnings create a \"disincentive for U.S. investment\" and need changing to be competitive with many U.S. trading partners. IBM did not respond. It's estimated that U.S. corporations have more than  $2 trillion in offshore earnings  that are not being taxed by the U.S. As my colleague Jesse Drucker has reported, companies funnel cash overseas to  lower their tax rates  and in some cases have figured out ways to  bring the money home tax-free  through acquisitions and other means. President Obama has waded into the issue. In February 2012 he proposed reducing the top corporate rate for most companies to 28 percent from 35 percent while eliminating tax breaks and changing other core features of the tax code.  One of the central concerns about a tax holiday is that it was tried before - in 2004 - and it  did little  to encourage the companies that took advantage of the break to create jobs or spur domestic investment, several independent economic studies have shown. However, the holiday did encourage companies to do one thing: to hoard overseas profits in expectation of another tax break.
