The district and union agreed to a contract that, for the first time, ties teacher evaluation to student performance. The Chicago Teachers Union, with 30,000 members, walked off the job Sept. 10 partly because of concern that longtime employees would be treated unfairly under such reviews.  The provision marks a win for Democratic Chicago Mayor  Rahm Emanuel , who has billed himself as a champion for \u201ceducation reform\u201d and a loss for tenured teachers who will see erosion in their  job security . The drama in Chicago -- the third-largest U.S. school district, with 400,000 students -- follows debate across the country about the validity of test-based evaluations.  \u201cAs more and more schools move in this direction, it\u2019s likely to move into the realm of the expected, rather than the exceptional,\u201d said Nancy Waymack, managing director of the  National Council on Teacher Quality , a Washington-based research and policy group.  Thirty-one states require that teacher evaluations include objective measures of student achievement, up from 15 in 2009, according to the council. As a result, 29 of the 50 largest districts have revamped their reviews, with most using test scores for part of the assessment.  \u2018Gaining Momentum\u2019  The inclusion of contentious teacher evaluation provisions promotes the movement toward using the approach for overhauling schools, said  Michelle Rhee , the former Washington schools chief who clashed with unions over such issues.  It also creates a group of potential losers: Teachers with seniority who once had near-unassailable job security and who now risk losing their jobs over poor evaluations.  \u201cIt is commendable and telling that a Democratic mayor was willing to take on special interests in his own party to fight for the civil rights of children,\u201d Rhee, who heads  StudentsFirst , a Sacramento-based education advocacy group, said in a statement. \u201cThe fact that critical issues, such as improving teacher quality and reforming tenure, were at the center of the strike shows the reform movement is gaining momentum.\u201d  Randi Weingarten , president of the  American Federation of Teachers , lamented what she called a \u201cgrowing obsession with high-stakes testing, denying kids the rich learning experiences they need.\u201d  \u201cTeachers continue to be denied the tools and conditions they need to do their jobs and then are blamed for every problem facing our schools,\u201d Weingarten said in a statement.  Economic Benefits  If the change improves education, the results could be significant. Boosting teacher quality yields long-term economic benefits for students, according to a 2011  study  by  Harvard University  and Columbia University researchers of 2.5 million children. Students with better teachers are more likely to go to college, get higher-paying jobs and save more for retirement, the study found. They are also less likely to become teenage parents.  Replacing a teacher in the bottom 5 percent -- based on improvement of students\u2019 test scores -- with one of only average quality increases the present value of children\u2019s lifetime earnings by $250,000, the study found.  Contract Details  Spelling out its version of an evaluation program tied to student achievement,  Chicago Public Schools  issued details of the contract last weekend. The district said that \u201cstudent growth\u201d -- or the improvement of children\u2019s test scores -- will account for 25 percent of a teacher\u2019s evaluation in the first two years of the pact, and 30 percent in the third. A new state law requires the 30 percent benchmark.  A \u201cstudent survey will be piloted\u201d in the contract\u2019s second year and would contribute to 10 percent of the teacher evaluation, according to the district.  Teachers are leery of the new method, said Maria Ferguson, executive director of the Center on Education Policy at George Washington University. In particular, instructors who work in low-income neighborhoods worry that the measures don\u2019t account for the difficulty of their classrooms.  \u201cThis is a change that shouldn\u2019t be crammed down their throats,\u201d Ferguson said in a telephone interview. \u201cTeachers need to be at the table.\u201d  Achievement Tests  Education researchers have found that the tests often aren\u2019t up to the task, said J.R. Lockwood, a senior statistician at Rand Corp., a researcher based in  Santa Monica ,  California .  State achievement tests are often designed to measure how many students are proficient in a subject, rather than how much a teacher has improved an individual student\u2019s performance, Lockwood said. Multiple teachers can contribute to students\u2019 results, making it difficult to pinpoint who should be rewarded, and exams don\u2019t adjust enough for the socioeconomic backgrounds of the students in the classroom, he said.  \u201cThe research community has fairly consistently been trying to put a brake on it,\u201d said Lockwood, who has studied such systems across the country for more than a decade. \u201cThey\u2019re not saying it\u2019s a bad thing. It\u2019s just that there are too many uncertainties. We\u2019re still trying to figure this out.\u201d  In  New York  City, the teachers union, citing flaws in the district\u2019s evaluation system, unsuccessfully went to court to stop Mayor  Michael Bloomberg \u2019s administration from releasing the names of educators and their ratings. The mayor is founder and majority owner of Bloomberg News parent Bloomberg LP.  Teachers have long been rewarded primarily on their years of experience and whether they\u2019ve secured an advanced degree.  Obama\u2019s Grants  Such provisions can be costly to cash-strapped districts. In November 2010, Microsoft Corp. Chairman  Bill Gates  urged top U.S. public-school officials to overhaul teacher pay, saying taxpayers are spending $59 billion a year on compensation plans based on seniority and degrees that don\u2019t improve student achievement.  Tying teacher evaluation to student performance was a requirement for winning grants in  Barack Obama  administration\u2019s $5 billion Race to the Top program, which led states to pass laws requiring such systems.  Public opinion polls support holding teachers accountable for student achievement, said Grover J. Whitehurst, director of the Brown Center on Education Policy at the  Brookings Institution , a Washington public policy and research group.  Currently, most systems don\u2019t make distinctions among teachers, so any change will be an improvement, Whitehurst said in a telephone interview.  \u201cTo not use the information is to throw away the best data that we have, imperfect though it is,\u201d Whitehurst said.","path":".\/2008_2012_msft_bloomberg_news\/chicago-strike-shows-rifts-over-move-to-grading-teachers.txt"},{"id":17657804,"title":"Google Said to Consider Financing an Offer to Acquire Yahoo","released_at":"<date>October 22 2011<\/date> <time>18:45:02<\/time>","content":"Google Inc. The Mexican tycoon has to decide whether trying to gain control of former national telecom operators in Europe is generally a good idea: They are too well-protected against hostile takeovers and agreeing with their own valuations would not leave Slim much of a profit potential. German parties  close  to coalition Angela Merkel's Christian Democrats and their former election rivals, Sigmar Gabriel's Social Democrats, are to reach a preliminary decision on forming a coalition after the third round of their exploratory talks on Oct. 17. If the talks go well, Social Democrat leaders will recommend that their Oct. 20 party convention support a \"grand coalition.\" The parties are expected to compromise on establishing a minimum wage, a demand put forwards by the Social Democrats but shunned by Merkel who believes it might destroy jobs. She believes the proposed $11.5 per hour rate is too high for eastern Germany. Merkel could appease her potential coalition partners by proposing higher subsidies for the German federal states. In any case, Gabriel and other Social Democratic leaders will do their best to keep the deal from falling through: Merkel could still go back to the Greens, who exited coalition talks earlier this week. Ubisoft shares  lose  26 percent over game delay The French digital game developer, Ubisoft, took a 26 percent plunge on the Paris stock exchange after announcing it would postpone the launch of its new game, Watch Dogs, by six months. One day's trading cost Ubisoft shareholders $400 million, because the delay will drive the company into the red for the financial year ending in March, 2014. Ubisoft management knew this would happen but still chose to give its developers more time to polish the game, intended for new generation gaming consoles from Sony and Microsoft. In the game development business, even established companies' fortunes hang on a single launch: They cannot afford to have a major product fail. As a result, it is one of the few industries where quality is truly the number one concern, well above such things as short-term stock market performance. Axa  sells  biggest catastrophe bond The French insurer Axa has successfully placed the biggest ever euro-denominated \"catastrophe bond,\" $473 million of repackaged major disaster risk. The issue brings the cat bond market closer to surpassing its 2007 record of $8 billion in total placements. Though the instrument is still considered exotic, any institutional investors would clearly rather deal with the risk of a hurricane or a flood that would render their investment worthless than with the irrationality and uncertainty of conventional bond and equity markets.  Russian  opposition  leader's jail term suspended In a long-awaited decision, a Russian court suspended the 5-year sentence of Alexei Navalny, a popular opponent to President Vladimir Putin. Navalny received the sentence in July for allegedly organizing the theft of lumber from a state-owned company, although the evidence was notoriously thin. While his lawyers appealed the verdict, Navalny ran for mayor of Moscow, and though he lost to the pro-Putin incumbent, he won 27 percent of the vote \u2013 enough to make imprisoning him politically uncomfortable. Though the suspended sentence allows Navalny to stay out of jail, the conviction was allowed to stand, and the opposition leader will not be able to take part in elections for the next five years. The challenge for Navalny now is to build a strong enough party to make gains without him actually running for political office. Putin, meanwhile, has calmed protest against Navalny's conviction while crippling a dangerous opponent. (Leonid Bershidsky, an editor and novelist, is a Bloomberg View contributor. The winning crew\ndonated the trophy to the  New York  Yacht Club, under the\ncondition that it be held in trust as a challenge trophy to\n\u201cpromote friendly competition among nations.\u201d  I\u2019m not sure exactly what they meant by that. With the trophy safely in hand, Ellison set\nabout realizing his deluded dreams.  Drunken Skipper  As the greatest prize in yachting, the cup has long been\ncoveted by the world\u2019s richest men. Tea magnate Thomas Lipton\ntried five times between 1899 and 1930 to win the cup and never\ndid. More recently,  Ted Turner  won it in 1977, though he\u2019s\nprobably better remembered for turning up drunk at his post-victory news conference than for the race itself. Now there is\nEllison, the founder and chief executive officer of Oracle\nCorp., who has spent hundreds of millions of dollars over the\nyears in pursuit of the cup. He won it three years ago and will\ndefend it this summer.  Ellison, however, is no ordinary billionaire. He is a\nSilicon Valley billionaire, and thus sees it as his sacred duty\nto disruptively innovate -- or is it innovatively disrupt? --\nevery industry he can, whether it be software or yachting. The\nAmerica\u2019s Cup was the perfect vehicle for his entrepreneurial\nevangelism: One of its quirks is that the winner of the last\nrace basically gets to set the rules for the next one.  What Ellison wanted was bigger, faster boats. Specifically,\n72-foot-long catamarans with massive, computer-controlled fixed\n\u201csails.\u201d (They\u2019re not sails that you or I would recognize, the\nsort that billow in the wind. More like the wing of a Boeing\n747, only upright and 13 stories tall.) The boats can travel up\nto 50 miles per hour, riding above the surface of the water on\nrudders and carbon-fiber blades. Is this even \u201csailing\u201d?  Ellison liked these big, fast boats because he thought they\nwould make better television. And  he was sure  that sailing\nbelonged on television. To that end, he hired the mastermind who\nbrought the virtual first-down line to the NFL\u2019s broadcasts and\nthe glowing hockey puck to the NHL\u2019s. Ellison was going to turn\nsailing into a spectator sport. Even if that meant buying the\nairtime himself to get any of the races leading up to the cup --\nthe \u201cAmerica\u2019s Cup World Series,\u201d as he called them -- on TV.  Where do Ellison\u2019s dreams of revolutionizing sailing stand\nnow, with the start of the competition just weeks away? Instead\nof 15 teams contending for the cup, as he had imagined, there\nare just four. (Bertarelli is among those who dropped out.)\nThere are two main reasons for this.  Frightened Crew  First, amazingly enough, it turns out that not even\nyachting billionaires are prepared to spend the $100 million it\ntakes to build and maintain boats that meet Ellison\u2019s absurd\nspecifications. Second, it turns out that sailors don\u2019t\nnecessarily want to sail them. Last month, one of the boats\ncapsized, killing the British Olympic gold medalist Andrew\n\u201cBart\u201d Simpson. (Like \u201csail,\u201d the term \u201csailor\u201d may need\nupdating: These aren\u2019t guys in polo shirts and Sperry Top-Siders. America\u2019s Cup racers now wear padded body armor and\ncrash helmets and carry oxygen tanks.)  Of course, no story of a megalomaniacal billionaire\nimposing his will on a sport would be complete without the\nfleecing of taxpayers. The city of  San Francisco  has spent\nmillions to redevelop its waterfront for the race, even as it\nhas come to grips with the reality that Ellison\u2019s promises of\n\u201ceconomic activity\u201d around the cup were mostly just hype.\nRussell Coutts, his team\u2019s CEO, is now acknowledging that\nmistakes have been made, and suggesting that whoever wins this\nyear\u2019s cup will probably opt for smaller, safer boats.  That\u2019s a start, but it\u2019s hardly enough. In Silicon Valley,\nthey  like to say  that failure is a prerequisite for success. In\nyachting the lesson is slightly different: Innovation doesn\u2019t\nalways equal progress. Also, it may be possible for one man to\nsinglehandedly destroy the sport\u2019s oldest and most famous race.  So no hard feelings, Larry. But maybe yachting would be\nbetter off if you spent a little more alone time on that\nHawaiian  island of yours . In the meantime, the America\u2019s Cup can\ngo back to wooden yachts and Newport,  Rhode Island , where it\nbelongs. Hearing arguments in a case that may test their\nunderstanding of popular culture and emerging technologies,\nseveral justices today said they knew enough to worry about the\nimplications were they to uphold the law. They asked whether\nstates could similarly shield children from exposure to movie\nand comic-book violence and to depictions of smoking and\ndrinking.  \u201cCould you get rid of rap music?\u201d Justice  Sonia Sotomayor \nasked the state lawyer. \u201cHave you heard some of the lyrics of\nsome of the rap music?\u201d  A decision upholding the measure might lead to similar laws\naround the country -- and new compliance costs for the video\ngame industry, which has $10.5 billion in annual sales. Six\nother states have enacted similar measures, and all have been\nstruck down in court.  California says its law, which has never been enforced, is\na way of helping parents shield their children from games the\nindustry itself has said aren\u2019t appropriate for minors. The\nmeasure is being challenged by two industry trade groups.  Compared to Pornography  Governor  Arnold Schwarzenegger  and Attorney General  Jerry Brown  contend that violent games are akin to sexual materials,\nwhich the government can restrict to protect children. Violent\ngames are \u201cno less harmful to the development of minors\u201d than\npornography, the state\u2019s lawyer, Zackery Morazzini, argued.  The law wouldn\u2019t prevent parents from buying the games for\ntheir kids.  Before a packed courtroom in Washington, several justices\nsaid the law might be too vague to pass constitutional muster.\nOthers resisted the state\u2019s contention that sales of violent\ngames to children don\u2019t warrant First Amendment protection.  \u201cIt has never been understood that the freedom of speech\ndid not include portrayals of violence,\u201d Justice  Antonin Scalia \nsaid. \u201cYou\u2019re asking us to create a whole new prohibition which\nthe American people never ratified when they ratified the First\nAmendment.\u201d  Justice  Anthony Kennedy  voiced similar concerns, saying\nCalifornia was \u201casking us to go into an entirely new area where\nthere is no consensus\u201d by carving out a violence exception to\nthe First Amendment.  Passing Familiarity  Justices  Ruth Bader Ginsburg  and  Elena Kagan  also voiced\nconcerns about the law. Kagan showed at least a passing\nfamiliarity with the video game business, asking whether the law\nwould restrict  Midway Games Inc. \u2019s \u201cMortal Kombat.\u201d  That was an \u201ciconic game, which I am sure half of the\nclerks who work for us spent considerable amounts of time in\ntheir adolescence playing,\u201d Kagan said. Her remark prompted\nScalia to quip, \u201cI don\u2019t know what she\u2019s talking about.\u201d  At the same time, several justices made clear they wouldn\u2019t\npreclude the state from taking any steps to shield children from\nviolent games.  Justice  Stephen Breyer  asked the video game industry\u2019s\nlawyer, Paul Smith, whether the state could block children from\nbuying games that depicted \u201ctotal gratuitous torture.\u201d  \u201cIf that\u2019s what it restricted, why is that such a terrible\nthing?\u201d Breyer asked.  Exposed to Gore  Chief Justice  John Roberts  read a description of the video\ngame \u201cPostal II,\u201d which includes scenes of decapitation and\nsetting people on fire, and said American society has long tried\nto shield children from that type of gore.  \u201cWe protect children from that,\u201d he said. \u201cWe don\u2019t\nactively expose them to that.\u201d  Outside the court, a handful of opponents of the law\ndemonstrated on the sidewalk. Some carried signs accusing\nSchwarzenegger, who starred in action movies before turning to\npolitics, of being a hypocrite for defending the law.  The video game industry says the California law\naccomplishes little in light of a voluntary rating system\nalready used by virtually all game publishers and the largest\nretailers. The system assigns one of eight age-specific  ratings \nto games -- with M signifying mature, or 17 and older, and AO\nindicating adults only, or 18 and older.  Smith argued that California \u201chas not shown there is a\nproblem, let alone a compelling problem requiring regulation.\u201d  Industry Support  The industry has lined up dozens of supporters. The\n Entertainment Merchants Association , which represents the home\nentertainment industry, joined the Entertainment Software\nAssociation in pressing the suit. Their allies include  Microsoft\nCorp. , which makes the Xbox game console;  Activision Blizzard\nInc. , the largest video game publisher; and the Motion Picture\nAssociation of America.  Nine states, responding to what supporters of the law  say \nwas an intense industry lobbying effort, are attacking the law,\ntaking the unusual position of opposing a fellow state and\narguing for restrictions on their authority. Eleven other states\nare backing California.  The American Academy of Pediatrics  said  last year that\nexposure to violence in video games and other media \u201crepresents\na significant risk to the health of children and adolescents.\u201d\nThe California chapter of the group is supporting the state at\nthe Supreme Court.  Labeling Games  The California law, meant to take effect in 2006, would\nrequire violent video games sold in the state to be labeled and\nwould ban their sale or rental to anyone under 18. (YHOO)  Chief Executive Officer Marissa Mayer, projected to report the first annual sales gain in four years today, is being urged by investors to explain how she\u2019ll build on that growth by luring users and advertisers.  The shares have  surged  30 percent since Mayer was named CEO in July, reflecting confidence in her ability to engineer a turnaround after market-share losses slammed momentum at the largest U.S. Web portal. His mystique is such that other security professionals avoid using wireless Internet near him. MJM himself suggests that those he meets allay their paranoia by taking batteries out of their mobile phones.  MJM -- Martin J. Muench -- is the developer of Andover, U.K.-based Gamma Group\u2019s FinFisher intrusion software, which he sells to police and spy agencies around the world for monitoring computers and smartphones to intercept Skype calls, peer through Web cameras and record keystrokes.  In the past year, the hacker-turned-executive has himself been under attack as the 2011 Arab Spring uprisings unravelled the cloak of secrecy he\u2019d operated behind.  FinFisher\u2019s once-elusive FinSpy tool has been exposed targeting activists from the Persian Gulf kingdom of Bahrain; decoded for the first time by computer-virus hunters; placed under export control by the U.K.; and traced to countries with poor human rights records, such as  Turkmenistan  in Central Asia.  As evidence mounts that repressive regimes routinely use surveillance gear to track and capture dissidents, FinSpy has been singled out as one of the most  invasive  weapons. The attention has subjected Muench to death threats, he says, and government scrutiny.  It\u2019s against this backdrop -- which Muench, 31, calls a \u201cwitch hunt\u201d -- that he\u2019s decided to explain himself, opening his Munich offices to a journalist.  \u2018Personified Evil\u2019  \u201cI\u2019m the personified evil,\u201d Muench says of his role as the face of FinFisher, which he defends as a tool for catching pedophiles and terrorists. Muench, who was born in northern  Germany  and grew up in a town (population 800) that he won\u2019t name out of concern for his family\u2019s security, started hacking at around age 13. As managing director of Gamma\u2019s German-based unit,  Gamma International  GmbH, he\u2019s developed FinFisher spyware since 2007, and leads its marketing.  \u201cThe product helps to catch serious criminals and helps to save lives,\u201d says Muench, who stands about 1.9 meters tall (almost 6 feet 3 inches), has close-cropped hair and is dressed in a black, collared shirt, distressed blue jeans and black shoes. He won\u2019t provide examples of crimes solved, saying it could jeopardize clients\u2019 methods. \u201cSo we have to live with the bad guy image,\u201d he says.  Other units of Gamma Group provide intelligence training and sell surveillance vans, wireless microphone systems and  interrogation rooms  outfitted with audio and video capabilities. The company is controlled by members of a British family, the Nelsons.  Transforming Surveillance  Of Gamma\u2019s products, FinFisher has become the flashpoint. It represents the leading edge of a largely unregulated trade in cybertools that is transforming surveillance, making it more intrusive as it reaches across borders and spies into peoples\u2019 digital devices, whether in their living rooms or back pockets.  A Bloomberg News investigation this year into the abuses of intrusion products and the threats of computer espionage has shown how technologies from companies such as Gamma and its competitor, Milan-based HackingTeam, represent the next step in a digital arms race between governments and the people they watch.  Political dissidents who discovered FinSpy trying to infect their e-mail inboxes heap scorn on Muench for what they say is complicity in rights abuses.  \u201cI have little respect for this man for his role in the violation of my  privacy rights  and for risking the work we are doing,\u201d says Ala\u2019a Shehabi, 31, a U.K.-born democracy advocate and economist hit by FinSpy in Bahrain this April and May.  Misunderstood Spyware  Muench responds that he and his spyware have been misunderstood, and that any product can be used for harm. \u201cSo can a can of fizzy drink or a car battery,\u201d he says.  To drive that point home, Gamma Group\u2019s communications director, Robert Partridge, points to a glass bottle of Coca- Cola in the middle of a table in the company\u2019s conference room. Carbonated beverages, he explains, could be very painful when poured in the noses of interrogation subjects who have been turned upside down.  Muench says Gamma acts responsibly by only selling FinFisher to governments and obeying the export laws of the U.S., the U.K. and Germany. After he sells a system, it\u2019s out of his hands, says Muench.  \u2018No Control\u2019  \u201cWe have no control; once it\u2019s out there it\u2019s basically with the country,\u201d he says during the five-hour interview that veered from a product demonstration in Gamma\u2019s conference room to lunch at a Bavarian  restaurant  serving specialties from Munich\u2019s  Oktoberfest  tents to getting lost driving his company\u2019s black BMW 528i sedan back to the office. \u201cThat\u2019s why we check, \u2018Are they bad guys?\u2019 before we deliver it.\u201d He doesn\u2019t reveal which governments have purchased FinFisher.  Muench, whose only formal education after high school was a part-time university course in jazz piano, is trying to set the record straight about himself and his company after a blistering year.  In May,  Bloomberg News  obtained spyware that had been sent to activists from Bahrain and gave copies to a San Francisco- based security expert, Morgan Marquis-Boire, for analysis. Marquis-Boire dissected the samples and found they were Muench\u2019s product. His research,  published  by the University of Toronto Munk School of Global Affairs\u2019 Citizen Lab, and Bloomberg News stories about it appeared in July.  Also in July, London-based Privacy International, which monitors surveillance abuses, informed the British government it planned to file a lawsuit to force regulation of surveillance technology sales, including those of FinFisher.  Targeting Dissidents  The next month, following the disclosures that the software had targeted dissidents, the U.K. government informed Gamma it must obtain export licenses to sell FinSpy outside the European Union.  At the same time, researchers including Claudio Guarnieri of Boston-based security risk-assessment company  Rapid7 ; Bill Marczak, a computer science doctoral candidate at the  University of California  Berkeley; and Marquis-Boire, whose day job is working as a security engineer at Google Inc., found computers that appeared to be command servers for FinSpy in at least 15 countries.  They also  documented  FinSpy\u2019s ability to take over mobile phones -- turning on microphones, tracking locations and monitoring e-mails.  The pressure has continued to build.  On Oct. 12, U.S. law enforcement officials  warned  smartphone users to protect themselves against FinFisher, calling it malware, or malicious software.  Government Warning  \u201cFinFisher is a spyware capable of taking over the components of a mobile device,\u201d the Internet Crime Complaint Center, a partnership between the  Federal Bureau  of Investigation and National White Collar Crime Center, said in a Website alert to the public. \u201cFinFisher can be easily transmitted to a Smartphone when the user visits a specific web link or opens a text message masquerading as a system update.\u201d  Muench has put himself forward as Gamma\u2019s point man on the issue, as Gamma\u2019s controlling shareholders, the Nelsons, remain in the background. He says they act only as investors, providing money and customer contacts for FinFisher.  The family declined requests to be interviewed for this story through Partridge, who acts as a spokesman for both Gamma and the Nelsons.  Before joining the Gamma group of companies 13 years ago, Partridge says, family patriarch  William Nelson , now 80, held a half ownership of Wallop Holdings Ltd., a pyrotechnics and defense company that made flares, riot-control equipment and smoke generators.  Iraq Questions  Questions that arose from Nelson\u2019s time at Wallop, also based in Andover in southern  England , foreshadowed the current FinFisher controversy.  Wallop twice denied published reports that it may have had dealings with Saddam Hussein\u2019s  Iraq . In one instance, the company said it had rejected an Iraqi request for rocket launcher samples in 1984. Then, in the 2003 invasion of Iraq, Scottish troops found grenades in boxes outside Basra bearing Wallop\u2019s name. That led Wallop to disclose that it had sold smoke grenades to  Kuwait  in 1986, and to suggest that the weapons must have been seized by Iraqi troops during their earlier occupation of the neighboring country, according to news reports at the time.  \u201cWallop Industries at no time supplied  Saddam Hussein  or Iraq,\u201d Gamma spokesman Partridge says. The items found in Iraq bore codes that matched the Kuwaiti sale, and Wallop never made rocket launchers, he says.  Surveillance Shift  Nelson sold his stake when new owners purchased Wallop in September 1987 in a deal that valued the company at 7.6 million pounds ($12 million), according to a company announcement.  After the sale, Nelson retired until 1999, when he joined Gamma, which had been founded in  Beirut  in 1990 as a trading company dealing in general and electrical goods, Partridge says. Today, under Nelson family control, the U.K. and German companies that comprise what is now Gamma Group specialize in surveillance and security.  The transformation shows why governments seeking to protect human rights must modernize their export controls to keep up with changing technology, says Ben Scott, a former policy advisor for innovation to U.S. Secretary of State  Hillary Clinton .  \u201cShipping guns and grenades over an ocean leaves a physical trail in a way that downloading software does not,\u201d says Scott, senior advisor to the Washington-based Open Technology Institute, a policy group that promotes affordable and universal communications networks and studies the social impact of new technologies.  Expanding Business  As Gamma expanded, it sold governments eavesdropping gear for intercepting communications, Muench says. In recent years, such passive surveillance, which includes phone tapping, became less effective as Internet communications boomed.  \u201cMore customers came and complained, basically saying \u2018Oh, we can\u2019t get this and that and that, so we need to find a way to intercept,\u2019\u201d Muench says.  By 2007, Muench had gained recognition as a developer of  BackTrack , one of the best-known free tool kits for computer penetration testing.  That year, Gamma approached him and, according to Muench, said, \u2019Listen we need professional government tools to face these kinds of challenges.\u2019\u201d He made the jump to corporate life.  Muench built the German business from a  home office  to a unit that now employs about 30 people on the second floor of a modern building with floor-to-ceiling windows in a neighborhood filled with technology companies. He owns 15 percent of the German-based Gamma International, he says.  Tables Turn  Muench stayed under the radar until the Arab Spring, which exposed surveillance technologies used by regimes across the  Middle East , turned the tables on him. As the purveyor of technology for secret stalking, he has himself become the hunted.  Muench and FinFisher first came under scrutiny after a sales pitch made to Egyptian state security for a system priced at 388,604 euros ($499,084) was  uncovered  following that country\u2019s February 2011 revolution. A sale was never completed, Muench says.  The secret FinFisher software became an object of fascination within the virus-hunting world. In March 2011, Mikko Hypponen, chief research officer at Helsinki-based data security company F-Secure Oyj, vowed that if a copy were ever found, he\u2019d write anti-virus protection against it.  Exposing FinSpy  From then, the attention didn\u2019t let up. In December, anti- secrecy website WikiLeaks posted Gamma promotional videos showing how police could plant FinSpy on a target\u2019s computer.  This year, the Citizen Lab and Bloomberg News reports about Bahrain on July 25 started the clock on a race between Muench, who needed to quickly rewrite his software, and the researchers and security companies, who began tracing where FinSpy was in use and crafting protection for its potential targets.  \u201cIt\u2019s a cat and mouse game,\u201d says Muench, who was in Brasilia that day pitching FinFisher at the Latin American installment of the  ISS World  surveillance tradeshow, known as the Wiretapper\u2019s Ball.  While Muench says the samples analyzed were demonstration versions, and not the operational software used by clients, they were close enough to require modifications, he says. Changing characteristics of the product would make it harder to detect by anyone who had seen the Bahraini samples. For the first time ever, he found himself in a position of having to put the company\u2019s emergency plan in action.  Emergency Plan  Colleagues in Munich opened a safe (the combination is \u201c666,\u201d he jokes) and removed a hard drive about the size of a large box of matches, which contained a modified version of the spyware, Muench says.  \u201cWe always have a spare, just in case,\u201d he says.  It took two days for programmers to prepare the new software for release on FinSpy systems around the world, and to inform customers of the update, he says.  To respond to the critics, Muench says he wants to demonstrate that FinSpy is a responsible product that includes features that make the data it gathers suitable for presentation in a court of law.  In the Munich conference room, where cabinets display black, plastic suitcases filled with cyber-interception gear, he fires up FinSpy on his Apple laptop, which projects what he\u2019s doing onto a screen at the front of the room. The  console  that intelligence agents use to monitor infected computers comes to life, in blue, black and white.  Live Demonstration  \u201cUnderstand, I can\u2019t show you 100 percent, but I\u2019ll show you most,\u201d Muench says.  He moves the arrow on his computer across the top of the screen, where tabs indicate two choices: \u201cPC Targets\u201d and \u201cMobile Targets.\u201d The targets for the live demonstration are Gamma computers used for such purposes, Muench says.  Clicking into the PC tab, he brings up a page filled with line after line of names and flags representing countries around the globe. The colors of  Brazil ,  Indonesia ,  Malaysia ,  Singapore  and the U.K. and several other nations are represented.  \u201cWhat we have here is an overview of PC targets that are currently infected,\u201d Muench says.  He clicks into one line and pulls up the transcript of a Skype text chat. Another click takes him to a recorded Skype call, on which he points to the timestamps. If the audio file is edited, the software will indicate how many seconds have been cut -- a safeguard against misuse, he says.  He then switches to \u201cMobile Targets,\u201d revealing a separate list, this time of handsets.  FinSpy Mobile can infect almost every kind of device, including Apple Inc.\u2019s iPhones and smartphones running Google\u2019s Android or Microsoft Corp.\u2019s Windows systems, according to a  pamphlet  Muench provides.  Asked if the publicity he\u2019s gotten for such surveillance powers inspires mistrust in the people he meets, Muench says he\u2019s given up on a social life for now. \u201cIf I meet a girl and she Googles my name, she\u2019ll never call back,\u201d he says. (MSFT)  used aggressive international tax maneuvers to avoid billions of dollars in taxes over the past three years.  The committee memo, released for a hearing today in Washington, said Microsoft used transactions with subsidiaries in  Puerto Rico , Ireland,  Singapore  and  Bermuda  to save at least $6.5 billion in taxes. The committee also revealed that  Hewlett- Packard Co. (HP)  has used a series of short-term internal loans that allowed the company to tap its offshore cash for domestic operations without paying taxes, according to the memo.  Senator  Carl Levin , a Michigan Democrat and chairman of the  Permanent Subcommittee  on Investigations, didn\u2019t accuse the companies of acting illegally, though he said he was \u201chighly dubious\u201d that HP was in compliance with the tax law.  Such financial maneuvers \u201cmay be in your temporary interest as a corporation,\u201d Levin told Bill Sample, Microsoft\u2019s corporate vice president for worldwide tax, at the hearing. \u201cIt increases your profits and reduces your taxes, but there\u2019s a heavy cost to the  United States ,\u201d Levin said.  Levin and the panel\u2019s top Republican,  Tom Coburn  of  Oklahoma , sent the memo to committee members.  Coburn described the moves as \u201cproperly legal  tax avoidance \u201d by companies taking advantage of a  tax code  that needs an overhaul.  \u201cOur report is about the symptoms of the disease, not the real disease,\u201d he said at the hearing.  Global Business  The report describes the ways companies can move profits outside of the country and keep them there to avoid U.S. taxes.  \u201cWe comply with U.S. and foreign tax laws,\u201d Sample said at the hearing. \u201cThat is not to say that the rules cannot be improved.\u201d  U.S.-based companies owe U.S. taxes on profits they earn around the world. They receive credits against that liability for taxes paid to foreign governments, and they don\u2019t have to pay U.S. taxes until they bring the money home.  The gap between the 35 percent U.S. corporate tax rate and lower tax rates in the rest of the world gives companies an incentive to book profits outside of the U.S. Levin said technology companies can easily move intangible assets such as patents outside of the U.S. with intra-company transactions at low prices.  Hard to Value  Those intangible assets are hard to value, and disputes about the correct price for such intra-company transactions are common. When foreign subsidiaries in low-tax countries pay too little, either up front or over time, they can get annual profits paid to them out of proportion to what they paid.  \u201cThe high-tech industry is probably the number-one user of these offshore entities to transfer intellectual property,\u201d Levin said.  In questioning Sample, Levin outlined how Microsoft uses transactions within the company, all with its own money, to assign about 47 percent of its income from U.S. sales to a Puerto Rico subsidiary, and how it shifts some income from around the world to a Bermuda subsidiary that has no employees.  Levin\u2019s investigators sent letters to companies and used subpoenas to get information that companies don\u2019t typically disclose. He said they focused on Microsoft and HP to show patterns that are common across U.S. companies.  IRS Enforcement  Levin attributed such tax avoidance in part to a lack of enforcement by the  Internal Revenue Service , gaps in IRS regulations and \u201cloopholes\u201d created by Congress.  Levin emphasized HP\u2019s use of loans to tap its offshore cash. The loans, the report said, are structured to comply with the letter of tax rules that allow short-term loans from subsidiaries in  Belgium  and the  Cayman Islands  to the parent company.  Although long-term loans would trigger tax consequences, the alternating-loan program provided a potential continuous stream of money for HP.  The memo, citing company documents, said as much as $5 billion was available to the parent company in 2008 and that the company borrowed from $6 billion to $9 billion in 2010. HP holds $29.1 billion in untaxed earnings outside the U.S., according to the company\u2019s most recent  annual filing .  Fiscal Calendars  IRS rules allow companies to take loans from foreign subsidiaries without tax consequences within a given fiscal quarter. The Belgian and Cayman subsidiaries have different fiscal calendars.  The company developed a schedule that allowed loans from the Belgian subsidiary within its fiscal quarters, and then loans from the Cayman subsidiary with a calendar that covered the periods when the Belgian subsidiary was crossing from one quarter to the next.  Lester Ezrati, a senior vice president for tax at HP, said at the hearing that the company did have gaps in its borrowing from the foreign subsidiaries. He also said the IRS didn\u2019t raise concerns when it examined the loans during a recent audit.  HP has fully complied with U.S. tax law, the company said in a statement.  \u201cWe are disappointed to see what appears to be a politically motivated attack on one of America\u2019s largest employers,\u201d it said. While every company would no doubt use this cash\ndifferently, the windfall could fund a return of capital to\nshareholders through increased dividends and share buybacks. Or\nit could be used to repay debt, fund capital expenditures or\nmake strategic acquisitions.  How the companies would deploy the money doesn\u2019t matter.\nThe important thing is that the cash would be put to work. So\nwhy hasn\u2019t this already happened?  The answer is clear: U.S. tax policies penalize the\nrepatriation of so-called foreign-source income, essentially the\nprofits earned by foreign subsidiaries of American corporations.\nThis cash pile isn\u2019t being hoarded or held on the sidelines, as\nmany pundits have suggested; rather, it is being kept offshore\nby our own tax structure.  Unlike most countries, the U.S. taxes the profits earned\noverseas by its corporations. The federal tax code then defers\nthe tax on the non-domestic profits until the corporation brings\nthose profits into the U.S. Since repatriating these profits\nmeans incurring a tax of as much as 35 percent, most overseas\nprofits remain offshore.  Given the weak economy and the debate over the need for\nadditional stimulus and further quantitative easing by the\nFederal Reserve, bringing home hundreds of billions, possibly\ntrillions, of dollars should be a priority. Although most\ncompanies would retain some overseas cash for their non-U.S.\noperations, clearly most companies have far more cash abroad\nthan is needed.  Largest Stimulus  Repatriation on such a scale would in effect be the largest\neconomic stimulus ever. Not only would the cash go right where\nit is needed the most -- the private sector -- but it wouldn\u2019t\nadd a single dollar to the  federal budget deficit . Actually, the\neconomic growth created through the use of this cash would\ngenerate billions in additional tax revenue.  Most successful U.S. multinational companies face the\ndilemma: Keep the cash overseas or bring the profits home and\npay the tax bill.  This isn\u2019t a merely theoretical debate about tax policy.\nLast month Microsoft Corp. said it would sell as much as $6\nbillion in debt to fund dividend payments even though it has\nabout $37 billion in cash and short-term investments on its\nbooks. Since most of its cash is overseas, borrowing makes\nbetter economic sense because the cost of borrowing is far lower\nthan the tax.  Cash on Sidelines  Microsoft isn\u2019t alone.  Cisco Systems Inc. , whose Chief\nExecutive Officer  John Chambers  is a vocal critic of U.S. tax\npolicy, has an estimated $30 billion in cash outside the U.S.\nDell Inc., Hewlett\u00adPackard Co., International Business Machines\nCorp. and Intel Corp. are other leading tech companies with\nsignificant cash overseas. Pharmaceutical giants Johnson &\nJohnson, Merck & Co., and Pfizer Inc. also have billions in un-\nrepatriated foreign profits.  A tax holiday on returning overseas cash isn\u2019t without\nprecedent. In 2004, the Homeland Investment Act reduced the tax\nrate on these profits to 5.25 percent from 35 percent. Granted a\nlower tax rate, U.S. corporations responded by shipping back an\nestimated $315 billion in 2004.  Critics of any reduction in taxes on repatriated overseas\nprofits, even a temporary one, argue that to do so would be\nrewarding companies for outsourcing U.S. jobs. Not surprisingly,\nlabor unions and their allies are the leading opponents of a tax\nholiday. In their view, overseas profits should be subject to\nU.S. tax even if those profits are never repatriated.  Obama\u2019s Support  President  Barack Obama  supports that position. The current\ntax provisions provide a loophole that \u201chas actually given\nbillions of dollars in tax breaks that encourage companies to\ncreate jobs and profits in other countries,\u201d according to the\npresident. Key members of Congress agree with the president.  This rhetoric is fueled by a broad mischaracterization of\nthe purpose and effect of international growth and investment by\nU.S. companies. Unions and their allies in Congress see all such\nmoves as simply outsourcing American jobs.  While that may be the case in a small percentage of\nsituations, the reality is different. Rather than weaken the\neconomy, successful multinational companies have been engines of\ngrowth. As Harvard Business School professor Mihir Desai has\nnoted, when U.S. businesses \u201cexpand abroad they expand at\nhome.\u201d  Companies that prosper internationally expand their\nresearch, development, management, human resources, information\ntechnology, marketing and financial teams, and most of those new\njobs wind up right here in the U.S.  Strings Attached  In fairness, not all labor leaders oppose lower taxes on\nrepatriation of overseas profits.  Andy Stern , president emeritus\nof the  Service Employees International Union , has proposed\ncutting the tax on repatriated overseas profits to 5.25 percent.\nThere\u2019s a big string attached: The tax revenue raised would fund\nprograms designed to create jobs in the U.S.  Others who oppose a tax holiday point to a  study  by the\nNational Bureau of Economic Research that showed a large\npercentage of the funds repatriated in 2004 were used for\ndividends and share buybacks.  While those findings are probably accurate, this misses the\npoint. Pumping new cash into the economy will have a positive\nimpact. Even if companies simply return the capital to their\nshareholders, that is a positive outcome since investors will\neither spend the cash or reinvest it.  Tax Holiday  Former Clinton Undersecretary of Commerce  Robert J. Shapiro \nagrees, concluding that \u201cthe repatriation of overseas profits\nwould certainly be in the economy\u2019s interest.\u201d  Amid a stagnant economy, high  unemployment , and ballooning\nfederal and state budget deficits, Congress and the president\nneed to eliminate or sharply reduce the taxes on the\nrepatriation of profits earned around the world.  With an era of slow growth here and rapid expansion in\nChina, India and Brazil, our tax policy needs to recognize that\nan increasing share of corporate profits will be earned outside\nthe country. U.S. tax policy should create incentives for\ncompanies to seek growth and expansion around the world,\nwherever and whenever those opportunities arise -- the sooner,\nthe better.  ( Frank Aquila  is a partner at the law firm Sullivan &\nCromwell. A version of this column appears on BusinessWeek.com.\nThe opinions expressed are his own.) (MDT) , the world\u2019s biggest maker of heart-rhythm\ndevices.  Medtronic does more than half of its $16 billion in annual\nsales of pacemakers, defibrillators and other devices in the\nU.S. It manufactures the equipment at this facility, legacy of a\ndefunct U.S. tax break designed to encourage investment on the\npoverty-stricken island. Yet, Medtronic credits the income to a\nmailbox in a Cayman Islands office building.  This isn\u2019t what the  U.S. Congress  had in mind when it did\naway with the federal tax credit for companies\u2019 Puerto Rican\nprofits. The break was attacked by Republicans and Democrats as\ntoo expensive, and as of 2006, it ended. So Medtronic and other\ncompanies found a solution: They are avoiding taxes by moving\nthose profits into shell subsidiaries in havens such as the\n Cayman Islands ,  Switzerland  and the Netherlands.  \u201cBy aggressively shifting income to offshore affiliates,\ncompanies appear to be getting U.S. tax benefits that are equal\nto or greater than the ones they did under the old Puerto Rico\ntax break,\u201d said Stephen E. Shay, former deputy assistant\nsecretary for international tax affairs at the  U.S. Treasury \nDepartment under President  Barack Obama , now a professor at\n Harvard Law School . \u201cThat almost certainly was not the intent\nof the repeal.\u201d  Less Than Half  The profits that used to benefit from the Puerto Rico\ncredit are now part of a mountain of tax-deferred offshore\nearnings totaling at least $1.38 trillion, according to a May\nreport by JPMorgan Chase & Co. Companies including  Apple Inc. (AAPL) ,\nGoogle Inc., Microsoft Corp. and Pfizer Inc. are lobbying\nCongress for a tax holiday to bring those profits home. Without\nsuch a break, any cash brought back to the U.S. would be taxed\nat the federal income-tax rate of 35 percent, with a credit for\nforeign income taxes already paid. (To see other articles from\nBloomberg\u2019s coverage of how corporations avoid taxes, click\n here .)  Medtronic, based in  Minneapolis , paid income taxes in\nfiscal 2011 at a rate of less than half that -- 16.8 percent.\nThat\u2019s also about half Medtronic\u2019s rate under the old Puerto\nRican tax credit.  As the Obama administration and congressional Democrats\ntake aim at tax breaks for everything from corporate jets to\nprivate-equity manager compensation, the aftermath of the Puerto\nRico credit\u2019s repeal shows just how difficult ending such breaks\ncan be -- and how determined well-funded tax planners and their\ncorporate clients are to create new ones.  \u2018Extraordinary\u2019 Profit  Now the  Internal Revenue Service  wants to collect some of\nthose lost taxes. It has identified as a top audit priority the\nsophisticated strategies U.S. companies used to shift income\nthat once benefited from the old tax break in Puerto Rico.  In a memo sent to IRS auditors in February 2007, the agency\ncalled profit levels \u201cextraordinary\u201d in many of the offshore\nunits created to take over for the subsidiaries that got the\nPuerto Rican break. In many cases, those units are generating\n\u201can inordinate amount of the profits, i.e., amounts in excess\nof what would be expected, based upon activity,\u201d according to\nthe IRS memo.  The agency is in a $958 million fight with Medtronic in\nU.S. Tax Court over how it reorganized its Puerto Rican\noperations, as well as a $452 million court dispute with Guidant\nLLC, now a part of medical device maker  Boston Scientific (BSX)  Corp.,\nover a similar move.  Transfer Pricing   Companies legally move profits offshore using \u201ctransfer\npricing,\u201d the system of allocating income between units in\ndifferent countries. This lets corporations like Medtronic say\nthat profit from a $5,000 pacemaker was earned in the Cayman\nIslands, even though the device was manufactured in Puerto Rico\nand sold in, say, Houston. The company has accumulated $14.9\nbillion in income allocated to its foreign subsidiaries on which\nit hasn\u2019t paid any U.S. income tax, according to its most recent\nannual report.  The profit shifting that can stem from transfer pricing\ncosts the U.S. government an estimated $90 billion a year,\naccording to  Kimberly Clausing , an economics professor at Reed\nCollege in  Portland ,  Oregon . That\u2019s about double the U.S.\nDepartment of Homeland Security\u2019s annual budget and dwarfs the\nrevenue loss from the various tax breaks currently under\nscrutiny. By comparison, changing the so-called carried-interest\nprovision that allows private-equity managers to pay taxes at a\nrate of 15 percent on most of their compensation would only\nraise about $2 billion per year for the federal government,\naccording to the Joint Committee on Taxation.  Cat and Mouse  Under U.S. transfer-pricing rules, offshore subsidiaries\nthat license rights from their parent companies are supposed to\npay an \u201carm\u2019s-length\u201d price, or what an unrelated company\nwould pay. Such transactions often involve the transfer of\nintellectual property rights and other so-called intangibles,\nfor which real world comparisons can be difficult to find. The\nIRS objects when offshore subsidiaries pay their parent company\na price that the agency claims is too low, which shifts taxable\nprofit out of the U.S.  \u201cWe are confident that Medtronic has met the requirement\nin establishing arm\u2019s-length pricing on all intercompany\ntransactions,\u201d said Amy von Walter, a spokeswoman for the\ncompany. She declined to comment on specifics of the IRS\ndispute.  Medtronic says in court papers that its offshore unit paid\nthe correct amount for rights moved out of the U.S.  The story of the Puerto Rico tax credit and its aftermath\nillustrates the cat-and mouse game companies and the U.S.\ngovernment play when Congress tries to close tax breaks. In this\ncase, even bipartisan support didn\u2019t stop companies from quickly\nfinding a new legal way to avoid paying taxes.  \u2018Cautionary Tale\u2019  \u201cIt is a cautionary tale,\u201d said Greg Ballentine, an\neconomist in  Washington  with Charles River Associates, a\nconsulting firm that advises companies on transfer pricing.\n\u201cThere is a very active and aggressive community of tax\nadvisers out there and they respond to whatever changes are\nmade, congressional or regulatory. So the IRS is frequently\nseveral steps behind.\u201d  Puerto Rico became a haven for the manufacturing operations\nof U.S. companies in the 1960s, when the federal government used\nvarious tax incentives to combat poverty and unemployment on the\nisland which now has almost 4 million residents.  In 1976, Congress added a tax credit that effectively\nexempted from federal income taxes the profits that U.S.\ncompanies attributed to Puerto Rico. The combination of the\nbreak, proximity to the U.S. and plentiful industrial sites\nprompted multinational companies to flock to the island, with\nmedical-device and pharmaceutical makers leading the way,\nincluding Pfizer,  Eli Lilly & Co. (LLY)  and Merck & Co.  Tax Holidays  Companies separately negotiated tax holidays from the\nPuerto Rican government -- eager to attract jobs to stanch\n unemployment  -- to be largely exempt from the island\u2019s\nequivalent of a national corporate income tax, often paying at\nrates in the low-to mid-single digits.  By the mid 1990s, critics led by Texas Representative Bill Archer, then the Republican chairman of the House Ways and Means\nCommittee, attacked the break as too expensive, costing the U.S.\nabout $3 billion a year. In some industries, the tax subsidy was\ncosting the U.S. as much as $72,000 per job, according to a\nstudy by the federal agency now called the Government\nAccountability Office. After a lobbying battle in 1996, the tax\nbreak was repealed, with a 10-year transition period for\ncompanies already benefiting from the credit.  \u201cIt pulled the rug from under our feet,\u201d said William\nRiefkohl, executive vice president of the  Puerto Rico\nManufacturers Association .  Raising $11 Billion  Archer, now a lobbyist for accounting firm\nPricewaterhouseCoopers LLP, which represents multinationals on\ntax issues, said: \u201cWe were determined to let everybody know we\nwere going to close corporate tax loopholes that clearly stood\nout as being appropriate for repeal.\u201d  The Joint Committee on Taxation projected that eliminating\nthe break would raise close to $11 billion for the U.S. Treasury\nover the next decade.  \u201cThere was certainly an expectation the companies would\nreact\u201d after the repeal, said Daniel M. Berman, a former deputy\ninternational tax counsel at the Treasury Department at the time\nof the dispute over the tax break. He is now a professor at\nBoston University\u2019s School of Law.  Berman was right. After losing the legislative fight, the\ntax-avoidance industry of accountants and lawyers sprung into\naction. While manufacturing facilities stayed in Puerto Rico,\ndozens of companies simply shifted the ownership of those assets\nto newly created subsidiaries in  tax havens  around the world.  Guidant Assets  Guidant, the medical-device maker once part of  Eli Lilly \nand now owned by Boston Scientific, transferred assets formerly\nowned by its Puerto Rico subsidiary to a unit in the\nNetherlands, records show.  Guidant says in its Tax Court filings that no taxes were\ndue on the transfer of assets overseas and that intracompany\nroyalties were priced properly. A spokeswoman for Boston\nScientific, the second-biggest heart-device maker, didn\u2019t reply\nto requests for comment.  One of the leading strategists behind the new tax maneuvers\nwas Ernest Aud Jr., a veteran international tax lawyer for\naccounting firm Ernst & Young LLP in  Chicago . Aud advised U.S.\nmultinationals on how to turn the potential tax jam into an\nasset.  \u201cI was probably the architect of a number of the early\nconversions,\u201d said Aud, now retired from Ernst & Young. \u201cWe\nwere the ones that made companies aware that there was an\nopportunity -- underscore opportunity -- to maybe do better\nunder\u201d the new arrangement than under the old Puerto Rico\nbreak.  Heart-Rhythm Equipment  Among those taking advantage of that opportunity was\nMedtronic. The corporation has grown from a medical repair shop\nfounded by a Minneapolis engineer in his garage to become the\nworld\u2019s biggest maker of heart-rhythm equipment. It also makes\nan array of other devices, including spinal technologies and\ninsulin- delivery systems.  Like dozens of pharmaceutical and medical-device makers\nthat flocked to Puerto Rico, attracted by the various tax\nbenefits, Medtronic opened its first factory in 1974 and\nexpanded twice after that.  Grand Cayman Subsidiary  In August 2001 -- about four years before the tax credit\nwould disappear for good -- Medtronic established a subsidiary\nin Grand Cayman, listing an address at an office now used by\nIntertrust Group Holding SA, a corporate-services provider that\nhelps companies establish shell subsidiaries in tax havens.  On paper, Medtronic transferred ownership of its Puerto\nRican assets to this new Cayman unit, called Medtronic Puerto\nRico Operations Co. The Cayman subsidiary is owned by a Dutch\narm, which is in turn owned by a Swiss subsidiary, court filings\nshow. In 2006, Medtronic transferred some of the Dutch company\u2019s\nassets to the unit in Zug, Switzerland, a popular destination\nfor companies seeking Swiss tax holidays.  The new Cayman entity also entered into an arrangement to\npay royalties to the U.S. parent to use intellectual property\nand other rights covering devices it manufactures in Puerto Rico\nand then sells back into the U.S. The IRS contends that\nMedtronic\u2019s Cayman unit underpaid for those rights, court papers\nshow, shifting offshore income from U.S. sales.  Offshore Profits  Taxes on such offshore profits are typically deferred\nindefinitely until the companies decide to bring the earnings\nback to the U.S.  Medtronic\u2019s tax rate has plummeted. In 1995, the year\nbefore congress abolished the Puerto Rico credit, the break cut\n4.2 percentage points off the company\u2019s effective tax rate,\nhelping to lower it to 33.5 percent. By 2011, Medtronic\u2019s tax\nrate was down to half that.  Overall, the savings from the low-taxed overseas income\nboosted Medtronic\u2019s net income in fiscal 2011 by 30 percent, to\n$3.1 billion, based on tax disclosures in the company\u2019s most\nrecent annual report.  The company has benefited from a \u201ctax incentive grant\u201d in\nPuerto Rico, according to the annual report, but doesn\u2019t\ndisclose that rate. Owning its Puerto Rican assets through a\nCayman shell company lets Medtronic move cash around the world\nwithout being subject to a Puerto Rican withholding tax,\naccording to two people familiar with such structures.  \u201cThe government underestimated how sophisticated and\naggressive multinationals would be in shifting truckloads of\nprofits out of the U.S.,\u201d Harvard\u2019s Shay said. Kanovsky and Bharara declined to identify lenders that\nmight face claims.  \u201cWe could see another potential big negative for the\nindustry out of this,\u201d said  Paul Miller , a former examiner for\nthe Federal Reserve Bank of Philadelphia and an analyst with FBR\nCapital Markets in Arlington, Virginia. \u201cIt\u2019s going to be a\ncontinued earnings drag on the industry.\u201d  Deutsche Bank said it will \u201cvigorously\u201d fight the\ngovernment\u2019s allegations.  \u201cWe believe the claims against MortgageIT and Deutsche\nBank are unreasonable and unfair,\u201d Renee Calabro, a spokeswoman\nfor the Frankfurt-based company, said by e-mail. \u201cClose to 90\npercent of the activity covered by the DOJ allegations happened\nprior to Deutsche Bank\u2019s acquisition of MortgageIT.\u201d  Deutsche Bank and MortgageIT concealed problem loans\nthrough \u201cegregious\u201d violations of HUD rules for analyzing the\nincome and creditworthiness of borrowers, according to the\nJustice Department\u2019s complaint filed yesterday in Manhattan\nfederal court. MortgageIT endorsed more than 39,000 loans for\nFHA insurance after 1999, making them \u201chighly marketable for\nresale,\u201d the U.S. said. Of those, 12,500 defaulted.  The Justice Department didn\u2019t file criminal charges or\nidentify employees.  The case is U.S. v. Deutsche Bank AG, 11-cv-2976, U.S.\nDistrict Court, Southern District of  New York  (Manhattan). Lawsuits\/Pretrial  Ex-Goldman Programmer Aleynikov Denied Freedom During Appeal  Goldman Sachs Group Inc. (GS)  computer programmer Sergey\nAleynikov won\u2019t be freed from jail while he appeals a 97-month\nprison term for stealing the firm\u2019s computer trading code, a\nfederal appeals court ruled.  Aleynikov was convicted by a jury in December of violating\nthe Economic Espionage Act and the Interstate Transportation of\nStolen Property Act. His lawyer,  Kevin Marino , told a panel of\nthree appeals court judges for the 2nd U.S. Circuit Court of\nAppeals that there was a substantial likelihood his client\u2019s\nconviction would be overturned.  On his last day of work at New York-based Goldman Sachs in\nJune 2009, Aleynikov uploaded hundreds of thousands of lines of\nsource code from the firm\u2019s trading system, the U.S. said. He\nthen circumvented Goldman Sachs\u2019s security system, sent the code\nto an outside server in Germany, compressed and encrypted it and\nlater took it with him to a meeting with new employers in\nChicago.  \u201cThere is a substantial question as to whether stealing\ncomputer source code violates either of these statutes,\u201d Marino\nsaid. \u201cGoldman Sachs never intended to place its high-frequency\ntrading system into the stream of commerce.\u201d  Marino argued during the trial that Aleynikov only took\nopen-source code he had written at Goldman Sachs and that\nnothing he took was proprietary. U.S. District Judge  Denise\nCote , who presided over the trial, rejected the argument, and in\nMarch, ordered Aleynikov jailed pending his appeal, saying he\nposed a risk of flight.  Assistant U.S. Attorney Joseph Facciponti yesterday told\nthe appeals court that Aleynikov still posed a flight risk.\nFacciponti said prosecutors were confident the conviction would\nbe upheld because the U.S. believes Aleynikov violated the\nstatutes by first taking the source code and then transporting\nit across state lines when he traveled to Chicago with it.  The case is U.S. v. Aleynikov, 1:10-cr-00096, U.S. District\nCourt, Southern District of New York (Manhattan). Household purchases, which account for about 70 percent of\nthe economy, rose 0.2 percent after a 0.4 percent gain the prior\nmonth, a Commerce Department report showed today in  Washington .\nThe median estimate in a Bloomberg survey of 72 economists\ncalled for a 0.3 percent rise. Incomes rose 2.6 percent, pushing\nthe saving rate up to a more than three-year high.  Lower fuel costs, job gains, holiday-season discounts and\nearly dividend payouts helped to accelerate Americans\u2019 spending\nlast quarter, even as a plunge in defense outlays and slower\nstockpiling led the economy to contract at a 0.1 percent annual\npace. An increase in taxes that began to shrink paychecks this\nmonth will pose a hurdle to sustaining gains in purchases.  \u201cConsumers closed out the year on a relatively strong\nnote,\u201d said Guy Berger, an economist at RBS Securities Inc. in\n Stamford ,  Connecticut , who correctly projected the gain in\nspending. \u201cWe have a fair amount of resilience in demand. But,\nthis quarter doesn\u2019t look great for spending as there will be\nsome intense headwinds.\u201d  Claims for  unemployment benefits  increased more than\nforecast last week, partially erasing a slide in the prior two\nweeks and reflecting the difficulty of adjusting the figures for\nswings at the start of a year, another report showed today.\nInitial jobless claims rose 38,000 to 368,000 in the week ended\nJan. 26, the Labor Department reported.  Spending Outlook  Consumer comfort declined for a fourth straight week as\nAmericans\u2019 outlook on spending soured, a sign the  payroll tax \nincrease that kicked in at the start of the year is starting to\nripple through the economy.  The Bloomberg Consumer Comfort Index dropped to minus 37.5\nin the period ended Jan. 27, the lowest reading since October,\nfrom minus 36.4 in the prior week. The measure\u2019s buying-climate\ngauge decreased to a four-month low. The Standard & Poor\u2019s 500 Index increased 0.1 percent to\n1,503.03 at 9:48 a.m. in  New York .  Projections for  consumer spending  in the Bloomberg survey\nranged from little changed to a 0.7 percent gain.  Incomes Jump  The Bloomberg survey median called for incomes to rise 0.8\npercent. The December gain was the biggest since December 2004,\nthe month Microsoft Corp. paid a special dividend. The November\nreading was revised up to show a 1 percent increase from a\npreviously reported 0.6 percent advance.  The saving rate increased to 6.5 percent, the highest since\nMay 2009, from 4.1 percent. Wages and salaries increased 0.6\npercent.  Disposable income, or the money left over after taxes,\nclimbed 2.8 percent after adjusting for inflation, the biggest\ngains since May 2008.  After-tax income rose at a 6.8 percent annual rate from\nOctober through December, the biggest increase since the second\nquarter of 2008, a report showed yesterday.  In addition to improving wages and salaries, some companies\npaid dividends and employee bonuses earlier than usual before\ntax rates went up this year. The Commerce Department estimated\nabout $26.4 billion of the increase in incomes last quarter was\nattributable to early dividend payments and another $15 billion\nreflected bonuses and other types of irregular pay.  First Quarter  That signals the surge in incomes last quarter will be\nreversed in the first three months of 2013, when those payments\ntook place in prior years.  Adjusting consumer spending for inflation, which renders\nthe figures used to calculate gross domestic product, purchases\nrose 0.2 percent after a 0.6 percent increase in the previous\nmonth, today\u2019s report showed.  Spending on durable goods, including automobiles, increased\n1.3 percent after a 2.9 percent advance.  The figures provide a monthly breakdown of the quarterly\ndata released yesterday, shedding more light on the trajectory\nof household spending entering 2013.  Consumer purchases grew at a  2.2 percent  pace in the fourth\nquarter, up from 1.6 percent in the previous three months, as\nAmericans bought more durable goods including automobiles.  Government Spending  The fourth-quarter drop in GDP was largely due to a decline\nin government outlays and a smaller gain in inventories that\nsubtracted a combined 2.6 percentage points from growth,\nCommerce Department data showed yesterday.  Today\u2019s report showed a price gauge tied to consumer\nspending, which are the figures tracked by Federal Reserve\npolicy makers, rose 1.3 percent in 2012 after advancing 2.4\npercent the prior year. It was the smallest annual increase\nsince 2008 and compares with the central bank\u2019s goal of 2\npercent.  Excluding food and energy costs, prices climbed 1.4 percent\nin 2012, down from a 1.9 percent increase the prior year.  The need to spur growth and end a four-year long period of\njoblessness above 7.5 percent, combined with little inflation,\nhelp explain why Federal Reserve policy makers yesterday\nrepeated they\u2019ll keep pumping money into the economy.  FOMC Statement  \u201cWith appropriate policy accommodation, economic growth\nwill proceed at a moderate pace and the  unemployment rate  will\ngradually decline,\u201d the central bank said in a statement.\nHousehold spending \u201cadvanced,\u201d though \u201cthe unemployment rate\nremains elevated,\u201d it said.  Amazon.com Inc. (AMZN) , the world\u2019s largest Internet retailer,\nthis week reported a 22 percent jump in fourth-quarter in sales\nas more shoppers turned to its broad product selection and\nspeedy shipping for holiday gifts.  Recent reports signal  consumer confidence  and spending may\ncool this quarter, in part due to changes in fiscal policy.\nCongress on Jan. 1 let the payroll tax revert to 6.2 percent\nfrom 4.2 percent while avoiding broad-based income tax\nincreases. Lawmakers are now wrangling over spending reductions\nscheduled for March 1 that threaten to further slow the economy. After years\nof gridlock and legislative disappointment, policy makers on\nboth ends of Pennsylvania Avenue are laying the groundwork for\nimmigration reform. The White House has been building a\ncoalition, including labor, business and advocacy groups, to\npower a final push. Meanwhile, a bipartisan bloc in the  U.S.\nSenate  has begun to outline comprehensive changes that have\nproved elusive in years past.  Although common ground among Democrats and Republicans is\notherwise limited, both parties have  ample cause  to put the\nimmigration debate behind them. Democrats are eager to deliver\non a long-delayed campaign promise; Republicans hope to shed a\npolitical liability and start fresh with the Hispanic and Asian\nvoters who will increasingly decide elections.  The goals are well understood: a path to legalization -- at\na minimum -- for about 11 million undocumented immigrants, eased\nrestrictions on legal entry, and stronger enforcement of the\nlaw, including a vastly improved employment verification\ncomponent.  Yet even mutual self-interest isn\u2019t enough to ensure\nsuccess in  Washington . Given the polarized politics generally,\nand the dysfunction of the  House of Representatives \nparticularly, the Senate seems the place to forge a compromise.\nSupport from a  nucleus  of Republican senators, including Marco Rubio of  Florida ,  John McCain  of  Arizona  and  Orrin Hatch  of\n Utah , will be crucial to a deal.  There is already broad agreement -- even in the House -- on\nthe  need to ease legal immigration  for highly skilled workers.\nBy shutting out desperately needed people with degrees in\nscience, technology, engineering or math, restrictive U.S.\npolicies are  damaging competitiveness , undermining  innovation \nand leaving gaps in the workforce.  Unfilled Jobs  Even with high U.S. unemployment, STEM jobs are going\nunfilled, in part because many qualified graduates of U.S.\ncolleges are foreigners who are unable to obtain the requisite\nworking papers. Microsoft has more than 6,000 job openings in\nthe U.S., more than half of them in high-paying core technology\nareas.  Senators should begin by increasing the number of visas for\nhighly skilled workers, along with green cards for permanent\nresidents and work permits for spouses. If Republicans and\nDemocrats can agree on such legislation, they can then build on\nthat foundation, adding a Dream Act to provide a pathway to\ncitizenship for young immigrants. If legislators find they can\nbear the weight of comprehensive reform, we will cheer. If the\npolitics take them only halfway, they should build as much as\nthey can now and revisit the most contentious issues later.  As a  report  released this week by the Migration Policy\nInstitute documents, the U.S. has spent $186 billion on\nimmigration enforcement over the past quarter century, with\nexpenditures spiking in recent years. Last year, the report\nsaid, the  Barack Obama  administration spent a whopping $18\nbillion on enforcement -- more than it spent on all other  law\nenforcement  combined. The  Border Patrol  has doubled its\npersonnel in the past seven years while investing heavily in\ntechnology.  Popular misconceptions and political rhetoric aside,\nillegal immigration has declined sharply even as the Obama\nadministration has conducted a record number of deportations.\nFewer efforts to cross the border illegally have led to a 53\npercent decline in detentions since 2008. It\u2019s time for the\nnation\u2019s debate -- and its laws -- to change with the facts on\nthe ground. With a brick-by-brick approach to reform, lawmakers\ncan build not a wall, but a better nation. The Federal Circuit, in a 2-1 decision, said no one was\nharmed from the more than nine years it took Cancer Research to\nobtain the patent and that there was no intent to deceive the\nagency when the inventor failed to disclose a paper he had\nwritten about the compound.  The case is Cancer Research Technology Ltd. v. Barr\nLaboratories Inc., 2010-1204, U.S. Court of Appeals for the\nFederal Circuit (Washington). Abbott, Bayer Ask Court to Narrow Patent-Misconduct Standard  Abbott Laboratories  urged a U.S. appeals court to make it\nharder for companies to block patent owners from enforcing their\nintellectual property rights because of misconduct in obtaining\nthe patent.  \u201cWhen people are making minor mistakes and the patent\nwould have been issued anyway, the public is not harmed,\u201d John\nWhealan, a law professor who is representing Abbott in the case,\ntold the nine-judge U.S. Court of Appeals for the Federal\nCircuit in Washington yesterday.  The court, which specializes in patent law, is trying to\nfind a standard that judges can use to determine when inventors\nhave committed inequitable conduct at the U.S. Patent and\nTrademark Office. The legal argument has often been used by\ngeneric-drug companies to challenge patents on medicines.  The case before the court is an appeal involving an  Abbott \ndispute with  Becton, Dickinson & Co.  and Bayer AG\u2019s health-care\nunit over a glucose-monitor design. An Abbott patent was deemed\nunenforceable as punishment for the Abbott Park, Illinois-based\ncompany giving contradictory information to the U.S. and\nEuropean patent offices on the same invention.  Whealan, the patent office\u2019s former top lawyer who\u2019s now an\nassociate dean at George Washington University, said the court\nshould have patents deemed unenforceable only if there has been\nfraud that was committed to obtain the patent.  His successor at the patent office, Raymond Chen, said that\nif it was too difficult to prove inequitable conduct, patentees\ncould \u201cengage in gamesmanship and mischief.\u201d  Chen said he wants the standard limited because the patent\noffice is overwhelmed with inventors presenting too much data\nfor fear they would later be found to have withheld information.  Allegations of inequitable conduct are raised in about a\nthird of lawsuits, yet sustained in few, said Circuit Judge\nPauline Newman. Chen called it a \u201cplague\u201d in litigation.  A lawyer for Leverkusen, Germany-based Bayer, Rachel\nKrevans from San Francisco\u2019s Morrison & Foerster LLP, said only\nfour cases of inequitable conduct have been upheld by the\nFederal Circuit, and judges have the option of throwing the\nissue out.  Sanofi-Aventis SA \u2019s patent on a $4 billion-a-year drug, the\nblood-thinner Lovenox, was ruled unenforceable when an appeals\ncourt in 2008 found the Paris-based company misled the U.S.\npatent office. The court, in a 2-1 decision, said Sanofi\nwithheld information on studies that compared the active\ningredient of Lovenox with a related compound to ensure the\npatent office believed the two were different.  The Pharmaceutical Research and Manufacturers of America,\nwhich represents drugmakers including  Pfizer Inc.  and  Merck &\nCo. , urged the court to clarify the standard.  \u201cThe oft-cited justification for the inequitable conduct\ndoctrine is to deter fraudulent conduct before the PTO,\u201d the\ntrade group said in a filing on the case. \u201cIn its present form,\nhowever, the doctrine has spiraled out of control.\u201d  Federal Circuit judges have been open with their belief\nthat the legal argument is overused. Chief Judge Randall Rader,\nin the April issue of the American University Law Review, said\ninequitable conduct has grown \u201cfrom a tiny bush on the patent\nlandscape that inhibited gross fraud into a ubiquitous weed that\ninfects every prosecution and litigation involving patents.\u201d  The case is Therasense Inc. v. Becton, Dickinson & Co.,\n2008-1511, -1512, -1513, -1514, -1595, U.S. Court of Appeals for\nthe Federal Circuit (Washington). Copyright  Two Defendants Dismissed from Harper Lee\u2019s Copyright Suit  Harper Lee, the 87-year-old author of \u201cTo Kill a\nMockingbird,\u201d has settled a copyright dispute with two of the\ndefendants she sued in a case over ownership of the copyright to\nher novel.
