Lee, who has failing eyesight and hearing, was residing in\nan assisted-living facility in 2007 after suffering a stroke\nwhen she signed a document assigning her copyright to Pinkus\u2019s\ncompany, according to the complaint. While the copyright was re-assigned to Lee last year after legal action and Pinkus was\ndischarged as Lee\u2019s agent, he was still receiving royalties from\nthe novel as of this year, according to the complaint.  \u201cPinkus knew that Harper Lee was an elderly woman with\nphysical infirmities that made it difficult for her to read and\nsee,\u201d Gloria Phares, Lee\u2019s lawyer, said in the complaint.\n\u201cHarper Lee had no idea she had assigned her copyright\u201d to\nPinkus\u2019s company.  \u201cTo Kill a Mockingbird,\u201d a story of racial injustice in\nthe American South, won a Pulitzer Prize for fiction and was\nmade into a film starring Gregory Peck, who won an Oscar for\nplaying the lawyer Atticus Finch. It is Lee\u2019s only published\nnovel. The book has sold more than 30 million copies worldwide.  According to a Sept. 5 court filing, the case against\nWinick and Posner was dismissed, with attorney fees and\nlitigation costs paid by each party. The dismissal was with\nprejudice, which means that the case can\u2019t be filed again\nagainst these two defendants.  The case remains active against Pinkus, whose answer to the\ncomplaint was due Aug. 16.  The case is Nelle Harper Lee v. Samuel L. The  International Association of Police Chiefs  wants\nCongress to update a federal law to compel more companies\nproviding communications services to build intercept tools that\nallow them to conduct surveillance with court orders.  \u201cWe just don\u2019t have the technology to keep up with what\u2019s\ngoing on,\u201d Peter Modafferi, chairman of the association\u2019s\ninvestigative operations committee, said in a phone interview.\n\u201cIt\u2019s not just Verizon and phone companies like that, there\u2019s\nTwitter and all kinds of methods for people to communicate.\u201d  Location-tracking data from an  Apple Inc. Skype didn\u2019t provide\ndata at all.  Facebook Inc. It fits into a shirt pocket and features a\n12 megapixel sensor, xenon flash and Carl Zeiss lens. If only\nthe rest of the wireless phone wrapped around it, the new N8,\nwere as good.  The world\u2019s largest smartphone maker has a lot riding on\nthe  N8 , which it\u2019s rolling out worldwide this month. The Finnish\ncompany has been hemorrhaging market share -- down to 37.4\npercent in the second quarter, from 45 percent a year earlier --\nrecently replaced its chief executive and has announced the\ndepartures of two key managers.  The N8 represents Nokia\u2019s biggest effort thus far to right\nthe ship. And though it improves on previous offerings, it\ndoesn\u2019t come close to matching the state of the art as defined\nby  Apple Inc. \u2019s iPhone 4 and the best devices from  Motorola\nInc. ,  HTC Corp.  and Samsung that use  Google Inc. \u2019s Android\noperating system.  Smartphones rise or fall on their hardware, software and\nthe apps and services available. The N8 does well on the first\nand decently on the third; where it falls short is on No. 2.  The N8\u2019s software, called Symbian^3, is an updated version\nof the software that\u2019s been powering Nokia phones for several\nyears. But \u201cupdated\u201d isn\u2019t the same as \u201cup to date,\u201d and\nwhile it has some nice touches it\u2019s still behind the times.  Down Memory Lane  For example, when you write an e-mail or send a text\nmessage and hold the phone in portrait -- that is, upright --\nposition, the touch screen defaults to a telephone-style numeric\nkeypad. For some users, that will be a trip down Wireless-Phone\nMemory Lane, back to those halcyon days when typing the letter\n\u201cs\u201d meant hitting the \u201c7\u201d key four times. Most people, however,\nwill likely be annoyed at always having to flip the phone\nsideways to get a QWERTY keyboard.  The N8 also sometimes requires you to go through a\nmultistep process to perform what ought to be a simple task.\nAnswering an e-mail, for instance, requires you to first hit an\n\u201cOptions\u201d button, then choose \u201cReply\u201d from a menu. And the\nsoftware feels sluggish at times, such as when sliding between\nthe three available home screens.  Physically, the phone is mostly impressive. The scratch-\nresistant, anodized-aluminum case makes it both look and feel\nlike a premium product. Not all of the five colors are to my\ntaste -- bright orange, anyone? -- but to each their own. The\nphone feels solid and good in the hand and, at 4.8 ounces,\nweighs just about the same as iPhone 4 even though it\u2019s thicker.  Protruding Camera  The reason for that extra thickness is also the most\nimpressive thing about the N8: the camera, which protrudes\nslightly from the back. It\u2019s among the best I\u2019ve seen in a\nmobile phone, not only for its resolution but for its operation\nin both idiot-proof mode (when I was using it) and under manual\ncontrol. There\u2019s autofocus, built-in face-detection technology\nand 2X digital zoom for still photos.  The N8 also shoots 720p video -- it includes an HDMI port\nand adapter cable for viewing on a high-definition TV -- and has\na front-facing, lower-resolution camera as well for video calls.\nI found the 3.5-inch screen acceptable but nowhere near as good\nas the displays found on Apple and  Samsung  handsets.  The N8\u2019s battery was able to get me through a full day of\nmoderate to heavy use. Good thing, because -- like the iPhone,\nand unlike just about every other smartphone -- the battery\nisn\u2019t replaceable by the user.  Eccentric Design  In Apple\u2019s case, the non-swappable battery is a reflection\nof  Steve Jobs \u2019s desire to control the entire user experience.\nHere, the decision just seems eccentric, like Saab putting the\nignition switch next to the shifter. I also found myself\nconcerned about the little trap doors covering the slots for\nyour carrier\u2019s SIM card and an SD storage card. I was afraid\nthey would snap off, though I eventually concluded they were\nsturdier than they seemed.  Nokia can\u2019t compete with the iPhone and Android devices in\nterms of the number of available applications. Still, I found\nits Ovi services -- which include a very good mapping\napplication, calendar and mail, among others -- to be thorough\nand well-integrated into the N8. Nokia is also building out Ovi\nas a platform for third-party developers, although to access\ntheir wares you first have to install the Ovi Store application\nitself; it doesn\u2019t come pre-loaded on the phone.  The N8 is in the process of being rolled out around the\nglobe. In the U.S., it\u2019s available for $550 unlocked in a\nversion that will run on either  AT&T Inc. \u2019s or  T-Mobile \u2019s\nnetwork; there\u2019s no word yet on whether a carrier-subsidized\nversion is on the way.  Nokia isn\u2019t the only smartphone maker struggling to reverse\na slide; Microsoft Corp. this week unveiled its new  Windows\nPhone 7  operating system as well. Given Nokia\u2019s No. 1 ranking in\nthe global market,  Stephen Elop , the former Microsoft executive\nwho took over as its CEO last month, is starting from a stronger\nposition than is his old boss,  Steve Ballmer . Elop\u2019s task will\nbe tough nonetheless: The N8, while an improvement on what\u2019s\ncome before it, still isn\u2019t good enough to stanch Nokia\u2019s\nbleeding. The new\nChromebook Series 5 laptop manages that impressive feat.  The Chromebook, born of a partnership between Samsung\nElectronics Co. and  Google Inc. (GOOG) , is the first commercially\navailable computer to run Google\u2019s Chrome Operating System. The\nidea is that you use \u201cthe cloud\u201d -- that is, the Internet --\nto replace many of the functions traditionally handled by the\n computer hardware .  It\u2019s a seductive notion, sort of like canceling your cable\nTV subscription and relying on the Net for all your video\nentertainment. But much like cable-cutting, it proves to be more\nattractive in theory than in fact.  The Series 5, which went on sale this week from  Amazon.com\nInc. (AMZN)  and Best Buy Co. at $500 for a 3G-enabled model and $430\nwith Wi-Fi only, is less than an inch thick and weighs 3.3\npounds. It has a 12.1-inch screen, two USB ports and a card\nreader. The keyboard is comfortable, and there\u2019s a track pad for\nnavigation that is generously sized but that had problems\nregistering some clicks accurately.  Outside of the operating system, software doesn\u2019t reside on\nthe computer itself; instead, you use online alternatives like\nGmail and Google Docs to create your word-processing,\nspreadsheet and other documents. And you don\u2019t store those\ndocuments locally on a hard drive; they live in the cloud too,\nwhere they\u2019re accessible to you through any Web-connected\ncomputer anywhere.  Under the Hood  Under the hood, not that it matters all that much, are an\n Intel Corp. (INTC)  microprocessor, two gigabytes of memory and 16\ngigabytes of solid-state storage, which is less than you\u2019ll find\non many smart phones.  Anyone who\u2019s ever suffered through the wait for a Windows\ncomputer to boot up -- which is to say, everyone who\u2019s ever used\na Windows computer -- will be grateful for the Series 5\nexperience.  Thanks to the lightweight nature of the operating system\nand the solid-state storage, I clocked the time from startup to\nlogin screen at a mere eight seconds. And battery life is good\nenough that you\u2019re more likely to just close the lid rather than\nturn the computer off, in which case you\u2019re back in business in\nthree seconds.  Samsung claims the battery will last 8 1\/2 hours in normal\nuse; I got more than six hours in my torture test, which\nincluded cranking up the screen brightness and streaming a\ncontinuous series of \u201cSimpsons\u201d episodes.  Ease of Use  As for ease of use, if you know how to work a Web browser,\nyou know how to work Chrome. All functions -- even accessing\nfiles, playing games or watching movies -- run through the\nbrowser. You can acquire new apps customized for the operating\nsystem, including the New York Times and \u201cAngry Birds,\u201d from\nthe online  Chrome Web Store . And upgrades to the operating\nsystem can come in the form of incremental, over-the-air\nimprovements.  But the Series 5\u2019s speed and ease of use were offset by a\nseries of problems I encountered that should fairly be laid at\nGoogle\u2019s feet rather than Samsung\u2019s.  I ran into the first one within moments of pulling the\ncomputer out of the box. Even though it had embedded 3G service\nfrom  Verizon Wireless , it required a Wi-Fi connection to\nactivate, and it wouldn\u2019t log on to Bloomberg\u2019s Wi-Fi network.  It isn\u2019t like there\u2019s anything exotic about our setup; I\u2019ve\nused it for legions of tablets, e-readers and even phones\nrunning Google\u2019s own Android operating system. But it turns out\nthat Google didn\u2019t include support for the authentication\nstandard we use -- a strange oversight in a device that, without\nan Internet signal, might be more accurately labeled a\nChromebrick.  3G Service  I finally activated the Chromebook by pulling out a spare\nwireless phone, calling the carrier to activate its mobile-\nhotspot function and using it to connect. Once I got over that\nhurdle, I was able to use the built-in Verizon service when I\nwas in the office or otherwise didn\u2019t have a usable Wi-Fi\nsignal.  The price of the 3G model includes 100 megabytes of data\nper month; beyond that, Verizon offers prepaid month-to-month\ndata plans starting at $20, and a $9.99 unlimited day pass.  An even bigger problem is the lack of an offline mode for\nGoogle Docs, Gmail and Google Calendar. So if you\u2019re on an\nairplane or someplace where you can\u2019t get an Internet signal,\nyou can for now forget about being able to do anything\nproductive. (Google says it expects to introduce offline\nfunctionality sometime this summer.)  At least you can lean back and watch a movie -- as long as\nyou\u2019ve remembered to download it first to an SD card or USB\nthumb drive.  Cloud Print  As for printing: It\u2019s complicated. In most cases, you\u2019ll\nfirst have to enroll the printer you want to use with Google\u2019s\nCloud Print service, then send it your document via the\nInternet. Hooking the Series 5 directly to the printer with a\nUSB cable won\u2019t work. It\u2019s all enough to make you yearn for the\nsimple pleasures of installing a Windows printer driver.  You might put up with the hassles if the Series 5 were\nreally, really cheap. It isn\u2019t: For the same cost, you can have\na choice of highly capable  Windows machines . (PC maker  Acer Inc. (2353) \nis coming out with a couple of slightly lower-priced\nChromebooks, but I haven\u2019t tested them yet.)  Someday, when the Internet is even more ubiquitous than it\nis now and connectivity is as available as oxygen, the\nChromebook may make sense. For now, though, it dwells in a\nnetherworld, neither as convenient as a tablet nor as potent as\na PC.  ( Rich Jaroslovsky  is a Bloomberg News columnist. The\nopinions expressed are his own.) Wall Street firms collected $3.73 billion from managing\ninitial public offerings and additional sales in the first three\nquarters, down 17 percent from a year ago, according to data\ncompiled by Bloomberg. Equity offerings slid 23 percent to $88.6\nbillion. Bond sales totaled $861 billion and high-yield debt\nissues rose 87 percent to a record $198 billion, the data show.  Companies are picking debt over equity as yields on U.S.\ninvestment grade corporate bonds sank to an all-time low of\n3.645 percent this week, according to data from Bank of America\nCorp.\u2019s Merrill Lynch. Diminished fees from stocks contributed\nto what may have been the worst quarter for investment banks\nsince the peak of the credit-market crisis.  \u201cYou have that perfect storm going against equity\nissuance,\u201d said  Peter Jankovskis , who helps manage $2.2 billion\nas co-chief investment officer at Oakbrook Investments in Lisle,\nIllinois. \u201cThe cost of debt is so much lower, and two, the\ncompanies aren\u2019t being very aggressive. There\u2019s not much the\nbanks can do about it. They\u2019re certainly losing out on fees.\u201d  The decline in fee income is coming in a business that has\ntraditionally been one of the most lucrative for the financial\nindustry. Banks earned fees of 4.21 percent from managing share\nsales in the U.S. this year, more than double those from\ncorporate bonds or mergers and acquisitions, according to data\ncompiled by Bloomberg.  Debt Versus Equity  MetLife Inc. , the largest U.S. life insurer, completed the\nbiggest share sale so far this year after raising  $3.62 billion \nin August to help finance its  acquisition  of a unit of New York-\nbased American International Group Inc. The life insurer also\nsold $3 billion of debt for the purchase.  For the share sale, Bank of America Corp.,  Credit Suisse\nGroup AG  of Zurich and four other banks hired by MetLife earned\n$93.1 million after charging 2.57 percent, Bloomberg data show.  That\u2019s almost six times more profitable than the 0.44\npercent fee from the  debt   offering , which gave the banks $13.3\nmillion, New York-based MetLife\u2019s filings with the Securities\nand Exchange Commission and data compiled by Bloomberg show.  Revenue from underwriting IPOs is even higher, with bankers\nearning an average of 6.53 percent this year, the data show.  \u2018More Lucrative\u2019  \u201cNo doubt the banks would rather do more equity deals,\u201d\nsaid  Michael Holland , who oversees more than $4 billion as\nchairman of Holland & Co. in New York. \u201cThere\u2019s no question the\nequity business is far more lucrative, but unfortunately for the\nbanks, it\u2019s not there right now for them.\u201d  Companies have raised 23 percent less from share sales in\n2010 versus the same period a year ago, according to data\ncompiled by Bloomberg. From 2007 to 2009, when U.S. equities\nfell as much as  57 percent  amid the worst financial crisis since\nthe Great Depression, they still sold at least $98.8 billion in\nstock in the first three quarters of each year, the data show.  Almost 70 percent of companies that completed IPOs in 2010\nhave raised less than they initially sought, while the average\namount of shares sold has decreased to an 11-year low of $152\nmillion per deal, data compiled by Bloomberg show. That\u2019s less\nthan half the size of an average initial offering last year.  Companies are taking advantage of the lowest borrowing\ncosts on record to issue debt.  Borrowing Costs  Near zero percent benchmark U.S. interest rates and the\nFederal Reserve\u2019s purchase of bonds pushed the average yield on\nU.S. investment grade debt to 3.645 percent this week, based on\nmore than 4,000 bonds in Bank of America Merrill Lynch\u2019s U.S.\nCorporate Master Index. That\u2019s the lowest since the data began\nin October 1986 and 25 percent less than at the end of 2009. While some of that testing happens in-house, developers often\noutsource some of the time-consuming task to low-cost shops that can throw a lot of\npeople at it to click all over the site looking for bugs and vulnerabilities.  In this case, Google wanted a robust test to attack the complex payment system,\nsimulating the battering it could expect in the real world. The search giant hired  Globant, \nthen a 350-employee Buenos Aires startup that had germinated in a bar in 2003. Within\na few months the software development and services company was back with\nsurprising results. It had mounted an unexpected attack (using PHP, a computer\nlanguage not typically used by Google but popular with app developers) to inject\ndeceptive information, successfully stealing money.  Impressed with the elegance of the hacking technique, Google\u2019s developer relations\nmanager, Patrick Chanezon, invited former Globant engineer Bruno Rovagnati to give a\ntalk at Google\u2019s Mountain View (Calif.) headquarters about how he uncovered the flaws.\n\u201cThe room was too small; all the engineering [people] wanted to hear,\u201d Chanezon\nrecalls. Five years later, Globant is one of Chanezon\u2019s \u201cfavorite outsourcing partners,\u201d\ncurrently working to refine Google\u2019s Chrome browser and its Android operating system.  \u201cWith Google as a customer, it became easier to introduce ourselves to other\ncompanies, so our growth exploded,\u201d says Martin Migoya, 43, Globant\u2019s chief executive\nand one of its four co-founders. At Google\u2019s recommendation, LinkedIn hired Globant in\n2007, when it needed temporary on-site engineering talent to prepare for the launch of\nOpenSocial, a programming platform that hosts social applications across multiple\nwebsites. Globant went on to design and build Outlook Social Connector for LinkedIn,\nwhich allows LinkedIn contacts to be imported into Microsoft Outlook. Globant now has\nseven engineers at LinkedIn\u2019s Mountain View headquarters, enhancing Internet browser\ntoolbars and LinkedIn\u2019s Android application. Globant is LinkedIn\u2019s only outside vendor\nthat writes source code for the popular professional networking tool, according to\nBrandon Duncan, LinkedIn\u2019s platform engineering director.  LATIN AMERICAN PIONEER  Globant now has some 150 customers, including Electronic Arts, MySpace, and ad\nagency JWT. Last year the company, which offers IT services ranging from\ndevelopment to quality testing, had $50 million in revenue; this year it could reach $90\nmillion, according to Migoya. Compliance Action  ICE Switches More Than 900 Swaps to Futures on Dodd-Frank Rules  Intercontinental Exchange Inc. (ICE) , the second-largest U.S.\nfutures market, has converted more than 900 over-the-counter\nenergy contracts to regulated futures in response to rules meant\nto prevent another financial crisis.  The Commodity Futures Trading Commission guidelines that\nwent into effect Oct. 12 require firms holding $8 billion of\nbilateral derivatives to register as swaps dealers and meet new\nperformance standards. The CFTC  granted  a reprieve to the  CME\nGroup Inc. (CME) , owner of the world\u2019s largest future exchange, on\nOct. 12 by saying the trading of its swaps won\u2019t be counted\ntoward the dealer minimum until Dec. 31.  The  Dodd-Frank Wall Street Reform and Consumer Protection\nAct  in 2010 gave the CFTC, which regulates futures contracts,\njurisdiction over the swaps markets with the aim of increasing\ntransparency.  Commodity futures are traded on exchanges that follow rules\nimposed by the CFTC, while swaps are negotiated directly between\ncounterparties and until now lacked many of the same\nrestrictions, including limits on the number of contracts one\ntrader could hold.  Swaps and futures are used by speculators and hedgers to\nplace bets on oil, natural gas and power prices. Swap dealers\nwill face capital, collateral, record-keeping and business\nconduct standards under Dodd-Frank. The rules force traders to\nreport over-the-counter transactions to regulators and process\nthem through third-party clearinghouses.  Atlanta-based ICE, which owns the largest European energy\nmarket, has converted all  cleared energy contracts  starting Oct.\n14.  For more, click here. Compliance Policy  Hedge Fund, Private Equity Bonus Rules Considered by FSA  The U.K. Financial Services Authority may set bonus rules\nspecifically for hedge fund and private equity managers as it\nworks to implement European Union regulations.  The FSA may write \u201ca remuneration code to apply\nspecifically to Alternative Investment Fund Managers, but\nmodeled closely on the existing code\u201d that applies to banks and\nother financial firms, the regulator said in a  statement  on its\nwebsite. While the FSA is obliged to comply with EU standards\nset by the European Securities and Markets Authority, that\nagency hasn\u2019t yet completed them.  European finance ministers in 2010 approved a law, known as\nthe Alternative Investment Fund Managers Directive, which gave\nParis-based ESMA power to set rules for  hedge funds  and private\nequity firms, regulating their pay and access to EU investors.  The aim of the rules would be to ensure managers \u201ccontrol\nrisk-taking behavior by reducing the potential adverse impact of\npoorly-defined remuneration schemes,\u201d the FSA said in a\ndiscussion paper. It\u2019s seeking input on the plans from the\nindustry and the public.  The FSA said its existing bonus code, which it expanded to\ninclude more than 2,700 firms at the end of 2010, may already be\ncompliant with the EU rules. Some U.K. funds are required to\ndisclose the size of their bonus pools for the previous year in\nregulatory filings.  Companies Face Fines as Much as 2% of Sales Under EU Privacy Law  Companies face fines as high as 2 percent of yearly global\nsales for losing personal data under an overhaul of European\nUnion privacy rules.  Data protection agencies in the EU\u2019s 27 countries would\ngain the power to sanction companies that violate requirements\nfor handling personal information proposed by the  European\nCommission  today. The measures, which also target online-\nadvertising and social-networking sites, update the EU\u2019s 17-\nyear-old data-protection policies.  The EU overhaul would also clamp down on data lapses such\nas  Sony Corp. (6758) \u2019s six-day delay in warning customers about a cyber\nattack that exposed more than 100 million customer accounts, the\nsecond-largest online data breach in U.S. history. Industry\ngroups with members including  Microsoft Corp. (MSFT)  and  Google Inc. (GOOG) \nhave warned against overly strict data-privacy rules that may\nstifle innovation.  Under the draft rules, serious violations, such as\nprocessing sensitive data without an individual\u2019s consent or\nwithout any legal justification, may be punished with penalties\nas high as 1 million euros ($1.3 million) or as much as 2\npercent of a company\u2019s yearly sales, the commission said. Less\nserious offenses would be punished with smaller fines.  Separately, Google, owner of the world\u2019s most popular\nsearch engine, is introducing a privacy policy covering the\nmajority of its products to simplify guidelines for users.  Google, which has had separate policies for more than 70\nproducts, said it will unify the approach for more than 60 of\nthem, including Android software for mobile phones, in a more-\nreadable format. The company also is reducing the number of\nterms of service, conditions users agree to when accessing\nGoogle products, and making them easier to read.  The  company , based in  Mountain View , California, is\ngrappling with increased government scrutiny amid concern that\nthe company needs to do more to safeguard customer privacy.\nThe changes will take effect on March 1. Google will preserve\nsome policies, for products such as Google Wallet and the Chrome\nbrowser.  Google may have changes to its privacy policy reviewed by\nIreland\u2019s data-protection agency. The agency will \u201cbe further\nassessing the implications of the changes now that they are\nlaunched to users,\u201d Gary Davis, the country\u2019s deputy data-\nprotection commissioner, said in an e-mailed statement. In terms of speed of adoption, only Apple's iPad has rivaled the Kinect. Aside from some tough comments on my blog, the long-term repercussions were low. That's pretty much what happens to a pundit who gets it wrong \u2014 nothing. Life is tougher for the strategist. A prescient call provides career rocket fuel, while the wrong one can be career limiting. So how to sift through the noise to evaluate the predictions that warrant the most careful attention? Watch out for the following four types of pundits. The non-user.  This pundit makes bold predictions about a product or service he's never used. Remember, a wide gulf separates a corporate press release or a carefully scripted demo and in-the-field reality. I ran into this trap when I  started getting excited  about Research in Motion's  Playbook  before the product had even been officially launched. The product's performance didn't live up to early press releases and has struggled in the market.  The projector.  This pundit makes predictions about markets that she doesn't participate in. For example, in 2008 a company called  Peek  launched a seemingly game-changing device that made it simple for people to access their email on the go. Many tech savvy reviewers said the product would take off because its simplicity would appeal to everyday users. The reviews convinced me to buy a Peek for my wife, but watching her use the device for five minutes led me to believe that as simple as the device seemed, it just didn't fit into my wife's life. That Christmas present quickly turned into a paperweight. The freeze framer.  Back in 2005 I wrote a piece [ PDF ] looking at a new video recorder introduced by Pure Digital Technologies, the Flip. I said the simple, easy-to-use product had one fatal flaw \u2014 customers had to drop it off at drugstores to get videos processed. How many would do that, I wondered? The mistake I made was assuming that Pure wasn't already working on its second version, which featured a simple mechanism to load video onto computers. The company took off and was ultimately acquired by Cisco for hundreds of millions of dollars. (Cisco strangely shut down Pure Digital this year, but that's  a different story .) Markets are dynamic, and if pundits don't take the long view they can make mistakes. This problem is one reason why I am skeptical of anything that is declared to be a \"killer.\" The opiner.  Michael Mauboussin, the Chief Investment Strategist at Legg Mason Capital,  eloquently describes  how the key thing to evaluate when looking at equity investors isn't  what  they buy but  how they choose  what to buy. In other words, ask \"What models do they use to make decisions? What process do they follow to gather data?\" The same holds true for pundits. Offering opinions without explaining underlying assumptions or mental models isn't helpful. The real world is complicated and any prediction ought to at least spell out the assumptions that would have to be true for a prediction to hold. Wrong predictions based on well-reasoned (at the time) assumptions are useful because they help strategists develop their own instincts for assessing future technologies. As an occasionally unhelpful pundit myself, I hope I've helped you dodge these dangerous characters \u2014 or at least put their opinions into perspective.","path":".\/2008_2012_msft_bloomberg_news\/four-strategy-gurus-to-avoid.txt"},{"id":47397193,"title":"U.S. Stocks Retreat as Bernanke Avoids Offering New Growth Plans","released_at":"<date>September 8 2011<\/date> <time>20:30:51<\/time>","content":"U.S. stocks fell, after the biggest\ngain in two weeks for benchmark gauges, as Federal Reserve\nChairman  Ben S. It announced plans in September\nto sell certificates to companies that vouch for an app\u2019s\nprivacy protection. Truste has since signed up more than a dozen\ncustomers, including GoDaddy.com Inc., Weather Channel\nInteractive Inc. and Yelp Inc.  Until now, Truste and rivals such as  Symantec Corp.  and\n VeriSign Inc.  have focused on personal-computer websites. The\ncompanies offer seals of approval that customers place on their\nsites -- something like a Better Business Bureau certificate --\nto show that consumers can safely shop there and share their\npersonal information.  Mobile Scams  The growth of smartphones and mobile apps has attracted\nscammers, who once stuck mostly to PCs, said  Maribel Lopez ,\nfounder of San Francisco-based  Lopez Research LLC , which tracks\nthe mobile industry. Less than half of\nrespondents said they felt very or somewhat safe. Almost a\nquarter said they used apps that track their location,\nand 12 percent regularly use their mobile phones for banking.  While Truste provides a seal of approval for an app\u2019s\nprivacy policies, it doesn\u2019t offer a guarantee of security. That\nmeans a user\u2019s credit card could still be stolen. It also isn\u2019t\nalone in verifying that apps protect users.  Apple Inc. , which\nruns the biggest app store, does its own vetting of software\ndevelopers. (BKS) \u2019s decision to stop competing in the tablet business potentially will accelerate a break-up of the largest U.S. bookstore chain.  With its Nook Media digital unit racking up more losses in its fiscal fourth quarter -- sending the shares down the most in almost two years yesterday -- the company said that to cut costs and limit inventory risk it will stop making tablets and partner with electronics manufacturers.  Since Barnes & Noble got into the tablet business in 2010, analysts questioned how it would maintain its initial success because the amount of investment to churn out devices to compete against the likes of Amazon.com Inc. and Apple Inc. would be difficult for a company of its size and acumen. This decision removes those hurdles, which could help make the Nook more viable on its own or as an acquisition target.  \u201cIt\u2019s a positive because anything they can do to cut back on that cash burn is a good thing,\u201d said  Michael Souers , an analyst for  Standard & Poor\u2019s  in New York. \u201cThat definitely has to be seen as a good thing and could potentially help find a buyer for Nook Media.\u201d  That in turn could allow founder  Leonard Riggio , the company\u2019s largest shareholder, to go ahead with his February proposal to buy the chain\u2019s retail arm.  The New York-based company has been exploring ways to increase its value for more than two years as management has said that investors weren\u2019t properly assessing its accomplishments with the Nook. The company started the digital content and mobile device division in 2009 to help navigate readers\u2019 shift away from paper books.  Possible Spinoff  Last year, the company created a subsidiary that included the Nook and college bookstore divisions and dubbed it Nook Media with an eye toward spinning it off into its own company.  Microsoft Corp. (MSFT)  and  Pearson Plc (PSON)  invested in the unit last year. That came after  Liberty Media Corp. (LMCA)  bought a stake in the entire company in 2011.  Then in February, Riggio said he planned to offer to buy the bookstore chain\u2019s retail assets, which included its more than 680 stores and website. That would leave Nook Media as a public company. It had a combined loss before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortization of $364 million in fiscal 2013 on revenue of $2.54 billion.  \u201cIt would be much easier to separate the businesses if Nook was doing better,\u201d said Souers, who recommends holding Barnes & Noble shares.  Nook\u2019s results looked much better last year when the idea of a spinoff took shape. While it was still losing money, revenue continued to grow.  Holiday Sales  That changed during this  holiday shopping season  as its lineup of new devices failed to connect with consumers. Sales at the Nook unit declined for the first time and the company had to write off excess inventory. That continued last quarter, leading to the decision to exit the tablet business.  \u201cWe\u2019ve been very focused here for the last three years on devices, and we realize we have to shift our focus to distributing the content more aggressively,\u201d through other platforms, Chief Financial Officer Michael Huseby said in an interview.  Barnes & Noble will keep making the black-and-white e-readers, on which it sells the majority of its e-books. It expects to generate more sales of digital content through its Nook application on other devices and sell more digital textbooks through the college unit, Huseby said.  Nook Color  The retailer started off well in the tablet business in 2010 when it released Nook Color. The seven-inch tablet quickly gained a foothold as one of the few inexpensive alternatives to Apple\u2019s iPad.  About a year after the Nook Color debut, Amazon\u2019s Kindle Fire arrived with a similar price and began grabbing customers. The competition only increased last year with Apple and Google Inc. offering seven-inch tablets.  Barnes & Noble responded by releasing its own 9-inch device, Nook HD+, for the holidays with the hope that a price 27 percent lower than an iPad would lure consumers. It didn\u2019t work, and the lack of demand prompted the company to write down inventory and led to a surprise loss during what is usually its most profitable quarter. Such writeoffs totaled $222 million in fiscal 2013, including $133 million last quarter.  \u201cWe want to move away from taking on all that risk ourselves,\u201d Chief Executive Officer William Lynch said on a call with analysts to discuss fourth-quarter results. \u201cAs we\u2019ve seen, the tablet market --especially in sub-8 inch -- got extremely competitive and it was very capital expensive to build our own tablets.\u201d  Funding Nook  The company expects Nook Media to keep funding itself with the reduction in costs from ceasing tablet production, selling current Nook inventory that has already been paid for and cash from Microsoft which agreed to make payments totaling $305 million over five years.  Barnes & Noble will sell its remaining inventory of Nook tablets through this holiday shopping season and then transition to the partnership model. The company declined to provide details on the plan beyond saying it is in talks with multinational technology firms.  The Nook division was part of a companywide net loss in the fiscal fourth quarter ended April 30 of $118.6 million, or $2.11 a share, from $56.9 million, or $1.06, a year earlier, Barnes & Noble said in a statement. Analysts projected 90 cents, the average of five estimates.  The shares rose 1.5 percent to $15.84 at 9:33 a.m. in  New York  after declining 17 percent yesterday for the biggest loss since Aug. 19, 2011. Trouble is, more than 40 percent of the job growth was\nattributable to a healthy expansion in  retail trade , which\nunderscores a larger economic problem. Although entrepreneurial\ninnovation usually leads to significant job creation, the great\nretail entrepreneurs of the past 30 years -- from  Amazon.com\nInc. (AMZN)  to Wal-Mart Stores Inc. -- have produced efficiency rather\nthan economywide employment.  Forty years ago, two jokers put up a  billboard  \u201cWill the\nlast person leaving SEATTLE -- Turn out the lights.\u201d Boeing\nCo., the region\u2019s industrial giant, had been cutting jobs, and\nthe city seemed about to become a Pacific outpost of the Rust\nBelt. But  Seattle  didn\u2019t go the way of Detroit, largely because\nof a string of remarkable entrepreneurs, who gave us, among\nother things, Amazon,  Costco Wholesale Corp. (COST) ,  Microsoft Corp. (MSFT) \nand Starbucks Corp. Today, the city is a success story, with  per\ncapita personal income  of more than $50,000 -- more than 20\npercent above the national average -- and an  unemployment rate \nbelow the national average.  As I discussed in a recent  City Journal article ,  Seattle \u2019s\nsuccess builds on a potent cocktail of education and\nentrepreneurship that provides a model for American rebirth.\nMore than 54 percent of Seattle\u2019s adults have college degrees,\nabout double the national average. The city\u2019s skill base seems\nto have been part of its attraction for both Microsoft\u2019s  Bill Gates  (a native son) and Amazon\u2019s  Jeff Bezos  (a transplant).  Starbucks Model  Even  Starbucks (SBUX) , which was founded by an English teacher, a\nhistory teacher and a writer, owes its existence to Seattle\u2019s\novereducated population. In the era when the high-end coffee\nchain was created, working-class guys were perfectly happy\nchugging down Chock full o\u2019Nuts.  All four of these Seattle-based companies are models of\nU.S. entrepreneurship. They have helped shape modern American\nlife, and their products sell around the globe. Yet Amazon and\nCostco may well have led to fewer, not more, jobs in the U.S.  Piecing together the full employment effects of any\nparticular company is close to impossible. Even the seemingly\nsimple task of estimating the impact of a new Wal-Mart store on\nlocal retail employment is terribly tricky. One  study  found that\neach  Wal-Mart (WMT)  increases retail employment by 50 jobs. Another    \npaper  makes the competing argument that the giant retailer puts\nstores in areas that are growing naturally, and that better\nstatistical techniques show that each new Wal-Mart decreases\ncounty level retail employment by 150 workers. The economywide\nimpact of Amazon is far harder to determine because it has\nbuyers and sellers everywhere.  But it isn\u2019t hard to spot the larger trend in retail trade\njob creation. The attached figure shows the time path of job-\ncreation rates for the economy as a whole and for retail trade\nin particular. The data comes from the  Census Bureau\u2019s Business\nDynamics Database , which defines the  job-creation  rate as the\nemployment growth at the establishment level divided by the\naverage of old and new employment.  The lower line shows the job-creation rate for the economy\nas a whole, which dropped from about 20 percent in the late\n1970s to 12 percent today. On average, the job-creation rate has\ndeclined by 1.4 percent per decade, which should scare anyone\nworried about our continuing ability to generate employment. The\nU.S. hasn\u2019t been producing fewer jobs than it used to, at least\nuntil the recent recession, but the number of jobs created\nhasn\u2019t increased with the overall size of the economy.  Service Economy  The top line shows the far steeper decline for retail\ntrade. The 1970s and 1980s were a great growth period for this\nsector, as the U.S. moved from manufacturing to a service\neconomy. When the economy roared back after the 1982 recession,\nthe job-creation rate in retail trade boomed at more than 20\npercent per year for each year from 1984 to 1988. The job-\ncreation rate in retail has never again broken 20 percent, and\nthe downward trend runs at 2.6 percentage points per decade.  I wouldn\u2019t want to blame Amazon or Costco for this trend,\nand I am a big fan of both retailers. There is a lot to like\nabout low prices and shopping over the Internet. But it\nshouldn\u2019t surprise us that tremendous improvements in retail\nefficiency have been associated with diminished job growth in\nthe e-tail sector.  Free markets have many virtues, and I have no sympathy for\nthose who want to preserve old retail jobs by banning\ninnovation. Preventing Wal-Mart from entering an urban\nneighborhood may protect a few local stores, but it is the poor\nwho suffer most when they have to pay unduly high prices. The\ncurrent crisis in the Mediterranean countries reminds us that\ngovernments that try to preserve old jobs by stifling new\nbusiness models eventually produce stagnation and decay.  Our best hope is that private entrepreneurs will figure out\nways to employ more Americans. The current 13.2 percent\n unemployment rate  for workers without high school degrees\nrepresents a failure of entrepreneurial imagination. Every out-\nof-work American provides an opportunity for some businessperson\nto figure out how to turn that person\u2019s wasted time into\neconomic profit.  The entrepreneurs who created Starbucks, especially Chief\nExecutive Officer  Howard Schultz , figured out how to solve that\nproblem. The company employs 149,000 people in its labor-\nintensive caffeine-delivery system. Its success as an employer\nrepresents a combination of product and process -- delivering\nwhat consumers want in a way that employs tens of thousands of\nbaristas worldwide.  What will it take for the U.S. to produce the entrepreneurs\nwho will create jobs for the millions who are still unemployed?\nThe government can act in three areas: regulation, taxation and\neducation.  Regulatory Barriers  Because budding entrepreneurs typically don\u2019t earn much at\nfirst, regulations can be the biggest barrier facing startups.\nSome of these rules are national, but many more are local.  All should be re-examined.  Detroit  should be welcoming\nevery new entrepreneur it can get, but the city\u2019s rules make it\nhard to open even a  food truck . The national government at least\nhas embraced the principle of applying cost-benefit analysis to\nexecutive branch regulations, but state and local governments\nlack the resources to properly evaluate their rules.  The federal government could help by setting up an\nindependent assessment agency, modeled on the  Congressional\nBudget Office , that offers cost-benefit analysis to lower levels\nof government to help identify and prune unnecessary\nregulations.  We also want to make sure that our  tax code  doesn\u2019t\ndiscourage companies from hiring new workers. I support the\ncontinuation of the  payroll tax cut  and the expansion of the\nearned income tax credit.  Finally, it makes sense to couple support for education\nwith the development of entrepreneurship and knowledge that\napplies in the job market. We can provide more aid for adult\neducation, as long as that aid is made contingent upon the\nacquisition of useful skills.  Despite the most recent numbers, the U.S. continues to have\nan employment problem. The main reason the unemployment rate\ndropped last week is that hundreds of thousands of people left\nthe  labor force . Entrepreneurship provides the best path to a\nhealthier economy, and the government\u2019s role in supporting\nentrepreneurs is to help train smart people, then get out of\ntheir way.  ( Edward Glaeser , an economics professor at  Harvard\nUniversity , is a Bloomberg View columnist. He is the author of\n\u201cTriumph of the City.\u201d The opinions expressed are his own.) It\u2019s the  PlayBook  tablet, and for  Research In Motion Ltd. (RIM) \nthe stakes could hardly be greater. With market share for its\npioneering smartphones falling, the company desperately needs\nthe PlayBook to be a success. And it deserves to be, once the\nsoftware catches up to the hardware.  The PlayBook, which arrives in stores April 19, is\ninitially available only with a Wi-Fi connection. It\u2019s priced\nthe same as the Wi-Fi-only models of  Apple Inc. (AAPL) \u2019s iPad 2: $499\nfor 16 gigabytes of storage; $599 for 32 GB and $699 for 64 GB.  It really, though, shouldn\u2019t be compared to the iPad,\nwhose bigger screen makes it better for watching movies and Web-\nsurfing, but is also 40 percent heavier.  The PlayBook\u2019s true competitors are the likes of Samsung\nElectronics Co.\u2019s Galaxy Tab and  Dell Inc. (DELL) \u2019s Streak 7, in a\ncategory that might be considered pocket-sized as long as you\u2019ve\ngot good-sized pockets. In that realm, the BlackBerry instantly\nraises the bar.  Like those competitors, the PlayBook is compact enough to\nbe held in one hand. It\u2019s roughly the size of a half-sheet of\npaper and weighs about 15 ounces. Along its top edge are a too-\nsmall power button and media-playback controls; the bottom\nincludes a micro-USB connection and an HDMI video port.  Full HD  The beautiful display measures seven inches diagonally with\na 1024 x 600 resolution, the same as the Galaxy Tab and much\nbetter than the Streak. Unlike the iPad 2, the PlayBook runs\nvideos that use  Adobe Systems Inc. (ADBE) \u2019s Flash technology. Its\ncameras are also better than the iPad\u2019s: three megapixels facing\nfront and five megapixels facing rear, and it\u2019s capable of\ncapturing video in full high-definition.  RIM says it expects the PlayBook battery to provide eight\nto 10 hours of use, which seems about right based on my\nexperience. After two days of using it for a variety of tasks,\nincluding Web surfing, watching YouTube videos and editing\ndocuments using the included  Docs to Go  suite of Microsoft\nOffice-compatible productivity apps, I had plenty of juice left.  While the Galaxy and Streak use a version of  Google Inc. (GOOG) \u2019s\n Android  software that was designed for mobile phones, the\nPlayBook uses a new operating system called the BlackBerry\nTablet OS. It\u2019s fast and easy -- once I got used to the unusual\nfact that the border as well as the screen is touch-sensitive.\nYou navigate by starting with your finger on the frame and then\nswiping it across the viewing area. Open apps can be dismissed\nfrom the screen with an oddly satisfying flick gesture.  Multitasking  The new operating system is strong on multitasking. If\nyou\u2019re watching a video and bring up the PlayBook\u2019s desktop, the\nvideo continues in a smaller window. Connect it to a high-\ndefinition TV or projector and you can continue to access the\nInternet or files on the tablet while your content plays\nuninterrupted on the big screen.  The main drawback is that the PlayBook feels unfinished.\nThat\u2019s because it is: A number of critical features and\napplications, while promised, aren\u2019t yet available.  For starters, there\u2019s currently no software for accessing\nall your e-mail, calendars or contacts in one place. RIM says it\nwill be available in the summer; in the meantime you can expect\nto be doing a lot of logging into websites to access your\npersonal information.  BlackBerry Bridge  The exception is if you already have a BlackBerry: A\nprogram called Bridge will let you wirelessly view your e-mail,\ncalendars and other data on the PlayBook\u2019s larger screen and\nshare the phone\u2019s wireless data plan between the devices.  Perhaps the most important missing feature, which won\u2019t\nshow up until later in the year, is software that RIM says will\nallow the PlayBook to run a limited selection from the vast\nuniverse of Android wireless-phone applications. The mobile\nmarketplace is increasingly a battle of app-fueled ecosystems,\nand while RIM says the PlayBook is launching with about 3,000\napps, offering Android compatibility hedges the risk that\ndevelopers won\u2019t continue to write for it if the tablet isn\u2019t an\nimmediate hit.  No one knows how well the emulation software will work; the\ncompany didn\u2019t make it available for preview. And there will be\nstrings attached: Only Android apps that RIM clears will work on\nthe PlayBook, and they will be available only through\nBlackBerry\u2019s  App World  store. PlayBook users won\u2019t be able to\naccess Google\u2019s thriving  Android Market .  Also yet to come are models that work over wireless  data\nnetworks . A version for  Sprint Nextel Corp. (S) \u2019s WiMax 4G network\nis promised for the summer, with ones for the 4G technologies\nused by  Verizon Wireless  and  AT&T Inc. (T)  in the second half of the\nyear.  It\u2019s impossible to say whether RIM\u2019s bet-the-company\nstrategy will pay off. Still, who would have thought that the\nmaker of some of the world\u2019s least exciting smartphones would\nhave produced a product this slick? The PlayBook makes\nBlackBerry relevant again. These days, any\ncomplaints about Quicken should be directed at Patzer himself.  \n Tired of getting its clock cleaned by his upstart\noperation, Intuit last year bought Mint and put Patzer in charge\nof its entire personal-finance operation. Now he and his new\nparent face the task of figuring out how the various pieces will\nfit together and rejuvenating Intuit\u2019s  Quicken  franchise.  \n Mint\u2019s greatest strength is its ability to create a budget\nfor people who don\u2019t have the time or patience to make one\nthemselves. Think of it as \u201cQuicken: Short-Attention-Span\nEdition.\u201d Once you provide log-ins for your bank accounts,\ncredit cards and other financial activities, the site gathers\nyour transactions, categorizes them, analyzes your spending\npatterns and says, \u201cOK, here\u2019s how much you have to play\nwith.\u201d  \n Now, I long ago got over any reluctance to trust software\nwith my financial information. Still, it felt a little weird to\nknow Mint was looking at my spending habits. It\u2019s much the same\nfeeling I get knowing Google Inc. is analyzing the contents of\nmy Gmail messages in order to show me ads.  \n No Input  \n There are two ways of looking at how good a job Mint does.\nOn the one hand, it\u2019s impressive to have a budget at all, given\nthat Mint constructs it with, essentially, no input from you. On\nthe other hand, you\u2019d think that a service that smart ought to\nknow that a teenage daughter\u2019s purchases from the  Sephora \ncosmetics chain are more likely to be in the \u201cpersonal care\u201d\nrealm than \u201cclothing.\u201d While Mint correctly guessed that\npurchases made at  Whole Foods Market  were likely to be\ngroceries, it couldn\u2019t figure out that transactions from Kings\nSuper Markets were, too.  \n So what do you do? You notice the problems and fix them\nyourself. In other words: You\u2019re refining your budget. After a\nwhile, you may even find yourself clicking over to the Planning\ntab and beginning to do more serious work on your financial\nfuture. The key is that you\u2019re doing it as you go along, and on\nyour own timetable.  \n Among other nice features, Mint provides a simple way to\ntrack the value of your investments, a useful companion  iPhone \napp and a set of e-mail or text alerts for low balances, pending\nbills and exceeding your budget.  \n Home-Equity Stumble  \n On the other hand, the service stumbled over handling a\nhome-equity line. Mint\u2019s customer-service department replied\npromptly via e-mail with a solution that turned out to be\nincorrect, but that set me on the path to solving the problem\nmyself.  \n Mint makes money by collecting bounties from financial\ninstitutions for steering you to their products based on your\nspending patterns. (It also provides aggregated consumer-\nspending data, including to Bloomberg LP, the parent company of\nBloomberg News.)  \n To Mint\u2019s credit, it clearly labels which offers come from\nits sponsors, and you\u2019ll find unsponsored ones mixed in as well.\nBeware, though: There may be less to some of those purported\n\u201csavings\u201d than meets the eye.  \n For instance, Mint suggested a credit card from its sponsor\n Discover  that would supposedly save me a bunch of money by\nshowering me with rewards and perks. But the comparison failed\nto take into account the rewards and perks of my current card.\nOnce I went back and added those details, a lot of the purported\nsavings evaporated.  \n Missing From Mint  \n Missing from Mint is the ability to make online payments,\nas are powerful investment-management tools. For that, you will\nstill need Intuit\u2019s Quicken, which comes in various editions\nranging in price from $29.99 to $89.99, including its first new\nMac version in three years.  \n Quicken, which is one of the longest continually produced\nPC programs this side of  Microsoft  Word, could use a dash of\nMint\u2019s more youthful DNA. The program\u2019s annual updates have\nbecome increasingly indistinguishable from each other, save when\nsome annoying new feature is introduced and you have to go\nhunting for the command to turn it off. (My least favorite was\nthe now-defunct Zipingo, which constantly prompted you to rate\npeople to whom you were making payments.)  \n Quicken also requires frequent software patches that are\nsometimes more trouble than they\u2019re worth. Update No. 7 for the\n2010 version promptly blew away my ability to download\ntransactions from or send payments through my main checking\naccount.  \n I\u2019ve got nothing against Quicken. It sort of runs in the\nfamily: One of my relatives works at Intuit in a non-product\nrole, and even my father was a devoted Quicken user.  \n But Dad passed away in 1989. For better or worse, Mint.com\nisn\u2019t my father\u2019s Quicken. Mostly for the better.  \n ( Rich Jaroslovsky  is a Bloomberg News columnist. The man who tops Bloomberg's  ranking  of the world's billionaires has  paid $155 million  for a 6 percent stake in Fomento de Construcciones y Contratas, a major Spanish construction and environmental services group that barely survived the financial crisis. Gates's stake in Microsoft, the company he co-founded in 1975, now counts for less than 18 percent of his total assets. The rest of his holdings consist increasingly of down-to-earth, solid companies providing relatively low-tech, unglamorous services. They include significant stakes in the Canadian National Railway, car dealer AutoNation, waste manager Republic Services, water and sanitary chemicals company Ecolab. The investments have done well, making money faster than Gates can give it away to charity. The Spanish investment represents one of the few Gates has made outside the Americas. Apart from the Canadian railroad stake, he owns about 3 percent of Femsa, the Mexican Coke bottler, and 3 percent of media company Grupo Televisa, also in Mexico. His European exposure has been limited to tactical purchases of shares in oil company BP. FCC, at first glance, is a strange choice. It lost more than $1.4 billion in 2012. True, most of that was a one-time writedown related to the failure of FCC's Austrian subsidiary, Alpine, after an unsuccessful Eastern European expansion. Yet 50 percent of the company's construction business was concentrated in Spain, a country that has not yet recovered from a burst real estate bubble. Nobody wants to build anything in Spain. The country's \"bad bank,\" Sareb, has its hands full trying to sell billions of dollars' worth of land and buildings it has acquired in an effort to clean up bank balance sheets. At the beginning of the year, FCC faced a mountain of debt -- almost $10 billion, 8 times its market value at the time. Esther Koplovitz, Spain's richest woman and the company's largest shareholder, took the reins as chairman of the board in a bid to turn things around. A newly appointed chief executive, Juan Bejar, outlined a plan to keep the company afloat, centered on the immediate sale of non-core assets to reduce debt.  The plan has worked remarkably well. FCC now expects to end the year with about $8 billion in debt, which it intends to completely refinance. In July, the company won the largest contract in the history of Spain's construction industry: a $6 billion deal to build three subway lines in Saudi Arabia's capital, Riyadh. It is becoming the kind of business Gates appears to like -- it even includes a highly profitable waste management operation.  It is still an optimistic bet. Economic growth in Southern Europe is now largely a promise. Spain is expected to post a 0.1 percent increase in its gross domestic product in the third quarter of this year, after seven quarters of continuous decline. Many investors believe it is time to buy the growth story as it begins to unfold. FCC's share price has doubled in the past six months. For anyone hesitating to jump on the bandwagon, Gates's deal is a clear sign that the European story is sound enough even for a conservative value investor.  From Gates's perspective, however, it's only a small bet. The entire investment, at $155 million, is no more than his portfolio fluctuates on an uneventful trading day. (Leonid Bershidsky, an editor and novelist, is a Bloomberg View contributor. While the source code, or method, used by a computer\nprogram to achieve a certain result can be protected, the result\nitself can\u2019t, Advocate General Yves Bot of the EU Court of\nJustice said in a non-binding opinion yesterday. The Luxembourg-\nbased court follows this advice in a majority of cases.  World Programming Ltd. infringed SAS\u2019s copyright by\ndeveloping a system that copied the company\u2019s manuals, SAS told\nthe EU court at a hearing in September. The case seeks to\nclarify the scope of copyright protection where software copies\nthe functions of a competing program without access to its\nsource code.  \u201cTo accept that a functionality of a computer program can\nbe protected as such would amount to making it possible to\nmonopolize ideas, to the detriment of technological progress and\nindustrial development,\u201d Bot said in the advisory opinion. He\nleft it up to a national court to decide whether WPL, in copying\nfunctionalities of the SAS system, reproduced a \u201csubstantial\npart\u201d of the elements that are SAS\u2019s own creation.  It\u2019s the first time the EU\u2019s top court has been asked to\ndefine the scope of copyright protection for computer software.\nThe  High Court  in  London  in 2010  referred the case  to the EU\ntribunal for guidance on how to interpret the region\u2019s  software \nand  copyright  laws. The court said WPL\u2019s system didn\u2019t breach\nSAS\u2019s copyright.  Rulings by the EU court usually follow within six months of\nan opinion.  The case is:  C-406\/10 , SAS Institute Inc. v. World\nProgramming Ltd.  For more, click here. (CSCO)  has cut its\nincome taxes by $7 billion since 2005 by booking roughly half\nits worldwide profits at a subsidiary at the foot of the Swiss\nAlps that employs about 100 people.  Now Cisco, the largest maker of networking equipment, wants\nto save even more -- by asking Congress to waive most federal\ntaxes due when multinationals bring such offshore earnings home.\nChief Executive Officer John T. Chambers has led the charge for\nthe tax holiday, which would be the second since 2004. He says\nit would encourage companies to \u201crepatriate\u201d as much as $1\ntrillion held abroad, spur domestic investment and create jobs.  Cisco\u2019s techniques cut the effective tax rate on its\nreported international income to about 5 percent since 2008 by\nmoving profits from roughly $20 billion in annual global sales\nthrough the Netherlands,  Switzerland  and Bermuda, according to\nits records in four countries. The maneuvers, permitted by tax\nlaw, show how companies that use such strategies most\naggressively would get the biggest benefit from the holiday,\nsaid Edward D. Kleinbard, a law professor at the University of\nSouthern California in  Los Angeles .  \u201cWhy should we reward firms for successfully gaming the\ntax system when we in turn are called on to make up the missing\ntax revenues?\u201d said Kleinbard, a former corporate tax attorney\nat  Cleary Gottlieb Steen & Hamilton LLP . \u201cMuch of these\nearnings overseas are reaped from an enormous shell game: Firms\nmove their taxable income from the U.S. and other major\neconomies -- where their customers and key employees are in\nreality located -- to tax havens.\u201d  Complying With Laws  \u201cCisco complies with all global tax laws,\u201d said John Earnhardt, a spokesman for the San Jose, California-based\ncompany, which makes switches, routers and other products, in an\ne-mailed statement. \u201cIn the past three years alone, Cisco\n(which has over 35,000 U.S. employees) has paid approximately\n$4.4 billion in U.S. federal corporate income taxes.\u201d The\ncompany reported an effective tax rate last year of 17.5\npercent, half the U.S. statutory rate.  Companies including  Google Inc. (GOOG) ,  Apple Inc. (AAPL)  and  Pfizer Inc. (PFE) \nare also pushing the proposed tax holiday, which would allow\nprofits to return to the U.S. at a discounted 5.25 percent rate.\nUnder current law, American companies can defer federal income\ntaxes on most overseas earnings indefinitely. When they do\nreturn to the U.S., they\u2019re taxed at the corporate rate of 35\npercent -- with credits for foreign income taxes paid. Thus,\ncompanies paying little overseas face higher U.S. tax bills upon\nrepatriation, and would get more benefit from the discount.  Competitors\u2019 Rates  \u201cCisco would like to bring its after-tax foreign earnings\nback to spend in the U.S., but cannot with the U.S. corporate\n tax rate  at 35 percent,\u201d Earnhardt said. \u201cOur foreign\ncompetitors are allowed to repatriate foreign earnings at rates\nof 0 to 2 percent.\u201d The tax-holiday push comes as the company\nfaces shareholder pressure to add to its cash outlays by paying\nhigher dividends to boost its stock price. It closed at $15.05\nyesterday, down 25.6 percent this year.  One way multinationals avoid taxes is through \u201ctransfer\npricing,\u201d transactions among subsidiaries that allow for\nallocating expenses to high-tax countries and profits to tax\nhavens.  As governments worldwide grapple with budget deficits --\n$1.4 trillion projected for the U.S. and 597 billion euros for\nthe European Union -- such income-shifting by multinationals\ncost the U.S. Treasury about $90 billion in revenue in 2008\nalone, according to a March article by Kimberly A. Clausing, an\neconomics professor at Reed College in Portland, Oregon.  \u2018Round-Tripping\u2019  Cisco transfers a portion of the patent rights to\ntechnology developed in the U.S. to a Dutch unit, which sells\nsome of the resulting products back to its parent for eventual\ndistribution in the U.S., according to annual reports filed by\nthe Amsterdam subsidiary. That means Cisco credits about $5\nbillion in U.S. sales annually to the Netherlands.  While that sort of structure allows for shifting income\nfrom U.S. sales to offshore subsidiaries -- a maneuver known as\n\u201cround-tripping\u201d -- Cisco pays all U.S. taxes on its profit from\nU.S. sales, said Earnhardt, the spokesman.  The company\u2019s overseas units move at least some of the\nincome back to their American parent via payments for the use of\nintellectual property and other services. Cisco does not\ndisclose whether any earnings from U.S. sales remain permanently\noffshore.  At the same time, most of the income from sales in\ncountries like  Germany ,  France  and  Japan , where statutory income\ntax rates average more than 30 percent, is ultimately\ntransferred to Switzerland, meaning the other nations lose\npotential tax revenue. The result: Cisco\u2019s international\nearnings have been taxed at about 5 percent since 2008, records\nshow.  Cost of Holiday  Chambers, 61, declined to be interviewed for this article.\nOver the past year, he has campaigned for a repatriation tax\nholiday, which the nonpartisan congressional Joint Committee on\nTaxation says would cost the U.S. Treasury $78.7 billion over\nthe next decade. That\u2019s about how much the federal government\nwill spend on cancer research over that time, based on current\nbudgets.  On earnings calls, in speeches and in national media,\nChambers has made the case for the tax break, saying it would\nhelp overcome a corporate tax system he calls \u201ca dinosaur\u201d and\n\u201cput more than two million Americans back to work.\u201d  It\u2019s unclear whether any jobs would come from Cisco, which\nannounced plans in May to shed an unspecified number of workers.\nEarnhardt, the spokesman, declined to comment on hiring plans\nfor the company, whose customers include  Verizon Communications\nInc. (VZ)  and  AT&T Inc. (T)   Cash Overseas  All told, Cisco has accumulated $31.6 billion in overseas\nearnings on which it has paid no U.S. income taxes yet, records\nshow -- part of more than $1 trillion in U.S. companies\u2019\noffshore profits, according to data compiled by Bloomberg. In\ntotal, almost 90 percent of Cisco\u2019s cash sits overseas.  \u201cI create jobs overseas,\u201d Chambers told interviewer\nLesley Stahl on the CBS News program \u201c60 Minutes\u201d in March.\n\u201cI build plants overseas and I badly want to bring that money\nback.\u201d  The company needs that cash to prop up its share price --\nwhich explains its support for the tax break, said Sandeep Shyamsukha, a communications analyst at Auriga USA LLC in  San\nFrancisco . Since 2006, Cisco has spent $43.5 billion on stock\nbuy-backs. In April, it paid its first shareholder dividend.\nConsumer advocate Ralph Nader, who owns Cisco stock, this month\ncalled for doubling the payout, as first reported in the Wall\nStreet Journal.  \u2018Tremendous Pressure\u2019  \u201cThe stock is struggling, the company has reached a mature\nphase and investors are demanding more returns,\u201d said\nShyamsukha, who has a \u201chold\u201d recommendation on Cisco shares.\n\u201cThere\u2019s tremendous pressure on the management to give out\ndividends and higher buybacks and that\u2019s probably what\u2019s pushing\nthem in this direction.\u201d  U.S. companies used $312 billion they repatriated under a\n2004 tax holiday largely for stock repurchases, while doing\nlittle direct hiring or domestic investment, according to a\npaper in the current issue of the Journal of Finance\u00a0by\nprofessors at the University of  Illinois , Harvard University,\nand the Massachusetts Institute of Technology. It was the latest\nin a series of studies that reached similar conclusions.  While Treasury Secretary Timothy F. Geithner has expressed\nskepticism about a new repatriation break, Representative Kevin Brady, a Texas Republican, introduced a bill on May 11 that,\nlike the 2004 measure, would not require companies to use their\ncash for hiring.  Lower the Gate  Brady declined to address why his measure does not include\na hiring requirement. \u201cWith millions of Americans seeking work\nit makes good economic sense to temporarily lower the tax gate\nand allow up to a trillion dollars of stranded American profits\nto flow back into our economy,\u201d he said in a statement.  The idea gained momentum last week after Senator Charles Schumer, a New York Democrat, said his party\u2019s caucus was\ndiscussing whether short-term revenue from the holiday could\nfund an \u201cinfrastructure bank\u201d to create jobs. Senator John Kerry, a Massachusetts Democrat, has also signaled that he may\nreconsider his previous opposition.  Cisco,  Oracle Corp. (ORCL) ,  Microsoft Corp. (MSFT)  and others formed a\ncoalition called WIN America Campaign that plans to spend\nseveral million dollars pushing the issue. The group is being\nadvised by SKDKnickerbocker, a Washington-based political\nconsulting firm for which Anita Dunn, President Obama\u2019s former\ncommunications director, is a managing director.  \u201cWe simply don\u2019t think it\u2019s a good idea to do nothing while\na trillion dollars sits overseas,\u201d said Doug Thornell, a vice\npresident for the firm who is advising the campaign.  Terra Cotta Hub  Cisco\u2019s overseas hub, in a terra cotta-faced office on the\noutskirts of Amsterdam, coordinates manufacturing, distribution\nand sales to  Europe ,  Asia  and other markets. Cisco Systems\nInternational BV employs about 2 percent of the company\u2019s global\nworkforce of roughly 70,000. It gets credit for more than half\nof Cisco\u2019s worldwide sales, including part of the U.S. business,\naccording to Dutch and U.S. filings.  Beginning in 1996, the Netherlands subsidiary began paying\nfor part of Cisco\u2019s ongoing research in the U.S. under a cost-\nsharing agreement, according to corporate records. Like other\nU.S. technology companies, Cisco qualifies for U.S. tax benefits\nby doing most of its research and development domestically. By\npaying for some of it, the overseas unit can remove a chunk of\nany subsequent profits from the U.S. and claim them offshore.  Buy-in Payments  Cisco\u2019s foreign operations also made so-called buy-in\npayments to the U.S. parent, acquiring an interest in some\nexisting intellectual property -- and a claim on future profits\nfrom it.  The company hasn\u2019t disclosed the amounts paid in those\ntransactions since 2002. The U.S. Treasury Department requires\nthat foreign subsidiaries pay an \u201carm\u2019s length\u201d price, or the\namount that would be paid by an unrelated party.  As a result of these arrangements, Cisco must buy from its\nown Dutch subsidiary some of the products it then sells to U.S.\ncustomers, even for equipment based on patents developed in the\nU.S. In 2008, for example, the Amsterdam unit reported $6.1\nbillion in sales to the U.S. and  Canada  -- equaling about 30\npercent of Cisco\u2019s total sales in those two countries.  The Dutch unit reported just a 1 percent profit margin on\nits total revenue of $22.1 billion in 2008. That\u2019s because most\nof Cisco\u2019s overseas earnings flow from the Netherlands to a\nseparate subsidiary in Switzerland under a sublicensing\nagreement for intellectual property.  Dutch Rules  Dutch tax rules make it cheaper for companies to route\npayments to their units in tax havens like Bermuda through the\nNetherlands instead of sending them there directly, said Richard Murphy, director of UK-based Tax Research LLP.  In Rolle, about 25 miles north of Geneva, a subsidiary\ncalled Cisco Systems International Sarl collects billions of\ndollars a year from its Dutch cousin. The town, which features\nsweeping views of the Alps and Lake Geneva, is home to units of\nseveral U.S. multinationals, lured by tax advantages. Rolle\u2019s\nmain pedestrian drag, Grand Rue, is lined by boulangeries and\nreal estate offices listing homes for millions of Swiss francs.  A short walk from 13th century buildings is Cisco\u2019s Swiss\nsubsidiary, housed in a five-story structure with horizontal\nmetal blinds that resembles a giant air conditioner.  Although Cisco does not disclose precise amounts paid to\nthe Swiss company, the Dutch unit reported paying $9.6 billion\nto other Cisco subsidiaries in 2008, including \u201croyalty\npayments for the license of intellectual property.\u201d The Swiss\nunit\u2019s tax rate has been less than 5 percent in recent years.  Other Countries\u2019 Rates  That beats the income-tax rates in many countries where\nCisco has sales: Germany\u2019s combined national-local rate is 30.2\npercent; France\u2019s 34.4 percent; Japan\u2019s 39.5 percent and the\nU.K.\u2019s 26 percent, according to figures from the Organization\nfor Economic Cooperation and Development.  While Switzerland\u2019s average combined statutory corporate\nincome tax rate is about 21 percent, some companies receive\nsignificant exemptions at both the federal level and the canton,\nthe Swiss equivalent of the state. A spokesman for the Swiss\nFederal Tax Administration declined to comment.  The unit in Rolle, which has roughly 100 workers, is owned\nby yet another Cisco subsidiary, registered at the offices of\nConyers Dill & Pearman, a law firm in Hamilton, Bermuda. For\nU.S. tax purposes, profits from the Swiss and Dutch units flow\nto this shell company, one of hundreds the law firm handles on\nBermuda, which has no corporate income tax.  Also Serving Google  One of the three directors listed for Cisco\u2019s Bermuda\nsubsidiary, a manager at Conyers Dill, is also a director for a\npair of units that helps cut the tax bills of another U.S.\ntechnology company: Google. The search engine giant used\nsubsidiaries in Bermuda, the Netherlands and Ireland to cut $3.1\nbillion from its worldwide tax bill over three years, Bloomberg\nNews  reported  in October.  The benefits from Cisco\u2019s foreign profits lopped 19.3\npercentage points off its total tax rate last year. Bloomberg\ncalculated Cisco\u2019s $7 billion tax savings since 2005 by applying\neach year\u2019s foreign tax benefit to pretax earnings as disclosed\nin U.S. filings. Results were combined for all years after the\ncompany restructured its overseas operations for tax reasons in\n2004.  While tax strategies have boosted Cisco\u2019s earnings, they\nmean less revenue for governments in countries where the company\noperates, a trend that may affect Cisco as well. The company is\nseeing slowdowns in its business with cash-strapped governments,\nChambers said during a May 11 earnings call.  Historically, the public sector has made up 20 percent of\nCisco\u2019s sales, Chambers said -- that\u2019d be about $8 billion in\ntaxpayer-funded sales last year. \u201cWe do not underestimate the\ntransition in front of us,\u201d he said.
