The immigrants from Taiwan also embody an argument for its opponents: They\u2019re older than 50.  Some 11 million undocumented workers would pay taxes to support government  health  and retirement programs if a rapidly aging nation gives them citizenship, advocates say. Yet a  study  by Princeton University researchers suggests a hidden cost. The newest Americans from Mexico, it found, are sponsoring older family members at a rate 16 times greater than such households did when the U.S. last rewrote immigration laws in 1986.  The trend of naturalized citizens sponsoring older parents for U.S. residency may offset some of the presumed payoff of turning millions of undocumented workers into legal taxpayers, according to the study. Some of those family members would be eligible for Medicaid, whose rising costs are part of the debate over U.S. fiscal solvency.  \u201cI understand the economic benefits,\u201d said Marta Tienda, a co-author of the report, presented last month. \u201cBut we have to be really up front about what it\u2019s going to cost us.\u201d  The Princeton study only attempted to measure the number of newcomers who are sponsored by naturalized citizens; it didn\u2019t put a price tag on absorbing an increasing number of older immigrants.  The Congressional Budget Office  said in a May 2 letter  to House Budget Committee Chairman Paul Ryan, a Wisconsin Republican, that it hadn\u2019t completed an analysis of proposed legislation debated this week in Congress.  Medicaid Expense  The CBO  estimated in 2006  that changes similar to those being considered would have increased spending by $53.6 billion during a 10-year period in categories including Medicaid, the state-federal health-insurance program for the poor and disabled.  At the same time, the CBO said, the legislation would have brought in a surplus of $65.7 billion through income and Social Security taxes, yielding a net surplus of $12.1 billion. The agency estimated the immigration measure would have increased gross domestic product 0.3 percent to 0.4 percent from 2007 to 2011, and 0.8 percent to 1.3 percent from 2012 to 2016.  The Princeton findings were echoed in part of a report released this week by the Heritage Foundation, a nonprofit research organization led by former U.S. Senator Jim DeMint, a South Carolina Republican and Tea Party leader. The foundation  warned  in its report that many older immigrants \u201cwould be poor and heavily dependent on taxpayers.\u201d  Business Forward  A  report  last month by Business Forward, an advocacy group whose sponsors include  Microsoft Corp. (MSFT)  (MSFT),  Citigroup Inc (C)  (C). and  Wal-Mart Stores Inc. (WMT)  (WMT), said contributions from undocumented workers make up almost 10 percent of the Social Security trust fund. The funds, which provide retirement or disability benefits to more than one in four U.S. households, are slated to begin running out of money in 2033. Medicare trust funds are on pace to run empty by 2024, according to a report last year by the trustees.  \u201cWe have to consider both sides of the equation,\u201d Nikhil Joshi, research director for the Washington-based group, said in a telephone interview. \u201cImmigrants tend to be younger and healthier than natives, and that will help us push those costs down.\u201d  Even so, Joshi acknowledged that \u201cimmigration reform can have unintended consequences. The stakes for getting it right are huge.\u201d  Latinos Doubling  The percentage of new legal permanent immigrants who are older than 50 has risen during the last quarter century, especially among newcomers from North America and Asia, according to Department of Homeland Security data analyzed by the Princeton researchers.  The percentage of older Asian immigrants has increased about 42 percent since 1985. About one in five of the 1.6 million Asian immigrants admitted from 2006 to 2009 were older than 50. Asians were the fastest-growing racial group in the U.S. in the last decade.  The rate for new North American residents, mostly from Mexico, the U.S.\u2019s largest source of immigrants, rose even faster. The percentage of North American immigrants older than 50 has more than doubled since 1985. Almost 17 percent of the 1.5 million immigrants admitted from 2006 to 2009 were older than 50, the researchers said.  In examining migration patterns among families, the Princeton researchers  found  the number of Mexican relatives older than 50 who were sponsored by naturalized citizens grew 16 fold from 1986 to 2000. The average naturalized citizen from Mexico sponsored 1.12 older family members in 2000, up from 0.07 in 1986.  New Arrivals  The report also found significant increases in parental sponsorship from 1991 to 2000 for new citizens born in China, India and the Philippines. The study only tracked those records up to 2000 because it typically takes a decade or more for a new arrival to become a naturalized U.S. citizen eligible to vouch for family members.  People born in Mexico sponsored 6.4 family members per naturalized citizen, the highest rate of any country in the study.  Naturalized citizens from China sponsored an average of two family members older than 50, and a total of 6.2 people each. People born in India or the Philippines sponsored 5.1 total family members, with an average of 1.7 older than 50.  Family Reunification  The dilemma raised by the Princeton research has its roots in a 1965 immigration overhaul championed by the late Senator Edward Kennedy, a Massachusetts Democrat. The 1965 law, enacted the same year Congress created Medicare, the federal universal health-insurance plan for the elderly, allowed naturalized citizens to sponsor immediate family members.  At the time, immigration reform was supported because it was expected to bring more Europeans to the U.S. Asians, who now make up about 5 percent of the population, constituted roughly 1 percent of the U.S. total then.  Kennedy\u2019s brother, then-Attorney General Robert Kennedy, said in congressional testimony that about 5,000 Asian immigrants would arrive in the first year, \u201cbut we do not expect that there would be any great influx after that.\u201d  The assumptions were based on \u201csentimental myopia or factual naivet\u00e9,\u201d wrote Tienda, the Princeton study co-author and daughter of an undocumented worker.  Deported Parents  In 2012, a record 33.7 million Hispanics of Mexican origin lived in the U.S., including 22.3 million born in this country, according to an  analysis  of Census data released May 1 by the Pew Research Center. Among them are children of immigrants who are eager to reunite with family members deported under current law.  Bianca Rojo, 22, who was born in San Francisco to undocumented Mexican immigrants, has lived apart from her parents since the age of 16, soon after they were denied asylum and deported to Mexico.  When she turned 21, Rojo, who lives in Richmond, California, with her two younger brothers, applied to sponsor their parents to return to the U.S. With the help of a grandmother, she\u2019s seeking a waiver to allow her parents to reenter the country.  \u201cIt\u2019s been very hard, not just emotionally hard but also physically and mentally draining,\u201d Rojo said. \u201cI still have to worry about how am I going to get to school. (BBRY) , the struggling Canadian smartphone maker, is considering putting itself up for sale after the lackluster debut of the BlackBerry 10 lineup dimmed its prospects as an independent company.  A special board committee will consider ways to enhance BlackBerry\u2019s value and scale, including joint ventures, partnerships or a sale of the company, according to a statement today.  JPMorgan Chase & Co. (JPM)  will serve as its financial adviser.  BlackBerry shares  gained 10 percent in  New York  trading.  The announcement builds on a move last year when BlackBerry hired JPMorgan and  RBC Capital Markets  to advise the company on strategic alternatives. At the time, Chief Executive Officer Thorsten Heins said a sale wasn\u2019t the \u201cmain direction\u201d he was considering. The company\u2019s outlook has worsened since then, with the revamped BlackBerry 10 -- the linchpin of a turnaround strategy -- meeting scant demand.  \u201cWhat BlackBerry is doing is the appropriate course of action,\u201d said  Charlie Wolf , an analyst with Needham & Co. in New York, who has the equivalent of a sell rating on the stock. The likelihood of a sale is at least 50 percent, he said. \u201cThe other options -- much less likely.\u201d  Heins will join fellow board members Timothy Dattels, Barbara Stymiest, Richard Lynch and Bert Nordberg on the new committee. Fairfax Financial CEO Prem Watsa, whose firm is BlackBerry\u2019s largest shareholder, will step down from the board to avoid conflicts that might arise from the discussions.  \u2018Right Time\u2019  \u201cGiven the importance and strength of our technology, and the evolving industry and competitive landscape, we believe that now is the right time to explore strategic alternatives,\u201d Dattels, a TPG Capital executive who will serve as the committee\u2019s chairman, said in the statement.  BlackBerry shares rose to $10.78 at the close in New York, marking the biggest one-day gain since March.  The company\u2019s days as a publicly held business may be numbered, said BlackBerry investor Brian Huen.  \u201cI think they\u2019re going to try to sell the company or take it private,\u201d said Huen, a managing partner with Red Sky Capital Management Ltd. in Toronto. His firm manages C$220 million in assets, including shares of BlackBerry.  Going Private?  Today\u2019s stock surge followed a 5.7 percent rise on Aug. 9, the previous trading day, when Reuters reported that the company was considering going private.  Heins and the board are coming around to the idea that going private would give them the leeway to fix problems out of the public view, Reuters reported, citing unidentified sources. Prior to Aug. 9, the stock had tumbled 22 percent this year.  Canada  Pension Plan Investment Board CEO  Mark Wiseman  said last week he would consider an investment in BlackBerry if the smartphone maker decided to go private.  \u201cIt\u2019s safe to say that any large deal in Canada or elsewhere is something that we would make sure we took a hard look at,\u201d Wiseman said in an interview. \u201cYou could say that about that asset.\u201d  Linda Sims, a spokeswoman for Canada Pension, which held 4.6 million  BlackBerry shares  at the end of March, declined to comment further today.  Silver Lake (SLR)   Before Heins became CEO in January 2012, the company  held talks  with private-equity firm  Silver Lake  Management LLC about possibly going private, a person familiar with the discussions told  Bloomberg News  last year.  The talks were preliminary and the two sides weren\u2019t able to agree on a potential valuation, the person said. Silver Lake, based in  Menlo Park ,  California , has had no meetings with BlackBerry in the past year, a person with knowledge of the discussions said last week.  Watsa\u2019s decision to resign from the board indicates that the Toronto-based businessman may be involved in some local attempt to rescue the company, Red Sky\u2019s Huen said. Such a move would face less scrutiny than a foreign bid. The Canadian government automatically reviews all foreign takeovers of companies with asset values of more than C$344 million ($334 million) to determine whether the transactions are a \u201cnet benefit\u201d to the country.  \u201cThere\u2019s a desire with folks like Prem Watsa and CPP to get involved and keep the thing together,\u201d Huen said. \u201cIt\u2019s a bit of a Canadian champion from a technology standpoint and there\u2019s going to be a desire to keep it together.\u201d  Paul Rivett , president of Fairfax, said he and Watsa declined to comment. Microsoft Corp., BlackBerry\u2019s rival in the smartphone-software market, isn\u2019t a probable buyer because of its partnership with mobile-phone maker  Nokia Oyj (NOK1V) , Wolf said.  If there was some indication BlackBerry\u2019s new phones were gaining traction, \u201ca buyer out of the PC or smartphone industry might emerge,\u201d he said. \u201cBut you got to believe that\u2019s not the case as yet.\u201d  Cost Cutting  BlackBerry fired 5,000 workers last year as part of a plan to eliminate $1 billion in operating costs. Analysts had expected the cutbacks to help the company post a profit last quarter. Instead, BlackBerry lost $84 million, dragged down by the sluggish sales of the BlackBerry Z10. The new touch-screen phone, introduced at a lavish event in New York in January, missed estimates by almost a million units last quarter. The company is projecting another loss for the current period.  \u201cIt could be a buyer from industry but it\u2019s more likely to be one from outside the industry and it would seem that the valuable assets are the patents and the NOC,\u201d said Wolf, referring to the secure network operating center, which the company operates for its clients. Penney Co.  expose the risks.  The number of companies making upfront payments surged to more than 70 this year from 41 in all of 2012, according to governance-advisory firm GMI Ratings Inc. J.C. Penney fired Johnson in April, 17 months after giving him a signing bonus of $52.7 million in shares to recruit him from Apple Inc.  J.C. Penney highlights the pitfalls of a practice that can reward executives who haven\u2019t done any work yet to the detriment of shareholders. Golden hellos, mostly paid in options and stock grants, got costlier amid rising stock markets after the recession ended in 2009. Among the biggest this year: Zynga Inc.\u2019s $45 million package to attract game-industry veteran  Don Mattrick  as chief executive officer.  \u201cInvestors should be skeptical of golden hellos, which represent pay decoupled from performance and provide no retention incentives,\u201d said  Lucian Bebchuk , a Harvard Law School professor in Cambridge, Massachusetts, who has researched CEO pay. \u201cEquity incentives that have not vested yet should best be viewed as ones that have not been earned yet.\u201d  Investors have so far paid less attention to golden hellos than to the large severance payouts known as golden parachutes. They should be concerned:  J.C. Penney  shares slumped 50 percent during Johnson\u2019s tenure, while Hewlett-Packard Co. dropped 46 percent under  Leo Apotheker , ousted in 2011 just 10 months after getting $8.6 million in signing bonus and relocation benefit. In total, Apotheker was entitled to about $34.7 million in cash and stock for less than one year\u2019s work.  Perform First  \u201cThe incentive should be they will come to the company and perform and be rewarded,\u201d said  Jon Luther , chairman of Arby\u2019s Restaurant Group Inc. and former Dunkin\u2019 Brands Inc. CEO.  Candidates for high-level positions who asked for signing bonuses to take jobs at companies where Luther was a board member have been rejected in favor of those who didn\u2019t, the executive said, declining to identify the companies and candidates for confidentiality reasons.  Luther said he never asked for such a bonus to take a job, and was never offered one: \u201cI said I\u2019ll get it done and you can take care of me when I succeed.\u201d  Golden hellos are often a sign of other compensation dysfunctions, said  Greg Ruel , a GMI senior research consultant. Companies cited by GMI for giving out upfront payments are graded a D in average for their overall pay practices -- on a scale of A to F. Take Chesapeake Energy Corp. and Best Buy Co., two companies that have been flagged by GMI for a golden hello: They also failed so-called say-on-pay votes in recent years, prompting changes in their compensation practices.  Thornton\u2019s Bonus  In April, the same month as Johnson\u2019s ouster, golden hellos were brought into the spotlight by Barrick Gold Corp. investors including Canada\u2019s six largest pension funds. They opposed an $11.9 million welcome package in cash to co-Chairman  John Thornton , the former Goldman Sachs Group Inc. president.  \u201cThis is the kind of situation where you are not getting anything in advance but yet you have to pay upfront for the hopes and the aspirations of what will be delivered down the road,\u201d  Robert Gill , a Toronto-based fund manager at Aston Hill Financial Inc., which manages C$8 billion ($7.7 billion) of assets including Barrick shares, said in an interview this month. \u201cWe don\u2019t like that. We don\u2019t think that\u2019s commensurate with how the industry should remunerate people.\u201d  GMI decided to include golden hellos as a possible negative mark in its rating system in April because of evidence the payments were increasing, Ruel said. In 2011, S&P 500 companies awarded 34 signing bonuses, a 26 percent jump from 2009, GMI found. The surprising gain prompted the governance firm to look beyond the index. The payouts have risen even as CEO turnover fell to the lowest since at least 2004 last year.  Outside CEOs  Companies often justify golden hellos by saying they cover for compensation that new CEOs had to forgo for leaving their previous employers. The payments partly explain why hiring an outside CEO costs about a third more than promoting from within, according to Chris McGoldrick, a senior research analyst at compensation tracker Equilar Inc.  Board compensation committees will have to weigh that reality as they search to fill CEO vacancies at  Microsoft Corp. , Lululemon Athletica Inc. and even J.C. Penney, which is seeking a replacement for its current interim CEO. Last year, about 26 percent of new S&P 500 CEOs were hired outside the company, according to executive recruiter Spencer Stuart.  \u201cThe board has to decide if they want to pay the freight to move the CEO from one job to another,\u201d said  David Larcker , a professor at the Stanford Graduate School of Business who has done research on executive compensation. \u201cIt\u2019s up to the board to make sure it\u2019s good for shareholders. I consider a request for cash a red flag, though.\u201d  \u2018Highly Desirable\u2019  Barrick founder and Chairman  Peter Munk  told investors who opposed Thornton\u2019s bonus at the April shareholders\u2019 meeting that he needed the former banker, \u201ca highly desirable, well-known commodity,\u201d to secure access to governments and protect against resource nationalism.  \u201cI do realize Thornton has a big name but now he really has to deliver,\u201d said Gill, the Aston Hill fund manager.  The board is in the process of strengthening governance practices through the addition of independent directors and improvements to executive compensation,  Andy Lloyd , a spokesman for the Toronto-based gold producer, said in an e-mail.  At Plano, Texas-based retailer J.C. Penney, Johnson got his November 2011 signing bonus, in restricted stock, to make up for what the executive had to leave at Apple, where he had led retail operations. Johnson couldn\u2019t be reached for comment.  Kristin Hays , a J.C. Penney spokeswoman, declined to comment.  Too Soon  Sometimes golden hellos do pay off for investors. Best Buy\u2019s shares have more than doubled since the consumer-electronics retailer lured  Hubert Joly  as chief executive in 2012 with a welcome package including a $3.5 million cash bonus and equity grants and options valued at almost $13 million.  For Zynga, a San Francisco-based social-gaming pioneer whose games have faded in popularity, it\u2019s too soon to tell. Although the stock has risen since Mattrick came on board in July and worked at cutting expenses and engineering a turnaround, it still trades at less than half the 2011 IPO price. Dani Dudeck, a Zynga spokeswoman, declined to comment.  Same goes for Chesapeake and health insurer WellPoint Inc., which awarded signing bonuses to their new CEOs this year.  \u201cThe board has to be careful not to fall in love with any one candidate,\u201d said  James Post , a corporate governance and ethics professor at Boston University School of Management. \u201cYou have to look for a good candidate at a good price, not a good candidate at any price.\u201d  To contact the reporter on this story: Jeff Green in Southfield, Michigan at  jgreen16@bloomberg.net   To contact the editor responsible for this story: Tom Giles at  tgiles5@bloomberg.net","path":".\/2008_2012_msft_bloomberg_news\/golden-hellos-surge-as-ceos-get-signing-jumbo-bonuses.txt"},{"id":7041835,"title":"HTC Said to Halt Larger Windows Phone on Display Resolution","released_at":"<date>December 18 2012<\/date> <time>03:48:33<\/time>","content":"HTC Corp. Traders seem to think Nokia got the better end of the deal: Its share price is up by more than one-third since the announcement, while Microsoft\u2019s market value has fallen by about 6 percent. Nokia shareholders certainly have reason to be happy: They ditched a money-losing division for cash, enabling the company to focus on the relatively more profitable business of selling network equipment. (Of course, they might have been in a  much better position  had Nokia decided to make phones using Google\u2019s Android operating system rather than Microsoft\u2019s Windows.) While I wouldn\u2019t want to question the judgment of the professionals who have money on the line, it\u2019s also possible that Microsoft made a good move as well. To see why, it helps to look back at the work of  Ronald Coase , a Nobel-winning economist who died yesterday at the age of 102. His prize was awarded in part for his research into the reasons why corporations exist. This might sound like an odd question to have to ask, but standard economics theory says that market prices provide the best signals for how to allocate resources. In theory, that means we ought to live in a world where everyone contracts out his labor and capital as needed. In practice, however, businessmen find it advantageous to organize people and machines and patents into corporations that are centrally managed. (A weird hybrid model can be found at  Sears .) Coase\u2019s  explanation  was that negotiations and auctions cost time and money: What does this have to do with Microsoft and Nokia? Nokia has been Microsoft\u2019s main partner for making Windows smartphones, but it has been losing so much money from that business that some people think it was on the verge of bankruptcy. (That\u2019s a sad state of affairs for the Finnish company, which first sold cell phones with e-mail capabilities  back in 1996 .) By contrast, Microsoft is still one of the world\u2019s most valuable companies -- its market capitalization is about the same as Google\u2019s -- and possesses tens of billions of dollars in cash (mostly  offshore ). Per Coase, the acquisition allows the tech giant to continue to invest in mobile technology without having to worry as much about whether it was making money right away. That might not turn out well -- Bloomberg View\u2019s editors think that Microsoft should  just give up and die  -- but it doesn\u2019t strike me as an obviously wrongheaded strategy for a company that has watched smartphones and tablets displace personal computers. After all, Nokia\u2019s low-end phones are extremely popular in poorer countries. Optimists  argue  that, given time, those low-margin devices could prove to be the first step on a ladder up to high-margin smartphones powered by Windows. That would be a sweet victory for Steve Ballmer, Microsoft\u2019s chief executive officer -- and also for Ronald Coase. (Matthew C. Klein is a writer for Bloomberg View. (GOOG) , joined by BlackBerry,\ntoday urged U.S. regulators to investigate whether some\ncompetitors violate antitrust laws by hiring companies to file\npatent-infringement suits for them.  There\u2019s been a rise of so-called privateers, which obtain\npatents from technology companies and then file infringement\nlawsuits against the sellers\u2019 competitors, Google and BlackBerry\nsaid in a filing with the U.S. Federal Trade Commission and\nDepartment of Justice. Internet service provider  EarthLink Inc. (ELNK) \nand  Red Hat Inc. (RHT) , the largest seller of Linux operating-system\nsoftware, also joined the submission.  The filing was part of broader  comments  by the companies on\nso-called patent assertion entities, which obtain patents for\nthe sole purpose of extracting royalties. Such companies\n\u201cimpose an ever-rising tax on innovative industries,\u201d Google,\nowner of the most widely used search engine, said in the filing.  \u201cWe are also concerned with, and suggest that the agencies\nshould seriously examine, the outsourcing of patent enforcement\nby operating companies - companies that develop technology and\nsell products - to PAEs and the competitive implications of such\nactivities,\u201d Google and  BlackBerry (BBRY)  wrote. \u201cSo-called\n\u2018privateering\u2019 amplifies the threat to innovation and\ncompetition already posed by PAEs.\u201d  Nokia Oyj (NOK) ,  Microsoft Corp. (MSFT) ,  BT Group Plc (BT\/A) \u2019s British Telecom\nand Alcatel-Lucent are among companies connected with these\nlicensing firms. Companies that would, in the past, assert their\npatents in lawsuits to protect their property now say they work\nwith privateers to make money from past research.  Privateer Arrangements  In a typical lawsuit, competing companies accuse each other\nof infringing patents and then reach a cross-licensing\nagreement, which lowers the amount of money that has to change\nhands. That type of resolution isn\u2019t possible when one side\ndoesn\u2019t make any products, and therefore doesn\u2019t have to fear a\nretaliatory lawsuit.  By transferring patents to such a firm, for a cut of any\nrevenue from a settlement or fees, a manufacturer can get a\nfinancial reward while insulating itself and its products from\ninfringement claims and limiting its legal costs, Google and\nBlackBerry said.  Google said assertion entities can increase the cost of\nlicensing because a portfolio can be split among multiple\nprivateers, each demanding a royalty. That\u2019s especially true\nwhen the larger company has patents that relate to technology\nused across the industry.  \u201cThese arrangements (and others) between operating\ncompanies and PAEs can, depending on the facts, transgress the\nantitrust laws,\u201d Google and BlackBerry wrote.  Google, FTC  Mountain View, California-based Google has been the target\nof an FTC investigation over the patent-licensing practices of\nits Motorola Mobility unit, which was accused of demanding\nunfairly high royalties for patents on industry standards.\nGoogle reached a settlement with the FTC on the issue in\nJanuary.  In the filing, Google and BlackBerry singled out a pledge\nNokia made to license all of its patents for mobile-phone\nstandards at a 2 percent royalty. Were a company like Nokia to\nsplit some of its standard patents among three different\nentities, it would increase the total cost to 8 percent, Google\nsaid.  An investigation into the privateering model \u201cwould\nprovide a foundation for the antitrust agencies to assess\nwhether the solutions to the competitive concerns patent\noutsourcing arrangements pose lie in antitrust enforcement, in\nchanges in the patent laws (where the antitrust enforcement\nagencies might play an important advocacy role), or elsewhere.\u201d  \u2018Important Channel\u2019  In a Dec. 10 hearing held by the FTC and DOJ, Espoo,\nFinland-based Nokia defended the practice.  \u201cOften we do not have the resources or otherwise are not\nbest positioned ourselves to exploit those inventions, either\nthrough our own products or through our own licensing\nactivities,\u201d Paul Melin, Nokia\u2019s chief intellectual property\nofficer, said on a panel. \u201cDivestments of patents have become a\nvery important channel for us to monetize and realize the value\nof our research and development.\u201d  Waterloo, Ontario-based BlackBerry and Nokia signed a\npatent-licensing deal in December to resolve disputes between\nthe two companies. That agreement didn\u2019t end a suit against\nBlackBerry by MobileMedia Ideas LLC, a licensing company that\nholds former Nokia and Sony Corp. patents. MobileMedia also won\na December trial against  Apple Inc. (AAPL) , which has a patent\nagreement with Nokia, too.  It can be difficult to identify who is profiting from a\npatent suit. One lawsuit against Google is by Suffolk\nTechnologies, whose owners include Goldman Sachs Group Inc.,\nGeneral Atlantic Partners LP and Boston Consulting Group Inc.,\naccording to a Dec. 7 court ruling on the ownership question. The\nfirm favors \u201cstuff that gives you a real yield,\u201d he said.  Even though the global economy is slowing and credit-rating\ndowngrades exceed upgrades, rising demand has allowed companies\nworldwide to sell about $2.16 trillion of bonds this year, the\nsecond-fastest pace on record based on data compiled by\nBloomberg. Instead of using the proceeds to expand and hire more\nworkers as desired by central banks that have cut interest rates\nto record lows, companies are mainly refinancing existing\nobligations or hoarding the money.  Cash Cushion  The ratio of cash to total assets for companies in the\nStandard & Poor\u2019s 500 Index rose to about 10 percent from 5.7\npercent five years ago, data compiled by Bloomberg show.  AT&T Inc. (T) , the Dallas-based wireless carrier and biggest\nU.S. nonfinancial issuer of debt securities, has extended the\nweighted average maturity of its bonds to 15.6 years from 13.3\nyears in 2009 while cutting the  average coupon  on its $64.4\nbillion of notes to 5.34 percent from 6.42 percent, according to\ndata compiled by Bloomberg.  \u201cPeople are saying the economy is sluggish, but it\u2019s not\nso bad that companies are going to start defaulting left and\nright and getting downgraded severely because they\u2019ve got a lot\nof cash and have funded out their debt maturities,\u201d  Martin Fridson , a global credit strategist in New York at BNP Paribas\nInvestment Partners who started his career as a corporate debt\ntrader in 1976, said in a telephone interview last week.  Double Yields  While investment-grade corporate bond yields are at record\nlows of about 3 percent, that\u2019s more than double what government\nsecurities pay, Bank of America Merrill Lynch indexes show. The\n gap , which ended last week at 2.05 percentage points, averaged\n0.71 percentage point in 2006 and the first half of 2007, before\nthe start of the worst financial crisis since the Great\nDepression.  Those rates are a powerful lure because government bond\nyields in the U.S., Germany and the U.K. are either below zero\non an absolute basis or after accounting for inflation. So-\ncalled real yields on 10-year Treasuries are about negative 0.2\npercent. Similar measures are negative 0.48 percent in Germany\nand negative 0.88 percent in the U.K.  Yields on 10-year Treasuries fell to a record 1.3960\npercent today, according to Bloomberg Bond Trader prices. Five-\nyear yields also reached an all-time low of 0.5411 percent.  The benchmark 10-year yield fell three basis points, or\n0.03 percentage point, to 1.43 percent at 12:44 p.m. in New\nYork. The 1.75 percent note due in May 2022 rose 9\/32, or $2.81\nper $1,000 face amount, to 102 31\/32.  BlackRock, Glenmede  \u201cGiven that the risk-free rate is very expensive, you\u2019ve\ngot to somehow generate some return,\u201d Roger Bridges, who\noversees $15.3 billion as the Sydney-based head of fixed income\nat Tyndall Investment Management Ltd., said in a July 16\ntelephone interview. \u201cCorporate bonds look very good.\u201d  Bridges said he was considering buying bonds sold in\nAustralia last week by Export-Import Bank of Korea. Loudi, home to 4 million people in Chairman  Mao Zedong \u2019s\nhome province of Hunan, is paying for the project with 1.2\nbillion yuan ($185 million) in bonds, guaranteed by land valued\nat $1.5 million an acre. That\u2019s about the same as prices in\nWinnetka, a Chicago suburb that is one of the richest U.S. towns,\nwhere the average household earns more than $250,000 a year.  In Loudi, people take home $2,323 annually and there are no\nOlympics here on any calendar.  \u201cThe debt isn\u2019t a problem as Loudi is not a developed\nplace,\u201d Yang Haibo, an official at the city\u2019s financing vehicle,\nsays as he sits with colleagues in a smoke-filled meeting room\nunder a No Smoking sign. \u201cIt\u2019s an emerging city.\u201d  A 3,300-mile (5,310-kilometer) tour of three cities in\n China , coupled with reviews of dozens of Chinese-language bond\nprospectuses that offer an unusually transparent view into local\ngovernment debt, shows just how widespread such borrowing has\nbecome. In China, as in the U.S. before the collapse of the\nsubprime mortgage market in 2007, local debt is backed by\ncollateral that is overvalued, may be hard to sell and, in some\ncases, doesn\u2019t exist.  Officials in Loudi, whose colonnaded government building is\nlocally nicknamed the White House, value their 18 tracts of land\nat almost four times what a similar plot sold for in May. In the\nnortheast city of Cangzhou, the man in charge of the assets\nfinancing a port expansion can\u2019t locate the land his company\nposted as collateral for a 1 billion-yuan bond sale. And a\nspending spree in Yichun, a district on the Russian border\ncovered by ice much of the year, is backed by promises of future\nland sales that officials acknowledge may never materialize.  \u2018Huge Myth\u2019  More than 400 billion yuan of municipal bonds sold since\n2008 -- part of as much as 14.2 trillion yuan in local borrowing\n-- show how much local officials rely on their own forecast that\nland prices will continue to rise. Efforts by the central\ngovernment to cool the  property market  so far have had no impact\non their bullish estimates.  Residential land sale values slumped 30 percent this year\nas local officials increased sales to pay back loans, according\nto  Credit Suisse Group AG. (CSGN)   \u201cIt\u2019s a huge myth that land sales are going to be able to\neven support the interest payments let alone the principal\npayments,\u201d says Stephen Green, the Hong Kong-based head of\nGreater China research at  Standard Chartered Plc. (STAN)  His research\nteam assumes that at least 4-6 trillion yuan of local government\nloans -- and possibly much more -- will ultimately not be repaid\nby the projects, Green wrote in a June 29 report on China\u2019s debt.  Echoes of U.S. Crisis  Local governments set up more than 10,000 so-called\nfinancing vehicles in the past decade to get around laws\nprohibiting them from taking direct loans. One third of them\ndon\u2019t have cash flow to service their loans, China\u2019s banking\nregulator says.  The similarities with special purpose vehicles in the U.S.\nhiding toxic repackaged mortgages from banks\u2019 balance sheets are\nincreasing. Subsequent losses prompted the U.S. government and\ncentral bank to lend, spend or guarantee a peak of $12.8\ntrillion in 2009 to rescue the financial industry, including a\n$45 billion direct investment to rescue  Citigroup Inc. (C) , then the\nbiggest U.S. financial services company.  \u2018Playing with Fire\u2019  \u201cIt means that China is playing with fire like we played\nwith fire when we had all those SPVs that took everything\nsupposedly off the books,\u201d says Carl Walter, who retired this\nyear as the chief operating officer in China for  JPMorgan Chase\n& Co. (JPM)  \u201cIt didn\u2019t take them off the books. Citibank went down.\u201d  Moody\u2019s Investors Service puts overall local government\nborrowing at 3.5 trillion yuan more than the 10.7 trillion yuan\nstated in a national audit published June 27. China\u2019s central\nbank on July 11 backed the official count, saying estimates of\n14 trillion yuan were \u201cobviously\u201d too large.  Banks cannot restructure all the local government loans on\ntheir books, Yvonne Zhang, a Moody\u2019s analyst in Beijing, says.\nRecapitalizing the banks by the central government will slow\ngrowth in the world\u2019s second-largest economy, says Vincent Chan,\nhead of China research at Credit Suisse in  Hong Kong .  The effects would reverberate around the globe in weakening\nthe country\u2019s appetite for U.S. Treasuries and European debt, as\nwell as driving down prices of oil and metals,  Fitch Ratings \nsaid in a June 28 report.  Touting Western Brands  The building binge fueled by this mound of debt is evident\na few hours\u2019 drive into the hills of Loudi from the provincial\ncapital of Changsha. Cranes abound amongst new high-rise\napartment complexes with names like Wealthy City, surrounded by\nbillboards showing pictures of Caucasian women strolling through\nshopping malls featuring brands like KFC and Microsoft.  Loudi City Construction Investment Group Co. plans to use\n21 percent of the proceeds from its bonds issued in March for\nthe stadium complex and the rest for a new expressway into town,\nwater treatment facilities and a park, according to its\nprospectus. The city is one of scores across the country\nbuilding roads, commercial centers and subways after being urged\nto spend their way out of the 2009 global recession.  On a sunny day in early June, Yang smiles as he talks of\ntransforming Loudi from an economy dominated by a single state-\nowned steelmaker into a bustling transport hub, a popular phrase\nthese days with officials who tout projects they say will bring\nprosperity to their cities.  High-Speed Railway  Set on a lush green hillside, Loudi will be a stop on a\nhigh-speed railway spanning more than 1,200 miles from  Shanghai \nin the east to Kunming in the west, near the border with the\nSoutheast Asian nation of Myanmar.  \u201cEvery train will stop here,\u201d says Yang, in his downtown\noffice at the company\u2019s headquarters. A Mao statue with a red\nkerchief draped around its shoulders stands in the lobby.  Outside, Yang points to a vacant plot in a swathe of land\nalready cleared and being drained to build apartment blocks.\nIt\u2019s one of the lots being used for collateral.  The company has pledged to repay debt by selling land it\nreceived from the city, leveraging local land prices that\ndoubled between 2007 and 2010, according to the prospectus. The\n9.69 million yuan an acre it values its land for the bond\ncompares with a tender price in May of 2.54 million yuan an acre\nfor a city plot zoned for commercial use, according to data from\nthe local State Land Resources Bureau.  Better Than Treasuries  Foreign ratings companies don\u2019t assess China\u2019s local bond\nmarket and domestic evaluations vary. Beijing-based Dagong\nGlobal Credit Rating Co. rates Loudi\u2019s bonds at its fourth-\nhighest investment grade, one level higher than it gives to U.S.\nTreasuries. That\u2019s in spite of its own December 2010 report that\nsaid: \u201cThe city\u2019s ability to balance the general budget is\ndecreasing and the results of the sales of land use rights will\nimpact the company\u2019s ability to invest and do construction.\u201d  Dagong gives a high rating to the bonds of local government\nfinancing vehicles because the central government has said\ninfrastructure debt will be repaid by local authorities,\nchairman Guan Jianzhong said July 11. Rapid growth in local\nfiscal revenue should enable them to pay debts, he said.  Loudi\u2019s investment vehicle had a negative operational  cash\nflow  of 187.1 million yuan in the first half of 2010, a period\nduring which it borrowed 284 million yuan. Beijing-based China\nInternational Capital Corp., often referred to as CICC, gives\nLoudi its third-lowest rating, a speculative or non-investment\ngrade.  The yield on Loudi\u2019s bonds reached a record high of 7.318\npercent on July 7, according to data from China Foreign Exchange\nTrade System.  Yang, the official, isn\u2019t worried. \u201cWhen we get to the end\nof our loan we\u2019ll just pay it back,\u201d he says.  Defaults Forecast  Across China, cities increasingly turned to the country\u2019s\nnascent bond market last year after the national government\nturned off the spigot for many bank loans. That\u2019s propelled a\nsix-fold increase in bond sales this year from three years ago,\naccording to CICC, an investment bank run by the son of former\npremier Zhu Rongji.  \u201cWe are forecasting a lot of local governments will have\nto default,\u201d says Jinsong Du, an analyst at Credit Suisse in\nHong Kong. About one-quarter of China\u2019s municipal debt is\nguaranteed with land sales revenue, Auditor General Liu Jiayi\nsaid June 27.  Mansions Among Smokestacks  In Cangzhou, almost 800 miles northeast of Loudi, on the\nshores of the  Bohai Gulf , luxury apartment complexes are\nsprouting up in view of more than a dozen smokestacks at one of\nChina\u2019s biggest coal depots. A billboard for Leader Mansion\npromises, in English, that it will bring the buyer a \u201chigh\ndegree of endorsement of a city life.\u201d  The city is expanding Bohai New Area, a port zone between\nTianjin and the border of Shandong province, by building roads\nand developing unspecified \u201cgreen\u201d projects with 1 billion\nyuan in bonds issued in May by Hebei Bohai Investment Co.\nThey\u2019re guaranteed by five tracts of land the company says is\nvalued at more than 1.54 billion yuan, or 462 yuan per square\nmeter. That\u2019s more than three times what it paid the local\ngovernment in December 2009, according to the company\u2019s land use\npermits viewed by Bloomberg News.  Ask Lu Chunjiang, a Communist Party member and head of the\nlocal investment company\u2019s asset management department, where\nhis assets are and he can\u2019t say.  \u201cIt\u2019s somewhere north of town, I don\u2019t exactly know\nwhere,\u201d Lu, 41, says in his second-floor office in Huanghua\nPort, built on saline marshes. \u201cIt\u2019s like the land outside the\ncity, you know, with the big piles of salt.\u201d  Inability to Pay  Hebei Bohai\u2019s bonds were skewered by Xu Xiaoqing, head of\nfixed income research at CICC, in a May 26 report.  \u201cThis issuer\u2019s own profit and cash flow is very little,\nits cash shortage is extremely big, its debt load is very heavy,\nand it doesn\u2019t possess the ability to pay this bond,\u201d Xu and\nhis team wrote. The local government\u2019s fiscal income \u201cis very\nlimited, there will be a lot of pressure on it to support the\npayment of this bond,\u201d they added.  Hebei Bohai\u2019s long-term debt of more than 7 billion yuan at\nthe end of 2010, before the bond was issued, was greater than\nthe city\u2019s annual revenue of about 5 billion yuan for that year,\naccording to the prospectus.  The debt-to-government revenue ratio was higher than that\nof Vallejo, the northern California city that filed for\nbankruptcy in 2008. Vallejo cited falling revenue from real-\nestate transactions as a reason for its bankruptcy.  Banks on the Hook  Banks including  Industrial & Commercial Bank of China (1398)  Ltd.\nand  China Construction Bank Corp. (939) , China\u2019s two biggest by market\nvalue, may have problematic loans equivalent to 30 percent of\ntheir books, says Victor Shih, a professor at Northwestern\nUniversity in Evanston,  Illinois , who studies China\u2019s local\ngovernment debt.  The banks also are among the leading holders of China\u2019s\nmushrooming corporate debt according to data compiled by\nChinabond, China\u2019s Beijing-based bond clearing house. This year,\nmutual funds have been the biggest buyers, according to CICC.\nThey\u2019ve snapped up half the corporate bonds issued in the first\nfive months of this year, 70 percent of which were to finance\nlocal government projects.  Buyers are attracted to high yields and have faith that\nthe central government will bail out any in trouble, says George Weisi Tan, head of bond investments at Fortune SGAM Fund\nManagement Co. in Shanghai.  \u201cThey think the interest is risk free,\u201d says Tan, who\nsays some brokerages leverage themselves as much as three times\ntheir capital. \u201cThis is really a big systemic risk.\u201d  Crisis \u2018Unlikely\u2019  Such pessimism is overblown, says  Nicholas Lardy , a senior\nfellow at  Washington \u2019s Peterson Institute for International\nEconomics who specializes in China\u2019s financial system. The\nbuildup of debt is slowing and many local infrastructure\nprojects will raise revenue and add to economic growth, he said.  \u201cA majority of the projects that are being undertaken by\nthese companies are probably projects that have very high\neconomic rate of return,\u201d Lardy says.  Wang Tao , a Beijing-based economist for UBS AG, wrote in a\nJune 7 report that a crisis from bad local debt is \u201cunlikely in\nthe near future.\u201d  Of most concern, she said, is borrowing obtained with no\ncollateral at all.  That\u2019s the case in Yichun, a Maryland-sized area of about\n1.3 million people deep inside the birch and pine forest on\nChina\u2019s border with  Russia .  Yichun is a poor city in a poor province. Income of Yichun\nresidents was little more than half the national average last\nyear. That hasn\u2019t stopped the government from going on a\nspending spree. The new local police headquarters has a\nminiature dome reminiscent of that on the Vatican\u2019s St. Peter\u2019s\nBasilica.  Shanty Towns  Yichun City Construction Investment & Development Co. sold\n1.2 billion yuan in bonds in 2009 backed only by a pledge from\nthe local government and possible future land sales. CICC gave\nit the lowest debt rating of any city financing vehicle. In\ncontrast, Dagong rates the bonds one level higher than  U.S. debt .  Money raised from the sale is being used for the\ndestruction of what the prospectus calls \u201cshanty towns.\u201d\nSingle-floor traditional wooden homes in the valley\nare being demolished to make way for thousands of low-income\napartments. The company has also financed a new reservoir, an\nairport terminal and parklands, one featuring faux Corinthian\ncolumns topped by winged warrior princesses and bronze\nsculptures of chariot-riding local gods.  Missing Chairman Mao  Wang Zhongbing, 77, a retired factory worker who spends the\nsummer days chatting with friends in a park next to the Yichun\nRiver, says the economic development is passing his family by.\nOnly one of his three adult sons has a job, he says.  \u201cI miss Chairman Mao,\u201d says Wang, sitting on a red plastic\nchair in front of a billboard for newly built Pinaster Town,\nfeaturing a picture of a woman in high heels stepping out of a\nRolls Royce. \u201cThe common people cannot afford these houses.\u201d  The Yichun financing vehicle would have lost money every\nyear from 2006 to 2008 except for direct government subsidies.\nAt its offices above a local bank branch in the center of town,\nSun Yunlan, 49, who according to the prospectus is deputy\ngeneral manager of the company, referred questions to the city\u2019s\nfinance department, which, in turn, referred questions back to\nthe company.  The prospectus promised that land from the city \u201cwill\nprovide a more substantial cash flow.\u201d Two years on, that\nhasn\u2019t come to pass, according to Wu Liangguo, the head of the\nYichun City Bureau of Land and Resources and its Communist Party\nsecretary.  \u201cThe land market in Yichun isn\u2019t that great,\u201d says Wu, 49,\nwho jogs even in minus 30 degrees Celsius (minus 22 degrees\nFahrenheit) chill of the Siberian winter. \u201cThe local government\nfinancing vehicle may get land in the future but it isn\u2019t a\ncertainty.\u201d  --Henry Sanderson, Michael Forsythe. To contact Bloomberg News staff for this story:\nHenry Sanderson in Beijing at 86-10-6649-7548 or\n hsanderson@bloomberg.net .\nMichael Forsythe in Beijing at +86-10-6649-7580 or\n mforsythe@bloomberg.net ;  To contact the editors responsible for this story:\nMelissa Pozsgay at \n mpozsgay@bloomberg.net .\nPeter Hirschberg at \n phirschberg@bloomberg.net ;","path":".\/2008_2012_msft_bloomberg_news\/china-cities-sell-land-at-winnetka-values-with-bonds-seen-toxic.txt"},{"id":74336385,"title":"U.S. Defends Data-Collection as Legal Anti-Terror Tool","released_at":"<date>June 7 2013<\/date> <time>08:31:00<\/time>","content":"The Obama administration confirmed the existence of a classified U.S. government program that gathers data on foreign nationals from Internet companies, defending the effort as legally authorized and essential to thwarting terrorist attacks.  The disclosure last night came a day after reports emerged of a secret court order compelling  Verizon Communications Inc. (VZ)  to provide the National Security Agency with data on all its customers\u2019 calls. While the revelations stirred outrage among privacy-rights advocates, U.S. lawmakers from both parties acknowledged earlier yesterday that they were aware of the Verizon order and backed the collection of telephone records as necessary to combating terrorism.  \u201cEverybody should just calm down,\u201d Senate Majority Leader  Harry Reid , a Nevada Democrat, said at a news conference in  Washington . \u201cIt\u2019s a program that\u2019s worked to prevent not all terrorism but certainly a vast majority of it.\u201d  Reports in the Guardian and Washington Post newspapers on telephone and Internet surveillance revived a debate that has repeatedly flared since the Sept. 11 attacks about the proper balance between American civil liberties and protection against terrorist threats. The news came as President  Barack Obama  is being challenged over his regard for individual privacy and constitutionally guaranteed freedom of the press.  U.S. Director of National Intelligence James Clapper acknowledged the Internet and telephone data-collection efforts in two statements circulated by the White House late last night. Responding to the Post and the U.K.-based Guardian reports, he called the surveillance a vital tool in fighting terrorism.  Protect Nation  \u201cInformation collected under this program is among the most important and valuable foreign intelligence information we collect, and is used to protect our nation from a wide variety of threats,\u201d Clapper said of the Internet effort.  The Post and the Guardian reported yesterday, citing classified documents, that the FBI and NSA had accessed the central servers of nine U.S. Internet companies, extracting audio and video chats, photographs, e-mails, documents and connection logs. Code-named PRISM, the program traces its roots to warrantless domestic surveillance efforts under former President  George W. Bush .  Microsoft Corp. (MSFT) ,  Yahoo! Inc. (YHOO) ,  Google Inc. (GOOG) ,  Facebook Inc (FB) ., and  Apple Inc. (AAPL)  were among the technology providers involved, the newspapers reported. The companies issued statements last night either denying that they had granted the government access to their servers or saying that they were unaware of the program.  Court Restrictions  The Post said the operation, which began in 2007, has grown exponentially and become the most prolific contributor to the president\u2019s daily intelligence briefing, providing raw material for almost one in seven reports. Part of the Defense Department, the NSA runs computer centers analyzing huge databases.  Clapper said the program to tap Internet companies\u2019 servers of \u201ccannot be used to intentionally target any U.S. citizen\u201d or anyone located within the U.S.  Both programs are authorized under the Foreign Intelligence Surveillance Act, Clapper said, and subject to supervision by members of Congress. Data collected are subject to limits by the Foreign Intelligence Surveillance Court, he said.  On the telephone program, he said, \u201cthe court only allows the data to be queried when there is a reasonable suspicion, based on specific facts, that the particular basis for the query is associated with a foreign terrorist organization.\u201d  The telephone surveillance, sought by the  Federal Bureau  of Investigation and approved by the court on April 25, requires Verizon to provide the NSA with information for three months on calls inside the U.S. and between the U.S. and other countries on a daily and \u201congoing\u201d basis, the Guardian reported.  Broad Support  The  American Civil Liberties Union  last night condemned the data collection described by the Post and Guardian as an abuse of power and called on U.S. lawmakers to investigate.  \u201cUnchecked government surveillance presents a grave threat to democratic freedoms,\u201d ACLU Deputy Legal Director Jameel Jaffer said in an e-mailed statement. \u201cThese revelations are a reminder that Congress has given the executive branch far too much power to invade individual privacy.\u201d  The  Justice Department , as part of its inquiries into leaks of national-security information, has also obtained secret search warrants for telephone records of journalists from the Associated Press and Fox News, prompting protests from U.S. lawmakers and media-advocacy groups.  Some lawmakers yesterday blasted the breadth of the surveillance. Senator  Charles Schumer , a  New York  Democrat, demanded an explanation for a program he called \u201cinvasive.\u201d  \u201cOne thing I have not heard is what the explanation is for needing to do this,\u201d Schumer told reporters.  \u2018Broad Support\u2019  House Speaker  John Boehner , an Ohio Republican, said Obama should explain to the American people what he\u2019s doing. The president has the \u201cresponsibility to outline what these tools are and how they are being used,\u201d Boehner told reporters.  Still, any effort to limit government surveillance authority \u201cseems unlikely given the broad support counter-terrorism programs have had from congressional leadership,\u201d said  Matt Miller , former public affairs director for the Justice Department under Obama and previously a staff member for House and Senate Democrats\u2019 campaign organizations.  \u201cSome of the criticism today is of the brand \u2018I can\u2019t believe you\u2019re doing this thing I authorized you today do,\u2019 which is just a little disingenuous,\u201d said Miller, now a partner in the policy and crisis management firm Vianovo LP.  Senate Intelligence Committee Chairman  Dianne Feinstein , a California Democrat, and  Saxby Chambliss  of  Georgia , the panel\u2019s top-ranking Republican, said that the telephone surveillance is legal and that they have been kept informed under the law.  \u2018Good Intelligence\u2019  \u201cTerrorists will come after us if they can, and the only thing we have to protect us is good intelligence,\u201d Feinstein told reporters. She said the telephone data had stopped multiple plots, though she would not provide any details.  The  Bush administration  started the so-called Terrorist Surveillance Program in the aftermath of the Sept. 11 attacks, when agencies began secretly conducting electronic surveillance on U.S. phone calls and e-mails without court warrants.  Congress passed a law in 2008 codifying parts of the program and authorizing intelligence agencies to get broad electronic surveillance orders from the Foreign Intelligence Surveillance Court. In 2012, there were 212 such FISA orders, known as \u201cbusiness records requests,\u201d according to a letter from the Justice Department to Reid. The letter doesn\u2019t specify the targets or scope of the requests.  \u2018Real Debate\u2019  That 2008 law updated the more than three-decade-old Foreign Intelligence Surveillance Act. It lets intelligence agencies monitor the e-mail, Internet activity and phone calls of non-U.S. citizens reasonably believed to be located outside the U.S. and involved in terrorist activities or other crimes. Congress voted last year to extend it until the end of 2017.  Senator  Ron Wyden , an Oregon Democrat who tried and failed to include stronger civil liberties protections the last time the law authorizing counter-terrorism surveillance was renewed, said he hoped disclosure of the monitoring would provoke \u201ca real debate in the Congress and the country.\u201d  Senator  Bob Corker  of Tennessee, the top Republican on the Senate Foreign Relations Committee said there could be a \u201cvery simple solution\u201d to address concerns Americans have about their data \u201cbeing stored, and potentially looked at, without them necessarily being singled out as someone who might be causing harm for our nation.\u201d He declined to elaborate.  Little Outrage  Still, there were few signs of outrage as senators filed out of a closed meeting held by the Senate Intelligence Committee on the program. Senators Marco Rubio, a Florida Republican,  Tom Coburn , an Oklahoma Republican, and  Al Franken , a Minnesota Democrat, told reporters that the surveillance program is operating under sufficient legal controls.  Feinstein and Chambliss, briefing reporters, said the telephone information collected is dumped into a government database and then used to respond to specific threats.  The surveillance program creates \u201ca telephone book\u201d of data and cannot be accessed without \u201creasonable, articulable suspicion that the records are relevant and related to terrorist activity,\u201d Feinstein said.  The court order covers telephone numbers as well as the location and duration of calls, but not the content of users\u2019 conversations, according to a copy of the order published by the Guardian and posted  on its website .  Supreme Court  The  Supreme Court  has never ruled on the constitutionality of such a sweeping surveillance program. In February, the court voted 5-4 to bar a challenge by lawyers and civil-rights activists to a federal law that allows government wiretapping of international phone calls and e-mails.  The majority didn\u2019t rule on the surveillance program itself, instead saying the opponents lacked \u201cstanding\u201d to sue because they hadn\u2019t shown they were being harmed.  \u201cThe stories published over the last two days make clear that the NSA -- part of the military -- now has direct access to every corner of Americans\u2019 digital lives,\u201d said the ACLU\u2019s Jaffer, who argued the case before the Supreme Court. \u201cPowers exercised entirely in secret, without public accountability of any kind, will certainly be abused.\u201d  Clapper last night criticized the release of previously classified information about surveillance efforts and said the Post and Guardian articles had left out important context about the usefulness of the programs and their privacy safeguards.  \u201cThe unauthorized disclosure of information about this important and entirely legal program is reprehensible and risks important protections for the security of Americans,\u201d Clapper said of the report on the Internet data. This week\u2019s document will form the basis or further\ndiscussion before draft legislation will be proposed in 2011\nwhich will then need the approval of EU nations and lawmakers.  \u201cWe are confident that an effective modern privacy\nprotection framework can support growth in the internet economy\nand can enable the free services that consumers value,\u201d said\nJustin B. Google Inc.\nwas fined 100,000 euros ($129,600) last year by  France , one of\nthe few European privacy agencies with the power to levy\nfinancial penalties, over the company\u2019s accidental collection of\npersonal information from wireless networks.  \u201cWe will finish with this scandal,\u201d  said  EU Justice\nCommissioner Viviane Reding at a press conference in Brussels.\n\u201cCompanies and organizations must notify serious breaches as\nsoon as possible which means for me 24 hours\u201d to the national\nregulatory authority and to the person whose data has been\ncompromised.  Under the draft rules, serious violations such as\nprocessing sensitive data without an individual\u2019s consent or\nwithout any legal justification, may be punished with penalties\nas high as 1 million euros or as much as 2 percent of a\ncompany\u2019s yearly sales, the commission said. Less serious\noffenses would be punished with smaller fines.  \u2018One-Stop Shop\u2019  The proposal will reduce the number of regulators a company\nneeds to contact for data-protection issues across the region as\nthe regulator of its home base will become a \u201cone-stop shop.\u201d\nIn practice, this will mean that Ireland\u2019s agency will be in\ncharge of regulating companies like  Google Inc. (GOOG)  and Facebook\nInc., which run their European operations from the country.  Wim Nauwelaerts, a lawyer at Hunton & Williams LLP in\nBrussels, said businesses welcome having one point of contact to\nreduce the legal uncertainty they currently face from multiple\njurisdictions.  \u201cInevitably some data-protection authorities are going to\nreceive more requests for clarifications,\u201d Nauwelaerts said.\n\u201cIt\u2019s going to be one of the challenges of data-protection\nauthorities going forward, to make sure that they are adequately\nequipped.\u201d  \u2018A Real Cost\u2019  Companies could save as much as 2.3 billion euros a year as\nredundant, contradictory or unnecessary reporting requirements\nare eliminated, Reding said. Businesses currently face \u201ca real\nextra cost\u201d from \u201ccontradictory data-protection\nrequirements,\u201d she said. (AAPL)  among its members, said the\nproposal\u2019s prescriptive approach to how data should be\ncollected, processed and stored may \u201cbog down companies with\nonerous compliance obligations which could inhibit digital\ninnovation.\u201d  To contact the reporter on this story:\nAoife White in Brussels at \n awhite62@bloomberg.net . (MSFT)  is paying a dot-com\nera price for Skype Technologies SA, almost 40 percent more than\nthe world\u2019s most popular Internet calling service itself says\nthe business is worth.  Microsoft, the world\u2019s largest software company, agreed to\npay $8.5 billion for Luxembourg-based Skype, which lost money in\nfour of the past five years even as it quadrupled sales. The\ntakeover, the largest for an Internet company since May 2000, is\n32 times Skype\u2019s adjusted earnings before interest, taxes,\ndepreciation and amortization, according to data compiled by\nBloomberg. It\u2019s just their misfortune\nthat, thanks to disclosure rules, they\u2019re among the most\nvisible.  This proxy season coincides with an electoral cycle in\nwhich  income inequality  has become a populist issue for\ncandidates in both parties, which means CEO paychecks will be\nscrutinized as never before. And what can\u2019t evade discovery is\nthat, even among the very rich, CEOs have been consistently\noverpaid.  By overpaid, I don\u2019t mean merely highly paid. We live in a\ncapitalist country, and talent is entitled to fetch its price.\nBut to take just one shining example,  Larry Ellison , CEO of\n Oracle Corp. (ORCL) , has gorged himself on more than $60\u00a0million in\nstock options every year since 2008, Bloomberg Businessweek\nreports in its Feb. 20 issue. Even if Ellison did groundbreaking\nwork and was a juggernaut of management brilliance, abusive\nwould not be too strong a word.  Fixing CEO pay -- making it more reflective of what\nexecutives are truly worth -- would go a long way toward\nrestoring America\u2019s faith in business, and in equal treatment.\nHow, is the $60\u00a0million question.  One myth should be cleared at the outset. In 2008, the CEOs\nwho run companies in the  Standard & Poor\u2019s 500 stock index \nearned, in total, less than 1\u00a0percent of what everyone who\u2019s a\n1\u00a0percenter earned. So it\u2019s unfair to blame CEOs alone for\nfostering inequality.  Movie Stars  Defenders of the system cite such data to advance a larger\nclaim. Pay for public company CEOs has risen, they say, for the\nsame reasons it has for movie stars, real estate moguls, and\nprivate entrepreneurs: Globalization and technology has created\na wider market.  Even President Obama, no friend of the very rich,\nacknowledged in December that \u201cover the last few decades, huge\nadvances in technology have allowed businesses to do more with\nless, and made it easier for them to set up shop and hire\nworkers anywhere in the world.\u201d Read thoughtfully, that implies\nthat 1 percenters are taking home more because, in an economic\nsense, they\u2019re earning it.  \u201cThe system has worked,\u201d says  Steven Kaplan , a professor at\nChicago Booth School of Business. From 2000 to 2010,\ncompensation for the median CEO in the Standard & Poor\u2019s 500\nIndex rose from $5\u00a0million to just over $8\u00a0million. (Those\nfigures represent actual dollars received; when calculated by\nthe value of options at the time of grants, pay over the period\nbegan and ended at $8\u00a0million.)  Pay for Performance  Kaplan asserts that CEOs are \u201cpaid for performance.\u201d In a\nliteral sense this is true; CEOs did earn more when their\ncompanies succeeded. But they earned so much, as well, for\nordinary and unquantifiable performance as to undermine the\nintended effect.  Apple Inc. (AAPL) \u2019s new CEO,  Tim Cook , may turn out to\nbe every bit as good as  Steve Jobs , or he may not. Apple\u2019s board\ndid not wait to find out. Cook got -- for his very first year as\nCEO -- a package worth $378\u00a0million.  The real explanation for sky-high pay lies in the \u201cagency\u201d\nproblem. Agents exploit their role as intermediaries. They\nthrive in imperfect markets in which pay scales do not respond\nquickly, if at all, to results. Hedge fund managers who deliver\nmediocre returns get rich thanks to their role as agents.\nMortgage traders employed by banks got huge bonuses in the fat\nyears but ducked responsibility for losses; they got a free ride\non their employers\u2019 capital.  Warped Market  So do some CEOs, though certainly not all.  Steve Ballmer  of\n Microsoft Corp. (MSFT) , for example, gets no options and total\ncompensation of $1.4 million. But all CEOs compete in a warped\nmarketplace. How often does the head of Company\u00a0X leave for\nCompany\u00a0Y? How often does a corporation sack its head? It\nhappens more than it used to, but the market remains inflexible,\nand firings are rarely for reasons of expense.  Consider that  Philippe Dauman , the chief executive of\nViacom Inc., speared $84\u00a0million in 2010, and that Eugene\nIsenberg of  Nabors Industries Ltd. (NBR)  was awarded $100\u00a0million last\nyear for agreeing to relinquish his job. These may be anomalies,\nbut it\u2019s hard to imagine them happening in any rational\nmarketplace.  The agency problem in the corner office is as old as public\nownership, though it was most famously brought to light in the\n1980s by  Harvard Business School  professor Michael Jensen, who\nobserved that CEOs, unlike private entrepreneurs, owned little\nstock and had scant stake in the common corporate purpose.  Options Shower  In a 1989 Harvard Business Review article, \u201cEclipse of the\nPublic Corporation,\u201d Jensen suggested that public shareholders\nhad become pass\u00e9. Of course, there was nowhere near enough\nprivate capital to replace the mass of public investors. For the\npublic companies that remained un-eclipsed, Jensen reckoned, the\nnext best thing would be to shower  stock options  on the\nexecutives, endowing them with the same incentives as their\npeers at private firms.  If Harvard Business School thought stock options were good\nfor America, corporate executives were perfectly willing to take\nthem. \u201cPay for performance\u201d was the mantra, but in the aftermath\nof the dot-com bubble it became abundantly clear, not least to\nJensen, that options hadn\u2019t performed as hoped.  Executives who were shielded from losses exposed their\nfirms to excessive risk -- Bernie Ebbers at WorldCom Inc. and\nKen Lay at Enron Corp. being just two examples. When bucketfuls\nof options were awarded year after year, executives had nothing\nto lose.  Pandit\u2019s Pay  In 2008, after promoting Vikram Pandit to CEO,  Citigroup\nInc. (C)  gave him $29\u00a0million in stock awards plus $8.4\u00a0million in\noptions. Alas, the stock cratered. Compensating Pandit (and not,\nof course, the public shareholders) for this bad luck, Citi\u2019s\ndirectors last year agreed to 500,000 more stock options and a\n$10\u00a0million stock award. These will reward Pandit for earning\nback the capital that, under his tenure, Citigroup had\npreviously lost.  The problem is systemic. From 2000 to 2010, shareholders\nlost 14\u00a0percent playing the  S&P 500 . But CEOs kept raking it in.  Jensen, still looking for solutions, has only gotten more\noutraged. In a blistering new paper, \u201cCEO Bonus Plans: And How\nto Fix Them,\u201d co-authored with Kevin Murphy, he observes that\n\u201calmost all CEO and executive bonus plans have serious design\nflaws.\u201d  The pair find, across the board, that bonuses are ripe for\ngaming and executives benefit from too much upside with little\ndownside. Jensen and Murphy propose that guaranteed salaries be\nlower and bonuses higher, with bonuses deposited into a notional\nbonus \u201cbank\u201d and paid out over time. Poor performance would\nreduce the executive\u2019s \u201cdeposit.\u201d  Overlapping Incentives  That\u2019s a fine start, but why stop there? It also makes\nsense to reduce the number of overlapping incentives. (Oracle\npaid its new president,  Mark Hurd , in six different ways in\n2011, totaling $78\u00a0million.) As Murphy says, \u201cIt was never our\nintention that companies would layer options for free on top of\nall these other forms of pay.\u201d Stock grants and options should\nbe dished out only at far less frequent intervals. Otherwise,\nexecs get a bump merely for recouping prior losses.  Also, huge exit packages, which make a mockery of Kaplan\u2019s\nclaim that failed CEOs suffer real punishment, have to be\ncurbed. The best way to ensure such reforms is for Congress to\nlegislate binding shareholder votes on any package worth more\nthan, say, $5\u00a0million. Let shareholders be their own agents. The opinions expressed are his\nown.) Luckily for\n Microsoft Corp. (MSFT) , it turns out not to be true.  Windows Phone 7, Microsoft\u2019s attempt to claw its way back\ninto the lucrative smartphone arena, was released a year ago to\nrespectful but hardly adulatory reviews. It was good, but not\ngood enough to go head-to-head with the big boys,  Apple Inc. (AAPL)  and\n Google Inc. (GOOG)   Now it is. Microsoft is rolling out Windows Phone 7.5, also\nknown as \u201cMango,\u201d an altogether more polished and potent\ncontender. The software began going out to existing users as a\nfree upgrade last week; new handsets from manufacturers\nincluding  HTC Corp. (2498)  and Samsung Electronics Co. will begin\nshowing up shortly. It deserves consideration if you\u2019re in the\nmarket for a new phone and not already committed to another\noperating system.  Once a dominant player in smartphones, Microsoft was slow\nto react to the 2007 release of Apple\u2019s iPhone and saw its\nmarket share implode.  Now, though, a combination of factors is giving it an\nopening.  Research In Motion Ltd. (RIM)  is struggling to hold onto its\nBlackBerry customers; Google\u2019s acquisition of Motorola Mobility\nHoldings Inc. may lead competing manufacturers to think twice\nabout their dependence on Android;  Hewlett-Packard Co. (HPQ)  pulled\nthe plug on its competing WebOS platform.  Steady Improvement  All that wouldn\u2019t matter much if the Windows Phone platform\ndidn\u2019t measure up. But Microsoft has steadily improved the\nsoftware, with interim updates and the 7.5 release adding\nfunctions that were notably absent at launch. Hello, copy-and-\npaste, Twitter support, Internet sharing; good to see you,\nvisual voicemail and multitasking. What kept you?  Unlike Apple\u2019s iOS, Google\u2019s Android and just about every\nother mobile-device operating system, a Windows phone doesn\u2019t\npresent you with rows of icons representing apps. Instead, the\nhome screen consists of a number of colorful tiles that\nrepresent the phone\u2019s key functions. These tiles can update\nthemselves with new information, so that, for example, you can\nsee your next appointment at a glance, or how many new e-mails\nyou\u2019ve received.  Some of the tiles lead to what Microsoft calls hubs --\ncollections of information and apps organized around a theme.\nThe People hub, for example, aggregates your contacts and\nsocial-network feeds, providing one-stop shopping for getting\nand staying in touch with people important to you.  Suggesting Apps  One of the cleverest features in the new version of the\noperating system is the way it integrates the search function\nwith the ability to discover and incorporate new apps.  For example, I used my test phone, a Samsung Focus, to find\nItalian restaurants near Bloomberg\u2019s  San Francisco  offices. The\nsoftware not only gave me the usual reviews and directions, but\nalso suggested I might want to download the OpenTable app for\nbooking reservations online. Once I did, future restaurant\nsearches gave me a reservation option that automatically\nlaunched the app.  Speech has also been integrated into the operating system.\nYou can dictate messages that are then read back to you and,\nonce you approve, dispatched as texts. Say \u201c\u2019Moneyball\u2019\nshowtimes\u201d and up pops a list of local theaters where the movie\nis playing, along with the option to buy tickets.  It\u2019s not as potent as Siri, the personal-assistant feature\nthat Apple is launching with its new iPhone 4S, but I found it\nmore useful and enjoyable than the voice features built into the\ncurrent version of Android.  Vetting the Marketplace  Microsoft says its Marketplace now has 30,000 apps, far\nfewer than the 500,000 or so available for iPhone or 250,000 for\nAndroid. At least Microsoft, like Apple and unlike Google, vets\nnew apps before they go into the Marketplace, providing a little\nhigher comfort level for the security-conscious.  A few things are still missing from Windows Phone 7.5. One\nis the ability to take advantage of the powerful multi-core\nprocessors that are showing up on high-end phones. Another is\nsupport for LTE, the fastest fourth-generation network\ntechnology, which  Verizon Wireless  and, more recently,  AT&T Inc. (T) \nhave begun rolling out.  Perhaps those features will show up in updates. In the\nmeantime, the Windows Phone platform may get another boost soon\nwhen  Nokia Oyj (NOK1V)  unveils the first devices developed under its new\nMicrosoft partnership.  Microsoft still has a long way to go to catch up with Apple\nand Google, and as this week\u2019s announcement of the latest iPhone\nillustrates, they\u2019re hardly standing still. Windows Phone 7.5,\nthough, at least confirms that Microsoft is pointed in the right\ndirection.  ( Rich Jaroslovsky  is a Bloomberg News columnist. The\nopinions expressed are his own.)  To contact the writer of this column:\nRich Jaroslovsky in San Francisco at \n rjaroslovsky@bloomberg.net .  To contact the editor responsible for this story:\nManuela Hoelterhoff at \n mhoelterhoff@bloomberg.net .","path":".\/2008_2012_msft_bloomberg_news\/-mango-makes-microsoft-relevant-in-phones-again-tech-by-rich-jaroslovsky.txt"},{"id":43355065,"title":"Nintendo to Halt Wii Production for Japan to Focus on U Console","released_at":"<date>October 2 2013<\/date> <time>02:15:51<\/time>","content":"Nintendo Co. Copyright  Software Copyright Allows Reverse Engineering, EU Court Says  Software companies can\u2019t rely on copyright rules to prevent\nrivals from \u201creverse engineering\u201d computer programs, the\nEuropean Union\u2019s highest court ruled.  SAS Institute Inc., the world\u2019s biggest closely held\nsoftware company, lost a bid at the EU Court of Justice to\nextend copyright protection to the functions of a computer\nprogram. World Programming Ltd. infringed SAS\u2019s copyright by\ndeveloping a system that copied the company\u2019s manuals, SAS said\nat a September hearing.  Copyright protection doesn\u2019t extend to the functionality of\na computer program or the programming language and the format of\na program\u2019s data files, according to a statement from the court\nyesterday.  \u201cThere is no copyright infringement\u201d when a software\ncompany without access to a program\u2019s source code \u201cstudied,\nobserved and tested that program in order to reproduce its\nfunctionality in a second program,\u201d the court said in the\nstatement.  SAS, based in Cary, North Carolina, is an independent maker\nof so-called business intelligence programs, which spot patterns\namid vast stores of data. WPL, based in Romsey, England, makes a\nsoftware product that analyzes and processes data.  It\u2019s the first time the EU\u2019s top court has been asked to\ndefine the scope of copyright protection for computer software.\nThe High Court in  London  in 2010 referred the case to the EU\ntribunal for guidance on how to interpret the region\u2019s software\nand copyright laws. The court said WPL\u2019s system didn\u2019t breach\nSAS\u2019s copyright.  Calls and e-mails to SAS offices in North Carolina and\nEngland weren\u2019t immediately answered before U.S. business hours.\nWPL didn\u2019t immediately respond to an e-mail seeking comment.  The ruling means \u201cthat competitive and interoperable\ncomputer programs can continue to be developed without threat of\nlegal liability,\u201d said  Thomas Vinje , a spokesman for the\nEuropean Committee for Interoperable Systems, a group\nrepresenting International Business Machines Corp.,  Oracle Corp. (ORCL) \nand other software developers.  The case is  C-406\/10 , SAS Institute Inc. v. World\nProgramming Ltd. The assembler of iPhones and iPads has resolved 98 percent of the 360 issues raised by the Washington-based Fair Labor Association, the group said in a report yesterday. The company has improved safety conditions, including testing sprinklers and maintaining equipment.  Inspections of the Taipei-based company\u2019s factories began last year after Apple Chief Executive Officer  Tim Cook  joined the FLA following the suicides of at least 10 Foxconn employees in 2010. Foxconn, the world\u2019s biggest contract manufacturer of electronics, more than doubled wages after protests from worker groups over conditions in a supply chain that includes Microsoft Corp. and Sony Corp.  \u201cThey have made a lot of progress, but they still have work to do,\u201d Auret Van Heerden, CEO of the Fair Labor Association, said in an interview. \u201cWe are up against the two toughest or most complicated action items: hours of work and union democracy.\u201d  Worker Shortage  A shortage of workers makes it difficult to completely fix the problems, Van Heerden said. Without enough employees to assemble electronics, Foxconn must rely on overtime work to get the job done, especially because Apple\u2019s production cycle is seasonal and gets busier around product introductions, he said. Many Chinese workers also only stay on the job for about a year, which diminishes their interest in getting involved in the union process, he said.  \u201cIt\u2019s becoming increasingly tight, and most factories are struggling to hire enough workers,\u201d he said.
