The Chinese government wages \u201ca large-scale cyber espionage campaign\u201d and \u201chas successfully targeted the networks of U.S. government and private organizations,\u201d the  U.S.-China Economic and Security Review Commission  concludes in its annual report to Congress released yesterday.  The commission for the first time said cloud computing, which connects Internet services, \u201crepresents a potential espionage threat.\u201d The report fails to cite any examples of the Chinese government using the technology in attacks.  \u201cOur focus has been on making sure that Defense Department or State Department data, or other government information, is secure,\u201d  William Reinsch , chairman of the commission, told reporters before the report\u2019s release. \u201cTo the extent those entities use the cloud as well, we think that they need to get a better grip on who\u2019s actually providing their services and where their data is going.\u201d  President  Barack Obama \u2019s administration and lawmakers have used diplomacy and a public shaming campaign to pressure Beijing to stop cyber-attacks that are estimated to cost the U.S. economy as much as $300 billion a year. Their efforts have been overshadowed by revelations since June that the  National Security Agency  eavesdropped on foreign leaders, hacked into the private networks of  Google Inc.  and  Yahoo! Inc.  abroad and spied on Americans and foreigners without warrants.  China Connection  China\u2019s Ministry of State Security, which is the country\u2019s main foreign intelligence collection agency, is \u201cclosely connected\u201d to a special cloud-computing zone in the city of Chongqing, the commission wrote. That represents a threat \u201cto foreign companies that might use cloud-computing services provided from the zone or base operations there,\u201d it concluded.  The only U.S. cloud provider singled out in the report as a possible risk for hacks sponsored by the Chinese government was Microsoft because the Redmond, Washington-based company has licensed its products to  21Vianet Group Inc. , a Beijing-based company selling online data center services.  The commission on Nov. 19 backed away from that assertion, saying in a statement it had \u201cbeen informed of new information and will be reaching out to all involved parties to determine what impact, if any, this has on the findings.\u201d  \u201cIf we inadvertently included incorrect information, we will make corrections as appropriate,\u201d according to the statement.  Microsoft Deal  The commission based its conclusions about cloud computing on a Sept. 5 report called  Red Cloud Rising  that it commissioned from a private U.S. intelligence and security company, Defense Group Inc., based in Vienna, Virginia.  The company was given incorrect information by Microsoft about its relationship with 21Vianet when it wrote the September report, Leigh Ann Ragland, one of the authors, said in an e-mail on Nov. 19. She said the company was contacting the commission to correct the report\u2019s language.  While Microsoft licenses its Windows Azure and Office 365 products to 21Vianet, the Chinese company doesn\u2019t have access to \u201cservices and datacenters operated by Microsoft outside of China,\u201d Doug Hauger, Microsoft\u2019s general manager for China commercial cloud services, said in an e-mail on Nov. 19.  Microsoft Azure and Office 365 \u201cinclude security technologies, systems and monitoring to mitigate malicious activities,\u201d Hauger said. \u201cIf we believe malicious activity is taking place, we investigate and take the appropriate action.\u201d  Zero-Day Exploits  Ragland said a theoretical cybersecurity concern still exists if the Chinese government can find unknown vulnerabilities, commonly referred to as zero-day exploits, in Windows Azure to attack users overseas.  \u201cCloud computing technology enables hackers to better obfuscate the source of their attacks, which also serves the strategic interests of certain organizations within the PRC military and government,\u201d she said. Accounts at Tel Aviv-based EToro, the largest social-investment network, have climbed to 2.85 million from 1.75 million in 2011.  ZuluTrade  in New York says users have more than tripled since 2011. About 17 percent of brokerages serving individuals offer the ability to copy other users\u2019 trades, according to a survey of 254 firms compiled by Aite Group LLC between October 2012 and April 2013.  In contrast to the secrecy that exists elsewhere in the investment world, where hedge funds protect their strategies and brokerages keep identities of private-banking clients confidential, the networks make positions visible to everyone. Users of  EToro  can duplicate bets made by the top traders, known as gurus, who may have as many as 100,000 followers and 10,000 copiers, raising concerns among professional investors.  \u201cI don\u2019t mind sharing what I\u2019m doing,\u201d said  Santosh Tiwari , a 37-year-old technology consultant from Reading,  England  who became an EToro guru as bets on the British pound helped produce a return of 11 percent over the past 12 months. \u201cEToro has evolved into such a big network, it has become a rich information source.\u201d  Disrupt Markets  Gurus may be able to disrupt markets as thousands of followers buy or sell the same securities, according to Justin Urquhart Stewart at Seven Investment Management Ltd. in London. Traders may just be seeing \u201cglimpses of someone\u2019s portfolio\u201d without being privy to a guru\u2019s overall trading strategy, Urquhart Stewart, who helps oversee about $6.8 billion, said in a telephone interview on June 3.  Copying someone based on past performance can be dangerous, according to Raimund Saxinger, a fund manager at Frankfurt-Trust Investment GmbH, which oversees about $22 billion.  \u201cIf you have a big universe to choose from, someone will always look good, just by the laws of numbers,\u201d Saxinger said in a telephone interview from  Frankfurt  on June 19. \u201cIt reminds me of Barton Biggs\u2019s account of a national coin-flipping contest where, after six months, there would be 32 contestants left from 200 million entrants. These 32 gurus would be interviewed on their finger-flipping technique and whether they used a special nail polish.\u201d  Biggs, the Morgan Stanley strategist who predicted the bull markets in U.S. stocks that began in 1982 and 2009 and urged investors to sell technology shares in the late 1990s before the dot-com bubble burst, died last year.  \u2018Survivorship Bias\u2019  Gains in global equities over the past four years may have increased the potential for \u201csurvivorship bias\u201d to create a distorted picture of leading gurus\u2019 skills, Saxinger said .  \u201cI\u2019m not sure if people are looking at the performance of trading gurus on a risk-adjusted basis,\u201d he said. \u201cInvestors need to take into account the risks taken by these gurus in order to obtain the returns that they make.\u201d  While gurus can earn as much as $10,000 a month in commissions for attracting people to duplicate their trades, they are often motivated by peer status in addition to money, according to Yoni Assia, EToro\u2019s founder and chief executive officer.  \u201cKnowing that there are thousands of users who think you\u2019re special in some way or other gives people the chance to experience a sense of self-fulfillment,\u201d Assia said. \u201cMost investment houses do not want to open up their customer base. On EToro, you can see who is buying and selling.\u201d  Mirror Trading  Social-investment networks started appearing in the middle of the last decade. Most focused on currency trading at first, as foreign-exchange markets allow 24-hour trading in highly liquid assets.  Tradency Inc. , a company founded by  Lior Nabat , began offering a mirror-trading platform in 2005. EToro, which started in 2007, made technology stocks such as Google Inc. and Apple Inc. available to its users in September last year and plans to add trading in well-known consumer companies.  Social investing attracts younger users and has a potential audience of hundreds of millions, according to Aite Group. Most clients have an interest in finance without the time or resources to be classed as a professional investor, Assia said.  ZuluTrade , a social network focused on currencies, says its user base has jumped 280 percent since 2011 to 500,000 members. Transaction volume reached about $40 billion a month, according to the company.  \u2018Strawberry Rhubarb\u2019  Collective2 allows customers to copy more than 15,000 trading programs designed by other subscribers. The  systems  have names such as \u201cEUR Scalper\u201d and \u201cStrawberry Rhubarb FX\u201d and can make buying and selling decisions for foreign exchange, equities and derivatives.  A program called \u201csp500-trading.com\u201d trades U.S. stock-index futures and claims an annual return of 75 percent. The \u201cenigma24 Eurostoxx\u201d system focuses on European equity derivatives and has posted an 8 percent annual loss.  \u201cThe Internet is great at breaking down barriers to entry, particularly in the financial world where going to the right schools and university still carry so much weight,\u201d Matthew Klein, CEO of Collective2 in New York, said in a phone interview. \u201cIf you are a genius who has developed a trading-software program in a basement in Moscow, you can use C2 as a distribution channel for the program you have developed to brokerages across the globe.\u201d  Virtual Money  At EToro, which plans to move its head office to  London  next week, clients can set up an account in minutes via their Facebook login. After practicing with virtual money, funds are deposited with a credit card. A minimum of $50 is required to start trading for real. Traders must also upload a copy of their passport and a utility bill.  \u201cWe don\u2019t think it is a fad,\u201d Assia said. \u201cSocial investing democratizes the world of investment. It allows people to see when people succeed and when they fail. You find all the secrets of the market.\u201d  EToro acts as a market maker, using derivatives known as contracts for difference to provide its users with exposure to stocks. CFDs are a leveraged product that allow people to bet on the movement of a stock without owning shares. The social investment network reached 50 million trades by users in May, 64 percent of which were copied.  Tiwari says becoming a guru felt like a natural progression and the status gives \u201cvalidation\u201d to his skills. He has about 3,500 copy traders and 72,000 followers, having used EToro since 2008, Tiwari said in a phone interview.  S&P Bets  Tiwari has a second account where he makes bets on the Standard and Poor\u2019s 500 Index and  Germany \u2019s  DAX Index (DAX) . He doesn\u2019t encourage people to follow these trades as he\u2019s just \u201ctrying out new ideas.\u201d The DAX climbed 1.7 percent to 7,940.99 at the close of trading in Frankfurt today. Describing himself on his  EToro profile  page as a part-time trader, Fernandez writes that he takes on little leverage, using technical and fundamental analysis to place bets on global currency markets.  \u201cWe invited him to attend a user event in  Barcelona  where he was warmly welcomed by all those attending, who wanted to finally meet him,\u201d Assia said. \u201cMalsolo is very much liked by the community and he regularly engages with his tribe to maintain and build his relationship.\u201d  Javier Paz, a senior analyst at Aite Group in  Boston , said social investing allows inexperienced investors to benefit from the wisdom of crowds. He is concerned about the amount of borrowing traders use to increase the size of their bets.  \u2018Dumb People\u2019  \u201cCrowd sourcing gives members of community linked insight as they pick up insight from each other,\u201d Paz said in a phone interview. \u201cLeverage means they risk losing a large portion of their original investment, which typically is a few hundred dollars. Smart people will make use of it in an intelligent way, dumb people will just use it too much.\u201d  Collective2\u2019s Klein said social investment networks need to promote responsible investing so uninformed traders don\u2019t suffer large losses. Users of EToro, which has obtained authorization under the U.K.\u2019s Financial Conduct Authority, can see the performance of a guru over the past year and the company is considering lengthening that, Assia said.  Social-network users still may not have sufficient information to judge the returns of fellow traders, according to David Jones, chief market strategist at IG, a London-based firm that offers spread betting, a way of placing wagers on stocks without owning them.  Closed Positions  \u201cSome companies only show the trading history of closed positions,\u201d Jones said in a telephone interview on June 5. \u201cA profit and loss could be skewed if some positions are still open. (MSFT)  and  Intel Corp. (INTC)  to combat  Apple Inc. (AAPL) \u2019s iPad in the $63.2 billion tablet market is getting off to a slow start.  Of more than a dozen tablets Microsoft and Intel touted for the new version of Windows, only five can be purchased for immediate U.S. delivery. Early demand for Microsoft\u2019s first computer, the Surface tablet, seems \u201cdisappointing,\u201d said Craig Berger, an analyst at FBR Capital Markets. And computer makers have been hampered in introducing tablets by limits Microsoft imposed on which manufacturers got a crack at prototypes, and by delays in Intel power-management software.  The holdup is making it harder for personal-computer makers, already beleaguered by plummeting demand, to challenge Apple and  Google Inc. (GOOG)  during the year-end holiday shopping season. While PC variants running Windows abound, tablets built on  ARM Holdings Plc (ARM)  technology-based chips or low-power processors from Intel are scarce.  \u201cYou can hardly even find one,\u201d said Bob O\u2019Donnell, an analyst at market researcher IDC in Framingham,  Massachusetts . \u201cSo even if you wanted to buy it, it would be difficult.\u201d  The list of Windows tablets is short. In addition to Microsoft\u2019s Surface,  Asustek Computer Inc. (2357) \u2019s Vivo Tab RT and  Lenovo Group Ltd. (992) \u2019s IdeaPad Yoga run the RT version of Windows and boast ARM-based chips.  Samsung Electronics Co. (005930) \u2019s ATIV Smart PC and  Acer Inc. (2353) \u2019s Iconia run Windows 8, and rely on Intel chips.  Microsoft Stores  Two of them, the Surface and the Acer device, are only available at Microsoft\u2019s own stores, which number just more than 60 for the holidays. FBR\u2019s Berger wrote in a note last week that Surface sales \u201chave underwhelmed expectations.\u201d Microsoft has declined to comment on Surface sales, which isn\u2019t a positive sign, said Wes Miller, an analyst at Directions on Microsoft.  \u201cWhen Microsoft is stealthy about numbers, that usually means something,\u201d he said. The PC market is forecast to shrink this year for the first time in more than a decade. Tablet shipments will pass notebooks in the second half of 2013, estimates Eve Jung, an analyst at Nomura. NPD DisplaySearch projects the tablet market will reach $162 billion in 2017, more than double its size this year.  Intel and Microsoft shares have suffered as concern rises about the future of the PC industry, exacerbated by the lack of Windows tablets on the market. Microsoft trades at a 29 percent discount on the same basis. Chipmaker Qualcomm Inc., benefiting from the surge in sales of mobile devices, trades at a 24 percent premium. Apple, before it introduced a new lineup of iPads, including the lower-cost iPad Mini, had  57 percent  of the market in the period. Licenses include copies corporations get as part of a multiyear contract, as well as those sold on new PCs and in retail, so the metric isn\u2019t a clear indication of demand.  More Choices  Intel, meantime, said consumers have more choices now, with tablets, ultrabooks and convertible devices that offer features of both.  \u201cWe have a number of innovative designs across the spectrum that offer a full Windows 8 experience, including new Intel-based tablets selling now from Samsung, Acer, Fujitsu and LG with several more on the way,\u201d Bill Calder, an Intel spokesman, said in an e-mailed statement.  Typical Windows releases are accompanied by hundreds of new machines. In this case, hardware manufacturers have done a better job delivering PC and notebook designs than tablets. While there are few tablets available, Microsoft has certified a total of 1,500 machines to run Windows 8.  U.S. retail sales of Windows PCs, including tablets, dropped 21 percent since the release of Windows 8 compared with the same period a year earlier, according to a  report  last week from market-research firm NPD Group Inc., whose data is based on a sampling of retailers and doesn\u2019t include Microsoft\u2019s own stores and therefore Surface sales. To contact the editor responsible for this story:\nNick Baker at   nbaker7@bloomberg.net .","path":".\/2008_2012_msft_bloomberg_news\/bets-against-u-s-technology-stocks-surge-following-apple-ibm-s-reports.txt"},{"id":55724448,"title":"Fight Google With Creativity, Not Antitrust Cases","released_at":"<date>December 18 2012<\/date> <time>18:39:29<\/time>","content":"Has the King of Search found a way out of a sticky antitrust settlement? Bloomberg News\u00a0 reports  that\u00a0 Google Inc. (GOOG)  is preparing to make voluntary concessions to end an almost two-year investigation of its business practices by the Federal Trade Commission. The federal scrutiny came in response to arguments from Google's competitors that the search company has abused its dominance in Internet search and given its own products and services an advantage. Google is said to be preparing a letter in which it will promise not to copy content from rival websites without permission, and will agree to allow advertisers to compare Google's ad-campaign data with other search-engine performance data. This would close the investigation without a lawsuit or settlement,  Bloomberg News  reports. In another investigation of Google, this one concerning patents, the FTC is likely to announce a consent decree this week in which Google would agree to license patents on reasonable terms. While Google seems to be slipping through settlement talks relatively unscathed in the U.S., in the European Union it may face more resistance from antitrust regulators  investigating  its dominance in the search market. In the U.S., Google handles about two-thirds of all Web searches. In several major European markets, Google accounts for more than 90 percent of searches. Google's easy-out in the FTC investigation would be a blow to competitor Microsoft Corp., whose Bing search engine accounts for about 16 percent of searches. Microsoft faced similar antitrust charges in 1998 when the U.S. Justice Department prevented it from using its  Windows operating system  to promote its Internet Explorer browser over competitors. Microsoft's loss in this antitrust case is often attributed to helping  advance  the rise of Google. So what's different in the case against Google today? It all comes down to the consumers. Google argues that its search ranking benefits users by providing top relevant content and that it doesn't hinder competitors because they are just \" one click away .\" In the Microsoft case, the judge  charged  that Microsoft was building a monopoly that harmed consumers by distorting competition and that raised the barrier of entry for Web developers, essentially limiting innovation. Today, we accept that the Web is an open place that cultivates creativity and innovation. Barriers to that openness harm our experience as users, so it's good that Google got a scolding and a reminder to play fair. It shouldn't copy information without permission, it should be transparent to\u00a0advertisers, and it should have fair terms for licensing patents essential for the industry. But what else can we expect? If consumers and advertisers have the necessary information to make choices among competitors, accusations of unfair monopoly on the Web fall flat.\u00a0Competitors might be better to leave off the litigation and try to knock Google off its throne the old-fashion way: with creative, user-conscious alternatives. (Kirsten Salyer is social media editor for Bloomberg View.  Follow  her on Twitter.) Seated across from Microsoft Corp.\u2019s billionaire co-founder on April 22 at a formal dining table in the Blue House, her official residence, Park picked the tech mogul\u2019s brain about how to nurture entrepreneurs to keep the world\u2019s 15th-largest economy humming.  \u201cIf there are more people like you, we will be able to create the world we dream of,\u201d Park, 61, told the smiling Gates.  By most measures, South Korea has already implanted itself among the globe\u2019s economic success stories, Bloomberg Markets magazine will report in its July issue. The one-time agrarian backwater has emerged as an icon of manufacturing, technology -- and cool.  More from the July issue of  Bloomberg Markets : Fifty million people have defied geography and history, rebounding from a 35-year Japanese occupation and the Korean War to create a thriving capitalist democracy along the world\u2019s most heavily fortified border. South Koreans in 1970 earned an average of $254 a year -- less than the $435 earned by their North Korean brethren. Last year, they averaged $22,708.  Overseas investors are embracing South Korea. They bought 55.6 trillion won ($49.2 billion) more Korean stocks and bonds than they sold in 2012.  The benchmark  Kospi Index (KOSPI)  has doubled to 2,001.20 as of May 29 from October 2008, when the subprime crisis roiled global markets.  Chaebols Rule  Family-controlled conglomerates known as chaebols, cranking out memory chips, liquid-crystal-display screens and tablet computers, have made Korea the seventh-largest exporting nation.  Samsung Group  sells more smartphones than Apple Inc., while Hyundai Motor Group, once known for unreliable cars, is aiming at Bayerische Motoren Werke AG in luxury vehicles. Sales of the top 30 chaebols equaled 82 percent of South Korea\u2019s $1.12 trillion gross domestic product in 2012, up from 53 percent in 2002.  Seoul, the work-obsessed capital of 10.4 million, is the epicenter of the buzz. Workers whose parents once toiled in uniforms making wigs and toys flock to office towers sporting Chanel and earbuds, traveling there in subways equipped with free Wi-Fi.  \u2018Pali, Pali\u2019  The world\u2019s most-wired country runs on \u201cpali, pali\u201d or \u201cquickly, quickly,\u201d as people in cafes along Garosu-gil Street swap quips or compete in a one-minute game called Anipang on ubiquitous mobile phones. Aspirations are soaring as parents hire English tutors for their children while indulging in plastic surgery for themselves in the Gangnam neighborhood south of the Han River. K-pop hits, soap operas and \u201cGangnam Style,\u201d rap artist Psy\u2019s record-setting video spoof of over-the-top consumption, spread the vibe worldwide.  \u201cKorea is going through a renaissance,\u201d says Richard Min, a Korean-American who moved to Seoul from Boston in 2000 and co-founded technology incubator Seoul Space Inc. \u201cIt\u2019s cool to be Korean.\u201d  Park, the Republic of Korea\u2019s 11th president and its first female leader, is striving for more than coolness. The daughter of late President Park Chung Hee, the military strongman who championed the country\u2019s industrial chaebols, says that to sustain growth, South Korea must move beyond those conglomerates and encourage small businesses.  \u2018Radically New\u2019  \u201cThe past economic model designed to catch up with advanced economies drove Korea\u2019s rapid growth, but it has lost steam,\u201d Park told Bloomberg Markets in a written reply to questions.  She seeks to add 2.5 million jobs during her five years in office -- 410,000 of them in areas overseen by her cumbersomely named Ministry of Science, ICT and Future Planning. (ICT stands for Information and Communications Technology.) She plans tax incentives for entrepreneurs and venture capitalists and an alternative stock market to help companies raise money.  \u201cThe president\u2019s drive to create new jobs started from a humble realization that we need to do something radically new,\u201d says Cho Won Dong, the president\u2019s senior secretary for economic affairs, discussing Park\u2019s strategy in his office near the Blue House.  Min, for one, is pumped.  \u201cPresident Park Geun Hye has decided creativity and innovation are the new keywords,\u201d the 39-year-old says. \u201cIf we grow the way Koreans love to grow, there is no reason why we can\u2019t be bigger than Silicon Valley.\u201d  Park\u2019s Mission  Dual forces lend urgency to Park\u2019s mission: Korea\u2019s aging population and falling birth rate and the economic dynamics of its neighbors.  While much of the world assumes that the South\u2019s most-vexing challenge is North Korea\u2019s volatile new leader Kim Jong Un, South Koreans themselves worry more about finding good jobs and staying economically competitive with the real giant to the north -- China, the No. 2 global economy. They are also looking anxiously at Japan, the country that China eclipsed, as Prime Minister Shinzo Abe drives down the yen.  Sixty years after the armistice that formally ended hostilities between the two halves of the Korean peninsula, only 15 percent of Southerners said North Korea was a priority, a February survey by Seoul\u2019s Asan Institute for Policy Studies found. Their top concerns were reducing household debt, in which South Korea ranks eighth in the world when measured against disposable income; lowering the 8.4 percent youth unemployment rate; and remaining in the middle class.  Creative Economy  Women, who are paid 39 percent less than men for the same job, are hoping Park will narrow an income gap that was the highest among 34 Organization for Economic Cooperation and Development members.  Park says the ticket to expansion is a creative economy underpinned by entrepreneurs and venture capitalists.  \u201cGrowth led by a few big firms and the government is bound to be limited,\u201d she told policy makers in April.  While Park is only now unrolling the details, investors like what they have seen so far.  \u201cPresident Park\u2019s goals are very good and, if achieved, will take Korea to the next stage,\u201d says  Mark Mobius , executive chairman of Templeton  Emerging Markets  Group, who oversees more than $50 billion in emerging-markets equities, about 4 percent of them Korean stocks.  China Looms  Park has her work cut out for her. The boom that has allowed people to splurge on luxuries is ebbing. One immediate challenge is a slowdown in China, which has become the largest buyer of South Korean exports. Longer term, China, with a research and development workforce of 2.3 million -- seven times greater than South Korea\u2019s -- looms as a formidable competitor.  \u201cChina has no fear of Korea anymore, so we now have to come up with something different,\u201d says senior economic secretary Cho, 56, who has a doctorate in economics from the University of Oxford and who served on former President Kim Dae Jung\u2019s economic team during the Asian financial crisis in 1998. \u201cPresident Park Geun Hye\u2019s solution is a creative economy.\u201d  South Korea\u2019s economy expanded by  2 percent  last year, the slowest pace since the 0.3 percent rate in 2009. The central bank has twice this year cut 2013 projections, with the estimate of 2.6 percent on April 11 a downgrade from its initial forecast of 3.2 percent.  Aging Koreans  Park is mindful of her country\u2019s demographic time bomb. The population is aging at the fastest pace of any advanced nation, the OECD says. The available workforce will dwindle starting in 2017. By 2026, one of five Koreans will be 65 or older, a level the U.S. won\u2019t reach until a decade later, Statistics Korea says.  Already, the middle class is shrinking and people are falling back into poverty as the division between rich and poor widens. The top 20 percent of South Koreans earn more than five times as much as the bottom 20 percent.  Park aims to have 70 percent of South Koreans in the middle class, with incomes that range today from $18,500 to $55,500, by term\u2019s end. She wants more Koreans to work, too. Her goal is to employ 70 percent of people ages 15 to 64, up from 64.2 percent in 2012.  \u201cThe new administration seeks to establish an economic system characterized by a virtuous cycle of growth, employment and distribution,\u201d Park told Bloomberg Markets.  Happiness Fund  The president administered an economic booster shot in April. She unveiled a 17.3 trillion won supplementary budget, the largest of its kind since the Asian financial crisis. She created the so-called National Happiness Fund to help low-income earners consolidate or refinance household debt, which totaled 959 trillion won, equal to 136 percent of disposable income at the end of 2012.  Park took her campaign for a creative economy to the U.S. in May. Stopping in New York, she extolled the late Korean video artist Nam June Paik.  \u201cThe U.S. invented the video,\u201d Park told supporters at the Waldorf-Astoria Hotel. \u201cJapan provided it to households. Korea made it art.\u201d  At a White House meeting, Park and President  Barack Obama  pledged to form a united front against North Korea\u2019s threats. She told the U.S. Congress she would \u201cwrite a sequel\u201d to Korea\u2019s transformation story.  Accompanied by a 51-member economic delegation that included Samsung Chairman Lee Kun Hee and Hyundai Motor Chairman  Chung Mong Koo , Park met U.S. business leaders on May 8. In Los Angeles, she brainstormed with Jennifer Yuh Nelson, the Korean-American director of \u201cKung Fu Panda 2;\u201d venture capitalists; and executives. She took advice from a participant to invest in a yet-to-be-determined U.S. venture capital fund, which would in turn invest in Korean startups.  Apple, Google  \u201cHopefully, we can create another Apple or Google on Korean soil,\u201d says economic adviser Cho, who accompanied the president to the U.S.  Park\u2019s entrepreneurship drive will be difficult in a country still dominated by conglomerates, says Bruce Cumings, a history professor at the University of Chicago.  Led by the chaebols, Korea\u2019s economy has expanded every year in the past five decades except for two: 1980, during the oil shock, and 1998, amid Asia\u2019s financial crisis. Outbound shipments by the 30 largest companies accounted for 84 percent of South Korea\u2019s exports in 2010.  \u201cCorporate bigness has been a key to Korean success, and the most successful chaebol, Samsung, now rivals Apple,\u201d says Cumings, who has written nine books on Korea, including \u201cThe Korean War\u201d (Random House, 2011). \u201cSamsung\u2019s prowess is not exactly an argument for small-bore entrepreneurship.\u201d  Fewer Jobs  Choi Seok Won, head of the research center of Hanwha Investment & Securities Co. in Seoul, counters that many chaebol jobs don\u2019t benefit Koreans. The overseas production of Korea\u2019s large manufacturers jumped to 16.7 percent of their total output in 2010 from 6.7 percent in 2005. Hyundai builds cars abroad, and Samsung Electronics Co. plans a Palo Alto, California, campus complete with startup incubator.  \u201cChaebols are phenomenally successful, but they no longer create jobs at home,\u201d Choi says.  Chaebols also have acquired a reputation for bending the rules, says  Shaun Cochran , head of Korea research at Hong Kong-based brokerage CLSA Asia Pacific.  \u201cPeople in Korea don\u2019t trust the power structure at the top because of a long history of leaders with special exemptions,\u201d he says. From 1990 to 2012, the heads of seven of the 10 biggest chaebols have been sentenced to prison for bribery, embezzlement and tax evasion. None spent more than a few months behind bars.  \u2018Full Circle\u2019  \u201cIf Park Chung Hee\u2019s legacy was nurturing the chaebols, it is his daughter\u2019s chance to come full circle,\u201d Cochran says. \u201cShe has to turn her back to close relationships her father had. She has to stand up and say those days are over.\u201d  While Park\u2019s policies regarding the chaebols are still evolving, she has shown backbone in dealing with the North. In April, North Korea threatened to rain nuclear missiles on South Korea and the U.S. and removed 53,000 workers from the Gaeseong industrial zone -- a jointly run operation just north of the border and the only existing symbol of Korean cooperation. After the North rejected talks, Park ordered all South Koreans to leave the complex, determined not to succumb to pressure designed to extract concessions.  \u201cThe Republic of Korea will never accept a nuclear-armed North Korea,\u201d Park told the U.S. Congress in May. \u201cPyongyang\u2019s provocation will be met decisively.\u201d  Less than two weeks later, North Korea test-fired six short-range missiles in defiance of international sanctions. Park\u2019s approval rating rose to about 56 percent in mid-May from 45 percent in late March.  Father\u2019s Determination  John Linton, a medical doctor who was born in South Korea to American parents, says Park\u2019s determination reminds him of her father\u2019s.  A fourth-generation resident, Linton, 53, lived through South Korea\u2019s transition to democracy from dictatorship and was a teenager when two tragedies befell the Park family. In 1974, Park Chung Hee was speaking at the National Theater of Korea when a North Korean agent named Mun Se Gwang opened fire. He killed First Lady Yuk Young Soo while aiming for the president. In 1979, Park Chung Hee was assassinated by intelligence chief Kim Jae Kyu for reasons that remain unclear.  Linton talked with Park Geun Hye in 2002. She had just returned from Pyongyang, where she met  Kim Jong Il , the current dictator\u2019s late father. Linton asked how she could have visited the man who engineered her mother\u2019s assassination. Park looked at him coldly.  \u201cMy family\u2019s interest is my family\u2019s interest, and my country\u2019s interest is my country\u2019s interest,\u201d he recalls her saying. \u201cThey are different.\u201d  Industrial Powerhouse  Park Chung Hee, a major general in the South Korean Army, spearheaded Korea\u2019s growth into an industrial powerhouse. From 1961 to 1979, he showered the chaebols with loans and tax breaks. In 1972, he unveiled a new constitution that increased a president\u2019s tenure and removed limits on re-election, marring his legacy. Students protested, and opposition leader Kim Dae Jung decried the move.  Kim, who died in 2009 at 85, became president in 1998. He won the Nobel Peace Prize in 2000 for his pro-democracy campaigns and work toward a historic inter-Korean summit.  Now, the strongman\u2019s daughter is unveiling incentives for the next wave of Korean businesses.  Encouraging Entrepreneurs  For companies three years old or younger, she\u2019s expanding tax breaks for angel investors and establishing a government-run Future Creation Fund, which, along with private contributions, will hold 200 billion won of seed money. She plans tax incentives to sellers or buyers of companies that are four to nine years old and a similar 300 billion won fund.  For firms 10 to 15 years old, Park is proposing a stock market called the Korea New Exchange, or Konex, for capital raising. It would supplement the  Kosdaq (KOSDAQ) , Korea\u2019s version of the tech-heavy Nasdaq.  \u201cAs a government, we cannot create creativity but an environment where startups can thrive,\u201d says Choi Mun Kee, 62, the new science and ICT minister.  Choi, as president of the Electronics and Telecommunications Research Institute, laid the foundation for Korea\u2019s mobile phone industry.  \u201cEntrepreneurs are going to be encouraged to take risks, allowed to fail and get another chance, raise capital easily and exit through mergers and acquisitions,\u201d he says.  Failure\u2019s Price  The price of failure is high in South Korea. A business owner has little chance of rebounding from bankruptcy. Korea\u2019s small and midsize companies raised 99 percent of their combined 472 trillion won of capital through loans last year, the government says.  \u201cIf you start a business and fail, that failure sticker will be with you for the rest of your life,\u201d says Daniel Shin, founder of TicketMonster Inc., South Korea\u2019s biggest shopping-deal website. He says Koreans define success as being a doctor or a lawyer, not an entrepreneur.  Choi wants to fight that perception by celebrating such startups as KakaoTalk, a free messaging service for smartphones with 88 million worldwide users. Seated in his office among framed commemorative stamps of Psy, Choi also praises  Golfzon (121440)  Co., creator of a virtual golf game that simulates outdoor courses, and Delight Co., which developed a hearing aid using a 3-D printer.  Silicon Seoul  The government, with its history of intervening in the economy, has a good chance of sparking a Korea-style Silicon Valley, CLSA\u2019s Cochran says.  \u201cKorea is one environment that is able to bring together a large number of industries,\u201d he says. \u201cThe government will get behind it, the banks will get behind it, and the companies will get behind it.\u201d  Park, like her predecessors, keeps a wary eye on the region\u2019s dominant forces: China and Japan. South Korea is eager to avoid the fate of Japan, which emerged as an economic superpower in the 1970s and 1980s on the strength of its exports. After the Plaza Accord of 1985 led to a surge in the yen\u2019s value, the central bank cut  interest rates , spurring speculation in real estate and stocks. The bubble popped in the early 1990s when the  Bank of Japan  lifted short-term interest rates. Ever since, Japan\u2019s economy has stagnated even as interest rates have fallen to virtually zero.  Japan\u2019s Moves  Abe, who took office in December, announced $100 billion in extra government spending and appointed a central bank governor who has vowed to pour money into the financial system to end Japan\u2019s lost decades.  One pillar of Abenomics is an effort to drive down the yen to help Japan\u2019s beleaguered exporters. The currency fell 18.9 percent against the  U.S. dollar  and 15.1 percent against the won in the six months through May 29, sparking concern in Korea and hurting its exporters.  \u201cCompared with the North Korea risk, a sliding yen is having a considerable impact on the real economy,\u201d Finance Minister Hyun Oh Seok told  Bloomberg News  on April 18.  China\u2019s newly confident companies are hurting Korea\u2019s exports with sheer competition. China has relegated 10 once-dominant export items, including petrochemicals, to second or third, the Korea International Trade Association says.  \u201cIn five to 10 years, China will have its technology, labor market and consumer market and will no longer need Korea,\u201d says Ted Chung, chief executive officer of Hyundai Card Co. and Hyundai Capital Services Inc. \u201cWe have to think about our next economic model -- ultimately, what kind of a country we want to make.\u201d  Chung, 53, sees promise in biotechnology and in combining information technology with South Korea\u2019s auto and other established industries.  Gender Inequalities  South Korea\u2019s women are hoping that any new economic model will mean more opportunities for them. Park got an unwanted reminder about the difficulty of addressing gender inequalities during her U.S. visit. A Washington-based intern accused the president\u2019s top spokesman, Yoon Chang Jung, of fondling her in a hotel. Park fired him and apologized to the public amid front-page stories in the Korean press. Yoon denied the accusations.  Kim Sung Joo is the rare woman who has made it to the top despite discrimination. In her case, Kim says, the bias was from her own father. Kim Su Geun, who headed energy conglomerate Daesung Group, favored his sons and expected his daughters to finish college and accept an arranged marriage. Kim says her father disowned her after she sought further education in the U.S. and wed the man of her choice.  Today, Kim, 56, calls herself a left-wing chaebol owner: Her luxury handbag company, MCM Holdings AG, is succeeding in a male-dominated society, and she devotes 10 percent of annual profits to train female business leaders and support North Korean defectors.  Little Guy  Park\u2019s effort to build small companies reflects not only an economic strategy but also empathy for the little guy -- a trait she shares with her late mother. Park was 9 when her father grabbed power from Prime Minister Chang Myon in a 1961 coup and she and two younger siblings moved to the Blue House. First Lady Yuk Young Soo established a foundation for children\u2019s welfare that ran a kindergarten and a science center. She once brought a young beggar to the presidential house to feed and bathe him, according to Park\u2019s autobiography, \u201cSteeled by Despair, Motivated by Hope.\u201d  Park was studying French in Grenoble, France, when her mother was killed. At 22, she adopted the role of first lady, hosting U.S. President  Jimmy Carter  in June 1979. Four months later, Park\u2019s father was assassinated. General Chun Doo Hwan took over and ruled until 1988, when he handed power to Roh Tae Woo.  Quitting Spotlight  Park retreated from the spotlight. The hardest thing was hearing loyal friends calling her father a dictator, she wrote in \u201cSteeled by Despair.\u201d She turned to Buddhism, meditation, reading and writing. She led the child-welfare foundation named for her mother and received 600 million won from her father\u2019s estate. She never married. Visitors to her house in 2002 were surprised to see an old TV and faded wallpaper, according to \u201cSolitary Leadership\u201d by Chun Young Shik.  Park entered politics in 1998 as the financial crisis rocked Asia. Thailand, struggling with current-account deficit and a property bubble, abolished its currency\u2019s peg to the dollar, causing the baht\u2019s collapse and a chain reaction in Malaysia, Indonesia and South Korea.  South Korea\u2019s economy, which had expanded at an annual average rate of 8.7 percent from 1980 to 1990, shrank 5.7 percent in 1998. Foreigners pulled out capital, businesses went bankrupt, and interest rates soared to 30 percent. The won plunged to a record low of almost 2,000 to the dollar in 1998. On May 29, it was trading at 1,133.  Deepest Recession  The country fell into its deepest recession since the war, threatening growth lauded as the Miracle on the Han River, after the waterway that bisects Seoul. Koreans rallied. When the government sought a $57 billion bailout from the  International Monetary Fund  in December 1997, citizens turned in gold jewelry to reduce the loan. The country fully repaid the IMF in August 2001, almost three years early. The economy grew 10.7 percent in 1999.  Park won parliamentary elections beginning in 1998. She became leader of the Grand National Party, which traces its history to her father\u2019s era, in March 2004. To defuse public outcry over an alleged bribery scandal involving the party\u2019s 2002 presidential candidate, Lee Hoi Chang, she moved the headquarters from Seoul\u2019s Yeouido financial district to a makeshift tent.  Face Slashed  Park almost lost her own life in 2006. She was campaigning in Seoul when an ex-convict who later said he was seeking attention slashed her face with a box cutter. It was a miracle that the 11-centimeter (4-inch) gash on her right cheek didn\u2019t touch the carotid artery, doctors told her after the attack.  Last December, Park defeated Moon Jae In in the presidential race, winning 51.6 percent to 48 percent. Donald Gregg, U.S. ambassador to South Korea from 1989 to 1993, says Park has adopted traits of her father and her mother.  \u201cThe new president has inherited both her parents\u2019 best qualities: her father\u2019s tenacity and intelligence and her mother\u2019s grace,\u201d says Gregg, who knew Park\u2019s parents and met with her several times.  Soon after she was elected, Park visited alleys behind Seoul\u2019s East Gate Market, where extreme poverty still exists in the thriving capital. The odor of urine from shared toilets permeates this area, where rooms just big enough to lie down in cost 180,000 won a month.  Eventual Reunification  \u201cPresident Park came here with a lunch box and distributed butane gas for cooking,\u201d says Lee Hak Soon, 74, who left North Korea during the war and settled in East Gate Market 44 years ago. \u201cShe reminded me of her mother.\u201d  As South Koreans adapt to Park\u2019s creative economy, some envision an even larger boom triggered by reunification. Thirty or 40 years after the Koreas reunite, their combined GDP could exceed that of France, Germany or Japan, predicts Kwon Goohoon, Goldman Sachs Group Inc.\u2019s chief economist for Korea.  Andrei Lankov , a professor at Seoul\u2019s Kookmin University, says merging the two Koreas will be jarring and painful.  \u201cMany South Koreans dream of gradual, managed unification, but in all probability, when the change does come, it will be dramatic and unpredictable,\u201d he says.  For now, the North, even with its bellicose leader whom many people believe hasn\u2019t yet turned 30, doesn\u2019t faze a new crop of businesspeople returning to Korea.  \u2018Best Time\u2019  \u201cIt is the best time ever to be in Korea right now to try and be an entrepreneur,\u201d says David Lee, a Korean-Canadian who came back to Seoul and founded video-editing company Shakr Media.  The experience of Shin, the 27-year-old Korean-American who started TicketMonster, shows hurdles still exist. He quit his consulting job at McKinsey & Co. in New Jersey to form his company. In Korea, he faced resistance when he tried to persuade a chaebol executive to offer a promotion on the shopping-deal site.  The executive wanted to know why a young man with a degree from the University of Pennsylvania\u2019s Wharton School was deviating from his McKinsey career. He said if his son took such a path, he\u2019d be very disappointed, Shin recalls. Shin sold TicketMonster -- valued at $300 million at the time -- for an undisclosed amount to LivingSocial Inc. in Washington in 2011.  Creative Couple  Husband-and-wife duo Bang Hyun Woo and Heo Yun Sil embody the creativity Park aims to unleash. Heo, 34, quit her job in 2007 as a mobile phone designer at LG Electronics Co. and formed Everyware Co. Bang, 34, has a Ph.D. in mechanical engineering.  The couple makes artworks that incorporate touch, sound, smell and sight. Viewers brush a blank canvas that changes color or throw balls at glass that seems to shatter. A TV takes photos to share on social networks. Samsung Everland Inc., SK Telecom Co. and Samsung Electronics have collaborated on several projects.  \u201cWe see limitless possibilities in technology and design to give joy to people,\u201d Heo says.  In their attic home-office atop a rundown Seoul building, Heo and Bang are doing just what Park says South Korea requires to expand its economy and keep China at bay.  \u201cKorea is pushing to make a transition to a pace-setting economic system by realizing a creative economy that will generate new added value and create jobs,\u201d she told Bloomberg Markets a week after releasing her blueprint for small businesses.  In Park\u2019s view, the South Korea that arose as an industrial giant under her father has the potential to become the next Silicon Valley.  \u201cOne person can change the world, like Bill Gates and  Steve Jobs ,\u201d she told top officials at the Blue House on April 18.  So says the general\u2019s daughter, the latest leader of a country that has survived war and privation and developed a decades-long habit of outsmarting its neighbors and confounding expectations. The ball is sharp, the girl\nblurry.  Now imagine being able to refocus the entire photo -- after\nthe fact.  That\u2019s the awesome thing about the  Lytro , the first\nconsumer camera to employ a technology called light-field\nphotography that until now was the province of scientific\nlaboratories.  Launched by a  Mountain View ,  California , start-up to\ncapitalize on  research  conducted at  Stanford University , the\nLytro introduces the concept of a living photo that can be\nadjusted on the fly by photographer and viewer alike.  Unlike a traditional digital camera, which depends on light\ndirectly hitting a sensor, the Lytro captures all the light in a\nscene traveling in any direction -- enough information to allow\nthe focus to be manipulated in any number of ways. Conventional\ncamera-makers talk about megapixels, the number of dots of\ninformation that make up an image; Lytro talks in terms of\nmegarays to describe the amount of light captured. The Lytro\nclaims a rating of 11 megarays, or 11 million rays.  Keeping It Simple  If the  technology  is unfamiliar and exotic, the Lytro\nitself, mercifully, isn\u2019t. For all its sophistication, it\u2019s a\npleasure to use. Not having to focus makes it easier than\ntraditional point-and-shoot cameras, or even your smartphone.\nThe Lytro turns on instantly and there\u2019s no shutter lag. My\nbiggest annoyance was a lens cap that kept popping off.  The camera, which fits easily into a jacket pocket, weighs\nless than eight ounces. A little more than four inches long, it\nresembles a squared-off spyglass. It\u2019s sold on the Lytro\nwebsite, which offers  two models . The 8-gigabyte version ($399)\ncomes in blue or graphite and can hold about 350 photos. The 16-\ngig model ($499) is red and holds about 750 photos.  At one end of the aluminum-clad body is the lens; at the\nother is a 1.46-inch square touchscreen viewfinder. You activate\nthe 8X optical zoom by running your finger back and forth along\nthe rubberized top of the camera; a quick tap of the screen\nadjusts the exposure. The shutter is an indentation atop the\ncamera, easy to find by touch and hard to hit by accident.  Windows Coming  Just how revolutionary the Lytro is doesn\u2019t really become\napparent until you connect it to your computer with the included\nUSB cable. As with  Cisco (CSCO) \u2019s late, lamented Flip videocam, the\ndesktop software you need is built into the camera and installs\nitself automatically. At the moment, it only works with  Apple (AAPL) \u2019s\nMac operating system; a  Windows (MSFT)  version is on the way.  Your photos are displayed iPhoto-like, but with one big\ndifference: Clicking anywhere on a picture refocuses it on that\nspecific point.  A photo I took of  San Francisco  Bay from the landmark Ferry\nBuilding allows me to choose between focusing on a close-in\npiece of iron railing or, off in the distance, the Bay Bridge or\nYerba Buena Island.  A shot of Rodin\u2019s \u201cBurghers of Calais\u201d on the Stanford\ncampus lets me change which of the burghers I want to emphasize.\nIn a close-up of a flower at a Palo Alto farmer\u2019s market, I can\nsharpen the focus on the pistil, or emphasize an individual\npetal.  Viewer\u2019s Choice  Don\u2019t like my choices? If I post my photos to the Lytro\nwebsite and share a link, anyone viewing them can make his  own\ndecision  about what to sharpen and what to blur.  At the outset, at least, the website and Facebook will be\nthe only ways to directly share Lytro\u2019s living pictures -- a\ndownside if you use some other site, like  Yahoo (YHOO) \u2019s Flickr or\n Google (GOOG) \u2019s Picasa, for your online storage and sharing. Lytro\u2019s\nsoftware does make it easy to tweet a picture in Twitter or +1\nit in Google Plus, but in each case it\u2019s just a link back to the\nversion on Lytro.com  You\u2019ll also find some things missing from the Lytro -- a\nflash, for example, and the ability to shoot video. But it does\noffer a \u201ccreative mode\u201d that gives the photographer more\ncontrol over a shot\u2019s refocus range, and the company says other\ncapabilities are in the works, including three-dimensional\nimages, light-field editing tools and the ability to make an\nentire photo in focus.  Introducing consumers to a completely new technology is\ninherently tricky, but Lytro has done an impressive job of\nkeeping things simple. You don\u2019t have to forget everything you\nknow about point-and-shoot cameras to use it -- just the part\nwhere you worry about ruining a shot because it\u2019s out of focus. T-Systems plans to lure customers by emphasizing the\nsecurity of its servers, over which it delivers its Internet-\naccessed computing services, Reinhard Clemens, the division\u2019s\nchief executive officer, told reporters in Bonn on Sept. 12.\nThis includes shielding clients from government access such as\nthat allowed by the U.S. Patriot Act, he said.  \u201cThe Americans say that no matter what happens I\u2019ll\nrelease the data to the government if I\u2019m forced to do so, from\nanywhere in the world,\u2019\u201d Clemens said. \u201cCertain German\ncompanies don\u2019t want others to access their systems. That\u2019s why\nwe\u2019re well-positioned if we can say we\u2019re a European provider in\na European legal sphere and no American can get to them.\u201d  Deutsche Telekom and other telecommunications companies are\npromoting cloud-computing offerings as a safe way for businesses\nto outsource their data centers. A government seal may fence off\nthe cloud offerings of T-Systems and European competitors such\nas Atos SA and  Cap Gemini SA (CAP)  and give them an advantage over\nU.S. rivals such as  Hewlett-Packard Co. (HPQ) ,  Microsoft Corp. (MSFT)  and\n International Business Machines Corp. (IBM)   Some of the surveillance powers of the U.S. Patriot Act,\npassed after the Sept. 11 attacks, have been opposed by some\nlawmakers and outside groups, including civil liberties\nactivists.  \u201cA German cloud\u201d would be a \u201csafe cloud,\u201d Clemens said.  U.S. Exit  Deutsche Telekom in March agreed to sell its T-Mobile USA\nunit for $39 billion to  AT&T Inc. (T)  The German company is\ncurrently trying to salvage the deal after the  Justice\nDepartment  sued Dallas-based AT&T and T-Mobile on Aug. 31,\nsaying a combination of the two companies would substantially\nreduce competition.  The global market for cloud services may surge to $148.8\nbillion in 2014 from $68.3 billion in 2010, according to\nresearcher Gartner Inc. T-Systems predicts it will generate 2\nbillion euros ($2.74 billion) more in revenue between 2009 and\n2015, mostly from delivering software and data storage to\ncustomers via the Internet.  A German certificate could be issued by the country\u2019s\nTechnical Inspection Association, based on guidelines developed\nby the Federal Office for Information Security, Clemens said.\nThe office is in talks with European Union officials to develop\ncommon standards across the region, which may result in a\nEuropean certificate, he said.  Reliability Issues  Telecommunications companies also need to convince clients\nabout the reliability of cloud services.  In May, SAP AG\u2019s head of global solutions, Sanjay Poonen,\nsaid an outage on  Amazon.com Inc. (AMZN) \u2019s cloud-computing services\nearlier this year, and a controversy around  Google Inc. (GOOG) \u2019s delays\nin providing e-mail services to 30,000 city employees in  Los\nAngeles  could make it harder for the  software industry  to\nconvince clients to use cloud computing services.  In the U.S., a group led by Salesforce.com and VCE, a cloud\nservices provider founded by Cisco Systems Inc. and EMC Corp.,\nsent a report to the government on July 26, urging it to\naccelerate government and commercial uptake of cloud\ntechnologies.  Apple Inc., aiming to capitalize on a shift away from\npersonal computers, this year introduced the iCloud service that\nstores music and other files online and keeps devices\nsynchronized wirelessly. The product will let users move their\n\u201cdigital life\u201d from PC hard drives to remote data centers in\nthe \u201ccloud,\u201d the company said at the time.  Talks About Standards  In the European Union, Commissioner  Neelie Kroes ,\nresponsible for the region\u2019s  Digital Agenda , has asked providers\nand users of cloud computing to participate in talks about data\nprotection and privacy as well as technical and commercial\nstandards.  \u201cThe cloud is critical to  Europe \u2019s growth,\u201d Kroes  said  in\nMarch. She said the European Union needs to develop the right\nlegal framework, encourage more technology research and push the\npublic sector to use cloud computing.  T-Systems\u2019 sales from cloud products are increasing by 49\npercent a year, Clemens said, without giving a total sales\nfigure. That\u2019s the word millions of Americans have been waiting to\nhear since  Apple Inc . and  Verizon Wireless  announced that the\niPhone 4 was at last coming to the Verizon network. Would it\nprovide a better experience than the version that runs on AT&T\nInc.\u2019s rival system?  My early conclusion is, it does. I\u2019ve been using the\n Verizon iPhone , available today for pre-order and in stores on\nFeb. 10, for about a week in various locales in Northern\nCalifornia, and it has yet to drop or fail to connect a call.\nThat\u2019s a sharp contrast with my AT&T iPhone, which continues to\nlose calls regularly.  You have to feel a little sorry for AT&T. When it won\nexclusive rights to the first iPhone in 2007, there was no way\nto know how popular it would prove to be -- or how much stress\nall those bandwidth-munching users would put on its network.  The result has been that many U.S. iPhone buyers have been\ntorn between delight with their cool gadget and a desire to hurl\nit into New York Harbor,  San Francisco Bay  or some other handy\nbody of water. And AT&T has become a punchline for comedians, as\nin  Jon Stewart \u2019s recent  rant  on  Comedy Central \u2019s   Daily Show .\u201d  No Slam-Dunk  Still, deciding between Verizon and AT&T isn\u2019t a slam-dunk,\nand current AT&T users who are able to switch shouldn\u2019t\nautomatically do so. The AT&T version is superior in some\nimportant respects, and you may have better service where you\nare than I do where I am. It does mean, though, that current and\npotential iPhone users in the U.S. finally have a choice. And\nthat\u2019s a very good thing.  The new iPhone is just that: a new iPhone. AT&T and Verizon\nuse different technologies, and a phone that runs on one\ncompany\u2019s network can\u2019t run on the other\u2019s. Still, the two\nhandsets have the same dimensions, display and user interface,\nand the physical differences are minimal. The Verizon version\nhas no SIM-card slot, the black bands in the metal rim that\nserve as the antenna are in different places and the mute switch\nis slightly lower -- meaning that some existing cases may not\nfit right.  The two phones seem comparable in their ability to connect\nto the Internet over their respective 3G  data networks . I found\nno clear pattern as to which was faster in terms of Google\nsearches, loading Web pages or running applications that access\nthe Net. Using  Speedtest.net \u2019s measurement app, sometimes one\nwas faster, sometimes the other. Neither phone is capable of\nusing the new 4G networks that carriers are beginning to roll\nout across the nation and that promise much faster data speeds.  Personal Hotspot  The Verizon phone offers one useful new feature called\nPersonal Hotspot, which for an extra monthly fee allows you to\nshare the iPhone\u2019s data connection via Wi-Fi with up to five\nother devices. It\u2019s simpler and more flexible than the so-called\ntethering function on AT&T iPhones, and I found it to work well\nwith a variety of gadgets, including laptops and an iPad. When\nother products are sharing the connection, you\u2019ll see a message\non the iPhone screen; when they are done using the phone to get\nonline, the Personal Hotspot shuts down to conserve battery\nlife.  There are two significant drawbacks to the Verizon iPhone.\nOne is that, unlike the AT&T version, you can\u2019t talk and access\nthe Internet over the 3G connection at the same time. So you\ncan\u2019t, for instance, check movie times while you\u2019re on a call\nwith a friend.  Don\u2019t Blame IPhone  This isn\u2019t the iPhone\u2019s fault -- it\u2019s a characteristic of\nthe technology Verizon uses, known as CDMA, and it\u2019s the same\nstory on Verizon 3G phones that run  Google Inc .\u2019s Android\noperating system and, later this year,  Microsoft Corp .\u2019s Windows\nPhone 7.  The other drawback is that CDMA, which was developed by\nQualcomm Corp., is far less widely used outside the U.S. than is\nthe standard AT&T uses, which is known as GSM. So if you need to\nuse your phone internationally, AT&T may make more sense.  The Verizon iPhone will cost $199.99 with a two-year\nservice contract for a model storing 16 gigabytes of music,\nmovies and data, and $299.99 for 32 gigabytes, which is\ncomparable to what AT&T charges. For now, Verizon will continue\nto sell an unlimited data plan for the device, but it\u2019s likely\nto follow AT&T to tiered pricing later this year.  Hopefully, Verizon executives have learned from observing\nAT&T\u2019s travails, and their network is ready for the onslaught of\ndata-hungry iPhone users. We\u2019ll soon find out. In the meantime,\na word to whoever it was in the Apple PR department who called\nmy AT&T iPhone while I was writing this column: Sorry about\nthat. The call failed. Try the Verizon number. To settle an antitrust investigation, Google is  agreeing  to distinguish between its own services and those of competitors in search results, Bloomberg News reports. This will slow -- though not stop -- the digital economy's gatekeeper from leveraging its dominance in search into market power in other areas. Currently, when a consumer looks for, say, flights on Google, the search engine provides a list of airfares offered by Google's advertisers. Next comes a box, dubbed a \"Google flight search,'' listing the major carriers and their prices. Only after that do online travel services, including Expedia, Kayak and TripAdvisor, appear; they often provide less expensive fares yet can require more time to filter through the many options. The same goes for shopping services. Google Shopping caught on slowly until the company began inserting the price-comparison site near the top of search results, pushing down competitors' listings and reducing the odds that a consumer would see or click on them.  Google also has created specialized search results that provide direct answers to queries before providing links to shopping search engines. The strategy has worked: Google Shopping ranks among the highest product sites, while traffic to rivals, including Nextag, Shopper.com and PriceGrabber, has plummeted.  Google says it's making life easier for us all by listing its specialized results and services first. Those wishing to use the discounters are free to keep clicking. The EU apparently disagrees and has \"invited\" Google to change its practices to avoid a lawsuit.  Google has proposed, and the EU appears willing to accept, a  three-part approach , according to the Financial Times: For sites on which Google doesn't sell ads, such as news and weather, it will label its in-house services as Google-owned. In other words, the EU wants consumers to consider results that give priority to Google's own services as if they were paid advertisements. For sites on which Google sells ads, including travel and local company reviews, it will more prominently display links to at least three competitors, such as travel-service rivals Expedia, TripAdvisor and Kayak. And for areas in which search results consist of paid ads, such as shopping, Google will hold auctions for competitors who wish to have their links displayed.  The upshot is that, because of the FTC's hesitance, searches in the U.S. will produce less consumer-friendly results. The FTC, after a two-year investigation, closed its case after concluding that Google was motivated more by wanting to improve the user's experience than by a desire to stifle competition. The FTC was giving Google the benefit of the doubt. EU Competition Commissioner Joaquin Almunia seems to have started from the opposite vantage point -- that Google is an aggressive competitor and will try to cement its Internet dominance whichever way it can. Google's market share for search is about 90 percent in the EU and more than 80 percent in the U.S.  Competitors who instigated the EU investigation can claim a partial victory, though  they aren't pleased  that Google won't have to change its algorithms. The company can keep giving preferred placement in results to in-house services so long as they're clearly labeled. The EU settlement also contains no finding that the company broke antitrust rules.  Still, the agreement is legally binding for five years, with a third party monitoring compliance. Google could face a fine of as much as 10 percent of annual sales for failing to keep its promises. The FTC's decision, on the other hand, isn't binding. In the U.S., Google voluntarily agreed to small changes having to do with advertising without signing a consent decree. If the EU-imposed changes fail to help rivals whose Internet traffic has been decimated because of Google's algorithms -- or if the labeling backfires and confers a special status on Google's services -- EU antitrust authorities could strike again. State attorneys general, consumer advocates and members of Congress will also be watching the EU's upcoming market test of Google's proposed changes.  The FairSearch Coalition, a group of technology companies including Microsoft, Expedia and Nokia, will make sure of that. They are among the companies that claimed Google gave itself preferential treatment in search results. FairSearch already has filed a separate complaint against Google over its Android operating system on mobile phones. And Google's Motorola Mobility unit is the subject of another EU probe related to patent licensing. This war -- Google versus everyone else -- is just warming up. (Paula Dwyer is a member of the Bloomberg View editorial board. That\u2019s the perfect combination of factors that leads to a\nbargain, according to two-year-old startup  SeatGeek .  The number-crunching website aggregates sports and\nentertainment tickets available on resale sites such as  StubHub ,\nthen mixes together millions of data points, some algorithms and\nan easy-to-use interface to help fans find the best deal.  The process of buying tickets on the secondary market can\nbe maddening, Bloomberg Businessweek reports in its May 30\nissue. Fly-by-night vendors and a lingering air of\nillegality -- sidewalk scalping is still against the law in many\nstates, while online reselling isn\u2019t -- make it hard to know\nwhom to trust, while price gougers make it tough to find a good\ndeal.  Resellers change ticket prices seemingly at random in a way\nthat maximizes their revenue and assumes \u201cmany consumers are\nnot strategic,\u201d said Andrew T. Sweeting, a  Duke University \neconomics professor.  Primary ticket sellers are getting in on the act, too, with\n Ticketmaster , sports teams and event promoters experimenting\nwith variable pricing.  \u201cIt\u2019s kind of overwhelming, the malice people have toward\nticketing,\u201d said SeatGeek Co-Founder Jack Groetzinger. \u201cThey\nconstantly feel like they are getting ripped off.\u201d  Groetzinger and his co-founder, Russell D\u2019Souza, both 26,\ncame up with the idea for SeatGeek in 2008 and started the site\na year later.  Celtics,  Red Sox   The former fraternity brothers were living in  Boston  and\nwanted to see the Red Sox and the Celtics play. Tickets for both\nteams are scarce and the college buddies were \u201coverwhelmed by\nthe bad experience of buying online,\u201d Groetzinger recalls. Sites such as  Kayak  and  Orbitz  have long aggregated and\nhelped buyers sort through airline deals. (MSFT) , which uses the technology in its  Bing  search\nengine.  Tricky Market  Groetzinger and D\u2019Souza quickly learned that making sense\nout of event tickets is trickier than in air travel. Andrew Decker,  Alan Schwartz  and Jim Ferency led the advisory team at Guggenheim, said a person with knowledge of the negotiations. The firms on both sides of the deal may get more than $240 million in fees, estimates from New York-based research group Freeman & Co. show.  The choice of smaller advisers underscores how more are taking lead roles on some of the most significant corporate transactions. The summer\u2019s last blockbuster deal, the $30 billion merger of Publicis Groupe SA and Omnicom Group Inc., didn\u2019t include a single large bank on its roster, with Rothschild and Moelis & Co. working with the French and U.S. companies.  Sharper Focus  Proponents of smaller firms say their focus on mergers and acquisitions advice helps them provide executives with impartial guidance, while dealmakers at big banks say their firms\u2019 global reach and broad role in the financial markets are advantageous.  The purchase of the wireless stake, if completed at $130 billion, would be the largest corporate transaction since Vodafone\u2019s acquisition of Mannesmann AG in 2000 and would surpass the 2001 merger of Time Warner Inc. and AOL Inc. The deal should close in the first quarter of next year, according to the statement today.  The move allows Verizon to take full control of its largest asset, enabling it to use the unit\u2019s cash flows to invest in faster networks to fend off challenges from  AT&T Inc. (T)  and Sprint Corp. For Vodafone, the deal will mean a windfall of more than $100 billion after tax that could fuel future acquisitions of cable operators.  League Tables  Before today\u2019s deal, Guggenheim Partners ranked 42nd in the global league tables for merger advice this year, working on about $10 billion in deals, according to data compiled by Bloomberg. The Verizon role puts Guggenheim Partners in ninth place for advising on M&A transactions globally, the data show. The firm grew out of the family investment office of the Guggenheim family, the namesake of modern art museums in  New York ,  Venice , and Bilbao,  Spain .  Taubman oversaw  investment banking  at  Morgan Stanley (MS)  before departing this year after 27 years at the firm. His exit followed three years of dual leadership of Morgan Stanley\u2019s investment bank with longtime competitor Colm Kelleher, who became sole head. The two clashed over how aggressively to pursue additional business with clients whom the bank was assisting with capital-markets deals, people familiar with the matter said last year.  Taubman, the son of an accountant, was born in New York and graduated from the  University of Pennsylvania \u2019s Wharton School in 1982, joining Morgan Stanley that year. He served as a lead adviser on Comcast Corp.\u2019s $58.7 billion purchase of AT&T Broadband in 2002 to create the world\u2019s largest cable operator. He also worked on Time Warner\u2019s combination with AOL and advised Microsoft Corp. on its 2008 bid for Yahoo! Inc.  Taubman\u2019s Roots  In the weeks after the bankruptcy of Lehman Brothers Holdings Inc. in September 2008, when his firm was close to collapse, Taubman helped negotiate a $9 billion investment from Tokyo-based Mitsubishi UFJ Financial Group Inc. that helped keep Morgan Stanley alive.  While it\u2019s unusual for a person to be credited individually as an adviser on a large transaction, Taubman\u2019s role isn\u2019t without precedent. Former Citigroup Inc. banker  Michael Klein  worked as a \u201cstrategic consultant\u201d to both Glencore and Xstrata in the 2012 deal that created Glencore Xstrata Plc, the world\u2019s largest combined mining and commodity-trading company. (APPL)  products in India, Chief Executive Officer\n Tim Cook  more or less wrote off the huge country.  He blamed a \u201cmultilayer distribution structure\u201d for making\nit too hard to reach consumers beyond elites in cities such as\nMumbai and Bangalore.  Apple (AAPL)  would look elsewhere for growth: \u201cIn\nthe intermediate term there will be larger opportunities outside\nthere,\u201d Cook said. Today, India -- with a  middle class  the size\nof the U.S. population -- accounts for less than 1 percent of\nApple\u2019s global sales.  By contrast, Samsung Electronics Co. saw plenty of\nopportunity in the subcontinent. The Korean company invested\nmassively in its brand and distribution in India. Rather than\nwaiting for the country to become rich enough to buy top-end\nsmartphones such as the  S4 , Samsung developed and sold a range\nof devices at different price points, some as cheap as $20. The\ncompany now dominates one of the fastest-growing smartphone\nmarkets in the world, outpacing not just Apple but  Nokia Oyj (NOK) ,\n BlackBerry (BBRY)  and others. Apple\u2019s stock, meanwhile, has swooned.  I don\u2019t mean to pick on Cook and Apple. Well-run and well-respected companies including  Sony Corp. (SNE) ,  Toyota Motor Corp. (TM) ,\n Daimler AG (DDAIF)  and  Caterpillar Inc. (CAT)  have similarly missed\nopportunities in India, writing it off as too poor, too corrupt,\ntoo hard. Always a difficult market, India has lately become\neven more challenging. Huge corruption scandals have virtually\nparalyzed the Congress Party government. A sclerotic bureaucracy\nand judicial system, primitive infrastructure and a gut-wrenching uncertainty around policies have killed any enthusiasm\nfor investment. Growth has  slowed  to less than 5 percent.  Moving On  Before, companies that were daunted by India focused on\n China , instead. Now, with the  Chinese economy  also shifting into\nlow gear, they are looking even further afield -- to Africa,\nIndonesia, even Myanmar. In each place, they typically encounter\nan initial burst in sales and enthusiasm. When that fades, they\nlook for the next hot emerging market.  Companies that decide to pass on India, however, are making\na big mistake. For one thing, they are leaving money on the\ntable. Faced with the same chaotic environment as Apple, not\njust  Samsung (005930)  but companies such as  Unilever NV (UNA) ,  Schneider\nElectric SA (SBGSY) , J.C. Bamford Excavators Ltd.,  Cummins Inc. (CMI) ,  Hyundai\nMotor Co. (005380)  and even  McDonald\u2019s Corp. (MCD)  are thriving in India. The\ncountry now accounts for one third of JCB\u2019s global sales and\neven more of its profit. Cummins derives 10 percent to 15\npercent of its profit from the subcontinent.  Secondly, chaos and corruption are hardly unique to India.\nThey are a defining feature of most  emerging markets , and\ncompanies that think they are going to have an easier ride\nelsewhere are in for a rude surprise.  To succeed in any emerging market, companies have to\ndevelop resilience. They have to learn to thrive in chaos. Where\nbetter to do so than in  India ? The country has huge potential --\nit\u2019s already one of the world\u2019s  top five economies  in\npurchasing-parity terms -- as well as good managerial and\ntechnical talent and reasonable institutions, which many smaller\ncountries lack. The lessons learned here can be applied across\nthe young, ambitious societies of the developing world.  The first thing to learn is to take a long-term approach to\nthe market. Firms such as Samsung, Cummins and McDonald\u2019s were\nwilling to wait almost a decade to see a return on their\ninvestments in local supply chains, local innovation capability\nand deep distribution networks.  At the same time, foreign brands must develop products that\nthe local market wants and sell them at disruptive price points.\nEngine manufacturer Cummins, for instance, confronted an\nunforgiving market. Indian drivers routinely overload trucks,\ndilute diesel with cheaper kerosene, fill their radiators with\nmuddy river water instead of coolant, and short out the\nelectronics by ignoring instructions. Yet they still expect the\nengines to perform and to last as long as they do in the U.S.\nAnd they are willing to pay only half as much for the\ntechnology.  Frugal Engineering  When I led Cummins in India, we radically modified our\ntruck engines to withstand tremendous abuse and to cost much\nless, and the company is now thriving in what has become the\nworld\u2019s second-largest truck market in unit terms. Success in\nIndia helped Cummins develop expertise in  frugal engineering , in\nmanaging joint ventures, and in creating a capable, low-cost\nsupply chain. All those skills are now serving the company well\nglobally.  Companies such as Cummins, JCB and Samsung don\u2019t wait for\nthe market to resemble what they are familiar with; instead they\nadapt to the realities of the market. This is a critical point\nlost on multinationals that see India as simply one more sales\noutlet for their products. Those companies wait for policies,\nregulation, infrastructure or the consumer to evolve to fit\ntheir well-tested global models. \u201cWe\u2019ll be back\u201d is the common\nrefrain. \u201cWe\u2019ll be back when India respects patents,\u201d say\npharmaceutical-company CEOs. Others have different benchmarks:\n\u201cWhen Indians stop pirating,\u201d \u201cwhen India has more efficient\ndistribution,\u201d \u201cwhen more Indians start eating meat.\u201d  This approach is risky, not prudent. It will be a long time\nbefore India looks like a developed market or even a terribly\nwelcoming place. It may even evolve in a fundamentally different\ndirection: Indian consumers, for instance, are bypassing\npersonal computers in favor of smartphones and the  mobile\nInternet . They are leapfrogging from a no-PC world to a post-PC\nworld. Where does that leave companies such as  Microsoft Corp. (MSFT) ,\n Intel Corp. (INTC) ,  Dell Inc. (DELL)  or  Hewlett-Packard Co. (HPQ) ?  By the time companies turn their attention back to India, a\ncompetitor will probably have taken an unassailable lead. This\nis the position that automobile makers, including Toyota,\n Volkswagen AG (VLKAY)  and  Nissan Motor Co. (NSANY)  are in; they are now locked\nin an expensive battle to claw back market share from  Suzuki\nMotor Corp. (7269) , Hyundai and  Mahindra & Mahindra Ltd. (MM)  This is what\nCaterpillar faces against the likes of JCB and Cummins, and it\nis what  Procter & Gamble Co. (PG)  is up against in competing with\n Unilever. (UN)   Companies shouldn\u2019t be beguiled by the romance of the next\nhot market. To thrive in the 21st century, getting past India\u2019s\n19th-century problems is a critical first step.  (Ravi Venkatesan is the former chairman of Microsoft India\nand Cummins India. His book, \u201cConquering the Chaos: Win in\nIndia, Win Everywhere,\u201d is out this week from Harvard Business\nReview Press.)
