Industry-standard technology helps ensure that different\nmanufacturers\u2019 products, such as mobile phone antennas and\nglobal-positioning system software, work together. Companies\nthat create technology that helps develop the agreed-upon\nindustry standard pledge to license patents for those inventions\non reasonable terms. Many of them\nare well-known companies with solid balance sheets and long\nhistories of profitability.  \n The  Standard & Poor\u2019s 500 Index , a decent gauge of the\noverall U.S. stock market, lost 11.4 percent for the last three\nmonths, even after taking dividends into account.  \n To me, things seem less grim than many investors think. The\nEuropean debt crisis of 2010 -- and probably 2011 -- may pass\nwithout lasting damage, as did the Asian currency crisis of\n1997-1998. That, too, provoked fears of a worldwide financial\nmeltdown. The Gulf of Mexico oil spill is a tragedy for\nwildlife, shrimpers, fishermen and tourism. Yet its economic\nimpact will be diluted with time.  \n Investors seem to forget that in the past 70 years we have\ngone through World War II, a cold war with the Soviet Union,\nradioactive fallout from nuclear testing, the Vietnam War, the\n2001 terrorist attack, the AIDS crisis and numerous recessions.  \n Overcoming Obstacles  \n And yet for the 70 years from 1940 through 2009, the U.S.\nstock market has provided a compound annual return of 10.8\npercent. We have always had problems, and always will -- yet\nenterprise, innovation and economic progress somehow continue.  \n Investors are fixated on whether we are about to have a\ndouble-dip recession. Double-dips are rare creatures, and not\nthe most likely outcome in my view. If you see stocks such as\nMicrosoft and  EBay Inc.  on the bargain counter, the wise thing\nin my opinion is to buy.  \n Microsoft, based in Redmond, Washington, fell 21 percent\nlast quarter. You can now pick up the shares for 12 times\nearnings. Over the past 10 years,  Microsoft  has sold for an\naverage of about 23 times earnings.  \n Enviable Performance  \n The hot fires that stoked Microsoft\u2019s earnings growth in\nthe mid-1990s have abated. Back then, the company had five\nstraight years in which earnings rose 20 percent or more. There\nis still some heat left. In the first quarter Microsoft earned\n$4 billion on sales of $14.5 billion. Its return on\nstockholders\u2019 equity was 42 percent, an envy-inspiring level of\nprofitability.  \n Analysts think Microsoft\u2019s  earnings  increased by about 27\npercent in the fiscal year that ended June 30. They foresee more\nmodest growth in the fiscal year that started last week.\nHowever, I think there is room for positive surprises, as\nMicrosoft benefits from demand for its latest operating system\nupgrade, Windows 7.  \n EBay , the online auction firm located in San Jose,\nCalifornia, is trading for less than $20, down from about $27\nthree months ago. In recent years, it has lost market share to\nAmazon.com in online retailing, but still is growing strongly.  \n The company has become the leading retailer in mobile\ncommerce, in which people order merchandise using Blackberry,\niPhone, Droid or similar smartphones, Colin Gillis, a New York-\nbased analyst at BGC Partners LP told Bloomberg News last week.  \n EBay Sets Records  \n EBay\u2019s 2009 revenue of $8.7 billion and earnings of almost\n$2.4 billion were both records. Sales and earnings were more\nthan double their 2004 levels, when the shares traded at more\nthan $50. The company is debt-free and the stock sells for 13\ntimes earnings.  \n General Dynamics Corp. , down 23 percent in total return for\nthe quarter, has been slammed as more people become convinced\nthat defense spending will have to be sliced as Congress tries\nto address the large federal deficit. The Falls Church,\nVirginia, military contractor makes planes, ships, weapons and\ninformation systems.  \n I agree that General Dynamics faces a difficult\nenvironment, but that is why its stock sells for less than 10\ntimes earnings. The company increased its earnings in eight of\nthe past 10 years; last year they were unchanged at $6.17 a\nshare, a record.  \n Investors also punished  American Eagle Outfitters Inc.  in\nthe last quarter. The clothing retailer for teenagers and young\nadults declined 36 percent, including dividends.  \n The stock faltered after American Eagle forecast second-\nquarter earnings below analysts\u2019 expectations. Yet I would put\nsome faith in the Pittsburgh-based company\u2019s long-term record,\nincluding positive earnings for 14 consecutive years.  \n I also like its  international expansion  push. Working with\nforeign partners, it opened stores this year in Dubai, Kuwait\nand Israel. It plans to enter mainland China and Hong Kong in\n2011.  \n Disclosure note: I own shares of General Dynamics\npersonally and for clients. I have no long or short positions in\nthe other stocks discussed in this week\u2019s column.  \n ( John Dorfman , chairman of Thunderstorm Capital in Boston,\nis a columnist for Bloomberg News. You\u2019ve already watched a  Netflix (NFLX)  movie, played \u201cAngry\nBirds\u201d and maybe even downloaded an e-book or two from\n Amazon.com (AMZN)  or Apple\u2019s iBooks. What next?  Here are three things you might not be aware you can do with\nyour new tablet:  USE IT AS A TELEPHONE: If you want to place a video call\nover a Wi-Fi connection, you\u2019ve got a lot of options, including\nMicrosoft\u2019s Skype and, for iPad users, Apple\u2019s FaceTime. But\nsuppose you want to make and receive voice calls, and not just\nwith other Internet-connected devices but with traditional\nphones as well?  You could set up a  Google (GOOG)  Voice account, which comes with\nits own phone number, and download its app -- which in the case\nof the iPad means an iPhone app blown up to twice its usual\nsize.  A more elegant solution is  Line2 , an app from the cleverly\nnamed Toktumi, a  San Francisco  company. For less than $10 a\nmonth, Line2 converts your iPad or Android device into a fully\nfunctioning phone with its own number, voicemail and a host of\nadvanced features.  It works not only over Wi-Fi but also 3G and 4G wireless\ndata networks -- giving you voice service any place and in any\nway your tablet can connect.  Multiple Devices  Even better, the service is transferable from device to\ndevice. Put the app on your phone too, and you\u2019ve now got a\nsecond, fully integrated line you can use for business or in\nother situations where you don\u2019t want to give out your personal\nnumber. Toktumi also provides software to let you place and\nreceive calls on your Line2 number from Windows PCs and Macs.  Line2 for Android provides a seven-day free trial before\nthe $9.95 monthly fee kicks in. For the iPad, the company,\nprodded by  Apple (AAPL) , is in the process of moving to a \u201cfreemium\u201d\nmodel, with a no-cost level for calls with other Line2 users and\na paid service for everyone else.  You\u2019ll also want to invest in a Bluetooth headset. You\u2019d\nlook awfully silly holding an iPad to your ear.  RUN WINDOWS AND MICROSOFT OFFICE: Several apps allow you to\ncreate, open and manipulate Microsoft Office files on a tablet,\nsuch as Documents To Go from Blackberry maker  Research In\nMotion (RIM) , Quickoffice and, for iPad users, Apple\u2019s iWork suite.\nLogMeIn Ignition allows you to view and control a specific\nWindows PC over an Internet connection, while  Citrix (CTXS)  Receiver is\naimed at enterprise users.  Free Windows  Now OnLive, a  Palo Alto , California-based online game\nservice, has launched an app called  OnLive Desktop  that puts a\nfully functional version of Windows 7, plus  Microsoft (MSFT)  Word,\nExcel and PowerPoint, on your iPad -- all for free.  The Microsoft programs aren\u2019t actually installed on your\ntablet. Rather, they are running on OnLive\u2019s servers, to which\nyou connect over the Internet. You\u2019ll need a Wi-Fi connection,\nwhere the programs run smoothly; while you can occasionally\nsqueeze in a few minutes over 3G, you can\u2019t count on it.  The documents you create are stored on OnLive\u2019s servers;\nsharing them with other computers, or uploading documents\ncreated elsewhere, is managed via the OnLive website. The free\napp provides 2 gigabytes of storage, and OnLive says a coming\n$10-a-month service will provide 50 gigabytes, plus the ability\nto add and run more Windows programs. Enterprise and Android\nversions are also in the works.  Wireless Keyboard  OnLive Desktop uses a touch-friendly version of Windows 7;\nan on-screen keyboard also is available. You\u2019ll almost\ncertainly, though, want to use it with a Bluetooth wireless\nkeyboard. It may now be possible to imagine The Great American\nNovel being written on an iPad - but not via fingers-on-glass.  ENTERTAINMENT REMOTE CONTROL: Here\u2019s perhaps the only area\nwhere some Android tablets are easier to use than iPads.  Most TVs are being sold with some ability to put them onto\na home network, either with built-in Wi-Fi or an adapter port.\nConnecting your TV to a network means, among many other things,\nthat you may be able to control it with an app on your Wi-Fi-\nconnected device. Millions of TVs, though, don\u2019t live on Wi-Fi\nnetworks. Owners rely on the infrared technology in traditional\nremote controls to change channels and adjust the volume.  Built-In Transmitter  Unlike the iPad, some Android tablets have a built-in IR\ntransmitter, allowing them to function as universal remote\ncontrols for TVs and home-entertainment gear right out of the\nbox. Probably the best I\u2019ve seen is the  Tablet S  from  Sony (6758) ,\nwhich includes an app that mimics the functions of the company\u2019s\nhigh-end standalone remotes, including controlling non-Sony\ngear. Other Android tablets with IR blasters include Vizio\u2019s\n Vtab  and  Samsung (005930) \u2019s  Galaxy Tab 7.0 Plus . Now, rechristened the Seaport district, construction cranes dot the landscape as builders put up high- end condominiums, offices and hotels in one of the biggest neighborhood transformations in Boston history.  \u201cThe waterfront is an overnight success that\u2019s taken nearly 30 years to come to fruition,\u201d said Brian Kavoogian, president and founder of Charles River Realty Investors LLC, which has developed or acquired more than 20 million square feet (1.9 million square meters) of real estate in the Boston metropolitan area. \u201cIt finally reached a tipping point.\u201d  Boston\u2019s real estate market, often overshadowed by the skyscrapers of  New York  and government-fueled growth in  Washington , is seeing a boom in construction as developers financed with cheap debt seek to profit from a growing workforce of educated young adults and strength in the technology and life-sciences industries. The office-vacancy rate is among the lowest of major U.S. markets and tenants are occupying new space at almost triple the national average.  Construction spending in Boston increased an estimated 37 percent in the year ended June 30 to $3.83 billion, the most since 2008, according to the mayor\u2019s office. The market is hot enough that some developers are considering building offices without having landed anchor tenants.  Largest Project  Work is planned or already underway on the $620 million redevelopment of the original Filene\u2019s department store property in Downtown Crossing, a $200 million  office tower  for State Street Corp. and the $800 million headquarters in the Seaport area for  Vertex Pharmaceuticals Inc. (VRTX)  -- at 1.1 million square feet, the nation\u2019s largest privately funded office-construction project.  \u201cYou have a city that has biotech and other thriving industries, and some big-name financial services,\u201d said John Garth, managing director at  Pembrook Capital Management LLC , a New York-based real estate investor looking to finance apartment construction in Boston. \u201cIt\u2019s a huge draw for young people, and that creates lots of demand for rental apartments as well as new office space and other construction.\u201d  The fourth-quarter office-vacancy rate in the Boston metro area was 10.9 percent, ranking it among the best-performing big markets in the country and less than the 15.4 percent nationwide average, according to brokerage CBRE Group Inc. Net absorption - - the increase in occupied space -- was 2.8 percent in 2012, compared with 1 percent nationwide. That\u2019s helping to spur building while construction in much of the rest of the country stagnates, said Arthur Jones, senior managing economist at the Los Angeles-based company.  New Cycle  \u201cThe fundamentals in Boston are favoring the move into another construction cycle,\u201d he said. \u201cVacancies are low, rents are improving and job growth is steady.\u201d  Boston has attracted major office owners including Tishman Speyer Properties LP and Blackstone Group LP. The largest U.S. office real estate investment trust,  Boston Properties Inc (BXP) ., is based in the city and owns marquee properties such as John Hancock Tower and Prudential Center.  Greater Boston is home to  50 universities  and colleges, among them  Harvard University  and  Massachusetts Institute of Technology , which provide a pipeline for graduates into the job market. In 2010, Boston had the biggest ratio of 20- to 34-year- olds among the 25 largest cities in the U.S., at 35 percent, according to a report from the mayor\u2019s office.  Job Growth  Boston\u2019s cumulative job growth, led by scientific and technical services, is projected to be 7.9 percent from 2011 to 2016, exceeding the state\u2019s 7.4 percent, according to the report. The city is home to financial firms such as Fidelity Investments, the second-biggest U.S. mutual-fund company, and State Street, the third-largest custody bank. Neighboring Cambridge, which has also seen a spike in new development, hosts employers such as biotechnology company  Biogen Idec Inc. (BIIB)  and technology giants Amazon.com Inc., Google Inc. and Microsoft Corp., said Peter Meade, head of the Boston Redevelopment Authority.  \u201cIn the last 24 months, suburban tech firms have been looking to relocate into town,\u201d said Andrew Hoar, president and co-managing partner at CBRE\/ New England , a joint venture partner with CBRE. \u201cFor many other markets it\u2019s the other way around. The young graduates in this town don\u2019t want to commute.\u201d  New Opportunities  The race to catch up with the city\u2019s growth is evident in the Seaport area, where about 3 million square feet of buildings is under construction, according to the redevelopment authority. The waterfront neighborhood, for decades isolated by Fort Point Channel and an elevated stretch of Interstate 93, has become more accessible after the Central Artery\/Tunnel Project rerouted the highway below ground. Known as the Big Dig, the 15-year-plus project was  completed  in 2007 after being plagued by delays and cost overruns.  \u201cThe opening up of areas like the waterfront is expanding opportunities to have developments occur in a way we have not seen in many years,\u201d Joseph Fallon, founder and chief executive officer of  Fallon Co ., developer of the Vertex buildings, said in an interview at his office in the Seaport, behind him the expansive view of Boston Harbor -- and cranes.  Fan Pier  The neighborhood, long targeted for growth, was slow to develop.  Fidelity Investments  and Drew Co. built the Seaport World Trade Center exhibition center there in 1986, joining  Anthony\u2019s Pier 4  restaurant, a local landmark. A larger-scale overhaul was hampered by the lack of infrastructure, a common vision for the area and economic downturns, according to the redevelopment authority\u2019s deputy director for planning, Richard McGuinness. Development of the district has been a top priority of Mayor  Thomas Menino  during his almost 20 years in office.  Fallon plans to complete the two Vertex structures in the waterfront area by the end of this year and has an adjacent parcel that may accommodate a third building. It will build a residential project if Vertex doesn\u2019t exercise the option to use the land, Fallon said. The developer\u2019s other projects in the Seaport neighborhood include a condo building and a 360,000- square-foot office for law firm Goodwin Procter LLP, both of which will break ground this year.  Exciting Neighborhood  Vertex (VRTX) , which has added more than 500 employees in  Massachusetts  in the past five years, is currently based in Cambridge. The company was attracted to the Seaport\u2019s proximity to Logan Airport and different types of transportation, as well as its mix of new businesses settling into the neighborhood, said Zach Barber, a spokesman for the drugmaker.  \u201cThe site and the neighborhood was exciting for us to be an anchor tenant in,\u201d Barber said.  New restaurants are popping up, such as Blue Dragon, an Asian eatery from Ming Tsai, host of the PBS cooking show \u201cSimply Ming.\u201d The outdoor Bank of America Pavilion showcases music events, while a convention center, completed in 2004, draws a regular stream of visitors, as does the  Institute of Contemporary Art , which relocated from the Back Bay in 2006.  Drew Co.  is building Waterside Place, a $120 million mixed- use project in the Seaport area that it expects to  complete  by year-end. It will include apartments, offices for startup companies and ground-floor retail, according to the authority.  Skanska Plans  Skanska USA, the American division of Stockholm-based construction and engineering firm  Skanska AB (SKAB) , in December acquired a parcel of land in the Seaport district from  Morgan Stanley (MS)  for $33 million and is planning an office building to accommodate spill-over demand from low-vacancy areas like East Cambridge, said Shawn Hurley, executive vice president. The company would build even without having a tenant signed first, known as speculative construction.  \u201cAt this point we\u2019d go ahead with a spec project,\u201d Hurley said in an interview at Skanska\u2019s Boston office. \u201cThe office market in East Cambridge is very healthy and has very little vacancy. This area becomes an alternative.\u201d  The risk of the accelerating growth in areas like the Seaport and Cambridge is that rising rents may drive tenants back into the suburbs, according to a fourth-quarter  report  by Cassidy Turley. In the Seaport, office rents for top-quality buildings have risen to $54 a square foot from $48 a year ago, putting rates on par with the historic Back Bay area, the brokerage said.  Less Affordable  \u201cWhile tech companies and startups are primarily responsible for South Boston\u2019s renaissance, we are watching to see what happens when their leases are up for renewal,\u201d Cassidy Turley said. \u201cThe Seaport may no longer be the affordable option it was even just 18 months ago.\u201d  The construction isn\u2019t solely in the Seaport. The  Longwood Medical and Academic Area  also has seen an increase in construction, driven by the expansion of medical facilities in the neighborhood. A partnership headed by local builder National Development  broke ground  in June on the $350 million Longwood Center, a research and development center with Dana-Farber Cancer Institute as anchor tenant.  New York-based  AREA Property Partners LP  and CV Properties LLC of Southport,  Connecticut , are building One Channel Center, the 500,000-square-foot office for State Street in the Seaport neighborhood. AREA expects to complete the project by July 2014, according to Chief Executive Officer Lee Neibart. (BA)   The changes include requiring the government to minimize\ncollection of information that could identify citizens in the\nprocess of sharing cyber threat data with the private sector,\nRogers and Ruppersberger said on a phone call. The lawmakers\nsaid they also want a provision saying companies only can use\ncybersecurity data to protect their networks, not for marketing\npurposes.  \u201cThe improvements that we plan to make to the bill at the\nmarkup will address several of the administration\u2019s concerns,\u201d\nRogers said. \u201cAnd we plan to keep talking and moving toward a\nconsensus that will allow us to get the bill signed into law.\u201d  The Intelligence Committee has scheduled an April 10\nclosed-door meeting to vote on the amendments and the measure.\nObama threatened to veto the bill last year partly over privacy\nconcerns.  The White House hasn\u2019t said whether it supports the bill\nwith revisions, Ruppersberger said.  Privacy Protections  Other changes include denying firms legal protections if\nthey use cyber threat information to hack each other; dropping\nlanguage allowing agencies to use information for national\nsecurity purposes; and creating roles for the government\u2019s\nprivacy and civil liberties board and federal privacy officers\nto review how information is shared and used, Rogers and\nRuppersberger said.  Congress is renewing its push to improve U.S. digital\ndefenses as warnings increase about computer attacks. A Feb. 19\nreport from security firm Mandiant Corp. concluded the Chinese\narmy may be behind a hacking group that has hit at least 141\ncompanies worldwide since 2006.  The  legislation , called the Cyber Intelligence Sharing and\nProtection Act, passed the House 248 to 168 last April. A\ndifferent cybersecurity bill didn\u2019t advance in the Senate, where\nit was blocked by Republicans who said it would lead to\nregulation.  Rogers has said Obama\u2019s cybersecurity executive order in\nFebruary, which sets up a system of voluntary computer-defense\nstandards for critical industries, created an opening to pass an\ninformation-sharing bill.  Corporate Support  Many of the House bill\u2019s corporate supporters are among the\ntop 20 contributors to Rogers\u2019 2011-2012 campaign committee,\naccording to the Center for Responsive Politics, a Washington-\nbased research group. They include AT&T,  Verizon Communications\nInc. (VZ) , Boeing and  Lockheed Martin Corp. (LMT)  employees and their\nfamilies.  Ruppersberger\u2019s top contributors in the same period also\ninclude Boeing and Lockheed employees and their families,\naccording to the center.  \u201cBoeing supports candidates with whom we have alignment on\nissues of importance to the company,\u201d Gayla Keller, a Boeing\nspokeswoman, said in an e-mail.  \u201cWith 82 percent of our company\u2019s sales derived from U.S.\ngovernment customers, we naturally have interactions with\nvirtually every standing committee in the United States\nCongress\u201d that has agency oversight, Rob Fuller, a Lockheed\nMartin spokesman, said in an e-mail.  Michael Balmoris, an AT&T spokesman, didn\u2019t respond to a\nrequest for comment. Edward McFadden, a Verizon spokesman,\ndeclined to comment.  Personal Data  The  American Civil Liberties Union  and other advocacy\ngroups have stoked online opposition to the House bill, saying\nit would allow Americans\u2019 personal data to be shared with the\nNational Security Agency and the military. The ACLU also\nobjected to allowing the government to use data for undefined\n\u201cnational security\u201d purposes.  Michelle Richardson, ACLU legislative counsel, called the\nbill a \u201cprivacy disaster.\u201d Congress should focus on \u201csmarter\nalternatives,\u201d she said in an interview before Rogers and\nRuppersberger announced the amendments.  The proposed changes don\u2019t include putting a civilian\nagency such as the Homeland Security Department in charge of\ninformation sharing, a priority of privacy advocates.  Representative Adam Schiff, a California Democrat on the\ncommittee, said he would introduce an amendment requiring\ncompanies to try to remove personal data before sharing.  Senate Action  Caitlin Hayden, a White House spokeswoman, declined to\ncomment on the House bill, referring to previous statements that\ncyber legislation should guard privacy, reinforce the\nappropriate roles of civilian and intelligence agencies, and\ninclude \u201ctargeted\u201d liability protections for companies.  A Feb. 13  petition  on the White House website protesting\nthe Rogers bill\u2019s lax privacy protections has gathered 100,000\nsignatures, the threshold to trigger a White House response.\nHayden declined to say how or when the White House would\nrespond.  The House bill\u2019s chances of passage depend on what action\nthe Senate takes, and Senate committee leaders haven\u2019t yet\ndecided on their cybersecurity strategy.  \u201cThe bill doesn\u2019t really go very far until the Senate has\nsomething that can match it, and they\u2019re not close to that,\u201d\nsaid  James Lewis , technology program director at the Center for\nStrategic and International Studies in Washington.  Facebook Inc. (FB) ,  Microsoft Corp. (MSFT)  and some technology trade\ngroups that endorsed the original House legislation have been\nmore tepid this year.  Facebook \u2018Encouraged\u2019  Facebook, owner of the world\u2019s largest social network, said\nin a letter last year the legislation \u201chelps provide a more\nestablished structure for sharing within the cyber community\nwhile still respecting the privacy rights and expectations of\nour users.\u201d  Asked for Facebook\u2019s current position, spokeswoman Jodi Seth said in an e-mailed statement the company is \u201cencouraged\u201d\nby the House interest and seeks a \u201clegislative balance\u201d that\npromotes information sharing and ensures the privacy of its\nusers. (GOOG) \u2019s Android software, the most widely used smartphone operating system, is making the leap to rice cookers and refrigerators as manufacturers vie to dominate the market for gadgets controlled via the Internet.  Android-based products ranging from Royal Philips Electronics NV\u2019s PicoPix pocket projector and  LG Electronics Inc. (066570) \u2019 Smart Thinq refrigerators to  Parrot SA (PARRO) \u2019s Asteroid car stereo systems and  Samsung Electronics Co. (005930) \u2019s Galaxy Camera will be on display this week at the annual International  Consumer Electronics Show  in Las Vegas.  Extending its free operating system to new devices could let Google collect more data to build its lucrative search business and one-up software rivals  Microsoft Corp. (MSFT)  and Apple Inc. Android also is an easy to-use-platform that helps appliance makers like Samsung and Philips add product features and benefit from demand for Internet-connected devices -- a market IDC predicts will reach more than $2 trillion in 2015.  \u201cAndroid is sitting pretty in this space to take more share from the incumbents,\u201d said IDC analyst Al Hilwa. \u201cThe fundamental advantage with Android is that the vendor can take a bigger chunk of the software and own it.\u201d  Since the first Android-based phones went on sale in 2008, devices based on the mobile operating system have surged in popularity. Smartphones running the software held 72 percent of the market in the third quarter, while Apple had 14 percent, according to Gartner Inc.  Intelligent Systems  Building Android directly into devices can make it easier for electronic equipment and appliances to exchange information with less human intervention. A television, for example, might show a pop-up message from a clothes dryer in the basement, indicating that the homeowner\u2019s jeans are not yet dry. The user could press a button on the TV remote to automatically add 15 minutes to the dryer cycle. A connected rice cooker could determine what type of rice is being used and set cooking instructions accordingly.  Making more intelligent, connected appliances and electronics has been a goal of manufacturers for years. And recent efforts to broaden Android beyond phones and computers haven\u2019t all panned out. Google tried to push into the living room via its Google TV product. The set-top boxes and software for televisions made by Sony Corp. and Logitech International SA didn\u2019t meet sales goals after their introduction in 2010. LG, Hisense Electric Co. and Vizio Inc. plan to demonstrate models that boast an updated version of Android for TVs in  Las Vegas .  Fragmented Market  This time will be different, manufacturers say. Companies are competing to develop operating systems that can span a variety of devices and attract a loyal base of developers and consumers.  The market for so-called intelligent systems, or devices capable of receiving and transmitting over the Internet, will double to almost 4 billion units in 2015 from more than 1.8 billion units and more than $1 trillion in revenue in 2011, according to IDC. The market now is fragmented among more than 30 software makers, including  QNX Software Systems Ltd.  and companies\u2019 home-grown development efforts.  \u201cThe Android circle is getting bigger,\u201d Android founder  Andy Rubin  said in May at a press conference. \u201cEverything should be Androidified -- is that the word?\u201d  Smartphone-Controlled  Android\u2019s proliferation offers broader access to hundreds of downloadable applications developed specifically for Web- connected gear, letting electronics makers create a family of products that can exchange information, said Frederic Albinet, marketing manager at Parrot, which began selling its $600 Asteroid Smart car system in October.  \u201cThere are many apps in the Android Marketplace we get access to, and our Asteroid developers have an operating system that everyone\u2019s becoming familiar with,\u201d he said.  Last year in  Japan , Panasonic Corp. began selling a range of home appliances, from microwaves to air conditioners, that can be controlled by smartphones while providing information to users. Its $600 Android-controlled SR-SX2 rice cooker lets users search for recipes on their Android phones and then transmit them to the cooker. It also provides information such as how much electricity it has used.  The company\u2019s NR series refrigerator counts the number of times that the door has been open and closed in order to make it run more efficiently, and it displays instructions on how to fix problems when they occur.  Samsung and LG, two of the earliest adopters of Android in smartphones, have begun integrating the software into cameras and appliances to stimulate sales in markets that haven\u2019t been growing rapidly.  Support Needed  While Android\u2019s free software allows for easy adoption, device makers may have to do more work than they would with software bought from a company like Microsoft, which supports development, testing and troubleshooting of such systems as Ford Motor Corp.\u2019s Sync information and entertainment-system software, said  Carl Howe , an analyst at  Yankee Group .  \u201cThe open part isn\u2019t as important as the reliability,\u201d Howe said. \u201cIt requires support and courting of customers. If Google has no interest, it\u2019s not going to go anywhere.\u201d  While Google only counts devices delivered by its network of 58 manufacturing partners, the company said in an e-mailed statement that the free Android operating system is available to any developers that wish to use it. Google declined to comment further on Android\u2019s expansion into electronics.  Intel\u2019s Customers  Intel Corp. (INTC) , the world\u2019s largest computer-chip maker, said it has no shortage of interest in Android-based systems. Intel\u2019s Wind River Systems software division is receiving an increasing number of customer requests, said  Jim Douglas , vice president of products and global marketing.  Electronics and appliance makers are taking advantage of falling prices for LCD screens and wireless technologies to consider connecting all manner of devices. Powerful processors that are becoming more affordable also are adding to the trend, Douglas said. He said the operating system could also be used in big-ticket industrial machines, though he declined to identify specific customers.  \u201cYou can now start to put pretty robust operating environments and applications on just about everything,\u201d he said. \u201cGoogle\u2019s done a nice job of building an open platform that it\u2019s easy to develop on top of it. Copyright  Righthaven Has No Standing to Sue, Judge in Denver Cases Rules  Righthaven LLC, the Las Vegas-based copyright-enforcement\norganization, was told it lacked standing to pursue a copyright\ninfringement case in federal court in Denver.  The ruling is significant because judge who made this\ndetermination is overseeing all 57 copyright infringement cases\nRighthaven filed in that court since Jan. 20.  Righthaven filed the cases on behalf of the Denver-based\nMediNews Group Inc. The suits related to the unauthorized use of\ncontent from MediaNews Group\u2019s \u201cDenver Post.\u201d  The owner of the itmakesense.com website was sued March 31\nfor using content from the newspaper on the  itmakessenseblog.com \nwebsite.  In each case Righthaven claimed to own the copyright to the\nwork that was allegedly infringed.  In his Sept. 27 ruling, U.S. District Judge John L. Kane\nsaid he gave a close reading to the copyright assignment\nagreement between MediaNews Group. He noted that under the\nagreement, Righthaven has no rights to the particular copyright\n\u201cother than the right to proceed in association with a\nrecovery.\u201d  This limitation means that Righthaven isn\u2019t an owner as\ndefined by copyright law, Kane said. As such \u201cit lacks standing\nto institute an action for copyright infringement.\u201d  He also said that because he wished to \u201cdiscourage the\nabuse of the statutory remedies for copyright infringement,\u201d so\nin addition to ruling there was no reason for the trial to go\nahead, he awarded attorney fees and litigation costs to the\ndefendant.  The case is Righthaven LLC v. Leland Wolf, 1:11-cv-00830-\nJLK, U.S. District Court, District of Colorado (Denver).  In a Sept. 8 court filing in a Righthaven case in a Nevada\nfederal court on behalf of Las Vegas-based Stephens Media Group,\na defendant who was awarded attorney fees has asked for seizure\nof Righthaven\u2019s intellectual property, real estate and bank\naccounts. (AAPL)  won an appeals court ruling upholding a lower-\ncourt order blocking Psystar Corp., maker of Macintosh computer\nclones, from selling copies of Apple Inc.\u2019s operating system.  The case, filed in federal court in  San Francisco  in 2008,\nwas related to a Psystar software product that made it possible\nfor customers to run the Mac Snow Leopard operating system on a\nnon-Apple computer.  Cupertino, California-based Apple had claimed that Psystar,\nbased in Doral,  Florida , was selling inferior computers and\nservers using unauthorized copies of the operating system. It\nwas also accused of selling downloadable updates for Snow\nLeopard.  The district court found that Psystar infringed the Apple\ncopyrights. While Psystar didn\u2019t appeal the infringement\nfinding, it asked the appeals court to reconsider the lower\ncourt\u2019s rejection of its contention that Apple\u2019s software\nlicense agreement was unenforceable.  Psystar had argued that the license provision requiring\nApple\u2019s operating system be run only on Apple computers was an\nunenforceable misuse of its copyright.  Apple argued that Psystar failed to prove copyright abuse\nbecause the license agreement didn\u2019t restrict creativity or\ncompetition. The appeals court agreed, and also affirmed the\nlower court\u2019s ruling barring future infringement.  The appeals court agreed with Psystar that Apple failed to\npresent an adequate argument for the sealing of Apple records in\nthe case file. It ordered the lower court to unseal those\nrecords.  The appeals court case is Apple Inc. v. Psystar Corp. 10-\n15113, U.S. Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit. The lower\ncourt case is Apple Inc. v. (CSCO) ,  Eli Lilly & Co. (LLY)  and\nQualcomm Inc., are considering the second set of  patent-law \nchanges in three years as the courts try to race ahead of\nCongress.  The goal is to rein in entities that buy patents and demand\nroyalties from as many companies as possible. Often derided as\n\u201ctrolls,\u201d such firms filed 19 percent of all patent lawsuits\nfrom 2007 to 2011, the Government Accountability Office found.  Finding a balance among protecting products from knockoff\ncompetition, rewarding inventors for making their ideas public\nand limiting nuisance suits has been debated for more than 200\nyears, even more so now that some lawsuits are targeting users\nof ubiquitous technology like e-mail and Wi-Fi.  \u201cThere\u2019s just a lot of pressure being put on Congress and\nthe courts to address the abusive practices,\u201d said Tim Molino,\nhead of government relations for BSA - the Software Alliance,\nbased in  Washington , whose members include  Microsoft (MSFT)  Corp. and\n Oracle Corp. (ORCL)  \u201cBoth sides are trying to assert their authority\nwhere they can to move the dial.\u201d  The U.S. Supreme Court is considering when to penalize\npatent owners for filing questionable claims, while the federal\ncourts\u2019 administrator has proposed disclosure  rules  that may\nlessen litigation costs.  The legislation Congress is considering would do some of\nthe same things -- make patent companies pay the other side\u2019s\nlegal fees if they lose and tell the courts to change their\ndiscovery rules.  Three-Way Split  \u201cYou do not need Congress to mandate things courts are\nalready willing to consider,\u201d Circuit Judge Kathleen O\u2019Malley\nof the  U.S. Court of Appeals  for the Federal Circuit, which\nhandles all patent appeals, said in a Sept. 17 speech to the\nIntellectual Property Owners Association.  The struggle between the courts and Congress has divided\ncompanies along the lines of who gets sued more often.  Google Inc. (GOOG) , Cisco and other technology companies in the\n Coalition for Patent Fairness  back legislation introduced Oct.\n23 by Representative Bob Goodlatte, a Virginia Republican who\nheads the House Judiciary Committee. It would allow collection\nof legal fees from licensing companies that lose at trial and\nrequire they provide more details about patents and how they\nwere infringed.  Companies like  Qualcomm Inc. (QCOM)  that own many patents and make\nmoney from licensing them say weakening patents would hurt their\nbusiness. The Qualcomm-backed Innovation Alliance seeks limited\ncongressional action, and is pushing lawmakers to stop diverting\nmoney from the U.S. Patent and  Trademark Office , which is funded\nentirely by user fees.  The Coalition for 21st Century Patent Reform -- made up of\nGeneral Electric,  Johnson & Johnson (JNJ) ,  Eli Lilly  and other patent\nholders -- says the Goodlatte bill takes some power from courts.  Venue Struggle  Industries reliant on patent protection for revenue, which\ninclude technology companies, drugmakers, and manufacturers, had\n3.9 million jobs and accounted for $763 billion, or 5.3 percent\nof gross domestic product, in 2010, according to a 2012 Commerce\nDepartment report.  Patent litigation is expensive. The cost of defending a\npatent suit through trial, not including damages, starts at\nabout $650,000 and can reach several million dollars, an\nAmerican Intellectual Property Lawyers Association study found.  A Senate Commerce subcommittee will hold a hearing Nov. 7\non the impact of royalty demand letters on small businesses,\nconsumers and innovators.  Goodlatte said at an Oct. 29 hearing his bill is the\nbailiwick of Congress and \u201cthe  Supreme Court  has long\nrecognized that the prescription of court procedure falls within\nthe legislative function.\u201d  2011 Law  Some companies say Congress is getting it wrong.  \u201cYou\u2019ve got this incredibly powerful organized lobby that\nwants to kill innovation because it\u2019s a threat to them,\u201d said\nLoudon Owen, chairman of I4i LP, a Canadian designer of software\nfor drug companies that won a $200 million verdict against\nMicrosoft in 2011.  A wide-ranging patent law passed in 2011, called the\nAmerica Invents Act, started as a push by companies like\nMicrosoft to make it easier to challenge patents and limit\ndamage awards. Those provisions never made it in the final law -\n- because the courts addressed the issues.  Microsoft curtailed its push for legislation after winning\nthree court rulings between 2007 and 2011 that limited damages\nin patent suits.  The public debate \u201cleads to legislative changes where\nlegislative change is needed,\u201d said  Horacio Gutierrez ,\nMicrosoft\u2019s head of intellectual property. \u201cIt crystalizes\nissues that can be resolved by courts in a faster and more\neffective way.\u201d  Sledgehammer, Scalpel  Companies are spending millions to influence lawmakers. In\n2011, three groups alone spent $2.4 million lobbying on the\nAmerica Invents Act. So far this year, they\u2019ve spent more than\n$1.1 million, according to Senate disclosure records. That\ndoesn\u2019t include campaign contributions or media buys.  The Coalition for Patent Fairness and the  National Retail\nFederation , a Washington trade group, paid for a newspaper\nadvertising campaign deriding \u201cpatent trolls\u201d this year.\nInnovation Alliance responded with \u201cWho\u2019s Trolling Who,\u201d\nsaying \u201cfringe abuses\u201d are being used to weaken  patent rights .  The Supreme Court announced Oct. 1 it would hear two cases\nthat would make it easier for targets of patent suits to collect\nattorneys\u2019 fees, which could deter groundless lawsuits.  The Federal Circuit is considering whether patent owners\ncan block competitors from selling products based on a finding\nof infringement of a feature of a complex device -- such as a\nway to scroll through pages on a smartphone.  The courts are limited because \u201cthey only can deal with\nthe facts of the cases and legal questions presented before\nthem,\u201d said  Mark Chandler , general counsel for  San Jose ,\nCalifornia-based Cisco.  While Goodlatte is pushing his committee to vote on the\nproposal quickly, the companies\u2019 split over certain segments may\ngive the courts time to tackle the so-called trolls.  \u201cIn general, courts are always a better way to fix things\nthan Congress,\u201d said Ron Laurie, managing director of Inflexion\nPoint Strategy, which counsels companies on intellectual\nproperty. \u201cCongress uses a sledgehammer and courts use a\nscalpel.\u201d  To contact the reporter on this story:\n Susan Decker  in Washington at \n sdecker1@bloomberg.net . Chromebook  For a couple of years, Google has been trying to establish\nits cloud-based Chrome operating system on laptop and desktop\ncomputers as an alternative to  Microsoft (MSFT) \u2019s Windows and Apple\u2019s\nOS X. Speaking for couch potatoes everywhere, I want to get out\nmore than I put in. Can\u2019t technology help?  Well, maybe. For the last several weeks, I\u2019ve been using a\n$100 gadget called a  Fitbit . It offers a limited but enticing\nglimpse of a future when the computing power already surrounding\nus works to keep us healthy -- even when we aren\u2019t consciously\ndoing anything to deserve it.  The Fitbit is an activity tracker about the size of a money\nclip and weighing next to nothing. You can stick it on a belt or\nbra, put it in your pocket or wear it on your wrist. Like a\npedometer, it counts your steps and measures distance traveled.\nIt also includes modes that estimate calories burned and monitor\nyour sleep patterns.  Best of all, the Fitbit doesn\u2019t depend too much on you.\nIt\u2019s simple, unobtrusive and automatically uploads the data it\ncollects to the Internet without your having to do anything more\ntaxing than walk past your computer.  Missed Opportunities  The consumer-technology industry has barely scratched the\nsurface in the health-and-wellness market, making it one of the\nleast-tapped opportunities in the tech bazaar. Most of us\nalready carry around supercomputers, disguised as smart phones\nand tablets, that are capable of monitoring when we exercise,\nwhat we eat and how well we sleep. Yet for the most part they\nsit there, wasted on phone calls and  text messages .  Meanwhile, sensors are growing smaller, cheaper and more\npowerful all the time. The typical mobile device has an\naccelerometer (the thing that makes it flip its screen when you\nturn it sideways) and a gyroscope, which orients it in three\ndimensions. Game devices like Nintendo Co.\u2019s Wii and  Microsoft\nCorp. (MSFT) \u2019s Kinect controller for the Xbox only begin to suggest the\nuses to which motion-sensing technology can be used to help get\nus on our feet.  It\u2019s easy to imagine a day in the not-too-distant future\nwhen cheap, unobtrusive, wearable sensors constantly monitor our\n heart rate ,  blood pressure  and activities and wirelessly\ncommunicate that data through our smart phones to the Internet,\nwhere it can be collated, analyzed and shared. Where we use our\nphones to snap pictures of our meals, which are instantly\nanalyzed for calorie count and nutritional value, then added to\nour online health profile. Where...sorry, I got carried away\nthere.  Nike\u2019s GPS Watch  The Fitbit does none of that. Nor is it likely to satisfy\nserious fitness enthusiasts, who have a range of more elaborate\nand expensive devices to choose from, such as  Nike Inc. (NKE) \u2019s $199\nSportWatch for runners, which includes a built-in GPS system.  What Fitbit does do is keep track of your normal daily\nactivities, giving you a benchmark and, perhaps, an incentive to\ndo more.  The sensor has a single button, which performs a multitude\nof functions; a tiny glowing blue display provides what passes\nfor a user interface. Push the button once, and the Fitbit gives\nyou a quick reading on your general activity level for that day\nin the form of a flower icon; the more active you\u2019ve been, the\nmore leaves on the flower\u2019s stem. Keep pushing the button, and\nyou\u2019ll get readings on the number of steps you\u2019ve taken today --\n10,000 is Fitbit\u2019s default goal -- as well as distance covered\nand calories burned.  Monitoring Sleep  A single long push puts the device into event-recording\nmode, useful for both tracking the effect of a specific activity\n-- how long a walk is it from here to town? -- and monitoring\nyour sleep.  The device comes with a belt clip, a base station and a\ncloth wristband. The thumb-size base station, which plugs into a\nUSB port on your computer, uses a low-power wireless technology\ncalled  ANT , from a unit of  Garmin Ltd. (GRMN) , that grabs information\nfrom the sensor and sends it to your personal Fitbit Web page.  There you can supplement the data with any additional\ninformation you want to enter yourself, ranging from activities\nthe Fitbit isn\u2019t good at sensing -- cycling is one -- to what\nyou\u2019ve had to eat. You can also choose to share your data via\nFacebook or  Twitter , or upload it to a personal health file at\n Google Health  or  Microsoft HealthVault .  The base station also serves as a power charger, though\nyou won\u2019t have to use it often in that role. In my tests, I got\nover a week of use on a single charge, and still had battery\nlife to spare.  Noticing Patterns  Over time, I began to notice some patterns. One is the\ngeneral benefit of simply getting up from my desk and taking a\nstroll. My 2.5 mile roundtrip walk from the office to an  Apple\nInc. (AAPL)  press event burned as many calories as a half-hour on the\nbike at the gym. I also learned that while I usually get only\nabout six hours of sleep a night, I\u2019m an efficient sleeper,\nrousing only a few times during a typical night.  Several things about the Fitbit need work. It still\nrequires a lot of tedious manual data entry to get the most out\nof it. (Let\u2019s see, what did I have for lunch Tuesday?) There\u2019s\nno iPhone or Android app, just a mobile website, and no way for\nthe Fitbit unit to use your phone to upload data.  The very obviousness of those shortcomings points the way\nforward for the consumer-technology industry. Fitbit is a good\nfirst step.  ( Rich Jaroslovsky  is a Bloomberg News columnist. Though the industry recovered and is prospering, today it faces a new technological challenge from \u201csmartwatches\u201d such as  Samsung Electronics Co. (005930) \u2019s $299 Galaxy Gear.  As with quartz four decades ago, the devices are being met with a shrug. According to a survey by consultants Deloitte, two-thirds of executives in the Swiss industry say smartwatches pose no threat.  \u201cHow would you like it if your boyfriend brings you a smartwatch instead of a nice pav\u00e9 diamond watch?\u201d said Johann Rupert, the billionaire controlling shareholder of  Cie. Swiss watchmakers \u201cshouldn\u2019t say too quickly it\u2019s a trend that won\u2019t affect them,\u201d said consultant Hofer, who checks his iPhone to be on time. \u201cThere should be some modesty.\u201d  \u2018An Anachronism\u2019  The high-end Swiss watch is so low-tech that from a practical standpoint, it should no longer exist. When battery-powered quartz watches arrived on the scene in the 1970s, many consumers abandoned older mechanical ones -- both those that require winding and self-winders, which tap energy from the motion of the wearer\u2019s wrist.  The number of Swiss employed in the industry fell from about 90,000 in 1970 to just over 30,000 in 1984, and companies decreased from 1,600 in 1970 to 600 today, according to the Federation of the Swiss Watch Industry, a manufacturers\u2019 group.  A big reason: Quartz watches were cheaper and more reliable. Even the most expensive mechanical watches lose several seconds a week and require maintenance every few years that can cost more than two new iPhones. Timezone, a watch-enthusiast website, calls them \u201can anachronism.\u201d  $2.9 Million Muller  Despite its continued reliance on centuries-old technology, the industry has fortified itself since the 1980s.  Switzerland \u2019s exports of timepieces rose 11 percent last year to a record 21.4 billion francs ($23.7 billion), based on wholesale prices, according to the Federation of the Swiss Watch Industry. Exports climbed 8.5 percent in September from a year ago, data from the federation showed today.  Mechanical watches made up a third of revenue in the $58 billion watch market last year, and the segment will expand 33 percent by 2016, researcher Euromonitor International forecasts. High-end Swiss watches can fetch stratospheric prices: Patek Philippe\u2019s Sky Moon Tourbillon runs $1.3 million and Franck Muller\u2019s Aeternitas Mega 4 is $2.9 million.  \u201cThe more you learn about watches, the more you realize there is real know-how behind them,\u201d said Gabriel Vachette, 30, who runs  a website  about watches and owns roughly 20. You don\u2019t get the same \u2018wow\u2019 factor with a smartwatch.\u201d  At greatest risk are low- and mid-range brands such as Swatch and Tissot, Cox said. With many timepieces in the $200-$400  price range , they\u2019ll often be in direct competition with smartwatches in the minds of buyers.  Samsung\u2019s watch \u201cshows nothing new,\u201d said Swatch Chief Executive Officer Nick Hayek. Swatch has made interactive watches for 20 years, he said, \u201cand has gained precious experience.\u201d Tissot, a Swatch unit whose watches have had electronic touch screens since 1999 and incorporate altimeters and electronic compasses for hikers and divers, has said it will continue adding technology. Swatch and Richemont shares have both outpaced Switzerland\u2019s benchmark SMI Index this year, and 20 analysts recommend buying Swatch while none recommend selling the stock.  Swatch shares  gained 0.4 percent to 588.50 Swiss francs in Zurich trading today while Richemont rose 0.9 percent to 94.40 francs. The SMI Index advanced 1.1 percent.  \u201cSo far the concept of the smartwatch is questionable,\u201d said Michel Keusch, a portfolio manager at Bellevue Asset Management AG in Kuesnacht, Switzerland, which holds Richemont and Swatch shares among its 2.2 billion francs of assets. \u201cYou need to charge it every day. It\u2019s a miniature screen. Everybody has a smartphone anyway.\u201d  Keusch said consumers may initially snap up smartwatches amid media hype, but that the product may fade like calculator watches did in the 1980s. He says sales may start around 2 million units a year -- a fraction of the 1 billion timepieces sold annually.  Fossil, Citizen  HTC Corp. (2498)  is developing a smartwatch that uses Google Inc.\u2019s Android software and can take pictures, according to a person familiar with the matter. The smartwatch will join a growing segment of wearable technology that already includes devices from Samsung and Sony Corp. (MSFT)  formed alliances in 2003 with Fossil and Citizen for watches that could receive information such as news, sports, weather, and stocks. Swatch and Tissot joined the software maker with similar products the following year. By 2008, they had all been pulled from the market. M&A is not.  Large acquisitions, led by  Verizon Communications Inc. (VZ) \u2019s\n$130 billion purchase of its wireless business from Vodafone\nGroup Plc, pushed mergers up 42 percent in the third quarter to\n$671 billion, data compiled by Bloomberg show. That belies\nstagnation in takeovers below $5 billion -- the heart of\ndealmaking -- where volumes fell about 2 percent. Those smaller\ndeals matter to bankers who count on them for close to 90\npercent of advisory fees, according to Freeman & Co.  The big deals, fueled by cheap debt, are concentrated in\nindustries including telecommunications and technology, where\ncompanies grappling with disruptive innovations or saturated\nmarkets are prepared to pay high prices to secure growth.\nSmaller companies, meanwhile, are holding off on deals because\nof lingering concerns about the economic recovery as a surge in\nstock prices makes targets expensive.  \u201cThe softness in M&A is evident in the $1 billion to $5\nbillion range,\u201d said Cary Kochman, head of North American M&A\nfor  Citigroup Inc. (C)  \u201cA number of large deals in 2013 could have\nbeen done five years ago or five years from now.\u201d  While the large deals grabbed headlines, there were only 15\nof them in the quarter, compared with about 6,500 valued at less\nthan $5 billion. The bigger acquisitions account for just 14\npercent of the $7 billion in fees that will be paid to\ninvestment banks for deals announced during the quarter,\naccording to estimates by  Freeman , a New York-based researcher.  During the buyout boom that preceded the 2008 recession,\nthe largest deals generated 18 percent of the fee pool at most.\nThe disparity occurs because banks typically charge a greater\npercentage of the value of smaller transactions.  Asian Slump  Buyers from  North America  were the most active among larger\nacquirers, accounting for 10 of the 15 big deals announced. In\n Asia , meanwhile, buyers both large and small were sidelined by\nfalling currencies and stock markets. The largest deals last quarter were struck by companies in\nthe technology, telecom and drug sectors -- industries facing\nrapid changes that drive them to pay high prices to gain size,\nnew technology or market reach.  \u201cThose are three sectors that are consolidating and the\nvalues tend to be large,\u201d said Michael Carr, head of Americas\nM&A for Goldman Sachs Group Inc., in a telephone interview. The nation will impose flexible fines that are multiple the\nvalues of infringed goods, moving away from fixed amounts, Vice\nChinese Commerce Minister Jiang Zengwei said at a briefing in\nBeijing today. China will amend its criminal law to make it more\neffective in fighting piracy, and improve evidence rules to aid\nowners of intellectual property, he said.  The moves build on a pledge by Vice Premier Wang Qishan\nlast month to improve monitoring of intellectual property rights\nin China. The nation is set to become the world\u2019s largest market\nfor copied software as it isn\u2019t reducing piracy quickly enough,\n Robert Holleyman , chief executive officer of the  Business\nSoftware Alliance , said in October.  \u201cWe are working to amend the relevant laws and regulations\nto increase punitive measures against law breakers so that they\nwill bear the corresponding legal responsibility for their\ncrimes of infringement and counterfeiting,\u201d said Jiang, who is\nalso office dean of China\u2019s National Leading Group for Combating\nIPR Infringement and Counterfeits.  Almost four out of five computer programs used in China are\npirated, according to the annual report of the alliance, a trade\ngroup representing companies in the  software industry , including\n Microsoft Corp. (MSFT)  and  Apple Inc. (AAPL)   \u2018Greatly Pushed\u2019  The central government has \u201cgreatly pushed forward\u201d its\neffort to use legal software nationwide, including the adoption\nof licensed programs at 135 state departments and some\nprovincial governments, the State Council said in a statement\ndistributed before Jiang\u2019s briefing.  The $7.78 billion commercial value of software pirated in\nChina last year was second only to the $9.52 billion lost in the\nU.S., the alliance said. Only 20 percent of software in the U.S.\nis pirated, compared with 78 percent in China, according to the\ngroup\u2019s report issued in May.  While the percentage of pirated software in China has\ndeclined, from 79 percent in 2009 and 92 percent in 2003, its\nvalue has increased as the Chinese software market expanded, the\nreport showed.  Chinese authorities investigated 16,000 cases of\ncounterfeiting involving 13.12 billion yuan ($2.1 billion) of\ngoods during the government\u2019s \u201cSharp Sword\u201d campaign, said the\nState Council, China\u2019s cabinet. The campaign, from October 2010\nto June 2011, led to prosecution in 2,176 cases, it said.  China will deploy enforcement inspections during the New\nYear and Lunar New Year holidays, according to the cabinet\nstatement.  Websites involved in counterfeiting and infringement will\nbe \u201crectified\u201d and companies producing unauthorized\nduplications of CDs and DVDs will be \u201csorted out,\u201d the State\nCouncil said. China will also crack down on the import and\nexport of counterfeit foods and drugs, it said. That\u2019s certainly proven to be\nthe case with the online music service  Spotify .  A big success in  Europe , it has developed a mystique among\nU.S. digerati unable to access it without resorting to elaborate\nworkarounds. Now it has arrived, and it turns out to be largely\nworthy of the buzz.  Spotify is cloud-based, meaning that its collection\nof some 15 million tracks is stored on and accessed over the\nInternet. It differs from services like  Apple Inc. (AAPL) \u2019s iTunes in\nthat you aren\u2019t purchasing and downloading individual tracks or\nalbums to your computer or smartphone. Instead, you decide what\nyou want to hear when you want to hear it, and stream it in real\ntime.  There are three tiers of service. The basic, free option,\nwhich is currently available on a by-invitation basis, gives you\naccess to the full Spotify catalogue. But you can only listen\nover a computer once you\u2019ve downloaded and installed its free,\niTunes-like software. Versions are available for both Microsoft\nWindows-based PCs and Apple Macs, though there\u2019s no option for\naccessing the service through a Web browser if you happen to be\naway from your own computer.  Ad-Free  The free service also carries ads, and after an\nintroductory period you\u2019ll be limited to 10 hours of listening a\nmonth and a maximum of five plays per track. Getting rid of the\nads and limits requires a $4.99-a-month \u201cunlimited\u201d\nsubscription. For $9.99, you also get to play Spotify tracks on\nyour smartphone or tablet, and to access the service through\nInternet-connected sound systems like Sonos wireless speakers\nand Logitech\u2019s Squeezebox line.  I\u2019ve been trying out the premium service for a couple of\nweeks, running it on both a PC and a Mac and installing its app\non both an iPhone 4 and an Android phone, Samsung\u2019s Droid\nCharge. While none of Spotify\u2019s individual features or\ncomponents is truly revolutionary, no one else has put those\npieces together in as simple and comprehensive a package.  As music services go, Spotify is a bit of a hybrid. As long\nas you\u2019re connected to the Internet, most songs are streamed,\nmeaning that they aren\u2019t hogging space on your device. The\npremium tier adds the option of saving songs locally, so they\u2019re\navailable even if you\u2019re on an airplane, subway or somewhere\nelse without  Internet service . Those songs go away if you drop\nyour Spotify subscription.  Importing ITunes  I started by installing Spotify\u2019s player software on the\nMac where I also keep my iTunes library. Spotify gave me the\noption of incorporating those purchased songs into its library\ntoo; I opted to bring only some of my playlists, encompassing\nseveral hundred cuts. The playlists promptly showed up on all\nthe other devices on which I had the software or app installed.  In cases where a track existed in Spotify\u2019s catalog, it\nmatched up its in-the-cloud copy with mine, making the song\ninstantly streamable on all my devices. For music that the\nservice didn\u2019t have, I had to go through a somewhat laborious\nprocess of putting both my computer and mobile device on the\nsame Wi-Fi network, opening the software on both and marking the\nplaylist to copy over the missing music.  For me, the real benefit of Spotify is in all those\nmillions of tracks that I didn\u2019t already own. I can play them\none-off, or organize my favorites into new playlists I can share\nwith other Spotify users via Facebook or Twitter.  No Beatles  You\u2019ll surely find music that appeals to you. Don\u2019t,\nthough, expect to find everything. For instance, like every\nother legal source of tracks except iTunes, it is BYOB -- Bring\nYour Own Beatles. Other old-school holdouts like Led Zeppelin\nand Metallica are missing too.  There are also holes in the catalogues of more recent, more\ndownload-friendly artists. For instance, I was able to find\nmultiple versions of Jason Mraz\u2019s 2008 hit, \u201cI\u2019m Yours,\u201d but\nonly a single live version of his 2002 \u201cThe Remedy (I Won\u2019t\nWorry).\u201d Spotify did provide a couple of karaoke versions, in\ncase I wanted to sing along. I didn\u2019t.  On the other hand, the service has an impressive collection\nof tracks from niche sources and artists who might be a little\noutside the pop mainstream.  A colleague was pleased to get hard-to-find tracks from\nfavorite performers like  James Blake , Nite Jewel and DaM-FunK.\nMyself, I was able to find remembered jazz chestnuts from\nartists like Ramsey Lewis and Vince Guaraldi, as well as a good\ndeal of Mississippi bluesman Johnny Rawls.  The digital-music market is undergoing its biggest changes\nsince the opening of the iTunes Store in 2003. Services like\nRhapsody, Grooveshark, Rdio and Pandora have all carved out\nnooks for themselves.  Amazon.com Inc. (AMZN)  and  Google Inc. (GOOG)  both\nrecently launched online-storage music services and Apple is\nabout to revamp ITunes to be more cloud-centric.  Even in this crowded field, Spotify stands out for its\nflexibility, depth and ease of use. It\u2019s one of those cases\nwhere the mystique is well-deserved.  ( Rich Jaroslovsky  is a Bloomberg News columnist. The\nopinions expressed are his own.) Smartphone buyers are increasingly snapping up devices with screens measuring 5 inches (13 centimeters) or more for easier Web browsing and video viewing, while others pick up a tablet to accompany their handset. Nokia is absent from both categories, dominated by  Samsung Electronics Co. (005930)  and  Apple Inc. (AAPL)   Nokia\u2019s failure to enter the large-screen market early on marks the third time in a decade the company has overlooked a major trend: In 2004 it was slow to embrace clamshell handsets, then a few years later it missed out on touch screens. This time, the company\u2019s future in smartphones is at stake as it seeks to sustain the nascent revival it has enjoyed with Lumia.  \u201cThis is a trend that can\u2019t be missed,\u201d said Francisco Jeronimo, an analyst at researcher IDC in  London . \u201cPeople are using smartphones in different ways now, consuming media by streaming over faster mobile networks. A 5-inch screen for a smartphone just feels right in the hand.\u201d  Sales of handsets 5 inches or bigger soared to 29.7 million units last year from 1.2 million a year earlier, Jeronimo said.  Stock Drop  While Nokia hasn\u2019t announced any bigger devices, the company is almost certainly preparing one and could release it within a few months, Jeronimo said. James Etheridge, a Nokia spokesman, declined to comment on plans for bigger-screen smartphones and tablets, saying that the company is still assessing consumer interest in them.  Nokia, based in Espoo, Finland, fell 0.5 percent to close at 2.51 euros in Helsinki trading. The stock  has lost  about 90 percent since the iPhone and Google\u2019s Android were introduced in 2007. Over the same period, Apple has almost tripled and Samsung has more than doubled. Nearly 20 percent of Nokia\u2019s shares are on loan -- borrowed stock is typically shorted --more than eight times the average among Euro Stoxx 50 members, according to Markit, a financial-information provider in London.  Nokia\u2019s flagship Lumia features a 4.5-inch screen, and the rest of its handsets have smaller displays. While the company has focused on the design and software of its smartphones, competitors have been getting bigger.  Galaxy S3  The 4.8-inch Galaxy S3 from Samsung, the world\u2019s largest handset maker, became the top-selling smartphone globally last year. The Galaxy S4, an updated version introduced last month, has a 5-inch screen.  Samsung\u2019s Note 2 has a 5.5-inch display.  ZTE Corp. (000063) \u2019s Grand Memo has a 5.7-inch display, and the Ascend Mate from  China \u2019s Huawei Technologies Co. boasts a 6.1-inch screen. Samsung in February unveiled  the Note 8.0 , an 8-inch device that works as a mobile phone. The industry often calls such devices \u201cphablets\u201d because they blur the line between phones and tablets.  Apple, which has dominated the 10-inch segment since it introduced the iPad three years ago, responded to phablet competition with the 7.9-inch iPad mini, unveiled in October. Apple has also increased the screen size of the iPhone, though it remains a relatively small 4 inches.  Nokia, which pioneered the mobile-phone market in the 1980s, clung to its so-called candy bar handsets a decade ago even as customers were flocking to clamshell phones made by Motorola Inc., Samsung and  Sony Ericsson . Its market share fell to a five-year low before recovering as the company released new clamshells and smartphones.  Microsoft Linkup  After 2007, Nokia\u2019s market share headed south again after it ignored consumer interest in touch screens, spurred by the iPhone. This time, there was no significant recovery.  Chief Executive Officer Stephen Elop started the current comeback effort two years ago, dropping Nokia\u2019s home-grown operating system in favor of Windows software from his former employer  Microsoft Corp. (MSFT)  He has also cut more than 20,000 jobs in a bid to revive Nokia after the company fell outside the top five in smartphone rankings and became  unprofitable .  The strategic shift has yet to reverse market-share losses, though Lumia sales did increase to 4.4 million units last quarter. In much the same spirit, once a\nyear this column also makes some predictions -- but only so\nthe economists have something to giggle over.  With that caveat in mind, here are 10 things that\nmight (or as likely not) happen in 2011:  No. 1. The bull market returns. Actually we\u2019ve already\nbeen in a bull market for more than a year. Just take a\nlook at the figures. But in the early stages of a rising\nequity cycle, no one says it\u2019s a bull market. First they\ncall it a dead-cat bounce. Then they call it a bear-market\nrally. By the end of 2011, the penny will have dropped.\nWe\u2019ll be officially back in bull territory. By the close of\nthe year, everyone will have started piling back into\nequities again.  No. 2. The alternative-investment industry crashes.\nThe main driver of hedge funds and private-equity funds was\nthe search for yield. With stock markets in the doldrums,\ninterest rates cut to almost nothing, and bond yields at\nrecord lows, investors were desperate for any kind of\nmeaningful return on their money. They were willing to\nlisten to slick hedge-fund managers who promised to make 30\npercent a year on high velocity yak-hide arbitrage. Next\nyear, interest rates will be rising, and so will bond yield\nand equity returns. Why bother paying a fortune to hedge-\nand private-equity fund managers, few of whom deliver on\ntheir promises, when you can get pretty decent returns from\nmainstream investments?  No. 3. Venture capital returns. The start-up industry\ntook a terrible beating from the  dot-com crash . But as a\nrough rule, a decade is long enough for the financial\nmarkets to forget everything. There are fantastic\nopportunities out there. Smartphone apps. Social\nnetworking. Alternative energy. Africa. The markets always\nhave space for some blue-sky optimists -- and 2011 will be\nthe year that venture capitalists fill that slot again.  No. 4. France gets smoked out in the euro crisis.\nSomehow France has managed to get itself grouped along with\nGermany as one of the strong euro nations. But it runs a\nbigger budget deficit than Italy. It has chronic\nunemployment and little growth. Crucially, it has the\ngreatest resistance to reform. The merest suggestion of\nextending working hours, or retirement ages, or reforming\npublic services, prompts massive demonstrations. It can\u2019t\nlast. Next year will be when France wallows with Ireland,\nGreece, Portugal and Spain.  No. 5. The  Apple Inc.  backlash starts. We used to\nthink International Business Machines Corp. was sort of\nsinister. Then it was Microsoft Corp. But which business\ntoday has far too much power, is run by control freaks and\nputs profits before principles? That\u2019s right. The world\u2019s\nthird-biggest company, measured by market value, is about\nto discover that the line between cool upstart and ugly\nmonopolist is a very thin one.  No. 6. The German model is back in fashion. The words\nGerman and fashion go together about as well as Greece and\nsolvent. But in a world trying to figure out how you get\nout of a debt crisis, the Rhineland model of capitalism is\nsuddenly going to seem very appealing. Lots of mid-size\ncompanies, with huge technical expertise, low debt and\nskilled workforces exporting niche products to the whole\nworld -- that sounds like a pretty good formula for success\nin the 2010s. By the end of 2011, expect every chief\nexecutive on the planet to start talking earnestly about\nhow they are looking to a German management model as their\nguide.  No. 7.  Lloyds Banking Group Plc  gets broken up. The\nhastily assembled merger between two of Britain\u2019s largest\nbanks, Lloyds and HBOS Plc, increasingly looks like one of\nthe more catastrophic decisions made during the height of\nthe credit crunch. It is too powerful. This will be the\nyear it gets split apart.  No. 8. Iceland teaches the world a lesson. Two years\nago, every government in the world bought into the idea\nthat you had to bail out your banks. If they collapsed, you\nwould go straight back to the Stone Age. One country defied\nthe consensus. Iceland couldn\u2019t afford to keep its banks\ngoing. What happened? There\u2019s been pain, sure, but from\nnext year on the economy should be growing again, inflation\nis under control and interest rates are coming down. If\nIceland keeps recovering, only one conclusion is possible:\nYou don\u2019t need to bail out banks after all.  No. 9. Russia puts the R back in BRIC. We\u2019ve heard a\nlot about the rising economic power of Brazil, India and\nChina. A lot less has been heard about the R in the BRICs -\n- Russia. It tends to get dismissed as a raw materials\nsupplier with an authoritarian government. But it\u2019s trying\nto recreate itself as a technology powerhouse -- look at\nthe plans to create a new Silicon Valley in the Moscow\nsuburb of Skolkovo. Crazy? Remember, this was the first\ncountry to put a  man into space . Russia has always been\nscientifically advanced. If it can bring its brains and\nbusinessmen together, it could yet outshine the B, I and C\nin the acronym.  No. 10. A backlash against Christmas e-cards. Do I\nreally need festive greetings from a small bank in Latvia\nI\u2019ve never spoken to? Is that Austrian management\nconsulting firm sincere in wishing me the best for the\nholiday season? I doubt it. Listen up guys. It\u2019s not\nthoughtful. It\u2019s not touching. It\u2019s spam. Frankly, I\u2019d\nrather get another e-mail from that friendly Ukrainian\ncompany that supplies Viagra without a prescription. By\nChristmas 2011, sending out e-cards will be socially\nunacceptable -- and not too soon.  ( Matthew Lynn  is a Bloomberg News columnist and the\nauthor of \u201cBust,\u201d a book on the Greek debt crisis. The\nopinions expressed are his own.)
