Its once tigerish economy is growing at\nits slowest rate in more than a decade. Newspapers are filled\nwith ever more depressing stories of rape, official plunder and\ngut-wrenching poverty. To an outsider the headlines can seem\nsurreal: Last week the cabinet actually voted to allow convicted\ncriminals to serve in Parliament and state legislatures, before\nbeing forced to back down.  Indians -- who know that almost a third of the members of\nthe lower house of Parliament face criminal charges -- can be\njaded about such things. But this kind of official brazenness\ncan hardly inspire confidence in companies looking to invest in\nIndia, which has long touted the rule of law as its one crucial\nadvantage over  China .  And what about affluent Indians, who unlike foreign\ncompanies have a big stake in their country and society? Can\nthey really continue to ignore the  chaos and dysfunction  that\nsurrounds them, the broken infrastructure and equally threadbare\nlaws? Can they thrive indefinitely in a country where most\npeople exist on less than $2 a day, where half the homes lack\ntoilets and three-quarters of the population doesn\u2019t have access\nto safe drinking water?  Broken Country  There is no question that India has great potential. Having\nbuilt successful operations for more than one multinational in\nmy homeland, I know it\u2019s quite possible to navigate India\u2019s\nchaos and build profitable businesses here. Indeed chaos --\nwhich is really shorthand for corruption, poor governance,\nuncertainty and volatility -- is a defining feature not just of\nIndia but also of many  emerging markets . Global companies that\nlearn to conquer it here will be well-prepared to succeed\nelsewhere.  But without a semblance of governance and the rule of law,\nIndia\u2019s rise is hardly inevitable.  Demographics  and talent --\nthe lodestones of India advocates -- don\u2019t automatically\noutweigh criminality, corruption and self-interest.  The culprits for this mess seem obvious: greedy\npoliticians, corrupt bureaucrats and the greasy oligarchs who\nflatter and fund them. Many middle-class Indians blame democracy\nitself, which gives the vote to the unwashed and easily bought\nmasses. Increasingly, though, I wonder if the problem isn\u2019t us:\neducated, relatively wealthy, urban Indians.  Millions of creative and resilient citizens have done well\nby finding ways around India\u2019s chaos rather than challenging it.\nWe send our children to private schools and abroad rather than\nto government schools. We patronize world-class private\nhospitals instead of the public health-care system. We live\nbehind the walls of gated communities, supplied by individual\nwells and powered by diesel generators.  Indeed, we take pride in our ability to succeed despite the\ngovernment. The less influence the state has in our lives, the\nbetter: We  don\u2019t vote  (turnout in elite areas is 35 percent or\nless) or pay taxes (less than 3 percent of Indians actually do).\nWe shudder at the thought of entering government or politics.  Our disengagement has made the erosion of India\u2019s public\ninstitutions possible. Now the fragile layer of insulation we\u2019ve\nwrapped around ourselves is also eroding. Even the affluent and\ninfluential can no longer escape the extortion and lawlessness\nthat the less lucky have always faced. I\u2019ve been trying to build\na house in Bangalore for more than two years, and have been\nstymied at every turn by rapacious demands for bribes. One\nfriend\u2019s home has been illegally occupied by a real-estate\ndeveloper with political connections; the legal process to evict\nhim has stalled because the judge hasn\u2019t showed up for a year.  \u2018Banana Republic\u2019  Another colleague, one of India\u2019s most respected and\ninfluential industrialists, has had to move out of his home in\nPune because an illegal mall sprouted a few feet outside his\ndoor. The state itself has turned predator. \u201cBribery and\nnepotism -- that\u2019s what it now takes to succeed,\u201d laments\nNarayana Murthy of Infosys, one of India\u2019s most respected\ncorporate leaders. \u201cThere is every possibility that India could\nslide down the path of becoming a  banana republic ,\u201d legendary\nindustrialist  Ratan Tata  has warned.  Let us be blunt: India\u2019s rise is not inevitable. As with\ncompanies, success isn\u2019t just about potential. It is about\nperformance. Performance requires good governance, strong\ninstitutions and, most of all, the rule of law. When politics\ndegenerates into family enterprises designed to plunder the\ncountry with the help of obliging businessmen and bureaucrats,\nwhen self-interest trumps national interest, sensible policies\nwill always lose out to the lure of graft and loot.  These problems will not fix themselves. Even now many urban\nIndians are hoping for the emergence of a benevolent strongman\nin Delhi, perhaps the opposition  Bharatiya Janata Party \u2019s\n Narendra Modi . Even if Modi is the strong leader he tries to\nportray, however, this is wishful thinking. The only way the\nsituation is going to change is if middle-class Indians -- those\nof us with education, money and a real stake in society -- work\nto change it.  We have to reclaim our country. That means becoming\nresponsible and truly engaged citizens for the first time. We\nhave to start following the law even when there are few\nconsequences for breaking it. We have to vote in elections and\npay taxes instead of bribes. We have to get out on the streets\nto protest publicly and vigorously against injustices -- not\njust once, when some  horrible scandal  moves us, but\nconsistently. We have to donate money and our time to strengthen\nNGOs and volunteer organizations.  Ultimately we have to have the courage to join the civil\nservice and to run for office. Unless honest and patriotic\nleaders replace the cynics and crooks, efforts to change the\nsystem will never gain sufficient momentum.  It\u2019s no longer appropriate for Indians to ignore the chaos\naround them the way a multinational might. We can\u2019t just wall\nourselves off, emigrate or send our money and kids abroad. Our\ndisengagement is producing a dysfunctional and unlivable\nsociety. If we don\u2019t conquer the chaos, chaos will conquer\nIndia.  (Ravi Venkatesan, the former chairman of Microsoft India,\nis the author of \u201cConquering the Chaos: Win in India, Win\nEverywhere.\u201d)  To contact the writer of this article:\nRavi Venkatesan at  ravi_venkatesan@hotmail.com . In the past 12 months, the micro-blogging social-networking\nservice played a role in changing the world, 140 characters at a\ntime. From  Egypt  to  Libya  to  Syria  and beyond, Twitter helped\nactivists thwart censorship dragnets, connect with the similarly\naggrieved and put underperforming leaders on the defensive.  Well, that was then. This will be remembered as the year\nTwitter  sold  its corporate soul at a time when the world needs\ngenuine transparency and the tools to realize it. By blocking\nmessages on behalf of governments, Twitter is both doing the\ndirty work for leaders from  Beijing (SHCOMP)  to Damascus and answering\nthe biggest question of the day: Will the Internet change the\nworld\u2019s authoritarian regimes, or will repressive governments\nchange the Web? Unfortunately, it looks like the latter.  Twitter said it would withhold a posting, or tweet, in a\ncountry where a particular kind of content is banned, but the\ncompany won\u2019t pull offending tweets from its entire audience.\nSuch claims are no more convincing than those of Google Inc.,\nwhich spent years rationalizing why it helped nations like  China \nstifle information. Google eventually developed a conscience and\nleft the most-populous nation.  Tough Spot  Granted, Twitter is in a tough spot as it goes from a\nscrappy Internet startup into a global power looking to win Wall\nStreet\u2019s blessing. Yahoo! Inc., Microsoft Corp. and Cisco\nSystems Inc. at times did their own bit for the Communist Party.\nI just wonder if there\u2019s a better way for technology executives\nto go -- one that doesn\u2019t enable the worst impulses of paranoid\nworld leaders in the name of market share and profit.  Egyptians who bravely took to Cairo\u2019s  Tahrir Square  to oust\nHosni Mubarak are lucky they did so last year. One shouldn\u2019t\noverhype the roles Twitter or Facebook Inc. played in toppling\nrogue regimes. Yet if Egyptians were to take to the streets in\n2012 rather than 2011, there\u2019s a genuine question about whether\nhistory might be different.  An even bigger issue is how governments undermine their own\nnations\u2019 economic performance. You won\u2019t read about this on\nTwitter or Facebook, but in the pages of George Orwell\u2019s 1949\nclassic \u201cNineteen Eighty-Four.\u201d Orwell invented concepts like\n\u201cBig Brother\u201d and \u201c\u2018thought crime\u201d and \u201cNewspeak\u201d and\noffered prescient insights into how the Internet would evolve.\nMake that devolve, as events in Asia become decidedly Orwellian.  Chilling Effect  The free flow of ideas and data has never been more\nimportant to raising living standards. Any country that censors\nthe conduits of those Information Age forces is handicapping\nitself and restraining the intellectual energy needed to drive\ngrowth. It was heartening to see Americans rise up against the\nStop Online Piracy Act, a law so vaguely written that it would\nhave had a chilling effect on free expression.  Asia  is going in the opposite direction. Take  South Korea ,\nwhich is among the most plugged-in nations, with broadband\nspeeds that are the envy of techies the world over.  Korea \u2019s\ncurbs on online communications are about social morals and good\nconduct. Yet there\u2019s plenty of doubt that such controls are\ncompatible with democracy and economic progress.  In  India  there\u2019s a move to block material deemed\nobjectionable. Who decides what meets that criteria and at what\ncost? In 2011, leaders were taken aback by an anti-corruption\ncampaign that caught fire on Twitter and Facebook. India\u2019s 1.2\nbillion people need more of that kind of social disruption.\n Indonesia ,  Singapore ,  Thailand  and  Vietnam  aren\u2019t above blocking\nwebsites or certain content.  Japan (JGDPAGDP)  and Malaysia are making\nsimilar noises.  China\u2019s Model  Imagine a world where technology giants weren\u2019t so quick to\nhelp governments censor. China should be of particular concern\nbecause its capital-markets, social-control model is attracting\nfans around the developing world.  What if you are an investor exchanging controversial ideas\nabout China\u2019s stability? Or an economist wondering about the\naccuracy of China\u2019s data? You may be less inclined to question\nthe conventional wisdom and the propaganda. It means the true\nstate of two of the biggest dangers to China\u2019s future --\ncorruption and pollution -- will become harder to discern.\nOfficials are clamping down on micro-blogging services like\nthose run by U.S.-listed Sina Corp.  \u2018#TwitterBlackout\u2019 Movement  One can argue that social media helped uncover conditions\nat the Shenzhen sweatshops that  Apple Inc. (AAPL)  relies on to churn\nout iPads and iPhones. These hypermodern gadgets are assembled\nin retrograde working conditions. The rash of suicides at\nFoxconn International Holdings Ltd.\u2019s factories tarnished the\nlate  Steve Jobs \u2019s legacy as the world was celebrating him as an\nunambiguous force for good.  Apple faces an Internet Age conundrum. The ubiquity of\ngadgets and Internet access gives voice to the masses, including\nthose angry about the human toll of Apple\u2019s fat profits. Some\nusers called for a Twitter boycott, using \u201c#TwitterBlackout\u201d\nas a hash tag, or labels that let people easily find tweets.\nOrganizations such as  Reporters Without Borders  are decrying a\nmove it says runs counter to the Arab Spring, in which Twitter\nserved as a sounding board and information exchange.  There\u2019s just one problem with calls to stop tweeting.\nTwitter can block those, too.  (William Pesek is a Bloomberg View columnist. The opinions\nexpressed are his own.) Legislation giving the U.S. Patent & Trademark Office in\nAlexandria, Virginia, more budget autonomy starting next fiscal\nyear clears the way for three new offices, in addition to a\nfourth in Detroit that had been in the works. Lawmakers\nincluding U.S. Representative Lloyd Doggett of Texas and Senator\nMichael Bennet of  Colorado  are lobbying for offices in their\ndistricts.  Moving the patent office beyond its suburban  Washington ,\nD.C., home base is intended to speed up an almost three-year-\nlong patent approval process, which requires face-to-face\nmeetings between inventors and agency examiners. The offices\nwould bring jobs, including 100 planned for Detroit in the first\nyear, and might serve as a magnet for companies looking to be\nnear the new offices.  \u201cIt\u2019s sort of like what Research Triangle did\u201d by landing\n International Business Machines Corp. (IBM) \u2019s research facility, said\nLaCharles Keesee, 46, a former patent examiner who is now\nexecutive director for the Denver Office of Economic\nDevelopment. \u201cYou could plant a scientific flag in the middle\nof your community and use that as a point of attraction to build\nan education community, an employment community.\u201d  Research Triangle Park, in the Raleigh-Durham area of  North\nCarolina , was created in the 1950s by a partnership of\nuniversities and corporations to boost the state\u2019s economy. The\ndevelopment has at least 170 companies including IBM,  Credit\nSuisse Group AG (CSGN)  and  Cisco Systems Inc. (CSCO) , with 38,000 full-time\njobs, according to the  foundation  that oversees the facilities. The gauge has climbed 13 points in two months, the biggest back-to-back advance since January-February 1992.  \u201cYou\u2019re seeing a significant pickup in demand for new residential dwellings,\u201d said Brian Jones, senior U.S. economist at Societe Generale in New York. His forecast of 55 was the most accurate in the Bloomberg survey. \u201cMortgage rates are moving higher and pulling people in. And I think that in general, the economy is getting better.\u201d  Prices Rise  The cost of living rose in June by the most in four months as gasoline prices climbed, figures from the Labor Department also showed today. The consumer-price index increased 0.5 percent after a 0.1 percent gain in May. The median forecast in a Bloomberg survey called for a 0.3 percent rise.  Excluding food and energy, prices climbed 0.2 percent for a second month.  Some Fed policy makers, including St. Louis Fed President James Bullard, have expressed concern inflation is too low, raising the risk of an outright decline in prices that would sap the recovery. Price readings closer to the Fed\u2019s goal will give the central bank the flexibility to move forward later this year with reductions in its $85 billion in monthly asset purchases designed to stoke the economy.  Fed Bank of Kansas City President Esther George today said the U.S. was on the \u201cright path\u201d for economic recovery and that cuts in the pace of stimulus are \u201cappropriate.\u201d George, speaking on Fox Business Network, also said inflation appears to be \u201cmoderate\u201d and the benchmark interest rate should not be held too low for too long.  Prices Climb  Consumer prices increased 1.8 percent in the 12 months through June, more than projected and up from a 1.4 percent year-over-year gain the prior month, the Labor Department\u2019s report showed.  \u201cA little more inflation, from the Fed\u2019s point of view and the economy\u2019s point of view, is actually desirable as long as it doesn\u2019t go too far,\u201d said PNC\u2019s Hoffman. \u201cIt\u2019s sort of a welcome note that we\u2019re not headed down a path to deflation.\u201d  Manufacturing production , which accounts for about 75 percent of total output, increased 0.3 percent in June, the most in four months, today\u2019s Fed data showed. It followed a 0.2 percent gain in May that was larger than previously estimated. Economists  projected  a 0.2 percent increase for June, according to the Bloomberg survey median.  Production among technology industries, including computers and semiconductors, increased 1.2 percent in June after advancing 2.3 percent in each of the prior two months.  Capital Spending  The gains indicate American companies are beginning to boost capital investments as they look past the specter of sequestration and global growth risks. Spending on information technology is up 4 percent this year compared with 2 percent last year, according to the median in a survey of 203 businesses by Computer Economics, a research company in  Irvine , California -- helping businesses such as Microsoft Corp.  Applied Materials Inc. (AMAT) , the largest seller of machinery used in the production of semiconductors and flat-screen displays, expects industry spending to pick up next year as chipmakers boost output to meet demand for mobile-device parts.  Competition among smartphone providers is driving demand for more advanced parts and improvement in the machines that make them, Chief Executive Officer Mike Splinter said at a July 8 analyst briefing in San Francisco.  The Fed\u2019s report today also showed motor vehicle production rose 1.3 percent in June following a 0.5 percent increase the month before.  Auto Sales  The automobile industry has been a bright spot for the economy, with the vehicle sales rate surging to 15.9 million in June, its best monthly pace since November 2007, according to data from Ward\u2019s Automotive Group.  The industry is not doing as well overseas. Car sales in Europe slumped to a two-decade low in June, the European Automobile Manufacturers\u2019 Association said today. Combined with other data showing German investor confidence unexpectedly dropped in July and euro-area exports fell in May for a second month, the figures added to signs the region is struggling to emerge from recession.  Slower-growing foreign markets may still temporarily crimp export-related activity at U.S. factories. The International Monetary Fund projects  China \u2019s growth will be 7.8 percent in 2013, down from an 8 percent April forecast, and the 17-country euro area will shrink 0.6 percent as the economies of France, Italy and Spain contract. The technology budget released today calls for $78.9\nbillion in spending next year, led by Defense Department\nreductions, as the administration promotes savings and\nefficiencies in federal-data programs. It\u2019s part of a $3.8\ntrillion election-year budget plan sent to Congress.  \u201cBy doing more with less, the administration is driving\nsavings across government and using those savings to reinvest in\ninformation technology and services that benefit the American\npeople,\u201d Obama said in a message accompanying the proposed\nbudget for fiscal 2013, the year starting Oct. 1.  The Obama administration has been trying to hold federal IT\nspending steady while increasing government efficiency through\nthe use of cloud computing and mobile devices. Information-\ntechnology expenditures rose 7.1 percent a year on average from\n2001 to 2009 and \u201chas effectively been halted\u201d with no growth\nfrom 2009 to 2013, according to the budget.  Information-technology spending includes purchasing\ncomputers, protecting government data, updating websites and\nhiring employees who provide technical support. The reduced\nexpenditures in 2013 will be driven by cutting the Pentagon\u2019s\ninformation technology investments 3.6 percent to $37.2 billion\nnext fiscal year, according to the budget.  \u2018Hot Areas\u2019  Spending on information technology by major civilian\nagencies will increase 1.1 percent to $41.7 billion, the budget\nshows.  The budget plan demonstrates a commitment to initiatives in\nprogress, which is good news for companies specializing in\ninformation technology products and services, said Alan Balutis,\ndirector of the Internet Business Solutions Group for  Cisco\nSystems Inc. (CSCO) , based in  San Jose ,  California .  \u201cThe hot areas will be cloud computing, data-center\nconsolidation, cybersecurity and mobile technology,\u201d Balutis\nsaid in an interview. He served as chief information officer for\nthe Commerce Department from 1995 to 2000 during the\nadministration of President  Bill Clinton .  Technology has largely stayed above the political fray\nheading into this year\u2019s elections, Balutis said. Politicians\ngenerally haven\u2019t attacked the idea of using technology to\nimprove government services or a reliance on companies for\nservices such as cloud computing, he said.  Innovation Focus  \u201cThere\u2019s a growing bipartisan recognition that technology\nis the vehicle that allows you to transform the way the\ngovernment does business,\u201d he said.  TechAmerica , a trade association in Washington, considers\nthe spending proposal to be a \u201csignificant commitment\u201d in the\nbudget to technology as total IT spending would be decreased,\nTrey Hodgkins, the group\u2019s senior vice president for national\nsecurity and federal procurement policy, said in an e-mail.  \u201cThis budget focuses on leveraging technology to increase\nefficiencies and savings,\u201d he said. \u201cWhile federal IT spending\nis going down, innovation in the federal government is going up.\nThis is a very positive thing.\u201d  The association represents companies including  Apple Inc. (AAPL) ,\n Dell Inc. (DELL)  and  International Business Machines Corp. (IBM)  Industry\nexecutives said they plan to review the budget to understand\nspecific IT cuts or spending increases.  More Cloud Computing  The administration seeks to shift more federal applications\nto cloud-computing networks operated by contractors, a move\naimed at saving money. The cloud is a Web-based pool of shared\ncomputing resources such as software and data storage.  Microsoft Corp. (MSFT) ,  Google Inc. (GOOG) ,  Amazon.com Inc. (AMZN)  and IBM are\namong companies competing for U.S. cloud-computing contracts.  Forty services have moved to the cloud while another 79 are\nscheduled for transition by June 2012, according to the budget.\nMore than 50 legacy systems have been eliminated.  \u201cThe adoption of cloud solutions has eliminated\nduplicative systems, while also integrating new levels of\nsecurity, reliability, and functionality, to include\ncollaboration, virtual meetings, and other innovations,\u201d\naccording to the administration\u2019s budget.  The administration began the  Federal Risk and Authorization\nManagement Program  in December to give U.S. agencies a one-stop\nshop when it comes to minimum security requirements and\ncontracting language for cloud computing.  Spending Curbs  \u201cThe federal government spends hundreds of millions of\ndollars a year securing the use of IT systems in a duplicative,\ninconsistent, and time-consuming manner,\u201d according to the\nbudget.  The White House also plans to curb IT spending by shrinking\nthe number of the data centers used by agencies to store large\namounts of information.  The U.S. government expects to close almost 1,100  data\ncenter  by 2015 to try to save $3 billion, according to the\nbudget. The administration said it plans to close 525 data\ncenters by the end of 2012.  \u201cMoving forward, the government will shift to a newer\noperating model that requires agencies to review existing data-\ncenter capacity for use before investing in a potentially\nduplicative capability,\u201d according to the budget.  The administration said it will take further steps to\nprotect federal computer systems from cyber attacks by foreign\ngovernments and hackers.  Securing Federal Networks  The Homeland Security Department will work with agencies to\nidentify areas in need of improvement to better defend computer\nsystems and develop risk mitigation strategies.  \u201cThreats to this infrastructure -- whether from criminal\nelements or nation-states -- continue to grow in number and\nsophistication, creating the potential that essential services\ncould be degraded or interrupted, and confidential information\nstolen or compromised, with serious effects,\u201d the\nadministration said.  The budget didn\u2019t provide an estimate for how much will be\nspent on cybersecurity in fiscal 2013. The patent is part of Microsoft\u2019s ActiveSync software that\nMotorola Mobility used to license before the two companies\nstarted fighting.  The case is part of a broader argument by Redmond,\nWashington-based Microsoft that Google\u2019s market-dominant Android\noperating system uses its technology. Motorola Mobility, which\nwas acquired by Google in 2012, is one of the biggest holdouts\nof a licensing program that Microsoft started three years ago.  While the synchronization was common with computers,\nsoftware engineers who thought \u201cwouldn\u2019t it be great to have\nthis on a mobile device\u201d were initially prevented by their\nlimited power, said Microsoft lawyer Constantine Trela.  Google, based in  Mountain View ,  California , is seeking to\nrevive Motorola Mobility\u2019s smartphone business. On Aug. 1 it\nannounced a new flagship Moto X smartphone with customizable\ncolors that will be assembled in the U.S. -- probably putting it\noutside the ITC\u2019s jurisdiction.  Microsoft contends any Motorola Mobility phone that has the\nsyncing feature infringes the patent, and has sued  U.S. Customs ,\nsaying its officials aren\u2019t stopping phones from crossing the\nU.S. border.  The cases are Microsoft Corp. v. ITC, 12-1445, and Motorola\nMobility LLC v. ITC, 12-1535, both U.S. Court of Appeals for the\nFederal Circuit (Washington). (SIE)   \u201cLump sum damages would act more as a deterrent than\nhaving two actuaries fight it out in a costly court case,\u201d\nWeertman said in a phone interview from  London . \u201cIt\u2019s a vicious\ncircle where the damages aren\u2019t deterrent enough.\u201d  In Europe, about 35 percent of software deployed on\npersonal computers was pirated every year since 2007, compared\nwith 20 percent in the U.S., according to a May study by BSA and\nresearcher IDC. Globally, the value of pirated software rose 14 percent to\n$58.8 billion last year, almost double the total in 2003. In\n China , almost four out of five programs in use are pirated, and\n65 percent in  Russia  is stolen, according to BSA.  The European Commission, the 27-nation EU\u2019s executive arm,\nlast year published a  report  showing that some provisions of the\ncurrent law, which was introduced in 2004, need \u201cfurther\nclarification and have resulted in diverging interpretations at\nnational level,\u201d said  Chantal Hughes , a spokeswoman for EU\nInternal Markets Commissioner  Michel Barnier . The commission is\nalso examining how to deal with the surge in online piracy.  Lobbying Efforts  Microsoft, the world\u2019s biggest software company, isn\u2019t\naiming to export the U.S. system around the world, said  Chris\nOldknow , the company\u2019s enforcement policy counsel. At the same\ntime, the risk for pirates is \u201cgreater that they\u2019ll wind up\nhaving to pay a substantial amount in America,\u201d Oldknow said in\nan interview. \u201cAnd lo and behold, America has the lowest rate\nof software piracy in the world.\u201d  Microsoft told the commission in March as part of a\n consultation  that lump sum or multiple damages, only available\nto some extent in 10 smaller EU member states such as  Belgium ,\nAustria and Malta, should be extended to the other 17 countries.  Fair damages should include lost profits and costs of\nenforcement, additional damages in the amount of economic\nbenefit of the infringer, and fixed-sum or multiple damages,\nRedmond, Washington-based Microsoft said. Corporate end users\nmay see an \u201ceconomic benefit\u201d in copying rather than buying\nsoftware if they are only made to buy the legitimate product\nonce caught or pay damages equal to the publisher\u2019s lost profit,\nthe company said.  Microsoft rose 0.5 percent to $27.12 and Adobe climbed 0.6\npercent to $26.39 as of 12:05 p.m. in  New York .  Under Licensing  Software firms such as engineering and design software\ncompany  Autodesk Inc. (ADSK)  say they also suffer from so-called under\nlicensing, where clients only pay for some of the programs used.  \u201cIt\u2019s a significant issue that does affect our bottom line\nand we take it very seriously,\u201d said spokesman Noah Cole.\nAutodesk, based in San Rafael,  California , uses internal\ntechnology to detect unauthorized use of its software.  The commission may make proposals on how to change the\ncurrent law in the first half of 2012, spokeswoman Hughes said.  \u201cSome claim that damages awards do not currently appear to\neffectively dissuade potential infringers from engaging in\nillegal activities,\u201d she said. \u201cThe commission services will\nexamine if changes are necessary.\u201d  In Germany,  Europe \u2019s biggest economy, there are neither\nstatutory nor punitive damages but it is up to the discretion of\nthe court whether to fine, with no fixed amount, Weertman said.\nThe highest total settlement in an \u201cend-user case\u201d was 1.5\nmillion euros, he said. In the U.K.\u2019s criminal courts, the\nmaximum statutory fine is 10,000 pounds ($15,800) and punitive\ndamages are not recognized, he said.  Punitive Damages  In the U.S., punitive damages are often awarded in piracy\ncases, with a statutory maximum rate per infringement of\n$150,000 if it is found to be willful, according to the BSA.  The low rate of piracy in Belgium, one of the EU countries\nwhere lump-sum or multiple damages are possible, backs up the\nsoftware companies\u2019 claim. The\nshows will be broadcast from IBM\u2019s lab in Yorktown Heights, New\nYork and air during the regular \u201cJeopardy\u201d time slot.  The project builds on IBM\u2019s work in the field of artificial\nintelligence, including the Deep Blue supercomputer that\ndefeated world champion Kasparov in a 1997 match. About four\nyears ago, executives at IBM, the world\u2019s largest computer-\nservices provider, decided to try another challenge that would\ngenerate public interest -- and this time with potential\ncommercial appeal, said Ferrucci.  The main task: make computers understand questions in\nnatural language, as opposed to the keyword searches common on\n Google Inc. \u2019s website or  Microsoft Corp. \u2019s Bing. While computers\ncan easily search databases, they have problems understanding\ncontext, innuendo and other subtleties common in most\ninformation, Ferrucci said.  How Watson Works  \u201cThe Holy Grail here is to create a technology that can\nunderstand what you\u2019re asking, the way you\u2019re asking it,\u201d he\nsaid. \u201cPeople want to do more with all the content we have.\u201d  For the \u201cJeopardy\u201d competition, Watson will receive each\nquestion through a typed entry at the same time host  Alex Trebek \nreads the queries to Jennings and Rutter. The computer will scan\na custom-made database for answers and then calculate its degree\nof confidence in an answer. If the confidence level exceeds a\ncertain threshold, it will buzz and speak the answer out loud.  \u201cWatson\u2019s a big step toward artificial intelligence that\ndirectly affects people\u2019s lives,\u201d  Paul Saffo , managing director\nat investment adviser Discern Analytics in San Francisco, said\nin an interview. \u201cIt will have the intended effect -- this is\ngoing to absolutely capture people\u2019s attention.\u201d  King Kong  Ferrucci developed the technology for Watson with a team of\nabout 20 other IBM scientists, including software engineers and\ncomputational linguists. They created their own database from\njournals, newspapers and other resources, rather than having the\ncomputer rely on the Internet. Then they developed algorithms\nthat look for relevant information, depending in part on\ncontext. The computer runs on IBM\u2019s Power 7 server system.  The project hit some snags. When asked to name the eighth\nWonder of the World, Watson came back, with \u201cemphatic\nconfidence,\u201d that the answer was King Kong -- which it found in\na description of the movie and failed to recognize it as\nfiction. The computer also struggled with words with double\nmeanings, like \u201ccushion.\u201d  \u201cYou could use \u2018bad\u2019 to mean bad, you could use \u2018bad\u2019 to\nmean good, you could mean \u2018bad\u2019 to mean cool, but there\u2019s an\nintended meaning\u201d Ferrucci said. \u201cLanguage is ambiguous, it\u2019s\ncontextual, it\u2019s tacit.\u201d  Track Record  The computer was fine-tuned during more than 50 games\nagainst former \u201cJeopardy\u201d contestants. Ferrucci declined to\ncomment on Watson\u2019s record from the games, saying that although\nWatson lost some games, the results gave IBM enough confidence\nto play on air against the two champions.  Jennings won 74 games in 2004 and 2005, setting the record\nfor most consecutive games played. Rutter won the highest total\never by a single player, earning $3.26 million.  IBM, based in Armonk, New York, added $1.54 to $145.82 at\n4:15 p.m. in New York Stock Exchange composite trading. The\nshares  have climbed  11 percent this year.  The company spends about $6 billion a year, or 6 percent of\nits sales, on research and development. It gets about $1 billion\nfrom licensing fees.  The machine has started to generate interest from\nbusinesses, particularly in customer support and health care,\nFerrucci said, declining to identify companies. The company is\nbuilding prototypes for specific applications, including health\ncare, he said, noting it would probably be at least three years\nbefore such a machine was used commercially.  There\u2019s also potential for mobile devices, if a search is\nable to show more precise responses on the smaller screen. The\ntechnology, which only works in English, will be translated into\nmultiple languages.  IBM has said that it will donate the $1 million to charity\nif Watson wins. Jennings and Rutter plan to give half of the\nproceeds to charity if they win. (AAPL) , making them among\nthe stars of the portfolio, said  David Mixon , a patent lawyer at\nBradley Arant Boult Cummings in Huntsville,  Alabama . That\u2019s fueling concern that electronics\nmakers can\u2019t count on  Asia  to counterbalance diminished demand\nin recession-ravaged  Europe  or in the U.S., where a recovery is\ntaking hold at a slower-than-predicted pace. With Intel and\nMicrosoft yet to gain market share in tablets against Apple\nInc., the PC industry may struggle to grow at all this year,\naccording to research by Robert W. Baird & Co.  \u201cThe current picture is lousy,\u201d said Pat Becker Jr., a\n fund manager  at  Portland , Oregon-based Becker Capital Management\nInc., which owns Intel and Microsoft shares. \u201cIt\u2019s Europe, it\u2019s\nthe  chain reaction  into the  emerging markets .  There have already been hints that China is affecting\ngrowth in the PC industry. Last week, Intel rival  Advanced Micro\nDevices Inc. (AMD)  disclosed that revenue unexpectedly slumped 11\npercent in the second quarter. AMD, Intel\u2019s only remaining\ncompetitor in PC processors, blamed weakness in China and Europe\nfor a revenue decline that contrasted with its previous estimate\nfor growth of as much as 6 percent.  China Growth  Applied Materials Inc. (AMAT) , Intel\u2019s largest  supplier , cut its\nannual targets last week, citing delayed orders for its\nchipmaking equipment because of weaker end-market demand for\nsemiconductors in the same regions.  China recorded its weakest expansion in three years in the\nsecond quarter when its economy advanced 7.6 percent from a year\nearlier, a government report in Beijing showed July 13.  In April,  Santa Clara , California-based Intel predicted\nsales of $13.6 billion, plus or minus $500 million, for the\nsecond quarter. Analysts on average project sales will rise\nabout 4 percent to match the midpoint of the company\u2019s forecast,\nwith per-share profit estimated to be 52 cents a share,\naccording to data compiled by Bloomberg. Gross margin, the only\nmeasure of profitability that Intel forecasts, was expected to\nbe about 62 percent, the company said. Redmond, Washington-based Microsoft\nwill follow on July 19 after the market closes.  \u2018Very Poor\u2019  While AMD\u2019s revenue disappointment may have been caused in\npart by market-share losses to Intel and Nvidia Corp. in\ngraphics chips, the magnitude of the miss shows just how quickly\nPC demand has dropped, said Mike Burton, an analyst at Northland\nSecurities Inc.  \u2018\u2018It\u2019s indicative of a very poor environment for PCs,\u201d\nsaid Burton, who has a market perform rating on Intel shares.\n\u201cIt\u2019s not just AMD.\u201d  Global PC shipments stalled in the second quarter,\ndeclining 0.1 percent to 87.5 million units, according to a July\n11 report from industry researcher Gartner Inc. The firm cited\nan uneven economic recovery in the U.S., slower spending in\n China  and Europe, and the encroachment of Apple\u2019s iPad and other\ntablets. Chris Caso, an analyst at Susquehanna International Group,\nsaid Intel is more likely to stick to projecting better market\nconditions that analysts estimate in an effort to convince its\ncustomers to keep ordering.  IPad Effect  \u201cIntel realizes that their view of the market influences\nthe market because they are the market,\u201d said Caso. \u201cThey\u2019re\ntrying to convince customers, investors and eventually the\nconsumer that they\u2019re right.\u201d  In an attempt to fire up demand for laptops and take on\ntablets, Intel last year began touting what it calls Ultrabooks,\nslim-line notebook PCs that resemble Apple\u2019s MacBook Air. (AAPL)   Take the new version of OS X, the Mac\u2019s operating system, called Mavericks after a fabled California surfing spot. Coupled with a new generation of the flagship MacBook Pro laptop, it provides the most powerful and polished experience in computing these days.  That\u2019s if you find its completely Apple-centric environment comforting rather than stifling and can afford the pricey hardware.  As OS X upgrades go, the most noteworthy thing about Mavericks may be its price: There isn\u2019t one.  The previous version of OS X cost $20, which was still much less than Microsoft charges for its major Windows upgrades. Mavericks, though, is available as a free download from the  App Store  for Macs running any of the three most recent editions of the operating system. (Those are Snow Leopard, Lion and Mountain Lion.)  I\u2019ve been using Mavericks on three Macs: the newly released 13.3-inch MacBook Pro With Retina Display, where it came pre-loaded, and recent-vintage models of the iMac and MacBook Air, where I installed it myself.  Bumpy Upgrade  Neither of the upgrades went entirely smoothly. The Air stopped in mid-download, informing me that \u201can error has occurred\u201d without specifying what the error was. (I was able to resume the process with no ill effects, however.)  And the iMac upgrade came to a screeching halt with a warning that my system was corrupted and I should immediately back up all my data, wipe the drive clean and mix a stiff drink. (OK, I made up that last part.)  I ignored the warning and tried again. This time, Mavericks installed without a hitch, and has been humming along for more than two weeks with nary a performance glitch. After examining logs from my computer, Apple said my experience was likely an anomaly.  The new operating system introduces two important apps, both migrating from Apple\u2019s iPads and iPhones: iBooks and Maps.  The books app works exactly the way it does on iOS devices. Purchases from the iBooks store can be stored in the cloud or locally, and bookmarks, highlights and notes are synced across all devices, so you can pick up on the Mac exactly where you left off on an iPad.  Memos, Papers  You may not read the great American novel on your Mac, but it\u2019s certainly useful for memos, school papers and the like.  Maps is similarly integrated through Apple\u2019s cloud services. Look up a location on the Mac and you can send the directions straight to your iPhone, where they automatically launch the Maps app.  While it\u2019s all very neat and seamless, it also points up what some people see as a major issue with the Apple ecosystem: While both iBooks and Maps are improving, neither is remotely the best of breed in its category.  Those honors belong to, respectively,  Amazon.com (AMZN) \u2019s Kindle family of apps and content and  Google (GOOG)  Maps. Both are available for Apple devices, but without the same level of integration, forcing you into a choice between quality and convenience.  Mavericks features a number of small but welcome enhancements, including the ability to assign tags to help locate related files, and recommendations for hard-to-crack passwords that are remembered by Apple\u2019s iCloud Keychain service.  Extended Life  Laptop buyers, though, will be more interested in how it works with  Intel (INTC) \u2019s latest microprocessors, called Haswell, to extend battery life on the updated MacBook Pros. The answer is: very nicely.  While Apple claims the new 13.3-inch model can go for up to nine hours between charges, I exceeded 10 without much difficulty. Apple puts the battery life of the updated 15.4-inch version at eight hours.  The new MacBook Pros are less expensive than their predecessors: Prices are 9 percent to 13 percent below comparable models from a year ago. Moreover, in a shot across  Microsoft (MSFT) \u2019s bow, Apple is now including its iWorks productivity suite, its answer Microsoft Office, with new Macs, along with its iLife photo, video and music apps.  Even with lower prices and bundled software, though, no one will describe the new MacBooks as value-priced. The 13.3-inch model starts at $1,299. My test unit, with eight gigabytes of memory and 256 gigabytes of fast flash storage, costs $1,499. The 15.4-inch version starts at $1,999.  Taken together, the MacBooks, Mavericks and the newly bundled applications -- knit together with the iPad-iPhone universe through Apple\u2019s cloud services -- create a start-to-finish experience that no competitor can match. The U.S. International Trade Commission yesterday in\nWashington  found  the Xbox doesn\u2019t infringe Motorola\u2019s patent for\na way to establish communication between the gaming-system and\naccessories, such as the controllers, ending a case filed in\nNovember 2010. The agency upheld a March ruling that cleared the\nXbox, which is made in  China , of the infringement claim.  The case is part of a global dispute between the companies\nover who is using whose patented inventions. Microsoft wants\nMotorola Mobility to pay royalties on smartphones running on\nGoogle\u2019s Android operating system. Google claims Microsoft owes\nMotorola Mobility royalties on the Xbox and Windows operating\nsystem.  Microsoft, based in Redmond, Washington, has argued that,\neven if it violates the Motorola patent, banning the Xbox would\nbe an extreme remedy that would reduce consumer choice and hurt\ngame developers.  \u201cThis is a win for Xbox customers and confirms our view\nthat Google had no grounds to block our products,\u201d Microsoft\nDeputy General Counsel  David Howard  said in a statement.  Matt Kallman, a spokesman for Google, said the company was\ndisappointed and evaluating its next steps. The case can be\nappealed to a court that specializes in  patent law .  Top Seller  The Xbox has been the top-selling U.S. game console for\nmore than two years. (6758) \u2019s PlayStation 4 and Nintendo Co.\u2019s Wii U, as well as new\ndevices from Apple Inc., Facebook Inc. and Amazon.com Inc. Countries at the top of the list had \u201csustained\ninvestment\u201d in IT from industry and their national governments\nduring \u201cthe leanest financial times IT producers have known in\na decade, and for many governments in at least a generation,\u201d\naccording to the study, which is conducted every two years.  With an overall score of 80.5 out of 100, the U.S. placed\n12.5 points ahead of second-ranked Finland, to maintain the top\nspot it held in 2009.  Singapore ,  Sweden  and the U.K. rounded out\nthe top five. The group represents technology\ncompanies including  Apple Inc. (AAPL) ,  Microsoft Corp. (MSFT)  and Symantec\nCorp.  The U.S. was 13.4 points behind leader Switzerland for the\nquality of its IT infrastructure and half a point behind\nAustralia for the legal environment, which includes data privacy\nand spam protection.  The study was conducted prior to President Barack Obama\u2019s\nSept. 16 signing of a patent reform law, which is expected to\nreduce the average 34 months it takes to issue a patent.  \u201cThe passage of the patent-reform bill will further\nstrengthen U.S. leadership both in the R&D environment but also\nin the legal environment,\u201d Holleyman said. Jean Veil , a lawyer for the Paris-based bank, said Societe\nGenerale is realistic about the chance of Kerviel repaying 4.9\nbillion euros. News  Debt Collectors Face Consumer Bureau Supervision in January  Large debt collectors, including law firms, will for the\nfirst time face supervision to assure they follow federal\nconsumer-protection laws beginning on Jan. 2, the U.S. Consumer\nFinancial Protection Bureau announced yesterday.  \u201cMillions of consumers are affected by debt collection,\nand we want to make sure they are treated fairly,\u201d  Richard Cordray , the agency\u2019s director, said in an e-mailed statement.\n\u201cWe want all companies to realize that the better business\nchoice is to follow the law -- not break it.\u201d  The regulation will cover any company that has more than\n$10 million in annual receipts from consumer debt collection.\nThat definition will capture about 175 collectors, representing\n60 percent of the industry\u2019s annual revenues, according to the\nCFPB.  The new rule could erode profits at major debt collectors\nincluding Norfolk, Virginia-based  Portfolio Recovery Associates\nInc. (PRAA) , the largest publicly held firm in the business, San Diego-\nbased  Encore Capital Group Inc. (ECPG)  and  Asta Funding Inc. (ASFI) , based in\nEnglewood Cliffs, New Jersey. It could also affect the largest\nplayer by revenue, NCO Group, a unit of New York-based  JPMorgan\nChase & Co. (JPM) \u2019s private equity arm, One Equity Partners.  The accounts-receivable industry had revenues of $17\nbillion in 2011, according to Kaulkin Ginsberg, a Rockville,\nMaryland-based consulting firm. In addition to debt collectors,\nthe industry includes debt buyers, who purchase written-off debt\nfrom creditors such as credit-card issuers. Debt collectors can\nbe independent agents, employees of buyers or members of law\nfirms.  The regulation closely tracks a Feb. 17 CFPB proposal that\nwas opposed by the debt-collection industry because of the $10\nmillion revenue threshold. ACA International, an association of\ndebt collectors, in an April 10 letter called the figure\n\u201carbitrary and capricious, an abuse of discretion and not\notherwise in accordance with law.\u201d  The regulation also includes partial coverage of collection\nlawyers. Earlier this year, groups including the National\nAssociation of Retail Collection Attorneys and the  American Bar\nAssociation  criticized the agency\u2019s initial proposal.  They said that Dodd-Frank exempts attorneys from Title X,\nthe section of the law creating the CFPB, on the grounds that\nthey are lawyers, not consumer financial services providers.  \u201cAs is clear from the legislative history of the act,\nCongress took pains to exclude attorneys engaged in the practice\nof law,\u201d the bar association wrote in an April 11 letter.  The final rule covers law firms meeting the agency\u2019s\ndefinition of debt collectors, namely those \u201cwhose principal\nbusiness activity is debt collection\u201d or who regularly engage\nin debt collection, according to the regulation. Firm News  Women Lawyers at Big Firms Struggle for Pay and Power  Despite the efforts of law firms to promote gender parity,\nwomen at the 200 biggest firms in the U.S. still lag men in\npower and pay, according to the seventh annual survey by the\nNational Association of Women Lawyers.  Women account for 15 percent of equity partners, about the\nsame percentage as in the first survey. Their compensation\ntrails behind men\u2019s at all levels, most notably at the equity-\npartner level, where women earn 89 percent of what men do, the\norganization said in a statement. Women hold 20 percent of the\npositions on a firm\u2019s highest governance committee, and women\nare firm-wide managing partner at 4 percent of firms. They make\nup 70 percent of the nonpartner track, lower paid, staff\nattorney positions, according to NAWL. That\u2019s the only category\nin which they are a majority.  Efforts to explain the pay differences were foiled by\ncompensation systems that lack transparency and could\nincorporate unintended bias, according the text distributed with\nthe survey.  \u201cThe gap between male and female compensation at the\nequity partner level does not correlate with male\/female\ndifferences in billable hours, total hours or books of business,\nbegging the question of how firms actually set compensation for\ntheir partners,\u201d NAWL Foundation President Stephanie Scharf, a\npartner at Scharf Banks Marmor LLC in Chicago, said in a\nstatement.  Moreover, the survey found the pay discrepancies begin at\nthe associate level, where new women lawyer earn 99 percent of\nwhat men earn and make less in bonuses. Women constitute nearly\n45 percent of the associate pool, yet they receive only 40\npercent of the bonuses, the report says.  If trends continue, the future looks dim, particularly\ngiven that for the second year in a row, the proportion of women\nentering big-firm practice has decreased, the report said. (GE)  redesign a tool to speed up the disassembly of gas\nturbines last year, is listed on the patent application as one\nof the inventors. Now, at the age of 20, he is working on a\nrocket-launch system in Alabama for  Boeing Co. (BA)   Peterson, a rising senior at Virginia Polytechnic Institute\nand State University in Blacksburg, is one of the hottest new\nproducts in corporate America\u2019s supply chain: a kind of futures\ncontract on high-skill labor.  Faced with a wave of retiring engineers and scientists and\nthe need for precise expertise, U.S. companies --including GE,\nBoeing,  United Technologies Corp. (UTX)  and  Microsoft Corp. (MSFT)  -- are\nreaching into colleges to make contact with students far earlier\nthan they ever have. Their involvement extends to advising and\nshaping curricula so graduates can plug into jobs faster with\nless training time and cost.  Universities \u201cneed to provide our students with hands-on,\nreal-world practical application from day one,\u201d said Rick Stephens, senior vice president of human resources and\nadministration at Boeing in  Chicago . \u201cSo when they show up at\nthe first job, not only can they find information, not only can\nthey develop it, they can actually do real work.\u201d Many schools\n\u201care getting that message.\u201d  Persistent Unemployment  The corporate initiatives will help resolve a skill\nmismatch that\u2019s contributed to persistently high unemployment\nsince the 18-month recession ended in June 2009. The jobless\nrate has stalled above  8 percent  for 40 consecutive months,\nrising to  8.2 percent  in May from 8.1 percent in April, and U.S.\nemployers created only 69,000 jobs last month, the fewest in a\nyear. The  unemployment rate  for youth between the ages of 16 and\n24 with a bachelor\u2019s degree or higher has averaged more than 9\npercent annually since 2009.  When the Labor Department released the jobs data on June 1,\nTreasuries rallied, driving 10-year yields below 1.5 percent for\nthe first time. That\u2019s a sign that long-term fixed-income\ninvestors see scant evidence of wage-driven inflation as the\nlabor market fails to match workers with jobs -- a trend that\u2019s\ncontributing to a loss of the dynamism for which U.S. employment\nhas long been known.  The stronger focus on applied learning in public\nuniversities such as  Virginia  Tech and  Georgia  Institute of\nTechnology in Atlanta also is driven by the harsh economics of\nstate budget constraints.  Raising Alarms  Despite alarms raised by policy makers about the need to\ndevelop a more educated American workforce, state legislatures\naren\u2019t coming up with the cash.  Taxpayer funding in Virginia has fallen 11 percent during\nthe past five years per full-time equivalent student after\nadjusting for inflation, while enrollment has climbed 21\npercent, according to  data  from the State Higher Education\nExecutive Officers association in Boulder, Colorado. Funding in\nGeorgia is down 23 percent in the same period, while enrollment\nis up 32 percent.  As taxpayer backing shrinks, costs shift to parents and\nstudents, who pay higher tuitions and take on more debt -- which\nmakes the goal of monetizing education with a solid job more\nurgent.  Tuition and fees for in-state students at public four-year\ncolleges and universities have climbed in the past decade at an\naverage annual pace of 5.6 percent beyond the rate of inflation,\naccording to the  College Board . Student-loan debt jumped to $904\nbillion in the first quarter of this year, the highest in\nrecords going back to 2003 tracked by the  Federal Reserve Bank\nof New York .  Reduced Spending  Steep payments for education loans hurt the economy, partly\nbecause they mean less  consumer spending  on purchases such as\nhouses, President  Barack Obama  told an audience of students,\nfaculty and local officials at the University of Nevada-Las\nVegas on June 7.  American companies are standing up to help with money,\nadvice and positions for job-seeking graduates. In return, they\nwant schools to take a more active role in training and skill\nformation.  \u201cWe do see employers who are interested in having students\nwho can come in and be productive right away,\u201d said Ralph\nMobley, director of career services at Georgia Tech. \u201cSmall to\nmid-sized companies, and even some larger ones, don\u2019t have\nbudgets for training like maybe they once did. They are looking\nto save some of that cost.\u201d  Sophomore Skills  While companies have for decades funded research and\nrecruited at institutions of higher learning, they now are more\ninvolved in what students do in some four-year technical\nprograms. They are making recommendations on curricula and\ninfluencing students\u2019 skills as early as sophomore year, said\nAmy Slaton, a professor of history at Drexel University in\nPhiladelphia.  \u201cIn the last five to eight years\u201d industry and academic\ncooperation \u201chas taken another notch up,\u201d Slaton said.\nBachelor\u2019s-level engineers \u201care coming out with a more focused,\npractical education that serves industry really well.\u201d  United Technologies  partners  with about a dozen U.S.\nuniversities and contributes about $5 million annually. The\nmoney may be in the form of a donated jet-engine part or cash\nthat funds a lecture series. The Hartford, Connecticut-based\ncompany recruits at schools such as  University of Connecticut \nand  Pennsylvania State University  for more than 1,000\ninternships a year.  \u2018Fair Share\u2019  \u201cI want more than my fair share\u201d of engineering talent,\n Louis Chenevert , chairman and chief executive officer of the\naerospace and building-products manufacturer, said in an\ninterview when asked about the return he gets on this\ninvestment. \u201cWe offer the best jobs in America to these\npeople,\u201d he said, noting that young engineers get a chance to\nwork on \u201cexciting stuff,\u201d such as the Black Hawk helicopter,\nmade by the company\u2019s Sikorsky division.  While Slaton says she worries universities are becoming too\nvocational -- with \u201cmuch of what we see getting produced as\nknowledge in the schools\u201d starting from \u201can industry-related\nfocus\u201d -- students interviewed for this story weren\u2019t\ncomplaining.  Peterson, the  Virginia Tech  student, said he structured his\ncourse work toward specializations that Boeing and GE need. When\nhe graduates with a mechanical-engineering degree in 2013, he\nwill have not only experience working at the two companies but\nalso hands-on involvement with some of their top projects.  Jobless Graduates  He says he sometimes wishes his classes took time to focus\non the theoretical underpinnings of engineering. Still, \u201cit\nmakes sense for universities to prepare their students the best\nway they can for the workforce,\u201d he said, adding that he knows\nof graduates from other schools who aren\u2019t getting offers.  The number of U.S. job openings rose to 3.7 million in\nMarch, the most since July 2008, even with  13 million  people out\nof work, according to Bureau of Labor Statistics data -- a sign\nthat some of the unemployed may not have skills that fit\nemployers\u2019 needs.  Georgia Tech helped start the trend toward more corporate\ninput into curricula in 2002, when the university hired Richard DeMillo,  Hewlett-Packard Co. (HPQ) \u2019s chief technology officer, as its\ndean of the College of Computing. He reorganized the curriculum\nbetween 2002 and 2005 with the intent of producing students\nbetter fit for industry.  The previous course load generated graduates who were less\nsuited to jobs in entertainment, health care and computer\nsecurity, he said. The new program allows students to choose\n\u201cthreads\u201d that allow them to mix computing with literature or\nanimation so they might be attractive to movie or gaming\ncompanies such as  Walt Disney Co. An EU settlement avoids any fines and a decision on whether\na company broke antitrust rules. Companies can be fined as much\nas 10 percent of their annual revenue if they break the terms of\na legally binding settlement. U.K. First  The company, which changed its name to BlackBerry yesterday to unify its branding, unveiled a touch-screen phone called the Z10 and a version with a physical keyboard named the Q10, both of which will run the retooled BB10 software. The Z10 goes on sale in the U.K. today, before appearing in  Canada  and the  United Arab Emirates  in the next 10 days.  Chief Executive Officer Thorsten Heins, who assumed the role of Steve Jobs-style pitchman at yesterday\u2019s event, said carriers were responsible for the BlackBerry\u2019s slow arrival in the U.S. The four largest mobile-phone services --  Verizon Wireless , AT&T Inc.,  Sprint Nextel Corp. (S)  and  T-Mobile USA  -- are taking longer to test the devices than their U.K. or Canadian counterparts, he said.  All the carriers got the final software for the phones, known as the \u201cgold code,\u201d at the same time, Heins said. (HPQ) \u2019s Canadian unit.  The Q10 won\u2019t appear until April because the company has focused its resources on getting the touch-screen model out first. In all, six analysts  recommend  buying the stock, 19 have a hold rating, and 21 advise selling, according to data compiled by Bloomberg. Foreclosure Errors May Cloud Ownership of U.S. Homes  U.S. courts are clogged with a record number of\n foreclosures . Next, they may be jammed with suits contesting\nproperty rights as procedural mistakes in the foreclosure cases\ncloud title establishing ownership.  \u201cDefective documentation has created millions of blighted\ntitles that will plague the nation for the next decade,\u201d said\nRichard Kessler, an attorney in Sarasota, Florida, who conducted\na study in Sarasota county that found errors in about three-\nfourths of court filings related to home repossessions.  Attorneys general in at least six states are investigating\nborrowers\u2019 claims that some of the nation\u2019s largest home lenders\nand loan servicers are making misstatements in foreclosures.\n JPMorgan Chase & Co.  is asking judges to postpone foreclosure\nrulings, while Ally Financial Inc. said Sept. 21 its GMAC\nMortgage unit would halt evictions. The companies said employees\nmay have completed affidavits without confirming their accuracy.  Such mistakes may allow former owners to challenge the\nrepossession of homes long after the properties are resold,\naccording to Kessler.  Ownership  questions may not arise until a\nhome is under contract and the potential purchaser applies for\ntitle insurance or even decades later as one deed researcher\ncatches errors overlooked by another. A so-called defective\ntitle means the person who paid for and moved into a house may\nnot be the legal owner.  \u201cIt\u2019s a nightmare scenario,\u201d said John Vogel, a professor\nat the Tuck School of Business at Dartmouth College in Hanover,\nNew Hampshire. \u201cThere are lots of land mines related to title\nissues that may come to light long after we think we\u2019ve solved\nthe housing problem.\u201d  Almost one-fourth of U.S. home  sales  in the second quarter\ninvolved properties in some stage of mortgage distress,\naccording to RealtyTrac Inc. In August, lenders took possession\nof record 95,364 homes and issued foreclosure filings to 338,836\nhomeowners, or one out of every 381 U.S. households, according\nto the Irvine, California-based data seller.  \u201cIf I were in the title industry, or a mortgage holder, or\nsomeone who bought a foreclosed property, this is something I\nwould be very worried about,\u201d said Michael Carliner, a Potomac,\nMaryland-based economic consultant specializing in housing.  Title insurers use their records and public documents to\nverify a seller is the home\u2019s true owner and that the  property \nis free from liens. They collect a one-time premium and pay\ncosts that may arise if someone challenges a new owner\u2019s right\nto the property. To obtain a mortgage, buyers are required to\npurchase a policy to protect the lender. Many people also get a\nso-called owners policy to protect themselves.  \u201cTitle is everything,\u201d said Susan Wachter, a real estate\nprofessor at the University of Pennsylvania\u2019s Wharton School in\nPhiladelphia. \u201cThere\u2019s no collateral without possession, and\nthat is title.\u201d  For more, click here. The lawsuit accuses Sony and Renesas of infringing a patent\nrelated to a way of making the packaging that goes around\nsilicon wafers so they can be used reliably in smaller\nelectronics, Tessera said in a statement. The company said it\nfiled the complaint Oct. 1 in federal court in Wilmington,\nDelaware.  Tessera Chief Executive Officer Hank Nothhaft has called\nthe company\u2019s patent litigation a \u201cstrategic\u201d effort to reach\nlicensing agreements after negotiations fail. The San Jose,\nCalifornia-based company got almost all of its  $299.4 million  in\nrevenue last year from royalty and licensing fees.  Sony, based in Tokyo, makes Bravia TVs, the PlayStation 3\ngame console, Vaio notebook computers and Blu-ray disc players.\nA Sony spokesperson didn\u2019t immediately return a call seeking\ncomment. Renesas, also based in Tokyo, makes chips that control\nproducts including DVD players and vehicle air bags.  The patent, issued in 2005, is different than ones asserted\nagainst companies including mobile-phone chipmaker Qualcomm Inc.\nand memory-chip maker Nanya Technology Corp.  Tessera lost a case before the U.S. International Trade\nCommission against memory-chip companies including Nanya, Acer\nInc., Elpida Memory Inc. and ProMos Technologies Inc. It won a\ncase against Qualcomm, Motorola Inc. and four other companies\nover chips used in wireless devices. Motorola later took a\nlicense to the Tessera patents.  Both the memory-chip and wireless-chip cases are on appeal. The seeds of the dispute, though, are at least three years old. That\u2019s when a set of key intelligence breakthroughs and devastating attacks, including a breach of  Google Inc. (GOOG) \u2019s computers, reshaped the White House view of China\u2019s cyber spying.  Although public information about the breach at Google and almost three dozen other companies was sketchy, that wasn\u2019t the case for the U.S. government, according to a person familiar with the investigation.  Within 24 hours of Google\u2019s January 12, 2010, announcement, U.S. investigators knew the attack had been state sponsored. Within three weeks, they had pinned it on a specific unit of the  People\u2019s Liberation Army , the person said. The attacks on Google and the other companies were especially worrisome because they targeted technology that makes up the underpinnings of the Internet.  The attack on Google, dubbed Operation Aurora by McAfee Inc. researchers, came about the same time that U.S. investigators were making a separate breakthrough. After years of trying, they identified several key individuals in the attacks against U.S. companies, placing them at the heart of China\u2019s intelligence apparatus.  The  Justice Department \u2019s national security division is now considering criminal indictments against some of those individuals, according to a second person familiar with the matter who asked not to be identified because it wasn\u2019t public.  No Chance  Prosecutors have virtually no chance of getting China\u2019s spies into a U.S. courtroom. Instead, a criminal indictment would lay out the detailed evidence of China\u2019s involvement in trade secrets theft -- a far more significant step than any the U.S. has taken so far.  \u201cThe decision to hold China publicly accountable reflects a high degree of confidence in the intelligence community as to who is responsible for the attacks,\u201d said Paul Tiao, a partner at Hunton & Williams LLP and until recently, senior counselor for cyber security to FBI Director  Robert Mueller . \u201cCertainty about attribution enables operational professionals and policy makers to explore different ways to deal with this threat.\u201d  The conflict over China\u2019s hacking puts the White House in a delicate position. The U.S. is trying to draw a bright line around economic espionage while still retaining the right to hack into foreign computer systems as part of more traditional spying efforts, which are focused on military secrets.  Managing Anger  American officials also must manage the anger of U.S. companies and voters, on one hand, and China, on the other, as they lay out the case that one of the country\u2019s largest trading partners and a rising power has been caught red-handed rifling the jewels of the  U.S. economy .  Over the last three months, that case has mostly consisted of a series of public remarks and visits to Asia by high-level officials, including the secretaries of Defense, Chuck Hagel, and Treasury,  Jacob Lew . In a speech in Singapore on June 1, Hagel said growing cyber-attacks on U.S. companies \u201cappear to be tied to the Chinese government and military.\u201d  In the days leading to this week\u2019s summit, China and the U.S. agreed to hold regular meetings, beginning in July, to establish norms when it comes to hacking and economic espionage.  Extracting Data  Less visible actions could be more significant in the long run. In February, the Department of  Homeland Security  released a set of indicators that companies could use to detect China espionage teams in their computers, among them computer IP addresses used by hackers to extract data.  The move was controversial within intelligence circles because it could tip off China to how the much the U.S. knows about the hacking, according to one former intelligence official. The White House intervened and pushed for the release, signaling the administration wanted to make a dent in China\u2019s activities, the former official said.  An indictment of some of China\u2019s cyber spies would go several steps beyond a recent Pentagon report that accused China of stealing weapons technology from U.S. defense contractors.  Evidence Chain  A detailed criminal indictment typically provides a chain of evidence and an account of why the person is accused of a crime. In this case, prosecutors would probably establish the theft of commercial or military technology and show what information the government has on the hackers\u2019 relationships to China\u2019s military intelligence organizations.  \u201cAnything that we can read ourselves, instead of having to take some official\u2019s word for it, is really powerful,\u201d Stewart Baker, former general counsel for the National Security Agency, said in a phone interview. \u201cThe more detail that comes out, the greater the pressure.\u201d  While U.S. spy catchers were zeroing in on Chinese hackers a few years ago, Operation Aurora demonstrated how the line was becoming blurred between traditional espionage and the theft of  trade secrets .  Google\u2019s willingness to announce publicly that it had been hacked was unusual. Still, the company kept secret that the hackers had accessed a server containing court orders, which could reveal the identity of U.S. government surveillance targets, including China\u2019 agents in the U.S. and elsewhere. That access was reported five weeks ago by a researcher at Microsoft Corp. and confirmed to  Bloomberg News  by a senior official involved in the investigation.  Raytheon, Intel  The wider list of victims was just as worrying. According to three people involved in the government and private investigations, the list included major defense contractors --  Raytheon Co. (RTN)  and  Northrop Grumman Corp. (NOC)  -- as well as a handful of technology companies including  Intel Corp. (INTC) ,  Adobe Systems Inc. (ADBE) ,  Yahoo! Inc. (YHOO) ,  Juniper Networks Inc. (JNPR) ,  Symantec Corp. (SYMC)  and Microsoft.  Morgan Stanley (MS) , the New York-based investment bank, was attacked, as was  eBay Inc ., the online auction site.  The investigation involved agents from the FBI, Defense Department and Department of Homeland Security, a response so broad that the agencies had to develop new rules to sort out their roles.  Once U.S. officials linked the attack to the PLA, the information was provided to senior executives of several companies, including Google co-founder  Sergey Brin , who was granted a temporary classified clearance to sit in on the briefing, according to a person familiar with the investigation.  In several cases -- including those of Google, Adobe and Intel -- investigators discovered that the attackers had accessed source code repositories.  Zero-Day Exploits  It\u2019s unlikely the hackers were trying to replicate Adobe or Google products, investigators believe. The real danger is that the hackers were mining for unknown flaws in the software\u2019s programming -- known as zero-day exploits. Those exploits can be used to take over computers, essentially giving China\u2019s cyber spies the keys to millions of computers worldwide as the software was shipped by major manufacturers. In the case of Intel, it would be hard-wired into the chip sets as firmware.  \u201cI don\u2019t think you can come to any other conclusion,\u201d said Stuart McClure, former chief technology officer for McAfee, which aided the government\u2019s investigation.  The seriousness of the attacks steeled the administration\u2019s resolve, while the intelligence breakthroughs provided the necessary proof.  Defending Networks  Over the next several months, the administration took several steps to help defend critical networks, including finalizing the Defense Industrial Base pilot project, which provided sensitive intelligence on China\u2019s hackers to defense contractors.  By then, however, administration officials had decided that a purely defensive approach wouldn\u2019t work. The only solution was pushing China to change its behavior. This weekend\u2019s meeting between the leaders of the two countries will be the best indicator so far of whether the plan is working.  \u201cThe idea of being victimized over and over again without taking action is not one you can stomach for very long,\u201d said Tiao, the former FBI agent. \u201cAfter a while you reach this boiling point, and we\u2019re finally seeing the response.\u201d  To contact the reporter on this story: Michael Riley in Washington at  michaelriley@bloomberg.net   To contact the editor responsible for this story: Michael Hytha at  mhytha@bloomberg.net","path":".\/2008_2012_msft_bloomberg_news\/secret-intelligence-fuels-u-s-hacking-fight-with-china.txt"},{"id":20860135,"title":"Nokia Predicts Higher Margin as Life Without Phones Looms","released_at":"<date>October 29 2013<\/date> <time>16:40:36<\/time>","content":"Nokia Oyj (NOK1V)  forecast rising profit margins at the network unit that will become its main business after the mobile-phone division it struggled to turn around is sold to  Microsoft Corp. Agency Model  While sales of e-books have exploded in the U.S., they still  make up  only 20 percent of the market, and those gains are slowing. Last year, e-book sales rose 44 percent to $3.04 billion after more than doubling in 2011, according to the Association of American Publishers.  The U.S. government and 33 state attorneys general sued Apple and five of the biggest publishers in April 2012, claiming the Cupertino, California-based company pushed publishers to sign agreements letting it sell e-books under a model that raised prices and harmed consumers.  Apple fought the lawsuit, seeking to fend off greater oversight and continue the agency model of letting content owners rather than retailers set prices, while generating income by taking a commission.  \u201cApple is using that agency model in a number of contexts and they chose to use it in part for e-books because they were using it in other contexts,\u201d said Scott Kessler, an analyst at S&P Capital IQ.  Price Points  Apple is the world\u2019s largest seller of music, and established the pricing model where tracks typically sell for 99 cents and albums for $9.99. With movies and television shows, where there is more competition from cable companies and online services such as  Netflix Inc. (NFLX)  and Hulu LLC, Apple has a less rigid pricing model.  By adopting a new model with higher e-book prices, Apple sought to force Amazon to change its pricing, the plaintiffs argued. At the time, the online retailer was selling titles for $9.99, often below cost. E-books now have a wider price range. More than 650,000 e-books sold by Amazon cost $4.99 or less and more than 1.2 million are $9.99 or less, the company said in May. Currently, the digital version of Dan Brown\u2019s \u201cInferno\u201d  sells  for $12.99.  U.S. District Judge Denise Cote said Apple lost the case, in part, because of statements by its deceased founder, Steve Jobs, that government lawyers said showed Apple was targeting Amazon. States are seeking triple damages for overcharges, according to Connecticut Attorney General George Jepsen\u2019s office. Another trial will be held to determine Apple\u2019s penalty. Amazon began selling e-books in 2007, and four years later, books for Kindle readers surpassed print sales. E-books will account for about half of that, he said.  Amazon\u2019s aggressive pricing means the online retailer\u2019s massive scale ends up benefiting customers, Kurnos said. Amazon has aligned itself with antitrust laws that seek to protect consumers, making its model difficult to contest, he said. It has the support of large\ncompanies including  Microsoft Corp. (MSFT) ,  International Business\nMachines Corp. (IBM)  and a group that represents  Johnson & Johnson (JNJ) ,\n Eli Lilly & Co. (LLY) ,  3M Co. (MMM)  and  General Electric Co. (GE)   The funding provision, which also would let the agency\nincrease fees paid by inventors and patent owners, is the\ncornerstone of the bill and has been a unifying issue even for\nthose who oppose other provisions. Since 1990, the agency says,\nmore than $800 million in fees have been diverted by lawmakers\nto non-patent purposes.  The patent office is funded entirely by user fees. The\nObama administration says the money is needed to hire more\nexaminers and improve agency computer systems to cut the current\n34-month wait for patent approval.  The U.S. Chamber of Commerce,  Washington \u2019s largest business\nlobbying organization, supported passage, as did the  United\nSteelworkers . A group representing large technology companies\nincluding Google Inc.,  Apple Inc. (AAPL) , and  Intel Corp. (INTC)  also  backed \nthe measure.  A group of technology companies that includes InterDigital\nInc. and  Tessera Technologies Inc. (TSRA)  had said the House-passed\nmeasure doesn\u2019t do enough to guarantee more funding for the\npatent office since the agency still has to get congressional\napproval to spend money it collects above its annual budget.  Groups  representing  small businesses say the legislation\nwill benefit large companies over independent inventors, create\na rush to the patent office and establish onerous review\nprocedures that will weaken the power of patents to protect\ninventions.  All newly issued patents may be subject to a challenge from\nthird parties, a variation of a process used by the  European\nPatent Office . Third parties would be allowed to submit\ninformation for consideration during the application process.  The bill also would limit patents on tax-avoidance\nstrategies, though companies including  Intuit Inc. (INTU)  and  H&R Block\nInc. (HRB)  have said they would retain protections for their tax-\npreparation software.  Banks including  Bank of America Corp. (BAC)  and  Citigroup Inc. (C) \nwould get new power to seek to cancel finance-related business\nmethod patents that they argue are of questionable validity.\nCompanies that own such patents, including DataTreasury Corp.\nand Trading Technologies International Inc., have accused the\nbanks of using their clout in Washington to avoid paying for\nusing someone else\u2019s inventions.  The trade group for generic-drug companies including Mylan\nInc. and Watson Pharmaceuticals Inc. opposes the bill because\nthere\u2019s a provision that lets patent owners retroactively\ncorrect errors that might otherwise lead a court to invalidate\nthe patents.  The Washington-based Generic Pharmaceutical Association\nalso objects to language in the bill that would ease deadlines\nfor seeking a patent-term extension granted to compensate\ndrugmakers for the time it takes to get regulatory approval.  The provision would provide a clear victory to  Medicines\nCo. (MDCO) , which won a court ruling that it was entitled to an\nextension even though it missed a deadline for an extension on\nthe main patent for its only drug, the anticoagulant Angiomax.  Fresenius SE (FRE) \u2019s APP Pharmaceuticals unit is appealing that\ndecision after the government said it wouldn\u2019t challenge the\njudge\u2019s decision in favor of Medicines Co.
