Trademark  Apple Wins Ruling on German Samsung Galaxy 10.1 Tablet Ban  Apple Inc., the world\u2019s most valuable technology company,\nwon backing from a German court for a ban on sales of Samsung\nElectronics Co.\u2019s Galaxy 10.1 tablet computer in the country.  A Dusseldorf court Sept. 9 upheld the temporary sales ban\nit issued Aug. 9, rejecting Samsung\u2019s bid to overturn it for the\nmost part. The judges won\u2019t ban sales in other European Union\ncountries as Apple had sought, Presiding Judge Johanna\nBrueckner-Hofmann said when delivering the verdict. The\nlegal dispute between Cupertino, California-based Apple and its\nclosest rival in tablet computers is intensifying as an\nincreasing number of consumers use devices such as tablets and\nsmartphones to surf the Web, play games and download music.  \u201cThe court is of the opinion that Apple\u2019s minimalistic\ndesign isn\u2019t the only technical solution to make a tablet\ncomputer, other designs are possible,\u201d Brueckner-Hofmann said.\n\u201cFor the informed customer there remains the predominant\noverall impression that the device looks\u201d like the design Apple\nhas protected in  Europe .  Samsung said it will appeal. The ruling \u201cseverely limits\nconsumer choice in  Germany \u201d and \u201crestricts design innovation\nand progress in the industry,\u201d the company said in a statement\ne-mailed after the ruling was issued.  The court didn\u2019t compare the Galaxy tablet with the actual\niPad and instead focused on a design Apple filed with the\nEuropean Union  intellectual property  agency in Alicante,  Spain ,\nBrueckner-Hofmann said.  Samsung\u2019s tablet didn\u2019t keep enough distance from the Apple\ndesign, the judge said. While the back of the Galaxy is\ndifferent from Apple\u2019s registered design, the important feature\nis the front, which is nearly identical, she said.  \u201cThe crucial issue was whether the Galaxy tablet looked\nlike the drawings registered as a design right,\u201d she said.\n\u201cAlso, our case had nothing to do with trademarks or patents\nfor technology.\u201d  The EU-wide ban was upheld for Samsung\u2019s German sales unit.\nThe court doesn\u2019t have jurisdiction to issue an EU-ban against\nSuwon, South Korea-based Samsung, itself, Brueckner-Hofmann\nsaid.  Strategy Analytics analyst  Neil Mawston  forecasts tablet\nsales could rise to about 2.4 million units in Germany this year\nfrom 0.6 million in 2010, making it Europe\u2019s third-largest\nmarket after the U.K. and  France .  The Dusseldorf court on Aug. 9 granted Apple a preliminary\nsales ban in 26 of the 27 EU member countries, only to scale\nback its reach a week later over jurisdictional issues. I\nuse real history, real locations, real science: I tell my\nreaders these are fictional characters but everything they\u2019re\ndealing with, it\u2019s real.  Lundborg: Does the thriller have a future?  Brown: We now have real-world thrillers at our fingertips\nalmost daily. What authors bring to reality is that they take\nout all the boring parts.  Writers create suspense by cutting up reality, putting it\nin a different order, dropping pieces out, putting in\nmisdirection. The story becomes fascinating as you try to\nconnect dots that aren\u2019t connected for you on the page.  Shadowy Consortium  Lundborg: Tell me about the secretive Consortium -- that\u2019s\nreal too?  Brown: There are a number of organizations like the\nConsortium. They essentially create alibis for people, or\nfictional realities. They make it easy to tell a very convincing\nlie.  Whether it\u2019s the Vatican, the White House or  Microsoft (MSFT)  --\nthey all need to manage public perception and sometimes that\ninvolves creating illusion or shaping the truth.  Lundborg: With \u201cThe Da Vinci Code\u201d you set the bar pretty\nhigh for yourself. Does that make it easier or harder?  Brown: In terms of research, I now have access to people\nand places I didn\u2019t before. But simultaneously, I\u2019m always\ntrying to keep what I\u2019m writing a secret, and so the people I\ntalk to are signing non-disclosures.  Misdirection  For every question I ask about the novel, I\u2019ll ask four\nabout other stuff entirely. I\u2019ll go on tours of places I know\naren\u2019t going to be in the book, just to keep people off the\ntrail. It\u2019s not very efficient.  Lundborg: So there\u2019s no point in asking what you\u2019re working\non now?  Brown: I\u2019d tell you, but it wouldn\u2019t be true.  Lundborg: What\u2019s the downside of \u201cDa Vinci\u201d?  Brown: There\u2019s a lot of pressure. There are a lot of people\nwho rely on me to turn in great books. Still, what a luxury to\nknow what you\u2019re putting on the page has a life.  Lundborg: Why are symbols so powerful?  Brown: They can convey enormous concepts without the\nbaggage of language. They are transparent and universal.  Lundborg: Why does Langdon wear a Mickey Mouse watch?  Brown: This very serious professor needs to remind himself\nnot to take it all that seriously. On some level, that\u2019s\nsomething, especially now, I remind myself almost on a daily\nbasis.  I take my work dead seriously, but what happens out in the\nworld with these books, I have to step away from. You run the\nrisk of losing your mind.  Lundborg: \u201cInferno\u201d is full of smart people -- but it\nseems the smarter they are, the more they suffer. Why is that?  Brown: On some level, ignorance definitely is bliss. The\nmore you understand the real world, the more you\u2019re concerned\nabout where we\u2019re headed.  On some level, we all live in denial.  To buy this book in North America, click  here . Tapping into a ready supply of geothermal energy and cool\ntemperatures, Bjorgolfur Thor Bjorgolfsson, Iceland\u2019s first\nbillionaire and the former owner of one of its largest failed\nbanks, is turning to the elements to attract customers to store\ndata on the island and capture a slice of a $41 billion market.  The Atlantic island has sought to reinvent itself as a safe\nand secure data haven halfway between Europe and North America\nas it recovers from the economic meltdown after the failure of\nthe country\u2019s top lenders in 2008. Its chance of success is set\nto improve with a link to the Emerald subsea cable between\n London  and  New York  that takes in Iceland for the first time.  \u201cIceland happens to be a rare spot on the earth where\nthere is a convergence of attributes that tick all the boxes,\u201d\nsaid Jeff Monroe, chief executive officer of Verne Global, the\n$700 million data center Bjorgolfsson opened for business last\nmonth in Keflavik. \u201cYou have 100 percent renewable energy. At full\ncapacity, the campus can accommodate the equivalent amount of\ncomputer power generated in a small town. Compliance Policy  Volcker Rule May Extend to Overseas Banks with U.S. Operations  Regulators writing a rule limiting proprietary trading by\nU.S. banks are considering extending the restrictions to\noverseas firms with operations in the country, according to four\npeople familiar with the proposal.  Officials next month will issue a proposal to carry out\nprovisions of the so-called Volcker Rule, part of the Dodd-Frank\nfinancial-regulation law. The proposal would clarify what types\nof offshore trading are exempt from the Volcker Rule, the people\nsaid.  The Volcker Rule, designed to reduce the types of risky\ninvestments blamed for triggering the financial crisis, has\nprompted U.S. banks such as  Goldman Sachs Group Inc. (GS)  to close\nproprietary-trading operations. Overseas banks say that a strict\ninterpretation of the rule may also force them to fire or\nrelocate U.S. employees who are involved in proprietary trading,\neven if no American money is at risk.  \u201cThere is no question that we would lose jobs,\u201d said\n Wayne Abernathy , vice president of the American Bankers\nAssociation in Washington. \u201cA lot of what the banks have been\ndoing in recent years to diversify their services are activities\nthat can easily be done by foreign competitors.\u201d  The rule, named for the former  Federal Reserve  Chairman\nPaul Volcker, includes exemptions for government-guaranteed\ninvestments, hedging, market-making and insurance-company\ntransactions. It also exempts proprietary trading conducted\n\u201csolely\u201d outside of the U.S.  The language of the bill is subject to interpretation by\nregulators at agencies including the Federal Reserve and the\nFederal Deposit Insurance Corp. Dodd-Frank, signed into law by\nPresident Barack Obama last year, requires regulators to adopt\nrules to carry out the provision by Oct. 18.  Regulators are considering how to define operations\nconducted \u201csolely\u201d outside of the country. Trading managed in\nthe U.S. or involving U.S.-based advisers may be subject to the\nrule even if it takes place overseas and has no U.S. investors,\nthe people said.  The proposal may still change, the people said. Five\nregulators, including the Fed, the Office of the Comptroller of\nthe Currency and the Securities and Exchange Commission and the\nCommodities Futures Trading Commission, must approve the\nproposal separately. The Treasury Department is responsible for\ncoordinating the regulation. The proposed rule will be released\nfor public comment and can be changed before it becomes final.  Colleen Murray, a spokeswoman for Treasury, and  Barbara\nHagenbaugh , a spokeswoman for the Fed, declined to comment.\nAndrew Gray, a spokesman for the FDIC, also declined to comment. Apple Inc. (AAPL) ,  Google Inc. (GOOG)  and  Microsoft Corp. (MSFT)  led the charge, saying they don\u2019t give the government access to servers where the data is kept. Some said yesterday they don\u2019t hand over user information without a court order. Others said that they hadn\u2019t even heard of the U.S. program, code-named PRISM.  Even without companies\u2019 consent, academics and computer-security specialists say, there\u2019s a broad range of ways the government can harness the systems of the largest technology providers to snoop on e-mail, photos and video chats coursing through the Web.  \u201cIt\u2019s likely that the denials from these companies are literally true, but they don\u2019t tell the whole story,\u201d said  Matthew Blaze , associate professor of computer and information science at the  University of Pennsylvania .  The administration of President  Barack Obama  confirmed the existence of classified programs to collect data on U.S. residents\u2019 telephone calls and foreign nationals\u2019 Internet activity on June 6, a day after the U.K.\u2019s Guardian newspaper reported on a secret court order compelling  Verizon Communications Inc. (VZ)  to provide the National Security Agency with data on customers\u2019 phone use. The Washington Post article was also published on June 6.  Obama has defended the practice, saying the government\u2019s efforts are \u201cmodest encroachments\u201d on privacy legally authorized by Congress and important to thwarting terrorist attacks.  \u2018Direct Access\u2019  AOL Inc., Apple and Paltalk.com all released statements saying they\u2019ve never heard of the PRISM program and don\u2019t give the government direct access to servers without a court order.  \u201cWe have not joined any program that would give the U.S. government -- or any other government -- direct access to our servers,\u201d  Mountain View , California-based Google said in a blog  posting . \u201cIndeed, the U.S. government does not have direct access or a \u2018back door\u2019 to the information stored in our data centers.\u201d  Facebook Inc (FB) ., Yahoo! Inc. and Microsoft said they only hand over data to the government when required by law to do so.  \u201cWhen companies like Yahoo or Apple say they do not provide \u2018direct access,\u2019 it is hard to know what they mean by \u2018direct,\u2019\u201d said David Wagner, a computer-science  professor  at the  University of California , Berkeley. \u201cMaybe they just mean that they believe there are protocols to limit access, but who knows how effective or stringent those protocols are, or who administers those protocols -- is the NSA overseeing themselves?\u201d  Big Database  Even without companies knowingly participating, there are a number of ways the government could gather data.  Some scenarios are straightforward, including the NSA assembling a massive database that cross-references public information on social media accounts with government records from tax filings and driver\u2019s licenses, according to  Avi Rubin , professor of computer science at  Johns Hopkins University .  \u201cA lot of the pages on Facebook and LinkedIn and Google Plus are open and public,\u201d he explained. \u201cA likely theory is that the NSA is just comparing that data to other open data like people\u2019s driver\u2019s licenses -- that would actually be a difficult undertaking requiring a lot of computing power, which the NSA would be completely capable of doing.\u201d  The NSA could also use readily available computer software and hardware to intercept electronic communications without the knowledge of Internet companies, Carl Herberger, a vice president for the network-security company  Radware Ltd. (RDWR) , said in an interview.  Without Notification  The technology can be installed at communication centers operated by Internet-service providers, said Herberger, whose company is based in  Tel Aviv ,  Israel , and has offices in  New Jersey .  The technology, which Radware sells, can intercept communications or make copies of communications, as well as break encrypted messages, Herberger said.  \u201cThere\u2019s no need to necessarily notify any of these Internet companies,\u201d Herberger said. \u201cToday, almost everything that\u2019s being done on the Internet has the capacity to be archived and reviewed.\u201d  Herberger said he had no direct knowledge of the PRISM program and that his company doesn\u2019t sell the intercept technology to the U.S. government.  Mining data associated with people\u2019s communications is hardly new for the government, said  Michael Reiter , a professor of computer science at the University of  North Carolina  at  Chapel Hill . The Patriot Act, which was passed in response to the terrorist acts of Sept. 11, 2001, authorized secret U.S. surveillance of phone calls and e-mails.  Courts, Hacks  Still, a government hack of corporate servers to obtain that type of information is unlikely, Reiter said.  \u201cIt\u2019s certainly more difficult to do that and far riskier to do that than it is to just go get the court order,\u201d he said. \u201cIt doesn\u2019t make sense to me that the government would try to do it.\u201d  Direct NSA access to the servers of Google, Facebook or other companies would likely require a secured space in their data centers known as a SCIF, for Sensitive Compartmented Information Facility. When AT&T Inc. provided the NSA access to customer phone calls as part of a secret  Bush administration  phone-tapping program, technicians reported seeing a secure room being constructed to protect the NSA\u2019s equipment, according to court documents.  At Facebook, owner of the largest social-networking service, no such SCIF exists, according to a person familiar with the company\u2019s data centers who asked not to be identified because the person wasn\u2019t authorized to speak on the matter.  Hardware, Cables  Another point of entry for the government might be working with Internet-service providers that manage hardware and cables over which data flows, according to  Aaron Massey , associate director of ThePrivacyPlace.org.  The NSA or another government agency could tap into the raw data feed running through these networks, with the cooperation of telecommunications providers.  In this way, it\u2019s \u201cpossible for the companies not to be involved at all,\u201d he explained. At the same time, this method makes it dramatically harder since the government \u201cwould have to decipher their data format,\u201d he said. While BlackBerry steadily lost market share over the past three years to  Apple Inc (AAPL) . and Samsung Electronics Co., it now has an opportunity to win back some consumers in the lull before the next iPhone arrives and after Samsung\u2019s Galaxy S4 got mixed reviews.  \u201cThe new BlackBerry handsets are holding up reasonably well against a number of recently released handsets,\u201d said  Andy Perkins , an analyst at Societe Generale SA in  London . The shares have  climbed  16 percent this year and have more than doubled since reaching a nine-year low in September. An international BlackBerry service disruption that month, which coincided for a second time with the introduction of a new iPhone, was the culmination of years of marketing fumbles, product delays and other missteps by the company.  Since taking over in January 2012, Chief Executive Officer Thorsten Heins has named new sales, marketing and legal chiefs and squeezed out $1 billion in operating costs by cutting six of 10 manufacturing sites, eliminating 5,000 jobs and selling one of two corporate jets.  BlackBerry surprised analysts in March by reporting a return to profitability for its fiscal fourth quarter, earlier than expected. The company probably had a profit of 9 cents a share excluding one-time charges and gains in the first quarter, which ended in May, reversing a loss of 37 cents a year earlier, according to analysts\u2019 estimates. BlackBerry has no comment on its performance last quarter, said Rebecca Freiburger, a company spokeswoman. The sun, on many days, hangs behind a haze of pollution,\nits light filtered down to a soupy dusk. The Internet is stuck\nbehind a government firewall, its main offerings obstructed to\nthose living in China.  That neither the sun nor the Web is fully gone, merely\ncrippled, makes dealing with their abbreviated selves especially\nannoying. You know their full versions are out there somewhere\nbecause they tease you most days. The sun\u2019s orange halo might\nappear briefly at dawn, only to be engulfed by the smog. Gmail\u2019s\nhomepage might begin to load tentatively, only to stumble and\nfreeze.  In many parts of the world (with some notable exceptions),\nwe have come to count breathable air and unfettered  Internet\naccess  among basic human conveniences, alongside indoor plumbing\nand access to education. That\u2019s why it is so jarring and\ndisorienting to suddenly lose them in Beijing to man-made forces\nof breakneck industrialization and censorship. No amount of\nreading or hearing about Beijing\u2019s air pollution and the Great\nFirewall, as the system of Internet censorship is inevitably\nknown, is enough to prepare you to deal with them.  For the moment, I\u2019ll leave the sun where I hope it still\nis, wrapped away in a blanket of smog so thick I can barely see\nthe high-rises less than a mile away. It smells faintly as if\nsomeone is burning tires.  Registration Required  The Great Firewall is a more complex and nuanced\nphenomenon, and it appears to be getting more capable in\ntripping up undesirable  Web connections .  Like many foreigners in  China , I signed up for a virtual\nprivate network, or VPN, geek-speak for a link to an overseas\nserver, which allows you to leapfrog the Chinese Internet and\nplug straight into the real thing, as if you were sitting in  New\nYork  or  London . Twitter, the New York Times and Gmail loaded\nseamlessly on my iPad, ending a tense couple of days of\nwithdrawal symptoms. And then it all crashed.  My VPN provider, a major player in the market, explained in\nan e-mail that the disruption was due to a recent update of the\nGreat Firewall, referred to as the GFW, which \u201cnow has the\nability to learn, discover and block VPN protocols\nautomatically.\u201d  The next day, the Global Times, a Chinese newspaper, ran an\narticle  headlined , \u201cForeign-run VPNs illegal in China: govt.\u201d\nIn it, the man known as the founding father of the Great\nFirewall was quoted as saying that foreign VPN providers needed\nto register with the government. \u201cI haven\u2019t heard that any\nforeign companies have registered,\u201d Fang Binxing, who is now\npresident of Beijing University of Posts and Telecommunications,\n told  the newspaper.  Fang gained notoriety in 2011 when a student threw a shoe\nat him while he was delivering a lecture on cybersecurity. The\nshoe connected with the target. The student fled the scene and\nwent into hiding, becoming an instant celebrity among the\ncountry\u2019s many opponents of Internet curbs. Sometime later,\nhackers broke into the homepage of Binxing\u2019s university and\ndefaced it with an image from something called Angry Shoes, a\nspoof on the wildly popular \u201cAngry Birds\u201d game. The birds at\nthe slingshot are replaced with shoes, and the pigs in the\nwooden house are  replaced  with Binxing\u2019s face.  The most recent VPN disruption seemed intended to target\nmobile devices, which are fast becoming an important way to\naccess the Internet. As my VPN provider promised to find a way\nto outwit the Great Firewall, several articles in state-run\nmedia reminded readers of the dangers lurking on the Web.  China\u2019s Rationale  On Dec. 18, for instance, a commentary piece on Xinhua,\nChina\u2019s official news agency,  called  for new laws to govern the\nInternet: \u201cIf there is no strict legal punishments on the\nviolators in cyber space, the negative factors will run wild to\ndestroy the Internet order and even incite online violence,\nwhich will bring great damage to people and society.\u201d This is\nthe Chinese government\u2019s original rationale for erecting the\nGreat Firewall, an elaborate network of blocks, network\nslowdowns and censorship rules that keep many of China\u2019s half-\nbillion Internet users in the dark about events in the world and\nin their own country.  The unease about the broader issue of curbs on free speech\nwas stoked anew recently when Mo Yan, the Chinese writer who won\nthis year\u2019s  Nobel Prize  for literature, seemed to liken\ncensorship to airport-security checks: an indispensable\nnuisance.  China\u2019s Internet is a strange place. Twitter and Facebook\nare blocked, their ability to disseminate unwelcome news and\nserve as organizing platforms for all sorts of protests deemed\ntoo grave a threat. Some of Google Inc.\u2019s services, including\nGmail, are intentionally slowed down to a snail\u2019s pace, which is\narguably even worse than being blocked outright because it gives\ncustomers an impression of poor service.  At the same time, Chinese clones of these American\ncompanies operate freely and load lightning-fast, their searches\ncarefully scrubbed for sensitive terms by in-house censors.\nWestern Internet companies that choose to enter the booming\nChinese market have to play by the government\u2019s rules.  The most striking example is Skype Inc., owned by  Microsoft\nCorp. (MSFT)  As detailed by Greatfire.org, a website tracking all\nthings related to the Great Firewall (and, of course, blocked by\nit), when you download Skype software in China, you are actually\ngetting a product tweaked in a crucial way. Chinese Skype, a\njoint venture majority-owned by a local company,  allows  the\ngovernment to monitor your chats.  Among the many curious things about the Chinese Internet,\none apparent contradiction stands out. Xinhua, the mouthpiece of\nthe government that insists on blocking Twitter, recently opened \na Twitter account, sending out more than 3,000 tweets, and \nattracting 8,000 followers -- following no one itself. Xinhua\u2019s \nappearance on Twitter, and the one-way nature of its boosterish \naccount, invited an avalanche of  ridicule  in the Chinese \nblogosphere.  Blocked Sites  Western news outlets that touch taboo subjects are blocked,\ntoo.  Bloomberg.com  and nytimes.com are both blocked because of\ntheir recent investigative reports on the financial dealings of\ntop Chinese leaders.  How effective is the Great Firewall, given the many ways of\nleaping over it? China\u2019s Internet sleuths aren\u2019t overly\nconcerned with how foreign companies and individuals access the\nWeb, or what they read there. They are concerned about Chinese\npublic opinion, and about ways to influence it by regulating\nwhat the Chinese people are and aren\u2019t allowed to see on the\nInternet.  By that second measure, the firewall achieves its\nobjectives just fine, despite the availability of VPNs and other\ntechnical tricks, many of them free.  Of China\u2019s 500 million Web users, only about 1 percent\n\u201cuse these tools to get around censorship, either because most\ndo not know how or because they lack sufficient interest in --\nor awareness of -- what exists on the other side of the \u2018great\nfirewall,\u2019\u201d Rebecca MacKinnon writes in \u201cConsent of the\nNetworked,\u201d a book on Internet freedom around the world.  Meanwhile, the wizards at my VPN provider finally found a\nway around the firewall\u2019s latest crackdown on smartphones and\ntablets. My iPad is useful again, until the firewall catches on\nand a new round of cat-and-mouse begins.  Sadly, there\u2019s no good news to report on breaching the wall\nof smog blocking the sun. No one has yet invented a virtual\nprivate network to transport one through the Beijing pollution. Apple's shares have gained more than 5 percent since then. It isn't the first time the legendary investor has made money by publicly haranguing corporate executives for failing to do their jobs. In the old days, he and others like him would send critical epistles to directors and executives that would eventually find their way into the press. Today it's faster and easier to peck a short message on a smartphone and within minutes set financial markets abuzz. While it's amusing to imagine an elderly billionaire having fun with a technology associated with the young, there are real lessons here about the uses and abuses of corporate cash. In 1986, Harvard University's Michael Jensen  argued  that public companies tend to waste money on empire-building acquisitions because it increases managerial pay and prestige at the expense of shareholders. Jensen recommended that activist investors force companies to improve returns by using excess cash to pay dividends and buy back stock. Recent research  supports this conclusion: Activists such as Icahn tend to make companies better.  According to Icahn , the best way to get promoted up the corporate hierarchy is to be likable but unexceptional -- the fraternity president who was always up for grabbing a beer but never seemed to find time to study. That suggests how he views Apple Chief Executive Tim Cook. (Another example is Dan Loeb, who is in the midst of trying to restore  Sony's former glory  after having helped out  Yahoo .) Although Apple has been mismanaged differently than the typical 1970s U.S. corporation, Jensen's argument still applies. Along with other tech giants, such as Google, Oracle and Microsoft, Apple has tens of billions of dollars in idle cash and short-term investments. Moreover, all of these highly profitable companies keep adding to their hoards, apparently because they have nothing better to do with the money. If there really is such a dearth of worthwhile investment opportunities, shareholders would be better off having the cash in hand to use as they see fit. People don't own shares in tech companies to sit on their savings when they can easily put their money into mutual funds that only buy T-bills. I am not in much of a position to judge whether shareholders will benefit more from Icahn's plan to hand the cash over to shareholders or whether they would be better off listening to Slate's Matt Yglesias, who  recommends  that Apple relocate from Cupertino, California, to Nebraska, among other things. I can say, however, that Icahn is supported by the finance academics. Tim Cook might not like having to deal with Icahn, but those who own a stake in Apple -- this includes everyone with exposure to the most common stock indexes -- should be glad that this fabled investor is getting involved. And if Cook has any bright ideas, maybe he's learned from Icahn how to let everyone know what they are. (Matthew C. Klein is a writer for the Ticker. The\nroadbeds rest on huge pontoons and sway a bit as you drive\nacross them on a windy day.  One is the last gasp of  Interstate 90  as it finishes its\njourney from  Boston  to the Puget Sound. The other is State Route\n520 or \u201c the 520 ,\u201d as it\u2019s known.  Which bridge to take from where, at what time, using which\nentrances and exits, has long been a major preoccupation of\nSeattleites and a frequent icebreaker with strangers. Technologically, the system is a marvel. There are no toll\nbooths. Indeed, there is no sign at all that this is a toll road\nexcept for actual signs that say so. The toll is collected in\nmyriad ways. You can sign up for an account and get a little\ncoded sticker for your windshield. Or you can wait until they\nbill you, using your license plate to track you down.\nApparently, it works. Unless your commute is between 11 p.m. and\n5 a.m., in which case it\u2019s free, you can\u2019t escape.  Except, of course, by taking I-90. That -- no surprise --\nis what has happened. Now the I-90 bridge is  more jammed  than\never, but if you have $7 to $10 a day to pay for the privilege,\nyou can sail on the 520 at any time.  Economists love this kind of thing. The money raised will\nbe used to rebuild the bridge. Thus this cost will be paid by\nthose who actually use the bridge, in direct proportion to how\nmuch they use it, rather than sticking it to the general\ntaxpayer. The market will sort out those who value their time at\nmore than $10 per commute from those who do not and give both\ndrivers what they prefer.  And of course, it\u2019s good for the environment: Some people\nwill reject both the toll and the increased congestion on the\nfree bridge, and use public transit or work from home.  Governments around the world are trying variations on this\napproach. In  London , there\u2019s  a daily fee  for every car driven\ninto the center of town. In Barcelona, there\u2019s  a tunnel  that\nspeeds you past the worst congestion, if you\u2019re willing to pay.\nIt\u2019s not a terrible idea. Unlike taxes, these fees are tied to a\nparticular benefit, which makes them easier to swallow. So does\nthe fact that they are voluntary.  In Seattle, since the toll was imposed, traffic on the toll\nbridge has dropped about 40 percent, while traffic on the free\nbridge has risen 10 percent. Overall traffic from the east side\nto and from the city has dropped about 6 percent.  Does this constitute success? That depends on your\ndefinition of success. As with the cigarette tax, the more\neffective a fee is in changing undesired behavior, the less\nmoney it brings in. Toll revenue from the 520 bridge is supposed\nto raise about $1 billion of the $4 billion-plus cost of the new\nbridge.  But the big problem with the new toll is that it is another\nsmall chipping way of our shared life as citizens, and another\narea where money makes the difference. It used to be that no\nmatter how rich you were, there were some things you could not\nbuy your way out of. Rush-hour congestion was one of them. The\nlaw, in its majesty, allowed rich and poor alike to get stuck in\ntraffic. I once heard  Steve Ballmer , chief executive of\nMicrosoft and worth many billions of dollars, talking about his\nstrategy for outfoxing the dread 520. (I tried it. It didn\u2019t\nwork.)  As  explained  by philosopher Michael Walzer, and somewhat\n more entertainingly  by my friend Mickey Kaus, there are two ways\nto deal with wealth and income inequality (if it  bothers you ,\nthat is). One is to reduce it, through the tax system. The other\nis to make money less important. Create national parks, open to\neverybody. Restore universal military service. And so on.  By this way of thinking, the two bridges side-by-side, one\ncostly to use and one free, constitute a small step backward,\ntoward making money more important. You might say: Wait a\nminute. What if there already was a toll on both bridges, and it\nwas lifted on one so that people willing to put up with crowds\ncould go across free? That wouldn\u2019t seem iniquitous, would it?\nBut it\u2019s the same thing, really.  And I would say, Great point! Let\u2019s continue this\ndiscussion over a drink downtown. And you would look at your\nwatch and say, It\u2019s too late. We\u2019ll never make it across the\nbridge before dinnertime.  ( Michael Kinsley  is a Bloomberg View columnist. The verdict, even for a patent jury award, was short-lived. The trial judge threw out the jury\u2019s decision the next month, finding Edison, New Jersey-based Mformation didn\u2019t provide enough evidence to support its claim against  RIM. (RIM)   Patent awards kept rising in 2012, with seven topping $100 million, including three of $1 billion or more. Those verdicts remain the most volatile, with courts reversing almost half of the 25 largest patent awards in U.S. history, according to data compiled by Bloomberg.  Verdicts have risen because \u201cthe value of technology has gone up as a driver of the economy,\u201d said  Amar L. Thakur , a lawyer with Quinn Emanuel Urquhart & Sullivan LLP in  Los Angeles  who represented Mformation in the RIM case, which is now on appeal. \u201cPeople have paid more attention to monetizing intellectual property and looking at it as an asset.\u201d  The three largest U.S. jury verdicts of 2012 and 11 of the top 50 were in patent-infringement cases, both for the first time, according to the Bloomberg data. The verdicts included three billion-dollar patent awards. There were a total of three patents verdicts of that size in all previous years combined.  Verdicts Targeted  Two of the 10 largest patent verdicts of 2012 have already been reversed, and almost all the rest are either targets of post-trial motions to set them aside or are already on appeal.  Patent litigation is a \u201ccauldron of reversals\u201d by trial judges and appeals courts because intellectual-property law is \u201cbeing developed right before our very eyes,\u201d said Douglas A. Cawley, an attorney who won a $368 million verdict in November for  VirnetX Inc. (VHC)  in an infringement claim against  Apple Inc. (AAPL)  over virtual-private-network technology.  Verdicts against corporations in other kinds of cases, such as antitrust or contracts, are less volatile because \u201cthese areas of the law are pretty well-formed,\u201d Cawley, of McKool Smith PC in  Dallas , said in a phone interview.  The U.S. Supreme Court and the  U.S. Court of Appeals  for the  Federal Circuit  in Washington, which hears all patent appeals, continue to decide pivotal cases, \u201csometimes several a year, that affect intellectual property,\u201d he said.  Biggest Award  The largest award last year, for $1.17 billion, was made in December by a jury in Pittsburgh federal court to  Carnegie Mellon University , which sued claiming  Marvell Technology Group Ltd. (MRVL)  infringed integrated-circuit patents. Marvell denied infringing and said it will ask that the verdict be set aside.  Apple won the second-largest in August when a jury in  San Jose ,  California , federal court awarded $1.05 billion for alleged infringement of smartphone technology patents by  Samsung Electronics Co. (005930)  Samsung denied infringement and said it would appeal.  Monsanto Co. (MON)  won a $1 billion verdict in August from a jury in St. Louis federal court in a suit against  DuPont Co. (DD)  over a patent for genetically modified soybeans. DuPont motions to set aside or reduce the verdict are pending.  For all types of lawsuits in 2012, the number of jury awards of $100 million or more jumped to 31 from 19, or 63 percent, over the previous year.  The verdicts included four medical malpractice and two nursing home negligence awards of $100 million or more. Three of the top 10 malpractice awards ever occurred in 2012, as did the largest-ever in a nursing home case -- $900 million against a Florida facility.  Trial Data  Most of the largest verdicts may be reduced or reversed on post-trial motions or through appeals-court decisions, based on the history of such litigation, according to Bloomberg data. Some have already been revised.  The patent cases face the greatest risk of reversal.  In 11 of the 25 largest jury verdicts ever in U.S. patent cases, the amount of damages or the entire judgments were set aside. The reversals included all three pre-2012 billion-dollar patent verdicts. New trials were ordered or judgments for the defendants replaced jury findings.  Four of the remaining 14 cases, all from 2012, haven\u2019t reached post-verdict decisions by trial or appellate courts.  Companies pursuing reversals of big patent awards have succeeded 56 percent of the time, a review of decisions in the biggest 25 such cases found. This compares with reversals in seven, or 28 percent, of the top 25 top awards in nonpatent cases involving corporations.  Federal Courts  Patent cases are decided in federal courts, where judges have been more likely to reverse the largest verdicts than their state-court counterparts, 36 percent versus 28 percent, according to the data.  With patent trials, \u201cif the defense loses, they say it\u2019s only halftime, and there\u2019s truth to that,\u201d said Richard Sayles, a Dallas lawyer who won a $1.67 billion verdict in  Johnson & Johnson (JNJ) \u2019s suit against  Abbott Laboratories (ABT)  in 2009 that was later erased. The Federal Circuit threw out the award to J&J, the largest ever in a patent case. The U.S. Supreme Court let stand its decision last year.  The Federal Circuit has reversed about half of the cases before it, largely because of reviews of so-called claims construction, Sayles said. The appeals court in those cases found the trial judges were wrong in how they defined key terms.  Trial judges hold pretrial hearings to determine exactly what the language of a patent covers. Then the Federal Circuit reviews the claims construction independently.  \u2018No Weight\u2019  \u201cThe district court opinion carries no weight,\u201d Sayles said. \u201cIt\u2019s a peculiar aspect of  patent law .\u201d  In some cases, damages were set aside as improperly calculated and new trials ordered. The Federal Circuit has issued rulings limiting the amount that can be collected when the infringing element is a small feature or component of a product.  The reversal rate is also connected to the willingness to fight over large markets, said William Lee of Wilmer Cutler Pickering Hale & Dorr LLP in  Boston , who was on Apple\u2019s team that won last year\u2019s $1 billion verdict against Samsung.  \u201cPatent litigation is being used to sort out a competitive marketplace,\u201d Lee said in an interview.  This is particularly true in areas where technologies converge, such as smartphones and computers, he said.  High Stakes  \u201cThese cases have high revenues, high damages,\u201d Lee said, and cases may be less likely to be resolved before appeals are completed. \u201cPlaintiffs and defendants are more willing to go to final determination to establish the rules of the game.\u201d  Judgments are rising because courts have changed how they deal with requests for injunctions and because more money is at issue than previously, said  Michael A. Carrier , a professor at Rutgers School of Law in  Newark ,  New Jersey .  \u201cThere are more patent lawsuits in areas of technology where there is a lot at stake,\u201d Carrier said in a phone interview. \u201cPatents are more frequently being enforced.\u201d  A  Supreme Court  decision in 2006 in a case involving  EBay Inc. (EBAY)  allowed judges greater discretion to reject requests to stop the use of infringing products. Defendants claimed patent owners were able to extract high settlement dollars because of the threat they could be shut down if they lost at trial.  With fewer such orders granted, more defendants are willing to fight at a trial, while more patent owners are looking to juries to give them high damage awards.  EBay Decision  \u201cThe Supreme Court\u2019s EBay decision has made it more difficult to get injunctions,\u201d said Cawley, of McKool Smith. \u201cIf you can\u2019t get that relief, you need to get damages.\u201d  Following the billion-dollar verdict in the Apple-Samsung smartphone patent dispute, U.S. District Judge Lucy H. Koh last month cited the EBay decision in rejecting Apple\u2019s bid for a permanent sales ban on 26 Samsung devices.  \u201cThough injunctions were once issued in patent cases as a matter of course,\u201d the U.S. Supreme Court changed the rules, requiring patent-holders to show an irreparable injury, that other remedies such as monetary damages weren\u2019t sufficient, and \u201cthat the public interest would not be disserved by a permanent injunction,\u201d she wrote.  Apple didn\u2019t meet these requirements, she ruled.  Patent verdict reversals may not mean a final victory for the defendant. Of the five patent verdicts of $500 million or more that were tossed out, in three cases the defendants that won the reversals nevertheless chose to settle.  Fleeting Victories  When a reversal involves setting aside damages or only part of a judgment, requiring a new trial, the patent-holder may still prevail and obtain an even bigger verdict the second time around.  SAP AG (SAP)  won a new trial in a patent case that first resulted in a $138.6 million verdict against it. The retrial in 2011 resulted in another loss to Versata Software Inc., this time with a $345 million award. The second judgment is now on appeal.  \u201cReversals are often by the Federal Circuit because of a mistake by a district judge and the trial has to be redone,\u201d Cawley said.  Settlements before retrials are common because the appellate decision has provided a road map of what might happen in a new trial, he said. \u201cOften the parties can see the handwriting on the wall,\u201d he said.  In most kinds of cases, the jury\u2019s award is the high-water mark. A settlement or final judgment is typically less -- often far less -- than the jury\u2019s assessment.  Patent Exception  Patent-infringement cases are an exception.  The judgments can grow with the addition of interest, enhanced damages for findings of willful infringement, or for continuing infringement after the trial.  Cawley in 2010 won a $105.8 million jury verdict against  Microsoft Corp. (MSFT) , again for VirnetX and over VPN technology. The case was settled before appeal for $200 million, he said.  Patent trials almost always are over the cost of the infringement up to the date of trial, Cawley said.  \u201cThe settlements may be greater than the verdict because the future may be greater than the past,\u201d he said. Talks Break Down","released_at":"<date>September 25 2013<\/date> <time>21:05:07<\/time>","content":"Alibaba Group Holding Ltd. is moving toward an initial public offering in the U.S. after talks for a Hong Kong listing broke down following management\u2019s proposal to keep control in a share sale, according to two people familiar with the matter.  China \u2019s largest e-commerce company is seeking U.S. law firms to help with an IPO and hasn\u2019t hired banks yet, said one of the people, who asked not to be identified because the process is private. Alibaba, which investment banks value at as much as $120 billion, is likely to choose to list its shares on the  New York  Stock Exchange, another person said.  Alibaba founder Jack Ma and partners want to control the Hangzhou-based company after the listing by effectively creating two groups of shareholders, with one group able to nominate a majority of board members. To protect the interests of ordinary shareholders, Hong Kong\u2019s exchange prohibits IPOs with different classes of shares, a structure that has been used by companies from  Facebook Inc. (FB)  to  Manchester United Plc (MANU)  in their U.S. initial offerings.  \u201cJack Ma really insisted on the partnership structure,\u201d said Billy Leung, an analyst at RHB Research Institute Sdn. in Hong Kong. \u201cIf you give it to them then you give it to everyone. Alibaba has been waiting for so long, they just said let\u2019s go to the U.S.\u201d  \u2018Emotional Arguments\u2019  Losing the Alibaba IPO would be a blow to Hong Kong, which hasn\u2019t hosted a first-time share sale of more than $4 billion since October 2010. The exchange is the fourth biggest equity market in the world, with companies trading there worth a combined $3.4 trillion in market value, according to data compiled by Bloomberg.  \u201cWe need to look objectively at the issues and not be swayed by emotional arguments or be distracted by specific circumstances of any given company or issue,\u201d Charles Li, CEO of Hong Kong Exchanges & Clearing Ltd., said in a  blog post  today. He didn\u2019t name Alibaba.  While the Nasdaq Stock Market dominated technology listings in the past, winning everything from Intel Corp. to Facebook, the New York Stock Exchange, or NYSE, has established itself as a challenger in the most recent wave of offerings. Since mid-2011, LinkedIn Corp., Pandora Media Inc. and Yelp Inc. have listed there, and Twitter Inc. is also leaning toward the NYSE, a person with knowledge of the matter said this week.  Alibaba declined to comment in an e-mail today. Lorraine Chan, a spokeswoman for Hong Kong Exchanges, declined to comment, citing a company policy against discussing individual cases.  NYSE Euronext (NYX)  spokesman Rich Adamonis also declined to comment on Alibaba\u2019s IPO plans as did William Briganti at Nasdaq OMX Group Inc.  Partnership Control  Alibaba may appoint underwriters by the end of this year, one of the people familiar said. While a final decision hasn\u2019t been made, the company may use a partnership structure similar to what it proposed in Hong Kong, the person said.  For weeks, Alibaba and the Hong Kong exchange discussed the proposal to let partners control most board nominations. That would let Ma, a former English teacher who owns 7.4 percent of the stock, and his managers run the company without worrying about being pushed out by an activist investor with a different strategy, a person familiar with the matter said last month.  The company had 28 partners as of Sept. 10, Ma said in an e-mail to employees this month. They include co-founder Joseph Tsai and Chief Executive Officer Jonathan Lu.  Investor Rights  Under Alibaba\u2019s partnership proposal, all shareholders would still vote on the proposed directors with partners being able to nominate an alternate if shareholders reject a candidate, the person familiar with Alibaba\u2019s thinking said.  No other investor rights would be changed, the person said. Deals involving company executives, major expenses and compensation would be voted on by all shareholders, according to the person.  \u201cThis is not a mere profit sharing mechanism, nor is it a vehicle of power to exert greater control over the company,\u201d Ma said in the Sept. 10 e-mail.  Hong Kong\u2019s bourse doesn\u2019t allow share classes with different voting rights, as exchanges in the U.S. do. Under Hong Kong\u2019s listing rules, new applicants must not include shares whose voting power doesn\u2019t bear a \u201creasonable relationship\u201d to the equity interest.  Manchester United  The dual-class structure helped Facebook\u2019s  Mark Zuckerberg  and Google Inc. co-founders  Larry Page  and  Sergey Brin  keep control of their companies after they went public. Manchester United, the English soccer club, also considered a share sale in Hong Kong before eventually settling on the U.S., where Class B shares owned by the Glazer family carry 10 votes apiece versus one vote each for the Class A shares sold in the IPO.  \u201cThey can go to the U.S. and accept the U.S. environment with more stringent reporting requirements and a class action litigation system and benefit from the dual-class voting structure,\u201d said David Webb, founder of local governance watchdog Webb-site.com and a former director of the exchange.  Ma started Alibaba in his Hangzhou apartment in 1999 with two dozen items for sale, and the company\u2019s expansion mirrors China\u2019s emergence as an  economic superpower . The company now has 24,000 employees and generates about 70 percent of package deliveries in China. Customers bought at least 1 trillion  yuan  ($163 billion) of goods via Alibaba last year.  That success has made Ma, 49, one of China\u2019s richest people with an estimated net worth of $3.7 billion, according to the Bloomberg Billionaires Index.  There is still room for growth. China has 591 million Internet users, greater than the population of any other country except  India , and McKinsey & Co. estimates China\u2019s Internet retail market will triple to $395 billion from 2011 to 2015.  Alibaba\u2019s Valuation  In a July 17 report, Evercore Group LLC estimated an Alibaba IPO could value the company at $120 billion, based on a forecast that operating profit could reach $7.1 billion in 2014. Goldman Sachs Group Inc. on July 22 put Alibaba\u2019s value at about $105 billion.  At $120 billion, Alibaba would be the third-biggest Internet company behind  Google (GOOG)  and  Amazon.com Inc. (AMZN)  based on market capitalization.  Alibaba could raise about HK$100 billion ($12.9 billion) in an initial sale, Ernst & Young LLP said June 28. That would make it the world\u2019s biggest IPO since Facebook raised $16 billion in May of last year, and Hong Kong\u2019s largest since  AIA Group Ltd. (1299) \u2019s $20 billion sale in October 2010, according to data compiled by Bloomberg.  The IPO of Facebook valued the company at $104 billion, and the shares lost as much as half their value in the first few months of trading before starting to recover.  Yahoo, SoftBank  Alibaba is considering a more conservative valuation than Facebook for its IPO, a person with knowledge of the matter said earlier this year.  Alibaba\u2019s profit in the latest quarter tripled from a year earlier to $669 million, Yahoo! Inc. said in July. Facebook earned $217 million in the same period and Tencent posted net income of 4.04 billion yuan.  Japan \u2019s  SoftBank Corp. (9984)  owns about 37 percent of Alibaba and Yahoo about 24 percent, the companies said separately in July. Hiroe Kotera, a Tokyo-based spokeswoman for SoftBank, declined to comment today about Alibaba\u2019s IPO plan.  After starting as a business-to-business marketplace on  Alibaba.com , where companies trade anything from shoelaces to steel, the company has morphed into a more consumer-focused operation. Its most popular platforms include Taobao Marketplace, which links individual buyers and sellers, and Tmall.com, which connects consumers to companies such as Microsoft Corp., Procter & Gamble Co. and Japanese clothing chain Uniqlo. Shares of three of the Web\u2019s top newly minted stocks --\nlocal-reviews site  Yelp Inc. (YELP) , online real-estate site  Trulia\nInc. (TRLA)  and social-networking giant  Facebook Inc. (ZNGA)  and Facebook, in particular, fomented an investor frenzy\nupon their IPOs -- only to suffer the consequences when skeptics\nquestioned how their newfangled businesses could sustain growth\nthrough virtual goods and daily deals, and without a way to make\nmoney from mobile. Groupon grappled with management\nsnafus and a slowdown in daily-deals sales, and Zynga plunged\nmore than 75 percent as consumers shifted away from some of its\ngames.  Now several months on, some of the companies are benefiting\nfrom pushes into mobile and local advertising. Tucker Bounds, a spokesman for  Menlo Park ,  California-based\nFacebook , declined to comment. Groupon, which started out promoting discounts via e-mail\nalerts, is bringing on new customers as more smartphone users\nturn to its mobile app, according to  Ross Sandler , an analyst at\nDeutsche Bank.  \u201cGroupon is surprisingly the most mobile penetrated e-commerce company we track,\u201d Sandler wrote in a research report\nin June. They were\nemployees of  American Superconductor Corp. , a maker of computer\nsystems that serve as the electronic brains of the device. From\ntime to time, AMSC workers are required to head out to a wind\nfarm in some desolate location -- that\u2019s where the wind usually\nis -- to check on the equipment, do maintenance, make repairs,\nand keep the customers happy.  On this occasion, the AMSC technicians were investigating a\nmalfunction. They entered the cylindrical main shaft of the\nturbine, harnessed themselves to a ladder, and climbed 230 feet\nin darkness up to the nacelle, an overpacked compartment that\nholds the machinery used to convert the rotation of the blades\ninto electricity. Devens, Massachusetts-based AMSC had been\nusing the turbine, manufactured by the company\u2019s largest\ncustomer, China\u2019s  Sinovel Wind Group Co. (601558) , to test a new version\nof its control system software.  The software was designed to disable the turbine several\nweeks earlier, at the end of the testing period. But for some\nreason, this turbine ignored the system\u2019s shutdown command and\nthe blades kept right on spinning. The AMSC technicians tapped\ninto the turbine\u2019s computer to get to the bottom of the glitch.  The problem wasn\u2019t immediately clear, so the technicians\nmade a copy of the control system\u2019s software and sent it to the\ncompany\u2019s research center in Klagenfurt, Austria, which produced\nsome startling findings, Bloomberg Businessweek reports in its\nMarch 19 issue. The Sinovel turbine appeared to be running a\nstolen version of AMSC\u2019s software. Worse, the software revealed\nBeijing-based Sinovel had complete access to AMSC\u2019s proprietary\nsource code. In short, Sinovel didn\u2019t really need AMSC anymore.  Bad News  Three days after that expedition in the Gobi, Daniel McGahn,\nAMSC\u2019s chief executive officer, got the news on his mobile phone\nwhile he was traveling in  Russia . Hired in 2006, McGahn helped\nrevamp the then-floundering company by focusing it on two things:\nChina and wind power. Those bets paid off for a while, as\nSinovel bought more and more turbine controllers from AMSC. Then\nin March\u00a02011, Sinovel abruptly and inexplicably began turning\naway AMSC\u2019s shipments at its enormous turbine assembly factory\nin Liaoning province.  On April\u00a05, AMSC had no choice but to announce that Sinovel\n-- now its biggest customer, accounting for more than two-thirds\nof the company\u2019s $315\u00a0million\u00a0in revenue in 2010 -- had stopped\nmaking purchases. Investors fled, erasing 40\u00a0percent of AMSC\u2019s\nvalue in a single day and 84\u00a0percent of it by September. The\ncompany\u2019s stock chart looks like the electrocardiogram of a\nperson rushing toward white light.  Sinovel Relationship  On June\u00a015, standing in a St. Petersburg office tower,\nMcGahn listened to the report from the Austrian team for\n30\u00a0minutes and felt the blood drain from his face. He had been\ntrying for months to save the relationship with Sinovel and was\nmaking almost no progress. By the time he ended the call from\nhis Austrian team, he knew why.  What McGahn says happened to AMSC may be incredibly brazen,\nbut it\u2019s hardly exceptional. There have been a large number of\ncorporate spying cases involving China recently, and they are\ncoming to light as President Barack Obama and the U.S., along\nwith  Japan  and the European Union, have filed a formal complaint\nto the World Trade Organization over China\u2019s unfair trading\npractices. The complaint includes the hoarding of rare earths,\nthe metals required for the manufacture of other green energy\ntechnologies such as batteries for hybrid vehicles.  Far-Reaching Campaign  In November, 14 U.S. intelligence agencies issued a report\ndescribing a far-reaching industrial espionage campaign by\nChinese spy agencies. This campaign has been in the works for\nyears and targets a swath of industries: biotechnology,\ntelecommunications, and nanotechnology, as well as clean energy.\nOne U.S. metallurgical company lost technology to China\u2019s\nhackers that cost $1\u00a0billion and 20\u00a0years to develop, U.S.\nofficials said last year. An  Apple Inc. (AAPL)  global supply manager\npled guilty in 2011 to funneling designs and pricing information\nto China and other countries; a  Ford Motor Co. (F)  engineer was\nsentenced to six years in prison in 2010 for trying to smuggle\n4,000 documents, including design specs, to China. Earlier this\nmonth, the National Aeronautics and Space Administration told\nCongress that China-based hackers had gained access to sensitive\nfiles stored on computers at the Jet Propulsion Laboratory.  As the toll adds up, political leaders and intelligence\nofficials in the U.S. and  Europe  are coming to a disturbing\nconclusion.  \u201cIt\u2019s the greatest transfer of wealth in history,\u201d General\nKeith Alexander, director of the National Security Agency, said\nat a security conference at  New York \u2019s Fordham University in\nJanuary.  Covering Digital Tracks  In other espionage cases, such as those involving  Google\nInc. (GOOG) ,  Lockheed Martin Corp. (LMT)  and DuPont Co., thieves did a far\nbetter job of covering their digital tracks. Sinovel, however,\nwas caught red-handed. AMSC has presented to law enforcement\nofficials in Austria and China computer logs and messages that\nshow Sinovel courting one of the U.S. company\u2019s employees and\npaying him to aid in the code heist.  \u201cIt\u2019s a red-hot smoking gun example,\u201d said John Kerry,\nchairman of the Senate Foreign Relations Committee and the\nDemocratic U.S. senator from AMSC\u2019s home state. \u201cIf this is the\nway the Chinese choose to do business, it\u2019s going to be very\ncontentious and tough sledding ahead for this relationship.\u201d  Intellectual Property Abuses  U.S. politicians and corporate executives have groused\nabout China\u2019s intellectual property abuses for years, to little\neffect. China often promises to take a harder stance against\nsuch thefts but rarely backs up the words with actions. For\nexample, Chinese officials have promised to crack down on the\ntheft of  Microsoft Corp.\u2019s (MSFT)  Windows operating system; the company\nsaid it\u2019s still seeing mass downloads of its software that were\nnever paid for. McGahn, though, has taken a highly unusual step.\nHe decided to fight back -- in China.  AMSC has filed four complaints against Sinovel in Chinese\ncourts -- where Sinovel has a steep home-field advantage --\nseeking $1.2\u00a0billion in damages. Sinovel has filed its own\ncountersuits claiming AMSC owes it $207\u00a0million for problems\nincluding defective equipment. Sinovel declined to make its\nchairman available for an interview or to comment for this story.\nAnd because Chinese courts don\u2019t make legal documents available\nto the public, it wasn\u2019t possible to read Sinovel\u2019s\ncounterclaims.  \u201cHow China responds to this is going to be central to how\nthey respond to other issues of concern between us,\u201d Kerry said.  Superconductive Material  AMSC was founded in 1987 by four professors at the\nMassachusetts Institute of Technology. The idea was to develop\npower transmission lines made from cooled superconductive\nmaterial, which dramatically reduces energy loss. At the time,\nsuperconductivity looked like science\u2019s latest gift to big\nbusiness. But the technology has never quite lived up to those\nearly hopes, and AMSC\u2019s business wallowed in the red for decades.\nIn 2006 the company hired McGahn, a gregarious executive with a\nmaster\u2019s degree in marine engineering from MIT, as a vice\npresident charged with exploring new businesses.  As McGahn surveyed AMSC\u2019s technology, he focused on the\ncompany\u2019s research into wind-turbine control systems. A modern\n1.5-megawatt turbine is the equivalent of a 160-ton, high-\nperformance pinwheel. Each gets stuffed with as much as $200,000\nworth of electronics, including a power converter and what\u2019s\ncalled a programmable logic controller, an industrial computer\nthe size of a couple of cigarette cartons. These devices are\nused to do everything from filling up the bottles in a Budweiser\nbrewery to controlling valves in oil pipelines. In the case of\nturbines, they can rapidly adjust the yaw and pitch of blades,\namong other functions. McGahn sensed an opportunity to take this\ntechnology and capitalize on China\u2019s efforts to harvest energy\nfrom the wind.  Clean Energy Law  The same year AMSC hired McGahn, China passed a clean\nenergy law calling for the creation of seven 10,000-megawatt\nwind farms in strategic zones throughout the country, including\nGansu, Zhejiang, Inner Mongolia, and Jiangsu provinces. The law\nmade China the hottest wind market in the world. In 2009,\naccording to a U.S. wind industry report, a new turbine was\ngoing up in China every hour. By 2020 just one of those wind\nfarms may produce as much power as 10 nuclear power reactors.  AMSC began packaging the electronic components and selling\nthem to China\u2019s small but growing domestic manufacturers, which\nhad plenty of capital and cheap labor to make the turbines\u2019\nsteel skeletons but lacked the sophisticated gadgetry to run\nthem. The arrangement was working the way it was supposed to:\nChina would turn out the commodity hardware -- the turbines --\nand a U.S. company would retain control of the high-margin\nintellectual capital-end of the business.  \u2018Symbiotic Relationship\u2019  \u201cWe always saw it as a symbiotic relationship of having\nChina\u2019s low-manufacturing cost coupled with Western\ntechnology,\u201d McGahn said. \u201cWe would grow as they grew.\u201d  McGahn was well aware of the dangers of working with\nChinese companies, which have become notorious for cutting out\ntheir partners after squeezing them for technology through\ntransfer agreements and other means. Now 40, McGahn built a\ncareer out of taking technology startups and building them into\nrevenue generators, often by finding customers among Asian\nmanufacturers. He used this approach with nanotube plastics for\nauto parts at a Cambridge, Massachusetts-based company called\nHyperion Catalysis International and with photovoltaic film at\nLowell-based Konarka Technologies.  Before arriving at AMSC, he had worked in Japan and  South\nKorea  and said he succeeded by carefully sizing up both partners\nand rivals. McGahn likes to tell people that almost all of\nhistory\u2019s wars started because political leaders misunderstood\ntheir adversaries.  \u201cI spend an inordinate amount of time studying my\ncounterparts,\u201d he said.  Secure Barriers  If McGahn was going to bet AMSC\u2019s future on partnerships\nwith Chinese companies, he wanted secure barriers around its\nintellectual property. He designed AMSC\u2019s China operations -- in\nfact, reorganized much of the company -- with that in mind. To\nhire AMSC\u2019s first 30 employees in China, McGahn interviewed 400\npeople, handpicking the ones he thought he could trust. When\nAMSC opened a factory in China\u2019s Jiangsu province to assemble\npower converters, McGahn made sure firmware and other\ntechnology-rich components were built in factories in the U.S.\nand then shipped to  Asia .  Software was sequestered at the company\u2019s research facility\nin  Austria , which has a booming clean energy sector much like\n Germany \u2019s. The source code to AMSC\u2019s control system software\nsits on a secure server in Klagenfurt. To protect the code from\nhackers, the server isn\u2019t accessible from the Internet.  Strategy From Beginning  \u201cThe idea of dividing up the intellectual property part of\nthe content and not having them in China was part of the\nstrategy from the beginning,\u201d he said.  McGahn thought he\u2019d planned for every contingency to keep\nAMSC safe. He also believed the company could find a way to have\nboth partners benefit. He was wrong on both counts.  Chinese businesses have proven very good at copying Western\ngoods and methods. This even appears to be true of espionage\nitself. China didn\u2019t invent intellectual property theft; it\u2019s\njust doing it on an unprecedented scale.  Willy Shih, a professor at Harvard Business School who has\ntestified before Congress about business dealings between the\nU.S. and China, takes a historical view of intellectual property\ntheft. In the 1870s, American textile companies would send\nemployees to work in British factories. They would take notes on\ntextile equipment and bring back the information. The Russians\nand East Germans stole U.S. computer and chip designs during the\nCold War.  \u201cAnd similar things have been true of Korean companies and\nJapanese companies,\u201d said Shih. \u201cI would argue that it\u2019s a\nnormal development pattern.\u201d  Good Timing  China\u2019s been helped by good timing. It\u2019s emerging as a\nglobal economic power at a time when nearly every secret worth\nstealing sits on a computer server. U.S. intelligence agencies\nfear that Chinese spies have already siphoned terabytes of data\nfrom thousands of Western companies.  Stealing information, however, isn\u2019t the same as being able\nto use it. The Soviets ended up generations behind their U.S.\nrivals in computing technology because they couldn\u2019t advance the\ncloned equipment fast enough. Shih said that for the Chinese to\nsucceed at the current game, they will need to build a research\nand development culture that can supersede their skills at\nmimicry.  \u201cMany countries go through an imitation phase, but the\nreal challenge is moving to an innovation phase,\u201d he said.  Found a Shortcut  Sinovel, arguably, found a shortcut to get there. Han Junliang, Sinovel\u2019s president, is 47 and wears thin-rimmed\nglasses below thick hair parted in the middle. His rather drab\nprofile doesn\u2019t match his status as one of China\u2019s most famous\nentrepreneurs. He rose over 17 years through the ranks of a\nstate-owned manufacturer, Dalian Heavy Industry Group Co., which\nbuilds steel-rolling equipment and other massive machinery. He\neventually became chairman of an electrical equipment division.\nWhen Han left in 2006 to start Sinovel, Dalian Heavy was among\nthe company\u2019s major shareholders and its biggest benefactor. Han\nhimself has a 13.3\u00a0percent stake in Sinovel through an\ninvestment that included personal loans and other means,\naccording to company documents and wind energy experts.  Unlike some of its Chinese rivals, there are no tennis\ncourts or Ping-Pong tables at Sinovel. The company isn\u2019t focused\non amenities, just rapid and relentless growth. Workers\nassembling the massive turbine bodies in the hangar-size factory\nin the northern province of Liaoning wear coats and hats on the\nplant floor because the facility isn\u2019t heated. In less than four\nyears, Han has made the company into the second-largest turbine\nmaker in the world, after the Danish manufacturer  Vestas Wind\nSystems A\/S. (VWS)   Not Alone  He didn\u2019t do it alone. Sinovel is one of the best-connected\nclean energy companies in China. Among its major investors is\nthe private equity group  New Horizon Capital (NEHICZ) , co-founded by Wen\nYunsong, also known as Winston Wen, son of China\u2019s premier, Wen Jiabao. Han was also close to  Zhang Guobao , until recently head\nof China\u2019s powerful National Energy Administration. According to\na former U.S. diplomat, who didn\u2019t want to be named because he\nstill works in China, Han\u2019s relation to Zhang may have given him\nan early look at yet-to-be-published government regulations and\nprovided Sinovel preference in the kinds of turbines chosen to\npower the state-planned wind farms.  When China finalized bids for a mega-wind project in 2008,\nSinovel won 47\u00a0percent of the deal, by far the biggest share of\nany manufacturer.  \u201cHan seems to have ridden the wave just perfectly,\u201d said\nLouis Schwartz, president of China Strategies, a firm that\nadvises Western companies on China\u2019s wind sector.  Visible Flaws  By late 2010 there were visible flaws in China\u2019s wind power\nindustry. The first was the production quality of the turbines.\nSince the government planners demanded quantity, and not\nperformance, wind farm developers tended to cut corners.\nThousands of China\u2019s turbines lack the more expensive technology\nthat keeps them operating when there is a disturbance on the\npower grid. In April\u00a02011, wind farms totaling 1,346 turbines\nshut down suddenly, a major technical failure that caused\ndisruptions on the electricity grid of two provinces.  The second problem was oversupply, which persists to this\nday. China has ended up with more than 80 wind turbine\nmanufacturers in a market that analysts believe can support\nabout 10. The price of a 1.5-megawatt turbine in the country has\ndropped about 40\u00a0percent and continues to fall, placing enormous\npressure on Han and his company. Sinovel had signed multiyear\ncontracts with AMSC, keeping what his company paid for a\nturbine\u2019s electronics suite steady even as Sinovel\u2019s prices\nplummeted. AMSC\u2019s products accounted for about 12\u00a0percent of a\nSinovel turbine\u2019s cost in 2008, according to public filings. By\n2011 they made up 18\u00a0percent, said Schwartz, the U.S. consultant.  \u2018See The Motivation\u2019  \u201cYou can see the motivation to acquire that technology,\u201d\nhe said. \u201cEverybody was getting squeezed except AMSC.\u201d  The semi-trailer load of ASMC electronic components that\nSinovel turned away March\u00a031 was worth $70\u00a0million, and the U.S.\ncompany claims it\u2019s owed another $70\u00a0million for components\nalready shipped. Sinovel and AMSC had several supply contracts\nextending to 2013 that together were worth more than\n$700\u00a0million. That all adds up to a very large chunk of AMSC\u2019s\ncurrent and future revenue stream.  The one piece of leverage that AMSC thought it had until\nlast June was proposed regulations in China that will require\nexisting  wind turbines  to be retrofitted with an updated\ntechnology called \u201clow voltage ride through,\u201d or LVRT.  LVRT capability keeps turbines from shutting down when\nthere is a large voltage dip on the grid, which can occur from\nlittle more than a tree falling on a transmission line. The\ntechnology would have prevented the April wind farm shutdowns.\nEven if Sinovel wanted to renege on its contracts, all its\nexisting 1.5-megawatt turbines were powered by AMSC electronics.\nIf the company wanted the upgraded LVRT software, Sinovel would\nhave to come to the table.  Different Plan  Han apparently had a different plan in mind. According to\ncourt documents, in 2010, Sinovel began recruiting Dejan\nKarabasevic, a Serbian software engineer who worked at AMSC\u2019s\nresearch facility in Klagenfurt. In December, Karabasevic sent\nhis existing contract with AMSC to Sinovel employees for review;\nby January\u00a02011, Sinovel was hunting for an apartment for him in\nBeijing.  Once in China, the engineer was pressed to create software\nthat could go on existing turbines as quickly as possible, using\nsource code taken from AMSC\u2019s server in Austria. For five days\nbeginning May\u00a010, Karabasevic said in a confession to Austrian\npolice, he worked steadily in his Beijing apartment and then\ntraveled to a wind farm with three Sinovel employees to test the\ncode in working turbines. By June it was done.  Pleaded Guilty  Karabasevic, who pleaded guilty, was sentenced in September\nto 1 year in jail and two years probation for distribution of\ntrade secrets. His attorney, Gunter Huainigg, declined further\ncomment.  In court filings in a Beijing copyright infringement case,\none of the four theft-related cases filed by AMSC in China, the\ncompany said it has evidence that the stolen code was already in\nmore than 1,000 Sinovel turbines by July. McGahn said he assumes\nit\u2019s been installed in many more since. Beginning in October,\nSinovel filed two countersuits totaling $207 million, claiming\nit stopped accepting the company\u2019s electronics because of\nquality problems.  In hindsight, it now appears that Han never planned to\nfulfill the kind of long-term partnership McGahn had envisioned.\nIn 2010, Han helped create a company called Dalian Guotong\nElectric, making himself chairman and giving Sinovel a\n20\u00a0percent stake.  Swapped Out  When AMSC investigators opened up a Sinovel turbine in a\nsecond location in July, they found that an AMSC power converter\nhad been swapped out and replaced with a nearly identical one\nmade by Guotong. It was running on a version of AMSC\u2019s control\nsystem software obtained the year before by Sinovel and\ndecrypted by its engineers. It looks like Han wanted to make\nGuotong Electric the Chinese version of AMSC.  Last June, after AMSC promoted McGahn from vice president\nto CEO, the executive began to learn the full extent of how\nwrong he was about Sinovel. As investigators scrambled to\ndetermine who had stolen the control system source code, they\nnarrowed the possibilities down to three people, all of whom\nworked at the Klagenfurt research facility. According to\ninterviews with people involved in the investigation and a\nreview of court documents, log files showed that the altered\ncode had been uploaded onto the Sinovel turbine on two different\ndays, June\u00a02 and June\u00a010. Two of the employees weren\u2019t in China\nat that time.  Vacation Days  The third, Karabasevic, had given notice at the end of\nMarch and started using vacation days the company still owed him.\nOne of AMSC\u2019s most valuable software engineers, Karabasevic and\nhis bosses had agreed he would stay in touch as they looked for\na replacement, so he retained a company e-mail account. The\ninvestigators discovered he was accessing the e-mail from\ncomputers in China. Next, they overlaid the computer addresses\nwith offices, production facilities, and wind sites linked to\nSinovel. The data sets matched.  In addition to its internal checks, AMSC brought in a\nconsulting firm that specializes in white-collar crime. The\ncompany hired a private investigator to tail Karabasevic in\nBeijing. Forensics experts examined his company laptop and\nrecovered data he had attempted to wipe from the machine. This\nled to the discovery of hundreds of messages about the code\nexchanged between Karabasevic and three Sinovel employees,\nincluding one e-mail in which the engineer sent AMSC\u2019s source\ncode to his Sinovel counterpart.  Austrian Authorities  AMSC eventually turned this evidence over to Austrian\nauthorities who took Karabasevic into custody. He admitted to\nbeing courted over several months by Sinovel, and to\nreprogramming the turbine-control system code from a Beijing\napartment Sinovel provided him. In a locked closet inside the\napartment, investigators found a six-year, $1.7\u00a0million\nconsulting contract with Sinovel and a related company. The\nsignature on the contract belonged to Han Junliang.  In terms of outright theft of intellectual property, there\nis growing evidence that China\u2019s intelligence agencies are\ninvolved, as attacks spread from hits on large technology\ncompanies to the hacking of startups and even law firms.  \u201cThe government can basically put their hands in and take\nwhatever they want,\u201d said Michael Wessel, who sits on the U.S.-\nChina Economic and Security Review Commission that reports to\nCongress. \u201cWe need to take more actions and protect our\nintellectual property.\u201d  Deflated Bubble  Those actions may create unexpected difficulties for\nSinovel in using AMSC\u2019s stolen code. At the end of 2010, as\nChina\u2019s wind-power bubble deflated, Sinovel had $1.7\u00a0billion in\nunsold inventory and was owed $2\u00a0billion by its customers. The\nobvious solution is to increase sales by looking overseas, part\nof Sinovel\u2019s long-term strategy in any case. The Chinese\ncompany\u2019s first major international deal, a contract in Ireland\nwith Dublin-based Mainstream Renewable Power Ltd., was shelved\nlast year after AMSC made its software theft public. If Sinovel\ndoes export turbines with the stolen code, AMSC said it can file\nlawsuits in those markets as well.  So far neither Sinovel nor China\u2019s government is giving any\nground. Police in Beijing, after reviewing a case file provided\nby AMSC, declined to open a criminal investigation against three\nSinovel employees named by Karabasevic. In the weeks leading up\nto the Feb.\u00a024 arbitration hearing in Beijing, the pressure on\nMcGahn and his company has grown. A fire in a turbine belonging\nto another AMSC customer in China killed two people, and a\nChinese media report, citing an anonymous source, blamed AMSC\u2019s\ncomponents. Jason Fredette, an AMSC spokesman, said that based\non information the company has obtained, its electronics weren\u2019t\nat fault.  Cyberattack  The day after the press report, AMSC computer networks in\nDevens were hit by a cyberattack. Forged e-mails were sent to a\nhandful of company executives; they contained spyware designed\nto copy confidential data, including documents and internal\ncommunications. Fredette said e-mails were expertly crafted and\nhad a fake link to a story about Sinovel\u2019s troubles, a bit of\nirony inserted by the attackers. The highest concentration of affected systems -- almost 60\npercent -- is in that country, according to data from  Symantec\nCorp. , the computer-security software maker. The worm\u2019s\nsophisticated programming and ability to hide itself suggest it\nmay have been built by a government-sponsored organization in a\ncountry such as the U.S. or Israel, said  Frank Rieger ,\ntechnology chief at GSMK, a maker of encrypted mobile phones. Iran, which has the world\u2019s second-largest oil reserves, is\nunder United Nations sanctions because it has refused to curtail\nuranium enrichment and the development of ballistic missiles\nthat might carry a weapon. The country started a 1,000-megawatt\nnuclear-power reactor near the city of Bushehr in August.  \u2018Hides in Windows\u2019  \u201cIt is theoretically possible that the U.S. government did\nthis,\u201d Falkenrath said during an interview today with Bloomberg\nTelevision. \u201cBut in my judgment, that\u2019s a very remote\npossibility. It\u2019s more likely that Israel did it.\u201d  A message left at the Israeli embassy\u2019s press office wasn\u2019t\nimmediately returned. The fix was downloaded\n12,000 times, and 15 customers said they were affected.  No new cases of Stuxnet infections have been reported since\nthe end of August, and Siemens was not able to determine the\nworm\u2019s country of origin, Machowetz said.
