To contact the editor responsible for this story:\nTom Giles at   tgiles5@bloomberg.net .","path":".\/2008_2012_msft_bloomberg_news\/ozzie-s-departure-from-microsoft-fuels-concern-about-ceo-ballmer-s-benc.txt"},{"id":80107421,"title":"Saving the Post Office One Stamp at a Time","released_at":"<date>March 28 2013<\/date> <time>22:00:06<\/time>","content":"In Robert Heinlein\u2019s classic novella \u201cThe Man Who Sold the Moon,\u201d an entrepreneur raises money for a lunar expedition by warning a soft-drink company that, without its support, he might have to turn to a competitor that will pay him to display its logo on the surface, where it will be visible from Earth.  The story came to mind when I read about the recent decision by the U.S. Postal Service to license the slogan \u201cRain Heat & Snow\u201d to a manufacturer of all-weather clothing. Much of the news media  misreported the story , suggesting the USPS was planning to sell its own line of apparel.  What makes this and other Postal Service  rumors  so eminently reportable is that the USPS is in big trouble, and everybody knows it. The Postal Service, which by  its own estimate  handles 40 percent of all the mail delivered in the world, lost $15.9 billion last year, on revenue of $65 billion. Its unfunded pension liabilities are close to $50 billion.  USPS receives no tax dollars. It has to eat what it kills. Yet new revenue is scarce, as are viable ideas for reducing spending. The Postal Service\u2019s  hasty sales  from its real estate portfolio haven\u2019t raised much money. Its plan to end delivery on Saturday would have saved $2 billion, but Congress killed the idea, at least through the end of September.  A Moonshot  Some say  the U.S. should follow the lead of the many other countries that have privatized the post office. Short of that politically unlikely solution, about the only money-making strategy left is to follow Heinlein\u2019s advice and sell the moon.  Which is to say: It\u2019s time for the Postal Service to monetize its most valuable tangible asset and offer advertising space on the 22 billion stamps it sells each year.  The idea isn\u2019t entirely new. In 1981, the USPS  proposed  selling advertisements on the booklets holding stamps (not on the stamps themselves), an idea that went nowhere. Beginning in the late 19th century, several other nations, including Great Britain, began to  allow advertising  on the obverse side of stamps, as well as on what is known as the selvedge (the page edges that are left when you tear out the stamps).  The postal service already has a \u201cvanity stamp\u201d program allowing users to pay for customized stamps for their own use: Anycorp can order stamps bearing its logo, a bride and groom can display their wedding date. The program was the subject of scandal early on, when customers began producing stamps bearing, for example, the  likeness  of Ted Kaczynski. In any event, it has  never produced  much revenue.  The program was a good idea, weakly executed. USPS should take it further, and sell space not on specially ordered vanity stamps but on stamps in general circulation. The idea would be that Anycorp\u2019s stamps, rather than being used simply on its own mail, would be for sale at every post office.  I have no idea what rates the market might bear. But private companies that print stamps carrying business logos often charge more than twice the face value of the postage. Were the USPS to emboss logos directly on first-class stamps at a cost of, say, 30 cents each -- not bad for a guaranteed view of the ad by the recipient -- the deficit could be cut by as much as $6.6 billion, or more than 40 percent. If USPS were to sell advertising on postmarks or bulk-rate cancellations, revenue could be higher still.  Now, you might immediately object that nobody will buy branded stamps -- that the customer at the counter, faced with a choice of a stamp bearing the Anycorp logo or a stamp bearing whichever historical figure USPS has most recently chosen to honor, will choose the commemorative. I\u2019m not sure. People plunk down good money for the honor of being allowed to dress as walking advertisements for Nike. A stamp bearing the Nike logo or images from \u201cMad Men\u201d might be a huge seller.  A Logo  Nevertheless, let\u2019s assume that the median stamp buyer would shun the Anycorp stamps, or even the Nike stamps. How then to monetize the considerable asset that the space on postage stamps represents?  Two solutions come to mind. First, the Postal Service might end the sale of commemorative stamps entirely, and sell only branded stamps. This might cause a revolution, especially at Christmas.  In the alternative, then, the USPS could place a logo in the corner of its commemorative stamps -- all its commemorative stamps. More to the point, USPS could auction off the right to sponsor some set of its stamps for a period of time. For three years, say, every stamp sold honoring a great American would be sponsored by Microsoft; every stamp honoring wildlife would be sponsored by Starbucks.  You might object that this would be disrespectful to  George Washington  or the  tufted puffin , to pick two currently available stamps. But is this necessarily so? If I buy a book about the first president or about the varieties of auks, and the name and logo of the publisher are embossed on the cover and the frontispiece, I don\u2019t worry about whether I\u2019ve become a toady of corporate America.  Selling advertising space would require a change in law, but so would most other tools by which USPS might increase revenue. As Walter Russell Mead has  put it , \u201cA Postal Service that can survive will need to be able to pursue new business opportunities without saying \u2018Congress, may I?\u2019 at every turn.\u201d  Still don\u2019t like the idea? Think stamps should be sacrosanct? Let\u2019s turn back to Heinlein\u2019s story. His protagonist, Delos Harriman, isn\u2019t trying to get rich. He just wants to go to the moon. \u201cI would cheat, lie, steal, beg, bribe,\u201d he says, with no sense of shame. He seeks corporate sponsors because he sees no other way to raise the capital he needs.  That\u2019s where the Postal Service finds itself. Certainly it would be nice to live in a world where stamps remain commercial- free. I\u2019m no fan of selling off our public spaces. But the Postal Service can no longer survive on its own. At some point, like Harriman, it will have to go where the money is.  (Stephen L. Carter is a Bloomberg View columnist and a professor of law at Yale University. He is the author of \u201cThe Violence of Peace: America\u2019s Wars in the Age of Obama,\u201d and the novel \u201cThe Impeachment of Abraham Lincoln.\u201d The opinions expressed are his own.)  To contact the writer of this article: Stephen L. Carter at  or  @StepCarter  on Twitter. It isn\u2019t completely satisfying, said Ron Montoya, the consumer-advice editor for Edmunds.com, an automotive data service in Santa Monica, California, who\u2019s tested the Siri-enabled system in the Chevrolet Spark.  \u201cIt works well enough for some things, but I personally think Siri doesn\u2019t work that well,\u201d Montoya said in a phone interview. \u201cIt frequently doesn\u2019t recognize my voice.\u201d  The Apple-enabled system in GM\u2019s subcompact cars wasn\u2019t as useful for navigation and other functions as systems automakers already offer, Montoya said.  \u201cSiri has not been designed for the car, where the cabin is often noisy,\u201d said Chris Schreiner, a research director for consultant Strategy Analytics Inc. and a former engineer for GM\u2019s OnStar telematics service. \u201cAutomakers tune voice systems for each car. Expecting Siri to work at the same level in every vehicle isn\u2019t practical.\u201d  \u2018Key Focus\u2019  Apple rose 1.2 percent to $453.32 at the close in  New York . Honda, Hyundai, Bayerische Motoren Werke AG, Daimler AG\u2019s Mercedes-Benz,  Land Rover , Jaguar,  Volkswagen AG (VOW) \u2019s Audi,  Toyota Motor Corp. (7203)  and the Chrysler Group LLC are also adding Siri Eyes Free capability in models that arrive this year.  Critical Demands  \u201cIn-car infotainment, connectivity, all these things, all the technology that\u2019s in the cabin of the car is becoming increasingly critical,\u201d said Karl Brauer, an industry analyst for Kelley  Blue Book  in  Irvine , California. \u201cApple has also got some real skin in the game. Apple\u2019s rivals have worked hard to establish a foothold inside the car that they will be reluctant to give up. Dell, 47, gains greater freedom to cut jobs and embark on strategy shifts at Dell Inc. without answering to public  shareholders . Still, the buyout imposes constraints, including saddling the company with $17 billion in debt. Interest payments will eat up  cash  that could be spent on  acquisitions  and research and development to take on  International Business Machines Corp. ,  Hewlett-Packard Co.  and  Oracle Corp.  That may also force Dell to keep the PC division, which drags on margins.  \u201cIt\u2019s a double-edged sword,\u201d said  Bill Whyman , an analyst at ISI Group. \u201cThey don\u2019t have the balance sheet to go up against IBM, HP or Oracle. Those companies spent billions of dollars to change the mix of their businesses.\u201d  Michael Dell and Silver Lake Management LLC are taking the Round Rock, Texas-based computer maker private in a transaction valued at $24.4 billion. Dell is regaining majority control of the company he started in an university dorm room, and will remain chairman and chief executive officer.  A quarter-century after its debut as publicly traded company, Dell\u2019s in a tough spot. The PC maker has spent $12.7 billion to buy 18 companies since 2009, including Compellent Technologies Inc. in data storage and Force10 Networks Inc. in networking. Yet Dell isn\u2019t bundling enough of those highly profitable products with the computer servers it sells. That would help it better cope with a PC sales slump.  Software Push  In software, a $1.5 billion business, Dell needs to make a bigger splash in cloud-computing tools for companies managing fleets of servers, networking gear, and business applications online, without hiring teams of expensive consultants. That could help Dell sell more software to mid-sized companies and enterprises seeking streamlined ways to manage their data centers, a $9.9 billion market occupied by heavyweights including IBM,  Microsoft Corp. , and  VMware Inc.   By going private, Dell could draw up a new playbook less contingent on satisfying shareholders. It can take steps to invest in the future, and emerge as a stronger company less reliant on PCs and able to claim a bigger slice of the technology industry\u2019s profits.  A closely held Dell would also save an estimated $556 million a year in  dividend payments . It could use that money for severance payments and restructuring costs.  Debt Costs  Without access to public-market capital, buying upstart firms with compelling technology becomes harder. Financing debt will also skim an estimated $1.2 billion a year, according to data compiled by Bloomberg. Dell\u2019s debt burden could increase if interest rates rise.  Lower credit ratings would also push financing costs higher. Moody\u2019s Investors Service lowered Dell\u2019s senior unsecured rating yesterday to Baa1 from A2, and Fitch Ratings cut Dell\u2019s long-term default rating to BB+ from A. Standard & Poor\u2019s put Dell\u2019s A- minus rating on negative watch.  The cost of servicing debt after the buyout over the next three years will be about the same, or slightly less, than Dell\u2019s dividend and share repurchase costs over the past three years, the company said in a filing yesterday with the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission.  Strategy Shift  One of the people likely to play a key role in reshaping Dell is  Marius Haas , recruited in August after Michael Dell pressed him to join. A 45-year-old Dutch national, Haas arrived after a year as an adviser at KKR & Co., and previously led mergers and acquisitions at Hewlett-Packard under former CEO  Mark Hurd .  Haas is trying to inject Dell with more urgency to pair storage and networking gear with the growing server business. Selling 2 percent more of high-margin gear with servers would add $1.2 billion in annual sales, said Haas, who says storage and networking products yield gross margins of 30 percent to 60 percent, compared with 22 percent for all of Dell.  Haas said he\u2019s been negotiating with Hurd, now Oracle\u2019s co- president, to get more Oracle database sales to run on Dell machines. About 60 percent of Oracle currently runs on Hewlett- Packard servers.  \u201cI would love to change that to 60 percent for Dell,\u201d Haas said. \u201cMark and I are very incented to work together.\u201d  Selling Servers  The enterprise efforts have paid off so far, with Dell emerging as one of the world\u2019s biggest makers of servers used to run websites, process financial transactions and analyze reams of business data. During the  third quarter , Dell sold about 565,000 mainstream Intel-based servers, according to Gartner -- just 65,000 less than market leader Hewlett-Packard.  Dell is poised to be No. 1 this year in the server market, CEO Dell said at a customer conference in December, giving the company a broad platform to pitch customers on its storage and networking products.  Gaining a larger share in enterprise computing won\u2019t be a slam dunk. A sizable portion of the server market has evaporated in recent years as huge volume customers such as  Google Inc.  and  Facebook Inc.  buy directly from no-name manufacturers such as  Quanta Computer Inc.   While putting more emphasis on data centers, Dell will need to grapple with what to do with PCs, an ailing division that accounts for about half of sales, according to  Shaw Wu , an analyst at Sterne Agee & Leach Inc.  PC Challenge  Within the PC market, Samsung Electronics Co., Lenovo Group Ltd., and Asustek Computer Inc. are challenging Dell at the lower end of its business, while demand for Apple\u2019s iPads and higher-end Macs remains buoyant.  \u201cAs we\u2019ve seen through history, it\u2019s tough to win a two- front war,\u201d Wu said.  Withdrawing from the scrutiny of public markets may be Michael Dell\u2019s gambit to restore his reputation as a technology pioneer. He  founded  Dell at 19, took it public at 23, and was worth $1 billion eight years later. What\u2019s to\ndebate when there\u2019s so much agreement -- or the semblance of it,\nat least?  Our frustration is quite the opposite: There is genuine\nagreement between Democrats and Republicans on some issues and\nyet that consensus fails to drive action. We see this playing\nout especially on immigration.  The larger immigration picture certainly remains\ncontentious, and unavoidably so. How to deal with 12 million\nillegal immigrants, most of them productive and law-abiding\nmembers of society? How to make the border more secure, and how\nmuch weight to give that imperfectly attainable goal?  Yet in one important area -- the treatment of highly\nskilled workers -- a strong consensus exists that a more liberal\npolicy is crucial for U.S. economic prospects. President  Barack Obama  and Republican challenger  Mitt Romney  agree. Almost\neveryone who has given the matter a moment of  intelligent\nthought  agrees. Yet nothing happens.  Human Capital  It would be hard to exaggerate the lunacy of the U.S.\u2019s\nrules on skilled immigrants. We know of no other  advanced\neconomy  that skews its policies so severely against the workers\nin greatest demand. Most countries see themselves as competing\nto attract that kind of immigrant, recognizing that human\ncapital is an important driver of economic success.  The U.S. has more to worry about than most. Its schools are\nunderperforming and its students have lost ground in comparison\nwith other countries. The educational quality of the U.S. labor\nforce, after decades of rapid improvement, has begun to\nstagnate.  Serious efforts to improve schools and develop a better-\ntrained labor force are under way -- we commend them\nwholeheartedly -- but it could be many years before we know the\nresults or see their effect on the economy. Meanwhile, strategic\nindustries, especially in information and communication\ntechnology, complain of skills shortages and are forced to meet\nthem by moving research and production abroad.  The U.S. compounds the idiocy of its cramped skilled-\nimmigrant quotas with impressive thoroughness. For instance, by\nlaw it allocates applications among countries according to a\nhalf-baked notion of diversity, rather than according to its own\neconomic needs. Many emigrants from  India  excel in engineering\nand other technical skills that American companies covet. Yet\nIndia\u2019s quota, small in relation to its pool of outstanding\napplicants, artificially restricts their numbers.  The U.S. attracts the best students from all over the world\nto its universities and then deports them soon after they have\nreceived degrees. If an immigrant is lucky enough to obtain an\n H1-B visa  -- the prized document sought by most foreign\ngraduates arriving to work for a U.S. employer -- it can take\nyears (if at all) to win permanent residency.  In the meantime, the immigrant is forbidden to change\nemployers and must become very acquainted with the legal system.\n(The rules are good for lawyers, at least.) Spouses, for the\nmost part, aren\u2019t allowed to work. And the  Internal Revenue\nService  has devised special tortures for immigrants who retain\nfinancial connections with their home countries, in effect\nregarding them as tax evaders unless they can prove otherwise.\nThe authorities have thought of everything.  Talent Magnet  Since its founding, the U.S. has been a magnet for the most\ntalented, ambitious and hard-working people in the world. This\nhas always been the nation\u2019s greatest strength. Highly skilled\nworkers have never been more valuable than they are today, and\nyet the U.S., in every way it can think of, now tells those\nwould-be Americans to get lost. They are beginning to get the\nmessage.  It is both remarkable and disgraceful that Congress\nunderstands the problem. It hears of little else from companies,\nincluding General Electric Co., Intel Corp. and Microsoft Corp.,\nand yet can\u2019t seem to separate the issue of highly skilled\nimmigrants from the wider and genuinely difficult aspects of\nimmigration policy.  Cold political calculations by both parties are holding\nback reform. House Republicans arranged a floor vote last month\non a measure that would have offered more residency visas to\nimmigrants with advanced science, technology, engineering and\nmath degrees, but set it up to fail by reducing the number of\nvisas overall (which Democrats oppose).  For their part, Democrats think it best to hold the\nskilled-immigration rules hostage until they can get a more\ncomprehensive agreement (which Republicans tend to resist). We\nfavor comprehensive reform, too, but not if the result is total\nparalysis, with intolerable costs to the economy.  Making progress where agreement is slender or nonexistent\nis hard enough, as Congress has proved. That was the mission for 130 tech executives, venture capitalists, educators and government officials who are flying today on British Airways' first in-flight, all-night hackathon called \"UnGrounded\" from San Francisco to London. The miles-high expectations? Come up with at least four ideas to alleviate a chronic shortage of  science, technology, engineering and math students  entering the global workforce. The dearth of qualified job candidates can stifle innovation. While the unique in-air networking session was created to get technology execs hooked on flying British Airways, the other motivation was to help solve, along with design firm IDEO, Google and several universities, an estimated shortage of 500,000 people who can fill computer-related jobs in the U.S. by 2020. A big part of that equation is figuring out how to fill more of these positions with women, who only represent 35 percent of the tech workforce, according to the airline. The group's four best ideas will be presented June 14 at the G8 summit's Innovation Conference and the concurrent United Nations' Decide Now Act conference in London. Afterward, Congress plans to return to Washington to seek a deal that avoids the fiscal cliff -- a combination of automatic tax increases and spending cuts scheduled to take effect in January.  In that time, the CEOs want Congress to come up with a framework for a long-range deficit reduction agreement with details to be worked out in early 2013.  The CEOs\u2019 principles call for Congress to overhaul Medicare and Medicaid, \u201cstrengthen\u201d  Social Security  and enact \u201ccomprehensive and pro-growth tax reform\u201d that lowers rates, broadens the tax base, raises revenue and cuts the deficit.  Obama has repeatedly called for a \u201cbalanced\u201d approach to deficit reduction that would include spending cuts and tax increases. Republicans insist on no tax increases in a deficit plan.  Simpson, Bowles  The deficit-reduction campaign group\u2019s founders -- Bowles, a Democrat and former White House chief of staff for President  Bill Clinton , and Simpson, a Republican and former senator from Wyoming -- proposed tax increases and spending cuts in 2010.  Still, asked specifically whether the campaign supports tax increases, Jon Romano, a spokesman for the group, referred to its stated principles and said it wasn\u2019t endorsing any particular proposal.  The campaign \u201cis looking for a plan that includes a comprehensive and pro-growth tax reform, which will broaden the base, lower rates, raises revenue and reduces the deficit,\u201d Romano said.  Linden said that if the CEOs \u201care out there endorsing the Bowles-Simpson framework of revenue and spending, then they are actually calling for more revenue than the president has.\u201d  \u201cThey are so much closer to where the president is than where the congressional Republicans are or where a potential\u201d President  Mitt Romney  would be, he said. The Office of the Director of National Intelligence\nreleased today an April 25 court document, along with two\nbriefing papers provided to Congress that describe the program\u2019s\nuse. Some text is redacted.  \u201cWe welcome a public debate about how best to safeguard\nboth our national security and the privacy of our citizens,\u201d\nDeputy Attorney General James Cole said in testimony before the\nSenate Judiciary Committee today. \u201cWe will be considering in\nthe coming days and weeks further steps to declassify\ninformation and help facilitate that debate.\u201d  The government\u2019s disclosures shed new light on the scope of\ntools utilized by intelligence and law-enforcement agencies\nafter the Sept. 11, 2001, terrorist attacks. Each of the\ndocuments calls the programs critical to halting future plots\nand presents the methodology and restrictions in place to guide\ntheir use.  They don\u2019t include the legal rationale for the programs\nwhich, along with the large-scale collection, has raised\nconcerns from lawmakers in both parties.  \u201cIf this program is not effective, it has to end,\u201d\nSenator Patrick Leahy, a Vermont Democrat and the chairman of\nthe committee, said today. \u201cSo far I\u2019m not convinced by what\nI\u2019ve seen.\u201d  \u2018Among Us\u2019  Top intelligence and law-enforcement officials are\ndefending the data-collection programs from criticism -- and\nproposals for legislative curbs -- since their disclosure by\nformer intelligence contractor Edward Snowden.  U.S. agencies are also facing pressure from technology\ncompanies including Yahoo! Inc.,  Google Inc. (GOOG) ,  Microsoft Corp. (MSFT) \nand  Facebook Inc. (FB) , to allow the disclosure of the role the\nprivate sector plays in the classified programs.  General Keith Alexander, the director of the NSA, said at a\nconference in Las Vegas today that intelligence agencies need to\nmaintain their access to the data.  \u201cTerrorists use our communications,\u201d Alexander said in a\nspeech at the Black Hat annual computer security conference.\n\u201cThey live among us.\u201d  Internet Surveillance  Snowden, who\u2019s currently in the Moscow airport and facing\ncharges of espionage and theft in the U.S., also disclosed the\nexistence of an Internet surveillance program, known as Prism,\nthat collects information on foreign citizens believed to be\noutside the U.S. and involved with terrorist organizations.  His disclosures, mostly released by the Washington Post and\nThe Guardian, have restarted a debate that had subsided in the\nwake of President George W. Bush\u2019s administration.  The Guardian today  reported  on another program disclosed by\nSnowden, called XKeyscore, which the organization said allowed\nNSA analysts to search databases containing e-mails, online\nchats and the browsing histories of individuals.  Lawmakers have zeroed in on the program that gathers\nmillions of phone records from U.S. citizens into government\ncomputers, authorized by the  Foreign Intelligence Surveillance\nCourt  under the Patriot Act. The court, which operates in\nsecret, has come under scrutiny for being too willing to approve\nintelligence-agency requests.  Senator Dianne Feinstein, a California Democrat and\nchairman of the Intelligence Committee, said today she would\nconsider including curbs on the phone-data program in the annual\nintelligence authorization bill.  Legislation Considered  Those changes, according to Feinstein, would include the\nrequirement of annual reports on the number of warrants obtained\nby the FBI to collect the content of calls, the number of U.S.\nphone numbers submitted as queries to a NSA database and the\nnumber of times per year a private company is required to\nprovide data as part of the program.  Top intelligence and law-enforcement officials have made\nrepeated trips to Capitol Hill, participating in public hearings\nand in classified closed-door briefings, to defend the\ninitiatives.  James Clapper, the director of national intelligence, said\nin a June 26 letter to senators that the phone record-collection\nprogram began in 2006 and is reauthorized by the the Foreign\nSurveillance Intelligence Court every 90 days. Clapper pointed\nto congressional reauthorization of the law permitting the\ncollection, as well as its oversight, in the letter.  Congress Briefed  Included in the information declassified today were\n briefing materials  provided by the Justice Department to\nlawmakers on the House and Senate Intelligence and Judiciary\ncommittees that described the phone-record program.  The materials, provided in 2009 and 2011, consist of five\npages that outline the use and restrictions imposed on the\nprogram. They also include the request that all members of\nCongress have an opportunity to access the contents in a\nclassified setting over a limited period of time.  The declassified documents include the outlines of a\nbroader effort to collect electronic communications of U.S.\ncitizens under the program -- a practice that U.S. officials say\nended in 2011.  Those programs \u201coperate on a very large scale,\u201d according\nto the documents provided to lawmakers in February 2011.  \u2018Compliance Problems\u2019  The briefing materials include the acknowledgment that\n\u201cthere have been a number of technical compliance problems and\nhuman implementation in these two bulk programs.\u201d The briefing\nsaid NSA and the surveillance court found no \u201cintentional or\nbad-faith violations.\u201d  The officials\u2019 efforts so far have failed to quell\nlawmakers\u2019 concerns that the programs undermine individual\nliberty, including privacy rights.  While lawmakers today said they appreciated the latest\ndeclassification effort, they also criticized its timing and the\nforced nature of the debate over the programs.  \u201cAd-hoc transparency doesn\u2019t engender trust,\u201d Senator Al Franken, a Minnesota Democrat, said during today\u2019s hearing.  Democratic Senators Mark Udall of  Colorado  and Ron Wyden of\n Oregon  have been among the programs\u2019 most vocal critics. They\u2019ve\nbeen joined by lawmakers from both parties.  Curtailment Urged  The two senators have called into question the testimony of\nintelligence officials that the phone-record program has been an\nintegral part of halting or disrupting terror plots. They have\ncalled on Obama\u2019s administration to end the program while\nproposing legislation to curtail its use.  A House proposal to defund the NSA programs came seven\nvotes short of passing July 24.  Democratic and Republican lawmakers across the political\nspectrum now say they\u2019re drawing plans to restrict data\ncollection, declassify court orders allowing the spying and\nchange the way the court\u2019s judges are appointed. The 17-page\norder released today was signed by Judge Roger Vinson.  Underpinning efforts to curb the NSA programs is a shift in\npublic opinion about government surveillance activities\nfashioned after the Sept. 11 attacks. A July 17-21 Pew Research\nCenter survey found 47 percent of adults polled have greater\nconcern over the reach of U.S. anti-terrorism policies, while 35\npercent were concerned they didn\u2019t go far enough.  That marked the first time civil liberties concerns have\ntrumped protection from terrorism since the organization began\nasking the question in 2004.  Transparency Sought  While House Democratic Leader Nancy Pelosi of  California \nvoted against the effort to defund the programs, she\nsubsequently asked the White House to seek changes. Pelosi and\n153 other House Democrats sent Obama a letter July 26, urging\ncurbs that would \u201cpreserve American\u2019s privacy and civil\nliberties while protecting our national security.\u201d  Top lawmakers on the House and Senate Judiciary and\nIntelligence committees, which have oversight of the programs,\nare working on proposals to curb or provide more transparency to\nthe NSA programs.  Representative Jim Sensenbrenner, a Wisconsin Republican\nwho sponsored the Patriot Act in 2001, and Democratic\nRepresentative Zoe Lofgren of California are working together on\nlegislation to allow businesses to disclose their involvement\nwith surveillance orders.  A separate Sensenbrenner bill would limit collection of\nphone data to targets of a federal terrorism investigation and\nput new restrictions on the surveillance court, said Ben Miller,\na Sensenbrenner spokesman.  Representative Adam Schiff, a California Democrat and\nmember of the House Intelligence Committee, has introduced two\nmeasures since the Snowden revelations that would revamp the\ncourt. One would change the selection process for the court\u2019s\njudges, taking it out of the hands of the U.S. Supreme Court\nChief Justice to allow White House input and Senate\nconfirmation. The other seeks to declassify many of the court\u2019s\nsecret rulings. He was a serial innovator whose illness cost the world a bright talent who was also a great company leader. I hope that the music from  the hymns of praise sung to him  in his waning days is playing on his iPod as he ascends into the firmament of the greatest American business leaders. If there were a Nobel prize for business, surely he would have won it.  He did what he set out to do and more. He saw the potential for computing power for the masses, useful and accessible to everyone. In a phrase that drove the early Apple,  he created bicycles for the mind. Jobs was all about mass personalization. The ubiquitous i of the iMac, iPhone, and iPad signaled individual as well as interactive in the user-friendly products he spawned.  In democratizing a technical field, Steve Jobs was the Henry Ford of his time. He turned computers into consumer products affordable by billions. Apple wasn't the biggest company \u2014 although Jobs lived to see a glorious moment when Apple's market cap shot ahead of Exxon's  to be number one.  But Apple consistently pushed the industry to change, playing the role of feisty fresh-faced free thinker. Apple was always a  counterculture challenging establishments  and going for the future \u2014 like the early emphasis on getting Apples into classrooms to help kids learn. Jobs was a co-founder but emerged as the business as well as technical leader. He didn't put his name on the door, although the Macintosh was named after his favorite apple, and company style reflected his tastes. That was Apple round I. Jobs also had a comeback story rivaling any in business, a model for leadership development. He lured a former PepsiCo executive, John Scully, to the young Apple company, as his \"adult supervision,\" only to find himself pushed out, in part due to excesses in the Mac division he headed. For a time it looked like Jobs was another faded icon, dabbling in a set of ventures hoping to recapture former glory or looking to prove Apple wrong. But he took advantage of opportunities, learned, and grew. He headed Pixar, a star in computer animation, and founded Next Computer. Next turned out to be his ticket back to Apple, when the underlying technology was sold to Apple.  His leadership pause refreshed and broadened him. As CEO of Apple round II, Jobs built a bigger and even more innovative company and it soared. Under the mature Jobs, Apple now understood how to enlist developers and other partners. Job's new bite of the Apple created products and platforms that made the computer less important than the content. He led the company into devices of the future, grabbing initial leadership in smartphones, and perhaps saved the online music business in passing. Even the Apple-Microsoft rivalry reflected the kind of competition that spurs innovation. Jobs didn't start a dynasty, and he didn't take on world problems. He focused on Apple. He  won't be known for the charitable foundations  bearing his name or the good done afterwards but for the value created through new products during his lifetime. Jobs brought design from backroom to forethought, shook industry boundaries, challenged giants, and excited consumers. That is an enormous legacy that will stand the test of history. Annette Bongiorno, who worked for Madoff for 40 years, would request trade dates and prices as much as a year old be used on account statements to reach pre-determined profit goals for customers, and cut out trade data to be taped onto some statements, Winnie Jackson, the defendant\u2019s former assistant, testified yesterday in federal court in Manhattan.  Bongiorno gave \u201cvery little explanation\u201d to Jackson when asked how the company\u2019s trading strategy worked, and Jackson, who started working for Madoff in the 1980s, didn\u2019t realize anything she was doing was fraudulent while she was following orders, she said.  Jackson said she never saw Bongiorno \u201ccut and paste\u201d trades onto account statements, though she said her former boss oversaw the creation of the statements and the practice wasn\u2019t uncommon or unusual.  Prosecutors showed Jackson and the jury examples of such statements, which included hand-written notes that Jackson identified as Bongiorno\u2019s. The example included trades for Microsoft Corp. in 2004 that had been taped onto the paper. No trades actually took place at the investment advisory business.  Madoff Hire  Bongiorno, who helped run the unit at the heart of the Ponzi scheme, has pleaded not guilty in the case. She joined Madoff\u2019s company straight out of high school when she was 19 years old, and argues Madoff tricked her into thinking she was part of a legitimate investment business.  Bongiorno and four other former Madoff employees are accused of conspiring for decades to hide Madoff\u2019s fraud by creating millions of fake documents to trick customers and regulators. Prosecutors are calling former workers, including some who have pleaded guilty, to testify against them.  Also on trial are Daniel Bonventre, who oversaw Madoff\u2019s broker-dealer and proprietary trading units; computer programmers George Perez and Jerome O\u2019Hara and Joann Crupi, who managed large accounts and worked closely with Bongiorno and Jackson. They have also pleaded not guilty. All five deny any wrongdoing and say Madoff duped them for years.  Warehouse Search  Bruce Dubinsky, a forensic accountant who in 2011 probed Madoff\u2019s fraud by examining millions of corporate documents and deconstructing computer code, testified yesterday that Madoff\u2019s firm was insolvent by December 2002. Dubinsky\u2019s investigation included searching thousands of boxes in Madoff\u2019s off-site warehouse, analyzing BlackBerry and e-mail data and hiring two former computer programmers who worked at International Business Machines Corp. decades ago to help retrieve data from Madoff\u2019s outdated storage devices and computer equipment.  Dubinsky, a managing director at Duff & Phelps LLC, testified that he will explain to the jury how Madoff\u2019s company became \u201cthe biggest Ponzi scheme in the history of the world.\u201d He started by explaining what a stock is and how a broker-dealer works. His testimony will continue Oct. 28.  Jackson testified Oct. 23 that her job included collecting historical trade data and prices for specific stocks over past weeks or months, and sometimes as long as a year, so that customer account statements could include backdated trades to reach specific profit requests sought by Bongiorno.  Jackson, who started working for Madoff in the 1980s, told the jury she also helped execute withdrawal requests for Bongiorno directly from her account, usually amounting to $2,500 in cash once or twice a month that she would personally deliver to her then-boss.  Fifth Witness  Jackson was the fifth witness to testify in the first criminal trial stemming from the world\u2019s biggest Ponzi scheme, which deprived investors of $17 billion in principal and billions more in fake profit. U.S. District Judge Laura Taylor Swain said the trial may last as long as five months.  Prosecutors yesterday showed Jackson a printout of a Madoff customer document for the Picower Foundation that included a handwritten note saying \u201cFake Sales\u201d at the top of one page and several handwritten numbers interspersed with printed ones. Jackson identified the writing as belonging to Bongiorno.  Jeffry Picower, who died in 2009, had been an investor with Madoff since the 1970s; his estate agreed to a $7.2 billion settlement with the U.S. and the trustee liquidating the Madoff firm.  \u2018Cancel\u2019 Trades  Under cross-examination, Bongiorno\u2019s lawyer, Roland Riopelle, showed additional pages from the same document, including another handwritten note on the last page that said to \u201ccancel\u201d the trades because they were being used to check for percentages.  Riopelle asked Jackson if, in her experience, the document appeared to be \u201cnefarious,\u201d prompting the U.S. to object over a witness being asked to opine about a document. Swain permitted the question, to which Jackson answered, \u201cNo.\u201d  After the jury left, Riopelle told the judge the \u201cFake Sales\u201d evidence was \u201cparticularly toxic\u201d without Jackson\u2019s interpretation.  Riopelle asked Jackson to identify a sample of about a dozen notes that were handwritten by Bongiorno on printed documents about customers\u2019 purported trades. While Peck\u2019s decision to let lawyers for both sides hash\nout the final details of Lehman\u2019s brokerage sale may have helped\nseal the deal, his blanket approval spawned an $11 billion\nlawsuit that threatens to undo the 2008 agreement.  Lehman alleges Barclays took advantage of the haste in\nwhich the deal was worked out to gain assets it never told the\njudge about. Now Peck may have to decide whether to undo his own\norder, or find another way to claw back some money for Lehman\ncreditors.  \u201cThose in charge of the sale decided, \u2018the whole financial\nsystem will collapse unless the sale is approved now,\u2019\u201d said\nGeorge Kuney, a professor at the University of Tennessee College\nof Law in Knoxville who teaches bankruptcy and contract law.\n\u201cOnce you proceed on that basis in a transaction of this size,\nthe process is going to be pretty sloppy and mistakes are\ninevitably going to be made.\u201d  Peck\u2019s assistant and courtroom deputy Lynda Calderon didn\u2019t\nreturn calls requesting comment from the judge. Under Peck, the\ntwo-year bankruptcy case has cost Lehman creditors $961 million\nin fees to managers and advisers through August, the most\nexpensive bankruptcy ever.  Randomly Assigned  Peck, a 65-year-old native New Yorker, was the Manhattan\ncourt\u2019s second most-junior bankruptcy judge in September 2008\nwhen he was randomly assigned the $639 billion Lehman\nbankruptcy, based on the firm\u2019s assets at the time.  Before Lehman, Peck\u2019s cases included the $500 million\nbankruptcy of Quebecor World (USA) Inc. in January 2008 and the\n$924 million bankruptcy of Sirva Inc., in February 2008. He was\nappointed to the bench in 2006.  Peck\u2019s Sept. 19, 2008, order approving the brokerage sale,\nsigned four days after the 158-year-old bank collapsed,\nspecifically allowed Lehman\u2019s and Barclays\u2019 lawyers to change\nany documents he\u2019d approved, or add documents that weren\u2019t\nfinished yet, though he said the changes shouldn\u2019t \u201chave a\nmaterial adverse effect on the debtors\u2019 estates\u201d and should be\nokayed by Lehman, its creditors and Barclays.  \u201cThe purchase agreement and any related agreements,\ndocuments or other instruments may be modified, amended or\nsupplemented by the parties thereto . . . without further order\nof the court,\u201d he wrote in his order.  Only Bidder  The 2009 lawsuit led to a trial that\u2019s been going on since\nApril. It pits Lehman, which examiner  Anton Valukas  has said hid\nbillions of dollars in risks before it failed, against Barclays,\nwhich was the only bidder for the brokerage.  Lehman accuses Barclays of taking a $5 billion \u201csecret\u201d\nprofit on a portfolio of securities it acquired with the\nbrokerage, and of making another $6 billion by writing up\nbusiness assets, skimping on promised payments and \u201cgrabbing\u201d\nmore financial assets belonging to Lehman. Some of the disputed\nassets were assigned to Barclays in a so-called clarification\nletter that should have been shown to Peck, Lehman says.  Barclays says it wants $3 billion of assets that were never\ndelivered. Lehman has no legal right to challenge the\ntransaction now because its advisers knew and documented all the\ndetails when the deal was struck, and defended it in a higher\ncourt when it was challenged, according to Barclays.  Lehman Creditors  Any money Peck might extract from Barclays would help\nLehman creditors, whom the company estimated in September stand\nto get about 15.8 cents on the dollar for their worldwide\nclaims, at the expense of Barclays, which reported net income of\n2.4 billion pounds ($3.8 billion) in the first half.  Peck may have indicated a changed position on orders\nearlier this year when Lehman\u2019s lawyers asked to restructure the\nfirm\u2019s biggest real-estate asset,  Archstone , a second time,\nsaying they couldn\u2019t proceed without his permission if the deal\nchanged.  \u201cAssume you don\u2019t have that authority,\u201d he told Lehman\u2019s\nlawyers at  Weil Gotshal & Manges LLP  in a May court hearing.  Closing arguments in the Barclays case are due in late\nOctober. Absent a settlement, Peck may rule in January or\nFebruary, lawyers in the case said. Britain\u2019s third-biggest bank\nmay not be competing on an even playing field, said  Lynn LoPucki , a bankruptcy-law professor at the University of\nCalifornia, Los Angeles.  \u201cBankruptcy courts tend to favor the debtors and the\ndebtors\u2019 lawyers\u201d who bring big cases to them, said LoPucki,\nauthor of Courting Failure: How Competition for Big Cases Is\nCorrupting the Bankruptcy Courts (University of Michigan Press).\n\u201cThat puts outsiders like Barclays at a disadvantage.\u201d  Lawyers and Witnesses  During the trial, Peck has been curt with Barclays\u2019 lawyer,\n David Boies , known for representing the Justice Department in a\n1998 antitrust case against Microsoft Corp., as well as U.S.\nVice President  Al Gore  in litigation over the 2000 presidential\nvote.  \u201cYou can tell us later how Barclays saved the world,\u201d\nPeck said once to Boies. When Barclays President  Robert Diamond ,\nwhose company employs about 147,000 people in 50 countries\naround the world, answered questions without first saying\n\u201cyes\u201d or \u201cno,\u201d Peck said the witness \u201cneeds to be kept on a\nvery tight leash.\u201d  In 2009, a U.S. district judge dismissed an appeal by\ninvestors including hedge fund Bay Harbour Management LC, saying\nthey hadn\u2019t proved Peck erred in approving the sale.  Speedy Sale  The U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission and the Federal\nReserve Bank of New York encouraged the speedy sale to Barclays\nto calm global securities markets that were spooked by the\nbankruptcy. Peck fended off Lehman creditors who said the sale\nwas moving too quickly and Barclays was underpaying, denying\ntheir objections.  Within days of the sale closing, London-based Barclays\u2019\nblue and white logo replaced Lehman\u2019s at its 32-story Manhattan\nheadquarters. Barclays paid $1.54 billion in the deal, as well\nas taking over a $45 billion loan from the Fed, with collateral\nnominally worth about $49.5 billion that took months to value in\nnearly frozen markets, Barclays executives have testified in\ncourt.  Peck isn\u2019t likely to overturn his entire sale order, said\n Chip Bowles , a bankruptcy lawyer at Greenebaum Doll & McDonald\nPLLC in Louisville, Kentucky. So-called 363 sales, which helped\nthe former General Motors Corp. and Chrysler LLC to reorganize\nin bankruptcy and created jobs for 10,000 Lehman employees at\nBarclays, normally are considered final in the courts, he said.  \u201cTo say the sale is invalid would be one of most\nimportant decisions in bankruptcy history,\u201d said Bowles.  Pension Fund Challenge  Lopucki said he saw no example in his 898-case bankruptcy\ndatabase at UCLA of a 363 sale ever being overturned.  Higher courts have usually upheld the finality of 363\nsales, said Kuney. In 2009, the U.S. Supreme Court dismissed a\nchallenge by pension funds to the White House-backed bankruptcy\nplan that let Chrysler sell assets to Italy\u2019s Fiat SpA.  What Peck might do is invalidate part of the documents he\ndidn\u2019t see, lawyers said.  \u201cThe judge could find the side agreements material, and\nexclude them,\u201d said  Stephen Lubben , a bankruptcy law professor\nat Seton Hall University School of Law in Newark, New Jersey, in\nan e-mail.  Lehman and Barclays have been fighting court battles over\nsuch terms as 15c3-3 assets -- a reference to securities\nregulations -- and ETD (exchange-traded derivatives) margin that\nwere featured in a last-minute document. The first refers to a\nLehman account with $769 million while the second contained $1\nbillion of margin backing Lehman\u2019s derivatives trades, which\nBarclays says it was entitled to when it assumed Lehman\u2019s\ntrades.  Signed, Never Saw  The margin was allocated to Barclays in a single bracketed\nphrase in the final document that at least one person who signed\nit,  James Giddens  of Hughes Hubbard & Reed LLP, the trustee for\nthe brokerage, claimed not to have seen. Giddens\u2019 lawyers signed\nthe document and testified in court on his behalf.  Peck might decide Barclays should give up those or larger\namounts, lawyers said.  \u201cThe judge said, \u2018Don\u2019t make any material changes,\u2019\u201d said\nBowles. \u201cIf it\u2019s $1 billion, that\u2019s real money.\u201d  Jonathan Schiller , a lawyer for Barclays, declined to\ncomment.  Robert Gaffey , Lehman\u2019s litigation lawyer, didn\u2019t\nreturn a call and e-mail seeking comment.  Abundance of Caution  Lehman\u2019s lead bankruptcy lawyer  Harvey Miller  said during\nthe trial that he sold Barclays a business, not a collection of\nassets, and didn\u2019t see any material changes that needed Peck\u2019s\napproval. Bowles said that if he had been in Barclays\u2019s shoes he\nwould have gone to Peck \u201cout of an abundance of caution.\u201d  Peck is handling three Lehman lawsuits against Barclays,\nincluding one by Giddens and one by creditors. Giddens is\nclaiming a total of $6.7 billion, including the $3 billion\nBarclays says he owes it.  Lehman\u2019s collapse and the lamentations of its creditors\nshould be laid at the door of its former management, said  Mark Williams , a lecturer at Boston University who wrote a book on\nLehman, \u201cUncontrolled Risk.\u201d  \u201cBarclays the opportunistic acquirer is being unfairly\npunished by creditor legal actions,\u201d Williams said. \u201cCreditors\nneed to hold Lehman executives and the board of directors\naccountable for financial loss.\u201d  The case is In re Lehman Brothers Holdings Inc., 08-13555,\nU.S. Bankruptcy Court, Southern District of New York\n(Manhattan). The world\u2019s largest retailer was on track to hit 36 of the 37 energy and environment goals Duke\u2019s predecessor set for the company in 2005. Not everyone in the audience responded with glee. \u201cWhen Mike Duke made that statement, my ears turned bright red. I felt my face flushing,\u201d said Charles Zimmerman, Wal-Mart\u2019s vice president of international design and construction. He was in charge of the one initiative among 37 that was failing to deliver. \u201cI felt eyes in the auditorium turning to me.\u201d The goal that Duke was unable to report progress on in 2009 was a pledge to reduce greenhouse gas emissions 20 percent by 2012 from the Wal-Mart stores, Sam\u2019s Clubs and distribution centers that existed in 2005. \u201cThis has been a target on my forehead for the last seven years,\u201d Zimmerman said. Three years later, the final results are in. Not only had Zimmerman caught up, but he hit the goal a year early. The company\u2019s 2011 data showed a drop in emissions 20.02 percent below its 2005 baseline for the existing facilities. Overall emissions have risen in the same time period as the company continues its global expansion, from about 19 million tons of carbon dioxide equivalent in 2005 to 22 million tons in 2010, the most recent year with published data. Its revenue has increased more than 50\u00a0percent since then, to $447 billion in 2012. How Zimmerman, 52, and his colleagues hit the mark a year early offers three key lessons in corporate sustainability: Make individuals responsible for specific sustainability goals and tie their compensation to it; reduce energy demand through more efficient products and practices; and switch to renewable energy where it\u2019s cheaper than conventional power. A Journey Begins Lee Scott, Mike Duke\u2019s predecessor as Wal-Mart CEO, fired the starter\u2019s pistol for corporate sustainability globally on Oct. 24, 2005, when he delivered a landmark address called \u201cTwenty First Century Leadership\u201d [ pdf ].\u00a0In it, he set out three aspirational goals -- think of them as Wal-Mart\u2019s North Stars for sustainability -- to buy 100 percent renewable energy, to create no waste and \u201cto sell products that sustain people and the environment.\u201d Thirty-seven specific initiatives followed. The sustainability program started out as a two-person office. Their job: Get the rest of the company to internalize the new goals and make sure they achieve them.\u00a0 Andrew Ruben was the Wal-Mart\u2019s first vice president for sustainability and is now a co-founder of Yerdle.com, a website that helps people tap their social networks to find and give away used goods. He organized the Wal-Mart kingdom into groups called Sustainable Value Networks, which encourage managers to interact with each other, suppliers and experts from universities, NGOs and governments. These structures\u00a0broke Lee Scott\u2019s massive challenge into easier-to-consume pieces. \u201cAt some point we realized that every time someone at Wal-Mart makes a decision, there are 100 unintended consequences,\u201d Ruben told the  Wal-Mart Sustainability Case Project , at the University of Arkansas Sam M. Walton College of Business. \u201cSo our goal became to help every business leader understand more of the unintended consequences so they would simply make better business decisions.\u201d Project 37 Charles Zimmerman spent the first few years of Wal-Mart\u2019s sustainability drive helping design more energy-efficient U.S. buildings. He was \u201ccaptain\u201d of the Sustainable Buildings Network, the work group (Sustainable Value Network) for Wal-Mart\u2019s facilities managers. In 2009, he helped the company knock off in 2009 its goal to build facilities that are 25 to 30 percent more efficient and that reduce greenhouse gases at least 30 percent below the 2005 baseline. Zimmerman had been in his new role at Wal-Mart for just a few months before the November 2009 sustainability powwow. In response to it, he founded what he called \u201cProject 37\u201d and purchased on his own dime what he admits are \u201ccheesy buttons\u201d emblazoned with a green 37 for colleagues to wear when meeting on the subject. \u201cIn 2009, it didn\u2019t look good,\u201d he said. In fact, in 2010, the company considered telling the NGO community and the public that it wouldn\u2019t be able to meet the goal. Watch\u00a0Wal-Mart's Growth Across the U.S.: Time-Series Map Zimmerman had more than professional pride at stake. Progress toward the 20 percent goal alone was responsible for \u00a0as much as 15 percent of his performance-review metrics. The group would meet once a quarter -- 6 a.m. Bentonville time to accommodate all the time zones -- so that country leads could compare notes on what was working, and what wasn\u2019t working, in the quest to reduce emissions. A few markets, Brazil and Japan in particular, were further behind the rest of the group, lacking the money to upgrade their facilities. When Doug McMillan, CEO and president for Wal-Mart\u2019s international stores, heard about this, he pulled out his checkbook. It was a no-brainer; upgrades pay themselves back in two or three years.\u00a0 Bentonville offered Brazil and Japan more than $50 million to pay for the energy-efficiency and greenhouse-gas reduction projects. Last year, Wal-Mart stores in Japan last year put installed LED bulbs on its sales floors. Brazil did lighting retrofits and put doors on its refrigerator cases. A Changing Rate of Change The pace of change has accelerated over the course of Wal-Mart\u2019s sustainability enterprise. It takes less time today, as Zimmerman put it, \u201cto globalize a good idea,\u201d particularly when it comes to deploying new, energy efficient technology. In 2005, sustainability planners decided to change the lighting in stores\u2019 freezer cases. Replacing existing bulbs with more efficient models served the dual purposes of reducing the energy needed for lighting and for refrigeration, since LEDs don\u2019t heat up like incandescent bulbs. It took three years from beginning the replacements in the U.S. until the last market completed it.\u00a0 In 2009, stores started doing the same with parking lot lighting. Early work turned out not to be worth the effort in the continental U.S., where electricity is relatively inexpensive. Puerto Rico\u2019s higher utility rates made the project pay for itself there. They retrofitted the island\u2019s stores and then moved on to some\u00a0350 parking lots in Central America. \u201cBy scaling this up one market at a time, it helped drive down the cost of the technology,\u201d Zimmerman said. By the time they\u2019d re-lit the rest of the world, the price had come down sufficiently that it finally made sense to do the U.S. They completed the project globally in 15 months.\u00a0 Along the way the lights themselves improved. Wal-Mart told General Electric, which manufactures road and area lights, \u201cIf you develop something that meets our expectations, we\u2019ll blow this through the roof for you,\u201d he said. \u2018Over the Top\u2019 Wal-Mart is the fifth-biggest U.S. user of clean energy in the U.S., according to a  ranking  by the Environmental Protection Agency. While just four percent of the company\u2019s electricity comes from what the EPA calls \u201cgreen energy,\u201d Wal-Mart\u2019s scale means that translates into a lot of energy -- more than 751 million kilowatts a year in the U.S. alone, enough to power about 65,000 homes. \u201cI think that\u2019s one of the things that really put us over the top,\u201d said Greg Trimble, Wal-Mart\u2019s senior director of global energy development and reporting. Some leading companies source vastly more than four percent of their own electricity from renewables. Intel, Staples and Kohl\u2019s Department Stores buy  100 percent green energy . Clean power makes up at least 30 percent of the electricity purchased by McDonald\u2019s, Lockheed Martin and Microsoft. The Unconvinced Not all environmentalists are on board with the greening of Wal-Mart. Stacy Mitchell is a senior researcher at the  Institute of Local Self-Reliance  and author of the 2006 book  Big Box Swindle: The True Cost of Mega-Retailers and the Fight for America\u2019s Independent Businesses . She published a critical report about Wal-Mart in March 2012, called \" Wal-Mart's Greenwash \"\u00a0(which Sustainability journalist Marc Gunther has written about\u00a0 here ). Mitchell emphasizes that Wal-Mart\u2019s emissions overall have grown as it continues to open stores around the world. The company\u2019s most recent  Global Responsibility Report , released in April, said that by the end of 2010 it had cut emissions 12.74 percent at the existing facilities\u2019 2005 baseline. The total greenhouse gas footprint grew 13.8 percent in that time.\u00a0 \u201cWhat Wal-Mart is doing on sustainability, I would argue, is more dangerous than greenwashing because to a degree there is a real impact to what their doing. What they do is they make improvements on the margin and because of the size of the company, they can often tout very big numbers in terms of waste reduced and that kind of thing,\u201d Mitchell said.\u00a0 \u201cIt\u2019s very easy for them to produce headlines that are very appealing, and seem hard to argue with. But when you really step back and look at the bigger picture, you see as a company that it really is in effect using sustainability as a growth strategy,\" she said. \"And Wal-Mart\u2019s growth is very bad for the environment.\u201d Many on Wall Street are skeptical that sustainability efforts at global companies are reflected in stock performance. Asked if sustainability is ever a factor in research, either as a proxy for management, or as a risk factor, Colin McGranahan, a retail sector analyst at Sanford C. Bernstein & Co., said in an email, \u201cNever a factor. Ever. Cannot rise to the level of materiality to the stock performance, which is our sole focus.\" No Rest for the Weary Charles Zimmerman bought cigars for Project 37 team members when their goal was in reach, last September. The cigar band carries the same green 37 that\u2019s emblazoned on their buttons. \u201cWe celebrated for a few minutes and now we\u2019re moving on to the next set of goals,\u201d he said. So far, the industry has been able to thwart\nthe most serious attacks and protect its clients, but hackers\nare adapting and growing more dangerous.  It is vital that Congress recognize the urgency of this\nsituation and take action to provide the private sector with the\ntools and support it needs to defend the millions of Americans\nit serves every day.  One of the most alarming trends is the increasing number of\ncyber-attacks on smaller financial institutions and businesses.\nThese organizations typically don\u2019t have the same resources or\naccess to information that larger companies do. This makes them\nmore vulnerable to a malicious attack that could disrupt capital\nmarkets and shake investor confidence in the financial system.  Hackers are also using individuals and smaller institutions\nas a gateway to infiltrate larger banking organizations.\nEveryone is a target.  Even in the absence of congressional action, cybersecurity\nis a top priority for the financial industry. It is devoting\nsignificant resources to build infrastructure and develop\nprocesses that protect clients, companies and the integrity of\ncapital markets.  Evolving Threats  My trade group, the Securities Industry and Financial\nMarkets Association, is organizing an industrywide exercise\ncalled \u201cQuantum Dawn 2\u201d on July 18. This exercise will\nsimulate a cyber-attack on the U.S. financial system. It will\nforce individual companies to test their response plans in order\nto maintain effective and orderly markets and protect client\ndata.  The simulation will include more than 50 companies and\nexchanges, as well as the U.S. Treasury Department, the\nSecurities and Exchange Commission and the Department of\nHomeland Security.  Industry efforts alone are insufficient. President  Barack\nObama  got it right in his Feb. 12  executive order , which\nencourages partnerships between the federal government and\nprivate-sector businesses. But we need more information from the\nU.S. government on the diverse and evolving threats we are\nfacing. Moreover, this information must be timely and\nactionable. The government has the resources to gather, process\nand disseminate intelligence on cyberthreats. Unfortunately,\nmost of the time it can\u2019t share that information with the\nprivate sector until after a cyber-attack has occurred. The\nindustry needs access to this threat information before an\nattack so it can proactively prepare and defend clients\u2019\ninformation and assets.  Likewise, if a financial company is the target of an attack\n-- whether successful or not -- or has intelligence on a new\nthreat, that information must be shared with government agencies\nand other companies that could be affected. Yet companies are\ncautious about sharing threat information that could be used to\nstop future attacks. Why? Currently there are no liability\nprotections for companies that share pertinent data. That has to\nchange. As Treasury Secretary Jacob Lew recently noted we need\nCongress to pass legislation that encourages and simplifies the\nflow of information between the government and the private\nsector.  Done right, information-sharing is the best way to keep our\nclients protected and our companies enabled to defeat the most\ncritical threats. For example, last month, Microsoft Corp. and\nthe Federal Bureau of Investigation successfully coordinated the\nglobal takedown of a ring that raided bank accounts around the\nworld and netted more than half a billion dollars.  Critics of information-sharing say that the practice raises\ntoo many privacy concerns. These are unfounded: The industry\ntakes client privacy very seriously and only shares information\nwhen absolutely necessary to address a threat. It also makes\nevery effort to keep shared data anonymous.  Ensuring Privacy  The reality is that we are dealing with attackers who have\nno respect for privacy and will try to access and exploit client\ninformation by any means. To not share threat information would\nbe like a citizen witnessing a robbery and not reporting it to\nthe police: Nobody gains.  Common-sense legislation would promote information-sharing,\nupdate the criminal penalties associated with cyber-attacks, and\nprovide protections for companies that share information and\nrespond to malicious activity. Of course, legislation must also\nensure the privacy of information that flows between companies\nand the government.  The government, the private sector and all Americans must\nremain vigilant in the face of cyber-attacks. The time is right\nfor Congress to pass legislation that will ensure the resiliency\nof the economy as we navigate this new frontier of criminal\nactivity.  (Judd Gregg, a former U.S. senator from New Hampshire, is\nchief executive officer of the Securities Industry and Financial\nMarkets Association.) Five years ago, Emergence  Capital Partners  made a $4\nmillion investment in  Veeva Systems Inc. (VEEV) , a startup that\ndevelops cloud software to help pharmaceutical companies manage\ntheir sales operations. After Veeva\u2019s debut today on the  New\nYork Stock Exchange (NYX) , the company was valued at $4.4 billion.\nEmergence, Veeva\u2019s biggest investor, owns a stake worth more\nthan $1.2 billion, a 300-fold return on its investment.  Assuming Veeva\u2019s stock holds or increases its value until\ninsiders can start selling in six months, the gains will be more\nthan six times the size of the $200 million fund that Emergence\nraised in 2007. That means big profits for the fund\u2019s investors,\nincluding the  California Public Employees\u2019 Retirement System  and\nthe  University of Michigan , Bloomberg.com reported on its  Tech\nDeals  blog.  Emergence is based in San Mateo, California -- halfway\nbetween San Francisco and the epicenter of Silicon Valley\u2019s Sand\nHill Road. The firm opened in the wake of the dot-com collapse\nin 2003, when technology investing had practically evaporated.\nIt\u2019s since raised $575 million over three funds.  Emergence\u2019s partners were betting that businesses would\nmove from paying for software licenses to buying Web-based\nservices on a subscription basis. That was the only way\n business-software  startups could generate revenue, because\ncustomers weren\u2019t willing to pony up millions of dollars\nupfront, Brian Jacobs, one of Emergence\u2019s three founders, said\nat a conference in July.  \u2018Tough Times\u2019  \u201cIn the very tough times of the bust, we saw that there\nwere companies that were succeeding and growing,\u201d Jacobs said.  For its first investment, Emergence bought a $1 million\nstake in Salesforce.com Inc. at about 40 cents a share (on a\nsplit-adjusted basis) the year before founder  Marc Benioff  took\nthe company public. The stock closed yesterday at $50.72.  Salesforce pioneered the software-as-a-service, or SaaS,\nmodel, a term that didn\u2019t even exist when Emergence was scouring\nthe market for deals. The firm went on to back SuccessFactors\nInc., which SAP AG bought for $3.4 billion in February 2012, and\nYammer Inc., snapped up a few months later by Microsoft Corp.\nfor $1.2 billion. Other companies still in the portfolio include\nBill.com Inc., Box Inc. and Lithium Technologies Inc.  \u201cEmergence deserves credit for betting their whole fund on\nSaaS long before it was popular,\u201d Yammer CEO David Sacks wrote\nin an e-mail.  Specialized Software  Gordon Ritter, a partner at Emergence and the chairman of\nVeeva\u2019s board, said the company\u2019s focus on a specific industry\nburdened by legacy systems has led to its rapid growth.  \u201cThis company got to a substantial revenue rate on less\ntime and fewer dollars than any other company I\u2019ve\nexperienced,\u201d Ritter said today in an interview.  In March, Ritter likened Veeva to a Salesforce for the\npharmaceutical industry. (7267) \u2019s aviation project 27 years ago at a hangar in Mississippi. Next year, Fujino, now president of the aircraft unit, says the project may finally get off the ground.  If so, Tokyo-based Honda would become the first newcomer to get U.S. approval in the $21 billion business-jet market since 2006. That would pit the carmaker against market leaders  Textron Inc. (TXT) \u2019s Cessna and  Brazil \u2019s  Embraer SA (EMBR3) , who have fended off threats from companies such as Bill Gates-backed Eclipse Aviation, which sought bankruptcy protection five years ago.  Though delivery of the HondaJet hasn\u2019t started, Fujino said he has clinched two to three years of orders for the $4.5 million plane and signaled the business will turn profitable before the end of the decade. The seven-seater plane, which Fujino calls a \u201cflying sports car\u201d or \u201cflying Acura,\u201d will be 15 percent more fuel efficient, have roomier cabin space and fly 10 percent faster than comparable aircraft, he said.  Skeptics abound.  \u201cThere are no newcomers to business aviation, only cautionary tales,\u201d said George Tsopeis, vice president at Montreal-based Zenith Jet, an aviation advisory firm. \u201cIf Honda manages to bring the HondaJet to market, that alone will be an accomplishment.\u201d  Aviator Glasses  Wearing aviator-style prescription glasses, Fujino said he expects the unconventionally designed jet -- the engines are on top of the wings -- to get clearance from the U.S. Federal Aviation Administration by next year.  He has said that before. Honda has delayed the debut of the plane every year since targeting deliveries in 2010 for reasons ranging from difficulties procuring components to parts damage caused by ice. The company says it\u2019s getting closer, in May announcing that its fifth FAA-conforming HondaJet successfully completed its first flight.  To get permission from the FAA, a manufacturer must demonstrate that the plane meets U.S. regulations on everything from the strength of the wings to how it lands in a crosswind. Most of the process is conducted behind closed doors because the test data and designs supplied by aircraft manufacturers are considered proprietary and confidential.  Certification is a \u201clong and arduous process\u201d that typically involves testing four to five aircraft for 2,000 flight hours, Tsopeis said. Once a company gets the nod from the FAA, it becomes easier to win certification from other aviation jurisdictions, he said.  Founder\u2019s Dream  The FAA doesn\u2019t comment on pending aircraft certification, it said in an e-mailed statement. Representatives at Cessna and Embraer didn\u2019t respond to e-mails seeking comment.  The start of deliveries would fulfill the wishes of the company\u2019s late founder, Soichiro Honda, who died in 1991. Though the carmaker doesn\u2019t expect the business to be a big profit contributor, it has pursued the project partly as a tribute to the founder, Chairman Fumihiko Ike said in an interview this month.  In the fiscal year ended March,  automobiles and motorcycles  accounted for 92 percent of Honda\u2019s revenue and 73 percent of operating profit.  Dead End  For Fujino, the jet\u2019s debut would come more than three decades after the company assigned him, then 26, to be the fifth member of a team dedicated to figuring out how to make planes -- a task he recalls seeming like such a dead end that he initially turned it down.  \u201cI joined Honda to make cars,\u201d he said. \u201cBut it\u2019s a company order so regardless of what I wanted, I was moved to the plane department. The finding was so bizarre that a friend at  NASA  advised him to drop it or risk ruining his career, he said. Fujino said he hesitated for half a year.  In 1996, in the midst of  Japan \u2019s first \u201clost decade,\u201d 35-year-old Fujino had to plead to Honda\u2019s board through several presentations not to scrap the unprofitable project. Chairman Harold A. Poling, filed for bankruptcy protection in 2008 as demand dried up.
