(WMT)  doesn\u2019t foreclose the ability of employees to bring\nsimilar suits for many other types of claims against companies.  The ruling \u201cis adding a higher burden\u201d of proof before an\nemployment discrimination class action can be certified, said\nCyrus Mehri, a Washington lawyer who represents workers in such\ncases. Plaintiffs lawyers said other class actions against\ncompanies, including those alleging bias over a written company\npolicy, product liability for items such as defective medicines\nor claims against banks for illegal fees, may not be affected.  \u201cTo get a class certified, there will have to be a closer\nlink between cause and effect,\u201d said Mehri, who recently won a\n$32 million settlement in a gender bias lawsuit against  Wells\nFargo & Co . \u201cIn the employment area, it\u2019s a steeper climb for\nplaintiffs.\u201d  Class certification allows workers to pursue their claims\nas a group, pooling resources and putting greater pressure on\ndefendants to settle. Companies often seek to avoid classes,\ninstead attempting to fight employees one-by-one, forcing them\nto use their own financial resources to litigate.  The Supreme Court today said lawyers for women suing\nBentonville, Arkansas-based Wal-Mart failed to point to a common\ncorporate policy that led to gender discrimination at thousands\nof its U.S. stores. The court said the women couldn\u2019t pursue\ntheir claims in a nationwide class action, or group suit, because \nthey hadn\u2019t shown a sufficient connection between their claims.  \u2018No Convincing Proof\u2019  \u201cBecause respondents provide no convincing proof of a\ncompanywide discriminatory pay and promotion policy, we have\nconcluded that they have not established the existence of any\ncommon question,\u201d Justice  Antonin Scalia  wrote for the\nmajority, reversing a lower court ruling. Use of statistical and\nanecdotal evidence to show managers discriminated and exercised\nthese decisions in a common way fell \u201cwell short,\u201d he said.  The ruling limits the ability of plaintiffs\u2019 lawyers to win\nmultimillion dollar damages through a single lawsuit,\nparticularly against employers. Units of Cigna Corp., Goldman\nSachs Group Inc., Bayer AG, Toshiba Corp., Publicis Group SA,\nDeere & Co. and Costco Wholesale Corp. all face gender\ndiscrimination complaints that seek class-action status.  More than 20 companies supported Wal-Mart at the Supreme\nCourt, including  Intel Corp ., Altria Group Inc., Bank of America\nCorp., Microsoft Corp. and General Electric Co.  Pattern of Discrimination  The lawsuit, filed in 2001, claimed Wal-Mart engaged in a\npattern of discrimination against women in pay and promotions\nnationwide and sought to cover every woman who worked at the\ncompany\u2019s stores from 1998 onward.  The court \u201creversed about 40 years of jurisprudence,\u201d\nsaid Joseph Sellers, attorney for the women suing Wal-Mart. The\ndecision forces a consideration of the merits of a claim at the\nclass certification stage, contrary to prior practice, Sellers\nsaid at a press conference today.  Sellers and co-counsel  Brad Seligman  said the lawyers would\nbe pursuing individual actions against the company and may\npursue smaller class actions.  \u201cThere are a number of options still available,\u201d he said.\n\u201cNone of them are as efficient\u201d as a nationwide class action.\n\u201cWal-Mart may regret the day\u201d it sought a rejection of class\ncertification, he said.  \u201cThe case is not over,\u201d said Seligman. \u201cWal-Mart is not\noff the hook.\u201d  Women Nationwide  About 12,000 women nationwide have contacted the lawyers\nsuing Wal-Mart to join the case, Seligman said. The company said\nin a statement that the ruling \u201ceffectively ends this class-\naction lawsuit.\u201d  \u201cThe plaintiffs\u2019 claims were worlds away from showing a\ncompanywide pay and promotion policy,\u201d Wal-Mart said.  Mehri said the justices added a new hurdle for plaintiffs.  Previously, employment lawyers seeking to have a class\naction allowed \u201chad to show that there is a common issue of\nfact,\u201d the lawyer said. Today\u2019s decision would require lawyers\nto \u201cshow that the common issue predominates,\u201d he said.  Plaintiffs\u2019 lawyers would have to provide more evidence\nbefore seeking a class certification decision, he said.  \u201cThere has to be greater proof of causation, so you see\nthe disparities,\u201d Mehri said in an interview.  The decision may have limited effect on some other pending\nbias class actions, said Seligman. He is also representing women\nsuing Issaquah, Washington-based Costco over gender\ndiscrimination. \u201cCostco was a much narrower case,\u201d covering\ntwo types of managers who were affected by decisions made above\nthe store level, he said.  \u2018Very Specifically\u2019  The justices \u201cfocus very specifically on our case,\u201d\nSeligman said of today\u2019s ruling. \u201cIt\u2019s not at all clear on the\nimpact\u201d on these other cases, he said.  Today\u2019s decision may change how plaintiffs\u2019 lawyers pursue\nclaims, Mehri said. While the decision doesn\u2019t affect cases\nalready settled, it may alter a lawsuit he\u2019s pursuing claiming\ngender bias against Ruth\u2019s Chris Steak House, Mehri said.  \u201cWe will be informed by the Supreme Court on how we shape\nour filings,\u201d he said. \u201cIt doesn\u2019t stop the case by any\nstretch.\u201d  The decision isn\u2019t likely to affect other class actions\nalleging other types corporate wrongdoing, said attorney Michael\nDonovan, who represents Wal-Mart workers in  Pennsylvania  suing\nthe company over wage-and-hour claims.  \u201cI don\u2019t think it has that much significance for most\ngeneral class actions,\u201d Donovan said in an interview. \u201cIt was\npretty much tied to whether the plaintiffs could prove a\ncompanywide policy or practice of discrimination.\u201d  Manager Discretion  The plaintiffs claimed in the Wal-Mart case that allowing\nindividual store managers\u2019 discretion to make their own\ndecisions may provide the basis of a disparate impact theory --\nthat women were affected more adversely than men by the policy.  While the judges found that such a theory can be pursued in\na class action lawsuit, that the claim can \u201cexist does not lead\nto the conclusion that every employee in a company using a\nsystem of discretion has such a claim in common,\u201d Scalia wrote.  The workers\u2019 lawyers \u201chave identified no \u2018specific\nemployment practice\u2019 -- much less one that ties all their 1.5\nmillion claims together,\u201d Scalia wrote. \u201cMerely showing that\nWal-Mart\u2019s policy of discretion has produced an overall sex-\nbased disparity does not suffice.\u201d  Donovan said this aspect of the ruling \u201cmakes it difficult\nfor employees to sue for corporate culture claims where there\nisn\u2019t any direct evidence but for the impact.\u201d Lawsuits outside\nthe employment arena often have business records plaintiffs can\nuse to prove claims, he noted.  Preclude Class Actions  The Supreme Court decision would only preclude class\nactions in lawsuits where there wasn\u2019t some sort of test or\npolicy or uniform condition, or business records pointing to\nthose items, Donovan said.  \u201cThere\u2019s not a whole lot of cases like that out there.\u201d  The court ruling makes pursuit of discrimination class\nactions \u201cvery difficult,\u201d said  David Sanford , a  Washington \nlawyer who won a $175 million settlement in a gender bias suit\nagainst Novartis AG.  \u201cIt\u2019s not impossible. It hasn\u2019t closed the door, but it\u2019s\nmade the challenge much harder,\u201d Sanford said in an interview.  \u201cThe Supreme Court has articulated a view that if you have\na policy of not discriminating, and if you have a company that\u2019s\nbig, and you\u2019re a plaintiff suing that company, if you cannot\nidentify a policy that suggests sex discrimination, then you\u2019re\nin trouble,\u201d he said.  Lawyers representing workers may begin filing claims with\nsubclasses, rather than as companywide actions, he said.  Multiple Bias Suits  Sanford has multiple bias lawsuits seeking class action\nstatus against companies including Philadelphia-based Cigna,\nBayer, Eaton Corp. and Toshiba. All these cases are in \u201cfairly\nearly stages of litigation,\u201d and motions for class\ncertification haven\u2019t been filed, he said.  The precise impact of today\u2019s decision on these cases\nhasn\u2019t been determined, he said.  \u201cWe\u2019re going to have to look at it very carefully,\u201d he\nsaid.  Sanford said he used the same theory of law in his Novartis\ncase that lawyers for the Wal-Mart plaintiffs used in theirs --\nthat the company\u2019s policies allowed a disparate impact on pay\nand promotions for women.  \u201cThat\u2019s a theory that plaintiffs won\u2019t be able to avail\nourselves of going forward,\u201d he said. \u201cWe\u2019re going to have to\nlook at ways to alter our theory.\u201d  Another change that may result from today\u2019s ruling is to\nthe plaintiffs\u2019 employment bar, Sanford said.  \u201cThere aren\u2019t many plaintiffs lawyers who do this work,\u201d\nhe said. \u201cThat number will shrink further.\u201d  The case is  Wal-Mart Stores  v. Managers will no longer be required to rate workers on a fixed scale of performance rankings, Lisa Brummel, Microsoft\u2019s executive vice president of human resources, said in a memo to the company\u2019s 99,000 staff.  \u201cGE and  Jack Welch  were leaders in this and Ford tried it, but it\u2019s never really caught on and the nature of work is changing,\u201d said Fred Foulkes, a professor of organizational behavior at the Boston University School of Management. \u201cYou can\u2019t just keep cutting the bottom 10 percent.\u201d  Microsoft\u2019s previous stack-ranking system required a fixed number of workers on a team to be graded poorly, with only a few awarded top ratings. While the policy has been tweaked over the years, the rank and file have long complained that the rules discouraged teamwork and forced poor scores onto good employees to meet quotas. The new initiative follows the \u201cOne Microsoft\u201d strategy unveiled by outgoing Chief Executive Officer  Steve Ballmer  in July, aimed at better cooperation among various products and initiatives at the world\u2019s largest software maker.  Forced Rankings  General Electric Co. (GE) , the world\u2019s largest maker of  jet engines  and diesel locomotives, backed away from forced rankings when Welch was CEO, Foulkes said. Such gradings have always been difficult in industries where measuring performance is subjective, he said.  Ford Motor Co. (F) \u2019s attempt to implement a program based on a fixed scale of performance grading forced managers to rank some employees as a \u201cC\u201d on a measure that started with \u201cA,\u201d and workers could face elimination if the grade didn\u2019t improve. It was scuttled in 2001, after some workers who were fired filed lawsuits and the system proved to be generally unpopular.  \u201cThese types of systems can really demoralize and disengage employees,\u201d said Lisa Gerhardt, a partner at recruitment firm Boyden Global Executive Search, who heads the human resources practice. \u201cWith companies having to do more with less people, if you don\u2019t have employees engaged, productivity is going to suffer.\u201d  \u2018Company Goals\u2019  Managers will be free to allocate compensation as they see fit within their budgets, Microsoft\u2019s Brummel wrote in the memo, which was obtained by Bloomberg and confirmed by Redmond, Washington-based Microsoft. The company is also doing away with performance ratings altogether and evaluating employees based on how well they work with others.  \u201cWe have taken feedback from thousands of employees over the past few years, we have reviewed numerous external programs and practices and have sought to determine the best way to make sure our feedback mechanisms support our company goals and objectives,\u201d Brummel wrote. \u201cThe changes we are making are important and necessary as we work to deliver innovation and value to customers through more connected engagement across the company.\u201d  Microsoft will still need to maintain a system to allow managers to rank good and bad employees, said Marc Effron, president of the Talent Strategy Group, a consulting firm. Facebook Inc. (FB) \u2019s founder will soon have to \u201clike\u201d China,\nwhere his website is banned. A post-initial-public-offering\nFacebook will have shareholders demanding that it tap China\u2019s\n1.3 billion people, and now. Such is life when your business\nmodel is predicated on ever-growing ranks of users updating,\nsharing and poking to make advertisers and  investors  rich.  Zuckerberg will certainly face difficulties. Facebook\u2019s\nrole in the Arab Spring movement caused many sleepless nights\nfor Communist Party bigwigs. Yet more focus should be on the\nthings  China (SHCOMP)  and Facebook have in common -- things that may not\njibe with Zuckerberg\u2019s claims of making the world a better\nplace.  Let\u2019s imagine a conversation between Zuckerberg and Chinese\nPresident  Hu Jintao . Zuckerberg might greet Hu as the supreme\nleader of world\u2019s biggest marketplace; Hu might refer to the\nhoodie-clad American as the supreme leader of the Internet\nworld.  \u201cContrary to what you might think, it will be great to\nhave Facebook in China,\u201d Hu might say. \u201cMy billion-plus people\nare used to having no privacy and relish losing even more of it\nthanks to your blue and white pages. That pleases me.\u201d  Privacy Lost  Zuckerberg (FB)  might retort: \u201cYes, Mr. President, you will be\nhappy to know that my people, just under a billion users mind\nyou, also look forward to sharing what\u2019s left of their privacy\nwith you and me.\u201d (Maniacal laughs all around.)  \u201cSee, Mr. Zuckerberg, we are not so different,\u201d Hu adds.\n\u201cWe both exert complete power over populations more eager to\nsurrender it than they realize.\u201d Adds Zuckerberg: \u201cAnd you\nhave to admit there\u2019s a silver lining here -- this will really\nstick it to  Google. (GOOG)  Neither of us likes them very much.\u201d  Moments after their meeting, Hu turns to his staff and\nsays: \u201cHe is the perfect foil for our designs on ruling\ncyberspace.\u201d Zuckerberg tells his own: \u201cHe is the perfect\nfoil for our designs on ruling cyberspace.\u201d  China\u2019s leaders will expect Facebook to bow to their\ncensorship demands the way Google Inc., Yahoo! Inc., Microsoft\nCorp. and Cisco Systems Inc. have. Twitter Inc. recently made an\nabout-face, announcing it will block posts on behalf of\ngovernments. And Facebook will look forward to mining what it\ncan from China\u2019s masses, just as it does America\u2019s.  That\u2019s probably not the Faustian bargain  Time magazine \nenvisioned in 2010 when it dubbed Zuckerberg \u201cPerson of the\nYear.\u201d For all the hype about Facebook as a force for\ndemocracy, its profit model is predicated on something very\ndifferent, and its side effects are still being counted.  Wall Street views Facebook as an unstoppable, limitless\nforce, much like economists thinking  China  can grow 10 percent\nforever. Facebook views our privacy as a commodity to be bought,\nsold and monetized, much as China\u2019s government benefits from\nkeeping close tabs on the masses. China\u2019s vast supply of low-\nwage workers comes from the nation\u2019s hinterlands; Zuckerberg\u2019s\ncheap-labor source is Facebook users.  Just like financiers wary of China, many Facebook users\nhave too much invested in the social-media juggernaut to walk\naway. Those miffed by Facebook mining their lives for profit\nthink it\u2019s too big of a phenomenon to blow off. It\u2019s one thing\nfor socially responsible investors to steer clear of tobacco and\noil stocks; China is quite something else.  Rights Surrendered  Facebook\u2019s governance structure resembles a dictatorship by\nrequiring investors to surrender rights to Zuckerberg. He now\ncontrols 56.9 percent of voting power and has the right to\nappoint his successor, a \u201cdisquieting factor,\u201d says Gamco\nInvestors Inc.\u2019s  Larry Haverty  in Rye,  New York . Yet asked in a\nFeb. 8 Bloomberg interview whether a growth-stock investor like\nhim wants to own Facebook, he said: \u201cabsolutely.\u201d  The bulls are so enthusiastic about China and Facebook that\nthey have no time for questions about whether either has peaked.\nChina proved it can grow for three years without U.S. and\nEuropean consumers. Doing so for two or three more years is\nanother story.  Critics question how many Facebook accounts are genuinely\nactive and how many are duplicates. I know loads of people who\nhave more than one account -- one for work, one for play. And\nwhat if China goes the way of  Japan  and  South Korea (KOSPI) , where\nsocial networkers prefer local offerings?  Facebook faces as existential a question as any  Internet\ncompany  does: Is it a virtual part of our lives or a real one?\nEven if it\u2019s true that some people are on Facebook for eight\nhours a day or more, does that ensure they will reach for their\ncredit cards? What if users become irate at the lack of\nopportunities to opt out of  Facebook \u2019s efforts to monetize them?  In a pre-IPO pledge not to sell out,  Zuckerberg said  he\nwants \u201cto change how people relate to their governments.\u201d Will\nsuch sophomoric idealism survive the Beijing challenge?\nFacebook\u2019s own China-like ways suggests that\u2019s highly doubtful. But this craft, built by a Dutch company called  U-Boat Worx , will carry three people as deep as 3,000 feet beneath the waves, allowing any billionaire to get his Captain Nemo on.  Megayacht owners are accustomed to their toys: Windsurfing boards, Jet Skis and helicopters are common. Submarines are just the latest addition to this aquatic arsenal,  Bloomberg Pursuits  magazine will report in its Autumn 2013 issue.  More from the Autumn issue of   Bloomberg Pursuits : \u201cYachting is not just about sitting in a marina and sipping martinis anymore,\u201d says Marc Deppe, vice president for sales and marketing at Vero Beach,  Florida \u2013based  Triton Submarines , one of a half-dozen companies globally producing so-called personal submersibles. \u201cOwners want the yacht to be an experiential platform where they go to unique places and see unique things and provide their families and guests with an adventure.\u201d  Among those known to harbor subs aboard their boats are Microsoft Corp. billionaire  Paul Allen , who owns the 414-foot (126-meter) Octopus, and Russian oligarch  Roman Abramovich , whose 537-foot Eclipse held the title of world\u2019s largest superyacht before being bested by the 590-foot Azzam, launched earlier this year by German luxury-boat builder Lurssen Werft GmbH, which declined to identify its owner.  Undersea Champagne  Unlike scuba diving, subs don\u2019t require passengers to complete certification courses, squeeze into neoprene, worry about the bends or even actually get wet. Once ensconced, occupants are sped along by electric propellers at 2 to 3 nautical miles (3.7 to 5.6 kilometers) per hour and can remain submerged for six to 16 hours, traveling farther, faster and for longer periods of time than even the most-accomplished conventional diver.  Although film director  James Cameron  famously reached the deepest point on the planet, the Mariana Trench, in an uncomfortably cramped, custom-built, single-occupancy vehicle, most submersibles aimed at the yachting set are appropriately plush: Passengers can kibitz while sunk into leather seats, play tunes through an iPod docking station and even sip Champagne pulled from an onboard chiller. Hydrophones allow passengers to listen in on dolphins, whales and other sea creatures. And many subs are outfitted with robotic arms or video-equipped remotely operated vehicles that can fly out to examine objects on the seabed.  Surveying Giant Squid  \u201cPeople see it as an expedition tool in terms of finding new things,\u201d says Bert Houtman, the former Dutch software entrepreneur who founded U-Boat Worx in 2005 largely to fulfill a boyhood dream of building his very own sub.  Although the most-brilliant tropical fish and corals are found in relatively shallow waters, personal submersibles can explore parts of the ocean that would otherwise remain beyond reach. In 2012, researchers used one of Triton\u2019s 1,000-meter-rated subs, lent by hedge-fund billionaire  Ray Dalio , to find and film a living giant squid for the first time. That same year, Allen lent his sub to an aborted attempt to salvage the bell from the Royal Navy cruiser HMS Hood, which was sunk during World War II. Richmond,  California \u2013based  Hawkes Ocean Technologies  even designed a sub capable of descending to 37,000 feet, which billionaire entrepreneur  Richard Branson  is using in his attempt to reach the deepest points beneath all of the world\u2019s oceans.  $1 Million And Up  Because the industry is largely unregulated, safety is an obvious concern, Houtman says. To reassure potential customers, the leading sub companies -- including Hawkes, Triton and U-Boat, along with Nautilus Submarines,  SEAmagine Hydrospace  and  Sub Aviator Systems  -- voluntarily submit their submersibles to rating by the American Bureau of Shipping, Lloyd\u2019s Register of Shipping, Germanischer Lloyd AG or  Italy \u2019s RINA. Most companies also require that would-be pilots complete a three-week training course and that at least one member of the yacht\u2019s crew other than the pilot knows how to launch, recover and monitor a sub\u2019s progress from the surface.  At a cost of about $1 million for a two-person capsule with the shallowest depth rating and upwards of $4 million for the largest, deepest-diving models, personal submersibles still constitute a relatively small market, with no more than 50 currently in operation worldwide, Houtman says.  Cranes Not Cost  However, in the short term, the biggest limit to growth in the market isn\u2019t cost, he says, but cranes. Rather than surfacing directly into the belly of its megayacht mother ship, a la  James Bond , minisubs spend their off-duty hours on deck, and most large yachts don\u2019t have the cranes capable of lifting and launching the vehicles, which can weigh from 6,000 to 18,000 pounds (2,700 to 8,200 kilograms).  To surmount this obstacle, Triton is now designing specialized tenders -- companion vessels costing from $2 million to $2.5 million and made specifically to store, launch and recover subs. Meanwhile, multiple yacht makers are pursuing the dream of launching directly from the bowels of a boat.  \u201cI have had a number of clients ask me about incorporating a personal submersible,\u201d says Luca Boldrini, head of sales and marketing at Italian yacht builder CRN. Cost and safety concerns tend to put them off, he says.  Houtman, however, compares the submersible market with yacht-based helicopters.  \u201cThirty years ago, people thought it was crazy to talk about putting helicopters on private yachts,\u201d he says. \u201cNow, it is not unusual for megayachts to have a helipad.\u201d  Abramovich\u2019s Eclipse has two. This particular race to the bottom, it would seem, is just getting started. Luxury\ncarmakers such as Daimler AG are benefiting from the euro\u2019s\nslide against the dollar, while the euro\u2019s weakness against the\nyen may have curbed earnings at Japanese technology firms.  \n Global Indicators  \n Sales at non-financial companies will be the best\nindicators of the economy\u2019s health worldwide, said  Sinan Akiman ,\nchief investment officer at Istanbul-based Garanti Asset\nManagement, which oversees $4.2 billion.  \n \u201cIf there is no, or very limited, increase in sales of\nnon-financial companies, that means the economy is still not\nrecovering,\u201d Akiman said. \u201cWe should especially look at big\nretail industry companies.\u201d  \n In the U.S., earnings gains for S&P 500 companies will\ncontinue through the second half of 2010 and average 34 percent\nfor the full year, analysts surveyed by Bloomberg project.  \n \u201cOur economy is beginning to repair itself, but it\u2019s by no\nmeans ready to run a marathon,\u201d said  Matt McCormick  of\nCincinnati-based Bahl & Gaynor Inc., which has $2.8 billion\nunder management. \u201cI do see earnings growth, but it\u2019s not going\nto be broad based.\u201d  \n Alcoa Inc. , the first company in the Dow Jones Industrial\nAverage to report earnings for the second quarter, may post a\nprofit for the first time in three quarters on July 12.  \n Materials Companies  \n Alcoa, based in New York, and other commodities companies\nmay see earnings growth of 46 percent in the three months\nthrough September, down from a projected 93 percent gain in the\nsecond quarter, analysts estimated. The leveraged buyout by  Silver Lake  Management LLC and founder  Michael Dell  would be the biggest since at least 2007, with an enterprise value of about $22 billion, according to data compiled by Bloomberg. The size of the deal probably will amplify potential buyers\u2019 confidence, spurring them to tackle more targets, said Sandler O\u2019Neill & Partners LP\u2019s Devin Ryan.  \u201cLBO activity historically has led the M&A markets more broadly,\u201d said Ryan, an analyst with the New York-based boutique investment bank. \u201cMore LBOs generally spark more strategic activity as well -- it all kind of ties into together.\u201d  Dell, also  chief executive officer , and Silver Lake announced today that they\u2019re taking the world\u2019s third-largest personal-computer maker private in a deal that values the equity at $24.4 billion, according to a statement. They\u2019re financing the transaction through a combination of cash and debt, including a $2 billion loan from Microsoft Corp. The biggest takeover of a computer maker was Hewlett-Packard Co.\u2019s purchase of Compaq Computer Corp. in 2002 for about $19 billion.  Silver Lake is taking advantage of record-low borrowing costs in the market for  junk bonds , where LBOs are financed. Banks arranged $638 billion of leveraged loans last year, compared with $592 billion in 2011, Bloomberg data show. Companies issued $359 billion in U.S. high-yield debt last year, the most in the country\u2019s history.  Debt Markets Open  \u201cThe debt markets are wide open,\u201d said Daniel Tiemann, head of transactions and restructuring services in the Americas for KPMG LLP. \u201cIt\u2019s like the party\u2019s all set and we\u2019re just waiting for the sellers to show up. Confidence is what is going to make the sellers show up.\u201d  While big LBOs will remain relatively rare, a handful of situations similar to Dell\u2019s are already in the works, said R.J. Hottovy, a senior analyst with  Morningstar Inc. (MORN)  in  Chicago . For example, Best Buy Co. founder Richard Schulze began negotiating last year to take the Richfield, Minnesota-based retailer private. Schulze, like Dell founder Michael Dell, owns part of his takeover target, with a  21 percent stake  as of December.  The Dell transaction builds on momentum from the fourth quarter, the only bright spot for M&A last year. While global volume shrank almost 9 percent to $2.2 trillion in 2012, the final three months of the year were the busiest for deals since 2008, with more than $700 billion in transactions, according to data compiled by Bloomberg.  Private-Equity Performance  There were more than $400 billion in private-equity deals last year, according to data compiled by Bloomberg, a 21 percent decline from a year earlier and the smallest amount since the depths of the financial crisis. The Dell acquisition dwarfs the LBOs over that period, such as the $7.15 billion takeover of El Paso Corp.\u2019s oil and natural gas exploration business, led by  Apollo Global Management LLC. (MSFT)  manager pushing the company\u2019s software onto 97 percent of the world\u2019s personal computers.  He spent his 13-year tenure as chief executive officer in the failed pursuit of an encore.  Ballmer, 57, said yesterday that he plans to retire within a year, capping a career that took him from a take-no-prisoners salesman once known for bringing a baseball bat to meetings into an embattled CEO of a company that couldn\u2019t keep pace with nimbler rivals and shifting customer tastes.  \u201cHe was a true company man,\u201d said  Tim Bajarin , president of market-research firm Creative Strategies, who first visited Microsoft when it had 28 employees in the early 1980s. \u201cThe bottom line is, he stayed too long at Microsoft with a position focused on PCs, and didn\u2019t really anticipate the dramatic impact of mobile computing.\u201d  Ballmer put his stamp on Microsoft by dint of his intellect, dogged pursuit of his goals and a close personal and business relationship with co-founder  Bill Gates  that saw the two executives complement each other\u2019s strengths and weaknesses through Microsoft\u2019s meteoric rise.  While Ballmer was clearly in charge, his tenure was marked by a list of missed opportunities: smartphones, Web search and tablet computing. While Microsoft built many of these products early on, it never came up with a hit. Its latest attempt to fight back, with Surface tablets, hasn\u2019t succeeded.  Industry Shift  The company, based in Redmond,  Washington , wrested control of the computer industry from  International Business Machines Corp. (IBM)  in the 1980s and made personal computing a reality for much of the world in the \u201990s.  During his time as CEO, Ballmer brought Windows, one of the world\u2019s most valuable brands, into the modern era. He was also instrumental in resolving a U.S. antitrust case that almost saw the company broken in two.  While Microsoft was already talking about a shift away from PC-based computing when Ballmer became CEO in 2000, the company has been eclipsed by  Apple Inc. (AAPL)  and  Google Inc. (GOOG) , as the industry\u2019s center of gravity shifted to handheld computers and software served via an Internet \u201ccloud\u201d instead of programs installed on the PCs that fueled Microsoft\u2019s two big franchises, the  Windows operating system  and Office productivity suite.  Ballmer\u2019s tenure hasn\u2019t worked out well for shareholders, either. An investment of $1,000 when Ballmer took over is now worth 13 percent less, including dividend returns, according to data compiled by Bloomberg. Since Microsoft\u2019s 1986 initial public offering through the end of the Gates era, $1,000 turned into $554,464.  Terrific Energy  \u201cMicrosoft had a great run for 30 years, but it\u2019s too much to expect somebody like Steve, who is more of a caretaker CEO than a visionary leader, to just bring Microsoft to the next level,\u201d said Michael Cusumano, a management professor at the  Massachusetts Institute of Technology , who wrote a 1995 book on the company.  Ballmer, raised outside  Detroit  and whose father was a manager at  Ford Motor Co. (F) , started at Microsoft in his 20s, dropping out of Stanford Graduate School of Business to join his Harvard friend Gates as Microsoft\u2019s first professional manager in 1980. The partnership would come to define the company and led to a string of historic success.  \u201cI\u2019ve met Steve a number of times. Gates correctly foresaw that the rise of cheap, plentiful machines using off-the-shelf parts rather than the custom-designed computers seen in the \u201960s and \u201970s would shift most of the value to software. Along with partner  Intel Corp. (INTC) , which had a chokehold on PC chips, Microsoft siphoned off much of the industry\u2019s profits.  Microsoft also dispatched Apple, whose Macintosh was considered by many users to be more elegant and better-designed. Windows PCs were cheaper, spawning a universe of software programs and add-on hardware that Apple couldn\u2019t match. Microsoft\u2019s  sales  grew 10,000-fold, from $7.5 million when Ballmer joined, to $78 billion last year.  High Octane  In the summer of 1995, Microsoft\u2019s shipment of Windows 95 was a turning point for the PC era, complete with a theme song from the  Rolling Stones  and midnight lines of customers waiting to buy the revamped operating system. Five years later, Windows 2000, in versions for PCs and servers, helped make Microsoft a viable alternative to Sun Microsystems and IBM in data centers.  Microsoft\u2019s market value soared from about $600 million when it went public in 1986, to more than $600 billion in 1999 at the height of its run.  \u201cMicrosoft was firing on all cylinders,\u201d Jack Gold, principal of market researcher J. Gold Associates, wrote in an e-mail.  With a booming voice and physically larger than most others in the room, the tenacious Ballmer often got his way. Yet he could also be a warm and gracious host, pouring sodas for guests and recalling his days as a young Duncan Hines brownie mix manager at  Procter & Gamble Co. (PG)  Ballmer also possessed a business savvy and grasp of data that belied his brusque style.  Critical Juncture  He could also be intemperate, working himself up into a froth, including his  sweaty rants  onstage at company conferences. During Microsoft\u2019s antitrust fight with the  Justice Department , his \u201cthe heck with Janet Reno\u201d comment about the U.S. attorney general didn\u2019t help the company\u2019s cause.  \u201cIn many ways he had a very hard job,\u201d said Cusumano. \u201cWhen Bill Gates stepped down in 2000, he left at a critical juncture,\u201d he said. Ballmer took over from Gates just as the Internet was creating new ways of computing and handheld devices were beginning to show promise.  \u201cAll of these changes, and Ballmer, who is much more of a sales guy than a technical leader or market visionary, was left holding the bag,\u201d he said. Microsoft had also started to splinter into fiefdoms of product groups that battled with each other instead of collaborating on hit products.  There have also been bright spots in Ballmer\u2019s tenure. He introduced the Xbox video-game console in 2001 and turned it into a  $7 billion business . The Windows 7 operating system in 2009 led to widespread upgrades of business PCs at a time when hardware sales were ebbing.  Apple\u2019s Revenge  With Microsoft awash in more money than any other U.S. company outside the financial industry, and facing pressure from shareholders to return cash, Ballmer began paying a dividend in 2003, a sign that the company was maturing. In 2004, he expanded on that, announcing the return of more than $75 billion to shareholders through buybacks and increased dividends.  Yet Ballmer couldn\u2019t turn Windows into a popular platform for mobile computing, as Apple had with the iPhone and iPad. Apple CEO  Steve Jobs  -- in his second career fight against the company -- took a page right from Microsoft\u2019s playbook, turning Apple into the hub of an industrywide ecosystem of software developers who wanted to write mobile applications for its platform.  \u201cI don\u2019t think anything will change at Microsoft as long as Ballmer is running it,\u201d Jobs said in Walter Isaacson\u2019s authorized biography, published in 2011. \u201cThey were very good at the business side of things. They were never as ambitious product-wise as they should have been.\u201d  Falling Short  Meanwhile Google had become what Microsoft had once been in the \u201990s -- a magnet for the most talented computer engineers. Google is now threatening Microsoft\u2019s business on several fronts, including Web search and advertising, mobile software, cloud-computing and productivity software.  Windows Vista, an ambitious operating system that was years late to market and plagued by technical difficulties, met with a terrible  reception  by businesses and consumers when it was released in 2006.  In tablets and smartphones, Microsoft\u2019s attempts to catch Apple and Google have fallen short. Its own Surface tablet has met with disappointing sales, and Windows 8, an operating system for tablet computers, has failed to gain significant market share on the devices. Various versions of Windows for smartphones haven\u2019t made much of a dent either. Inc. (YHOO)  in 2008 -- have left Microsoft without much sway in the consumer space, where Google and  Facebook Inc. If two heads are better than\none, then a hundred heads are even better, and once we are\ndealing with thousands, a good answer starts to look inevitable.\nThis idea has major implications for business decisions, stock\nmarkets, political movements and democracy itself.  In 1907, Francis Galton provided a  memorable example . He\nasked about 800 people to guess the weight of an ox. None of\nthem gave the correct answer (1,198 pounds), but the mean\nresponse was eerily accurate (1,197 pounds). Many experiments\nhave replicated Galton\u2019s finding, showing that if a large group\nis asked to make some numerical estimate, the mean answer (and\nsometimes the average) is remarkably good.  This kind of crowd wisdom seems like a parlor trick, but it\nhas important practical lessons. Suppose we want to make a\nprediction about a presidential election, gross domestic product\ngrowth, the  unemployment rate  or the sales of a new commercial\nproduct. If we have a large number of predictions, we might want\nto aggregate them and use something like the average. Indeed,\nthis is a significant part of the approach taken by Nate Silver\nin his  highly publicized , and stunningly successful, work on\nrecent elections.  Predictive Value  Alternatively, we might want to create a \u201cprediction\nmarket,\u201d in which people make wagers on what they think will\nhappen and the market\u2019s odds emerge from those wagers. The  Iowa\nElectronic Markets  have long done something like this for\npresidential elections. Google Inc., Microsoft Corp.,  Hewlett-Packard Co. (HPQ)  and other businesses have been experimenting with\nprediction markets as well.  In general, the resulting forecasts have proved extremely\naccurate. With respect to economic forecasts, prediction markets\noutperform both professional forecasters and polls. The  most\ndramatic finding  is that market prices often operate as\nprobabilities. Some research has found that when prices suggest\nthat events are likely to occur with 90 percent probability,\nthey occur 90 percent of the time; when prices suggest a\nprobability of 80 percent, the events happen 80 percent of the\ntime; and so forth.  An appreciation of crowd wisdom suggests that social\nnetworks hold special potential, because they can aggregate\ndiverse views with astonishing speed. These networks make it\neasy to find out whether people like certain goods and services,\nand if a lot of people do, perhaps we have reason for confidence\nabout those goods and services. But  recent research  raises\ncautionary notes. It turns out that crowds may have much less\nwisdom when their members are listening to one another. In such\ncases, we can end up with forms of herding, or social cascades,\nthat reflect serious biases.  Researchers have long known that crowds can be misled if\ntheir members influence one another. But the  new research  goes\nfar beyond this simple point. Lev Muchnik, a professor at Hebrew\nUniversity of  Jerusalem , and his colleagues used a website that\naggregates stories and allows people to post comments, which can\nin turn be voted \u201cup\u201d or \u201cdown.\u201d An aggregate score comes\nfrom subtracting the number of down-votes from the number of up-votes.  The researchers created three conditions: \u201cup-treated,\u201d\nin which a comment, when it appeared, was automatically and\nartificially given an immediate \u201cup\u201d vote; \u201cdown-treated,\u201d\nin which a comment, when it appeared, was automatically and\nartificially given an immediate \u201cdown\u201d vote; and \u201ccontrol,\u201d\nin which comments did not receive an artificial initial signal.\nMillions of site visitors were randomly assigned to one of the\nthree conditions.  Surprising Results  You might think that after so many visitors (and hundreds\nof thousands of ratings), the single initial vote could not\npossibly matter. If so, you would be wrong. After seeing an\ninitial up-vote, the first viewer became 32 percent more likely\nto give an up-vote himself. What\u2019s more, this effect persisted\nover time. After a period of five months, a single positive\ninitial vote artificially increased the mean rating of comments\nby 25 percent. It also significantly increased \u201cturnout\u201d (the\nnumber of ratings).  With respect to negative votes, the picture was not\nsymmetrical. The initial down-vote did increase the likelihood\nthat the first viewer would also give a down-vote. But the\neffect was rapidly corrected, and after a period of five months,\nthe artificial down-vote had no effect on median ratings (though\nit did increase turnout). Muchnik and his colleagues conclude\nthat \u201cwhereas positive social influence accumulates, creating a\ntendency toward ratings bubbles, negative social influence is\nneutralized by crowd correction.\u201d They believe that their\nfindings have implications for product recommendations, stock-market predictions and electoral polling.  We should be careful before drawing large lessons from a\nsingle study, particularly when no money was on the line. But\nthere is no question that some products, people, movements and\nideas have enjoyed social success only because of the functional\nequivalent of early up-votes. On the Internet and elsewhere,\nthere are lessons here about the essential unpredictability of\ncrowds -- and about their occasional  lack of wisdom .  (Cass R. Sunstein, the Robert Walmsley University professor\nat  Harvard Law School , is a Bloomberg View columnist. He is the\nformer administrator of the White House Office of Information\nand Regulatory Affairs, the co-author of \u201cNudge\u201d and author of\n\u201cSimpler: The Future of Government.\u201d)  To contact the writer of this article:\nCass R. The flashy effort is drawing gawkers, but the Google Loon project could fall short of its goal of spreading knowledge, and bringing cultural and economic improvements to the third world. Bill Gates says Google is full of hot air. The uber philanthropist -- and still the largest individual shareholder of Google's aging rival, Microsoft --  criticized Loon  in the latest issue of Bloomberg Businessweek, saying it's \"not going to uplift the poor.\" Still, it's hard to argue that giving people access to information would be a bad thing, and Google isn't the only one to recognize this. Here are three other ways that could help poor countries get reliable online connections: Backup for Blackouts:  Described as a \"backup generator for the Internet,\" BRCK is a portable device with a large battery that can connect to a variety of Internet sources. When a landline connection drops out, the device can switch to a nearby Wi-Fi signal or cellular-data network if either is available. While it can be used at home like an ordinary router, the battery lasts for eight hours to allow users to work from the field or stay online during power outages. Blackouts are a common occurrence throughout Africa, home to the nonprofit Ushahidi, which makes the gray  BRCK  (pronounced \"brick\"). The product was crowdfunded via Kickstarter, and the first 2,000 units are expected to ship to backers by November, Nathaniel Manning, Ushahidi's director of business development, said in an interview. Surfing via Satellite:  From a business standpoint, connecting the vast, underdeveloped world through traditional means is often impractical. That's probably why Google is building balloons instead of laying fiber cables in these countries. But what about aiming even higher -- with rockets? O3b Networks, which counts Google as one of its backers, plans to build a low-cost, high-speed data network using satellites. Based in Jersey, a British crown dependency, O3b (for the \"other 3 billion\" Internet users) launched its first four satellites into orbit on June 24 and plans to send another four next month. The goal, according to the company, is to enable people across Africa, Asia, Latin America, the Middle East, and elsewhere to get speedy and affordable Internet access. Local Roads for the Data Superhighway:  Networks in emerging markets can be especially slow and expensive because they're not designed efficiently. Service providers in less-developed nations often decide, incorrectly, that it's more cost-effective to run their domestic traffic over international lines, a  study  published last year by researcher Analysys Mason found. It would be like an entire city's auto traffic being largely confined to freeways (think: Los Angeles). The study, commissioned by the trade group Internet Society, pointed to a better route: Companies in sub-Saharan Africa had built physical infrastructure called Internet exchange points. Like highway interchanges, they not only save money, but they can significantly speed things up. If one of these efforts beats Loon to enhancing connectivity in third-world countries, maybe Gates will foot the bill for high-altitude party balloons to celebrate. This story was first published in Bloomberg's Global Tech Today newsletter. Targeting management adds to decades-old routine activist demands for mergers, breakups or dividends to boost equity prices. Just three days ago, Microsoft CEO  Steve Ballmer  said he\u2019s retiring within a year -- four months after activist fund manager ValueAct Capital Partners LP\u2019s Jeffrey Ubben disclosed a $1.9 billion Microsoft stake. J.C. Penney (JCP)  is probably the most notable failure. There are several other situations where the jury is still out.\u201d  The emboldened approach comes amid a general rise in activism. Assets managed by activist funds have more than doubled over the past five years, to about $73 billion as of the first quarter, from about $32 billion in 2008, according to data compiled by Hedge Fund Research.  Board Representation  So far this year, the most popular activist strategy was seeking board representation, followed by the removal of a CEO or director, according to data from Activist Insight, which tracks the industry. As recently as 2010, removing the CEO was sixth, the data show.  They are also tormenting bigger targets. Companies with a market capitalization of more than $10 billion rose to 5.7 percent of targets this year, from 2.6 percent in 2010. Companies with a market value of $2 billion to $10 billion represent 28 percent of the targets so far in 2013, compared to 12 percent in 2010, Activist Insight said in the report.  \u201cThe real new thing here is that they are going after companies with a market cap larger than $1 billion and targeting CEOs specifically,\u201d said Steven Balet, managing director at FTI Consulting in New York, who has been advising on proxy fights for 19 years. \u201cIn the past they were seeking mergers or sales.\u201d  Judging from recent stock performance, the strategy has been a good thing for shareholders in slightly more than half the campaigns included in Bloomberg\u2019s analysis.  Outperformance  Among 23 companies where activists have either won executive or director changes in the past 18 months, 15 outperformed the  Standard & Poor\u2019s 500 Index (SPX)  and 8 fell behind since the change was completed, according to data compiled by Bloomberg. Another seven companies are in the midst of activist fights seeking management changes. All but one, Agrium Inc., North America\u2019s third-biggest fertilizer producer, have so far outperformed the S&P, the data compiled by Bloomberg show.  Changing CEOs comes with risk, and new executives often take years to build credibility, said Ralph Whitworth, co-founder of Relational Investors LLC who\u2019s been fighting for changes at companies for more than two decades.  \u201cSituations where the shareholders become the most frustrated and where there is enough dissatisfaction to cause a CEO change -- those are likely the ones that need it,\u201d said Whitworth, 58. \u201cIt\u2019s often an easy answer when things aren\u2019t going well for people to default to, \u2018Well, we need a new CEO,\u2019 but it\u2019s usually more complex than that.\u201d  Second Overhaul  Whitworth has been Hewlett-Packard Co.\u2019s chairman since April, part of the second board overhaul in two years while Chief Executive  Meg Whitman  struggles to turn around a business facing a historic industry slump in personal-computer sales. Rewarding Investors  Ackman, one of the most aggressive activists in seeking management changes, is among the best and worst in rewarding stockholders.  J.C. On Aug. 13, Ackman, 47, stepped down from the board after his demand to hasten the search for a long-term replacement CEO was rebuffed by Chairman Tom Engibous and fellow directors.  Ackman has also delivered recent successes.  Hunter Harrison , his candidate at  Canadian Pacific Railway Ltd. Procter & Gamble Co. replaced CEO Bob McDonald less than a year after Ackman bought a $1.8 billion stake in the consumer-products company and began agitating to oust the chief executive.  Creating Value  Among the 8 companies that underperformed the S&P 500 in the data is  Occidental Petroleum Corp. Office Depot Inc. (ODP)  and J.C. Penney both criticized campaigns by their respective largest shareholders --  Jeffrey Smith  and Ackman -- as \u201ccounterproductive,\u201d with mixed results. Revenue in the current period will be as much as $13.4 billion, the  Santa Clara , California-based company said yesterday in a statement.  Analysts (INTC)  on average had predicted sales of $12.8 billion, according to data compiled by Bloomberg.  Improving demand for powerful chips at the heart of corporate networks will blunt the impact of falling PC sales and help Intel boost revenue for the year, Chief Financial Officer Stacy Smith said. While a consumer shift to smartphones and tablets from PCs contributed to Intel\u2019s third straight decline in quarterly  revenue , its server-chip sales have benefited from the increased Internet traffic these mobile devices bring.  \u201cPCs and notebooks are being replaced by tablets and smartphones,\u201d said  Cody Acree , an analyst at Williams Financial Group Inc. who has a hold rating on Intel shares. \u201cThat is impacting the consumer side, but it\u2019s not impacting servers and is actually driving heavier server traffic.\u201d  Intel  shares  fell less than 1 percent to $21.72 at 10:40 a.m. in  New York , compared with a 2.7 percent decline for the Philadelphia Semiconductor Index. For the uninitiated, that\u2019s the trend among  search engines \ntoward including results from Facebook contacts, Twitter\nfollowees and other digital buddies among the traditional blue\nlinks. Given my skepticism, you\u2019d think I wouldn\u2019t like the new\nsocial-centric version of Microsoft\u2019s Bing, the perpetual No. 2\nto Google.  That\u2019s not the case. In making social-search results more\nprominent, Bing has at the same time reorganized its screen\nlayout to make them easier to ignore when they aren\u2019t relevant.\nThe result is a cleaner, calmer interface that lets users focus\nmore specifically on finding the online information they need.  Some searches naturally invite others\u2019 opinions. What are\nthe best Chinese restaurants on the  San Francisco  Peninsula? Is\n\u201cThe Avengers\u201d worth seeing in 3D?  For many others queries, though, the social component is\nuseless. If I want to know the current student enrollment at\n Yale University , it doesn\u2019t really matter that four of my\n Facebook (FB)  friends studied there, and another lists it as a\n\u201cLike.\u201d  Jammed In  Until now, Bing displayed that kind of information amid its\nmain results in the form of a row of tiny Facebook profile\npictures. The thumbnail photos were so small they were\nunrecognizable, and the social-search components, along with\nother extraneous material jammed in, resulting in more\nscrolling.  In the new layout, the screen is broken into three\ncomponents. The left-hand column, the widest, is a clean list of\nrelevant blue links -- the kind of thing Google used to be known\nfor before it began salting its results with stuff like the\n \u201cSearch, plus Your World\u201d  integration with its  Google (GOOG) + social\nnetwork.  If you\u2019ve signed in to Bing with your Facebook ID, a gray\nthumbs-up icon appears next to any link endorsed by a friend.\nHovering over the icon opens a bubble identifying who it is.\nOtherwise, the results are mercifully clear of clutter.  Next to the main results, a column Microsoft calls Snapshot\nincludes not only the expected text-based ads and related\nsearches, but also relevant information that changes as you\nhover over an entry with your mouse.  Carlyle\u2019s Rates  When I searched for Manhattan hotels, for instance, the\nSnapshot displayed a map locating the top hits. When I hovered\nnext to the entry for the Carlyle, the Snapshot displayed\nreviews from  TripAdvisor  and links to let me check room rates\nand availability.  The biggest change, though, is the new third column, a gray\nbar running down the right-hand side of the screen. It\u2019s called\nthe Sidebar and it\u2019s all about social.  When you enter a query, the Sidebar immediately suggests\ncontacts under the heading \u201cFriends Who Might Know.\u201d For now,\nthese results are limited to your Facebook friends, but\n Microsoft (MSFT)  says other social networks, such as LinkedIn, Quora\nand Foursquare, will be added over time. Clicking on any name\nopens a window allowing you to post an inquiry directly to the\nfriend\u2019s Facebook wall.  For some searches, the Sidebar will also suggest people\noutside your own networks -- bloggers, Tweeters and others --who\nmight be authoritative sources. When I entered \u201c Ashton Kutcher ,\u201d for instance, Bing displayed a link to the actor\u2019s\nTwitter account.  Easy to Hide  Perhaps the best thing about the Sidebar is that it\u2019s easy\nto hide. One click collapses it into a thin, gray, non-\ndistracting band; another click slides it back out to its full\nwidth, for those times when you may be looking for advice along\nwith your information.  As for the relevance of that advice, a week of using the\nnew Bing suggests that the social component is still very much a\nwork in progress.  When I searched for \u201cPalo Alto lunch spots,\u201d Bing not\nonly gave me the expected  Yelp  links but also suggested two\n\u201cFriends Who Might Know:\u201d Julia, who works on the nearby\nStanford University campus, and Felicity, who lives in\nneighboring Portola Valley. I decided not to put them on the spot by asking for\nrecommendations.  Some Bing users already see the new layout and features\nwhen they log in. Over time, I expect Bing to grow smarter about finding\nuseful information for me from my social network. For now, at\nleast, I\u2019m grateful that it also knows how to get out of my way. Or voluntarily, like the U.K. and\nGermany. Or slowly and reluctantly, like the U.S. One way or\nanother, it has to happen. You can\u2019t run deficits of 10 percent\nof gross domestic product or more forever.  \n But what does that mean for investors?  \n The  U.K. stock market  has already priced in earnings shocks\nfrom companies that have run into trouble because of reduced\ngovernment spending. And, in most developed countries, the cuts\nare only just starting. We\u2019ll see a lot of corporate-profit\ndeclines across Europe and the U.S. in the next couple of years.  \n To survive that you need to short companies that depend on\ngovernment spending; think about the regions that will avoid the\nworst of the pain; and focus on businesses that can save the\ngovernment some money. Follow those simple rules, and your\nportfolio should make it through the years of belt-tightening.  \n There is already plenty of evidence from the U.K. about the\nimpact that the austerity drive can have on share prices. Cable\n& Wireless Worldwide Plc, the telecommunications provider, said\nlast week that spending cuts by  David Cameron \u2019s new coalition\ngovernment would lower earnings.  Its shares  dropped 17 percent\non the day. Last month, Connaught Plc, which maintains social\nhousing, told shareholders the same message. Its shares dropped\nas much as 41 percent on the day.  \n 50 Percent  \n It\u2019s no great surprise that austerity drives will hit a lot\nof companies hard. State spending accounts for 30 percent to 50\npercent of the economy, depending on which country you look at.\nStart hacking away at half of your GDP, and a lot of people will\nfind life much tougher.  \n So how should you steer your portfolio through the age of\nausterity? Here are four principles to keep in mind:  \n One: Keep away from government contractors. In the last\ndecade, the state has outsourced a lot of its work. There have\nbeen big contracts awarded -- and, as we know, governments are\nvery bad at getting value for money, so most of those contracts\ncame with fat profit margins. Likewise, defense companies will\ndo it tough -- wars are a real luxury when you need to cut\npublic spending by a quarter. You don\u2019t want to be holding\nshares in companies such as defense manufacturer  BAE Systems Plc \nin that kind of environment. All of them are going to suffer.\nClear them out of your portfolio -- then short them.  \n Regional Focus  \n Two: Focus on regions. Government spending is always\nconcentrated in particular areas, either because they are poor,\nor because it is where the governing party\u2019s voters happen to\nlive. In the U.K., that is Scotland, Wales and the north of\nEngland, the heartland of the Labour Party, which held power for\nthe last 13 years. But every country has a region of high public\nspending. Avoid them, because they will be hit hardest. But\nother places such as prosperous London and the south-east of the\ncountry will do fine. Invest in businesses that focus on those\nplaces and you won\u2019t regret it.  \n In the U.K., take a look at  Ocado Group Plc . The online\ngrocery retailer got a rough ride in its initial public offering\nlast week. Yet the wealthy shoppers of the south-east of England\nwho make up its core market are going to get through the\nausterity drive better than most people.  \n Cheap New Ways  \n Three: Look for better mousetraps. Governments won\u2019t just\nbe able to cut their way out of trouble. The deficits are just\ntoo big for that. They will have to innovate as well, finding\nnew ways of doing the same things more cheaply. The private\nsector is much better at that than the public sector. So look\nfor companies in health care, education or outsourcing that can\ncome up with new, more-efficient ways of doing things. They will\nhave plenty of demand for their services.  \n One example.  Capita Group Plc , which provides a criminal-\nrecords service for the U.K. Home Office, is pitching money-\nsaving ideas to the British government. If they are good, they\ncan expect an enthusiastic reception.  \n Four: Don\u2019t forget about growth. The historical record\nshows that times of austerity are also ones of great\nentrepreneurial energy. During the 1930s, new industries such as\nconsumer electronics and plastics were created. In the turbulent\nmid-1970s, the personal-computer industry was born, as companies\nsuch as Microsoft Corp. and Apple Inc. were founded. When times\nare hard, a lot of smart people don\u2019t have any choice but to set\nup their own business. And they will have to do it on the cheap\nas well, which is usually the best way.  \n New Opportunities  \n So don\u2019t be too defensive. Even amid austerity, there will\nbe some terrific new companies getting started. It is a good\ntime to be looking for businesses to back.  \n Where should you be looking? How about  Nathaniel Rothschild \u2019s new mining company, Vallar Plc, which has just\nlisted its shares in London? The best brand name in global\nfinances should be able to open a few doors, and resources are a\ngrowth industry.  \n Some of those investments may do well, others badly. But\nstick to those four principles and your portfolio should survive\njust fine. Ignore them, and you can expect to get burned.  \n ( Matthew Lynn  is a Bloomberg News columnist and the author\nof \u201cBust,\u201d a forthcoming book on the Greek debt crisis. The four firms, ranked among the world\u2019s top 20 law firms,\nhave extensive global networks and expertise in key practice\nareas that will support Singapore\u2019s economy and the development\nof its legal services, the ministry said.  \u201cWe\u2019ve seen a substantial increase in the frequency and\ncomplexity of transactions negotiated from Singapore,\u201d said\nSushma Jobanputra, partner-in-charge of Jones Day\u2019s Singapore\noffice, which has 27 lawyers. \u201cWe have fairly aggressive plans\nfor Singapore.\u201d  Mergers and acquisitions in Southeast Asia rose 45 percent\nto $140.9 billion in 2012, according to data compiled by\nBloomberg. The license will \u201copen up further opportunities for\nSingapore lawyers in international practice and help\ninternationalize the Singapore legal profession,\u201d Kevin Wong,\nmanaging partner of Linklaters\u2019 Singapore office, said in an e-\nmailed statement today. Singapore started opening its legal market in 1981 by\nallowing foreign banks to bring in lawyers from New York, London\nand Hong Kong to advise on some offshore transactions. Wrong Question","released_at":"<date>July 8 2012<\/date> <time>22:30:06<\/time>","content":"Google  responded last week  to\nEuropean antitrust regulators investigating a long list of\nclaims against the world\u2019s largest search engine. Whether or not\nthe complaints against Google are valid, they may be looking\nbackward. Increasingly, Google is not a search engine.  Yes, Google accounts for 80 percent of all Web searches in\n Europe . It is facing criticism (some of it prompted by\nMicrosoft) for favoritism toward Google\u2019s own specialty search\nproducts -- travel, finance, hotels, restaurants, maps -- that\nmay put its competitors at a disadvantage. In the U.S., the\nFederal Trade Commission has also been investigating Google for\nthe past year.  As pressure mounts on Google to change its practices, it\u2019s\nnot clear whether antitrust regulators are asking the right\nquestions. Although European Commission authorities are focused\non Google\u2019s familiar Web pages of blue links, and  the prominence\nof  Google products on those pages, Google seems to be heading in\na different direction. It wants to be whispering to individual\nusers by way of its Google devices.  Whether competition law has anything to say about this is\nan open question. Do we require  Chevrolet  to allow all car-radio\nmanufacturers to install their devices in its vehicles? (No, we\ndon\u2019t.)  Perfect Search  In November 2009, Google\u2019s vice president of search\nproducts and user experience,  Marissa Mayer ,  described  the\nperfect search engine: \u201cIt would be one that could understand\nspeech, questions, phrases, what entities you\u2019re talking about,\nconcepts. It would be able to search all of the world\u2019s\ninformation, [find] different ideas and concepts, and bring them\nback to you in a presentation that was really informative and\ncoherent.\u201d  Two years later, Apple introduced its voice-recognition\nsoftware, Siri, for the iPhone. It seemed to fit that job\ndescription. Except for one detail: Siri is  inaccurate  almost a\nthird of the time.  Last month Google made a series of  intriguing announcements \nsignaling that deeply contextualized, personalized information\nservices aimed right at Siri will be rolled out this month in an\nupdate to Android phones. Users won\u2019t have to ask specific\nquestions because their device will already know where they are\n-- and even what their calendar says they\u2019re doing. Google Now\nwill display transportation information, weather, sports scores,\nrestaurant locations and presumably any other contextually\nrelevant information. A soothing Siri-like voice will answer a\nmurmured query if Google Now hasn\u2019t already figured out the\nuser\u2019s needs.  Just as the term \u201chorseless carriage\u201d was overtaken by\n\u201cautomobile,\u201d \u201csearch engine\u201d will soon sound primitive to our\n21st-century ears. Instead, you will have a digital deputy that\ntravels with you and is simpler to use and tailored to your\nwants and needs.  Because Android phones already command more than 50 percent\nof the U.S. market for handheld devices, all Google has to do is\nhang on to its Android customers in order to have the scale and\nscope it needs to be successful. If its pilot fiber optic\ninstallation in  Kansas City ,  Kansas , and Kansas City,  Missouri ,\nworks and can be replicated, Google can also avoid dependence on\nany wireless carrier: Unlicensed wifi hotspots connected to\nfiber nodes will provide users with mobile connectivity, and\nGoogle won\u2019t have to ask permission from AT&T or Verizon to\nintroduce a new device or service.  Vertical Integration  Google is not alone in climbing the heights of vertical\nintegration. Apple and Facebook are  working together  more\nclosely, with Facebook the default calendar and contact app in\nApple\u2019s latest operating system. And Facebook is supposedly\nplanning  its own phone .  What competition law has to say about the personalized,\nvertically integrated ecosystems now being built by Apple,\nFacebook and Google is far from clear. Consumers will have a\nchoice of competing handsets, as they do now. But their\nsubsequent options (what calendar, what map, what apps) may be\nsharply limited. Signing up with a particular brand of personal\nassistant will lead to a cascade of path-dependent filters, as\nsoftware learns more about its users and serves them more\ndirectly.  In response to European and U.S. competition authorities,\nGoogle is likely to agree to better labeling of its search\nresults to more clearly show Google\u2019s commercial relationships\nto particular links. This may be a solution to a fading problem.\nAs \u201csearch\u201d becomes an anachronism and personalization the new\nnormal, we\u2019ll have deeper issues to deal with.  (Susan P. Crawford is a contributor to Bloomberg View and a\nvisiting professor at the Harvard Kennedy School of Government\nand  Harvard Law School . She is a former special assistant to the\npresident for science, technology and innovation policy. The\nopinions expressed are her own.)  Read more opinion online from  Bloomberg View . (MSFT)  and  Google Inc. (GOOG)  have discovered a common foe: patent owners who try to sue their customers or go after an entire industry.  Both companies are seeking to curb the litigation practices of firms that buy patents with the sole purpose of demanding royalties from as many end-users as they can, even if it means suing a pizza parlor or non-profit. Anger has united a cross section of retailers, finance companies, public-transit operators and hotels, and even caught the attention of President  Barack Obama , who last month announced corrective measures.  Focusing on that core issue could create pressure in Congress for legislation and action by U.S. courts -- as long as companies avoid the squabbling that marred the previous effort to change patent law. That took almost a decade and pitted industries, and even technology companies, against each other.  \u201cGoing after bad litigation behavior is an approach we can all agree on,\u201d said Tim Molino, director of government relations for Washington-based BSA - The Software Alliance, whose members include Microsoft and Oracle Corp.  Google spokesman Matt Kallman referred questions about patent legislation to the Coalition for Patent Fairness, a Washington-based lobbying group backed by Google, Cisco Systems Inc. and Intel Corp. Each month, the group has a meeting with an increasing number of organizations to discuss ways to get legislative change.  \u2018Patent Trolls\u2019  \u201cIt\u2019s tech and retail and restaurants and hospitals and cable companies -- you name it,\u201d said Matt Tanielian, executive director of the coalition. \u201cThere are patrol trolls -- the patent assertion entities -- that have gone way too far and that\u2019s what the focus is. This is no longer just about patent law. It\u2019s about the economy and consumer protection.\u201d  The increased political attention is due to patent owners who started going after product end-users, demanding cheap settlements from a large number of companies. A White House-commissioned report estimated that more than 100,000 companies were threatened last year, including members of politically connected  Washington  trade groups like the National Retail Federation and Financial Services Roundtable.  Members of Congress have proposed legislation to limit some patent owners from seeking product import bans at the U.S. International Trade Commission, expand reviews of business method patents and force certain patent owners who lose at trial to pay legal fees of those they accused of infringement.  Court Actions  The courts have also been trying to curb abuses. The ITC, a quasi-judicial agency in Washington, set up a program to resolve certain patent cases more quickly. The chief judge of the federal appeals court that specializes in patent law co-wrote a New York Times opinion piece advocating sanctions for litigation abuses.  Getting a consensus could mean avoiding more controversial issues such as curbing software patents, and ensuring that any changes don\u2019t have unintended consequences that hurt universities needing legal protection for their research and patent-reliant businesses.  \u201cYou do not want to try to fix things that are broken and in the process break something that\u2019s important to American competitiveness,\u201d said Horacio Gutierrez, deputy general counsel of Redmond, Washington-based Microsoft.  There are major issues among technology companies that could create fissures. Mountain View, California-based Google wants to cut back on software patents that it says are being unfairly used in cases, for instance, that target mobile phones running on its Android operating system. Microsoft and Oracle, which both have infringement claims against Google, have pledged to fight any efforts to limit software patents.  Xboxes, IPhones  Microsoft wants to curb the use of patents that relate to widely used technological standards, a key issue in its fight with Google over inventions used in its Xbox video-gaming system and Windows operating system.  Apple Inc. (AAPL) , another Google foe, is fighting to prevent an import ban on some of its older iPhone 4s found to infringe a Samsung Electronics Co. patent on an industry standard.  Gutierrez, like others interviewed for this story, is a veteran of the debates that occurred before Congress in 2011 passed the most sweeping overhaul of the U.S. patent system in at least a half-century.  That measure started as a wish list drawn up by those who wanted help fighting off the myriad patent suits from companies that bought patents from bankrupt dot-coms or people who tinkered on their own with computers.  Legislative Hang-Over  Some of the proposals went too far for companies such as Scotch tape manufacturer 3M Co., consumer-products maker Procter & Gamble Co., drugmaker Pfizer Inc. and conglomerate General Electric Co., which said a weakening of patent rights could hurt their businesses and the economy.  Those companies have been silent in the latest push for new patent legislation, as have smaller firms that rely on intellectual property protection to start new businesses, said former PTO Director David Kappos.  The new effort should hone in on practices that are seen as abusive, rather than stigmatizing every patent owner who doesn\u2019t make a product, he said.  \u201cThere\u2019s almost a little bit of a mob atmosphere -- we\u2019ve got to do more, we\u2019ve got to do something dramatic,\u201d said Kappos, now with Cravath Swain & Moore in New York. \u201cWe don\u2019t hear the voices we need who will say, \u2018I\u2019ve got an important business that\u2019s built on the strengths of the IP system and I don\u2019t want it to be so skewed so much it disrupts my legitimate business model.\u2019\u201d  Less Contentious  In 2011, Congress focused on the less-contentious issues like changes to how patents are reviewed because of key rulings from courts that addressed many of the litigation controversies brought up a decade ago.  Court rulings helped by altering the calculation of damages for small parts in complex products, making it easier to prove a patent is a variation of earlier know-how and making it harder for patent owners who don\u2019t make products to get court orders preventing others from using an invention.  \u201cThe courts have played a very helpful role over the years and they will continue to do that, and they can work more quickly than Congress,\u201d Gutierrez said.  In the end, it will probably be a combination of the courts and Congress that curb patent abuses, particularly if industries can find common ground.  \u201cThere is a growing sentiment among people who deal with this business that there are tactics and strategies that are inappropriate and hurt the entire system,\u201d Molino said. (6758) \u2019s new PlayStation 4 device.  \u201cThis is a great opportunity for Don, and I wish him success,\u201d Ballmer wrote in a memo sent to Microsoft employees and posted on its website today.
