One financing idea -- getting $150 million from Seattle-area taxpayers -- ran afoul of state Representative Ross Hunter. The state was reducing college funding, and tuition was surging.  \u201cWe were cutting billions of dollars out of our budget, and we are going to build a stadium. Really?\u201d says Hunter, 51, a Democrat from Medina who is chairman of the House Ways and Means Committee. \u201cI was OK with saying \u2018No.\u2019\u201d  That didn\u2019t prevent taxpayers in Seattle and the rest of the U.S. from subsidizing the $250 million project anyway. Tax breaks on municipal bonds issued for the stadium, donations for construction and increased contributions tied to ticket purchases will cost the U.S. Treasury $154 million over 30 years, based on data compiled by Bloomberg. Without the exemptions, Athletic Director Scott Woodward says, he couldn\u2019t have financed the overhaul.  Related:  In Stadium Building Spree, U.S. Taxpayers Lose $4 Billion As the school\u2019s football team prepares for a bowl game Dec. 22 in Las Vegas, the field at Husky Stadium is dotted with earth movers and  dump trucks . The construction shows how even some of the most soundly run college football programs benefit from indirect tax subsidies totaling hundreds of millions of dollars. In addition to the deductions that helped fund this project, sports departments are exempt from taxes on ticket, television and other income generated by their stadiums.  Arms Race  The system of taxpayer subsidies is contributing to a financial arms race among the 120 schools in the top division of football, the most lucrative college sport. Within that group, the median athletic budget is $38 million, according to an October  report  by the  National Collegiate Athletic Association . The richest programs generate revenue of almost four times as much, approaching $150 million. Only 23 programs  turned a profit  in fiscal 2011, according to the NCAA.  Tax preferences reduce the cost of athletic programs, allowing schools to build bigger facilities and pay coaches more. Breaks targeted at fans reduce the cost of tickets, allowing schools to raise prices. Dennis Coates, an economist at the University of Maryland Baltimore County, said college sports may not be the best use of tax exemptions.  \u201cIf we are going to allow charitable donations, we should think about what the ultimate purpose of those donations happens to be,\u201d Coates said in an interview. \u201cWhen one thinks of charity, they don\u2019t think of charity flowing to the head football coach of a big state university.\u201d  Coates also questioned muni financing for stadiums. \u201cUsing the borrowing power of the state and tax-exempt interest to build stadiums for sporting events isn\u2019t the real purpose of the university, either,\u201d he said.  Stadium Renovations  Maximizing revenue by creating premium seating -- such as Husky Stadium\u2019s new luxury suites -- is part of the funding strategy. The University of  Washington  project is just one of dozens of stadium or arena overhauls in the past decade.  The  University of California , Berkeley, unveiled a $321 million  renovation  to its football stadium in August that upgraded seating and concession stands, widened concourses and brought the structure into compliance with seismic standards. The  University of Alabama  in Tuscaloosa spent $65 million adding 9,000 seats and 36 sky boxes to Bryant Denny Stadium in 2010. And for $226 million, the  University of Michigan  in 2010 added 82 suites, 3,000 club seats, a new press box and other amenities.  Federal Deficit  As Congress contemplates a revision of the  tax code  next year to close the federal  budget deficit , some of the decades- old exemptions that benefit college sports may face elimination, according to U.S. Representative Dave Reichert, a Washington Republican on the Ways and Means Committee. Deductions for donations to education cost the Treasury $5.7 billion this year, according to Congress\u2019s Joint Committee on Taxation. There isn\u2019t an estimate for lost revenue from sports-related exemptions.  \u201cEverything has to be on the table,\u201d Reichert said in an interview. \u201cWe feel like the momentum is there\u201d to overhaul the tax system, he said. \u201cStadiums are paid for a certain way today. But there could be a better way to pay for them.\u201d  The University of Washington has been playing football in horseshoe-shaped Husky Stadium since 1920. The vista from the 72,500-seat venue, the largest in the Pacific Northwest, includes Lake Washington, Mount Rainier and downtown Seattle. On football Saturdays, some fans arrive by boat and anchor nearby. A wave to the dock summons a ride ashore with the school rowing team, winner of four of the past six men\u2019s national championships.  Model Program  By most measures, the 42,500-student university runs a model sports program. The athletic department\u2019s $70.2 million budget supports 10 men\u2019s and 11 women\u2019s teams. The school doesn\u2019t require  student athletic fees .  UW athletes tied with those of the University of Utah for the third-highest graduation rate in the Pacific 12 Conference over the past four years with 81 percent, behind No. 1  Stanford University  and the University of  California ,  Los Angeles . The school finished in the top 25 of the Learfield Sports Director\u2019s Cup -- an award that measures the success of the entire program -- in four of the past five years.  This year\u2019s football team won 7 games and lost 5, and it will play in its third straight postseason game when it faces  Boise State University  in the MAACO Bowl. All of the school\u2019s other fall semester teams qualified for the NCAA postseason.  Seismic Retrofit  Around six years ago, however, it became clear that the sports program\u2019s biggest income source would have to be updated. The oldest football stadium in the Pac-12 needed renovations to withstand earthquakes, comply with the Americans With Disabilities Act and replace crumbling sidewalks and railings. The university also wanted to add revenue-generating premium seats and electronic displays, and update the structure\u2019s technological infrastructure.  The price tag was going to be $450 million. The university proposed covering $150 million of that by extending county taxes on food and beverages, rental cars and lodgings, which had been used to finance stadiums for the  National Football League \u2019s Seahawks and  Major League Baseball \u2019s Mariners.  Representative Hunter, a former Microsoft Corp. manager whose district doesn\u2019t include the stadium, and other lawmakers turned thumbs down. The legislature would have had to assent, and it never came to a vote. Starting in fiscal 2008, the state\u2019s revenue fell 5.6 percent over the ensuing five years, according to the Washington State Budget & Policy Center in Seattle.  Tuition Increases  Over that period, state funding for the University of Washington declined 50 percent, while tuition and mandatory fees for resident undergraduates jumped 66 percent to  $10,574 , according to the school.  All of that left Woodward, the athletic director, to rehabilitate the stadium without funds from the county, the state or the university. Now 49, Woodward set out to cut the costs. He got permission to bypass the university\u2019s usual committee-laden approval process and obtained proposals directly from developers for preset prices, rather than through architects and builders separately, says Chip Lydum, the associate athletic director for operations and capital projects.  Developers are more efficient in negotiating with builders -- getting them to work for less in return for getting hired on other projects -- and substituting less expensive materials that still meet building codes. That, plus recession-borne lower borrowing costs, reduced the price.  For $250 million, the school is adding 30 luxury suites, 65 patio suites, 2,500 club seats and an 88,000-square-foot football operations department. It is lowering the field by four feet (more than a meter) and rebuilding the lower bowl and south-side upper deck. There will also be a 200-car parking garage that wasn\u2019t originally planned.  Muni Bonds  The financing includes $50 million in private donations. While that means the money isn\u2019t coming directly from taxpayers or students, it does reduce revenue to the  U.S. Treasury . Contributions for university facilities are usually 100 percent deductible. Assuming that donors were in the 35 percent tax bracket -- for those with taxable earnings of more than $388,350 a year -- the cost to the Treasury may total as much as $17.5 million.  Woodward borrowed the remaining $200 million by selling municipal bonds. Investors in muni bonds don\u2019t have to pay U.S. income taxes on interest. Their tax break will reduce federal revenue by $1.3 million this year, or $28.5 million when all the bonds mature in 2043, based on data compiled by Bloomberg and reflecting yields as of Nov. 30. The state of Washington also is forgoing taxes on residents with interest income from at least some of the bonds.  \u201cI\u2019m not smart enough to tell you I know all the answers to  tax reform ,\u201d Woodward says. \u201cWhat I do know is that our donors are generous in this current tax structure, and we\u2019re the only country that has this tremendous philanthropic giving. Are the breaks still needed by college athletics? I think so.\u201d  Ticket Buyers  The renovated stadium will create additional tax breaks for Washington football fans when it reopens Aug. 31. That is because the school requires some of those who buy season tickets to make donations to the athletic department in addition to the face value of the seats. Under U.S. tax law, fans can deduct 80 percent of these contributions from their taxes.  The Huskies estimate that the new suites and premium seating will raise $16 million a year in donations. Assuming a 28 percent tax rate -- the third-highest, for married couples reporting taxable income between $142,700 and $217,449 -- that would cost the Treasury as much as $3.6 million a year initially, increasing over time as contribution minimums rise.  Tax Policy  \u201cThat deal may not be good federal  tax policy , but it\u2019s the best available and most responsible deal for the university and its stakeholders,\u201d said Justin Marlowe, a professor of public finance at the University of Washington\u2019s Evans School of Public Affairs, in an interview.  Additionally, the athletic department projects that other stadium-related revenue -- such as ticket sales, naming rights and concessions -- will increase by $17 million, or 57 percent, to $47.5 million annually, according to Assistant Athletic Director Carter Henderson. That will more than cover payments on the stadium debt of $15.9 million, the school says.  One group that isn\u2019t benefiting from Woodward\u2019s stadium project is students. After the renovation, their section will move to the end zone from the lower level between the 30-yard lines. Student tickets used to go for $120 a season. Now Woodward will sell those seats to the public for as much as $1,249 a season, including the mandatory donation, according to the university.  No Vote  The students didn\u2019t have a vote on the move and didn\u2019t like the idea of a 10-fold price increase, says  Evan Smith , 21, the president of the student government organization. The senior from Gig Harbor, Washington, who is studying economics and government, said students felt like poor neighbors.  \u201cIt was dropped on us in the final stages of approving the renovation,\u201d Smith says. \u201cThe sentiment was, \u2018Wait, the football team is our team, it\u2019s our college, they play for us.\u2019 When they are running onto the field, they are looking at the student section, and we are cheering them on.\u201d  The students did get the athletic department to lower their season ticket price to $99 for the end-zone seats.  \u201cIn the end, they took the approach that: \u2018We look at all of our customers the same. We can charge more for these seats and you can\u2019t afford it, so we will charge those who can,\u2019\u201d Smith says. \u201cIt was kind of tough hearing that.\u201d  Community Heroes  Economists and politicians debate the benefits of taxpayer subsidies for stadiums, professional or college. Job creation and business development promised by proponents usually fall short of estimates, said Marlowe, the UW public finance professor. The projects often move money that would have been spent at one venue to another, without adding significant new economic activity, he said. At the same time, tax breaks for the wealthy often encourage investment, allowing benefits to filter down and create value for all, he said.  \u201cThe Huskies are heroes to the community,\u201d Marlowe says. \u201cIs that enough of a benefit? Is the tax break to the rich enough to underwrite the effort, through fundraising, investment and high-priced tickets, worth it to generate pride in the community? We\u2019re living through some difficult economic times and these are the kinds of questions being asked.\u201d  Hunter, the state lawmaker who argued against tax money for Husky Stadium, says there is something to learn from Woodward\u2019s ability to get the project done anyway.  \u201cThis is like one of those times when you say \u2018No\u2019 to your kid, and he says, \u2018Darn, I really want that,\u2019 and so he decides to mow a bunch of lawns and babysit,\u201d Hunter says. \u201cIn the end, they are getting a great stadium that will last for years.\u201d  To contact the reporter on this story: Curtis Eichelberger in Wilmington,  Delaware  at  ceichelberge@bloomberg.net . At OpenWorld, Oracle will seek to show there\u2019s an alternative path to cloud computing -- where programs are stored and managed remotely -- than the no-hardware approach espoused by rivals such as  Salesforce.com Inc. (CRM)  and  Workday Inc. (WDAY)   \u201cThis will be an important week for them coming up, to declare they\u2019re in the cloud,\u201d said  Rick Sherlund , an analyst at Nomura Holdings Inc., who recommends buying Oracle shares. \u201cLarry\u2019s getting with the program in a big way.\u201d  The 12c database will let Oracle serve multiple companies\u2019 data-processing needs from the same information storehouse and will arrive by early next year, Ellison told analysts on a Sept. 20  conference call . The company\u2019s Exadata and Exalogic systems, plus its database, Java development tools and social media- analysis software, can be delivered to businesses as a service Oracle manages over the Internet, Hurd said.  Services Shift  \u201cWe\u2019ll be giving you a cloud with the Exadata infrastructure,\u201d Hurd said in the interview at the company\u2019s  Redwood City ,  California , headquarters. \u201cYou have the ability to change the economics dramatically.\u201d  As  International Business Machines Corp. (IBM) ,  Microsoft Corp. (VMW)  and VMware Inc. also shift toward selling products aimed at letting companies manage more of their systems and software as a service, it\u2019s important that Oracle adapt as well. The new 12c database -- the c stands for \u201ccloud\u201d -- includes the ability that lets the software handle multiple jobs using \u201cvirtualization\u201d technology, an advantage in cloud computing.  It has been  five years  since the company introduced a new version of the database, and Oracle is pitching its customers on the benefit of being able to move their computing jobs from their data centers to the cloud if the need arises, Hurd said.  Private Clouds  Oracle can remotely manage customers\u2019 applications,  database software , and server computers in so-called private clouds sitting inside companies\u2019 own data centers to increase the peace of mind of chief information officers, said Sherlund, who is based in  New York . Customers would get the benefit of Oracle\u2019s package of technology without having to perform the installation and maintenance themselves.  Oracle is relying on the new products to help reverse a slowdown in growth and a stock price that has underperformed those of its rivals. Sales declined 2.3 percent in the fiscal first quarter, which ended Aug. 31, dragged down by a drop in the hardware business acquired from Sun Microsystems in 2010. New software license sales, a measure of freshly signed business, tapered to 5.1 percent growth from more than 16 percent a year earlier.  Oracle\u2019s stock has risen 22 percent this year,  compared with gains  of 35 percent for SAP, and a 51 percent climb for shares of Salesforce.com.  Acquisition Strategy  Oracle has expanded sales and profit through its acquisition strategy. The company has spent more than $50 billion on more than 80 deals to add business programs that mostly run on servers and personal computers.  Still, it may be harder to grow through acquisitions in cloud computing, because those companies sell by subscription and don\u2019t have steady streams of maintenance revenue that Oracle can immediately add, said Pat Walravens, an analyst at JMP Securities LLC.  \u201cCloud companies don\u2019t lend themselves well to a rollup strategy,\u201d said Walravens, who has a market perform rating on Oracle shares. \u201cYou just don\u2019t get the same efficiencies.\u201d  Software-as-a-service providers also tend to trade at higher multiples of sales than the businesses Oracle has traditionally bought, making deals relatively more expensive, said John O\u2019Farrell, a partner at venture capital firm Andreessen Horowitz. Bloomberg LP, the parent of  Bloomberg News , is an investor in Andreessen Horowitz.  \u2018Savvy Company\u2019  Oracle has said it has signed $1 billion of cloud-computing business, including from its Oracle Cloud service, which includes Fusion human-resources and customer-relations applications as well as online programs from  acquired  companies Taleo and RightNow Technologies. The company will give an updated figure at a meeting with analysts on Oct. 4, Hurd said.  By contrast, Salesforce in its last quarterly report boasted a $4.1 billion backlog of signed contracts. Brian Acker, the Toronto-based\nmanager of a fund that buys large U.S. companies and beat 94\npercent of peers in the past year, says he\u2019s found the secret to\nbeating  Wall Street : staying away.  Acker, whose Acker Finley Select U.S. Value 50 Fund has\nreturned 31 percent since the end of 2009, says being about 560\nkilometers (350 miles) from the New York Stock Exchange keeps\nhim away from the buzz of corporate news that could throw off\nhis quantitative strategy, which relies on statistical analysis\nto pick shares.  \u201cEveryone wants to get on the hottest stock, the hottest\nnews, and I think returns from that are marginal at best,\u201d\nAcker, 51, said. His company manages about C$560 million ($586\nmillion). \u201cThe market is wired in such a way, all the\nadvantages are gone from the floor being close,\u201d he said. \u201cThe\nfarther away, the better.\u201d  Among 205 funds that purchase the biggest American\ncompanies from outside the U.S., only three have gained more\nsince April 2010 than the Select U.S. Value 50 Fund. Among 85\nlarge-cap funds based in  Canada , only the  Montrusco Bolton\nQuantitative Canadian Equity Fund (MONTBQCE)  had a higher return in 2010.  Acker, the chief executive officer of  Acker Finley Inc. ,\nachieved the returns even though the fund had more invested in\ntechnology and health-care companies than in other industries.\nThose groups lagged behind the rest of the U.S. stock market\nover the past year.  Value Stocks  The C$47 million fund focuses on value stocks, or companies\nwith low share prices in relation to earnings. U.S. large-cap\nvalue stocks have lagged behind  growth stocks  -- or companies\nwith the fastest profit increases -- over the past year,\naccording to Russell Investments indexes.  Acker bought stocks such as Woonsocket, Rhode Island-based\n CVS Caremark Corp. (CVS) , the largest U.S. provider of  prescription\ndrugs , as well as Redmond, Washington-based  Microsoft Corp. (MSFT)  and\n Walgreen Co. (WAG)  of Deerfield,  Illinois , the biggest U.S. drugstore\nchain. He invested in the companies following declines and sold\nbefore they declined again.  He bought Microsoft, the world\u2019s largest software maker,\nfor $24.65 a share in October and sold it at $27.81 on Jan. 4.\nMicrosoft has fallen 6.9 percent to $25.98 in 2011.  Acker uses a formula when choosing stocks, calculating a\n\u201cmodel price\u201d for each Standard & Poor\u2019s 500 Index company\nbased on three factors: \u201cintrinsic business value\u201d or what its\nbalance sheet says about its ability to generate profit; how\nlikely the balance sheet is to be affected by changes to the\nshare price; and projected earnings growth.  Ranking Companies  He then ranks the largest 100 companies and the other 400\ncompanies in the  S&P 500  by how much they would have to gain to\nmatch their model price. The 10 or so highest-ranked companies\nfrom the first group and 40 highest-ranked companies from the\nsecond group are added to or kept in the fund. (RIG) , the offshore driller, and  Kinder Morgan Energy\nPartners LP (KMP) , a pipeline company, that are ineligible for the\nindex.  \u2018Holier Than Thou\u2019  \u201cWhat I see constantly that drives me crazy is people say\nthey beat the S&P 500, but they don\u2019t have S&P 500 companies in\nthe portfolio,\u201d he said. \u201cI don\u2019t want to sound holier-than-\nthou, but I have a perverse feeling of satisfaction that I can\nactually beat the S&P 500 with S&P 500 names.\u201d  The fund added  Freeport-McMoRan Copper & Gold Inc. (FCX) , the\nworld\u2019s largest publicly traded copper producer, in early March,\nwhen it was trading at about $52 a share. Acker\u2019s model came up\nwith a valuation of $79.27 for the Phoenix-based company. Acker\nsaid other investors have probably driven down the shares amid\nspeculation Chinese economic growth will slow, curbing demand\nfor metals.  \u201cWe don\u2019t make any macro guesses,\u201d Acker said. \u201cWe\ninvest the way we invest all the time.\u201d  Acker said he plans to reinvest in Microsoft over the next\nmonth because his model price is 47 percent above the software\ncompany\u2019s current share price. The stock has fallen 10 percent\nsince Jan. 27, when the company reported second-quarter unearned\nrevenue, a measure of multiyear contracts, below the average\nanalyst estimate.  Intrinsic Value  Microsoft\u2019s balance sheet indicates the shares have an\nintrinsic value far higher than the current market value, he\nsaid. Microsoft has 19.95 cents in debt for each dollar of\nequity, 21 percent less than the S&P 500 Information Technology\nIndex as a whole. The company had $4.02 billion in cash on Dec.\n31.  Acker said he\u2019s not the only investor who recognizes that\nMicrosoft shares are undervalued.  \u201cPeople aren\u2019t really missing it, it\u2019s just that no one\nreally cares,\u201d he said. \u201cEveryone\u2019s turned into a momentum\nguy. Away From  New York   While Acker may benefit from his location, other fund\nmanagers aren\u2019t taking advantage of their distance from New\nYork. (AAPL) \u2019s trial against Samsung Electronics Co., Apple\u2019s\ndeep ties to Samsung are becoming more apparent even as the two\ncompanies clash in court.  As the trial enters its second week, Apple is producing\ntestimony intended to prove that the South Korean company copied\npatented technology for smartphones and tablet computers.  \u201cThere are a number of Samsung phones and two Samsung\ntablets that are substantially the same as those\u201d described by\nApple patents,  Peter Bressler , an inventor of 70 design and\nutility patents, said yesterday before a jury in federal court\nin  San Jose ,  California . The next biggest is Hewlett-Packard Co.,\nproviding 3.2 percent.  Samsung and Apple\u2019s interdependence traces its roots to the\nbeginning of the iPhone. Ahead of the 2007 debut, Apple realized\nit needed a processor better tailored to the device. A\nmicroprocessor acts as the brains of a device, determining how\nfast it runs and letting it perform critical tasks. Apple turned\nto Samsung, then ramping up a division that makes so-called\nlogic chips, which handle the devices\u2019 other functions.  The two companies, which had already worked together in\nscreens and memory chips, cut a deal that resulted in Samsung\nbecoming the sole manufacturer of the so-called A-series of\nchips, which are at the heart of the iPhone and iPad. There are signs Apple is taking steps away from Samsung.\nSome of the memory components in the iPhone 4S, which was\nreleased last year, come from SK Hynix Inc., said Stuart Robinson, an analyst who studies the smartphone-component\nindustry for  Strategy Analytics . New screen technology that will\nbe part of the next version of the iPhone, to be released this\nyear, is being made by LG Display Co., Sharp Corp. and Japan\nDisplay KK, according to Sanford Bernstein & Co. research.  \u201cThey are trying to reduce their dependency on Samsung as\nmuch as possible,\u201d Robinson said. Shifting to\nanother manufacturer would make Apple vulnerable to more\nlitigation or force it to pay license fees, he said. California Plan to Regulate Fracking Stirs Trade Secrets Battle  A California proposal to regulate the chemicals used by oil\ncompanies in hydraulic fracturing is stirring a battle over\nindustry assertions of trade secrets protection and\nenvironmentalist calls for disclosure to shield public health.  State officials developing rules for fracking say they have\nto walk a fine line to avoid lawsuits by both the public and the\nindustry, circumscribing their proposal.  \u201cWhat we\u2019re doing with the regulation is limiting how\noften we would get sued,\u201d said Jason Marshall, chief deputy\ndirector of California\u2019s Conservation Department, which oversees\noil and natural gas production.  California, the fourth-largest oil-producing state, is\nwrestling with the potential hazards of fracking to unlock an\nestimated 15.4 billion barrels of oil in a deposit known as the\nMonterey shale. The state is the latest attempting to regulate\nthe fluids used in fracking, which shoots a mixture of water,\nsand and chemicals underground to access dense rock formations.  Texas ,  Louisiana ,  Montana , New Mexico and North Dakota are\namong those requiring the chemicals to be disclosed, while\nleaving it to energy companies to decide what they label secret.  The industry \u201cis attempting to exempt itself from the\nbasic regulation of its activities by virtue of arguing that its\ncommercial interests will be damaged if secrets are revealed,\u201d\nsaid David Levine, a law professor at Elon University in\nGreensboro, North Carolina, who specializes in intellectual\nproperty.  Dealing with trade secrets is nothing new for states,\nLevine said, citing regulations that require voting-system\nvendors to reveal the source code in their machines to election\nofficials, even if it\u2019s privileged information, to assure the\nintegrity of balloting.  California\u2019s initial proposal on fracking, released in\nDecember, would call for companies to disclose a trade secret to\na public agency if it\u2019s needed to investigate or respond to a\nspill. It would also require disclosure to a physician to\ndiagnose or treat a patient or respond to a medical emergency.  \u201cWe would be having it available when we need it,\u201d\nMarshall said. \u201cThe operators are required to maintain that\ninformation, they just don\u2019t have to tell it to us until we need\nit as regulators.\u201d  California\u2019s constitution requires public access to\ngovernment records unless exempted by law. The agency could face\na lawsuit from the public if it withheld requested data, or a\nlawsuit from an oil company for violating trade-secret\nprotections if it released the information. Dan Loeb, the billionaire founder and\nprincipal owner of Third Point LLC, the $14 billion activist\nhedge fund, has made about $1 billion for himself and his\ninvestors from a two-year crusade to increase  Yahoo! Inc. (YHOO) \u2019s\nstock price. He\u2019s been extraordinarily  successful ; the shares\ntrade for about $33 these days, up from about $13.50 when Loeb\nstarted buying them in September 2011.  But while Loeb was busy cashing in, what benefit did\nYahoo\u2019s 627 million unique monthly visitors (me among them) get\nfrom his 26 months (and counting) of ownership?  The answer: not much, except for some major new headaches.\nThis raises the legitimate concern that the saber-rattling by\ncertain activist hedge-fund managers is designed to benefit\nthem, not the companies they target or their customers.  In his typically  aggressive  fashion, Loeb indeed rattled\nevery possible Yahoo cage. He  criticized  the board for hiring\n Carol Bartz  as chief executive officer. He said the board made a\ngross error by turning down Microsoft Corp.\u2019s $31-a-share offer\nfor Yahoo in 2008. (The stock was trading at $13.61 at the\ntime.)  He accused Yahoo founder  Jerry Yang  and board chairman  Roy Bostock  of \u201cstrategic bungling.\u201d He  described  Bostock as \u201ca\nlame duck outgoing Chairman.\u201d Loeb famously uncovered the\n\u201cdiscrepancies\u201d in the education record of new Yahoo CEO  Scott Thompson , who had claimed his degree from Stonehill College,\noutside  Boston , was in accounting and computer science when it\nwas just in accounting. \u201cNow more than ever Yahoo! investors\nneed a trustworthy CEO,\u201d Loeb  wrote  in May 2012.  CEO\u2019s Resignation  He called for Thompson\u2019s dismissal; 11 days later, Thompson\n resigned . In July 2012, Loeb recruited high-profile Google\nInc. executive  Marissa Mayer  to lead Yahoo. According to company\nfilings, the Yahoo board offered her a pay package of $60\nmillion, including future bonuses and other compensation, to\nmake up for what she lost by leaving Google.  Loeb\u2019s payoff for all this hard work came a year later,\nwhen the company announced an unusual arrangement: It would buy\ntwo-thirds of Loeb\u2019s 60 million shares at the market price of\n$29.11 per share, for a total of $1.2 billion. (MSFT)  a shot.  The software maker began a trial in the northeastern province of Limpopo last month that taps unused slices of television spectrum to provide online access to remote townships. Potential partners include state-controlled  Telkom SA SOC Ltd. (TKG)  and MWEB ISP, a unit of  Africa \u2019s biggest media company  Naspers Ltd. (NPN) , said two people familiar with the matter, asking not to be identified because the discussions are confidential.  South Africa remains one of the world\u2019s stragglers in Internet access, with average broadband speeds lagging behind smaller economies including Uganda and Azerbaijan, according to  netindex.com . The latest test is a chance for Redmond, Washington-based Microsoft to catch up with  Google Inc. (GOOG)  in the country\u2019s smartphone and cloud-computing markets. Google is also testing the use of so-called white spaces with a project spanning 10 schools in the Cape Town area.  \u201cWe are being led by a generation that does not fully understand the value of this IT infrastructure,\u201d Microsoft South Africa Managing Director Mteto Nyati, 48, said in an interview this month. \u201cThe barrier for people to either get our services or buy our services is the connectivity.\u201d  Multiple Partners  In an e-mailed statement, MWEB ISP said its chief executive officer, Derek Hershaw, has held discussions in recent weeks with Microsoft, although the company isn\u2019t currently involved in the project. A representative for Telkom declined to comment. A Microsoft spokeswoman in Johannesburg said the  software company  is looking for multiple partners for the project.  Naspers retreated 1 percent to 865.50 rand as of 4:02 p.m. in Johannesburg trading, while Telkom advanced 0.4 percent to 22.50 rand.  Slow connections limit the ability of businesses to grow and hurts South Africa\u2019s economy, which will probably expand by 2 percent in 2013, compared with 5.6 percent in sub-Saharan Africa, according to the  International Monetary Fund .  The ruling  African National Congress  has pledged to extend broadband access to every citizen by the end of this decade, a mission that has been entrusted to Telkom, South Africa\u2019s largest fixed-line operator. The ANC came to power under President  Nelson Mandela  after the end of white minority rule in 1994.  Telkom was awarded a near-monopoly five-year exclusive license in 1997 to expand fixed-line access in exchange for commitments including bringing cable to rural areas. That plan backfired because without competition, Telkom was able to price its packages above what people wanted to pay, according to Kate Turner-Smith, a BPI Africa Capital Ltd. analyst.  Little Competition  \u201cBecause there was no fixed-line competition Telkom priced their service too high, so the majority of people opted not to go for broadband because they couldn\u2019t afford it,\u201d she said.  Telkom charges 856 rand ($83) a month for 4 megabytes per second of uncapped Internet in a country where the average  household income  is $12,000. That compares with $30 offered by  TalkTalk Telecom Group Plc (TALK)  in the U.K., where the  average  household income is $49,000.  Of every 100 people in South Africa, 2.18 has a broadband fixed-line subscription in 2012, less than half the number in Vietnam and Peru, according to the  World Bank . That compares with 15.8 percent broadband penetration for all methods of accessing the Internet in South Africa, according to research and consultancy firm World Wide Worx.  Video Streaming  For Adi Nduka-Agwu, whose job is to sell the output of  Nigeria \u2019s $800 million-a-year Nollywood movie industry in South Africa, the affordability of decent Internet presents more of an obstacle than the widespread availability of pirate DVDs that undermine her business.  \u201cThe Internet is pretty poor,\u201d said Nduka-Agwu, head of Africa Business Development for iRoko Partners, a Nollywood film distributor. Broadband connections that are fast and reliable enough to stream movies are \u201cquite rare\u201d among low- and medium-income groups, she said.  South Africans  are increasingly turning to the country\u2019s two biggest wireless carriers,  Vodacom Group Ltd. (VOD)  and  MTN Group Ltd. (MTN) , as their primary provider of  Internet access , as the number of smartphone users grows.  MTN had 13.5 million mobile-data users in South Africa as of June 30 compared with 11.9 million a year earlier, while Vodacom had 14.4 million at the end of March, an increase of 18 percent from a year earlier.  MTN and Vodacom may compete with Microsoft in bidding for unused TV spectrum, according to BPI\u2019s Turner-Smith. \u201cIt\u2019s much cheaper to roll out a wireless broadband system than it is to roll out a wired one,\u201d she said.  Solar Powered  A spokesman at Vodacom declined to comment, while an MTN representative didn\u2019t respond to an e-mailed request for comment.  As part of its white spaces project, Microsoft is bringing solar-powered wireless Internet and free tablet computers to schools in five rural South African townships in Limpopo, about 196 miles (315 kilometers) from Johannesburg. The signals are broadcast from solar-powered base stations and picked up by a receiver.  \u201cOur agenda is to come up with a business model,\u201d Microsoft\u2019s Nyati said. Sony Corp. (6758) ,  Microsoft Corp. (MSFT)  and Nintendo Co. have\nhelped to build a market worth $24.1 billion in the U.S. in\n2011, according to NPD Group Inc. Regan in New York at \n mregan12@bloomberg.net ;\nLu Wang in New York at \n lwang8@bloomberg.net   To contact the editor responsible for this story:\nLynn Thomasson at \n lthomasson@bloomberg.net","path":".\/2008_2012_msft_bloomberg_news\/asian-stocks-climb-for-fourth-day-on-stimulus-won-strengthens.txt"},{"id":58774025,"title":"The Real U.S. Map, a Country of Regions (Part 4): Colin Woodard","released_at":"<date>October 4 2011<\/date> <time>00:00:50<\/time>","content":"In 2100, will the political map of\nNorth America look the same as it does today? Will the continent\nstill be divided into three enormous federations (the U.S.,\n Mexico ,  Canada )?  Or will it have morphed into something else? A Balkanized\nset of nation-states along the lines of 20th-century  Europe ? A\nloose E.U.-style confederation stretching from Monterrey,\nMexico, to the Canadian Arctic? A unitary state run according to\nbiblical law as interpreted by the spiritual heirs of Jerry Falwell? A postmodern utopian network of semi-sovereign self-\ncontained agricultural villages freed by technological\ninnovations from the need to maintain larger governments at all?  No one who\u2019s being both thoughtful and honest has any idea.\nBut a meaningful assessment of the future depends on an accurate\nappraisal of the past and present. We must acknowledge that --\ndespite both the myth of a united America and politicians\u2019 cries\nfor states\u2019 rights -- this country\u2019s most meaningful fissures\nhave little to do with our 50 state demarcations or other\nofficial political boundaries.  Instead, the U.S. can best be examined as a federation\ncomposed of 11 regional nations shaped by immigration patterns,\noriginal shared values and the gradual drifting together of\npeople with similar values and complementary commercial\ninterests. Previous discussions in this series have covered\neight of the 11 nations (Yankeedom, New Netherland, the\nMidlands, Tidewater, Greater Appalachia, the Deep South, El\nNorte and New France). This installment will focus on the other\nthree: the Left Coast, the Far West and First Nation.  From the American Revolution and the Civil War to the\ntumultuous 1960s and the blue-state, red-state maps of recent\npresidential elections, intra-national differences among the 11\nnations have been important. The nations divided themselves into\ntwo hostile, feuding blocs -- the Deep South, Tidewater and much\nof Greater Appalachia versus Yankeedom, New Netherland, the\nMidlands and the Left Coast. Their cultural battles simmered for\na century after Appomattox and, in the late 1950s and early\n\u201960s, broke into open conflict.  Cultural Uprising  At this point, each coalition underwent an internal civil\nwar: In the Dixie bloc, blacks rose up against segregation and\nthe caste system. At the same time, the northern alliance faced\na cultural uprising led by the youth. Both revolts started as\nhomegrown phenomena, but soon drew interventionists from the\noutside.  In the civil rights movement, assistance from the Northern\nnations proved decisive, as federal troops forced whites in\nTidewater, Appalachia and especially the Deep South to dismantle\ntheir racial caste system. And in the \u201860s cultural revolution,\nDixie-based political leaders opposed young revolutionaries from\nthe Left Coast, New Netherland and Yankeedom whose agenda was\ndiametrically opposed to everything the Deep South and Tidewater\nstood for.  Weakened by revolution at home, Dixie-bloc leaders were\nunable to stop the youth movement in the short term, but they\nhave since spearheaded efforts to roll back much of what the\nrebellion accomplished. Resentments stemming from these twin\nuprisings widened the divide between the nations, poisoning\nefforts to find common ground in 20th-century America.  The \u201cculture wars\u201d of the 1990s and 2000s were, in\nessence, a resumption of the \u201860s-era struggle, with a majority\nin the four Northern nations generally supporting social change\nand an overwhelming majority in the Dixie bloc defending the\ntraditional order. (Opinions in El Norte and the Far West\nvaried, based on the issue at hand.) Northern-alliance campaigns\nfor civil liberties, sexual freedom,  women\u2019s rights , gay rights\nand environmental protection all became divisive sectional\nissues, just as Dixie\u2019s promotion of creationism, school prayer,\nabstinence-only sex education, abortion bans and states\u2019 rights\ndid.  The Northern alliance vs. Dixie bloc chasm today remains\nthe greatest chasm among the 11 nations and, as the fallout from\nworldwide economic trouble hit the U.S. in the rest of this\ndecade, the tensions between nations can only become more\nintense, and might lead to an increasingly divided future.  Crucial to this future are three of the nations, one that\nis already influential and two others in transition.  The Left Coast  A Chile-shaped nation pinned between the Pacific Ocean and\nthe Cascade and Coast mountain ranges, the Left Coast extends\nnorth from Monterey,  California , to Juneau, Alaska, and includes\nfour decidedly progressive metropolises: San Francisco,\n Portland ,  Seattle  and  Vancouver . A wet region of staggering\nnatural beauty, this region was colonized by two groups: New\nEngland merchants, missionaries and woodsmen arrived by sea and\ngained control of the coastal towns, and farmers, prospectors\nand fur traders from Greater Appalachia arrived by wagon and\ndominated the countryside.  Originally slated to become a \u201cNew England on the\nPacific\u201d -- and the target of a dedicated Yankee missionary\neffort -- the Left Coast retained a strong strain of New England\nintellectualism and idealism even as it embraced a culture of\nindividual fulfillment.  Today, it combines Yankee faith in good government and\nsocial reform with a commitment to individual self-exploration\nand discovery, a fecund combination. The Left Coast has been the\nbirthplace of the modern environmental movement and the global\ninformation revolution. It is home to Microsoft, Google, Amazon,\nApple, Twitter and Silicon Valley. And it has been a co-founder\n(along with New Netherland) of the gay rights movement, the\npeace movement and the 1960s cultural revolution.  Ernest Callenbach\u2019s 1975 sci-fi novel, \u201cEcotopia,\u201d\nimagined the U.S. portion of the region as having broken off\ninto a separate, environmentally stable nation at odds with the\nrest of the continent. A modern secessionist movement seeks to\ncreate the sovereign state of Cascadia by adding in British\nColumbia and southern  Alaska  as well, forming a \u201cbioregional\ncooperative commonwealth.\u201d Yankeedom\u2019s closest ally, the Left\nCoast battles constantly against the libertarian-corporate\nagenda of its neighbor, the Far West.  The Far West  Climate and geography have shaped all the 11 nations to\nsome extent, but the Far West is the only one where\nenvironmental factors have truly trumped ethnic ones. High, dry\nand remote, the interior West presented conditions so severe\nthat they effectively destroyed would-be settlers who tried to\napply the farming and lifestyle techniques they had used in\nGreater Appalachia, the Midlands and other nations. With minor\nexceptions, this vast region couldn\u2019t be effectively colonized\nwithout the deployment of vast industrial resources: railroads,\nheavy mining equipment, ore smelters, dams and irrigation\nsystems.  As a result, the colonization of much of the region was\nfacilitated and directed by large corporations based in distant\n New York ,  Boston ,  Chicago  or  San Francisco , or by the federal\ngovernment itself, which controlled much of the land.  Even if they didn\u2019t work for one of the colonizing\ncompanies, settlers were dependent on the railroads for\ntransportation to and from far-off markets and manufacturing\ncenters. Seaboard nations treated the region as an internal\ncolony, exploiting it for their benefit. And the region remains\nin a state of semi-dependency, despite significant\nindustrialization during the World War II and the Cold War.  Its political class tends to revile the government for\ninterfering in its affairs -- a stance that often aligns it with\nthe Deep South -- while demanding that it continue to receive\nfederal largesse. Yet the Far West rarely challenges its\ncorporate masters, who retain near-Gilded Age levels of\ninfluence over the region.  Today, this nation encompasses all of the interior U.S.\nwest of the 100th meridian, from the northern boundary of El\nNorte up to the southern frontier of First Nation. It includes\nnorthern  Arizona ; the interiors of California,  Washington  and\nOregon; much of British Columbia,  Alberta , Saskatchewan,\nManitoba and Alaska; portions of the Yukon and the Northwest\nTerritories; the arid western halves of the Dakotas, Nebraska\nand Kansas; and all or nearly all of Idaho, Montana,  Colorado ,\nUtah and  Nevada .  First Nation  Like the Far West, First Nation encompasses a vast area\nwith a hostile climate: the boreal forests, tundra and glaciers\nof the far north. The difference, however, is that the\nindigenous inhabitants are still in the area -- most of them\nhaving never given up their land by treaty -- and still retain\ncultural practices and knowledge that allow them to survive in\nthe region.  American Indians have recently begun reclaiming their\nsovereignty. In Alaska and Nunavut, they have won considerable\nautonomy. And in Greenland, the indigenous people now have a\nself-governing nation-state, which stands on the threshold of\nfull independence from Denmark. First Nation\u2019s people now have a\nchance to put native  North America  back on the map culturally,\npolitically and environmentally.  First Nation is rapidly taking control of large portions of\nwhat once were the northern fringes of the Far West, including\nmuch of Yukon, the Northwest Territories and Labrador; the\nentirety of Nunavut and Greenland; the northern tier of Ontario,\nManitoba, Saskatchewan and Alberta; much of northwestern British\nColumbia; and the northern two-thirds of  Quebec .  Tomorrow: the turbulent future.  (Colin Woodard, a correspondent for the Christian Science\nMonitor and the Chronicle of Higher Education, is the author of\n\u201cThe Lobster Coast,\u201d \u201cThe Republic of Pirates\u201d and \u201cOcean\u2019s\nEnd.\u201d This is the fourth in a five-part series excerpted from\nhis new book, \u201cAmerican Nations: A History of the Eleven Rival\nRegional Cultures of North America,\u201d published Sept. 29 by\nViking. (CBS) , derided by rivals for\nattracting TV viewers too old for advertisers to care about,\nsays 54 is the new 49.  The last of the U.S. baby boomers turn 48 this year, moving\ninto the sweet spot for luxury cars, financial services and\npharmaceuticals, three of CBS\u2019s largest ad categories.  The shift is forcing marketers to reconsider how they\ntarget the $12.7 billion that researcher Kantar Media says they\nspent on prime-time network TV ads last year. As boomers --\npeople born from 1946 through 1964 -- leave the 18-to-49-year-\nold group that has long dominated  television advertising ,\ncompanies are focusing more on older consumers.  \u201cWhile we enjoy winning in all the categories, 18-to-49 is\nnot the end-all it\u2019s made out to be,\u201d Nina Tassler, CBS\u2019s head\nof entertainment, told TV critics last month in  Beverly Hills ,\n California .  With the  National Football League \u2019s Super Bowl and a key\nNFL playoff game in the TV season starting next month, CBS will\nprobably lead in 18-to-49-year-old viewers for the first time in\n20 years. Still, the most-watched network overall will generate\nmore sales from ads targeting 25-to-54-year-olds, Tassler said.  Though the groups mostly overlap and represent a large\nchunk of the population, the younger skew of those 18 to 49 has\nmade them a desirable audience since the 1970s. That\u2019s when\nadvertisers began to focus on the 75-million plus U.S. baby\nboomers, who were reaching maturity and forming households,\nseeing younger consumers as more open to new products and less\nlikely to have established loyalties.  Time, Economics  Time and economics are changing that. Most Americans don\u2019t\nset up households until after college, according to Pat McDonough, senior vice president of insights, analysis and\npolicy at Nielsen, which reports the audience ratings used to\nset advertising rates. And more people in their 50s are willing\nto try new products, she said.  \u201cRealistically, most 18-year-olds aren\u2019t determining what\nlaundry detergent they\u2019ll use,\u201d McDonough said.  With an average age of almost 57, CBS has the oldest\naudience of the four largest broadcast networks, according to\nNielsen. Fox is youngest, with a median age of 45, while NBC\u2019s\nmedian is 50 and ABC\u2019s is 52.  The perception that 50 is \u201cancient\u201d is changing,\naccording to Peter Gardiner, national media buyer at Deutsch, a\nunit of New York-based  Interpublic Group of Cos.  that lists\n Microsoft Corp. (MSFT)  and  Johnson & Johnson (JNJ)  as clients. Most have\ngrown children, are in their peak earnings years and are still a\ndecade or more from retirement, he said.  \u201cIt\u2019s not that the younger demographic is less\nimportant,\u201d said Gardiner, who notes half his clients have\nbegun to target 25-to-54-year-olds in recent years. \u201cIt\u2019s that\nthe older audience is becoming more important.\u201d  Buying Power  The buying power of older viewers has also grown, said\nDavid Poltrack, CBS\u2019s chief research officer, while 18-to-24-\nyear-olds have been hit hard by the slow recovery.  The 45-to-64-year-old age group was least affected by the\nrecession, according to Census data. The group\u2019s 2010 median\nannual income of $60,700 was 2.1 percent less than before the\nrecession. Those under age 25 suffered a 9.7 percent decline, to\n$24,140. Ive\u2019s industrial design group works differently. The model sustainable company generally looks like this. It has a phenomenal track record of stock growth and a full bucket of cash. It militantly roots out inefficiency from its operations and supply chain and invents new products that take into account social change and resource availability. It increases the transparency of its operations and invites outside scrutiny to make sure it\u2019s in compliance with the highest legal and social standards. Factor in the ability to scale change and the rankings change dramatically. The model company, in short, might be Apple. I first taught a graduate-level Sustainability & Investing class at Columbia University\u2019s Earth Institute in 2009. The class was composed of students from diverse backgrounds, including specialists in hedge-fund management, conservation, utilities, fashion, supply chains, and others. We assembled a portfolio of our picks for the most sustainable companies -- those that understand new global risks and opportunities, and innovate accordingly.\u00a0And we selected companies that were best positioned to push improvements in resource efficiency throughout the global economy. Apple was one of our core 20 holdings; it was trading at $192 by the end of 2009. The portfolio outperformed the market that year and went on to outperform the S&P 500 in 2010 and 2011. Studies more rigorous than my students\u2019 portfolio experiment suggest that companies that build a \u201c culture of sustainability \u201d perform better in the long-term than those that don\u2019t. More than ever, companies are turning to sustainability to gird against volatility and as a strategy to feed middle-class consumption expanding in China, India, Brazil and beyond. No company embodies innovation and success more than Apple. The company traded in the $7 to $12 range from 2001 to 2003, has since catapulted to the $500-600 range, and peaked at $644 in April. It's now the only company in the world with a market value of more than a half trillion dollars. There are two types of equity portfolios, those that rode at least some of Apple\u2019s success, and those that missed out. The relative returns of each of these portfolios have largely been driven by this one factor. Apple has issued annual reports on its supplier relationships since 2007. It publishes product-specific environmental reports, which are more detailed than those of most competitors, covering climate change, energy efficiency, materials use, packaging, avoidance of restricted substances, and recycling. The company's iPad 2 Environmental Report reports that the tablets exceed the strict European Directive on the Restriction of the Use of Certain Hazardous Substances in Electrical and Electronic Equipment by avoiding mercury in its display, arsenic in its glass, BFRs (brominated flame retardants) and PVCs (polyvinyl chloride). Critics have no shortage of ammunition to challenge this argument. Apple and other global companies can no longer avoid scrutiny anywhere they operate, from activists, investors, governments, and journalists. Ma Jun, a Chinese environmental activist and founder of China's Institute of Public and Environmental Affairs, pretty much singlehandedly caused Apple to address problems in its supply chain by bringing them into the public spotlight. Worker suicides at Foxconn, Apple's Chinese manufacturing partner, in recent years focused attention on the company's long hours, unsafe conditions and packed living quarters. Apple joined the Fair Labor Association earlier this year, the first technology company to do so. The FLA's subsequent investigation found at least 50 breaches of Chinese labor laws as well as the code of conduct the group signed with Apple. Many of the most damning critiques of Apple's worker conditions rely heavily on data and examples brought to light by Apple itself. The tough love is to be expected; by housing the bulk of its manufacturing operations in China, the company draws increased scrutiny to a country known for cheap, unregulated labor. What matters more is how the company responds. So far, Apple has improved worker conditions at its Foxconn facilities and, through its transparency and influence, is improving conditions across China. Apple's forthrightness helps shield it from detractors and helps it become a stronger company. Apple\u2019s public disclosure of its suppliers in the last year was welcome transparency and should be seen as an investment confidence-builder akin to buying back shares. Sustainable companies are mindful of more than just supplier relations and working conditions. Environmental issues -- which many people in the U.S. wrongly assume to be the entirety of sustainability -- offers Apple room for growth. In 2011, the Carbon Disclosure Project noted that Apple and nine other companies with large market caps didn't respond to the group's annual survey. Greenpeace tossed a dart at the company in April, concluding in its environmental assessment of cloud-computing companies, \u201cThree of the largest IT companies building their business around the cloud -- Amazon, Apple and Microsoft -- are all rapidly expanding without adequate regard to source of electricity, and rely heavily on dirty energy to power their clouds.\u201d The report prompted a vociferous response from Apple, which in May announced it was approved to build a 20-megawatt solar power facility across the street from its data center in Maiden, North Carolina. The site will be powered completely by renewable sources by the end of 2012. Apple ranked 50 th  in the 2011 Newsweek Green Rankings, assembled in part by TruCost, where I am Senior Vice President. This ranking reflects Apple's substantial energy consumption. What it does not reflect is the company\u2019s potential to scale sustainability innovation, which will drive even more change than their current performance shows. Can Apple keep it up? Only if authenticity, transparency and responsiveness grow and thrive. Legitimate efforts at sustainability are creating and defending value. Apple needs sustainability -- and sustainability needs examples like Apple\u2019s. Krosinsky is Senior Vice President of TruCost. (GAI)  The majority said the patentholder\nmust prove the defendant knew about the infringement or at least\nwas \u201cwillfully blind\u201d to it. Edward Joyce, a spokesman for Globus, didn\u2019t immediately\nreturn voice and e-mail messages seeking comment on the suit.  The case is Synthes USA v. Globus Medical Inc., 11-cv-652,\nU.S. District Court, District of Delaware (Wilmington).  Pronova, Teva Agree to Dismiss Patent Litigation in U.S.  Pronova BioPharma ASA and Teva Pharmaceuticals USA Inc.\nagreed to dismiss patent litigation in the U.S. District Court\nin Delaware, according to a Pronova statement. Terms of the\nagreement weren\u2019t disclosed  The suit, filed in September 2010, is related to three of\nPronova\u2019s U.S. patents pertaining oil purification. IV Objects to Characterization of \u2018Patent Troll on Steroids\u2019  Intellectual Ventures , the company founded by  Microsoft\nCorp. (MSFT) \u2019s former Chief Technology Officer  Nathan Myhrvold ,\nobjected its portrayal last week on the National Public Radio\nprogram \u201cThis American Life.\u201d  The episode, titled \u201c When Patents Attack ,\u201d looked at\npatent litigation brought by patent-owning companies. At one\npoint Intellectual Ventures was characterized as a \u201cpatent\ntroll on steroids.\u201d  In an e-mailed statement from Intellectual Ventures\nspokeswoman Kasey Halmagyi, the Bellevue, Washington-based\ncompany said it disagreed with what it said was the program\u2019s\npremise that patents have a negative effect on innovation. That\nnotion \u201cflies in the face of centuries of evidence,\u201d Halmagyi\nsaid in the statement.  At one point in the report, non-practicing entities --\ncompanies that have patents, but do not produce products based\non those patents -- are characterized as being Mafia-like. IV\nsaid in the statement that the program \u201cuses some colorful and\ndramatic devices\u201d and that \u201csome of the characterizations in\nthe piece are frankly absurd.\u201d  Among the people interviewed on the show were  Peter N.\nDetkin , who ran the IP litigation at  Intel Corp . before he\nbecame one of IV\u2019s founders and vice chairman;  John M. Demaris ,\na former partner at  Chicago \u2019s Kirkland and Ellis and now the\nowner of 4,000 patents he bought from Micron Technology Inc.;\nand  Michael C. Smith , a partner in  Siebman, Burg, Phillips &\nSmith LLP , who has litigated patent cases in Marshall,  Texas  on\nbehalf of both plaintiffs and defendants.  Smith took \u201cThis American Life\u201d reporters on a tour of an\noffice building near the courthouse in Marshall, Texas, that\nhouses many of the plaintiffs in cases tried in that court. He\ncalled the building \u201cground zero\u201d for companies that file\ninfringement suits and don\u2019t make the products covered by their\npatents.  He said the building was filled with empty offices that had\nonly a name plate on the door.  Intellectual Ventures said in its statement that rather\nthan being a so-called troll, it provides \u201can efficient way for\npatent holders to get paid for the inventions they own, and in\nturn, for technology companies to gain easy access to the\ninvention rights they need now or may need as they enter new\nmarkets.\u201d  Intellectual Ventures completed a licensing agreement with\n Chunghwa Picture Tubes (CGHD)  Ltd., it said in a  statement  yesterday.\nIn addition to having access to 35,000 patents, the agreement\nadmits the Taoyan County, Taiwan-based company to what IV calls\nits \u201cIP for Defense\u201d program, according to the statement.  The program provides customers accused of patent\ninfringement \u201cthe ability to obtain patents from IV\u2019s portfolio\nto support counter-assertions, enabling more efficient\nnegotiations in order to reduce liabilities and achieve\nfavorable licensing terms,\u201d according to the statement. The  gap  between yields on 10-year notes issued by state-\ncontrolled companies with top debt ratings and similar-dated\ngovernment bonds grew 16 basis points to 104 basis points, the\nbiggest increase since Lehman Brothers Holdings Inc. filed for\nbankruptcy in September 2008, according to Chinabond data. The\nspread was 81 on Nov. 5, the narrowest since July 2007, and\naveraged 135 in the past three years.  \u201cAs liquidity becomes tighter, brokerages and mutual\nfunds, who trade more frequently than banks and insurers, are\nselling corporate debt for cash-type securities,\u201d said  Jiang Chao , a Shanghai-based analyst at Guotai Junan Securities Co.,\nChina\u2019s largest brokerage by revenue. \u201cThe yield gap may widen\nfurther in the short run in reaction to tightening measures.\u201d  Policy makers ordered lenders to set aside more funds as\nreserves twice this month and raised interest rates in October\nfor the first time since 2007, seeking to rein in credit growth\namid the fastest inflation in two years. That\u2019s leaving finance\ncompanies with less to invest in corporate debt after the value\nof outstanding notes in the interbank market jumped 39 percent\nin the last 10 months to 3.36 trillion yuan ($506 billion).  Drains Cash  The People\u2019s Bank of China ordered banks to set aside\nlarger reserves for the fifth time this year on Nov. 19,\nboosting the proportion of deposits that must be set aside by\nhalf a percentage point to 18 percent for the nation\u2019s largest\nlenders. The move will drain about 350 billion yuan from the\nfinancial system, Bank of America Merrill Lynch estimates.  \u201cThe bond market still needs time to digest the impact of\nthe central bank\u2019s reserve-ratio increase, and we are not\noptimistic on the direction of the bond market in the short-\nterm,\u201d  Citic Securities Co.  analysts  Wang Mingfeng  and  Guo Qinmiao  wrote in a research note yesterday.  The yield on 10-year government  bonds  climbed five basis\npoints yesterday to 3.92 percent, while the rate on  corporate\ndebt  rated AAA increased 6 basis points to 4.97 percent, data\nfrom Chinabond, the nation\u2019s largest debt-clearing house, show.\nThe difference between the two has narrowed 34 basis points this\nyear as regulators eased restrictions on corporate-bond\nownership, enabling insurers to hold more of the securities and\nallowing approved overseas banks to invest.  U.S. Yield Gap  Top-rated U.S. corporate bonds with maturities of seven to\n10 years yielded 68 basis points more than Treasuries at the end\nof last week, 10 basis points more than at the start of 2010,\naccording to Bank of America Merrill Lynch\u2019s U.S. Corporate\nIndex. Microsoft Corp.\u2019s 3 percent notes due October 2020\nyielded 3.34 percent, 47 basis points more than similar-maturity\nTreasuries, according to data compiled by Bloomberg.  The 5.28 percent bond due April 2020 issued by China Datang\nCorp., the nation\u2019s second-largest power producer, yielded 4.91\npercent yesterday, 107 basis points more than government bonds,\naccording to data from the National Interbank Funding Center.\nThe spread was 86 at the end of October.  Lending curbs reduce liquidity in the corporate-bond\nmarket, eroding the attraction of the securities, according to\n Chen Jianbo , a fixed-income analyst at BOC International (China)\nLtd.  \u201cIt\u2019s harder to sell corporate bonds for cash than\ntreasury debt when liquidity is becoming tighter,\u201d said Chen,\nwho is based in Beijing. \u201cBanks also reduce purchases of\ncorporate bonds toward year-end to meet annual reporting\nrequirements for capital-adequacy ratios, intensifying liquidity\npressure for those bonds.\u201d  Yuan Outlook  Speculation the yuan will strengthen is helping attract\noverseas investors to China\u2019s bonds, supporting the market, said\n Tan Weisi , who oversees about 400 million yuan as head of\nFortune SGAM Fund Management Co.\u2019s fixed-income arm in Shanghai.  \u201cChina\u2019s bond market is much more attractive for overseas\nthan domestic investors, given expected yuan appreciation,\u201d Tan\nsaid. \u201cThey get at least 6 percent from company bond yields and\nyuan appreciation is about 5 percent, so we are talking about 10\npercent from bond investment. Previously,\noverseas firms could put funds only into China\u2019s exchange-traded\ndebt using quotas allowed under the Qualified Foreign\nInstitutional Investors program.  Rate Rises  Corporate debt traded on China\u2019s interbank market has\nhanded investors a  loss  of 1.7 percent this month, trimming\ngains for the year to 5 percent, Chinabond data show. That\ncompares with a 1 percent loss on  government securities .  Bonds slumped in the past month after the central bank\nraised its benchmark one-year lending and deposit rates by a\nquarter of a percentage point on Oct. 19, the first  increases \nsince 2007, to help contain inflation. Consumer prices rose 4.4\npercent from a year earlier in October, the biggest gain since\nSeptember 2008.  One-year interest-rate  swaps , the fixed cost needed to\nreceive the floating seven-day repurchase  rate , jumped 21 basis\npoints yesterday to a two-year high of 2.99 percent. Five-year\nswaps climbed 7 basis points to 3.87 percent, according to data\ncompiled by Bloomberg. While the world\u2019s biggest firms have struggled to develop products targeted at older consumers, a group led by former  Apple Inc. (AAPL) ,  Microsoft (MSFT)  Corp. and EBay Inc. employees yesterday unveiled Lively. The system of tiny sensors helps the elderly maintain their independence, letting far-flung relatives know whether they take their pills on time or exit the house.  Related Stories Lively marks the first result of an effort by Sarasota,  Florida  -- which boasts the highest concentration of elderly people of any large U.S. county -- to transform the region into a test market for companies eager to tap into the $8 trillion buying power of seniors. The  Institute for the Ages , a Sarasota nonprofit, played a key role in Lively\u2019s creation, connecting the San Francisco-based company with residents who provided feedback to improve its product.  They included Bill Tavolga, a 91-year-old self-described tech geek who helped Lively\u2019s developers find bugs in the system. The outcome was a tool that helps shrink the 350-mile (560-kilometer) distance between Phyllis Bek-gran, 89, and her son by letting him know when she doesn\u2019t pick up her TV remote.  To Sarasota\u2019s elderly, \u201cwe\u2019re saying we want to capture your voice, so that any issue that you\u2019ve got insights on, we\u2019ll find the connections that can make that voice valuable,\u201d said  Tom Esselman , 52, a former Hallmark Cards Inc. executive who now heads the Institute for the Ages, which is part think tank, part market research company.  Silver Valley  For years, businesses have conducted trial runs in cities such as Columbus,  Ohio , where the population breakdown mirrors that of the U.S. overall. In an  aging  world, Sarasota is seeking to become the new Columbus -- and, in time, the new, innovative Silver Valley counterpart to Silicon Valley in what is called the \u201caging space.\u201d  With the massive baby boom generation beginning to move into the ranks of the elderly, companies are trying to front-run the trend by figuring out the next hot products for seniors. So far their search has remained largely unfulfilled because of a marketing conundrum: Graying boomers, even more than previous generations, don\u2019t want to be identified as elderly.  Neglected Areas  The idea for the Institute for the Ages emerged after Scope, a nonprofit community group whose name stands for Sarasota County Openly Plans for Excellence, sought advice from hundreds of residents on the topic of aging in 2008. Sarasota County Commissioners approved $1.2 million to get the institute off the ground, and a recruiting firm found Esselman. He was 22 years into a career at  Kansas City , Missouri-based Hallmark, where he had helped invent talking greeting cards and served as director of innovation.  Meanwhile in Silicon Valley, Iggy Fanlo was looking for opportunities in large, growing yet neglected areas of business. He had spent the past dozen years at Internet companies, including  San Jose , California-based  EBay. (EBAY)   \u201cWhat jumped off the page was aging,\u201d said Fanlo, 51. Finding the existing market for passive home monitors for the elderly expensive and clunky, he decided to start there.  At a forum early last year sponsored by Maveron LLC, a venture capital firm that Starbucks Corp. founder  Howard Schultz  helped create, Fanlo met David Glickman, 42. Glickman, then an entrepreneur-in-residence at Maveron, had worked at Apple, where he helped develop the Newton, a 1980s precursor to the iPad.  Soon after, Fanlo and Glickman, along with Keith Dutton, a former software engineer at Microsoft, founded  Lively , and its eponymous first product was born.  Seniors\u2019 Feedback  In the startup\u2019s hunt for market-research firms, Sarasota\u2019s institute stood out. For one, it was cheaper -- at about $25,000. Yet its primary appeal was the promise of qualitative feedback through hands-on access to seniors, Glickman said.  \u201cThere\u2019s nothing more valuable than putting things in front of people and actually being in peoples\u2019 homes to talk about it,\u201d he said. Between him and and Fanlo, they visited all 30 pilot study participants -- chosen because they lived alone - - after arriving in Sarasota in February.  One was Bek-gran, whose husband of 68 years died in 2010. Lively sensors throughout Bek-gran\u2019s two-bedroom condo now log when she opens her refrigerator and exits the front door. The data is then transmitted to a secure website for her youngest son, Peter, to view from his home in  Key West , Florida.  TV Remote  \u201cI also had one on my TV remote, because we all know if I didn\u2019t pick that up, there\u2019s something wrong with what\u2019s going on in the world,\u201d Bek-gran recalled with a laugh.  One day, Bek-gran didn\u2019t open her pillbox by 11 a.m. An e-mail alert popped into Peter\u2019s inbox, and on Lively\u2019s website, a red, frowning face replaced a green smiling one next to Bek-gran\u2019s medication icon. Her phone soon began ringing; it was Peter, with a reminder to take her pills.  For Bek-gran, who\u2019s been active all her life and still shows her paintings at art exhibitions, maintaining her independence is crucial. Lively helps her do that, part of the growing \u201caging in place\u201d market for products and technology, such as walk-in bathtubs and higher toilet seats, that assist people at home as they get older. The market is forecast to rise 10-fold to $20 billion by 2020, according to a  report  by research firm Aging in Place Technology Watch.  Finding Bugs  Fellow participant Tavolga, a former marine biologist, wasn\u2019t shy about pointing out the system\u2019s flaws.  \u201cI added a sensor on the front door,\u201d Tavolga wrote to Glickman in a Feb. 26 e-mail. \u201cWorks O.K., but I cannot change the name from \u2019Custom #4.\u2019\u201d  Three days later: \u201cO.K. I found out why the label change would not take. It would not accept \u2019Front Door\u2019 as two words.\u201d  Sensors throughout Tavolga\u2019s home often failed.  \u201cThe Medication sensor is still red-face\u201d online, which indicates inactivity, he wrote. \u201cThis time I took my pills before 7 a.m.\u201d On March 26, he noted that it needed to be \u201cstrongly shaken\u201d in order to register.  \u201cIt was fun; for one thing, I\u2019m a computer geek,\u201d recalled Tavolga, who e-mails his \u201csweetheart\u201d every morning from a Samsung tablet, reads books on a Kindle and updates the online music archives of a local library twice a week.  In addition to logging a senior\u2019s daily routine, Lively solicits news and photos weekly from designated family members and friends via e-mail. It compiles them into a booklet, called a LivelyGram, and snail mails it to the senior\u2019s home. The concept was developed with Glickman\u2019s late grandmother in mind, he said. She wasn\u2019t online, and when family members mailed photos to her, it made her feel more connected.  Peace of Mind  The system gives both sides peace of mind without feeling intrusive, users say.  \u201cIt doesn\u2019t feel like monitoring because it\u2019s not the specifics of what I\u2019m doing -- it doesn\u2019t say where I\u2019m going or what I\u2019m doing,\u201d Bek-gran said.  Next year, Lively plans to add a feature that could detect falls or allow the senior to call for help in the event of an emergency -- the most-requested add-on during the trial run, including by Bek-gran, Glickman said. Lively now sends two pillbox sensors, up from one initially, after learning in Sarasota that most seniors use more than a sole dispenser, he said.  Sarasota County  Located in southwest Florida on the  Gulf of Mexico , Sarasota -- the name shared by the county and its second-biggest city -- has long been known as a go-to place for retirees after their working years have ended.  One in three of its 386,000 residents is 65 years or older, the highest proportion of any county with a population of at least 250,000, according to the U.S. Census Bureau. That\u2019s a snapshot of what the rest of the developed world will look like by 2050, according to  RTI International , a nonprofit research institute based in Research Triangle Park,  North Carolina .  Sarasota has advantages as a research center: It\u2019s wealthier, healthier and better educated than most retiree hubs, according to  data compiled by Bloomberg . Worldwide, 60-and-older consumers spent more than $8 trillion in 2010; by the end of this decade, they will spend $15 trillion, according to data tracker Euromonitor.  Creating Jobs  When Sarasota County approved $1.2 million in development grants in 2011, it was based on the promise that the Institute for the Ages would help create 840 jobs and contribute $159 million in economic impact for the area within 10 years. The institute will also measure itself based on the size of its volunteer senior database. It\u2019s currently at 1,500; by 2016, it hopes to have as many as 10,000 and, eventually, 50,000.  In July, the institute signed a deal with a joint venture between  Intel Corp. (INTC)  and  General Electric Co. (GE)  to test a product called Connect Caregiver, which helps keep track of an elder\u2019s doctors\u2019 appointments and diet, among other things, via an online portal. Juvent, a device to boost bone density made by  Palm Beach Gardens , Florida-based American Medical Innovations LLC, will be next, Esselman said.  Instead of money, the men and women who took part in the Lively study were offered a free yearlong subscription for the product. They also attended a pizza party with 10 pies Esselman made from scratch using his Italian family recipe.  \u201cWe couldn\u2019t think of a more genuine way to thank them in a personal way -- these people had become like family,\u201d Esselman said. \u201cAt one point, three of the older ladies came up to me while I was punching the dough and shared stories of them baking bread in their kitchens with their mothers.\u201d  To contact the reporters on this story: Esme E. (TWX) \u2019s Warner Brothers Entertainment achieved\npartial victory in a case involving the use of movie publicity\nstills.  The studio sued five companies that license images taken\nfrom publicity materials for the films \u201cGone With the Wind,\u201d\n\u201cWizard of Oz,\u201d and several \u201cTom and Jerry\u201d animated\nfeatures. In that order, U.S. District Judge Henry Edward Autrey said\nthe defendants were like \u201cnaughty selfish children\u201d  for\ncontinuing to gain \u201cunfairly and illegally\u201d from Warner\nBrothers\u2019 protected works.  The defendants appealed. On July 5, the 8th U.S. Circuit\nCourt of Appeals said that the trial court reached too far with\nits order. The movie publicity stills were in the public domain\nand no reasonable jury could find that \u201cmerely printing a\npublic domain image on a new style of surface\u201d infringed, the\ncourt said.  The defendant companies were still barred from creating\nthree-dimensional images or from juxtaposing those images with\ncontent taken from underlying works, such as phrases from the\nbooks on which the films are based.  The court said that such use would be adding new elements\nof expression to the protected content in the films and would\ntherefore infringe.  The case in the trial court is Warner Brothers\nEntertainment Inc., v. Dave Grossman Creations Inc., 4:06-cv-\n00546-HEA, U.S. District Court, Eastern District of Missouri\n(St. Louis). The appeal is Warner Brothers Entertainment Inc. v.\nX One X Productions, 10-1743, U.S. Court of Appeals for the\nEighth Circuit.
