Google\u2019s income shifting -- involving strategies known to\nlawyers as the \u201cDouble Irish\u201d and the \u201cDutch Sandwich\u201d --\nhelped reduce its overseas tax rate to 2.4 percent, the lowest\nof the top five U.S. technology companies by market\ncapitalization, according to  regulatory filings  in six\ncountries.  \u201cIt\u2019s remarkable that Google\u2019s effective rate is that\nlow,\u201d said  Martin A. Sullivan , a tax economist who formerly\nworked for the U.S. Treasury Department. \u201cWe know this company\noperates throughout the world mostly in high-tax countries where\nthe average corporate rate is well over 20 percent.\u201d  The U.S. corporate income-tax rate is 35 percent. In the\nU.K., Google\u2019s second-biggest market by revenue, it\u2019s 28\npercent.  Google, the owner of the world\u2019s most popular search\nengine, uses a strategy that has gained favor among such\ncompanies as Facebook Inc. and Microsoft Corp. The method takes\nadvantage of Irish tax law to legally shuttle profits into and\nout of subsidiaries there, largely escaping the country\u2019s 12.5\npercent income tax. (See an interactive graphic on Google\u2019s tax\nstrategy  here .)  The  earnings  wind up in island havens that levy no\ncorporate income taxes at all. Companies that use the Double\nIrish arrangement avoid taxes at home and abroad as the U.S.\ngovernment struggles to close a projected $1.4 trillion  budget\ngap  and European Union countries face a collective projected\ndeficit of 868 billion euros.  Countless Companies  Google, the third-largest U.S. technology company by market\ncapitalization, hasn\u2019t been accused of breaking tax laws.\n\u201cGoogle\u2019s practices are very similar to those at countless\nother global companies operating across a wide range of\nindustries,\u201d said  Jane Penner , a spokeswoman for the Mountain\nView, California-based company. Penner declined to address the\nparticulars of its tax strategies.  Facebook, the world\u2019s biggest social network, is preparing\na structure similar to Google\u2019s that will send earnings from\nIreland to the Cayman Islands, according to the company\u2019s\nfilings in Ireland and the Caymans and to a person familiar with\nits plans. A spokesman for the Palo Alto, California-based\ncompany declined to comment.  Transfer Pricing  The tactics of Google and Facebook depend on \u201ctransfer\npricing,\u201d paper transactions among corporate  subsidiaries  that\nallow for allocating income to tax havens while attributing\nexpenses to higher-tax countries. Such income shifting costs the\nU.S. government as much as $60 billion in annual revenue,\naccording to Kimberly A. Clausing, an economics professor at\nReed College in Portland, Oregon.  U.S. Representative  Dave Camp  of Michigan, the ranking\nRepublican on the House Ways and Means Committee, and other\npoliticians say the 35 percent U.S. statutory rate is too high\nrelative to foreign countries. International income-shifting,\nwhich helped cut Google\u2019s overall effective tax rate to 22.2\npercent last year, shows one way that loopholes undermine that\ntop U.S. rate.  Two thousand U.S. companies paid a median effective cash\nrate of 28.3 percent in federal, state and foreign income taxes\nin a 2005 study by academics at the University of Michigan and\nthe University of North Carolina. The combined national-local\nstatutory rate is 34.4 percent in France, 30.2 percent in\nGermany and 39.5 percent in Japan, according to the Paris-based\nOrganization for Economic Cooperation and Development.  The Double Irish  As a strategy for limiting taxes, the Double Irish method\nis \u201cvery common at the moment, particularly with companies with\nintellectual property,\u201d said  Richard Murphy , director of U.K.-\nbased Tax Research LLP. Murphy, who has worked on similar\ntransactions, estimates that hundreds of multinationals use some\nversion of the method.  The high corporate tax rate in the U.S. motivates companies\nto move activities and related income to lower-tax countries,\nsaid Irving H. Plotkin, a senior managing director at\nPricewaterhouseCoopers LLP\u2019s national tax practice in Boston. He\ndelivered a presentation in Washington, D.C. this year titled\n\u201cTransfer Pricing is Not a Four Letter Word.\u201d  \u201cA company\u2019s obligation to its shareholders is to try to\nminimize its taxes and all costs, but to do so legally,\u201d\nPlotkin said in an interview.  Boosting Earnings  Google\u2019s transfer pricing contributed to international tax\nbenefits that boosted its earnings by 26 percent last year,\ncompany filings show. Based on a rough analysis, if the company\npaid taxes at the 35 percent rate on all its earnings, its share\nprice might be reduced by about $100, said  Clayton Moran , an\nanalyst at Benchmark Co. in Boca Raton, Florida. He recommends\nbuying Google stock, which closed yesterday at $607.98.  The company, which tells employees \u201c don\u2019t be evil \u201d in its\ncode of conduct, has cut its effective tax rate abroad more than\nits peers in the technology sector: Apple Inc., the maker of the\niPhone;  Microsoft , the largest software company;  International\nBusiness Machines Corp. , the biggest computer-services provider;\nand Oracle Corp., the second-biggest software company. Those\ncompanies reported rates that ranged between 4.5 percent and\n25.8 percent for 2007 through 2009.  Google is \u201cflying a  banner  of doing no evil, and then\nthey\u2019re perpetrating evil under our noses,\u201d said  Abraham J. Briloff , a professor emeritus of accounting at Baruch College in\nNew York who has examined Google\u2019s tax disclosures.  \u201cWho is it that paid for the underlying concept on which\nthey built these billions of dollars of revenues?\u201d Briloff\nsaid. \u201cIt was paid for by the United States citizenry.\u201d  Taxpayer Funding  The U.S.  National Science Foundation  funded the mid-1990s\nresearch at Stanford University that helped lead to Google\u2019s\ncreation. Taxpayers also paid for a scholarship for the\ncompany\u2019s cofounder, Sergey Brin, while he worked on that\nresearch. Google now has a stock market value of $194.2 billion.  Google\u2019s annual reports from 2007 to 2009 ascribe a\ncumulative $3.1 billion tax savings to the \u201cforeign rate\ndifferential.\u201d Such entries typically describe how much tax\nU.S. companies save from profits earned overseas.  In February, the  Obama  administration proposed measures to\ncurb shifting profits offshore, part of a package intended to\nraise $12 billion a year over the coming decade. While the key\nproposals largely haven\u2019t advanced in Congress, the IRS said in\nApril it would devote additional agents and lawyers to focus on\nfive large transfer pricing arrangements.  Arm\u2019s Length  Income shifting commonly begins when companies like Google\nsell or license the foreign rights to intellectual property\ndeveloped in the U.S. to a subsidiary in a low-tax country. That\nmeans foreign profits based on the technology get attributed to\nthe offshore unit, not the parent. Under U.S. tax rules,\nsubsidiaries must pay \u201carm\u2019s length\u201d prices for the rights --\nor the amount an unrelated company would.  Because the payments contribute to taxable income, the\nparent company has an incentive to set them as low as possible.\nCutting the foreign subsidiary\u2019s expenses effectively shifts\nprofits overseas.  After three years of negotiations, Google received approval\nfrom the IRS in 2006 for its transfer pricing arrangement,\naccording to filings with the Securities and Exchange\nCommission.  The IRS gave its consent in a secret pact known as an\nadvanced pricing agreement. Google wouldn\u2019t discuss the price\nset under the arrangement, which licensed the rights to its\nsearch and advertising technology and other intangible property\nfor Europe, the Middle East and Africa to a unit called Google\nIreland Holdings, according to a person familiar with the\nmatter.  Dublin Office  That licensee in turn owns Google Ireland Limited, which\nemploys almost 2,000 people in a silvery glass office building\nin central Dublin, a block from the city\u2019s Grand Canal. The\nDublin subsidiary sells advertising globally and was credited by\nGoogle with 88 percent of its $12.5 billion in non-U.S. sales in\n2009.  Allocating the revenue to Ireland helps Google avoid income\ntaxes in the U.S., where most of its technology was developed.\nThe arrangement also reduces the company\u2019s liabilities in\nrelatively high-tax European countries where many of its\ncustomers are located.  The profits don\u2019t stay with the Dublin subsidiary, which\nreported pretax income of less than 1 percent of sales in 2008,\naccording to Irish records. That\u2019s largely because it paid $5.4\nbillion in royalties to Google Ireland Holdings, which has its\n\u201ceffective centre of management\u201d in Bermuda, according to\ncompany filings.  Law Firm Directors  This Bermuda-managed entity is owned by a pair of Google\nsubsidiaries that list as their directors two attorneys and a\nmanager at Conyers Dill & Pearman, a Hamilton, Bermuda law firm.  Tax planners call such an arrangement a Double Irish\nbecause it relies on two Irish companies. One pays royalties to\nuse intellectual property, generating expenses that reduce Irish\ntaxable income. The second collects the royalties in a tax haven\nlike Bermuda, avoiding Irish taxes.  To steer clear of an Irish withholding tax, payments from\nGoogle\u2019s Dublin unit don\u2019t go directly to Bermuda. A brief\ndetour to the Netherlands avoids that liability, because Irish\ntax law exempts certain royalties to companies in other EU-\nmember nations. The fees first go to a Dutch unit, Google\nNetherlands Holdings B.V., which pays out about 99.8 percent of\nwhat it collects to the Bermuda entity, company filings show.\nThe Amsterdam-based subsidiary lists no employees. The New York-based\ndrug manufacturer claims that most of its profits are earned\noverseas even though its sales are almost entirely in the U.S.\nForest later disclosed that its transfer pricing was being\naudited by the IRS.  Since the 1960s, Ireland has pursued a strategy of offering\ntax incentives to attract multinationals. A lesser-appreciated\naspect of Ireland\u2019s appeal is that it allows companies to shift\nincome out of the country with minimal tax consequences, said\nJim Stewart, a senior lecturer in finance at Trinity College\u2019s\nschool of business in Dublin.  Getting Profits Out  \u201cYou accumulate profits within Ireland, but then you get\nthem out of the country relatively easily,\u201d Stewart said. \u201cAnd\nyou do it by using Bermuda.\u201d  Eoin Dorgan, a spokesman for the  Irish Department of\nFinance , declined to comment on Google\u2019s strategies\nspecifically. \u201cIreland always seeks to ensure that the profits\ncharged in Ireland fully reflect the functions, assets and risks\nlocated here by multinational groups,\u201d he said.  Once Google\u2019s non-U.S. profits hit Bermuda, they become\ndifficult to track. The subsidiary managed there changed its\nlegal form of organization in 2006 to become a so-called\nunlimited liability company. Under Irish rules, that means it\u2019s\nnot required to disclose such financial information as income\nstatements or balance sheets.  \u201cSticking an unlimited company in the group structure has\nbecome more common in Ireland, largely to prevent disclosure,\u201d\nStewart said.  Deferred Indefinitely  Technically, multinationals that shift profits overseas are\ndeferring U.S. income taxes, not avoiding them permanently. The\ndeferral lasts until companies decide to bring the earnings back\nto the U.S. In practice, they rarely repatriate significant\nportions, thus avoiding the taxes indefinitely, said Michelle\nHanlon, an accounting professor at the Massachusetts Institute\nof Technology.  U.S. policy makers, meanwhile, have taken halting steps to\naddress concerns about transfer pricing. In 2009, the Treasury\nDepartment proposed levying taxes on certain payments between\nU.S. companies\u2019 foreign subsidiaries. The\nWhite House still proposes to tax excessive profits of offshore\nsubsidiaries as a curb on income shifting, she said. This is a new one for the software giant, which debuted its next-generation console today in  13 countries . The original Xbox and Xbox 360 did not run Windows, Microsoft's flagship computing platform. Previous iterations of the system had a single custom operating system focused primarily on playing games. The Xbox One has a game-centric operating system, too. But it also has a stripped-down version of Windows 8, designed to be more flexible and optimized for non-gaming applications like Skype and Hulu. The third operating system is a layer that connects the two, enabling fast switching between games and apps. It's not the first video-game system that has a version of Windows loaded onto it \u2014 Sega's Dreamcast, which launched in 1999, ran Windows CE. But it's the first Xbox. The 360 wasn't really capable of running Windows, according to Boyd Multerer, director of development for Xbox.  The triple-platform play is part of a plan to leverage technologies and products from various divisions of Microsoft to get a leg up on  Sony  and Nintendo. Microsoft views the Xbox One as a test case for its new One Microsoft strategy, which is  outgoing CEO Steve Ballmer 's scheme to make the company work better together. Check out my story in the latest issue of  Bloomberg Businessweek  for more on that.  \"There's been this tremendous mindset change,\" Multerer said. \"We're getting more attention and more help and more love from the Windows team than we've ever seen before.\" Because game hardware is only updated every five to 10 years, consoles need to be able to adapt to changing usage habits and features that might not exist when they came out. When the Xbox 360 was released eight years ago, nobody could have foreseen Kinect or the advent of apps. To future-proof the Xbox One, Microsoft turned to a technology typically used in data centers. Virtualization software \u2014 a program called hypervisor, specifically \u2014 allows the hardware to run different operating systems without one impacting the other. The structure will enable Microsoft to add to and experiment with the apps side of the machine without wrecking existing games, Multerer said. On the Xbox 360, apps can only run one at a time, and the first batch of programs had to be custom-built by Microsoft because the tools were so complicated.  Microsoft brought in some of its big guns to work on the third operating system and programming tools that tie the whole thing together. For example, Dave Cutler, the father of Windows NT, was shifted to Xbox to build the hypervisor. Multerer himself is a key part of gaming history at Microsoft as the man who started the Xbox Live online service. J Allard, one of the earliest Xbox executives, brought him to the company's nascent gaming division in 2000. In his pitch, Allard pointed to the back of the original Xbox hardware and said, \"We've decided to put an Ethernet port in. Go figure out what it talks to,\" recalled Multerer.  Marc Whitten, the chief product officer at Xbox, said the idea of Windows in an Xbox might elicit a few groans. Microsoft hasn't always done a good job of combining products elegantly, he said. \"Collaboration, when done well, is a magical thing,\" he says. \"When it's done poorly, it can feel a little pasted together.\" Thankfully, Microsoft has taken extra steps to minimize the chance of deathmatches getting interrupted by blue screens of death.","path":".\/2008_2012_msft_bloomberg_news\/xbox-one-has-not-one-but-three-operating-systems.txt"},{"id":1617247,"title":"Nokia Tells U.K. Court HTC Is Copying Handset Texting Technology","released_at":"<date>October 7 2013<\/date> <time>15:35:51<\/time>","content":"Nokia Oyj (NOK1V) , the Finish company selling\nits handset business to Microsoft Corp, told a London court that\nTaiwanese phonemaker HTC Corp. was copying its technology\ndesigned to help transmit voice and text messages. Microsoft\u2019s version of the Surface tablet that is most\ncomparable to the iPad won\u2019t be able to run older Windows apps,\nforcing developers to start from scratch.  \u2018Playing Catch-Up\u2019  Windows 8 is the first Microsoft operating system that will\nwork on computers running chips based on  ARM Holdings Plc (ARM) \ntechnology. The NERD building, located in Cambridge\u2019s Kendall Square,\nlets Microsoft maintain a base near the  Massachusetts Institute\nof Technology  and  Harvard University  as well as offices\nbelonging to Google,  VMware Inc. In June the  U.S. Senate  passed an immigration bill that\nallows more H-1Bs while also increasing their cost and barring\nsome companies from placing holders of the visa with customers.\nIndia\u2019s software-export industry relies on an army of such guest\nworkers to service clients in the U.S., its biggest market. The bill \u201cis fairly detrimental to our business model,\u201d\nAshok Vemuri, the head of Americas at Infosys Ltd., India\u2019s\nsecond-largest software exporter, said in a July 12 interview.\n\u201cIt\u2019s really action for the creation of jobs\u201d for U.S.\nworkers. Infosys (INFO)  is\ntrying to alert U.S. clients to the threat the bill poses to the\nSouth Asian country\u2019s technology industry, he said.  $87 Billion  India will export as much as  $87 billion  of information\ntechnology services in the year ending March 2014, according to\nNASSCOM, an industry lobby. Sales are equivalent to about 4.5\npercent of India\u2019s $1.8 trillion gross domestic product.  The backbone of that trade is the H-1B, a non-immigrant\npass that lets companies in the U.S. temporarily hire workers in\nspecialist fields. The permit lasts for up to three years and\nthe maximum extension is usually 36 months.  U.S.-registered units of Indian companies apply for the\nvisas and then often locate the recipient at a client\u2019s company\nto support the software.  Indians received more than half the 106,445 first-time\nH-1Bs issued in the year ending September 2011, according to a\nU.S. Department of Homeland Security  report . The main goals of the Senate bill, the most significant\nrevision of U.S. immigration law in a generation, are to create\na path to citizenship for about 11 million undocumented\nimmigrants and direct $46.3 billion toward securing the border\nwith  Mexico .  The legislation is now before the  House of Representatives ,\nwhose leaders have expressed opposition to the Senate measure\nand say they favor separate, piecemeal bills.  Potential Casualties  Infosys and other Indian outsourcers, such as larger rival\n Tata Consultancy Services Ltd. (TCS)  in Mumbai, have emerged as\npotential casualties of clauses that change rules governing H-1B\nand L-1 visas intended for high-skilled workers.  While the legislation raises the annual H-1B cap to as much\nas 180,000 from 65,000, it increases visa costs five-fold for\nsome companies to $10,000. It also bans larger employers with 15\npercent or more of their U.S. workforce on such permits from\nsending H-1B staff to client\u2019s sites.  The aim is to balance the U.S. economy\u2019s need to fill\ngenuine skills gaps with protection for U.S. citizens from\nbusinesses that may use the guest-worker program to bring in\ncheaper labor, Neil Ruiz, a senior policy analyst at the\n Brookings Institution  in  Washington , said in an interview.  Schumer\u2019s View  \u201cThe goal of the H-1B program is to have American\ncompanies hire foreigners to fill gaps in their employment needs\n-- not to simply bring in lower-cost labor from overseas,\u201d\nSenator  Charles Schumer , a  New York  Democrat who is the bill\u2019s\nprincipal sponsor, said in an e-mail.  \u201cThat\u2019s not what some\ncompanies have been doing. Losing Sleep  \u201cI\u2019m losing sleep over it,\u201d said Sripal, who earns about\n$5,500 a month. \u201cI\u2019ve seen more people get rejected this year\nthan ever before. No one becomes a software engineer for an\noutsourcing company because they love coding or consulting. It\u2019s\nfor the status back home -- so my parents can brag about their\nson and find me a nice wife. Time\u2019s running out I guess.\u201d  Sripal sends at least $1,000 a month to his family in\nBangalore and Mullapudi, whose H-1B expires in the fall of 2015,\nabout $650 for his sister\u2019s education in  New Delhi . They asked\nthat their Indian employers not be named as they aren\u2019t\nauthorized to speak to the media.  India \u2019s central bank  estimated  in 2010 that the U.S. and\n Canada  account for about 38 percent of remittances to the\ncountry, citing transfers by information technology workers.\n Remittances  overall were $62 billion in the year ended March.  Trade Barriers  The potential effect of the Democratic-led Senate\u2019s rules\non such transfers and export earnings would ripple through\n Asia \u2019s No. 3 economy, stoking losses of $6 billion to $8 billion\nin the 12 months to March 2015, JPMorgan estimated in a June 24\nnote.  Indian Finance Minister Palaniappan Chidambaram told\nmembers of the House during a trip to the U.S. earlier this\nmonth that the possible curbs on knowledge workers amount to\nnon-tariff trade  barriers .  Chidambaram is trying to keep capital flowing into India to\nrevive its economy, which grew at the slowest pace in a decade\nin the year ended March. The country also needs funds to finance\na  record  current-account deficit and to steady the rupee. The\ncurrency sank to an all-time low versus the dollar July 8.  Sangeeta Kumar, for one, hopes India convinces U.S.\nlawmakers to think again. The New Delhi-based 32-year-old\nanalyst at Tata Consultancy Services has set her sights on\nworking in the world\u2019s biggest economy.  \u201cThe immigration bill is a major blow to my career\naspirations,\u201d she said. \u201cGoing to the U.S. doesn\u2019t just mean\nmore money, but also work experience that improves your long-term job prospects.\u201d  Possible Reprieve  For now, India may get a reprieve after the Republican-led\nHouse delayed consideration of immigration bills until the fall.  House Republicans\u2019 decision to act in a piecemeal fashion,\ninstead of on one comprehensive bill, points to a drawn-out\nprocess, diminishing the chances that President  Barack Obama \nwill sign his top domestic priority into law by year\u2019s end.  Current draft House legislation also lacks the clause\nbarring visa-dependent employers from client sites, said\nBrookings\u2019 Ruiz. The shape and timing of the final law remain\nunclear, he said.  A clampdown may have a silver lining for India by ensuring\nskilled workers stay in or return to the country sooner, said\nShubhada Rao, chief economist at  Yes Bank Ltd. (YES)  in Mumbai.  \u201cI don\u2019t think it\u2019ll be a challenge for those people to\nfind appropriate work here,\u201d Rao said in an interview. Yet both have battled back from unemployment to\ncreate successful businesses, with the sort of government\nsupport that could help thousands of other jobless people, too.  Allie  manages  apartment buildings in  Portland ,  Oregon ;\nCostlow owns four creperies in  Maryland . To get started, each\ndrew on business coaching and income support from an unusual\nstate-funded jobless initiative. These  self-employment\nassistance  programs provide 26 weeks of income support,\ntypically about $10,000. Participants try to start enterprises,\nrather than being required to look full time for traditional\njobs.  Founding a business isn\u2019t for everyone. Hours are long,\ninitial earnings puny, and the failure rate high even in boom\ntimes. A weak economy makes everything harder.  For some displaced workers, however, self-employment may be\ntheir best hope. Entrepreneurial aid to the jobless is typically\naimed at older, educated workers who lost good jobs in battered\nindustries. With the national  unemployment rate  above 9 percent,\nsuch candidates face slim odds of finding appropriate work\nthrough a standard job hunt.  In  Oregon , people opting for self-employment get business\npointers as well as detailed reviews of their startup plans.\nExaminers look for clear ideas about pricing, supplies,\ncustomers and competition. Only candidates judged to have at\nleast a moderate chance of success can proceed.  Oregon\u2019s Successes  Oregon recently surveyed 369 people who have participated\nin its program since 2000. Seventy percent had started a\nbusiness; nearly half of those were hiring workers. The small\nsurvey\u2019s responses might be skewed toward recipients who\nthrived. Even so, Oregon\u2019s successful entrepreneurs each created\nan average of 2.63 additional jobs.  In  New Jersey , about 600 jobless people a year try self-\nemployment. Data on success rates is fragmentary, but state\nofficials say participants have started businesses in at least\n33 fields, including computer services and catering. When such\nventures thrive, founders don\u2019t just earn income -- they keep\nhiring, becoming job multipliers.  Self-employment aid closely matches the cost of regular\n unemployment benefits , which can run $400 a person per week.\nBritain, France and  Sweden  have operated similar entrepreneurial\nassistance programs since the 1980s, with good results. In the\nU.S., though, only about a dozen states have followed suit, and\nmost programs are tiny.  Bureaucracy is partly to blame. Current state and federal\nrules don\u2019t allow unemployed workers to pursue self-employment\naid right away; instead they must qualify for regular jobless\nbenefits first, which takes weeks. States also worry that some\nstartup dreams might fizzle quickly, wasting taxpayer money.  Living With Risks  Making the entrepreneur\u2019s path risk-free is impossible.\nStill, that shouldn\u2019t stymie such aid. Three of the biggest\nstates -- California, Texas and  Florida  -- are home to 30\npercent of America\u2019s unemployed. Two other changes could help make entrepreneurship a\nlikelier path back to work. In some cases\nthis year\u2019s hobby can be built into next year\u2019s business.  When 4.7 people are out of work for every job opening,\nunemployed Americans deserve better odds of becoming their own\nbosses. Two-thirds of the 862 surveyed described the global economy as either stable or improving. That\u2019s up from just over half who said that in September and is the most since May 2011.  The U.S. came out on top for the eighth straight quarter when investors were asked which markets will offer the best opportunities over the next year. China ranked second, reversing a decline to fourth in the September poll of investors, analysts and traders who are Bloomberg subscribers. The European Union, beset by a debt crisis, was seen offering the worst returns.  \u201cThe global economy is improving, recovering and healing, thanks to the U.S. and the  emerging markets ,\u201d said Andrea Guzzi, a poll respondent and vice president of IST Investmentstiftung fuer Personalvorsorge, which manages money for Swiss pension funds. \u201cMore people are becoming wealthy, less and less are poor.\u201d  Stocks were seen as the asset of choice, with more than one in three of those surveyed on Nov. 27 forecasting equities would have the best returns in the coming year. Real estate came in second: Just less than one in five investors singled it out favorably, the best showing since the quarterly poll began in July 2009. Bonds were seen as offering the worst returns.  Fed Purchases  The  Federal Reserve  is expected to provide continued support to the  bond market  after its Operation Twist program ends next month, according to the poll. About three in four said the U.S. central bank will begin outright purchases of  Treasury securities  after its plan for  swapping  short-dated securities for longer-dated ones expires.  A plurality -- two in five -- said the Fed also will continue buying mortgage-backed securities into 2014, a strategy dubbed QE3 by investors, shorthand for the third round of quantitative easing by the central bank.  \u201cThe Fed is being very clear about monetary policy,\u201d Gala Prada, a poll respondent and portfolio and asset manager for Fiatc Mutua de Seguros y Reaseguros, a Barcelona-based insurance company, said in an e-mail. \u201cIf the economy doesn\u2019t improve, there will be a QE4 or more asset purchases.\u201d  Tighter Rules  The growing optimism among investors about the world economy was not reflected in their views of the prospects for the financial services industry. About seven in ten said they expect large banks to reduce payrolls further in the next year after cutting at least 188,000 jobs over the last two years. A majority blame regulatory changes for the reductions.  Banking authorities have tightened rules and raised capital standards on banks after the worst financial crisis since the Great Depression forced governments to spend billions of dollars to rescue ailing financial institutions.  \u201cMany countries have oversized banking sectors, which need to go back to more sustainable sizes,\u201d Guzzi said in an e-mail from Zurich.  The optimism on the world economy is based in part on an expectation that the U.S. will avert $607 billion in automatic spending cuts and tax increases scheduled for Jan. 1. Three out of four surveyed anticipate that President  Barack Obama  and Congressional leaders will reach a short-term agreement to avoid the fiscal cliff.  OECD Warning  The 34-nation Organization for Economic Cooperation and Development in Paris warned this week that the world economy would tip into recession if the U.S. failed to act.  Close to half of investors said they plan to increase their exposure to equities over the next six months, up from less than two in five in September.  Respondents are most bullish about U.S. equities. A majority forecast that the Standard & Poor\u2019s 500 Index will rise during that time frame. S&P 500 futures rose 0.6 percent to 1,415.8 at 7:08 a.m. in  New York  amid optimism President Barack Obama will reach an agreement with Congress over a new budget. The stock gauge has increased 12 percent this year.  \u201cU.S. companies have better profit potential, balance sheets and access to capital,\u201d Christian Thwaites, a poll respondent and president and chief executive officer in New York of Sentinel Investment, which manages more than $27 billion, said in an e-mail.  Property Prices  U.S. property prices also are heading up, investors said. More than three in five forecast that housing values would be higher six months from now. A minority responded that way in the last poll in September.  Home prices  rose in the year ended in September by the most since July 2010, climbing by 3 percent, according to the S&P\/Case-Shiller index of property values in 20 cities.  The housing market has been supported by the Fed, which has said it expects to hold overnight interbank rates near zero until at least the middle of 2015.  Forty-five percent of investors said the U.S. central bank would enhance understanding of its policies and help the economy if it tied its pledge to keep rates low to specific thresholds for unemployment and inflation. One in four said such a move would be confusing if such a goal-oriented commitment replaced the Fed\u2019s current calendar-specific rate promise.  The Fed itself is split over the issue. Fed Vice Chairman  Janet Yellen  and Chicago Fed President  Charles Evans  have supported a switch, while Philadelphia\u2019s  Charles Plosser  and the Dallas Fed\u2019s  Richard Fisher  have voiced doubts.  Commodities, Bonds  Commodities lost some favor in the latest survey. Only 12 percent said it will be the best-performing asset class over the next year, down from 18 percent in September.  Investors remain downbeat on bonds. Forty-eight percent intend to reduce their holdings of U.S. Treasury bonds over the next six months, the most since the poll began asking that question in May 2011. By a slim margin -- 50 to 45 percent -- respondents viewed Treasuries as a safer investment than AAA- rated U.S. corporate bonds, such as those of Microsoft Corp. and Exxon Mobil Corp.  More than two of five investors expect European Union markets to offer the worst opportunities over the next year. That was the most negative reading in the poll, followed by  Japan , with 23 percent, and the  Middle East , with 17 percent, up from 7 percent in September.  Iran Strike  Forty percent of respondents are less likely to put money into  Egypt  since President Mohamed Mursi took over in July -- 10 times the amount who said they are more likely to invest.  Protesters and police clashed in Cairo on Nov. 28 as Egypt\u2019s opposition resolved to stand firm against Mursi and the Muslim Brotherhood in a showdown over his self-decreed powers.  Half of those surveyed said they don\u2019t expect a military strike against  Iran\u2019s nuclear program  in 2013.  Israeli Prime Minister  Benjamin Netanyahu  has repeatedly warned that time is running out to prevent an Iranian nuclear bomb, which he expects to be aimed at  Israel .  Iranian President  Mahmoud Ahmadinejad , who regularly denounces Israel as an illegitimate regime that should \u201cdisappear,\u201d says his country\u2019s nuclear program is for peaceful purposes.  The poll of Bloomberg customers was conducted by Selzer & Co., a  Des Moines , Iowa-based company. The survey has a margin of error of plus or minus 3.3 percentage points. She told the managers she hadn\u2019t approved\nthe transfer. The problem was, her computer had.  As Allison, chief executive officer of Sterling Heights,\nMichigan-based Experi-Metal Inc., was to learn, her company\ncomputer was approving other transfers as she spoke. During\nhours of frantic phone calls with her bank, Allison, 45, was\nunable to stop this cybercrime in progress as transfer followed\ntransfer. By day\u2019s end, $5.2 million was gone.  She turned to her bank, a branch of  Comerica Inc. (CMA) , to help\nrecover the money for her metal-products firm. It got all but\n$561,000 of the funds. Then came the surprise: the bank said the\nloss was Experi-Metal\u2019s problem because it had allowed Allison\u2019s\ncomputer to be infected by the hackers.  \u201cAt the end of the day, the fraud department at Comerica\nsaid: \u2018What\u2019s wrong with you? How could you let this happen?\u2019\u201d\nAllison said.  In increments of a few thousand dollars to a few million\nper theft, cybercrooks are stealing as much as $1 billion a year\nfrom small and mid-sized bank accounts in the U.S. and Europe\nlike Experi-Metal, according to Don Jackson, a security expert\nat Dell SecureWorks. And account holders are the big losers.  \u2018Losing More Now\u2019  \u201cI think they\u2019re losing more now than to the James Gang\nand Bonnie and Clyde and the rest of the famous gangs\ncombined,\u201d said U.S. Senator Sheldon Whitehouse, a Rhode Island\nDemocrat who chaired a Select Committee on Intelligence task\nforce on U.S. cybersecurity in 2010.  Organized criminal gangs, operating mostly out of Eastern\nEurope, target small companies, school districts and local\ngovernments that maintain fat commercial bank accounts protected\nby rudimentary security measures at community or regional banks.\nThe accounts typically aren\u2019t covered by insurance as individual\naccounts are.  \u201cIf everyone knew their money was at risk in small and\nmedium-sized banks, they would move their accounts to JPMorgan\nChase,\u201d said James Woodhill, a venture capitalist who is\nleading an effort to get smaller banks to upgrade anti-fraud\nsecurity for their online banking programs.  JPMorgan Chase & Co. (JPM) , the second-largest  U.S. bank , is the\nonly major U.S. bank that insures commercial deposits against\nthe type of hacking that plagues smaller banks, Woodhill said.  \u201cChase has invested substantially in fraud prevention and\ndetection capabilities for our clients,\u201d Patrick Linehan, a\nJPMorgan spokesman, said in an e-mail. \u201cIf there is fraud on an\naccount, we work with our clients on a case-by-case basis.\u201d  Smaller Banks  Smaller banks as well as many of the victims tend not to\nmake the thefts public, according to interviews with the\ncustomers and experts such as Woodhill. As the threat becomes\nbetter known, small-business customers and other target entities\nmay shift their business to large, national banks, which can\nbetter absorb the losses to maintain customer relations and\nwhich have better security policies to protect clients from such\ncrimes.  \u201cIt\u2019s frightening for small businesses because they have\nno clue about this,\u201d said Avivah Litan, an analyst at Stamford,\nConnecticut-based Gartner Inc., which does computer analysis.\n\u201cThey just don\u2019t have any clue, and everyone expects their bank\nto protect them. Businesses are not equipped to deal with this\nproblem, and banks are barely equipped.\u201d  Customers used to being made whole when they are victims of\ncredit-card fraud or ATM thefts have had to sue small and\nmedium-size banks to recover losses after being blamed by their\nbranches for permitting the crime, as Allison was.  Law Enforcement  The traditional help of law enforcement hasn\u2019t been there\neither for such customers. In the heyday of bank robberies in\nthe 1930s, the FBI became famous for Tommy-gun shootouts with\nthe bad guys, who were put on the Most Wanted list. In most\ncases, the identities of the John Dillingers and Pretty Boy\nFloyds of the 21st Century aren\u2019t known because of online\nanonymity, and the bureau doesn\u2019t disclose statistics on how\nmuch these cybercrooks are stealing.  Victims in the last two years have ranged from Green Ford\nSales, a car dealership in Abilene,  Kansas , to Golden State\nBridge Inc., a construction company in  California  wine country.\nNo need to use a mask or gun. These criminals can steal millions\nfrom the comfort of their homes dressed in their pajamas.  The crime profits can be staggering and the risks minimal.\nJackson, the security expert, said three sophisticated gangs\neach haul in at least $100 million a year. That dwarfs the $43\nmillion taken in all conventional bank heists in the U.S. last\nyear, from stick-ups to burglaries, according to the FBI.  A $100 Million Hit  \u201cA $100 million hit on a bank or a series of banks,\u201d\nWhitehouse said. \u201cThat\u2019s a pretty big bank robbery. And it\ndoesn\u2019t even make the press. It just trickles through in FBI tip\nsheets.\u201d  To law enforcement officials, cybercrime is a new priority.\nBoth the  Federal Bureau of Investigation  and the U.S. Secret\nService, which has jurisdiction over financial crimes, have\nboosted manpower to combat computer-enabled robberies and have\nformed partnerships with foreign law-enforcement agencies.  Those efforts have been swamped by the explosion in e-\ncommerce, said Chris Swecker, a former FBI assistant director\nwho advises companies on cybersecurity. As millions of customers\nhave shifted online, criminals have followed, their hacking\ntools and nimble criminal organizations racing ahead of old-\nschool law enforcement models.  \u201cThrough cybercrime, transnational criminal organizations\npose a significant threat to financial and trust systems,\u201d\nincluding banking, stock markets and credit-card services,\naccording to a National Security Council report issued in July.  National Security Threat  Cybercrime has risen to the level of a national security\nthreat, according to the report, citing a \u201ccritical shortage of\ninvestigators with the knowledge and expertise to analyze the\never increasing amounts of potential digital evidence.\u201d  The banking industry\u2019s reluctance to confront this problem\nhead-on has allowed criminals to reinvest some of their booty to\ncreate better, more effective malicious software, known as\nmalware, according to Woodhill.  Malware is what hurt Earl Goossen, business manager for\nGreen Ford Sales, when he logged on to the company\u2019s payroll\naccount at First Bank Kansas at 7:45 a.m. central standard time\non Nov. 3, 2010. Just two days earlier he\u2019d used his computer to\narrange for the bank to send out the $63,000 payroll to employee\naccounts. Everything went smoothly at first. Goossen responded\nto a follow-up e-mail request from First Bank Kansas to okay the\npayroll, just as he did on the 1st and 15th of every month.  Malicious Software  Unbeknownst to Goossen, malicious software had infected the\ncomputer with a so-called worm, which had the ability to grab\npasswords, user names and credit-card data.  Some malware allows hackers thousands of miles away to take\nremote control of machines it infects, as if they were sitting\nat the keyboard. This malware is affordable and easy to obtain.\nA basic version sells for less than $5,000, Jackson said. Many\nmodels, licensed like commercial software from Microsoft Corp.\nand Adobe Systems Inc., even come with tech support, he said.  The worm on Goossen\u2019s machine allowed thieves to log onto\nthe website of the auto dealer\u2019s bank using Goossen\u2019s\ncredentials and set up a second payroll batch for the usual\namount for nine non-existent employees. The additional payroll\nwas sent out overnight by First Bank.  The software allowed the hackers to grab Goossen\u2019s e-mail\npassword and banking details. All they had to do was change the\nnotification e-mail address to a name under their control.  Gun-Toting Robbers  When an amount like Green Ford\u2019s $63,000 is taken from a\nbank by gun-toting robbers, the FBI would typically dispatch\nspecial agents to cordon off the crime scene and interview\nwitnesses. No agents arrived in Abilene on Nov. 4, and no one at\nthe company was ever interviewed by the bureau about the theft.  Green Ford\u2019s owner, Lease Duckwall, filled out a report\nwith local police, who don\u2019t have a cybercrime unit. The Kansas\nBureau of Investigation examined his computer and found nothing\nof use. Frustrated, Duckwall turned detective, interviewing bank\nemployees, victims of similar crimes and whoever knew anything\nabout cybertheft. In the end, the trail went cold.  Representatives of the FBI and the Secret Service insist\nthey are not overwhelmed.  \u201cI don\u2019t think it\u2019s right to conclude that because there\nare not a lot of arrests that law enforcement is not doing its\njob,\u201d said Gordon Snow, the FBI\u2019s assistant director of the\ncyber division.  Fighting Cybercrime  The FBI and Secret Service have increased the number of\nagents dedicated to fighting cybercrime. Last September, as part\nof \u201cOperation Trident Beach,\u201d U.S. prosecutors in  Manhattan \narrested a gang of money mules in connection with a wide-ranging\ncyberfraud ring that had stolen $70 million from banks and tried\nto grab another $150 million in the U.S. and Western  Europe . No\nringleader was arrested, even though five were questioned by\npolice in Ukraine, according to the FBI.  The inability to put handcuffs on suspects in Eastern\nEurope is a source of frustration for law enforcement, according\nto representatives of the FBI and Secret Service.  \u201cWe can\u2019t let that stop us from continuing to move\nforward,\u201d said Pablo Martinez, who heads the cybercrime unit at\nthe Secret Service. \u201cYou have to go after every target.\u201d  Mules, used by hackers as cutouts, are an obvious target,\neven the unwitting ones. When thieves stole the money from\nDuckwall\u2019s dealership, some of the money first went to Shawn\nYoung\u2019s account in upstate  New York . Young thought it was a\nlegitimate transaction -- at first.  Assistant Manager  Young, 35, was officially an assistant manager for R.E.\nCompany Back Office. He got his job in October through a\nCareerbuilder website ad that said an Australian office services\ncompany was looking to expand into New York state. He was\nselected to scout locations in the Binghamton area. It did seem\nodd his new employer never asked for his Social Security number,\nhe said in an interview.  Part of his job was to transfer payments made by some of\nthe company\u2019s U.S.-based clients to various programmers. He\ncorresponded with his boss, Samantha Simons, exclusively through\nthe company\u2019s intranet site.  At 8:45 a.m. on Nov. 3, Young got his first payment-related\nassignment. He logged into the R.E. Company Back Office intranet\nsite and learned from his supervisors that $4,975 had been\ndeposited into his account at M&T Bank in Endicott, New York.\nThe sender was Green Ford Sales.  Act Quickly  His boss said he could keep $145 of the money if he acted\nquickly. Within 10 minutes, he withdrew the funds and drove to\nthe closest  Western Union Co. (WU)  office, a few miles away. Young\npulled into the Western Union parking lot and his cell phone\nrang. It was a manager from the M&T Bank branch where he\u2019d made\nthe withdrawal. She said the bank had discovered the wire\ntransfer wasn\u2019t authorized. It was only then that Young realized\nsomething might be wrong, he said.  On his way back the bank, his phone rang again. It was\nSimons, calling from a Syracuse telephone area code to see if\nthere was a problem with the transfer. Young, who had never\nspoken with his boss, told her he\u2019d been asked to return the\nfunds. In a matter-of-fact manner, Simons said OK and hung up,\nhe said.  After learning from his bank that the wire transfer from\nGreen Ford had been unauthorized, Young tried to log into the\nR.E. Company Bank Office website, but his access had been\nterminated.  \u201cI was lucky I did not send the money,\u201d Young said. \u201cI\ndodged a bullet there.\u201d  Christine Palmer wasn\u2019t as fortunate. In February, the\nsingle mother from  New Britain , Connecticut who moonlights as\nthe manager of a band, Enemy Remains, applied for a position\nadvertised on Careerbuilder.com.  Flexible Gig  A woman named \u201cJennifer\u201d from CS Office Services called\nto say she had the job, a flexible gig that paid by the\nassignment and required her to help process transactions.  On March 3, after a few weeks of online training, Palmer\nwoke up to find that $98,000 had been deposited into her account\nat  Bank of America Corp. (BAC)  An e-mail instructed her to withdraw\n$9,000 in cash and wire it to three individuals in the Ukraine\nvia Western Union.  Then, Palmer was to transfer the rest of the funds to a\nUkrainian bank account. As a fee, Palmer could keep $1,800 of\nthe total. Before she\u2019d completed the wire transfer, a man with\nan Eastern European accent called, urging her to speed things\nup.  \u201cHe sounded very concerned, which made me think I was\ngoing to lose my job,\u201d Palmer said.  Stolen Funds  It wasn\u2019t until a few days later, when  Charlotte , North\nCarolina-based Bank of America halted the wire transfer and told\nher the funds had been stolen, that Palmer realized CS Office\nServices didn\u2019t really exist, and that her employers were part\nof a criminal scheme.  Bank of America closed Palmer\u2019s account and told her she\nwas responsible for paying back the $9,000 she\u2019d wired overseas.  Palmer said she no longer looks for jobs advertised on web\nsites.  Unwitting money mules aren\u2019t the only ones to have gotten\nwake-up calls in the new world of bank cybercrime. Customers\nsometimes find their friendly bank has become an adversary,\nquoting the fine print of account contracts about who is\nresponsible for what.  On May 7, 2009, cyberthieves hacked into the bank account\nof Patco Construction Inc., based in Sanford,  Maine , and\ninitiated a series of wire transfers totaling $56,594. Some\ntransfers bounced back, causing Ocean Bank to send owner Mark\nPatterson a routine return notice via the U.S. Postal Service.  Transfer Money  Over the next several days, the crooks continued to\ntransfer money out of Patco\u2019s account, removing almost $500,000\nbefore Patterson received the mailed letter from Ocean Bank. The\nbank eventually recovered a portion of the transfers, leaving\nPatco with a loss of $345,444, according to Patterson.  Patterson said Ocean Bank rebuffed his attempts to reach a\nsettlement, so in January 2010 he sued. He argued the bank\nshould have done a better job monitoring the company\u2019s bank\naccount. Ocean Bank argued that its protections were\n\u201ccommercially reasonable,\u201d in keeping with general guidance\nissued by the U.S. banking industry in 2005.  In May, a federal magistrate judge in  Portland , Maine,\nfound for Ocean Bank, now known as People\u2019s United Bank, a unit\nof Bridgeport, Connecticut-based  People\u2019s United Financial Inc. (PBCT)   U.S. District Judge D. Brock Hornby in Portland affirmed\nthe magistrate\u2019s decision today.  Infuriated  The magistrate\u2019s ruling infuriated Woodhill, who co-founded\nAuthentify, a cybersecurity firm, in 1999. He is trying to\nchange the law governing liability in hacking cases.  \u201cI can\u2019t fathom how one could consider a security\nprocedure that makes it easy for people to steal money from\nschool districts, churches and small businesses to be\ncommercially reasonable,\u201d Woodhill said.  Woodhill faulted banks for downplaying or hiding the scope\nof bank heists, a posture he attributes to fear of undermining\nconfidence in an online banking system that saves financial\ninstitutions tens of millions of dollars a year in transactions\nthat don\u2019t have to be processed by a human teller.  Last year, Woodhill came to the rescue of Karen McCarthy,\nwhose marketing firm was victimized by hackers in February 2010.\nMcCarthy, who made one wire transfer on the same day every\nmonth, for $1,000, noticed a problem with her computer on Feb.\n10. The screen had turned blue and appeared frozen, while other\ncomputers in her firm seemed to function normally.  McCarthy\u2019s Plans  In the weeks leading up to the frozen-screen episode,\nMcCarthy had reached an agreement to sell her firm, Little &\nKing. She\u2019d bought out her lease, sold her office equipment and\nsupplies and was preparing to join the new company as an\nemployee, leaving behind the worries of business ownership.  After her computer froze, she printed out statements from\nToronto Dominion Bank in preparation for the sale of her\ncompany. Over the Feb. 13-15 Presidents Day weekend, she\ncouldn\u2019t figure out discrepancies between recent bank statements\nand the amount in her company\u2019s checking account. Finally, on\nthe Monday evening, a national holiday, she checked her online\nbanking account and saw five unauthorized wire transfers.  She called TD Bank in a panic. Because of the holiday, she\nwas told no one was available. The next morning she marched into\nher TD Bank branch, in Massapequa, New York, and asked an\nassistant manager for help.  Calls Not Returned  At first the manager told her the bank would get her money\nback, she said. Once it became clear the funds were stolen, the\nbank stopped returning her calls, McCarthy said.  The theft derailed the sale of McCarthy\u2019s company, forcing\nher to raid her children\u2019s college funds for needed cash. Of the\n$164,000 stripped from her account, TD Bank recovered almost\n$95,000, leaving her about $70,000 in the hole -- and without an\noffice or equipment, she said.  When she learned TD Bank was to hold a fraud-prevention\nseminar on May 13, 2010, in Burlington,  Vermont , she hopped on a\nplane and slipped into the meeting. During the morning\npresentation, when an expert in wire transactions was talking\nabout ways that small businesses could protect themselves from\nthe dangers posed by cybercriminals, McCarthy raised her hand.  Why wasn\u2019t TD Bank doing a better job protecting its small-\nbusiness clients, she asked. How had TD Bank allowed $164,000 to\nbe wired out of her account even though she hardly every made\nwire transfers? As the speaker tried to respond, McCarthy kept\npeppering him with questions about his bank\u2019s responsibilities\nto its clients.  Let\u2019s Talk Outside  Two bank representatives, including TD Bank\u2019s head of\ncorporate security and investigations, walked over to McCarthy\u2019s\ntable and suggested they continue the subject outside. McCarthy\ntold the head of security it was good to meet him finally, since\nshe\u2019d been calling him for weeks following the robbery and had\nnever gotten through.  Jennifer Morneau, a spokeswoman for TD Bank, confirmed\nthat there was such an incident involving a \u201cwoman from Long\nIsland\u201d at one of its anti-fraud seminars, and didn\u2019t have any\nfurther information.  \u201cWe constantly monitor and assess the security of our\nsystems,\u201d Morneau said in an e-mailed statement. \u201cWe also\nbelieve that educating our customers is one of the best ways to\nhelp them defend against online fraud and identity theft,\nbecause even the best security measures can only prevent fraud\nif customers are also vigilant about employing the necessary\nsafeguards to protect their information.\u201d  Anti-Bank Website  With Woodhill\u2019s support, McCarthy started a website she\ncalls www.yourmoneyisnotsafeinthebank.org and has organized\nother cybercrime small-business victims across the country. In\nindustry presentations, Woodhill uses her as an example in\ndescribing what\u2019s wrong with online banking and the current\nrules governing the commercial accounts of small businesses.  \u201cIf every small-business account holder in America knew\nwhat Karen McCarthy had gone through, there would be a run on\nthe banks,\u201d he said.  Last year Woodhill supported a proposed law, introduced by\nU.S. Senator Chuck Schumer, a New York Democrat, that would have\nextended protections enjoyed by individual bank depositors to\npublicly funded entities such as school districts and town\ngovernments. Congress adjourned before any vote was taken.  Woodhill is now pushing for a federal law that would\nrequire regional and community banks to warn their commercial\nclients explicitly of the dangers of cyber fraud. He\u2019s hired\nformer Louisiana congressman Billy Tauzin, a Democrat turned\nRepublican who chaired the House Energy & Commerce committee, to\nrepresent him.  Bank Opposition  The American Banking Association has opposed attempts to\nextend cyberfraud protection from depositors to small-business\nclients. Until recently, the association\u2019s position has\nprevailed.  Then came the Experi-Metal lawsuit brought by Valiena\nAllison against Dallas-based Comerica. In June, U.S. District\nJudge Patrick J. Duggan ruled in  Detroit  in favor of Allison and\nExperi-Metal, agreeing Comerica\u2019s response to the fraud didn\u2019t\nmeet standards of good faith and fair dealing. Comerica agreed\nto pay Allison almost the entire amount stolen.  Other cybercrime victims have taken note of this precedent,\nsaid Brian Krebs, who has written about the Little & King case\nand other cyberthefts on his blog (www.krebsonsecurity.com).  Village View, an escrow company based in Redondo Beach,\nCalifornia, that was robbed of $465,558 by cyberthieves in March\nof 2010, sued Professional Business Bank just two weeks after\nthe Experi-Metal decision.  Bank Attitudes  The last thing community banks want is to be at odds with\ntheir clients, said  Doug Johnson , a senior policy analyst for\nthe  American Bankers Association .  \u201cBanks don\u2019t like to sue their customers and customers\ndon\u2019t like to sue their banks,\u201d he said. \u201cWhen disputes occur,\nit\u2019s best to try to work together for an appropriate result.\u201d  Woodhill said the banking industry is behind the curve on\nthis matter, just as it was in 1978 when it opposed the\nElectronic Funds Transfer Act, which protects consumer bank\ndeposits from fraud.  \u201cThat\u2019s one of the biggest favors Congress ever did for\nbanks, even though they were against it,\u201d he said. \u201cBanks\ntruly do not understand what their own interests are. Nasdaq  was forced to freeze trading in stocks it lists for three hours on Aug. 22 when data lines malfunctioned, and share and options venues from New York to  Chicago  have paused or suspended trading in the past three weeks due to errors.  NYSE\u2019s Improvement  For NYSE, the debut was an opportunity to encroach further on Nasdaq\u2019s tech dominance. Between the start of 2011 and Nov. 5, NYSE won 46 technology and Internet IPOs, with $8.7 billion raised, according to data compiled by Bloomberg. Nasdaq secured 44 companies raising $24.7 billion, including the $16 billion that Facebook received.  Although there are 13 exchanges among the more than 50 venues where U.S. stocks trade, NYSE and Nasdaq are the only two where companies go public. Competition for IPOs is critical for both, which get about a fifth of revenue from listing fees and related services.  Scrutiny was high because IPOs have seen some of the biggest market-structure catastrophes. Nasdaq Stock Market member firms lost tens of millions of dollars in Facebook\u2019s debut after the computer matching the first trade went into a loop and the open was delayed. Missing trade confirmations and confusion about prices were the first signs of trouble for a stock that  fell  more than 50 percent in less than four months.  SEC Fine  Nasdaq was fined $10 million by the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission and faces $41.6 million in claims from members. The exchange, home to tech pioneers including Apple Inc. and Microsoft Corp., learned last month that it wouldn\u2019t be listing Twitter.  Two months before the  Facebook IPO , Bats Global Markets Inc., an all-electronic exchange operator based in Lenexa,  Kansas , stunned  Wall Street  by failing to get its own IPO trading hours after it was priced. Flawed software was blamed by CEO Joe Ratterman, who pulled the listing and now is in the process of merging with a rival, Direct Edge Holdings LLC.  In the past three months, exchanges have reported multiple instances of information lines being snarled. Price dissemination among options venues broke down on Sept. 16 when the central conduit operated by an NYSE Euronext unit that links a dozen exchanges faltered, forcing them all to shut briefly.  Credit Risk  The mishaps have become so frequent and serious that  Standard & Poor\u2019s  said in September that credit ratings for exchanges worldwide may be cut if they\u2019re not addressed. After Nasdaq\u2019s Aug. 22 data-feed error prevented thousands of U.S. stocks from trading for three hours, SEC Chairman Mary Jo White demanded an industry response.  Breakdowns \u201cinvolved relatively basic, albeit serious, errors,\u201d she  said  at a Security Traders Association conference in  Washington  on Oct. 2. \u201cMany could have happened in a less complex market structure, but the persistent recurrence of these events can undermine the confidence of investors and public companies.\u201d  Trading of over-the-counter stocks -- or companies not listed by either the NYSE or Nasdaq -- was halted for three-and-a-half hours today after a network failure at the main venue prompted regulators to order a shutdown. Pay-for-Delay Drug Deals Said to Be Target for Rule at FTC  The U.S. Federal Trade Commission is considering using its\nrule-making power to stop so-called pay-for-delay deals between\nbrand-drug manufacturers and makers of generic medicines after\nfailing to get judges or Congress to act, three people familiar\nwith the process said.  FTC Chairman Jon Leibowitz, pushing to abolish these deals,\nis studying how the agency could prohibit brand-name\nmanufacturers such as  Cephalon Inc. (CEPH)  and Sanofi Aventis SA from\npaying generic-drug makers such as  Watson Pharmaceuticals Inc. (WPI) \nto drop patent lawsuits that might get generics to market\nfaster, the people said. Leibowitz estimated in an interview May 3 that the deals\ncost consumers about $3.5 billion a year in higher prescription\ndrug prices by slowing the introduction of generics.  A rule to block certain patent settlements would be unusual\nfor the FTC because it would involve antitrust rather than\nconsumer protection and it could be made on the agency\u2019s own\ninitiative under its basic statutory authority rather than at\nCongress\u2019s specific direction, said Bert Foer, president of the\nAmerican Antitrust Institute in  Washington .  Efforts by the FTC to challenge the settlements in federal\ncourts have failed and Congress hasn\u2019t moved to outlaw them. Generic drugs  account  for 78 percent of all retail\nprescriptions in the $307.4 billion-a-year U.S. pharmaceuticals\nmarket, according to the IMS Institute for Healthcare\nInformatics. (FB)  so soon after the company\u2019s initial public offering has few precedents in Silicon Valley, where venture capitalists typically hold shares longer.  Thiel, a Facebook director and its first outside investor, divested 72 percent of his remaining shares three months after it went public. Of the 40 biggest U.S. technology IPOs since the end of 2010, only Facebook and its underwriters let some backers sell so soon, with every other company adopting a so-called lock-up period about twice that long.  While venture capitalists commonly sell their stakes after helping startups reach the public markets, they usually whittle their holdings over a period of quarters or even years. That\u2019s to avoid flooding the market with too much new stock, which can drive down the shares, and to show continuing support for the company. Thiel\u2019s timing was particularly precarious, because Facebook was already down about 50 percent from the IPO.  \u201cWith the benefit of hindsight, you could say that the underwriters probably regret agreeing to an early release of the shares,\u201d said Ted Hollifield, a partner at  Alston & Bird LLP  in Menlo Park, California, and an expert in  venture capital . \u201cThe stock still seems to be searching for an actual trading range and you would ideally like to see that take place before there\u2019s additional selling pressure.\u201d  Facebook  rose  1.5 percent yesterday to $19.44 in Nasdaq Stock Market trading. The shares have dropped 49 percent since first being sold for $38 apiece on May 17. The company said in July that sales growth slowed and its profit margins narrowed, two months after telling investors that revenue growth wasn\u2019t keeping up with user growth on mobile devices amid more mobile  adoption.  Early Investor  Thiel first invested $500,000 in Facebook in 2004, when the website was limited to college students,  a scene that was depicted  in \u201cThe  Social Network ,\u201d the fictionalized history of the company. He has made more than $1 billion from his early bets on Facebook, and put a plan in place at the time of the IPO to sell most of his stake when the lock-up expired.  Board members adopt selling plans in part to avoid potential insider trading allegations. Still, it\u2019s surprising for an investor and board member to set up a plan that involves selling so much so quickly, said Sam Hamadeh, chief executive officer of PrivCo LLC, a New York-based research firm that specializes in private companies\u2019 financial data.  John Doerr , who led  Kleiner Perkins  Caufield & Byers\u2019s early investment in  Google Inc. (GOOG) , has been incrementally selling shares since the Internet search company\u2019s 2004 IPO.  First Opportunity  LinkedIn Corp.\u2019s biggest venture backers,  Sequoia Capital  and  Greylock Partners , still held half their shares in the professional social network 11 months after the company\u2019s May 2011 IPO, according to regulatory filings.  Eight months after  Zynga Inc. (ZNGA) \u2019s IPO, top venture investor Kleiner Perkins hasn\u2019t reported selling any of its 21 million shares.  Groupon Inc.\u2019s (GRPN)  biggest venture backer, New Enterprise Associates, hasn\u2019t disclosed any sales in the nine months since the daily deal site\u2019s offering.  Including the shares Thiel sold in the  Facebook IPO , he has now unloaded more than 80 percent of his pre-IPO stake.  \u201cIt\u2019s a bit stunning that at the earliest opportunity it was sold and the volume that was sold,\u201d said Hamadeh. \u201cTheir job is to liquidate, but typically it\u2019s a little more gradual.\u201d  Thiel wasn\u2019t alone in selling Facebook stock early.  Accel Partners , the venture firm that bought a $12.2 million stake in 2005, sold in the IPO and then distributed more shares to its investors last week. The firm has unloaded more than half the 201.4 million shares it owned prior to the offering.  Harvesting Gains  In some instances, underwriters reserve the right to release some shares before the lock-up expires. In  Zillow Inc. (Z) \u2019s IPO, holders were allowed to sell a quarter of their shares after 90 days if certain conditions were met in the stock performance.  Like the partners at Accel, Thiel can\u2019t be faulted for locking in gains from a highly speculative bet, said  James Cox , a securities law professor at  Duke University  in Durham, North Carolina.  \u201cWe do expect early investors like him to harvest their gains,\u201d Cox told Bloomberg Television\u2019s \u201cMoney Moves\u201d on Aug. 21. \u201cThat\u2019s what provides the seed capital for companies like Facebook to get going.\u201d  In this case, it looks bad, because of all the publicity around Facebook and the poor performance of the shares, he said. For retail investors to step in, they\u2019ve \u201cgot to be pretty optimistic and perhaps more optimistic than the insiders who are selling,\u201d he said.  Broad Investments  Jeremiah Hall, a spokesman for Thiel, declined to comment. Rich Wong, a partner at Palo Alto, California-based Accel, didn\u2019t respond to a request for comment. Ashley Zandy, a spokeswoman at Facebook in Menlo Park, declined to comment.  Fred Wilson , a partner at Union Square Ventures in New York and early Zynga investor, defended Thiel and Accel in an Aug. 21  blog post . He said venture capitalists are measured by how much money they return to their investors, so sitting on billions of dollars of stock is risky. Furthermore, they\u2019re \u201cterrible public market investors,\u201d and many have a policy of getting out of public stocks as soon as possible, he wrote.  Thiel, who co-founded PayPal Inc. and made millions from its 2002 sale to EBay Inc., is a partner at Founders Fund in  San Francisco . His investments include data and security software maker Palantir Technologies Inc., Yammer Inc., which was acquired last month by Microsoft Corp., and Space Exploration Technologies Corp., which in May became the first company to dock a craft at the International Space Station.  Even if Thiel is selling Facebook stock to focus more on early-stage investments, the size of the deal causes some concern, said  Martin Pyykkonen , an equity analyst covering Internet companies at Wedge Partners Corp. in Greenwood Village, Colorado.  \u201cIt raises a little bit of skepticism in terms of his opinion\u201d of Facebook, said Pyykkonen. \u201cHe\u2019s made some smart investments as a VC and a guy in the valley over the years. Intel told the EU General Court to throw out the European\nCommission\u2019s ruling that its use of rebates violated EU\nantitrust rules. Intel  said  the EU failed to use mitigating\nevidence or to allow it respond to all of the allegations.  \u201cThe burden of proof on the commission is a heavy one\u201d\nand \u201cthe commission simply has not met the burden of proof,\u201d\nNicholas Green, a lawyer for Intel, said to the court in\nLuxembourg. \u201cThe commission\u2019s analysis is simplistic and static\nand fails to capture the dynamics of competition.\u201d  The fine was levied after  Advanced Micro Devices Inc. (AMD) \ncomplained that the rebates were unfair.  Santa Clara ,\nCalifornia-based Intel agreed to pay AMD $1.25 billion in 2009\nto end a U.S. lawsuit and the company reached a separate\nsettlement with the U.S. Federal Trade Commission. Intel expects\n2012 to be a year of \u201crecord revenues,\u201d with growth in the\nmobile-phone market adding to its 80 percent market share for\nchips in personal computers.  \u2018Threatening Effect\u2019  At the time, had companies such as  Dell Inc. (DELL)  and Hewlett-\nPackard Co. turned to Intel rival AMD, it \u201cwould have had a\nthreatening effect\u201d so Intel shut out AMD, said commission\nlawyer Nicholas Khan. \u201cThe industry was rife with the sort of\npractices which were condemned by this decision.\u201d  Intel\u2019s appeal cites numerous errors with the EU decision,\nincluding its failure to make notes of a witness who was\n\u201chighly likely\u201d to provide evidence supporting Intel\u2019s\nargument that its rebates to PC makers weren\u2019t conditional on\nexcluding AMD from the market. It also says the EU should have\nsought documents from AMD that were \u201cpotentially exculpatory\u201d\nand given Intel an additional hearing to defend itself.  The competition ruling has already been criticized by the\nEU\u2019s own ombudsman, who said in 2009 that the antitrust agency\nwas guilty of \u201cmaladministration\u201d for failing to record notes\nof the meeting with Dell. The report wasn\u2019t binding on the\ncommission, which disagreed on the need for formal minutes.  The antitrust fine was the EU\u2019s biggest, more than double\nthe 497 million-euro penalty against  Microsoft Corp. (MSFT)  in 2004. It\nrepresented about 4 percent of Intel\u2019s $37.6 billion in  sales  in\n2008, below the maximum penalty of 10 percent of yearly sales\nregulators can impose.  Procedural Grounds  Intel\u2019s chances of getting the fine cut or canceled \u201clie\nmore on procedural than on substantive grounds,\u201d putting the\nfocus on Intel\u2019s arguments that regulators didn\u2019t respect basic\ndue process, said Alfonso Lamadrid, a lawyer at Garrigues in\nBrussels.  The EU\u2019s eight-year investigation found that Intel impeded\ncompetition by giving rebates to computer makers from 2002 until\n2005 on the condition that they buy at least 95 percent of chips\nfor PCs from Intel. It said Intel imposed \u201crestrictive\nconditions\u201d for the remaining 5 percent, supplied by AMD, which\nstruggled to overcome Intel\u2019s hold on the market for processors\nthat run PCs.  The case may be less likely to affect the law on rebates\nbecause the EU\u2019s approach on refunds linked to sales volumes has\nchanged since the Intel case, with a greater emphasis on\nregulators proving that the alleged abusive behavior has\nconcrete effects on competition.  Loyalty Reducing  \u201cTraditionally, it was sufficient for the commission to\nshow that the rebate had a loyalty-reducing effect to establish\na violation of competition rules,\u201d Lamadrid said. \u201cIn the\nIntel case, the commission claimed that negative effects on\ncompetition could be shown in the foreseeable future.\u201d  The computer makers coaxed to not use AMD\u2019s chips included\nAcer Inc., Dell, Hewlett-Packard, Lenovo Group Ltd. and NEC\nCorp., the commission said in 2009. The EU also said Intel made\npayments to electronics retailer Media Markt on the condition\nthat it only sell Intel-based PCs. It also ordered Intel to stop\nusing illegal rebates to thwart competitors, an instruction that\nIntel complained was unclear. Sunnyvale, California-based AMD, which initiated the EU\nantitrust case, is no longer involved and won\u2019t intervene at\nthis week\u2019s hearing after settling with Intel. Decisions by\nthe EU court can be appealed a last time to the  European Court\nof Justice , the 27-nation bloc\u2019s highest court, which is also in\nLuxembourg.  The case is T-286\/09 Intel v Commission. (MSFT) \u2019s nine-year-old\nantitrust agreement with the U.S.  Justice Department , set to\nexpire today, permanently changed the software marketplace,\nmaking it more open, fair and innovative, the agency said.  The final judgment in the Microsoft case, in effect since\n2002, prevented the company from using its monopoly  Windows\noperating system  for personal computing to quash competition,\nthe department said yesterday in a statement.  The court\u2019s decree \u201chelped create competitive conditions\nthat enabled new kinds of products, such as cloud computing\nservices and mobile devices, to develop as potential platform\nthreats to the Windows desktop operating system,\u201d the\ndepartment said.  The Justice Department, joined by 19 states and the\nDistrict of Columbia, sued Microsoft in 1998, alleging the\ncompany unlawfully protected its Windows monopoly by keeping\ncomputer makers from promoting browsers that competed with\nMicrosoft\u2019s  Internet Explorer .  The government contended Microsoft hindered access to the\nNetscape Navigator browser because its Java programming language\nlet programmers write applications that ran on any operating\nsystem, not just Windows.  \u201cMicrosoft got into antitrust trouble because it fell\nbehind as an innovator and then tried to catch up by flexing its\nWindows monopoly rather than competing on the merits,\u201d said\nAndy Gavil, an antitrust professor at Howard University Law\nSchool in  Washington . \u201cIt did that most extremely with Internet\nbrowsers and media players.\u201d  New Software  The settlement protected development and distribution of\nnew software and barred Microsoft from continuing the behavior\nthat triggered the antitrust lawsuit.  \u201cOur experience has changed us and shaped how we view our\nresponsibility to the industry,\u201d Microsoft spokesman  Kevin Kutz \nsaid in an e-mailed statement. \u201cWe are pleased to bring this\nmatter to successful resolution.\u201d  Microsoft submitted to court oversight of its practices\nunder a decree issued by U.S. District Judge Colleen Kollar- Kotelly. The supervision included periodic reviews to ensure the\ncompany complied with terms of the settlement to give computer\nmakers freedom to promote rival products.  Harry First, a professor at  New York University School of\nLaw  in  Manhattan , said he questions how much was accomplished.  Market Share  \u201cEverything that was done didn\u2019t really disrupt\nMicrosoft\u2019s position,\u201d he said. \u201cIt\u2019s still a Windows world\nand Internet Explorer still has a major share of the browser\nmarket.\u201d  Internet Explorer has 55 percent of the browser market,\nwhile Mozilla\u2019s Firefox has 22 percent, according to research\nfirm Netmarketshare\u2019s website.  Google Inc. (GOOG) \u2019s Chrome has 12\npercent and Apple Inc.\u2019s Safari has 7 percent, Netmarketshare\nreports.  Still, Kollar-Kotelly said at the last oversight hearing on\nApril 27 that the compliance committee had worked well and could\nbe used as a model for cases in the future.  The European Commission accused Microsoft in 2004 of\nabusing its dominant position by deliberately restricting the\nability of non-Microsoft software on larger computers to work\nwith its Windows operating system. Microsoft\u2019s bundling of the\nmedia player with Windows was also deemed unfair by the\nCommission, which fined the company a record 497 million euros\n($706 million), ordered it to share secret programming data with\ncompetitors and offer a version of Windows without a music and\nvideo player.  \u201cThe most important thing about the case was that it put\nMicrosoft under incredible scrutiny for how it was going to\ntreat firms coming to life around the browser,\u201d said Timothy Wu, an information industries scholar from  Columbia University \nwho is on leave to advise the U.S. Federal Trade Commission.  Wu said the antitrust case helped Internet companies such\nas Google and Facebook Inc. flourish, while products such as\nWordPerfect and Lotus 1-2-3 software lost momentum due to\nMicrosoft\u2019s dominance.  The case is U.S. v. Microsoft, 98-cv-01232, U.S. District\nCourt,  District of Columbia  (Washington). Captain Beefheart , whose real name was Don Glen Vliet,\nperformed with Zappa early in their careers, before they became\nestranged over artistic issues. Cote, who will decide the case without a jury, interrupted\nSnyder repeatedly with questions. The government is seeking an order barring Apple from\nalleged anticompetitive actions, including price fixing, in the\nmarket for digital books. The U.S. isn\u2019t asking for money\ndamages.  A group of states is also seeking fines and unspecified\ndamages. If Apple is found liable in the trial, damages will be\ndetermined in a separate proceeding. A win for the government\nmay fuel class actions by private plaintiffs seeking triple\ndamages permitted under antitrust law.  The case is U.S. v. Apple Inc., 12-cv-02826, U.S. District\nCourt, Southern District of New York (Manhattan).
