(GS)  and  Citigroup Inc. (C)  stepped up warnings to shareholders about cyber attacks as the U.S. prodded banks and government agencies to bolster their defenses.  Online and mobile banking give new points of entry that can be used to disrupt or penetrate operations, the two New York- based firms said last week in annual regulatory filings. The companies said they\u2019re vulnerable to tactics that overload websites to shut off public access, such as assaults that disrupted the nation\u2019s largest lenders late last year.  U.S. banks are speculating that foreign nations, organized crime or terrorists are behind efforts to cripple their websites and warning that costs to keep intruders at bay will rise. President  Barack Obama  directed the government on Feb. 12 to develop voluntary security standards for companies running vital infrastructure and is pushing Congress to set formal rules.  \u201cWe are going to see more disclosures, and that\u2019s a warning sign that things are really getting bad,\u201d said Lawrence Ponemon, chairman of Ponemon Institute LLC, a Traverse City, Michigan-based security research firm, which predicts a 30 percent increase in expenses tied to cyber intrusions this year.  Attacks in December hit  Bank of America Corp. (BAC) ,  JPMorgan Chase & Co. (JPM) , U.S. Bancorp,  Wells Fargo & Co. (WFC)  and  SunTrust Banks Inc. (STI) , two executives at security companies said at the time. PNC Financial Services Group Inc., the second-biggest regional bank, said in its annual filing that cyber attacks may hurt customer confidence and increase costs at the Pittsburgh-based company.  Security Breaches  The intrusions aren\u2019t limited to financial firms, with Microsoft Corp., the largest software maker, saying Feb. 22 a small number of its computers were infected by malicious software in a cyber attack similar to those experienced by Facebook Inc. and Apple Inc.  Cyber security gained renewed national attention in the past few years with revelations about a security breach of a U.S. Federal Reserve website, intrusions at the  New York Times (NYT)  and other news organizations attributed to Chinese hackers, and a wave of so-called denial-of-service attacks that disrupted the websites of the biggest U.S. banks and payment networks.  The tactic can disable a website by flooding it with traffic. While that doesn\u2019t give intruders access to cash or personal data, regulators warned banks in December the attacks might be used to distract staff while accounts are penetrated, or to block banks and customers from informing each other.  New Threat  \u201cWe know hackers steal people\u2019s identities and infiltrate private e-mail; we know foreign countries and companies swipe our corporate secrets,\u201d Obama said in his  State of the Union  speech. \u201cNow our enemies are also seeking the ability to sabotage our  power grid , our financial institutions and our air- traffic-control systems.\u201d  MasterCard Inc. (MA) , the second-biggest U.S. payments processor, said in its Feb. 14 annual filing the firm routinely receives threats, \u201cand our technologies, systems and networks have been subject to cyber attacks.\u201d So far, the impact hasn\u2019t been material, according to the Purchase, New York-based firm.  U.S. Bancorp, ranked fifth by deposits among commercial banks, told regulators Feb. 22 it had been  targeted , and that it might not be able to stop all attackers \u201cbecause the techniques used change frequently or are not recognized until launched, and because security attacks can originate from a wide variety of sources.\u201d The Minneapolis-based lender cited organized crime, terrorists and hostile foreign governments, and said risks increase as it adds more Internet and mobile-banking options.  Testing Defenses  Wells Fargo, the biggest U.S.  home lender , reiterated in its Feb. 27 filing that attacks against banks may be meant to \u201ctest their cyber security in advance of future and more advanced cyber attacks,\u201d and said preventing or cleaning up after intrusions may get expensive for the San Francisco-based firm. It didn\u2019t specify the cost.  Bank of America, whose customers complained that websites run by the Charlotte, North Carolina-based company were repeatedly slowed or knocked offline, previously acknowledged it had faced a series of denial-of-service attacks and may be required to spend significant amounts to address future attacks.  The bank, ranked second by assets, didn\u2019t add any detail in its latest filing, and spokesmen for all the lenders declined to elaborate on their cyber-security measures.  \u2018Frightening Number\u2019  Non-U.S. companies also felt the impact. HSBC Finance Corp., the Illinois-based unit of Europe\u2019s largest bank by market value,  HSBC Holdings Plc (HSBA) , said in today\u2019s regulatory filing it faced several denial-of-service attacks last year across Latin America, Asia and North America.  Royal Bank of Canada (RY) \u2019s CEO  Gordon Nixon  told shareholders last week the number of attacks faced daily by his Toronto-based company is \u201cfrightening.\u201d  \u201cThe good news is they don\u2019t get through the firewalls and our various protective measures have served us extremely well,\u201d Nixon said at the bank\u2019s Feb. 28 annual meeting.  With incidents becoming widespread, banks are putting aside rivalries and collaborating more closely on how to block intruders, said Ed Powers, a principal at  Deloitte & Touche LLP  in New York who specializes in information security and risk management.  \u201cThese attacks have started to go beyond nuisance,\u201d Powers said in an interview. While none has resulted in a \u201ccatastrophe,\u201d it\u2019s reasonable to foresee something much more disruptive ahead, he said.  Spy Agencies  Mobile and online banking are adding vulnerability, as are customers and vendors who link directly to data systems, Fed Governor  Sarah Bloom Raskin  told bankers and regulators last week during an Atlanta speech. That has led to \u201cconcerted cooperative work between government and financial institutions,\u201d and the Department of  Homeland Security  has provided firms with technical assistance, she said.  The biggest U.S. banks work closely with the Central Intelligence Agency, National Security Agency, Defense Department and governments around world to address \u201chundreds of thousands\u201d of cyber attacks, according to  Jamie Dimon , chief executive officer of New York-based JPMorgan.  \u201cIt\u2019s a big deal; it\u2019s going to get worse,\u201d Dimon, 56, said during an Oct. 10 panel discussion at the  Council on Foreign Relations . \u201cComputers in 10 years are going to be a hundred thousand times faster. And so they\u2019ll be able to do calculations quicker and get through quicker.\u201d  Opportunity Cost  Cyber threats could cost firms the opportunity to improve their systems and save money. Travelers Cos., which represents the  insurance industry  in the  Dow Jones Industrial Average , said Feb. 19 it  may forgo  new and more efficient technologies if they further expose the New York-based company to attacks.  A group calling itself Izz ad-Din al-Qassam Cyber Fighters has claimed responsibility for the most recent intrusions on U.S. banks, saying they\u2019re in response to a video uploaded to Google Inc.\u2019s YouTube ridiculing the  Prophet Muhammad  and offending some Muslims. NBC News and former Senator  Joseph Lieberman , a Connecticut independent, have said Iran may have been behind these attacks.  The group hit U.S. bank websites with a new round of denial-of-service attacks on Feb. 25, according to Rodney Joffe, senior vice president at Neustar Inc. of Sterling, Virginia, and Carl Herberger, a vice president of security solutions at Tel Aviv-based Radware Ltd., who both provide security to some of the targeted banks.  In a statement posted on the website pastebin.com on Feb. 26, the group said it targeted more than 11 banks for new assaults including Bank of America and PNC.  Obama\u2019s Edict  The U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission  told companies  in October 2011 they should disclose real or potential cyber attacks capable of disrupting business operations or financial stability and should address the threat if a network breach is \u201creasonably likely\u201d to have a material effect.  Obama\u2019s executive order includes parts of Senate legislation that failed to pass last year. Republicans and the U.S. Chamber of Commerce, the nation\u2019s largest business lobby, said the bill\u2019s standards would amount to burdensome regulation.  The Obama administration soon will submit priorities for cyber security legislation to Congress to build on his executive order, said Caitlin Hayden, a White House spokeswoman.  \u201cAlthough this executive order will help raise the nation\u2019s cyber defenses, it does not obviate the urgent need for legislation,\u201d Hayden said last week via e-mail. She didn\u2019t specify the priorities or the timeframe for sending them to Congress. I\u2019ve long agreed with those who say Apple must invade the\nTV market to maintain its phenomenal growth. Jobs may have as\nwell: Walter Isaacson, in his best-selling biography, quoted him\nsaying he had \u201cfinally cracked\u201d the challenge of creating \u201can\nintegrated television set that is completely easy to use.\u201d  The company has already pretty much nailed the set-up part.\nThe new Apple TV, a black square roughly the size of a hockey\npuck, has just two wires to worry about: the power cord, and a\ncable connecting it to a high-definition port on your\ntelevision. (It also has optional ports for a hard-wired\nInternet link and for connecting the unit to a home-theater\naudio system.)  Just seven minutes after I removed the shrink-wrap, I was\nwatching a video. It would have been faster if I had shorter\nlog-ins for my ITunes Store account and Wi-Fi network.  User Interface  The box sports a revamped user interface, which has  drawn\ncriticism  from some Apple purists, but I found it useful for\nbrowsing through the thousands of movies and TV episodes on the\niTunes Store.  I could quickly scroll by category and genre, and\nselections began playing within moments. (How quickly, of\ncourse, depends on the speed of your Internet connection.) I\nalso had instant access to all the content I previously\npurchased on other Apple devices.  My main beef with the interface, one that will have to be\nsolved in any fully integrated Apple set, was the painful search\nprocess when using the included three-button remote control.  It required me to laboriously enter my search term by\nscrolling through a grid of letters, choosing one at a time,\nuntil what I was looking for showed up on an ever-changing list\nof possible matches.  The process is much easier if you have an iPhone, iPad or\niPod touch and download Apple\u2019s free Remote app, which lets you\nsimply type your query on your device. But not every viewer of\nan Apple-branded set might have an Apple mobile device -- or\nhave it handy.  More for Siri  What if you could simply tell your TV what you wanted to\nwatch, and it understood and fetched it? The technology already\nexists in  Siri , the iPhone 4S virtual assistant. Implementing it\nin a future Apple-branded television would eliminate the current\ncomplications without the need for a full-scale keyboard, which\nwas one of the things that sunk  Logitech (LOGN) \u2019s Google-based adapter.  The new Apple TV\u2019s biggest change from the previous model\nis a boost in video quality to 1080p from 720p. As a practical\nmatter, this means it\u2019s now approaching the quality of a Blu-ray\nplayer -- without, of course, the hassle of managing Blu-ray\ndiscs. A  Wallace & Gromit  film downloaded from iTunes looked\nspectacular on my 1080p TV, as did photos streamed from my\ncomputer and movies from  Netflix. (NFLX)   Apple as Gatekeeper  Speaking of which, you can now sign up for, access and pay\nfor a Netflix account using your Apple ID. That doesn\u2019t sound\nimportant, but it could be another indicator of Apple\u2019s approach\nto building a full-scale television: setting itself up as the\ngatekeeper, just as it does on its iOS devices. After all,\nalmost the entire appeal of  Amazon.com (AMZN) \u2019s Kindle Fire tablet is\nin how much content is available seamlessly with a single Amazon\nlog-in.  There are many ways to access Internet video these days.\nMost new TVs offer ways to connect, though some require an\nextra-cost adapter and suffer from jumbled interfaces. Game\nconsoles like  Microsoft (MSFT) \u2019s Xbox have morphed into home-\nentertainment portals. And, most notably, the  Roku 2 XD  offers\nApple-like simplicity and video quality, plus many more content\nsources and a lower ($80) price.  But if you\u2019re already committed to the Apple universe of\ndevices and content -- or want to get ready for the integrated\nset that might be coming -- the little Apple TV is a good\nchoice. (MSFT) \nfrom selling its Xbox gaming software in  Germany , a U.S. appeals\ncourt ruled.  A three-judge panel in  San Francisco  upheld a  Seattle \njudge\u2019s order blocking Motorola Mobility\u2019s enforcement of the\nsales ban it won in May in its lawsuit against Microsoft pending\nin Germany. The panel said the lower court\u2019s order was narrowly\ntailored.  Motorola Mobility and Microsoft are locked in legal battles\nover patents for Xbox and smartphone software in the U.S. and\nGermany. Microsoft contends all devices that run on Google\u2019s\nAndroid operating system use its technology and seeks royalties\nfrom Motorola Mobility. Motorola Mobility says it\u2019s owed\nroyalties on the Xbox for use of the company\u2019s Wi-Fi and video-\ncompression technology.  To enforce the German sales ban, Motorola Mobility would\nhave to post a security bond covering potential damages to\nMicrosoft, the appeals court said. Microsoft could also avoid\nthe injunction by taking steps towards entering a licensing\nagreement with Motorola with a specific rate or rate determined\nby Motorola.  Representatives of  Mountain View , California-based Google,\ndidn\u2019t respond to an e-mail message to the company\u2019s media\noffice seeking comment on the ruling.  Seattle Judge  Microsoft obtained the Seattle judge\u2019s order blocking\nMotorola Mobility form enforcing a German injunction before\nMotorola Mobility won the lawsuit in Germany.  U.S. District Judge James Robart in Seattle said an\nexisting contract lawsuit between the two companies in his\ncourthouse will help determine a royalty rate, so putting the\nGerman injunction on hold is appropriate, the appeals court\nsaid.  \u201cIt is clear that there is a contract, that it is\nenforceable by Microsoft, and that it encompasses not just U.S.\npatents but also the patents at issue in the German suit,\u201d the\nappeals court said.  Motorola Mobility, based in Libertyville,  Illinois , has\nsubmitted offers to license its patents, some of which relate to\nstandards established by industry groups for video compression\nand Wi-Fi technology. It also has offered to take a license to\nthe coordination feature known as ActiveSync, that it has\npreviously licensed from Microsoft before 2007.  Standard Demand  Motorola Mobility sent letters to Microsoft with what it\nsaid was a standard demand for a 2.25 percent royalty on the end\nprice of products that use the inventions, including the Xbox\nand Windows products. Microsoft contends that would add as much\nas $4 billion in annual royalties, a figure Motorola Mobility\ndisputes.  Microsoft contends the offer doesn\u2019t meet Motorola\nMobility\u2019s obligation to license such patents on fair and\nreasonable terms, and the licensing offer should be based on\n\u201cmarket rates.\u201d It filed a breach of contract suit that\u2019s\nscheduled for trial in November in federal court in Seattle,\nnear Microsoft\u2019s headquarters in Redmond,  Washington .  \u201cWe\u2019re pleased that Judge Robart\u2019s decision has been\naffirmed by the Ninth Circuit Court of Appeals, preventing\nMotorola from enforcing an injunction in Germany until its use\nof standard essential patents can be closely examined,\u201d  David\nHoward , corporate vice president and deputy general counsel for\nMicrosoft, said in an e-mail. \u201cIt continues to be our hope that\nGoogle and Motorola live up to their promises to standards\norganizations.\u201d  The case is Microsoft Corp. v. Motorola Mobility Inc.,\n12-35352,  U.S. Court of Appeals  for the Ninth Circuit, San\nFrancisco. It\u2019s also creating a new class of mutant\npersonal computers.  Nowhere is this clearer than in the laptop segment, where\nthe long-dominant clamshell design is yielding to new forms:\ncomputers that bend, tilt and swivel, with touch screens that\nare clearly inspired by, even if they don\u2019t directly compete\nwith, handheld tablets like  Apple (AAPL) \u2019s iPad.  With that in mind, I\u2019ve been trying several of these new\nconvertible-tablet hybrids. All are of the \u201cUltrabook\u201d\ncategory: They run on  Intel (INTC)  chips, are thin and light as these\nthings go, have no DVD drives and use solid-state  flash memory \nin place of a traditional hard disk.  Of the first wave, my favorite so far is  Lenovo (992) \u2019s IdeaPad\nYoga, which as its name implies can be folded into all sorts of\ninteresting positions.  At first glance, the Yoga, which starts at $999, looks like\na fairly standard clamshell, .67 inch (1.7 centimeters) thick \nand weighing 3.4 pounds (1.5 kilograms). It\u2019s solidly built, \nwith hinges strong enough to keep the 13.3-inch screen from \nflopping around -- one of my laptop pet peeves.  If you use the screen only in that position, though, you\u2019re\nmissing the whole point.  Touchscreen Tablet  Fold the Yoga over and it becomes a touchscreen tablet --\ntoo heavy to hold for long, but useful to watch a video or take\nadvantage of Windows 8\u2019s full-screen applications. (The\nkeyboard, which faces out, is automatically disabled to avoid\nerrant presses.)  You can also stand the screen up, using the inverted\nkeyboard as a base, or prop it up like a tent.  The major drawback, one that afflicts its competitors as\nwell, is the minimal storage capacity -- or, more specifically,\nthe amount of it claimed by Windows 8 system files. Fewer than\nhalf the 128 gigabytes on my test machine were available for my\nown applications, files and content. The least expensive model\nwith a more plausible 256 GB, available in the U.S. only through\n Best Buy (BBY) , is $1,400.  Eccentric Sony  Sony devices these days range in design from\nstraightforward to what-were-they-thinking eccentricity. The Duo\n11, which starts at $1,200, falls into the latter category.  At rest, the Duo is a tablet .71 of an inch thick. At 2.87\npounds, it is more manageable than the Yoga. But it becomes\nconsiderably less satisfying when, after fumbling around to\nfigure out how to open it, you lift and slide the 11.6-inch\ntouch screen to expose the keyboard.  The problem is the design, which means that the propped-up\nscreen covers almost half the base. The result is a cramped\nkeyboard with no place to rest your palms, nor even a track pad.\nInstead, there\u2019s a tiny round pointing device wedged in between\nthe G, H and B keys.  It makes for a thoroughly unpleasant typing experience.\nWhile  Sony (6758)  tries to mitigate the input problems by including a\nstylus, there\u2019s no place on the Duo 11 to store it.  In general, the Duo 11 is much better for consuming content\nthan for producing it: The high-resolution screen makes viewing\nhigh-definition videos in tablet mode a pleasure. But my test\nunit was plagued by a balky accelerometer that sometimes took an\ninordinate amount of time to reorient the screen when I flipped\nit from landscape to portrait.  Un-Flashy Toshiba  Over the years, Toshiba has developed a reputation for\nsolid, decidedly un-flashy, laptops. Windows 8 has given it the\nopportunity to finally break out, and Toshiba has seized the\nmoment to deliver the Satellite U925t, a convertible starting at\n$1,150 that is -- sorry -- solid and decidedly un-flashy.  At 3.4 pounds, the Satellite is actually a little lighter\nand has a smaller footprint than the Yoga. But it feels bulkier,\nowing to its slightly greater thickness and less elegant design.  Like the Sony, and unlike the Lenovo, the  Toshiba (6502) \u2019s screen\nis always exposed, meaning that you may want some sort of sleeve\nor cover to protect it from dirt when not in use.  Also like the Sony, you slide the screen up to put the\nSatellite into laptop mode. But at least you have an adequately\nsized keyboard, a touchpad and a little extra space for your\nwrists. You also have a larger screen -- 12.5 inches -- though\nits 1366-by-768-pixel display lags behind both the Duo 11 and\nYoga. And while long battery life isn\u2019t an outstanding\ncharacteristic of this entire category, the Satellite was\nmarginally better than either of the others.  The coming months will see the arrival of scores of similar\nWindows hybrids, most notably including a new, more powerful\nversion of Microsoft\u2019s Surface. Whether these new devices can\nstave off the PC\u2019s long, slow decline remains to be seen, but in\nthe meantime they are introducing some welcome novelty into the\nmarket.  ( Rich Jaroslovsky  is a Bloomberg News columnist. The\nopinions expressed are his own.) (MSFT)  Chief Executive Officer  Steve Ballmer  adds to\nthe drumbeat for change at the top of technology bellwethers.  Boards at increasingly large hardware and software makers\nare replacing CEOs to help their companies repel threats from\nupstarts such as Facebook Inc. and  Apple Inc. (AAPL)  The aim is to keep\nfrom getting left behind in emerging technologies including\nsocial networking, mobile computing and the delivery of software\nover the Internet, via the so-called cloud.  Hewlett-Packard Co. (HPQ) , Google Inc. and  Advanced Micro Devices\nInc. (AMD)  lead technology companies with a combined $265 billion in\nmarket value on the Standard & Poor\u2019s 500 Index that have\nchanged CEOs since August. That\u2019s up from companies worth $75\nbillion a year earlier. Privately held Twitter Inc. replaced its\nCEO in October, a month after Finland\u2019s  Nokia Oyj (NOK1V)  did the same.  Investors may clamor for new leadership at companies\nincluding  Cisco Systems Inc. (CSCO)  and  Research In Motion Ltd. (RIM) , said\nBill Coleman, a  partner  at venture capital firm  Alsop Louie\nPartners  in San Francisco.  \u201cThe companies that haven\u2019t moved are under a lot of\npressure, and one of the first places you look to change things\nis at the top,\u201d said Coleman, the former CEO of BEA Systems\nInc., which was acquired by  Oracle Corp. (ORCL)  \u201cThere are lots of\ncompanies like Nokia and RIM and AMD and Cisco that have fallen\nbehind and lost at least some of their competitive edge.\u201d  Ballmer is being criticized as Redmond, Washington-based\nMicrosoft loses market share to Apple and Google in mobile\nphones and Apple\u2019s iPad takes sales from personal computers\nrunning Microsoft\u2019s Windows.  Ballmer Dinged  The board docked Ballmer some of his potential bonus last\nyear for falling short in mobile and new forms of computers.  Einhorn, president of hedge fund Greenlight Capital Inc.,\nsaid Ballmer has failed to seize on Microsoft\u2019s opportunities\nand overspent on efforts to remedy shortcomings.  \u201cHe\u2019s allowed competitors to beat Microsoft in huge areas,\nincluding search, mobile-communications software, tablet\ncomputing and social networking,\u201d Einhorn said at a conference\nthis week. \u201cEven worse, his response to these failures has been\nto pour tremendous resources into efforts to develop his way out\nof these holes.\u201d  During Ballmer\u2019s 11-year reign as CEO, shares have declined\nmore than 50 percent, even though sales have more than tripled\nand profit has risen 141 percent.  While investors\u2019 patience with Ballmer is wearing thin,\nMicrosoft\u2019s board may not quickly agitate for change, said Pat Becker Jr., principal of  Portland , Oregon-based Becker Capital\nManagement, which holds Microsoft.  \u2018Losing the Tech World\u2019  \u201cHe doesn\u2019t have the investor base and my fear is he\u2019s\nlosing his customer base and losing the tech world in general,\u201d\nsaid Becker, whose firm has about $2.5 billion in assets. \u201cThe\ninvestor base would welcome new leadership, but whether the\nboard wants him to go is a different thing.\u201d  Ballmer\u2019s supporters could point to the company\u2019s sales and\nprofit growth on his watch, said Michael Cusumano, a  professor \nat the  Massachusetts Institute of Technology \u2019s  Sloan School of\nManagement  in Cambridge.  \u201cFinancially Microsoft has really done quite well,\u201d\nCusumano said. \u201cThey are still printing money essentially.\u201d  Frank Shaw , a spokesman for Microsoft, declined to comment.  Other boards have shown less resistance to change. Hewlett-\nPackard directors pushed out former CEO Mark Hurd in August\nafter an investigation found he violated the company\u2019s code of\nbusiness ethics by concealing a personal relationship with a\nfemale contractor.  Hewlett-Packard, AMD, Google  Hurd\u2019s successor,  Leo Apotheker , said this month that he\ninherited a company ill-equipped to win business from companies\nthat want to switch to cloud computing. AMD board members ousted\nCEO Dirk Meyer in January amid frustration with the company\u2019s\nlack of progress in chips for tablets.  Google turned to one of its co-founders, Larry Page, 38, to\nsucceed  Eric Schmidt , 56, who ran the company for a decade. The\nmove was aimed at helping Google bolster its defenses against\nFacebook and recapture the entrepreneurial ethos that fostered\nthe creation of the most-used search engine.  Some companies aim for executives who, by dint of age or\nstrategic vision, convey the sense they can cater to younger,\ntechnology-savvy consumers, said Paul Saffo, managing director\nat investment adviser  Discern Analytics .  Under CEO Steve Jobs, Apple has gained share in the\ndigital-music and mobile-phone industries with products that\ndemonstrate his appreciation of customers\u2019 preferences, says\nSaffo, whose firm is based in  San Francisco . S&P is poised to provide AAA grades to 59 percent of\nSpringleaf Mortgage Loan Trust 2011-1, a set of bonds tied to\n$497 million lent to homeowners with below-average credit scores\nand almost no equity in their properties. New York-based S&P\nstripped the U.S. of its top rank on Aug. 5, saying Washington\npolitics were making the country less creditworthy.  Treasuries gained about 1.95 percent and U.S. borrowing\ncosts have fallen to record lows as investors repudiated the\ndowngrade, according to Bank of America Merrill Lynch indexes.\nS&P has awarded AAAs to more than $36 billion of securities in\nthe U.S. this year that were created by bankers who continue to\ngather thousands of loans, bundle them into bonds of varying\nrisk and pay ratings firms a fee to assign credit rankings.  \u201cEverybody has been led to believe over the years that AAA\nmeans AAA means AAA across the board,\u201d Gregory W. Smith, the\ngeneral counsel for the $41 billion Public Employees\u2019 Retirement\nAssociation of  Colorado , said in a telephone interview on Aug.\n24. \u201cAnybody that didn\u2019t learn in the 2008 crisis that doesn\u2019t\napply should find another line of work.\u201d  Inflated Grades  Money managers are lending to the government at rates that,\nin some cases, are about a third of what they demand to hold\ntop-rated mortgage notes, four months after Congressional\ninvestigators said S&P helped spur the longest economic\ncontraction since the 1930s by assigning inflated grades to the\nbonds from 2005 through 2008.  More than 14,000 securitized bonds in the U.S. are rated\nAAA by S&P, backed by everything from houses and malls to auto-\ndealer loans and farm-equipment leases, according to data\ncompiled by Bloomberg.  S&P has said it made mistakes in structured finance since\nthe crisis including misunderstanding cash flows and using\nconflicting methods to analyze the securities. Its owner, New\nYork-based McGraw-Hill Cos., depended on credit ratings for 27\npercent of its $6.19 billion of revenue last year, down from 33\npercent of $6.77 billion in 2007, Bloomberg data show.  \u201cThese are errors that could cause airplanes to crash if\nthis was aerospace engineering,\u201d said Sylvain Raynes, a\nprincipal at R&R Consulting in New York and a former analyst at\nMoody\u2019s Investors Service.  Senate Report  Securitization enabled by S&P contributed to more than $2\ntrillion in losses and writedowns at the world\u2019s largest\nfinancial institutions and the collapse of Lehman Brothers\nHoldings Inc. three years ago, causing credit markets to seize\nup and leading to the global recession.  A  report  by the Senate\u2019s Permanent Subcommittee on\nInvestigations said that S&P, Moody\u2019s and  Fitch Ratings  helped\ntrigger the financial crisis when they cut thousands of mortgage\nsecurities they rated AAA to junk status. The raters had engaged\nin a \u201crace to the bottom\u201d to win business, lawmakers said.  Bank of America Corp. and Royal Bank of Scotland Group Plc\nsold $242.7 million of the Springleaf mortgage bonds today that\nare set to get S&P\u2019s top ratings, according to people familiar\nwith the matter, who declined to be identified because the terms\nhaven\u2019t been set.  The transaction was reworked after marketing began to give\nthose securities more protection against losses than S&P\nrequired, a sign investors may not have trusted the grades. An\nadditional $49.7 million of the deal ranked AAA that will suffer\nlosses first was split from the rest and not sold.  The safer debt was sold at a yield of 4 percent and has a\nprojected average life of 2.44 years, one of the people said.\nThat\u2019s about 20 times the rate demanded on two-year Treasuries.  Springleaf Bonds  The underlying mortgages represent 96.6 percent of the\ncurrent value of the homes, the issuer estimates. Borrowers may\nhave an incentive to walk away from the debt and leave investors\nwith sizable foreclosure losses should the economy slow further\nand  house prices  continue to decline.  The securities were created by Springleaf Finance Corp., a\nlender to borrowers with risky credit that\u2019s majority owned by\nprivate-equity firm Fortress Investment Group LLC and partly by\nformer parent American International Group Inc., according to\nthe people familiar with the offering.  \u201cWe didn\u2019t even start to look at the deal,\u201d  Paul Norris ,\na senior money manager at Dwight Asset Management Co. in\nBurlington, Vermont, which manages and advises on about $54\nbillion of assets, said on Aug. 25. \u201cFor the funds we would buy\nthis in, we need a AAA rating and we don\u2019t have any confidence\nS&P would hold this rating for any period of time.\u201d  Better Record  Underlying loans for the bonds are on average five years\nold, according to a document sent to investors. Credit scores of\nthe borrowers, none of whom has missed a payment over the past\ntwo years, average 651. The U.S. median is 711, according to\nFair Isaac Corp., which creates the  formulas  behind FICO scores.  The transaction may get investment-grade ratings on 79\npercent of the debt, meaning losses on the underlying loans can\nreach 21 percent before portions rated BBB or better lose\nprincipal, according to the term sheet. Springleaf plans to\nretain all but the most-senior debt, said two of the people.  Of the $12.8 billion of loans made by the firm over the\npast decade that are still outstanding, 11.5 percent are 60 days\nor more delinquent, the term sheet shows. That\u2019s a better track\nrecord than rivals, with the rate on subprime mortgages packaged\ninto bonds averaging almost 37 percent, Bloomberg data show.  Ed Sweeney , an S&P spokesman, declined to comment on the\nSpringleaf transaction. \u201cWe believe our ultimate success will\nbe driven by the value investors derive from our ratings and\nanalysis,\u201d he said.  Ability to Tax  S&P says structured finance securities  can deserve  the top\ngrades if they\u2019re backed by enough collateral to weather a U.S.\ndefault. The company said it downgraded the U.S., which, unlike\ncorporations, has the authority to set tax rates and print\nmoney, because politicians are becoming \u201cless stable, less\neffective and less predictable.\u201d Government debt of the world\u2019s\nlargest economy is now rated AA+, the same as Belgium.  \u201cI\u2019m trying to sort out why debt backed by the ability to\ntax in the  United States  is rated lower than securities that are\nbacked by no particular ability to have additional revenue,\u201d\nsaid  John Milne , who oversees about $1.8 billion as chief\nexecutive officer of JKMilne Asset Management in  Fort Myers ,\n Florida , in a telephone interview on Aug. 23. To contact the reporter on this story:\nRita Nazareth in Sao Paulo at \n rnazareth@bloomberg.net   To contact the editor responsible for this story:\nNick Baker at \n nbaker7@bloomberg.net","path":".\/2008_2012_msft_bloomberg_news\/u-s-stock-index-futures-gain-as-european-ministers-hold-debt-crisis-talks.txt"},{"id":12464457,"title":"Don't Let Predictability Become the Enemy of Innovation","released_at":"<date>May 15 2013<\/date> <time>17:00:20<\/time>","content":"Unhappily shocked by Sputnik's unexpected 1957 success, President Eisenhower quickly pushed the Pentagon to establish the  Defense Advanced Research Projects Agency (DARPA) . Its ostensible mission: \" to prevent technological surprise to the U.S. military, and to create surprises of its own .\"  Anticipating and enabling \" technological surprise \" has become even more challenging, DARPA director  Arati Prabhakar  recently told an MIT audience, because more people in more places have more access to more technology that ever before.  Surprises can come from anywhere. In an era of greater global trade, knowledge transfer and transparency, Prabhakar unsurprisingly reports DARPA's core value proposition demands disproportionately greater imagination and ingenuity. Predictability breeds complacency. Predictability is DARPA's cultural, technical and organizational enemy.  The more Prabhakar talked, the clearer it became that DARPA's intimate historical relationship with surprise offered a powerful conceptual model for serious innovators worldwide. What role should surprise play in defining one's innovation brand in the minds of customers and competitors?  To surprise or not to surprise?  That is the innovation question.  (This question  from a marketing perspective  was recently explored on this site.) For Apple, the iPhone and iPad were unquestionably strategic surprises explicitly intended to disrupt established industries and disorient entrenched competitors. Steve Jobs, who had always sought to surround his company in auras of mystery and secrecy, was a master of injecting the unexpected into the zeitgeist. Indeed, Apple assiduously cultivated \"expect the [delightfully] unexpected\" as part of its innovation brand.  While seen neither as flashy nor as glamorous as Apple's offering, Amazon's Kindle and Fire platforms similarly signaled strategic surprise. Jeff Bezos transformed perceptions surrounding Amazon as a global retailer by making clear they wanted to be a global innovation ecosystem as well. Amazon had made itself accessibly and invitingly unpredictable.  After initially dismissing tablets as inferior to laptops, Microsoft surprised a number of its partners and developers by introducing Surface. A defensive surprise, to be sure, but one acknowledging Microsoft's competitive environment had completely changed. But the greatest determinant of effective innovative surprise is not technical capability \u2014 it's expectations.  Surprise is about expectations. Successful surprises subvert, destroy and\/or exceed expectations. The great innovation tension in business is appropriately managing expectations.  With apologies to  Clay Christensen , this other \"innovator's dilemma\" asks, \"Is it better to be 'predictably surprising' or 'surprisingly predictable'?\" That is, do customers and clients prefer the comforts of predictable improvements and enhancements that fall squarely within educated expectations? Or would they rather the thrill and novelty of innovations that challenge and intrigue them in unexpected ways? If you're an Apple or a Samsung or an Amazon, is your brand better off building expectations around \"no surprises\" innovations that happily soak your customers in the warm bath of familiarity? Or do you gain greater brand equity by creatively disrupting the very expectations they're predisposed to bring to your products and services? The simple thought-experiment and test I advise innovators to explore is substituting the phrase \"pleasant surprise\" for \"innovation\" whenever they discuss new offerings and upgrades. There's a world of UX difference between a significant innovation and a significant pleasant surprise.  In fact, as many innovators discover to their sorrow, many of their most innovative features and functions are frequently regarded as unpleasant surprises.  How intimately do your designers and marketers link and measure the value of an innovation to the pleasure of its surprise? The great paradox, of course, is that the more people expect surprises, the less surprising those surprises are.  And surprise, like any other differentiator, can quickly hit diminishing returns. But, as DARPA's successful history as a surprise-based innovator suggests, understanding the differences and distinctions between \"proactive\" surprise and \"reactive\" surprise can pay huge dividends. What's surprising is how few innovators appreciate that.","path":".\/2008_2012_msft_bloomberg_news\/don-t-let-predictability-become-the-enemy-of-innovation.txt"},{"id":85377279,"title":"Yahoo Said to Be in Talks to Resolve Facebook Patent Suit","released_at":"<date>June 5 2012<\/date> <time>04:01:00<\/time>","content":"Yahoo! While Cohen wasn\u2019t charged, a grand jury indicted the fund he founded, saying it had become \u201ca magnet for market cheaters.\u201d The U.S. alleged there had been a \u201cfailure by the fund owner and others\u201d at SAC, and described separate insider trading schemes by eight SAC fund managers and analysts. Pending Deal  To date, 83 people have been charged by Manhattan U.S. Attorney Preet Bharara\u2019s office with insider trading, with 74 either pleading guilty or being convicted at trial. Eight have pleaded not guilty and are awaiting trial while one man is a fugitive.  Bharara said yesterday Aggarwal is charged with one count of conspiracy to commit securities fraud and one count of conspiracy to commit  wire fraud  for passing along an inside tip about the Yahoo!- Microsoft venture.   \u201cAggarwal leveraged his contacts in the technology industry to obtain an illegal edge in the form of inside information about a highly anticipated development, then lied about his criminal conduct,\u201d Bharara said in a statement.  Aggarwal provided material nonpublic information about the companies\u2019 strategic partnership in Internet search and advertising to two different hedge funds, including SAC, the U.S. alleged in a criminal complaint.  Within Weeks  According to the U.S., on July 9, 2009, Aggarwal learned from a friend at Microsoft about the partnership discussions and that a transaction was likely to be announced within weeks.  The next day, Aggarwal gave the information to Lee, then at SAC, and told him he had heard it from a source, whom Aggarwal described as \u201ca senior guy\u201d at Microsoft, according to the U.S.  Aggarwal told Lee that Yahoo executives had been meeting with senior Microsoft officials at Microsoft\u2019s offices and that an announcement would be made on the agreement within two weeks, the U.S. alleged in the complaint.  Aggarwal spoke to about 14 traders or portfolio managers at various hedge funds about the Microsoft-Yahoo partnership, the U.S. said. Prosecutors also alleged in the criminal complaint that a Microsoft executive working in the Bing division is a co-conspirator in the case. They didn\u2019t name the executive.  Retired Employee  One of the hedge funds was Millennium Management LLC, the person familiar with the matter said. According to the criminal complaint, FBI agent Ronan Byrne interviewed Aggarwal, who later allegedly told him that, prior to becoming a research analyst, he\u2019d worked at Redmond, Washington-based Microsoft.  Tripp Kyle, a spokesman for New York-based Millennium, declined to comment. Peter Wootton, a spokesman for Microsoft, didn\u2019t immediately return a call seeking comment about Aggarwal\u2019s case.  As a result of Aggarwal\u2019s tips, SAC Capital on July 10, 2009, bought \u201cseveral hundred thousand shares of Yahoo stock\u201d while Lee bought 25,000 Yahoo shares in his personal account, according to court papers.  Hedge Funds  When questioned by his employer on July 20, 2009, about tips he was providing to hedge funds, Aggarwal denied having any inside information and claimed his source was a person who had been retired from Microsoft for years, prosecutors alleged.  Lee pleaded guilty on July 23 to trading on information provided by a source at Yahoo and is cooperating with the U.S.  Aggarwal, who faces as long as 25 years in prison if convicted on both charges, is also being sued by the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission.  He made an initial appearance yesterday before U.S. Magistrate Judge Nandor Vadas in federal court in  San Francisco . The judge agreed to release Aggarwal on a $500,000 personal recognizance bond and ordered him to appear in federal court in New York on Aug. 2.  \u201cHe\u2019s willingly returning to New York,\u201d said Sam Braverman, a lawyer in New York who\u2019s representing Aggarwal in both the SEC and the criminal cases. During the phone call, Aggarwal conveyed material nonpublic information about the Yahoo-Microsoft partnership, prosecutors said.  Lee, who managed a $1.25 billion portfolio at SAC and worked at the firm until March, focused on \u201cspecial situations\u201d including mergers and acquisitions, private-equity buyouts and corporate restructurings in publicly traded companies, Bharara\u2019s office said.  He pleaded guilty to conspiracy and  securities fraud , admitting that in 2009 he got illegal tips about Yahoo and 3Com Corp., generating more than $1.5 million in profits for the hedge fund, according to the SEC\u2019s lawsuit.  The SEC filed an amended complaint in Lee\u2019s case yesterday, adding Aggarwal as a defendant and saying that its investigation is continuing.  The criminal case is U.S. v. Brazilian lawmakers are under orders from President Rousseff to pause all other legislative proceedings until they hash out a proposal that would require Google and other providers of online services to keep local-user information in data centers within the country.  The measure is at the forefront of a growing backlash against American Internet companies, with allegations emerging last month and as recently as last week that the NSA gained access to e-mails between world leaders and their staffs, raising questions about the data held by U.S. Internet companies. European lawmakers are considering their own penalties for companies that share unauthorized information.  Google (GOOG)  says the data-center requirement would hinder expansion in Brazil, the world\u2019s sixth-largest market for Internet users, because the infrastructure would be complicated to develop. Violating the rule would cost Google 10 percent of its annual sales in Brazil, where it is the most-visited website, according to research firm  ComScore Inc. (SCOR)   While Google doesn\u2019t disclose its Brazilian revenue, the country is the third-largest market for the company\u2019s Android smartphone software and the nation with the fifth-most YouTube users. On a monthly basis, 92 percent of Brazilian Internet users visit Google sites, according to ComScore.  \u2018Much Later\u2019  \u201cBrazilian users would ultimately be harmed because they couldn\u2019t access new tools, new services,\u201d said  Marcel Leonardi , public policy director for Google in Brazil, in a telephone interview from  Sao Paulo . \u201cCompanies would choose to implement those services at a much later stage, if at all.\u201d  Rousseff\u2019s support for the measure underscores the tendency toward protectionism in Brazil, which has raised taxes on foreign investment and car imports under her administration. It also provides a way for her to show she\u2019s fighting on behalf of Brazilians amid nationwide protests against political corruption and the government\u2019s spending priorities.  Yet she\u2019s far from alone in calling for greater scrutiny of the NSA\u2019s practices. German  Chancellor Merkel  and French President  Francois Hollande  called last week for closer cooperation on espionage after documents gathered by former NSA contractor Edward Snowden revealed U.S. authorities hacked Merkel\u2019s mobile phone in 2010. Mexico is probing allegations of U.S. eavesdropping on former President  Felipe Calderon .  EU Overhaul  The 28-nation European Union is debating a complete overhaul of its data protection rules dating back to 1995. A proposal put forward last year by the European Commission, the EU\u2019s regulator, would also hold U.S. companies such as Google, Facebook Inc. and  Apple Inc. (AAPL)  liable for violations such as unauthorized transfers of data on EU citizens to non-EU countries. Fines could be as high as 100 million euros ($138 million), according to draft rules backed last week by a European Parliament committee.The EU plans need the support of lawmakers and national governments before they can become law.  Brazil\u2019s data-center requirement would be tacked onto a bill called  Marco Civil  that establishes legal guidelines for  Internet providers , such as neutrality in the services consumers can access on their networks. Rousseff marked the bill as urgent on Sept. 11, less than two weeks after documents leaked by Snowden revealed the agency monitored her communication with her staff. The urgent designation means lawmakers must set aside all other business to consider the measure, which would get similar priority in the Senate if it\u2019s approved in the lower house.  Next Week?  The bill will be discussed in the lower house on Nov. 5 and will be voted the following day, said  Alessandro Molon , its sponsor, in an interview today. He attributed the weeklong wait more to a separate debate over Internet neutrality. Whether the proposal will include the data-center measure is undecided, he said. He is scheduled to meet with Rousseff this week.  In an interview last week with Radio Itatiaia of  Belo Horizonte , Brazil, Rousseff said Marco Civil \u201cclearly shows Brazil\u2019s position\u201d that data should be stored within the country, not \u201cin the  United States  as it is today.\u201d  Google said in an e-mailed statement that it supports the broader Marco Civil law while opposing the data-center proposal. Google rose 2.1 percent to $1,036.24 at the close in New York.  Internet trade associations and the  International Chamber of Commerce  said in an  open letter  to the Brazilian congress that the data-center proposal would hurt the country\u2019s competitiveness, increase the cost of doing business, lead to slower growth and make Brazilian  Internet users  more vulnerable to hacking.  Less Secure?  Even if it were possible to identify users based on nationality or location, isolating their data would make them less -- not more -- secure, said  Zahid Jamil , a lawyer who works with the International Chamber of Commerce and other groups on cybercrime and technology in  emerging markets . Part of Google\u2019s security strategy to protect user data from computer crashes and cyber attacks is to \u201cchunk and replicate the data over multiple systems to avoid a single point of failure,\u201d according to the company\u2019s  website .  \u2018No Relevance\u2019  A hacker targeting a Brazilian would know exactly where to look for information if it were confined to one data center, said Jamil, the chairman of the Developing Countries Center for Cyber Crime Law, a Pakistan-based group.  \u201cLocalization of data has no relevance whatsoever on security or fighting cyber crime,\u201d Jamil said from Karachi in an Oct. 15 telephone interview. \u201cThe argument that data is this one thing, and you only have one copy in Brazil and therefore it\u2019s safe, is a false argument based on a 20th century understanding of physical things.\u201d  Molon, the bill\u2019s sponsor, said the priority of the data-center measure is to make Internet companies subject to Brazilian law, which safeguards citizens against monitoring. Storing data locally gives Brazil legal control of user information, he said.  Unlike emerging markets China, Russia and South Korea, Brazil doesn\u2019t have a well-developed domestic Internet industry. Rousseff\u2019s local data-center proposal would protect Brazilian citizens while encouraging the growth of local companies to challenge Google, said  Pablo Ortellado , a public-policy professor at the University of Sao Paulo.  \u201cConsidering the implications of the spying allegations, I think it\u2019s preferable that we develop a national industry, even if it\u2019s not initially of the same quality as the American market,\u201d Ortellado said.  China Clash  Google has clashed with governments before, leading the company to make choices to adapt to local laws while still pursuing its  mission  to make information universally accessible. In China, where officials can block websites that don\u2019t comply with media regulations, Google decided in 2010 to stop altering its search results, redirecting users to a Hong Kong site, limiting its ability to expand in China.  In  Latin America , Google is building a $150 million data center in  Chile , on the outskirts of Santiago. The  facility  will be operating by the end of this year. Chile was chosen for Google\u2019s first data center in the region because of \u201can ideal combination of reliable infrastructure, a skilled workforce and a commitment to transparent and business friendly regulations,\u201d according to a company statement.  Expresso E-Mail  Google isn\u2019t the only company affected by Brazil\u2019s response to the NSA spying allegations. Government agencies won\u2019t renew their contracts with  Microsoft Corp. (MSFT)  to use Outlook e-mail services, Communications Minister  Paulo Bernardo  told reporters Oct. 14. Government-controlled  Telecomunicacoes Brasileiras SA (TELB3)  is working on its third version of a domestically developed e-mail service called Expresso, which will be ready for full adoption in November. Mimi Newman, a Microsoft spokeswoman, had no immediate comment.  Even as it pursues the data-center measure, Brazil plans to use Google\u2019s technology for education and Web access, including a project to  blanket  the Amazon with Internet coverage using balloons. And right now,  Barnes & Noble (BKS)  has one of the best ones going.  It\u2019s the Nook HD+, the nine-inch color tablet the struggling bookseller introduced late last year to compete with  Apple (AAPL) \u2019s iPad and, especially,  Amazon (AMZN) \u2019s 8.9-inch Kindle Fire HD.  At its launch, the Nook was hampered by a lack of content beyond B&N\u2019s own e-book offerings and by the absence of key apps. But the company has addressed some of those shortcomings while augmenting the device\u2019s attractive price with special deals that make it worth a look.  The  HD+  comes in two versions: one with 16 gigabytes of storage for $269, the other with 32 gigabytes for $299. Those are the same prices Amazon touts for the  Kindle Fire HD , but with a couple of important differences.  To get that price on the Kindle, you have to be willing to accept ads; it\u2019s $15 extra for commercial-free versions.  The Nook also includes a wall charger and cable -- Amazon gives you just the cable -- and includes a slot for a microSD card to expand its storage capacity up to 96 gigabytes. The Kindle isn\u2019t expandable; Amazon expects you to store a lot of content online using its Cloud services.  Content Credit  But what really makes the Nook attractive is a $50 credit toward content purchases made within 30 days, lowering its effective price to $219. That\u2019s only a few bucks more than the no-ads version of the seven-inch Kindle Fire HD, which has a 40 percent smaller screen.  The credit is available only on Nooks purchased at one of Barnes & Noble\u2019s 670 or so stores, or online at  Nook.com ; it doesn\u2019t cover devices purchased through retail partners like  Wal-Mart (WMT)  and  Staples (SPLS) . Barnes & Noble says the offer is good indefinitely, though it did suspend it for a week recently when it gave away a free monochrome e-reader with each purchase.  While the Nook is nowhere near as potent as the iPad or  Microsoft (MSFT) \u2019s Surface, it also costs far less. The least expensive iPad, the base-model iPad mini, is $329, while the cheapest Surface, the RT, is $500.  Not Cheap  The Nook neither looks nor feels cheap. It weighs about 18 ounces, about two ounces lighter than the Kindle Fire HD, and its battery should get you through a day of normal use.  The screen is a beauty. It has a resolution of 1920 by 1280 pixels and can display video in full high-definition. Not only is it better than the Kindle, its 256 pixels-per-inch density nearly matches that of the iPad\u2019s vaunted Retina display.  Its biggest missing feature, relative to its Amazon competition, is a camera. So even though Microsoft is an investor in the Nook business, forget about using its Skype service.  The Nook, like the Kindle, runs a version of  Google (GOOG) \u2019s Android operating system, although -- again like the Kindle -- it\u2019s so heavily modified that you might never know it. One result is that it doesn\u2019t have access to the 700,000 or so apps in the  Google Play store ; instead, you\u2019re limited to apps that have been tailored specifically for Barnes & Noble.  Still Weak  That\u2019s been a weakness of the Nook from the beginning, and it still is, but a little less so. There are native Nook apps for  Facebook (FB) , Twitter, Netflix and Spotify, plus a Web browser.  It has also expanded its sparse video catalog through recent deals with  Lions Gate (LGF) ,  MGM (MGMB)  and  Viacom (VIAB) \u2019s Paramount, among others. MGM\u2019s \u201cSkyfall\u201d came preloaded on my test device, and James Bond was pretty impressive on that nice screen.  Still, the Nook ecosystem pales next to Amazon, which has smartly made the Kindle a seamless entry point to its enormous collections of movies, music, television shows and books. And the Kindle has vastly more apps too -- so many more that Barnes & Noble won\u2019t even release a count of Nook apps.  It also has more configurations, including an extra-cost option to connect to  AT&T (T) \u2019s fast 4G LTE network; the Nook works only over a Wi-Fi connection.  All things being equal, the Kindle is the superior device. But all things aren\u2019t equal as long as you can get a Nook HD+ for, effectively, $219 -- making it worth consideration if you\u2019re shopping for a good tablet that won\u2019t break the bank. In an increasingly mobile world, though, the most important characteristic may be longer -- as in, how long the battery lasts between charges.  And longer is what makes  Apple (AAPL) \u2019s latest MacBook Air worth talking about. Utilizing new, lower-power chips from Intel, the Air takes battery life to places it\u2019s never been on a lightweight laptop computer.  Earlier MacBook Airs broke new ground in both portability and performance, with solid-state chips in place of mechanical hard drives to store programs and data. Using  Microsoft (MSFT) \u2019s Windows 8 operating system,  Samsung (005930) ,  Sony (6758) , Toshiba and others have since produced even thinner and lighter models.  No one, though, comes close in longevity -- and won\u2019t until the new chips become standard.  The base-model 11.6-inch MacBook Air retains the $999 price tag of its predecessor, but doubles the amount of storage to 128 gigabytes; a 256-gigabyte version pushes the price to $1,199. The larger Air, which has a 13.3-inch screen, costs $100 less than last year: $1,099 for 128 gigabytes, $1,299 for 256.  Lookalike Models  Externally, the new models are indistinguishable from their predecessors. They have the same striking machined-aluminum bodies and wedge-shaped designs, only .11 of an inch at the thinnest point, and weigh just 2.38 pounds and 2.96 pounds.  The big change is under the hood. Primarily thanks to Intel\u2019s brand-new \u201cHaswell\u201d generation of chips, the 13.3-inch MacBook Air can go up to 12 hours between charges, according to Apple, while the smaller unit lasts up to nine hours.  I cranked up the brightness on my 13.3-inch test device -- equipped with an i5 chip, four gigabytes of system memory and 128 gigabytes of storage -- disabled power-saving settings, made sure Bluetooth and Wi-Fi were both active and launched a constant stream of  Netflix (NFLX)  movies and TV shows.  Understated Estimate  With all that, I managed from nine to more than 10 hours of use, suggesting that the company may be slightly understating the battery life you\u2019ll see in the real world.  The Haswell chips actually clock in marginally slower than the processors used in previous-generation Airs. But you\u2019d never know it, perhaps because of other changes Apple has made, including using new, faster flash-memory chips to perk up the process of accessing and storing data, plus speedier graphics.  The Air also supports 802.11ac, the latest and fastest Wi-Fi connection. Because the standard is brand-new, few people yet have routers that will allow them to take advantage of the greater speeds. Over time, though, users will see faster downloads and enhanced range.  Although the MacBook\u2019s design holds up well against newer competitors, there are still a couple of areas that could stand improvement.  Chief among these is the screen, where the Air continues to lack the ultra-sharp Retina display found on Apple\u2019s MacBook Pro, to say nothing of iPads and iPhones.  The Air\u2019s screens are still very nice: The smaller model has a resolution of 1366 by 768 pixels, the larger 1440 by 900. But to get a better display, you\u2019ll have to move up to the heavier, costlier Pro -- or to competing models like the Toshiba Kirabook or Google\u2019s Chromebook Pixel.  Of course, a better display would also consume more power, reducing the new Air\u2019s chief advantage over those rivals. So maybe it\u2019s a tradeoff worth making. Ben Allgrove, a partner at law firm  Baker & McKenzie LLP  in\n London , said the gap is a result of the legal challenges for\ncopyright owners. Last year, France lost $2.6 billion in pirated software,\nwhile Germany lost $2.1 billion, Italy $1.9 billion and the U.K.\n$1.8 billion. The four nations were among the 10 most pirated\nworldwide. Across the EU, Bulgaria recorded the highest rate of\nsoftware piracy in 2010 at 65 percent, while Luxembourg had the\nlowest at 20 percent, according to BSA.  The  European Commission  may make proposals on how to change\nthe current law in the first half of 2012, said  Chantal Hughes ,\na spokeswoman for EU Internal Markets Commissioner  Michel\nBarnier  said. CFTC Approves Rule Expanding Access to Swaps Clearinghouses  Swaps clearinghouses will be required to open access to\ncompanies with at least $50 million in capital under Dodd-Frank\nAct rules completed by the U.S.  Commodity Futures Trading\nCommission .  The rule was hailed by CFTC chairman  Gary Gensler  as \u201cone\nof the most significant rulemakings to lower risk in the\nfinancial system.\u201d  CFTC commissioners voted 3-2 yesterday to implement\ngovernance of member-funded clearinghouses that will guarantee\ntrades between buyers and sellers in the $601 trillion swaps\nmarket. Dodd-Frank, the financial-regulation overhaul enacted\nlast year, included the rulemaking in the agency\u2019s mandate after\nlargely unregulated trades helped fuel the 2008 credit crisis.  The rules will govern clearinghouses that develop plans to\ncover a default by their largest member. The CFTC and other\nregulators may adopt separate rules for clearinghouses deemed\nsystemically important, which would have to create plans to\ncover the possible default of the two largest members. The  European Securities and Markets Authority , which\ncoordinates national market regulators in the EU, will give a\nnon-binding opinion on whether a national regulators\u2019 decision\nto drop the ban makes sense. One home in Washington attracted 168 offers in December and sold for almost twice the asking price. About 70 people lined up last month for a lottery to select buyers for four available houses in a San Ramon,  California , subdivision where, in August, bidders camped for weeks to secure purchases.  A plunge in U.S. home listings to a 12-year  low  is driving up prices and preventing transactions from returning to historically normal levels. Many potential sellers are holding off until values rise more, while investors are snatching up distressed properties before they reach the market. Builders, reporting their best orders in years, can\u2019t increase production fast enough. As buyers seek to take advantage of record-low mortgage  rates , the supply and demand imbalance threatens to further limit deals as the key spring selling season approaches.  \u201cThere is just no inventory for buyers,\u201d said Bob Cilk, an agent with Re\/Max Accord in Pleasanton, California, where only 27 single-family houses are available for sale, about a third of the normal level. \u201cThere are lots of losers in the marketplace now. When you have multiple offers, there are several losers and only one winner for each home.\u201d  Price Gains  U.S. home prices rose 8.3 percent in December from a year earlier, the biggest jump since May 2006,  Irvine , California- based CoreLogic Inc. reported today. Existing home sales  fell  1 percent to a 4.94 million annual rate in December as tight supply put a lid on deals, according to the National Association of Realtors. A normal level is 5 million to 5.5 million transactions, said Walter Molony, a spokesman for the group in Washington.  While rising values eventually compel would-be sellers to list their homes, inventories may remain tight for a year or two because prices need to rise another five or 10 percent before enough sellers can cover mortgage and transaction costs, said Mark Zandi, chief economist for Moody\u2019s Analytics Inc. in West Chester,  Pennsylvania .  \u201cNobody wants to sell at the bottom and everybody wants to buy at the bottom,\u201d said  Paul Diggle , property economist for Capital Economics Ltd. in  London . \u201cThat might create some kind of standoff until home prices rise sufficiently so that sellers come back to the market at a larger scale.\u201d  Biggest Concern  About a third of homeowners say their biggest concern about selling now is that they will miss out on future price gains, according to a January  survey  by Redfin, a Seattle-based brokerage. That surpassed the economy as the top worry.  New listings in 21 of the largest U.S. cities plunged 21 percent last month from a year earlier, led by declines of more than 35 percent in the San Francisco Bay area, Las Vegas and Atlanta, Redfin said. At the end of 2012, about 28 percent of home listings nationally went under contract within 14 days, with cities in California\u2019s Silicon Valley and Los Angeles areas exceeding 40 percent. In Washington, Seattle and Denver it was more than 30 percent.  While more homeowners usually list properties after the start of the year, the buyer and seller logjam probably will continue into the spring as the appetite for real estate increases, said Jed Kolko, chief economist of San Francisco- based  Trulia Inc. (TRLA) , which operates an online property-listing service.  \u201cInventories start growing in February and peak in July, but without even more new construction and more homeowners willing to sell, inventory will stay tight through this housing season,\u201d Kolko said.  Homebuilder Demand  For homebuilders, the spring selling season is traditionally viewed as starting the weekend after the National Football League\u2019s Super Bowl, which was held two days ago. The companies can\u2019t increase production fast enough because of labor shortages and rising competition for lots in the best locations, said Brad Hunter, chief economist of Metrostudy, a Washington- based research firm that tracks construction.  \u201cThey\u2019re barely keeping up with the demand and their backlogs are growing,\u201d Hunter said. \u201cAnd that emboldens them to raise prices.\u201d  PulteGroup Inc. (PHM) , the largest U.S. homebuilder by market value, is \u201cpurposefully slowing our rate of sales as we focus on maximizing margin over driving volume,\u201d and raising prices in areas such as Phoenix and  Florida , Chairman and Chief Executive Officer Richard Dugas said on a conference call with analysts last week. The Bloomfield Hills, Michigan-based company reported a 27 percent jump in fourth-quarter orders as profit quadrupled.  Distressed Decline  Much of the dropoff in listings of existing properties is tied to fewer foreclosure deals and short sales, where the homeowner sells for less than is owed on the mortgage, said Tim Ellis, real estate analyst with Redfin.  Listings for short sales fell in more than 60 percent of 102 major metropolitan areas in 2012 from the previous year, matching the share for bank-owned properties, according to RealtyTrac, an Irvine, California-based data provider. The processing of delinquent loans slowed starting in late 2010 after allegations that lenders used workers to sign foreclosure documents without verifying the paperwork.  Distressed listings may increase in 2013 because foreclosure filings began picking up last year, especially in states that require court approval for repossessions, such as New York, New Jersey,  Illinois ,  Ohio  and Florida, said  Daren Blomquist , vice president of RealtyTrac. It takes about 600 days, on average, from the time a property enters the foreclosure process until a bank sells it, Blomquist said.  New Supply  \u201cWe would anticipate in the markets with the biggest increases in foreclosure activity in 2012, the supply shortage will be eased somewhat in 2013 as those properties are listed for sale,\u201d Blomquist said.  In Washington, a 2,850-square-foot (265-square-meter) foreclosed home near Union Station went on the market in late November for $337,000 and attracted 168 offers during a 10-day bidding period that was closed to investors, said Michelle Johnson of Tri-State Realty LLC in Bowie,  Maryland , who is representing the Department of Housing and Urban Development in the sale of the property.  \u201cWhen it was on the market, you could go there any hour and you would think it was happy hour -- there were always agents and buyers there, even at night,\u201d Johnson said.  Private Equity  Private-equity firms such as  Blackstone Group LP (BX)  began purchasing thousands of foreclosed homes last year, taking them out of the for-sale inventory and converting them into rentals. New York-based Blackstone, the largest investor in the business, has spent more than $2.5 billion on 16,000 homes and is buying in nine markets, from Miami to Phoenix.  \u201cThe incredible emergence of big money is a significant reason why we have less supply,\u201d said Thomas Lawler, a former Fannie Mae economist who\u2019s now a housing consultant in Leesburg, Virginia.  Rising prices may spur some investors to test the sales market, along with \u201creluctant landlords\u201d who needed to move for jobs or family changes but chose not to sell during the downturn, Lawler said.  Elyn Yao became a landlord five years ago after moving out of her two-bedroom townhouse in Seattle\u2019s Fremont neighborhood to the Madrona area, seeking to be closer to her job at Microsoft Corp. While the rent hasn\u2019t completely covered her costs, she was waiting for the market to improve. Her agent, Kevin Lisota, listed the home in early January and it was under contract four days later for $450,000, $5,000 above the asking price.  New Places  \u201cThe market was starting to pick up and it was a good opportunity to get out of the business of being a landlord,\u201d said Yao, who bought the property in 2004 for $452,000.  In the tightest markets, homeowners are worried that if they sell, they may not be easily able to find a place to buy, Lisota said. The improving  job market  and restrictive lending standards are also pushing up rents for  apartments  across the country.  \u201cThe seller\u2019s No. 1 concern is, \u2018Can I get the price I want,\u2019 followed up by \u2018Will I be able to find a replacement in a reasonable time frame,\u2019 Lisota said.  In Silicon Valley, demand is so brisk that some buyers are agreeing not to make deals contingent on successful financing, inspection or appraisal, and are accepting properties in \u2018\u2018as is\u2019\u2019 condition, said Mary Pope-Handy, an agent in Los Gatos, California. Some buyers are allowing sellers to remain in the home after closing for months without paying rent, she said.  Camping Out  At the Solaire at Gale Ranch community in San Ramon, prospective buyers camped out in tents for as long as two weeks in August before the developer released nine houses for sale, said Sonal Basu, an agent with Redfin.  The builder, Shapell Homes, shifted to a lottery system this year after neighbors complained about people living outdoors for weeks, Basu said. The company has since discovered it has a wider global\napplication.  \n ``We looked and found we can use it in Europe, Asia and\nSouth America and we went ahead to do so,'' Oyegbola said.  \n One Laptop acknowledged it did buy at least one Konyin\nkeyboard, but never used the software that accompanied the\nkeyboard, according to its court papers.  \n Konyin software is for use with  Microsoft Corp. 's Windows,\nand the One Laptop computer is  Linux -based, so the Konyin\nsoftware would not work, One Laptop said in its pleadings.  \n Because it never used the software, One Laptop never agreed\nto the license agreement, and therefore could not have breached\nthe agreement by developing the XO laptop's multilingual\nkeyboard, according to court papers.  \n One Laptop also denied that it had misappropriated any\nKonyin trade secrets. The layout of the Konyin keyboard is\n``publicly available to anyone who inspects the keyboard'' and is\nalso available at the www.konyin.com Web site, One Laptop said in\nits pleadings.  \n Intel Corp. left One Laptop's board in January after\nreaching what Intel spokesman  Chuck Mulloy  said was ``a\nphilosophical impasse'' with the foundation. There have been more than $240 billion of tech and telecom takeovers this quarter, led by  Verizon Communications Inc. (VZ) \u2019s $130 billion buyout of  Vodafone Group Plc (VOD) \u2019s stake in their wireless venture, according to data compiled by Bloomberg. That puts the three-month period on pace to be the busiest since 2000, when AOL Inc. and Time Warner Inc. announced their merger, then valued at as much as $186 billion.  Tech and telecom deals have already helped push total mergers and acquisitions volume this quarter past the previous one, with more than $520 billion in transactions worldwide, data compiled by Bloomberg show. The activity underscores how more companies are finally making strategic moves to counter technological disruption, said Jennifer Nason, global chairman of tech-media-telecom  investment banking  at JPMorgan Chase & Co.  \u201cThe fast pace of innovation, increasing competitive dynamics and the potential for increasing capital costs have created the perfect storm for strategic moves which had been contemplated for a while,\u201d said Nason, 53, who advised Verizon on the wireless venture buyout and worked on Nokia Oyj\u2019s proposed sale of its mobile-phone business to  Microsoft Corp. (MSFT) , both announced Sept. 2. \u201cOnce you see a few deals happen, you can expect more.\u201d  Vodafone\u2019s Moves  Vodafone\u2019s sale of the stake in Verizon Wireless gives it billions of dollars to make its own acquisitions while simultaneously making the U.K. wireless operator a potential target, according to analysts. The transaction also puts pressure on competitors such as  AT&T Inc. (T)  to accelerate strategic changes. AT&T, second in U.S. mobile-phone customers to  Verizon Wireless , said this year that  Europe  may offer attractive options for  expansion .  Among handset makers, BlackBerry Ltd. said last month it\u2019s weighing a sale, following the lackluster debut of the BlackBerry 10 lineup.  Lenovo Group Ltd. (992) , the world\u2019s largest maker of personal computers, also said this month it\u2019s looking for acquisitions in PCs and smartphones.  Innovations from smartphones to social media are creating new opportunities for some companies and ruining the business models of others, driving dealmaking in both cases. Verizon\u2019s deal with Vodafone crowns a summer that saw Publicis Groupe SA and Omnicom Group Inc. agree to combine to create a $35 billion advertising powerhouse, as well as Microsoft\u2019s $7.2 billion bid for the Nokia mobile business and patents.  Nokia\u2019s Future  Verizon and Vodafone had discussed a buyout of the wireless stake on and off for a decade, according to people familiar with the talks. For the U.S. company, the case for full ownership became more compelling with growth in mobile-data use by high-spending customers, allowing it to increase its offer to a level acceptable to Vodafone, they said.  Nokia\u2019s (NOK1V)  future, meanwhile, has been a subject of speculation almost from the moment Apple Inc. debuted the iPhone in 2007. Once the world\u2019s leading mobile-phone manufacturer, Nokia has fallen badly behind Apple and Samsung Electronics Co., and the Windows Phone operating system its devices run accounts for less than 5 percent of new smartphones, according to researcher IDC.  Telecom companies such as  Telefonica SA (TEF) , which is attempting to merge its German business with that of Royal KPN NV, are looking to consolidate as growing data use demands more expensive networks and regulators restrict fees for services like roaming.  Good Climate  \u201cThe dynamism in the wireless sector is quite strong, and as it moves to video capability the industry requires upgrades,\u201d said Eli Noam, a professor of finance and economics at  Columbia Business School , as well as the director of the Columbia Institute for Tele-Information. That\u2019s putting pressure on mobile carriers to build scale by expanding their global footprint, he said.  For boards and chief executive officers wary of making big decisions amid volatile economic conditions and markets, recent weeks have offered a respite. While the fiscal problems of  Greece ,  Spain , and other struggling Euro-area countries are far from solved, none has caused a market-roiling crisis since Cyprus\u2019s bailout in March. The economy of the 17-nation currency bloc returned to growth in the second quarter, driven by increased exports.  News like that has helped global stock-market indexes stay buoyant, with the  S&P 500   rising  about 15 percent since the start of the year and  London \u2019s FTSE 100 up about 10 percent.  Borrowing Costs  The expectation that  interest rates  will rise has also spurred some companies to act. Verizon took advantage of the favorable interest rate environment to borrow about $60 billion to fund the wireless venture buyout.  While yields have climbed from earlier record lows, they\u2019re well below historic averages. The average yield investors demand to hold bonds in the Bank of America Merrill Lynch U.S. Telecommunications Index, which includes debt from AT&T and Vodafone, was 3.88 percent as of Sept. 2, up from an unprecedented 2.92 percent last October. The average over the past 10 years was 5 percent.  For the Vodafone deal, Verizon will probably issue $40 billion to $50 billion in bonds, according to a person with knowledge of its plans. Depending on how the borrowing is structured, its first offering could set a new record for the largest-ever U.S. bond issue, surpassing Apple\u2019s $17 billion sale in April, the person said.  Silicon Valley  Apple and rival  Google Inc. (GOOG) , whose mobile software powers more than 90 percent of new smartphones, are the source of many of the disruptions that are encouraging deals. Publicis CEO  Maurice Levy  cited the need for consolidation to confront the growing power of the Silicon Valley firms when he announced the Omnicom deal, which will create the world\u2019s largest advertising agency.  Given encouraging signs for the economic environment, deal activity may continue, particularly in tech and telecom, said Pip McCrostie, global vice chair of transaction advisory services at EY, formerly called Ernst & Young LLP.  \u201cActivity will be very much based on the fact that as companies and CEOs get more confident, in a sustainable growth picture, we\u2019ll see more M&A,\u201d McCrostie said.
