The greatest\nthinkers challenge what everyone believes to be obvious. They\nallow us to see the world anew.  We may be primed for another lesson, this time in\neconomics. It has been \u201cobvious\u201d to most people over the past 30\nyears that the creative dynamism of the free market, the energy\nof private individuals pursuing their own dreams, is the best\ndriver of economic innovation. The global economy carries the\nindelible imprint of the brilliant visionaries who created\ncompanies such as Microsoft Corp., Apple Inc. and Google Inc.\nInnovation is a private affair, best left free of the typically\nsluggish and wasteful interference of government.  What seems so obvious might also be completely wrong. This\nis the point that economist Mariana Mazzucato makes in her\nrecent  book , \u201cThe Entrepreneurial State: Debunking Private vs.\nPublic Sector Myths.\u201d  Think of the Internet, biotechnology, electronics,\nphotonics, materials science and nanotechnology -- all the\ncrucial technologies of our age. Go back further to oil, rail,\nthe airlines and nuclear energy. None of these would be as\ndeveloped as they are, and some would hardly exist, without the\nfounding vision and directed action of government agencies.  Long-Term Vision  Consider the Internet and the World Wide Web, energized by\ncompetition among behemoths such as Google and Facebook Inc. and\ncountless garage-style startups such as Clarity and Avaaz. This\nfrontier of market freedom was brought into existence by\ngovernment pursuing a long-term vision that no company would\nhave attempted. People at the  Defense Advanced Research Projects\nAgency  had the imagination to support a consortium of\nuniversities and research firms to build a network of computers\nable to exchange information, and undertook the sustained effort\nrequired to make it happen.  What about Google? The genius and inspiration of the\ncompany\u2019s founders,  Sergey Brin  and  Larry Page , played a big\nrole in making it happen. So did funding from the U.S. National\nScience Foundation, which let the two computer scientists\ndevelop the algorithm that so transformed Web search and\npropelled the company ahead. Forward-thinking leaders at the\nfoundation offered funding in precisely this area because they\nthought it would pave the way to a world of new technologies.  Even Apple, normally viewed as the singular creation of the\nlone genius of  Steve Jobs , owes much to government. Mazzucato\npoints out that Apple received crucial finance in its early\nyears from the U.S. government\u2019s small-business investment\nprogram. Every one of the most important technologies in Apple\u2019s\nsmart products, including the iPhone and iPad, were developed\nelsewhere and largely thanks to state funding.  The picture is similar throughout the economy. Of the\nroughly 100 most important innovations from 1971 to 2006, as\nidentified by R&D Magazine, almost 90 percent depended heavily\non federal research support, according to Mazzucato. And\nwhatever big pharmaceutical companies might say about the risks\nthey take and amounts they spend to develop new drugs, most of\nthe really innovative discoveries the past few decades have come\nfrom publicly funded laboratories.  The point isn\u2019t that Jobs wasn\u2019t a genius, or that the\nenergy and creativity of the private sector aren\u2019t necessary.\nIt\u2019s that governments have had a huge and widely unappreciated\ninfluence on our economic well-being. They can often achieve\nthings the private sector cannot, creating new technologies and\nentirely new markets.  It\u2019s a point that  John Maynard Keynes  made long ago: \u201cThe\nimportant thing for Government,\u201d he observed, \u201cis not to do\nthings which individuals are doing already, and to do them a\nlittle better or a little worse; but to do those things which at\npresent are not done at all.\u201d  White Elephants  Governments do have flaws. They are prone to pursue white-elephant projects and to suffer from stifling bureaucracy. These\nare problems to battle against, while benefiting from the best\nthings government can do.  Mazzucato warns that the perception of government impotence\nin innovation can be self-fulfilling. Uncertainty in policy is a\nrecipe for failure. Government is most effective when it acts\nwith confidence, as evidenced in places such as China and\n Brazil , which have successfully developed technologies for the\nanticipated \u201cgreen revolution\u201d with the help of state aid.  As long as we remain under the spell of myths and don\u2019t\nrecognize the potential for visionary government action to help\nlead society forward -- as it has in the past -- we are likely\nto suffer. Viewed correctly, government should be an invaluable\npartner of the private sector, one that is willing and able to\ntake the crucial risks that business won\u2019t.  (Mark Buchanan, a theoretical physicist and the author of\n\u201cThe Social Atom: Why the Rich Get Richer, Cheaters Get Caught\nand Your Neighbor Usually Looks Like You,\u201d is a Bloomberg View\ncolumnist.) (TWTR)  ahead of its planned initial public offering. It\u2019s got a dearth of patents, too.  The microblogging service said in its prospectus this week that it has nine issued U.S. patents. That compares with 774 cited by Facebook Inc. before its initial public offering in May 2012 and International Business Machine Corp.\u2019s 6,478 patents accrued last year alone. Twitter\u2019s smaller patent trove reflects its philosophy of letting engineers and designers own their inventions.  While Twitter\u2019s policy is an effort to limit patent litigation, some investors and analysts are concerned it could backfire. Evidence shows that intellectual property can help companies raise more funds in their offerings, as patents enable investors to quantify the value of technological breakthroughs. Those safeguards are important for potential Twitter investors, amid the company\u2019s widening losses and a lack of other financial metrics to go by.  \u201cThe lack of a large number of issued patents is a little concerning,\u201d Maulin Shah, managing director at Envision IP LLC, an advisory and research firm in  New York , said by phone. \u201cIf Twitter does deal with patent-infringement lawsuits, they don\u2019t have too many patents to lean on to countersue. That does put Twitter at a disadvantage.\u201d  Innovator Agreement  Twitter says in its prospectus that many competitors have \u201csubstantially larger patent\u201d portfolios, which could make it a target for litigation.  At the same time, Twitter has said that too many patents may hinder innovation. In May, the San Francisco-based company implemented the  Innovator\u2019s Patent Agreement , or IPA, to keep ownership of inventions in the hands of the people who created them. As part of the policy, Twitter can\u2019t pursue offensive litigation without the inventor\u2019s permission. The IPA ensures that the patents \u201cwill be used only as a shield rather than as a weapon,\u201d according to Twitter\u2019s website.  The IPA will help the company lure and retain more talented engineers, said Robert Clarkson, a partner in the  capital markets  practice at corporate law firm  Jones Day . More than 5,000 patent actions were filed last year, the highest number ever recorded, according to a 2013 study by  PricewaterhouseCoopers LLP .  \u201cTwitter has taken a somewhat different approach in that agreement,\u201d Clarkson said in a phone interview from  San Francisco . \u201cThis helps them attract leading individuals. They get more by attracting the best and brightest.\u201d  Investor Risk  The policy\u2019s biggest risk is that employees will take their inventions with them, posing a competitive threat if they leave, according to Jeff Sica, president and chief investment officer of Sica Wealth Management LLC.  \u201cThis is a radical way of dealing with patents, which is far different than anything investors have seen before,\u201d said Sica, who oversees about $1 billion under management. \u201cPeople may appreciate the openness and invitation of competition.\u201d  Sica, who\u2019s considering buying shares of Twitter, said that the company has developed a strong enough brand to withstand the competition.  Jim Prosser, a spokesman for Twitter, declined to comment.  Twitter is seeking to raise more than $1 billion in its IPO, people familiar with the situation said last week, and will probably start a roadshow to market the offering in the last week of October. The company pegged the fair value of its common stock at $20.62 a share in August.  Active Users  Twitter\u2019s potential, as it lures advertising with more than 230 million monthly active users, means it could fetch $50 a share by the end of 2014, according to Robert Peck, an analyst at SunTrust Robinson Humphrey Inc. That user base is also critical to defending Twitter from competitors, he said.  \u201cInvestors are asking if Twitter\u2019s not protecting their business,\u201d Peck said by phone. \u201cI think there\u2019s a business risk there, but at this point, the network effect protects Twitter.\u201d  Adding patents ahead of an IPO can help a company  raise  a higher amount in its market debut, according to a study of 234 software firms in the U.S. An additional patent obtained prior to the debut increased proceeds by about 0.9 percent, according to a working paper presented last year by Diego Useche, a researcher at the University of Bordeaux.  \u201cThe more that IP is protected, the less infringement opportunity there is, and therefore, would increase the valuation,\u201d said Peter Adriaens, a professor of entrepreneurship and strategy in the Stephen M. Ross School of Business at the University of Michigan.  Patent Boost  Facebook placed a large focus on strengthening its patent portfolio before going public to protect itself from potential infringement cases, according to Envision IP. The  social network  acquired about 750 patents from IBM and another 650 from Microsoft Corp. prior to its IPO, Envision IP said in a Sept. 13 note.  While  LinkedIn Corp. (LNKD) , the professional-networking website, and  Zynga Inc. (ZNGA) , maker of the online social game \u201cFarmVille,\u201d both went public with two or fewer patents, they were each profitable before their IPOs. Twitter\u2019s net loss widened to $133.9 million in the first nine months of this year.  Twitter has been named in more than a dozen patent-infringement lawsuits, according to data compiled by Bloomberg. So far, it has successfully fended off the cases.  In August, Twitter won a U.S. appeals court ruling that it didn\u2019t infringe a patent owned by Eaton Corp.\u2019s Cooper Notification for a mass messaging system. In April 2012, it won a jury verdict that it didn\u2019t infringe patents owned by closely held VS Technologies for a way to build virtual communities.  TechRadium Inc., a closely held company that provides a system for emergency response services, sued in 2009 after municipalities said they were opting for Twitter\u2019s system. The two sides settled in December 2010, according to court records.  Patents Pending  Twitter may have access to eight more patents through its recent acquisitions of TweetDeck, Bluefin Labs and Dasient, though these patents have yet to be legally assigned to the company, according to Envision IP\u2019s  research  note. Twitter also said in the regulatory filing that it has about 95 patent applications pending in the U.S. and abroad.  The company\u2019s lack of offensive litigation could cut down on expenses. Each patent lawsuit can cost as much as $5.5 million, depending on the size of IP at risk, according to a 2013 study by the  American Intellectual Property Law Association .  \u201cIt does help the company to reduce the litigation costs to reduce patents,\u201d said the  University of Michigan \u2019s Adriaens. \u201cYou need to have enough to project confidence to investors in terms of what you have in the way of intellectual property.\u201d  To contact the reporter on this story: Leslie Picker in New York at  lpicker2@bloomberg.net   To contact the editor responsible for this story: Jeffrey McCracken at  jmccracken3@bloomberg.net","path":".\/2008_2012_msft_bloomberg_news\/witter-pre-ipo-patent-paucity-seen-posing-investor-risk-tec.txt"},{"id":38333507,"title":"Russia\u2019s Buffett-Gates Follower Charts a Path to Charity","released_at":"<date>August 11 2013<\/date> <time>20:01:00<\/time>","content":"In his suite at the Four Seasons hotel in New York shortly before Christmas 2010,  Bill Gates , now the world\u2019s richest person, got some advice from the world\u2019s No. 82.  Russian billionaire Vladimir Potanin says he told Gates how the  Microsoft Corp. (MSFT)  co-founder could persuade the wealthiest people on the planet to hand over much of their fortunes to charity under the Giving Pledge program organized by Gates and  Warren Buffett , Bloomberg Markets will report in its October issue.  More from the September issue of  Bloomberg Markets : \u201cI advised him to try and move this initiative from American soil,\u201d Potanin says during an interview in the offices of his Interros Holding Co. across the Moscow River from the Kremlin. \u201cI said, \u2018Bill, make it a real international initiative.\u2019\u201d  Potanin is now leading the way in his home country. In February, the 52-year-old nickel magnate became the first Russian billionaire to sign up for the Giving Pledge, promising at least half of his wealth to philanthropic causes. Potanin was worth $12.3 billion as of Aug. 8, according to the  Bloomberg Billionaires Index .  Interest in charitable giving is growing among the richest Russians, according to data compiled by Bloomberg from 15 of the wealthiest of the country\u2019s billionaires and from annual reports issued by their companies and charitable foundations.  Profligate Spenders  Many of these Russians prospered on assets they purchased in the post-Soviet era of the 1990s. Some are now seeking to throw off their reputations as profligate spenders more interested in yachts than philanthropy, especially because, as Potanin says, \u201cThe gap between the poor and the rich is so huge.\u201d  From Jan. 1, 2010, to Dec. 31, 2012, 15 Russian billionaires who provided documentation to  Bloomberg News  donated a total of $1.64 billion to philanthropic projects, according to their submissions.  In acquiring data on 15 of  Russia \u2019s richest men -- and they are all men -- Bloomberg News submitted surveys to 23 billionaires; eight declined to provide information. The combined worth of the 15 was $155 billion as of Aug. 8, or about 8 percent of the Russian economy. The 15 philanthropists who provided data gave away about 1 percent of their aggregated fortunes during the three-year period.  Russian Largesse  On average, according to their submissions, they donated 40 percent more in 2012 than they did in 2010. Their monetary gifts went to a variety of charitable efforts, including education, sports, culture and health care.  The Russians\u2019 largesse is small compared with the philanthropy of Gates and Buffett. The  Bill & Melinda Gates Foundation , which is funded by Gates, his wife and Buffett, gave away almost twice as much money in a single year as all 15 Russians did over three years.  The Gates Foundation gave $3.2 billion in grants in 2011, according to its annual report. Gates and Buffett, the two richest people in the U.S., have a combined net worth of $133.3 billion, or just $21.7 billion less than that of all 15 Russians.  Charitable giving in Russia remains among the least developed in the world, according to the West Malling, England-based Charities Aid Foundation.  In December, a 2012 CAF survey ranked Russia 127th out of 145 countries assessed on the basis of their citizens\u2019 charitable contributions and volunteer work. Russian philanthropy is at least moving in the right direction, says Maria Chertok, head of the CAF\u2019s Moscow office.  \u2018Radical Change\u2019  \u201cPotanin\u2019s promise puts Russian philanthropy on the world stage,\u201d she says. \u201cIt may not lead to a radical change of attitude in Russia, but it will definitely encourage others.\u201d So will planned tax breaks for individuals and corporations, she says.  Russia\u2019s most munificent billionaire is Roman Abramovich. The bulk of his $12.6 billion fortune is derived from his 1996 purchase of a controlling interest in oil company OAO Sibneft, which is now part of state-run natural gas company OAO Gazprom.  During the three-year period examined, Abramovich, 46, owner of the English Premier League\u2019s Chelsea Football Club and the 77th-richest person in the world, donated about $310 million to philanthropic causes ranging from a nationwide program to advance soccer in Russia to the art foundation run by his partner and mother of their two children, Darya Zhukova.  State Assets  Abramovich\u2019s trajectory from post-Soviet businessman to charitable billionaire is in many ways typical of the other 14 in the Bloomberg ranking. With few exceptions, the billionaires acquired some of Russia\u2019s biggest enterprises at bargain prices during  Boris Yeltsin \u2019s presidency following the collapse of the  Soviet Union  in 1991.  Under a loans-for-shares arrangement, as it came to be known, leading Russian businessmen lent the cash-strapped government money in exchange for the right to buy state assets cheaply when Yeltsin\u2019s administration failed to repay the loans. Abramovich purchased his share of Sibneft for $100 million and sold it to Gazprom for almost $10 billion in 2005.  Potanin, the sixth-largest donor among the 15 billionaires, was one of the architects of the loans-for-shares practice.  In 1997, together with  Mikhail Prokhorov , his then-business partner, he acquired 38 percent of OAO GMK  Norilsk Nickel (GMKN) , the world\u2019s largest producer of the metal, for $270 million; his stake, now reduced to 27.9 percent, was worth $6 billion as of Aug. 8.  Two Helipads  Potanin, who gave away $110 million during the survey period, defends loans-for-shares as a salutary mechanism that allowed for the privatization of an economy that was plagued by inefficiencies and was in the grip of the Soviet-era nomenklatura, or elite.  Ever since the stubble-bearded Abramovich bought  Chelsea FC  a decade ago for 142 million pounds ($217 million), the U.K. tabloids have focused on him less for his philanthropy than for a lifestyle that contrasted starkly with the living standards of the general population in Russia, where the average monthly income is about $900.  Abramovich has residences in London, in Cap d\u2019Antibes on the French Riviera, on the Caribbean island of St. Barts and in Aspen, Colorado. Equipped with two helipads, a minisubmarine and two swimming pools, his yacht Eclipse was until earlier this year the longest in the world.  The wealthiest Russians, including Abramovich, have frequently made civic -- as opposed to charitable -- contributions.  Brooklyn Nets  The superrich, for example, have been called upon by the government of President  Vladimir Putin  to help build facilities for soccer\u2019s 2018  World Cup  and next year\u2019s Winter Olympics in Sochi on the  Black Sea . These expenditures, which aren\u2019t so much donations to charity as investments that may or may not pay off, aren\u2019t counted in the Bloomberg ranking.  Russia needs to change the culture of philanthropic giving from a government-led, top-down system to one driven by rich Russians making their own decisions, Irina Prokhorova says. She runs the charitable foundation set up by her brother, Prokhorov, 48, the ninth-largest giver in the survey and an owner of the Brooklyn Nets basketball team.  \u201cIt is important to let people of wealth support what they want to support and not what they are obliged to do,\u201d she says. \u201cWe know of quite a lot of cases where rich people have to donate money to institutions because they are asked to do it.\u201d  Patriotic Giving  The changes that Prokhorova endorses seem to be under way. During the survey period,  Alisher Usmanov , who, with a fortune of $19.9 billion, is Russia\u2019s richest man and the second-largest benefactor, gave away $247 million to institutions such as the Moscow State Institute of International Relations and the capital\u2019s Pushkin Museum of Fine Arts.  Usmanov, 59, is the majority shareholder in OAO Metalloinvest Holding Co., Russia\u2019s largest iron ore producer.  Suleiman Kerimov, 47, the third-largest giver, whose assets include a stake in  Polyus Gold International Ltd. (PLZLY) , says he will plow all profits from companies he owns into his Lucerne, Switzerland-based Suleyman Kerimov Foundation, which has built schools in Russia and funded medical operations for indigent Russians.  Some of the giving is markedly patriotic. Fifth-largest giver Andrey Skoch, 47, a partner of Usmanov\u2019s, donated $117 million; some of the money went into restoring monuments to Russia\u2019s war dead.  Cultural Relics  Potanin gave away $110 million, mainly to educational and cultural institutions, including the State Hermitage Museum in  St. Petersburg .  Fourth-ranked  Viktor Vekselberg , 56, has spent some of his $14.9 billion fortune to repatriate cultural relics, including 18 pre-revolutionary Russian Orthodox church bells and a collection of bejeweled Faberge eggs. Vekselberg gave away $160 million to support, among other things, a high school basketball championship and the Jewish Museum and Tolerance Center in Moscow.  The charity impulse is spreading to wealthy individuals who made their fortunes more recently than during the spate of post-Soviet privatization.  Gennady Timchenko , 60, a longtime Putin associate who is the 12th-largest giver, acquired much of his wealth through oil trading during the 2000s. During the three years surveyed, he spent $48 million on projects such as free housing for 36 Russian families who had adopted 110 orphaned children.  \u2018New Level\u2019  Timchenko\u2019s wife, Elena, says he may eventually sign up for the Gates-Buffett pledge. She manages her husband\u2019s philanthropic activities from her 41st-floor office in the Moscow building that houses Gunvor Group Ltd., Timchenko\u2019s oil-trading firm.  \u201cWe, of course, are following this initiative closely,\u201d she says, wearing a diamond bracelet. \u201cIt takes the idea of philanthropy to a new level.\u201d  Usmanov says he believes it\u2019s better to give the money away now than to pass it along to future generations.  \u201cIt may happen that I won\u2019t leave any bequest at all,\u201d says Usmanov, who has no children. \u201cI would prefer to do everything I can to make this world better myself and right now, rather than someone else doing it after me, as I don\u2019t know whether he will do it better than me.\u201d  Potanin, who has a daughter and two sons, shares that view. Looking relaxed in a blue sweater, Potanin says the realization that he could give large sums to charity first came to him about a decade ago, when he saw that his children didn\u2019t need a lot of his money to achieve success.  \u2018Without Me\u2019  At the time, his daughter, Anastasia, now 29, and son Ivan, 24, started to win medals at home and abroad in a  Jet Ski  sport called aquabike.  \u201cThey became champions,\u201d Potanin says. \u201cI understood they can do something without me.\u201d  Potanin, the son of a high-ranking Soviet trade official, says his heirs may get as little as $10 million each. He says he will transfer the bulk of his wealth to charitable purposes in seven years.  In  a February 2010 interview  with the Russian newspaper Komsomolskaya Pravda, Anastasia Potanina said she supports her father\u2019s decision.  \u201cMy dad brought me up so that I wanted to achieve something myself, to prove to myself and others that I can also do a lot, so that I am not only seen as the daughter of an oligarch,\u201d she said. \u201cMy father believes that the society which enabled him to achieve a lot has the right to expect something in return.\u201d  Potanin Scholars  The  Vladimir Potanin  Foundation dispenses $150-per-month scholarships to 1,200 students a year to help cover living costs at their tuition-free universities. Twice a year, it also donates up to $6,600 apiece for student-run projects that have social, educational or scientific value.  For a few days in July, Sergey Pereverzev and Olga Sabylinskaya, who are enrolled at Belgorod State University near the Ukraine border, joined about 350 scholarship winners from 28 universities across Russia at a summer symposium for Potanin Foundation scholars outside Moscow.  Last winter, Pereverzev, 23, and Sabylinskaya, 21, got $1,200 from the foundation to set up a blood bank at their university. Having signed up 220 blood donors, the pair came to Moscow to brief their colleagues on the project\u2019s progress.  Suspicious Russians  \u201cThese schools give an opportunity to meet with clever and interesting people,\u201d Pereverzev, a law student, says. For Sabylinskaya, a journalism student, the get-together was a reminder of what counts in life:  \u201cI understood that my diploma means nothing. Only my ability to think matters.\u201d  Pereverzev and Sabylinskaya say they\u2019re grateful to Potanin. Whether the rest of Russian society will ever come to appreciate his and other billionaires\u2019 generosity remains an open question, Potanin says. Russians are suspicious of the men they see as oligarchs.  \u201cThe problem in Russia is that philanthropy is not well perceived by society,\u201d Potanin says. \u201cMany people think that it\u2019s not coming from the heart.\u201d  It\u2019s up to the richest Russians to prove their comrades wrong. I\u2019ve been using the iPad Air, which goes on sale Nov. 1,\nfor a week now, and it\u2019s hands-down the best tablet on the\nmarket. Apple has recrafted the hardware and packed in new\nsoftware and services that make it more useful for creating\ncontent, not just consuming it. In fact, it\u2019s now\njust five ounces more than the latest  iPad mini , which grew\nmarginally heavier to accommodate a bigger battery. (I\u2019ll look\nat the mini in a later column.)  Three Nickels  The Air is also slimmer, both side-to-side -- the bezels\nhave been sliced by about a third of an inch each -- and front-to-back. It\u2019s now a mere .29 inches thick, a little more than\nthree nickels. Yet its aluminum-and-glass construction makes it\nfeel far more solid than competing devices from  Samsung (005930) , for\ninstance.  Apple says the Air is the lightest full-size tablet on the\nmarket, but that depends on your definition of \u201cfull-size.\u201d\n Amazon.com (AMZN)  immediately  disputed  the claim, though its Kindle\nFire HDX has a considerably smaller screen. As on the 5s,\nthere aren\u2019t many apps beyond a few games that tap into that\nincreased processing power, though that may change over time.  Speed Boost  Users who connect over Wi-Fi, on the other hand, will see\nan immediate impact from the Air\u2019s dual antennas and updated\nwireless technology. I actually grew impatient trying to exhaust the battery in\nmy tests; you should get a lot more than a full day of normal\nuse on a charge.  The iPad Air retains the same 2,048-by-1,536 pixel Retina\ndisplay of previous models. On a strictly by-the-numbers basis,\nthe display -- so dazzling when it debuted -- has been passed by\nthe likes of Google and Samsung. Since the human eye can\u2019t\nreally distinguish between 264 pixels per inch and 300, you\u2019re\nnot likely to have any complaints about the screen.  Missing Feature  One thing that\u2019s not here that should be is Touch ID, the\nfingerprint sensor on the latest iPhone. Apple won\u2019t say why it\nwas left out, but it\u2019s arguably even more important on a larger\ndevice, which may be used to access more sensitive personal\ninformation. I expect to see it on future iPads, and will be\nglad when it shows up.  Not that long ago, the iPad so dominated the tablet market\nthat it would have been unthinkable to buy something else. With\nthe rise of quality tablets from Google, Amazon and others, it\u2019s\nno longer the only choice. But it\u2019s still the best choice.  ( Rich Jaroslovsky  is a Bloomberg News columnist. (AAPL)  and its\nchief executive officer,  Tim Cook , for getting serious about\nreturning unneeded capital to shareholders. As for the details,\nsome of them don\u2019t seem well thought out.  The maker of iPhones and iPads this week said its board\napproved a sixfold increase in its stock-repurchase plan to $60\nbillion. Not long ago, even discussing the idea of large share\nbuybacks was a nonstarter for Apple. Now that its stock has\n tanked , the company is acting like they are a must-do, no matter\nwhat else the future might bring. At about $408 a share, down 42\npercent since its record high in September, Apple has a  stock-market value  of $383 billion.  \u201cThis is the largest single share repurchase authorization\nin history and is expected to be executed by the end of calendar\n2015,\u201d Apple said in an April 23  news release , the same day the\ncompany  reported  its first quarterly profit decline in a decade.  How could Apple be so confident it will spend the whole $60\nbillion by then? That\u2019s hard to say. The company is under no\nobligation to complete the repurchase program, although it\nobviously wants the markets to believe it will. Apple\u2019s\nstatements this week suggested it would carry out the plan\nwithout regard to price, which should be the most important\nconsideration of all.  Shunning Repurchases  Nobody knows what Apple\u2019s stock will do next month or next\nyear. Would Apple keep doing buybacks if its  price-earnings\nratio  tripled? That would be a high-class problem to have if the\nP\/E soared because of a rising share price, but not if the main\nreason was a plunge in profits. Either way, you have to think\nApple would reconsider its plans, except Apple didn\u2019t say what\nmight cause its expectations to change. The stock now trades for\na mere 9.8 times earnings for the past four quarters.  Berkshire Hathaway Inc. (BRK\/A) , the conglomerate run by  Warren Buffett , also used to shun buybacks. Like Apple, it, too,\nchanged tacks recently. In 2011, Berkshire  said  it would begin\nrepurchasing shares for as much as a 10 percent premium to its\nbook value, or common shareholder equity. The company\u2019s board\nraised the limit in December to 20 percent. (Berkshire had paid\nabout $1.4 billion to buy back stock as of the end of last\nyear.)  Unlike Apple, Berkshire provided well-defined parameters\nfrom the outset. The  stock  currently trades for a 41 percent\npremium to book, so investors have a clear understanding that\nBerkshire isn\u2019t a buyer at today\u2019s prices. The company has said\nit wouldn\u2019t do buybacks if they would reduce Berkshire\u2019s cash to\nless than $20 billion. It also has said it expects the program\nto continue indefinitely. There is no timetable.  Apple\u2019s  buybacks  are part of a program to return $100\nbillion to shareholders by the end of 2015, including $11\nbillion of annual dividend payments. The company had $12 billion\nin cash and $133 billion of  marketable securities  as of March\n30. About 70 percent of that was held offshore, which means the\ncompany would face a large tax bill if it repatriated the assets\nunder current laws. Because of that, Apple this week said it\nplans to borrow money to help pay for returning capital to\nshareholders. The company has no debt now.  Criticisms of Apple\u2019s disclosures may seem minor, compared\nto the important step the company is taking to bring some\nrationality to its  capital structure . Apple doesn\u2019t need $145\nbillion of cash and securities on its balance sheet earning next\nto nothing. No company does. Most of it belongs in the hands of\n shareholders  who can put the money to better use.  That said, there\u2019s little to be gained from creating long-range expectations that later might prove unwise to fulfill.\nSure, Apple used wiggle words to describe its intentions. It\nalso created a needless risk to its credibility in the event\nthat circumstances warrant a change. The board would have been\nbetter off simply authorizing more buybacks and describing the\nconditions under which Apple would follow through with them. An\nApple spokesman, Steve Dowling, declined to comment.  Buyback Missteps  Plenty of technology companies, notably Dell Inc., have\nhurt themselves by repurchasing huge quantities of their own\nstock at inflated levels. (For more on Dell\u2019s disastrous\nbuybacks, see this excellent  column  from January by Floyd Norris\nof the  New York  Times.) In recent years, Brazil has become a major source of malware that steals online banking passwords, a development that may surprise you given the attention paid to attacks originating in Eastern Europe and Asia. To understand why Brazil is a magnet for hackers, it helps to consider the country's long history in electronic banking, according to a  report  by Trend Micro, a Tokyo-based security firm. For decades, Brazil's banks have been on the forefront of online finance, pioneering electronic systems in the 1980s to help speed transaction times and stabilize a troubled economy, Trend Micro said. The country is now home to the world's second-largest ATM market, according to the report.  It's also home to surging cybercrime. Brazil's large online population - 88.5 million people, or more than 40 percent of the population - makes for a big target. And $1.4 billion was lost in the country in 2012 to electronic fraud, according to the Brazilian Federation of Banks, which also said a wave of successful heists is likely to push the total higher this year. As with many developing economies, growth in people getting online combined with financial institutions enabling Internet banking lead to increased risks for consumers. Brazil is home to the famous -- at least in the security world -- Bancos Trojans, a family of malware that steals banking information from Latin American consumers. And lately, other popular banking Trojans such as ZeuS, SpyEye and CARBERP, which were uncommon in Brazil, have now been spreading quickly there, according to Trend Micro. A big part of the reason is many people don't patch their systems. Brazil is still plagued by the Conficker worm, which infected millions of machines worldwide in 2009, because many people are using pirated versions of Windows, according to Trend Micro. The security hole that Conficker exploited in Windows was patched by Microsoft in 2008, before the attacks became widespread. Computers that aren't patched are still vulnerable. The challenge facing Brazil in fighting off hackers holds a lesson for other developing economies. The emergence of online banking has given both the country's financial institutions and consumers easier access to one another. Long live\nKindle.  \n OK, maybe the Kindle isn\u2019t actually dead. After all,\n Amazon.com Inc.  announced two new models of its e-reader this\nweek after selling boatloads of the previous version: Kindle\nsales accelerated in every month of the second quarter, the\ncompany said July 19.  \n The problem is what it said three days later, on July 22:\nProfit in the period missed analysts\u2019 expectations, and\noperating income in the third quarter will also be below\nprojections. That\u2019s in part because of the price cuts that have\nslashed the cost of its flagship model by 45 percent, to $189,\nin little more than a year.  \n A big reason is  Apple Inc. \u2019s success in selling iPads:\nalmost 3.3 million since its April debut, the company said in\nJune. The iPad, with its vivid color screen and multimedia\ncapabilities, provides a richer reading experience and also runs\nthousands of applications, plays movies and music, and is far\nbetter at surfing the Web and handling e-mail.  \n The Kindle, by contrast, has a grayscale screen and is\nessentially good only for downloading and reading books. While\nit\u2019s much lighter and easier to use in direct sunlight, its\nbiggest head-to-head advantage over the iPad is price: The iPad\ncosts from $499 to $829. And if price is your major weapon,\nprofit margins are going to suffer.  \n Poised to Reign  \n Still, there\u2019s more to the Kindle than just the hardware.\nThere\u2019s also Kindle software and Amazon\u2019s e-bookstore. Whatever\nhappens to profits on Kindle the device, Kindle the service is\npositioned to reign supreme in the realm of e-reading for a long\ntime to come.  \n Unlike Apple, which has tied its iBookstore service to its\niPad, iPhone and iPod touch hardware, Amazon has pursued a\nKindle-everywhere strategy. In addition to its own gadget,\nAmazon has made Kindle reading software and e-books available on\nApple\u2019s mobile devices as well as on Mac and  Microsoft  Windows\ncomputers,  Research In Motion  Ltd.\u2019s BlackBerrys, and most\nrecently smartphones running  Google Inc. \u2019s Android operating\nsystem.  \n Further, the software syncs across all platforms, meaning a\nreader can set down a Kindle e-book on an iPad and resume\nreading on, say,  Motorola Inc. \u2019s Droid X right where he or she\nleft off. Books purchased from Apple, meanwhile, sync only on\nApple devices.  \n Publishers\u2019 Loathing  \n Amazon\u2019s low-price strategy extends to e-books themselves.\nMany publishers regard the company with almost as much\nresentment as music companies have for Apple. They viewed the\n$9.99 price that Amazon slapped on most e-books to jumpstart the\nmarket to be too low, and welcomed Apple\u2019s entry and different\nbusiness model as a way to push up e-book prices.  \n The number of current bestsellers priced between $10 and\n$12.99  did rise to 30  in July from 17 in May, according to the\nKindle Nation Daily blog. And while there\u2019s no guarantee that\nhigher prices will stick -- even Amazon Chief Executive Officer\n Jeff Bezos , in a recent Fortune magazine interview, expressed\nskepticism -- any increase would presumably help Amazon\u2019s\nmargins along with everyone else\u2019s.  \n On the hardware front, the forecast is for more turmoil.\nAmazon\u2019s new Kindle design is thinner, lighter, with a better\ndisplay and longer battery life than the one it\u2019s replacing. The\n$189 model adds the ability to connect over Wi-Fi as well as 3G\ndata networks; a new $139 model will have Wi-Fi only.  \n Non-Apple Competitors  \n Now let\u2019s see how the Kindle\u2019s non-Apple competitors\nrespond. If there are profits\nto be made in selling e-books, Amazon is best-positioned to make\nthem.  \n ( Rich Jaroslovsky  is a Bloomberg News columnist. The Organisation for Economic Co-operation & Development,\nwhich represents 34 countries, released yesterday the 2009\n Programme for International Student Assessment . For the first\ntime, the triennial test broke out China\u2019s Shanghai region --\nwhich topped every country, in all academic categories. Earnings  excluding certain items declined to 40 cents a share, compared with analysts\u2019 39-cent estimate.  Yesterday\u2019s results suggest Chief Executive Officer  Michael Dell  has made headway in his campaign to transform the company into a provider of a broad range of business-technology products. Dell\u2019s earlier struggle to gain share in mobile devices and a late entrance into cloud computing contributed to a 31 percent decline in its stock in 2012, prompting Dell to seek a buyout.  \u201cThe strength in the enterprise business indicates their focus on that business is working as they had thought,\u201d said  Abhey Lamba , an analyst at Mizuho Securities USA Inc., who has a  neutral  rating on Dell. \u201cTheir focus is on the high-margin businesses, which is showing up in the results.\u201d  Dell  rose less than 1 percent to $13.83 at the close in New York. Some  stockholders  want a higher price, and the results could strengthen their hand, Lamba said. Dell, the world\u2019s third-largest PC maker, is suffering from declining demand for desktops and laptops. Global  PC shipments  declined 4.9 percent in the fourth quarter of 2012, according to market researcher Gartner Inc., and Dell\u2019s shipments fell 21 percent.  PC Slump  The company hasn\u2019t capitalized on consumers\u2019 and businesses\u2019 shift toward smartphones and tablets, which are replacing traditional PCs for many tasks. Windows 8, the version of Microsoft Corp.\u2019s PC operating system that\u2019s designed to run on tablets as well, has gotten off to a slower-than-expected start since its October arrival, an executive at Dell rival Hewlett-Packard Co. said in January. With business customers, Dell is benefiting from continued replacements of older PCs running Microsoft Corp.\u2019s Windows XP and Windows Vista, to the more than three-year-old Windows 7, Gladden said. Dell\u2019s PC business helps spark sales of other products, he said.  \u201cThat\u2019s an important part of our business model,\u201d he said. Earnings excluding some items may decline 2 percent to $1.68, according to data compiled by Bloomberg.  Michael Dell and private-equity firm Silver Lake seek to take Dell private amid stiffening competition in mobile and cloud computing. Rowe Price Group Inc. and Southeastern Asset Management, which together own more than 10 percent of the stock, have said Dell is worth more than the buyers have offered. The computer maker is setting up meetings with shareholders to assess their demands for getting the buyout done, people with knowledge of the situation have said. The shot, known as RTS,S, would be the first vaccine\nagainst malaria. It protected 56 percent of 6,000 children aged\nfive months to 17 months old from developing symptoms 12 months\nafter receiving their third dose and 47 percent from suffering\nsevere malaria, according to data from a final-stage study\npublished online today by the New England Journal of Medicine.  \u201cThe overall picture is this is a project that has the\npotential to halve malaria in young children,\u201d David\nSchellenberg, one of the study\u2019s authors and a professor of\nmalaria and international health at the  London School of Hygiene\nand Tropical Medicine  in London, said in a telephone interview.\n\u201cIt\u2019s an enormous achievement which has taken decades and huge\namounts of resources.\u201d  There were 225 million cases of malaria, a mosquito-borne\nparasite of the human liver and blood, globally in 2009,\naccording to the  World Health Organization . The illness causes\nfever, chills and flu-like symptoms, or shock, anemia and organ\ndamage if untreated. Malaria is prevented now with insecticide-\ntreated bed nets. Drugs are prescribed after infection.  About 781,000 people died from the disease in 2009, most of\nthem children under the age of five in sub-Saharan  Africa ,\naccording to the WHO.  Side Effects  The data published today are the first results from a study\nof 15,460 children aged as young as six weeks in seven African\ncountries that began in March 2009.  Children were given either RTS,S or a non-malaria vaccine.\nThe number of serious adverse events was about the same in each\ngroup, according to the researchers and London-based Glaxo.\nEighteen percent of those receiving the experimental vaccine\nsuffered a serious side effect, compared with 22 percent of\nthose receiving the control vaccine, Glaxo said.  Results from a smaller, mid-stage trial published in 2007\nshowed the vaccine reduced new malaria infections -- as\nconfirmed in blood tests -- in African infants by about two-\nthirds.  The vaccine\u2019s level of protection ultimately needs to be\nhigher, Eric Mouzin, a medical epidemiologist at the  Roll Back\nMalaria Partnership , a network of malaria organizations based in\nGeneva, said in a telephone interview.  \u201cIdeally you would want a vaccine to be 100 percent\neffective,\u201d he said. \u201cThat\u2019s not what we have at the moment.\nIt doesn\u2019t mean we won\u2019t get it one day.\u201d  \u2018Complete Non-Starter\u2019  Another researcher,  Adrian Hill , director of the Jenner\nInstitute in Oxford,  England , said additional data in the study\nraised a question about whether the vaccine would prove\nworthwhile. The researchers found the vaccine was 35 percent\neffective against severe malaria after 11 months in a combined\ngroup of five- to 17-month-olds and six- to 12-week olds. That\nsuggests the vaccine won\u2019t be cost-effective against severe\nmalaria in the younger group to whom it is designed to be given,\nmaking it \u201ca complete non-starter,\u201d Hill said. Gates Meeting  \u201cWe have better vaccines than RTS,S,\u201d Hill said in a\ntelephone interview. \u201cThere are a lot of vaccines in the clinic\nnow that when combined with RTS,S get high levels of efficacy.\nWe could do better. The measure also allows for safe-harbor programs, in which\nsome information-collecting companies may receive an exemption\nfrom some elements of the bill. If Medicare was capped and couldn\u2019t shoot up\nautomatically, unemployment would probably be in double digits.  Out-of-control health-care spending is the only stimulus\nthe Republicans can\u2019t stop. What else is there? Go out late at\nnight in some of the darkest American cities. Whether it\u2019s\n Cleveland , Baltimore or  St. Louis , it seems the only thing left\nto light up the gloom is a big hospital, shining like a 12-gated\ncity, inlaid with MRIs like precious jewels, and for that we can\ngive thanks to  Medicare  and Medicaid.  Imagine Cleveland without the  Cleveland Clinic , or\nBaltimore without  Johns Hopkins . Even in Chicago, with a more\ndiversified base, the city would seem flat without the expansion\nat Northwestern Memorial Hospital and Rush University Medical\nCenter -- with all that hammering and sawing as they get ready\nfor Obamacare.  If Medicare, in particular, wasn\u2019t out of control, many\ninner-city high-school grads would find it even harder to get\njobs. According to research  cited  in the Harvard \u201cPathways to\nProsperity\u201d report in 2011, health care by itself added a half-million jobs even in the recession -- not just ones for high-school grads as security guards and cooks, but jobs for those\nwith \u201csome college,\u201d such as respiratory technicians.  Stimulus Effect  It\u2019s not the WPA, but all this health-care spending creates\nthe kind of \u201cmiddle-skilled\u201d jobs we have to push now in lieu of\nassembly lines. Many high-school grads -- or those we may\neuphemistically  say  have \u201ccredentials short of an associate\u2019s\ndegree\u201d -- earn more than those with college diplomas. Thanks to\nentitlements being out of control, there is still at least one\nway into the middle class.  All this also has a Keynesian-type effect to make up for\nthe way state and local governments keep cutting back spending.\nThis was the first recession where we responded by  cutting \npublic-sector jobs. Government employment has fallen to its\nlowest level since 1968, Bloomberg\u2019s BGOV Barometer shows. The\ncutbacks forced by balanced-budget clauses in many state\nconstitutions only hold back a real recovery.  On the other hand, Medicare goes on its merry uncapped way,\nand has a synergy effect with all the other health-care\nspending. In some sense, the jobs that come out of this\nautomatic federal stimulus are public-sector jobs, in that\nplenty of people in health care owe their employment to Medicare\nspending that keeps going up.  To a social-democrat type like me, the problem, at least in\nthis current economy, is not that health-care entitlements are\nout of control, but that all this spending seems to entitle us\nto less and less. My older friends are groaning: \u201cWait -- I\u2019m\ngoing to turn 65, and I\u2019m still going to have to pay for half of\nmy health care?\u201d It\u2019s inefficient, and it\u2019s wasteful, partly\nbecause there\u2019s not enough Medicare and Medicaid -- let alone a\nsingle-payer system across the board -- to let the government\ndictate prices. The smaller its share in paying for health care\nin the U.S., the less able the government is to hold down prices\n-- which is how most  social democracies  in northern  Europe  and\n Canada  and elsewhere keep their costs under control.  That is, Medicare and Medicaid are wasteful because even in\ncombination they aren\u2019t big enough to let the government dictate\nprices and use a bigger club to make the system more efficient.  Jobs Program  But for the moment, look at the bright side: At least the\nbucks keep going out the door. One can think of public spending\nthat could have a much bigger multiplier effect -- for example,\na dollar to stop a teacher or a cop from being fired. But that\u2019s\ndiscretionary state and local spending, while Medicare\nentitlements can\u2019t be stopped.  If one thinks of our whole health-care industry as a public\nsector in disguise, it starts to seem that the free-market U.S.\nis almost as statist as  France . After all, health care is about\n18 percent of the U.S.\u2019s gross domestic product, soon to be 20\npercent or more.  In my own Cook County,  Illinois , the big employer is the\ncounty itself, which is partly because it runs the Stroger\nHospital, Chicago\u2019s behemoth public medical center. The largest\nprivate employer is  Advocate Health Care , a hospital chain. Much\nof our \u201cprivate\u201d enterprise, the whole  drug industry , depends on\na sector being pumped up by Medicare. Where would an orthopedic-device  maker  in Warsaw,  Indiana , be without Medicare partly\nkicking in?  Health care is our King Coal. If we were  Russia , it would\nbe our Gazprom. If the U.S. is in a \u201ccontrolled\u201d depression,\nMedicare spending is doing the controlling, keeping the bottom\nfrom falling out of the economy. McDonald\u2019s Corp., Wendy\u2019s Co.,\n Microsoft Corp. (MSFT) , General Electric Co., even Caterpillar Inc. in\na way depend on the  consumer spending  from millions of Americans\nwho only have jobs because entitlements are out of control.  Medicare may even make the U.S. more globally competitive.\nAlthough chief executive officers are shedding nonwage benefits,\nsuch as retiree medical plans, some companies still cover a\nshare of the costs. And it\u2019s not just because of union pressure.\nTo attract the most-skilled workers, some of the best U.S.\ncompanies offer some supplemental retiree health benefit.  Cut Medicare, and nonwage labor costs go up. Limit it to\nvouchers, and you will see more companies offering at least\nsomething. Yes, it\u2019s just one more nonwage cost, and retiree\nhealth care would be one of the most unpredictable of all. How\nwould we induce investment to create high-end jobs if we create\neven more uncertainty about these costs?  Republican Plan  The Republicans -- with Representative  Paul Ryan \u2019s budget\nplan -- would do just that. Don\u2019t think Ryan\u2019s plan would simply\nbe shifting health-care costs to the poor, or even the middle\nclass, or even to his mother. Inevitably we would be shifting\nsome of these costs to our global corporate champions, too.\nIsn\u2019t the  U.S. trade deficit  big enough?  At the moment, though, the Ryan plan isn\u2019t law, and at\nleast we have some stimulus the  Tea Party  can\u2019t stop. Americans\nshould be grateful that they live in a country where\nentitlements are out of control.  And it may be the one thing that saves Obama\u2019s presidency. (MSFT)  was warned by European Union regulators to modify how it presents Internet Explorer in its new Windows 8 operating system to avert another antitrust clash, Competition Commissioner  Joaquin Almunia  said.  Microsoft said it would implement changes to Windows 8 before the new version of its operating system goes on sale in two days. The world\u2019s largest software maker was also sent EU antitrust objections today over its failure to comply with a settlement of an earlier probe requiring it to display a choice of rival web browsers.  \u201cWe have raised issues with Microsoft relating to Windows 8,\u201d Almunia told reporters in Brussels today. \u201cIf a user decides to set a rival browser as a default browser, there should not be an unnecessary warning in Windows or confirmations by the user and the  Internet Explorer  icon should also be unpinned from the Start screen. We expect Microsoft to address these issues.\u201d  Microsoft has already been fined 1.68 billion euros ($2.17 billion) in EU antitrust probes, including an 899 million-euro penalty for failing to obey an order to share data with competitors. The Redmond, Washington-based company agreed in 2009 to offer access to rival browsers as a part of a settlement to repair its relationship with the bloc\u2019s regulators. It told regulators last December that it was complying with its commitments.  Browser Choice  Robin Koch, a spokesman for Microsoft in Brussels, said the company was changing \u201csome aspects of the way the browser choice screen works on Windows 8 and will have those changes implemented\u201d before the product goes on sale on Oct. 26.  Almunia said he\u2019d contacted Microsoft about Windows 8 and told management \u201cat the highest level possible what are my concerns and what kind of presentation should be avoided if they don\u2019t want to take the risk of new investigations.\u201d  Today\u2019s statement of objections is a step toward possible fines over Microsoft\u2019s failure to comply with its earlier pledge to display a choice of web browser. The EU can fine companies as much as 10 percent of yearly revenue if they \u201cbreached commitments made legally binding,\u201d according to its statement.  Microsoft takes the statement of objections listing the EU\u2019s antitrust concerns over compliance with the settlement \u201cvery seriously,\u201d Koch said.  Technical Error  Almunia said in July that Microsoft may have misled regulators by failing to display a browser choice screen to users of the  Windows operating system  since February 2011. The company blamed a technical error for not showing the screen to some users and offered to extend until March 2016 a commitment to show it.  Microsoft is strengthening its internal procedures to help prevent a repeat of the technical error, Koch said. The company \u201cwill continue to cooperate fully with\u201d the commission.  The company  said  in July it only learned that month that it didn\u2019t offer its browser choice software to some 28 million computers running Windows 7 Service Pack 1, or 10 percent of the computers that should have received it. It distributed a software fix to computers that were affected.  Under the terms of Microsoft\u2019s 2009 pledge, consumers who buy personal computers were given a choice of the 12 most widely used browsers to install in addition to, or instead of, Microsoft\u2019s Internet Explorer.  Repeat Offenses  Any fines for Microsoft may take into account repeat offenses, Almunia said in July in a reference to the EU\u2019s 2008 penalty for the company\u2019s failure to obey an earlier EU decision. That ruling also ordered it to provide information to software developers to make compatible products.  Almunia said there were \u201cno grounds\u201d for EU officials to intervene on Microsoft\u2019s Windows RT software for tablets. The software, to be introduced on Oct. 26, prohibits any browser except for Internet Explorer, according to a May blog post by Mozilla Corp., maker of the rival Firefox browser.  Companies have raised \u201cvarious issues about other aspects of Microsoft\u2019s compliance\u201d that regulators had examined and didn\u2019t see any reason to pursue, Almunia said.  \u201cWe will remain vigilant and we will continue to monitor all aspects of Microsoft\u2019s compliance with the commitments in the future,\u201d Almunia said. The company gets an average of 276 inquiries per listing\nand 16 bidders per auction. The beige boxes and generic laptops of a few years ago are\ngiving way to new generations of sleek machines running\n Microsoft (MSFT) \u2019s Windows 7 -- and ready for Windows 8 later this\nyear.  For evidence, take a look at Sony\u2019s Vaio Z, a 13-inch\nnotebook potent enough to replace a desktop, and  Samsung (005930) \u2019s\nlatest Series 9, the thinnest 15-incher you can buy. Yes,\nthey\u2019re expensive, but they\u2019re also beautiful.  A lot of the credit goes to Apple. The entire laptop\ncategory has been in a state of upheaval since the iPad\u2019s launch\ntwo years ago. Meanwhile, the MacBook Air raised the bar on\ndesign and spawned a new class of Windows PC competitors, called\nUltrabooks, featuring Intel microprocessors, speedy solid-state\nstorage and much faster boot-up and shut-down times than hard-\ndrive-based computers.  Windows 8 may accelerate the trend. It\u2019s being designed to\nrun on touch-based tablets as well as PCs. Microsoft and its\npartners say they hope to spawn new kinds of hybrid devices that\ncombine the best of both. Maybe so. Still, it\u2019s comforting to\nknow that the new operating system is promised to work on any\nhardware running Windows 7.  Breathtaking  Apple (AAPL) \u2019s success has also shown that buyers are willing to\npay premium prices for features and style. And \u201cpremium\u201d\ndoesn\u2019t even begin to describe the Vaio Z and Series 9. A better\nword would be \u201cbreathtaking.\u201d  The  Vaio Z  is one of the most adaptable ultraportables out\nthere, allowing you to add layers of functionality depending on\nyour needs of the moment. Closed, the Vaio Z is just .66 inches\nhigh, measures 13 inches by 8.27 inches and weighs a mere 2.57\npounds. The tapered case further shrinks its footprint, making\nit convenient to use in tight spaces, such as an airplane tray.  Compared to other laptops, less of the Vaio\u2019s weight is in\nthe screen, giving it a springy feel when closed that makes it\nfeel less solid than it probably really is. ( Sony (6758)  says the extra\ngive is deliberate, to help cushion the computer from the rigors\nof travel.) When the screen is opened, its hinges prop up the\nunit\u2019s rear, ever-so-slightly angling the backlit keyboard.\nThat\u2019s a good thing, because the low-lying keys had too little\ntravel for my liking. Tilting the keyboard helped.  Expanding Power  The real power in the Vaio Z comes from its expandability.\nThe unit comes with a compact external docking station for\ndesktop use that provides easy access to its high-definition\nvideo and USB 2.0 and 3.0 ports, with options for a DVD burner\nor Blu-ray drive. And a $150 screw-on sheet battery, augmenting\nthe Vaio\u2019s minimalist four-hour life, provides enough juice to\nget through more than a full day\u2019s untethered work while still\nkeeping it less than an inch thick.  Here\u2019s where the bad part of \u201cbreathtaking\u201d comes in: The\nprice may leave you gasping. Sony is currently selling the base-\nmodel Vaio Z -- with an  Intel (INTC)  Core i5 chip, four gigagbytes of\ninstalled memory and a 128-gigabyte solid-state drive -- for\n$1,700. That\u2019s rich enough, but outfit it with an i7 processor,\na more usable six gigabytes of memory and 256 gigabytes of\nstorage, Blu-ray and the extended battery, and you\u2019re suddenly\nat $3,000.  Staggering  A top-line model, with more memory and SSD storage, is a\nstaggering $4,500. I\u2019d like to meet the person willing to spend\nthat much on a PC.  By comparison, the Samsung Series 9 almost feels like a\nbargain at $1,500 for a model with a 15-inch screen, Core i5,\neight gigabytes of memory and 128 gigabytes of storage. (There\u2019s\nalso a 13-inch model for $100 less.)  The  Series 9  weighs about 3 1\/2 pounds and measures 14\ninches wide by 9.3 inches deep. But the number that jumps out is\nits thickness: .58 of an inch. How thin is that? Really, really\nthin. Crazy thin. Thinner than the already-impossibly-thin\nMacBook Air.  It\u2019s so thin, in fact, that it can\u2019t accommodate Ethernet\nor standard high-definition video cables, though it does have\nspace enough for, among other things, three USB ports and a slot\nfor an SD expansion card.  One of my complaints about last year\u2019s 13-inch Series 9 was\nthe poor, 4-hour battery life. The new model allows for a larger\nbattery that should give you six to seven hours, depending on\nwhat you\u2019re doing. And the charcoal-gray aluminum alloy body\nfeels more solid than the Sony\u2019s.  When I looked at the previous model of the Series 9 last\nsummer, I described it as \u201cgorgeous and capable.\u201d The\ndescription applies equally to this new, bigger version. Loeb\u2019s Third Point hedge fund asked Sony, which had seen its market value shrink almost 90 percent from its peak, to sell as much as 20 percent of the entertainment business in an initial public offering and focus on its struggling electronics unit, according to a letter to Chief Executive Officer Kazuo Hirai. (YHOO)  last year, efforts by U.S. investors from T. Boone Pickens to Cerberus Capital Management LP to wring higher returns from Japanese companies have met with limited success.  \u201cIn Japan, you\u2019re dealing not just with a different governance system, but almost a different form of capitalism,\u201d said Rakesh Khurana, a professor at Harvard Business School who has studied such efforts. \u201cJapanese companies try to balance the interests of finance, labor and government, while the U.S. in recent decades has become investor-centric, so raiders and activists are more tolerated.\u201d  Sony  shares  rose 10 percent to 2,072 yen at the close of trade in Tokyo, the highest level since July 2011. Activism in Japan dates back to at least 1991, when the oilman Pickens acquired a 26 percent stake in  Koito Manufacturing (7276) , an auto parts dealer affiliated with  Toyota Motor Corp. (7203) , and tried to obtain a board seat. Pickens ended up abandoning his quest, and selling the stake at no profit, after Koito spent the equivalent of $4.4 million to block his efforts, the Wall Street Journal reported at the time.  Deja Vu  Almost two decades later, a similar scenario played out at  Sapporo Holdings Ltd. (2501) , Japan\u2019s fourth largest brewer. Margin Boost  Sony, which invented the Trinitron cathode-ray tube TV in the 1960s and began selling the Walkman portable music player a decade later, saw its market value reach more than  $120 billion  in 2000. The company failed to stem share-price declines that began in 2000 after Welsh-born U.S. citizen Howard Stringer became Sony\u2019s first non-Japanese CEO in 2005. But in December 2009, the Air Force\u2019s Rapid\nReaction Innovation Team at Wright-Patterson Air Force Base in Dayton,  Ohio , tried an\nunconventional approach: It asked workers at the Air Force Research Laboratory with less than\nfive years on the job to develop their own proposals. Then some 2,000 personnel voted on the\nbest ideas; ultimately the Air Force awarded $75,000 for prototyping each of the two winners.  David Shahady, the deputy director of the Rapid Reaction Innovation Team responsible for the\nexperiment, says the ideas resulted in better cameras in drones and a radar system that remotely\ndetects human vital signs from 10 times the distance of previous systems. With demonstrations\ncompleted this summer, he expects to evaluate them outside the lab over the next year. \u201cWe have\nbeen trying to find different ways to inspire [our young scientists and engineers] to come up with\nnew ideas ... within our own walls,\u201d says Shahady. \u201c[This project] allowed us to energize this\nworkforce.\u201d  To manage the idea generation and approval process, Shahady hired  Lumenogic , a Westport,\nConn., consulting firm that specializes in developing and customizing online systems for large\norganizations to use to gather so-called collective intelligence from their employees. Lumenogic\u2019s pitch: The data will help clients\nfunction better because they will be better informed. Thomas W. Malone, director of MIT\u2019s\nCenter for Collective Intelligence at the  Sloan School of Management , says the burgeoning field\n-- first popularly explored in James Surowiecki\u2019s 2004 book, \u201cThe Wisdom of Crowds\u201d -- can\noffer businesses a competitive edge.  Like its approximately half-dozen competitors in the U.S., Lumenogic provides its clients\ntraining on how to use the customized online platforms, makes refinements, and collects and\ninterprets the data, for fees that range from tens of thousands of dollars to hundreds of thousands\nof dollars. The information collected ranges from the open-ended, such as strategic directions a\ncompany should take, to the specific, like expected sales. Dr. Emile Servan-Schreiber, a\nLumenogic managing director, estimates annual spending for collective intelligence is roughly\n$150 million to $250 million, with U.S. companies accounting for about 40 percent.  Online Prediction Markets  Besides harvesting good ideas, collective intelligence consultants often set up online prediction\nmarkets that employees can use to bet on crucial outcomes -- such as product delivery schedule,\ndemand, or sales.  Hewlett-Packard (HPQ)  was one of the first technology behemoths to\nexperiment with an internal market, dramatically improving the quality of its printer sales\nforecasts in the mid-1990s.  Cisco Systems  (CSCO),  Google (GOOG) , and  Microsoft (MSFT) \nhave since followed suit. Knowledge about complex issues is often scattered in a large crowd\namong different disciplines and perspectives, says Alpheus Bingham, who directed  Eli Lilly \u2019s\n(LLY) early experiments in prediction markets a decade ago and now consults for the\npharmaceutical industry.  Rather than just sell software, like some of its rivals, Lumenogic also serves as a consultant,\nhelping clients unearth beneficial information and determine how to analyze it and put it to use,\nsays Edward Rhoads, another Lumenogic managing director. \u201cEvery company faces the\nchallenge of [finding out] what our company really knows -- how do I access it, when I need it,\nhow I need it -- to help drive decision-making or results,\u201d he says. Lumenogic was established in\n2008 when two managing partners from the New England Consulting Group, also in Westport,\nteamed with Paris-based NewsFutures, a prediction markets software pioneer co-founded by\nServan-Schreiber. Rhoads says the five-employee firm, with clients including  Johnson &\nJohnson (JNJ) ,  Pfizer (PFE) ,  L\u2019Oreal (OR) ,  Siemens (SI) , and  ArcelorMittal (MT) , expects\nrevenue of $2 million this year, double that of 2010.  MIT\u2019s Malone says it\u2019s a \u201cpuzzle\u201d why more companies have not made use of prediction markets\nthat have proved beneficial to early adopters. He notes one likely obstacle is resistance to sharing\ninformation internally within companies. That didn\u2019t stop  Syngenta (SYT) , the $11.6 billion\nSwiss seed and crop protection company, from hiring Lumenogic in 2010 to improve forecasts\nfor its chemicals. The factors affecting growers\u2019 demand are far more than just fickle weather,\nand because production decisions must be made six months ahead of actual use, forecasting\naccuracy affects profitability and market share. Visala James, a Syngenta executive in Basel,\nsays Lumenogic\u2019s prediction market exercises are proving more accurate than forecasts the\ncompany made through traditional surveys that can take many weeks instead of days. The\nimprovements in predicting growers\u2019 demand by country and region, which will take a few years\nto confirm, would be \u201chugely valuable,\u201d says James. BitTorrent Founder Seeks U.S. Patent on Live Video Streaming  A new application published in the database of the U.S.\nPatent and  Trademark Office  covers a technology enabling live\nvideo streaming anyone can perform without elaborate equipment.  Application  20130066969 , published in the database March\n14, lists  Bram Cohen  of Mill Valley, California, as the\ninventor. He is best known as the author of the BitTorrent\nprotocol that is used for peer-to-peer file sharing.  According to the application, the technology will divide\ncontent into multiple data blocks that are transmitted to what\nthe inventor says are \u201cclubs.\u201d Each person involved in the\ntransaction will belong to at least two of these clubs. When the\ncontent comes to one person, that person will distribute the\ndata block to others in the club, and also to people in others\u2019\nclubs. That person will also receive data blocks assigned to\nother clubs from members of those clubs. Earnings have exceeded analyst estimates at 72 percent of\nthe 68 companies in the S&P 500 that have reported results so\nfar, according to data compiled by Bloomberg. Profits have\nslumped 3.3 percent for the group and the entire index is\nprojected to report a 2.1 percent decrease in earnings.  Credit Suisse Group AG (CSGN)  cut its year-end forecast for the\nS&P 500 to 1,425 from 1,440, citing the potential of a U.S.\nrecession induced by so-called fiscal cliff.  Andrew Garthwaite ,\nglobal equity strategist, said he sees a 10 percent chance of\nthe economy contracting should lawmakers do nothing to prevent\nabout $607 billion of tax increases and spending cuts from\nkicking in at the end of the year.  The dollar weakened against 10 of 16 major peers, losing\nmore than 0.3 percent versus the Japanese yen, Swedish krona and\nAustralian dollar. The U.S. currency was little changed at\n$1.2284 per euro.  Commodities Gain  Natural gas surged as much as 8 percent, leading gains in\n22 of 24 commodities tracked by the S&P GSCI Index, amid\npredictions of a smaller-than-normal increase in stockpiles.\nCattle futures and hogs gained more than 2 percent on\nspeculation that the declining U.S. herd size caused by rising\nfeed costs will lead to a shortage of supplies.  Wheat rose for a sixth straight session on forecasts that\ndry weather will persist for the next week, further cutting the\ncondition of U.S. crops.  Among European stocks, Credit Suisse jumped 4.5 percent\nafter it announced measures to cut costs and boost capital by\n8.7 billion Swiss francs ($8.9 billion). Puma SE tumbled 4.8\npercent after Europe\u2019s second-largest sporting-goods maker cut\nforecasts for sales and profit in 2012.  Analysts are cutting European profit forecasts at the\nfastest rate since 2009 as the region heads for a recession and\ngrowth in  China  slows for a sixth quarter. It\u2019s thin, light and made of machined aluminum, but\nit isn\u2019t a MacBook. It\u2019s got a beautiful touch screen, but it\nisn\u2019t a  Microsoft (MSFT)  Surface Pro.  It\u2019s the Google Chromebook Pixel, and the most striking\nthing about it is neither the design nor the screen. It\u2019s the\nprice tag.  Google\u2019s spent the last few years trying to establish its\nChrome Operating System as a viable competitor to Windows and\n Apple (AAPL) \u2019s OS X by partnering with manufacturers like Samsung, Acer\nand  Hewlett-Packard (HPQ)  to produce inexpensive laptops.  But with the Pixel, it\u2019s taken on the hardware\nresponsibility itself and gone decidedly upscale in the process.\nThe new machine, available from  Google Play  online and at  Best\nBuy (BBY)  stores, costs $1,299 (1,049 pounds in the U.K.) for a Wi-Fi-\nonly model with 32 gigabytes of flash-memory storage, or $1,449\nfor one with 64 gigabytes and the ability to also connect to\n Verizon (VZ)  Wireless\u2019s speedy 4G LTE network.  That\u2019s a lot of money for a computer whose usefulness is\nlimited when it isn\u2019t connected to the Internet, and that costs\neven more than comparable Apple- and Windows-powered machines\nunencumbered by that concern.  The Chrome OS is, essentially, a Web browser. The idea\nbehind it is that most everything you do exists not on the\ncomputer itself, but on the Internet.  Google Docs  Need to write something or create a slideshow? Open the\nword-processing or presentation applications in Google Docs.\nWant to save it? Use your online storage space in Google Drive.\nWant more apps? Choose them from the Chrome Web store, use them,\nand they go away when you\u2019re done until you summon them again.  Living in the cloud like that doesn\u2019t require a lot of\ncomputing power; pretty much all you need is an Internet\nconnection.  Acer (2353)  is currently selling a Chromebook for as little\nas $199 that does nearly all that the six-times-costlier Pixel\ndoes.  You do get a lot with the Pixel, starting with a whopping\nterabyte of online Google Drive storage free for three years,\nand a dozen free sessions of  GoGo (GOGO) \u2019s in-flight Internet access to\naddress one of the most common connection-less situations.  Physically, the new Chromebook is as handsome as any laptop\nthis side of a MacBook. It weighs 3.35 pounds and, with the lid\ndown, measures little more than half an inch thick. A thin strip\nof lights across the back glows with Google\u2019s signature colors,\nor delivers coded status reports. (Red means \u201ccharge me.\u201d)  Dazzling Display  Lift the lid and you meet the Pixel\u2019s dazzling touch\ndisplay. The 12.85-inch screen is unusually proportioned, with a\n3:2 aspect ratio that  Google (GOOG)  says was chosen to optimize it for\nviewing Web pages over, say, widescreen videos. It\u2019s gorgeous,\nwith a pixel density of 239 per inch that the company says is\nthe highest on any laptop.  Under the hood are components that compare well with other\nhigh-end competitors, including the solid-state storage, an\n Intel (INTC)  Core i5 processor and four gigabytes of memory. But here\u2019s\nthe thing: In a Chromebook, a lot of this stuff is unnecessary.  Having a touch screen is certainly nice -- but Google Docs\nisn\u2019t particularly optimized for touch, nor are many Web pages.\nA Core i5 is useful when you\u2019re powering through Windows 8 or\nMac applications, but here it\u2019s overkill, plain and simple.  Costly Overkill  And overkill at a cost that isn\u2019t just reflected in the\nprice: Perhaps a less potent processor would be less of a drain\non the Pixel\u2019s battery life.  Google claims it gets five hours of use, which is 23\npercent less than even the $249 Chromebook from partner  Samsung. (005930) \nI got even less: not much over four hours when I was doing\nnothing more strenuous than streaming video over Wi-Fi. I also\nfound the battery drained after a couple of days in sleep mode,\na stark contrast to, say, Apple\u2019s MacBook Air, which can sleep\nfor weeks and still hold its charge.  As for the Chrome OS, it\u2019s much more usable than in its\nearly days. There are more things you can do offline, and\nsynchronization with the cloud is transparent when you are\nconnected.  Still, I continued to encounter odd glitches and ambiguous\nerror messages, particularly when the Pixel was in the process\nof reconnecting to the cloud after being awakened from slumber.  My guess is that Google doesn\u2019t really expect to sell a\nbunch of Pixels. It seems more like a statement that Chromebooks\ncan be high-end as well as low, and that Google is capable of\ncrafting beautiful hardware that compares favorably with its\ncompetitors.  Personally, I\u2019d find the statement a lot more compelling at\nhalf the price.  ( Rich Jaroslovsky  is a Bloomberg News columnist. The\nopinions expressed are his own.)
