A mission-critical subordinate makes disparaging remarks about the strategy or other team members, and the chief executive must decide how to handle it. Those remarks might not get  printed in a sensationalist magazine like  Rolling Stone  and echoed throughout international media. The mission might not be as critical in its consequences as the war in Afghanistan. The players might not be a sitting U.S. President and a battle-hardened General. But the issues are familiar, whether you are a company founder dealing with the sales manager, a hospital CEO with the director of nursing, or a program head with an aggressive staff member. You have to determine the boundaries of acceptable conduct and a course of remedial action.  \n\n Is attitude important for accomplishment?    \nGeneral McChrystal's skills were not in question, and he was getting results \u2014 albeit in a very difficult and controversial situation. The issue for President Obama, it appeared, was attitude, including the lapse in judgment involved in talking in front of a reporter. Even in a world of flattened, networked, first-name-using organizations in which the language of superiors and subordinates has long disappeared, \"insubordination\" is still considered a violation of standards. Solidarity is important to execution, especially when the outside world \u2014 competitors, customers, or the public \u2014 is watching. Concerns or alternative views should be offered at appropriate times and in appropriate ways. The mission, not politics or petty personal grievances, should be the most important consideration. We all know that there are cynical saboteurs ready to strike in any organization, but that doesn't mean that the leader has to tolerate them. \n\n What is the impact on the rest of the organization?    \nThe foot soldiers doing the work in the trenches can find dissension at the top disturbing, especially if they are risking lives or livelihoods. In the Obama-McChrystal case, this is more than metaphor. The respect of his troops is a reason some former military officers gave me at a recent debate for wishing the President could have disciplined McChrystal while keeping him in command. But business executives at that debate pointed to the many team members that the President needed to support.  Letting one executive slide because his or her work is mission-critical can send a bad message to the people in other functions. \n\n Is there a qualified replacement? \nPresident Obama replaced General McChrystal with a highly-experienced superior,  General David Petraeus . Knowing that there is a qualified replacement waiting in the wings is clearly important. But in this case, even with a vast army (so to speak), the President had to reach up for an officer to step into McChrystal's job, leaving a void in higher command. At Microsoft, Steve Ballmer has been known to step in personally to manage a troubled unit, in addition to his CEO duties. It would be far better to reach below for replacements, into a full bench of already-trained and qualified replacements for any mission-critical job. In some large companies, such as the global cement company CEMEX, training replacements is considered a part of every manager's job. In small organizations, this might be handled by a buddy system in which key managers work closely together, learn enough about a colleague's work to be able to take over in an emergency. \n\n In an ideal world, such issues would be prevented by good organizational practices. The chief and the officer would have worked out their differences in private. In the real world of Presidents with huge staffs working on multiple fronts, Generals rising for their military skills not their diplomacy, and media outlets eager to find fights that make good stories, there will inevitably be Obama-McChrystal moments. In every part of the world, leaders should ask themselves what they would do if confronted with insubordination in their own organizations.","path":".\/2008_2012_msft_bloomberg_news\/obama-mcchrystal-moments-handling-insubordination.txt"},{"id":55150604,"title":"ARM Surges After Microsoft Accord Signals It May Replace Intel in Tablets","released_at":"<date>July 23 2010<\/date> <time>20:21:15<\/time>","content":"ARM Holdings Plc  rose the most in\nalmost two years in London trading after announcing a licensing\ndeal with  Microsoft Corp.  that may give its technology a shot at\nreplacing Intel Corp.\u2019s chips in new Windows tablet computers.  \n ARM, whose chip designs are already in  Apple Inc. \u2019s iPad,\nwill expand the use of its technology in Microsoft devices, the\nCambridge, England-based company said today in a statement. Such\nfuture-focused imagery suggests an aggressive corporation on the\nmove.  Bill Gates , the  Microsoft Corp. (MSFT)  founder, and his wife,\nMelinda, pursue their philanthropic goals with the same\nimpatient fervor that he brought to achieving world domination\nby Windows. With $33.5 billion in assets (which is growing\nquickly through gifts from  Warren Buffett ), the foundation aims\nto transform global health, agriculture and education.  By contrast, the 900,000-square-foot campus located near\nthe foot of the Space Needle north of downtown seems designed to\nplay down the urgency and breadth of that mission. The Seattle-\nbased architecture firm on NBBJ supplies a generic glass-and-\nmetal corporate niceness with comforting wood floors and neutral\ncarpeting. From the street, it looks like a standard-spec office\nbuilding.  The lofty glassy lobby overlooks an alluring plaza that\nunites two six-story boomerang-shaped buildings with lush\nplantings heavy on native ferns and ponds spanned by wooden\nbridges. The ponds, designed by landscape architect  Gustafson\nGuthrie Nichol  Ltd., store rain runoff to water plants in dry\nmonths. Cool underground water storage reduces power demand for\nair-conditioning.  Sharing Ideas  I strolled down sun-filled corridors that run along the\ntightly curved inside face of the buildings. Lined by small\nmeeting spaces and lounges, these hallways subtly encourage\npeople to stop and share ideas. Coffee and snack areas are\norganized around spacious stairways showered in daylight at the\napex of the boomerangs, so that people trying to end AIDS will\ncross paths with education reformers.  Most people work near a window because the buildings\u2019\nprofiles are narrow, and the light quality is superb compared to\nyour average cubicle farm. Gates people call this \u201cdaylight\nequity.\u201d It also saves lighting energy.  From a high balcony I gazed into a huge space that serves\nas a cafeteria and \u201ccivic room,\u201d as NBBJ managing partner Steve\nMcConnell calls it, because it also hosts large meetings of\ngrantees and other global partners. Receptions spill outside to\nthe lush plaza. In addition, there\u2019s a large conference center.  The planned and informal socializing aspires to lead to\neureka moments. Too bad they feel ticked off a checklist rather\nthan exuding engagement with the necessary passion and urgency.  Default to Blandness  Artifacts from many countries hang on the wall and\nstrategically placed screens play videos of work being done, but\nthey are background ambience, not front and center. The place is\nalmost aggressively impersonal, as if any meaningful\narchitectural gesture might offend someone or be read as\ncolonialist bullying.  A visitor center will open next year, but it\u2019s conceived as\na museum, and may feel like a defense against interested\ncitizens rather than an invitation to them.  The default to blandness is a lost opportunity.  It put me in mind of  Livestrong , Lance Armstrong\nFoundation, whose recently built home in Austin I had toured not\nlong ago.  Founded by the bicycling champion, the organization\nsupports people with cancer. The San Antonio architecture firm\n Lake\/Flato  remodeled an old metal warehouse, and bathed its\ncavernous interior with daylight from bands of windows built\ninto the roof. Informally arranged cubicles flow around boxlike\nwooden structures enclosing conference spaces.  Joy of Giving  Touching testimonials from grateful partners and supporters\n-- heavily bicycle-themed -- clutter the place. The joy of\ngiving and the connection to people served is palpable.  Livestrong offers conference space free to nonprofits\naround the city. In this way it builds community connections not\nonly through its core mission but by mingling with other\ncharitable organizations.  At 30,000 square feet, Livestrong is tiny compared to\nGates, with a simpler mission focused on people in deep\ndistress. Rather than fence off emotion, the foundation and its\narchitecture invite it in, with the result that the place has a\ncheerful energy utterly invisible at the posh, sober Gates.  (James S. Research In Motion Ltd. (RIM) \u2019s decline\nhas die-hard BlackBerry fans harking back 15 years to the days\nwhen another fruit-themed company was losing market share,\nposting losses and spurring talk of its imminent demise.  In 1997,  Apple Computer Inc. (AAPL)  lost more than $1 billion, saw\nsales tumble 28 percent and was as little as 90 days away from\nbankruptcy. Co-founder Steve Jobs returned to Apple that year\nand did many of the things RIM is attempting now: He simplified\nthe company, embraced a new operating system and revamped the\nculture to focus on products that were true breakthroughs.  RIM faces long odds in trying to replicate Apple\u2019s success\nstory -- for one, it lacks  Steve Jobs . A RIM comeback also\nhinges on challenging a hit product that Jobs himself\nintroduced: the iPhone. Still, RIM has rabid fans and can rely\non Apple\u2019s approach of controlling both hardware and software,\nletting it make products that tightly integrate the two pieces.  \u201cApple and RIM are both innovative companies with very\nloyal customers,\u201d said Ron Adner, an  associate professor  of\nstrategy and entrepreneurship at the  Tuck School  of Business at\n Dartmouth College  in  New Hampshire . \u201cFor RIM to follow that\nstory line, they need a lot of innovation in not a lot of time\n-- not impossible, but not likely.\u201d  RIM Chief Executive Officer Thorsten Heins took the helm in\nJanuary and made some big changes, including a plan to fire\nalmost a third of the  workforce  and shut down manufacturing\nsites. The Waterloo, Ontario-based company also hired JPMorgan\nChase & Co. and  RBC Capital Markets  to study strategic options.\nHeins says selling the company isn\u2019t the goal of the review. RIM\nwould prefer to find a partner or license its operating system.  \u2018Own Path\u2019  With the changes under way, Heins, 54, says his company\nwill surprise critics with its transformation.  \u201cThe trait that distinguishes innovative companies is the\nability to keep conventional wisdom in perspective and focus\ninstead on the unique value they provide customers,\u201d he said in\nan e-mail interview. \u201cThey follow their own path, which is what\nRIM is doing -- and we know we must get it right.\u201d  Even so, Heins\u2019s product changes haven\u2019t been as big as\nthose enacted by Jobs, who died last year. Immediately after\ntaking over Apple in 1997 following a 12-year absence, Jobs cut\nabout 70 percent of the company\u2019s products -- including printers\nand the Newton personal digital assistant. He trimmed research\nspending and eliminated the corporate-development department.  Board Shakeup  Jobs also replaced most of the board and began reworking\nthe corporate structure and supply chain. The common theme:\nfocus only on what was necessary to maintain the company\u2019s hold\non its loyal fans.  From that position of retrenchment, Jobs pursued an\nambitious expansion. He personally helped create Apple\u2019s \u201cThink\nDifferent\u201d campaign -- not just to get customers to buy current\nproducts but to inspire Apple\u2019s own employees to build them.\nApple released the iPod music player and iTunes in 2001, the\niPhone in 2007 and the iPad in 2010. The company dropped the\nword \u201ccomputer\u201d from its name in 2007, reflecting that\ntransformation. Four years later, it overtook  Exxon Mobil Corp. (XOM) \nto become the world\u2019s most valuable business.  RIM needs to show that it\u2019s not just trying to play catch-\nup, said Adner, author of \u201cThe Wide Lens: A New Strategy for\nInnovation.\u201d Take the example of the BlackBerry PlayBook. When\nthe Apple iPad tablet took off, RIM hurried to offer its own\ndevice. The result of that rush job was a product that lacked\nbuilt-in e-mail -- one of the BlackBerry\u2019s main selling points.  \u201cIt was lunacy,\u201d Adner said.  \u2018Bold Retreat\u2019  Instead, RIM needs to make a \u201cbold retreat\u201d to get out of\nmarkets where it can\u2019t win, such as consumer technology,\nfocusing instead on its corporate customers, he said.  Charlie Wolf , an analyst who has covered Apple since 1985\nand watched its comeback unfold, isn\u2019t counting out RIM yet. The\nreal test will be whether its new BlackBerry 10 software can\ndeliver, he said.  \u201cI don\u2019t think we should dismiss BB10 -- it would be\nfoolish,\u201d said Wolf, who works for Needham Securities Inc. in\n New York . \u201cBut to begin to attract new users, it\u2019s got to be\nsuperior and markedly superior to the iPhone. And it\u2019s an\nincredibly tall order.\u201d  Like Apple\u2019s bruising at the hands of  Microsoft Corp. (MSFT)  in\n1996, RIM has been battered by competitors. Sales fell 43\npercent last quarter from a year earlier, as U.S. and Canadian\nconsumers dumped their BlackBerrys in favor of Apple\u2019s iPhone\nand devices based on  Google Inc. (GOOG) \u2019s Android platform. The company\nexpects a second straight operating loss this quarter.  Market Share  The sales declines may slow as RIM\u2019s customer base is\nwhittled down to the BlackBerry faithful, though that\u2019s no\nrecipe for growth, said Daniel Kunstler, a former technology\nanalyst who was among the first to upgrade Apple to a buy rating\nin August 1997.  Fifteen years ago, Apple\u2019s market share was plunging. Its\nportion of the personal-computer market had fallen by almost\nhalf over a three-year period, according to  Standard & Poor\u2019s .\nThe stock also was getting battered, falling to a split-adjusted\n$3.19 in July 1997. It now trades at almost $575. RIM shares,\nmeanwhile, are currently trading below $7, down 95 percent from\ntheir mid-2008 peak of $147.55.  Kunstler, based in  San Francisco , says the comparison\nbetween RIM and Apple is flawed because the Canadian company\nlacks a couple of key ingredients: Jobs\u2019s own imagination and\nhis ability to coax and cajole his teams into executing their\nideas and delivering products on time.  Product Fumbling  \u201cBefore Jobs returned, Apple had been fumbling very badly\nfor a number of years on the product side,\u201d Kunstler said. The\nproduct discipline he instilled in the company is hard to\nreplicate, he said.  In a bid to tighten its product focus, RIM plans to sell\nfewer BlackBerry models when the new generation arrives --\nprobably no more than four, Heins says. Even so, the products\nwill be late. Last month, Heins delayed the arrival of RIM\u2019s\nfirst BB10 phone until early 2013, meaning it will now debut\nmore than a year after it was originally expected.  Heins took over as CEO from  Mike Lazaridis  and  Jim Balsillie , who ran the company as a team. Lazaridis, RIM\u2019s\nfounder, remains a director, is vice chairman and heads up the\nboard\u2019s innovation committee -- its own attempt to think\ndifferent. The company\u2019s next breakthrough may be just as hard\nfor outsiders to predict as its initial success, Lazaridis said\nin an e-mail.  \u2018Game-Changing Innovation\u2019  \u201cOne thing we\u2019ve seen over the years is that game-changing\ninnovation can come from anywhere, including a company that got\nits start over a bagel shop in Waterloo, Ontario,\u201d he said.  Jobs had instant credibility with Apple employees because\nhe helped start the business and wasn\u2019t around during most of\nthe lean years. Lazaridis doesn\u2019t have that distinction: RIM\ngained and then lost most of its value under his stewardship.\nHe\u2019s also been criticized for not anticipating the popularity of\ncamera phones and mobile browsers. By stepping aside this year,\nLazaridis put Heins, a former Siemens AG executive who joined\nRIM almost five years ago, in the role of would-be savior.  RIM declined to say if Heins is taking cues from Jobs\u2019s\ncareer. His inspiration comes from 78 million BlackBerry fans,\nwho want to see the company succeed, Heins said.  \u201cThe excitement and commitment that all of these people,\nour customers, fans and employees, show on a daily basis gives\nme all the inspiration I need to navigate through this period\nand guide RIM to once again transform the way people communicate\nand to generate long-term value for our shareholders,\u201d Heins\nsaid in an e-mail.  NeXT Software  The linchpin of Apple\u2019s operating-system comeback was NeXT,\nan OS Jobs had built while in exile from Apple. The company\nacquired the business and then retooled it to create the basis\nof the Mac OS X. Similarly, RIM bought QNX Software Systems for\n$200 million in 2010 and began reconfiguring it as the basis for\nBB10. To contact the editor responsible for this story:\nMichael Hytha at   mhytha@bloomberg.net .","path":".\/2008_2012_msft_bloomberg_news\/allen-novozymes-samsung-eu-customs-lady-gaga-intellectual-property.txt"},{"id":93970466,"title":"Women Win in Venture Capital When They Don\u2019t Sue","released_at":"<date>May 30 2012<\/date> <time>23:00:48<\/time>","content":"Kleiner Perkins  Caufield & Byers is\nanti-woman.  That\u2019s the position of Ellen Pao, a junior partner at the\nventure capital firm who filed a lawsuit in San Francisco\nSuperior Court contending \u201cdiscriminatory treatment of Plaintiff\nand other female employees, specifically in advancement and\ncompensation because of their gender.\u201d Pao is also saying she\nwas sexually harassed and that after she complained to higher-\nups she suffered retaliation.  The greater question here isn\u2019t whether certain executives\nat Kleiner Perkins treated  Pao  poorly. That\u2019s entirely possible.\nThis column isn\u2019t suggesting otherwise. The question is whether\nsuch a lawsuit is pro-woman -- whether its consequences will be\ngood for women in the specific field of venture capital on a net\nbasis, as they say in business schools. The answer is: probably\nnot.  You can make the case that Pao\u2019s action may work against\nwomen who want to be entrepreneurs.  There are two kinds of companies in the U.S.: square ones\nand wild ones. The former have the advantage that they follow\nmany rules; their disadvantage is that they aren\u2019t always\ncreative. The wild type, common in  venture capital , does\neverything differently, starting with the open office.  Over the years, creative rebels have often behaved poorly\nin their creative workplaces. Do most of us approve? Hardly.\nNobody likes, say, the way the great creator of  Apple Inc. (AAPL) ,\n Steve Jobs , treated many colleagues.  Growth or Responsibility  But creative environments boast an advantage: They\ncontribute more growth than the old dinosaurs. The venture\ncapitalists give money to entrepreneurs, including women. As the\ncowboy firms age, they tend to develop their own culture of\nresponsibility. It\u2019s their returns and their optimism that lured\ntop students such as  Pao  in the first place.  A brilliant electrical engineer, Pao didn\u2019t go straight\nfrom college (Princeton, class of 1991) to a job with a\nMidwestern manufacturer or the U.S. Department of Labor. She\naimed higher:  Harvard Law School ,  Harvard Business School  and\nthen venturesome companies such as  Microsoft (MSFT)  Corp. and  Kleiner\nPerkins . If these workplaces were wild, there was glamour in\nwildness.  Her action may reduce the very kind of access she enjoyed\nfor those who followed her. Setting Kleiner Perkins aside,\nconsider the rest of the sector. Human-resources specialists\naren\u2019t idiots. They see how much Pao, still merely alleging, is\ncosting a firm such as Kleiner Perkins: time, image and\ndistraction from its main work, finding value. Other businesses\nwill work harder to avoid a litigious hire. They will scour\ncandidates\u2019 resumes for similarities to Pao\u2019s. Her husband,\nAlphonse Fletcher Jr., had filed lawsuits. Any job candidate\nwith a record of suing, or with a litigious spouse, will get a\ncooler reception. Starting last week. In other words, some\nhighly qualified candidates will be excluded. Will HR\ndepartments admit what they are doing? Never.  Pao complains that Kleiner Perkins excluded her from top-\nlevel meetings. At venture capital firms across the U.S.,\nexecutives are probably rejiggering their e-mail and chat\nsettings to be sure that every junior partner at the Pao rank\ngets CC\u2019d. But there are still some meetings, alas, to which\neveryone isn\u2019t invited. Management\u2019s main response will be to\nensure that next time the junior partners don\u2019t even know those\nmeetings exist. That is exactly the opposite of the open office.  Global Divide  The same trade-off between \u201csafe\u201d and \u201ccreative\u201d exists\namong countries. Apparently it is difficult for a nation to be\nboth intensely fair and intensely friendly to entrepreneurs.\nCompare the two premier surveys on entrepreneurship and gender\nfairness, the  World Bank \u2019s  Doing Business  survey, and Unesco\u2019s\nhighly regarded  Global Gender Gap Report .  Singapore , Hong Kong and  China ,  New Zealand , the U.S.,\n Denmark ,  Norway , the U.K., and South Korea rank at the top in\nthe 2011 edition of the World Bank survey. Less highly ranked\nfor \u201cdoing business,\u201d according to the same survey, are  Finland ,\nIreland, Iceland, Canada, Australia and  Japan . Business\nconfronts more hassles in these countries.  Yet the very same countries that rank lower on the\nentrepreneurship charts star when it comes to gender equality.\nIceland, Finland,  Sweden  and Ireland are top countries in the\n2011 update of Unesco\u2019s survey. Singapore, No. 1 for business\nopportunity, ranks 57th of 135 countries, below Jamaica,\nNamibia, Russia and Honduras on the gender-gap index. The U.S.\nranks fourth when it comes to doing business, but only 17th when\nit comes to measuring the gender gap.  In the U.S., litigation isn\u2019t great for growth and  job\ncreation . The tort system, according to  estimates  by the\nconsulting firm  Towers Watson (TW) , cost the country $264.6 billion\nin 2010. When you leave out the Gulf of Mexico oil spill,\ngenerally such tort costs are slightly down, in part because\nstates have changed laws after recognizing the financial burden\nof lawsuits.  A case such as Pao\u2019s might do more damage in the venture-\ncapital sector than elsewhere. Such action forces the U.S.\nventure capitalists over a bit on the spectrum toward safety,\nand away from risk. It makes the old VC firms more like the\npublic sector or traditional American corporations.  This isn\u2019t to say that sexism or sexual harassment is\nacceptable, or that Pao should tolerate it, or that Kleiner\nPerkins shouldn\u2019t take action against wrongdoers. It is to\nsuggest that there is a cost to remedying the problem with\nshowcase litigation.  Pao may think her legal action will create opportunities\nand top jobs for the next generation of girls. In fields such as\nthe one she chose, there might be more jobs if there were fewer\ndiscrimination lawsuits.  ( Amity Shlaes  is a Bloomberg View columnist and the\ndirector of the Four Percent Growth Project at the Bush\nInstitute. The opinions expressed are her own.) Once inside, he called\n Miles Nadal , his boss in Toronto, and resigned.  \n Bogusky was 46. Adweek had named him creative director of\nthe decade, and the advertising agency he helped build,  Crispin\nPorter + Bogusky , had more than $1 billion in billings. He held\na dream title of his own making, chief creative insurgent. His\nsalary was close to $2\u00a0million, a person familiar with the\nevents tells Bloomberg Businessweek in its Aug. 2 edition.  \n The conversation with Nadal, the owner of CP+B parent\ncompany MDC Partners, was followed by an e-mail that Nadal made\npublic on his personal blog. Bogusky, who helped create the\nantismoking \u201cTruth\u201d ad campaign, said he appreciated that\nNadal saw him \u201cas a friend who wants to try something new.\u201d He\nsigned it, \u201cLove, Alex.\u201d  \n Then Bogusky and his wife, Ana, spent much of the afternoon\nsitting on their porch contemplating what he had just done.  \n MDC relied on CP+B for at least a quarter of its\n$546\u00a0million in revenue last year, and Nadal often referred to\nBogusky as the  Steve Jobs  of the industry.  \n In a statement to Bloomberg Businessweek, MDC concluded:\n\u201cOur future has never looked brighter and neither has Alex\u2019s.\u201d\nMDC wouldn\u2019t grant an interview to discuss exactly how bright\nits future would be without the most famous name in advertising.  \n Blog Posts  \n Bogusky declined to comment for this story as well. Even\nso, clues to his state of mind are revealed in interviews with\nindustry peers, co-workers and family members. There are also\nhints about why clients such as Best Buy Co.,  Burger King\nHoldings Inc. , Domino\u2019s Pizza Inc., Microsoft Corp. and Kraft\nFoods Inc., which had just awarded its Macaroni & Cheese account\nto CP+B, didn\u2019t want to say much about him.  \n Perhaps the most telling of Bogusky\u2019s statements before\nresigning was a blog post calling for a ban on advertising to\nkids. In it, he pointed to the child-friendly marketing at\nMiami-based Burger King, one of CP+B\u2019s biggest accounts. Bogusky\nhad a reputation for pushing clients, employees and even\nconsumers right to the edge. This time he went over.  \n Bogusky spent his entire career at one agency, one he had\nknown since he was a child. His father, Bill, was a graphic\ndesigner in Miami whose main client was a local firm, Crispin\nPorter. Bill Bogusky says that at age 3 Alex drew \u201can\nincredibly perfect caricature\u201d of him, which Bill still has in\nhis home studio. As a teenager, Alex devoted himself to dirt\nbike racing and motocross.  \n Rising Star  \n \u201cI thought the racing was outrageously stupid,\u201d says\nBill, who nonetheless served as Alex\u2019s crew and sponsor. \u201cThen\none day he said he wanted to be a graphic artist like me. He\nsent off his bikes and went to art school in Atlanta.\u201d  \n After a semester, Alex returned to Miami and joined the\nBogusky studio, where he soon caught  Chuck Porter \u2019s attention.\nIn 1989, when he was 26, he was invited to join Porter\u2019s agency.\nHe was Employee 16. Five years later he became creative\ndirector; by 1997, he was a partner.  \n While Crispin Porter was small and unknown to Madison\nAvenue, Bogusky and Porter were ambitious. (Sam Crispin retired\nin 1991.) The agency\u2019s first big break came in the late 1990s\nwhen it put together a series of antismoking ads for teenagers\nin Florida funded by the cigarette companies\u2019 settlement with\nthe U.S. government. The Truth campaign told kids they were\nbeing played by tobacco executives, and the number of young\nsmokers dropped.  \n Truth Campaign  \n Bogusky\u2019s creative partner when the campaign went national\nwas Pete Favat, now chief creative officer at Arnold Worldwide.  \n \u201cAlex called us brothers born in outer space who came to\nearth to screw with the ad world,\u201d Favat says.  \n The Truth campaign won industry honors, including an Effie\nAward, which brought all sorts of clients and employees to\nMiami. It also brought Nadal, who in 2001 paid about $20\u00a0million\nin cash and stock for a 49\u00a0percent stake in the agency. He now\nowns it outright.  \n CP+B\u2019s first attention-getting corporate account was\nBayerische Motoren Werke AG\u2019s Mini Cooper. Bogusky introduced\nAmericans to the cars by putting them on top of SUVs, in stadium\nseats and outside department stores as kids\u2019 rides; he produced\nan online mockumentary about how to spot a counterfeit Mini.  \n When CP+B won the Burger King account in 2004, America\u2019s\nsecond-largest burger chain had been trying with scant success\nto revive the brand.  \n Subservient Chicken  \n \u201cThe guys at CP+B absolutely loved the fact that we were a\nchallenger,\u201d says  Brian Gies , who was a senior executive in\nBurger King\u2019s marketing department at the time and has since\nleft the company. They conceived of  Subservient Chicken , the\nwebsite that invites viewers to order around a man dressed in a\nchicken costume. It was one of the first ad sites to go viral,\ngetting more than 15\u00a0million hits in the first five days and\nalmost half a billion since.  \n \u201cWe wanted to develop our social currency, to stimulate\ncuriosity,\u201d Gies says. \u201cSubservient Chicken was a pretty\nunexpected but compelling approach to talk about \u2018Chicken Your\nWay.\u2019 \u201d  \n After that, Bogusky got Burger King executives to\nreintroduce the King as a masked character who was creepy and\nsilent and hard to ignore. He was just as bold with Volkswagen\nAG, persuading the carmaker to run ads featuring a realistic\ncrash in which no one was hurt. The tagline: \u201cSafe happens.\u201d  \n Controlled Message  \n Bogusky was in total control in the office in Coconut Grove,\nwhich was just minutes away from the ocean by skateboard or\nbike. Bogusky himself might come in on Mondays with a bloody\nbruise from biking. He was charismatic and intense, good-looking\nenough to command attention and talented enough to make his\nunconventional style acceptable.  \n For years, he checked every piece of work. His opinions were\norders, and when he reviewed a campaign, the veterans knew to\ntake notes.  \n \u201cHe wasn\u2019t trying to be an a--hole,\u201d says  Evan Fry , a\ncreative director who left CP+B last fall to start his own shop.\n\u201cIf you were secure, you would have no trouble.\u201d  \n A sign on Bogusky\u2019s door read: \u201cIf you want someone to\nmake you happy, see your therapist. If you want someone to make\nyour ads better, see me.\u201d  \n As the agency grew to almost 1,000 employees and won award\nafter award, Bogusky became a somewhat reluctant icon for an\n advertising industry  going through tumultuous times.  \n In 2006, Bogusky and his wife, whom he had met at the\nagency, decided they wanted to raise their two kids in Boulder.\nHe threatened to quit if not allowed to open an office there.\nLater that year, he took about 50 members of the creative team\nwith him to Boulder. Before long, some 550 people had relocated.  \n Beginning to Disengage  \n Then something changed for Bogusky. In early 2008 he began\nto disengage, giving up day-to-day responsibilities but keeping\nan eye on the creative work.  \n While CP+B was making ads about \u201cWhopper freakouts\u201d and\nperfecting ways to order Domino\u2019s pizzas from a laptop on a\ncouch, Bogusky was finishing a book. In late 2008 he released\n\u201cThe 9-Inch \u2018Diet\u2019: Exposing the Big Conspiracy in America.\u201d  \n The back cover promises: \u201cThe best tricksters in the\nindustry explain how you as a consumer are being duped and how\nyou are actually part of the conspiracy to make you fat.\u201d  \n Many assumed the book was satire or even an elaborate\nadvertisement. It was neither. The \u201c9-Inch\u201d of the title\nrefers to the average diameter of a dinner plate in America in\n1970; today the size is one-third larger. Bogusky hadn\u2019t told\nany clients, or Nadal, that he was writing a book.  \n 9-Inch Diet  \n \u201cBurger King and other clients didn\u2019t ever figure into our\ndiscussions,\u201d says Daniel Power, whose powerHouse Books\npublished the book. \u201cHis idea was: \u2018We have obligations to our\nclients, but we can be active agents in the world. Some things\nwe do for a living, and some things have to be challenged.\u2019 \u201d  \n In a 2008 interview with BusinessWeek, Bogusky called the\ndisconnect between his book and his Burger King work \u201cmaybe a\nbit of creative tension.\u201d Fry, who worked closely with him,\nsays Bogusky \u201chad to do some damage control.\u201d  \n A Burger King spokeswoman declined to comment.  \n Bogusky continued to move farther away from the corporate\nhand that had been feeding him. He became interested in climate\nchange. He read about the industrialization of food, the\npoliticization of education. He invested in a Boulder company,\nJustin\u2019s Nut Butter, that makes organic peanut butter sold in\njars and single-serve packs.  \n Founder Justin Gold recalls the adman asking him the first\ntime they met, \u201cDoesn\u2019t it suck that you have this amazing\norganic product in this totally unsustainable package?\u201d Says\nGold: \u201cIt was the thing you don\u2019t want to talk about. He went\nright for it.\u201d  \n Ready to Leave  \n By the end of 2009, Bogusky was ready to leave CP+B, but\nNadal wasn\u2019t ready to let him go.  \n According to a person familiar with the matter, Nadal\noffered him a three-year contract potentially valued at\n$20\u00a0million. Bogusky wasn\u2019t interested. Eventually they worked\nout an agreement: Bogusky would take one step further back from\nthe agency and become the part-time chief creative insurgent at\nMDC. Nadal declined to comment.  \n On Jan.\u00a07, Bogusky called  Colin Drummond , then head of\naccount planning at CP+B, into his office to tell him the news.  \n \u201cI was shocked,\u201d Drummond recalls. \u201cAlex was pretty\nmatter-of-fact. He wasn\u2019t emotional. I knew of his desire to\nlook beyond advertising. He thinks about something for a long\ntime, but he keeps quiet. Then when he makes a decision, he acts\nvery swiftly.\u201d  \n Next Steps  \n They talked about what Bogusky might do next, which seemed\nwide open and didn\u2019t have much to do with MDC. Except in this\nway, says Drummond: \u201cHe said that he told Miles to fire him if\nhe said anything that would potentially upset any MDC clients.\u201d  \n The next morning the seven CP+B partners held a town hall\nmeeting in Boulder. \u201cAlex didn\u2019t say he was leaving the agency\nquite as directly as he did with me,\u201d Drummond recalls. \u201cHe\nsmoothed it over, saying that he would still have an office at\nCP+B. He wanted the clients and employees to feel that it wasn\u2019t\na big deal, and the industry too.\u201d  \n Bogusky continued to influence life at CP+B. He got the\nagency involved in a bike-sharing program in Denver and brought\nin a Buddhist to lead mindfulness sessions.  \n The dissonance between his avocation and his vocation was\nincreasing. When he spoke at a gathering of environmentalists in\nCalifornia in April, Bogusky opened: \u201cMany of us are in this\nimperfect situation where we make decisions within corporations\nand then we go outside and have to deal with it.\u201d That month he\nalso received at least $10\u00a0million for his remaining CP+B stake.  \n Turning on the Industry  \n By June it was clear Bogusky wasn\u2019t just leaving the\nindustry, he was turning on it. While most of his peers were at\nthe annual Cannes Lions International Advertising Festival, he\nwas advocating on his blog for a ban on advertising to kids.  \n He named names, citing Oak Brook, Illinois-based McDonald\u2019s\nCorp. and Burger King, still a CP+B client. Then he sent the\npost by e-mail to Porter in Cannes.  \n Porter has spoken about Bogusky and the piece just once, to\nAdvertising Age: \u201cI told him it was well written and made some\ngreat points, but I also said he needs to make a choice because\nit\u2019s not [compatible with the business we\u2019re in]. And the next\nmorning he sent me a note saying, \u2018I resigned like you\nrecommended.\u2019\u201d  \n In the days after his resignation, there was among his\ncolleagues a sometimes uneasy recognition of the dilemma Bogusky\nhad found himself in.  \n Aware of Conflict  \n \u201cHe was definitely aware that there would be a conflict\nwhen he expressed these thoughts,\u201d Drummond says. \u201cHe wants to\nsee systems change. Who wouldn\u2019t?\u201d  \n Bogusky\u2019s decision leaves CP+B without its Jobs, and the\nfirst big test of its ability to cope is likely to be with\nBogusky\u2019s signature client. Burger King recently appointed a new\nhead of marketing and is fighting with its franchisees, in part\nover the direction of its advertising.  \n \u201cMiles says the relationship with Burger King is solid,\nbut I don\u2019t believe it is completely stable,\u201d says Jim Edwards,\nthe former managing editor of Adweek who now writes about the ad\nworld for BNET Industries. \u201cIf CP+B can stabilize it and sales\ngo up, then all is well. If they lose Burger King, then they\u2019ve\nlost their biggest client and their spiritual father. And that\u2019s\na lot of trouble to be in.\u201d  \n From FearLess Cottage, Bogusky sends out periodic messages\nto the world, offering glimpses of his future ambitions in\nsometimes cryptic blog posts and homemade videos. In mid-July he\ninterviewed Robyn O\u2019Brien, author of \u201cThe Unhealthy Truth: How\nOur Food Is Making Us Sick -- And What We Can Do About It,\u201d and\nfocused on genetically modified soybeans.  \n \u201cGod created all these seeds but never got around to\nmonetizing that s--t. God\u2019s a bad capitalist. So we said, let us\nshow you how it\u2019s done,\u201d he said, to the bemusement of his\nguest. \u201cWe have a right to critique a food system created by a\ncorporation.\u201d  \n \u201cWhat if things don\u2019t turn out well and your kids come to\nyou and ask: \u2018What did you do to try to stop this?\u2019\u201d  \n To contact the reporter on this story:\n Susan Berfield  in New York at \n sberfield@bloomberg.net   \n          \n          \n\n\n  \n     \n       \n     \n           \n                                                 \n                     \n                     Enlarge image \n                     \n                     \n                       Bogusky Turns Back on Career  \n                       \n                         \n                           alexbogusky.com via Bloomberg \n                         \n                         Alex Bogusky, former creative director of Crispin Porter & Bogusky advertising agency. \n                       \n                     \n                                        \n           \n                     Alex Bogusky, former creative director of Crispin Porter & Bogusky advertising agency. The agreement will bolster the Devices & Services unit\u2019s\nsecond-quarter profitability, Espoo, Finland-based Nokia said in\na statement yesterday. The details of the contract, under which\nApple will pay Nokia an undisclosed sum and royalties for the\nterm of the agreement, are confidential, the Finnish company\nsaid.  The two mobile-phone makers have been in litigation since\nOctober 2009, when Nokia filed a lawsuit accusing Cupertino,\nCalifornia-based Apple of infringing patents. Robert T. Emmel was accused of making improper disclosures\nof News Corp.\u2019s News America Marketing In-Store unit. He was a\nformer account director for retailers who was fired in 2006.  Emmel allegedly brought confidential information to a\nnumber of state and federal offices, including the New York\nAttorney General\u2019s Office, the U.S. Securities and Exchange\nCommission and the U.S. Senate Finance Committee.  News America agreed in February to pay $125 million to\nsettle a suit from  Insignia Systems Inc. (ISIG)  accusing the company of\nanti-competitive behavior. It earlier agreed to pay $500 million\nto  Valassis Communications Inc. (VCI)  on similar claims, and $29.5\nmillion to settle a claim from Floorgraphics Inc.  In the suit filed in April 2007 in federal court in\nAtlanta, Emmel was accused of \u201cthe devious and unauthorized\nretention\u201d of computer data and hard-copy documents. News\nAmerica said he gave this information to a competitor and\nindicated he would supply it to others.  Emmel responded by telling the court that he was convinced\nhis ex-employer \u201cwas engaged in widespread illegal activity\nagainst its customers, competitors and shareholders\u201d and that\nNews America management refused to do anything about it. He\ndescribed the information he took as evidence of News America\u2019s\n\u201cextensive billing and revenue-sharing fraud against its\ncustomers,\u201d and \u201cpredatory and anti-competitive schemes\nagainst competitors.\u201d  The data also proved that News America engaged in\n\u201cfraudulent inflation of its reported earnings,\u201d he said.  When Emmel left News America in December 2006, he signed an\nagreement not to disclose his employer\u2019s confidential data or to\ndisparage the company. That agreement was signed on Dec. 21.  The day before he signed the agreement, he sent a package\nof News America\u2019s confidential documents to a staffer for the\nU.S. Senate\u2019s Finance Committee. He said later in a deposition\nthat his goal \u201cwas to make sure the information got out before\nI would be signing an agreement.\u201d  The court issued an order in March 2009 barring further\ndisclosures of the confidential information. Emmel then\nappealed.  The 11th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals looked at the\nlanguage of the agreement and said that because all the promises\nEmmel made when he signed the contract were in future tense,\nthey wouldn\u2019t apply to his actions before the signing date.  \u201cThe specific promises undertaken were couched in language\nthat applies only prospectively,\u201d the court said in its June 8\nruling. \u201cThe simple past tense\u201d could have been used in the\ncontract to capture Emmel\u2019s pre-contract actions, the court\nsaid. (AAPL) \u2019s MacBook Air set the bar.  No one else even came close -- until now. Thanks to a new\ngeneration of notebooks running  Microsoft Corp. (MSFT) \u2019s Windows 7\noperating system, new laptops featuring stylish designs, more-\npowerful processors and speedy storage have taken on Apple in\nthis rarefied niche.  Don\u2019t get me wrong: The latest Air, introduced last year,\nremains the gold standard. It uses chips rather than a\nconventional hard drive to store data, making it lightning swift\nto start up, while even the larger of its two models, with a 13-\ninch screen, weighs just 2.9 pounds (1.32 kilograms).  Its smaller sibling, which has an 11-inch screen and weighs\n2.3 pounds, is my main traveling companion these days. Using\nApple\u2019s free Boot Camp program, I\u2019ve been able to easily run\nWindows and Microsoft Office on it despite its constrained, 128-\ngigabyte storage capacity.  You, however, may not need or want the Air\u2019s Mac-ness. In\naddition, you may want more up-to-date hardware (at least until\na likely update this summer, the Air uses two-generation-old\nmicroprocessors).  Here are three of the most capable Windows-only\nalternatives.  Samsung Series 9  It\u2019s black where the Air is silver, and wavy where the Air\nis razor-edged. But if you want the closest Windows equivalent\nto the Apple experience, look no further. The Series 9 from\nSamsung Electronics Co. is both gorgeous and capable.  At 2.89 pounds, the Series 9 is a hair lighter than the\nAir. The 13-inch screen lives up to Samsung\u2019s reputation for\nbright and beautiful displays. And it features  Intel Corp. (INTC) \u2019s\nlatest-generation \u201cSandy Bridge\u201d microprocessor, four\ngigabytes of memory and a 128-gigabyte solid-state drive.  Unfortunately, it all comes at a price, figuratively and\nliterally. The nice screen and CPU cut down on battery life: I\nwas able to coax just 4 hours while streaming a Netflix movie\nover Wi-Fi. And, at $1,650, the Series 9 costs $250 more than an\nAir with comparable screen, memory and storage.  Lenovo ThinkPad X1  Ever since the days when  International Business Machines\nCorp. (IBM)  owned the brand, ThinkPads have defined a certain class of\nportable computers: sturdy business companions that make up in\nreliability what they lack in pizzazz. That\u2019s still the case\nunder  Lenovo Group Ltd. (992) \u2019s ownership. The X1, with its  Corning\nInc. (GLW)  Gorilla Glass screen and solid construction, certainly has\nthe sturdy part down. But the X1 brings a little unaccustomed\nflash to the party too.  Start with that classic keyboard. Sure, it has the\nThinkPad\u2019s trademark orange eraser-like pointer protruding from\nbetween the G and H. But the keys themselves are generously\nsized and slightly concave, making for a comfortable typing\nexperience. And at less than an inch at its thickest part, it\u2019s\nthe skinniest ThinkPad ever.  At 3.7 pounds, the X1 is almost a pound heavier than some\nof its competitors. And Lenovo opted for the higher capacity of\na physical hard drive -- 320 gigabytes at 7200 RPM in the $1,399\nbase model -- over faster but more limited-capacity solid-state\nstorage.  The X1 still emphasizes function over form, but the form\nhas gotten a lot nicer.  Toshiba Portege R830  What  Toshiba Corp. (6502) \u2019s Portege line lacks in elegance, it\nmakes up for in value. The lightweight R830 offers the broadest\nrange of MacBook Air-substitutes, with models starting at under\n$800.  At those prices, there\u2019s some obvious corner-cutting. The\nR830 case lacks the elegant design and solid feel of the\nSamsung, for example, and the lower-end models use poky 5400 RPM\nhard drives, a far cry from the solid-state storage that makes\nthe MacBook and Samsung feel so zippy.  Moving up the price ladder, however, you get the R830-\nS8330. It\u2019s $1,649, and comes with SSD storage, a top-flight\nIntel i7 processor and even a DVD drive, something that\u2019s\nmissing from the competition. The Samsung has it beat for\nportability and elegance, but the Toshiba comes the closest to a\ndesktop replacement in an ultra-portable package.  ( Rich Jaroslovsky  is a Bloomberg News columnist. Compliance Policy  Audio Records of Swaps and Futures Trades Required by CFTC Rule  Derivatives traders will be required to keep audio records\nof commodities transactions under U.S. Commodity Futures Trading\nCommission  rules  completed in a private vote yesterday.  The regulation, revised by commissioners to limit the\nimpact on smaller brokers, could help CFTC\u2019s enforcement unit\ndetermine traders\u2019 intent when later probing claims of market\nmanipulation and false reporting, the agency said in a\nstatement. It is already common practice for equities traders to\nmake such audio recordings.  Under the rule approved in a 5-0 vote, derivatives brokers\nand certain members of exchanges and swap-execution facilities\nwill be required to record quotes, bids, offers, trading and\nprices that lead to transactions whether communicated by\ntelephone, voice-mail, mobile or other electronic media.  The CFTC backed away from requiring records of oral\ncommunications that lead to trades in grains, according to a\nstatement. Companies will have a year to comply with the\nregulation.  The agency delayed consideration of the rule in September\namid resistance from industry groups representing trading firms\nand exchanges. Klein said Microsoft\u2019s\nproducts other than Windows have \u201ca lot of headroom\u201d to grow\nand shore up results while Windows struggles.  Klein, who said he\u2019s leaving Microsoft to spend more time\nwith his family and doesn\u2019t have immediate plans, said he\u2019ll be\nreplaced by a new CFO from Microsoft\u2019s internal finance team in\nthe next several weeks.  To contact the reporter on this story:\nDina Bass in Seattle at \n dbass2@bloomberg.net   To contact the editor responsible for this story:\nTom Giles at \n tgiles5@bloomberg.net","path":".\/2008_2012_msft_bloomberg_news\/icrosoft-third-quarter-profit-exceeds-estimates-on-cost-contro.txt"},{"id":88897577,"title":"Amazon\u2019s Bezos Fuels Tablet Wars With $199 Kindle","released_at":"<date>September 28 2011<\/date> <time>13:45:48<\/time>","content":"Jeff Bezos  is channeling  Steve Jobs . It\u2019s mid-September and the wiry billionaire founder of\n Amazon.com Inc. (AMZN)  is at his brand new corporate headquarters in\nSeattle, in a building named \u201cDay One South\u201d after his\nconviction that 17-year-old Amazon is still in its infancy.  Almost giddy with excitement, Bezos retrieves one by one\nthe new crop of dirt-cheap Kindle e-readers --- they start at\n$79 --- from a hidden perch on a chair tucked into a conference\nroom table. When he\u2019s done showing them off, he stands up, and,\nfor an audience of a single journalist, announces, \u201cNow, I\u2019ve\ngot one more thing to show you.\u201d He waits a half-beat to make\nsure the reference to Jobs\u2019 famous line from  Apple Inc. (AAPL) \npresentations hasn\u2019t been missed, then gives his notorious\nbarking laugh.  With that, Bezos pulls out the Kindle Fire, Amazon\u2019s long-\nanticipated tablet computer --- and the first credible response\nto the Apple iPad,  Bloomberg Businessweek  reports in its Oct. 3\nedition.  Unlike a wave of other tablets that have emerged hopefully\nonly to flop, such as the  Hewlett-Packard Co. (HPQ)  TouchPad, the\nMotorola Mobility Holdings Inc. Xoom, and the  Research in Motion\nLtd. (RIM)  PlayBook, the Kindle Fire has a good shot at turning the\nnewest theater of war in high-tech into a two-tablet battle.  $199 Fire  With a 7-inch display, the Fire is about half the size of\nthe iPad. At $199, it\u2019s also less than half the price of the\ncheapest Apple model. Amazon has painted over the rough surfaces\nof  Google Inc. (GOOG) \u2019s Android operating system with a fresh and easy-\nto-use interface and tied the device closely to its own large\nand growing content library. Kindle Fire owners can watch the\nfilm \u201cRio,\u201d scroll through magazines such as The New Yorker or\nEsquire, and access their music collection on Amazon\u2019s servers.  \u201cWhat we are doing is offering premium products at non-\npremium prices,\u201d Bezos says. Other tablet contenders \u201chave not\nbeen competitive on price\u201d and \u201chave just sold a piece of\nhardware. We don\u2019t think of the Kindle Fire as a tablet. We\nthink of it as a service.\u201d  To demonstrate the Kindle Fire, Bezos pulls up a chair. He\nproudly shows off a lightning-fast Web browser that runs on\nAmazon\u2019s EC2 cloud computing engine and Amazon\u2019s version of the\nAndroid app store, with over 10,000 games, e-mail programs,\nshopping guides, and the like.  Bezos pauses briefly to exhibit his dexterity at a game\ncalled \u201cFruit Ninja,\u201d zapping watermelons and kiwis that fly\nacross the screen, and appears to momentarily lose himself in\nthe effort. \u201cI do find it strangely therapeutic, uncomfortably\ntherapeutic,\u201d he says.  No Camera  There are some limitations to the Kindle Fire. Unlike the\niPad 2, it doesn\u2019t have embedded cameras or a microphone, and\nthere\u2019s no 3G cellular connection, only Wi-Fi.  Its diminutive size, which makes it so handy for stashing\nin a coat pocket, also makes it unlikely to satisfy more than\none antsy kid on a long car ride.  The versatile iPad 2, with its video chatting capabilities\nand exquisite screen resolution, is a lifestyle-defining objet\nd\u2019art.  The stripped-down Fire is more of a sit-back-on-the-sofa-\nand-shop device. It crystallizes the difference between Apple,\nwhich tends to keep prices -- and profit margins -- high, and\nAmazon, which likes to start low and drive lower in an effort to\nknee-cap the competition. The tablet is symbolic of Amazon\u2019s\nability to adapt and reluctance to cede the future to anyone. If\nthe Fire and its inevitable sequels are successful, they will\nadd even more might to one of the fastest-growing retail\noperations the world has ever seen.  Largest Bookstore  Amazon\u2019s 1990s slogan -- \u201cEarth\u2019s largest bookstore\u201d --\nstood for an ambition that now seems cute. Amazon boasted of its\nunlimited selection of books, even though in most cases it was\nsimply having them shipped directly from distributors.  Today, Amazon sells millions of goods and services, from\ntoys and high-definition televisions to server space for other\nInternet companies and digital reading devices for book lovers.\nBorders Group Inc. found it impossible to match Amazon\u2019s\nselection and went out of business earlier this year.  Best Buy Co. has watched Amazon undercut it and commoditize\nwhole product categories, and is now trying to shrink the square\nfootage of its superstores.  Wal-Mart Stores Inc. (WMT)  has struggled\nto match the ease and reliability of Amazon\u2019s shipping network,\nand posted nine straight quarters of declining same-store sales.\nWebsites that have matched Amazon in selection, price, and\ncustomer service -- Zappos, Diapers.com -- Bezos has quickly\nacquired.  `Hyper Competitor'  \u201cAmazon is not a fight-on-their-knees kind of company,\u201d\nsays Rob Glaser, the Seattle-based entrepreneur behind\nRealNetworks and now also a venture -capitalist at  Accel\nPartners . \u201cJeff\u2019s a hyper competitor.\u201d  As its rivals steadily asphyxiate, Amazon is ringing up 50\npercent growth in quarterly revenues, and may reach $50 billion\nin sales this year.  Wal-Mart needed almost twice the time --- 33 years --- to\ncross that threshold.  \u201cAmazon is such a smart learning organization,\u201d says Nancy F. Koehn, a professor of business administration at Harvard\nBusiness School. \u201cIt\u2019s like a biological organism that through\nnatural selection and adaptation just keeps learning and\ngrowing.\u201d  Amazon is also facing a new kind of challenge that\ncompetitors like Wal-Mart are intimately familiar with ---\ncultural backlash, or at least the early signs of it. The\ncompany has been criticized for waging an expensive state-by-\nstate battle to avoid collecting sales taxes, and more recently\nfor skimping on air conditioning in its East Coast distribution\ncenters during a brutally hot summer.  Growing Dominance  If the Kindle Fire is half as good as it looked in Bezos\u2019\nconference room, it will fan the fears about Amazon\u2019s growing\ndominance. The tablet funnels users into Amazon\u2019s meticulously\nconstructed world of content, commerce, and cloud computing.\nJust like owners of Kindle e-reading devices tend to start\nbuying all their books from Amazon, Kindle Fire owners are\nlikely to hand over an increasing chunk of their entertainment\nbudget to Jeff Bezos.  Tablets represent an opportunity for Bezos not only to sell\na new kind of device but also to entice people to buy more\nstuff.  Even with only 28.7 million iPads sold, e-commerce sites\nsay they see an increasing amount of traffic coming from\ntablets. Forrester Research reported that online purchases made\non tablets now account for 20 percent of all mobile e-commerce\nsales, and that almost 60 percent of tablet owners have used\nthem to shop.  `Huge Tailwind'  Bezos says tablets \u201care a huge tailwind for our business.\u201d  Amazon once saw spikes in traffic during the workday lunch\nhours. Now traffic is more evenly distributed as people pick up\ntheir tablets anytime of the week, buying the books and albums\nthey see on television and making impulsive decisions about\nreplacing their dishwashers.  The Kindle Fire (internal code name: Otter) is designed to\nensure that even more of those purchases go to Amazon. The\ncompany has built a tablet-optimized shopping application, with\nsimplified and streamlined pages with none of the clutter of the\nmain website. The app is pre-installed and sits at the bottom of\nthe Fire\u2019s main screen (users can get rid of it if they want).  The device also comes with the enticement of a 30-day free\ntrial of Amazon Prime, the company\u2019s $79-a-year two-day delivery\nprogram that tends to convert members into Amazon addicts who\ntriple or even quadruple the amount they spend on the site.\nSince March, Amazon has also administered its own app store for\nAndroid devices, culling Google\u2019s more comprehensive selection\nand removing everything that\u2019s offensive and unreliable.  Twitter, Facebook  Kindle Fire owners will have access to apps from Pandora\nMedia Inc., Twitter, Facebook, and  Netflix Inc. (NFLX)  Although other\ncompetitors like  Barnes & Noble Inc. (BKS)  can submit their apps, it\nwill be much easier for Kindle Fire owners to find Amazon\u2019s own\ncontent. That\u2019s one reason Amazon is in the best position to turn\nthe tablet battle into a two combatant war.  The other is price. Analysts speculating on the new device\npegged the Kindle Fire at $250 to $300. (Companies like Samsung\nand RIM have entered the tablet race with similar devices at\nthose prices and above.)  Bezos is able to go lower because he can make his profits on\nmedia content and with additional subscriptions to Amazon Prime,\nwhich then will drive additional purchases of toys, toasters,\ndiapers, etc. He\u2019s also exploiting his company\u2019s popular cloud\ncomputing initiative, called Amazon Web Services.  `Extremely Low Margins'  Amazon saves money on the Kindle Fire by packing it with\nonly eight gigabytes of memory (the costliest version of the iPad\nhas 64 gigs), but owners of the device get to store as many\nbooks, songs, movies, and personal documents on Amazon\u2019s cloud\nservers as they like for free.  Bezos won\u2019t say whether he thinks he\u2019ll lose money on the\ndevice itself, only that he\u2019s at ease flirting with red ink.  \u201cCertainly this is a for-profit business,\u201d he says. \u201cLet\u2019s\nput it this way. We are and always have been very comfortable at\noperating at extremely low margins.\u201d  Though the decision to design and build its own hardware is\na high-stakes bet, it\u2019s equally true that Bezos had no choice but\nto enter the tablet business.  About 40 percent of Amazon\u2019s revenue comes from media ---\nbooks, music, and movies --- and those formats are rapidly going\ndigital.  Amazon was late to understand the speed of that transition;\nApple, which introduced the iPod in 2001 and iTunes two years\nlater, wasn\u2019t. The iPad has only strengthened Apple\u2019s hold over\ndigital media.  Kindle App  Although there\u2019s a Kindle app for the iPad, Apple takes a 30\npercent slice of all e-books Amazon sells on it and has\nrestricted Amazon and other app makers from directing iPad users\nto their websites in order to avoid giving Apple its cut. Doing\nbusiness on the iPad threatens Amazon\u2019s already thin profit\nmargins.  Bezos says he doesn\u2019t think defensively.  \u201cEverything we do is driven by seeing opportunity rather\nthan being worried about defending,\u201d he says. Given Apple\u2019s\ninroads into the media business, that\u2019s hard to believe. Bezos is\nmagnanimous toward Jobs.  \u201cOn a personal level we have a tremendous amount of respect\nfor Apple and Steve. I think that\u2019s returned,\u201d he says. \u201cOur\ncultures start in the same place. Both companies like to invent,\nboth companies like to pioneer, both companies start with the\ncustomer and work backwards. There\u2019s a like-mindedness.\u201d Pause.\n\u201cAre two companies like Amazon and Apple occasionally going to\nstep on each other\u2019s toes? Yes.\u201d  E-Book Store  Amazon has recovered more quickly than other tech companies\nin the race to catch up with Apple in digital media. Amazon\nintroduced an online TV and movie store in 2006, the Kindle e-\nbook store in 2007, and the MP3 digital music store in 2008.  Earlier this year, Amazon also aimed its sights on Netflix\nwith an Instant Video streaming service that\u2019s free for members\nof Amazon Prime, and it\u2019s now spending hundreds of millions to\nincrease its catalog with TV shows and movies from studios like\n News Corp. (NWSA) \u2019s Fox and NBC Universal.  The music and video stores haven\u2019t been huge hits. That may\nchange on the Kindle Fire. On a tablet those apps will give users\nthe impression that most songs, TV shows, and movies are just a\nclick away.  \u201cWe are leaning into this,\u201d Bezos says. \u201cIt\u2019s not a small\ninitiative for us.\u201d  Amazon is also among the companies in the final round of\nbidding for the online video site Hulu, according to people with\nknowledge of that process who were not allowed to speak on the\nrecord.  IPod Lessons  Apple\u2019s success with the iPod taught the entire tech\nindustry another valuable lesson. There were other digital music\nplayers on the market back in the 1990s, but Apple\u2019s device,\nwhich seamlessly blended hardware, software, and eventually an\nonline service in iTunes, made the experience simple and\nunintimidating for non-techies.  There is a sense, as one easily holds the Kindle Fire in one\nhand (try doing that with an iPad), that Bezos is working from\nthe same set of principles as Jobs: Content matters. Simplicity\nis key. How do companies allow users to easily buy songs, movies,\nand other digital goodies? They persuade customers to entrust\nthem with their credit cards--as both Amazon and Apple have done.\nHow do they ensure that the device is easy to use? They design\nand build it themselves.  Making Own Hardware  \u201cWhat should Amazon be doing in 20 years?\u201d  That was the first question Bezos asked Jateen Parekh, a\nSilicon Valley systems engineer who had worked for the digital\nvideo recorder pioneer Replay-TV, an early TiVo rival, and\nPhilips Research, a division of the Dutch consumer electronics\nmaker.  It was August 2004, and Bezos and his new senior vice-\npresident in charge of worldwide digital media, Steven Kessel,\nwere exploring what seemed like a radical idea for an online\nretailer: making their own hardware.  \u201cThe question impressed me,\u201d recalls Parekh, who is now the\nfounder and chief technology officer of digital radio startup\nJelli. \u201cThe fact that the CEO was thinking that far out was\nhuge.\u201d  Parekh joined Amazon that September, becoming the first\nemployee of Lab126, a secret Silicon Valley skunkworks. At\nfirst, Parekh didn\u2019t have an office to report to: He and the few\nindustrial designers and engineers hired soon after, including\nGregg Zehr, a former vice-president of hardware engineering at\nPalm Computing, set up shop in an empty room in the offices of\nA9, Amazon\u2019s  Palo Alto , California-based search subsidiary.  Build an E-Reader  Parekh recalls spending his first few weeks investigating the\npossibility of building Internet-connected set-top boxes and\neven an MP3 player.  Bezos loved reading far more than listening to music, and\nAmazon had deep expertise in the book market, so the next\ndecision was a natural one. Amazon\u2019s new hardware geeks would\nbuild an e-reader. Parekh and Zehr, who became president of the\nnew division, researched existing e-readers of the time, such as\nthe Sony Librie, which required AAA batteries, sold poorly, and\nnever made it out of  Japan . They concluded the market was wide\nopen.  \u201cIt was the one thing that wasn\u2019t being done well by anyone\nelse out there,\u201d Parekh says.  First though, Amazon\u2019s engineers needed a better name for\nthe original \u201cA2Z Development Corp.\u201d Parekh and his colleagues\nhated it, and thought it ill-suited to luring the best and\nbrightest engineers from places like Apple and Palm.  Lab126 Project  They eventually settled on the more mysterious \u201cLab126.\u201d\nThe 1 stands for a, the 26 for z, a geeky naming convention\ninside Amazon where groups like the personalization team are\nreferred to by the abbreviation P13N. (If you\u2019re confused by\nthat, count the letters in the word \u201cpersonalization.\u201d)  Other people who worked for Lab126 in those early years\nrecall it as a loosely managed startup. The group piggybacked on\nA9\u2019s infrastructure for most the next year. When the search\ndivision moved to the former offices of a Palo Alto law firm,\nLab126 moved with them and took up residence in the old law\nlibrary.  Lab126 was eventually given almost unlimited resources. It\nalso had to contend with the unfettered imagination of Bezos.\nAmazon\u2019s founder wanted his new -e-reading device to be drop-dead\nsimple to use and argued that configuring devices to Wi-Fi\nnetworks was too complicated for non-tech-savvy users.  No PC Connection  He also didn\u2019t want to force customers to connect the\ndevice to a PC, so the only alternative was to build cellular\naccess right into the device, the equivalent of embedding a\nwireless phone in the hardware. Nothing like that had been\ntried before. Bezos insisted that customers should never have\nto know the wireless connection was there or even pay for access.  \u201cI thought it was insane, I really did,\u201d Parekh recalls.  The effort to develop the first Kindle ended up taking more\nthan three years. Almost everything went wrong. The black and\nwhite displays from E Ink, an offshoot of the Massachusetts\nInstitute of Technology Media Lab that makes screens resembling\nthe printed page and require very little power, would look good\nfor one month and then degrade alarmingly.  Qualcomm Inc. (QCOM) , which was set to provide the wireless chips,\nwas sued by a competitor,  Broadcom Corp. (BRCM) , and for months was\nenjoined by a judge from selling its wares in the U.S.  The Lab126 team repeatedly urged Bezos to make their project\neasier by considering a Wi-fi-only connection for the Kindle. He\nrejected the idea, constantly suggesting new ones for complicated\nfeatures, like the notion that customers\u2019 annotations of books\nshould be backed up on Amazon\u2019s servers.  Code-Name `Fiona'  That original Kindle, code-named \u201cFiona\u201d after a character\nin Neal Stephenson\u2019s futuristic novel \u201cThe Diamond Age,\u201d was\nfinally ready to go in the fall of 2007.  Still, Amazon almost blew it. Modeling demand after the\nfirst-year sales of the original iPod, Amazon underestimated what\na hit the Kindle would turn out to be. The first batch sold out\nin just a few hours. Amazon then discovered that one of its\nTaiwanese suppliers had discontinued a key part and spent months\ngetting a replacement.  \u201cYou look at the history of the Kindle, they developed some\nreal skills around the creation of that product. They\u2019ve cut\ntheir teeth so to speak,\u201d says Brian Blair, a New York-based\nanalyst at Wedge Partners.  Making four successive versions of the Kindle e-reader also\nled Amazon down the path toward the Kindle Fire. For years the\nengineers at Lab126 tried to create a workable and reader-\nfriendly color Kindle, according to three former employees.  New Color Displays  New color display technologies like Qualcomm\u2019s Mirasol and\nanother MIT IT-offshoot called Pixel Qi proved unreliable and\ndifficult to produce in large quantities. In January 2010, the\niPad demonstrated the broad appeal of a new kind of color LCD\ntablet with better image quality, wider viewing angles, and,\nnear to Amazon\u2019s heart, Apple\u2019s own selection of e-books. People\nclose to Lab126 say that work on tablets, including the Kindle\nFire, started soon after.  Amazon\u2019s devices division now employs around 800 hardware\nand software engineers in Cupertino,  California , who fill up all\nbut one floor of an entire eight-floor office building and part\nof a second building in the same office park, less than a mile\nfrom Apple\u2019s corporate headquarters.  In the unit\u2019s industrial design lab, according to a person\nwho has visited that top-secret floor but was not authorized to\nspeak on the record, naked e-ink displays hang from the walls\nwith images from books imprinted on their screens.  E-Ink Screens  They\u2019re used to demonstrate to potential new hires how an\ne-ink screen can hold an image indefinitely without being\nconnected to a power supply.  There\u2019s also another office of Kindle employees at Amazon\u2019s\nnew corporate campus in the South Lake Union district of\nSeattle, in a building nostalgically named \u201cFiona.\u201d The group is\ncordoned off from other Amazon employees, whose company badges\ndo not grant them access.  Bezos won\u2019t say what kind of devices he\u2019s cooking up next.\nPeople with knowledge of the division\u2019s plans say that the\nKindle Fire is only the first of a line of Amazon tablets, not\nan isolated product, and that the group has always considered\nthe possibility of building Amazon cell phones and Internet-\nconnected TVs.  \u201cWe are a company with a lot of ideas,\u201d Bezos says, when\nasked directly about his plans. And then, of course, he laughs\nuproariously.  Kindle Fire Impact  For those already competing with Amazon, the Kindle Fire\nwon\u2019t be good news.  Kevin Ryan, the co-owner of Green Apple Books, a 44-year-\nold bookstore in  San Francisco , says that Amazon has lowered the\nprices in the book business beyond his ability to match them.\nAmazon has also locked up several big authors to publishing\ncontracts, and though it says it will produce their books in\nprint as well as digital formats, that has competing retailers\nnervous.  \u201cThey\u2019re bullies. They really are. I think they really want\nto be a monopoly,\u201d Ryan says from the 8,000-square-foot store\nthat features tribal masks over the bookshelves, and which has\nwatched sales drop for much of the last decade.  Of the growing group of authors like George R.R. Martin\nwhose books have sold over a million digital copies through\nAmazon, he says, \u201cYou have to assume that people joining the\nmillion book Kindle club is taking business away from you.\u201d  ShopRunner Program  In the past year major chains like Toys \u201cR\u201d Us Inc., Sports\nAuthority, and  RadioShack Corp (RSH) .have teamed up to combat Amazon\u2019s\nmight, forming a free shipping program called ShopRunner that,\nlike Amazon Prime, also offers free two-day shipping for $79 a\nyear. It\u2019s not clear yet how ShopRunner is doing; the group\nwon\u2019t release subscriber numbers.  Fiona Dias, ShopRunner\u2019s chief strategy -officer, says that\nby locking in a new wave of customers with the Kindle Fire,\nAmazon will make their jobs even harder.  \u201cIt\u2019s a phenomenal concentration of power,\u201d she says. \u201cIf\nwe were scared of Amazon in the Web world, we should be\nabsolutely terrified of them in the tablet world.\u201d  It\u2019s not just competitors that are assessing Amazon\u2019s\ndominance. Over the past year, lawmakers, the media, and even\nsome customers have begun weighing Amazon\u2019s growing sales and\nsize against the impact for communities, commerce, and the local\njob market.  Amazon has brought some of this scrutiny on itself. It\ntouts its hiring of workers for its growing network of shipping\ncenters, yet those jobs aren\u2019t exactly plumb: They start at\naround $11 an hour (with health benefits), and conditions can be\ntough.  Few Perks  The recent newspaper account in the Allentown, Pennsylvania\nMorning Call said that temperatures over the summer in a local\nAmazon facility reached 120 degrees Fahrenheit (49 degrees\nCelsius), and that workers who were slowed by the heat felt\npenalized by their bosses. (Amazon has promised to put in air\nconditioners.)  The report is consistent with a company that gives\nemployees few perks aside from 10 percent off $1,000 in annual\npurchases. Unlike Google and Apple, Amazon doesn\u2019t subsidize\nmeals or provide free sodas. Even the pet dogs of Amazon\nemployees get a better deal: There\u2019s a bucket of free milk bones\nat the front desk of every company building in Seattle.  The multi-state battle over state sales tax has created\nperhaps the most controversy around Amazon. Legislators in more\nthan a dozen states, pressed by such politically connected\ncompetitors as Wal-Mart, have been pushing Amazon to collect the\nsales tax that their customers technically already owe on online\npurchases, to better repair widening budget deficits and pay\nfiremen and school teachers.  California Compromise  Bezos has fought that effort, saying that only federal\nlegislation can overrule a U.S. Supreme Court ruling from 1992\nthat retailers with no physical presence in a state should not\nhave to pay sales tax there. Critics have charged he\u2019s just\nstringing out his price advantage as long as possible.  On Sept. 7, Amazon finally compromised in California,\nagreeing to start collecting sales tax in the state by November\n2012. Bezos says that by then the federal government will\nuniformly set nationwide standards for the collection of online\nsales tax.  \u201cYou have to do what you think is correct,\u201d he says.\n\u201cObviously we care about perception but we also value substance\nand the right place to fix this is in federal legislation.\u201d  Losing the tax advantage may not be such a bad thing. If and\nwhen Amazon starts collecting sales tax, it will be free to set\nup distribution centers right outside major cities, which would\nenable even faster deliveries than it offers now.  Same-Day Deliveries  As part of Amazon\u2019s deal with California, for example, the\ncompany has pledged to spend $500 million on new warehouses\nand hire 10,000 full-time workers and 25,000 seasonal employees.  Customers in California may soon end up getting same-day\ndeliveries of products and even produce. Amazon\u2019s experimental\n\u201cFresh\u201d grocery program is now active in Seattle, where the\ncompany already collects sales tax.  Nancy Koehn of Harvard Business School says Amazon may be\ngetting big enough for people to finally start considering the\nramifications -- for towns, shopping centers, and jobs --- of a\nworld dominated by online buying. She recently discussed Amazon\non Wisconsin Public Radio --- not the most neutral forum --- but\nwas surprised when almost all of the phone calls from listeners\nwere critical of the company.  \u201cAmericans get very nervous about centralized power that -\naffects their communities,\u201d she says. \u201cWe get a little bit\nnervous about bigness, yet we want the convenience and the -\npricing and the material plenty that bigness allows.\u201d  11 New Buildings  Amazon\u2019s new Seattle campus testifies to that growing size.\nThe company has leased 11 brand new buildings in the burgeoning\nSouth Lake Union neighborhood from real estate developer and\n Microsoft Corp. (MSFT)  co-founder Paul Allen. It\u2019s classic Amazon:\nunostentatious, and no -company signs on any of the buildings.\nThe entire campus is due to be completed by 2013 and will host\nseveral thousand employees, but the company is growing so fast,\nit\u2019s already looking for even more space.  In Day One South, Bezos would clearly rather discuss the\nKindle Fire than real estate, sales taxes, or air conditioning.\nFormer employees of Lab126 say the chief executive officer\nspends an -unusual amount of his time delving into the gritty\ndetails of his fledgling hardware business, and can happily talk\nfor hours about the location of this or that button on a device.  \u201cI spent a huge amount of time working on Kindle Fire,\u201d he\nsays. Edelman, founder of the\nworld\u2019s largest independent public-relations firm, with a client\nlist that includes Microsoft Corp., Wal-Mart Stores Inc. and\nGeneral Electric Co., has died. He was 92.  He died yesterday of heart failure, according to a\nstatement from his company, citing his wife, Ruth Edelman.  The firm that Edelman started in 1952 in  Chicago  now has 66\noffices and more than 4,500 employees worldwide, according to\nits  website . It is part of closely held Daniel J. Edelman Inc.,\nof which he remained chairman.  Edelman \u201cwas the acknowledged leader in public relations\nfor consumer products and gained fame in the USA as the creator\nof the media tour -- a PR technique in which a company\nspokesperson visited key markets, performed store openings, did\nradio and newspaper interviews and, most important of all,\nparticipated in a talk show on local television,\u201d  according to \n\u201cThe Global Public Relations Handbook: Theory, Research and\nPractice\u201d (2009), edited by Krishnamurthy Sriramesh and Dejan\nVercic.  Edelman\u2019s choice of Vincent Price as spokesman for the\nCalifornia wine industry in 1966 was one of the first\ndeployments of a celebrity in a PR campaign, according to the\nfirm.  Firm\u2019s Milestones  Other milestones the firm cites include repositioning\nKentucky Fried Chicken as KFC in 1975, establishing the first\nfree consumer help-line with the Butterball Turkey Talk-line to\nhelp holiday-season cooks in 1981, managing the release of the\nIraq Study Group Report in 2006 and helping Starbucks run its\n40th anniversary campaign in 2011.  Edelman retired as chief executive officer in 1996, handing\nthe reins to his son, Richard Edelman.  Daniel Joseph Edelman was born on July 3, 1920, in New York\nCity. He graduated from Columbia University in 1940 and earned a\nmaster\u2019s degree in journalism a year later from its Graduate\nSchool of Journalism.  He worked as a reporter in Poughkeepsie, New York, before\nserving in World War II in a psychological warfare unit --\n\u201cdoing a lot of writing and nightly analysis of German\npropaganda,\u201d he recalled in an  interview  with the Arthur W.\nPage Center for Integrity in Public Communication, part of Penn\nState University.  Before founding his firm on Oct. 1, 1952, in an office in\nChicago\u2019s Merchandise Mart, Edelman wrote news for CBS and\nhandled public relations for a hair-care company that later was\nacquired by Gillette Co. The legislation is opposed by public employee unions,\nwhich say it would mark a costly intrusion into the taxing\nauthority of local governments.  The varying state laws can be a burden to employees who\nmust file taxes in multiple jurisdictions and businesses that\nmust keep track of where their income is earned.  Dozens of companies, including  AT&T Inc. (T) ,  Hewlett-Packard\nCo. (HPQ)  and  Lockheed Martin Corp. (LMT)  signed a letter to congressional\nleaders urging them to pass the measure. Supporters said it will\nsimplify tax rules at odds with an increasingly mobile\nworkforce.  Not all workers would benefit. The limits won\u2019t apply to\nthe earnings of athletes, entertainers and public figures who\ncommand hefty speaking fees, which states would be allowed to\ntax as they do currently. The measure\u2019s effects will depend on the difference\nbetween the amount states lose by taxing visiting workers and\nhow much comes back from their residents.  States such as  New York  that draw a large number of\ntraveling workers would lose the most, the budget office said,\nwhile nearby states such as Connecticut and New Jersey probably\nwould gain  tax revenue .
