(PFE) , is taking more control of his fortune.  Lubin, 52, chairman of Upsher Asset Management, a so-called single-family office that oversees the assets of his family and three others descended from his grandfather, is shifting capital from outside funds into direct investments. Family offices increased their direct allocations to private companies and real estate last year to an average of 11 percent from 6 percent in 2009, according to a study to be released today by the  Wharton Global Family Alliance .  \u201cIf you have a third or half of your portfolio where you\u2019re paying 2 and 20, suddenly you\u2019re saying, \u2018You know what, these guys are eating up half of my return,\u2019\u201d Lubin said of fees charged by many private equity and hedge funds, traditionally 2 percent of assets and 20 percent of profits. \u201cThat doesn\u2019t make any sense. There\u2019s got to be a better way.\u201d  Single-family offices are investing directly because of declining fund returns and concerns that some outside managers charge high fees and may have conflicts of interest, according to Wharton. The offices generally are dedicated to the investment oversight and financial planning of one clan. They usually serve families worth at least $100 million, such as those of computer maker  Michael Dell  and  Microsoft Corp. (MSFT)  co- founder Bill Gates.  Upsher Asset Management devotes about 7 percent of its assets to direct investments in private companies or  real estate , compared with none five years ago, said Lubin, who is also managing partner of the New York-based venture-capital firm Radius Ventures LLC.  \u2018Profound Changes\u2019  \u201cThere are profound changes that occurred as a result of the 2008 and 2009 economic recession and financial crisis,\u201d said Raphael \u201cRaffi\u201d Amit, chairman of the Wharton Global Family Alliance, a unit of the University of Pennsylvania\u2019s Wharton School in Philadelphia that focuses on wealthy families and their businesses.  Families reported a fivefold increase in their allotments to art collections and precious metals, which made up 5 percent on average in 2011, according to the study.  They cut their average outlay for private equity funds to 9 percent from 11 percent two years earlier. The average portion in hedge funds stayed the same at about 12 percent, while investments dedicated to funds of funds dropped to almost zero.  Conflict Potential  \u201cWe see almost a move completely out of fund of funds,\u201d Amit said. \u201cThese trends are a result of poor performance of fund of funds and the deep concern that family offices have about conflicts of interests at large financial-service companies. That\u2019s something that the big banks have to take notice of.\u201d  Funds of hedge funds lost an average of 3 percent annually in the four years through 2011, according to  Bloomberg\u2019s indexes for funds . Funds of funds seek to minimize risk a client would have from investing with a single manager. They generally add a layer of fees on top of the cost of the underlying investments. Funds of funds charge an average 7.6 percent performance fee and 1.3 percent management fee, according to data compiled by Bloomberg.  The Wharton report is based on a survey of 106 families from 24 countries conducted last year. About 41 percent of the respondents were based in the Americas. Amit declined to release country-specific data to preserve confidentiality. Sixty-three percent of respondents held more than $500 million in assets.  Privacy, Control  Advantages of single- family offices  include privacy, control and customization. There probably are about 400 in the U.S. with more than $500 million in assets that provide investment management, administrative and family services as independent firms with their own staffs, Amit said.  \u201cPeople were a little less focused on what it cost to invest and what we were paying managers to get their expertise,\u201d before 2008, said Lubin. Since then many family offices have become more focused on risk management, liquidity and fees as returns declined.  Along with paying management and incentive fees, clients in private-equity and hedge funds may be required to commit their money for a period of years.  The median private-equity fund that made its first investment in 2003 produced a 12 percent internal rate of return as of the end the first quarter, compared with 8.8 percent for funds that started in 2008, according to data compiled by Seattle-based researcher  PitchBook Data Inc .  Real Estate  Lubin\u2019s family office brought in a new adviser for its hedge-fund strategy, hired managers to add investments in commodities and precious metals, and is building its own real estate portfolio, he said. The firm has done more direct deals in industries it\u2019s familiar with such as health care since the financial crisis rather than using a fund that may charge high fees and have a lock-up period.  The single-family office this year purchased units in New York\u2019s  condominium market  to rent, he said.  \u201cWe will continue to methodically add to the portfolio over the next several years,\u201d Lubin said.  \u201cFamilies found that some of their providers really were conflicted\u201d by fees from certain products or trading revenue, said Laird Pendleton, co-founder of the  CCC Alliance LLC , a private consortium of single family offices based in  Boston . \u201cPeople are in-sourcing much of that now.\u201d  Adding Staff  Single-family offices saw a 25 percent increase in staff hired to select investment managers and a 12 percent expansion in those dedicated to monitoring performance, according to the Wharton  study .  Pendleton also is co-founder and principal of Cairnwood Cooperative Corp., an office that manages his family\u2019s wealth into its sixth generation. Pendleton, 57, said his great- grandfather in 1883 started Pittsburgh Plate Glass Co., known today as  PPG Industries Inc. (PPG)  The family has increased its direct investments in venture capital and private companies since 2008, he said.  \u201cThe crisis showed that a lot of hedge funds and other investments in the alternative area are really a handshake deal,\u201d Pendleton said. \u201cThere is in many cases a very weak mechanism for being able to go in and remove your assets from a fund.\u201d  He and Lubin declined to disclosed their family offices\u2019 assets under management.  Dell, Gates  Dell, the founder, chairman and chief executive officer of computer maker  Dell Inc. (DELL) , formed a money-management firm called  MSD Capital LP  in 1998 dedicated to investing his family\u2019s assets. The firm has more than $12 billion under management and a staff of about 80 people. It is focused solely on investments for the family in asset classes including publicly traded securities, private equity and real estate.  Todd Fogarty, a spokesman for New York-based MSD, declined to comment on the firm\u2019s investments.  Cascade Investment LLC is the personal holding company dedicated to Microsoft co-founder Gates\u2019s investments. The Kirkland, Washington-based firm oversees about three-quarters of Gates\u2019s $64.6 billion fortune, according to data compiled by the  Bloomberg Billionaires Index . Bridgitt Arnold, a family spokeswoman, declined to comment.  About 52 percent of single-family offices reviewed their investment policies this year, compared with 40 percent in 2011, according to a separate study released yesterday by the  Family Wealth Alliance , a research and consulting firm. About 27 percent made changes such as placing more emphasis on capital preservation, short-term liquidity and diversification, said Robert Casey, senior managing director for research at the Wheaton, Illinois-based firm.  Ideal Structure  The Family Wealth Alliance study is based on responses from 34 offices, Casey said.  The most successful single-family offices are structured with investment-policy statements, succession-plan documents, education for younger generations and staff dedicated to selecting investment managers and monitoring portfolios, the Wharton study found. That puts the region, with a population of about 26 million, well ahead of countries such as  Spain , which has about 47 million people, and  Italy , with about 61 million.  \u201cIf I\u2019m selling a business with lots of exposure to  France , the interest goes down fast,\u201d said Kristian Terling, who handles the Nordic business for Los Angeles-based investment bank Houlihan Lokey. \u201cI say \u2018 Sweden ,\u2019 the mood softens.\u201d  Sweden\u2019s economy has grown by more than 10 percent since 2009, according to government records. While Sweden\u2019s growth for 2012 is projected to have slowed to 0.9 percent, it\u2019s still expected to beat the euro region, which is contracting. All of the Nordic countries boast triple-A credit ratings and the region overall is projected to expand by 2.1 percent this year.  \u201cThe countries are very well established with good growth records, they speak English, and they have stable politics,\u201d says Pip McCrostie, global vice chair of transaction advisory services at Ernst & Young, based in London. \u201cMoney always flows to the safe haven when it\u2019s looking to avoid risk.\u201d  Global Footprint  Foreign buyers are especially drawn by the global footprint of the region\u2019s companies.  \u201cMany Nordic-headquartered businesses have specific technologies and products with global reach,\u201d says Tom Bernhardsen, a director at  Credit Suisse Group (CSGN) \u2019s investment bank handling Nordic countries and energy services.  In December, Deerfield, Illinois-based  Baxter International (BAX)  agreed to pay about $4 billion to acquire Swedish medical- equipment maker Gambro, which has 13 production facilities in nine countries and sales in more than 100 nations.  That same rationale applies to speculation of an eventual takeover of Finnish mobile-phone maker  Nokia Oyj (NOK1V)  by  Microsoft Corp. (MSFT) , which already collaborate on smartphones, analysts and bankers have said. Another deal that could break: Nokia Siemens Networks, Nokia\u2019s equipment joint venture with Siemens AG, may reignite takeover interest after the company topped Nokia\u2019s earlier quarterly estimates, analysts said.  Among the Scandinavian countries, Sweden draws the most buyers, with $113 billion of acquisitions since 2007 by companies with headquarters abroad, followed by  Norway  with $95 billion, according to data compiled by Bloomberg. About 631,000 Swedish companies, amounting to more than 20 percent of the country\u2019s private sector, were owned by foreign companies in 2011, compared with less than 5 percent in 1980, according to a report from the country\u2019s official statistics bureau.  Little Opposition  Stefan Folster, chief economist at the Confederation of Swedish Enterprise, said the country appreciates the new capital, ideas, and markets that come with foreign ownership.  \u201cThe history of Volvo Cars is a very good example of a company people believe wouldn\u2019t have survived had it remained Swedish,\u201d he said.  Ford Motor  bought Volvo in 1999, then sold it to  China \u2019s Zhejiang  Geely Holding (175)  Group in 2010. There\u2019s been little opposition to the fallout from cross-border deals in Scandinavia, in contrast to increasing protest elsewhere in Europe, says Folster. Volvo saw minimal resistance when it cut production in Sweden while seeking to expand operations in China.  Acquisitions by Nordic buyers in 2012 fell 42 percent from 2008 levels, to $45 billion, according to Bloomberg data, even though Scandinavian companies hold about $103 billion of cash, 30 percent more than they did four years ago.  \u201cThey have the financial strength for deals but are worried about the economic outlook,\u201d Terling, of Houlihan Lokey, said.  Statoil  One company that may look outward is  Statoil ASA (STL) , Norway\u2019s biggest energy explorer and 67 percent-owned by the government. It\u2019s hunting for targets in the U.S., people familiar with the company have said. It would have the financial muscle to pursue companies such as  EOG Resources Inc. (EOG) , a $34 billion Houston- based crude oil producer whose chief executive officer, Mark Papa, is retiring in June, analysts said earlier this year.  Meanwhile, local companies are showing no skittishness in acquiring one another -- for the same reasons that attract foreign buyers. Fiskars, a 363-year-old Finnish maker of kitchenware, agreed to buy Danish porcelain maker  Royal Copenhagen (RBREW)  in December for 66 million euros ($89 million) in a push to become more global, said Kari Kauniskangas, Fiskars\u2019s chief executive officer.  \u201cWe\u2019ll build on Royal Copenhagen\u2019s position in  Asia , and can access new markets such as central Europe,\u201d he said. Amid multicolored beanbags, web designers, animators and cartoonists are toiling away on this July day, Bloomberg Markets magazine reports in its October issue. Were it not for dozens of Apple Macintosh screens atop desks, the warehouselike space might be mistaken for a student common room.  Omar Al Abdallat, a well-known political cartoonist, clicks on one of his latest creations for  Kharabeesh , Think Arabia\u2019s website: a drawing of a terrified child peeking out of a hole shaped like a map of  Syria . Al Abdallat, 32, is recruiting top cartoonists from across the  Middle East  to provide animated video content for the Arab world.  Founded in 2008 by blogger Wael Attili and some friends, Kharabeesh, which means doodles in Arabic, is creating videos that attract 20 million views a month.  Before there was an Arab Spring, there was a quiet revolution of sorts brewing in  Jordan .  The country experienced a tech boom that gained speed as young Arabs toppled regimes from  Egypt  to  Tunisia  and millions were driven online for the first time. Jordan now hosts about three-quarters of all Arabic content on the Internet, according to the Geneva-based International Telecommunication Union (ITU).  \u2018Not Free\u2019  Can it last? Doubts grew in September when the Jordanian parliament passed a law curtailing freedom of expression on the Internet and giving the government broad powers to block websites it deems inappropriate.  \u201cThe law is so vague you could drive a truck through it,\u201d says Abdelmajeed Shamlawi, chief executive officer of the  Information and Communications Technology Association  of Jordan.  The law, which was passed a few days after demonstrators took to the streets in Amman to protest an anti-Islam video that originated in the U.S. and was broadcast on the Internet, was deplored by groups such as  Human Rights Watch  as an instance of state censorship.  On a scale of 1 (most free) to 7 (least free), Jordan scores 5.5, or \u201cnot free,\u201d according to the Freedom in the World 2011 report published by  Washington-based Freedom House .  Still, even with large Palestinian and Iraqi communities inside its borders, and flanked by a deepening civil war in Syria, Jordan remains relatively stable by regional standards.  Silicon Wadi  While online enterprises crop up from Cairo to  Qatar , Amman is the closest thing the Middle East has to a Silicon Valley outside  Israel  and has been dubbed Silicon Wadi (Arabic for valley).  The capital, as a hub for Internet businesses, has the potential to benefit from a growing regional market. Only 29 percent of the Middle East\u2019s population used the Internet last year compared with 68 percent in  Europe  and 78 percent in the U.S.,  according to the ITU .  With roughly two-thirds of the population under 30 years old, the region has one of the fastest-growing Internet penetration rates in the world.  From June 2010 to June 2012, the number of people in the Middle East using social media such as Facebook almost tripled to 45.2 million from 16 million, according to the  Dubai School of Government .  In Jordan, entrepreneurs have been thriving, aided by an educated, English-speaking professional class and, compared with the pricier Persian Gulf capitals, affordable living costs.  Brain Gain  The surge in business activity is luring Jordanian expatriates back to the fold; there\u2019s even a LinkedIn group called Jordan\u2019s Brain Gain, with more than 2,700 members as of September.  Israel, home to the largest number of startup companies per capita in the world, is unchallenged as the region\u2019s information and communications technology powerhouse. Its ICT industry generated 82.5 billion Israeli shekels ($20.5 billion) in revenue in 2011, or 12.1 percent of the country\u2019s gross domestic product, according to the government\u2019s Central Bureau of Statistics.  Although comparable businesses in Jordan produced a relatively small amount of revenue in 2010 -- $2.2 billion -- they represented 14 percent of the country\u2019s GDP, the same share as tourism, and the fastest-growing part of the economy, according to the technology association.  The country remains poor. Jordan had a per capita GDP of $4,666 in 2011, placing it 103rd among nations, one notch above  Ecuador  and one below  Turkmenistan , according to the  World Bank . Unlike some of its neighbors, Jordan has no significant  oil deposits .  \u2018ICT Leader\u2019  King Abdullah  II, who came to power in 1999 after the death of his father, King Hussein, has for years proclaimed his modernization goals. He has tried to create incentives for entrepreneurs to build businesses from e-commerce companies to Web-based media.  Abdullah, who was educated in the U.K. and the U.S. and whose wife, Queen Rania, worked briefly for Apple Inc. and Citigroup Inc., presided over the deregulation of the Jordanian telecommunications industry and increased funding for computer education at schools and universities.  \u201cWe are the ICT leader in the Arab world,\u201d King Abdullah said in an e-mail in response to questions. \u201cAs a small country that accounts for only 2 percent of the region\u2019s population, imagine what it means to us that we produce and manage 75 percent of all Arabic-language Internet content.\u201d  \u2018Chilling Effect\u2019  And yet it was the king who endorsed the new rules that have alarmed Jordan\u2019s growing community of Internet entrepreneurs.  The law requires any website hosted in Jordan whose \u201cactivity includes publishing news, investigative reports, articles and comments related to the internal or external affairs of the Kingdom\u201d to be licensed by the government and holds the sites responsible for the accuracy of their content and for user comments posted there.  \u201cIt will have a chilling effect,\u201d says Christoph Wilcke, Jordan researcher for  Human Rights Watch . \u201cWe are seeing a regression on the king\u2019s reform agenda.\u201d King Abdullah didn\u2019t respond to requests for comment on the law.  For now, Jordanian entrepreneurs are creating some of the Middle East\u2019s biggest e-commerce platforms such as Souq.com and MarkaVIP to feed consumer demand -- including demand from wealthy Arab women in countries such as Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates.  \u2019Gold Rush\u2019  \u201cThis is the last Internet gold rush to be had,\u201d says Khaldoon Tabaza, the founder and CEO of Amman-based Zad Capital, a  venture capital  firm, who is building a new holding company for e-commerce startups called iMENA.  Amman is the birthplace of the Arab world\u2019s most successful Internet venture: Maktoob, a portal that in 2000 made it possible to send and receive e-mail in Arabic for the first time. In 2009, Maktoob founders Samih Toukan and Hussam Khoury sold the company to  Yahoo! Inc. (YHOO)  for $175 million.  The deal was a boon to investors. The private-equity arm of Chase Coleman\u2019s New York-based Tiger Global Management LLC cashed in its more than 40 percent stake, which it had begun acquiring in 2006. Tiger Global topped Bloomberg Markets\u2019 2011 ranking of the world\u2019s best-performing large hedge funds.  The result was a \u201cMaktoob effect,\u201d demonstrating that the Internet in the Middle East offers business potential, says Fadi Ghandour, a Jordanian who founded Dubai-based  Aramex PJSC (ARMX) , the largest courier company in the region.  Paving the Way  \u201cMaktoob has become the rallying call for young entrepreneurs,\u201d Ghandour says.  Ghandour, 53, helped pave the way. He was a founding investor in Maktoob and is a backer of four-year-old Kharabeesh along with a dozen other startups. He\u2019s also chairman of  Wamda , an Internet platform that tracks entrepreneurship, and has a fund to invest in startups in conjunction with Dubai-based Abraaj Capital Ltd.  Startup success is constrained by Jordan\u2019s size, a lack of venture capital and an obstructive patchwork of multiple customs and immigration authorities in the region. Jordan\u2019s population of 6 million people means that tech startups need to target bigger and wealthier markets for profit.  \u201cNobody is building for Jordan; they\u2019re building for the region and the world,\u201d says Emile Cubeisy, who manages Accelerator Technology Holdings\u2019 $30 million Badia Impact Fund, which provides early-stage finance for Jordanian tech startups. \u201cWe are a region of 300 million people that share one common culture and common language, yet as markets we are completely disconnected.\u201d  Rich Propsect  Still, Fawaz Zu\u2019bi, Jordan\u2019s minister of telecommunications from 2000 to 2004, says the country\u2019s tech industry could be generating about $4 billion a year by 2017. He founded Amman- based Accelerator Technology, which has raised a total of $80 million from investors such as Chicago-based real estate tycoon Sam Zell and C-SPAN co-founder  John Evans .  Zu\u2019bi and Cubeisy have jointly invested in 20 companies, mostly in the Middle East.  One of their most successful investments is Rubicon Group Holding, an Amman-based computer animation company set up by Randa Ayoubi in 1994 with just $150,000. Ayoubi\u2019s firm is generating about $40 million of revenue annually. GrowthGate Capital Corp., a Bahrain-based private-equity firm, took a 30 percent stake in Rubicon for an undisclosed sum. Ayoubi says she\u2019s considering taking her company public.  Investors such as Tabaza of iMENA say creating Arabic content is a rich prospect. While almost 5 percent of all  Internet users  are Arabic speakers, less than 2 percent of content is in Arabic, according to the ITU.  Proving Ground  E-commerce in the Middle East is in its infancy, with only about $11 billion worth of sales, according to Amman-based Arab Advisors Group. Europe, the largest e-commerce market in the world, posted sales last year totaling 246 billion euros ($309 billion), according to the  European Multi-channel and Online Trade Association .  Perhaps the most dynamic proving ground for technology startups in the Arab world can be found on the outskirts of Amman at  King Hussein  Business Park, home to Microsoft Corp., Hewlett-Packard Co. and a new, homegrown technology incubator called Oasis500.  Led by Usama Fayyad, 49, who was Yahoo\u2019s global chief data officer from 2004 to 2008, Oasis500 is aiming to create 500 companies in five years by providing something Fayyad says is missing in the Middle East: seed-stage and early-stage money.  \u201cA lot of ideas get suppressed or die in the desert of early-stage investment,\u201d Fayyad says.  \u2018Boot Camps\u2019  To nurture startups,  Oasis500  offers entrepreneurs five- week-long \u201cboot camps\u201d and cash infusions of $15,000 apiece in exchange for small slices of equity. From early 2010 to June 2012, Oasis500 raised about $6 million for early-stage financing. Since September 2010, it has invested in about 55 companies, double the number Fayyad originally projected; only three companies had failed as of September 2012.  Oasis500 has already cashed out of one of its incubated investments, an e-commerce site called Run2sport.com, which bills itself as the first online sports shop in the Middle East.  Last year, after an Oasis500 angel-network event, Fayyad personally invested in Amman-based  MarkaVIP , a Middle East- focused, invitation-only shopping site. Offering discounts on designer goods, MarkaVIP says it has 2 million users and is on track to report $100 million of revenue in 2012.  Battling Distrust  MarkaVIP encapsulates the opportunities and difficulties of Amman startups.  It raised $10 million in April from investors, led by Amsterdam-based Prime Ventures. That funding came on top of $5 million in November 2011 from New York-based Invus Financial Advisors; Antwerp, Belgium-based Hummingbird Ventures; and San Francisco-based Lumia Capital -- all of which demonstrates the region\u2019s potential, says Martin Gedalin, a partner at Lumia who sits on MarkaVIP\u2019s board.  \u201cThe Middle East was a region that was being underappreciated by investors in the States,\u201d he says.  On the downside, e-commerce sites such as MarkaVIP have had to battle the distrust in the Middle East of using credit cards online. About 80 percent of its sales are made in cash-on- delivery terms.  Amer Abulaila, one of MarkaVIP\u2019s founders, and his partner Ahmed Alkhatib have spent the past year building hand-delivery and payment systems in Jordan and the U.A.E. and are in the process of setting up Qatar and Saudi Arabia.  \u2018First Wave\u2019  \u201cWe are trying to make this business scalable,\u201d Abulaila says, chain-smoking as a Mac screen on his desk displays the pleasing sight of that day\u2019s sales ticking rapidly upward.  The Middle East tech business is a work in progress, Gedalin says.  \u201cThere\u2019s a lot of consumer demand in these markets, so you see online commerce as the first wave of innovation,\u201d he says. Whether other waves keep on coming will depend to some extent on the future of freedom of expression in Jordan. To contact the reporter on this story:\nAdam Satariano in  San Francisco  at \n asatariano1@bloomberg.net   To contact the editor responsible for this story:\nTom Giles at \n tgiles5@bloomberg.net","path":".\/2008_2012_msft_bloomberg_news\/apple-s-ipad-leads-surge-in-tablet-shipments-research-firm-says.txt"},{"id":84494199,"title":"Publicis-Omnicom Merger Won't Save the Madmen","released_at":"<date>July 29 2013<\/date> <time>19:41:14<\/time>","content":"A \"merger of equals\" is how Omnicom Group Inc. and Publicis Groupe SA  describe  their trans-Atlantic combination. It's true in the sense that the companies are equally doomed -- for reasons that their Madmen Merger won't do much to forestall. To paraphrase the chief executive officers, Maurice Levy of Publicis and John Wren of Omnicom, the rationale behind their surprise deal can be summed up as the three S's: size (good for pricing muscle), synergies (good for cost-cutting) and software (good for Big Data analysis). But the problems facing the two advertising giants, and traditional advertising in general, have little to do with a lack of size or an absence of synergies. They have a lot to do with revolutionary changes in the advertising landscape, including the arrival of new media giants like Google Inc., Facebook Inc. and Twitter Inc., the explosion of Big Data and changes in consumer behavior.  In recent years, these changes have brought forth such innovations as automated trading of ad space and data-driven analysis of consumer buying habits. Messages can be tailored to individuals like never before, because companies are collecting and analyzing mass quantities of data that consumers reveal about themselves as they surf the Web, compose blogs, post personal details on social media and purchase items with credit cards.  The ability to push an ad for engine tune-up service to the mobile device of someone who just searched the Web for the nearest auto repair shop is more important than the relationships of yore -- among corporate ad buyers, ad agencies' creative talent and media space buyers, and the sales staffs for newspapers and TV and radio outlets.  Television is still the major beneficiary of U.S. ad spending, with about $66 billion this year. Yet  online ads  are gaining, with about $43 billion. Of that, mobile devices are the biggest target, with about $4 billion in ads and growing fast, according to eMarketer.  Automated ad buying, or programmatic purchasing, is in its infancy, with about $3.4 billion in sales. But it will grow quickly because real-time bidding for space is efficient and less costly -- precisely because it cuts middlemen like Publicis Omnicom out of the picture.  Such digital disintermediation has forced wrenching change in many an industry, including music, television, book publishing, newspapers, stock exchanges and financial services. Many companies tried to forestall those changes by merging -- a strategy that is expensive and largely proven not to work.  Google is the biggest digital winner of all. The top five ad agencies would have to merge before their annual sales added up to Google's 2012 revenue of $50 billion, most of which came from its advertising business. Google sells online search ads and operates one of the biggest automated advertising marketplaces, which works much like a Nasdaq for online ad space. Facebook is another big winner. It has more than 1 billion users posting reams of personal details every month, allowing Facebook to build a massive database on buying habits that advertisers can use to target messages. True, traditional ad agencies now work with Google, Facebook and Twitter, but the tech companies can easily bypass the agencies to work directly with, say, Ford Motor Co. or PepsiCo Inc.  The integrated ad agency, moreover, is under attack from still other new entrants, including IBM Corp., Oracle Corp. and Microsoft Corp. All have spent heavily to acquire the talent and develop the software to analyze consumer data for large companies. The merger of Publicis and Omnicom may give the new company market muscle when it comes time to buy space for clients looking to cut their advertising costs. But it won't do much to help them compete against the force of creative destruction known as Silicon Valley. (Paula Dwyer is a member of the Bloomberg View editorial board. Today's  story  by Bloomberg News's Michael Riley presents a new question: should we be upset that companies voluntarily assist U.S. cyber-attacks on other countries?  Under what's called the ``trusted partners'' program, thousands of American corporations, including Internet and technology companies, hardware and software makers, banks and Web security providers are voluntarily turning over sensitive information to U.S. national security agencies, Riley reported. In return, U.S. companies get favors from the government, ranging from a pat on the back to access to classified intelligence about issues affecting their businesses.  The government can use that information to infiltrate or attack the computers of foreign governments or other organizations. For example, Microsoft tells American intelligence agencies about bugs in its software programs before they're fixed, which lets the government exploit the flaws. One tech executive called the data voluntarily provided to the government \"highly offensive\" in value. After last week's news that the National Security Agency is tracking Americans' e-mails and phone calls, there's a temptation to view this latest story in the same vein of conspiracy and government overreach. But the data being shared don't include the private communications of the companies' customers, according to Riley's sources.  Nor is it clear that U.S. companies are in breach of any ethical obligations by voluntarily cooperating with national security officials. (There's no allegation of a breach of the law, or of customers' privacy.) You could argue that companies such as Microsoft shouldn't aide attacks on foreign governments, but the principle behind that view looks more like pacifism than any clear reading of business ethics. If these revelations raise new worries, they're for shareholders. By allying with the U.S. government to enable cyberattacks on other countries, these companies become participants in those conflicts, and so may be at greater risk of retaliation by the organizations the U.S. targets. Submitting to legally binding demands for data is one thing; signing up as a voluntary member of the country's cybersecurity forces is another. Executives may conclude those risks are outweighed by the business value of whatever they get in return, or they may feel they're doing their patriotic duty. Either way, because of the secretive nature of these arrangements shareholders aren't aware of that decision, let alone given the chance to sign off on it. The dilemma increases in the case of foreign investors, who may own shares in companies that are helping to undermine their countries' cyberdefenses. And some shareholders may simply prefer that executives stick to the job of running their companies, not role-play in a John le Carre novel. Getting into bed with the national-security apparatus raises questions about the appropriateness of executives choosing to play in an arena they may not understand, with consequences they might not be able to predict, and without the knowledge of their shareholders. The tradeoffs may be worth it, but in these early days of cyberwarfare it isn't clear how anyone can say so with confidence.  (Christopher Flavelle is a member of the Bloomberg View editorial board. Maybe a degree from the  London School  of\nEconomics.  It\u2019s been awhile since a new version of Office stirred a\nlot of excitement. So much has already been built into the\nworld\u2019s most popular productivity suite over the years that it\u2019s\nhard to get too worked up over new features. Threaded comments\nin Word! Recommended PivotTables in Excel!  Still, the new Office is worth paying attention to for a\ncouple of reasons. It\u2019s the first one designed for use in the\nera of cloud-connected devices, touchscreens and tablets. And\nMicrosoft is radically changing how it\u2019s priced and sold to\nconsumers.  The cloud -- in this case, Microsoft\u2019s  Office.com  website\nand SkyDrive service -- is integral to the new offering.  Facing a threat from  Google (GOOG) \u2019s online suite of productivity\napplications, Microsoft has adopted a hybrid model. Unlike the\nGoogle Docs approach, major Office components are still\ninstalled locally on your computer, giving you full access and\nflexibility even when you are offline.  If you\u2019re signed into Office.com, your files, formatting\nand preferred settings will be seamlessly saved to  SkyDrive ,\ngiving you access to your work even if you\u2019re signing in from\nanother computer -- or a Windows Phone, for that matter. If\nyou\u2019re not online, changes you make locally to a file will be\nautomatically synced the next time you connect.  Touch-Friendlier  New features are designed to make Office friendlier to\nusers of tablets and touchscreens. For example, a toolbar option\nlets you space icons farther apart to make them easier to poke\nwith a finger.  One option I found particularly appealing on a touchscreen\ntablet display is Word\u2019s new Read mode that automatically\nreflows text. And OneNote lets you draw or write on screen using\na finger or stylus and gives you a full-screen view in the new\nWindows 8 style.  The biggest change to Office, though, is in how it\u2019s sold.\nMicrosoft wants you to think of it not as a product you purchase\nonce every several years, but as a service you subscribe to and\npay for every year, called Office 365 Home Premium.  Blurred Line  The concept is in keeping with the times, where the line\nbetween software and services is increasingly blurred. But it\ncan make the process of figuring out what\u2019s best for you almost\ninsanely complicated.  OK, stay with me now.  A subscription to Office 365 will cost $100 a year. For\nthat, PC users will get the full complement of Office programs:\nWord, PowerPoint, Excel, Outlook, OneNote, Access and Publisher.  You may install them on up to five computers, so one\nsubscription can take care of an entire family. You also get\naccess to Web-based versions of the programs, in case you\u2019re\nworking on someone else\u2019s computer, and 27 gigabytes of SkyDrive\nstorage, rather than the seven gigabytes Microsoft gives away\nfor free.  Plus 60 minutes of worldwide phone time per month via\n Skype . Plus, if there\u2019s an  Apple (AAPL)  user in the family, he or she\ncan get the Mac version of Office on the same subscription.  Whew! Sounds like quite a deal, and it may be -- if you\nneed all that. But many may find it overkill. How often does\nJunior really need to create a relational database in Access for\nhis homework?  One-Time Purchase  For most consumers, the alternative will be a one-time-only\npayment of $140 for a version called Office Home & Student,\nwhich includes Word, Excel, PowerPoint and OneNote. For the\nprevious version of Office, that one-time purchase bought you\nthe right to install it on three computers. But for the 2013\nedition, Microsoft has reduced it to one.  So to figure out the best deal for yourself, you have to\ntake into account how many computers you have, how many of the\nOffice component programs you\u2019re likely to use, whether and how\nmuch you want to use the cloud for storage, and how often you\ncall overseas -- just for starters.  And, of course, how you feel about committing yourself to\npay $100 a year, every year, or else see your Office files\ndegraded to a read-only form you can continue to access, but not\nedit.  I foresee consumers the world over logging on to\nMicrosoft\u2019s online store, or standing slack-jawed in their\nneighborhood  Staples (SPLS)  or  Best Buy (BBY) , trying to sort everything out.  Or maybe building a database in Access to keep track of all\nthe variables.  ( Rich Jaroslovsky  is a Bloomberg News columnist. The\nopinions expressed are his own.) No, really. Well, sort of.  The phone in question is the new Atrix 4G from Motorola\nMobility Holdings Inc., for which  AT&T Inc . will begin taking\norders on Sunday. To be honest, I didn\u2019t actually do any writing\non the Atrix\u2019s four-inch touchscreen. Instead, I used the new\nMotorola Laptop Dock, which converts the phone, Transformers-\nstyle, into the brain of a netbook computer.  These are challenging times for AT&T, which this week lost\nits role as the exclusive U.S. source for  Apple Inc .\u2019s iPhone\nand needs to generate some buzz to counter the iPhone\u2019s arrival\non archrival Verizon Wireless\u2019s network.  While the Atrix is no iPhone-killer, it does deserve a\nlittle buzz. Yes, it\u2019s on the costly side, it\u2019s kind of geeky\nand its audience may be a bit narrow -- after all, how many\npeople really need a new phone and a new computer at exactly the\nsame time? -- but it\u2019s also innovative and, with a few\nexceptions, well-designed.  What makes the Atrix plausible as a netbook replacement is\nthe growing power being packed into smartphones. Many of the\nphone\u2019s specifications, including a dual-core processor and a\ngigabyte of memory, aren\u2019t out of place in an inexpensive\nlaptop.  Betting on Android  The Atrix, which costs $199.99 with a two-year AT&T\ncontract, is of a piece with the quality handsets Motorola has\nbeen producing since it bet its future on  Google Inc .\u2019s Android\noperating system two years ago. It includes a 5-megapixel rear\ncamera with dual LED flash that\u2019s also capable of shooting high-\nresolution video, a front-facing camera to allow video calling,\nand even a fingerprint reader. Unlike the iPhone, it will\ndisplay content that uses  Adobe Systems Inc .\u2019s Flash technology.  The Atrix is, in other words, a very nice smartphone. But\nthere are lots of very nice smartphones these days. What sets\nthis one apart is the laptop dock. AT&T is selling it in a\nbundle including the phone for $499.99 after a $100 rebate; it\nrequires an extra $20-a-month data-tethering plan that also lets\nthe phone share its Internet connection via Wi-Fi with other\nnearby devices.  The dock consists of an 11.6-inch screen, a near-full-sized\nkeyboard, a large trackpad, two mouse buttons and two USB ports.\nIt weighs less than three pounds with the phone and is quite\nuseless without it.  Coming to Life  To activate the dock, you plug the Atrix into a cradle that\nfolds out from behind the screen. Immediately, the laptop comes\nto life. A replica of the phone\u2019s screen gives you access to all\nits functions and apps. You can also surf the Web with Mozilla\nCorp.\u2019s  Firefox  browser, while a rudimentary file manager lets\nyou locate and navigate through information on the phone as if\nit were a PC.  The dock provides you with a number of productivity\noptions. The phone itself comes preloaded with  QuickOffice , an\napp that lets you create or open Microsoft Office-compatible\nfiles. You can also use Firefox to access  Google Docs  or\nMicrosoft\u2019s  Office Web Apps , which offer word processing,\nspreadsheet and other software that runs in the cloud -- on\ndistant Internet servers -- rather than locally on your own\ndevice.  In practice, you probably won\u2019t want to write the Great\nAmerican Novel on the  Atrix  dock. Among other things, printing\nfrom it is easiest if you have a wireless printer, which not\neveryone does. Still, it works very well for tweaking a\npresentation or memo, surfing the Web or updating your Facebook\nstatus.  Emergency Jolt  The dock has its own battery and will recharge the Atrix\neven if it isn\u2019t plugged into the wall. So if you manage to\nexhaust the phone\u2019s battery -- Motorola claims nine hours of\ntalk time -- you can pop it in for an emergency jolt.  The principal drawbacks I encountered centered around how\nyou can, or can\u2019t, use the phone while it\u2019s docked. Making or\nreceiving calls automatically puts the Atrix into speaker-phone\nmode, with the sound coming out of the dock\u2019s stereo speakers.\nWhile incoming calls were clear, they were also quiet, even with\nthe volume turned up as high as it would go.  Moreover, callers consistently complained that I sounded\nmuffled and distant unless I closed the laptop. In addition,\nbecause the screen blocks the phone and the dock has no camera,\nyou can\u2019t use it for video calls.  Besides the laptop dock, Motorola is also offering a\n$189.99 entertainment kit that provides a wireless keyboard and\nmouse, remote control and multimedia dock that lets you toss the\nphone\u2019s contents onto your big-screen TV.  Some people, I suspect, won\u2019t see much advantage in all\nthis expandability. In particular, the $500 price on the laptop\ndock if you buy it separately from the phone makes little sense\nwhen the same amount of money can net you a more-than-adequate\nlaptop that comes with its own brain and doesn\u2019t have to borrow\nyour phone\u2019s.  Still, as smartphones grow ever more powerful and\nubiquitous, expect to see more blurring of distinctions among\nmobile devices. The Atrix is clearly at the forefront of the\ntrend.    Rich Jaroslovsky  is a Bloomberg News columnist. The\nopinions expressed are his own.)  To contact the writer of this column:\nRich Jaroslovsky in  San Francisco  at \n rjaroslovsky@bloomberg.net . From\nits beginnings, the Information Age has been about better,\neasier access to new data, more and more kinds all day long and\nwherever we go.  According to the  University of California  at  San Diego \u2019s\nappropriately named  How Much Information  project, we now consume\nabout 100,000 words each day from various media. That\u2019s a\nwhopping 350 percent increase, measured in bytes, over what we\ncrunched back in 1980.  There\u2019s a lot of griping about TMI and ADD, but\nanthropologist Robert Kozinets suspects that most of it pertains\nto the workplace, where a person might indeed feel overwhelmed\nby unwelcome rings, pings and flashing lights.  \u201cIt\u2019s almost as if we live in two worlds,\u201d he says,\n\u201cbecause in our leisure time, we\u2019re more and more focused.\u201d His\nfavorite example is the expansion of fandom. These days, using\nthe Internet, sports and celebrity fanatics can revel in almost\ninstantaneous information.  Internet Expertise  Internet access , coupled with eminently portable laptops\nand smartphones, also liberates us in certain ways from\ntraditional categories. The old boundaries between the home and\nthe workplace or school grow fuzzier by the day. Thanks to blogs\nand websites like YouTube and Amazon, the lines between\n\u201camateur\u201d and \u201cprofessional\u201d have also blurred: Anyone can\nconsume culture and develop expertise, or hone their latent\ntalents. About 15 percent of Americans now engage in serious\nphotography, videography or filmmaking.  But now that the Internet provides so much art for free,\nmany creative people worry about survival, as do the flagging\nindustries that formerly supported them. Rather than seeing\nartists as an endangered species, however, marketing guru Seth Godin says, \u201cThey\u2019re the only people who are going to make money\n10 years from now, because the way you make money is from your\nideas.\u201d  Shepard Fairey  earns millions each year, even though his\nart is free -- unless you want a signed, limited-edition piece\nor an image to put on a corporate T-shirt. Those cost a lot,\nsays Godin, \u201cbut the only reason people pay is because his free\nideas are everywhere.\u201d Similarly, although the music business is\nailing, there is more music than ever being made and listened\nto. \u201cThe digital thing took away the requirement that you need\nan orchestra to write a symphony,\u201d Godin says.  Eric von Hippel, an innovation expert at the  Massachusetts\nInstitute of Technology \u2019s  Sloan School of Management , conducted\nresearch in  England  showing that individual consumers, often\naided by the Internet, spent twice as much money over a three-\nyear period as U.K. companies did on inventing new products and\ntweaking existing ones, particularly scientific tools and sports\nequipment. In a creative response to their generation\u2019s\ndisastrously high  unemployment rate , an eclectic group of\nmillionaires in their 20s who founded their own Internet\nbusinesses recently formed the nonprofit Young Entrepreneur\nCouncil, which advises others on how to start companies rather\nthan wait around for traditional jobs.  \u2018Collective Intelligence\u2019  That\u2019s only the beginning.  Information technology  has given\nus an immediate, you-are-there way to see everything from\nrevolutions to oil spills, and to react negatively or offer a\nhelping hand. Our smart tools also pull us together in new\ncommunities oriented around important issues. The notion of\n\u201ccollective intelligence\u201d first surfaced in the early 20th\ncentury, when American entomologist William Morton Wheeler\nobserved that a colony of ants could cooperatively act as a\n\u201csuperorganism.\u201d The term has gone through many iterations, but\nnow mostly refers to the cognitive surge that occurs when people\nand their computers are connected to one another. Instead of\njust thinking singly, we cogitate as a hive.  Neophiliacs  -- people who are strongly attracted to change\nand anything new -- are particularly attuned to the sociological\ntransformations under way in the Information Age. One example is\nthe way we think about culture: In what some critics view as a\nsociety ever more superficial, anthropologist Grant McCracken\nsees a tumultuous, yet vibrant, work in progress in which the\nold modifiers of \u201chigh\u201d and \u201clow\u201d no longer apply. \u201cThese kids\nare so good at media that they don\u2019t have any of that hesitation\nof \u2018Oh, this isn\u2019t something I can afford to take seriously --\nit\u2019s not high culture,\u2019\u201d McCracken says. \u201cThey gave up that\nambivalence and embrace pop culture as culture, which makes a\nbig difference in your life.\u201d  A surprising number of works from this more expansive\nculture not only entertain us but also offer the kind of\nspiritual and philosophical uplift traditionally supplied by\nhigh art and religion. Hugely successful films such as \u201cAvatar,\u201d\n\u201cLord of the Rings\u201d and the Harry Potter tales are full of bits\nof ancient wisdom, psychology, sociology and theology. Their\nfans are interested not only in sex and violence, but also in\nexistential and moral questions. Such entertainments have become\nmyths and sagas that, like the Bible and the Bhagavad Gita, help\npeople grapple with big issues, life\u2019s meaning included. \u201cFrom\none perspective, Cain and Abel is just a story, too,\u201d Kozinets\nsays.  Some of our more fast-paced entertainments help us figure\nout our more complicated lives by providing new information on\nhow other people cope. In the popular fascination with how the\nrich and famous handle marriage and adultery, obesity and\nanorexia, McCracken sees our desire to \u201caudition the change\u201d\ninstead of trying it at home.  \u2018Experimental Creatures\u2019  \u201cBy serving as vehicles of self-transformation,\u201d he says,\n\u201cthe stars allow us to watch others explore life\u2019s options\nalmost like they were in a laboratory. They change themselves so\nthat we don\u2019t have to.\u201d The  Air Force  puts an X before the names\nof its experimental aircraft, such as the  X-15  fighter jet, and\nMcCracken thinks that actress  Lindsay Lohan  deserves an X before\nher name, too. \u201cShe\u2019s an experimental creature who becomes a\nkind of object lesson in transformational activity.\u201d  Before the likes of \u201cThe Bachelor\u201d and \u201cTemptation Island,\u201d\nsays media scholar  Robert Thompson  of  Syracuse University , our\ninsight into what actually went on when people were romantically\ninterested in each other was limited to personal experience and\nthe secondhand, furtive and limited information gained from\nfriends\u2019 reports, overheard comments, steamy novels and scripted\nmovies. As much as he enjoyed \u201cSleepless in  Seattle \u201d and \u201cYou\u2019ve\nGot Mail,\u201d he says, \u201cthose films are to real relationships what\na Greek temple is to a ranch house.\u201d  Its many benefits aside, the new technology supplies\ninformation, not knowledge or meaning. Aristotle said a society\nshould be judged on its capacity for contemplation as well as\nproductivity and pleasure. Facts alone are not enough to\nestablish real understanding, which requires context and\nreflection.  As psychologist  Barry Schwartz  of Swarthmore College says,\n\u201cThe experience that comes from thinking hard for a while about\na subject is no longer available to some people, because they\ndon\u2019t stay on the task long enough to get to that point.\nCommitment has become a kind of dirty word.\u201d The Internet\u2019s\ncapacity to generate superficial novelty is epitomized by the\nmeme: a cultural tidbit, from a catchy anecdote to a joke to an\nimage that spreads rapidly through society, now usually\nelectronically.  Some memes are amusing, creative or informative, like the\nself-explanatory song called \u201c United Breaks Guitars ,\u201d which\ncaused a brief, but precipitous, drop in the airline\u2019s stock.\nHowever, memes can also cause harm -- as racist and misogynistic\nones do -- spread falsehoods and waste time.  Political Memes  \u201cOne thought in the mimetic community is that ideas are\nparasites that don\u2019t care what they do to their host as long as\nit helps them to spread,\u201d Godin says. \u201cThe  Tea Party  -- or the\nCommunist Party -- is a political meme that doesn\u2019t care if it\ndestroys the country, because its only job is to reproduce.\u201d  Technology\u2019s way of undermining deep thinking was the focus\nof a much-remarked-upon front-page  story  in the New York Times\ntitled \u201cWe Have Met the Enemy and He Is PowerPoint.\u201d The piece\nexamined the consequences of the military\u2019s increasing\ndependence on the Microsoft program, which magically reduces the\nmost complicated matters to wonderfully clear talking points and\ncharts. As Brigadier General H. R. McMaster, a veteran of the\nwar in  Iraq , put it, PowerPoint is \u201cdangerous because it can\ncreate the illusion of understanding and the illusion of\ncontrol. Some problems in the world are not bullet-izable.\u201d  Even on campus, the hope that our society can satisfy\nAristotle\u2019s criterion of contemplation seems endangered.\nOriginal thinking arises from a foundation of serious learning,\nbut college professors complain that the concept of research has\ncontracted to the point that really good students go to the\nfourth or fifth page of a  Google search , while most settle for\nthe first one or two.  Neuroscientist Jane Joseph of the University of  South\nCarolina  is struck by the way in which some young people\ncasually resort to plagiarism without realizing that it\u2019s a\nproblem: \u201cThey just paste in something they got online as an\nanswer on a test. Then they say, \u2018What? That\u2019s wrong?\u2019\u201d\nLike the proverbial kids in the candy store, we neophiles need\nto think about our consumption of data in much the same way we\nthink about food. Multinational companies can legally structure transactions\nso they don\u2019t pay tax anywhere, creating \u201cstateless income\u201d that\nis coming under attack as countries seek to fill budget gaps.\nThe Obama administration, Organization for Economic Cooperation\nand Development and tax officials from other countries want to\nreach a consensus on how to combat the issue, with more than a\ndozen proposals being weighed, Bloomberg BNA reported.  \u201cEvery country is revenue-hungry,\u201d said Edward Kleinbard, a\nprofessor at the University of Southern California\u2019s Gould\nSchool of Law who has written several papers and testified\nbefore Congress on the subject. \u201cCountries see very large gaps\nin their corporate tax collections.\u201d  The heightened scrutiny offers a chance to take action.\nThe largest U.S.-based companies expanded their untaxed offshore\nstockpiles by $183 billion last year, or 14 percent, according\nto data compiled by Bloomberg. In the U.S., Senator Carl Levin\nheld hearings taking companies like  Apple (AAPL)  Inc.,  Microsoft (MSFT)  Corp.\nand  Hewlett-Packard (HPQ)  Co. to task for structures that let them pay\nlittle or no tax on billions in profits. Representative Dave Camp is leading a tax rewrite that he says will fix the system.  \u201cEverything is up for grabs right now, including a\nsubstantial rewrite of the international tax rules,\u201d Kleinbard\nsaid. \u201cWhen the dust settles, U.S. multinationals will pay a\nhigher effective tax rate tomorrow than they do today.\u201d  \u201cIncreasing Recognition\u201d  Stateless income is one driver behind a plan to stop profit\nshifting unveiled in July by the OECD, which calls on countries\nto take action in more than a dozen areas over the next two\nyears. Treasury Secretary Jacob Lew hailed the plan. Leaders of\nthe wealthiest economies, the Group of Eight nations, have\nagreed to tackle tax evasion by multinational companies anew.  There is \u201cincreasing recognition\u201d that tax rules in many\ncountries have been designed so companies can avoid tax on an\ninternational scale, said Rafaelle Russo, a senior adviser at\nthe OECD Centre for Tax Policy and Administration.  \u201cThere has never been so much support for doing work in\nthis area, from senior tax officials to finance ministers,\u201d said\nRusso. \u201cYou see that in the tone of the work.\u201d  The solutions are likely to be difficult and consensus on\nhow to address it may be tough to achieve, former Treasury\ninternational tax counsel John Harrington said.  \u201cThere\u2019s not a global, universal way of dealing with\nstateless income,\u201d said Harrington, now a partner with Dentons\nin  Washington . \u201cYou have to look at individual situations. In\nsome cases the benefits of going after stateless income may not\nbe worth the cost.\u201d  Apple\u2019s Cook  Levin\u2019s subcommittee spent months of examining the tax\nframeworks used by Microsoft and Hewlett-Packard. Another issue focused\non Hewlett-Packard\u2019s use of loans from foreign subsidiaries to\nthe U.S. parent to essentially repatriate billions in foreign\nearnings without having to pay U.S. taxes on the money. Employment rose 236,000 last month after a revised 119,000 gain in January that was smaller than first estimated, Labor Department figures showed today in Washington. The median forecast of 90 economists surveyed by Bloomberg projected an advance of 165,000. The jobless rate dropped to 7.7 percent, the lowest since December 2008, from 7.9 percent.  \u201cIt really should cause people to rethink their weak first-half growth estimates,\u201d said  Drew Matus , deputy U.S. chief economist at UBS Securities LLC in  Stamford ,  Connecticut , who correctly forecast the unemployment rate. \u201cPeople counted out the U.S. consumer a little too easily on the payroll-tax increases.\u201d  Stocks, the dollar and Treasury yields all rose on signs the world\u2019s largest economy is gaining strength in the face of  federal budget  cuts and higher payroll taxes. The report may fuel debate among Federal Reserve policy makers considering how long to maintain record stimulus to boost growth and employment.  Matus said the report is likely to convince Fed policy makers \u201cthat they\u2019re doing exactly the right thing by stimulating the economy.\u201d  Stocks, Treasuries  The Standard & Poor\u2019s 500 Index rose 0.5 percent to 1,551.18 at the close in  New York . Treasuries declined, pushing up the yield on the benchmark 10-year note to 2.04 percent from 2 percent late yesterday. The dollar extended gains versus the yen to the highest level since 2009.  Hiring in construction jumped by the most in almost six years. Payrolls also climbed at retailers and professional and business services such as temporary-help firms.  An improving labor market has enhanced the job prospects of college seniors, who are now searching for post-graduation employment. Most of those on track to graduate from the Georgia Institute of Technology in Atlanta have job offers two months before May, when they leave, said Jasmine Lawrence, 21, a computer science major who has been hired by Microsoft Corp., where she had an internship last summer.  \u201cIt is a great time for engineers right now,\u201d said Lawrence, who said she had four offers, including one from Google Inc. and Gulfstream Aerospace Corp. \u201cLots of companies want to hire tech students.\u201d  Private Payrolls  Private payrolls, which don\u2019t include jobs at government agencies, rose by 246,000 in February after a revised gain of 140,000 the previous month. Economists forecast they would grow 170,000 following an initially reported 166,000 gain in January.  As the U.S. economy gains momentum,  Europe \u2019s is contending with a debt crisis that is weighing on company spending and investment. Germany industrial production unexpectedly stagnated in January, a report today showed.  In  China , exports exceeded forecasts in February, an indication that improving global demand may help to sustain the rebound in the world\u2019s second-biggest economy.  Projections for U.S. payrolls ranged from gains of 121,000 to 260,000 following an initially reported 157,000 increase in January, according to the Bloomberg survey. Revisions subtracted a total of 15,000 jobs to the employment count in December and January.  The  unemployment rate , derived from a separate survey of households, was forecast to hold at 7.9 percent, according to the Bloomberg survey median. The decline reflected both a gain in employment and an increase in people leaving the  labor force . The decline in unemployment reflected both a gain in employment and an increase in people leaving the labor force. The participation rate, or the share of working-age people in the labor force, dropped to 63.5 percent, matching the lowest since September 1981, from 63.6 percent.  At the same time, higher wages will give American consumers more to spend as they contend with an increase in the payroll tax. Average hourly earnings rose 0.2 percent to $23.82 in February, today\u2019s report showed. The average work week for all employees increased six minutes to 34.5 hours. Employment at private service-providers jumped 179,000 and retailers took on 23,700 employees.  Government payrolls decreased by 10,000 last month. Payrolls at government agencies and the companies they contract will be further tested in 2013. At the start of the month, Congress let $85 billion in across-the-board budget cuts, known as sequestration, proceed because it couldn\u2019t compromise on  deficit reduction .  \u201cToday\u2019s numbers show that the recovery is gaining traction,\u201d Alan Krueger, chairman of the White House Council of Economic Advisers, said on Bloomberg Television. Personal computer sales have slumped industrywide since the new operating system was released a year ago, while the company had to take a $900 million charge in July to account for unsold Surfaces.  Now it\u2019s trying again, with revised software and new versions of the two Surface models. All are notably improved, though not really enough to change many minds.  From the beginning, Windows 8 has suffered from schizophrenia. The Start screen, with its big, colorful tiles designed to bring Windows into the era of touch-friendly tablets, is largely disconnected from the more traditional desktop, where most productive work actually takes place.  There are two versions of some applications, like  Internet Explorer , while others will run in one environment but not in the other.  Provided as a free download, Windows 8.1 introduces a few welcome tweaks that make moving back and forth a little less jarring.  One is the return of the familiar Start button on the desktop. Pressing and holding it brings up a menu of tasks you can perform directly -- including, saints be praised, shutting down the computer.  Less Flexible  It isn\u2019t as flexible as the menu in Windows 7 -- there\u2019s no way to add shortcuts to often-used programs, for instance -- but it addresses a common complaint of non-touch-screen users and people who do most of their work in desktop applications.  You can, if you locate the deeply buried setting, now order the operating system to launch directly into desktop mode. And you can choose the same background for both it and the tile interface -- a seemingly small thing that subtly reduces the discombobulation.  Windows 8.1 also incorporates a host of enhancements that add flexibility and address previous user pain points. You can play with the size of the tiles on the Start screen, for instance, and -- depending on your screen size and resolution -- display four apps running side by side in adjustable windows. The search functionality has been improved, and there\u2019s deeper integration with Microsoft\u2019s SkyDrive for storing your documents and data online.  Underlying Problems  The changes are for the most part good ones. They simply don\u2019t come close to addressing the underlying problems.  The changes to the Surface tablets are also welcome but similarly modest.  Far and away the most important one is under the hood of the Surface Pro 2, the full-fledged Windows PC version: the inclusion of  Intel (INTC) \u2019s newest microprocessors, dubbed \u201cHaswell.\u201d These chips, which debuted on the most recent version of  Apple (AAPL) \u2019s MacBook Air, provide much better power management than previous generations.  The impact of the new chips plus a bigger battery is readily apparent. I used barely half the power on a four-plus hour flight between  San Francisco  and Atlanta, even with the screen brightness cranked up and the inflight Wi-Fi going constantly. I could get eight hours between charges without using the power-saving mode or taking any extra steps to conserve battery life. By contrast, it took heroic efforts to coax more than five hours from its predecessor.  Few Changes  Beyond extending the battery life -- and a new, second position for the built-in kickstand that finally allows the computer to be used on a lap -- the changes are few. The Surface Pro 2 retains the same dimensions, approximate weight (two pounds) and bright, beautiful 1920-by-1080-pixel 10.6-inch display. And there\u2019s still no place to stow the included stylus.  It also costs the same as the previous model before a recent price cut, starting at $899 for a model with 4 GB of memory and 64 GB of storage. But that\u2019s just the beginning.  You\u2019ll almost certainly want the backlit Type Cover 2 snap-on keyboard ($130), which converts the tablet into a true laptop -- unless you opt for the new $200 Power Cover, which includes a battery that Microsoft says more than doubles longevity. And more memory and greater storage can push you toward the stratosphere.  If you\u2019re looking for something a little less pricey and are willing to make compromises, Microsoft would like to introduce you to the Surface 2. It\u2019s the successor to last year\u2019s Surface RT, the attempt to be a combination iPad-killer and lightweight PC that ended up failing at both.  Better Screen  The new Surface, which starts at $449 for a model with 32 GB of storage, physically resembles the Surface Pro 2, especially since its screen has been upgraded to the same resolution.  But it\u2019s thinner, lighter -- 1.5 pounds -- and doesn\u2019t have an Intel microprocessor. Instead, its brain is an  Nvidia (NVDA)  Tegra of the kind most often found in tablets and smartphones.  As a result, it doesn\u2019t run the millions of programs written for earlier versions of Windows, just the far smaller number -- Microsoft says about 110,000 -- written specifically for the tile interface.  It does have one major asset: a full, built-in version of Microsoft Office that for the first time includes Outlook for e-mail and calendaring. Of course, to take full advantage of Office you\u2019ll need either the Type Cover or the $120, pressure-sensitive Touch Cover 2.  I generally liked the previous Surface for lightweight productivity tasks, and generally like this one too. That said, the first one was a flop and there\u2019s little here to make users revise their opinions.  ( Rich Jaroslovsky  is a Bloomberg News columnist. The opinions expressed are his own.) R.R.\nDonnelley had filed a draft of the document without\nauthorization, Google later said on its blog.  The timing raised concerns about Google\u2019s ability to\nrelease sensitive financial data through proper channels, said\nDavid Larcker, a corporate-governance professor at the Stanford\nGraduate School of Business. Before trading was halted, a 9\npercent drop in Google shares wiped more than $22 billion from\nits market capitalization in minutes.  \u201cIt is highly unusual for this thing to be cut loose ahead\nof time,\u201d Larcker said. \u201cThis is a big deal. The markets hinge\non appropriate disclosure, following the process. You worry\nabout some people getting the news earlier than others.\u201d  The snafu upstaged another Google event, the release of a\nChromebook computer, hitting during a press conference in  San\nFrancisco  and prompting several reporters to rush out to cover\nthe results. Google requested the halt in  trading  of its shares\nas it made final touches to the results, which showed profit and\nsales that fell short of analysts\u2019 projections.  R.R. Donnelley Investigates  Profit excluding some items was $9.03 a share, the  Mountain\nView , California-based company said. Excluding sales passed to\npartner sites, revenue was $11.3 billion. Analysts on average\nhad estimated profit of $10.65 a share on sales of $11.8\nbillion.  Google shares fell 8 percent to $695 at the close in New\nYork.  R.R. Donnelley  fell  less than 1 percent to $10.76 at the\nclose after earlier erasing as much as 6.5 percent immediately\nafter Google\u2019s statement was released. R.R. Donnelley said it\u2019s\ninvestigating the matter.  \u201cWe are fully engaged in an investigation to determine how\nthis event took place and are pursuing our first obligation --\nwhich is to serve our valued customer,\u201d Chicago-based R.R.\nDonnelley said in a statement.  Google\u2019s filing included the phrase \u201cPENDING LARRY\nQUOTE,\u201d just above a summary of results. The mishap quickly\nturned into a commonly discussed and joked-about theme on\nTwitter.  Microsoft\u2019s Numbers  Google isn\u2019t the only company to have its results released\nbefore planned.  Microsoft Corp. (MSFT) \u2019s earnings were released more\nthan an hour before schedule in January 2011, after Selerity\nInc., a New Jersey market-information company, used software it\ndeveloped to obtain Microsoft\u2019s press release from a public area\nof the software maker\u2019s site.  Embarrassing as the incident was, it may not give Google\ncause to sue Donnelley, said  Stuart Grant , a Wilmington,\nDelaware-based  lawyer  who represents investors in securities\ncases.  \u201cOf course it\u2019s possible to sue,\u201d Grant said in an\ninterview. \u201cBut I\u2019m not sure if a company has to put out\ninformation at any specific time.\u201d  Still, the timing left investors without the added\nexplanation that comes in the conference call that typically\noccurs soon after a release hits newswires, said Kerry Rice, an\nanalyst at Needham & Co.  Lacking Context  \u201cThere\u2019s not a lot of context around the earnings right\nnow, so people make the conclusion one way or the other and it\nmay not be right,\u201d he said in an interview. \u201cThe uncertainty\nbreeds a sense of fear and people automatically sell.\u201d  Public companies can file their documents with the\nSecurities and Exchange Commission directly through a website\ncalled EdgarLink Online. They have to request access codes to\nuse the site, including a Central Index Key, or CIK, from the\nagency. CIKs are used on the SEC\u2019s computer systems to identify\ncorporations and individuals who have filed disclosure\ndocuments.  Instead of filing themselves, some corporations use agents\nto submit documents on their behalf -- in part because the\nprocess can be complicated. The SEC requires public companies to\nsubmit documents created with HTML software, which has more\nstringent technical requirements than other formats, such as\nMicrosoft\u2019s Word software or  Adobe Systems Inc. (ADBE) \u2019s PDF.  Documents that are tied to specific transactions, such as a\nstock or bond offering, are often submitted to filing agents\nwithout much notice. In contrast, filing agents typically\nreceive advance notice on documents that are more predictable,\nincluding Form 8-Ks that are filed in tandem with earnings\nreleases. A Form 8-K must be submitted within four days of the\nevent that is being disclosed in the filing, such as an earnings\nrelease. Honestly, we didn\u2019t think anyone was. If he intended to be reassuring, his words had the opposite effect. The president\u2019s  remarks  in defense of the government\u2019s vast electronic surveillance programs help explain why U.S. citizens -- and, not incidentally, U.S. businesses -- should be so unnerved by them.  The first point is that we don\u2019t necessarily know what is happening. According to the  Washington Post  and  the Guardian  newspaper, the National Security Agency and the  Federal Bureau of Investigation  are sifting through vast amounts of data -- including audio, video, e-mail, photographs, documents and much else -- produced by nine U.S. technology companies. The program, code-named Prism, allegedly spied on content being shared by foreign users.  Such programs -- in addition to Prism there is the vast effort, also revealed this week, to collect phone data from Verizon Communications Inc. customers -- naturally raise questions about the proper balance between privacy and security. \u201cWhen you actually look at the details, then I think we\u2019ve struck the right balance,\u201d the president said today. OK, fine: So how about some details?  Congress -- where fear of being labeled weak on terrorism affords the security-industrial complex a supine majority -- must rediscover its national-security prerogatives. It shouldn\u2019t be too hard. The 2011 vote to extend provisions of the Patriot Act produced 153 nays in the House and 23 in the Senate. That\u2019s a skeptical base on which to build effective oversight.  Senators  Ron Wyden  of Oregon and Mark Udall of  Colorado , both Democrats, offered an amendment to the 2011 reauthorization that would have compelled the attorney general to \u201cpublicly disclose the United States Government\u2019s official interpretation of the USA Patriot Act.\u201d  Understanding how the government interprets the law is prerequisite for this debate. Let\u2019s get that on the record, then see where the discussion leads.  At the very least the public debate should be routed through the intelligence committees in the House and Senate. It is no longer enough for them to give vague blessings to government spying. They should issue annual, unclassified reports certifying that they have reviewed secret government programs and they endorse their basis in law and their validity on national-security grounds. The reports should include minority dissents. The public needn\u2019t see secrets; we do need to know more about how Congress is scrutinizing the process.  Aside from concerns about privacy and government power, Prism is also cause for economic anxiety. The companies reportedly compliant with the NSA\u2019s snooping look like a Who\u2019s Who of 21st-century American innovation: Apple Inc., Yahoo! Inc., Google Inc., Microsoft Corp. and Facebook Inc. all joined the party.  The companies involved have been offering carefully worded denials, but even hints of acquiescence in this program should be cause for  deep worry  from a business perspective. Foreign governments, already inclined to protect homegrown technology businesses, might find such surveillance a convenient excuse to increase regulatory or antitrust pressure on Silicon Valley hegemons. More legitimately, they might also want to protect their citizens and businesses from foreign espionage.  And they\u2019d be right to: Spying on foreign citizens is the explicit justification offered for this program by U.S. Director of National Intelligence James Clapper. If these companies are soon subjected to far more onerous privacy provisions in foreign countries, they shouldn\u2019t be surprised in the least. There\u2019s  some indication  the program may have violated European Union  privacy rules .  International users of such services might be at ease with sharing their photos and videos with family and friends. Sharing them with  Uncle Sam , however, is a different matter entirely. That\u2019s not to say that these revelations alone will lead to a global revolt against Facebook. But combined with Facebook\u2019s penchant for violating user privacy, some people may start looking at competing services that do a better job of protecting their data -- and that aren\u2019t known to be bugged by the U.S. intelligence community.  It may not be realistic to have expected these companies to decline the government\u2019s invitation to help it spy (although Apple appears to have resisted for several years). But they had to have known the potential for controversy.  In a 2009 debate on Patriot Act provisions, Democratic Senator  Dick Durbin  of Illinois predicted the program would run into trouble. \u201cSomeday the cloak will be lifted, and future generations will ask whether our actions today meet the test of a democratic society -- transparency, accountability and fidelity to the rule of law and our Constitution,\u201d he said.  Durbin was prescient, but his timing was off. His questions aren\u2019t for future generations -- they\u2019re for us. Tablet computers are being tested across all military\nbranches, according to interviews conducted by Bloomberg\nGovernment since May 17. The services pay $500 to $600 per\ntablet, less than half the cost of laptops that are\n\u201cruggedized,\u201d or enhanced with a shell and toughened to\nwithstand harsh environments. (DELL) , RIM and other tablet makers are vying to\ntap the military market for computers, laptops and servers worth\n$2.9 billion in the government\u2019s 2010 fiscal year. Of that\namount, spending on enhanced laptops was $33 million. The\ndepartment spent $37 million on tablets in the same fiscal year,\naccording to Bloomberg data.  \u2018Disruptive Technology\u2019  Tablets are a \u201cdisruptive technology\u201d that can replace\nheavier and more expensive equipment, Dosmann said. \u201cAs an\ninfantry soldier, the last thing I want is something more to\ncarry.\u201d  To secure the devices so they can only be accessed using\nthe common access card carried by all military service members\nand Defense employees, the services must install additional\nsoftware or hardware, Gary Winkler, the Army\u2019s former program\nexecutive officer for  enterprise  information systems, said in a\nJune 20 telephone interview. Winkler oversaw about $4 billion,\nor 56 percent, of the Army\u2019s information-technology budget.  \u201cIt\u2019s very tough to drive the manufacturers to make the\ntablets and the devices with the embedded security that only the\nDefense Department needs or only parts of the federal government\nneeds because the market just isn\u2019t big enough,\u201d said Winkler,\nwho now heads Fairfax, Virginia-based Cyber Solutions and\nServices Inc., a government consulting and contracts support\ncompany.  Secure Servers  The iPhone and iPad already interact with the common access\ncard, or  CAC , and will be approved soon, possibly this month,\nWinkler said. Security engineering is under way for  Google\nInc. (GOOG) \u2019s Android operating system.  Microsoft Corp. (MSFT) \u2019s Windows\nMobile operating system was CAC-enabled more than a year ago.  BlackBerry smartphones, which run on RIM\u2019s secure servers,\nalready are approved by the Defense Department and in use on the\nbattlefield. The PlayBook runs on the same servers, Dosmann\nsaid.
