(GOOG) , avoiding a potentially costly legal battle with U.S. regulators, ended a 20-month antitrust probe by pledging to change some business practices and settling allegations it misused patents to thwart competitors in smartphone technology.  The Federal Trade Commission voted 5-0 to close its investigation into whether Google unfairly skewed its search results, with the company saying it would voluntarily remove restrictions on the use of its online search advertising platform and offer companies the option of keeping their content out of Google\u2019s search results.  Under a consent decree regarding patents, Google will be limited in its ability to seek court orders barring competitors\u2019 products when the company has agreed to license its technology on reasonable terms.  \u201cThe changes Google has agreed to make will ensure that consumers continue to reap the benefits of competition in the online marketplace and in the market for innovative wireless devices they enjoy,\u201d FTC Chairman  Jon Leibowitz  said today at a news conference in  Washington . \u201cThis was an incredibly thorough and careful investigation by the commission, and the outcome is a strong and enforceable set of agreements.\u201d  No Enforcement  The agency\u2019s decision to close its probe of Google\u2019s search practices without any enforcement action is a blow to competitors including  Microsoft Corp. (MSFT) ,  Yelp Inc. (YELP)  and  Expedia Inc. (EXPE)  An alliance of such e-commerce and Web-search companies pressed the agency to bring a lawsuit, claiming Google\u2019s dominance of Internet search, combined with the company favoring its own services in answers to queries, violates antitrust laws.  \u201cGoogle\u2019s competitors are looking at this as though it\u2019s a slap on the wrist,\u201d said Jeffrey Jacobovitz, an antitrust litigator with Arnall Golden Gregory LLP in Washington. \u201cIt\u2019s clear the FTC thought this was the best deal they could get and if they had gone to court, they may not have been as successful.\u201d  Google said in a blog posting today that it agreed in a  letter  to the FTC that websites will be allowed to remove their own content such as reviews from search-results pages including those for local, travel and shopping services. Advertisers will also be able to compare data from other  search engines  within third-party services that use Google\u2019s AdWords software, Google said in the posting.  \u2018Universal Search\u2019  The FTC decision gives a green light to Google to continue with what it calls \u201cuniversal search,\u201d where it mixes its own answers to queries with links to other sources of information. Critics complained that by pushing other websites farther down in search rankings, Google was hurting competition and consumers.  \u201cWe\u2019ve always accepted that with success comes regulatory scrutiny,\u201d Google said in the blog post. \u201cWe\u2019re pleased that the FTC and the other authorities that have looked at Google\u2019s business practices have concluded we should be free to combine direct answers with Web results.\u201d  Beth Wilkinson , the Washington litigator hired by the FTC to oversee a potential lawsuit, said that the evidence didn\u2019t show Google\u2019s actions were against the law.  \u201cUndoubtedly, Google took aggressive actions to gain advantage over rival search providers,\u201d Wilkinson said in an FTC statement. \u201cHowever, the FTC\u2019s mission is to protect competition, and not individual competitors.\u201d  Google Reports  The agreement requires Google to give the FTC reports on its compliance with the agreement for five years. The agency has the right to review company documents and interview Google employees if it suspects non-compliance, Peter Levitas, a deputy in the bureau of compliance, told reporters.  FTC Commissioner Tom Rosch, a Republican, said in a separate statement that while he believed Google\u2019s behavior didn\u2019t warrant any action, the agreement the agency accepted \u201ccreates very bad precedent and may lead to the impression that well-heeled firms such as Google will receive special treatment at the commission.\u201d  \u201cInstead of following standard commission procedure and entering into a binding consent agreement to resolve the majority\u2019s concerns, Google has instead made non-binding commitments with respect to its search practices,\u201d said Rosch, who steps down tomorrow and will be replaced by Joshua Wright, a law professor at  George Mason University .  \u201cAfter promising an elephant more than a year ago, the commission instead has brought forth a couple of mice,\u201d he said.  Urging Delay  Google critics, including FairSearch.org, the alliance of Google competitors, had urged the FTC to delay a decision until Google submitted a detailed proposal to the European Commission\u2019s antitrust probe.  \u201cThe FTC\u2019s decision to close its investigation with only voluntary commitments from Google is disappointing and premature\u201d given that the European Commission is seeking to resolve \u201cfour abuses of dominance\u201d it identified, FairSearch.org said in an e-mailed statement.  Leibowitz said European law differs from that in the U.S.  \u201cWe have to do what\u2019s right under our own laws,\u201d Leibowitz said in an interview with Bloomberg Television. \u201cWhen an investigation is ready to be closed, we like to close it.\u201d  Consent Decree  The agency voted 4-1 on the patent settlement, a formal, 10-year consent decree that restricts the situations in which Google can seek court injunctions against competitors\u2019 products that rely on so-called standard-essential patents. Google would still be able to try to block rivals from using those patents if it can\u2019t reach a licensing agreement, the agency said.  Companies that create technology that helps to develop an agreed-upon industry standard pledge to license associated patents on \u201cfair, reasonable and nondiscriminatory\u201d terms.  Industry-standard technology helps ensure products such as mobile phone antennas and global-positioning system software can operate together when made by different manufacturers.  Today\u2019s settlement comes amid a surge in patent litigation as handset and device makers vie to increase their shares of the worldwide mobile-technology market, projected to almost double to $847 billion by 2016, according to estimates by  Yankee Group , a Boston-based research firm.  Industry Standard  At issue are Google\u2019s efforts to bar U.S. imports of Microsoft and  Apple Inc. (AAPL)  products by claiming the devices, which rely on industry-standard technology, infringe patents owned by Google\u2019s Motorola Mobility unit.  Google, based in  Mountain View ,  California , paid $12.5 billion for Motorola Mobility, in part to get its trove of more than 17,000 patents and applications. Some of those patents cover fundamental technology on how mobile electronics operate, so it would be difficult for Apple to work around the inventions.  Before today\u2019s consent decree, judges in Seattle and  Chicago  had already said Motorola Mobility isn\u2019t entitled to an order blocking sales of products based on the use of standard- essential patents. The U.S. International Trade Commission in Washington, which has the power to block imports, is considering whether it will adopt similar rules.  The agreement still could mean that Motorola Mobility will have to drop some of its claims against Microsoft at the ITC, said Jorge Contreras, an associate law professor at American University in Washington. The commission already has cleared Apple of claims it was infringing Motorola Mobility patents for wireless technology.  Microsoft, Apple  Both Microsoft and Apple have pledged not to seek court bans based on the use of standard-essential patents. While it was seeking regulatory approval to buy Motorola Mobility, Google said it would continue the handset maker\u2019s policy of not pursuing such orders as long as negotiations were under way. The settlement with the FTC requires Motorola Mobility to take extra steps including offering binding arbitration of royalty disputes.  The FTC agreement won\u2019t change the overall litigation between Motorola Mobility, Apple and Microsoft, said James Kulbaski, a patent lawyer with Oblon Spivak in Alexandria, Virginia.  \u201cThere was always a likelihood an injunction could not be obtained\u201d on the standard-essential patents, Kulbaski said. \u201cThere are some good non-standard essential patents which will not fall under this FTC ruling.\u201d  To contact the reporter on this story: Sara Forden in Washington at  sforden@bloomberg.net   To contact the editor responsible for this story: Michael Hytha at  mhytha@bloomberg.net .","path":".\/2008_2012_msft_bloomberg_news\/google-investigation-by-ftc-ends-with-voluntary-changes.txt"},{"id":71581020,"title":"Sony Network Breach Puts Hirai to the Test as Succession Looms","released_at":"<date>April 29 2011<\/date> <time>01:27:47<\/time>","content":"The day after  Sony Corp. Armonk, New York-based  International\nBusiness Machines Corp. (IBM) , had a market capitalization of $202\nbillion, data compiled by Bloomberg show.  After returning, Jobs had led Apple\u2019s transformation into a\nseller of everything from smartphones to music. He engineered\nthe company\u2019s comeback by honing its industrial design, tightly\nintegrating software and hardware, and pushing into new markets.  The iPhone, introduced in 2007, has become Apple\u2019s best-\nselling product and turned the company into the world\u2019s biggest\nsmartphone maker. After winning customers away from  Research In\nMotion Ltd. (RIMM)  and  Nokia Oyj (NOK1V) , Apple is now sparring with Google for\nleadership in the market for mobile-phone software.  Jobs was appointed chairman this week after resigning as\nCEO and recommended appointing Cook, 50, as his successor. He\nwas on medical leave since Jan. 17 after combating a rare form\nof cancer since 2003 and surviving a liver transplant in 2009.  Day of Reckoning  \u201cI have always said if there ever came a day when I could\nno longer meet my duties and expectations as Apple\u2019s CEO, I\nwould be the first to let you know,\u201d Jobs, 56, said in a\nstatement on Aug. 24. \u201cUnfortunately, that day has come.\u201d  Apple may now need to spend more money acquiring products\nto replace those built using Jobs\u2019s ideas, said  Malcolm Polley ,\nwho oversees $1 billion as chief investment officer at Stewart\nCapital in Indiana, Pennsylvania. You could do that via acquisition.\u201d  \u2018Blunt the Force\u2019  The company is going to have to add products to \u201cblunt the\nforce\u201d of Google\u2019s Android platform, said  Michael Yoshikami ,\nchief executive officer and founder of YCMNet Advisors, which\nmanages $1.1 billion in Walnut Creek,  California .  Android was the  best-selling  smartphone operating system\nworldwide in the second quarter with sales rising more than\nfourfold to give it 43.3 percent of the market, led by Samsung\nand HTC Corp., according to Gartner Inc., the research firm\nbased in Stamford, Connecticut.  Netflix Inc. (NFLX) , based in Los Gatos, California, would allow\nApple to boost revenue from streaming live videos and television\nshows and keep users dependent on its products for a wider range\nof media, the University of North Carolina\u2019s Malhotra said.  Steve Swasey , a spokesman for Netflix, declined to comment\non whether it would consider a sale to Apple or whether the\ncompany has been approached by Apple about an acquisition. Presentations to attract investors had collided with a\n2,000-point plunge in the  Dow Jones Industrial Average  during\nthe previous 14 trading days. Carbonite was determined to go\npublic, even though 10 other companies had postponed their\ndebuts, Bloomberg Markets magazine reports in its November\nissue.  Michael Stark, who runs San Francisco-based Crosslink\nCapital Inc., knew Carbonite. He\u2019d invested $12 million in\nJanuary as part of a venture-capital deal.  After Carbonite lowered its price, Stark placed an order of\n1 million shares at the IPO, doubling his stake to 8.3 percent,\nsplit between hedge and venture investments. By the closing\nbell, Carbonite had gained 24 percent to $12.35. The stock\nclimbed further, giving Crosslink a 28 percent return in a\nmonth, trouncing the 3.3 percent gain for the Nasdaq Computer\nIndex. On Oct. 3, the shares traded at $12.  Stark\u2019s Carbonite investment is quintessential Crosslink.\nThe firm, with $2.15 billion under management, tries to make\nmoney from a hybrid strategy of providing venture funding for\nprivate companies and hedge-fund investments to profit from\npublic ones. The setup lets the firm double its bets when it\nperceives good opportunities.  \u2018Full Picture\u2019  In September 2005, Crosslink made a $13.3 million\ninvestment in Provo, Utah-based  Ancestry.com Inc. (ACOM) , a Web-based\ngenealogy company, in return for 2.4 million shares valued at\n$5.60 each.  When Ancestry.com went public, Stark bought an additional\n200,000 shares. He controlled 7.3 percent of the company by May\n2010, reducing that stake to 3.7 percent as of the end of June.\nOn Oct. 3, Ancestry.com was trading at $21.98.  \u201cWe look at growth companies and don\u2019t limit ourselves to\nwhether a company is public or private,\u201d he says.  From his 22nd-floor Embarcadero Center office in  San\nFrancisco \u2019s financial district, Stark expands on that thought.\nHe points toward San Francisco Bay from one window and then\nmotions toward another set of windows, where his gaze drifts\nover the city to the iconic Coit Tower.  \u201cI can see what\u2019s going on by looking both ways,\u201d he\nsays. \u201cI can see the full picture and not a half picture.\u201d  \u2018Looking for an Education\u2019  Crosslink\u2019s full-picture approach has largely paid off.\nStark\u2019s venture funds have $1 billion under management.\nCrosslink Ventures IV, which started investing in 2000, has\nreturned an average of 28 percent a year since then.  The $510 million Crosslink Emerging Growth Fund, the\nflagship hedge fund, has returned an average of 13.4 percent\nafter fees annually from September 1999 through August,\naccording to an investor.  Crosslink\u2019s crossover funds put about 40 percent of assets\ninto venture deals and the rest into hedge-fund investments.\nCrosslink Crossover III, which started in September 1999, has\nreturned an average of 13.6 percent a year through June, the\ninvestor says.  Crosslink\u2019s strategy of getting an early peek at promising\ntechnologies gives it an edge, says Michael Weisberg, a\nCrosslink investor who runs Crestwood Capital Management LP, a\n$1 billion hedge fund in  New York .  \u201cStark is looking for an education, to get a sense of\nwhere the technology is going,\u201d Weisberg says.  Subprime Miss  Stark has barriers between his funds to avoid any\nregulatory headaches. He doesn\u2019t trade in a company at which\nCrosslink has a board seat, which could provide access to\ninsider information.  Although venture firms aren\u2019t required to register with the\nU.S. Securities and Exchange Commission, Crosslink has\nregistered as an investment adviser and has passed SEC audits,\npartner Isabelle Fymat says. The firm tracks stock trades of\nemployees and their household members.  Stark has had his failures. His immersion in the world of\ntechnology trends meant he didn\u2019t see the subprime crisis until\nit was too late. The Emerging Growth Fund lost 29 percent in\n2008, even as it held onto  Apple Inc. (AAPL) ,  Google Inc. (GOOG)  and  Qualcomm\nInc. (QCOM)  It still beat the 38.5 percent tumble in the Standard &\nPoor\u2019s 500 Index that year.  \u201cWe like to make long-term bets, but sometimes events\nsurprise us,\u201d he says.  Vulnerable  Stark\u2019s faith in technology growth companies makes\nCrosslink vulnerable when a boom he expects doesn\u2019t pan out. The\nhedge fund bought a stake in Sunnyvale, California-based network\nsecurity company  Fortinet Inc. (FTNT)  in August 2010 for about $8 a\nshare. On July 6, the shares closed at a 52-week high of $28.17.\nThen, on July 19, Fortinet reported earnings that disappointed\nanalysts. The stock fell 19 percent to $21.61 the next day.\n\u201cVolatility in growth companies can be brutal,\u201d Stark says.  Supporters say Stark has a rare talent: He unearths\ncompanies that may pay off in a few years while managing the\ndaily ups and downs of his hedge fund.  \u201cIt\u2019s hard to find someone who\u2019s good at picking stocks,\nwho can also pick stocks to short and understands industry\ntrends to select startups for the venture side,\u201d says Robert\nManilla, chief investment officer at the $3.2 billion  Kresge\nFoundation  in Troy,  Michigan . Manilla has invested in Crosslink\nsince 2003.  Tech IPOs  \u201cStark and his team are thoughtful investors with a vision\nof where the world is going,\u201d he says.  Stark\u2019s skills are in demand as more technology startups\nplan initial public offerings. Groupon Inc., a Chicago-based\ndiscount coupon seller, and Zynga Inc., a San Francisco social-\ngaming company, have filed for IPOs. Crosslink\u2019s marquee name,\nonline radio service Pandora Media Inc., started trading shares\non June 15. Overall, 135 U.S. companies had IPOs this year\nthrough the end of August, 21 percent more than at that point\nlast year, according to Bloomberg data.  \u201cYear to date, 2011 was the strongest year for tech IPOs\nsince 2007,\u201d says Kathleen Smith, a principal at Greenwich,\nConnecticut-based Renaissance Capital LLC, an IPO investment\nadvisory firm.  Market turmoil since the end of July has made some\ninvestors pause. The average technology IPO fell 18 percent this\nyear through the end of September, according to Renaissance\nCapital.  \u201cThe recent volatility has taken the wind out of companies\nthat were not ready for prime time,\u201d says Lise Buyer, an IPO\nconsultant and founder of Class V Group LLC in Portola Valley,\n California .  \u2018Wealth Building\u2019  Still, with more than 300 offerings lined up, the pipeline\nis strong. \u201cThere\u2019s definitely a sense of renewed IPO\noptimism,\u201d she says.  Stark is enthusiastic about social networking, Chinese\nInternet firms and infrastructure companies active in cloud\ncomputing -- using remote computers to store and retrieve\ninformation.  \u201cYou can have dramatic wealth building in a relatively\nshort period of time, and that\u2019s what we are trying to\ncapture,\u201d he says.  Beijing-based Baidu Inc.,  China \u2019s largest Internet company,\nwent public in August 2005. Its shares have soared an average 50\npercent a year, rewarding Stark with more than 20 times his\ninvestments in the company started by Robin Li and Eric Xu.  \u201cWe like Chinese nationals educated in the U.S. who are\nentrepreneurs and go back home to set up their own companies,\u201d\nhe says.  Intel Analyst  Stark grew up in Quincy, Illinois, with old-school\ntechnology in his blood: His father was a technician for phone\ncompany Illinois Bell. His mother was a secretary. An only\nchild, he arrived at Northwestern University as the first member\nof his family to attend college. After getting a civil\nengineering degree, he earned an MBA with honors from the\nUniversity of Michigan.  Stark headed west in 1980 to join chipmaker  Intel Corp. (INTC) \njust as the computer and semiconductor industries were on the\ncusp of exponential growth. He worked as a financial analyst and\non special projects, studying potential equipment suppliers for\nIntel.  In 1983, that background helped him land an analyst\nposition covering the semiconductor industry at what was to\nbecome Robertson Stephens & Co., the San Francisco investment\nbank that specialized in tech companies. In 1989, he was on a\nteam that created Omega Funds, a venture fund within the bank.  Cold Calls  The group later started a crossover fund to invest in\npublic and private companies. BankAmerica Corp., now  Bank of\nAmerica Corp. (BAC) , acquired Robertson Stephens and then sold it off.  Stark and Seymour Kaufman, an investment banker who co-\nmanaged Omega Funds, bought out the fund, with its $300 million\nin assets, in 1999. They changed the name to Crosslink Capital.\nKaufman, a mentor to the firm, isn\u2019t involved in the running of\nthe company.  Crosslink offices, with prospectuses, annual reports and\noffering documents strewn across every working space, are far\nfrom the fabled VC mecca of Sand Hill Road in Menlo Park, south\nof San Francisco. Crosslink\u2019s location makes its 37-person team\nwork harder, says Jim Feuille, who heads venture operations.  Feuille\u2019s group ferreted out Pandora only after spending a\nyear making cold calls. The venture fund\u2019s initial $33 million\ninvestment was valued at $500 million at the end of September,\neven after Pandora shares declined 8.4 percent since the IPO.  Genesis of Pandora  The idea that led to Crosslink\u2019s investment in Pandora came\nfrom an unexpected quarter. In October 2003, Steve Jobs, then\nApple\u2019s CEO, said the company\u2019s iTunes service would be\navailable for  Microsoft Corp. (MSFT) \u2019s Windows operating system.  Feuille predicted that digital music would take off because\nmore than 90 percent of the world\u2019s PCs ran on Windows. Stark\nbought Apple shares for the hedge fund, making almost 50 times\nhis investment when he closed the position in February. Feuille\nlater bet on Ecast Inc., a San Francisco startup that offered\ndigital jukeboxes, for the venture fund.  \u201cYou see an idea and want to figure out what\u2019s the next\nevolution,\u201d Feuille says.  To sniff out more digital music opportunities, Feuille had\nan associate call dozens of companies before Crosslink spotted\nSavage Beast Technologies in 2005. The startup had developed a\ndatabase and algorithms that let users customize music searches.\nIf a listener liked  Pink Floyd,  the software would suggest other\nbands he might enjoy.  Going Free  Savage Beast changed its name to Pandora in 2005 and\nembarked on a business to stream music over the Internet.\nTrouble was, it had begun a subscription model, offering members\n10 hours of free music and then charging a $3-per-month fee.  \u201cI told Pandora\u2019s board there is too much free music out\nthere,\u201d recalls Feuille, wearing a blue shirt under a black\nsleeveless fleece with Crosslink\u2019s logo of two interlocking Cs.\nThe subscription strategy was unlikely to make much headway, he\nsays.  \u201cGood-enough free music will always beat a little bit\nbetter,\u201d he says.  Feuille offered to fund the venture if Pandora\u2019s board\nswitched to a free radio service backed by ads. The board\neventually agreed.  \u201cCrosslink was pivotal to our success,\u201d says  Tim Westergren , Pandora\u2019s co-founder and chief strategy officer. He\nsays Feuille saw Pandora\u2019s potential before its board could.  \u201cJim advocated for a free service, which at the time was\nfar from obvious,\u201d Westergren says.  Home Runs  Today, Pandora has more than 100 million registered users.\nRevenue for the quarter ended on July 31 doubled to $67 million.\nAbout half came from mobile devices, CEO Joseph Kennedy says.\nThe company lost $3.2 million as it paid half of the revenue in\nroyalties to record companies. Pandora makes 87 percent of its\nsales from ads on listener devices and the rest from\nsubscriptions.  Stark has made other bets against prevailing wisdom.\n Equinix Inc. (EQIX) , a Redwood City, California-based provider of data\ncenters, had to restructure its debt and raise money in 2003.\nManagers held more than 80 meetings with private-equity, VC and\n hedge funds , Chairman Peter Van Camp says.  Crosslink was the only U.S. company that offered anything:\na $10 million investment from the venture fund, which it\nexchanged for shares valued at about $3.34 each. On Oct. 3,\nEquinix shares traded at $84.27, producing a 25-fold return.  \u201cThey looked beyond the immediate economics of the company\nand could see where the technology was heading,\u201d Van Camp says.  Solar Bets  Stark figured that  First Solar Inc. (FSLR) , the world\u2019s biggest\nmaker of thin-film solar panels, would eventually find its\ntechnology overtaken.  \u201cWe knew technologies would emerge to make First Solar\nobsolete, but that would not happen in 2006,\u201d he says.  Crosslink started buying after First Solar\u2019s IPO that\nNovember, snapping up shares at $24 each. At the end of 2007,\nshares of the Tempe, Arizona, company were trading at $267.14.  \u201cWe got a 10 bagger because we understood the technology,\nwe understood the situation,\u201d he says, meaning he made 10 times\nhis investment. Ballmer, whose skills were in many ways complementary to Gates', took the helm of an already massive organization as it entered an era of relentless disruptive innovation by competitors. He managed to hold the stock price on a pretty even keel, but no better than that.  It's worth taking a step back to look at what all the chatter is about.  The debate has focused almost entirely on the leadership of innovation.  Read just a few of the articles \u2014 some of the buzzier ones have been  a condemnation  by  The New Yorker 's Nicholas Thompson,  an incisive critique  by Derek Thompson of  The Atlantic , and  a counterargument  by Timothy Lee in  The Washington Post . There's a pattern in them. They argue over whether Bing was a respectable competitive response to Google or not; they give Xbox its due, while tending to cordon it off as a special case; they accuse Microsoft of being oblivious to the threat posed by Web and mobile apps, or point to evidence that it was responding. Ballmer is being damned or defended wholly on the string of innovative (or not) products released on his watch.   So the big lesson other CEOs should take away from this public trial is a cautionary one: this is how you, too, will be judged.  We have known for a long time that innovation is the name of the game now. Peter Drucker  made the point in HBR's pages  18 years ago, writing that \"Core competencies are different for every organization .... But every organization needs one core competence: innovation.\"  We've known even longer that our legacy organizations are not geared to excel at innovation.  This was the point of James March's classic 1991 paper  Exploration and Exploitation in Organizational Learning . He pointed out that companies had much more to gain in the short-term, and therefore were tooled to compete, by exploiting opportunities already found than by exploring the business landscape for new ones. It's a point that Clay Christensen put his own twist on with  The Innovator's Dilemma :   Even when leaders know intellectually that groundbreaking innovation is imperative, they find themselves investing in incremental refinements to please their most sophisticated customers, and leave themselves wide open to disruption by upstarts.   Geoffrey Moore  once compared big companies trying to innovate to right-handed people writing with their left hands.  All the apparatus may be in place, but if the organization isn't in the habit of doing it constantly, it will always be an awkward affair. Despite two decades of seeing the problem, very few CEOs have thought seriously about how their organizations should be reinvented if innovation matters more than anything else.  Well, guess what: it does. Two other observations can be made about the public autopsy of Ballmer's career:  It may constitute another small way that Steve Jobs left a dent in the universe. And it might be more about us in the end than about Ballmer \u2014 or any CEO. I can't remember people obsessing about a CEO's legacy this much before Steve Jobs' decline forced the issue in his case.  But I suspect this will not be the last departing CEO we will put under a glaring spotlight.  And I predict, too, that the attention won't only follow titanic departures in the tech sector. We're figuring out that innovation is the be-all and end-all in every kind of business, and that the quality of leadership is a big factor in determining where it happens. At the same time, we have all gained access to immediate national conversations on the matters that interest us.  And the fact is that the matter does interest us.  In the United States, there is a terrible anxiety about losing the innovative edge that has been our source of competitive advantage and can be our only salvation. Tyler Cowen's  The Great Stagnation  is a prime example; his reading of history convinces him that the U.S. has reached a \"technological plateau\" and reenergizing economic growth will be extremely hard to do. Peter Thiel, who innovated as a co-founder of PayPal, is similarly worried - and also worrying about the worry. \"It would be hard to imagine the President of the United States declaring war on Alzheimers,\" he  told a business crowd on Nantucket last year , \"because our pessimism about technology has started to seep into the system.\"  This obsession over national competitiveness isn't only an American one. Smart people worldwide fret that the era of discovery is over and, economically speaking, we're now in for a rough ride.  It makes me wonder if what we're really talking about, when we talk about Ballmer, is the fear of our own failure to innovate.","path":".\/2008_2012_msft_bloomberg_news\/steve-ballmer-s-big-lesson-for-the-rest-of-us.txt"},{"id":39933205,"title":"African Investor Takes Silicon Valley Tough Love to Kenya","released_at":"<date>February 7 2013<\/date> <time>21:53:43<\/time>","content":"Mbwana Alliy  is sitting in a conference room in a Nairobi,  Kenya , tech center, an Apple MacBook close by. Though only 23 percent of houses there have electricity and just 9 percent of roads are paved, mobile-phone penetration is 75 percent in the country, up from 5 percent in 2003. The rapid gains have spawned innovation. For example, pretty much anything in Kenya can be bought via text message, which is convenient in a place where credit cards are rarely accepted and carrying cash can make one a target for robbery.  Alliy moved back to Africa in April after four years in Silicon Valley and three as a product manager for Microsoft in  Seattle . He\u2019s convinced he can make money by schooling local tech entrepreneurs in the ins and outs of venture capitalism.  200 Pitches  Getting his Savannah Fund started was his first challenge. He had to pitch more than 200 times before he found someone to back it. Now, even with names like Russ Simmons, the co-founder of Yelp Inc.; Dave McClure of 500 Startups; and Tim Draper, of New York-based Draper Fisher Jurvetson, among Savannah\u2019s investors, Alliy hasn\u2019t reached his target of $10 million.  Alliy spends his days talking to budding entrepreneurs about term sheets,  capital structure  and other basics of corporate governance.  \u201cOne startup asked me, \u2018What is a board? Why do you need a board?\u2019\u201d he says. \u201cWe spent an hour and a half going through that.\u201d  Many of those who come to him have been operating on grants from charitable groups such as the  Bill & Melinda Gates Foundation  and have little concept of how to make a profit.  Alliy\u2019s first investment was in  BiNu Pty , an Australia-based company that developed a program that strips down smartphone applications so they work on the very basic phones that most Africans carry. He put in an undisclosed amount of money himself and helped raise a total of $1.5 million in a first round of funding. He also recently put an undisclosed sum into MPrep.  Accelerator Program  Alliy has also started a so-called accelerator program through the Savannah Fund that gives entrepreneurs management advice and a small amount of cash in exchange for a 15 percent equity stake. The program has helped launch three companies:  Ahonya.com Ltd. , a Ghanaian enterprise that aims to be the Amazon.com of Africa;  Kola Studios , a mobile-game developer in  Uganda ; and Kenya-based  SafariDesk , which helps plan African vacations.  Savannah Fund investor Draper, who put in $250,000, says he\u2019s eager to get in at the onset of Africa\u2019s tech development.  \u201cWe were among the first  venture capital  investors in places like  India , Eastern Europe and  China ,\u201d he says. \u201cThis kind of early fund can have an enormous impact in a region. Entrepreneurship spreads, and wealth and jobs follow.\u201d  Jim Forster, a former Cisco engineer with investments in Ghana, Kenya and Somalia, says he gave Alliy money partly because he admired his commitment to helping Africa.  Investment Models  \u201cThe question that was in my mind, and to some degree still is, is how is the investment model that has worked in Silicon Valley going to work there?\u201d  Alliy\u2019s fortunes may turn on the growing interest of multinationals in Africa.  Google Inc. (GOOG) ,  International Business Machines Corp. (IBM) ,  Nokia Oyj (NOK1V)  and  Samsung Electronics Co. (005930)  have all given time or money to iHub, the Nairobi mall turned tech center that Alliy works out of. They give the budding entrepreneurs phones for testing and send executives to give talks at the mall\u2019s top-floor coffee shop.  And at tech conferences from  Nigeria  to  South Africa , startups are giving demo pitches and seeking venture capital or grant funding.  In his determination to succeed, Alliy spends countless hours working for no pay -- calling prospective investors in the U.S., mentoring entrepreneurs even after he has rejected them for funding and gathering market data. He had to interview local retailers himself to learn which is the most popular smartphone in Kenya: It\u2019s the N3 from Hong Kong-based Tecno Telecom Ltd., running on Android.  \u2018I\u2019m Doing It\u2019  Potential investors both in Africa and Silicon Valley are eager to pick Alliy\u2019s brain.  \u201cI\u2019m doing it,\u201d Alliy says with frustration. \u201cBut I can\u2019t be the only guy doing calls, every night, with investors abroad.\u201d  If his and other African ventures are to succeed, he adds, investors have to take the risk and put down their money. We  get a dopamine rush when we are presented with confirming data  similar to what we get when we eat chocolate or fall in love. On Facebook  we defriend those with different political views to our own . On Twitter we follow people just like us. Yet a vast body of research now points to the import of contemplating diverse, dissenting views. Not just in terms of making us more rounded individuals but in terms of making us smarter decision-makers.  Dissent, it turns out, has a significant value. When group members are actively encouraged to openly express divergent opinions they not only share more information, they consider it more systematically and in a more balanced and less biased way. When people engage with those with different opinions and views from their own they become much more capable of properly interrogating critical assumptions and identifying creative alternatives. Studies comparing the problem-solving abilities of groups in which dissenting views are voiced with groups in which they are not  find that dissent tends to be a better precondition  for reaching the right solution than consensus. Yet how many leaders actively seek out and encourage views alien and at odds to their own?  All too few.  President Lyndon Johnson notoriously discouraged dissent, with many historians  now believing that this played a significant role  in the decision to escalate U.S. military operations in Vietnam. Excessive  group-think is now recognized to have underpinned  President Kennedy's disastrous authorization of a CIA-backed landing at Cuba's Bay of Pigs.  Former employees of the now defunct Lehman Brothers have talked about how  voicing dissent there was considered a career-breaker . Yale economics professor Robert Shiller  explained  that when it came to warning about the bubbles he believed were developing in the stock and housing markets just before the financial crisis he did so only \"quietly\" because: \"Deviating too far from consensus leaves one feeling potentially ostracized from the group with the risk that one may be terminated.\" Is this the feeling the \"clubby\" environment in your boardroom is inadvertently engendering? Or are you actively signaling that you want to hear views different and diverse and in opposition to your own? We need to have the confidence to allow our own ideas and positions to be challenged.  Eric Schmidt, the Executive Chairman of Google,  has talked about how he actively seeks out  in meetings people with a dissenting opinion. Abraham Lincoln's renowned \" team of rivals \" was comprised of people whose intellect he respected and were confident enough to take issue with him when they disagreed with his point of view. Stuart Roden, Co Fund Manager of Lansdowne Partners' flagship fund, one of the world's largest hedge funds, tells me he sees one of his primary roles as being the person who challenges his staff to consider how they could be wrong, and then assess how this might impact on their decision-making. Who in your organization serves as your Challenger in Chief? Interrogating the choices you are considering making? Making you consider the uncontemplated, the unimaginable and that which contradicts or refutes your position?  And also challenging you?  For we are not the robotic emotionless decision-makers of economics text books, bound to make the rationally best choices. Instead we're prone to a whole host of thinking errors and traps. Did you know that when we're given information that is better than we expected \u2014 i.e. that our chance of being targeted for burglary is actually only 10% when we thought it was 20% \u2014 we revise our beliefs accordingly. Whereas if it's worse \u2014 i.e. if we're told that rather than having a 10% chance of developing cancer, we actually have a 30% chance \u2014 we  tend to ignore this new information ? Are you aware of the extent to which our emotions or moods can skew our choices? You may already know that stress leads to excessive tunnel vision, but did you know that studies of both judges and doctors  reveal that when stressed they typically revert  to their unconscious racial stereotyping biases?  Or that if we go 24 hours without sleep or spend a week sleeping only four or five hours a night,  our thinking is as compromised as if we were drunk ? Whilst studies in which people are presented with financial choices reveal that people make worse decisions when their blood sugar has dipped, but also when they're feeling hot under the collar.  Male students presented with a financial decision after having been shown either a \"neutral\" image such as a rock or a \"hot\" image of a lingerie clad Victoria's Secret model,  made significantly poorer choices after having looked at the \"hot\" image . And how about our propensity to become overly attached to the past?  You remember how huge Nokia was. From the 1990s onwards, Nokia dominated the mobile phone industry. At its peak the company had a market value of $303 billion and by 2007 around four in 10 handsets bought worldwide were made by Nokia.  But when Apple introduced its game changing iPhone in 2007, Nokia was caught sleeping on the job. Despite having themselves developed an iPhone-style device \u2014 complete with a colour touchscreen, maps, online shopping, the lot \u2014 some seven years earlier. They never released the product. Instead they decided better to stick with what they knew worked \u2014 good, solid, reliable mobile phones. As a former employee working in the development team at the time  said of that decision , \"Management did the usual. They killed it!\" When the iPhone was introduced, Nokia engineers  sneered at the Apple devices' inability  to pass their \"drop test\" in which a phone was dropped onto concrete from a five-foot height. Nokia management believed that their successful past would continue to provide a reliable guide to the future, but as we now know it didn't. In the six years since the iPhone was introduced Nokia lost about 90% of its market value. And when Microsoft bought Nokia's phone business this month, the fire sale price it paid for it, only half what Google paid for Motorola last year, firmly reflected just how far it had fallen. Your Challenger in Chief needs to be alerting you to such thinking errors and foibles. And you need to be listening to him or her.","path":".\/2008_2012_msft_bloomberg_news\/every-leader-needs-a-challenger-in-chief.txt"},{"id":14538609,"title":"U.S. Stocks Advance Before Alcoa Kicks Off Earnings Season","released_at":"<date>July 12 2010<\/date> <time>21:01:35<\/time>","content":"U.S. stocks rose, adding to gains\nfrom the biggest weekly rally in a year for the Standard &\nPoor\u2019s 500 Index, as analyst upgrades of technology companies\nboosted optimism before the start of the earnings season.  \n SanDisk Corp.  surged 6.8 percent as UBS AG advised buying\nthe shares, while Qualcomm Inc. jumped 3.5 percent as Goldman\nSachs Group Inc. added the stock to its \u201cconviction buy\u201d list.\nHewitt Associates Inc. surged 32 percent after Aon Corp. agreed\nto buy the consulting company. Should we view them as the twin flagships of Microsoft\u2019s\nnew Windows Phone 8 operating system? By that standard, they\u2019re\nimpressive: two polished, highly capable new devices that show\noff Microsoft\u2019s colorful, innovative software to great effect.  Or do we take into account external issues, like the\nbusiness struggles of both companies and the fact that WinPhone\n8 versions of such critical applications as Spotify, Instagram\nand Pinterest are missing in action? In that case, these look\nmore like desperate efforts by two also-rans in hardware to\nhitch their fates to an also-ran in mobile-device software.  I prefer to think the former. But a little caution is in\norder.  On the surface, Windows Phone 8 looks a lot like its\npredecessor, Windows Phone 7. It preserves the same distinctive,\ntile-based interface, albeit with a few tweaks.  You can now, for instance, choose from three sizes of\ntiles, giving you additional control over your start screen. New\n\u201cKid\u2019s Corner\u201d parental controls let you lock down certain\nfeatures and content before you hand the phone over to Junior to\nplay with.  While the visible changes are few, things are vastly\ndifferent beneath the hood. Essentially,  Microsoft (MSFT)  pulled out\nthe engine and rebuilt it from scratch.  Powerful Processors  The operating system now supports more powerful processors\nand higher-resolution screens than Windows Phone 7 could\nhandle.\u00a0The flip side is that apps written for the new software\nwon\u2019t run on WinPhone 7 hardware.  As for the new phones, if you put the Lumia 920 and 8X side\nby side, it isn\u2019t easy to tell them apart. The Lumia has a\nmarginally larger screen -- 4.5 inches, versus 4.3 inches for\nthe 8X -- but both displays are beautiful, with bright colors,\ndeep blacks and even more pixels per square inch than the iPhone\n5\u2019s 4-inch Retina display.  The glass is also rounded at the corners and framed by very\nthin bezels. Both phones have polycarbonate bodies and are\navailable in a selection of colors.  Pick them up, though, and a big difference becomes\napparent: The Lumia is a brick.  Heavy Duty  At 6.5 ounces, it\u2019s one of the heaviest current-model\nsmartphones -- 65 percent heavier than  Apple (AAPL) \u2019s iPhone 5 and 39\npercent heavier than the  Samsung (005930)  Galaxy S III, which has a\nlarger screen. It\u2019s even heavier than Samsung\u2019s Galaxy Note II,\nwhich, with its enormous 5.5-inch screen, is almost more tablet\nthan phone.  And speaking of tablets, the Lumia is almost 50 percent\nthicker than an iPad mini. In short, this is one big hunk of\nhardware.  There are, however, offsetting benefits.  Start with the price: In the U.S., the Lumia costs only\n$100 on a two-year contract with AT&T. For that, you get a\ngenerous 32 gigabytes of storage, a  Qualcomm (QCOM)  Snapdragon S4\nprocessor and, a specialty of Nokia\u2019s, a high-quality 8.7-\nmegapixel camera with Carl Zeiss optics.  It also runs over  AT&T (T) \u2019s ultrafast 4G LTE network, if\nyou\u2019re lucky enough to live in one of the 100 or so markets\nwhere the service has been rolled out.  Neat Extras  Then there are the extras. One is the ability to charge the\nphone wirelessly simply by laying it on top of an optional $49\ncharging pad. (AT&T is including the pad for a limited time at\nno extra cost.) And there\u2019s an excellent maps application.\n(Nokia owns Navteq, one of the world\u2019s major providers of\ngeographic data.)  While the Lumia 920 is so far available only on AT&T, HTC\u2019s\n8X is appearing on both AT&T and Verizon Wireless, where it can\naccess LTE, as well as on  T-Mobile (DTE) , whose non-LTE \u201c4G\u201d network\ngenerally provides slower speeds. The  Verizon (VZ)  version also\nsupports wireless charging, though I wasn\u2019t able to try it out\nsince my test unit was from AT&T.  The 8X has the same processor as the Lumia 920 but costs\ntwice as much for half the storage: $200 for 16 gigabytes. (AT&T\nis also offering an eight-gigabyte model for $100.) It also has\na less-beefy battery (though both should get you through a full\nday of normal use) and an eight-megapixel camera that\u2019s OK, but\nthat I didn\u2019t like as much as the Lumia\u2019s.  On the other hand, the 8X is a far more compact package,\nboth lighter -- 4.6 ounces -- and thinner. And HTC has put some\nextra effort into the audio, including  Beats  technology and an\namplifier for cranking up the volume.  So that\u2019s your choice: value, power and camera versus\ncomfort, elegance and sound. With just a little question mark\nabout what the future holds for all three companies.  ( Rich Jaroslovsky  is a Bloomberg News columnist. The\nopinions expressed are his own.)  Muse highlights include Lance Esplund on  art  and Greg Evans\non  television . (VZ) , and TechAmerica,\nwhose members include  International Business Machines Corp. (IBM)  and\n Microsoft Corp. Talk: Amity Shlaes","released_at":"<date>January 26 2010<\/date> <time>02:00:00<\/time>","content":"When President  Barack Obama  delivers\nhis State of the Union address tomorrow, he\u2019ll do it in English.\nBut what he says would sound just fine in Japanese.  \n That\u2019s because the policies the president will outline are\ncloser to those of traditional Japan than those of traditional\nAmerica. The promulgation of such policies may help the\npresident\u2019s party in the short term, but isn\u2019t optimal for the\ncountry\u2019s long-term future.  \n Consider what the president is likely to do. The first\nthing is bow to a long list of established interest groups. The\npresident is certain to devote time in the speech to flattering\norganized labor. Labor\u2019s political support is all the more\ncritical after the president\u2019s health-care setback. You also can\nbet teachers will get a mention, along with the middle class.  \n The private sector will get a nod too. The president\nlearned last week that bashing business leads to instant losses\nin the stock market. So he\u2019ll leave it to the Democratic lobbies\nto call out  Goldman Sachs  greed.  \n Instead he will praise an enlightened company or two, as\nwell as its founder or chief executive. There will probably be\none old-line outfit -- say General Electric and  Jeff Immelt  --\nand a newer company, maybe Microsoft and  Bill Gates , or Google\nand  Sergey Brin .  \n Expect the president to elaborate on the importance of\ngreen keiretsu, though he probably won\u2019t use that Japanese word.\nHe will talk about how companies can work together with each\nother and government to achieve greener economic growth.  \n National Harmony  \n All this is highly Japanese -- the idea that the country,\nand also the economy, is made up of groups, not individuals, and\nthe idea that the nation as a whole benefits most from a harmony\nof such groups.  \n Next Obama will talk a little bit about infrastructure,\nsuch as the rumored high-speed rail funding for Florida. Word\nhas it that Obama has a plan to create green construction- or\ntechnology-related jobs.  \n To the Japanese this will sound more than familiar. When\ntheir economy hit troubles in the early 1990s, they turned to\ninfrastructure spending to stimulate growth. By the end hundreds\nof billions had been spent. The coast was lined with concrete\nand Japan had new airports and bridges to nowhere.  \n But the  stock market  wasn\u2019t back to its old levels, and\n unemployment  more than doubled, from 2.1 percent in 1990 to 4.6\npercent in 1999.  \n Finally there\u2019s financial reform. The president will talk\nabout the need to halt risk-taking such as proprietary trading\nat commercial banks so that depositors won\u2019t be hostage to\nfoolhardy derivatives bets. You will hear about safe, federally\nguaranteed deposits at banks or thrifts.  \n Missing Opportunities  \n This idea is the most Japanese of any he will present, in\nboth a good and bad sense. The president is right: depositors\nshould be able to count on most of their deposits being there.\nBut to establish a system in which\u00a0insured deposits of citizens\nreside at banks or thrifts that can\u2019t participate in many of the\nopportunities of the global economy is to replicate the bad\naspects of the Japanese postal bank system.  \n That sounds appealing given the ruction of the past two\nyears. But over the course of history Japan\u2019s postal banks, as\nwell as their analogues in Germany, have offered limited returns\nto their depositors. It will cut depositors out of some of the\nopportunity that lies ahead. The result of the sequestering of\ntheir cash has been a safe life, but a lower standard of living,\nfor the Japanese.  \n Too Big  \n The real reason that the administration feels the need to\npush for such protections is also Japanese -- an unwillingness\nto do something more fundamental, end the too big to fail\ndoctrine. If there were no too big to fail doctrine, and banks\nwere allowed to fold, many banks would indeed evaporate. Others\nwould reconfigure themselves, and some would thrive.\u00a0The market\nwould clear.  \n As difficult as it is to imagine, a few big failures would\nlead to a healthier scenario, in which our financial\ninstitutions are small enough not to cause catastrophe when they\nswoon.  \n But Washington prefers to keep things murky. No one in the\nU.S., or anywhere else, is going to have any idea of what the\nU.S. financial sector is really worth. The industry\u2019s values\nwill move up, and  prices  will move down, but in a less reliable\nfashion than they would if markets alone were determining them.\nThat means, as in Japan, that over time people will be wary of\ninvesting in it.  \n This Japanification -- an America that is anxious but safe,\nor safe but anxious -- may appeal to the president\u2019s Democratic\nconstituents. It will offer the promise, but only the promise,\nof a place like America in the 1950S.  \n Not Worth It  \n But Japanification isn\u2019t worth it, for it is more likely to\nyield an economy like Japan\u2019s in the 1990s, with an average\ngrowth  rate  of about 1.5 percent, than America\u2019s in the 1950s,\nwhen growth zipped along.\u00a0By postponing dealing with many of our\neconomic problems we are ensuring stagnation.  \n Economist  Martin Feldstein  is predicting average annual\ngrowth of 1.9 percent for the U.S. in the coming decade. That\u2019s\nalready below the 3 to 4 percent averages that Americans used to\ntake as their birthright in the days of  Bill Clinton  or before.\nBut what proposals like Obama\u2019s effectively are saying is: we\u2019d\nlove 1.9 percent, but we\u2019d be fine with 1 percent, or 0.5\npercent, as long as there were no global economic crises. And\nthat resignation is the most Japanese of all.  \n ( Amity Shlaes , senior fellow in economic history at the\nCouncil on Foreign Relations, is a Bloomberg News columnist. The\nopinions expressed are her own.)  \n Click on \u201cSend Comment\u201d in the sidebar display to send a\nletter to the editor.  \n To contact the writer of this column:\nAmity Shlaes at  amityshlaes@hotmail.com","path":".\/2008_2012_msft_bloomberg_news\/obama-ready-to-short-u-s-with-japan-inc-talk-amity-shlaes.txt"},{"id":2419564,"title":"Obama Defends Data Spying as Modest Privacy Encroachment","released_at":"<date>June 7 2013<\/date> <time>18:23:07<\/time>","content":"President  Barack Obama  defended classified programs to collect data on U.S. residents\u2019 telephone calls and foreign nationals\u2019 Internet activity as \u201cmodest encroachments\u201d on privacy legally authorized by Congress and essential to thwarting terrorist attacks.  \u201cIn the abstract, you can complain about Big Brother, and how this is a potential program run amok,\u201d Obama told an audience in San Jose,  California . \u201cBut when you actually look at the details, then I think we\u2019ve struck the right balance.\u201d  The Obama administration confirmed the existence of the programs last night, a day after reports emerged of a secret court order compelling  Verizon Communications Inc. (VZ)  to provide the National Security Agency with data on all its customers\u2019 telephone use. While the revelations stirred outrage among privacy-rights advocates, U.S. lawmakers from both parties acknowledged earlier yesterday that they were aware of the Verizon order and backed the collection of telephone records as necessary to combating terrorism.  The revelation reignited a debate over the proper balance between civil liberties and security that has flared repeatedly since the Sept. 11, 2001, terrorist attacks. Yet the public backing the Obama administration received from lawmakers in the aftermath of the disclosures makes it unlikely Congress will act to limit the surveillance.  Making Choices  \u201cYou can\u2019t have 100 percent security and also then have 100 percent privacy and zero inconvenience.\u201d Obama said. \u201cWe\u2019re going to have to make some choices as a society.\u201d  The Washington Post and the U.K.-based Guardian newspapers reported yesterday, citing classified documents, that the  Federal Bureau  of Investigation and the NSA had also accessed the central servers of nine U.S. Internet companies, extracting audio and video chats, photographs, e-mails, documents and connection logs. Code-named PRISM, the program traces its roots to warrantless domestic surveillance efforts under former President  George W. Bush .  Microsoft Corp. (MSFT) ,  Yahoo! Inc. (YHOO) ,  Google Inc. (GOOG) ,  Facebook Inc (FB) ., and  Apple Inc. (AAPL)  were among the technology providers involved, the newspapers reported. The companies issued statements last night either denying that they had granted the government access to their servers or saying that they were unaware of the program.  \u2018Hype\u2019 Coverage  Obama dismissed some of the coverage as \u201chype,\u201d saying the telephone program only collects billing data such as the telephone numbers making and receiving calls and the duration of calls. Any monitoring of telephone conversations involving U.S. residents requires a separate court order, he said.  \u201cNobody is listening to your telephone calls. That\u2019s not what this program\u2019s about,\u201d Obama said. The monitoring of Internet communication, which the Post reported includes e-mails and audio and video chats, \u201cdoes not apply to U.S. citizens and it does not apply to people living in the United States.\u201d  The surveillance programs \u201cmake a difference to anticipate and prevent possible terrorist activity,\u201d the president said.  Obama stressed that the surveillance is authorized by federal judges on the secret Foreign Intelligence Surveillance Court and that members of Congress have been regularly informed of it.  \u201cWhen it comes to telephone calls, every member of Congress has been briefed,\u201d Obama said. The House and Senate intelligence committees are regularly briefed \u201cwith respect to all these programs,\u201d he said.  Raw Material  The Post reported that the Internet surveillance, which began in 2007, has grown exponentially and become the most prolific contributor to the president\u2019s daily intelligence briefing, providing raw material for almost one in seven reports. Part of the Defense Department, the NSA runs computer centers analyzing huge databases.  U.S. Director of National Intelligence James Clapper acknowledged the Internet and telephone data-collection efforts in two statements circulated by the White House late last night.  Clapper said the program to tap Internet companies\u2019 servers \u201ccannot be used to intentionally target any U.S. citizen\u201d or anyone located within the U.S.  Both programs are authorized under the Foreign Intelligence Surveillance Act, Clapper said. Data collected are subject to limits set by the surveillance court, he said.  On the telephone program, he said, \u201cthe court only allows the data to be queried when there is a reasonable suspicion, based on specific facts, that the particular basis for the query is associated with a foreign terrorist organization.\u201d  Verizon Calls  The telephone surveillance, sought by the FBI and approved by the court on April 25, requires Verizon to provide the NSA with information for three months on calls inside the U.S. and between the U.S. and other countries on a daily and \u201congoing\u201d basis, the Guardian reported. Lawmakers said the order was part of a surveillance ongoing since 2007. Outside analysts said the program probably also included other telephone carriers.  The  American Civil Liberties Union  last night condemned the data collection described by the Post and Guardian as an abuse of power and called on U.S. lawmakers to investigate.  \u201cUnchecked government surveillance presents a grave threat to democratic freedoms,\u201d ACLU Deputy Legal Director Jameel Jaffer said in an e-mailed statement. \u201cThese revelations are a reminder that Congress has given the executive branch far too much power to invade individual privacy.\u201d  The  Justice Department , as part of its inquiries into leaks of national-security information, has also obtained secret search warrants for telephone records of journalists from the Associated Press and Fox News, prompting protests from U.S. lawmakers and media-advocacy groups.  Explanation Demanded  Some lawmakers yesterday criticized the breadth of the surveillance. Senator  Charles Schumer , a  New York  Democrat, demanded an explanation for a program he called \u201cinvasive.\u201d  \u201cOne thing I have not heard is what the explanation is for needing to do this,\u201d Schumer told reporters.  House Speaker  John Boehner , an  Ohio Republican , said Obama should explain to the American people what he\u2019s doing. The president has the \u201cresponsibility to outline what these tools are and how they are being used,\u201d Boehner told reporters.  Still, any effort to limit government surveillance authority \u201cseems unlikely given the broad support counter-terrorism programs have had from congressional leadership,\u201d said  Matt Miller , former public affairs director for the Justice Department under Obama and previously a staff member for House and Senate Democrats\u2019 campaign organizations.  \u201cSome of the criticism today is of the brand \u2018I can\u2019t believe you\u2019re doing this thing I authorized you to do,\u2019 which is just a little disingenuous,\u201d said Miller, now a partner in the policy and crisis management firm Vianovo LP.  Calm Urged  \u201cEverybody should just calm down,\u201d Senate Majority Leader  Harry Reid , a Nevada Democrat, said at a news conference in Washington. \u201cIt\u2019s a program that\u2019s worked to prevent not all terrorism but certainly a vast majority of it.\u201d  Senate Intelligence Committee Chairman  Dianne Feinstein , a California Democrat, and  Saxby Chambliss  of Georgia, the panel\u2019s top-ranking Republican, said that the telephone surveillance is legal and that they have been kept informed under the law.  \u201cTerrorists will come after us if they can, and the only thing we have to protect us is good intelligence,\u201d Feinstein told reporters. She said the telephone data had stopped multiple plots, though she declined to provide any details.  Sept. 11 Aftermath  The  Bush administration  started the so-called Terrorist Surveillance Program in the aftermath of the Sept. 11 attacks, when agencies began secretly conducting electronic surveillance on U.S. phone calls and e-mails without court warrants.  Congress passed a law in 2008 codifying parts of the program and authorizing intelligence agencies to get broad electronic surveillance orders from the Foreign Intelligence Surveillance Court. In 2012, there were 212 such FISA orders, known as \u201cbusiness records requests,\u201d according to a letter from the Justice Department to Reid. The letter doesn\u2019t specify the targets or scope of the requests.  That 2008 law updated the more than three-decade-old Foreign Intelligence Surveillance Act. It lets intelligence agencies monitor the e-mail, Internet activity and phone calls of non-U.S. citizens reasonably believed to be located outside the U.S. and involved in terrorist activities or other crimes. Congress voted last year to extend it until the end of 2017.  Senator  Ron Wyden , an Oregon Democrat who tried and failed to include stronger civil liberties protections the last time the law authorizing counter-terrorism surveillance was renewed, said he hoped disclosure of the monitoring would provoke \u201ca real debate in the Congress and the country.\u201d  Little Outrage  Senator  Bob Corker  of Tennessee, the top Republican on the Senate Foreign Relations Committee said there could be a \u201cvery simple solution\u201d to address concerns Americans have about their data \u201cbeing stored, and potentially looked at, without them necessarily being singled out as someone who might be causing harm for our nation.\u201d He declined to elaborate.  Still, there were few signs of outrage as senators filed out of a closed meeting held by the Senate Intelligence Committee on the program. Senators Marco Rubio, a Florida Republican,  Tom Coburn , an Oklahoma Republican, and  Al Franken , a Minnesota Democrat, told reporters that the surveillance program is operating under sufficient legal controls.  Feinstein and Chambliss, briefing reporters, said the telephone information collected is dumped into a government database and then used to respond to specific threats.  The surveillance program creates \u201ca telephone book\u201d of data and cannot be accessed without \u201creasonable, articulable suspicion that the records are relevant and related to terrorist activity,\u201d Feinstein said.  Supreme Court  The  Supreme Court  has never ruled on the constitutionality of such a sweeping surveillance program. In February, the court voted 5-4 to bar a challenge by lawyers and civil-rights activists to a federal law that allows government wiretapping of international phone calls and e-mails.  The majority didn\u2019t rule on the surveillance program itself, instead saying the opponents lacked \u201cstanding\u201d to sue because they hadn\u2019t shown they were being harmed.  \u201cThe stories published over the last two days make clear that the NSA -- part of the military -- now has direct access to every corner of Americans\u2019 digital lives,\u201d said the ACLU\u2019s Jaffer, who argued the case before the Supreme Court. \u201cPowers exercised entirely in secret, without public accountability of any kind, will certainly be abused.\u201d  Clapper last night criticized the release of previously classified information about surveillance efforts and said the Post and Guardian articles had left out important context about the usefulness of the programs and their privacy safeguards.  \u201cThe unauthorized disclosure of information about this important and entirely legal program is reprehensible and risks important protections for the security of Americans,\u201d Clapper said of the report on the Internet data. By buying mortgage-related securities, the Fed aims to\nfurther drive down house-loan rates to encourage refinancing and\ninduce home buying. Yet  mortgage rates  have already declined\ntremendously with no obvious impact on housing activity, and\nhomebuyers certainly didn\u2019t show the enthusiasm for the first\ntwo rounds of quantitative easing that equity investors did.  Some observers believe the Fed wants to use inflation and\nnegative real rates to reduce the burden of the Treasury\u2019s huge\ndebt by paying bond holders negative real returns. I am\nskeptical that the Fed has any sinister motivation. This notion\nof a policy of \u201cfinancial repression\u201d belongs in the same\ncategory as the mistaken belief that the Fed is hyping its\nbalance sheet and bank reserves to generate serious inflation as\na way to reduce the real value of federal debt, also at the\nexpense of government-security owners. Such strategies are the\nhallmark of the likes of  Zimbabwe  or banana republics.  Yet the absence of sinister motivations doesn\u2019t mean the\nFed\u2019s actions haven\u2019t had distorting effects on the economy.\n Interest rates  close to zero create deviations from the norm and\nproduce a new set of relationships that few forecasters and\npolicy makers fully understand. This low- or no-interest-rate\nworld also has winners and losers.  Negative Rates  Let\u2019s look at the beneficiaries. At a zero  federal funds\nrate , the Fed can\u2019t cut any further in reaction to economic\nweakness. If deflation occurs, the central bank can\u2019t push real\nrates negative to stimulate borrowing. Furthermore, the lack of\nresponse to almost-zero interest rates by lenders and borrowers\nis what compelled the Fed, and earlier the  Bank of Japan , into\nthe new world of quantitative easing. This and other non-\ninterest rate actions taken previously also have pushed the Fed\nuncomfortably close to fiscal policy and threatened its\nindependence.  While I doubt that the Fed in any way intended to ease the\nfederal debt and  deficit , it is important to keep in mind that\nlow interest rates keep the cost of financing the debt low, even\nas the amount of borrowing leaps. I wouldn\u2019t suggest, of course,\nthat these low financing costs encourage Congress and the\nadministration to delay dealing with the mushrooming federal\ndebt.  Still, after deducting its own operating expenses, the Fed\nreturns the interest it receives on the holding of Treasuries\nand agency securities to the Treasury, helping to offset the\ndeficit. In a recent speech, Bernanke said that in the past\nthree years the Fed has remitted $200 billion to the Treasury.\nCentral banking is a neat game. The Fed creates money out of\nthin air, uses it to buy securities and then sends the interest,\nafter expenses, back to the government. How do the rest of us\nget in on it?  Central-bank rates close to zero also promoted the strange\nphenomenon of negative returns on  short-term government\nsecurities . Then there is the recent negative 0.75 percent yield\non 10-year Treasury inflation-protected securities, whose\nreturns are adjusted for inflation. If annual consumer-price\nincreases over the next decade turn out to be 2.5 percent, as\nforecast by the spread between 10-year TIPS and 10-year Treasury\nnotes, the return on the TIPS would be slightly less than 2.5\npercent annually.  The federal government, of course, isn\u2019t the only borrower\nbenefiting from low interest costs and negative real rates.\nResidential  mortgagors , if they can qualify for loans, obviously\nare getting a break with 30-year rates at 3.4 percent.  Corporate Debt  Investment-grade corporations have been able to issue debt\nand refinance at low rates, and many are doing so. In July, $75\nbillion was issued, a record for any July, at 3.2 percent\naverage yields, a record low, and particularly noteworthy\ncompared with an average 7.2 percent yield over the last 30\ndays. In the third quarter, $257 billion was issued, 64 percent\nmore than a year earlier. To be sure, low corporate-bond yields\nare partly due to individual investors\u2019 disdain for stocks; and\ninvestment-grade corporates also have appeal as havens.  Low interest costs as well as tax deductibility make it\nattractive to issue bonds instead of equity. Some entities are\nissuing century bonds. Last year, the  Massachusetts Institute of\nTechnology , Norfolk Southern Corp., Berkshire Hathaway Inc.,\n Procter & Gamble Co . and Coca-Cola Co. all locked up borrowing\nthat doesn\u2019t mature for 100 years.  In August 2011, the University of  Southern California \nissued $300 million in century bonds with a 5.25 percent coupon\nyield, compared with a 3.4 percent yield at the time on 30-year\nTreasuries. The relatively small premium for an additional 70\nyears suggests that buyers of that issue don\u2019t see a danger of\ninflation for many years.  Another winner from low interest rates, and especially QE3,\nare agency securities. On Sept. 13, when QE3 was announced,\n Fannie Mae (FNMA)  mortgage-backed securities with a 3 percent interest-\nrate coupon jumped 1-10\/32 points, outperforming the 10-year\nTreasury note by 1-4\/36 points. Normally, the performance\ndifference in a trading day is less than 5\/32 point. The Fed\u2019s\n$40 billion-a-month purchase of agency debt via QE3 is the\nequivalent of a major part of the normal $140 billion monthly\nissuance.  Dividend-paying stocks have also benefited from low\ninterest rates, despite average yields of only 2.1 percent for\n Standard & Poor\u2019s 500 Index (SPXL1)  stocks. Furthermore, the equities\ncollapse in 2008 and the S&P 500\u2019s zero net gain from 1998\nthrough 2011 and no gain in 2011 have steered many institutional\nand individual investors to bonds and to stocks that pay high,\nsustainable and increasing dividends. These investors want\nincome here and now as opposed to pie-in-the-sky  capital\nappreciation  sometime in the future.  Dividend Payouts  Investors are putting increasing pressure on corporate\nmanagements to pay dividends, and in August, S&P 500 companies\npaid out a record $34 billion. This pressure is also reflected\nin stock repurchases. Although they aren\u2019t always completed, the\ntiming of actual purchases is uncertain and repurchases\nsometimes simply offset new issuances to employees,  S&P 500\ncompanies (SPX)  have announced $429 billion in equity buybacks for\n2012. That\u2019s down, however, from $555 billion last year.  Companies such as  Microsoft Corp. (MSFT)  and Wal-Mart Stores Inc.\nthat are no longer perceived as  growth stocks  are under heavy\npressure to pay dividends.  Wal-Mart\u2019s (WMT)  dividends have risen 5.3\ntimes in the past decade and the dividend yield is now an\naverage 2.1 percent, even as the stock price has risen only\nabout 50 percent in that time.  Interestingly, the total return on dividend-paying stocks\nbeat nonpayers in every year since 2000, except 2003 and 2009.\nIf $10,000 had been invested in nondividend-paying stocks in\n1979, it would have been worth $250,000 in 2010, but the same\namount invested in dividend-payers would have risen to $413,000.\nPart of this superior result, of course, is the compounding of\nreinvested dividends.  Interest rates close to zero have also made highly\nleveraged speculation in commodities very cheap. Still,\ncommodity prices have been declining on balance since early\n2011, suggesting that low-cost financing, droughts and other\npositive factors have been more than offset by the global\nrecession and hard landing in  China .  I have always been agnostic on gold. Its price is\ninfluenced by so many forces that it is hard to figure out how\nthey play out on balance, and often they cancel each other out.\nThink about political risk, economic uncertainty, inflation and\ndeflation, central-bank holdings, Indians who buy gold in good\ntimes and trade down to silver in bad, new gold-mining\ntechniques, the gold bugs who hold a gold bar in one hand and an\nAK-47 and dried food in the other.  In the inflationary 1970s, gold leaped to more than $800\nper ounce as it was sought as an inflation hedge. Then its price\nfell for two decades. The current jump seems to be a haven play\nand also reflects distrust for paper currencies in general.\nThere has been little inflation lately, and the dollar has been\ntrending up, so those factors aren\u2019t responsible. Gold is also\nprobably being propelled by low interest rates, which reduce its\ncarrying costs, and the uncertain atmosphere that surrounds zero\nor even negative rates. Still, gold returns nothing, and even at\nzero interest rates, costs money to keep secure and to store.  Tomorrow, I will describe the negative effects of low\ninterest rates.  (A. The number of American college graduates holding\nbusiness degrees jumped 6.2 percent from the end of the\nrecession in 2009 to last year.  More than 12 million Americans, or one in five college\ngraduates, have a business degree, according to data from the\n U.S. Census Bureau . Four times as many adults hold business\ndegrees as liberal arts and history majors among the nation\u2019s\nalmost 59 million people who have undergraduate degrees.  \u201cBusiness is a safe harbor,\u201d Kevin Burns, director of\n career services  at  Arizona  State University\u2019s W.P. The government began providing\ninformation about undergraduate degrees for people 25 years and\nolder in its 2009 American Community Survey, an annual poll of 3\nmillion households. The growth in science and engineering majors also surpassed\nthat of undergraduate business-degree holders. More Flexibility  The ranks of liberal arts and history degree holders fell\nto 3 million, down 100,000 from 2009. (AMZN) , the largest online retailer, will offer users free digital copies of CDs bought on its site, as it competes with  Apple Inc. (AAPL)  and  Google Inc. (GOOG)  to attract music lovers choosing to store their songs on the Web.  The new service, called Amazon AutoRip, gives access to MP3 versions of tracks from an initial batch of 50,000 albums, including \u201cOverexposed\u201d by Maroon 5 and Pink Floyd\u2019s \u201cThe Dark Side of the Moon,\u201d Amazon said today in a statement. The service is retroactive, so anyone who has bought CDs from Amazon since it started selling music in 1998 can claim a copy.  While Amazon was the first company to move music to the cloud -- storing content on the Internet for access on any device -- its Cloud Player is still trailing Apple\u2019s iTunes and has new rivals in Google and Spotify Inc. In the second quarter, Apple had 64 percent of the market for digital music, compared with 16 percent for Amazon and 5 percent for Google, according to research firm NPD Group Inc.  \u201cWe\u2019ve known for a while that there is kind of a hole in the customer experience,\u201d Steve Boom, vice president of digital music at Amazon, said in an interview. \u201cA lot of the music people are putting in the cloud is music that they ripped from CDs. We\u2019re providing a service that\u2019s reducing friction.\u201d  Digital Books  The effort may foreshadow a similar option for e-books, said  Scott Devitt , an analyst at Morgan Stanley. Amazon, which makes Kindle electronic readers and tablets, could profit from paying publishers a subsidy to make a digital copy of all the books available on its online store, he said.  \u201cHaving a digital library that is accessible only on the Kindle platform essentially locks a customer into the Kindle ecosystem forever,\u201d he wrote today in a note to clients. \u201cIf executed, it would possibly be the largest coup in company history.\u201d  Seattle-based Amazon has spent much of the past year making sure Cloud Player users can access music from more devices -- phones and tablets -- and more platforms, including Google\u2019s Android and Apple\u2019s iOS. The online retailer also made it possible to listen to music on  Roku Inc.  boxes and Samsung Electronics Co.\u2019s televisions, and for customers to import music into their Amazon libraries from iTunes and Microsoft Corp.\u2019s Windows Media Player.  Spotify\u2019s Rise  Still, there\u2019s plenty of competition. Spotify, which lets users access music without owning it for a monthly fee, is taking share away from Apple, and the model is something Amazon and Google should emulate, said Brian Blair, an analyst at Wedge Partners Corp. in New York.  \u201cAmazon has done a decent job, but Spotify is disrupting iTunes a little bit everyday,\u201d Blair said. \u201cAmazon Cloud Player, Google Play -- I\u2019ve seen no evidence that suggests you\u2019re seeing a migration of users away from iTunes to those services.\u201d  The e-commerce company worked with \u201cmajor\u201d record labels to create AutoRip, Boom said. By giving users digital content they didn\u2019t previously have, there\u2019s less incentive to download illegal music, giving labels a reason to join, he said. Amazon will focus mostly on new releases and popular albums as more titles are added going forward, Boom said.  The digital copies of CDs are stored for free in users\u2019 Amazon Cloud Player libraries and don\u2019t count toward storage limits. While customers can legally make a copy of any CD they\u2019ve bought, Amazon\u2019s developers worked to match the digital music available in its MP3 store to physical CDs for sale to make it easier, Boom said. (7203) \u2019s\nsuppliers, halting worldwide production, the automaker had to\ndecide where to focus its resources. It picked the Prius.  \u201cWe were rapidly burning through cash,\u201d said Atsushi Niimi, head of production, in an interview. \u201cWe decided we had\nto get things going bit by bit to survive through this, so we\nprioritized the cars our customers wanted most.\u201d  The carmaker started calling suppliers across the country\nto find parts for the Prius and luxury-brand Lexus hybrids. By\nMarch 28, Toyota\u2019s Tsutsumi and Kyushu factories were producing\nthe models again at 30 to 40 percent of capacity, Niimi said. General Motors Co.
