(F)  and  Hyundai Motor Co. (005380)  in the U.S. market, which is\nrecovering from its deepest postwar slump.  \u201cThe last several years have been a triple shock for\nToyota,\u201d said Masatoshi Nishimoto, a Tokyo-based automotive\nanalyst for global consulting company  IHS Inc. (IHS)  \u201cIt\u2019s now at a\nmajor turning point.\u201d  Lost Share  The fallout from the earthquake and the unprecedented\nrecalls devastated Toyota sales, which are down 7.8 percent in\n2011 through August in the U.S., while GM, Ford, Hyundai and\nChrysler increased shipments by 16, 12, 21 and 21 percent\nrespectively, according to Autodata Corp. Toyota was outsold in\nthe U.S. by GM, Ford and the Fiat-Chrysler group in August,\naccording to data compiled by Bloomberg Industries.  While GM\u2019s share of the U.S. market in the first eight\nmonths increased 1 percentage point to 20 percent and Hyundai\u2019s\nrose a half percentage point to 5.2 percent, Toyota lost 2.5\npercentage points to 12.7 percent.  The 74-year-old company that Ford Chief Executive Officer\nAlan Mullaly once praised for \u201cthe finest production system in\nthe world,\u201d plans to regain market share with at least 11 new\nmodels over the next two years. Analysts including IHS\u2019s\nNishimoto say Toyota\u2019s advances in fuel economy will underscore\nits recovery even as rivals narrow the gap in quality and\noutsell the Japanese company in emerging markets such as  China .  New Prius Cars  Toyoda\u2019s effort to win back market share, which includes\nthree new versions of the Prius, the world\u2019s top-selling hybrid,\nand electric or dual-power versions of other models, is as much\nabout the company\u2019s strategy to regain its lead as it is about\nthe Japanese economy\u2019s failure to return to prosperity after two\ndecades of anemic growth.  The revamped line-up begins this week with the release of\nthe 2012 model of the Camry, the best-selling car in the U.S.\nfor 13 of the past 14 years. Toyota has promised another four\nreleases this year and at least six in 2012.  \u201cBack in the 80s, if someone said Toyota, the first thing\nthat popped in your mind was Corolla,\u201d said  Jim Lentz ,\npresident of Toyota\u2019s U.S. sales, in an interview. \u201cThrough the\n90s, it was probably Camry. China Sales  The production hiatus after the disaster relegated Toyota\nto No. 5 in China by sales of passenger vehicles in the first\nseven months of this year, trailing  Volkswagen AG (VOW) , GM, Nissan\nand Hyundai, according to an August report on the country by\nconsumer ratings company J. Toyota sold 2,261 Prius cars in China in the last four\nyears, compared with 632,000 Camrys and 809,000 Corollas.  Yen Pain  Toyota\u2019s come-back will be burdened by Toyoda\u2019s commitment\nto keeping jobs in Japan as the strongest yen against the dollar\nin six decades and looming power shortages make it harder for\nthe automaker to escape the same fate as Japan\u2019s economy:\nsliding competitiveness and stagnant growth. Toyota makes more\nvehicles domestically than rivals Honda Motor Co., Nissan Motor\nCo. and Suzuki Motor Corp. combined, making it the most-affected\nJapanese automaker when the earthquake struck.  Suppliers of 1,260 parts and materials used in Toyota cars\nwere crippled by the magnitude-9 temblor and tsunami, leading\nofficials initially to predict a production loss of 2 million\nvehicles, or a quarter of the company\u2019s global output last year. In the weeks following the earthquake on March 11 -- known\nas \u201csan ten ichi ichi\u201d or 3\/11 in Japanese -- Toyota worked to\nrebuild its manufacturing network. While its darkened plant near\nSendai, in Miyagi prefecture, suffered little damage, many\nsuppliers had plants destroyed. Japan\u2019s national effort to recover from the quake helped\nbring factories back on line quicker than expected. Toyota now\nestimates a shortfall of only 150,000 units this fiscal year.  Even without the damage from the quake, Japanese companies\nhave had to cope with a domestic economy that has grown at an\naverage 1.2 percent annually in the past 21 years.  More than two decades of government spending to revive\ngrowth have saddled the country with the world\u2019s highest level\nof public debt. Japan has had deflation for more than a decade,\nand has the world\u2019s oldest society with a median age of 44,\naccording to the United Nations. Downward pressure on wages has\nsapped consumer spending on cars, televisions and appliances.  Growth Downgraded  Japan\u2019s economy contracted at an annualized 2.1 percent\nrate in the three months ended June, its third consecutive\nquarter of decline. The government downgraded its growth\nforecast to 0.5 percent in the year started April, from 1.5\npercent, to reflect the quake\u2019s effect.  The stronger yen has sapped exporters\u2019 profits. A 15-yen change in the rate over the past year has \u201cblown\noff\u201d 300,000 yen, or $3,900, in profit on a $20,000 car,\nTakahiko Ijichi, Toyota\u2019s senior managing officer, said on Aug.\n2. That cut Toyota\u2019s fiscal first-quarter operating profit by 50\nbillion yen, he said.  Japan\u2019s former finance minister,  Yoshihiko Noda  unveiled a\n$100 billion effort on Aug. 24 to help companies cope with the\nyen\u2019s rise, releasing foreign-exchange reserves to the state-run\nJapan Bank for International Cooperation to aid exporters, hours\nafter Moody\u2019s Investors Service lowered the nation\u2019s debt rating\nfor the first time since 2002. Edward Felten , known for cracking the music industry\u2019s\ndigital-copyright protection code, was hired by FTC Chairman\n Jonathan Leibowitz  to help determine how user privacy can be\nprotected in the $26 billion online advertising industry, which\ncollects Web-surfing habits to deliver personalized ads.  Felten, 47, a professor of computer science and public\naffairs at Princeton University in Princeton, New Jersey, will\nbe the agency\u2019s first chief technology officer. He starts full-\ntime Jan. 1.  If advertisers ask consumers what they want directly,\n\u201cthat information may be more accurate than what the company\nhas deduced about the user,\u201d Felten said in an interview at the\nFTC\u2019s Washington office. \u201cAnd the user may have a higher\ncomfort level deciding what information to provide rather than\nworrying about what inferences might be made from what they\u2019ve\ngathered.\u201d  Growth of the online advertising industry, led by companies\nsuch as  Microsoft Corp. , Google Inc.,  Yahoo! Inc.  and  AOL Inc. ,\nis at stake as advocacy groups and regulators question how\ninformation about the online behavior of consumers is collected,\nanalyzed and distributed.  \u2018Feasible Options\u2019  A privacy report issued by the FTC on Dec. 1 urged creating\na do-not-track option. It would let consumers block their\nbrowsing habits from marketers.  Felten is studying the workings of such blocking\nmechanisms, including a tracking-protection option offered in\nMicrosoft\u2019s Explorer 9 browser released Dec. 7 and Google\u2019s\nadvertising-preferences manager. A group of researchers at\nStanford University in Palo Alto, California, also has developed\na way for browsers to notify websites that a visitor doesn\u2019t\nwant information collected.  \u201cThese are feasible options,\u201d Felten said. \u201cThe question\nof what is best is something we are still discussing. I don\u2019t\nget the sense the FTC is in a rush to mandate a unified\nsystem.\u201d  Felten, who reports directly to FTC Chairman Leibowitz, won\na challenge in 2001 from the music industry\u2019s Secure Digital\nMusic Initiative Foundation, which asked researchers to test the\n\u201cdigital watermarks\u201d that secured music files to discourage\ncopying and distribution of pirated material.  Code-Cracker  The watermarks are inaudible messages hidden in music that\nprovide copyright information to MP3 players and recorders. The\ndevices won\u2019t copy music with the security code.  Felten cracked the code, and when he said he would make the\nresults public, the foundation threatened to sue him. The cookie\ncan collect information including the person\u2019s unique computer-\nidentification number, terms used for searches and names of\nwebsites visited. The data can be combined with demographic and\npurchasing information to create profiles of people that are\nsold to businesses to target ads for specific products and\nservices.  \u2018Nothing Sinister\u2019  Marketers say they can do a better job of delivering\nrelevant advertisements if they know the individual\u2019s interests. Marketing based on an individual\u2019s\ninterests can be valuable to both consumers and companies if\ndone in ways that make people comfortable, he said.  The administrations of Bill Clinton and George W. Bush\ndidn\u2019t place constraints on Internet data collection in order to\nencourage development of the online economy. Now regulators and\nlawmakers are taking a closer look at what rules are needed.  The Commerce Department issued a report Dec. 16 urging Web\ncompanies to work with the government and consumer groups to\ncraft privacy measures to protect online users.  Felten, who says he likes to run and cook Mexican food in\nhis spare time, is taking a leave of absence from Princeton to\njoin the FTC. The largest maker of business-management software has a\nrealistic chance of overtaking IBM in database revenue in the\nnext three years as it wins customers with new applications,\nintegration with mobile and real-time technology, and lower\nprices, said John Chen, head of Sybase, the database and mobile-\nsoftware maker that SAP bought for $5.8 billion in 2010.  SAP\u2019s push into  database software  opens up a battlefield\nwith archrival Oracle and is giving the Walldorf, Germany-based\ncompany a fresh source of revenue growth. To become a longer-\nterm threat to its bigger rivals, SAP also needs to plan for\nadvances further out, such as self-correction mechanisms or\nbuilt-in security layers, Chen said.  \u201cI used to run an underdog for a long time, and I never\nunderestimate competitors,\u201d Chen said in a phone interview on\nAug. 7. \u201cWe seem to have something that could mesh well\ntogether. It\u2019s an iPad, only... smaller.  Beyond that, there may not be much more to say about the\nlatest addition to  Apple (AAPL) \u2019s tablet family. But I\u2019ll think of\nsomething.  OK, how about this?  Apple\u2019s most important products created their own markets:\nPeople didn\u2019t know they wanted or needed an iPhone until Steve Jobs & Co. showed it to them. The iPad mini, by contrast, is an\nattempt to follow competitors rather than find a new audience.\n Amazon.com (AMZN) \u2019s Kindle Fire and Google\u2019s Nexus 7, to name two, have\nshown that users want something smaller than the 9.7-inch screen\nthat\u2019s been on every iPad until now.  Which isn\u2019t to say Apple has compromised the iPad\nexperience. For the most part, it has simply shrunk it.  The mini\u2019s screen measures 7.9 inches diagonally. Though\nthat\u2019s 35 percent larger than the competing Amazon and  Google (GOOG) \ndevices, which have 7-inch screens, I still found it small\nenough to hold comfortably in one hand.  Like its big-brother iPad, the mini accommodates six rows\nand four columns of app icons. The icons here are smaller, but\narrayed with enough space between them that even my large\nfingers had no difficulty landing on the one I wanted.  Crazy Light  The most striking thing about the mini is in how thin and\nlight it is. It is really thin and light. Crazy thin and crazy\nlight, even.  Despite the mini\u2019s larger screen, at under 11 ounces it\nweighs a full 21 percent less than the Kindle Fire HD, and 9\npercent less than the Nexus 7. It\u2019s also 30 percent thinner than\neither of them, thinner, in fact, than a pencil.  With those dimensions, the mini is extraordinarily easy to\nslip into a purse or jacket pocket. I was even able to smuggle\nmy review unit into  Microsoft (MSFT) \u2019s Surface tablet launch event in\nNew York last week in my sports coat. No one noticed.  Besides the size and price tag -- more about that later --\nthe most notable thing about the mini is the quality of its\ndisplay, which can be best described as adequate. Unlike the big\niPad (just refreshed with a faster processor and graphics chip,\nplus Apple\u2019s new Lightning connector), the iPad mini lacks\nApple\u2019s ultra-sharp Retina display.  Instead, the mini\u2019s screen has a resolution of 1024 by 768\npixels. That\u2019s the same as on the iPad 2, but less than either\nthe Kindle or Nexus.  Fine Print  I didn\u2019t see a huge difference in some uses, such as\nwatching videos or reading e-books. But I found it noticeably\nharder to read some Web pages, particularly those with fine\nprint. If you\u2019ve got eyesight at all like mine, be prepared to\ndo a lot of pinching and zooming.  Beyond that, the mini offers few surprises to anyone who\u2019s\never used an iPad. Battery life will vary depending on your\nactivities, but I found it comparable to the all-day performance\nof the 9.7-inch model. And the mini ran all my iPad apps without\ndifficulty -- a particularly big advantage, given the paucity of\napps available for either the Kindle Fire or the Nexus 7.  Google claims 600,000 apps for the Nexus 7. But almost all\nof those are simply smartphone apps running on the bigger\nscreen, as opposed to the 275,000 designed specifically to take\nadvantage of the iPad\u2019s capabilities. And the Google Play store\ncan\u2019t approach Apple\u2019s iTunes Store in terms of its selection of\nmovies, music and other content.  App Selection  Amazon, with its huge content selection, can plausibly\ncompete with Apple on that score. But its selection of apps,\ndepending on how you want to count, is even worse than Google\u2019s.  Which raises the question: How much is Apple\u2019s superiority\nin software and content worth to you? How about $130?  That\u2019s the price difference between the iPad mini, which\nstarts at $329 for a Wi-Fi model with 16 gigabytes of storage,\nand a comparably equipped Nexus 7 or Kindle Fire HD, which both\ngo for $199. The mini is also available with 32 and 64 GB\ncapacities, each for an extra $100. And, for an another $130, it\nwill come in versions capable of connecting to the  AT&T (T) ,  Verizon (VZ) \nor  Sprint (S)  4G LTE wireless networks.  There are a few extra benefits as well. The mini has both\nfront and rear-facing cameras; the Kindle and Google tablets\nhave only front-facers. The cellular-enabled models also have a\nGPS chip.  I can tell you the iPad mini is the best small tablet you\ncan buy. The question you\u2019ll have to answer for yourself is\nwhether it\u2019s that much better. The rules were set to take effect this year. The EPA\nproposed in December that they be deferred and yesterday\u2019s\nnotice makes that decision final. The rules will be delayed\nuntil March 31, 2013, for some substances and two years later\nfor others.  Facilities that emit 25,000 metric tons or more a year of\ngreenhouse gases, such as carbon dioxide, are required to submit\nannual reports to the EPA on those releases. On Aug. 22, the EPA\nstarted a new program that lets 7,000 power plants, refiners and\nother manufacturers file their emissions data electronically.\nThe information must be submitted by the end of September.  Employers Must Tell Workers of Right to Unionize, NLRB Says  U.S. employers must post notices informing workers about\ntheir legal rights to form a union and bargain on contracts, the\nNational Labor Relations Board said in a rule that may help\nefforts to organize employees.  Companies that use posters to tell employees about\npersonnel rules or policies must add a notice about their\ncollective bargaining rights, according to a statement yesterday\nfrom the NLRB. The posting must be completed Nov. 14.  \u201cThe notice does make it easier for labor to make\ninroads,\u201d Doreen Davis, a partner in the labor and employment\npractice at Morgan, Lewis & Bockius LLP in  New York  and\nPhiladelphia, said in an interview.  The board proposed the rule to spell out for employees\ntheir rights under federal laws that let workers choose to form\nand join a labor union. Business groups protested the proposal\nand said the rule shows that the agency favors unions.  \u201cIt\u2019s arbitrary, it\u2019s capricious,\u201d Peter Schaumber, a\nformer NLRB chairman appointed by Republican President George W.\nBush, said in an interview. \u201cIt shows just how activist they\u2019re\nprepared to be.\u201d  \u201cThe NLRB rule simply brings the National Labor Relations\nAct in line with other workplace laws that require employers to\npost a notice in the workplace of their employees\u2019 rights,\u201d\nPeter Colavito, director of government relations at the 2.2\nmillion-member Service Employees International Union, said in a\nstatement. U.S. Banks Said to Seek Relief From Regulators as Deposits Swell  U.S. regulators have asked some banks to take more deposits\nfrom large investors even if it\u2019s unprofitable, and lenders in\nreturn are seeking relief on insurance premiums and leverage\nratios, according to six people with knowledge of the talks.  Deposits are flooding into the biggest U.S. banks as\ncustomers seek shelter from  Europe \u2019s debt crisis and falling\nstock prices. That forces lenders to raise capital for a growing\nbalance sheet and saddles them with the higher deposit insurance\npayments. With short-term  interest rates  so low, it\u2019s hard for\nfinancial firms to reinvest the new money profitably.  Regulators have asked banks to take the deposits anyway,\nthree people said, with one lender accepting $100 billion. The\nregulators want lenders to take the deposits because it improves\nthe stability of the financial system, according to one of the\npeople, who said U.S. banks are viewed as places of strength.  Some of the largest ones have talked with regulators about\nsoftening rules for ratios that measure capital and assets,\naccording to the people, who declined to be identified because\ntalks are private. At least one asked for a waiver on paying\nhigher premiums to the Federal Deposit Insurance Corp., which is\nless likely to be granted, one of the people said.  \u201cIf the helicopter comes raining money on your bank and\nit\u2019s only temporarily there, it could be excessively costly and\ndisruptive,\u201d said  Robert Litan , a vice president of research\nand policy at the Kansas City, Missouri-based Kauffman\nFoundation, which promotes entrepreneurial business practices.  The extra deposits are problematic because they\u2019re subject\nto withdrawal, so banks have to park the money in low-yielding\nshort-term investments, Litan said. With few other choices\navailable, banks have stashed their excess deposits at the Fed,\nwhich means the cash gets counted as assets.  This expands their balance sheets and thus pushes down\ntheir leverage ratio, which measures Tier 1 capital divided by\nadjusted average total assets; the lower the ratio, the weaker\nthe bank, at least in theory. In reality, regulators regard U.S.\nlenders as relatively strong with sufficient capital cushions,\nthe people said.  Lenders have held discussions with officials at the Fed,\nFDIC, Office of the Comptroller of the Currency and the Treasury\nDepartment, according to four of the people. Spokesmen for the\nfour agencies declined to comment.  Shannon Bell, a Citigroup spokeswoman,  Howard Opinsky  at\nJPMorgan, Ancel Martinez at Wells Fargo and Bank of America\u2019s\nJerry Dubrowski declined to comment.  Relaxing the rules or enforcement could be a slippery\nslope, said  Lou Crandall , chief economist at Wrightson ICAP LLC,\na Jersey City, New Jersey-based unit of London-based ICAP Plc,\nthe world\u2019s largest inter-dealer broker.  \u201cAsking for a free pass on the leverage ratio for bank\ndeposits by itself isn\u2019t something that regulators would\nconsider,\u201d Crandall said. \u201cThe question is whether banks\nshould be able to exclude reserve balances since they are a\nrisk-free asset.\u201d  For more, click here.  Facebook Faces Confusion From Multiple Privacy Agencies, EU Says  Facebook Inc. and other Internet companies face legal\nconfusion from local and national European regulators with\ndifferent approaches to data protection, the European Commission\nsaid.  These differences \u201cshow the risk that the same company and\nservices will be treated in an inconsistent manner by different\nauthorities,\u201d said  Matthew Newman , a spokesman for the European\nCommission, in an e-mail. The Brussels-based regulator will\npropose draft rules later this year for all data protection\nagencies across the 27-nation bloc to follow.  Facebook\u2019s like button and facial-recognition features were\ncriticized by two German regional regulators this month, with\nofficials in Schleswig-Holstein saying the like button may\n violate  European Union and German data protection law while\nHamburg\u2019s data protection agency said the company may break\nprivacy rules by recording biometric data.  Facebook is among U.S. companies that have faced scrutiny\nin the EU for possible privacy breaches.  Google Inc. (GOOG) ,  Microsoft\nCorp. (MSFT)  and Yahoo! Inc. have been pushed by European data-\nprotection officials to limit the amount of time they store\nonline users\u2019 search records. The group of regulators, known as\nthe Article 29 Data Protection Working Party, has also\ncriticized Facebook for policy changes that could harm users\u2019\nprivacy. For many, it represents their \u201cbank\u201d far more than\nrows of tellers standing behind tall counters.  The story of the ATM\u2019s rapid rise to ubiquity is also one\nof a revolution in retail banking.  It begins with the embrace of automation that\ncharacterized the mid-century economy and gave rise to vending\nmachines, self-service gas stations and other innovations. In\nthe case of the ATM, much of the initial impetus began with\nEuropean bankers concerned about increasing unionization and\nrising labor costs. To economize, they solicited engineers to\ndevelop a solution for after-hours cash distribution.  In 1967, two British banks installed prototypes of today\u2019s\nATM. The same year, Swedish savings banks unveiled a similar\ninvention called the Bankomat. By 1971, manufacturers were\nmushrooming and building ATMs around the world, including in\nthe U.S. and  Japan .  These early devices were all stand-alone, clunky,\nunfriendly and inflexible. They could do one thing only:\ndispense cash when activated by a token. Some banks would keep\nthe token in the machine and return it to the customer (by\npost) once the account was debited. Many machines proved\nunreliable: Rarely had electronic equipment been put to the\ntest by weather in such a way. Security was also a problem, as\nthere was no easy way to make sure that whoever deposited a\ntoken was indeed the owner of the bank account.  Moving Online  Chubb, the British lock maker, pioneered the use of a\npersonal identification number. Chubb (along with several other\ncompanies) also introduced card-like plastic tokens with a\nmagnetic strip. Yet this wasn\u2019t enough to reassure bankers.  For these reasons, the development of online communication\nwith a central computer became an overriding concern.\n International Business Machines Corp. (IBM)  was a pioneer in this\nregard. IBM started the first online trials in  Sweden  and\nfollowed up with an online device in the U.K. for Lloyds Bank\nin 1972. For most of the 1970s, IBM engineers worked to develop\nthe rails, pipes and standards on which other elements of the\npayments ecosystem -- such as credit cards and point-of-sale\nterminals -- would eventually depend.  By the early 1980s, however, ATM manufacturers such as\nChubb, De La Rue Plc and Docutel Corp. had failed to keep up\nwith developments in computing and electronics. Others hadn\u2019t\nyet achieved a critical market share. Citibank had effectively\nabandoned a plan to commercialize devices of its own patented\ndesign. Even IBM, which had the marketing muscle, engineering\nexpertise and business contacts to take over the market,\ndecided against further investment in payment technology.  Around this time, two Ohio-based companies,  NCR Corp. (NCR)  and\n Diebold Inc. (DBD) , were working on technology that would enable them\nto effectively dominate the world\u2019s supply of ATMs for the next\ntwo decades.  Capitalizing on deregulation and the banking industry\u2019s\ngrowth across retail markets, NCR and Diebold were instrumental\nin turning the dinosaur cash dispenser into today\u2019s sleek,\nmulti-function ATM. The companies\u2019 innovations included new,\ncustomer-friendly video-display units; programmable buttons\nalongside the screen; a shift toward dispensing cash\nhorizontally, which reduced jams; and a growing menu of\noptions, including money transfers and balance inquiries.  Explosive Growth  These advances soon freed staff at retail-banking branches\nto engage customers in higher-value services, such as\ninsurance, mortgages and stock-market trading. ATMs thus proved\nto banks that there were alternative distribution channels to\nbrick and mortar branches; became the backbone of the payments\nsystem; and opened the door to telephone and Internet banking.\nIn this sense, ATMs enabled the explosive growth of retail\nfinance during the last decades of the 20th century.  ATMs, however, remained expensive to operate. The need for\ndedicated phone lines still limited them largely to bank\nbranches or high-traffic locations such as train stations and\nairports. Operating systems and microprocessors had to be\ncustom-made. All this changed with the advent of digital\ntelephony and personal computers, and the introduction of\n Microsoft Corp. (MSFT)  software as the core operating system. The ATM\nthen effectively became a terminal of banks\u2019 central computers,\nenabling online verification at the point of transaction.  In the mid-1990s, Triton Systems Inc. and Tidel\nEngineering LP introduced lighter and cheaper machines that\nused dial-up communications. Unlike ATMs attached to a bank,\nthese new cash dispensers could send and receive encrypted data\nover regular phone lines. As a consequence, new organizations\ncalled independent ATM deployers (better known as IADs) began\ninstalling stand-alone ATMs in grocery stores, bars,\nuniversities and casinos that dispensed cash for a fee.  The IADs also introduced the practice of self-\nreplenishment: The owner of a bar, for example, could deposit\ncash received from customers directly into the ATM, increasing\nsales while reducing the need to transport cash to and from the\nbank.  More recently, in what is perhaps the dawn of another new\nera, some banks have explored the possibility of connecting\nATMs to mobile-telephone networks. This level of sophistication\nisn\u2019t bad for a machine that had decidedly humble beginnings\nalmost 50 years ago.  But the ATM has always been more than a convenient way to\nget cash. It revolutionized the way banks think about\ncustomers, the way the financial world thinks about technology,\nand the way we pay for almost everything we buy.  ( Bernardo Batiz-Lazo  is a professor of business history\nand bank management at Bangor University in  Wales  and the\nauthor, with Tom Harper, of \u201cCash Box: The Invention and\nGlobalization of the ATM.\u201d The opinions expressed are his own.) Brian Holland, Nasdaq \u2018Marketing Ace\u2019 Behind Ads, Dies at 67","released_at":"<date>August 23 2012<\/date> <time>23:00:00<\/time>","content":"L. Brian Holland, the marketing\nexecutive who fueled the growth of the  Nasdaq (NDAQ)  Stock Market by\nharnessing the power of  television advertising  to build a brand,\nhas died. He was 67.  Holland died of a heart attack on Aug. 14 at his farm in\nGreensboro,  Maryland , according to his daughter, Megan.  He arrived at  Nasdaq  in 1989 as senior vice president of\nmarketing after working at ad agencies J. Walter Thompson USA\nand Wells Rich Greene and at Chase Manhattan Bank. Nasdaq -- the\nNational Association of Securities Dealers Automated Quotations\n-- had opened for business in 1971 as the first electronic stock\nmarket, focusing first on over-the-counter shares.  In 1989, \u201cthe exchange was in the shadow of the 1987 crash\nand had lost 10 percent of its companies,\u201d Holland recalled in\na 2000  interview  with Industry Week. \u201cMy task was to stop that\noutflow and to increase market share of new companies that were\nlisting.\u201d  In particular, Nasdaq was trying to keep its much-better-\nknown competitor, the  New York  Stock Exchange, from luring away\nany of its \u201cfearsome foursome\u201d listed companies, Microsoft\nCorp., Cisco Systems Inc.,  Intel Corp . and Dell Inc., Charles\nGasparino wrote in his 2007 book, \u201cKing of the Club:  Richard\nGrasso  and the Survival of the New York Stock Exchange.\u201d  As the in-house \u201cmarketing ace\u201d at the Washington-based\nNational Association of Securities Dealers, founder of Nasdaq,\nHolland was asked by then-president Joseph Hardiman to devise\nthe first advertising campaign by an equity market, according to\nGasparino.  Ad Slogan  The ads, calling Nasdaq \u201cthe stock market for the next\nhundred years,\u201d focused on success stories of listed companies\nsuch as Microsoft and depicted the  NYSE (NYX)  as yesterday\u2019s news.  \u201cIt is said he is to computer software what Thomas Edison\nis to the light bulb,\u201d began one 30-second commercial that\nspotlighted the achievements of Microsoft founder  Bill Gates .  It ended: \u201cWhere in today\u2019s world do you find companies\ncapable of such astonishing growth? Actually, there\u2019s a list of\nthem printed every day. Nasdaq -- the stock market for the next\nhundred years.\u201d  Holland worked with the New York advertising firm of\nMessner Vetere Berger Schmetterer, which today is part of Euro\nRSCG Worldwide Inc. Founding partner Tom Messner wrote in Adweek\nin 2005 that Nasdaq was \u201cthe first great campaign the agency\ndid,\u201d turning the market \u201cinto a brand that would drive the\neconomy of the 90s.\u201d  On Broadway  Holland was also a driving force behind  MarketSite , the\nseven-story cylindrical tower in New York\u2019s Time Square that\nserves as Nasdaq\u2019s broadcast facility and high-tech advertising\nbillboard for its member companies.  Describing MarketSite to the trade publication Brandweek in\n1997, Holland said: \u201cAs we have attracted numerous companies\nwhich are definitely household names, like Staples, Starbucks,\nBed Bath & Beyond, and of course, technology names like\nMicrosoft and Intel, we saw an opportunity to demystify the\nNasdaq for a lot of people, as well as make us more appealing to\nthe news media.\u201d  Lee Brian Holland was born on Jan. 8, 1945, in  Chicago  and\nwas raised in Hockessin,  Delaware , a suburb of Wilmington. He\ngraduated from  Georgetown University  in Washington, in 1967.  Growing Corn  After leaving Nasdaq in 2001, Holland worked for Pipeline\nTrading Systems LLC, a New York-based broker-dealer that\nspecialized in electronic block-trading of securities. He\nretired two years ago and lived at the Maryland farm that had\nbeen his summer home since 1988, raising crops such as soybeans\nand corn, his daughter said.  Nasdaq, the second-largest U.S. equity exchange, is\ncurrently owned by Nasdaq OMX Group Inc., which went public in\n2002.  Besides Megan, Holland is survived by a son, Christopher,\nand a second daughter, Siobhan, from his first two marriages,\nwhich ended in divorce, and by his third wife, Dianna Lawrence. Petrobras, based in Rio de Janeiro, sold 2.4 billion common\nshares for  29.65 reais  each and priced 1.87 billion preferred\nstock at 26.30 reais apiece. The company sold 115 billion reais\n($67 billion) of shares and banks have an option to buy another\n5 billion reais, according to a statement sent late yesterday.  Petrobras is spending about $224 billion over the next five\nyears to boost production to 5.38 million barrels a day by\ntapping deposits trapped under a layer of salt beneath the ocean\nfloor. The share sale was priced at a 2 percent discount to\nyesterday\u2019s close, suggesting investors are backing Petrobras\u2019s\nplans to overtake industry rivals such as Chevron Corp.  \u201cMany of the other global majors are being challenged\nbecause their reserves are being depleted,\u201d said  Ron Holt ,\nchief executive officer of Hansberger Global Investors Inc. in\nFort Lauderdale, Florida, which manages $8 billion. \u201cIf you\nlook at the potential capital expenditures that the company has\nplanned for the next several years, that is a very significant\npotential exploration project for them.\u201d  The company is tapping demand for emerging-market assets to\ndevelop deposits including Tupi, the largest discovery in the\nAmericas in three decades. The field, and the nearby Libra\ndeposit in the so-called presalt region off the Brazilian coast,\nmay each contain as many as 8 billion barrels of oil.  Exxon, Apple, PetroChina  After the sale Petrobras jumped to the fourth-biggest\ncompany in the world, behind  Exxon Mobil Corp.,   Apple Inc.  and\n PetroChina Co.,  data compiled by Bloomberg shows. Petrobras has\na market value of $214 billion, more than companies including\nMicrosoft Corp. and Wal-Mart Stores Inc.  \u201cGiven Petrobras\u2019s superior asset base and growth profile\nversus global oils, we believe the stock should trade at a\npremium relative to peers,\u201d Bank of America analyst  Frank McGann  said in a note to clients.  Petrobras  has slumped 28 percent this year on concern the\nsale will cut  earnings  and boost state interference. After the\nshare sale, investors will focus on Petrobras\u2019s exploration\nprogram to exploit the discoveries, said  Mirela Rappaport , who\nhelps manage about $100 million at Investport in Sao Paulo.  Brazil will add the most oil production of any country\noutside of the Organization of Petroleum Exporting Countries, or\nOPEC, over the next 25 years and surpass Venezuela and Mexico to\nbecome the second-largest producer in the Americas, behind the\nUnited States, the EIA said in its  International Energy Outlook .  Production Targets  Petrobras has doubled output in the past 10 years and will\nsurpass Exxon\u2019s current production by 2015 if it meets targets\nset in its current business plan.  Petrobras plans to boost production 7.8 percent this year,\nwhile Exxon is targeting an increase of 3 percent to 4 percent\nthis year. Chevron plans to increase 1 percent a year for the\nnext five years.  Still, Petrobras has missed production targets in the past\nand extracting oil from deep waters \u201ccould be slower and more\nexpensive than anticipated,\u201d McGann said. \u201cRisks are oil\nprices, project execution, and politics.\u201d  The company\u2019s  preferred shares  fell 50 centavos, or 1.9\npercent, to 26.30 reais at 5:07 p.m. in Sao Paulo trading, while\nthe common stock dropped 2 percent to 29.65 reais.  As part of the share sale, Petrobras issued about $42.5\nbillion of stock to Brazil\u2019s government in exchange for the\nrights to develop 5 billion barrels of oil reserves. The sale\nincludes an over-allotment option by underwriters to sell 188\nmillion shares, or about $3 billion, over the next 30 days.  Increased Control  The sale may signal President  Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva  is\npaving the way for greater control over the Brazilian economy\nbefore the likely election of his chosen successor  Dilma Rousseff  next month.  \u201cIt wasn\u2019t in Frankfurt, it wasn\u2019t in New York, it was in\nour Sao Paulo exchange that we carried out the biggest\ncapitalization in the history of capitalism,\u201d Lula said at an\nevent in Sao Paulo today.  Production at Shell, based in The Hague, was about 3.15\nmillion barrels a day in 2009, down from 3.25 million a year\nearlier, according to its annual report. Exxon\u2019s output was\nabout 3.93 million barrels in 2009, up from 3.92 million a year\nearlier.  Prior to the sale, Petrobras was valued at 8.03 times its\nestimated earnings for this year, according to data compiled by\nBloomberg. That compares with 10.6 times for Beijing-based\nPetroChina Co., Asia\u2019s biggest company by market value, and 10.8\ntimes Irving, Texas-based Exxon, the world\u2019s largest company by\nmarket capitalization, the data showed.  Government Stake  A total of 18 equity offerings were completed this year by\nBrazilian companies before Petrobras\u2019 sale, raising $12.4\nbillion, data compiled by Bloomberg show. The shares have gained\n20 percent, on average.  The government increased its stake in the company to 48\npercent from 40 percent after the share sale, Finance Minister\n Guido Mantega  said at an event in Sao Paulo today. That includes\nminority stakes held by state-owned banks.  Before the sale, the government controlled the company\nthrough 55.6 percent of voting shares. Petrobras didn\u2019t disclose\nthe government\u2019s voting stake after the offering.  Lula is tightening the state\u2019s grip on the domestic oil\nindustry after Tupi was discovered in 2007, the largest find in\nthe Western Hemisphere since Mexico\u2019s Cantarell in 1976. He says\nBrazil is relying on the country\u2019s oil wealth to help raise the\nnation\u2019s 192 million residents out of poverty. Trademark  Amazon.com Seeks Dismissal of Apple Lawsuit Over \u2018 App Store \u2019  Amazon.com Inc. (AMZN) , responding to a trademark lawsuit by Apple\nInc. over its use of the words \u201cApp Store,\u201d said the term is\ngeneric and denied that the iPhone maker has exclusive rights to\nthe phrase.  Amazon, the world\u2019s largest online retailer, said it isn\u2019t\nrequired to obtain a license or authorization to use \u201cApp\nStore\u201d because the term is \u201cunprotectable\u201d and won\u2019t be\nconfused or unfairly compete with Apple\u2019s App Store service,\naccording to a filing yesterday in federal court in Oakland,\nCalifornia. App is short for application.  \u201cBased on their common meaning, the words \u2018app store\u2019\ntogether denote a store for apps, such as the app stores\noperated by Amazon and Apple,\u201d Amazon said in the filing. Kristin Huguet, an Apple spokeswoman, didn\u2019t immediately\nreturn a voice-mail message seeking comment.  Apple\u2019s App Store, started in 2008, offers downloads of\nprograms from the company and third-party developers to users of\niPhones, iPod media players and iPad tablet computers.  Apple, based in Cupertino, California, applied to register\nApp Store as a trademark in the U.S., and the U.S. Patent and\nTrademark Office approved the application, Apple said in the\nlawsuit. The mark hasn\u2019t yet been formally registered and\n Microsoft Corp. (MSFT)  is opposing the application.  Both Microsoft and Apple have brought in linguistics\nexperts who filed reports to the patent office supporting their\nopposing contentions about whether \u201capp store\u201d is a generic\nterm or a proper noun.  The case is Apple Inc. v. Amazon.com Inc., 11-1327, U.S.\nDistrict Court, Northern District of California (Oakland). Wegmans, based in Rochester,  New York , has in-store\npharmacies in five states, and Walgreen complained that the\nsimilarity of the two logos would lead consumers to a false\nbelief that the two companies had an affiliation.  Terms of the settlement weren\u2019t disclosed in a court\nfiling. Wegmans said in a  statement  that it would quit using the\n\u201ccircle W\u201d symbol on its Wegmans brand packaging by the end of\nJune 2012. It will retain the right to use \u201cWegmans\u201d in\nscript, it said.  \u201cThe cost of making relatively minor changes to a limited\nnumber of products was much less than the cost of litigating\nthis case to the end,\u201d Jo Natale, a Wegmans spokeswoman, said\nin the statement.  Wegmans never had any intent to make its products or logos\nresemble Walgreen\u2019s, she said.  The case is  Walgreen Co. (WAG)  v. Wegmans Food Markets Inc.,\n1:10-cv-01216-TSE-TCB, U.S. District Court, Eastern District of\nVirginia (Alexandria).  Obituary  Norman Latker, Prime Mover for Bayh-Dole Act, Dies at 79  Norman J. Latker, who played a key role in the passage of\nthe 1980  Bayh-Dole Act  that allows universities and research\ninstitutes to take title to inventions stemming from federally\nfunded research, has died. He was 79.  When Latker was a patent counsel with the National\nInstitutes of Health, he published a study showing that of\n30,000 federally owned patents, almost none had been\ncommercialized. U.S. senators Birch Bayh and Robert Dole used\nthe data to support their bill.  As a result of the bill\u2019s passage, $100 billion worth of\ntechnology was released for licensing to the private sector,\nBruce Merrifield, former Assistant Secretary of Commerce in the\nReagan Administration, said in a statement posted on the online\nguestbook accompanying Latker\u2019s April 17  obituary  in the\nWashington Post.  \u201cNorm left behind an enduring legacy that he and his\nfamily can be proud of,\u201d Robin Rasor, president of the\nAssociation of University Technology Managers,\nsaid in an e-mail. AUTM presented Latker with its Driving\nInnovation award at a December celebration of the 30th\nanniversary of Bayh-Dole.  After leaving NIH, Latker worked in the Small Business\nAdministration\u2019s Office of Advocacy and, later, the Office of\nFederal Procurement Policy and the Department of Commerce, where\nhe developed implementing regulations for Bayh-Dole.  He also\ndrafted the 1986 Federal Technology Transfer Act.  Latker also headed the Interagency Committee on Technology\nTransfer, established to implement the 1986 law.  After he left\ngovernment service, Latker practiced at Washington\u2019s Brody &\nNeimark PLLC.  He had an undergraduate degree in chemical engineering and\na law degree from the University of Illinois. He also received\nhonorary doctorates from the University of Illinois and the\nUniversity of Wisconsin in recognition of his contributions to\ntechnology transfer.  Latker, who lived in Bethesda, Maryland, at the time of his\ndeath, was survived by his wife and two children. His family\nrequested that memorial donations be made to the  Tuberous\nSclerosis Alliance . (NFLX)  has become the best\nperforming U.S. stock in the Standard & Poor\u2019s 500 Index in 2013\nand the second most expensive, and therein lies a tale of\ndisagreement.  Investors who dig into company filings can find negative\nfree  cash flow , a surge in liabilities for new movie and TV-show\ncontent and a long-term increase in unpaid subscribers.\nMoreover, perceived limits on customer numbers and the high\nprice of shares have led 26 of the 37 Bloomberg-listed a nalysts \ncovering the stock to advise investors to sell or hold stakes. Earnings Call  Chief Executive Officer  Reed Hastings  may get questions\nabout the Los Gatos-California-based company\u2019s performance when\nhe hosts a videoconference today to discuss second-quarter\nearnings. Content Spending  Front and center in such an analysis is how much Netflix,\nwith a market capitalization of almost $15 billion, spends on\ncontent. It pays about $500 million a quarter, while running a\ndeficit in free cash flow in the past two quarters, company\nfilings show.  It has $5.7 billion of binding contracts to pay for and\nlicense streaming content, of which about $2.4 billion is\npayable in less than a year, according to its first-quarter\nfiling. Hastings has said he doesn\u2019t favor that. No wonder.\nIn 2011, Netflix announced it would separate its DVD-by-mail and\nstreaming plans, with each available for $7.99 a month.\nCustomers with joint streaming and DVDs plans saw bills jump to\n$15.99 from $9.99. After that 60 percent bump, about 800,000\nsubscribers canceled. The stock hit a low in November of that\nyear of $63.86, down from a 2011 high of about $299. It\u2019s still\nnot back to that level.  If Hastings doesn\u2019t budge on streaming prices, he might\nhave to keep selling stock or debt. That wouldn\u2019t be good for\nshareholders, Pachter said. In February, Netflix sold $500\nmillion of  junk bonds  to help fund programming and retire debt.  Netflix also is adding business risks as it licenses more\noriginal series that don\u2019t have a proven track record like the\nhit AMC \u201cMad Men\u201d series it offers.  \u201cThere is always the chance any particular show could\nflop,\u201d said an April report by New York-based Jefferies Group\nLLC, a securities and investment-banking firm. \u201cPrior content\ndeals offered a more predictable return profile.\u201d  Internet TV  One of Hastings\u2019s key messages to investors has been about\nthat growth Pachter says Internet investors are focused on. Other key metrics in assessing the company include revenue,\nsubscriber numbers and, in the long term, profit. Netflix\nrevenue was $3.6 billion last year, up from $3.2 billion the\nyear before. Those who pay up for the privilege of owning an Apple product feel like they are part of an elite organization that, somehow, anyone can join. That has been the secret sauce that allows Apple to charge premiums of as much as 50 percent over the prices of comparable computers and phones sold by competitors, which in turn has let it earn outsized profits despite selling a relatively small number of devices. Now, however, executives in Cupertino, California, are betting that it's time to abandon this strategy. Competitive pressure from Google has pushed Apple to dilute its brand by offering a cheaper iPhone, known as the 5c, which will cost about half as much as the new 5s. This gambit may work, but it will not be without some long-term drawbacks. Apple has introduced a hierarchy of quality and price within the community of iPhone owners. Apple's mobile market share has already peaked in rich countries as consumers are now warming to the high-end smartphones and tablets made by Samsung and powered by Google's Android operating system. In the rest of the world, Apple has aspirational appeal among the upper-middle class but is too expensive for most people. Nokia's \"dumb phones\" and, to a lesser extent, cheaper Android phones made by Samsung, HTC, LG and others are all vastly more popular in India, Africa, and Latin America. Unlike Apple's premium phones and tablets, those products are barely profitable. However, there is some evidence that people who like their lower-end devices will upgrade to high-margin ones made by the same company. This is  one explanation  for why Microsoft was willing to purchase Nokia's money-losing handset division, which was announced last week. A few billion euros is a small price to pay for what could be more than a billion potential Windows phone customers. This also explains why companies like Samsung are willing to live with profit margins just half of what Apple earns in exchange for relentless growth in market share. They sell cheaper phones that get consumers up the ladder toward higher-end products. Apple has long resisted this strategy, but the 30 percent decline in its  market value  over the past 12 months and the  pressure from activists like Carl Icahn  may have gotten it to change its tune. That could be good for the company's long-term growth, but it will come with a cost that the executives in Cupertino may not fully appreciate. (Matthew C. Klein is a writer for Bloomberg View, and owns an iPhone. (6758)  and Microsoft Corp., lackluster sales of its new Wii U and a shift by casual game players to smartphones and tablet computers.  Yamauchi succeeded his father as president in 1949, and the company almost was forced to file for bankruptcy in the late 1960s after several failed attempts to expand its product lineup into toy guns, baby carriages and fast food, according to several books written on Nintendo\u2019s history. A few are top performers, and are eligible for promotion and larger bonuses. Most are average. The rest are denied bonuses and often asked to leave. The performance reviews that determine these rankings occur every six months. As Kurt Eichenwald explained in an  article  in Vanity Fair magazine, the system encourages workers to undermine each other, to avoid taking risks and to spend more time sucking up to bosses than working. Even worse, it removes many of the incentives for collaboration. Despite these downsides, ranking systems are surprisingly popular at  big companies . That's all the more remarkable considering that research shows that performance-based pay is only good for people who are doing  routine tasks . That's because these workers don't benefit much from cooperating. Other workers, however, perform better when they aren't judged against their peers. Economists used to think it was obvious that people would work better if you give them greater financial incentives to succeed, although psychologists knew that choking under pressure was a real phenomenon. High stakes often produce nervousness and anxiety. Think of all the public-speaking advice you hear about imagining audience members in their underwear. In 2005, several economists combined this intuition with some  clever experiments  and found that \"the highest levels of rewards produced lower performance.\" Even more relevant for Microsoft is a recent  paper  that studies how teams perform under three different compensation plans: one where there were no bonuses for individual effort, one where there were small bonuses and one where each team member was paid almost exclusively for performance. They found that \"the presence of a high relative reward seems to crowd out voluntary cooperation (i.e., the willingness to exert effort above the individual rational level),\" although this is somewhat offset by the fact that each team member works harder to grab the biggest possible share of the bonus pool. The upshot for Microsoft and other companies is that they could benefit from a more cooperative compensation model. Microsoft's new management might be able to realize the company's  potential  with the help of some behavioral economics. (Matthew C. Klein is a writer for Bloomberg View. But in a cavernous room in  New York \u2019s SoHo district, a\ngroup of entrepreneurs is working to render the entire\nWashington conversation over Obamacare obsolete. There,\nObamacare is no longer a political controversy: It\u2019s a business\nopportunity. And a trio of young technologists have raised $40\nmillion to take advantage of it.  For Joshua Kushner, the epiphany came when he opened his\ninsurance bill. \u201cI realized I had absolutely no idea what it\nmeant,\u201d he said. \u201cI\u2019m overeducated. I run a growing business,\nbut I don\u2019t know what my benefits are, I don\u2019t know what doctors\nor hospitals I have, I don\u2019t know how to file a claim. So I\npicked up the phone and called 10 or 12 of my friends and asked\nif they had any idea how to navigate this amazing expense. None\nof them did.\u201d  Transforming Industries  To Kushner, that signaled a business opportunity -- and a\nsocial one. The 28-year-old Harvard graduate is the founder of\nThrive Capital, which invests in Internet and media companies,\nincluding Kickstarter and Instagram. \u201cWe hope to transform\ntraditional industries,\u201d he said.  But he was afflicted by the ennui that\u2019s infected the\nlatest crop of young coders. He quotes Jeff Hammerbacher, one of\nFacebook\u2019s early employees, saying, \u201cThe best minds of my\ngeneration are thinking about how to make people click ads, and\nthat sucks.\u201d  So Kushner called his friend Kevin Nazemi, formerly of\nMicrosoft Corp., and Mario Schlosser, of the Latin American\nsocial gaming giant Vostu Ltd., and they decided in January 2012\nto take on one of the biggest, most hidebound industries of all:\nhealth care. The way to do it, they decided, was by transforming\nhealth insurance. \u201cIt\u2019s just a beautiful vantage point for\naddressing these issues,\u201d Schlosser said.  Starting a new health insurer is a nice thought, but an\nalmost impossible task. At least, it used to be. That was before\nObamacare upended part of the industry.  Come Oct. 1, all 50 states and the  District of Columbia \nwill open health insurance marketplaces (sometimes called\n\u201cexchanges\u201d) to serve people who don\u2019t get coverage from their\nemployer or a government program. The insurers in these online\nmarketplaces won\u2019t be able to discriminate based on existing\nconditions. They have to offer a core package of essential\nbenefits and clear pricing information. And they\u2019re about to see\na flood of first-time customers.  In New York City, one of those insurers will be Oscar.\nThat\u2019s the name Kushner and his co-founders chose, hoping it\nwould help humanize their company. \u201cI don\u2019t think we could do\nthis without Obamacare,\u201d Schlosser said. \u201cYou\u2019d have to break\ninto a market that\u2019s been pretty \u2018oligopolized\u2019 with big\ninsurers catering to brokers, agency houses and big employers.\nBut now we have a direct connection to the consumer.\u201d  Breeding Familiarity  The idea behind Oscar is that using your insurance should\nbe as easy and intuitive as using your Facebook account or your\nTumblr page. As Nazemi puts it, \u201cWe have a responsibility to\ntake the friction and pain of engagement out of the process.\u201d\nThe experience is familiar to anyone who uses today\u2019s leading\nsocial networks (the former head of engineering at Tumblr now\nworks for Oscar). But for anyone who\u2019s used the websites of\nAetna or Cigna or Blue Cross Blue Shield, it\u2019s something of a\nrevelation.  Sign into your Oscar insurance account online and you\u2019ll\nsee a few carefully chosen options on a page that\u2019s otherwise\nwhite and clean. At the top, you can type in your symptoms and\nbe taken immediately to a guided set of options, including a\nbutton that lets you talk to a doctor. Click it, and a doctor\nwill call you, wherever you are, whatever time of day it is,\nwithin 20 minutes. If you need to see someone, the site will\noffer a list of nearby providers, tell you which ones are\nrecommended for your condition and tell you how much each is\nlikely to cost.  It\u2019s an elegant interface, but elegance isn\u2019t its sole\npurpose. It\u2019s built to funnel you toward the choices Oscar wants\nyou to make. The same big-data methods at work in every major\ntechnology business are eagerly embraced at Oscar. Over time,\nthe insurer hopes to get much, much better at knowing what\npeople should do for a given set of symptoms and helping them\ndecide to do that thing.  Schlosser tells the story of an analysis his team ran on a\ndatabase of six years\u2019 worth of anonymous medical claims. The\nteam looked only at episodes that began with a headache and\nended on the same day they started, which means no follow-up\ncare was needed.  \u201cFive percent of those episodes accounted for 35 percent\nof the costs,\u201d Schlosser marveled. \u201cThe people in that 5\npercent all ended up at the emergency room. That was probably\npeople who had a headache on Sunday night at 4 a.m. when the\ndoctor wasn\u2019t there. If you could just take that issue and move\nit to a different layer of care, a nurse coming to visit you or\ngoing online with a televisit, that\u2019s win-win-win. It\u2019s a win\nfor the consumer. It\u2019s a win for the providers. And it\u2019s more\ncost-efficient.\u201d  Building Trust  That\u2019s the larger ambition of the founders: to change\nhealth care by building an insurance website that people trust\nto guide them through their care decisions.  Will it work? Who knows? Plenty of starry-eyed optimists\nhave tried and failed to revolutionize health care. Perhaps\npeople won\u2019t want to sign up with an insurer they\u2019ve never heard\nof. Or perhaps Oscar\u2019s website will prove glitchy and its care\nnetwork unreliable. Or maybe Oscar will appeal only to the young\nand the techy -- in which case it\u2019ll end up skimming off the\npeople who need care least.  But the Oscar team is ready to try. They\u2019ve attracted\nserious talent from the health-care industry, including Charlie Baker, the former chief executive officer of Harvard Pilgrim\nHealth Care Inc., and Aran Ron, the former chief medical officer\nof EmblemHealth Inc. They\u2019ve been approved for the  New York City \nmarket, with premiums that are smack in the middle of the\ncompetition.  Whether new entrants such as Oscar can compete in the\ninsurance marketplaces, and whether they will force incumbents\nto up their game in response, is the big test for Obamacare. If\nthe marketplaces succeed, they could, over time, take over\nAmerican health care. States can begin adding large employers to\nthem in 2017, and already some Republicans are proposing plans\nto move Medicare or Medicaid beneficiaries into them in the\ncoming decades.  It\u2019s this opportunity to change American health-care\nforever -- an opportunity that carries the potential for both\nhuge profits and huge social benefits -- that\u2019s dominating the\nhealth-care industry and even parts of the venture-capital\nindustry. And Oscar isn\u2019t alone in trying to take advantage of\nit: Data released by the  Department of Health  and Human Services\nshows that a quarter of the companies applying to offer coverage\nin the federally run marketplaces are entering the individual\ninsurance market for the first time.  The competition begins Oct. 1. Perhaps Washington can stop\nbickering over the politics long enough to pay attention?  ( Ezra Klein  is a Bloomberg View columnist.) Buffett endured scorn from Republicans this month after he\ncalled the Tea Party approach to budget talks \u201cinsane\u201d and\nproposed raising $500 billion by taxing the richest Americans.\nBuffett, chief executive officer of  Berkshire Hathaway Inc. (BRK\/A) , was\ncited as an exemplar by Obama at least three times since July.  \u201cWhenever Buffett says something, you can almost put money\non the fact that within the next 48 hours, Obama\u2019s going to use\nthe phrase, \u2018My good friend Warren Buffett says blah, blah,\nblah,\u2019\u201d said David Rolfe, chief investment officer of Berkshire\nshareholder Wedgewood Partners Inc. \u201cIf you\u2019re going to tread\ninto those waters, you need to expect the brickbats.\u201d  Buffett\u2019s criticism contrasts with praise he offered in the\nlast decade to former California Governor Arnold Schwarzenegger\nand the political appointees of former President George W. Bush.\nThe Tea Party movement, which made gains in last year\u2019s\nelections, was faulted by Buffett for silencing other Republican\nvoices. Buffett plans to hold a Sept. 30 fundraiser in  New York\nCity  for Obama\u2019s re-election bid, Democratic officials said.  Support for Republicans  Buffett, 81, has championed causes like abortion rights and\nthe estate tax through his career, even as he cultivated\nrelationships with Republican leaders. Buffett, a Democrat, was\nan economic adviser for Schwarzenegger\u2019s 2003 campaign and\nrepeatedly praised Bush\u2019s picks, including former Treasury\nSecretary  Henry Paulson  and Federal Reserve Chairman Ben S. Bernanke, for their handling of the 2008 credit crunch.  Buffett raised his voice as Democrats and Republicans\nsparred over a budget deficit of more than $1 trillion and\nworked on campaigns for the 2012 presidential election. Buffett,\nwhose fortune is valued at more than $35 billion, has delved\ninto public policy since July in a New York Times op-ed and\ninterviews with CNBC, Bloomberg Television and Charlie Rose.  \u201cThe speak-softly approach wasn\u2019t working, and he didn\u2019t\nthink enough people were paying attention,\u201d said  Whitney Tilson , co-founder of Berkshire shareholder T2 Partners LLC and\na member of Patriotic Millionaires for Fiscal Strength, which\nadvocates higher taxes on the rich. \u201cHe\u2019s doing it because he\nbelieves in it, not because it\u2019s in his self interest.\u201d  \u2018A Sound Bite\u2019  Buffett built Omaha, Nebraska-based Berkshire from a\nfailing textile mill into a $180 billion seller of insurance,\nenergy and freight hauling with more than 250,000 employees.  \u201cI think Mr. Buffett needs a day job,\u201d Representative Joe Walsh, an Illinois Republican elected with Tea Party support,\nsaid today in an interview on Bloomberg Television\u2019s \u201cInside\nTrack.\u201d \u201cThese millionaires and billionaires are the folks\nthat try to create jobs and grow the economy. He said billionaires\nhad been \u201ccoddled long enough\u201d by Congress and proposed\nincreasing some government revenue from capital gains that are\ncurrently taxed at 15 percent.  \u201cBuffett has always been in favor of taxes, and he\u2019s\nalways been in favor of a progressive scale,\u201d said Roger Lowenstein, the journalist and author of \u201cBuffett: The Making\nof an American Capitalist.\u201d \u201cWhat\u2019s new is that the Republican\nParty has moved to the right of Genghis Khan.\u201d  Republicans want to use their control of the House and\ntheir ability to block bills in the Senate to continue tax cuts\npassed under Bush and extended last year under Obama. De Beers Infringement Suit Against Adwar Casting Dismissed  A New York-based jewelry casting company won the dismissal\nof a patent-infringement lawsuit brought by diamond producer De\nBeers.  De Beers sued Adwar Casting Co. and three other defendants\nfor infringing design patents for its Everlon Love Knot\nCollection. The lawsuit, filed in federal court in Kansas City\nMissouri, on Aug. 25, alleged that \u201clove knot\u201d jewelry\ncastings made by Adwar infringed the patents.  Adwar  and Dinaro Creations LLC, also of New York, were both\ndismissed from the case, according to a Nov. 1 court filing.  The jewelry caster said in an e-mailed statement that it\nhad been selling \u201clove knot\u201d castings for 30 years, and has\nthe right to continue to manufacture and sell the line. Gregg\nAdwar, Adwar Casting\u2019s president, said that even though the suit\npertained to \u201conly a small handful\u201d of his company\u2019s products,\n\u201cwe are please the De Beers decided to dismiss this case so\nquickly, after we provided evidence of our long-standing\nproduction of the pieces.\u201d  The case is De Beers UK Ltd. v. Adwar Casting Co, 4:10-cv-\n00843-GAF, U.S. District Court, Western District of Missouri\n(Kansas City).  Abbott Challenges $1.67 Billion Patent Loss to J&J Over Humira  Abbott Laboratories  urged a U.S. appeals court to throw out\na $1.67 billion patent-infringement verdict, the largest in U.S.\nhistory, set after a jury found the company used  Johnson &\nJohnson \u2019s technology to develop the rheumatoid arthritis drug\nHumira.  Abbott is focusing its appeal on the validity of its patent\n7,070,775, co-issued to New York University and J&J\u2019s Centocor\nunit. Humira, Abbott\u2019s biggest drug, includes human antibodies\nthat aren\u2019t covered by the patent, a lawyer for the Abbott Park,\nIllinois-based company said.  \u201cIt was Abbott who invented the first fully human\nantibody\u201d used to treat arthritis, William Lee of WilmerHale in\nBoston told the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Federal Circuit in\nWashington yesterday. Abbott also contends that even if the\nverdict is upheld, the damage award is excessive.  A federal jury in Marshall, Texas, in June 2009 said the\ncompany owed $504 million in patent royalties to J&J based on\nsales of Abbott\u2019s Humira arthritis drug, plus $1.17 billion to\ncompensate J&J for decreased sales of its competing treatments.\nThe trial judge later added $175.6 million in interest, bringing\nthe total to $1.84 billion.  Humira generated $4.67 billion in sales in the first nine\nmonths of the year, 19 percent of Abbott\u2019s total revenue, the\ncompany reported Oct. 20. That includes $2 billion in U.S.\nsales, a jump of 14 percent from the year-ago period.  \u201cThe damage award was as large as it was because the\ninfringing product, Humira, is as big as it is,\u201d Dianne\nElderkin, a Centocor lawyer at Akin Gump in Philadelphia, told\nthe three-judge panel.  Humira, which costs about $19,000 a year, blocks action of\ntumor necrosis factor, or TNF, which is linked to inflammation.  Abbott said the patent doesn\u2019t cover the human antibodies\nthat are used in Humira, and they are invalid because scientists\ncouldn\u2019t make fully human antibodies against TNF in a laboratory\nin 1994, the date set by the court as the time of the invention.  In 1994, \u201cno one anywhere on the face of the earth had a\nfully human antibody\u201d that would work against TNF, Lee said.\n\u201cA lot of people tried and they had failed. How can you have a\nwritten description that says you have something that you don\u2019t\neven know exists?\u201d  J&J sells the competing medicine Remicade, made with a\ncombination of mouse and human antibodies. J&J and NYU contend\nthe patent covers both the combination and fully human\nantibodies against TNF. When the body produces too much TNF, it\ncan cause the immune system to attack healthy tissue and leads\nto inflammation.  \u201cWhat was invented here was a specific class of\nantibodies,\u201d Elderkin said. Abbott\u2019s expert witness at trial\nmade the same arguments as Lee and the jury \u201crejected his\ntestimony,\u201d Elderkin said.  Abbott has filed its own lawsuit against Centocor, claiming\nJ&J\u2019s arthritis drug Simponi, made with human antibodies and\nfirst sold last year, is infringing an Abbott patent. Abbott\nalso claims a J&J psoriasis medicine, Stelara, violates two\nother patents. Those cases are pending in federal court in\nWorcester, Massachusetts.  The case is Centocor Inc. v. Abbott Laboratories, 10-1144,\nU.S. Court of Appeals for the Federal Circuit (Washington). The\nlower court case is Centocor Inc. v. Abbott Laboratories,\n07cv139, U.S. District Court, Eastern District of Texas\n(Marshall). A U.S. appeals\ncourt rejected that argument, ruling that all illegal\ndownloaders, regardless of their motives, are subject to the\nsame range of penalties.  The Recording Industry Association of America, acting on\nbehalf of major record labels, sued more than 12,000 people and\nsent notices to thousands of others it claimed were illegally\nsharing music.  Tenenbaum and a woman from Minnesota took their cases to\ntrial, and both lost. An appeals court plans to hear arguments\nin the Minnesota case in June.  The trial judge in Tenenbaum\u2019s case reduced the jury award\nto $67,500, saying the larger amount was unconstitutionally\nexcessive. The 1st U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals in Boston\nreinstated the award and said the record companies would be\nentitled to a new trial if the judge cut the award again.  Suing Tenenbaum were  Sony Corp. (6758)  and its Arista Records,\nWarner Music Group\u2019s Warner Bros. and Atlantic labels and\n Vivendi SA\u2019s (VIV)  Universal Music Group. They said he made songs\navailable on various sites including Napster, Morpheus, Kazaa\nand LimeWire, distributing songs to millions of other people.  The Supreme Court had ruled in 2005 that Internet file-\nsharing networks may bear responsibility when users illegally\ndownload music and movies, giving the recording industry new\npower to shut down such sites.  Tenenbaum\u2019s lawyers said a 2008 study estimated that the\naverage teenager illegally downloaded 800 songs, which would\nexpose that person to damages of as much as $120 million.  The Obama administration defended the statute, saying\nTenenbaum\u2019s argument that the recording industry should have to\nshow how much it was harmed by his actions would defeat the\nlaw\u2019s purpose of deterring copyright infringement.  The government urged the court not to take the case, saying\nsome issues remained unresolved, including what the judge might\ndo to the $675,000 damage award.  The case is Tenenbaum v. Raikes, then president of Microsoft\u2019s business\ndivision (now chief executive officer of the Bill and Melinda\nGates Foundation), had helped create a computer\nscience-entrepreneurship program for the university in the late\n1990s. He suggested its students create 3D training software for\nthe coaches as a class project.  The three undergraduates who signed on, David Graaf, Brian\nKaiser, and John Wirtz, quickly discovered that streaming video\nof the football players themselves was more effective than\ncomputer graphics. So they pivoted, developing software for\ncoaches to use to create video clips highlighting athletes\u2019\nstrengths and weaknesses. \u201cThey were smart enough to throw out my\nidea,\u201d says Raikes, who led a $1.25 million angel investor round\nin 2007 to turn their software into a business.  Today about 200,000 coaches from high schools, universities,\nand professional teams in the U.S. use the software, called Hudl,\nsays Wirtz, who serves as chief product officer. The appeal? Hudl\nsolves the biggest hurdles coaches face when using videos for\ntraining: editing time and sharing them securely. Wirtz says a\ncoach can use the software to edit, annotate, and post a video\nfor his players in less than an hour. Users can capture video\nfrom any device. And Hudl\u2019s apps for smartphones and tablets\nenable them to stream and download videos.  \u201cTraining is much more efficient because [Hudl] captures\neach play as its own entity,\u201d says Ross Tucker, a former NFL\nplayer whose business, Go Big Recruiting, helps high school\nathletes get their tapes to college coaches. He doesn\u2019t use the\nsoftware himself but says his clients who do are fans. \u201cRather\nthan a practice or game and many plays you\u2019d have to fast-forward\nor rewind to, each play is its own video file,\u201d he says.  Unlike traditional editing programs, Hudl automatically\nmatches camera angles and footage to speed the process and\norganize footage into specific plays. The system also compiles\ndata about each play\u2014for example, who threw the football, who\ncaught it, and the distance it was carried. Once coaches upload\ntheir videos to Hudl\u2019s site, players enter log-ins to watch them.\nAnnual subscriptions start at $800 for high school coaches and\n$3,000 for college coaches. Subscribers can assign log-ins to up\nto 40 athletes, who pay nothing.  Now the 65-employee Lincoln (Neb.) business, which Wirtz\nsays became profitable in 2010, is trying to expand its services\noverseas in about 20 sports, from cricket to soccer. Wirtz says\nfootball and basketball, which are more conducive to splicing up\nthan other sports, make up a \u201cbig portion\u201d of Hudl\u2019s use in the\nU.S. But he notes Hudl already has 600 teams using its system\noutside the country, mostly through word of mouth.  To increase its reach, Hudl snapped up major competitor\nDigital Sports Video last year and this year bought Apex. The\nacquisitions helped increase revenue to $9 million in 2011, from\n$2.5 million in 2010, and Wirtz projects $17 million this year.\nHe won\u2019t say whether Hudl would like to buy one of its remaining\nbig competitors, Krossover.  Hudl wants to make its service available instantly\neverywhere, but the laws of physics aren\u2019t helping. That\u2019s\nbecause signals traveling at the speed of light across oceans and\ncontinents don\u2019t provide the real-time experience Hudl aims to\ngive coaches and athletes, says Wirtz. Right now, for example, if\na soccer team uploads a video while playing in  China , it can\u2019t\nget instant feedback from a coach in the U.S. because Hudl\u2019s\nservers are on the East Coast. Allen, a co-founder of\n Microsoft Corp. (MSFT) , pledged an additional $300 million to the brain\ncenter that bears his name to study how vision works.  The  Allen Institute for Brain Science , based in  Seattle  and\nfounded in 2003, will begin a 10-year project to map the visual\nsystem. That brings Allen\u2019s total contribution to $500 million,\nsaid Allan Jones, the chief executive officer of the institute,\nin a telephone interview.  The project, starting in mice, will involve several hundred\nscientists and will apply knowledge from genomics, anatomy,\ncomputer modeling and physiology. A map of the visual cortex,\nthe place in the brain that receives and processes the messages\nof sight, may help improve understanding of higher brain\nfunction, said Christof Koch, chief scientific officer of the\nAllen Institute and R. Clay Reid of Harvard University Medical\nSchool in  Boston , in an editorial today in the  journal Nature .  \u201cAlthough the institute\u2019s project will focus on visual\nstimuli in mice, it will capture fundamental aspects of higher\nbrain functions: perception, conscious awareness and decision-\nmaking, and how they lead to action,\u201d Koch and Reid, who is\njoining the Allen Institute, said in the article.  Once understood in mice, scientists may turn to the human\nvisual system, the researchers said. Human brains have a mass of\nabout 3 pounds, while mouse brains are .001 pounds. Human brains\nhave 86 billion neurons, mice have only 70 million.  Neural Networks  Researchers will catalog neurons and measure the electrical\nactivity of the cells as they transmit messages into and out of\nthe visual cortex. Using techniques of genetic engineering that\nmake the neurons light up, they will watch circuits activate\nwhenever the animal makes a decision, enabling them to chart the\nanatomy of neural networks.  \u201cThe Allen Institute has found a unique niche to do these\nthings at a large scale,\u201d Jones said. Usually in academic\nsettings, individual researchers\u2019 questions drive the science.\nThis allows for a more-systematic approach, he said.  To support the initiative, the Institute plans to double\nits current staff to more than 350 people over the next four\nyears. Today\u2019s donation will fund the first four years of the\nnew project.  In April 2011, the Institute created a gene map of the\nhuman brain and made it freely available to assist researchers\nstudying disorders such as Parkinson\u2019s disease and autism. That\neffort followed a 2006 map of the mouse brain.
