The billionaire co-founder of PayPal and chairman of electric carmaker Tesla Motors Inc. stopped participating with FWD.us earlier this month. \u201cWe want a political system that is less cynical over time, not more,\u201d Musk said.  Technology entrepreneur Anil Dash, who declined to join the group, was more blunt, writing on his blog, \u201cIf we\u2019re finally moving past our innocent, naive and idealistic lack of engagement with the actual dirty dealings of legislation, then let\u2019s try to figure out how to do it without losing our souls.\u201d  With the Senate planning to begin debate on immigration the week of June 10, the feuding with FWD.us risks diluting the strength of and sapping energy from organizations seeking to promote the bill\u2019s passage.  High Stakes  The stakes are high, as the  technology  industry for a decade has sought more temporary visas for skilled employees, saying there aren\u2019t enough qualified Americans to do such jobs as software engineering. Labor unions dispute that, arguing that Silicon Valley companies want to deflate wages by importing cheaper workers.  Introducing FWD.us in an April 11 essay in the  Washington  Post, Zuckerberg wrote that FWD.us would focus on immigration and also help on issues such as improving science, technology, engineering and math teaching in schools and increasing funding for scientific research.  As a social-welfare group, FWD.us isn\u2019t required to reveal its donors and is limited in the amount of political work it can do. FWD.us lists 36 founders and major contributors on its website, without disclosing how much money they\u2019ve given or the group\u2019s total budget.  Political Background  The backers are a who\u2019s who of the digital age. Among them: Microsoft Corp. chairman  Bill Gates , LinkedIn Corp. executive chairman  Reid Hoffman , Netflix Inc. chief executive officer  Reed Hastings , Yahoo! Inc. CEO Marissa Mayer and Google Inc. executive chairman  Eric Schmidt .  Some of them are seasoned political contributors. Schmidt, for example, is a top donor to President  Barack Obama  and Senator  Orrin Hatch , a Utah Republican and tech advocate.  Zuckerberg, 29, is newer to politics, having never written a check to Obama or any other federal candidate, according to the Center for Responsive Politics, based in Washington.  In April, the FWD.us offshoots spent more than $1 million on a trio of TV commercials which aired for about a week in home states of senators.  In one TV spot, Graham, a South Carolina Republican, says he wants to build the Keystone pipeline to transport tar-sands oil from  Canada . In another, a narrator reminds viewers that Begich, an Alaska Democrat, wants to drill for oil in a wildlife refuge. Neither commercial mentions immigration.  Tested Strategy  The Graham ad reflects a time-tested political strategy, said  Haley Barbour , an adviser to FWD.us\u2019s Republican group and Mississippi\u2019s former governor.  \u201cIt\u2019s very appropriate to remind people of his judgment so that, as voters learn about immigration, they listen to him,\u201d Barbour said in an interview. \u201cIt\u2019s a proven concept, used in all kinds of advertising. And for good reason -- it\u2019s logical.\u201d  Musk and another former FWD.us donor, David Sacks, who founded business networking site Yammer Inc., concluded otherwise and quit Zuckerberg\u2019s group. Sacks declined to comment through Yammer spokeswoman Belinda Wong.  At the time those ads were airing, FWD.us\u2019s Silicon Valley-based president Joe Green, was pitching other tech entrepreneurs for support. After having lunch with Green, Dash and Josh Miller, a founder of startup company  Branch , both wrote online essays expressing their reservations.  Silicon Outrage  The group\u2019s approach, \u201cthough pitched as \u2019pragmatic\u2019 and \u2019smart\u2019 by Beltway insiders, is typically only practiced by large pharmaceutical companies, gun manufacturers, and the like,\u201d Miller wrote in an  essay  posted to the website Buzzfeed.com.  Venture capitalist Vinod Khosla has more sharply criticized Fwd.us, asking May 5 in a Twitter message why the the group was willing to \u201cprostitute climate destruction & other values to get a few engineers hired & get immigration reform?\u201d  Keith Rabois, a partner at  Khosla Ventures , is a contributor to Fwd.us. The company didn\u2019t respond to requests for comment.  In addition to the Graham and Begich ads, Zuckerberg\u2019s group is running radio and TV spots that emphasize the \u201ctough\u201d aspects of the immigration plan.  Limbaugh Ads  A minute-long ad airing now on the national talk-radio shows of  Rush Limbaugh  and Sean Hannity begins: \u201cOur immigration system is a joke, and the whole world knows it.\u201d  It goes on to say that Senator  Marco Rubio , a Florida Republican, and Representative  Paul Ryan , a Wisconsin Republican, \u201care working on plans to change that. It all starts with real border security, more fencing, more manpower and high-tech surveillance.\u201d  Of those ads, Rob Jesmer, the FWD.us campaign manager, said, \u201cThere\u2019s a lot of conversation about immigration happening on talk radio. We\u2019d be foolish not to get our message out over that medium.\u201d  Opponents of FWD.us\u2019s tactics recently started using some of the same social-media sites that made the group\u2019s backers wealthy. (AAPL)  and  Google Inc. (GOOG)  in the smartphone market are dimming amid lackluster demand for its flagship touch-screen device.  Corporate information-technology departments have long wanted a third alternative to Apple\u2019s iPhones and devices based on Google\u2019s Android operating system, to ensure innovation and price competition. Yet many businesses are dropping support for BlackBerry as employees flock to touch-screen devices from Apple,  Samsung Electronics Co. (005930)  and others, according to makers of software used by companies to manage smartphones at work.  That trend was underscored last week when BlackBerry missed analysts\u2019 estimates for phone shipments and profit. Now the Waterloo, Ontario-based company could see further declines as businesses grow more skeptical of its brand, said Bob Tinker, chief executive officer of MobileIron Inc., a maker of smartphone-management software used by 5,000 companies. That makes  Microsoft Corp. (MSFT) \u2019s Windows Phone a likelier third option.  \u201cMost of our customers have been planning to support three mobile operating systems -- iOS, Android and either Windows Phone or BlackBerry,\u201d said Tinker, whose products compete with the enterprise servers BlackBerry offers its clients. \u201cThe recent results indicate that BlackBerry is not going to be the third.\u201d  BlackBerry last week disclosed weaker-than-expected sales of its flagship Z10 handset, which was designed to exploit its new BB10 software to take on high-end phones such as the iPhone and Samsung\u2019s Galaxy S4. The stock plunged the most in 13 years after the news and has lost a third of its value since the announcement. BlackBerry fell 0.5 percent to $9.65 at the close in  New York , its fifth consecutive day of declines.  Microsoft Boost?  The disappointing results give a shot in the arm to Microsoft, which has gained ground on BlackBerry in recent years in the struggle for third place. In the global smartphone market, BlackBerry\u2019s share shrank to 2.9 percent last quarter from 6.4 percent a year earlier, according to research firm IDC. Apple and Android together held 92 percent of the market. Microsoft\u2019s Windows Phone bumped BlackBerry into fourth place.  BlackBerry\u2019s worldwide  subscriber base  slipped to 72 million last quarter, from 76 million and 79 million in the preceding quarters, and the company last week said it will no longer disclose a user tally.  With limited employee demand for BlackBerry devices, some companies are deciding to turn off the BlackBerry Enterprise Server, which is the back-office software that lets BlackBerry users securely get e-mail and synchronize appointments in the corporate network, rather than upgrade to the new version for the BB10 operating system, said Tinker. That saves monthly charges and lowers IT costs. Without BES, BlackBerry devices lack most of the features that made them so popular with IT departments and many users.  Already Installed  \u201cWe have seen a very enthusiastic response to BES10 from our customer base,\u201d said Pete Devenyi, senior vice president of enterprise software for BlackBerry, who said 18,000 companies have downloaded or deployed the software since it was released in January. A BES10 server can manage 15,000 BlackBerry phones, versus about 2,000 for the previous generation. \u201cThe adoption of BB10 has been very much in accordance with our expectations,\u201d he said.  Microsoft cites a growing library of 160,000 apps for Windows Phone devices as evidence of the platform\u2019s strength.  \u201cWe agree with the industry experts who say Windows Phone has claimed the third spot in the mobile space and is gaining traction,\u201d Tony Mestres, a vice president in Microsoft\u2019s Windows Phone unit, said in an e-mailed statement. Yesterday, it was revealed that the authors' methodology, choice of data and competence with the Microsoft Excel spreadsheet were all  found wanting . When it comes to policymaking, this news changes very little: the Reinhart-Rogoff paper was always a flimsy justification for fiscal austerity. Reinhart and Rogoff never explicitly said that high levels of public debt retard economic growth. Instead, the professors merely identified a weak correlation between the two variables. Their paper also refrained from addressing some important questions: How specifically does public indebtedness affect economic growth, if at all? Are countries with their own currency, including the U.S., the U.K. and Japan, fundamentally different from those without, such as members of the euro area? How should countries near the magic threshold of 90 percent public debt to GDP behave in order to maximize long-term growth?  Politicians -- particularly those with an atavistic fear of government budget deficits -- rarely grasped these subtleties. Regrettably, the professors did not overexert themselves correcting misinterpretations of their work, so advocates of tax increases and spending cuts eagerly cited Reinhart and Rogoff for years. It turns out, though, that even someone who uncritically accepts the implications of \"Growth in a Time of Debt\" shouldn't support fiscal tightening when the economy is weak. The reason is that the policies of austerity don't affect the ratio of public debt to national income in a straightforward way. That ratio has two parts: the level of income and the level of debt. Fiscal austerity affects both. When the economy is weak, the negative effect of tax hikes and spending cuts often outweighs the reduced level of borrowing. In other words, fiscal tightening actually increases, rather than decreases, the level of public indebtedness. Similarly, tax cuts and spending increases can lower the ratio of public debt to national income under certain circumstances. This point was cleverly made by the International Monetary Fund in its October 2012  World Economic Outlook . In box 1.1, Olivier Blanchard, the IMF's chief economist, and Daniel Leigh looked at the \"fiscal multiplier\" that relates changes in government spending and taxation against changes in overall economic output. The IMF and national governments forecast economic activity, public debt-to-GDP ratios and budget deficits on a regular basis. Those forecasts all require assumptions about the size and direction of the fiscal multiplier. Blanchard and Leigh compared these forecasts against what actually happened and found that \"the negative short-term effects of fiscal cutbacks have been larger than expected because fiscal multipliers were underestimated.\" Those forecasting errors had real policy implications. Overly optimistic projections were regularly used to justify controversial -- and ultimately counterproductive -- policies in the U.K. and the euro area. Those policies failed to produce the desired results because, as Blanchard and Leigh explain, \"the multipliers used in generating growth forecasts have been systematically too low since the start of the Great Recession.\" That finding explains why Reinhart and Rogoff never made a strong case for austerity. The easiest way to avoid crossing some magic threshold of public debt to GDP is to avoid raising taxes and cutting spending when the economy is weak. In other words, serious believers in Reinhart and Rogoff should have been the strongest opponents of fiscal tightening. (Matthew C. Klein is a contributor to the Ticker. The fresh inquiry, which follows the FTC\u2019s decision to close a review of Google\u2019s search business in January without taking action, is in the preliminary stages and may not expand into a larger probe, said the people, who asked not to be named because the matter hasn\u2019t been made public.  FTC investigators are examining whether Google is using its position in U.S. display ads -- a $17.7 billion industry that includes the sale of banner ads on websites -- to push companies to use more of its other services, a practice that can be illegal under antitrust laws, the people said. Google has been drawing regulatory scrutiny around the world as it bolsters its market share of digital advertising.  Canada\u2019s Competition Bureau is preparing to start a formal inquiry into Google\u2019s search practices, the company disclosed last week. The European Union is investigating Google for the way it operates the search business and also has opened a probe into its handset unit, Motorola Mobility, over the licensing of its patents to rival device makers. Antitrust agencies in Argentina and South Korea are also scrutinizing the company.  Niki Fenwick , a spokeswoman for Google, and Peter Kaplan, a spokesman for the FTC declined to comment on the probe.  Google\u2019s shares fell 1.1 percent to $873.32 at the close in New York, extending a decline of almost 1 percent yesterday after news of the probe was released.  Earlier Probe  Google, avoiding a potentially costly legal battle with U.S. regulators, ended a 20-month probe in January of whether it unfairly skewed search results by pledging to change some business practices and settling allegations it misused patents to thwart competitors in smartphone technology.  The company said it would voluntarily remove restrictions on the use of its online search-advertising platform and offer companies the option of keeping their content out of Google\u2019s search results.  The FTC\u2019s resolution of its search-practices probe came as a blow to Google\u2019s competitors including Microsoft Corp., Yelp Inc. and Expedia Inc. An alliance of such e-commerce and Web-search companies pressed the agency to bring a lawsuit, claiming Google\u2019s dominance of Internet search, combined with the company favoring its own services in answers to queries, violates antitrust laws.  Microsoft isn\u2019t involved in the FTC\u2019s review of the display advertising market, one of the people said.  Justice Department  The FTC secured clearance to move forward with the new investigation in the display-advertising market from the antitrust division of the Justice Department under a process that ensures the two agencies don\u2019t investigate the same matters at the same time, one of the people said.  For the past two years, the antitrust division and the FTC have split investigations of the Mountain View, California-based company, with the FTC conducting a broad probe of whether Google\u2019s business practices hurt competition and the antitrust division reviewing its  acquisitions .  In the new probe, the FTC is exploring concerns about Google\u2019s growing market share with some of its digital advertising tools and services, including technology that places display ads on websites, the people said.  Competing Products  The FTC is looking at whether Google is using its tools to force companies to bypass competing products and use other Google properties, including a marketplace for buying and selling Internet display ads, and features that help companies maximize revenue, the people said. The agency is also reviewing Google\u2019s potential to use its dominance in search advertising to squeeze out competitors in the display advertising market, the people said.  Some of the advertising tools came from Google\u2019s purchase of DoubleClick Inc., which received antitrust approval at the end of 2007. The FTC, which voted 4-1 to  approve the merger , said competition among display-ad networks was \u201cdynamic,\u201d according to a statement at the time.  \u201cWe will closely watch these markets and, should Google engage in unlawful tying or other anticompetitive conduct, the commission intends to act quickly,\u201d the FTC said in the statement.  Market Share  Google\u2019s share of the display ad market reached 24 percent during the first quarter in the U.S. with its closest competitors, Yahoo! Inc. and Facebook Inc., each holding less than 10 percent market share, according to research firm IDC.  Facebook, the largest social-networking service, lost its lead to Google last year and is expected to expand its market share at a slower pace. Facebook will grab 16 percent in 2015, up from 15 percent last year and less than 3 percent in 2008,  EMarketer , another research firm, estimates.  Google took 47 percent of total U.S. digital ad spending in the first quarter of this year, according to IDC.  \u201cThe market positions of Google and DoubleClick suggest that the combined firm could engage in a number of potential anticompetitive strategies to further enhance its positions in the various markets at issue,\u201d the FTC wrote in its DoubleClick statement.  The practice of tying, or bundling, products and services together may be a violation of antitrust laws if the company in question has the market power to force customers to acquire products or services together that they might prefer to buy from different providers, said  Spencer Waller , an antitrust law professor at Loyola University Chicago.  Microsoft Case  One of the most high-profile tying cases was the lawsuit the U.S. brought against  Microsoft  in 1998, when it claimed the company unlawfully protected its Windows monopoly by keeping computer makers from promoting Web browsers that competed with Microsoft\u2019s Internet Explorer.  The government contended Microsoft hindered access to the Netscape Navigator browser because its Java programming language let programmers write applications that ran on any operating system, not just Windows. The final judgment, a settlement in which Microsoft agreed to end the anticompetitive conduct, put the company under court supervision until 2011.  \u201cSpecialty producers may be very good at what they do, but if they can\u2019t get access to their customers, that\u2019s a legitimate harm that antitrust has addressed historically and should continue to address,\u201d Waller said. It shows a new EU resolve to crack down on rent-\nseeking by  Russia\u2019s  natural-gas behemoth and, at long last, to\nheed the complaints of the bloc\u2019s smaller ex-Soviet members.  The European Commission  accuses  Gazprom of stifling\ncompetition in European markets by restricting the interstate\ntrading of natural gas, limiting the diversification of gas\nsupplies by blocking rival gas-pipeline projects, and pegging\nthe price of natural gas to  oil prices  in long-term contracts.  These practices reflect Gazprom\u2019s decades-old strategy of\nseeking a monopoly, rather than competing under the free-market\nrules that the EU has been developing as it tries to create a\nsingle, 27-nation energy market.  Gazprom (OGZD) \u2019s business model has\nlong been to buy gas cheap from Central Asian producers that\nhave no alternative route to reach  Europe . Gazprom then moves\nthe gas through Russian pipelines and sells it to EU energy\ncompanies at twice or three times the purchase price.  Such monopolistic arrangements have generated  enormous\nrevenue  for Gazprom and the Russian state, some of whose top\nofficials also sit on the boards of large Russian energy\ncompanies. The monopoly profits that result are being earned at\nthe expense of European consumers and Central Asian producers.  The EU has long understood these market abuses and said it\nwanted to right them. But because Russian leaders were able to\ndivide the Europeans by offering special deals to larger buyers\nsuch as  Germany , little was done.  Diversifying Supplies  Now the EU is supporting several new options to diversify\nits gas supplies. These include building more liquefied-natural-\ngas terminals in order to open EU markets to more suppliers and\na network of new gas pipelines from the Caspian basin to Europe,\nvia  Turkey . The EU\u2019s Sept. 4 antitrust case against Gazprom is\nanother element in this broader quest to diversify Europe\u2019s\nsupplies of natural gas.  The decision to confront Gazprom contrasts sharply with the\nEU\u2019s approach when  Gerhard Schroeder  was the German chancellor.\nIn October 2005, Schroeder threw his country\u2019s full support\nbehind Gazprom\u2019s  Nord Stream  pipeline, which now bypasses the\nBaltic nations and  Poland , thus weakening their hands in\nnegotiations with the company and the Russian state. He joined\n Nord Stream \u2019s board after leaving office.  Radek Sikorski, the Polish defense minister at the time,\ndubbed Nord Stream the \u201cMolotov-Ribbentrop pipeline,\u201d reflecting\nthe deep sense of betrayal that was felt by millions of\nEuropeans from Poland to  Estonia . Sikorski was referring to the\nsecret 1939  nonaggression pact  that allowed  Adolf Hitler  to\ninvade Poland and carved up Eastern Europe between the  Soviet\nUnion  and  Nazi Germany .  The EU\u2019s biggest players appear finally to have recognized\nthat by standing together and resisting Gazprom\u2019s monopolistic\nquest to divide and conquer their smaller allies, the bloc has\nsufficient leverage to bring meaning to its well-worn statement\nthat Gazprom needs Europe as much as Europe needs Gazprom.  Europe and Gazprom really do need each other. But Europe\ndoes not need the type of Gazprom that exists today. Rather, the\nEU needs a reliable commercial partner that may drive a hard\nbargain, but operates according to market principles. So the\nEU\u2019s goal is not, and should not be, to punish Gazprom, but to\nuse the force of competition to elicit market-based behavior.  Restraining Monopolies  Predictably, Russian leaders have  cried  foul. They say the\nEU is singling out Gazprom in a fit of anti-Russian prejudice.\nThey should remember that the EU not long ago took on another\nforeign behemoth, Redmond, Washington-based  Microsoft Corp. (MSFT) , to\nend what it considered monopolistic behavior. Equally, in 1911\nthe U.S. government broke Standard Oil Co. into several\ncompeting companies, some of which still exist as  Exxon Mobil\nCorp. (XOM) ,  Chevron Corp. (CVX)  and  ConocoPhillips. (COP)   Today, the EU isn\u2019t calling for Gazprom\u2019s breakup. And even\nif it were, Russia\u2019s leaders could take comfort in the success\nof the U.S. oil companies that emerged from Standard Oil. If the\nEuropean Commission can keep its nerve and compel Gazprom to\nfollow EU antitrust laws, then Gazprom would be forced to hone\nits competitive edge rather than rely on rent-seeking to pad its\nbalance sheet.  The result would be a stronger, more reliable and cheaper\nnatural-gas supplier for consumers, in Europe and Russia alike.\nGazprom would gradually have to improve its delivery of services\nand open up its pipelines for independent Russian natural-gas\ncompanies to use. Finally, a Gazprom that operates according to\nmarket, rather than monopolistic, forces is less likely to be\nused by the Kremlin as a geopolitical tool. The company played\ndirectly into such fears in its statement after the EU\u2019s\nannouncement on the antitrust investigation. Gazprom said it was\n\u201c a business  entity empowered, according to the legislation of\nthe Russian Federation, with special social functions and the\nstatus of a strategic organization, administered by the\ngovernment.\u201d President  Vladimir Putin  followed a few days later\nwith a decree that forbids Gazprom, or any other Russian state-\nowned company, from providing information to investigators\nwithout the state\u2019s permission.  In the past, such  Russian tactics  bullied Europe\u2019s largest\ncountries into ignoring their smaller Eastern neighbors\u2019 pleas\nfor support. In 2006, for example, when  Lithuania  was planning\nto sell its sole oil refinery to Poland\u2019s PKN Orlen SA, rather\nthan to a Russian company, the Russian pipeline supplying crude\nto the plant allegedly suffered an accident that shut it down.\nThe sale went through and the pipeline never reopened. Lithuania\nnow imports oil for the refinery by sea.  Lithuania\u2019s Example  Lithuania  appears  to have triggered the European\nCommission\u2019s decision to act, after the Baltic nation of about\n3.2 million people carried out EU recommendations to \u201cunbundle\u201d\nits domestic natural-gas and electricity markets, which would\nprohibit energy producers from also owning transmission or\ndistribution networks. That affected Gazprom, and the company\nresponded by threatening, and then imposing, higher natural-gas\nprices on Lithuania.  The threats failed, and Gazprom since came to a deal on\nunbundling its Lithuania assets that will come into effect in\n2014. The commission and the EU\u2019s bigger members should take\nnote and stick with the antitrust case. It is the best route to\na relationship with a Gazprom that is no longer able to divide\nand conquer within European energy markets. (MSFT)  event in Washington,\nD.C. \u201cIt\u2019s going to be a continuing issue and a big one.\u201d  By some estimates, 114 billion e-mails and 24 billion  text\nmessages  are sent globally each day, as well as more than 12\nbillion phone calls made, according to Trey Hodgkins, a senior\nvice president for TechAmerica, a Washington-based trade group\nwhose members include Verizon,  AT&T Inc. The myth is that the U.S. should be doing a better job of\npreparing underprivileged high school students, so they can win\nscholarships to Yale, Harvard and other top schools. Then they\ncan  march across  commencement stages into prosperous careers.\nThis is worse than a myth. It\u2019s a joke.  The Ivy League -- Brown, Columbia, Cornell, Harvard,\n Princeton , Pennsylvania and Yale universities, plus  Dartmouth\nCollege  -- has a total of 38,464 undergraduate slots. If you add\nin the 31-college cabal, the Consortium on Financing Higher\nEducation, which includes the  Ivy League  members and is the\nprivate elite colleges\u2019 own selection of the best of the best,\nyou have 118,784 total undergraduate seats.  If you then add the  University of California  at Berkeley;\nthe  University of Michigan  at  Ann Arbor ; the  University of Texas \nat Austin and the  University of Illinois  at Champaign-Urbana,\nthe total potential myth-actualizing undergraduate population\nrises to 242,905.  To demonstrate the folly of the myth, note that if students\non  Pell grants  took every undergraduate seat at these selective\ncolleges, that would still leave us with 9.157 million for whom\nwe have no plan. A total of 9.4 million students in college\nreceive  Pell grants , the bedrock federal aid for low-income\nstudents. They are the ones who might work two -- even three --\njobs to support families, and who may have been lucky to\ncomplete the semester, never mind a degree.  Scary Numbers  The scary truth is that letting these 9.4 million founder\nis our -- we, the people\u2019s -- active national higher-education\nplan. We know it leads to  fewer jobs  for the 9.4 million, many\nwithout health insurance or a living wage, and we know we will\npay later in Medicaid and  food stamps .  This plan isn\u2019t in a single report to download. It is the\nsum of our inactions and stale policies. Solutions require\naccountability, and in America\u2019s systems no one is responsible\nfor educating the poor.  In the marketplace of democracy and capitalism, who would\ndirectly profit from educating, say, 1 million more able, but\nlow-income, students? No one. A balanced budget with reserves in\nthe bank is the reasonable goal of any college president.\nHigher-education leaders, whatever their goodwill, have no\nincentive to  educate  the poor.  Funding abounds for research papers, conferences and ideas.\nWhat\u2019s missing is anyone willing to be responsible for seeing\nthat more of these 9.4 million people complete their education,\ndegree or certificate, or just obtain a skill. Is the world too\nmessy for such big plans? U.S. President  Lyndon Johnson  would\nhave disagreed. He enacted the Civil Rights Act of 1964, the\nVoting Rights Act of 1965, and the Higher Education Act of 1965\n-- the backbone of today\u2019s federal higher-education policies --\nall with the  Vietnam War  under way.  Taking responsibility for educating 9.4 million students\nbludgeoned by poverty is a daunting problem. I know this from\nthe hundreds of them I have seen over six years in my College\nWriting I  class  at Bunker Hill Community College in  Boston .  I will celebrate any individual triumph for what that is --\none success with millions of students to go. A year ago, I\nscreamed with joy as an Iraq veteran, a Lakota Sioux in my very\nfirst College Writing I class, accepted his diploma from\nDartmouth. That was a \u201cmakes life worth living\u201d moment. The rest\nof that class? Only one other I know of completed college.\nAmbitions and motivation  crumbled  under jobs, health issues and\nfamily problems.  Forget Yale  In early returns for this year, my colleagues and I have\nhelped students who will be heading this year to Amherst, Mount\nHolyoke and Wellesley colleges, as well as  Tufts University .\n( Williams College  and Yale, Harvard and Princeton won\u2019t visit to\nlook for students.)  However gratifying the triumphs of these few students, we\nknow we are  failing  because we know the others. That would\ninclude a student coming to my 7 a.m. class from an overnight\nshift. Or the one leaving a midnight class at 2:30 a.m. for a\nseasonal job at Logan Airport, de-icing planes.  We all struggle to retrain ourselves to meet the needs of\nsuch students. My major professional development this year has\nbeen learning to recertify students for food stamps.  I will yield to the cries that all these millions don\u2019t\nneed a full four-year degree. My alarm is that our national\ndiscussions on an educated citizenry have lost touch with the\nskills that even entry-level jobs in the U.S. require today.  Look at courses in  community colleges . Running an MRI\nmachine requires an anatomy and physiology course in the same\ndetail that a pre-medical student would take. A basic Microsoft\nExcel course involves understanding finance for those functions\nand formal logic for the IF functions.  Using Excel pivot tables, my colleagues tell me, is a skill\nthat all but guarantees a decent entry-level job for a\ncommunity-college graduate. As I learned in the 629-page entry-level Excel textbook that I\u2019m muddling through, pivot tables are\nfor data mining. This, the book tells me, is the process of\n\u201canalyzing large volumes of data using advanced statistical\ntechniques.\u201d  How many graduates with bachelor\u2019s degrees know finance,\nlogic and advanced statistical techniques? What is the plan for\neven half of the 9.4 million on  Pell grants  to learn these\nentry-level job skills? We don\u2019t have one. The few who might win\nscholarships at selective colleges won\u2019t transform the nation\u2019s\nworkforce.  Two recent studies show how blinkered our thinking is. In a\nBrookings Institution paper titled \u201cThe Missing \u2018One-Offs\u2019: The\nHidden Supply of High-Achieving, Low Income Students,\u201d Caroline Hoxby of  Stanford University  and Christopher Avery of Harvard\naffirmed that there are talented poor students with high SAT\nscores who, shockingly enough, have never heard of Harvard or\nWilliams.  Wrong Investments  The take-away in discussions of this study is that we\nshould do a better job of getting them into wealthier colleges\nthat will pay their way.  Why not say that they are worth the\npublic investment, no matter what school they go to.  Finding more spots for low-income students at selective\ncolleges may be impossible in any case. A New America Foundation\nstudy by  Stephen Burd  details what students from families that\nmake $30,000 a year or less have to pay out of their own\npockets, even after financial aid is taken into account. While\nAmherst sets the standard on generosity, with a net price of\n$448 a year for Pell grant recipients, Williams charges $5,402\nand Princeton $7,545, according to the study.  My favorite graduations aren\u2019t the ceremonies that\nperpetuate the myth. They are at community colleges, where the\nimages are flipped. Parents and grandparents are receiving the\ndegrees with their children and grandchildren in the audience\ncheering. I will share their joy, however incomplete the\nachievement for now. And one day, I hope I will see something to\ncelebrate for millions more of them. White House  Monti\u2019s unelected government of non-politicians has kept a\npledge by Berlusconi to erase the budget gap in 2013, pushing\nthrough 20 billion euros ($26 billion) in tax increases and\nspending cuts as well as measures aimed at spurring anemic\nItalian growth through deregulation and reducing red tape. He has\nsince pushed Merkel to help nations like Italy and Greece offset\nthe impact of austerity measures and asked the EU to make\neconomic growth a formal priority alongside fiscal virtue. He again pointed to\nprevious German and French violations of EU deficit rules in\npushing for more comprehension for  Greece .  \u2018Resentments\u2019  \u201cThe very tough approach being taken toward Greece today\nmay lead us to regard this as being excessive, and it probably\nis,\u201d Monti said, warning \u201cresentments\u201d fueled by the crisis\nrisked breaking apart the 27-nation EU. \u201cThere are no good guys\nand bad guys. We all need to feel jointly responsible.\u201d  While Merkel has praised Monti for his \u201cremarkable\nmeasures,\u201d she was less charitable when asked about enjoining\ngrowth and fiscal discipline as a cornerstone of EU policy.  \u201cI\u2019m still looking for what more we should do,\u201d she told\nreporters in Berlin on Jan. 18. \u201cWhen I have figured that out,\nI will tell you what it is.\u201d  Still, Monti\u2019s role in Europe\u2019s crisis debate is growing as\nSarkozy digs into his re-election battle while trailing in the\npolls and Merkel risks being distracted from the crisis by the\nresignation of Wulff. Monti\u2019s next challenge is to make good on a pledge to\noverhaul Italy\u2019s rigid labor market by the end of March. His\nability to see that through, while ensuing lawmakers don\u2019t\ndilute his earlier measures on deregulation and red tape, may\ndecide whether his government lasts to the end of the current\nlegislature in spring 2013.  That effort will also help determine whether Italian bond\n\u201cyields can revert on a permanent basis to lower levels, which\nwill in turn help to achieve the  budget surplus  that is needed\nto start bringing down Italian government debt to a sustainable\nlevel,\u201d Ostwald said. Twenty-six projects are under way, from glass towers in downtown  San Francisco (ROFFSFRV)  to suburban office parks in Sunnyvale and  Santa Clara ,  California , according to brokerage CBRE Group Inc. About 3.4 million square feet (316,000 square meters) of the new development, or more than half, is speculative, meaning landlords broke ground without signing tenants, CBRE data show.  The building boom comes after three years of expansion by companies including Google Inc., Apple Inc. and  Salesforce.com Inc. (CRM)  spurred a surge in rents, making San Francisco the top U.S. office market in 2012 based on forecasts for future increases, according to Green Street Advisors Inc. Growth has cooled, with leasing down 43 percent in the city and two quarters of occupancy losses in Silicon Valley in the past year, raising the prospect that tenants won\u2019t be easy to find at higher rates.  \u201cCompanies decided to lock up space before rents climbed further, so they accelerated their normal leasing,\u201d said Donald Wise, chief executive officer of Metzler Realty Advisors Inc., a Seattle-based investor whose $445 million purchase of an  office tower  in  San Francisco \u2019s South of Market district was the city\u2019s priciest deal per square foot in 2012. \u201cDemand is now muted.\u201d  Newly occupied space in San Francisco totaled 80,850 square feet in the first quarter, down from a quarterly average of 118,000 square feet in the trailing 12 months and 526,000 square feet in 2011, according to data from Los Angeles-based CBRE. In Silicon Valley, roughly the area between San Francisco and  San Jose  about 45 miles south in Santa Clara County, occupancy tumbled by a net 94,000 square feet from the fourth quarter, with the vacancy rate rising to 11.4 percent from 11.2 percent.  Luring Talent  Some software, social-media and mobile-application firms have rented too much space for their current needs, said Steve Barker, San Francisco branch manager for Studley Inc., a tenant brokerage. Large firms are assessing global markets for mobile devices, online services and cloud storage on the Internet before signing more leases, while smaller companies take longer to consider deals as landlords raise rates to see what tenants will bear, said Todd Shaffer, managing director in Santa Clara for broker Cornish & Carey Commercial Newmark Knight Frank.  \u201cPeople are getting all worried, but it\u2019s a good sign that they\u2019re thinking things through,\u201d said Shaffer, referring to office renters. \u201cI\u2019ll be concerned if we\u2019re having this conversation at the end of the third quarter.\u201d  Cost Increase  San Francisco\u2019s leasing boom drove up costs for the most desirable  office space  -- including rent, local taxes and service charges -- by 36 percent in the year through September, the biggest jump among 133 global markets, CBRE said. Technology firms accounted for more than half of all deals, with San Francisco-based  Salesforce.com (CRM) , the biggest provider of online customer-management software, leasing 1.3 million square feet, the most by one company in a year since at least 2000, the brokerage said.  Asking rents in San Francisco rose 18 percent in the first quarter from a year earlier to $50.79 a square foot, the 12th straight gain, and in Silicon Valley they climbed 7.9 percent to $37.68, the highest since 2001\u2019s third quarter, CBRE said.  During the recession, rents bottomed in San Francisco at $30.50 a square foot, and vacancy peaked at 16.2 percent, in the first quarter of 2010, according to CBRE. Silicon Valley rates hit a low of $27.71 a square foot in the third quarter of 2010, with vacancy peaking at 21 percent a year earlier.  \u2018Fifth Inning\u2019  Across the country, office leasing in central business districts fell 5.3 percent in the first quarter from a year earlier, and vacancies were little changed at 13 percent, according to brokerage Cushman & Wakefield.  San Francisco\u2019s office market is now in the \u201cfifth inning\u201d of a nine-inning recovery, with \u201cdecelerating\u201d growth that\u2019s dropped its five-year outlook for rent increases to second in the U.S. based on revenue per square foot,  Michael Knott , managing director of  Newport Beach , California-based research firm Green Street, wrote in an e-mail.  West Los Angeles (MODCMMAP)  is the top office market based on forecasted rent growth through 2017, he said.  The current development wave, the most since 9.1 million square feet were added in 2001, include speculative projects in San Francisco such as Tishman Speyer Properties LP\u2019s  Foundry Square III , with large floors that \u201ccreate a sense of voluminous space illuminated by floor-to-ceiling glass,\u201d and a tower by Boston Properties Inc., at 535 Mission St., with \u201cexcellent natural light\u201d and a \u201cdramatic two-story lobby,\u201d according to the developers.  Corporate Campus  In Silicon Valley, Menlo Equities LLC and Beacon Capital Partners LLC are constructing three buildings at 3333 Scott Boulevard in Santa Clara, which the firms describe as \u201ca traditional Silicon Valley mid-rise corporate campus with ample parking and stand-alone identity.\u201d Jay Paul Co. is developing the second property of a planned six-building  campus  in Sunnyvale, dubbed Technology Corners, with \u201clandscaped plazas, fountains and walkways,\u201d the company said.  San Francisco\u2019s office market has a \u201cgenuine groundswell of demand\u201d that justifies site development and building that\u2019s \u201ca little bit more aggressive,\u201d Boston Properties Chairman  Mort Zuckerman  said on the firm\u2019s May 1 earnings call. Google, Microsoft Corp., Yahoo! Inc. and San Francisco-based startups Square Inc. and AppDynamics are all looking for large blocks of space, said Doug Linde, president of the Boston-based landlord.  Rising Employment  Job growth is still robust, with employment rising for the 33rd straight month in both San Francisco and Silicon Valley. This year through March, 33,000 new jobs were added in the city and 28,900 in the valley, according to California\u2019s Employment Development Department. Two-thirds of professional and business-services positions came from the technology industry, the agency said on April 19.  Companies are willing to pay triple the cost of suburban space to locate in the city because workers prefer an urban environment, said Carl Bass, CEO of Autodesk Inc. The  San Rafael , California-based maker of computer-aided design software signed three leases last year at San Francisco\u2019s One Market and Pier 9 that will almost double its occupancy to 287,000 square feet by mid-2014.  \u201cIf you get better people, it\u2019s worth it,\u201d Bass said in an interview.  Landlords are contending with smaller space needs from tenants across industries, down by almost a third to 170 square feet per employee, on average, said Studley\u2019s Barker. Technology firms in San Francisco need 30,000 more hires to fill space that\u2019s already been leased, he said.  Space Race  \u201cThis tech market has been driven by a race to control contiguous space and pre-empt rising rates,\u201d Barker said in an interview. \u201cThey\u2019ve massively over-leased. It remains to be seen whether they can fill it.\u201d  The rise in San Francisco rents means that offices comparable to those leased at $30 a square foot in early 2012 are now asking $50 a square foot, according to Barker. Spec buildings under construction will require rents of $60 to $70 a square foot at minimum to cover development costs, he said.  Each project has its own financing structure, starting with the price of land, that can dictate success in a fast-moving market, said Henry Bullock, chairman of  Palo Alto , California-based Menlo Equities. Low-rise construction in Silicon Valley, at $375 to $425 a square foot, is cheaper than urban towers in San Francisco, Bullock said. Menlo and Boston-based Beacon Capital will seek rents of $35 a square foot at the Scott Boulevard project in Santa Clara.  \u2018Not Worried\u2019  \u201cThere\u2019s not a lot of development as a percentage of the existing inventory, so we\u2019re not worried,\u201d Bullock said in a telephone interview. The  three buildings  will be \u201cshell-ready\u201d by mid-August, with \u201cname-brand companies\u201d in discussions to lease one or all of them, he said.  Among San Francisco spec projects, the  535 Mission St . tower by Boston Properties, the biggest U.S. office real estate investment trust, will cost $700 a square foot, Green Street said in a Feb. 6 note. That\u2019s 15 percent more than Kilroy Realty Corp. is spending to develop nearby 350 Mission St., a high-rise that\u2019s no longer spec after being fully preleased to Salesforce.com.  The Boston Properties investment, with an expected 6 percent yield, \u201cseems just OK\u201d compared with Los Angeles-based Kilroy\u2019s 6.5 percent or more and a guaranteed tenant, Green Street said in its note. \u201cWithout any known preleasing, these economics seem so-so on a risk-adjusted basis,\u201d the firm said.  Spec builders probably believe the potential for profit is greater by \u201cdeveloping to core, rather than buying to core,\u201d said Wise of Metzler Realty, whose acquisition last year on behalf of a German pension worked out to $802 a square foot.  \u201cThere\u2019s strong reason to be optimistic,\u201d Wise said. \u201cI don\u2019t think the market has gotten so overheated that new supply will outstrip reasonable expectations of demand.\u201d  To contact the reporter on this story: Dan Levy in San Francisco at  dlevy13@bloomberg.net   To contact the editor responsible for this story: Kara Wetzel at  kwetzel@bloomberg.net","path":".\/2008_2012_msft_bloomberg_news\/san-francisco-leasing-slows-amid-office-boom-real-estate.txt"},{"id":98959065,"title":"Buffett \u2018In the House\u2019 Gets 50,000 Followers on Twitter","released_at":"<date>May 2 2013<\/date> <time>18:09:58<\/time>","content":"Warren Buffett , the chairman of  Berkshire Hathaway Inc. Gupta was stepping down after nine years as managing\ndirector of the global consulting firm, and his colleagues were\ngathered to celebrate his tenure and wish him the best in the\nnext phase of his career.  They offered champagne toasts and took photos of Gupta,\nstanding next to the elephant, which was draped in a brightly\ncolored shawl called a jhool. The decorated elephant represented\nthe Hindu god Ganesh, who bestows good fortune on new ventures.\nGupta smiled as he rested his arm on its trunk, Bloomberg\nMarkets magazine reports in its July issue.  Today, some of those same people say they\u2019re stunned by\nwhat they\u2019ve since learned about Gupta. In March, the U.S.\nSecurities and Exchange Commission filed an  administrative order \nagainst him saying that he had passed confidential information\nto hedge fund billionaire  Raj Rajaratnam , the central figure in\nthe biggest crackdown on insider trading in U.S. history.  Rajaratnam was convicted on 14 counts of conspiracy and\nsecurities fraud on May 11 and could face 19 years in prison,\npending his July 29 sentencing in federal court.  Double Life  Government wiretaps and phone records show that Gupta\ncalled Rajaratnam nine times in 2008 and 2009, giving the hedge\nfund manager information to make trades for his New York-based\nGalleon Group LLC.  Gupta, 62, who divides his time between his Connecticut\nhome, a Manhattan apartment and a Florida getaway, has lived a\ndouble life. For 34 years until 2007, he worked for  McKinsey ,\nincluding nine years as the top executive of one of the world\u2019s\nmost trusted and prestigious consulting firms.  He was the confidant of chief executive officers such as\n Goldman Sachs Group Inc. (GS) \u2019s  Lloyd Blankfein  and  Procter & Gamble\nCo. (PG) \u2019s former head A. G. Lafley. Gupta sat on the boards of both\nof those companies -- and he was a director at four other\npublicly traded corporations.  As a philanthropist, Gupta raised millions of dollars for\neducation and health care, especially in  India  where he was born\nand to which he wanted to give back. He\u2019s done charitable work\nwith Microsoft Corp. co-founder  Bill Gates , former U.S.\nPresident Bill Clinton and Indian Prime Minister Manmohan Singh.\nFriends describe him as brilliant and humble.  Keeping Secrets  At McKinsey, a firm known for keeping secrets, Gupta\nharbored a few of his own. As the managing director and then as\nsenior partner of McKinsey for four more years before he\nretired, he ran his own consulting business on the side -- a\nviolation of McKinsey rules.  He and Anil Kumar, a former McKinsey partner who last year\npleaded guilty to passing confidential information to\nRajaratnam, set up their own consulting company. Gupta also\nindependently advised  Genpact Ltd. (G) , a Gurgaon, India-based firm\nthat manages business processes for other companies. That work,\ntoo, broke McKinsey\u2019s rules.  \u201cIt has always been a clear violation of our values and\nprofessional standards for any firm member to provide consulting\nor advisory services outside of McKinsey for personal monetary\ngain,\u201d says Michael Stewart, a McKinsey partner and director of\ncommunications.  McKinsey conducted an internal investigation of Gupta and\nKumar, and has cooperated with prosecutors and the SEC.  Off Track  During the past decade, Gupta, who was already a\nmillionaire, began to veer off track. He spent more time with\nWall Street money managers. He told colleagues that he wanted to\nbe a dealmaker, not just a consultant. Gupta declined to comment\non what he told his colleagues or on anything else reported in\nthis story.  While Gupta was devoted to his philanthropy in India, his\nquest to amass great wealth led him to lapses in judgment, says\nBala Balachandran, dean of the  Great Lakes Institute of\nManagement  in Chennai, India, and a friend for almost three\ndecades.  \u201cHe wanted a billionaire\u2019s life and the question for him\nwas how could he become a billionaire in a short time,\u201d\nBalachandran says.  Gupta, a man to whom corporate chieftans turned for advice\nand counsel, chose poorly when it came to investment partners.  In December 2006, two years before he reached McKinsey\u2019s\nmandatory retirement age of 60, Gupta co-founded private equity\nfirm New Silk Route Partners with investors, three of whom had\npreviously paid fines to settle SEC actions against them.  The Fines  Among the three was Rajaratnam, whose Galleon Group paid a\n$2 million fine and forfeited profits to the government in May\n2005 to settle an SEC  complaint  it had made improper trades. He\nneither admitted nor denied wrongdoing.  Two other investors in New Silk Route, Parag Saxena and\nVictor Menezes, like Gupta, had connections in the U.S. and\nIndia.  Saxena, a former money manager, paid a $250,000 fine in\n1994 to  settle  civil claims that he had received pre-initial-\npublic-offering stock in companies at big discounts and then\nrecommended the shares to his clients at Chancellor Capital\nManagement Inc., after the companies went public.  In January 2006, Menezes, a former  Citigroup Inc. (C)  senior\nvice chairman, paid $2.7 million in a fine and forfeited trading\nprofits to the U.S. to settle  SEC charges  that he sold Citigroup\nholdings ahead of an announcement of losses from a subsidiary in\nArgentina. Both men neither admitted nor denied wrongdoing.  Balachandran says he warned Gupta of his choice of business\npartners.  \u2018The Chicken Flu\u2019  \u201cYou\u2019re an eagle, so why do you want to be with these\nchickens who can\u2019t fly?,\u201d Balachandran says he told Gupta.\n\u201cYou\u2019ll get the chicken flu.\u201d  Gupta hasn\u2019t been charged with a crime in the Galleon\ninsider trading scandal. The SEC administrative action against\nhim is a civil complaint -- and the most that could happen to\nhim is a fine and a consent decree that could bar him from\nserving on public company boards in the U.S.  Gupta and Rajaratnam have known each other since the 1990s,\nand their relationship is both personal and professional. Gupta\ninvested $10 million of his own money with Rajaratnam, according\nto Gupta\u2019s lawyer,  Gary Naftalis . Gupta gave Rajaratnam more\nthan money; he passed along information on Goldman and P&G,\nprosecutors said during Rajaratnam\u2019s trial in Manhattan.  Unindicted Co-Conspirator  Justice Department prosecutors called Gupta an unindicted\nco-conspirator. They presented wiretap evidence to the\nRajaratnam jury showing that Gupta had told the hedge fund\nmanager that in 2008 Goldman Sachs\u2019s board was discussing\npossible acquisitions of American International Group Inc. or\nWachovia Corp.  Gupta also gave Rajaratnam early word on earnings at\nGoldman Sachs and P&G, the SEC says in its action.  Gupta sent an e-mail in late February to fellow directors\nof the Indian School of Business, declaring his innocence.  \u201cI have done nothing wrong,\u201d he wrote to the board of the\nschool, which he co-founded in 2001 in Hyderabad. \u201cThe SEC\u2019s\nallegations are totally baseless.\u201d  For the 85-year-old McKinsey, the Kumar conviction and the\nSEC action against Gupta have been a blow to its elite image.\nThe firm counts among its clients hundreds of the world\u2019s\nleading corporations, including Bloomberg LP, and governments.  Old Boys\u2019 Club  Consultants never talk about their clients in public, and\nthe firm won\u2019t even disclose customers\u2019 identities. Leaders of\nmajor companies have started their careers at McKinsey,\nincluding Boeing Co. CEO Jim McNerney, former American Express\nCo. head Harvey Golub and one-time International Business\nMachines Corp. CEO Lou Gerstner.  For decades, until the 1970s, the firm was the ultimate old\nboys\u2019 club, where consultants were required to wear hats and\nlong, dark-colored socks, with white, button-down cotton shirts\nand conservative suits. Gupta was the first nonwhite and non-\nU.S.-born elected managing director of the firm.  McKinsey veterans have been deeply troubled by Gupta\u2019s run-\nin with the SEC.  \u201cI was shocked, totally and completely shocked, at the\nnews of the allegations,\u201d says Ian Davis, who succeeded Gupta\nas McKinsey\u2019s managing director from 2003 until 2009 and is now\na director of BP Plc and Johnson & Johnson.  Gupta got caught up in envy and emulation of the super-\nrich, says Terry Connelly, dean of the Ageno School of Business\nat Golden Gate University in San Francisco.  \u2018Seductive Power\u2019  \u201cYou can never underestimate the seductive power of three\nor more zeroes added to net-worth numbers,\u201d says Connelly, a\nformer managing director at Salomon Brothers Inc. \u201cYou can be\nsuccessful, but if you\u2019re in hedge fund managers\u2019 circles and\nyou\u2019re not rich like them, you can start asking, \u2018Why can\u2019t I\nget that? I\u2019m every bit as smart.\u2019\u201d  Smart is a word people often use when describing Gupta. His\nascent from lower-middle-class roots in Kolkata to the top of\nMcKinsey is a triumph of brainpower and drive.  He was born in December 1948, 14 months after India became\nindependent of British rule. His father, a journalist who worked\nfor two newspapers, fought for India\u2019s independence and was\njailed several times for his political activism. His mother was\na teacher in a Montessori school.  The family moved to New Delhi when Gupta was five. He, his\ntwo sisters and younger brother attended  Modern School,  one of\nIndia\u2019s few English-language, Western-style high schools at the\ntime -- located off what was then New Delhi\u2019s most exclusive\nshopping district,  Connaught Place .  Orphaned at 18  Gupta was orphaned at age 18 after both his parents died of\nnatural causes within two years of each other. He persuaded an\nunmarried aunt to live with him and his siblings, according to a\n1994 interview Gupta gave to \u2018Business Today,\u2019 an Indian\nmagazine.  He said he was shattered by his father\u2019s death and became\nvery studious, careful never to make a mistake that could cost\nhim his high school scholarship.  Gupta ranked in the top 20 applicants among hundreds of\nthousands of Indian youth who took the entrance examination in\n1966 for a spot at the elite  Indian Institute of Technology ,\naccording to an interview he gave to the \u201cEconomic Times\u201d of\nIndia when he became head of McKinsey.  He chose the Delhi campus, which kept him close to home\nand, in 1971, he earned a bachelor\u2019s degree in mechanical\nengineering. His main leisure activity was acting in plays in\nthe school\u2019s drama club, where he met his future wife, Anita\nMattoo, an electrical engineering student.  Choosing Harvard  In the socialist India of the 1970s, white-collar positions\noutside the civil service were scarce. Gupta got his first job\noffer from  ITC Ltd. (ITC) , a British-owned company that sold\ncigarettes and ran hotels. He turned it down when he was\nadmitted to  Harvard Business School  on scholarship.  The academic workload was unrelenting for most but not for\nGupta, says John Carberry, who lived in the same Boston\ndormitory and was Gupta\u2019s friend.  \u201cSometimes we\u2019d still be doing cases at 2 a.m., but he\u2019d\nbe done by 11 p.m. and lying on his bed, watching Johnny Carson,\u201d says Carberry, who\u2019s now president of Wellesley,\nMassachusetts-based  F.L. Putnam Investment Management Co . \u201cBut\nif you had problems with your schoolwork, he\u2019d always help.\u201d  At a time when students at Harvard Business School were\noverwhelmingly white, Gupta stood out culturally and\nintellectually, Carberry says.  \u201cGupta was unassuming and humble,\u201d he says. \u201cWhen he\nspoke in class, though, everyone put their pencils down and\nlistened. He was the smartest guy in my section, just\nbrilliant.\u201d  Baker Scholar  Gupta became a Baker Scholar, a distinction earned by the\ntop 5 percent of students in his graduating class in 1973. With\nhis Master of Business Administration degree, he applied for a\nspot with McKinsey.  Even with his stellar academic record, the firm turned him\ndown. Walter Salmon, one of Gupta\u2019s professors who had McKinsey\nconnections, wrote Gupta a recommendation, and the consulting\nfirm decided to hire him in  New York .  Gupta advanced steadily, becoming a McKinsey partner in\n1980 and moving to Copenhagen the following year. In 1984, Gupta\nbegan overseeing all of the firm\u2019s business in Scandinavia. He\nmoved to McKinsey\u2019s  Chicago  office in 1987 and became head there\nin 1989. The office served many of the region\u2019s manufacturing\nand consumer products companies.  James Kilts, a former CEO of Nabisco Group Holdings Corp.\nand Gillette Co., says he was impressed when he first met Gupta\nin Chicago in the late 1980s. Kilts was then an executive at\n Kraft Foods Inc. (KFT) , and Gupta advised him about strategy for\ncheese products.  \u2018Self-Deprecating\u2019  \u201cHe was very thoughtful and self-deprecating,\u201d Kilts\nsays. \u201cHe could take a complicated subject and simplify it.\u201d\nKilts kept in touch with Gupta as both men advanced. \u201cYou could\nalways learn something from him,\u201d he says.  Gupta\u2019s big career leap came in 1994, when McKinsey held\nelections for a new leader, something that happens every three\nyears. The firm\u2019s 427 partners nominated seven of their peers in\nthe order they preferred. After several rounds of ballots,\nGupta, who was 45 at the time, was elected. He became McKinsey\u2019s\nyoungest managing director.  McKinsey grew rapidly under his leadership. He won re-\nelection twice, and during his three terms, the maximum the firm\nallows, revenue increased to $3.4 billion from $1.2 billion. The\nnumber of partners rose to 891, according to  Kennedy Information\nLLC , a research firm that tracks the consulting industry.  McKinsey opened 26 new offices globally under Gupta,\nwho pursued global expansion in India,  China  and other emerging\nmarkets where the firm\u2019s biggest clients increasingly were doing\nbusiness.  Internet Startups  As the tech boom took hold in the 1990s, Gupta pushed\nMcKinsey to take on Internet startups as clients, even when they\ncould pay only in stock. That broke from the firm\u2019s tradition of\nserving mostly blue-chip clients who paid fees. The equity,\nwhich McKinsey accepted from about 150 fledgling firms, went\ninto a profit pool for partners, according to former partners.  Client demand for McKinsey services declined following the\nbursting of the Internet bubble in 2000.  Global Crossing Ltd. (GLBC) ,\nKmart Corp., Swiss International Air Lines AG and other\ncompanies McKinsey had advised filed for bankruptcy. The biggest\npublic embarrassment was Enron Corp.\u2019s collapse.  The Houston-based energy trader, which had been the\nseventh-largest company by assets in the Standard & Poor\u2019s 500\nIndex, lost almost all of its value when regulators found the\ncompany had used accounting gimmicks to create a massive fraud.  Outside Interests  Enron had McKinsey in its bloodlines. Jeffrey Skilling, the\nfirm\u2019s CEO, had once been a McKinsey partner, and the consulting\nfirm had advised the company for 18 years as it transformed\nitself from an oil pipeline operator to a derivatives trader.\nSkilling was convicted of fraud in 2006 and sentenced to 24\nyears in federal prison.  As McKinsey\u2019s spate of woes swelled, so did Gupta\u2019s outside\ninterests. He raised personal donations from India\u2019s top\nbusiness executives, including  Infosys Technologies Ltd. (INFO) \nChairman N.R. Narayana Murthy, to start the Indian School of\nBusiness.  He also tapped McKinsey consultants based in India,\nincluding Anil Kumar, who would later get caught up in the\nGalleon scandal. The school, which has become the most prominent\none-year business school in India, opened in July 2001.  When an earthquake struck the Indian state of Gujarat in\nApril 2001, Gupta co-founded the  American India Foundation  to\nraise funds for victims. The foundation has since raised\nmillions of dollars from Hollywood stars, executives and money\nmanagers to aid India\u2019s poor.  Secret Business  Rajaratnam and his wife donated $1.5 million to the\nfoundation in 2006 for an HIV-AIDS program, and made more\ndonations later.  Gupta\u2019s McKinsey partners supported his philanthropic\nefforts. They didn\u2019t, however, know about the for-profit work he\ndid while still at the firm, according to Stewart, McKinsey\u2019s\ndirector of communications.  In 2001, Gupta and Kumar set up their own consulting\ncompany, Mindspirit LLC, in the names of their wives, Anita\nGupta and Malvika Kumar, according to a filing with the SEC by\nOmaha-based InfoGroup Inc. The two men, working for Mindspirit,\ngave advice to the company\u2019s CEO, according to the SEC filing.  InfoGroup, a database company, compensated Mindspirit with\n200,000 stock options, which the consulting company exercised\nfor an undisclosed amount, the filing said.  Bill Clinton, honorary chairman of the American India\nFoundation and another InfoGroup consultant, according to the\nfiling, was granted 100,000 stock options he never exercised.  All-Female-Crew  The same filing disclosed the settlement of a shareholder\nsuit against InfoGroup\u2019s CEO Vinod Gupta for his use of company\nfunds for personal pleasures. He had 28 club memberships, 20\ncars, a yacht with an all-female crew and a private jet he used\nto fly his family and friends to Africa, Cancun and Italy.  Vinod Gupta, who\u2019s not related to Rajat Gupta, had\ncollaborated with Rajat Gupta in building the American India\nFoundation. He resigned as CEO in August 2008 and repaid\nInfoGroup $9 million, according to the filing.  Another company that Gupta independently advised was\nGenpact Ltd., a Gurgaon, India-based company that had been spun\noff from General Electric. Genpact\u2019s sole client initially was\nGE, to which it provided back-office support.  Stock Options  Gupta was an advisory director from 2005 to 2007, for which\nhe was granted 81,405 stock options, valued at 93 cents each\nthen, according to Genpact\u2019s 2008 proxy statement. He hasn\u2019t\nexercised the options which expire in 2015, according to company\nfilings. Genpact shares traded at $16.88 on May 16.  Gupta became enamored of private equity as he saw others on\nWall Street earning far more than he could make at McKinsey. In\n2006, he co-founded New Silk Route Partners, which eventually\nraised $1.3 billion to invest in India and other emerging\neconomies, company filings show. Rajaratnam dropped out as a\npartner before New Silk Route opened. He invested $50 million in\nthe firm. He withdrew his stake last year, according to Kathleen\nLacey, an outside spokesperson for New Silk Route.  After retiring from McKinsey in 2007, Gupta globe-trotted\nconstantly. He traveled to India to look for investments for New\nSilk Route and to cities throughout the U.S. and overseas for\nmeetings at the five public companies and many nonprofit boards\non which he was a director.  Galleon\u2019s Headquarters  When Gupta was in New York, he spent time with Rajaratnam.\nAccording to testimony at Rajaratnam\u2019s trial, Gupta and his New\nSilk Route co-founders initially worked in cubicles at Galleon\u2019s\nheadquarters. New Silk Route later leased an office on Madison\nAvenue that was less than a block and a half from Galleon\u2019s.  Gupta, in 2007, joined Rajaratnam and a third partner to\nform GB Voyager Multi-Strategy Fund, an investment fund,\ncontributing $10 million of his own money. The $50 million fund\ninvested in Galleon hedge funds, including those that traded on\nGupta\u2019s allegedly illegal tips, the SEC says.  Gupta passed confidential information to Rajaratnam in 2008\nand 2009, the SEC says. He disclosed information on two calls to\nRajaratnam in September 2008 about the $5 billion investment in\nGoldman Sachs from Warren Buffett\u2019s Berkshire Hathaway Inc., the\nregulator says.  Rajaratnam\u2019s Galleon Technology funds, which held no\nGoldman Sachs investments before those calls, bought 120,000\nGoldman Sachs shares after Gupta talked to Rajaratnam, the SEC\nsays. On a telephone conference call at 3:15 p.m. on Sept. 23,\nthe Goldman Board approved Berkshire\u2019s $5 billion investment.  Passing the Word  \u201cGupta participated in the board meeting telephonically,\nstaying connected to the call until approximately 3:53 p.m.,\u201d\nthe SEC wrote. \u201cImmediately after disconnecting from the board\ncall, Gupta called Rajaratnam from the same line.  \u201cWithin a minute after this telephone conversation, at\n3:56 p.m. and 3:57 p.m., and just minutes before the close of\nthe markets, Rajaratnam caused the Galleon Tech funds to\npurchase more than 175,000 additional Goldman shares,\u201d the SEC\nwrote.  Galleon made more than $900,000 on the Goldman stock bought\nin advance of the announcement of Berkshire\u2019s stake, according\nto the SEC.  A month later, Gupta called Rajaratnam 23 seconds after a\nGoldman Sachs board call during which senior executives informed\ndirectors of poor results by the bank, the SEC says.  Gupta also knew that Kumar, who was still employed at\nMcKinsey, was being paid by Rajaratnam from offshore accounts,\naccording to phone calls tape-recorded by federal investigators.  \u201cYou know, Rajat, I\u2019m paying him a million a year for\ndoing literally nothing,\u201d Rajaratnam told Gupta in a July 2008\ncall recorded by federal investigators.  \u2018Very Generous\u2019  \u201cI think you\u2019re being very generous,\u201d Gupta replied. \u201cHe\nshould sometimes thank you for that, you know?\u201d  Kumar, in pleading guilty, said Rajaratnam paid him $1.75\nmillion to $2 million.  For himself, Gupta wanted at least a 10 percent stake in\nthe Galleon International Fund, one of Rajaratnam\u2019s hedge funds,\nin exchange for attracting investors. In a May 2008 wiretapped\ncall, Rajaratnam told Kumar that he was ready to offer this to\nGupta.  \u201cHe\u2019s not giving me the luxury of saying, \u2018Why don\u2019t you\ncome up with a package?\u2019\u201d Rajaratnam said. \u201cHe\u2019s telling me,\n\u2018I want so much.\u2019\u201d  Gupta never got that stake, according to testimony at\nRajaratnam\u2019s trial. The $10 million he invested in the Voyager\nfund with Rajaratnam was wiped out in the 2008 global subprime\nfinancial meltdown.  No Profit  Gupta\u2019s New Silk Route private equity fund hasn\u2019t turned a\nprofit with exits on any of its investments to date, according\nto  Venture Intelligence , a Chennai-based research firm that\ntracks private equity in India.  Rajaratnam was arrested in October 2009. Gupta left Goldman\nSachs\u2019s board in 2010, remaining a director at AMR, Genpact,\n Harmon International Industries Inc ., P&G and  Sberbank of\nRussia. (SBER)   In January 2011, the SEC notified Gupta that it had tied\nhim to Rajaratnam and would file an administrative action\nagainst Gupta. He gave no hint of his legal perils when, on Feb.\n27, he joined friends and business colleagues in a corporate box\nat Bangalore\u2019s Chinnaswamy Stadium.  India was facing England in a group stage match in the\nCricket  World Cup .  \u201cHe was chatty and looked dapper and cheerful,\u201d says\nShoba Narayan, an Indian author and acquaintance of his. There is no\nreason for me to suddenly deviate from a lifetime of probity and\nhonor.\u201d  Gupta flew back to New York after the match, which ended in\na tie. House Leaders Reach Deal on Letting Patent Office Keep Fees  House leaders agreed yesterday to give the U.S. Patent and\nTrademark Office greater control over its own funding, paving\nthe way for a floor vote on legislation to overhaul the U.S.\npatent system.  Under the deal announced yesterday, a special fund would be\nestablished to hold user fees collected in excess of the\nagency\u2019s budget. The fund could only be tapped by the patent\noffice, which would have to submit a spending plan to Congress\nto access the money.  Guaranteed access to all the fees collected by the agency\nis the cornerstone of a wide-ranging bill, H.R. 1249, that\nmirrors a measure passed by the Senate on a 95-5 vote in March.\nIf passed, the legislation would mark the biggest change to the\nU.S. patent system since 1952.  Like the Senate bill, the House measure seeks to end\nlawmakers\u2019 longstanding practice of steering fees collected by\nthe patent office toward non-patent purposes. Since the passage\nof a 1990 law requiring the agency to fund itself, Congress has\nretained more than $800 million in user fees.  The diversion of fees has been linked to an increase in the\nnumber of patent applications awaiting first review by agency\nexaminers. It takes, on average, about 34 months to complete a\nreview, and more than 700,000 applications have yet to receive a\nfirst response from the agency.  Companies from a range of industries, including drugmaker\n Eli Lilly & Co. (LLY)  and chipmaker  Intel Corp. (INTC) , as well as\nuniversities, venture capital firms, unions and the U.S. Chamber\nof Commerce have expressed support for ending fee diversion.  The legislation, the result of more than six years of\nnegotiations, testimony, and compromise, continues to have some\ndetractors.  Some small businesses have objected to language that would\ngrant patents to the first inventor to file an application.\nUnder existing law, patents go to the first person to invent\nsomething, which has led to often years-long fights over the\ntiming of ideas. The patent office, which supports the change,\nsays it would align U.S. law with the rest of the world.  Another provision would create a new process to review\npatents after they\u2019ve been issued. Independent patent owners or\nfirms that often sue big companies, like Acacia Research Corp.,\nsay it gives big companies another way to intimidate independent\ninventors and avoid paying for the use of someone\u2019s technology.\nLarge technology companies including  Cisco Systems Inc. (CSCO)  and\n Google Inc. (GOOG)  say it would help weed out patents of questionable\nvalidity.  The trade group representing generic-drug companies\nincluding Mylan Inc. and  Teva Pharmaceutical Industries Ltd. (TEVA) \nopposes a provision that would let patent owners who make errors\nor withhold information from the agency go back and make\ncorrections. The generic-drug makers say it would help brand-\nname companies avoid having their patents deemed unenforceable\nas punishment for misleading the agency.  The Senate bill is S. 23.
