Now, as he seeks to take  Dell Inc. (DELL)  private, the same investment firm may provide pivotal financing for what would be the largest buyout since 2007.  It wouldn\u2019t be the first time that Dell, who ranks 63rd on the  Bloomberg Billionaires Index  with $14.1 billion, has relied on MSD Capital LP to increase his holdings in the computer company. Between January 2006 and March 2011, he bought $625 million of Dell stock with cash provided by MSD Capital, according to a person familiar with the firm, who asked not to be identified because its operations are private.  Dell\u2019s fortune is key to pulling off the LBO. He\u2019s expected to contribute about half of the estimated $8 billion to $9 billion in equity needed for the deal, with private-equity firm  Silver Lake  Management LLC and Microsoft Corp., whose software powers many of Dell\u2019s machines, each contributing $1 billion to $2 billion, people with knowledge of the deal said.  \u201cGiven the difficulty of raising capital for new funds, some general partners would be reluctant to put big checks into one company like that,\u201d said Marc Bonavitacola, the head of U.S. private equity at SVG Advisers Inc. in  Boston . \u201cYou need two sponsors plus Michael Dell\u2019s equity.\u201d  Buying Stock  Since peaking more than a decade ago, the computer company that Dell founded with $1,000 in 1984 while attending the  University of Texas  has lost three quarters of its  market value . Michael Dell\u2019s 15.7 percent  stake  in the  Round Rock , Texas-based computer company is valued at $3.6 billion today. MSD Capital\u2019s assets have surged beyond $12 billion.  A spokesman for MSD Capital, whose initials stand for Michael Saul Dell, declined to comment.  David Frink , a spokesman for the computer company, said Michael Dell doesn\u2019t comment on his personal investments. Frink also declined to comment on the potential buyout.  Housed on the 21st Floor of 645 Fifth Avenue in  Manhattan , MSD was formed by former  Goldman Sachs (GS)  Group Inc. executives John Phelan and Glenn Fuhrman in 1998. Today, the firm has five investment groups, including a private-equity unit that seeks to invest in leveraged buyouts of companies with \u201cworld class management teams,\u201d according to its website.  Dedicated Team  Dell hired Phelan and Fuhrman about 10 years after Goldman Sachs took his computer maker public through a $30 million stock offering. During the intervening years, Dell\u2019s market value had soared, leaving him with a personal stake valued at close to $20 billion in early 2000.  Michael Dell had previously invested proceeds from the sale of Dell stock with various money managers, a process that led him to conclude that he needed a dedicated investment team, said the person familiar with the firm.  The opportunity came when he had lunch with Phelan, who had formerly worked as an analyst in Goldman Sachs\u2019s investment banking unit as well as for real estate investor  Sam Zell  and hedge-fund manager  Edward Lampert .  During the lunch, Phelan outlined plans to start his own firm, only to have Dell say \u201cWhy don\u2019t you do this for me?\u201d according to a January 2010 interview published by the student union newspaper at the  London School  of Economics, the money manager\u2019s alma mater. Phelan teamed up with Fuhrman, who had worked at Goldman Sachs\u2019s Special Investments Group, to co-found MSD Capital with an initial contribution of $400 million in capital from Dell, the article said.  Fuhrman said in an e-mail that he wasn\u2019t available for comment.  Alternative Assets  Created just as the Internet stock boom was gathering force, MSD Capital initially made venture capital investments, alongside other strategies, building a portfolio of 50 technology companies ranging from FTD.com to E-Steel, according to a January 2001 press release.  After the dot-com bust at the turn of the century, MSD Capital curtailed its venture investing. Even before, the firm had begun diversifying into other types of alternative assets. Today, more than 100 employees in offices in  New York ,  Los Angeles  and  London  run money in five different investment groups, including ones that invest in distressed securities, hedge funds, real estate and publicly traded stocks, as well as the private-equity team.  LBO Advantage  Taking his company private would give Michael Dell the flexibility to invest more heavily in mobile computing, according to Rich Kugele, an analyst at Needham & Co. Dell shares have declined 35 percent during the past five years, as consumers opted to replace desktop and notebook computers with smart phones and tablets manufactured by the likes of Apple Inc. and Samsung Electronics Co.  Even with the stock market decline, a leveraged buyout of Dell would require raising more equity and debt than any deal since 2007. In addition to the equity put up by Michael Dell, Silver Lake, and Microsoft, the buyout would be financed by debt and possibly some of the $11 billion in cash that the computer company had on its balance sheet as of Sept. 30.  \u201cIt\u2019s a tough transaction to get done,\u201d said John Orrico, co-portfolio manager of the $3 billion  Arbitrage Fund (ARBFX) , run by Water Island Capital LLC in New York. \u201cYou have to be concerned about their ability to transform themselves in the context of being heavily debt laden.\u201d  Investment Units  In addition to purchasing stock in his company, Michael Dell has used MSD to pay his taxes and make charitable contributions, said the person close to the firm.  Some of the firm\u2019s capital is locked up in illiquid investments such as private equity and real estate. Those holdings are marked at cost, meaning gains or losses on the investments aren\u2019t reflected in the company\u2019s assets under management, according to the person.  The private-equity unit, led by Eric Rosen, a former managing director at Onex Corp., usually invests $100 million to $250 million per deal, but will consider larger as well as smaller opportunities \u201cdepending on the particular investment profile,\u201d according to MSD Capital\u2019s website.  In July 2009, Phelan and Fuhrman set up a separate firm called MSDC Management LP to run  hedge funds  with capital from outside investors as well as the Dell family. At the end of 2011, the firm had $4.4 billion in assets under management and ran three funds that specialized in credit opportunities, distressed European debt and energy. It also has a special purpose vehicle that holds stock in the former IndyMac Bancorp, now known as OneWest Bank FSB, which MSD Capital acquired along with Paulson & Co. and JC Flowers & Co. for $13.9 billion in January 2009.  Stock Holdings  The credit opportunity fund, which MSD initially started in January 2002 as an internal strategy, has produced a compounded annual growth rate of 9.6 percent since that time, compared with 5.9 percent for  hedge funds  globally, according to Chicago-based Hedge Fund Research Inc. The energy fund\u2019s annual growth rate has been 23 percent since October 2008, compared with 6.5 percent for hedge funds.  MSD Capital held at least $561 million worth of stock in eight companies traded on U.S. exchanges as of Sept. 30, including DineEquity Inc., the parent to the Ihop pancake chain, and Wright Express Corp., which last quarter changed its name to WEX Inc., according to a regulatory filing. Many of MSD Capital\u2019s other holdings are long-term investments, according to news reports and public filings.  MSD Capital\u2019s real estate holdings include the Four Seasons Resort Maui at Wailea Hotel in Hawaii as well as the Heritage Fields, a shuttered marine base with 3,724 acres (1,507 hectares) in El Toro,  California . MSD Capital teamed up with the real estate arm of Cerberus Capital Management and homebuilder Lennar Corp., as well as other investors, to buy the former marine base for $650 million in February 2005.  Other previous investments include a 50 percent stake in Gap Radio Broadcasting, an operator for 111  radio stations , and the subordinated bonds of Simmons Bedding Co. European Council President Herman van Rompuy submitted the gadgets for testing to EU security services in Brussels, and they asked German experts for help. The technicians from Bonn allegedly found the devices infected with Trojans capable of gathering and transmitting information from computers and phones. It was not clear which guests of the summit received the USB drives: The British prime minister's office, for one, said  David Cameron  had not been given one. In any case, Russia denied the allegations. President Vladimir Putin's spokesman Dmitri Peskov called them an attempt to distract attention from U.S. spying on world leaders. The U.S. National Security Agency now also  denies  that it spied on millions of Europeans, saying European intelligence services voluntarily supplied phone records to the U.S. Be that as it may, any politician with sensitive information on his computer or phone ought to have them checked for spyware. It is also safe to assume that any phone conversation is unsafe. One bunch of spooks or another will be interested. France  suspends  \"ecotax\" French Prime Minister Jean-Marc Ayrault announced the suspension, for the third time, of the \"ecotax\" on large vehicles that was due to come into effect from 2014. The decision followed clashes between protesters and police in Brittany last weekend. Ayrault stressed that the levy has not been abolished, merely postponed -- the government wants to rework it, introducing different tax rates for different regions. The message from the French people is clear: A tax burden of 46 percent gross domestic product is as much as they can bear. The highly unpopular Socialist government has lost its ability to raise taxes, and the only way it can cut the budget deficit is by curbing spending.  Italian  recession  enters third quarter Antonio Golini, head of Italy's official statistical agency Istat, said the nation's gross domestic product fell by \"a limited amount\" in the third quarter of 2013. Official quarterly data are not expected for another two weeks, but Golini's statement makes it clear that Italy, unlike Spain, is not yet out of recession. Industrial production in the euro area's third biggest economy is still 25 percent below the pre-crisis peak, and public debt is expected to top 132 percent of GDP by the end of the year. Prime Minister Enrico Lette has succeeded this month in derailing his fractious coalition ally Silvio Berlusconi's bid for an early election, but all the fight seems to have gone out of him after the victory, just when it was time to present a budget. The government's version is complacently high on the spending side. Nokia  sells  record number of smartphones The Finnish mobile phone producer said it sold 8.8 million Lumia smartphones in the third quarter of 2013, more than ever before and 19 percent more than in the previous quarter. That is still below the company's break-even target, 50 million Lumias a year, but it is an optimistic sign for Microsoft that the take-up rate of its mobile operating system, which the Lumias run, is increasing. Nokia's deal with Microsoft, in which the latter acquires the Finnish firm's mobile phone business, will not be closed until the first quarter of 2014, so the Finnish company is still carrying the phone unit's losses. Its management's thoughts, however, are far away: the discussions at Nokia are all about what to do with Microsoft's cash, $7.2 billion of it, when it finally comes in. As to that, nothing has been decided yet. Some of the cash will probably be distributed to shareholders, and the rest could be used to bolster the company's large and modestly profitable network equipment business. Europe's biggest CO2 emitter  changes  strategy Peter Terium, chief executive of German energy company RWE, Europe's biggest CO2 emitter, announced a radical change of strategy, saying that from now on the company will only grow in renewable energy. Terium vowed that RWE would no longer open any power plants running on fossil fuel and that it would bring down energy production from conventional sources from more than 50 percent of the total to 20 percent by 2020. The strategy shift is hardly voluntary: Germany's heavily subsidized renewable energy industry has brought down energy prices so that up to 40 percent of RWE's conventional plants are losing money. The company's cash flow is barely sufficient to service its $48 billion debt. RWE is planning an asset sell-off and job cuts to avert a cash crunch. Under the circumstances, the new policy is largely a declaration by the management that it accepts the new reality and will try to make sure it does not kill the company. The ruling is scheduled to come by June.  Universities face the prospect of having to find new ways\nto maintain racially diverse campuses, potentially including\nclass-based affirmative action. The logic behind\nthat stance was questioned by Justices Sonia Sotomayor and\nStephen Breyer, both Democratic appointees, who said they saw\nlittle difference between the Texas policy and the University of\nMichigan Law School plan upheld in 2003.  The 2003 decision, Grutter v. Bollinger, said colleges and\ngraduate schools could consider race as long as they do so\nthrough a broad review of a student\u2019s application and don\u2019t\nmechanistically award extra points to every minority.  \u201cYou don\u2019t want to overrule Grutter,\u201d said Sotomayor, the\ncourt\u2019s first Hispanic justice. \u201cYou just want to gut it.\u201d  A central question in the Texas case is whether\nuniversities can adequately diversify without resorting to\nracial preferences. The University of Texas admits three-\nquarters of its freshman class each year on the basis of high\nschool class rank -- the \u201ctop 10 percent rule.\u201d  That system, the product of a 1997 state law, ensures a\nsignificant number of minorities because it guarantees slots to\nstudents at predominantly Hispanic and black schools. The\nuniversity considers race only in admitting the rest of the\nclass.  Many Options  The court has multiple options for resolving the case short\nof barring all affirmative action policies. The justices could\nsay the top-10 program achieves sufficient diversity by itself,\nmaking explicit racial preferences unnecessary.  Such a ruling would potentially force other universities to\nlook more closely at race-neutral approaches, including socio-\neconomic affirmative action and the abolition of legacy\npreferences, which disproportionately favor white students.  Another possibility would be to require a stronger showing\nfrom universities as to why their programs are necessary, said\n Richard Sander , a professor at the UCLA School of Law in Los\nAngeles who attended the argument. The justices spent part of\nthe hour-plus argument trying to sort out exactly how the Texas\npreference works.  Lack of Information  \u201cWhat struck me is how frustrated they were with the lack\nof information,\u201d said Sander, who filed a brief urging the\ncourt to put limits on affirmative action. \u201cNobody had any idea\nof how large the preference was.\u201d  The Texas program is being challenged by Abigail Noel\nFisher, who applied unsuccessfully to Texas in 2008 and later\nenrolled at Louisiana State University. A graduate of a Houston-\narea public high school, she says she was passed over by UT in\nfavor of minority classmates with lower grades and fewer\nextracurricular activities.  Texas has support in the case from some of the most\npowerful institutions in the U.S. The 59 companies that signed\nthe brief backing the university also include Gap Inc., Pfizer\nInc., Shell Oil Co. and  Viacom Inc. (VIAB)   Those corporations are in the unusual position of arguing\nalongside the Obama administration, which has  cast  affirmative\naction as a national security issue. The administration says\nrace-conscious admissions, both at the country\u2019s military\nacademies and at universities with Reserve Officers\u2019 Training\nCorps programs, help ensure a diverse group of officers.  \u2018Effective Citizens\u2019  \u201cThe core of our interest is in ensuring that the nation\u2019s\nuniversities produce graduates who are going to be effective\ncitizens and effective leaders in an increasingly diverse\nsociety, and effective competitors in diverse global markets,\u201d\nsaid U.S. Solicitor General Donald Verrilli, the\nadministration\u2019s top Supreme Court lawyer.  Texas also drew support from Justice Ruth Bader Ginsburg,\nas well as Sotomayor and Breyer.  \u201cThis program certainly is no more aggressive than the one\nin Grutter,\u201d Ginsburg said. \u201cIt\u2019s, in fact, more modest.\u201d  Alito faulted the Texas program for potentially giving a\npreference to the minority child of two corporate lawyers. The\nplan helps Hispanics and blacks \u201cwho come from privileged\nbackgrounds,\u201d he said.  Justice Elena Kagan isn\u2019t taking part in the case. She was\nthe Obama administration\u2019s top courtroom lawyer when the\nadministration filed a brief at the appeals court level.  Akin to Quota  In his 2003 dissent, Kennedy said the University of\nMichigan Law School policy at issue in that case was akin to a\nquota. At the same time, he said in that case that universities\ncould constitutionally make racial diversity a goal.  Although Kennedy directed the bulk of his questions at the\nlawyers defending affirmative action yesterday, he also balked\nat Rein\u2019s criticism of Texas\u2019s policy for adding only a handful\nof minority students to the school.  \u201cIf it\u2019s so few, then what\u2019s the problem?\u201d Kennedy asked.  Kennedy \u201crecognizes the continuing challenges that the\nnation has in the area of race,\u201d said Debo Adegbile, acting\npresident and director-counsel of the NAACP Legal Defense Fund.\nAt the same time, \u201che has expressed skepticism in several\ncontexts about what the remedies are to address it.\u201d  Bollinger said he was cheered that Fisher\u2019s lawyer didn\u2019t\nask the court yesterday to overturn the Grutter ruling.\nBollinger was president of the University of Michigan during\nmuch of that case, leading the defense of its affirmative action\nprogram.  \u201cI am perhaps more hopeful than I was six months ago,\u201d\nBollinger said.  The case is Fisher v. University of Texas at Austin,\n11-345. Since then, the UN, politicians and climate campaigners all have labored to get the world\u2019s major economies to curb the use of fossil fuels. They haven\u2019t had much success. President Obama failed in his first year of office to move national climate legislation through Congress. Australia did recently enact a national greenhouse gas law, and several U.S. states, including California and parts of the Northeast, have cap-and-trade programs. China, Vietnam, Costa Rica, and at least a dozen other emerging nations are implementing emissions trading. Even these nations are not making a dent in the problem. Annual global emissions of greenhouse gases have grown by nearly 45 percent since the 1992 Earth Summit. Atmospheric concentrations of carbon dioxide, the most important greenhouse gas, are climbing steadily. The past decade was the hottest globally on record, followed by the 1990s, followed by the 1980s. The longer we wait to address climate risks, the harder they'll be to address. With roughly 50,000 assembling for the Rio+20 Summit, maybe it\u2019s time for a new approach. Amid a faltering global economy, no country wants to stop burning oil, coal and natural gas. Might there instead be a way to clean up--or recycle--the CO2 they generate? That\u2019s precisely what a handful of scientists and entrepreneurs are aiming to do. They have launched startup companies that are building machines to capture CO2 from the air, with the backing of well-to-do investors including Bill Gates and Edgar Bronfman Jr.\u00a0 They hope to develop what are called \u201cnegative emissions technologies\u201d -- a technical phrase for machines that suck carbon dioxide out of the air. At least in theory, they could dial back CO2 concentrations if they exceed safe levels, as some scientists say they already have. Direct air capture of CO2 \u201copens up the possibility of capturing more CO2 than is being emitted by point sources \u2013 in other words, taking them carbon negative, not just carbon neutral,\u201d says Nicholas Eisenberger, a strategic advisor to Global Thermostat , an air-capture company started by his father, Peter Eisenberger, a physicist and the founding director of the Columbia Earth Institute. No one doubts that CO2 can be drawn down through chemical processes. That\u2019s essentially how CO2 is removed from submarines or spaceships, so that people can continue to breathe.\u00a0 The trouble is, using today\u2019s technology, it\u2019s very expensive. Two peer-reviewed studies published in 2011 pegged the cost at $600 to $1,000 per ton of CO2. Since a mid-sized car emits about six tons a year, that means it would cost $3,600 to $6,000 a year just to recycle the CO2 from a, say, a Ford Taurus. Scientists working on direct air capture think they can drive the costs down much lower.\u00a0 Carbon Engineering , a startup based in Calgary, Alberta, offers a \u201cconservative estimate\u201d\u00a0 on its website  of\u00a0 \u201cless than $250 per ton.\u201d\u00a0 Others peg the costs at $150 a ton, or less. Cost is key to the future of carbon capture because there\u2019s substantial unmet demand for CO2, at prices that can top $100 a ton. Most of the demand comes from the oil industry, which injects CO2 deep into the ground to extract oil, a well-established process known as enhanced oil recovery.\u00a0 Algae biofuel companies are also in the market for CO2 because it helps algae grow more quickly. Four companies are trying to turn direct air capture of CO2 into a business.\u00a0 Kilimanjaro Energy  was founded by the industry pioneer, Columbia University physicist Klaus Lackner, initially financed with $8 million from Gary Comer, the founder of Lands\u2019 End. (Comer died in 2006.) Last year, Kilimanjaro raised another $3.5 million in venture capital. Carbon Engineering is led by David Keith, a physicist and climate scientist who has a joint appointment at the University of Calgary and at Harvard\u2019s Kennedy School. Bill Gates is an investor, as is his friend Jabe Blumenthal, a former Microsoft executive who designed the first version of Excel. (The size of their investments hasn\u2019t been disclosed.) Global Thermostat was formed by physicist Peter Eisenberger and Graciela Chichilnisky, an economist and mathematician. Its biggest investor is Edgar Bronfman Jr., the Warner Music CEO and heir to the Seagram\u2019s fortune, who has put in $15 million. Finally, there\u2019s\u00a0 Climeworks , which was spun out of ETH Zurich, a university where its co-founder, Christophe Gebald was a graduate student. Their technologies and business plans vary. Kilimanjaro\u2019s CEO, Ned David, is bullish on enhanced oil recovery. CO2, he says, could do for the oil business what hydrofracking has done for natural gas, unleashing vast amounts of fossil fuels that might otherwise remain in the ground. \u201cA money gusher,\u201d he calls it. Meantime, Boeing has been studying the technology to see if it could be used to make fuels at the military\u2019s Forward Operating Bases (FOBs). That would be very expensive, but the military may be willing to pay a steep price to avoid the attacks on convoys that are used to move fuel through unstable regions. Ultimately, direct air capture could be a way to recycle emissions. CO2 pulled from the air and hydrogen extracted from water can be combined to make hydrocarbons--transportation fuels. If the entire process is powered by low-carbon energy, the result would be low-carbon or carbon-neutral gasoline, diesel or jet fuel. \u201cClosing the carbon cycle\u201d is how Peter Eisenberger describes it. He says , air capture will enable any country, anywhere in the world to make its own sustainable transportation fuels. It may sound farfetched--but, after two decades of trying, so does the idea that the world is going to give up fossil fuels anytime soon. Nicholas Eisenberger's last name has been corrected. It can take anywhere\nfrom one month to one year to find what they\u2019re looking for.\u201d  Robb says book buyers these days fall into two categories:\nThey\u2019re either seeking something special for themselves or a\nrare printed treat to offer a client.  First Carol  \u201cIt\u2019s an interesting selection, like a 95,000 pound copy\nof an 1807 volume of \u2018Doctor Thornton\u2019s Flower Book\u2019 or a 19,500\npound first edition of  Charles Dickens \u2019s \u2018A Christmas Carol,\u2019\u201d\nRobb says.   James Bond  is big, too, a sign of the times, I\nsuspect.\u201d  Robb says another significant signpost is  Google Books , the\nInternet library of logorrhea that since 2004 has digested 15\nmillion of the estimated 130 million titles published since the\n15th-century invention of the printing press, according to a\n2010  Harvard University  study by Jean-Baptiste Michel.  \u201cInternet publishing adds to the difficulty of assessing\nwhat books, printed today on paper will become the investments\nof the future,\u201d Robb says. \u201cIt\u2019s impossible to calculate the\ntrue growth potential of a modern first edition.\u201d  Wizard Editions  There are exceptions. Chief among them are first editions\nof   Harry Potter  and the Philosopher\u2019s Stone,\u201d the opening\nsalvo of J.K. Rowling\u2019s seven-volume wizard franchise. \u201cOnly\n500 first editions of Philosopher\u2019s Stone were printed,\u201d Robb\nsays. \u201cThey now sell for between 7,000 and 10,000 pounds. This\nis a gilt that will go up in price.\u201d  Robb says the  Dow Jones Industrial Average  of his market\nincludes original volumes written by Jane Austen, Charles Darwin, Beatrix Potter, Dickens, William Shakespeare and  Winston Churchill .  Recent market movers -- U.K. art dealer Michael Tollemache\nlast year paid $11.5 million at a Sotheby\u2019s London auction for\nan original four-volume edition of John James Audubon\u2019s \u201cBirds\nof America\u201d and Microsoft Corp. founder  Bill Gates  shelled out\n$30.8 million in 1994 for  Leonardo da Vinci \u2019s \u201cCodex\nLeicester\u201d -- are fluky super-events.  Clark Kent  Yet the superhero market remains robust, particularly for\nthose who invested in an original copy of Action Comics 1.\nPublished in June 1938 for 10 U.S. cents, the story that\nlaunched Clark Kent\u2019s career sold for $317,000 in 2009. The storm comes in the wake of  Auburn University  English\nprofessor Alan Gribben\u2019s decision to have  NewSouth Books  roll\nout a bowdlerized version of  Mark Twain \u2019s \u201cAdventures of\nHuckleberry Finn,\u201d replacing the word \u201cnigger\u201d with \u201cslave\u201d\nto foster political correctness among new readers of the\nAmerican classic.  Boosting Value  \u201cOverly precious,\u201d is how Robb describes U.S. euphemism\npolice sanitizing Twain\u2019s passages, descriptions that\nnonetheless continue to accurately mirror 19th-century American\nattitudes. \u201cExpurgating Twain\u2019s words in all new editions will\nonly increase the value of the old editions.\u201d  For Robb, the cascade effect of the U.S.\u2019s Huckleberry Finn\ncontroversy is palpable and sitting on the Edwardian table in\nfront of him. It\u2019s called \u201cNegro.\u201d  It was published in 1934 by Nancy Cunard, the daughter of\nluxury-passenger-line owner Bache Cunard. Robb describes the\n855-page book as a \u201cmonumental anthology of commentary and\narticles on many aspects of black life, culture and politics.\u201d  Dedicated to the black American jazz musician \u201cHenry\nCrowder, my new Negro friend,\u201d Cunard\u2019s coffee-table-sized tome\nis perhaps the earliest historical compilation of the treatment\nof blacks globally. The pages of \u201cNegro\u201d include rarely seen\nofferings by Langston Hughes, William Carlos Williams and W.E.\nDubois.  Beckett Translation  The 5,800 pound book, in which the N-word pops up with the\nfrequency of a rap song, comes with maps, sheet music, essays,\nphotographs and the observations of black boxing champions and\nthe singer Josephine Baker. Loeb's Third Point fund, which holds $1.1 billion of Sony shares, is  prodding  the Japanese giant to sell as much as 20 percent of its entertainment business and focus on electronics.   But other than film blockbusters such as \"Skyfall\u201d or \u201cThe Amazing Spider-Man,\u201d what does Sony really have going for it? When the company posted its first profit in years in the fiscal year ended March 31, entertainment was among the only bright spots. Its electronics business is missing in action. Years after Apple Inc. changed the world,  Sony  still hasn't come out with a globally competitive answer to the iPod, iPhone or iPad.   Sony's problem isn't the economy or the strong yen, but that it long ago stopped dreaming up game-changing products. That left a void that Apple and South Korea's  Samsung Electronics Co.  easily filled. Instead of focusing on innovation, Sony's chief executives, Howard Stringer and, more recently, Kazuo Hirai, sought to cut costs and streamline operations.   Yet the company needs drastic change to avoid irrelevance and it's hard to see how an insider such as Hirai can engineer it. It is even more difficult to understand why investors such as Loeb don't see that. Frankly, the only answer for  Sony  may be for it to be acquired.  It's blasphemy even to raise this possibility. Sony is synonymous with Japan's rise from the ashes of World War II and has a unique place in the national psyche. Yet Apple has what Sony once did: the \"cool factor\" sought by consumers. But Sony has what Apple doesn't: mountains of content. The word \"synergies\" makes eyes roll, though Apple and Sony are a good match. Perhaps Samsung, too.  These days, Sony is looking like Microsoft Corp., which was slow to realize how Google Inc. and Apple were making it more Old Economy than New Economy. It took Sony far too long to understand the threat from more innovative and nimble competitors. Just wait until China's technology industry gets its act together.   Investors such as Loeb are free to recommend half measures in hopes of returning Sony to greatness. But there's no ignoring that a company that once prided itself on being the one and only is now just one of many. And a troubled one at that.  (William Pesek is a Bloomberg View columnist. The Space Needle, Monorail and Bubblelator of \u201cCentury\n21\u201d not only pointed to an exciting technology-driven future.\nThe fair did what great urban spectacles like the Olympics are\nsupposed to do: It put the city on the map, jump-starting a\nhalf-century of transformation.  The history of Olympic bids and World\u2019s Fairs is littered\nwith costly failures. Beijing\u2019s Olympics site is dominated by\nthe spectacular empty husk of the Birds Nest stadium. Athens\u2019s\nstunning venues by  Santiago Calatrava  attract aficionados of\nruin porn.  Hoping to avoid such fates, London focused its Olympics\nplanning on revitalizing an ignored swath of its East End. The\ncosts rose, however, to as much as 9.3 billion pounds ($14\nbillion) from 3.4 billion pounds.  Cities are reassessing Olympics bids. Recession-wracked\n Madrid , looking longingly on Barcelona\u2019s 1992 success, promises\na shoestring games if it\u2019s selected for 2020.  I thought about what Seattle did right -- for about $500\nmillion in today\u2019s dollars -- as I walked the 74-acre fair site.\nThe iconic Space Needle still dominates the city, with an\nathletic design that sums up the era\u2019s faith in the futuristic\nwith purposefully elegant engineering.  Science Pavilion  The fair\u2019s centerpiece was the science pavilion, boxlike\nexhibition structures arranged around a sparkling pool from\nwhich elegant fretwork arches rise. It showed visitors the\ndegree to which the city was evolving from hick timber town to\nengineering hub. ( Boeing Co. (BA) , which dominated Seattle\u2019s economy\nin the 1960s the way cars dominated  Detroit , had inaugurated its\n707 -- the plane that ushered in today\u2019s era of mass air\ntransportation -- in 1958.)  The much-modernized Pacific Science Center remains one of\nthe best designs of architect Minoru Yamasaki in his signature\nModernist Gothic style. He would find global fame designing  New\nYork \u2019s World Trade Center.  I walked past the  Seattle Repertory Theater  and the  Seattle\nOpera , both founded the year after the fair\u2019s success allowed\nSeattle to chase big-city cultural dreams.  A distinctive arena with angular columns holding up a\nhandsome cable-suspended roof has served well for hockey and\nbasketball, though San Francisco hedge-fund manager Christopher\nHansen now seeks to replace it.  Talented Locals  The fair was charmingly modest, and lucky to get far better\narchitecture from talented locals (Victor Steinbrueck, Paul\nThiry) than  New York City \u2019s overblown extravaganza of 1964. It\nwas said to have made money.  The site still hosts numerous festivals and celebrations.\n Frank Gehry  designed the Experience Music Project for  Microsoft\nCorp. (MSFT)  co-founder  Paul Allen . It showcases a strange amalgam of\nrock-music history and science-fiction memorabilia. This past\nspring a collection of Dale Chihuly glass art opened in a\ngreenhouse-style pavilion erected at the base of the Space\nNeedle.  Ten million people visited the fair in what was then an\nunpretentious middle-class city. A lot of them liked the\nmountains, picturesque bays and slow pace. There was a civic-\nbuilder class preparing the city for the future with\nregionalized planning and sewers that cleared up the crown jewel\nof Lake Washington.  Seattle also had a powerful engine of innovative growth in\nthe form of Boeing, and a growing customer-focused retail chain\ncalled  Nordstrom Inc. (JWN)  So people came.  Fledgling Companies  Seattle looked like a write-off around 1970, though, when\nBoeing was forced to lay off two-thirds of a workforce of about\n80,000. And yet those who stayed and worked had the skills to\ntake on new challenges a decade later when fledgling companies\nlike Microsoft,  Starbucks Corp. (SBUX) , and  Amazon.com Inc. (AMZN)  were ready\nto grow fast.  Almost everyone who was around then recognizes the fair as\na turning point. It was an expression of civic energy and an\nemerging urban identity. The fair didn\u2019t invent that identity,\nit proclaimed it to a world that didn\u2019t know.  Barcelona hosted the most successful recent Olympics, but\nit spent big on transformative infrastructure, as London did.  The lesson of Seattle\u2019s budget World\u2019s Fair is a subtle\none. If a city doesn\u2019t have an economy and amenities to draw\npeople, neither the glitziest fair pavilions nor the most\nglamorous stadiums will make a difference.  (James S. Russell writes on architecture for Muse, the arts\nand culture section of  Bloomberg News . He is the author of \u201cThe\nAgile City.\u201d The opinions expressed are his own.) Compliance Action  Boeing Fined $13.6 Million by U.S. for Tank Guidance Delays  The U.S. Federal Aviation Administration proposed to fine\n Boeing Co. (BA)  $13.6 million, its second-largest penalty ever, for\ndelays in telling airlines how to prevent fuel-tank explosions\non 383 aircraft. The Chicago-based company missed the deadline\nfor 747s by 301 days, and was 406 days late for 757s, according\nto the FAA release.  \u201cWe are committed to ensuring the safety of the flying\npublic,\u201d U.S. Transportation Secretary Ray LaHood said in the\nstatement. \u201cManufacturers must provide the necessary\ninstructions so the airlines can comply with this important\nsafety regulation.\u201d  The fine is the largest proposed by the FAA since it sought\n$24.2 million from  AMR Corp. Airbus SAS, Boeing\u2019s main competitor for civilian aircraft,\nmet the deadline, according to the statement. Compliance Policy  MF Global, Peregrine Spur CFTC Call for Electronic Bank Access  U.S. regulators, seeking to bolster protection of futures\ncustomer funds after shortfalls at  MF Global Holdings Ltd. (MFGLQ)  and\nPeregrine Financial Group Inc., are seeking electronic access to\nbanks\u2019 accounts to monitor records.  \u201cWe need to ensure regulators have direct daily access to\nbank accounts and custodial accounts of the futures commission\nmerchants,\u201d Commodity Futures Trading Commission Chairman  Gary Gensler  said Friday in a telephone interview. \u201cIn addition, I\nthink we need direct access to acknowledgment letters and\nconfirmations, and that all of this should be 24 hours a day, 7\ndays. That means electronic access.\u201d  The CFTC and the National Futures Association, an industry-\nfunded self-regulator, are facing new scrutiny from lawmakers\nand market participants amid allegations of a $200 million\nshortfall in customer funds at Peregrine. The agency sued the\nbrokerage over the alleged shortfall less than a year after\nbeing scolded for poor oversight following the collapse of MF\nGlobal, which left an estimated $1.6 billion fund gap.  The drive for electronic access to monitor customer funds\nhas gained bipartisan support on the five-member CFTC.  Scott\nO\u2019Malia , a Republican commissioner, has called a July 26 meeting\nof the agency\u2019s technology advisory committee to consider an\nindustry-funded solution for electronic oversight.  Bart Chilton, a Democratic commissioner, said the agency\nneeds \u201crobust data dives\u201d to protect customer funds.  \u201cWe shouldn\u2019t take the word of a firm, but rely upon\nelectronic banking with secure communications,\u201d Chilton said in\nan e-mail.  The CFTC on Friday approved changes proposed by the NFA to\nrequire additional reporting by brokers about customer funds.\nThe rules will bar futures brokers from using an alternative\nmethod for calculating how much margin to keep in accounts used\nfor trading on foreign exchanges. In the U.S., brokers must keep\nfunds sufficient to handle liquidation of an account.  IRS Ends Deals That Let U.S. Companies Skip Repatriation Tax  The U.S. Internal Revenue Service will prevent companies\nfrom entering into transactions that allow them to tap their\noffshore cash stockpiles without paying taxes, the government\nsaid.  \u201cThe IRS and the Treasury Department believe that these\ntransactions raise significant policy concerns,\u201d the agencies\nsaid in a notice Friday. The rules, once written, will be made\neffective as of July 13.  Companies owe U.S. taxes on income they earn around the\nworld after receiving credits for foreign taxes paid. Under U.S.\ntax law, they must pay those taxes only when they repatriate the\nincome.  That system has led companies including  Google Inc. (GOOG) ,\n Microsoft Corp. (MSFT)  and  Pfizer Inc. (PFE)  to keep foreign profits outside\nthe U.S. Data compiled by Bloomberg in March showed that 70\ncompanies have $1.2 trillion in untaxed profits around the\nworld, up 18.4 percent from a year earlier.  Those companies and others lobbied Congress unsuccessfully\nin 2011 for a temporary tax holiday on repatriated profits.\nRepublicans including presidential candidate Mitt Romney favor\nchanging the tax system permanently to allow companies to bring\nmost overseas profits into this country without facing the\nresidual U.S. tax.  The IRS notice describes two types of transactions it is\ntrying to prevent and says the agency is \u201caware\u201d that\ntaxpayers are engaging in them. One involves selling a patent\nfrom a U.S. company to a foreign subsidiary without triggering\nan immediate U.S. tax.  In the other type of transaction, a company uses its\noffshore money to purchase a U.S. company and quickly\nreorganizes to move the purchased company outside the U.S.  In the Courts  Visa, MasterCard Settle Swipe-Fee Antitrust Suit With Merchants  Visa Inc. (V) ,  MasterCard Inc. (MA)  and some of the biggest U.S.\nbanks agreed to a settlement of at least $6.05 billion in a\nprice-fixing case brought by retailers over credit-card swipe\nfees.  The total value of the settlement is $7.25 billion to a\nclass of about 7 million merchants in the U.S. that accept Visa\nand MasterCard credit cards and debit cards, a law firm for the\nmerchants, Robins Kaplan Miller & Ciresi LLP, said in a\nstatement.  Visa, the world\u2019s biggest payments network, said its share\nof the settlement filed July 13 in federal court in Brooklyn,\nNew York, was about $4.4 billion. Visa said the proposed\nsettlement payments, including costs incurred by MasterCard Inc.\nand card-issuing banks, would be about $6.6 billion. That amount\nwould include about $525 million for individual claims.  \u201cWe believe settling this case is in the best interests of\nall parties,\u201d Visa Chief Executive Officer Joseph W. Saunders\nsaid in a statement.  Noah Hanft, MasterCard\u2019s general counsel, said in a\nstatement that, \u201cOur decision to settle is based on our belief\nthat MasterCard and our stakeholders are best served by an\namicable resolution.\u201d  The agreement, which provides for a temporary reduction in\nrates for merchants and allows them to impose surcharges on\ncustomer purchases, follows a seven-year legal battle with U.S.\nretailers that accused the two largest payment networks of\nconspiring with banks to fix swipe fees, or interchange.  \u201cIt\u2019s been an extraordinarily intense and difficult\nsettlement to reach,\u201d K. Craig Wildfang, a lead lawyer for the\nplaintiffs, said in a phone interview.  The dispute began in 2005, a year before MasterCard\u2019s\n initial public offering  and three years ahead of San Francisco-\nbased Visa\u2019s. Merchants alleged the companies violated antitrust\nlaw by fixing the swipe fees, which average about 2 percent of\nthe purchase price. Proceeds generate more than $40 billion a\nyear for U.S. banks.  The case had been set for trial in September before U.S.\nDistrict Judge John Gleeson in Brooklyn.  The settlement includes a $6.05 billion cash payment,\naccording to a July 13 filing. That amount would be reduced if\nsome plaintiffs don\u2019t agree to participate.  The settlement also provides for a temporary rebate of\nabout one-tenth of a percentage point on the fees charged\nretailers, according to the filing. The agreement includes\nmodifications in Visa and MasterCard rules to allow merchants to\ntack surcharges on to bills based on the fees.  The case is In re Payment Card Interchange Fee and Merchant\nDiscount Antitrust Litigation, 05-md-01720, U.S. District Court,\nEastern District of New York (Brooklyn).  For more, click here.  Mortgage Database MERS Reaches Settlement With Delaware  Merscorp Holdings Inc. , which operates a mortgage registry,\nsettled a lawsuit brought by the Delaware Attorney General  Beau Biden  that accused the company of engaging in deceptive\npractices.  Merscorp Holdings agreed to conduct regular audits of its\nrecords for accuracy and maintain a database that allows\nhomeowners to learn who owns their mortgage, Biden said July 13\nin a statement.  The MERS system, which tracks ownership interests in\nmortgages and servicing rights, has been targeted in lawsuits by\nthe attorneys general of New York and Massachusetts. Biden\ncontended in his lawsuit in Delaware Chancery Court in\nWilmington that the company\u2019s records were inaccurate and that\nit impeded the ability of homeowners to fight foreclosures and\nobtain loan modifications from lenders.  Banks created MERS to reduce costs and speed up the process\nof bundling mortgages into securities, according to Biden. The\ncompany built \u201can unregulated shadow mortgage registry\u201d that\nallows mortgage records to be changed without any oversight,\nBiden said in court papers.  Merscorp Holdings\u2019 shareholders include  Bank of America\nCorp. ,  Wells Fargo & Co. (WFC)  and mortgage-finance companies Fannie\nMae and Freddie Mac, according to its website. Bank of America\nand Wells Fargo were among five banks that reached a $25 billion\nsettlement with state and federal officials this year over\nforeclosure practices.  Biden said his settlement will increase the transparency\nand accuracy of mortgage records.  The settlement agreement requires Merscorp Holdings to\nmaintain a database accessible online and by phone that allows\nhomeowners to see who owns their mortgage and services the loan,\naccording to Biden\u2019s office. Records of the MERS system must be\naudited, with the results reported to Biden\u2019s office, the\nattorney general said.  Merscorp Holdings already has implemented the measures in\nthe settlement nationally except the reports to Biden\u2019s office,\nJason Lobo, a company spokesman, said in a phone interview. The\nReston, Virginia-based company didn\u2019t admit to wrongdoing.  \u201cWe are pleased to have come to an agreement with the\nstate of Delaware that both serves the best interests of\nDelaware homeowners and protects the value Merscorp Holdings\nbrings to its members,\u201d Chief Executive Officer Bill Beckmann\nsaid in an e-mailed statement.  The case is Delaware v. Merscorp Inc., CA6987, Delaware\nChancery Court (Wilmington). The justices  said  the\nEnvironmental Protection Agency was better equipped than federal\njudges to assess the costs and benefits of reducing greenhouse\ngases.  \u201cIt is altogether fitting that Congress designated an\nexpert agency, here, EPA, as best suited to serve as primary\nregulator of greenhouse-gas emissions,\u201d Justice Ruth Bader\nGinsburg said for the court. Justice Sonia Sotomayor didn\u2019t take\npart in the case.  Through the federal Clean Air Act, Congress has entrusted\nthe EPA and state regulators to determine greenhouse-gas\nregulations for industries, according to the court.  The ruling bolsters EPA\u2019s position as the focal point for\ncurbing heat-trapping emissions from vehicles and industrial\npolluters such as power plants, according to David Doniger,\npolicy director for the climate center at the Natural Resources\nDefense Council, an environmental group based in New York. The Standard & Poor\u2019s 500 Index has traded at an average price-earnings multiple of 13.9 this year, 0.18 times the mean level of the Thomson Reuters\/ University of Michigan  final index of consumer sentiment, according to data compiled by Bloomberg. The gap is the widest since 1995, when the  S&P 500  gained 34 percent for its biggest annual rally of the last five decades.  Bears say the discounted valuations are still too high and anticipate the slowing U.S. recovery will lead to a repeat of last year, when equities lost 19 percent in five months. Bulls say price-earnings ratios as low as during the financial crisis make no sense with housing and industrial production expanding and the U.S. Federal Reserve standing ready to act should employment worsen.  \u201cThe world is profoundly underinvested in U.S. equities,\u201d said  Jeffrey Saut , chief investment strategist at Raymond James & Associates in  St. Petersburg , Florida. His firm oversees $350 billion. \u201cWe\u2019re in a confidence crisis, so Mr. Market is unwilling to put a big, higher P\/E ratio on it.\u201d  Fed Action  The S&P 500 advanced 0.4 percent  last week  to 1,362.66 and gained 7.4 percent this year, as Fed Chairman  Ben S. Bernanke  said he is prepared to act to boost growth should the labor market fail to improve. The comments helped offset a lowered forecast for 2013  global growth  from the  International Monetary Fund , giving the S&P 500 its first back-to-back weekly advance since June. The U.S equity benchmark retreated 0.9 percent to 1,350.52 today.  Earnings for the 123 companies in the S&P 500 that have reported quarterly results so far are  beating  analyst projections by an average 4.6 percent, data compiled by Bloomberg show. That\u2019s masking weaker sales growth in the most recent quarter as companies improve margins to top estimates. Only 41 percent of the reported companies have topped analysts\u2019 estimates on sales, while 73 percent have beaten on profit, the data show.  Beating Forecasts  EBay Inc. (EBAY) , the world\u2019s biggest auction site, and Coca-Cola Co., the largest soft-drink maker, rose after posting profit and sales last week that beat forecasts. Microsoft Corp., the biggest software maker, reported higher earnings than projected and rose 2.5 percent last week. The maker of the  Windows operating system  missed analysts\u2019 sales estimate by less than 1 percent.  McDonald\u2019s Corp., the world\u2019s No. 1 restaurant chain by value,  Lockheed Martin Corp. (LMT) , an aerospace company that counts the U.S. government as its biggest  customer , and AT&T Inc., the second-largest phone company by market value, are among the more than 172 companies reporting earnings this week.  While more than  $2.5 trillion  has been added to American equity values since the start of 2010, the gains came as the S&P 500\u2019s price-earnings ratio contracted 23 percent, data compiled by Bloomberg show. The index\u2019s multiple, a gauge of investor sentiment because it reflects expectations for earnings growth, was 13.9 last week, down from 18.9 in January 2010 and compared to the 16.4 average since the 1950s.  Consumer confidence  as measured by the University of Michigan survey has increased, climbing to an average of 75.3 in 2012 from 71.8 in 2010 and reaching a four-year high of 79.3 in May, data compiled by Bloomberg show. The gauge has tracked stocks during swings in the market, holding above 90 from June 1996 to March 2000 when the S&P 500 rallied 128 percent.  Sentiment Gauge  The sentiment gauge averaged 67.4 in 2011, a year when the mean valuation for  S&P 500 companies  was almost a point higher, data compiled by Bloomberg show. The last time valuations were this low relative to consumer confidence was in 1995, during an eight-year  bull market  in which the  S&P 500 quadrupled .  Stock prices already reflect the worst outcome for the economy and there are signs it will be avoided, according to  Lawrence Creatura , who helps oversee $367 billion as a Rochester, New York-based fund manager at Federated Investors Inc. New home starts last month climbed to an almost four-year record and light-vehicle sales signal the auto market is on pace for the best year since 2007, while economists say the U.S. may expand faster this year than last.  \u201cYou\u2019ve already paid as a stock holder for a part of any recession which may or may not occur,\u201d Creatura said in a July 19 phone interview. \u201cI don\u2019t think that investors are right to be shying away from stocks. The low valuations are enough to justify buying.\u201d  Volatility Aversion  Stock  volatility  may be preventing buying after U.S. equity declines of at least 15 percent began in the last two Aprils. The S&P 500 has gained or lost about 1 percent  each day  in the past 12 months, almost twice the rate in the previous year. The average since the 1960s is 0.7 percent, according to data compiled by Bloomberg.  Investors are bracing for a repeat of the 2008 financial crisis, which wiped out as much as $10.8 trillion of U.S. equity value, according to James Swanson, chief investment strategist at Boston-based  MFS Investment Management , which oversees $278.2 billion. The S&P 500 dropped 2.5 percent on June 1 after the Labor Department said  unemployment  rose to 8.2 percent and payrolls missed estimates. It lost 1.6 percent on June 25 as European leaders gathered to address a banking crisis in Greece.  2008 Repeat  \u201cPeople had a near-death experience in 2008 and 2009 with the crisis, and they are afraid that could happen again,\u201d Swanson said in a July 18 phone interview. Investors \u201care afraid of the markets, when I don\u2019t think they should be,\u201d he said. \u201cIt\u2019s probably a good time to look at the market.\u201d  The lack of confidence can be seen in the outperformance of defensive industries since the S&P 500\u2019s 2012 high on April 2. Phone stocks, utilities, consumer staples and health care companies were the only ones to gain among the  10 groups . Investors have been buying dividend stocks at a time when more companies are paying them. In the second quarter, 369 companies in the S&P 500 raised or maintained their dividends, the most since at least 2004, data compiled by Bloomberg show.  Event Risk  Mutual funds that invest in U.S. equities saw $1.47 billion in net outflows for the week ending July 11, after 14 straight months of withdrawals that totaled about $200 billion, according to data from the Washington-based  Investment Company Institute . Strategists are telling clients choosing portfolios to put the least amount into U.S. stocks since 1997, according to the average of Wall Street firms surveyed by Bloomberg.  \u201cThe main things investors are focusing on are the ongoing crisis in  Europe  and weaker economic data for the U.S.,\u201d Wayne Lin, a  money manager  at Baltimore-based Legg Mason, said in a July 20 phone interview. His firm oversees $627 billion. \u201cThere\u2019s a lot of event risk that can lead to volatility, and that\u2019s the big worry these days.\u201d  While investor sentiment deteriorates, chief executive officers are more optimistic about the future of the economy than they were last year. The CEO Confidence Index, which plots expectations for overall business conditions on a scale of 1 to 10 and is compiled by Chief Executive Group, reached 5.56 last month, compared with 4.88 in September, data compiled by Bloomberg show. Today\u2019s level is 4.3 percent higher than the average since June 2009, when the worst recession since the  Great Depression ended .  Home Prices  Home prices are stabilizing and starting to increase. The S&P\/Case-Shiller index of property values adjusted for seasonal variations rose 0.7 percent in April, the third straight gain. U.S. homebuilder confidence climbed in July by the most since September 2002, a report last week showed.  The U.S. may expand 2.1 percent this year, the same projection economists held when surveyed in January, data compiled by Bloomberg show. Forecasts last year had come down 0.7 percentage point to 2.5 percent by this time last year.  \u201cGiven that our view is slow growth, if that\u2019s correct, it\u2019s a positive thing that expectations are already down,\u201d Christian Andreach, co-head of global equities at Manning & Napier Advisors based in Fairport,  New York , which manages about $40 billion, said in a July 19 telephone interview. Microsoft Corp. and General Electric Co. slipped at least 1.8 percent to pace declines among large companies. Caterpillar Inc. slumped 3.4 percent after its global retail machine sales dropped for a ninth consecutive month. BlackBerry Ltd. plunged 17 percent after announcing 4,500 job cuts.  AK Steel Holding Corp. (AKS)  sank 8 percent, leading declines among steelmakers, after predicting a third-quarter loss.  The  Standard & Poor\u2019s 500 Index (SPX)  fell 0.7 percent, the most since Aug. 27, to 1,709.91 at 4 p.m. in New York. The  Dow Jones Industrial Average (INDU)  lost 185.46 points, or 1.2 percent, to 15,451.09 for the biggest retreat since Aug. 15. Both gauges slid for a second day after reaching a record Sept. 18.  \u201cIt\u2019s probably a little confusing to the market what\u2019s coming out of the Fed,\u201d John Kvantas, a San Antonio, Texas-based  executive director  who helps manage more than $16 billion at USAA Investments, said in a phone interview. \u201cMaybe the Fed is trying to send a message that \u2018yeah we didn\u2019t taper, but it doesn\u2019t mean we will never taper and maybe actually will taper still quite soon.\u2019\u201d  About 8.9 billion shares changed hands on U.S. exchanges, the most since June 28, as futures and options contracts expired in a process known as quadruple witching. Announced index changes, such as the addition of Visa Inc., Goldman Sachs Group Inc. and Nike Inc. to the Dow and the  S&P 500 \u2019s inclusion of Vertex Pharmaceuticals Inc. and Ametek Inc., took effect after the markets close. The operator of the S&P 500 also rebalanced the index, a quarterly move to adjust member weightings.  More Evidence  The S&P 500 climbed 1.3 percent this week, continuing a rebound from its worst month since May 2012, after the central bank unexpectedly refrained from reducing monetary stimulus. The  Federal Open Market Committee  said it wants more evidence of an economic recovery before paring its bond purchases. The stimulus helped boost the equity index 155 percent higher since March 2009.  The Fed is now expected to begin tapering asset purchases in December, with 24 of 41 economists surveyed Sept. 18-19 saying the central bank won\u2019t take the first step in slowing its $85 billion in monthly bond buying until then.  Fed Bank of St. Louis President  James Bullard , a voter on policy this year who has backed the bond buying, said earlier today the decision not to taper was a close call and \u201csmall\u201d cuts are possible next month. Policy makers meet Oct. 29-30.  \u2018Let\u2019s Wait\u2019  \u201cWeaker data came in,\u201d Bullard said on Bloomberg Television\u2019s \u201cBloomberg Surveillance\u201d with  Tom Keene ,  Michael McKee  and Sara Eisen. \u201cThat was a borderline decision,\u201d and \u201cthe committee came down on the side of, \u2018Let\u2019s wait.\u2019\u201d With inflation low, Bullard said, \u201cwe can afford to be patient.\u201d  Kansas City Fed President Esther George, who was the lone dissenter in the last FOMC meeting, said today at the  Manhattan Institute  for Policy that she sees \u201csubstantial\u201d progress in the labor market. She said policy makers\u2019 decision to maintain the pace of bond purchases \u201ccreated confusion, created a disconnect.\u201d  The debate on when to cut stimulus and by how much has  whipsawed  stocks since May, when Fed officials first indicated reductions could start this year. The S&P 500 tumbled 5.8 percent from a record on May 21 through June 24. It rebounded 8.7 percent to close at a fresh high on Aug. 2 before slumping 4.6 percent as investors increasingly anticipated cuts at the September meeting. The gauge rallied 5.8 percent from that Aug. 27 low to its latest record.  Government Shutdown  Investors are also watching the political wrangling over the approaching limit on federal spending. Government funding expires Oct. 1 and the Treasury is expected to exhaust its ability to borrow funds in mid-October, when it will hit the statutory debt limit.  The U.S. House voted today to finance the federal government through mid-December and choke off funding for President  Barack Obama \u2019s health-care law, setting up a showdown with the Senate and the White House. The Senate will consider its version of the funding measure next week. The White House said Obama would veto the House bill.  \u201cWhen you look at political uncertainty and a fight going forward and the government really faces a shutdown, I don\u2019t know how that can be construed as a positive in the market\u2019s mind,\u201d Bill Schultz, chief investment officer who oversees about $1.1 billion at McQueen Ball & Associates in Bethlehem,  Pennsylvania , said by phone. \u201cIf anything, it just means potentially less economic activity.\u201d  Barclays Projection  The Fed\u2019s decision to maintain the pace of stimulus prompted Barclays Plc to boost its estimate for the S&P 500 to 1,800, the highest 2013 projection among Wall Street equity strategists.  \u201c\u2018Lower for longer\u2019 monetary policy is more probable than we believed a week ago,\u201d Barry C. Knapp, the firm\u2019s head of U.S. equity strategy, wrote in a note today.  The new forecast implies a 5.3 percent gain from today\u2019s close and tops the average strategist projection of 1,706, according to data compiled by Bloomberg. Intel and AMD\nhave engaged in patent and antitrust battles with each other\nsince the early 1990s.  \u201cThis case is utterly hopeless and should never have been\nbrought,\u201d Nicholas Green, a lawyer for Intel, told the EU\u2019s\nsecond-highest court on the third day of hearings.  The EU probe concluded Intel impeded competition by giving\ncomputer makers rebates from 2002 until 2005 on the condition\nthat they buy at least 95 percent of their chips for personal\ncomputers from the Santa Clara, California-based company. Intel\nimposed \u201crestrictive conditions\u201d for the remaining 5 percent,\nsupplied by AMD, which struggled to overcome Intel\u2019s hold on the\nPC processor market, the EU said. The infringement continued\nuntil at least December 2007, the EU said.  Accusations that Intel paid Lenovo, the world\u2019s second-\nlargest computer maker, in 2006 to delay AMD-based notebooks and\ngave the manufacturer rebates in 2007 under an agreement not to\nbuy from AMD were wrong and the commission ignored evidence that\nshowed otherwise, Green told the court yesterday.  The 2006 payments \u201cwere to win business, not to cancel a\nlaunch\u201d of AMD-based notebooks, Green said. Lenovo also told\nthe investigators the 2007 deal wasn\u2019t exclusive and \u201cthere was\nserious concern that AMD was not a reliable supplier and\nbusiness partner,\u201d Green said.  The EU began investigating after AMD complained in 2000.\nIntel agreed to pay AMD $1.25 billion in 2009 to end all civil\nlitigation. Sunnyvale, California-based AMD is no longer\ninvolved in the case and won\u2019t intervene at this week\u2019s hearing.  The antitrust fine was the EU\u2019s biggest, more than double\nthe 497 million-euro penalty against Microsoft Corp. in 2004. It\nrepresented about 4 percent of Intel\u2019s $37.6 billion in sales in\n2008, below the maximum penalty of 10 percent of annual sales.  Any decision by the EU General Court can be appealed to the\nEU Court of Justice in Luxembourg.  The case is T-286\/09  Intel Corp. (INTC)  v. Commission. (GOOG)  and  Facebook Inc. (FB)  are finding the prospects cloudier this week as they gather along the French Riviera to schmooze and raise cash.  Executives mingling on hotel terraces for the annual  Monaco  Media Forum are grappling with tight financing after missteps by industry heavyweights and disruption caused by the rise of smartphones. The landscape has changed for startups looking to raise  venture capital , list their shares or get acquired by a larger company, investors and executives said.  \u201cNow it\u2019s about reality and it\u2019s show-me-the-money time,\u201d said Ian Maude, a media analyst at Enders Analysis in  London . \u201cThere are huge changes in the venture-capital market. Investors are now more concerned about returns.\u201d  Facebook\u2019s stock has plunged since its May share sale, Google has missed analysts\u2019 estimates and social gaming company  Zynga Inc. (ZNGA)  lost at least nine senior managers as its price fell more than 75 percent since its December offering. With consumers increasingly shifting to smartphones from personal computers, ad-supported sites are finding it especially hard to generate new revenue, said Maude.  \u2018Overpriced Market\u2019  For venture-capital investors, \u201cthe market was overpriced in the first half of this year\u201d as Facebook\u2019s pre-IPO valuations filtered down into the rest of the technology world, Tomasz Czechowicz, managing partner at Warsaw-based tech investment firm MCI Management, said in Monaco. \u201cRight now the market is at a good balance.\u201d  The Monaco Media Forum in  Monte Carlo  attracts executives from Google, Facebook and  Microsoft Corp. (MSFT) , along with venture investors and startup entrepreneurs looking to pitch ideas. The three days of speeches, seminars and extended cocktail hours cover topics from measuring online audiences to appealing to tech-savvy members of the \u201cmillennial\u201d generation. For new businesses basing their models on advertising, \u201cnow you can only do niches,\u201d such as targeted services for certain professionals, Czechowicz said.  Increased scepticism about tech companies\u2019 prospects has a precedent. Following the 2001 dot-com bust, which followed flops such as Pets.com, investors also became more conservative.  \u2018Tougher Questions\u2019  \u201cI\u2019m sure everyone is asking tougher questions\u201d now, especially about later-stage companies considering an IPO, said Daniel Waterhouse, a partner at venture firm Wellington Partners. \u201cPeople are more critical of the fundamentals of the business.\u201d  Advertisers and Web companies struggling to attract cash and users\u2019 attention are also finding more difficulty as people shift to mobile devices. Nokia mobile phone unit  acquired  by Microsoft. Microsoft agreed to acquire Nokia's mobile phone business, including all its patents, for $7.2 billion in cash. Nokia chief executive Stephen Elop, a Microsoft alumnus, is part of the deal: He will return to Microsoft as head of the mobile business. Outgoing Miscrosoft CEO Steve Ballmer is thus tying Microsoft into his \"devices and services\" strategy. The acquisition will cost Microsoft about 10 percent of its cash, a big bet on a business with only a little more than 3 percent share of the smartphone market. For the Finnish company, the deal prevents a potential cash crisis and eliminates a messy, money-losing division that was fighting an uphill battle in a highly competitive environment. Nokia can now concentrate on its lucrative network equipment business and try to forget that as recently as 2011, its revenue equaled 20 percent of Finland's gross domestic product. Ayrault  circulates  intelligence report on Syria chemical attack. During a meeting with party leaders ahead of a parliamentary debate on military intervention in Syria, French Prime Minister Jean-Marc Ayrault unveiled an intelligence file asserting that the August 21 chemical attack in Syria came from government-controlled areas and left 281 people dead. The document is available to the public on government and media sites. So far, France has been the staunchest U.S. ally in the plan to launch a retaliatory strike on the forces of Syrian President Bashar al-Assad. President Francois Hollande's Socialist Party holds a majority in the French parliament, and, unlike their British counterparts, the legislators are likely to back intervention if asked. That, however, is likely to be the extent of any offers of military (as opposed to political) support from Europe for President Barack Obama, as he goes to congress for approval of airstrikes. Eurozone PMIs  indicate  optimism. The research firm Markit released fresh purchasing managers' indices for euro area countries, showing improvements throughout the region except in France, which together with Greece is the only country to score a PMI below 50 percent, indicating expectations of negative growth. For the euro area as a whole, the PMI stands at 51.4, a 26-month high, up from 50.3 percent a month ago. Employment, however, is not growing. These are valid reasons for the European Central Bank to keep its main interest rate at 0.5 percent when its governors meet this week: The signs of recovery are too fragile to follow U.S. regulators' example in talking of monetary tightening. French  banks  among Europe's riskiest, study says. According to a study of systemic risk by the University of Lausanne's Risk Management Center, European banks and insurers will need an additional $1.3 trillion in capital in case of a new financial crisis, defined as a 40 percent decline of the world stock market in a six-month period. The study ranked financial sector companies by systemic risk level, and three of the worst five institutions were French: Credit Agricole, BNP Paribas and Societe Generale. This is likely to be the result of their focus on investment banking, which calls for higher debt levels. While a major financial shock is unlikely in the near future, the study shows that French bankers have learned fewer lessons from the 2008 crisis than their peers in Germany, the U.K., Spain and Switzerland. Greek supermarkets  allowed  to sell expired food. In the sixth year of Greece's recession, supermarkets have been allowed to sell food after its expiry date. Starting September 2, stores can set up separate clearly marked racks where such products will be sold at discount prices. The measure is designed to help both retailers, hard hit by falling demand, and impoverished consumers. Indignant commentators in the Greek press have denounced the conservative government's move as a cruel reminder of the growing divide between the rich and the poor, but it makes sense. Greeks took too long to realize that what happened to its economy was a direct result of living beyond their means. The new discount racks are about austerity rather than inequality. The U.S. territory\u2019s leaders are seeking to lure mainland residents such as hedge-fund billionaire John Paulson. Moving to Puerto Rico could allow Paulson and other top-earning taxpayers to shield future income from the Internal Revenue Service without giving up their passports.  Puerto Rico, eager for economic growth, is making an unusually direct pitch to wealthy Americans that risks a political backlash from Congress, said John Buckley, a former tax counsel for Democrats on the House Ways and Means Committee.  \u201cThey\u2019re walking a fine line,\u201d Buckley said. \u201cThis would be the first time that Puerto Rico would kind of deliberately erode the U.S. tax base for individuals.\u201d  Already, 10 Americans have taken advantage of a year-old Puerto Rico law that lets them avoid local and U.S. capital gains taxes by signing agreements with the territory\u2019s government. Paulson, a 57-year-old New Yorker, is considering such a move, according to four people who have spoken with him about it, Bloomberg News reported March 11.  The law was designed to promote investment in the island territory. The unemployment rate there was 14 percent in December 2012, compared with 10.2 percent in Nevada and Rhode Island, the states with the highest unemployment, according to the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics.  Puerto Rico\u2019s gross domestic product per capita in 2010 was $16,300, about the same as Botswana or Belarus, according to the  CIA World Factbook .  Lost Manufacturing  Puerto Rico wants to diversify its economy, which has lost some of its manufacturing base to low-wage countries such as the Dominican Republic and China, said Gabriel Hernandez, one of the framers of the Puerto Rican tax law and head of the tax division of BDO Puerto Rico PSC.  \u201cIt\u2019s our reaction to what happened, that the world got more connected,\u201d said Hernandez, who likened the effort to tax incentives used by states to lure businesses.  The U.S., he said, should embrace \u201cthe whole concept of trying to make our economy more independent or more stable or more self-reliant.\u201d  The law takes advantage of the longstanding interaction between the tax codes of the U.S. and Puerto Rico. Under laws previously passed by Congress, all income earned in Puerto Rico by island residents is exempt from U.S. taxation. Residents still owe the IRS taxes on any U.S. income.  Untaxed Income  By moving to Puerto Rico, wealthy Americans can transform potential U.S. capital gains income taxed at up to 23.8 percent into untaxed Puerto Rican income. They must meet residency tests, including spending 183 days a year in Puerto Rico and having social and personal connections on the island.  By contrast, renouncing U.S. citizenship by moving to another country is much more punitive for wealthy taxpayers. They must surrender their U.S. passports and pay an exit tax on the value of unrealized capital gains. As a simplified example, someone giving up citizenship who has $100 million in untaxed stock gains could pay $23.8 million upon departure.  Even with potential tax advantages, Paulson and others considering a move to Puerto Rico should be wary, said Argeo Quinones Perez, a professor of economics at the University of Puerto Rico\u2019s Rio Piedras campus.  \u2018Third-World Environment\u2019  \u201cFor people as wealthy as Mr. Paulson and the like, spending half a year in this provincial, third-world environment would be like spending half a year in minimum-security prison,\u201d he said in an e-mail. \u201cThe tax breaks Mr. Paulson and other people and entities enjoy in this fiscal paradise are at the heart of the long-term fiscal crisis and economic stagnation we suffer.\u201d  Puerto Rico, which has a population of about 4 million and is smaller geographically than Connecticut, has been a part of the U.S. since the  Spanish-American War  in 1898. The commonwealth has a non-voting resident commissioner, Pedro Pierluisi, who represents residents in Congress and caucuses with House Democrats.  In an interview yesterday, Pierluisi blamed Puerto Rico\u2019s unresolved status between statehood and independence. As a state, he said, Puerto Rico would get more federal funding, which would be an acceptable tradeoff for bringing residents\u2019 income under the federal income tax. Residents and employers do pay federal payroll taxes.  Mirror Code  \u201cShort of statehood, this is what you do,\u201d he said, adding that a struggling Puerto Rico economy just encourages migration in the opposite direction, to Florida, Texas and North and South Carolina.  Puerto Rico\u2019s separate tax system makes it different from several other U.S. territories. Guam, the U.S. Virgin Islands and the Northern Mariana Islands all use what is called a \u201cmirror code,\u201d in which they use the U.S. tax code and substitute the name of the territory each time the law says United States. The District of Columbia is treated generally like a state for tax purposes.  The Virgin Islands attempted to lure hedge-fund managers more than a decade ago, using authority Congress granted the territory to encourage economic development.  That effort fizzled after Congress changed the law in 2004 to make it more difficult to recharacterize U.S. income as island-based, and the IRS began auditing more aggressively.  Harmonizing Rules  Puerto Rico\u2019s attempts to lure U.S. taxpayers could draw more scrutiny of taxation in the territories, which hasn\u2019t received much attention lately, said Senator Charles Grassley, former chairman of the Finance Committee, who led the effort against the Virgin Islands maneuvers.  \u201cHarmonizing the tax rules of the territories could be something to look at if Congress and the president undertake comprehensive tax reform,\u201d the Iowa Republican said in an e- mailed statement this week. \u201cOr if Puerto Rico maintains a separate tax system, that could be conditioned on accepting certain rules to prevent tax evasion.\u201d  The hybrid system of Puerto Rican taxation has implications for companies, too. Until 2006, the U.S. offered companies a credit against U.S. income taxes for investments in the territories. Companies also have access to the U.S. market, patent protection and the U.S. legal system, Hernandez said.  After that break expired, companies restructured their Puerto Rican operations to take advantage of the fact that it\u2019s considered a foreign jurisdiction for tax purposes.  Companies such as Amgen Inc.,  Pfizer Inc. (PFE)  and Microsoft Corp. receive local tax benefits from their operations on the island, according to regulatory filings. As with profits in another country, the companies can earn and leave money in Puerto Rico without paying U.S. corporate income taxes.  \u201cThe same thing that Paulson is getting, corporations are getting in the manufacturing sector,\u201d Pierluisi said.  At a hearing last year, Senator Carl Levin, a Michigan Democrat, said Microsoft\u2019s method of routing profits through Puerto Rico saved the company $4.5 billion over three years.  Bill Sample, the company\u2019s corporate vice president for worldwide tax, testified at the hearing that Microsoft follows all tax laws.  For U.S. lawmakers concerned about the budget deficit, the Puerto Rico law could be a boon, said Buckley, who now teaches tax law at Georgetown University in Washington. A legislative attempt to prevent Paulson and others from tax-free moves to Puerto Rico could generate revenue for the U.S. Treasury.  \u201cYou could get a score here,\u201d Buckley said, \u201cAnd I doubt a lot of people are going to stand up and defend him.\u201d  To contact the reporter on this story: Richard Rubin in Washington at  rrubin12@bloomberg.net   To contact the editor responsible for this story: Jodi Schneider at  jschneider50@bloomberg.net","path":".\/2008_2012_msft_bloomberg_news\/puerto-rico-beyond-irs-reach-woos-paulson-sized-fortunes.txt"},{"id":97521923,"title":"Israel-Based Football Website Is Turning Fans' Love of the Game Into a New Media Business","released_at":"<date>September 9 2013<\/date> <time>10:04:18<\/time>","content":"Behind one of the biggest sources of news and analysis on the English Premier League are Israeli entrepreneur Asaf Peled and his more than 1,400 enthusiasts, who are happy to share their football knowledge for free.
