The paper, released by the  Justice Department  and U.S.\nPatent and  Trademark Office , says that, in some instances,\npatent owners shouldn\u2019t be allowed to block sales or imports of\nproducts based on the use of standards that help products from\ndifferent manufacturers work together. The U.S. Federal Trade\nCommission, which reached a consent agreement with  Google Inc. (GOOG) \nlast week restricting its use of standard-essential patents, has\ntaken a similar position.  The paper puts added pressure on the U.S. International\nTrade Commission, which is considering the issue as part of a\nrequest by  Samsung Electronics Co. (005930)  to halt imports of  Apple Inc. (AAPL) \nproducts made in  Asia . A final decision is expected Feb. 6.  The ITC\u2019s approach \u201cwill be important to the continued\nvitality of the voluntary consensus standards-setting process\nand thus to competitive conditions and consumers in the  United\nStates ,\u201d the two agencies wrote, without citing specific cases.  The agencies, in a joint policy paper,  said  that, while\npatent owners have the right to exclude others from using their\ninventions, the public benefit of allowing that is limited when\nit comes to so-called standard-essential patents.  The Washington-based trade commission is investigating\nother complaints filed by owners of standard-essential patents,\nincluding one by Google\u2019s Motorola Mobility unit against\n Microsoft Corp. (MSFT) , an  InterDigital Inc. (IDCC)  case against Huawei\nTechnologies Co. and one filed by  Ericsson AB (ERIC)  against Samsung.  Setting Standards  Companies participate in groups to establish technical\nspecifications that can be used across platforms for things like\nhow video images are transmitted or what type of plug is used\nfor phone chargers. Those who establish the standards pledge to\nlicense any relevant patents on fair, reasonable and non-\ndiscriminatory terms, or FRAND.  Apple and Microsoft, which are involved in patent fights\nwith Motorola Mobility, have said they would never seek to block\nuse of their patented inventions when it applies to such\nindustry standards. Google and Samsung maintain they have the\nright to seek such orders in instances where a licensing\nagreement can\u2019t be reached.  The FTC agreement with Google limits the ability of the\n Mountain View , California-based company to ban competitors\u2019\nproducts unless it first takes steps to reach licensing\nagreements. It does allow Google to seek such orders in response\nto patent suits filed against it by competitors.  \u2018Two Wrongs\u2019  \u201cGoogle should not be permitted to abandon its FRAND\ncommitment just because another firm is suing for an injunction\non a standard-essential patent,\u201d David Heiner, Microsoft\u2019s\ndeputy general counsel, said in a statement. \u201cTwo wrongs don\u2019t\nmake a right.\u201d  Niki Fenwick, a spokeswoman for Google, said the company\nhad no comment. Officials with Samsung and Apple didn\u2019t\nimmediately return messages seeking comment.  The Justice Department and patent office laid out\nguidelines that should be met before an exclusion order is\ngranted by the trade commission. The agencies said the standard\nalso should apply in district court lawsuits. Judges in Seattle\nand  Chicago  have already said Motorola Mobility isn\u2019t entitled\nto orders halting U.S. sales of products based on the use of\nstandard-essential patents.  Trade Practices  The ITC\u2019s job is to protect U.S. markets against unfair\ntrade practices. It must consider the impact of import bans on\nthe competitive conditions in the U.S. When a company accused of\ninfringing a patent hasn\u2019t refused to license the standard-\nessential patents, \u201cthe public interest may preclude the\nissuance of an exclusion order,\u201d the two agencies said.  In some instances, the commission could delay the effective\ndate of an import ban to give licensing negotiations between the\nparties another chance, they said.  Still, they said, the decision \u201cshould be made against the\nbackdrop of promoting both appropriate compensation to patent\nholders and strong incentives for innovators to participate in\nstandard-setting activities.\u201d  To contact the reporter on this story:\nSusan Decker in Washington at \n sdecker1@bloomberg.net   To contact the editor responsible for this story:\nBernard Kohn at \n bkohn2@bloomberg.net","path":".\/2008_2012_msft_bloomberg_news\/u-s-agency-advised-to-limit-patent-based-import-bans.txt"},{"id":81189180,"title":"Carlyle\u2019s Rubenstein Says Many Large LBOs Don\u2019t Succeed","released_at":"<date>January 24 2013<\/date> <time>18:09:47<\/time>","content":"David Rubenstein , co-chief executive officer of  Carlyle Group LP (CG) , said a leveraged buyout of the size being considered for computer maker  Dell Inc. Cohen ignored the red flag as well as objections from his own legal department and hired him the following year, according to an indictment yesterday that accused Cohen\u2019s SAC Capital Advisors LP of securities fraud and wire fraud. The government said SAC created an environment in which employees were encouraged to use illicit information and the compliance office identified only one example of suspected insider trading in its history.  Lee, 34, was charged with securities fraud for trading in stocks including Yahoo! Inc. and 3Com Corp. and has pleaded guilty. He is at least the 11th person to be linked to insider trading while working at the SAC, and his actions as late as 2010 represent some of the most recent examples of alleged wrongdoing at firm, occurring after the government\u2019s probe was publicized.  \u201cThe particular story of Richard Lee\u2019s time at SAC is emblematic of the broader culture problem at the fund,\u201d Manhattan U.S. Attorney Preet Bharara said yesterday at a news conference.  Government\u2019s Evidence  Lee\u2019s hiring was among the evidence cited by the government to allege that SAC, based in  Stamford ,  Connecticut , enabled and promoted insider trading from as early as 1999 through at least 2010. Lee, who co-managed a $1.25 billion portfolio at SAC, including borrowed money, joined Cohen\u2019s firm in April 2009 and left in June 2011 before returning for a second stint last year.  Jonathan Gasthalter, a spokesman for SAC at Sard Verbinnen & Co., declined to comment on the allegations against Lee.  The hedge-fund company denied that it encouraged or tolerated insider trading and said it will continue to operate as it works through the matter.  \u201cThe handful of men who admit they broke the law does not reflect the honesty, integrity and character of the thousands of men and women who have worked at SAC over the past 21 years,\u201d the firm said in an e-mailed statement.  Studious, Bookish  Lee, who wears glasses and has a slender build, was described by a former SAC employee who knew him as studious and bookish. He wasn\u2019t the aggressive, hyper-competitive type usually found at hedge funds, said this person, who asked not to be identified. Lee graduated from Brown University in Providence, Rhode Island, in 2001 with a bachelor\u2019s degree in economics, according to school records.  The person who spoke to Cohen about Lee referred to him as part of an \u201cinsider trading group\u201d at Citadel, the government said. The firm, run by Ken Griffin, hasn\u2019t been accused of any wrongdoing.  \u201cCitadel does not have, and never has had, an \u2018insider trading group,\u2019\u201d  Katie Spring , a spokeswoman for Citadel, said in an e-mailed statement. \u201cCitadel has strict rules against, and oversight designed to prevent, insider trading. He worked within a special situations group that seeks to profit by predicting triggers for stocks and bonds such as corporate restructurings and acquisitions.  Expert Network  Lee initially interviewed with SAC in 2006 and at that time told a senior executive that his investment process included consulting with an expert network. It isn\u2019t an idle question. The company is touting the\n Surface , its shiny new tablet-PC hybrid, as something of an\niPad-killer. After a week of using it, I\u2019m not so sure. But it\nmay just be the slickest laptop I\u2019ve used in a very long time.  Technically, the Surface isn\u2019t a PC at all, since it\ndoesn\u2019t run on the  Intel (INTC)  microprocessors that are the industry\nstandard. Instead, it uses an  Nvidia (NVDA)  chip of the kind commonly\nfound in tablets and wireless phones, and its operating system\nis a variant of Microsoft\u2019s new Windows 8 called Windows RT.  To many users, though, that may be a distinction without a\ndifference. The Surface, which goes on sale Oct. 26, is\npreloaded with new versions of  Microsoft (MSFT)  Word, Excel, PowerPoint\nand Internet Explorer and has a desktop mode that feels a lot\nlike traditional Windows. Outfitted with one of Microsoft\u2019s\nsnazzy new $120 keyboard covers, and perhaps a USB thumb drive\nto expand the storage, it becomes a powerful, lightweight\nproductivity tool.  The Surface starts at $499 for a Wi-Fi-only model with 32\ngigabytes of storage. In theory, that\u2019s $100 cheaper than a\ncomparable iPad. But only in theory.  For one thing, not all that space is accessible to the\nuser; only 44 GB of my 64 GB test model was actually available\nfor my own stuff.  Expensive Accessories  Moreover, the accessories needed to use it as a PC are\nexpensive and available only from Microsoft: that colorful cover\nthat doubles as a flat, pressure-sensitive keyboard, or -- my\nfavorite -- a $130 model with actual keys. (A bundle with a\nblack flat keyboard is $599 for 32 GB, $699 for 64 GB.)  There are a few big differences between the Surface and the\nflood of new Windows 8 PCs hitting the market. One is the\nlimited storage; the other is the absence of Outlook,\nMicrosoft\u2019s e-mail and calendar client.  The biggest difference, though, is that it can\u2019t run\nexisting software written for previous versions of Windows, like\n Adobe (ADBE) \u2019s Photoshop or  Intuit (INTU) \u2019s QuickBooks. (A costlier Surface\nthat will run Windows 8, use Intel chips and handle legacy\nsoftware is due early next year.)  The Surface\u2019s split personality is evident as soon as you\npull it out of the box. It\u2019s a sleek black rectangle weighing\n1.5 pounds with a 10.6 inch widescreen touch display -- both\nslightly more than the current-generation iPad -- and front- and\nrear-facing cameras. Turn it on, and you\u2019re greeted with the new\nWindows Start screen, full of big, colorful tiles that display\nupdated information and launch apps.  Beautiful Bauble  Then you\u2019re asked to give your beautiful new bauble a name.\nYou might want something friendly, like maybe \u201cRich\u2019s\nSurface.\u201d Oops, sorry, you\u2019re not allowed to use a space, an\napostrophe or other \u201cspecial characters.\u201d Same old Microsoft.  In tablet mode, the Surface is swift and responsive,\nwhether you\u2019re launching new apps or scrolling between open\nones. Though not quite in the iPad\u2019s league, the screen is nice\nenough -- and the integrated kickstand allows you to prop it up\nat a comfortable angle, perfect for viewing, say, a movie on an\nairline tray table. The kickstand snaps shut with a pleasing\nclick, indicative of the overall solid feel of the device.  But while I generally like the touch interface, and give\nMicrosoft props for not aping the iPad, it simply isn\u2019t as clean\nand intuitive as  Apple (AAPL) \u2019s iOS. As just one small example, it took\nme a very long time to figure out how to change the default\nlocation for the Weather app, followed by multiple steps and\nswipes.  App Selection  Nor can the Surface compete with the iPad on the number and\nvariety of available apps, at least until existing Windows\nprograms get rewritten for the new environment.  I also had issues with its power system, ranging from the\nawkward placement of the connector to a mysterious episode in\nwhich a nearly full battery on Saturday drained to completely\nempty by Monday morning.  Depending on what I was doing, I sometimes coaxed\nMicrosoft\u2019s promised eight hours of battery life out of the\nSurface. But it isn\u2019t as long-lived as the iPad, even with its\noverly aggressive default screen-dimming settings.  The biggest question is how users familiar with previous\nversions of Windows adapt to the new interface, whether on the\nSurface or the other Windows RT and Windows 8 devices to follow.  Something like the traditional Windows desktop environment\nstill exists. But it\u2019s now, essentially, an app launched via a\ntile on that colorful Start screen.  Seeing Double  The potential for confusion is considerable. For instance,\nthere are now two separate versions of Internet Explorer 10: one\nin the new style, for when you\u2019re using the Surface as a tablet,\nand a separate, more traditional one for when you\u2019re working on\nthe desktop.  The Start screen also behaves inconsistently: Some tiles\nlaunch new-style apps while others, such as those for the\npreview versions of Word, Excel, PowerPoint and OneNote, toss\nyou into the desktop environment.  While I initially regarded the desktop as a kind of penalty\nbox, I found myself gravitating towards it. In some ways, using\nit on the Surface reminded me of netbooks, those cheap little\nWindows PCs that enjoyed a brief vogue a couple years ago. But\nthis is what a netbook should have been: versatile, with a\nmodern design and an appealing, well-made look and feel.  Microsoft is taking several enormous gambles with the\nSurface. Are users willing to embrace a Windows so different\nfrom what they\u2019ve known for nearly 20 years? How will Intel and\ncomputer makers react to the fact that their software partner is\nnow a direct competitor?  It may just be that the company didn\u2019t have a choice if it\nwanted its flagship software to remain relevant. With the world\nmoving inexorably toward mobile devices, the Surface is the\nfirst Windows PC of the post-PC era.  ( Rich Jaroslovsky  is a Bloomberg News columnist. The\nopinions expressed are his own.)  Muse highlights include Ryan Sutton on  dining  and Philip\nBoroff on  theater . The four executives are Bob Mansfield, Bruce Sewell, Jeffrey Williams and  Peter Oppenheimer , according to fiscal 2012 compensation figures for top earners filed with the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission. About 80 percent of  S&P 500  companies had submitted their numbers as of April 12.  Last year was the second in a row that payouts at Cupertino, California-based Apple ranked among the most generous. Apple directors, who put CEO  Tim Cook  at the top of the heap last year, are using compensation to keep the team that transformed the iPhone maker into the most valuable technology company under co-founder Steve Jobs, who died in 2011. The urgency has increased in recent months as Samsung Electronics Co. and Google Inc. challenge Apple.  \u201cIt\u2019s a retention strategy to keep the key executives who were present in the Steve Jobs era,\u201d said  Greg Sterling , an analyst at San Francisco-based Opus Research. \u201cThey want to be sure the actual talents that they bring to the company are retained, and also from a perception standpoint to retain confidence in the leadership.\u201d  Pay Disclosures  Apple\u2019s Mansfield received $85.5 million, almost entirely in stock, the second-largest 2012 compensation package in the S&P 500. The total was boosted by the value of a related accounting charge and options that vested earlier than other Apple executives. Mansfield\u2019s base salary was $805,400, matching that for Oppenheimer, Sewell and Williams. Their pay jumped after receiving 150,000 in restricted stock units shortly after Jobs passed away.  Steve Dowling, a spokesman for Apple, declined to comment on compensation. In its regulatory filing, Apple\u2019s board said the stock grants should be \u201cmeaningful in size in order to retain the company\u2019s executive team during the CEO transition.\u201d  The pay-package data compiled by Bloomberg include base salary, bonus, equity and other benefits for the 2012 fiscal year, which in Apple\u2019s case  ended  in September. Apple executives who became enriched as the stock surged under Jobs might have been tempted to leave, their wealth intact, in the wake of his death and the passing of the reins to Cook, said McCall, who also co-founded compensation advisory firm Compensia Inc. A federal judge last month reduced the award by $450.5 million, ordering a new trial on damages for some products.  Williams , 49, senior vice president of operations, came in fourth at $68.7 million. Under Moonves, CBS \u201cposted record results in 2012, with its highest revenues, operating income, and EPS since it became a standalone company in \u201906,\u201d the company said in a statement. I don\u2019t have any rhythm, so you guys can score amazing.\u2019  \u201cThey were laughing,\u201d he said yesterday. \u201cIt was good, the families really appreciated that.\u201d  Ganem and Donnelly work with the  Semper Fi Fund , a charity set up to help ex-military personnel who\u2019ve been wounded, which often means a lost limb. The fund has given away $74 million to help soldiers with their lives post-injury, adapting their homes, getting prosthetics and providing support.  Iraq, Afghanistan  The Semper Fi Fund veterans came to Boston, they said, because the aftermath of the bombing, \u201clooked exactly like something we saw in Iraq and  Afghanistan ,\u201d Ganem said. \u201cAmerica responded for us, and it\u2019s our time to give it back to the civilians.\u201d  Joe Blansfield, a nurse practitioner at Boston Medical Center\u2019s trauma practice who is also an Army reserve colonel and served in Iraq, said the two veterans made a strong impression on the patients they visited.  \u201cWhen they got to the area where the patients were, it was magic,\u201d Blansfield said in a telephone interview. \u201cThe message is that \u2019Hey, it\u2019s going to be alright. Life goes on.\u2019 These guys were even saying they\u2019re doing things now that they didn\u2019t do before they were injured and lost a limb.\u201d  It also gave patients a chance to see what prosthetic technology can do with sport- and mobility focused limbs made of carbon fiber and titanium, he said.  48 Hospitalized  A week after the attack, 48 people were still hospitalized citywide, according to figures provided yesterday by six Boston hospitals that dealt with most of the seriously injured. At least 13 survivors lost a limb, including some who had multiple amputations, said the hospitals, which include Brigham & Women\u2019s Hospital, Beth Israel Deaconess Medical Center, Tufts Medical Center, and Massachusetts General Hospital.  Five people lost seven limbs at Boston Medical Center, medical officials said yesterday in a news conference. Already, though, they are undergoing rehabilitation that includes some walking and exercises to make them more mobile, doctors said. They lauded the veterans for volunteering their time.  The veterans \u201cwalked through the halls and showed these patients their life isn\u2019t over,\u201d Jeffrey Kalish, Boston Medical Center\u2019s director of endovascular surgery said at a press briefing.  Temporary Prostheses  The next phase for the Boston victims will be temporary prostheses, which can be fitted two to three months after the injury followed by permanent ones about a year later, said Simona Manasian, a rehabilitation doctor at Boston Medical.  After that, a more permanent prosthesis will be made, or multiple ones like Ganem and Donnelly have.  \u201cThey know that part of you better than anyone else,\u201d Ganem said of his prosthetic specialist. \u201cOutside of your marriage or your close family, it\u2019s one of the closest relationships you have.\u201d  The Semper Fi Fund expanded its mission after the Boston explosions -- it will now give the same support it gives to wounded soldiers to victims of terrorism in the U.S. It has started a separate fund to help raise resources.  \u201cIt\u2019s my ninth year, and I still have bad days,\u201d Ganem said. \u201cBut I can call Bobby, or I can call hundreds of other guys and gals. We\u2019re there to pull each other through the dark places and push each other.\u201d  The fund will do the same for the Boston victims they met with, he said.  \u2018Call Us\u2019  \u201cWe gave them our cards and our numbers, and told them, \u2018It doesn\u2019t matter what time it is. If it\u2019s 2 a.m. and you need some support, or you just want to bitch about something and you don\u2019t want to bitch at the person you\u2019re with because they\u2019re taking care of you\u2019\u201d that they could call, said Ganem.  Both ex-soldiers said that being physically active has been a help in their recoveries, in part with the phantom pains that are common in those who\u2019ve had amputations. Patients who\u2019ve lost limbs can feel a burning or itching sensation that\u2019s no longer there. Or painful jolts can shoot up the body from the damaged leg or arm.  \u201cI tried some of the medicine in the beginning, I never liked it,\u201d Ganem said. \u201cStaying active does help keep the phantom pain away.\u201d  Triathlon Legs  Some of the artificial legs owned by the two men are built for comfort, others for action, they said.  Ganem has broken several of them while weight lifting, he said, and uses an older one to get wet -- like when he\u2019s competing in the Tough Mudder, an obstacle course endurance race. Donnelly had one made for the triathlons he competes in -- a carbon fiber arc that has a running tread built into the bottom, with a cut-out for cleat to attach the prosthetic to his road bicycle. He also sails.  During an interview, Donnelly took off his prosthetic leg and handed it to a reporter.  \u201cIt\u2019s a running foot with a heel, so you can wear a shoe,\u201d he said. \u201cIt\u2019s all carbon -- so light -- it\u2019s great.\u201d  The legs attach to the limb using a sleeve that holds a pin in place. That pin then slots into a carbon fiber shell, connected to a leg that can be designed for running, heavy weight bearing, comfort, cycling or just about anything. Ganem even has one he uses to play golf, and has taken others to extreme conditions like ice climbing in  Wyoming  or dog sledding. (GOOG)  can\u2019t wield some patents to block the sale of  Microsoft Corp. (MSFT)  products may point toward resolution of a fundamental question underlying the global smartphone wars -- what constitutes a fair and reasonable royalty?  In cases across the U.S. and  Europe , Google, Microsoft and other companies are battling over the power of patents used in industrywide standards for technologies, such as Wi-Fi, that let competing products work together. Patent owners who help set those specifications pledge to license their inventions on \u201cfair, reasonable and non-discriminatory terms.\u201d  No court has defined that concept, helping spark conflict when companies can\u2019t agree on a fee. U.S. District Judge James Robart in  Seattle  may become the first.  \u201cThere is so much litigation going on trying to determine what a reasonable royalty is,\u201d said  James Kulbaski , a patent lawyer with Oblon Spivak in Alexandria, Virginia. \u201cEveryone has agreed to pay it, but no one knows what it is.\u201d  Robart ruled on Nov. 30 that, because Google\u2019s Motorola Mobility had agreed to license its standard-essential patents, it was only entitled to seek fair royalties from Microsoft, not to ask the court to forbid sales of Microsoft products that use standards including those patents. The judge\u2019s next step is to figure out what fees Microsoft should pay.  That threshold question is bedeviling the U.S. Federal Trade Commission, the European Commission, the U.S. International Trade Commission and courts on four continents. While the concept of fair and reasonable royalties for essential technologies has been around for decades, the debate heated up with the global legal actions over smartphones and tablet computers.  \u2018Important Step\u2019  \u201cSomehow, this judge is going to have to define fair and reasonable,\u201d Kulbaski said. Defining what\u2019s reasonable \u201cis a key question to all patents related to standards\u201d and will \u201cbe an important step in future license negotiations.\u201d  Google paid $12.5 billion to buy Motorola Mobility, an early pioneer in the mobile phone market, in part to get access to its patents on industry-standard technologies. The FTC, in a broad-ranging probe of Google, is looking at whether the Mountain View,  California , company is improperly using those patents to stifle competition.  Most of the patents in the smartphone wars don\u2019t relate to industry standards. Still, defining fair and reasonable -- eliminating that contentious issue -- could be a springboard for resolving lawsuits over other patents.  Inefficient Litigation  \u201cThe litigation we\u2019re seeing, which is costing hundreds of millions, if not billions of dollars, is inefficient and it would be good to reduce the litigation if possible,\u201d said Jorge Contreras, an associate law professor at American University in Washington.  When a company agrees to license its patents on fair terms, \u201cthe patent holder has told the market that it does not need exclusivity and is willing to accept money in return,\u201d Contreras said. \u201cThe only question is how much money it is owed, a question that the court should answer soon.\u201d  Apple Inc. (AAPL) , based in Cupertino, California, and Redmond, Washington-based Microsoft argue owners of standard-essential patents shouldn\u2019t be able to obtain orders that block the use of inventions, a position backed by Robart\u2019s decision.  Limits on the patents could discourage companies from participating in groups that set specifications that make electronics work more efficiently, said  Adam Mossoff , a George Mason University law professor.  Low-Cost Infringement  \u201cThe people who are saying it\u2019s a problem have dominated the public discourse to the point where everyone says there\u2019s a problem, but the facts on the ground don\u2019t support that,\u201d Mossoff said. The companies \u201care using the legal system to get away with infringement at a lower cost.\u201d  Mossoff said these types of disputes have been around for decades, and companies decide what\u2019s fair without governmental intervention.  \u201cThere is zero evidence of any actual harm to consumers,\u201d Mossoff said. \u201cWe all have our smartphones, tablets exist and there is amazing technology that comes out every week.\u201d  Motorola Mobility contends it met its obligations and neither Microsoft nor Apple would bargain. The Libertyville, Illinois-based handset maker made an opening request for 2.25 percent of the retail price of Apple and Microsoft products, a figure both companies called exorbitant as they filed breach-of- contract claims.  Apple Suit  Apple\u2019s case in  Wisconsin  was thrown out after the iPhone maker said it would agree to a court-determined royalty only if it was less than $1 per unit. Microsoft, which has agreed to pay a royalty rate set by Robart, has told the judge that an appropriate figure would be for pennies per unit, or less than $1 million a year.  ITC Judge David Shaw is scheduled to hear arguments this week in a dispute between Motorola Mobility and Microsoft over some of the same patents that are involved in the Seattle federal-court lawsuit.  The agency, which has the power to block U.S. imports of products that infringe American patents, is considering whether it should issue bans on products based on standard-essential patents in a case filed by Samsung Electronics Co. against Apple. At the same time, Samsung is accused by Ericsson AB of refusing to pay fair royalties on wireless standards.  The Federal Trade Commission and members of Congress have argued that patent owners shouldn\u2019t be able to use the threat of a U.S. import ban as a weapon in disagreements about royalty payments.  Standard Setting  The FTC has signaled it wants a greater role in determining what\u2019s fair and reasonable. The agency, in a 3-2 decision Nov. 26,  forced  Robert Bosch GmBh to make standard-essential patents for air conditioners available to competitors as a condition for approving acquisition of the patent owner.  \u201cThe FTC is right to take a look at this because we don\u2019t have any overarching group looking at the standard-setting organizations,\u201d said Robert Stoll of Drinker Biddle in  Washington . \u201cThe consumer is harmed if the other companies can\u2019t use those standards. The purpose of \u2018fair and reasonable\u2019 is to give everyone an even playing field.\u201d  To contact the reporter on this story: Susan Decker in Washington at  sdecker1@bloomberg.net   To contact the editor responsible for this story: Bernard Kohn at  bkohn2@bloomberg.net","path":".\/2008_2012_msft_bloomberg_news\/icrosoft-google-patent-fight-rests-on-defining-fairness.txt"},{"id":94699840,"title":"Asian Stocks Rise, Led by Tech Companies as Nokia Loses Share; Tepco Drops","released_at":"<date>June 1 2011<\/date> <time>10:23:56<\/time>","content":"Asian stocks rose, driving the\nregional benchmark index to its highest level in three weeks, as\nrivals of Nokia Oyj gained after the mobile-phone maker lowered\nits sales and profit forecasts. The broadly positive news likely helped this week's stock rally to continue, but those looking at the economy over the longer term should keep a wary eye on disposable income. Real personal income after taxes grew by 0.4 percent in May. If that pace can be maintained, it would translate into a 12-month gain of about 4.9 percent. Excluding a few unusual bumps (including the dividend payments made last year in advance of the tax hikes associated with the \u201cfiscal cliff,\u201d as well as Microsoft\u2019s enormous special dividend in 2004) this would be the  fastest  annual growth rate in household spending power since the late 1990s. Encouragingly, the Bureau of Economic Analysis revised its estimate for real disposable income growth in April to 0.3 percent, up from the original 0.1 percent. Spending has been growing more slowly than income since January. Initially, the savings rate plunged to 2.2 percent in January, from an average of about 4.2 percent in October and November. (The dividend payments in December mean that some of the data from that month need to be interpreted with caution.) However, the personal savings rate has steadily increased from that low level to 3.2 percent, despite the hefty tax increases. That could be bad, since each person\u2019s spending ends up as someone else\u2019s income somewhere. Right now, however, it means that U.S. households are saving more, and thus the rest of the economy -- foreigners, the government and businesses -- has to be saving less. Given the continued  narrowing  of the federal budget deficit, this suggests that corporate investment and net exports are finally starting to pick up some of the slack. That would be a welcome development. We can do better. Personal income comes from a few different sources: employee compensation, financial assets, ownership of small businesses, transfers from the government. (Unsurprisingly, interest income has ticked noticeably higher in the past couple of months.) Despite relatively rapid growth, the level of pretax employee compensation is still below where it was in December, 2012. Some of that probably reflects the distortion caused by tax hikes as some employers probably paid larger year-end bonuses. Still, the pretax wages and salaries of employees in private industries were less than half of one percentage point higher in May 2013 than in November 2012. It\u2019s worse after taxes and inflation are taken into account. Real disposable personal income in May is 0.6 percent lower than it was in November. Considering that the economy is still growing relatively slowly and that unemployment remains unacceptably high, those tax increases seem like a needless self-inflicted wound. (Matthew C. (ORCL)  is casting aside longstanding rivalries with  Microsoft Corp. (MSFT)  and  Salesforce.com Inc. (CRM) , with partnerships to bolster its cloud-computing services aimed at businesses moving their software online.  In one alliance, Microsoft\u2019s Windows Azure cloud-computing service will run Oracle\u2019s  database software , Java programming tools and application-connecting middleware, Microsoft Chief Executive Officer  Steve Ballmer  and Oracle co-President  Mark Hurd  said. Under a separate nine-year  pact , Salesforce is buying Oracle hardware and software to power its applications.  \u201cWhen customers choose cloud applications they expect rapid low-cost implementations,\u201d Ellison said in a statement today announcing the Salesforce partnership. \u201cThey also expect application integrations to work right out of the box -- even when the applications are from different vendors.\u201d  Oracle is mending fences with former foes as it shifts focus to subscription-based online software rather than programs installed on customers\u2019 own machines, a transition forced in part by nimbler cloud-computing rivals including Salesforce. Microsoft is competing with  Google Inc. (GOOG)  and  Amazon.com Inc. (AMZN)  as it seeks new sources of revenue from online services, as demand for personal computers slumps.  \u201cIt\u2019s about time, and we\u2019re really glad to have the chance to work in this much newer and more constructive way with Oracle,\u201d Ballmer said. \u201cThe partnership has an immediate benefit to customers of every size and shape.\u201d  Compatible Software  Microsoft and Oracle\u2019s collaboration would lure customers seeking more  technical compatibility  between products. Oracle plans to support versions of its database and Java software that customers run through the online Azure service, and when using Microsoft\u2019s Hyper-V virtualization software, which lets servers run more efficiently, Hurd said. Oracle also will let customers use their current  software licenses  on Azure, he said.  Oracle\u2019s database, which will be upgraded later this year as a new version called 12c, competes with Microsoft\u2019s own SQL Server. Companies using Microsoft\u2019s Azure cloud service, which lets companies build and run programs online, will be able to put information into Oracle\u2019s database.  The alliance with Microsoft lets Oracle offer its customers the option of sticking with its database and middleware at a time when businesses are moving more of their software to cloud-computing services. Oracle reported on June 20 that fiscal fourth-quarter software license and subscription sales grew just 1 percent, less than analysts had projected.  Database Market  Oracle controlled 45 percent of the $28.2 billion worldwide database market in 2012, compared with 20 percent for Microsoft and 18 percent for  International Business Machines Corp. (IBM) , according to IDC.  Azure\u2019s main competitor is Amazon Web Services, in a growing area called infrastructure as a service, which lets companies rent computing power, storage and database software via the Internet. That\u2019s the fastest-growing part of the cloud market, according to Gartner Inc., which estimates sales in the market segment to surge by an average of 38 percent annually to $30.6 billion by 2017, from $6.17 billion last year.  Microsoft, which said in April that revenue from Azure and related software sales topped $1 billion annually, has pledged to match Amazon Web Services\u2019 prices.  \u2018Platform Wars\u2019  \u201cThis deal gives Microsoft clear competitive advantages against two of its top rivals,\u201d James Staten, an analyst at Forrester Research, said in a  blog post . It bolsters Microsoft\u2019s efforts to compete with  VMware Inc. (VMW) , the market leader in virtualization software, and \u201cgives Windows Azure near-equal position against Amazon Web Services in the cloud platform wars,\u201d he said.  Oracle also will make its version of the open-source Linux operating system available through Azure.  \u201cThe cloud is the tipping point that made this happen,\u201d Hurd said. \u201cThis made a lot of sense for both of us.\u201d  The two companies have a long history of competition stretching back to the dawn of personal computers in the 1970s. Oracle CEO  Larry Ellison , who first publicized the alliance on his company\u2019s earnings conference call last week, used to deride Redmond, Washington-based Microsoft as a \u201cconvicted monopolist\u201d after it was found guilty in federal court of illegally defending its Windows monopoly to squelch competition.  Trash Inspection  In 2000,  Redwood City , California-based Oracle said it hired detectives to comb the trash of two organizations supporting Microsoft in its antitrust trial. Ellison added that he\u2019d be happy to ship his garbage to Redmond for inspection.  Still, Microsoft and Oracle have cooperated before. Oracle\u2019s database also runs on Windows, and developers using Microsoft\u2019s Web services software can  build applications  using Oracle\u2019s software tools.  Ballmer said that the companies would continue to compete, and that much of their cooperation so far had been done out of public view. The very nature of cloud computing, in which software applications span multiple companies\u2019 infrastructure software and Web sites, meant that approach was no longer sufficient, he said.  \u201cThat behind-the-scenes collaboration is not enough. Benioff, who used to work for Ellison as an Oracle salesman, has been winning business from Oracle with online tools for customer management, marketing and human resources. Salesforce will use Oracle\u2019s financial management and HR software internally, and the two companies\u2019 applications will share some data.  \u201cLarry and I both agree that Salesforce.com and Oracle need to integrate our clouds,\u201d Benioff said. (GOOG) \u2019s Chromebook was dismissed as a bare-bones laptop with limited appeal when it debuted two years ago. Now it\u2019s defying skeptics and gaining share as the rest of the personal-computer market shrinks.  Chromebooks have in just the past eight months snagged 20 percent to 25 percent of the U.S. market for laptops that cost less than $300, according to NPD Group Inc. The devices, which have a full keyboard and get regular software updates from Google, are the fastest-growing part of the PC industry based on price, NPD said.  The surge marks Chromebooks as one of the few types of computers able to attract consumers while  Dell Inc. (DELL)  and other traditional PC makers undergo a shakeout. The industry has already seen notebook-PC sales eroded by the popularity of smartphones and tablets such as  Apple Inc. (AAPL) \u2019s iPad. As a result of the shift, worldwide PC shipments  fell  4 percent in 2012 and are forecast to decline 7.8 percent this year, the largest annual drop on record, according to researcher IDC.  \u201cWhile we were skeptical initially, I think Chromebooks definitely have found a niche in the marketplace,\u201d  Stephen Baker , an analyst at NPD, said. \u201cThe entire computing ecosystem is undergoing some radical change, and I think Google has its part in that change.\u201d  The growth follows the unveiling of low-cost Chromebook models from Google\u2019s hardware partners  Acer Inc. (2353)  and  Samsung Electronics Co. (005930)  last October, at prices starting at $199, down from about $300 or more.  Stripped Down  Chromebook\u2019s rising market share is impressive given how the cards appeared stacked against the devices when they were introduced in 2011. At the time, Chromebooks\u2019 lack of built-in software was considered unusual compared with laptops based on  Microsoft Corp. (MSFT) \u2019s Windows operating system.  While Windows laptops have software that is loaded onto the devices themselves, Chromebooks are based on Google\u2019s Chrome operating system. Customers access tools from the cloud -- online programs that include Google\u2019s own word processing, e-mail and spreadsheets -- so the machines are essentially stripped-down computers. The cloud services drive more data and, ultimately, more advertising back to Google.  Google and other electronics companies separately make tablets and smartphones based on its Android mobile-operating system. Initially, the bare-bones nature of Chromebooks didn\u2019t win over critics, some of whom said the devices made them long for Windows-based laptops.  Low Cost  \u201cWhile the Chromebook is a bold idea that may be a harbinger of the future of computing, it\u2019s too limited and buggy today to be the main computer relied upon by mainstream users,\u201d Walt Mossberg of AllThingsD and The Wall Street Journal wrote in a review of a Samsung Chromebook in 2011.  Now, early adopters and buyers in the education market are driving sales of Chromebooks, lured by their low cost, ease of use and transport, and Web-based services. Chromebooks are also benefiting as the market for laptops that cost less than $300 is set to grow more than 10 percent in 2013, Baker said.  Google has also stepped up its support for Chromebooks with new manufacturing partners and retailers, while spending marketing dollars to broaden the devices\u2019 appeal.  Traditional Microsoft allies  Lenovo Group Ltd. (992)  and  Hewlett-Packard Co. (HPQ)  both began offering Chromebook models in recent months. And Chromebooks moved into retail locations last October with  Best Buy Inc. (BBY)  and recently added  Wal-Mart Stores Inc. (WMT)  and  Staples Inc. (SPLS)   Small Portion  Chipmaker  Intel Corp. (INTC) , another longtime Microsoft partner, also has more than 1,000 software engineers who spend at least some of their time working on Chrome OS, adding to it and making sure it works with the chipmaker\u2019s microprocessors, according to Imad Sousou, vice president of Intel\u2019s Software & Services Group.  \u201cWe\u2019re seeing tremendous growth, without a doubt -- massive, massive growth,\u201d said Caesar Sengupta, head of product development for Chromebooks.  Google declined to comment on Chromebooks\u2019 sales figures.  Chromebooks still remain a small portion of the total U.S. market for laptops and netbooks. The devices had about 4 percent to 5 percent share in the first quarter, though that was up from 1 percent to 2 percent in 2012, according to Mikako Kitagawa, an analyst at Gartner Inc.  Google intends to woo more customers with updates to the machines\u2019 operating system every six weeks, delivered over the Internet. The company also has made Chromebooks more like traditional PCs by including tools that let users run programs even when they aren\u2019t connected to the Internet.  Bigger Screens  Google\u2019s next step may be to take Chromebooks more upscale, including new models that appeal to more expensive tastes, Baker said. That could include bigger screens, improved keyboards and more built-in storage. During arguments today in  Washington , the court\u2019s\nRepublican-appointed majority scrutinized the University of\nTexas\u2019s admissions program, which uses race as a consideration\nin admitting as much as one quarter of each class.  \u201cWhat you\u2019re saying is that what counts is race above\nall,\u201d Justice Anthony Kennedy, the likely swing vote, told the\nlawyer defending the plan. \u201cYou want underprivileged of a\ncertain race and privileged of a certain race.\u201d  At stake are policies that have been a fixture on U.S.\ncampuses since the 1960s. All but a handful of the nation\u2019s\nselective colleges and professional schools consider race as\nthey seek to ensure a diverse student body. A ruling against\nTexas would raise new legal questions about those programs --\nand perhaps even wipe them out. The court will rule by June.  Roberts, who once described racial classifications as \u201ca\nsordid business,\u201d signaled he would support a broad ruling. He\nrepeatedly voiced discomfort with the idea of identifying\nstudents by racial group.  \u201cShould someone who is one-quarter Hispanic check the\nHispanic box or some different box?\u201d he asked.  Ruling Jeopardized  The  Texas  case may undermine or overturn a 2003 Supreme\nCourt decision that reaffirmed the right of universities to\nconsider race in admissions as a means of ensuring campus\ndiversity. The court\u2019s composition has changed since then, most\nnotably through the retirement of Justice Sandra Day O\u2019Connor,\nwho wrote the 5-4 ruling.  O\u2019Connor, who was in the audience today, was succeeded by\nJustice Samuel Alito, a skeptic of racial preferences.  Bert Rein, the lawyer challenging the Texas program on\nbehalf of a rejected white applicant, stopped short of directly\nasking the court to overturn its 2003 ruling. The logic behind\nthat stance was questioned by Justices Sonia Sotomayor and\nStephen Breyer, who said they saw little difference between the\nTexas policy and the University of Michigan Law School plan\nupheld in 2003.  Class Rank  The 2003 decision, Grutter v. Bollinger, said colleges and\ngraduate schools could consider race as long as they do so\nthrough a broad review of a student\u2019s application and don\u2019t\nmechanistically award extra points to every minority.  \u201cYou don\u2019t want to overrule Grutter,\u201d said Sotomayor, the\ncourt\u2019s first Hispanic justice. \u201cYou just want to gut it.\u201d  A central question in the Texas case is whether\nuniversities can adequately diversify without resorting to\nracial preferences. The University of Texas admits three-\nquarters of its freshman class each year on the basis of high\nschool class rank -- the \u201ctop 10 percent rule.\u201d  That system, the product of a 1997 state law, ensures a\nsignificant number of minorities because it guarantees slots to\nstudents at predominantly Hispanic and black schools.  The university considers race only in admitting the rest of\nthe class. Rein today said that\u2019s unnecessary, given the success\nof the class-rank method.  \u201cRace should have been a last resort,\u201d he argued. \u201cIt\nwas a first resort.\u201d  Rejected Applicant  Rein\u2019s client, Abigail Noel Fisher, applied unsuccessfully\nto Texas in 2008 and later enrolled at Louisiana State\nUniversity. A graduate of a Houston-area public high school, she\nsays she was passed over by UT in favor of minority classmates\nwith lower grades and fewer extracurricular activities.  Texas has support in the case from some of the nation\u2019s\nmost powerful institutions. Fifty-nine companies -- including\n Microsoft Corp. (MSFT) ,  Wal-Mart Stores Inc., (WMT)  Gap Inc.,  General\nElectric Co. (GE) , Pfizer Inc., Shell Oil Co. and  Viacom Inc. (DELL) \u2019s path from personal- computer leader to buyout candidate mirrors the descent of an industry left behind by a raft of upstarts better equipped to capitalize on shifting consumer and business technology demands.  In a deal valued at $24.4 billion, the PC maker is going private in a leveraged buyout by Silver Lake Management LLC and Chief Executive Officer Michael Dell, who regains majority control of the company he founded in 1984.  Dell pioneered low-cost manufacturing and direct-to-buyer shipping, helping transform computers from bulky office machines costing thousands of dollars apiece to devices that every household could afford. It rode that focus on expense reduction to the top of the PC industry. Yet the company, along with many of its peers, failed to adapt as customers lost their appetite for desktops and even slimmed-down laptops, opting for a new class of mobile machines -- smartphones and tablets.  \u201cEverything in our high-tech industry that was once driven by a PC is now driven by a smartphone,\u2019 said Jim McGregor, an analyst at Tirias Research. \u2018\u2018Dell more than anything changed the business model of the PC market. But when you look at all the innovation that\u2019s gone on recently, it hasn\u2019t been on the PC.\u201d  Michael Dell  and Silver Lake will pay $13.65 a share for the PC maker, the companies said yesterday in a statement.  Microsoft (MSFT)  Corp., a Dell partner whose software runs more than 90 percent of the world\u2019s PCs, is contributing a $2 billion loan to the buyout, which will give Dell more latitude to cut jobs and steer strategy.  Dell\u2019s Heyday  The computer industry is facing its second consecutive decline in annual sales this year while tablets and smartphones continue to surge. PC shipments fell 4 percent in 2012 and will slide a further 1.5 percent this year, JPMorgan Chase & Co. analysts estimate. Tablet unit sales, by contrast, rose 72 percent last year and will surge 54 percent this year, they project.  Dell\u2019s rise from dorm-room startup to more than $100 billion market-value company in the middle of the last decade exemplified a time when innovation in electronics was focused on the PC. By selling directly to consumers and companies and letting them specify their own components, the Round Rock, Texas-based company helped bring down the average selling price of a PC from more than $2,000 in 1995 to less than $700 in 2011, according to market-research firm IDC.  IBM\u2019s Path  In the process, Dell elbowed aside the industry\u2019s founder,  International Business Machines Corp. (IBM) , contributing to that company\u2019s exit from the business in 2005 in a spinoff to  Lenovo Group Ltd. (992)  Freed of the commodity PC business, IBM recast itself as a computer software and services company, a move that Dell has tried to replicate through acquisitions.  IBM now gets about 80 percent of its revenue from services and software, helping its gross margin -- a measure of profitability that equals the percentage of sales left after deducting production costs -- reach 52 percent in the most recent quarter. That\u2019s more than twice the gross margin at Dell, which still relies on PCs for half of its revenue.  The past two years are littered with examples of a changing of the guard among the companies that dominate technology.  Qualcomm Inc. (QCOM) , the largest maker of chips that run phones, unseated  Intel Corp, (INTC)  the No. 1 provider of processors for PCs, as the biggest U.S. chipmaker by market capitalization.  Mobile Era  With the emergence of tablets and smartphones, PCs now represent just 29 percent of all Internet-connected devices, according to a December report by Goldman Sachs Group Inc. That means that Microsoft, whose operating system ran 97 percent of computing devices in 2000, now has just 20 percent of the total consumer-computing market. Google Inc.\u2019s Android mobile operating system has 42 percent, and Apple Inc. has 24 percent.  \u201cThe bigger question is: Are personal computers dinosaurs?\u201d said Daniel Morgan, a senior portfolio manager at Synovus Trust Co.  What the industry and Dell in particular missed was the shift from corporations to consumers as the drivers of growth in computing, according to Bob O\u2019Donnell, an analyst at IDC. While businesses dominated orders, Dell\u2019s focus on lowering the costs of manufacturing helped it prosper. When innovation in products was needed, the company suffered.  \u201cThe design piece was something where they fell behind on,\u201d said O\u2019Donnell. \u201cDell has kind of gotten in some markets early, but barely dipped their toes in and then backed away. That was true for mobile phones, that was true for tablets.\u201d  Product Flops  Dell\u2019s attempts to fire up consumer interest in PCs such as the Adamo in 2009 flopped when the $2,000 price of the slimline notebook limited sales. The Dell Streak smartphone went on sale in June 2010 and was discontinued the following year. Likewise, the Dell DJ music-file player and iPod rival debuted in 2003, then was withdrawn in 2006.  Dell\u2019s limited efforts contrast with  Apple (AAPL) \u2019s success at reinventing itself and becoming the world\u2019s largest publicly traded company. Apple, one of the pioneers of personal computing, now gets less than 15 percent of sales from its Macintosh computer line, while more than 70 percent comes from smartphones and tablets.  \u201cI don\u2019t see them all of a sudden introducing a new product that gets everyone excited,\u201d Synovus\u2019s Morgan said of Dell. \u201cI just haven\u2019t seen much from Dell.\u201d  The lack of appeal to consumers may spill over and hurt corporate PC sales as BYOD -- bring your own device -- accelerates, according to IDC\u2019s O\u2019Donnell. Consumers are increasingly taking easier-to-use iPads and smartphones to work, potentially undermining demand for devices traditionally provided by employers.  Cost Focus  Another constraint on Dell\u2019s ability to innovate was its focus on reducing  costs  and lower prices, which increasingly drove its business toward lower levels of profitability as Asian manufacturers followed with similar approaches, according to O\u2019Donnell. By choosing to discount and manufacture cheaper rather than improve designs, PC makers became involved in a \u201crace to the bottom,\u201d which Dell is no longer winning.  Dell, once No. 1 in PCs, lost the industry crown to  Hewlett-Packard Co. (HPQ)  in 2006, and Lenovo leapfrogged it to take second place in 2011. Dell is now third with 10.7 percent of the 352.7 million-unit market in 2012, after suffering a 12 percent shipment decline, the largest drop among the top five producers, according to Gartner Inc.  And while Hewlett-Packard has returned to the top spot, that company is also struggling because of its failure to crack the tablet or phone markets, after its acquisition of Palm Inc. didn\u2019t produce products that companies or consumers wanted. Hewlett-Packard saw PC shipments decline 6.7 percent in 2012 and has considered divesting the unit.  Cash Engine  Dell, meantime, isn\u2019t likely to shed PCs anytime soon. It relies on the division, which provides about half of its revenue, to generate cash needed to make payments on the debt incurred to buy out shareholders, said Abhey Lamba, an analyst at Mizuho Securities USA Inc.  \u201cThey would need to continue running the PC business to generate a certain threshold of cash, and the PC industry is increasingly getting commoditized,\u201d said Lamba. \u201cThe thing with a commodity business is you lower cost by getting scale, and you get scale by lowering price, so it\u2019s a vicious cycle.\u201d  To contact the reporters on this story: Ian King in San Francisco at  ianking@bloomberg.net ; Dina Bass in Seattle at  dbass2@bloomberg.net   To contact the editor responsible for this story: Tom Giles at  tgiles5@bloomberg.net","path":".\/2008_2012_msft_bloomberg_news\/dell-s-drop-mirrors-descent-of-pc-industry-in-mobile-world-tec.txt"},{"id":49835349,"title":"Microsoft Seeks to Invalidate Motorola Patent in U.K. Trial","released_at":"<date>December 10 2012<\/date> <time>14:12:08<\/time>","content":"Microsoft Corp. (MSFT)  unveiled a new version of its software for smartphones today, redoubling an effort to regain market share lost to  Apple Inc. (AAPL)  and  Google Inc. (P)  app with a year of advertising-free Internet radio, a program that helps customers use less of their wireless data capacity and an app that lets parents control what programs and features their children can use, Microsoft Vice President Joe Belfiore said today at an event in  San Francisco .  Windows Phone 8 software, running on devices with better screens and more powerful chips, will rely for the first time on the same underlying programming code as the flagship Windows operating system. Microsoft, with just 3.5 percent share of the  smartphone market  in the second quarter, seeks to close a gap with Apple\u2019s more popular iOS and devices from  Samsung Electronics Co. (005930)  and other makers that use Google\u2019s Android.  \u201cThe platform looks very competitive,\u201d Al Hilwa, an analyst at research firm IDC, said of Microsoft\u2019s new lineup. Carrier Push  Microsoft Chief Executive Officer  Steve Ballmer  said the new phones go on sale in  Europe  this weekend and in the U.S. in November at  AT&T Inc. (T) ,  Verizon Wireless  and T-Mobile USA stores, as well as Microsoft\u2019s own retail outlets.  Aside from improving phone hardware and adding features to the software, Microsoft\u2019s biggest challenge lies in how to market its mobile products, particularly in the stores of U.S. carriers where salespeople often recommend iPhones and Android devices.  Carriers and handset makers have been providing sales staff with their own Windows Phones in an effort to get them excited about the products, said Thom Gruhler, a vice president recruited in March from McCann Worldgroup to improve the Windows Phone\u2019s marketing.  \u201cI don\u2019t want to say we\u2019ve got it all solved, but the important thing for us is there\u2019s excitement among retail sales personnel,\u201d he said. \u201cThis isn\u2019t a panacea. Gruhler also noted that Verizon, which had previously sold only one Windows Phone model in the two years the devices have been on the market, is showing a new level of commitment by selling three different models this holiday.  Helping to boost Microsoft\u2019s case with consumers, Windows Phone now has 120,000 apps, including 46 of the top 50 on rival phones, Microsoft\u2019s Belfiore said. Pandora, for example, had been a long-time holdout.  There are more than 700,000 apps on Apple\u2019s store, including more than 275,000 specifically for the iPad tablet computer. There are about 700,000 apps for Android devices, Google said.  Apple\u2019s Popularity  Operating on phones with a dual-core chip and high- definition screens, Windows 8 supports near-field communication technology, which lets customers use phones to make payments. Redmond, Washington-based Microsoft initially discussed some of the features in June.  The new Windows Phone 8-based devices are aimed squarely at Apple\u2019s iPhones, which have a market share of 17 percent, as well as smartphones based on Google\u2019s Android software, which accounted for 68 percent of the market, according to Framingham, Massachusetts-based IDC.  The iPhone 5 sold 5 million units in its debut weekend, or about the same number of Windows Phone devices shipped in the entire second quarter, based on IDC\u2019s data.  Consumers heading into the U.S. year-end holiday shopping season are being offered a bounty of choices. Apple began selling the iPhone 5 last month with a bigger screen, lightweight body design and faster processor, and Google today unveiled new versions of its Nexus smartphone and tablet, which showcase Android\u2019s latest features. There is some growth, with second quarter market share climbing from 2.3 percent a year earlier, according to IDC. For the first time in a decade, the total PC market will contract this year, by 1.2 percent to 348.7 million units,  according  to IHS ISuppli.  Microsoft, which is revamping its software across the board, introduced Windows 8, a new version of its software for PCs, last week. The remark\nwas part of a broad rebuke of Google\u2019s competitors that accused\nthem of a \u201chostile, organized campaign\u201d against Android, which\nhas emerged as the top operating system for smartphones.  Google\u2019s rivals are joining forces to purchase patents to\nkeep them out of the  Mountain View , California-based company\u2019s\nhands and taking other steps to make it more expensive for\nhandset makers to use Android, he said yesterday. Drummond cited\nMicrosoft and Apple working together to acquire Novell\u2019s patent\nportfolio as an example of the campaign against Google.  Microsoft\u2019s Response  Microsoft General Counsel  Brad Smith  responded yesterday by\nsaying Google had been asked to participate in the Novell bid.\nMicrosoft also released an e-mail from Google turning down the\noffer.  That prompted today\u2019s update from Drummond.  \u201cMicrosoft\u2019s objective has been to keep from Google and\nAndroid device-makers any patents that might be used to defend\nagainst their attacks,\u201d Drummond said. \u201cA joint acquisition of\nthe Novell patents that gave all parties a license would have\neliminated any protection these patents could offer to Android\nagainst attacks from Microsoft and its bidding partners.\u201d  Frank Shaw , a spokesman for Redmond, Washington-based\nMicrosoft, reiterated today that the company asked Google to\njoin the Novell partnership.  \u201cWe offered Google the opportunity to bid with us to buy\nthe Novell patents; they said no,\u201d Shaw said in a series of\nmessages on Twitter. \u201cWhy? The regulator didn\u2019t pay attention to warning signs or\nreact fast enough to reports of problems with Libor rates,\nlawmaker George Mudie told Financial Services Authority Chairman\n Adair Turner . The disclosures are \u201cnot only very troubling in themselves\nbut they have the effect of undermining public confidence in\nfinancial markets,\u201d Bernanke said during testimony yesterday to\nthe Senate Banking Committee in Washington.  The Fed didn\u2019t have information to suggest that banks were\nmanipulating rates \u201cfor profit,\u201d only that some were\n\u201cpossibly submitting low rates to avoid appearing weak\u201d during\nthe financial crisis, Bernanke said. Others","released_at":"<date>July 10 2013<\/date> <time>22:01:00<\/time>","content":"Willi Kuhlmann remembers the day the  Berlin Wall  was erected on Aug. 13, 1961, and how the system of spying on East German citizens by secret police known as the Stasi intensified.  His experience as a border guard along the Wall that divided  Germany \u2019s capital city for 28 years makes him mistrustful of the data-gathering carried out by the U.S. National Security Agency, revealed in a series of disclosures to publications including Germany\u2019s Der Spiegel by fugitive Edward Snowden in recent weeks.  Kuhlmann, a 77-year-old retired forester, is among ordinary Germans who draw parallels between the NSA\u2019s activities and the surveillance carried out by the Stasi. One in two of the country\u2019s citizens regard Snowden as a hero, according to a June 29 survey of 504 people by Emnid for  Bild am Sonntag  newspaper.  \u201cYou don\u2019t spy like that on your friends,\u201d said Kuhlmann in a telephone interview.  Chancellor Angela Merkel , whose government has rejected the leaker\u2019s application for asylum to Germany, spoke with U.S. President  Barack Obama  over the phone last week after  Der Spiegel  reported that the NSA spied on German citizens and European diplomats. Germany was the top destination among European countries for the intelligence gathering, with about 500 million phone calls, e-mails and SMS being monitored and recorded by the NSA every month, the magazine said.  WikiLeaks Support  Snowden, who has been offered legal and logistical support by anti-secrecy website WikiLeaks as he faced U.S. requests for extradition in  Hong Kong  and  Russia , also said NSA officials were \u201cin bed together with the Germans.\u201d According to  Der Spiegel , the NSA has a partnership with Germany\u2019s foreign intelligence service, or BND, with the Americans providing \u201canalysis tools\u201d for the BND to use as it monitors streams of data passing through Germany.  Interior Minister  Hans-Peter Friedrich  will fly to the U.S. today to join high-level talks about Snowden\u2019s revelations as European Union and U.S. officials seek to clarify the allegations. Friedrich is scheduled to meet Attorney General Eric Holder and presidential adviser  Lisa Monaco  tomorrow in  Washington .  \u201cThere\u2019s nothing wrong about telling the truth,\u201d said Janina Cieply, 22, an anthropology student at Berlin\u2019s Free University. \u201cIt looks like the NSA picked up where the Stasi left off. Of course this is a delicate topic in Germany, and rightfully so. It\u2019s the government\u2019s duty to protect the people from such attacks.\u201d  Wau Holland  While some Germans voice their support for Snowden, people around the world are less willing to offer financial backing to WikiLeaks and causes such as Snowden\u2019s. Donations to the Wau Holland Foundation, the Hamburg-based main financing channel for WikiLeaks, remained well below levels seen in 2010, when the group published diplomatic and military documents obtained by U.S. Army Private Bradley Manning.  Mindful of state surveillance by the Stasi under communism and the Gestapo under the Nazis, Germans are more sensitive than people in other nations to the powers of surveillance by government agencies.  Communist East Germany\u2019s Staatssicherheit, or Stasi secret police, was the regime\u2019s enforcer whose motto was \u201cShield and Sword of the Party.\u201d The Stasi had 93,000 full-time agents and at least 189,000 part-time informers in 1989, the year the  Berlin Wall  fell before the 1990 German reunification, Joerg Drieselmann, director of Berlin\u2019s  Stasi Museum , said in a phone interview. East Germany had a population of about 16.4 million in 1989.  \u2018Collective Memory\u2019  \u201cThe Stasi is the ultimate expression of spying in Germany\u2019s collective memory,\u201d he said.  Drieselmann said 120 kilometers (75 miles) of Stasi files still exist and that this is thought to be 65 percent to 70 percent of the total files before the Stasi\u2019s frantic shredding and burning of its archives shortly before the communist state\u2019s collapse.  \u201cWe still can\u2019t compare the Stasi with the NSA,\u201d he said. \u201cI certainly don\u2019t want to even try to compare them as institutions but let\u2019s be clear: the NSA has gathered vastly more information than the Stasi ever did.\u201d  In an interview with Die Zeit newspaper published yesterday, Merkel said she rejects any parallel between the Stasi and espionage practices of democratic states.  Spy Drama  The Stasi legacy still resonates and was dramatized in a film \u201c The Lives of Others ,\u201d about an agent spying on a writer and his lover, which won an Oscar for Best Foreign Language Film in 2007.  Germany has a long tradition of data protection laws dating back to the 1970s. The state of Hesse introduced the first data protection law worldwide in 1970, according the Hesse State Commissioner for Data Protection  website .  In 1983, the country\u2019s top court said Germany\u2019s constitution grants individuals a right to \u201cinformational self-determination.\u201d A system \u201cin which citizens can no longer know who knows what and when and on which occasion about them,\u201d is incompatible with the constitution, the judges ruled. As a result, data can\u2019t be collected without authorization under a law that determines and limits the scope and purpose.  Stasi and Nazi abuses which were followed by this legal framework lead many Germans to react strongly to data security violations.  \u201cI think it\u2019s a catastrophe that this is possible in this supposed free world,\u201d said Josef Geuecke, 50, a farmer. \u201cWe have to try to stop this at all levels. We\u2019ve become very sensitive after 1945, but that\u2019s our duty.\u201d  Exclusion Risks  Yet Jan Techau, head of the Carnegie Endowment\u2019s Brussels office, said the German government is unlikely to heed the call of some members of the public and politicians in Berlin to trim back data exchanges with the U.S.  \u201cGerman intelligence would lose access to American intelligence which has been useful in the past,\u201d Techau said in a phone interview. \u201cIt would catapult Germany outside of America\u2019s privileged inner circle. Sure, there\u2019s a certain amount of hysteria and over-reaction in Germany but you can\u2019t just dismiss this because there is a breach of trust.\u201d  German industry, reliant for its exports on a technological edge over products made in lower-cost countries, is concerned the snooping may damage its competitiveness.  Play \u2018Hardball\u2019  \u201cBerlin should invest heavily in cyberdefense and anti-espionage activities, give more resources to its intelligence agencies and join in the game of hardball,\u201d Markus Kerber, the Federation of German Industry\u2019s director general, wrote in an opinion piece in the Financial Times. \u201cIn a world of realpolitik, only the strong are taken seriously.\u201d  The U.S. Patriot Act allows authorities to demand punctual access to information from U.S. companies. Reports leaked by Snowden said the NSA has been able to access servers of Google Inc., Facebook Inc., Apple Inc., Microsoft Corp. and others at any time since 2007. Other leaks pointed to the U.K.\u2019s GCHQ tapping into and analyzing data from fiber-optic cables carrying  Internet traffic , as well the U.S. bugging EU offices in Washington.  \u201cWhen someone tells the truth like that, our government should protect him,\u201d said Norbert Mayer, a 66-year-old retiree from  Frankfurt . \u201cBut we\u2019re clearly governed from Brussels and Washington. And it seems like even Merkel has no choice but to give in to Obama.\u201d  Kuhlmann, the former  Berlin Wall  border guard, said intelligence gathering today in democracies takes place under totally different -- and much higher -- standards than what he knew in the East Bloc under communism.  \u201cSpies exist in every nation and today we need to keep close watch on terrorists and organized crime,\u201d he said. \u201cBut we learned in East Germany that spying must be controlled and in this case it doesn\u2019t seem like it was.\u201d  To contact the reporters on this story: Cornelius Rahn in Berlin at  crahn2@bloomberg.net ; Leon Mangasarian in Berlin at  lmangasarian@bloomberg.net   To contact the editors responsible for this story: Kenneth Wong at  kwong11@bloomberg.net ; James Hertling at  jhertling@bloomberg.net","path":".\/2008_2012_msft_bloomberg_news\/germans-hail-snowden-as-nsa-evokes-stasi-seizing-lives-of-others.txt"},{"id":27095910,"title":"Microsoft Co-Founder Allen Gives $26 Million to Washington State","released_at":"<date>December 2 2010<\/date> <time>18:23:26<\/time>","content":"Paul Allen , the co-founder of\nMicrosoft Corp., will give Washington State University $26\nmillion for its  School for Global Animal Health . To contact the reporter on this story:\n Oliver Staley  in New York at \n ostaley@bloomberg.net   To contact the editor responsible for this story:\nJonathan Kaufman at \n jkaufman17@bloomberg.net","path":".\/2008_2012_msft_bloomberg_news\/billionaire-paul-allen-donates-26-million-to-washington-state-university.txt"},{"id":79089810,"title":"Pricing, not Piracy, Hurts Culture Trade (Part 3): William Patry","released_at":"<date>December 29 2011<\/date> <time>00:00:22<\/time>","content":"The universal nature of music, art\nand literature explains their enduring appeal and allows their\ncreators the opportunity to reach a global audience.  The ability of copyright owners to be paid for exploitation\nof their works beyond their own national boundaries has been\nimportant since at least the late 18th and early 19th centuries.\nBeethoven, Haydn, Mozart and other composers entered into\nsimultaneous publication agreements in order to prevent\nunauthorized printing of their works in other countries.  Including intellectual property within trade agreements is\na relatively recent strategy -- originally developed by the U.S.\nin the early 1980s. In such agreements, intellectual property\nissues are subsumed within a larger trade agenda. For large,\nintellectual property-exporting countries such as the U.S.,\nobtaining ever-stronger rights is seen as a way to obtain ever-\nstronger control over foreign markets. But what are the benefits\nfor countries that are net importers of intellectual property?\nFew if any. On the contrary, they experience a net loss.  When the  United States  was itself a developing country, it\nrejected the pleas of Britain and other developed countries to\nprotect foreign authors. From 1790 to 1891, the U.S.\ndeliberately denied protection to foreign published works, and\nthis policy greatly benefited American economic development.  Not surprisingly, developed countries argue for strong,\nuniform intellectual-property laws worldwide. A rising tide\nlifts all boats, they say.  Rising Tide  That metaphor promises equality for all, and if the yachts\nare lifted up a bit more than dinghies, the dinghies might not\ncomplain so long as they are lifted up, too. The implied promise\nis that developing countries will end up with the same access to\npharmaceutical drugs, the same creative works and so on as\ndeveloped countries have. Yet countries that lack an educated\ncitizenry, adequate domestic research-and-development companies,\nmeaningful participation in financial markets and effective\nmeans to bring domestic innovations to market will not realize\nthe benefits.  Consider, for example, how a small domestic record industry\nin a developing country can be easily eliminated if the\nfloodgates are opened to foreign  record companies .  The rising-tide metaphor can also be thought of in\nconventional economic terms. In the 18th century,  Adam Smith \nclaimed that an increase in the size of markets leads to\nincreases in the diversity of offerings. Trade among countries\nincreases this diversity by introducing people in one country to\nthe goods, services and cultures of others.  In the 19th century, however, Alexis de Tocqueville took a\ndifferent view. After studying life in the U.S., he concluded\nthat \u201cmarket growth serves as a magnet, pulling creators\ntowards mass production and away from serving niches.\u201d And he\nsaid this results in \u201ca culture of the least common\ndenominator.\u201d  De Tocqueville\u2019s view seems to have prevailed. There is\nconsiderable evidence that our best-selling creations are dumbed\ndown. (In 2010, the top-grossing film in the U.S. was \u201cToy\nStory 3.\u201d)  At the same time, large markets such as  New York City  do\nprovide diverse, niche offerings. And the growth of Internet\nplatforms such as YouTube and blogs has provided fantastic\nofferings for specialized tastes. The economist Tyler Cowen had\nit right when he said, \u201cMarkets bring more homogeneity and more\ndiversity. This dual trend characterizes consumer taste as well\nas cultural products generally.\u201d  Cultural Dominance  Yet dominance of U.S. cultural works leads to a dominance\nof U.S. culture, and it is easy to see why. No country can\nfoster the creativity of its own citizens if the financing,\nproduction and distribution of works is controlled by large,\nwealthy foreign corporations.  The conventional notion in the U.S. that stronger copyright\nlaws can deter bootlegging of DVDs and the like is a fallacy.\nUnauthorized markets arise when demand for copyrighted works is\ncreated but not met. So the best way to prevent the sale of\nunauthorized goods is to flood the market with authorized goods.\nThe vast unauthorized markets that exist around the world are\nnot a sign of moral shortcomings among people in those\ncountries; they\u2019re simply the result of copyright owners\nclinging to failed business models.  Multinational corporations make the bulk of their profits\nin developed-country markets, and thus have little interest in\nserving other ones, especially when doing so means that they\nneed to compete in terms of price.  In a comprehensive study of how media is consumed around\nthe world, the  Social Science Research Council  concluded:\n\u201cMedia piracy has been called \u2018a global scourge,\u2019 an\n\u2018international plague,\u2019 and \u2018nirvana for criminals,\u2019 but it is\nprobably better described as a global pricing problem.\u201d  Where goods owned by multinational corporations are sold at\nall in  developing countries , they are offered at the same prices\nas in developed countries, or at comparable prices that place\nthe goods out of reach of all but the wealthiest consumers.  This pricing problem is strikingly absent from most\ndiscussions of intellectual property. Policy makers are still\nfocused on enforcing tough copyright and trade regulations. Yet\nthe Social Science Research Council found \u201cno evidence -- and\nindeed no claims -- that enforcement efforts to date have had\nany impact on the overall supply of pirated goods.\u201d In none of\nthe nations studied was the comparative price -- the price that\nreflects cost-of-living differences --the same as in the U.S.  Soybeans for Software  Consider the example of Microsoft\u2019s Office 2007: In 2004,\nMarcelo D\u2019Elia Branco,  Brazil \u2019s liaison between the open source\ncommunity and the government, estimated that one license for\nMicrosoft\u2019s Office suite meant Brazil had to export 60 sacks of\nsoybeans. As then-President  Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva  observed,\n\u201cFor the right to use one copy of Office plus Windows for one\nyear or a year and a half, until the next upgrade, we have to\ntill the earth, plant, harvest and export to international\nmarkets that much soy. When I explain this to the farmers, they\ngo nuts.\u201d  The solution here is simple: Offer the same goods at\ndifferent prices in different countries, based on people\u2019s\nability to pay. There will still be those who engage in large-\nscale unauthorized copying. And going after the very small\nnumber of those who are doing most of the harm is entirely\njustified. What\u2019s unjustified is threatening the broad\npopulation with lawsuits and crippling penalties.  Copyright owners should support the good guys by providing\nreasonably priced and convenient authorized goods. If they can\u2019t\ndo this, no copyright law can help them.  (William Patry, senior copyright counsel at Google Inc., is\nthe author of \u201cMoral Panics and the Copyright Wars\u201d \u201cPatry on\nCopyright\u201d and \u201cPatry on Fair Use.\u201d This is the first in a\nthree-part series of excerpts from his new book, \u201cHow to Fix\nCopyright,\u201d to be published Jan. 5 by  Oxford University Press .\nThe opinions expressed are his own. Read  Part 1  and  Part 2 .)  To contact the writer on this article:\nWilliam Patry at  williampatry@yahoo.com .  To contact the editor responsible for this article:\nMary Duenwald at   mduenwald@bloomberg.net .","path":".\/2008_2012_msft_bloomberg_news\/pricing-not-piracy-hurts-copyright-part-3-commentary-by-william-patry.txt"},{"id":29561104,"title":"Apple's Surge May Make It `Too Big to Succeed': Chart of the Day","released_at":"<date>June 22 2010<\/date> <time>14:05:04<\/time>","content":"The 38-fold surge in Apple Inc.\nshares that drove the iPhone seller past Microsoft Corp.\u2019s\nmarket value means the company may be \u201ctoo big to succeed,\u201d\naccording to research from  Rob Arnott .  \n Research Affiliates LLC found that since 1953, shares of\nthe biggest Standard & Poor\u2019s 500 Index company in an industry\ntrailed the average stock by 2.4 percent a year in the next\ndecade.
