Adafruit Industries, which sells do-it-yourself\nelectronics kits, would give $1,000 to the first person to\nunlock Kinect\u2019s sophisticated motion sensors from the Xbox so\nthat any tinkerer could repurpose the technology for such\nprojects as building robots. In a week Adafruit had a winner, a\nSpanish engineer who got Kinect to work with his laptop just\nhours after it was released in  Europe . \u201cNow it\u2019s unlocked for\ncreativity,\u201d Fried  wrote .  That could be the tagline for Adafruit, the company Fried\nfounded in 2005 while getting her masters in electrical\nengineering and computer science at the  Massachusetts Institute\nof Technology . The electronics kits she sells are \u201copen-source\nhardware,\u201d meaning that Adafruit shares the designs that\ncompanies usually keep secret. \u201cWe\u2019re giving away all our\nintellectual property for free,\u201d says Fried, 31. The eight-\nemployee company will ship more than $3 million worth of kits\nthis year from its top-floor loft four blocks north of  Wall\nStreet  in New York\u2019s financial district.  The  software industry  has embraced open source over the past\ndecade, with such companies as Red Hat built around code that is\npublic and free for others to modify. The idea is newer to\nmanufacturing. About 50 companies worldwide are selling open-\nsource hardware, estimates Ayah Bdeir, who helped organize the\nfirst  Open Hardware Summit  in September at the  New York  Hall of\nScience. The business case for publishing product designs is\n\u201ccounterintuitive for any person [who] invests or works in\nproduct development,\u201d she says. These companies succeed by\nproviding support and service to customers that distinguishes\nthem from competitors who could make identical products using\ntheir designs. \u201cThe world knows they are experts in what they\ndo, and [customers] want to purchase from them,\u201d Bdeir says.  LEANING TOWARD THE FANCIFUL  The strategy helped Adafruit double its revenue from 2009 to\n2010, and Fried projects it nearly to double again next year, to\n$5 million to $6 million. With no outside investment, Fried\nlaunched the company with $10,000 her parents designated for her\nMIT tuition to buy parts for her first kit, a synthesizer. \u201cAs\nsoon as we made a profit, I had to take it out to pay tuition,\u201d\nshe says. Adafruit now sells two dozen unique electronics kits\nto hobbyists and students and ships some 100 orders a day. The\nprojects, which range from about $20 to $100, tend to be\nfanciful, such as the MintyBoost, a portable charger for cell\nphones and other devices that fits inside an Altoids tin, and\nthe TV-B-Gone, a remote that can shut off televisions in a 150-\nfoot radius.  For each kit, the company publishes the computer-aided design\nfiles, schematics for circuit boards, and the firmware or\nsoftware code that runs inside a device. Anyone can use this\nmaterial under a  Creative Commons  license, provided they credit\nthe source and publish any related works under a similar open-\nsource license.  In addition to publishing designs, the company offers online\ntutorials, and Fried co-hosts a weekly video chat with Adafruit\ndesigner Phillip Torrone to teach lessons and answer questions.\n\u201cShe\u2019s really educating people. It\u2019s almost like she\u2019s running a\nschool in addition to everything else she\u2019s doing,\u201d says Alicia\nGibb, another organizer of the Open Hardware Summit who works as\n\u201cgadget wrangler\u201d at Bug Labs, an open-source hardware company\ndeveloping wireless devices. (NKE)  wants to make improving your golf game easier.  The world\u2019s largest producer of sporting goods obtained a  patent  Sept. 4 to put data-collecting sensors on  golf clubs  to improve personalization. In one scenario, the analysis of a swing is shown on a display screen embedded on the back of the club\u2019s head. That would make getting fit for golf clubs faster and more precise, the company said.  \u201cCustom fitting is outdated, and can be inaccurate,\u201d Nike said in  documents  posted on the website of the U.S. Patent and Trademark Office. While most fitting is done indoors on a hard surface, the new club would allow golfers to measure a swing out on a course, which would garner more accurate data, Nike said.  Nike has been integrating digital technology into sports equipment as a way for users to measure and improve results. It also increases the time consumers spend with the brand, which can increase loyalty and sales. The company this year introduced a wristband that tracks daily activity and shoes equipped with sensors that can record such metrics as how high a basketball player jumps during a dunk.  Mary Remuzzi, a spokeswoman for Nike, declined to comment on the patent and when such products might come to market.  The Beaverton, Oregon-based company also received a  patent  last week for a data collection system that places sensors and transmitters in shoes that automatically track the distance and time of a run or walk. The data would then be shared with the user by sending it to a mobile device or computer.  Marketing Potential  Beyond measuring performance, there is also marketing potential. In one example, a person walks into a store and the shoe sensor tells the salesman the kind of sneaker, the shopper\u2019s identity and how long he or she has worn the shoe. Advertising based on that data is then shown to the person wearing the shoes through an in-store terminal or is sent to a mobile device.  The system may also allow Nike to offer promotions based on how much the shoes are used. In one scenario from the patent document, a person buys shoes and registers for a contest that offers a prize if they run 100 miles in a month.  Revenue from Nike\u2019s running category surged 32 percent to $3.7 billion in its fiscal year ended May 31st, while golf rose 10 percent to $726 million. The company\u2019s total revenue was $24.1 billion.  While golf equipment has become more sophisticated, including balls designed to cater to a player\u2019s strengths, fitting is largely a trial-and-error process, Nike said.  Radar System  This patent would remove that uncertainty by using accelerometers and gyroscopes to measure as many as 100 data points to record such measurements as the angle of the club face, Nike said.  Nike obtained a patent last month for a computerized radar system that places sensors on soccer balls and other equipment as a way to offer data analysis for team sports. It may be able to track two soccer players at the same time with sensors on their shoes as well as the ball to measure how well they pass to each other. The INSA polling organization showed AfD getting more than the 5 percent of the vote required to win seats. Other polls put it just below the 5 percent mark. Chancellor Angela Merkel's coalition partners, the Free Democrats, are also in the gray area, unsure of a place in parliament. With Merkel's Christian Democrats poised to remain the largest party in the Bundestag but without an outright majority, the question is what coalition it will be able to form. At this point, a \"grand coalition\" with the second most popular party, the Social Democrats, is highly likely because the eurosceptics are taking away votes from the Free Democrats. Paradoxically, the AfD's success may lead to a more pro-European government than the current one. Nokia chief to get big payout as he  moves back  to Miscrosoft  Outgoing Chief Executive Stephen Elop will get $25.4 million as a parting gift, 30 percent of it from Nokia and the rest from Microsoft. The package includes Elop's salary for the rest of his contract and issue equity compensation of $19.8 million. It is fitting that Microsoft has agreed to pay a lion's share of the compensation. A former Microsoft employee, Elop first committed the Finnish company to the production of Windows smartphones and then engineered the sale of its mobile phone business to Microsoft. The Redmond, Washington, company is now bringing him over to manage the new division. On the one hand, the payout reinforces suspicions -- shared by Finnish government officials -- that Elop was Microsoft's \"Trojan horse\" from the start. On the other hand, Windows Phone is an unpopular operating system and Nokia's handset business is a deeply troubled enterprise, so the sweetener may be a way to encourage Elop to do his best with it. Air France KLM  mulls  Alitalia acquisition   The Franco-Dutch airline is considering a takeover of the Italian flag carrier, Alitalia, when the consortium that saved it from bankruptcy in 2008 is allowed to sell its shares in October. Its board of directors may decide on the plan next week. The consortium consists of companies whose primary business has nothing to do with aviation: a bank, a highway operator and a diversified industrial holding, and Alitalia has not fared well under its ownership: 2013 will be its sixth loss-making year in a row, and it may run out of cash by the end of the year. Air France KLM itself is in the midst of a restructuring program that includes drastic cost cuts, but at least it has a vision of what needs to be done to save a traditional airline. Interest from Air France KLM would be welcome news both to the investors and to Alitalia itself, but not to many of its staff, if the massive layoffs at AirFrance are any indication. Adidas  issues  profit warning  Germany's Adidas, the world's second biggest sportswear manufacturer after Nike, warned investors they should expect a dividend payout of no more than $1.15 billion for 2013, down from the previous minimum estimate of $1.2 billion. The company, whose Adidas and Reebok brands are strong in Russia, Brazil, Argentina and Turkey, is suffering from the weakening of emerging-markets currencies and a slowdown in the golf market. Besides, the company is having difficulty moving to a new distribution facility near Moscow and has to lower its Russian sales projections. It is commonly thought that globalization is the best cure for European companies facing lower demand at home, but Adidas's troubles highlight the pitfalls of global expansion. The company, however, is still in great shape financially and in terms of sales: It is just that investors' expectations may have been too high. France  calls for  EU regulation of U.S. Internet companies  France is calling on the European Commission to work out rules for Internet companies to ensure the profits they make in Europe are taxed in the EU. That would mean, in effect, taxing international data flow. French Technology Minister Fleur Pellerin, who is behind the proposals, also wants the EU to decree that digital entities like e-books and user profiles contained within closed ecosystems like Google's, Apple's and Amazon's be made transferable between systems. That, according to Pellerin, would help European companies compete with U.S. Internet giants. The plan, however, is not likely to be adopted by Brussels: It looks too much like an extortion attempt victimizing successful companies that won market share in Europe without any help from the local regulators. (Leonid Bershidsky, an editor and novelist, is a Bloomberg View contributor. Dell\u2019s early success came from slashing pennies from component prices and tightening supply chains to trim days off delivery times -- not from inventing product categories or adopting bold new strategies. As chief executive officer, he avoided investing heavily enough in smartphones or music players, and he was late to the shift to cloud computing.  The strategy caught up with Dell, leaving the company he built from a university dorm room ill-equipped to adapt to changing demands from consumers and businesses or to vie with nimbler competitors in mobile and data-center technology. After years of market-share losses and  tumbling shares , Dell orchestrated a $24.4 billion buyout using his own wealth, his stock in the company, a loan from  Microsoft Corp.  and investment by private-equity firm Silver Lake Management LLC.  Even after going private, the company won\u2019t be making radical moves overnight, Chief Financial Officer  Brian Gladden  said in a Feb. 5 interview.  Patience Required  \u201cIt\u2019s going to take more time,\u201d Gladden said. \u201cIt will take more patience and investment for us to deliver.\u201d  Dell also isn\u2019t considering parting with its low-margin PC division, the company said in a regulatory filing.  \u201cWe have the resources and the backing to do incredible things and to lead our company on to great successes,\u201d Dell said before a crowd of staff members yesterday in Las Vegas. \u201cI\u2019m very excited. I think the upside for our company is huge.\u201d  The remarks evoked a Michael Dell of a  bygone era , like the one who at the age of 12 set up a national mail-order stamp auction that netted $2,000. He later dashed his parents\u2019 hope that he\u2019d become a doctor. Instead he dropped out of the  University of Texas  to focus on his dorm-room business of cobbling together PCs at a lower cost than market leaders  International Business Machines Corp.  and Compaq Computer Corp. Rather than maintaining expensive networks of dealers and retailers, he drove a frat-like corps of 20-something tele-sales representatives to revolutionize how PCs were sold.  Dell Box  After the Netscape browser made the Internet mainstream, Dell devised processes to let customers easily configure, order and track PC purchases with no human interaction. Over time, Dell expanded from basic corporate desktops and laptops into the more lucrative server business.  \u201cHe takes it very seriously that his name\u2019s on the side of every box that goes out,\u201d said  Phil McKinney , the former chief technology officer in Hewlett-Packard\u2019s PC division who\u2019s now CEO of CableLabs, a provider of cable technology.  Having forced rivals to adopt its low-cost operating model, Dell established itself as a leader in consumer PCs as well. It developed a brand so strong that the company was able to overcome  snafus  such as the 2003 arrest of Ben Curtis, the company\u2019s \u201cDell Dude\u201d pitchman, after trying to buy marijuana.  More recently, though, Dell has responded more slowly and less successfully to new threats. Years after Apple Inc. unveiled the iPod, Dell introduced its Dell Digital Jukebox music player and then discontinued it three years later.  Phones, Adamo  It started  selling  Dell-branded big-screen TVs in 2003 before scrapping the effort in 2007. A smartphone introduced in 2010 lasted only a year. Dell dabbled in retail kiosks with limited success.  Dell also stumbled with the 2009 introduction of the Adamo, a $2,000 laptop meant to tap into an imagined luxury market for Windows PCs, marketed with modernist black-and-white ads. The product failed to find many buyers, in part because Dell\u2019s sales force focused on low-priced machines to compete with Acer Inc. and Asustek Computer Inc., according to a former executive.  \u201cThat didn\u2019t go so well,\u201d Dell said in a 2011 interview in his private conference room at Dell\u2019s Round Rock, Texas headquarters, speaking in his trademark staccato style. \u201cMistakes were made, lessons were learned, and move on, keep going.\u201d  EMC Considered  Michael Dell was also reluctant to pursue transformative acquisitions.  Kevin Rollins , who was operating chief before becoming CEO in 2004, wanted the company to acquire EMC Corp., the world\u2019s biggest maker of storage computers, according to a person with knowledge of the matter. Dell said the deal was too risky, said the person, who asked not to be identified because the discussions were private.  EMC, with a  market capitalization  north of $50 billion, is a leader in business computing and benefits from its majority ownership of VMware Inc., the biggest maker of software that lets computers run multiple operating systems.  Dell favored more modest deals, acquiring Alienware Corp., which made souped-up PCs for video gamers, in 2006.  Under Dell, the company resorted to cutting costs too aggressively at times to shore up a failing business model, Hayward said.  Intel, Outsourcing  In the early part of the last decade, faced with increasing pressure from low-cost Asian rivals such as Acer and Lenovo Group Ltd., Dell outsourced much of its customer-support operations to India. After a much-publicized backlash, the company pulled some of these call centers back to the U.S.  In 2010, Dell  paid  $100 million to settle accounting-fraud charges brought by the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission that the company had failed to tell investors it accepted payments from Intel Corp. for refusing to use chips from other suppliers. The payments allegedly helped Dell meet earnings projections from 2001 to 2006.  Dell has rarely publicly expressed concerns about his company\u2019s strategic direction. He\u2019s well-liked by other technology CEOs, and is known for rapidly responding to e-mails and for spending hours chatting with analysts over cocktails at investor conferences.  The affable demeanor belies a prickly side. When an analyst showed that the company had lost $38 million using risky currency hedging practices in 1992, Dell threatened to sue.  HP Tweet  When Hewlett-Packard said publicly in 2011 that it might sell off its PC business, Dell sent a  Twitter message  saying, \u201cGoodbye HP, Sorry you don\u2019t want to be in PCs anymore. But we do more than ever.\u201d  Dell handed the CEO reins to Rollins in 2004, and while he remained engaged with the company, he also spent more time on personal pursuits, such as building an 18,500 square-foot  home  in Hawaii and taking a stake in Kona Village Resort, a Hawaiian resort long favored by tech luminaries including  Steve Jobs .  In 2007, with Dell\u2019s business quickly deteriorating, Rollins was pushed out and the company declared the return of Michael Dell -- even though the two executives had been working closely and shared few major differences of opinion, according to executives who know Dell.  Upon his return, Dell set about girding his company for the new realities of the technology landscape, spending $12.7 billion on 18 acquisitions since 2009.  \u201cClearly the next phase of Dell\u2019s evolution as a company is all about growing beyond where we started, and very deeply into services and software and solutions,\u201d Dell said in the 2011 interview. \u201cThat keeps me plenty energized and plenty excited.\u201d  Dell has considered taking the company private for years, talking publicly about the prospect in 2010. Before settling on an LBO he also considered breaking up the company, separating PCs from the areas focused on data centers and other products for businesses, people with knowledge of the matter have said.  A 31 percent decline in his company\u2019s share price in 2012 made a buyout all the more affordable -- and necessary. Over the past year, the money\nflowing into them has surged so much that their assets under\nmanagement are up more than 50 percent, while those of hedge\nfunds as a whole have risen less than 15 percent.  What is driving the growth of activism? The most immediate\nreason is that the funds are performing well, as  a report  from\nCitigroup Inc.\u2019s Financial Strategy and Solutions Group, of\nwhich I am chairman, shows. Since the beginning of 2009,\nactivist hedge funds, on average, have earned an annual return\nafter fees of almost 20 percent, compared with 13 percent for\nthe stock market as a whole and 8 percent for all hedge funds.\n(That\u2019s right: After fees are taken into account, hedge funds\nhave underperformed the market.) The managers of the most\nsuccessful funds are becoming legends by combining outsize\nreturns with colorful personalities.  These funds are also growing in number, and they\u2019re aiming\nfor larger and larger companies. This year, for example,  Carl Icahn  bought a large share of Apple Inc. stock, ValueAct\nHoldings LP has targeted Microsoft Corp., and Trian Fund\nManagement LP has pursued DuPont Co. Although most activist\ncampaigns still occur in the U.S., foreign activity is rising\nrapidly, too.  Even strong stock market performance is no longer\nprotection against an activist effort. This year, more than half\nof targets had outperformed their peers before the activist\ncampaigns began. Activists clearly believe that, with changes,\nsuccessful companies can perform even better in the future.  Added Value   Activists are increasingly turning their attention to\nconglomerates with multiple lines of business and low\ninvestment. And many companies are targeted multiple times; 60\npercent of the companies activists went after this year had been\nthe subject of previous campaigns.  What impact do the activist funds have on the companies\nthey invest in? It would be impossible for activists to earn\nsuch high returns if their campaigns did not increase the value\nof the shares they buy. And that is indeed what happens: On\naverage, from a month prior to the campaign through two years\nafter it starts, targeted companies receive returns about 20\npercent to 30 percent higher than those of their untargeted\npeers.  This average, however, masks substantial variation in the\ntargeted companies, research by the Financial Strategy and\nSolutions Group shows. Indeed, more than half of them experience\nreturns that lag the market. Activists often invest in several\ncompanies simultaneously, and big returns from one more than\noffset weak returns from the others and bring the average well\nabove the market.  Productivity Change  All of this makes you wonder: What lasting differences do\nactivist hedge funds make in the way targeted companies operate\nand in the lives of the people working there?  Alon Brav of Duke University, Wei Jiang of Columbia\nUniversity and Hyunseob Kim of Cornell University  have explored \nthese questions for manufacturing companies in the U.S. On\naverage, the researchers find, activism causes a temporary\ndecline in productivity, presumably as the company reorganizes,\nbut within three years, productivity rises significantly.  That scenario is consistent with the financial returns, and\nresearch shows an important mechanism for the improvement:\nActivists often push for the sale of less productive plants and,\nunder new owners, those plants become noticeably more\nproductive.  What about the effect on workers? Brav and his co-authors\nfind it is decidedly negative. While the workers\u2019 productivity\nrises -- on average, 7 percent -- their hourly wages remain the\nsame.  Furthermore, the number of workers and the hours per worker\nboth fall, for a total decline of more than 10 percent in labor\nhours. Brav and his co-authors conjecture that the workers may\nhave previously enjoyed wages above their market value, and that\nthe activist intervention removes this wage premium. Note also\nthat they examined only averages; given the variation in\nfinancial returns, one might expect the effects on business\nperformance and workers to also vary significantly.  As activists become ever more prominent, and the easier\ntargets are exhausted, their average excess financial returns\nmay diminish. And even (or especially) where activism helps to\nproduce better value, workers do not seem to share in the\nbenefits.  ( Peter Orszag  is vice chairman of corporate and investment\nbanking and chairman of the financial strategy and solutions\ngroup at Citigroup Inc. and a former director of the Office of\nManagement and Budget in the Obama administration.)  To contact the writer of this article:\nPeter Orszag at  orszagbloomberg@gmail.com .  To contact the editor responsible for this article:\nMary Duenwald at   mduenwald@bloomberg.net .","path":".\/2008_2012_msft_bloomberg_news\/activist-investors-help-companies-not-workers.txt"},{"id":34013134,"title":"Apple to Yahoo Deny Providing Direct Access to Spy Agency","released_at":"<date>June 7 2013<\/date> <time>23:42:58<\/time>","content":"U.S. technology providers from  Apple Inc. (AAPL)  to  Yahoo! Inc. (YHOO)  said they don\u2019t give the U.S. government direct access to their systems, responding to newspaper reports of a top-secret electronic surveillance program.  The National Security Agency and the  Federal Bureau  of Investigation access the central servers of nine U.S. Internet companies, extracting audio and video chats, photographs, e-mails, documents and connection logs, the  Washington  Post and the U.K.-based Guardian reported late yesterday, citing documents they obtained.  Code-named PRISM, the program traces its roots to warrantless domestic surveillance efforts under former President  George W. Bush . The nine companies include  Microsoft Corp. (MSFT) ,  Google Inc. (GOOG) ,  Facebook Inc. (FB)  as well as Apple and Yahoo, the Post report said, citing a slide presentation dated April 2013.  \u201cWe have never heard of PRISM,\u201d said Steve Dowling, a spokesman for Cupertino, California-based Apple. \u201cWe do not provide any government agency with direct access to our servers, and any government agency requesting customer data must get a court order.\u201d  The news emerged a day after the Guardian reported that the NSA was culling millions of telephone records from  Verizon Communications Inc. (VZ)  under a clandestine court order. The disclosure of Verizon data collection stirred protests from privacy-rights advocates and renewed questions about the regard President  Barack Obama \u2019s administration has for civil liberties.  Intelligence Briefings  The  American Civil Liberties Union  condemned the Internet surveillance efforts described by the Post as an abuse of government power and called on U.S. lawmakers to investigate.  \u201cUnchecked government surveillance presents a grave threat to democratic freedoms,\u201d ACLU Deputy Legal Director Jameel Jaffer said in an e-mailed statement. \u201cThese revelations are a reminder that Congress has given the executive branch far too much power to invade individual privacy.\u201d  Obama didn\u2019t mention the surveillance reports during a fundraising dinner last night at the Portola Valley,  California , estate of Sun Microsystems Inc. co-founder Vinod Khosla. Today, the president defended the collection of data on U.S. residents\u2019 telephone calls and foreign nationals\u2019 Internet activity, calling the efforts a \u201cmodest encroachment\u201d on privacy that\u2019s been legally authorized by Congress.  Make Choices  \u201cYou can\u2019t have 100 percent security and also then have 100 percent privacy and zero inconvenience,\u201d Obama said in  San Jose . \u201cWe\u2019re going to have to make some choices as a society.\u201d  U.S. Director of National Intelligence James Clapper defended the program as crucial and said procedures ensure only foreign nationals outside the U.S. are targeted.  \u201cInformation collected under this program is among the most important and valuable foreign intelligence information we collect, and is used to protect our nation from a wide variety of threats,\u201d he said in a statement circulated via e-mail by the White House.  Clapper also said that any telephone data collected is subject to court restrictions.  \u201cThe court only allows the data to be queried when there is a reasonable suspicion, based on specific facts, that the particular basis for the query is associated with a foreign terrorist organization,\u201d he said. The program \u201ccannot be used to intentionally target any U.S. citizen\u201d or anyone located within the U.S., Clapper said.  Exponential Growth  The Post said the NSA operation, which began in 2007, has grown exponentially and become the most prolific contributor to the president\u2019s daily intelligence briefing, providing raw material for almost one in seven intelligence reports. The NSA runs computer centers for analyzing huge databases.  An earlier version of the Post report said the companies, \u201cknowingly participate in PRISM operations.\u201d Later versions on the newspaper\u2019s website omitted that language and added new text indicating the companies were unaware of the program.  Acknowledging the companies\u2019 denials, the Post said it\u2019s \u201cpossible that the conflict between the PRISM slides and the company spokesmen is the result of imprecision on the part of the NSA author.\u201d  U.S. agencies have vastly expanded surveillance efforts since 2001 in a bid to avoid a repeat of the Sept. 11 terrorist attacks on  New York  and the Pentagon. The  Bush administration  started the so-called Terrorist Surveillance Program under which agencies began secret electronic surveillance on U.S. phone calls and e-mails without court warrants.  Legal Authorization  In 2008, Congress passed a law codifying parts of the program and authorizing intelligence agencies to get broad electronic surveillance orders from the Foreign Intelligence Surveillance Court.  That law, updating the more than three-decade-old Foreign Intelligence Surveillance Act, lets intelligence agencies monitor the e-mail, Internet activity and phone calls of non-U.S. citizens reasonably believed to be located outside the U.S. and involved in terrorist activities or other crimes. Congress voted last year to extend it until the end of 2017.  The telephone surveillance, reported by the Guardian, was sought by the FBI and approved by the court on April 25. It requires Verizon to provide the NSA with information about calls inside the U.S. and between the U.S. and other countries on a daily and \u201congoing\u201d basis.  \u2018Unauthorized Disclosure\u2019  While Clapper didn\u2019t deny the Post reports that the NSA and FBI operate a separate initiative tapping into Internet companies\u2019 servers, he criticized the release of previously secret information.  \u201cThe unauthorized disclosure of information about this important and entirely legal program is reprehensible and risks important protections for the security of Americans,\u201d he said. The campaign finance picture has shifted since the 2008 race. I say this for two main reasons. First, for the enormously transformative impact MOOCs can have on literally billions of people in the world. Second, for the equally disruptive effect MOOCs will inevitably have on the global education industry.  While at Davos, I was fortunate to attend an amazing panel \u2014 my favorite of the conference \u2014 with a murderer's row of speakers. Moderated by Thomas Friedman of  The New York Times , the list of speakers: Larry Summers, former president of Harvard; Bill Gates; Peter Theil, a partner at Founder's Fund;  Rafael Reif, president of MIT; Sebastian Thrun, CEO of Udacity; Daphne Koller, CEO of Coursera, and a 12-year-old Pakistani girl who has taken a number of Stanford physics classes through Udacity. Below is a collection of some of the highlighted comments from this remarkable panel as well as a couple from audience members who were given an opportunity to comment.  Why this disruption is happening:  Peter Thiel, partner, Founders Fund \n\"In the United States, students don't get their money's worth. There's a bubble in education as out of control as the housing bubble and the tech bubble in the 1990s. Education costs have gone up 400% since 1980. That's the highest escalation of costs--higher than health care. There's now a trillion dollars in student debt. And thanks to the way bankruptcy laws were restructured under George W Bush, you can't get out of the college loan even if you become bankrupt. This is deeply broken.  \"You have to ask yourself, 'What is the nature of education as a good?' Ideally you want it to be learning. But it also functions as insurance. Parents will pay a lot of money for insurance against cracks in our society. Education as insurance has something to be said because it connects to the economy. You know computer science, you can get a job. But education also functions as a tournament. You do well if you go to a top school but for everyone else the diploma is a dunce hat in disguise. People need to understand what they're trying to do? Is it insurance? A tournament? Learning?\" Where we are in the evolution of this change: Larry Summers, former President of Harvard \n\"It's important to remember this really wise quote when thinking about the transition to online education: 'Things take longer to happen than you think they will and then they happen faster than you think they could.' If you had a discussion with dentists on tooth decay in 1947 it would have been about brushing your teeth and dental care, but the most important thing to happen with fighting tooth decay was fluoridated water and this is similar. It's hard to know when it will happen but at some point this will be transformative. The first stage is when it does what was being done before but better. That's what is happening now. But we're going to where we don't need to have two semesters, classes of same length, grading on the basis of things called exams. You can't think of another industry where a list of top 10 providers is perfectly correlated to what it was in 1960.\" Daphne Koller, founder of Coursera \n\"We're at 2.4 million students now. The biggest lesson I've learned on this is I underestimated the amount of impact this would have around the world. I really didn't envision this scale and this impact this quickly.\" Raphael Reif, president of MIT \n\"We manage this transition very carefully. How can MIT charge $50,000 for tuition going forward? Can we justify that in the future? We see three components to MIT- first there's the student life, then there's the classroom instruction, but for us, the projects and labs activity is where real education occurs. But I don't think we can charge that much for tuition in the future and it's a big pressure point for us.\" Bill Gates, chairman of Microsoft \n\"When people first put courses online people thought they could charge money and no one bought them. They put them online but from a global perspective, all these high numbers of students we're hearing about today, the effective number of people who use them is zero. It's not widely used as a percentage of the global population. Our whole notion of 'credential', which means you went somewhere for a number of hours, needs to move to where you can prove you have the knowledge and the quality of these online courses need to improve. Over the next few years the quality will improve. 90% of these courses will be long forgotten and never viewed. Over the next five years this transformation will be phenomenal but only through a pretty brutal winnowing out process.\"  On what an online education world means for hiring and talent for educators: Rafael Reif \n[On the question of how to hire professors in the MOOC era] \"Can you hire MIT professors who know that they need to teach 150,000 people and not 150? We have spectacular researchers who are lousy teachers. That's sad. A teacher in the future will become more like a mentor. The model of on campus education will be more about mentorship and guidance with research as an important factor.\"  We can't presume to know what format will work in the future: Larry Summers \n\"It's important to remember that we're not so good at understanding the subtleties of environments that make them attractive to people. Look at football for example. One way to watch a game is to sit on a cold bench with no good food and bad bathrooms, the other is in your own living room, with replay, and food you like at your convenience. And then ask yourself- which would you guess people pay for? Which do people cheer for? You'd get it wrong. There are aspects of bringing people together in groups that we can't quite understand and judge. The working out of this will depend a lot on formulas for making it attractive and collaborative. And as football example suggests, it won't be immediately obvious what those models are.\" What's next in this space? Bill Gates \n\"Who is going to jump first into granting a degree that doesn't have the seat time requirement that we do today that employers will see as credible? Where does the credibility come from?  Sebastian Thrun, CEO of uDacity \n\"I think the question is how do you make the credential have currency that an employer knows? We've had good success. We have 350 companies who have hired our students. Employers worry about soft skills and we can measure that and it's on equal performance with hard skills. The credential thing is interesting- we launched a class for credit with California schools for remedial math. We priced them at 10-15 percent of what college costs. There are lots of improvements to be made, but the outcome tends to be better today with us.\" Jimmy Wales, founder, Wikipedia \n\"The overall quantity and quality of formal education hasn't changed whereas the informal education has skyrocketed in the last 30 years. People used to go to library and now go to Wikipedia. We haven't really begun to understand the impact on that.\" Muhammad Yunus, Nobel Peace Prize Winner, Founder Grameen Bank \n\"What does this all mean? The technology gives us tremendous power to solve this stark problem all around us. We need to design these so no child is left out of this. What need to ask, what is education after all? We need to resolve that. What are we getting our young people ready for? It's for the purpose of our life. And we need to make sure we give people a purpose to their life. It won't be done by current system. It will be done by people who have nothing to do with current system.\"","path":".\/2008_2012_msft_bloomberg_news\/eight-brilliant-minds-on-the-future-of-online-education.txt"},{"id":84039165,"title":"Klawe Turns Harvey Mudd College Into Haven for Women in Tech","released_at":"<date>September 23 2011<\/date> <time>15:11:37<\/time>","content":"As Harvey Mudd College President\nMaria Klawe strolled her Southern  California  campus recently,\nshe stopped to talk with Lillian de Greef, a senior eager to\ndiscuss her plans for a graduate degree in computer science. Klawe\u2019s transformation of this small liberal arts college\n35 miles east of  Los Angeles  has sent ripples from  Seattle  to\nSilicon Valley, where startups and technology giants are\ndesperate to find talented developers, even as the unemployment\nrate hovers above 9\u00a0percent. If you\nalready have an iPad 2, there\u2019s little need to upgrade.  It isn\u2019t that the new iPad lacks impressive features --most\nnotably, a vastly better display and an ultra-fast Internet-\nconnection option. It\u2019s just that it seems designed to maintain\n Apple (AAPL) \u2019s huge lead in the tablet wars, rather than to extend it.  The closest parallel might be the iPhone 4S, a similarly\nincremental updating of its predecessor. The 4S, though, had one\ngenuinely breakthrough feature: Siri, the voice-based personal\nassistant. For all its improvements, there\u2019s no comparable\ninnovation in this year\u2019s iPad.  The new tablet, which Apple is just calling \u201cthe iPad,\u201d\nis in many ways indistinguishable from its predecessor, the iPad\n2. The pricing is unchanged, ranging from $499 to $829,\ndepending on storage capacity and network options. It\u2019s a wee\nbit thicker -- two-hundredths of an inch -- and less than two\nounces heavier. Otherwise, it\u2019s the same height and width, with\nthe same-sized 9.7-inch screen.  Sweet Pixels  But oh, what a screen. For this new edition, Apple has\nreplaced the previous, perfectly nice one with the same so-\ncalled Retina Display it introduced on the iPhone 4. The new\nscreen provides 2048 x 1536 resolution, which is to say four\ntimes the number of pixels of the old one, and more even than a\nhigh-definition TV set.  While the Retina Display on the iPhone wasn\u2019t an earth-\nshaking advance, the impact is far more evident on the iPad\u2019s\ngreater real estate. Even the text in an e-book is crisper,\nhigh-def video is sharper and photos are crystal clear.  The visual improvements extend to newly enhanced graphics\nprocessing as well as a better photographic experience. Apple \njunked the iPad 2\u2019s primitive rear-facing camera in favor of a \nnew one with a five-megapixel sensor, plus optics and features \nborrowed from the iPhone 4S that include image stabilization \nand the ability to shoot full high-def video. And it\u2019s \nintroducing a $4.99 iPad version of its popular  iPhoto  Mac \napp that, combined with the stunning screen, makes editing\nand sharing photos a pleasure.  Charged Up  In a week of using the new model, I found battery life to\nbe quite comparable to the iPad 2. That doesn\u2019t sound like big\nnews -- but it is. That\u2019s because the new edition introduces\nsupport for the power-hungry 4G  data networks  known as LTE that\nare being rolled out in the U.S. by  Verizon (VZ)  Wireless and AT&T.  Especially in these early days, when the networks aren\u2019t\ncrowded, LTE can deliver thunderous performance. On my test\nmodel, which runs on the AT&T network, I\u2019ve clocked speeds over\n40 megabits per second, which is faster than most home cable-\nmodem connections.  Apple says the iPad provides up to 10 hours of use over Wi-\nFi, and nine hours on a cellular network. Based on my tests,\nthat may actually be a little conservative. After near-constant\nLTE use, including Web surfing and an hour or two of streamed\nvideo, I still had power to spare at the end of the day.  With battery life no longer a concern, the principal issues\naround LTE involve price and coverage. An LTE-equipped iPad\ncosts $130 more than the Wi-Fi-only one, and data plans, which\nvary by carrier, range from $15 to $50 a month. (No long-term\ncontract is needed.) Moreover, LTE is so fast you may find\nyourself consuming more data than you\u2019re used to.  Verizon or  AT&T (T) ?  You\u2019ll also have to choose whether you want a Verizon or\nAT&T model, since their LTE networks aren\u2019t compatible. Verizon\nhas broader coverage and lets you share the connection with\nother devices. But AT&T\u2019s $30-a-month plan allows you more data\nthan Verizon\u2019s, and its fallback network when LTE is unavailable\nis faster.  The new iPad\u2019s 2012 enhancements -- not to mention its wide\nlead over all rivals in terms of the number and quality of\navailable apps -- keep Apple easily ahead of all other tablet-\nmakers. In fact, by keeping the iPad 2 alive and cutting its \nstarting price by $100, to $399, Apple has instantly made it the \nsecond-best tablet you can buy.  When the company launched the iPad 2 a year ago, it was\nremarkable how few changes were needed to keep it the No. 1\ntablet. Since then, devices running  Google (GOOG) \u2019s Android operating\nsystem have flooded the market, while  Microsoft (MSFT)  is poised to\nintroduce a new generation of competitors running the next\nversion of Windows. Yet once again, Apple has -- with a minimum\nof effort -- lapped the field.  ( Rich Jaroslovsky  is a Bloomberg News columnist. The\nopinions expressed are his own.) (AAPL)   Samsung won\u2019t seek injunctions to block sales of\nsmartphones and tablets using its standard-essential patents for\nfive years against companies willing to seek fair licensing\nterms, according to proposals outlined by the European\nCommission in a  statement  today.  \u201cAbuses must be prevented so that standard-setting works\nproperly and consumers do not have to suffer negative\nconsequences from the so-called patent wars,\u201d EU Competition\nCommissioner  Joaquin Almunia  said in the statement. \u201cIf we\nreach a good solution in this case, it will bring clarity to the\nindustry.\u201d  The EU is cracking down on patent abuses as  Google Inc. (GOOG) \u2019s\nMotorola Mobility unit,  Microsoft Corp. (MSFT) , Apple and Samsung trade\nvictories in divergent court rulings across the world on\nintellectual property. Almunia has said he\u2019s targeting \u201crules\nof the game\u201d to prevent companies from unfairly leveraging\ntheir inventions to thwart rivals.  The proposed commitments \u201cwill not affect Samsung\u2019s\ndistribution practices or production capabilities in any way,\u201d\nRhee So-eui, a company spokeswoman in  Seoul , said by e-mail.  \u2018Balanced Approach\u2019  \u201cSamsung is committed to fair and reasonable licensing of\nour technologies and believes a balanced approach to patent\nlicensing will promote innovations to the benefit of consumers\nand the industry,\u201d she said. \u201cWe are confident that the\nproposed commitments are a constructive reflection of this.\u201d  Seeking an injunction on a patent used in a standard\nagreed by an industry may break EU antitrust rules if the\npatent-holder previously promised to license the patents on\nfair, reasonable and non-discriminatory terms and a licensee is\nwilling to pay a fair fee, the commission said in its statement.  Almunia said forthcoming decisions on other standards cases\nwill give more guidance, including two involving  Motorola\nMobility (MMI)  Holdings. \u201cThere are some other elements that will\ncome in the next ones,\u201d he told reporters in Brussels today.  Samsung must negotiate licenses for up to 12 months and\nagree to terms set by a court or an arbitrator if no agreement\ncan be reached. Samsung and a potential licensee will have to\naccept arbitration if they can\u2019t agree on a court or arbitrator.  Reduced Choice  Consumers are harmed by increased prices, reduced product\nchoice and less innovation when companies seek royalty rates or\nbroad cross-licenses that a competitor won\u2019t agree to, the EU\nsaid.  If Samsung\u2019s rivals and customers agree that the company\u2019s\noffer allays antitrust concerns, regulators can make the offer\nbinding on Samsung and end the EU probe as well as any threat of\na fine. Samsung\u2019s commitments would be monitored by an\nindependent trustee. Samsung would risk fines of as much as 10\npercent of yearly revenue if it breaks its pledge.  The EU began probing Samsung last year on injunctions it\ntook in 2011 to block sales of Apple products using Samsung\u2019s 3G\nUMTS patents. Regulators say Apple was willing to license the\npatents on fair terms and Samsung\u2019s injunctions violated\ncompetition rules. Samsung withdraw injunctions in December,\nbefore the EU sent it an antitrust complaint. The commission in May sent a formal complaint to Motorola\nMobility saying it suspects the company is abusing its dominant\nposition by \u201cseeking and enforcing\u201d injunctions against Apple\nin  Germany  based on standard-essential patents. Load it up with full versions of Microsoft\u2019s\nWindows and Office software. Now try running everything at the\nsame time, including the Mac\u2019s operating system, without\ncrashing or slowing things to the speed of the Long Island\nExpressway on a summer weekend.  Parallels Desktop 7 , the latest version of Parallels Inc.\u2019s\nWindows-in-a-Mac software, successfully navigated my little\ntorture test with nary a hiccup. There\u2019s no better solution for\nMac users who want Windows compatibility and don\u2019t mind spending\n$80 extra (plus the cost of Windows itself) to get it.  You don\u2019t need Parallels to run Windows on a Mac. Ever\nsince  Apple Inc. (AAPL)  switched to using the same  Intel Corp. (INTC)  chips\nthat run most Windows personal computers, it has had a free\nprogram called Boot Camp that lets you switch back and forth.  Boot Camp, though, has several limitations. You have to\nchoose which operating system you want to start up, and reboot\nif you want to go back and forth. And there\u2019s no easy way to\nshare files between the two sides, or to transfer information\nfrom one to the other.  Parallels allows the two to co-exist, letting you switch\nbetween them seamlessly, even cutting and pasting between\napplications. You can run an entire PC in a window on your Mac\ndesktop, complete with Windows 7\u2019s \u201cAero\u201d user interface with\nits translucent borders. Or you can choose a mode called\nCoherence that hides Windows, making PC programs feel and behave\nalmost like native Mac applications.  Two Generations Old  To try out the software, I used a year-old 11-inch MacBook\nAir with a now two-generations-old Intel Core 2 Duo processor,\nfour gigabytes of memory and 128 gigabytes of storage. I had\npreviously installed Windows and Office, using Boot Camp to run\nthem when needed.  I started out using Parallels with the Snow Leopard version\nof the Mac\u2019s OS X, then upgraded to the latest version, Lion.\nThe installation process under Snow Leopard went smoothly, with\none exception: a somewhat disconcerting Microsoft message\ninforming me that my fully, honestly bought-and-paid-for copy of\nWindows wasn\u2019t legit.  Parallels said the warning was probably triggered because\nWindows had been installed before its software was. In any\nevent, I was allowed to proceed with the set-up despite my\nimpugned integrity.  Imaginary PC  Recognizing that I had already partitioned the Mac\u2019s flash-\nmemory storage to accommodate the two operating systems,\nParallels incorporated my existing Windows programs and files\ninto its \u201cvirtual machine\u201d -- the imaginary PC it creates\nwithin the Mac environment. If I hadn\u2019t already owned Windows,\nParallels would have allowed me to buy and download a copy from\nits new online Convenience Store, which includes a variety of\nutilities, games and other programs as well.  The software proved to be both low-overhead and low-\nmaintenance. It took up less than a gigabyte of my constrained\nstorage capacity and speedily launched Microsoft programs in\nCoherence mode from a drop-down Windows start menu accessed via\na Parallels icon on the Mac\u2019s top bar.  All my custom macros for Microsoft Word worked without a\nhitch. I was also able to easily run the special software used\nfor accessing the Bloomberg Professional Service, and even ran -\n- slowly --  Take-Two Interactive Software Inc. (TTWO) \u2019s Major League\nBaseball 2K11 game.  Hiding the Seams  Even better, Parallels has successfully hidden many of the\nseams that existed in earlier versions of the program. The Mac\u2019s\ncamera, for instance, can now be shared between Windows and Mac\nprograms without reconfiguring it.  Many of Lion\u2019s new features are enabled for PC programs,\nincluding gesture-based navigation, full-screen mode and the\nability to pin Windows icons to the Launchpad screen. And you\ncan even choose to replace Windows programs\u2019 borders with a Mac\nlook, completing the illusion of complete integration.  In conjunction with the release of Parallels Desktop 7, the\ncompany also upgraded Parallels Mobile, its iPad app ($5 for a\nlimited time, eventually $20) that allows you to remotely\ncontrol your virtual machine and, now, the rest of your Mac as\nwell. In general, I found that the app worked well but had no\nparticular advantage over other services that offer much the\nsame functionality.  Linux and Lion  If you have a more robust Mac than my little Air, you can\nuse Parallels Desktop 7 to manage multiple virtual machines --\nnot just Windows but Linux and even Lion, which could prove\nuseful to Mac developers seeking to try out code in a controlled\nsetting.  For us normal people, though, its value comes in the\nmeshing of the Windows applications we may need for business\nwith the pleasures of the Mac hardware and operating system. If\nit doesn\u2019t completely end the endless Windows-Mac debate, it\ncomes pretty close: Just imagine one of those \u201cI\u2019m a Mac, I\u2019m a\nPC\u201d commercials with the two of them walking off arm-in-arm.  ( Rich Jaroslovsky  is a Bloomberg News columnist. The\nopinions expressed are his own.) Baucus released a draft bill yesterday that would lower the\ncorporate tax rate by an unspecified amount, end a rule that has\nencouraged companies to accumulate about $2 trillion in earnings\nin their foreign subsidiaries and impose a 20 percent tax on\nthose stockpiled profits.  The Finance panel chairman, who has been criticized by\nfellow Democrats for being too friendly to business, is\nencountering opposition from some of the multinational\ncorporations he has courted. The trade council, whose board of directors includes\n Microsoft Corp. (MSFT)  and  United Technologies Corp. (UTX) , said it was\n\u201cdisappointed\u201d in Baucus\u2019s plan.  \u2018Penalize Multinationals\u2019  \u201cThis draft appears to penalize multinationals and will\nmake it more difficult for companies to compete globally,\u201d\nCatherine Schultz, the group\u2019s vice president for  tax policy ,\nsaid in a statement.  Baucus, of Montana, who plans to release drafts on other\ntax topics today and tomorrow, wants to make the biggest tax\ncode changes since 1986 before he leaves Congress at the end of\n2014. He and his House Republican counterpart,  Dave Camp  of\nMichigan, have been stymied by the partisan divide over whether\nthe government should collect more revenue.  \u201cI\u2019m just trying to make something happen by taking the\ninitiative,\u201d Baucus said yesterday. \u201cTax reform has more\npolitical potency than a lot of people at first believe.\u201d  Technically Complex  The international tax system is one of the most technically\ncomplex areas of the U.S. tax code and potential changes are\nbeing watched closely by companies that have significant global\nbusinesses, including Pfizer Inc., Apple Inc. and The  Procter &\nGamble Co. (PG)   For more than two years, many companies have been lobbying\nCongress for a system that would lessen the tax burden on U.S.\ncompanies\u2019 overseas income. They make the argument that most\nother industrialized countries don\u2019t require their companies to\npay home-country taxes on foreign income.  Baucus\u2019s plan would make it harder for companies to shift\nprofits from the U.S. and require a type of minimum tax that\nwould limit the benefit of earning income in low-tax countries.  Some of the criticism stems from the plan\u2019s vagueness on\nthe corporate tax rate. Unlike Camp\u2019s proposal, which favors a\n25 percent rate without specifying how he would offset the\nbudgetary cost, Baucus has said only that he hopes to get the\nrate below 30 percent, down from 35 percent now. Corporations\nwould find the changes more palatable with a lower rate.  Groups aligned with labor unions, such as Americans for Tax\nFairness and Citizens for Tax Justice, said yesterday that\nBaucus\u2019s plan doesn\u2019t go far enough because he\u2019s insisting that\ncorporate tax changes should be revenue-neutral instead of\nraising the taxes companies pay.  Lew\u2019s Support  Baucus garnered supportive or neutral statements from\nTreasury Secretary Jacob J. Lew and at least four members of his\ncommittee -- Democrats  Ron Wyden  of Oregon,  Sherrod Brown  of\nOhio and  Jay Rockefeller  of West Virginia, along with Republican\nRob Portman of Ohio.  Baucus\u2019s plan would make it tougher for companies to claim\nthat profits are earned in low-tax countries, said Ed Kleinbard,\na tax-law professor at the University of  Southern California .  Under the Baucus plan, technology and pharmaceutical\ncompanies would no longer be able to pay single-digit effective\ntax rates on their foreign income, he said.  \u2018Income Strategies\u2019  \u201cThe package reduces the opportunities for large-scale\nstateless income strategies both by U.S. multinationals and by\nforeign multinationals doing business in the United States,\u201d\nsaid Kleinbard, a former chief of staff of the congressional\nJoint Committee on Taxation.  Under current law, U.S. companies owe taxes at the federal\nrate of 35 percent on all income they earn around the world.\nThey receive tax credits for payments to foreign governments and\ncan defer U.S. taxation until they repatriate the money.  That system has encouraged companies to accumulate untaxed\nearnings in foreign subsidiaries. It also creates incentives for\ncompanies to move intellectual property out of the U.S. and into\nlow-tax jurisdictions.  Many other countries, including the U.K. and Japan, have\nshifted to what\u2019s known as a territorial system in which\ncompanies owe little or no taxes on their foreign income. In the\nopposite direction, industrialized countries have been moving to\nprevent companies from using accounting maneuvers to shift\nincome outside their borders.  The Baucus plan is \u201ca cautious, modest step in the\ndirection of territorial taxation,\u201d said Alan Viard, a resident\nscholar at the  American Enterprise Institute , a research group\nin Washington that advocates for small government.  Hybrid System  Baucus, in suggesting a hybrid between current law and a\nterritorial system, is proposing two options for his minimum\ntax. The first would tax all income from foreign sales and\nservices immediately at a rate equal to 80 percent of the new\nU.S. rate.  Baucus has said he wants a new tax rate of less than 30\npercent. If it were set at 28 percent, for example, the minimum\ntax would be set at 22.4 percent.  That rate would apply to a company\u2019s earnings in each\njurisdiction, so that companies operating in high-tax areas\nwould owe no incremental U.S. tax on their foreign earnings. A\ncompany operating in Ireland, by contrast, would effectively\nhave to pay the U.S. the difference between the Irish tax rate\nof 12.5 percent and 22.4 percent.  The second option would set a lower minimum tax rate, 60\npercent of the U.S. rate, while narrowing the definition of\nincome eligible to only income from active business operations.\nOther income would be taxed at the full U.S. rate immediately.  Accumulated Earnings  The earnings that companies have accumulated under the\ncurrent system would be taxed at 20 percent over eight years,\nregardless of whether companies have the money in liquid form\nand regardless of whether they bring it back to the U.S.  That tax would generate more than $200 billion, and Baucus\nhasn\u2019t decided what to do with the revenue. Some could be used\nto ease the transition to the new system. Some could be used, as\nPresident  Barack Obama  has suggested, for infrastructure.  Baucus is seeking comments from companies and senators by\nJan. 17.  Senator  Orrin Hatch  of Utah, the top Republican on the\nFinance Committee, said he disagreed with Baucus\u2019s decision to\nrelease the drafts while Democrats are proposing tax increases\nin a budget conference committee.  Today\u2019s draft is expected to address tax administration\nissues, including tax filing and  identity theft . Tomorrow\u2019s\nproposal is expected to focus on capital-cost recovery and\ndepreciation rules. Companies that work to establish standards have the advantage of knowing their inventions have to be used in all products in an industry. In turn, they pledge to license any relevant patents on fair and reasonable terms.  Economic Role  There\u2019s a risk standard-patent holders could be gaining \u201cundue leverage and engaging in \u2018patent hold-up,\u2019 i.e. asserting the patent to exclude an implementer of the standard from a market to obtain a higher price for use of the patent than would have been possible before the standard was set,\u201d Froman said.  \u201cThe administration is committed to promoting innovation and economic progress, including through providing adequate and effective protection and enforcement of intellectual property rights,\u201d Froman said. That type of battery is used in\nhearing aids, garage-door openers and small electronic devices. The visa, intended for skilled workers, allowed him to stay in the U.S. after earning a master\u2019s degree in electrical engineering from the  University of Alabama  in 1991. Later, the H-1B provided a steady supply of foreign-born employees for a technology-services company where he worked as an executive.  Today, Gupta is an outspoken critic of the program that helped start his career and that technology moguls, including  Microsoft Corp. (MSFT) \u2019s  Bill Gates  and  Facebook Inc. (FB) \u2019s  Mark Zuckerberg , want Congress to expand.  \u201cSomewhere along the way, the program\u2019s been hijacked,\u201d says Gupta, 45, chief executive officer of Systems in Motion, a closely held company based in Newark,  California .  As lawmakers consider the first major overhaul of U.S. immigration law since 1986, the high-technology industry is divided over the H-1B program. While both industry leaders and startups seek the world\u2019s most innovative thinkers, outsourcing firms, hired by corporate clients to help cut costs, got more than half the 85,000 visas available last year.  Gupta, a native of  India  who\u2019s now a U.S. citizen, says the H-1B is leading to \u201ceconomic abuse.\u201d Outsourcing companies -- such as  Cognizant Technology Solutions Corp. (CTSH)  and  Infosys Ltd. (INFO)  -- use the program to import thousands of lower-paid information- technology workers instead of employing Americans, even as the program fails to meet the talent demand at firms such as  Google Inc. (GOOG)  and Facebook, he says.  His company -- using American workers based in Ann Arbor,  Michigan  -- competes against the outsourcing companies.  Surging Demand  The demand for the visas was underscored this month, when companies exceeded the annual H-1B cap within five days of the start of the annual application process, meaning a government lottery will be held later this year to determine visa winners.  The outsourcing companies\u2019 dominance of the H-1B visa pool is \u201ccreating a big squeeze,\u201d says Luis Arbulu, managing director of Hattery, a San Francisco-based venture capital and product-development firm. \u201cIt\u2019s putting pressure on everyone, from the Googles and Intels of the world to startups.\u201d  The inflow of H-1Bs -- more than enough workers each year to staff a new Apple or Google -- also is hurting American workers, some studies show. Skilled immigrants using H-1Bs and other visas take one-third to one-half of new IT jobs each year, and their presence is keeping inflation-adjusted industry wages at late-1990s levels, according to  a study  by the labor union- funded  Economic Policy Institute  in  Washington .  Raising Cap  Congress created the H-1B program in 1990 to help U.S. companies fill job vacancies with skilled foreign workers. Proposed legislation drafted by a bipartisan group of eight senators would raise the annual visa cap to 135,000 and allow for further expansion to 180,000 depending upon economic conditions.  The draft bill also aims to discourage companies from outsourcing computer jobs via the H-1B route by barring the program\u2019s heaviest users from obtaining additional visas and raising fees for \u201cH-1B-dependent\u201d employers. And it would require companies to advertise the jobs first before hiring foreign workers.  \u201cMore home-grown American talent is something we all should applaud,\u201d Senator  Richard Durbin  of Illinois said at a Judiciary Committee hearing on April 22.  Two Populations  From its inception, the H-1B program has included two different populations: global all-stars who command salaries well in excess of $100,000 to develop products, and journeymen engineers working for outsourcing firms that take over computer operations for clients, including  JPMorgan Chase & Co. (JPM) ,  Citigroup Inc. (C)  and Commerzbank AG.  \u201cWe\u2019re very, very different companies,\u201d says Damien Patton, chief executive of social media startup Banjo, which employs several H-1B holders. \u201cWe\u2019re your innovators. They\u2019re your -- I don\u2019t know -- your labor pools.\u201d  Cognizant, of Teaneck, New Jersey, the largest single user of  H-1B visas  in fiscal 2012, says its use of employees based in both the U.S. and India allows its more than 820 clients to benefit from \u201cintellectual arbitrage\u201d -- the ability to tap technology specialists in both countries. The company\u2019s share price has doubled over the past five years while the Standard & Poor\u2019s 500 Stock Index has risen less than 14 percent.  More H-1Bs are needed because the tech industry can\u2019t find enough top American computer experts, industry executives say. The jobless rate in March for workers in computer and mathematical occupations was 3.5 percent, according to the Bureau of Labor Statistics, compared with the national figure of  7.6 percent .  10,000 Openings  Four companies --  International Business Machines Corp. (IBM) ,  Intel Corp. (INTC) , Microsoft and  Oracle Corp. (ORCL)  -- have 10,000 U.S. job openings, according to the Silicon Valley Leadership Group, an industry lobby.  Potential workers with the best credentials enjoy a seller\u2019s market. On the Palo Alto campus of  Stanford University , recruiters line up outside the Gates Computer Science Building - - named for Microsoft co-founder Bill Gates -- to hand out pamphlets advertising job openings.  \u201cI got one,\u201d said Mehran Sahami, an associate professor of computer science. \u201cI said, \u2018I already have a job!\u2019 But, our students come out with multiple job offers.\u201d  H-1Bs provide significant numbers of skilled workers for some of the country\u2019s top technology firms. About 5 percent of  Intel (INTC) \u2019s 53,000 U.S. employees hold such visas, according to  Peter Muller , government-relations director for the computer chip maker. \u201cWe depend on it,\u201d he said in a phone interview.  Constant Search  Skilled workers from overseas can be especially critical for startups, which have less of a margin for error in filling out their small staffs.  At Banjo, Patton employs 16 corporate recruiters and a team of immigration attorneys in a constant search for employees. The company, which makes a location-based social media application, competes with Google,  Netflix Inc. (NFLX)  and PayPal Inc. for talent and often can\u2019t find American workers with the skills it needs.  Banjo requires computer specialists conversant in state-of- the-art programming languages. Many American workers have outdated skills or are older and thus unlikely to adapt to the demands of a startup, he says.  \u201cWe won\u2019t hire someone who\u2019s marginal,\u201d Patton says. \u201cWe don\u2019t hire 6s or 7s. We hire 9s and 10s.\u201d  About one-quarter of the 20-month old startup\u2019s 25-person staff holds an H-1B visa.  Dying Languages  Hattery\u2019s Arbulu, 39, a veteran of six years at Google, says he can\u2019t use middle-aged computer scientists who cut their teeth on dead or dying programming languages such as Cobol or Fortran.  \u201cNow, it\u2019s Python, HTML 5, Ruby-on-Rails,\u201d he says, referring to three cutting-edge programming tools. \u201cThey didn\u2019t exist 10 years ago.\u201d  The startups\u2019 argument is echoed by a 2012 Microsoft  strategy paper  that identifies \u201cthe best and the brightest innovators in the world\u201d as the intended recipients of the additional H-1B visas.  Yet Microsoft and other major companies only get a minority of the annual H-1B allotment. The biggest users of the program are tech-outsourcing companies, such as Cognizant, Tata Consultancy Services and Infosys.  Cognizant has streamlined IT operations for six of the top 10 U.S. banks, including JPMorgan, which named the company one of its top suppliers for 2005. Four of the 10 largest European Union institutions also rely on Cognizant.  Indian Nationals  \u201cThe vast majority\u201d of the business and technology relying on visas and work permits, the company said in its 2012 10-K filing.  Alan Alper, a  Cognizant (CTSH)  spokesman, declined to answer questions about H-1Bs beyond a prepared statement saying the proposed legislation would \u201cdo more harm than good to our economic recovery, global competitiveness and customer service.\u201d  Spokesmen for Tata and Infosys weren\u2019t immediately available for comment.  Critics of the H-1B program, such as Ron Hira, a professor at the Rochester Institute of Technology in  New York , say those companies capitalize on immigration-law loopholes to undercut American workers.  They do so by employing computer specialists from India who earn 15 percent to 20 percent less than comparable U.S. workers, according to Norman Matloff, a computer science professor at the  University of California , Davis. A 2011 Government Accountability Office  report  found that 54 percent of H-1Bs went to workers who were paid \u201centry-level wages.\u201d  Wage Pressure  For American workers, the availability of foreign labor puts pressure on wages and working conditions.  Lee Cook, 58, of Durham,  North Carolina , has felt the effects firsthand. Since taking early retirement from IBM in 2009, Cook has worked on contract jobs performing IT assignments for employers such as Bank of America Corp. and the U.S. Department of  Homeland Security .  The availability of H-1B visa holders allows employers to offer less and demand more, he says. If Cook balks at relocating or working without benefits, foreign competitors will be happy to accept.  \u201cThey\u2019ll be in the North Pole on Monday if there\u2019s a job,\u201d Cook says.  Almost four years ago, Gupta opted to put his knowledge of outsourcing to work building a business model based on domestic labor. Instead of using foreign workers, he hires a mix of new college graduates and laid-off automotive engineers to handle IT projects. The stock change would create a new class of nonvoting\nshares that will be distributed to existing shareholders in what\nis effectively a 2-for-1 stock split. Google aims to prevent employee stock compensation and\nstock-based acquisitions from diluting the voting power of its\nfounders. The  Mountain View , California-based company wants the\nflexibility to be able to make long-term investments, using its\nshares, without the risk of losing control. The move builds on\nGoogle\u2019s dual-class stock structure, created when the company\nwent public in 2004, that already limited investor influence.  \u201cWe have put our hearts into Google and hope to do so for\nmany more years to come,\u201d Chief Executive Officer  Larry Page \nand co-founder  Sergey Brin  said today in a statement posted\nonline. \u201c So we want to ensure that our corporate structure can\nsustain these efforts and our desire to improve the world.\u201d  First Quarter  First-quarter profit, excluding certain costs, was $10.08 a\nshare, the company said on  its website . Analysts had  projected \n$9.64 on average, according to data compiled by Bloomberg.\nExcluding revenue passed on to partner sites, sales rose to\n$8.14 billion, matching estimates.  Page, who became CEO a year ago, has pushed Google deeper\ninto display advertising and mobile services. This year the\ncompany will account for 16.5 percent of the U.S. market for\ndisplay ads, which include banners and videos, according to\nEMarketer Inc. By next year, Google is projected to grab almost\n20 percent, unseating Facebook Inc. as the market leader.  \u201cThe viability of Google is still very, very strong,\u201d\nsaid Ron Josey, an analyst at ThinkEquity LLC in  New York . He\nrecommends buying the stock, which he doesn\u2019t own himself.\n\u201cThere\u2019s still a lot of room for growth across its multiple\nbusinesses.\u201d  Google\u2019s shares  were little changed in late trading after\nthe announcement. They had risen 2.4 percent to $651.01 at the\nclose in New York.  \u2018Google\u2019s Story\u2019  The desire to maintain control has always been a driving\nforce at Google, said  Colin Gillis , an analyst at BGC Partners\nLP in New York.  \u201cThat\u2019s been Google\u2019s story,\u201d he said.  While the new proposal will be subject to a vote at\nGoogle\u2019s annual meeting on June 21, Page, Brin and Chairman  Eric Schmidt  control the majority of voting power.  \u201cWe expect it to pass,\u201d  David Drummond , Google\u2019s chief\nlegal officer, said in the statement.  Investors will receive one share of the new stock for each\none they hold. So a share valued at $600 when the split takes\neffect would become two shares, each valued at $300. Unlike with\na typical stock split, though, voting power in the company won\u2019t\nchange, said  Charles Elson , director of the University of\n Delaware \u2019s John L. Weinberg Center for Corporate Governance.  \u201cA true stock split would give the holder a share with the\nsame voting right as the share they held,\u201d Elson said. \u201cThis is\nmore of a stock dividend.\u201d  Google Paranoia?  Paul Hodgson , a researcher at  GovernanceMetrics\nInternational Inc. , a  corporate-governance  consulting firm in\nNew York, said the approach isn\u2019t ideal because it puts\nunnecessary limits on shareholders.  \u201cThat is anti-best practice as far as best governance, but\nso was the dual-class structure in the first IPO,\u201d Hodgson said.\n\u201cThere are plenty of companies that have a single class of\nshares, one vote per share, and they aren\u2019t paranoid that\nshareholders are going to somehow influence the future strategy\nof the company.\u201d  Page and Brin said they recognize that some people won\u2019t\nsupport the change.  \u201cWe understand that other companies have been very\nsuccessful with more traditional governance models,\u201d they said\nin the statement. \u201cBut after careful consideration with our\nboard of directors, we have decided that maintaining this\nfounder-led approach is in the best interests of Google, our\nshareholders and our users.\u201d  Cash Holdings  Some investors have been asking Google to consider a cash\ndividend or a stock buyback. The company has $49.3 billion in\ncash and short-term investments, up from $44.6 billion in the\n previous quarter .  When asked why Google isn\u2019t returning cash to its\nshareholders, Chief Financial Officer Patrick Pichette said the\nmoney could be used for strategic investments, such as the\nplanned $12.5 billion  acquisition  of Motorola Mobility Holdings\nInc. He said there were nothing new to announce on that front.  Google still gets most of  its revenue  from Internet-search\nads -- the text links that appear in query results. The average\ncost per click declined 12 percent in the first quarter after\nfalling 8 percent in the fourth quarter. The number of paid\nclicks rose about 39 percent.  The company posted first-quarter  net income  of $2.89\nbillion, or $8.75 a share, compared with $1.8 billion, or $5.51\na share, a year earlier.  Mobile search ads have become a bigger piece of Google\u2019s\nbusiness. Companies will probably commit 23 percent of their\nsearch-based ad spending to mobile devices by the end of this\nyear, according to  Marin Software , which helps manage about $3.5\nbillion annually in online ads. Jonathan Blackman and Carmine Boccuzzi, partners at  New\nYork \u2019s  Cleary Gottlieb  Steen & Hamilton LLP, have represented\nArgentina in litigation that began in 2002. The two share a\nhistory with U.S. District Judge Thomas Griesa, the  Manhattan \njurist who has presided over the fate of billions of dollars of\nArgentine debt over the same period.  The work, on behalf of a government that has criticized and\nignored Griesa, has put the lawyers in a difficult position with\nthe 82-year-old judge who oversees litigation over the defaulted\nbonds. Their conflict with opposing counsel and even the judge\nmay only intensify as the landmark case heads toward a dramatic\nhearing before a federal appeals court early in the new year.  At a Nov. 9 court conference, Griesa asked Boccuzzi about\npress statements by Argentine President Cristina Fernandez De Kirchner and Economy Minister Hernan Lorenzino that the Republic\nwouldn\u2019t pay what it called the \u201cvulture funds\u201d that are\ntrying to collect on the defaulted bonds.  \u201cIs that the position of the president of the Republic?\u201d\nGriesa asked. \u201cIs that the position of the economic minister,\nMr. Boccuzzi?\u201d  Argentina\u2019s Defiance  Boccuzzi made several attempts to argue that Argentina\u2019s\nofficials weren\u2019t publicly announcing their defiance of Griesa\u2019s\ncourt and the  U.S. Court of Appeals  in New York. More recently they\njoined forces to challenge California Proposition 8, the voter-\napproved measure that banned gay marriage in that state and is\nnow before the U.S. Supreme Court.  NML Capital  Olson represents Elliott Management Corp.\u2019s NML Capital\nLtd., which is trying to collect on its defaulted bonds in a\ncase involving $1.3 billion of debt and interest. Boies\nrepresents a group of investors who traded their defaulted bonds\nfor new ones, at a discount, when Argentina restructured its\ndebt.  Argentina issued the bonds beginning in 1994. Since the\n2001 default, its government has refused to make any payments on\nprincipal or interest.  In 2005 and 2010, Argentina offered an exchange to holders\nof the defaulted bonds. The investors could trade for new\nexchange bonds, at a discount of as much as 75 percent. Holders\nof more than 91 percent of Argentina\u2019s defaulted debt\nparticipated, according to the appeals court. Argentina has made\nall required payments on the exchange bonds while continuing to\nrefuse payment to the holdout bondholders.  Some of the holders of the defaulted bonds bought them\nbefore they were repudiated by Argentina and have held them\nsince. Others, including  Paul Singer \u2019s Elliott Management and\nAurelius Capital Management, bought the bonds later, as\ndistressed debt. They are the investors Argentina\u2019s officials\ncall \u201cvultures.\u201d  Court\u2019s Order  The U.S. Court of Appeals in New York on Oct. 26 ruled that\nArgentina must pay the holdouts if it goes forward with\nscheduled payments to holders of the exchange bonds, affirming\nrulings by Griesa. The appeals court noted Argentina\u2019s\n\u201ccontinual disregard\u201d of the rights of its creditors and the\nauthority of the U.S. courts considering the litigation. The\ncourt sent the case back to Griesa to clarify two issues.
