Griesa\u2019s Nov. 21 ruling that Argentina had to pay $1.3\nbillion into an escrow account if it went ahead with the \nscheduled payments of about $3 billion sparked a rout in \nArgentine bonds and prompted Fitch to cut ratings on the \ncountry\u2019s debt.  Nixon Appointee  Griesa was appointed to the bench in 1972 by President\n Richard Nixon , a Republican. In New York, he\u2019s one of about 40\njudges in the federal courthouse in Manhattan. In Argentina,\nhe\u2019s famous for his rulings in the case.  In 2010, when Griesa refused to block an $18.3 billion bond\nswap, he was portrayed as a hero in Buenos Aires newspapers.\nLater, when he ruled in favor of a bid by NML Capital to seize\n$105 million in Argentine assets held in New York, an Argentine\nbusiness daily printed a caricature of him with a vulture on his\nshoulder.  Boccuzzi and Blackman are experts on laws that give foreign\ncountries immunity from being sued in the U.S. under some\ncircumstances, a key defense for Argentina. While many investors\nhave won judgments for the money they claim the country owes\nthem on their bonds, they\u2019ve had much less success in trying to\ncollect on the government\u2019s assets located in the U.S. and\nelsewhere.  Boccuzzi, who received his undergraduate and law degrees\nfrom  Yale University , joined Cleary Gottlieb in 1994 and became\na partner nine years later. The process starts in China, where pallets of iPhones are moved from factories in unmarked containers accompanied by a security detail. The containers are then loaded onto trucks and shipped via pre-bought airfreight space, including on old Russian military transports. The journey ends in stores where the world's biggest technology company makes constant adjustments based on demand, said people who have worked on Apple's logistics and asked not to be identified because the process is secret. The multi-pronged operation has been built up under Cook, who oversaw Apple's supply chain before being tapped as Steve Jobs's successor in 2011. Getting iPhones seamlessly moved from factories to customers is critical for the Cupertino, California-based company, which derives more than half of its annual revenue from the flagship product. Apple also relies on a sales spike after a product's release. It sold more than 5 million units in the debut weekend for the iPhone 5 last year. \"It's like a movie premiere,\" said Richard Metzler, chairman of the Transportation Marketing and Communications Association and a former executive at FedEx and other logistics companies. \"It all needs to arrive at the exact same time everywhere.\" The task is even more challenging this year, with Apple adding new iPhone models -- including a lower-priced smartphone -- and colors. The company has signed a  deal with NTT DoCoMo in Japan  and is also  close to adding China Mobile , which would boost Apple's customer base by hundreds of millions. Any snafu can mean lost sales or increased costs. Steve Dowling, a spokesman for Apple, declined to comment. Apple's worldwide logistics operation is now overseen by Michael Seifert, an Amazon.com veteran who joined the company in 2010. He reports up through the organization to Jeff Williams, Apple senior vice president of operations who runs the company's supply chain. The logistics for a new gadget start months before it is unveiled, said the people with knowledge of the process. Apple first coordinates flights and trucks to move components from suppliers to  assembly plants in China . Teams from sales, marketing, operations and finance collaborate to forecast how many devices the company expects to sell, said the people. The internal estimate is crucial. An example of how that can go wrong is  Microsoft's recent $900 million writedown  because of unsold Surface tablets. Microsoft, the world's largest software maker, is now  buying Nokia , adding employees with more experience building such hardware products. \"Software is a different deal altogether than an actual physical product that is going to be sold,\" said Metzler. \"There are a lot more steps and different disciplines.\" Once a forecast is made, millions of iPhones are manufactured, said the people with knowledge of the process. The handsets remain in China while Apple's software team at headquarters  finishes work on the iOS software  that runs on the device, said a former Apple manager who declined to be named because the process is private. Once a final version is finished, the software is loaded on the phones. Before Apple's formal unveiling on stage, iPhones are shipped to distribution centers around the world, including Australia, China, the Czech Republic, Japan, Singapore, the U.K. and the U.S., said one of the people with knowledge of the matter. Security personnel are with the devices every step of the way, from truck depots, airports, customs and storage warehouses until the product is finally unveiled, two people said. FedEx ships Apple handsets to the U.S. mainly using Boeing 777s, according to Satish Jindel, a logistics-industry consultant and president of SJ Consulting Group. Those planes can make the 15-hour flight from China to the main U.S. hub for freight shipments in Memphis, Tennessee, without refueling, Jindel said. The 777s can carry about 450,000 iPhones and cost about $242,000 to charter, with fuel accounting for more than half the expense. Apple has used less conventional aircrafts to transport its gadgets in the past. Before the debut of new iPods last decade, Apple packed an old Russian transporter plane with the media players to get them to stores on time, said a person familiar with the flight. The iPhone's high price and light weight mean Apple can still reap big margins while packing many devices into air shipments, instead of using sea cargo as was historically the case with consumer electronics, said Mike Fawkes, a former supply-chain executive at Hewlett-Packard. \"If you have a product like a printer that costs $100 and is pretty big, you can't air ship that because it destroys the economics,\" he said.  Once the iPhone goes on sale, Apple must manage the flow of orders from people looking for a specific color, memory size and even engravings, said the people with knowledge of the matter. The iPhone 5S will come in three colors and the 5C in five. Online orders are received at factories in China, where workers customize the smartphones and put them on pallets with others destined for customers in a similar part of the world. \"People like to talk about how the key to Apple's success is their products,\" said Fawkes. \"While I agree with that, their operational capabilities, and their ability to scale and bring new products to market efficiently, are unprecedented and a huge competitive advantage.\" By monitoring sales from its retail stores, website and third-party resellers, Apple reallocates handsets based on where demand is strongest, one of the people said. IPhones coming off the assembly line in China originally destined for retail stores in Europe could be used to fill a bump in online orders, for instance. The process involves crunching a lot of data. \"The information about a shipment is as important as the physical movement,\" said Metzler, the former FedEx exec. \"If you know where your inventory is at all times, you can make changes along the way.\" Once the launch madness subsides, it's not quite time to celebrate at Apple. Following every release, the company's logistics team debriefs at the Apple headquarters to study what went wrong, two of the people said. AuthenTec makes fingerprint sensors that corporations use to secure access to  computer networks , technology that it has been expanding for use on smartphones and tablets. Apple is stepping up efforts to demonstrate its devices are safe from malware and other threats as the iPhone and iPad gain popularity with business customers and in case it decides to introduce features for making payments with a phone.  \u201cAuthentication is a giant padlock or dead bolt on the front door of an iPhone and iPad,\u201d said Sathvik Krishnamurthy, the president and chief executive officer of Voltage Security Inc., a maker of iPhone and iPad e-mail security technology. A fingerprint is a much safer feature than the current four-digit pin customers use to unlock iPhones and iPads, he said. \u201cIt\u2019s a natural addition.\u201d  Higher Bid  AuthenTec surged 66 percent to $8.42 at the close in  New York , the biggest gain since its 2007 initial public offering, suggesting investors may anticipate a higher bid. Apple increased 1.8 percent to $585.16.  The deal may hurt Samsung Electronics Co., Apple\u2019s biggest competitor in smartphone sales, which  last week  said it would start using AuthenTec\u2019s technology in new devices. Samsung is unlikely to continue with plans to use AuthenTec under Apple\u2019s ownership, said Jay Chaudhry, CEO of  Zscaler Inc. , a computer security company.  Given that, Samsung might consider bidding for AuthenTec, said Richard Shannon, an analyst at Craig-Hallum Capital Group, who has a buy rating on AuthenTec\u2019s shares. Like Apple, Samsung may need to upgrade security features on its devices, he said.  \u201cMobile devices are becoming more Internet and data centric, which means they are no different in some ways than a PC, which exposes them to risks related to security,\u201d said Anil Doradla, an analyst at William Blair & Co. who has a buy rating on Apple\u2019s shares. \u201cBy acquiring this company, Apple is basically going after the security portfolio.\u201d  Breakup Fee  AuthenTec\u2019s other customers include  Nokia Oyj (NOK1V) , Cisco Systems Inc., and  Texas Instruments Inc. (TXN) , according to the company\u2019s website company.  The deal, which still requires the approval of shareholders and regulators, is expected to close in the third quarter of this year, according to the filing. AuthenTec would pay Apple a breakup fee of $10.95 million if it accepts a superior proposal.  Apple might deploy AuthenTec\u2019s technology to introduce new ways to make purchases with an iPhone, said Chaudhry. Fingerprints could be used in lieu of signatures, he said.  \u201cIn mobile payments, strong authentication becomes very important,\u201d Chaudhry said. \u201cNow Apple will own that technology and it becomes easier for them to embed it in their devices.\u201d  Security Policy  Adding AuthenTec\u2019s technology also will help Apple increase sales to businesses, whose information-technology departments require more security capabilities than consumers using the devices for personal use, said Krishnamurthy of Voltage Security.  \u201cIf your security policy says you need a 15-character password with numbers and special characters, you\u2019re going to lose a lot of usability with that policy,\u201d Krishnamurthy said. \u201cBy doing that with fingerprint authentication you have a simple way to recognize users and bypass that cumbersome process.\u201d  Steve Dowling, a spokesman for Cupertino, California-based Apple, declined to discuss the company\u2019s strategy.  \u201cApple acquires smaller technology companies from time to time,\u201d Dowling said. \u201cWe generally do not disclose our purpose or plans.\u201d  Apple has made 12 purchases in the past five years, according to data compiled by Bloomberg. They include this year\u2019s purchase of Anobit Technologies Ltd., an Israeli company that makes flash memory drives for the iPhone and iPad, and Chomp Inc., a maker of a search engine for discovering iPhone and iPad applications.  Its biggest purchase was the $4.5 billion purchase of a patent portfolio from Nortel Networks Corp. last year, which Apple did jointly with Microsoft Corp. and other technology companies.  Piper Jaffray & Co. was AuthenTec\u2019s financial adviser, with Alston & Bird LLP acting as legal adviser. House Ways and Means Committee Chairman  Sander Levin  and Senator  Charles Grassley , the Senate Finance\nCommittee\u2019s top Republican, both called for the U.S. to file a\ntrade complaint.  \n China\u2019s currency has \u201cappreciated only modestly\u201d since\nlast month\u2019s policy shift, he said. \u201cThere is no real question\nthat China\u2019s exchange-rate policy is unfair, contributes to\nglobal trade imbalances, and costs the United States jobs and\neconomic growth, particularly in the manufacturing sector.\u201d  \n The report increases the chances of an October showdown,\nwhile also pushing off calls for action until January, when a\nnew Congress may be less likely to press the issue, said  Derek Scissors , a research fellow at the Heritage Foundation in\nWashington.  \n \u201cThe administration can more easily opt to call\nmanipulation in October, saying they gave Beijing every chance\nto implement real policy change,\u201d Scissors said. \u201cBut the\nmanipulator tag itself does nothing but trigger talks.\u201d  \n Full Document  \n The Treasury said the report covers the second half of 2009\nand includes some information from the first half of 2010. Authorities had allowed the yuan to rise 21 percent\nin the three prior years.  \n \u201cChina\u2019s exchange-rate reform must be reinforced by\nmacroeconomic policies that support domestic demand and other\nstructural reforms to create a strong foundation for\nconsumption-led growth,\u201d the Treasury said. \u201cExchange-rate\nappreciation should play an important role in rebalancing\nChina\u2019s economy.\u201d  \n U.S. Criticism  \n Companies in Asia and in the U.S. have called on China this\nyear to let the yuan rise. Chinese executives including  Yang Yuanqing , chief executive officer of Beijing-based computer\nmaker Lenovo Group Ltd., and Qin Xiao, chairman of China\nMerchants Bank Co., said in March that China could benefit from\nan appreciation of the currency.  \n U.S. companies have criticized what they view as favoritism\nof Chinese firms over foreign competitors.  \n A January letter to the White House from the U.S. Chamber\nof Commerce, the Business Software Alliance, and more than a\ndozen other groups representing companies such as Microsoft\nCorp., Boeing Co., Motorola Inc., Caterpillar Inc., and United\nTechnologies Corp. warned of \u201csystematic efforts by China to\ndevelop policies that build their domestic enterprises at the\nexpense of U.S. firms.\u201d  \n Geithner opted to delay the report until after a series of\nmeetings between U.S. and Chinese officials in Beijing and as\npart of Group of 20 policy discussions. After last month\u2019s G-20\nsummit in Toronto, President  Barack Obama  said the U.S. will be\nmonitoring markets to make sure that China follows through.  \n Market Forces  \n \u201cWe do expect that as more and more market forces come to\nbear, that given the enormous surpluses that China has\naccumulated, that the renminbi is going to go up and it\u2019s going\nto go up significantly,\u201d Obama said.  \n In its previous report in October, the Treasury criticized\nChina for the \u201clack of flexibility\u201d of the yuan and a buildup\nof foreign-exchange reserves while declining to call the nation\na manipulator of its currency. It said China\u2019s yuan policies\nwere a \u201cserious concern\u201d and pledged to negotiate with China\nat the G-20 and the bilateral meetings.  \n China\u2019s  reserves  rose to a record $2.447 trillion in the\nfirst quarter of 2010, according to the People\u2019s Bank of China.\nHoldings jumped $22.5 billion in March, after gaining $9.4\nbillion in February and $16 billion in January, data posted on\nthe central bank\u2019s  website  in April showed.  \n Under a 1988 law, the Treasury is required to report to\nCongress twice a year on international economic conditions and\nexchange-rate policies. The Treasury is required to enter direct\ntalks with a country deemed to be manipulating its currency, and\nalso seek redress through the International Monetary Fund. The\nlast country labeled a manipulator was China, in 1994.  \n To contact the reporter on this story:\n Rebecca Christie  in Washington at \n rchristie4@bloomberg.net \n Ian Katz  in Washington at \n ikatz2@bloomberg.net   \n          \n          \n\n\n  \n     \n       \n     \n           \n                            \n                     \n                     U.S. treasury secretary Timothy Geithner. (GOOG)  and  United Continental\nHoldings Inc. (UAL)  won two patent-infringement trials this year in a\ncourthouse where that\u2019s not supposed to happen.  The courts in the Eastern District of Texas, which includes\nthe Tyler courthouse where Google and United defended\nthemselves, have delivered half the largest U.S. patent verdicts\nagainst corporations in history. A quarter of defendants in U.S.\npatent cases filed in 2011 were sued there.  The recent defense victories, along with changes in U.S.\npatent law from courts and Congress, have chipped away at the\ndistrict\u2019s title of top location for patent suits. Since\nSeptember, more infringement suits have been filed in\nWilmington,  Delaware , than in eastern Texas, according to an\nanalysis co-authored by  James Pistorino , a lawyer with Perkins\nCoie LLP in  Palo Alto ,  California .  \u201cIt\u2019s more problematic to file a case here than it was\nthree years ago,\u201d said Sam Baxter, a patent lawyer with McKool\nSmith PC in Marshall, Texas, who represented Versata Software Inc.\nin a $345 million verdict it won last year against  SAP AG (SAP) , the\n10th-largest patent verdict in U.S. history.  Delaware had more patent suits filed in 2011 while more\ncompanies were sued in eastern Texas. There were 484 suits\ninvolving 2,458 defendants in Delaware and 418 suits with 3,163\ndefendants in Texas, according to Pistorino\u2019s study.  United, Amazon  Patent owners still have the advantage in east Texas cases\nthat come to trial. They\u2019ve won about two-thirds of the trials\nin 2011 and so far this year, according to LegalMetric Inc., a\nSt. Louis-based company that compiles data on litigation. Of the\n22 trials since Jan. 1, 2011, patent owners won 15, said  Greg\nUpchurch , director of research.  This year, though, airlines including United won a March\nverdict in Tyler, Texas, that invalidated patents for a way to\nreserve seats online. A month earlier, another Tyler jury\ninvalidated a patent challenged by companies including Google\nand  Amazon.com Inc. (AMZN)  over a way to make the Internet more\ninteractive.  Google has won three of its four trials in east Texas,\nCatherine Lacavera, director of litigation for the  Mountain\nView , California-based company, said. In the fourth, the jury\nawarded $5 million and the companies settled. All have been in\nthe past two years.  \u201cI heard about the statistical reputation that plaintiffs\nare far more successful, but we\u2019ve had a very good experience\nthere,\u201d Lacavera said. Court Changes  The biggest change affecting the  Texas  courts was the\npatent-law overhaul signed in September, Pistorino said. It\nincluded a provision that bars filing a single suit against\ndozens of unrelated companies. That makes it more expensive to\nsue a large number of companies in hopes of getting quick\nsettlements.  The September law followed years of court rulings that\nnarrowed the power of patents and chipped away at the appeal of\nthe courts in Marshall and Tyler. The  Supreme Court , in a series\nof rulings since 2006, made it easier to challenge a patent and\nharder to block an infringer from using the invention, which led\nto more trials.  The  U.S. Court of Appeals  for the Federal Circuit, which\nhandles patent appeals, made it easier to  transfer  cases and\nlimited the amount of money that can be collected when the\ninvention covers just a small feature of a product such as a\ncomputer. It\u2019s also not as fast to reach trial, with some now\ntaking upwards of three years. Having left the heavy-lifting to technology companies until early this year,  San Francisco \u2019s non-tech employers are playing a growing role in the city\u2019s  labor recovery . Positions in everything from retail to construction to hospitality now comprise about 75 percent of the city\u2019s job growth, helping the Northern Californian hub add jobs at among the fastest rates in the nation and reduce its  unemployment rate  to 6.5 percent.  San Francisco\u2019s experience is also seen in broadening expansions in other U.S. technology centers such as  Seattle  and  Boston , easing concerns that innovation would create work for only the most highly-skilled and highly-paid while others get left behind. Every new technology job in a city creates five additional local jobs outside the sector over time, according to an analysis by Enrico Moretti, an economics professor at the  University of California , Berkeley.  \u201cPeople were missing the big picture,\u201d said Moretti, author of \u201cThe New Geography of Jobs\u201d published in May. \u201cTech cannot offer jobs to the average worker, but every software engineer attracted to Twitter will indirectly support many more service jobs. My research suggests that this multiplier effect is particularly large for high-tech jobs.\u201d  Shares fell as U.S. leaders prepared to negotiate a budget deal to try to avert the so-called fiscal cliff of tax increases and budget cuts slated to take effect next year if lawmakers don\u2019t act. The Standard & Poor\u2019s 500 Index dropped 0.2 percent to 1,406.29 at the close of trading in  New York , paring a decline of as much as 0.8 percent.  \u2018Misplaced Faith\u2019  In the face of a manufacturing contraction accelerated by the 2007-2009 recession, even the biggest names in American technology worried so-called knowledge work wouldn\u2019t be able to sustain U.S. employment.  Andy Grove , co-founder of  Santa Clara , California-based  Intel Corp. (INTC) , warned in July 2010 of \u201cour own misplaced faith in the power of startups to create U.S. jobs.\u201d  \u201cThe great Silicon Valley innovation machine hasn\u2019t been creating many jobs of late,\u201d Grove wrote in an article in Bloomberg Businessweek. \u201cWhat kind of a society are we going to have if it consists of highly paid people doing high-value-added work -- and masses of unemployed?\u201d  Grove wasn\u2019t available for comment, said Tom Waldrop, an Intel spokesman.  In 2010, computer systems design was the only industry in the San Francisco metropolitan area that added more than 2,000 jobs. The city lost 12,200 positions across all industries.  Broadening Gains  Two years later, the home of some of the world\u2019s best-known Internet companies, including Twitter Inc. and  Yelp Inc. (YELP) , has been transformed. Jobs in most  major industries , aside from the government, grew in October from the same month in 2011, including a 5.6 percent surge in the retail sector and 3.2 percent gain in construction. Three-fourths of the city\u2019s job growth took place outside the industries of information, computer systems design and computer and electronic manufacturing, compared with 40 percent as recently as January. Seasonally unadjusted unemployment in the metropolitan area -- also including the counties of  San Mateo  and Marin -- is now a full percentage point lower than the  national average .  Signs of the spreading recovery are evident in record ridership on the Bay Area Rapid Transit rail system and construction sites sprouting in once abandoned corners of the city.  Home values  in San Francisco have been growing on a year- on-year basis for four consecutive months, accelerating to a 5.3 percent increase in August, the biggest 12-month gain in almost two years, according to the S&P\/Case-Shiller index. That compares with a 2 percent gain in 20 U.S. cities.  \u2018Full-Fledged\u2019 Recovery  \u201cThat can\u2019t be driven by just one sector, which actually isn\u2019t that big a sector,\u201d said Ted Egan, chief economist of San Francisco\u2019s city government, referring to technology companies. \u201cIt\u2019s a full-fledged recovery.\u201d  Nationwide, technology was among the early drivers of the economic recovery, and, as in San Francisco, continues to outpace other sectors. Jobs in computer systems design services started rising from a year earlier in April 2010, while it took another five months for total payrolls to begin increasing.  Technology has a wider reach than traditional sources of jobs both because those companies tend to need more business services to operate and their workers have bigger salaries to spend, UC Berkeley\u2019s Moretti said.  For every new technology job, two positions in professional work -- doctors, lawyers -- and three others in non-professional occupations -- waiters, store clerks -- are supported over time, according to Moretti\u2019s analysis of 11 million U.S. workers in 320 metropolitan areas. Technology\u2019s multiplier of five compares with 1.6 for manufacturing, Moretti said.  Innovation Centers  From greater Seattle, home of  Amazon Inc. (AMZN)  and  Microsoft Corp. (MSFT) , to Boston, to Austin,  Texas , and Raleigh,  North Carolina , jobs in the country\u2019s other innovation centers are growing at a faster pace than the national average. A similar dynamic is at play in all of these areas, where early technology-driven growth in employment is now spreading to local services, UC Berkeley\u2019s Moretti said.  Driving economic growth in the tech clusters are programmers like Simon Murtha-Smith, co-founder of San Francisco-based  Singly Inc. , which provides software services to engineers. He says he spares few expenses, including a $9 half- gallon of orange juice from his local Whole Foods store every week. He and his fiancee also have been spending an additional $150 on rent since August, when they moved into a one-bedroom apartment with a hilltop view of the city.  His company also drops plenty of money in the local economy, he said.  Contracting Help  \u201cWe have someone who delivers catering to our office four days a week, and on the fifth day we eat out in the Mission,\u201d Murtha-Smith said, referring to the office\u2019s neighborhood lined with organic-produce restaurants and bars serving craft beers. \u201cWe have accountants, we have lawyers, all in the local area. We outsource all of it. We also hire designers on a contract basis to do specific things for us.\u201d  Benefiting from the spillover are workers such as Elana Polichuk, 28, who ended three months of unemployment in the middle of September.  Polichuk says with the contract jobs from creative temporary staffing companies and freelance work editing graduate school applications, she will be earning more than she ever did in  Minnesota , from where she moved in July.  \u201cThere are way more opportunities here and way more competition, and it\u2019s exciting because it helps me up my game,\u201d said Polichuk, who hopes to secure full-time work. \u201cI just bought a sweater. I have gas money to go up to Marin to go hiking. I was able to buy my friend a cup of coffee. It\u2019s all these small things that I couldn\u2019t afford to do a couple months ago.\u201d  To contact the reporter on this story: Aki Ito in San Francisco at  aito16@bloomberg.net . Seeking more lucrative work through tapping skills she\u2019d learned as a kid building websites, she went to TrainSignal Inc., which provides web-based computer training for $49 a month. A month later, she was hired as a systems specialist at a consulting company in  Chicago .  \u201cIt\u2019s becoming less and less about formal education,\u201d said Wallace, 25, who moved to  Washington  in the middle of last year for a higher-level tech support specialist job at The Public Health Institute. \u201cPeople just want to know that you can do the job.\u201d  While online courses have been around since the early days of the Internet, job training has remained the purview of community colleges and vocational schools, requiring students to spend thousands of dollars to learn word processing, financial spreadsheets and web development. With  unemployment  hovering at 7.6 percent, companies like  TrainSignal  and  Lynda.com Inc.  are pitching what they call a more efficient and affordable route for people who need retraining on their own schedule.  They\u2019re part of a revival in web education startups. Venture capitalists poured $632.3 million into the market in 2012, up 41 percent from the previous year, and the most since the dot-com bubble\u2019s peak in 2000, according to the  National Venture Capital Association . Lynda, based in Carpinteria,  California , raised $103 million in January led by Spectrum Equity and  Accel Partners , the largest venture funding on record for an education company, based on NVCA data.  Momentum Building  For job training, momentum for online education is building. Richard Gallanti, a vocational counselor at  Rehabilitation Perspectives Inc.  in Burke,  Virginia , offers Lynda.com to every client, mostly professionals, like police officers and firefighters, who were injured on the job and need skills for office work.  Clients using Lynda can learn Microsoft Corp.\u2019s Word, Excel and PowerPoint programs and  Autodesk Inc.\u2019s (ADSK)  AutoCAD software for architects, and typically find jobs in about half the time that it takes for those who stick with traditional classroom training, Gallanti said.  Follow Progress  Subscriptions start at $25 a month per person. A single course at a local community college on basic Word or Excel would be more expensive and may be available only at a particular time and place, he said. He can also follow clients\u2019 progress to make sure they\u2019re doing the necessary assignments.  \u201cCost is one thing, but it\u2019s not the only thing -- it\u2019s availability,\u201d Gallanti said. \u201cI need it now. I can\u2019t wait for the next semester or the next class.\u201d  Requiring Americans who are receiving  unemployment insurance  to enroll in classes, including online courses, would save the government money, James Sherk, a senior policy analyst at the Washington-based  Heritage Foundation , wrote in a Feb. 26  report .  Improving skills would make the jobless more employable, he wrote. And because online progress can be easily tracked, it would encourage the 5 percent to 10 percent of people on assistance he estimates who are abusing the system by not seeking work to take a job. Had the program been in place this year, it would have saved $1.5 billion to $3 billion, he said.  Ridding Fraud  \u201cIt\u2019s a conservative lower-bound estimate that comes just by getting rid of fraud,\u201d Sherk said in an interview. He derived his estimate of the number of people abusing the system and money saved based on various state studies, including in Maryland and  Utah , that show more-stringent training or job-search requirements to remain on unemployment insurance reduced the number of those receiving benefits or shortened the duration of assistance. The Heritage Foundation, a nonprofit headed by former Republican Senator  Jim DeMint  of  South Carolina , advocates for smaller government.  \u201cWe haven\u2019t seen a lot of this implemented on a large scale,\u201d Sherk said. \u201cPart of the reason we put out the report was to try and encourage policy makers to think about this as an option.\u201d  Retraining is a growing niche for Lynda, which gets most of its business selling subscriptions to universities and corporations. Lynda has more than 2 million users, and is finding increasing traction with job seekers, said co-founder Lynda Weinman.  \u201cIn a super-competitive job market like today, it\u2019s not as simple as you go to school and get certification,\u201d Weinman said. \u201cThe personalized aspect of online is incredibly powerful and efficient, because nobody has the time and a lot of people don\u2019t have the money.\u201d  New Marketplaces  Lynda and Schaumburg, Illinois-based TrainSignal have both been around for more than a decade, and have recently moved from mailing out instructional DVDs to offering on-demand services on the Web. Startups like  Skillshare Inc.  and  Curious.com Inc.  have established new marketplaces, allowing experts in subjects such as photography, basic car repair and computer programming to put low-cost courses online for anyone to take.  Online programs alone can\u2019t solve the training needs of the jobless. At the Henry Street Settlement in  New York , a 120-year-old social service center, some 5,000 job seekers from the city\u2019s Lower East Side neighborhood come through every year. Many don\u2019t own a computer and lack any Internet proficiency, said David Garza, the  executive director . He offers the example of a building superintendent who lost his job after 20 years and needed to first learn how to launch a browser.  Lack Skillset  \u201cPeople don\u2019t necessarily have the skillset or ability to focus on the tools to navigate through some of these online courses,\u201d Garza said. A big part of the curriculum is providing training so clients can apply for restaurant and retail jobs online, he said. Henry Street has a computer lab, sponsored by Microsoft, which provides the software for free.  Community colleges \u201cdo a tremendous amount of online training themselves,\u201d said David Baime, senior vice president for government relations for the  American Association  of Community Colleges in Washington. \u201cThere is something about being in a classroom that some people like,\u201d he said. \u201cIt really depends on the individual.\u201d  For Ina Lee, Internet-based education proved to be the transition she needed after losing her job of 12 years as a graphic designer in 2009. While doing some freelance work, Lee heard about Lynda from a friend who persuaded her to register. She took courses on  Adobe Systems Inc.\u2019s (ADBE)  Dreamweaver for website development and Apple Inc.\u2019s Final Cut Pro for video editing.  New Skills  That gave her the skills to get hired last year as director of creative services at the Elizabeth House Family Life Center Inc., a nonprofit in Wilmington,  Delaware . \u201cIt helped me greatly,\u201d said Lee, 49. \u201cDreamweaver really gave me the power to talk to Web developers with confidence,\u201d she said.  Yet Lee isn\u2019t convinced that classrooms are a thing of the past. While unemployed, she also took a two-week course at a community college, gaining some basic web development skills. In addition to the benefits of an in-person instructor, she made some connections that could prove beneficial in the future. \u201cI love meeting people face to face,\u201d she said.  On TrainSignal, novices who come to the site with no background in computers can be ready for an entry-level job in three months from the training they get in hardware, operating systems and networks, said Chief Executive Officer Scott Skinger. TrainSignal offers the classes and a third party administers the certification.  Promote Services  TrainSignal has chosen not to raise venture money. The company expects to almost double this year to $12 million in sales and jump to $20 million next year, according to Skinger. The growth will better enable the company to promote its services to employment agencies, Skinger said.  \u201cIt\u2019s a matter of when, not if,\u201d he said. \u201cWe need more time to reach out and make people aware of it. It\u2019s a logical fit.\u201d  As Wallace, the former acupuncturist, was looking to change careers, she chose TrainSignal because she could get basic training for computer maintenance and then learn more as she was ready to advance.  Wallace\u2019s improved skills landed her a higher-level job, moving her to Washington from Chicago, and almost doubling her pay to $55,000 a year. Since starting at the Public Health Institute a year ago, she\u2019s taken TrainSignal classes on  VMware Inc. (VMW)  virtualization technology and is looking into getting certified on using Cisco Systems Inc.\u2019s routers and switches.  \u201cI see myself moving towards being an I.T. director, moving up through the ranks,\u201d said Wallace. \u201cThe more skills I have the more marketable I become.\u201d  To contact the reporter on this story: Ari Levy in  San Francisco  at  alevy5@bloomberg.net   To contact the editor responsible for this story: Tom Giles at  tgiles5@bloomberg.net","path":".\/2008_2012_msft_bloomberg_news\/unemployment-prompts-online-training-challenging-colleges-jobs.txt"},{"id":71427879,"title":"Bankers Join Billionaires to Debunk \u2018Imbecile\u2019 Attack on Top 1%","released_at":"<date>December 20 2011<\/date> <time>05:01:00<\/time>","content":"Jamie Dimon , the highest-paid chief\nexecutive officer among the heads of the six biggest U.S. banks,\nturned a question at an investors\u2019 conference in New York this\nmonth into an occasion to defend wealth.  \u201cActing like everyone who\u2019s been successful is bad and\nbecause you\u2019re rich you\u2019re bad, I don\u2019t understand it,\u201d the\n JPMorgan Chase & Co. The owner of KFC and  Pizza Hut  restaurants is seeking lower tariffs on chicken wings exported to feed hungry Europeans.  Lobbying by companies is accelerating as the U.S. Trade Representative\u2019s office prepares to negotiate with the 27-nation European Union to form the world\u2019s largest free-trade region.  Wal-Mart Stores Inc. (WMT) ,  Intel Corp. (INTC) , the United Steelworkers union and the Sierra Club are among 367 parties weighing in as the agency opened two days of hearings today.  Because the talks will cover a wide range of merchandise and services, they run the risk of being stalled by special interests. Officials plan to move quickly, beginning the talks in July and reaching an agreement by the end of 2014.  \u201cWe must get the substance right,\u201d Dan Mullaney, assistant U.S. trade representative for Europe and the  Middle East , said at today\u2019s hearing. \u201cWe acknowledge that a negotiation that drags on is in no one\u2019s interest.\u201d  Government leaders and business groups are pursuing the pact, known as the Trans-Atlantic Trade and Investment Partnership or T-TIP, as a way jump-start their sluggish economies. Negotiators want to eliminate most tariffs and streamline the thicket of regulations in the two regions that generate $28 trillion in annual economic output, almost half the world\u2019s total.  Farms, Health  Old differences, which have in part prevented the two sides from advancing to an agreement before now, are again surfacing. The U.S. and the EU, which have the world\u2019s largest bilateral economic relationship, have long been at odds over farm policy, health standards, regulations for manufactured goods and country-specific names for products.  \u201cWe emphasize geographic indications, and we do not like it very much when on a wine label from the U.S., we see \u2018Champagne,\u2019\u201d French Trade Minister Nicole Bricq told reporters through a translator during a visit to Washington last month.  \u201cThe agreement itself will set the bar for free-trade agreements worldwide,\u201d  Peter Westmacott , the U.K. ambassador to the U.S., said during a speech in Washington in April. \u201cThe sheer size of the two economies of the European Union and the United States, and the amount of trade between them, means that T-TIP will be unprecedented in its scale.\u201d  Significant Investments  An agreement would reduce costs for companies and industries -- such as automotive, pharmaceuticals, medical equipment and chemicals -- that already have significant direct foreign investment in the regions, according to a May 21 Bloomberg Government  study .  The accord will cover issues including agriculture, financial regulations, telecommunications and rules for digital goods that haven\u2019t even been invented yet. With the stakes high, groups representing industries from automakers to soft drinks are seeking to influence the talks.  \u201cCustoms duties should be eliminated on automobiles and parts thereof,\u201d according to a filing by the lawyer for Ferrari North America Inc., the Maranello, Italy-based car company\u2019s U.S. distributor.  The American Automotive Policy Council, a Washington-based group that represents  Ford Motor Co. (F) ,  General Motors Co. (GM)  and  Fiat SpA (F) \u2019s Chrysler Group LLC, is among other groups seeking tariff elimination and a convergence between EU and U.S. rules.  Wing Supplies  Yum! Brands Inc. KFC sends U.S. poultry to Europe \u201cto supplement local supply,\u201d which is often too low to meet its demand, the company said.  Yum has to pay 1,024 euros ($1,327) a ton on frozen chicken wings shipped from U.S. processing plants to Europe, according to the company\u2019s filing.  The transatlantic accord \u201cneeds to be an agreement that reflects today\u2019s world,\u201d Peter Allgeier, president of the Coalition of Services Industries, said at today\u2019s hearing. The Washington-based group\u2019s members include  JP Morgan Chase & Co. (JPM) , Microsoft Corp. and  FedEx Corp. (FDX)  The pact should ensure that state-run businesses including postal carriers, don\u2019t have an unfair advantage over private competitors, Allgeier said.  Industry Requests  Company requests for provisions are largely specific to an industry. Atlanta-based  Coca-Cola Co. (KO)  wants to prevent duplication of regulations for the safety of the flavoring used in soft drinks. Intel Corp. of  Santa Clara , California, wants to ensure that rules for communications technology don\u2019t favor local providers. Wal-Mart, the world\u2019s largest retailer, is seeking immediate elimination of  import duties , fewer rules for grocery labeling and a framework that encourages electronic commerce.  \u201cThe retail industry continues to evolve from a traditionally \u2018brick and mortar\u2019 industry to a new multi-channel \u2018brick and click\u2019 industry,\u201d the Bentonville, Arkansas-based company said in its filing.  Not everyone is content with streamlining the rules. Too much convergence might eliminate necessary regulations and \u201cpose a serious threat to the environment, working families and communities,\u201d the  Sierra Club  said in comments. The San Francisco-based environmental group said it is also concerned that the accord would deprive the U.S. Energy Department of oversight for exports of liquefied natural gas to the EU.  Labor Requests  The AFL-CIO, the largest U.S. labor federation, wants to make sure the accord avoids rules governing air and maritime transport. The steelworkers\u2019 union said rules of origin for merchandise should be focused on enhancing  job creation  in the U.S. and the EU.  Public Citizen , a Washington-based consumer group, wants the text of the negotiations to be made public and it wants provisions dealing with copyrights and data protection left out of the text.  Before they negotiate, legislatures on both sides of the Atlantic are assessing public sentiment. Foreign Talent  By finding loopholes surrounding different visas, the\ncompanies can employ more foreign workers in the U.S., helping\nthem boost revenue and avoid hiring higher-priced local labor,\nsaid  Rajiv Khanna , a Virginia-based immigration lawyer. Now, come lie for me.\u201d  \n That, he says, was the start of a career which took him to\n UBS AG  and  BNP Paribas SA  before returning home in 2000 to\nbecome the nearest thing Ireland has to a celebrity economist.  \n His newspaper columns, three books and documentaries draw\ntogether the economic dots for the common man. Now, he\u2019s taking\nhis shtick to the Peacock stage at the  Abbey , as part of the\nnational theater\u2019s admirable effort to engage with today\u2019s\nissues rather than focus on money-spinning revivals of classics.  \n There\u2019s no shortage of material, given the collapse of\nIreland\u2019s economic and to a lesser extent, social fabric in the\nlast five years. The Abbey has chosen well in asking McWilliams\nto explain how, in his words, the Irish economy \u201cevaporated.\u201d  \n As ever with McWilliams, his work divides opinion. One\nreviewer on the Abbey\u2019s  website  described the show as a \u201ctrain\nwreck.\u201d Another called it \u201cstunning.\u201d  \n The truth is somewhere in between.  \n The show is entertaining and fluent. The sparse staging,\nwith a gantry crane and orange hard hat, captures the obsession\nwith real estate.  \n Seeking Solutions  \n Yet McWilliams is no economic messiah, and the 90-minute\nmonologue comes unstuck when he seeks solutions.  \n First, the good. Dressed in an open necked shirt and suit,\nhis analysis sparkles with anecdotes and one-liners.  \n Essentially, Irish banks borrowed from Germans --\npersonified by McWilliams as Gunther, the careful BMW accountant\nwhose only eccentricity is an annual visit to a nudist colony in\nCroatia.  \n The banks fed Gunther\u2019s cash to the Irish, who used it to\nbuild, buy and sell property to each other, buy worthless\napartments in Bulgaria and send their children to private\ncreches with names like \u2018Little Harvard.\u2019  \n Now Gunther wants his money back, and Ireland can\u2019t pay.  \n McWilliams offers an alternative to the Irish government\u2019s\nposition that somehow the debt must be paid, even if that means\npouring billions of taxpayers\u2019 money into a banking black hole.  \n Insider Bailout  \n According to McWilliams, that amounts to a bailout of the\ninsiders, the bankers, the developers and the lawyers that\nbrought Ireland to the abyss. The outsiders, the rest of us,\nwill pick up the tab in the shape of higher taxes,  rising\nunemployment  and emigration for generations to come.  \n What to do? First, default on the bank debt, says the ex-\nbanker. Second, exit the euro as the region falls asunder,\ndevalue our way out of our very own Great Depression and sell\nour banks to the French and Germans.  \n Then, somehow persuade the Googles and  Microsofts  which are\ndotted across Ireland to put 10 percent of their profits into\nstart-up local companies in what McWilliams calls a \u201cJoycean\nfusion\u201d of U.S. money and Irish brainpower.  \n This would somehow be underwritten by the Irish diaspora,\nan untapped network stretching from New York to Shanghai.  \n It\u2019s here that the show loses momentum. His plan is oddly\nreminiscent of the government\u2019s big idea of creating an ill-\ndefined \u2018smart-economy.\u2019 For the first time, McWilliams\u2019\ndelivery grows wooden, as if he\u2019s not completely convinced\nhimself.  \n \u201cOutsiders\u201d reinforces the sense that the contrarian is a\nbit of a national treasure, a hugely talented communicator. It\u2019s\njust not that clear if, on the bigger question of how we save\nthe Irish economy, he has much to say.  \n Through July 3 at the Abbey Theatre, Middle Abbey Street,\nDublin 2. Just as ambitious: do it with college students in\n South Carolina , far from the engineering hotbeds of Silicon\nValley, New York or Austin,  Texas .  The company, based at the  University of South Carolina  in\nColumbia, can create an app in five days with \u201cpremade\nprogramming Lego blocks,\u201d said Chief Executive Officer Steve Leicht, one of three non-students at the company who work for\nfree. That means a chunk of code can quickly add GPS features or\nthe ability to share content on  Facebook  or  Twitter , helping the\nsmall team compete with experienced developers.  \u201cWhat they are doing is very cool,\u201d said  Vivek Wadhwa , an\nentrepreneurship and public-policy lecturer who has  academic\nroles  at Stanford, Duke and Emory universities. \u201cThe startup\nscene in South Carolina is very small, but there are sparks of\nlight, and this is one of them.\u201d  The company highlights how the app era has allowed\ninnovation to thrive in new and unexpected locales. With\nsimplified development tools, just about anyone with mid-level\nprogramming skills can build mobile applications.  About one in three apps are made by individuals or\ncompanies with fewer than five employees, according to App\nAnnie, a company that helps publishers track their own  app store \nmetrics.  Fertile Ground  Colleges and universities, with their legions of\nsmartphone-toting students, offer particularly fertile ground.\nStudent efforts are often spurred by school policies that\nencourage professors and students to create companies. At least\n36 colleges across the U.S. have business incubators that make\nmobile apps, according to the National Business Incubator\nAssociation.  \u201cApp development has become very much popular among\ncollege students,\u201d said  Agata Chydzinski , Director of\nOperations at the  USC\/Columbia Technology Incubator , who has\nworked with business incubators for 10 years. \u201cIt starts in\nhigh schools.\u201d  \u201cWhen you find a student who has ideas, or skills, or who\ncan design, and other students who are in business school, it\ncould make a hugely successful company,\u201d Chydzinski said.  The technology incubator offers workspace and mentorship\nopportunities to dozens of companies, including 52apps. The\nUniversity of  North Carolina  at  Chapel Hill  has offered to fund\nthe development of a mobile application that uses university\nresearch.  Austin Incubator  An incubator at the  University of Texas  at Austin is home\nto mobile apps including Next One\u2019s on Me, which allows users to\ntreat their friends to coffee or lunch, and Drivve, which\nfacilitates document management on smartphones. And at\n Northwestern University  near  Chicago , a startup incubator is\ncurrently home to 18 companies, including mobile app maker\nSweetPerk, which developed an app that enables merchants to\nadvertise more effectively.  Of course, colleges have long been fountains of Internet\ninnovation.  Mark Zuckerberg  started Facebook out of his dorm at\nHarvard. Aaron Levie founded Box, a cloud storage company, at\nthe University of  Southern California . Silicon Valley investor\n Peter Thiel  even pays student entrepreneurs as much as $100,000\nto drop out of college and pursue their ventures full-time.  Today\u2019s crop of students have it easier than ever,\nespecially when it comes to mobile apps. Tutorials for learning\nhow to code and make applications are readily accessible online\nand you need little more than a computer and an Internet\nconnection to get started.  Weekly Celebration  In Columbia, the 52apps team meets in its offices each\nMonday to choose that week\u2019s application. Programmers start\ncoding before lunchtime, and by Thursday, a beta version is\ntested. On Friday, the software is sent to  Apple Inc.\u2019s App\nStore .  \u201cEvery Friday when an app goes out, the whole group hangs\nout and celebrates,\u201d said Christopher Thibault, who co-founded\nthe company with former high-school classmate Brendan Lee. So\nfar, the company has received more than 100 ideas, and expects\nto use at least 10 of them. She heard about 52apps from a friend on\nFacebook.  Texting Idea  \u201cI would describe myself as a lazy texter, and if I had\nthis app, it would be a lot easier for me,\u201d Boineau said.\n\u201cThey positioned it as, make a good idea, and they\u2019ll make the\napp for you.\u201d  The company plans to make apps for all the major platforms,\nincluding Google Inc.\u2019s  Android  and Microsoft Corp.\u2019s new\n Surface  tablet. The team also is building a content-management\nsystem to sell to universities to simplify distance learning and\nadministrative tasks. The transfer overseas of these kinds of rights\nhas enabled Google to attribute earnings to foreign units that\npay lower taxes, Bloomberg News reported a year ago.  While Google\u2019s potential liability isn\u2019t clear, similar\ndeals between companies and offshore arms are often the subject\nof disputes over hundreds of millions of dollars in taxes, said\nDaniel Frisch, an economist at Horst Frisch Inc. which advises\nbusinesses on  transfer pricing  -- the allocation of income\nbetween units in different countries. In 2006, the IRS settled a\ncase with drugmaker  GlaxoSmithKline Plc (GSK)  for $3.4 billion.  \u201cThe very biggest transfer-pricing tax disputes are over\ntransfers of intangibles to offshore subsidiaries,\u201d said\nFrisch, whose firm is based in  Washington .  Google, owner of the world\u2019s most popular search engine,\nhas cut its worldwide tax bill by about $1 billion a year using\na pair of strategies called the \u201cDouble Irish\u201d and \u201cDutch\nSandwich,\u201d which move profits through units in Ireland, the\nNetherlands and  Bermuda . Google reported an effective tax rate\nof 18.8 percent in the  second quarter , less than half the\naverage combined U.S. and state statutory rate of 39.2 percent.  Tax Holiday  \u201cThis is a routine inquiry,\u201d said Jim Prosser, a\nspokesman for  Mountain View , California-based Google. He\ndeclined to comment further.  Dean Patterson, a spokesman for the IRS in Washington, said\nfederal law prohibits the agency from discussing specific\ntaxpayers.  U.S. companies are sitting on at least $1.375 trillion in\nearnings in their foreign subsidiaries on which they have paid\nno federal income taxes, according to a May report by JPMorgan\nChase & Co. Companies including Google,  Cisco Systems Inc. (CSCO) ,\n Pfizer Inc. (PFE) ,  Apple Inc. (AAPL)  and  Microsoft Corp. (MSFT)  are lobbying\nCongress for a tax holiday on bringing home those profits, which\nwould otherwise be subject to U.S. income tax at the 35 percent\ncorporate rate with a credit for foreign taxes already paid.  The Obama administration is opposed to that tax break and\nhas been stepping up criticism of tax preferences for various\nindustries and millionaires. Last week, Senate Democrats\nproposed a new surtax on people earning at least $1 million a\nyear, a move that would generate an estimated $453 billion over\nthe coming decade.  France Probe  The  French tax authority  also began reviewing Google\u2019s\nincome shifting in December, examining transactions between the\ncompany\u2019s French and Irish subsidiaries, according to two people\nwith knowledge of the probe. The French inquiry was prompted by\nthe October 2010 Bloomberg article on the company\u2019s tax-cutting\nstrategy, the people said.  A spokesman for the French budget ministry, which oversees\nthe tax authority, declined to comment, saying the agency cannot\ndiscuss individual cases.  Multinational companies cut their tax bills by shifting\nearnings into subsidiaries in offshore  tax havens , a strategy\nthat is drawing increased scrutiny from the IRS.  In May, the IRS appointed its first  transfer-pricing \ndirector, Samuel Maruca. Last year, it announced the assignment\nof additional agents and attorneys to examine a few large\ncompanies as part of a pilot program. The IRS wouldn\u2019t discuss\nwhether Google is one of those companies.  Valuable Patents  Moving profit abroad is particularly important for cutting\nthe tax bills of technology and pharmaceutical companies because\nof their valuable and easily transportable collection of patents\nand copyrights. Google, Cisco, Facebook Inc., Microsoft and\n Forest Laboratories Inc. (FRX) , maker of the blockbuster\nantidepressant Lexapro, have used tax-cutting strategies that\nmove profits into units -- often with no employees or offices --\nin havens such as Bermuda, the Cayman Islands and Switzerland,\nBloomberg has reported.  In recent years, the IRS has engaged in a number of high\nprofile disagreements with multinational companies over their\ntransfer pricing. In 2006, the agency announced it was settling\nits dispute with GlaxoSmithKline.  In 2009, the IRS lost a closely watched U.S. Tax Court case\nwith Veritas, now a part of computer-security software maker\n Symantec Corp. (SYMC)  In that dispute, over intellectual property\nrights moved to an offshore subsidiary, the IRS sought $545\nmillion.  Enforcement Setback  The win for Veritas was a major setback for the IRS\u2019s\nability to enforce transfer-pricing rules, according to H. David Rosenbloom, an attorney at Caplin & Drysdale in Washington, and\ndirector of the International Tax program at  New York  University\nSchool of Law.  Income shifting by multinational companies cost the U.S.\n$90 billion in federal  tax revenue  during 2008, according to a\nMarch article in the trade journal Tax Notes by  Kimberly\nClausing , an economics professor at  Reed College  in Portland,\nOregon.  Google cuts its tax bill by about $1 billion a year using a\ntechnique that allocates profits to a unit managed out of a  law\nfirm  in Bermuda, where there is no corporate income tax. In\n2009, the most recent year for which records are available, this\nsubsidiary collected 4.34 billion euros (about $6.1 billion) in\nroyalties from a Google unit in the Netherlands, according to a\nDutch corporate filing.  As of June 30, Google held $18.8 billion in cash in its\nforeign subsidiaries, almost half its total $39.1 billion in\ncash and marketable securities.  \u2018Buy In\u2019  The IRS has already approved a major part of Google\u2019s\nstrategy. In 2006, the agency signed off on a 2003 intracompany\ntransaction that moved foreign rights to its search technology\nto an Irish subsidiary managed in Bermuda called Google Ireland\nHoldings. That deal -- known as a \u201cbuy in\u201d in tax parlance --\nmeant subsequent profit overseas based on those copyrights has\nbeen attributed to foreign subsidiaries rather than to Google in\nthe U.S. where the technology was developed.  The IRS approval came in an accord known as an  advance\npricing agreement . Those arrangements are part of an agency\nprogram intended to forestall disputes with companies, including\ndisagreements over the price paid by offshore units for patent\nand other intellectual property rights.  Google Acquisitions  That deal between the IRS and Google only covered rights\nthe company held as of the 2003 licensing deal with its Irish\nunit. It didn\u2019t cover copyrights subsequently acquired by the\nU.S. parent and then moved abroad.  Following that 2003 transaction, Google made several\nacquisitions, spending $1.65 billion for online-video site\nYouTube in 2006; $625 million for e-mail security service\nPostini in 2007; and $3.2 billion for web-advertising company\nDoubleClick Inc. in 2008. The IRS now is examining the prices\npaid by the foreign subsidiaries for the rights to software and\nother intangibles moved offshore that formerly belonged to those\nthree companies.  According to U.S. Treasury Department rules, foreign units\nlicensing rights from their U.S. parents are supposed to pay an\n\u201carm\u2019s length\u201d price, or the amount that would be paid by an\nunrelated company. If the offshore subsidiary pays too little,\nthat has the effect of shifting income overseas, thus helping\nthe parent avoid U.S. income taxes.  SEC Review  Google\u2019s taxes have also drawn government scrutiny from the\nSecurities and Exchange Commission. Last December, the SEC asked\nthe company for \u201cgreater detail\u201d about the profit it said it\nhad earned in countries with lower tax rates and the impact on\nits effective  tax rate , according to correspondence released by\nthe agency in March. The SEC said in a February letter that it\nhad completed its review of Google\u2019s filings. It is unclear what\naction, if any, the agency took.  In August, Google announced it was spending $12.5 billion\nto acquire Motorola Mobility Holdings Inc., the Libertyville,\nIllinois telecom-equipment and mobile-phone maker. Google said\nit was doing the deal primarily for Motorola\u2019s collection of\nvaluable patents. Prosser didn\u2019t respond to a question about\nwhether Google would be moving any of those  patent rights \noffshore. Top Patent Area Silicon Valley Getting Its Own Satellite Office  Apple Inc. (AAPL) ,  Google Inc. (GOOG)  and  Intel Corp. (INTC)  soon won\u2019t have to\ntravel across the U.S. to get patent protection on their latest\ninventions.  Silicon Valley,  Dallas  and Denver have been selected as the\nnew homes for regional patent offices as part of an effort to\ncut down on a backlog of applications awaiting review, the U.S.\nPatent and Trademark Office said yesterday.  The agency, which is opening a satellite office in  Detroit \non July 13 and has declared a \u201ccritical need for electrical\nengineers,\u201d is trying to hire more examiners to cut into the\n640,000 applications awaiting a first review. By expanding\nbeyond its Alexandria, Virginia, campus, the patent office is\nseeking to take advantage of a pool of engineers who understand\ntechnology and can work closer to where inventors are located.  The additional offices were authorized under an overhaul of\nthe patent system signed into law last year. About 600\napplications were submitted, and the selections were based on\ngeographic diversity, economic impact, the local workforce and\nproximity to companies that are submitting applications.  \u201cThe single most important step we can take to support an\neconomy built to last is to bring new inventions to market as\nquickly as possible,\u201d said David Kappos, director of the Patent\nand Trademark Office.  The regional offices -- one for each time zone -- would\nbecome hubs with \u201ca tangible impact on each city\u2019s innovation\neconomy,\u201d he said.  The four offices also could develop their own expertise to\nreflect local communities -- Detroit for automotive, metallurgy\nand paints; Dallas for energy; Denver for aerospace; and Silicon\nValley for electronics and biotechnology. Denver also was\nselected in part because it has a large number of veterans with\nadvanced degrees, and President  Barack Obama \u2019s administration\nhas a policy to hire more veterans, Kappos said.  The Silicon Valley area, which also includes Sunnyvale and\nSanta Clara, is the top recipient of patents, with more than\n10,000 issued in 2010, agency figures show. The region\ncomprising San Francisco, Oakland, and Fremont adds another\n6,290 patents, the third-most behind the  New York  and northern\nNew Jersey region. (INTC) , the world\u2019s largest semiconductor maker, slashed its third-quarter sales forecast, citing declining demand for personal computers from corporate customers in a weakening economy.  Sales will be $12.9 billion to $13.5 billion, down from a prior projection of $13.8 billion to $14.8 billion, the Santa Clara, California-based company said in a statement yesterday. Analysts on average had estimated sales of $14.2 billion, according to  data  compiled by Bloomberg.  PC makers are reducing orders for Intel\u2019s chips at a time of the year when they normally buy more to build products for the  holiday shopping season . Intel said demand for chips used in business machines and orders in  emerging markets  are lower than expected, compounding concern that the PC market may not grow this year as consumers flock to smartphones and tablets.  \u201cIt\u2019s worse than everyone expected,\u201d said  Patrick Wang , a New York-based analyst for  Evercore Partners Inc. (EVR)  \u201cTheir consumer PC business is getting whacked.\u201d  Intel declined 3.6 percent to $24.19 at the close in New York yesterday, leaving the  stock  little changed this year.  Advanced Micro Devices Inc. (AMD) , Intel\u2019s largest rival in PC processors, fell 5.7 percent to $3.45.  Nvidia Corp (NVDA) , which makes graphics chips used in computers, decreased 2.4 percent to $13.40.  Gross margin, the only measure of profit that Intel forecasts, will be 61 percent to 63 percent in the period, down from the prior forecast of 63 percent, plus or minus a \u201ccouple of percentage points.\u201d Analysts had projected 63 percent, according to Bloomberg data. Gross margin is the percentage of sales left after deducting the cost of production.  Withdrawn Forecasts  Intel also withdrew all full-year forecasts and said it will provide updated projections with its third-quarter earnings report on Oct. 16.  The company in July scaled back its annual sales forecast as personal-computer demand fails to rebound among consumers in the U.S. and Europe. Revenue will rise 3 percent to 5 percent in 2012, Intel said that month, lower than an earlier projection for a gain at a percentage in the high single digits.  Yesterday\u2019s announcement indicates that sales in the PC market are unlikely to grow this year, according to  Daniel Berenbaum , an analyst at MKM Partners LLC. Intel\u2019s customers may be cutting back on inventory ahead of the debut of  Microsoft Corp. (MSFT) \u2019s new Windows operating system, the first specifically designed to work on tablets with a touch-screen interface, he said.  \u2018Bear Case\u2019  Intel also faces the prospect of losing customers as more consumers access the Internet via smartphones and tablets. Microsoft and  Google Inc. (GOOG)  are introducing tablets in a market already crowded with devices challenging  Apple Inc. (AAPL) \u2019s iPad.  Market researcher Gartner Inc. predicts the PC market will grow 2 percent to 372.3 million units in 2012. Next year the market will expand 12 percent to 415.5 million units.  \u201cThe problem is PC makers don\u2019t know what to build,\u201d said Berenbaum. \u201cThe bear case is that this indicates that people are not going to buy PCs, they\u2019re buying tablets.\u201d  Microsoft, with its entry in the tablet market, is for the first time creating versions of its  Windows operating system  that will work on chips using technology from companies other than Intel. That is causing PC makers to hold off on processor orders, unsure of which type of computer will catch on with consumers, according to Berenbaum.  Intel is also planning to spend less on new plants and equipment this year. Instead of a blessing, it\u2019s turned into a curse.  As part of the MSCI  Emerging Markets  Index, Israel had a weighting of 2.7 percent, the 11th highest and an outsized proportion for investors focused on developing economies. Now it makes up 0.2 percent of the MSCI World Index of 33 developed nations, forcing Israeli companies to compete with those from the U.S., Europe and Japan for fund managers\u2019 attention.  While Israel has more  startups  per capita than any country and the benchmark TA-25 Index delivered the developed world\u2019s second-best risk-adjusted returns, at the  Tel-Aviv  Stock Exchange, top officers have resigned, trading is down 44 percent since MSCI\u2019s endorsement and big companies are leaving. The chief executive officer of one of those,  Mellanox Technologies Ltd. (MLNX) , says the exchange may need to be sold.  \u201cWe went from a significant place in a market we wanted to move from to no-man\u2019s land,\u201d Daniel Goldstein, the global head of sales at IBI-Israel Brokerage and Investments Ltd., which manages more than 27 billion shekels ($7.6 billion), said on July 28 by phone from Tel Aviv. \u201cThere are lots of interesting things happening here, but this is not necessarily reflected on the  TA-25 index. (TA-25)  There is nothing high-tech.\u201d  Resignations  Israel\u2019s TA-25 Index rose 8.6 percent since the MSCI reclassification took effect in May 2010 versus a 67 percent jump for the  Nasdaq Composite Index. (CCMP)  That year alone, investors pulled $795 million from the Israeli market. The 44 percent tumble in volumes through the end of 2012 compared with an average 18 percent global decline, the Bank of Israel said in a March 12 report.  Initial public offerings have dried up. In June,  Kadimastem Ltd. (KDST) , a developer of stem cell therapies, became the first company to list on the Tel Aviv bourse since the end of 2011, compared with a record 56 IPOs in 2007, exchange data show.  Companies that pulled off the exchange, which had 549 stocks in 2012, included Hot Telecommunication System Ltd., a telecommunications company, and ELAD Canada Inc., a real estate company owned by billionaire Isaac Tshuva.  Israel Chemicals Ltd. (ICL) , the Tel Aviv-based company that extracts minerals from the Dead Sea to make fertilizers and potash, said yesterday it\u2019s preparing for a dual listing in part to shield itself from worsening conditions on the local bourse.  \u2018Wake-Up Call\u2019  The drop in volumes prompted a feud between regulators and exchange officials over who was to blame. Former Tel Aviv Stock Exchange Chief Executive Officer Ester Levanon resigned on July 17 and Saul Bronfeld, the chairman since 2006, followed the next week. Bronfeld, a former Bank of Israel chief economist, cited government regulations and slower economic growth for the exodus of investors and companies. Israel Securities Authority Chairman Shmuel Hauser says the bourse\u2019s management is also responsible.  \u201cThe decline in volume and prices on the Tel Aviv bourse is due to excessive regulation and the change in the pace of economic growth, not the operations of the bourse,\u201d Bronfeld said in an interview Aug. 5 in Tel Aviv. \u201cMy resignation is a wake-up call for Jerusalem,\u201d where Prime Minister  Benjamin Netanyahu \u2019s government is based, he said.  The resignations are coinciding with a shuffle at the central bank, where two candidates nominated by Netanyahu to replace former Governor  Stanley Fischer  have withdrawn.  Jacob Frenkel , a former central bank chief, and Leonardo Leiderman, the chief economist at  Bank Hapoalim Ltd. (POLI) , dealt a blow to Netanyahu by giving up their nominations. Fischer\u2019s handpicked deputy, Karnit Flug, is acting as a caretaker in the meantime.  More Sanguine  Israel\u2019s outlook was more sanguine four years ago. The nation\u2019s economy recovered from the 2008 crisis faster than most advanced nations with gross domestic product expanding by 14.7 percent between 2009 and 2012, compared with 3.2 percent growth in the U.S. and a contraction of 1.5 percent in the euro region.  In 2009, investors bought a net $1.7 billion of shares and the TA-25 Index soared 75 percent, the most in at least 16 years and the fourth-best performance among benchmark indexes tracked by Bloomberg in Europe and Africa.  The benchmark TA-25 Index has produced the second-best risk-adjusted returns among developed stock benchmarks after Australia\u2019s S&P\/ASX 200 Index in the past decade, helped by a technology-driven economy that has attracted global leaders in the industry.  Google Buys  Google Inc., the world\u2019s biggest search engine, said on June 11 that it\u2019s acquiring Israeli map-software provider Waze Inc. after international investors including  Warren Buffett  bought local companies.  \u201cIsrael has been a center of innovation for the better part of its existence and you see that today,\u201d Zach Herzog, the head of international sales at Psagot Investment House Ltd. in Tel Aviv, said in a phone interview on Aug. 2. \u201cAny high-tech company in the world like Google, like  Intel Corp. The Yokneam Elit-based company trades on the  Nasdaq  Stock Market in New York, as well as in Germany.  More companies from Israel trade in the U.S. than from any foreign country except China. (ADHD) , a Tel Aviv-based developer of a drug for treating attention deficit hyperactivity disorder, listed on Nasdaq in May. The index provider also looks at liquidity and the accessibility of the country\u2019s markets to foreign investment. Once a nation\u2019s status is changed, investors tracking the MSCI index\u2019s benchmarks have to rebalance their portfolios.  Levanon, who became CEO of the exchange in 2006, said in an interview three years later that winning MSCI\u2019s approval was like breaking the glass ceiling for investment in Israel. \u201cWe\u2019re playing with the big boys now,\u201d she said after MSCI announced its decision.  Both Levanon and Bronfeld failed to update trading systems and products at the bourse and didn\u2019t find solutions for the lower volumes, according to a copy of a letter sent by Hauser to the exchange last month. Sharona Mazalian, an ISA spokeswoman, declined to comment further. New management will \u201cstrengthen the bourse,\u201d Hauser said July 25 in an e-mailed statement. (NICE) , the Ra\u2019Anana-based provider of analytical tools for recording service transactions, is the only technology company in the 25-member benchmark index.  \u201cThe advantages of a dual listing are no longer great, and it\u2019s much more logical for us to be listed only on Nasdaq,\u201d Nice Chief Executive Officer Zeevi Bregman said in an interview today with business daily Globes. Greenberg, the former\n American International Group Inc. (AIG)  chief executive officer, seeks\nto break new ground in lawsuits challenging the U.S. takeover of\nthe insurer in a bailout that reached $182 billion.  Greenberg\u2019s Starr International Co. sued the government\nNov. 21, calling the public assumption of 80 percent of stock in\nthe insurer in 2008 an unconstitutional \u201ctaking\u201d of property\nthat requires $25 billion in compensation.  Starr also sued the Federal Reserve Bank of New York,\nsaying it breached its duty to AIG shareholders by loaning $85\nbillion at 14.5 percent while offering better terms to banks in\na \u201cbackdoor bailout.\u201d AIG almost collapsed after bets tied to\nthe housing market soured, and the bailout was revised at least\nfour times before reaching $182 billion.  Both complaints were filed by attorney  David Boies , who\nrepresented the U.S. in its Microsoft Inc. 1999 antitrust trial\nand  Al Gore  in the Florida presidential recount litigation in\n2000.  \u201cAny time David Boies is asking for $25 billion, I would\nsay this is not a normal case,\u201d said Robert H. Thomas of the\nHonolulu firm  Damon Key Leong Kupchak Hastert .  \u201cHe takes cutting edge cases in unexplored areas of law,\u201d\nsaid Thomas, who specializes in land-use and eminent domain.\n\u201cIt\u2019s audacious. As someone who represents plaintiffs in these\nkinds of cases, I\u2019d say more power to him. But it\u2019s a stretch.\u201d  Boies convinced a judge that Microsoft Corp. was a\nmonopolist and successfully defended Starr against an AIG claim\nin 2009 that it looted the insurer of $4.3 billion in stock. He\nalso worked for National Basketball Association players in labor\ntalks that just concluded.  Boies Response  Boies didn\u2019t respond to requests for comment on his chances\nof success in the Starr cases.  He sued the Federal Reserve in U.S. District Court in New\nYork, and the takings case is in the U.S. Court of Federal\nClaims in  Washington . That court handles cases against the\nfederal government for money, including claims that the U.S.\ntook private property for public use without just compensation\nin violation of the Fifth Amendment to the Constitution.  Most of those cases involve the loss of property value\nthrough regulation, Thomas said.  Starr, AIG\u2019s largest shareholder at the time of the\nbailout, claims that in the midst of the financial crisis in\nSeptember 2008, the U.S. took 80 percent of AIG\u2019s equity while\nviolating the constitutional rights of shareholders to due\nprocess and equal protection of the law.  Bailout\u2019s Flaws  While the bailout was \u201costensibly designed to protect the\n United States  economy and rescue the country\u2019s financial\nsystem,\u201d Starr claims, \u201cthe ends could not and did not justify\nthe unlawful means employed by the government to achieve that\ngoal.\u201d  Greenberg led AIG for almost four decades though 2005,\nresigning amid an investigation by  New York  Attorney General\n Eliot Spitzer  into accounting practices. Greenberg is also\nchairman and CEO of C.V. Starr & Co.  Before recovering compensation for a taking, Starr must\naccept the government\u2019s underlying premise for the action and\nnot challenge its validity, according to attorney Jerry Stouck\nof Greenberg Traurig LLP in Washington.  \u201cIt\u2019s assumed that if they took your property, they did it\nfor a good reason,\u201d Stouck said. \u201cThe issue is whether the 80\npercent equity in AIG was taken from its owner under\ncircumstances that require the government to pay for that\nstake.\u201d  Power to Take  Takings cases have produced mixed results at the  Supreme\nCourt  in recent years. In 1992, it ruled in Lucas v. South\nCarolina Coastal Council that a landowner is entitled to\ncompensation when regulators  bar all development  on a parcel.  In 2005, the court gave local governments broad power to\ntake over private property to make way for shopping malls,\noffice parks and sports stadiums.  Government agencies can constitutionally take property as\npart of an economic development plan and transfer it to another\nparty, as long as the landowner is compensated, the court ruled\nin a case involving development in  New London ,  Connecticut .  Starr argues that AIG was caught in a liquidity crisis\nhastened by the Fed\u2019s denying the insurer access to lending\nthrough its so-called discount window.  The central bank struck the AIG equity deal a day after the\nLehman Brothers Holdings Inc. bankruptcy on Sept. 15, 2008.\nStarr claims the U.S. could have lent money without demanding\nequity, as it did with foreign banks and other lenders.  Treasury Official  \u201cIt is important to remember that the government provided\nassistance to AIG -- and stopped it from collapsing -- in order\nto prevent a meltdown of the entire global financial system,\u201d\nsaid Tim Massad, assistant secretary for financial stability at\nthe  U.S. Treasury . \u201cOur actions were necessary, legal and\nconstitutional. We are reviewing the lawsuit and expect to\ndefend our actions vigorously.\u201d  Jack Gutt , a spokesman for the New York Fed, said the\nallegations have no merit.  \u201cAIG\u2019s board of directors had an alternative choice to\nborrowing from the  Federal Reserve , and that choice was\nbankruptcy,\u201d Gutt said. \u201cBankruptcy would have left all AIG\nshareholders with worthless stock. The Federal Reserve\u2019s actions\nwith regard to AIG helped to restore financial stability in the\nUnited States during a period of intense volatility and\nvulnerability in the  U.S. economy .\u201d  Starr must show that it suffered an injury that requires\ncompensation, said Vermont Law School professor  John Echeverria .  Assets\u2019 Value  \u201cThat depends on a showing that the assets were worth X\nbefore the government acted and X minus Y after the government\nacted,\u201d Echeverria said. \u201cThe suit is on its face unappealing\nand unattractive. The court will look with great skepticism on a\nclaim seeking billions of dollars in taxpayer funds.\u201d  Regulators have \u201ctremendous discretion\u201d to act, said\nattorney Thomas M. Buchanan of Winston & Strawn LLP in\nWashington.  \u201cI don\u2019t think I\u2019ve seen any takings cases that have\nsucceeded in a financial crisis,\u201d Buchanan said. \u201cThis is\nobviously a pretty novel theory.\u201d  Winning a regulatory takings case is very difficult, said\n Robert H. I\u2019ve been using the new software since last week and find\nit useful and attractive. At the same time, it\u2019s somewhat\noverbearing in controlling how you interact with your phone. I enjoyed being able to quickly flip through a series of\nupdates, registering Facebook \u201clikes\u201d simply by double-tapping\nthe screen. This people-centric approach resembles the \u201clive tiles\u201d\nMicrosoft features in its Windows Phone operating system.
