The rise of\nsmartphones and online marketing convinced him to try again.  \u201cThere is very significant opportunity for new entrants to\ncome in with innovation and gain significant traction, but these\nthings are lightning in a bottle,\u201d said Lou Kerner, a social\nmedia analyst at Wedbush Securities Inc. \u201cGroupon has grown\ndramatically faster than anyone thought they would.\u201d  Chen\u2019s challenge is ensuring DailyGobble.com stands out\namong hundreds of online coupon sites, led by Groupon and\nLivingSocial. The 330 restaurants posting discounts on\nDailyGobble.com so far are Chen\u2019s proof his concept has\npotential. Within a year, he projects quarterly revenue of as\nmuch as $7 million and net income of $250,000.  Limit Discounts  DailyGobble\u2019s pitch to restaurateurs is that they only pay\nfor coupons diners use, and they can limit discounts to specific\ntimes of day when tables typically sit vacant. Many established\ncoupon sites, LivingSocial among them, charge up-front fees for\nlistings and don\u2019t permit time restrictions.  \u201cWe can use DailyGobble for times that the restaurant is\nnot full,\u201d said Darren Wan, 36, owner of Red Egg in  New York ,\nwhich is offering a 20 percent rebate on Chen\u2019s site on Tuesdays\nand Sundays from 8 p.m. to 11 p.m.  DailyGobble charges eateries fees of 5 percent of food\nsales to list deals -- a smaller cut than most other coupon\nsites take -- and requires discounts of at least 20 percent,\nChen said. Diners get rebate checks in the mail after spending\nenough to amass $25 in savings or can send funds to a PayPal\naccount.  Rebates Versus Coupons  The refund model sets DailyGobble apart from Groupon and\nLivingSocial, among other deal sites, where buyers purchase the\ndiscounted items up front, then use coupons when they dine out.  \u201cI think there will be some resistance and hesitation in\ngetting the money back later,\u201d said  Greg Sterling , an analyst\nwith Opus Research Inc. in  San Francisco . \u201cThere\u2019s a trust\nissue initially. If it\u2019s easy to get the money, it will create a\nlot of stickiness and loyalty.\u201d  Chen says diners will like avoiding the hassle and\npotential embarrassment of coupons, particularly in the two\nfood-obsessed cities his site targets: New York and San\nFrancisco.  A sales force is paramount to make such sites viable, said\n Sucharita Mulpuru , an analyst at Forrester Research. DailyGobble\nhas nine employees on its sales team so far, Chen said.  \u201cIt\u2019s very, very labor intensive,\u201d Mulpuru said. \u201cYou\nhave to get the word out to customers and you have to do it in a\nway that\u2019s not predictable.\u201d  Smartphone Apps  The site now works through an iPhone application that lets\ndiners photograph receipts and e-mail them to DailyGobble.\nEmployees at the company\u2019s one-room New York office verify the\nbill and start a rebate tab for customers.  Apps for  Google Inc. (GOOG) \u2019s Android software should be available\nwithin a week, and software for  Research in Motion Ltd. (RIM) \u2019s\nBlackBerry will be released in four to six weeks, Chen said.  Other deal companies offer businesses delayed returns,\nusually giving the eatery 50 percent of its money within three\nto 10 days and the rest as many as 40 days after the deal, said\nAlberto Gonzalez, 46, owner of New York-based  GustOrganics . They\nalso don\u2019t let businesses pick the time customers can use the\ndeal, he said. A flood of coupon-carrying clients can overwhelm\nan unprepared small business.  \u201cOne of the issues we normally have with other deals is\nall the people with the deals come when we\u2019re the busiest,\u201d\nGonzalez said. \u201cWe have to run the vouchers, and that takes\ntime, and sometimes it gets complicated.\u201d  Gonzalez, who is offering 25 percent off meals between 8\na.m. and 11 a.m. with DailyGobble, said other deal companies\nhe\u2019s used, including Groupon,  DailyCandy Inc.  and Gilt Groupe\nInc.\u2019s  Gilt City , take as much as 25 percent of sales generated\nthrough their sites, versus DailyGobble\u2019s 5 percent. Thurber, director of the Center for Congressional and\nPresidential Studies at American University in Washington.  Though the studies found that money brought home in 2004\nended up benefiting a narrow set of shareholders, support is\ngrowing in Congress for the tax holiday as companies expand\ntheir roster of lobbyists. One case they are making is that the\npotential flood of cash will boost the faltering U.S. economy.  Complex Issues  \u201cThere are many issues that are very important but are\ncomplex and don\u2019t seem of great importance to the wider public -\n- those are the issues primed for having people who formerly\nworked on the Hill or executive branch intervening in making\npolicy,\u201d Thurber said.  Those with Capitol Hill connections who are lobbying for\nthe repatriation tax break include former Louisiana\nRepresentative Jim McCrery, who until 2009 was the top\nRepublican on the U.S. House\u2019s tax-writing Ways and Means\nCommittee; Dena Battle, the former legislative director for that\ncommittee\u2019s current chairman, Representative  Dave Camp , a\nMichigan Republican; and at least four former staffers for House\nSpeaker  John Boehner .  Michael Steel , a spokesman for Boehner, an  Ohio Republican ,\nsaid former staff members don\u2019t influence policy. \u201cThe speaker\nmakes such decisions based on what is best for his constituents\nand the American people,\u201d Steel said.  \u2018Regenerate the Economy\u2019  Advocates for the break say a repatriation holiday would\nbring more than $1 trillion to the U.S. now held overseas.  \u201cIt would do much to regenerate the economy,\u201d said Robert Livingston, a former Republican chairman of the House\nAppropriations Committee and speaker-designate who is now\nlobbying for  Oracle Corp. (ORCL)  \u201cA total of $1.5 trillion from all\naffected U.S. companies would go a long way to pull us out of\nthe doldrums.\u201d  There are more insiders pushing for the tax holiday than\nthose in Bloomberg News\u2019 tally of at least 60. That figure\nincludes only registered lobbyists who worked for a sitting\nmember of Congress and disclosed lobbying on the issue for the\nWIN America Campaign, the group of  companies  seeking the break,\nor for one of the companies or associations in the coalition.  WIN America is coordinated by SKDKnickerbocker, a\nWashington political consulting and public relations firm, which\nincludes as a managing director Anita Dunn, former\ncommunications director for President  Barack Obama . Dunn isn\u2019t a\nregistered lobbyist.  Longtime Fixtures  The list of more than 160 lobbyists includes other longtime\nfixtures in Washington, such as former Representative\nLivingston; Democratic fundraiser Tony Podesta; and Kenneth Kies, former chief of staff of the congressional Joint Committee\non Taxation.  The proposed break has gained momentum in recent months,\nwith several prominent Democrats, including Senator  Charles Schumer  of New York, expressing a willingness to consider the\ntax holiday. Meanwhile, Republican presidential candidates\n Michele Bachmann , a House member from Minnesota, and Texas\nGovernor  Rick Perry  have called on Congress to let companies\nbring home offshore earnings at a reduced  tax rate .  The Obama administration has said it is opposed to a stand-\nalone tax holiday for repatriated profits, pointing to the 2004\nexperience. Obama has been taking aim at tax breaks benefiting\ncertain industries, such as oil and gas, and deductions and\nexclusions claimed by millionaires. He has embraced changes\nsuggested by billionaire  Warren Buffett , who has said he pays\ntaxes at a lower rate than his secretary.  U.S. multinational companies have amassed more than $1.375\ntrillion in profits overseas on which they have paid no federal\nincome tax, according to a recent report by  JPMorgan Chase & Co. (JPM) \nWhen the earnings are returned to the U.S. -- or repatriated --\nthey are taxed at the top corporate rate of 35 percent, with\ncredits for foreign income taxes paid.  Reprising 2004 Holiday  The companies are pushing to reprise the 2004 holiday that\nallowed them to bring home offshore earnings at a low tax rate\nof 5.25 percent. Under that break, companies repatriated to the\nU.S. $312 billion, largely for stock repurchases rather than\ndirect hiring or investment, according to a recent paper in the\nJournal of Finance, the latest in a series of studies that\nreached similar conclusions.  The proposed holiday would reward the companies that have\nmost aggressively parked profits in  tax havens  such as Bermuda,\nthe Cayman Islands and Switzerland, said Martin A. Sullivan, a\nformer Treasury Department economist and contributing editor for\nthe non-partisan Tax Notes.  \u201cA lot of what companies report as foreign profit is\nreally U.S. profit that should be subject to U.S. tax,\u201d\nSullivan said. \u201cThose earnings didn\u2019t get overseas by accident.\nMany of these companies intentionally put them there to avoid\npaying U.S. taxes.\u201d  Tally of Lobbyists  Bloomberg\u2019s tally covers individuals who were registered to\nlobby on the repatriation issue at some point in the first half\nof this year, the period for which records are available. Some\nof the lobbyists have since left their firms. The figures don\u2019t\ninclude those who were listed as lobbying on general tax issues\nfor companies in the WIN America coalition, except where the\nlobbyists confirmed to Bloomberg News that they were working on\nrepatriation.  Newer members of the revolving-door community are involved,\nsuch as Danielle Maurer, a lobbyist at the Republican firm of\nFierce, Isakowitz & Blalock. It has been paid $160,000 so far\nthis year by Oracle to lobby on a variety of tax issues, and the\nWin America coalition recently hired the firm. Maurer had been\ndirector of member services for Boehner, helping assign House\nmembers to committees.  Baucus Alumni  In all, three former staffers of Baucus, the Finance\nCommittee\u2019s chairman since 2007, are lobbying on the\nrepatriation holiday. Besides Forbes, there\u2019s Nick Giordano of\nWashington Council Ernst & Young, a longtime Cisco lobbyist.\nMicrosoft has retained Timothy E. Punke, a former adviser to\nBaucus on trade issues who is active in Democratic politics.  The WIN America campaign\u2019s manager is Karen Olick, former\nchief of staff to Senator  Barbara Boxer , a California Democrat.\nOne of the spokesmen for the group is  Doug Thornell , who most\nrecently was a staffer for Representative  Chris Van Hollen , a\nMaryland Democrat who is a member of the House leadership. Like\nAnita Dunn, Thornell and Olick aren\u2019t registered lobbyists.  \u201cOur economy needs all the help it can get, and leaving\nthis money in foreign banks when we could bring it home now\nmakes no sense,\u201d Thornell said. The measure, which the president has repeatedly cited in\nspeeches promoting his economic policies, gives the U.S. Patent\nand Trademark Office more control over its funding and makes\nfundamental changes in how patents are processed and reviewed.\nIt passed the House in June and won final approval Sept. 9 on an\n89-9  vote in the Senate.  \u201cBy creating a faster process for the approval of patents\nand reducing the amount of uncertainty, it will increase\ninvestment in the economy today and start creating jobs today,\u201d\n Jason Furman , deputy director of the National Economic Council\nsaid yesterday in a conference call with reporters.  The patent office, which is funded entirely by user fees,\nwill be able to set its own fees, with any money in excess of\nthe budgeted amount going to a fund that can only be used by the\nagency. The office plans to hire as many as 2,000 more examiners\nin the coming fiscal year, revamp an outdated information\ntechnology system that it has described as \u201cbeyond horrific,\u201d\nand open satellite offices across the country to tap into local\nworkforces.  The goal is to address a backlog of almost 700,000\n applications  awaiting first review and decrease the average 34\nmonths it takes to issue a patent. Reducing the time it takes to\ngive inventions legal protection will speed new products to the\nmarket, helping economic growth, according to the bill\u2019s\nsupporters.  Research Promotion  The president also plans to announce new programs to\npromote the commercial use of work done by scientists at\nuniversities and government research labs. The  National\nInstitutes of Health  will help companies cut the time and cost\nfor developing new drugs and the  National Science Foundation \nwill establish a prize to reward the university that makes the\nmost progress in accelerating job growth, Furman said.  Obama is scheduled to sign the legislation at Thomas\nJefferson High School in Alexandria, Virginia. The suburban\n Washington  town is home to the patent office headquarters and\nthe school is named for the third U.S. president who, as\nsecretary of state under  George Washington , signed the nation\u2019s\nfirst patent law in 1790.  Fast Track  The patent office already has been working to speed up the\napplication process, including giving green technology fast-\ntrack reviews. DuPont Co., the Wilmington, Delaware-based\nchemical company, used the program to obtain patents on\nbiofuels, said DuPont Chief Executive Ellen Kullman, who is a\nmember of the president\u2019s Council on Jobs and Competitiveness  \u201cPace is really critical here,\u201d she said. \u201cIf you can\nget the pace of the patents going, you can accelerate the pilot\nlaunch; you can accelerate the production.\u201d  The legislation is the culmination of more than a decade of\ndiscussions and six years of negotiations and lobbying by every\nindustry. It covers each step of the patent process, setting new\nprocedures to review issued patents while curtailing some\nlitigation. It has the support of companies including  Microsoft\nCorp. (MSFT) ,  International Business Machines Corp. (IBM)  and a group that\nrepresents  Johnson & Johnson (JNJ) ,  Eli Lilly & Co. (LLY) ,  3M Co. (MMM)  and\n General Electric Co. (GE)   Furman said that the breakthrough came during a December\nmeeting Obama held with business leaders, including Lilly Chief\nExecutive Officer John Lechleiter and Cisco Systems Inc. CEO\n John Chambers , who disagreed over how much the bill should deal\nwith changes in litigation. Then-Commerce Secretary  Gary Locke \nfollowed up to resolve the differences, Furman said.  Big Companies  Some small business have criticized the legislation as\ngiving big companies an unfair advantage in obtaining patents\nand creating new hurdles to enforcing  patent rights  against\ncompanies that copy inventions without compensation.  Supporters have expressed reservation on the funding issue,\nsaying it doesn\u2019t go far enough to protect the patent office\nfrom having funds siphoned off to other priorities. Congress has\ndiverted almost $1 billion from the agency since a 1990 law\nrequired the patent office to pay for itself.  Under the bill, patents would be granted to the first\ninventor to file an application, ending an often time-consuming\nprocedure to determine who came up with an idea first and\nbringing the U.S. in line with patent laws in other countries.  All newly issued patents may be subject to a challenge from\nthird parties, a variation of a process used by the  European\nPatent Office .  The bill also would limit patents on tax-avoidance\nstrategies, though companies including  Intuit Inc. (INTU)  and  H&R Block\nInc. (HRB)  have said they would retain protections for their tax-\npreparation software.  The trade group for generic-drug companies, including Mylan\nInc. and Watson Pharmaceuticals Inc., opposed the bill because\nthere\u2019s a provision that lets patent owners retroactively\ncorrect errors that might otherwise lead a court to invalidate\nthe patents. Chief Executive Officer  Andrew Miller \nsaid in June that the newspaper, which also led coverage of the\nWikiLeaks disclosure of classified U.S. diplomatic cables, may\nrun out of cash in three to five years without a reorganization.  \u201cThese investigative stories are very expensive and really\ndon\u2019t have much impact on the trajectory of the business,\u201d said\nDouglas McCabe, a media analyst at Enders Analysis in London.\n\u201cAll this may do is slow the decline temporarily.\u201d  Circulation Falls  July figures from media researcher ABC show a 10 percent\nyear-on-year decline in print circulation for the Guardian,\nversus an average of 8.8 percent for U.K. broadsheets. The\nGuardian said the decline reflects a decision to stop counting\ninternational editions, which will be discontinued later this\nyear. Excluding international sales and bulk distribution,\ncirculation fell 2.2 percent, and rose 5.1 percent on a month-\nto-month basis, it said.  Hayley Dunlop, a Guardian spokeswoman in  London , said that\nannual decline still made the newspaper the strongest year-on-\nyear performer among U.K. broadsheets. She added that by early\ninternal measures the newspaper\u2019s average daily U.K. Web traffic\nrose 3.1 percent in July from the previous month.  Advertisers, meanwhile, are shifting more spending to the\ncheaper, thinner tabloids as circulation declines across the\nindustry, said  Alex DeGroote , a media analyst at Panmure Gordon\nin London. \u201cThe rate of decline is a lot lower in mass-market\ntabloids versus broadsheets.\u201d  Sunday Mirror  Those tabloids\u2019 appeal to advertisers will grow as they\nbenefit from the demise of the News of the World, with almost\n2.7 million readers a week before its final edition on July 10.  The Mail on Sunday, the  Daily Mail \u2019s sister paper, recorded\na 17 percent surge in circulation in July, making it the most\npopular U.K. Sunday newspaper with 2.26 million readers\naccording to ABC.  The Sunday Mirror climbed 64 percent to almost 1.79 million\nreaders while the Observer, the Guardian\u2019s Sunday title, saw\noverall circulation little changed along with other Sunday\nbroadsheets, though Dunlop said the paper\u2019s preferred measure of\ncirculation showed a 6.6 percent increase. Improved advertising\nrevenues are likely to follow for both the Mail and Mirror,\ncredit agency Fitch Ratings said Aug. 16.  So far the Guardian has been insulated from the worst of\nnewspapers\u2019 woes by an old-fashioned source of support:\nclassified advertising. Guardian Media Group co-owns Trader\nMedia Group, which publishes ads under the AutoTrader brand,\nwith private-equity firm Apax Partners LLP.  \u201cThe stake in AutoTrader is providing the cash to keep the\npaper afloat,\u201d said Dominic Buch, a media analyst at Numis\nSecurities Ltd. in London.  Liquidity  Earlier this year Guardian CEO Miller said an initial\npublic offering of Trader Media, which brought in 120 million\npounds in operating profit before one-time items in year ended\nApril 3, was a possibility. Guardian Media Group had 14.8\nmillion pounds in cash and short-term  bank deposits  at year-end.\nIncluding an investment fund that the company can draw on when\nneeded, liquidity reached 197.4 million pounds, down from 260.8\nmillion pounds a year earlier.  After more than two years following how News of the World\njournalists hacked into the voicemails of celebrities and\npoliticians, the Guardian on July 4 broke the story that the\npaper had targeted the phone of murder victim Milly Dowler.  The revelation, and subsequent scoops on police corruption\nand other hacking victims, led to the resignation and arrest of\n News Corp. (NWSA)  executives including Rebekah Brooks, CEO of the News\nInternational U.K. newspapers unit.  Digital Push  The long-term investigation that let the Guardian break the\nhacking story was typical for the paper, which was founded as\n the Manchester Guardian  in 1821 in the aftermath of Peterloo\nMassacre of workers protesting the government amid famine and\nunemployment. After surviving a bruising 1980s and \u201890s\ncirculation battle with the Independent, it\u2019s now Britain\u2019s\nfourth most popular daily broadsheet. Guardian Media Group is\nowned by the London-based Scott Trust, which reinvests its\nearnings in the Guardian and Observer\u2019s journalism.  The Guardian has consistently supported left-of-center\npolitical parties in Britain, endorsing the Liberal Democrats in\nthe 2010 general election after backing either Labour or a\ncombination of Labour and the Liberal Democrats in 1997, 2001,\nand 2005. It last endorsed the Conservatives in 1955.  The Guardian has pursued an aggressive digital strategy,\ngoing further than any other British paper in establishing its\nwebsite as a global hub for commentary and analysis. In addition\nto applications for  Apple Inc. (AAPL) \u2019s iPhone and iPad as well as for\nAmazon.com Inc.\u2019s Kindle e-reader, the Guardian\u2019s Comment is\nFree website has become a Huffington Post-style hub for\ncommentary and analysis with hundreds of contributors and a U.S.\nsub-site.  Paywall Supporters  The newspaper has shied away from following rivals like the\nNew York Times and News Corp.\u2019s London-based Times in erecting a\npaywall to charge online readers for access. The  New York Times\nCo. (NYT)  last month posted earnings that beat analysts\u2019 estimates,\nhelped by its online barrier set up March 28, which asks readers\nto sign up for a subscription after 20 free articles in a month. (GOOG)  has scored a huge blow against its archenemy.  Yes, Google+ delivers features and functionality that\n Microsoft Corp. (MSFT) \u2019s Bing search engine can\u2019t touch.  Wrong archenemy, you say? Google+ is supposed to be a\n Facebook -killer? Ehhh, not so much.  At least not now. While Google+ brings some welcome new\nfeatures to the social-networking space, there\u2019s no great\ninnovation that would make you want to use it as your primary\nonline identity, or that Facebook couldn\u2019t emulate if it chose\nto.  Google+ , which launched about a month ago, is officially a\nbeta, or test,  service ; to join, you need an invitation from\nsomeone who\u2019s already a user. Judging from the evidence, invites\naren\u2019t very hard to come by: Less than three weeks after launch,\nChief Executive Officer  Larry Page  announced that the service\nhad already signed up 10 million members.  That sounds like a lot, and it is. But considering that\nFacebook is up around three-quarters of a billion, Google+ has a\nlong way to go before your friends are as likely to be hanging\nout there as they are on the competition.  Instantly Familiar  The core of Google+ will be familiar to Facebook loyalists.\nUsers can post items that friends can comment on, just like\nFacebook\u2019s Wall. There\u2019s also what Google calls the Stream, a\nflow of items posted by others -- essentially, Facebook\u2019s News\nfeature. On Facebook, if you see a post you like, you can \u201cLike\u201d\nit; on Google+, you can \"+1\u201d it.  And it isn\u2019t just Facebook that Google+ borrows from. In\naddition to people you know, you also have the ability to latch\non to those you don\u2019t, as on Twitter, and add their posts to\nyour Stream.  The Google+ system for managing all this is its most\ninteresting feature: Circles. They\u2019re an easy and logical way\nfor you to organize the people in your network and decide whose\nstuff you want to see, and who you want to see your stuff. In\nsome ways, it isn\u2019t all that different from Facebook\u2019s \u201cFriend\nLists,\u201d but Google+ makes Circles far simpler to establish and\nmanage.  Moving in Circles  You start off with four pre-configured circles, labeled\nFriends, Family, Acquaintances and Following. You also have the\nability to easily create and name additional circles.  People in your address book, or potential contacts that\nGoogle suggests, are represented by small rectangular tiles with\ntheir profile pictures. All you do is drag and drop a tile into\none or more of your circles. Those you add are notified that\nyou\u2019ve put them in a circle, but not told which one. So they\u2019ll\nhave no idea if they\u2019re in People I Idolize or Former Co-Workers\nI Never Want to See Again.  When you post something, or upload photos, you decide which\nof your circles you want to share with. Those embarrassing party\nphotos? Let\u2019s keep \u2018em away from the professional circle.  On the other hand, if you want a wider audience, you can\nmake a post visible to \u201cextended circles\u201d -- people in the\ncircles of people in your circles -- or to the general public.  Working Both Ways  Circles works both ways: You can filter your Stream to see\nonly posts from your family, for example, or only those from\nprofessional colleagues.  It all serves to make your online connections different,\nand more nuanced, in Google+ than in Facebook. The latter is\nlargely a reciprocal relationship, where both sides have to\nagree before you become friends. In Google+, it\u2019s more like two\nseparate relationships, mine with you and yours with me, that\nmay or may not be parallel, since I may choose to share less\nwith you than you do with me.  On the other hand, Google+ affords opportunities for other\ntypes of interaction. One is the ability to start a Hangout,\nwhich is a multiparticipant video chat room to which you can\ninvite others. It\u2019s a neat idea that requires you to know folks\nwho want to participate -- which, until there are many more\nusers on the system, may be in short supply.  Tying Things Together  One unexpected result of using Google+ was that I found\nmyself much more likely to use other parts of the Google\necosystem. Things like Gmail and the Picasa photo-sharing site,\nwhich have been around longer than Google+, felt less like\ndisparate products and more like features of a unified, personal\nservice.  Google describes its new network as a \u201cproject,\u201d and I\nencountered a number of issues that made clear this is very much\na work in progress. For example, I was unable to install the\nhangouts feature on a Mac using  Apple Inc. (AAPL) \u2019s Safari web browser;\nI finally got it working in Google\u2019s Chrome browser.  Until the bugs are worked out and the service is opened to\nall comers, we have no way of knowing whether people really want\nor need another social network -- and if so, whether this one\u2019s\nfeatures are compelling enough to attract them.  For Google, the best-case scenario is that the service\nproves so flexible and easy to use that it creates a network\neffect, where more and more people join because so many of their\nfriends are already on it.  The worst case is that Google+ becomes to Facebook what\n Bing  is to Google, less a real competitor than simply an\nalternative with some interesting features that aren\u2019t\nsufficiently compelling to ever lift it above being a distant\nNo. 2.  ( Rich Jaroslovsky  is a Bloomberg News columnist. The\nopinions expressed are his own.) (AMZN) , is\nthe latest technology business to consider changing its\ncorporate status to cut hundreds of millions of tax dollars. As Equinix\u2019s data centers --\nessentially computer-age warehouses -- continue to sprawl, the\nproperty required to house them has convinced Chief Executive\nOfficer  Stephen Smith  that the time may be ripe to redefine the\nbusiness as a real estate investment trust, a designation set\naside for companies that invest heavily in real estate.  \u201cTax efficiency is the most important attribute of being a\nREIT, so that\u2019s certainly a positive,\u201d said  Clayton Moran , an\nanalyst at Delray Beach, Florida-based Benchmark Co., who\nrecommends buying the shares. \u201cREITs are valued at a premium\ngiven that they\u2019re highly recurring dividend plays.\u201d  REITs typically are subject to lower taxes and pay higher\ndividends than other companies, so the conversion would help\nSmith return more money to shareholders, he said in an\ninterview. More technology-related companies that make money\nfrom owning and operating facilities are making the switch to\nREITs. Recent examples are storage services provider Iron\nMountain Inc. and  American Tower Corp. (AMT) , which leases wireless\ncommunications tower space.  Outpacing Peers  Equinix\u2019s stock has beaten every large U.S. technology\ncompany in the past year as demand for its services drove a\nfour-fold  rise in revenue  since 2007.  Even though Equinix belongs to tech indexes run by  Standard\n& Poor\u2019s (S4INFT)  Financial Services LLC, Russell Investments and NASDAQ\nOMX Group Inc., it gets more than three-quarters of sales from\nrenting out server space in more than 100 facilities worldwide,\nmeeting  criteria required to become a REIT . If it converts, the\ncompany would pay most of its income to shareholders in the form\nof a dividend, while also joining a favored asset class -- the\nBloomberg REIT Index has  topped  the  S&P 500 Index  in nine of the\npast 12 years.  Equinix, based in Redwood City,  California , has surged 60\npercent in the last 12 months, the  second-biggest gain  among the\n116 members of the  Russell 1000 Technology Index (RGUSTL)  after\n SolarWinds Inc. (SWI)  and about six percentage points better than\n Apple Inc. (AAPL)  The stock fell 3.2 percent to $162.48 yesterday in\nNasdaq Stock Market trading.  Tax Break  Even with its recent gain, Equinix trades at a discount to\nREITs, according to data compiled by Bloomberg. For 2013,\nEquinix has an estimated enterprise value to Ebitda (earnings\nbefore interest, taxes, depreciation and amortization)  ratio of\n10 , compared with 17 for the  Bloomberg REIT index , a group that\nincludes owners of malls, storage facilities, apartment\ncomplexes and medical buildings.  Data center operators  Digital Realty Trust Inc. (DLR)  and  DuPont\nFabros Technology Inc. (DFT) , which are not in the index, have ratios\nof 15 and 13, respectively. American Tower has jumped 17 percent\nsince converting into a REIT on Dec. 31. Iron Mountain is up 11\npercent since approving a plan to become a REIT on June 6.  \u201cThe path has been laid for additional companies to elect\nto operate as a REIT,\u201d said Mark Decker, the head of real\nestate investment and corporate banking at BMO Capital Markets\nin  Chicago .  The conversion would eliminate Equinix\u2019s corporate tax and\nthe company would send about 90 percent of income to investors,\nwho would be taxed on the dividend received. Colby Synesael, an\nanalyst at Cowen & Co., estimates the change would save the\ncompany $312 million in taxes between 2015 and 2016, the first\ntwo full years that a plan would be in place.  \u2018Arms Merchants\u2019  Equinix provides data center space to more than 4,300\ncompanies, including AT&T,  Microsoft Corp. (MSFT)  and Amazon, which\nrents space in some areas to deliver its Web hosting service.  Kevin Landis  owns $3.3 million in Equinix shares and counts\nit as the 10th-biggest holding in his Firsthand Technology\nOpportunities Fund. He\u2019s betting on the company\u2019s ability to win\nsales from the world\u2019s largest businesses as the need for space\nand connectivity increases.  \u201cAs an investor, I love arms merchants,\u201d said Landis,\nwhose firm is based in  San Jose , California. \u201cAs servers get\nbanished from the enterprise, can you even imagine a scenario in\nwhich data centers don\u2019t get more and more important?\u201d  Landis said he didn\u2019t have any special insight into the\nREIT question, though he expects to get additional details\ntomorrow, when Equinix  reports  second-quarter results. The\ncompany is expected to say that  sales  in the period climbed 18\npercent to $467.2 million from $394.9 million a year earlier,\naccording to the average estimate of analysts\u2019 forecasts\ncompiled by Bloomberg.  Revenue Growth  That follows revenue  growth  in 2011 of 32 percent to $1.61\nbillion from $1.22 billion in the previous year. Equinix is\nforecasting sales of $3 billion by 2015.  \u201cWe don\u2019t want to do anything that would damage our growth\nprofile,\u201d Smith said in an interview. \u201cThat\u2019s the biggest\ndebate with the board.\u201d  Smith told investors in February that Equinix had hired\nadvisers to help explore a conversion, and during last quarter\u2019s\nearnings call in April he added that the company will incur a $2\nmillion expense this year for the analysis. Bank Bonus, Capital Rules Are 2012 Priorities for EU Agency  The European Union\u2019s top bank regulator will focus on\ndeveloping tougher rules for lenders\u2019 capital, bonuses and\nliquidity this year.  The  European Banking Authority  will use data on bankers\u2019\nbonuses \u201cfor the design of the technical standards that it will\ndevelop in 2012-2013,\u201d the agency said in a  document  posted on\nits website yesterday. The London-based EBA will make rules for\nbanks to hold \u201cbetter quality capital\u201d as part of the region\u2019s\nimplementation of global standards known as Basel III.  The EBA told banks last month to raise 114.7 billion euros\n($147.3 billion) in fresh capital by the end of June as part of\nmeasures introduced to respond to the euro area\u2019s sovereign-debt\ncrisis. Lenders should look to bolster reserves by cutting\nbonuses, retaining earnings or issuing shares, it said.  The EBA\u2019s predecessor, the Committee of European Banking\nSupervisors, set bonus rules in December 2010 that limited\nupfront cash payouts to around a quarter of the total bonus to\nlink incentives to the long-term performance of the firm.  Banks were quizzed on the number of employees who make more\nthan 1 million euros as part of the data collection exercise\nthis year.  The authority will also collect information to develop\nrules for a maximum leverage ratio by 2015, and draft\ndefinitions and impact studies for liquidity regulations. (AAPL)  would be drama-free.  \u201cHe goes, \u2018I never want you to ask what I would have done,\u201d\u2019 Cook recalls in the Dec. 10 issue of Bloomberg Businessweek. \u201c\u2018Just do what\u2019s right.\u2019 He was very clear.\u201d  In Cook\u2019s first 16 months on the job, Apple has released next-generation iPhones and iPads and seen its  stock price  rise 43 percent. Though it hasn\u2019t yet expanded into new  product categories  (still no Apple TV set), the company has changed in significant ways, largely because of Cook\u2019s calm and steady influence. In his most wide-ranging interview as CEO, Cook explains how Apple works now, talks about the perception that he\u2019s \u201crobotic,\u201d and announces the return of Apple manufacturing to the U.S.  Question: How has Apple changed since Oct. 5, 2011?  Cook: The first thing to realize is that all the things that have made Apple so special are the same as they have always been. That doesn\u2019t mean that Apple is the same. Apple has changed every day since I have been here. But the DNA of the company, the thing that makes our heart beat, is a maniacal focus on making the best  products  in the world. Not good products, or a lot of products, but the absolute best products in the world.  Slideshow:  Tim Cook at Apple In creating these great products we focus on enriching people\u2019s lives -- a higher cause for the product. These are the macro things that drive the company. They haven\u2019t changed. They\u2019re not changing. I will not witness or permit those changes because that\u2019s what makes the company so special.  More Transparency  There are lots of little things that change, and there will be lots of little things that change over the next year and the years thereafter. We decided being more transparent about some things is great -- not that we were not transparent at all before, but we\u2019ve stepped it up in places where we think we can make a bigger difference, where we want people to copy us. So there are things that are different, but the most important thing by far is, the fiber of the place is the same.  Question: The decisions that you\u2019re alluding to -- more transparency into the  supply chain , doing corporate matches for employees\u2019 charitable donations -- were those things that you\u2019d thought, \u201cYou know, I want to bring that to the culture. I can\u2019t wait to introduce them.\u201d How did those inflection points come up?  Personal Philosophy  Cook: My own personal philosophy on giving is best stated in a (John F.) Kennedy quote, \u201cTo whom much is given, much is expected.\u201d I have always believed this. Always. I think that Apple and Apple\u2019s employees have done enormous good and can do even more. One of the things that we have done is match our employees\u2019 charitable contributions, where they select who they want to give to. So it\u2019s not some corporate committee deciding, but it\u2019s our  80,000 employees  deciding what they want to do, and then we match it.  You know, it\u2019s clearly something I wanted to do, yes. But others wanted to do it, too. Our transparency in supplier responsibility is an example of recognizing that the more transparent we are, the bigger difference we would make. We want to be as innovative with  supply responsibility  as we are with our products. That\u2019s a high bar. The more transparent we are, the more it\u2019s in the public space. The more it\u2019s in the public space, the more other companies will decide to do something similar. And the more everybody does it, the better everything gets. It\u2019s a recognition that we need to be super-secretive in one part about our products and our road maps. But there are other areas where we will be completely transparent so we can make the biggest difference. That\u2019s kind of the way we look at it.  Interim CEO  Question: You were CEO on an interim basis twice before. How is the experience of being permanent CEO different from those two stints?  Cook: There were actually three times. There was Steve\u2019s first surgery back in \u201904. Then a medical leave for half a year and then \u201911. Not that there wasn\u2019t public focus on those, but that public focus tended to be quick, and then it sort of flipped back to Steve. This has been different. This, you know. (Pause.) This has been different. So I have had to adjust to that. I\u2019m a private person, so that\u2019s been a bit of a surprise for me, not something I would have predicted. Maybe I should have.  Question: Rex Tillerson is the CEO of  Exxon (Mobil Corp.) (XOM) , which is at any given moment the second-most valuable company in the world. I\u2019m guessing 10 percent of our readers know who he is. I\u2019m guessing less than 1 percent could spot him on sight. By virtue of Steve Jobs and his legacy and by virtue of Apple living in everyone\u2019s pocket, you\u2019re famous. I mean, really, globally famous.  Confronting Fame  Cook: I don\u2019t feel famous. You know, I lead a simple life. My life is incredibly simple. But what\u2019s changed is that, yeah, people recognize me. They may think, \u201cI have seen him before. You know, the CEO of Apple\u201d or whatever. And so it has been a bit of adjustment for me, because for years I had the privilege of being anonymous. There is a great privilege in that if you\u2019re a private person. So it\u2019s a bit different. I love Apple deeply, and I\u2019m having the time of my life. Obviously, if I could rewind the clock, Steve would still be here. He was a dear friend -- much more than a boss. But I love being  CEO of Apple . I love it. It\u2019s just something I have to, and continue to, adjust to. If you have some ideas there of how I can do it better, I would love to hear it. (Laughs.)  Question: Would you describe yourself as a shy person? If so, what would you tell a shy person about how to go about not just being a public face, but also being a source of inspiration for 80,000 employees?  Personal Recognition  Cook: Would I describe myself as being shy? (Pause.) No, I wouldn\u2019t say I\u2019m shy. I don\u2019t think a shy person would stand on a stage and give a presentation or do communications meetings with numerous people and this sort of thing. But I\u2019m not a person that puts value in being recognized. This doesn\u2019t drive me. I am driven by great work and seeing people do incredible things and having a part in that. So it\u2019s more of a feeling inside that drives me, not a public recognition that drives me. Maybe that makes me a bit different.  You mentioned the Exxon CEO. It\u2019s interesting to me -- and I think this is a privilege for Apple -- just like we\u2019re sitting down at this table today, I get e-mails all day long, hundreds, thousands per day from customers who are talking like you and I are talking, almost like I\u2019ve gone over to their home and I am having dinner with them.  Customer Connections  They care so deeply about Apple they want to suggest this or that or say, \u201cHey, I didn\u2019t like this,\u201d or, \u201cI really love this,\u201d or tell me that FaceTime has changed their lives.  I received an e-mail just today where a customer was able to talk to their mother who lives thousands of miles away and is suffering from cancer, and they couldn\u2019t see her any other way.  But the point is they care so much they take the time to say something. It\u2019s not a letter like you might think is written to a CEO. It\u2019s not this formal kind of stuff. It\u2019s like you and I are having a discussion, and we\u2019ve known each other for 20 years, and I want to tell you what I really think. I love it. I don\u2019t know if there\u2019s another company on earth this happens with. It\u2019s just not people from the U.S. These are people from all over the world. I look at it, and I go, \u201cThis is a privilege.\u201d  Is there another company in the world where their customers care so much they do this? I don\u2019t think there is. Other companies I\u2019ve worked at, you might get a letter every six months, and it was, you know, \u201cI want my money back,\u201d or something sort of terse. There was no emotion in it. So I think this is really something incredible.  Emotional Ties  It\u2019s one of the things that I knew about Apple even back 15 years ago when I was in the interview process with Steve. Apple was this company going through all of these hard times. Customers got angry with Apple and would yell and scream -- but they would keep buying. If they got mad at Compaq they would just buy from Dell. There was no emotion there. It was a transaction.  With Apple, my first day at work I crossed a picket line to get in the building! There was a picket line of customers who were protesting, because Steve had decided to kill the Newton device. And it was because they cared so deeply about it. And I thought, \u201cThis is amazing.\u201d I still remember it like it was yesterday. I was walking to the lift that day and thinking, \u201cOh my God, my life is different.\u201d It was so great. It was so great.  Product Introductions  You know, I have been involved in hundreds of new product announcements, hundreds of product withdrawals. At one of the companies I worked at, not to mention any names, we\u2019d put (new products) in the lobby. We\u2019d get on the employee intercom system and say, \u201cCome look at them,\u201d and nobody came. They didn\u2019t even care.  So I think you\u2019re right. I don\u2019t know the gentleman from Exxon. But I think the likelihood that\u2019s going on there is zero. I\u2019ve talked to many other CEOs who look at me like I have three heads when I talk about getting hundreds or thousands of customer e-mails in a day. It\u2019s a privilege. It\u2019s like you\u2019re sitting at the kitchen table. You\u2019re a part of the family. And we have to continue to honor that.  Question: You seem to be an enormously responsible person. Is that accurate?  Cook: I love the company. A significant part of my life is Apple. Maybe some people would say it\u2019s all of my life. I would say it\u2019s a significant part. And you know, I feel both a love for it (and) I feel a responsibility. I think this company is a jewel.  Personal Biography  I think it\u2019s the most incredible company in the world, and so I want to throw all of myself into doing everything I can do to make sure that it achieves its highest, highest potential.  Question: Nothing hardens faster than the details of a CEO\u2019s bio. Every story about you mentions the following: You\u2019re a Southern gentleman. An  Auburn football  fan. Always early to work, always the last one to leave. None of it is negative, but do you recognize yourself in those descriptions or do you find yourself a little bit distorted?  If so, would you like to correct a few things?  Cook: I think when you start reading about yourself, it\u2019s almost -- it\u2019s like a caricature. It begins to sound like someone else. That\u2019s probably a better question to ask people that really know me versus me. I hate talking about me. You know, it\u2019s not something I do well or do a lot. I generally avoid it.  Disciplined Robot  But I would say that the person you read about is robotic. There are some good things about that, perhaps. (Laughs.) Discipline comes to mind. But it sounds like there is just no emotion. People that know me, I don\u2019t think they would say that. I certainly am not a fist-pounder. That isn\u2019t my style. But that and emotion are two different things. One is just a way of expressing it, basically. So, anyway.  Question: How many products does Apple have now?  Cook: Well, we have few. You could almost place every product that we (make) on this table. I mean, if you really look at it, we have four iPods. We have two main iPhones. We have two iPads, and we have a few Macs. That\u2019s it. And we argue and debate like crazy about what we\u2019re going to do, because we know that we can only do a few things great. That means not doing a bunch of things that would be really good and really fun.  That\u2019s a part of our base principle, that we will only do a few things. And we\u2019ll only do things where we can make a significant contribution. I don\u2019t mean financially. I mean some significant contribution to the society at large.  Product Refinement  You know, we want to really enrich people\u2019s lives at the end of the day, not just make money. Making money might be a byproduct, but it\u2019s not our North Star.  Question: How does that calculus work when you\u2019re considering product refinements versus new product lines?  Cook: The way we look at things is we will argue and debate about what to do with both existing products and new product lines. And when we get an idea that\u2019s great enough, we put all of our energy into executing that. We\u2019re fortunate. We find ourselves in two markets right now that are extremely fast- growing and extremely large -- that\u2019s the  phone space  and the tablet space. The PC space is also large, but the market itself isn\u2019t growing. However, our share of it is relatively low, so there\u2019s a lot of headroom for us.  The MP3 market has shrunk. It\u2019s shrinking because people are listening to music on their phones, but it\u2019s still big. We sold 35 million iPods last year, and we love music. I still use a dedicated music player in the gym every day, and I think many people do. Clearly they do, with what we\u2019re selling.  Fostering Debate  So each of those product lines has a great future by themselves, but obviously we also talk about what else we can do. We always have. And we\u2019ll argue, debate and collaborate. And I mean argue and debate in the greatest sense of the words because they -- you know, I never wanted to remove that. It\u2019s a great culture. And it\u2019s clear that we can do more. At the right time, we\u2019ll keep disrupting and keep discovering new things that people didn\u2019t know they wanted.  Question: I\u2019m not going to ask you about an Apple TV, because I know you\u2019re not going to say if it exists or when it\u2019s coming. But what I do want to know is -- there must be enormous pressure, both on you and on your teams, to continue to create breakthroughs. How does that affect you?  Cook: There\u2019s more pressure that comes from within than from the outside. Our customers have an incredibly high bar for us. We have an even higher bar for ourselves.  World Class  So we want to do great work -- and yeah, people are always talking about what we may do next and when it might happen -- but honestly we\u2019re driven much more internally by great people who want to do great work.  As I look around the table at the  executive team , arguably, at least in my opinion, we have the best designer in the world, the top silicon expert in the world, the best operational executive in the world, and the best leaders in marketing, software, hardware and services. These are people that have very high standards that are driven to do things beyond what other people have thought. And I think it\u2019s that ambition and that desire and that thrust for excellence that make creating new things even more likely.  Question: Let me drill down on this one more time.  Cook: Please. Go ahead.  Question: Even superheroes brood, right? Even people with superpowers who are used to doing miraculous stuff -- I\u2019m putting myself in their shoes and imagining that the masses are out there giving Apple love because you\u2019ve created behavior- altering technology. I would imagine that would get to people at Apple once in a while, and that it\u2019s partly your job to figure out a way to say to them, \u201cTrust the process. Trust us.\u201d  No Process  Cook: Two things. One, I wouldn\u2019t call it a process. Creativity is not a process, right? It\u2019s people who care enough to keep thinking about something until they find the simplest way to do it. They keep thinking about something until they find the best way to do it. It\u2019s caring enough to call the person who works over in this other area, because you think the two of you can do something fantastic that hasn\u2019t been thought of before. It\u2019s providing an environment where that feeds off each other and grows.  So just to be clear, I wouldn\u2019t call that a process. Creativity and innovation are something you can\u2019t flowchart out. Some things you can, and we do, and we\u2019re very disciplined in those areas. But creativity isn\u2019t one of those. A lot of companies have innovation departments, and this is always a sign that something is wrong when you have a VP of innovation or something. You know, put a for-sale sign on the door. (Laughs.)  Head Cheerleader  Everybody in our company is responsible to be innovative, whether they\u2019re doing operational work or product work or customer service work. So in terms of the pressure, all of us put a great deal of pressure on ourselves.  And yes, part of my job is to be a cheerleader, and getting people to stop for a moment and think about everything that\u2019s been done. I mean, just take this year. You know, take the last 60 days: iPhone 5, whole new iPods, including a new iPod touch and iPod nano, a fourth-generation iPad, the new iPad mini, a to-die-for MacBook Pro that\u2019s the best Mac we\u2019ve ever done. And so you look at all this, and you go, \u201cOh my God. How could one company do all of this?\u201d And it\u2019s not like we have that many people. As a matter of fact, that\u2019s a secret. You know, small teams do amazing things together.  All of the people around the table have been there for a while, and they\u2019ve lived through different cycles. So they have a maturity, but they still have their boldness. They\u2019re still ready to burn the bridge. And this is great. Because there is no other company like that anymore.  One-Day Transformations  I mean, no company would have done what we did this year. Think about it. We changed the vast majority of our iPhone in a day. We didn\u2019t kind of -- you know, change a little bit here or there. IPad, we changed the entire lineup in a day. The most successful product in consumer electronics history, and we change it all in a day and go with an iPad mini and a fourth- generation iPad. Who else is doing this? Eighty percent of our revenues are from products that didn\u2019t exist 60 days ago. Is there any other company that would do that?  Question: But as a technology consumer and user, and a heavy one, I\u2019m always interested in the new. So unlike, say, ( Procter & Gamble Co .), where there\u2019s a dependability factor, a lot of your brand is \u201cHere comes something new. We\u2019re going to change your behavior again.\u201d  Cook: This is the reason we exist. This is the reason we keep working, and it\u2019s the reason people want to work at Apple.  Replacing Managers  Question: In the past few weeks you replaced two members of your senior executive team, mobile software head  Scott Forstall  and retail chief  John Browett . How did those moves make Apple better, which is a polite way of saying, what was wrong?  Cook: The  key in the change  that you\u2019re referencing is my deep belief that collaboration is essential for innovation --and I didn\u2019t just start believing that. I\u2019ve always believed that. It\u2019s always been a core belief at Apple. Steve very deeply believed this.  So the changes -- it\u2019s not a matter of going from no collaboration to collaboration. We have an enormous level of collaboration in Apple, but it\u2019s a matter of taking it to another level. You look at what we are great at. There are many things. But the one thing we do, which I think no one else does, is integrate hardware, software and services in such a way that most consumers begin to not differentiate anymore. They just care that the experience is fantastic.  Management Team  So how do we keep doing that and keep taking it to an even higher level? You have to be an A-plus at collaboration. And so the changes that we made get us to a whole new level of collaboration. We\u2019ve got services all in one place, and the guy that\u2019s running that has incredible skills in services, has an incredible track record, and I\u2019m confident will do fantastic things.  Jony (Ive, senior vice president of industrial design), who I think has the best taste of anyone in the world and the best design skills, now has responsibility for the human interface. I mean, look at our products. (Cook reaches for his iPhone.) The face of this is the software, right? And the face of this iPad is the software. So it\u2019s saying, Jony has done a remarkable job leading our hardware design, so let\u2019s also have Jony responsible for the software and the look and feel of the software, not the underlying architecture and so forth, but the look and feel.  I don\u2019t think there\u2019s anybody in the world that has a better taste than he does. So I think he\u2019s very special. He\u2019s an original. We also placed Bob (Mansfield, senior vice president of technologies) in a position where he leads all of silicon and takes over all of the wireless stuff in the company. We had grown fairly quickly, and we had different wireless groups.  \u2018Cool Ideas\u2019  We\u2019ve got some really cool ideas, some very ambitious plans in this area. And so it places him leading all of that. Arguably there\u2019s no finer engineering manager in the world. He is in a class by himself.  And Craig (Federighi, Apple\u2019s senior vice president of software engineering) is unbelievable. We don\u2019t subscribe to the vision that the OS for iPhones and iPads should be the same as Mac. As you know, iOS and Mac OS are built on the same base. And Craig has always managed the common elements. And so this is a logical extension. Customers want iOS and Mac OS X to work together seamlessly, not to be the same, but to work together seamlessly.  These moves take collaboration to a whole different level. We already were, to use an industry phrase that I don\u2019t like, best of breed. But it takes us to a whole new level. So that\u2019s what it\u2019s all about. I know there has been a lot written on that, but that\u2019s really what\u2019s behind it.  Jony Ive  Question: What\u2019s your relationship like with Jony Ive? What bonds you to him?  Cook: I love Jony. He\u2019s an incredible guy, and I have a massive amount of respect for him. What bonds us? We both love Apple. We both want Apple to do great things. We both subscribe to the same principles. We believe in the simple, not the complex. We believe in collaboration. We both view Apple as here to make the best products in the world. So our values are the same.  And whether you ask me about \u201cTim and Jony\u201d or \u201cJony and Bob\u201d or whatever, my answer would be the same. If you look at the top 100 people at Apple, you\u2019re going to find very different people, very different personalities, very different styles. We\u2019re not a Chiclet company. We don\u2019t put people through a machine where they come out and talk the same, look the same, think the same. We really value diversity with a capital D.  Different Styles  We want diversity of thought. We want diversity of style. We want people to be themselves. It\u2019s this great thing about Apple. You don\u2019t have to be somebody else. You don\u2019t have to put on a face when you go to work and be something different.  But the thing that ties us all is we\u2019re brought together by values. We want to do the right thing. We want to be honest and straightforward. We admit when we\u2019re wrong and have the courage to change.  And there can\u2019t be politics. I despise politics. There is no room for it in a company. My life is going to be way too short to deal with that. No bureaucracy. We want this fast- moving, agile company where there are no politics, no agendas.  When you do that, things become pretty simple. You don\u2019t have all of these distractions. You don\u2019t have all of these things that companies generally worry about.  No Silo  You don\u2019t have silos built up where everybody is trying to optimize their silo and figuring out how to grab turf and all of these things. It makes all of our jobs easier so we\u2019re freed up to focus on the things that truly matter.  You know, I\u2019ve got experience with other companies. Apple\u2019s a jewel. It\u2019s a privilege to be in an environment like that. I have seen the results of things not being like that. It\u2019s no fun. It sucks the life out of you, and so I guard that. There is nothing I won\u2019t do to guard that. Let me just put it like that.  Question: How do you interact with design? You don\u2019t have meetings. You don\u2019t have a formal process. Do you just wander down, and you and Jony look at stuff?  Cook: I wouldn\u2019t say we don\u2019t have meetings. I wouldn\u2019t go that far. I\u2019m talking about how the kernels of ideas are born. We want ideas coming from all of our 80,000 people, not five or three. A much smaller number of people have to decide and edit and move forward, but you want ideas coming from everywhere. You want people to explore. So that\u2019s what I was talking about before.  Executive Meetings  We have an executive team meeting. It\u2019s every Monday at 9 a.m. Religiously, all of us are in that meeting. We spend four hours together. We talk about everything in the company that\u2019s important -- everything. We go through every product that\u2019s shipping, how it\u2019s doing. We go through every  new product  that\u2019s on the road map -- what\u2019s going on, how the teams are doing, and any key issues there are. We might argue and debate current issues. We might argue and debate future road maps.  We may get to a point where we say, \u201cYou know, this one we\u2019ve got to go off site and really brainstorm about it in a bigger way.\u201d By keeping that cadence and being religious about it -- people don\u2019t travel during that time; everyone is there, and they\u2019re not delegating -- it makes the company run a lot smoother. You don\u2019t get out of sync because you\u2019re constantly coming together.  Now that\u2019s just one thing. Here\u2019s another example. Every Wednesday we\u2019re meeting with product divisions. So a subset of the (executive team) will meet with the Mac division and spend several hours going through Mac. The following Wednesday we\u2019ll spend several hours going through iPhone, and then we\u2019ll go tick-tock, tick-tock again. And so you have meetings like this not just for yourself, although it\u2019s critical for yourself, but you do it because it helps the company run.  Visiting Stores  Question: Do you get walking-around time?  Cook: Yeah, and it\u2019s critical. And it\u2019s not just not walking around on campus. We have a lot of stores. So I\u2019ll walk around our stores. You can learn a tremendous amount in a store. I get a lot of e-mails and so forth, but it\u2019s a different dimension when you\u2019re in a store and talking to customers face to face. You get the vibe of the place.  Not allowing yourself to become insular is very important -- maybe the most important thing, I think, as a CEO. Now fortunately, I think it would be really hard for a CEO of Apple to become insular, but maybe it could happen. I don\u2019t know. But between customers and employees and the press, you get a lot of feedback. The bigger thing is processing and deciding what to put in the distraction category versus where the nuggets are.  Question: How is Apple\u2019s tablet strategy different from Samsung (Electronics Co.)\u2019s or Amazon\u2019s or Microsoft\u2019s?  Product Details  Cook: Again, if you look at our North Star, we\u2019re focused on making the best products, so ours is very product-centric. We care about every detail. We\u2019re also marrying hardware, software, and services. If you think about Android, it\u2019s more like the Windows PC model. The operating system comes from company A. Company B is doing some integration work, and maybe the services come from yet somewhere else. I think we know the kind of customer experience that produces.  In fact, there are all these tablets that have come out -- there were a lot of tablets that came out last year as well -- and the usage of them appears to be very low. Certainly the data that I\u2019m seeing suggests -- and this is all third-party data -- that over 90 percent of the Web-browsing traffic from tablets are from iPad. You may have seen the data over the weekend from IBM that was Black Friday sales that showed the iPad was used in more e-commerce transactions than any other device. And that\u2019s more than all Android devices combined, tablets and smartphones.  User Experience  Since these statistics do not correlate with unit sales, it suggests to me that the iPad user experience is so far above the competition. The iPad has become a part of their lives, instead of a product that they buy and place in a drawer.  And so the advantage for us in having some competition is the more products that are out there, the more attention a category gets. The more attention the category gets, the more people that are in the buying and consideration process. I think that\u2019s actually good for us.  Question: Have you played with the Surface or Galaxy?  Cook: I have, yes. Both of those -- and some others. What I see, for me, is that some of these are confusing, multiple OSs with multiple UIs (user interfaces). They steer away from simplicity. We think the customer wants all the clutter removed. We want the customer to be at the center of everything. I think when you start toggling back and forth between OSs and UIs, etc., I don\u2019t think that\u2019s what customers are looking for.  I think that customers want tablet-optimized apps. You know, we have 275,000-plus apps that have been optimized for the tablet. If you just stretch out a smartphone app on a tablet, it\u2019s an awful experience. It\u2019s not what customers want. I think it\u2019s another reason that usage is so low on these other tablets.  Tablet Competitors  I don\u2019t doubt that there will be units sold in other tablets. It\u2019s happening today. It will happen in the future. But what I strongly believe is that many people that are doing so might feel good initially if they pay a low price, but will bring it home and start to use it, and they\u2019re no longer satisfied. That good feeling is gone. And those people don\u2019t repeat purchases.  Let me give you an example of this. I was thinking about this the other day. Look at netbooks. Many people thought netbooks were the coolest thing ever. Many companies hyped them. In fact, the sales boomed, and then what happened? They crashed, because they were awful! They were flimsy products with crappy, cramped keyboards. They were underpowered. They were just awful.  Pricing Strategy  So we never went into that category. We never put any time into it. A great product doesn\u2019t mean an expensive product. It means a fair price. The iPad mini is all the way down to $329. This isn\u2019t an expensive product. So when we can do great products and achieve a great price, we feel great. But what we wouldn\u2019t do is say, \u201cWe\u2019ve got to have something for this price, and then let\u2019s see what we can do for it.\u201d  That\u2019s not how we think. We think about the product and making a great product that we want to use. When we can do that and achieve another price point, that\u2019s great. But our customers have a high expectation, and we\u2019re not going to try to pass off something -- we would never do that. That\u2019s not how we think.  Question: It strikes me that Apple Maps was a very rare instance of Apple thinking about corporate strategy before thinking about the customer experience. Is that fair?  Cook: No. No, it\u2019s not how I would characterize it. I would characterize -- well, let me back up for a minute. The reason we did Maps is we looked at this, and we said, \u201cWhat does the customer want? What would be great for the customer?\u201d We wanted to provide the customer turn-by-turn directions. We wanted to provide the customer voice integration. We wanted to provide the customer flyover. And so we had a list of things that we thought would be a great customer experience, and we couldn\u2019t do it any other way than to do it ourselves.  \u2018Screwed Up\u2019  We set on a course some years ago and began to do that. So it wasn\u2019t a matter of saying, \u201cStrategically it\u2019s important that we not work with company X.\u201d We set out to give the customer something to provide a better experience. And the truth is it didn\u2019t live up to our expectations. We screwed up.  So what are we doing? We\u2019re putting all of our energy into making it right. And we have already had several software updates. We\u2019ve got a huge plan to make it even better. It will get better and better over time. But it wasn\u2019t a matter that we ... decided strategy over customers. We screwed up. That\u2019s the fact.  Question: Samsung is one of your biggest suppliers. They\u2019re also one of your biggest competitors and an opponent in litigation. Is that awkward?  Patent Litigation  Cook: Life is a complex thing sometimes, and yes, it\u2019s awkward. It is awkward. I hate litigation. I absolutely hate it. For us, this is about values. What we would like, in a perfect world, is for everyone to invent their own stuff. We love competition.  But we want people to have their own ideas and invent their own stuff. So after lots of trying, we felt we had no other choice. We tried every other avenue, and so we\u2019ll see what happens in the future.  Question: You know the Lee family at Samsung. Does it affect how you interact with them? How do you defuse that when you have to talk as partners?  Cook: We can separate in our minds the different portions of their company. They\u2019re a big company and have different divisions and so forth. So that\u2019s kind of how I try to think about it.  Competing Interests  I\u2019m not saying this is the same, but for years we have worked with people who we also compete with. I mean, Microsoft is an example. They provide Office, and so they\u2019re a developer- partner, but they\u2019re also a competitor. Intel is a partner on the Mac, but they are obviously trying to get into the mobile business.  So it\u2019s not different for us. It\u2019s not unique. It\u2019s not the first time where we have competed and cooperated. This is something that we get up every day doing. The thing that is different is the added litigation burden. I hope this works out over time.  Question: You\u2019ve done a lot of work to add transparency to the manufacturing process, in particular to the conditions of people who are working on Apple products. You\u2019ve known Terry Gou at Foxconn (Technology Group) for 20 years.  Cook: A long time.  Question: When you asked him to change some things, what specifically did you ask him to change and how receptive was he?  Auditing Foxconn  Cook: I found him to be very receptive. We had been in the auditing mode for some time and publishing annual reports and working very hard to correct things that we found, and so forth. We\u2019re still doing tremendous auditing, but in addition to that we\u2019ve enlisted the Fair Labor Association to provide additional audits. They bring expertise of looking at different industries.  It\u2019s total transparency. They publish their own results and so forth. We\u2019re the only technology company that\u2019s doing that.  Terry agreed to open his facilities to our auditors and the FLA auditors. It was a requirement from us, but he agreed.  If you look at our website, we\u2019re publishing working hours for almost a million people across our supply chain. Nobody else is doing this. We are very much managing this at a micro level. And you know, maybe as important as that, we are training workers on their rights. We have trained 2 million people, and we\u2019ve brought college courses to the factories where people can begin to earn their degrees.  Foxconn Dorms  So we\u2019re doing a number of things that I think are really great, really different and industry-leading. I think no one is looking at this as deeply as we are or going as deep in the supply chain. We\u2019re back to the mines. We\u2019re going all the way, not just at the first layer. And in addition to that, we\u2019ve chosen to be incredibly transparent with it. I invite everyone to copy us.  Question: I understand there are Apple employees staying in the dorms at these factories.  Cook: We have executives that have stayed in dorms. It\u2019s not unusual. Honestly, this wasn\u2019t to see what life was like in a dorm. It was that we worked so closely with these manufacturing partners and in the manufacturing plants (that) it\u2019s convenient to do. And actually several of our people wind up doing that.  In addition, we have hundreds of people that reside in  China  in the plants on a full-time basis that are helping with manufacturing and working on manufacturing process and so forth. The truth is we couldn\u2019t innovate at the speed we do if we viewed manufacturing as this disconnected thing. It\u2019s integrated. So it\u2019s a part of our process.  Supply Chain  Question: You said you now track down to the mines. What\u2019s left in the supply chain that\u2019s unknowable?  Cook: There are always things that are unknowable. I think that anyone that thinks they have it all down is not looking hard enough, not looking deep enough, or not raising the bar. From our point of view, we don\u2019t want to find zero issues. If we\u2019re finding zero issues, our bar is in the wrong place. So we begin to raise the bar to find issues, and we keep doing this. If you\u2019re doing that, you\u2019re always finding something. That\u2019s the way we look at it.  It sort of goes back to that Kennedy point I made with regard to our matching contributions. We have been given a lot. We earned it, but we have a responsibility to leave the world a better place.  Question: You were instrumental in getting Apple out of the manufacturing business. What would it take to get Apple back to building things and, specifically, back to building things in the U.S.?  U.S. Manufacturing  Cook: It\u2019s not known well that the engine for the iPhone and iPad is made in the U.S., and many of these are also exported -- the engine, the processor. The glass is made in  Kentucky .  And next year we are going to bring some production to the U.S. on the Mac. We\u2019ve been working on this for a long time, and we were getting closer to it.  It will happen in 2013. We\u2019re really proud of it. We could have quickly maybe done just assembly, but it\u2019s broader because we wanted to do something more substantial. So we\u2019ll literally invest over $100 million. This doesn\u2019t mean that Apple will do it ourselves, but we\u2019ll be working with people, and we\u2019ll be investing our money.  Question: On that subject, it\u2019s 2012. You\u2019re a  multinational.  What are the obligations of an American company to be patriotic, and what do you think that means in a globalized era?  Cook: (Pause.) That\u2019s a really good question. I do feel we have a responsibility to create jobs. I don\u2019t think we have a responsibility to create a certain kind of job, but I think we do have a responsibility to create jobs.  Corporate Obligations  I think we have a responsibility to give back to the communities, to pick ways that we can do that ... and not just in the U.S., but abroad as well.  I think we have the responsibility to make great products that we can recycle and that are environmentally friendly. I think we have a responsibility to make products that have a greater good in them.  That\u2019s the one that is most important of all, because a cigarette company could give back things and environmentally dispose of their product or something like that. But we want to provide a product that changes people\u2019s lives in some way. We spend a lot of energy focusing on education. We created iBooks Author and gave it away for free. We wanted to reinvent the textbook and reinvent the classroom and try to really go a long way to solving the student engagement problem. It doesn\u2019t solve every problem in education, but it solves a very important one, right?  Job Creation  And so I think we do have a responsibility for all these things. I\u2019ve never thought a company\u2019s measurement of  job creation  should be limited to the number of employees working directly for them. That\u2019s a very old-time way of measuring. Our iOS platform allows developers to work as entrepreneurs and sell their applications to a worldwide market that didn\u2019t exist previously. The mobile  software industry  was nascent before the iPhone. Now you\u2019ve got hundreds of thousands of developers out there.  Unlike other companies -- at least I know of no other large companies -- almost all of our R&D is sitting in  California . It\u2019s a part of our model. We do this because it\u2019s important for people to run into each other and discuss ideas and collaborate. We\u2019re building a multibillion-dollar headquarters to house them in what we think will be the center of creativity. We\u2019re building a campus in Austin for people in  Texas . We\u2019re building three data centers -- adding to the one we have in Maiden ( North Carolina ) and establishing new sites in  Oregon  and in  Nevada .  600,000 Jobs  So jobs can come in many different ways. I think if you fairly look at it -- we\u2019ve had this estimated by other parties - - we\u2019ve created about 600,000 jobs in the U.S. They all don\u2019t work for Apple. We\u2019re part of a global economy. Over 60 percent of our sales are outside the  United States . So we have a responsibility to others as well. But this is our home market, and I take all of those very seriously -- jobs, education, giving back, the environment.  Question: Not many people know that Apple has a hedge fund, Braeburn Capital.  Cook: I wouldn\u2019t call it a hedge fund.  Question: How would you describe it?  Cook: It\u2019s an entity that manages  Apple\u2019s cash . So I wouldn\u2019t call it a hedge fund because -- at least the way I think of a hedge fund, it\u2019s -- if you look at (Braeburn\u2019s) investments you would find the most conservative investments known to man in there. (Laughs.)  Braeburn Capital  Question: And from what I hear about the returns ...  Cook: That\u2019s intentional. We don\u2019t view ourselves as an investment bank or a mutual fund with an aggressive charter. The goal is capital preservation. I have to say, in the last several years that has not been an easy task. I think the guys have done a remarkable job in this.  Question: How often do you check in on it?  Cook: I don\u2019t get into the decision to invest in this municipal or this corporate bond or this T-bill or anything like that. We have a treasury department and a chief financial officer that\u2019s fantastic, and they do those things.
