Question: One of the few negative things said about you is that you\u2019re not a product guy. You\u2019re a logical guy. You\u2019re a systems guy. You have an engineering background. Given that you\u2019re a product company, does that cut you? Is that something you would refute?  Seeking Opinions  Cook: I think people should decide how they want to describe me themselves. But I\u2019ll tell you what I do. Whether there\u2019s something that I think I know really well or I don\u2019t know at all -- and there\u2019s a huge range there -- I always enlist other people, because the people around the table are phenomenal people.  And I\u2019ve always found even when I thought I knew the most that there was something more that could be added and make it even better.  I\u2019ve never felt that I had to know it all, do it all, any of those things. I think you could have an S on your chest and a cape on your back and not be able to do all those things. I know of no one that can do all that. Maybe there are, but I\u2019m not. So I rely on a lot of people for a lot of different things.  Intuition Counts  Question: What\u2019s the role of intuition in your job?  Cook: It\u2019s critical. It\u2019s extremely critical. The most important things in life, whether they\u2019re personal or professional, are decided on intuition. I think you can have a lot of information and data feeding that intuition. You can do a lot of analysis. You can do lots of things that are quantitative in nature. But at the end of it, the things that are most important are always gut calls. And I think that\u2019s just not true for me, but for many, many people. I don\u2019t think it\u2019s unique.  Question: An anecdote that\u2019s now part of your biography is that  Steve Jobs  told you, \u201cDon\u2019t think what I would do.\u201d Is that true, and if so, can you tell the story?  Cook: Yeah, sure. One weekend he called me, and he said, \u201cI\u2019d like to talk to you.\u201d This was in summer of \u201911.  I said, \u201cFine. When?\u201d  In typical Steve fashion he said, \u201cNow.\u201d  \u201cGreat. I\u2019ll be right over.\u201d (Laughs.)  Steve Jobs  So I go over to his house, and -- I still remember how he started this discussion. He said, \u201cThere has never been a professional transition at the CEO level in Apple.\u201d He said, \u201cOur company has done a lot of great things, but has never done this one.\u201d The last guy is always fired, and then somebody new comes in.  And he goes, \u201cI want there to be a professional CEO transition, and I have decided, and I am recommending to the board that you be the CEO, and I\u2019m going to be the chairman.\u201d  Of course, we had talked about me being a successor before, so it wasn\u2019t the first time I had heard that, but the conversation occurred at a period of time when I felt Steve was getting better, and I think he felt this way as well. So from that point of view, I was a little surprised. I asked again, \u201cAre you sure?\u201d He said, \u201cYes.\u201d I would go, \u201cAre you sure,\u201d and he said, \u201cYes. Don\u2019t ask me anymore.\u201d  So we started talking about what it meant. Again, this is when I am thinking, and I\u2019m certain he\u2019s thinking, that this is going to go on for a long, long period where he\u2019s the chairman and I am CEO. So I\u2019m trying to understand -- how does he see this working? He had obviously thought very deeply about it.  Disney Example  And as a part of this, I asked him about different scenarios to understand how he wanted to be involved as chairman. He said, \u201cI want to make this clear. I saw what happened when  Walt Disney  passed away. People looked around, and they kept asking what Walt would have done.\u201d He goes, \u201cThe business was paralyzed, and people just sat around in meetings and talked about what Walt would have done.\u201d  He goes, \u201cI never want you to ask what I would have done. Just do what\u2019s right.\u201d He was very clear.  He was making this point, and he says, \u201cI hope you listen to my input if I want to input on something.\u201d I said, \u201cOf course.\u201d (Laughs.) But he was so clear, and I have to tell you that it\u2019s probably removed a tremendous burden from me that would have been there otherwise. And he repeated this much closer to his passing. I think in the second instance, I think he did that because he knew it would lift a burden. It was his way of making sure Apple would not be burdened by the past.  More so than any person I ever met in my life, he had the ability to change his mind, much more so than anyone I\u2019ve ever met. He could be so sold on a certain direction and in a nanosecond (Cook snaps his fingers) have a completely different view. (Laughs.) I thought in the early days, \u201cWow, this is strange.\u201d  Old Ideas  Then I realized how much of a gift it was. So many people, particularly, I think, CEOs and top executives, they get so planted in their old ideas, and they refuse or don\u2019t have the courage to admit that they\u2019re now wrong. Maybe the most underappreciated thing about Steve was that he had the courage to change his mind. And you know -- it\u2019s a talent. It\u2019s a talent. So, anyway.  Question: Do you miss him?  Cook: I do, every day. He was a friend, and it\u2019s -- I guess the external view of that is that he\u2019s a boss, but when you work with someone for that long, for me anyway, the relationship is really important. You know? I don\u2019t want to work with people I don\u2019t like. Life is too short. So you do become friends. Life has too few friends. In the largest LBO since the financial crisis, Chief Executive Officer  Michael Dell  and Silver Lake Management LLC are paying $13.65 a share, the companies said yesterday in a statement. That\u2019s 25 percent more than the closing price of $10.88 on Jan. 11, the last trading day before Bloomberg News reported the discussions.  Michael Dell is taking back majority control of the company he started in a University of Texas dormitory almost three decades ago after struggling to equip the PC maker for a new generation of competitors in mobile and cloud computing. He\u2019s wagering that he can more effectively transform Dell into a provider of a broad range of products for corporations outside the scrutiny of public investors, even while encumbering it with about $17 billion in additional debt.  \u201cBefore this agreement the company\u2019s core PC business was deteriorating more than its new enterprise business and the net effect was weak revenue growth,\u201d  Shebly Seyrafi , an analyst at FBN Securities, said in an interview. \u201cNow they have the opportunity to be more aggressive and flexible, fix things and turn it around. Normally for deals like this we see a 15 to 25 percent premium, so I think this price is reasonable.\u201d  Microsoft Contribution  Even as being private shields Round Rock, Texas-based Dell from answering to public shareholders on a quarter-by-quarter basis, it subjects the company to new constraints, including the addition of debt. Following the transaction, Michael Dell will be chairman and chief executive, maintaining \u201csignificant equity,\u201d according to the statement.  Microsoft Corp. , the top software maker, is contributing a $2 billion loan, according to the statement. The investment helps to support \u201cthe long term success of the entire PC ecosystem,\u201d Microsoft said in a separate statement. Microsoft won\u2019t be involved in day-to-day operations, Dell Chief Financial Officer  Brian Gladden  said in an interview.  Microsoft opted to lend Dell the money to avoid having a stake in one of its PC-maker partners, a move that would have been viewed as favoritism, potentially rankling rival computer companies that also have close ties with Microsoft, according to a person familiar with the matter.  Silver Lake  Silver Lake, a technology-focused private-equity firm, was working with partners to line up about $15 billion in funds for the buyout, people familiar with the matter have said.  Dell, which trails Hewlett-Packard Co. and Lenovo Group Ltd. in the PC market, rose 1.1 percent to $13.42 at the close in New York. Its stock plummeted 31 percent last year as it struggled to adapt to the industrywide shift to smartphones, tablet computers and cloud computing services.  \u201cThey obviously see the writing on the wall,\u201d said  Daniel Morgan , a senior portfolio manager at Synovus Trust Co. in Atlanta. \u201cThey understand what the challenges are and realize they need to refurbish what they are doing.\u201d  Michael Dell recused himself from all discussions on the board of directors concerning the deal and from the vote. A special committee handled negotiations with the help of independent financial and legal advisers.  The agreement gives the company 45 days to solicit other potential offers, in what\u2019s known as a go-shop period. A successful counter-suitor would have to pay a termination fee of $180 million. Dell directors considered breaking up the company before opting for the LBO, people familiar with the matter said.  Counter-Bidders Unlikely  Evercore Partners Inc., which is advising the special committee of the board, also approached other potential buyers and received no alternative bids, a person with knowledge of the matter said last month.  \u201cWe believe the board has likely evaluated other options and another bidder is unlikely to emerge at this point,\u201d said  Abhey Lamba , an analyst at Mizuho Securities USA Inc.  Dell has seen its fortunes rise and fall since holding an initial public offering in 1988. CEO Dell, who founded the company with $1,000 in 1984, was viewed as an industry wunderkind, demonstrating that he could sell complex products more efficiently and conveniently than was thought possible.  By cutting out middlemen and honing manufacturing so companies and consumers got exactly the PC configuration they wanted, Dell grabbed share and piled up profit even with lower operating margins than rivals like IBM and Compaq Computer Corp., fueling an almost two-decade boom. Eight years after the IPO, Dell\u2019s stake was worth more than $1 billion.  \u2018Pruning\u2019 PCs  Dell ceded the CEO role to Chief Operating Officer  Kevin Rollins  in 2004 only to return to the helm in 2007 after the company lost its top PC spot to Hewlett-Packard and earnings fell short of estimates. The company was also beset at the time by an accounting scandal that later resulted in a $100 million settlement with the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission.  Since his return, Dell has talked publicly about \u201cpruning\u201d his PC business while using the cash it generates to snap up companies in computer networking, storage, and enterprise software. Global PC sales fell 3.5 percent last year to 352.7 million units, market researcher Gartner Inc. said. Dell\u2019s market share fell 12.3 percent to 10.7 percent.  Consumers and companies are shunning PCs in favor of mobile devices made by Apple Inc. and Samsung Electronics Co., and Dell lags behind Oracle Corp., Cisco Systems Inc. and International Business Machines Corp. in data-center hardware, software and services.  \u2018Just Words\u2019  The company\u2019s travails are reflected by falling profit. Dell will earn $2.98 billion excluding some items in fiscal 2013, compared with $3.49 billion in 2012, according to analyst estimates compiled by Bloomberg.  There\u2019s no guarantee that Dell will do better as a private business. Companies including networking-equipment maker Avaya Inc. and disaster-recovery software company SunGard Data Systems Inc. have struggled since going private last decade. Chipmaker Freescale Semiconductor Ltd. went public in May 2011 after a 2006 LB0, though its stock tumbled by 19 since then, through Feb. 4.  \u201cMichael Dell has never stated what he wants to do to save the company that he can\u2019t do because Dell is a public company,\u201d said  Erik Gordon , a clinical assistant professor at the University of Michigan\u2019s Stephen M. Ross School of Business. \u201c\u2018More latitude\u2019 is the standard rationale for going private, but it\u2019s just words unless someone has an idea that couldn\u2019t be implemented as a public company.\u201d  Technology Buyouts  Other technology companies have attempted to go private and had the talks fall through over valuations or difficulty in financing deals. That was the case for disk-drive maker Seagate Technology Plc in late 2010 -- though it did have a successful LBO a decade earlier. Fidelity National Information Services Inc.\u2019s buyout talks unraveled in 2010 after the company sought a higher price than private-equity firms were willing to pay.  Emphasizing data-center products and services has helped Dell stave off margin erosion. Gross margin is projected to be 22.4 percent in fiscal 2014, compared with 22.3 percent in 2012.  Still, the transformation into a provider of a range of business services, designed to lessen Dell\u2019s dependence on the PC market, didn\u2019t come swiftly enough to prevent going private from being the more attractive option.  The transaction has an enterprise value of $22.2 billion, reflecting $11.3 billion in cash and $9.03 billion in debt. Excluding Michael Dell\u2019s 14 percent stake, the deal\u2019s  equity value  is about $21 billion.  Biggest Since Hilton  If completed, the leveraged buyout would be the biggest since Blackstone Group LP\u2019s $26.2 billion acquisition of Hilton Worldwide Inc., which was announced in July 2007. That deal was struck just as credit markets were seizing up amid a surge in subprime-mortgage defaults. Banks, stuck with loans they couldn\u2019t sell to investors, backed away from financing leveraged takeovers.  While debt markets have loosened up since 2010 as interest rates have fallen, the biggest LBO since 2007 was the $7.2 billion KKR & Co. paid for Samson Investment Co., the Tulsa, Oklahoma-based oil and gas producer, in 2011. A year ago,  Google (GOOG)  and its hardware partner, Samsung,\nintroduced a bold effort to drive a stake through the heart of\nWindows: the Chromebook laptop.  Here was a simple, easy-to-use computer that relied on the\nInternet to handle every task, from running programs to storing\ndocuments -- all without a line of Microsoft code.  Both the product and its reception in the marketplace were\nless than stellar. Now Google and Samsung are back with a new\npair of computers, the Chromebook Series 5 laptop and Chromebox\nSeries 3 desktop computer. They\u2019ve improved from last year, but\nnot enough.  At the heart of the computers is Google\u2019s  Chrome Operating\nSystem , which is essentially a web browser. Instead of\ninstalling programs on the computer, you run web apps --\nprograms that are located online and accessed through the\nbrowser. Google maintains a  website  where you can find links to\nseveral thousand of them and install shortcuts on your computer.  There are a number of advantages to this set-up. The\noperating system on your computer is never out of date. (In\nfact, Google has already pushed out multiple updates since last\nyear\u2019s launch.)  All your apps are online and your documents are\nautomatically backed up to the cloud, so you can access them\nfrom any Internet-enabled computer.  No Net  But there are disadvantages as well, principally if you\u2019re\nsomewhere without an Internet connection, when the Chromebook\u2019s\nusefulness plummets. Another limitation is its capacity: a mere\n16 gigabytes, less than many smartphones.  Physically, the Chromebook is solid if nondescript. It\nweighs 3.3 pounds, is .8 of an inch thick, has a 12.1-inch\nscreen and a battery  Samsung (005930)  says will last for six hours.  The base, Wi-Fi-only model costs $450; for $100 more, you\ncan get one with built-in 3G service from  Verizon (VZ)  Wireless. The\nprice of the 3G model includes a minimal 100 megabytes of data\nper month. Plans with higher limits are available at extra cost.  New this year, the Chromebox costs $329, but you provide\nyour own screen and keyboard; it\u2019s comparable to  Apple (AAPL) \u2019s Mac\nMini. Both Chrome computers use  Intel (INTC) \u2019s lightweight Celeron\nmicroprocessor, a chip you can find in many comparably priced\nWindows PCs with far greater capabilities.  Screeching Halt  The first thing I did with the Chromebook was try to\nactivate it in Bloomberg\u2019s  San Francisco  offices. A year ago,\nthis seemingly simple task came to a screeching halt because --\nunlike every iPhone, iPad, Kindle and even phones running\nGoogle\u2019s own Android operating system -- the Chrome OS couldn\u2019t\nhandle the common authentication method we use on our network.  This time: success. Sort of. I still couldn\u2019t do it, but\nthree members of our technical-support team, after a fair amount\nof fiddling and fumbling, were able to make it work.  Except for that, the Chromebook is easy to use. Google has\nalso added a couple of features that make it look and feel a\nlittle more like a traditional computer, including a task-bar-\nlike launcher for opening new Chrome or app windows. You can\nalso have multiple windows open at once and drag them where you\nlike them.  Offline Mode  I was also able to try out a new feature promised for next\nmonth: an offline mode that will allow you to work on a document\neven when you\u2019re not online, then sync the changes automatically\nnext time you connect.  Using a test document Google shared with me via Google\nDocs, I shut down my Internet connection, tweaked the file -- a\nmock job resume for  Harry Potter  -- and saw my changes reflected\nonce I re-enabled access to the network.  I ran into trouble, though, when I attempted to open a\n Microsoft (MSFT)  Word file I had emailed to myself using Google\u2019s\nGmail.  Three times, the download failed and I received an error\nmessage inviting me to help Google debug the problem. While I\ncame up with a workaround, it\u2019s the sort of thing that doesn\u2019t\ninstill confidence.  Over all, the new version of the Chromebook improves on its\npredecessor, and will be even better with the offline\nfunctionality. But \u201cbetter than it was\u201d isn\u2019t the same as \u201ca\ncompelling experience.\u201d  Of all companies, Microsoft seems to get it.  While this week\u2019s announcement of its new Surface tablets\nleft huge questions unanswered, it\u2019s a dramatic attempt to\nreimagine Windows computing -- and considerably more intriguing\nthan what Google and Samsung have to offer, even the second time\naround. Show me another industry\nwhere the boss isn\u2019t really the boss, where he and the company\nare subject to the whims of one.  \n Dan Gilbert  owns the National Basketball Association\u2019s\nCleveland Cavaliers. So, too,\nwill the value of Gilbert\u2019s investment.  \n One question keeps popping into my mind while watching the\nfree-agent frenzy unfold: Why, other than ego, would anyone want\nto own a professional sports franchise? (EA)  that played on dedicated machines and sold for $60 each. His next project promises console-quality action for free to anyone with an iPad.  Cousins\u2019s journey reflects the turmoil roiling the $67 billion video-game industry more than 40 years after \u201cPong\u201d lit up black-and-white screens. The largest U.S. publishers face a talent drain as big-game veterans like Cousins bring their skills to cheaper and easier-to-develop mobile platforms including  Apple Inc. (AAPL) \u2019s iOS. and  Google Inc. (GOOG) \u2019s Android.  \u201cIt\u2019s anarchy out there, and these big companies are finding it difficult to steer their supertankers,\u201d said Cousins, 38, now general manager of Tokyo-based social-game maker  DeNA Co. (2432) \u2019s Scattered Entertainment.  RELATED NEWS Consumer tastes have shifted at warp speed away from higher-priced packaged discs, and developers are following. Fifty-eight percent of North American developers are planning their next games for smartphones and tablets, based on a  survey  of 2,500 for the Game Developers Conference, which starts today in  San Francisco . Just 11 percent expected to work for  Sony Corp. (6758)  or  Microsoft Corp. (MSFT) \u2019s upcoming consoles, and 6.4 percent for  Nintendo Co. (7974) \u2019s Wii U, out since November.  Newer products such as Cousins\u2019s horror-themed shooting title, \u201cThe Drowning,\u201d threaten to undermine console sales before big publishers like Electronic Arts and  Activision Blizzard Inc. (ATVI)  can move to new platforms.  Mobile Rise  Revenue from free mobile games and those downloaded to computers surpassed annual sales of packaged titles in 2012, when follow-on spending for weapons and other in-game items are included, according to a December survey of U.S. gamers\u2019 playing trends by Frank Magid Associates Inc.  Changes in player preferences recently forced publisher THQ Inc. into bankruptcy and Electronic Arts CEO John Riccitiello out of his job. Former Electronic Arts executive John Schappert, who became chief operating officer at  Zynga Inc. (ZNGA)  when social games on Facebook were gaining popularity, stepped down last August as momentum shifted to mobile.  Google\u2019s Android operating system is the latest big threat. Three of four handsets sold in the $260 billion global smartphone market are powered by Android, and developers are moving to capitalize.  Adding momentum to the shift are coming machines that give Android developers an outlet for more powerful features and add mobility to PC game-play.  Ouya, Razer  Ouya, a $99 Android console, will be released on March 28. Handhelds from  Nvidia Corp. (NVDA) , Wikipad Inc. and San Diego-based Razer Inc. will appear before the next PlayStation or Xbox arrives. In  Seattle , closely held  Valve Corp. , which has built its Steam online store for PC games to more than 50 million members, is working on a home hub for games and media, CEO Gabe Newell said in January.  Cousins left  Redwood City , California-based Electronic Arts in March 2011 after working on console and free-to-play versions of \u201cBattlefield.\u201d EA, which calls the title one of its core franchises, is expected to unveil a new version on March 26. (GE)  and  Pfizer Inc. (PFE)  stockpiled an additional $187\nbillion in untaxed overseas profits over the past year, boosting\ntheir offshore holdings by 18.4 percent, according to data\ncompiled by Bloomberg.  The 70 U.S.-based companies studied hold $1.2 trillion in\nprofits around the world. GE and Pfizer have built up the most\nmoney outside the U.S., with $102 billion and $63 billion\nrespectively, according to securities filings.  Apple Inc. (AAPL) ,\n Google Inc. (GOOG)  and  Microsoft Corp. (MSFT)  were among the companies that\nincreased their accumulated overseas profits by more than 40\npercent in 2011.  As U.S.-based companies expand globally, they keep profits\noverseas, legally out of the reach of the Internal Revenue\nService. Lawmakers from both political parties point to the\nstockpiling as a symptom of a failed corporate tax system, even\nwhile they remain deadlocked over whether the U.S. should impose\nhigher or lower taxes on its companies\u2019 global profits.  \u201cYou\u2019re seeing more and more business go on overseas,\nbecause that\u2019s where an increasing amount of the global\npurchasing power is,\u201d said  Matt Miller , director of public\npolicy at the  Business Roundtable , a Washington-based\nassociation of chief executives at large companies that backs\nlower taxes on overseas profits. \u201cWe need to get a competitive\ntax system that is not antiquated and has all the complexities\nwe have today.\u201d  Worldwide Profit Tax  Under the U.S. tax code, the top corporate rate is 35\npercent on worldwide profits. Companies receive credits for\npayments to other governments, and they can defer taxation while\nthe money accumulates. When companies bring their profits home,\nthey pay U.S. taxes after subtracting the foreign tax credits.  Democrats, including President Barack Obama, maintain that\nthe system encourages companies to move jobs and profits\noverseas. He has proposed a global minimum tax on foreign\nprofits.  Republicans, including  Dave Camp  of  Michigan , the top tax-\nwriter in the House of Representatives, make the opposite\nargument. They say the residual tax that U.S. corporations face\nmakes them less competitive in global markets and discourages\ncompanies from reinvesting their profits at home.  Andrew Williams, a spokesman for Fairfield, Connecticut-\nbased GE, said the company\u2019s operations around the world support\nU.S. facilities that produce goods for export.  Broader Tax Base  \u201cWe believe fundamental tax reform would increase domestic\ninvestment, create high-quality jobs and encourage U.S.\nmultinationals to reinvest more overseas earnings in the U.S.,\u201d\nhe said in an e-mailed statement. \u201cWe support a broader tax\nbase, lower statutory corporate tax rate and adoption of a\nterritorial tax system even if it means higher taxes for\ncompanies like GE.\u201d  Bloomberg analyzed the public filings of 70 U.S.-based\ncompanies that had reported at least $4 billion in untaxed\noverseas profits as of this time last year. The data include\ninformation from the two most recent annual reports -- covering\nthe years ending Dec. 31, 2011, and Dec. 31, 2010, for most\ncompanies.  A May 2011 study by JPMorgan Chase & Co. found that U.S.\ncompanies had $1.375 trillion in undistributed foreign earnings.\nLast year\u2019s total of $1 trillion held overseas by the 70\ncompanies in the data compiled by Bloomberg made up about three-\nquarters of the total amount cited by JPMorgan.  Low-Tax Countries  As a result, the latest data suggest that, in all, U.S.\ncompanies have more than $1.6 trillion outside the country. The\ntotal includes cash and investments in assets such as factories\nand active businesses.  Companies typically bring home money earned in high-tax\njurisdictions that can be offset with foreign tax credits and\nkeep profits earned in low-tax countries outside the U.S., said\nEdward Kleinbard, former chief of staff of the congressional\nJoint Committee on Taxation.  \u201cThe companies continue to reap the harvest of their years\nof aggressive tax planning to locate as much of their profits as\npossible in low-tax foreign jurisdictions,\u201d he said.  Representatives of several of the companies, including\nPfizer and  Citigroup Inc. (C) , said they keep money outside the U.S.\nto support their international businesses.  \u2018Matter of Course\u2019  \u201cCiti maintains a presence in more than 100 countries and\nsome of its earnings are retained outside of the U.S. to provide\nthe necessary capital to fund its international operations,\u201d\nsaid Jon Diat, a spokesman for Citigroup, which increased its\naccumulated overseas profits to $35.9 billion from $32.1\nbillion.  Joan Campion, a Pfizer spokeswoman, said the company\nrepatriates profits \u201cas a matter of course.\u201d That strategy\ngives Pfizer a higher effective tax rate than its competitors,\nits chief financial officer, Frank D\u2019Amelio, told investors on a\nconference call Jan. 31.  Some tax policy analysts, including law professor Thomas\nBrennan of  Northwestern University  in  Chicago , say companies are\nholding money outside the U.S. in part because they are waiting\nfor Congress to repeat a 2004 tax holiday law that set a maximum\ntax rate for repatriation of 5.25 percent.  \u201cWhy not do it?\u201d he said. \u201cIt\u2019s pure upside. In the\nworst-case scenario, you\u2019re going to be taxed as you would have\nbeen in any event.\u201d  Issuing Debt  Many large companies can meet their cash needs by issuing\ndebt in the U.S. without tapping their offshore holdings,\nBrennan said.  A coalition of U.S.-based companies, including Google,\n Cisco Systems Inc. (CSCO) ,  Qualcomm Inc. (QCOM)  and  Oracle Corp. (ORCL) , has been\nlobbying for the past year for a repatriation holiday.  \u201cGoogle\u2019s practices are very similar to those at countless\nother global companies operating across a wide range of\nindustries, such as technology, pharmaceuticals and retail,\u201d\nGoogle said in an e-mailed statement.  The temporary repatriation proposal hasn\u2019t advanced in\nCongress. Obama opposes a one-time tax holiday, arguing that it\nwould be a giveaway to big corporations.  Doug Thornell , an adviser to the pro-repatriation\ncoalition, called the inaction a \u201cmissed opportunity\u201d for\nCongress.  \u201cThe money keeps piling up while Washington fiddles,\u201d he\nsaid in a statement.  Permanent Change  Other companies, including International Business Machines\nCorp., have emphasized a permanent change and not a one-time\nholiday.  Camp has said he prefers to address repatriation as part of\na tax-code overhaul. His draft proposal would shift the U.S. to\na territorial tax system that exempts 95 percent of foreign\nprofits. That would resemble the systems of other major\neconomies, such as the U.K.,  Japan  and  Germany .  All four Republican presidential candidates have endorsed a\nterritorial tax system. In an essay in the Boston Herald\nyesterday, Mitt Romney wrote that companies will continue to\npark profits outside the U.S.  \u201cWith our high rates and our punitive incentives, we are\nshooting ourselves in the foot with a machine gun,\u201d he wrote.\n\u201cThis has to end and I will end it.\u201d  Under the Obama or the Camp approach, the accumulated\noffshore profits must be addressed, said Kleinbard, now a law\nprofessor at the University of  Southern California  in  Los\nAngeles .  Camp Proposal  \u201cIt would be extraordinarily and unnecessarily complicated\nto imagine a world in which old earnings were taxed one way and\nnew earnings taxed a different way,\u201d he said.  Camp has proposed a 5.25 percent tax on the accumulated\noffshore profits to finance a transition to a territorial\nsystem. In his proposal, that one-time revenue would help offset\nthe cost of the territorial system.  Representative Kevin Brady, a Texas Republican, has\nsponsored a bill for a repatriation tax holiday. He said the\npunitive nature of the U.S. tax code is illustrated by the\ngrowth in offshore holdings.  \u201cIt\u2019s both a cry for immediate repatriation and an\nassurance for fundamental  tax reform  that there will still be\nstranded profits,\u201d Brady said in an interview. \u201cThe pot will\nstill be large and I think it will continue to grow\nexponentially.\u201d  To contact the reporter on this story:\nRichard Rubin in Washington at \n rrubin12@bloomberg.net   To contact the editor responsible for this story:\nJodi Schneider at \n jschneider50@bloomberg.net","path":".\/2008_2012_msft_bloomberg_news\/cash-horde-expands-by-187-billion-in-untaxed-offshore-accounts.txt"},{"id":65749439,"title":"Hewlett-Packard Plunges as Whitman Projects Profit Drop","released_at":"<date>October 3 2012<\/date> <time>20:28:55<\/time>","content":"Hewlett-Packard Co. News  Comcast Backed by High Court on Philadelphia Antitrust Suit  Comcast (CMCSA)  Corp., the nation\u2019s largest cable-television\ncompany, doesn\u2019t have to defend against an $875 million\nantitrust lawsuit on behalf of as many as 2 million\nPhiladelphia-area customers, the U.S. Supreme Court ruled.  The justices, voting 5-4 to reverse a lower court, said the\ncase against Comcast was too unwieldy to proceed as a single\nclass-action lawsuit.  The Philadelphia-based company was accused of monopolizing\nits hometown market. The suing customers said Comcast swapped\nterritories and subscribers with competitors to ensure it could\ncontrol the market and charge higher prices. Comcast has denied\nthe allegations.  The high court, in an opinion by Justice Antonin Scalia,\nsaid the customers didn\u2019t meet requirements for outlining a\ncommon method that could be used to determine monetary damages\nfor each of the thousands of individual parties to the lawsuit.  Proof about a common methodology for measuring damages is\nneeded before the case can proceed as a class-action suit\ncovering many individual claims, the court said. The customers\nfell short when they produced a general theory about alleged\novercharges from lack of competition without more detailed\ninformation about the impact of the specific antitrust\nallegation in the lawsuit, the court ruled.  \u201cWe are pleased that the Supreme Court found that a class\nshould not have been certified in this case,\u201d Jenni Moyer, a\nComcast spokeswoman, said in an e-mail.  Scalia\u2019s majority opinion was joined by Chief Justice John Roberts and Justices Anthony Kennedy, Clarence Thomas and Samuel Alito.  Justices Ruth Bader Ginsburg, Stephen Breyer, Sonia Sotomayor and Elena Kagan dissented.  Miguel Estrada a partner at Gibson Dunn & Crutcher LLP,\nargued the case for Comcast. This\nwill help ensure that only those cases truly suited for\ncollective adjudication will be certified as class actions.\u201d  Barry Barnett, a partner at Susman Godfrey LLP, argued for\nthe consumers seeking class status. The companies surveyed, including  Google Inc. (GOOG) ,  Microsoft\nCorp. (MSFT)  and  Cisco Systems Inc. (CSCO) , have been lobbying Congress for a\nreduced tax rate on bringing back profits to the U.S., and they\nmaintain that such a tax holiday would spur economic growth.  \u201cThey want to avoid paying taxes,\u201d Levin told reporters\nin  Washington . \u201cIt\u2019s just pretty obvious what they want to\ndo.\u201d  Levin\u2019s staff compiled the report based on surveys they\nsent to the companies earlier this year. The companies gave\nLevin data that they don\u2019t publicly disclose in securities\nfilings about how they invest their overseas assets.  Under U.S. law, multinational companies with operations\noverseas don\u2019t have to pay U.S.  corporate income  taxes of as\nmuch as 35 percent on that income until they bring the money\nhome. They can receive credits for taxes paid to other\ngovernments.  U.S. Tax Rules  The tax code lets companies invest those tax-deferred\nearnings -- estimated at more than $1 trillion for all of the\ncompanies -- in U.S. assets such as Treasury bonds, bank\naccounts and stocks of other companies. Levin has previously\nproposed preventing companies from investing offshore funds in\nthe U.S. without paying the residual tax.  Levin\u2019s report found that nine of the companies in the\nstudy, including  Qualcomm Inc. (QCOM) , Johnson & Johnson and  EMC Corp. ,\nhave more than 75 percent of their untaxed overseas earnings in\nU.S. assets. The report doesn\u2019t include data for each company.  \u201cAlmost half of the so-called offshore funds were really\nonshore,\u201d Levin said.  According to the report, companies said in the surveys that\nthey invest in U.S. assets because of the dollar\u2019s stability,\npotential accounting issues related to currency fluctuations and\nsuppliers\u2019 requests to be paid in U.S. dollars.  Safety and Liquidity  \u201cWe follow the strategy of investing in U.S. securities\nwith our overseas cash because we want to maximize the safety\nand liquidity of our investments,\u201d said Al Wasilewski, a\nspokesman for  New Brunswick , New Jersey-based  Johnson & Johnson. (JNJ) \nThe maker of Listerine and Tylenol had $37 billion permanently\ninvested outside the U.S. as of Jan. 2, 2011, according to its\nfinancial statement.  Levin said the companies are taking advantage of the U.S.\nfinancial system without contributing enough to it.  The report didn\u2019t include  General Electric Co. (GE) , which leads\nU.S.-based companies with $94 billion in profits outside the\ncountry. It also didn\u2019t include banks such as Bank of America\nCorp. with accumulated foreign profits. The totals include items other than cash,\nsuch as the value of factories and other permanent investments\nthat companies have made outside the U.S. Levin\u2019s report didn\u2019t\nbreak out the portion of earnings that are liquid assets. It\u2019s\na lovely little device for watching movies, listening to music\nand playing games. Slim, sleek, sophisticated -- and irrelevant.  That\u2019s because the Zune HD was released two years after the\ndebut of  Apple Inc. \u2019s iPod Touch. By the time it joined the\nbattle, the war was already lost.  In technology, being late can be as disastrous as being\nwrong. And that\u2019s the battle  Microsoft Corp.  is now fighting\nwith the release of Windows Phone 7, its new smartphone\noperating system. The good news is that the software is\ngenerally a winner: fun, easy to use and not just another iPhone\nwannabe. The bad news is that the good news may not matter.  Microsoft hasn\u2019t just lost market share since the iPhone\ninaugurated the modern smartphone era, it has seen its position\nimplode, falling to 5 percent in the second quarter from 22\npercent in 2004.  The company simply can\u2019t afford to be shut out of the\nbooming market. Morgan Stanley analyst  Mary Meeker  predicts that\nwithin five years, more users will connect to the Internet on\nmobile devices than the desktop computers that Microsoft has\ndominated for decades. Unless the company can establish a\nbeachhead in mobile, it\u2019s facing a long slow slide into\nirrelevance.  Android Threat  As devastating as the iPhone\u2019s arrival proved, Microsoft\u2019s\ntrue mortal threat comes from  Google Inc. \u2019s Android software,\nwhich in little more than a year has skyrocketed. Google says it\nis now activating more than 200,000 new Android devices a day.\nWhile Google gives its software to manufacturers, Microsoft\ncharges for its.  To make Windows Phone 7 a success, Microsoft also is\nspending massively on marketing and offering its business\npartners other inducements that Google doesn\u2019t. Phones equipped\nwith the new operating system go on sale early next month.  Chief Executive Officer  Steve Ballmer \u2019s previous attempts\nto stem the Android-iPhone tide resulted in embarrassment upon\nembarrassment, including a roundly panned update of Microsoft\u2019s\nprevious mobile operating system in 2009 and, earlier this year,\nthe dismal failure of its Kin line, two phones built around\nsocial networking that were killed off less than two months\nafter they were introduced.  In other words, the stakes could hardly be higher. And\nbecause of that, Microsoft -- which is exerting a great deal of\ncontrol over manufacturers in terms of the look and feel of the\nnew Windows Phone 7 handsets -- deserves a lot of credit for\nbeing willing to do a few things that go against the prevailing\nsmartphone norm.  Live Tiles  The difference is apparent from the moment you power up a\nWindows Phone. Instead of screen after screen of application\nicons, as with the iPhone and Android phones, you\u2019re presented\nwith a set of colorful rectangles Microsoft calls \u201clive\ntiles.\u201d Some of these provide information and summon basic\nfunctions, such as the phone tile that tells you how many calls\nyou\u2019ve missed and brings up the dial pad; some are links to\nprograms, such as a mobile version of Microsoft\u2019s Internet\nExplorer Browser; and some are entry points for what Windows\nPhone 7 calls \u201chubs.\u201d  To the extent that  Windows Phone 7  has a Big Idea, hubs is\nit. These are collections of programs, information and functions\norganized around a single theme. There are six of them: People,\nPictures, Music and Video, Marketplace, Microsoft Office and\nGames.  Accessing Music, Photos  The People hub, for instance, agglomerates your address\nbook, Facebook friend list and updates in one place. Music and\nVideos is based on the Zune software, which is easy to use and\nsyncs with content on your computer. Games brings the  Xbox Live \nservice to mobile phones, allowing you to play against other\nusers, though I personally prefer not to share with others\nevidence of my startling lack of ability. The Pictures hub is\nboth a home for your own photos and videos and a portal for\nviewing and commenting on others\u2019 Facebook photos.  The idea sounds more complicated than it is. I found the\nhubs generally logical and easy to grasp; their major\nshortcoming is that they are too limited.  Facebook, for example, is well integrated into the People\nhub -- but Twitter isn\u2019t. For that, you have to leave the tile\nview to scroll through a tiresome vertical list of apps.  The Pictures hub is great if you and your friends all use\nFacebook or Microsoft\u2019s Windows Live to store photos online. Use\n Yahoo \u2019s Flickr or some other service? Not so lucky.  Microsoft has a good idea here, but it has to do much more\nto make its phones friendlier to the things I want to use on it,\nnot what it and its partners want me to use.  Business Considerations  That, in fact, is my biggest complaint about Windows Phone\n7: Too much about it seems dictated by business considerations\nrather than user experience. For instance, the two AT&T Inc.\nphones I tested -- the  HTC  Surround and the  Samsung  Focus --both\nincluded a fat first-screen tile touting  AT&T \u2019s U-verse\ntelevision service.  Office, which includes limited-function productivity\nsoftware, seems to be a hub because, well, Microsoft owns\nMicrosoft Office.  The Surround and HTC\u2019s HD7, which is appearing in the U.S.\non the T-mobile network, both have tiles leading to an \u201cHTC\nHub\u201d that, confusingly, includes its own interface and featured\napps.  Playing Catch Up  Because Windows Phone 7 is, essentially, an entirely new\nsmartphone platform, it will take a while before we have any\nsense of whether and how quickly third-party developers write\napps for it. (The new Marketplace hub is still in the process of\nbeing populated.) Certainly  Microsoft , with its deep pockets,\nwill do all it can to provide inducements, but it\u2019s safe to say\nthat it will lag far behind the iPhone, Android devices and even\nResearch In Motion Ltd.\u2019s BlackBerry for a long time to come.  Similarly, Microsoft has a lot of catching up to do in\nterms of basic functionality. Among other things, Windows Phone\n7 doesn\u2019t yet offer a visual listing of voicemail messages, as\nAndroid phones and iPhones do, nor is it equipped to share\nits Internet connection with other devices.  Facing a field crowded with well-entrenched competitors,\nMicrosoft smartly decided it stood little chance with a me-too\nentry. Its gamble to do things differently resulted in a product\nthat, all things being equal, provides a plausible alternative.\nBut at this late date, all things aren\u2019t equal, and Windows\nPhone 7, while much better than previous Microsoft offerings,\ndoesn\u2019t do any one thing so much better that it makes you have\nto have it.  ( Rich Jaroslovsky  is a Bloomberg News columnist. The\nopinions expressed are his own.)  To contact the writer of this column:\nRich Jaroslovsky in San Francisco at \n rjaroslovsky@bloomberg.net . Hewlett-Packard Co. (HPQ)  is the latest to enter the fray. Its\npurchase of Palm Inc. last year brought with it the company\u2019s\nwell-regarded webOS operating system. Now HP has launched the\nTouchPad, a tablet gunning for  Apple Inc. (AAPL) \u2019s iPads, iPhones and\niOS software.  I\u2019ve been a fan of the polished, easy-to-use webOS software\nsince its debut on Palm smart phones, and the good news is that\nit makes the leap from phone to tablet beautifully. Moreover,\nthe TouchPad comes with some cool new capabilities and\naccessories that might make even an Apple-lover envious.  Unfortunately, there\u2019s not-so-good news too. You\u2019d expect\nthe world\u2019s largest computer maker to know a thing or three\nabout hardware. But that, surprisingly, is where the TouchPad\ncomes in a little light.  Make that, a little heavy. Among other problems, the\nTouchPad weighs in at about 1.6 pounds (740 grams), which is a\nwhopping 23 percent heavier than the comparable iPad 2, and\nheavier even than the original iPad.  Same Screen  There are many similarities to the iPad. Both have 9.7-inch\nscreens and their height and width are nearly identical. They\u2019re\npriced the same too: $500 for a Wi-Fi-only model with 16\ngigabytes of storage; $600 with 32 gigabytes. TouchPads with\nbuilt-in wireless data service from  AT&T Inc. (T)  are promised for\nlater in the year.  By controlling both the software and the hardware, HP can,\nlike Apple, create a largely seamless user experience. Learn the\nwebOS interface -- with its \u201ccard\u201d metaphor, you simply flick\na window to dismiss an application -- on one device, and you\nknow how to use it on any.  In some areas, HP has even Apple beat. For instance, you\ncan pair the TouchPad and HP\u2019s coming Pre 3 phone just by\ntapping them together, and then pass information wirelessly\nbetween them. Once I got the hang of it, which took a while, I\ncould find a Web site on the Pre, then toss it onto the\nTouchPad\u2019s larger screen.  With the Pre in my pocket, I was also able to answer\nincoming calls and receive and send  text messages  directly on\nthe TouchPad.  Sluggish Response  For all those whiz-bang features, though, the TouchPad\nsometimes struggles with the basics. The tablet, which is run by\na  Qualcomm Inc. (QCOM)  microprocessor, can feel sluggish and\nunderpowered. When I turned it from portrait to landscape mode,\nit took a moment for the screen to properly reorient itself, and\nat one point I had one horizontal stack of cards and one\nvertical stack on the desktop at the same time.  Battery life was less than stellar. While HP says you can\nexpect 8 to 9 hours of video-watching and Web surfing, I got\nonly 4 1\/2 hours in my stress testing, which involved running\nvideos continuously with the screen at maximum brightness, and\nWi-Fi and Bluetooth both active. And the screen, even at the\nmax, was markedly dimmer than those of the iPad 2 and Samsung\nElectronics Co.\u2019s similarly sized Galaxy Tab 10.1, which runs\nthe tablet version of  Google Inc. (GOOG) \u2019s Android operating system.  Fingerprint Magnet  The TouchPad also lacks the rear-facing camera that\u2019s\nbecome standard on competing tablets, most useful for shooting\nvideo. And the glossy black plastic case is a major fingerprint\nmagnet.  Palm\u2019s pre-HP challenge was attracting enough users to make\nit worthwhile for developers to write apps for it. That problem\nis likely to dog the TouchPad as well. Apple claims more than\n90,000 programs written specifically for the iPad; HP says the\nTouchPad will have about 300 at launch, plus a few thousand more\noriginally written for its phones and tweaked for the tablet.  The company is determined to lure developers by promising\nno mere app store but something called \u201cPivot,\u201d a handsome,\nmagazine-like online catalog. And HP says it will eventually put\nwebOS on many more devices, including printers and computers\nthat run  Microsoft Corp. (MSFT) \u2019s Windows operating system, in hopes of\nreaching the critical mass that will make its ecosystem\ncompetitive. In turn, they reinvest that money in local entrepreneurs, who may go on to achieve success themselves and fund the next wave of innovators. But the problem for  London's Tech City  is the entrepreneurs have yet to get that cycle started. Despite the emergence of high-profile companies such as Mind Candy and Songkick, none of the hub's startups have gone public.  Achieving a breakout IPO will be \"the true measure of Tech City's success,\" according to Ben Drury, the co-founder and CEO of  7Digital , an online music service located in that area. To help kickstart things, Drury and others are looking for answers from the U.K.'s original tech hub, which sits just 80 kilometers (50 miles) north of Tech City -- Cambridge. Aside from boasting a world-class research university, Cambridge is the birthplace of some of the U.K.'s biggest tech companies, such as chip designer ARM, which surpassed $23 billion in market value earlier this year. \"The U.K.'s got a new ecosystem in east London, but we aren't learning from our pre-existing tech heritage,\" Drury said. \"The two areas need to share knowledge and collaborate more openly on ideas.\" A spokesman for the University of Cambridge said that  collaboration  is \"at the heart of the Cambridge cluster,\" and the university lets outside companies, including those from Tech City, use its lab equipment and other facilities. Tech City could use the help. Among the challenges, a shortage of talent tops the list. A recent survey of the area's startups found that 77 percent of them believe a lack of skilled workers was hampering their growth, according to  research firm GfK . Also, 29 percent said a dearth of capital was causing them to miss significant expansion opportunities. Despite its proximity, accessing Cambridge's business and academic know-how may not be easy. While the university's spokesman says that collaboration is the mantra, tech investor Hussein Kanji has had a different experience. \"Cambridge University has a pecking order that is completely proprietary,\" said Kanji, an alumnus of Stanford University, which played a central role in the growth of Silicon Valley and is known for its culture of openness. \"The hierarchy kind of works against itself, and if you're an outsider, you're an outsider.\"  The university's \"us versus them\" mentality extends into the investment environment, Kanji said. \"In investor meetings I've noticed Cambridge guys get annoyed that Tech City gets the publicity it does,\" he said. \"Cambridge's angel investors remain in Cambridge, and there's a resistance to outside capital. It's extremely insular.\"  One group that's trying to change that is the Cambridge Angels investment group, which announced an effort earlier this year to hold events designed to build bridges between the two tech clusters, according to  Business Weekly . Another group attempting to forge stronger ties between Tech City and Cambridge is  Entrepreneur First , which tries to lure talented graduates to London's startup scene, and away from the well-beaten path of a high-paid job at an investment bank or a law firm. Larson-Green\u2019s obstacles are about to get bigger, now that she\u2019s been put in charge of all hardware at the world\u2019s largest software company. As head of the devices and studio engineering group, she is responsible for Microsoft\u2019s push into gadgets such as tablets, which so far is faltering as consumers and businesses shun the company\u2019s nine-month-old Surface computer in favor of the iPad from Apple Inc. and mobile machines from Samsung Electronics Co.  Larson-Green is at the center of a sweeping overhaul by Microsoft Chief Executive Officer  Steve Ballmer , unveiled yesterday, which is intended to streamline management and rev up growth in areas like mobile devices. The task is urgent as Microsoft, with its Office and Windows software products dominant on personal computers, deals with a PC slump caused by consumers\u2019 increasing preference for mobile devices.  Cutting Through  Jensen Harris, the Microsoft software designer who Larson-Green shoved out of the way during the 2001 earthquake -- even though she\u2019s about a foot shorter than he is -- said she makes quick work of any obstacle. The temblor \u201cwas my first experience with Julie,\u201d said Harris, who has worked for her for the past 10 years overhauling Office and Windows. \u201cJulie has this immediate ability to cut through things.\u201d  Microsoft is increasing its bet on hardware as its  revenue  growth has slowed and its stock price has underperformed the Standard & Poor\u2019s 500 Index in five of the past six quarters. Tablets, a market where 3.7 percent of machines run Microsoft\u2019s Windows, are poised to outsell PCs by 2015, market research firm IDC said.  Yet Microsoft\u2019s move into hardware has been shaky. The Redmond, Washington-based company\u2019s Surface tablet, which is its first-ever computer and the only piece of hardware Larson-Green has worked on, sold just 900,000 units in each of Surface\u2019s two quarters on the market, according to IDC.  Xbox Woes  Larson-Green will also have to help Microsoft\u2019s Xbox video-game business, its more established hardware effort, recover from missteps in the unveiling of its latest console, the Xbox One. The company recently angered gamers by announcing a requirement to connect the Xbox One to the Internet daily and by placing some restrictions on transferring used games and then reversing course. The device, which goes on sale in the fall, costs $499, or $100 more than its rival from Sony Corp.  The newly anointed senior leaders will meet weekly to make sure efforts are coordinated, Ballmer said in an interview.  \u201cYou have to agree on what the cadence is on which devices and services,\u201d he said.  Microsoft declined to make Larson-Green available yesterday to discuss her specific plans for hardware. In an interview last month, Larson-Green said she\u2019s fascinated by all manner of devices -- she had a Samsung Galaxy phone on her desk and an HTC Corp. One in her bag. She also listed wearable technology and living room devices as interesting and new challenges for Microsoft.  \u201cTechnology is going to be everywhere and we want to be relevant to your life, and so we are going to be everywhere,\u201d she said. Larson-Green has taken on huge product challenges before. She helped spearhead a radical redesign of Microsoft\u2019s flagship operating system, Windows 8, which was released in October and aroused the ire of some longtime users. Critics said Windows 8, which is designed to work with touch-screen devices, came too early for a PC market that\u2019s still dominated by machines without touch-screens.  Larson-Green took the view that the greater risk was staying on a path of incremental updates, said Harris.  Two Roads  \u201cThere are two roads you can go on. Larson-Green, a native of logging town Maple Falls, Washington, joined Microsoft in 1993 and rose through the ranks. She became a vice president in the Office division in 2006.  By 2009, Larson-Green was in charge of the look and feel of Windows -- and closely watching the threat that new types of devices could pose to Microsoft and the PC industry. At the 2009  Consumer Electronics Show  in Las Vegas, she saw touch devices and e-readers that were adding computing functions. It was clear consumers would prefer portable touch devices to desktop computers for many tasks, she said.  Underdog Position  The rest of the Windows team also saw their software falling behind because of trends like mobile and touch, Harris said. Lawsuits\/Pretrial  Higher Court Will Decide Whether Picard Can Sue JPMorgan  A bankruptcy judge doesn\u2019t have the authority to decide\nwhether the trustee liquidating Bernard Madoff\u2019s firm has the\nright to sue JPMorgan Chase & Co. for $6.4 billion, a higher\ncourt said.  U.S. District Judge  Colleen McMahon  in New York said she\nwould determine whether trustee  Irving Picard  has standing to\nsue the bank on behalf of the con man\u2019s customers, as JPMorgan\nrequested. The question of Picard\u2019s status requires\n\u201csignificant interpretation\u201d of federal non-bankruptcy law\nthat isn\u2019t the province of a bankruptcy court, she said in a\nwritten opinion yesterday explaining her May 4 decision to take\nthe case. JPMorgan argued that Picard was hired to liquidate the\nMadoff firm, and wasn\u2019t empowered by law to mount a class-action\nsuit to recover money on behalf of Madoff customers. Picard,\nclaiming that he was suing as a single entity, not a class,\n\u201cmisses the point,\u201d the judge said.  \u201cThe issue is whether seeking damages on behalf of more\nthan 50 persons or prospective class members triggers\u201d a law\nthat might bar Picard from bringing his suit, the judge said.  McMahon\u2019s opinion is another challenge to Picard, who has\nfiled more than 1,000 suits claiming $100 billion for investors\nin the Ponzi scheme. He said he would decide whether Picard can bring common-\nlaw claims such as unjust enrichment and can sue on behalf of\ncustomers, since his job is to liquidate the Madoff firm.  Picard, whose firm was paid $146 million through March for\nwork since Madoff\u2019s 2008 arrest, has fought to keep his cases in\nbankruptcy court. JPMorgan \u201cno doubt hopes to distance itself\nboth from the thousands of victims of that scheme and from other\nalleged wrongdoers\u201d by going to district court, Picard said in\na March filing. Ensco and the government\nasked for the delay in a joint filing on May 20.  Both sides said an 11-day temporary delay of the judge\u2019s\nMay 10 order would \u201cprevent further unnecessary litigation.\u201d\nIf they can\u2019t reach a settlement by June 20, they may seek to\nextend the stay to continue talks, according to the filing. The Interior Department opposed Ensco\u2019s suit, saying that a\ndelay in issuing new permits was needed to give the industry\ntime to boost safety and spill-response capabilities after the\nDeepwater Horizon drilling rig off the Louisiana coast exploded\nin April 20, 2010. Trials\/Appeals  Microsoft Appeal of 899 Million-Euro Fine May Limit EU Powers  Microsoft Corp. (MSFT) \u2019s challenge to an 899 million-euro ($1.26\nbillion) European Union penalty for failing to comply with an\nantitrust ruling may lead to a curb on regulators\u2019 powers.  The world\u2019s largest software company will tell judges at an\nappeal hearing today that in 2008 the European Commission failed\nto give it sufficient guidance to avoid the fine.  Microsoft is the only company in more than 50 years of EU\ncompetition policy to be penalized for failing to comply with an\norder. The Brussels-based commission said it breached an earlier\nruling by overcharging for licenses that rivals needed to\nconnect products to Windows computers. As the first appeal of\nsuch a decision, the judges at the  EU General Court  in\nLuxembourg will clarify the scope of the commission\u2019s power.  \u201cIt\u2019s not about the money for Microsoft, it\u2019s not about\nthe money for the commission or the other applicants,\u201d said\nNicolas Petit, a competition law professor at the University of\nLiege in Belgium. \u201cAt the heart of the case is whether a\nregulator can find and penalize infringements without really\nsaying what the substance of the law is.\u201d  The commission, the EU\u2019s antitrust authority, imposed the\n899 million-euro fine as a so-called periodic penalty payment on\nRedmond, Washington-based Microsoft for failing to comply with a\n2004 antitrust order.  Under the initial decision, Microsoft was fined 497 million\neuros and ordered to provide data to competitors to allow\nservers to connect to computers using the Windows operating\nsystem.  Microsoft was also required to limit to a \u201creasonable\u201d\namount the royalties it charged for the technology. An EU court\nin September 2007 rejected Microsoft\u2019s appeal of that decision.  Today\u2019s case is the last remnant of years of disputes with\nthe commission that resulted in fines totaling 1.68 billion\neuros. Microsoft agreed to a settlement in 2009 in a bid to\nclose a long chapter in the company\u2019s uneasy relationship with\nthe EU regulator.  Amelia Torres, a spokeswoman for the commission, declined\nto comment.  The case is T-167\/08, Microsoft v. European Commission.  For more, click here. The fight stems from one of the largest defense procurement\nfiascos in U.S. history. The trade groups filed separate lawsuits and appeals\nchallenging the regulation. That reveals \u201ctheir life experience or attitude that\nmay have an impact on how they view the facts of the case.\u201d  The practice adds fuel to the debate over social-networking\nprivacy and whether Internet postings should be used to reject\nsomeone from a job or academic program -- or a seat in the jury\nbox. Facebook has more than 500 million users, while Twitter\nmembers post 140 million messages daily. That yields a wealth of\ndata that lawyers can use to screen people or hone arguments. Verdicts\/Settlement  Fed Releases Discount-Window Loan Records Under Court Order  The Federal Reserve released thousands of pages of secret\nloan documents under court order, almost three years after\nBloomberg LP first requested details of the central bank\u2019s\nunprecedented support to banks during the financial crisis.  The records -- 894 files in PDF form that must be\nindividually opened and read -- reveal for the first time the\nnames of financial institutions that borrowed directly from the\ncentral bank through the so-called discount window. The Fed\nprovided the documents after the U.S. Supreme Court last month\nrejected a banking industry group\u2019s attempt to shield them from\npublic view.  \u201cThis is an enormous breakthrough in the public\ninterest,\u201d said Walker Todd, a former Cleveland Fed attorney\nwho has written research on the Fed lending facility. \u201cThey\nhave long wanted to keep the discount window confidential. They\nhave always felt strongly about this. They don\u2019t want to tell\nthe public who they are lending to.\u201d  The central bank has never revealed identities of borrowers\nsince the discount window began lending in 1914. The Dodd-Frank\nlaw exempted the facility last year when it required the Fed to\nrelease details of emergency programs that extended $3.3\ntrillion to financial institutions to stem the credit crisis.\nWhile Congress mandated disclosure of discount-window loans made\nafter July 21, 2010, with a two-year delay, the records released\nyesterday represent the only public source of details on\ndiscount-window lending during the crisis.  The Fed documents released yesterday show the central bank\nproviding credit to borrowers large and small. A page described\nas \u201cPrimary Credit Originations, February 5, 2008\u201d lists the\nNew York branch of Deutsche Bank AG with a loan of $455 million\nfrom the New York Fed. On the same day, Macon Bank is listed\nwith a $1,000 loan from the Richmond Fed.  Lending through the discount window soared to a peak of\n$111 billion on Oct. 29, 2008, as credit markets nearly froze in\nthe wake of the bankruptcy on Sept. 15, 2008, of  Lehman Brothers\nHoldings Inc. (LEHMQ)  While the loans provided banks with backstop cash,\nthe public has never known which banks borrowed or why. Fed\nofficials say all the loans made through the program during the\ncrisis have been repaid with interest.  Former Fed officials, lawyers representing the central\nbank, and even some Fed watchers have expressed concern that\nrevealing the names of discount-window borrowers could keep\nbanks away from the facility in the future. Madoff trustee Irving Picard and\nhis law firm were paid about $102 million in the 21 months from\nDecember 2008, when Madoff was arrested, through September 2010,\nit said.  As the liquidations are far from over, \u201cfees paid to date\nfor both the Lehman and Madoff liquidations are a mere fraction\nof the amounts that will eventually be sought,\u201d the report\nsaid. Yet the SEC failed to set up a review schedule and scope\nfor inspections, the Inspector General said. SIPC\u2019s board \u201cconstantly monitors the SIPC fund to assure\nthat the corporation has sufficient assets to fulfill all of\nSIPC\u2019s statutory missions,\u201d Stephen Harbeck, SIPC\u2019s president,\nsaid in an e-mail. York","released_at":"<date>June 7 2011<\/date> <time>04:01:05<\/time>","content":"When Syria\u2019s government unblocked\nFacebook, YouTube and Blogspot in February, many activists saw\nthe move as an overture to protesters, possibly one offering a\nsemblance of the freedoms won by insurgents in Egypt and\n Tunisia .  Others saw it as a potential means of surveillance. They\nwere right: Within weeks, reports began to emerge from detained\nSyrian activists who said that authorities had demanded their\nFacebook passwords. Others inside the country noted that their\nfriends\u2019 Facebook walls had been compromised and now contained\npro-regime sentiment.  On Twitter, Syrian protesters have noted the emergence of\npro-regime \u201cspambots\u201d: accounts set up with automated feeds\nthat post benign content, including links to attractive\nphotographs of Syrian landscapes, to the hashtag used by\nprotesters and supporters, presumably to flood it with\ncontradictory information. Activists believe the bots have been\ncreated by regime supporters, paid or otherwise.  The potential for authorities to use tools like Twitter and\nFacebook to track down insurgents is very real. Many\ndemonstrators chose early on not to hide their identities,\nemboldened by the success of  Egypt \u2019s mostly peaceful\nuprising.\u00a0When coupled with Facebook\u2019s requirement that users\ncreate profiles using their real names, pro-democracy activists\nare at risk of being unmasked on social networks.  As writer Evgeny Morozov has argued, the Internet can be as\nmuch a tool of repression and control as of liberation. As\nMorozov writes in his 2011 book, \u201cThe Net Delusion,\u201d\u00a0Belarus\nauthorities have used Facebook to monitor its citizens, assuming\nthey\u2019ll share plenty of personal information on the social\nnetwork.  Upper Hand  In  Iran , despite news media proclamations of a \u201cTwitter\nrevolution,\u201d the regime had the technological upper hand, not\nonly censoring websites but harnessing the widespread use of\nsocial media tools to their advantage to track down activists.  That  Syria  would pursue a digital crackdown seems\ninevitable. What\u2019s less clear is the technology that companies\nand governments are -- or could be -- adopting to mitigate\ntechnological repression.  In January, when Tunisians uploaded videos of street\nprotests to Facebook to share with the world, authorities\nmodified Facebook landing pages, inserting extra code and\nredirecting Tunisian users to a different page in order to\ncapture their passwords. Facebook responded favorably, adding\nadditional security measures for Tunisian users, including\nrouting all requests for  http:\/\/facebook.com  to\nhttps:\/\/facebook.com, a more secure login page for the site.\nLater, Facebook offered an opt-in HTTPS version of the site to\nusers everywhere.  Alarm Sounded  In this case, Facebook acted after Tunisian activists and\nnon-governmental organizations sounded alarms. In another case\nin 2009, the U.S.  State Department  called upon Twitter to halt a\nsite update during a crucial time for Iranian protesters. Though\nthe move allowed activists to continue using Twitter during a\ntime of day when protests were prevalent, the State Department\u2019s\nrequest also provided fodder to the Iranian regime to blame the\nprotests on foreign interference.  While those efforts were helpful, governments and Internet\ncompanies could do more.\u00a0Facebook, for example, could prompt\nSyrian users to create new passwords and to stop using old ones\nthat may have been compromised. That is a low-cost measure, but\neven it has potential drawbacks. Some detained Syrians have\nrecently reported that authorities threatened to hurt their\nfamilies if they changed their passwords.  No Pseudonyms  Sometimes a company\u2019s policies are the problem.\u00a0Facebook\nremoves users caught with pseudonyms from the site.\u00a0When a\nperson using his real name finds his account erroneously\nremoved, Facebook requires proof of identification via e-mail, a\nmove that presents risks for users in authoritarian states.  The U.S. is one of the few countries actively promoting an\nInternet freedom agenda.\u00a0As a recent paper from the  Center for a\nNew American Security  points out, this agenda, which includes\npushing U.S. companies to create policies oriented toward free\nexpression, would be strengthened by collaboration with other\ndemocratic governments. A new strategy released by the White\nHouse in May, the International Strategy for Cyberspace, calls\nfor such cross-border partnerships.  By forming a coalition, the U.S. could deflect concerns\nthat the initiative is a cover for its own geopolitical goals --\nand remove the stigma some activists fear comes with accepting\nmoney from any single government.  A Step Ahead  A coalition could also more quickly train experts and\nsupply tools to activists, helping them stay a step ahead of\nrepressive regimes looking to block their use of networks as\nwell as track, harass and arrest them. Broader government\nparticipation would also allow for a wider exchange of\ninformation and technology among activists from different\ncountries.  NGOs also have a role to play in ensuring the safety of\nsocial media users. The  Global Network Initiative  has convened\nhuman-rights groups, academics, investors and Internet\ncompanies, including Google, Yahoo and Microsoft, in an effort\nto advance free expression and privacy online. My organization,\nthe Electronic Frontier Foundation, is a participant.  Organizations can play other parts as well, distributing\ntools like HTTPS Everywhere, which enforces HTTPS encryption on\nmajor websites. The program was developed by the EFF and the Tor\nProject, a global network of servers offering anonymous Web\nsurfing.  In the end, there is no single solution. Government\nregulation is difficult to get right, and can harm the very\npeople it\u2019s intended to help.  While companies are often at the\nfront lines, they need public scrutiny to stay in check and\nensure user privacy. Ultimately, the burden falls hardest on\nusers to stay vigilant and look out for themselves. Often, no\none else will.  (Jillian C.
