They were belting down the freshly groomed corduroy, carving fast, giant-slalom turns last year when--bam!--they collided, hard.  The impact cracked both their helmets. Byrne, whose buyout firm, CrossHarbor Capital Partners LLC, owns the private Montana resort, broke a ski in half. Collins, the club\u2019s head of sales, flew into the trees. The pair wobbled into the lodge and learned later that they had sustained concussions,  Bloomberg Pursuits  magazine reports in its Fall issue.  For Byrne, 47, it was just another brush with danger. Last year, he rode the Baja 1000 race route in  Mexico  on a Honda motorcycle until a friend crashed and collapsed a lung. In 2007, the mast on Byrne\u2019s 82-foot (25-meter) racing yacht Captivity  snapped at midnight  during an 811-mile Caribbean regatta in 25 knots of wind. With just the backup motor, the crew pointed the yacht toward bright lights on the coast of Cuba, the nearest land. They got lucky. The beams came from the U.S. base at Guantanamo Bay. The boat was damaged beyond repair.  \u201cI go hard at whatever I do,\u201d says Byrne, whose congenial grin and graying hair parted on the left make him look more like a banker in  Boston , where CrossHarbor is based, than an adrenaline junkie. He shakes his head and laughs at his exploits, which emerge in conversations like other people\u2019s accounts of beach vacations.  Bulk Purchase  The  Yellowstone Club , a private enclave tucked into the Madison Range south of Bozeman, is Byrne\u2019s latest thrill ride. Instead of just buying a house at the resort, like other wealthy ski freaks, he purchased all 13,600 acres (5,504 hectares) and everything on them--15 lifts, three lodges, a golf course--for $115 million after the club went bankrupt in 2008. And he did it during the worst recession since the 1930s.  For its money, CrossHarbor got more than just a secluded getaway with Switzerland-in-America views and uncrowded slopes and fairways. It also got wealthy members, including  Bill Gates  and  Barry Sternlicht , CEO of Starwood Capital Group LLC. Since taking over, Byrne has added to the A-list, bringing in  Justin Timberlake  -- who\u2019s an excellent snowboarder -- Google Inc. Chairman  Eric Schmidt  and Peter Berg, actor and director of the 2004 movie \u201cFriday Night Lights.\u201d  \u201cIt\u2019s a very interesting and eclectic group of people,\u201d Berg says. \u201cI\u2019ve got a lot of new best friends.\u201d  Mandatory Property  The cost of membership is steep: You have to buy a piece of real estate, be it a condominium for $2.5 million or a 357-acre  ranch  for $18 million. Started in the late 1990s by one-time timber baron Tim Blixseth and his wife, Edra, the club attracted hedge-fund managers such as Cliff Asness and Jeffrey Ubben and political figures, including former U.S. Vice President Dan Quayle and the late Representative  Jack Kemp .  Byrne visited in 2005, bought a lot to build on, and then snapped up four more to develop and sell. Then he went deep and purchased Sunrise Ridge, a planned cluster of 58 duplexes and triplexes, 15 of which were under construction.  Soon after Byrne\u2019s arrival, a Kardashian-style drama turned the Yellowstone Club into a reality show staged in Montana courts. The club had borrowed $375 million in a syndicated loan from Credit Suisse Group AG and the Blixseths used it to buy luxuries outside of the club, including a private island in the Caribbean for $28 million, according to a 2006 lawsuit by former cyclist  Greg LeMond , a member and part owner at the time.  Then the Blixseths divorced. Edra got the club in a settlement, just as the global financial system seized up, wiping out the market for $10 million ski chalets. CrossHarbor, which manages money for the Smith College endowment and other institutions, loaned the club $23 million to keep it operating in bankruptcy before buying it outright.  Reluctant Spokesman  After five years of brand-destroying bad press, the club required a leader with turnaround skills who could show that better days were ahead.  \u201cThis place needed a face,\u201d says Byrne, who has always shunned the media but has played that role this time. \u201cIt wasn\u2019t by design or desire.\u201d  Byrne and his partners, including billionaire Ronald Burkle, have spent $100 million on improvements to the club. They cleared out the Persian rugs, velvet-covered chairs and beaded lamps that made the mountain lodge, with its tall stone fireplace and elk on the menu, look more like a 19th-century bordello.  They added tennis courts, a clubhouse on the golf course, a new fitness center and 20 Below, a kids zone with a soda fountain, basketball court and movie theater. A new village around the lodge, with spas, bars and shops, is on the way, says Mike Meldman, CEO of  Discovery Land Co. , which manages the club and owns a piece of it.  Real Skiing  \u201cIt will feel like a mini mountain town,\u201d he says.  You would expect a ski resort for millionaires to be all about  Dom Perignon  and truffle crostini at 10,000 feet. Such indulgences are found here. But make no mistake, the skiing is the real draw. The steeps are steep, and the powder-loaded chutes at the top of the mountain, with 100-mile (161-kilometer) views, are every bit as good as the wine list at the club\u2019s Warren Miller Lodge, named after the legendary ski filmmaker and member. You can go faster than at Vail or Aspen, too, because there are so few skiers.  \u201cThe skiing is as good as anything in the world,\u201d Berg says.  That is Byrne\u2019s reward for buying the club. More than yacht racing, more than motorcycling, even more than working, Byrne loves to ski.  Fresh Snow  On Presidents\u2019 Day weekend, a storm is dumping 8 inches (20 centimeters) of fresh snow, luring Byrne from visits with potential buyers and onto the hill. He drops into the Rainbow Lodge, the rustic alternative to the grander main one, and says a quick hello to some members who are watching an English Premier League game between Sunderland and Arsenal. Byrne meets Collins, the colleague he collided with last year, and heads out into the blizzard.  At the Mountain Lift, Byrne says hello to Jim Davidson, co-founder of  Silver Lake , the Silicon Valley buyout firm that tripled its money selling Skype Technologies SA to Microsoft Corp. last year. Davidson and his wife head down under the lift.  Byrne is nursing an ankle he broke in a November basketball game. Still, he skis toward the chutes below Pioneer Ridge: First Hour Glass, Second Hour Glass and Elevator Shaft. He has The Who\u2019s Quadrophenia pumping on his in-helmet headphones. All the music at the club -- in the bar, in the restaurant, at the lift -- is classic rock.  \u201cWe gotta make the old guys feel young,\u201d he says.  Lone Peak  Byrne scans the chutes, finds an untracked line between two spines of rock and pushes off. He makes deft turns through the fresh snow. If the ankle still hurts, it doesn\u2019t show. At the bottom, Byrne looks up at Lone Peak, the 11,166-foot mountain that looms over the club to the north. Its steep, above-timberline faces are draped with tantalizing snow. Byrne talks about putting a chairlift up the side of it.  \u201cThat\u2019s big-boy skiing up there,\u201d he says.  After the snow melts in the summer, the club holds Camp Yellowstone, where families gather for a long weekend of sack races, tug of war and other old-school field day games. Tragedy struck the camp in August, when member James Sinclair Welch, 19, took a midnight ride in a four-wheel-drive all-terrain vehicle with Parker Regan, his prep-school roommate. Welch made a left on a road in the club and tossed Regan from the ATV, according to the Montana Highway Patrol.  Regan, also 19, died at the scene. Welch was charged with negligent vehicular homicide under the influence of alcohol. He posted $50,000 bail on Aug. 3, and pleaded not guilty at his arraignment on Sept. 24.  First Sale  Byrne, who grew up in Marblehead,  Massachusetts , has been making money in property since the age of 16 or 17, when he got his license to sell it. Working at his mother\u2019s real estate office one summer day, he stepped in for an agent who had taken the day off and sold a home listed for more than $1 million.  \u201cI got a check for $22,000,\u201d Byrne recalls. \u201cI said, This is pretty good!\u201d  As a high school student, he peddled $60 ficus trees and carpet remnants to college kids and their parents to decorate dorm rooms of Boston-area schools.  After Byrne graduated in 1986 from  Tufts University , a year early, he took a job restructuring bad loans at Bank of New England Corp. and then left to start CrossHarbor in 1992. He was 26. One of his first deals was a $190 million distressed loan on a building called One Kendall Square in Cambridge, near  Massachusetts Institute of Technology . Byrne had a contract to buy the loan for $63 million. But he didn\u2019t have $63 million.  Geneva Pitch  A friend told him about a group from the  Middle East  that was looking for real estate investments, and Byrne traveled to Geneva to pitch them. Two months later, he had the money. Almost every other Sunday, for six years, Byrne flew to Geneva to meet with his investors. The commute almost cost him his life. One Sunday -- Sept. 2, 1998 -- Byrne was set to fly to Geneva but felt crappy and didn\u2019t go. Shortly after takeoff, the cockpit of  Swissair Flight 111  caught fire and the MD-11 plunged into the ocean, killing all 229 people on board. It was the most serious near miss for a guy who\u2019s had a few of them.  \u201cMy phone was ringing off the hook that night,\u201d he says.  African Reunion  These days, Byrne spends as much time as he can at the club, for work and pleasure. In February, he attended a reunion with Tanya and Mikey Carr-Hartley, owners of a high-end  safari company  in  Kenya . A club member threw a dinner for them and other members who had been on their trips in  Africa  over the years. The group of about 30 met at Rainbow Lodge, had a few drinks and then climbed into heated snow cats for a ride to the mid-mountain Timberline Cafe for scallops and pheasant.  Many of the guests were friends of Byrne\u2019s, including Tom Healey, who was on board Captivity when its mast snapped near Cuba and who crashed his motorcycle in Baja.  \u201cI\u2019m in AA,\u201d Healey says, by way of introduction. \u201cAlways attacking!\u201d  The same is true of Byrne. \u201cHe likes excitement,\u201d says Google\u2019s Schmidt, a skier.  The next day, Byrne is back on the slopes, this time with Scot Schmidt, one of the first professional extreme skiers -- people who rip down absurdly steep terrain on camera. Now, he\u2019s a full-time ski guide at the club.  \u201cI show people how to play the course,\u201d he says. Schmidt takes off from the top of Pioneer Mountain and arcs fast turns through the powder. The white peaks of nearby Wyoming reach into the southern horizon. Byrne watches, then pushes off down the side of a mountain he bought -- at least in part -- for the thrill of it. The smartphone maker said yesterday it reached a tentative agreement for a $4.7 billion buyout by a group led by  Fairfax Financial Holdings Ltd. (FFH) , its biggest  shareholder . Including net cash, the proposal values the Waterloo, Ontario-based company at an 80 percent discount to its book value and just 0.17 times its sales, the cheapest revenue multiple on record among similar-sized North American telecommunications or technology acquisitions, according to data compiled by Bloomberg.  While the company has six weeks to seek other bids,  Pacific Crest  Securities said investors should be happy to get the $9 a share that Fairfax is offering. Chief Executive Officer Thorsten Heins, who took over in January 2012, didn\u2019t publicly disclose the company was for sale until last month after almost a year of canvassing potential buyers. Now, BlackBerry has posted a string of quarterly  sales  declines and lost almost $79 billion in market value as it fell behind Apple Inc. and Google Inc. Last week, BlackBerry said it will cut a third of its workforce and take a writedown of as much as $960 million.  \u201cIt is being valued like a broken company,\u201d Anil Doradla, a Chicago-based analyst at William Blair & Co., said in a phone interview. \u201cThey had a chance to potentially execute on an M&A deal when these guys were doing better. So by the time Thorsten Heins came on board, I think it was too little, too late.\u201d  Deal Value  Including the $2.8 billion of  cash  and equivalents BlackBerry had in the most recent quarter, the proposal values the company at about $1.9 billion. The group led by Toronto-based Fairfax is still seeking financing for the offer, which is subject to due diligence and further negotiation.  Fairfax owns about 10 percent of BlackBerry\u2019s  common stock . BlackBerry didn\u2019t name the other members of the takeover consortium. Fairfax CEO Prem Watsa said in an interview that the consortium at this point doesn\u2019t include  Mike Lazaridis , inventor of the BlackBerry and former co-CEO of the company, who has a 5.7 percent stake in the company.  Lisette Kwong, a spokeswoman for BlackBerry, declined to comment on the Fairfax bid and reiterated that the deal includes a go-shop period that may reveal other offers.  \u201cOur offer represents compelling value, particularly by comparison to recent transactions like Microsoft and Nokia,\u201d  Paul Rivett , president of Fairfax, said in an e-mailed response to questions.  Microsoft Corp., the world\u2019s largest software company, agreed this month to buy Nokia Oyj\u2019s handset business for $7.2 billion. Microsoft paid 0.42 times Nokia\u2019s trailing 12-month revenue from devices and services, according to data compiled by Bloomberg that include net debt.  Deep Discount  When BlackBerry shares were halted yesterday before news of the deal, the stock\u2019s 20-day average price was $10.31, higher than Fairfax\u2019s $9-a-share cash bid. The offer is a 3.2 percent premium to the closing price on Sept. 20, when the stock plunged after BlackBerry said it\u2019s cutting 4,500 jobs and will record an inventory writedown, mostly for the new Z10 touch-screen devices.  The transaction would value BlackBerry at an 83 percent discount to the $11.3 billion of revenue it generated in the past 12 months, according to data compiled by Bloomberg. That\u2019s a lower sales multiple than any other technology or telecommunications takeover struck in  North America  for more than $1 billion, the data show.  Those deals had a median book value multiple of 5.3, while the BlackBerry buyout would be for just 0.2, the data show.  Other Bidders?  For shareholders, a deal still may be wishful thinking because there isn\u2019t yet a firm offer on the table, MKM Partners LLC\u2019s Michael Genovese said. There\u2019s a chance that Fairfax will reduce its offer after scrutinizing BlackBerry\u2019s books, and other bidders are unlikely to step in, the  Stamford , Connecticut-based analyst said.  He values BlackBerry at $7 a share, excluding its cash, which the company is projected to burn through in the coming quarters.  \u201cIf you own the stock, your upside is capped at $9,\u201d Genovese said in a phone interview. \u201cThis is not yet a real deal. Hopefully, for people who are long BlackBerry, it will result in one, but that\u2019s very far from certain.\u201d  Today, BlackBerry shares fell 3.3 percent to $8.53, their lowest closing level since last November.  BlackBerry\u2019s dimming prospects led the company to form a special board committee last month to evaluate all possible options, including joint ventures, partnerships or an outright sale.  \u2018Pretty Attractive\u2019  That announcement followed almost a year of bankers from JPMorgan Chase & Co. and  RBC Capital Markets  quietly contacting possible bidders, said two people with knowledge of the matter, who asked not to be named because the talks were private. The advisers found little interest in buying the whole company, the people said at the time.  It\u2019s unlikely that other suitors will emerge with higher offers for BlackBerry, according to Doradla of William Blair.  \u201cI would be surprised if someone would come in and outbid Fairfax,\u201d the analyst said. \u201cIf someone were to buy them out, by now they would have made that decision. I don\u2019t know why they\u2019d go after the asset today rather than one year or six months ago. Nothing has really changed.\u201d  That means $9 a share may be the best BlackBerry shareholders are going to get, said  James Faucette , a Portland, Oregon-based analyst at Pacific Crest.  \u201cI actually think this is a pretty attractive offer for shareholders,\u201d he said in a phone interview. \u201cHonestly, if they were to let it go a few quarters, it would be meaningfully worse.\u201d  True Value  While there\u2019s value in BlackBerry\u2019s intellectual property and enterprise platform, it\u2019s difficult to envision a competitor or another technology company stepping in with a rival bid for the whole company, Oppenheimer Holdings Inc.\u2019s  Ittai Kidron  wrote in a report yesterday after the Fairfax offer was announced.  \u201cThat said, it is possible a company could come out of the woodwork or potentially another financial entity\/consortium would find value in pursuing a deal,\u201d the New York-based analyst wrote.  The Wall Street Journal  reported  that there are other parties still considering making a bid for BlackBerry, citing an unnamed person familiar with the matter. It was unclear how the Fairfax news would impact the deliberations, the newspaper said. Licensing Obligations  The cases were to be the first in which courts were asked\nto define licensing obligations of patent owners who help create\ntechnological specifications.  The focus now turns to the trial in Microsoft\u2019s complaint\nagainst Google, scheduled to start next week in  Seattle , said\nJorge Contreras, an associate law professor at American\nUniversity in Washington. The Wisconsin trial was sidetracked on the issue of whether\nany decision by the judge would resolve the companies\u2019 dispute\nabout what amount of royalty would fit the definition of fair\nand reasonable -- the standard for payments on standard-\nessential patents. Soon after, serious talks began, moving from Round Rock,\nTexas, where Dell is based, to California to New York. The code\nname for the potential deal: Mr. Denali. The discussions broke\nup several times over price, especially in the final weeks of\nthe deal, according to the people. The price ranged from an\ninitial offer of $12 a share to the final price of $13.65.  After six months of negotiations, Dell and private-equity\nfirm Silver Lake Management LLC agreed yesterday to buy the\ncomputer company for $24.4 billion in the biggest leveraged\nbuyout since 2007. While other leveraged buyouts are often\ninitiated by LBO firms, this was Michael Dell\u2019s deal from the\nstart, an effort to ensure his legacy and reinvent the\nstruggling company he founded in a University of Texas dormitory\nalmost three decades ago.  Michael Dell is committed to his job as chairman and chief\nexecutive officer, said Dell Chief Financial Officer  Brian Gladden .  \u201cFinancially, he\u2019s putting a lot of capital into this\nprocess,\u201d Gladden said.  Dell advanced 0.1 percent to $13.43 at 10:45 a.m. in New\nYork trading. In the last 52 weeks the stock traded between\n$8.69 and $18.36, data compiled by Bloomberg show.  Under the deal, Dell will contribute his 14 percent  stake ,\nvalued at about $3.4 billion, as well as $700 million, a person\nfamiliar with the matter said, giving him a majority stake in\nthe company. Silver Lake will invest about $1.4 billion in the\nbuyout and Microsoft Corp. will invest about $2 billion, one of\nthe people said. Another $13 billion will be financed by banks.  Industry Shift  Going private will enable CEO Dell, 47, to reposition the\ncompany amid shrinking personal computer sales and the\nindustry\u2019s shift to mobile and cloud computing without the\nscrutiny and stock fluctuations that come with being publicly\ntraded.  The deal took several twists as board members tried to\nensure that shareholders were protected in a buyout that was\nbeing led by management. Dell recused himself from the board to\nlet it work independently on the potential deal, according to\npeople familiar with the situation.  Alex Mandl , the board\u2019s lead director, formed a special\ncommittee with three directors,  Laura Conigliaro ,  Ken Duberstein \nand  Janet Clark . The committee hired as financial advisers three\nof JPMorgan Chase & Co.\u2019s top dealmakers --  James B. Jennifer Zuccarelli , a spokeswoman for JPMorgan, and  David Frink , a spokesman for Dell, declined to comment.  One of the first moves by the board was to make Dell agree\nhe would work with any and all potential partners, said one of\nthese people. Whether it was Silver Lake or TPG Capital or\nanother private-equity firm, Michael Dell would have to\nnegotiate with them in good faith if they made the best offer,\nsaid this person.  Possible Alternatives  Meanwhile, the board had hired Boston Consulting Group Inc.\nto consider alternatives, according to people familiar with the\nmatter. One idea discussed by BCG and Dell executives: Break the\ncompany in two, splitting off the personal computer business\nfrom units that focused on data-center hardware and software,\nthe people said. Microsoft Ties  There was also a tie between Durban and Microsoft. Durban,\nwho joined Silver Lake in 1999, had led the firm\u2019s buyout of\nSkype Technologies SA, which Microsoft later bought. Microsoft\njoined the Dell talks and agreed to contribute a $2 billion loan\nto help finance the deal. Microsoft opted for a loan rather than an equity investment\nto avoid rankling other PC that use Windows, said one of the\npeople, who asked not to be named because the matter isn\u2019t\npublic. Nokia CEO Stephen Elop is returning to Microsoft as part of the asset sale, making him Ballmer\u2019s most likely successor and signaling that the company is in smartphones for the long haul, Sanford C. Bernstein & Co. said, even as some shareholders say that strategy is misplaced.  \u201cI can\u2019t say I\u2019m too thrilled about the deal,\u201d Tim Schwartz, a  money manager  at  Bloomfield Hills , Michigan-based Schwartz Investment Counsel Inc., which oversees $1.3 billion and owns Microsoft, said in a phone interview. \u201cThe perception is that this is going to be a continuation of the old management and old-school Microsoft mentality.\u201d  Ballmer Exit  Microsoft shares surged 7.3 percent on Aug. 23 after Ballmer, who has been CEO since 2000, said he will retire within 12 months. Some investors were eager for his replacement to be an outsider who might make bold moves to reverse a shrinking market value, such as spinning off consumer-centric units like Xbox and shifting its focus back toward software and services for businesses.  The Nokia purchase instead has fueled speculation that Elop, a former Microsoft executive, is being groomed to take the helm and will continue with Ballmer\u2019s strategy of keeping enterprise and consumer products under one roof. The  stock  has dropped 6.6 percent since announcing the Nokia deal, sending Microsoft\u2019s market value down to $260 billion yesterday.  Today, Microsoft shares climbed 0.1 percent to $31.23 at 9:50 a.m.  New York  time.  \u201cThere have been a meaningful proportion of investors who had hoped that Microsoft would de-emphasize its consumer businesses and focus on its more profitable, more predictable corporate businesses,\u201d Chris Hickey, a London-based analyst at Atlantic Equities, said in a phone interview. \u201cThis acquisition obviously makes that possibility extremely unlikely\u201d and \u201cties the hands\u201d of the next CEO, he said.  Critical Market  Microsoft said adding Nokia\u2019s handset business will let it make more money from Windows Phones and help the software maker move faster and create better products in a market that is critical to its success. The company sees \u201csignificant long-term revenue and profit opportunities\u201d for shareholders, Ballmer said in the press release announcing the deal.  \u201cPhones are the most personal of the personal devices people use today and success in phones is important for success in tablets and PCs,\u201d  Brad Smith , Microsoft\u2019s general counsel, said in an interview Sept. 3. \u201cWe need to move faster.\u201d  Tony Imperati, a spokesman for Microsoft, declined yesterday to comment further.  The timing of the deal limits activist shareholder ValueAct Holdings LP\u2019s ability to fight the deal, according to  Rick Sherlund , a New York-based analyst at Nomura Holdings Inc. ValueAct last week won an agreement that would give it a seat on Microsoft\u2019s board next year and guaranteed regular meetings with \u201cselected Microsoft directors and management.\u201d In return, the investor won\u2019t pursue or participate in a proxy contest.  Response Options  A person with knowledge of the matter has said that ValueAct wants Microsoft to focus on its business software and Internet-based cloud services rather than consumer technology. Representatives for ValueAct didn\u2019t return calls for comment on the Microsoft-Nokia deal.  \u201cNow that ValueAct has entered its standstill agreement, it is not clear what alternatives ValueAct may have to respond to shareholder dissatisfaction with the Nokia deal,\u201d Sherlund wrote in a note Sept. 3.  Much of the dissatisfaction is due to \u201cnot the deal itself but what it could mean,\u201d Mark Moerdler, a New York-based analyst at Bernstein, said in a phone interview. \u201cIt may not be the end of the investments Microsoft makes in trying to chase after the consumer market, an area that the Street may or may not feel is the best use of Microsoft\u2019s resources.\u201d  More Deals?  Microsoft still needs more applications and services if it wants to fulfill Ballmer\u2019s strategy of integrating its services with its devices, similar to what Apple has done,  Jason Maynard , a San Francisco-based analyst at  Wells Fargo & Co ., wrote in a Sept. 3 report.  BlackBerry Ltd.\u2019s strong presence in the enterprise market could still attract interest from Microsoft, according to people familiar with the matter who asked not to be identified. Shares of the Canadian smartphone maker, which is weighing a sale, have risen 6.2 percent since Microsoft\u2019s Nokia announcement.  Microsoft paid 0.42 times Nokia\u2019s trailing 12-month revenue from devices and services, according to data compiled by Bloomberg that include net debt. That revenue multiple would imply an enterprise value of $4.8 billion for Blackberry. The device maker\u2019s equity and net cash are currently  valued  at $2.8 billion.  The acquisition will put an even bigger spotlight on the struggles in Microsoft\u2019s consumer-devices business, which are likely to continue as it faces off against stronger rivals Apple and Google, Hickey of Atlantic Equities said.  Declining Asset  The deal doesn\u2019t offer much more to Microsoft than it already had as part of its partnership with Nokia, according to Nandan Amladi, a New York-based analyst at Deutsche Bank AG.  \u201cThey already had a partnership in place, so people are wondering why they bought an asset with a declining revenue base and pretty challenging margins,\u201d Amladi said in a phone interview.  Microsoft is paying a much higher premium for the Nokia assets than \u201ceven optimistic estimates suggested they were worth,\u201d said  Todd Lowenstein , a Los Angeles-based fund manager at HighMark Capital Management Inc., which oversees about $19 billion and owns Microsoft shares.  \u201cThe deal handcuffs the next CEO somewhat,\u201d Lowenstein said in an e-mail. \u201cThis feeds into the perception Microsoft lacks capital discipline, overpays on deals, and chases growth in areas where they aren\u2019t competitive at their core.\u201d  To contact the reporters on this story: Tara Lachapelle in New York at  tlachapelle@bloomberg.net ; Brooke Sutherland in New York at  bsutherland7@bloomberg.net   To contact the editor responsible for this story: Sarah Rabil at  srabil@bloomberg.net","path":".\/2008_2012_msft_bloomberg_news\/icrosoft-out-18-billion-on-ballmer-nokia-deal-real-m-a.txt"},{"id":5954918,"title":"Go Daddy Names Irving as CEO","released_at":"<date>December 11 2012<\/date> <time>15:33:23<\/time>","content":"Go Daddy Group Inc., an Internet\ndomain-name hosting company, appointed Blake Irving chief\nexecutive officer. The Dec. 14 ruling resolves a dispute over whether  Bikram\u2019s\nYoga College of India  -- the chain of studios owned by Bikram\nChoudhury that offers yoga in a hot setting -- can receive U.S.\ncopyright protection for yoga exercises. Bikram sued several\nyoga studios and their owners last year alleging that their use\nof his choice and order of poses violated his copyright.  The  U.S. Copyright Office  in June said that a sequence\ncouldn\u2019t be protected under copyright laws. \u201cA compilation of\nexercises or the selection and arrangement of yoga poses will be\nrefused registration,\u201d the agency said in a release published\nin the Federal Register.  In the Dec. 14 ruling, U.S. District JudgeOtis Wright\nnoted that while books or photographs depicting a compilation\ncan be copyrighted, federal protection doesn\u2019t cover the\nselection, coordination or arrangement of exercise. Wright held\nthat \u201ceven if the manner in which Choudhury arranged the\nsequence is unique, the sequence would not be copyrightable\nsubject matter because individual yoga poses are not\ncopyrightable subject matter.\u201d  The ruling won\u2019t end the litigation because the suit also\nclaims trademark infringement, copyright of the dialogue that\naccompanies the sequence and a violation of the teacher-\ncertification agreements. A trial is still scheduled for Jan. 29\non those remaining claims, said Eric Maier, a partner at Maier\nShoch LLP who represents  Evolation Yoga .  Yoga to the People , a New York studio that employed the\nsequence of poses in a hot studio and was also sued by Choudhury\nlast year, settled its lawsuit on Dec. 3. According to a joint\nstatement, Yoga to the People will stop offering the same\nsequence of 26 poses by Feb. 15. Jordan Susman, who represents\nYoga to the People, didn\u2019t respond to an e-mail yesterday\nseeking comment on Wright\u2019s ruling.  Robert Gilchrest, a lawyer at Silverman Sclar Shin & Byrne\nPLLC in Los Angeles who represents Bikram Yoga and Choudhury,\nalso didn\u2019t respond to an e-mail yesterday seeking comment.  Maier said his client had discussed settling with Bikram\nYoga before talks stalled. \u201cThey insisted that we had to agree\nthat they had a copyright over the sequence,\u201d Maier said. \u201cWe\nrefused because we believed there was no such copyright.\u201d  The case is Bikram\u2019s Yoga College of India LP v. Evolation\nYoga LLC, 11-cv-05506, U.S. District Court, Central District of\nCalifornia (Los Angeles). The case that settled Dec. 3 is\nBikram\u2019s Yoga College of India LP v. Yoga to the People Inc.,\n11-cv-07998, U.S. District Court, Central District of California\n(Los Angeles). A third case still pending is Bikram\u2019s Yoga\nCollege of India LP v. Raiz, 11-cv-7377, U.S. District Court,\nCentral District of California (Los Angeles).  Patents  AstraZeneca Can Block Generic Version of Crestor until 2016  AstraZeneca Plc (AZN) , the U.K.\u2019s second-biggest drugmaker, won\nan appeals court ruling that will block generic versions of its\ntop-selling cholesterol medicine Crestor in the U.S. until July\n2016.  The patent on the medicine is valid and enforceable, the\n U.S. Court of Appeals  for the Federal Circuit in Washington said\nin an  opinion  posted on its website Dec. 14. The court rejected\nchallenges made by generic-drug makers including  Mylan Inc. (MYL)  and\n Teva Pharmaceutical Industries Ltd. (TEVA)   The ruling ensures AstraZeneca won\u2019t lose sales of a\nproduct that brought in $2.3 billion in U.S. revenue in the\nfirst nine months of the year. Total sales of Crestor, whose\nchemical name is rosuvastatin, account for 22 percent of London-\nbased AstraZeneca\u2019s revenue.  The generic-drug companies, except Apotex Inc., conceded\nthat they infringed the patent for the compound rosuvastatin and\nfocused their challenge on claims the patent covered an obvious\nvariation of earlier compounds.  They also claimed AstraZeneca and patent partner  Shionogi &\nCo. (4507) , based in Osaka, Japan, didn\u2019t disclose important\ninformation to the U.S. Patent and  Trademark Office . Failure to\nreport information that could bear on the originality of a\nproduct could lead to a patent being thrown out.  The appeals court panel in a 2-1 decision upheld a lower\ncourt ruling that rejected those arguments, and that Apotex\u2019s\ncopy would infringe the patent. The challengers also included\n Aurobindo Pharma Ltd. (ARBP) , Par Pharmaceutical Cos. and  Sun\nPharmaceutical Industries Ltd. (SUNP)   The Federal Circuit in February upheld the dismissal of\nCrestor suits over patents that expire in 2018 and 2021 that\ncover the methods of using the active ingredient for certain\ntypes of patients.  The case is In Re Rosuvastatin Calcium Patent Litigation,\n2010-1460, U.S. Court of Appeals for the Federal Circuit\n(Washington).  The lower court combined case is In re Rosuvastatin Calcium\nPatent Litigation, 08-1949, U.S. District Court, District of\nDelaware (Wilmington).  To see the patent: RE37,314.  Intel Wins First Round in Patent Fight That Threatens Chips  Intel Corp. (INTC)  won the first round of a patent-infringement\ncase that some lawmakers said may threaten jobs at the company\u2019s\nU.S. manufacturing plants.  The world\u2019s largest semiconductor maker didn\u2019t infringe the\npatents of closely held  X2Y Attenuators LLC , U.S. International\nTrade Commission Judge  David Shaw  said in a  notice  posted on the\nagency\u2019s website on Dec. 14. The next step is a possible review\nof the judge\u2019s findings by the full commission, which has the\npower to block imports of products if they infringe U.S.\npatents.  Lawmakers from both U.S. political parties have taken\ninterest in the outcome, saying a loss for Intel could harm U.S.\njobs. That\u2019s drawn the case into a broader dispute over whether\npatent owners that don\u2019t make products should be able to use the\nITC\u2019s import-ban power in fights over licensing fees.  After workers in the U.S. do initial manufacturing work,\nIntel uses plants in other countries for final assembly, leaving\nits chips and the products that use them vulnerable to an ITC\nimport ban.  Hewlett-Packard Co. (HPQ)  and  Apple Inc. (AAPL) , which use Intel\nchips, are also named in the ITC complaint.  The X2Y patents cover ways to overcome electromagnetic\ninterference that can damage electronics. The company, which\ndevelops methods for improving the performance of circuits,\nlicenses its inventions to Samsung Electronics Co., the world\u2019s\nbiggest maker of computer-memory chips.  \u201cX2Y remains confident that the Commission will protect\ntrue innovation regardless of the size of the innovator and will\ncontinue to vigorously enforce its  intellectual property  against\nthese infringers,\u201d X2Y said in an e-mailed statement\ndistributed by a spokeswoman, Anne Standley.  Civil suits that X2Y filed in federal court in its hometown\nof Erie, Pennsylvania, are on hold pending the outcome of the\nITC case. The commission has set a target date of April 15 to\ncomplete the investigation.  \u201cWe are gratified with this result and will continue to\ndefend ourselves in the case pending in U.S. district court,\u201d\n Chuck Mulloy , a spokesman for Santa Clara, California-based\nIntel, said in an e-mailed statement. UN Telecom Treaty Approved Amid U.S. Web-Censorship Concerns  An agreement to update 24-year-old United Nations\ntelecommunications rules was approved against the opposition of\ncountries including the U.S. and the U.K., whose officials\nwalked out on the talks on concerns about Internet regulation\nand censorship.  The new pact includes measures that would give countries a\nright to access international telecommunications services and\nthe ability to block spam. The delegations that declined to sign\nthe amended text, including Canada, Denmark, Australia, Norway\nand Greece, argued those measures would pave the way for\ngovernment censorship.  The countries that won\u2019t sign the new treaty will continue\nto be bound by the 1988 version, said Sarah Parkes, a\nspokeswoman for the International Telecommunication Union.  \u201cWhat is clear from the ITU meeting in Dubai is that many\ngovernments want to increase regulation and censorship of the\nInternet,\u201d Google Inc., the world\u2019s biggest search engine, said\nin a statement. \u201cWe stand with the countries who refuse to sign\nthis treaty and also with the millions of voices who have joined\nus to support a free and open web.\u201d  Talks at the World Conference on International\nTelecommunications in Dubai this week were marked by\ndisagreements between anti-regulation countries, including the\nU.S. and many European states, and a group that argued for some\nInternet measures to protect and advance networks, including\nRussia, China and several Middle Eastern nations. Industrial Espionage  HP Boardroom Investigator Sentenced to Three Months Prison  Bryan Wagner, a private investigator who helped steal\ntelephone records for an internal investigation into media leaks\nby Hewlett-Packard Co. board members, was sentenced to three\nmonths in prison.  Wagner was sentenced Dec. 13, according to a statement from\nU.S. Attorney Melinda Haag in San Francisco on Dec. 14. Wagner\npleaded guilty in 2007 to conspiracy and aggravated identity\ntheft. He admitted to using the Social Security number of an\nunidentified journalist to obtain the reporter\u2019s telephone\nrecords to pursue the source of the leak, a practice called\npretexting.  Hewlett-Packard Chairman Patricia Dunn was fired in 2006\nfor approving the boardroom spying, which spurred a national\ndebate over identity theft. Hewlett-Packard contracted with\nAction Research Group in Florida. Action Research hired Wagner\nof Littleton, Colorado, who posed as the targets of the\ninvestigation to obtain their phone records.  The probe of Hewlett-Packard and its investigators moved\nCongress and the California Legislature to pass laws prohibiting\nthe release of phone records without consent. Hewlett-Packard,\nbased in Palo Alto, California, in 2008 settled with reporters\nover claims their privacy was invaded by the company\u2019s\ninvestigation.  Cynthia Chin Young Lie, a federal public defender who\nrepresented Wagner, didn\u2019t immediately return a call to her\noffice for comment on the sentence.  The case is U.S. v. Wagner, 07-00016, U.S. District Court,\nNorthern District of California (San Jose). Only UBS paid more, $1.5 billion, last year. The cooperative lender will pay U.S. and U.K. regulators as well as the Dutch central bank. Rabobank had made a provision for a Libor fine, helping to drive down its profit in the first half of 2013, by 14 percent. The actual penalty, however, is bigger than the bank foresaw, meaning that its earnings will take a further hit. Rabobank is determined to put the 2009 affair behind it, having recently abolished bonuses for its top staff in an attempt to stress its conservative values. Other banks implicated in the Libor scandal should react in the same spirit. Demonstrating responsibility pays: former RBS chief John Hourican, who was not implicated in the Libor scandal but resigned, refusing a $8 million bonus, has now been  hired  to turn around the bailed-out Bank of Cyprus, a job as high-profile and challenging as they get. Loeb takes  position  in Nokia, expects payout Activist investor Daniel Loeb announced that his hedge fund Third Point has taken a position in the telecom equipment maker Nokia, in the expectation that after the sale of its phone business to Microsoft the Finnish company will return some of its $8 billion cash to investors. Loeb's fund has performed well lately and other investors will want to follow his lead, making it easier for him to pressure Nokia management for a buyback or special dividend. Distributing the cash may not be the company's best option, however. It might need the money to follow in the footsteps of Ericsson, the Swedish company that also got out of the mobile phone business to consolidate its leadership in the network equipment market. If Nokia used part of the proceeds from the Microsoft deal to acquire its ailing French competitor, Alcatel Lucent, it would become a much more formidable competitor to both Ericsson and Chinese companies such as ZTE and Huawei. Peugeot  reconsiders  project with GM The French car maker PSA Peugeot Citroen said it had placed a joint project with GM \"under review.\" It is now unlikely that the two companies will work together on a new platform for small cars as planned, meaning that the $1 billion in annual synergies PSA and GM targeted will not be achieved. That is bad news for PSA, which just announced weak third quarter results: a 3.7 percent drop in sales compared to the same period of 2012, caused by a 10 percent drop in Europe and slumps in Russia and Brazil. The French company has pinned its hopes on China, where its sales grew 28.5 percent in the third quarter. PSA recently opened two factories in China, and partnership with local car producer Dongfeng may hold more promise for the French automaker than any joint efforts with GM. ECB to ask banks to  increase  reserves as part of review As it prepared to review the balance sheets of 130 euro area banks, the European Central Bank told them to set aside 8 percent of their risk-adjusted capital against potential losses. The review is scheduled to begin in November, with the ECB aiming both to revive trust in the euro area's financial system and to uncover any balance sheet holes that may have escaped notice. The real test for the ECB will come if the massive exercise does result in recapitalization demands for some of the banks: How these capital increases will be handled will determine the ECB's effectiveness as a banking regulator. Greek  neo-fascist Golden Dawn   loses  state funding The Greek parliament voted overwhelmingly to withdraw state support from anti-immigrant Golden Dawn party, which was entitled to $1.2 million in 2013 because it had been elected to parliament. The party's leader Nikolaos Michaloliakos and two members of the party's parliamentary faction are in jail on charges of participating in a criminal organization. The Greek authorities cracked down on Golden Dawn, which unabashedly used Nazi symbols, after the murder of a left-wing rapper by one of the far-right party's supporters. So far, Greece has been the only European country to fight back resolutely against the rise of ultranationalism, but then Golden Dawn was particularly odious and violent. Its successors will be more cautious and probably more successful: The sentiment that got the party elected has not gone away. (Leonid Bershidsky, an editor and novelist, is a Bloomberg View contributor. From Scratch  The machines that are most comparable to the iPad -- which\nboasts more than 200,000 apps -- won\u2019t be able to run older\nWindows apps, forcing Microsoft to start from scratch. Windows 8 is the first Microsoft operating system for\ncomputers that use chips based on  ARM Holdings Plc (ARM)  technology.\nThese chips are widely used in mobile devices, including the\niPad. Trouble is, Microsoft\u2019s ARM-based devices will run only\napps designed specifically for Windows 8 -- and none of the\nmillions of programs already available for Intel-based machines.  Hence the app-building drive. For much of February, app\ndevelopers could come to Building 20 at Microsoft\u2019s Redmond,\nWashington campus and turn their app over to a Windows engineer\nwho tries it out and provides feedback. Now Microsoft has taken\nthat program on the road, visiting 87 cities, including New\nYork, Paris and Guangzhou,  China .  Developers who are earlier in the process -- those with an\nidea yet no app -- can attend a different program called an App\nAcceleration Lab to get advice on shaping their product.  Moonlighting Staff  Another Microsoft-led effort has been in place since\nSeptember. The company has trained more than 80 design firms to\naid or build apps for developers who aren\u2019t familiar with\nWindows\u2019 new design or design in general, said Catherine Brooker, a spokeswoman for Microsoft.  As with Windows Phone, Microsoft encouraged its own\nemployees to write apps by waiving so-called moonlighting\nrestrictions on workers, which keep staff from writing apps on\ntheir own time. Unlike with Windows Phone, Microsoft is not\npaying app developers to build for Windows 8.  The company is also running a 12-week paid internship\nprogram called the Foundry at its  New England Research and\nDevelopment Center , NERD for short. There, 22 college students\nin the program will build Windows 8 apps while getting training,\nproduct reviews and mentorship from Microsoft.  With traditional PCs, it wasn\u2019t hard to convince developers\nto build programs for Windows, the dominant operating system.  Convincing Skeptics  Microsoft\u2019s tablet challenge is steeper. It must win over\napp firms and developers that grew up building programs for\nsmartphones and tablets, where Microsoft has little and no\nshare, respectively.  Microsoft\u2019s pitch: Unlike the old apps that don\u2019t work with\nsome Windows 8 devices, the new ones will be available not only\nto buyers of tablets, but also to the more than 300 million\nbuyers of Windows PCs. That won over SigFig, a maker of a\nprogram that lets users track investments.  Some programmers remain unconvinced of the need to make\ngames, magazines or other online tools for a software maker more\nthan two years late to the tablet market.  Facebook Inc. (FB) , the largest social network, has no plans to\nmake a Windows 8 app even though it makes apps for the iOS and\nAndroid, according to a person with knowledge of the matter.  Flipboard, whose CEO is ex-Microsoft executive Mike McCue,\nisn\u2019t planning a Windows 8 version, said Marci McCue, head of\nmarketing at the  Palo Alto , California-based company.\nFlipboard\u2019s app, which aggregates a user\u2019s social-networking\nfeeds, has built apps for the iPad and tablets that run Android.  Waiting Game  Other big app makers, including  Zynga Inc. (ZNGA) ,  PopCap Games ,\nTwitter Inc.,  Pandora Media Inc. (P)  and  Amazon.com Inc. (AMZN) , declined\nto comment on their plans for Windows 8.  Companies such as SigFig or graphic-design software maker\nCorel Corp., make apps that work well on both tablets and PCs.\nFor them, writing for Windows 8 is a no-brainer.  Other developers of tablet-focused applications will wait\nto see whether enough consumers purchase Windows tablets, said\nLaurent Bugnion, a senior director for European operations at\n IdentityMine , one of the agencies in Microsoft\u2019s program that is\nworking on Windows 8 apps for clients that declined to name.  \u201cThe Apple fanatics, who anyway won\u2019t touch a PC with\nchopsticks, they won\u2019t be interested,\u201d he said. \u201cBut the\npragmatic people will probably wait for a while and suddenly\nwhen we see a few good devices come out they will start\ndeveloping.\u201d  Digital Chocolate  Netflix Inc. (NFLX)  is another one of the companies working on\napps for Windows 8, people with knowledge of the matter said.\nSome of the initial apps will be in the Windows store with the\nadvent of the Release Preview.  Mobile games maker Digital Chocolate Inc. also plans to\nhave games available for Windows 8 at launch, said Chief\nExecutive Officer Trip Hawkins, while declining to specify\nfurther. Corel is working on several.  Before Pop started building its app for Major League\nSoccer, the team and employees of the professional soccer\nfederation spent a day at Microsoft\u2019s campus getting guidance\nfrom the company, said Kaylynn Kelley, who oversees Pop\u2019s work\nwith Microsoft. Pop had an engineer and a designer assigned to\nhandle questions, which included nighttime calls that went on\nfor two hours. The free app, which includes news, videos and\nstandings, will probably be available in the next few days.  Microsoft\u2019s \u2018Handholding\u2019  SigFig, whose app is already in the Windows Marketplace,\nreceived \u201cconcierge-like service\u201d from Microsoft, said Patrick Cushing, the company\u2019s product manager for mobile. For example,\nMicrosoft looked over SigFig\u2019s code and showed ways to make use\nof Windows 8 features they hadn\u2019t thought of using. When hospitals look to Microsoft Corp., it's no longer\njust for the latest in office software. Some are getting help\nfrom the technology giant in diagnosing their patients.  Medical providers are experimenting with new ways to sift\nthrough their data and find patterns. The results can be\nsurprising: Microsoft recently examined health records from a\nresearch partner, MedStar Washington Hospital Center in\nWashington, D.C., and found that the location of patients'\nrooms is one factor in whether they get sick. Such insights\ncan help identify hot spots for bacteria and illness and stop\ntheir spread.  As hospitals digitize patient records and amass huge\namounts of data, many are relying on companies such as\nMicrosoft, SAS Institute Inc., International Business Machines\nCorp. and Oracle Corp., whose data-mining technologies can\nhelp them detect patterns and improve medical care.  The analytics industry generated more than $30 billion in\nrevenue last year, according to research firm IDC. That is\nforecast to increase to $33.6 billion this year as the\nhealth-care industry becomes a bigger customer.  The use of data-mining technology has already led to some\nmeasurable improvements in patient care.  New York-Presbyterian Hospital has reduced the rate of\npotentially fatal blood clotting in patients by using\nanalytics software, Dr. Nicholas Morrissey, a surgeon involved\nin the effort, said in an interview.  As patients were being admitted, the hospital started\nusing Microsoft software in 2010 to scan records for risk\nfactors, such as cancer, smoking and the amount of time\npatients were bed-bound. By letting the software rather than\nthe hospital staff make the assessment, doctors saved time and\nmade better evaluations, Morrissey said.  The clotting now happens at a rate of 0.23 incidents per\n1,000 patient days, versus 0.33 incidents per 1,000 patient\ndays before implementation of the software, Morrissey said. He\nstressed that further study of the software's impact is\nneeded.  \"I wouldn't be out there saying we've solved the\nproblem, but we're definitely making progress -- that was a\nsignificant drop,\" he said.  Seton Healthcare Family, a hospital system in central\nTexas, started using data-mining software from IBM last year\nto sift through transcribed doctors' notes and other\n\"unstructured data,\" such as numbers printed on medical\nimages, for ways to lower readmission rates for congestive\nheart failure patients.  It found some surprising themes. Two of the strongest\npredictors of whether a patient would be rehospitalized were\nlack of an emotional support network and the presence of a\nbulging jugular vein -- two things hospital staff can easily\nlook for when admitting patients.  \"We've gotten some really tremendous results,\" said Ryan\nLeslie, Seton's vice president of analytics and health\neconomics. The hospitals narrowed a list of 113 predictors\nthat medical staff thought would be important down to 18, and\neven identified some that weren't on the original list, such\nas the bulging vein.  Besides improving patient care, hospitals' use of\nanalytics software can make them eligible for millions of\ndollars in government funding if they can demonstrate\n\"meaningful use\" of their computer systems. The payments are\npart of the Obama administration's $14.6 billion program to\nprod health-care providers to adopt electronic medical\nrecords.  Federal law prohibits medical providers from disclosing\ncertain health information without patient consent, but there\nis an exemption for activities that fall under \"quality\nimprovement,\" said Susan McAndrew, deputy director for health\ninformation privacy at the U.S. Department of Health and Human\nServices' Office for Civil Rights.  That means health-care providers generally don't have to\ntell patients that their records are being analyzed for the\npurpose of improving care, which has raised some privacy\nconcerns.  \"People do not like to have researchers of any stripe\nusing their electronic health records,\" said Deborah\nPeel, founder of Austin, Texas-based Patient Privacy Rights.\n\"As a matter of respect and autonomy and\npatient-centeredness, patients want to be asked. When they are\nasked, by and large they support this. It's the not being\nasked stuff that's really bad.\"  She pointed to a 2007 survey that found just 1 percent of\nrespondents felt researchers didn't need to seek permission\nbefore using their medical data.  Some privacy experts disagree, warning of the dangers of\nover-notification.  Deven McGraw, director of the health privacy project with\nthe Center for Democracy & Technology in Washington, said\nnotifying patients too often could be unnecessarily confusing.  \"You ask for it when it's used in ways that people might\nnot expect,\" she said.  New York-Presbyterian Hospital and Seton Healthcare\nFamily didn't notify their patients. MedStar Washington\nHospital Center did not respond to a request for comment.  Morrissey of New York-Presbyterian, which published some\nof its results, emphasized that no personal information is\never publicly disclosed. He said the benefits outweigh the\nconcerns.  \"I think we're going to impact things that are most\nlife-threatening,\" he said, emphasizing that while the results\nneed further research, \"it seems real, and it's significant.\"","path":".\/2008_2012_msft_bloomberg_news\/data-mining-in-doctor-s-office-helps-solve-medical-mysteries.txt"},{"id":70545401,"title":"Google Unveils $199 Tablet in Bid to Vie With Apple, Amazon","released_at":"<date>June 27 2012<\/date> <time>22:43:30<\/time>","content":"Google Inc. It also provides a useful introduction to what I call the \"Innovator's Paradox.\" \n\n Blodget's article was provocative. He argued that Microsoft is in a no-win situation. It isn't sitting on any idea that is on the cusp of turning into a multi-billion dollar business. The personal computer is losing its dominance to mobile devices and tablets. The company's core profit drivers (Windows and Office) are under disruptive assault from Google's freely available applications and operating system. At best, Microsoft will respond with its own free products and erode its profit margin. \n\n The most telling thing in Blodget's post was a chart that showed the sources of Microsoft's profits over the past few years. Microsoft's core business has continued \u2014 despite continued proclamations of the company's coming demise \u2014 to throw off cash and to grow. But new growth businesses that were specks in 2006 (entertainment and devices and online services) remain tiny, and Microsoft hasn't created any material new businesses over the past few years. \n\n So the real problem isn't what Microsoft is doing today. It's what Microsoft did, or didn't do, five, or even 10 years ago. At the time, its base business was a bastion of strength. Today's threats were in their infancies. It would have been the perfect time to plant seeds that today would be blooming profit generators.  \n\n Why didn't it? It's The Innovator's Paradox: When you don't need the growth, you act in ways that lead to you not getting the growth you will need. And when you do need the growth, you can't act in ways that deliver it. \n\n Got that? \n\n I use this chart to illustrate this point. It's helpful to stimulate discussion among a company's leadership team. \n\n As the chart shows, when times are going great (\"exploitation\"), companies have ample resources to invest in growth. But because times are going great, innovation efforts tend to be undisciplined. New growth efforts get flooded with cash. Companies don't worry about iterating to find a successful business model. Overpriced acquisitions occur. \nThen, inevitably, maturation sets in. The need for new growth intensifies. But resources are harder to come by. Acquisition targets would rather join forces with the new kid on the block whose rapidly appreciating stock acts as a powerful acquisition currency. The acute need for growth gives an almost gravitational pull to large, existing markets. After all, that's where the money is. But large, existing markets are an innovator's fool's gold; glimmery, shiny, but not of much value. \n\n So what do you do about the Innovator's Paradox? Consider what my colleague Clark Gilbert found in his  doctoral research . He looked at how newspaper companies responded to the Internet, intersecting the disruptive innovation research of Clayton Christensen and the famous behavioral research of Amos Tversky and Daniel Kahneman. \n\n Some companies in Gilbert's study viewed the Internet as a threat. That led to them committing resources to innovation efforts. However, they responded in very rigid ways (typically creating replicas of the newspapers online). Other companies viewed the Internet as an opportunity. That framing allowed for more expansive response strategies, but made it difficult to support serious resource allocation. Gilbert summarized this challenge by saying, \"Absent a sense of threat, response to disruptive opportunities is inadequate; but with threat, the fully funded response is too rigid.\" \n\n The trick, Gilbert argued, was to decouple the allocation of resources from the use of the resources. Breaking the Innovator's Paradox requires similar logic. Companies have to recognize that their  core business, no matter how great it seems today, has a limit . That recognition should drive consistent allocation of resources to new growth efforts, especially when times are good. But those resources can't be burdened with a \"bunker\" mentality, or else they will struggle. As one friend told me, \"No great growth business was built from a defensive crouch.\" Further, companies have to make sure they avoid the  \"curse of abundance\"  that can lead overly resourced growth efforts to struggle. \n\n So, all you have to do is invest when you don't need to, break psychological barriers that might unintentionally inhibit creativity, and somehow avoid the abundant resources that would seem to be your primary source of competitive advantage.  \n\n No one said this was going to be easy.","path":".\/2008_2012_msft_bloomberg_news\/icrosoft-and-the-innovator-s-paradox.txt"},{"id":42274806,"title":"Microsoft, AmEx Said to Compete for Foursquare Stake","released_at":"<date>August 30 2013<\/date> <time>21:18:58<\/time>","content":"Microsoft Corp. Greenlight said the market abuse was \u201cinadvertent.\u201d The\nNew York-based firm and Einhorn were fined a total of 7.2\nmillion pounds by the regulator for insider trading. The fine\nand legal fees are being paid by Greenlight and Einhorn and\nwon\u2019t affect investors, he said in a letter yesterday.  \u201cEinhorn\u2019s defense, good as it is, does not change the\nfact that the fund avoided significant losses ahead of other\nuninformed market participants and investors who did suffer\nlosses,\u201d said Joe Seet, a senior partner at Sigma Partnership\nin  London , which advises  hedge funds  on compliance.  According to the FSA, a week before Punch announced the\nsale, some shareholders and potential investors were notified of\nthe share sale by a company the FSA referred to as \u201cFirm X.\u201d\nThe firm contacted Greenlight about the Punch issuance, and\nEinhorn declined to discuss it on a \u201cwall crossed\u201d basis,\nwhere it\u2019s agreed to share inside information on the condition\nthat it\u2019s not acted on, the regulator said.  Following Day  The following day, a corporate broker from Firm X and Punch\nmanagement had a 45-minute conference call with Einhorn, during\nwhich inside information was disclosed to him, the FSA said.\nEinhorn was told the sale would probably happen in about a week.  Goldman Sachs Group Inc. (GS)  and Merrill Lynch & Co. arranged\nthe share sale, according to a filing at the time of the stock\noffering. The broker who briefed Einhorn was Merrill Lynch\u2019s\nAndrew Osborne, a member of its corporate broking unit in\nLondon, according to two people with knowledge of the case. He\nhas since left the firm, which is now part of Bank of America,\nsaid one of the people. Both people declined to be identified\nbecause the regulator hasn\u2019t disclosed the broker\u2019s identity.  Found only in the U.K., corporate brokers are appointed by\ncompanies to liaise with institutional shareholders and offer\nstrategic advice, often leading to underwriting and corporate-\nfinance work.  Osborne wasn\u2019t immediately available for comment. A\ncolleague who answered the telephone at his former office\ndeclined to provide his contact details. He is listed on the\nFSA\u2019s register as being \u201cinactive\u201d since Nov. 30. CityAM\nreported Osborne\u2019s involvement yesterday.  Bank of America  John Mcivor, a Bank of America spokesman, and Jo Carss, a\nGoldman Sachs spokeswoman, declined to comment on the FSA probe.  The FSA, which said the trade wasn\u2019t deliberate or\nreckless, is imposing stricter supervision after being\ncriticized for failing to prevent the U.K.\u2019s worst financial\ncrisis since World War II. The fine against Einhorn, 3.64\nmillion pounds ($5.7 million), is the second-largest civil\npenalty levied against an individual by the FSA after a $9.6\nmillion fine against Dubai-based investor Rameshkumar Goenka in\nNovember.  FSA spokesman  Chris Hamilton  said related enforcement\nactions against third parties in the Greenlight case are\ncontinuing, declining further comment on the targets.  Einhorn and the firm \u201ccompletely disagree\u201d with the FSA,\nthe  fund manager  told investors in his letter yesterday. He also \nsaid he didn\u2019t violate any U.S. securities laws.  \u2018Don\u2019t Believe Now\u2019  \u201cI didn\u2019t believe in 2009, and I don\u2019t believe now, that\nthere was anything wrong with our conduct,\u201d Einhorn said. \u201cWe\ndid not enter into any confidentiality agreement, we explicitly\nrequested that we not be given confidential information, and we\ndon\u2019t believe we were given any.\u201d  John Nester , a spokesman for the U.S. Securities & Exchange\nCommission, declined to comment on whether the agency has\ninvestigated the trades.  \u201cImmediately\u201d after the call, Einhorn told Greenlight\ntraders to sell all Punch shares, the FSA said.  The firm sold 11.65 million shares, reducing its holding\nfrom 13.3 percent to 8.9 percent over the next four days. The\nfirm, which bought Punch shares between June 2008 and January\n2009, had never sold or tried to sell them before that day.  Einhorn\u2019s firm had initially invested in Punch because it\nthought the shares were mispriced by the market and was unlikely\nto issue equity, according to the UK regulator.  Wholly-Owned  Greenlight, wholly-owned by Einhorn, had around 31\nemployees in 2009, according to the FSA. The $7.8 billion\nGreenlight Capital LP fund returned 2.9 percent last year and\nhas produced annualized returned of 20 percent since the fund\nstarted in May 1996, according to a letter sent to investors.  Einhorn, who profited from a bet against Lehman Brothers\nHoldings Inc. before that firm collapsed in 2008, in May called\nfor Microsoft Corp.\u2019s board to replace Chief Executive Officer\n Steve Ballmer . Also last year, he offered $200 million for a 33\npercent stake in the New York Mets baseball team before\nwithdrawing the bid. In 2006, he finished 18th in the  World\nSeries  of Poker\u2019s main event.  Einhorn said yesterday that Greenlight would offer\ninvestors a \u201cone-time opportunity\u201d to redeem by March 31. The\nfirm also plans to open its funds to existing partners and to\nnew investors to replace any redemption requests they receive\nuntil March 1.  \u2018Experienced Professional\u2019  \u201cEinhorn is an experienced professional with a high\nprofile in the industry,\u201d said Tracey McDermott, the FSA\u2019s\nacting enforcement chief. \u201cWe expect someone in his position to\nbe able to identify inside information when he receives it and\nto act appropriately. His failure to do so is a serious breach.\u201d  On a conference call yesterday with investors and the\nmedia, Einhorn gave his version of events. A Greenlight analyst\nwas approached by an investment banker for Punch, asking if\nGreenlight, as the second largest shareholder, would be willing\nto have a conversation, he said. The analyst said Greenlight\nwould be happy to talk but wouldn\u2019t sign a non-disclosure\nagreement and didn\u2019t want to receive any information that would\nrestrict it from trading the stock.  The call took place on June 9, with Einhorn, Punch\u2019s chief\nexecutive and chief financial officers, and the investment\nbanker, Einhorn said. Two other investment bankers were\nlistening on the call, though they didn\u2019t take part in the\nconversation, he said.  Stock Offering  On the call, the CEO said he was considering a stock\noffering, and Einhorn said he thought it was a bad idea for\nshareholders and a good idea for bankers, Einhorn said. In\nresponse to Einhorn\u2019s question about whether Punch stock was\nfairly valued, the CEO replied the valuation was fair, though he\nwould \u201cput a discount on it,\u201d given the risks of not being\nable to make debt payments that were coming due in 18 months,\nEinhorn said.  \u201cThis was a sobering moment,\u201d Einhorn said. He said he\nasked the CEO if the decision had been made to issue more stock,\nand the CEO replied that no decision had been made, and the\ncompany was just exploring its options as it looked to raise\nmoney.  A spokeswoman for Punch Taverns yesterday declined to\ncomment on the FSA fine or the case.  Einhorn, who said he turned over a tape of the conversation\nto the FSA, said the experience would cause him to \u201crethink our\nefforts when speaking with UK companies.\u201d  At the end of the call, Einhorn said he told the CEO that\nhe planned to sell his shares. The CEO offered to tell him more\nif he signed the non-disclosure agreement, and again Einhorn\ndeclined, the hedge fund manager said.  \u201cThis resembles  insider trading  as much as soccer\nresembles football,\u201d said Einhorn. Companies including VantagePoint Capital Partners and  Khosla Ventures  are stepping up funding for systems to manage electricity, which are typically less capital intensive than solar-panel factories. Venture capital and private-equity financing for renewables dropped to its lowest in at least six years in 2012, according to data compiled by Bloomberg.  Competition for the best investments from Blackstone Group LP to  Warren Buffett  along with a plunge in profit from the solar and wind industries prompted the shift. It pushed Silicon Valley into taking smaller stakes in emerging technologies that help squeeze efficiency and flexibility from power supplies.  \u201cWe are going through a repositioning of cleantech,\u201d said Wal van Lierop, founder of Chrysalix Energy Venture Capital, which is based in Vancouver. \u201cThe big sectors -- solar, wind and LEDs -- are in the process of being consolidated. They\u2019re maturing, so they fall out of the cleantech opportunity basket. We now are trying to find the next hot spots.\u201d  Investment flowing from private equity and venture capital firms into renewable energy fell 34 percent to $5.75 billion last year, according to Bloomberg New Energy Finance, the lowest since at least 2006. That accounted for 2.2 percent of the $268.7 billion invested in the clean  energy industry , down from as much as 6.5 percent in 2008.  Grid Technology  Chrysalix invested in the energy-management providers Enbala Power Networks and AlertMe Ltd. Khosla funded LightSail Energy Inc., which is developing energy storage devices.  \u201cOur specialty is with large technology risk, where if the technology works there\u2019s a big economic breakthrough,\u201d  Vinod Khosla , the billionaire founder of Khosla Ventures in Menlo Park,  California , said in an interview. \u201cThat\u2019s what we keep looking for in all areas.\u201d  Alan Salzman, chief executive officer of VantagePoint Capital Partners, said systems that allow energy to be used more efficiently and help the grid cope with variable supplies from wind and solar plants represent the richest new areas.  Energy storage is \u201can essential component\u201d for renewable energy to thrive, Salzman said. \u201cThat\u2019s an area that has been hugely underserved historically that we think remains hugely interesting,\u201d he said.  Energy Efficiency  VantagePoint, based in San Bruno, California, backed Next Step Living Inc. and Tendril Networks Inc., which developed  energy-efficiency  software to reduce power consumption.  \u201cOne of the disappointments in the U.S. is that our utility smart-grid deployments have really slowed,\u201d Salzman said. Deployments have \u201cshifted overseas right now, away from the U.S., because of our regulatory environment,\u201d he said. \u201cIt doesn\u2019t mean that our archaic system -- see  Hurricane Sandy  -- isn\u2019t ripe for updating.\u201d  So-called energy smart technologies including efficiency products and equipment for the electricity grid amounted to $2.2 billion of the clean energy investment from  venture capital  and private equity tracked last year by New Energy Finance. That accounted for 38 percent of VC\/PE funding for clean energy last year, up from 15 percent in 2008. Solar investments were $1.58 billion last year.  Renewables Dwindling  Profits have drained away from renewable energy in the past three years as manufacturing capacity surged quicker than demand.  Solar cell  prices plunged 74 percent since the end of 2010 to 40 cents from $1.46 for each watt of capacity. The cost of power from wind  turbines on land  fell 15 percent to $81.44 per megawatt-hour since mid-2009, according to Bloomberg New Energy Finance estimates.  That reduced the industry\u2019s attractiveness for venture capital companies. With solar, now that the technology is proven, the industry\u2019s biggest challenge is driving down costs, said Raj Prabhu, managing partner at Mercom Capital Group in Austin,  Texas .  Solyndra LLC got more than $1.2 billion in venture capital funding. Then it liquidated after competition from Chinese manufacturers priced its tubular solar modules out of the market. Panel maker MiaSole Inc. was sold in January to Hanergy Holding Group Ltd. for about $30 million. That\u2019s a fraction of the $494.4 million poured into it by Kleiner, Vantage Point and Firelake Capital, according to Mercom Capital Group.  VC Misfires  Another misfire for the VC investors was  A123 Systems Inc. (AONEQ) , a provider of batteries for electric cars. It filed for bankruptcy in October as sales of the vehicles failed to meet expectations. It got at least $278 million from VC firms including North Bridge Venture Partners LP and CMEA Ventures.  \u201cVCs are really good at finding new technologies but not so good at manufacturing,\u201d Prabhu said. \u201cThey\u2019ve learned that they need to stick to picking technology winners, not building factories. The new money is going downstream to help build markets. The industry is now mainstream.\u201d  As venture capital moves away from traditional renewables, mainstream investors are starting to move in. Buffett\u2019s MidAmerican Energy Holdings Co. decided in January to spend as much as $2.5 billion on two large solar farms, after forming a unit dedicated to wind and solar holdings last year.  The private equity company  Blackstone Group LP (BX)  in September bought Vivint Inc. for $2 billion, giving it access to a home- security and energy-management provider with more than 670,000 North American customers. Vivint says the networks that manage these services complement its growing residential solar systems by smoothing the flow of solar power onto the electricity grid and into homes.  Solar\u2019s Gleam  A few parts of the solar industry remain attractive for investors, even after the slump in the costs of panels. Elon Musk\u2019s  SolarCity Corp. (SCTY)  has more than doubled since its initial public offering on Dec. 12. It develops rooftop solar systems, which are more economical to install since the price of cells plunged.  Technology to store and conserve energy also is gaining attention among VC investors. Utilities are taking more of their power from renewables.  Wind turbines  produce power when there\u2019s a breeze, and solar only when the sun is up. Integrating those power flows into distribution grids used to coping with steady supplies from coal and nuclear plants requires new systems that give engineers more flexibility.  Black Coral  In December, Next Step Living, a residential energy- efficiency company, raised $18.2 million from VantagePoint, Black Coral Capital and the Massachusetts Green Energy Fund LP.  The month before, billionaire  Peter Thiel  led a $37.3 million fundraising for LightSail Energy Inc. It\u2019s developing storage systems that compress air in tanks and generate power when the air is released, backed by Khosla and Microsoft Inc. founder  Bill Gates . Arbitration Backed as High Court Rules for American Express  The U.S.  Supreme Court  reinforced companies\u2019 power to\nfunnel legal disputes into arbitration, ruling in favor of\n American Express Co. (AXP)  in an antitrust clash with retailers over\nthe credit cards they must accept.  The justices, voting 5-3, said merchants seeking to sue\nAmerican Express are bound by an agreement they signed to pursue\ndisputes individually before an arbitrator. A federal appeals\ncourt had refused to enforce the arbitration accord, saying its\nbar on class actions would make it infeasible for the merchants\nto press their claims.  Writing for the majority, Justice  Antonin Scalia  said\ncourts must respect arbitration agreements -- and bans on class\nactions -- even when the cost of pressing an individual case\nwould exceed the potential damages.  In dissent, Justice Elena Kagan said the ruling would let\nwrongdoers immunize themselves against lawsuits. She said\nAmerican Express had used its market clout to foist the contract\non retailers.  Justices Ruth Bader Ginsburg and  Stephen Breyer  joined\nKagan in dissent. Justice  Sonia Sotomayor , who was involved with\nthe case as an appellate judge, didn\u2019t take part in the Supreme\nCourt\u2019s decision.  Chief Justice  John Roberts  and Justices Anthony Kennedy,\n Clarence Thomas  and  Samuel Alito  joined Scalia in the majority.  The decision extends a 2011 Supreme Court ruling that said\ncompanies can use arbitration accords to block employees and\nconsumers from pressing claims as a group. Both cases turned on\nthe 1925 Federal Arbitration Act, which says courts must enforce\narbitration accords the same as any other contract.  Yesterday\u2019s ruling \u201cpreserves the availability of\narbitration as a fair, efficient and cost-effective way to\nresolve disputes,\u201d American Express said in an e-mailed\nstatement.  \u201cThe decision is catastrophic for the antitrust laws, as\nwell as for civil rights, consumer rights and many other\nstatutory rights,\u201d said Paul Bland, an attorney with Public\nJustice, a Washington-based advocacy group.  The case is American Express v. Italian Colors Restaurant,\n12-133.  For more, click here.
