Steve Park , a spokesman for Apple in  Seoul , declined to\ncomment.  The court started a new round of trials between Apple and\nSamsung in the Netherlands in September, concerning multiple\npatents and proceedings as Apple seeks a ban on Galaxy devices\nin the country, where the Suwon, South Korea-based company has\nits distribution center for Europe. The companies compete in a\nglobal smart phone market that grew 62 percent to $219 billion\nlast year, according to data compiled by Bloomberg Industries.  Samsung Infringes Four Apple Patents, U.S. Trade Judge Says  Samsung Electronics Co. infringes four Apple Inc. patents,\nincluding one for the design of the iPhone and one for touch-\nscreen technology co-invented by  Steve Jobs , a U.S. trade judge\nsaid in a decision that gives Apple another legal victory over\nits biggest smartphone competitor.  Two other patents, including one for the exterior shape of\nthe iPhone, weren\u2019t infringed, U.S. International Trade\nCommission Judge Thomas Pender said in a notice on the agency\u2019s\nwebsite. The judge\u2019s findings are subject to review by the full\ncommission, which has the power to stop goods that infringe U.S.\npatents at the border.  The agency has twice before forced companies to alter\nforeign-made smartphones if they wanted to keep selling them in\nthe U.S. HTC Corp. phones were held up at the border in May\nafter Apple won a trade case, and the Cupertino, California-\nbased company has an enforcement action pending that accuses HTC\nof violating the trade agency\u2019s exclusion order. Google Inc.\u2019s\nMotorola Mobility unit was ordered to remove a feature to\ncoordinate schedules from its phones after they were found to\ninfringe a Microsoft Corp. patent.  The case in yesterday\u2019s ruling is one of more than three\ndozen between the makers of about half of the world\u2019s\nsmartphones, who have run up hundreds of millions of dollars in\nlegal bills. Samsung, which lost a $1 billion jury verdict in\nAugust against Apple, is challenging a different ITC judge\u2019s\nfindings that its own patents weren\u2019t infringed by Apple.  The ITC, as an independent agency under the executive\nbranch, isn\u2019t bound by the legal standard used in that decision.\nIts job is to protect U.S. markets from unfair trade practices,\nincluding patent infringement, and its only power lies in the\nability to keep products from entering the U.S.  Samsung has submitted documents to Pender about a way to\nchange its designs to address the patent dispute, though the\npapers are confidential so it isn\u2019t known what changes to its\nphones are involved. Apple is seeking to block U.S. imports of\nmore than a dozen models of Samsung phones and tablets,\nincluding Galaxy Tab, Galaxy Nexus, Galaxy SII, and Galaxy Note.  The Apple case against Samsung is In the Matter of\nElectronic Digital Media Devices, 337-796, and Samsung\u2019s case is\nIn the Matter of Electronic Devices, Including Wireless\nCommunication Devices, Portable Music and Data Processing\nDevices, and Tablet Computers, 337-794, both U.S. International\nTrade Commission (Washington). A man\u2019s gotta retain some shred of\ndignity.  So you won\u2019t see me in my floppy college sweatshirt\ngrinning like an idiot as I land a few uppercuts in the \u201cKinect\nSports\u201d boxing game. Or leaping to maneuver my raft in the\n\u201cRiver Rush\u201d game in \u201cKinect Adventures.\u201d And regarding my\nmoves in \u201cDance Central,\u201d well, the less said the better.  Without the photographic evidence, you\u2019ll just have to take\nmy word for it that the $149.99  Kinect  -- which turns your\nentire body into a video-game controller -- is a wonderful\nantidote to couch potato-itis. While it may not satisfy hard-\ncore gamers, for normal people the device is a gas.  It\u2019s also something of a technological marvel. Motion-based\ngaming was pioneered by Nintendo Co. with its 2006  Wii . More\nrecently,  Sony Corp . introduced the Move system for its\n PlayStation 3  console. Both of those require you to hold or move\na controller. The Kinect doesn\u2019t -- you\u2019re interacting directly\nwith the game, which makes for a quite different, and much more\nimmersive, experience.  Microsoft has been working on the Kinect and talking about\nit for so long, giving demonstrations at tech conferences, that\nits release last week felt a bit anticlimactic. At least until I\nhad a chance to play with it, when it became clear that this\ngadget provides the now 5-year-old  Xbox 360  with an entirely new\ndimension.  Black Bar  The Kinect is a motorized black bar housing a camera,\ninfrared projector, depth sensor and microphones, about 11\ninches wide (28 centimeters) and 3 inches deep, that sits on a\nsmall stand. You can place it either above or below your\ntelevision, anywhere from 2 feet to 6 feet off the ground.\nMicrosoft recommends putting it on a shelf or other stable\nsurface, though I balanced mine on the top edge of my TV.  Physical set-up is a snap: If you\u2019ve got the latest version\nof the Xbox, a single cable connects the two products. Owners of\nolder Xboxes must use the included brick-like power adapter.  Configuring the device is more involved. The Xbox prompts\nyou in a sort of Simon Says routine -- Stand here! No, there!\nRaise your hand! Wave! -- as it places you properly and learns\nto identify you. Once it does, Kinect remembers who you are\nwhenever you start to play, even to the point of recognizing you\nif you jump into a game to replace another player.  \u2018Eye of the Tiger\u2019  You\u2019ll need a sufficiently big area to play in, as every\ngame tiresomely reminds you. Microsoft recommends that a single\nplayer stand 6 feet away from the sensor, 8 feet if two are\nplaying. If you get too close in the heat of battle, as I did in\na few boxing matches -- I\u2019ve clearly got the \u201c Eye of the\nTiger \u201d -- you\u2019re prompted to move back until you\u2019re again\nwithin proper range.  Many game options and commands are gesture-based: You\nchoose which game you want, how many players and the like by\nhovering your hand in midair so that an icon on the screen makes\nthe appropriate selection. Move your hand too soon, and you have\nto start over again, which gets old fast. Raising an arm to the\nside will pause the game; so will simply walking out of the\nKinect\u2019s line of sight.  Noticeable Time Lag  While the game play is smooth, there\u2019s sometimes a\nnoticeable lag between your action -- kicking at an on-screen\nsoccer ball, timing a leap -- and the corresponding move of your\non-screen avatar. The delay isn\u2019t enough to be annoying, and\nafter a while you\u2019ll find yourself automatically compensating\nfor it -- just ask my table-tennis opponent once I got my timing\ndown on my sidearm smashes. But it does raise the question of\nhow suitable the Kinect will prove for serious, sophisticated\ngamers, for whom a few milliseconds can be a big deal.  For now, at least, that isn\u2019t an issue: The first crop of\nKinect games, which cost about $50 each, aren\u2019t aimed at them\nanyway. Instead, many of them are cartoony or otherwise family\nfriendly. About a dozen and a half titles were available at\nlaunch, and many more are on the way.  Titles so far include Microsoft\u2019s \u201cKinect Adventures,\u201d\nwhich is included with the device, and \u201cKinectimals,\u201d where\nyou adopt, train and play with cuddly jungle creatures; \u201cDance\nCentral,\u201d from  Viacom Inc .\u2019s MTV Games; and  Ubisoft\nEntertainment \u2019s \u201cYour Shape: Fitness Evolved,\u201d which provides\nan array of routines from cardio workouts to tai chi.  The Kinect adds several other bells and whistles, including\nlimited voice recognition, video chatting and the ability to\nshare those pictures of you playing -- sort of a stop-action\nvideo -- with your friends via the Xbox Live online service. New\nKinect Guide and Kinect Hub screens act as portals to some of\nthese features -- but, unfortunately, also add to an Xbox\nnavigational jumble that\u2019s enough to make you nostalgic for\nWindows 3.0.  But none of those cavils really matter. What does is that\nKinect takes gaming to a totally new place -- and provides a ton\nof fun along the way.    Rich Jaroslovsky  is a Bloomberg News columnist. The\nopinions expressed are his own.)  To contact the writer of this column:\nRich Jaroslovsky in  San Francisco  at \n rjaroslovsky@bloomberg.net . Deborah Hellinger , a spokeswoman\nfor  Redwood City , California-based Oracle, declined to comment\non whether it was considering buying Quest.  Insight\u2019s agreement with Quest has a relatively low break-\nup free, which could draw out bidders and may have been designed\nto encourage competing offers, according to Alec Levine, an\nequity derivatives strategist at Newedge group SA in  New York . Just about every set maker has its own \u201csmart TV\u201d system\nfor connecting to the Internet to access programs from  Netflix (NFLX) \nand other online services.  And just about every one of these \u201csmart TVs\u201d is pretty\nstupid, with clumsy interfaces, limited choices and sometimes\npainful set-up processes. The most recent one I grappled with, a\n Panasonic (6752) , had me debugging DHCP problems. If you don\u2019t know\nwhat that means, trust me, you\u2019re better off.  By contrast, the $100 Roku is a model of simplicity and\nchoice, with a relatively painless set-up process and a new,\neasier-to-navigate interface.  Getting up and running with the unobtrusive, hockey-puck-\nlike Roku 3 took me about 20 minutes. I connected it to an HDMI\ninput on my TV, plugged it in and, following the on-screen\ninstructions, introduced it to my Wi-Fi network. (There\u2019s also\nan Ethernet port for wired networks.)  The most laborious part of the process was enabling my\nexisting programming services, which required me to log into\neach one through a web browser on my computer or mobile device\nand enter a code generated by the Roku on the TV screen.  Unfortunately, Roku comes with its own remote -- no one\nwants yet another remote to juggle. But Roku\u2019s has something to\nease the pain: a headphone jack. Plug in a headset, and the TV\u2019s\nspeakers are immediately silenced as the audio output is\ntransferred to the remote.  Silent Viewing  It\u2019s a neat feature, allowing you to watch in bed without\nthe sound disturbing a sleeping partner. Roku even includes a\nset of earbuds, though I would have preferred the company skip\nthem -- I have enough of those already -- and instead include\nthe HDMI cable you\u2019ll need.  A number of companies make products that access online\nprogramming, including  Western Digital (WDC)  (the WD TV Play) and  D-\nLink (2332)  (the Boxee Box). But Roku\u2019s most important competitor by\nfar is the $99  Apple TV , which offers fewer choices but better\nintegration with  Apple (AAPL)  devices and content -- including the\nability, through Apple\u2019s AirPlay technology, to stream movies\nand TV shows directly from computers and iDevices.  Wi-Fi Scheme  Roku is working on adding a similar feature, using a new\nWi-Fi scheme called  Miracast , but no telling how long that will\ntake or what devices it will work with.  Both boxes offer access to pay services including Netflix,\nMajor League Baseball games and Hulu Plus. And each has some\nimportant video sources missing from the other:  Amazon (AMZN)  Instant\nVideo only on Roku, iTunes and  Google (GOOG) \u2019s YouTube only on Apple\nTV.  But Roku has a far larger selection, more than 700, the\ncompany says, many of them free and\/or highly specialized in\nnature: the Indian Food channel; Hypnosis TV; and Rustavi 2,\nwhich provides \u201ca diverse range of top quality TV programming\u201d\nin \u201cthe native language of the Republic of  Georgia .\u201d  It also comes with the Angry Birds in Space game built in,\nthe remote doubling as a handheld controller.  In terms of performance, the Roku 3 has a more powerful\nprocessor and better Wi-Fi than its top-of-the-line predecessor,\nthe Roku 2 XS. I\u2019m not sure how much difference that makes in\npractical terms, since I never had serious performance issues\nwith previous models, but it may allow for additional\ncapabilities later.  Hi-Def Streaming  Like the 2 XS and the $80 2 XD, the new Roku streams video\nat up to 1080p full high-definition. (Two cheaper models, the\n$50 LT and $60 HD, top out at 720p.) The new interface is indeed\nless cumbersome than the old one -- it will be offered on the\nprevious models as a software update -- and moves along smoothly\non the 3.  There are, of course, many other ways to connect your TV to\nthe Internet, including via gaming consoles like  Microsoft (MSFT) \u2019s\nXbox and  Sony (6758) \u2019s Playstation. Every one of them poses the\nimplicit question: Why should you need a separate device at all?  But until the TV makers get smarter about smart TVs, or\nApple delivers its long-rumored set, Roku is one of the easiest\nand most elegant ways to add intelligence.  ( Rich Jaroslovsky  is a Bloomberg News columnist. The\nopinions expressed are his own.)  Muse highlights include Jason Harper on  cars  and Martin\nGayford on  art . (MAR)  plans to add three hotels to the seven it now operates in Egypt and wants assurance that the country\u2019s new Islamist-dominated government will welcome tourists and the alcohol they like to consume.  Egypt did both under President  Hosni Mubarak , who ruled for 30 years before being ousted last year during the Arab Spring revolutions that swept the  Middle East . Executives for Marriott plan to join a trade delegation to Egypt this week to see if those policies will change under the newly elected President Mohamed Mursi, whose Muslim faith generally shuns alcohol.  \u201cWe\u2019re hoping to learn from the minister of tourism what his strategy is for tourism,\u201d Alex Kyriakidis, president and managing director of Bethesda, Maryland-based Marriott\u2019s Middle East & Africa business, said in a phone interview. The trip provides an opportunity for learning about \u201cthe strategy for the new government in industry,\u201d he said.  Kyriakidis will be among more than 100 executives from 49 U.S. companies including  Exxon Mobil Corp. (XOM) ,  Microsoft Corp. (MSFT) ,  Morgan Stanley (MS)  and  Pfizer Inc. (PFE)  scheduled to participate in what the U.S. Chamber of Commerce said is its largest business delegation ever to visit Egypt. The Washington-based industry group and its affiliate, the U.S.-Egypt Business Council, are leading the Sept. 8-11 trip.  Political Instability  President  Barack Obama \u2019s administration is moving ahead with a $1 billion aid package, including debt relief, to help Egypt\u2019s economy, slowed by political instability that reduced tourism and investment. A military council ruled after Mubarak\u2019s February 2011 ouster, and the current government is seeking a $4.8 billion International Monetary Fund loan.  The June election of Mursi, who was the Muslim Brotherhood\u2019s candidate, has raised uncertainty for businesses and created a delicate situation for the Obama administration. Mursi\u2019s victory and the rise of the Brotherhood as a political force have left U.S. officials wary of helping an Islamist group with militant elements versus taking the risk that others, such as Iran, might step in to fill any void.  The trade mission \u201cis a critical aspect of dealing with a very rapidly changing political structure,\u201d  Anthony Cordesman , an analyst at the Center for Strategic and International Studies in Washington, said in a phone interview. Strong ties with Egypt are essential \u201cif you\u2019re going to be trading in the Middle East and you want to have a future in the Middle East,\u201d he said.  Merchandise Trade  While the $8.3 billion in merchandise trade between the U.S. and Egypt in 2011 was less than 1 percent of the $3.7 trillion in global U.S. trade, the Arab nation grants U.S. military planes fly-over rights and provides access to the  Suez Canal , a key channel for oil shipments and American military transport to the Persian Gulf.  G. Steven Farris, chief executive officer of  Apache Corp. (APA) , a Houston-based oil and natural gas producer, is chairman of the U.S.-Egypt Business Council and a leader of the U.S. delegation, according to the Chamber of Commerce.  Ken Hyatt, the U.S. Commerce Department\u2019s acting deputy under secretary for international trade, will focus on development of Egypt\u2019s travel and tourism industry during the trip, agency spokesman Tim Truman said in a phone interview.  The trip is a \u201cgoodwill mission\u201d that will \u201cdeepen our overall commercial relationship with this important trading partner,\u201d Hyatt said in an e-mailed statement.  Tourism Workshop  At the Cairo Marriott Hotel, located on an island in the Nile River, U.S. executives will meet with Egyptian officials including Hisham Zazou, the tourism minister, on Sept. 9 for a workshop before dinner at the hotel, according to Marriott officials.  \u201cEgypt has been on the receiving end of bad news for the past 16 to 17 months,\u201d Kyriakidis said. A central question facing hotels, airlines and tour operators is, \u201cHow do we bring back the face of Egypt that was being promoted to the world\u201d prior to Arab Spring, he said.  Marriott operates seven hotels in Egypt and plans to open three more within the next four years, including the 331-room Nile Ritz-Carlton in Cairo scheduled for 2013.  The company wants ensure that the government won\u2019t make changes to past policies that encouraged cultural, archaeological and religious tourism. It also wants to establish a dialog to promote the industry, after a decline in visitors during the political upheaval, according to Kyriakidis.  \u201cThese are the practical things that we\u2019re hoping we can walk away with,\u201d he said.  Visitor Statistics  Official statistics show the number of tourists reached 5.08 million in the first half of 2012, up 23 percent over the same period last year, though still lower than record levels reached in 2010, according to the state-run Ahram Online website.  Other companies participating in the trade mission include  Boeing Co. (BA)  of Chicago;  Citigroup Inc. (C)  of New York;  Coca-Cola Co. (KO)  of Atlanta;  General Electric Co. (GE)  of Fairfield, Connecticut;  Google Inc. (GOOG)  of Mountain View, California; and  FedEx Corp. (FDX)  of Memphis, Tennessee, according to the U.S. Chamber of Commerce.  Egypt\u2019s \u201ctransition to a more transparent and accountable governance will set the stage for even greater engagement by U.S. companies,\u201d Lionel Johnson, the industry group\u2019s vice president for Turkey, Middle East and North Africa affairs and a leader of the delegation, said in a  statement .  \u201cFor us, this is about supporting an important relationship that goes back more than 40 years,\u201d Tim Neale, a Boeing spokesman, said in an e-mail. The U.S. company has sold commercial jets to Egypt Air since 1968 and has provided its military with aircraft since 1979, he said.  Strategic Concern  Government officials participating in the trade mission include Deputy Secretary of State Thomas Nides, a co-leader of the delegation, and Deputy National Security Adviser  Michael Froman .  Secretary of State  Hillary Clinton  announced the delegation\u2019s visit in July during a trip to Cairo in which she focused on Egypt\u2019s economic challenges and outlined the details of the $1 billion aid package Obama announced last year, including loans and loan guarantees for small- and medium-sized businesses.  Egypt\u2019s economic and political stability is a crucial strategic concern for the U.S., in part because of its influence on the region. Accumulating great wealth often speaks to a person\u2019s\npersistence and career-management skill. Yet when a company\nachieves the same feat, it often goes unnoticed.  I like to spotlight such companies from time to time by\ncompiling a list of U.S. companies that are balance-sheet\npowerhouses.  To make the list, a company must have:  -- Stock-market value of $1 billion or more;  -- Cash or near-cash of $300 million or more;  -- Long-term debt of $200 million or less;  -- Total debt no more than 10 percent of stockholders\u2019\nequity;  -- A current ratio (current assets divided by current\nliabilities) of 2.0 or more;  -- Fully diluted earnings of at least 10 cents a share in\nthe latest fiscal year.  This year, 28 companies made my Balance Sheet Powerhouse\nlist. That\u2019s pretty good considering the economy is recovering\nfrom a dreadful recession. In 2006, 42 companies passed these\ntests while 38 were on the list in 2005.  Strength in Numbers  I compiled this list for six years from 2001 through 2006,\nand then abandoned it for a while. I am bringing it back because\nI believe investors pay too much attention to short-term\nfluctuations in earnings, and not enough attention to longer-\nterm qualities such as balance-sheet strength.  To make this list is an honor. Yet it\u2019s not equivalent to a\nstock recommendation.  That\u2019s because companies that make the list are often so\noutstanding their excellence is already recognized with a high\nstock price. To make money in the stock market, you need to find\neither a great company at a good price, or a good company at a\ngreat price.  A few companies have graced the Balance Sheet Powerhouse\nlist several times.    Forest Laboratories Inc . is the only company that has made\nthe list all seven years I have compiled it. The  drug company \nhas been an uninspired investment for the past decade. It trades\nat about $32, little changed from its level 10 years ago.  Going forward, I believe New York-based Forest Labs will be\nan excellent investment. The drugmaker is debt free and its\nshares trade at seven times earnings. The company has just\nenhanced its pipeline by agreeing to acquire Clinical Data Inc.\nof Newton Massachusetts for $1.2 billion.  Next Best-Seller  That will give Forest Labs the rights to Clinical Data\u2019s\nnew antidepressant Viibryd, which was approved by the U.S. Food\nand Drug Administration in January. Viibryd could be a possible\nsuccessor to Lexapro, which loses patent protection in 2012.\nLexapro has been Forest\u2019s best-selling drug, accounting for more\nthan half of sales.  Forest Labs was formerly tied with Microsoft Corp. at six\nappearances on this list. Microsoft missed the debt-to-equity\nratio cutoff this year. Its debt is about 20 percent of equity.  San Diego-based  Qualcomm Inc ., the communications-\ntechnology company, is back for a sixth appearance. One of its\nlatest ventures involves interactive graphics, a project it dubs\naugmented reality. One example is a virtual-reality basketball\ngame in which players can move their mobile phones around to\nshoot from various angles.  EBay Inc., which had previously tied with Qualcomm at five,\nmissed the cut this time, tripping on the same hurdle as\nMicrosoft. (Ebay\u2019s debt is 12 percent of equity.)  Not Good Enough  Both Microsoft and EBay still have strong balance sheets in\nmy opinion, just not quite excellent enough to meet the\nPowerhouse criteria.    Google Inc ., the largest company on this year\u2019s list in\nterms of market value, has made the list each year it was\neligible. Google went public in 2004.  In addition to Forest Labs, I think  AVX Corp . looks\nattractive as a purchase. Based in Fountain Inn,  South Carolina ,\nAVX makes components that store and regulate electrical energy.  AVX shares trade at 12 times earnings and 1.4 times book\nvalue (corporate net worth per share). Those are attractive\nvaluations, especially for a company that stayed profitable\nduring the recent recession. Analysts expect it to post a 67\npercent earnings increase this fiscal year.  I also like Dallas-based  Texas Instruments Inc ., which is\nmaking the roster for the first time this year, and which I\nrecommended in a column last month. However, I consider it less\nof a bargain than Forest Labs and AVX.  Below is the list of 28 stocks that are Balance Sheet\nPowerhouses. Now, they\u2019re trying to claw back lost ground.  Seeking to avoid being just pipes that carry services and\napplications from Apple,  Google  and others, operators are\nstarting to go beyond ringtones and links to radio and\ntelevision channels to offer apps of their own.  Companies like Apple \u201cneed our investment to exist, but\nthat\u2019s not enough for us to grow,\u201d France Telecom Chief\nExecutive Officer  Stephane Richard  said in an interview in\nParis. \u201cWe need to find ways to be more useful to our clients,\nlike through mobile banking and electronic health.\u201d  The services tug-of-war will be discussed at the Morgan\nStanley Technology, Media & Telecommunications Conference\nstarting in Barcelona today. The stakes are high. The worldwide\nmarket for games, entertainment and workplace tools for mobile\ndevices may balloon to $40 billion by 2014, compared with $14.3\nbillion this year, according to consulting firm Booz & Co.  Operators have only a small piece of this pie. Revenue at\nFacebook, the world\u2019s largest social-networking site, may double\nto at least $1.4 billion this year. Apple\u2019s revenue from apps\nsold through its iTunes Store rose 22 percent in the latest\nquarter to about $1.2 billion, while Google\u2019s sales surged about\n23 percent to about $7.3 billion.  Smartphone Rise  In contrast, many large telecommunications companies\u2019\nrevenue is stagnant or declining, with  Telefonica SA , Europe\u2019s\nsecond-largest operator, and  AT&T Inc. , the U.S.\u2019s largest\ncarrier, seeing sales slide by 2.1 percent and 0.8 percent\nrespectively last year.  Mobile devices have become the fastest-growing piece of the\ntelecommunications market. Smartphone shipments are set to pass\n268 million units this year, from 122 million reported by\n Gartner Inc.  in 2007, when Apple unveiled its iPhone and spawned\na new industry.  Users who play games, watch video, send messages and surf\nthe Internet are showing an insatiable appetite for such\nservices. Phone companies have steadily increased bandwidth to\nenable consumers to access services at super-fast speeds.\nThey\u2019re discovering, however, that much of the money to be made\nis in add-on services.  More Than Speed  \u201cIt\u2019s not only about the speed, it\u2019s about what you offer\nwith that speed,\u201d said  Olivier Baujard , chief technology\nofficer at  Deutsche Telekom AG , Europe\u2019s biggest phone company.\n\u201cThe rule will be value-added services in order to maintain the\nsame ARPU,\u201d or average revenue per user.  In the early days of smartphones, the operators had control\nof the user experience. The online portals they managed\ntypically gave users access to a selection of services such as\ngames, ringtones and news, with the extra fees going to the\noperators themselves.  Apple opened the App Store in 2008, stocked with third-\nparty software. It has since grown to include more than 250,000\napps, inspiring similar services from Google and  Microsoft Corp.   Operators \u201chad high hopes until 2007 or 2008,\u201d said\nPatrik Karrberg, a researcher in the London School of Economics\u2019\nDepartment of Management. The hopes dimmed after the emergence\nof iPhones and improved data speeds that made the Internet\ndirectly accessible on handsets.  Portal Death  \u201cThey gave up the idea of controlling the entry point,\u201d\nKarrberg said. \u201cThat was the death of the portal.\u201d  Most smartphone users now access online services through\nportals operated by Google, whose Android operating system for\nmobile devices was the most popular in the U.S. in the third\nquarter, according to market researcher Canalys, or via Apple\nand  Research In Motion Ltd.\u2019s  offerings.  Apple gives 70 percent of the revenue from App Store sales\nto developers, keeping the rest. Google gives developers 70\npercent of Android Market revenue and takes some of the rest in\na \u201ctransaction fee,\u201d saving a slice for carriers.  Phone operators\u2019 attempts to drum up interest for their own\nbranded services have a mixed record of success. Vodafone, the\nworld\u2019s largest mobile-phone operator by revenue, last year\nintroduced Vodafone 360, a social networking and apps portal\navailable on specially designed handsets.  The portal has 790,000 registered users, compared with more\nthan 500 million on Facebook. When  Pieter Knook , the head of the\n360 project, quit in September, Vodafone didn\u2019t replace him.  Payment Platforms  The portal \u201cwas an attempt to regain control in this\nlandscape, but I think it\u2019s quite clear that it hasn\u2019t been\nsuccessful,\u201d said  Paolo Pescatore , an analyst with CCS \nInsight in London. \u201cFundamentally people just want Facebook. \nThey don\u2019t want to sign up to other services and platforms.\u201d  Operators also are experimenting with mobile payment\nplatforms and home entertainment. Third-Party Billing  Payment platforms are a key opportunity, said  Adolfo Hernandez , the president for operations in Europe, the Middle\nEast and Africa for network equipment builder  Alcatel-Lucent SA .\n\u201cYou could visit an online video shop and just say, \u2018charge my\nphone bill,\u2019\u201d he said. Nevertheless,\nit took an outsider -- none other than Energy Secretary  Steven Chu , who has a Nobel Prize in physics -- to come up with the\nidea of peering inside the malfunctioning blowout preventer on\nthe sea floor with high-energy gamma rays.  \n BP tried Chu\u2019s idea -- after a few snickers and Incredible\nHulk jokes, according to the Washington Post -- and lo and\nbehold, it worked. The probe that Chu recommended was \u201ccrucial\nin helping us understand what is happening inside the BOP\n(blowout preventer) and informing the approach moving ahead,\u201d\n Jane Lubchenco , head of the National Oceanic and Atmospheric\nAdministration, reported on June 2.  \n The gamma ray incident is symptomatic of a problem that\u2019s\nbigger than London-based BP: Energy companies worldwide are far\nless science-oriented than one might expect from an industry\nthat is heavily dependent on technology for safety and profit,\nBloomberg Businessweek reports in its June 21 issue. In the\nU.S., energy companies\u2019 spending on research, development, and\ndeployment amounts to just 0.3\u00a0percent of sales.  \n That\u2019s barely more than a tenth what the auto industry\nspends as a share of sales and is dwarfed by the pharmaceutical\nindustry, which spends almost 19\u00a0percent of sales. (American\nPetroleum Institute chief economist  John Felmy  says R&D measures\nunderstate his industry\u2019s \u201coverall investment for the future.\u201d)  \n R&D Spending  \n Many economists argue that government needs to step in when\nthe private sector isn\u2019t providing the socially optimal amount\nof something like research. But government R&D spending on\nenergy has been scarce, too. It was less than 0.03\u00a0percent of\nU.S. gross domestic product as of 2007, about one-third the\nshare in Japan. The dearth of investment in energy R&D, private\nand public, helps explain why the world is still getting its\nenergy by punching holes in the sea floor rather than from\nsafer, renewable sources such as the sun and the wind.  \n In his Oval Office speech on the Gulf spill on June\u00a015,\nPresident  Barack Obama  cited a rapid boost in energy R&D as one\nof several ideas that \u201chave merit and deserve a fair hearing in\nthe months ahead.\u201d That was a paler endorsement than some R&D\nboosters hoped for. On June\u00a011, the new American Energy\nInnovation Council  called  for a gradual increase to $16\u00a0billion\nin annual federal R&D energy spending, from around $5\u00a0billion\nnow, including more money to help commercialize out-of-the-box\nideas.  \n The seven-member council, which includes Microsoft Chairman\n Bill Gates , General Electric CEO  Jeffrey Immelt , and Silicon\nValley venture capitalist  John Doerr , said that, left unchanged,\nthe U.S. energy system \u201cwill condemn our children to a seriously\nconstrained future.\u201d  \n Deficit Obstacle  \n The drive for more energy R&D is up against formidable\nobstacles, starting with the federal budget deficit.\nRepresentative  Ralph Hall , the ranking Republican on the House\nScience and Technology Committee, tried in May to cut about\n$40\u00a0billion from the $86\u00a0billion sought by House Democrats for\nthe America COMPETES Act, which funds all kinds of federal\nresearch as well as math and science education.  \n \u201cWe must be mindful of our spending if America is to\ncontinue to compete globally,\u201d Hall said then. The House\neventually voted to reauthorize the act without Hall\u2019s cuts,\nwhile the Senate hasn\u2019t yet acted. Even if Congress agrees to\nauthorize the full $86\u00a0billion, funding could still be cut in\nthe appropriations process.  \n Money isn\u2019t the only problem. On the right, many\nRepublicans say the federal government should be involved only\nin basic science, not steps toward commercialization. On the\nleft, many Democrats hope to kick-start research and investment\nin green energy via measures such as carbon caps that would make\ncoal and oil more expensive.  \n \u2018Disruptive Technologies\u2019  \n Hanging in the balance are small, new initiatives such as\nARPA-E, a 20-employee Energy Department program that funds what\nDirector  Arun Majumdar  calls \u201creally high-risk, high-reward,\ndisruptive technologies.\u201d ARPA-E is modeled on DARPA, the\nPentagon\u2019s Defense Advanced Research Projects Agency, which\nhelped launch the Internet and the global positioning satellite\nsystem.  \n Like DARPA, the Energy program is free from civil-service\nhiring rules, so it can bring in top scientists and engineers\nfor short stints. It began operations last year with a two-year\nallocation of $400\u00a0million in stimulus funds. With that money\nlargely spent, the Obama Administration is seeking $300\u00a0million\nfor ARPA-E from the regular budget for the fiscal year beginning\nOct.\u00a01.  \n Defying Bureaucracy  \n Defying bureaucratic convention, ARPA-E is funding an\nunorthodox technique for producing ethanol from plant matter\neven though it competes with another arm of the Energy\nDepartment, the Joint BioEnergy Institute. \u201cThat\u2019s the kind of\nenvironment we want,\u201d Majumdar said in a June\u00a014 interview. \u201cI\u2019d\nrather have the competition inside the U.S. than outside the\nU.S.\u201d  \n What looks like fruitful competition to Majumdar can look\nlike wasteful redundancy to a Congress that\u2019s worried about\n deficits . He says that\u2019s a problem. \u201cFrankly we haven\u2019t done a\ngood enough job of explaining what we\u2019re about. It\u2019s a new\nmodel.\u201d  \n The American Energy Innovation Council argues that ARPA-E\nmerits $1\u00a0billion a year. Majumdar, who worked under Chu at\nLawrence Berkeley National Laboratory, says he\u2019d be happy just\ngetting the requested $300\u00a0million given the big budget deficit.  \n On the other hand, other nations are finding the funds\nnecessary to leap ahead in fields such as lithium-ion batteries\nand wind turbines. Energy\u2019s Chu testified last year that China\nis spending $9\u00a0billion a month on clean energy investments. Says\nEnergy Under Secretary  Kristina Johnson : \u201cWe\u2019re competing with\nsome very fierce competitors that are throwing everything they\nhave behind being successful in this clean energy economy.\u201d  \n ( Peter Coy \u2019s column will appear in Bloomberg Businessweek\u2019s\nJune 21 issue. Called Haswell, the chip design delivers 50 percent more battery life than Intel\u2019s previous model, enabling thinner, lighter notebooks and machines that convert to tablets. PC makers including Hewlett-Packard Co. will show devices with the chip this week at Computex, the biggest annual computer event.  As Intel enters a predicted second straight year without  revenue  growth, Chief Executive Officer Brian Krzanich is counting on Haswell and other energy-efficient processors in the pipeline to bolster laptop sales and win more business in tablets. By 2015, global tablet shipments are expected to eclipse PCs as consumers flock to smaller, more affordable machines, according to researcher IDC.  \u201cFor the first time there will be lower price points and new form factors that will help PCs,\u201d said  Tristan Gerra , an analyst at Robert W Baird & Co. in San Francisco. \u201cIn notebooks, Haswell is the first laptop chip that\u2019s going to provide enough battery life.\u201d  Haswell is Intel\u2019s latest attempt to move away from producing processors that suck as much electricity as small TVs to make chips that can let laptop users watch three movies on a single battery charge. Credit Suisse Bonus Bonds Lead Embrace of \u2018Capital Relief\u2019  Credit Suisse Group AG (CSGN) \u2019s $750 million in bonuses given this\nyear in the form of bonds, while compensating employees, also\nplayed a role in shifting risk in derivatives trading.  The securities shielded the Zurich-based bank from\npotential losses on $16 billion of derivatives trades -- and\nreduced its capital needs -- by shifting some of the risk onto\nemployees, people with knowledge of the matter said. Instead of\nthe company bearing the full brunt of any trades where customers\nfailed to pay up, bonus recipients will share the cost.  The bonds are part of a resurgence in \u201cregulatory capital\nrelief transactions,\u201d created by bankers looking to cut risk\nand build cushions against losses without diluting shareholders,\nselling assets or scaling back trades and loans. Some of\nEurope\u2019s biggest banks including  Barclays Plc (BARC) ,  Standard\nChartered Plc (STAN)  and Commerzbank AG are paying investors and\nemployees interest rates as high as 15 percent in return for\nagreeing to share losses on at least $30 billion of assets.  Using techniques similar to the ones that packaged\nmortgages into bonds, lenders are turning holdings of corporate\nloans, export-import credit or derivatives-trading gains into\ntriple-A securities.  The practice has drawn scrutiny from regulators in the U.K.  For more, click here. Closely held companies with undisclosed profits and obscure\nnames like Getco LLC, Hard Eight Futures LLC and Quantlab\nFinancial LLC, are beginning to act more like Wall Street banks,\ncutting checks to politicians, forming trade groups and hiring\nlobbyists and ex-regulators. They\u2019re looking to fend off tighter\nrules and appease lawmakers who say the firms disadvantage small\ninvestors and contribute to wild swings in stock prices.  While the companies, which use high-powered computers to\nexecute thousands of trades in milliseconds, aren\u2019t approaching\nthe big banks in Washington spending, they have more than\nquadrupled their political giving over the last four years, a\nBloomberg News analysis shows. The top recipients include  Eric Cantor , set to become House majority leader, and several\nincoming senators who won in last week\u2019s Republican rout.  \u201cThey are under attack as an industry and they are\nfighting back,\u201d said  James Angel , a professor at Georgetown\nUniversity\u2019s business school who is on the board of Direct Edge\nHoldings LLC, which operates stock exchanges. \u201cThere is an old\nsaying in Washington that if you are not at the table, you are\non the table.\u201d  In just over a decade, high-frequency trading has evolved\nfrom a little-known investment strategy practiced by\nmathematicians to a force that accounts for the majority of U.S.\nstock trades. The companies, which prefer to be called automated\nproprietary trading firms, say they benefit all investors by\nkeeping markets liquid and transaction fees low.  Periods of Stress  The  Securities and Exchange Commission  is less certain of\nthe benefits. The agency is considering a requirement that high-\nfrequency traders keep buying and selling shares during periods\nof stress, instead of just abandoning the market. The SEC is\nalso evaluating whether it should slow down computers that\nsubmit and cancel thousands of orders in milliseconds by\nrequiring bids to stand for a minimum amount of time.  While regulators may need to address some issues, any rules\nshouldn\u2019t get in the way of innovation, said  David Hirschmann ,\npresident of the U.S. Chamber of Commerce\u2019s  Center for Capital\nMarkets Competitiveness .  \u201cThere are those who really want to turn the clock back to\n1980,\u201d said Hirschmann, whose trade group\u2019s members include\nstock exchanges, financial firms and public companies.  Levin Warning  The SEC and members of Congress already were examining the\nbusiness when the May 6 market plunge temporarily wiped out $862\nbillion of share value in 20 minutes. Although an investigation\nby regulators didn\u2019t put direct blame on high-frequency firms,\nthe volatility of stock prices focused more attention in\nWashington on their operations.  \u201cThose with powerful computers are able to use them to\ntheir own financial advantage,\u201d Senator  Carl Levin , a Michigan\nDemocrat, said Sept. 28 on the Senate floor. \u201cThose who exploit\nour markets to the detriment of long-term investors and the real\neconomy will not be able to do so without a battle from the\nSenate.\u201d  In addition to writing proposed rules, the SEC\u2019s\nenforcement division is investigating whether computer-driven\ntraders have manipulated prices. \u201cYou have to be concerned\nevery time there\u2019s a lack of transparency into a market\npractice, particularly one like high-frequency trading that is\nso prevalent,\u201d  Robert Khuzami , the SEC\u2019s enforcement chief,\nsaid in an interview.  The scrutiny has spurred the industry to seek friends in\nWashington. Managers and employees of 21 of the largest\ncomputerized-trading firms, including Getco, Allston Trading LLC\nand Infinium Capital Management LLC gave about $490,000 for this\nyear\u2019s congressional elections, compared with just over $100,000\nin 2006, according to federal election reports filed through\nOct. 15.  In 2000, when some of the firms didn\u2019t yet exist,\ncontributions totaled about $10,000.  Schapiro\u2019s Plans  Although high-frequency trading wasn\u2019t addressed by\nCongress in the Dodd-Frank regulatory overhaul, SEC Chairman\n Mary Schapiro  in September 2009 began issuing proposals to\ncurtail market developments that cater to the industry.  After the May 6 stock plunge, she went even further by\nsaying the SEC will examine whether it should restrict a\npractice by high-frequency firms of canceling most of the orders\nthey submit.  Last January, Representative Cantor of Virginia, the second\nhighest-ranking Republican in the House, sent Schapiro a letter\nsaying her agency\u2019s ideas for regulating fragmented, electronic\nmarkets, including a proposal that would prohibit exchanges from\ngiving high-frequency traders and other market participants a\nsplit-second peek at stock orders, \u201cappeared ad hoc in\nnature.\u201d  \u2018Collect the Facts\u2019  The SEC should \u201ccollect all the facts and develop coherent\nand rational policy objectives before adopting any potentially\nfar-reaching rulemaking proposals,\u201d Cantor wrote in the Jan. 27\nnote.  Cantor, who helped spearhead his party\u2019s successful\ncampaign to win the House back from Democrats, has been among\nthe largest recipients of contributions from the industry, with\nhe and his political action committee taking in $23,000 since\nlast year, records show.  On Oct. 5, 2009, for example, eight top executives from\nChicago-based Getco, including the chief executive officer,\ngeneral counsel and chief financial officer, gave Cantor more\nthan $10,000, records show.  He collected $1,400 the same day from  James Simons , the\nlegendary founder of Renaissance Technologies Corp., a hedge\nfund that engages in high-frequency trading. Other firms whose\nemployees have contributed money to Cantor include Tradelink LLC\nand Traditum Group LLC.  No one at Getco has asked Cantor to discuss regulatory\npolicy with the SEC, spokeswoman Sophie Sohn said.  \u2018Share Our Experience\u2019  Getco supports some rules for high-frequency trading under\nconsideration by the SEC, Sohn said. She said the company\nalready faces obligations to buy and sell stock at the best\noffer price, because it\u2019s a designated market maker at the New\nYork Stock Exchange.  \u201cAs a major participant on many of the world\u2019s leading\nexchanges, we believe it is important to share our experience\nwith regulators, lawmakers, fellow industry participants and\nmembers of the press who are seeking to improve their\nunderstanding of market structure,\u201d she said.  Jonathan Gasthalter , a spokesman for Renaissance, declined\nto comment on Simons\u2019s political contributions.  Cantor also wrote to the SEC after the agency responded to\nthe May crash by urging stock exchanges to implement so-called\ncircuit breakers that halt trading of any stock with a 10\npercent price-swing in less than five minutes.  \u2018Holistic Review\u2019  \u201cI am concerned that this was done before conducting a\nholistic review of the causes of the disruption,\u201d Cantor wrote\nin his second letter dated May 21. Cantor wasn\u2019t available to\ncomment, said his spokesman John Murray.  Another advocate for electronic trading has been\nRepresentative  Jeb Hensarling , a Texas Republican who sits on\nthe House Financial Services Committee.  Hensarling and Representative  Spencer Bachus , the Alabama\nRepublican in line to become chairman of the financial services\npanel, advised Schapiro in an Aug. 24 letter to get a better\nunderstanding of what caused the crash before \u201cassigning blame\nto algorithmic or high-frequency trading firms.\u201d  Hensarling received $4,800 last month from  Suhas Daftuar \nand Alexander Morcos, two managing directors of Hudson River\nTrading LLC, a New York high-frequency trading firm. Hudson\nRiver Trading didn\u2019t respond to a request for comment.  In an interview, Hensarling said he\u2019s concerned the SEC is\nacting \u201cprecipitously\u201d in singling out high-frequency trading.\n\u201cI\u2019m not necessarily saying they are wrong, but the\naccountability function of Congress is to ensure there is\njustification for what you\u2019re doing,\u201d he said.  Donations to Democrats  Other politicians who were the biggest recipients of\ndonations from high-frequency traders include  Mark Kirk , a\nRepublican who won a U.S. Senate seat in Illinois, Senator\n Charles Schumer , a New York Democrat, Representative  Melissa Bean , an Illinois Democrat, and  Robin Carnahan , a Democrat who\nlost her race for a U.S. Senate seat from Missouri.  In June, about two dozen high-frequency trading firms\nformed a trade association to respond to legislative and\nregulatory proposals. Known as the Principal Traders Group, the\nassociation said it plans to reach out to the media to improve\nits understanding of electronic trading.  \u201cThey felt their voice was missing in the press,\u201d said\n James Overdahl , a vice president at NERA Economic Consulting in\nWashington who advises the group. The firms want to make sure\nthat any proposed rules are \u201cdata driven and responding to\nactual evidence,\u201d he said.  Lobbying  The Principal Traders Group is a part of the Futures\nIndustry Association, which advocates on behalf of financial\ncompanies in Washington. The unit doesn\u2019t lobby, said Overdahl,\na former chief economist at the SEC and Commodity Futures\nTrading Commission.  Still, a number of high-frequency firms, including members\nof the Principal Traders Group, have retained former aides to\nlawmakers to push their interests in Washington.  Getco in April 2008 hired the Rich Feuer Group, which\nrepresents financial titans such as Goldman Sachs Group Inc. and\nCredit Suisse Group AG. Getco has paid Rich Feuer at least\n$730,000 in the past two years to lobby Congress and the SEC on\nrules affecting electronic trading and U.S. market structure,\naccording to federal disclosure records.  RGM Trading LLC, a high-frequency trader based in Austin,\nTexas, hired Patton Boggs LLP\u2019s  Micah Green  this year and has\npaid his firm $180,000. Green, who was head of the Bond Market\nAssociation, also lobbies on behalf of Quantlab, a computerized-\ntrading firm based in Houston.  RGM and Quantlab didn\u2019t respond to requests for comment.  Former Dodd Aide  Alex Sternhell, a former aide to Senate Banking Committee\nChairman  Chris Dodd , has been paid $310,000 since last year to\nlobby for Hudson River Trading, records show.  Some of the companies have also employed former regulators.\nGetco hired SEC lawyer  Elizabeth King  in June, adding to a\nroster of agency alumni that includes  John McCarthy , the\ncompany\u2019s general counsel, and former SEC Chairman  Arthur Levitt , who\u2019s a consultant.  Cameron Smith , Quantlab\u2019s general\ncounsel, worked at the SEC in the 1990s.  Levitt is a board member of Bloomberg LP, the parent\ncompany of Bloomberg News.  The high-frequency trading firms\u2019 Washington education is\nfollowing a well-worn path, traveled by such companies as\nMicrosoft Corp. and Google Inc. that avoided the political\nprocess until they grew too big to escape notice.  \u201cLike so many other cutting edge technologies that have\nrun into the media and regulatory whipsaw, high-frequency\ntrading firms would be smart to engage in the Washington public\npolicy discussion,\u201d said  Israel Klein , a lobbyist at the\nPodesta Group who represents financial companies. (ARW)  and  Avnet Inc. (AVT)  to see if corporate technology\nspending will grow more than forecast this year.  Expenditures worldwide on data-center systems -- comprising\nservers, storage and network equipment -- will increase about\n2.4 percent this year to $127.3 billion, based on projections\nfrom Gartner Inc., an industry researcher. That follows gains of\nalmost 2.6 percent last year.  This estimate has remained stable, and halfway through the\nyear it\u2019s \u201con pace with every other indicator we track,\u201d said\nJohn Lovelock, a research vice president in Toronto at Gartner.  Arrow\u2019s global enterprise-computing solutions business and\nAvnet\u2019s technology-solutions unit provide good barometers of\ninformation-technology hardware spending, according to Shawn Harrison, an analyst in Independence,  Ohio , at Longbow Research\nLLC. Real-time indicators such as cancellation rates -- along\nwith guidance from the companies\u2019 executives -- are useful to\ninvestors who track incremental changes in demand, he said.  These companies are bellwethers also because they\u2019re not in\nthe personal-computer business, so they aren\u2019t exposed to the\nweakening demand for these products that has hurt  Microsoft\nCorp. (MSFT)  and  Intel Corp. (INTC) , he added.  Arrow is scheduled to report second-quarter results\ntomorrow. Avnet plans to release its fiscal fourth-quarter\nreport on Aug. 7.  Slowly Improving  After demand for the products they sell slowed in mid-summer and early fall last year, there are signs that some\nmetrics, such as the bookings rate, are \u201cslowly improving,\u201d\nHarrison said. \u201cIT budgets appear to be holding firm.\u201d  The Federal Reserve Bank of  Dallas  noted progress in the\nJuly 17 Beige Book business survey, saying \u201chigh-tech orders\nand production were flat to slightly up\u201d since the June 5\nreport. The San Francisco Fed\u2019s Tech Pulse Index also reflects\nthe shift, rising for a fourth consecutive month to 98.67 in\nJune, the highest since 2008. This index tracks the health of\nthe U.S. IT industry using investment, consumption, employment,\nindustrial-production and shipment data.  The pace of tech-hardware spending is picking up as\n\u201cpurchasing managers are starting to press on the gas a\nlittle,\u201d said Christian Bertelsen, who oversees more than $1.5\nbillion in assets as chief investment officer of Global\nFinancial Private Capital in Sarasota,  Florida . Companies are\ninvesting in part to replace old equipment after purchases were\ndelayed last year, he said. It forecasts second-quarter sales will be between $1.75\nbillion and $1.95 billion, compared with almost $1.7 billion a\nyear ago.  Worldwide sales in Phoenix-based Avnet\u2019s technology-solutions business fell 0.9 percent from a year earlier to about\n$2.5 billion in the three months ended March 30, it reported\nApril 25. Now, for the first time, there are two: the new flagship iPhone 5s, and the lower-cost, colorful iPhone 5c, both of which arrive in stores Sept. 20.  After a week of using them, my view is simple: If you like Apple products, you\u2019ll like these; if you don\u2019t, you won\u2019t.  With its ease of use, enormous wealth of high-quality apps and content and well-integrated online services, the iPhone still provides the best overall user experience of any smartphone. But while Apple has never introduced this many iPhones, it\u2019s also never changed so little from the previous generation.  The 5s is the current iPhone 5 -- same size, shape, metal body and 4-inch Retina display -- with upgraded internals and one terrific new feature. The iPhone 5c is to all intents and purposes the current iPhone 5 housed in a new plastic body.  Both phones run iOS 7, a new version of Apple\u2019s mobile operating system that becomes available today for downloading to iPads and older iPhones. The software\u2019s look and feel have been overhauled, with flat, brightly colored icons replacing the more textured look of previous releases.  Users of iOS 7, which I\u2019ll discuss at greater length in a separate column, will find some things different. For example, you now close an app running in the background by flicking a thumbnail of it with your finger. And they\u2019ll find some new things, like iTunes Radio, which takes on the likes of  Pandora (P)  and  Spotify , and a new Control Center that gives you quick access to key settings -- something phones with  Google (GOOG) \u2019s Android software have had for some time.  Incremental Changes  But the phones themselves are mostly about incremental changes and perhaps about laying the groundwork for future, bigger innovations.  The most important new feature in both is the 5s Touch ID fingerprint sensor, which elegantly addresses a significant pain point for mobile users: security.  Mobile devices are increasingly the repositories of some of our most sensitive data. Yet most people don\u2019t have passcodes set up, because it\u2019s just too annoying to enter them dozens of time a day.  The Touch ID is built into the 5s home button. Once you\u2019ve scanned your fingers -- I used both thumbs -- a light press of the button wakes the phone and simultaneously unlocks it. It works far better than any other biometric device I\u2019ve used, not requiring your finger to be positioned just so. It makes security transparent and even pleasurable.  Mobile Payments  The Touch ID also works for purchases from Apple\u2019s iTunes and App Stores, yet another small step -- after the Passbook feature introduced last year -- toward establishing the company as a force in the nascent field of mobile payments.  Apple is taking pains to reassure users that the fingerprint data, which is stored in mathematical form rather than as a graphical image, never leaves the phone. It\u2019s stored in a special area of the new A7 microprocessor that powers the 5s, and Apple says it isn\u2019t uploaded to its servers or anywhere else.  Apple says the A7 is the first 64-bit chip in a smartphone, something that\u2019s of far more interest to technophiles than average consumers. But you may see evidence of the greater power in things like the complex graphics of some visually intensive games and the speed of the 8-megapixel camera\u2019s autofocus. And, like a new motion processor, its value may become clearer as new apps take advantage of it.  Upgraded Camera  Speaking of the camera, it\u2019s been upgraded with a larger sensor, wider aperture and a new flash for taking better photos in less-than-ideal lighting conditions. Images captured in a darkened restaurant were much warmer and more natural than on the current model.  The camera app has also been extensively reworked to add features like a burst mode for taking multiple rapid-fire shots and auto image stabilization. They work well, but will hardly be novel to anyone who\u2019s used a recent Android device or even one of  Microsoft (MSFT) \u2019s Windows phones.  Other changes are similarly welcome if not revolutionary. There\u2019s a new gold color (joining silver and gray), slow-motion video, an improved front-facing camera for better video calls using Apple\u2019s FaceTime, and support for more non-U.S. carriers\u2019 ultra-fast LTE networks.  Visible Changes  The 5c\u2019s changes are more visible, if less significant. The big one is the new body. Though it\u2019s plastic, there\u2019s nothing cheap-feeling about it, and the cartoon-like iOS 7 somehow feels more at home when it\u2019s surrounded by one of the five bright new colors: blue, pink, yellow, green and white. (Even the software\u2019s background color is set to match the color of the case.)  The 5c\u2019s other departures from the 2012 model are exceedingly modest. It, too, has the new FaceTime camera and expanded LTE support. Battery life should be about the same as on the 5 and 5s, good enough to easily get through a full day of normal use.  Otherwise, the biggest change is in the price. On the  Verizon (VZ) ,  AT&T (T)  and  Sprint (S)  networks in the U.S., the 5s starts at $199 on a two-year contract for a model with 16 gigabytes of storage, while the 5c is the least expensive new iPhone ever: $99 for the 16-gigabyte version. On the contract-free  T-Mobile (TMUS)  network, the 5s starts at $649, the 5c at $528.  There\u2019s nothing wrong with either phone. But there\u2019s not much that\u2019s pulse-quickening about them either.  (Rich Jaroslovsky is a Bloomberg News columnist. The opinions expressed are his own.) Turning the computer maker into a private company would allow  Michael Dell  and his private-equity backers to manage the company\u2019s finances differently, said a person familiar with the matter. For example, they could borrow money by securitizing accounts receivables, a move a public board and public shareholders would likely reject, said this person.  Dell needs more urgency and focus, said  Erik Gordon , a professor of law and business at the  University of Michigan . \u201cIt hasn\u2019t diddled too long in PC-land because public stockholders tied its hands,\u201d Gordon said in an e-mailed statement. \u201cIt was free to go into tablets and services, as did its competitors, but management chose not to.\u201d  TPG Capital  David Frink , a spokesman for Dell, and Gemma Hart, a spokeswoman for Silver Lake, declined to comment. Officials at Credit Suisse, JPMorgan, Barclays, Bank of America, and Royal Bank declined to comment.  TPG Capital, which earlier looked at participating in a transaction, is unlikely to be part of any deal with Silver Lake, said a person familiar with the matter.  KKR & Co. (KKR) , which considered a deal with Dell last year, also isn\u2019t likely to bid at this time, said another person. Representatives at TPG and KKR declined to comment.  Silver Lake has ammunition some other buyout firms don\u2019t: It just raised $7 billion for a new fund that could swell to as much as $10 billion, two people familiar with the matter said this week, and that fund can only invest in technology companies. Michael Dell also was one of the early investors in Silver Lake\u2019s initial fund of $2.3 billion.  Dell\u2019s Stake  Under the current negotiations, Michael Dell, the top  shareholder  in the computer maker, would roll his stake into the buyout, said one of the people. Dell, 47, owns about 15.7 percent of the company, according to data compiled by Bloomberg, valuing his stake at $3.45 billion, based on yesterday\u2019s closing price.  He and  Glenn Hutchins , co-founder and Co-CEO of Silver Lake, are scheduled to attend the  World Economic Forum , which takes place in Davos,  Switzerland  from Jan. 22 to Jan. 27.  Based on the company\u2019s market value, a deal could be the largest buyout of a technology company since 2007, when KKR bought First Data Corp. for more than $25 billion, according to data compiled by Bloomberg. It might also be the biggest acquisition in the computer industry since Hewlett-Packard Co. bought Compaq Computer Corp. for about $19 billion more than a decade ago, the data show.  Technology Buyouts  Large leveraged buyouts have been scarce since the financial crisis. The biggest for the technology sector in the past two years was Blackstone Group LP\u2019s $3 billion purchase of health-care billing company Emdeon Inc., according to data compiled by Bloomberg.  Other technology companies, including disk-drive maker Seagate Technology Plc, have tried to go private and seen talks collapse over valuations or financing difficulties.  Silver Lake has been investing in technology companies since its founding in 1999. Its latest fund, Silver Lake Partners III LP, was generating an 18 percent net internal rate of return, according to data from  California Public Employees\u2019 Retirement System , a limited partner.  In 2009, the  Menlo Park , California-based firm bought a majority stake in Skype Technologies SA from EBay Inc. in a deal that valued the calling service at $2.75 billion. Less than two years later, Microsoft Corp. agreed to buy Skype for $8.5 billion.  While Skype yielded a threefold return for Silver Lake, another big bet didn\u2019t. Silver Lake\u2019s 2007 investment in communications equipment maker Avaya Holdings Corp. was marked at cost as of Dec. 31, 2011, meaning the firm has yet to book a profit on the deal, according to a marketing document. Hearing arguments yesterday in Washington, a majority of\nthe nine justices suggested that Monsanto has broad rights to\ncontrol the use of seeds that contain its patented technology.\nThe genetically modified seeds are used to grow more than 90\npercent of the nation\u2019s soybeans.  \u201cWhy in the world would anybody spend any money to try to\nimprove the seed if as soon as they sold the first one anybody\ncould grow more and have as many of those seeds as they want?\u201d\nChief Justice  John Roberts  said.  He and other justices signaled that they view seeds\nharvested from patented crops as new products with fresh patent\nprotections. A victory for Monsanto would potentially let patent\nholders restrict use of self-replicating products beyond the\nfirst generation, benefiting producers of live vaccines,\ngenetically modified salmon, and bacteria strains used in\nmedical research.  Monsanto, the world\u2019s biggest seed company, forbids farmers\nfrom saving seeds for replanting instead of buying new ones each\nseason. The company is battling Vernon Hugh Bowman, an Indiana\nfarmer.  Biotechnology, Software  Biotechnology companies, software makers and research\nuniversities say a ruling for Bowman would weaken their patent\nprotections. On the other side, makers of replacement auto parts\nand the American Antitrust Institute argue against restricting\nhow patented products are used.  Monsanto, based in St. Louis, inserts genes into crops that\nlet them withstand application of the herbicide Roundup. Farmers\nwho buy so-called Roundup Ready seeds agree to restrictions on\ntheir use. Monsanto has sued 146 U.S. farmers for saving Roundup\nReady soybeans since 1997, winning all 11 cases that went to\ntrial, said  Kelli Powers , a Monsanto spokeswoman.  Bowman, 76, said he complied with the rules for the spring\nplanting of soybeans, which he bought from  DuPont Co .\u2019s Pioneer\nunit, a Roundup Ready licensee. For the second crop of the\nseason, which is susceptible to low yields because of its late\ntiming, Bowman planted beans he bought from a grain elevator.\nBowman estimated he saved $30,000 for his farm.  No Written Restrictions  Bowman says he did nothing wrong since there were no\nwritten restrictions on purchasing soybeans from the elevator.\nHe contends Monsanto\u2019s patent rights expired after farmers\nbought the original seeds.  The U.S. Court of Appeals for the Federal Circuit  ruled \nagainst Bowman in September 2011. He just can\u2019t plant,\nharvest, and then replant.\u201d  Monsanto has said a loss would force the seed industry to\nshift research away from crops such as soybeans, canola and\nwheat that produce exact replicas of themselves because they are\nself-pollinating.  Grain from hybrid crops such as corn isn\u2019t typically\nreplanted because the offspring are less productive.  Genetic traits require an average of $136 million to\ndevelop and commercialize, a process that takes 13 years,\naccording to  CropLife International , an industry group. Monsanto\nin 2012 reported $1.51 billion in research and development\nspending.  $19.9 Billion  U.S. farmers spent $19.9 billion on seeds in 2012,\naccording to data compiled by Bloomberg Industries.  The Center for Food Safety, a Washington-based group that\nis critical of genetically engineered foods, suggested in a\ncourt brief that Monsanto could use sales contracts and Plant\nProtection Act certificates, rather than patents, to prevent\ncopying while permitting farmers to save seed for themselves.  The Obama administration is largely backing Monsanto in the\ncase. To rule that the first sale of a seed ends Monsanto\u2019s\nintellectual property rights would \u201ceviscerate patent\nprotections,\u201d Melissa Arbus Sherry, a Justice Department\nlawyer, told the justices.  \u201cThere would be no incentive to invest, not just in\nRoundup Ready soybeans or not even agricultural technology,\u201d\nSherry said.  BSA - The Software Alliance, with members including  Apple\nInc.  and  Microsoft Corp ., said in court papers that eliminating\npatent protection for self-replicating seeds could aid software\npiracy. Diagnostic companies including Agilent Technologies Inc.\nand Life Technologies Corp. said they often sell items for\nresearch use only. That allows them to charge lower prices by\npreventing replication of their products. They asked the court\nto uphold Monsanto\u2019s conditions. He was about to begin a new job as Barack Obama\u2019s campaign\nmanager, and being a diligent student with access to some very\nsmart people, he arranged a rolling series of personal seminars\nwith the CEOs and senior executives of companies including  Apple\nInc. (AAPL) ,  Facebook Inc. (FB) ,  Zynga Inc. (ZNGA) ,  Google Inc. (GOOG) ,  Microsoft Corp. (MSFT) ,\n Salesforce.com Inc. (CRM) , and DreamWorks SKG, Bloomberg Businessweek\nreports in its June 18 issue.  \u201cI went around the country for literally a month of my\nlife interviewing these companies and just talking about\norganizational growth, emerging technologies, marketing,\u201d he\nsays at Obama\u2019s campaign headquarters in Chicago.  In two long, private conversations, Steve Jobs tore into\nMessina for all the White House was doing wrong and what it\nought to be doing differently, before going on to explain how\nthe campaign could exploit technology in ways that hadn\u2019t been\npossible before.  Segmented Voters  \u201cLast time you were programming to only a couple of\nchannels,\u201d Jobs told him, meaning the Web and e-mail. \u201cThis\ntime, you have to program content to a much wider variety of\nchannels -- Facebook, Tumblr, Twitter, YouTube, Google --because\npeople are segmented in a very different way than they were four\nyears ago.\u201d  When Obama declared for president, the iPhone hadn\u2019t been\nreleased. Now, Jobs told him, mobile technology had to be\ncentral to the campaign\u2019s effort.  \u201cHe knew exactly where everything was going,\u201d Messina\nsays. \u201cHe explained viral content and how our stuff could break\nout, how it had to be interesting and clean.\u201d  At DreamWorks Studios,  Steven Spielberg  spent three hours\nexplaining how to capture an audience\u2019s attention and offered a\nnumber of ideas that will be rolled out before Election Day.  An early example of Spielberg\u2019s influence is\nRomneyEconomics.com, a website designed by the Obama team to\ntell the story -- a horror story by their reckoning -- of\npresumptive Republican presidential nominee Mitt Romney\u2019s career\nat Bain Capital LLC.  Spielberg Team  Afterward, Spielberg insisted that Messina sit down with\nthe DreamWorks marketing team. Hollywood movie studios are\nexpert, as presidential campaigns also must be, at spending huge\nsums over a few weeks to reach and motivate millions of\nAmericans.  An awestruck tone surfaces when Messina talks about these\nencounters and what they taught him. At 42, he is tall and\nslightly stooped, with an innocent face, a flop of blond hair,\nand a sheepdog friendliness made somewhat surreal by the arsenal\nof profanity he deploys when not speaking for the record.  Messina, who\u2019s from Denver, managed his first campaign as\nan undergraduate at the University of  Montana  and in the 20\nyears since has never lost a race. Before joining Obama in 2008,\nhe alternated between running campaigns and working on Capitol\nHill.  He made his name as chief of staff to Senator Max Baucus of\nMontana, becoming known as \u201cBaucus\u2019s muscle\u201d for his skill as\na behind-the-scenes enforcer. In 2005 he ran the Democrats\u2019\nsuccessful pushback against George W. Bush\u2019s plan to privatize\nSocial Security.  Drugmaker Deal  \u201cHe had a talent for getting K Street to see that it was\nto their advantage to get on board with whatever Baucus was\ndoing,\u201d says Jim Manley, a former top aide to Senate Majority\nLeader Harry Reid. At the White House, Messina was instrumental\nin cutting the deal with the pharmaceutical industry that helped\nclear the way for the health-care overhaul law.  Messina is unusual in  Washington , at once a hard-bitten\npolitical fixer known for handling unpleasant tasks -- \u201cIn the\nWhite House he was given all the, pardon my French, the s--t\nwork,\u201d says Baucus -- and also earnestly devoted to self-\nimprovement in a way few Washington operatives would want\nrevealed.  A sign on his old computer in Baucus\u2019s office, hung with no\nevident irony and left there by the staff as a token of\nfondness, reads, \u201cBe Better Today Than You Were Yesterday.\u201d  Along with his conversations with chief executive officers,\nMessina\u2019s regimen for the new job included reading a hundred\nyears\u2019 worth of campaign histories piled on a shelf above his\ndesk. Still, his obsession runs to the future, not the past, and\nto business as much as politics.  New Model  Messina is convinced that modern presidential campaigns are\nmore like fast-growing technology companies than anything found\nin a history book and his own job like that of the executives\nwho run them.  \u201cWhat they\u2019ve done is more readily applicable to me,\nbecause they all started very small and got big very quickly,\u201d\nhe says.  Messina came to this insight through a relationship with\nsomeone keenly attuned to these changes and famous for having\ngroomed two other young men to run a very large enterprise:  Eric Schmidt , Google\u2019s executive chairman. Messina considers him a\nmentor.  \u201cJim and I met in the 2008 campaign and just hit it off on\na personal basis,\u201d Schmidt says. \u201cWe became very good\nfriends.\u201d Schmidt was an early sounding board and later\narranged many of the meetings with CEOs.  Fading Idealism  Obama can use the help. Re-election campaigns are\nunglamorous. For many supporters, the thrill of electing him has\nfaded, and the idealism that once vitalized them has given way\nto disillusionment.  In 2008, Obama\u2019s campaign earned acclaim for using\ntechnology to harness, in volunteers and dollars, the excitement\nsurrounding his candidacy. He routed the Republican nominee,\n Arizona  Senator John McCain, outspending him almost 3 to 1.  This race will be different. Romney and his allies may hold\nthe financial upper hand, not least because the  Supreme Court \u2019s\nCitizens United decision in 2010 allowed for a flood of\ncorporate cash. The unspoken hope in  Chicago  is that superior\nstrategy and a shrewd use of technology can make up for Obama\u2019s\ndiminished stature and more formidable opponent. So Messina has\nspent 18\u00a0months studying and building.  Two Visions  The Nov. 6 election will be a contest between two different\nvisions of government and between competing ideas about how to\nreach voters. Romney\u2019s campaign will take a traditional\napproach, heavy on television advertising and backed by a\nmassive war chest.  Obama\u2019s will rely on organization, scaling up to a national\nlevel the type of grassroots effort Messina once ran for Baucus\nin Montana. His big bet is that Schmidt, Spielberg, and the rest\nare right about how far technology has advanced -- that it\u2019s\ncome far enough to mitigate Obama\u2019s disadvantages and solve what\n David Plouffe , the White House adviser who ran the last\ncampaign, calls \u201cour Electoral College Rubik\u2019s Cube.\u201d  In that sense, the campaign is about how best to run a\nlarge, complex enterprise, while under tremendous pressure and\npublic scrutiny. Messina is wagering Obama\u2019s second term on the\nidea that the collected wisdom of technology\u2019s biggest titans\ncan outsmart Romney, whose executive savvy has made him rich and\nbrought him to the cusp of the presidency.  Spinning Fantasy  Presidential campaigns are rarely what they seem. For all\nthat the candidates crisscross the country, offering sweeping\nnational visions and vowing to represent everyone, they really\nfocus on only a handful of states. A campaign manager\u2019s job is\nto spin the fantasy and not fall for it.  The last election was unusual in that Obama conducted a\nnational campaign, expanded the electorate, and won a broad\nswath of voters. This election will mark a return to the mean,\nas is already evident in Obama\u2019s strategy, which aims to\npersuade a sliver of the electorate, not expand it.  Messina is focused on seven states -- Florida, Ohio,\nVirginia, Iowa, North Carolina, Colorado, Nevada -- that\nprobably hold the key to the election. Neither the nature of the\nrace nor the means of reaching voters will be quite the same.  Messina often tries to convey this to donors by telling the\nstory of how he came to be campaign manager. It\u2019s December 2010.\nHe\u2019s wading through chest-high surf in Hawaii with the\npresident. Obama summons him over.  \u2018Got a Favor\u2019  \u201cI\u2019ve got a favor I want to ask,\u201d he says. \u201cI\u2019d like you\nto run the re-elect.\u201d Messina replies that he\u2019s flattered, yet\nhe\u2019ll only take the job on one condition: \u201cYou have to\nunderstand, this will be nothing like the last campaign.\u201d  \u201cI thought the last one went pretty well.\u201d  \u201cIt did. But everything is different now.\u201d  The story is a windup to a sermon Messina likes to give\nabout the importance of technology in reaching voters -- a sort\nof TED talk that echoes a point about which Schmidt, too, is\nadamant. Last January, as Messina was beginning his new job,\nSchmidt stepped back from Google and Larry Page took over as\nCEO. Since then, Schmidt has become a kind of guru to Messina,\nan executive coach and kindred spirit.  The two became acquainted during the last campaign, just\nafter  Hillary Clinton  dropped out of the race, when Messina,\nthen Plouffe\u2019s right hand, was preoccupied with ramping up for\nthe general election.  3-Hour Talk  \u201cI said to him, \u2018You\u2019ve done what I\u2019m being asked to\ndo,\u201d\u2019 Messina says. \u201cHe said, \u2018Yes, I have. Let me sit down\nwith you, and we\u2019ll talk.\u2019 For three hours we sat in a\nconference room, and he just gave me advice about all the\nmistakes he\u2019d made, about purchasing supply chains, about HR,\nabout the blocking and tackling of growing fast and making sure\nyou have organizational objectives.\u201d  \u201cWhat I like about Jim,\u201d Schmidt says, \u201cis that he\nstarts the day thinking, \u2018What are the analytical measurements\nthat I should make decisions on?\u2019 Many people in politics have\nno concept of what I just said. They\u2019re intuitive thinkers, and\nthey\u2019re often right. But the difference is that to run a large\noperation in today\u2019s world, the best way to do it is\nanalytically. And you have the tools now.\u201d  Even with the last campaign\u2019s success using the Internet,\nSchmidt says the world hadn\u2019t yet reached the point where\ntechnology could transform how people run for president.  \u201cIn 2008 most people didn\u2019t operate\u201d on Facebook and\nTwitter, he says. \u201cThe difference now is, first and foremost,\nthe growth of Facebook, which is much, much more deeply\npenetrated into things.
