You can run political campaigns on the sum of those\ntools.\u201d  Channel to Supporters  In his memoir of the 2008 election, Plouffe discusses\ntechnology\u2019s importance. The 13\u00a0million e-mail addresses Obama\ncollected were a potent way to raise money and a valuable means\nof talking to supporters as well.  \u201cWe had essentially created our own television network,\nonly better,\u201d he writes, \u201cbecause we communicated directly\nwith no filter to what would amount to about 20\u00a0percent of the\ntotal number of votes we would need to win -- a remarkably high\npercentage.\u201d  Both Schmidt and Messina share a fondness for the metrics\nthat highlight these changes: Facebook users have grown tenfold\nsince the last campaign, to more than 900\u00a0million. In 2008 most\nusers were in their teens or twenties; the fastest-growing\nsegment now is people over 50.  Twitter Followers  On Election Day, Obama sent two Twitter messages to his\n116,000 followers; today, he has 16\u00a0million followers, and his\ntop advisers are all prolific Twitter messagers and minor\nsocial-media celebrities.  Extrapolating a bit, it isn\u2019t hard to imagine the campaign\nhaving a direct line to 50\u00a0percent or 70\u00a0percent -- or maybe\nmore -- of the voters it will need to win.  To reach this expanding universe of potential supporters,\nthe Obama team spent nine months building a platform it calls\nDashboard, which allows field staffers and volunteers to access\nand update the campaign\u2019s voter database from an app on their\nphones.  Canvassers can visit a neighborhood and see which houses\nare targets and which are a waste of time. Everything is updated\nin real time -- no need to lug around a clipboard or check in at\nan office. And for voters, no more annoying knocks on the door\nwhen they\u2019ve just gotten a phone call or e-mail.  \u2018Snowflake\u2019 Organization  Dashboard is an important component of what the campaign\nrefers to as the \u201csnowflake\u201d model of organizing, the idea\nthat each paid staffer creates and oversees an expanding network\nof volunteers -- a snowflake.  Last year, Obama\u2019s fundraisers pushed big donors to\ncontribute the annual maximum of $35,800 right away. This would\ncover the salary of one paid field staffer, who oversees five\nunpaid \u201cneighborhood team leaders,\u201d each of whom brings in\nfive team members, who then recruit 20 volunteers apiece. Total:\n500\u00a0people.  The campaign estimates each of the Obama snowflakes will\nproduce an extra 1,000 votes. The earlier they did this, the\nmore voters they would reach.  \u201cMy advice was to think about it in terms of quarters,\u201d\nsays Schmidt. \u201cYou really have six quarters between\u201d the\nspring of 2011 \u201cand the election. So essentially all of the key\npersonnel decisions are made in the first quarter. And then you\nbuild from there.\u201d  Measurable Politics  As Plouffe put it: \u201cPolitics always has room for feel and\ninstinct. But there is so much now that is measurable. We think\nfrom a technology and data perspective that what Jim has built\nwill be the best that politics has ever seen.\u201d  Silicon Valley\u2019s influence is evident even in the layout of\nthe campaign\u2019s headquarters. Designed with input from Facebook\nexecutives, the floor plan has few private offices and lots of\nbig, collaborative open spaces where staffers work in pods.  This avoids a common Washington problem. The history of\nAmerican presidential campaigns is full of infighting, hatred,\nand rivalries. Then Vice President Al Gore\u2019s 2000 campaign and\nthen-Senator Hillary Clinton\u2019s 2008 bid were riven with\nfactionalism among status-obsessed aides on different floors.\nObama\u2019s staff is spread across a single floor -- to outward\nappearances, happily.  At Schmidt\u2019s suggestion, Messina bypassed the political\npros who usually handle campaign technology and opted to build\nit in-house.  Innovators Needed  \u201cEric said to me, for a lot of these positions, you don\u2019t\nwant political people,\u201d Messina says. \u201cYou need innovators,\npeople who can get stuff done quickly.\u201d  The campaign\u2019s chief technology officer, Harper Reed, is a\nfriendly, bearded startup veteran with lots of tattoos, who\u2019d\nnever worked in politics and was brought in from the online T-\nshirt vendor Threadless.com.  \u201cHe looks like he\u2019s the heavy-metal lead guitarist in\nMetallica,\u201d Messina says. \u201cBut he\u2019s a genius. He threw out all\nthe old conventional wisdom and said, \u2018Show me what you want on\na white board. I\u2019ll build it for you.\u2019\u2009\u201d  Under Reed, the Obama team has built systems for\nregistering voters, organizing volunteers, and generally\nvacuuming up and analyzing every available bit of personal data\n-- voting patterns, political contributions, and consumer\npreferences as well as what people read and share, and how they\nrespond to e-mails, ads, Twitter messages, and other\nsolicitations.  Fashion as Revenue  At the suggestion of another of Messina\u2019s advisers, Obama-\nthemed merchandise has become a lucrative revenue source. Early\non, Messina met, and was dazzled by, Anna Wintour, the editor of\nVogue and inspiration for \u201cThe Devil Wears Prada,\u201d who created\na spreadsheet to convince him that fashion could generate\nserious money for the campaign.  \u201cWhat is the one thing everyone has from \u201908? A T-shirt,\u201d\nMessina says.  Wintour drew conservatives\u2019 scorn for appearing in an\nonline video soliciting donors for a fundraising dinner for the\nfirst couple with Sarah Jessica Parker.  Her influence actually runs much deeper. Last fall the\ncampaign held a runway show in Manhattan to unveil a luxury\nclothing line by celebrity designers, including Vera Wang and\nDiane von Furstenberg.  Messina, whose own fashion sense borders on the tragic, was\nintroduced on the runway by Scarlett Johansson. Republicans\ngleefully mock Obama\u2019s designer collection as an exercise in\nnarcissism, while the Romney campaign also sells merchandise,\nmostly the standard T-shirts, hats, and buttons.  Money, Voters  Messina sees only the influx of millions of dollars --\nalthough he won\u2019t say how many millions. Sure, the $95 Thakoon\nPanichgul scarf and $75 Tory Burch tote bag are outlandish, yet\nthey net a lot more than $10 Hanes T-shirts.  \u201cRaise money, register voters, and persuade voters,\u201d\nMessina says. \u201cEverything has to feed into those three\nthings.\u201d  From the outside, it isn\u2019t clear that will be enough. On\nJune\u00a07, the Romney campaign said it raised $76\u00a0million in May,\ntopping Obama\u2019s $60\u00a0million and marking the first time in five\nyears that Obama had been outraised. Even with Spielberg\u2019s input\non the Bain ad, elite opinion was that it mostly flopped, after\ncampaign surrogates, including  Bill Clinton  and Cory Booker,\nveered off message and commended Romney\u2019s business record, to\nthe delight of Republicans and cable news producers.  Bain Attack  Messina is adamant that the Bain attack succeeded among the\nuncommitted voters he\u2019s concerned with, who ignore pundits and\nare only now beginning to form opinions of Romney.  \u201cWhen people say \u2018How\u2019s the Bain thing playing?\u2019 it\ndoesn\u2019t matter what the set of Morning Joe has to say about\nit,\u201d Plouffe says. \u201cBut if you\u2019re a 45-year-old swing voter in\nToledo, Ohio, what are you seeing? What\u2019s in your local\nnewspaper? What ads are running? And what\u2019s going on in the\nlocal field operation? That\u2019s what really matters.\u201d  These voters will probably decide the election. All the\ntechnology, money, and management theory really amount to an\nelaborate, determined effort to discredit Romney and win their\nsupport. By virtue of his background, Messina may be especially\nwell suited to that job.  Messina will go a long way to win, as the two leading\nstories from his Montana career suggest. Both involve the 2002\nSenate race he ran for Baucus, a Democrat seeking re-election in\na terrible year for Democrats.  Fringe Candidate  To protect Baucus, Messina had him refuse to participate in\nany debate that didn\u2019t also include a fringe third-party\ncandidate who\u2019d inadvertently dyed his skin blue with homemade\nantibiotics -- a guaranteed distraction.  The other story involved his Republican challenger, a state\nsenator named Mike Taylor, who was the target of an ad so\ndevastating it got national attention.  The ad charged Taylor with having embezzled student loans\nfrom a cosmetology school he\u2019d owned in the 1980s. The ad\u2019s\nforce lay in the music and imagery. Set to a porn soundtrack, it\nfeatured snippets of an old television ad for Taylor\u2019s hair\nsalon that showed the candidate clad in a medallioned, open-\nshirted disco outfit, massaging lotion into another man\u2019s face,\nand then appearing to reach toward the man\u2019s crotch, as a\nnarrator intoned, \u201cNot the way we do business in Montana.\u201d  \u201cJim is tough,\u201d Baucus says. \u201cI\u2019ll never forget when he\nshowed me that ad. We were in Bozeman in a motel. The curtains\nwere drawn. He said, \u2018Max, what do you think?\u2019 They were afraid\nI wasn\u2019t going to like it. I loved it!\u201d  \u2018No Honor\u2019  Humiliated, Taylor quit the race, and Baucus sailed to\nvictory. \u201cI found out quickly from Messina that there was no\nhonor in politics,\u201d Taylor says in an e-mail.  Starting out in Montana provided a broad education in all\naspects of a campaign. A rural state with fewer than 1 million\nresidents, Montana is so cheap even a legislative candidate on a\n$20,000 budget can run a sophisticated campaign with radio and\ntelevision ads, direct mail, and phone banks.  Districts are small enough that candidates can, and are\nexpected to, knock on every door. Messina became known as a\n\u201cfield guy\u201d for his dogged emphasis on voter contact.  \u201cIt taught me very early on,\u201d he says, \u201cthat you can win\nif you run good enough grassroots and you\u2019re very clear about\nthe differences with your opponent.\u201d  Because Montana typically votes Republican for president,\nit\u2019s often regarded as a red state. Still, it\u2019s almost evenly\ndivided between the parties.  Competitive Politics  \u201cPolitics here is competitive,\u201d says Dave Hunter, a local\nconsultant and early mentor to Messina. \u201cDemocrats usually\nperform at around 47 or 48\u00a0percent, so candidates have to run a\nlittle better campaign than Republicans to win statewide.\u201d  The state also lacks a significant minority presence.  \u201cWe really don\u2019t have African-Americans or a Hispanic\npopulation,\u201d Hunter says. \u201cYou win in Montana by convincing\nwhite, independent voters to turn out for you. It\u2019s good\nexperience for presidential politics because it\u2019s not about\nturning out your base; it\u2019s about persuasion.\u201d  Ten years later, Messina is trying to do the same thing,\nonly at a much higher level. Montana is out of reach. Yet the\nseven states he\u2019s targeted, as well as a few more he hopes won\u2019t\nend up in play, all lie within striking distance of either\ncandidate.  If the European crisis explodes or an attack on Iran drives\nup  oil prices , the  U.S. economy  may tank and render moot all of\nMessina\u2019s careful planning. Or the recovery could pick up steam,\nor the old gaffe-prone Romney could return and hand Obama an\nunexpectedly easy win.  A likelier scenario, though, is that the race will be\nclose. Messina may see that happening.  \u201cJim has said to me, \u2018This is the most important thing I\nwill do in my lifetime,\u201d\u2019 says  Penny Pritzker , the national\nfinance chairwoman of the last campaign.  Should it come to that, Messina will have a chance to do\nwhat every campaign manager dreams of doing, what most\nWashington operatives brag about doing, and what only an elect\nfew have ever actually done -- make the difference in a\npresidential election. Then, the CEOs will come to him for\nadvice. (GOOG)  to  Valero Energy\nCorp. (VLO)  sit on record cash stockpiles and payouts remain at three-\nyear lows.  Standard & Poor\u2019s 500 Index companies paid 27 percent of\nearnings in dividends in the second quarter, down from 30\npercent in 2008 and below a 30-year average of 41 percent,\naccording to Wells Fargo & Co. Company cash, equivalents and\nshort-term marketable securities jumped 63 percent to $2.77\ntrillion in the same period, according to Bloomberg data.  \u201cCompanies are hoarding a lot of cash and they\u2019re getting\na very low return for it,\u201d said Richard Sichel, chief\ninvestment officer at Philadelphia Trust Co., which manages $1.6\nbillion. \u201cThat\u2019s all the more reason for them to pay bigger\ndividends.\u201d  Investors gave dividends less importance while stocks\nsoared during the middle of the last decade, said Gina Martin Adams, a Wells Fargo equity strategist in New York. Now\ninvestors want companies to pay out more of the cash they are\nholding to make up for low equity returns in the past year, said\n Keith Wirtz , who helps manage $16.7 billion as chief investment\nofficer at Fifth Third Asset Management Inc. in Cincinnati.  The  S&P 500 \u2019s ratio of net debt to earnings before\ninterest, taxes, depreciation and amortization has dropped to\n2.6 from 5 in mid-2008, data compiled by Bloomberg show.\nAnalysts surveyed by Bloomberg project this year\u2019s earnings will\nincrease 18 percent to about $100 a share.  Total Return  \u201cWhy are they sitting on all this cash, earning close to\nzero, when they could at least be putting it in the hands of\nshareholders?\u201d said Michael Mullaney, who helps manage $9.5\nbillion at Fiduciary Trust Co. in Boston.  Companies are harboring cash because the economic and\npolitical outlook remains cloudy, said  David Sowerby , a fund\nmanager with Bloomfield Hills, Michigan-based Loomis Sayles &\nCo., which manages $150 billion. Before dividends are increased,\nSowerby said he wants more share buybacks from companies that\nsee their stock as cheap.  The cash also would come in handy for acquisitions in\nmarkets with slow organic growth, said  Dan Veru , chief\ninvestment officer at Fort Lee, New Jersey-based Palisade\nCapital Management LLC, which manages $3.4 billion. Companies\nwould have to use cash instead of shares because of depressed\nequity values, he said.  \u201cWe\u2019re going to be faced for some time with a slow\nenvironment for organic-type growth,\u201d he said.  General Electric  General Electric Co. (GE) ,  CBS Corp. (CBS)  and  Citigroup Inc. (C)  were\namong companies that cut dividends during the recession as\nglobal financial-industry losses and writedowns from the credit\ncrisis surpassed $1 trillion in December 2008. Shareholder\npayouts haven\u2019t been brought back to pre-recession levels.  GE in 2009 lowered its quarterly dividend for the first\ntime since 1938 to 10 cents a share from 31 cents. The world\u2019s\nbiggest provider of power-generation equipment and services has\nincreased the payment three times since to 15 cents and Chief\nExecutive Officer Jeffrey Immelt has told investors that raising\nthe dividend and accelerating share repurchases will be\npriorities over large acquisitions in the \u201cnear term.\u201d  Cash and short-term investments at Fairfield, Connecticut-\nbased GE rose to $136 billion at the end of the second quarter,\nfrom $89 billion in the first quarter of 2009.  CBS, Valero  CBS, owner of the most-watched U.S. television network,\ntrimmed its dividend 81 percent in 2009 to 5 cents from 27\ncents. The New York-based broadcaster bought back stock and\nlifted the payout this year to 10 cents after trimming debt and\nas profit margins improved. Cash and near cash items have risen\nto $1.3 billion in the latest reported quarter from $239 million\nat the beginning of 2009.  Valero, the largest independent U.S. crude refiner, has\nmore than doubled its cash holdings since 2009 to $4.1 billion.\nThe San Antonio-based company cut its 15 cents dividend in 2010\nto 5 cents, where it remains today.  \u201cDistribution of dividends and other forms of income\nstreams will become even more important over the balance of this\ndecade in contribution of total return,\u201d Wirtz of Fifth Third\nsaid of companies in general. \u201cThat\u2019s very much on our mind.\u201d  Companies are earning almost nothing by sitting on cash at\na time when the stock market may be entering another lost decade\nsimilar to the 1970s, Fiduciary Trust\u2019s Mullaney said. They\nshould be a \u201cbit more generous with their payouts,\u201d he said.  Attracting Investors  The S&P 500 has dropped 17 percent in the five years ended\nyesterday. In the 1970s, it gave an average annual return of 2.4\npercent. The index has tumbled 11 percent this year, and is down\n18 percent from a 52-week closing high on April 29.  With an outlook of low growth for stocks over the next few\nyears, the time for higher dividends has arrived, said  Barry James , president of James Investment Research Inc. in Xenia,\nOhio, which manages $2.5 billion of securities. James favors\ncompanies like Indianapolis-based drugmaker  Eli Lilly & Co. (LLY) ,\nwhich has a dividend yield of about 5.3 percent.  A more aggressive dividend policy would help attract\ninvestors, who are migrating to fixed income, back to equities,\nMullaney said.  \u201cThat\u2019s one way companies can differentiate themselves as\nfar as being better total-return prospects if they do pay up\nmore in dividends during rough times,\u201d he said.  Share Buybacks  The S&P 500\u2019s dividend yield had risen to 2.31 percent as\nof yesterday, the most since November 2009, according to data\ncompiled by Bloomberg. The rate is higher than the yield on 10-\nyear Treasuries, only the second period since the 1950s in which\nthat was the case. Dividends topped U.S. government bonds in\n2008 and 2009, after Lehman Brothers Holdings Inc.\u2019s bankruptcy\nspurred the worst financial crisis since the Great Depression.  At least 60 companies in the S&P are likely to raise their\ndividends, including  Wal-Mart Stores Inc. (WMT) ,  Walt Disney Co. (DIS)  and\n Nike Inc. (NKE) , according to a Bloomberg analysis of seven criteria\nincluding company guidance, dividend history, regression\nanalysis and put-call parity.  Some companies including  CVS Caremark Corp. (CVS)  and Intel Corp.\nhave turned to share buybacks, giving each remaining share a\nbigger slice of earnings.  S&P 500 companies were paying out about 1.92 percent of\ntheir stock price in dividends at the end of the second quarter.\nWhen the value of share repurchases is added in, the stock yield\njumped to 4.88 percent, according to data from S&P. That\u2019s up\nfrom 3.4 percent in the first quarter of 2010 and down from\nabout 7.5 percent at the end of 2008.  Financial Companies  A lot of the dividend malaise can be blamed on financial\ncompanies, said Martin Adams of Wells Fargo. U.S. banks are\nholding cash as Europe grapples with the threat of sovereign\ndebt defaults and as they await clues on changes in financial\nregulations, she said.  Citigroup, the U.S. bank that received the largest\ntaxpayer-funded bailout, had a quarterly payout as high as $5.40\nin 2007, trimming it in 2008 before discontinuation in 2009. The\nNew York-based bank reinstated the dividend in June of this year\nat 1 cent a share, after a reverse split of common stock. The 1-\ncent quarterly payout produces an annualized dividend yield of\nabout 0.08 percent, among the lowest of S&P 500 companies that\npay a dividend, according to data compiled by Bloomberg.  JPMorgan Chase & Co. (JPM) , which had the largest cash holdings\namong S&P 500 companies with $414 billion, raised its quarterly\ndividend to 25 cents a share this year from 5 cents. The payout\nis less than the 38 cents the New York-based bank paid at the\nbeginning of 2009.  Technology Companies  Technology companies also have been hesitant to pay\ndividends because they\u2019re seen as a symbol of dwindling growth\nprospects, Martin Adams said. Google, which has increased its\ncash pile to $39 billion from $16 billion in 2008, and  Apple\nInc. (AAPL) , which sits on $28 billion of cash, don\u2019t pay dividends.  Dell Inc. (DELL) , which had the 13th-highest cash-to-assets ratio\nin the S&P 500 at midyear, also pays no dividend. The Round\nRock, Texas-based company has about $1 of cash for every $3 of\nassets on its balance sheet, according to Bloomberg data. That\u2019s\nmore than double the ratio of  Caterpillar Inc. (CAT) , which pays a\ndividend of 46 cents, and three times the ratio of Hewlett-\nPackard Co., which increased its dividend this year to 12 cents.  \u201cDividends are going to grow more and more important, and\nyou\u2019ll see more companies paying them and more investors focused\non them,\u201d James said. \u201cTen years ago the dividend yield was an\nafterthought.\u201d  Getting Louder  Microsoft Corp. (MSFT) , the largest holder of cash among non-\nfinancial S&P 500 companies at the end of June with $52.8\nbillion, boosted its quarterly dividend 25 percent to 20 cents a\nshare this year. Neil Herman, an analyst at Ticonderoga\nSecurities LLC, had urged the Redmond, Washington-based software\nmaker to double the dividend as a way to juice the share price.  Microsoft has a \u201cbalanced approach to allocating capital\u201d\nthat includes investment in its markets, acquisitions, share\nbuybacks and dividends, Chief Financial Officer Peter Klein told\nanalysts last month, according to the transcript of the meeting.  \u201cAs time goes on, investors will get increasingly louder\nthat they want the dividend, that they want some form of yield\noff their equity investment,\u201d Martin Adams said. Companies in the IT industry eclipsed financials in total\ndividend payouts for the first time in the third quarter. That\nmarks a change as IT companies generally have held onto cash so\nthey could reinvest it in research and development or make\nacquisitions. Now, facing pressure from yield-starved\nshareholders, firms such as Cisco Systems Inc. and Microsoft\nCorp. are choosing to disburse some of that cash by introducing\nor increasing dividends.  \u201cTech has excess cash and the ability to pay, whereas\nfinancials will take a long time to get back to where they\nwere,\u201d said  Howard Silverblatt , a senior index analyst at\nStandard & Poor\u2019s in New York.  IT stocks accounted for 9.2 percent of the almost $210\nbillion in  dividends  paid out as of Oct. 7 compared with 8.9\npercent for financial stocks, according to data compiled by S&P.\nIn 2007 before the recession, financial stocks made up 30\npercent of dividends and IT was 5.7 percent.  Companies in the IT sector are also maturing, which means\n cash flow  has risen and capital needs have fallen, said James\nMeyer, chief investment officer of investment management firm\nTower Bridge Advisors in West Conshohocken, Pennsylvania, whose\ntypical clients have $1 million or more in investable assets.  As of Oct. 6, 73 stocks in the  S&P 500 Index  paid dividends\nexceeding the average corporate bond yield of 3.6 percent, more\nthan at any time in at least 15 years, data compiled by\nBloomberg and Bank of America Corp. show. The average yield for\na stock in the IT industry that pays dividends is 1.9 percent\ncompared with 1.4 percent for a financial stock, based on data\nfrom S&P.  Reduced Payouts  Many financial companies reduced or eliminated their\npayouts because they accepted funds from the Troubled Asset\nRelief Program and are concerned about meeting certain capital\nrequirements before paying them again, said  Jeff Rubin , director\nof research at Westport, Connecticut-based Birinyi Associates, a\nmoney management and research firm.  Low fixed-income rates are also fueling the hunt for higher\nyields. The  two-year  Treasury note yield fell to a record low of\n0.3512 percent yesterday. The  10-year  security\u2019s yield dropped\nto 2.3552 percent on Oct. 6, the lowest level since January\n2009.  Clients are seeking dividend-paying stocks of high quality\nbecause they want income and companies \u201cthat they can go to\nsleep with at night,\u201d said  Hank Smith , chief investment officer\nof Radnor, Pennsylvania-based Haverford Trust Co., which manages\nabout $6 billion.  Haverford\u2019s Quality Growth Portfolio , which\nhas about $3 billion invested in dividend-paying companies,\nallocates 21 percent to technology stocks and 13 percent to\nfinancials.  Telecommunications Yields  Although more IT stocks are paying dividends, investors\nshould remember they still pay less than other industries, Rubin\nof Birinyi Associates said. Telecommunications and  utilities \noffer the highest yields of 6.1 percent and 4.5 percent,\nrespectively. And banks may start paying higher dividends again\nas soon as 2011, he said.  Helen Modly , a fee-only financial planner at Focus Wealth\nManagement in Middleburg, Virginia, said she\u2019s adding dividend\nexchange-traded funds to portfolios for the first time because\nof clients\u2019 requests for yield. She said she prefers  SPDR S&P\nDividend ETF , which has returned 13 percent this year, and\n Vanguard Dividend Appreciation ETF , which has returned 7.2\npercent, because they\u2019re less risky than owning individual\nstocks.  The SPDR S&P  fund , which yields 3.3 percent, has attracted\n$1.36 billion in net new inflows during the first eight months\nof the year, said  Jim Ross , global head of ETFs at State Street\nGlobal Advisors in Boston. The greatest allocation in the fund\nis to utilities, at 21 percent.  Tax Implications  In one of Vanguard Group Inc.\u2019s actively managed dividend\nfunds, the  Equity Income Fund , IT has increased to 8 percent\nfrom 2 percent of assets, said  Linda Wolohan , a spokeswoman for\nthe Valley Forge, Pennsylvania-based mutual fund company.  Last week Fidelity Investments changed the benchmark for\nits  Strategic Dividend and Income Fund  to the MSCI USA High\nDividend Yield Index from the Russell 3000 Value Index to\nincrease yield, said  Chris Sharpe , co-portfolio manager of the\nfund, who\u2019s based in Boston.  The move resulted in holdings in the financial industry\ndropping and IT increasing. As of June 30, the MSCI Index had\n3.5 percent in financials compared with 30 percent in the\n Russell Index  and IT had 5.8 percent compared with 5 percent in\nthe Russell Index, according to Fidelity.  For investors who opt to put money in dividend-paying\nstocks, there are tax implications to consider. Many dividends\nhave been taxed at a federal rate of 15 percent since 2003. Next\nyear, if Congress doesn\u2019t act, they may be taxed as ordinary\nincome, as high as 39.6 percent. Along with its first female members, the 80-year-old\nprivate club in Augusta, Georgia, has its initial corporate-\nhospitality pavilion and a newly hired woman executive to help\nchairman  Billy Payne  expand the business of golf\u2019s opening\nannual major championship. In the past seven years, Payne has\nforged new sponsorship and broadcast deals, licensed a Masters\nvideogame, and built $13 million of facilities for corporate\npartners and club members to entertain clients.  Augusta National\u2019s members include  Berkshire Hathaway Inc. (BRK\/A) \nChairman  Warren Buffett  and  Microsoft Inc. (MIC)  co-founder  Bill Gates . After decades of reflecting the genteel values of  Bobby Jones , Augusta National co-founder and golf\u2019s lone Grand Slam\nchampion, this Who\u2019s Who of American business is starting to run\nits signature tournament like a business.  \u201cThis is a natural progression of the recognition that the\nMasters is a commercial enterprise,\u201d said Casey Alexander, a\ngolf industry analyst and research director of New York-based\nGilford Securities.  \u201cThe world is not the same as when Mr.\nJones ran the Masters. Things that do not evolve die.\u201d  Jones and his successors charged patrons, as spectators\nare called, low prices and forbade sponsors\u2019 logos on the\ngrounds. The cost of a Masters ticket, or badge, for all four\nrounds starting  April 11  is still $250, compared with $400 for\nthis June\u2019s  U.S. Open . Corporate signs remain absent, and to 100\nmillion global TV viewers who watch the tournament with few\ncommercials, the Masters seems unchanged. Hidden from the\ncameras\u2019 view are more than 100,000 square feet of new\ncorporate-hospitality buildings.  Olympics Lesson  While referring often to Jones, the 65-year-old Payne\noperates as he did when leading another tradition-laden sports\nevent: the Olympics. The 1996 Games he oversaw in Atlanta were\nthe most sponsor-intensive in history.  The Masters\u2019 growth has trumped maintaining club tradition\nunder Payne, in leading an institution that\u2019s been slow to\nchange. Augusta National admitted its first black member in\n1990. The club staged the 2003 and 2004 Masters without\nsponsors, after the companies were pressed by a group of women\u2019s\norganizations to support ending all-male membership.  Payne\u2019s ability to leverage and accommodate sponsors may\nexplain why he admitted former Secretary of State Condoleezza Rice and philanthropist Darla Moore as the club\u2019s first female\nmembers, according to Marcia Chambers, who has studied Augusta\nNational and written about golf-club discrimination. (IBM) , whose four male\npredecessors were all club members. Casey Coffman, formerly\nof  Madison Square Garden Co., (MSG)  became the club\u2019s senior director\nof business affairs, Payne\u2019s lieutenant on Masters sponsorships\nand broadcast matters.  Payne\u2019s Team  Coffman, whom an Augusta National spokesman declined to\nmake available for an interview, was a senior vice president for\ncorporate strategy and development at MSG and, prior to that,\nchief operating officer of Hicks Sports Group, parent of\nbaseball\u2019s Texas Rangers and hockey\u2019s  Dallas Stars . Changing Times  Until Payne\u2019s arrival, lodging on the grounds, 10 white\nbuildings known at the club only as cabins, was for the use of\nmembers, with each bearing the names of distinguished ones, such\nas the Eisenhower Cabin.  In 2007, Augusta National began building  cabins  for\nsponsors. The first three, near the 10th hole, were for IBM,\nExxon Mobil and AT&T.  Their average size is about 3,300 square\nfeet, according to county tax assessor records, and they are\nvalued at a total of $1.4 million.  In 2009, the club added  facilities  off the first fairway\nfor two new international sponsors, Rolex and Mercedes-Benz, and\nits U.S. broadcaster since 1956,  CBS. (CBS)  They\u2019re valued at a total\nof $2.7 million by the tax assessor and encompass 16,500 square\nfeet.  Tough Ticket  The Masters, said sports business consultant Peter Stern,\nis \u201cthe Holy Grail of sponsorships, because of the prestige of\nthe tournament and the limited supply of Masters badges.\u201d  A\ncompany\u2019s ability to invite top customers to golf\u2019s most\nlegendary tournament -- which is also one of sport\u2019s toughest\ntickets -- is a feat, according to Stern, president of\nStrategic, a New York-based sponsorship advisory company.  For years, sponsors griped about their limited ability to\nentertain customers on Augusta National\u2019s grounds. As in, it certainly is\na consumer-tech wonder. And also as in, I wonder if the content\nproviders who may determine its success are prepared to take\nfull advantage of it?  \n The half-hour or so I spent playing with the iPad at its\nSan Francisco unveiling yesterday was much too short a time to\nevaluate it authoritatively. What I can say is that it\u2019s fast,\nbeautiful and loaded with potential.  \n The half-inch-thin iPad looks something like an iPod Touch\non steroids. While it uses the iPhone\/iPod Touch operating\nsystem -- meaning it runs just about all the 140,000 or so\napplications already written for those pocket-sized devices --\nyou can sense a little Mac DNA as well in the machined aluminum\nback. It feels solid and substantial in your hand -- and also,\nat about a pound and a half, is considerably heavier than a\ntypical e-book reader, one of its core functions.  \n Indeed, the iPad is about consumption of media in all its\nforms, from storing and viewing your photos to watching high-\ndefinition movies on the lovely 9.7-inch touch screen.  \n I was struck by its speed and responsiveness. In the photo\napplication, for instance, I could race through hundreds of\nphotos in a blur. Apps originally written for the iPhone, such\nas Electronic Arts Inc.\u2019s car-racing game Need for Speed Shift,\nlooked terrific when expanded to fit the iPad screen. They may\nlook better still once developers begin writing specifically to\nthe new dimensions and the capabilities of the custom Apple-\ndesigned chip that powers the unit.  \n Turning the Page  \n Books in the new iBooks application look much more paper-\nlike than they do on devices such as Amazon.com Inc.\u2019s Kindle or\nBarnes & Noble Inc.\u2019s Nook. Turning a page is so smoothly\nanimated that if you stop in the middle of the process, you see\nboth the content of the page being turned and that of the new\npage peeking out from underneath, just as if you were holding a\nphysical book.  \n While Apple is hardly known for the value pricing of its\nproducts, the iPad may be the exception. It will be available in\nsix models, with the least expensive -- including 16 gigabytes\nof flash-memory storage and Wi-Fi connectivity -- starting at\njust $499. It and two other Wi-Fi models with more memory go on\nsale in March.  \n 3G Connectivity  \n A month later, three more iPads will go on sale, adding\nconnectivity over AT&T Inc.\u2019s 3G wireless network in the U.S.\nThe top-of-the-line model, with both 3G and 64 GB storage, will\ncost $829. AT&T will offer no-contract data plans costing $14.99\nfor up to 250 megabytes per month, or $29.99 for an all-you-can-\neat plan.  \n At those prices, and if the iPad also fulfills Jobs\u2019s\nbattery-life promises -- 10 hours of heavy-duty use, and even\nlonger for lower-impact functions like listening to music --\nApple will have delivered a true achievement. Then the question\nwill be whether the publishing industry, which up to now hasn\u2019t\nbeen known for forward thinking, will do the same.  \n Will book publishers, for example, get to work producing\nadded-value interactive versions that include author interviews\nand DVD-style extras to take advantage of the iPad\u2019s multimedia\ncapabilities? Or will they be content to use Apple\u2019s new iBooks\nstore to sell the same plain-vanilla e-books they currently\nproduce, in hopes of simply lessening their dependence on\nAmazon.com?  \n Life Preserver  \n What about newspaper and magazine publishers? These, after\nall, are the same geniuses who decided to give away their\nproduct for free, then expressed shock when their audiences\nended up valuing it no more highly than they did. Will they now\nrecognize the life preserver Apple has thrown them and produce\nversions optimized for the new platform, with features that will\nexcite their customers and re-engage their advertisers?  \n To a larger extent than with most of Apple\u2019s other\nproducts, the iPad\u2019s fate is out of the company\u2019s hands. Without\ncompelling new content, it risks having no reason to be.  \n If that\u2019s the case, it may turn out that Apple\u2019s decision\nto bring iWork, its Mac productivity suite, to the iPad will be\ncrucial. The three iWork programs -- a word processor,\nspreadsheet and presentation software -- will sell for $9.99\neach. With them and a Bluetooth keyboard, or perhaps the new\ncombination keyboard-dock that Apple showed off this week, the\niPad becomes a sophisticated alternative to inexpensive netbook\ncomputers running Microsoft Corp.\u2019s Windows software.  \n While that might still sell a fair number of iPads, it\nwould signal failure in the ambitious goals Jobs has set out for\nthe device. To be truly \u201crevolutionary,\u201d which was the word he\nused to describe it, the iPad needs content as cool as it is.  \n (Rich Jaroslovsky is a Bloomberg News columnist. The\nopinions expressed are his own.)  \n Click on \u201cSend Comment\u201d in the sidebar display to send a\nletter to the editor.  \n To contact the writer of this column:\nRich Jaroslovsky in New York at \n rjaroslovsky@bloomberg.net .  \n          \n          \n\n\n  \n     \n       \n     \n           \n                            \n                     \n                     The Apple iPad tablet is pictured in this undated handout photograph provided to the media on Jan. 27, 2010. Under the legislation, copyright owners will have exclusive\ncontrol over how works are made available on the Internet.\nOwners will be able to apply \u201ctechnological protection\nmeasures,\u201d commonly known as digital locks, to prevent\nunauthorized access of copyrighted material.  \u201cCanadians will soon have modern copyright laws that\nprotect and help create jobs, promote innovation, and attract\nnew investment to Canada,\u201d Industry Minister Christian Paradis\nsaid in a statement. \u201cWe are confident that this bill will make\nCanada\u2019s copyright laws forward-looking and responsive in this\nfast-paced digital world.\u201d  The proposed law will implement treaties, signed by Canada\nin 1997, that establish rights and protections recommended by\nthe World Intellectual Property Organization.  The legislation is similar to earlier versions introduced\nby the governing Conservatives that were blocked by opposition\nparties. The bill may pass this time after Prime Minister\nStephen Harper\u2019s Conservatives won a majority of seats in the\nHouse of Commons in the May 2 general election. Seizure and liquidation of Righthaven\u2019s assets \u201ccould\nresult in the software being purchases by a competitor of\nRighthaven,\u201d according to the filing. (BRK\/A)  locked in a gain on its  Intel Corp. (INTC)  bet by selling its stake less than a year after making the investment, shunning the buy-and-hold strategy favored by Chairman  Warren Buffett .  Berkshire\u2019s Geico unit accumulated 11.5 million shares of  Santa Clara , California-based Intel in the second half of 2011 for an average price of about $22 each, according to National Association of Insurance Commissioners data compiled by Bloomberg. Buffett\u2019s firm sold the stake in the world\u2019s largest semiconductor maker for an average price of $27.25 this year through May 8, netting about $60 million in profit.  The holding period is short for Omaha, Nebraska-based Berkshire, which Buffett built through acquisitions and by accumulating the biggest stakes in companies such as American Express Co. The billionaire has been handing more responsibility over the $86.2 billion  stock portfolio  to his deputies, Ted Weschler and Todd Combs, as part of a  succession plan . The back- up stock pickers are responsible for Berkshire\u2019s smaller holdings, while Buffett manages larger stakes.  \u201cWarren has always had an opportunistic arbitrage appetite, and the new investors share some of that,\u201d Tom Russo, partner at Berkshire investor Gardner Russo & Gardner, said in a phone interview. The Intel trade reflects an \u201cold and more traditional\u201d style of value investing that relies on buying attractively priced stocks and selling when shares rise to a target, he said.  Intel Investment  Berkshire accumulated 5.66 million Intel shares in the days through Aug. 8, 2011, for an average price of $22.05, the NAIC data show. Buffett\u2019s company bought an additional 5.84 million shares through Oct. 20 that year for an average price of $21.46. At those prices, the investment would have generated a 25 percent gain, or $63.2 million in profit.  Liquidating the full stake by May 8 helped Berkshire avoid a 15 percent  slide  in the semiconductor maker\u2019s stock in the last four months. The company cut its third-quarter sales estimate on Sept. 7, forecasting $12.9 billion to $13.5 billion, down from a prior projection of $13.8 billion to $14.8 billion, citing declining demand. Intel said demand for chips used in business machines and orders in  emerging markets  are lower than expected, compounding concern that the PC market may not grow this year as consumers flock to smartphones and tablets. Intel doesn\u2019t discuss stock transactions by investors and declined to comment on revenue guidance and business conditions, said  Laura Anderson , a company spokeswoman. Berkshire declined to comment.  Some of Berkshire\u2019s largest holdings, including stakes in Coca-Cola Co. and  Wells Fargo & Co ., date back more than a decade. Buffett has criticized so-called high-frequency trading, in which computer algorithms exploit small variations in prices, as a tax on investors. In February, the billionaire wrote that holding large amounts of stock in  \u201cfirst-class businesses\u201d  over the long term will generate better returns than bonds, gold and other assets often deemed safe.  Hold Forever  \u201cWhen we own portions of outstanding businesses with outstanding managements, our favorite holding period is forever,\u201d he said in a  1989 letter  to shareholders after Berkshire began accumulating Coca-Cola shares. \u201cWe are just the opposite of those who hurry to sell and book profits when companies perform well but who tenaciously hang on to businesses that disappoint.\u201d  Not all Berkshire investments have been for the long haul. They sold when the value climbed to levels commensurate with other giant  oil companies , he said. Part of that strategy involved hiring Weschler, 51, and Combs, 41, to help oversee investments. When stakes are built across multiple days, the NAIC allows companies to consolidate acquisitions under the date of the last purchase. This big  crude-oil price manipulation lawsuit  is gibberish but that doesn't mean it's wrong. The gibberish might be inherent in how crude oil is priced. Which makes sense; I suppose that the harder it is to explain a market the easier it is to manipulate. The story is that some guys who trade oil derivatives on New York Mercantile Exchange are suing a bunch of physical oil traders including Royal Dutch Shell, BP, Statoil, Morgan Stanley, Trafigura, Phibro and Vitol, claiming that those traders manipulated the Dated Brent physical oil price benchmark set by Platts, the price reporting agency. The Platts benchmark, which affects those Nymex etc. derivatives prices,  is set  in a semi-subjective way, based on transactions executed, and bids and offers made, between 4 and 4:30 p.m. London time each day for crude delivery 10 to 25 days out. The claim is that this window was pretty thinly traded and subject to manipulation, and that Shell and BP and the rest took advantage of the opportunity to manipulate the benchmark price in ways that helped their derivatives positions, and hurt those of the plaintiffs.* It is tempting to start from the premise that the oil price benchmark is dumb and should have been less manipulable but let's resist that temptation. You know what is a great benchmark? The S&P 500. There are these 500 stocks, and they're a big chunk of the stock market, and they trade just a whole whole lot, and all the shares of each stock are perfectly identical, and all the trades are perfectly commensurable and instantly publicly reported, and you can add them up in a sensible market-cap-weighted way and then bang, you have an index. And I'm sure there are people with S&P 500 derivatives positions who are like \"ooh what I will do is I will trade those 500 stocks uneconomically to make money on my derivatives positions\" but this is not a thing people worry about for two reasons: Then there's oil.  This complaint  is full of the technicalities of renting ships to pick up oil cargoes. Reading it you occasionally get a whiff of salt air, though I guess if you're on a boat in the North Sea loading oil it probably smells more like a gas station? Anyway, the point is that there is oil under the ocean and somebody sticks a tube way under the ocean and the oil flows up the tube into a big tank in the middle of the ocean and every couple of days a big boat comes up to the tank and you move the oil onto the boat and the boat goes on its merry way to deliver the oil to someone who will turn it into gasoline and eventually light it on fire. There are important differences between this and a stock price, and they include the oil and the tanks and the boats. You don't need to rent a boat to buy shares of Microsoft. Your shares of Microsoft aren't waiting for you in a tank in the middle of the ocean. Stock trades are all very clean and computery and fungible. Nobody gets wet, or lit on fire. Physical oil trades are different, and the job of the oil price reporting agencies, like Platts, is to compress all this messy nautical activity into a nice simple number and call that number a price. That is just hard in a way that the S&P isn't. So you have to make decisions and those decisions will be necessarily arbitrary and someone will necessarily game them a bit. Platts reports its Dated Brent price as of 4:30 p.m. London time, and it takes into account transactions and bids and offers during a window, called the \"Platts window,\" that starts at Time X and ends at 4:30. Time X happens to be 4 p.m., meaning that trades at 3:59 p.m. are arbitrarily excluded, but I guess Time X has to be  some  time, meaning there's going to be  some  arbitrary exclusion.*** Similarly, Dated Brent takes into account trades in cargoes for delivery between 10 and Y days out. Y is 25, though it was 21 before 2012. This arbitrarily excludes cargoes for delivery Y+1 days out but what are you going to do, that is true for any Y. Did the big traders game those things a bit? I mean, I don't know, probably, right? If nothing else your derivative positions will affect your timing decisions: If you are short derivatives -- that is, you want Dated Brent prices to go down -- and you are also selling physical oil, you will try to sell that oil at 4:01 and will be willing to take a lower price. If you are long derivatives, you'll try to sell the oil at 3:59, to keep the sale out of the Platts window. If you're short, and you're looking to buy oil in a few weeks, you might pick a delivery day 26 days out. If you're long, you might go with 25. The complaint is one part making a lot of hay over those arbitrary distinctions,**** one part expressions of astonishment at sub-one-percent price moves that must have sounded better when they wrote them,***** one part complaining that the big oil companies would buy oil and rent tankers without telling everyone what they were up to, and like 10 parts quoting trader whining as evidence of manipulation. Here is a representative passage: That manipulation is: Shell and Statoil put some boats in the North Sea to move oil, which remember is their business. But they wouldn't tell everyone what they were doing with the boats. Also some traders were confused. Manipulation! I mean, maybe? But it's not evidence. I am no expert but there's nothing here that looks like a smoking gun. There are claims that the defendant oil companies did uneconomic physical transactions, presumably to make derivatives profits, but they're pretty vague.****** There are some accusations -- like one about \"the large physical cargo position accumulated by Shell as it manipulated prices lower\" -- that seem to defy economic sense,******* though again that doesn't mean they're wrong. It means either that they're wrong or that this market defies economic sense, which I guess is sort of the point of the lawsuit. More generally, you can't confuse the weakness of this case with wrongness. These guys don't seem to have any proof that anyone manipulated oil prices, but they have reason to hope that they'll happen upon some. The European Commission, the U.K. Serious Fraud Office, and the U.S. Federal Trade Commission are all looking into allegations of manipulation by some of the same oil traders here. Maybe they'll find something! These plaintiffs sure hope so; they say \"The foregoing investigations are expected to yield information from Defendants' internal records ( e.g. , instant messages, e-mails, telephone records, Brent Crude oil trading data, etc.) that provide further support for Plaintiffs' claims.\" At which point they'll be all, \"we told you so! Also, pay us.\"  Like the plaintiffs' lawyers here, I will look forward to the results of those investigations, and like them I will hope that those results include lots of dumb IM conversations to the effect of \"yo bro nice job manipulating oil prices thx!!!1!,\" because like them I more or less make my living off those dumb IM conversations. In that capacity I am saddened by the fact that this lawsuit contains no real proof of manipulation. I guess they are too. It's a disappointing lawsuit, but there's no reason why it wouldn't be. These plaintiffs were big market participants -- one of them was on Nymex's board of directors and executive committee -- but that doesn't seem to have gotten them any privileged understanding of how the market worked, or didn't work. After all, they were the guys on the other side of BP's and Shell's and Statoil's and so forth's allegedly manipulative trades. They were the ones who got fooled. It'd be too much to hope that they'd be the ones to provide the evidence of how they were fooled. * The derivatives here seem to be mostly short-term contracts for differences but also forwards and futures, though it's a bit vague. ** How important is #2 compared to #1? I don't know. It's sort of my  pet theory of Libor ; Libor had no #1 at all -- it is basically not a traded thing -- but arguably has some #2, in that there are big banks on both sides of Libor swaps. *** I suppose it could be, like, 4:31 p.m. the previous day, so every trade counts, but then your price starts looking a little stale. **** There are, for instance, claims that Platts used, say, a too-low price from a trade by one of the defendants during the 10-to-25-day window, but ignored another much higher price from an independent trade for delivery in 26 days or whatever. But that's just how the benchmark works! A trade in the window counts, a trade outside the window doesn't, even if someone after the fact claims that the outside-the-window trade was more economical. ***** \"Dated Brent, which priced off the Forties, fell an astounding $0.375 on that day  [September 24, 2012]  to minus $0.325 under North Sea Dated Strip. This was the largest one-day fall in the Forties crude prices since June 12, 2012,\" or in about three months, which, like, the biggest thing in three months happens roughly every three months. Also that's $0.375 on a price of over $100 a barrel so it's not  that  astounding. ****** For instance, BP sold a bunch of cargoes in the Platts window one time, and the plaintiffs say \"BP's conduct was not economically rational for a company that had a large number of unsold cargoes,\" since such a company would actually sell over a full trading day rather than selling all at once in the half-hour Platts window. Which sounds plausible, but you can't really hold BP to the standard of \"trade in a way that some other guys on Nymex think in hindsight would be most efficient,\" even if their argument for its efficiency seems pretty good. Also, even if they're right, and the BP trader came in and knew he had to sell 6 cargoes that day for good fundamental reasons but decided to do it inefficiently at the close because that would be better for his derivatives positions -- is that manipulation? If the trader was like \"I'm going to do uneconomic trades solely to help my derivatives,\" sure, manipulation; but if he was like \"I gotta do these trades anyway and they're going to move the price against me on physical, so I might as well at least do that in a way that helps my other-way derivatives positions,\" that seems kind of okay to me? I'm open to persuading on this point. ******* I mean. Last week, the EU opened an investigation into  Google Inc. \nfor allegedly discriminating against competing services in its\nsearch results. Last year, it hit Intel Corp. with a 1.06\nbillion euro ($1.33 billion) fine. Earlier this decade,\nMicrosoft Corp. got socked with a fine by the EU of almost 500\nmillion euros.  At this rate, the people at Facebook Inc. and Twitter Inc.\nmust be feeling distinctly nervous.  Can the EU really play policeman to the global technology\nindustry? Of course not.  There are two big problems. First, the EU\u2019s  trust-busters \ndon\u2019t seem to have much of a clue as to the difference between a\nmonopoly and a really, really successful company. Second, it\nlooks like sour grapes, at best, and at worst, revenge. Europe\u2019s\nregulators keep picking on the most accomplished U.S. companies\nwhile failing to do much to encourage competitors from their own\ncountries. Antitrust policy shouldn\u2019t be a way of leveling the\nindustrial score between continents.  Google is only the latest in a long line of U.S. technology\ncompanies to get into trouble with Europe\u2019s regulators. Intel,\nthe world\u2019s largest computer chipmaker, was fined for allegedly\nimpeding competition in the computer-chip market. In 2004,\nMicrosoft was fined after the EU ruled that it was taking\nadvantage of its dominant position in the computer-operating\nsystems used to run personal computers.  One More Probe  In July, the EU started an investigation into  International\nBusiness Machines Corp.  over whether it was abusing its position\nas the dominant supplier of mainframe computers. Back in 2001,\nthe EU blocked General Electric Co.\u2019s $47 billion purchase of\nHoneywell International Inc. on competition grounds, even though\nneither company was European. The list goes on and on.  The rights and wrongs of all those particular cases are for\nthe lawyers to argue over. But there are two big issues that\ndeserve a wider debate.  First, does the EU have a clue whether a technology company\nis dominating a market and abusing its power?  The one thing we have learned over the four decades during\nwhich the digital economy has emerged is that it has a natural\ntendency toward monopoly. We also know that these monopolies\noften are fleeting, with the time on top growing ever shorter.  IBM looked like a monopoly for a long time, before getting\nwhacked by Microsoft and a host of companies that could make\ncomputers cheaper. Then Microsoft looked all-powerful, until the\narrival of Google and the revival of  Apple Inc.  Google may seem\ndominant now, but Facebook is gaining ground fast. Will Google\nbe as strong in a decade\u2019s time as it is today? You would hardly\nwant to bet on it.  Two Forces  In fact, two forces are at work. In technology, there is a\nhuge first-mover advantage. The company that gets a product to\nthe market first takes a massive lead over everyone else. There\nalso is a network effect. People use Microsoft operating systems\nbecause everyone else does. It\u2019s the same for Facebook. We log\non that social network because it\u2019s where our friends are. A\nnatural consequence of both forces is very high market shares.  If a cement maker controlled 90 percent of the market, you\nmight well suspect there was something murky going on that\nsqueezed rivals out of the industry. But when a technology\ncompany has a 90 percent market share, that\u2019s often just the\nresult of it getting there first and everyone wanting to use the\nsame website, search engine or software program.  It doesn\u2019t necessarily follow that the technology company\nis abusing its position, or bullying rivals. It just happened to\ncome up with an idea first and be really good at what it does.  EU\u2019s Job  And, of course, the market is fluid. Something else gets\ninvented really quickly. Rival entrepreneurs are likely to crack\nthe monopoly, if that is what it is, far faster than any\nfunctionary in Brussels.  Next, is it really the job of the EU to police the global\ntechnology industry?  For starters, it looks like sour grapes for the EU to\nconstantly attack the most successful U.S. companies. Europe has\nbeen very bad at producing new, high-tech champions. The mobile\nphone manufacturer Nokia Oyj is the only real winner, and it\nlooks like it\u2019s on the retreat after falling behind in\nsmartphones.  Legal Assaults  Europeans probably wouldn\u2019t be too impressed if the U.S.\nkept launching legal assaults on, say, Europe\u2019s luxury\nautomobile manufacturers or its fashion houses. They can\u2019t be\nsurprised if Americans look at the way the EU attacks the most\ninnovative U.S. companies and start wondering if this isn\u2019t more\nabout hitting back at perceived American dominance of the\ntechnology industry than opening up the market. It sure looks\nthat way -- and that is hardly the image the EU should be\ncreating for itself.  If Google or Intel or IBM were true monopolists rather than\njust successful at what they do, then wouldn\u2019t it be better to\nhave a coordinated global approach to curbing their power? The\nEU can reshape the European electricity industry, or dairy\nindustry, or whatever, but it can\u2019t hope to re-shape the global\ntechnology industry. It makes itself look stupid and impotent by\ntrying.  The EU would be better off spending its time and money\nthinking about how Europe could start producing a few more\ntechnology giants, rather than attacking the American ones.  Maybe Google is a monopolist, and maybe it isn\u2019t. We need\nat least another decade before we can really start to reach a\njudgment on that. Even if it is, it\u2019s unlikely that Brussels is\nthe best place to start breaking it apart.  ( Matthew Lynn  is a Bloomberg News columnist and the author\nof \u201cBust,\u201d a forthcoming book on the Greek debt crisis. The\nopinions expressed are his own.) These technologies\nimprove productivity and facilitate better  living standards \nwhen they penetrate into societies. Among them, information\ntechnology (IT) has become the most dominant; IT has\nrevolutionized almost every aspect of our lives, public and\nprivate, by connecting individuals, institutions and\ngovernments in mutually dependent ways. With its ease of\nadoption, this interdependence has scaled rapidly, unlike any\nother technology in modern history. In Africa, for\nexample, despite decades of using electricity, no one can\nclaim that the continent has fully adopted it. The same\napplies to the aerospace and biochemical industries, among\nothers.  IT is good for developing countries \u2014 it empowers people\nand improves their lives. But, in many African countries, the\nsuccesses afforded by IT can backfire if it becomes a\ntoo-dominant focus. Take  Nigeria  for example: Despite decades\nof crude oil exploration, it cannot claim that it has\ndeveloped indigenous domain expertise in that industry. If the\nMNCs depart, Nigeria will cease to remain an oil-producing\nnation, as it lacks the local ability to explore, extract and\nsustain production. But in the IT industry, most Nigerian\nfirms are well-positioned for any challenge.  The success of IT in Africa has reached a level where it\nis being dangerously over-emphasized. From The  World Bank  to\nThe  African Union , everyone is talking about IT. IT events are\nvery common everywhere, not to mention the\nGoogle, Microsoft, and Blackberry platform-based competitions\nthat are being endlessly unleashed as these brands jockey for\nposition on the continent. The Nigerian government has created\na new ministry to focus solely on IT and related areas. And\nAfrican leaders are neglecting most non-IT technologies.\nAcross most African universities, the only funded and active\nlabs are the IT labs. University administrators are happy to\ntout how they equipped IT labs, though everything else is\nbroken. Agricultural engineering students are more focused on\nIT than on learning to build next-generation farm machinery.\nIt's a troubling pattern, as everyone wants to be seen as\nIT-savvy.  While IT can be applied to any field, the way  Africa  is\npromoting it sets a dangerous precedent. In my\ncontinent, \"information technology\" has become synonymous with\n\"technology\" itself. If you don't know IT, you're not a\ntechie. You can master  diesel engines  and polymer\ntechnology, but without expertise in IT, few believe that you\nbelong in the technology sector.  So, what's the danger? Everyone wants to be an IT guy. No\none remembers that we still need food. At the University of\nNairobi, I recently asked a group of agricultural science\nstudents about their plans upon graduation. Only one wanted to\nstay in agriculture; others are making apps for farmers.\nYes, they know more about mobile operating systems and mobile\npayments than they do about farming! The farms are now IT\nlabs. And while you can simulate farming on tablets, you can't\neat the virtual fruit.  Pick up a typical newspaper on the continent, and you'll\nfind that the technology column has been changed to an IT\ncolumn. Newspapers write about Google, Blackberry, Facebook\nand Apple in the technology section, but non-IT companies \u2014\nthough they're technology firms \u2014 are rarely reported on. Tech\njournalism is now IT journalism. Even the governments have\nconfused technology policy with IT policy.  I firmly believe that IT has helped Africa, and that it\nhas a role to play as the continent advances. But, there needs\nto be a balance. The continent needs techies in\nmining, geology, semiconductors, agriculture, chemicals, and\nother areas besides IT, and government must ensure that IT\ndoes not create a situation that will destroy the continent's\ncapacity to feed her citizens and compete in the future.","path":".\/2008_2012_msft_bloomberg_news\/information-technology-s-dangerous-trend-in-africa.txt"},{"id":45450174,"title":"Bershidsky on Europe: Berslusconi Party Splits","released_at":"<date>October 2 2013<\/date> <time>08:50:27<\/time>","content":"Here's today's look at some of the top stories on markets and politics in Europe: Italian government may  survive  confidence vote Enrico Letta's coalition may survive the Oct. 2 confidence vote in parliament, forced by Silvio Berlusconi. The former prime minister's party appears to be splitting: Angelino Alfano, until recently one of Berlusconi's most powerful allies, who served as Letta's deputy in the coalition cabinet, insists that the party must vote in favor of the government. Another defector, Senator Carlo Giovanardi, said about 40 of his colleagues in the senate were prepared to switch sides, more than enough to carry the day for Letta. Alfano's last-minute talks with Berlusconi on Oct. 1 were fruitless, and the former premier reaffirmed his commitment to bringing down the government. He may not have the votes: Many of his supporters are tired of government crises and unsure of what they are supposed to be fighting for. The markets are tired, too: yields on Italian government debt barely edged up and then dropped back to last week's levels, reflecting either growing investor indifference or a belief that the cabinet will survive. Italian shares, too, bounced back when the split in Berlusconi's party became obvious. Il Cavaliere's star may finally be setting. Google  closer  to EU antitrust settlement EU Competition Commissioner Joaquin Almunia said Google has come up with new proposals to stave off antitrust procedures similar to those that led to Miscrosoft paying a $794 million fine in 2004. The U.S. company offered to make rival services' offerings more prominent in search results and allow competitors to bid for extra exposure. It is not clear whether this will satisfy complainants, who include Microsoft, TripAdvisor, Expedia and other household names as well as smaller European companies. This time, however, Almunia does not want to subject the Google proposals to a full-scale market test because he says he already knows the sides' positions. Almunia, who is due to leave his post next year, wants a settlement by the spring. Google may have given him just enough to put the matter to rest. Ousted Intesa chief to get $6 million  parachute Another golden parachute scandal is brewing in Europe. The Italian banking group Intesa Sanpaolo said it would not fire Enrico Cucchiani, who has been forced to step down as chief executive, for another six months. He would receive the same salary as he made in his role as CEO while having no responsibilities at the bank. That comes to $1.2 million for the six months. The total value of Cucchiani's severance package is about $6 million, though he only worked at the bank for 21 months before his work displeased large shareholders. Staying on until April 2014, allows the 63-year-old to receive pension benefits specified in his contract \u2013 and possibly to collect the maximum pension from the Italian government. That would go beyond Intesa's charitable desire to be fair to a former top manager. European companies ought to be mindful of a recent Swiss referendum that banned golden parachutes altogether: If they do not curb their generosity, an indignant public may force similar restrictions on them. ECB vice president  says  euro area banks are undervalued   Just as the European Central Bank prepared to start a big asset review of the euro area's banking system, the man responsible for the exercise, ECB Vice President Vitor Constancio, said European banks were undervalued compared to their U.S. counterparts. According to Constancio, the big banks in the euro area had, on average, better capital ratios than big U.S. banks. The ECB official appeared to be sending a signal to bankers that the ECB was their ally: It is important for the central bank to establish a working relationship with them as it prepares to start supervising them a year from now. Constancio, however, was only talking about the large banks, which have been the focus of post-crisis restructuring efforts. He must be aware that smaller institutions will require much attention from the regulator: It is because of them that the massive asset review is necessary in the first place. French unemployment  drop  caused by computer bug In August, the French government announced triumphantly that the number of unemployed had dropped by 50,000 in the month. Even as the announcement went out, however, Labor Minister Michel Sapin was worried that the number was somehow too big. He ordered Pole Emploi, the state employment service, to investigate and sure enough, the sudden employment boom turned out to be the result of a computer bug at mobile operator SFR that prevented 170,000 unemployed from receiving text messages reminding them to renew their claims. Because of that, between 32,000 and 41,000 people failed to renew on time and were not reflected in the statistics. That means unemployment was down in August, but only slightly. It's OK to be optimistic, but much about the current European recovery needs to pass the too-good-to-be-true test. (Leonid Bershidsky, an editor and novelist, is a Bloomberg View contributor. Anyone who wants or needs a tablet isn\u2019t likely to be\nsatisfied with the Nook Color for too long. The more you use it,\nthe more apparent its functionality and performance issues\nbecome. (AMZN) \u2019s servers to wage cyber attacks such as\nthe one that crippled  Sony Corp. (6758) \u2019s PlayStation Network and led\nto the second-largest online data breach in U.S. history.  A hacker used Amazon\u2019s Elastic Computer Cloud, or EC2,\nservice to attack Sony\u2019s online entertainment systems last\nmonth, a person with knowledge of the matter said May 13. The\nintruder, who used a bogus name to set up an account that\u2019s now\ndisabled, didn\u2019t hack into Amazon\u2019s servers, the person said.  The incident helps illustrate the dilemma facing Chief\nExecutive Officer  Jeff Bezos : Amazon\u2019s cloud-computing service\nis as cheap and convenient for hackers as it is for customers\nranging from  Netflix Inc. (NFLX)  to  Eli Lilly & Co. (LLY)  Last month\u2019s attack\non Sony compromised more than 100 million customer accounts, the\nlargest data breach in the U.S. since intruders stole credit and\ndebit card numbers from Heartland Payment Systems in 2009.  \u201cAnyone can go get an Amazon account and use it\nanonymously,\u201d said Pete Malcolm, chief executive officer of\nAbiquo Inc., a  Redwood City , California-based company that helps\ncustomers manage data internally and through cloud computing.\n\u201cIf they have computers in their back bedroom they are much\neasier to trace than if they are on Amazon\u2019s Web Services.\u201d  Network Resumption  Sony on May 14 partially restarted its PlayStation Network\nand Qriocity services, which had been shut since April 20\nbecause of the intrusion. The company has hired three security\nfirms to investigate and is working with the law enforcement\nofficials. Sony has faced a backlash from regulators and\ncustomers over the time it took to warn customers that their\ndata may have been stolen.  Drew Herdener, a spokesman for Seattle-based Amazon, the\nworld\u2019s largest online retailer, declined to comment. Amazon\ndidn\u2019t respond to a request to speak with Bezos. Patrick Seybold, a U.S. spokesman for Tokyo-based Sony, declined to\ncomment beyond public statements made on the matter.  The  Federal Bureau of Investigation  will likely subpoena\nAmazon or seek a search warrant to access the history of\ntransactions, trace who had access to the specific Internet\naddress at the time and get details on payment data, said E.J.\nHilbert, president of the security company Online Intelligence\nand a former FBI cyber-crime investigator.  FBI Probe  FBI Special Agent Darrell Foxworth, a spokesman for the\nagency\u2019s  San Diego  office, said he couldn\u2019t comment on whether\nthe bureau served Amazon with a search warrant or subpoena and\nthat investigators are following up \u201ceach and every lead.\u201d\nAmazon\u2019s Herdener declined to say whether his employer had been\nsubpoenaed or served with a search warrant.  Amazon Web Services leases computing space to companies so\nthey don\u2019t have to buy their own servers to store data and\nhandle a surge in visitors.  Prices for EC2 range from 3 cents to $2.48 an hour for\nusers on the east coast of the U.S., according to its website.\nSigning up to the service requires a name, e-mail address,\npassword, phone number, billing address and credit card\ninformation. Users get an automated call from Amazon and are\nasked to dial in a four-digit verification code to complete the\nregistration process.  That\u2019s not enough to scare off hackers seeking to conduct\nattacks anonymously, and Amazon doesn\u2019t have the means to detect\nillegal uses of its servers, Abiquo\u2019s Malcolm said.  Good Versus Bad  \u201cRealistically, Amazon can\u2019t do anything to prevent it,\u201d\nMalcolm said. \u201cThere is no way of telling who\u2019s a good guy and\nwho\u2019s a bad guy.\u201d  Web Services generated about $500 million in revenue for\nAmazon in the past year, according to estimates at  Barclays\nCapital . That\u2019s about 1.5 percent of 2010 sales at Amazon, which\ndoesn\u2019t disclose sales from the unit.  Amazon fell $10.05, or 5 percent, to $192.51 at 4 p.m. New\nYork time on the Nasdaq Stock Market. Sony was little changed\ntoday in Tokyo trading.  As companies from Amazon to  Microsoft Corp. (MSFT)  build server\nfarms worldwide, the services can help hackers hide their\ntracks, said Hilbert.  Cloud services are also attractive for hackers because the\nuse of multiple servers can facilitate tasks such as cracking\npasswords, said Ray Valdes, an analyst at Gartner Inc. Amazon\ncould improve measures to weed out bogus accounts, he said.  Hijacked Servers  The use of hijacked or rented servers to launch attacks is\ntypical for sophisticated hackers, according to Hilbert. Chinese\nhackers used the servers of a major U.S. Internet service\nprovider in 2008 to break into a government agency and several\ndefense contractors, according to a secret Nov. 3, 2008, cable\nexposed by Wikileaks.  The hackers \u201cused at least three separate systems at the\nunnamed ISP in multiple network intrusions and have exfiltrated\ndata via these systems,\u201d according to the cable.  In some cases, hackers hide their tracks beneath several\nlayers of proxy servers that can span the globe. A recent attack\nagainst computers in  South Korea  was controlled from servers in\nmore than 20 different countries, according to Georg Wicherski,\na security analyst at  Santa Clara , California-based  McAfee Inc. (MFE) \nThe identity of the offenders is unknown, he said.  Rethinking Cloud  Malicious attacks  in the U.S. are on the rise. They made up\n31 percent of data breaches in 2010, up from 24 percent a year\nearlier, with each event costing U.S. businesses an average of\n$7.2 million, according to a March report by the Ponemon\nInstitute. The study found that about 85 percent of all U.S.\ncompanies have experienced one or more attacks.  Last month\u2019s incursion was \u201cvery carefully planned, very\nprofessional, highly sophisticated criminal cyber attack,\u201d Sony\nhas said. To contact the reporters on this story:\n Mark Lee  in  Hong Kong  at \n wlee37@bloomberg.net ;\nDiana ben-Aaron in Helsinki at \n dbenaaron1@bloomberg.net   To contact the editors responsible for this story:\nYoung-Sam Cho at   ycho2@bloomberg.net ;\nKenneth Wong at   kwong11@bloomberg.net","path":".\/2008_2012_msft_bloomberg_news\/apple-no-1-smartphone-vendor-in-second-quarter-researcher-says.txt"},{"id":54090916,"title":"When Organizational Memory Stands in the Way","released_at":"<date>March 11 2013<\/date> <time>16:00:20<\/time>","content":"Your company's organizational memory might be holding it back. Consider the following parable: Two monks \u2014 one old and one young \u2014 were walking to a village far from their monastery. Along the way they saw a beautiful, young woman waiting at the edge of a stream, too afraid to cross. The young monk reminded himself of his vow not to touch women and continued walking. But to his amazement, the elder monk sped right past him while carrying the young woman, safely across the stream, on his back!  When the old monk put her down on the other side of the stream, she thanked him with a respectful bow. The old monk, in turn, gave her a bright smile, and continued walking. The young monk considered and reconsidered the old monk's action back at the stream. He could not stop churning. His thoughts grew angrier and angrier. Finally, hours later, he ended up shouting at the old monk, \"You broke your sacred vows! You are not supposed to touch a woman! How can you forgive yourself? You should not be allowed back in the monastery!\" Surprised at his outburst, the old monk replied calmly, \"I dropped her hours ago. Why are you still carrying her?\" Like the young monk, many organizations carry a heavy burden, and for far too long. The result \u2014 obsolete policies and practices, outdated assumptions and mind-sets, and underperforming products and services. This organizational memory creates biases that get embedded in planning processes, performance evaluation systems, organizational structures and human resource policies. This becomes a big burden when non-linear shifts occur. Examples of the burden of such organizational memory include Blackberry \u2014 it could not forget about the physical keyboard when the world had moved on to touch screens, and Microsoft \u2014 it could not forget about the desktop as the key computing device when the world had moved on to mobile devices on the one hand and cloud-based services on the other. How can established organizations be more like the elder monk \u2014 and transcend the clutches of the burden of organizational memory when there is a need to respond to non-linear shifts?  Let us look at how  Infosys succeeded in this transformation . Infosys initially provided only IT services. However, they noticed that their most demanding clients were frustrated by having to work simultaneously with multiple service firms, each lacking full accountability. They realized that in this frustration lay the seeds of a non-linear shift \u2014 and that they would either have to respond quickly and master the shift or become victims of it. They perceived the need for an organization that would provide management consulting services, redesign operations, and write specifications for new IT systems; then develop, test, install and maintain it; perhaps even accept responsibility for executing routine client operations such as transaction processing.  They also realized that the current organizational memory would be a burden for this new reality. So they created a parallel world with different people and distinct processes. \nThey focused on three key areas: All these changes helped Infosys overcome the burden of the organizational memory of a very successful IT services company, while retaining all of the essential elements that were responsible for its success. As a result of this successful transformation, Infosys grew 25-fold over the decade from 2000 to 2010 \u2014 from $200 million to $5 billion. If you too sense big non-linear shifts in your markets, remember that \"organizational forgetting\" may be essential to meeting the challenges successfully.","path":".\/2008_2012_msft_bloomberg_news\/when-organizational-memory-stands-in-the-way.txt"},{"id":5299282,"title":"Congress Gets Failing Marks on Economy","released_at":"<date>December 16 2011<\/date> <time>19:38:36<\/time>","content":"Congress is ending what may be its\nleast productive year on record after government shutdown\nthreats, the collapse of debt-reduction talks and little action\nto fix the worst  U.S. economy  since the Great Depression.
