Jamie Montgomery, 53, will keep managing the firm\u2019s\nexisting $50 million in venture-capital investments, such as\nVantage Media and ServiceMesh. He will also be advising Signal\nHill on the establishment of its operations on the West Coast.\nHis brother Michael Montgomery, 58, will step back from his day-\nto-day responsibilities as president of the company and complete\nthe active mandates with clients.  Signal Hill  Signal Hill , which advises on raising capital and focuses\non high-growth companies, opened offices last year in Boston and\nBangalore,  India .  \u201cSan Francisco was the last missing piece of our puzzle in\nthe U.S.,\u201d Scott Wieler, Signal Hill\u2019s chairman and founder,\nsaid in a telephone interview. \u201cTechnology mergers and\nacquisition is as frothy as we have seen in a long time.\u201d  In March, Signal Hill advised Coyote Point Systems Inc. on\nits sale to Fortinet Inc. It also advised Arbitron Inc. last\nyear in its $1.2 billion sale to Nielsen Holdings NV, and\nIncentive Targeting Inc. when it was sold to Google Inc. in\nNovember.  So far this year, $69.6 billion in technology and Internet\ndeals have been announced, according to data compiled by\nBloomberg, up 72 percent from $40.44 billion a year earlier.  \u201cWe are in the sweet spot, as the top-10 technology\ncompanies are continuing to add to their portfolio at an\naccelerating rate,\u201d Wieler said.  To contact the reporter on this story:\nSerena Saitto in  New York  at \n ssaitto@bloomberg.net   To contact the editor responsible for this story:\nJeffrey McCracken at \n jmccracken3@bloomberg.net","path":".\/2008_2012_msft_bloomberg_news\/ontgomery-sells-san-francisco-office-as-it-unwinds-m-a-advisory.txt"},{"id":60989092,"title":"Trading Pennies Into $7 Billion Drives High-Frequency\u2019s Cowboys","released_at":"<date>October 6 2010<\/date> <time>04:01:00<\/time>","content":"A cowboy-hat-wearing robot with\n\u201cSell\u201d emblazoned across its chest adorns a wall-length mural\nin the lounge of RGM Advisors LLC in Austin,  Texas . Another\nrobot, with \u201cBuy\u201d on it, wobbles toward a green  Wall Street \nsign as two machines tote spark-emitting high-speed cables.  \u201cWe explained to a local artist that we wanted a mural\nthat represented our business, and he came up with the design,\u201d\nRGM Chief Executive Officer Richard Gorelick says in an airy\n16th-floor office that calls to mind a Scandinavian design firm\nrather than a company that trades hundreds of millions of shares\na day, Bloomberg Markets magazine reports in its November issue.  As a cue to RGM\u2019s staff of 120 mainly scientists, software\ndevelopers and information technology graduates that their job\nis to eke out a fraction of a cent profit on each of those\ntrades, five stone urns in the lobby are stuffed with pennies.  \u201cIt\u2019s a lot easier for us to teach really smart scientists\nabout markets and trading than to teach traders about\nprogramming,\u201d Gorelick, 39, says.  High-frequency firms such as Gorelick\u2019s are the rebellious\nnew force in U.S. securities markets. Armed with algorithms and\ncomputers that shave milliseconds off the speed of a trade,\nprogrammers, math whizzes and even some former dot\u00adcommers like\nGorelick have set up shop from Austin to  Chicago  to Red Bank,  New Jersey . These firms don\u2019t analyze a company\u2019s value or bet\non financial news. They use computers to scour public and\nprivate markets for deviations from historical prices and leap\non discrepancies, rather than betting on the value of a company,\ncurrency or commodity.  All About Speed  \u201cSpeed is now the defining characteristic of the market,\u201d\nsays  Adam Sussman , the New York-based director of research at\n Tabb Group LLC , who has researched the role of high-frequency\nfirms in financial markets.  Fast-paced trading played a role in the 10-minute U.S.\nstock market crash on May 6. The automatic execution of a sale\nof futures contracts valued at about $4.1 billion helped trigger\nthe plunge, according to an Oct. 1 report by the U.S.  Securities\nand Exchange Commission  and Commodity Futures Trading\nCommission. The initial sales of the contracts led to a burst of\ntrading among high-frequency firms, the report said.  Some high-frequency companies set themselves up as market\nmakers, offering prices to buy and sell shares. Others exist\nspecifically to profit from mismatches among stocks.  \u2018Quick Killing\u2019  Nanex LLC  says some activities are underhanded. Researchers\nat the Winnetka, Illinois, data firm have found instances in\nwhich thousands of quotes a second in a particular stock are\nfired and canceled immediately, overwhelming trading systems.\nThis process has added the term \u201cquote stuffing\u201d to the\nlexicon.  \u201cHigh-frequency traders are not interested in the\nfundamental worth of a company,\u201d says George Feiger, CEO of\n Contango Capital Advisors Inc. , a San Francisco money management\nfirm with $2\u00a0billion in assets. \u201cThey are only interested in\nmaking a quick killing and moving on.\u201d  Regulators are fumbling with how to rein in the HFT crowd\nand its computers that generate more than half of all U.S. stock\ntrades each day. The SEC is looking into establishing and then\nenforcing a minimum time period, such as 50 milliseconds, that a\nquote to buy or sell a stock would have to remain valid,\naccording to firms who have met with the SEC. Such a move could\nlimit the number of cancellations. The SEC also is considering\nwhether to require high-frequency firms to remain in a market,\nrather than pulling out when times get tough, to maintain a\nsupply of stock.  \u2018Wild Wild West\u2019  Democratic Senator Ted Kaufman of  Delaware  wants the SEC to\nlimit the number of quote cancellations. The SEC has proposed\nrules to monitor firms that trade more than 2 million shares a\nday.  Such changes assume that enforcers are as agile as high-\nfrequency firms.  \u201cTechnological advances have outstripped our ability to\nregulate them,\u201d says Andrew Lo, director of  Massachusetts\nInstitute of Technology\u2019s  Laboratory for Financial Engineering\nand chief scientific officer of quantitative-analysis hedge fund\nAlphaSimplex Group LLC. \u201cIt\u2019s like the Wild Wild West.\u201d  The burgeoning HFT industry has spawned legions of jeans-\nwearing techies who arm their machines to outwit rivals.\nProgrammers write formulas to sniff out the buy and sell\nintentions of mutual funds and jump in ahead of them in a\npractice called gaming. Institutional investors use strategies\nsuch as iceberging: breaking a single large order into chunks,\nand leaving just a small order, or the tip, visible. The gamers,\nalso called sharks, unleash small buy and sell orders to uncover\nthe hidden ones.  May 6  The event that triggered the intense interest of regulators\nwas the crash on May 6. The Dow Jones Industrial Average --\nalready down about 350 points on concern that  Greece  would\ndefault on its 210 billion euro ($290 billion) debt -- nose-\ndived 600 points in less than 10 minutes. Just as quickly, it\nrebounded to finish the day 347 points lower. The plunge\ntemporarily erased $862 billion from U.S. equities in the Dow\u2019s\nbiggest-ever intraday drop.  In a May 18 report, the SEC and  CFTC  said they\u2019re focusing\non six areas -- including whether declines in index futures and\nexchange traded funds may have created waves of share sales.  In the Oct. 1 report, the regulators said an unidentified\nfirm set off the plunge by selling 75,000 contracts on the\nStandard & Poor\u2019s 500 Index known as E-mini futures. Two people\nwith knowledge of the findings identified the firm as Waddell &\nReed Financial Inc., an Overland Park, Kansas-based mutual-fund\ncompany. The automated sales of the contracts created a flurry\nof trading among HFT firms, according to the report.  \u2018Hot Potato\u2019  \u201cHFTs began to quickly buy and then resell contracts to\neach other, generating a \u2018hot-potato\u2019 volume effect as the same\npositions were rapidly passed back and forth,\u201d according to the\nreport. Between 2:45:13 and 2:45:27, \u201cHFTs traded more than\n27,000 contracts, which accounted for about 49 percent of the\ntotal trading volume, while buying only about 200 additional\ncontracts,\u201d the report says.  The report is unlikely to end the debate over the role of\nhigh-frequency firms. \u201cIf there is a time advantage, there is a\nmonetary advantage,\u201d says Nanex founder Eric Scott Hunsader.  In a run-up to the crash, some high-frequency traders\nsubmitted and then canceled tens of thousands of buy and sell\norders a second, overloading trading systems, Hunsader says. The\nSEC hasn\u2019t accused any firm of quote stuffing and no firm has\nowned up to unleashing their computers on the day of the crash.  Quote Stuffing  Quote stuffing hasn\u2019t gone away. On an average day, 15 to\n20 stocks get more than 5,000 quotes a second that never turn\ninto a trade, Hunsader says.  \u201cIf the number of quote-stuffing incidences continues, one\nor more systems will get saturated,\u201d he says.  After May 6, the SEC and CFTC sought advice from traders,\ninvestors, academics, exchange officials and HFT executives on\nwhat to do.  \u201cThis is truly the brave new world we are trying to\nregulate,\u201d CFTC Commissioner Scott O\u2019Malia says.  SEC Chairman  Mary Schapiro  said in a September speech to\nthe  Economic Club of New York  that the agency may impose rules\non high-frequency traders.  During the past decade, the SEC moved to lower trading\ncosts and create competition between exchanges. Some SEC\nchanges, such as electronic communications networks, automated\ncomputer trading systems that match buyers and sellers, have\nvirtually eliminated traditional market makers -- the people who\nused to stand on the floors of exchanges and offer buy and sell\nprices for a stock. That has left market-making activity\ndominated by HFT firms with few rules to govern them.  Boost the Economy  \u201cThe function of the capital markets is to facilitate\ncapital formation and boost the overall economy, not to assure\nthe profitability of any group of market professionals,\u201d says\nDaniel Gray, assistant director of the SEC\u2019s division of trading\nand markets.  Proponents of high-frequency trading -- and the companies\nthemselves -- say they lubricate the gears of capitalism, making\nmarkets more efficient and slashing trading costs.  \u201cThe equity market has created an intense and healthy\ncompetition in providing liquidity,\u201d says Liam Connell, CEO of\n Allston Trading LLC,  a Chicago high-frequency firm that deals in\noptions, futures contracts and foreign exchange. \u201cWe\u2019re ripping\neach other\u2019s throats for fractions of a penny.\u201d  $7.2 Billion Profit  They deny quote stuffing. In fact, most HFT firms say they\nslowed trading -- or shut down altogether -- as May 6 unfolded\nbecause they were unsure of whether the quotes they were seeing\nwere accurate. Now some are balking at any requirement that\nwould force them to remain in the market during such times.  For all of their impact, there aren\u2019t all that many high-\nfrequency traders. HFT firms, some with just a handful of\nemployees, make up about 2 percent of the 20,000 hedge funds,\nbrokers and mutual funds active in U.S. equities, according to\nTabb Group.  Last year, they accounted for 60 percent of the daily U.S.\nstock market volume of 9.8 billion shares and about 40 percent\nof futures and foreign-exchange trading, according to Tabb.\nTheir trading profit: about $7.2 billion in 2009, Tabb says. By\ncontrast, just one investment bank,  Goldman Sachs Group Inc .,\nmade $13.3 billion in net profit last year. Goldman traders\ngenerated more than $100 million on 17 separate days during this\nyear\u2019s second quarter.  Warp-Speed Trading  This warp-speed universe is eons away from the days when\ntraders in colorful jackets convened at the premier trading\nmarketplace, the  New York  Stock Exchange. Today, the Big Board\nis one of 11 U.S. exchanges that display quotes publicly. Two\nmore are coming this month. More than 30 dark pools, which allow\nbuyers and sellers to operate without showing their actions to\nothers, and 200-plus venues operated by banks and brokerages\nmatch buyers and sellers privately.  Five years ago, almost 80 percent of the shares of NYSE\ncompanies were traded on that exchange. Today, the NYSE controls\n26 percent of the shares traded on its trading platforms.\n(Bloomberg LP, the parent of Bloomberg News, owns Bloomberg\nTradebook, an ECN that operates a dark pool.)  On a broiling August afternoon in Austin, about 30 T-shirt-\nand jeans-wearing RGM engineers 1,700 miles (2,700 kilometers)\naway from Wall Street watch a map of network traffic flowing\nacross major markets on a 52-inch (132-centimeter) screen. Long\nequations scribbled in red and blue markers decorate glass\noffice dividers. Outside, shops sell \u201cKeep Austin Weird\u201d\nsouvenirs.  Algorithmic Models  RGM\u2019s researchers build models for all of the stocks,\nfutures and options the company trades to continuously determine\na fair price. To value oil giant  Chevron Corp ., a high-frequency\nprogram might monitor not only Chevron\u2019s stock price but compare\nit with crude oil, a basket of oil company shares and  interest\nrates . Computers would monitor bid and ask spreads, the gap\nbetween the price that a buyer wants to receive and what a\nseller will pay, across all trading venues to gauge demand.  \u201cHigh-frequency firms work to tighten the spreads,\u201d\nGorelick says. \u201cIf the price has moved away from fair value,\ntraders try to push it back.\u201d That means buying or selling,\ndepending on the direction of the move.  Another strategy, called pairs trading, is based on the\nidea that prices of related stocks should be correlated. Soda\nrivals  Coca-Cola Co . and PepsiCo Inc. tend to fluctuate around\nthe same news. When that relationship breaks down so that the\nprice of one stock increases while the other falls, it means\nopportunities to profit.  Dot-Com Heritage  \u201cThink of prices of different correlated instruments as\nbeing held by rubber bands,\u201d Gorelick says. \u201cOnce these rubber\nbands get stretched, that\u2019s how we make our money.\u201d  High-frequency traders didn\u2019t have their HFT acronym when\nGorelick started  RGM  in 2001 with Robbie Robinette and Mark\nMelton, the R and M of the firm.  Gorelick, who has a law degree from  Georgetown University \nin Washington, had been general counsel and later chief strategy\nofficer for message board search and shopping-comparison website\nDeja.com Inc. After the technology bubble burst in 2000,\nDeja.com shelved its IPO plans and sold its shopping service to  EBay Inc . and its newsgroup search archives to  Google Inc .  \u201cNot one of us was a trader,\u201d Gorelick says. He met\nRobinette, a software developer, at Deja.com; Melton, who\nspecialized in data mining and pattern recognition, was\nRobinette\u2019s cycling buddy.  The three started a company to apply mathematical models to\ndetect trading patterns. \u201cWe liked a business where solving\ndifficult technical problems led very directly to business\nsuccess,\u201d Gorelick says.  \u2018Three Guys From Texas\u2019  The trio thought they could beat technical traders, who\nrely on charts to identify historical price patterns. They pored\nover trading books and wrote their first program. Gorelick\nheaded to Wall Street to meet brokers. People didn\u2019t understand\nwhat they were doing, he recalls.  \u201cWe were three guys from Texas, with no trading experience\nand little money,\u201d Gorelick says over a Cobb salad lunch. \u201cIt\nprobably looked pretty flaky.\u201d  Finally, a New York day-trading firm let them open an\naccount. The partners loaded their program, which looked at\nstatistical relationships among stocks, on a Compaq computer.  \u201cOur first day, we did four trades and made $17,\u201d\nGorelick says. \u201cOur second day, we lost a few hundred dollars\nand had to make adjustments.\u201d By the spring of 2002, their\nstrategy was working well enough to allow them to rent offices\nand recruit programmers and researchers.  Rise of Computers  RGM was preceded by a line of firms conceived by computer-\nsavvy mavericks. Portfolio insurance traders were the early whiz\nkids of the 1980s until they got blamed for the 1987 stock\nmarket crash, says Bernard Donefer, who ran Fidelity\nInvestments\u2019 electronic trading desk from 1996 to 2002 and is\nnow a professor at  Baruch College  in New York.  In the 1990s, day traders using the Small Order Execution\nSystem, a computer network that automatically executed trades of\nup to 1,000 shares, were called the SOES bandits because they\nswooped in before market makers could update prices.  \u201cIt was not economical to use a human market maker when\ncomputers can do it much cheaper,\u201d Donefer says.  SEC Innovations  The SEC paved the way for today\u2019s high-frequency traders in\n1998. Then-Chairman Arthur Levitt authorized Regulation ATS,\nwhich spawned ECNs to match buyers and sellers. (Levitt is on\nthe board of Bloomberg LP.)  The SEC ordered the introduction of decimalization in 2000,\nlowering the minimum spread between what a seller will accept\nand what a buyer wants to pay to a penny from an eighth of a\ndollar, or 12.5\u00a0cents. The SEC\u2019s aim was to reduce the cost of\ntrading for retail investors.  In the 1990s, if you had wanted to buy a share of  International Business Machines Corp ., the price would have been\n$129, $129.125, $129.25 and so on. Today, the gap between the\nbuyer and seller of a popular stock is often around a penny.  In another attempt to make markets more democratic, the\nSEC\u2019s Regulation NMS in 2007 stipulated that orders be posted\nelectronically and immediately executed at the best price\navailable nationally. The combination of lower spreads and\ngreater competition sent traditional market makers fleeing.\nMarket making on the NYSE moved to computer screens from\nexchange floors.  Fleeting Opportunities  \u201cOpportunities that in the past would last three days now\nlast only five minutes or less,\u201d says Irene Aldridge, author of\n\u201cHigh-Frequency Trading: A Practical Guide to Algorithmic\nStrategies and Trading Systems\u201d (Wiley, 2009). \u201cThere is too\nmuch information for a human trader to process.\u201d  Automation introduced normally staid institutional\ninvestors to the high-frequency world. For mutual funds that\ndeal in blocks of stock, there\u2019s always danger in having rivals\ndetect a trade. Once a high-speed firm discovers a fund\u2019s large\nbuy order, HFT computers may instantly move to snap up the\navailable stock on other exchanges, expecting to sell it to the\ninstitution at a higher price.  The massive volumes generated by HFT firms scouring various\nmarkets can also send false trading signals.  \u201cI am not sure if the quote at any time accurately\nreflects the balance of supply and demand,\u201d says Kevin Cronin,\ndirector of global equity trading at Atlanta-based mutual fund\nfirm  Invesco Ltd ., which has $560 billion under management.  \u201cI see a quote, and many times it disappears in an instant\nwithout anything trading,\u201d adds Cronin, who spoke at the SEC\nhearing and wants the commission to restrict HFT activities.  HFT Backers  High-frequency trading has won supporters, even in the $12\ntrillion mutual fund industry. George Sauter, chief investment\nofficer at Vanguard Group Inc., the biggest U.S. mutual fund\nmanager, with $1.4\u00a0trillion in assets, says HFT has lowered\ncosts. Decimalization, the absence of middle\u00admen and competition\nsparked by high-frequency traders have shrunk spreads.  \u201cMy transaction costs have fallen by 50 percent over the\npast 10 years,\u201d says Sauter, who also spoke at the SEC hearing\nand disagrees with curbs on HFT. \u201cYou cannot throw out high-\nspeed trading with the bath water.\u201d  Institutions have to adapt to reality, says Jose Marques,\nwho joined  Deutsche Bank AG  as global head of electronic equity\ntrading this year from  Credit Suisse Group AG .  \u201cWe have gone from machines looking for patterns to\nmachines looking for other machines looking for patterns,\u201d says\nMarques, who fends off high-frequency players for the bank\u2019s\nelectronic trading clients.  Hide-and-Seek  \u201cWe take the very techniques the high-frequency crowd use\nto detect activity and use that knowledge to defend our\nclients,\u201d he says. \u201cIf we make a trade and see prices start to\nmove, we\u2019ll stop trading. High-frequency players will lose\ninterest and move on. At that stage, we resume our trading.\u201d\nThe aim is to keep trading without attracting attention.  It\u2019s still a struggle to trade without being detected, says\nHenri Waelbroeck, research director at New York-based electronic\nbrokerage Pipeline Financial Systems LLC.  \u201cOver time, all algorithms will leave a signature, a\nfootprint that could be read by others,\u201d he says.  Manoj Narang became interested in faster trading when he\nsuspected somebody was deciphering his trades. Narang, 40, an\nMIT graduate who\u2019d worked for Goldman Sachs and Credit Suisse,\nwas running a $200 million hedge fund above a Restoration\nHardware store in Red Bank. He speculated that companies with\nsimilar strategies were firing off trades faster than he was.  \u2018Taking Opportunities\u2019  \u201cFirms were jumping ahead of us in trades, taking\nopportunities,\u201d says Narang, dressed in a blue T-shirt, jeans\nand a Yankees cap as about 25 people, mostly men in their 20s,\nwork at computers in near silence. Narang measured his holding\ntime in three or four days, not seconds or even minutes, and was\nmissing out on profits.  Narang, who had founded  Tradeworx Inc.  to sell trading\nsoftware in 1999 and had started his hedge fund in 2001, hired\nengineering and math graduates. He began a $5\u00a0million high-\nfrequency operation in January 2009. Today, he trades as many as\n60 million shares a day, with an average holding time of 2\nminutes, compared with 10 minutes in the summer.  Narang walks to a whiteboard to explain one of his\nstrategies. All he needs is the price relationship between two\nstocks. Once his computers detect that the price of one stock is\nmoving more than others, the machines go into action. If the\nprice of  Microsoft Corp . is rising, Tradeworx sells Microsoft\nshares and buys the SPDR S&P 500 ETF Trust.  \u201cYou don\u2019t need to look at anything other than the price\nof Microsoft to determine if it is rich or cheap,\u201d he says.  Low Risk, Low Reward  There are plenty of chances to scalp a penny or two. A\nfluctuation in Microsoft shares will change the price of\nMicrosoft options, as well as indexes that track Microsoft and\nthe Standard & Poor\u2019s 500 futures contract. Narang\u2019s machines\nsell the SPDR ETF fund and buy Microsoft, closing the trade for\na profit.  \u201cThis is not a swing-for-the-fences strategy but a low-\nrisk, low-reward operation,\u201d he says.  The trick is to generate enough volume to make it a\nsustainable business. Allston\u2019s Connell left behind 14 years on\nWall Street to join the Chicago firm in 2004, a year after it\nwas formed. A native of Dublin who, with his rumpled white shirt\nand steel-gray hair, resembles actor Dennis Quaid, Connell won a\n1988 U.S.\u00a0Green Card lottery, a government program that offered\npermanent residency. He headed to Salomon Brothers Inc. in New\nYork to set up fixed-income-trading systems.  Price Discrepancies  Connell says he quit Salomon in 1998 because he felt\ndestined for a life in middle management. He joined Chicago-\nbased Hull Trading Co., which was a pioneer in electronic\ntrading in options and futures. Goldman Sachs bought Hull for\n$531 million in 1999, making him managing director for equities\nderivatives trading systems. He spent four years there, took a\nyear off and then joined Allston.  Seated in an office in the Chicago Board Options Exchange\nbuilding with the blinds drawn against the glaring August\nsunlight, Connell says his team constantly looks for ways of\nidentifying price discrepancies.  One approach would be to look at a stock\u2019s historical\ntrading pattern and buy or sell whenever the stock moves out of\nits range. Another is comparing a stock\u2019s movement to a basket\nof related stocks. By contrast, a traditional asset management\nfirm may look at year-ahead earnings, price-earnings ratio and\ncash-flow expectations to determine fair value.  Without knowing anything about Goldman Sachs\u2019s profit or\ncash flow, a firm could still make money trading the shares. To\nillustrate how this might be done, Connell shows a spreadsheet\nwith two days of Goldman Sachs price movements.  Buy and Sell Spikes  He points out where sudden spikes go back to an average\nprice. These spikes are most likely short-term discrepancies in\nbuy and sell orders, he says. By selling when the stock rose\nsharply and buying when the price fell sharply, a firm could\ntheoretically make a profit. A company could apply this rule to\nspreads between similar stocks or baskets of stocks, says\nConnell, who declines to discuss Allston\u2019s strategies.  At RGM, Gorelick has the same reticence. When asked about\nprofits, he\u2019s tight-lipped.  \u201cThat\u2019s one of the benefits of being a private company,\u201d\nhe says.  From RGM\u2019s first operating day when it did four trades and\nmade $17, it now trades hundreds of millions of shares a day. If\nit makes 0.1 cent to 0.2 cent a share, or 1 to 2 mil in industry\nparlance, that could mean $75 million to $150 million a year in\nrevenue from its trades. With options, futures and foreign\nexchange, trading profit could top $200 million.  \u201cWe\u2019re not Goldman Sachs, but this is a good business,\u201d\nhe says.  Genie Out of Lamp  Supporters and opponents agree on one thing: High-frequency\ntrading is here to stay.  \u201cYou can\u2019t put the genie back in the lamp,\u201d says Tim Sargent, CEO of Quantitative Services Group LLC, a Naperville,\nIllinois, company that analyzes trading costs.  The trick for regulators will be to weave some magic of\ntheir own to keep financial markets humming without letting fast\ncomputers bent on quick profits get the upper hand. (005930) , the world\u2019s\nlargest television maker, acquired  Boxee Inc. , a New York-based\nstartup whose set-top box can record broadcasts and stream\nonline video. (AAPL) \u2019s iOS operating systems, in addition to\nthe software that powers its connected TV box. Samsung said\nclosely held Boxee can help it develop Internet-enabled devices.  \u201cSamsung has acquired key talent and assets from Boxee,\u201d\na spokeswoman for the Suwon, South Korea-based company said in\nan e-mailed statement. \u201cThis will help us continue to improve\nthe overall user experience across our connected devices.\u201d  Consumers\u2019 living rooms are turning into a major\nbattleground for technology companies this year. Roku Inc.,\nanother closely held TV-box maker, has managed to gain some\nsuccess with its streaming players that are sold for as little\nas $50.  Boxee has found itself in several battles with media giants\nsince the company was started in 2007. OK, it's a very\nnice phone.  \n But nothing about the new Nexus One smartphone from Google\nInc. comes close to warranting the mass hysteria that attended\nits unveiling last week.  \n The Nexus One isn't revolutionary. Nor is it an iPhone\nkiller -- a phrase we should banish to the Tech Writers' Hall of\nCliches. It is, instead, a sleek phone with some advancements in\ndisplay and processor technology that will surely be matched and\nthen overtaken by others in the months ahead.  \n True, the rapidly evolving competition among Google, Apple\nInc., Microsoft Corp. and Research in Motion Ltd. is fascinating\nto watch. And Google's plunge into e-tailing -- the Nexus One\ncan only be bought directly from the company over the Web -- has\nthe potential to shake up how phones are sold.  \n Me, though, I find it hard to swoon over a business model.  \n The Nexus One, manufactured by Taiwan's HTC Corp. to\nGoogle's specifications, is similar in both size and shape to\nthe iPhone -- a smidge thinner and lighter, a trifle longer. It\nruns a new version of Google's Android operating system that\nmakes modest tweaks to the software that debuted on Motorola\nInc.'s Droid two months ago.  \n Thing of Beauty  \n If anyone ought to feel threatened by the Nexus One, it's\nMotorola, which committed to using Android for all its\nsmartphones and now has powerful new competition from its own\npartner. Just to cite one area, the Droid's screen used to be my\nfavorite: super-bright, with higher resolution than the iPhone.\nBut the Nexus One uses new technology that provides an even\nricher display, with deeper colors and blacker blacks. It's a\nthing of beauty.  \n Under the hood, the Nexus One uses a Qualcomm Inc.\nprocessor that's the most powerful ever put in a phone. It also\nhas enhanced 3-D graphics, expanded speech-to-text features --\nyou can now dictate your Facebook or Twitter updates rather than\ntype them -- a replaceable battery and a memory-card slot.  \n At the same time, the Nexus One shares the shortcomings of\nprevious Android and HTC phones.  \n The number of Android apps trails far behind the iPhone. So\ndoes Android's ability to sync with Microsoft Outlook for e-\nmail, calendars and contacts, though it does provide the\ncapability to view and work with Microsoft Word, Excel and\nPowerPoint files through technology from Quickoffice Inc. and\nDataViz Inc.'s Documents To Go.  \n Accidental Launches  \n Its app icons, which now whiz onto the desktop instead of\nrolling up window shade-style, are too small and close together;\nI too often accidentally launch an app when all I'm trying to do\nis scroll through them. The included 4 gigabytes of storage is\ntoo small and inflexible, with only 190 megabytes set aside for\napps.  \n You can't pinch your fingers together or move them apart to\nzoom in or out on a screen. The home, back, menu and search\nbuttons below the screen require too much pressure to push, and\nthe trackball seems superfluous except when it glows to signal a\nnew call or message.  \n The company's real innovation is in how it's selling the\nNexus One and the other Google-branded phones to follow.  \n Most phones in the U.S. are purchased tied to a specific\ncarrier, which subsidizes the cost of the handset in return for\nyour commitment to a service contract. Google is seeking to\nseparate the handset from the service. You can buy it with a\nservice plan for $179, or pay $529 and purchase service\nseparately.  \n T-Mobile  \n At launch, there isn't much of a choice: The only carrier\ncurrently offering a plan is T-Mobile USA, the U.S. mobile-phone\ndivision of Deutsche Telekom AG, which charges $79.99 per month.\nIn theory, you can also use a SIM card from AT&T Inc., but the\nphone wouldn't be able to use AT&T's 3G network for data, only\nits older, slower Edge network. Outside the U.S., Google is\nshipping the unlocked Nexus One to the U.K., Hong Kong and\nSingapore.  \n The choices will multiply over time. This spring will see a\nNexus One that runs on the Verizon Wireless network, which uses\na different technology than AT&T and T-Mobile. Also in the\nspring, Vodafone Group Plc is lined up to offer a service plan\nfor the Nexus One in Europe.  \n Google is responsible for delivering the phone -- the one I\nordered on launch day last week arrived in less than 48 hours --\nand will be the first point of contact if anything goes wrong.  \n Weakening the carriers' control and compelling them to\ncompete with each other may eventually put more power into\nconsumers' hands -- and, of course, Google's.  \n While all this is interesting, it's hardly earth-\nshattering. When Apple introduced the iPhone in 2007, it changed\nthe entire way people thought about wireless devices, ushering\nin the era of the mobile Web.  \n The Nexus One? It's just a very nice phone.  \n (Rich Jaroslovsky is a Bloomberg News columnist. Discussions probably will cover the cross-border movement\nof financial data, information and communications services,\nmaritime, environmental and energy services and government\nprocurement.  Nkenge Harmon, a spokeswoman for the USTR in Washington,\ndeclined to comment, saying by phone: \u201cWe haven\u2019t notified\nCongress, and when we notify Congress, we\u2019ll notify Congress.\u201d  It would be the first new trade negotiation since Obama was\nre-elected in November.  Discussion Topics  An agreement should address the free movement of data\nbecause manufacturers rely on the flow of information and\nservices to facilitate their cross-border operations, according\nto the Coalition of Service Industries, a Washington-based trade\ngroup. Its members include  JPMorgan Chase & Co. (JPM) ,  Verizon\nCommunications Inc. (VZ) ,  Walmart Stores Inc. (WMT) ,  Microsoft Corp. (MSFT) ,  AT&T\nInc. (T) ,  Visa Inc. (V) , and  FedEx Corp. (FDX)   Peter Allgeier, a former U.S. ambassador to the WTO who is\nnow head of the CSI, last month called the agreement on a\nframework for the talks encouraging and praised \u201cthe degree of\ncollaboration and cooperation.\u201d  He said he hopes the talks produce an ambitious agreement\nthat creates new trade opportunities rather than just\nconsolidating concessions in existing bilateral accords.  Five Goals  A group of 21 governments agreed on five goals for the\ndiscussions of an accord to liberalize services last month, and\npledged to begin negotiations this year.  Unlike other WTO talks, only those countries that choose to\nparticipate are part of the discussions. So far, Brazil, China\nand India, three of the world\u2019s fastest-growing economies, have\ndeclined to participate in the talks. The 21 governments, which represent 50 countries, account\nfor about 70 percent of global commerce, according to the CSI.  John Clancy, the European Commission\u2019s spokesman for trade\nin Brussels, declined to comment about what the U.S.\nnotification would mean for the services talks. Windows Phone software head Terry Myerson will add responsibility for the Windows and Xbox operating systems.  Ballmer is concentrating divisions around hardware and Internet services to appeal to customers who increasingly use mobile devices for tasks once done on desktop machines. As demand for Microsoft\u2019s flagship Windows software ebbs amid a global personal-computer slump, Ballmer needs to slice away management layers that have hampered product development.  \u201cFirst and foremost this is an attempt to address the fact that they are behind in tablet and mobile,\u201d said  Colin Gillis , an analyst at BGC Partners LP in  New York . \u201cThey\u2019re effectively saying, \u2018We have some problems we need to address and we need to make radical changes to accomplish it.\u2019\u201d  The shares rose 2.8 percent to $35.69 in New York, the highest closing price since 2007. Cloud Efforts  Microsoft is also trying to challenge Amazon.com Inc. and Google Inc. in cloud services as more customers opt for software that\u2019s run over the Web instead of installed on corporate machines. Initially the society sued Leadscope in Ohio federal court\nin May 2002. Leadscope responded to that suit, seeking dismissal\non the grounds that the court lacked jurisdiction. ACS then\nrefilled the complaint in Ohio state court in July 2002.  The state court jury rejected the trade-secret claims and\nawarded Leadscope $26.5 million on its counterclaims of unfair\ncompetition and defamation. ACS then appealed.  The Ohio high court found that the jury properly determined\nthat Leadscope had been harmed by the ACS actions and was\nentitled to compensation. Leadscope\u2019s defamation claim did not\nhold up, nor did the $15 million of the jury award that was\nrelated to that claim.  The case is American Chemical Society V. It will\nhelp Apple customers stream and store music and videos remotely,\nvia the so-called cloud, rather than having to download files to\na hard drive, said  Gene Munster , an analyst at Piper Jaffray in\nMinneapolis. Google Inc. , owner of the world\u2019s largest search\nengine, already has a facility in a neighboring county.  Microsoft, Google Centers  \u201cNames like Google and Apple indicate you\u2019re in the 21st\ncentury and open for business, so we hope to propel this to\nsomething greater,\u201d said  Kitty Barnes , chairman of the Catawba\nCounty Board of Commissioners.  U.S. technology companies increasingly are setting up shop\nin small-town America.  Microsoft Corp. , Facebook Inc. and\nTwitter Inc. all are placing data centers in sparsely populated\nregions, drawn by tax incentives, inexpensive labor, cheap\nelectricity and abundant space.  Microsoft, based in Redmond, Washington, weighs more than\n35 different issues when selecting a site, said Kevin Timmons,\n general manager  of the company\u2019s data center operations. The\ncompany plans to build a $500 million data facility in Virginia,\nGovernor  Bob McDonnell \u2019s office  said  in August.  \u201cTopping the list were factors such as its close proximity\nto our customers, fiber-optic networks, a large pool of skilled\nlabor and an affordable energy source,\u201d Timmons said. To land its Apple facility, North Carolina\u2019s legislature\napproved $46 million in tax breaks for the company. Local\ngovernments also trimmed Apple\u2019s real property taxes by half and\nslashed personal property taxes by 85 percent,  records show .  Some local officials say companies, not communities,\nbenefit most as big providers locate operations in rural areas.  \u201cI have a problem with government giving large\nmultinational corporations millions of dollars in handouts,\u201d\nsaid T.J. The popularity of smartphones and tablets has put the\ncompanies on a collision course. The market for mobile-phone\nchips will grow 40 percent to $29.9 billion by 2015, according\nto  the Linley Group . With more consumers using handheld devices\nas their primary access to the Internet, Intel can\u2019t afford to\nstay only in the realm of personal computers, said  Jim McGregor ,\nchief technology strategist for research firm In-Stat.  \u201cFor Intel, it\u2019s a \u2018we have to be there,\u2019\u201d he said.\n\u201cNever bet against a computing device that fits in your pocket.\nI do more on my smartphone than any other device.\u201d  For years, Intel processors failed to win orders in the\nmobile-phone market, mostly because they were too energy-hungry\nto work in a device that consumers expect to last days between\ncharges. ARM Technology  The success of Apple Inc.\u2019s iPad, which runs smartphone\nchips based on  ARM Holdings Plc (ARM)  designs, proved to consumers\nthat phone processors could deliver enough performance for\ncomputing tasks. Microsoft Corp., the top software maker, also\nis putting pressure on Intel to adapt. Intel is counting on the effort to help maintain its\nleadership in the notebook market, said Lazard\u2019s Amir.  \u201cYou need to be sure that you\u2019re not losing the\nnotebook,\u201d said Amir, who has a  \u201cneutral\u201d rating (INTC)  on Intel. Doctorate Holders  At issue is how many, and what sort of, immigrants the U.S.\nought to be admitting. The legislation passed today would\nreserve 55,000 visas for those with doctorates in the designated\nfields, though graduates with master\u2019s degrees could benefit if\nnot all of those green cards are taken. The bill would also make\nit easier for recipients\u2019 spouses and under-age children to join\nthem by allowing them to wait in the U.S. after spending one\nyear on the green card wait list.  The bill wouldn\u2019t result in an increase in total\nimmigration because it would eliminate a similar number of visas\noffered through a program designed to encourage diversity among\nimmigrants.  That program -- which sets aside green cards for countries\nwith low rates of immigration to the U.S., such as  Ethiopia ,\n Nigeria , Uzbekistan, Albania,  Ghana  and  Morocco  -- was created\nin 1990 as a counterweight to immigration policies biased toward\napplications of people who either already have family in the\nU.S. or fill certain employment needs. I'm going to be away the next couple days, but the updates will return on Monday: India's new central banker won't get a  honeymoon . Standard & Poor's put India's deepening financial crisis in stark relief: There is more than a one-in-three chance the country will be downgraded within two years, a risk that will grow as officials in New Delhi dither ahead of a May election. Until then, all eyes will be on Raghuram Rajan, India's new central bank governor, who starts tomorrow. If the respected economist hoped for a honeymoon period, a chance to get his bearings, he can forget it. The rupee is flirting with 70 to the dollar, and with politics paralyzed, the onus for action has fallen on him. Rajan will have to impress world markets right out of the gate if he's to have any hope of success. Fitch calls Malaysia out for economic  baby steps . In July, the ratings company cut its outlook for Southeast Asia's third-largest economy to negative, citing rising debt and lack of budgetary reform. More recently, as the market turmoil engulfing India and Indonesia ricocheted Malaysia's way, Prime Minister Najib Razak curbed subsidies that were stretching government budgets. Yet Fitch isn't impressed. \u201cFurther steps to improve fiscal sustainability and long-term macroeconomic stability could see the ratings revert to stable outlook,\u201d says Fitch analyst Andrew Colquhoun. At a time when global investors are scrutinizing national balance sheets more aggressively than in the last 15 years, Najib must do better than fiscal baby steps. Is China's Li the  second coming  of Zhu Rongji? Reform-minded Chinese officials hope so. But Premier Li Keqiang is pledging to do two contradictory things: execute a top-to-bottom shift in the nation's export-addicted economy, while maintaining 7 percent-plus growth. If this balancing act sounds impossible, that's because it is. To succeed, Li needs to develop some of the toughness demonstrated by Zhu, the man who held his job from 1998 to 2003. Zhu knew that making China more innovative, productive and stable meant creating a vibrant private sector, and he was willing to cause pain -- throwing tens of millions of Chinese out of work -- to get there. Li is still talking as though China can reform without suffering markedly slower growth. That's wishful, not wise thinking.  Sony's ' sense of crisis ' makes it takeover target. Poor Sony just can't get a break. The one-time innovative powerhouse this year finally introduced a smartphone some Japanese want to buy and hopes to bring the Xperia global -- just as the market for pricey handsets has become saturated. \u201cWe have a high sense of crisis,\" Yasuhiro Ueda, a Sony senior vice president, tells Bloomberg News. As the company that once changed the world with the Walkman fights irrelevance, shareholders may may have to take hope from Microsoft's purchase of Nokia. With each passing year, content-rich Sony's only real future is as a takeover target, especially as its board digs its head into the proverbial sand. Nimbler rivals Apple and Samsung have the hardware, Sony owns music and movies galore. Merger, anyone? Myanmar is  behind schedule  on stock exchange. This will sound like bad news to many. Multinational companies and investors alike are clamoring to cash in on Myanmar's opening after decades of isolation and economic neglect. But it's best if Burmese officials move carefully and methodically to ensure they are ready for the coming onslaught of capital. Myanmar needs a stable and deep capital market to thrive and it turned to Japan to help build an equities bourse. Tokyo-based officials say Myanmar is behind schedule to open trading by 2015. And that's fine; it's more important to get things right than meet an arbitrary deadline that's more about today than tomorrow. (William Pesek is a Bloomberg View columnist. On April\u00a024, Google Inc. unveiled its long-awaited Drive\nservice, which lets people store files online and synchronize\nthem across all their devices. Drew Houston, the chief executive\nofficer of file-syncing service provider Dropbox Inc., goaded\nthe juggernaut with a tweet: \u201cIn other news, @Dropbox is\nlaunching a search engine.\u00a0:)\u201d  Box Inc., another cloud-storage provider, hosted a\npreviously planned party on a Manhattan rooftop on April\u00a025.\nChief Executive Officer Aaron Levie shimmied in suit and\nsneakers while Elijah Wood -- yes, that Elijah Wood -- manned\nthe turntable. Technology \u2018Everyone Needs\u2019  \u201cThis is the kind of technology -- a la the phone, Web\nbrowser, and e-mail -- that everyone needs, and there just\naren\u2019t many products like that,\u201d said Josh Stein, a managing\ndirector at Draper Fisher Jurvetson.  Box and Dropbox -- along with about a dozen other startups\nas well as  Microsoft Corp. (MSFT) , Amazon.com Inc., and  Apple Inc. (AAPL)  --\nare engaged in a fight with huge ramifications for the future of\ncomputing.  Every year, people create more and more photos, videos,\nWord documents and other files. Increasingly, those data are\nscattered across phones, tablets, computers and other devices.\nThe storage startups and their competitors are vying to be the\ncentral control panel for all this information.  \u201cAll of these companies see this future where your devices\nare basically portals to all your stuff,\u201d said Tom Kleinpeter,\nthe former chief technology officer at FolderShare, a file-\nsyncing service acquired by Microsoft in 2005. \u201cAnd whoever\nholds on to all that stuff has a huge advantage.\u201d  The story of FolderShare shows how hard it is to get a\nsimple-seeming technology such as cloud storage to work\nproperly. Founded in 2002, the company let people sync as many\nfolders as they wanted among multiple computers -- a freedom\nthat was overwhelming to some.  \u2018Big Mistakes\u2019  \u201cOne of our big mistakes was letting people do whatever\nthey wanted,\u201d said Kleinpeter. Many customers failed to even\ngrasp the basic syncing concept: that their computers needed to\nbe online at the same time to swap files.  San Francisco-based  Dropbox , founded in 2007, picked a\nsimpler approach. When users install its desktop or mobile apps,\nthe service creates a single folder -- a dropbox -- on each\ndevice. Anything saved in that file is available on every other\ndevice.  While FolderShare required an Internet connection to work,\nDropbox stores copies of each file on the computer or mobile\ndevice where it was created and on servers the company rents\nfrom  Amazon. (AMZN)  That means users can work offline and sync\neverything later.  Single Folder  \u201cDropbox was brilliant picking that single folder thing,\u201d\nsaid Kleinpeter. Microsoft Corp. (MSFT) \u2019s Windows Azure software and related programs have surpassed $1 billion in annual sales for the first time, a sign of progress in the effort to challenge  Amazon.com Inc. (AMZN)  in cloud computing.  The sales milestone for Azure -- which stores business information and programs on remote servers and lets customers access them over the Web -- was reached in the past 12 months, said Curt Anderson, finance chief for Microsoft\u2019s server and tools unit.  Microsoft, the largest software maker, is counting on Azure and other Internet-based business programs to bolster growth as a global personal-computer slump erodes demand for Windows software installed on desktop machines. About 20 percent of companies tapping the cloud use  Azure , compared with 71 percent usage for Amazon, according to James Staten, an analyst at  Forrester Research Inc. (FORR)  Within a year, Microsoft can command as much as 35 percent, he said.  \u201cI expect them to double annually from here,\u201d Staten said of Microsoft\u2019s Azure revenue. \u201cMicrosoft probably has more net new growth opportunity sitting in front of them than probably anyone in the market.\u201d  Microsoft\u2019s $1 billion sales figure includes Azure, as well as software provided to partners to create related Windows cloud services, Anderson said in an interview. Azure customers use the services to run corporate programs, websites and applications from Microsoft\u2019s data centers, rather than spending on their own servers, storage machines and workers to maintain them.  Amazon\u2019s Beachhead  Azure subscriptions have risen 48 percent in the past six months, said Takeshi Numoto, Microsoft\u2019s vice president for marketing for the server and tools division. That unit, which encompasses Azure, has posted nine straight quarters of  sales  growth of at least 10 percent, he said. Windows sales were $18.4 billion last year, down 5.7 percent from a peak in 2010.  Gaining ground against Amazon won\u2019t be easy. Microsoft will need to do a better job of convincing existing  customers , as well as newer companies seeking to reduce computing costs, why they should opt for Azure, Staten said.  \u201cThe majority of people thinking about cloud weren\u2019t thinking of Azure first,\u201d Staten said. \u201cThat\u2019s been an uphill climb for them, and even though Microsoft is now matching the prices of Amazon and some of the capabilities, they haven\u2019t really answered the question of \u2018Why Azure?\u2019\u201d  Startups, which tend to be early adopters of new technology, may be an especially hard sell, he said.  \u201cThey haven\u2019t excited the front-line developers -- the ones who made Amazon who they are,\u201d he said. \u201cThose will be hard to influence.\u201d  Making Progress  Take Forest Key, an ex-Microsoft manager who is now chief executive officer of hotel-software startup  Buuteeq Inc.   Even after Key\u2019s firm participated in a Microsoft program that gives free software to startups, he chose Amazon\u2019s cloud service two and a half years ago. Now that Azure is more on par with Amazon, Key said he doesn\u2019t want to switch.  Anne Temme, a spokeswoman for Seattle-based Amazon at  Weber Shandwick , didn\u2019t respond to a request for comment.  Still, Microsoft is making progress, said Scott Maxwell, senior managing director at OpenView Venture Partners in  Boston . The company is teaming up with venture firms and investment groups, often giving away its services so that as startups grow, they\u2019re already Microsoft customers. More of his companies are bringing up Azure as an option, and he\u2019s encouraging them to look into it, he said.  \u2018Huge Moves\u2019  \u201cMicrosoft is getting really focused and making huge moves in the market,\u201d he said. \u201cThey\u2019re really trying to get more companies on the platform.\u201d  Microsoft shares rose 2.6 percent to $32.61 at the close in  New York . The stock has increased 22 percent this year.  Earlier this month, Microsoft rolled out a new set of cloud services designed to more directly challenge Amazon and vowed to match the online retailer\u2019s lowest prices for competing products. Since then, Azure added 10,000 customers, Numoto said.  With the latest offering, Microsoft entered a niche known as Infrastructure as a Service, which lets companies move applications to the cloud by renting storage and servers -- instead of older versions of Azure that required customers to write programs from scratch.  $30.6 Billion Market  It\u2019s the fastest-growing part of the cloud market, according to Gartner Inc., which estimates that sales of infrastructure services will surge by an average of 38 percent annually to $30.6 billion by 2017 from $6.17 billion last year.  \u201cNot that many people have quite figured out that the Azure of today is not the same as two years ago,\u201d  David Smith , an analyst at Gartner, said in an interview. \u201cIt\u2019s changed a lot and the issue is getting people to give it a second look.\u201d  One early convert is  Goodyear Tire & Rubber Co. (GT) , which last year moved a North American program that tracks tire performance and wear to Azure from an internal system. The application, which has almost one million data points on various tires for vehicles ranging from trucks to school buses, helps Goodyear catch safety issues and propose the best products for typical road conditions in a specific region at a given time of year.  Goodyear, the largest U.S. tiremaker, opted for Azure over Amazon because it already used Microsoft\u2019s database and programming tools, said Johnny McIntosh, director of Goodyear\u2019s fleet headquarters in  North America .  Goodyear Singapore  When Goodyear wanted a similar system in  Singapore , it took less than an hour to set up, he said.  \u201cIt\u2019s not all been rainbows and sunshine -- we were an early adopter so you know there will be some growing pains,\u201d he said. \u201cBut overall it\u2019s heavily used and it\u2019s held up well.\u201d  The total cloud market, which includes categories like advertising, where Azure and Amazon don\u2019t compete, is forecast to rise to $237.2 billion in 2017 from $108.9 billion last year, according to Gartner. Amazon Web Services\u2019 annual revenues could reach $20 billion by 2020 from $1.8 billion last year, Carlos Kirjner, an analyst at Sanford C. Bernstein & Co., estimated in a research report earlier this month.  One area where Microsoft has an edge over Amazon is in the so-called private cloud, which lets customers run Web-based programs via their own data centers. Microsoft also links Web- based applications to its traditional software. Amazon hasn\u2019t focused much on the private cloud, Staten said.  Xerox Programmers  Microsoft\u2019s flexibility helped win over  Xerox Corp (XRX) , which is barred by some government customers from running its programs in the public cloud. Azure enables Xerox programmers in Bangalore,  India , to coordinate with users in the U.S., said Raman Padmanabhan, chief information officer for Xerox\u2019s business services unit.  Under the old system, U.S. customers often discovered bugs when it was the middle of the night in India. Now, Indian engineers run virtualization software that replicates systems running in the U.S. to speed development and test new software, he said. (AMZN) \u2019s new Seattle headquarters from terminal dullness.  The e-commerce giant is building the city\u2019s largest commercial development, a 3.3-million-square-foot complex called Rufus 2.0 after a dog owned by two early employees.  The bubbles are the shiny centerpiece for what John Schoettler, Amazon\u2019s director of global real estate and facilities, calls an \u201curban campus.\u201d It\u2019s tailored to a young workforce that rejects both the sterile self-importance of corporate downtown towers and the grinding commute and isolation of suburban office parks.  Besides the domes, the campus comprises three 38-story glass towers that rise from three city blocks north of downtown Seattle. Amazon wants the towers to fade into the downtown-edge background, but they are so lacking in character that they stick out embarrassingly.  Local architect  NBBJ  has devised hivelike \u201ccenters for energy\u201d within the towers that unite multiple floors with stairways so that employees can\u2019t help encountering each other and sharing ideas. The uniformly skinned towers reflect none of that internal vitality.  The campus \u201cis not insular,\u201d Schoettler says. Landscaped passages wander through each block, inviting the public to share greenery, a playing field and a dog park.  Green Lifestyles  The amenities are aimed at the sought-after young professionals, who want green urban lifestyles and are adept at spinning ideas into growth.  Too bad only the five-story greenhouse bubble building, which will entwine meeting and dining spaces with tall indoor trees and draping vines, attracts attention. Its 1960s sci-fi look is at least distinctive.  Amazon\u2019s headquarters complex takes its cues from the rapidly growing South Lake Union neighborhood, which hosts a mix that is hot in urban development now: technology businesses, the  Fred Hutchinson Cancer Research Center  and a constellation of related medical companies.  Amazon and its neighborhood stir together every hip urban ingredient. Bike lanes? Check. Decorative trolley line? Check. Car-sharing? Check. Sidewalk cafes featuring artisanal-sounding sandwiches? Check.  Already 20 sites in South Lake Union have been renovated or built new in more than two dozen blocks that had languished for decades as a sorry blend of parking lots, warehouses and crumbling wooden houses.  Imagination Deficit  Imagination on the part of the architects (NBBJ, Callison LLC, and  LMN Architects ) failed to make the checklist, however, and so the result, as with Amazon\u2019s towers, is leaden.  Microsoft co-founder Paul G. Allen, through his Vulcan Real Estate, is the dominant figure in South Lake Union\u2019s renaissance. Amazon is the chief tenant.  The buildings vary only in trivial details, like whether the rectangular windows are oriented vertically or horizontally. The brick-and-metal exteriors fail to evoke the authentic grit and variety of the slickly remodeled warehouse districts they imitate.  Instead of sculpting buildings to grab  Seattle \u2019s dim daylight and stunning views, the dumb exteriors face other dumb exteriors across narrow alleys.  Amazon\u2019s canopied and landscaped passages are derived from those found winding through the blocks of South Lake Union. Dotted with trees, cafe tables and forgettable artwork, they are listless.  It Matters  Does this mediocrity matter? It\u2019s the norm in commercial development, after all.  Yes, I fumed as I walked these blocks. Seattle is a creative-class capital, where innovation and steely resolve have nurtured leading companies from Boeing Co. to Microsoft Corp., Nordstrom Inc. to Starbucks Corp.  Why must architecture go missing?  In terms of sustaining cities, boring buildings are death. Seattle has been on a roll since the emergence of Microsoft in the 1980s, and it has largely forgotten how it recovered from a precipitous decline in the 1970s by nurturing the neighborhoods that had a rich history of architecture and real amenity.  The Amazon campus and South Lake Union gall because their urban ingredients could make such a rich mix. In the hands of insightful designers, these streets could wondrously reinvent formulaic downtown and suburban commercial monocultures.  Hope Bubbles  Amazon\u2019s bubble domes are cause for hope. They replace one of the low boxy buildings of an earlier design, after local design-review officials belatedly recognized that some uniqueness or expression of innovation was called for.  And NBBJ has breathed more life into them in a late-August plan-review submission. Now the glass panels are framed by struts and spokes that resemble sports-car wheels nested together.  This injection of engineering bling fits the jet-age technological optimism embodied by the nearby Space Needle and monorail train. It hints at the energy that could jolt the entire complex to life.  I hope it means Amazon now recognizes that dullness can be a curse.  (James S. Russell writes on architecture for Muse, the arts and culture section of  Bloomberg News . The former Illinois senator who in 2008 campaigned for president pledging to curb the role of money in politics has decided to accept unlimited corporate dollars for his second inauguration. His shift from four years ago, when he banned company funding, marks an early strategic step toward building the organization that will finance his presidential library, foundation and other post-White House aspirations, advisers say.  Slideshow:  Yes, He Will -- The 57th Presidential Inauguration \u201cWith a two-term president, you have the luxury of planning time,\u201d said Skip Rutherford, who helped raise $165 million for former President  Bill Clinton \u2019s library and works as dean of the University of Arkansas Clinton School of Public Service. \u201cI would not be surprised if the Obama foundation would probably incorporate some time this year.\u201d  For his second inauguration, Obama plans to raise $50 million from individuals and corporations. Financing his career after leaving office will cost orders of magnitude more: The price tag of his presidential library alone could easily exceed $500 million, according to presidential library experts.  Related: Aides, who asked for anonymity to discuss strategy, say raising that amount of money will be impossible unless they build bridges to corporate donors -- and give their exhausted, long-time political campaign supporters a break.  Individual Cap  Along with refusing corporate donations for his first inauguration, Obama capped individual gifts at $50,000.  The decision to accept unlimited corporate money \u201cis a step backwards,\u201d said  Fred Wertheimer , president of the Washington-based campaign finance overhaul advocacy group Democracy 21. \u201cThey saw no reason to do that in 2008 and they have no justifiable basis for doing it in 2012.\u201d  Obama\u2019s acceptance of company cash for his swearing-in festivities excludes donations from lobbyists or political action committees.  Still, that hasn\u2019t stopped lobbyists from making their presence known: mCapitol Management, which paid $2.4 million to lobby the federal government during the first nine months of 2012, and Barnes and Thornburg, which spent $2.1 million on lobbying, are among the sponsors of the Illinois State Society\u2019s black-tie inaugural gala on Jan. 19.  Obama\u2019s List  After financing the most expensive campaign in presidential history -- Obama, an allied super-political action committee and the  Democratic National Committee  collected $1.1 billion -- many of his contributors are feeling tapped out. Aides concluded that accepting corporate dollars for the inauguration would give their wealthiest supporters a needed break, in order to collect their donations later. Microsoft today urged the justices in a one-hour hearing in\nWashington to overturn a jury verdict won by closely held  I4i\nLP , which sued the larger company for patent infringement. In upholding the verdict, the  U.S. Court of Appeals  for the\nFederal Circuit said Microsoft didn\u2019t prove that the disputed\npatent, which covers a feature that lets large companies add\nspecial data to Word files, was based on technology that was\nalready in the marketplace. Change in the Law  \u201cWhen the Patent Office didn\u2019t even consider the evidence,\nit makes absolutely no sense\u201d to use the clear-and-convincing\nstandard, Microsoft\u2019s lawyer, Thomas Hungar, argued. Software, Enterprise  Most of the focus now will be on reviving the printing business to generate more cash, while expanding the enterprise computing businesses, Whitman said.  \u201cThe two growth engines of our company are going to be the software business and the enterprise business,\u201d Whitman said. \u201cOur customers make long-term investments. The push to boost sales to corporate customers comes as  China \u2019s  Lenovo Group Ltd. (992)  is poised to supplant Hewlett-Packard as the top PC supplier. Its share of PCs dropped to 14.9 percent in the second quarter, while Lenovo\u2019s increased to 14.7 percent, according to  Gartner Inc. (IT)   The PC market will expand less than 1 percent this year, the worst performance since it shrank in 2001, according to IDC, complicating Whitman\u2019s turnaround effort. Research, Cloud  Whitman has been spending more on research and development and directing funds toward areas of the computing market where she says Hewlett-Packard can gain an edge, including managing growing volumes of business data and helping companies transition to cloud computing over the Internet.  While the research investment may pay off down the line, it\u2019s partly responsible for the unexpected profit drop Hewlett- Packard projected for 2013, said  Amit Daryanani , an analyst at RBC Capital Markets.  In the enterprise computing market,  Oracle Corp. (ORCL)  is creating a cloud service that lets companies rent processing power, storage, database software and business applications from the company instead of buying them outright, a threat to Hewlett-Packard\u2019s server and disk drive businesses. (VMW)  are also vying to supply more of the platform software that can help companies switch to cloud computing. In the tablet market dominated by Apple\u2019s iPad, Hewlett- Packard is seeking to appeal to corporate clients with an emphasis on security and the ability to run business applications. Hewlett-Packard said it will introduce a tablet for business users, the ElitePad 900, in January that runs Microsoft\u2019s Windows 8 software.  In her drive to shore up profit hammered by sales of low- margin PCs, Whitman has announced plans to cut 29,000 jobs by the end of fiscal 2014 to save as much as $3.5 billion a year. Many of the reductions are from the company\u2019s underperforming enterprise services unit, which former CEO Mark Hurd added with the 2008 acquisition of Electronic Data Systems. What about the actions of the companies themselves -- have they met their ethical obligations to their customers and society as a whole? Do they even have any? The  Washington Post  reported that the National Security Agency collects data \"directly from the servers\" of Microsoft, Yahoo, Google, Facebook, PalTalk, AOL, Skype, YouTube and Apple. While some companies issued carefully worded denials of involvement, it's hard to imagine they were unaware of the  arrangement , however they choose to describe it. Assuming that the companies found the program an infringement on our liberties, could they have declined to provide the government the information it requested? Ultimately, probably not; it seems unlikely they would have met the requests had they not faced a legal obligation to comply. But legal and ethical obligations aren't necessarily the same thing.  Take the recent case of Apple's use of  Irish subsidiaries  with no tax residency to avoid U.S. taxes; the tactics may be legally sound, but ethically dubious. Now turn that around: If companies are willing to go to such lengths to get around U.S. tax law, is it too much to ask that they apply the same creativity to avoiding the surrender of their customers' private information?  In Apple's case, that may have happened. Apple looks to have resisted the government's requests for years. What does that say about other companies, which complied more quickly: Are they better corporate citizens, or worse?  The role and obligation of the corporation in American society is an unsettled question. When Mitt Romney proclaimed that  \"corporations are people\"  in 2011, he sparked a combination of ridicule and outrage. But Apple, Facebook and Google occupy an increasing space in popular culture, and they're judged not only for the products they sell or the profits they generate, but also the way they treat their workers, pay their taxes and even design their  headquarters .  The surveillance debate raises the question of whether our expectations of these companies and their leaders should also extend to the defense of our civil rights. Imagine, for an instant, that Steve Jobs, Sergey Brin, Larry Page and Mark Zuckerberg had held a press conference in 2007, when the government first began seeking this access, and said to the public, \"The government has asked for your information, and we don't think that's right.\"  Faced with that kind of corporate civil disobedience, what would the government have done? Arrested them? Closed down their operations? Taken the companies over? It seems unlikely. More likely, the government would have backed down, at least temporarily. And the next time Congress tried to co-opt the nation's most prominent companies in its intelligence gathering, it might have thought twice. The point isn't that these companies should have stopped this program from starting. It is that they probably had the power to do so, when so few others had that power. The line about great power and great responsibility is apt: Does the ethical burden increase with the consequences of a company's decisions? This week's revelations demonstrate the centrality of Silicon Valley to American life, in ways we never imagined. In the face of that expanded role, maybe it's time to revisit what it means for a company to be a good corporate citizen, and whether that includes acting as a check on the government when no one else can. (Christopher Flavelle is a member of the Bloomberg View editorial board. Sewage-derived power supplies 22 percent of Severn Trent\u2019s energy, almost double that of 2005. At United Utilities, it\u2019s 14 percent. British utilities are shifting fecal matter to vats of bacteria that consume the waste, releasing biogas that\u2019s burned to drive water treatment. The result is lower energy bills and surplus power sent to the grid that heat more U.K. tea kettles.  Water businesses in Britain aren\u2019t the only ones finding value in waste. Companies in Europe and China are turning more to biogas to counter fossil-fuel costs and energy price volatility. Microsoft Corp., the largest software maker, uses effluents to help power a data center in  Wyoming . Skiers in northern  Arizona  speed down slopes on artificial snow made entirely from treated wastewater.  \u201cWe live in a resource-constrained world, we\u2019re going to have to squeeze more and more out of our waste,\u201d said Christopher Gasson, the publisher of Global Water Intelligence in Oxford,  England . Sewage sludge \u201csmells like money to an increasing number of entrepreneurs.\u201d  Some investors in Europe see an opportunity in such a market. Last year,  Bayerische Motoren Werke AG (BMW)  heiress Susanne Klatten, Germany\u2019s wealthiest woman, bought 20 percent of Paques BV, a Dutch biogas technology business.  There are about 2,250 facilities in Europe now using sewage sludge to produce biogas that can generate power, according to the European Biogas Association.  Germany  and Switzerland have the highest concentration with 980 and 463. The U.K. and  Sweden  have at least 100 each.  Berlin Water  Berliner Wasserbetriebe, Germany\u2019s biggest water provider that serves 3.7 million people in and around the capital, has turned sewage sludge into power and heat for at least two decades, said Stephan Natz, a spokesman.  Last year it produced 22 percent of the electricity the utility consumed, mainly from sewage sludge. The company produces power and heat from sewage sludge at all six of its wastewater-treatment plants, Natz said on Feb. 18.  While Gasson estimates more than two-thirds of wastewater utilities in northern Europe are investigating the technology compared with less than 10 percent in 2008, that\u2019s not quite the case in the U.S.  American Water Works Co. (AWK) , the largest U.S. publicly traded water company, has no plants that produce energy from sewage. It\u2019s being considered and is at a very preliminary stage of discussion, the company said by e-mail in response to questions.  \u2018Minority Taste\u2019  Sewage sludge is broken down in a process called anaerobic digestion, which is also used to convert food waste into power.  Aqua America Inc. (WTR) , the second-biggest U.S. water utility by market value, said it has one anaerobic digestion facility that doesn\u2019t produce electricity and they\u2019re unlikely to build any such plant for power.  \u201cThe technology remained a minority taste until about five years ago,\u201d according to Gasson of GWI, a U.K. market research firm. Rising gas prices in Europe forced wastewater utilities to focus on energy bills \u201cat the same time renewable energy was attracting serious investment: Anaerobic digestion technology suddenly came back to life.\u201d  The European Biogas Association and Gasson both say Europe is leading the way with the most established market while  China  is one of the fastest-growing areas.  Waste Streams  The proportion of wastewater collected and treated in China more than doubled from 2004 to 2010 from 33 percent to 74 percent. The nation will spend about $68 billion to 2015 collecting and treating wastewater, showing \u201csignificant\u201d potential for energy from biogas, Gasson said.  By 2020, electricity produced from waste streams may be equivalent to meeting the energy demands of about 2.5 million British homes, or 10 percent of U.K. households, according to a Ernst & Young LLP report that cites the think-tank CentreForum.  Water companies already treat about 66 percent of Britain\u2019s sewage sludge using this process.  Fluctuating energy prices and the rise in fuel costs are helping spur utilities\u2019 investments.  The shift is a \u201cmind-set change\u201d as the industry starts to view the by-product of the wastewater process as something of value rather than an inconvenience that\u2019s costly to dispose of, said Mark Turner, water sector leader at Ernst & Young.  Pennon Group Plc (PNN)  through its Viridor Ltd. unit is investing about 1 billion pounds to 2015 developing at least 300 megawatts of facilities that turn waste from homes and businesses into energy. That project pipeline will drive the company\u2019s growth, Chairman Ken Harvey said in November.  Biogas Beetle  United Utilities, which has biogas plants at 23 of its sites, said this makes \u201cgood\u201d business sense and it plans to invest more. Diverting waste from landfills saves regional provider Wessex Water Services Ltd. millions of pounds, it said.  Seeking to exploit rising landfill taxes, water businesses are expanding their expertise to generate power from food waste. Wessex Water built a food waste pre-treatment facility to help chains find an alternative way to dispose of scraps.  Wessex Water said clients including supermarkets also ask whether sewage-gas can be used to power their trucks. It showed the technology by operating a Volkswagen Beetle car on biogas.  Severn Trent, based in Coventry, treats excrement from about 4 million homes and businesses and turns it into electricity equivalent to power 50,000 U.K. households. Wessex Water said it produces sewage-derived electricity equivalent to power 12,000 homes.  \u2018Delivering Value\u2019  Southern Water Plc processes human waste equal to 1,120 Olympic-size swimming pools, plans to start four new plants in 2013, and Anglian Water Group Ltd. last year generated energy equivalent to supplying 11,500 U.K. homes with power for a year.  \u201cIt\u2019s about controlling our costs and ultimately delivering value to our customers and it\u2019s about doing the right thing for the environment and the U.K. in terms of renewables and carbon reduction,\u201d said Jonathan Davies, general manager for group business development at Severn Trent.  Severn Trent and Anglian Water have seen a cost-reduction from their facilities partly through government incentives that currently grant them two Renewable Obligation Certificates per megawatt-hour of electricity produced, equating to about 82.96 pounds ($128) a megawatt-hour at current ROC prices.  Southern Water Ltd. exports about 10 percent of its electricity and United Utilities last year fed 9 percent into the grid.  Biogas gas be used as a fuel to generate electricity and power cars as well as for heating and cooking.  Which means that \u201ctechnically you could wake up one morning and be cooking your breakfast with gas derived from human waste,\u201d said Mohammed Saddiq, general manager of Geneco, Wessex Water\u2019s clean-energy unit. In 2008, 153 propositions were placed on\nballots, compared with 204 in 2006.  In Colorado, voters will consider amending the constitution\nto ban state borrowing beginning in 2011. If approved, Colorado\nwould be the only state prohibited from issuing bonds to fund\ninfrastructure projects, according to a report by the\nlegislative conference. The measure also would limit future\nborrowing by municipalities and school districts.  The state and its enterprises issue an average of $2.9\nbillion in new bonds annually and spend about $2 billion a year\nto repay debt, according to a Sept. 13 booklet released by the\nLegislative Council of the Colorado General Assembly.  No Prepayment Penalty  The proposal would require debt issued by local governments\nto be subject to prepayment without penalty at any time,\nincreasing the cost of capital to issuers, Fitch Ratings said in\nan Oct. 14 news release.  The amendment requires local governments to decrease tax\nrates when debt is repaid, \u201cfurther complicating the prospect\nof maintaining steady revenue capacity for local governments\u2019\nfuture capital needs,\u201d Fitch said.  In Washington, which doesn\u2019t have an income tax, voters\nwill consider imposing a levy on the adjusted gross income of\nindividuals earning more than $200,000 and couples earning more\nthan $400,000. The revenue would offset a cut in state property\ntaxes and an increase in the business and occupation tax credit.
