Chairman  Bill Gates \nurged top U.S. public-school officials to overhaul teacher pay,\nsaying taxpayers are spending $59 billion a year on compensation\nplans that don\u2019t improve student achievement.  Teachers should be rewarded for results, not for seniority\nor advanced degrees, Gates said today in a speech to the  Council\nof Chief State School Officers  in Louisville, Kentucky.\nRevamping teacher pay will free up scarce money to help improve\neducational performance, said Gates, co-chair of the $36.4\nbillion Bill & Melinda Gates Foundation.  The speech marks the first time Gates has broached the\nsubject of state budgets in his quest to tie teacher pay to\nacademic results -- a goal he shares with the Obama\nadministration. His effort may pit him against teachers\u2019 unions,\nwhose contracts generally provide higher pay for seniority and\nadvanced degrees.  \u201cThe effort to improve schools will be in the context of\nvery tight budgets,\u201d Gates told the schools chiefs. \u201cIt\u2019s\nsomething you look at and think about every day. This conflict\nof dealing with tough financial situations while making the\nreforms that can improve student achievement has never been\ntougher than it is right now.\u201d  A 2008  survey  of members of the American Federation of\nTeachers found that 87 percent supported awarding additional pay\non the basis of an advanced degree such as a master\u2019s or\ndoctorate, and 82 percent said pay should be tied to seniority.\nTwenty-one percent said compensation should be linked to gains\nmeasured by standardized test results. The Washington-based\nunion represents 1.5 million members nationwide, according to\nits website.  Seniority Privileges  Teacher seniority provisions make up 10 percent of school\nexpenditures, or $50 billion a year, according to research by\nthe Seattle-based Gates foundation. Giving teachers a pay bump\nfor getting master\u2019s degrees costs $9 billion a year, the\nfoundation says. The two items account for one-quarter to one-\nthird of teacher compensation, the foundation estimates.  Pensions that let teachers retire as early as 48 years old\nmay also be too costly when budgets are tight, Bill Gates said\nin the interview.  School systems will have to find the money for merit pay\nfrom within existing budgets, Gates said. He suggested shifting\nmoney set aside for rewarding teachers on the basis of seniority\nor from those who attain advanced degrees. To study and develop\neffective ways to award merit pay, the Gates foundation is\ninvesting $290 million over seven years in the Tampa, Florida;\nMemphis, Tennessee; and Pittsburgh school districts, as well as\na charter-school consortium in Los Angeles.  Class Size  Schools may also save money by increasing class size, Gates\nsaid. U.S. student-teacher ratios dropped to 15-to-1 today from\n26-to-1 in 1960, without improving student results, according to\nthe foundation. Schools would save more than $10,000 per\nclassroom by increasing class size by four pupils. They could\nuse the money to pay the best teachers more, according to the\nfoundation.  Increasing class size is likely to be unpopular with\nparents and politicians,  Michelle Rhee , former chancellor of the\nDistrict of Columbia public schools, said in an interview\nyesterday in Cambridge, Massachusetts. Data show that smaller\nclass sizes don\u2019t necessarily improve student performance, she\nsaid.  \u201cIf you reduce the number of teachers and provide money to\nthe most highly effective teachers to take on five more kids,\nthat probably ultimately is going to be the best utilization of\nthose resources,\u201d Rhee said. \u201cHe\u2019s absolutely right.\u201d  While more effort is needed to improve student performance,\nincreasing public-school class sizes and shifting money from\nmore-experienced and more-educated teachers won\u2019t help,  Randi Weingarten , president of the American Federation of Teachers,\nsaid today in a statement.  \u2018Culture of Collaboration\u2019  \u201cThe school districts that have a strong culture of\ncollaboration and provide teachers with the support and\nresources they need have both low teacher attrition and high\nstudent performance,\u201d Weingarten said. Republican senators who endorsed a bipartisan framework for the most significant revision of immigration law in almost three decades criticized a White House plan for not requiring tighter border security as a condition of a path to citizenship.  \u201cOne of the things that\u2019s very important to me is to make sure that the enforcement mechanisms happen,\u201d Senator  Marco Rubio  of  Florida , one of four Republicans backing the Senate blueprint, said in an interview. \u201cThe mistake that\u2019s been made in the past is that while the legalization happened, the enforcement didn\u2019t, and it led to the 11 million people that are here.\u201d  President  Barack Obama  is seeking to harness political momentum following his strong support from Hispanic voters in November to enact new immigration policy. Democrats say they are encouraged that an increasing number of Republicans have dropped their opposition to providing a path to citizenship as part of such a move.  \u201cThe good news is that, for the first time in many years, Republicans and Democrats seem ready to tackle this problem together,\u201d Obama told a cheering audience yesterday at Del Sol High School in  Las Vegas . \u201cAt this moment, it looks like there\u2019s a genuine desire to get this done soon.\u201d  Still, differences between the president\u2019s outline and the Senate framework are coming into focus, most notably over conditions for allowing those already in the country illegally to become citizens.  Border Security  In addition to tightened border security, Republicans want a citizenship path to hinge on tracking people in the U.S. on visas. A commission of governors, community members, and attorneys general living on the Southwest border would make a recommendation when the security measures are completed.  The White House plan doesn\u2019t link citizenship to security, out of concerns that a longer process could make it almost impossible for those immigrants to gain full status.  U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement deported 396,906 people in fiscal year 2011 and a record 409,849 in fiscal 2012 according to figures released by the agency, part of the Department of Homeland Security.  Obama also supports equal treatment of same-sex couples when one partner is from outside the U.S. That provision isn\u2019t included in the Senate framework and may be opposed by some Republicans.  \u201cWe hope the president is careful not to drag the debate to the left and ultimately disrupt the difficult work that is ahead in the House and Senate,\u201d  Brendan Buck , a spokesman for House Speaker  John Boehner , said following Obama\u2019s remarks.  Hispanic Voters  Boehner, of Ohio, is among Republicans who have said the party must find a more positive approach to immigration policy. Hispanics, a rapidly growing group of U.S. voters, cast 71 percent of their votes for Obama on Nov. 6, according to exit polls.  The increasing political clout of Hispanic voters, who make up 10 percent of the electorate and 16.7 percent of the population, has prompted Republicans who long opposed an immigration overhaul to reevaluate their position.  An immigration rewrite has drawn the backing of religious organizations,  law enforcement , and companies including  Wal-Mart Stores Inc. (WMT) , Goldman Sachs,  Microsoft Corp. (MSFT) ,  Intel Corp. (INTC) , and  Google Inc. (GOOG)  as they seek to hire more foreign workers.  Labor Force  Of the 47 million new workers entering the  labor force  between 2010 and 2050, a projected 37.6 million will be Hispanic, according to an October 2012 Bureau of Labor Statistics report. The percentage of Hispanics in the workforce will grow to 18.6 percent by 2020 and to 30 percent in 2050, doubling from 15 percent in 2010, according to the report.  Speaking yesterday at a school where more than 62 percent of the students are Hispanic, Obama warned that if immigration legislation is bogged down in Congress, he would send his plan to the Capitol and insist lawmakers vote on it \u201cright away.\u201d  Senate Majority Leader  Harry Reid , a Nevada Democrat, cautioned that the president \u201chas put his arms around the four senators on the Democratic side and the Republican side, but with the caveat he\u2019s not going to wait around forever to actually have legislation that we move on.\u201d  Obama gave tentative endorsement to the framework that the Republican and Democratic senators unveiled Jan. 28, saying the proposal was \u201cvery much in line with the principles I proposed and campaigned on.\u201d  \u2018Measurable Increases\u2019  Another of the Republicans who crafted the Senate plan,  Arizona  Republican Jeff Flake said he will insist that citizenship can happen only after a \u201cmeasurable increases in border security.\u201d  \u201cThis provision is key to ensuring that border security is achieved, and is also necessary to ensure that a reform package can actually move through Congress,\u201d Flake said in a statement.  Flake called on Obama to embrace a temporary worker program that the senator said is necessary \u201cto ensure that future labor needs are addressed.\u201d  The Republican senators negotiating a plan include his 2008 presidential opponent, Senator  John McCain  of Arizona, along with Rubio, a top surrogate for 2012 Republican presidential nominee  Mitt Romney  who also is seen as a possible 2016 presidential contender.  Immigration legislation signed by President  Ronald Reagan  in 1986 made three million undocumented workers eligible for legal status and created a market for fraudulent documentation. Illegal immigration soared, casting a shadow of subsequent efforts to legalize immigrants.  2007 Effort  An effort by President  George W. Bush  in 2007 to rewrite immigration law failed amid public ire over illegal immigration.  \u201cImmigration reform, like tax and Social Security reform, is very complex,\u201d said Stephen Yale-Loehr, an immigration law expert and professor of law at  Cornell University . \u201cEven if everyone wants reform, it may still take a long time to get a bill through Congress.\u201d  The plan may face its toughest test in the Republican-led House, which is dominated by lawmakers who\u2019ve expressed little interest in immigration laws beyond tightening border security.  \u201cUntil the administration creates a comprehensive border security plan that includes a reasonable definition of operational control we can measure, we cannot quantify success or failure,\u201d House  Homeland Security  Chairman Michael McCaul, a Texas Republican, said in a statement. \u201cThe Senate blueprint appropriately made securing our borders a priority, while the administration appears content to once again neglect to do so.\u201d  To contact the reporters on this story: Kathleen Hunter in Washington at  khunter9@bloomberg.net ; Lisa Lerer in Washington at  llerer@bloomberg.net   To contact the editor responsible for this story: Jodi Schneider at  jschneider50@bloomberg.net","path":".\/2008_2012_msft_bloomberg_news\/obama-works-to-turn-election-win-into-immigration-force.txt"},{"id":51706678,"title":"Hong Kong Stocks Drop Ahead of Fed; City Developers Gain","released_at":"<date>September 18 2013<\/date> <time>08:38:47<\/time>","content":"Hong Kong  stocks  fell for a second\nday before the U.S. Federal Open Market Committee\u2019s announces\nwhether it will pare record stimulus. Duffey Jr. said yesterday in a summary judgment\nin Atlanta. The \u201cfailure to predict the market does not amount\nto securities fraud.\u201d  The SEC sued Morgan Keegan in July 2009, claiming it\nencouraged brokers to push the debt before the $330 billion\nmarket froze in February 2008, and customers weren\u2019t told about\nthe growing risk the securities could become difficult to sell.\nSince then, dozens of banks have returned billions of dollars to\nharmed investors.  John Nester , an SEC spokesman, said the agency is\nconsidering whether to appeal. A phone call after normal\nbusiness hours to Tim Deighton, a spokesman for Birmingham,\nAlabama-based Regions, wasn\u2019t immediately returned.  Federal and state regulators have sanctioned banks for\nselling auction-rate securities as safe, cash-like investments.\nThe instruments are typically municipal bonds, corporate bonds\nand preferred stocks whose rates of return are periodically\nreset through an auction.  The SEC cited testimony of four customers claiming they\nwere misled by Morgan Keegan brokers who allegedly said ARS were\n\u201ccash equivalents\u201d and \u201ccompletely liquid,\u201d according to the\njudgment. Duffey faulted the agency for arguing those investors\u2019\nclaims were true for others.  \u201cThe SEC is attempting to bootstrap the investor-specific\nimpact of the misrepresentations alleged by four individual\ninvestors as a grounds to seek relief for a whole class of\ninvestors without any evidence that the other investors received\nsimilar oral misrepresentations,\u201d Duffey said in the judgment. Butler was to be resentenced yesterday. In a letter June 27\nto U.S. District Judge Jack B. Weinstein in Brooklyn, New York,\nhis lawyers said Butler couldn\u2019t be resentenced yet because of\nprocedural issues. They also said Butler would agree to have the\nfraud charge remain in federal court in Brooklyn, even after the\nappeals court said it belonged in federal court in Manhattan.\nThe agreement apparently means that the conviction would stand.  \u201cThe defendant will agree to venue in the Eastern District\nof New York,\u201d they wrote.  Butler and his partner,  Julian Tzolov , were convicted of\nintentionally misleading clients about securities purchased on\ntheir behalf.  One of Butler\u2019s lawyers, Steven F. Molo, confirmed the\nadjournment in a phone interview and said the parties would have\nto discuss the procedural issues.  Robert Nardoza  , a spokesman\nfor U.S. Attorney Loretta Lynch, declined to comment.  The case is U.S. v. Tzolov, 08-cr-370, U.S. District Court,\nEastern District of New York (Brooklyn). Instead the list is dominated by the big technology winners of the past 20 years that have built innovation into their DNA (Apple, Google, Amazon, Samsung, Microsoft), and a lot of smaller, newer start-ups. The main exceptions are Target, Coca Cola, Corning, Ford, and Nike (the company that topped the list).  It's not surprising that younger  entrepreneurial firms are considered more innovative . After all, they are born from a new idea, and survive by finding creative ways to make that idea commercially viable. Larger, well-rooted companies however have just as much motivation to be innovative \u2014 and,  as Scott Anthony has argued , they have even more resources to invest in new ventures. So  why doesn't innovation thrive  in mature organizations? To get some perspective on this question, I recently talked with  Steve Blank , a serial entrepreneur, co-author of The Start-Up Owner's Manual, and father of the \"lean start-up\" movement. As someone who teaches entrepreneurship not only in universities but also to U.S. government agencies and private corporations, he has a unique perspective. And in that context, he cites three major reasons why established companies struggle to innovate. First, he says, the focus of an established firm is to execute an existing business model \u2014 to make sure it operates efficiently and satisfies customers. In contrast,  the main job  of a start-up is to search for a workable business model, to find the right match between customer needs and what the company can profitably offer.  In other words in a start-up, innovation is not just about implementing a creative idea, but rather the search for a way to turn some aspect of that idea into something that customers are willing to pay for.  Finding a viable business model is not a linear, analytical process that can be guided by a business plan. Instead it requires iterative experimentation, talking to large numbers of potential customers, trying new things, and continually making adjustments. As such,  discovering a new business model is inherently risky, and is far more likely to fail than to succeed.  Blank explains that this is why companies need a portfolio of new business start-ups rather than putting all of their eggs into a limited number of baskets. But with little tolerance for risk, established firms want their new ventures to produce revenue in a predictable way \u2014 which only increases the possibility of failure. Finally, Blank notes that the  people who are best suited to search for new business models and conduct iterative experiments usually are not the same managers who succeed at running existing business units.  Instead,  internal entrepreneurs are more likely to be rebels  who chafe at standard ways of doing things, don't like to follow the rules, continually question authority, and have a high tolerance for failure. Yet instead of appointing these people to create new ventures, big companies often select high-potential managers who meet their standard competencies and are good at execution (and are easier to manage).  The bottom line of Steve Blank's comments is that the process of starting a new business \u2014 no matter how compelling the original idea \u2014 is fundamentally different from running an existing one. So if you want your company to grow organically, then you need to organize your efforts around these differences.  Watch for Steve Blank's upcoming article in the April issue of the Harvard Business Review.","path":".\/2008_2012_msft_bloomberg_news\/steve-blank-on-why-big-companies-can-t-innovate.txt"},{"id":66571431,"title":"Google to Microsoft\u2019s New Import May Be Cyber Standards","released_at":"<date>April 26 2013<\/date> <time>04:01:00<\/time>","content":"Efforts by  Google Inc. They founded what is now  Apple Inc. (AAPL)  in 1976 to sell their\ncreations. Apple, based in Cupertino, California, surpassed\nMicrosoft Corp. in 2010 to become the world\u2019s most valuable\ntechnology company.  A timeline of Jobs\u2019s career follows:  Feb. 24, 1955: A boy is born in San Francisco to college\ngraduate students Joanne Carole Schieble and Syrian immigrant\nAbdulfattah \u201cJohn\u201d Jandali. Jobs said in a 1997 New York Times\nMagazine article that he wouldn\u2019t talk about his biological\nparents, citing privacy. He is adopted by Clara and Paul Jobs,\nwho name him Steven Paul Jobs and raise him in the suburbs of\n Mountain View  and Los Altos, California.  1972: Jobs graduates from Homestead High School, the Cupertino\nschool that is also the alma mater of Wozniak, his future\nbusiness partner. Jobs enrolls at  Reed College  in  Portland ,\n Oregon , and drops out after one semester. \u201cThe minute I dropped\nout I could stop taking the required classes that didn\u2019t\ninterest me and begin dropping in on the ones that looked\ninteresting,\u201d he said during a June 2005  commencement speech  at\n Stanford University .  1974: Jobs returns to California and works as a designer at\nAtari Corp., the video-game company. He later travels to  India \nin search of spiritual enlightenment.  1975: Jobs and Wozniak hang out at Homebrew Computer Club, an\ninformal gathering of engineers and hobbyists who swap parts and\nideas. The two show off the Apple I and Apple II computers at\nthe club meetings, according to  an article  written by Wozniak.  April 1, 1976: Jobs, Wozniak and Ron Wayne found Apple. Wayne,\nwho worked with Jobs at Atari, gives up his 10 percent share of\nApple less than two weeks later.  April 16, 1977: Wozniak and Jobs introduce the Apple II, which\nbecomes one of the first successful personal computers.  May 1978: Jobs\u2019 girlfriend, Chrisann Brennan, gives birth to a\ngirl, Lisa Brennan-Jobs. Chrisann raises Lisa mainly on her own.\nJobs later reconciles with Lisa.  Dec. 12, 1980: Apple goes public at $22 a share. Adjusted for\nsplits since then, the initial public offering price is $2.75.\nApple closed yesterday at $378.25.  February 1982: Jobs, 26, is featured on the cover of Time under\nthe headline, \u201cStriking It Rich, America\u2019s Risk Takers.\u201d He\nappears on the  magazine\u2019s cover  more than a half dozen times.  January 1983: Apple releases the Lisa, the first commercially\nsold computer with a graphical user interface. The Lisa, with a\nprice tag of $9,995, is a commercial failure.  January 1984: Apple announces the new Macintosh computer with an\nad that airs only once, during the  Super Bowl . The ad shows a\nwoman throw a hammer at a giant screen as a voice reads, \u201cOn\nJanuary 24, Apple Computer will introduce Macintosh and you\u2019ll\nsee why 1984 won\u2019t be like \u20181984.\u2019\u201d The Mac, which sells for\n$2,500, becomes the first commercially successful personal\ncomputer to have a graphical user interface and mouse.  September 1985: After being stripped of responsibilities amid a\npower struggle with Chief Executive Officer John Sculley and the\nboard, Jobs resigns as chairman. He tells the board: \u201cI\u2019ve been\nthinking a lot and it\u2019s time for me to get on with my life. It\u2019s\nobvious that I\u2019ve got to do something. I\u2019m 30 years old,\u201d\naccording to Sculley\u2019s book, \u201cOdyssey: Pepsi to Apple.\u201d Jobs\nsoon starts NeXT Computer Inc., which builds high-powered\neducational computers.  February 1986: Jobs buys George Lucas\u2019s computer-graphics shop\nfor $10 million and renames it Pixar Inc.  March 18, 1991: He marries Laurene Powell at a hotel in Yosemite\nNational Park. Their first child, Reed, is born in September,\nfollowed by daughters Erin in 1995 and Eve in 1998.  February 1993: NeXT decides to stop making computer workstations\nand lays off more than half of its 540 employees.  November 1995: Pixar releases its first feature film, \u201cToy\nStory,\u201d which grosses more than $360 million and is nominated\nfor three Oscars. In the same month, the company goes public.\nJobs would say in a 1998  BusinessWeek article , \u201cI think Pixar\nhas the opportunity to be the next Disney -- not replace Disney\n-- but be the next Disney.\u201d  Dec. 20, 1996: Apple says it will buy NeXT for $400 million and\nrehire Jobs as a consultant to help the company revamp its\nflagship Macintosh software. The third-largest PC maker says it\nwill incorporate NeXT\u2019s technology into the next version of the\nMac operating system. Apple was in such dire straits before the\nreturn of Jobs that BusinessWeek in February ran a cover article\ntitled, \u201cThe Fall of an American Icon.\u201d  July 9, 1997: After 17 months as Apple\u2019s chairman and chief\nexecutive officer, Gilbert Amelio is forced to resign. Jobs\nlater becomes interim CEO while Apple searches for a new leader. (AAPL) \u2019s new iPhone 4S and the previous\nmodel. Until you turn it on.  In a week of using the 4S, I found so many new things\nunder the hood that, with a few cosmetic changes, the company\ncould legitimately have called it \u201ciPhone 5\u201d and no one would\nhave blinked.  The speech-recognition capabilities are vastly better than\non any other mobile device. The camera is much improved, not\njust in specs but in ease of use. And though the phone runs over\n3G, or third-generation,  data networks , it\u2019s faster than some\nphones that are being marketed as 4G.  The new iPhone -- available for order now and in stores on\nOct. 14 -- is physically identical to the iPhone 4. In the U.S.,\nit costs $199 for a model with 16 gigabytes of storage on a two-\nyear contract, $299 for 32 gigabytes and $399 for 64 gigabytes.\nThe phone comes with the new  iOS 5  operating system, which I\u2019ll\ndiscuss in a future column.  The 4S runs on the networks used in the U.S. by  Verizon\nWireless  and  Sprint Nextel Corp. (S) , as well as on those used by\n AT&T Inc. (T)  and most of the rest of the world. That\u2019s particularly\nimportant for Verizon and Sprint users who travel\ninternationally and who won\u2019t have to worry about their phones\nbecoming bricks outside the U.S.  Meeting Siri  The most interesting new feature is  Siri , the voice-\nrecognition system. You\u2019ve long been able to run searches on\nphones using  Google Inc. (GOOG) \u2019s Android software, and  Microsoft Corp. (MSFT) \nhas embedded speech-based features throughout the latest version\nof its Windows Phone 7 operating system. Those phones, though,\nhave a limited vocabulary and often require you to phrase your\ninquiries very carefully.  Siri is something different. Remember the scene in the old\n \u201cStar Trek\u201d movie  where a time-traveling Scotty tries to\ndirect a Mac by picking up the mouse and casually speaking into\nit? Imagine it with just the mouse and not the Mac, and you\u2019ve\ngot the essence of Siri: natural language integrated with the\nphone\u2019s sensors and software.  When I asked Siri, \u201cWill I need an umbrella tonight?\u201d its\nrobotic female voice informed me, \u201cThere\u2019s no rain in the\nforecast,\u201d while the screen displayed the weather report for my\nlocation. When I told it to find me a good Mexican restaurant in\nmy neighborhood, it displayed a listing ranked by Yelp ratings.  No Football Scores  When Siri couldn\u2019t immediately provide an answer, as when I\nasked for the score of the  San Francisco  49ers football game, it\noffered a Web search. You can also use it to make appointments,\nset reminders, dictate outgoing messages and read incoming ones.  Siri did occasionally trip up, sometimes because I confused\nit with homonyms or ambiguous phrasing. For example, when I\nasked it for \u201cwalking directions to 9 Lombard Street,\u201d it\nheard the \u201cto\u201d as \u201ctwo\u201d and provided directions to 29\nLombard instead. And when I was about to go outside and asked,\n\u201cDo I need a jacket?\u201d it presented me with directions to the\nnearest Men\u2019s Wearhouse.  Still, it\u2019s smart enough to be occasionally spooky, as when\nI simply told it to text \u201cDavid\u201d -- and it correctly deduced\nwhich of the 12 Davids in my address book I meant.  If not quite as awesome as Siri, the iPhone 4S camera is\nstill as good as you\u2019re likely to find in a wireless phone,\nsurpassing my previous favorite, the Nokia N8.  More Light  The headline number -- the increase in megapixels to eight\nfrom five -- doesn\u2019t tell the whole story. More striking is\nwhat\u2019s been done with the optics and software, including a\nlarger lens aperture that lets more light hit the sensor, face\ndetection and the ability to shoot video in full 1080p high-\ndefinition.  Sadly, the camera isn\u2019t able to turn a mediocre\nphotographer into a good one. But I particularly appreciated the\nability to take pictures even when the phone was locked, and\nthat I could zoom in and out by pinching and zooming the image,\nfar more intuitive in a touchscreen device than the former\nslider control.  The camera is also noticeably faster, thanks to the phone\u2019s\nnew dual-core A5 processor, the same brain used in Apple\u2019s iPad\n2. Indeed, the faster processor, combined with changes to the\ngraphics, software and antennas, makes the iPhone 4S zippier\nacross the board -- in launching and running apps and even in\ndownloading data.  Beating Samsung  The 4S isn\u2019t a \u201c4G\u201d device, but my tests showed it to be\nas fast or faster on AT&T\u2019s network as phones being sold as\n\u201c4G.\u201d (Verizon and Sprint users won\u2019t see that kind of\nperformance, owing to those carriers\u2019 slower 3G networks.)  Using Ookla\u2019s  Speedtest  app, I compared the 4S with Samsung\nElectronics Co.\u2019s new Galaxy S II, which AT&T labels as 4G. In\ndozens of tests in and around San Francisco, the iPhone 4S\nregistered faster download speeds more than two-thirds of the\ntime.  It achieved that performance without any apparent\ndegradation in battery life. Apple says the new device provides\nup to 8 hours of 3G talk time, an hour longer than the iPhone 4.\nIn regular though not constant use, I was able to go about a day\nand a half between charges.  The phone\u2019s new antenna design seems to have reduced the\nnumber of dropped calls over AT&T\u2019s much-maligned network,\nthough my sample was admittedly limited.  With the iPhone\u2019s continuing advantage in number of apps\n(500,000 and counting), its arrival on the Sprint network and\nits ability to function as a world phone, the 4S doesn\u2019t leave\nmany holes for the competition to plug.  And then there\u2019s this: The 4S is the first phone you\u2019ll\never be tempted to ask for the secret of life. Go ahead --\nyou\u2019ll get an answer, too. It isn\u2019t from \u201c Star Trek ,\u201d though\nscience-fiction readers will recognize, and get a chuckle from,\nthe response.  ( Rich Jaroslovsky  is a Bloomberg News columnist. Intelligence leaders yesterday encountered pushback from\nkey constituencies as they tried to mend fences in the wake of\nformer NSA contractor Edward Snowden\u2019s disclosures about the\nscope of classified programs that collect bulk data on phone and\nInternet use.  NSA Director Keith Alexander was heckled during a speech at\nthe Black Hat conference yesterday in which he appealed to\nhackers to examine \u201cthe facts\u201d about the spy programs and to\nkeep working with his agency on cybersecurity defenses.  Senior intelligence officials were subjected to pointed,\nskeptical question by lawmakers in  Washington  yesterday after\nthe director of national intelligence declassified parts of\ndocuments describing how and why the NSA collects records of\nmillions of Americans\u2019 phone calls.  \u2018Not Convinced\u2019  The documents included a surveillance-court ruling\nunderlying a requirement that a unit of Verizon Communications\nInc. provide all of its customers\u2019 phone-calling logs to the NSA\nunder an order renewed every three months.  They also included congressional briefings from 2009 and\n2011 outlining the scope of that program and one that until 2011\nallowed collection of bulk electronic communications including\ne-mails.  Snowden revealed that the U.S. government was secretly\ncollecting the telephone calling information through the secret\nVerizon court order, and operating a program known as Prism that\ncollects Internet data from Apple Inc., Google Inc., and other\ncompanies to monitor online activity of foreigners believed to\nbe plotting terrorist attacks. The five-page congressional briefings, provided to\nlawmakers on the Intelligence and Judiciary committees in 2009\nand 2011, outline the scope of the program, as well as one that\nalso allowed collection of bulk electronic communications. U.S.\nofficials have said that aspect of the program ended in 2011. And on Dec. 3 the government probably will say that the\nU.S. unemployment rate is stuck at 9.6 percent, according to the\nmedian estimate of 57 economists surveyed by Bloomberg News,\nwhich will translate to anemic pay gains.  Not at  Google Inc.  The search-engine behemoth, looking to\nstem the defection of key workers to other hot Silicon Valley\nemployers, announced last month that its workforce of about\n22,000 employees will get a 10 percent wage hike starting in\n2011. (Imagine, when will the average employee feel it\u2019s a\nreasonable gamble to walk into the boss\u2019 office and demand a 10\npercent raise or threaten to walk?)  \u201cGoogle has to preempt the desire for its talented\nemployees to seek work elsewhere,\u201d says  Richard Florida ,\ndirector of the  Martin Prosperity Institute  at the University of\nToronto. \u201cI\u2019ve seen talented employees flee the previous\nemployer of the moment for the next employer of the moment --\njust ask Microsoft.\u201d  With about $33 billion in cash and short-term investments,\nand a  stock-market capitalization  of almost $180 billion, Google\ncan afford to throw money and shares at its employees. Yet the\nsignificance of Google\u2019s across-the-board pay raise extends far\nbeyond corporate competition. It reflects a war for brains and\ntalent that is heating up throughout the information technology\necosystem.  Scrambling for Position  Web-based search-engine companies, mobile Internet\nproviders, application developers, wireless companies and other\ninnovative communication firms are jockeying for position in\ngrowing, and profitable, markets. And while the implosion of\nhousing, the bank bailouts, and the divisive politics of fiscal\nand monetary policy received most of the headlines since 2007,\nthose years also marked the acceleration of the information-\nintensive creative economy.  Google\u2019s  growth  and shared prosperity serve as a\npunctuation point. \u201cI have been convinced for some time that we\nare going through a major restructuring of the economy that is\nmuch bigger than the difficult time we are going through right\nnow,\u201d says  Erik Brynjolfsson , director of the MIT Center for\nDigital Business.  Certainly, compared with most parts of the economy,\ninnovation is flourishing in the communications and information\necology. Think  Apple Inc.  and apps.  Amazon.com Inc.  and online\nretailers.  Payrolls Expand  That growth is showing up in jobs and wages. From October\n2009 to October 2010, the number of jobs in computer systems\ndesign and related services rose by 7.5 percent, according to\nthe  Bureau of Labor Statistics . Telecommunications employment\nwas up (0.9 percent), as was data processing, hosting and\nrelated services (0.5 percent), computer and peripheral\nequipment (0.7 percent), and communication equipment (0.7\npercent).  The split shows up in geography as well. Workers in the\nmost cosmopolitan cities are seeing wage gains. For instance,\nthe average weekly wage increase for all private industry\nworkers in the U.S. from the first quarter of 2009 to the first\nquarter of 2010 was 1 percent, according to the BLS. Yet average\nweekly wages in tech-heavy San Francisco over the same time\nperiod increased 5.4 percent. The gain in information-rich\nWashington was 2.8 percent. New York City saw an 11.9 percent\nincrease, with the biggest pay earned in finance (22.7 percent)\nand professional business services (10.9 percent).  \u2018Knowledge Work\u2019  \u201cThis isn\u2019t about information technology,\u201d says  Paul Saffo , a long-time Silicon Valley consultant and a managing\ndirector at Discern Investment Analytics. \u201cThis is about\nknowledge work.\u201d  It\u2019s intriguing to note that almost a century ago another\npay raise signaled a coming transformation of the U.S. economy.\nHenry Ford announced on Jan. 5, 1914, that he would double his\nfactory workers\u2019 wages to $5 a day. (He also reduced daily hours\nworked from 9 to 8.)  Ford Motor Co. , like Google, had good\nbusiness reasons for its move: The Model-T assembly line was a\nbrutal place and in 1913 Ford had to hire 50,448 people to\nmaintain a workforce of 13,623, according to  Richard Tedlow ,\nbusiness historian at the Harvard Business School.  Paying workers a better wage than they could get elsewhere\nencouraged loyalty. But the $5 wage also marked the passage\ntoward a mass-production economy where factory workers were\nworking class on the job but middle class at home, once they\nshared in the remarkable productivity bounty of manufacturing.\nAnd since smokestack America was such a dominant part of the\neconomy, the benefits spilled into industries outside\nmanufacturing.  Creative Class  Fast forward to today: The wealth of the emergent knowledge\neconomy or creator economy is largely being pocketed by\nemployers and employees in the creative industries. It\u2019s a\ngrowing sector of the economy with knowledge work or creative\nwork -- people who are paid to think -- including everyone from\nsoftware programmers to scientists to graphic designers.  According to Florida, the creative class made up 32 percent\nof the American workforce in 2009, up from 29 percent in 1998.\nIn contrast, service jobs -- typically low-paying work --\ncomprise about 45 percent of the workforce.  It\u2019s an open question as to whether America will persist as\na house divided between a relatively well-off knowledge sector\nelite and everyone else. There\u2019s no doubt that the knowledge\neconomy is one of the few bright spots in the private-sector\nlabor market and is giving a lift to a struggling economy. These subsidiaries can help U.K.-based multinationals shift income to mailboxes in tax havens.  \u201cHere is a blatant incentive inside the U.K. tax system to move profits previously in London into a tax haven,\u201d said  Richard Murphy , director of Tax Research LLP in Norfolk, England. \u201cIt is just absurd. At the same time, we have people like Osborne saying \u2019I\u2019m going to crack down on  tax avoidance .\u201d\u2019  As politicians in Europe and the U.S. talk tough on corporate tax dodging, several of their governments are helping multinationals lower tax bills. They have been cutting corporate rates, introducing laws that encourage tax avoidance, and rejecting proposals to close loopholes. Even amid growing public outrage in Europe against austerity policies, the gulf between rhetoric and reality on taxation means individuals rather than businesses are often bearing the brunt of higher taxes.  \u2018Avoidance Game\u2019  At a time when unemployment in the European Union is at record levels, nations eager for jobs remain hesitant to alienate multinational companies by raising their taxes. Instead, countries such as Spain, Greece, and Hungary have imposed hefty sales tax increases, a hit borne most severely by poor people.  \u201cI am skeptical whether the different countries have the political courage to take on the corporate tax avoidance game,\u201d said Sven Giegold, a member of the EU parliament from Germany\u2019s Green Party. \u201cYou need consensus of the participating partners, and I do not see the leadership to force through a global model.\u201d  In December, the European Commission, the governing body of the EU, declared war on tax evasion and avoidance, which it said costs the EU 1 trillion euros a year. It encouraged its members to create \u201cblacklists\u201d of tax havens.  Still, the commission instructed them to single out only non-EU countries as havens -- even though member-nations such as Luxembourg, the Netherlands, and Ireland encourage multinational companies to legally dodge billions of dollars in taxes around the world.  Helpless EU  Similarly, the Organization for Economic Cooperation and Development, an influential publicly funded think tank on international tax policy, used to cite potentially harmful tax behavior by member states, including Luxembourg, the Netherlands, Ireland, Belgium and others. It stopped issuing those reports in 2006 because of \u201ca lack of political interest\u201d from member nations, said Pascal Saint Amans, director of the OECD\u2019s Center for Tax Policy and Administration.  \u201cThe Europeans say one thing and do another,\u201d said H. David Rosenbloom, the head of the international tax program at  New York  University\u2019s law school and an attorney at Caplin & Drysdale in Washington. \u201cThe EU can\u2019t do anything as long as it\u2019s got Luxembourg and the Netherlands and Ireland\u201d within the union.  EU spokeswoman Natasja Bohez-Rubiano said its member states have agreed to not introduce any new tax loopholes, thus making internal blacklists unnecessary.  Regimes Undermine  \u201cWhat is clearly needed, however, is greater coordination in taxation, to prevent one national regime from undermining another, and to address loopholes and mismatches. That is precisely what the Commission is proposing,\u201d she said.  Some action may yet emerge from all the talk. The OECD says it will release an \u201caction plan\u201d on profit shifting by July. The agency expects to address policies by member states that help corporations avoid taxes, Saint Amans said.  The European Commission is now re-examining a set of key EU rules that makes it easier for companies to dodge taxes. The most important are a pair of directives allowing units of multinationals to shift profits into subsidiaries free of withholding taxes -- regardless of whether the units receiving the cash ever pay any taxes on it.  \u201cThese two directives are sort of the infrastructure for the tax dodging,\u201d said Giegold, the parliament member from Germany.  French President  Francois Hollande  recently said he wants companies there to disclose more details on foreign units, including profits and taxes in haven subsidiaries. Hollande\u2019s former budget minister last month acknowledged hiding much of his wealth offshore.  Efforts Stalled  Countries are increasingly announcing agreements to share information about individual tax dodgers, prodded in part by a new U.S. law that requires foreign banks to report information on accounts to the Internal Revenue Service.  Yet efforts to make corporations pay more taxes are largely stalled.  Since 2007, countries including Italy, Spain, the U.K., Germany, Greece and Sweden have cut their corporate tax rates, seeking to compete with neighbors for profits and jobs. In some cases, countries are keeping tax incentives in place for native corporations, even as they eliminate loopholes for foreign multinationals.  In that vein, France last year tightened a law that permitted foreign multinationals to use French subsidiaries there to rack up big deductions on interest expense. While the country has changed some laws for domestic companies as well, the rules for such deductions for native French businesses remain generous, practitioners said.  Profit Shifting  \u201cGovernments don\u2019t like it when profit shifting is happening to them. But since they want their own multinationals to be successful, they\u2019re effectively helping them engage in profit shifting-type transactions in other countries,\u201d said Les Samuels, a former assistant U.S. Treasury secretary for tax policy under President  Bill Clinton . \u201cIt could be considered a beggar thy neighbor tax policy.\u201d  In January, the Netherlands held a parliamentary debate to examine its own role as an enabler of tax avoidance. The country\u2019s extensive tax treaty network and permissive policies have encouraged companies to shift as much as $13 trillion a year through paper units there, much of it en route to island havens. As previously reported by Bloomberg, companies including Google,  Yahoo! Inc. (YHOO) ,  Dell Inc. (DELL) , Merck & Co.,  Cisco Systems Inc. (CSCO) ,  Microsoft Corp. (MSFT)  and  Forest Laboratories Inc. (FRX)  have made use of such shelters, with nicknames like the \u201cDutch Sandwich.\u201d  Cosmetic Change  At that debate, the parliament rejected a pair of motions to tighten loopholes for companies in the Netherlands, including requiring them to have employees in the country to be eligible for favorable tax treatment.  Instead, parliament made a cosmetic change by rejecting the term \u201ctax haven\u201d to describe the Netherlands. In April, the parliament asked the  finance ministry  to develop an \u201caction plan\u201d to address Dutch tax dodging, but hasn\u2019t taken up any anti-tax haven legislation since.  Meanwhile, Ireland, already an attractive destination for multinational companies, is making it even easier for them to avoid taxes.  Last year, for example, Irish revenue authorities agreed to let Google make billions of dollars in royalty payments directly to a Bermuda subsidiary, helping to cut the company\u2019s tax bill by at least $2 billion a year, according to U.S. and overseas securities filings. Previously, Google had routed those payments through a shell company in the Netherlands to avoid a 20 percent Irish withholding tax on payments destined for island havens. According to a person with knowledge of the arrangement, Ireland agreed to accept an additional tax well below 20 percent in exchange for the favorable treatment.  Even Germany  Even Germany, considered relatively vigilant in policing tax avoidance, permits multinationals to bring profits home from havens -- especially other EU countries -- without any additional levy.  \u201cIt would be very important for Germany to do something about this,\u201d said Markus Meinzer, a senior analyst for  Tax Justice Network , based in Marburg, Germany.  While lacking Europe\u2019s public uproar over corporate tax avoidance, the U.S. has seen the same gap between policy makers\u2019 talk and action.  \u201cEvery multinational company should have to pay a basic minimum tax,\u201d President  Barack Obama  said last year in his  State of the Union  speech. \u201cNo American company should be able to avoid paying its fair share of taxes.\u201d  Loopholes Open  Along those lines, the Treasury Department in April unveiled a list of global tax loopholes that it wants to close, many of which it is targeting for the fifth year in a row. With the exception of one provision changing the way U.S. multinational companies take credits they get for paying income taxes abroad, none of the major initiatives have become law.  In late 2011, Representative  Dave Camp , chairman of the House Ways and Means Committee, surprised industry groups by announcing a set of international tax proposals, many of which could have hampered corporate shelter strategies. Almost nineteen months later, the Michigan Republican still hasn\u2019t introduced a bill to turn those ideas into law. A spokesman for Camp said the committee will bring forward a tax reform bill this year, including the international proposals.  \u2018Bedroom Tax\u2019  Nowhere is the public anger over corporate tax dodging more visible than in the U.K. Protesters have organized repeated marches and public demonstrations, including occupations in December of Starbucks coffee shops. In April, demonstrators rallied outside the homes of U.K. government officials over the so-called \u201cbedroom tax\u201d -- serving one of the officials with a mock eviction notice. The bedroom tax is not actually a tax, but a reduction in government housing benefits for people deemed to have too much living space.  In their public comments, British leaders are responding. The House of Commons has said it will ask Google to return for a second hearing this coming Thursday to explain its low U.K. tax bill. Prime Minister  David Cameron  wrote to the president of the European Council in late April that he wants Europe to lead a fight on tax dodging.  \u201cAs you know, the loss of  tax revenue  resulting from tax evasion and aggressive avoidance is staggering,\u201d he wrote. \u201cIn a period of fiscal consolidation where hard-working citizens and businesses are being asked to bear extra burdens, we need coordinated, truly global action to address these issues.\u201d  At a meeting of the Group of Seven nations on Saturday in Aylesbury, outside London, Chancellor of the Exchequer Osborne said it is \u201cincredibly important that companies and individuals pay the tax that is due.\u201d The G-7, which includes the U.S., agreed to act together to stop tax avoidance, he said.  Double Speak  Yet the U.K. is aggressively moving to make it easier for multinationals to avoid taxes. Beginning in 2009, the country began switching from taxing worldwide income to solely taxing profit that companies claim are earned within the country, a so-called \u201cterritorial\u201d system. It eliminated taxes on dividends paid to a U.K. company, even if coming from a subsidiary in a tax haven.  Beginning last month, the U.K. slashed the tax rate to 10 percent from the regular 23 percent rate on profit attributed to patents and intellectual property to lure research and technology jobs.  Yvette Hodgson, a spokeswoman for the U.K. Treasury, said the government is \u201ccommitted to creating the most competitive corporate tax system in the G20.\u201d  \u201cGlobal tax rules have stood still for almost a century,\u201d Hodgson said. \u201cBritain is leading the international effort to bring them into the twenty first century.\u201d","path":".\/2008_2012_msft_bloomberg_news\/europe-eases-corporate-tax-dodge-as-worker-burdens-rise.txt"},{"id":61792307,"title":"Strategic Hotels Turns From Penny Stock to Deal Target","released_at":"<date>June 20 2013<\/date> <time>20:33:50<\/time>","content":"Strategic Hotels & Resorts Inc. A. Intellectually stimulating and gratifying.  B. Excellent pay for new bachelor\u2019s degree grads.  C. A career dead-end.  The correct answer (with a \u201cyour mileage may vary\u201d\ndisclaimer) is: D. All of the above.  Although the very term \u201ccoding\u201d evokes an image of\ntedium, it is an intellectually challenging activity, creative\nand even artistic. If you like puzzles and are good\nanalytically, software development may be your cup of tea. You\nnot only get to solve puzzles for a living, but in essence you\ncompose them.  Wages for new computer-science graduates working as\nsoftware engineers are at, or near, the top of most surveys,\ncertainly compared with new humanities grads. We hear about\nthe gap a lot this time of year, as students compare job\noffers.  You had better be good to get that first job in computer\nengineering, because you will probably be asked to  code on\ncommand  during job interviews; employers have been burned too\noften by those with high grades yet low ability. But those who\nare chosen are generally paid well and love the work.  The downside? Well, say you interview as a graduating\ncollege senior at  Facebook Inc. (FB)  You may find, to your initial\ndelight, that the place looks just like a fun-loving dorm --\nand the adults seem to be missing. But that is a sign of how\nthe profession has devolved in recent years to one lacking in\nlongevity. Many programmers find that their employability\nstarts to decline at about age 35.  Gone by 40  Employers dismiss them as either lacking in up-to-date\ntechnical skills -- such as the latest programming-language\nfad -- or \u201cnot suitable for entry level.\u201d In other words,\neither underqualified or overqualified. That doesn\u2019t leave\nmuch, does it? Statistics show that most software developers\nare out of the field by age 40.  Employers have admitted this in unguarded moments.  Craig Barrett , a former chief executive officer of  Intel Corp .,\nfamously remarked that \u201cthe half-life of an engineer, software\nor hardware, is only a few years,\u201d while  Mark Zuckerberg  of\nFacebook has blurted out that young programmers are superior.  Vivek Wadhwa , a former technology executive and now a\nbusiness writer and Duke University researcher,  wrote  that in\n2008 David Vaskevitch, then the chief technology officer at\n Microsoft Corp. (MSFT) , \u201cacknowledged that the vast majority of new\nMicrosoft employees are young, but said that this is so\nbecause older workers tend to go into more senior jobs and\nthere are fewer of those positions to begin with.\u201d  More than a decade ago, Congress commissioned a  National\nResearch Council study  of the age issue in the profession.\nThe council found that it took 23.4 percent longer for the\nover-40 workers to find work after losing their jobs, and that\nthey had to take an average pay cut of 13.7 percent on the new\njob.  Why do the employers prefer to hire the new or recent\ngrads? Is it really because only they have the latest skill\nsets? That argument doesn\u2019t jibe with the fact that young ones\nlearned those modern skills from old guys like me. Instead,\nthe problem is that the 35-year-old programmer has simply\npriced herself out of the market. As Wadhwa notes, even if the\n45-year-old programmer making $120,000 has the right skills,\n\u201ccompanies would rather hire the younger workers.\u201d  Whether the employers\u2019 policy is proper or not, this is\nthe problem facing workers in the software profession. And\nit\u2019s worsened by the  H-1B  work-visa program. Government data\nshow that H-1B software engineers tend to be much younger than\ntheir American counterparts. Basically, when the employers run\nout of young Americans to hire, they turn to the young H-1Bs,\nbypassing the older Americans.  Fewer Managerial Jobs  With talent, street smarts and keen networking skills,\nyou might still get good work in your 50s. Moving up to\nmanagement is also a possibility, but as Microsoft\u2019s\nVaskevitch pointed out, these jobs are limited in number.\nQualifications include being \u201cverbally aggressive,\u201d as one\nmanager put it to me, and often a willingness to make late-\nnight calls to those programmers in  India  you have offshored\nthe work to.  Finally, those high programmer salaries are actually low,\nbecause the same talents (analytical and problem-solving\nability, attention to detail) command much more money in other\nfields, such as law and finance. A large technology company\nmight typically pay  new law-school graduates  and  MBAs  salaries\nand compensation approaching double what they give new\nmaster\u2019s degree  grads in computer science .  If you choose a software-engineering career, just keep in\nmind that you could end up working for one of those lowly\nhumanities majors someday.  (Norman Matloff is a professor of computer science at the\n University of California , Davis. The opinions expressed are\nhis own.)  Read more opinion online from  Bloomberg View . The term is used today to describe businesses that obtain\npatents from technology companies and then file infringement\nlawsuits against the sellers\u2019 competitors. Tech companies use\nprivateers to distract their adversaries or collect royalties on\nthe patents without provoking retaliatory litigation, said Ron Laurie, managing director of Inflexion Point Strategy LLC in\n Palo Alto ,  California .  Nokia Oyj (NOK) ,  Microsoft Corp. (MSFT)  and Alcatel-Lucent are among\ncompanies connected with these licensing firms. Companies that\nwould, in the past, assert their patents in lawsuits only to\nprotect their property now say they work with privateers because\nthey\u2019re obligated to make money from past research.  \u201cThe moral stigma of being associated with patent\nassertion isn\u2019t what it used to be,\u201d said Laurie, who advises\ncompanies on intellectual-property purchases. \u201cThe whole\npatent-assertion business is becoming more and more legitimized\nthrough these privateering operations.\u201d  The practice of selling patents and retaining the rights to\nshare in lawsuit proceeds probably will grow as early innovators\nin mobile-phone development, such as Nokia and Ericsson AB, lose\nmarket share to the likes of Apple and Samsung Electronics Co.  It can also make it hard to figure out who actually owns a\npatent. The U.S. Patent and  Trademark Office  plans at a  meeting \ntoday to discuss possible rules requiring more disclosure about\nthe \u201creal party in interest\u201d in patents and applications.  Litigation Strategies  \u201cEvery large company is selling patents today,\u201d said  Ron Epstein , chief executive officer of patent brokerage Epicenter\nIP Group LLC.  \u201cWhen they are selling, they are looking for the best\npossible price,\u201d he said. \u201cDoes an intelligent manager of a\nresource called a patent have a responsibility of getting the\nhighest possible return for these assets, or do they have to\nworry about how it will harm competitors?\u201d  Yesterday, a Nevada licensing company,  Unwired Planet Inc. (UPIP) ,\nsaid Ericsson had sold it 2,185 phone-related patents and\napplications in return for \u201ccertain ongoing rights in future\nrevenues.\u201d  MobileMedia Ideas LLC, a licensing company holding former\nNokia patents, last month won a jury verdict against  Apple Inc. (AAPL) ,\nwhich has an agreement allowing use of different patents Nokia\nowns.  BT Group Plc (BT\/A)  and Alcatel-Lucent also have transferred\n patent rights  to entities filing infringement suits, and are\nentitled to share their licensing proceeds.  MobileMedia is \u201csolely responsible for their own licensing\nand litigation strategies,\u201d said Mark Durrant, a spokesman for\nthe Finnish handset maker.  Fewer Risks  Companies that sell patents don\u2019t face the costs of\nlitigation or the possibility of a countersuit against their\nproducts, Laurie said.  When Nokia sued Apple in 2009, the iPhone maker lodged\ninfringement claims against Nokia. The companies, which could\nhave faced limits on sales of their products if they lost,\nnegotiated an agreement two years later.  Five years ago, any connections with patent-assertion\ncompanies reflected poorly, Laurie said. \u201cNow that\u2019s kind of\nhistory and everyone\u2019s singing \u2018How can I get in on this\naction?\u2019\u201d he said.  Patent Pool  MobileMedia owns patents that originated with Nokia, Sony\nCorp. and MPEG LA, the licensing administrator for a pool of\npatents used by consumer-electronics makers. Those three\nretained a stake in MobileMedia, according to a June 21, 2010,\nfiling in the Apple case.  A federal jury in  Delaware  found on Dec. 13 that Apple\u2019s\niPhone infringed three patents held by MobileMedia. A second\ntrial will be held to determine how much Cupertino, California-\nbased Apple should pay.  Research in Motion Ltd., which makes the BlackBerry phone,\nlost a Swedish arbitration court case in November challenging\nMobileMedia\u2019s right to sue. RIM and Nokia announced a licensing\ndeal Dec. 21 that resolves other litigation. The MobileMedia\ncase is continuing.  Paris-based Alcatel-Lucent set up a fund called MultiMedia\nPatent Trust to hold Lucent patents. A jury on Dec. 13 cleared\nApple and LG Electronics Inc. of the trust\u2019s infringement\nclaims.  Redmond, Washington-based Microsoft and Nokia will get a\nshare of licensing proceeds from Nokia patents transferred to a\nCanadian firm, Mosaid Technologies Inc.  Google Inc. (GOOG)  filed a\ncomplaint with European regulators in June saying the Mosaid\nagreement improperly thwarts competition.  Nokia\u2019s Reasons  \u201cOften we do not have the resources or otherwise are not\nbest positioned ourselves to exploit those inventions, either\nthrough our own products or through our own licensing\nactivities,\u201d said Paul Melin, Nokia\u2019s chief intellectual\nproperty officer. \u201cDivestments of patents have become a very\nimportant channel for us to monetize and realize the value of\nour research and development.\u201d  Melin said the company has transferred patents more than 20\ntimes over the past five years, many going to companies whose\nmain business is to derive licensing revenue.  David Cuddy, a Microsoft spokesman, and  Mary Ward , an\nAlcatel-Lucent spokeswoman, had no comment.  Blurred Connections  The changing ownership of a patent can make it hard to\ndetermine who benefits from a lawsuit.  In a case against Google and  AOL Inc. (AOL)  in Alexandria,\n Virginia , a judge confronted what he called the \u201cincreasingly\ncommon but always vexing\u201d question of who has \u201call substantial\nrights\u201d to a patent. That information is needed, District Judge\nT.S. Ellis said, to make sure the firm that brought the case,\nSuffolk Technologies LLC, had standing to sue.  Suffolk Technologies is owned by a group that includes\nGoldman Sachs Group Inc., General Atlantic Partners LP and\nBoston Consulting Group Inc., the judge said. The Bakers, who started Dragon in their Boston-area home, had seen it grow into a company with $68 million in sales, more than 350 employees and operations in the U.S.,  Germany , U.K,  France  and  Japan . They wanted to sell to a company that would let them continue to develop the technology they had spent their professional and married lives creating.  \u201cThis was the most important business decision of our lives,\u201d Janet Baker said in an interview in the couple\u2019s home in West Newton,  Massachusetts . \u201cWe chose Goldman because of their global reach and their reputation as the world\u2019s most important investment bank.\u201d  In a federal trial that began yesterday in  Boston , the Bakers claim that shoddy work by Goldman Sachs on the $580 million all-stock sale of Dragon to a Belgian competitor, Lernout & Hauspie Speech Products NV, cost them their company and their fortune.  Within months of the sale\u2019s June 2000 close, Lernout & Hauspie collapsed in an accounting scandal and its shares that the Bakers took as payment for their 51 percent stake in Dragon were worthless.  \u2018Like Our Child\u2019  Worse, according to Jim Baker, they no longer had access to the speech-recognition technology they had created. The patents underlying Dragon products including their popular dictation program, Dragon NaturallySpeaking, were sold at a bankruptcy auction.  \u201cDragon Systems and the Dragon technology was like our child,\u201d Jim Baker said in the interview in May.  Goldman Sachs says it isn\u2019t to blame. The fraud at Lernout & Hauspie, which the bank said it couldn\u2019t have been expected to discover, caused the Bakers\u2019 losses, Goldman Sachs argued in court papers.  The bank also said its contract was with Dragon, which no longer exists, and argued that the Bakers themselves lack legal standing to sue. The New York-based bank said it advised Dragon to get its accountants, Arthur Andersen LLP, to probe Lernout & Hauspie\u2019s financial status.  The four-man Goldman Sachs team assigned to the transaction provided Dragon with competent advice, the bank said in court filings.  Same Approach  \u201cThere\u2019s no difference in the quality or the standard or the approach that we take in working on assignments for small companies or large companies,\u201d Gene T. Sykes, Goldman Sachs\u2019s head of mergers and acquisitions, said in a 2011 deposition in the case. \u201cEvery client, whether large or small, gets the same high-quality approach.\u201d  The Bakers claim the opposite is true. Jim, a mathematician, and Janet, a biophysicist, said they methodically considered what area of research to spend their lives pursuing. They were looking for a field in which they could make a concrete contribution within 40 years or so -- the span of a professional career, Janet Baker said. They chose computer speech recognition.  Dragon Decor  Much of the couple\u2019s early work was done at the dining-room table in their Victorian home, which is still filled with dragons -- dragon kites, a dragon sculpture by the door, the Bakers\u2019 dragon-pattern wedding china.  After founding Dragon, the Bakers\u2019 work proceeded apace with the development of desktop computers with ever-increasing memory and processing speeds.  Jim\u2019s work in mathematics led them to apply a mathematical principle called Hidden Markov Models to predict what word would follow another.  In the 1980s, Dragon sold an early voice recognition program to a U.K. company called Apricot Computers Ltd. In 1990, the company introduced DragonDictate, a commercial dictation program.  \u201cYou had to pause ... between ... each ... word,\u201d Jim Baker said, describing the limits of the program.  Grateful Customers  From the start, the Bakers got feedback from early adopters of the technology, including many disabled people. They\u2019ve kept letters from grateful customers who credited Dragon\u2019s products with giving them new powers of communication.  The ultimate goal, a large-vocabulary, continuous speech recognition product that could register words as they were spoken, remained out of reach until 1997 when Dragon introduced  Dragon NaturallySpeaking .  NaturallySpeaking had a dictionary-sized vocabulary and was available in six languages. Users could speak at a normal speed. Pauses were no longer necessary. Oscar-winning actor Richard Dreyfuss, a fan of the Dragon program, volunteered as master-of- ceremonies when it was introduced.  Industry Awards  The product was a hit with consumers and won dozens of industry awards. The current version of Dragon NaturallySpeaking is sold by Burlington, Massachusetts-based  Nuance Communications Inc. (NUAN)   The success of NaturallySpeaking brought Dragon into  competition  with companies including  International Business Machines Corp. (IBM)  and  Microsoft Corp. (MSFT) , which were interested in developing  their  own speech-recognition products.  The Bakers, who were getting unsolicited offers to buy Dragon, knew they needed capital to develop their technology. That led to Goldman Sachs, the sale to Lernout & Hauspie and the loss of Dragon itself.  \u201cIt was devastating,\u201d said Janet Baker. \u201cYou spend round the clock working on something for decades. And the train stops.\u201d  Their case will be considered by a jury of six, with as many as six alternates, who were selected yesterday in the courtroom of U.S. District Judge Patti Saris. Saris, appointed by President  Bill Clinton , has presided over civil and criminal cases, including one in which she accepted in April, Merck & Co.\u2019s agreement to pay a $321.6 million criminal fine and $628.3 million to resolve civil claims that it sold Vioxx for unapproved uses and improperly touted its safety.  Co-Founders, Witnesses  Some potential jurors gasped when Saris said the trial may take until Jan. 25 to complete. She told them the court will take a break from Dec. 21 to Jan. 2 for the Christmas and New Year holidays.  After opening statements, the first witness will be Jim Baker, Cotler told Saris yesterday.  The Bakers\u2019 witnesses will include Paul Bamberg and Robert Roth, Dragon co-founders who held minority shares in the company. Bamberg\u2019s and Roth\u2019s claims against Goldman Sachs will be tried along with the Bakers\u2019 in the trial.  Both sides said they will show jurors recorded testimony from Sykes. They also plan to present expert witnesses to testify about investment banking practices and to offer their opinions on Goldman Sachs\u2019s conduct in the Dragon transaction.  Goldman Sachs didn\u2019t take part in a crucial March 8, 2000, meeting set to put together final terms of the sale, according to the Bakers. The leader of the Goldman Sachs team was on vacation and said he couldn\u2019t phone into the meeting, they said. It was at that meeting that Dragon agreed, disastrously, to the Belgian company\u2019s request to change its half-cash, half-stock offer into one that paid only in Lernout & Hauspie stock.  Inconsistent Statements  The Bakers claim the Goldman Sachs team failed to investigate inconsistencies in Lernout & Hauspie\u2019s financial statements that should have prompted them to steer Dragon away from the deal.  The Bakers point to press reports showing that Lernout & Hauspie\u2019s reported revenue in  Asia  jumped from $9 million in 1998 to $138 million the following year.  Later, after the Dragon sale closed, the Wall Street Journal said reporters had contacted a group of Korean companies that Lernout & Hauspie identified as customers. Many of the companies said they didn\u2019t do any business with the company.  The Bakers may tell jurors that Goldman Sachs considered investing $30 million of its own money in Lernout & Hauspie in 1998, before it was hired to advise Dragon. The firm abandoned the idea, which it called \u201cProject Sermon,\u201d after pursuing due diligence, including calls to customers of the Belgian company. The Goldman Sachs team made no such calls in preparation for the Dragon transaction, the Bakers said in court filings.  \u2018Huge Red Flag\u2019  \u201cIf Goldman had made even one such phone call to one of the many fake Asian customers that L&H was claiming were sources of huge amounts of new revenue, it would have raised a huge red flag that would have stopped the merger,\u201d the Bakers argued in court papers.  According to the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission, Lernout & Hauspie created bogus customers, booked circular transactions with shell companies and recorded loans as sales from 1996 to 2000. The company was forced to restate $373 million in earnings and filed for bankruptcy in November 2000.  The suit against Goldman Sachs was put on hold by agreement of both sides for years while the Bakers sued other Lernout & Hauspie and participants and advisers in the deal. They\u2019ve reached a total of about $70 million in settlements, Cotler told Saris earlier.  Damages Sought  Based on the value of Dragon at the time of the sale, the Bakers lost as much as $288.8 million in the sale and its aftermath, they said in court filings. Bamberg and Roth have said they lost as much as $50 million.  In court filings, Goldman Sachs said the plaintiffs damages are less than the amount they\u2019ve already recovered in settlements.  The judge yesterday denied a request by Goldman Sachs to delay the trial because of statements made by Cotler to the press.  She ordered the lawyer not to talk to reporters about the case.  \u201cYou cannot talk to the press,\u201d she told Cotler, who was quoted last week in a Boston Globe column about the case. \u201cYou cannot. I don\u2019t know why you did.\u201d  She ordered Goldman Sachs to remove from its website arguments it posted about its defenses.  The case is Baker v. Goldman Sachs & Co., 09-cv-10053, U.S. District Court, District of Massachusetts (Boston).  To contact the reporter on this story: Bob Van Voris in  New York  at  rvanvoris@bloomberg.net . For just as long, the generation that put up the early cash rarely appreciated what its descendants got in return.  From 1803, when  Thomas Jefferson  negotiated the Louisiana Purchase, to the creation of the Internet in our day,  Washington  has invested in ventures that at the time seemed folly. Instead, they ended up spawning businesses small and large. Many of these investments didn\u2019t just re-engineer the economy;  they transformed society.  Today, the promise of a similarly sized game changer may be crushed if lawmakers respond too harshly to calls for deep cuts in federal spending. No doubt there are many good reasons to trim the government\u2019s fiscal wings, but there can only be bad outcomes if the federal government abandons the angel\u2019s role.  The Internet shows federal seed money can put innovation into motion. Hundreds of millions of dollars invested in the Internet\u2019s precursors from the 1960s to the 1990s laid groundwork for  e-commerce , which is forecast to reach more than $1 trillion by the end of this year.  Government agencies nurtured the Internet and the Web as a platform on which businesses could grow and make money. Startup companies based solely on the Internet have grown into global giants, with names like  Amazon.com (AMZN) ,  eBay  and  Google. (GOOG)   Some of us are old enough to remember life without e-mail, mobile phones and global search. Ask a 20-year-old to imagine that and you\u2019ll get a look of total amazement. Picture what a 5- year-old will be able to do and learn as a result of the next new thing.  The reason the Internet became such a central part of people\u2019s lives is because it\u2019s a \u201cgenerative technology,\u201d in the words of Jonathan Zittrain, a professor of law and computer science at  Harvard University . Anyone can now develop never- before-imagined products and applications that ride on the Internet.  The personal computer, GPS -- even duct tape -- are all examples of generative technologies. What makes them work are open standards, which mean any company can use them to invent new products and services that work with other companies\u2019 innovations to create a competitive marketplace.  To understand why generative technologies are important, consider the French government\u2019s investment 30 years ago in a national data network. Working with  France Telecom (FTE) , the national phone company, the government created the Minitel, a computer French citizens could use to do everything from checking the yellow pages to signing up for online dating.    Today, the U.S. government has two generative technology investment opportunities that promise even more economic growth than the Internet. The first is cloud computing, which provides cheaper, more flexible computing power and storage in data centers worldwide. Think  Apple (AAPL) \u2019s iTunes,  Netflix (NFLX)  and Google\u2019s Gmail. Advances in cloud technology will enable thousands of new applications.  Second is the \u201ccloud of things,\u201d which combines cloud computing with hundreds of billions of appliances and inexpensive sensors that will collect a flood of new data and video. Companies and governments can use these ubiquitous sensors to improve just about everything we do, from quickly rerouting traffic from clogged highways to monitoring the health of patients and synchronizing every electronic function in our homes.  The federal government funds research in sensors as well as the education of computer scientists and engineers. If the next president and Congress choose to cut federal spending in the name of austerity, U.S. leadership in cloud computing and the cloud of things just may go with it -- as will the jobs. Companies are expected to create at least 7 million new cloud- related jobs globally by 2015, according to an IDC Corp. study sponsored by  Microsoft Corp. (MSFT)   The next president should channel Thomas Jefferson. Faced in 1803 with stinging criticism and economic uncertainty, Jefferson raised $15 million, more than the  federal budget  at the time, to buy 820,000 square miles in the North American heartland. The deal doubled the size of the fledgling U.S. and gave farmers, and later companies, access to some of the world\u2019s most fertile and resource-rich land, treasures that would later fuel the U.S. industrial boom.  Another boom awaits, driven by data and the cloud.  ( Mike Nelson  is a technology analyst with Bloomberg Government. The views expressed are his own.) The Paris-based Organization for Economic Cooperation &\nDevelopment, which represents 34 countries, today released the\n2009  Program for International Student Assessment . For the first\ntime, the test broke out the performance of China\u2019s Shanghai\nregion, which topped every country in all academic categories.\nThe U.S. government considers the test one of the most\ncomprehensive measures of international achievement.  The results show that U.S. students must improve to compete\nin a global economy, Education Secretary  Arne Duncan  said\nyesterday in a telephone interview. President Barack Obama\u2019s\nadministration is promoting national curriculum standards and a\nrevamping of teacher pay that stresses performance rather than\ncredentials and seniority.  \u201cThe brutal fact here is there are many countries that are\nfar ahead of us and improving more rapidly than we are,\u201d Duncan\nsaid. \u201cThis should be a massive wake-up call to the entire\ncountry.\u201d  \u2018Key Schools\u2019  China\u2019s success in Shanghai results from the government\u2019s\nabandonment of a system of \u201ckey schools\u201d for elites and the\ninstitution of \u201ca more inclusive system in which all students\nare expected to perform at high levels,\u201d the OECD said in the\nreport.  China also raised teacher pay and standards and reduced\nrote learning, while giving students and local authorities more\nchoice in curriculum.  Shanghai was the first city in China to achieve universal\nprimary and junior-secondary education, and more than 80 percent\nof students of college age are admitted into higher-education\ninstitutions, compared with the national figure of 24 percent,\naccording to the report. The U.S. is traditionally ranked against other OECD\ncountries. U.S. math scores rose from 474 in 2006, when they ranked\n25th of 30 OECD countries.  The average U.S. reading score of 500 ranked 14th among\nOECD countries, which were led by South Korea, Finland and\nCanada. Shanghai students scored 575. The U.S., which\nscored 489 in 2006, ranked 21st among 30 OECD countries that\nyear.  The U.S. faces educational challenges from its immigrant\nand heterogeneous population, an OECD report said. Compliance Policy  Denmark Is Biggest Loser in Basel Plan Redefining Assets  Denmark\u2019s mortgage system, already fighting global\nliquidity rules the industry warns would spell its demise, is\nnow battling a plan to redefine trading assets it says ignores\nthe Nordic country\u2019s centuries-old framework.  A proposal by the Basel Committee on Banking Supervision\nwould require banks to shift all mark-to-market assets to\ntrading books. That would force Denmark\u2019s $480 billion mortgage\nindustry to reclassify home loans as traded assets, even though\nthey\u2019re not resold. The plan also ignores the fact that a\nmortgage\u2019s interest-rate risk is passed on to the bondholder,\nleaving issuers with a capital shortfall as big as $61 billion,\naccording to the Association of Danish Mortgage Banks.  Denmark\u2019s home-loan industry, which backs the world\u2019s\nthird-largest mortgage-bond market, is still trying to persuade\nregulators in Europe to change Basel liquidity rules it says\nwould force banks to dump mortgage assets.  The Basel Committee\u2019s deadline for accepting comments on\nthe proposal was this month. Denmark\u2019s central bank and\nFinancial Supervisory Authority, in a  letter  dated Sept. 11,\nsaid such a requirement would raise Danish mortgage bank capital\nneeds by \u201cseveral multiples\u201d without reflecting lenders\u2019\nactual risk levels.
