Compliance Action  RBS Managers Condoned Libor Manipulation During Expansion  Royal Bank of Scotland Group Plc  managers condoned and\nparticipated in the manipulation of global interest rates,\nindicating that wrongdoing extended beyond the four traders the\nbank has fired.  In an instant-message conversation in late 2007, Jezri\nMohideen, then the bank\u2019s head of yen products in Singapore,\ninstructed colleagues in the U.K. to lower RBS\u2019s submission to\nthe London interbank offered rate that day, according to two\npeople with knowledge of the discussion. No reason was given in\nthe message as to why he wanted a lower bid. The rate-setter\nagreed, submitting the number Mohideen sought, the people said.  Mohideen wasn\u2019t alone. RBS traders and their managers\nroutinely sought to influence the firm\u2019s Libor submissions\nbetween 2007 and 2010 to profit from derivatives bets, according\nto employees, regulators and lawyers interviewed by  Bloomberg\nNews . Traders also communicated with counterparts at other firms\nto discuss where rates should be set, one person said.  RBS, 81 percent owned by the British  government , is one of\nat least a dozen banks being probed by regulators worldwide over\nallegations that traders colluded to manipulate the benchmark\ninterest rate so they could profit from bets on interest-rate\nderivatives.  Regulators are now probing RBS\u2019s yen, Swiss franc and U.S.\ndollar sales-and-trading businesses, all part of the fixed-\nincome division, said two people who asked not to be identified\nbecause the bank\u2019s internal investigation, begun more than two\nyears ago, is still in progress. Investigators are focusing on\nthe firm\u2019s swaps, inflation-trading and foreign-exchange teams,\nas well as on money-market traders who made daily Libor\nsubmissions, the people said.  The process of setting rates was open to abuse because RBS\nfailed to establish guidelines until June 2011, four people\nfamiliar with the business said. Managers encouraged rate-\nsetters to discuss Libor with traders across the company as a\nway of ensuring the bank\u2019s submissions reflected market\nconditions, particularly after money markets froze in 2007, the\npeople said. These communications -- by e-mail, instant messages\nand telephone -- are the focus of regulators\u2019 probes.  David Greene, a senior partner at law firm Edwin Coe LLP in\nLondon said this kind of activity \u201cwas widespread in the\nindustry\u201d and a lot of traders didn\u2019t consider it to be wrong. Germany\u2019s lawmakers have yet to\nratify the agreement due to take effect from 2013 amid\nopposition from the Social Democratic Party.  Grinberg made the statements in a written  submission  to the\nParliament before a  hearing yesterday  in Berlin.  Grinberg favors building a global automatic information\nexchange system through measures such as the U.S. Foreign\nAccount Tax Compliance Act, which requires banks to report\ninformation on consenting American account holders directly to\nthe Internal Revenue Service. Switzerland  agreed  in June to\nimplement the FATCA legislation, while Swiss lawmakers also\nvoted this month to allow group requests for information on\nAmericans with cross-border accounts in the Alpine nation.  Those measures equate to automatic information exchange,\naccording to Grinberg. That\u2019s\naccording to analysis by Ghostery, a browser plug-in that detects hidden scripts running\non Web pages. Readers needn\u2019t worry, though, because the data -- browser type,\ndemographics, language settings, page views -- is anonymous. In fact, this type of data\ncollection is standard practice for just about every website on the Internet. Marketers\nuse it to deliver more relevant ads to users. It would be better, privacy advocates argue,\nif users could opt out of being tracked or at least see what data is being collected.\nEighty percent of general election voters in the U.S. support a \u201cDo Not Track\u201d list,\naccording to a 1,000-person poll released last July by nonprofit advocacy group\nConsumer Watchdog.  Now lawmakers are looking to impose rules that take those online privacy concerns into\naccount, with three \u201cDo Not Track Online\u201d bills making their way through Congress. The\nfirst, Representative Jackie Speier\u2019s (D-Calif.) bill, introduced in February, requires\nadvertisers to disclose what information is collected and how it\u2019s used, as well as\nprovide tools that enable users to block data collection. Senators  John Kerry  (D-Mass.)\nand  John McCain  (R-Ariz.) introduced a similar bill in April and Senator John D. Rockefeller IV (D-W.Va.) brought forward a third bill on May 9. Lawmakers, privacy\nadvocates, and industry leaders expect a version of the legislation to be signed into law\nin the near future but are vague on specifics.  So it would seem  Bizo,  a three-year-old online marketing firm that collects and sells\ndata on 85 million business professionals to publishers, marketers, and advertising\nagencies would fight it, keeping in line with much of the industry that wants self-\nregulation instead of the government stepping in. Instead, its founder and chief\nexecutive officer, Russ Glass, is leading the charge on regulation. In February, Glass\nwrote the Federal Trade Commission a letter to propose how it can regulate responsibly\nto ensure consumer choice and data collection openness. \u201cWe didn\u2019t come from the ad\nindustry,\u201d says Glass, 35, the former vice-president of marketing and product\nmanagement at ZoomInfo, a business information search engine. \u201cIt was just obvious to\nus that transparency and the ability for people to own their own data made a ton of\nsense.\u201d  MORE APPEALING  Glass is adamant that giving individuals the ability to modify their data will make Bizo\u2019s\nservices more appealing to those being tracked -- and those tracking them. About 70\npercent of his 34-employee San Francisco company\u2019s revenue comes from its ad\nnetwork, which marketers pay to use to target business professionals with ads as they\nnavigate the Web.  Unlike Google AdWords, which targets users based on keywords, Bizo\u2019s network uses\ncookies. These packets of data are used to create anonymous user profiles based on\ndemographic data Bizo collects from about 1,200 different sources, including contact\ndirectory Jigsaw and business information and marketing firm Access Intel. As with\nLinkedIn, customers use Bizo to target businesspeople based on what industry they\u2019re\nin, how senior they are, what job function they hold, or what size company they work for.\nThe difference is Bizo allows marketers to reach professionals across the Web, not just\nwithin LinkedIn\u2019s network. Bizo\u2019s other business line is selling its business demographic\ndata to publishers and other ad networks to make their targeting more effective.  Cultivating trust is important to Glass. Without it, a company\u2019s brand is less valuable,\nparticularly in the ad industry, which is already hampered by massive consumer\nmistrust, he says. When Glass launched Bizo in 2008, he says, it was the first on the\nmarket with a tool allowing Web surfers to see what information was being collected\nalong with the ability to correct facts or to opt out of being tracked. For example, if a\nbusiness executive notices an ad served by a Bizo user she doesn\u2019t find relevant, she\ncan click on an \u201ci\u201d icon in an overlay or a descriptive link above or below the ad to make\ncookie changes so that it stops appearing. In April, Bizo recorded roughly 25,000 opt-\nouts across its platform, about 0.01 percent of its monthly unique audience. Google\nreleased its tool about three months later, and others have since followed suit with\nsimilar opt-out features on ads they serve.  IMPROVED EFFICIENCY  Of course, no matter how transparent the explanation of how their data will be used,\nsome people don\u2019t want to be tracked. That means Bizo, its few competitors like\nbusiness-to-business advertising network BBN Networks, and thousands of data\ncollectors won\u2019t be able to target those individuals as they click their way around the\nWeb. While there are exemptions for the collection of business-related data in Speier\u2019s\nbill, the opt-out tracking standards would affect Bizo the same as any other online\ntracker. Glass says rules will improve efficiency since users who opt out \u201cwouldn\u2019t have\nconverted anyway,\u201d referring to sales. The latest versions of  Microsoft\u2019s Internet\nExplorer (MSFT)  and Mozilla\u2019s Firefox include do-not-track features. Based on its\ndeveloper release,  Apple\u2019s Safari 6 (AAPL)  will add them this summer. Google has an\nopt-out plug-in for Chrome, though do-not-track functionality isn\u2019t a built-in feature.  \u201cI think the ball is rolling and there\u2019s going to have to be some sort of regulation to\nplease the constituencies that want it,\u201d says Bob Felsenthal, vice-president and\npublisher of BtoB, a business-to-business marketing magazine with offices in  Chicago \nand  New York City . \u201cI think what you don\u2019t want is something nearly as radical for the\nInternet industry as ended up for the consumer telemarketing industry.\u201d He\u2019s referring to\nthe Federal Trade Commission\u2019s National Do Not Call Registry, which went into effect in\nFebruary 2008. The service lets individuals avoid telemarketing calls, a development\nFelsenthal says \u201cdestroyed\u201d the industry. \u201c[It] probably went too far too quickly, but after\nyears of doing nothing,\u201d Felsenthal adds.  This time, lawmakers are taking action on Internet marketers much more quickly.\nFelsenthal agrees with Glass that the online marketing industry should welcome\ngovernment oversight rather than just self-regulation measures. Felsenthal also notes\nthat because Bizo limits its services to targeting business readers, the company likely\nwon\u2019t be adversely affected by  government regulation . \u201cI don\u2019t think that business\nreaders, like consumers, are as concerned about having ads on the page because it\u2019s\nusually of business information that\u2019s of interest to them -- so I think that makes [Bizo]\nunique and different.\u201d  Convinced relatively few of the individuals he relies on will opt out should legislation\nbecome law, Glass is optimistic about growth. Bizo has 1,000 publisher partners that\nshare revenues from advertisements served, including  Yahoo! (YHOO),   Nielsen\n(NLSN),  and  Dun & Bradstreet (DNB),  plus more than 300 marketer customers. Glass\nsays renewal rates are up more than 30 percent from a year earlier. As clients\u2019\nadvertising budgets expand, Glass expects revenue to hit $15 million in 2011, up more\nthan double from $6.8 million last year. I\u2019ve been trying out two of the new boxes, Sony\u2019s NSZ-GS7 -- rolls trippingly off the tongue, doesn\u2019t it? -- and Vizio\u2019s Co- Star. While they\u2019re considerable improvements over the previous generation, Google TV still has a long way to go.  The devices join a crowded field that already includes the $99 Apple TV and the Roku family of players, which range from $50 to $100. Meanwhile,  Microsoft (MSFT) \u2019s Xbox and Sony\u2019s own PlayStation have morphed from game consoles into full-fledged entertainment hubs, while many TVs come with Wi-Fi and their own \u201csmart TV\u201d software.  The new Sony and Vizio units -- along with an announced Google TV set-top box from  China \u2019s Hisense and a TV from  LG (066570)  with the software  built in  -- aim to differentiate themselves by not merely connecting your TV to the Internet, but by integrating online video content with programming from traditional sources like cable and satellite.  Extra Complexity  The theory is that it shouldn\u2019t matter to you where the content resides; one interface -- and one remote -- should be able to locate it. In practice, though, Google TV also adds an extra layer of complexity to installation and use.  In my case, for example, I messed up my first attempt to introduce the NSZ-GS7 into my home video set-up. The mistake stemmed from my efforts to connect the player to my cable-TV box, something that simpler streaming devices don\u2019t ask you to do.  At one point, I found I had to lie to the installation process, telling it I could see a certain channel on the screen when I couldn\u2019t, to get the cable programming guide configured. That\u2019s probably because I had neglected to attach an extra wire that the  Sony (6758)  player required. (In contrast, the Vizio setup process went more smoothly.)  While the Vizio and Sony players share the underlying Google software, there are some important differences in connectivity, features and cost between the two.  Black Box  The  NSZ-GS7  -- let\u2019s just call it \u201cthe Sony box\u201d -- is a flat black rectangle, about half the size of a Blu-ray player. The back includes high-definition video input and output ports, an optical digital port for running the sound through a receiver and two USB connectors to accommodate external drives for accessing photos, music or other content.  There\u2019s also an Ethernet port for use with a wired network, though most people are likely to take advantage of the built-in Wi-Fi.  A huge weakness of previous Google TV devices was the remote control. While Apple and Roku both feature minimalist versions, the  Logitech (LOGN)  box came with -- no lie -- a full-size keyboard. And the remote for the Sony TV set that had the Google software built into it was its own  special kind of horror .  With the new player, Sony has done a lot of streamlining: On one side of the remote is a keyboard, useful for entering Wi- Fi passwords, search terms and the like. The flip side has a limited set of buttons built around a laptop-style trackpad.  It\u2019s also smart enough to sense which side you\u2019re using and disable the other to avoid accidental clicks. Alternatively, you can also use free Sony remote apps for iPhones and Android phones.  Big Drawback  The Sony\u2019s biggest drawback may be its price: $200, not only double the  Apple (AAPL)  and top-of-the line Roku devices but also twice as much as the  Vizio Co-Star .  Physically, as well as in price, the $100 Co-Star more closely resembles the hockey-puck-like  Apple  and  Roku  adapters. Compared with the Sony, you can tell where corners have been cut. There\u2019s only one USB port, for instance, and no optical audio. In addition, the Vizio remote is chunkier and clunkier.  On the other hand, the Co-Star has some nice touches the Sony lacks. I appreciated the labeled, dedicated buttons on its remote that take you directly to\u00a0Amazon.com\u2019s Instant Video\u00a0service and Netflix. And the Vizio\u00a0supports the OnLive service for playing console-quality video\u00a0games without a console, negating the need for a separate\u00a0adapter.  Only a geek could have loved the original Google TV. With this new generation, it has certainly become more accessible. But there remain easier and cheaper ways to watch online content on your television.  ( Rich Jaroslovsky  is a Bloomberg News columnist. The opinions expressed are his own.) In a 7-1 ruling yesterday, the justices ordered a federal appeals court to scrutinize again the  University of Texas  at Austin\u2019s affirmative-action program. While leaving intact a 2003 decision that reaffirmed the right of colleges to use race in admissions, the majority told the lower court to rule on whether the school had exhausted \u201crace-neutral alternatives.\u201d  Even as civil-rights leaders hailed the court for preserving affirmative action, colleges will be under pressure to justify their programs under the ruling and may find that the decision emboldens other spurned students to sue, legal scholars and university officials said. More schools may choose to use income and other measures to attract a broad array of students, said  Richard Kahlenberg , a senior fellow in Washington with the Century Foundation, a public policy research group.  \u201cIt will have a big impact,\u201d said Kahlenberg, whose research supports the use of family income, rather than race, in admissions. \u201cUniversities will have to be very careful before they resort to racial preferences.\u201d  Such measures are bound to fall short, based on the experience of the University of  California  and other systems that have tried them,  Lee Bollinger , president of  Columbia University  in New York, said in an interview.  Less Effective  \u201cYou will not get the degree of racial and ethnic diversity that we need for the educational benefits we seek by only focusing on low-income applicants,\u201d said Bollinger, who as president of the  University of Michigan  in the late 1990s and early 2000s led the defense of its affirmative action programs in the 2003 case.  Follow the Supreme Court's Blockbuster Week: Live Blog Affirmative action has been a fixture on U.S. campuses since the 1960s, diversifying what had been many virtually all-white student bodies. Most of the nation\u2019s selective colleges and professional schools consider race as they seek to ensure a multiracial student body. Blacks and Hispanics now make up more than a quarter of U.S. college students.  The University of  Texas  admits three-quarters of its freshman class each year on the basis of high school class rank -- the \u201ctop 10 percent\u201d rule. That system, while race-neutral on the surface, ensures a significant number of minorities because it guarantees slots to students at predominantly Hispanic and black schools.  Majority View  The university considers race only in admitting the rest of the class. Opponents of preferences say that\u2019s unnecessary, given the success of the class-rank method. Texas counters that even with race-based admissions, a high percentage of its classes have few if any black and Hispanic students.  Justice  Anthony Kennedy , writing for the majority, said that while courts should defer to universities in determining whether diversity is essential to their educational mission, judges should closely scrutinize the means schools use to bolster minority enrollment.  \u201cThe university must prove that the means chosen by the university to attain diversity are narrowly tailored to that goal,\u201d Kennedy wrote. \u201cOn this point, the university receives no deference.\u201d  Richard Sander, a law professor at the University of California, Los Angeles who has been critical of affirmative action, said Kennedy\u2019s language calling for facts supporting the use of race could set up universities for legal battles.  \u2018Low Bar\u2019  \u201cHe\u2019s setting a very low bar for future litigation,\u201d Sander said in a phone interview.  The University of Texas said the ruling won\u2019t force any immediate changes in its admissions policies. University President Bill Powers said in a statement that the system \u201cfully satisfies\u201d the standards laid out by the Supreme Court.  Civil-rights groups hailed the decision, saying it represents a victory for equal opportunity.  The court set a \u201csharper and tighter\u201d standard for using race in admissions, said  Sherrilyn Ifill , president and director-counsel of the NAACP Legal and Educational Fund.  \u201cThe University of Texas can meet it,\u201d Ifill said in a briefing with reporters. \u201cOther universities can meet it as well.\u201d  University of Texas students overwhelmingly support the school\u2019s admissions policies, Student Body President Horacio Villarreal III said in a phone interview. He cited a vote last year in which 35 members of the student government unanimously supported a resolution praising the admissions standards.  Student Support  \u201cThe whole university benefits from a diverse student body,\u201d said Villarreal, 22, a political science major and rising senior from  Corpus Christi , Texas. \u201cWe are doing things the right way.\u201d  The 2003 decision, Grutter v. Bollinger, said colleges and graduate schools could consider race as long as they do so through a broad review of a student\u2019s application and don\u2019t mechanistically award extra points to every minority.  Affirmative action has \u201cbeen a very important part of the great success of American education that is admired around the globe,\u201d Bollinger said. \u201cIt would be great pity to retreat at this stage when the work is not over.\u201d  The Texas policy was challenged by Abigail Noel Fisher, who applied unsuccessfully to the Austin campus in 2008 and later enrolled at  Louisiana State University . A graduate of a Houston-area public high school, she said she was passed over by UT in favor of minority classmates with lower grades and fewer extracurricular activities.  Corporate Backing  Texas had support in the case from some of the nation\u2019s most powerful institutions. Fifty-nine companies -- including  Microsoft Corp. (MSFT) ,  Wal-Mart Stores Inc., (WMT)  Gap Inc.,  General Electric Co. (GE) , Pfizer Inc., and  Viacom Inc. (VIAB)  -- filed a  brief  saying they rely on universities to prepare a racially diverse workforce.  \u201cPeople educated in diverse settings are better equipped to make the kinds of valuable contributions to the workforce that result from exposure to a variety of viewpoints and backgrounds,\u201d  Seth Martin , a spokesman at Fairfield, Connecticut-based GE, said in an e-mail.  Yesterday\u2019s decision will intensify the debate between people who say affirmative action is crucial for recruiting disadvantaged minorities and those who argue that targeting low-income families or those who haven\u2019t attended college can be equally effective.  Justifying Programs  Colleges are going to have to make sure they can justify their affirmative action programs, according to  Ada Meloy , general counsel of the American Council on Education, a Washington nonprofit group representing more than 1,800 college presidents. The move \u201cmay accelerate\u201d efforts to use income, rather than race, to recruit diverse classes, she said.  In a report last year, the Century Foundation examined states such as Washington, Florida and Arizona that had eliminated racial and ethnic preferences at public universities because of voter referenda, executive orders or legislative actions. Seven of 10 institutions were able to produce as much or greater black and Hispanic representation using race-neutral means, such as family income, Kahlenberg said.  Yet, officials at the  University of California  say their efforts have fallen short. Since highly selective UC Berkeley stopped considering race in admissions for undergraduates in the 1998-1999 school year, the percentage of blacks enrolled fell by half to 3 percent in the 2012-2103 period. The percentage of Hispanic students held steady, at 13 percent, though their population has been increasing.  \u2018Limited Success\u2019  Since the ban, the University of California expanded its outreach to high schools in pursuit of students from low-income families or those with little or no experience with higher education. It also decreased the weight given to standardized tests and admitted a specific number of top graduates from each high school -- a plan similar to Texas\u2019s \u201ctop 10 percent\u201d program, the system\u2019s lawyers wrote.  Still, those measures \u201cenjoyed only limited success\u201d because they haven\u2019t reversed the \u201cprecipitous decline in minority admission and enrollment,\u201d the University of California wrote in a brief supporting Texas.  Admissions directors say they are confident their current programs operate in sync with the law and would survive any legal challenge.  \u201cWe have had our processes reviewed by independent sources,\u201d said Tom Parker, dean of admission and financial aid at  Amherst College  in Massachusetts. \u201cWe will continue to do what we\u2019ve always done.\u201d  Massachusetts Institute of Technology  has always considered \u201cmultiple forms of diversity,\u201d according to  Stuart Schmill , dean of admissions at the Cambridge, Massachusetts school.  \u201cI don\u2019t see us doing anything different now,\u201d Schmill said.  The case is Fisher v. University of Texas at Austin, 11-345. (AAPL) \u2019s bid to limit  Google\nInc. (GOOG) \u2019s use of certain patents as a tool to block imports of the\niPhone and iPad may be getting traction at a U.S. trade agency,\npossibly altering the global battle over smartphones.  The U.S. International Trade Commission  said  yesterday it\nwill review whether Apple, which gets about 75 percent of its\nrevenue from the iPhone, iPad and related products, infringed\nfour patents held by Google\u2019s Motorola Mobility unit. A trade\njudge in April said Apple infringed one of the patents.  The commission also asked lawyers in the case, and the\npublic, for comments on how to proceed when infringed patents\ncover aspects of technology that are adopted by an entire\nindustry so electronic devices work across platforms.  \u201cThere\u2019s some sort of movement to reduce \u2018competition\nthrough litigation,\u2019\u201d said  Will Stofega , a program manager at\nresearcher IDC in Framingham,  Massachusetts . \u201cThey really want\nto bring this whole issue to a head. Patent litigation is part\nof the ordinary due course of business, but this has gone beyond\nthat.\u201d  The U.S. Federal Trade Commission, a half-dozen members of\nCongress and companies including  Intel Corp . and Cisco Systems\nInc. have in recent weeks questioned whether companies that\nhelped develop standards should be able to get orders from the\nITC to block competitors\u2019 use of the technology.  The ITC will review aspects of all four Motorola Mobility\npatents in the case against Apple. Of the 13 questions it posed\nto lawyers yesterday, eight are related to handling standard-\nessential patents. Should it side with Motorola Mobility, the\nagency has the power to order  U.S. Customs  and Border Protection\nto stop iPhones and iPad computers made in Asia from entering\nthe U.S.  75 Percent  The iPhone generated $22.7 billion in sales in the quarter\nended March 31 for Apple, or 58 percent of the company\u2019s total\nrevenue. It was the best-selling smartphone in the U.S., with 29\npercent of the market, while Motorola Mobility had 10 percent,\nresearcher NPD Group  said  May 2.  Apple\u2019s iPad dominates the tablet computer market, with 72\npercent of the market, according to  researcher DisplaySearch .\nThe iPad and related products brought in $6.6 billion for Apple,\nalmost 17 percent of its revenue, in the second quarter.  A ruling for Apple on the smartphone issue would limit the\nammunition that Motorola Mobility has hurled at its rivals.\nApple and  Microsoft Corp. (MSFT)  have said the patents they asserted at\nthe ITC against Motorola Mobility are for features, not industry\nstandards.  3G, Wi-Fi  Two of the patents in Motorola Mobility\u2019s case against\nApple relate to the industry standard for 3G generation\ntechnology. The 3G patent that was found to be infringed covers\na way to eliminate noise so signals are clearer.  \u201cWe remain confident in our position and look forward to\nthe further confirmation of Apple\u2019s violation of Motorola\nMobility\u2019s intellectual property when the full commission rules\nin August,\u201d  Jennifer Erickson , a spokeswoman for Libertyville,\nIllinois-based Motorola Mobility, said in a statement. A judge said three of\nthe standard-essential patents and another Motorola Mobility\npatent were infringed. The commission said it needs another\nweek, until July 2, to determine how it will handle the next\nsteps in that case.  Allowing the owner of a standard-essential patent to seek an\nimport ban would undermine the purpose of establishing industry\nstandards, Apple\u2019s lawyers wrote in a June 8 letter to the ITC\nsupporting Microsoft. Any dispute over royalties should be\nhandled in civil court, the company said.  Pre-Emptive Strike  \u201cEnabling hold-up of the industry could undercut the\ndevelopment of industry standards and reverse the gains in\nproductivity that standardization produces, thereby damaging not\nonly companies like Microsoft, but also U.S. consumers and the\npublic in general,\u201d Apple wrote.  Motorola Mobility filed its complaint against Apple in\nOctober 2010 as a pre-emptive strike after the iPhone maker made\npublic statements that phones running on Google\u2019s Android\noperating system were copying features of its products. The\ndispute is part of a broader global battle for supremacy in the\nsmartphone and tablet computer markets that also pits Apple\nagainst Android-device manufacturers Samsung Electronics Co. and\n HTC Corp. (2498)   Bargaining Power  Android is the most popular platform for smartphones, with\n61 percent of the market, NPD said. Google\nbought Motorola Mobility in part to gain access to its trove of\n17,000 patents, many on phone technology.  In the Chicago case, U.S. Circuit Judge  Richard Posner  said\nhe wouldn\u2019t ban a product that follows an industry standard\nunless Apple refused to pay a fair rate.  \u201cOnce a patent becomes essential to a standard, the\npatentee\u2019s bargaining power surges because a prospective\nlicensee has no alternative to licensing the patent; he is at\nthe patentee\u2019s mercy,\u201d Posner wrote.  EU Complaint  Cupertino, California-based Apple also has filed a\ncomplaint against Motorola Mobility at the European Union,\naccusing the handset manufacturer of misusing patents that\nrelate to industry standards. It also filed a lawsuit accusing\nMotorola Mobility of breaching its contractual obligation to\nlicense any standard-essential patents on fair and reasonable\nterms.  Apple contends Motorola Mobility never made a fair offer,\nwhile Motorola Mobility has said that Apple won\u2019t negotiate.  The case against Apple is In the Matter of Wireless\nCommunication Devices, Portable Music and Data Processing\nDevices, Computers and Components Thereof, 337-745, and Apple\u2019s\ncase against Motorola Mobility is In the Matter of Mobile\nDevices and Related Software, 337-750, both U.S. International\nTrade. (BB) \u2019s sales\ntumbled in recent years, the company continued amassing patents,\nbuilding an intellectual-property hoard that\u2019s now central to\nits effort to entice bidders.  The struggling smartphone maker received 986  patents  last\nyear, a 49 percent increase from 2011, according to figures\ncompiled by the Intellectual Property Owners Association.\nBlackBerry\u2019s patents are valued at anywhere from $1 billion to\n$3 billion, depending on how many of them have already been\nlicensed out, analysts and patent experts estimate.  Working in BlackBerry\u2019s favor: The patents cover similar\ntechnology as Apple Inc.\u2019s intellectual property, and much of\nthe portfolio is only a few years old. The downside is that the\nmarket for such assets has cooled. Previous patent buyers such\nas  Apple (AAPL)  and Google Inc. amassed broad portfolios in patent\ndeals two years ago.  \u201cThis is an incredibly volatile market,\u201d said Ron Laurie,\nmanaging director of  Palo Alto , California-based Inflexion Point\nStrategy, who advises companies on patents. \u201cIt all depends on\nperceived demand and strategic value.\u201d  A higher patent valuation would help the company as it\nseeks offers better than  Fairfax Financial Holdings Ltd. (FFH) \u2019s\ntentative $4.7 billion buyout proposal, even if it means\nbreaking the company up to get the fullest value for the assets.  Patent Mentions  Apple, whose iPhone is now the best-selling smartphone,\ncites BlackBerry\u2019s technology 1,295 times in its own patent\napplications, according to MDB Capital Group LLC, a  Santa\nMonica , California-based patent-investment bank. The rivals\ncredit each other more than any other two North American device\nmakers. Companies are required to identify competing technology\nto ensure they aren\u2019t claiming something already patented.  Lisette Kwong, a Waterloo, Ontario-based spokeswoman for\nBlackBerry, and Kristin Huguet, a spokeswoman for Apple,\ndeclined to comment.  Given its connections to Apple and an average patent age of\njust 3.4 years, the portfolio may fetch $2 billion to $3\nbillion, according to MDB. That value may be lower if BlackBerry\nhas already licensed much of its technology, said Erin-Michael Gill, managing director of MDB Capital. Widely licensed patents\nhave less use for new deals or court challenges.  \u2018Trivial Amount\u2019  \u201cIf that\u2019s the case, the financial buyers no longer have\nmuch interest -- and the strategics don\u2019t need them,\u201d Gill\nsaid. \u201cThen it would go from multibillion dollars to a trivial\namount, probably just a few hundred.\u201d  MDB\u2019s estimate reflects what the patents would fetch as\nstand-alone assets without liabilities a buyer of the whole\ncompany would face. The cost of shutting the hardware unit could\nbe $800 million, according to BMO Capital Markets.  Raymond James Financial Inc. (RJF)  pegs the value of BlackBerry\u2019s\npatent portfolio at about $1.6 billion, with the phonemaker\u2019s\nenterprise network of servers at $550 million to $1.1 billion.\nAdd those assets to the $2.6 billion in cash the company had at\nthe end of last quarter, and you get close to the $4.7 billion\nFairfax is offering.  BlackBerry, which redefined what a phone could do more than\na decade ago, has been eclipsed by Apple and  Samsung Electronics\nCo. (005930) , which offered a slicker range of smartphones and tablets.\nBlackBerry\u2019s share of the global smartphone market shrank to 2.9\npercent in June -- down from 19 percent four years earlier --and\nlast quarter sales plunged 45 percent from a year earlier.  BlackBerry slipped 1.6 percent to $8.25 at the close in  New\nYork . The stock has fallen almost 31 percent this year and\nremains more than 90 percent below its 2008 peak.  Potential Bidders  Fairfax, BlackBerry\u2019s largest shareholder, is trying to\nline up financing and partners for its bid to take the company\nprivate. BlackBerry co-founders  Mike Lazaridis  and Douglas Fregin, who together control 8 percent of BlackBerry\u2019s shares,\nsaid this month they\u2019re also mulling a bid. Lazaridis holds 178\nBlackBerry patents, according to MDB.  After signing a nondisclosure agreement, Cerberus Capital\nManagement LP is in the early stages of considering an offer to\nacquire all of BlackBerry, a person with knowledge of the\nsituation said last week. Lenovo Group Ltd. also signed a\nnondisclosure agreement and is actively considering a bid, the\nWall Street Journal reported last week. Patents last 20 years from the date of their application,\nmaking BlackBerry\u2019s 3.4-year average appealing, Gill said.  \u201cThere\u2019s 15-plus years of useful life to this portfolio,\nwhich is significant,\u201d he said. \u201cAnybody that cares about\nApple is going to care about this portfolio -- including\nApple.\u201d Not all patents are created equal. Everyone wants to know what John Paulson or David Einhorn or David Tepper is loading up on and what they're getting rid of. And yes, there's an exchange-traded fund to feed that fascination. It's up 52 percent since its inception less than a year ago -- 18 percent more than the S&P 500 Index. The Global X Top Guru Holdings Index ETF ( GURU ) sounds a bit gimmicky, but its inner workings are more sophisticated than its name. GURU's methodology is to scour 13F filings and buy the biggest stock holding from each hedge fund. Filters are put in place to eliminate funds that have high turnover rates -- those that do a lot of rapid-fire buying and selling -- and the ETF considers only hedge funds with concentrated top holdings. In other words, it screens for stocks that hedge funds are committed to, which makes it a sort of greatest hits of hedge fund stock picks. The outperformance of GURU, which has 80 percent of its assets in U.S. stocks, over the S&P 500 is partly due to the fact that it is an equal-weighted portfolio. That means that smaller juggernaut stocks like Pandora ( P ) and GameStop Corporation ( GME ) are given roughly a 2 percent weighting just like giants such as Microsoft ( MSFT ) and AIG ( AIG ). By contrast, market-cap-weighted ETFs tend to drown out small stocks' gains and get hit harder by overvalued larger stocks coming back down to earth.  One successful example of GURU's methodology is Liberty Media ( STRZA ). GURU picked up the stock in November of 2012 when it was JAT Capital Management's top holding. During the next quarter, the stock was spun off and gained 50 percent in value. The ETF sold it a quarter later for a huge profit when the next round of 13F filings showed that it was no longer JAT Capital's top holding. A big selling point for GURU is convenience. It would take a lot of legwork to download and read through every 13F filing and find cases like Liberty Media. There are hundreds of 13Fs filed quarterly, and it's no picnic to read through them. Whether GURU is a cheap or expensive ETF depends on your perspective. With an expense ratio of 0.75 percent, it's much cheaper than an actual hedge fund, which typically charges a 2 percent management fee and a 20 percent performance fee. On the other hand, 0.75 percent is about double the average cost of a U.S. equity ETF. For a $10,000 investment, that's $75 a year in fees. When you can get the Schwab U.S. Broad Market ETF for an expense ratio of 0.04 percent, or $4 on a $10,000 investment, $75 seems like highway robbery. At $38.8 million in assets, GURU is one of the smaller ETFs, which scares some investors. That said, it has seen $36 million of inflow in the past six weeks, and the total value traded this past April was $1.4 billion, a big jump compared with $27 million in December. With smaller ETFs it is always reassuring to see investors arriving at the party rather than going home. Is GURU a good investment? Like every ETF, it depends on an investor's purpose and time horizon. At the end of the day, it comes down to how comfortable you are taking on more U.S. stock exposure that may overlap with your existing portfolio -- and how much you believe in the investing prowess of hedge funds. Eric Balchunas is an exchange-traded fund analyst for Bloomberg. Comments Sought on \u2018Economically Significant\u2019 Inventions Secrecy  The U.S. Patent and Trademark Office is seeking comments on\nthe feasibility of placing \u201ceconomically significant\u201d patents\nunder a secrecy order.  According to a statement from the patent office, it\u2019s\nconsidering possible changes to existing policies for reviewing\napplications that are potentially detrimental to national\nsecurity.  The office is responding to a request from Congress asking\nwhether national-security screening of patent applications\nshould be extended to cover economically significant patents\nfrom discovery by foreign entities.  A report from the Commerce, Justice, Science and Related\nAgencies Subcommittee issued in July 2011 said that the lag\nbetween publication of the application and the issuance of the\npatent enables competitors to design around U.S. technologies\nand \u201cseize markets before the U.S. inventor is able to raise\nfinancing and secure a market.\u201d  The subcommittee has told the patent office to develop\ncriteria \u201cto evaluate the national security applications of\npatentable technologies.\u201d  The patent office said it\u2019s seeking comments from \u201cthe\ninnovation community\u201d on whether an economic security screening\nprocedure should be considered.  Presently all patent applications are screened to determine\nwhether publication or disclosure of the application would be\ndetrimental to national security. Those applications are\nforwarded to the Defense Department and other agencies\ndesignated by the president.  Foreign patent filings for applications under a secrecy\norder are prohibited without the concurrence of the reviewing\nagency that requested the secrecy order.  One of the 16 questions on which the patent office is\nseeking input is whether patent practitioners presently try to\nmake an end run around possible secrecy orders by drafting\npatent applications in such a way as \u201cnot to raise national\nsecurity implications of such an invention.\u201d  Comments must be submitted by June 19, according to the\nstatement. King, developer of \u201cCandy Crush Saga,\u201d yesterday reached 150.4 million monthly users on Facebook Inc. -- surpassing \u201cFarmVille\u201d maker Zynga, which has 150.2 million, according to online tracker  AppData . That ended Zynga\u2019s five-year reign as the top game maker on Facebook\u2019s social network.  Zynga is hiring Mattrick, former head of Microsoft Corp.\u2019s entertainment division, to take over from founder  Mark Pincus , who will remain chairman. It\u2019s an effort to recharge revenue growth at the game developer, whose shares have tumbled by more than two-thirds since its 2011 initial public offering as demand fizzled for games like \u201cMafia Wars.\u201d Mattrick\u2019s challenge as CEO will be twofold: winning Facebook gamers back from King, and wooing players who favor mobile devices with titles designed for smartphones and tablets.  \u201cIt\u2019s like trying to turn a ship around that\u2019s been going in the wrong direction,\u201d said  Sean McGowan , an analyst at Needham & Co. who recommends buying Zynga shares. \u201cMobile is a different animal -- it\u2019s different from anything Mattrick has done.\u201d  Pincus will take a diminished role at the San Francisco-based company he founded, a sign that his hard-charging management style and negotiating prowess -- once described by  Google Inc. (GOOG)  Chairman  Eric Schmidt  as \u201cfearsome\u201d -- may have clashed with the needs of a large, publicly traded business. Zynga reached a peak 327 million users on Facebook in October before entering its first extended period of  decline , according to AppData. Zynga has lost more than 100 million players in the past year -- about the same number gained by King -- because it has continued to rely too much on old hits, said Michael Pachter, an analyst at Wedbush Securities Inc.  Those losses stemmed from \u201cletting many games get stale and not really innovating, and from King growing like a weed,\u201d Los Angeles-based Pachter wrote in an e-mail.  King\u2019s Strategy  King\u2019s approach of testing out a variety of new games on its own site before releasing them on Facebook has helped it lure users like Linda Gaden, a resident of Tacoma,  Washington , who gave up on Zynga years ago and currently has two games of  \u201cCandy Crush Saga\u201d  going.  \u201cAfter I found King, I left everything -- King is where my passion is,\u201d Gaden said in a phone interview. \u201cThey come out very often with new games that you\u2019re not going to find anywhere else.\u201d  Zynga rose 6.5 percent to $3.27 at the close in  New York . The stock has dropped 67 percent since debuting in December 2011.  Mattrick may help Zynga create new, appealing games by drawing on his experience at EA, where he worked for more than a decade and was responsible for creating original content, McGowan said. The executive resigned from Microsoft at the end of last week, a person with knowledge of the matter said.  Mobile Gaming  The new CEO will also seek to reinvigorate Zynga\u2019s efforts in mobile games, where it has failed to produce a lasting hit. Talent Exodus  A leadership change may also help Zynga do a better job attracting and retaining top engineers and executives. The company has lost more than a dozen top managers in recent months as the value of equity used to compensate workers has declined. Many staffers have left to create their own mobile game startups that are poised to vie with Zynga.  About half of Zynga\u2019s employees say they would recommend working at the company to a friend, compared with 91 percent of  Google Inc. (GOOG)  workers, 77 percent of Microsoft and 67 percent of staff at Electronic Arts, according to surveys done by job-hunting site  Glassdoor Inc . Pincus joins other technology entrepreneurs who have lost or ceded top jobs within a few years of taking a company public. Earlier this year,  Groupon Inc. (GRPN) \u2019s board of directors fired  Andrew Mason , the co-founder and former CEO, as growth slowed.  Pincus Collaboration  In a memo to Zynga employees today, Mattrick said he plans to work closely with Pincus to restart growth.  \u201cZynga is a great business that has yet to realize its full potential,\u201d Mattrick said in the memo, which was posted on Zynga\u2019s blog. \u201cI\u2019m really proud to partner with a product focused founder like Mark and work with the executive team to grow the DNA of the company and lead this transition.\u201d  Mattrick, who  joined  Microsoft in 2007, became president of the interactive-entertainment business in October 2010. The executive had been leading the effort to introduce the next-generation Xbox One home-entertainment and gaming console that will compete with  Sony Corp (6758) .\u2019s new PlayStation 4 device.  Yet the unveiling of the next Xbox wasn\u2019t without hiccups. Mattrick reversed course on a policy last month for Microsoft\u2019s new console that would have required users to connect to the Web at least once every 24 hours to keep playing a game, and the company lifted restrictions on reselling, trading and lending used game titles.  Microsoft CEO  Steve Ballmer  had been planning a reorganization of the world\u2019s largest software maker aimed at reducing the number of business units and putting more focus on devices and services, people familiar with the matter said last month. He was planning to give more responsibility to Mattrick, the people said at the time. The House may take up the measure some time next month,\naccording to the office of Majority Leader Eric Cantor, a\nVirginia Republican.  A key provision of the legislation would give the patent\noffice more power over its funding by allowing the agency to\nalter its fee structure and keep Congress from diverting fees\nfor non-patent purposes.  \u2018America\u2019s Innovators\u2019  \u201cThis structure is critical to enable the USPTO to better\nmeet the needs of America\u2019s innovators,\u201d Locke wrote,\nsuggesting there should be technical changes to allow the patent\noffice to make interim fee adjustments \u201cso it can best use this\nnew authority on day one.\u201d  The measure also calls for granting patents to the first\ninventor to file an application, eliminating an often years-long\nprocedure to determine who first came up with an idea. The\nfirst-to-file system is used in most countries.  \u201cWe strongly support the proposed transition of the  United\nStates  to a first-inventor-to-file system,\u201d Locke wrote. It\nwould help U.S. businesses \u201cby providing a more transparent and\ncost-effective process that puts them on a level playing field\nwith the rest of the world.\u201d  Among the companies supporting the proposal are  General\nElectric Co. (GE) , DuPont Co., Eli Lilly & Co.,  Microsoft Corp. (MSFT) ,\n International Business Machines Corp. (IBM)  and Advanced Micro Devices\nInc. Some technology companies, including  Google Inc. (GOOG)  and  Apple\nInc. (AAPL) , have expressed reservations about certain provisions in\nthe legislation even as they have supported changes to how the\npatent office is funded.  Other sections supported by the administration include a\nnew procedure to review issued patents and allowing third\nparties to submit information on pending applications. Locke\nsaid the administration will work with the committee to address\nother provisions.  The House patent bill is H.R. 1249. With changes in\nlegislation that limited the number of defendants in a single\nsuit, that number increased even more in 2012.  Congress is considering proposals that would limit some\nlitigation practices by patent-licensing firms. (T)  and Verizon Wireless,\nworking to wring more profit from their next-generation  data\nnetworks , face a new obstacle: Smaller competitors are offering\nsimilar services for free.  FreedomPop, a company funded by Skype founder  Niklas Zennstrom , will sell an iPhone case that gives consumers free\naccess to 1 gigabyte of data from Clearwire Corp.\u2019s 4G wireless\nnetwork. Another Clearwire partner,  United Online Inc. (UNTD) \u2019s\nNetZero, is offering 200 megabytes a month for free for as long\nas 12 months -- so long as users buy a wireless modem, which can\ntake the form of a small USB stick that plugs into the device.  The freebie approach lets new carriers hook bargain-hunting\ncustomers -- with the aim of getting them to pay for extra\nbandwidth later -- while helping  Clearwire (CLWR)  recoup some of the\nbillions of dollars spent building its network. For Verizon and\nAT&T, the top U.S. wireless carriers, the move threatens the\ncombined $12.2 billion they took in from data last quarter.  \u201cFreedomPop could, over time, put pricing pressure on the\nincumbents,\u201d said Kevin Smithen, an analyst at Macquarie\nSecurities USA Inc. in New York. \u201cThey have the potential to be\ndisruptive.\u201d  The phone industry suffered through a similar shakeup in\nthe last decade, when services such as Skype emerged. Founded in\n2003, Skype offers free calling between personal computers -- a\nfeature that forced phone companies to cut their long-distance\nand international calling rates. With  170 million connected\nusers  last year, Skype has become the world\u2019s largest\ninternational long-distance service. In 2011,  Microsoft Corp. (MSFT) \nacquired the company for  $8.5 billion .  \u2018Revolutionizing Catalyst\u2019  What Skype did for voice, Clearwire and partners want to do\nfor data. The idea is to undercut the prices for the service\nplans that let smartphones and tablets surf the Web and download\napplications. For now, though, the effect won\u2019t be as dramatic\nas with Skype, since Clearwire\u2019s network only covers about 70\nU.S. cities.  NetZero began a marketing campaign this month, including TV\nspots and online ads. It also will promote the service to the\nmore than 70 million people who use other offerings from parent\ncompany United Online, an  Internet service provider .  \u201cOur goal is to be a revolutionizing catalyst to the\nmarket,\u201d said Mark Goldston, chief executive officer of\n Woodland Hills , California-based United Online. \u201cWe think we\nhave a pretty big appeal.\u201d  Budget Consumers  He expects the service to attract budget-conscious\nconsumers who use public Wi-Fi hot spots for  Internet access , as\nwell as the growing number of people with tablets, though those\ntablets, too, would need to hook up to a modem. After customers\nuse up the free 200 megabytes, they would have to pay for data.\nPrices start at $9.95 a month for 500 megabytes.  FreedomPop, meanwhile, offers additional data for a penny a\nmegabyte -- beyond the free 1 gigabyte. The company could\nattract 1 million subscribers in about two years, Smithen\nestimates. Tony Miller, a spokesman for Los Angeles-based\nFreedomPop, declined to discuss the company\u2019s marketing plans.  Clearwire stands to benefit if either service catches on.\nFreedomPop probably pays Clearwire about $10 per gigabyte of\ncapacity, Smithen said.  \u201cIt could be worth a couple of hundred million dollars a\nyear, with high margins,\u201d he said.  The Bellevue, Washington-based company could use the boost.\nClearwire\u2019s stock has fallen 93 percent since peaking in 2007.\nThe company lost more than $2.5 billion over the past five years\nas it built out its network.  Sprint Nextel Corp. (S)  is currently\nits largest customer.  Price Hikes  The new services may attract users who are frustrated by\nrate increases at AT&T and other carriers. In January, AT&T\nraised the price of its data plans for new customers by $5 a\nmonth. Verizon announced plans for a $2 fee on some users in\nDecember, then backed away from the proposal after complaints\nfrom outraged customers. Verizon also stopped offering unlimited\ndata plans to new users last year.  Carriers are coping with burgeoning data traffic, forcing\nthem to be more vigilant about customers\u2019 data usage, said  Steve Clement , an analyst at  Portland , Oregon-based Pacific Crest\nSecurities LLC.  \u201cThe trends recently have been to increase prices to deal\nwith scarcity,\u201d he said. Without a viable competitive threat,\nprices will at least stay at current levels, if they don\u2019t rise\nhigher, he said.  Mark Siegel , a spokesman for Dallas-based AT&T, and  Brenda Raney , a representative for  Basking Ridge , New Jersey-based\n Verizon Wireless , declined to comment.  Wireless \u2018Duopoly\u2019  In recent years, the U.S. wireless market has turned into\n\u201ca duopoly,\u201d with AT&T and Verizon grabbing most new wireless\nsubscribers, according to  Craig Moffett , an analyst at Sanford\nC. Bernstein & Co. The two companies have generated 85 percent\nof the industry\u2019s free cash, not including funds that were\nreinvested back into building out networks, he said.  Other companies are competing on price, even without going\nthe freebie route.  Republic Wireless , a division of\nBandwidth.com Inc., offers unlimited voice, text and data for\n$19 a month. The company, which resells network capacity from\nSprint, is rolling out a trial version of the service and filled\nup all the available spots in eight hours. The service doesn\u2019t\nrequire users to sign up for a contract.  \u2018Freedom Model\u2019  \u201cTraditional telecom is all about control,\u201d said Republic\nWireless General Manager Brian Dally. \u201cOn the Internet, we are\nused to a freedom model. We stand for bringing those Internet\nvalues to telecom.\u201d  Lower-priced wireless services are already putting the\nsqueeze on existing carriers in other countries. In  Canada , for\ninstance, new entrants to the market have undercut data pricing\nby 83 percent, according to a  report  last year from Convergence\nConsulting Group. Convergence expects new carriers to have 4\nmillion subscribers, or 12 percent of Canada\u2019s wireless market,\nby the end of 2014. That\u2019s up from 5 percent at the end of 2011.  Across the border, U.S. consumers also are increasingly\nlooking beyond the main four carriers, said Emily Smith, an\n analyst  at Pyramid Research. Young people in particular may be\ninterested in something like FreedomPop, she said.  \u201cThere\u2019s a growing awareness among American consumers that\nthere are cheaper alternatives to the top four,\u201d Smith said. (GOOG) , which says it gets about 1,400 requests a month from U.S. authorities for users\u2019 e- mails and documents, is organizing an effort to press for limits on government access to digital communications.  The company has been talking to advocacy groups and companies about joining a lobbying effort to change the 1986 Electronic Communications Privacy Act, said  Chris Gaither , a Google spokesman. He declined to elaborate.  \u201cGiven the realities of how people live and where things are going in the digital world, it\u2019s an important time for government to act\u201d to update the law,  David Drummond , Google\u2019s chief legal officer, said in an interview. \u201cIt\u2019s a bipartisan issue and I think the momentum is going to build because citizens are expecting this.\u201d  Google officials say changes in the law are needed to prevent law enforcement from obtaining certain e-mails and other content without search warrants, and to give documents stored on cloud services the same legal protections as paper documents stored in a desk drawer. Cloud services, which didn\u2019t exist when the privacy law was passed, let users store and process data on remote servers via the Internet.  Spending on public cloud services is expected to reach $100 billion globally by 2016, from $40 billion last year, according to technology research firm IDC.  Last year, the owner of the world\u2019s largest search engine helped lead an Internet protest movement that derailed anti- piracy legislation in both houses of Congress. It began drawing attention to the privacy law last week, disclosing that more than two-thirds of 8,438 requests for user data it received from U.S. authorities in the second half of last year took place without a search warrant.  Netflix Bill  The privacy law sets out how law enforcement can get access to e-mails and other forms of digital communication. Senate Judiciary Committee Chairman  Patrick Leahy , a Vermont Democrat and one of law\u2019s original architects, said it\u2019s been made outdated by technology advances and expanded government surveillance powers.  Leahy\u2019s committee, over the objections of law enforcement groups, passed a proposal in November requiring government officials to get a search warrant to obtain e-mails and other communications regardless of their age.  That eliminated a provision in the law, written at a time e-mail was rarely stored by service providers, allowing authorities to obtain messages more than 180 days old with only a subpoena.  Law Enforcement  Leahy attached the change to a measure backed by  Netflix Inc. (NFLX)  to allow online sharing of video-rental information. The language was stripped out before the Netflix bill passed both chambers of Congress in December and was signed by President  Barack Obama .  The senator, in a Jan. 16 speech, said he\u2019ll reintroduce electronic-privacy legislation this year. He said he stayed on as judiciary committee chairman to continue that effort.  Groups representing federal, state and local law enforcement officers say Leahy\u2019s proposal could impede investigations.  \u201cIt changed the rules and operating procedures without conferring any advantages,\u201d said Konrad Motyka, president of the FBI Agents Association, an Alexandria, Virginia-based group representing 12,000 current and former FBI special agents. \u201cDon\u2019t just make our jobs more difficult.\u201d  Motyka said any move to increase the legal standard should be paired with measures to aid  law enforcement , such as requiring companies to respond to warrants within a specified period of time, and making exceptions for cases of child abuse, violent crimes and terrorism.  Justice Department  The U.S.  Justice Department  provided \u201ctechnical assistance\u201d on Leahy\u2019s bill, including \u201cexamples of problems that would be created for the executive branch in order to comply with legislative mandates,\u201d Beth Levine, a spokeswoman for Iowa Senator  Charles Grassley , the Judiciary Committee\u2019s top Republican, said in an e-mail.  Tracy Schmaler , a Justice Department spokeswoman, didn\u2019t respond to a phone call and e-mail requesting comment.  Google is part of an existing coalition, called Digital Due Process, formed in 2010 to seek changes to the privacy law. The coalition cuts across political ideology, with members including the  American Civil Liberties Union  and Americans for  Tax Reform , the anti-tax group led by  Grover Norquist . The U.S. Chamber of Commerce, the nation\u2019s largest business lobby, joined last month.  Other members include  Facebook Inc. (FB) ,  Amazon.com Inc. (AMZN) , and  Microsoft Corp. (MSFT)   \u2018Same Rights\u2019  \u201cIt\u2019s critical that we start to have the same rights in the online world that we do in the offline world,\u201d Chris Calabrese, ACLU legislative counsel, said in an interview. A paper letter has more protection against government searches than an older e-mail under current law, he said.  House Judiciary Committee Chairman Bob Goodlatte, a Virginia Republican, has said Congress should look at the privacy law, while saying he hasn\u2019t committed to specific changes. He said he expects to hold a hearing on the law this year.  Goodlatte, who sponsored the Netflix bill, said his willingness to work on the privacy law helped convince Leahy to get the video-sharing measure passed and \u201cnot hold it hostage\u201d to broader privacy changes.  Leahy and Goodlatte backed the anti-piracy bills in Congress that Google opposed and helped defeat last January. Google said the measures would lead to online censorship and chill innovation.  Google spent $16.5 million on lobbying last year, up from $9.7 million in 2011, according to Senate lobbying disclosures. Google\u2019s political action committee gave $9,500 to Goodlatte during the 2012 election.  Gmail, YouTube  The U.S. made the most requests for Google user information among governments in the second half of 2012, according to the company\u2019s transparency  report  released Jan. 23. Google is posting additional information for users today about what kinds of data it discloses to U.S. agencies from its Gmail, YouTube, Google Voice and Blogger services under ECPA legal processes.  While the law \u201cseems to allow\u201d the government to force service providers to turn over some digital content with a subpoena or court order, Google requires a search warrant before disclosing e-mail text, private videos or blog posts, and voicemail messages, according to a company fact sheet.  Google will release information other than content, such as user registration data and Internet-protocol addresses, under subpoenas or court orders, the company said. The technology juggernaut's problems, though, stem in part from a decision made long before Ballmer was in charge. In the early 1980s, Microsoft and Apple defied the expectations of industry experts by choosing to build proprietary operating systems for personal computers, rather than relying on Unix, a system initially developed in 1969 at Bell Labs. The extremely flexible Unix, which could be adapted to any hardware, became the domain of open-source geeks. They tweaked it to produce Linux, a free operating system popular largely among network administrators and Web developers. When Steve Jobs returned to Apple from a long exile in 1996, he changed the company's course. The successful Mac OS X operating system evolved from the Unix-based system used by Next, Inc., the company Jobs founded after his ouster from Apple in 1985. Clearly, the advantages of Unix, particularly its stability and processing power, had not been lost on Jobs.  Today, Unix-like systems dominate the smartphone market. Both leading mobile operating systems, iOS and Android, are based on Unix. The latter uses a Linux kernel at its core. Technology analyst Benedict Evans recently  noted  in his blog that at the end of 2012, about 900 million of the world's 1.1 billion smartphones were running either the iOS or Android versions of Unix.  \"It is pretty striking that almost a fifth of the earth's adult population has a Unix box in their pocket,\" wrote Evans. Unix has won a technological victory over Microsoft's approach, largely based now on Windows NT, a platform originally developed in 1992.  It's hard to fault Ballmer for Microsoft's defeat. By the time he became CEO in 2000, Microsoft was firmly locked into a business model that excluded the use of open-source software. License fees were -- and remain today -- the company's main revenue source. Of Microsoft's $77.9 billion in revenue in fiscal 2013, only $13.4 billion came from other sources. By contrast, Apple makes most of its money selling gadgets, and almost all of Google's revenues come from advertising. In both cases, it is much easier to build on open-source solutions than if your business depends on selling software.  \"Some companies compete with us using an open source business model by modifying and then distributing open source software at nominal cost to end-users and earning revenue on advertising or complementary services and products,\" Microsoft wrote in its latest annual report. \"These firms do not bear the full costs of research and development for the software.\" Access to more nimble technology, which builds on the experience of a large, creative developer community, has allowed Microsoft's competitors to get their products to market much faster. Windows Phone 8, based on a Windows NT kernel, had some technological advantages over Android and iOS, but it came out too late for users to care. The system has garnered only a 3.3 percent share of the smartphone market. Within the constraints of Microsoft's business model, Ballmer has performed well. Corporate customers are not switching to alternative open-source products, because they like to deal with a specific, established supplier. Ballmer can hardly be blamed for refusing to chase technological leadership at the cost of undermining a lucrative core business. The company has been extremely profitable, accumulating a cash position of $77 billion as of June. Despite its underperformance in the stock market, its price-to-earnings ratio, at 11.3, is similar to Apple's 11.8.  Ballmer is also right not to give up on consumer products. At the very least, working on them allows Microsoft to better understand its business customers' needs. In the corporate market, speed is not as important as in the consumer segment, and Microsoft certainly has the money to keep developing its proprietary platform. Lagging a step or two behind may be irritating, but it's still profitable. (Leonid Bershidsky, an editor and novelist, is a Bloomberg View contributor. These programs, whose participants are known as trusted partners, extend far beyond what was revealed by Edward Snowden, a computer technician who did work for the National Security Agency. The role of private companies has come under intense scrutiny since his disclosure this month that the NSA is collecting millions of U.S. residents\u2019 telephone records and the computer communications of foreigners from  Google Inc. (GOOG)  and other Internet companies under court order.  Many of these same Internet and telecommunications companies voluntarily provide U.S. intelligence organizations with additional data, such as equipment specifications, that don\u2019t involve private communications of their customers, the four people said.  Makers of hardware and software, banks, Internet security providers, satellite telecommunications companies and many other companies also participate in the government programs. In some cases, the information gathered may be used not just to defend the nation but to help infiltrate computers of its adversaries.  Along with the NSA, the Central Intelligence Agency, the  Federal Bureau  of Investigation and branches of the U.S. military have agreements with such companies to gather data that might seem innocuous but could be highly useful in the hands of U.S. intelligence or cyber warfare units, according to the people, who have either worked for the government or are in companies that have these accords.  Microsoft Bugs  Microsoft Corp. (MSFT) , the world\u2019s largest software company, provides intelligence agencies with information about bugs in its popular software before it publicly releases a fix, according to two people familiar with the process. That information can be used to protect government computers and to access the computers of terrorists or military foes.  Redmond, Washington-based Microsoft and other software or Internet security companies have been aware that this type of early alert allowed the U.S. to exploit vulnerabilities in software sold to foreign governments, according to two U.S. officials. Microsoft doesn\u2019t ask and can\u2019t be told how the government uses such tip-offs, said the officials, who asked not to be identified because the matter is confidential.  Frank Shaw , a spokesman for Microsoft, said those releases occur in cooperation with multiple agencies and are designed to give government \u201can early start\u201d on risk assessment and mitigation.  In an e-mailed statement, Shaw said there are \u201cseveral programs\u201d through which such information is passed to the government, and named two which are public, run by Microsoft and for defensive purposes.  Willing Cooperation  Some U.S. telecommunications companies willingly provide intelligence agencies with access to facilities and data offshore that would require a judge\u2019s order if it were done in the U.S., one of the four people said.  In these cases, no oversight is necessary under the Foreign Intelligence Surveillance Act, and companies are providing the information voluntarily.  The extensive cooperation between commercial companies and intelligence agencies is legal and reaches deeply into many aspects of everyday life, though little of it is scrutinized by more than a small number of lawyers, company leaders and spies. Company executives are motivated by a desire to help the national defense as well as to help their own companies, said the people, who are familiar with the agreements.  Most of the arrangements are so sensitive that only a handful of people in a company know of them, and they are sometimes brokered directly between chief executive officers and the heads of the U.S.\u2019s major spy agencies, the people familiar with those programs said.  \u2018Thank Them\u2019  Michael Hayden , who formerly directed the National Security Agency and the CIA, described the attention paid to important company partners: \u201cIf I were the director and had a relationship with a company who was doing things that were not just directed by law but were also valuable to the defense of the Republic, I would go out of my way to thank them and give them a sense as to why this is necessary and useful.\u201d  \u201cYou would keep it closely held within the company and there would be very few cleared individuals,\u201d Hayden said.  Cooperation between nine U.S. Internet companies and the NSA\u2019s Special Source Operations unit came to light along with a secret program called Prism. According to a slide deck provided by Snowden, the program gathers e-mails, videos, and other private data of foreign surveillance targets through arrangements that vary by company, overseen by a secret panel of judges.  U.S. intelligence agencies have grown far more dependent on such arrangements as the flow of much of the world\u2019s information has grown exponentially through switches, cables and other network equipment maintained by U.S. companies.  Equipment Specs  In addition to private communications, information about equipment specifications and data needed for the Internet to work -- much of which isn\u2019t subject to oversight because it doesn\u2019t involve private communications -- is valuable to intelligence, U.S. law-enforcement officials and the military.  Typically, a key executive at a company and a small number of technical people cooperate with different agencies and sometimes multiple units within an agency, according to the four people who described the arrangements.  Committing Officer  If necessary, a company executive, known as a \u201ccommitting officer,\u201d is given documents that guarantee immunity from civil actions resulting from the transfer of data. The companies are provided with regular updates, which may include the broad parameters of how that information is used.  Intel Corp. (INTC) \u2019s McAfee unit, which makes Internet security software, regularly cooperates with the NSA, FBI and the CIA, for example, and is a valuable partner because of its broad view of malicious Internet traffic, including espionage operations by foreign powers, according to one of the four people, who is familiar with the arrangement.  Such a relationship would start with an approach to McAfee\u2019s chief executive, who would then clear specific individuals to work with investigators or provide the requested data, the person said. The public would be surprised at how much help the government seeks, the person said.  McAfee firewalls collect information on hackers who use legitimate servers to do their work, and the company data can be used to pinpoint where attacks begin. The company also has knowledge of the architecture of information networks worldwide, which may be useful to spy agencies who tap into them, the person said.  McAfee\u2019s Data  McAfee\u2019s data and analysis doesn\u2019t include information on individuals, said Michael Fey, the company\u2019s worldwide chief technology officer.  \u201cWe do not share any type of personal information with our government agency partners,\u201d Fey said in an e-mailed statement. \u201cMcAfee\u2019s function is to provide security technology, education, and threat intelligence to governments. This threat intelligence includes trending data on emerging new threats, cyber-attack patterns and vector activity, as well as analysis on the integrity of software, system vulnerabilities, and hacker group activity.\u201d  In exchange, leaders of companies are showered with attention and information by the agencies to help maintain the relationship, the person said.  In other cases, companies are given quick warnings about threats that could affect their bottom line, including serious Internet attacks and who is behind them.  China\u2019s Military  Following an attack on his company by Chinese hackers in 2010,  Sergey Brin , Google\u2019s co-founder, was provided with highly sensitive government intelligence linking the attack to a specific unit of the  People\u2019s Liberation Army , China\u2019s military, according to one of the people, who is familiar with the government\u2019s investigation. Brin was given a temporary classified clearance to sit in on the briefing, the person said.  According to information provided by Snowden, Google, owner of the world\u2019s most popular search engine, had at that point been a Prism participant for more than a year.  Google CEO  Larry Page  said in a blog posting June 7 that he hadn\u2019t heard of a program called Prism until after Snowden\u2019s disclosures and that the  Mountain View , California-based company didn\u2019t allow the U.S. government direct access to its servers or some back-door to its data centers. He said Google provides user data to governments \u201conly in accordance with the law.\u201d  Leslie Miller, a spokeswoman for Google, didn\u2019t provide an immediate response June 13.  The information provided by Snowden also exposed a secret NSA program known as Blarney. As the program was described in the  Washington Post (WPO) , the agency gathers metadata on computers and devices that are used to send e-mails or browse the Internet through principal data routes, known as a backbone.  Metadata  That metadata includes which version of the operating system, browser and Java software are being used on millions of devices around the world, information that U.S. spy agencies could use to infiltrate those computers or phones and spy on their users.  \u201cIt\u2019s highly offensive information,\u201d said Glenn Chisholm, the former chief information officer for  Telstra Corp. (TLS) , one of Australia\u2019s largest telecommunications companies, contrasting it to defensive information used to protect computers rather than infiltrate them.  According to Snowden\u2019s information, Blarney\u2019s purpose is \u201cto gain access and exploit foreign intelligence,\u201d the Post said.  It\u2019s unclear whether U.S. Internet service providers gave information to the NSA as part of Blarney, and if so, whether the transfer of that data required a judge\u2019s order.  Less Scrutiny  Stewart Baker, former general counsel for the NSA, said if metadata involved communications between two foreign computers that just happened to be crossing a U.S. fiber optic cable \u201cthen the likelihood is it would demand less legal scrutiny than when communications are being extracted one by one.\u201d  Lawmakers who oversee U.S. intelligence agencies may not understand the significance of some of the metadata being collected, said Jacob Olcott, a former cybersecurity assistant for Senator John D. Rockefeller IV of West Virginia, the Democratic chairman of the Senate Commerce Committee.  \u201cThat\u2019s what makes this issue of oversight so challenging,\u201d said Olcott, now a principal at Good Harbor Security Risk Management in Washington. \u201cYou have a situation where the technology and technical policy is far outpacing the background and expertise of most elected members of Congress or their staffs.\u201d  While companies are offered powerful inducements to cooperate with U.S. intelligence, many executives are motivated by patriotism or a sense they are defending national security, the people familiar with the trusted partner programs said.  Einstein 3  U.S telecommunications, Internet, power companies and others provide U.S. intelligence agencies with details of their systems\u2019 architecture or equipment schematics so the agencies can analyze potential vulnerabilities.  \u201cIt\u2019s natural behavior for governments to want to know about the country\u2019s critical infrastructure,\u201d said Chisholm, chief security officer at  Irvine , California-based Cylance Inc.  Even strictly defensive systems can have unintended consequences for privacy. Einstein 3, a costly program originally developed by the NSA, is meant to protect government systems from hackers. The program, which has been made public and is being installed, will closely analyze the billions of e-mails sent to government computers every year to see if they contain spy tools or malicious software.  Einstein 3 could also expose the private content of the e-mails under certain circumstances, according to a person familiar with the system, who asked not to be named because he wasn\u2019t authorized to discuss the matter.  AT&T, Verizon  Before they agreed to install the system on their networks, some of the five major Internet companies --  AT&T Inc. (T) ,  Verizon Communications Inc. (VZ) , Sprint Nextel Corp.,  Level 3 Communications Inc. (LVLT)  and  CenturyLink Inc. (CTL)  -- asked for guarantees that they wouldn\u2019t be held liable under U.S. wiretap laws. Those companies that asked received a letter signed by the U.S. attorney general indicating such exposure didn\u2019t meet the legal definition of a wiretap and granting them immunity from civil lawsuits, the person said.  Mark Siegel , a spokesman for Dallas-based AT&T, the nation\u2019s biggest phone carrier, declined to comment. Edward McFadden, a spokesman for New York-based Verizon, the second-largest phone company, declined to comment.  Scott Sloat , a spokesman for Overland Park, Kansas-based Sprint, and Monica Martinez, a spokeswoman for Broomfield, Colorado-based Level 3, didn\u2019t immediately respond to requests for comment.  Linda Johnson, a spokeswoman for Centurylink, formerly Qwest Corp., said her Monroe, Louisiana-based company participates in the Enhanced Cybersecurity Services program and the Intrusion Prevention Security Services program, which includes Einstein 3. Both programs are managed by the U.S. Department of  Homeland Security .
