So when he notes in a  farewell interview  that, thanks to social media, there's now \"an instant referendum on everything; I think it's going to make governing more difficult,\" private sector managers better get nervous, too. The Arab Spring and other Twitter-credited uprisings get virtually all the headlines, but the C-suites and high-profile executives at enterprises worldwide are increasingly conducting \"instant referenda\" on their presentations, decisions, and actions. The digital institutionalization of the instant referendum makes leadership and management more difficult, as well. The more controversial or confusing the leadership decision, the harsher and more influential the instant judgments of that referendum can be. Don't think for a moment that mid-level J.C. Penney managers and employees weren't sharing their unhappiness and concerns during  Ron Johnson's troubled tenure  there. At Microsoft, no sooner had Steve Ballmer's resignation set the company's digital tongues a'wagging than another internal debate broke out in the wake of the company's  multi-billion-dollar Nokia acquisition . Are Google's employees running comparable referenda on the impact that a  cofounder's relationship status  may have on their company? The water cooler hasn't vanished; it's simply become virtual, transported into the cloud. What's fundamentally different, of course, is the new speed and scalability of sentiment. Where rumors and reactions once took weeks to coalesce into enterprise attitudes, internal networks and \"gray market\" social media now compress into days. Global firms \u2014 indeed, any organizations of size and\/or scale \u2014 are now captive to social-mediated  \"information cascades\"  that can turn quiet doubts into open skepticism and reluctant accommodation into passive resistance.  Managing \u2014 or at least influencing \u2014 information cascades will become one of the core communications competencies of top-level executives. Facilitating favorable cascades will matter as much as killing one in its virtual tracks. If information is cascading in private Twitter, Facebook, and\/or LinkedIn networks, executives may indeed have to ask to \"friend\" or \"follow\" hub colleagues and subordinates. At one European global financial firm, I saw heavily lawyered internal communications about an internal problem managed so poorly that managers across the enterprise collectively lost respect for the senior executive tasked with handling it. The instant referendum in the aftermath almost instantly devalued that executive's brand within the firm. He had to rehabilitate himself in face-to-face meetings throughout Europe to make up for losing that referendum. Needless to say, he and the corporate communications folks monitored the internal chatter that followed his make-up sessions. Issues of privacy and anonymity for these informal \"off-network\" referenda become managerially challenging, as well. In instant referenda environments, being likable and\/or highly competent counts for a lot. Leaders and managers want to be seen as either nice or credible enough to get the benefit of the doubt for a difficult decision or a controversial choice. Being more accessible or responsive can help. Similarly, so might \"information inoculation\" strategies and tactics where \u2014 like with a good vaccine \u2014 people get exposed to just enough of the decision or conflict to prevent uncontrollable outbreaks of negative sentiment.  Does this create the real risk that managers and leaders appear afraid of negative reactions from their subordinates? Yes, it does. Does it also create the possibility that employees and colleagues will be even angrier and more resistant to leaders who behave as if their reactions don't much matter? Why, yes. Michael Bloomberg knows things have changed. In the  digital enterprise  where  BYOD  has become the new normal, instant referenda are an emergent phenomenon that leaders and managers ignore at their peril. The more important \u2014 and controversial \u2014 the decision, the more important that instant referendum will prove.  Poker players worldwide understand the admonition that if you can't spot the fish at the table in the first half hour, then you're the fish. In the socially mediated enterprise, leaders who aren't really aware of their internal referenda aren't really leading.","path":".\/2008_2012_msft_bloomberg_news\/e-instant-referendum-that-s-undermining-your-leadership.txt"},{"id":85587704,"title":"Bill Gates Seeks $1.5 Billion More to Eradicate Polio by 2018","released_at":"<date>April 25 2013<\/date> <time>10:23:36<\/time>","content":"Bill Gates , chairman and co-founder\nof  Microsoft Corp. In that filing\nhe said that the defendants\u2019 \u201cdownplaying similarities is a\ntactic that is expected but should not be construed as\naccurate.\u201d  In a July 9 order, U.S. District Judge Julie E. Carnes said\nthat Marquardt\u2019s book failed to meet copyright law\u2019s standards\nfor infringement due to \u201csubstantial similarity,\u201d and\ndismissed the case.  The case is Marquardt V. Trade Secrets\/Industrial Espionage  DoubleLine\u2019s Gundlach Says He Offered to Buy TCW in 2009  DoubleLine Capital LP\u2019s  Jeffrey Gundlach  testified that in\nSeptember 2009 he offered to buy TCW Group Inc., the asset-\nmanagement company that fired him three months later.  Gundlach, who started DoubleLine weeks after TCW fired him\nin December 2009, told a Los Angeles jury yesterday that he\noffered about $350 million for 51 percent of the firm. TCW\nclaims that Gundlach and three other former TCW employees stole\nits trade secrets to open a rival business. Gundlach says TCW\nfired him to avoid paying hundreds of millions of dollars in\nfees.  TCW, the Los Angeles-based unit of  Societe Generale (GLE)  SA,\nsued Gundlach, 51, in January 2010, a month after more than half\nof TCW\u2019s fixed-income professionals had joined his new firm. TCW\nseeks $375 million in damages, claiming Gundlach stole its trade\nsecrets, including client portfolio data, to start DoubleLine.  Gundlach, who had worked at TCW for 25 years and who was\nnamed Morningstar\u2019s Fixed Income Manager of the Year in 2006,\ncountersued, saying that TCW fired him to avoid having to pay\nmanagement and performance fees for the distressed-asset funds\nhis group managed and that went \u201cthrough the roof.\u201d Gundlach\nseeks about $500 million.  TCW argues that Gundlach wouldn\u2019t have been able to get\nDoubleLine started so quickly if he hadn\u2019t had access to the\ntrade secrets and confidential information. Gundlach today disputed testimony by Cris Santa Ana, a co-\ndefendant and counter-claimant, detailing the kind of TCW\ninformation he wanted collected.  Gundlach also said he spoke with Western Asset Management\nCo. earlier in 2009 about moving the funds he managed at TCW to\nthe rival company. The talks were prompted by Paris-based\nSociete General\u2019s announced intention to get out of the asset-\nmanagement business and the arrangement he contemplated would\nhave been beneficial to TCW as well, Gundlach said.  A proposed June 12, 2009, compensation arrangement by\nWestern Asset Management, based on an estimated $150 million in\nrevenue from his business, was a non-starter and he didn\u2019t read\na follow-up proposal, Gundlach said.  The case is Trust Co. of the West v. Gundlach, BC429385,\nCalifornia Superior Court, Los Angeles County. Even with the recent stock plunge, it is the most valuable company in the world, with a market capitalization of about $412 billion.  After the release of the iPhone, Apple\u2019s ads focused less on emotions and more on illustrating what its products could do. Most showed an Apple gadget with a finger demonstrating their use -- say, how to pinch to enlarge a Web page -- against a clean white background and upbeat music.  Now Apple has realized that its products no longer sell themselves so easily, given competition from devices with the same or additional features at lower prices, said the people with knowledge of the company\u2019s advertising plans. Since co-founderJobs\u2019s death in October 2011, Apple\u2019s only new product line has been the iPad mini, itself an evolution from the aging iPad.  Samsung\u2019s Rise  Since then,  Samsung Electronics Co. (005930)  has taken the global lead in smartphones, thanks to strong sales of its Galaxy devices. One  pokes fun at geeky Apple fans standing in line waiting to get a new iPhone that lacks features already available in Samsung\u2019s Galaxy.  \u201cWe measured response to Samsung and Apple ads the week after that ran, and the scores for Apple dropped like a rock,\u201d said Peter Daboll, CEO of Ace Metrix Inc., a consulting firm that surveys TV viewers on the effectiveness of ads.  Big Brother  Apple\u2019s partnership with Chiat\\Day began in the 1980s, stemming from Jobs\u2019s relationship with creative director Lee Clow. Clow, known for his long beard and laid-back approach, led development of the \u201c1984\u201d Macintosh ad, which symbolized Apple\u2019s challenge to International Business Machines Corp. by depicting a runner throwing a hammer into a TV screen featuring a Big Brother-like speaker. He\u2019s also credited with creating the Energizer Bunny and other iconic campaigns.  Though the agency lost Apple\u2019s business when Jobs was ousted in 1985, Jobs called Clow after he returned in 1997 to work on the \u201cThink Different\u201d campaign.  In the ensuing 14 years, the companies settled into a groove that revolved around Jobs, who dominated the company\u2019s advertising strategy -- and Apple and Media Arts Lab have struggled to adapt to life without him.  For years, Media Arts Lab executives, including James Vincent, traveled to Cupertino from  Los Angeles  most Wednesdays to discuss ideas and get Jobs\u2019s feedback, people said.  Schiller\u2019s Marketing  Since his death, the meetings are run by Philip W. Schiller, senior vice president of marketing, which has meant less clarity about what the company wants its ads to say, people familiar with Apple\u2019s advertising said.  Once Jobs had made a decision, no one at Media Arts Lab argued for long. Now, its creative staff becomes frustrated more often when Schiller shoots down ideas, they said.  Apple declined to make Schiller available for this story. A campaign featuring one of Apple\u2019s Genius Bar customer-service representatives, started during the 2012 Olympics, was halted after just a few weeks. During the late 17th century, they were the birthplace of Lloyd\u2019s of London and the London Stock Exchange -- two institutions that helped make the square-mile City of London a global financial capital.  Today, just north of where one of the City\u2019s ancient gates once stood, the latest chapter in London\u2019s economic history is being written in a new generation of coffeehouses, Bloomberg Markets will report in its June issue.  More from the June 2013 issue of Bloomberg Markets: At Shoreditch Grind on the Old Street roundabout, a gritty traffic circle, and at Ozone Coffee Roasters, a few blocks away, bearded young men and nose-ringed women huddle around laptops and discuss ideas for startup companies.  The surrounding offices, many of them in converted warehouses, are so crammed with technology startups -- at least 300 -- that the area has been dubbed, in mock seriousness, Silicon Roundabout.  Increasingly, that nickname is losing its irony: Established technology players are moving in.  Google Inc. (GOOG)  recently opened Campus London, a kind of clubhouse for digital entrepreneurs, not far from the roundabout.  Inside, techies hobnob in the bustling cafe and attend lectures and other free events; they can gain access to hot desks, printers and conference rooms operated by another company, TechHub, for a 375 pound ($560) annual fee. Springboard and Seedcamp Ltd., European tech incubators, rent space on two of Campus\u2019s floors.  \u2018Flat White\u2019  Following Google\u2019s lead,  Microsoft Corp. (MSFT)  and  Cisco Systems Inc. (CSCO)  are opening their own Campus-like innovation centers close to the roundabout, while  Amazon.com Inc. (AMZN)  has put its first engineering center outside the U.S. a few blocks west. There, hundreds of developers work on Amazon\u2019s video-streaming services.  Taking in the adjacent neighborhoods, the government estimates there are now more than 1,300 digital or media startups in the once-dreary hinterland of East London.  Welcome to the \u201cflat white economy.\u201d The term was coined by Rob Harbron, an economist at the London-based Centre for Economics and Business Research in winking reference to the Australian-inspired espresso-and-steamed-milk drink popular in East London\u2019s cafes.  Encompassing media, Internet and creative businesses such as film, music and advertising, the flat white economy accounted for 4.5 percent of British gross domestic product in 2011, up from 2.8 percent in 2008, according to the latest U.K. government analysis.  Bright Spot  The flat white economy is a rare bright spot in an otherwise dismal economic landscape. Having emerged from a double-dip recession in the summer of 2012, the U.K. economy has  struggled  to find its footing. GDP grew a meager 0.3 percent in the first quarter of 2013.  A policy of harsh government spending cuts is only starting to be felt three years into Conservative Prime Minister  David Cameron \u2019s government. Unemployment, at 7.8 percent in January, remains high. In February, rating firm Moody\u2019s Investors Service stripped the country of its vaunted Aaa bond rating.  In contrast to the caffeinated buzz of Silicon Roundabout, the mood in the City remains downbeat five years after the onset of the global financial crisis. Here, pinstriped men and women trudge to work at dawn through the half-light of a British spring, past steel and glass towers full of empty desks.  \u2018Main Drivers\u2019  Financial services, the dominant industry in London since the 1980s, has been in decline, slipping from more than 10 percent of British GDP in 2008 to 9.4 percent in 2011.  \u201cWe don\u2019t expect employment in financial services to grow very fast even as the economy recovers,\u201d Harbron says.  The British government is desperate to find sectors to fill the hole.  \u201cThe main drivers of growth over the past 10 years were property, financial services,  consumer debt  and  government borrowing ,\u201d says Rohan Silva, 32, a senior policy adviser to Cameron. \u201cWe have got to move the economy to a more resilient footing: life sciences, green tech and digital technology.\u201d  Yet even as the flat white economy gains ground, venture capitalists say it will take time for London to rival more-established tech hubs such as Silicon Valley,  Boston \u2019s tech corridor or  Tel Aviv .  \u201cNone of the European tech hubs compare to the U.S. or  Israel ,\u201d says Hussein Kanji, a London-based angel investor.  Uphill Struggle  Startup founders in London were \u201cless ambitious\u201d than their U.S. counterparts and were 31 percent more likely to target smaller markets, according to a 2012 report by Startup Genome, a website that analyzes tech entrepreneurship.  London companies also struggled to find seed investors willing to put $500,000 to $2.5 million into startups, the report said. As a result, by the time they had found proven markets for their products, these companies raised on average 81 percent less capital than their equivalents in Silicon Valley.  City Meets Tech , a group whose co-founders include James Rowsell, chief executive officer of Cantor Fitzgerald  Europe , has been trying to get bankers involved in seeding fledgling tech companies. The group organizes pitch days that introduce startups to investors from London\u2019s financial community.  It\u2019s an uphill struggle, says Steve Karmeinsky, a startup consultant and co-founder of City Meets Tech.  \u201cIf you are a broker making 100-million-pound trades a day, the idea of putting 30,000 or 40,000 pounds into a tech startup seems too difficult,\u201d he says. \u201cIt\u2019s easier to go and buy your second Porsche.\u201d  The rap on London has long been that its business culture isn\u2019t supportive of entrepreneurs -- that failure carries too much stigma.  Seed Funding  \u201cI think most of that has changed,\u201d says Ben Holmes, a partner at Index Ventures in London, a firm that has a 350 million euro ($455 million)  early-stage fund . The cost of failure has fallen.  \u201cFor just tens of thousands -- or even a few thousand pounds -- you can build and test a prototype,\u201d Holmes says.  The recent recession also lowered opportunity costs: With young graduates hard-pressed to find jobs, would-be entrepreneurs have little to lose on a startup.  And, while there\u2019s still a gap in seed funding, overall  venture capital  has become more plentiful, though still lagging far behind the U.S. In 2012, the U.K. was the most active European hotbed, with $1.8 billion raised, up from $1.4 billion in 2009, according to Ernst & Young LLP.  Holmes says London now has all the ingredients of a successful tech hub except one: an initial public offering or acquisition with a valuation of $1 billion or more. In the world of venture capitalism, the $1 billion exit is seen as an important milestone for a tech center, cementing its reputation and creating enough millionaires to seed another round of startups.  Snakeskin Boots  Exemplifying London\u2019s tech resurgence is a shaggy-haired 38-year-old entrepreneur with a penchant for loud shirts and snakeskin boots named Michael Acton Smith.  Acton Smith had minor success during the first dot-com boom with a company that sold gifts and gadgets online; its most popular item was a chess set made of shot glasses.  In 2004, he convinced a group of investors to back him in an online games company called  Mind Candy . In three years, the company burned through 5 million pounds developing a treasure-hunt game that flopped.  With what little cash Mind Candy had left, Acton Smith gambled on a new idea: Moshi Monsters, a site that would allow children to adopt, personalize and care for a digital creature.  Moshi Monsters  After a slow start in the depths of the 2008 financial crisis, during which Mind Candy almost went bankrupt, Moshi Monsters became a phenomenon. Kids have created more than 75 million of them. Mind Candy has signed more than 100 Moshi Monsters merchandising deals ranging from stuffed animals to music.  In three rounds of venture funding, Mind Candy has received about 12 million pounds, most of it from the London office of Accel Partners Ltd., a  Palo Alto , California-based VC firm, and Index Ventures. In 2011, the last year for which audited financials are available, Mind Candy made a profit of 7.4 million pounds on revenue of 29 million pounds. In 2012, revenue doubled, the company says.  Mind Candy\u2019s first offices were in Battersea in South London. Lured by a mixture of cheap real estate and bohemian atmosphere, the company moved east to Shoreditch in 2009, soon followed by a wave of digital startups.  \u201cWe like this part of town because it is a little bit grubby,\u201d says Divinia Knowles, 34, Mind Candy\u2019s chief operating officer.  Twisting Slide  While average commercial rents in Shoreditch have increased nearly 40 percent to 42.50 pounds a square foot from the end of 2008, they\u2019re still about half the price of those in London\u2019s West End, according to real estate brokerage  Cushman & Wakefield  Inc.  Mind Candy occupies 2,700 square meters (30,000 square feet) on the top two floors of a rehabbed 1960s office building on Bonhill Street, less than a five-minute walk from the Old Street roundabout and directly across from Google\u2019s Campus.  The offices feature green AstroTurf-like flooring, rainbow-colored Moshi Monster murals, a faux treehouse and even a twisting metal-tube slide so employees can swish down to the third floor from the fourth.  Nearly 5 kilometers (3 miles) to the west, inside the Georgian drawing rooms of 10 Downing Street, Cameron has been trying to give London\u2019s growing tech hub a helpful nudge.  Thatcher\u2019s Footsteps  In doing so, he\u2019s following in the footsteps of  Margaret Thatcher , who died on April 8, says Sara Kelly, executive director of the Coalition for a Digital Economy, a trade association. The late prime minister\u2019s privatization of British Telecommunications Plc and Cable & Wireless Ltd. in the 1980s, for example, created opportunities for smaller companies.  \u201cHer policies made becoming an entrepreneur an acceptable alternative career path,\u201d Kelly says.  With policy adviser Silva acting as his de facto liaison to the tech community, Cameron has pushed through a raft of policies aimed at boosting entrepreneurship, including an income tax credit of up to 50,000 pounds on the first 100,000 pounds invested in a startup and an exemption from capital gains taxes. The government also created a so-called entrepreneur\u2019s visa that makes it easier for foreigners to come to the U.K. to start businesses.  Despite almost across-the-board spending cuts in the 2012 budget -- including 3.2 billion pounds in local government and 1.8 billion pounds in defense -- in an effort to balance the U.K.\u2019s books, Cameron has found money for East London\u2019s tech hub.  Shared Offices  He\u2019s committed 25 million pounds to improving broadband connections and  pledged 50 million pounds  to erect a landmark building in the middle of the Old Street roundabout with classrooms, auditoriums, shared offices and 3-D printing labs. The project is due to be completed by 2016. The government will fund one-half to two-thirds of the project\u2019s cost, with the rest coming from private donations, Silva says.  Late last year, Silva hired Joanna Shields away from her job heading  Facebook Inc. (FB) \u2019s European operations and named her chief executive of the  Tech City Investment Organisation , charged with promoting London as a tech center.  In April, Silva announced he planned to leave Downing Street at the end of June to found his own digital education startup.  Cameron isn\u2019t the only one looking for tech to replace some of the losses from financial services. Real estate companies that once catered to banks see profits in tech startups. Tech and media companies now account for 35 percent of all commercial real estate demand in London, more than any other industry group, according to Cushman & Wakefield.  Incubator Space  In March, Canary Wharf Group Plc, which has been developing a financial district east of the City since the 1990s, launched  Level39 , an incubator space for startups focusing on financial applications, or fin tech, among other areas.  Ironically, the very institution that made London a global financial center has been among the biggest impediments to making it a global tech hub: the London Stock Exchange.  The LSE\u2019s main market required companies going public to sell at least 25 percent of their shares. This rule turned off venture-backed startups fearful of diluting existing investors. By contrast,  Nasdaq \u2019s minimum float is 5 percent.  In March, the LSE created a  High Growth Segment  within its main market that will allow companies to sell fewer shares -- just 10 percent -- provided they have had 20 percent annual revenue growth for three years running.  Tech Ingenue  While that may help London, the U.S. retains other advantages, Index Ventures\u2019 Holmes says.  \u201cIt is a difficult choice for many companies,\u201d he says. \u201cDo you go to the U.S., where there is a bigger comparable set of businesses, more analyst coverage and the valuation models are better understood? In 2003, Congress took back 130,000 temporary work visas. Four years later, Silicon Valley was surprised when proposed legislation didn\u2019t come close to addressing companies\u2019 skilled-worker needs.  After the 2007 loss, the industry took a new tack. Tech leaders helped write legislative drafts spelling out what they wanted; they broadened their pitch about immigration to include legalizing undocumented immigrants in the country; and they now are using social media to press their case.  \u201cWe knew we had to get into the game early and go strong,\u201d said Robert Hoffman, senior vice president of government relations for the  Information Technology Industry Council , which lobbies for technology companies. \u201cWe knew we had to think several steps down the road.\u201d  Silicon Valley\u2019s role in pushing for changes in immigration law adds economic urgency to a debate that for more than a decade has focused mostly on the treatment of 11 million undocumented residents. The tech community\u2019s engagement also brought to the table companies with the power to mobilize thousands of supporters to join ranks with the Latino community.  Hatch\u2019s Support  The gains from the new approach were on display yesterday when Senator  Orrin Hatch , a Utah Republican and industry ally, backed a broad revision of  immigration  law in the Senate Judiciary Committee after the adoption of an amendment making it easier for technology companies to hire more temporary workers. The panel also approved the full immigration bill 13-5.  A \u201cvirtual march\u201d today and tomorrow is designed to \u201cleverage the power of innovative digital tools and technology to influence the policy debate in  Washington ,\u201d said Jeremy Robbins, director of the Partnership for a New American Economy. The group is also leading a social-media campaign that encourages Twitter users to contact their lawmakers.  In the first few hours of the movement, which uses the Twitter hashtag \u201ciMarch,\u201d the government account for the White House shared seven messages about how immigration affects business and technology.  Borrowed Tactic  March organizers are taking a page from an online movement last year that stopped an effort to crack down on Internet usage of intellectual property.  Google Inc. (GOOG)  and Wikipedia led a blackout of Internet sites that included a directive to call Congress and tell them to reject the anti-piracy legislation.  Helping amplify voter voices is corporate money: The computer and Internet sector made $64 million in federal contributions during last year\u2019s election, more than twice its giving in 2004, according to the Center for Responsive Politics based in Washington. The industry employed 1,142 lobbyists last year to spend more than $133 million pushing its agenda, the center found. Google spent $16 million on advocacy last year, quadrupling its investment in just three years.  Tech has led a surge of lobbying registrations this year on immigration, according to a report today by the Sunlight Foundation, a Washington-based political money tracker. Technology interests accounted for more than one-quarter of the 37 organizations that registered lobbyists this month and last, the report found.  Matured Industry  \u201cThe industry has matured about Washington,\u201d said Jack Krumholtz, a managing director at The Glover Park Group\u2019s Washington office and who was government relations manager for Microsoft for 14 years. \u201cThere is awareness now of the need to engage policy makers at all levels of government.\u201d  And tech-savvy billionaires have invested their reputations and riches into the immigration issue.  Facebook\u2019s  Mark Zuckerberg  and LinkedIn\u2019s  Reid Hoffman  started a political group called FWD.us that has paid for TV ads to boost and protect immigration backers including Senator  Marco Rubio , a Florida Republican.  Apple Inc. (AAPL)  co-founder  Steve Jobs \u2019s widow, Laurene Powell Jobs, will be part of Partnership\u2019s online drive, called the March for Innovation. And  New York  Mayor Michael Bloomberg funds Partnership, which includes dozens of computer and Internet company chief executives. The mayor is founder and majority owner of Bloomberg News parent Bloomberg LP.  More Engaged  \u201cThe tech community is more engaged in public policy than at any time that I\u2019ve been in Congress,\u201d said Republican Senator Jerry Moran, who served as a Kansas congressman from 1997 until he was elected to the Senate in 2011. \u201cThey\u2019re paying attention, and they\u2019re trying to influence the debate.\u201d  When Congress reconvened in January, technology advocates worked with Moran, Hatch and other lawmakers on tech-friendly immigration bills that the bipartisan Gang of Eight senators could refer to as they wrote the immigration legislation.  The I-Squared Act, sponsored by Hatch, would raise the number of temporary visas available to skilled workers, such as computer engineers, and the Start-Up Act, sponsored by Moran, would make it easier for foreign-born entrepreneurs to stay in the country. Elements of both are included in the legislation.  \u201cThese bills were templates for what we wanted to see in immigration,\u201d said Senate  Amy Klobuchar , a Minnesota Democrat who co-sponsored I-Squared and the Start-Up Act. \u201cThey are helpful because they bring a business focus to immigration.\u201d  \u2018Favored Child\u2019  Congressional consensus on the principles of tech\u2019s must-haves empowers the industry to act as a chief lobbyist for the overall bill. Tech has become a \u201cfavored child\u201d in the push for a revision of immigration laws, said Scott Corley, executive director of Compete America, a coalition that represents companies and trade associations on immigration.  \u201cIt has been an endless source of frustration over 10 years, and it has taken some time for tech leaders to realize this, but if you care about high-skilled workers, you have to care about broader immigration reform,\u201d said  Steve Case , the CEO of Revolution LLC and a co-founder of  AOL Inc. (AOL)   Case also served on President  Barack Obama \u2019s jobs council and has testified about immigration issues facing tech. \u201cThe political dynamic is such that none of the specifics get passed without being part of a bigger bill,\u201d he said.  Bad Breaks  Until now, tech leaders and trade groups have been beset by bad timing and bad breaks.  In 1998, Microsoft, Intel and other companies persuaded Congress to increase the number of  H-1B visas  from 65,000 to 115,000 and then to 195,000 as computer companies were rapidly growing. Then the dot-com bubble burst and economy dipped, resulting in a glut of qualified technology workers and H-1B visas that were left unused.  Congress made no move to extend the temporary visa increase, and it reverted to 65,000 in 2004, though that year Congress did approve an additional 20,000 visas for foreign nationals holding a master\u2019s or doctoral degree from a U.S. university.  As the economy picked up, tech trade groups resumed lobbying Congress to let them hire more foreign-born workers, including a failed push to persuade Congress to let companies apply for H-1Bs that hadn\u2019t been used during the  slow economy .  Microsoft Chairman  Bill Gates  met with congressional leaders in 2006 to urge them to increase the number of visas available. That effort failed. In 2007, President  George W. Bush  led the \u201cgrand bargain\u201d on immigration, an effort that didn\u2019t include many outside voices or allow for amendments.  Burned by the failure of a broad rewrite of immigration laws, technology companies tried to go it alone by focusing only on their need for skilled workers. In each of the past five years, they tried and failed to win additional visas. The rule\nhas sparked two years of debate since the 2010 Dodd-Frank Act\nmandated that the SEC impose the rule, with some business groups\nrailing against the costs of tracking thousands of suppliers\nthrough every link of a chain that leads to their source mines.  Once the rule is in place, the agency estimates 6,000\npublicly-traded companies -- mostly manufacturers and retailers\n-- must report to the SEC where they get their tin, tantalum,\ntungsten or gold. The rule is meant to halt the flow of mining\nmoney to those committing atrocities in the  Democratic Republic \nof Congo by pressuring manufacturers to protect their\nreputations -- not by issuing an outright ban on using the\nconflict metals.  The offices of Republican commissioners Troy Paredes and\nDaniel Gallagher, didn\u2019t respond to messages seeking comment on\nthe vote.  John Nester , an SEC spokesman, declined to comment.  Ubiquitous Metals  The metals are in virtually any device with an on-switch.\nElectronics firms such as  Apple Inc. (AAPL)  use most or all of the\nmetals, and the rule would also affect jewelry makers such as\n Tiffany & Co. (TIF) , aerospace companies such as  Boeing Co. (BA)  and\nretailers including  Wal-Mart Stores Inc. (WMT)  and  American Apparel\nInc. (APP)  Since it was proposed by the SEC, the rule has drawn about\n40,000 public comment letters. The rule\nwill provide a phase-in period for companies to comply, she\nsaid, and \u201cwill try to give latitude and flexibility in some\nareas.\u201d She said her agency was \u201clooking close\u201d at the\nguidelines already in place at the Paris-based Organisation for\nEconomic Co-operation and Development. As of Dec. 14, the index\u2019s best performer for 2010 was\n Cummins Inc. , a Columbus, Indiana, manufacturer of engines and\npower generators. The stock is up about 136 percent so far this\nyear.  I have owned Cummins for clients on and off over the years.\nI think the  management  team under Chief Executive Officer\n Theodore Solso  is sensible and takes the long view. Analysts\nestimate the company will post diluted earnings per share of $5\nthis year, a record.  I do not own Cummins currently, however. There is a vast\ndifference between a good company and a good stock. At about\n$108, I think Cummins is fully priced. It now trades at five\ntimes book value (corporate net worth) and 23 times earnings.  Here is a rundown on some other leaders and laggards in the\nS&P 500 this year:  Akamai Technologies Inc. , located in Cambridge,\nMassachusetts, helps to deliver content and monitor traffic on\nthe Internet. This is a stock in which fortunes have been made,\nand lost.  From a high of more than $327 a share in 1999, Akamai fell\nto less than $1 a share in 2002. Since then it has regained\ntraction and risen to about $50. The good-company, bad-stock\nsyndrome applies here. I consider the shares overpriced at 51\ntimes earnings and almost nine times revenue.  In the Clouds  Then there\u2019s  Salesforce.com Inc. , which is as popular with\ninvestors as Akamai was 11 years ago. A leader in cloud\ncomputing for businesses, Salesforce saw its revenue grow to\n$1.1 billion last year from $51 million in fiscal 2003.  Shares in the San Francisco-based company have advanced\nabout 86 percent so far this year.  Computing that involves storing files and programs on a\nhost\u2019s servers is here to stay. It allows salespeople in\ndifferent cities to share notes and observations easily. Yet I\ncan give you three good reasons not to invest in Salesforce.  First, at 245 times the past four quarters\u2019 earnings, it\nhas huge expectations built into the stock price. Second,\nanalysts expect its fully diluted earnings per share to fall\nmore than 20 percent this fiscal year, ending January 2011,\nbefore growth resumes in the next two years. Third, Microsoft is\ntaking explicit aim at its market.  Betting on China  Wynn Resorts Ltd.  likewise seems overvalued. The operator of\nluxury casinos in Las Vegas, its headquarters city, and Macao,\nChina, is priced as a hot growth stock at 83 times earnings. Yet\nits best earnings result, $5.63 a share, came in 2006. This year\nanalysts expect it to earn about $1.14.  Priceline.com Inc. , based in Norwalk, Connecticut, is up\nabout 85 percent. I think it offers a useful online shopping\nservice, and its ads starring actor  William Shatner  are funny.\nBut pay 12 times book value and 42 times earnings? No way.  One might expect to find better bargains among the S&P\n500\u2019s laggards. This year\u2019s crop of underachievers doesn\u2019t\nexcite me much, but I do think there is rebound potential in H&R\nBlock Inc. and Apollo Group Inc.  The biggest loser in the index is  Dean Foods Co. , down\nabout 55 percent so far this year. The Dallas-based food and\nbeverage company is cheap at eight times earnings, but its debt-\nto-equity ratio of 271 percent is too high.  Yes, I know dairy products, Dean\u2019s specialty, are supposed\nto be a steady business that can easily support a heavy debt\nload. But experience suggests that debt never matters -- until\nit does.  Rebound Potential  H&R Block , the largest U.S. tax preparer, is down about 43\npercent this year. The Kansas City, Missouri, company has\nproblems -- mopping up after a messy foray into mortgage\nlending, and more competition from sellers of tax-preparation\nsoftware -- but I think it has comeback potential. At eight\ntimes earnings, I believe H&R Block is a good candidate both for\na quick January bounce and a good year in 2011.  Apollo Group is down about 36 percent. I wrote about this\ncompany and its competitors last month. In my judgment Apollo is\nmore capable than most for-profit education companies of meeting\nproposed federal standards. Shares in the Phoenix-based company\ngo for seven times earnings.  Debt Heavy  SuperValu Inc. , a grocery and pharmaceutical-distribution\ncompany based in Eden Prairie, Minnesota, is trading for only\nfive times earnings. That\u2019s tempting, but I worry about the\ncompany\u2019s debt, which is almost five times equity. The stock is\ndown about 31 percent.  Finally,  PulteGroup Inc. , a home builder in Bloomfield\nHills, Michigan, is down about 30 percent. I think it will take\na while for homebuilders to make money again because of\noverbuilding from 2000 to 2006 and because of the large number\nof foreclosed homes now coming onto the market. With debt at 187\npercent of equity, and with the company\u2019s earnings still\nnegative, I would wait.  This column has mostly focused on stocks I would avoid.\nNext week I\u2019ll look at the other side of the coin -- my 10\nfavorite stocks for 2011. BlackBerry\u2019s once-lucrative services business and hardware unit would have zero value in a breakup as phone losses erode fee-based revenue earned from each subscriber, according to Raymond James Ltd. If a buyer closed the hardware unit in favor of its own technology, it would cost about $800 million, said BMO Capital Markets. BlackBerry\u2019s patents, software and a secure network are each worth more than $1 billion, BMO said, and the company has about $2.8 billion in  cash .  The Waterloo, Ontario-based company appointed board members last week to analyze a sale or new partnerships to try to turn the company around. The value of the hardware unit may plummet further as customers shy from buying a device whose future is up in the air, leading acquirers to gravitate to BlackBerry\u2019s other assets,  Brian Huen , managing partner at Red Sky Capital Management, said by phone on Aug. 19.  \u201cYou\u2019re effectively killing that business by saying \u2018I\u2019m up for sale,\u2019\u201d said Huen, whose Toronto-based firm manages about C$220 million ($212 million) in assets including BlackBerry shares. \u201cNobody is interested in buying the entire entity. BlackBerry hired JPMorgan Chase & Co and RBC Capital Markets 17 months ago to explore its strategic options as sales of the company\u2019s once-iconic phones tumbled amid competition from  Apple Inc . and  Samsung Electronics Co . Those bankers contacted possible bidders late last year and found little interest in buying the whole company, particularly from private-equity firms, said two people familiar with those discussions. Android, Apple  The hardware business, which helped fuel net income of $3.4 billion in 2011, lagged behind as the industry shifted to touchscreen devices with a wide variety of applications available for download. BlackBerry\u2019s share of the global smartphone market fell to 2.9 percent in the second quarter from 4.9 percent a year earlier, behind Microsoft Corp.\u2019s Windows Phone platform, Apple Inc.\u2019s iOS and Google Inc.\u2019s market-leading Android, according to IDC, based in Framingham, Massachusetts.  Speculation that the company might be taken private to be restructured or broken up out of the public spotlight accelerated after the Aug. 12 announcement, in which  Prem Watsa , a Toronto-based businessman and BlackBerry\u2019s largest shareholder, said he would step down from the board. The company didn\u2019t mention going private as an option at the time.  BlackBerry fell 2.8 percent to $10.25 at the close in New York, cutting its market value to $5.37 billion. The shares have dropped 14 percent this year, leaving BlackBerry down more than 90 percent from its 2008 high. The company had 72 million smartphone subscribers at the end of June.  Tim Long , an analyst at BMO Capital Markets in New York, puts the cost of shutting down BlackBerry\u2019s hardware unit at about $800 million, or $1.50 a share. He rates BlackBerry a hold.  Nortel\u2019s Fate?  The company\u2019s cash reserves will be worth about $2.6 billion at the end of this fiscal year; its patents and other intellectual property might fetch $1 billion; the network would be worth $1.2 billion; and the software about $1.5 billion, Long said in an Aug. 13 note to clients. Subtracting the $800 million estimated cost of shutting down the handset businesses, that would give BlackBerry a sum-of-the-parts value of about $5.5 billion, or $10.50 a share.  Raymond James put the value of BlackBerry\u2019s patents higher, as much as $1.6 billion. In an Aug. 12 note, Raymond James\u2019s  Steven Li  said BlackBerry is probably worth about $4.5 billion, or $8.70 a share, if broken up. Toronto-based Li rates BlackBerry a hold. Cash Trove  \u201cWhat happened with Nortel, where they just started selling bits of it, that could happen,\u201d Compeau said. \u201cThere\u2019s not that many players who can extract value from all those different parts.\u201d  Unlike Nortel, BlackBerry has never issued debt and had $2.8 billion worth of cash and cash equivalents at the end of June, more than enough to ward off bankruptcy. The company posted a $646 million loss in fiscal 2013, its first annual loss in a decade.  Sales of the new BlackBerry Z10 touch-screen phone missed analysts\u2019 estimates by close to a million units last quarter. Facing two straight quarters of declining profit and a  stock  that\u2019s down by more than a quarter from a September 2012 record, Apple is facing a similar challenge with the iPad as it has with the iPhone, battling lower-cost rivals and proving that incremental changes to existing products are enough to draw customers. The company will also show new Mac software and a new Mac Pro high-end desktop computer at tomorrow\u2019s event, a person with knowledge of the plans has said.  Tablet Era  Even as tablet sales growth slows, the industry shift that\u2019s been under way since  Steve Jobs  unveiled the iPad in 2010 shows no signs of abating.  Microsoft Corp. (MSFT) ,  Intel Corp. (INTC) ,  Hewlett-Packard Co. (HPQ)  and Dell Inc. are grappling with shrinking demand for their computer software and hardware as consumers and businesses move more day-to-day tasks to handheld devices.  \u201cThe tablet market is going to be bigger than the traditional computing market,\u201d said Horace Dediu, a market researcher who runs Asymoco.com. (MSFT)  is weathering slumping personal-computer sales by focusing on Xboxes, business software and cloud services, as departing Chief Executive Officer  Steve Ballmer  seeks to make the company less dependent on its  Windows operating system .  Microsoft reported fiscal first-quarter sales and profit yesterday that topped analysts\u2019 average  estimates  on demand for Office programs and database servers. The company\u2019s revenue forecast for the current quarter was also ahead of projections.  The world\u2019s largest software maker is undergoing unprecedented changes, conducting its first-ever CEO search and starting an organizational overhaul aimed at bolstering sales by focusing on devices and services. Companies are snapping up products such as Web-based cloud services and the Lync instant messaging and voice software, bolstering sales even as consumers purchase fewer PCs running Windows.  \u201cIt\u2019s good revenue growth, but the question going forward with these new initiatives is, will they generate the billion-dollar numbers we need to drive the top line number and to say Microsoft is really invigorated,\u201d said Daniel Morgan, a  fund manager  at Synovus Trust Co. in Atlanta, which owns Microsoft shares.  Microsoft, based in Redmond,  Washington , rose 6 percent to $35.73 at the close in  New York , the biggest increase in two months. The shares fell 3.7 percent last quarter, compared with a 4.7 percent  increase  in the Standard & Poor\u2019s 500 Index.  Corporate Sales  Net income in the period that ended Sept. 30 rose to $5.24 billion, or 62 cents a share, from $4.47 billion, or 53 cents, a year earlier, Microsoft said. Sales climbed 16 percent to $18.5 billion. Analysts on average had predicted profit of 54 cents on $17.8 billion in revenue, according to  data  compiled by Bloomberg.  For the current quarter, Microsoft forecast higher sales of its commercial products and services, which includes corporate sales of Office and server software, as well as strong Xbox demand as a new game console is rolled out. While the company didn\u2019t provide a projection for total revenue, at the low end of the ranges provided for each of five divisions, sales for the fiscal second quarter would exceed the $22.9 billion average estimate of analysts polled by Bloomberg.  Microsoft\u2019s first-quarter revenue got a lift from products such as the SQL database server, SharePoint, Exchange for e-mail, and Lync for corporate messaging and telephony. Revenue from commercial cloud products more than doubled.  Future Revenue  In the commercial division, which includes these corporate products, licensing revenue jumped 7.3 percent to $9.59 billion, and other corporate revenue, including Internet cloud-based programs, rose to $1.6 billion. That compares with average analysts\u2019 estimates of $9.42 billion and $1.58 billion, respectively, based on four estimates compiled by Bloomberg.  Unearned revenue, which comes from sales of multiyear deals that will be recognized in the future, was $20.2 billion for the quarter, compared with the $21.1 billion average  analyst  projection, according to data compiled by Bloomberg.  Consumer demand for PCs wasn\u2019t as bad as Microsoft had expected, particularly in developed markets, and corporate PC sales are showing signs of stabilizing, Chief Financial Officer Amy Hood said in an interview. PC sales in  China  continue to be weak because of excess inventory. Similar trends should persist in the current quarter, she said.  Consumer Devices  First-quarter sales from devices and consumer hardware, including Surface tablets and Xbox  game consoles , increased 37 percent to $1.49 billion, more than the $1.14 billion average estimate. Devices and consumer licensing, which includes Windows pre-installed on computers, fell 7.2 percent to $4.34 billion, compared with analysts\u2019 average estimates for sales of $4.24 billion.  Surface did better than some analysts projected. Microsoft said it sold $400 million worth of the tablets in the period. Goldman Sachs Group Inc. had estimated the devices and their accessories would pull in $181 million in sales. Microsoft sold more than two times the number of Surface units as the previous quarter, Hood said.  \u201cIf you think about all the news that has been going on outside the company, people here have been very focused,\u201d she said. \u201cThe team is really dedicated to delivering no matter what.\u201d  New Xbox  The release of the  Xbox One  in November is likely to be larger in terms of sales than the two previous Xbox console introductions, Hood said.  Commercial licensing sales will be $10.7 billion to $10.9 billion in the second quarter, Hood forecast on a conference call yesterday. Other commercial revenue, which includes the company\u2019s corporate cloud programs, will be $1.7 billion to $1.9 billion, she projected.  In the consumer and devices unit, licensing sales will be $5.2 billion to $5.4 billion; revenue from hardware, which includes the new Xbox, will be $3.8 billion to $4.1 billion; and other consumer products will bring in $1.7 billion to $1.8 billion, she said.  The software maker\u2019s sales growth had been hurt in recent quarters as the PC market contracted amid a transition to mobile devices for surfing the Internet. Worldwide PC shipments fell 8.6 percent last quarter, researcher Gartner Inc. said earlier this month, amid lackluster demand from students returning to school.  In July, the company\u2019s profit in the fiscal fourth quarter missed projections by the the biggest margin in at least 10 years. Results also were hurt by a $900 million writedown of inventory of Surface tablets. The company cut prices for the devices, which first went on sale a year ago, to clear inventory ahead of the introduction of updated models this week.  Ballmer\u2019s Departure  A week before the fourth-quarter earnings miss, Ballmer unveiled Microsoft\u2019s biggest management shuffle in more than a decade, a bid to align the company around hardware and Internet-based services and an attempt to halt the slide of Windows.  Then, in August, the company said that Ballmer, who took over as CEO from co-founder  Bill Gates  in 2000, will step down from that role within a year. People with knowledge of the matter said earlier this month that the board is aiming to have a successor in place by the end of 2013. Don\u2019t: Rich Jaroslovsky","released_at":"<date>November 7 2012<\/date> <time>21:00:00<\/time>","content":"I\u2019ve made a lot of computer blunders over the years. The biggest was taking a perfectly well- functioning  Sony (6758)  Vaio and upgrading it from Windows XP to Windows Vista, which left it so crash-prone as to be all but useless.  So please believe me when I offer this word of advice on installing Microsoft\u2019s shiny new Windows 8 operating system:  Don\u2019t.  Windows 8 is far from the disaster Vista was. But unless you have a very recent personal computer with a touch screen, there are few benefits -- and some significant drawbacks in terms of learning curve and usability -- to upgrading from Windows 7.  Microsoft is doing its best to make the process attractive. Buyers of Windows 7 PCs between June 2, 2012, and Jan. 31, 2013, can upgrade for $15, while owners of older computers can download a copy from  Microsoft (MSFT) \u2019s online store for $40.  I decided to go old school, buying the traditional boxed DVD of Windows 8 Pro at the neighborhood  Staples (SPLS)  for $70. My guinea-pig machine was one I use specifically for testing software and services, a three-year-old  Hewlett-Packard (HPQ)  Pavilion desktop purchased at  Costco (COST)  -- just the sort of thing many families might have at home.  Bumpy Path  I began the upgrade at 9:45 a.m. and finished it an hour and 37 minutes later, not counting another 15 minutes or so spent solving a couple of lingering issues. The process wasn\u2019t entirely smooth.  Most of the time was spent staring at the screen, which was populated by various all-but-indistinguishable status updates: \u201cgetting devices ready,\u201d \u201cgetting ready,\u201d \u201cwhile we\u2019re getting things ready,\u201d and finally, more than an hour into the process, \u201cwe\u2019re getting your PC ready.\u201d Wait, what have you been doing up to now?  The final message was accompanied by \u201cthis will take a few minutes.\u201d No kidding.  Theoretically, I could have just started the process and walked away. But as it turned out, that would have been a mistake.  Shortly after I began, the installer mysteriously quit and returned me to the Windows 7 desktop with no explanation. I restarted the process, which at least picked up where it had left off.  Manual Intervention  Then, more than an hour into the effort, the Pavilion\u2019s hardware-diagnostic program prevented a required restart of Windows until I manually intervened. Had I not been sitting in front of the screen monitoring developments, it would have taken even longer before I was up and running.  Finally, upgrade complete, I rebooted into the new Windows 8 Start screen. I was greeted with its colorful tiles -- and an error message that read \u201c.Net 3.5 Client Profile Runtime has stopped working.\u201d When I tried to summon Microsoft\u2019s online help service for a solution, I discovered my PC no longer had  Internet access , thanks to an incompatibility with the version of  Symantec (SYMC) \u2019s Norton Firewall software I was using. (Most of my other existing programs, though, seemed to run fine with the new operating system.)  Once I sorted out those issues, I noticed an immediate benefit. Prior to the upgrade, it took the Pavilion about 2-1\/2 minutes to boot from a cold start. Windows 8, though, was much faster: about 50 seconds.  The upgrade also gave me tiles to access Microsoft\u2019s new Xbox Music service and a not-yet-very-populated app store for programs written for the new interface.  Touch Screens  The other Start-screen tiles were filled with self-updating information from my social networks, calendar and other applications. While I was able to navigate through them using the mouse, it\u2019s clear the interface is really aimed at users with touch screens.  Those are likely to be standard equipment on most new Windows PCs, including the new Windows tablets from manufacturers including, for the first time, Microsoft itself. But the millions of individuals and businesses with older, mouse-driven systems -- and even many with laptops that have a touchpad but no touch screen -- may find themselves needing to memorize keyboard shortcuts for many common tasks, a throwback to earlier days of computing.  While there\u2019s still a Windows 7-like desktop, it\u2019s been demoted: You launch it from one of the tiles on the Start screen. And missing from the desktop is the familiar button that would allow you to shut down or restart the PC. Instead, you\u2019re expected to summon what Microsoft calls \u201ccharms\u201d -- a set of buttons running down the side of the screen -- choose Settings and power down from there.  Summoning Charms  That\u2019s fine for touch screens and for Windows tablets, which -- like  Apple (AAPL) \u2019s iPad -- you shouldn\u2019t have to power down or reboot very often. But it\u2019s clumsy for users of more traditional PCs, who will have to learn just where to move the cursor on the screen to bring up the charms.  Further, there\u2019s no option to boot directly into the desktop environment, or restore the Start menu. And, adding to the sense of schizophrenia, Windows 8 has two separate versions of the Internet Explorer web browser, one written in the new style, the other a more traditional one that shows up when you\u2019re working on the desktop.  For buyers of new computers, Windows 8 will be inescapable, and may make sense for the new generation of hardware it\u2019s spawning. But if you don\u2019t already have something close to the latest and greatest PC and you\u2019re reasonably happy with Windows 7, my guidance is simple:  Skip it.  ( Rich Jaroslovsky  is a Bloomberg News columnist. The opinions expressed are his own.)  Muse highlights include  Jason Harper  on  cars  and Lance Esplund on  art . Gains of 20 percent or more pushed  Boeing Co. (BA)  and Amgen Inc. past $100 in 2013, joining 64 companies in the Standard & Poor\u2019s 500 Index above the threshold, twice the level in 2010, according to data compiled by Bloomberg. Ten companies have split their stock this year, compared with 42 annually since 1996, data from S&P show, helping send the average share price to $65.96 last quarter, the highest on record.  Splits have been diminishing since the  bull market  began as pressure eases to hold prices at levels that make it easier to amass shares. While the practice has been considered a sign of confidence in future growth, executives at companies such as  Apple Inc. (AAPL)  say it does no good for shareholders and have refrained from the action since the start of the rally.  \u201cAs retail investors become less important to the investor base, the behavioral reasons for splitting the shares are less compelling,\u201d Ravi Dhar, a professor at the  Yale School of Management  who has studied financial markets, said in an Aug. 12 phone interview. \u201cThese companies didn\u2019t want to encourage too many individual investors or day traders. They wanted to keep the price high.\u201d  Getting Expensive  Ninety-eight S&P 500 companies have surpassed the price at which they last split, with the median  stock trading  27 percent higher, according to data compiled by Bloomberg. The split price has been about $96 on average, based on data from 389 firms since 1981.  Priceline.com (PCLN)  Inc.,  trading  at $940, has never divided its shares. Google Inc. is the second-highest priced company in the S&P 500 at $869.81, and Apple, at $498.50,  last split  in 2005. MasterCard Inc. has never taken the action, even after reaching a record $654 this month.  Splits, for decades a way of enticing individuals by lowering share prices, have declined as professional investors increased their role in the  U.S. equity market . Ownership of stocks by institutions rose to about 67 percent in 2010 from 34 percent in 1980, according to a study by Marshall Blume and Donald Keim at the Wharton School at the  University of Pennsylvania .  Price Agnostic  Those figures exclude exchange-traded funds, securities that track equity indexes and trade like shares throughout the day. The ETF industry has seen assets invested in stocks expand 56 percent since 2010 to $1.17 trillion, based on data from the Washington-based  Investment Company Institute  through June 30.  \u201cIf a lot of the equities are being held in some institutional intermediary, I don\u2019t think the price is that critical,\u201d Ernie Cecilia, the chief investment officer who helps oversee $7 billion at  Bryn Mawr  Trust Co. in Bryn Mawr,  Pennsylvania , said in an Aug. 7 telephone interview.  Exxon Mobil Corp. (XOM)   reached  $95.20 last month, exceeding the level from the last split more than a decade ago. International Business Machines Corp. hasn\u2019t done it since 1999, after its stock reached $246. In 1997, the Armonk, New York-based company split two-for-one when the shares hit $179.25. IBM traded at $187.53 yesterday.  Splits \u201cdo nothing\u201d for shareholders, Apple Chief Executive Officer  Tim Cook  said in February 2012, in response to an investor question. Cupertino, California-based Apple became the world\u2019s largest company in January 2012, and its stock rallied to a record $702.10 by September 2012, bringing the market value to more than $650 billion.  Cheaper Stocks  \u201cRetail investors in general don\u2019t really understand that it doesn\u2019t really matter if a stock has been split,\u201d Brett Bartman, a Beverly Hills, California-based senior vice president -- financial adviser at  RBC Capital Markets , said in a telephone interview. His firm oversees $1.2 billion. \u201cThey seem to still view a stock that trades at $5 or $10 as being a cheaper stock than a stock trading like Apple, which is not the case at all.\u201d  Investors are increasingly surrendering stock selection to fund managers and ETFs. More than $38 billion went into U.S. ETFs last month, the fourth-highest inflow ever, as the  S&P 500  climbed to a record, according to data since 2000 compiled by Bloomberg. Almost $30 billion of the deposits went to funds that buy and sell American equities.  ETF Expansion  \u201cIf I want immediate and broad exposure to a sector, the ETF lets us get in there immediately and get it done,\u201d Richard Saperstein, a managing director and principal who helps oversee about $8 billion at HighTower Advisors LLC\u2019s Treasury Partners in  New York , said in an Aug. 1 phone interview.  Concern about future economic growth and memories of the 2008 financial crisis and volatility in 2011, when equity swings approached records, may be keeping executives from reducing share prices, according to Eric Teal, who helps oversee $5 billion as the chief investment officer at First Citizens BancShares Inc.  \u201cThere\u2019s been so much volatility, managements have been hesitant to split their stocks,\u201d Teal said in a telephone interview from Raleigh,  North Carolina . \u201cThey\u2019re unsure if an economic downturn could follow or more global uncertainty could unfold, so they don\u2019t want to do splits right now.\u201d  Stocks that  split shares  since 2011 have performed about the same as the S&P 500 during the three months since the action, according to data compiled by Bloomberg. The median company rose 6 percent, compared with a 4.5 percent gain for the benchmark gauge.  Past Rallies  Salesforce.com Inc. (CRM) , the largest maker of online customer-management software, rose 2.1 percent in the three months since the April 18 four-for-one split, compared to a 9.6 percent S&P 500 rally. Whole Foods Market Inc., the largest natural-goods grocer in the U.S., added 2.7 percent since distributing one share for each owned on May 30. The S&P 500 is up 1.9 percent since then.  Cabot Oil & Gas Corp. (COG) , based in Houston, was the 10th company to split shares this year when it  divided  the $74.78 stock in two today.  The advance that began in March 2009 is lifting more companies than past rallies, contributing to the increase in stocks trading above $100. A version of the S&P 500 that  strips out biases  related to market value has gained 220 percent during that stretch, compared with 149 percent in the weighted gauge. The index fell 1 percent to 1,669.02 at 9:44 a.m. New York time today.  Trading Brake  Previous bull markets were narrower, with gains confined to fewer stocks. In the last 50 months of the 1990s technology bubble, the S&P 500 increased 146 percent, almost double the increase in the Equal-Weighted Index, as computer companies such as  Microsoft Corp. (MSFT)  and Cisco Systems Inc. monopolized the rally.  In isolation, fewer splits and record prices reduce equity  market volume  by lowering the number of shares that can be bought and sold for the same amount of money. About 5.67 billion shares of U.S. equities traded hands each day on all U.S. exchanges since June 30, compared to 6.03 billion in the same period last year. At the same time, the  value  of traded shares climbed to $203 billion a day from $190 billion.  Lower prices attract so-called high-frequency traders who buy and sell hundreds of shares in fractions of a second, attempting to profit from the price disparities. For companies  that trade above $100 , an average of 1.7 million shares changed hands daily, according to three-month data compiled by Bloomberg. The volume for stocks less than $25 was 11.5 million.  Reverse Split  Citigroup Inc. (C)  reverse split its stock in May 2011, turning 10 shares into one and bringing the price above $40. CEO Vikram Pandit said part of the reason was to \u201cencourage institutional and other long-only buyers of the stock to invest in our company and also to discourage high-frequency trading that fuels volatility.\u201d  Volume for Priceline.com dropped 23 percent since the shares crossed $600 on Feb. 28, 2012, compared with the prior 12 months, according to data compiled by Bloomberg. The Norwalk, Connecticut-based travel reservation system is the highest-priced stock in the S&P 500. Regeneron Pharmaceuticals Inc., the Tarrytown, New York-based drug maker, closed at more than $100 a share in early 2012. Trading has averaged 925,000 shares a day since then, down from 1.2 million the year before. (MSFT)  got a judge to\norder a group of unidentified hackers to stop running networks\nof infected computers known as botnets that allegedly hijack\nonline bank accounts.  U.S. District Judge Sterling Johnson Jr. in Brooklyn, New\nYork, today issued a preliminary injunction against 39 John Does\nwho use hacker aliases such as \u201cMonstr\u201d and \u201cGribodemon\u201d to\ncreate a network of botnets running malicious software known as\nZeus.  A botnet is a network of infected computers programmed to\nsend data automatically from their hard drives to a server\ncontrolled by hackers. Hackers infect computers with software\nthat can steal online banking logins and passwords, which they\ncan use to transfer money to their own accounts.  \u201cThat\u2019s the primary purpose of this scheme,\u201d said  Gabriel\nM. Ramsey , a lawyer for Redmond, Washington-based Microsoft,\nwhich claims the Zeus botnets controlled by the John Doe hackers\nhave taken more than $100 million.  Microsoft, the world\u2019s biggest software maker, sued the\nunnamed hackers on March 19. The case was made public March 27,\nthe day after Microsoft said it had seized computer servers in\nPennsylvania and  Illinois , while escorted by U.S. Marshals, to\npreserve evidence.  Record Keystrokes  The Zeus software allows a hacker to monitor a victim\u2019s\nonline activity and record keystrokes, according to a March 26\nstatement from Microsoft. The company said it has detected more\nthan 13 million suspected infections of Zeus software worldwide\nsince 2007, and 3 million in the U.S.  \u201cMicrosoft and its partners took down two Internet\nProtocol addresses behind the Zeus command and control\nstructure, and Microsoft is currently monitoring 800 domains\nsecured in the operation, which are helping identify thousands\nof computers infected by Zeus,\u201d the company said in the\nstatement.  Ramsey said Microsoft and other plaintiffs are speaking to\n law enforcement  about the matter. He declined to comment on the\ncase after the hearing.  A botnet is a collection of computers \u201crunning software\nthat allows communication among those computers and that allows\ncentralized or decentralized communication with other computers\nproviding control instructions,\u201d according to Microsoft\u2019s\ncomplaint.  Same Codes  Botnets running Zeus software share the same code and\ninfrastructure, according to the complaint. The names of the\nbotnets\u2019 creators are unknown, according to the complaint. No\ndefendants\u2019 representatives appeared at today\u2019s hearing.  Microsoft said the raids this month marked the second time\nit has conducted physical seizures in a botnet operation. Some\nZeus botnet computers are in the Eastern District of New York,\nthe U.S. jurisdiction that includes the  Brooklyn  federal court,\naccording to the complaint.  The company also said it believed the lawsuit is the first\nto use the Racketeer Influenced and Corrupt Organizations Act\nagainst a botnet operation. The federal RICO law was passed to\nfight organized crime.  Plaintiffs joining Microsoft in the case are Reston,\nVirginia-based FS-ISAC Inc., which represents banks and other\nfinancial-services companies in combating cyber threats, and\nHerndon, Virginia-based National Automated Clearing House\nAssociation, which manages the ACH Network, \u201cthe backbone for\nthe electronic movement of money and data,\u201d according to the\ncomplaint.  The case is Microsoft Corp. v. John Does 1-39, 12-cv-01335,\nU.S. District Court, Eastern District of New York (Brooklyn). It\u2019s 1981. Most people have never heard of Silicon Valley.\nThe country\u2019s most famous businessman is Lee Iacocca, the head\nof Chrysler Corp. He\u2019s famous because in 1979 he engineered a\ngovernment bailout -- loan guarantees -- that saved the company.\nHe\u2019s also famous because, unlike his peers, Iacocca is colorful.\nHe seems to believe in what he\u2019s doing.  In 1981, business executives aren\u2019t known for either\npersonality or passion. The general public sees business as a\nboring, impersonal, possibly suspect activity. Its significance\nseems purely financial.  \u201cBusinessmen,\u201d Tom Wolfe tells the Wall Street Journal, \u201cno\nlonger have the conviction that what they\u2019re doing is exciting\nand glamorous, which is, I guess, another way of saying\nintrinsically worthwhile.\u201d  That was all about to change.  In the 1980s, entrepreneurs became heroes, celebrities and\nrole models. The Apple whiz kids, Steve Jobs and  Steve Wozniak ,\nwere the new face of business.  Money was, of course, part of the appeal -- millionaires in\ntheir 20s! -- but there was much more to it than that. The\naspirations for pleasure and self-expression that the\nsociologist Daniel Bell had condemned as the \u201ccultural\ncontradictions of capitalism\u201d turned out to be its fuel.  \u201cIt\u2019s a neat way to play,\u201d said Dave House, who was the\nmanager of  Intel Corp. (INTC) \u2019s microprocessor division in 1982 when he\nposed for a magazine in a hot tub with his girlfriend,\napparently naked. House wasn\u2019t talking about his hot-tub\nfrolics. He was explaining why he kept working once he had more\nmoney than he knew what to do with.  In the 1980s, business became a realm of passion and\npersonality and, above all, surprises. Big changes could come\nfrom anywhere -- from backwaters such as  Bentonville, Arkansas \nand  Memphis ,  Tennessee , and  Portland Oregon.  Or, of course,\n Cupertino, California  and  Redmond, Washington . The ethos of\nSilicon Valley became, if not workaday reality, then the\ncultural norm.  \u201cApple was about as pure of a Silicon Valley company as you\ncould imagine,\u201d Jobs said in an interview with  Newsweek  after he\nwas fired in 1985. If he had been born and raised in  New York ,\nwe probably would never have heard of him. But Jobs grew up\nknowing about David Packard and Bill Hewlett starting a business\nin their garage. When he was barely a teenager, he cold-called\nHewlett, whose home number was listed in the phone book, and\ntalked his way into a job at HP.  \u201cOur role model was Hewlett-Packard,\u201d he said in 1985.\nApple just grew a lot faster.  Although the HP Way was Silicon Valley lore, it wasn\u2019t a\ntouchstone to the general public. Apple\u2019s rapid success, by\ncontrast, made quite an impression. Before long, the ideal of\nthe loyal company man working his way to the top was being\nreplaced by the ideal of the brilliant, arrogant college dropout\nconquering the world before he was 30: the entrepreneur as\nAlexander.  Business became more like sports or fashion: a topic of\nsocial conversation, a source of rooting interest and an\nexpression of personal taste. The cultural, or even religious,\nwar between Apple and Microsoft devotees would have been as\ninconceivable in 1981 as a \u201cbrand evangelist\u201d or a corporate\nchieftain who appeared in public without a tie.  Now, by contrast, people far removed from the executive\nsuite, working in entirely different companies or even\ncompletely different industries, have strong opinions about what\nstrategies Apple or Microsoft or General Motors or Wal-Mart or\nAmazon should pursue.  \u201cYour work is going to fill a large part of your life, and\nthe only way to be truly satisfied is to do what you believe is\ngreat work,\u201d Jobs said in a 2005  Stanford University\ncommencement speech , which has been much quoted in recent days.\n\u201cAnd the only way to do great work is to love what you do. If\nyou haven\u2019t found it yet, keep looking. Don\u2019t settle.\u201d  That inspiring philosophy offers the promise of greatness\nand self-fulfillment, but also perpetual dissatisfaction. If\nbusiness isn\u2019t just about making money, if it is about finding a\nversion of true love and leaving a cultural mark, the stakes are\nmuch higher. Your work becomes your identity.  Nobody ever asked why Steve Jobs kept working after he was\nrich. Everyone understood.  (Virginia Postrel is a Bloomberg View columnist. She is the\nauthor of \u201cThe Future and Its Enemies\u201d and \u201cThe Substance of\nStyle,\u201d and is writing a book on glamour. The opinions expressed\nare her own. This column, which was published on Aug. 26 after \nSteve Jobs stepped down at Apple, is all the more timely with \nhis death on Oct. 5.)
