In the 21st century only IBM's Sam Palmisano has done\nso.  When Palmisano retired this month, the media chronicled\nhis success by focusing on IBM's 21% annual growth in earnings\nper share and its increase in market capitalization to $218\nbillion. But IBM hasn't flourished because it kowtows to  Wall\nStreet . In fact, five years after Palmisano took over, IBM\nstock was stuck where it had been when his tenure began.  The real story behind IBM's success is the course\nPalmisano set for 21st century global enterprises. Recognizing\nthat the company's command-and-control culture wouldn't work\nin the 21st century, he defined leadership as leading by\nvalues and created a unique collaborative organizational\nstructure.  In 2002 Palmisano succeeded a legendary leader in Lou\nGerstner, who saved IBM from being broken up and put it on a\nviable course. Whereas Gerstner famously declared \"the last\nthing IBM needs is a vision,\" Palmisano had a clear vision for\nthe company. He saw its unique strength as offering complete\nsolutions tailored to customers' needs \u2014 something no other\ncompany could match. To concentrate on customer\nsolutions, Palmisano spun off personal computers and disk\ndrives and acquired PriceWaterhouseCoopers' consulting\nbusiness.  Executing this strategy required seamless integration of\nIBM's product capabilities with its geographic reach. This\nmeant abandoning IBM's existing organization, in which product\nsilos and geographic entities operated independently and\nfrequently were more competitive than collaborative. Palmisano\nreorganized IBM into a \"globally integrated enterprise\"\nfocused on worldwide collaboration. He cajoled, pushed, and\npulled the company into a client-centric, agile structure able\nto customize delivery of IBM's software assets, hardware\nassets, and intellectual property.  With 440,000 employees in 170 countries, Palmisano\nrecognized that IBM couldn't be run solely from the top;\nrather, it needed thousands of leaders operating\ncollaboratively around the globe to fulfill its customers'\ndiverse needs. His first act was to abolish IBM's corporate\nexecutive committee.  Palmisano understood that reorganizing IBM's formal\nstructure wouldn't be sufficient; he had to thoroughly\ntransform the company's culture and do so in a sustainable\nway. His ingenious first step toward creating a collaborative\nculture was a massive, global collaboration. In 2003 he\nlaunched an online, interactive \"values jam\" involving all\nemployees for 72 hours to determine what IBM's values should\nbe. The\u00a0three principles that emerged from that event guided\ndecision-making throughout the organization, giving IBM's\nhuge, globally dispersed workforce the discipline necessary to\nexecute the company's new strategy.  Palmisano could not have succeeded at placing values at\nthe center of IBM's operations without strong principles of\nhis own. These are the qualities I believe made him the best\nCEO, so far, of the 21st century:  Humility and openness. Palmisano has an engaging manner\nand keen sense of humor. Colleagues say his humility and humor\nare disarming. In a speech on IBM's 100th anniversary, he\nsaid:  The old model of the heroic superman is increasingly\narchaic. The most active and successful leaders today see\nthemselves as part of the global community and peer groups.\nThey listen as well as they speak. Never confuse charisma with\nleadership. The first job of a leader is to enable an\norganization to survive without him or her. The key to that is\nto build a sustainable culture.  He practiced this by listening intently to employees\nthroughout the organization. He also talked to customers on a\ndaily basis and circumnavigated the globe six times a year to\nmeet customers in person. These relationships were essential\nin gaining the confidence of customers who had qualms about\noutsourcing to IBM.  Patience and a long-term view. Palmisano warned against\nprioritizing shareholders or other constituents, calling this\n\"a false choice,\" and explaining that \"Long-term management is\na serious challenge in a world driven by short-term thinking.\nForward-thinking leaders are not just achieving measurable\nsuccess in the short-term. They are innovating in ways that\ncreate virtuous circles for a generation or more.\" He was\ncomfortable making smart bets to position IBM for decades-long\ngrowth, such as creating the Emerging Business Organization to\nincubate new businesses and shield them from P&L pressures.\nAnd his time leading IBM's Asia-Pacific business taught him\nabout the value of building long-term relationships, not just\ndoing transactions.  Directness. Palmisano believes the technology industry\nrequires \"a high-performance, in-your-face, speak-your-mind\nculture.\" He's personable, but blunt. Known for walking out of\nlong meetings to make sales calls, he shortened IBM's\ntwo-month annual budget process to six days. Instead of formal\nperformance reviews, he regularly engaged in short\nconversations, focusing on key initiatives. Many who know him\ncite his impatience as a strength; it kept him relentlessly\nfocused on execution.  Pragmatism. When the U.S. government cut back on work\npermits for foreign nationals, IBM had thousands of Indian\nemployees forced to return to their home country. He turned\nthat problem into competitive advantage by relocating most of\nIBM's software operations to  India  as its Indian operations\ngrew from 3,000 to 100,000 employees. He also forced partners\nand distributors to commit in writing to uphold IBM's strict\nethical standards. In 2009 he called off the $7 billion\nacquisition of Sun Microsystems in part due to Sun's egregious\ngolden parachutes.  As Palmisano built  IBM  into the world's leading\ninformation technology company, its competitors dithered. HP\nsuffered from a progression of strategic missteps and failed\nleaders. Microsoft's enterprise services stagnated. Cisco now\nsells mostly commoditized products. In contrast, IBM kept\nlaser-like focus on building the global organization to\nexecute its strategy, and financial results followed.  Palmisano once said, \"The CEO is not the brand! It is not\nabout you. You are a temporary steward of a wonderful\nenterprise, so leave it in better shape than you find it.\" As\nhe concludes his career, he leaves his successor, Virginia\nRometty, with an iconic giant poised to dominate its industry\nfor decades to come.  This post draws upon several resources, including: the\nIBM archives; Palmisano's own\narticle, \"The Globally Integrated Enterprise\" in\u00a0 Foreign\nAffairs  and his speech on the Future of Leadership; a Harvard\nBusiness Review\u00a0interview with\nPalmisano, \"Leading Change When Business is Good;\"<a\nhref=\" http:\/\/hbr.org\/product\/leaders-who-make-a-difference-sam-palmisano-s-smar\/an\/311701-MMC-ENG \">Rosabeth\nMoss Kanter's case on IBM<\/a> and\nJoseph Bower and Sonja Ellington Hout's case on IBM. Carlos Slim , the telecommunications magnate who controls Mexico\u2019s  America Movil (AMX)  SAB, maintained his title as the richest person on Earth for the entire year. The 72-year-old\u2019s net worth rose $13.4 billion -- or 21.6 percent -- through Dec. 31, making him the second-biggest gainer by dollars.  Gains by Slim\u2019s industrial conglomerate, Grupo Carso SAB, and Grupo Financiero Inbursa, his banking and insurance operation, more than offset the decline posted by America Movil, his biggest holding. Everything it does is interpreted as evil.  In the 1950s, it was General Motors. GM\u2019s CEO,  Charles\n\u201cEngine Charlie\u201d Wilson , became a national figure of ridicule\nfor telling a congressional committee, \u201cWhat\u2019s good for General\nMotors is good for America.\u201d Except that he actually said, \u201cFor\nyears I thought that what was good for the country was good for\nGeneral Motors and vice versa\u201d -- which is quite a different\nproposition.  In the 1990s, the goat was Microsoft. That antitrust case\nlooks a bit silly in retrospect, don\u2019t you think? Turns out it\nwasn\u2019t Microsoft that was about to take over the world: It was\nGoogle. (And just so you know, I once worked for Microsoft.)  Who is the goat today? Clearly it\u2019s Wal-Mart. Does anybody\nreally love Wal-Mart? Well, I\u2019m a pretty big fan. It\u2019s fun to\nroam the aisles and see what people are buying. Nineteen-inch\nflat-screen TVs for $98! That\u2019s pretty great. Wish I needed one.  Last week, my colleague  Jeffrey Goldberg  launched a\n ferocious attack  on  Sam Walton \u2019s daughter, Alice (net worth:\n$21 billion), for building a billion-dollar art museum in\nBentonville,  Arkansas , where Wal-Mart has its headquarters, and\nstocking it with American art. He calls it a \u201cmoral tragedy.\u201d\nWhy? Because Alice Walton\u2019s money is tainted by its source: Wal-\nMart.  What is Wal-Mart doing that\u2019s so wrong? Critics like\nGoldberg say that Wal-Mart employees are underpaid and that many\ndon\u2019t get health care. They see the museum as a symbol of the\ngrowing gap between the haves and the have-nots.  Lady Bountiful  As for what Walton can do about any of this,  Goldberg\nsuggests  she could fund day-care centers or mobile dental\nclinics for employees. This smacks of Lady Bountiful delivering\nturkeys to the serfs at Christmastime. Wal-Mart is a profitable\nbusiness. It shouldn\u2019t get subsidized by charity. Nor should its\nemployees have to depend on charity. I also suspect that most of\nthem are thrilled to have the new museum in town, and don\u2019t see\nit as a symbol of  income inequality .  The  growing income gap  is a big problem, but how is Wal-\nMart contributing to it? Presumably Wal-Mart pays what it has to\nin order to attract workers, and doesn\u2019t pay a lot more if it\ncan be avoided. Presumably, Wal-Mart scours the globe looking\nfor bargains, and if  China  is the cheapest producer, China gets\nthe business. That\u2019s capitalism, and if we don\u2019t like the\nresults, we can use the tools of government, primarily the  tax\ncode , to improve them. True, Wal-Mart has a reputation for being\nespecially ruthless in its dealings with employees and\nsuppliers. Goldberg talked to one employee who said she was paid\nso little that she had to live in her car. Did he talk to no one\nwho said he or she liked working for Wal-Mart?  As for benefits, no company is obliged to offer health\ncare. Critics often note that Wal-Mart doesn\u2019t offer health\ninsurance to employees who work less than 24 hours a week. You\ncould turn that around and say that Wal-Mart does offer health\ncare to employees who work at least 24 hours a week. Check with\nyour own company. My experience is that you become eligible for\nbenefits at about half-time. That would be 20 hours. So is 24\nhours so unreasonable? It\u2019s also true that Wal-Mart is raising\nthe premiums for many employees who do get health insurance. But\nmost companies in the U.S. are probably planning to increase the\nemployee contribution in the coming year. Certainly it\u2019s nothing\nunique to Wal-Mart.  There are those whose objections to Wal-Mart are more\naesthetic than economic: the barnlike quality of the stores, the\nimpact of a Wal-Mart  on old downtowns , even the whole culture of\nconsumption that some people find distasteful. They\u2019re welcome\nto those views as long as they acknowledge that higher prices at\nnon-Wal-Mart stores are bad for consumers -- especially poor\nconsumers.  Small-Business Myths  Wal-Mart\u2019s employees seem to me at least as cheerful as\nthose in Target or Costco. But perhaps the company has\nhypnotized them -- or possibly me -- in some sort of  Stepford\nWives  scenario.  Big companies make fat targets, but a more deserving target\nmight be small companies. Instead, we have the ever-inflating\nmyth of small business. Small businesses come and go, creating\nand eliminating jobs along the way. Yes, they are an important\npart of the economy, and often they come with inspiring tales of\nhard-working immigrants and so on. But they\u2019re in it to make a\nprofit, just like Wal-Mart. And I doubt that many offer health\ncare to people working less than 24 hours a week. A successful\nsmall-business owner is more likely to be in the notorious 1\npercent than an employee (or even a stockholder) of a big\ncorporation. They don\u2019t need to be coddled with special tax\nbreaks.  Walton could have put her museum in  New York , where this\nsort of thing belongs. Most of us don\u2019t get to Bentonville as\noften as we\u2019d like. Or she could have decided not to build it at\nall, for fear that journalists would start comparing her to\n Marie Antoinette . Would that have been better?  ( Michael Kinsley  is a Bloomberg View columnist. The\nopinions expressed are his own.)  To contact the writer of this article:\nMichael Kinsley at  mkinsley@bloomberg.net . The  U.S. Court of Appeals  for the Federal Circuit in\nWashington, which handles all patent appeals, issued a 135-page\n decision  by 10 circuit judges that included five viewpoints and\n\u201cadditional reflections\u201d from Chief Judge Randall Rader.  \u201cWe have propounded at least three incompatible standards,\ndevoid of consensus, serving simply to add to the unreliability\nand cost of the system of patents as an incentive for\ninnovation,\u201d Circuit Judge Pauline Newman wrote.  Google Inc. (GOOG) ,  Facebook Inc. (FB)  and  JPMorgan Chase & Co. (JPM)  are\namong the companies that argued that patent standards for\nsoftware are too lax. A group whose members include software\nmakers  Microsoft Corp. (MSFT)  and  Oracle Corp. (ORCL)  warned the appeals court\nthat limiting protection for software could hurt the nation\u2019s\neconomy.  The case centered on patents owned by Melbourne-based Alice\nCorp. over ways to minimize risk in certain computerized-trading\nplatforms. The court ruled CLS Bank International won\u2019t have to\nface patent-infringement claims by Alice, which is owned by\n National Australia Bank Ltd. (NAB)  and Alice Ventures Pty.  A majority of the 10 judges said aspects of Alice\u2019s patents\ncovering a method of performing the idea weren\u2019t eligible for\nprotection, while the court was evenly split regarding systems\nto implement that idea. Five of the judges said they would send\nall or part of the case back to the trial judge for further\nreview.  Help Cry  The U.S. Supreme Court also has struggled to determine what\ntypes of innovations qualify for patent protection. In 2010, the\ncourt issued a 5-4 decision on patents for methods of conducting\nbusiness, and last year limited patents for diagnostic medical\ntests. With such a fractured ruling on software, the issue\nprobably is headed to the high court again.  A petition \u201ccould simply attach the decision with a one\nword argument -- \u2018Help!\u2019 -- and have a good chance for Supreme\nCourt review and guidance,\u201d said David Long, a patent lawyer\nwith Dow Lohnes in  Washington .  Circuit Judge Alan Lourie, writing for five of the judges,\nsaid courts should consider \u201cwhether steps combined with a\nnatural law or abstract idea are so insignificant, conventional,\nor routine as to yield a claim that effectively covers the\nnatural law or abstract idea itself.\u201d  Circuit Judge Kimberly Moore, writing for four judges, said\nthe decision by Lourie would cause \u201ca free fall in the patent\nsystem.\u201d  Non-Precedent Precedent  \u201cLet\u2019s be clear: if all of these claims, including the\nsystem claims, are not patent-eligible, this case is the death\nof hundreds of thousands of patents, including all business\nmethod, financial system, and software patents as well as many\ncomputer implemented and telecommunications patents,\u201d Moore\nwrote.  Judge Richard Linn, in another opinion, said companies\nconcerned that there is a proliferation of software patents\nshould turn to Congress.  Although the court issued the full ruling as a precedential\nopinion, Rader said the decisions were so split that \u201cnothing\nsaid today beyond our judgment has the weight of precedent.\u201d  The case is CLS Bank v. Alice Corporation, 11-1301, U.S.\nCourt of Appeals for the Federal Circuit (Washington). The\nlower-court case is CLS Bank International v. Alice Corp.,\n07cv974, U.S. District Court for the  District of Columbia \n(Washington). The new pact includes measures that would give countries a right to access international telecommunications services and the ability to block spam, which delegations declining to sign the amended text argued would pave the way for government censorship and control over the Web.  Canada ,  Denmark ,  Australia ,  Norway ,  Costa Rica ,  Serbia ,  Greece ,  Finland  and others followed the U.S. in refusing to sign on these grounds. (GOOG) , the world\u2019s biggest search engine, said in a statement. \u201cWe stand with the countries who refuse to sign this treaty and also with the millions of voices who have joined us to support a free and open web.\u201d  Talks at the World Conference on International Telecommunications in Dubai this week were marked by disagreements between anti-regulation countries, including the U.S. and many European states, and a group that argued for some Internet measures to protect and advance networks, including  Russia ,  China  and several Middle Eastern nations.  Google Opposition  The conference has attracted criticism because of its one- country-one-vote model that ignores population size. Internet companies including Google have complained that they don\u2019t get a voice in the negotiations. While technology groups are allowed to participate in the discussions and have joined as parts of delegations, they don\u2019t get a vote in the proceedings.  \u201cIt\u2019s with a heavy heart and a sense of missed opportunity that the U.S. must communicate that it\u2019s not able to sign the agreement in its current form,\u201d the U.S. delegation said in a statement at the plenary after the final changes were adopted last night. \u201cWe candidly cannot support an ITU treaty that is inconsistent with the multi-stakeholder model.\u201d  The  International Telecommunication Union , a UN agency, earlier had agreed that no measures would be adopted that gave the body increased control over the Web or the  member states  the ability to censor content. It has succeeded in bringing unprecedented public attention to the different and important perspectives that govern global communications.\u201d  Tax Changes  Other articles that were passed address changes in the way telecommunications companies should be taxed and compensated in a system that has moved from phone companies that were largely government-owned monopolies to one with private mobile-phone companies. He is also a conscientious citizen, risking\ncareer and liberty to expose what he believes to be grave\nwrongdoing. This is the paradox underlying government\nsurveillance programs in general, and in particular the shaky\nfoundations of the U.S. national security apparatus.  Snowden, an employee of Booz Allen Hamilton working in\n Hawaii  as a contractor for the National Security Agency, has\nrevealed himself as the source of leaks about a program called\nPrism, which allows the NSA to collect and mine user data from\ncompanies such as Google Inc., Facebook Inc. and Microsoft Corp.\nUntil recently, according to news media reports, Snowden was\nholed up in a Hong Kong hotel; he says  he intends  to seek asylum\nfrom \u201cany countries that believe in free speech.\u201d  There\u2019s a compelling case to be made against Snowden\u2019s\nactions. If Prism played the central role that officials claim,\nthen revealing its existence could significantly harm Americans\u2019\nsafety. If Snowden didn\u2019t want to be part of such a program, he\ncould have simply left his job. If he thought the program was\nbeing run improperly, he could have taken his concerns to the\nagency\u2019s inspector general or to Congress.  Leakers\u2019 Dilemma  But anyone seeking to pass judgment on Snowden should try\nto understand the dilemma he describes. He says he didn\u2019t want\nto live in a society that engages in the sort of program he\nworked on. Based on statements from President  Barack Obama  and\nmembers of Congress, it seems unlikely that Snowden would have\nfound much support from inside government for his view that the\nprogram was abusive. So he concluded -- perhaps irresponsibly,\nperhaps arrogantly -- that going public was the only way to\nforce a change.  Snowden\u2019s case highlights the difficulty, if not\nimpossibility, of debating U.S. national security policy in this\nage of ubiquitous technology: How do you build informed public\nconsent for surveillance when the only people who know about\nthose programs can\u2019t talk about them? And without the public\u2019s\nconsent, how can those programs be legitimate in a democratic\nsociety?  Those questions aren\u2019t new, but Snowden\u2019s revelations give\nthem new importance. Those who think what he did was wrong need\nto do more than just criticize his actions. The goal should be\nto make it easier for others like him to follow their\nconsciences without breaking the law. And we need to have the\npublic debate that Snowden concluded was lacking -- a point that\ncan\u2019t reasonably be contested, even by his angriest detractors.  The Obama administration may be tempted to respond to\nSnowden\u2019s actions by intensifying its policy of intimidating\nwould-be leakers through prosecutions. Yet as this case\ndemonstrates, the prospect of imprisonment doesn\u2019t deter\neveryone. The administration and Congress should instead\nacknowledge that members of the intelligence community need\nbetter avenues for reporting practices they find to be abusive -\n- if only because, absent such avenues, there will be more\nEdward Snowdens.  Snowden hasn\u2019t alleged any illegal activity. Yet there are\nreforms that could be useful, even if they wouldn\u2019t apply in his\ncase.  One option would be to give contractors with access to\nclassified information the same whistle-blower protections that\ngovernment intelligence personnel received under a presidential\n directive  issued last year. Another would be to expand the role\nof the Office of Special Counsel or similar body to include the\ninvestigation of the type of privacy abuses Snowden says he\nobserved. If would-be leakers think they can get a fair hearing\nfor their complaints without going to the media, they may make\ndifferent choices.  Classified Expansion  The fact that Snowden was an employee of Booz Allen\nHamilton has also  raised questions  about the appropriateness of\nturning over so much of our national security and intelligence\nwork to private contractors. That may be a legitimate point, but\nits relevance is to the vast expansion of the surveillance state\n-- and the explosion of classified information. There were about\n1.3 million people with top-secret security  clearance  last year,\nmore than a third of them government contractors.  Instead of asking whether the government should rely less\non companies such as  Booz Allen , the Snowden affair compels us\nto ask a different question: Whether the U.S. national security\napparatus is now too big, and its techniques too sweeping, to\nmaintain the level of secrecy the government claims it needs --\nand what size, and which means, are appropriate for a democratic\nrepublic.  To contact the Bloomberg View editorial board:\n view@bloomberg.net .","path":".\/2008_2012_msft_bloomberg_news\/edward-snowden-criminal-or-model-citizen-.txt"},{"id":39464057,"title":"\u2018Do-Right\u2019 Buffett Plants a Misplaced Kiss: Jonathan Weil","released_at":"<date>April 6 2011<\/date> <time>23:15:04<\/time>","content":"Long ago when I was a young reporter\ncovering the Arkansas legislature for the local paper in  Little\nRock , there was a line I\u2019d hear in the hallways periodically\nabout the prevailing moral standard some lawmakers lived by when\ndoing the people\u2019s business, called \u201cthe do-right rule.\u201d  It went like this: If I\u2019m the one doing it, then it must be\nall right. This brings us to the subject of  Warren Buffett , a\nlongtime adherent to his own version of the do-right rule, which\nhas no particular meaning other than that it is flexible and\nsounds folksy. The problem with this rule is it works well,\nuntil it doesn\u2019t. And lately for Buffett, one of the greatest\nvalue creators ever, it hasn\u2019t been working so hot.  Witness the harsh public reaction to the goodbye kiss\nBuffett planted last week on  David Sokol , 54, the head of\nseveral  Berkshire Hathaway Inc. (BRK\/A)  subsidiaries who had been widely\nviewed as Buffett\u2019s successor in waiting.  In his letter disclosing Sokol\u2019s surprise resignation,\nBuffett praised Sokol\u2019s \u201cextraordinary\u201d contributions. He told\nhow Sokol had bought millions of dollars of  Lubrizol Corp. (LZ)  stock\nfor himself, shortly before he suggested (successfully) to\nBuffett that Berkshire buy the company. It was all legal,\nBuffett opined. Buffett also told us that Sokol had said his\nLubrizol purchases \u201cwere not a factor in his decision to\nresign,\u201d as if that were credible.  It wasn\u2019t until the end of his letter that I began\nwondering if Buffett had lost his mind. \u201cI have held back\nnothing in this statement,\u201d he said. \u201cTherefore, if questioned\nabout this matter in the future, I will simply refer the\nquestioner back to this release.\u201d  Great Oz  So, it wasn\u2019t just some questioners who would get the\n\u201c Great Oz Has Spoken \u201d treatment from Buffett. All questioners\nwould, which is nuts. I mean, what\u2019s he going to do if and when\nthe Securities and Exchange Commission asks him about Sokol\u2019s\ntrades? Take the Fifth?  This should be a defining moment for Buffett, and for the\npublic whose  rock-star  adulation he craves. Maybe now the world\nwill realize we never should have held him up -- or bought his\nact -- as some moral paragon for business.  Sure, we can admire his talent for securities analysis, and\nhis success at building an empire and making himself and lots of\nother investors rich. But let\u2019s put to rest the exaltations\nabout his plain talk and his eye for strong character. He\u2019s a\ncorporate chief executive officer, for goodness sake. These are\nthe kinds of dodges we\u2019ve come to expect from many CEOs.  Buffett, whose record of reputational hits is long and\nvaried, is no exception.  Moody\u2019s, Coke, Gen Re  He was on the audit committee of  Coca-Cola Co. \u2019s board when\nthe SEC found the company had misled investors about its\nearnings during the 1990s. He stayed silent about  Moody\u2019s Corp. (MCO) \nas it sold the public down the river with countless AAA ratings\non garbage subprime mortgage bonds while Berkshire was its\nlargest shareholder.  Four former executives of Berkshire\u2019s Gen Re unit were\nsentenced to prison for helping American International Group\nInc. commit accounting fraud a decade ago. At least in that\ninstance, after Gen Re paid $92 million last year to settle\ninvestor claims and end government investigations, Buffett\npublicly acknowledged that the company had done something  wrong .  And how much does Berkshire\u2019s board really care about its\ntrusted insiders\u2019 trading anyway? The company kept  Deloitte &\nTouche  as its outside auditor after learning in 2008 that\nDeloitte\u2019s vice chairman had been trading in and out of\nBerkshire\u2019s stock while he was the  advisory partner  on\nBerkshire\u2019s audit. That caused Deloitte and Berkshire to violate\nthe SEC\u2019s auditor-independence rules, the agency said last year.  That\u2019s Independence  Rather than change firms, though, Berkshire concluded\nDeloitte was independent anyway. The SEC went along with it,\nwhich ultimately is what mattered, not some higher Berkshire\nvirtue of keeping up pristine appearances. (The former Deloitte\npartner last year paid about $1 million to settle fraud\n allegations  by the SEC.)  Sometimes Berkshire\u2019s whoppers are more subtle. The\ncompany\u2019s latest proxy lists Microsoft Corp. Chairman  Bill Gates \nas an \u201cindependent\u201d director, even though Buffett has  pledged \nmost of his $47 billion fortune to the  Bill & Melinda Gates\nFoundation . That may be OK under the SEC\u2019s definition of\nindependent, just not under a common-sense standard.  Another supposedly independent director is Walter Scott,\nwho owns 9.4 percent of the voting shares in Berkshire\nsubsidiary MidAmerican Energy Holdings, from which Sokol is\nresigning as chairman. Berkshire\u2019s proxy assures us these\nmatters were duly considered.  Related Parties  Berkshire steers millions of dollars of fees each year to\nVice Chairman Charlie Munger\u2019s old law firm, Munger, Tolles &\nOlson, where Berkshire director Ronald Olson is a partner. Other\ndirectors include Buffett\u2019s son, Howard. At most public\ncompanies such dealings would be held up as examples of weak\ngovernance. Because this is Buffett, Berkshire usually has\ngotten a pass.  There is one benchmark by which the 80-year-old Buffett has\nbeen wildly successful: \u201cIn Berkshire\u2019s case, we long ago told\nyou that our job is to increase per-share intrinsic value at a\nrate greater than the increase (including dividends) of the  S&P\n500 ,\u201d Buffett wrote in his latest  annual letter  to\nshareholders.  That, along with finding an able successor, is the standard\nby which investors should and will judge him. Anyone searching\nfor a folk hero to idolize should look somewhere else. They now have a second thing in common: The  Transformer AiO P1801  from  Asus (2357) , a fully functional Windows 8 desktop computer that\u2019s also a giant, fully functional Android tablet.  The question is of course: Why?  Who needs to be able to flip from running  Microsoft (MSFT)  Excel to  Google (GOOG)  Now at the touch of a button?  After spending time with this weird, $1,299 hybrid, which goes on sale in the U.S. in April, I have the answer: No one.  But, almost in spite of myself, I came to see how it might be useful, if not for the manufacturer\u2019s quality-control issues.  The name \u201cAiO\u201d -- for \u201call in one\u201d -- is misleading. The computer actually consists of two pieces: a detachable 18.4-inch screen and the separate \u201cPC station\u201d it slides onto.  The PC station holds the guts of what\u2019s needed to make the Transformer a potent Windows 8 desktop: an  Intel (INTC)  Core i5 microprocessor, eight gigabytes of memory,  Nvidia (NVDA)  graphics, a one-terabyte hard drive and a DVD drive. A wireless mouse and keyboard complete the package.  Mode Switch  Boot up the PC, and you\u2019re greeted by the colorful Windows 8 desktop, with its familiar tiles, plus one that isn\u2019t familiar. It features a little green robot and is labeled \u201cMode Switch.\u201d  Poke it, and the screen goes dark for three seconds. When it returns, Presto! You\u2019re looking at the home screen for Android 4.1, which Google calls \u201cJelly Bean.\u201d  The electronics for the tablet side are contained within the screen itself: Nvidia\u2019s Tegra 3 processor and 32 gigabytes of solid-state storage.  The Android home screen also features an app called \u201cMode Switch.\u201d Tap it, and three seconds later you\u2019re back in Windows 8.  So why would you ever want this capability? I can think of one big reason: apps.  After an early burst of activity, growth has slowed in the Microsoft app store for the new Windows 8 user interface. At last count, there were only about 50,000. By contrast, the number of Android apps is now  about 700,000 .  Super-Size  To be sure, most of them were designed for smartphones and aren\u2019t optimized for tablets, let alone a super-size one like the Transformer. Still, even a blown-up smartphone app is better than no app at all.  For example, I was able to watch college basketball playoff games in real time, using the NCAA March Madness Live Android app. If I were moving around the home or office, it was easy to pop the screen out of the PC station and carry it with me into the next room, using the integrated kickstand to prop it up.  Of course, at 5-1\/2 pounds -- roughly equivalent to eight  Apple (AAPL)  iPad minis -- I certainly wouldn\u2019t want to carry it far.  When used off the dock, you can expect battery life of about five hours, though Asus has thoughtfully provided a second power supply for when the Transformer roams from home base.  Because the PC hardware resides in the docking station, you aren\u2019t able to use the Transformer as a full Windows 8 tablet. Instead, Asus has included software that\u2019s supposed to allow it run Windows remotely over short distances.  Failed Connection  Unfortunately, it proved problematic: Whenever I removed the screen from the dock, the Windows connection failed and the tablet flipped over into Android mode. Asus eventually replaced the first unit with a second one, which had the same problem until a company technician managed to get it working properly.  That was just one of several vexing issues I encountered with both machines. The \u201cMode Switch\u201d app would routinely drop me into Windows\u2019 desktop mode instead of the Start Screen -- an annoying and unnecessary extra stop. (If you began on the Start Screen, you\u2019re supposed to be returned there.) (MSFT)  is telling employees that a reorganization plan by departing Chief Executive Officer  Steve Ballmer  will go ahead, seeking to reassure senior managers who are concerned that the search for a successor will throw turnaround efforts into disarray.  Some members of Microsoft\u2019s senior leadership team e-mailed their staff on Aug. 23 to say they remain committed to Ballmer\u2019s vision and the reorganization, said three people with knowledge of the matter. Some Microsoft executives have seen an increase in outside job offers since the July restructuring plan and others may be tempted to leave after stock grants and bonuses are awarded in late August, said the people, who asked not to be identified because the communications were private.  Even as it hunts for a CEO who may change tack, Microsoft\u2019s board needs managers to stay focused on the reorganization plan, the biggest shift in more than a decade. Ballmer is emphasizing hardware and Internet-based services, shifting away from software for the declining personal-computer industry and putting Microsoft on better footing to compete with  Google Inc. (GOOG) ,  Facebook Inc. (FB)  and  Apple Inc. (AAPL)  in mobile devices and online advertising.  \u201cThey need to change everything, everything,\u201d said Ivan Feinseth, chief investment officer of Tigress Financial Partners LLC in  New York . \u201cThey need to be better in social, mobile, analytics and cloud, and they really have very little to offer in those areas.\u201d  Ballmer Departs  Ballmer said on Aug. 23 that he intends to retire within 12 months after leading Microsoft since January 2000. During the CEO\u2019s tenure, Microsoft has battled to stay relevant as consumers have shifted from using its core Windows software for PCs toward mobile devices from Apple and others. Facebook and Google have also pushed ahead in social networking and online advertising, areas where Microsoft remains weak.  Tony Imperati, a spokesman for Redmond, Washington-based Microsoft, declined to comment on the executive e-mails.  Microsoft can ill afford to wait and see if a new CEO alters the Ballmer plan. With the company behind in mobile and tablets and as core revenue from its flagship Windows product shrinks, the stock is down about 37 percent under Ballmer\u2019s watch. Last month, Microsoft also reported sales and profit that missed analysts\u2019 estimates.  Microsoft shares declined 2.6 percent to $33.26 at the close in New York.  While embarking on a new CEO search, Microsoft will also have to contend with retaining employees and tamping down unease that for some began with the July reorganization.  More Uncertainty  \u201cThere\u2019s going to be more confusion near-term,\u201d said  Sid Parakh , an analyst at McAdams Wright Ragen in  Seattle . \u201cIt just seems like now there\u2019s the question of how\u2019s the new person going to look at these changes. Some executives unhappy with their new roles may leave after the stock grants and bonuses at the end of August, said another person.  Some Microsoft executives are also getting more feelers from recruiters and companies to leave since the reorganization and expect that to accelerate as the next CEO remains to be chosen, said another person with knowledge of the matter.  Calming Nerves  Ballmer\u2019s reorganization, which put all of Microsoft\u2019s hardware into one unit and shifted the Windows and Windows Phone operating systems under the same executive, was undertaken with the knowledge that a new CEO might end up at the company\u2019s helm, said another person with knowledge of the matter. It didn\u2019t make sense to put the changes on hold for as long as a year until a new CEO was in place, the person said.  The same day as Ballmer\u2019s retirement announcement, Microsoft\u2019s leadership team held a previously planned meeting, after which some senior executives e-mailed their staff to say they are committed to the restructuring, said the people with knowledge of the matter. The paper, released yesterday by the  Justice Department  and\nU.S. Patent and Trademark Office, says that, in some instances,\npatent owners shouldn\u2019t be allowed to block sales or imports of\nproducts based on the use of standards that help products from\ndifferent manufacturers work together. The U.S. Federal Trade\nCommission, which reached a consent agreement with Google Inc.\nlast week restricting its use of standard-essential patents, has\ntaken a similar position.  The paper puts added pressure on the U.S. International\nTrade Commission, which is considering the issue as part of a\nrequest by Samsung Electronics Co. to halt imports of  Apple Inc. (AAPL) \nproducts made in  Asia . A final decision is expected Feb. 6.  The ITC\u2019s approach \u201cwill be important to the continued\nvitality of the voluntary consensus standards-setting process\nand thus to competitive conditions and consumers in the United\nStates,\u201d the two agencies wrote, without citing specific cases.  The agencies, in a joint policy paper, said that, while\npatent owners have the right to exclude others from using their\ninventions, the public benefit of allowing that is limited when\nit comes to so-called standard-essential patents.  The Washington-based trade commission is investigating\nother complaints filed by owners of standard-essential patents,\nincluding one by  Google Inc. (GOOG) \u2019s Motorola Mobility unit against\nMicrosoft Corp., an  InterDigital Inc. (IDCC)  case against Huawei\nTechnologies Co. and one filed by  Ericsson AB (ERIC)  against Samsung.  Companies participate in groups to establish technical\nspecifications that can be used across platforms for things like\nhow video images are transmitted or what type of plug is used\nfor phone chargers. Those who establish the standards pledge to\nlicense any relevant patents on fair, reasonable and non-\ndiscriminatory terms, or FRAND.  The Justice Department and patent office laid out\nguidelines that should be met before an exclusion order is\ngranted by the trade commission. The agencies said the standard\nalso should apply in district court lawsuits. Judges in Seattle\nand Chicago have already said Motorola Mobility isn\u2019t entitled\nto orders halting U.S. sales of products based on the use of\nstandard-essential patents. The German suits over the design of the products are\nscheduled to be put on hold until the process in Spain is\ncompleted. Stocks began short-term declines in April of each of the last three years. Still, the benchmark measure has  surged 130 percent  from a 12-year low in 2009 as the Federal Reserve embarked on three rounds of bond purchases to stimulate the economy.  Thirteen S&P 500 companies including General Electric Co. posted quarterly earnings today. The court will consider whether patent owners can control\nthe use of products that can make copies of themselves, such as\nsoybean seeds producing plants bearing new seeds, genetically\nmodified salmon, live vaccines, or stem cells and bacteria\nstrains used in medical research.  The Supreme Court has scheduled arguments Feb. 19 in an\nappeal of a patent-infringement case by Vernon Hugh Bowman, a\nfarmer who planted soybean seeds harvested from plants that were\ngrown from Monsanto\u2019s engineered seeds. The world\u2019s biggest seed\ncompany said Bowman violated a policy forbidding farmers from\nsaving seeds for replanting rather than buying them anew each\nseason from Monsanto or a licensee.  Monsanto, based in St. Louis, inserts genes into crops that\nallow them to withstand application of the herbicide Roundup.\nFarmers who buy so-called Roundup Ready seeds agree to\nrestrictions on their use.  A victory for Bowman \u201cwould potentially kill the seed\nindustry,\u201d said Peter Corless of Boston\u2019s  Edwards Wildman\nPalmer LLP , who specializes in biotechnology patents. \u201cNo one\nwould bother doing the research. To contact the reporter on this story:\n Mark Lee  in  Hong Kong  at \n wlee37@bloomberg.net   To contact the editor responsible for this story:\nMichael Tighe at \n mtighe4@bloomberg.net","path":".\/2008_2012_msft_bloomberg_news\/qihoo-360-quarterly-profit-declines-as-spending-increases.txt"},{"id":59490681,"title":"Stolen Credit Cards Go for $3.50 at Amazon-Like Online Bazaar","released_at":"<date>December 20 2011<\/date> <time>05:01:34<\/time>","content":"In mid-September, a European hacker\nnicknamed Poxxie broke into the computer network of a U.S.\ncompany and, he said, grabbed 1,400  credit-card  numbers, the\naccount holders\u2019 names and addresses, and the security code that\ncomes with each card.  With little trouble, he sold the numbers for $3.50 each on\nhis own seller\u2019s site, called CVV2s.in, to underworld buyers who\nhave come to trust the quality of his goods, he said.  \u201cThe main thing in any business is honesty,\u201d Poxxie said,\nwithout any trace of irony.  The Traverse City, Michigan-based  Ponemon Institute , which\nresearches data security, estimates that thieves annually steal\n8.4 million credit-card numbers in the U.S. alone. How do\ncyberbandits, who have turned hacking into a volume business,\nunload all those numbers? A lot like  Amazon.com (AMZN) , it turns out.  Customers on CVV2s can search for card numbers by bank,\ncard type, credit limit and zip code, loading them into a\nvirtual shopping basket as they go. The site offers the ability\nto search by bank identification number. That means customers\ncan choose cards by institutions known to have weak security,\nPoxxie said. CVV2s even has an automated feature that lets\nclients validate the numbers in real time, to make sure the bank\nhasn\u2019t canceled the card.  Sites like Poxxie\u2019s make up the cyberunderworld\u2019s version\nof a pirate\u2019s cove, offering their online booty at cut-rate\nprices. Hundreds of millions of dollars in stolen data are\nbought and sold in underground\u2019s chat rooms and forums every\nyear, a fencing operation that becomes more robust annually,\naccording to RSA, the security division of  EMC Corp. (EMC) \nCrackHackForum.com, one of the sites, even mimics  EBay Inc. (EBAY) ,\nrating buyers and sellers with starred reviews.  $114 Billion a Year  Symantec Corp. (SYMC) , the cybersecurity firm, estimates that\ncyberthieves steal data worth $114 billion a year. By\ncomparison, the  Federal Bureau of Investigation  said the take\nfrom all bank robberies in the U.S. in 2010 was just\n$43 million. The global market in cocaine is an estimated\n$85 billion, according to the  United Nations .  \u201cThe problem is getting worse faster than we\u2019re getting\nbetter,\u201d said Tony Sager, chief operating officer of the\nInformation Assurance Directorate at the National Security\nAgency, which includes some of the U.S. government\u2019s best\ncyberexperts. \u201cWe\u2019re not keeping pace.\u201d  To look inside the cyberbazaar, to find details on prices\nand goods for sale, Bloomberg News gathered information through\npublicly available websites and in restricted forums, aided in\nthis search by cybersecurity experts. Some of the information\nwas provided through online interviews with participants, who\nprotected their real identities as they discussed details on\ntheir lives and criminal operations.  How to Verify  The cyberunderground thrives because of anonymity: Hackers\ncan devise any persona to conduct business and use a variety of\ntechnical tricks to hide their tracks. Their stories were\nverified to the extent possible by security experts who have\nwatched the careers and methods of specific hackers for years.  As recently as 2008, the fight between those who protect\n computer networks  and those who attack them was about evenly\nmatched. That\u2019s no longer the case, according to the cybercops.\nThe defenders are losing the battle because of a combination of\ntheir opponents\u2019 technical achievements and rapid advances in a\nglobal supply chain of theft.  In 2009, Symantec cataloged 2.8 million new viruses\ninfecting computers. A year later, that number had jumped to\n286 million. One reason for the hundredfold growth is that\nsophisticated viruses now change their digital signatures as\nthey infect new machines. Because anti-virus software uses a\ncatalog of known signatures to stop infections, the dominant\ncybersecurity technology in many cases is useless as a result.  Cheap Malware  Some of the market\u2019s most advanced malware -- stealth\nsoftware that steals data or lets hackers take remote command of\na computer -- can be bought for a few thousand dollars.\nSophisticated spam operations implant the malware in computers\nfor pennies per victim.  Black-market vendors test malware against the latest anti-\nvirus programs; provide hosting for command-and-control servers\nin countries that can\u2019t be touched by U.S.  law enforcement ; or\nstart a directed denial-of-service attack on a commercial or\nother website priced by the number of hours the site is down.  One enterprise, advertised recently on the Israeli forum\nSecondZion, has created a language-aid call center for hackers\nwho need to pose as U.S. bank customers or communicate with a\nGerman-speaking money mule, as currency transporters are called.\nThe hackers provide a script; operators do the rest. \u201cGood\nafternoon, ladies and gentleman crooks,\u201d the site says, noting\nthat its translators are \u201call operators with extensive\nexperience.\u201d Two users followed up with comments praising the\nservice as excellent.  Illicit Chat Rooms  Distribution of goods and services is organized through\nthousands of illicit chat rooms and invitation-only forums. Some\nare publicly accessible: Any beginner looking to learn the\nbasics of a so-called SQL injection hack -- a basic attack on\nthe security of a website -- can join a forum like OpenSC and\nask for tips. Others are private and access is strictly\nprotected.  The most serious criminals congregate on forums such as\nMaza. Membership to the forum is granted only by a vote of all\nof its senior members and only after an eight-day waiting\nperiod, according to researchers who have tried to infiltrate\nit. Most deals done on the forum are large, so members use an\nescrow system. Cash or goods are held either by a trusted senior\nhacker or one who has retired from the business. In a criminal\nworld in which conspirators almost never meet and trust is in\nshort supply, the escrow system has evolved as a way for elite\nhackers to do big business.  \u2018Five Figures\u2019  \u201cMost of the transactions of in those forums will be in the\nfive figures,\u201d said a security investigator who has infiltrated\nseveral such forums. \u201cThe escrow system is the only way to make\nthose transactions viable.\u201d  Public hacker sites, including CrackHackForum and\nHackForums, usually have rules against selling stolen data.\nEnforcement of sales postings is often weak and varies widely.  Poxxie\u2019s site, which is well known to security experts, was\nrun until recently from a server in  India , where U.S. law\nenforcement carries little weight with local authorities when it\ncomes to computer crime. The site was recently moved or shut\ndown, a common security practice among hackers.  Poxxie has been in business long enough to see the price\nfor a stolen credit card plummet because of over-supply and more\nsophisticated safety precautions by banks. Why charge $3.50 for\na stolen card number with the purchasing power to buy a car? The\ncard could be canceled at any time after purchase, he said, and\nthere are inherent risks in using it.  Crime Wave  \u201cIn this whole carding scene, nothing is guaranteed,\u201d\nPoxxie said via ICQ, the online messaging network that is a\ncommon platform for doing business in the cyberunderground.  Poxxie\u2019s business is a boutique firm in an industrial-scale\ncrime wave. Although the targets of cybercrime are still\nconcentrated in the U.S. and  Europe , the perpetrators are\nglobal. Some are independent operators who make a few thousand\ndollars a month, often supplementing their income with a day\njob. Others are members of large criminal organizations.  Hex Nightmare falls somewhere in between. When you conduct\nbusiness with the 20-something cyberthief, the first -- and only\n-- thing you see is an avatar on ICQ: an anime version of a girl\nin hip huggers and a tank top. A person who has tracked her over\nseveral years said Hex Nightmare has managed to gain an\nimpressive pedigree in the cyberunderground, learning quickly\nand moving in some of the most trusted circles of top\ncyberthieves.  Take-Home Pay  Her take-home from cybertheft, which concentrates mostly on\nstealing credit-card numbers and online banking credentials,\ncompares with the pay of some lower-level corporate executives,\nshe said via ICQ -- keeping her true identity secret. \u201cI can\npossibly make an extra $8k a month on top of my regular income,\u201d\nshe said.  To the young hacker, cybertheft is like a second job, one\nshe juggles, she said, with going out to clubs on weekend nights\nand waitressing during the week. Her legitimate job is also a\nway to launder illicit income, she said. Hex Nightmare said she\ndidn\u2019t want the debt of a university education and instead spent\ntwo years on the forums learning her trade. The hacker faces\nnone of the violence associated with other organized crime and\notherwise leads a relatively normal life.  \u201cThey have no idea what I do,\u201d she said of friends and\nacquaintances. The details of the cyberthief\u2019s personal life --\nincluding her real gender and age -- couldn\u2019t be verified but\nher business model and activities were corroborated by a\nsecurity professional and fit the profile typical of young\nhackers, according to Eric Strom, an FBI special agent who heads\nan elite cyber team based in Pittsburgh.  Like Universities  \u201cThese are marketplaces, but they are also like\nuniversities,\u201d Strom said. \u201cYou have newbies on there, you have\nseasoned guys. It\u2019s a meeting place, it\u2019s a social networking\nplace, everything wrapped into one.\u201d  Working out of an office in a tech hub along the\nMonongahela River, Strom wears short-sleeves and loose pants,\nthe uniform of a man who fights crime at a computer keyboard.\nHis unit has a storied place in that world. It was behind\nDarkMarket, an elite English-language hackers forum that turned\nout to be an FBI sting when 56 of its members were arrested in\n2008.  Before turning to the cyber world, Strom spent most of his\nFBI career fighting the Mafia. It\u2019s was good training, he said.  Like the Mob  \u201cThe stance we take is looking at it through the lens of\norganized crime,\u201d he said. It took the better part of the 1980s\nand early 1990s for federal authorities to understand and begin\nto dismantle the U.S. mafia: develop investigative capacity,\npenetrate complex enterprises, pass new laws. It will take time\nwith global cybercrime as well, Strom said.  \u201cWe\u2019re trying to keep pace with how the crime is evolving,\u201d\nhe said.  Facing sophisticated cartels, the FBI and European law\nenforcement officials have created new cybersquads and launched\nmajor investigations. In October 2010, the FBI began one of its\nmost ambitious cybercrime operations. Code-named Trident Breach,\nauthorities broke up an international crime ring responsible for\nstealing $70 million from online bank accounts of small\nbusinesses and local government throughout the U.S. and Europe.\nThere were arrests in four countries, including 39 in the U.S.  Frustrations  That success was accompanied by frustrations faced daily by\ninvestigators: There is almost no chance the world\u2019s top\ncybercriminals -- residing in haven countries like Belarus,\n Romania , and Ukraine -- will ever be brought to justice. Most of\nthe individuals detained last year were international students\nwho, acting as so-called mules, withdrew money from the hackers\u2019\nU.S. bank accounts and forwarded it home. Five people who were\ndescribed as kingpins were detained for questioning in Ukraine.\nAll five were eventually set free without seeing the inside of a\ncourtroom, the FBI said in September.  \u201cCybergangs, mainly in Eastern Europe and the former  Soviet\nUnion , are making money that rivals some drug cartels,\u201d said\nRichard Clarke, former special adviser on cybersecurity to U.S.\nPresident  George W. Bush , at an October conference on network\nsecurity. \u201cThere is frankly nothing the FBI and Secret Service\ncan do about it.\u201d  In April, the  Department of Justice  dismantled one of the\nlargest known criminal botnets, a network of infected computers\nprogrammed to send data automatically from their hard drives to\na server controlled by hackers. The department declared the\nbreak-up of Coreflood, as the botnet was known, a major victory.  The Russians  It said almost nothing about the criminals who ran it.\nResearchers at Dell SecureWorks, the Atlanta-based security firm\nthat aided the investigation, said the kingpins behind Coreflood\nare three Russians last known to be living comfortably in\nRostov, a mid-size city on the Don River.  \u201cOur relationship with the Russians is always a work in\nprogress,\u201d Strom said.  No one personifies  Russia \u2019s place at the top of the cyber\nunderworld more than Gribo-demon, a Russian programmer, around\n30 years old, U.S. investigators estimate. He is one of the few\ncybercriminals who is the focus of a his own FBI special\noperation. Gribo-demon is the author of SpyEye, a sophisticated\nmalware package first released in late 2009 and upgraded several\ntimes since then.  Once downloaded on a machine, the malware can be used by\nhackers to take remote command of key functions. Using SpyEye, a\ncyberthief can hijack an online banking session in real time,\ntransfer funds to accounts they or their mules control, and\nadjust the balance displayed so nothing seems amiss.  Seems Legit  The transaction looks legitimate because, in computer\nterms, it is. All the bank can tell is that it was made from\ntheir customer\u2019s computer, using their correct password. A basic\nversion of SpyEye costs around $2,000, according to the hacker\nsites.  \u201cSpyEye provides military-grade intrusion capabilities for\nthe price of a TV,\u201d said Gunter Ollmann, vice president of\nresearch at Damballa Inc., the Atlanta-based security firm\nthat tracks major cyberthreats.  Gribo-demon\u2019s real innovation stems from what he didn\u2019t do:\nkeep SpyEye to himself. Hackers used to write their own code.\nGood tools were  trade secrets . Gribo-demon instead licenses\nSpyEye, mimicking Microsoft and Oracle, a business model that\narguably opened cybercrime to the masses.  The model was pioneered by a competitor and fellow Russian\nwho created popular malware called ZeuS, according to security\nexperts. ZeuS first appeared in 2008. Both programmers provided\nclients with  customer service , offering an array of enticing\nmodules to add functionality for an additional price.  Beta Testing  The ZeuS author, known as Slavik, even Beta-tested new\nversions with elite users, according to Don Jackson, a\nSecureWorks researcher. Slavik disappeared in late 2010, but not\nbefore he handed the ZeuS source-code to Gribo, who incorporated\nsome of its features into his own product, Jackson said.  Security experts say it\u2019s hard to overestimate impact of\nSlavik\u2019s and Gribo-demon\u2019s handiwork. In September, the Tokyo-\nbased cybersecurity firm Trend Micro publicized a dossier on a\n20-something Russian cyberthief who goes by the name Soldier,\ntracing his activities in the underground forums over several\nmonths. Using SpyEye, soldier stole $3.2 million from U.S.\ncustomers of three banks in just six months -- about $17,000 a\nday -- Trend Micro said.  Going Price  The hacker used bank-account information scraped from more\nthan 25,000 victims\u2019 computers, in some cases renting other\ncyberthieves\u2019 networks of infected computers. He created\ncounterfeit checks with banking data and mailed them to money\nmules throughout the  United States . They cashed them, then\nforwarded the funds untraceably to Russia. He even used stolen\ncredit card numbers vacuumed from the victims\u2019 hard drives to\nbuy pre-paid postal-service labels for the packages.  \u201cFrom start to finish, this guy leveraged every bit of\ndata,\u201d said Alex Cox, an investigator for Netwitness, a\ncybersecurity division of  EMC Corp. (EMC) , which has also been\ntracking Soldier\u2019s activities.  The most remarkable thing about the theft -- and this is,\nto experts in the field, the most worrisome development of the\npast few months -- was that Soldier didn\u2019t need any special\nexpertise with computers. All he needed was a shopping list.  \u201cHe\u2019s not a lone hacker,\u201d said Trend Micro\u2019s  David Perry .\n\u201cHe didn\u2019t write any code.\u201d  Shopping List  Strom said the FBI is also tracking Soldier and is\nconfident they\u2019ll get him. \u201cThese guys are very sophisticated,\nbut often times they slip up,\u201d Strom said.  Strom and other investigators have one significant\nadvantage: the hackers have a habit of turning their skills on\none another. The FBI\u2019s DarkMarket sting started with a hacker\nwar between a hacker, calling himself Iceman, who ran\nCardersMarket, and JiLsi, the DarkMarket administrator, whose\nreal name was Renukanth Subramaniam, the FBI said.  \u201cWe took advantage of that animosity,\u201d Strom said,\neventually persuading JiLsi to turn over the site to the FBI and\ngiving the bureau control over all communications involving\nDarkMarket\u2019s 2,500 members. As a result, Subramaniam was\nsentenced to more than four years in prison in the U.K.  Maza, the elite Russian forum, was recently hacked and its\ndatabase dumped online. It presented a priceless opportunity for\nlaw enforcement. The forum\u2019s database held membership lists, e-\nmail addresses, IP addresses, and passwords -- the kind of\ninformation the world\u2019s top cyber thieves try very hard to keep\nsecret. The main suspect in the Maza attack is the administrator\nof a rival site, Hex Nightmare said.  Learned a Lot  \u201cWe learned a lot of lessons with DarkMarket, and we\u2019ve\npassed that experience on not only to other offices within the\nFBI but to our counterparts overseas,\u201d Strom said. \u201cWe\u2019re\ndefinitely taking the fight back to them.\u201d  Hex Nightmare agrees the FBI may eventually make more\nprogress. Nokia\u2019s R&D was always about a checklist of features, not\nan experience the way Apple\u2019s is, says a former Nokia Research\nCenter developer who didn\u2019t want to be identified because he\nstill works in the mobile-phone industry. But you know, my leadership team is  smart . And they've been hugely successful. So  why  are they doing things that are just so obviously wrong?\" The answer we came to was a simple one. The company's core control mechanisms \u2014 the means by which it decides how to allocate resources, start and stop projects, and so on \u2014 were organized to do one thing: minimize mistakes. No one would ever say it that way, but it clearly explained why even seemingly simple decisions required consensus and multiple rounds of meetings. There's nothing necessarily wrong with control mechanisms to minimize mistakes. In fact, when problems can be tightly defined, mistake-minimizing mindsets are very valuable. There have been plenty of recent examples where shareholders would have been well served by systems to curtail wild risks. Even Google, one of the poster children of a fundamentally different control mindset \u2014 call it \"experimentation encouraging\" \u2014 hears calls to \"get its house in order.\" Mistake-minimizing companies have their limits, however. They particularly struggle to handle industry transitions when answers come not from the Microsoft suite of products but from somewhat disorderly discovery in the marketplace.  In those circumstances, companies need to find a way to balance mistake-minimizing approaches that ensure the core business stays in control and produces vital cash flow for growth with experiment-encouraging approaches that spur the creation of new growth. The fundamental challenge, then, is finding the right way to balance this tension. Academics offer up at least three answers: Each theory has its advocates, but each feels incomplete. The Christensen doctrine helped Dayton-Hudson create Target, Hewlett-Packard succeed in inkjet printing, and Qantas create its discount JetStar airline. But companies that follow this approach don't develop a  capability  to create new growth businesses.  Tushman and O'Reilly essentially punt: if you have a leader like Amazon.com's Jeff Bezos, you can succeed; if you don't, you are in trouble.  While Govindarajan and Trimble's guidance makes sense at a high level, coloring in the details related to portfolio management, decision making, and managing distinct cultures presents challenges. \nThere is an interesting idea coming out of the work my colleague Clark Gilbert is doing to transform the  Deseret News  and  Deseret Digital  (both owned by the Mormon Church). Gilbert says he has found success from creating a \"modular exchange\" between the old and new business. Visualize an airlock chamber on a ship. Innovators exploring new businesses enter the airlock, seal the door behind them, borrow the equipment that will help them with a tight seal from stopping unintentional contamination, and then start to explore. When they return, they can then \"decontaminate\" before re-entering the mother ship.  Gilbert's instincts are generally spot-on, and his early results are impressive, so I'm eager to see what he and my colleagues Matt Eyring and Dick Foster do as they continue to develop this idea. In the meantime, corporate leaders should at least step back to assess the degree to which their corporations are governed by mistake-minimizing systems. Exhorting people to be more innovative when all soft and hard systems point towards incrementalism doesn't do much good.","path":".\/2008_2012_msft_bloomberg_news\/negotiating-innovation-and-contro.txt"},{"id":18414329,"title":"Neiman Marcus Takes Fight to \u2018Intolerable\u2019 Patent Suers","released_at":"<date>May 28 2013<\/date> <time>04:01:00<\/time>","content":"To Neiman Marcus Group Inc.\u2019s\nlawyers, the letter from an unnamed inventor\u2019s representative\noffering to negotiate patent licenses after an \u201canalysis\u201d of\nits technology was all too familiar. Rising stakes in patent litigation over smartphones and\nother technologies have led to an increase in businesses, often\nderided as \u201ctrolls,\u201d that make money by licensing patents\nrather than providing products and services. A subset have found\nthat approaching users of technology, rather than the producers,\ngets settlements that avoid the cost and risk of going to court.  Retailers, hotel owners and municipalities say they\u2019re fed\nup receiving royalty demands for using common technology like\nWi-Fi connections to the Internet, tracking customer shipments\nand scanning documents to send via e-mail.  Forest, Trees  Some technology providers like Cisco Systems Inc., Adobe\nSystems Inc., Google Inc. and Microsoft Corp. are filing\nlawsuits seeking to invalidate patents owned by holders who\u2019ve\ngone after their customers. Lawsuits against users would be put\non hold if manufacturers intervene, under proposals by leaders\nof judiciary committees in both houses of Congress.  \u201cThe demands for settlements are designed to be well below\nthe cost of litigation,\u201d French said. \u201cThe lawyers know this\nand that\u2019s why they come after retailers.\u201d  Neiman Marcus had no comment for this story because of the\nlitigation, said Ginger Reeder, a company spokeswoman.  ArrivalStar SA, a company based in Luxembourg that owns\npatents for systems to track vehicles, has filed hundreds of\nlawsuits against companies such as pharmacy retailer Rite Aid\nCorp., railroad Union Pacific Corp., electronics maker Sharp\nCorp. and even the city of Vacaville, California.  In most instances, the cases are quickly settled.  \u201cAny company that we contact has actively gone out and\nimplemented our technology,\u201d said  Anthony Dowell  of Taft\nStettinius & Hollister in Indianapolis, who represents\nArrivalStar, in an interview. \u201cWe would prefer to go after the\ncompany that developed the technology and whenever we can, we\ndo. We want to go after the forest, the big picture, and not the\ntrees.\u201d  Targeting Customers  Federal law says a patent infringer is anyone who makes,\nsells or uses a protected invention. In 2008, the U.S. Supreme\nCourt limited patent holders from extracting royalties from\ncompanies at each stage of the distribution process. That forced\nthem to choose where in the chain to make their legal stand.\nThey could go after manufacturers, distributors or customers,\nnot all three.  The court ruling \u201creally started focusing people on the\ncustomers,\u201d said James Yoon, a patent lawyer with Wilson\nSonsini in Palo Alto,  California , in an interview. \u201cIf people\nsued the suppliers and they settled, all the customers\ndownstream would be protected.\u201d  Lawsuits like the one filed April 30 by Neiman Marcus are\nrare because they cost a lot of money. A patent suit with less\nthan $1 million at stake typically incurred about $650,000 in\nlegal costs in 2011, according to a study by the American\nIntellectual Property Law Association in Arlington, Virginia.  Loser Pays  As part of a 2011 law, Congress prevented patent owners\nfrom filing one suit against dozens of companies, intending that\nthe cost of filing individual suits in multiple courts would\ndeter some cases. That makes it hard to quantify whether the\nnumber of patent cases against end-user companies has grown.  Among the proposals in the U.S. House and Senate are ones\nthat would make patent owners pay legal costs if they lose a\ncase, increase reviews of software patents, and require patent\nowners to provide more data rather than filing boilerplate\nsuits.  Retailers want more protections, including a requirement\nthat technology users can\u2019t be sued unless the manufacturer is\nnamed as well, French said.  Serial Pioneer  The late Jerome Lemelson, who owned patents related to\nmachines that scanned products for defects and prices, was a\npioneer in suing end users. He first sued automakers in the late\n1990s and then pursued hundreds of retailers.  Before his patents were thrown out by an appeals court in\n2005, a foundation in his name had collected more than $1.5\nbillion in settlements. The money has gone in part to pay for a\n program  at Massachusetts Institute of Technology and a  section \nof the Smithsonian\u2019s National Museum of American History.  \u201cHe wanted to sue the deep-pocketed end users,\u201d said\nJesse Jenner of Ropes & Gray in New York. Jenner represented the\nmanufacturers, including Cognex Corp., who joined to fight the\nLemelson patents. \u201cEverybody has agreed it\u2019s changed the nature\nof patents and patent enforcement.\u201d  Sending letters to companies asking them to talk about\nspecific patents can help avoid litigation, said Erich\nSpangenberg, chief executive officer of IP Navigation Group LLC,\nthe Dallas-based patent licensing firm that sent the letter to\nNeiman Marcus.  While he wouldn\u2019t identify his client, Spangenberg said the\nletter to the retailer was a \u201clet\u2019s talk\u201d request that could\nhave resulted in no payments by Neiman Marcus. He said that\nstrategy helps avoid litigation and isn\u2019t involved in the\n\u201cshakedown\u201d tactics of mass letter-writers.  Court Guidance  The U.S. Court of Appeals for the Federal Circuit needs to\nprovide more guidance to judges on when to put the user suits on\nhold, Yoon said. The appeals court, which handles all patent\ncases, has backed sanctions against patent owners who file\nfrivolous suits or those seeking what the court has called\n\u201cnuisance value settlements,\u201d he said.  Until there are changes in the law, \u201clittle guys need to\nreach out to the community of other little guys to see if they\ncan\u2019t get together into a joint defense group to spread out the\ncosts,\u201d Jenner said.  The Senate bills are S.1013 and S.866. The House bills are\nH.R. 845 and H.R. 2024. Cisco Systems Inc .,  Microsoft Corp . and  Google Inc . account\nfor the biggest portion of the $943 billion stockpile, Moody\u2019s\nsaid yesterday in a report. That\u2019s up from $937 billion at the\nend of 2009 and $775 billion in the prior year. Borrowers have bolstered their finances by slashing\nspending and raising cash, selling $945.8 billion of U.S.\ncorporate bonds this year, following a record $1.23 trillion in\n2009, according to data compiled by Bloomberg. While that\u2019s\nhelped corporate  credit quality  improve, a reluctance to use the\nmoney for hiring and investing until more signs of growth emerge\nisn\u2019t helping shorten a \u201cjobless recovery,\u201d Moody\u2019s said.  \u201cThe mantra is better safe than sorry,\u201d said Mark Luschini, chief investment strategist at Philadelphia-based\nJanney Montgomery Scott LLC, which has $50 billion of assets\nunder management. \u201cCompanies have been very aggressive in\nfinding ways to do business without having to hire.\u201d  \u2018Human Side\u2019  Americans\u2019 views on job availability and wage prospects\nsoured in October, according to a report yesterday from the New\nYork-based Conference Board, highlighting the risk that 9.6\npercent unemployment will limit  consumer spending , which\naccounts for 70 percent of the world\u2019s biggest economy.  Corporate borrowers, concerned last year they wouldn\u2019t be\nable to tap debt markets following the worst financial crisis\nsince the Great Depression, now fret over prospects for economic\ngrowth, said  John Milne  of JKMilne Asset Management  \u201cIt would be naive to believe that the human side of\nrunning a business is insulated from the low confidence that\nconsumers have,\u201d said Milne, who oversees about $1.8 billion as\nchief executive officer for the firm in  Fort Myers ,  Florida .  Elsewhere in credit markets, the extra yield investors\ndemand to hold company bonds instead of similar-maturity\ngovernment debt fell 1 basis point to 165 basis points, or 1.65\npercentage point, according to Bank of America Merrill Lynch\u2019s\nGlobal Broad Market Corporate Index. Leveraged Loans  Credit swap indexes typically fall as investor confidence\nimproves and rise as it deteriorates. Contracts pay the buyer\nface value if a borrower fails to meet its obligations, less the\nvalue of the defaulted debt. Microsoft has $36.8 billion and  Mountain View ,\nCalifornia-based Google has $30.1 billion.  Corporations will eventually have to use that cash amid\nshareholder demands to boost returns, reversing the improvement\nin their balance sheets, Oman said. Yields on new bonds fell to within 15 basis points, or 0.15\npercentage point, of existing securities on average last month,\naccording to data from JPMorgan Chase & Co., the biggest\nunderwriter of the debt. Spreads, Returns  The extra yield investors demand to own U.S. investment-\ngrade corporate debt narrowed 5 basis points from the end of\nJuly to 184 basis points on Sept. 17, Bank of America Merrill\nLynch index data show. A benchmark indicator of corporate credit risk in the U.S.\nfell for a second day. That\u2019s the lowest level since a new series of the index\nwith new maturities started trading Sept. 20. The measure\ntypically falls as investor confidence improves and rises as it\ndeteriorates. A\nbasis point equals $1,000 annually on a contract protecting $10\nmillion of debt. Which is actually too bad\nfor would-be buyers, because the new Note doesn\u2019t measure up to\nthe competition.  The tablet builds on Samsung\u2019s Galaxy Note 5.3, a similarly\nstylus-equipped smartphone that came out earlier this year and\nprovides a certain level of geeky fun on a five-inch screen.  Something about its size, and the fact that as a phone it\u2019s\nalways with you, seems to encourage a grab-and-go spontaneity\nthat\u2019s missing from the tablet version. The Galaxy Note 10.1\noffers a lot more screen, but a lot less fun.  Unlike its smaller cousin, the 10.1 is a Wi-Fi-only device.\nThere\u2019s no option to connect over a cellular network, as you can\nwith the phone or with the  AT&T (T)  or  Verizon (VZ)  Wireless versions of\nthe iPad. It starts at $500 for a model with 16 gigabytes of\nstorage, the same as a Wi-Fi iPad.  At 0.35 of an inch thick and 1.31 pounds, the Galaxy Note\nis a smidgen thinner and lighter than the iPad. But the way\nSamsung achieves its advantage is by making the tablet seem\nplasticky and cut-rate.  Not only can you actually feel the back flex when you push\non it, which raises some questions about its durability, but\nthere\u2019s even a visible distortion on the screen where your\nfinger is pressing. I\u2019ve never seen that on a tablet before.  Skimpy  The Galaxy Note also skimps on the screen, which is usually\namong the strongest selling points for any  Samsung (005930)  device. (Just\ncheck out the dazzling display on, say, Samsung\u2019s Galaxy S III\nsmartphones.)  The tablet\u2019s 1280 by 800 resolution means its picture is\nmade up of a little over a million pixels. That sounds like a\nlot -- until you realize that the Retina Display on the iPad\npacks more than three million pixels into a similar amount of\nreal estate.  There isn\u2019t anything hugely wrong with the screen: Movies\nand photos look all right. But in an area where Samsung products\nnormally excel, it\u2019s just pedestrian.  The Galaxy Note\u2019s most distinguishing characteristic is, of\ncourse, the stylus, which Samsung calls an S Pen. It hides so\nwell in a corner of the tablet that there\u2019s a sticker on the\nback to show you where to find it. Just keep close track of it:\nA replacement costs $40.  Pen Apps  Remove the pen, and a menu automatically pops up showing\nthe pre-loaded apps that take advantage of it. These include\nSamsung\u2019s S Note, which lets you draw pictures and offers some\niffy handwriting recognition, and  Adobe (ADBE) \u2019s Photoshop Touch\nediting software.  The Galaxy Note runs \u201cIce Cream Sandwich,\u201d the next-to-\nnewest version of  Google (GOOG) \u2019s operating system, on top of which\nSamsung has added its own interface and features.  Some of its tweaks are useful, like the ability to split\nthe screen to show some apps running side by side. I was able,\nfor instance, to display a  Microsoft (MSFT)  Word-compatible document in\nthe included Polaris Office app right next to the e-mail client,\nand drag content from one to the other.  Other Samsung-specific enhancements are more questionable,\nlike the extra software button added to the standard Android\nnavigation that snaps a screenshot. It\u2019s handy when you want to\ngrab a picture of a web page so you can annotate it with the\nstylus; you can also permanently capture that masterpiece you\ndoodled. But I sometimes found myself hitting it by accident\nwhen I was going for one of the neighboring, far-more-often-\nuseful Android controls.  Stereo Sound  The Galaxy Note has some nice touches. It has a pair of\nspeakers, as opposed to the single one on the iPad, and they\nfire forward rather than downward. The result is audio that, if\nit isn\u2019t very loud, is recognizably stereo and of better quality\nthan you\u2019ll find on many other tablets.  A microSD slot allows you to expand storage capacity.
