If enrollment in the online marketplaces repeats the pattern set in the Massachusetts exchange that was the model for Obamacare, the young people vital to the plan\u2019s financial stability are paying little attention to the federal website\u2019s mishaps as they wait for the March 31 deadline to sign up.  When Massachusetts started its health-insurance exchange in 2007, younger and healthier people were the most likely to procrastinate until the final weeks to obtain coverage. By November of that year, the last month to sign up to avoid a penalty, the portion of enrollees age 35 or younger had more than doubled to 36 percent from February, one analysis showed.  \u201cThe young and healthy are going to be the last to enroll,\u201d said Michael Perry, a partner at PerryUndem Research, which has done market analysis for Planned Parenthood and the Robert Wood Johnson Foundation on the new exchanges. \u201cWho knows, in February, when they\u2019ll probably start getting around to this, or March, what the story will be?\u201d  Critics of Obamacare, such as  Douglas Holtz-Eakin , the chief economic adviser to 2008 Republican presidential nominee  John McCain , question the comparison with Massachusetts, saying a relatively small portion of the state\u2019s population lacked insurance at the time, and the law was less politically charged.  Central Focus  Enrolling those under 35 has been the focus of the Obama administration\u2019s strategy on the online exchanges all year long. Buy-in from the young is essential to establishing a sound actuarial pool and keeping premiums affordable because the law bans discrimination against people with pre-existing conditions; otherwise those with chronic health problems could swamp the system and send rates soaring.  Related News: The program\u2019s rocky start was underscored last week when the government  said  that in the first month of enrollment about 106,000 people signed up for private insurance through Obamacare -- including only 26,794 for private plans through the federal website. The government had an early target of 800,000 sign-ups for the first two months, though it scaled back expectations as the online exchange was beset with software flaws.  The White House anticipates Obamacare enrollment patterns will follow the same trajectory as Massachusetts, said  David Simas , a deputy senior adviser to Obama who works on health policy. \u201cThe Massachusetts experience, both in terms of the initial levels of low enrollment as well as later engagement by younger folks, is the best road map,\u201d Simas said.  Healthy Waiting  In Massachusetts, healthy people of all ages waited longer to enroll than those with chronic medical conditions, according to the analysis of monthly applications by professors  Amitabh Chandra  of Harvard,  Jonathan Gruber  of the Massachusetts Institute of Technology and Robin McKnight of Wellesley College.  The portion of enrollees without chronic conditions rose from 64 percent in the first half of 2007 to 70 percent during the next five months and 76 percent in the months following the mandate\u2019s November deadline, according to a 2011 article by the three professors in the New England Journal of Medicine.  Monthly enrollments by healthy residents peaked at just over 6,000 during December, immediately after the deadline, according to  the article .  By 2011, 96 percent of Massachusetts residents had insurance, compared with 84 percent of the U.S. population, an  analysis  of census data by the Kaiser Family Foundation shows.  \u2018Be Patient\u2019  \u201cThe Massachusetts data teaches us to be patient,\u201d said Gruber, who advised the Obama administration on its health-care plan and was one of the architects of the Massachusetts law passed under then-Republican Governor  Mitt Romney . \u201cThe younger, healthier people were more motivated by the have-to than want-to and they came in later.\u201d  Holtz-Eakin sees limits to using the Massachusetts pattern to predict how people will respond to the exchanges under the Affordable Care Act, which has been the target of relentless Republican attacks since Obama signed it into law in March 2010.  In Massachusetts, the startup wasn\u2019t beset with the same technical difficulties, said Holtz-Eakin, now president of the American Action Forum, a policy research group.  And young, healthy people are a \u201ctough crowd\u201d to sell on the immediate value of health insurance, he said. \u201cAny bad news with this group has to concern you. As a going-in proposition, you have to be nervous about them showing up.\u201d  New Wrinkle  The initial open enrollment period also was longer in Massachusetts. While the Obama health-care plan has a six-month sign-up period for coverage in the first year ending March 31, Massachusetts opened enrollment in stages 15 months ahead of the coverage deadline.  One new wrinkle Obama added last week was his decision to allow private insurers to extend existing individual policies for up to a year even if they don\u2019t comply with the minimum standards required for insurance sold on the federal exchanges.  Karen Ignagni , president of America\u2019s Health Insurance Plans, an industry group, said the last-minute change might have a disproportionate impact on sign-ups by younger and healthier people. Unlike Obamacare plans, those policies can keep premiums lower by excluding people with health problems and covering fewer services.  \u201cIf now, fewer younger and healthier people choose to purchase coverage in the exchange, premiums will increase and there will be fewer choices for consumers,\u201d Ignagni said in an e-mailed statement.  Enrollment Shortfall  Earlier this year, the White House set a goal of getting 2.7 million 18- to 34-year-olds to sign up for insurance policies through the online exchanges, based on a  projection  by the Congressional Budget Office of a total enrollment of 7 million people in the first year.  More than a month after the start of  healthcare.gov , the federal website that handles insurance sign-ups in 36 states, workers on the front lines in the drive to enroll people say the site remains inconsistent, balky and crash-prone.  Jeffrey Zients , the former White House budget chief whom Obama appointed on Oct. 22 to help sort out the website problems, has said the site will work smoothly by the end of November.  Uninsured Americans have until March 31 to purchase policies to avoid penalties under Obamacare and until Dec. 15 to obtain insurance if they wish to begin coverage at the beginning of the year.  Website Fixes  If the administration can improve the website\u2019s performance in time, younger consumers will quickly look past the early glitches, said  Tim Bajarin , president of San Jose, California-based  Creative Strategies  who has followed consumer electronics startups for 35 years.  \u201cThe stories that there is a hiccup, these guys don\u2019t care,\u201d Bajarin said. \u201cThey know technology will get fixed. Their faith in technology is a lot greater than their parents\u2019 generation.\u201d  Apple Inc.  broke its quarterly sales record for smartphones in 2010 even after starting the period by acknowledging antenna problems with its iPhone 4 in an episode that  Steve Jobs  dubbed \u201cAntennagate,\u201d Bajarin said.  Microsoft Corp.  won a wide following for its Windows 95 and Windows XP operating systems after early flaws, he said.  A tangential impact of the website woes has been a temporary pullback in the Obama administration\u2019s efforts to market the online insurance exchanges, said  Dan Mendelson , chief executive officer of the Washington-based consultancy Avalere Health LLC. Because of the priority placed on signing up those younger than 35, the marketing campaign is disproportionately geared toward the young, he said. Their operating styles, however,\nare a study in contrasts.  At  Oracle Corp. (ORCL) , Ellison has stormed into new markets,\nmaking daring acquisitions and denouncing his competitors. At\n Microsoft Corp. (MSFT) , Ballmer has maintained a lofty cash balance\nwhile generally adopting a less strident view of his peers, at\nleast in public. Can this schism be explained entirely by\nstrategic differences between the two companies -- or are CEOs\u2019\npersonalities and life circumstances relevant, too?  Determinants of corporate investment have been studied for\ndecades. In economics, most such analyses assumed that company\ncharacteristics and circumstances play a dominant role, with\neverything else relegated to the background. There is growing\nevidence, though, that the personal characteristics of chief\nexecutive officers can be quite important. In a recent  paper , we\nhypothesized that CEOs\u2019 concern for social position may result\nin different attitudes toward risk, and thus affect their\ncompanies\u2019 investment policies.  Since their earliest days, humans have been concerned about\nrelative position. Your rank in relation to your peers has been\nimportant for, among other things, the choice of a mate. If\nrelative success determines ability to find a desirable mate, it\nmay explain some of the drive to outdo the competition even if\nyou have more money than you know how to spend. Such competition\ncreates a kind of tournament, raising your tolerance for taking\nlarge financial risks.  Daredevil Drivers  Indeed, evidence in psychology indicates that mating\nconcerns are important for risk-taking, at least among males.\nAuto insurers have long realized that single people behave more\naggressively, charging them higher premiums to compensate for\ngreater risk.  We were curious whether this behavior could be found in an\nenvironment where the stakes are high and consequences far-\nreaching. Do status concerns help explain CEO behavior? If\nmarriage market competition is indeed important, then single\nmanagers, who are presumably active in the market for mates,\nshould act more aggressively in hopes of making it really big.\nMarried ones should be more risk-averse.  We collected data on the marital histories of the CEOs of\n1,500 publicly traded companies, including Oracle\u2019s Ellison\n(currently single; married four times) and Microsoft\u2019s Ballmer\n(married since 1990). We found that companies whose CEOs are\nsingle invest substantially more than other companies, in\nparticular when it comes to investments subject to the greatest\nuncertainty, such as acquisitions or research and development.\nThese companies\u2019 stock returns are also substantially more\nvolatile, indicating that they are indeed exposed to greater\nrisk.  We tested our findings to make sure that we weren\u2019t just\nfinding greater appetites for risk among younger managers, who\nare less likely to be married, or at smaller companies, which\nare more volatile. We found this relationship between marital\nstatus and companies\u2019 risk-taking persists even after adjusting\nfor age and company size.  Beating the Market  Extending our analysis to mutual-fund managers, we find\nevidence that single managers take more idiosyncratic risk --\nthat is, attempt to beat the market more aggressively -- than\nmarried ones.  Of course, it is possible that getting married and starting\na family has a direct effect on lowering one\u2019s risk appetite.\nPerhaps people become more conservative simply because they are\nconcerned about not having enough money to provide for their\nspouse and children. But most CEOs have enough wealth to ensure\na comfortable life for their families even if their company goes\nbankrupt.  Does this mean corporate boards should require a new CEO to\nbe married to avoid excessive risk-taking? Not necessarily.\nAfter all, risk is in the nature of business, and without risk-\ntaking, innovation and economic growth are impossible. The key\nis to have the right person for the right job. A young company\nlooking for a big break might be well served by an ambitious\nyoung CEO looking to take the place of Ellison as the most\neligible bachelor on the Forbes 400 list.  Marital status obviously can\u2019t explain everything. Look at\nLehman Brothers Holdings Inc., which collapsed in spectacular\nfashion in 2008, even though its CEO,  Dick Fuld , famously\npromoted a  corporate culture  that prized successful marriages.\nEven so, the disparity between single and married leaders\ndeserves recognition as a hidden factor that can influence\ncorporate behavior and risk.  (Nikolai Roussanov and Pavel Savor are assistant professors\nof finance at the  University of Pennsylvania \u2019s Wharton School.) Burger King Worldwide Inc.\u2019s (BKW)  first foray into  France  failed, and it just returned in December after a 15-year absence. Dell\u2019s existing bonds don\u2019t have terms limiting total\nindebtedness at the Round Rock, Texas-based company, leaving\ncreditors vulnerable to new obligations that may rank senior to\ncurrent debt, according to research firm CreditSights Inc. As the World Economic Forum\u2019s annual meeting began today in\nSwitzerland and Federal Reserve policy makers convene in\nWashington, 48 percent of respondents predict the U.S. will be\namong the world\u2019s best-performing markets this year, according\nto the  quarterly poll  of 1,209 investors, analysts and traders\nwho are Bloomberg subscribers that was conducted Jan. 23-24.\nThat\u2019s the highest rating for the U.S. since the poll began in\n2009 and it\u2019s more than twice that of Brazil and China, the\nsecond-ranked markets.  The  U.S. economy  is improving in the eyes of half those\nsurveyed, compared with 18 percent who are positive about world\ngrowth. Investors have yet to embrace tentative gains in\nfighting  Europe \u2019s debt crisis, with 48 percent identifying the\neuro area as one of the worst to invest in and 67 percent\npredicting that any perceived improvement is temporary and the\ncrisis will deepen again.  \u201cThe difference between the U.S. and Europe is almost\nnight and day,\u201d said Paul Winghart, a poll respondent and\nsenior fixed-income strategist at RBC Wealth Management in\nMinneapolis, which oversees about $227 billion. \u201cWe have been\nrecommending that investors stay within the U.S.\u201d  Americans Optimistic  Americans were the most optimistic about their own markets,\nwith 62 percent citing it one of the best investment\nopportunities, up from 53 percent in December. Twenty-five\npercent of euro-area residents also picked the U.S., compared\nwith 40 percent who chose the EU. Almost half of U.S.\nrespondents said their economy was improving; 17 percent of\neuro-area residents said the same of their own.  The U.S. economy will grow 1.8 percent this year, while the\neuro-region will shrink 0.5 percent, the  International Monetary\nFund  said yesterday in an update of its World Economic Outlook.  That two-speed sentiment is reflected in what investors are\nbetting on in the next six months. Fifty-nine percent say they\nexpect the  Standard & Poor\u2019s 500  Index to be higher by the\nmiddle of the year and 32 percent say they intend to buy more\ndollars. By contrast, 43 percent predict the Euro Stoxx 50 Index\nwill be lower over the same timeframe and 9 percent plan to\nincrease their exposure to the euro.  Favoring Stocks  Investors increasingly favor stocks, with 46 percent\nsaying they will offer the highest return this year -- the most\nsince the poll began. Thirteen percent identify commodities as\nthe most attractive asset, with 12 percent choosing gold and 11\npercent preferring currencies.  Thirty-nine percent of respondents say bonds will offer the\nworst return and 9 percent say they are increasing holdings of\n U.S. Treasuries , with 46 percent predicting the yield on the 10-\nyear note will rise by mid-year. Just under half say they will\ncut their exposure to European sovereign debt.  Pluralities say the prices of gold and oil will both be\nhigher in the next six months as will the MSCI Asian Pacific\nIndex and the FTSE 100.  As investors become more confident, their \u201cmoney will\nenter the stock market,\u201d said Todd Cowle, a poll participant\nand managing partner at Ultimate Tier Advisors LLC in Plano,\nTexas, which manages about $100 million. \u201cWe\u2019re setting\nourselves up for a rally\u201d in the U.S. equity market, he said.  U.S. Outlook  Fifty percent of the respondents said the economy in the\nU.S. is improving, compared with 10 percent who said so in a\npoll in September. This confidence provides Fed Chairman  Ben S. Bernanke  and his colleagues with a reason to hold off on another\nround of stimulus when they conclude their two-day meeting\ntoday.  It also hands an election-year fillip to President Barack Obama.  \u201cNo, we will not go back to an economy weakened by\noutsourcing, bad debt, and phony financial profits,\u201d Obama said\nin the prepared text of his State of the Union address last\nnight. \u201cTonight, I want to speak about how we move forward, and\nlay out a blueprint for an economy that\u2019s built to last -- an\neconomy built on American manufacturing, American energy, skills\nfor American workers, and a renewal of American values.\u201d  Some 55 percent of those asked, nevertheless, say they are\npessimistic about Obama\u2019s policies.  Job Growth  Payrolls in the U.S. grew by 200,000 workers last month\nafter a gain of 100,000 in November, the Labor Department\u2019s\nreport showed on Jan. 6. The jobless rate unexpectedly declined\nto 8.5 percent, the lowest level since February 2009, from 8.7\npercent the prior month. An improving job market and freer\ncredit may underpin American consumer sentiment and spending\njust as the debt crisis in Europe prompts additional belt-\ntightening overseas.  Signs of U.S. renewal and the continued weakness in Europe\nmay set the tone for the five-day gathering of 2,600 business,\nfinancial and political leaders in the Swiss ski resort of\nDavos. Delegates include U.S. Treasury Secretary  Timothy F. Geithner , Microsoft Corp. co-founder  Bill Gates  and billionaire\ninvestor  George Soros .  \u201cWe are very bullish about the United States,\u201d Starwood\nHotels & Resorts Worldwide Inc. President Matthew Avril said in\nan interview in Davos today. \u201cEverybody recognizes that there\nare some challenges and difficulty in Europe that have to be\nworked through.\u201d  More Support  The U.S. may provide more support for slumping global\ngrowth as 37 percent conclude the world economy is deteriorating\nand the same amount share that view about  China , which helped\npower the recovery from the recent credit crisis. Still, 67\npercent say the world won\u2019t suffer a recession this year and 79\npercent predict the same of the U.S. The IMF sees global growth\nof 3.3 percent, with Chinese growth slowing to 8.2 percent.  Investors are less upbeat about the euro region even after\nits debt markets started the year showing signs of stabilizing.\nFor the first time, a majority -- 56 percent -- say one or more\nnations will leave the single currency in the next 12 months and\n6 percent say its economy is improving. Less than 30 percent say\nthe worst of the debt crisis is over.  Still, 81 percent say the currency bloc won\u2019t collapse this\nyear and 64 percent doubt the region\u2019s banks will suffer a\nmeltdown in 2012. Policy makers may also have succeeded in\nreducing the fear of default as the number of respondents\nanticipating sovereign bankruptcies in Portugal, Ireland, Italy\nand  Spain  all decline. So what do you get when you marry the two and put the\nresult on the best 4G network? The Galaxy Nexus, a superphone\nthat is still somehow a little less than the sum of its\nconsiderable parts.  The Galaxy Nexus, which costs $299 on a two-year contract\nfrom  Verizon Wireless , is the first device to ship with Android\n4.0, or in Google\u2019s dessert-based nomenclature, \u201cIce Cream\nSandwich.\u201d It is supposed to blend the separate cell-phone\n(\u201cFroyo,\u201d \u201cGingerbread\u201d) and tablet (\u201cHoneycomb\u201d) flavors\nof Android\u2019s operating systems.  The idea is to simplify things both for developers, who\notherwise have to worry that apps written for one version of\nAndroid won\u2019t run on another, and for consumers, giving them a\nsimilar experience no matter what kind of device they\u2019re using.\n Apple (AAPL) , not surprisingly, set the bar here with one operating\nsystem -- iOS -- running iPads, iPhones and iPod Touches.  Lard-Free  The Nexus phone is mercifully free from the proprietary\nuser interfaces and apps that manufacturers and carriers often\nlard atop Android. And Ice Cream Sandwich brings some welcome\nenhancements.  Physical buttons are out. In their place are on-screen\nback, home and recent-apps controls that rotate along with the\ndisplay when you turn the phone into portrait mode. You can also\ncreate folders of apps by stacking them one atop the other, and\n-- as on Honeycomb tablets -- summon thumbnail images of open\napps with the recent button. If you see one you don\u2019t need, a\nsideways finger flick dismisses it.  One major innovation isn\u2019t so successful: Face Unlock,\nwhich theoretically allows you to unlock your phone simply by\nholding it up to your face and letting it recognize you. It\u2019s a\nneat trick when it works, but I repeatedly got error messages\ntelling me I couldn\u2019t be recognized. Take it from me: Few things\nin technology are as depressing as being rejected by your own\nphone.  Insecure  Some users, meanwhile, have reported being able to fool the\nfeature by holding up a photo of themselves; even  Google (GOOG)  warns\nduring the set-up process that Face Unlock is less secure than\nother ways of protecting your phone.  As for the Galaxy Nexus hardware, it\u2019s handsome without\nbeing particularly distinctive. The nicest feature is the big\n4.65-inch screen that, typically for Samsung devices, is\nabsolutely gorgeous, with deep blacks and ultra-rich colors. My\nmain complaint was the automatic-brightness level, which is\nsupposed to adjust to ambient light but that I found\nconsistently too dim for my tastes. Eventually, I went into the\nsettings and disabled it.  Under the hood is a dual-core  Texas Instruments (TXN)  processor,\nplus a gigabyte of memory and 32 gigs of storage. There are also\n1.3-megapixel front and 5-megapixel rear-facing cameras, and it\nshoots video in full 1080p high-definition. The whole package is\nstill only a third of an inch thick and weighs about 4.8 ounces.  Power Outage  In the U.S., the Galaxy Nexus runs on  Verizon (VZ) \u2019s LTE 4G\nnetwork. LTE is the fastest network technology, and Verizon has\nthe broadest coverage. But there\u2019s a catch: LTE also gobbles\nbattery life. I\u2019ve generally found that Samsung does the best\njob among LTE handset-makers in managing power. But I\u2019d be\ntempted to take advantage of the fact that -- unlike iPhones --\nthe Galaxy Nexus\u2019s battery is user-replaceable, and carry a\nspare.  A version of the phone is also in the works for  Sprint (S) ,\nwhich will start rolling out LTE this year. A model with 16\ngigabytes of storage and using HSPA+ -- yet another network\ntechnology -- is available in other nations where LTE isn\u2019t\nwidespread. Carriers offering this version of the phone include\n Vodafone (VOD)  and  Telefonica (TEF) \u2019s O2.  Because of Google\u2019s open-to-all-manufacturers approach,\nit\u2019s hard for any Android phone to match the seamlessness of an\niPhone,  Research In Motion (RIM) \u2019s BlackBerry or even devices running\n Microsoft (MSFT) \u2019s Windows Phone 7. Perhaps that will change after\nGoogle takes control of handset-maker  Motorola Mobility\nHoldings (MMI) . Until then, the Galaxy Nexus comes closer than\nanything yet to providing the definitive Android experience.  ( Rich Jaroslovsky  is a Bloomberg News columnist. The\nopinions expressed are his own.) Chief Executive Officer Hubert Joly, who is known as a turnaround expert, seems finally to have staunched the bleeding that  I reported on last year : This time around, the results are surprisingly good: Gross margins expanded to 26.5 percent this year, beating estimates of 23.3 percent. So does that mean that the patient is back on the road to health? Not yet. At this point, Joly is simply better managing the decline. Same-store sales fell by 0.6 percent, and overall revenue was down 0.4 percent. This despite aggressive price moves by Joly, who set up a permanent price-matching policy in an attempt to win back sales from Amazon. The company expanded its profits by cutting costs. And in the long term, I just don\u2019t see how Best Buy can cut costs enough to stay competitive with Amazon. For one thing, Amazon isn\u2019t even trying to be really profitable; it plows everything back into warehouses, servers and other capacity-building investments. The company can now site and build a warehouse in under a year.  In some sense, Best Buy\u2019s big advantage is that it doesn\u2019t have to do this kind of investment; it already has all its \u201cwarehouses,\u201d aka stores, so it can return that money as profit to its shareholders. To be sure, the company is retooling to bring a more boutique feel to its stores -- specialty sections for prime manufacturers such as Microsoft, Apple and Samsung, high-end appliance and sound-system areas. But that\u2019s not nearly as big a cost as putting up a giant new building. Something like 90 percent of the U.S. population lives within a few minutes of a Best Buy. But at Best Buy\u2019s stage of life, all that investment is as likely to be a liability as an asset. As I noted in last year\u2019s piece, every retailer is ultimately undone the same way: Its real estate, once its greatest asset, becomes an expensive albatross. As sales fall, the company\u2019s cash flow is drained away by long-term mortgages or leases that cannot be shed without paying penalties that they don\u2019t have the cash for, which is, after all, why they need to shed the leases. Moreover, every dollar that Amazon invests makes Best Buy\u2019s real estate less valuable. It increases Amazon\u2019s economies of scale, or moves the warehouses closer to Best Buy\u2019s customers, cutting shipping times and costs and making them even more competitive against the big-box retailers. I went into reporting that piece looking for the way that the big boxes could restore their former glory, but I came away pretty pessimistic. Oh, Best Buy may survive -- but it will do so by shrinking, and upscaling. It cannot match Amazon on selection, and while it can match the prices, in the long run it\u2019s hard to see how it can make money doing so. Best Buy does offer instant gratification that Amazon can\u2019t match; on the other hand, I can\u2019t go to Best Buy in my pajamas. If Best Buy is going to survive, it will have to provide a service. The days of the commodity brick-and-mortar appliance and electronics retailers are numbered -- and in my opinion, the number isn\u2019t all that large. Ultimately, Joly\u2019s job is to keep the company alive while turning it into something else -- something with a value proposition that Amazon can\u2019t match. Early signs so far are as encouraging as they could be. But danger remains. To survive, he\u2019s being forced to cut costs deeply. This slash-and-burn approach may clear the way for a fruitful next stage. But there\u2019s always a risk, with these sorts of moves, that you will deeply damage the brands and the human capital that you need to carry you forward.","path":".\/2008_2012_msft_bloomberg_news\/best-buy-s-last-hurrah-.txt"},{"id":50939861,"title":"Hewlett-Packard Sales Slump Shows CEO Whitman\u2019s Challenge","released_at":"<date>August 23 2012<\/date> <time>14:16:33<\/time>","content":"Hewlett-Packard Co. Web users will be given the option to bar companies from\nsending them ad messages based on tracking of their previous\nonline searches, according to a  statement  today by the trade\ngroups led by the  American Association of Advertising Agencies \nand the  American Advertising Federation .  The industry initiative is based on guidelines recommended\nlast year by the U.S. Federal Trade Commission. The FTC\u2019s\nproposals stemmed from the agency\u2019s continuing inquiry into how\ncompanies tailor their advertising to individuals and whether\npractices based on consumer Web browsing intrude on privacy.  \u201cThe goal of the program is to make Internet advertising\nmore transparent and allow consumers to have a choice about the\nads they receive,\u201d said  Stuart Ingis , a partner at  Venable LLP \nin Washington, which is advising the groups, which include the\n Association of National Advertisers , the  Direct Marketing\nAssociation  and the  Interactive Advertising Bureau .  \u201cThe public votes every day with their clicks,\u201d Ingis\nsaid in an interview. \u201cThis program is to make sure that is\npreserved and can be expanded responsibly.\u201d  Coca-Cola, Microsoft  Members of the American Advertising Federation include\nProcter & Gamble, the world\u2019s largest consumer-product company,\nas well as  Coca-Cola Co.,  Microsoft Corp., and  American Airlines \nand advertising agencies such as Interpublic Group of Co.\u2019s\nMcCann Worldgroup and  WPP Plc \u2019s Young & Rubicam Inc., according\nto  the group\u2019s website .  The groups said they will promote widespread adoption of\nthe plan by businesses through a national education campaign.\nBeginning next year, the Council of Better Business Bureaus and\nthe Direct Marketing Association will enforce compliance among\nmember companies that choose to join the program. The Direct\nMarketing Association will also make participation mandatory\namong its members, according to the initiative.  Privacy advocates such as the Center for Digital Democracy,\nwhich criticized the FTC\u2019s recommendations last year as\nineffective, said today\u2019s industry proposal also fell short.  \u201cThis is too little too late and doesn\u2019t solve the\nproblem,\u201d  Jeff Chester , executive director of the Washington-\nbased group, said in an interview today. The initiative appears\n\u201ctimed to head off more comprehensive recommendations to be\nmade by the FTC in the upcoming weeks,\u201d Chester said.  The previous FTC recommendations  encourage  customer\ncontrol, transparency, data security and a limited period for\nkeeping the customer information.  Web Icon  Under the new trade-group program, an icon will be\ndisplayed near online advertisements and Web pages where\nconsumer data is collected and used for \u201cbehavioral\nadvertising,\u201d according to a statement released today.  Consumers will be able to click on the icon for information\nabout such practices and choose whether they want their data\nused to receive target ads.  Companies with more than $2 million in annual Internet\ninterest-based advertising will pay $5,000 to add the icon to\ntheir Internet ads, while those spending less can use the icon\nfor free, Ingis said. Participating in the opt-out page will\ncost $10,000 for larger companies and less for smaller firms, he\nsaid. The justices today said they will review a federal appeals\ncourt decision that approved a single suit to cover women who\nworked at the retailer\u2019s 4,400 Wal-Mart and Sam\u2019s Club stores\nsince 2001. Wal-Mart, facing billions of dollars in potential\nliability, contends the lower court made it too easy for workers\nwith different job histories to band together in a single case.  A decision throwing out the suit, the largest-ever U.S.\nemployment class action, might affect several pending cases. A\nsuit on behalf of more than 700 women against  Costco Wholesale\nCorp.  is on hold until the Supreme Court resolves the Wal-Mart\ncase. Tobacco companies including  Altria Group Inc.  say the Wal-\nMart case may affect their challenge to a Louisiana court order\nrequiring them to spend more than $270 million on a smoking\ncessation program.  The lower court ruling \u201cwould dramatically broaden the\ncircumstances where classes can be certified in all types of\ncases against all types of companies,\u201d Wal-Mart\u2019s lawyer,\n Theodore Boutrous , said in an interview.  Wal-Mart faults the lower courts for allowing a type of\nclass action generally used when plaintiffs are seeking an\ninjunction, rather than damages.  No Damage Estimate  Wal-Mart hasn\u2019t set funds aside to pay any damages in the\ncase, according to a regulatory filing released in September,\nand said it can\u2019t estimate what the amount would be. The\ncompany, the world\u2019s largest retailer and the largest U.S.\nprivate employer, had $15 billion in profit and more than $400\nbillion in sales over the past 12 months.  The Bentonville, Arkansas-based company fell 13 cents to\n$54.49 at 4 p.m. in trading on the New York Stock Exchange.  Wal-Mart is accused in the nine-year-old suit of paying\nwomen less than men for the same jobs and giving female workers\nfewer promotions. Six women are seeking to serve as class\nrepresentatives, including Betty Dukes, a Wal-Mart greeter in\nPittsburg, California.  Too Much Discretion  The women say that at the time the suit was filed Wal-\nMart\u2019s corporate policies gave local managers too much\ndiscretion over hiring and pay decisions. The result was a \u201ctap\non the shoulder\u201d system that let managers steer opportunities\ntoward their male colleagues, said  Joseph Sellers , who\nrepresents the women.  \u201cThere\u2019s a large body of social science research that\nshows, when left to their own devices, people tend to pick\npeople like themselves,\u201d Sellers said in an interview.  Wal-Mart says that any problems were isolated ones and that\nthe claims of women around the country would be too varied to\nproceed fairly as part of a single case. The workers in the\nclass come from 41 regions and 400 districts and carry 170\ndifferent job classifications, the company said in its appeal.  Wal-Mart says the case would be so unwieldy it would\nviolate the procedural rules that govern civil cases in federal\ncourt and the Constitution. The company argues that it should\nhave a chance to defend against the allegations on a case-by-\ncase basis.  1.5 Million Workers  A federal trial judge certified a class of as many as 1.5\nmillion past and current employees, saying that \u201crough justice\nis better than the alternative of having no remedy at all for\nany class member.\u201d  The San Francisco-based 9th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals,\non a 6-5 vote, upheld that ruling as to women who were working\nwhen the lawsuit was filed. The appeals court said the trial\njudge might be able to create an additional class for former\nemployees.  Writing for the 9th Circuit majority, Judge  Michael Daly Hawkins  said that a class action was better than \u201cclogging the\nfederal courts\u201d with individual suits. \u201cMere size does not\nrender a case unmanageable,\u201d Hawkins said.  In dissent, Judge  Sandra Ikuta  said, \u201cNever before has\nsuch a low bar been set for certifying such a gargantuan\nclass.\u201d  Nineteen companies, including  Bank of America Corp.  and\n Microsoft Corp. , urged the justices to take up the Wal-Mart\nappeal. They said the lower court opinion makes it too easy for\nworkers challenging employment practices to secure class-action\nstatus and then extract large settlements.  Corporate Policies  One of the companies,  DuPont Co. , said it weighed in \u201cto\nreinforce the important role that corporate policies and\nguidelines play in creating a workplace that embraces diversity\nat all levels.\u201d DuPont\u2019s chief executive officer,  Ellen Kullman , is the first woman to hold that role in the company\u2019s\n208-year history.  Wal-Mart said in a statement it was pleased the Supreme\nCourt granted review. \u201cThe current confusion in class-action\nlaw is harmful for everyone - employers, employees, businesses\nof all types and sizes and the civil justice system,\u201d the\ncompany said.  Sellers said the plaintiffs welcomed review. \u201cWe are\nconfident that the decision to certify the class was sound,\u201d he\nsaid in a statement.  The justices will hear arguments early next year, most\nlikely in March or April, and probably rule by July. The case\n\u201clikely will be the most important business case this term,\u201d\nsaid  Carter Phillips , a Washington lawyer who filed a brief\nbacking Wal-Mart on behalf of DRI, a defense-attorney group.  \u2018Might Be Huge\u2019  \u201cIf the court were to affirm, it would be an enormous\ndecision,\u201d Phillips said. \u201cIf it reverses, then it might be\nhuge or it might be relatively limited.\u201d  One issue in the case is a technical one involving the\nrules that govern lawsuits in federal court. The trial judge\ncertified the class action under Rule 23(b)(2) of the Federal\nRules of Civil Procedure. Classes certified under that provision\nare mandatory, meaning potential plaintiffs can\u2019t opt out of the\ncase or file their own suit.  Wal-Mart says workers should have had to meet the stricter\nstandards that normally apply to class actions seeking damages.  The justices also suggested they would consider broader\nissues, telling the two sides to discuss the prerequisites for\nany type of class action. (005930)  patent\nfor a way data is transmitted.  No president has overturned an ITC import ban since Ronald Reagan did it in 1987, in a case involving Samsung. Cupertino,\nCalifornia-based Apple is counting on Obama\u2019s increased interest\nin patent disputes to win another exception.  \u201cI would hope that if he decides to wade in, that he would\ndo so in a way that aims for more reasonable and coherent\nintellectual property policies to remove some of the\ngamesmanship,\u201d said Charles Golvin, an analyst with Forrester\nResearch. \u201cThat would be a lot more helpful than if it was seen\nas protecting a U.S. company versus a Korean one.\u201d  If no action is taken by the deadline, Apple would have to\nstop selling the affected devices on its website and its stores,\nand wouldn\u2019t be able to bring any new devices into the U.S.\nPhones and tablets already on store shelves for companies like\nAT&T Inc. or  Best Buy Co. (BBY)  could remain for sale.  The import ban applies to the iPhone 4 and iPad 2 3G models\ndesigned for networks run by AT&T, T-Mobile US Inc. and two\nregional carriers in Texas and  Alaska .  IPhone 4 models sold for other networks weren\u2019t impacted,\nnor were newer devices including the iPad mini and iPhone 5.\nApple counts on older iPhone models, often given away with a\ntwo-year contract, to entice people it hopes will become loyal\ncustomers.  Ecosystem Enticement  \u201cThey rely on some of the older models to feed the\necosystem and get people into the wonderful world of Apple,\u201d\nsaid  Will Stofega , program director at researcher IDC in\nFramingham,  Massachusetts . Not having that\nproduct to sell to those customers would be a big impediment.\u201d  Standard Patents  The Samsung patent is for a way data is transmitted over\ncommunications networks. It\u2019s a feature in a widely used\ntechnological standard established by a number of companies.  Companies that get together to establish industry standards\nhave the advantage of ensuring their inventions are included in\nthat standard so everyone uses them. In turn, they pledge to\nlicense any relevant patents on \u201cfair, reasonable and non-discriminatory\u201d terms.  Obama\u2019s administration in January sent the ITC proposed\nguidelines to consider before issuing import bans based on a\nfinding that standard-essential patents were infringed.  It said that while patent owners have the right to exclude\nothers from using their inventions, the public benefit of\nallowing that is limited when it comes to standards patents. The\nU.S. Federal Trade Commission filed a similar paper with the\nagency last year.  \u2018Unwilling Licensee\u2019  Four senators wrote to Froman on July 30, asking him to\n\u201cassess the substantial public interest considerations\u201d\nregarding the use of standard-essential patents at the ITC. The\nsenators were Democrats Amy Klobuchar of  Minnesota  and Barbara Boxer of  California , and Republicans Mike Lee of Utah and James Risch of  Idaho .  Apple and Microsoft Corp. have promised not to use any\npatents they have on industry standards to block competing\nproducts. Samsung and  Google Inc. (GOOG) , which owns Motorola Mobility\nand the Android operating system that\u2019s the most popular\nplatform for mobile phones, reserved the right to use them if\nthe other side is considered an \u201cunwilling licensee.\u201d  Samsung, based in Suwon, South Korea, said Apple has\nrefused to negotiate licensing terms, and overturning the trade\nagency\u2019s finding of infringement would \u201ccreate incentives for\nimplementers to unreasonably refuse to negotiate.\u201d  Samsung demanded 2.4 percent of Apple\u2019s iPhone and iPad\nrevenues, which would come to about $18 per phone -- a figure\nApple called unreasonable.  Global Outlier  Companies won\u2019t want to create new products that comply\nwith industry standards if they fear a patent owner demanding\nhigh royalties, Apple argued in its filing with the trade\nrepresentative. It said the ITC was an \u201coutlier internationally\nand domestically\u201d on the issue.  Samsung, which is under investigation by European\nregulators on allegations of patent misuse, agreed to not seek\nsales bans based on any of its standard-essential patents on\nthat continent. It made no such promise in the U.S. and defended\nits position, saying Apple refused to a licensing deal on any\nterms.  Two U.S. judges have said Google\u2019 Motorola Mobility unit\ncan\u2019t use standard-essential patents to seek bans of products.  One of those rulings, against Apple, is scheduled for\narguments at the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Federal Circuit\nin Washington on Sept. 11. The other involves a  Microsoft Corp. (MSFT) \nbreach-of-contract complaint against Google that\u2019s scheduled for\ntrial in  Seattle  later this month.  Apple can ask that court to put the current order on hold\nuntil the underlying infringement finding is reviewed. While the\nFederal Circuit doesn\u2019t often grant such requests, it might in\nthis case because of the case coming up in September, said\nRodney Sweetland, a patent lawyer with Duane Morris in\nWashington.  The Apple case against Samsung is In the Matter of\nElectronic Digital Media Devices, 337-796, and Samsung\u2019s case is\nIn the Matter of Electronic Devices, Including Wireless\nCommunication Devices, Portable Music and Data Processing\nDevices, and Tablet Computers, 337-794, both U.S. International\nTrade Commission (Washington). To contact the reporter on this story:\nBlanche Gatt in London at \n bgatt@bloomberg.net   To contact the editor responsible for this story:\nColin Keatinge at \n ckeatinge@bloomberg.net .","path":".\/2008_2012_msft_bloomberg_news\/nokia-s-ollila-says-board-expects-market-share-loss-ft-reports.txt"},{"id":69212670,"title":"Coke Gets Hacked And Doesn\u2019t Tell Anyone","released_at":"<date>November 4 2012<\/date> <time>23:01:00<\/time>","content":"FBI officials quietly approached executives at  Coca-Cola Co. (KO)  on March 15, 2009, with some startling news.  Hackers had broken into the company\u2019s computer systems and were pilfering sensitive files about its attempted $2.4 billion acquisition of  China Huiyuan Juice Group (1886) , according to three people familiar with the situation and an internal company document detailing the cyber intrusion. The Huiyuan deal, which collapsed three days later, would have been the largest foreign takeover of a Chinese company at the time.  Coca-Cola, the world\u2019s largest soft-drink maker, has never publicly disclosed the loss of the Huiyuan information, despite its potential effect on the deal. It is just one in a global barrage of corporate computer attacks kept secret from shareholders, regulators, employees -- and in some cases even from senior executives.  When hackers last year waged a large-scale attack on  BG Group Plc (BG\/) , raiding troves of sensitive data, the British energy company never made it public. Luxembourg-based steel maker ArcelorMittal also kept mum when intruders targeted, among others, its executive overseeing  China . As did  Chesapeake Energy Corp. (CHK) , after cyber attackers made off with files from its investment banking firm about natural gas leases that were up for sale.  Each of these cases was detailed to Bloomberg News either by people involved in remediating the situation or executives briefed on the details, who asked not to be identified because the information wasn\u2019t public; or in computer logs compiled by researchers monitoring the activities of hackers in China.  Concealing Breaches  Digital intruders are increasingly targeting information about high-stakes business deals -- from mergers and acquisitions to joint ventures to long-term supply agreements -- and companies routinely conceal these breaches from the public, say government officials and security companies.  Such thefts are tilting the playing field, putting compromised companies at a disadvantage in business negotiations and, in turn, leaving investors in the dark, they say.  \u201cInvestors have no idea what is happening today,\u201d says Jacob Olcott, a former cyber policy adviser to the U.S. Congress. \u201cCompanies currently provide little information about material events that occur on their networks.\u201d  In the U.S., the Securities and Exchange Commission last year  said  that companies are required to report any material losses from such attacks, and any information \u201ca reasonable investor would consider important to an investment decision.\u201d  Investors Care  \u201cWe don\u2019t credit the idea that no one would care,\u201d says Meredith Cross, director of the SEC\u2019s division of corporation finance. \u201cWe think reasonable investors could care depending on the specific facts and circumstances.\u201d  Yet no company has publicly disclosed the theft of sensitive deal-related information from a computer intrusion, says Olcott, a principal at  Good Harbor Consulting , an Arlington, Virginia-based company that provides security risk management services.  Many companies worry that such news could batter their reputation and stock price, according to more than a dozen information-security managers.  \u201cThey fear that bringing this to the public will do them more harm than good,\u201d says Michael Oberlaender, who has worked as the top information-security executive at companies in the U.S. and  Germany .  Little Known  A striking aspect of the wave of corporate hacking is how little is sometimes known about the information taken, much less who is taking it and how it\u2019s being used, say security researchers.  Without complete answers, it can be difficult for companies to attach a dollar figure to the losses. Most don\u2019t deem hacks to be a material event, which would require disclosure to shareholders, says Stewart Baker, a partner at Steptoe & Johnson LLP and former assistant secretary for policy at the Department of Homeland Security.  \u201cAll of the ambiguities stack the deck against disclosure,\u201d he says.  Despite the  estimated  $60 billion invested by corporations and governments in network security systems, hackers continue to circumvent them.  Chilling Account  The Coca-Cola report provides a rare and chilling account of the intricate and determined ways that hackers raided its files -- from pilfering internal e-mails to gaining the ability to access almost any  Microsoft (MSFT)  Windows server, work station or laptop on the network with full remote control.  Computer hackers made daily incursions through Coca-Cola networks over a period of at least one month, often using systems that were first compromised by infected e-mails sent to company executives. The messages were disguised to look authentic but actually contained malicious software, or malware, that gave intruders a pipeline into the company\u2019s networks, according to the report.  Once inside, the hackers struck quickly. In the first two days, they uploaded a dozen tools allowing them to steal e-mails and documents, installed a keystroke logger on the machine of a top executive in Hong Kong, and stole computer account passwords for other Coca-Cola employees, including those with administrative powers, to help them move freely across the company\u2019s network, according to the report.  Acquisition Demise  It is unclear whether the attack played a role in the demise of the Huiyuan acquisition.  Coca-Cola spokesman  Kent Landers  said the company wouldn\u2019t discuss \u201csecurity matters,\u201d but in a statement said it \u201cmanages security risks in conjunction with the appropriate security and law enforcement organizations around the world.\u201d  \u201cWe make disclosures in our public filings when we believe they are appropriate and in accordance with the requirements of the federal securities laws,\u201d he added.  Jenny Shearer, a spokeswoman for the  Federal Bureau of Investigation  in  Washington , declined to comment.  Like many other corporate cyberattacks, it appears that hackers in China were behind the Coca-Cola breach.  While the internal Coke report says the intruders were state-sponsored, its details, including the types of malware and techniques used, suggest they are part of Comment group, one of the most prolific hacking groups based in China, according to  AlienVault , a San Mateo, California-based security firm.  China Hackers  \u201cIt\u2019s very clear that Comment is behind it,\u201d says Jaime Blasco, head of AlienVault\u2019s security lab.  Comment has extensive reach, Bloomberg News  reported  in July, having penetrated computer networks from the European Union Council to powerful Washington law firms to workers at a U.S. nuclear power plant.  Companies doing business in China or competing against Chinese rivals should expect hackers will go after their most confidential files, says James Lewis, a senior fellow who studies cybersecurity at the Center for Strategic and International Studies in Washington.  \u201cThis has been a part of their plan to catch up to the West,\u201d Lewis says. \u201cYou steal their technology, you steal their business secrets.\u201d  The theft of deal-related information has become widespread even as it remains mostly secret, so much so that U.K. Foreign Secretary William Hague said in a  speech  in October that it has the potential to affect the trajectory of the global economy.  \u2018Devastating Impact\u2019  \u201cIf these attacks are left unchecked, they could have a devastating impact on the future earning potential of many major companies and the economic well-being of countries,\u201d Hague said.  The Chinese Foreign Ministry said accusations that China engaged in broad hacking efforts are unfair \u201cwithout concrete evidence and investigation.\u201d  \u201cChina is also a major victim of cyberattacks,\u201d ministry spokesman Hong Lei said at a press briefing last week. \u201cWe hope to engage in active and practical international cooperation so as to jointly ensure Internet security.\u201d  China\u2019s Ministry of Commerce didn\u2019t respond to a request for comment.  Many companies tightly restrict knowledge of computer breaches to a select handful of staffers and swear consultants to confidentiality, requiring them to destroy documents and erase hard drives upon finishing their work, according to the more than dozen information-security managers.  Massive Breach  Take, for instance, an intrusion last year at  BG Group  that has never been disclosed to shareholders. The company, which posted $21 billion in revenue in 2011, discovered a breach in its computer networks described as massive by four people knowledgeable about it, with vast quantities of data taken.  The hack targeted information such as geological maps and drilling records, as well as far-flung data from the company\u2019s worldwide network going back at least a year, that could impact sensitive deals, according to one of the people who worked on cleaning up the intrusion.  Despite the scope of the breach, it was kept under wraps inside the company, according to three of the people. Most of the company\u2019s information-technology staff weren\u2019t told about the intrusion, according to one of the people, who described how colleagues at adjacent desks had no clue anything was wrong.  Risk Factor  Since the end of 2010, Reading, U.K.-based BG Group has included for investors a one-sentence risk factor in its regulatory filings: \u201cInformation security breaches may also result in the loss of BG Group\u2019s commercially sensitive data.\u201d  BG Group spokesman Mark Todd said he wouldn\u2019t respond to \u201crumor and speculation, or upon media stories based on anonymous sources.\u201d  The company \u201chas robust security measures across its business to protect its information technology,\u201d he said in an e-mailed statement. \u201cBG Group fully complies with all relevant market disclosure guidelines and regulatory requirements. When we have something material to announce, we do so via the established disclosure channels.\u201d  Companies listed on the  London  Stock Exchange are under rules, similar to those in the U.S., to disclose to investors anything that will have a material impact on the company\u2019s financial situation, says Chris Hamilton, a spokesman for the  Financial Services Authority , the U.K. financial watchdog.  800 Million Pounds  In one case, officials estimated the cost of lost data from a British company while concealing the firm\u2019s identity from the public. Jonathan Evans, head of Britain\u2019s MI5 domestic security service, said in a  speech  in June that digital intruders targeting a \u201cmajor London listed company\u201d had caused a loss of 800 million pounds ($1.3 billion), in part because of the resulting disadvantage in \u201ccontractual negotiations.\u201d  Investor advocates are trying to prod companies into publicly disclosing the breaches, even if they can\u2019t estimate their cost. If information worth a few million dollars is compromised, the same security weaknesses could be exploited to steal data worth hundreds of millions of dollars, says Michael Connor, executive director of  Open MIC , a New York-based non- profit that focuses on media policies and supports shareholder activists.  \u201cThe extreme reaction of not talking about it at all seems to me not very productive, particularly if you have whole industries that are being attacked,\u201d says Connor.  Targeting Outsiders  To gain access to confidential deal information, hackers often target links in a chain of outside organizations that handle such information on the company\u2019s behalf, such as banks and law firms. China-based cyberthieves, for instance, hacked into the computer networks of seven law firms in 2010 to get more information about BHP Billiton Ltd.\u2019s ultimately unsuccessful $40 billion bid to acquire Canadian company Potash Corp. of Saskatchewan, Inc., Bloomberg  reported  in January.  Intruders took a similar approach last year in a breach that ultimately targeted Chesapeake Energy, the second-largest U.S. natural gas producer, according to a person familiar with the situation and computer logs viewed by Bloomberg News. The logs indicate that Comment group obtained information about Chesapeake\u2019s efforts to sell natural-gas leases by hacking into an office of  Jefferies Group Inc. (JEF) , which is  advising  on the sales.  At just after noon on Sept. 22, 2011, the logs show, hackers gained access to the computer system of Kyle Guidry, an investment banker in Houston who handles energy deals for New York-based Jefferies. The intruders rooted around in Guidry\u2019s system for about three hours, departing at 3:17 p.m. local time. Among the files they took were those titled \u201cCHK Mississippian,\u201d \u201cCHK Utica JV Utica,\u201d \u201cSinopec CA - Executed.docx\u201d and \u201cGeneral - China SHG\\deals\\STA.\u201d  Chesapeake Files  Chesapeake, whose ticker on the  New York  Stock Exchange is CHK, was in the midst of selling stakes in the Utica shale deposit in  Ohio  at the time, and is still trying to find buyers for assets in the Mississippi Lime in Kansas and  Oklahoma .  Neither Chesapeake nor Jefferies disclosed the hack to shareholders.  Chinese energy companies have been on an energy buying spree in the U.S. and  Canada . Fu Chengyu, chairman of China Petroleum & Chemical Corp., or Sinopec, said in May the company has held talks with Chesapeake and others about shale investments.  Lv Dapeng, a Sinopec spokesman, didn\u2019t respond to phone calls seeking comment.  A Chesapeake spokesman, Jim Gipson, didn\u2019t reply to requests for comment. The company hasn\u2019t publicly disclosed any loss of deal information, nor does it list data breaches as a risk-factor in SEC filings.  \u2018High Priority\u2019  \u201cInformation security is a high priority at Jefferies and we make all appropriate effort to safeguard client information,\u201d says Richard Khaleel, a spokesman for Jefferies.  Kyle Guidry declined to comment.  In its most recent annual report, Jefferies warned investors of a hypothetical risk: \u201cOur computer systems, software and networks may be vulnerable to unauthorized access, computer viruses or other malicious code,\u201d which could jeopardize clients\u2019 confidential information.  Records show that cyber intruders also have managed to penetrate the computers of top dealmakers.  In July 2011, Comment group rifled through the computer networks of  ArcelorMittal (MT) , according to computer logs compiled by researchers tracking the hackers.  Hacking ArcelorMittal  Among their targets: Sudhir Maheshwari, the executive in charge of corporate finance, and mergers and acquisitions for the world\u2019s largest steel maker.  The logs show Comment intruders broke into Maheshwari\u2019s computer on July 14, 2011, at 12:08 p.m. Eastern Standard Time. Once inside, they searched through a folder called \u201cChina.\u201d After examining a draft version of a PowerPoint presentation Maheshwari gave at a JPMorgan Chase & Co. conference in Beijing the month before, the hackers zipped up, encrypted and downloaded all the PowerPoints, the logs show.  The intruders then bundled up his e-mail messages from June 22 to July 14, 2011. A security researcher who analyzed the logs says he assumes that the e-mails were downloaded, though the log files don\u2019t confirm that. He requested anonymity because he was discussing confidential material.  While confirming that a breach occurred last year on Maheshwari\u2019s laptop, Giles Read, an ArcelorMittal spokesman, says an internal investigation found it was not a widespread compromise of the computer networks and the company believes a firewall prevented documents from being removed. In addition, it conducted a review of the targeted e-mails and documents and determined that none of them contained highly sensitive information, Read says.  Damage Risk  ArcelorMittal , which trades in Amsterdam, has never publicly disclosed a serious breach of its computer networks. In February, the steelmaker began referencing the possibility of such a threat in its regulatory filings. The warning wasn\u2019t instigated by any particular breach, Read says.  \u201cAn increasing number of companies, including ArcelorMittal, have recently experienced intrusion attempts or even breaches of their information technology security,\u201d says the annual report. Such an incident could allow hackers to \u201cmisappropriate confidential information, cause interruptions in the company\u2019s operations, damage its computers or otherwise damage its reputation,\u201d it says.  Hacker Prowess  Hackers showed similar prowess in penetrating the networks of Coca-Cola.  In 2008, shareholders of Huiyuan, the biggest fruit and vegetable juice company in China, hired Goldman Sachs to find a buyer for the company. After months of due diligence, Atlanta- based Coca-Cola made the highest offer at $2.4 billion. The deal was publicly  announced  on Sept. 3, 2008, pending approval from China\u2019s Ministry of Commerce.  Two weeks later, Paul Etchells, then the deputy president of Coca-Cola\u2019s Pacific Group, met with U.S. officials from the American Embassy in Beijing and expressed confidence that the deal would clear China\u2019s internal antitrust review, according to a U.S. State Department  cable  published by Wikileaks.  Over the next six months, Coca-Cola supplied written information to China\u2019s Ministry of Commerce on 12 occasions and interacted a further 18 times with China\u2019s regulators, according to another State Department  cable  released by  Wikileaks .  Sensitive Information  Amid this review, the company learned that its computer systems had been breached and sensitive deal information taken from the computer account of Etchells on March 3, 2009, according to the internal report on the attack.  The investigation traced the breach back to an e-mail that appeared in Etchells\u2019s in-box on Feb. 16, 2009, according to the report.  The message contained the subject line \u201cSave power is save money! (from CEO)\u201d and appeared to come from the work e-mail account of Bernhard Goepelt, at the time a legal executive in the company\u2019s Pacific Group and today, senior vice president and general counsel.  Coca-Cola\u2019s brass had been striving to meet company-wide energy reduction targets. The body of the e-mail contained a link to a file that purported to contain a message from the chief executive officer.  When Etchells clicked on the link, malware was surreptitiously loaded onto his machine, giving hackers full access to Etchells\u2019s computer via the Internet, according to the internal report. They installed a keystroke logger, which captured everything the executive typed.  Adobe Vulnerability  Once in control of the computer, the hackers installed various other programs, gaining access to the company\u2019s corporate network and using Etchells\u2019s machine as a staging point to store and download data taken from other computers.  Etchells, who left Coca-Cola in 2010, didn\u2019t reply to requests for an interview.  Shortly after Etchells\u2019s computer was compromised, hackers targeted other Coca-Cola executives in the region. On March 13, 2009, a disguised malicious e-mail was sent to Brenda Lee, a public affairs executive in China. The message appeared to be a media advisory from the Beijing office of the World Bank. When Lee opened the attached PDF file, however, malware exploited a vulnerability in  Adobe (ADBE)  Reader software and gave hackers access to her machine, according to the report.  Hackers installed a keystroke logger and sought out e-mails related to the Huiyuan deal, forwarding them to a Gmail account whose owner couldn\u2019t be identified, the report said.  Deal Rejected  Lee, who left Coca-Cola in 2011, declined to comment. Coca-Cola issued a statement that day saying it respected the Ministry\u2019s decision and wouldn\u2019t appeal. (CMCSA)  and\nMcAfee Inc., now part of  Intel Corp. (INTC) , as well as Google Chief\nExecutive Officer  Eric Schmidt , have written letters in support\nof legislation.  Those companies have now become silent in the wake of the\nleaks on whether they still support it. Delaying action leaves\nthe rules unclear about what data can be shared and whether the\ncompanies can be sued by customers for providing data to the\ngovernment.  Google, based in  Mountain View , California, was among the\nInternet companies said to be providing data for the Internet\ncommunications monitoring effort, known as Prism. The company\nhas asked the surveillance court for permission to disclose\nintelligence agencies\u2019 requests for user data.  Prior to Snowden\u2019s leaks, lawmakers and officials from\nPresident  Barack Obama \u2019s administration were calling with\nincreasing urgency for legislation to defend banks, utilities\nand telecommunication networks from potentially devastating\ncomputer attacks.  \u201cThis has become a radioactive fallout zone for a while in\nterms of new legislation,\u201d said Stewart Baker, former general\ncounsel for the NSA, in an interview.  House Measure  The House in April passed a bill, H.R. 624, that would\nshield companies from lawsuits for sharing information about\nhackers with each other and the government, and authorize\ncorporations to receive classified data from U.S. intelligence\nagencies about threats.  Companies had been asking the Senate, which hasn\u2019t\nintroduced a bill this year, to follow the House.  Sena Fitzmaurice, spokeswoman for Philadelphia-based\nComcast, declined to comment about whether the company still\nsupports the House bill. Verizon spokesman Edward McFadden\ndidn\u2019t respond to phone calls and e-mails for comment.  Michigan Democrat  Carl Levin , chairman of the Senate Armed\nServices Committee, said passing a cybersecurity measure has\nbecome more difficult in the Senate.  \u201cPeople\u2019s demand for transparency has definitely\nincreased,\u201d said  Jan Schakowsky , of Illinois, the top Democrat\non the House Intelligence Oversight and Investigations\nsubcommittee.  NSA Role  Senator  Dianne Feinstein , a California Democrat and\nchairwoman of the Senate Intelligence Committee, said she plans\nto introduce similar legislation to the House bill, though\nwouldn\u2019t say when.  Feinstein is reviewing whether companies should be allowed\nto directly share information about online attacks with the NSA\nor be required to interact with a civilian agency, like the\nHomeland Security Department.  Legislation is needed \u201cto ensure that voluntary\ninformation sharing is lawful,\u201d Feinstein said an e-mailed\nstatement. She said it should include liability for companies\nand privacy protections for citizens.  McCaul said his bill will require companies to share data\nwith Homeland Security. Last year, Senate Republicans blocked\ncybersecurity legislation in part because of objections that the\ndepartment would be the contact point for data sharing and\nsetting the rules.  \u201cPeople get spooked by the fact that the NSA has housed\neverybody\u2019s phone records,\u201d he said.  Information Sharing  The scope of information companies are sharing with the\ngovernment under the spy programs isn\u2019t clear, said Michelle\nRichardson, legislative counsel for the  American Civil Liberties\nUnion  in Washington.  The ACLU has opposed cybersecurity legislation on grounds\nthat citizens\u2019 personal information might not be protected if\nturned over to the government as part of sharing data on cyber\nthreats. Richardson questioned whether a new law is needed given\nthe amount of data already being exchanged.  The government can order telecommunications and Internet\ncompanies to provide data related to national security\ninvestigations under sections of the Patriot Act and Foreign\nIntelligence Surveillance Act. The companies are given legal\nprotections for doing so.  In some cases, data is used to defend  computer networks \nfrom hacking attacks, according to the  Office of the Director of\nNational Intelligence . These communications have \u201cprovided\nsignificant and unique intelligence regarding potential cyber\nthreats to the  United States  including specific potential\ncomputer network attacks,\u201d the office said  June 8 .  Lumped Together  Frank Shaw , a spokesman for Redmond, Washington-based\n Microsoft Corp. (MSFT) , and Michael Fey, McAfee\u2019s worldwide chief\ntechnology officer, said their companies also voluntarily\nprovide intelligence agencies additional data on threats to\ncomputer networks.  It\u2019s wrong to lump together the type of information being\nshared under the spy programs with what would fall under a\ncybersecurity bill, said  Michael Chertoff , Homeland Security\nsecretary under President  George W. Bush .  \u201cThey\u2019re completely different things and they shouldn\u2019t be\nconfused, although inevitably they will be,\u201d Chertoff said in\nan interview.  \u201cWhat you\u2019re looking for in cyber is information about\nwhat\u2019s in the packets moving across the Internet and the\nmalicious code,\u201d said Chertoff, who founded a security\nconsulting company in Washington. \u201cThe collection of phone data\ndoesn\u2019t help you with cyber. The other stuff only looks at\nforeign communications.\u201d  Legislation to defend computer networks would enable\nautomated sharing about new hacking attacks and involve more\ncompanies than are covered under the spy programs, such as\nutilities, Chertoff said. (MSFT) \u2019s next leader, just boosted his chances by helping orchestrate the $7.2 billion deal that makes him a senior executive at the software maker he once helped run.  The 49-year-old Canadian, who has been chief executive officer at  Nokia Oyj (NOK1V)  for three years, will move back to Microsoft as it buys the Finnish company\u2019s mobile-phone unit. The one-time head of the software maker\u2019s business division returns with experience competing head-on in mobile devices against  Apple Inc. (AAPL)  and  Google Inc. (GOOG)   Microsoft needs a leader to help it add market share in smartphones, tablets and search as CEO  Steve Ballmer  prepares to step down. While Elop did little at Nokia to erode Apple and Google\u2019s lead, he was a loyal Microsoft partner who negotiated the agreement that landed Windows on millions of phones.  \u201cElop is on the short list of possible CEO candidates,\u201d said Sami Sarkamies, an analyst at Nordea Bank AB in Helsinki. \u201cHe has the right experience from working both inside and outside the company.\u201d  Elop nonetheless has detractors who decry his failure to make Nokia profitable, and its shares have declined by half on his watch. Ballmer, one of Microsoft\u2019s largest owners with about 4 percent of its outstanding shares, declined to say yesterday whether Elop is a candidate to succeed him as CEO.  No Shoo-In  \u201cGiven the performance of Nokia under Elop\u2019s stewardship, getting the CEO job would seem a pretty big reward,\u201d said Charles Golvin, an analyst at Forrester Research Inc. in Cambridge,  Massachusetts . \u201cFrom a financial perspective, it wasn\u2019t a stellar performance.\u201d  Microsoft, based in Redmond,  Washington , has said it will consider internal and external candidates to replace Ballmer. If Microsoft brings in a leader from outside, analysts have suggested candidates including  EBay Inc. (EBAY)  CEO John Donahoe and Sheryl Sandberg,  Facebook Inc. (FB) \u2019s chief operating Officer.  Microsoft and Espoo, Finland-based Nokia have had a close relationship through Elop, who was in charge of Microsoft\u2019s Office products and helped lead the division\u2019s cooperation with its Finnish handset partner. He left the software maker in September 2010 to take the top job at Nokia.  Burning Platform  At Nokia, Elop took over as the mobile-phone pioneer\u2019s market-share losses to the iPhone and Google\u2019s Android devices threatened to accelerate. At the time, he likened Nokia\u2019s position to a person standing on a burning oil platform on the verge of being engulfed in flames, facing the option of staying aboard or jumping to the ocean to have a chance to survive.  In February 2011, Elop struck a deal with Ballmer to switch Nokia\u2019s smartphones from its own Symbian operating system to Windows Phone. In exchange, Microsoft paid more than $1 billion to Nokia for marketing and development of products on Windows.  Before his careers at Microsoft and Nokia, Elop ran Macromedia Inc., focusing on Flash Internet software and helping to arrange the company\u2019s $3.4 billion sale to  Adobe Systems Inc. (ADBE)  in 2005.  During his year as COO at  Juniper Networks Inc. (JNPR) , he oversaw reorganizations that helped expand profit margins and boost sales, closing the gap with networking leader  Cisco Systems Inc. (CSCO)  Then, days before Juniper was to name him CEO in 2008 -- the press release had already been written -- Elop quit to join Microsoft.  Nokia Outsider  At Nokia, Elop became the first non-Finn to run the company and challenged its slower-moving, consensus-driven culture. He took over from a 30-year Nokia veteran.  Elop\u2019s effort to transform Nokia\u2019s handset business hasn\u2019t led to an earnings recovery, with the company losing more than 5 billion euros ($6.6 billion) in nine quarters. Even as sales of the Lumia smartphone brand -- introduced under Elop -- have started to rise, Nokia has made scant market-share gain against Google\u2019s Android and Apple\u2019s iPhone.  Among the victories Elop can claim: In the first quarter, on the strength of Lumia, Microsoft beat out  BlackBerry (BBRY)  as the third-largest smartphone operating system, according to a  Gartner Inc. report . Elop has also helped attract new application developers through Lumia\u2019s nascent sales gains.  Lumia Brand  The Lumia brand will follow Elop to Microsoft, which also will license the Nokia brand for 10 years to be used in cheaper, more basic phones. That means Elop gets to work with many of the same partners and customers he knows from Nokia.  \u201cWe can invest more resources into the effort, and we can build on the momentum that has already been established,\u201d Elop said yesterday on Ballmer\u2019s conference call with analysts.  Elop also has experience overhauling a major corporation. He has cut tens of thousands of jobs in a bid to revive Nokia after the company fell outside the top five in smartphone rankings and became unprofitable.  After the sale to Microsoft, Nokia\u2019s biggest business will be a network-equipment division that competes with  Ericsson AB (ERICB) , Alcatel-Lucent SA and China\u2019s Huawei Technologies Co.  Microsoft\u2019s  profit  in the latest quarter missed analysts\u2019 projections by the most in at least a decade as the Windows business shrank. Poor sales of the Surface tablet computer led to an inventory writedown of $900 million, more than the $853 million in Surface sales in the latest fiscal year.  Stocks Languish  Neither Elop nor Ballmer has been a boon to his company\u2019s shares.  Nokia stock  has dropped by half since Elop was hired on Sept. 10, 2010, even with yesterday\u2019s 34 percent gain to 3.79 euros in Helsinki. The stock added 0.5 percent today. Microsoft declined 2.2 percent to $31.20 at the close in New York, and the stock is down more than percent since Ballmer  became CEO  in 2000.  To revive Microsoft\u2019s mobile business, Elop will face the same challenge he faced at Nokia: getting more consumers to give Windows devices a chance.
