At least the authors of the five-word summary above --\nmembers of the AFL\u2019s knife-sharpening union -- could say they\nspent 1910 crafting a decent pun.  A century later the idea of a dull work-year is quaint\nverging on incomprehensible.  Global trade connects the fate of every industry and\nlaborer, no matter how small or seemingly self-sufficient, to\nthe decisions of bureaucrats in China, shipbuilders in Korea,\nand bankers everywhere. It\u2019s hard to have a quiet year in the\nshop when the shop has no borders.  Even the structure of a year seems enlarged and more\ncomplex. The depth of our interconnectedness, the constancy of\nmedia, means that themes and moods tend to hang around past\ntheir season.  By the admittedly squishy metrics of pessimism and\ndisruption, 2010 feels as if it started a long time ago.  Maybe that\u2019s because we\u2019re still breathing the fumes\nof 2008. Lehman Brothers\u2019 collapse 27 months ago brought on more\nthan just a teetering economy: It created a cloud that has\nsettled over many Western economies and, in 2010, wrought a kind\nof seasonal affective disorder on their citizens.  Fact Disconnect  In a Bloomberg poll conducted in October, two out of three\nlikely voters in the Nov.\u00a02 midterms said that taxes had gone\nup, the economy had shrunk, and the billions lent to banks as\npart of the Troubled Asset Relief Program would never be\nrecovered. A September poll showed that 77\u00a0percent of global\ninvestors expected the European monetary union would crumble and\nat least one struggling government would default, all despite a\n$1\u00a0trillion euro zone backstop.  What\u2019s revealing about these responses is the chasm\nbetween feelings and facts.  Congress and the Obama Administration have cut taxes by\n$240\u00a0billion since 2009. Growth continued without interruption\nin 2010 in the U.S. and most major economies. The Treasury\nexpects to turn a $16\u00a0billion profit on the TARP rescue. Greece\nand Ireland may have stared into the white light of fiscal\ndeath, but they were yanked back to earth by their neighbors and\nare now trying to rehabilitate (with wounded fury, but -- so far\nat least -- without default).  By the end of the third quarter, U.S. nonfinancial\ncorporations were sitting on a record $436 billion in cash.\nThrough Dec. 14, the  Standard & Poor\u2019s 500 Index  was up\n11\u00a0percent for the year. And Wall Street was racking up its\nfourth-largest profit ever, a projected $19 billion for the\nyear, according to the New York State Comptroller\u2019s office.  Jobs, Houses  So if things aren\u2019t nearly as bad as they seem, why do\nthey seem so bad? Jobs and houses have a lot to do with it.  In the U.S., 17\u00a0percent of the workforce either couldn\u2019t\nfind employment or was surviving on part-time jobs. Their\ncollective frustration and scrimping are contagious. Despite\ninterest rates so low they would shock previous generations, the\n housing market  has all the bustle of a Pompeii bazaar; there\nwere 202,000 new homes on the market at the end of October, the\nfewest since June 1968.  Mix in an unrelenting  foreclosure  crisis, in which the\ncenturies-old concept of title was thrown into doubt by faulty\nrecord-keeping, and it\u2019s easy to understand why so many people\nfeel like they\u2019ve lost a degree of control over their lives:\nThey have.  How Quaint  The notion that trusted institutions can restore our sense\nof security is as quaint as that 1910 yearbook. Governments\ncan\u2019t stop leaks -- of oil or information -- let alone regulate\nbehavior. Passage of the Dodd-Frank financial bill in July may\nhave constrained investment banks by putting limits on\nproprietary trading, but as  Michael Lewis  wrote for this news\nservice: \u201cWhat\u2019s really striking is how little ability the\noutside world retains to find out what is going on inside these\nplaces -- even after we have learned that what we don\u2019t know\nabout them can kill us.\u201d  The Tea Party, which resists meaning as ferociously as it\nresists  Ben Bernanke , makes sense when seen as an exercise in\nfist-shaking. Two years after hope and change, it fumed at such\neconomic abstractions as quantitative easing and bending the\ncurve and asked a simple question: Why can\u2019t we have our country\nback?  Long Gone  Here\u2019s the thing: That America has been gone for years.\nCheap labor and plentiful resources combined with ease of travel\nand communication have given emerging markets more than just a\nplace at the table.  In 2010, the U.S. added 937,000 jobs; Foxconn, the Taiwan-\nbased maker of nearly every consumer electronic product you\u2019ve\never wanted, added 300,000.  Fueled by gold, copper and coal, the most robust currency\nof the year against the dollar was the Mongolian tugrik.  In India, competition for deals has become so intense that\nbillionaire  Ravi Ruia  is branching out to Africa -- buying coal\nmines in Mozambique and part of a Kenyan oil refinery.  Competition is one of the pleasures of business and one of\nthe foundations of America. That right hasn\u2019t been rescinded --\nit\u2019s been extended to people around the world. In a way, we\u2019ve\nwon. Now the game starts again.  Capitalism lives off of change. The new challenge is to\nshake off the trauma of a decade that started with the ultimate\nloss of control and get to work on winning the new century.  From Here to Infinity  There\u2019s a lesson to be found in the two most-talked-about\ncompanies of the year.  On May 26, Apple blew past Microsoft to become the second-\nmost-valuable company in the world (it\u2019s currently No. 3)\nlargely by selling beautiful devices that let you control a\nuniverse with a swipe.  Google, which began the decade offering a pathway to\ninfinity, now fights to keep its employees from defecting to\nFacebook, which chops infinity into an endless series of cul-de-\nsacs. Apple and Facebook figured out something about the\nconsumer psyche -- then they innovated to fill the need with\nastonishing results.  Bloomberg Businessweek\u2019s year-end issue published this week\ntakes some inspiration from that approach.  It tries to take all the contradictions and complexity of\n2010 and make sense of them. Grouping the year into chapters\nentitled Normal, Jobs, Spills, Stuck, Currency, and Gaga, we try\nto show all the ways in which diverse stories link up, sometimes\nin linear fashion, sometimes with unexpected leaps -- such as\nthe price of gasoline, measured in bacon.  Like 2010, the magazine we think is full of surprises. One\nthing\u2019s for sure: It ain\u2019t dull.  ( Josh Tyrangiel  is editor of Bloomberg Businessweek. A\nversion of this column appears in the Dec. 20 issue available on\nnewsstands today. The opinions expressed are his own.) Among the 100 non-financial companies with the most cash\nand marketable securities, 31 that disclose funds parked in\nforeign units have sold $103 billion of dollar-denominated bonds\nsince the start of 2012, according to data compiled by\nBloomberg. Cupertino, California-based Apple, which issued a\nrecord $17 billion of bonds on April 30, leads borrowers from\n Microsoft Corp. (MSFT)  to  Nike Inc. (NKE)  paying an average of 2.38 percent\nannually to borrow for about 12 years.  Raising domestic funds with debt instead of repatriating\nnon-U.S. holdings allows companies to exploit both record-low\nyields and tax-deductible interest payments while also avoiding\na government levy of as much as 35 percent on the cash.\n Washington \u2019s tax code has failed to keep up with the digital age\nby making it too costly to bring money home, Cook said last week\nin congressional testimony. Of the iPhone maker\u2019s $145 billion\nof cash, 70 percent is held overseas.  Boost Leverage  \u201cThere\u2019s this giant arbitrage game going on,\u201d Edward Kleinbard, a tax law professor at the University of Southern\nCalifornia, said in a telephone interview from Los Angeles. By\nissuing dollar debt, \u201cfirms are leaving their worldwide\ninterest expense in the United States, where they\u2019re deducting\nthat interest against their highest-taxed income in the world,\nand getting cash to fund dividends or stock buybacks,\u201d he said.  Global demand for information-technology multinationals has\nleft the businesses with at least $340 billion abroad, the most\nof any industry, Bloomberg data show. The companies have issued\nabout $40 billion of bonds since the beginning of last year.  Conditions are ripe for technology borrowers to boost\nleverage to fuel equity returns that have underperformed the\nbroader market, Barclays Plc analysts including Danish Agboatwala wrote in a May 16 report. The gauge widens\nwhen investors seek the perceived safety of government\nsecurities and narrows when they favor assets such as corporate\nbonds. Trade Secrets\/Industrial Espionage  Obama to Increase Diplomatic Pressure Against Trade-Secret Theft  The U.S. will put diplomatic pressure on countries\nimplicated in thefts of  trade secrets  and seek stronger\ninternational enforcement of intellectual-property protections,\naccording to a government report released yesterday.  President  Barack Obama \u2019s administration pledged to share\nmore intelligence with companies about the countries involved in\neconomic espionage and methods used to steal corporate\ninformation, and to study the need for stronger U.S. laws\nagainst trade-secret theft.  It comes a day after the computer-security firm Mandiant\nCorp. said in a report that the Chinese army is probably the\nsource of hacking attacks against at least 141 companies\nworldwide since 2006.  The trade-secret strategy looks at more than computer-based\ntheft. It says the pace of economic espionage is accelerating\nthrough recruitment of current and former employees of\ncompanies, as well as cyber intrusions against U.S. businesses,\nlaw firms, universities and financial institutions.  While it doesn\u2019t single out China, yesterday\u2019s report cites\nexamples of economic espionage in which corporate secrets were\npassed to Chinese institutions.  \u201cTrade secret theft threatens American businesses,\nundermines national security, and places the security of the\n U.S. economy  in jeopardy,\u201d the document says. \u201cThese acts also\ndiminish U.S. export prospects around the globe and put American\njobs at risk.\u201d  The administration will intensify efforts to apply\ndiplomatic pressure on countries \u201cwhere there are regular\nincidents of trade secret theft\u201d and press them to strengthen\nenforcement action, according to the strategy document. In trade\nnegotiations, the U.S. will seek agreements for other countries\nto provide protections for corporate secrets similar to those in\nU.S. law.  The Director of National Intelligence will oversee\nincreased sharing of U.S. intelligence on trade-secret theft\nwith the private sector, including information on foreign\ngovernments involved in espionage and the types of technology\ntargeted, the document says.  The administration will promote voluntary industry best\npractices on protecting intellectual property, and the  Federal\nBureau  of Investigation is expanding efforts to fight computer\nintrusions involving trade-secret theft, according to the\nadministration\u2019s strategy.  The separate cybersecurity report released yesterday said\ncomputer intrusions from China, mainly directed at U.S.\ncompanies, were carried out by a group that is \u201clikely\ngovernment sponsored\u201d and is similar \u201cin its mission,\ncapabilities, and resources\u201d to a unit of the  People\u2019s\nLiberation Army .  A spokesman for China\u2019s Foreign Ministry, Hong Lei, denied\nany military involvement and said his department is opposed to\ncomputer hacking and has been a victim of attacks itself. (MSFT)  Chief Executive Officer  Steve Ballmer  isn\u2019t letting his departure plans stand in the way of a complete overhaul of the software-centric strategy he spent decades putting in place.  Even after saying last month he will retire from Microsoft within the next year, Ballmer is accelerating the company\u2019s move into hardware with a $7.2 billion deal to buy  Nokia Oyj (NOK1V) \u2019s handset unit yesterday. That\u2019s an area the Redmond, Washington-based company waded into in the past 18 months, including last year\u2019s introduction of the Surface tablet.  Now the company, which built a dominant position in personal-computing operating systems by focusing on software and relying on multiple partners to offer hardware, is diving into its own smartphone line, a low-end handset business and manufacturing operations. With rivals like  Apple Inc. (AAPL)  and  Google Inc. (GOOG)  leading in mobile, Microsoft executives said the company had few options except to break from its software past.  \u201cWe were in software exclusively and that was a logical thing to do for a long period of time, but the reality today is that\u2019s no longer possible,\u201d Microsoft Chief Financial Officer Amy Hood said in an interview.  Ballmer had no choice, said  Carolina Milanesi , an analyst at Gartner Inc. Even combined with Nokia, Microsoft has less than a 4 percent share in smartphones and is running out of time to carve out a piece of a market ruled by Google\u2019s Android and Apple\u2019s iOS.  Urgent Change  \u201cThere must be a sense of urgency that Microsoft feels about how much longer it will take them to make it in mobile and they need to make it in mobile,\u201d Milanesi said. \u201cThere is a sense that they have to move faster than they have been and the only way they can do that is by integrating the hardware and software.\u201d  Within Microsoft\u2019s headquarters, Ballmer realized last year that the company needed to dump its traditional playbook and make its own phones, said a person familiar with the matter.  At the time, Microsoft\u2019s Windows Phones were still at a percentage in the low single digits. It became clear that the company couldn\u2019t gain on competitors or turn phones into a significant moneymaker if Microsoft only made the operating system, said the person, who asked not to be identified because the talks were private.  Six Weeks  Soon Ballmer was on the phone with Nokia Chairman  Risto Siilasmaa , resulting in a meeting in February at the  Mobile World Congress  show, said the person. Various forms of a deal were rejected by both boards and talks seemed dead in June before being revived about six weeks ago, the person said.  Peter Wootton, a spokesman for Microsoft, declined to comment on specifics of the talks.  With the deal, Microsoft becomes the last major developer of smartphone operating systems to get into phone hardware. Apple makes its own handsets that use its iOS operating system. Google acquired Motorola Mobility last year for about $12.4 billion, giving the company its own lineup of phones.  \u201cPhones are the most personal of the personal devices people use today and success in phones is important for success in tablets and PCs,\u201d  Brad Smith , Microsoft\u2019s general counsel, said in an interview. \u201cWe need to move faster.\u201d  Ballmer helped Microsoft co-founder  Bill Gates  formulate much of the strategy that led the company to dominate PC operating systems in the 1990s. As Microsoft\u2019s first business manager, Ballmer negotiated some of the company\u2019s initial deals to put its software on partners\u2019 computers.  Strategy Shift  The formula: focus on software that supports a multitude of devices, give customers choice, hone in on the part of the market that has very high margins and leave the low-margin hardware to others.  Microsoft has developed Xbox game consoles since 2001 and took that on because partners weren\u2019t interested. Elsewhere it hewed to the strategy -- it avoided making its own music player, for example, until it was too late to catch Apple\u2019s iPod.  Microsoft has increasingly deviated from the formula in recent months. In October 2012, it started selling the Surface tablet. That same month, Ballmer wrote a shareholder letter announcing a new strategy focused on devices and services. In July, he instituted the biggest reorganization in more than a decade to align divisions around his vision.  \u201cIt\u2019s a big transformation, but that\u2019s kind of what you need to do in the technology world to move forward,\u201d Ballmer told  Tom Keene  on Bloomberg Television\u2019s \u201cThe Pulse.\u201d  Trickier Partnerships  Microsoft isn\u2019t completely changing its stripes, and it will still license its Windows Phone software to other handset makers. Yet that will be trickier because Microsoft now has to reassure hardware partners that it isn\u2019t putting Nokia devices ahead of their products.  Terry Myerson, head of Microsoft\u2019s operating systems, this week authored a blog post claiming the deal would benefit all Windows Phone partners. He ended with a lyric from the  rock band  The Killers: \u201cI don\u2019t shine if you don\u2019t shine.\u201d  The move to devices and services means a change for Microsoft\u2019s margins. Internet-based services and hardware are costlier to deliver than software, and margins will decline, Hood said. Microsoft will still be able to increase revenue and profit by selling more, even at a lower margin, she said.  Shareholder Reaction  For phones specifically, Microsoft\u2019s traditional strategy of working with equipment manufacturers wasn\u2019t very profitable, Hood said. The phone unit had to fork over more than $1 billion to Nokia as part of a 2011 deal that got the Finnish phone maker to use the software. Hood said the Windows Phone business will end up with higher operating income once Nokia is integrated than it had without the hardware business.  Neither the prospective margins nor Microsoft\u2019s further entrenchment in consumer hardware thrilled shareholders, some of whom favor a focus on  business software . The company\u2019s shares fell 4.6 percent yesterday to close at $31.88.  This is \u201cnot good for investors that were hoping the company would narrow their focus to the enterprise,\u201d said Pat Becker Jr., a  fund manager  at  Portland , Oregon-based Becker Capital Management Inc., which oversees $2.6 billion including Microsoft shares. \u201cWhy not let the next CEO make this call?\u201d  The deal is also serving to jolt investors who read Ballmer\u2019s retirement as a sign Microsoft would reverse course on its devices strategy.  \u201cAnyone who thought that would be put on hold while a new CEO was sought has to accept that now,\u201d said Tony Ursillo, an analyst at Loomis Sayles & Co. in  Boston . They negotiate which will handle major antitrust\ninvestigations, with the decision often turning on their\nrespective expertise in an industry. Delaware Needs a Fifth Federal Judge, U.S. Judicial Panel Says  Delaware, home to courts that specialize in business cases\nand a popular venue for patent cases, needs a fifth federal\njudge to help the district court keep up with increasing\ncorporate litigation, a panel of judges concluded.  If the recommendation by a subcommittee of the Judicial\nConference of the U.S. is accepted in March, Congress will be\nasked to create a position as the number of U.S. patent suits is\nrising.  \u201cIt makes sense to add capacity for dealing with this\nsituation, which most of us expect to persist,\u201d Frank\nScherkenbach, a patent attorney whose clients included  Microsoft\nCorp. (MSFT) , said in an e-mail. \u201cIt makes sense to add that capacity\nin one of the courts most affected by these recent trends.\u201d  Delaware handles more patent cases per judge than any of\nthe other 93 federal districts, with 179 cases filed for each of\nthe four judges from September 2011 to June 2012, according to\nthe Judicial Conference. During the same period, all types of\ncases climbed in the state, putting the load at 1,077 cases per\njudge, second-highest in the U.S.  The subcommittee met in December and issued a memorandum\noutlining its recommendation earlier this month.  Business costs rose more than fourfold since 2005 over\nroyalty demands filed by patent owners seeking quick profits,\naccording to a study by Boston University School of Law.  Companies face $29 billion in expenses from 5,842 claims of\ninfringement filed in 2011 by so-called non-practicing entities,\npatent owners collecting license fees instead of making\nproducts. That\u2019s up from 1,401 claims and $6.6 billion in costs\nin 2005, according to the study, published in June.  The court in Delaware was considered the second-most\nfavorable to patent owners from 1995 to 2011, based on a 42\npercent success rate and a median damage award of $20.6 million,\naccording to an October 2011 report by PricewaterhouseCoopers\nLLP. The Eastern District of  Virginia , which also is considered\nthe fastest for getting cases to trial, ranked first.  Delaware is tied with New Jersey courts for the busiest\nwhen it comes to litigation over generic drugs, according to\nPriceWaterHouseCoopers.  It also vies with the Eastern District of  Texas  as the\nbusiest courthouse when it comes to new patent-infringement\nfilings, according to an April 2012 study by James Pistorino, a\nlawyer with Seattle-based Perkins Coie LLP.  Congress  last created  a federal judgeship in Delaware in\n1984. Senate confirmation is required to fill a post, and there\nare currently 85 judicial vacancies and 33 nominees awaiting\napproval. Zuru President Nick\nMowbray, who started the toy company with his brother in New\nZealand eight years ago, said the engineer worked on the\ntechnology in his home for 13 years and left Innovation First\nafter being rebuffed three times over two years in efforts to\nbuild a robotic fish.  \u201cThey realize they made the wrong move by not licensing\nthis technology,\u201d Mowbray said. \u201cThey can\u2019t make it work, so\nput out press releases saying that we copied them.\u201d  To contact the reporter on this story:\nVictoria Slind-Flor in Oakland, California, at   vslindflor@bloomberg.net .  To contact the editor responsible for this story:\nMichael Hytha at   mhytha@bloomberg.net .","path":".\/2008_2012_msft_bloomberg_news\/cascades-apple-megaupload-hexbug-intellectual-property.txt"},{"id":4002398,"title":"Business Looks to Republicans to Block Obama on Rules, Taxes","released_at":"<date>November 3 2010<\/date> <time>19:44:49<\/time>","content":"The Republican victories in Congress\nmean U.S. companies from  Goldman Sachs Group Inc . to  WellPoint\nInc . may be able to weaken or block what they consider President\n Barack Obama \u2019s anti-business policies on health care, the\nenvironment, taxes and financial reform.  Republicans retook the House of Representatives yesterday\nwith a gain of at least 60 seats, their biggest increase since\n1938. The party will use its first majority in the House since\n2006 to try to eliminate funding for parts of Obama\u2019s health\ncare bill opposed by business as well as curb regulations and\ngovernment spending,  Jay Timmons , executive vice president of\nthe  National Association of Manufacturers , a Washington-based\nlobbying group, said in an interview before the election.  \u201cAmericans voted for jobs and economic growth\u201d and\n\u201cresoundingly rejected\u201d Democrats\u2019 policies on taxes and\nregulation,  Thomas Donohue , president of the  U.S. Chamber of\nCommerce , the biggest business lobbying group, said in a\nstatement last night.  Republicans also scored a net gain of at least six seats in\nthe Senate, though Democrats retained control of that body.  The results will bolster Republican efforts to extend Bush-\nera tax cuts for those earning more than $250,000 and to defeat\nObama\u2019s proposals to increase taxes on companies\u2019 overseas\nprofits.  Stabilizing Taxes  \u201cWhen you have 9.6 percent  unemployment  it\u2019s not the time\nto be raising taxes,\u201d  John Engler , NAM\u2019s president and the\nformer Republican governor of Michigan, told reporters today.  On health care, they are \u201creally going to be pushing back\non the regulations,\u201d said  Kim Monk , managing director at the\ninvestment advisory firm  Capital Alpha Partners LLC  in\nWashington. \u201cThere could be some serious blowback from a\nRepublican Congress.\u201d  Republicans also are likely to use their new leadership of\nHouse committees to tie up administration officials in hearings\nto explain and delay proposed rules on pesticides, ozone\nstandards and mining, said  Kenneth Green , resident scholar at\nthe American Enterprise Institute in Washington, a group\ncritical of Environmental Protection Agency regulations.  The efforts may backfire, especially if Republicans carry\nout threats to subpoena members of the Obama administration and\nif their push to cut spending results in a government shutdown,\nsaid  Jack Pitney , a political science professor at Claremont\nMcKenna College in Claremont, California.  Harder Line  \u201cThere will be a large number of new members who will\npress for a harder line,\u201d Pitney said. \u201cBut the new members\nare like gasoline: they provide the fuel for the party but they\nare also very combustible and can provoke explosions.\u201d  More-ambitious goals sought by some lawmakers and\nbusinesses, such as completely overturning Obama\u2019s health-care\noverhaul, probably will remain out of reach for Republicans\nbecause of the Democratic majority in the Senate and Obama\u2019s\nveto power.  High-profile objectives, such as repealing the health-care\nmeasure, won\u2019t progress past \u201csymbolic, messaging votes,\u201d said\n Bruce Josten , the top lobbyist for the U.S. Chamber.  The Washington-based Chamber, which led the fight against\nObama on health care and financial regulation and budgeted a\nrecord $75 million promoting pro-business candidates, says it\nhopes the acrimony of the election campaign can be put aside and\nRepublicans can work with Obama to cut the deficit, promote\nnuclear power and energy efficiency, and pass long-stalled free\ntrade agreements.  Bipartisan Potential  Other items may gain support from both the administration\nand Congress, such as scaling back business taxes imposed by the\nhealth-care bill, providing highway funding, creating renewable-\nenergy standards and boosting nuclear power, he said.  \u201cThere is a potential here for some bipartisan movement,\u201d\nJosten said.  The results of the election are positive for companies in\npharmaceuticals, air-freight and financial services as well as\nrestaurants, according to a report today by Thomas Lee, chief\nequity analyst at  JPMorgan Chase  & Co. in New York. Alternative-\nenergy stocks such as  First Solar Inc . and  EnergySolutions Inc .\nmay take a hit because the election makes less likely added\ngovernment subsidies or legislation that would drive renewable-\nenergy demand, Lee wrote in his report.  Bank of America Corp.,  Visa Inc ., Pfizer Inc.,  FedEx Corp .\nand  Duke Energy Corp . are among 23 stocks Lee predicts may gain\nbecause a Republican victory means less pressure on them in\nWashington.  Credit Expansion  \u201cWe could start to see credit expansion next year as a\nresult of extension of the Bush-era tax cuts,\u201d Lee said on a\nconference call today. \u201cThis all argues for the markets to hit\n1,300 by year end.\u201d  The Standard & Poor\u2019s 500 Index, which closed at the\nhighest level since May 3 yesterday, rose 0.12 percent to\n1195.52 at 3:01 p.m. New York time today.  \u201cThe Republican victory in the House means there will be\nan absolute halt to the Obama agenda,\u201d Tom Block, founder of\nTom Block Consults and the former head of government relations\nfor JP Morgan, said on the call organized by Lee.  Following are assessments of what the new Congress means\nfor selected industries and issues.  FINANCE  The election will put Republicans in charge of the House\nFinancial Services Committee that Massachusetts Democrat  Barney Frank  has headed since 2007. A Wall Street critic, Frank and\nSenator  Christopher Dodd , a Connecticut Democrat who is\nretiring, wrote the law aimed at reining in abuses that they say\ncontributed to the financial crisis. The legislation represents\nthe biggest overhaul of financial regulations in more than seven\ndecades.  Republicans\u2019 new power gives them the ability to shape more\nthan 240 rules that may be needed to implement the Dodd-Frank\nlaw, including regulations establishing the direction and\nindependence of the new Consumer Financial Protection Bureau.\nRulemaking by the Commodity Futures Trading Commission and other\nagencies on bank capital standards, derivatives and proprietary\ntrading also will draw increased scrutiny.  \u201cWe don\u2019t want them to regulate capriciously, arbitrarily,\nwithout engaging in a cost-benefit analysis,\u201d Representative\n Jeb Hensarling , a Texas Republican on the financial services\npanel, said in an interview.  The regulatory oversight and ability to weaken rules may\nbenefit banks including Goldman Sachs,  JPMorgan  and  Bank of\nAmerica , all of which lobbied against elements of the Dodd-Frank\nlaw, saying they would hurt profits.  On housing, Republicans including Hensarling say they want\na free-market approach that would phase out federal support for\nFannie Mae and Freddie Mac, the mortgage companies taken over by\nthe government after their losses soared.  A legislative stalemate may be fine with financial\ncompanies as well as investors, said  Alison Williams , a\nBloomberg Research analyst. \u201cIn general, investors just want\ngridlock so the government will be less of a threat,\u201d she said.  HEALTH CARE  House and Senate Republicans have written at least  30 bills \nthat would roll back provisions of the health-care overhaul\nObama signed into law in March.  Such efforts may help WellPoint and rival health insurers\nescape regulations on how much they spend on patient care and\nlet  Boston Scientific Corp . and other medical-device makers\ndodge $20 billion in tax increases over the next decade.  \u201cYou can literally open the bill and point your finger to\na page and say, \u2018Here\u2019s something we should go after,\u2019\u201d said\nRepresentative  Michael C. Burgess  of Texas, a Republican who\nserves on the House Energy and Commerce health subcommittee.\n\u201cIt\u2019s all bad.\u201d  The Republicans\u2019 push will force Democrats to vote on\nwhether to defend the most controversial parts of the law, such\nas requiring insurance for all Americans, said  Tom Scully , the\nformer chief of the Medicare program under President  George W. Bush .  Republicans also want to go after a requirement that\nbusinesses of all sizes report to the Internal Revenue Service\nany expenditures of more than $600, and they probably will\ntarget the budgets of agencies that are implementing the law.  The split Congress ensures there won\u2019t be an outright\nrepeal of the law that Republicans such as Representative  John Boehner , who is in position to become the new speaker of the\nHouse, have called for, Scully said.  \u201cVery little will happen in the next two years, but it\nwill be a big political battle,\u201d said Scully, senior counsel at\nthe Washington office of Alston & Bird LLP.  DEFENSE  House Republicans have pledged to cut $100 billion in\ndomestic discretionary spending, the outlays set by Congress on\na yearly basis that aren\u2019t mandated by law.  Don\u2019t look for them to take the ax to defense spending very\nsoon, though.  Wary of the growing military might of China, Republicans\nare likely to be more aggressive in spending in ways that\nrespond to that country\u2019s capabilities in naval warfare,\nballistic missiles and air power, even if the overall U.S.\ndefense budget doesn\u2019t increase.  \u201cWe have to look at the totality\u201d of China\u2019s efforts,\nsaid Representative  Randy Forbes , a Virginia Republican who may\nbecome head of the House Armed Services Committee\u2019s readiness\nsubcommittee. Once lawmakers focus on the emerging challenges,\nthey will agree on the need for \u201creadiness capability,\u201d he\nsaid.  That would entail devoting more money to weapons programs\nbenefiting contractors making sea-based, anti-missile systems,\nsuch as  Lockheed Martin Corp.  and  Raytheon Co. , said  Loren Thompson , defense analyst with the Lexington Institute in\nArlington, Virginia.  Also standing to gain are ship- and submarine-makers\n Northrop Grumman Corp.  and  General Dynamics Corp ., said  James McAleese , a consultant to defense companies.  New Republican House defense leaders will also try to\nprotect military contractors in lawmakers\u2019 districts, Thompson\nsaid.  Representative  Howard McKeon , a California Republican, is\nlikely to become chairman of the Armed Services Committee.  Bill Young , a Florida Republican, may head the panel of the\nAppropriations committee that approves defense spending.  Northrop Grumman was the top defense contractor in McKeon\u2019s\nCalifornia district with contracts worth $1.01 billion in 2009,\naccording to data compiled by Bloomberg. Lockheed was second\nwith $253.2 million.  General Dynamics was the largest defense contractor in\nYoung\u2019s Florida district, receiving $286.2 million, followed by\nRaytheon\u2019s $221.8 million.  ENERGY  On energy policy, the first order of business for\nRepublicans will be to block the Environmental Protection\nAgency\u2019s plan to limit carbon emissions.  Congressional Democrats from coal-producing states have\njoined Republicans in seeking to stop or postpone EPA regulation\nof carbon emitted by power plants and factories. EPA\nAdministrator  Lisa Jackson  has said Obama \u201cwould veto any\nattempt to take away authority here.\u201d  The failure to pass his cap-and-trade measure, which would\nreduce carbon emissions and create a market in pollution\nallowances, may force Obama to take smaller steps to reshape\nU.S. energy policy. \u201cWe may end up having to do it in chunks,\nas opposed to some sort of comprehensive omnibus legislation,\u201d\nthe president said in an  interview  published in the Oct. 15\nissue of Rolling Stone magazine.  Efforts to reach a compromise on energy legislation may\nfocus on enacting national requirements for the use of non-\npolluting renewable energy.  Electricity producers such as  NRG Energy Inc.  may benefit\nas Republicans push to include nuclear power in such a standard\nalong with the wind turbines and solar panels favored by\nenvironmentalists, said  David Crane , chief executive officer of\nPrinceton, New Jersey-based NRG.  TRANSPORTATION  Airlines such as  United Continental Holdings Inc.  and  Delta\nAir Lines Inc.  may gain from the shift in congressional power\nbecause Republicans oppose proposals to limit the outsourcing of\nmaintenance work abroad and to subject global airline alliances\nto antitrust regulation.  House-approved legislation to finance the Federal Aviation\nAdministration, still pending, would require drug testing and\nadditional inspections at overseas maintenance centers used by\nU.S. carriers, potentially raising costs and making outsourcing\nless attractive to the airlines.  The legislation also would restrict global airline\nalliances by ending their exemption from antitrust prosecution\nafter three years. Carriers such as  AMR Corp. \u2019s American\nAirlines and  British Airways Plc , and Delta and  Air France-KLM ,\nuse alliances to act as single entities in setting prices and\nschedules on international routes.  \u201cThe current Congress has been anti-airline,\u201d  William Swelbar , a research engineer specializing in air transport at\nthe Massachusetts Institute of Technology in Cambridge,\nMassachusetts, said in an interview. \u201cThere will be a new set\nof ears to listen to the industry.\u201d  The shift in House lawmakers shaping transportation policy\nmay benefit FedEx, operator of the world\u2019s largest cargo\nairline, by ending Democratic efforts to ease union organizing\nat the company\u2019s Express unit.  Rival  United Parcel Service Inc.  and the Teamsters Union\nbacked the provision sponsored by Democratic Representative\n James Oberstar  of Minnesota, chairman of the  Transportation and\nInfrastructure Committee , who was defeated in yesterday\u2019s\nelection.  Automakers such as  Toyota Motor Corp.  of Toyota City,\nJapan, which recalled 8 million vehicles in the past year, may\nface less scrutiny with the House Energy and Commerce Committee\nlikely to be led by  Fred Upton , a Michigan Republican, said\n Michael Stanton , president of the Association of International\nAutomobile Manufacturers, a trade group based in Arlington,\nVirginia. The current committee chairman is Democratic\nRepresentative  Henry Waxman  of California, who led hearings into\nToyota\u2019s handling of the recalls.  TRADE  Republican control of the House may provide the best chance\nto pass free-trade agreements with South Korea, Colombia and\nPanama since they were approved by President Bush in 2007. Obama\nhas shied away from pushing the deals in Congress as drafted\namid high unemployment and opposition from some fellow Democrats\nand labor unions.  \u201cThis is one area where Republicans and Democrats can work\ntogether,\u201d said  William Lane , government relations director for\n Caterpillar Inc ., the world\u2019s biggest construction-equipment\nmaker, which favors free trade.  For companies such as Caterpillar, UPS,  Boeing Co . and\n Citigroup Inc ., getting the agreements passed would broaden\naccess to markets abroad, with the South Korean deal alone\nboosting U.S. exports by $10.9 billion a year, according to the\nU.S. International Trade Commission.  Republican leaders such as Kentucky Republican Senator\n Mitch McConnell  and Michigan Republican  Dave Camp , positioned to\nbe the incoming chairman of the House Ways and Means Committee,\nsay they want to help Obama get the pending trade deals\napproved.  \u201cUnder a Republican House leadership, if the president is\nserious about moving forward on trade, he will have a serious\npartner on Capitol Hill,\u201d Texas Republican  Kevin Brady , the\nlikely chairman of the trade subcommittee of the Ways and Means\nCommittee, said at a meeting in Washington Oct. 25. \u201cWe believe\nthe three agreements are critical.\u201d  The South Korean accord, the most important of the three\npending pacts in volume of goods affected, may draw especially\nstrong bipartisan support. \u201cKorea has broader implications,\u201d\nsaid Laura Lane, head of international government affairs at New\nYork-based Citigroup, said in an interview.  With almost $68 billion in two-way trade, the deal would be\nthe U.S.\u2019s largest free-trade pact since the North American Free\nTrade Agreement in 1994 and may be critical to helping Obama\nmeet his goal of doubling American exports in five years.  TAXES  International Business Machines Corp ., Microsoft Corp.,\n Blackstone Group LP  and  Occidental Petroleum Corp . all have\nlobbied against the Obama proposals to increase taxes on\noverseas profits. The election gives them some important allies.  \u201cRepublicans have pretty much staked their claim that\nthey\u2019re not going to raise taxes,\u201d said  John Feehery , who was\nan adviser to former House Speaker  Dennis Hastert , the last\nRepublican to hold that top post. \u201cRepublicans are much more\ncognizant and care more about the financial impact of these\ntaxes on jobs.\u201d  Republican control of the House may make it impossible for\nObama to succeed in his bid to boost taxes on profits companies\nmake overseas. And the gridlock that may result from a divided\nlegislature would also stave off separate changes proposed by\nthe administration that would cost oil companies, including\nOccidental, tens of billions more a year by raising taxes on\ntheir non-U.S. operations.  \u201cThe punitive-type tax changes against the energy industry\nwill be much more difficult to pass with Republicans in charge\nof the House,\u201d said Gerald McPhee, senior vice president of\nfederal relations at Los Angeles-based Occidental, the fourth-\nlargest U.S. oil company by market value.  The Republican victory also may allow private-equity firms,\nsuch as New York-based Blackstone, to kill a four-year effort by\ncongressional Democrats to raise taxes on the incentive pay\nearned by their executives known as carried interest.  Besides blocking prospective increases, businesses may find\na ripe political environment for getting some long-sought tax\nbenefits through Congress. Companies such as San Jose,\nCalifornia-based  Cisco Systems Inc.  may find new support for a\ntemporary tax holiday on their foreign earnings that was\nrejected by the Senate in 2009.  Businesses \u201care not going to be seen as a pool of funds to\nbe pillaged by Congress anymore,\u201d said Curtis Dubay, a senior\ntax policy analyst at the Washington-based Heritage Foundation,\na research institution that often sides with Republicans on tax\nissues.  IMMIGRATION  Immigration is one area where the Republican ascendency may\nprove disappointing to some companies, including  Intel Corp.  and\n Hilton Worldwide Inc.  They want to increase the flow of legal\nforeign workers through changes to immigration law.  Republican lawmakers, who will lead the debate on the issue\nin the House, plan to focus on border security and cracking down\non illegal immigration first. They say they will consider the\nmeasures sought by business only after fewer illegal immigrants\nare coming across the U.S.-Mexico border.  Representative  Steve King , an Iowa Republican slated to\nhead the House Judiciary subcommittee on immigration policy,\nsays he opposes lifting visa caps for lower-skilled foreign\nworkers because that would depress U.S. worker wages. He would\nsupport increasing visas for higher-skilled workers only if they\nmeet criteria to boost the U.S. economy.  That means they should be young, well-educated and able to\nspeak English, King said. \u201cThat\u2019s the indicator of whether they\ncan assimilate into the broader society.\u201d  Intel and other technology companies such as  EBay Inc . and\n Cognizant Technology Solutions Corp . want Congress to lift the\ncap on H-1B visas for skilled workers. The annual limit has been\n65,000 since 2004, after expiration of a temporary increase from\n2001 to 2003 that raised the cap to 195,000. In fiscal 2010, the\ncap was reached in nine months.  Companies also want to lift the 140,000 limit on\nemployment-based green cards that prove permanent residency.  At Intel, about 6.5 percent of 40,000 workers in the U.S.\nare in the country on temporary visas. The company helps those\nworkers apply immediately for green cards, said Peter Muller,\ndirector of government relations. \u201cWe want to keep them,\nideally for their entire career,\u201d he said.  The restaurant and hotel industries need more seasonal,\nlower-skilled workers.  Jonas Neihardt , a Hilton lobbyist, is\npushing for a simpler system to verify the legal status of\nworkers and a boost in H-2B visas for non-farm seasonal\nemployees, now capped at 66,000.  \u201cWe\u2019re anticipating when things get better we\u2019ll need more\nof those types of workers,\u201d Neihardt said.  Corporations say they hope the importance of the Latino\nvote in the 2012 presidential elections will cause congressional\nRepublican leaders to support a broad bill.  \u201cIt will be an uphill battle, but it could be that the\nRepublicans would see that it\u2019s to their advantage to get this\nissue behind them,\u201d said  Randy Johnson , vice president for\nlabor policy at the U.S. Chamber of Commerce.  LABOR  Organized labor faces tougher times on Capitol Hill.  \u201cThe election profoundly reshapes labor\u2019s agenda,\u201d said\n Harley Shaiken , a professor of labor relations at University of\nCalifornia at Berkeley.  Unions face little chance of achieving legislative goals\nenvisioned from a Democratic-majority Congress, such as easier\norganizing rules, mandatory paid sick leave, and bigger fines\nfor workplace safety violations, he said.  Labor leaders are now likely to scale back their\nlegislative ambitions and increase efforts to make gains through\nregulatory agencies. Unions may still have enough supporters to\nmake it difficult for business to achieve anti-union\nlegislation, particularly in the Senate.  \u201cOn labor issues, it\u2019s going to be very difficult to move\nthe ball in either direction,\u201d said Glenn Spencer, who handles\nlabor matters at the  Chamber of Commerce .  The biggest short-term impact may be for unions\nrepresenting construction-trades and public-sector workers.\nRepublicans have generally opposed union-backed federal stimulus\nspending, such as measures that created construction jobs and\nsaved jobs of teachers, police officers and other public-sector\nworkers. (MSFT) \u2019s decade-long\nstruggle against a European Union antitrust probe that led to\nmore than 1.68 billion euros ($2.1 billion) in fines will enter\nits final phase tomorrow when an EU court rules on the company\u2019s\nchallenge.  The world\u2019s largest software company asked the EU General\nCourt to void an 899 million-euro fine imposed after Microsoft\nfailed to comply with a 2004 antitrust order to provide rivals\nwith data to help them work with the company\u2019s operating-system\nsoftware. The fine was on top of Microsoft\u2019s earlier penalties\nof 497 million euros and 280.5 million euros and surpassed only\nby a 1.06 billion-euro levy against  Intel Corp .  \u201cThe two fines for Microsoft and Intel certainly sent a\nmessage,\u201d said Ted Henneberry, a lawyer at Bingham McCutchen\nLLP in  Washington  who has previously worked for Microsoft on\nmatters not related to the EU case. \u201cThis thing is history now.\nToday companies realize that you\u2019re better served trying to work\nthings out with the\u201d European Commission.  Microsoft\u2019s Windows software powered 95 percent of\npersonal-computers in 2004, when EU regulators fined the company\na record 497 million euros and ordered it to offer a version of\nthe software without a music and video player. Now, amid a\nglobal slump in PC sales, Microsoft is preparing to manufacture\nits first tablet to challenge Apple\u2019s Inc.\u2019s iPad.  Microsoft is the only company in more than 50 years of EU\ncompetition policy penalized for failing to comply with an\norder. The Redmond, Washington-based company agreed to a\nsettlement in 2009 in a bid to repair the company\u2019s relationship\nwith the European Commission. License Guidance  Microsoft argued at a hearing last year that regulators\nshould have given it more guidance to avoid the fine. Under the\ninitial decision, Microsoft was ordered to provide data to\ncompetitors to allow servers to connect to computers using the\n Windows operating system . It was also required to limit to a\n\u201creasonable\u201d amount the royalties it charged.  The fine was a so-called  periodic penalty  calculated\nbecause Microsoft was in breach of the EU order for 488 days,\nregulators said in 2008. The case is T-167\/08, Microsoft v. European Commission. (MSFT)  challenged as\n\u201cunfair\u201d a European Union penalty of 899 million-euros ($1.26\nbillion) it received for failing to comply with an antitrust\nruling.  The world\u2019s largest software company told judges at an\nappeal hearing today that the 2008 European Commission fine was\n\u201cespecially unfair\u201d because the regulator failed to give it\nsufficient guidance to avoid the fine. The court should annul\nthe \u201cunnecessary, unlawful and totally disproportionate\npenalty,\u201d Microsoft lawyer Jean-Francois Bellis told the court.  Microsoft is the only company in more than 50 years of EU\ncompetition policy to be penalized for failing to comply with an\norder. Today\u2019s case is the last remnant of years of disputes\nwith the commission that resulted in fines totaling 1.68 billion\neuros. Microsoft agreed to a settlement in 2009 in a bid to\nrepair the company\u2019s uneasy relationship with the EU regulator.  The Brussels-based commission said Microsoft breached an\nearlier ruling by overcharging for licenses that rivals needed\nto connect products to Windows computers. As the first appeal of\nsuch a decision, the judges at the  EU General Court  in\nLuxembourg will clarify the scope of the commission\u2019s power.  \u201cThis case would not have arisen if the commission had\nbeen as explicit with respect to the rates which it wanted\nMicrosoft to charge as it had been with all the other aspects of\nthe licensing terms proposed by Microsoft,\u201d Bellis told a\nthree-judge panel.  Periodic Penalty  The commission, the EU\u2019s antitrust authority, imposed the\n899 million-euro fine as a so-called  periodic penalty  payment on\nRedmond, Washington-based Microsoft for failing to comply with a\n2004 antitrust order.  The punishment \u201cserved no purpose other than pressuring\nMicrosoft into coming up with an outcome\u201d that the EU could\nhave come up with \u201cfrom the outset,\u201d Bellis said.  Under the initial decision, Microsoft was fined 497 million\neuros and ordered to provide data to competitors to allow\nservers to connect to computers using the  Windows operating\nsystem .  Microsoft was also required to limit to a \u201creasonable\u201d\namount the royalties it charged for the technology. An EU court\nin September 2007 rejected Microsoft\u2019s appeal of that decision.  \u201cThis is a case about a gambler who doubled up on a losing\nbet, lost again and now wants his money back,\u201d Nicholas Khan, a\nlawyer for the commission, told the court. The 2007 EU court\ndecision \u201cmeant that the gamble failed\u201d and \u201cMicrosoft wants\nto unwind the bet. These gambling instincts persist in the\nmanner of conducting these proceedings.\u201d  Compete With Microsoft  The only reason why competitors wanted the inter-\noperability information from Microsoft was not to add features\nto their products, it was because rivals needed to be able to\ncompete, said Thomas Vinje, a lawyer who spoke on behalf of some\nof the interveners, including  International Business Machines\nCorp. The\ncommission\u2019s case is supported by seven interveners, including\nIBM and Oracle.  488 Days  The EU assessed Microsoft\u2019s proposals for 306 days of the\nEU\u2019s 488-day periodic penalty, said the company\u2019s lawyer Bellis,\nwho works at law firm  Van Bael & Bellis  in Brussels.  \u201cWhy did it take the commission so long to review them?\u201d\nasked Bellis. \u201cHow can the commission fine Microsoft for\nfailing to apply reasonable rates from June 2006 to October 2007\nwhen the final parameters were only determined on October 22,\n2007?\u201d  Microsoft also questions the validity of the EU\u2019s\nassessment reports prepared by a trustee charged with monitoring\nthe company\u2019s compliance with the 2004 decision. While the decision was unanimous,\nthe justices divided 5-4 in their reasoning, with the majority\ndeclining to bar all patents on methods of conducting business.  \n \u201cThis is a victory for people in favor of broader patents\ngenerally, including software,\u201d said patent lawyer  Edward Reines  of Weil Gotshal in California, who was watching the case.\n\u201cThe stakes are high, the technology is evolving rapidly and\nit\u2019s really difficult to make all-purpose rules in this area.\u201d  \n The justices voting in the majority said there needs to be\na flexible test for emerging technologies. The case drew record\ninterest for a business dispute before the highest U.S. court,\nwith  Microsoft Corp.  and  Morgan Stanley  among dozens of\ncompanies filing briefs. The fight split industries, dividing\ncompanies that rely on their own intellectual property from\nthose aiming to head off expensive infringement lawsuits.  \n The dispute involved Bernard L. Bilski and Rand A. Warsaw,\nfounders of a Pittsburgh company that sells customized consumer\nenergy products. The Supreme Court was reviewing a decision by\nthe U.S. Court of Appeals for the Federal Circuit against Bilski\nthat said methods can be patented only if they have some\nphysical component, through either a connection to a machine or\ntheir power to transform an item into a different state.  \n Rewording the Patent  \n Writing for the Supreme Court, Justice  Anthony Kennedy  said\nthe federal circuit\u2019s standard was only a \u201cuseful and important\nclue\u201d and isn\u2019t the sole test that should be used in\ndetermining whether a process is eligible for a patent. He did\nsay business methods \u201craise special problems in terms of\nvagueness and suspect validity.\u201d  \n The decision leaves it up to the federal circuit, which\nspecializes in patent law, to create a more flexible test.  \n Michael Jakes , the lawyer who represented Bilski and\nWarsaw, said it may just mean a rewording of the patent\napplication to \u201cmake the claims less abstract.\u201d  \n \u201cFor most patent owners, it\u2019s a very good decision,\u201d\nJakes, a lawyer at Finnegan Henderson in Washington, said in a\ntelephone interview. \u201cIt eliminates the federal circuit\u2019s very\nrestrictive test and leaves open patents for things that are not\nphysical\u201d inventions.  \n Abstract Idea  \n Companies that argued that the lower court standard was too\nrestrictive included  Bank of America Corp. ,  Medtronic Inc. ,\nNovartis Corp.,  Palm Inc.  and Accenture Plc. Small software,\nfinancial services and electronic commerce companies also backed\nbroad patent rights.  \n Those urging restrictions on method patents included\nMicrosoft, Morgan Stanley,  Google Inc.  and  J.C. Penney Co.  The\nObama administration also advocated a high standard for granting\nmethod patents, as did Bloomberg LP, the New York-based parent\ncompany of Bloomberg News.  \n Patents can be granted for machines, articles of\nmanufacture, compositions of matter, and processes. It is the\ndefinition of a \u201cprocess\u201d that was the subject of the dispute.  \n Justice  John Paul Stevens , joined by justices  Ruth Bader Ginsburg ,  Steven Breyer  and  Sonia Sotomayor , said that \u201ca claim\nthat merely describes a method of doing business does not\nqualify as a process\u201d that is eligible for a patent.  \n \u201cIf business methods could be patented, then many business\ndecisions, no matter how small, could be potential patent\nviolations,\u201d Stevens wrote. \u201cBusinesses would either live in\nconstant fear of litigation or would need to undertake the costs\nof searching through patents that describe methods of doing\nbusiness, attempting to decide whether their innovation is one\nthat remains in the public domain.\u201d  \n The case is Bilski v. It\u2019s a radical shift as Microsoft overhauls its Internet-based programs, seeking to stay in sync with the fast-changing technology industry.  For much of Microsoft\u2019s 38-year history, infrequent upgrades made sense for businesses seeking predictable improvements. That\u2019s changed as nimbler entrants such as Dropbox Inc., Box Inc.,  Jive Software Inc (JIVE)  (JIVE). and Google Inc. refine features and deliver automatic updates over the Web. That tinkering has helped lure customers and put pressure on margins at Microsoft\u2019s biggest division, which accounted for $24 billion in sales last year, or a third of the total.  \u201cMicrosoft, on this every-three-year schedule for the massive wave of new products, looks like a dinosaur,\u201d said  Melissa Webster , an analyst at market-research firm IDC, based in Framingham,  Massachusetts . \u201cThree years is a lifetime in tech these days.\u201d  That message has gotten through. Within a year, users of Internet-based versions of Office productivity software, as well as e-mail, telephony and collaboration tools, will have parts of their software refreshed weekly, Jeff Teper, an Office vice president, said in an interview. Microsoft has been moving toward more frequent updates with other programs, including Windows.  Later today at a company conference, Microsoft will showcase how software developers can build programs that take advantage of the Web-based Office 365, Chief Executive Officer  Steve Ballmer  said in a speech at the show yesterday.  Risky Switch  To pave way for the Office shift, the company is tapping the experience of a team of data scientists it gained in July with the acquisition of Yammer Inc. The 5-year-old startup convinced its customers the frequent updates were an advantage, because it gave them the latest and greatest features.  Moving fast also carries risks. While Yammer has 7 million users, 80 percent of them unpaid, Office has more than 1 billion, and the vast majority pay for the software. A half-baked or unpopular change in Office will be met with widespread scrutiny and complaints.  \u201cThis is where folks who have been at Microsoft for a while are envious of Yammer -- their mistakes go relatively unnoticed,\u201d Teper said.  Quality Matters  Raman Padmanabhan, chief information officer for  Xerox Corp. (XRX) \u2019s business-services unit, has been briefed on Microsoft\u2019s move to faster updates. He said he\u2019s supportive as long as product quality doesn\u2019t suffer. Xerox uses both Office and Microsoft\u2019s SharePoint collaboration software.  \u201cIt\u2019s all about service and quality,\u201d Padmanabhan said. \u201cYou have to have a have a certain quality or it just kills your business.\u201d  Office is the biggest part of Microsoft\u2019s business division, where  revenue  increased 25 percent in fiscal 2012 compared with 2010 amid growth in areas like SharePoint, which helps workers collaborate, and Lync, programs that enable Internet-telephone calls. Office 365, a collection of Office programs accessible through the Web, is now a $1 billion business.  Yammer releases updates to users twice a week. Facebook Inc., by comparison, operates at a rate of twice a day. Yammer is moving to three times a week and ultimately intends to adopt a system of continuous updates, said Adam Pisoni, Yammer\u2019s chief technology officer and co-founder, who now serves as general manager of engineering for Office.  Draft Picks  Microsoft and other traditional software companies would once spend months planning new features, and months more building and testing them. Customers knew roughly how often Microsoft would release a new version, and they were free to skip updates. Problem was, besides being slow, the system relied on engineers who often did a poor job predicting how customers actually behave, Pisoni said.  \u201cWhat you realize when you begin to be very data-driven is a very large percentage of our ideas are bad,\u201d said Yammer\u2019s Pisoni.  Pisoni asked Yammer\u2019s data chief, Peter Fishman, who has a Ph.D. in economics and started his career helping the  Philadelphia Eagles  make draft decisions, to make it a top priority to help Microsoft with its own data analysis. Fishman meets with the Office sales group, research and development and engineering teams. Some parts of Office already are doing things \u201cthe Yammer way,\u201d with rapid updates that are closely tracked for satisfaction and user engagement, Teper said.  \u2018Foundational Shift\u2019  \u201cA lot of focus is on close to real-time,\u201d said Bobby Kishore, an 18-year Microsoft veteran who leads engineering and operations for Office 365. \u201cWe just can\u2019t rely on some focus groups. We have to be led by data. That is a foundational shift that is permeating through the organization.\u201d  The Internet-based Office 365 software is already being updated on about a monthly basis. Patent Fees  The patent office, which is funded entirely by user fees,\nwill be able to set its own fees, with any money in excess of\nthe budgeted amount going to a fund that can only be used by the\nagency. Rowling and the Chamber of Literary Fame","released_at":"<date>July 19 2013<\/date> <time>15:15:51<\/time>","content":"Last weekend\u2019s  revelation  that  J.K. Rowling  is the author of the critically acclaimed and -- until now -- commercially unsuccessful crime novel \u201cThe Cuckoo\u2019s Calling\u201d has  electrified  the book world and solidified Rowling\u2019s reputation as a genuine writing talent: After all, if she can impress the critics without the benefit of her towering reputation, then surely her success is deserved.  And yet what this episode actually reveals is the opposite: that Rowling\u2019s spectacular career is likely more a fluke of history than a consequence of her unique genius.  Whenever someone is phenomenally successful, whether it\u2019s Rowling as an author,  Bob Dylan  as a musician or  Steve Jobs  as an innovator, we can\u2019t help but conclude that there is something uniquely qualifying about them, something akin to \u201cgenius,\u201d that makes their successes all but inevitable.  Even when we learn about their early setbacks -- Rowling\u2019s original manuscript for \u201cHarry Potter and the Sorcerer\u2019s Stone\u201d was  rejected  by no fewer than 12 publishers; Columbia Records Inc. initially  refused  to release Dylan\u2019s \u201cLike a Rolling Stone\u201d; Jobs was  booted  from Apple Inc. in the mid-1980s -- we interpret them as embarrassing oversights that were subsequently corrected rather than evidence that their success may have somehow been a product of luck or happenstance.  The Experiment  Several years ago, my colleagues  Matthew Salganik  and  Peter Dodds  at  Columbia University  and I challenged this conventional wisdom with an unusual  experiment . We set out to prove that market success is driven less by intrinsic talent than by \u201ccumulative advantage,\u201d a rich-get-richer process in which early, possibly even random events are amplified by social feedback and produce large differences in future outcomes.  To test our cumulative-advantage hypothesis, we recruited almost 30,000 participants to listen, rate and download songs by bands they had never heard of. Unbeknownst to the participants, they were randomly assigned to one of two groups: an \u201cindependent\u201d group, which saw only the names of the bands and the songs, and a \u201csocial influence\u201d group, whose participants could see how many times songs had been downloaded by others in the group. In addition, those in the social-influence group were assigned to one of eight different \u201cworlds\u201d that were created concurrently, allowing us to effectively \u201crun\u201d history many times.  If quality determined success, the same songs should have won every time by a margin that was independent of what people knew about the choices of others. By contrast, if success was driven disproportionately by a few early downloads, subsequently amplified by social influence, the outcomes would be largely random and would also become more unequal as the social feedback became stronger.  What  we found  was highly consistent with the cumulative-advantage hypothesis. First, when people could see what other people liked, the inequality of success increased, meaning that popular songs became more popular and unpopular songs become less so. Second and more surprisingly, each song\u2019s popularity was incredibly unpredictable: One song, for example, came in first out of 48 we sampled in one \u201cworld,\u201d but it came in 40th in another.  In the real world, of course, it\u2019s impossible to travel back in time and start over, so it\u2019s much harder to argue that someone who is incredibly successful may owe their success to a combination of luck and cumulative advantage rather than superior talent. But by writing under the pseudonym of Robert Galbraith, an otherwise anonymous name, Rowling came pretty close to recreating our experiment, starting over again as an unknown author and publishing a book that would have to succeed or fail on its own merits, just as  Harry Potter  had to 16 years ago -- before anyone knew who Rowling was.  False Results  Rowling made a bold move and, no doubt, is feeling vindicated by the  critical acclaim  the book has received. But there\u2019s a catch: Until the news leaked about the author\u2019s real identity, this critically acclaimed book had sold somewhere between 500 and 1,500 copies, depending on which report you read. As they say in the U.K., that\u2019s rubbish! What\u2019s more, had the author actually been Robert Galbraith, the book would almost certainly have continued to languish in obscurity, probably forever.  \u201cThe Cuckoo\u2019s Calling\u201d will now have a happy ending, and its success will only perpetuate the myth that talent is ultimately rewarded with success. What Rowling\u2019s little experiment has actually demonstrated, however, is that quality and success are even more unrelated than we found in our experiment. It might be hard for a book to become a runaway bestseller if it\u2019s unreadably bad (although one might argue that the Twilight series and \u201cFifty Shades of Grey\u201d challenge this constraint), but it is also clear that being good, or even excellent, isn\u2019t enough. As one of the hapless editors who turned down the Galbraith manuscript  put it , \u201cWhen the book came in, I thought it was perfectly good -- it was certainly well-written -- but it didn\u2019t stand out.\u201d  Ironically, that\u2019s probably how those 12 editors felt about the original \u201cHarry Potter\u201d manuscript. Now, of course, they look like idiots, but what both our experiment and Rowling\u2019s suggest is that they might have been right all along.  Had things turned out only slightly different, the real Rowling might have met with the same success as the fake Robert Galbraith, not the other way around. As hard as it is to imagine in the Harry Potter-obsessed world that we now inhabit, it\u2019s entirely plausible that in this parallel universe, \u201cHarry Potter and the Sorcerer\u2019s Stone\u201d would just be a \u201cperfectly good\u201d book that never sold more than a handful of copies; Rowling would still be a struggling single mother in Manchester,  England ; and the rest of us would be none the wiser. Colors, Shape  Design rights are a form of intellectual property that have protection similar to trademarks under European law. Apple successfully used its iPad design rights to block at least some Samsung tablet sales in Germany. He achieved that mostly by\ninvesting in big-name companies such as Apple Inc. and News\nCorp.  \n Since then, many stocks have turned against him, especially\nthose of Citigroup Inc. and Time Warner Inc. The Saudi royal\u2019s\nfortune has been trimmed to $16.6 billion, based on the value of\nhis Kingdom Holding Co. stake on March 31 and his personal\nassets as of Feb. 10.  \n \u2018Buffett of Arabia\u2019  \n Alwaleed often refers to himself as the \u201cBuffett of\nArabia,\u201d although the comparison to Warren Buffett, chairman of\nBerkshire Hathaway Inc., doesn\u2019t hold up. Berkshire Hathaway\u2019s\nClass A shares more than doubled in the same span of almost ten\nyears, swelling Buffett\u2019s stake to $48.7 billion.  \n Alwaleed, who\u2019s a nephew of Saudi King Abdullah, is\nplotting a rebound. Publicly traded stock, which made up at\nleast 79 percent of Alwaleed\u2019s assets in 2000, now constitutes\nonly about 23 percent of his wealth.  \n 371-Room Palace  \n Alwaleed\u2019s most ambitious undertaking is the 1-kilometer-\ntall (0.62-mile-tall) Kingdom Tower in Jeddah. When completed,\nthe skyscraper will be the world\u2019s tallest, surpassing the\ncurrent record holder -- Dubai\u2019s Burj Khalifa -- by 21 percent.  \n The prince says his shift in strategy at Kingdom Holding,\nwhich he controls with a 95 percent stake, may put him on a path\nto surpass the riches of the 79-year-old Buffett.  \n \u201cWhen he was my age, he was not as big as me,\u201d Alwaleed\nsays. \u201cI still have 20 years.\u201d  \n Alwaleed\u2019s preoccupation with his status and wealth, which\nincludes four jets, a 281-foot (86-meter) yacht and a 371-room\npalace, is also on display at Kingdom Holding\u2019s headquarters.  \n The glass tower that he built has an oval-shaped hole in\nthe top that resembles the eye of a sewing needle. Alwaleed then got down to business.  \n \u201cNeedless to say, I should be pleased to consider\nparticipating in any of your future investments that you may\ndeem pertinent,\u201d the prince wrote.  \n A Laggard  \n Buffett, who grew rich by investing in consumer brands such\nas American Express Co. and Coca-Cola Co., wrote back three days\nlater. He said he would be delighted to team up with the prince.\nHe also piled on the praise.  \n \u201cIn Omaha, I\u2019m known as the \u2018Alwaleed of America\u2019 -- which\nis quite a compliment,\u201d Buffett wrote.  \n In December 1999, Alwaleed told Buffett in a letter that he\nfound news coverage of a slump in Berkshire\u2019s stock \u201chighly\nobjectionable\u201d and had written to editors to defend him.  \n \u201cDear Prince Alwaleed,\u201d Buffett responded the next day.\n\u201cYou\u2019re terrific!\u201d  \n A decade later, it\u2019s the prince\u2019s investments that need a\nboost. As of March 31, Alwaleed\u2019s net worth had dropped 21\npercent from May 2000, the tally shows.  \n Citigroup shares, which fell 90 percent during the period,\ndid the most damage to his fortune. The prince even fell behind\nthe Dow Jones Industrial Average, which returned 27 percent,\nincluding reinvested dividends.  \n \u201cHe\u2019s become a laggard,\u201d says Laszlo Birinyi, founder of\nequity research firm Birinyi Associates Inc. in Westport,\nConnecticut. \u201cAs an investor, his record is not worth\nfollowing.\u201d  \n Unrealized Losses  \n Sitting at his gray-marble desk in his office, Alwaleed\ndefends his stock picking, saying most of his losses came in\n2008 as a wave of subprime-mortgage defaults convulsed the\nfinancial world.  \n He grabs a copy of Richard J. Connors\u2019s book \u201cWarren\nBuffett on Business\u201d (Wiley, 2009) and flips it open to a\npassage he has highlighted with a green marker.
