In 2008,\neveryone had a hiccup. He went down also.\u201d  \n Buffett declined to comment for this story.  \n Alwaleed\u2019s decline may be worse than his accounting shows.\nIn its 2008 annual report, Kingdom Holding classified more than\n$4 billion of its $7.45 billion of stock market losses as\ntemporary -- and therefore didn\u2019t subtract them from its\nearnings.  \n Ernst & Young Note  \n Kingdom Holding\u2019s auditor in Riyadh, Ernst & Young,\nqualified its approval of the accounts, saying it couldn\u2019t\ndetermine whether the company took a big enough deduction for\nthe market losses, according to its notes on the company\u2019s\nstatements. Ernst & Young didn\u2019t say the company had violated\naccounting standards generally accepted in Saudi Arabia.  \n A year later, as the unrealized loss shrank to $3.53\nbillion, Ernst & Young didn\u2019t attach any qualification to its\naudit of Kingdom Holding.  \n Even though the unrealized loss has come down, the\nauditor\u2019s notes suggest that the value of Kingdom Holding may be\nless than its market capitalization of $9.49 billion as of April\n26, says Steven Bankler, a San Antonio-based forensic accountant\nwho examined the company\u2019s financial statements at the request\nof Bloomberg News.  \n Kingdom Holding\u2019s Sanbar says the company correctly judged\nthe size of its unrealized loss and that it expects its stock\ninvestments to bounce back.  \n Kingdom Oasis  \n Alwaleed also hopes to boost his fortune in the desert of\nSaudi Arabia. Northeast of Riyadh, the prince\u2019s armored GMC\nSuburban bumps over rocks as he prepares to inspect his latest\nproject: Kingdom Oasis, a development that includes an\nequestrian resort, a banquet facility and villas. Oasis is part\nof the 16.8-square-kilometer (6.5-square-mile) Kingdom City\nRiyadh planned community.  \n His driver, who has a black pistol holstered under his arm,\nturns past what will be a safari park and lake and stops in\nfront of a clubhouse next to horse stables.  \n Alwaleed ducks inside the clubhouse and spots a flaw: Two\nPing-Pong tables in the recreation room instead of one. He\nthrusts his wooden walking stick at one of the tables.  \n \u201cThis should be removed,\u201d he barks at his project managers.\n\u201cAnd put in billiards.\u201d  \n When he\u2019s not inspecting his investments, Alwaleed\nsometimes meets with foreign officials and heads of state as\npart of his role as a Saudi royal.  \n Saudi King  \n \u201cI\u2019m a businessman, but that\u2019s only a platform,\u201d he says.\nWhen asked if he wants to be king, he said he would serve his\nnation in any capacity if asked.  \n In a country with thousands of princes and an autocratic\nregime with no firm order of succession, Alwaleed doesn\u2019t have a\nclear path to the throne. Unlike his cousins from other lines of\nthe Saud family, he lacks a formal role in government.  \n Alwaleed\u2019s father, Talal Bin Abdulaziz, does sit on the\nkingdom\u2019s commission for succession, which helps pick the crown\nprince after the death of a king.  \n Talal became a black sheep of the royal clan after pressing\nunsuccessfully in the 1950s for more democracy in Saudi Arabia.\nHe later founded the Arab Gulf Program for United Nations\nDevelopment Organizations in 1980 and currently serves as its\npresident. The group raises money to support reproductive health\neducation in Mauritania and women\u2019s entrepreneurship in the Gaza\nStrip.  \n Princess Ameerah Altaweel  \n Alwaleed has followed his father\u2019s example by advocating\nfor greater freedom for Saudi women, who must wear neck-to-toe\nrobes to mask their figures in public.  \n The prince has hired a mostly female staff at his offices,\ncreating workplaces rarely seen in Saudi Arabia. The women he\nemploys dress in Western clothing and hold jobs managing his\nconstruction projects, piloting his jets and directing catering\nat his palace.  \n Three times divorced, the prince has a son, 32, and a\ndaughter, 27. Alwaleed is now married to Princess Ameerah\nAltaweel, 27, who speaks fluent English with an American accent\nshe picked up from watching the television show \u201cFriends.\u201d  \n The princess, who\u2019s vice chairman of the Alwaleed Bin Talal\nFoundations for Charity and Philanthropy, says she wants to be\nthe first Saudi woman to drive on public roads -- if it becomes\nlegal.  \n \u201cShe\u2019s the vanguard,\u201d Alwaleed says.  \n Starting with $30,000  \n The prince says his liberal views were nurtured in the\nU.S., where in 1979 he received an undergraduate degree in\nbusiness administration from Menlo College in Atherton,\nCalifornia.  \n After Alwaleed returned to Riyadh, his father jump-started\nthe prince\u2019s investment career by giving him a $30,000 loan and\na house, which he mortgaged. As the prince started to build his\nfortune, he earned a master\u2019s degree in social science from\nSyracuse University in Syracuse, New York, in 1985.  \n Alwaleed says he made his first billion by 1989 from\ninvestments in Saudi real estate and banking as well as\ncommissions he earned as a local agent for foreign construction\ncompanies. In the next two years, the prince began investing in\nCiticorp, which was then drowning in bad real estate loans.  \n After Citicorp Chief Executive Officer John Reed asked\nAlwaleed for a cash infusion, the prince in 1991 added $590\nmillion to his stake. That brought his total investment to $797\nmillion, making him the bank\u2019s biggest individual shareholder --\na position the prince says he still holds today.  \n Technology Splurge  \n Seven years later, the bank merged with Travelers Group\nInc. to form Citigroup, and by 2000, Alwaleed\u2019s shares were\nworth $8.6 billion, even after he\u2019d sold off some of his\noriginal holding.  \n \u201cHe took a big risk and it paid off,\u201d says David Webb, head\nof the finance department at the London School of Economics.\n\u201cBig fund managers didn\u2019t buy the stock, and then some guy from\nthe Middle East puts all his eggs in one basket. We all could\nhave been rich, looking backwards.\u201d  \n The billionaire used his new riches to splurge on U.S.\ntechnology shares in the first half of 2000. Just as stock\nmarkets were beginning to plunge that year, with the Nasdaq\nComposite Index falling 78 percent through October 2002,\nAlwaleed bought $400 million of Compaq Computer Corp. shares and\n$200 million of WorldCom Inc.  \n He also purchased shares of Amazon.com Inc. and DoubleClick\nInc. as well as household names such as AT&T Corp., McDonald\u2019s\nCorp. and Coca-Cola. The prince told Bloomberg News at the time\nthat he was buying all of these stocks on the cheap.  \n Praise from Murdoch  \n As he spread his money around corporate America, Alwaleed\nwon many friends. News Corp. Chairman Rupert Murdoch was among\nthe 355 guests who gathered at the Plaza Hotel to honor the\nprince in November 2000 at an awards dinner thrown by the Arab\nBankers Association of North America.  \n After the guests took their seats in the Grand Ballroom,\nAlwaleed entered the room with his retinue and walked to the\nhead table, drawing applause. He sat next to Murdoch, and the\ntwo men chatted over a dinner of lobster tails and rack of lamb.  \n Then the media mogul took the podium to praise the Saudi\nroyal for his investment in News Corp., at the time an\nAustralian company that had U.S.-traded shares. From his initial\nNews Corp. investments of a combined $600 million in 1997 and\n1999 through that evening in 2000, Alwaleed had almost doubled\nhis money.  \n \u201cVery proud, we are, that Prince Alwaleed is one of News\nCorp.\u2019s largest shareholders,\u201d Murdoch said.  \n Selling Apple  \n After six tribute speeches, Alwaleed returned to the\nhotel\u2019s Suite 537, decorated with gilded furniture, where\njournalists quizzed him about ill-timed investments he had\nannounced about six months earlier.  \n \u201cWe don\u2019t see any further investments in the Internet,\u201d\nAlwaleed said. \u201cMany companies are going to go bankrupt.\u201d  \n In 2002, the same year in which WorldCom went belly up, the\nprince deployed another $1 billion in three companies whose\nstock he already owned: AOL Time Warner Inc., Priceline.com Inc.\nand Citigroup.  \n Priceline.com was the only winner: The shares he\u2019s held on\nto have jumped fourfold to about $175 million, based on data in\nKingdom Holding documents.  \n The investor would be worth several billion dollars more\ntoday had he not chucked the bulk of his stake in Apple in 2005.\nHe had poured $115 million into the computer maker in 1997.\nUnder founder and CEO Steve Jobs, the company introduced the\niPod four years later.  \n Returning to Saudi  \n At Alwaleed\u2019s Hotel George V in Paris in November 2005, the\nprince told Bloomberg News his motive for selling his Apple\nstake.  \n \u201cThe benefit of iTunes and all the good moves that Steve\nJobs has done have already been put in the price,\u201d Alwaleed\nsaid.  \n He was wrong. The rapidly selling iPod was followed in 2007\nby the iPhone, which transformed mobile devices, and the iPad in\n2010. The prince missed a sevenfold rally starting from the\nmiddle of 2005. His holding would have been worth about $6.75\nbillion as of today.  \n As Alwaleed was selling his Apple shares, he began moving\nmoney from the U.S. into Saudi Arabia, which itself was in\ntransition. In 2005, King Fahd, who had ruled for 23 years, died\nat age 82, propelling Alwaleed\u2019s uncle -- Crown Prince Abdullah\n-- to the throne.  \n \u201cThe prince made a commitment to the king,\u201d Sanbar, 62,\nsays. \u201cHe said, \u2018Instead of having 80 percent of my wealth\noutside, I\u2019m going to bring it here.\u2019\u201d  \n Kingdom IPO  \n In 2007, Alwaleed put together an initial public offering\nfor Kingdom Holding on the Saudi stock exchange. The 240-page\nprospectus, which appeared on Kingdom Holding\u2019s Web site only in\nArabic, said the company\u2019s listed assets had achieved lifetime\nannual returns of 19.9 percent through March 30, 2007.  \n The figure included only shares held at the time, omitting\nmoney losers such as WorldCom that Alwaleed had already sold.  \n \u201cThese historical results do not represent all of the\ninvestments that Management has made during the relevant\nhistorical periods,\u201d the prospectus said.  \n The prospectus contained one number that concerned\npotential shareholders, Sanbar says. Some 40 percent of its\nassets were in Citigroup stock, which was just starting to slip\nfrom its record high of $56.41 in December 2006. Kingdom Holding\nassured investors it would pare back the Citigroup stake.  \n \u201cThe answer was, we were going to start selling and shift\nto regional and Gulf investments,\u201d Sanbar says.  \n Citigroup Crashes  \n Kingdom Holding\u2019s stock jumped 20 percent on its first day\nof trading on July 29, 2007, giving the company a market value\nof about $20 billion. But Kingdom never sold its Citigroup\nshares as planned. From the IPO to the end of 2007, as credit\nmarkets tightened, the bank\u2019s stock plunged by more than a\nthird.  \n \u201cBuy-and-forget can be deadly to a portfolio,\u201d says\nFrederic Dickson, who manages $25 billion, including Citigroup\nshares, as chief market strategist at D.A. Davidson & Co. in\nLake Oswego, Oregon.  \n As the deepening credit crisis sent Citigroup shares\ntumbling 77 percent in 2008, Alwaleed had one reason to cheer.\nAt Microsoft\u2019s annual CEO summit in May in Redmond, Washington,\nthe prince finally got to meet his pen pal, Buffett.  \n During the event, a beaming Alwaleed posed with Buffett for\na photo taken by the prince\u2019s personal photographer. Buffett\nhammed it up for the camera, handing his black wallet to the\nprince as the flash went off.  \n Photo With Buffett  \n After the conference, Alwaleed sent Buffett a copy of the\nphoto, and Buffett wrote back to thank the prince. In signing\noff, he continued their banter about collaborating.  \n \u201cI hope we can come up with something in which we can work\ntogether,\u201d Buffett said in the June 2008 letter.  \n Alwaleed could use some help from the Oracle of Omaha. In\n2008, Kingdom Holding reported a net loss of $7.98 billion. That\nyear, as the U.S. government injected $45 billion into Citigroup\nto save it, the prince began to buy more of the bank\u2019s shares.  \n \u201cAt $3, you have to buy,\u201d Alwaleed says. His purchases from\n2008 and 2009 turned a profit as Citigroup shares rose to $4.61\non April 26.  \n While Kingdom Holding rebounded to a profit of $107 million\nfor 2009, it also reported the unrealized loss of $3.53 billion\nthat carried over from 2008\u2019s rout. Bankler, the forensic\naccountant, says the profit could vanish, slashing the company\u2019s\nmarket value and Alwaleed\u2019s net worth, if even a small portion\nof those unrealized losses became permanent.  \n Fairmont, Four Seasons  \n \u201cOne of the factors of market value is earnings per share,\nand they didn\u2019t take that hit,\u201d Bankler says.  \n Alwaleed\u2019s fortunes are improving this year. On April 19,\nCitigroup posted a first-quarter profit after two years of\nlosses, and the next day, Kingdom Holding also reported a gain.\nBut the company\u2019s shares remain in the doldrums. Since its first\ntrading day in 2007, Kingdom Holding\u2019s stock has fallen 54\npercent to 9.6 Saudi riyals on April 26.  \n \u201cAlwaleed is a major player, always will be,\u201d says Four\nSeasons CEO Isadore Sharp, who became fast friends with the\nprince after they met on Alwaleed\u2019s yacht in 1994. \u201cThe markets\nare turning. Things are getting back on track.\u201d  \n Alwaleed says he plans to take his hotel businesses public\nin the next few years. He bought his first stakes in Toronto-\nbased Fairmont Raffles Holdings International and Four Seasons\nin 1994. Fairmont also runs the Plaza Hotel, which is jointly\nowned by Kingdom Holding and Israeli billionaire Isaac Tshuva\u2019s\nElad Properties.  \n Hotels made up 63 percent of the assets in the prince\u2019s\ncompany in 2009, according to its year-end report.  \n \u2018He\u2019s a Hotelier\u2019  \n \u201cHe\u2019s a hotelier,\u201d Bankler says. \u201cThis is a hotel company.\u201d  \n Alwaleed\u2019s partners in Fairmont, which runs more than 90\nhotels worldwide, include Qatar\u2019s sovereign wealth fund and\nColony Capital LLC, the Los Angeles-based buyout firm founded by\nbillionaire Thomas J. Barrack.  \n The prince is in business with Gates at Four Seasons, which\noperates 83 hotels globally. Kingdom Holding and Gates\u2019s\ninvestment company, Cascade Investment LLC, each hold 47.5\npercent of the hotel management company. Sharp, who founded Four\nSeasons, retains a 5 percent stake.  \n Fairmont and Four Seasons may be ripe for an IPO as the\nrecession eases and companies stop trimming travel expenses,\nsays Smedes Rose, an analyst who covers hotels at Keefe,\nBruyette & Woods Inc. in New York.  \n Kingdom Tower  \n \u201cTrends are turning much better for them, and you\u2019d want to\ngo public into the momentum of a recovering market,\u201d he says.\n\u201cFour Seasons has a lot of legs.\u201d  \n Alwaleed says that within two years he also plans to hold\nan IPO for his Riyadh-based media company, Rotana Holding, which\nincludes Arabic movie and music channels and a record label. In\nFebruary, Murdoch\u2019s News Corp. agreed to buy 9.1 percent of\nRotana for $70 million.  \n The prince\u2019s Kingdom Tower project in Jeddah, Saudi\u2019s\ncommercial hub on the Red Sea, faces several obstacles. The\nspike-shaped skyscraper anchors a project that includes shopping\nmalls, a marina, hotels, villas and parks. Alwaleed, who says\nthe tower will be completed in four to five years, plans to\nraise some of the $20 billion that the complex will cost from\nequity investors and the sale of Islamic bonds.  \n And he has hired Emaar Properties PJSC -- the Dubai-based\ncontractor that erected Burj Khalifa -- to manage the project.  \n \u201cThe beef is in Saudi Arabia,\u201d Alwaleed says. \u201cIn 2010,\nwe\u2019re seeing ourselves coming out of it.\u201d  \n Burj Khalifa opened in January, just after the Arab emirate\nwent from being the world\u2019s best-performing real estate market\nto the worst. Prices for apartments in the tower have dropped to\nless than half of their 2008 peak during the credit crackup.  \n $32.1 Billion Difference  \n Alwaleed may have an even tougher time filling his\nskyscraper in Saudi Arabia, says Saud Masud, head of Middle East\nresearch at UBS AG in Dubai. Masud says Saudi laws and customs,\nincluding restrictions on travel, women\u2019s attire and the\npurchase of local securities by foreigners, deter visitors and\nbusinesses from entering the nation.  \n \u201cIt\u2019s not going to be a straightforward build-it-and-they-\nwill-come,\u201d Masud says. \u201cWhat the market needs now is affordable\nhousing and not kilometer towers.\u201d  \n As the prince rides in his GMC truck around the site of his\nKingdom City residential development, he once again draws\ncomparisons between himself and Buffett: The prince says they\nboth buy undervalued assets. The offices of Kingdom Holding and\nBerkshire Hathaway have roughly the same square footage, and\nboth companies have small staffs at their headquarters.  \n Pepsi Versus Coke  \n \u201cI drink Pepsi; he drinks Coke,\u201d Alwaleed says, with a\nlaugh.  \n The biggest difference between the two men: The investor\nfrom Omaha is worth about $32.1 billion more than the Saudi\nprince. Alwaleed\u2019s sluggish performance over the past decade\nhasn\u2019t crimped his style, though.  \n In 2012, he\u2019ll take delivery of a custom-fitted double-\ndecker Airbus A380, becoming the first private buyer of the\nworld\u2019s biggest airliner. While he may not be the world\u2019s\nrichest man, he knows how to act like he is.  \n To contact the reporter on this story: Vernon Silver in Rome at\n   vtsilver@bloomberg.net   \n          \n          \n\n\n  \n     \n       \n     \n           \n                                                 \n                     \n                     Enlarge image \n                     \n                     \n                       The cover of the June 2010 issue of Bloomberg Markets  \n                       \n                         \n                           Kingdom Holding Co. via Bloomberg \n                         \n                         The cover of the June 2010 issue of Bloomberg Markets magazine shows a photo of Saudi Prince Alwaleed Bin Talal, left, with Warren Buffett, chief executive officer of Berkshire Hathaway, at Microsoft Corp.'s 2008 CEO summit in Redmond. \n                       \n                     \n                                        \n           \n                     The cover of the June 2010 issue of Bloomberg Markets magazine shows a photo of Saudi Prince Alwaleed Bin Talal, left, with Warren Buffett, chief executive officer of Berkshire Hathaway, at Microsoft Corp.'s 2008 CEO summit in Redmond. (F)  in the race for tech-savvy drivers.  BMW and  Daimler AG (DAI) \u2019s Mercedes-Benz are adding Internet and\nsmartphone access to their vehicles as environmental concerns\nand consumer addiction to mobile devices shift the emphasis to\nhigh-tech gadgetry from horsepower.  \u201cMobile connectivity is playing an increasing role in all\nour lives,\u201d BMW sales chief  Ian Robertson  said at an event in\nMunich. \u201cThese services will continue to grow. It\u2019s a component\nof a competitive advantage.\u201d  Luxury-auto makers were slow to link their cars to the\nInternet because of concern about safety and allowing unfiltered\ndata into their vehicles. The proliferation of mobile devices\nlike  Apple Inc. (AAPL) \u2019s iPhone is changing that, while  oil prices \nabove $100 a barrel increases pressure on carmakers to find a\nselling point that isn\u2019t associated with burning fuel.  Mercedes began offering  Internet access  in vehicles for the\nfirst time this year with the upgraded C-Class and revamped SLK\nroadster. BMW last month introduced a smartphone application\nthat allows iPhone users to access playlists and browse tweets\nfrom the car\u2019s display.  Volkswagen AG (VOW) \u2019s Audi will add real-time\ntraffic data to its navigation service in  Europe  this summer. Between its November introduction and the end of March, Nintendo sold 3.45 million Wii Us. That compares with 18.6 million Wii consoles and 120 million games for it in its first year, the bank said. Through Unity, programmers get software for games and animation and other tools to adapt titles that already run on mobile devices. Unity says the Wii U kit may be released this year. Free Games  Michael Pachter , an analyst at Wedbush Securities Inc. in Los Angeles, doubts whether the Unity partnership will be enough to reinvigorate the Wii U. EU data-protection watchdogs for the first time would be\nempowered to fine companies as much as 2 percent of yearly\nglobal sales for \u201cintentionally or negligently\u201d violating the\nrules under the commission proposal. Google, Facebook and other\nInternet companies have faced investigations by regulators\naround the world as authorities grapple with how to better\npolice corporate use of personal data.  Data protection \u201cis a fundamental right\u201d that needs to be\nprotected, so \u201cif you want my data, ask me for consent,\u201d\nAlbrecht told journalists at a press conference in Brussels\ntoday. His proposal would create \u201cmore transparency\u201d on data\nhandling, individual rights and the duties of companies that\nprocess personal information.  \u2018Very Complex\u2019  \u201cWhat was already a very complex piece of draft\nlegislation has become by far the strictest, most wide-ranging\nand potentially most difficult to navigate data-protection law\never to be proposed,\u201d Eduardo Ustaran, the head of the privacy\nand information group at law firm Field Fisher Waterhouse LLP in\n London , said in a  blog  posting today. One of Kundra\u2019s goals in the initiative was to\nreplace contracts that have locked agencies into proprietary\nsystems developed and operated by a few contractors, a situation\nthat he said keeps the government\u2019s technology costs high.  Kundra estimated that $20 billion the government spends on\nfederal technology systems can be moved to the cloud, in which\nnetworks of computing resources are shared by multiple users.\nThat would account for 25 percent of the $80 billion that the\nU.S. government spends annually on information technology.  Kundra\u2019s replacement, former  Microsoft Corp. (MSFT)  executive\nSteven VanRoekel, has said he will continue Kundra\u2019s cloud\ninitiative. Kundra is now a joint fellow at the John F. (IBM)  and Microsoft, contractors that make up\n\u201ca very vibrant and healthy ecosystem,\u201d said Kundra, who\nattended last week\u2019s Dreamforce cloud-computing conference in\nSan Francisco. The event is Salesforce.com\u2019s annual conference.  Agencies should write contracts that allow them to easily\nshift data from one vendor\u2019s storage space to another, creating\ncompetition and keeping contractors\u2019 pricing transparent, Kundra\nsaid. Data transfer should be as simple as transferring contacts\nfrom one e-mail system to another, he said.  If agencies can switch cloud providers, it will create\n\u201chealthy market pressure\u201d that will keep the cost for a cloud\nservice low, David Bonnette, president of closely held\n BigMachines Inc. , a Deerfield, Illinois-based product and\nservice configuration company that uses a cloud platform, said\nin an interview.  \u2018IT Cartel\u2019  That will avoid the creation of a cloud-based version of\nwhat Kundra calls the \u201cIT cartel,\u201d a small number of\ntraditional technology contractors that make billions of dollars\na year by operating federal networks. Agencies cannot shut down\nthose systems or shift to other systems, including the cloud,\nbecause the networks run on outdated technology that makes it\ndifficult and costly to transfer the data. To contact the editor responsible for this story:\nManuela Hoelterhoff at \n mhoelterhoff@bloomberg.net .","path":".\/2008_2012_msft_bloomberg_news\/scene-in-d-c-lott-dole-howard-baker-daschles-biden.txt"},{"id":10816575,"title":"U.S. Surveillance Is Not Aimed at Terrorists","released_at":"<date>June 23 2013<\/date> <time>22:00:00<\/time>","content":"The debate over the U.S. government\u2019s monitoring of digital communications suggests that Americans are willing to allow it as long as it is genuinely targeted at terrorists. What they fail to realize is that the surveillance systems are best suited for gathering information on law-abiding citizens.  People concerned with online privacy tend to calm down when told that the government can record their calls or read their e-mail only under special circumstances and with proper court orders. The assumption is that they have nothing to worry about unless they are terrorists or correspond with the wrong people.  The infrastructure set up by the National Security Agency, however, may only be good for gathering information on the stupidest, lowest-ranking of terrorists. The Prism surveillance program focuses on access to the servers of America\u2019s largest Internet companies, which support such popular services as Skype, Gmail and iCloud. These are not the services that truly dangerous elements typically use.  Read More:   Leonid Bershidsky on  Snowden's Moscow Layover   In a January 2012  report  titled \u201cJihadism on the Web: A Breeding Ground for Jihad in the Modern Age,\u201d the Dutch General Intelligence and Security Service drew a convincing picture of an Islamist Web underground centered around \u201ccore forums.\u201d These websites are part of the Deep Web, or Undernet, the multitude of online resources not indexed by commonly used search engines.  No Data  The Netherlands\u2019 security service, which couldn\u2019t find recent data on the size of the Undernet, cited a 2003 study from the University of California at Berkeley as the \u201clatest available scientific assessment.\u201d The study found that just 0.2 percent of the Internet could be searched. The rest remained inscrutable and has probably grown since. In 2010, Google Inc. said it had indexed just 0.004 percent of the information on the Internet.  Websites aimed at attracting traffic do their best to get noticed, paying to tailor their content to the real or perceived requirements of search engines such as Google. Terrorists have no such ambitions. They prefer to lurk in the dark recesses of the Undernet.  \u201cPeople who radicalise under the influence of jihadist websites often go through a number of stages,\u201d the Dutch report said. \u201cTheir virtual activities increasingly shift to the invisible Web, their security awareness increases and their activities become more conspiratorial.\u201d  Radicals who initially stand out on the \u201csurface\u201d Web quickly meet people, online or offline, who drag them deeper into the Web underground. \u201cFor many, finally finding the jihadist core forums feels like a warm bath after their virtual wanderings,\u201d the report said.  When information filters to the surface Web from the core forums, it\u2019s often by accident. Organizations such as al-Qaeda use the forums to distribute propaganda videos, which careless participants or their friends might post on social networks or YouTube.  Communication on the core forums is often encrypted. In 2012, a French court found nuclear physicist Adlene Hicheur guilty of, among other things, conspiring to commit an act of terror for distributing and using software called Asrar al-Mujahideen, or Mujahideen Secrets. The program employed various cutting-edge encryption methods, including variable stealth ciphers and RSA 2,048-bit keys.  The NSA\u2019s Prism, according to a classified PowerPoint presentation  published  by the Guardian, provides access to the systems of Microsoft Corp. (and therefore Skype), Facebook Inc., Google, Apple Inc. and other U.S. Internet giants. Either these companies have provided \u201cmaster keys\u201d to decrypt their traffic - - which they deny -- or the NSA has somehow found other means.  Traditional Means  Even complete access to these servers brings U.S. authorities no closer to the core forums. These must be infiltrated by more traditional intelligence means, such as using agents posing as jihadists or by informants within terrorist organizations.  Similarly, monitoring phone calls is hardly the way to catch terrorists. They\u2019re generally not dumb enough to use Verizon. Granted,  Russia \u2019s special services managed to kill Chechen separatist leader Dzhokhar Dudayev with a missile that homed in on his satellite-phone signal. That was in 1996. Modern-day terrorists are generally more aware of the available technology.  At best, the recent revelations concerning Prism and telephone surveillance might deter potential recruits to terrorist causes from using the most visible parts of the Internet. Beyond that, the government\u2019s efforts are much more dangerous to civil liberties than they are to al-Qaeda and other organizations like it.  (Leonid Bershidsky is an editor and novelist based in Moscow. The opinions expressed are his own.)  To contact the writer of this article: Leonid Bershidsky at bershidsky@gmail.com. The  data  were extracted from 29,000 pages of documents and\n18 Fed-prepared Microsoft Excel spreadsheets listing more than\n21,000 transactions. The records were made public in batches on\nDec. 1, 2010, and March 31 and July 6 of this year. The Fed\nreleased some of them under the 2010 Dodd-Frank Act and the rest\nin responses to Freedom of Information Act requests by media\noutlets including Bloomberg News and related federal court\norders. The data covered money borrowed from the central bank\nfrom August 2007 through April 2010.  More than a dozen lending programs were deployed by the Fed\nin response to the crisis. From those, Bloomberg News selected\nthe seven available to a broad set of banks, brokerage firms and\nother companies. They included the Fed\u2019s discount window, the\nlast-resort lender for troubled banks, and six temporary\nmeasures: the Asset-Backed Commercial Paper Money Market Mutual\nFund Liquidity Facility; the Commercial Paper Funding Facility;\nthe Primary Dealer Credit Facility; the Term Auction Facility;\nthe Term Securities Lending Facility; and so-called single-\ntranche open market operations.  (View the Bloomberg  interactive graphic  to chart the Fed\u2019s\nfinancial bailout.)  Many firms borrowed from two or more programs through\nmultiple subsidiaries, all disclosed separately in the Fed data.\nThe central bank didn\u2019t detail how much each borrower had\noutstanding from all programs on any given day, a measure of\nvulnerability during the crisis.  Daily Total Balances  Bloomberg News combined the Fed\u2019s loan data, including the\namounts, dates and payoff deadlines, into a master Excel file to\ncalculate daily total loan balances for each parent company.  Fed officials provided Bloomberg News with early payoff\ndates for a handful of loans, which are reflected in the\nanalysis. Discount-window figures are based on daily\noutstanding-balance reports. Reports for 18 business days were\nmissing from the Fed\u2019s release. While money was likely owed\nduring those gaps, it wasn\u2019t feasible to determine how much, so\ndiscount-window balances were zeroed out for those days. As a\nresult, some companies\u2019 daily totals show sudden dips and\nspikes. In all other instances, the loans were assumed to have\nbeen paid off on their due dates.  Emergency measures that targeted specific companies -- Bear\nStearns Cos.,  American International Group Inc. (AIG) ,  Citigroup Inc. (C) \nand  Bank of America Corp. (BAC)  -- were disclosed at the time and so\nwere excluded. Loans to these companies from the other seven\nprograms were included.  TSLF Loans  Loans from the TSLF program were included only after\nborrowers exercised rights purchased from the TSLF Options\nProgram; options purchased but not used were excluded. The\nCentral Bank Liquidity Swap Lines, which lent dollars to foreign\ncentral banks so they could in turn pass on the liquidity to\ninstitutions operating in their own countries, were omitted\nbecause the companies that ultimately got those funds haven\u2019t\nbeen disclosed.  The analysis includes 394 companies that took loans from at\nleast one of the six temporary programs and 13 more that were\namong the top discount-window borrowers. About 1,600 additional\ndiscount-window borrowers were excluded because their loan\nbalances averaged less than $20 million a day.  Abbreviated Names  The Fed data identified many borrowers using abbreviated\nnames. In many instances, different banks had similar or even\nidentical names. To differentiate the institutions and determine\ntheir parents, identifying characteristics in the documents such\nas cities and Fed districts were compared with Bloomberg\u2019s\nglobal database of companies and subsidiaries, which include\nFederal Deposit Insurance Corp. and U.S. Securities and Exchange\nCommission filings.  Firms acquired during or after the financial crisis are\nlisted separately from their new parents. Loans to Merrill Lynch\n& Co., for example, weren\u2019t combined with those to Bank of\nAmerica, which purchased the New York-based brokerage on Jan. 1,\n2009. (SFLY)  The\nauctioned patents -- more than 1,100 related to the capture,\nmanipulation and sharing of digital images -- were previously\nestimated by advisory firm 284 Partners LLC to be worth as much\nas $2.6 billion.  \u201cThis is a fraction of our overall patent portfolio,\u201d\nsaid Chris Veronda, a spokesman for Rochester, New York-based\nKodak. \u201cWe retain ownership of about 9,600 other patents for\nour ongoing businesses.\u201d  The agreement resolves all patent-infringement lawsuits\nbetween Kodak and the 12 licensees, Veronda said. That includes\nsuits Kodak had against Apple, RIM, Fujifilm, HTC, Samsung and\nShutterfly. In a May filing, Kodak had said Apple alone owed it\nmore than $1 billion in patent royalties.  Competing Consortiums  Before uniting as one bidding group, Apple and Google had\nled competing consortiums bidding for Kodak\u2019s patents, people\nfamiliar with the situation said earlier this year.  The two groups joined forces in August as the initial\nauction date approached, a person familiar with the process said\ntoday. Combining allowed each company to only pay for the\npatents and protection it needed.  Unlikely partnerships occur in patent sales because they\nallow competitors to neutralize potential infringement\nlitigation. A group including Apple, Microsoft and RIM bought\nNortel Networks Corp.\u2019s more than 6,000 patents for $4.5 billion\nout of bankruptcy last year. Google lost the auction for those\npatents after making an initial offer of $900 million.  A May ruling against Kodak by the U.S. International Trade\nCommission dealt a blow to the company\u2019s pursuit of a higher\nprice for its patents. The decision, the result of a two-year\nlegal fight against Apple and RIM over a patent for previewing\ndigital images on cameras, was upheld in July. It dashed Kodak\u2019s\nplans to pursue royalty payments from Apple and RIM it once\nestimated at more than $1 billion.  Lost Interest  After the ITC ruling, bidders lost interest in buying the\npatents to pursue infringers for compensation and licensing\nfees, the person familiar with the process said today, asking\nnot to be identified because the details aren\u2019t public. The sale\nbecame defensive as buyers offered to pay only enough to cover\ntheir potential exposure to litigation with Kodak, the person\nsaid.  Kodak needed to sell the patents for at least $500 million\nunder a November agreement -- codenamed Komodo -- to obtain $830\nmillion in financing to exit bankruptcy in the first half of\n2013. That funding also requires progress in the sale of two\nbusiness units and resolution of U.K. pension obligations. The\npatent sale had to be agreed upon by Jan. 31 and must close by\nFeb. 28.  In court documents, Kodak said it had generated more than\n$3 billion in revenue by licensing some of the patents to\noutside users, including Samsung,  LG Electronics Inc. (066570) , Google\u2019s\nMotorola Mobility unit and  Nokia Oyj. (NOK1V)   Selling Businesses  Chief Executive Officer Antonio Perez has been selling\nbusinesses to shrink Kodak and fund its shift into commercial\nprinting and packaging after seeking Chapter 11 protection in\nJanuary. The company is also selling its consumer-film, photo-\nkiosk and commercial-scanner businesses and shuttering its\nconsumer inkjet-printer unit.  Kodak filed for bankruptcy after years of burning through\ncash while the rise of digital photography eroded its film\nbusiness. The company has announced almost 4,000 job cuts this\nyear and spent $3.4 billion on restructuring before bankruptcy,\nincluding payouts to fire 47,000 employees since 2003.  The 132-year-old imaging company listed $5.1 billion in\nassets and $6.75 billion in debt in its bankruptcy filing.  The bankruptcy case is In re  Eastman Kodak Co. (PG) \u2019s move this week\nto hire back A.G. Lafley as its chief executive officer recalls\nthe successful returns of former leaders from  Steve Jobs  to\n Starbucks Corp. (SBUX) \u2019s  Howard Schultz .  Yet for every  Apple (AAPL)  or Starbucks, there\u2019s a  Dell Inc. (DELL)  or\nYahoo Inc., where comebacks couldn\u2019t reverse sagging fortunes.  While bringing back an old hand isn\u2019t a guarantee of\nsuccess, it\u2019s a clear sign that something has gone haywire. In\nthe case of Cincinnati-based P&G, ex-CEO Bob McDonald struggled\nto turn around the world\u2019s largest consumer-products maker, lost\nmarket share to rivals like Unilever and was under pressure from\nactivist investor  Bill Ackman , who pushed for his exit.  \u201cIt\u2019s always an emergency when this happens,\u201d said  Jay Lorsch , a professor at  Harvard Business School  in Boston who has\nstudied boards and management for 25 years. \u201cYou don\u2019t go back\nto the old guy unless you made a mistake and it means you didn\u2019t\nhave another candidate ready to go.\u201d  Investors shouldn\u2019t lose sight of the fact that in most\ncases, even successful ones, bringing back a former leader means\nthe board failed to groom a solid successor, Lorsch said.  McDonald, 59, who was handpicked by Lafley, lowered  profit\nforecasts  three times in 2012. Ackman, who bought a stake about\nnine months ago, wanted him out.  Lots of Forewarning  \u201cThey had so much forewarning, so how could they be in\nthis spot of not having a clear successor,\u201d said  Jeffrey Sonnenfeld , senior associate dean at the Yale School of\nManagement. \u201cThis company has groomed so many top executives\nthat it\u2019s hard to understand why they\u2019re in this spot.\u201d  Now that Lafley is back, he got a vote of confidence from\nP&G shareholders: the stock rose 4 percent yesterday, the\nbiggest gain since October 2009, following the announcement of\nhis return. Codenamed \u201c Route 66 \u201d for the storied American highway, the $2.2 billion deal for Siemens\u2019s 50 percent stake in  Nokia Siemens  Networks was struck after the industrial group opted against continuing its quest for a private-equity investor, said people familiar with the situation. The owners had considered options ranging from an initial public offering or a spinoff to a buyout of the partnership by Siemens, the people said, asking not to be identified discussing confidential deliberations.  The transaction, announced yesterday, will give Nokia full control of a once-struggling provider of networking equipment whose earnings are improving as wireless carriers increase spending on high-speed data systems. It allows Siemens to part ways with a business that has accumulated 5 billion euros ($6.5 billion) in operating losses over six years and which it has long characterized as peripheral to its industrial investments.  Leading the negotiations were Siemens Chief Financial Officer Joe Kaeser and his counterpart at Nokia, Timo Ihamuotila, the people said.  Parallel Sale Process  The German company, advised by  Goldman Sachs Group Inc (GS) ., was also running a parallel process to look for a private-equity buyer, the people said. One potential option was for Siemens to buy all of Nokia Siemens Networks and to then immediately sell a majority stake to buyout firms, the people said.  While Siemens discussed a transaction with Advent International, KKR & Co. and TPG Capital, it was clear such a deal would take months to execute -- a timeline at odds with its desire to exit Nokia Siemens as soon as possible, they said. Siemens\u2019s private-equity talks also prompted Nokia to take action because the Finnish company was keen to benefit from Nokia Siemens\u2019s cash flow and rising earnings, the people said.  The two sides then reached an accord on price last week, they said.  Bloomberg News  reported the agreement late Sunday, with the companies confirming the deal seven hours later.  Schroeter\u2019s Exit  Siemens\u2019s efforts to sell its stake accelerated after Marco Schroeter, the venture\u2019s chief financial officer, was pushed out in February, a person familiar with the situation told Bloomberg News in May. Schroeter was an ally of Kaeser, the person said. The appointment of former operating chief Samih Elhage in Schroeter\u2019s place led to a deterioration in relations between Munich-based Siemens and Espoo, Finland-based Nokia, according to the person.  Nokia also favored a speedy agreement as the handset maker came under financial pressure, according to people familiar with the matter. Led by former Microsoft Corp. executive Stephen Elop, Nokia is seeking to re-orient its strategy around high-end smartphones under the Lumia series. The company\u2019s earnings and shares have been hammered by competition from  Apple Inc (AAPL) . and Samsung Electronics Co., whose iPhone and Galaxy devices are the most popular.  In announcing the deal yesterday, Nokia said its 4.5 billion euros in net cash at the end of March shrank by between 300 million euros and 800 million euros during the second quarter. Speaking on a conference call, Elop said a range of options remain open for Nokia Siemens.  Options  Those possibilities include an IPO, a stake sale to private-equity or state investors or a linkup with Alcatel-Lucent SA, said one of the people familiar with the transaction. No decision has been made, the person said.  Nokia Siemens\u2019s employee representatives have been seeking job guarantees in  Germany  as the company evaluates a potential sale of manufacturing plants in  Finland ,  India  and  China  and to outsource production, people familiar with the matter said. The plan is preliminary and may not result in a transaction.  The 1.7 billion-euro purchase price for Nokia Siemens values the venture at 3.4 billion euros. Hannu Rauhala, a Helsinki-based analyst at Pohjola Bank, estimated Nokia Siemens was worth more than 5 billion euros.  Nokia was little changed at 2:13 p.m. in Helsinki, after rising 3.7 percent yesterday. Siemens slipped 0.5 percent to 79.24 euros in  Frankfurt , after yesterday\u2019s 2.6 percent gain.  JPMorgan Financing  JPMorgan Chase & Co. (JPM) , which advised Nokia on the deal, is structuring financing for the transaction and will be seeking to syndicate its bridge loan to other banks in the coming weeks, according to people familiar with the matter. Given its financial constraints, Nokia is likely to require refinancing in the medium term, with options including the issuance of a high-yield bond or a sale of new shares being considered, the people said.  French rival Alcatel-Lucent, which closed a 2 billion-euro loan deal with Credit Suisse Group AG and Goldman Sachs earlier this year, last week sold 630 million euros in bonds that can be converted or exchanged for its stock.  James Etheridge, a spokesman for Nokia, and Philipp Encz, a Siemens spokesman, declined to comment on how the deal came together. Representatives for Advent, TPG and KKR also declined to comment.  Part of the payment under the agreement will come from a 500 million-euro secured loan from Siemens due one year after the transaction is completed.  Abandoned Talks  Nokia Siemens\u2019s parents abandoned talks with private-equity companies including TPG Capital and Gores Group LLC in 2011 after the buyout firms failed to come up with a compelling offer. The owners then said Nokia Siemens would become a more independent entity.  Private-equity firms are taking a cautious approach to the network equipment industry, which has been upended by competition from Chinese suppliers such as Huawei Technologies Co. and  ZTE Corp (763) . The Chinese companies have come to dominate  emerging markets  and make inroads into  Europe , though Nokia Siemens and Alcatel-Lucent have preserved their position in the U.S. due to security concerns.  Siemens\u2019s choice of codename for the sale of Nokia Siemens was appropriate for an asset it was eager to unload. Route 66 was a U.S. road linking  Chicago  to  Los Angeles  that was immortalized in John Steinbeck\u2019s \u201cThe Grapes of Wrath\u201d and the 1946 song \u201c(Get Your Kicks On) Route 66.\u201d Yet after being supplanted by the more modern Interstate Highway System, the road no longer exists as a single artery. More Bloomberg coverage of the 2013 Davos World Economic Forum As businesses mature or shift focus and leaders fall victim to scandal or mismanagement, the cast of roughly 2,600 at the annual gathering changes as well. More than 230 people with the title of chairman or CEO who attended in 2012 are skipping 2013, according to the attendee lists. About the same number will participate this year who weren\u2019t on the 2012 list.  \u201cYou go to Davos with an agenda, and if you feel like that agenda is not being filled, there\u2019s little reason to go,\u201d said John Kao, founder of the  Institute for Large Scale Innovation , who has attended Davos about a dozen times at the invitation of organizers and is skipping this year. \u201cIt\u2019s inconvenient to get to. There\u2019s a lot of friction. It\u2019s cold. There are a lot of people there. The logistics of just going down the street can be very daunting.\u201d  Too Busy  Kao said he didn\u2019t seek an invitation this year because he\u2019s working on a couple of e-learning startups and is too busy. When he was first building his company, which helps countries increase innovation, Davos was a good way to meet world leaders. Now he has relationships with 46 different countries.  \u201cA company gets to a point where they kind of go, \u2018OK, am I going to get much more from where I am in my growth trajectory from Davos at this point?\u201d\u2019 said Alan Marcus, senior director and head of information technology and telecommunications industry for the World Economic Forum. Some companies may skip a few years and then \u201cthey are back in because they are at a different point.\u201d  In addition to Zuckerberg, other no-shows this year include Google co-founder  Larry Page  and LinkedIn Corp. co-founder Reid Hoffman, who last made the trip in 2009, according to official lists of attendees. Google co-founder Sergey Brin was last at Davos in 2008. Evan Williams, co-founder of  Twitter Inc. (TWTR) , last went in 2010.  \u2018Tech Pioneer\u2019  \u201cGoogle came in originally as a tech pioneer, became a global growth company and became now a big substantial economic presence on the planet,\u201d Marcus said. \u201cAs any company does, of any size, they go through various stages of growth.\u201d  He said Google\u2019s shift from hosting a large, popular party at Davos to organizing private dinners is another example of the transition.  Davos gives so-called Technology Pioneers a significant discount off the normal forum membership to allow them to get a start on the world stage, Marcus said.  For two years, the pioneers pay a discounted 25,000 Swiss francs ($26,900) for an annual membership, compared with the 50,000 to 500,000 Swiss franc annual membership for larger businesses, he said. Without the discount, each attendee also has to pay 25,000 Swiss francs to attend, he said.  \u201cIt\u2019s an awesome business opportunity,\u201d said Ilja Laurs, founder and CEO of GetJar Inc., a San Mateo, California, company that operates an independent mobile applications store for smartphones. In his two years as a Technology Pioneer, 2011 and 2012, he was able to meet Vodafone Group Plc CEO Vittorio Colao and Skype co-founder  Niklas Zennstrom , among others, he said. Now that he has to pay the full amount, he\u2019s skipping.  \u2018Same People\u2019  \u201cThere are diminishing returns in terms of scale, because they tend to mostly be the same people, the chance to meet people new is less each year,\u201d Laurs said. \u201cI would say it\u2019s 25 percent less valuable each year. You realize it does cost money, and you could do something else with that money.\u201d  This year, a lot of the Technology Pioneer focus is on smaller health, security and mobile companies, Marcus said. Mc10 Inc., which makes wearable, flexible electronics for uses such as measuring the force of a blow to a hockey player\u2019s head, and Lookout Mobile Security are among those getting the discount this year, he said.  There is perhaps \u201ca little less of the social network now because we\u2019ve done that the last four or five years,\u201d he said. Now Davos is \u201clooking at some of these other challenges and trends.\u201d  Social Media  Social media pioneers such as LinkedIn and Facebook have clearly grown. Facebook has more than 1 billion users. LinkedIn just surpassed 200 million members, and Twitter scatters its 140-character prose to 140 million globally. No one from LinkedIn or Twitter was included in this year\u2019s list. LinkedIn said Hoffman isn\u2019t attending because of a scheduling conflict.  Twitter, Dropbox Inc.,  ComScore Inc. (SCOR) , Kayak Software Corp., Palantir Technologies Inc., Kaspersky Lab and Yandex NV are also among past recipients of the Technology Pioneer program, which started in 2000, Davos\u2019s Marcus said.  Focusing on new technology will ensure the next Zuckerberg or Hoffman get a chance at Davos, said Michael Useem, director of the Center for Leadership and Change Management at Wharton School of the University of Pennsylvania, who attended his first forum in 1996.  High Visibility  \u201cDavos can be a place for companies to be more visible because it\u2019s a pretty good place to strut your stuff and market a new company,\u201d said Useem, who will return this year. \u201cFor companies with brands that are already globally known, there is less need for publicity.\u201d  For larger corporations, Davos is more attractive to business-to-business companies, such as Microsoft Corp.,  Cisco Systems Inc. (CSCO)  or Dell Inc., than consumer-facing social media companies, he said. Dell CEO  Michael Dell  and Cisco CEO John Chambers are both listed as attendees this year. Microsoft Chairman Bill Gates attends on behalf of his foundation.  Facebook Chief Operating Officer Sheryl Sandberg, a co-chair of the event last year, is one of two employees of the social-networking company on this year\u2019s list, and Google has six, including Margo Georgiadis, president of Americas operations. Yahoo! Inc. CEO Marissa Mayer is participating this year and attended the past three years while at Google, according to the list.  \u201cBig, global companies, which deal with governments around the world or are concerned about issues like health care, energy and climate change, get to Davos regularly,\u201d said  William George , a professor at Harvard Business School who will attend this week.  Big Banks  Goldman Sachs Group Inc. CEO Lloyd Blankfein and Rex Tillerson, CEO of Exxon Mobil Corp., are both on the list this year. Harvard\u2019s George sits on the board of both companies. The CEOs of JPMorgan Chase & Co.,  Bank of America Corp. (BAC) , Citigroup and  Morgan Stanley (MS)  are slated to attend in 2013, as in past years.  Muhtar Kent , CEO of Coca-Cola Co., the world\u2019s largest soft drink maker, is a co-chairman of the event this year. Indra Nooyi, CEO of PepsiCo Inc., the rival beverage company and world\u2019s largest snack-food maker, is listed as an attendee.  The discussions at Davos are important to \u201ccrack the algebra of growth\u201d and help the world create sustainable business growth and sustainable job creation, Kent said at an opening press conference for the forum.  Even among established companies, fortunes and profiles at Davos will change, Marcus said. The shift in demand to mobile chips from PC chips means  Intel Corp. (INTC)  doesn\u2019t send quite as large a contingent as it did in the past, while  Qualcomm Inc. (QCOM)  has stepped up, he said.  Fortunes Shift  \u201cYou have to shift with the times and recognize that while Intel is still a massively powerful company, Qualcomm has become far more interesting. We have to accommodate and recognize that, and sometimes it does mean a shift in who is there.\u201d  Qualcomm CEO  Paul Jacobs  continues to be sought after constantly, Marcus said.  The gathering still attracts a global spotlight, with some of the largest contingents each year coming from media companies such as Thomson Reuters Corp. and Bloomberg LP, the parent of Bloomberg News. Each is sending about 11 people, among the most for any organization, according to the preliminary list.  Some companies, such as Apple Inc., never send executives. And for many CEOs, it either stops making sense or never will make sense to attend, said Jeff Sonnenfeld, senior associate dean at the Yale School of Management. He doesn\u2019t attend Davos.  Wasted Time  \u201cLarge confabs are a waste of their time because they don\u2019t need to be seen,\u201d he said. \u201cA sense of self-anointed aristocracy is not what they\u2019re looking for. They don\u2019t need the affirmation of who else is there to feel like they\u2019re significant players in the world.\u201d  The \u201celites\u201d at Davos need to focus more on looking forward to make the event more relevant, Mohamed El-Erian, CEO of Pacific Investment Management Co., said in a Bloomberg Radio interview Jan. 18.  \u201cI don\u2019t go to Davos, honestly, because I have more things to do here at Newport Beach that serves the clients,\u201d he said. \u201cI\u2019d rather read about Davos than be there and run around. It\u2019s not my type of place. I don\u2019t do well in these sorts of places. I\u2019d rather be behind the screen or in smaller groups where you can have more interesting discussions.\u201d  No-shows often reflect current events, such as the reduced number of bankers in 2009 after the global financial meltdown. Individuals in the spotlight for unfavorable reasons will skip Davos, even if they had been regular attendees, said Wharton\u2019s Useem.  Surprise Appearance  One executive who wasn\u2019t on the current official list and turned up at Davos anyway is  Steven A. Cohen , who also attended in 2011 and 2012 and was seen in the past dancing at the Google party. His SAC Capital Advisors LP hedge fund is at the center of an investigation into illegal trading activity on Wall Street. Cohen hasn\u2019t been accused by the government of any wrongdoing.  Several high-profile banking executives who lost jobs last year are understandably absent. Marcus Agius, who stepped down as chairman of Barclays Plc, and  Bob Diamond , its former CEO, were among top executives who weren\u2019t on the list to attend this year. A spokesman for Diamond didn\u2019t respond to an e-mail or phone call seeking comment.  Bank Resignations  Clemens Boersig, the former Deutsche Bank chairman, is scheduled to miss his first Davos since at least 2007 after stepping down last year. Former Citigroup CEO Pandit, who left the job in October, is also off the list after attending in 2010, 2011 and 2012. He was a co-chairman in 2012. Kaspar Villiger, chairman of UBS, stepped down in May. He attended in 2010, 2011 and 2012 and isn\u2019t on the 2013 list. Contact information for Agius and Villiger wasn\u2019t available. Pandit didn\u2019t respond to an e-mail seeking comment.  Boersig stepped down as chairman of Deutsche Bank\u2019s supervisory board at the end of May, according to a spokesman for the bank. Anshu Jain and Juergen Fitschen, the bank\u2019s co-CEOs, and Paul Achleitner, Deutsche Bank\u2019s supervisory board chairman, are scheduled to attend the gathering in Switzerland.  Pierre Duhaime, former CEO of Canada\u2019s SNC-Lavalin Group Inc., attended last year and isn\u2019t on this year\u2019s list. He was arrested and charged in November with fraud, fraud conspiracy and forgery, Quebec police said at that time. Michel Massicotte, a Montreal lawyer representing Duhaime, didn\u2019t immediately respond to a Jan. 23 e-mail seeking comment.  Reasons to stay home can be more benign. Francisco D\u2019Souza, CEO of Cognizant Technology Solutions Corp., is skipping for the first time in many years because of a knee injury, he said in an e-mailed response.  Always There  For some folks, it\u2019s still an event that can\u2019t be missed. More than 450 people were on the list of attendees for the past five years and are listed on the preliminary 2013 list, including Microsoft\u2019s Gates, Facebook\u2019s Sandberg, financier George Soros,  Volkswagen AG (VOW)  CEO Martin Winterkorn and Carlos Ghosn, CEO of Renault SA and Nissan Motor Co. About half of the people listed appear only once as attendees.  In the end, you have to want to come to Davos because attending is anything but cushy and pampering and can be intimidating, said Kathy Bloomgarden, CEO of New York public relations company Ruder Finn Inc., who has been going to the forum for the past 11 years and will attend this week.  \u201cDavos is crowded, there are transportation hassles getting there and being there, and people who don\u2019t go don\u2019t like to wander through throngs and stop to talk to people they don\u2019t know,\u201d she said. \u201cAnd you won\u2019t be staying in a luxury hotel. It\u2019s more like a camping experience in the mountains, which some CEOs don\u2019t like.\u201d  Davos Allure  Still, the allure of Davos is strong, said Innovation\u2019s Kao, who said he may be back again next year if he\u2019s invited.  \u201cDavos is a special event and sometimes it\u2019s good to take a year off, so when you go back, your palate is cleansed and you have a sharper appreciation,\u201d he said. \u201cThe idea of just going for the sake of going, because you can afford to pay the freight, doesn\u2019t seem quite as attractive because we\u2019re all very busy.\u201d  To contact the reporter on this story: Jeff Green in Southfield, Michigan, at  jgreen16@bloomberg.net . (VMW)  rose the most in eight\nmonths after Chief Executive Officer Pat Gelsinger forecast\naccelerating revenue growth, easing investor concern that he\u2019s\nnot moving swiftly enough into new businesses.  VMware\u2019s stock advanced 8.1 percent to $81.37 at the close\nin New York, the biggest gain since July 18.  EMC Corp. (EMC) , VMware\u2019s\nmajority owner, also issued an outlook for annual sales growth\nof at least 8 percent, lifting its shares by 1.8 percent to\n$24.90.  VMware\u2019s revenue will increase 15 percent in 2014 and as\nmuch as 20 percent in the following two years, the company said\ntoday at a meeting with analysts. VMware also plans an initial\npublic offering for Pivotal, a joint venture with EMC. Restructuring Plan  VMware, based in  Palo Alto ,  California , had plunged 25\npercent in the past 12 months through yesterday, and was trading\nat its lowest value  relative  to the Morgan Stanley Technology\nIndex on a price-to-earnings basis since December 2009,\naccording to data compiled by Bloomberg.  The company had issued a forecast on Jan. 28 that first-\nquarter revenue will be $1.17 billion to $1.19 billion,  below \nthe range of analysts\u2019 estimates, sending the stock down the\nmost since 2008. (MSFT)  and the freely\nvirtualization software  Xen Hypervisor  are also taking some\nshare and pushing down prices. VMware said today that Pivotal will have 1,250 employees\nand make its public market debut after about 12 months or more,\nVMware said today. Some investors are also concerned that the\nspinoff of Pivotal will rob VMware of future sales, according to\nAbhey Lamba, an analyst at Mizuho Securities USA Inc. He rates\nthe stock a buy.  The Pivotal spinoff probably benefits parent EMC more than\nVMware, and is part of a series of steps to \u201cmake a more\nefficient EMC portfolio,\u201d Staten said.  Investors will have to wait at least a quarter or two\nbefore deciding whether January\u2019s sales forecast turns out to be\na shift in the market environment or the new management team\nsetting a low bar, said Mizuho\u2019s Lamba. Delta , which handles more air freight than any other U.S.\nairline, will have a \u201cperfectly decent\u201d holiday season, Neel\nShah, cargo unit vice president, said in a Sept. 8 interview.\nShipments are \u201csolid\u201d at FedEx, the world\u2019s second-largest\npackage-shipping company, Chief Executive Officer  Fred Smith \nsaid on a Sept. 16 conference call.  \u201cIt\u2019s a lot better than last year, our orders are way\nahead,\u201d  Bruce Rockowitz , president of Hong Kong-based  Li & Fung\nLtd. , said in an interview on Sept. 17 in New York. The company\nis the biggest supplier of clothes and toys to U.S. retailers\nsuch as  Wal-Mart Stores Inc.  and  Target Corp.   Shipments are being fueled by retail inventories that are\nclose to record lows at the current sales pace, meaning stores\nmust replenish shelves ahead of the biggest shopping period of\nthe year. While the recession ended in June 2009, the loss of\nmore than 8 million jobs has prompted retailers to discount\nmerchandise to attract customers.  \u2018Better Place\u2019  \u201cWe expect a very, very competitive and aggressive\nChristmas and holiday selling season, price-focused,\u201d  William Simon , head of Wal-Mart\u2019s U.S. stores, said at an analyst\npresentation on Sept. 15. \u201cCustomers are focused on their\nsavings,\u201d and \u201cchallenged\u201d by unemployment close to a 26-year\nhigh, he said.  While \u201cnobody knows what the consumer\u2019s going to do,\u201d\nretailers, with leaner inventories this year, \u201care in a better\nplace,\u201d Li & Fung\u2019s Rockowitz said. The Baird U.S. Truck Freight Index rose 4.7\npercent, while it was down 9.4 percent in August 2009.  Constrained by Jobless  Retailers\u2019 holiday sales from November through January will\nrise 2 percent from a year earlier, according to Deloitte LLP\u2019s\nretail group, following a 1 percent gain in 2009. A year ago,\nAmericans had no plans to boost spending, which accounts for\nabout 70 percent of the economy, after retrenching during the\nworst recession since the 1930s, a Bloomberg News survey showed\nat the time.  \u201cHousehold spending is increasing gradually, but remains\nconstrained by high unemployment, modest income growth, lower\nhousing wealth, and tight credit,\u201d Federal Reserve policy\nmakers said in a statement on Sept. 21. They kept the benchmark\ninterest rate near a record low and said they\u2019re willing to ease\nmonetary policy further to spur growth.  With consumers waiting later and later to make purchases,\nretailers may step up the last-minute deals, said  Walter Todd ,\nwho helps manage $850 million at Greenwood Capital Inc. in\nGreenwood, South Carolina.  Last-Minute Deals  \u201cShippers are going to get paid regardless of whether the\nmerchandise at retailers sells,\u201d said Todd, whose holdings\ninclude shares of Wal-Mart, Target and  United Parcel Service\nInc.  \u201cIf the stock market continues to do well, and once the\nelections are over, consumers may begin to feel better, and that\ncould give a boost to holiday sales.\u201d  That indicates \u201cupside\u201d to the share price of companies\nranging from Target, the second-biggest U.S. discount retailer,\nto luxury chains  Tiffany & Co.  and  Coach Inc. , \u201cwhere there\u2019s\nrisk but potentially more reward,\u201d he said.  Target shares have gained more than 12 percent this year.\nCoach shares have gained almost 20 percent, while Tiffany has\nincreased more than 9 percent. Target gained 14 cents today to\nclose at $54.53, while shares of Tiffany gained $1.25 to $47.11\nand Coach gained $1.14 to $43.71.  Stores are restocking as their inventory-to-sales ratio\nfell to 1.33 in March and April, the lowest since comparable\nrecords began in 1992. The latest data show chains in July had\nenough goods on hand to meet 1.38 months\u2019 worth of sales at the\ncurrent pace. So that will\ngive you confidence that this holiday season should be pretty\ngood.\u201d  Richfield, Minnesota-based Best Buy Co.\u2019s stockpiles are up\n6 percent from a year earlier.  The inventory \u201cputs us in great position for the\nholidays,\u201d  Brian Dunn , chief executive officer of Best Buy, the\nworld\u2019s largest consumer-electronics retailer, said in a Sept.\n14 interview.  Success at ordering enough of the key products, without\nhaving too much left over to discount, will determine the\nseason\u2019s winners and losers. Best Buy is expanding offerings of\nApple Inc.\u2019s iPad to all its U.S. locations and devoting more\nspace to the so-called tablets category.  Toys \u2018R\u2019 Us  will operate 600 mall-based temporary stores\nfor the holidays. No, this isn\u2019t an exercise in entrapment. The insider\nknowledge I\u2019m referring to is legal. Corporate officers,\ndirectors and major shareholders must report their trades in\ntheir company\u2019s stock to the Securities and Exchange Commission\nwithin two business days.  The figures are available to anyone who wants to study\nthem. Many people don\u2019t bother, and as a money manager, I try to\ntake advantage of the prevailing neglect. This legal insider\ntrading data is one of the signals I use to decide whether to\nbuy a stock.  Dell Inc. (DELL) , once a market darling, is largely ignored by\ninvestors now. Dell stock, which traded for more than $58 when\ntechnology stocks peaked in March 2000, fetches about $15 today.  Against this gloomy backdrop,  Michael Dell , chairman and\nchief executive officer, purchased more than 10 million shares\nin March. This brought his total holding in the company he\nfounded to about 273 million shares. He owns 14 percent of the\n Round Rock , Texas-based company, a stake worth about $4.1\nbillion.  Dell doesn\u2019t actively trade shares in his own company,\ntrying to time the stock\u2019s gyrations. He is more of a patient\naccumulator.  Under Investors\u2019 Radar  I think his latest judgment is sound. While the stock\nlanguishes, the company has reported two consecutive quarters\nwith the highest quarterly earnings per share in its history.\nInvestors seem not to have noticed.  For the fiscal year that ended in January, Dell reported a\n39 percent return on stockholders\u2019 equity. Apple Inc.\u2019s\ncomparable figure is 35 percent. Yet Dell sells for only 11\ntimes earnings, a moderate multiple.  At  AOL Inc. (AOL) , the large but struggling Internet portal site\nthat was spun off from Time Warner Inc., insiders also bought\nshares last quarter. The biggest transaction was the purchase of\n477,000 shares by Timothy Armstrong, chairman and chief\nexecutive.  New York-based AOL\u2019s revenue fell in five of the past seven\nquarters. As they become more Internet-savvy, many people no\nlonger feel a need for a portal. Search engines are easy to use.\nFor those who want a portal, AOL faces competition from Yahoo\nInc. and Microsoft Corp.\u2019s MSN service.  Vote of Confidence  Armstrong\u2019s purchase, amounting to about $10 million,\nsuggests that he thinks these problems can be solved.  AOL stock looks cheap by some measures: 0.9 times book\nvalue (corporate net worth per share) and 0.9 times revenue. It\nis not cheap on earnings, however, with a price\/earnings ratio\nof 26. The balance sheet looks strong, with debt less than 4\npercent of equity.  The company suffered a loss of $7.34 a share in 2010. This\nyear, analysts expect it to bounce back and show a profit of\nabout $1 a share.  Transactions by top executives such as Dell and Armstrong\nare my favorite form of insider intelligence. I believe that\ntrades by chief executive officers and chief financial officers\nare the ones that best predict future stock movements.  Several other types of insiders must also file reports with\nthe SEC. Corporate officers, directors, and owners of 5 percent\nor more of a corporation\u2019s stock all must disclose their trades.  I view trades by these other insiders are predictive, but\nnot to the same degree as C-level executives.  Verizon\u2019s Buyback  In some cases, a company itself qualifies as an insider.\nThat happened this month with  Verizon Communications Inc. (VZ) , which\nwas buying back a chunk of its own stock.  Verizon, based in  New York , is the second-largest U.S.\ntelecommunications company by market value, after AT&T Inc. On\nApril 7, the company bought more than 17 million of its shares.  The buyback, executed when the U.S. stock market was down\nslightly as aftershocks rocked  Tokyo , is part of a larger plan.\nIn February, Verizon\u2019s board authorized the company to buy back\nas many as 100 million shares, about 3.6 percent of all\noutstanding shares, by early 2014.  Such buybacks are usually a good sign for shareholders.\nThey signal that a company\u2019s board thinks its stock is\nundervalued, and that management thinks the present moment is an\nopportune time to buy.  To me, the best thing about Verizon shares is the dividend\nyield, currently more than 5 percent. Shares fetch 14 times\nearnings, which is not too pricey.  Real Estate Play  On the negative side, the company\u2019s debt exceeds\n shareholders\u2019 equity .  General Growth Properties Inc. (GGP) , a Chicago-based real estate\ninvestment trust that owns shopping centers, emerged five months\nago from the largest real-estate bankruptcy in U.S. history.\nBefore going through bankruptcy, it owed $27 billion.  General Growth Properties\u2019 malls are home to about 24,000\nstores. The REIT is struggling to regain profitability. In 2010,\nit lost $1.4 billion, the year before, $1.3 billion. Yet this\nREIT knows how to make money: It turned a profit for 17 years in\na row before its recent rough patch.  Brookfield Asset Management Inc. (BAM\/A) , a publicly traded company\nthat invests mainly in real estate, acquired 233 million shares\nin January, almost doubling its stake. It now owns almost 24\npercent of the company. I regard Brookfield\u2019s executives as\nsmart people. The fact that they are interested in General\nGrowth makes me interested.
