(AAPL) \u2019s use of offshore tax shelters called attention to how U.S. companies lower their taxes, and underscored the difficulty Congress confronts when trying to end the practice.  Companies with multinational operations have lobbied for years to lower corporate  tax  rates in exchange for bringing some of their offshore cash home. Their efforts have been given a fresh push with the formation of new coalitions, including one organized by the Business Roundtable, an association of chief executive officers of leading U.S. companies with more than $7.3 trillion in combined annual revenues.  The hearing by the Senate Permanent Subcommittee on Investigations yesterday focused on the $102 billion in assets that Apple, the most valuable U.S. technology company, has stored in offshore entities. Apple executives defended their practices, with Chief Executive Officer  Tim Cook  saying the company complies with all laws and has no plans to repatriate earnings kept abroad.  \u201cWe pay all the taxes we owe -- every single dollar,\u201d Cook said.  Apple\u2019s appearance before the panel was intended to draw maximum attention to the flawed U.S. tax system and jump-start discussions in Congress about rewriting the  tax code , said Senator  Carl Levin , a Michigan Democrat who heads the panel. \u201cWe\u2019ve got to change this system,\u201d Levin said. \u201cIn order to change it we\u2019ve got to understand it, not deny it.\u201d  Tax Overhaul  Senator  John McCain  of Arizona, the panel\u2019s top Republican, said he and Levin are seeking to craft a bipartisan proposal that would end some tax benefits for companies, although the timing of an agreement isn\u2019t clear.  The push to rewrite tax laws has cooled as the pace of  deficit  growth has slowed and lawmakers have become preoccupied with advancing immigration law revisions and investigations of accusations that the  Internal Revenue Service  improperly gave more scrutiny to anti-tax groups seeking nonprofit status.  U.S. companies are shifting more of their revenues overseas. The nation\u2019s 83 biggest companies increased their untaxed offshore holdings by 14.4 percent to $1.46 trillion in the past year, according to data compiled by Bloomberg. The U.S. captured just 9 percent in 2010 of its federal tax revenues from companies, down from 32 percent in 1952, according to a 2011 Congressional Research Service report.  The Senate hearing was called to air accusations the iPhone, iPad and iPod maker has created a web of offshore entities to avoid paying $9 billion and more in payments.  Defending Apple  In the last four years, Apple has avoided paying taxes on $44 billion in income, McCain said. He called the company \u201cone of the biggest tax avoiders in America.\u201d  Three entities set up in Ireland hold 60 percent of Apple\u2019s profits and claim to be tax residents \u201cnowhere in the world,\u201d McCain said. \u201cIt\u2019s completely outrageous.\u201d  Another concern raised by lawmakers is that Apple paid lower taxes to the U.S. government than it reported to shareholders -- and the difference between those two amounts widened in recent years.  \u201cWhile legitimate reasons may exist for differences between a corporation\u2019s financial statements and its tax returns, the Subcommittee found large and growing differences in each of the three years it examined with respect to Apple,\u201d according to the panel\u2019s report.  Apple\u2019s federal tax provision, cited in regulatory filings, was $6.9 billion in fiscal 2011, compared with $2.5 billion reported on the company\u2019s U.S. tax returns, the report said. The difference that year was $4.4 billion, wider than $2.6 billion in fiscal 2010 and $1.4 billion two years earlier.  \u2018Awful\u2019 Code  Not all lawmakers supported summoning Apple executives to the hearing. Senator Rand Paul, a Kentucky Republican, said Apple was dealing with an \u201cawful\u201d tax code.  Apple, in written testimony, denied any wrongdoing and said the company was one of the largest taxpayers in the U.S., having paid $6 billion last year.  Cook called for a simplified U.S. corporate tax code that would allow capital to flow back to the U.S., \u201cfully recognizing that this would likely result in an increase in Apple\u2019s U.S. taxes.\u201d  The hearing \u201cclearly raises the issue that we have a broken tax system,\u201d said Claire Buchan Parker, spokeswoman for a newly formed coalition called  LIFT America . The Washington-based coalition includes  Cisco Systems Inc. (CSCO)  and  Honeywell International Inc. (HON) , and advocates for a simplified U.S. tax code with rates comparable to other countries.  \u2018Clear\u2019 Rules  \u201cWe need to have a tax code that allows these companies to compete and win internationally because that\u2019s actually tremendously helpful for U.S. workers,\u201d Buchan Parker said in a phone interview.  The coalition doesn\u2019t have a formal position on what the U.S. tax rate should be on companies that repatriate foreign earnings. Rather, the group believes the current 35 percent corporate tax rate is too high and supports a hybrid system that has \u201cclear, manageable rules to ensure that companies pay their taxes at home and abroad,\u201d Buchan Parker said.  The  Business Roundtable , based in Washington and representing international brand names like  The Coca-Cola Co. (KO)  and  Microsoft Corp. (MSFT) , has started a lobbying campaign called  The Campaign for Home Court Advantage  to advance lower rates.  Companies owe U.S. taxes on income they earn around the world after receiving credit for foreign taxes paid. Under U.S. tax law, companies can defer U.S. taxation of profits earned outside the country until they bring the money back. Then, they must pay corporate taxes of as much as 35 percent minus tax credits for payments to foreign governments.  Tax Holiday  The current system has led companies, including  Google Inc. (GOOG)  and Pfizer Inc., to keep foreign profits outside the U.S. Those companies and others lobbied Congress unsuccessfully in 2011 for a temporary tax holiday on repatriated profits.  \u201cWe can\u2019t solve this problem on our own by punishing our companies,\u201d said Robert Atkinson, president of The  Information Technology  and Innovation Foundation, a nonpartisan research group in Washington.  The chances for a broad tax deal may be as good as they\u2019ve been, mainly because key lawmakers want it as part of their legacy, Atkinson said in a phone interview. \u201cI do think the stars are aligned better than they\u2019ve been in 25 years for corporate  tax reform ,\u201d he said. \u201cThat doesn\u2019t mean it\u2019s going to happen.\u201d  Good Timing  Senator  Max Baucus , a Montana Democrat who heads the Senate Finance Committee, isn\u2019t seeking re-election and Republican Representative  Dave Camp  of Michigan, who heads the House Ways and Means Committee, will lose his chairmanship because of term limits. Both men want to pass a tax-code revision package.  Political and institutional barriers complicate their efforts.  \u201cCutting taxes for corporations doesn\u2019t sound really good politically\u201d amid a \u201ctight budgetary environment,\u201d said Curtis Dubay, a senior tax policy analyst at the Heritage Foundation, a Washington-based group headed by former Republican Senator  Jim DeMint  of South Carolina. \u201cObama is just not going to sign into law a bill that cuts taxes for corporations,\u201d Dubay said.  President  Barack Obama  has proposed a revenue-neutral tax overhaul that would lower the corporate rate to 28 percent from 35 percent. Republicans are pushing for a deeper reduction.  If an agreement can be reached on how much to cut the rate, that move would be paired with elimination of some other tax provisions used by companies to reduce their payments. U.S. corporations received $181 billion in income tax breaks in 2011, about as much as they paid in taxes, according to a report last month by the Government Accountability Office in Washington.  \u2018Political Differences\u2019  Cutting tax preferences means \u201cyou have to take away some benefits that are currently there,\u201d said Robert Pozen, a senior fellow in economic studies at the  Brookings Institution , another Washington-based think tank.  There also are \u201cbig political differences\u201d between lawmakers who want to impose a 35 percent tax on corporate income and those who want to adopt a territorial tax system that would impose a lighter tax burden on companies\u2019 foreign income, Pozen said. \u201cThat\u2019s a pretty big gap,\u201d he said.  Camp\u2019s committee this year will consider a measure that would implement a territorial tax system and also call for profits to return to the U.S. at a 5.25 percent tax rate.  No Consensus  The business community also lacks a consensus on how to amend the tax code. Companies that operate only in the U.S. have less interest in how overseas earnings are taxed than multinational corporations, especially those that secure favorable tax treatment through intangible properties like patents and intellectual property, Pozen said.  \u201cThere are a lot of differences among companies as to what\u2019s the best strategy\u201d for amending tax laws, he said.  While there\u2019s a consensus that corporate tax rates should go down, the challenge is doing so in the context of a broader tax restructuring, said Edward Kleinbard, a tax law professor at the University of  Southern California  and a former chief of staff of the congressional Joint Committee on Taxation.  \u201cWhat\u2019s really hard is to do a corporate bill on a stand-alone basis when, at the moment, people see it as wrapped up in a larger tax reform package,\u201d Kleinbard said. Google Inc. (GOOG)  is buying Motorola Mobility Holdings\nInc., many observers say, so it can integrate hardware and\nsoftware to be like Apple (and to enlarge its patent pool).  Last week,  Joel Ewanick , the global chief marketing officer\nat General Motors,  declared  that \u201cit\u2019s time to clearly\ndifferentiate our brand and align closer to a true global brand\nlike Apple.\u201d Translation: We want to be like Apple.  Apple has topped Fortune magazine\u2019s list of \u201cMost Admired\nCompanies\u201d four years running. This month it was briefly the\nmost valuable company in the world. Even holding the No. 2\nmarket capitalization is pretty amazing for a company that\nalmost died in 1997, when it was valued at less than $3 billion.  To many people, Apple\u2019s success seems like magic. Others\nattribute it to cool products, good marketing, and  Steve Jobs \u2019s\ncharisma or presentation skills. Critics credit the Apple co-\nfounder\u2019s ability to project a \u201c reality distortion field .\u201d  In his new book \u201cGood Strategy, Bad Strategy: The\nDifference and Why It Matters,\u201d  Richard P. Rumelt , a strategy\nprofessor at UCLA\u2019s Anderson School of Management, offers\nanother explanation: the ruthless execution of good strategy.  Strategy is not what many people think it is. It is not a\nfill-in-the-blanks mission statement blathering about how XYZ\nCorp. will ethically serve its stakeholders by implementing\nbest-in-class integrated sustainable practices to grow as a\nglobal leader while maximizing shareholder value. Such bafflegab\nis  \u201cDilbert\u201c-fodder  that generates cynicism and contempt. It\nis, at best, a big waste of time.  Neither is strategy a declaration that the ABC Co. will\nincrease sales by 20 percent a year for the next five years,\nwith a profit margin of at least 20 percent. Strategy is not the\nresolve to hunker down and try harder -- what Kenichi Ohmae of\nMcKinsey criticized in a 1989 Harvard Business Review  article  as\n\u201cdo more better.\u201d Effort is not strategy. Neither are\nfinancial projections. And neither are wishes.  A strategy \u201cis a way of dealing with a high-stakes\nchallenge,\u201d Rumelt told me in an interview. \u201cIt\u2019s a way around\nthe obstacles or problems in a difficult situation.\u201d  Every good strategy, he writes, includes what he calls the\nkernel: a \u201cdiagnosis\u201d of the challenge (\u201cWhat\u2019s going on\nhere?\u201d), a \u201cguiding policy\u201d for dealing with that challenge\n(the core idea often called a strategy), and a set of \u201ccoherent\nactions\u201d to carry out that policy (the implementation).  For his friend Stephanie\u2019s corner grocery, Rumelt writes,\nthe diagnosis was competition from a large 24-hour supermarket,\nthe guiding policy was \u201cto serve the busy professional who has\nlittle time to cook,\u201d and the coherent actions included\nstocking more prepared meals and opening an extra checkout stand\nat 5:00 p.m.  This strategy not only told Stephanie what to do but what\nshe had to stop doing. Selling more prepared meals meant taking\nspace away from the munchies for her many student customers. To\nfocus labor expenses on the peak times for her professional\ncustomers, she closed earlier, meaning no sales from late-night\nstudy breaks. \u201cStrategy is scarcity\u2019s child and to have a\nstrategy, rather than vague aspirations, is to choose one path\nand eschew others,\u201d writes Rumelt.  A strategy is not a goal like maximizing  shareholder value \nor keeping America safe from terrorism. It\u2019s not even a plan. It\nis a design -- a coherent approach to defining and solving a\nparticular problem, in which the different elements have to work\ntogether.  In this analysis, Steve Jobs is not only a connoisseur and\nsponsor of good design. He is himself a successful designer --\nnot of products but of business strategies.  Apple\u2019s recent success has made people forget not only how\nclose the company came to failing but also what Jobs did to turn\nit around when he returned as chief executive in 1997. He\ndiagnosed Apple\u2019s problem: It was hemorrhaging cash and its\nproduct lineup was too diverse, confusing and expensive.  In response, Rumelt explains, Jobs \u201credesigned the whole\nbusiness logic around a simplified product line sold through a\nlimited set of outlets.\u201d He cut product offerings down to two:\na desktop and a laptop, and no peripherals. He moved most\nmanufacturing to  Taiwan , cut software development, and\neliminated all but one national retailer, opening a Web store to\nsell directly to consumers.  And, yes, Jobs also got  Microsoft Corp. (MSFT)  to invest $150\nmillion in Apple and to commit to continuing to make Mac\nversions of key software. But that agreement wouldn\u2019t have\nhelped much without the rest of the strategy. \u201cI don\u2019t know how\nhe learned that ruthlessness,\u201d Rumelt says. But it worked.  What Jobs did not do, the book suggests, is equally\ntelling. He avoided all the management responses that masquerade\nas strategies. \u201cHe did not announce ambitious revenue or profit\ngoals; he did not indulge in messianic visions of the future,\u201d\nRumelt writes. \u201cAnd he did not just cut in a blind ax-wielding\nfrenzy.\u201d  The organization\u2019s new, coherent design bought the company\ntime and gave it a clear identity on which to build. Apple\u2019s\ngutsy decision to open its own retail stores in 2001 made sense\nonly in the context of its new strategy.  Rumelt, who is a business consultant as well as one of the\nmost-cited scholars in his field, met Jobs in 1998, while\nworking for  Telecom Italia SpA. (TIT)  Rumelt congratulated Jobs on the\nturnaround but expressed skepticism about Apple\u2019s chances of\novercoming the Windows-Intel lock on personal computers. \u201cWhat\nare you going to do in the longer term?\u201d Rumelt asked. \u201cWhat\u2019s\nthe strategy?\u201d  Jobs, he recalls, \u201cjust smiled and said, \u2018I am going to\nwait for the next big thing.\u2019\u201d  Jobs recognized that Apple couldn\u2019t change the realities of\nthe PC business. It needed a change in the environment that\nwould make possible a new strategy, oriented toward growth this\ntime rather than survival. He found that opportunity with the\niPod and online music.  \u201cStrategy is not a magic potion for overcoming any\nobstacle,\u201d says Rumelt. \u201cThe part that\u2019s hard to write about,\nthat people reject, that they don\u2019t want to hear me say, is that\nyou may be facing an obstacle you can\u2019t deal with. Choose a\ndifferent obstacle. Play games you can win.\u201d  Rumelt says he was motivated to write his book in part\nbecause he believes \u201cbad strategy\u201d -- or, perhaps more\naccurately, pseudo-strategy or even anti-strategy -- has become\nincreasingly pervasive, not only in business but in all sorts of\nnon-commercial organizations. Feeling obliged to articulate a\n\u201cstrategy\u201d (or compelled to by orders from the board or\nCongress), people cook up statements that lack the clear-eyed\nanalysis, real choices and coherent actions that good strategy\ndemands.  For example, in 2008 the  Los Angeles Unified School\nDistrict  adopted seven  \u201ckey strategies,\u201d  including to \u201cbuild\nschool and District leadership teams that share common beliefs,\nvalues and high expectations for all adults and students and\nthat support a cycle of continuous improvement to ensure high-\nquality instruction in their schools.\u201d  That is a hope, a goal, or perhaps a prescription for North\nKorean-style totalitarian conformity. Whatever it is, the\nstatement is not a strategy. It offers no guide to action. It is\nall too typical of \u201cstrategy\u201d -- in the private sector as well\nas the government, in huge multinational corporations and small\nlocal charities.  Bad strategy, Rumelt writes, goes wrong in four common\nways. Many bad strategies are just superficial nonsense\nexpressed in big words, which Rumelt very politely calls\n\u201cfluff.\u201d Others fail to define the challenge. Some mistake\ngoals or wishes, for strategy. And some set impossible\nobjectives rather than focusing on modest but achievable ones.  Even when it doesn\u2019t lead to bad decision-making, Rumelt\nargues, formulating bad strategy hurts organizations. \u201cYou use\nup the psychological and intellectual resources that could be\nused for figuring out what we should actually be doing around\nhere, creating these things,\u201d he told me. \u201cIf the very top\nmanagement of the company puts together a retreat for the top 50\nexecutives and what they come out with is a financial forecast,\nthat\u2019s a misuse of the knowledge and energy in the group.\u201d  So if you really want to be like Apple, drop the fluff-\nfilled vision statements and magical wishes. Pretend your\ncompany\u2019s existence is at stake, coldly evaluate the\nenvironment, and make choices. Stop thinking of strategy as\nmeaningless verbiage or financial goals and treat it as a\nserious design challenge.  (Virginia Postrel is a Bloomberg View columnist. (MSFT) , the city said.  The New York Police Department worked with Redmond,\nWashington-based Microsoft, the world\u2019s biggest software maker,\nto develop the Domain Awareness System, which aggregates and\nanalyzes information from cameras, license-plate readers,\nsensors and law enforcement databases, according to a statement\ntoday from Mayor  Michael Bloomberg \u2019s office.  \u201cThe system is a transformative tool because it was\ncreated by police officers for police officers,\u201d NYPD\nCommissioner Raymond Kelly said in the statement.  The system was unveiled by Bloomberg and Kelly at the\nheadquarters of the Lower  Manhattan  Security Initiative a few\nblocks south of  Wall Street , where personnel from the NYPD and\nits partners examine feeds from surveillance cameras, alerts\nfrom license-plate readers and reports from 911 calls.  There are about 3,000 closed-circuit television cameras\nconnected to the Domain Awareness System, most of which are\nlocated in lower and midtown Manhattan, along with 2,600\nradiation detectors carried by officers on patrol and several\nhundred license-plate readers mounted on police cars and\ndeployed at bridges, tunnels and streets, Bloomberg said.  Instant Information  The system allows investigators to instantly see\ninformation including arrest records, 911 calls associated with\na suspect and related crimes occurring in a particular area,\naccording to the statement. It also allows investigators to map\ncrimes to reveal patterns and track where a car associated with\na suspect is located and has been in the past.  It also helps in counterterrorism efforts, such as allowing\nthe NYPD to examine video feeds to determine who left a\nsuspicious package at a location or help assess whether a\nradiation detector was set off naturally, by a weapon or by a\nharmless isotope used in medical treatments.  Under the agreement, the city will receive 30 percent of\ngross revenue on future sales of the system, which cost about\n$30 million to $40 million to develop, said Jessica Tisch,\ndirector of policy and planning for the NYPD\u2019s counterterrorism\nbureau.  \u201cWe realized we had the opportunity to create a powerful\nand coordinated domain awareness system to help us combat both\nterrorism and conventional crime,\u201d Kelly said at a press\nconference. \u201cNot just dealing with the matters in financial\nsystem, but citywide by coordinating our alert systems with vast\namounts of data. The system allows us to connect the dots by\ninstantly tapping into the details of crime records, 911 calls,\nlicense plate readers, videotape footage and more.\u201d  \u2018Our Expenses\u2019  Bloomberg said that selling the system to other cities may\nallow  New York  to \u201crecoup all of our expenses over a period of\ntime and maybe even make a few bucks.\u201d  Tisch showed how the system worked to alert officers to a\n911 report of a suspicious package -- a box with Jack Daniel\u2019s\nwhiskey markings found outside a Union Square theater a few days\nago -- and allow them to call up cameras within 500 feet to\ndetermine when the package was left and by whom. The package\nturned out to be trash that had blown away from another\nlocation.  \u201cThe idea is to get the information out into the field as\nquickly as possible,\u201d Tisch said.  Privacy advocates such as the  American Civil Liberties\nUnion , which has  asked  police departments and agencies in 38\nstates to provide information on how they use license-plate\nreaders, said the system may give the police information on\ninnocent  New Yorkers .  New Yorkers  \u201cWe fully support the police using technology to combat\ncrime and terrorism, but law-abiding New Yorkers should not end\nup in a police database every time they walk their dog, go to\nthe doctor or drive around Manhattan,\u201d Christopher Dunn,\nassociate legal director of the New York Civil Liberties Union,\nsaid in a statement.  The mayor pointed out that the private sector has used\nsimilar technology for a long time, and that many buildings\nalready have security cameras posted inside and at entrances and\nexits. He also said facial recognition isn\u2019t being used in New\nYork\u2019s system.  \u201cThe bad guys have everything that we do too and if you\nreally want to worry about security and freedoms, that\u2019s the\nfirst thing,\u201d Bloomberg said. \u201cThere\u2019s a lot of evidence that\nthere are a lot of bad guys around the world that are devoting a\nlot more resources than we are to taking away our freedoms.\u201d  The mayor is the founder and majority owner of Bloomberg\nLP, the parent company of Bloomberg News. As some members of Congress condemned the program as an intrusion in the lives of innocent Americans, the White House said Congress was regularly updated and all rules were followed. Lawmakers confirmed they knew of the classified court order compelling  Verizon Communications Inc. (VZ)  to provide data on its customers\u2019 calls, continuing a George W. Bush administration policy that sparked a national controversy.  The publication of the secret court order by the U.K.-based Guardian newspaper renewed a political debate that has repeatedly flared since the Sept. 11, 2001, attacks about the proper balance between traditional American civil liberties and protection against terrorist threats. It came as President  Barack Obama  is being challenged over his regard for individual privacy and constitutionally guaranteed freedom of the press.  The Justice Department, as part of its inquiries into leaks of national-security information, has also obtained secret search warrants for telephone records of journalists from the Associated Press and Fox News, prompting protests from U.S. lawmakers and media-advocacy groups.  FBI Request  The telephone surveillance, sought by the Federal Bureau of Investigation and approved by the court on April 25, requires Verizon to provide the National Security Agency with information about calls inside the U.S. and between the U.S. and other countries on a daily and \u201congoing\u201d basis. The NSA runs computer centers for analyzing huge databases.  The  Washington  Post reported this evening that the NSA and FBI also are tapping directly into the central servers of nine leading U.S. Internet companies, capturing audio, video, photographs, e-mails, documents and connection logs. The Post said the operation, which began in 2007, has grown exponentially and become the most prolific contributor to the president\u2019s daily intelligence briefing, providing raw material for almost 1 in 7 intelligence reports.  Microsoft Corp. (MSFT) ,  Yahoo! Inc. (YHOO) ,  Google Inc. (GOOG) ,  Facebook Inc (FB) ., PalTalk,  AOL Inc. (AOL) , Skype Technologies SA, Google\u2019s YouTube, and  Apple Inc. (AAPL)  participate in the program, the Post reported. The White House did not immediately return telephone and e-mail requests for comment.  Disrupting Plots  White House deputy press secretary  Josh Earnest , commenting earlier today on the telephone surveillance program to reporters traveling with Obama on Air Force One, said any such monitoring is carried out \u201cwith the knowledge and oversight of Congress.\u201d It doesn\u2019t include listening to telephone calls, and he said the president\u2019s paramount goal is to \u201cdisrupt plots that may exist.\u201d  Earnest said the data collected relates to call details, such as the telephone numbers of the caller and recipient and the length of their conversation. Neither he nor lawmakers would say whether the government monitors calls through other telephone companies, though outside analysts said that was probably the case.  Senate Intelligence Committee Chairman Dianne Feinstein, a California Democrat, and Senator Saxby Chambliss of  Georgia , the panel\u2019s top-ranking Republican, told reporters that the surveillance is legal and that they have been kept informed under the law. The court order lasts three months and was a regular renewal of the legal authority, which has been going on for seven years, Chambliss said.  Attacks Thwarted  \u201cTerrorists will come after us if they can, and the only thing we have to protect us is good intelligence,\u201d Feinstein said.  House Intelligence Committee Chairman Mike Rogers, a Michigan Republican, said telephone records collected under the surveillance program were used to thwart a \u201csignificant\u201d terrorist plot within the \u201cthe last few years.\u201d He declined to provide any details on the incident.  Some lawmakers blasted the breadth of the domestic surveillance. Senator Charles Schumer, a New York Democrat, demanded an explanation for a program he called \u201cinvasive.\u201d  \u201cOne thing I have not heard is what the explanation is for needing to do this,\u201d Schumer told reporters.  Senator  Rand Paul , a Kentucky Republican, called the program \u201can astounding assault\u201d on the U.S. Constitution.  \u2018New Low\u2019  \u201cAfter revelations that the Internal Revenue Service targeted political dissidents and the Department of Justice seized reporters\u2019 phone records, it would appear that this administration has now sunk to a new low,\u201d Paul said in a  statement  posted on his congressional website.  The order from the Foreign Intelligence Surveillance Court covers telephone numbers as well as the location and duration of calls, according to the order published by the Guardian and posted  on its website .  Feinstein and Chambliss, briefing reporters, said the information collected is dumped into a government-maintained database and then used to respond to specific threats.  The surveillance program creates \u201ca telephone book\u201d of data and cannot be accessed without \u201creasonable, articulable suspicion that the records are relevant and related to terrorist activity,\u201d Feinstein said.  Senate Majority Leader Harry Reid, a Nevada Democrat, joined them in defending the monitoring, saying it wasn\u2019t new.  \u201cEverybody should just calm down,\u201d Reid said.  Obama \u2018Responsibility\u2019  His counterpart in the House, Republican Speaker John Boehner of  Ohio , said Obama should explain to the American people what he\u2019s doing that requires the intrusion. Obama has the \u201cresponsibility to outline what these tools are and how they are being used,\u201d Boehner told reporters in Washington.  Representative James Costa, a California Democrat, told a Bloomberg Government breakfast this morning that the monitoring of telephone data \u201ctests the faith and credibility of Americans about our government.\u201d  Former vice president and Democratic presidential candidate Al Gore criticized the monitoring in a message to Twitter followers: \u201cIn digital era, privacy must be a priority. Is it just me, or is secret blanket surveillance obscenely outrageous?\u201d  The disclosure may put further pressure on U.S. Attorney General Eric Holder, who is under fire for targeting reporters in the crackdown on leaks. It also may weigh on the nomination of Obama\u2019s choice as the next FBI director, James B. Comey.  Disclosure Sought  Privacy-rights advocates issued swift protests upon learning of the Guardian report, calling the data collection an intrusion on millions of Americans. The American Civil Liberties Union called for the Obama administration to halt the program and disclose its scope and asked Congress to investigate.  Paul Bresson, an FBI spokesman, and Verizon spokesman Ed McFadden declined to comment.  The Verizon data-collection order was signed 10 days after the Boston Marathon bombing killed three people and injured more than 260 in the highest-profile terrorist incident on U.S. soil since 2001. U.S. agencies vastly expanded surveillance efforts during the past 12 years in a bid to avoid a repeat of the attacks on New York and the Pentagon.  The Bush administration started the so-called Terrorist Surveillance Program in the aftermath of the Sept. 11 attacks, when agencies began secretly conducting electronic surveillance on U.S. phone calls and e-mails without court warrants.  2008 Law  Congress passed a law in 2008 codifying parts of the program and authorizing intelligence agencies to get broad electronic surveillance orders from the Foreign Intelligence Surveillance Court.  That law, updating the more than three-decade-old Foreign Intelligence Surveillance Act, lets intelligence agencies monitor the e-mail, Internet activity and phone calls of non-U.S. citizens reasonably believed to be located outside the U.S. and involved in terrorist activities or other crimes. Congress voted last year to extend it until the end of 2017.  \u201cWe\u2019ve been saying for over a decade that the law is incredibly broad and could be interpreted to allow something like this, but people didn\u2019t believe it,\u201d said Michelle Richardson, legislative counsel of the ACLU. \u201cNow that there is hard proof, hopefully this will force Congress to take a look at it.\u201d  Law Challenged  The Supreme Court has never ruled on the constitutionality of such a sweeping surveillance program. In February, the court voted 5-4 to bar a challenge by lawyers and civil rights activists to a federal law that allows government wiretapping of international phone calls and e-mails.  The majority didn\u2019t rule on the surveillance program itself, instead saying the opponents lacked \u201cstanding\u201d to sue because they hadn\u2019t shown they were being harmed.  In 2012, there were 212 such FISA orders, known as \u201cbusiness records requests,\u201d according to a letter from the Justice Department to Reid. The letter doesn\u2019t specify the targets or scope of the requests.  The Guardian report marks the first time since broad surveillance was authorized in 2008 that an unredacted order has come to light.  \u201cIt confirms the worst fears that these tools are not being used in a targeted manner just against suspected terrorists and spies,\u201d Richardson said.  Senators led by Paul and Oregon Democrat Ron Wyden tried and failed to amend last year\u2019s legislation extending FISA so it would have included what they said were needed provisions to protect the constitutional rights of U.S. citizens.  \u201cThis sort of widescale surveillance should concern all of us and is the kind of government overreach I\u2019ve said Americans would find shocking,\u201d Senator Mark Udall, a Colorado Democrat, said in an e-mailed statement. (DELL)  marks the return of credit-busting takeovers as the\ncost of financing the deals gets ever cheaper.  The cost to protect against losses on  Quest Diagnostics\nInc. A benchmark gauge of U.S. corporate credit risk rose on\nthe speculation, according to Bank of America Merrill Lynch\ncredit strategists.  Record-low borrowing costs in the market for junk bonds,\nwhere LBOs are financed, is combining with rising confidence in\nthe financial system to boost bets that a successful Dell deal\nwill be followed by others. Private-equity funds have $360\nbillion of committed unspent capital dedicated to buyout funds\nin the global market, according to data from London-based\nresearch firm Preqin Ltd., providing plenty of firepower for\nmore LBOs.  \u201cIt\u2019s really now that, for the first time, uncertainty has\ndeclined so much that private equity firms have the confidence\nto pull off LBO deals,\u201d Bank of America Merrill Lynch credit\nstrategist Hans Mikkelsen said in a telephone interview. The measure typically falls as investor confidence improves\nand rises as it deteriorates. The contracts pay the buyer face\nvalue if a borrower fails to meet its obligations, less the\nvalue of the defaulted debt. A basis point equals $1,000\nannually on a contract protecting $10 million of debt.  The U.S. two-year interest-rate swap spread, a measure of\ndebt-market stress, increased 1.07 basis points to 16.44 basis\npoints as of 11:31 a.m. in New York. The gauge widens when\ninvestors seek the perceived safety of government securities and\nnarrows when they favor assets such as company debentures.  \u2018Tough Road\u2019  Bonds of  Charlotte , North Carolina-based Bank of America\nCorp. are the most active dollar-denominated corporate\nsecurities today, accounting for 5.7 percent of the volume of\ndealer trades of $1 million or more as of 11:31 a.m. in New\nYork, according to Trace, the bond-price reporting system of the\nFinancial Industry Regulatory Authority. Leveraged loans and high-yield, high-risk bonds\nare rated below Baa3 at Moody\u2019s Investors Service and lower than\nBBB- at S&P.  Issuance of collateralized loan obligations, which group\nhigh-yield, high-risk loans and slice them into securities of\nvarying risk and return, peaked in 2007, pooling about $105\nbillion to invest in junk-grade loans, according to Wells Fargo\n& Co., which estimates that as much as $80 billion could be\nraised this year. That would surpass the $55 billion of new CLOs\nin 2012, which topped the bank\u2019s original forecast for just $12\nbillion in 2012.  Record Pace  Investors have funneled cash into junk bonds at a record\npace, pushed into higher-risk assets as the Federal Reserve\nholds benchmark interest rates between zero and 0.25 percent and\nbuys back bonds to suppress borrowing costs. (ADBE) \u2019s customers prey to hackers simply\nwasn\u2019t a top company priority.  At Adobe, whose Acrobat and Reader programs for creating\nand viewing PDF documents sit on most of the planet\u2019s personal\ncomputers, \u201csecurity never made the list,\u201d says Brad Arkin,\nsenior director of security for products and services at the San\nJose, California-based company.  Then, in 2009, what became known as the JBIG2 flaw created\nan existential crisis for the company. For the first time,\nhackers were found to be using a crack in the armor of Acrobat\nand Reader to infiltrate major corporations and Adobe had no\navailable fix.  \u201cThat was the big wake-up call,\u201d Arkin says. \u201cWe needed\nto make some big changes to protect our users.\u201d  The company realized it had to defend itself against a new,\nsophisticated type of hacker-spy targeting the software\u2019s\ncorporate users and their secrets, Arkin says.  In one instance, attackers used the JBIG2 defect to get\naccess to the computer of a  Coca-Cola Co. (KO)  executive in  China \nthrough an infected Adobe PDF they e-mailed to her, according to\nan internal Coca-Cola document obtained by Bloomberg. The\nbeverage maker was involved in what would have been the largest\nforeign takeover of a Chinese company at the time.  After finding there were too many imperfections to fix,\nArkin says he instead erected a virtual wall around the\nprograms, and focused on keeping that defense intact.  Eschewing Vigilance  It might not be enough.  \u201cImagine a castle wall as long as the Great Wall of\nChina,\u201d says Kyle Randolph, a former senior manager of product\nsecurity at Adobe, who worked there from 2008 until this year.\n\u201cAll you need is one hole and the whole thing is compromised.\u201d  Flaws  in the ubiquitous software on PCs, tablets and\nsmartphones have empowered cyber intruders and plagued\nbusinesses, governments and political dissidents with sabotage,\ntheft and physical attacks, a year-long series by  Bloomberg News \nshows. In part, it is the legacy of companies that eschewed\nvigilance, putting profit before safety.  That it took a series of attacks on corporate customers to\nshock the U.S. software company into making security a priority\nhelps illustrate why today -- two decades after the Internet age\ntook off -- computer users are at risk whenever and wherever\nthey\u2019re online.  Protective Walls  Products used on virtually all computers, from Adobe,  Apple\nInc. (AAPL) ,  Microsoft (MSFT)  Corp. and  Oracle Corp. (ORCL) , consistently dominate\nindustry rankings of programs most vulnerable to attack. The\nresulting Swiss cheese of imperfections has made every citizen a\npotential crack in the security walls meant to protect their\ngovernments, employers and anyone with whom they do business.  Across the industry, software makers say they are taking\nsecurity seriously and making improvements to address the\nincreasingly sophisticated hacker threat. For instance,\nMicrosoft and Adobe have made it easier for users to get updates\nthat patch defects, and Google Inc. fends off attacks by\nencrypting traffic on its Gmail service.  Adobe\u2019s Arkin says the company\u2019s strategy makes the\nsoftware easier to defend by requiring it to safeguard about\n8,000 lines of code that hackers could use to breach the\nprotective wall, instead of tens of millions of lines in the\nunderlying programs. While the programs won\u2019t be perfect\nforever, Adobe is working to keep ahead of the hackers by making\ntheir jobs harder and more expensive, Arkin says. \u201cOur end goal\nis to protect users of our software,\u201d he says.  Chamber Resistance  The flaws have nevertheless flourished in the absence of\nindustry standards or product liability.  Attempts to force the architects of the Internet to improve\nthe safety of users have so far failed, in part because the U.S.\nChamber of Commerce has pushed back on behalf of its business\nmembers. It helped defeat a cyber security bill backed by the\nWhite House this year that included regulation of the small\nfraction of corporate computer systems that, if hacked, could\ncause mass casualties or economic damage. Chamber lobbyists cast\nthe bill as unnecessary and overreaching, and said government\nmeddling would only make the problem worse.  In response to questions about its opposition to the bill,\nthe Chamber provided a letter it sent last month to the  U.S.\nSenate , favoring a \u201cworkable\u201d bill focused on information\nsharing, and voicing \u201cserious concerns\u201d about government\ninterference with the private sector.  U.S. Defense Secretary  Leon Panetta  invoked Pearl Harbor in\nan Oct. 11 speech warning that extremist groups or a rival\nnation might use cyber tools to attack.  Lagging Security  In America and the U.K., about 1-in-3 computer users had\ncontact with malicious software, just between July and September\nthis year, according to data Moscow-based anti-virus software\nmaker  Kaspersky Lab  collected from its customers.  The implications of lagging security go beyond PCs to\ncritical infrastructure and industry, such as power grids and\nrailroads, and to increasingly networked lives, including phone\nsystems and videoconferencing that run over the Internet.  \u201cSooner or later, the people who are exploiting these\nsecurity flaws will go from stealing information to breaking\nsystems -- because they can -- and then it\u2019s going to be obvious\nto everybody how bad things are,\u201d says Stewart Baker, former\ngeneral counsel for the  National Security Agency , the U.S. spy\nagency, which monitors foreign communications.  Global Abuses  Increasing the security of millions of lines of code\nunderlying some of the world\u2019s most popular software would be\ntime-consuming and expensive. Behind closed doors, software\nmakers consistently argue that while consumers may appreciate\nmore security, there is little evidence they\u2019d sacrifice\nfunctionality, time-to-market or cost to get it, according to\nthree policy makers who regularly attend meetings with software\ncompany chief executive officers. They asked not to be named\nbecause the meetings were confidential.  In a series of stories that showed the global abuses and\ncosts of cyber weapons and espionage, Bloomberg News uncovered a\ndiverse array of attackers and targets: A hacker group linked by\nU.S. intelligence to the Chinese military, according to a U.S.\ndiplomatic cable released by Wikileaks, stole U.S. corporate\nsecrets and pilfered bureaucrats\u2019 e-mails in Brussels, while\ncommercial spyware made in Europe hit Persian Gulf activists;\nand Syrians fought a cyber war via online chats and webmail with\nrudimentary tools and deadly results.  Single Thread  As different as the examples are from each other, a single\nthread runs through them all: flawed software or network design\nenabled the hacks.  The March 2009 Coca-Cola hack, which was first reported by\nBloomberg News in November this year, used the Adobe JBIG2\nvulnerability a month after Adobe alerted customers to the\nproblem.  Spyware identified as being from Milan-based HackingTeam,\nwhich targeted activists in the United Arab Emirates and\n Morocco , used imperfections in Microsoft and Adobe software.  A commercial spy program sold to governments -- and\ndiscovered by Bloomberg News to have been used in the\nsurveillance of Bahraini democracy activists -- had  advertised \nthat it was able to gain control of computers through an Apple\niTunes flaw that was publicly known for three years before Apple\npatched it in November 2011. The manufacturer of the  FinFisher \nsoftware, U.K-based Gamma Group, pins the blame on Apple.  \u201cThey could have protected users,\u201d says Martin J. Muench,\nthe managing director of Gamma\u2019s German unit. \u201cSecurity wasn\u2019t\ntheir highest priority.\u201d  \u2018Good Impact\u2019  Apple spokesman  Bill Evans  said the iTunes security\nproblem has been fixed and declined to comment on Muench\u2019s\nstatement.  Microsoft has taken steps to keep customers safer, says\nMatt Thomlinson, general manager of product security at the\nRedmond, Washington-based company. It ramped up the effort in\n2002 with the establishment of its  Trustworthy Computing \ninitiative, which deals with security and privacy issues. Since\n2004, Microsoft has made automated updates a standard setting\nfor users of its  Windows operating system .  \u201cWe\u2019ve had some really good impact on driving down attacks\nthrough vulnerabilities, but that doesn\u2019t mean the attackers are\ngoing away,\u201d he says.  \u201cI don\u2019t think you\u2019re ever going to get to the point where\nthere are zero vulnerabilities,\u201d says Thomlinson, who has been\nwith Microsoft since 1994. \u201cWe can remove vulnerabilities from\nthe code, and that\u2019s what we\u2019ve attempted to do.\u201d  \u2018Moving Target\u2019  As companies such as Microsoft harden their defenses,\nhackers find new ways to get in, improving their skills or going\nafter other products, says Steven M. Christey, principal\ninformation security engineer at  MITRE Corp. , a non-profit group\nbased in Massachusetts and Virginia that tracks vulnerabilities.  \u201cSoftware security is a rapidly moving target,\u201d he says.\n\u201cThe result is a perpetual arms race between the software\nvendor and the attacker.\u201d  In the continuous battle, an informal army of hackers,\nsecurity firms, academics and other bug hunters seeks out\nimperfections in programs that an attacker can use to compromise\na computer. Some privately alert software makers to flaws they\nfind. Others devise methods for using those defects -- known as\nexploits -- and then sell or publicize them as hacking tools.  Despite new priorities for security, some software makers\ngive hackers head starts by failing to fix the problems quickly.  This year, Oracle didn\u2019t patch a bug in Java, its computing\nplatform for a range of games, trading and other programs, until\nalmost five months after researchers alerted it about the\nvulnerability.  Alerting Hackers  On April 2, Polish firm  Security Explorations  told Oracle\nit had discovered a defect in the product. Months went by with\nno solutions from Oracle, the world\u2019s largest supplier of\n database software .  That began to change on Aug. 26, when an alert went up on a\nwebsite that tracks software vulnerability. The site, run by the\nsecurity firm  FireEye Inc. , said that a new Java flaw had been\nspotted in targeted  attacks .  The next day, computer code for using that flaw to invade\nmachines running Java was added to a hacking tool kit available\nfor free online, called Metasploit. Virtually any hacker could\nnow download the exploit and use it.  HD Moore, chief security officer at  Rapid7 , the Boston-\nbased company that runs Metasploit, says publishing exploits\nforces companies to be accountable. \u201cIt\u2019s hitting the vendor\nover the head with a hammer,\u201d he says. \u201cWhen everybody has\naccess to it, they need to take it seriously.\u201d  Most Targeted  On Aug. 28, Milpitas, California-based FireEye found\nevidence of the \u201cfirst indication of a large scale attack\u201d\nwith the new exploit. AlienVault, a security firm, linked the\noriginal attacks to China-based hackers.  Then, two days later, Oracle  issued  patches to protect\ncustomers.  Hackers have piled on, making Java the most targeted\napplication during the third quarter of 2012, accounting for 56\npercent of exploits blocked by  Kaspersky  Lab anti-virus\nsoftware. Adobe took second place, with 28 percent.  \u201cThis year, yes, Oracle has been the worst,\u201d says Jaime\nBlasco, head of the security lab at AlienVault.  Oracle spokeswoman  Deborah Hellinger  declined to comment on\nthe Java flaw identified by Polish researchers or its system for\npatching vulnerabilities.  Arkin said the Kaspersky ranking catches many attacks aimed\nat problems in older versions that have been fixed but which\nhaven\u2019t been updated by users. \u201cThat\u2019s the milk carton with last\nyear\u2019s date on it,\u201d he says. \u201cWe say, \u2019We hear you, we\u2019ve\nlistened and here\u2019s the solution.\u2019\u201d  Reducing Dangers  While hacking\u2019s dangers can\u2019t be eliminated, they can be\nreduced, as the evolution of the  auto industry  has shown.  In 1965, consumer rights advocate  Ralph Nader  published\n\u201cUnsafe at Any Speed,\u201d detailing how U.S. automakers, fearing\nhigher costs, resisted measures such as seat belts and ignored\ncrash-test findings. The book spawned congressional hearings and\nmodern safety requirements -- and since then the U.S. per-capita\ndeath rate from auto accidents has been cut by more than half.\nCars still crash, but new ones come with air bags.  Almost a half century later, Nader says the government and\nonline service providers should do more to safeguard consumers\nfrom the new threat. \u201cIt does seem they can\u2019t keep up with the\ngenius nature of the hackers,\u201d says Nader. \u201cBasically it\u2019s the\ncost of doing business.\u201d  Safety Crossroads  For the Internet, the current safety crossroads has roots\nin the fine print that comes with most software licenses, which\nlargely absolve makers of the products underpinning the Internet\nof liability.  Legal liability can wreck an industry or move it offshore,\nBaker, the former NSA general counsel, says.  \u201cSoftware security is uniquely resistant to the kind of\nlaw making and standard setting that courts do,\u201d he says.  Today the onus is on consumers to protect themselves so\nthey don\u2019t become the conduit that lets attackers into their\nbusinesses, utilities or governments. To help reduce those\nrisks, there are several steps technology companies can take to\nadd virtual seat belts and air bags to their products and give\ncustomers safer choices.  In one simple solution already adopted by some suppliers,\nsoftware makers can automate the patches for flaws, rather than\ndepending on users to figure out how to do it themselves, says\nStefano Ortolani, a security researcher for Kaspersky Lab Italy.  Automated Patches  Even with the Java patch issued in August, for instance,\nthere was no automated update process for all users, so many had\nto either deploy the fix themselves or disable Java to be\nprotected. Today about 65 percent of Java users lack the latest\nversion, which includes patches of security holes, according to\nRapid7.  Service providers and software makers can change the ways\npeople use computer programs by keeping applications off devices\naltogether, and running them in a new network of remote\ncomputers, known as the cloud. With word processing or\naccounting programs in the cloud, rather than individual\nmachines, software makers can ensure security fixes are applied\nfor all users and are done more quickly, says Rob Rachwald,\ndirector of security strategy at  Imperva Inc. , a Redwood Shores,\nCalifornia-based web security company.  \u201cYou\u2019re using it on the Web, not your desktop,\u201d he says.  Roadmaps Deprived  Software makers could provide another fix that would\ndeprive hackers of the predictable roadmaps they use to navigate\npeoples\u2019 computers by purposely jumbling where programs and data\nare stored in a machine\u2019s memory. That defensive move doesn\u2019t\nstop hackers from getting in, but can keep them from taking\ncontrol, says Andy Chou, chief technology officer of San\nFrancisco-based Coverity Inc., which finds and fixes software\ndefects for clients.  Consumers themselves have options to mitigate risk, some\nborrowed from the world of hacking, from encrypting their e-\nmails to using special Web browsers that disguise their\nidentities.  Using sites whose addresses start with HTTPS -- an\nencrypted version of HTTP -- adds a layer of protection. Most\nwebmail providers, such as Google\u2019s Gmail, have made HTTPS\nstandard, while  Yahoo! Inc. (YHOO)  until recently had held out. The San\nFrancisco-based  Electronic Frontier Foundation  has said Yahoo\nputs users at risk, especially in repressive countries.  Shaming Yahoo!  \u201cThey deserve to be shamed loudly and at length,\u201d EFF\u2019s\nInternational Freedom of Expression Coordinator Eva Galperin\nsaid in a Nov. 28 e-mail.  In response to questions about EFF\u2019s position, Yahoo said\nthat it has begun offering the technology behind HTTPS and will\ncontinue to do so over the next few months, and that it is\ndeveloping and testing more secure platforms. \u201cYahoo! is\ncommitted to protecting the security and privacy of our users,\u201d\nthe statement said. The EFF\u2019s Galperin said, \u201cI am glad they\nare finally getting started.\u201d  To achieve the cyber equivalent of crash-testing, industry\nstandards for vetting programs would tip the balance toward\nsafety, says Sean Coyne, a Washington-based cyber-security\nresearcher who has worked for government and corporate clients.  \u201cNobody is holding the manufacturers\u2019 feet to the fire,\u201d\nCoyne says.  Minimum security standards might lead software makers to\nbeef up the now paltry ranks of programmers dedicated to making\nsure products are safe. It\u2019s not unusual for software makers to\nhave one security person per every 500 to 1,000 developers, says\n Coverity \u2019s Chou.  Fixable Flaws  \u201cThose 1,000 developers are writing code every day -- how\ncan that one poor guy keep up?\u201d he says.  As corporate customers fend for themselves, they also can\ndo more to keep safe. Many of the hacks uncovered this year by\nBloomberg News showed basic -- and fixable -- flaws in internal\nsecurity.  In the 2009 Coca-Cola hack, an internal investigation found\nthat it was the work of state-backed hackers, and that the\ncompany neglected to take several protective steps. Details in a\ncompany document detailing the attack indicate the intruders\nwere part of a prolific China-based hacking group, according to\nresearchers interviewed by Bloomberg.  Coca-Cola needed to patch Adobe Reader vulnerabilities to\naddress immediate holes and, for the longer term, establish a\ncomprehensive program for managing fixes, according to the\nreport.  Fighting JBIG2  When inadequate records prevented them from reconstructing\nthe hack, investigators recommended the company implement\nsystems to perform centralized logging of what occurs on the\nnetwork. Coca-Cola spokesman  Kent Landers  declined to comment\nwhen asked this week about any follow-up to the incident.  The story behind the Coca-Cola hack is also the tale of\nAdobe\u2019s fight against the JBIG2 bug. Adobe\u2019s challenge, as told\nby former and current employees, provides a window into the\ntension between profit and safety that has shaped the Internet.  Tom Ferris, an Adobe researcher from 2006 to 2010, worked\nfinding security failures and triaging all the security\nvulnerabilities streaming in. He recalls that when he started,\nthey\u2019d find 10 to 15 flaws a week that needed a fix. \u201cI told my\nmanagers this was a big problem,\u201d he says.  They ignored him, until the JBIG2 bug hit, he says. The\nflaw causes the Adobe Reader and Acrobat applications to crash,\nallowing an attacker to take control of the system.  \u201cEverything changed,\u201d Ferris says.  Hackers Pounce  The ordeal began on Feb. 19, 2009, when researchers at\nSymantec Corp., the world\u2019s biggest security-software maker,\nsaid they\u2019d  discovered  the bug, and alerted Adobe. That day,\nAdobe issued a security warning, saying a fix wouldn\u2019t be\navailable until the following month.  In China, and possibly elsewhere, hackers pounced. On March\n3 and 4, 2009, U.S. defense contractor Lockheed Martin Corp.\u2019s\nincident response team  intercepted  intrusion attempts that used\nthe vulnerability in e-mails purporting to be about an\naeronautics conference and a meeting on U.S. missile defense,\naccording to a paper the company researchers wrote.  It took until March 10 for Adobe to come out with an\nupdated program that users could download to mitigate the flaw.  Three days later, hackers hit an executive in China for\nCoca-Cola, which was awaiting approval for its $2.4 billion\nacquisition of China Huiyuan Juice Group. It was one of several\nhacks using different means that compromised company executives\nat the time.  \u2018Not Economical\u2019  On March 18, 2009, the Chinese Ministry of Commerce\nrejected Coca-Cola\u2019s acquisition citing antitrust grounds.  Inside Adobe, the security push had just begun. Yet fixing\nevery line of the programs wasn\u2019t in the cards because the\ncompany wasn\u2019t willing to take on the expense, says Ferris and\nhis former colleague, Randolph.  \u201cIt\u2019s just not economical,\u201d Randolph says. \u201cThey\u2019re\nstill making money and they\u2019re doing what\u2019s best for their\nshareholders.\u201d  Arkin says the company heavily automated its process for\nreleasing a patch, reducing the time lag from weeks to an\naverage of five days. They turned off risky features, leaving it\nto users to decide if they wanted them.  The best bet, Arkin says he decided, was to find a way to\nquarantine programs. In the design, called sandboxing, a hacker\nmight manage to take over Adobe\u2019s Reader, but would need to\nescape the virtual sandbox to do further damage on a user\u2019s\ncomputer.  In November 2010, Adobe released Reader X, promoting the\nsandbox as a way to better protect customers. \u201cTo date, we\u2019re\nnot aware of any customer anywhere who is running Adobe Reader X\nwho has ever been attacked in the real world,\u201d Arkin says.  That\u2019s the kind of challenge hackers love. The activities are \u201cconducted under authorities widely\nknown and discussed, and fully debated and authorized by\nCongress,\u201d Clapper said in a statement released in  Washington \nyesterday. \u201cTheir purpose is to obtain foreign intelligence\ninformation, including information necessary to thwart terrorist\nand cyber-attacks against the United States and its allies.\u201d  The Internet program, code-named PRISM, can\u2019t be used to\nintentionally target U.S. citizens or anyone known to be in the\nU.S., according to a declassified summary of the program also\nreleased yesterday. Only a\nfew years later, it both defined and dominated the personal-\ncomputer market, changing the way the world worked while\ngenerating vast fortunes for its two founders.  Now one of them,  Paul Allen , sheds his long-standing public\nreticence with a new memoir, \u201c Idea Man .\u201d In it, he recreates\nthe spirit of those early days in all their energy and tumult,\nproviding a fascinating look at what it took to build the\nMicrosoft behemoth. And he offers a guided tour of the personal\nfascinations and foibles that have shaped his life in the almost\n30 years since he stepped away from the company.  Most of all, \u201cIdea Man\u201d reacquaints us with his friend\nfrom boyhood,  Bill Gates  -- not today\u2019s epic philanthropist, but\nthe single-minded, chair-rocking, brilliant, sometimes ferocious\nvisionary who built the fortune he is now so determinedly giving\naway.  This is the Gates who would occasionally doze off during\nall-night programming sessions, his nose touching the keyboard\nfor a couple hours, then \u201copen his eyes, squint at the screen,\nblink twice and resume precisely where he left off -- a\nprodigious feat of concentration.\u201d  It\u2019s also the Gates who was so socially maladroit he would\neat chicken with a spoon, who would abuse subordinates and who\nmost of all maintained a fearsome focus on crushing competitors\nand building Microsoft into the colossus it became.  Coke-Bottle Glasses  In one of the book\u2019s most memorable scenes, he and Allen,\non a business trip to  Tokyo , find themselves in a hotel elevator\nnext to \u201ca long-haired guy with Coke-bottle eyeglasses and a\nJapanese woman with curly black hair.\u201d Allen, struck dumb until\nthey leave the elevator, asks, \u201cDid you see that? That was  John Lennon  and  Yoko Ono .\u201d \u201cReally?\u201d Gates replies. \u201cOh, yeah,\nyou might be right.\u201d  That was Gates, Allen observes: \u201cthinking about the\nsoftware business first, second, and third.\u201d  The author\u2019s self-portrait is in some ways nearly as\nunflattering as his portrait of Gates, albeit for very different\nreasons. The Microsoft-era Allen emerges in these pages as a\npassive-aggressive figure, beaten down by Gates\u2019s bullying and\nnursing private resentment as his partner maneuvers to reduce\nhis share of the company to 40 percent, then 36 percent. Only\nwhen, battling cancer, he overhears Gates and protege  Steve Ballmer  planning to dilute his holdings still further does he\ndraw the line. Bursting in on them, he shames them into backing\ndown, but the damage to his relationship with Gates and\nMicrosoft is already done.  \u2018Scheming\u2019  \u201cI helped start the company and was still an active member\nof management, though limited by my illness, and now my partner\nand my colleague were scheming to rip me off,\u201d he writes. \u201cIt\nwas mercenary opportunism, plain and simple.\u201d By 1983, he was\ngone from the company he helped build.  The Allen of the book\u2019s later chapters, freed by his\ndeparture and wealth from the need to be passive-aggressive,\nsometimes seems just, well, passive -- a genuinely creative\nthinker lacking the Gatesian fire to impose his vision on the\nworld around him.  Recognizing early the coming era of global connectivity --\nlong before the Internet, he dubs it \u201cthe Wired World\u201d --Allen\nacquires a huge stake in  America Online , then dumps it amid\nhostility from the company and potential competition from\nMicrosoft, effectively leaving $40 billion on the table when AOL\nlater merges with Time Warner.  Bad Bets  He bets big on cable as a key component in his Wired World,\nbut his Charter Communications spirals into bankruptcy amid poor\ndecisions and management scandals. The leadership he installs at\nhis National Basketball Association team squanders fan goodwill\nwith a roster that earns the nickname \u201cthe Portland Jail\nBlazers,\u201d while its arena ends up in -- you guessed it --\nbankruptcy.  Allen\u2019s scientific and philanthropic ventures have fared\nmuch better: funding cutting-edge research into how the brain\nworks; backing the project that won the X Prize for building a\nprivate spacecraft; fueled by his Jimi Hendrix fixation,\ncommissioning  Frank Gehry  to design  Seattle \u2019s  Experience Music\nProject  museum. Pay no attention to\nits fight with  Apple Inc.  over smartphones, or to any other tech\nrivalry.  The search giant\u2019s war with  Microsoft Corp.  is The Big One,\nthe confrontation that will determine what kind of future\nMicrosoft has, and maybe if it even has a future. And the two\nnew weapons Google unsheathed last week carry an unmistakable\nmessage of mortal peril.  First came the  Nexus S , the new Google-labeled smartphone\nand the first to run \u201cGingerbread,\u201d Google\u2019s latest Android\noperating system. Then came a plain black laptop called the Cr-\n48, the first computer to run the company\u2019s Web-based Chrome\nOperating System.  On the surface, neither seems particularly menacing. The\nNexus S, made by  Samsung , is the successor to one of the most\nhyped and least successful products of 2010, the lovely and ill-\nfated Nexus One. And the Cr-48 isn\u2019t even for sale. It\u2019s a\ngeneric prototype that Google is making available to thousands\nof developers, companies and others to get them familiar with\nthe concept of the new operating system before commercial\nversions from manufacturers such as Samsung Electronics Co. and\n Acer Inc.  show up next year.  Enormous Threat  Still, the two devices represent an enormous threat to\nMicrosoft and its chief executive officer,  Steve Ballmer . The\nsuccess of Android is rapidly foreclosing Microsoft\u2019s growth\nprospects as more computing is done on mobile devices.\nMeanwhile, Chrome OS takes dead aim at its great twin cash cows:\nthe Windows and Microsoft Office franchises.  Of the two new offerings, the Nexus S is the one most\nvisible to consumers. The phone went on sale in the U.S.\nyesterday at Best Buy Co. stores and online for $199 on a two-\nyear contract from  Deutsche Telekom AG \u2019s T-Mobile USA, and for\n$529 with no contract.  The phone, a variation on Samsung\u2019s popular Galaxy S line,\ncomes with a gorgeous four-inch touch screen, front- and rear-\nfacing cameras for video chatting and a passel of Google apps\nand services. Its potential killer application is Near Field\nCommunication, a technology that allows it to read encoded\ninformation from special chips that can be embedded in signs, on\nT-shirts or other objects.  Mobile Payments  Putting NFC support into Android is the biggest step yet\ntoward using the mobile phone as a way of paying for things. And\nit comes at a time when Microsoft is still playing catch-up.\nHaving frittered away its early strength in smartphones, it\nsuffered a series of stumbles, including a line of youth-\noriented phones called Kin that it introduced this year and\npulled from the market after less than two months. Its latest\neffort, the Windows Phone 7 operating system, is a great\nimprovement -- but still lacks such basics as cut-and-paste\nfunctionality.  It\u2019s possible for Google and Apple to both succeed in\nmobile phones. It\u2019s harder to imagine Google and Microsoft both\nthriving. Google\u2019s business model, which calls for getting\nmanufacturers to use its operating system, is far closer to\nMicrosoft\u2019s than to Apple\u2019s strategy of making money on the sale\nof proprietary hardware. And, of course, Google offers Android\nto manufacturers at a price that Microsoft can\u2019t beat: free.  While Android is all about limiting Microsoft\u2019s future,\nChrome OS takes dead aim at its present: the Windows and Office\nbusinesses that, in the quarter that ended Sept. 30, earned $6.7\nbillion of the company\u2019s $7.1 billion in operating income.  In the Cloud  At first glance the Cr-48 -- Cr being the symbol for the\nelement chromium -- looks like a basic laptop. The differences\nbecome evident once you turn it on. With no large programs or\ndevice drivers to load, it boots in 15 seconds. The operating\nsystem is, essentially, just a Web browser that you can never\nclose. Forget about a hard drive: Everything you use, all your\nprograms and all your data, reside in the cloud, on Google\u2019s\ndistant servers. And it uses not a bit of Microsoft software.  Nor is Microsoft the only one threatened. What kind of chip\npowers the Cr-48? Who cares? For the record, the Cr-48 has an\nAtom microprocessor from  Intel Corp. , but it\u2019s no more relevant\nthan what kind of chip powers your smartphone. How about makers\nof flash memory chips, like  Toshiba ? A Chrome OS machine needs\nlittle -- the Cr-48 has only 16 gigabytes -- since nothing is\nstored on the computer itself.  Useless Brick  Chrome completely commoditizes the hardware; the only\nthings that count are being connected to the Internet, and at\nwhat speed. For now, that\u2019s Chrome\u2019s biggest weakness. While the\nCr-48 works either over a Wi-Fi network or its built-in  Verizon \nWireless 3G service, you can\u2019t always count on getting a\nconnection. On a cross-country flight this week, the Cr-48 was a\nuseless, inert brick.  On the other hand, that isn\u2019t likely to be a permanent\ncondition as Internet connections become ever more ubiquitous.\nSome airlines, such as Virgin America Inc., have already started\nrolling out onboard Wi-Fi.  Since Chrome OS, like Android, is free, it\u2019s logical to ask\nwhat Google gets out of it. Company executives talk about the\nbenefits of tying users to Google services and gaining valuable\ndata to help refine its search algorithms. It remains to be seen\nwhether those users will be troubled by the privacy implications\nand whether Google\u2019s business model will work for manufacturers.  You can\u2019t help thinking that the real point of Chrome is\nthe threat it poses to Windows. From its founding, Google has\ndefined itself as the anti-Microsoft. Its \u201cdon\u2019t be evil\u201d\ncorporate mantra never needed to specify what it meant by\n\u201cevil,\u201d because everyone already knew. The fact is, Google\ndoesn\u2019t actually need Chrome OS to succeed. Microsoft, though,\ndesperately needs it to fail.  ( Rich Jaroslovsky  is a Bloomberg News columnist. To contact the editor responsible for this column:\nJames Greiff at   jgreiff@bloomberg.net .","path":".\/2008_2012_msft_bloomberg_news\/google-aims-twin-daggers-at-microsoft-s-heart-rich-jaroslovsky.txt"},{"id":78703479,"title":"Just How Valuable Is Google's \"20% Time\"?","released_at":"<date>August 20 2013<\/date> <time>14:40:11<\/time>","content":"Reports of the  death  or  deliquescence  of Google's \"20% time,\" which allows employees to devote one day a week to side projects, may well be exaggerated. They certainly inspire less controversy than  Yahoo's targeted euthanizing of telecommuting . But both emphasize the importance of Silicon Valley's most precious value-added differentiator: technical talent. The care, feeding, and culture of productive talent deserve all the attention and debate they get \u2014 and more. Virtually everyone who's made money from the App Store or competed against a  Salesforce.com  or  SurveyMonkey  viscerally understands the huge differences between \"pretty good\" developers and those best described as \"terrific.\" \" Acqu-hiring \" has become both a buzzword and a best practice for a reason. Relative to the enormous economic value talent can deliver, gluten-free gourmet cafeterias and concierge service represent a small price to pay. But employing talent is one thing. Keeping it productively innovative and innovatively productive is another. What happens to self-image and individual expectations as enterprise definitions of \"productively innovative\" and \"innovatively productive\" change? If people believe they've been promised the opportunity to devote up to one day a week pursuing disruptive innovation insights, they're arguably entitled to feel a little cheated or miffed when told to \"double down\" on their day jobs. At a certain point, innovation cultures are as much about \"credibility\" as creativity and ingenuity. That's why Google presents such a special case. No one doubts founders Larry Page and Sergey Brin are passionately committed \u2014 intellectually and emotionally \u2014 to innovation as core to their entrepreneurial identities and effectiveness. That sensibility made Google Google. Yet it's also true the company  shut down Google Labs , its popular intrapreneurial playground and beta site, to the surprise and disappointment of employees and customers alike. More than a few Googlers also feel that  Google X  \u2014 the \"disruptive\/new paradigms\"  skunkworks  operation launched in 2010 \u2014 now owns \"big think\" innovation hearts and minds of their founders. Google X innovation gets to create the future, they observe, while Google innovation gets to improve the business. Their innovation discretion shrinks while Google X's horizons expand. Is this perception unfair or inaccurate? Certainly, many people inside the company and out agree that Larry Page took the  late Steve Jobs's advice  and admonitions very seriously: \"The main thing I stressed was focus,\" Jobs said. \"Figure out what Google wants to be when it grows up. It's now all over the map. What are the five products you want to focus on? Get rid of the rest, because they're dragging you down. They're turning you into Microsoft. They're causing you to turn out products that are adequate but not great.\" Neither Steve Jobs nor Apple culture encouraged, nurtured, or celebrated 20% time among employees to inspire innovation. To the contrary, Apple's clarity of vision and relentless dedication to user experience and design assured that the company's world-class talent would overwhelmingly focus their efforts on delivery, not novelty. Apple innovation culture was more top-down alignment of talent than facilitation of bottom-up empowerment. But successfully delivering that vision to overwhelming market approval proved intoxicating and addictive for much of the company's top technical talent. But I don't think the story is Page or Brin becoming more Jobs-like or that Google's innovation culture has pruned individual discretion in favor of greater organizational alignment. My view \u2014 reflected in the  comments of many Googlers  \u2014 is that the company is internally debating how its most talented employees generate the most valuable innovation. Do they productively innovate better by more rigorously focusing on their ongoing projects? Or do curiosity-driven and\/or passion-driven initiatives lead to measurably better innovation outcomes? Google has publicly defined itself as an organization that wants to be data driven in its most important business decisions. The company has put  people analytics  of individual talent and team performance alike at the core of managing itself. Yes, there's flakiness and inherent subjectivity in many of the metrics. But the simple truth is that Google as both a culture and a global enterprise wants to take more data more seriously. The obvious result? Google's innovation culture is being shaped as much by the performance data of its people as by their technical intuitions and insights. In other words, tomorrow's Google won't embrace 20% \"free time\" for everyone; innovation best practice will mean some individuals and teams will have as much discretionary time as they need while others will have virtually nil. You've got a problem with that? Well, the data suggest you shouldn't. I don't doubt for a minute that Google's founders and top leadership will ultimately rely on their gut instincts and intuitions \u2014 albeit richly informed by data \u2014 when the time comes to hire, fire, and\/or acquire. Nor do I doubt that the care, feeding, and culture of technical talent will increasingly be determined and defined by data. That's where credibility will come from and, yes, that's what will sharpen entrepreneurial focus, as well.","path":".\/2008_2012_msft_bloomberg_news\/just-how-valuable-is-google-s-20-time-.txt"},{"id":82378127,"title":"Soros Increases Holdings in Teva to Most Since 2010","released_at":"<date>November 22 2013<\/date> <time>22:23:48<\/time>","content":"Soros Fund Management LLC, the\nfamily office of billionaire  George Soros , increased its\nholdings in  Teva Pharmaceutical Industries Ltd. Microsoft Research economist David Rothschild has a project called  PredictWise  that sifts through zillions of data points scooped up from the Internet to predict outcomes of various public events like Eurovision, the Academy Awards, and elections. Its Eurovision predictions take odds from gambling sites such as PaddyPower and Betfair, as well as Youtube views and mentions in social media, Rothschild says. Those, he said on his blog, are predictors of the votes of judges drawn from the dozens of countries competing.
