We\u2019ve seen PCs that bend, PCs that slide, even PCs that convert to Android tablets. Now come two more, one enormous and the other compact. Each in its own way tries to redefine what a Windows-based computer can be.  Lenovo (992) \u2019s 27-inch IdeaCentre Horizon Table PC can be used as a standard, if gigantic, desktop computer. It comes with a wireless keyboard and laser mouse, and a hinge that props it up at a comfortable viewing angle for productivity applications.  But the real fun, and the Horizon\u2019s reason for being, happens when you collapse the stand and lay it flat on a tabletop. Suddenly, Windows 8 is gone, replaced by a Lenovo-designed multi-user interface called Aura, and the Horizon becomes a digital game board.  The computer comes with nine games pre-installed, including Air Hockey and Monopoly. More are available through a partnership with  Electronic Arts (EA)  and  Ubisoft (UBI) , and it can also run games written for  Google (GOOG) \u2019s Android mobile operating system, thanks to a technology called BlueStacks.  It has three kinds of game controllers: a pair of strikers for the hockey game, joysticks that attach via suction cups, and digital dice for traditional board games.  Heavy Going  The Horizon weighs about 18 pounds, making it luggable if not exactly portable, and the screen has a battery if you want to set it up for a quick session of Texas Hold \u2019Em and don\u2019t have a power outlet handy.  As a PC, the Horizon is full-powered, with a choice of  Intel (INTC) \u2019s Core i7 or i5 processors, one-terabyte hard drive and eight gigabytes of random-access memory.  Lenovo is currently selling the Horizon via its website at $1,849 for the i7 version and $1,699 for the i5; it says those prices will fall to $1,599 and $1,499 when it hits  Best Buy (BBY)  store shelves in June.  The Horizon isn\u2019t cheap, but it\u2019s a fun and flexible take on the concept of the \u201cfamily computer.\u201d  Flashy Toshiba  Toshiba has long had a reputation for delivering solid, unflashy laptops. Now it has decided to bring the bling, with the pricey, tricked-out Kirabook 13.3-inch notebook.  It\u2019s ultra-thin, ultra-light and built around Intel\u2019s Core i5 and i7 chips. Seven tenths of an inch thick and 2.66 pounds - - less than the 13-inch MacBook Air -- it comes with eight gigabytes of memory and 256 gigabytes of solid-state storage.  With its magnesium alloy body, the computer is nice to look at, though the design -- with two rounded corners and two squared-off ones -- may be an acquired taste for some.  The really gorgeous aspect of the Kirabook is the screen, with a resolution of 2560 by 1440 pixels that works out to 217 pixels per inch. Imagine taking the dazzling Retina display from  Apple (AAPL) \u2019s full-sized MacBook Pro and transplanting it to the lightweight MacBook Air, and you\u2019ll begin to get the picture.  The Kirabook\u2019s screen is almost too nice, if that\u2019s possible. The  subpar appearance  of some Windows programs and web content that weren\u2019t designed to be viewed at such high resolutions is annoying. But that can\u2019t fairly be blamed on the Kirabook.  With that beautiful display and nice-sounding  Harman Kardon (HAR)  speakers,  Toshiba (6502)  aims to go upscale with the Kirabook. My enthusiasm, though, was dampened by problems with my i7-equipped review unit.  Noisy Fan  One was the extraordinarily noisy fan, which had a tendency to kick on soon after boot-up and periodically thereafter. Another was the battery; though it\u2019s supposed to last for six hours, it sometimes plunged from nearly full to zero while the computer was asleep overnight.  Toshiba says it hasn\u2019t received other such complaints, and it may have just been bad luck that I got a defective unit. Still, it definitely detracted from the premium experience the company was attempting to deliver, as did a touch screen that proved a smudge magnet despite its alleged fingerprint-resistant coating.  Then there\u2019s the price. The base-model Kirabook costs $1,600, but doesn\u2019t come with a touch screen, which I consider to be required for Windows 8. The touch screen adds $200 to the price, while my test model, with the Core i7, is $2,000.  It\u2019s a nice machine, but for that much money you expect more, and you should get it. The company has registered to meet with lawmakers to\ndiscuss the Investment Canada Act, which sets rules for foreign\nacquisitions of local companies, according to federal lobbying\ndocuments. The government automatically reviews any takeover bid\nof more than C$344 million ($332 million).  The push comes amid speculation that Toronto\u2019s  Fairfax\nFinancial Holdings Ltd. BlackBerry executives made the disclosure about discussing\nthe  Investment Canada Act  with lawmakers and government\nofficials in the past week, according to the lobbying register.\nBefore that, the act hasn\u2019t been listed as a subject of interest\nto the company for years. Lenovo, the world\u2019s largest personal-computer maker, said\nin January that it was assessing potential acquisition targets,\nincluding BlackBerry. At the time, Canadian Finance Minister Jim Flaherty said certain local technologies were off-limits to\nforeign buyers. The government would look \u201ccarefully\u201d at a bid\nfrom Lenovo, he said. BlackBerry operates secure servers for the\nCanadian and U.S. governments, which would put additional\nscrutiny on a Chinese deal. Pairing BlackBerry\nwith Nokia would let the software company roll up the industry\u2019s\nsmaller competitors, potentially creating more of a threat for\nApple and Android.  Still, sealing a deal for BlackBerry may not be easy --\neither at home or abroad.  JPMorgan Chase & Co. Fairfax held a 9.9 percent\nstake in BlackBerry as of June 30. Swaps to insure Fairfax debt against default indicate\ndeclining risk and lower odds the company will lead a buyout\nthat could saddle Fairfax with debt. The contracts fell eight\nbasis points this week to 164 basis points, the narrowest in\nalmost seven months.  Credit-default swaps narrow as confidence in a borrower\nimproves and the cost of protecting the debt drops. Swaps pay\nthe buyer face value if a borrower fails to meet its\nobligations, less the value of the defaulted debt. One basis\npoint equals $1,000 annually on a contract protecting $10\nmillion of debt.  Disappointing Sales  BlackBerry\u2019s board began discussing a possible sale after\nits revamped BlackBerry 10 operating system struggled to gain\ntraction. With the deal, announced Oct. 15, Japan\u2019s third-biggest\nmobile-phone operator is looking to benefit from a shift to\nfaster mobile networks using long-term evolution, or LTE.  Here are answers to some frequently asked questions about\nLTE. The information is drawn from research by the International\nTelecommunications Union under the UN, IHS iSuppli, ABI Research\nand NgnGuru Solutions\u2019 LTEWorld.org Website.  Q: What is it?  LTE is a standard for higher-speed mobile services being\nadopted by carriers around the world. The technology offers peak\ndownload rates of at least 100 megabits per second that can go\nas high as 300Mbps, compared to a maximum of 50Mbps for current\n3G standards, according to the  ITU . Upload rates are at least\n50Mps and as high as almost 100Mbps, compared with a maximum of\nless than 30Mbps for 3G. Latency, or round-trip delay, is 50\npercent to 80 percent shorter than existing standards.  The latest versions of LTE, known as LTE-Advanced, have\nbeen  designated by the ITU  as 4G technologies with earlier\niterations considered to be 3.9G.  There\u2019s also a competing 4G technology called WiMAX\noriginally backed by  Intel Corp. (INTC)  Carriers, including Sprint\nNextel Corp., that announced a plan in 2006 to build a\nnationwide WiMAX network now favor LTE because it\u2019s faster and\nmore compatible with existing 3G mobile standards.  Q: What can it do for consumers?  LTE offers faster downloads and streaming, allowing users\nto quickly load videos from websites such as  Google Inc. (GOOG) \u2019s\nYouTube and watch high-definition clips without a hitch. To put\nit in context, you can enjoy downloads and Internet browsing\nthat seem as fast as WiFi connections at home. The faster\nservice comes with a price -- LTE plans cost consumers about 20\npercent more than similar 3G products,  according to  ABI\nResearch.  Q: Who offers it?  Mobile operators globally, from Sprint in the U.S. to  NTT\nDocomo Inc. (9437)  in Japan to  SK Telecom (017670)  in  South Korea , have rolled\nout LTE networks, with more deployments to follow in the next\ntwo to three years, according to ITU.  You need devices designed to run on LTE networks to enjoy\nthe service.  Apple Inc. (AAPL) \u2019s latest iPhone 5 supports LTE, while\nother phone makers including  Samsung Electronics Co. (005930)  and  HTC\nCorp. (2498)  have also introduced LTE phones.  There will be more LTE devices:  Asustek Computer Inc. (2357) ,\nmaker of the Eee PC, will offer LTE when it becomes one of the\nfirst companies to offer tablets running  Microsoft Corp. (MSFT) \u2019s\nWindows RT platform this month.  Nokia Siemens Networks Oy is the largest maker of LTE\nequipment bought by operators, followed by Huawei Technologies\nCo. and Ericsson,  according to   ABI Research . LTE will be the\nmain driver of an 8.3 percent growth this year in mobile network\nequipment revenue to $45.5 billion,  according to  IHS iSuppli.\nFourth-generation infrastructure will rise from $8.6 billion\nglobally this year to $25.2 billion next year, comprising the\nmajority of all expenditure, IHS said.  Q: Why is this a big deal?  As more people download apps, games and movies on their\nmobile devices, faster mobile connections will be required to\nserve the data. The average size of an Apple iOS app grew 16\npercent in the six months to September, with games getting 42\npercent larger, ABI  said . Global LTE subscriptions will reach\n1.2 billion by 2016, compared with 16.9 million in 2011,\naccording to IHS iSuppli.  New mobile networks cost carriers billions of dollars a\nyear, hence the financial support Sprint sought from its deal\nwith Softbank. The agreement allows Sprint to fund a faster\nexpansion of LTE networks and take on bigger competitors  Verizon\nWireless  and  AT&T Inc. (DD)  over a patent for genetically\nmodified soybeans may be vulnerable, mostly because of the\namount of the damages.  The award, handed down Aug. 1 by a federal jury in\nMonsanto\u2019s hometown of  St. Louis , was the largest in the U.S.\nthis year and the fourth biggest patent verdict in U.S. history.\nTwo of the three awards that exceeded that amount were thrown\nout on appeal and the other was cut by almost two-thirds after a\nsettlement.  \u201cNo court is going to let a billion-dollar verdict stand\nwithout a hard look,\u201d said John Dragseth, a patent lawyer with\nFish & Richardson in  Minneapolis .  Monsanto and DuPont are the two biggest companies in the\n$34 billion commercial seed market. The St. Louis jury took just\n45 minutes to reject DuPont\u2019s challenges to a Monsanto patent on\ngenetically modified crops that survive the weedkiller Roundup.\nThe panel decided DuPont willfully infringed the patent by\nmaking soybeans that combined the Roundup Ready trait with a\nsimilar DuPont technology known as GAT.  DuPont, which generated $38 billion in revenue last year,\nsaid in a statement that it will appeal, focusing on the\nMonsanto patent, the amount of damages and \u201cfundamental\nerrors\u201d in the case. For example, Monsanto told the jury in\nclosing arguments that DuPont\u2019s decision not to commercialize\nsoybean seeds that combine the two traits was irrelevant,  Daniel Turner , a company spokesman, said in a telephone interview.  Startling Size  \u201cI\u2019m startled by the size of the verdict in the absence of\nany commercial sales,\u201d said Warren Woessner, a lawyer who\nspecializes in biotechnology patents at Schwegman, Lundberg &\nWoessner in Minneapolis. \u201cInfringement has historically been\nfound in cases like this, but there are no damages awarded.\u201d  DuPont rose 0.9 percent to $49.47 at the close in  New York .\nMonsanto fell 0.4 percent to $87.04.  Monsanto argued that DuPont violated a licensing agreement\nand infringed the Roundup Ready patent when it began making\nsoybeans that added the GAT trait. DuPont made the combination\nto patch problems with GAT, Monsanto said. DuPont argued that\nMonsanto deceived the U.S. Patent and  Trademark Office  to obtain\nits patent, rendering it invalid and unenforceable.  Roundup Ready  DuPont infringed the Roundup Ready patent six years before\nits expiration, Monsanto told the jury. DuPont expected to\ngenerate $3 billion of revenue from soybeans that tolerate GAT\nand Roundup over those six years, which translates into $800\nmillion to $1 billion in damages to Monsanto, the company\u2019s\nlawyers argued.  Federal law defines infringement as anyone making, using,\nselling, offering to sell or importing a patented invention.  The law indicates DuPont shouldn\u2019t have begun to work with\nthe Roundup Ready trait until the patent expires in September\n2014,  Mark Gulley , a New York-based analyst with Gulley &\nAssociates, said in a note to clients.  The jury determined the award by calculating a reasonable\nroyalty rate from the time the infringement was said to begin,\nsaid  Oskar Liivak , an associate professor at Cornell Law School\nin Ithaca, New York, who specializes in intellectual property.\nMonsanto said at the trial that DuPont rebuffed an offer for a\n$1.5 billion license.  \u2018Large Figure\u2019  \u201cThe fact that DuPont ultimately never sold the seed was\nnot relevant for the reasonable royalty calculation and, as the\ndamages showed, that reasonable royalty added up to a rather\nlarge figure,\u201d Liivak said.  DuPont will get a chance to make its arguments first to\nU.S. District Judge Richard Webber, who presided over the trial.\nWhichever side loses may then seek review before the  U.S. Court\nof Appeals  for the Federal Circuit in  Washington , which\nspecializes in U.S. patent law. Monsanto will be able to argue\nthe award should be higher because the jury found the\ninfringement was intentional.  An appeal by DuPont may force the Federal Circuit court to\ndecide where the line is between permissible experimentation to\nimprove upon an invention, and a violation of a patent owners\u2019\nright to exclude others from using it, Woessner said.  \u201cUsually you are entitled to improve on a patented gene or\nwork on it, even with commercial purposes in mind,\u201d Woessner\nsaid. \u201cIt\u2019s certainly a highly appealable issue.\u201d  The largest U.S. patent verdict to be upheld on appeal was\na $200 million jury award that grew to $300 million with added\nroyalties and interest, against Microsoft Corp. over a feature\nin Word, part of the Office software used by more than 1 billion\npeople.  New Trials  Microsoft won new trials in three cases where the original\nverdicts exceeded $368 million, including two that centered on\nthe calculation of damages. All of those cases were later\nsettled, with terms never disclosed.  \u201cThe size of the verdict will give the panel that gets the\ncase over at the Federal Circuit a reason to look hard at the\nbasis of it,\u201d said Dirk Thomas, a patent lawyer with  McKool\nSmith  in Washington. \u201cThey\u2019re not immune to a lot of zeros on\nthe left side of the decimal. A very large verdict like that is\ngoing to garner greater scrutiny than a small verdict.\u201d  The appeals court has been curbing damage awards over the\npast five years, particularly as they relate to the value of\nsmall components compared with the entire price of a computer,\nThomas said.  Of the top 10 patent verdicts , four were against\nMicrosoft, according to data compiled by Bloomberg. Two others,\nagainst Apple Inc. and Johnson & Johnson, are on appeal before\nthe Federal Circuit. A $345 million verdict against SAP Inc.,\nwhich dropped off the top 10 list with the addition of the\nMonsanto decision, is on appeal.  Biggest Verdicts  The biggest two verdicts in history -- $1.67 billion won by\nJohnson & Johnson against Abbott Laboratories over technology\nunderpinning an arthritis drug, and $1.52 billion against\nMicrosoft over digital music -- were thrown out based on the\nfacts of the cases.  The only other verdict exceeding $1 billion, a dispute\nbegun in 1990 between Litton Systems Inc. and Honeywell Inc.\nover aircraft navigation gyroscopes, was settled in 2001 for\n$440 million.  Dragseth, who was part of the team that got the $1.52\nbillion verdict against Microsoft overturned, said the sheer\nsize of the jury award was a factor in that victory.  \u201cIf they had come in on $30 million on that invention,\nthere\u2019s a good chance we would have lost,\u201d he said. Copyrights on Foreign Works Upheld by U.S. Supreme Court  The U.S. Supreme Court upheld a federal law that gave\ncopyright protection to millions of foreign-produced books,\nmovies and musical pieces and may undermine Google Inc.\u2019s effort\nto create an online library.  Yesterday\u2019s 6-2 ruling takes works by Alfred Hitchcock,\nPablo Picasso, Igor Stravinsky and J.R.R. Tolkien out of the\npublic domain, barring use without permission of the copyright\nowner. The justices rejected arguments from orchestra conductors,\neducators, performers, film archivists and movie distributors.\nThey argued that the 1994 law violates the constitutional\nprovision that lets Congress set up a copyright system, as well\nas the Constitution\u2019s free-speech guarantee. But before I dive in, some quick thoughts.It was an odd year for green business, and it began with some mixed signals about how far companies were coming on sustainability. A\u00a0 GreenBiz report \u00a0indicated that progress had slowed or even regressed, but\u00a0 MIT and BCG also declared \u00a0that sustainability had reached a \"tipping point\" with more companies putting sustainability \"on the management agenda.\" In reality, both views were right. Corporate sustainability lost some of its sexiness from previous years, as it grew more entrenched in day-to-day business. Some parts of the agenda \u2014 eco-efficiency and resource conservation for example \u2014 are widely accepted now, and it's rare to find a big-company CEO who doesn't have sustainability on his or her radar. The mega forces driving sustainability deep into business \u2014 such as climate change, resource constraints, and transparency \u2014 are getting stronger. We may not be keeping pace with these pressures, but leading companies continue to evolve more sustainable strategies and tactics. Let's look at some top macro- and company-level stories. Macro Trends 1. Historic drought and Hurricane Sandy sweep away (some) climate denial For many people this year, climate change moved from theoretical to painfully real. Mega weather took many lives and cost over $120 billion in the U.S. alone ( $50 billion for the drought ,\u00a0 $71 billion for Sandy ). After Sandy raged across the eastern coast,\u00a0 Businessweek \u00a0blared on its cover \" It's Global Warming, Stupid .\" New York Mayor Bloomberg, a Republican, endorsed President Obama in the election, titling his open letter, \" A Vote for a President to Lead on Climate Change .\" As bad as Sandy was, the relentless drought across the middle of the country may prove more convincing in the long run.\u00a0 Corn yields per acre fell 19% , food prices rose, and water disappeared \u2014\u00a0 the Mississippi River may soon struggle to support commerce . Individual companies are feeling the bite: analysts at Morningstar estimate that\u00a0 input costs at Tyson Foods will rise by $700 million \u00a0\u2014 more than its\u00a0 2012 net income . Over one-third of the world's largest companies surveyed by the Carbon Disclosure Project are\u00a0 already seeing the impacts of climate change on their business . So with life-and-death consequences and vast costs, we must have moved quickly to tackle climate change, right? Sort of... The year\u00a0 ended with the failure, yet again , of the international community to come to some agreement on climate change. But country-level and regional policy moved forward:\u00a0 Australia passed a carbon tax ,\u00a0 South Korea approved carbon trading , and\u00a0 California just began its own trading experiment . Many countries also committed serious funds to build a clean economy:\u00a0 Saudi Arabia pledged $109 billion for solar ,\u00a0 Japan declared that a $628 billion green energy industry would be central to its 2020 strategy, and\u00a0 China targeted $372 billion \u00a0to cut energy use and pollution. In the U.S.,\u00a0 a backdoor approach to climate policy took over . The Obama administration issued\u00a0 new standards to double the fuel economy of cars and trucks , and the National Resources Defense Council (an NGO)\u00a0 proposed using the Clean Air Act to reduce emissions from power plants by 25% . 2. The math and physics of a planetary constraints get clearer Arithmetic had a big year: Nate Silver's nearly perfect predictions of the election gave him the oxymoronic status of rock-star statistician. The\u00a0 math and physics of sustainability \u00a0got some serious attention as well. Writer and activist Bill McKibben wrote a\u00a0 widely-read piece in\u00a0 Rolling Stone \u00a0about climate math \u2014 how much more carbon emissions the planet can take \u2014 and followed it up with a national awareness-building tour. Based on similar numbers, both\u00a0 McKinsey \u00a0and PwC UK calculated how fast we must reduce the carbon intensity of the global economy ( PwC's number is 5 percent\u00a0per year until 2050 ). And on the resource constraint front,\u00a0 Jeremy Grantham , co-founder of the\u00a0 asset management firm GMO \u00a0($100 billion invested), continued his relentless numbers-based assault on the fallacy of infinite resources. In his\u00a0 November newsletter , he demonstrated exactly how much of a drag on the U.S. economy commodity prices have become. Nobody can really deny that, in principle, exponential growth must stop someday. Grantham, McKibben, and many others are making the case that someday has arrived. 3. The clean economy continues to explode The rapid growth of natural gas production (the biggest energy story of the year) and the high-profile failure of one solar manufacturer (Solyndra) have\u00a0 confused people about the prospects for clean tech . In reality, the clean economy is winning. The share of U.S. electricity coming from non-hydro renewables doubled to 6% in the last 4 years. On May 26,\u00a0 Germany set a world record \u00a0when it produced 50% of its electricity needs from solar power alone. In a mini political tipping point, six Republican senators publicly supported an extension to the wind production tax credit in the U.S. (which will expire in days), and got an earful from a\u00a0 Wall Street Journal \u00a0editorial . It wasn't just energy. One auto analyst declared 2012 the \" Year of the Green Car ,\" with more high-MPG models, 500,000 hybrid sales in the U.S., and\u00a0 plug-in sales up 228 \u00a0percent. To cap the year, the pure electric\u00a0 Tesla Model S was selected as the Motor Trend Car of the Year . Company Stories This year, there were countless eco-efficiency stories about companies\u00a0 saving millions of dollars \u00a0and developing new tools to make buildings, fleets ( Staples and UPS, for example ), and manufacturing much leaner. Aside from that overall theme, the following stories grabbed me because of their connection to larger trends. 4. The green supply chain gets some teeth: Walmart changes incentives for buyers\u00a0 This year, Walmart finally added a key element to its impressive green supply chain efforts. The retail giant's powerful buyers, or merchants, now have\u00a0 a sustainability goal in their performance targets and reviews . For example, the laptop PC buyer set a goal that, by Christmas, all of the laptops Walmart sells would come pre-installed with advanced energy-saving settings. It was by no means a hiccup-free year on sustainability issues for Walmart, with\u00a0 deep concerns \u00a0about corruption in its Mexican operations. But the subtle change in buyer incentives is a big deal. 5. Transparency and tragedy raise awareness about worker conditions Early in 2012, Apple took some serious heat for the\u00a0 working conditions at Foxconn , the giant company that assembles a huge percentage of our electronics. Later in the year, tragedy struck Dhaka, Bangladesh when a\u00a0 fire at the Tazreen Fashion factory \u00a0killed or injured hundreds of people. The company that owns the factory serves Walmart, Carrefour, IKEA, and many others (but in fact,\u00a0 some companies didn't even know that Tazreen was a supplier ). It's unclear if any of these human and PR disasters will affect the companies downstream, but transparency and knowledge about the lives of the people who make our products will continue to rise. 6. Data gets bigger and faster: PepsiCo and Columbia speed up lifecycle assessments The\u00a0 rise of Big Data \u00a0was an important theme in business in general this year, but especially in sustainability. And nowhere is good data needed more than in the onerous and expensive task of calculating a product's lifecycle footprint.\u00a0 PepsiCo has had great success with the method , finding ways to reduce cost and risk for key brands, but execs wanted to apply the tool across thousands of products. To make the exercise feasible and affordable, they turned to Columbia University, which developed a\u00a0 new algorithm for fast carbon footprinting . This isn't just a wonky exercise: As PepsiCo exec Al Halvorsen told me, \"the real reason you do an LCA is improve the business, to put more efficient processes in place, and innovate in the supply chain.\" 7. Sustainability innovation opens up: Unilever, Heineken, and EMC ask the world for help This new world of social media, where everyone has a voice, can be tough on companies. Consumers can gather around a green issue and pressure companies to change their behavior. Some notable change.org campaigns this year\u00a0 challenged Universal Pictures \u00a0(about its green messaging around\u00a0 The Lorax ),\u00a0 Crayola \u00a0(recycling markers), and\u00a0 Dunkin' Donuts \u00a0(Styrofoam cups). But companies can also use \"open\" innovation tools to generate new ideas and invite the world to solve problems together. Unilever, which has my vote for leader in corporate sustainability right now, held an online discussion or \"jam.\" Then the company posted a list of \" Challenges and wants \" and asked for ideas on solving big issues such as how to bring safe drinking water to the world's poorest regions.\u00a0 Unilever has received over 1,000 ideas \u00a0and is \"pursuing 6 to 7 percent of these with internal teams.\" Other notable open innovation models this year included\u00a0 Heineken's $10,000 sustainable packaging contest \u00a0(which yielded some very fun ideas like a roving tap truck) and\u00a0 EMC's eco-challenge with InnoCentive on e-waste . 8. The economy gets a bit more circular: M&S, H&M, and Puma experiment with closing loops\u00a0 On the heels of\u00a0 Patagonia's \"Don't Buy This Jacket\" campaign \u00a0( one of my top 10 stories from last year ), British retailer M&S began a program called \" Schwop \" that asked customers to bring back old clothes every time they bought new ones. This month, H&M also rolled out a\u00a0 global clothing collection and recycling effort . Puma, after making last year's list with it's Environmental P&L, kept the momentum going and\u00a0 announced a new \"InCycle\" collection \u00a0with biodegradable sneakers and shirts, and recyclable jackets and backpacks. Remanufacturing has been around a long time, but closing loops is getting more popular every year. 9. Dematerialization gets sexier: Nike's knitted shoe shows off sustainable style\u00a0 Keeping the apparel theme, um, running, check out\u00a0 Nike's new shoe with FlyKnit technology . The upper part of the shoe is constructed from a single strand, which greatly reduces waste and lightens the shoe dramatically. It's a great thing when a more sustainable design also coincides perfectly with customer needs. Enough said. 10. Zero becomes more the norm: DuPont, GM, and John Elkington show the way\u00a0 The idea that organizations should send zero waste to landfill was once a niche idea, but it's quickly becoming the ante to enter the waste management game. Announcements on waste may not be exciting, but they demonstrate how companies can turn a cost center into a source of profit. DuPont's Building Innovation Products business\u00a0 reduced its landfill waste from 81 million pounds to zero in three years . GM announced that it would ramp up its already extensive waste reuse and recycling efforts, which are now generating\u00a0 $1 billion a year . And a plug for a fellow writer: In a new book, sustainability thought leader John Elkington made the case that the future would belong to the \" Zeronauts ,\" the \"new breed of innovators determined to drive problems such as carbon, waste, toxics, and poverty to zero.\" Five Questions For 2013 Some other promising stories are in the \"too early to tell\" stage, but bring up some key questions: 1. \u00a0Can we standardize sustainability, which some smart folks began to do around rankings ( GISR ) and accounting ( Sustainability Accounting Standards Board )? 2. \u00a0Will we find a way to value externalities like ecosystem services and internalized, intangible benefits? (A focus of some of my work as an advisor to PwC US). For example, Microsoft launched an\u00a0 internal carbon tax \u00a0and some major companies (Coca-Cola, Nike, Kimberly-Clark, etc.)\u00a0 pledged to value natural capital \u00a0at Rio+20. 3. \u00a0Will government get in the way or help, like when the\u00a0 U.S. Senate allowed the military to keep investing in biofuels ? 4. \u00a0Hertz and B&Q (Kingfisher) have delved into collaborative consumption (see WWF's Green Game-Changers \u00a0report), but will the sharing economy make a dent on sustainability issues? 5. \u00a0Finally, how much will we challenge the nature of capitalism, and what will that mean for how companies operate? (This is the focus of my next project.) So many stories, so little time... on to 2013. Happy holidays and have a safe and wonderful New Year! Winston is the co-author of the best-seller\u00a0 Green to Gold \u00a0and the author of\u00a0 Green Recovery . The report, provocatively titled \"We Have Met the Enemy and He is Us\" [ PDF ], summarizes its findings thus: One of those narrative fallacies relates to the most basic thing that investors care about: results. Most of the funds in which Kauffman invested failed to beat public market indices, despite the higher-risk nature of their work. Kauffman found that larger funds in particular provided disappointing returns. Kauffman didn't say it was opting out of venture capital. Rather, it plans to seek smaller funds, shift some of its money towards public equities, and co-invest in later-round deals with seasoned investors. It also called on investors to work to better align investor and venture capitalist incentives. Within Innosight, where I lead venture investing, the report led to an invigorating debate about the industry. We debated two possible stories behind some of the report's statistics. The first story relates to plain old-fashioned competition. Over the past decades, foundations, pensions, and other investors have poured money into venture capital, particularly in the United States. The number of funds has exploded. If one assumes that the number of great startup ideas is relatively stable at any given time (a contentious but simplifying assumption), increased supply has to decrease returns. A result that is exacerbated by the simultaneous decrease in the cost of innovation and the rise of new approaches, like  Y Combinator's  systematic incubation factory,  Kickstarter's  crowd-funding platform, and super angels like  Ron Conway . Barriers to entry are decreasing and disruptive entrants are surging, a recipe that both Michael Porter and Clayton Christensen could agree augurs poorly for industry returns. The alternative and potentially more troubling story is that the venture capital approach is fundamentally flawed. The industry has unquestionably helped to support the formation of world-changing companies such as Microsoft, Cisco Systems, Google, Facebook, and countless others. Yet over the past decades, venture capitalists have shown signs, despite all their experience and skills, that they've not gotten better at what they do.  Maybe that's just the way it is. You can't know  ex-ante  which idea is the right one. If that's the case, though, it would be far better to simple spur more Y-Combinator-like incubators that follow the Steve Blank gospel of getting out of the building and iterating to discover product\/market fit.  A related possibility is that a majority of venture capitalists use flawed theories of startup success. Clayton Christensen likes to describe how, in the early stage of theory development, people make predictions based on observed correlations. For example, people observed that things that flew had feathers. So people hoping to fly created large feathered wings. More advanced theories pinpoint causal mechanisms. For flight, that was Bernoulli's Principle, a theory that explained the concept of lift and why modern aircraft are not covered in feathers. Much of the venture capital industry seems stuck in the feathers-and-wings stage of theory development. Many successful venture capitalists observe directional patterns. \"Every time I have succeeded,\" they might think, \"I've backed an 'A team,' that has targeted a hot market space.\" There's no doubt that's true, but that is a statement of correlation, not causality. Even worse, the narrative fallacy means that people are likely to construct stories about the past that might not have been precisely true, making future predictions even more dubious.  Google Ventures is an intriguing example of a venture organization putting more science behind its correlative analysis. As detailed in a recent  Fast Company article , it has a team of statisticians crunching data to determine patterns of success in startups. For example, its team found the perceived wisdom that failure is beneficial isn't backed by data. Almost 30% of businesses founded by someone who had succeeded once succeed again, versus 15% of businesses founded by someone who failed once.  The Google Ventures approach has its limits. Without understanding  why  a pattern exists, making reliably accurate predictions is hard, at best. This is where good business theory comes in. Work by Christensen and other innovation thought leaders has built a body of theory about why certain ideas succeed and others fail. Other academics, in particular  Noam Wasserman  at the Harvard Business School, have provided useful theories to inform the critical choices facing entrepreneurs.  It's not hard to see the venture capital industry trifurcating. There will always be top-tier firms who give their seal of approval to a select group of startups. Expect to see continued growth among incubators that support fast-cycle iteration. And in between, look for a rise of companies that take the Google Ventures approach even further to approach the funding of startup companies scientifically. The rest? Well, Darwin has a way of working out such problems.","path":".\/2008_2012_msft_bloomberg_news\/is-venture-capital-broken-.txt"},{"id":20697510,"title":"AT&T Embraces Startup Speed-Dating to Spur Innovation","released_at":"<date>April 2 2012<\/date> <time>04:01:00<\/time>","content":"AT&T Inc. Obama\u2019s campaign entered the general election race with $88.8 million in cash, compared to $50.4 million for Romney coming out of the  Republican National Convention . The president raised $84.8 million in August, while Romney raised $66.6 million and borrowed an additional $20 million secured by general-election campaign donations -- most already in the bank -- to pay expenditures until he officially became his party\u2019s nominee at the convention.  In total, Obama has raised a total of $441.3 million for his re-election to $283.6 million for Romney, who used some of his cash to pay bonuses to his top aides. The figures are based on disclosures filed yesterday with the  Federal Election Commission .  When national political parties and allied super-political action committees are included, though, Romney entered September with more cash to spend on his side than Obama, $165 million to $101 million.  The  Republican National Committee  overcame Romney\u2019s campaign fundraising deficit, bringing in $35.6 million last month and entering September with $76.6 million in the bank. The  Democratic National Committee  raised just $5.6 million and reported taking an $8 million loan, finishing the month with $7.1 million in cash.  Party Money  The disparity between the parties\u2019 national committee accounts is largely because the Democrats -- with an undisputed nominee -- have already been investing in swing-state voter turnout initiatives.  The DNC has distributed $60.7 million this year to state parties, most of it in presidential swing states, while the RNC has transferred $15 million. In  Ohio , which no Republican has ever won the White House without carrying, the DNC transferred more than $2.5 million last month to the state party. The RNC gave just over $550,000.  Obama, meanwhile, spent $66 million on ads last month, more than tripling Romney\u2019s $18 million.  Romney Bonuses  The Romney campaign made payments totaling more than $200,000 to at least nine senior campaign staff members that supplemented their regular salaries. Political director  Rich Beeson  received $37,500 and campaign manager Matt Rhoades, policy director Lanhee Chen and communications director  Gail Gitcho  were among six aides who each received $25,000. Two others got $10,000 each. All of the payments were made Aug. 31, the end of the monthly reporting period and the day after the Republican convention ended.  A co-founder of the Boston-based private-equity firm  Bain Capital  LLC, Romney has relied on financial support from Wall Street. His eight biggest sources of contributions in August came from financial-services employees, according to a Bloomberg News computer-assisted analysis of FEC data.  Leading the way were employees of  Goldman Sachs Group Inc. (GS) , who have been Romney\u2019s biggest source of campaign donations and contributed another $172,780 last month. Since he announced his candidacy last year, Romney has received $848,860 from Goldman employees and their families. (AAPL) \u2019s rivals aren\u2019t rushing\nto emulate the iPhone maker\u2019s decision to subject supplier\nfactories to audits by a labor group. Instead, they\u2019re sticking\nto internal checks that may leave room for violations -- and\nnegative public relations fallout.  Apple said on Feb. 14 the Fair Labor Association had\nstarted independent audits amid criticism of conditions at its\n plants  in  China . Companies including  Microsoft Corp. (MSFT) ,  Dell Inc. (DELL) ,\nHewlett-Packard Co. and Samsung Electronics Co. rely on their\nown evaluations, based in part on guidelines from the Electronic\nIndustry Citizenship Coalition, which they say are sufficient to\nprevent abuses.  Though Apple\u2019s decision to join FLA may not root out all\ninstances of labor abuse, the EICC\u2019s  member  companies may open\nthemselves to even harsher criticism. While the EICC sets\nstandards for ethics, worker safety and labor practices, it\ndoesn\u2019t require members to disclose findings and it lacks\nenforcement powers. The result is a disjointed system of self-\nimposed regulations that fail to hold companies accountable when\nabuses arise, according to labor advocates and technology\nexecutives.  \u201cThey are absolutely toothless,\u201d said Tom Fallon, chief\nexecutive officer of  Infinera Corp. (INFN) , a Sunnyvale, California-\nbased maker of telecommunications equipment that hasn\u2019t joined\nthe EICC because Fallon says the group isn\u2019t effective. \u201cI\ndon\u2019t think they do meaningful work.\u201d  Wendy Dittmer, a spokeswoman for EICC, said she doesn\u2019t\nknow of any instance of a factory losing business, permanently\nor temporarily, for failing to live up to the group\u2019s code of\nconduct. The  EICC  doesn\u2019t require companies to share those\ndetails about their relations with business partners, she said.  Foxconn  Technology companies are under scrutiny for working\nconditions at  Foxconn Technology Group (2354)  and other manufacturers\u2019\nChinese plants, where the world\u2019s best-selling gadgets are\nassembled. Workers making Apple products log 11 hours of work a\nday, six days a week, while production speeds are so high that\nworkers aren\u2019t able to rest while making iPads, according to New\nYork-based  China Labor Watch . Employees have been exposed to\ndangerous aluminum dust, the group said. Foxconn installed\nsafety nets and hired counselors and psychologists in response\nto multiple suicides in 2010.  Apple\u2019s FLA Membership  Amid the criticism, including a  New York  Times\ninvestigation highlighting Foxconn\u2019s labor conditions, Apple\nopened factories to the FLA, a Washington-based nonprofit\norganization, and said that the group would inspect plants owned\nby three of its largest manufacturing partners. Apple in January\nalso listed its suppliers for the first time. The company has\ndisclosed instances of rights violations in an annual progress\nreport since 2006, though it has never specified where or at\nwhich suppliers the violations occurred.  Foxconn also said on Feb. 18 that it was raising wages to\n$290 a month, double the level of three years ago.  No other technology company has sought membership in the\nFLA, said CEO Auret van Heerden. Founded in 1999 to address\nworking conditions in the apparel industry, most of the group\u2019s\n34  member companies  come from that business, including Nike Inc.\nand Adidas AG.  Unlike the EICC, FLA member companies must agree to\ndisclose their suppliers and to submit to unannounced visits\nfrom the FLA or third-party auditors. The FLA also posts results\nof all audits on its website.  The  67-member  EICC, a Washington-based trade group founded\nin 2004, doesn\u2019t require companies to stop using suppliers or\nmanufacturers regardless of their record on treatment of\nworkers. It dictates only that \u201cmembers commit to continuous\nimprovement,\u201d said Dittmer, the group\u2019s spokeswoman. Cupertino,\nCalifornia-based Apple also is a member of the EICC.  Internal Audits  When it comes to ensuring factories\u2019 ability to reliably\nmake a quality product, most companies in the EICC insist that\nall factories earn certifications to ensure a plant can reliably\ndeliver high-quality products.  The  EICC  doesn\u2019t require any such certification regarding\nthe treatment of workers. Member companies may choose an EICC-\nsanctioned outside auditor, usually paid by the company. Yet,\ncompanies aren\u2019t required to make the results of their audits\npublic or share them with the EICC. Each company owns the\nresults of its audits, Dittmer said.  A drawback to both the FLA\u2019s and EICC\u2019s approach is\ninspections often don\u2019t include suppliers further down the\nsupply chain, said Mike Fawkes, a former supply-chain executive\nat  Hewlett-Packard. (HPQ)  A handheld product like the iPhone has\n hundreds  of parts, many of them made by small companies in\nChina.  Defining \u2018High-Risk\u2019  Even the FLA only requires companies to audit about 5\npercent of companies in their supply chains, down from 30\npercent when the organization was created, said Heather White,\nwho founded workplace-auditing firm Verite in 1995 and is now a\nfellow at Harvard\u2019s Edmond J. Safra Center for Ethics.  Until recently, the EICC hadn\u2019t required member companies\nto audit a specific percentage of its suppliers, the EICC\u2019s\nDittmer said. In 2010, the EICC members voted to create a\ncompliance program to include a requirement that members audit\nsome percentage of \u201chigh risk\u201d factories owned by the company\nor important suppliers. The board voted on Feb. 17 on what\nnumber of high-risk suppliers would need to be inspected, though\nit hasn\u2019t released the result. She says the definition of high-\nrisk is up to each company.  Need for \u2018Vision\u2019  The technology industry\u2019s inconsistent approach illustrates\nthe need for a more comprehensive strategy to prevent excessive\novertime, poor pay and dangerous chemical exposure, said Scott\nNova, executive director of Worker Rights Consortium, a group\nthat investigates factory conditions.  \u201cWe don\u2019t see that kind of vision,\u201d said Nova, who is\nbased in  Washington . \u201cWe see it with technological innovation,\nwith design and marketing, but we don\u2019t see it when it comes to\nhuman rights.\u201d  The EICC was formed when large U.S. technology companies\nsought to create an industry code of conduct. Almost all of them\nhad outsourced most of their production in the previous decade,\nand had watched as Nike and other apparel makers came under\ncriticism for child-labor violations and other workplace issues.  \u201cNone of us wanted to get Nike\u2019d,\u201d said Fawkes, the\nformer executive at Hewlett-Packard, the world\u2019s largest maker\nof personal computers.  Getting Started  Fawkes said the founding members of the EICC, including\nDell and  International Business Machines Corp. (IBM) , sincerely wanted\nto improve working conditions at their suppliers. The companies\ndebated whether to let members satisfy the code of conduct as\nthey saw fit, or to implement a more explicit certification\nprocess. In the end, they went with the less rigorous approach.  \u201cWe felt we had to get something started, because this was\ngoing to be a long journey,\u201d said Fawkes, who is now a venture\ncapitalist at  VantagePoint Capital Partners . \u201cThese supply\nchains are 10 levels deep, and we intuitively knew that the\nlower you got, the worse the conditions got.\u201d  Some executives said it\u2019s unfair to demonize Western\ntechnology companies, which outsourced production to  Asia  to\ndeal with competitive pressure to keep prices low, since\nworkplace norms are so different in China. In addition, many\nworkers in China were young people from the countryside who\nwanted to make as much money as quickly as they could, said\nMichael Marks, former CEO of  Flextronics International Ltd. (FLEX) , the\nworld\u2019s largest contract manufacturer before Foxconn\u2019s rise a\ndecade ago.  \u201cMost Chinese workers at that point in time wanted as much\novertime as they could get,\u201d he said. \u201cIf we tried to limit\nthem to 50 hours, we\u2019d get complaints.\u201d  Microsoft, Dell, Samsung  Companies that are part of the EICC defend their practices\neven if they don\u2019t plan to partner with FLA. Dell, the third-largest maker of personal computers, has\nemployees inspect suppliers\u2019 operations, including Foxconn\u2019s,\nsaid  David Frink , a spokesman. \u201cIt\u2019s an ongoing process,\u201d he\nsaid. \u201cWe\u2019re encouraged by the progress.\u201d  Samsung, the world\u2019s biggest smartphone maker last year,\nsaid it has a \u201climited\u201d relationship with Foxconn. In the company\u2019s 2010 corporate responsibility report it\nsaid it found child-labor violations at 1 percent to 10 percent\nof its audited sites, and excessive working hours at more than\nhalf. The  Palo Alto , California-based company didn\u2019t provide\nmore specifics about the violations.  \u2018Hands-On\u2019 Assessment  Companies that aren\u2019t members of EICC also have internal\ninspections under way.\u00a0 Nokia Oyj (NOK1V) , the world\u2019s second-largest\nmaker of mobile phones, said it works with aid organization\n Oxfam  and the  International Metalworkers Federation  to ensure\nproper conditions. That's what I called the SPDR S&P Health Care Services ETF ( XHS ), because out of all exchange-traded funds it had the most exposure to hospitals -- the biggest beneficiary of Obamacare -- while not owning any big brand-name drug companies or medical device makers, both of which will see new taxes under the health insurance law. Soon after the article came out, I noticed this tweet from Hardeep Walia (@hardeepw): Enrolling in the Ultimate Obamacare ETF. Nah our #motif is better. That intrigued me. How could his \u201cmotif\u201d be a better choice than the ETF I wrote about? And what was a motif? A little Googling revealed that Walia is chief executive officer of online broker Motif Investing Inc., which was launched in June 2012. Backers include Goldman Sachs Group Inc.; board members include former Securities and Exchange Commission chairman Arthur Levitt and former Wall Street executive Sallie Krawcheck. (Levitt is a board member of Bloomberg LP, the parent of Bloomberg News.) The former president of ETrade Financial Corp. is an adviser. Walia, 40, was general manager of enterprise-services business and director of corporate strategy and development at Microsoft. All right, then, definitely worth a phone call. Pretty good, but not perfect -- that was Walia's verdict on XHS as an Obamacare play. The first thing he said about it? \"XHS has a veterinary supply stock in it,\" which is not a factor in Obamacare. I wasn't going to argue with that. More broadly, I had to admit his \"motif\" was more finely tuned than the ETF I'd written about.  It has about 20 percent in hospitals, like XHS. It also has 43 percent in pharmacy benefit managers and 18 percent in generic drug makers. Generic drugs will benefit from government incentives to substitute them for brand names. It has 12 percent in electronic medical records companies, and 1.5 percent in an insurance exchange. So far this year, it's up 36 percent; XHS is up 32 percent.  Motif allows everyday investors to create what are, with a few key differences, sector- or theme-based baskets (motifs) of up to 30 stocks or ETFs for a total $9.95 commission. Investors own each stock in the basket they create and trade and can change the weightings of the stocks. In interviews, Walia has suggested his company be thought of as \"the Apple App Store, but with motifs\" and \"as ETF 2.0.\"  In all fairness, XHS wasn\u2019t made to profit from Obamacare, but to provide exposure to health care service companies, which it does well. So far there are 120 set motifs that include many real-world themes. Here are some of the more intriguing motifs designed by the firm:  Motif also lists some 15,000 \u201ccommunity\u201d motifs made by other investors. They can be used by anyone on the site, and each has a chat room. If an investor purchases your motif, you get a $1 royalty. These homegrown motifs range from the compelling to the inane, and that's just looking through the W's: Motifs, unlike ETFs, have no management fee and trade on no exchange. Investors pay $4.95 if they trade one stock or $9.95 to rebalance or buy or sell multiple securities within a motif. All trades can be made intra-day and an account can be set up with a minimum of $250.  One disadvantage of motifs compared with ETFs is that when you change the securities in them, you incur capital gains and will be taxed. When ETFs are rejiggered and rebalanced, very rarely do investors pay capital gains taxes. Walia says Motif is working on a tax-optimization solution.  Whether or not you end up using Motif, you may want to surf around its website. Making investing more interactive, social and fun is a victory in itself. Eric Balchunas is an exchange-traded-fund analyst at Bloomberg. (GOOG) , Facebook Inc. and  LinkedIn Corp. (LNKD)  wound up in Ireland because they could reduce their tax bills. Their success is leading European and U.S. politicians to label the country a tax haven that must change its ways.  The grand architect of much of that success: Feargal O\u2019Rourke, the scion of a political dynasty who heads the tax practice at PricewaterhouseCoopers in Ireland. He advises both multinational companies and the government on tax policy and has emerged as his country\u2019s leading defender.  \u201cUnder no circumstances is Ireland a tax haven,\u201d O\u2019Rourke said recently at his corner office on the River Liffey in Dublin, a ritual stop for many tech companies in their Irish quest. \u201cI\u2019m a player in this game and we play by the rules.\u201d  In that game, multinational companies find ways to legally avoid income taxes in the countries where most of their customers are. Google cuts billions off its tax bill each year by sending profits through Ireland to a mailbox in  Bermuda ;  Facebook (FB)  sends them through Ireland to Grand Cayman; LinkedIn uses Ireland en route to the Isle of Man. O\u2019Rourke advised each company on its arrangements, according to two people familiar with the matter.  He also persuaded regulators to eliminate a withholding tax on profits that corporations move out of the country -- while separately advising his cousin who was finance minister.  Political Backlash  Such concessions now expose Ireland to a political backlash. Across Europe, officials have grown increasingly frustrated with corporate tax avoidance as individuals are asked to pay more and sacrifice in the name of austerity. German politicians are urging Ireland, a recipient of international bailouts, to alter the tax system that lured multinationals like  Apple Inc. (AAPL)  and Google. The European Union is even probing Ireland\u2019s corporate tax deals.  Cracking down on tax avoidance by multinational companies has emerged as a priority for the Group of 20 nations and the European Commission. It costs the U.S. and Europe at least $100 billion a year, with O\u2019Rourke\u2019s clients among the biggest beneficiaries.  The lost revenue \u201chas to be made up by you and me and every other taxpayer who can\u2019t afford high-flying attorneys and accountants to shift our income into places with low taxes,\u201d said Robert B. Reich, a professor of public policy at the University of  California  at Berkeley, and former labor secretary in the Clinton administration.  Way Station  While Ireland recently announced plans for a modest tightening of its corporate tax rules in response to the criticism, the country remains highly attractive to multinationals as a way station for their profits.  O\u2019Rourke and other accountants like him \u201cthink up these tax strategies and the impact is tens of billions in lost tax revenue in Europe, the U.S. and less-developed countries,\u201d said Jim Stewart, an associate professor of finance at  Trinity College \u2019s school of business in Dublin. \u201cHe\u2019s a very aggressive leader of the tax-avoidance industry here.\u201d  O\u2019Rourke often speaks loudly and excitedly, gesturing with his hands, yet is careful not to let disagreements turn into arguments. He said the finger-pointing at Ireland and at his profession is misdirected, and politicians around the world complaining about tax avoidance have only themselves to blame.  \u201cWhy should Ireland be the policeman for the U.S.?\u201d he asks. \u201cThey can change the law\u201d -- he snaps his fingers -- \u201clike that! I could draft a bill for them in an hour.\u201d  Bypassing Politics  O\u2019Rourke rebuffed entreaties to enter politics early in his career after getting degrees in commerce and accounting. He made partner at PWC in 1996, just as a U.S.-driven tech boom was transforming Ireland. The son of Mary O\u2019Rourke, perhaps the country\u2019s best-known female politician, he sees himself as also serving the public good, attracting foreign investment and high-paying jobs. U.S. multinational companies employ about 100,000 people in Ireland. He jousts with critics on  Twitter Inc. (TWTR)  (another client), radio and newspaper op-ed pages.  \u201cI like selling Ireland,\u201d said O\u2019Rourke, 49, who has bright blue eyes and a bushy mane of black hair tinged with flecks of white. \u201cWe have a lot to offer.\u201d  O\u2019Rourke has pursued this mission with vigor. Over the years, he has pushed for regulatory changes to help cut his clients\u2019 tax bills and advised the Irish government on tax policy. He was instrumental in creating an Irish tax-credit program that subsidizes the research of companies like  Intel Corp. (INTC)  -- another client.  O\u2019Rourke declined to discuss his clients. His roster was confirmed by people outside the firm who are familiar with his practice.  Seeking Advice  Paul Haran, a former Irish government official who introduced major elements of Ireland\u2019s corporate tax system, said he often consulted O\u2019Rourke.  \u201cI\u2019d naturally pick up the phone and ask him,\u201d Haran said, about \u201ctax and how it operates in the real world.\u201d  An annual ritual has long showcased O\u2019Rourke. Since the mid-1990s, the Irish finance minister has given several hundred business leaders an overview of the new government budget at a PWC-sponsored breakfast at one of Dublin\u2019s top hotels. For years, that was Charlie McCreevy, a top politician in the Fianna Fail party, who would then turn over the proceedings to the real expert on the budget\u2019s key tax provisions: O\u2019Rourke.  \u201cI used to use him to get advice on technical tax issues and he\u2019d give that advice freely,\u201d said McCreevy, the country\u2019s finance minister from 1997 to 2004.  Dual Roles  O\u2019Rourke sees no conflict in his dual roles representing private industry and advising the government on issues that benefit his clients. Just having a pipeline to the government doesn\u2019t guarantee results.  \u201cAdvisers advise, ministers decide,\u201d he said.  Attracting foreign companies has been integral to Ireland\u2019s economic success. It boomed in the 1990s as companies like Apple, Intel, Dell Inc. and  Microsoft Corp. (MSFT)  took advantage of its cheap and educated workforce. U.S. multinationals doubled their employment of Irish workers and helped cut Ireland\u2019s  unemployment rate  to less than 4 percent from almost 14 percent.  After the tech bubble burst in 2000, Ireland morphed from a vigorous economy into a tax haven with slower job growth, said Stephen Kinsella, an economics lecturer at the  University of Limerick \u2019s business school.  Mailbox Subsidiaries  Ireland\u2019s transformation into a hub for tax avoidance can be seen in U.S. Commerce Department data. In 2010, U.S. companies attributed $95 billion in profits to Irish subsidiaries, up more than sevenfold from $13 billion in 2000. Actual employment at those units barely grew during that decade, and the companies\u2019 reported tax rate plummeted to 3 percent from 9 percent.  Many of the Irish subsidiaries have no offices or employees and pay no income taxes. They are merely ways to move profits out of countries where sales take place to mailbox subsidiaries in zero-tax island havens.  \u201cWhat we celebrate is that we attract more foreign direct investment than anyone else in the world,\u201d Kinsella said. \u201cWhat we don\u2019t celebrate is that we deliberately turn a blind eye to companies using tax loopholes that we are probably aware of to avoid tens of billions in taxes around the world.\u201d  O\u2019Rourke\u2019s office on the second floor of the PWC building features photos of him with Muhammad Ali and Bill Clinton. Obsessed with U.S. politics, he\u2019s read every presidential autobiography since Truman, and all of Robert A. Caro\u2019s four-part Lyndon B. Johnson biography. He identifies himself as a \u201cJFK Democrat or a Rockefeller Republican.\u201d  Double Irish  At PWC, O\u2019Rourke oversees a staff of 500 tax accountants and lawyers, including teams stationed in San Francisco, San Jose, New York and  London . He has an apartment he rents out in the south of  France , near Cannes, and lives with his wife and two children in a suburban Dublin house that was listed recently for almost 1.4 million euros ($1.9 million). The house is no longer on the market.  The O\u2019Rourke client whose tax strategies have attracted the most attention is Google, based in Mountain View, California. It uses an elaborate structure that routes its European sales through a subsidiary in Dublin. The unit in turn pays billions in royalties to another Irish company for the rights to Google\u2019s various patents.  Because the second unit is managed in Bermuda, it isn\u2019t \u201ctax resident\u201d in Ireland and thus doesn\u2019t owe Irish taxes. This technique, known as a \u201cDouble Irish,\u201d results in the majority of Google\u2019s worldwide profits avoiding income tax anywhere in the world and reduced the company\u2019s worldwide income tax bill by $2.2 billion last year.  Dutch Sandwich  For years, Irish tax policy impelled Google to take one extra step. If those payments from the Irish unit went directly to Bermuda, they were subject to an Irish withholding tax, because Ireland doesn\u2019t have a tax treaty with Bermuda. So Google, like some other companies, has avoided the 20 percent withholding tax by moving those payments through a unit in the Netherlands, a tactic known as a \u201cDutch Sandwich.\u201d  O\u2019Rourke set out to simplify those structures, eliminating the need for a Dutch intermediary.  In October 2007, he met at Google\u2019s Dublin headquarters on Barrow Street with Tadhg O\u2019Connell, the head of the Irish Revenue division that audits tech companies, according to a person familiar with the meeting.  O\u2019Connell rejected O\u2019Rourke\u2019s request that royalties like Google\u2019s should be able to flow directly to units in Bermuda and Cayman without being taxed. O\u2019Connell, who left the Irish Revenue earlier this year to work for Deloitte, a competitor to O\u2019Rourke\u2019s firm, declined to comment. A Google spokesman declined to comment.  High Places  In 2008, O\u2019Rourke\u2019s cousin Brian Lenihan Jr. became the country\u2019s finance minister, setting policy for the Irish Revenue office. Two years later, after continued entreaties by O\u2019Rourke, the revenue office announced that it would no longer impose withholding taxes on such transactions.  \u201cWe take the view that if there is valuable intellectual property outside of Ireland, it\u2019s not reasonable for us to jump on that,\u201d said Eamonn O\u2019Dea, who now oversees the corporate, business and international division of the Revenue Office.  While acknowledging he considered himself an adviser to his cousin -- who died of cancer in 2011 -- O\u2019Rourke said they never discussed the withholding tax and it didn\u2019t come under the finance ministry\u2019s purview. He didn\u2019t want to be accused of exploiting his family ties to benefit clients, he said.  Family Background  \u201cI have been extraordinarily careful over the years to ensure that no one could ever make a valid criticism of me that I got to where I am because of my family background,\u201d he said.  On a crisp September afternoon, O\u2019Rourke joined his mother for lunch at the  Hodson Bay Hotel  in Athlone, the working-class town on the River Shannon where he grew up. The daughter of an Irish tax inspector and businessman who once owned the hotel, Mary O\u2019Rourke served almost 30 years in Parliament for Fianna Fail and held three cabinet positions.  Over bacon, lettuce and tomato sandwiches, Mary spoke in a way that suggested her view of Ireland\u2019s best economic interest doesn\u2019t always mirror her son\u2019s. She complained that the Irish banks had pared their lending since the financial crisis.  \u201cThe banks are telling lies like they always did,\u201d she said, evoking the populist rage that helped make her folksy 2012 autobiography, \u201cJust Mary,\u201d an Irish bestseller. Her son, whose firm advises major banks, remained silent.  Campaign Trail  After lunch, he drove to the village of Ballynahown. There he parked his silver Mercedes Benz outside a church where more than 30 years earlier he had campaigned for his mother after Sunday Mass. A nervous 17-year-old, O\u2019Rourke had perched precariously on a chair and shouted into a bullhorn connected to loudspeakers on a car\u2019s roof, exhorting residents to support her first run for  Irish Parliament . He coined her slogan: \u201cA strong voice for you and a strong voice for your area.\u201d  His father, Enda O\u2019Rourke, ran a midsized oil distribution company, where Feargal helped dispatch trucks to deliver heating oil. The elder O\u2019Rourke, who died in 2001, was also president of the local amateur rugby club, meaning Feargal spent his childhood helping set up the pitch and pick up dirty jerseys in the locker room after a match. He has a collection of Rugby team match programs dating back to 1888 --more than 2,000 -- in leather-bound volumes in his suburban Dublin home.  In Parliament, Mary O\u2019Rourke joined her brother, Brian Lenihan, who would later become the country\u2019s deputy prime minister. She became minister of education, then health, then public enterprise. (In Ireland, only Parliament members serve as cabinet ministers; they then serve in both positions simultaneously.) Meanwhile, two of Lenihan\u2019s sons -- O\u2019Rourke\u2019s cousins -- would be elected to Parliament, including Brian Lenihan Jr., the future minister for finance.  Wide Popularity  Feargal O\u2019Rourke also won wide political favor. In 1998, the deputy prime minister from the opposing party appointed him to a position with Forfas, a state policy body to promote science and technology. There, O\u2019Rourke recommended the government create a generous system of tax credits for research and development spending, he said. That credit benefits his clients, including one in particular: Intel, the semiconductor maker based in Santa Clara, California.  The program -- which allows companies to claim a tax credit at double the normal Irish tax rate for research expenses -- cost the Irish government 250 million euros in 2011. That\u2019s equivalent to about 7 percent of the 3.5 billion euros in corporate income taxes that Ireland collected that year.  \u2018Right Thing\u2019  The program was \u201cthe right thing for Ireland,\u201d said O\u2019Rourke, who declined pay for his service on the Forfas board.  Intel, which employs about 5,200 people in Ireland, has \u201cconsistently supported these types\u201d of tax credits worldwide, spokesman Chuck Mulloy said.  Earlier this year, Ireland\u2019s Department of Finance announced a review of the credit program \u201cto ensure the credit represents value for money for the Irish taxpayer.\u201d Last month, the  Irish Times  reported the research tax credits were being improperly claimed in 80 percent of the cases examined in a government audit.  In 2012, the \u201cBig Four\u201d accounting firms reported almost $25 billion in worldwide revenue from tax advising. Like PWC, the others have large tax practices in Dublin. O\u2019Rourke\u2019s competitors include KPMG veteran Adrian Crawford, who shuttles between the firm\u2019s midtown Manhattan office and Dublin, and has advised clients like Microsoft, which has accumulated about $76 billion in offshore profits.  At Ernst & Young, a former Irish revenue official named Joe Bollard has advised  Forest Laboratories Inc. (FRX) , maker of blockbuster antidepressant Lexapro, which has moved billions of dollars in profits through Ireland to a Bermuda mailbox.  Barnstorming Tours  Four times a year, O\u2019Rourke makes weeklong barnstorming tours to the West Coast. He recently touched down in San Francisco after a 16-hour trip, and visited Facebook and Twitter, according to his social media postings.  Along the way, he promoted investing in Ireland to prospective clients. He is often accompanied on such visits by locally stationed  Irish Development Agency  officials.  \u201cThere\u2019s a real vitality, a real buzz in the U.S.,\u201d said O\u2019Rourke, who is immersed in U.S. popular culture and considers  Breaking Bad  one of the best television shows ever.  \u201cIt is the era of the antihero,\u201d O\u2019Rourke said of the main character, Walter White, who makes and loses millions cooking methamphetamine. \u201cI don\u2019t know what it says that we can be rooting for a guy on the dark side of the law.\u201d  EU Probe  On Sept. 12, the morning after the Financial Times reported that the European Union was probing Ireland\u2019s tax practices, O\u2019Rourke appeared on a popular Irish radio show, jousting with Richard Murphy, a U.K. tax accountant and blogger.  \u201cThere\u2019s been a lot of guff talked out there about Ireland being a tax haven,\u201d said O\u2019Rourke. When the EU inquiries are done, \u201cIreland will be found to have not done any tax deals, no matter what way you define them.\u201d  Murphy retorted: \u201cIreland sells harmful tax practices that undermine the revenues of other countries.\u201d  O\u2019Rourke interrupted: \u201cThat\u2019s untrue.\u201d  Their squabbling continued on Twitter until O\u2019Rourke struck a conciliatory note: \u201cMust have you over -- always want our tax people to hear contrary views.\u201d  Even as he promotes his country\u2019s current tax practices, O\u2019Rourke foresees a new order. Changes in Ireland and worldwide are inevitable, he said, primarily because the Organization for Economic Cooperation and Development is targeting tax avoidance. He predicts his country will eventually prohibit companies like Google and Apple from setting up units in Ireland that don\u2019t owe income taxes there.  If O\u2019Rourke\u2019s prediction comes true, the \u201cDouble Irish\u201d will disappear from the tax avoidance lexicon.
