(GOOG) \u2019s  Android\nMarket  listing the same incorrect author.  Kytomaki ran tests, identified the mislabeled software as a\nfast-moving attack and published the findings online.  Google responded swiftly. It yanked the apps from the\nmarketplace and, using a little-known tactic to keep the malware\nfrom spreading, flipped a kill switch that reached into more\nthan 250,000 infected Android smartphones and removed all\nvestiges of the software.  \u201cI was positively surprised by how fast Google got the\napps removed from the market and how fast they were able to roll\nout a tool for removing the malware,\u201d Kytomaki said.  Google,  Apple Inc. (AAPL)  and  Microsoft Corp. (MSFT)  have with little\nfanfare embraced technology that lets technicians instantly and\nremotely purge unauthorized content from users\u2019 machines. So-\ncalled kill switches are standard on Android handsets and\niPhones, the smartphone leaders. The capability will soon become\nmore widespread with the release of Microsoft\u2019s Windows 8\nsoftware for tablets and computers.  While their stated use is for the removal of harmful\ncontent, there\u2019s no standard definition of what that means, and\ncompanies aren\u2019t required to disclose when and how the tools are\nemployed. The technology could be harnessed by a hacker to\nunleash a virus, a company to pry into a user\u2019s private\ninformation or a government body to repress free speech, said\n Eric Goldman , director of the  High Tech Law Institute  at Santa\nClara University\u2019s law school.  \u2018Dictator-Philosopher-King\u2019  \u201cWe have the benevolent dictator, philosopher-king type of\nmodel,\u201d Goldman said. \u201cYou have someone who has absolute\ncontrol over my hard drive in ways I may have never anticipated\nor consented to. If they use that power wisely, they actually\nmake my life better. We don\u2019t know if they use the power wisely.\nIn fact, we may never know when they use their power at all.\u201d  Kill switches are technologically unsophisticated\nadministrative programs that run silently in the background.\nThey have long existed in controlled networks, like at work,\nwhere technical staff has power over every machine. They haven\u2019t\nbeen widely used on personal computers, whose users are online\nsporadically and inconsistently update security patches -- a\nfailure that has fostered the spread of malware such as the\nConficker worm, which has infected millions of Windows machines.  Smartphone users, on the other hand, are online all the\ntime and must download applications from tightly controlled\nstores. By design, mobile software gives computer companies a\nsecond chance on security, said  Kevin Mahaffey , co-founder of\nLookout Inc., a San Francisco security firm for smartphones.  \u2018Overcorrection\u2019  \u201cThe remote-removal tools are very much a response to the\nmistakes of the PC era,\u201d Mahaffey said. \u201cWhether or not it\u2019s\nan overcorrection, I think history will tell us. It can be done\nright, but we as an industry need to tread carefully. It\u2019s easy\nto imagine several dystopian futures that can arise from this.\u201d  One concern is that Google, Microsoft and others could face\nexternal pressure to engage kill switches.  Governments are getting increasingly aggressive in\ndemanding help from technology companies in censoring e-mail and\nthe Internet, as BlackBerry maker  Research In Motion Ltd. (RIM) \nlearned in 2010 when  India ,  Saudi Arabia  and the  United Arab\nEmirates  pressured it to open customer communications to\ninspection.  \u201cIf you build a control into a device that the\nmanufacturer and carrier can control, it will be used by\ngovernments,\u201d said  Chris Wysopal , co-founder of Veracode Inc.,\na security firm in Burlington,  Massachusetts .  Benefits, Drawbacks  Hackers are also getting more sophisticated at infiltrating\nprotected networks, and privacy breaches are more common as\npersonal data becomes the coin of the Internet realm. A kill\nswitch feature carries clear benefits, and potentially dangerous\ndrawbacks, Wysopal said.  \u201cIt can really be used to add security, but it can also be\nused to deny people their rights to communicate,\u201d he said.\n\u201cThis is a place where there\u2019s no clear doctrine. We haven\u2019t\nheard anything clearly come out from an Apple or a Google\nsaying, \u2018Here\u2019s when we\u2019ll use our kill switch and when we\nwon\u2019t.\u2019\u201d  Representatives of  Mountain View , California-based Google\nand Microsoft, based in Redmond,  Washington , said they have used\nkill switches a handful of times, though they declined to\nprovide specifics.  Tricking \u2018Twilight\u2019 Fans  The kill switch is reserved for \u201creally egregious, really\nobvious cases\u201d of harmful content, said  Hiroshi Lockheimer ,\nGoogle\u2019s vice president of Android engineering.  \u201cWe\u2019ve always viewed remote removal as the final option,\u201d\nhe said. \u201cIt\u2019s not something we want to use.\u201d  One instance came after  Jon Oberheide , a 28-year-old\nsecurity researcher from  Ann Arbor ,  Michigan , duped fans of the\n\u201c Twilight \u201d teen vampire movies. Oberheide uploaded a fake app\non the Android Market and billed it as a preview of the latest\nfilm in the series. The software was empty, except for a single\nscreen shot.  Still, the app, which had been downloaded 200 times,\nprovided an entr\u00e9e that might have let Oberheide introduce\nmalware onto devices. It also helped Oberheide goad Google into\nusing its kill-switch option.  \u201cIt finally happened,\u201d Oberheide said.  Google, taking a lesson from PC industry bouts with\nmalware, has built in more aggressive protections since the\nfirst versions of Android, which began appearing in phones in\n2008. Google\u2019s partners have sold more than 250 million Android\ndevices, while Apple has sold more than 180 million iPhones.  Hacking Risk  Security experts said users would be at risk if hackers\nwere able to hijack the mechanism Google uses to push software\nto the devices. Lockheimer said Google takes security of the\nmechanism seriously and has built-in protections.  Microsoft, which enabled the feature in Windows smartphones\nseveral years ago, said its takedowns have not involved malware.\nThe violations concerned \u201ctechnical issues and content\nissues,\u201d said Todd Biggs, a director of  product management  at\nMicrosoft.  \u201cRevocation is a last resort, and it\u2019s uncommon,\u201d Biggs\nsaid. \u201cWe take that as a signpost that we\u2019re on target toward\nour goal, which is safe, reliable apps for consumers.\u201d  Microsoft disclosed last year that it was adding a kill\nswitch to desktop and laptop software. It did so by posting the\n terms of use  for an application store, a new feature for Windows\n8.  Amazon\u2019s \u20181984\u2019 Moment  RIM\u2019s  licensing documents  for vendors say that RIM reserves\nthe right to remove applications from users\u2019 devices \u201cfor any\nreason whatsoever.\u201d Marisa Conway, a spokeswoman for Waterloo,\nOntario-based RIM, declined to comment.  Tom Neumayr , a spokesman for Cupertino, California-based\nApple, also declined to comment.  Steve Jobs , Apple\u2019s deceased\nco-founder, confirmed the existence of a kill switch in a 2008\n interview  with the Wall Street Journal. Jobs said it would be\n\u201cirresponsible\u201d for Apple not to have a way to protect users\nfrom malicious applications. The comment appeared at the bottom\nof a story about iPhone app sales, in response to research that\nuncovered clues that such a feature existed on Apple devices.  The incident that encapsulates the danger of using a kill\nswitch is  Amazon.com Inc. (AMZN) \u2019s use of the feature to delete some\ncopies of  George Orwell \u2019s \u201c1984\u201d and \u201cAnimal Farm\u201d novels\nfrom Kindle devices in 2009 after discovering a publisher had\nsold them without the necessary rights.  \u2018Stupid, Thoughtless, Out of Line\u2019  Customers were infuriated, and CEO  Jeff Bezos  called it\n\u201c stupid , thoughtless and painfully out of line with our\nprinciples.\u201d The company vowed it would never delete books from\nKindles again.  Amazon representatives didn\u2019t respond to requests for\ncomment.  While the emergence of kill switches shows the growing\ncontrol that technology companies have assumed over users\u2019\ndevices, it also exposes the shortcomings of other methods of\nkeeping users\u2019 computers clean.  Stephanie Stambaugh, a 47-year-old freelance writer from\nDenver, has been battling a so-called botnet infection on her\nhome PCs since December. Her Internet provider,  Comcast Corp. (CMCSA) ,\nalerted her to the infection, a type of program where a machine\nis controlled without the user\u2019s consent that is becoming more\ncommon. She said that while she has run a dozen different\nantivirus and other cleanup programs, she is still getting\nalerts that her machine is infected.  Giving Up Privacy  Stambaugh said she can\u2019t afford the $130 virus cleanup\nservice that Comcast offers, and is considering reinstalling her\noperating software, the nuclear option of virus cleanups.  Cable-network operators such as Comcast have insight into\nwhich computers are compromised, since they can see when\nmachines are silently reaching out to malicious sites. Yet they\ndon\u2019t have the same capabilities as companies such as Google,\nMicrosoft and Apple. Aside from alerting customers, they are\nlimited to quarantining poisoned computers, or restricting the\namount of bandwidth they consume. It\nrose again in 2009, placing 13th in Bloomberg Markets\u2019 annual\nhedge-fund ranking, with a 42 percent return. That, however,\nonly made up for 2008 losses.  Down to $9 Billion  Spooked investors asked for their money back. These days,\nFalcone manages just $9 billion, a third of his boom-time pile.  Many hedge funds have had a lackluster 2010. The private\npools of cash -- raised from wealthy families, pensions and\nendowments -- returned 1.45 percent on average in the first\neight months of 2010, according to  Hedge Fund Research Inc.  in\nChicago.  Mom-and-pop investors in the  Pimco Total Return Fund , the\nworld\u2019s biggest bond fund, earned 8.7 percent in the same\nperiod, including reinvested dividends.  Managers who are still in the game -- 2,900 hedge funds\nclosed from the beginning of 2008 to June 30 -- are paring risk.\nMany are shunning investments in private companies, which have\nproved hard to sell since the credit markets went into\nconvulsions two years ago.  Taking on Verizon  Falcone is trying to recover with his biggest bet ever.\nHe\u2019s building a wireless network powered by satellites and cell\ntowers that will cover the entire U.S. and compete with AT&T\nInc.,  Verizon Communications Inc.  and billionaire  Craig McCaw \u2019s\n Clearwire Corp.  to deliver fast Internet service to smartphones.  Falcone says Harbinger has spent $2.9 billion on its\nbroadband company, LightSquared, which in turn plans to pay\nNokia Siemens Networks $7 billion to build and operate its\nnetwork over the next eight years.  \u201cI\u2019ve always been a believer in wireless,\u201d Falcone says in\na rare interview at his office 30 stories above Park Avenue in\nNew York. He also acknowledges that his clients see LightSquared\nas a giant gamble because it accounts for much of Harbinger\u2019s\nportfolio. \u201cThis has been a hot button for some of my investors,\nthe biggest issue for me in the last 12 months,\u201d Falcone said in\nmid-September.  Falcone\u2019s is one of at least three big hedge funds that\nhave stumbled since their career-making wins in the mortgage\ncollapse. Paulson & Co., the $31 billion fund that earned $15\nbillion in 2007 betting against mortgages, was down 11 percent\nthis year as of August.  Pellegrini Downsizes  Founder  John Paulson \u2019s former top lieutenant,  Paolo Pellegrini , set up his own firm, PSQR LLC, in 2009. After\ngaining 62 percent that year, he lost 11 percent in 2010 through\nAugust and then decided to return money to outside investors and\njust manage his own funds, according to a person briefed on the\ndecision.  \u201cJust because a manager got the subprime trade right, it\ndoesn\u2019t necessarily mean he\u2019s a skilled manager,\u201d says  Brad Balter , managing partner of Balter Capital Management LLC, a\nBoston-based firm that invests in hedge funds for clients.\n\u201cThere have been several funds that benefited from that bet in\n2007 whose performance was mediocre before and continues to be\nmediocre today.\u201d  These days, Falcone is literally blasting his investors\u2019\nmoney into space. Late in 2010 or early in 2011, LightSquared\nplans to launch its first communications satellite aboard a\nRussian-built rocket fired from Kazakhstan. A second bird will\ngo up sometime after that, giving the company the ability to\nprovide mobile Internet access anywhere in the U.S.  Investor Lockup  The risk for Falcone is alienating investors who thought\nthey were putting money into a hedge fund that traded securities\nthat were easy to buy and sell, not one that locks up their\nmoney in a private wireless company that could take years to\nbuild and years longer to turn a profit.  \u201cHe\u2019s changed the very focus of the fund,\u201d says  Geoffrey Bobroff , president of Bobroff Consulting, an investment fund\nconsultant in East Greenwich, Rhode Island. \u201cIf you do that, you\nneed to afford people the opportunity to exit.\u201d  Like many hedge-fund managers, Falcone declined to give\ninvestors all of their money back in 2008 because he would have\nhad to sell assets at bargain-basement prices, if he could sell\nthem at all. Those clients are still waiting for more than 90\npercent of the money he withheld, they say.  Taste for the Offbeat  Falcone has always had a taste for offbeat investments. His\nportfolio includes a 49 percent stake in African Medical\nInvestments Plc, a London-based startup company that operates\nclinics for middle-class Africans and expatriates across the\ncontinent. Harbinger is also an investor in a casino in Vietnam.  The Falcones are hedge-fund celebrities in New York,\ncovered in gossip pages and photographed at charity dinners,\nwhere Lisa turns up in diaphanous gowns and short skirts,\nusually with a different bejeweled cross around her neck for\neach event.  Phil shook up the city in 2008 when he became the biggest\nshareholder of New York Times Co. and tried to wrest strategic\nchanges from the controlling Sulzberger clan.  Tabloids pounced when the Falcones\u2019 former butler, a gay\nman, alleged in a lawsuit that Lisa sexually harassed him. She\ndenies it.  This year, Lisa produced  \u201cMother and Child,\u201d  a film that\nstars  Annette Bening  and  Naomi Watts  and that deals with\nadoption issues.  Make or Break  The wireless play could save or break Falcone and his\ndwindling fund. Falcone started 2009 with just $6.5 billion, an\ninvestor says, after losses and the return of billions of\ndollars to anxious clients. Falcone has at least $800 million of\nhis own money in the Capital Partners fund, according to\ninvestors.  In 2009, he borrowed $113 million from his Special\nSituations Fund to pay his personal taxes, a move that could\ninvite scrutiny from the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission\nbecause the fund wasn\u2019t allowing investors to take money out at\nthe time, says Bobroff, a former SEC attorney.  \u201cRegulators would love to jump on that,\u201d he says.  Falcone says the loan was proper. \u201cThat\u2019s been disclosed\nand discussed with investors,\u201d he says.  Falcone is going all in on wireless. LightSquared and other\ntelecommunications investments account for about 90 percent of\nnet assets in the Capital Partners fund and more than 50 percent\nof the Special Situations Fund, which together hold about $5.5\nbillion, according to investors.  Rapid Build-out  Falcone declined to confirm the numbers.  Harbinger has to move fast. The Federal Communications\nCommission is requiring LightSquared to build out a network that\ncan serve 100 million people by Dec. 31, 2012. If it doesn\u2019t,\nthe FCC can nullify LightSquared\u2019s licenses for the radio\nfrequencies it needs to operate.  Building a network will cost about $5 billion, says Credit\nSuisse Group AG telecom analyst  Jonathan Chaplin . Falcone will\nhave to cover another $3 billion in losses while he hustles for\ncustomers, Chaplin says. \u201cIt\u2019s going to take a lot of capital to\nget it built, and I\u2019m not sure the capital is available,\u201d he\nsays.  Falcone secured a piece of what LightSquared needs in\nSeptember, getting a $750 million, four-year loan from  UBS AG ,\naccording to two people familiar with the matter.  Option to Sell  One option for Falcone is to sell his licenses now and\nforget the fuss of building a network, Chaplin says. Harbinger\ngot the licenses when it completed its purchase of a money-\nlosing satellite company called  SkyTerra Communications Inc.  in\nMarch.  The licenses are probably worth $9 billion today, according\nto Chaplin. They cost Falcone about $4 billion, including leases\non wireless frequencies he signed to complement SkyTerra\u2019s,\nChaplin says. Any transaction would need approval from the FCC.  Investors will have to wait longer, perhaps for an initial\npublic offering, if Falcone keeps building. McCaw\u2019s Kirkland,\nWashington-based Clearwire, which sold shares to the public in\nApril 2007, has a  market value  of $7.3 billion.  Whether he builds a telecom system or sells his spectrum,\nFalcone needs a winner. His $3.4 billion Capital Partners fund\nis struggling. In 2008, it lost billions making bullish bets on\niron-ore producers, including Perth, Australia-based  Fortescue\nMetals Group Ltd. , whose stock was down 74 percent for that\nyear. Harbinger lost still more investing in Houston-based power\ncompany  Calpine Corp. , whose shares fell 56 percent in 2008.  Up and Down  Harbinger recouped those losses in 2009, when Calpine,\nFortescue and other stocks rebounded. This year, Falcone is down\nagain. As of the end of August, Harbinger\u2019s flagship fund had\nlost 16 percent, partly because of a plunge in the stock of\n TerreStar Corp. , another satellite communications company.  Harbinger owned 31 percent of TerreStar as of June 30; its\nshares were down 49 percent for the year as of Sept. 28, to 48\ncents. In August, the company warned in a regulatory filing that\nit would have to declare bankruptcy if it couldn\u2019t borrow more\nmoney to operate a satellite that it launched in July 2009.  Investors have already lost patience. Falcone is\nliquidating about 80 percent of his $2 billion Special\nSituations Fund, which holds a chunk of the LightSquared\ninvestment, at the request of clients, investors say. Falcone\nhas been trying since June to raise $1 billion to $1.5 billion\nfor LightSquared from investors who would be willing to commit\ncapital for several years, according to potential investors who\nhave seen the marketing documents.  Spectrum Shortage  That money would be used to buy some of the wireless bet\nfrom his two hedge funds. As of mid-September, he had no takers.\nFalcone declined to comment on the matter.  Falcone is betting that the boom in wireless data triggered\nby  Apple Inc. \u2019s iPhone and  Google Inc. \u2019s Android operating\nsystem for mobile phones will create a shortage of spectrum --\nthe radio frequencies needed to transmit phone calls, Web pages,\nYouTube videos and Twitter updates over the air.  \u201cSpectrum, by its nature, is a finite resource,\u201d Falcone\nsays. \u201cI\u2019m a big believer in finite resources.\u201d  The U.S. government leases rights to the frequencies. Data\ntraffic on  AT&T \u2019s network, where the iPhone operates, grew 5,000\npercent in the three years after that device came out, the\nDallas-based company says.  Unlike AT&T and Verizon, LightSquared won\u2019t run its own,\nbranded wireless service. It will sell space on the network at\nwholesale prices to other carriers, retailers and media\ncompanies.  Selling Wholesale  If Apple wanted to sell iPhones that run on an Apple-\nbranded network, for example, it could contract with\nLightSquared for the capacity.  Investors who stick with Falcone must accept that he makes\nbig bets that don\u2019t always work out. Falcone\u2019s most public\nblunder was paying an estimated $500 million for almost 20\npercent of the New York Times\u2019s publicly traded Class A shares.\nThe company is controlled by the family of Times publisher\n Arthur Ochs Sulzberger Jr . through their Class B shares, which\ngive them the right to appoint 9 of the 13  directors .  Falcone bought the stake in 2008, when he was fresh from\nhis mortgage killing and the newspaper\u2019s  revenue  was falling as\nadvertisers migrated to the Internet. In January 2008, he\noffered a slate of four new directors and urged the company to\nsell extraneous assets, such as its stake in the Boston Red Sox\nbaseball team, and to use that money to build its online\nbusiness.  Times Incursion  Two of Falcone\u2019s nominees won election to the board:  Scott Galloway , founder of Firebrand Partners, a consulting firm that\nadvised Falcone on the purchase, and  James Kohlberg , chairman of\nKohlberg & Co. and son of  Jerome Kohlberg , a founder of private-\nequity giant KKR & Co.  Falcone hasn\u2019t been able to turn around New York Times\u2019s\nslumping stock. Since Galloway and Kohlberg joined the board on\nApril 22, 2008, the company\u2019s  shares have fallen  60 percent as\nof Sept. 28, to $7.82. Falcone still owned 9 percent of the\nClass A shares as of June 30. Kohlberg remains on the board;\nGalloway left this year.  People who know Falcone say he\u2019s a hard-working guy who\nretains his Midwestern values.  \u201cPhil is a product of his upbringing,\u201d Galloway says. \u201cHe\nhas good manners. He\u2019s not a chair thrower. I\u2019ve never seen him\nyell.\u201d  When Harbinger was looking for office space a few years\nago, Falcone\u2019s broker found a prime location on which another,\nsmaller hedge fund had put a deposit. The broker told Harbinger\nit could certainly outbid them.  \u2018Bad Karma\u2019  \u201cPhil\u2019s words were, \u2018That\u2019s bad karma; I don\u2019t want to push\nout a smaller firm,\u2019\u201d Galloway says.  Family is important to Falcone, Galloway says. His twin\ndaughters come to lunch at his office, 10 blocks south of their\nhome, every Friday. Galloway says he once set up a meeting for\nFalcone with a billionaire investor who was interested in\nHarbinger. Falcone said he couldn\u2019t make the meeting because he\nhad to go see his mother.  Falcone was wide-eyed when he arrived at Harvard in 1980,\nsays hockey teammate Greg Olson, who\u2019s now a dentist in\nMinnetonka, Minnesota.  \u201cHe was a deer in the headlights,\u201d Olson says.  After recovering from the initial shock, Falcone made\nhimself something of a campus don. Hockey teammates called him\n\u201cFashion Phil\u201d because he cared so much about his clothes, Olson\nsays. He had a blue, three-piece suit that he wore often, and he\nalways wore stylish shoes.  Hockey Intensity  The center on the hockey team, Falcone practiced hard and\nstudied hard.  \u201cHe took a lot of ribbing because of his intensity,\u201d says\nteammate Brad Karp, a former energy executive in Santa Fe, New\nMexico.  In his freshman year, Falcone won the George Percy award,\ngiven to first-year players for enthusiasm and sportsmanship.\nHarvard went to the NCAA championships in 1983, Falcone\u2019s junior\nyear. The team lost to Wisconsin, 6-2.  After graduating with a B.A. in economics, Falcone played\nhockey for a professional team in Malmo, Sweden, for a year. He\nquit when he injured his leg. He returned to the U.S. and went\nto work for investment bank Kidder, Peabody & Co. in New York,\nwhere he traded high-yield debt for about five years.  In 1990, Falcone and Edward Garden, a friend from Harvard,\npooled their money, got some loans and bought AAB Manufacturing\nCorp., a struggling Newark, New Jersey-based maker of brushes\nand combs. Then a drugstore chain that was one of AAB\u2019s biggest\ncustomers went bankrupt, taking the combmaker\u2019s receivables with\nit.  Going Broke  In congressional  testimony  on hedge funds\u2019 role in the\nfinancial crisis, Falcone said he was so broke he couldn\u2019t pay\nhis electric bill.  Falcone returned to Wall Street, trading distressed debt\nfor several firms, including  Barclays Plc.   In 2001, Harbert Management Corp., a Birmingham, Alabama-\nbased money management company, was looking for someone to start\na fund to trade distressed debt and came across a PowerPoint\npresentation from Falcone. Harbert hired him to start what\nbecame Harbinger, staking him with $25 million.  Falcone was a valuable commodity. Harbinger returned 18.7\npercent a year on average over the next five and a half years\ncompared with 15 percent for competing distressed-asset funds.  Buying Insurance  In 2006, he put on the trade that would make his name. Like\nPaulson and other mortgage mega-bears, he bought credit-default\nswaps, contracts that rose in value as the price of interest-\npaying securities constructed from individual home mortgages\nlost value. Also like Paulson, Falcone bought many of the swaps\nfrom a salesman named  Greg Lippmann  at Deutsche Bank AG,\naccording to a person familiar with the purchases.  When the housing market collapsed in 2007 and defaults\nsoared, Falcone got rich.  Falcone\u2019s wealth has made him and his wife, Lisa, highly\nvisible newcomers to big-time philanthropy. Lisa rattled the\ntitans of charity in June 2009 at a party for donors to the High\nLine, a new park in Manhattan built atop a disused elevated\nrailway. In the middle of a speech by  High Line  founder Joshua\nDavid, Lisa, clad in a gray, shimmery minidress tied at the\nwaist with a white bow, strode to the front of the crowd, asked\nfor the microphone and said she would match a $10 million gift\nto the High Line that had just been announced by  Barry Diller ,\nchief executive officer of IAC\/InterActiveCorp., and his wife,\nfashion designer  Diane von Furstenberg .  Lisa Lawsuit  Lisa\u2019s upbringing was even more hardscrabble than her\nhusband\u2019s: She grew up in Spanish Harlem and was raised by a\nsingle mother on welfare. She was working as a model when she\nmet Phil Falcone through mutual friends at a Manhattan\nrestaurant in the late 1980s. They were married in 1992.  Lisa is now the overseer of the Falcones\u2019 properties, one\nof which is a compound on the island of St. Barts in the\nCaribbean that the Falcones bought for $39 million in 2008 --\nthe most expensive home purchase in the island\u2019s history,\naccording to  Sotheby\u2019s  International Realty, the listing agent.  William Gamble, the former manager of their homes, says in\na complaint filed in February in New York State Supreme Court\nthat Lisa sexually harassed him on a trip to St. Barts in March\n2008. First, she told him to wear a smaller bathing suit to help\nimprove his tan, he says in the suit. Days later, she put her\nhand down his pants while drunk and, when rebuffed, hit him with\nher hand three times, leaving bruises on his abdomen, the suit\nsays.  Falcone Denial  The Falcones denied Gamble\u2019s charges in a response filed in\ncourt on April 20. \u201cPlaintiff\u2019s job performance during his\nemployment by the defendants was unsatisfactory,\u201d the response\nsays.  Falcone bought the St. Barts house just before he got\nclobbered by the credit crisis and the subsequent slowdown in\nthe economy. That\u2019s when his Calpine bet, among others, went\nsouth. Like other hedge funds, Harbinger had to fight its way\nthrough the crisis, selling assets to limit losses and to return\nmoney to anxious investors.  \u201cPeople looked at us like an ATM,\u201d Falcone says.  Harbinger wouldn\u2019t let investors have all the money they\ndemanded from the flagship Capital Partners fund. He broke the\nnews in an e-mail around midday on Christmas Eve 2008, saying he\nwould limit redemptions to two-thirds of investors\u2019 requests.  Falcone put 15 illiquid private-equity investments into a\nsegregated account called a side pocket, according to investors.\nThe holdings would be sold off over time, with investors getting\ncash back as sales were made.  7 Percent Solution  As of late September, investors had received only 7 percent\nof the money in the side pocket, they say.  Falcone declined to comment on the matter.  While denying clients, Falcone in October 2009 took a $113\nmillion loan from the Special Situations Fund to pay his\npersonal taxes, according to investors who learned of the loan\nin the fund\u2019s 2009 financial statements. Investors say they\nwould have preferred having excess cash returned to them. The\nfund allowed no redemptions after the 2008 bankruptcy of  Lehman\nBrothers Holdings Inc. , which was the fund\u2019s broker and held its\nassets.  Falcone\u2019s funds are too narrowly focused for some\ninvestors. Executives that manage a fund for  PNC Financial\nServices Group Inc.  in Pittsburgh asked for the return of their\nwhole investment -- an unspecified amount -- from Harbinger\nCapital during the fiscal year ended on March 31, according to a\nregulatory filing. Harbinger \u201cgot caught up in concentrated,\nilliquid situations in 2008,\u201d managers of the PNC Long-Short\nMaster Fund LLC said in the filing.  New York Pulls Out  The New York State Common Retirement Fund is pulling its\nentire $68 million investment in Harbinger. It asked for $27\nmillion at the start of 2010 and the remaining $41 million in\nmid-September, spokesman  Dennis Tompkins  says. He declined to\nsay why the fund decided to redeem.  Falcone, in an August 2009 investor conference call,\npledged to reduce the amount of stock and private-equity\ninvestments in the Capital Partners fund to about 50 percent of\nassets, moving more into bonds, according to investors who were\non the call. They say that didn\u2019t happen.  Falcone declined to comment on the matter.  One investor is taking the big bets in stride.  Mark Yusko ,\nchief investment officer at Morgan Creek Capital Management LLC\nin Chapel Hill, North Carolina, says betting lots of money on a\nfew ventures isn\u2019t necessarily bad.  \u2018An Outstanding Investor\u2019  \u201cConcentration indicates passion and conviction,\u201d Yusko\nsays. \u201cI can manage around concentration because I don\u2019t have\nall my money with him. Philip is an outstanding investor. He has\nthe intestinal fortitude and patience to stick with an\ninvestment.\u201d  Falcone\u2019s satellite play started out as the kind of\ndistressed-debt investment typical of Harbinger. The licenses\nhe\u2019s using to build his network have been bouncing from one\nowner to the next since 2000, when Motient Corp., a company that\nsold package-tracking services to  United Parcel Service Inc. ,\nset up a partnership with other investors called Mobile\nSatellite Ventures LP (MSV) to try to build a network. It sold\npart of its stake in the unit in October 2001 and then sought\nbankruptcy protection.  Apollo Global Management LLC, the private-equity firm run\nby  Leon Black , bought a piece of an Internet software company\ncalled Rare Medium Group Inc. in 1999. Two years later, Rare\nMedium bought into MSV. As the Internet boom went bust, Rare\nMedium morphed into a satellite communications company, changing\nits name to SkyTerra Communications in 2003 and going on to\naccumulate a majority of MSV in May 2006.  Buying SkyTerra  Falcone started acquiring SkyTerra shares about the same\ntime, according to regulatory filings. He\u2019s been on a telecom\nbender ever since. He says buying wireless spectrum is a better\nbet than buying media properties.  \u201cDo you want to own the Lincoln Tunnel or the cars that go\nthrough it?\u201d he asks. \u201cYou want to own the road.\u201d  In April 2008, Falcone paid Apollo $10 apiece for 16.4\nmillion shares of SkyTerra. By the end of 2008, the shares had\ndropped 86 percent, to $1.79. Harbinger bought the shares of\nSkyTerra it didn\u2019t already own in March of this year for another\n$262.5 million.  Falcone renamed the Reston, Virginia-based company\nLightSquared in July. He hired  Sanjiv Ahuja , former chief\nexecutive officer of  France Telecom SA \u2019s Orange Group mobile\nphone unit, to run it.  Satellite Play  In addition to Light\u00adSquared and his stake in cash-strapped\nTerreStar, Falcone bought a 28 percent stake in Inmarsat Plc, a\nLondon-based competitor to SkyTerra that has 11 satellites\nproviding worldwide voice and data service.  Falcone wanted all of Inmarsat. He said in a July 2008\npress release that Harbinger and  SkyTerra , then independent,\nwould team up and bid for the company after getting regulatory\napproval. Global credit markets seized up months later, and\ndealmaking halted. If Falcone bid, it wasn\u2019t made public.  Controlling Inmarsat would make Falcone\u2019s investment much\nmore valuable, says  Patrick Comack , an analyst at Zachary\nInvestment Research & Management LLC in Miami Beach, Florida.\nInmarsat controls wireless spectrum that\u2019s interwoven with\nLightSquared\u2019s. Having broader swaths of spectrum means you can\nsend more information over the air. If LightSquared is to use\nits spectrum for broadband Internet, it must be separated into\ncontiguous blocks, Comack says.  Dirty Spectrum  \u201cThey\u2019ve got a huge amount of high-quality spectrum, but\nthe majority isn\u2019t usable until they clean it up,\u201d he says.  To solve that problem, LightSquared said in August that it\nwould pay Inmarsat $337.5 million over 18 months to modify its\nnetwork so the frequencies can be untangled.  The FCC originally set aside the SkyTerra spectrum strictly\nfor satellite use. The FCC encourages satellite systems because\nthey aren\u2019t affected by hurricanes, earthquakes or other events\nthat can knock out cell towers. The downside of satellites is\nthat they don\u2019t provide good connections in cities, where\nbuildings can block transmissions, and that all of the expense\nis upfront: SkyTerra\u2019s two satellites will cost $300 million\neach to build and launch, Credit Suisse analyst Chaplin says.  The SkyTerra spectrum became more valuable in November\n2004, when the FCC ruled that its satellite system could be\naugmented with land-based cell towers, making it more attractive\nto mobile phone users.  Falcone still must launch satellites in order to comply\nwith the FCC licenses. Lots of companies have tried to build\nsatellite networks and failed. One of the first, Teledesic LLC,\nplanned to dish up Internet service from space with 288\ninexpensive satellites by 2002.  Wireless and Risk  It was backed by McCaw, Microsoft Corp. co-founder  Bill Gates  and, later, Saudi Arabian  Prince Alwaleed Bin Talal . The\nbackers halted funding, and the network never got built.  Falcone knows the risks. Yet he takes pride in never losing\nhis calm. \u201cYou tell me I need a heart transplant and then I\u2019ll\nget stressed out,\u201d he says.  Galloway of Firebrand agrees that his friend keeps his\ncool. \u201cHe doesn\u2019t scare easily,\u201d Galloway says. \u201cHe does a lot\nof homework, makes a decision and doesn\u2019t look back.\u201d  Falcone better hope his investors don\u2019t scare easily\neither. The ride they\u2019re on could be bumpier than Falcone\u2019s\ncross-country trip in that battered Mercury. The court noted that the term \u201cumami\u201d comes from the\nJapanese language, and is used to describe a so-called fifth\ntaste in addition to sweet, salt, bitter and sour. He said that Umami Burger\u2019s\nmarket is \u201cyoung, hip gourmands colloquially known as\n\u2018foodies.\u2019\u201d They are consumers who \u201cinvest considerable time\nand energy in being \u2018foodies\u2019 in much the same way young people\nput great effort into following obscure bands of dubious\nmusicality.\u201d  These consumers, he said, are likely to be familiar with\nUmami Burger\u2019s brand and not likely to be confused by the pizza\nrestaurant\u2019s name.  Umami Burger doesn\u2019t yet have a presence in Austin, while\nthe pizzeria is already open for business, he said. The pizzeria\nwould lose the effects of its preopening promotion, goodwill and\nbrand awareness if it was forced to change its name, according\nto the ruling.  The case is Umami Burger Licensing USA LLC v. Umami Mia\nPizzeria LLC, 13-cv-00511, U.S. District Court, Western District\nof Texas (Austin). (HPQ)  added three directors, including former  Microsoft Corp. (MSFT)  software head Ray Ozzie, as Chief Executive Officer Meg Whitman tries to bolster sales with new technology and services amid a global PC slump.  Ozzie will be joined on the board by Jim Skinner, the former CEO of  McDonald\u2019s Corp. (MCD)  and current chairman of  Walgreen Co. (WAG) , and Dob Bennett, the ex-CEO of  Liberty Media Corp. (LMCA) , the Palo Alto, California-based company said today. The additions expand the board to 12 members from nine.  Hewlett-Packard is shoring up its board following a shake-up in April when Ray Lane stepped down as chairman after an $8.8 billion writedown of a company acquired on his watch. With the third board overhaul since 2011, Whitman is gaining expertise in software and marketing as she expands in mobile computing to reach users who are abandoning PCs for smartphones and tablets.  \u201cIt doesn\u2019t hurt to have a software guru on the board,\u201d said Brian White, an analyst at Topeka Capital Markets who has a sell rating on the shares and a $12 target price. \u201cSoftware is becoming more important. That\u2019s one area that HP really needs to beef up.\u201d  Lotus Creator  Ozzie has a long and distinguished history in the computer industry, though his tenure at Microsoft was relatively brief. He is best known as the creator of Lotus Notes, a pioneering e-mail system that was acquired by International Business Machines Corp. He later founded software maker Groove Networks, which Microsoft acquired in 2005.  When Microsoft co-founder Bill Gates announced in 2006 that he would step down from his day-to-day role, Ozzie was one of two executives tapped to chart the course of the world\u2019s largest software maker. Yet by the time Ozzie left Microsoft in 2010, he had been less visible and his departure wasn\u2019t considered a surprise.  More recently, Ozzie has been running  Talko Inc. , a cloud computing company he founded.  \u201cAs we move forward with our turnaround, it\u2019s a huge benefit to be able to get advice from a board made up of such experienced business and technology leaders,\u201d Whitman said in the statement. \u201cFor their part, Dob, Ray and Jim have just about seen it all during their careers.\u201d  Additional Directors  The company will continue seeking additional directors and a nonexecutive chairman in the coming months, Ralph Whitworth, interim chairman, said in a  blog  post.  Whitworth became temporary head of the board in April in a shake-up that also led Lane\u2019s exit and the departures of directors G. Kennedy Thompson and John Hammergren. Lane gave up his chairmanship after investors re-elected him in a narrow majority of votes, issuing a rebuke of his oversight of the botched acquisition of software maker Autonomy Corp.  Skinner was CEO of McDonald\u2019s from 2004 to 2012, and oversaw a  sharp rise  in the company\u2019s stock. He led the world\u2019s largest restaurant chain through the U.S. economic recession by scaling back new store openings and expanding the menu to include premium coffee drinks to lure higher-income consumers while introducing healthier options like oatmeal and smoothies.  Bennett was CEO of Liberty Media from 1997 to 2005, and previously served as finance chief at the company, which  invests  in a variety of entertainment and sports ventures. He also led Liberty Media\u2019s initial public offering in 2001.  \u2018Strategic Sense\u2019  Of the three, Ozzie is the most welcome addition, according to  Jayson Noland , an analyst at Robert W. Baird & Co. Ozzie became chief software architect at Microsoft in June 2006, directing development of new versions of the company\u2019s operating systems and services, according to the statement. Before that, he was chief technical officer.  \u201cIt\u2019s hard for a few new directors to make a big difference in a company this size,\u201d said Noland, who has a neutral rating on the shares and a $25 target price. \u201cRay Ozzie makes the most strategic sense. Software is certainly a key initiative.\u201d  Lane joined the board in November 2010 in the aftermath of the departure of CEO Mark Hurd, who left that August after the board said he violated Hewlett-Packard\u2019s code of business ethics. Lane\u2019s reign came to be associated with the ill-fated tenure of CEO Leo Apotheker, who was ousted after 11 months on the job; strategy shifts, such as a flip-flop over whether to sell the PC division; and acquisitions, including Autonomy, that did little to revamp Hewlett-Packard.  A board shake-up in January 2011 added executives with ties to Apotheker, aiming to quell criticism over they way directors had handled Hurd\u2019s departure.  Hewlett-Packard shares have rallied 85 percent this year amid tentative signs that Whitman is making headway in her efforts to reignite growth. They rose less than 1 percent to $26.38 at the close in New York. So what makes investors believe  Nintendo Co. (7974) \u2019s  Super Mario  can take on  Tencent Holdings Ltd. (700) \u2019s giant, undead spider Vilemaw in its Chinese lair?  Nintendo shares have risen 33 percent since state-run China Daily on Jan. 28 said the country was ready to end a 13-year ban on consoles. Meant to shelter China\u2019s youth from the violence and perceived corrupting influence of video games, the ban instead spawned a generation of gamers grown used to a free online model and increasingly migrating to mobile devices.  Console vendors Nintendo,  Sony Corp. (6758)  and  Microsoft Corp. (MSFT)  face an uphill slog to get consumers to pay hundreds of dollars for hardware they never knew they\u2019d missed, said Shanghai-based Spicy Horse Games founder American McGee. With the U.S. industry mired in a two-year slump, console makers are looking to  China \u2019s $10 billion market for a boost that may never come.  \u201cYou are basically trying to take an elephant to a Ferrari race,\u201d said McGee, who set up Spicy Horse in 2006 to make games for PlayStation and Xbox before moving to online and mobile in 2011. \u201cThis is a market where free-to-play online and mobile has already won. These guys will be coming to the fight when the fight is already over.\u201d  Not only that: piracy, censorship and regulatory costs will add to their challenges.  Consoles like Nintendo\u2019s Wii U, released in November, and the upcoming Sony PlayStation 4 and Microsoft Xbox One, were banned by China in 2000. That let online titles dominate, like market-leader Tencent\u2019s \u201c League of Legends ,\u201d featuring Vilemaw.  China Rising  The Shenzhen-based company holds 21 percent of China\u2019s video-game market, which grew 30 percent to 38.5 billion  yuan  ($6.3 billion) in the first six months, Analysys International data show. U.S. sales of video-game hardware, software and accessories fell 15 percent in June from a year earlier to $593.3 million, according to NPD Group Inc.  While \u201cLeague of Legends\u201d and many online games in China are free to play, operators charge users to stock up on or upgrade virtual weapons and armor. That model has carried over well to tablets and smartphones: Analysys said mobile gaming more than doubled to 5 billion yuan.  Touchscreen handheld devices such as  Apple Inc. (AAPL) \u2019s iPad and iPhone aren\u2019t seen as gaming products in China, which last year overtook the U.S. as the world\u2019s biggest smartphone market.  Black Market  If Chinese consumers are scrambling to go mobile, a trip to Li Jianwei\u2019s Game-You shop in Beijing illustrates the lack of pent-up demand for consoles. Li sells smuggled Xbox 360s with Kinect motion sensor for 2,300 yuan. His glass countertop is littered with binders displaying hundreds of pirated titles.  Li and an assistant playing \u201cNBA2K13\u201d basketball on a widescreen TV are the only people there. Three neighboring shops were also empty.  Chinese mobile gamers will rise 30 percent to 280 million this year, while there are only about 1 million users of black-market consoles, according to Analysys estimates.  Hopes for  market access  were further stoked last month when  China Daily  cited unidentified government officials saying foreign vendors would be allowed to sell their products in China if they are made in the  Shanghai  Free Trade Zone.  \u201cIt\u2019s encouraging news and we look forward to learning more,\u201d said Joanna Li, a spokeswoman in Beijing for Redmond, Washington-based Microsoft. Sony sees China as \u201can attractive market\u201d where the Tokyo-based company always considers opportunities, spokesman Satoshi Nakajima said. (HOT) \nand insurer  Aviva Plc (AV\/)  that have appeared this year, the blog\nalso solicits donations for Five Star.  \u2018Wide Audience\u2019  The blog has the elements of \u201ca great place to make\nmoney,\u201d said Pietro Paganini, who teaches business\nadministration at John Cabot University in Rome. \u201cIt has a very\nwide audience.\u201d  The blog\u2019s web address, beppegrillo.it, appears on the Five\nStar logo that adorns campaign posters and official ballots in\nthe voting booth. The blog has a page  dedicated  to Five Star,\ncontaining electoral lists, a forum and its policy program. That\npage didn\u2019t have advertising this week.  Five Star refused to accept the 42.8 million euros ($55\nmillion) in public funding it says it is entitled to for the\nnearly 9 million votes it won in the Feb. 24-25 general\nelection. The party\u2019s lawmakers, political neophytes swept to\npower under Grillo\u2019s banner, are required by Five Star\u2019s code to\nreturn a portion of their salaries to the state.  Party Donations  The party  collected  774,208 euros from 9,789 donors through\nApril 11, according to the website. Grillo travelled Italy in a\ncamper during the campaign, making stops in more than 70 cities\nand broadcasting his rallies live through the website.  Grillo\u2019s campaign against the use of public subsidies\npushed Letta last week to announce his government is preparing a\nbill to abolish state financing for parties. Grillo has taken to his blog this month to assert that\nBerlusconi oversees \u201cthe obscene partnership between illegality\nand democracy,\u201d and dubbed Letta \u201cCaptain Findus\u201d after a\nbrand of freezer-stored fish-sticks. Ignazio Marino, of Letta\u2019s Democratic Party, took\n43 percent, while Giovanni Alemanno, the incumbent from\nBerlusconi\u2019s coalition, got 30 percent.  Grillo, 64, was a success as an entrepreneur before\nfounding the blog eight years ago with the website\u2019s curator,\nGianroberto Casaleggio. In the 1980s and 1990s, Grillo was a\npolitical satirist who built his celebrity pitching Yomo yogurt\nin a series of TV spots. That notoriety, combined with his\nwebsite posts and rallies, helped him gain a following for his\nblog, and then turn Five Star into the country\u2019s third-biggest\npolitical force.  DVD-Funded  \u201cWe started the blog in 2005 and initially funded it with\nthe DVD of one of my shows,\u201d said Grillo. \u201cThen we went ahead\nwith the movement.\u201d  The website is where Grillo\u2019s rallies are broadcast, and\nthat\u2019s where his 1.2 million followers on Twitter Inc. end up\nwhen they click on links in his posts. Grillo\u2019s Facebook page,\nwhich has more than 1.3 million \u201clikes,\u201d also contains links\nto the blog. Parliamentary events involving Five Star members\nare shown live in streaming. Starr knew how to\ncultivate relationships with powerful people, and he did it in\nthe most transparent way -- by serial name-dropping.  \n Dining with Starr in the Grill Room at the Four Seasons in\nNew York meant listening to him reel off bold-face names as fast\nas he guzzled Diet Cokes, according to one occasional lunch\ncompanion who asked not to be identified.  \n Certain people would come up again and again in his boasts,\naccording to a story in the June 21 issue of Bloomberg\nBusinessweek. Starr would say he had lunch with Peter Peterson,\nco-founder of the private-equity firm Blackstone Group LP, or\nthat he and \u201cPete\u201d were talking at the Council on Foreign\nRelations, long chaired by Peterson, or that he had done\nsomething with \u201cPete,\u201d according to the companion.  \n Starr managed money for a living, and his relationship with\nPeterson was one of his key assets. Rachel \u201cBunny\u201d Mellon, the\n99-year-old widow of the bank heir and philanthropist Paul\nMellon was a longstanding client, according to Alex Forger,\nMellon\u2019s lawyer. It was his connection to the Mellons that\nstarted Starr on his path to wooing the rich, according to\npeople who knew Starr and who asked not to be identified.  \n Starr\u2019s career famously came to an end last month when\ngovernment agents arrived at his home on Manhattan\u2019s Upper East\nSide and found him hiding in a closet, prosecutors in Manhattan\nsaid on the night of his arrest. His $7.5 million condominium,\nwhich he shared with his fourth wife, Diane Passage, a pole\ndancer, featured floor-to-ceiling windows, a granite lap pool,\nand a 1,500-square-foot garden, financed with what prosecutors\nsaid was plundered cash, according to a criminal complaint.  \n \u2018Secret\u2019 Interest  \n Days after his arrest, a grand jury indicted Starr for\ncheating 11 clients -- Jim Wiatt, the former head of the William\nMorris Agency, and actress Uma Thurman among them -- out of $59\nmillion.  \n Starr pocketed half that amount, while the other half was\nplaced in investments in which he or his friends had a secret\ninterest, prosecutors said. Starr has denied wrongdoing and is\nbeing held at the Metropolitan Correctional Center in lower\nManhattan. The Securities and Exchange Commission brought its\nown civil fraud lawsuit against Starr and Passage, seeking the\nreturn of tens of millions of dollars.  \n The two haven\u2019t yet responded to the SEC suit. A judge last\nweek extended the freeze on the couple\u2019s assets at a hearing\nattended by Passage, who looked uncharacteristically demure in a\npink cardigan and a black skirt. She declined all reporters\u2019\nquestions except for one from Bloomberg Businessweek, about her\nage.  \n \u201cThirty-four,\u201d she said. \u201cYou can take a couple of years\noff that if you want to.\u201d  \n Elite Crowd  \n The disintegration of Starr & Co., which once managed more\nthan $700 million for about 175 wealthy individuals, exposes an\nuncomfortable truth about the elite crowd he preyed on -- that\nwealthy, sophisticated people could be such easy marks for\nfraud. While the numbers involved aren\u2019t on the scale of Bernie\nMadoff\u2019s Ponzi scheme, Starr shared Madoff\u2019s ability to create\nan aura of exclusivity around himself that appealed to the\nelite.  \n His allure was augmented by Starr\u2019s attendance at\ninvitation-only business gatherings, such as Allen & Co.\nPresident Herbert Allen\u2019s annual media conference in Sun Valley,\nIdaho.  \n Still, there is no special trick to Starr\u2019s alleged con\ngame that one can glean from his indictment or the SEC\ncomplaint. So how is it so many people so willingly allowed\ntheir pockets to be picked?  \n The Herd  \n \u201cEveryone follows the herd,\u201d said Ken Springer, a former\nFederal Bureau of Investigation agent and founder of New York-\nbased investigative firm Corporate Resolutions. \u201cEveryone says\nthis guy is the best, and no one vets the people.\u201d  \n Starr & Co. rose by buzz and fell by buzz. A court-\nappointed receiver has reported that only 30 to 40 clients\nremained with the firm, after scores of others left amid\nrepeated incidents of unauthorized client wire transfers and\nmoney-losing investments.  \n Individuals once affiliated with Starr have typically gone\nmum -- Peterson declined to comment on either his relationship\nwith Starr or the accusations against him -- or distanced\nthemselves from him. Millennium Technology Ventures, a venture-\ncapital firm that grew out of one co-founded by Starr and\nPeterson, addressed the issue in a June 4 letter to investors.  \n \u2018Not Involved\u2019  \n \u201cHe has not been involved in investment decisions for the\nfund and has not been actively involved in any operational or\nstrategic decision-making capacity with the fund for many years\nnow,\u201d wrote Daniel Burstein, one of Millennium\u2019s two managing\npartners who were once with Blackstone. In addition, he wrote,\n\u201cMr. Starr has been removed from his role as a member of the\nSpecial Advisory Board.\u201d  \n Peterson remains a special advisory partner with\nMillennium, according to the firm\u2019s website. Burstein declined\nto comment for this story.  \n Starr\u2019s connections to Blackstone go back to the early\n1990s, when the firm was considerably smaller than it is now.\nBlackstone received $90 million from clients of Starr & Co.,\naccording to a lawsuit filed in 2009 by the estate of former\nStarr client Joan Stanton.  \n Actor Wesley Snipes, for instance, put $1 million into\nBlackstone, according to testimony in the actor\u2019s 2008 tax-\nevasion trial. Injecting himself as a middleman, Starr charged\nclients for placing their money with the firm and pooled their\ninvestments in partnerships he controlled, prosecutors said. The\nStanton complaint doesn\u2019t claim that Blackstone was aware of\nStarr\u2019s motives.  \n \u2018Excessive\u2019 Fees  \n The Stanton estate\u2019s suit decried \u201cexcessive fees,\u201d which\ncame on top of Starr\u2019s regular ones. His annual charges rose\nfrom $120,000 in the years after he began working with Stanton\nin 1987 to $228,000 in 2004. The suit also accused Starr of\nusing the partnerships to prevent Stanton from having direct\ncommunication with Blackstone.  \n Stanton committed $5.1 million to a fund called Blackstone\nDomestic Capital Partners II, a Blackstone entity, her estate\nalleged. Her money didn\u2019t go straight to Blackstone Domestic,\naccording to the lawsuit. Stanton\u2019s money was instead put with\nthat of other Starr clients in a $12.4 million pool he formed\ncalled Blackstone Investors Partnership, which wasn\u2019t affiliated\nwith the Peterson Blackstone, according to the complaint.  \n Stanton\u2019s Blackstone Domestic returns were supposed to go\nto a trust whose assets would be distributed tax-free to heirs.\nThose Blackstone returns went to purposes unknown, according to\nthe Stanton estate\u2019s complaint.  \n Venture Firm  \n By 1997, Starr and Peterson had grown close enough to\ncreate and co-invest in a tech venture firm called P.S. Capital,\naccording to filings and a person familiar with the enterprise.\nThe vehicle\u2019s chief financial officer and general counsel was\nRonald Starr, a son from Ken Starr\u2019s first marriage, and it\ncreated two investment funds totaling $13 million, according to\nthis person.  \n As Internet fever spiked around the year 2000, P.S. Capital\nmorphed into the more ambitious Millennium Technology Venture\nFund, which, according to press releases, raised $160 million of\ninvestor capital, yielded more than two dozen technology\nstartups, and included \u201cspecial limited advisory partners\u201d\nPeterson and Starr.  \n Dan Burstein, who previously had been a senior adviser to\nBlackstone and chief investment officer of P.S. Capital, became\na managing partner of Millennium, as did Richard Kimball, then\nPeterson\u2019s son-in-law.  \n Settled Suit  \n The firm\u2019s location in the same office building as Starr &\nCo. enabled Starr to be active in the firm. He was \u201cactively\ninvolved in managing personnel matters,\u201d according to a former\nMillennium secretary named Mystery Masiello, who filed a\ndiscrimination lawsuit against the company in 2003. She alleged\nthat when she told the firm\u2019s leaders she was pregnant in July\n2001, Starr said, \u201cOh great, now Dan is going to have to get a\nnew assistant,\u201d referring to Burstein. The case was settled on\nundisclosed terms in 2003.  \n The Millennium fund, launched just before the Internet\nbubble burst, proved to be a dud. Its few successes -- such as\nthe Internet security company Phobos, which was sold to\nSonicWALL in 2000 -- were overshadowed by big losses. About half\nof the original $160 million has been returned to investors,\naccording to a person familiar with its finances who asked not\nto be identified. Millennium is in the process of being wound\ndown, according to the June 4 letter to investors.  \n \u2018Land Rush\u2019  \n \u201cThey were caught up in the Oklahoma land rush\u201d along\nwith many other Internet investors, says Neil Livingstone,\nformer chief executive officer of GlobalOptions Group Inc., a\nsecurity company. GlobalOptions, which he said was the\nMillennium Fund\u2019s only non-tech investment and its top-\nperforming portfolio company after the bubble burst, went public\nin 2005. It owed much of its success to business it received\ndirectly from Millennium during the post-bubble malaise.  \n \u201cWe shut down a lot of their Silicon Valley companies,\u201d\nsaid Livingstone, who is now CEO of Washington security firm\nExecutiveAction. The firm was an early example of Starr\u2019s\ngrowing propensity to invest client funds \u201cin questionable and\nsuspicious investments, often with a direct benefit to himself,\nhis wife,\u201d or friends, prosecutors said last month in Starr\u2019s\ncriminal complaint.  \n Starr also put his clients\u2019 money straight into\nGlobalOptions stock. In\nits new incarnation it has had some success, investing in\ncompanies that were later bought by Amazon.com Inc., Microsoft\nCorp. and AT&T Inc., and in April it closed a new $280 million\nfund to new investors, according to Millennium\u2019s press releases.  \n Starr was listed on the Millennium website as a \u201cspecial\nlimited advisory partner\u201d until February 2008. He effectively\nceased involvement when Burstein changed the concept, according\nto people familiar with the firm.  \n Starr met Bunny Mellon when he was a young certified public\naccountant with Manhattan-based Oppenheim, Appel, Dixon & Co.\nThe Bronx-born graduate of Queens College and Brooklyn Law\nSchool loved the idea of handling taxes for one of America\u2019s\nrichest families, according to a person familiar with the\nsituation.  \n Modest Dress  \n He absorbed his clients\u2019 methods and desires, though he\ndressed inexpensively himself. The Stantons\u2019\napartment served as a salon to many of the city\u2019s elite. Joan\nStanton was an actress who had played Lois Lane in The\nAdventures of Superman radio show, and their home was often\nfilled with performing artists, according to a person familiar\nwith the matter.  \n When their daughter turned 21, Leonard Bernstein led the\nsinging of Happy Birthday, the daughter, Jane Stanton Hitchcock,\nonce recounted in an interview. Film director\nMike Nichols and stage director Hal Prince became Starr clients.\nArthur Stanton died in 1987, leaving $60 million to his widow,\nand Starr pitched himself to manage it for her, according to a\nperson familiar with the matter.  \n \u2018Predator\u2019  \n The lawsuit brought against Starr by Joan Stanton\u2019s estate\n22 years later, soon after her own passing at age 94 in May\n2009, portrayed him as a predator who defrauded her of \u201ctens of\nmillions of dollars.\u201d \u201cMrs. Stanton\u2019s lack of financial acumen\nwas known to Mr. Starr,\u201d according to the complaint. \u201cMr.\nStarr began to cultivate Mrs. Stanton as a client who would come\nto rely on his services exclusively.\u201d  \n Starr left Oppenheim in 1987 to start his own firm, he said\nin testimony at the 2008 tax-evasion trial of client Wesley\nSnipes. Skills honed on the Mellons and Stantons served him well\nin building a larger clientele, according to a person who has\nknown him professionally for years. The person describes Starr\nas a master of ingratiating himself with people. He wasn\u2019t\nsuave; he wasn\u2019t a Madoff in appearance and charm; he was rather\nabrupt.  \n Detailed Investments  \n So what was the appeal? This person describes Starr as very\nbright and says he came across as sincere. He could sit down\nwith a piece of paper and map out detailed investments.  \n Starr\u2019s reputation took its first public beating in 2002\nwhen his client Sylvester Stallone sued him for keeping him\ninvested in Planet Hollywood from 1997 to 2001, as the\nrestaurant chain spiraled toward bankruptcy and the value of his\n4 million shares withered. The actor accused Starr of putting\nhis friendship with Keith Barish, a founder of Planet Hollywood,\nahead of his fiduciary duty to clients, and sought at least $10\nmillion in damages.  \n The litigation, settled on undisclosed terms in 2003, was\nan example of what prosecutors later said was Starr\u2019s habit of\nmaking decisions without his clients\u2019 approval. In 2006, Starr\nformed Starr Investment Advisors; regulatory filings indicate he\nhad 26 to 100 clients and 11 to 50 employees.  \n Two Funds  \n Starr placed $6.5 million of Bunny Mellon\u2019s fortune into\ntwo investment funds from 2005 to 2007 without informing his\nlongtime client that they were \u201chighly speculative and risky,\u201d\naccording to prosecutors. He also failed to \u201cdisclose certain\nconflicts of interest,\u201d according to indictment against Starr.\nBarish didn\u2019t return a call seeking comment.  \n Only in August 2009, when investigators asked Mellon\u2019s\nattorney about these illiquid investments, did her\nrepresentative become aware of the funds. Starr returned $4.3\nmillion to Mellon that month, according to the indictment.  \n Starr\u2019s behavior outside the office also turned erratic\nafter taking up with Passage in 2005. He began to forsake his\nown counsel about modest appearances, spending more than\n$400,000 on jewelry from Jacob & Co., aka Jacob the Jeweler,\nduring the span of several months in 2006, according to the\ncriminal complaint.  \n Pole Dancer  \n In May 2007, he divorced Marisa Starr. He did so by filing\ncourt documents without her knowledge that claimed she agreed to\nend 16 years of marriage, according to her 2009 lawsuit. Starr\u2019s\nfourth wife was a flashy, jarring presence in Manhattan society\n-- tattooed, provocatively dressed and a pole dancer. She put on\na Poledance Superstar competition in New York in October 2009 to\nraise money for a charity she started called S.P.I.N. (Single\nParents In Need), according to a website promoting the event.  \n Starr was proud of her, too, showing iPhone pictures of her\ngyrating on a pole to fellow attendees at a Tribeca Film\nFestival function in 2008, according to people who were there.  \n In early 2008, Starr recruited Jacob the Jeweler, whose\nreal name is Jacob Arabo, as an investment client. His money was\ninvested in \u201csure deals\u201d that included Glassnote Entertainment\nGroup, which gave Passage a $150,000-a-year job, and Martin\nBregman Productions, a movie venture involving Marty Bregman, a\nStarr client and a veteran producer of films such as Scarface,\naccording to the criminal complaint.  \n Prosecutors said Passage wanted to make the film version of\n\u201cThe Desert Rose,\u201d Larry McMurtry\u2019s novel about an aging Las\nVegas showgirl. The two doomed ventures represented $2.7 million\nof the $13 million of which Arabo was defrauded by Starr,\naccording to the complaint.  \n Strange Behavior  \n The same network that made Starr rich quickly undid him, as\nstories of losses and strange behavior spread. Clients left the\nfirm, including Mike Nichols and his broadcaster wife, Diane\nSawyer, according to a person familiar with the matter.  \n Four months after Stanton\u2019s death, her estate sued Starr\nfor \u201cgross abuse of trust and confidence\u201d over 20 years. The\nStanton complaint, combined with some individual complaints,\nspurred the Manhattan District Attorney\u2019s office and the SEC to\nstart asking questions.  \n Starr settled with the Stanton estate for an undisclosed\nsum in January, according to a person familiar with the\nsituation. He also reached a $4 million settlement that month\nwith an unidentified playwright and screenwriter who complained\nof being fraudulently induced to invest in a failed restaurant\nchain, according to the indictment.  \n Top Clients  \n Starr raided other clients\u2019 accounts to make the payment,\nprosecutors said. In another winter development, a veteran\naccount manager for Starr named Arnold Herrmann left for rival\nfirm Citrin Cooperman & Co. and took some of his top clients,\naccording to a Feb. 11 Citrin Cooperman press release. One of\nthe clients was Barbara Walters, according to a person familiar\nwith the matter.  \n As his firm disintegrated, Starr tried to maintain\nappearances. In February he borrowed $2.6 million from Los-\nAngeles-based City National Bank, according to a lawsuit filed\nby the bank on June 16, two weeks after Starr missed a $9,385\ninterest payment. At a March 10 meeting with federal\ninvestigators, he said his firm had 200 clients. While that\nwould have almost been true at its peak, the list had dwindled\nto less than a quarter of that by the time of his arrest,\naccording to the criminal complaints and a document filed in\ncourt by the Starr & Co. receiver, Aurora Cassirer.  \n Final Straw  \n In April, prosecutors said, Starr bought the $7.5 million\ncondominium. This proved to be the final straw. On May 25, the\nlawyer for Bunny Mellon, Starr\u2019s first big client and one of his\nlast, was looking through her financial statements. He saw a\nseries of mid-April wire-transfers out of her Starr & Co.\naccount, totaling $5.75 million, according to prosecutors. Starr\nhad allegedly raided the account to close on his condominium.\nThe lawyer called the authorities. Two days later, federal\nagents were removing him from the closet.  \n The civil case is SEC v. Starr, 1:10-cv-04270, and the\ncriminal case is U.S. v. The company is designing computers that require less space\nand power than conventional machines yet perform just as well.\nThe idea is to fill a gap left by  Hewlett-Packard Co. (HPQ)  and  Dell\nInc. (DELL) , which have curtailed research and development, SeaMicro\nChief Executive Officer Andrew Feldman said in an interview.  \u201cWe stepped into a market that isn\u2019t very good at R&D and\nisn\u2019t very good at innovation,\u201d said Feldman, whose company\nbegan shipping its first products a year ago. \u201cThey became\nsupply-chain companies. They stopped doing engineering.\u201d  SeaMicro is focusing on the type of servers used by\nFacebook Inc. and  Google Inc. (GOOG)  to provide so-called cloud\nservices over the Internet -- a market that will almost double\nby 2015, according to IDC. By producing machines that uses a\nquarter of the power and a sixth of the space, SeaMicro has seen\nsales boom, said Feldman, 42. While he declined to give revenue\nfigures, Feldman estimates that SeaMicro set a sales record for\na Silicon Valley computer-hardware startup in its first year of\nshipping products.  The company recently hired its 100th employee and has moved\ninto a bigger space in  Sunnyvale, California . The new\nheadquarters is a sea of gray cubicles -- many yet to be\noccupied -- an environment more reminiscent of Silicon Valley\npioneers like  Intel Corp. (INTC)  than dot-com startups.  Giant Rivals  Maintaining SeaMicro\u2019s growth will hinge on whether the big\nserver makers, including Hewlett-Packard and Dell, pursue the\nsame innovations, said Jeffrey Hewitt, an analyst at Stamford,\nConnecticut-based Gartner Inc. The company has made strides in\nstreamlining the way processors work together, helping SeaMicro\ncarve out a niche for itself, he said.  \u201cThe jury is still out as to whether HP and Dell are\nasleep at the wheel,\u201d Hewitt said.  The market for SeaMicro\u2019s servers is still in its early\nstages, he said. As it grows, Hewlett-Packard and Dell may place\nmore emphasis on it, Hewitt said.  Jim Ganthier, a vice president of  Palo Alto , California-\nbased Hewlett-Packard, said his company isn\u2019t worried about\nSeaMicro. SeaMicro will remain a small\nplayer with niche technology, he said.  \u2018On an Island\u2019  \u201cThey\u2019re going to be left on an island with their shiny\nlittle box,\u201d Ganthier said.  Even so, Hewlett-Packard\u2019s research budget is smaller today\nas a percentage of sales than it was 15 years ago. The company\nspent 2.6 percent of revenue on R&D in the most recent fiscal\nyear, down from 7.1 percent in fiscal 1996.  Dell, meanwhile, says it\u2019s also exploring new technologies.\nIt \u201cspends a ton of time talking to customers\u201d and builds\nproducts that cater to specific needs, said Steve Cumings, who\nhandles marketing for data centers at the  Round Rock , Texas-\nbased company. Dell also resells some SeaMicro servers, making\nthe companies partners and competitors.  \u201cWe\u2019ve been very successful in the market,\u201d Cumings said.\n\u201cWe look at a lot of new technologies.\u201d  Dell spent 1.1 percent of revenue on R&D in the last fiscal\nyear, versus 1.8 percent 15 years ago.  SeaMicro was founded in 2007 with investments from Khosla\nVentures, Draper Fisher Jurvetson and Crosslink Capital Inc. The\ncompany\u2019s customer list includes  Skype Technologies SA (MSFT) ,\nEHarmony.com Inc., Nippon Telegraph & Telephone Corp. and France\nTelecom SA. It also serves all of the major companies that use\ndata centers to provide cloud services, Feldman said.  Design Innovation  SeaMicro\u2019s biggest innovation is its chip design, he said.\nThe company\u2019s application-specific integrated circuit, or ASIC,\nreplaces as much as 90 percent of the separate components on a\nserver motherboard and links the processors together.  SeaMicro servers rely on Intel\u2019s Atom processor -- a chip\ndesigned for battery-powered devices. That means it doesn\u2019t\nrequire a lot of electricity. The processor isn\u2019t one of Intel\u2019s\nmore powerful products, though by using a lot of them, SeaMicro\ncan get the necessary performance with less power.  Often the servers are handling simple tasks, such as\ndelivering e-mail or a Facebook page. The big computer makers\nhaven\u2019t adapted to this world of cloud services, Feldman said.  Instead of buying powerful computers designed for the\ncomplex needs of a few internal users, cloud-service providers\nwant servers to handle millions of customers. That means they\nwant a much bigger array of cheap, efficient machinery, he said.  \u201cThe nature of the work changed,\u201d Feldman said. \u201cIt\nchanged from a small number of users to many users, and from\nhard problems to easy problems.\u201d  To contact the reporter on this story:\nIan King in  San Francisco  at \n ianking@bloomberg.net   To contact the editor responsible for this story:\nTom Giles at   tgiles5@bloomberg.net","path":".\/2008_2012_msft_bloomberg_news\/seamicro-aims-for-startup-stardom-with-old-school-innovation.txt"},{"id":14689516,"title":"Kings Sale, Move May Be Formality Without Counter Offer, Arena","released_at":"<date>January 23 2013<\/date> <time>05:00:35<\/time>","content":"The approvals needed by the group\nseeking to buy the Sacramento Kings and move the franchise to\nSeattle may be a formality without a concrete counter offer and\narena deal in  California \u2019s capital city.
