He\u2019s doing it by lending money to strangers online. An\naccountant by day, Qiu has turned out to be a better loan\nmanager by night than most banks. Only two investments out of\nhis 80,000  yuan  ($12,525) total, each worth 100 yuan, have gone\nunpaid. Nonperforming loans at a Chinese lender, on average,\nwould be almost four times as much.  \u201cI don\u2019t care what the money is used for because that\u2019s\nbeyond my control,\u201d said the 30-year-old certified financial\nplanner who jumped into online lending in May by registering at\n Ppdai.com , one of China\u2019s largest such sites. \u201cFor me, the key\nis to identify those who have at least a willingness to honor\ntheir debt, so I need to keep my eyes wide open.\u201d  Peer-to-peer lending is taking off in China as traditional\nmethods of private lending among family and acquaintances, part\nof the country\u2019s unregulated $2.4 trillion shadow-banking\nsystem, move online. More than 2,000 websites have been set up\nnationwide since 2007,  China  National Radio reported in May.\nLoans brokered online increased 300-fold to 6 billion yuan in\nthe first half of 2011, the latest figures available, from the\nfull year total in 2007, the  report  said.  \u2019Innovative Lending\u2019  Akin to  LendingClub.com  or  Prosper.com  in the U.S., China\u2019s\npeer-to-peer lenders let individuals invest a minimum of 50 yuan\nin projects ranging from small-business expansion to funding\nnewlyweds\u2019 honeymoons for as much as 23 percent interest, the\nhighest rate allowed under Chinese law. While the returns are\nhigher than parking the money in bank accounts earning 3\npercent, they\u2019re dwarfed by some underground shadow-banking\ninvestment yields that can go as high as 100 percent.  \u201cThis is an interesting and innovative lending platform\nwith a lot of goodwill,\u201d said Liao Qiang, a Beijing-based\ndirector for financial institutions at  Standard & Poor\u2019s .  Existing outside of regulators\u2019 jurisdiction, online\nlending sites aren\u2019t without risks. The China Banking Regulatory\nCommission in September issued a  warning  about web-based\nbrokers, cautioning that their bad-loan ratio is \u201csignificantly\nhigher\u201d than that of banks -- without specifying the figure --\nand that they can cross the line into illegality such as fraud,\nfunding illegitimate businesses or money laundering.  A Beijing-based spokesman for the banking regulator said\npeer-to-peer lending isn\u2019t under its official purview.  \u201cThere is no discipline at all,\u201d Liao said, calling it a\n\u201cshort-lived fad\u201d that won\u2019t affect the role banks play in the\neconomy. \u201cThere\u2019s no enforcement should borrowers default.\u201d  Prosper Marketplace  Online peer-to-peer lending started in the U.K. in 2005 and\nspread to the U.S.,  Germany  and elsewhere. Prosper Marketplace\nInc., the first such U.S. lender, reported a 179 percent\nincrease in volume in 2011 and has almost 1.4 million members\nfunding $369 million in loans.  Lending online became popular in China after a tightening\nof  bank credit  in 2010 following two years of stimulus spending\nto fight the global financial crisis. With total loan volume\nless than $1 billion, it\u2019s still a tiny part of the country\u2019s\nshadow-banking universe -- along with underground lending, off-\nbalance-sheet financing by banks and investments by trust firms\n-- that policy makers led by Premier  Wen Jiabao  are trying to\nbring under government oversight.  The total amount that circulates as loans among friends,\nfamilies and companies is $1.3 trillion, according to estimates\nby research firm  IHS Global Insight Ltd. (IHS) , an amount equal to\nlast year\u2019s U.S. budget deficit.  Microfinance Inspiration  The Ppdai site, which calls itself China\u2019s first and\nlargest, was founded by former Microsoft Corp. engineer Zhang\nJun and three former classmates from  Shanghai  Jiaotong\nUniversity. Zhang said they found inspiration when Bangladeshi\neconomist  Muhammad Yunus  and his Grameen Bank won the Nobel\nPeace Prize in 2006 for lifting millions out of poverty by\nmaking small loans through what is known as microfinancing.  Reeling from a failed YouTube-like website, the friends\ndecided to pool their remaining savings of 200,000 yuan to\nconnect borrowers with investors via the Web. The catch: None of\nthe founders, including one who was a corporate lawyer at the\ntime, knew if it was legal.  \u201cWe went ahead because we couldn\u2019t find any regulation\nthat specifically bans it,\u201d Zhang, 35, said in an interview at\nhis Shanghai Ppdai Financial Information Services Co. office in\na shared space for startup companies at a high-tech park in\nShanghai\u2019s Pudong district. \u201cWe knew the demand was there. So\nwas the supply.\u201d  Loan Requests  Like San Francisco-based Prosper, Ppdai requires borrowers\nto list basic personal information and details of their\nfinancing needs. Investors review the requests and make\ninvestments that meet their criteria. About 80 percent of the\ntotal 400 million yuan of lending brokered by Ppdai since 2007\nhas gone to small businesses, Zhang said.  Only 3 percent of China\u2019s 42 million small and medium-sized\nfirms are able to get loans from banks, according to an estimate\nby Citic Securities Co., while 36.7 trillion yuan of  household\nsavings  are parked in banks. Half of that amount earns as little\nas  0.35 percent  a year in checking accounts, with the remainder\nearning a 3 percent savings rate, which the government lowered\nfrom 3.5 percent in June.  A recent loan request by an online sportswear retailer in\n Hunan province  asked for 11,970 yuan to buy inventory for the\nfall season, paying 20 percent interest. Another borrower in\nShandong province is seeking 50,000 yuan to purchase\nmanufacturing equipment, paying 18 percent.  Default Risk  Ppdai, which in Chinese is short for \u201clending through\nauctions,\u201d claims more than 1.1 million registered users. Loan\namounts start at 3,000 yuan and are capped at 500,000 yuan, with\nlenders contributing a minimum of 50 yuan. The maximum  interest\nrate  by law, 23 percent, can\u2019t exceed four times the benchmark\nlending rate, now 6 percent for  one-year loans . Credit cards\nusually charge 18 percent.  \u201cIt\u2019s fairly easy to get consumer loans and credit cards\nfrom banks nowadays,\u201d S&P\u2019s Liao said. \u201cIf someone is\nunqualified for that, he may very likely end up being a borrower\nonline and the default risk is extremely high.\u201d  About 3.5 percent of Ppdai\u2019s loans aren\u2019t paid off on time,\nZhang said, while 1.2 percent have been overdue for at least 90\ndays, the definition of nonperforming at Chinese banks. That\ncompares with the 0.9 percent bad-loan ratio of the nation\u2019s\ncommercial banks as of the end of March, according to data from\nthe banking regulator. The rate by investor Qiu of 0.25 percent\nis considerably lower than Ppdai\u2019s average.  Online Rescue  The default rate of  LendingClub Corp. , a U.S. peer-to-peer\nlending site which issues consumer loans of as much as $35,000\nfor everything from home repair to exotic vacations, has been\nbelow 3 percent since its inception in 2007, while at Prosper\nthe loan-loss rate is about 5 percent, according to the\ncompanies\u2019 websites.  One Chinese borrower, 29-year-old Xu Xiaolong, counts\nherself a beneficiary after a lending website helped her family\nsurvive a difficult period in May. Xu\u2019s husband had a car\naccident and needed 30,000 yuan to pay his medical bills.  Days before the accident, the couple had put 1 million\nyuan, their entire savings plus some loans from relatives and\nfriends, into a nonrefundable investment. They bought 30-year\nrights to eight acres of green-tea fields in  Fujian province .  Hongling Chuangtou Ecommerce Co. , which operates the\nMy089.com lending website from Shenzhen, increased Xu\u2019s\nborrowing limit after learning what happened. She was able to\nraise all the money she requested in one day at an 18 percent\nannual rate.  \u2018Great Platform\u2019  \u201cIt\u2019s a great platform to resort to if you have urgent\nneeds,\u201d Xu, who had been a borrower and lender previously, said\nin a telephone interview. \u201cI am truly thankful for it.\u201d  Ppdai, which charges borrowers a fee of as much as 4\npercent of their loans, began to break even early last year,\nZhang said. Almost 80 percent of the company\u2019s monthly revenue\nof 500,000 yuan goes to the salaries of its 40 employees, while\nthe rest is reinvested in the business, he said.  Renrendai Business Consulting (Beijing) Corp., which\noperates renrendai.com, brokered about 130 million yuan of loans\nonline in the first half this year, an increase of more than 10\nfold from a year earlier, according to its  earnings report \nposted last week. Borrowers are paying between 10.3 percent and\n16.6 percent interest on loans with maturities of three months\nto 24 months.  Credit Scoring  China\u2019s lack of a credit-scoring system makes risk\nmanagement difficult for peer-to-peer lending, giving potential\nlenders no way to gauge borrowers\u2019 creditworthiness.  For most online platforms in China, risk-control measures\ninclude checking whether the personal identification or business\nlicense of the borrower has been photo-shopped. Those who have\ndefaulted have their names and contact numbers disclosed on the\nfront page of the website.  \u201cComing from a technology background, it took us a while\nto realize that risk management is key to the business,\u201d Zhang\nsaid. \u201cBut we can do just enough to reduce default and prevent\nfraud, so we urge investors again and again not to put all their\neggs in one basket.\u201d  \u2018Ponzi Scheme\u2019  Some peer-to-peer sites have shut down. Hahadai.com, a\nShanghai-based online loan broker with almost 100,000 registered\nusers, closed in July 2011, about 18 months after it started,\nbecause the company didn\u2019t have enough capital, the Economic\nObserver  reported .  Taojindai.com, which went live on June 3, became\ninaccessible five days later, with more than 1 million yuan in\ninvestments from at least 80 users missing, the China Business\nNews  reported  last month, calling it the first \u201c Ponzi scheme \u201d\nin the country\u2019s peer-to-peer lending business.  \u201cUnlike banks, these middlemen are unable to collect\ninformation on borrowers and manage loans afterwards,\u201d the\nregulator warned in September. \u201cIn the event that illegal\nactivities such as malicious fraud or even  money laundering \noccur, it will endanger the entire society.\u201d  The same concerns have haunted the sites\u2019 U.S.\ncounterparts. Prosper in November 2008 stopped all new lending\nafter the  U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission  issued a\ncease-and-desist letter characterizing the website as a seller\nof investments, a label Prosper had resisted by arguing it was a\nmarketplace matching lenders and borrowers.  Five months later, California regulators  allowed  the\ncompany to resume raising money in the state and lending it out\nunder a system that lets borrowers and lenders use bids to set\nthe interest rates on loans.  Suicides, Bankruptcies  China\u2019s policy makers are trying to regulate the excesses\nof private lending after a spate of suicides and bankruptcies\naround the country led to defaults, lawsuits and protests.  \u201cInformal lending through various forms has been an\nintegral part of China\u2019s financial system because not all of its\nfunctions can be replaced by banks,\u201d said He Wenguang, an\neconomics professor at China Agricultural University in Beijing,\nwhose research focuses on rural and microfinancing. \u201cIt will\ncontinue to exist with or without government interference.\u201d  Beyond Lending  CreditEase, established as a peer-to-peer lending site in\n2006, has now become a provider of wealth-management services,\ncredit ratings and rural financing, drawing investment from\nventure-capital firm IDG Capital Partners and Morgan Stanley\u2019s\nAsia fund. The company doesn\u2019t have the licenses required by the\nbanking and securities regulator for these services.  \u201cWe are a company that provides all types of services,\nincluding financial planning,\u201d said Tang Ning, founder and CEO\nof CreditEase. \u201cWe don\u2019t consider ourselves simply a lender.\u201d  Tang, who went to  Bangladesh  to study microfinance under\nYunus, said Beijing-based CreditEase is registered as a service\ncompany, not a lending organization.  To ensure that it could continue to grow in the absence of\nclear regulation, Ppdai sought an operating license as a\nprovider of \u201cfinancial-information services,\u201d Zhang said.\nAfter numerous visits by officials from the central bank and\ncity government, Ppdai was granted the license in May by\nShanghai\u2019s Administration for Industry & Commerce, he said.  Providing financial information isn\u2019t what peer-to-peer\nlending is about, raising more questions from users such as Qiu.  \u201cI am still not sure whether my investment is legal or\nnot,\u201d said Qiu, whose loans included 500 yuan for a borrower\u2019s\napartment renovation and 400 yuan to a paint seller in\nChongqing. \u201cI can manage default risks by screening borrowers,\nbut there is nothing I can do if the whole website turns out to\nbe a scam. So finally, who\u2019s the police on this place if that\nreally happens?\u201d  --Luo Jun. (T)  and\nJohnson & Johnson are paying less tax than before the recession\neven as profits have rebounded, buoyed by breaks and expansion\nin overseas markets, where the tax burden is lower.  Cash tax payments by non-financial companies in the\n Standard & Poor\u2019s 500 Index (SPX)  fell 13.2 percent to $222 billion in\n2010 from 2007, according to data compiled by Bloomberg, while\nnet income rose 12.5 percent to $612 billion. Cash taxes are the\namount paid in taxes to all jurisdictions in a given year.  The pattern has implications for the U.S. government and\nfor companies, said  Jim Paulsen , chief investment strategist at\nMinneapolis-based Wells Capital Management. With domestic job\ngrowth still anemic, Congress may want to keep tax breaks such\nas accelerated depreciation, while companies may continue growth\noutside the U.S. because of strong demand, Paulsen said.  \u201cIn this recovery, there are so much more foreign profits\nas a proportion of the total for the large companies,\u201d said\nPaulsen, whose firm manages about $340 billion. \u201cThere are just\ngreater business opportunities abroad with the emerging world\ngrowing faster.\u201d  The  Congressional Budget Office  estimates that U.S.\n receipts  from corporate income will drop to $181 billion in\nfiscal 2011 from $191 billion in 2010, and rebound to $279\nbillion in the fiscal year ending Sept. 30, 2012. Corporate tax\ncollections were $353.9 billion in fiscal 2006 and $370.2\nbillion in fiscal 2007.  The decline since 2007 adds to the pressure on Congress as\nlawmakers squabble over how to narrow the U.S. budget deficits.  Offsetting Current Taxes  Some of the drop in tax receipts can be traced to the 18-\nmonth recession through June 2009 and longstanding provisions of\nthe U.S. tax code that allow companies to use losses from lean\nyears to offset their current taxes.  Corporate earnings also have been boosted by Congress\u2019s\nmove in 2008 to increase by 50 percent the amount of\ndepreciation for  capital spending  that can be deducted in one\nyear. The measure, designed to stimulate spending and create\njobs, was raised to 100 percent expensing in September 2010. The\naccelerated depreciation write-down is set to revert to 50\npercent in 2012.  \u201cEspecially for companies like AT&T and Verizon that are\ncapital-intensive, the government put in place tax shelters in\nan effort to get them to accelerate some of their capital\nspending, and they\u2019ve certainly benefited,\u201d said Ben Abramovitz, an analyst with Kaufman Brothers LP in  New York , who\nhas a hold recommendation on AT&T.  AT&T posted profit of $19.9 billion in 2010 and paid cash\ntaxes of $3.5 billion, lower than taxes of $4 billion in 2007 on\nnet income of $12 billion.  Capital Spending  It\u2019s unclear how much the tax break enticed companies to\nboost capital spending. Companies in the  S&P 500 , excluding\nfinancial corporations, reported less spending in 2009 and 2010\nthan peak capital spending of $523 billion in 2008, according to\ndata compiled by Bloomberg. In the past 12 months, spending has\nrebounded to $535 billion.  \u201cIt\u2019s really in the best interest of the economy for the\nU.S. government to entice those companies to spend on something\nthat creates a long-term economic benefit and that primarily is\ninfrastructure in the country,\u201d Abramovitz said.  Dallas-based AT&T\u2019s capital expenditures fell in 2009 to\n$16.6 billion from $19.7 billion the previous year. Spending\nrebounded to $19.5 billion in 2010 and is forecast to reach\n$20.1 billion this year for the second-largest U.S. wireless\nprovider and largest U.S. telephone company, according to the\naverage estimate from 17 analysts surveyed by Bloomberg.  Lingering Effect  The effect of net losses on cash taxes can linger for years\nbecause companies can gradually deduct them from subsequent\nprofits, said  Michelle Hanlon , associate professor of accounting\nat the Sloan School of Management at the Massachusetts Institute\nof Technology in Cambridge.  After eliminating non-financial companies that had losses\nin 2008 and 2009, cash taxes for S&P 500 members fell to $200\nbillion in 2010 from $217 billion three years earlier. Profit in\nthose periods rose to $547 billion from $512 billion, according\nto the data compiled by Bloomberg.  Johnson & Johnson (JNJ) \u2019s cash tax bill dropped to $2.4 billion\nlast year from $4.1 billion in 2007 while net income rose to\n$12.3 billion from $10.6 billion. Part of the reason for the\nreduced tax bill of the world\u2019s second-biggest seller of health\nproducts is expansion in countries such as China, Brazil and\n India , where the corporate  tax rate  is lower than the U.S., said\n Jeff Jonas , an analyst with Gabelli & Co. in Rye, New York.  Growth Outside U.S.  \u201cThe bulk of their growth has come outside of the U.S.,\u201d\nsaid Jonas, who has a buy recommendation on  New Brunswick , New\nJersey-based J&J. \u201cThey really stepped up their investment in\n emerging markets .\u201d  Profits earned abroad are levied at rates in those\njurisdictions, with a credit given for foreign taxes paid, and\naren\u2019t subject to U.S. taxes until brought home.  At  Danaher Corp. (DHR) , a maker of medical and measurement\nequipment, the percentage of revenue from emerging markets\njumped to 22 percent from 10 percent in 2005. That share may\nclimb to 40 percent over time, Chief Executive Officer Larry Culp said in a Nov. 8 presentation to analysts.  \u201cCompanies are even more aggressive in terms of\nidentifying the countries in which they earn the income,\u201d said\n Robert Willens , a corporate tax consultant in New York.\n\u201cThey\u2019re able to shift more profits to tax haven kind of\ncountries that have lower rates.\u201d  Bringing Profits Home  The catch is that multinational companies can\u2019t repatriate\nthose profits to the U.S. without paying corporate tax on them.\nWith a top corporate U.S. rate of 35 percent, cash held abroad\nhas been piling up. About $20 billion of Johnson & Johnson\u2019s $31\nbillion in cash and short-term investments is held outside the\nU.S., Jonas said.  U.S. companies, including  Microsoft Corp. (MSFT)  and  Oracle Corp. (ORCL) ,\nare pushing for a tax break to repatriate more than $1 trillion\nof earnings held abroad. In the last 18 months of his life, Jobs, who died on Oct. 5\nat age 56, was obsessed with crushing Android. He explained to\nhis authorized biographer, Walter Isaacson, that the litigation\nagainst device manufacturers was meant to communicate an\nunmistakable message: \u201cGoogle, you f--king ripped off the\niPhone, wholesale ripped us off. Grand theft.\u201d  \u2018Dying Breath\u2019  Jobs swore he would \u201cspend my last dying breath\u201d and\n\u201cevery penny\u201d in  Apple\u2019s coffers  \u201cto right this wrong. I\u2019m\ngoing to destroy Android, because it\u2019s a stolen product. I\u2019m\nwilling to go to thermonuclear war on this.\u201d  One problem with nuclear attacks, even those of the\nmetaphoric variety, is that the targets may retaliate with nukes\nof their own. That is precisely what has happened.  For every Apple allegation, a rival has countered that\nApple isn\u2019t as uniquely innovative as Jobs liked to boast. To\nthe contrary, Samsung, Motorola and others insist that some of\nApple\u2019s most valuable patents -- such as those protecting the\nminimalist design of the iPhone and iPad -- were never valid in\nthe first place.  By pushing the launch button on his legal ICBMs, Jobs\nbequeathed a significant risk to his successors. Apple may\nsucceed in forcing competitors to deactivate a few phone\nfeatures, or maybe even yank an entire model or two from a major\nmarket. But Apple has many rivals: If one falters, others will\nstep in.  134 Phones  Samsung\u2019s website lists no fewer than 134 phone models.\nApple, by contrast, has only two core products at issue in the\npatent war: the iPhone and iPad. Unlikely as it might seem, if a\ncompeting manufacturer manages to convince a judge or a trade\ncommission somewhere in the world that Apple has relied on a\nfaulty patent for something important, the Cupertino,\nCalifornia-based juggernaut could suffer profound reputational\ndamage and -- more important to stakeholders -- market-share\nerosion.  From a distance, the mobile-device patent wars resemble a\nmad free-for-all, but the salient strain of conflict can be\ntraced to Cupertino in early 2010.  With Apple\u2019s iPhone continuing to sell millions of units,\nJobs in January of that year introduced the slender iPad tablet\ncomputer. Both devices run iOS, Apple\u2019s proprietary operating\nsystem that coordinates individual software programs and enables\nApple devices to communicate with one another.  Closed System  Jobs famously sought to keep Apple\u2019s operating systems\nexclusive -- closed off from rivals--and tightly integrated with\nApple hardware. Google designed Android, by contrast, based on\nopen-source code, which Google makes available for free to\nmultiple hardware manufacturers to install on phones and\ntablets.  Google spreads Android to make money from the online\nadvertising that trails Android wherever it goes, not from\ndevice sales. It\u2019s the same strategy Google uses with its\nubiquitous Internet search service.  Android\u2019s very existence offended Jobs. \u201cWe did not enter\nthe search business,\u201d he told Apple employees during a meeting\nat the company\u2019s headquarters in January 2010, according to the\nIsaacson biography. \u201cThey entered the phone business. Make no\nmistake. They want to kill the iPhone.\u201d  Jobs\u2019s outrage reflected his formative corporate experience\nin the 1980s, when he refused to license the Macintosh operating\nsystem for Apple\u2019s stylish desktop computer. His nemesis, Bill Gates, licensed  Microsoft Inc. (MSFT) \u2019s competing Windows operating\nsystem and DOS before that to numerous PC manufacturers.  Microsoft Products  Jobs disdained Windows as an inferior product, but snob\nappeal notwithstanding, Microsoft stomped Apple in the desktop\nsoftware marketplace. Would something similar come to pass with\niOS and Android?  What particularly irked Jobs about Google\u2019s operating\nsystem was that Android phones offered so many features he felt\nApple had created, including the overall look of the devices and\ntheir use of multitouch finger swiping.  In 2008, Jobs had visited Google\u2019s Palo Alto offices to\ntell founders Larry Page and Sergey Brin that if they backed\noff, perhaps Apple would grant Google access to a couple of\nicons on the iPhone\u2019s home screen. If they developed Android to\ncompete with iOS, Jobs warned, he would go to court.  Apple\u2019s Share  While Apple remains the world\u2019s most valuable business, as\nmeasured by market capitalization, and its iPad dominates rival\ntablets, Android has blown past Apple\u2019s share of the phone\noperating-system business. Phones with Android software\naccounted for almost 51.6 percent of smartphone shipments\nworldwide in the final quarter of 2011, according to research\nfirm Canalys. The iPhone had 23.4 percent.  Jobs\u2019s notion of channeling his pique into a federal case\nfaced several obstacles. As a practical matter, a judge couldn\u2019t\norder Google to stop selling copycat phones because Google, now\nbased in  Mountain View , California, didn\u2019t sell phones in the\nfirst place. Likewise, Google couldn\u2019t be forced to pay money\ndamages related to allegedly contraband phones manufactured and\nmarketed by other companies.  On a symbolic level, stabbing straight at Google\u2019s jugular\nmight have provoked antipathy toward Apple among consumers and\nthe Silicon Valley elite.  So in March 2010, Jobs attacked an Android proxy, accusing\nHTC, based in Taoyuan City, Taiwan, of violating 10 patents in\nproducts such as the Nexus One, Touch Pro and Droid Eris.  \u201cWe can sit by and watch competitors steal our patented\ninventions,\u201d Jobs declared at the time, \u201cor we can do\nsomething about it.\u201d  HTC Partnership  Founded in 1997, HTC had used its Android partnership with\nGoogle that began in 2007 to evolve from a contract manufacturer\nof gear for other brands to a major smartphone seller in its own\nright. It punctuated its advertising with the understated\nslogan, \u201cQuietly Brilliant.\u201d  Apple chose to accuse HTC before the International Trade\nCommission, a quasi-judicial  Washington  agency that moves more\nquickly than congested federal courts and has authority to\nexclude imports by intellectual-property wrongdoers.  \u201cApple went after what looked like a soft target,\u201d said\nWilly Shih, an intellectual property scholar and professor of\nmanagement practice at Harvard Business School. Wounding HTC\nwould send a signal to other Android-affiliated manufacturers.  HTC turned out to be tougher than expected. It hired\ntopflight outside legal counsel, including the San Francisco-\nbased firm  Quinn Emanuel Urquhart & Sullivan LLP (496224L) , which also had\nrepresented Google.  Undercutting Competition  The Taiwanese company contended in its filings that it had\ndone nothing wrong and Apple was fighting in court to undercut\nits competition.  Before trial, Apple began to back off, dropping several of\nits allegations. An ITC administrative law judge further\nnarrowed the case when he found preliminarily that HTC infringed\njust two Apple patents.  In December, the full commission whittled the case down\nagain, concluding that HTC violated only a sole patent covering\na minor feature allowing a smartphone to recognize a number so\nit can be called instantly. HTC met this news by announcing that\nit had designed a work-around that would allow it to avoid the\nimport ban Apple sought.  Following the final commission decision and a  stock-buyback \nannouncement, HTC\u2019s shares shot up 7 percent, the maximum\npermitted during a single day\u2019s trading on the  Taiwan Stock\nExchange .  Dubious Outcome  For this dubious outcome, Apple paid a price: HTC and other\nphone makers began filing patent claims against Apple.  Motorola Mobility didn\u2019t wait for Jobs to move first. In\nOctober 2010, the Libertyville, Illinois-based manufacturer,\nrepresented by Quinn Emanuel, filed a trio of lawsuits and an\nITC complaint accusing Apple of infringing its patents.  Apple responded with an ITC action that Motorola phones\nrunning Android -- the Droid, Droid 2, Droid X -- copied the\niPhone. For procedural reasons, Apple\u2019s claim moved more\nswiftly, and in January of this year, an ITC administrative law\njudge ruled that Apple had failed to show any violations by\nMotorola Mobility. On March 16, the commission upheld Motorola\nMobility\u2019s victory.  In this tit-for-tat fashion, the patent war spread from\nWashington to Chicago to Delaware, and on to Britain, France,\n Germany , Holland, Italy and  Australia . New motions, hearings,\nand appeals occur on a daily basis.  Mannheim Court  In one ruling, a court in Mannheim, Germany, decided in\nFebruary that Apple had infringed a Motorola patent for a\nfeature that automatically \u201cpushes\u201d incoming e-mail messages\nonto a phone\u2019s screen. Days later, in a court in Munich, Apple\nwon an injunction against Motorola related to \u201cslide-to-\nunlock\u201d technology. Each side is appealing each ruling, with no\nend in sight.  A mobile-phone pioneer for decades, Motorola Mobility\npossesses a trove of basic patents essential to building most\ndigital devices. So valuable is the company\u2019s intellectual\nproperty that in August, Google announced it would pay $12.5\nbillion to acquire its mobile-phone operation and its 17,000\npatents.  The deal, said Google CEO Page, will \u201cenable us to better\nprotect Android from anticompetitive threats from Microsoft,\nApple and other companies.\u201d  In other words: You sue us, we sue you. In February, Apple\nlodged a complaint with the European Commission, alleging that\nMotorola Mobility is using so-called standard essential patents\nto try to block competing products -- a claim that  Motorola\nMobility (MMI)  contests.  \u2018Copycats\u2019 Year  In March 2011, during the gala unveiling of the iPad2,\nSteve Jobs turned his often-cruel attention to Samsung. He made\nfun of its Galaxy Tab and gave the Korean company top billing in\na chart proclaiming 2011 the \u201cYear of the Copycats.\u201d A month\nlater, Apple sued Samsung in San Jose.  Until the turn of the 21st century, Samsung and other\nfamily-controlled Korean conglomerates, or chaebols, were widely\nviewed as congenital imitators: manufacturers of unimaginative\nelectronics, kitchen appliances and cars. Without much fanfare,\nSamsung grew into the world\u2019s largest tech company as measured\nby revenue and one of the biggest suppliers of memory chips,\nmicroprocessors and smartphone displays.  Today Samsung generates about one-fifth of all Korean\nexports and wields extraordinary influence in its home country.\nIn 2008, Chairman Lee Kun-hee, one of Korea\u2019s richest men, was\ncharged with tax evasion and breach of trust. Convicted of both\ncrimes, he managed to avoid prison, receive a presidential\npardon, and return to the company\u2019s helm.  Samsung\u2019s Galaxy  Unlike HTC, which embraced the Android operating system in\n2007, Samsung waited another couple of years to introduce its\nAndroid-equipped Galaxy line of phones.  According to an Apple legal filing, Samsung skipped the\ndifficult task of original research and development and simply\naped \u201cApple\u2019s innovative technology, distinctive user\ninterfaces, and elegant and distinctive product and packaging\ndesign.\u201d  Apple alleges that when Samsung announced its Galaxy i9000\nphone in March 2010, it had copied \u201cevery aspect of the\ndistinctive and minimalist Apple iPhone 3G trade dress: a\nrectangular product with four evenly rounded corners, a flat\nclear face covering the front of the product, (and) a large\ndisplay screen under the clear surface.\u201d  \u2018Steal Our Ideas\u2019  Steve Dowling, an Apple spokesman, said, \u201cThis kind of\nblatant copying is wrong, and we need to protect Apple\u2019s\nintellectual property when companies steal our ideas.\u201d  Samsung doesn\u2019t deny that, at some level, its smartphones\nlook and function like Apple\u2019s. The Korean company instead\nargues in legal papers that competing products -- be they\nmicrowave ovens or the latest, coolest phones -- often resemble\neach other. And, anyway, just how amazingly innovative are\nrounded corners on a rectangular communication device?  Apple, according to Samsung, is trying to use litigation to\nobtain something no competitor should have: \u201cperpetual\ndomination of the smartphone and mobile-computer market.\u201d  James Chung , a Samsung spokesman, said, \u201cSamsung will\ncontinue to defend our intellectual property to serve our\ncustomers and ensure our continued innovation and leadership in\nmobile communications.\u201d  Several Asian manufacturers were noodling around with\nsimilar-looking rectangular smartphones before the iPhone came\nto market. Tipping its hat to a fellow Korean manufacturer,\nSamsung said that in 2006, almost a year before the iPhone\nappeared, LG Electronics announced the round-cornered LG\nChocolate, with \u201cvirtually all of the (design) features Apple\nclaims\u201d to have patented.  \u2018Naturally Evolving\u2019  In December 2006, before Apple released images of the\niPhone, Samsung itself filed a design patent in Korea for a\nsimilar rectangular phone called the F700. Smartphone and\ntablet-computer design was \u201cnaturally evolving\u201d in the\ndirection Apple claims it has exclusive rights to use, according\nto Samsung.  If true, that matters because patent law states that if an\nidea is \u201cobvious\u201d to an \u201cordinary observer\u201d at the time of\nits invention, it doesn\u2019t deserve patent protection. By\nattacking Samsung, Apple has inadvertently put its own patents\ninto play.  \u201cPatent suits are a double-edged sword,\u201d said Harvard\u2019s\nShih.  J&J Verdict  If anyone has any doubt, they need only look at the largest\npatent-infringement verdict in history. In 2009,  Johnson &\nJohnson (JNJ) \u2019s Centocor unit won a $1.67 billion victory over  Abbott\nLaboratories. (ABT)  But J&J overreached.  Last year an appellate court threw out the verdict, ruling\nthat the J&J patent for human antibodies used in arthritis drugs\nhad been invalid all along.  The appeals court disparaged the J&J patent as, at most,\n\u201ca wish list of properties\u201d that the antibodies might possess\nand, in the process, provided critical legal protection for\nAbbott\u2019s competing remedy, Humira.  Shih himself bears some scars from IP fights during a long\ncorporate career as an executive at  International Business\nMachines Corp. (IBM) , Digital Equipment Corp.,  Silicon Graphics\nInternational Corp. (SGI)  and  Eastman Kodak Co. (EKDKQ)   Since joining the faculty at Harvard five years ago, Shih\nhas turned a cozy, book-lined campus office into an informal\nmuseum of digital gadgetry. His shelves and closets contain\nrudimentary computer motherboards, intricate telephone chip sets\n(genuine and Chinese fakes), anachronistic pocket cameras, and,\nincongruously, a scale model of an F-18 fighter jet.  \u2018Pyramid of Innovation\u2019  \u201cMost modern technology exists at the top of what I like\nto call a pyramid of innovation,\u201d Shih said. A smartphone has\nso many components building on earlier inventions that \u201cit\u2019s\nimplicating countless patents someone could sue over,\u201d he said.\n\u201cIt\u2019s genuinely difficult to look down the pyramid from the top\nand see comprehensively all of the building blocks.\u201d  \u201cIt\u2019s a recipe for litigation,\u201d he said.  Since the early 1600s, Anglo-American law has granted\ntinkerers and visionaries temporary monopolies on inventions.\nSomeone willing to disclose an innovation via the modern U.S.\npatent system generally may exclude others from exploiting it\nfor 20 years.  Public disclosure, in theory, alerts others who might want\nto take advantage of a patented advance, for which they could\noffer a licensing fee. And this theory has often held up in\npractice -- especially in computer technology -- but not always.  License Negotiations  For one thing, license negotiations sometimes break down.\nApple said in its legal papers that it approached Samsung in\n2010 to seek licensing fees, but the discussions concluded\nwithout agreement. Samsung lawyers have confirmed in court there\nwere such negotiations, without going into detail.  Shih suggests that a mobile-device patent war may have been\ninevitable. Gargantuan rivals with deep pockets converged on the\nmarket from several directions: Apple and Microsoft out of the\ncomputer business, Google from the Internet search-and-\nadvertising business, Asian manufacturers from\ntelecommunications. Suing over patents became just another\nweapon, like marketing or pricing.  Another factor has contributed to a boom in tech\nlitigation. Beginning in the early 1990s, the U.S. Patent and\nTrademark Office instituted policies that encouraged patent\nproliferation. One required examiners to provide written\njustification for denying applications but not for granting\nthem. Annual patent grants have risen 150 percent since 1990 --\nfrom 99,077 to 247,713.  Ties Continue  Odd as it may seem to outsiders, Shih said, Apple and\nSamsung will probably continue their  supply-chain  relationship\neven as they slug it out in court. Although the companies\ngenerally decline to discuss their ties, just last year, in the\nmidst of all the high-volume litigation, Samsung began shipping\nA5 logic chips -- the brain of the latest iPhones and iPads --\nfrom a new factory in Austin, Texas. The A5 is twice as fast as\nits predecessor, the A4, which is also made by Samsung.  In addition, the Korean company sells Apple the highly\ntouted screens that provide supervivid images on the third-\ngeneration iPad. Apple turned to Samsung after  LG Display Co. (034220) \nand  Sharp Corp. (6753)  didn\u2019t meet its stringent quality requirements,\nan analyst with iSuppli said in March. \u201cThe display\nspecifications on the new iPad are very demanding in terms of\nthe very high resolution,\u201d the analyst, Vinita Jakhanwal, said.\nFor all the scorn Apple heaps on Samsung as an also-ran tech\ninnovator, it remains reliant on it.  \u2018Irreparable Harm\u2019  Four months after Judge Koh joked about sending the lawyer\nto a mediator with boxes of chocolate, she held another hearing,\nthis one on Apple\u2019s motion for a preliminary injunction to stop\nSamsung from selling three phones -- the Galaxy S 4G, Infuse 4G\nand Droid Charge -- and the Galaxy Tab 10.1 tablet in the U.S.\nApple claimed that without the judicial order it would suffer\n\u201cirreparable harm.\u201d  \u201cThere is a battle going on between the Android operating\nsystem and the iOS,\u201d explained McElhinny, Apple\u2019s lead attorney\nand a partner with the San Francisco-based law firm  Morrison &\nFoerster LLP (1124L) .  \u201cA large percentage of the American public has yet to\nchoose a smartphone,\u201d he said. \u201cOnce people make that choice,\nthey remain loyal to that operating system, and they are likely\nto make their future purchases in that environment.\u201d  Worldwide, Apple shipped a top-ranked 37 million\nsmartphones in the fourth quarter of 2011, a 128 percent\nincrease over 2010, according to research firm IDC. Samsung\nshipped 36 million smartphones, for an even more impressive 275\npercent gain.  \u2018Earthshakingly New\u2019  In the preliminary injunction hearing, Apple relied on four\nof its patents to argue that its phones are \u201cearthshakingly\nnew, completely novel.\u201d For good measure, McElhinny said the\niPad tablet had \u201ccreated an entirely new product category.\u201d  Two of the patents cover the iPhone\u2019s exterior design.\nPatents are referred to by their last three digits, and this\npair is known as the D\u2019087 and the D\u2019677. The claim covered by\nthe D\u2019087 is simply that of \u201cthe ornamental design of an\nelectronic device,\u201d as depicted in a series of 48 schematic\ndrawings.  A third patent, D\u2019889, covers the visual characteristics of\na tablet device, as described by similarly basic schematic\ndrawings.  A fourth patent, \u2018381, issued on Dec. 23, 2008, has no\n\u201cD\u201d prefix because it covers a function rather than a design -\n- specifically, a method \u201cfor list scrolling and document\ntranslation, scaling, and rotation on a touchscreen display.\u201d  Bounce Back  For shorthand, this function is known as \u201cbounce back.\u201d\nWhen a user places her finger on a device screen and drags an\nimage or document past the screen\u2019s edge, and then releases her\nfinger, the image or document bounces back to fill the full\nscreen. All three of the Samsung phones, as well as the Galaxy\nTab 10.1, have bounce back.  Kathleen M. Sullivan, a Quinn Emanuel partner speaking on\nbehalf of Samsung, pointed out to Koh that all kinds of devices\npredating Apple\u2019s products -- phones and tablets -- look, and in\nsome regards, work like the iPhone and iPad. Apple is seeking an\nunjust monopoly on rectangular smartphones and tablets with a\nflat surface and rounded corners, Sullivan said.  The judge interrupted at one point and held up the\ncompeting Samsung and Apple tablets. Could Sullivan tell them\napart?  \u201cNot at this distance, your honor,\u201d the lawyer admitted.\nJudge and attorney were about 10 paces apart.  Closer View  \u201cAll right, I\u2019ll bring it up closer,\u201d the judge said.\n\u201cWhich one is which?\u201d  Finally, Sullivan correctly identified the iPad.  \u201cIt took a long time to make that distinction,\u201d the judge\nsaid. Her point was that inattentive consumers might confuse the\nSamsung for an Apple. Consumer confusion is an important\ncriterion in determining whether patent infringement has\noccurred.  \u201cYour Honor,\u201d Sullivan protested, \u201cwith respect, I\u2019m\nstanding far away from you and you covered up the brand logo.\u201d  Sullivan said, \u201cThe D\u2019889 patent is for the whole device,\nand you didn\u2019t show us the back.\u201d  Koh, as it turned out, hadn\u2019t made up her mind. Samsung,\nshe suggested, may have imitated Apple, but Apple may have\nimitated a much earlier and commercially unsuccessful device\nintroduced in 1994 by the newspaper publisher Knight-Ridder.  \u201cWell, then, we\u2019ll accept that, your honor,\u201d Sullivan\nresponded.  Clear Ruling  On Dec. 2, Koh issued a 65-page ruling that for its\nclarity, if nothing else, could be the core text for a law\nschool patent course.  \u201cJudge Koh was an IP litigator before she joined the\nbench, so she is very knowledgeable about these issues,\u201d said\n Mark Lemley , a professor at Stanford Law School and director of\nits program in law, science and technology.  The judge\u2019s findings were tentative. All she ruled on was\nApple\u2019s request for a preliminary injunction blocking the sale\nin the U.S. of Samsung devices pending a final determination at\na trial scheduled to begin in July. Koh\u2019s opinion avoided both\nApple\u2019s heroic self-regard and Samsung\u2019s irreverence toward\nApple\u2019s singular aura as a brand.  As a first step, the judge reaffirmed that while a product\ndesign is patentable, aspects \u201cdictated by functionality\u201d\naren\u2019t.  Obvious Design  Apple\u2019s patents  don\u2019t give it ownership of the idea of\nmaking smartphones small enough to hold conveniently. If they\ncould, no one else would ever be able to sell a usable\nsmartphone. Similarly, Apple can\u2019t preclude rivals from having a\nscreen large enough for the user to control with the touch of a\nfinger, or a speaker in the upper portion of the device\u2019s front\nface so it can be placed next to the ear.  Turning to the concept of \u201cobviousness,\u201d Koh showed\nsympathy for Samsung\u2019s argument that Apple\u2019s claims of\n\u201cearthshaking\u201d innovation may be exaggerated. She analyzed a\nJapanese patent issued to the Japanese company Sharp on June 6,\n2005, well before Apple obtained its relevant patents.  Foreign patents can be cited as \u201cprior art\u201d to undercut\nU.S. patents. Illustrating her opinion with sketches from U.S.\nPatent Office records, Koh said the Sharp patent, like Apple\u2019s\nD\u2019087, has \u201crounded corners, a bezel, a similarly shaped\nspeaker, and similar proportions of screen and border.\u201d The\nSharp patent \u201cdiscloses an overall simple, minimalistic\ndesign.\u201d  She added, \u201cAn ordinary observer would likely consider\n(Apple\u2019s) D\u2019087 to be substantially the same\u201d as  Sharp (6753) \u2019s\npatent.  Summer Trial  Without reaching a firm conclusion -- that will come at\ntrial this summer -- the judge ruled that \u201cSamsung has met its\nburden and raised substantial questions regarding the validity\nof the D\u2019087 patent.\u201d  By picking this fight, Apple jeopardized a potentially\ncrucial piece of intellectual property. In practical terms, that\nmeans the company\u2019s belligerence may have diminished its\nleverage in future litigation or cross-licensing negotiations.  Patent law analysis follows convolutions that can leave the\nlayman with a headache.  Assuming that the other Apple design patent would be found\nvalid at trial, Koh said it was likely that Samsung\u2019s S 4G and\nInfuse 4 phones infringed it. But she chose not to halt the\nsales of those phones, in part because she saw the issue of\ninfringement as a \u201cclose question\u201d requiring more evidence.  Apple Loss  Samsung, she continued, \u201cfaces the distinct possibility of\nwrongly having to withdraw two of its cell phones from the\nmarket.\u201d For the moment, she denied Apple\u2019s bid to bar the two\nSamsung phones from being sold in the U.S.  Apple got even more discouraging results on its iPad\ndesign. Again peppering her ruling with handy graphic\nillustrations, Koh showed how the crude-looking 1994\nFidler\/Knight Ridder tablet, designed for reading newspapers\ndigitally, created \u201cthe same basic visual impression\u201d as\nApple\u2019s D\u2019889 patent for the iPad.  \u201cThe court,\u201d she wrote, \u201ctherefore finds that Samsung\nhas raised a substantial question regarding the validity of the\nD\u2019889 patent on obviousness grounds.\u201d That could mean the\niPad\u2019s design is up for grabs. In any event, Koh declined to\nenjoin Samsung\u2019s Galaxy Tab 10.1.  Undeterred, Apple hired an additional law firm, Los\nAngeles-based  Gibson, Dunn & Crutcher LLP (1128L) , and dispatched it\nalong with Morrison & Foerster to file the new suit in February,\nalleging that Samsung\u2019s latest products infringe additional\nApple patents.  Claims, Counterclaims  The inevitable counterclaims and replies to counterclaims\nensued; Koh\u2019s docket for smartphones and tablets continues to\nexpand, as do corresponding dockets in courts in other cities\nand countries.  People familiar with the situation note that top-level\nexecutives at both Apple and Samsung have communicated lately\nabout potential settlement options. Apple CEO Tim Cook doesn\u2019t\nseem to share his predecessor\u2019s passion about laying all foes to\nwaste. Cook appears to view litigation as a necessary evil, not\na vehicle of cosmic revenge.  Still, the larger contest between Apple and Google is\nnowhere near resolution. And it isn\u2019t just about smartphones and\ntablets. While they struggle for dominance in mobile devices,\nApple and Google are protecting their flanks from Microsoft and\ngirding for a coming clash over the market for digital hubs that\nintegrate the Internet with television.  In the short run, the tech giants could save themselves\nconsiderable legal fees and distraction if they were to lock\ntheir lawyers in a hallway of conference rooms and refuse to\nrelease them until they had crafted a series of comprehensive\ncross-licensing pacts. This process eventually resolved similar\nlitigation in the desktop computer field.  Such a solution \u201cis still probably what will happen\nhere,\u201d said Stanford\u2019s Lemley. \u201cBut in the meantime, these\ncompanies have paid their lawyers more than $400 million\u201d over\nthe last several years. \u201cIt\u2019s not clear what they\u2019re getting\nfor that money.\u201d  The case is Apple Inc. v.  Samsung Electronics Co. (005930) , 11-\n01846, U.S. District Court, Northern District of California (San\nJose).  To contact the reporter on this story:\nPaul M. Analysts projected a 3.6\npercent gain.  \u201cThe street believes the market has limited downside but\nis still waiting for Prime Minister Shinzo Abe and his\nstructural reforms before it gets too bullish again,\u201d said\nStuart Beavis, head of institutional equity derivatives at\nVantage Capital Markets in  Hong Kong . The median forecast of economists\nsurveyed by Bloomberg was for a 2.2 percent gain. Separately,\njobless claims dropped more than forecast. Trademark  Pernod Ricard Loses Ruling in Bacardi \u2018Havana Club\u2019 Fight  Pernod Ricard SA, the world\u2019s second-biggest liquor maker,\nlost an appeals court ruling in its 17-year battle with Bacardi\nLtd. over the right to use the name \u201cHavana Club\u201d on rum in\nthe U.S. market.  The  U.S. Court of Appeals  in Philadelphia ruled yesterday\nthat a lower-court correctly ruled that consumers wouldn\u2019t be\nconfused into thinking Bacardi\u2019s Havana Club rum was made in\nCuba because the label states it was made in  Puerto Rico .  \u201cNo reasonable interpretation of the label as a whole\ncould lead to the conclusion that it is false or misleading,\u201d\nU.S. Circuit Judge Kent Jordan said in an opinion that affirms\nthe 2010 ruling by the U.S. District Court in Wilmington,\n Delaware .  \u201cWe\u2019re certainly disappointed with the decision,\u201d David\nBernstein, a lawyer representing Pernod Ricard, said in a\ntelephone interview. \u201cIf there\u2019s any basis for an appeal, we\u2019ll\nconsider it.\u201d  Pernod has been fighting with  Bacardi  over rights to the\nname in the U.S. since 1994, when Bacardi applied for a U.S.\ntrademark for Havana Club. That application was suspended by the\nU.S. Patent and Trademark Office pending the results of\nlitigation, Bernstein said. Pernod, based in Paris, sells  Havana\nClub  throughout the world, except in the U.S.  \u201cOur conclusion in this case says nothing of whether the\nwords \u2018Havana Club\u2019 are eligible for registration as a\ntrademark,\u201d Jordan said in the opinion yesterday.  Pernod argued in its appeal that U.S. District Judge Sue\nRobinson \u201crefused even to consider\u201d the results of a Pernod-\ncommissioned survey showing that about 20 percent of U.S. rum\nconsumers were misled or confused by Bacardi\u2019s Havana Rum\nbottle.  In yesterday\u2019s opinion, the appeals court said, \u201cSurvey\nevidence has no helpful part to play on the question of what the\nlabel communicates regarding geographic origin.\u201d  Bacardi, based in Pembroke, Bermuda, argued that the survey\nwas \u201cfatally flawed\u201d and that the front of its liquor bottle\nclearly states \u201cPuerto Rican rum.\u201d  \u201cBacardi applauds the appellate court\u2019s decision which\nreaffirms that Bacardi has accurately portrayed both the\ngeographic origin and Cuban heritage of our Havana Club rum,\u201d\nPatricia Neal, a spokeswoman for Bacardi USA, said in an e-\nmailed statement.  Cuban trademarks have importance in anticipation of an end\nto the 1963 embargo by the U.S. that blocks most trade between\nthe countries. Cuban-made rum can\u2019t be legally sold in the U.S.  The Havana Club trademark was first used in the 1930s by\nCuba\u2019s Arechabala family, whose distilling company was\nconfiscated by Fidel Castro\u2019s revolutionary government. After\nthe trademark owned by the Arechabalas lapsed, the state-owned\nCubaexport registered it in the U.S. in 1976 and assigned it to\nthe Pernod joint venture in 1993.  In 1998, Congress passed legislation making trademarks\nconfiscated by the Cuban government unenforceable in the U.S.\nThe law has been applied only to the Havana Club mark.  The U.S. Court of Appeals for the D.C. Circuit in\n Washington  upheld that law in March. It said the U.S. Treasury\nhas the right to refuse to allow a Cuban state-owned group to\nrenew its U.S. trademark for Havana Club. Pernod sells Havana\nClub throughout the world, except in the U.S., under that 1993\nventure with Cubaexport.  Bacardi bought rights to the Havana Club name from the\nArechabala family and distills rum in that name in Puerto Rico\nusing the recipe of Jose Arechabala, court papers state. It has\nbeen available in the U.S. since 2006 only in  Florida .  Pernod turned Cuba-made Havana Club into the world\u2019s\nfourth-most-popular brand of standard rum, selling about 3.5\nmillion cases a year, up from 400,000 cases sold in 1993,\naccording to the research report.  Without access to the U.S. market, Pernod\u2019s Havana Club had\n5 percent of the world\u2019s rum sales, according to the report. In\nthe U.S., Bacardi\u2019s brands led the rum market with about 40\npercent of sales, according to court papers.  In  Spain , Bacardi sued Pernod in 1999, claiming it was the\nrightful owner of the Havana Club trademark.  Two Spanish courts ruled that the joint venture with Pernod\nwas the proper owner because the Arechabala family had neglected\nits rights, both in allowing its trademark to expire and waiting\ntoo long to challenge ownership. Spain\u2019s  Supreme Court  ruled in\nPernod\u2019s favor in February, saying Bacardi had no claim to the\nHavana Club name in that country.  London-based Diageo Plc is the world\u2019s largest distiller.  The appeal is Pernod Ricard USA LLC v. Bacardi USA Inc.,\n10-2354, 3rd U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals (Philadelphia). The\nDelaware case is Pernod Ricard USA LLC v. Bacardi USA Inc., 06-\ncv-505, U.S. District Court, District of Delaware (Wilmington). The board noted that when the Mississippi school replaced\nan elongated eagle head logo with one with a more rounded shape,\nthe number of vendors selling marked products increased\n\u201cdramatically\u201d and items marked with the new logo became best\nsellers. Copyright  U.K.\u2019s Ofcom Looking at Reducing Cost of Infringement Appeals  The cost of processing appeals under the U.K.\u2019s Digital\nEconomic act could be about 400 British pounds each, according\nto a  report  released by the government regulatory authority for\nbroadcast and telecommunications, known as Ofcom.  This could lead to an annual processing cost of 40 million\npounds ($65 million), according to the report.  The high cost of pursuing these appeals could potentially\nprovide a barrier to some copyright owners\u2019 participation in the\nenforcement process, the report suggested. A \u201cvexatious system\nof coordinated appeals\u201d could bring this whole system down, if\na lobby group were to be successful in attempts to persuade\nconsumers to appeal every single infringement notification made\nunder the act, according to the Ofcom report.  Ofcom said in the report it\u2019s considering seeking bids from\nvarious entities that already operate adjudication and\narbitration systems as a way of getting what it called\n\u201cinnovative and cost-focused bids.\u201d Another cost-cutting\npossibility might be the removal of the right of appeal\naltogether, Ofcom said, noting that this could be \u201cfrustrating\nfor subscribers.\u201d  For more copyright news, click here. Other documents he was accused of taking weren\u2019t\nconfidential or he sent home for his own use, he said.  Both sides agreed to dismissal of the suit, according to\ncourt papers filed July 7. (7974) , maker of the Wii video-gaming system, won a U.S. appeals court ruling that makes it\nharder for patent-licensing companies to seek an import ban on\nproducts as a way to demand royalties.  Motiva LLC, which claimed Nintendo infringed its patents\nfor a system to track a game user\u2019s position, didn\u2019t meet the\nrequirements to file a trade complaint, the Court of Appeals for\nthe Federal Circuit said May 13 in a decision posted on its\nwebsite. The ruling backs the U.S. International Trade\nCommission\u2019s decision against the Dublin, Ohio-based company.  The ITC\u2019s goal is to protect U.S. markets from unfair trade\npractices, and it requires patent owners to prove they have\nsomething worth protecting. The agency said Motiva\u2019s three-year-old lawsuit against Kyoto, Japan-based Nintendo in a district\ncourt didn\u2019t pass that test, and the appeals court agreed.  The ITC had found Nintendo didn\u2019t infringe the patents. The\nFederal Circuit, rather than ruling on that issue, made its\ndecision on the question of whether a case should have been\nallowed at the commission.  The ITC has the power to block products that infringe U.S.\npatents. Companies such as  Google Inc. (GOOG)  and Apple Inc. have said\nthat potential threat is being used too often by patent-licensing firms to force legal settlements.  The ITC has only issued four import bans to companies that\ndon\u2019t make products, and in each of the cases, the patent owner\ndeveloped the technology, according to an April report from the\ncommission.  Motiva was founded in 2003 by two men who sought to\nintegrate fitness and video games through motion detection,\naccording to the complaint. They were unsuccessful in\ncommercializing any product.  In November 2006, Nintendo began selling the Wii, which\nfeatures a motion-sensor controller that allows users to\nreplicate movements like swinging a tennis racquet on screen.  Motiva sued Nintendo in 2008 in federal court in Tyler,\nTexas, a district with a history of decisions favoring patent\nowners. Nintendo succeeded in having the case transferred to a\nfederal court in Seattle, and then having it put on hold while\nthe U.S. Patent and  Trademark Office  reviews the validity of the\npatents.  The ITC complaint was filed in September 2010, which both\nthe agency and the Federal Circuit said was too late if Motiva\nwanted to show it was interested in preserving its ability to\ncommercialize the inventions.  The case is Motiva LLC v. ITC, 12-1252,  U.S. Court of\nAppeals  for the Federal Circuit (Washington). The ITC case is In\nthe Matter of Video Game Systems and Controllers, 337-743, U.S.\nInternational Trade Commission (Washington). Should Apple win permission to add the Galaxy S4 smartphone\nthat Samsung released last month, it will drop one of the other\ndevices from the list, according to the filing.  Samsung, too, submitted a 22-product list to Koh,\nidentifying as alleged infringers five models of Apple\u2019s iPhone,\nfive versions of the iPad tablet computer, three types of iPod\ndigital-music players and the MacBook Pro and MacBook Air\ncomputers. The earlier case is Apple Inc. v.  Samsung Electronics Co. (005930) \nLtd., 11-cv-01846, and the second case is Apple Inc. v. Samsung\nElectronics Co., 12-cv-00630, U.S. District Court, Northern\nDistrict of California (San Jose). Metso\u2019s invention relates to\nconveyors that can be folded into the side so the machine can\ntravel on roadways.  Terex, the Westport, Connecticut-based maker of cranes and\nlifts, argued that the invention was little different from the\nolder Masterskreen Dominator developed by the same inventor. The\nFederal Circuit agreed. It was \u201cordinary skill and common sense\nrather than innovation\u201d that led to the patented invention, the\nthree-judge panel said.  Metso, based in Helsinki, makes paper machines in addition\nto rock crushers.  The case is Metso Minerals Inc. v. Powerscreen\nInternational, 11-cv-01572, U.S. Court of Appeals for the\nFederal Circuit (Washington). The lower court case is Metso\nMinerals Inc. v. Trademark  Forever 21\u2019s Trademark Case Against Discounters Set for May 28  Forever 21 Inc.\u2019s trademark lawsuit against discount\nclothing stores is set to go to trial in federal court in  Los\nAngeles  on May 28.  The Los Angeles-based clothing company sued the off-price\nstores, claiming they were selling Forever 21 merchandise\nwithout authorization, even if they cut out the Forever 21\nlabels or substituted new labels.  Investigators for Forever 21 shopped at the off-price\nstores and purchased items that contained some of the chain\u2019s\ntrademarks, the company said. In a complaint filed in February\n2012, Forever 21 said the sales violated its exclusive rights to\nsell goods under its marks, and that consumers would be confused\nby the similarity.  Defendants have responded in court filings, saying that\nwhen they buy clothing bearing brands, the practice is to remove\nall identifying marks before the items are placed on the selling\nfloor. They also said that Forever 21 waited too long to place\nits claim and had misused its trademarks.  The case could have \u201cresounding effects\u201d on the off-price\nclothing market,  according to  California Apparel News.  The case is Forever 21 Inc. v. The bill unveiled today by Senator Patrick Leahy, a Vermont\nDemocrat, would set a national standard for notifying consumers\nthat replaces data-breach reporting requirements in 47 states.\nLeahy, who chairs the Senate Judiciary Committee, cited recent\ncyber attacks at companies including  Sony Corp. (6758)  and  Lockheed\nMartin Corp. (LMT)  as he introduced the measure.  \u201cThe many recent and troubling data breaches in the\nprivate sector and in our government are clear evidence that\ndeveloping a comprehensive national strategy to protect data\nprivacy and security is one of the most challenging and\nimportant issues facing our country,\u201d Leahy said in a\n statement .  Under the measure, anyone who \u201cintentionally or\nwillfully\u201d conceals a data breach would be subject to criminal\npenalties including a fine or up to five years in prison,\naccording to a fact sheet released with the bill.  The bill, known as the Personal Data Privacy and Security\nAct of 2011, is co-sponsored by three other Democratic senators:\n Charles Schumer  of  New York , Ben Cardin of  Maryland , and Al Franken of  Minnesota . Leahy introduced similar cybersecurity\nmeasures in 2005, 2007 and 2009 that failed to advance in the\nSenate.  \u2018Compliance Burdens\u2019  The measure parallels the cybersecurity proposal issued by\nthe Obama administration on May 12. Like the administration\u2019s\nplan, the Senate bill introduced today calls for creating a\nuniform federal law for informing consumers about data breaches,\na provision welcomed by the technology industry.  The proliferation of state laws has caused \u201cconfusion for\nconsumers and unnecessary compliance burdens for companies,\u201d\nRobert Holleyman, president of the  Business Software Alliance ,\nsaid a statement. The group represents software makers including\n Apple Inc. (AAPL)  and  Microsoft Corp. (MSFT)  Holleyman urged Congress to pass\n\u201ca single, national standard to replace the unwieldy state\npatchwork we have today.\u201d  The security breaches at Sony and Lockheed Martin have\nsharpened U.S. government scrutiny of how businesses safeguard\nconsumer data and notify the public about cyber attacks. Sony\nhas been criticized by U.S. lawmakers for taking six days to\nwarn customers about the breach.  The Leahy measure does not give a specific timeframe for\nmaking such reports and says that companies should disclose data\nbreaches \u201cwithout unreasonable delay.\u201d Businesses would be\nexempt from public disclosure if they determine that no consumer\ndata were compromised and share that information with the U.S.\nSecret Service.  Government Contractors  The legislation also requires businesses to create a\nprivacy and security program to protect \u201csensitive\u201d data.\nFederal agencies would be required to evaluate the data security\npractices of government contractors and assess privacy\nprovisions of third-party data services under the bill.  Lockheed Martin, the world\u2019s largest defense contractor,\nwas hit by a cyber attack on May 21 that the company later said\nresulted from a March data theft at RSA, a provider of security\ntokens. RSA\u2019s parent company, EMC Corp., offered today to swap\nthe SecurID tokens that RSA provides to defense contractors and\ngovernment agencies.  The Leahy bill addresses \u201cthe growing need to establish\nprivacy protections when government agencies transfer personal\ndata to private contractors,\u201d  Marc Rotenberg , executive\ndirector of the Electronic Privacy Information Center, said in\nan e-mailed statement.  Data Brokers  The bill would allow consumers to obtain reports from data\nbrokers such as  Acxiom Corp. (ACXM)  and  Reed Elsevier Plc (REL) \u2019s Lexis Nexis\nunit about the personal information that has been collected on\nthem. Consumers would be allowed to dispute and correct any\ninaccuracies in the digital records. Data brokers that fail to\nfollow the rules would be subject to fines of up to $250,000 per\nviolation.  House lawmakers including Representative Mary Bono Mack, a\nCalifornia Republican who chairs a subcommittee on commerce,\nmanufacturing and trade, also are working on legislation aimed\nat protecting consumer data. Bono Mack also has called for a\nnationwide data-breach reporting standard.  \u201cConsumers have a right to know when their personal\ninformation has been compromised, and companies have an\noverriding responsibility to promptly alert them,\u201d Bono Mack\nsaid at a June 2 hearing on data security. (MSFT)  and  Sony Corp. (6758)  this week as the console makers battle to show they\u2019ve got the best plan for selling pricey machines in the age of cheap play on phones and tablets.  Both present today at E3, the video-game industry\u2019s annual conference running through June 13 in  Los Angeles , with the $67 billion game market in the grip of two-year slump. Consumers have cut purchases of consoles and costly packaged games for inexpensive Web-delivered titles like Rovio Entertainment Oy\u2019s \u201cAngry Birds,\u201d defined as more casual, mobile and social.  Microsoft\u2019s Xbox One and Sony\u2019s PlayStation 4, set to be in stores for the U.S. holidays, tackle the shift differently. Sony is trying to coax casual and hard-core gamers to line up early for blockbuster titles and smaller exclusives that can develop into hits. Microsoft positioned Xbox One as the center of living-room entertainment, with programming from director  Steven Spielberg , ESPN and Hollywood studios -- leaving gamers to question whether it\u2019s their best console choice.  \u201cThey\u2019re having to resell to their consumer base again,\u201d said  David Cole , an analyst at industry research firm DFC Intelligence. \u201cIt\u2019s going to be very much a challenge for both of those companies to capture a casual consumer who is on the fence about replacing their console and buying a new system.\u201d  With  Nintendo Co. (7974) \u2019s Wii U player, introduced last November, selling below company expectations, Sony and Microsoft\u2019s plans for console prices, game resales and recharging sales have broad implications for the industry.  Faster Change  In the year since 50,000 gamers last gathered at E3, change has accelerated.  THQ Inc. (THQIQ) , the maker of \u201cSaints Row\u201d and other titles, filed for bankruptcy and sold most of its assets, while  Activision Blizzard Inc. (ATVI) , the largest U.S. game company, lost more than 1.3 million subscribers from its storied \u201cWorld of Warcraft\u201d multiplayer online game during the first quarter.  Even the maker of casual games for  Facebook Inc. (FB) ,  Zynga Inc. (ZNGA) , which once looked to be the biggest threat to traditional developers, missed a shift to mobile play and has been forced to fire several hundred employees.  U.S. retail spending on games, including used games and rentals, fell 9 percent to $1.37 billion in the first quarter from a year earlier, according to industry researcher NPD Group. Digitally delivered content rose 8 percent to $1.59 billion.  Sony Chief Executive Officer  Kazuo Hirai , under pressure from billionaire investor  Daniel Loeb  to restructure the Tokyo-based company, said in late May the PlayStation 4 \u201cis first and foremost\u201d a game console that must establish itself with all players before assuming a broader livingroom role.  Design Specs  At E3, the company probably will unveil the machine\u2019s actual design specs and elaborate on its online strategy for games and other entertainment, said  Michael Pachter , an analyst at Wedbush Securities in Los Angeles.  Both Xbox One and PlayStation 4 use personal-computer architecture from  Advanced Micro Devices Inc. (AMD) , meaning developers won\u2019t have to tweak games for a particular system, and the titles will look similar on both machines.  As a result, the competition for developers and gamers centers around services, exclusive titles and incentives for game-makers.  The PlayStation 4 will support free-to-play and episodic titles. Sony\u2019s acquisition of cloud-gaming service Gaikai will allow users browsing the PlayStation Store to try a portion of a game before purchasing and eventually will make previous libraries, including older PlayStation 3 games, available on the new console, said Dan Race, a spokesman.  Indie Swag  Sony also is stepping up use of its Sony Pub Fund, created in 2009, to offer financial and marketing support to independent developers who might otherwise create games for  Apple Inc. (AAPL)  devices or Samsung Galaxy phones. Its companion Incubation Program delivers  office space , equipment and technical support, Race said.  \u201cSony has come out and given very clear signs to independent developers that they support us and that we\u2019re going to have an easier time developing on that platform,\u201d said Brian Choi, 20, a junior at USC\u2019s Interactive Media and Games school.  Smaller games offer less potential return than blockbuster titles, according to Pachter. He said they can become an incentive for a consumer to stick with a console after buying it for other reasons.  \u201cI don\u2019t think indie development is worth investing a lot of money from Microsoft\u2019s perspective, but Sony obviously thinks so,\u201d Pachter said.  Xbox Exclusives  Sony has also begun promoting its $49.99-a-year PlayStation Plus subscription, a premium tier of its PlayStation Network with additional services such as game demos, automatic software updates and free content.  PlayStation Plus, introduced in 2010, has lagged behind Microsoft\u2019s popular  Xbox Live . Race didn\u2019t say whether the company will add products from Gaikai to the paid service.  Microsoft, in unveiling the Xbox One on May 21, said its new console will be the centerpiece of living-room entertainment. Hard-core gamers and independent developers initially cried foul as the Redmond, Washington-based company appeared to shift its focus to delivering exclusive content from Hollywood, sports and other forms of entertainment.  The company said its studios are spending more than ever on new content, working on 15 exclusive game titles, including eight entirely new properties, that will be introduced during the Xbox One\u2019s first year of sales.  \u2018Close Sale\u2019  The company plans to showcase some of the games this week, Letty Cherry, a spokeswoman, said in an e-mail.  \u201cMicrosoft needs to close its sale to the core gamer,\u201d said Doug Creutz, a San Francisco-based analyst at Cowen & Co.  Ahead of E3, Microsoft clarified its position on the thorny issue of the Xbox One\u2019s used-games policy. Developers have said they\u2019re losing millions of dollars through trade-ins at specialty retailers such as GameStop Corp. Gamers like being able to resell titles they\u2019ve used, or buy a used game they wouldn\u2019t pay $60 for new.  Microsoft said it won\u2019t stop gamers from trading in used games for Xbox One, while leaving it up to  Electronic Arts Inc. (EA) , Activision Blizzard and other outside publishers to set their own policies. The company did set limits on the ability to swap games among friends.  For its own titles such as \u201cHalo,\u201d Microsoft said it won\u2019t charge a fee for resales.  Cable Deals  Microsoft aims to sell more Xbox One players than the current installed base of Xbox 360s, estimated at 76 million worldwide by the company. It could get a boost if pay-TV providers such as  British Sky Broadcasting Group Plc (BSY)  and  Comcast Corp. (CMCSA)  subsidize the potential $400 price, letting users purchase the new player for $200 and pay the rest in higher monthly bills, Creutz said.  \u201cIt becomes a lot less of a stretch,\u201d Creutz said in an interview. \u201cMicrosoft\u2019s focus on the living-room experience has the potential to broaden the appeal to a very mass market.\u201d  Microsoft has a number of pricing options. One deal offered with the  Xbox 360  let a buyer pay less upfront for the device in exchange for a two-year, premium-priced commitment to Xbox Live, said  David Dennis , a Microsoft spokesman. He declined to discuss specifics for Xbox One.  Even with new strategies, Nintendo, Sony and Microsoft probably will sell 10 percent to 20 percent fewer consoles than the previous generation, with Nintendo\u2019s Wii U losing market share against the Xbox One and PlayStation 4, Pachter said.  \u201cWe\u2019ve been waiting impatiently for new machines, and we\u2019re really pleased to see them coming to market,\u201d said Tony Key, senior vice president of sales and marketing for Ubisoft SA, maker of titles such as \u201cAssassin\u2019s Creed.\u201d \u201cThe industry needs a wake-up, and hopefully this time next week everyone is better informed about what lies ahead for this next generation of hardware.\u201d  To contact the reporter on this story: Cliff Edwards in  San Francisco  at  cedwards28@bloomberg.net   To contact the editor responsible for this story: Anthony Palazzo at  apalazzo@bloomberg.net","path":".\/2008_2012_msft_bloomberg_news\/sony-microsoft-battle-goes-to-e3-as-tablets-dent-consoles.txt"},{"id":88297721,"title":"Boeing, Callaway, Microsoft, News Corp., Smart Balance: U.S. Equity Movers","released_at":"<date>June 15 2010<\/date> <time>20:31:07<\/time>","content":"Shares of the following companies\nhad unusual moves in U.S. trading.
