The grape grower sued the Agriculture Department and its\nlicensee, the  California Table Grape Commission , in federal\ncourt in Fresno,  California , in November 2007.  Delano, joined by two other growers, claimed the patents,\nwhich covered three varieties of table grapes, weren\u2019t valid\nbecause they had been known, used and sold before the patent\napplications were filed. They also claimed that federal\nantitrust law was violated.  In dispute are patents PP15,891, for the Sweet Scarlet\ngrape variety; PP16,229, for Scarlet Royal grapes; and PP16,284,\ncovering the Autumn King variety.  The Agriculture Department had licensed the patents to the\ngrape commission, a marketing agency whose mission is to promote\nthe state\u2019s table-grape industry. The commission is funded by a\ntax levied on each box of table grapes produced in California.  The three plaintiffs claimed the commission contacted\nCalifornia table-grape growers in 2004, telling the growers they\ncould keep their vines and avoid a lawsuit if they admitted they\npossessed them, paid the commission $2 per vine they reproduced\nand $2 a box of grapes they previously shipped and promised not\nto propagate any more of those varieties.  This letter was sent before the patent applications were\nfiled, and the letter wasn\u2019t disclosed in the patent\napplication, according to court papers.  In response to the suit, the Agriculture Department said it\ncouldn\u2019t be sued under a legal doctrine that bars such actions\nagainst the federal government. The trial court agreed, held\nthat unless the Agriculture Department was a party to the suit,\nthe patent claims couldn\u2019t proceed, and dismissed the case.  The growers then appealed, arguing that the federal agency\nwasn\u2019t a necessary party to the patent claims. They also claimed\nthat their patent case against the government wasn\u2019t barred\nunder the so-called sovereign immunity doctrine.  The appeals court said that because license between the\ngovernment and the commission didn\u2019t give the commission any\nright to enforce the patent against infringement, the government\nhad to be a party to the suit.  It found that federal law waiving sovereign immunity for\nnon-monetary claims against federal agencies is broad enough to\npermit the growers to pursue patent-invalidation actions against\nthe Agriculture Department.  The appeals court did uphold the trial court ruling barring\nthe antitrust allegations. It said the growers failed to provide\na plausible basis for finding the patent grape varieties formed\na relevant antitrust market.  The growers\u2019 case was argued by  Lawrence M. Hadley  of\n Hennigan Dorman LLP  of  Los Angeles . The California Table Grape\nCommission\u2019s argument was made by Randolph D. Moss of\nWashington\u2019s Wilmer Cutler Pickering Hale & Dorr LLP. California\nTable Grape Commission, 1:07-cv-01610-OWW-SMS, U.S. District\nCourt, Eastern District of California (Fresno). The appeal is\nDelano Farms Co. v. The PC era is ending. More evidence\nof the monumental shift away from personal computers will come\nwhen  Dell Inc. (DELL)  reports results later today, and  Hewlett-Packard\nCo. (HPQ)  announces its earnings next week.  As more consumers and businesses flock to smartphones and\ntablets, companies led by Hewlett-Packard, Dell and  Microsoft\nCorp. (MSFT)  that long benefited from demand for PCs are feeling the\npain. Dell will report a 10 percent  drop  in sales, while\nHewlett-Packard\u2019s revenue fell 6 percent in the most recent\nquarter, estimates compiled by Bloomberg show.  The declines mark a reversal from the 1980s, when Microsoft\nco-Founder Bill Gates and Dell Founder  Michael Dell  helped usher\nin the PC age with low-cost machines that transformed how\ncompanies work and made it easy for consumers to use computers.\nThe PC shunted aside bigger, pricier, more complex minicomputers\nand mainframes that once dominated the industry.  \u201cPC makers are succumbing to the fate of those who don\u2019t\nlearn from history, not even their own,\u201d said  Erik Gordon , a\nprofessor at the Stephen M. (IBM) \u2019s software-research lab in Beijing, I observed dozens of Chinese employees moving about seemingly free of any security-related limitations. I asked the lab\u2019s manager two questions:  \u201cDo you have any way of knowing whether any of your Chinese staff is also working for the Chinese government?  \u201cDo you have any way of knowing whether any of your Chinese staff is a spy?\u201d  The manager unhesitatingly answered \u201cNo\u201d to both. He hastily added, \u201cBut you can be sure that we at IBM work very hard to protect our core intellectual property.\u201d  This episode could occur at any of the many U.S. corporate facilities in  China . It highlights an underreported feature of recent cyberattacks: Much of China\u2019s hacking power was Made by the U.S.A.  For decades, U.S.-owned technology giants have set up state-of-the-art factories, laboratories and training programs in China. Their aim was to use a super-cheap, lightly regulated production base to supply Chinese and world markets, and to harness Chinese scientific talent. Greater profits were the top priority, but the companies also claimed that a more computer- and Internet-savvy China would become more peaceful and democratic.  Access Price  Chinese authorities demanded some technology as the price of access to their market. Yet most transfers were made voluntarily to Chinese partners. China\u2019s hacking prowess makes clear that, as critics warned, the government and military benefited from widespread sharing of know-how directly applicable to spying, sabotage and theft of business secrets.  Paradoxically, the first known victims of China\u2019s U.S.- enabled cybercapacities were Chinese citizens. These include dissidents who were tracked with technology sold by  Cisco Systems Inc. (CSCO)  and  Yahoo! Inc. (YHOO)  (YHOO), as well as ordinary people whose online content has been censored with products provided by  Microsoft Corp (MSFT)  (MSFT). and  Google Inc (GOOG)  (GOOG).  Those four companies, and many others, still supply official Chinese customers with capabilities easily used against U.S. government or business targets. (Google itself has repeatedly complained about attacks from China-based hackers.) These companies also continue to strengthen the technology base of a nation designated by the Defense Department as the greatest potential foreign threat to U.S. security.  Cisco, for example, says that its goals include maintaining \u201cclose relationships with government\u201d and notes that the regime\u2019s \u201cgood will\u201d is important for operations, \u201cenforcement,\u201d sales and policy. IBM touts its capacity to \u201cimprove the way government\u201d works, \u201csolve problems and challenges in public administration,\u201d and aid China\u2019s \u201cdrive to build a harmonious society.\u201d  Intel Corp. (INTC)  says its mission includes \u201cstrategic technology collaborations\u201d with the government. Microsoft considers itself \u201ca partner in developing the local IT ecosystem with the Chinese government.\u201d  Like IBM, companies such as Cisco,  Hewlett-Packard Co. (HPQ) , Intel, Google, Microsoft, Oracle Corp. and Yahoo have established large research centers in China. Thousands of engineers are working to develop capabilities that could easily be drafted for cyberwarfare.  Innovation Center  IBM also runs a China-based Global Rail Innovation Center that \u201cfocuses on every aspect of modern rail systems, such as track surveillance and infrastructure.\u201d Undoubtedly, that knowledge could help disrupt U.S. transportation networks. IBM also has sold a wide range of advanced hardware and software to Huawei Technologies Co., whose reported extensive ties with the Chinese government and military led the  House Intelligence Committee  to brand it a national security threat.  Finally, U.S.-owned companies have nurtured Chinese talent. As of 2010, Cisco was on track to build 300 of its acclaimed  Networking Academies  to train 100,000 Chinese students, and planned to use its curriculum to build 35 Model Software Colleges with the Education Ministry. IBM has created partnerships with more than 60 Chinese universities, and Intel is working with Chinese schools to develop their \u201cresearch program and talent pool.\u201d  Texas Instruments Inc (TXN) .\u2019s worldwide Leadership University includes two leading Chinese technical institutions.  Google\u2019s China University Relations program has forged ties with at least 15 Chinese institutions. Microsoft has established research partnerships with more than 30 Chinese universities focused partly on \u201ctalent development\u201d and programs that have trained, among others, more than 1,000 doctorate holders.  President  Barack Obama \u2019s new cyberdefense program can help safeguard U.S. security and commercial secrets. But its effects will be limited if American companies continue to shower China with hacking-related know-how. Significant new restrictions must replace today\u2019s failed security controls.  Companies will complain about lost business opportunities. The U.S. should solicit the cooperation of other trade partners in limiting China\u2019s technology access. But even simply curbing the availability of America\u2019s world-leading capabilities would enhance U.S. security. And the White House should tell allies that efforts to take advantage of the limits on U.S. exports will be treated as unfriendly acts.  Before China\u2019s cyberoffensive, U.S. companies could legitimately argue that they, and America, would be enriched by technological engagement. The new security threats, however, now trump any plausible economic benefits. Doing business with China can continue. Business as usual can\u2019t.  (Alan Tonelson is a research fellow at the U.S. Business and Industry Council, which represents almost 2,000 domestic manufacturing companies. He is the author of \u201cThe Race to the Bottom: Why a Worldwide Worker Surplus and Uncontrolled  Free Trade  Are Sinking American Living Standards.\u201d The opinions expressed are his own.) Compliance Policy  CFTC Proposes Clearing Determinations Under Dodd-Frank Act  The U.S. Commodity Futures Trading Commission proposed\nwhich  interest-rate  and credit-default swaps must be guaranteed\nby clearinghouses as soon as November to help reduce risk in the\n$648 trillion global market.  The proposal approved 5-0 by CFTC commissioners in a\nprivate vote, would require that four types of  interest-rate\nswaps  denominated in U.S. dollars, euros, British pounds and\nJapanese yen be settled at clearinghouses that stand between\nbuyers and sellers, according to an agency statement released\nyesterday. The measure would govern swaps conducted by companies\nincluding  JPMorgan Chase & Co. (JPM) ,  Goldman Sachs Group Inc. (GS)  and\nCargill Inc. Credit swaps in two indexes would face clearing\nrequirements under the proposal, the CFTC said.  \u201cOne of the primary benefits of swaps-market reform is\nthat standard swaps between financial firms will move into\ncentral clearing, which will significantly lower the risks of\nthe highly interconnected financial system,\u201d CFTC Chairman  Gary\nGensler  said in a statement.  The 2010 Dodd-Frank Act directed the CFTC and Securities\nand Exchange Commission to reduce risk in the market after\nlargely unregulated swaps helped fuel the 2008 credit crisis\nthat led to the collapse of Lehman Brothers Holdings Inc. and\nU.S. bailouts of companies including  American International\nGroup Inc. (AIG)  The agencies are striving to meet an end-of-year\ndeadline set by Group of 20 member nations to bolster oversight.  The CFTC has 90 days to complete proposed determinations,\nwhich may lead the first swaps to face mandatory clearing in\nlate October or early November. Clearinghouses operated by  CME\nGroup Inc. (CME) ,  IntercontinentalExchange Inc. (ICE)  and LCH.Clearnet Group\nLtd. guarantee swaps. The proposal will be open for 30 days of\npublic comment.  The measure would require clearing of credit swaps tied to\nNorth American and European indexes. Clearing wouldn\u2019t be\nrequired for tranches of credit indexes.  The CFTC may later decide to require clearing for energy,\nagricultural and equity indexes, the agency said.  In a separate 5-0 vote, CFTC commissioners approved a rule\ngoverning when banks and other firms must comply with clearing\nrequirements. The rule requires swap dealers to be first among\nfirms required under Dodd-Frank to clear swaps.  FDIC Issues Creditworthiness Rule for Savings Banks\u2019 Investments  The U.S. Federal Deposit Insurance Corp. approved a final\nrule yesterday to put new risk limits on corporate bonds in\nwhich federal and state savings associations can invest.  A savings bank isn\u2019t allowed to invest in a corporate bond\nwhen the issuer can\u2019t show it\u2019s able to meet financial\ncommitments for the security\u2019s projected life, according to the\nrule approved by FDIC directors in a written ballot. The new\nstandard replaces the use of credit ratings, which were banned\nfrom federal regulations by the 2010 Dodd-Frank Act.  \u201cThe FDIC does not expect the final rule to change the\nscope of permissible corporate debt securities investments,\u201d\nthe agency said in  guidance  issued about the rule, which goes\ninto effect Jan. 1. If a bond worked as an investment under the\nold system, \u201ca bond with similar default probabilities will be\npermissible under this rule.\u201d  On June 26, the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency\napproved a new standard for national banks that similarly\njettisoned the use of credit ratings. Also by Jan. 1, OCC-\nregulated national banks will need to use a combination of\ninternal analysis, third-party research and analytics that use\nexternal credit ratings in order to conclude a security is\ninvestment grade, the OCC said.  Overstated credit ratings contributed to the 2008 financial\ncrisis, leading U.S. lawmakers to require regulators stop using\nthem.  SEC Said Poised to Make Companies Report Business With Warlords  Companies would have to disclose whether they buy metals\nfrom central African warlords under a rule the U.S. Securities\nand Exchange Commission is poised to adopt next month, said a\nperson with knowledge of the agency\u2019s deliberations.  The so-called conflict minerals rule is opposed by the two\nRepublicans on the five-member commission, according to the\nperson, who spoke on condition of anonymity because the\ndiscussions leading up the Aug. 22 vote are private. The rule\nhas sparked two years of debate since the 2010 Dodd-Frank Act\nmandated that the SEC impose the rule, with some business groups\nrailing against the costs of tracking thousands of suppliers\nthrough every link of a chain that leads to their source mines.  Once the rule is in place, the agency estimates 6,000\npublicly traded companies -- mostly manufacturers and retailers\n-- must report to the SEC where they get their tin, tantalum,\ntungsten or gold. The rule is meant to halt the flow of mining\nmoney to those committing atrocities in the  Democratic Republic \nof Congo by pressuring manufacturers to protect their\nreputations -- not by issuing an outright ban on using the\nconflict metals.  The offices of Republican commissioners Troy Paredes and\nDaniel Gallagher, didn\u2019t respond to messages seeking comment on\nthe vote.  John Nester , an SEC spokesman, declined to comment.  The metals are in virtually any device with an on-switch.\nElectronics firms such as  Apple Inc. (AAPL)  use most or all of the\nmetals, and the rule would also affect jewelry makers such as\n Tiffany & Co. (TIF) , aerospace companies such as  Boeing Co. (BA)  and\nretailers including  Wal-Mart Stores Inc. (WMT)  and  American Apparel\nInc. (APP)  Since it was proposed by the SEC, the rule has drawn about\n40,000 public comment letters. The slavery index is being developed by a co-founder of Free the Slaves, Kevin Bales, Professor of Contemporary Slavery at the Wilberforce Institute at the University of Hull in the U.K., and Fiona David, a visiting fellow at the Centre for International and Public Law at the  Australian National University . Risk Measures  The index is based on data on slave numbers from governments, international organizations and surveys, supplemented with statistical analysis and estimation, Walk Free said in an e-mail. Big\ntakeovers. Nerdy 20-somethings getting rich quickly. To borrow a\nphrase from an old Prince song, the markets are suddenly\npartying like it\u2019s 1999 again.  The tech bubble is back. Facebook Inc. is commanding an\nenormous valuation. So are Groupon Inc., Twitter Inc. and\nLivingSocial.com. Even Rovio Mobile Oy, the small Finnish\ncompany behind the hit app Angry Birds, looks like it will soon\nbe worth a fortune.  The trouble is, everyone still remembers how the bubble\nburst last time around. Investors know there is a lot of money\nto be made from technology. They also know there is just as much\nto be lost when the bubble bursts.  To steer a way through that -- backing the winners, and\navoiding the obvious calamities -- there are some simple rules\nwe should draw from the last tech boom: Don\u2019t worry too much\nabout business models; look for emerging monopolies; back the\ngreediest entrepreneurs; and buy after the hype subsides.  That way, one should still be able to make money out of\nwhat remains the world\u2019s most lucrative growth industry.  There is little question that some verve and excitement\nhave returned to the technology markets. It might not be quite\nback to the levels of mania that surrounded the  dot-com boom  --\nbut it is getting close.  $50 Billion  Facebook is valued at $50 billion, on the basis of its most\nrecent stock sales. Groupon, the Chicago-based daily-deals site,\nhas held talks about an IPO that would value it at as much as\n$25 billion, according to people familiar with the matter. Its\ncompetitor LivingSocial may follow it to the market. Twitter\nvalued itself at $3.7 billion at the end of last year, and may\nbe worth a lot more by now.  AOL Inc. (AOL) , a company that knows a fair bit about Internet\nbubbles, has pumped some excitement into a moribund  media\nindustry  with its $315 million purchase of the Huffington Post\nwebsite. Even humble app designers are now hot properties. Rovio\nMobile is preparing itself for an IPO, and last month received\n$42 million in funding. At this rate, it may one day overtake\nthat fallen star of the Finnish technology industry: Nokia Oyj.  Not everyone thinks it will end happily.  \u201cMost of them will be overpriced,\u201d said  Warren Buffett ,\nchairman and chief executive officer of Berkshire Hathaway Inc.,\nspeaking about social-networking valuations last month.  Fortunes Lost  True enough. Among investors with a memory stretching back\nmore than a decade, the simple combination of words \u201ctech\u201d and\n\u201cIPO\u201d conjure visions of valuations spinning out of control --\nand everyone losing a fortune on a lot of companies that,\nlooking back, were about as solid as a bowl of chicken broth. It\nis certainly possible that this tech boom will end up with more\nAngry Stockholders rather than Angry Birds.  Against that, the likes of  Google Inc. (GOOG) , Amazon.com Inc. and\n Apple Inc. (AAPL)  are now among the biggest companies in the world. The\nInternet economy is expanding all the time. If you invested in\nthe right businesses last time around, you made a lot of money.  So the trick is to back the right horses -- and to do that\nyou need to learn the lessons of the last tech bubble to steer\nyour way through this one.  Here are four good places to start.  First, don\u2019t worry about business models. Google didn\u2019t\nhave one to start with. Neither did Facebook. The advertising\nfollowed later. Both concentrated on making a great product that\nwould have a huge audience, and figured that so long as they had\nthat the  revenue  would follow. So don\u2019t spend too much time\nfretting about how the business doesn\u2019t make any money yet. So\nlong as the audience is there, it will be fine.  Network Effect  Two, look for monopolies. The Internet has an in-built\ntendency to create companies with massive market share. There is\na simple reason for that: the network effect. We all use\nMicrosoft operating systems because everyone else does.\nLikewise, we go to Facebook because that is where all our\nfriends are. So it\u2019s best to look for sites or software systems\nthat everyone flocks to -- not because they are necessarily that\ngreat but just because everyone else does.  Three, skip the companies selling shares too soon. The best\nInternet entrepreneurs are greedy. They know they are on to\nsomething good, and they won\u2019t be giving away equity until they\nhave to. Watch for the businesses where the founders are only\nselling stock when they really need to -- and skip the ones\nwhere they are cashing out too early.  Four, buy after the IPO. There is an inevitable cycle of\nhype and disappointment before the really strong businesses\nemerge. The company goes public on a wave of excitement, then\nthere is disappointing news, and the shares crash. Make sure you\nbuy on the disappointment rather than the hype.  It remains the case that technology is where the real\nfortunes of the next decade will be made. Investors just need to\nmake sure they tread carefully -- because there will be some\nspectacular turkeys out there as well as some great businesses.  (Matthew Lynn is a Bloomberg News columnist and the author\nof \u201cBust,\u201d a book on the Greek debt crisis. The opinions\nexpressed are his own.) (AAPL) \u2019s  share price , a persistent question has lingered:\nWhy is the stock still so  cheap ? One overlooked answer may be\nthat Apple\u2019s accounting isn\u2019t as conservative as it used to be.  After topping $500 a share this week, the iPhone and iPad\nmaker now has a $468 billion  market capitalization . Yet Apple\ntrades for only 14.3 times its earnings for the previous four\nquarters -- about the same as the  Standard & Poor\u2019s 500  Index\u2019s\nprice-earnings ratio -- in spite of growth that\u2019s far above\naverage. Revenue last quarter rose 73 percent to $46.3 billion,\nwhile earnings more than doubled to $13.1 billion.  Many theories have been floated for why such a rapidly\nexpanding company with such loyal customers would trade for so\nlittle. Perhaps investors believe Apple will cling to its $97.6\nbillion hoard of cash and marketable securities, rather than pay\na fat dividend. Others have suggested a lack of confidence about\nthe future. It\u2019s a consumer-electronics company, after all, and\ncompetition is brutal.  While each of those points has merit, here\u2019s an explanation\nthat hasn\u2019t gotten enough attention: Thanks to an  accounting-\nrule  change for which it lobbied, Apple gets to book revenue\nfrom sales of bundled products such as iPhones -- which include\nhardware, software, services and upgrade rights -- more quickly\nthan it used to. In short, one reason Apple\u2019s earnings have been\nso high is accounting inflation, and the market realizes this.  Restated Numbers  The easiest way to see the rule change\u2019s impact is to look\nback at the  two sets  of numbers Apple reported for fiscal 2009.\nOriginally, the company said it had $5.7 billion of net income\nfor the year on $36.5 billion of revenue. Then in January 2010\nApple retroactively adopted the new accounting principles and\nrestated its previous numbers. The restatement boosted Apple\u2019s\nfiscal 2009 net income 44 percent to $8.2 billion. Revenue was\nrevised to $42.9 billion, 17 percent higher than originally\nreported.  Nothing changed economically, of course. Only the\naccounting did. On the surface, though, Apple\u2019s valuation looked\ncheaper under the new reporting regime than under the old one.  On Dec. 31, 2009, for instance, Apple had a market\ncapitalization of about $191 billion. Using the fiscal 2009\nearnings that Apple initially reported, its price-earnings ratio\nthat day was about 33. Using its restated numbers, the ratio\nwould have been about 23. My guess is a similar effect is\noccurring today: Had it not been for the rule change, Apple\u2019s\nP\/E ratio would be higher, because the \u201cE\u201d would be lower.  \u201cIt would appear that the market continues to consider a\nsignificant component of Apple\u2019s revenues and gross profit to be\npresently unearned and not deserving of a normal market\nmultiple,\u201d said Charles Mulford, an accounting professor and\ndirector of the Financial Reporting and Analysis Lab at Georgia\nInstitute of Technology in Atlanta.  Apple was one of a  handful  of companies that  lobbied  the\n Financial Accounting Standards Board  for the new rules in 2009.\nThe impact for Apple seems to have been greater than for most\nothers, probably because of the nature of its products.  Dell\nInc. (DELL)  said the rule switch had no material impact on its results.\n Microsoft Corp. (MSFT)  and  Oracle Corp. (ORCL)  said the same.  Hewlett-Packard\nCo. (HPQ) \u2019s earnings got a slight boost.  The FASB rule change had two main parts. One related to so-\ncalled  multiple-deliverable arrangements , while another covered\n software  sales. When Apple sells an iPhone, for example, the\nhardware and software are delivered at the time of sale. Other\ndeliverables include the rights to future software upgrades and\nother features.  Economic Life  The old accounting rules required Apple to defer large\nchunks of its revenue and recognize the amounts gradually over\neach product\u2019s economic life. While the details are complicated,\nthe gist under the new rules is that Apple is allowed to record\nmore revenue upfront.  What\u2019s unknowable is how much different Apple\u2019s latest\nresults would have looked had the FASB not amended its\nstandards. There\u2019s no way to tell from the company\u2019s\ndisclosures. Plus, Apple adopted the new accounting principles\nright before it  introduced  the iPad. An Apple spokeswoman,\n Kristin Huguet , didn\u2019t return phone calls seeking comment.  Let me be clear: I\u2019m not opining on whether Apple is\novervalued or undervalued, and I\u2019m certainly not making any\npredictions about its stock price. The point here is that it\nmakes sense for Apple\u2019s earnings multiple to have declined\nsignificantly once you consider how the company\u2019s accounting has\nchanged.  The bottom line: Not all iEarnings are created equal.  ( Jonathan Weil  is a Bloomberg View columnist. The opinions\nexpressed are his own.)  Read more opinion online from  Bloomberg View . But adversity (almost) always creates economic opportunity. Digital media continue to be springboards for global innovation and enterprise. North America's fracking fever has proviked experts (who once feared the world had passed  Hubbert's Peak ) to predict the US will soon be a net energy exporter. Human ingenuity \u2014 increasingly augmented by technical amplifiers \u2014 remains the most remarkable renewable resource. So here are four innovation ideas \u2014 themes, really \u2014 sure to gain significantly greater mind- and market-share over the coming year. What do they all have in common? Individual empowerment. 'Badges? We Don't Need No  Stinkin' Badges! ' With apologies to John Huston , yes we do. From Khan Academy to Coursera to edX to the O'Reilly School of Technology, badges increasingly enjoy consideration  as human capital's coin of the the realm for online education . Valid and verifiable accreditation is an exponentially growing challenge for virtual educators \u2014 and their students \u2014 worldwide. What should it mean to employers that someone has successfully completed a core course in Machine Learning or Hadoop? What does an executive education badge from an Instituto de Empresa, an Insead or Hitotusbashi say about the curricular competences of its holder? What badges will dramatically increase a job candidate's hireability or promotability? Linked-In endorsements are lovely, but the demand for meaningful and measurable affirmation and accreditation will have profound effects  on both higher and executive education . Badging bandwidth will further expand as the IBMs, Accentures, Schlumbergers and professional societies decide that they, too, want to brand the expertise of their training programs and people. Craft unions and other skilled labor organizations also seem destined to bring badging to their memberships. Will badges require successful course completion? Or will be badges be won by passing a demanding array of standardized virtual tests? Course content, quality and participation won't ultimately determine the triumph of the online educational revolution. The ability  to measure and assess real learning and skills acquisition  in virtual environments will. Badges \u2014 not digital diplomas \u2014 seem to be the best and likeliest bet on accreditation's future. What policies and programs is your organization developing around badges? Do your hiring\/promotion processes recognize badges? Badges will be key variables in human capital evaluation. Is HR your best badgemeister? Second Screens  and Monetizing Multitasking Attention is no longer undivided. Multitasking rules. Kindle readers tweet commentary about the ebooks and magazines they're reading; folks chatting on their iPhones use their tablets to turn real-time conversations into livestreamed blogs. The mix of device mobility and multiplicity makes people into multimedia 'prosumers;'  nobody is doing 'just one thing' anymore.  Hollywood and content creators worldwide  have taken notice  and readjusted their business models accordingly. Television shows are no longer broadcast \u2014 or streamed \u2014 to be watched; they're supposed to be tweeted and\/or otherwise reengaged. \"Late Night with Conan O'Brien\" invites its viewers to download a 'watchalong' app.  Disney 'Second Screen' offers 'playalong' apps for movie classics ranging from 'Bambi' to 'The Lion King.' Bravo encourages and expects viewers of its cult shows to tweet their real-time reactions to the world. Instead of forcing people to overwhelmingly focus their time and attention on a single screen, broadcasters, sports teams and \"appreneurs\" increasingly seek to monetize divided attention spans by promoting multidevice engagement. Multitasking has evolved from a distraction and diversion to a financial focus wherever digital content lives. The phenomenon is global: Chinese and Indian yuppies increasingly carry two devices. So do the emerging middle classes in Brazil and Colombia. Monetizing multitasking will be mass media challenge, not a province of the elites. Of course, \"second screening\" won't be just a consumer behavior. Personal productivity both at home and at work will depend on finding ways to integrate  how multiple devices work together  to amplify individual performance. Designing for multidevice\/multitasiking second- (and third-) screen engagement is in its earliest phases. But the designs it inspires are exactly what Apple, Amazon, Google, Samsung, Nokia and Microsoft are looking for. Taking 'Recofriendations' More Seriously What friends and colleagues \"like\" is useful to know. But is it enough? While recommendation engines have been fantastically successful for the Amazons and Netflixes, they remain relative underachievers given their technical and algorithmic potential. Both in theory and practice, social media platforms like Facebook, Twitter, Pinterest, Yelp and Reddit have the data and analytics to transform  how \"likes\" get \ntranslated into insight and advice . \"Recommenders\" that go beyond alerting\/notifying you that \"friends you know\" like  this  movie or have read  that  article are emerging. Just as Gmail now begins to suggest \"other\" people you might send that email to, Facebook,  Amazon  and LinkedIn will increasingly make recommendations based on your \"successful\" web behaviors. \" Social Reader \"-like notifications will give way to more sophisticated reasons and rationales for recommendation. Recommendations will be more like \"Here's why...\" than \"Hey!\" Find a particularly helpful answer on Quora? You'll have a recommender suggest who on Outlook\/Gmail\/Linked-In and\/or Facebook should be forward an excerpt. Did you just book a flight on Expedia or enter travel plans on your Calendar? Then your recommender will suggest which friends and\/or acquaintances you might wish to contact when you're there. Preparing PowerPoint\/Keynote presentations with a few facts a tad fuzzier than you might like? Your recommender offers up names drawn from your social networks of possible \"reviewers\" for your iffier slides. Simply put, recommendation engine technology will be repurposed  to better align what you're digitally doing  with which particular friends\/colleagues\/acquaintances would likely be most interested in learning about it \u2014 and vice versa.  As with multitasking above, \"recofriendation engines\" may prove as valuable for professionals seeking a productivity boost as for people looking to go beyond \"notifications\" and tweets for engaging friends. Will there be battles and skirmishes about \nthe privacy implications? There always are. Otherwise, what's not to \"like?\" Fed Up Entrepreneurship Critics  harshly declare Ben Bernanke's Federal Reserve  hates savers and retirees . Certainly, equity investors believe the Fed's low interest rate policies make the stock market a better bet for higher returns. \"The [Fed] has created an environment where there is no effective alternative to stocks,\" Omega Advisors CEO Leon Cooperman  told CNBC the week before Christmas . \"...Half the stocks in the market are now yielding more than fixed income. You have to go back to 1958 to see that kind of condition.\"  Controversies about  the efficacy of the Fed's policies  at stimulating economic growth notwithstanding, Bernanke's declaration that  interest rates will be kept low until unemployment rates dramatically improve  signal a profound shift in the investment environment. Investors looking for higher returns will increasingly look to more \ninnovative alternatives. Will lower interest rates make venture capital a more appealing option? Preliminary data suggest not. According to  a PriceWaterhouse Coopers preliminary review , 2012 venture funding has actually declined. \"Investment for the first three quarters of the year was $20 billion into 2,661 deals, a level well below this point last year, making it likely that 2012 will fall short of 2011 in terms of both dollars and deal volume,\" the PwC release asserted. The numbers don't lie. However, a slower-growth economy and near-zero interest rates strongly suggest that entrepreneurs may find it easier to make the case that their ventures \u2014 even on a risk-adjusted basis \u2014 might be worth serious consideration. Entrepreneurship as an \"alternative investment\" may hold growing appeal to institutional investors seeking \"growth stories\" and diversification options.  While everyone, of course, looks for the next Google and Facebook, the reality is that  globally, innovation opportunities in bio\/nano\/info-technologies continue to emerge. Who would have picked hydraulic fracturing as a disruptive business\/technology breakthrough in 2002?  How angel investment, corporate venturing or institutionalized venture capital innovatively responds to Fed policy remains to be seen. But the relative paucity of returns on more traditional investments and the increasingly appeal of innovation opportunities suggest that there may never be a better time to be a charismatic entrepreneur with a scalable prototype.","path":".\/2008_2012_msft_bloomberg_news\/four-innovation-trends-to-watch-in-2013.txt"},{"id":24645974,"title":"FastShip, Live Nation, Google, VW, CA: Intellectual Property","released_at":"<date>March 22 2012<\/date> <time>11:01:01<\/time>","content":"FastShip Inc. (MSFT)  released a new version of\nInternet Explorer, and while we wait to hear from the security\nexperts how it fares against hackers, it\u2019s already taken a big\nstep forward on the privacy front.  Internet Explorer 9, which is available as a  free download \nfrom Microsoft, replaces IE\u2019s previous, largely ineffectual\nscheme for preventing snoopy content providers from\nsurreptitiously tracking your online movements. The goal may be\nbenign -- gathering usage data for analytic purposes, for\ninstance -- but such data can also generate a profile of you,\nbased on your behavior, which can be used for ad-targeting or\nother more nefarious purposes.  The new version of Microsoft\u2019s browser offers controls\nthat, while far from perfect, make it easier to choose what\ninformation about your behavior you\u2019re willing to share with\nonline content providers.  While IE remains one of the most widely used pieces of\nsoftware on the planet, it doesn\u2019t wield the clout it once did.\nFor years now, new generations of competing browsers -- Google\u2019s\nChrome, Apple\u2019s Safari, Mozilla\u2019s Firefox and Opera Software\u2019s\nOpera, to name four -- have out-innovated and out-performed it.  With IE9, which is all-around faster, slicker and more\nenjoyable than its predecessor, Microsoft finally deserves to be\nfront-of-mind again for anyone lucky enough to be able to run\nit.  Not for Everyone  Therein lies an important point: Not every Web surfer -- in\nfact, not even every Microsoft-using Web surfer -- will be\ncapable of running the new software. In a bold move, the company\nhas made IE9 compatible only with Windows 7, the current version\nof its desktop operating system, and with its immediate\npredecessor, Vista. About half of all Windows users, who are\nstill on the nine-year-old XP operating system, are out of luck.  Microsoft says that step was made necessary by the new\nfeatures of IE9 that integrate it more deeply with the operating\nsystem than previous versions, or, in earlier years, antitrust\nregulators would allow.  Among other things, IE9 blurs the line between programs\nrunning on your computer\u2019s hard drive and content from the Web.\nWebsite icons can now be permanently affixed to Windows\u2019s task\nbar, where they both look and, if the site developer supports\nit, act much like applications located on your PC.  Jump Lists  Pin the Yahoo! icon to your task bar, for instance, and a\nright-button mouse click opens a menu called a jump list that\nlets you go directly to the site\u2019s widely used mail, finance and\nsports services.  The New York Times  menu gives you links to its\ntop 10 headlines, plus shortcuts to its home page and search,\nvideo and most-popular functions.  The new browser is also much speedier. Its Windows-only\norientation means Microsoft didn\u2019t have to make compromises to\nassure it would run the same on other operating systems; by\ncontrast, Chrome, Safari, Firefox and Opera all have versions\nthat run on Macs as well as PCs, and all except Safari have\nversions for the open-source Linux operating system too.  The most important part of Microsoft\u2019s Windows-only\napproach is that IE can harness your PC\u2019s hardware to give\nitself a significant speed boost for performing certain kinds of\nfunctions -- running  animated graphics , for instance.  IE9\u2019s new privacy features, meanwhile, represent an upping\nof the ante for other browser developers. The previous version\nof Explorer had a tool called \u201cInPrivate Filtering\u201d that\nproved to be deeply flawed. Among other things, it was disabled\nby default; to trigger it, users had to deliberately switch it\non, and every time they closed their browser, the setting would\nrevert to the off position.  More Powerful  While IE9 still requires the user to choose tracking\nprotection, this time it\u2019s easier to do, more powerful and\npersists across browsing sessions.  To enable the feature, you\u2019ll click on the settings icon on\nIE9\u2019s  newly streamlined interface , and choose the \u201cSafety\u201d\noption from the pull-down menu. The software uses two methods\nfor blocking tracking. One instructs your browser to tell\ncontent providers that you don\u2019t wish to be tracked. While\nreputable services should comply, there\u2019s no protection against\nthe unscrupulous ones.  The second method requires a little more work on your part,\nhopefully just once, by allowing you to easily subscribe to\nonline \u201ctracking protection lists.\u201d These lists are maintained\nand updated by online-privacy organizations such as  TRUSTe  and\n PrivacyChoice , which monitor content providers and their\ntechnologies, and are supposed to actually block their efforts.  Cat and Mouse  The big question is how well the new tools work, or whether\nthey\u2019ll trigger cat-and-mouse moves by less-than-reputable sites\nto circumvent them. Indeed, one risk with Microsoft\u2019s new\nfeatures is that they\u2019ll result in a false sense of security.  Still, they represent a welcome step to put privacy issues\nfront and center -- and not just for Microsoft. The next version\nof Firefox will include \u201cdo not track\u201d functionality, for\ninstance, while Google recently made an  anti-tracking add-on \navailable for its new Chrome 10 browser.  With President Barack Obama\u2019s administration and Congress\nbeginning to debate the need for online-privacy legislation,\nMicrosoft\u2019s efforts with IE9 may be just the opening salvo in a\nfeature war among all the browser makers to make Web surfing\nsafer and more private. We can only hope.  ( Rich Jaroslovsky  is a Bloomberg News columnist. The\nopinions expressed are his own.) Especially when it comes to sustainability.\u00a0 Companies best known for sustainability -- Apple Inc., FedEx Corp., Toyota Motor Corp.\u00a0-- aren't the ones leading their peers on real, company-wide gauges of sustainability performance. That\u2019s one conclusion reached in a new report published last week by Brandlogic and CRD Analytics that compares how 100 top companies perform, and are perceived to perform, on sustainability.\u00a0 The report also found that most companies are making real operational improvements that key audiences are not\u00a0factoring into their perceptions. Ninety-three of the 94 companies that also appeared in the 2011 report showed measurable sustainability performance improvements this year. (Six companies were replaced for the 2012 study.) Yet only a third of those companies showed improved perception scores, a possible consequence of consumers being hit with too much information that they're not in a position to evaluate.\u00a0 To find companies' \u201cSustainability Reality Scores,\u201d researchers rated their performance on environmental and social issues and corporate governance, as defined by\u00a0141 metrics, ranging from energy and water use, human rights, employee diversity, and commitment to transparency and disclosure.\u00a0 They then surveyed thousands of professional investors, purchasing managers and university and college students, to see how their perceptions stood up against the more objective metrics. The survey results inform the \u201cSustainability Perception Scores.\u201d Purchasing managers were by far the hardest graders, although all three classes of respondents marked companies' scores down. \"As people become more aware, and actually see more information, they actually become more skeptical,\" James Cerutti, a Brandlogic senior partner suggested in a telephone interview. \"They don't know what the facts really may be\u2026 It may just be a natural reaction to say, well, I'm gonna be a little cynical, a little skeptical here.\" Both the reality and perception scores are translated onto 100-point scales for each company. The methodology is explained in the full report,\u00a0 here .\u00a0The 100 companies each fall into one of four quadrants on a\u00a0\"sustainability IQ matrix\u201d: Leaders, who rate high in both performance and perception, fill the upper right quadrant; Challengers, who score well in performance and below the mean in perception, fill the upper left quadrant; Promoters, who are perceived to be sustainability leaders but who rate below the mean on actual performance, fill the lower right quadrant; and Laggards, who trail the both means for both performance and perception, fill the lower left quadrant. The study enables comparisons between companies within a sector. United Parcel Service, Inc. (UPS), for example, earned one of the study\u2019s highest marks for company-wide operational performance on environmental, social and corporate governance issues. Its competitor, FedEx, scored half as well on overall\u00a0performance, but manages a much stronger overall perception of sustainability. Other noteworthy results:\u00a0 Apple has the highest perception rating of the 100 companies, which is surprising given that the company, \u201cthough improved, continues to rate below the mean on real performance,\u201d Cerutti said on a conference call when the report launched last week. Technology companies such as\u00a0Dell Inc., Hewlett-Packard Co., International Business Machines Corp. (IBM)\u00a0and Microsoft Corp. all rated higher than Apple on their \"sustainability reality score.\" One explanation is that Apple\u2019s phenomenal success in sales and branding has created a kind of halo effect that encouraged survey respondents to perceive it as a sustainable company.\u00a0In reviewing their data, researchers found that companies' scores on environmental and social issues and governance account for only 50 percent or 60 percent of the perception that survey respondents had of them. In the case of a company like Apple, having wildly successful products might make people willing to overlook supply chain or environmental questions and credit it with being more sustainable, Cerutti said in our interivew. Toyota trails Bayerische Motoren Werke AG (BMW), Volkswagen AG and Ford Motor Co. in overall sustainability\u00a0performance, but leads them, substantially, in perceived performance.\u00a0 Pharmaceutical companies were among the leaders on the \u201cSustainability Perception Score\u201d in 2011, but fell out of that role this year.\u00a0 Last year, 15 companies had perception scores that led their performance scores by more than 20 points. This year, Facebook Inc. and Amazon.com, Inc. are the only two.\u00a0 Companies with high perception scores tend to embed their sustainability achievements directly in what Cerutti called overall \u201cbrand communication.\u201d Sustainability reports may now be routine for most global companies, but that doesn\u2019t mean many people read them.\u00a0 Visit\u00a0 www.bloomberg.com\/sustainability \u00a0for the latest from Bloomberg News about energy, natural resources and global business.","path":".\/2008_2012_msft_bloomberg_news\/apple-fedex-toyota-lead-in-perceived-sustainability.txt"},{"id":47454753,"title":"HP to Keep Supporting \u2018Not Dead\u2019 WebOS Software, Executive Says","released_at":"<date>August 20 2011<\/date> <time>04:00:07<\/time>","content":"Hewlett-Packard Co. The deal, along with six others so far this month, wasn\u2019t subject to any oversight by financial authorities, yet would help establish the price for more than half the world\u2019s oil.  Trading in oil cargoes from the  North Sea  set benchmark prices published by Platts, a unit of McGraw Hill Financial Inc., that ultimately help determine the amount refiners pay for crude, which in turn affects what consumers pay for gasoline and diesel fuel. Last week, Europe\u2019s top antitrust official barged into this lightly regulated corner of the market, raiding the offices of  Royal Dutch Shell Plc (RDSA) , BP and Statoil, and requesting records from some of Europe\u2019s biggest trading houses, including Vitol Group, Gunvor Group Ltd. and Glencore Xstrata Plc.  The investigation targets possible collusion to manipulate benchmark energy assessments reported by Platts. The probe is being led by European Union Competition Commissioner  Joaquin Almunia , who also is pursuing price-fixing allegations related to the London interbank offered rate, or Libor, and in the market for  credit derivatives . Commodities regulators have little authority to police price-reporting companies.  \u201cThey have a hammer, and they\u2019re going around looking for nails to pound with it,\u201d Craig Pirrong, director of the  University of Houston \u2019s Global Energy Management Institute, said by phone last week. \u201cLibor showed them how powerful a hammer they had, and in particular it showed them what can happen when you get access to company records. It\u2019s amazing the kinds of things you can find there.\u201d  Pricing Probes  Pricing mechanisms are under scrutiny around the world after U.S and U.K. investigators uncovered widespread attempts by banks to manipulate Libor, the benchmark lending rate tied to $300 trillion in securities worldwide.  Royal Bank of Scotland Group Plc , UBS AG and  Barclays Plc (BARC)  have been fined $2.5 billion and at least a dozen firms remain under investigation. Regulators are also looking for evidence of price fixing in ISDAfix, the benchmark rate for the $379 trillion swaps market.  \u201cThis is nothing like Libor,\u201d Adrian Binks, chairman of  Argus Media Ltd. , a reporting company and Platts competitor in London, said in an e-mail May 20. \u201cPrice reporting agencies are independent companies that compete with each other. It\u2019s really industry\u2019s choice to use our quotations. We\u2019re not receiving money for the trades. We\u2019re not like the banks.\u201d  Independent Reviews  The price-reporters said they ordered independent reviews of their methods after calls by regulators last year to safeguard against market manipulation. Platts\u2019s will start in June and be completed this year. Argus and Reed Business Information\u2019s  ICIS  said their evaluations would be completed by October. The process, which preceded and is separate from the EU inquiry, will examine whether the reporters comply with their own stated assessment methods, the companies said this week.  The appraisals are a response to calls by international regulators for \u201crobust\u201d controls to prevent manipulation and distortion of wholesale prices for commodities from crude to gasoline. Auditors will assess whether the reporting companies have adhered to principles set out last October by the International Organization of Securities Commissions. The Madrid-based group, which brings together regulators from more than 100 countries, said that benchmark assessments are vulnerable to manipulation.  \u201cA review by an external auditor as called for by the  IOSCO principles  will demonstrate to regulators the strength of Platts\u2019s internal controls,\u201d Dan Tanz, the company\u2019s vice president of editorial, said yesterday in an e-mailed statement from London. Platts has a long track record of \u201cstrong internal governance,\u201d he said.  Constrained Regulators  London-based BP spokesman David Nicholas declined to comment on BP crude trades. Shell spokeswoman Julia Dudley also declined to comment. Morten Eek, a spokesman for Statoil, said the company doesn\u2019t comment on specific trades.  Bloomberg LP, the parent of  Bloomberg News , competes with Platts and other companies in providing energy markets news and information.  Almunia\u2019s probe sidesteps the legal limits that have constrained commodities regulators, and instead focuses on potential antitrust violations, one of the most powerful enforcement weapons in the European regulator\u2019s arsenal. He\u2019s employed the same tactic in the investigations into credit derivatives and Libor.  \u2018Creative, Encouraging\u2019  \u201cIt\u2019s not only creative, it\u2019s encouraging,\u201d  Bart Chilton , commissioner with the U.S. Commodity Futures Trading Commission, said in an interview May 20. \u201cUltimately these prices that are being posted impact consumers around the world. It\u2019s a big hairy deal.\u201d  Platts\u2019s Dated Brent crude assessment is based on the price of trades, bids and offers on four grades of North Sea crude and related contracts. Platts gathers information from traders through emails, phone calls, instant messages and Platts electronic system, called the eWindow. Then the company calculates the day\u2019s price as of 4:30 p.m. London time.  That benchmark price affects the value of over-the-counter oil derivatives, Brent futures traded on the ICE Futures Europe Exchange in London, and cargoes of crude from Canada to Australia. On May 9, the day Statoil sold the tanker of Norwegian Oseberg to BP, Dated Brent declined $1.83 a barrel to $103.69, erasing $1.1 million from the value of a standard 600,000 barrel shipment.  Worldwide Impact  That loss would be amplified worldwide. About 200 billion barrels of oil and related contracts are priced using Brent each year, Liz Bossley, chief executive officer of London-based Consilience Energy Advisory Group Ltd., and author of \u201cTrading Crude Oil: The Consilience Guide,\u201d said by phone yesterday. That\u2019s $20.6 trillion a year based on yesterday\u2019s settlement price of $103.02 a barrel.  Total Oil Trading, an arm of the French  oil company   Total SA (TOT) , said in an August letter to IOSCO that Platts prices are used to determine the value of as much as 95 percent of crude transactions linked to price reporting, 90 percent of refined products and 90 percent of derivatives in the over-the-counter market. The prices are \u201cout of line with our experience of the day\u201d several times a year, the company said.  \u201cIn commodity markets, if you look at the role of Platts, it\u2019s enormous,\u201d  Karel Lannoo , chief executive officer of the Centre for European Policy Studies in Brussels, said by phone last week. \u201cIn Europe, nobody is looking at this because we have no specific derivatives market regulators or commodity market regulators.\u201d  Loosened Control  Benchmark energy assessments like those published by Platts helped break the pricing control held by oil producers before exchanges offered publicly traded futures contracts. Argus and ICIS also gather information from buyers and sellers about the day\u2019s transactions and publish price assessments for subscribers.  Platts publishes thousands of daily assessments across multiple commodities, which are used to price gasoline, diesel, biofuels, natural gas, electricity and petrochemicals.  \u201cPlatts believes the transparency we have brought to oil markets over the last 20 years and the valuable and timely insights into global oil trading activity that we have been able to provide as a result has been of significant benefit to all involved and the public,\u201d Dave Ernsberger, Platts global director of oil, said in an e-mail this week.  Monti\u2019s Crusade  The company\u2019s London offices were searched on May 14 by investigators dispatched by Almunia, a Spanish socialist who is one of the most powerful antitrust enforcers in Europe. The competition office, once led by former Italian Prime Minister  Mario Monti , has in the past decade pursued allegations against companies including  Microsoft Corp., (MSFT)  the world\u2019s largest software maker, and  Google Inc., (GOOG)  operator of the world\u2019s largest Internet search engine.  Almunia has made policing financial benchmarks a priority. He has opened investigations into Goldman Sachs Group Inc., JPMorgan Chase & Co. and other investment banks over Libor, and he\u2019s examining possible collusion among banks and brokers to manipulate benchmark lending rates in Swiss francs, the yen and the euro.  The EU has treated collusion on benchmark lending rates as a price-fixing cartel that can be punished under its antitrust rules. Fines can be as much as 10 percent of a company\u2019s yearly global revenue and are based on its annual sales in the market where it tried to fix prices.  Limited Jurisdiction  Almunia has stepped in where commodities regulators can\u2019t. The CFTC has limited jurisdiction over the physical trades that underlie the benchmarks. Those transactions are deemed forwards, or bilateral deals that provide for physical delivery between commercial parties, such as an oil producer and refiner, and are exempt from regulation.  \u201cWe have no view or surveillance into what they do,\u201d Chilton said. \u201cWe\u2019ve tried. We\u2019ve been rebuffed in court. So there definitely needs to be more transparency.\u201d  That\u2019s why Almunia\u2019s inquiry is so important, he said. Chilton declined to comment on whether the CFTC was cooperating with the European Commission inquiry or pursuing its own investigation into price reporting.  The suspected violations are related to Platts price assessments for crude, refined products and biofuels, and may have been going on since 2002, Statoil said in a May 14 statement.  Finnish Refiner  In addition to BP, Shell, Statoil and Platts, EU investigators last week raided fuel trader Argos Energies, the company said May 17. Traders including  Glencore Xstrata (GLEN) , Vitol and Gunvor were asked to give information, though they aren\u2019t being investigated, according to three people familiar with the situation, who asked not to be identified because the matter is private.  Neste Oil Oyj (NES1V) , Finland\u2019s only refiner, said May 16 that it was asked to provide information regarding potential manipulation of global crude and biofuel markets.  As investigators plow through 11 years of instant messages, phone records and emails, the inquiry will probably entangle more participants in Platts energy pricing, a list that includes dozens of banks,  hedge funds ,  oil companies  and trading houses, Pirrong said.  \u201cIt has a lot of people nervous,\u201d he said. Lawsuits\/Pretrial  CFTC Position Limits Rule Lawsuit Dismissed by Appeals Court  Two Wall Street groups\u2019 challenge to a U.S. Commodity\nFutures Trading Commission rule on position limits must first be\nconsidered in a trial court, a federal appeals court ruled,\ndismissing the case.  A three-judge panel of the U.S. Court of Appeals in\nWashington said Jan. 20 that it doesn\u2019t have jurisdiction to\nconsider the case because the Commodity Exchange Act and last\nyear\u2019s Dodd-Frank law \u201care silent\u201d on whether the rule can be\ndirectly challenged to the appeals court.  \u201cInitial review occurs at the appellate level only when a\ndirect-review statute specifically gives the court of appeals\nsubject-matter jurisdiction to directly review agency action,\u201d\nJudges Judith Rogers, Merrick Garland and Janice Rogers Brown\nsaid, citing circuit precedent. \u201cThere is no express\ncongressional authorization of direct appellate review\napplicable to the petition for review in this case.\u201d  The  International Swaps and Derivatives Association Inc. \nand  Securities Industry and Financial Markets Association  filed\nan emergency request Jan. 9 urging the appeals court to put the\nrule on hold while the court considers their legal challenge.\nThe groups asked the court to issue a ruling by Jan. 27.  By dismissing the case, the judges also rejected that\nrequest.  The groups, in one of the financial industry\u2019s highest-\nprofile efforts to weaken last year\u2019s Dodd-Frank law, filed\nlawsuits challenging the rule in two federal courts in\nWashington last month. Martian Watches  and  Meta Watch Ltd.  are trying similar approaches.  Wearable Battle  Apple\u2019s watch foray would also open a new front in its competition with Google -- this time, in the area of wearable technology. Google is developing Google Glass, a computing device that resembles spectacles and is worn on the face. Owners of the glasses will be able to speak commands to snap photos, record videos or ask for directions, among other tasks.  Apple, more than any other company, has proved its ability to move into mature markets and remake them with new, easy-to- use innovations. Before Apple created the iPhone, cell phone makers were enjoying record sales of devices based less on technological innovation than on fashion and brand. Apple\u2019s iPhone 5 was the bestselling smartphone in the fourth quarter,  according  to Strategy Analytics, and its mobile operating system commanded 21 percent of the market,  according  to IDC.  The watch business is experiencing a renaissance reminiscent of the cell phone industry before the iPhone. Shares of Fossil and  Movado Group Inc. (MOV)  have more than tripled since the end of 2009.  Stock Rally  Both companies enjoy gross margins greater than 55 percent, owing to brisk demand for fashionable watches.  Swatch Group AG (UHR) , the biggest maker of Swiss timepieces, surged to a record last month after reporting accelerating profit growth and expanded production capacity.  Such gains lessen the incentive for companies to incur the costs and risks associated with bringing out more technologically capable smart watches. Apple\u2019s shares retreated 2.4 percent to $420.05 at the close in New York.  Fossil, which built smart watches in partnership with Sony Ericsson as well as with Microsoft in the last decade, currently has no plans to do more, CEO Kosta Kartsotis said.  \u201cWe do have a number of things we\u2019re looking at and watching,\u201d he said on a recent conference call. Still, he added, conventional watches are \u201ca much bigger opportunity.\u201d  Besides brand and retail outlets, another advantage for Apple is its unmatched ability to drive down the price of components such as displays, batteries and circuit boards.  Ive Interested  Success in the watch business could provide some relief from gross-margin pressure that has dragged on shares.  A main concern is whether the company can find a product to compensate for slowing sales of the iPhone, which has gross margins of around 55 percent, roughly twice that of iPads and Macs. An Apple watch could carry margins that high, said Bloomberg Industry\u2019s Srinivasan.  Apple design chief Jony Ive has long had an interest in watches. Besides owning many high-end models himself, he had his team visit watch factories and ordered boxes of a sports watch made by  Nike Inc. (NKE)  in the mid-2000s, said Wilson, who was then Nike\u2019s  creative director .  Coming up with a single watch to appeal to millions of consumers will test even Apple\u2019s design mettle. While consumers are discriminating about which phone they carry, they may prove even more fussy about something worn every day. The buying public may opt for different types of timepieces, depending on the occasion -- for instance, a high-priced Swiss watch for a black-tie affair, or a sports-oriented smart watch on weekends.  \u201cApple can merge fashion with function,\u201d said Marshal Cohen, an  analyst  at NPD Group. \u201cAn Apple watch could triple the size of the watch business in a year or two. (MSFT)  Chief Executive Officer Steve Ballmer has been contemplating his departure from the world\u2019s largest software maker for at least three years.  Ballmer and the company\u2019s board started discussing succession planning as early as 2010, said a person with knowledge of the matter, who asked not to be identified because the deliberations were private. The conversations centered on what attributes Ballmer and other board members wanted in a new CEO. That led to Ballmer exposing internal CEO candidates to the board and also meeting with external candidates, said the person.  The exit plans gathered steam about three to four months ago, when Ballmer approached the board and said he was considering stepping down and asked directors to examine what an official succession process would look like, said the person. Ballmer finalized his decision with the board on Wednesday.  The CEO, 57, will now retire within 12 months, Microsoft said yesterday in a statement. The Redmond, Washington-based company\u2019s lead independent director, John Thompson, will oversee the search for his successor, heading a committee that will also include Microsoft co-founder Bill Gates. Investors applauded the move, sending the shares up the most since 2009.  Industry Decline  Ballmer\u2019s announcement reflects the changes roiling the computing industry his company helped pioneer. Microsoft, which supplies the software running most personal computers, lost almost half its value on Ballmer\u2019s watch. The stock hasn\u2019t closed above $50 since his first year on the job amid competition from  Google Inc. (GOOG) ,  Apple Inc. (AAPL)  and  Facebook Inc. The mantle of technology leadership has instead been taken up by Google, Apple and Facebook, which have over the past decade moved the landscape toward mobile, search and social networking -- all areas where Microsoft is weak.  \u2018Lightning Rod\u2019  Amid these shifts, Microsoft last month reported quarterly profits and sales that missed analysts\u2019 estimates. Congressional leaders decided to eschew the\ntraditional July 4 recess ostensibly to try to force\nthemselves and their colleagues to come up with ways to\nbegin to close the gaping federal budget deficits -- a\nvirtual necessity if a credit-rating downgrade on the\n United States  government is to be avoided. There is said to be more than $1.5 trillion in cash\nsitting in the overseas coffers of American corporations.\nWhy not give these corporations the incentive to bring that\nmoney home with a tax break, but in exchange demand that\nthey use the cash to, among other things, build new plants\nand equipment, hire new employees, and invest in research\nand development? According to the New York Times, Apple has some\n$12 billion in cash or cash equivalents overseas. Microsoft\nhas $29 billion. Google has $17 billion. Cisco has nearly\n$32 billion abroad.  If these companies simply repatriate the money, of\ncourse, they are subject to tax rates of up to 35 percent.\nIf they leave it and use it overseas, they don\u2019t pay any\nU.S. taxes on the money. A one-time break on the 35 percent\nrate -- as occurred most recently with the Homeland\nInvestment Act of 2004 -- would encourage companies to\nbring the money back home and spend it here while pumping\nnew tax dollars into the Treasury to help reduce the\ndeficit.  Many of these corporations sense the opportunity at\nhand and are lobbying Congress for a one-time \u201ccash\nrepatriation\u201d tax rate of 5.25 percent. Those against the\nrepatriation tax holiday cite what happened after the 2004\ntax holiday as a reason to resist giving companies another\nbreak this year.  No New Jobs  \u201cRepatriations did not lead to an increase in domestic\ninvestment, employment or R&D -- even for the firms that\nlobbied for the tax holiday stating these intentions and\nfor firms that appeared to be financially constrained,\u201d\naccording to a June 2009  study  of the 2004 act published by\nthe nonpartisan  National Bureau of Economic Research .  What happened with the cash? \u201cInstead, a $1 increase\nin repatriations was associated with an increase of almost\n$1 in payouts to shareholders,\u201d the report found.  The\npharmaceutical giant Merck repatriated nearly $16 billion\nbut ended up using most of it, according to regulatory\nfilings, to reduce its work force, increase its dividends\nto shareholders, and buy back its own stock.  While it is regrettable that after 2004 these\ncompanies defied the intent of the tax break, there is\nnothing necessarily wrong with shareholders getting the\nmoney. Shareholders spend money, too, don\u2019t they?  Don\u2019t Look Back  Still, rather than obsess about why the 2004 tax\nholiday failed to achieve its goals, how about learning\nfrom that experience to design a better tax break for 2011?\nLast week, the editors of Bloomberg View suggested that a\ndeal be struck at 15 percent if companies could also\nprovide verifiable job growth over a three-year period,\nwhich could generate something like $200 billion for the\nTreasury if the bulk of that $1.5 trillion held overseas\ncame home.  While unlikely to happen at that magnitude -- tech\ncompanies like Cisco and Apple have relatively far fewer\nworkers than traditional manufacturing firms and thus might\nnot be interested -- anything like that kind of money going\ninto the Treasury would help assure increasingly wary\ninvestors (and credit-rating agencies) that lawmakers might\nactually be serious about trying to reduce budget deficits.  It might also help to lower the tensions around the\nincreasingly rancorous debate about whether spending should\nbe cut or taxes raised. (My answer? Both must happen: taxes\nshould be raised on the wealthy and spending should be\nreduced, particularly in the military.)  Variety of Rates  There is nothing magical about the 15 percent rate\nproposed by the View editors, or about limiting the tax\nbreak to companies that hire new workers. Congress could\ncome up with a variety of reduced rates for companies that\npump up research and development or build new offices and\nfactories and a smaller break for those that simply return\nit to investors.  The point is that those companies that are serious\nabout helping to put Americans back to work and investing\nin their futures -- as opposed to sitting on piles of cash\n-- would get rewarded for it. The companies that can\u2019t get\ntheir minds -- or their economic analyses -- around the\nidea of spending their cash in the United States can now\neither keep it overseas or bring it back home, subject to\nthe regular 35 percent tax rate.  Congress should use its ruined Independence Day\nholiday to solve our nation\u2019s serious economic problems,\nand a one-time tax holiday with the appropriate safeguards\nand incentives would be a great act of patriotism.  (William D. Cohan, a former investment banker and the\nauthor of \u201cMoney and Power: How Goldman Sachs Came to Rule\nthe World,\u201d is a Bloomberg View columnist. (FB) , will function as the common capital for both states for a period of 10 years, according to the decision by Singh\u2019s cabinet. Control of Hyderabad is a key reason behind the protests, Reddy told CNN-IBN television news channel on Oct. 6.  Hyderabad has seen a three-hour daily power cut as about 60,000 utility workers have stayed home to protest the new state, according to a top official in the local government\u2019s electricity department who requested anonymity as he isn\u2019t an authorized spokesman. That has removed 3,600 megawatts of generation capacity, or 20 percent of the state\u2019s total, he said.  Grid Risk  Failure to contain the demonstrations may prompt further distribution cuts to sustain a  power grid  that connects all of southern India. Talks with the labor unions of state power plants are on to prevent a repeat of last year\u2019s collapse of the northern power grid that left an area inhabited by almost half of the population without electricity.  \u201cEverything is intact,\u201d said G. Anbunesan, chief of disaster management in the region at  Power System Operation Corp. , which operates the grid. \u201cSo far, there\u2019s no problem.\u201d  In the worst case, authorities would have the option of isolating Andhra Pradesh from the southern grid, according to Debasish Mishra, head of energy practice at Deloitte Touche Tohmatsu India Pvt. in Mumbai.  \u201cBecause of the blackouts, the load has already gone down significantly,\u201d he said. \u201cAs long as they are able to match the demand and supply, the grid should be fine.\u201d  Representatives of Google and Dr. Reddy\u2019s Laboratories said the companies have yet to be affected. Waze would let Google, owner of the world\u2019s most popular search engine, eliminate a threat to its home-grown navigation app. It would also keep a growing provider of mapping software away from other companies, including Facebook, the world\u2019s largest social network. The service also notifies drivers of road work, speed traps other potential hazards, using input from users. With free tools available over the Web and on mobile devices, Waze generates revenue via location-based advertising. A carried interest is an ownership interest in a\npartnership that entitles the partner to a percentage of the\nprofits but doesn\u2019t obligate the partner to provide any capital.\nIt is the other partners who provide the necessary capital, and\nthey are thereby \u201ccarrying\u201d the partner who does not.  A carried interest can arise in many contexts. It is fairly\ncommon on Main Street. My dad was a veterinarian who, as he got\nup in years, brought a young veterinarian into his practice.\nAlthough my dad did not call it that, the young veterinarian had\na carried interest -- that is a percentage of the profit with no\nobligation to invest capital.  Income from being a veterinarian is ordinary income, and\nthus the young partner with the carried interest paid  tax  on his\nshare of the partnership income at ordinary income rates. If the\nunderlying activity of the partnership, however, is an activity\nthat produces capital gains, then the partner with the carried\ninterest will have a share of the underlying capital gains and\nwill pay tax on that income at a 15 percent rate.  Different Income  That is the situation with a private-equity partnership\nwhose business is to buy companies and (it hopes) sell those\ncompanies a few years later at a profit. So, the only difference\nbetween an investor with a carried interest in a private-equity\npartnership and my dad\u2019s young veterinary partner is that the\nunderlying activity in private equity produces capital-gain\nincome, and Congress has chosen to tax capital-gain income at 15\npercent.  For a couple of years after President  Ronald Reagan \u2019s tax\nreforms were adopted in 1986, capital gains were taxed at the\nsame rate as ordinary income. That was very unusual. In most\nrecent years, capital gains have been taxed at a lower rate than\nordinary income, and the differential was increased by the Bush\ntax cuts. You can argue whether capital gains should be taxed at\n15 percent, but that is a big issue having only a little to do\nwith carried interest.  In all the years that capital gains have enjoyed a\nfavorable  tax rate , there has been a simple definition of what\nis a capital gain. It is simply gain on the sale of investment\nproperty, such as stock. The distinction between capital gain\nand ordinary income has never been based on the amount of sweat\nthat went into producing the income. The workaholic investor who\nspends 60 hours per week researching stocks still earns capital\ngains that are no different, in the tax law, from the gains of\nan investor who gives little thought to his portfolio.  Bill Gates  has a capital gain when he sells  Microsoft Corp. (MSFT) \nstock even though, by most accounts, Microsoft would not exist\nwithout his considerable effort. Similarly, the distinction\nbetween capital gains and ordinary income has never been based\non the amount of money invested or, indeed, whether there was\nany investment at all. An entrepreneur who starts a business\nwith no investment (or more likely an investment by someone else\nwith money) still generates capital gains on the sale of her\nbusiness, and it is sometimes said that this fact accounts for\nthe vibrancy of the tech economy in the  United States .  What then would be the basis for saying that a private-\nequity executive with a carried interest should have his\npercentage of the capital gain from the sale of an underlying\ninvestment recharacterized as ordinary income? Is it because he\nsweats and the other investors don\u2019t?  Well, maybe, but what about the full-time investor who\nsweats over his stock portfolio or the entrepreneur who slaved\nover her startup business. It is hard to make a distinction\nbased on effort.  Plus, most private-equity executives earn large cash\nsalaries that are taxed as ordinary income. Do we have to value\nthe executive\u2019s effort and see if it exceeds her cash salary,\nand then attribute that excess to the carried interest?  Tax Law Perspective  From the perspective of tax law, it just doesn\u2019t make sense\nto have a tax distinction based on the sweat of the private-\nequity executive. A distinction based on the fact that the\nprivate-equity executive with the carried interest provides no\ncapital to the partnership seems hard, too.  Do we really want a tax law in which only people who\nalready have money can earn a capital gain? And, if earning a\ncapital gain requires an investment, then how much? Does it have\nto be a big investment? Can it be borrowed from the other\npartners? Isn\u2019t a carried interest in effect just a loan from\nthe moneyed partners?  These are difficult questions that affect the entire\nstructure of capital-gains taxation -- not just carried\ninterest. It would be very hard to draw a fair line between the\ntype of private-equity investment that is deserving of capital\ngain treatment and that which is not.  It is perhaps not an accident that the carried interest\ndiscussion is taking place in the political arena -- over Mr.\nRomney\u2019s tax returns -- rather than the worlds of tax law or  tax\npolicy , and that the advocates of taxing carried interest at\nhigher rates are not tax experts who understand the complexity\nof the issue and the difficulty of drawing fair lines. That compared with\nthe $8.41 billion average  estimate  of analysts, according to\ndata compiled by Bloomberg. Profit before certain costs was\n$9.50 a share, missing the $10.50 average estimate. The  shares \nplunged as much as 10 percent.  Chief Executive Officer  Larry Page  is moving into new\nmarkets to ignite growth outside Google\u2019s traditional search-\nbased business. That effort contributed to an 8 percent drop in\nthe average price Google gets when users click an ad, because it\ncharges less for ads on mobile devices and in  emerging markets ,\nsaid  Herman Leung , an analyst at Susquehanna Financial Group. A\nstronger dollar also eroded the value of international sales.  \u201cGoogle is not invincible,\u201d said San Francisco-based\nLeung, who doesn\u2019t own the stock. \u201cEvery company is going to be\nsubject to growing pains.\u201d  Google  shares  tumbled to as low as $573 in extended trading\nafter the report. They had gained 1.1 percent to $639.57 at the\nclose in  New York . The stock climbed 8.7 percent last year.  International Sales  International sales made up 53 percent of revenue in the\nquarter, down from 55 percent in the third quarter, the company\nsaid. Online ad sales in  Europe  increased about 5 percent in the\nfourth quarter, compared with a 20 percent increase in the first\nhalf of last year, said Clay Moran, an analyst at Benchmark Co.,\nwho is based in  Delray Beach ,  Florida .  \u201cIn large part, it is due to Europe,\u201d  Sameet Sinha , an\nanalyst at B.
