Google\u2019s net income rose to $2.71 billion, or $8.22 a\nshare, compared with $2.54 billion, or $7.81 a share, a year\nearlier, the  Mountain View , California-based company said.\nOperating expenses rose to $3.38 billion, or 32 percent of\nrevenue, in the recent period. In the year-earlier quarter,\noperating costs equaled 30 percent of revenue, Google said.  \u201cOne of the major concerns here is given the performance\non the top line, what does the margin picture look like going\nforward?\u201d said Ken Sena, an analyst at Evercore Partners Inc.\nin New York, who rates Google shares \u201coverweight.\u201d  The number of total clicks on ads rose 34 percent during\nthe quarter, Google said.  Search Upgrades  The company has been working to offer customers more\noptions in mobile and display advertising, faster-growing\nmarkets than search-based ads. Google also has been investing in\nits search engine to improve the quality of results and bolster\nmarket share to stay ahead of  Microsoft Corp. (MSFT) \u2019s Bing service.  In  December , Google\u2019s share of U.S. searches rose to 65.9\npercent from 65.4 percent the previous month, according to\n ComScore Inc . Microsoft had 15.1 percent of searches, up from 15\npercent, while  Yahoo! Inc. (YHOO) \u2019s search engine accounted for 14.5\npercent.  Google is betting it can maintain its dominance in search\nby offering users faster, more personal query results. Last\nyear, Google rolled out the \u201cInstant Pages\u201d feature, which\naims to cut the time of searches for users by about 2 to 5\nseconds.  Social Searching  Earlier this month, Google introduced \u201cSearch, Plus Your\nWorld,\u201d intended to give users more personalized search results\nby tapping content from the Google+ social-networking service.\nThe search service lists items that users may have put on\nGoogle+ or related results from friends\u2019 posts on the social\nsite, which competes with Facebook Inc. The Google+ service now\nhas 90 million users globally, more than double the amount in\nOctober.  Still, Google\u2019s efforts to attract users have drawn\nregulatory scrutiny. More recently, the FTC expanded its antitrust probe of\nGoogle to include scrutiny of Google+, two people familiar with\nthe situation said last week. BlackRobe is one of a growing number of third-party\nlitigation financiers that fund lawsuits in exchange for a share\nof the recovery. The company targets investments of $2 million\nto $8 million in complex commercial litigation cases, including\nintellectual property, antitrust and breach of contract\ndisputes, that have the potential for damages in excess of $50\nmillion, Coffey said.  In addition to BlackRobe and Juridica, New York-based\nBurford Group also operates in the space targeting commercial\ndeals. The global market for litigation financing has grown to\nabout $5 billion, Clive Ward, managing director for Tangerine\nInternational Ltd., the promoter of a namesake lender to U.K.\nlaw firms, said last month.  While the firm doesn\u2019t provide legal advice, the three\npartners plan to be more actively involved in cases than just\nfinancing them, Coffey said. In addition to Chepiga, BlackRobe\nhas hired a handful of retired former litigators who help part-\ntime to evaluate cases. The firm, which is raising funds, has\nlooked at about 80 cases since last year and has closed\ninvestments in two, Coffey said. He declined to identify the\ninvestments. Now he\u2019s worried that a trade deal being negotiated by nine\nPacific-region nations including the U.S. may curtail access to\nthose cheap drugs in favor of patented pharmaceuticals, raising\ncosts to survive HIV\/AIDS in developing nations.  \u201cThis agreement is good for the rich countries,\u201d Low, 45,\nsaid during an interview in Washington. \u201cIt\u2019s not good for the\npoor countries.\u201d  Protecting the patents of drug makers including  Abbott\nLaboratories (ABT) ,  Bristol-Myers Squibb Co. (BMY)  and  GlaxoSmithKline Plc (GSK) \nas part of the Trans-Pacific Partnership has drawn criticism\nfrom groups such as Doctors Without Borders and  Public Citizen .\nThe proposed accord has also spurred calls from U.S. lawmakers\nfor greater transparency about the negotiations, while\ntechnology companies including  Microsoft Corp. (MSFT)  and  Symantec\nCorp. (SYMC)  are urging fewer restrictions on cross-border data flows.  While the advocacy groups claim the U.S. position in the\ntalks favors patented medicines, not just those for HIV\/AIDS,\nadministration officials say affordability and innovation aren\u2019t\nmutually exclusive goals.  Twin Goals  The U.S. cited two goals in the talks: \u201cPreserving the\nintellectual property protections that spur innovation in the\npharmaceutical industry in a way that also drives access to\nmedicines in the developing world,\u201d  Carol Guthrie , a\nspokeswoman for the U.S. Trade Representative\u2019s office, said in\nan e-mail.  The multilateral talks, the main accord being pursued by\nPresident  Barack Obama \u2019s administration, would create an\neconomic zone with $20.5 trillion in output, according to a\nCanadian estimate. Talks that began with Australia, Brunei,\nChile, Malaysia,  New Zealand ,  Peru , Singapore, the U.S. and\nVietnam may expand after the parties invited Canada and Mexico.  A final agreement probably will encompass traditional\nissues including agriculture and intellectual property, as well\ninvestment and protections for businesses that compete against\nstate-owned enterprises, according to the trade office.  HIV Populations  The number of people living with HIV in the nine nations\nvaries from a low of 49 in Brunei, or about 0.01 percent of its\npopulation last year, to 1.2 million, or 0.39 percent of the\n U.S. population  in 2010, according to reports submitted by the\ncountries to the  UNAIDS  Secretariat in Geneva.  U.S. negotiators in September proposed eliminating duties\non medicines and setting a deadline for drug companies to bring\ntheir products to market by giving them access to nations in the\npact and creating a \u201cpathway\u201d for generics. The strategy is\naimed at promoting access to medicines while protecting\nintellectual property for the products.  \u201cAn effective, transparent and predictable intellectual\nproperty system is necessary for both manufacturers of\ninnovative medicines and manufacturers of generic medicines,\u201d\naccording to a U.S. briefing document.  \u201cWe\u2019ve gotten a lot of comments and criticism about our\nproposal that we are reflecting upon very carefully,\u201d Deputy\nU.S. Trade Representative Demetrios Marantis said today at a\nconference in Washington.  HIV patients take a daily  regimen  of at least three\nantiretroviral medications -- such as Bristol-Myers\u2019 Sustiva,\nGlaxo\u2019s Ziagen and Abbott\u2019s Kaletra -- from two or more\ndifferent drug classes to manage the virus, according to the\n U.S. Department of Health  and Human Services.  Generic Costs  The price of initial treatments in developing countries has\ndeclined about 99 percent, to less than $150 per person a year\nfrom $10,000 in 2000 as generic medicines become more prevalent,\naccording to a July analysis by humanitarian organization\nDoctors Without Borders.  Under a 1995 multilateral agreement, which sets minimum\nintellectual-property standards, patents are protected for at\nleast 20 years. U.S. Trade Representative  Ron Kirk  has said the\nU.S. and the partner nations will implement the agreement in a\nway that supports public health.  Advocacy and development groups that have seen documents in\nthe negotiations said the U.S. position offers too many\nprotections to existing patent holders, such as letting\nmanufacturers extend their patents by modifying existing brand-\nname products. The U.S. Trade Representative\u2019s office hasn\u2019t\nconfirmed the authenticity of those documents.  Deter Copies  Broader patent protections deter production of generics,\nand treatment costs rise as patients switch regimens after\ndeveloping resistance to their original medications, according\nto Burcu Kilic, legal counsel for Public Citizen\u2019s Global Access\nto Medicines program in Washington.  \u201cWe need the generic companies to enter the market\u201d to\nbring down the price for HIV\/AIDS drugs, she said in a phone\ninterview.  Karl Uhlendorf, a spokesman for the  Pharmaceutical Research\nand Manufacturers of America , the Washington-based industry\ngroup for patent holders including Bristol-Myers,  Pfizer Inc. (PFE) ,\nAbbott and  Merck & Co. (MRK) , said in an e-mail that intellectual-\nproperty protection isn\u2019t a barrier to patient access to\nmedicines.  \u2018High Standards\u2019  \u201cThe negotiations should sustain the high standards on\nintellectual-property rights that are a hallmark of U.S. law,\u201d\nSenator  Claire McCaskill , a Missouri Democrat, said in an Aug. 6\nletter to Obama, echoing statements by Democrats from\nMassachusetts and Washington state.  Intellectual-property revenue is \u201cone of America\u2019s big\nstrengths in the world economy\u201d and patent protections provide\nincentives for future medicines, said Edward Gresser, a policy\nadviser at USTR during President  Bill Clinton \u2019s administration.  \u201cYou really need to look illness by illness\u201d to determine\nif there\u2019s an issue with access to medicines, he said in a phone\ninterview. \u201cThere\u2019s vastly more income being provided to low-\nincome cases\u201d of HIV\/AIDS than 10 years ago, he said.  \u201cTrade policy alone cannot solve the challenges relating\nto access to medicines,\u201d the agency said in its report dealing\nwith pharmaceuticals in the Pacific talks. Poor drug\ndistribution networks and infrastructure systems in  developing\ncountries  also limit access to HIV treatments, it said.  The next round of talks is set for Sept. 6-15 in Leesburg,\nVirginia. The public, industry, health and development experts\nand federal agencies can attend, as they have in the past,\naccording to the trade representative\u2019s office.  Groups that work with HIV\/AIDS patients say it\u2019s important\nthat negotiators get the balance right between access and\ninnovation.  \u201cIt\u2019s a matter of life or death,\u201d Low said. In a conversation with a reporter, Amelio compared Apple to a ship loaded with treasure, but with a hole in the bottom, leaking water. \"My job is to get everyone to row in the same direction.\" When Steve Jobs  later recounted the story  at a conference panel in 2010, the audience erupted in laughter. But the metaphor, while it may seem bungled at first glance, actually describes the way many leaders approach strategy. There's a big hole in the enterprise \u2014 a gap that, until it is filled, will not let them meaningfully execute any strategy. Instead of trying to figure out what they're missing, and solve their biggest issues, they focus on finding a direction, any direction, to try to steer their ship.  The history of business strategy \u2014 which is  still a relatively new field , emerging only in the last 50 years \u2014 is essentially a series of theories of how to create value. Most strategists through the years have been similarly focused on picking a direction and getting everyone to steer in harmony. While the many schools of strategy, from adjacency positioning (\"we'll expand to similar markets\") to the  search for blue oceans  (\"we'll serve a market no one else does\") have different ideas about what direction is best, most of them involve the same underlying quest for some sweet theory of success that, once it's found, will be all leaders needs to know where to steer the company. It's understandable that decision makers want to start there, because most business choices seem, at first glance, to deal with the destination: Where shall we grow? Which industries should we expand to? What markets should we serve?    But in the real world, the choice of a direction is just one element of strategy. It must be integrated with choices about one's identity, purpose, and capabilities. Strategy is what Harvard Professor Cynthia Montgomery calls a \"fundamental question that any company's leader must ultimately answer: What will this firm be, and why will it matter?\" The value proposition may be based on a theory of success, but it can also be based on a company's capabilities \u2014 what it does particularly well \u2014 or on some other aspects of a company's history and proficiency. If there's an internal gap, or an internal problem preventing the company from realizing its potential, that can be as powerful a strategic barrier as any market failure.  Those who want to be effective strategists thus have a lot to sort through \u2014 multiple value creation theories, and scores of approaches on creating strategy (with hundreds of books with advice on the topic). What if, instead of looking for one solution that works for everything, business strategists looked for ways to improve their own judgment and strategic focus? We think one approach to building this judgment is to look more freshly at the companies in your own industry. Who is winning and how are they doing it? What are the key drivers of your company's success? These are not simple questions, and that is why the topic of strategy still seems quite unsolved to many. But if you spend some time thinking about companies this way, you will find your own discernment \u2014 of internal and external factors \u2014 can improve.  We've discovered that, for ourselves, in an online survey we designed in which we invite people to look at company strategies. Most people, for example, recognize that different companies in the same industry approach strategy in very different ways \u2014 and this difference, in itself, drives their competitive advantage. This has been particularly evident in the personal computer industry, where  Apple's success,  is generally attributed to its capabilities \u2014 including its innate, artistic understanding of design and human behavior \u2014 while Microsoft's success is driven by great market resonance of a few powerful products.  Or consider the financial services and insurance sector, where companies may, in the future, owe their success less to their ability to manipulate capital, and more to their abilities in customer service and product innovation. Perhaps that's why we're finding that many respondents believe that most of the companies in their industry \u2014 including their own company \u2014 lack what they need to compete and create value in the marketplace.   We invite you to join us in learning more about the fundamental strategic choices companies make and how successful these have turned out to be.  The survey that we developed  \u2014 which takes about 10 minutes to complete \u2014 poses the question \"What drives a company's success?\", based on the companies that you observe (and that you work for). If you take it, we'll provide you with an analysis of what you and your competitors see as the key strategic success factors in your industry. As a side effect \u2014 or maybe as the primary outcome \u2014 you will be able to test your strategic judgment against those of others, and perhaps gain a better sense of the right direction for your enterprise. Microsoft Corp. (MSFT) ,  Apple Inc (AAPL) . and  Google Inc (GOOG) . each added to their non-U.S. holdings by more than 34 percent as they reaped the benefits of past maneuvers to earn and park profits in low- tax countries. Combined, those three companies alone plan to keep $134.5 billion outside the U.S. government\u2019s reach, more than double the $59.3 billion they held two years earlier.  The build-up of offshore profits -- totaling $1.46 trillion for the 83 companies examined -- is increasing because of incentives in the U.S.  tax code  for booking profits offshore and leaving them there. The stockpiles complicate attempts to overhaul the tax system as lawmakers look for ways to bring the money home and discourage profit shifting.  \u201cThe corporate system is broken and it\u2019s broken primarily because of international,\u201d said Edward Kleinbard, a tax law professor at the University of  Southern California .  The ability to defer U.S. taxes until profits are brought home, the ease of shifting profits to low-tax countries and the world\u2019s highest statutory corporate rate have all contributed to the growing stockpiles outside the U.S.  A report last year by analysts at  JPMorgan Chase & Co (JPM) . estimated that all U.S.-based companies had $1.7 trillion in accumulated offshore profits. In the data compiled by Bloomberg, 83 companies had about 75 percent of last year\u2019s total, which suggests that the total for all companies now exceeds $1.9 trillion.  $108 Billion  General Electric Co (GE) . again leads all U.S. companies with $108 billion held offshore, up from $102 billion a year earlier. Pfizer Inc. is second with $73 billion, followed by Microsoft, Merck & Co.,  Johnson & Johnson (JNJ)  and International Business Machines Corp. The data comes from companies\u2019 annual regulatory filings.  Eleven companies, including Apple,  Cisco Systems Inc. (CSCO)  and Citigroup Inc., have at least $40 billion in profits reinvested overseas, up from six companies that had crossed that mark last year and three the year before that.  The data compiled by Bloomberg examined 83 U.S.-based companies that each reported holding more than $4 billion in earnings outside the country indefinitely in one of the past two years.  Foreign Parents  It excluded companies such as Eaton Corp. that now have foreign parents, and it also excluded  United Technologies Corp (UTX) ., which disclosed a $22 billion balance this year and hadn\u2019t reported the numbers before then.  The analysis relies on the most recent filings for the companies. Those with fiscal years that end Dec. 31 filed their 10-Ks over the past few weeks.  Apple,  whose stock  has fallen 38.7 percent from its Sept. 19 closing high of $702.10, has been under pressure to return cash to investors in the form a dividend or buyback. Chief Executive Officer  Tim Cook  has said the money isn\u2019t burning a hole in the company\u2019s pockets and that it\u2019s considering different strategies to reward investors with a new payout.  A reason for the overseas cash growth can be linked in part to Apple\u2019s performance. Sales in  Asia ,  Europe  and  Australia  rose 43.7 percent to $80.2 billion in fiscal 2012. Unlike most other U.S.-based companies, Apple has already taken  accounting charges  for eventual taxes on some of its unrepatriated foreign holdings and reports an associated deferred tax liability of $14.7 billion.  Cash Holdings  The company\u2019s permanently reinvested overseas earnings were $40.4 billion while its foreign cash holdings were $82.6 billion, as of Sept. 29, 2012.  Steve Dowling, a spokesman for Apple, declined to comment.  The Securities and Exchange Commission has asked some companies, including Google, to assert that they have enough liquidity in the U.S. to justify their contention that the offshore money will stay overseas indefinitely.  Google wrote in its  annual filing  that $31.4 billion, or 65.3 percent, of its liquid holdings were outside the U.S.  \u201cOur current plans do not demonstrate a need to repatriate them to fund our U.S. operations,\u201d the filing said.  Niki Fenwick, a spokeswoman for Google, declined to comment.  Twelve of the 83 companies in the analysis reduced their offshore holdings from the previous year\u2019s level, including  Exxon Mobil Corp (XOM) .,  Las Vegas Sands Corp (LVS) . and  General Motors Co (GM) .  Vegas Sands  Las Vegas Sands in 2012, according to its filing, repatriated $1.37 billion tax-free because it had enough foreign tax credits. The company said it would consider future foreign earnings not to be indefinitely reinvested, and its total accumulated earnings declined to $4.3 billion from $5.6 billion the year before.  Exxon Mobil\u2019s holdings declined to $43 billion from $47 billion, in part because of a restructuring of its operations in  Japan .  The U.S. operates what is known as a worldwide tax system, which means the country applies its 35 percent corporate tax rate to profits that U.S.-based companies earn around the world. Most other industrialized nations impose minimal taxes, if any, on their companies\u2019 foreign earnings.  Tax Credits  U.S. companies receive foreign tax credits for payments to other countries, meaning that they can bring home previously taxed earnings with little residual tax owed to the U.S. They also can defer the U.S. tax until they bring the profits home.  \u201cIf you lowered the corporate tax rate, some of these problems, they don\u2019t go away, but they\u2019re reduced,\u201d said Rob Atkinson, president of the  Information Technology  and Innovation Foundation, a Washington-based group that promotes policies favoring technological innovation. The group\u2019s board includes executives from Microsoft, Apple, Cisco and  Intel Corp (INTC) .  In their annual regulatory filings, companies are required to report foreign profits that haven\u2019t been repatriated and for which they haven\u2019t provided for U.S. taxes.  The balances aren\u2019t necessarily held in cash and may never realistically be subject to U.S. taxes, particularly if invested in physical assets in high-taxed foreign countries, said Susan Morse, a tax law professor at the  University of California , Hastings.  \u201cIn many cases, it really is permanently reinvested and it\u2019s not an earnings management game,\u201d she said.  A 2011 report by Senator  Carl Levin , a Michigan Democrat, found that 46 percent of offshore assets held by a subset of 27 companies was invested in U.S. banks or assets, suggesting that it does flow to some extent through the  U.S. economy .  Intangible Assets  The incentive to accumulate overseas profits in cash is acute for technology and pharmaceutical companies that generate income from intangible assets such as patents. They can sell the patents to their foreign subsidiaries and then shift them to low-tax jurisdictions and book the profits there.  \u201cThey\u2019re using the law to their advantage, as all companies do,\u201d Atkinson said. \u201cAnd it\u2019s easier to do that with intangible income.\u201d  That pattern is evident from the filings of the minority of companies that disclose how much they would have to pay if they brought their offshore profits home.  Microsoft, for example,  reported that  it would owe $19.4 billion if it repatriated its $60.8 billion in offshore holdings. That 31.9 percent rate indicates that Microsoft has paid as little as 3.1 percent in foreign taxes, or somewhat more if the $19.4 billion includes state taxes and foreign withholding taxes.  \u2018Outdated\u2019 System  In testimony before a Senate subcommittee last year, Bill Sample, Microsoft\u2019s corporate vice president for worldwide tax, said the U.S. tax system is \u201coutdated,\u201d uncompetitive and provides disincentives for U.S. investment.  \u201cMicrosoft\u2019s tax results follow from its business, which is fundamentally a global business that requires us to operate in foreign markets in order to compete and grow,\u201d he said. \u201cIn conducting our business at home and abroad, we abide by U.S. and foreign tax laws as written.\u201d  Citigroup reported that it would owe $11.5 billion if it repatriated its $42.6 billion, suggesting a foreign  tax rate  as low as 8 percent.  \u2018Know How\u2019  \u201cMore companies know how to do it,\u201d said Kleinbard, a former chief of staff of the congressional Joint Committee on Taxation who said international tax-avoidance techniques are spreading. \u201cThey\u2019ve learned the technologies from the innovative leaders, the tax technology leaders.\u201d  U.S. lawmakers are examining changes to international taxation as part of a tax-code rewrite that would have to address the built-up earnings in a transition to a new system.  Senators  Ron Wyden , an Oregon Democrat, and  Rob Portman , an  Ohio Republican , said last month that they saw room for an international system that would lower the U.S. tax rate, let companies bring home new profits mostly tax-free and limit companies\u2019 ability to move profits out of the U.S.  That would mirror the proposals offered by Senator  Mike Enzi , a Wyoming Republican, and Representative  Dave Camp , a Michigan Republican and chairman of the House Ways and Means Committee.  Camp\u2019s proposal  would impose a 5.25 percent tax on the accumulated earnings, whether repatriated or not, payable over eight years.  That plan, released in 2011, will eventually be part of a tax code overhaul that Camp plans to push through his committee this year. Legislation that created the Securities and Exchange Commission in 1934 also deemed the main venues self-regulatory organizations, or SROs, overseeing their member firms and trading. (MSFT)  is sticking with a\ndecision to make it harder to track users\u2019 online behavior,\nearning plaudits from privacy groups while drawing fire from the\nadvertisers its money-losing Web unit needs most.  After months of criticism that the new tools cut off\nvaluable customer-targeting information, the software maker has\nno plans to change the automatic setting in its newest Internet\nExplorer browser that tells websites not to track user behavior,\nGeneral Counsel Brad Smith said in an interview.  \u201cWe crossed the Rubicon and are completely comfortable\nbeing on the other side of the river,\u201d he said. \u201cWe have no\nintention of going back and have no intention of engaging in\ndiscussion on that possibility.\u201d Smith will provide an update\non the company\u2019s position today in a  blog posting .  The so-called Do Not Track feature has been at the center\nof privacy debates over browsing data and how websites and\nmarketers use it to make money. For Microsoft and the\nadvertisers, at stake is a $31.7 billion U.S. Internet ad market\nthat  grew  22 percent in 2011, according to the Interactive\nAdvertising Bureau, much of it generated by ads tailored to user\nbehavior. Inc. (YHOO) , who say they\nwill ignore privacy signals transmitted by Internet Explorer 10.  \u2018Achilles Heel\u2019  \u201cAdvertisers have invested a lot in their ad platforms and\nthe Achilles heel is the consumers aren\u2019t aware that their data\nis being bought and sold,\u201d said  Anthony Mullen , an analyst at\nForrester Research Inc. \u201cThat being exposed, which is what this\nMicrosoft initiative does, is healthy, but I can see why the ad\nindustry is nervous.\u201d  Microsoft wants to engage in talks with advertisers and\nstandards bodies to assuage some concerns, Smith said. For Redmond, Washington-based Microsoft, the world\u2019s\nlargest software maker, the kerfuffle is the latest challenge to\nits ad business. The company wrote down $6.2 billion from the\nunit in the quarter that ended June 30, and Microsoft\u2019s U.S.\ndisplay business is forecast to grow 13 percent this year, while\nthe total U.S. market for display ads expands by more than 20\npercent, according to data from EMarketer Inc.  Limited Use  For now, a lot of the debate over Do Not Track is just\nsaber-rattling. Internet Explorer 10 was released on Oct. 26\nwith the newest Windows software, so it\u2019s not in use on many\nsystems yet. Advertisers are unlikely to pull listings from\nMicrosoft\u2019s websites in retaliation if the ads make money, said\nClark Fredricksen, a vice president at EMarketer.  Still, advertising industry groups are concerned that\nMicrosoft may crimp future ad-spending growth by creating a\nlarger group of Web users who object to being tracked.  Almost all sites collect browsing data and track Web\nsurfers\u2019 habits to decide which ads to show consumers, and use\nthe demographic information to persuade advertisers to buy\nspace. Without this information, ads would be far less\neffective, making it harder to generate the ad revenue that\nLiodice said pays for much of the content on the Internet.  Privacy Complaints  In response to a 2007 complaint by privacy groups such as\nthe Electronic Frontier Foundation and the Consumer Federation\nof America about the tracking and selling of private user data,\nthe U.S. Federal Trade Commission began examining the idea of a\nDo Not Track list. Do Not Track now works by having a browser\nsend a signal to websites, stating that the user doesn\u2019t want\nhis or her behavior to be monitored. As the feature was\nenvisioned, advertisers would voluntarily comply.  All the major browser makers -- Microsoft,  Google Inc. (GOOG)  and\nMozilla Corp. -- have incorporated Do Not Track signals into\ntheir products. Google and Mozilla have the setting turned off\nas a default, requiring users to actively turn it on to block\ntracking.  For now it\u2019s not even clear how advertisers wanting to\ncomply with Do Not Track should behave. A World Wide Web\nConsortium working group tasked with devising a standard for Do\nNot Track has labored for about 18 months without coming to an\nagreement.  Surprise Decision  Microsoft\u2019s move was surprising to people both inside and\noutside the company. The Internet Explorer team made the\ndecision over the objections of some of Microsoft\u2019s advertising\nofficials, said people familiar with the matter, who asked not\nto be named because the decision was confidential.  Before the announcement, even Microsoft officials on the Do\nNo Track working group had raised questions about whether it\nmade sense to turn the signal on by default, said Jonathan Mayer, a member of the group and a Stanford University graduate\nstudent who is one of the researchers who came up with the\ninitial idea for the standard.  The Internet Explorer group itself, though, decided that\nstarting with the setting activated was the best way to protect\nconsumers.  \u201cSeventy-five percent of the consumers we surveyed in the\nU.S. and  Europe  said they wanted DNT on by default,\u201d\nMicrosoft\u2019s Smith wrote in an October blog post.  Google Challenge  Microsoft may also be aiming to use privacy as a stick to\nbeat rival Google with, Mayer said. Google\u2019s Chrome browser has\n gained  share, rising to 15 percent of the market last month from\n10 percent at the end of 2010, according to Net Applications.\nInternet Explorer fell to 48 percent from 57 percent. Google is\nalso poised to seize the No. 1 spot in the display-ad market\nthis year from Facebook, EMarketer forecasts.  Still, it\u2019s not clear whether the more consumer-oriented\napproach will win Microsoft any Chrome users, and it has already\nalienated one group -- big advertisers.  In its October  letter  to Microsoft, Liodice\u2019s Association\nof National Advertisers said the default Do Not Track setting\nwill hurt advertising, reduce the amount of Internet content\nsupported by those ads and ultimately \u201cundermine American\ninnovation and leadership in the Internet economy.\u201d  Both that association and the Digital Advertising Alliance\nare recommending advertisers ignore Do Not Track signals coming\nfrom Internet Explorer 10. Yahoo, the biggest U.S. Web portal\nand Microsoft\u2019s partner in search, has said it will ignore the\nsetting.  Consumer Information  \u201cThe Internet is funded by advertisers,\u201d Liodice said.\n\u201cThe ability to reach our consumers requires that we absorb\ninformation from them.\u201d  And even if Microsoft and the advertisers can make peace,\nDo Not Track still faces major challenges. Every Wednesday at 9\na.m. San Francisco time, Mayer spends 90 minutes on a conference\ncall with other members of the workgroup and any advertisers or\nindustry members that want to join. There\u2019s been no progress\ntoward agreeing on a standard to guide advertisers on how to\nabide by Do Not Track, he said.  \u201cEverything that could be said has been said,\u201d he said.\n\u201cThere are fundamental differences of opinion.\u201d  To contact the reporter on this story:\nDina Bass in Seattle at   dbass2@bloomberg.net   To contact the editor responsible for this story:\nTom Giles at   tgiles5@bloomberg.net","path":".\/2008_2012_msft_bloomberg_news\/icrosoft-rankles-advertisers-with-web-user-privacy-plan.txt"},{"id":8760256,"title":"Microsoft-Sony Battle Broadens to Romance Games at Show","released_at":"<date>September 18 2013<\/date> <time>09:58:35<\/time>","content":"Microsoft Corp. The agreement allows customers to review privacy policies\nfor apps before they download it rather than after, and it\nrequires the companies to disclose to consumers what information\nthey collect, how they use it and who it is shared with,\naccording to the statement.  In six months, the companies will meet with Harris to\n\u201cassess privacy\u201d in mobile networks, she said in the\nstatement. As a warning, it\u2019s\ndistinctly unnerving.  \u201c Worm \u201d is the story of Conficker, a nasty piece of\nsoftware injected into the Internet\u2019s bloodstream in 2008. Since\nthen it has infected millions of computers worldwide, assembling\nthe largest-ever \u201cbotnet\u201d -- a drone army of machines that,\nunknown to their owners, might be ordered at any time to unleash\ndigital havoc that could bring down global communications\nsystems, power grids, perhaps the very Internet itself.  Where did Conficker come from, and who was or is behind it?\nNo one knows, including Bowden, the author of \u201c Black Hawk\nDown .\u201d Perhaps it\u2019s the Ukrainians, or the Chinese, or a \u201cdark\nSymantec\u201d -- a commercial criminal enterprise established as\nthe mirror image of the well-known Internet security firm.\nWhoever they were, though, they clearly knew what they were\ndoing.  The worm combined the best-of-breed malevolence from\nprevious malware exploits -- chronicled here in sometimes mind-\nnumbing detail -- with unique advancements of its own. Once it\ninfected a computer, it would repair the Microsoft Windows\nsecurity breach it had exploited, preventing competitors from\ncoming in behind it. It would also stealthily thwart any effort\nby the computer\u2019s owner to install a cure. And then, like a\nterrorist sleeper cell, it would simply await instructions from\nits unknown master.  Justice League of Nerds  Combating this mortal threat was an ad hoc group of\nsecurity experts calling itself the Cabal -- in Bowden\u2019s\ntelling, a sort of  Justice League of America  of computer nerds\ndesperately racing against time, official indifference and its\nown internal divisions to head off computergeddon.  They included representatives from Microsoft, think-tanks\nand the loosely organized bodies that pass for the Internet\u2019s\ngoverning authorities, as well as assorted other industry\nconsultants.  Conspicuously absent was any representative of the U.S.\ngovernment, despite repeated efforts to engage it. The silence\nfrom official quarters proved baffling, until the truth dawned\non the Cabal. \u201cThe real reason for the feds\u2019 silence was ...\nthey had nothing to offer!\u201d Bowden writes. \u201cThey were in way\nover their heads.\u201d  With a deadline of April 1, 2009, when the botnet was\nprogrammed to become operational, the Cabal struggled to unpeel\nConficker\u2019s protective layers, figure out how it worked and head\nit off.  Checking In  Every day, the worm would create and check in with long\nlists of randomly generated Internet domains, behind any one of\nwhich its master might lurk. Only as the date approached on\nwhich the zombie army would rouse to life did the populace at\nlarge become aware of its peril. The New York Times ran\narticles. \u201c60 Minutes\u201d did a segment. The world held its\nbreath.  And then ... nothing. The mighty beast shuddered, sent a\nlittle spam and then lapsed back into whatever digital muck\nspawned it.  Or did it? Bowden makes a case that the unknown botmaster\u2019s\ngoal wasn\u2019t to unleash a single crippling attack but to create\nan infrastructure that can be exploited at will in the future.  \u2018Marshaled for Attack\u2019  \u201cThe Conficker botnet, this enormous concentration of\ncomputer power, had been assembled and was still in the hands of\nits mysterious creators,\u201d he writes. In hacker jargon, the\nmillions of infected machines remained \u201cpwned, or owned, and\nthey could be turned to any task the botmaster defined. They\ncould be leased for plunder or marshaled for attack.\u201d  The author does his best to maintain the story\u2019s dramatic\ntension. But a combination of factors -- the lengthy history of\nmalware near the beginning of the book, the lack of knowledge on\nwho perpetrated Conficker and why -- all conspire to make\n\u201cWorm\u201d an oddly unsatisfying yarn.  So, too, does a series of annoying factual errors. Personal\ncomputers were widely available in 1984, contrary to the book\u2019s\nassertion. Microsoft\u2019s first product, for the pioneering Altair\nmicrocomputer, was a BASIC language interpreter, not an\noperating system. And so on.  As a cautionary tale, though, \u201cWorm\u201d is worth attention.\nGovernment officials up to and including President Obama have\ntaken notice of Conficker and begun to address some of the\nissues it raised. But you\u2019ll probably put \u201cWorm\u201d down with the\nthought that cyberspace is just as dangerous as the physical\nworld we inhabit.  \u201cWorm: The First Digital World War\u201d is published by\nAtlantic Monthly Press (245 pages, $25). Because we hold others accountable for disclosure, we expect the same of ourselves. While disclosing errors of judgment may be embarrassing, the sooner the lapses are reported, the sooner there is nothing more to say.\u201d  We are defined by our words -- and they applied to us when a Bloomberg LP customer expressed concern that  Bloomberg News  reporters had access to limited client information. Our client is right. Our reporters should not have access to any data considered proprietary. I am sorry they did. The error is inexcusable. Last month, we immediately changed our policy so that reporters now have no greater access to information than our customers have. Removing this access will have no effect on Bloomberg news-gathering.  Now let\u2019s also be clear what our reporters had access to. First, they could see a user\u2019s login history and when a login was created. Second, they could see high-level types of user functions on an aggregated basis, with no ability to look into specific security information. This is akin to being able to see how many times someone used Microsoft Word vs. Excel. And, finally, they could see information about help desk inquiries.  Why did reporters have access to this in the first place? The recent complaints go to practices that are almost as old as Bloomberg News. Since the 1990s, some reporters have used the terminal to obtain, as the Washington Post reported, \u201cmundane\u201d facts such as log-on information. There was good reason for this, as our reporters used to go to clients in the early days of the company and ask them what topics they wanted to see covered. Understanding how clients used the terminal was more important then. We still do that today, which is why we have feedback tabs on our news-related terminal functions. Equally important is our commitment to transparency, which is why \u201cThe Bloomberg Way\u201d is a public document.  As we\u2019ve grown, and as data privacy has become a central concern to our clients, we should go above and beyond in protecting data, especially when we have even the appearance of impropriety. And that\u2019s why we\u2019ve made these recent changes to what reporters can access.  This leads to a second point lost in much of this weekend\u2019s conversation: The protection of important customer data has been essential at Bloomberg since our founding more than 30 years ago. We have never compromised the integrity of that data in our reporting.  At no time did reporters have access to trading, portfolio, monitor, blotter or other related systems. Nor did they have access to clients\u2019 messages to one another. They couldn\u2019t see the stories that clients were reading or the securities clients might be looking at.  Like all other Bloomberg employees, our reporters, upon hiring, enter into a confidentiality agreement that strictly prohibits them from discussing non-public Bloomberg documents and proprietary information about the company and its clients in their reporting.  Our editorial and reporting standards have been among the most stringent in the business for more than 20 years. We apologize for our error as it does not reflect on our culture or our heritage. And we will strive to continue to uphold the highest standards while adhering to the best practices in the industry as long as we may be fortunate to serve our customers as they would have us serve them.  ( Matthew Winkler  is the editor-in-chief of Bloomberg News. The opinions expressed are his own.)  Read Bloomberg chief executive officer Daniel L. The group, which is scrutinizing the data harvesting by the\nNational Security Agency, relies on the government\u2019s spy office\n-- the very people it\u2019s supposed to be examining -- for its\nstaff and logistics. Panel members are Richard Clarke, a former U.S.\ncybersecurity adviser; Michael Morell, a former deputy CIA\ndirector; Geoffrey Stone, a  University of Chicago  law professor;\nCass Sunstein, a Harvard Law School professor who once worked in\nthe administration; and Peter Swire, who served on Obama\u2019s\nNational Economic Council.  \u201cThey\u2019re driven by an earnest desire to do right that is\nthrough the lens of an incredibly biased perspective,\u201d Meinrath\nsaid. \u201cThey either are directly or have been part of the\nintelligence community or the Obama administration.\u201d  Stakeholder Concerns  The panel\u2019s final report, due to the president by Dec. 15,\nfollows interim findings delivered orally at the White House\nearlier this month and two private meetings held in September,\naccording to participants.  The options for changes at the NSA, floated by\nstakeholders, lawmakers and the administration, cover everything\nfrom limiting the scope of the surveillance programs to\nexpanding public disclosure and strengthening oversight.  Two qualifications each panelist had on his side when Obama\ntapped him: a security clearance to review the NSA\u2019s classified\nprograms -- and being steeped in Washington policy or politics.  One example of those ties: At a Nov. 14 awards banquet for\nthe Middle East Institute, Clarke, who is chairman of the board\nof governors, was hailed by Obama\u2019s National Security Adviser\n Susan Rice . Stone, a former faculty colleague of Obama\u2019s at the\nUniversity of Chicago law school, also was involved in an effort\nto consider establishing the president\u2019s library at the campus,\naccording to a 2012 story in  Politico .  Swire, who also served in the Clinton administration as a\nprivacy expert, was tapped last year as co-chairman of a World\nWide Web Consortium working group charged with defining a\nprotocol to protect privacy.  The panelists declined to be interviewed. Revelations of NSA spying may cost the U.S. cloud industry\nas much as $35 billion by 2016, the  Information Technology\nIndustry Council , which represents more than 50 companies,\nincluding Google and Facebook, and the Software Information\nIndustry Association told the panel in a letter.  Losing Market  They cited an August report by the  Information Technology \nand Innovation Foundation, which predicted the U.S. would lose\nas much as 20 percent of the foreign market for cloud computing\nto competitors as a result of the NSA\u2019s surveillance programs. In mapping the ways the genes link to the brain\u2019s\nstructures, researchers at the  Allen Institute for Brain\nScience , funded by  Microsoft Corp. (MSFT)  co-founder Paul Allen, found\nthat the vast majority of the 20,000 genes in the human genome\nplay a role in the organ\u2019s function and architecture. That\u2019s\nmore than in any other organ in the body, according to the\nreport published today in the journal  Nature .  Figuring out how the brain is built and organized may help\nscientists studying diseases, by pointing out which part of the\norgan uses a gene that previous research has shown to be faulty,\nsaid Seth Grant, a professor at Edinburgh University and a study\nauthor. The data outlines 400 to 500 distinct brain areas in\neach hemisphere.  \u201cThe human brain is the most complex structure known to\nmankind,\u201d Grant said in a telephone interview. \u201cThis allows us\nfor the first time to overlay the human genome on the human\nbrain.\u201d  Two brains from male donors ages 24 and 39 were mapped, and\nthe genes\u2019 expression between the two were very similar. Before\ntoday it wasn\u2019t clear how alike any two brains would be. These\ntwo organs were of similar age, gender, and ethnicity. Their\nhigh degree of similarity suggests a \u201cstrong underlying common\nblueprint\u201d for all human brains, the scientists wrote.  Ambitious Project  The group analyzed tissue from about 900 sites of the\nbrains as well as a half of a third specimen and used more than\n60,000 gene expression probes to establish the information,\naccording to the report.  \u201cIt\u2019s breathtaking in its ambition,\u201d said  Steve\nMcCarroll , the director of genetics for the Stanley Center for\nPsychiatric Research at the Broad Institute in Cambridge,\n Massachusetts . He wasn\u2019t involved in the study. \u201cI was amazed\nto see how many anatomically defined sites they\u2019d actually\ndissected out of each brain. In the effort to make a geographic\natlas of regional gene expression it goes really far beyond\nanything that\u2019s been done before.\u201d  Scientists have begun to identify a number of genes with\nclear relevance to mental illness, McCarroll said. However, most\nresearchers aren\u2019t sure what these genes do in the body, and\nhaving the atlas may help for future steps, he said. For\ninstance, if a gene is identified as a schizophrenia risk\nfactor, knowing where it\u2019s expressed in the brain may help\nexplain why patients behave the way they do.  Brain Differences  There will probably be differences between male and female\nbrains, said  Ed Lein , a co-investigator at the Allen Institute,\nand one of the study authors. The group started with male brains\nbecause there were more of them available, he said. Previous\nwork the Institute has done in rodents suggests there would be\ndifferences.  The Institute\u2019s previous  gene atlas  of a mouse brain, when\ncompared to today\u2019s human blueprint, may help drug companies\ndevelop better psychiatric medicines, Lein said. Since many\ntreatments work well in mouse models and fail in human trials,\nknowing how the two systems differ on a fine-grained level may\nhelp pharmaceutical companies avoid expensive failures in the\nfuture, Lein said.  Paul Allen and his sister Jody Allen Patton founded the\nSeattle-based institute to undertake neuroscience research.  Paul\nAllen  has committed $500 million to the institute as of 2012,\naccording to its  website . No one has seen the\nNational Security Agency leaker since he landed at Sheremetyevo\nTerminal E on June 23, intending to go on to  Ecuador , where he\nhad requested political asylum. Now he isn\u2019t going there: On\nJuly 1, the Russian consul at Sheremetyevo reported that the\nnight before, Snowden asked for asylum in  Russia .  Dithering by the Ecuadorean authorities and, apparently,\nsome prompting from the Russian special services have\ntransformed the former NSA contractor full of romantic notions\nabout Internet privacy and information freedom into a modern-day\n Kim Philby , destined to live out his life in a country waging a\ncold war against his homeland.  Russia seemed to be a safe stopover for Snowden, wanted in\nthe U.S. for exposing the NSA\u2019s top secret efforts to monitor e-mails and chats using the infrastructure of American Internet\ngiants such as  Google Inc. Ecuador has, after all, harbored WikiLeaks founder\nJulian Assange in its  London  embassy. Patent Fees  Congress passed legislation in 2011 that changed how patent\napplications were handled from the moment they entered the\nAlexandria, Virginia-based agency and added new review processes\nfor patents already issued.  At the center was a provision allowing the patent office to\nset its own rates and have greater control over its money. Patent Fee Changes \u2018Critical\u2019 to Economy, Commerce Tells House  Letting the U.S. Patent and Trademark Office set its own\nfees and keep all the money it collects is \u201ccritical\u201d to\npromoting innovation, according to the Commerce Department,\nwhich oversees the agency.  The House is considering a measure known as the America\nInvents Act that would mark a fundamental change in how patents\nare reviewed and the biggest revision to U.S. patent law since\n1952. Commerce Secretary Gary Locke wrote in support of the\nproposed legislation in letters yesterday to Representative\nLamar Smith, a  Texas  Republican who chairs the House Judiciary\nCommittee, and Michigan Representative John Conyers, the panel\u2019s\ntop-ranking Democrat.  The Senate passed a similar measure in a 95-5 vote on March\n8. Locke said the administration, which supported the Senate\nversion, wants \u201cprompt passage\u201d of legislation, saying it may\nhelp promote  job creation .  \u201cEnactment of a balanced bill is an important part of the\nadministration\u2019s goal of \u2018out-innovating\u2019 our economic\ncompetitors and winning the future -- and it can be done with no\ncost to taxpayers and no addition to the deficit,\u201d Locke wrote.  The House may take up the measure next month, according to\nthe office of Majority Leader Eric Cantor, a Virginia\nRepublican.  A key provision of the legislation would give the patent\noffice more power over its funding by allowing the agency to\nalter its fee structure and keep Congress from diverting fees\nfor non-patent purposes.  \u201cThis structure is critical to enable the USPTO to better\nmeet the needs of America\u2019s innovators,\u201d Locke wrote,\nsuggesting there should be technical changes to allow the patent\noffice to make interim fee adjustments \u201cso it can best use this\nnew authority on day one.\u201d  The measure also calls for granting patents to the first\ninventor to file an application, eliminating an often years-long\nprocedure to determine who first came up with an idea. The\nfirst-to-file system is used in most countries.  The House patent bill is H.R. 1249.  SEB Wins U.S.  Supreme Court  Patent Fight With Global-Tech  The U.S. Supreme Court, in a decision limiting the rights\nof some patent holders, upheld a $5 million award against a\nhome-appliance maker for persuading retailers to sell a copycat\nversion of an  SEB SA (SK)  deep fryer.  The 8-1 ruling set a high bar for claims that one company\ninduced another to infringe a patent, while saying SEB met that\nstandard in its suit against Hong Kong-based  Global-Tech\nAdvanced Innovations Inc. (GAI)  The majority said the patentholder\nmust prove the defendant knew about the infringement or at least\nwas \u201cwillfully blind\u201d to it. (RHT) ,\nGeneral Motors Co., Yahoo! Inc.,  EBay Inc. (EBAY)  and  Hewlett-Packard\nCo. (HPQ)  \u201cIn a world with products that are so versatile and\nflexible, a higher standard to prove inducement of infringement\nmakes sense.\u201d  The case divided businesses along what have become familiar\nlines in patent cases -- with large technology companies\nincluding  Google Inc. (GOOG)  and  Microsoft Corp. (MSFT)  urging limits on\ninfringement suits, and the drug industry arguing for robust\npatent protection.  Writing for the Supreme Court, Justice  Samuel Alito  said a\nlower court standard made it too easy for patentholders to win\nsuits alleging inducement to infringe.  At the same time, Alito said SEB met the Supreme Court\u2019s\nnew standard. Two companies that offer high-encryption e-mail services, Lavabit and Silent Circle, have\nannounced they will  cease providing it . Foreign firms interested\nin cloud computing, widely viewed as tech\u2019s next profit machine,\n are seriously considering  Asian and European providers instead\nof U.S. ones.  In each case, the decision was made after concerns were\nraised about security. And the concerns in question were about\nthe security policies of the U.S. government.  You can consider the National Security Agency\u2019s data-gathering programs a grim necessity to protect the nation or an\noutrageous violation of privacy. What is unquestionable is that\nthey are reshaping the tech marketplace.  Yet it should have been obvious that so extensive a system\nof surveillance, no matter how benignly intended, would have\nunintended consequences. Some of the ill consequences are even\npredictable.  Consider cloud computing. Worldwide spending on the cloud\nis expected to double over the next three years to more than\n$200 billion. U.S. firms have been leaders in developing the\ntechnology. According to  a new report  from the Information\nTechnology & Innovation Foundation, however, global worries\nabout NSA surveillance are likely to reduce U.S. market share.  Scary Numbers  The report\u2019s admittedly loose estimate is that U.S. cloud-computing firms will lose $21 billion to $35 billion in revenue\nbetween now and 2016. According to the report, some 10 percent\nof non-U.S. members of the  Cloud Security Alliance  said they\u2019ve\ncanceled a project with a U.S. company since the disclosure of\nthe NSA\u2019s surveillance. In addition, 56 percent indicated \u201cthat\nthey would be less likely to use a U.S.-based cloud computing\nservice.\u201d  These are scary numbers for one of the few true growth\nareas in the tech sector. But they are precisely what should\nhave been expected in the wake of the disclosures. \u201cIf I were\nan American cloud provider, I would be quite frustrated with my\ngovernment right now,\u201d  Neelie Kroes , the European Union\u2019s\ncommissioner for digital affairs, said in the ITIF report.  It\u2019s true that the NSA never intended for its data-collection activities to become public knowledge. It\u2019s also true\nthat many of the European allies who are complaining about the\nprograms have fewer legal protections for data than the U.S.\ndoes. But optics -- the way something looks when at last it\u2019s\nexposed -- can also turn out to be an unintended consequence.  Remember that all of this controversy is arising at the\nvery moment when the brave knight of  Internet security  may be\ndying in his armor. We have learned already that it turns out to\nbe easier than many experts imagined to hack even  thoroughly\nhashed passwords . At this year\u2019s Black Hat USA security\nconference in  Las Vegas , experts said that recent mathematical\nbreakthroughs mean that the major encryption protocols on which\nInternet security rests are likely to be cracked within  five\nyears or less . (The NSA, which should know,  recommends  that\nbusinesses switch to more secure protocols that are based on\nsomething called elliptic curve cryptography.)  The government\u2019s fast-growing suite of tools to get around\nthe security of communications represents a threat to privacy\nnot in the modern sense of a litigable right, but in the old-fashioned sense of a general belief that one remains anonymous\nwhile moving through the world. When  Abraham Lincoln , in his\nsearch for Confederate spies, authorized the seizure of copies\nof all telegrams sent and received in the North, even his own\nsupporters were outraged -- not because he had violated their\nconstitutional rights (there was no right to privacy), but\nbecause he had violated the unspoken compact between the\ngovernment and the governed.  Scary Powers  It\u2019s being violated again. Few are likely to shed tears for\nthe child-pornography defendant whose powerfully encrypted hard\ndrives are, after repeated failures,  finally cracked  by the\nfederal government. Yet we mustn\u2019t forget that it is in the\nnature of bureaucracies to search for more nails to strike once\nthey\u2019ve finished polishing their hammers.  That\u2019s why  some commentators  worry about another unintended\nconsequence of the NSA disclosures: Typically, the way to keep a\nsurveillance program secret is through a sort of triage -- that\nis, by not acting on most of what you uncover. That way, those\nyou are trying to watch can\u2019t reverse-engineer the contours of\nyour system. They might not even know you are tracking them.  But with knowledge of the NSA\u2019s programs now public, law-enforcement agencies at all levels are demanding access to its\ninformation. But the larger the audience sifting through the\ndata, the greater the disturbance to the uneasy balance between\nenforcing the law and respecting the sphere of privacy -- and\nthe greater the likely harm to domestic technology companies.  President  Barack Obama  has asked us to trust him to use\nwisely whatever has been collected, and there is no reason to\ndoubt his sincerity. The American tradition, however, is more\nthe other way around: It\u2019s the government that\u2019s supposed to\ntrust the people.  (Stephen L. Carter is a Bloomberg View columnist and a\nprofessor of law at  Yale University . He is the author of \u201cThe\nViolence of Peace: America\u2019s Wars in the Age of Obama\u201d and the\nnovel \u201cThe Impeachment of Abraham Lincoln.\u201d Follow him on\nTwitter at  @StepCarter .) The EU is already drafting new regulations to force these companies to protect their European customers data more adequately. Bundesbank  warns  of real estate bubble According to a Bundesbank study, apartments in Frankfurt, Munich and Frankfurt are overpriced by about 20 percent. Germans traditionally prefer to rent housing, which has led to a lethargic real estate market. In the last three years, however, low interest rates and a flight to value as debt markets disappointed investors have triggered a boom. German authorities are not overly worried about a nationwide housing bubble because the price spikes have only occurred in a few large cities. Germany is, however, concerned that the European Central Bank is keeping rates too low in an attempt to boost growth, and Angela Merkel's government will use the bubble data to argue for a monetary tightening. Eni head says U.S. shale  a threat  to Europe Paolo Scaroni, head of Italian energy giant Eni, said the U.S. shale boom was threatening European heavy industry. \"Why would anyone invest in anything energy intensive [in Europe] rather than go to Texas, where the cost of electricity is half and gas a third?\" he questioned. Scaroni and others in the European energy sector believe the difference between oil and gas prices in Europe versus the United States is here to stay, because shale projects will take off more slowly in Europe. This could result in rapid U.S. re-industrialization as the old continent seeks growth opportunities in less energy-intensive businesses. Hediard files for  bankruptcy  as Russian owner fails  The celebrated, 160-year-old luxury grocery chain Hediard, which has its flagship store in Paris' Place de la Madeleine opposite arch-rival Fauchon, has filed for bankruptcy. Hediard seemed unsinkable after Russian billionaire Sergei Pugachev, then seen as close to President Vladimir Putin, bought it in 2007. Pugachev's business empire has since gone bust, however. His Russian bank, Mexhprombank, failed in 2010, and his industrial assets were sold or seized for debts. Pugachev once promised Hediard international expansion, but he has proved unable to finance either that or the restructuring of the loss-making company. Russian tycoons got rich quickly, but their money can disappear just as fast \u2013 a cautionary tale for the owners of prestigious but money-losing European assets, who dream of Russian capital injections. To contact the editor responsible for this story:\nMichael Sillup at   msillup@bloomberg.net .","path":".\/2008_2012_msft_bloomberg_news\/iger-woods-s-video-game-cover-companions-to-be-picked-online-by-fans.txt"},{"id":11048584,"title":"IPad, IPhone Tackle \u2018What-to-Watch\u2019 Dilemma: Rich Jaroslovsky","released_at":"<date>July 13 2011<\/date> <time>20:00:00<\/time>","content":"With flat-screen televisions, smart\nphones and tablets, there have never been more ways to watch\nmovies and TV shows. And with Netflix, Hulu and their ilk, there\nhave never been more sources.  The missing piece is figuring out easily what content is\nactually available and getting it to the screen you want to\nwatch it on.  I\u2019ve been trying out a pair of very different approaches to\ntackling that problem from two Silicon Valley startups, both\nmaking use of  Apple Inc. (AAPL) \u2019s iPad, iPhone and iPod touch.  One,  Fanhattan , is a free app that acts as the ultimate TV\nGuide, helping you locate movies and shows for viewing on, or\nvia, your iPad. The other,  Peel , is a $100 \u201cappcessory,\u201d a\ngadget-plus-app combination that turns your iPhone or iPod touch\ninto a super-smart remote control for the stuff coming to your\ntelevision via cable, satellite or Internet connection.  While neither represents a complete solution, both are\nuseful, depending on your viewing habits.  Fanhattan\u2019s view of the world is content-centric, aiming to\nbring together in one place not only every option you have for\nviewing a movie or show, but also reviews, trailers, and even\nlinks to buy tchotchkes.  From the main screen, you choose either movies or TV shows,\nand are then presented with options to search for a specific\ntitle or browse a variety of categories and criteria, from genre\nto critics\u2019 picks. Select one, and Fanhattan aggregates\ninformation from online sources and displays it in a visually\nrich environment.  Appropriate Apps  If you choose a viewing option the iPad and Fanhattan\nsupport -- Netflix\u2019s instant-view service, for instance, or  Hulu\nPlus  -- Fanhattan will launch the appropriate app if you already\nhave it, or prompt you to install it if you don\u2019t.  This being the season for big, noisy action movies, I\nentered \u201cTransformers\u201d and chose the 2009 installment,\n\u201cRevenge of the Fallen.\u201d Under \u201cWatch Now,\u201d I was given\noptions to view the trailer and to rent or buy the video from\nApple\u2019s iTunes store for immediate download.  Also listed were a variety of other options for acquiring\nthe film, including pricing information for buying the DVD or\nBlu-ray from  Amazon.com Inc. (AMZN) , or for renting or buying it from\nthe video-on-demand services of Amazon,  Wal-Mart Stores Inc. (WMT) \u2019s\nVudu and  Microsoft Corp. (MSFT) \u2019s Zune.  Action Figure  But there was also much more: a summary of the plot, to the\nextent there is one; critics\u2019 reviews from Rotten Tomatoes;\ninformation on the cast and crew (sadly, the YouTube selection\nfor \u201cMegan Fox Sexy Movie Scenes\u201d was disabled); and even a\nlink to purchase the Transformers 2 Revenge of the Fallen Movie\nScout Class Action Figure Breakdown ($9.99 from Amazon).  I had some issues with Fanhattan. The navigation, handled\nby a variety of taps and up-and-down and side-to-side swipes,\nwas overly complicated. And when I searched for an episode of\nLarry David\u2019s \u201cCurb Your Enthusiasm,\u201d my only viewing options\nwere to buy it from iTunes or rent it from Amazon -- even though\nit was also available through  Time Warner Inc. (TWX) \u2019s  HBO  Go app,\nalready installed and active on the same iPad. (Fanhattan says\nit hasn\u2019t yet established a relationship with HBO, so its\nresults don\u2019t show up in the app.)  While Fanhattan has to get more comprehensive, its looks\nand general approach make it an appealing starting point. That\nbrings me to Peel, which attacks the what-to-watch issue through\nthe device you\u2019re still most likely to be watching on: your\ntelevision set.  Colorful Tiles  The Peel app, which is free, learns your viewing tastes based\non information you provide, as well as its analysis of what you\ntend to watch and even what time of day you like certain kinds\nof programming. Having told the app what cable system I\u2019m in, it\nfound and displayed appropriate programs as colorful tiles on my\niPhone, refining its suggestions the more it learned about me.  Its real value, though, comes when it\u2019s paired with the\n$100 palm-size gadget that looks vaguely like a pear. It allows\nthe app to control your TV and the devices hooked up to it\nwithout the need to plug anything into either them or your\niPhone.  Instead, you plug a special cable into a port on your home\nrouter, then position the battery-powered pear near your video\ngear. A one-time set-up routine introduces the app to your\ntelevision, cable or satellite box, home theater, Blu-ray player\nand whatever else you\u2019ve got. No more figuring out which TV\ninput which device is plugged into; you simply choose the device\nyou want to control, and you\u2019re presented with an appropriate\nremote on your mobile device\u2019s screen.  Ordered by Interests  Now, when the app locates programs for you, just poke one\nof those colored tiles -- ordered by your interests, not to the\narbitrary channel numbers of a grid -- and you\u2019ll flip straight\nto the program.  I found the Peel generally worked pretty well, though once\nor twice I lost the virtual controls on my iPhone and just faced\na blank gray screen. In addition, Peel recommends locating its\nrouter cable within 25 feet of the pear, which may not work in\nyour particular layout.  For the moment, Fanhattan, with its online orientation, and\nthe TV-centric Peel don\u2019t directly compete. But the lines are\nrapidly blurring. Fanhattan is working on a version for\nInternet-connected TVs, while the Peel already can control\ndevices that hook you into the Net, like Apple TV. And both are\nworking on versions of their apps to run on mobile devices using\n Google Inc. (GOOG) \u2019s Android operating system.  The struggle to control how you\u2019ll access entertainment in\nthe future has barely begun. Fanhattan and Peel, each in its own\nway, have successfully staked out a piece of the turf.  ( Rich Jaroslovsky  is a Bloomberg News columnist. The\nopinions expressed are his own.) The Win America Campaign, which included  Cisco Systems\nInc. (CSCO) ,  Microsoft Corp. (MSFT)  and  Apple Inc. The effort fizzled as some Republicans focused on\npermanent  tax policy  and Democrats warned of the potential\nrevenue loss.  The group wanted Congress to reprise a 2004 tax holiday\nthat let companies bring home offshore profits at a discount.\nCritics, including the Obama administration, said the proposal\nwould cost the government money, encourage companies to move\nprofits offshore and undermine efforts to overhaul the U.S. tax\ncode.  Not Promising  Prospects for the legislation weren\u2019t promising,\ncontributing to the group\u2019s decision to end operations, said a\nlobbyist who worked on the effort and wouldn\u2019t discuss the\ndecision publicly.  At one point last year, the repatriation effort looked\n\u201cunstoppable\u201d in Congress, said Steve Wamhoff, legislative\ndirector of  Citizens for Tax Justice , a Washington group that\nopposed the proposal.  \u201cThis is a great sign for anyone who cares about tax\nfairness,\u201d he said. \u201cA lot of people have figured out that\nthis is a proposal that really would offer the greatest benefits\nto some of the worst abusers of the corporate tax system, the\ncompanies that are really shifting their profits to  tax\nhavens .\u201d  Doug Thornell , who had been a spokesman for the campaign,\ndeclined to comment.  Under current law, companies can defer U.S. taxation of\nprofits earned outside the country until they bring the money\nback. Then, they must pay  corporate taxes  of as much as 35\npercent minus tax credits for payments to foreign governments.  Overseas Profits  U.S. companies have stockpiled more than $1 trillion in\nuntaxed profits outside the country. Seventy companies with the\nmost money outside the U.S. held a total of $1.2 trillion\noverseas, according to data compiled by Bloomberg last month.\nThose companies increased their offshore holdings by 18.4\npercent over the past year. (PFE)   The companies maintain that a repatriation holiday -- like\none enacted in 2004 that allowed profits to return to the U.S.\nat a 5.25 percent tax rate -- would inject money into the U.S.\neconomy. Representative  Kevin Brady , a Texas Republican,\nsponsored a bill that would have repeated the 2004 holiday.  The Joint Committee on Taxation, the nonpartisan\nscorekeeper of tax bills for Congress, estimated that the\nrepatriation proposal would cost the government $78.7 billion in\ntax revenue over a decade, because companies would stockpile\nprofits outside the U.S. in anticipation of another tax holiday.  Tax-Code Overhaul  The repatriation campaign ran into resistance in part\nbecause the money held outside the U.S. was seen in Congress as\na way to help finance an overhaul of the  tax code , the lobbyist\nsaid.  Dave Camp , chairman of the House Ways and Means Committee,\nproposed an overhaul of the international tax system that would\nend most taxation of overseas profits. It would require\ncompanies to pay taxes on their untaxed offshore balances as if\nthey were brought home and taxed at a 5.25 percent rate.  Camp, a Michigan Republican, didn\u2019t endorse a stand-alone\nrepatriation holiday bill. The matter will probably be covered informally over dinner Oct. 9 or before presentations begin on Oct. 10, said the person, who asked not to be identified because board gatherings are private.  Executive Chairman Bill Ford, Mulally and Chief Operating Officer Mark Fields -- the heir apparent to the top Ford job -- all have reiterated Ford\u2019s plan for no leadership change through 2014 for the second-largest U.S. automaker. Getting clear direction from the CEO will be crucial to the board\u2019s efforts to pull off a smooth switch to a post-Mulally era, whenever he leaves. Ford\u2019s history of transitions is bumpy.  \u201cThis is not something that can be just left hanging,\u201d said Maryann Keller, an auto-industry consultant who has served as director on six boards. \u201cIf there\u2019s going to be a new leader for Ford, then that new leader has to be appointed and named quickly.\u201d  Microsoft Search  Microsoft CEO  Steve Ballmer  announced in August that he was retiring within a year. Directors, led by Chairman Bill Gates, have discussed as CEO candidates Mulally, 68, former Nokia Oyj CEO Stephen Elop, Microsoft business development and evangelism chief Tony Bates, and former Microsoft No. 3 executive Paul Maritz, according to people with knowledge of the matter.  The search process is still in the early stages and the board isn\u2019t close to making a decision, said the people, who asked not to be identified because the process is confidential.  \u201cNothing has changed from what we announced in November,\u201d Jay Cooney, a Ford spokesman, said by telephone. \u201cAlan is focused on continuing to execute the One Ford plan, and we don\u2019t engage in speculation or publicly discuss board matters.\u201d  For Ford, \u201cit\u2019s a highly distractive element that enters into the conversations that go on,\u201d said Jon Luther, chairman of Roark Capital\u2019s Arby\u2019s Restaurant Group Inc., who has managed CEO transitions both as a director and as a former CEO of Dunkin\u2019 Donuts. \u201cYou have a very high-level, public board that has to address these issues, because so many constituents of the Ford business are affected by it.\u201d  Tumultuous History  The stakes are high for Dearborn, Michigan-based Ford, which has had just 10 leaders in its 110-year history, and some of the transitions resulted in tumult.  Founder Henry Ford overstayed through poor health and mounting losses in the 1940s. His oldest grandson, Henry Ford II, in the 1970s feuded with and pushed out Lee Iacocca, who became an icon at Chrysler Corp.  Alex Trotman in the 1990s avoided preparing multiple successors. His heir, Jacques Nasser, attempted to remake Ford into a consumer-products company and failed, with his tenure ending after crises with sport-utility vehicle rollovers caused by Firestone tires.  This time will be different, Bill Ford, 56, said last week in an interview with Bloomberg Television. He called his company\u2019s top management  team  the best in his 34-year career.  \u201cWhoever the next CEO is, it will be seamless,\u201d Bill Ford said. \u201cThey\u2019ve loved working in this style with this vision since 2006,\u201d when Mulally arrived from Boeing Co. \u201cThere is no appetite within the management team for deviating.\u201d  Grooming Talent  The Ford board has sought to groom internal talent since Bill Ford went outside the company to recruit Mulally away from Boeing following a 37-year career at the Chicago-based aircraft manufacturer. Bill Ford yielded the CEO post he had held since replacing Nasser in late 2001.  \u201cThis is a board that has been dealing with succession issues for some years,\u201d said Keller. \u201cThey know who the heirs-apparent are. They put in place a process a year ago that was meant to create a logical and orderly transition for Mulally\u2019s replacement.\u201d  Ford fell 1.6 percent to $16.81 at the close in New York. The shares have surged 30 percent this year, outpacing an 18 percent gain for the Standard & Poor\u2019s 500 Index.  Late last year, Ford elevated Fields to chief operating officer, positioning him as the top candidate to succeed Mulally. Fields, 52, told reporters last month that Ford\u2019s business-plan review meetings, conducted every Thursday and initiated by Mulally, have been \u201ccore to changing the culture at Ford.\u201d  Watershed Moment  It was during one of the earliest of these meetings in 2006 that Fields, the head of Ford\u2019s Americas operations, strayed from the company\u2019s internal track record of hiding problems. In sharing that a balky tailgate was interrupting production of the Edge utility vehicle, he won Mulally\u2019s early praise.  Mulally and other executives within Ford have shared this anecdote countless times as a watershed moment that marked a turning point in Ford\u2019s culture. The automaker last month bought a software startup called Livio to help it devise systems that better link car passengers\u2019 mobile phones to their vehicles.  Mulally has delivered multiple keynote speeches at the annual  Consumer Electronics Show  in Las Vegas. In September, when Mulally reiterated the plan to continue as Ford CEO through 2014, he was in Berlin at the IFA technology show.  \u2018Perform Better\u2019  \u201cAnywhere he wants to be in charge in the CEO job, he will make the company perform better,\u201d said Aaron Gellman, a professor of management and strategy at Northwestern University\u2019s Kellogg School of Management in Evanston,  Illinois . Mulally made almost $21 million in 2012, according to data compiled by Bloomberg.  Whether Mulally leaves Ford before or after the end of 2014, it\u2019s unlikely he would just retire, said Gellman, who has known Mulally for decades. He said he was unaware of his friend\u2019s plans.  \u201cIt would be hard to keep him on the bench for very long,\u201d Gellman said by telephone.  \u2018Love Fest\u2019  Admiration of Mulally extends beyond his friends. Lime Wire Judge Limits Copyright Damages Labels Can Seek  A federal judge limited the number of recordings for which\nmusic labels can seek monetary damages in the copyright\ninfringement case against website Lime Wire LLC.  U.S. District Judge  Kimba Wood  said that the record labels\ncan\u2019t demand statutory damages for each individual song that\nappears on an album, according to a filing yesterday in\n Manhattan . A trial for damages is to begin May 2.  Wood found Lime Wire and its founder,  Mark Gorton , liable\nfor inducing copyright infringement last year. The Lime Wire\nwebsite allowed users, without authorization from copyright\nowners, to download recordings and share them with others on\ntheir computers. As the case has moved into the damages phase,\neach side is trying to increase or limit the number of\nrecordings liable for monetary awards.  Total damages could reach hundreds of millions of dollars,\naccording to court papers.  Music labels, including  Sony Corp. (6758) \u2019s Arista Records and\n Warner Music Group Corp. (WMG) \u2019s Atlantic Records, have identified\n11,205 recordings that they say Lime Wire users infringed, and\nsaid they\u2019ll seek statutory damages for 9,715. Copyright law\nallows statutory damages of up to $150,000 per infringed work,\nwhich meant a possible liability of more than $1 billion.  Wood said that an album constitutes one infringed work. The\nexception to that is a track from the album released as a single\nrecording to be sold through Apple Inc.\u2019s iTunes or some other\nretailer.  Wood ruled in March that the labels were entitled to only\none statutory damage award for each work infringed, regardless\nof how many people downloaded the recording. The labels\u2019 demands\ncould have meant damages of trillions of dollars, which she said\nwas an \u201cabsurdity.\u201d  Wood ordered the labels to submit their final list of\nrecordings by April 15.  Lime Wire was ordered last year to shut down its music\nfile-sharing site.  The case is Arista Records LLC v. Lime Wire LLC, 06-05936,\nU.S. District Court, Southern District of New York (Manhattan).  For more copyright news, click here.
