In a 7-1 ruling, the court left intact a 2003 decision that reaffirmed the right of universities to use race as a criterion for admissions. The majority instead said a federal appeals court hadn\u2019t properly applied the standards laid out in the 2003 ruling.  Today\u2019s decision provides a limited victory to opponents of racial preferences, giving them new grounds to challenge university admission policies around the country. The majority said universities must prove that their means of attaining diversity meet a demanding constitutional test known as \u201cstrict scrutiny.\u201d  \u201cStrict scrutiny imposes on the university the ultimate burden of demonstrating, before turning to racial classifications, that available, workable race-neutral alternatives do not suffice,\u201d Justice Anthony Kennedy wrote for the majority.  Affirmative action has been a fixture on U.S. campuses since the 1960s, diversifying what had been many virtually all-white student bodies. Most of the nation\u2019s selective colleges and professional schools consider race as they seek to ensure a multiracial student body. Blacks and Hispanics now make up more than a quarter of U.S. college students.  10 Percent  At the core of the debate was whether universities can adequately diversify without resorting to racial preferences. Under Texas\u2019s Top Ten Percent Law, the university\u2019s flagship Austin campus admits three-quarters of its freshman class each year solely on the basis of high school class rank. That system, while race-neutral on the surface, ensures a significant number of minorities because it guarantees slots to students at predominantly Hispanic and black schools.  The university considers race only in admitting the rest of the class. Opponents of preferences say that\u2019s unnecessary, given the success of the class-rank method. Texas counters that even with race-based admissions, a high percentage of its classes have few if any black and Hispanic students.  Kennedy said that while courts should defer to universities in determining whether diversity is essential to their educational mission, judges should closely scrutinize the means schools use to bolster minority enrollment.  \u2018No Deference\u2019  \u201cThe university must prove that the means chosen by the university to attain diversity are narrowly tailored to that goal,\u201d Kennedy wrote. \u201cOn this point, the university receives no deference.\u201d  Edward Blum, who organized the challenge to the University of Texas policy, said the court had established \u201cexceptionally high hurdles\u201d for colleges to meet.  \u201cIt is unlikely that most institutions will be able to overcome these hurdles,\u201d said Blum, the director of the Project on Fair Representation in Alexandria,  Virginia , in an e-mailed statement. \u201cThis opinion will compel the Fifth Circuit to strike down UT\u2019s current use of race and ethnicity.\u201d  Texas said the ruling won\u2019t force any immediate changes in its admissions policies. Bill Powers, the university\u2019s president, said in a statement that its system \u201cfully satisfies\u201d the standards laid out by the Supreme Court.  Current Practices  Current admissions practices at universities can continue for at least another year as the case works its way again through the courts, said Michael Olivas, a University of Houston law professor who helped draw up the University of Texas admissions plan. Proponents of affirmative action will be relieved by the ruling, he said.  \u201cThis could have been so much worse and may yet be,\u201d Olivas said in a telephone interview. Affirmative action \u201clives on, but all of us believe it\u2019s under an impending death penalty.\u201d  The 2003 decision, Grutter v. Bollinger, said colleges and graduate schools could consider race as long as they do so through a broad review of a student\u2019s application and don\u2019t mechanistically award extra points to every minority. The author of that 5-4 ruling, Sandra Day O\u2019Connor, retired in 2006.  Joining Kennedy\u2019s opinion today were Chief Justice John Roberts and Justices Antonin Scalia, Samuel Alito, Clarence Thomas, Stephen Breyer and Sonia Sotomayor. Sotomayor, the court\u2019s first Latina justice, is a supporter of affirmative action who says she benefited from it during her career.  \u2018Discriminatory Past\u2019  Writing in dissent, Justice Ruth Bader Ginsburg said Texas had followed the model the court approved in the 2003 case. She said government actors, including state universities, need not be blind to the lingering effects of \u201can overtly discriminatory past.\u201d  In a concurring opinion, Thomas said he would have outlawed the use of race by university admissions offices.  \u201cIf the court were actually applying strict scrutiny, it would require Texas either to close the university or to stop discriminating against applicants based on their race,\u201d he wrote. \u201cThe court has put other schools to that choice, and there is no reason to treat the university differently.\u201d  Justice Elena Kagan didn\u2019t take part in the case. She was the Obama administration\u2019s top courtroom lawyer when the administration filed a brief at the appeals court level.  Supporters of affirmative action expressed relief that the court didn\u2019t go further.  \u2018Great Success\u2019  \u201cIt\u2019s been a very important part of the great success of American education that is admired around the globe,\u201d said Columbia University President Lee Bollinger, who as president of the University of Michigan in the late 1990s and early 2000s led the defense of its affirmative action programs. \u201cIt would be a great pity to retreat at this stage when the work is not over.\u201d  The Texas policy was challenged by Abigail Noel Fisher, who applied unsuccessfully to the school in 2008 and later enrolled at Louisiana State University. A graduate of a Houston-area public high school, she said she was passed over by UT in favor of minority classmates with lower grades and fewer extracurricular activities.  The Supreme Court decision is a \u201cnet plus\u201d for opponents of affirmative action, said Roger Clegg, president and general counsel of the Center for Equal Opportunity, a Falls Church, Virginia, nonprofit group opposed to racial preferences. The language of the court\u2019s decision should continue to push universities to use alternatives to race -- such as income -- to improve diversity on campus, he said.  \u2018It\u2019s Disappointing\u2019  \u201cIt\u2019s disappointing the court had the opportunity today to say definitively that considering race in admissions is not justified,\u201d Clegg said in a telephone interview.  Texas had support in the case from some of the nation\u2019s most powerful institutions. Fifty-nine companies -- including  Microsoft Corp. (MSFT) ,  Wal-Mart Stores Inc. (WMT) , (WMT) Gap Inc.,  General Electric Co. (GE)  (GE), Pfizer Inc., Shell Oil Co. and  Viacom Inc. (VIAB)  (VIAB) -- filed a  brief  saying they rely on universities to prepare a racially diverse workforce.  Those corporations were in the unusual position of arguing alongside the Obama administration, which  cast  affirmative action as a national security issue. The administration said race-conscious admissions, at the country\u2019s military academies and at universities with Reserve Officer Training Corps programs, help ensure a diverse officer corps.  Texas argued that its program is a model of the type of plan the high court approved in the Grutter ruling.  The case is Fisher v. University of Texas at Austin, 11-345. Navy Systems  A product of the U.S. Navy\u2019s Space and Naval Warfare\nSystems Center, the document exposed sensitive details of\ninfrastructure changes for outfitting the base with a new sensor\nsystem. The mirror site said only that the file \u201cwas first\npublicly revealed by WikiLeaks working with our source.\u201d  Boback said the retrieval and posting follows a pattern his\nresearchers have tracked over and over. They estimate that as\nmuch as half of the postings by the group could originate from\ninformation siphoned from peer-to-peer users, he said.  \u201cThere are not that many whistleblowers in the world to\nget you millions of documents,\u201d Boback said. \u201cHowever, if you\nare getting them yourselves, that information is out there and\navailable.\u201d  Tiversa provided its findings to U.S. agencies to aid what\nBoback called the early stages of an investigation into the\nmatter. A separate criminal probe is being conducted by a U.S.\ngrand jury in  Virginia  regarding tens of thousands of diplomatic\ncables and other secret material allegedly provided by U.S. Army\nprivate Bradley Manning, Stephens said in December.  Swedish Allegations  WikiLeaks founder Julian Assange is in the U.K. fighting\nextradition to Sweden, where he faces allegations of sexual\nmolestation and rape. Lawyers for Assange have said the\naccusations in Sweden are politically motivated and tied to the\nactions of WikiLeaks.  The U.S.  Justice Department  declined to comment on whether\nthere was an official investigation regarding the downloads\nTiversa concluded were done by WikiLeaks, said Dean Boyd, a\nspokesman.  Lime Group, which owns the rights to LimeWire software,\nshut its operations in December and an e-mail to Tiffany\nGuarnaccia, a spokeswoman, couldn\u2019t be delivered. The network\ncan be used by anyone who previously downloaded the software,\npeer-to-peer experts said. Sharman Networks, which owns Kazaa,\nreferred inquiries to ICON Communications in Sydney,  Australia ,\nwhich didn\u2019t return e-mails seeking comment.  U.S. Probes  The U.S. investigations could provide authorities an\nalternate path for prosecuting WikiLeaks and Assange, said Paul\nOhm, an expert in cyber crime at the University of  Colorado  in\nBoulder.  Boback, whose firm has made such searches for the  Federal\nBureau of Investigation  and the  Internal Revenue Service  to\ntrace unauthorized downloads, argued that such conduct is just\ninformation scavenging, not illegal hacking.  Assistant U.S. Attorney Kathryn Warma in  Seattle , who\nsuccessfully prosecuted similar cases of unintended searching,\nsaid the systematic pillaging of computer contents through peer-\nto-peer networks could be pursued under federal anti-hacking\nstatutes.  Even if not criminal, such conduct, if traced to WikiLeaks,\nwould contradict its stated mission as a facilitator of leaked\nmaterial by insiders, whose identities, Assange has said, the\ngroup takes measures not to know. The group provides an\nencrypted drop box on its website that it said prevents any\ntracing back to the source of documents.  Receptacle for Leaks  \u201cIf their information gathering doesn\u2019t consist simply of\nbeing a receptacle for leaks but of this more aggressive effort\nto go out and cull this information, then you\u2019re moving a clear\nstep further from anything that resembles traditional\njournalistic practice,\u201d said Mark Jurkowitz, the associate\ndirector for the Washington-based Project for Excellence in\nJournalism.  The evidence could also be used by congressional\ncommittees, which Boback said are pursuing a separate inquiry to\nundermine WikiLeaks\u2019 claim that it\u2019s a legitimate media\norganization with protections under the First Amendment.  \u201cThere is a difference between being given information\nthat may have been obtained in violation of some agreement or\nlaw versus the media itself violating the law or an agreement in\norder to obtain information,\u201d said Sandra Baron, the executive\ndirector of the Media Law Resource Center in  New York . \u201cThe\nmedia is not allowed to steal.\u201d  Thousands of Documents  The WikiLeaks site has posted hundreds of thousands of\ndocuments in the past four years. With the exception of\nclassified material allegedly provided by Manning, the source of\nits leaked documents has never been publicly identified.  On Jan. 17, a former Swiss banker, Rudolf Elmer, turned\nover information to Assange on almost 2,000 account holders\nElmer claims are guilty of  tax evasion  and other crimes. The\ndata has yet to be published by WikiLeaks.  Assange based the group\u2019s primary servers in Sweden because\nof the strength of that country\u2019s media laws, which prohibit\nauthorities from inquiring about journalistic sources, he has\nsaid. The group said in 2010 that the  Swedish Pirate Party ,\nwhich aims to reform copyright law and ensure citizens\u2019 right to\nprivacy, would host some of the group\u2019s servers as well.  Assange has told interviewers he aims to make leaks\nuntraceable to avoid retaliation against providers by\ngovernments or others harmed by the information.  Sourcing Information  \u201cWe cannot comply with requests for information on sources\nbecause we simply do not have the information to begin with,\u201d\nWikiLeaks has said on its website.  The vulnerability of vast amounts of confidential and\nsecret information on peer-to-peer networks is a risk well-known\nto researchers and security experts, as well as to information\nscavengers and foreign intelligence agencies, according to  Eric\nJohnson , an expert on peer-to-peer technology at Dartmouth\nCollege\u2019s Tuck School of Business in Hanover,  New Hampshire .  The networks are popular with U.S. soldiers in Iraq and  Afghanistan , who use them to download music and videos, as do\nteenagers who sometimes download material on their parents\u2019\ncomputers, Johnson said. A Congressional subcommittee held\nhearings in 2007 and 2009 on inadvertent sharing on such sites.  In 2009, Tiversa found the entire blueprints and avionics\npackage for Marine One, the presidential helicopter, on a\ncomputer linked to  Iran , according to Boback\u2019s 2009 testimony at\nthe hearings. His firm also found a leak of a file of a LimeWire\nuser that showed the safe-house location of the president\u2019s\nfamily.  Terrorism Targets  In late 2009, WikiLeaks published a spreadsheet detailing\nvulnerable, potential terrorist targets in Fresno County\ncompiled by State of California security officials and the U.S.\nDepartment of  Homeland Security . It noted locations for caches\nof bomb-grade fertilizers; the location of large gasoline and\npropane reserves; and the coordinates of key military and law\nenforcement sites and their functions.  Asked to aid in the investigation of the leak by U.S.\nauthorities that the company declined to identify, Tiversa found\nthe spreadsheet was inadvertently exposed by a California state\nemployee using a peer-to-peer network in August 2008, more than\na year before WikiLeaks posted it.  A WikiLeaks post of Army intelligence documents in 2009\nincluded reports on Taliban leaders and their movements, as well\nas confidential notes of meetings where complaints were voiced\nabout the performance of Iraqi police. Those documents were\nexposed to unauthorized searching on peer-to-peer networks more\nthan eight months earlier in September 2008, Tiversa\ninvestigators found after they were asked to investigate the\nmatter by a client the company declined to identify.  Order of Battle  The Pentagon\u2019s 58-page Afghanistan Order of Battle was\nexposed in a file-sharing network in January 2009 and posted on\nWikiLeaks four months later. For a downloaded list of every\nChevron Corp. property in the U.S. and  Canada , the posting gap\nwas two months -- from March to May 2009, the firm found.  Confidential documents can be mined from peer-to-peer\nnetworks using malicious software that sucks out information\nunrelated to the song, photo or other material users want to\nshare. In most cases, Johnson said all that is needed is weak\nsecurity settings or user mistakes that allow searchers to dig\ninto the computers of users who don\u2019t realize that confidential\nfiles on their hard drives can be tapped.  Congressional Legislation  The U.S. House of Representatives last year approved a bill\nthat would prohibit peer-to-peer file sharing software on any\nU.S. government computer.  If federal prosecutors can definitely link the theft of\nconfidential information directly to WikiLeaks and its core of\npaid staffers and volunteers, they would still face significant\nchallenges. The legal tools available to them for a criminal\nprosecution aren\u2019t firmly tested, according to lawyers and peer-\nto-peer experts.  \u201cIt\u2019s not a slam dunk either way\u201d said Ohm, a former\nJustice Department prosecutor.  In 2008, a  federal court  in  Oklahoma  found that removing\npornographic pictures from a computer by an FBI agent using\nLimeWire didn\u2019t constitute an illegal search. In contrast, Warma\nsuccessfully prosecuted two Seattle cases recently involving\nindividuals who retrieved financial information through LimeWire\n\u201cin excess of authorization.\u201d Warma said retrieving\nconfidential information through peer-to-peer networks could be\nprosecuted under the federal  Computer Fraud and Abuse Act .  \u201cI can almost guarantee you there is a task force at the\nDepartment of Justice that\u2019s been tasked with creatively coming\nup with theories to use against WikiLeaks,\u201d Ohm said. \u201cI\u2019m\nsure that in those conversations the Computer Fraud and Abuse\nAct has come across the board, especially with this new twist of\npeer-to-peer networks.\u201d  To contact the reporter on this story:\nMichael Riley in  Washington  at   michaelriley@bloomberg.net . No, wait, a Mac. Now an iPad. And now a Windows\nPC.  My digital flexibility is thanks to  Connect by Quickoffice ,\na new service and set of applications that let me keep all my\nimportant documents constantly updated on whatever device I\nhappen to have with me.  Quickoffice is familiar to many mobile-device users for its\napps that create, open and edit files compatible with\nMicrosoft\u2019s Office formats. Connect, which I\u2019ve been using in\npre-release form for the last couple of weeks, provides an easy-\nto-use conduit to make sure the various versions of those files\nare always in sync, regardless of where they happen to\nphysically reside.  The proliferation of smartphones and tablets has made it\neasier than ever to make changes on the go to a memo,\nspreadsheet or presentation, and online-storage sites like\n Google (GOOG)  Docs and Dropbox let you upload a document from, say,\nyour desktop Windows PC, pull it down onto your iPad for a few\nquick tweaks, then send it back to the Cloud.  But that means you now have two versions of your document\nfloating around: the latest one, on your iPad and the online\nsite, and the previous one, still residing on your PC\u2019s hard\ndrive. Each additional device you use creates more opportunities\nfor confusion.  Completing the Circuit  Connect aims to solve that problem by completing the\ncircuit for you automatically. Any changes you make to a file\nwill be reflected on all your enrolled devices, assuring that\nwhatever version you summon, from wherever, will always be the\nlatest.  The concept is familiar to users of  Apple (AAPL) \u2019s iWork\napplications -- Pages, Numbers and Keynote -- who already enjoy\nsimilar functionality on their iPads and iPhones through Apple\u2019s\n iCloud  service. But there\u2019s not even an easy way yet to extend\nthat convenience to Mac computers. And Apple, of course, has\nvery little incentive to make it easier for you to use Android\nphones and Windows PCs. That\u2019s where Connect comes in.  The first step is to download the Connect software to each\nof your various devices -- from the Apple App Store and Google\nPlay for iOS and Android devices, respectively, and from the\nQuickoffice website for Windows PCs and Macs.  Automatic Upload  On each device, the software creates a folder called \u201cMy\nConnect.\u201d Any document you place in it is automatically\nuploaded to the Quickoffice service, then pushed out to the My\nConnect folders on all your other devices. In my tests, mostly\ndone before the service became publicly available, new or\nchanged documents were usually updated on other devices within\nfive minutes, though I sometimes experienced longer delays.  In addition to My Connect, you can also designate specific\nfolders on your computer to be available through Connect, and\nyou can allow other people access for collaborating purposes.\nYou can also tie in your existing cloud-storage accounts,\nincluding Google Docs,  Microsoft (MSFT) \u2019s  SkyDrive ,  Dropbox ,  Evernote \nand  Box .  Besides passing this column around from device to device as\nI was writing it, I designated a folder on my Windows PC whose\ncontents I wanted to make available on whatever gadget I\nhappened to be carrying. I also used Connect to import a\nPowerpoint presentation from Google Docs onto an iPad, where I\nused the Quickoffice editing tools to modify it, added it to the\nMy Connect folder and later summoned it on a Windows PC for some\nfurther polishing.  Bumpy Process  The process was sometimes bumpy. For example, a Microsoft\nWord document from my PC popped up normally on all my devices\nexcept for my  Samsung (005930)  Droid Charge phone, where it appeared\ngrayed out and inaccessible, though other Word files showed up\nfine. For a while, I could access Connect documents on my Mac,\nbut the ones I created there weren\u2019t reaching my other devices.\nA company engineer eventually helped me clear up that problem.  My issues may have stemmed from the fact that I was mostly\nusing early versions of the software, and when I encountered\nproblems I could still remotely search my devices for the file I\nneeded. Still, for Connect to live up to its promise, it will\nneed to deliver a more seamless experience than I encountered.  Connect has three levels of service. The free version is\nlimited to syncing two devices, and doesn\u2019t include the tools\nfor making changes on your mobile devices. A premium edition --\n$20 a year for now, eventually $45 -- is more useful, adding\nediting capabilities and allowing you to enroll up to four\ndevices. A $70 tier allows six devices and additional features\nthat include being able to retrieve older versions of a\ndocument.  If you\u2019re already paying for cloud-based storage from\nDropbox or some other provider, you may decide that you can\nmanage to keep things straight on your own. But the more devices\nyou have, the more valuable you\u2019ll find Connect.  ( Rich Jaroslovsky  is a Bloomberg News columnist. The\nopinions expressed are his own.) Simon, 38, and his father, Paddy Kelly,\n66, were once among Ireland\u2019s most audacious real estate\ndevelopers. During the boom years, they borrowed about\n700\u00a0million euros ($950 million) from  Anglo Irish Bank Corp.  to\nbuy golf resorts and build hotels.  Today, the Kellys are 800 million euros in debt, Anglo\nIrish has been nationalized, and the Kellys\u2019 former assets\nlitter the streets of Dublin, Bloomberg Businessweek reports in\nits Nov. 22 edition. Discussing the Morrison, Simon says\ncasually, \u201cOh, I own part of the hotel. Well, not anymore. Now,\nNAMA owns it.\u201d  The National Asset Management Agency, or Ireland\u2019s \u201cbad\nbank,\u201d was created by the government in 2009 to help stanch a\ncrisis within the Irish banking system that has pushed the\ncountry to the edge of insolvency. Ireland\u2019s finance minister\nappointed NAMA\u2019s board -- a former bank manager, two accountants,\nand former government officials -- which now controls the loans\nfor hundreds of hotels, offices and resorts. It remains to be\nseen whether NAMA will take over the rest of developers\u2019\npersonal assets.  \u201cWhere NAMA is unable to work with debtors,\u201d either by\nvirtue of their refusal to cooperate or the hopelessness of\ntheir financial position, \u201cthen NAMA will pursue all avenues to\nrecover what they can for the taxpayer,\u201d says spokesman Ray\nGordon.  Building Bailout  NAMA, excluded from Freedom of Information laws, is famous\nfor its opacity. Its actions have not stopped the momentum of\nthe crisis. The Irish spent the past week bracing for the\narrival of European Union and International Monetary Fund\nofficials to negotiate a possible emergency bailout of the Irish\neconomy. While Ireland hasn\u2019t yet asked for assistance, in an\ninterconnected euro zone, its neighbors may not allow it the\nluxury of resisting.  \u201cIreland is our closest neighbor, and it\u2019s in Britain\u2019s\nnational interest that the Irish economy is successful and we\nhave a stable banking system,\u201d says  George Osborne , the U.K.\nchancellor. \u201cSo Britain stands ready to support Ireland in the\nsteps that it needs to take to bring about that stability.\u201d  Irish Finance Minister  Brian Lenihan  has pledged to work\nwith the EU and IMF while asserting his country\u2019s stability.\n\u201cOur budgetary policy has full confidence among European\npartners,\u201d Lenihan told reporters on Nov. 17. \u201cBut in relation\nto banking, steps taken to date require further support. What\nmay be required may not be in fact an actual transfer of money\nnow but a demonstration of how much money can be made available\nif further difficulties materialize.\u201d  Government Funding  The Irish underestimated the severity of the losses for the\npast two years. In September, the government said that the bank\nbailout may cost as much as 50\u00a0billion euros. NAMA says it will\nabsorb an estimated 73\u00a0billion euros of loans from the banks at\na discount of about half of their value.  The figures sound small relative to the U.S. rescue of its\nbanking system, except that Ireland\u2019s population hovers at 4.4\nmillion, according to the World Bank; the bailout so far equals\n30\u00a0percent of the country\u2019s 158\u00a0billion-euro gross domestic\nproduct. EU officials say Ireland\u2019s emergency aid package may\ntally $136\u00a0billion, roughly the same amount given to Greece in\nMay.  While the U.S. economy was driven off a cliff by the\nreckless securitizing of subprime mortgages and Greece collapsed\nunder the burden of misrepresented government spending, the\nIrish traveled a simpler road to ruin: by taking out enormous,\nunregulated loans. Ireland\u2019s economy has contracted for three\nconsecutive years, and the Irish Central Bank governor has\ndeclared his country\u2019s fiscal deterioration \u201cworse than almost\nany other country.\u201d  Rising Yields  The yield on 10-year Irish bonds climbed to almost\n9\u00a0percent in mid-November, compared with 11\u00a0percent for Greece.  There were hardly any critics of the Celtic Tiger from 1995\nto 2007, when  GDP  growth averaged 5\u00a0percent to 10\u00a0percent and\npushed Ireland into the ranks of the world\u2019s leading economies.  Now seemingly everyone in Ireland recalls a symbolic moment\nwhen they realized things had gone too far. For David Byrne, a\nrepossessed-car auctioneer, it was the sight of his fellow\ncountrymen swilling expensive wine. For Simon Ensor, a real\nestate agent, it was the day the owners of a 1,000-square-foot\nDublin carriage house insisted on selling it for 2.5\u00a0million\neuros, as opposed to the agent\u2019s suggested 2\u00a0million euros ---\nand then the house went for 3\u00a0million euros at auction. For many,\nit was the day the Savoy Hotel in London was bought by Irish\nproperty developer  Derek Quinlan .  After the Fall  Today, according to former Central Bank of Ireland\neconomist David McWilliams, the average Irish family owes\n132,000 euros to banks. Ireland\u2019s Economic and Social Research\nInstitute estimates that housing prices have fallen 36\u00a0percent\nfrom their peak in 2006.  Unemployment  has increased to 14\npercent from 4\u00a0percent during the boom years.  Many Irish people won\u2019t be able to pay off their debts in\ntheir lifetime, and almost all commercial developers are broke.\nThe nation once described by New York Times columnist  Thomas L. Friedman  as the second richest in Europe has become the country\nwith the region\u2019s largest deficit.  More poignantly, a people who fought against the British\nEmpire for their sovereignty may lose control of their financial\nfuture.  Brian Lucey , an economist at Trinity College Dublin,\nsays the government miscalculated the size of the crisis.  \u201cThe banks destabilized the sovereign and the sovereign\nhas destabilized the euro zone,\u201d Lucey says. \u201cThe banks are\ntotally dependent on the European Central Bank for existence.\u201d\nOf a potential bailout, he adds: \u201cWe won\u2019t have much of a\nchoice.\u201d  Wasteland Tour  Inside an old black Land Rover bursting with pens and\nwrappers and trash, Simon Kelly conducts a wasteland tour of the\nDublin boom years. \u201cWe built this thing ourselves,\u201d Kelly says\nas he passes glittering glass buildings. \u201cWe were trading with\nourselves. And everything was being funded by the Germans\nthrough the European Central Bank. So nothing\u2019s really changed,\nif you think about it. We\u2019re still being funded by the Germans\nthrough the European Central Bank.\u201d  According to the Irish Property Council, as many as 29\nIrishmen involved in real estate --- from property barons to\nconstruction workers --- have committed suicide. The Kellys have\nsteeled themselves against the pain caused by the financial\ncollapse in a uniquely Kelly way: by leaning into it.  Paddy was the first of the go-go developers to say in court,\nin 2009, that \u201cmy liabilities exceed my assets.\u201d On Oct.\u00a028,\nSimon published a book about his misadventures in finance called\n\u201cBreakfast with Anglo.\u201d  \u2018Gone Bonkers\u2019  Simon spends much of his time helping NAMA manage his\nproperties, now estimated to be worth 700\u00a0million euros, down\nfrom a high of 2.8\u00a0billion euros, and flying to England every\nfour months for a business course on corporate responsibility\nand sustainability. He hopes someday to create a company that\nproduces something other than glass and steel.  \u201cHalf of the developers have gone bonkers, half left the\ncountry,\u201d Kelly says. \u201cMost of the men are 65 years old, so\nthey don\u2019t need a new life. I\u2019m 38 years old and have five kids.  \u201cMy wife thought we were all nuts,\u201d he adds. \u201cShe was\nfrom a farming family. \u2018Why do you want all this money?\u2019 she\nwould ask.\u201d  Two neighborhoods on Kelly\u2019s tour best represent the bubble\nthat overwhelmed Ireland. The Docklands, a stretch along both\nsides of the River Liffey that was once the dodgiest part of\ntown, now has gleaming office buildings, apartment complexes,\ntheaters and convention centers. It\u2019s also where the empty shell\nof Anglo Irish\u2019s new headquarters sits and inoperative cranes\nloom like morbid giraffes.  Futuristic Project  At night, the lit-up glass offices, the Samuel Beckett\nBridge designed by  Santiago Calatrava , and the neon rings of\nConvention Centre Dublin all look like a futuristic project from\nan architect\u2019s computerized modeling system.  Ballsbridge is the home of Shrewsbury Road, the poshest\nstreet in Dublin, where 6,000-square-foot homes once sold for\n55\u00a0million euros. The neighborhood also yielded one of the\ncrash\u2019s few success stories: the sale of Jurys hotel in 2005, a\nbonanza for the property\u2019s owner, hotelier John Gallagher.  The site consisted of about five acres, and developers were\nsaid to be considering bidding 60\u00a0million euros to 70\u00a0million\neuros an acre, the same price that Chelsea Barracks, the\ndesirable real estate in west London, was going for at the time.\nFew seemed to notice that while the bidders for Chelsea Barracks\nincluded a Qatari real estate investment firm and an American\nprivate equity fund, the bidders for Irish properties were\nalmost always Irish.  Bidding War  Driving past Jurys, a five-story brick behemoth rising over\nleafy streets, Kelly talks about the bidding war with nostalgia.\n\u201cIt was as if the person who bid the highest was a genius,\u201d he\nsays. The Kellys offered 273\u00a0million euros, but Jurys, along\nwith an adjacent site, sold to a developer named  Sean Dunne  for\n380\u00a0million euros. Gallagher, meanwhile, sold much of his hotel\nchain and escaped the crash with a 1.1\u00a0billion-euro profit.  Kelly calls the episode \u201cmy awakening moment.\u201d \u201cI would\nlook at the Americans, look at Apple and Microsoft, and think\nthey\u2019re brilliant, because they produce all this stuff,\u201d he\nsays. \u201cWe buy buildings. We buy products in Germany and turn\nthem into buildings.\u201d  The Irish were long dispossessed of land by an Anglo\nProtestant ruling class. Simon Kelly\u2019s great-great grandfather\nwent to prison in 1882 for promoting land reform during a period\nknown as the Land War.  Common Wisdom  Simon\u2019s grandfather was a builder and refurbished elite\nGeorgian houses. For the Kellys, the ultimate goal in life was\nto become landlords; the notion that one would never go hungry\nif one owned land was common wisdom for a generation.  Paddy and his seven brothers did well building houses in\nthe 1960s and 1970s. Then he went bust for the first time during\nthe 1970s oil crisis, and like many Irish builders, Paddy moved\nto England during Ireland\u2019s recession in the 1980s, where he\nenjoyed an affluent life in Mayfair. By this time, Simon, the\noldest of four children, demonstrated a knack with spreadsheets\nand was involved in the business. When the economy collapsed in\nthe late 1980s, Paddy went broke again and came home.  This time, a new opportunity awaited him. In the late 1980s\nand early 1990s, U.S. corporations such as Intel, Microsoft and\nDell arrived in Ireland to take advantage of the nation\u2019s\neducated, English-speaking workforce and 12.5\u00a0percent corporate\ntax rate. (Multinationals account for about a fifth of Ireland\u2019s\nGDP.)  \u2018Honest Endeavor\u2019  Foreign companies required buildings and helped start the\nboom that got the Kellys back on their feet. Simon calls the\nearly 1990s their \u201chonest endeavor phase\u201d as more and more\nbuilders -- men who didn\u2019t go to school, calculated sums on the\nbacks of envelopes and adopted the American term \u201cdevelopers\u201d\n-- became rich. Soon they would also become national heroes.  The other beast born in the late 1980s was  Sean FitzPatrick \u2019s Anglo Irish, which, being a smaller bank amid old\nstandbys like  Allied Irish Banks Plc  and Bank of Ireland Plc,\nneeded to distinguish itself. Anglo Irish began to aggressively\noffer loans for property development.  \u201cWe\u2019d have a lovely breakfast at 7 in the morning at the\nShelbourne, and I\u2019d say to my lender, \u2018I need some money,\u2019 and\nhe\u2019d give me 10\u00a0million quid,\u201d Simon recalls. \u201cI could have\ngamed the whole system if I wanted. There was no amount of money\nI wouldn\u2019t have been lent.\u201d  Deals and Speculation  Simon\u2019s memoir details endless deals and speculations with\nacres bought, developed or flipped. The Kellys couldn\u2019t keep\ntrack of them all: a ski resort in Italy, a hotel in Malta, the\nwaterfront in Sarasota, Florida. \u201cIn the end, I found it\nvulgar,\u201d he says. \u201cIt became like Wall Street.\u201d  The actual boom ended in 2001, when productivity growth\nfell to 5\u00a0percent. After that, the Fianna F\u00e1il government, which\nhas led Ireland throughout the boom and bust, maintained growth\nby keeping credit flowing easily to keep up property prices.  \u201cAfter 2001, we went into this credit-fueled boom,\u201d says\nLucey of Trinity College. \u201cAlthough people conflate the booms,\none was based on exports and competitiveness, and the other was\na decision to keep that going by pouring credit into the markets\nand not regulating the financial-services industry.\u201d  Soon, everyone joined the party. Newspapers published real\nestate sections 50 pages thick, developers began to travel by\nhelicopter, and men traveled to Antwerp for bachelor parties.\nIreland\u2019s GDP, which had been $25\u00a0billion in the 1980s, soared\nto $267\u00a0billion in 2008.  Like Cupcakes  Even more meaningfully, a country that had seen large\nnumbers leave for America, Australia and England now had close\nto zero unemployment. The Irish now speak of those years with\nself-deprecating affection. \u201cGetting a mortgage was really like\nqueuing up for cupcakes,\u201d says Byrne, the car auctioneer.\n\u201cOrdinary people were telling their neighbor they\u2019re buying a\nthree-bedroom with a private pool in Spain! Ordinary people!\u201d  The Irish banks that made all those second houses possible\nweren\u2019t investment banks or hedge funds. They were traditional\nbanks, which found themselves suddenly flooded with cheap credit.\n\u201cThere was a lot of money sloshing around,\u201d says Lucey. \u201cPlus,\nthere were historically low interest rates in the euro zone.\u201d  FitzPatrick was an early adopter, aggressively loosening\nloan restrictions at Anglo Irish. Other banks implemented the\nsame strategy to keep up. Financier Niall McFadden told the\nSunday Business Post that one bank accepted a personal guarantee\nfor a 6.3\u00a0million-euro loan without ever bothering to meet with\nhim.  \u201cThey did it because they could, because the regulator was\nnonexistent and the government was perfectly happy to engage in\nbubble financing of the public sector,\u201d says Lucey. \u201cWhen the\nbubbles went away, the whole thing fell apart.\u201d  Lehman Bankruptcy  The 2008 collapse of New York-based Lehman Brothers\nHoldings Inc. accelerated Ireland\u2019s slide, as property prices\ncontinued a drop that started in 2007. \u201cAs a small, open\neconomy, Ireland was always going to be vulnerable to global\nswings,\u201d says  Ray Kinsella , an economist at University College\nDublin. \u201cBut this is predominantly a self-inflicted crisis.\u201d  On Sept.\u00a029, 2008, with shares of financial companies\nplummeting, the government declared it would guarantee the debts\nof the banks. Regulators, who had done little for the past\ndecade, didn\u2019t realize the extent of those debts, and bankers\ndidn\u2019t help illuminate the scale of the crisis.  \u2018Thank You\u2019  A few days after the guarantee, FitzPatrick said during a\nradio interview that everything was fine: \u201cThe cause of our\nproblems was global, so I can\u2019t say sorry with any degree of\nsincerity and decency, but I do say thank you,\u201d he said.  On Oct.\u00a06, something unusual happened to Eugene McErlean:\nThe Central Bank of Ireland\u2019s new financial regulator,  Matthew Elderfield , apologized to him.  McErlean, 52, had worked for five years as an auditor for\nAllied Irish Bank. In 2002, he prepared a report for the\nnation\u2019s then financial regulator making a case that his\nemployer had overcharged on hourly rates for the amount of time\nthat bank managers spent with customers. (The range of\novercharges tallied about 88\u00a0million euros.) The Central Bank\ndecided against launching an investigation, and a year later,\nMcErlean was removed from his job.  \u201cThe banks believed their own publicity, that Irish banks\nwere the best in the world,\u201d he says over coffee in the lounge\nat Buswells Hotel. \u201cI had worked other places. And my job as\nauditor was to give an independent opinion.\u201d  Elderfield apologized last month for the McErlean case.\n\u201cSome of the matters could have been handled better by the\npublic authorities involved, and as a result of that I am sorry\nfor any unintentional distress caused to Mr. McErlean,\u201d he said\nbefore a committee in Parliament.  Wall Street  Irish banks operated in a culture of deference and\nuniformity, and, due to the sharp increase in business and the\narrival of a Wall Street culture of performance-based pay,\nbankers went from making 150,000 euros a year to millions.  As Simon Kelly describes it, bankers also stopped paying\nattention to their loans. Ireland had 10 to 15 major property\ndevelopers who could drive the market, and everyone wanted to\nloan money to them.  McErlean says the regulator at the Central Bank, who got\nreports on this activity at least once a quarter, didn\u2019t pay\nclose attention. \u201cIf normal checks and balances had been in\nplace, none of this would have happened,\u201d he says.  The Irish still don\u2019t really know what went on inside their\nbanks.  Shane Ross , a senator and author of two best-selling\nfinancial books, says criminal activity wasn\u2019t the cause of the\ncrash. \u201cIt was a simple circle of being interdependent on each\nother,\u201d he says, referring to the politicians, developers,\nregulators, and bankers. \u201cThe country would have gone bankrupt\nwithout spectaculars like Sean FitzPatrick.\u201d  Dr. Doom  Few whistleblowers or truth-tellers have emerged as heroes\nin Ireland. David McWilliams and an economist named  Morgan Kelly ,\nIreland\u2019s Dr. Doom, were mocked during the bubble years when\nthey predicted a reversal in the country\u2019s fortunes.  Bertie Ahern , Ireland\u2019s Prime Minister from 1997 to 2008,\nfamously dismissed the naysayers at a trade union conference in\n2007: \u201cSitting on the sidelines cribbing and moaning is a lost\nopportunity. I don\u2019t know how people who engage in that don\u2019t\ncommit suicide.\u201d  Now the very idea of Ireland seems at stake. \u201cThis is now\nabout sovereignty,\u201d says Diarmaid Ferriter, an historian and\nauthor of \u201cThe Transformation of Ireland.\u201d \u201cCan we actually\nsurvive? Have we lost control? We\u2019re very proud of our\nindependence.\u201d  He continued: \u201cThis was a country that fought a Land War\nand got rid of an English class of landlords, and that was\nreplaced by an Irish class of landowners, speculators, and\nbankers even more invidious. That\u2019s a terrible tragedy.\u201d  High Court  The grand front entrance of Four Courts, an 18th\u00a0century\nbuilding that houses the High Court of Dublin, recently reopened\nto the public. Inside, the mood is grim. On a busy morning in\nthe bankruptcy and home repossessions courts, the judge,  Brian McGovern , sat on a bench in a small, wood-paneled courtroom.  Six globe lights hung from the ceiling; carafes of water\nwere placed on the tables and benches. The room soon filled with\nlawyers in black capes; debtors in jeans hid in the back row.  The bankruptcy session ran long. \u201cI\u2019m sorry,\u201d the judge\nsaid to lawyers waiting for the foreclosures portion of the\nmorning. \u201cThe bankruptcy list unfortunately has grown in\nsize.\u201d There were some 50 cases that day.  Then it was time to deal with home repossessions. In 2007\nthere were fewer than 10 cases heard in a week; now there are 90.\nAccording to the Independent Mortgage Advisers Federation, there\nare 700,000 active mortgages in Ireland; industry trackers like\nMorgan Kelly estimate that 100,000 are under water, and one in\n20 is at least three months in arrears.  Civil War  In court, most lawyers requested that their clients\u2019 cases\nbe deferred for six months, and the judge showed a bias toward\ngranting debtors some breathing room. \u201cThere\u2019d be a civil war\nin Ireland if legislators let financial institutions repossess\npeople\u2019s homes,\u201d says Byrne, the repossessed-car auctioneer.  Because of its history with landownership, when it comes to\nhouses, Ireland maintains a relatively generous forbearance\npolicy, although in 2009, repossession orders were up 27\u00a0percent\nfrom the year before.  The tradition of leniency made the two couples who stood\nbefore McGovern volunteering to relinquish their homes that much\nmore surprising. The judge inquired about their finances, their\nemployment and their children, and then almost pleaded with the\ncouple to hold off, to try and get their funds together.  \u201cWe\u2019re ready to move on,\u201d one woman said, her voice\nbreaking. \u201cIt\u2019s dragging us down.\u201d  Social Conflict  In a Nov.\u00a08 column in the Irish Times, Morgan Kelly wrote:\n\u201cIf one family defaults on its mortgage, they are pariahs: if\n200,000 default they are a powerful political constituency. The\ngathering mortgage crisis puts Ireland on the cusp of a social\nconflict on the scale of the Land War.\u201d  One of Paddy and Simon Kelly\u2019s biggest projects was\ntransforming Carton House, a castle-like estate that once\nbelonged to lords of Ireland, into a hotel and residential\ndevelopment. While Carton House is now 72\u00a0million euros in debt\nand partially owned by NAMA, Paddy enjoys playing on its golf\ncourse.  It\u2019s unclear whether NAMA will initiate bankruptcy\nproceedings against developers. For that reason, and because\nIreland\u2019s bankruptcy laws are harsh, many developers have\nskipped town. Paddy and Simon haven\u2019t, though Simon admits to\nbeing more nervous these days about the prospect of bankruptcy.\nIn the meantime, they expect to receive civil servant salaries\nto help NAMA manage their businesses.  Celtic Tiger  Paddy, white-haired and pink-faced, sits in the golf\nclubhouse dressed in a yellow sweater over a pink button-down\nshirt. Talking about the Celtic Tiger years, his eyes light up\nlike an aging rock star remembering the 1960s. He says they\n\u201cwere magic.\u201d  Asked if at any point he had become depressed by the crash,\nhe screws up his face and says, \u201cAre you joking?\u201d  \u201cWhen I was younger, I was the best marble player, and\nthen I hurled them all away,\u201d he says. \u201cSomeone asked me why?\nThey had no value. The fun was in the game.\u2019\u201d  Paddy, who last went bust in 1987, knows that tomorrow\nisn\u2019t a total a mystery. \u201cLearn to protect yourself, and have\nsafety nets,\u201d he says. \u201cThree years ago I came back from the\nUnited States, and I said, \u2018Everything in America has shut down.\nWhen America gets a cold, we get the flu; let\u2019s tidy up, see if\nwe\u2019re O.K.\u201d He says he knew what was going to happen 18 months\nbefore he went under. \u201cWe\u2019re comfortable,\u201d he says.  Tons of Cement  Then he tells another story: \u201cWhen we were building houses\nwith my father and there\u2019d be 20 tons of cement delivered,\nDaddy\u2019d always take a bag and hide it. When we\u2019d go to finish\nthe job, we\u2019d say, \u2018Daddy, we run out.\u2019 And he\u2019d come with the\nbag. He taught us all: You have to have savings. You have to\nhave hidden strength and hidden assets. And overall, your first\nduty is as a family.\u201d  Should the developers feel responsible for what happened to\ntheir country?  \u201cNo question,\u201d says Paddy. \u201cBut I think the blame game\nessentially doesn\u2019t work. If you take the last few years, we\nhaven\u2019t borrowed any money. Why didn\u2019t we borrow money? Because\nit was not available. It starts with the minister of finance,\nbut he didn\u2019t know what was going on. And the regulator didn\u2019t\nknow what was going on. And the European bankers didn\u2019t know\nwhat was going on. They kept pushing money into Ireland.\u201d  While Paddy Kelly is talking about new projects, Simon is\nless enthusiastic. \u201cI\u2019m an example of corporate excess,\u201d he\nsays. When Simon\u2019s small son climbs into the car at the end of\nthe Celtic Tiger Graveyard tour, Simon looks at him and says he\ncan\u2019t help hoping he finds a future far away from the\ndevelopers\u2019 trade: \u201cI hope he goes to Harvard.\u201d  To contact the reporter on this story:\nSuzy Hansen at  hansen.Suzy@gmail.com   To contact the editor responsible for this story:\nSheelah Kolhatkar at   skolhatkar@bloomberg.net","path":".\/2008_2012_msft_bloomberg_news\/ireland-risks-becoming-another-greece-as-europe-s-economic-superstar-fades.txt"},{"id":75373151,"title":"Samsung Sent EU Antitrust Complaint Over Apple Injunctions","released_at":"<date>December 21 2012<\/date> <time>19:54:41<\/time>","content":"Samsung Electronics Co. (AAPL)  and legions of software developers are girding for fines and rules that analysts say threaten to stifle growth.  The U.S. Federal Trade Commission, which this month fined Path Inc., a social-networking site, $800,000 for unauthorized collection of user data, is investigating a rising number of mobile apps for privacy violations. California Attorney General  Kamala Harris  is stepping up scrutiny of app makers, and congressional lawmakers are planning legislation that would require programmers to bolster disclosure and data protection.  Developers rely on tools that track users\u2019 whereabouts, surfing habits and buying preferences to pack their apps with ads and features. Yet, with vast amounts of personal data bought and sold over the Web, user privacy is at risk. Therein lies a conundrum: More fines and tighter rules to protect consumers could boost costs for small companies whose apps are fueling demand for mobile advertising, tablets and smartphones.  \u201cPrivacy measures could directly impact the development of the mobile-advertising market,\u201d said John Jackson, an analyst at Framingham, Massachusetts-based researcher IDC. \u201cAny legislative actions could lead to very heavy setbacks.\u201d  That has big implications for Google and Apple, which together account for 91 percent of smartphone operating systems. Google\u2019s Android is the most widely used software for the devices, followed by Apple\u2019s iOS,  according  to IDC. The companies keep part of the revenue generated by app sales while making money from ads embedded in certain applications. Facebook Inc. and Twitter Inc. also make app versions of their social- media services available for download on mobile devices.  Safeguarding Data  These companies are taking steps to safeguard user data and lessen the likelihood of a raft of new rules.  Apple\u2019s efforts include \u201climited ad tracking and the ability for customers to manage their privacy settings for location, contacts, photos and more,\u201d said  Tom Neumayr , a spokesman for Cupertino, California-based Apple.  The company vets all apps before they\u2019re made available in its  App Store  and offers a tool called Restrictions, which lets parents prevent kids from installing or deleting apps, making in-app purchases and accessing certain other features.  Google updated its developer program policy in August to prohibit apps that disclose personal information without user consent. Facebook lets customers adjust settings so they can search and filter each piece of content that\u2019s shared publicly.  Increased Enforcement  Increased enforcement and the cost of complying with new regulations could eventually push small developers out of business, Erica Sadun, an author of books on mobile-app development, said via e-mail. Even small fines can add up for fledgling companies that, according to  estimates  by GigaOM Pro, on average generate less than $500 a month from sales of downloadable apps.  \u201cOne-man shops may be driven under or may simply start avoiding anything that involves any user identification whatsoever,\u201d Sadun said. \u201cAn onerous requirement would be a tipping point that could potentially sink the independent developer, and a hazy one would open them up to potential lawsuits.\u201d  App makers are already feeling the heat. Path, which lets people form tight-knit online social networks, was penalized for collecting information from children without the consent of their parents. In response, Path closed its services to children under 13, and, by terms of  the settlement , must commission independent privacy assessments every other year for the next 20 years.  \u2018Apps Failed\u2019  The FTC  fined  W3 Innovations LLC $50,000 in 2011 for letting children publicly post personal information on message boards via apps like Emily\u2019s Girl World.  According to an FTC  review  of 400 apps for kids, \u201cmost apps failed to provide any information about the data collected through the app, let alone the type of data collected, the purpose of the collection, and who would obtain access to the data. Even more troubling, the results showed that many of the apps shared certain information with third parties -\u2013 such as device ID, geolocation, or phone number -\u2013 without disclosing that fact to parents.\u201d  More strictures are coming. The FTC\u2019s revised Children\u2019s Online Privacy Protection Rule,  taking effect  in July, will require app makers to get parental consent to collect information from children. That will result in about $10,000 in legal costs per developer, costing $270 million for makers of education apps for Apple devices alone, said Morgan Reed,  executive director  of the the  Association for Competitive Technology , whose members include Apple, Facebook and Microsoft Corp.  Sensitive Information  \u201cWe recognize that app developers are small, but their size should not excuse their responsibility to consumers, given the sensitive information they may handle,\u201d Christopher Olsen,  assistant director  at the FTC\u2019s division of privacy and identity protection, said in an interview. \u201cCertainly we\u2019ll be active on the enforcement front.\u201d  The FTC formed a mobile-technology unit about two years ago and has staff members looking at mobile apps at various divisions, such as the one focused on advertising, he said. The agency issued a 36-page  report  Feb. 1 with  recommendations  on how developers and app stores should protect users\u2019 privacy.  Among the recommendations: companies such as Apple, Google, Microsoft, Amazon.com Inc. and  Research In Motion Ltd. (BB)  should set more privacy requirements for developers. For instance, it asked for real-time notifications to users whenever their personal information is accessed.  Trust Questioned  Congressional lawmakers are working on legislation this year that would tighten mobile privacy protection and improve disclosure. The  Apps Act  will be referred to a House Energy and Commerce Committee subcommittee, according to Andy Phelan, communications director for Representative Hank Johnson, a Democrat from  Georgia .  The Apps Act  asks  developers to obtain users\u2019 consent to terms and conditions governing collection of user data. It also gives the government oversight of how and when privacy notices should be provided to users.  States, led by  California , are devoting attention to mobile apps as well. California Attorney General Harris  sued  Delta Air Lines Inc. in December for not posting a privacy notice within its \u201cFly Delta\u201d mobile app. The suit seeks to stop Delta from distributing the app without a privacy policy and includes penalties of up to $2,500 for each violation.  \u201cIt was clear to us that a lot more could be done to improve the disclosures,\u201d Olsen said. \u201cApps need to do more to avoid raising consumer trust concerns -- raising questions as to whether apps in general can be trusted.\u201d  To contact the reporter on this story: Olga Kharif in Portland at  okharif@bloomberg.net   To contact the editor responsible for this story: Tom Giles at  tgiles5@bloomberg.net","path":".\/2008_2012_msft_bloomberg_news\/google-to-apple-gird-for-ftc-led-mobile-privacy-crackdown-tec.txt"},{"id":10067728,"title":"Nokia's Green Seeks R&D Edge Back From IPhone, Android","released_at":"<date>September 21 2010<\/date> <time>08:12:55<\/time>","content":"Nokia Oyj  Chief Technology Officer\n Rich Green  says he wants his team to be in \u201cdirty jerseys\u201d as\nthe Finnish company seeks to regain the edge in smartphones from\nApple Inc. and Google Inc.  \u201cThey should be in the game, playing, and not on the\nsidelines with a clean jersey telling people what to do,\u201d Green\nsaid in an interview. Nokia\u2019s  research and development budget  of 5.9 billion\neuros ($7.7 billion), including 3 billion euros for devices and\nservices, is the largest in the industry. The company spent\nalmost six times as much as Apple on R&D last year. Although it\nemployed more than 17,000 R&D workers in devices and services,\nNokia still isn\u2019t leading the charge in smartphone innovation.  \u201cWhy can you not see that they have the biggest R&D budget\nwhen you get their products?\u201d said  Bengt Nordstroem , the CEO of\nStockholm-based consulting company Northstream AB. \u201cSomething\u2019s\nnot working when the people who have the biggest budget and the\nmost resources cannot translate that strength into something\nthat means something to customers.\u201d  Nokia\u2019s R&D efforts are symptomatic of the broader\nstructural challenges that lie ahead for Green and Elop, both\nnewcomers to the Espoo, Finland-based company. It may be among\noperations that risk being shrunk as competition intensifies.  Research Center  \u201cIf financial pressures on the company increase, Nokia may\nbe obliged to review its software R&D strategy, perhaps\npartnering, outsourcing or even selling off selected elements,\u201d\nsaid  Gavin Byrne , an analyst with researcher Informa Telecoms &\nMedia in London. The  Nokia Research Center , which conducts research with a\nhorizon of three to 10 years in a dozen locations from Berkeley\nto Nairobi, employs 500 people. The company\u2019s smartphone development efforts have also been\nsplit among three potentially competing platforms, Symbian 3,\nSymbian 4 and MeeGo. It\u2019s also expanding the Series 40 platform\nfor the low-end phones that make up the bulk of its shipments\nand are gradually approaching smartphones in sophistication.  R&D Centers  A plethora of devices with varying software and interfaces\nhas turned off developers. Modest economic growth and tight cost controls enabled\ncompanies to record a 2 percent increase in revenue and\nunchanged  cash flow  from operations in the year ended September\n2012, according to the report. High cash balances are positive\ncredit factors and ensure companies can retire near-term\nmaturing debt if the  capital markets  are disrupted and withstand\ndeterioration in business conditions.  \u201cThere are a few key drivers to the record cash levels\nincluding good financial performance, steady growth for the\naggregate of non-financial companies, a modest increase in\nrevenues and supplementing funding needs through raising debt in\na market last year that was very receptive to debt issuance,\u201d\nLane, senior vice president at Moody\u2019s said in a telephone\ninterview. Companies need to be able to manage cash so they are\nprepared to handle unforeseen macroeconomic or financial\nchallenges, and \u201cmaintain the ability to invest in product\ndevelopment, research and development and  capital expenditures ,\nwhich are the foundation for companies to stay competitive over\nthe long-term,\u201d he said. (AAPL)  is counting on the popularity of its devices and political pressure to thwart efforts by  Google Inc. (GOOG) \u2019s Motorola Mobility to block imports of the iPhone and iPad, two of the best-selling electronic devices in the U.S.  The U.S. International Trade Commission in Washington is scheduled to announce today whether iPhones and other Apple devices infringe Motorola Mobility patents and, if so, whether it will stop them from being imported into the U.S. from  Asia .  As part of its review, the ITC is weighing whether to limit use of import bans in disputes over patents that relate to industrywide standards. Some members of Congress, the U.S. Federal Trade Commission and companies including  Intel Corp . have urged such a step.  \u201cI do not think, in the current legal and political climate, that there is any possibility that the iPhone will be excluded from importation,\u201d said Rodney Sweetland, a patent lawyer with Duane Morris in Washington who specializes in ITC cases.  Motorola Mobility says Apple products infringe four patents, two of which relate to industry standards for 3G wireless and Wi-Fi technologies, and that Apple has rebuffed offers to license the standard-essential patents. The other two patents aren\u2019t standard-essential, nor are the seven patents that are the subject of a new complaint Motorola Mobility filed Aug. 17.  Apple denies infringing the patents and contends they\u2019re invalid. Even if the commission finds a patent violation, Apple says in filings that its devices shouldn\u2019t be stopped at the U.S. border.  \u2018Neat\u2019 Products  \u201cThe commission is under some political pressure not to keep \u2018neat\u2019 products out of the country,\u201d said Scott Daniels of Westerman Hattori in  Washington , who does ITC cases. \u201cNormally, politics and Congress have very little impact on commission rulings. In the case of something so central to the economy, there could be an impact.\u201d  A trade judge in April said Apple, which this week became the most valuable U.S. company in history, violated one patent that\u2019s essential to 3G. The commission is reviewing his findings.  The iPhone\u2019s $47.1 billion in sales and $20.4 billion in iPad sales together made up more than 62 percent of Cupertino, California-based Apple\u2019s fiscal 2011  sales , according to data compiled by Bloomberg. The second standard-essential patent in Motorola Mobility\u2019s complaint also would cover Mac computers, the iPod Touch and Apple TV.  Congressional Pressure  Members of Congress including House Judiciary Committee Chairman  Lamar Smith , a Texas Republican, wrote the ITC in June saying the benefits of adopting standard technologies \u201cmay be undermined\u201d if patent disputes threaten the ability to sell products in the U.S. The Senate Judiciary Committee held a July 11  hearing  on the issue.  Patent owners whose technologies are adopted as industry standards, such as specifications that let wireless phones communicate with one another, agree to charge fair and reasonable licensing fees. In those kinds of cases, the FTC urged the trade commission to take other steps, such as pushing for mediation of royalty amounts, before considering a ban on imports.  Blocking imports based on infringement of a standard- essential patent \u201chas the potential to cause substantial harm to U.S. competition, consumers and innovation,\u201d the FTC wrote in a June 6 filing with the agency. It said companies could be coerced into unreasonable licensing fees in a practice known as a \u201cpatent holdup.\u201d  Motorola Mobility says it fulfilled its obligation to make a reasonable royalty offer and Apple refuses to negotiate.  \u2018Unwilling Licensee\u2019  \u201cApple and others -- without analyzing the facts of this case -- point to the problem of \u2018hold up,\u2019\u201d Motorola Mobility told the commission in a July 16 filing. \u201cBut they ignore the counter problem of \u2018hold out\u2019 -- an unwilling licensee being rewarded for its intransigence in a manner that will deprive patent owners of value and create disincentives for innovative companies from participating in standards setting.\u201d  The case represents one battle in a broader global legal war over patents, including more than a dozen complaints at the ITC over the past two years, as companies vie for increased shares of a smartphone market that grew 62 percent to $219 billion last year.  Apple, in one of the high-profile cases, is awaiting a California jury\u2019s verdict in a separate dispute claiming that Samsung\u2019s Android phones copied patented iPhone features.  Korean Ban  In  South Korea  today, the Seoul Central District Court ruled that Apple and Samsung infringed each other\u2019s patents and told them both to stop selling some versions of their products in that country.  Google, based in  Mountain View , California, is counting on Motorola Mobility\u2019s long history with mobile phones -- and its trove of 17,000 patents -- to force Apple into a settlement of the ITC case that could also encompass handset makers using Google\u2019s Android operating system, including Samsung Electronics Co. and  HTC Corp. (2498)   Motorola Mobility approached Apple in 2007 about a patent license, demanding a royalty of 2.25 percent of the price of Apple products. Motorola Mobility has said that\u2019s the standard offer it makes, and expects the figure to change during negotiations. Apple and Microsoft Corp., which has its own legal fights with Motorola Mobility, said the demand was unreasonable.  Presidential Review  President  Barack Obama  could review a commission decision and reject any import ban on public policy grounds. In the past, patent owners have lost efforts to block imports for health- related products, for devices that reduced gasoline consumption during the 1970s oil crisis, and when the government was in the midst of trade negotiations.  ITC Judge Thomas Pender, who presided over the trial, recommended that the agency issue an import ban on any product found to infringe the Motorola Mobility patents. He said Apple should pay the 2.25 percent royalty rate during the 60-day presidential review period.  \u2018Extreme Solution\u2019  Qualcomm Inc., (QCOM)  which makes and designs chips for mobile phones and gets more than one-third of its revenue from licensing, said the FTC\u2019s suggestion for limiting import bans based on standard-essential patents is \u201can extreme solution in search of a problem.\u201d  The commission could say that an import ban isn\u2019t in the public interest, or delay imposing a ban to give Apple and Motorola Mobility time to resolve their differences or to have other courts hear their cases, said David Long, a patent lawyer with Dow Lohnes in Washington.  \u201cTheir challenge would be to create what relief they can if there is a violation,\u201d Long said. \u201cIt\u2019s up to Congress to establish whether standard-essential patents are welcome at the ITC, and Congress hasn\u2019t done that.\u201d  The case is In the Matter of Certain Wireless Communication Devices, Portable Music Data, Processing Data Devices, Computers and Components Thereof, 337-745, U.S. International Trade Commission (Washington). Taubman,\nco-heads of Morgan Stanley\u2019s biggest business, work on opposite\nsides of an ocean, disagree about strategy and share an enmity\nthat has become the subject of company jokes.  At a meeting of more than 100 managing directors at the\nRitz-Carlton Battery Park hotel in New York last year, Robert Kindler, the bank\u2019s head of mergers and acquisitions and brother\nof stand-up comedian Andy Kindler, drew laughs and whistles when\nhe ribbed the two men about their relationship, according to two\npeople who attended the session.  \u201cSo how\u2019s that co-head thing going?\u201d Kindler asked,\ngesturing at Kelleher and Taubman, who are in charge of\n investment banking , sales and trading and were seated onstage\nwith other members of the firm\u2019s operating committee.  Neither Kelleher, 54, a gregarious former fixed-income\nsalesman, nor Taubman, 50, a reserved investment banker,\nresponded to the taunt, said the people, who asked not to be\nidentified because they weren\u2019t authorized to speak. In the aftermath of the terrorist bombing there on April 15, Boston Police Commissioner Edward Davis wants even more cameras to boost street-level surveillance, said spokeswoman Cheryl Fiandaca. Other cities, too, now may be spurred to expand their systems, which security specialists said will fuel sales growth in the $3.2 billion video surveillance industry.  Such actions increase tensions between law enforcement officials and privacy advocates, who say they worry about Big Brother intrusions into people\u2019s legal activities. The  American Civil Liberties Union  in  San Francisco  raised such concerns after Police Chief Greg Suhr cited Boston last week in saying he wants additional cameras for downtown Market Street to give police a better look during parades and other public events.  \u201cWe shouldn\u2019t rush into mass surveillance of San Franciscans as they go about their everyday lives,\u201d Abdi Soltani, executive director of the ACLU of Northern California, said on the group\u2019s  website .  The role of video surveillance drew national attention as the  Federal Bureau  of Investigation used law enforcement and private security cameras -- plus smartphone images provided by hundreds of people -- to identify the suspected bombers, brothers Tamerlan and Dzhokhar Tsarnaev. Since the al-Qaeda attacks on  New York  and the Pentagon in 2001, U.S. cities have deployed video and other sensors purchased with the help of billions of dollars in federal counterterrorism funding.  \u2018Terrible Reminder\u2019  \u201cThe Boston bombing is a terrible reminder of why we\u2019ve made these investments -\u2013 including camera technology that could help us deter an attack, or investigate and apprehend those involved,\u201d New York City Mayor  Michael Bloomberg  said in remarks April 16.  The extent of government video surveillance capabilities in U.S. cities currently is hard to determine since the information is generally not made public. Chicago authorities have access to about 10,000 public and private video surveillance cameras, according to a 2011 report by the American Civil Liberties Union of Illinois. San Francisco has cameras in high-crime areas that are reviewed for evidence after a crime has occurred.  In the U.S., closed-circuit television and video surveillance equipment is an estimated $3.2 billion market this year, up from $3 billion in 2012, according to IMS Research, part of  IHS Inc. (IHS)  of Englewood, Colorado.  Projected Growth  The market is projected to grow to $4.1 billion by 2016, Paul Everett, senior manager for the IHS security research group in Austin,  Texas , said in a phone interview.  Historically, terrorist attacks have spurred growth, and the Boston bombing also may have that effect, Everett said.  \u201cAs the event happened out in the open, the market may see more in the way of city surveillance projects,\u201d he said.  While New York and some other cities have expanded the number of cameras using grants from the Department of  Homeland Security , other cities such as Los Angeles have opted against widespread use of cameras, in part because of the cost, said  Marc Rotenberg , executive director of the Washington-based Electronic Privacy Information Center.  \u201cPeople have accepted some degree of public surveillance, but at the same time I just don\u2019t see a big push for a dramatic increase,\u201d Rotenberg said in an interview.  London Watching  There are far fewer closed-circuit television cameras in U.S. cities than in  London , where attacks by bombers seeking to drive the British out of Northern Ireland predate threats from Islamic extremists. London boroughs and the city\u2019s transit network together have deployed more than 91,000 CCTV cameras, according to 2011 data obtained by  Big Brother Watch , a civil liberties group. More than 1,800 cameras monitored the athletic village during the 2012  Olympic Games  hosted by the city.  There\u2019s no authoritative estimate of how many tens of thousands of other cameras are operated privately at stores, office buildings and other locations in the U.K. capital, where closed-circuit cameras are easily visible on street poles, in shops, in the subway and on buses. In London, it\u2019s estimated that on average, an individual may be recorded by more than 300 cameras in a single day, according to a 2012 report by Big Brother Watch.  \u201cLondon is probably the most surveilled city in the world,\u201d the group\u2019s director, Nick Pickles, said in a telephone interview.  Catching Criminals  In London, cameras helped track down criminals in riots across the city in August 2011, and the terrorists who attacked the bus and subway system in July 2005 were recorded on camera buying supplies for their bombs. In total, only one U.K. crime is solved for every 1,000 cameras because the majority of the 4.25 million CCTV cameras installed nationwide deliver low-quality images, according to a 2012 report by Bsria Ltd., a U.K. research and consulting firm.  One  law-enforcement  ambition is to couple real-time video with artificial intelligence software able to act before a terrorist bombing or other crime occurs. Such systems would alert police to warning signs, such as an abandoned backpack or recognized face, in time to avert a potential terrorist attack.  New York, a target for terrorist plots more frequently than any other U.S. city, is advancing toward that capability with its so-called Domain Awareness System, an effort developed with  Microsoft Corp. (MSFT)  of Redmond,  Washington , that\u2019s described as drawing real-time information from about 3,000 CCTV cameras and other sensors in lower and midtown Manhattan.  Detecting Abnormalities  The camera network \u201cnow has the capacity to alert police to abnormalities it detects on the street, such as an abandoned package,\u201d said Bloomberg, who is founder and majority owner of Bloomberg LP, the parent of  Bloomberg News .  In a WOR Radio interview last month, before the Boston attack, Bloomberg remarked on the advance in surveillance technologies -- including police use of drones -- and its implications for individual privacy.  \u201cYou\u2019re going to have face recognition software, people are working on that,\u201d Bloomberg said March 22. \u201cWe\u2019re going into a different world, uncharted.\u201d  \u201cWe\u2019re going to have more visibility and less privacy,\u201d he said. \u201cIt\u2019s not a question of whether it is good or bad, I just don\u2019t see how you can stop that.\u201d  Marathon Surveillance  Boston-area authorities had almost 150 cameras in the local network as of 2007, according to the most recent figures provided to the ACLU of  Massachusetts . Carol Rose, the group\u2019s executive director, warns against what she considers the temptation to see increasing video surveillance as a solution to the terrorist threat.  \u201cPeople have to understand there was a lot of surveillance at the finish line of the Boston Marathon,\u201d she said in a telephone interview. \u201cNeither there nor in the many studies that have been done is there any evidence that surveillance is going to stop or deter someone from a violent act.\u201d  To the extent that surveillance can help to track a perpetrator, she said \u201cthere is no objection to that so long as there are appropriate checks and balances.\u201d  \u201cIf we permit our fear to lead us down a path where everyone becomes a suspect, not only are we violating fundamental principles of democracy, but we also are undermining public safety because when everyone is a suspect, then no one is a suspect,\u201d she said.  Wary Americans  Her concerns are shared by many Americans, according to a Washington Post poll after the Boston bombing. The poll found 48 percent of people worry that the government \u201cwill go too far\u201d to investigate terrorism versus 41 percent who said the government \u201cwill not go far enough.\u201d The poll of 588 adults has an error margin of plus or minus five percentage points.  Government officials have considerable legal leeway to expand the use of video cameras in public places, said Christopher Swift, a lawyer and an adjunct professor of national  security studies  at  Georgetown University \u2019s School of Foreign Service in Washington.  Many people misjudge the extent of their Fourth Amendment privacy rights outside the home, he said.  \u201cLet\u2019s be honest here; the government can fly a helicopter over your house and hover there and take pictures of what\u2019s going on in your backyard, and the  Supreme Court  has said that is legal,\u201d he said in an interview. He was referring to a 1989 case, Florida v. Riley, in which the high court held that police don\u2019t need a warrant to observe an individual\u2019s property from public airspace.  Small Drones  That ruling may have greater consequences than the justices realized at the time, as law enforcement agencies evaluate the possible use of small, unmanned aircraft in police work. Cities as small as Monroe, North Carolina, population 33,000, have been seeking to acquire drones.  Once prices drop, \u201cpeople will think it\u2019s crazy not to use them for policing,\u201d said Stewart Baker, a lawyer at  Steptoe & Johnson LLP (1372L)  and former assistant secretary for policy at the Homeland Security Department. \u201cYou can see how it would have been very useful to have drones fly over Boston during the manhunt.\u201d  Drone use was a source of privacy concerns well before the Boston attack.  The federal government uses Predator drones to help patrol the border, an area so broadly defined that it includes New York City and Chicago, said Rotenberg of the Electronic Privacy Information Center.  U.S. Customs  and  Border Protection , part of the Homeland Security Department, has outfitted those aircraft with technology to intercept mobile phone signals and identify people on the ground, according to documents Rotenberg\u2019s group obtained under the Freedom of Information Act.  Rotenberg\u2019s organization is seeking to suspend the drone program until privacy rules are put in place.  To the extent drones are used in emergency situations, like the Boston manhunt, \u201cI don\u2019t think anyone is going to object to that,\u201d Rotenberg said. \u201cAs a form of routine surveillance 24-7 for the general public, there\u2019s a problem.\u201d  To contact the reporters on this story: Terry Atlas in Washington at  tatlas@bloomberg.net ; Greg Stohr in Washington at  gstohr@bloomberg.net   To contact the editor responsible for this story: John Walcott at  jwalcott9@bloomberg.net","path":".\/2008_2012_msft_bloomberg_news\/surveillance-cameras-sought-by-cities-after-boston-bombs.txt"},{"id":15612601,"title":"U.S. Stocks Fall Amid Concern U.S. Economy Is Faltering","released_at":"<date>August 10 2011<\/date> <time>13:31:03<\/time>","content":"U.S. stocks fell at the start of\ntrading, as measured by the Standard & Poor's 500 Index, at 9:31\na.m. New York time.
