So it\u2019s no coincidence that B&O is bringing its high-style\nethos to the market for peripherals designed to work with\n Apple (AAPL) \u2019s iPhones, iPads and Macs. The result is the  Beolit 12 , a\nportable speaker that uses Apple\u2019s AirPlay technology to\nwirelessly stream music throughout your home.  The Beolit 12 introduces B&O Play, a new line that in the\nB&O world will pass for budget-priced -- in this case, $799.  Now, in the world of most mortals, $799 is a lot of money\nfor a speaker. Even high-end manufacturers like  Klipsch ,  Bowers\n& Wilkins  and  Bose  sell similar products for hundreds less.\nStill, if you\u2019ve got the coin and want the cachet, B&O offers\nvery good sound in a striking package.  The Beolit 12 resembles a compact, aluminum-clad picnic\nbasket. It measures about nine inches by five inches, and stands\nabout seven inches tall, with a rubberized top that provides\neasy access to the power, volume controls and wireless-network\nindicator. At about six pounds, it\u2019s easily transportable\nwithout being featherweight; a leather shoulder strap completes\nthe basket metaphor.  Plays Well With Apple  At the back are USB and line-in ports, should you want to\ndirectly connect an iPad, iPhone or iPod touch (or a non-Apple\nphone or MP3 player). But the Beolit works and plays best with\nthe Apple ecosystem, specifically  AirPlay , its proprietary\nsystem for media sharing across devices.  Airplay is what allows you to, for example, beam photos or\na movie from your iPad onto a big-screen television equipped\nwith the company\u2019s $99 Apple TV gadget. Choose it,\nand the music begins to play. That\u2019s it.  Unfortunately, it takes a good deal of effort to get to\nthat effortless point. Setting up the Beolit is a pain.  Awkward Set-Up  You start by opening a door on the speaker\u2019s back,\nrevealing a large empty compartment and exposing two ports: one\nfor the power cable and the other for an included Ethernet\ncable. You\u2019ll need a computer, which can\u2019t be connected to the\nInternet during set-up. Enter information about your Wi-Fi\nnetwork, disconnect the computer and wait for the speaker to\nrestart, amid much blinking of orange and white lights.  Once done, you\u2019re rewarded with sound that\u2019s surprisingly\nrich coming from such a compact package, thanks to the 120-watt\namplifier driving a pair of two-inch tweeters and a four inch-\nwoofer that provides solid bass.  The sound is by no means audiophile-quality. As with the\none-box solutions from B&O\u2019s competitors, there\u2019s no real stereo\nseparation to speak of, and squeezing everything into such a\nsmall package inevitably imposes compromises. Still, for what it\nis, you\u2019re likely to be happy.  Time Out  B&O says the Beolit will play for eight hours with a device\ndirectly plugged in, but only four hours if you\u2019re using\nAirplay. That would be pretty disappointing if it were true.  During my test, the estimate proved much too conservative.\nWith the volume loud enough to fill a large, fully furnished\nroom, I got more than 6-1\/2 hours of continuous listening\nbetween charges.  Is the Beolit 12 worth the money? Only if you understand\nthe premium you\u2019re paying to buy into the B&O lifestyle. If so,\nyou\u2019ll get some very nice sound along with it. No wonder, though: Ballmer oversaw Microsoft during what's been called its  lost decade , and here's a look at opportunities missed -- and botched -- during his tenure. 1. Mobile Microsoft achieved dominance at a time when everyone wanted to own a personal computer tethered to his or her desk at home or at the office. It forged lucrative relationships with major PC-makers and optimized its software around the Intel processors, thumping the competition along the way (including, mind you, Apple). That strategy worked brilliantly until other devices started taking screen time away from the desktops and laptops that were Microsoft\u2019s bread and butter. (See also the fate of Dell, Hewlett-Packard and Intel.) As users have developed a decided preference for computing anytime and anywhere they want, PC sales have suffered and have been in an  outright decline  for more than a year. The biggest threat came from smartphones, a market that is growing by about  50 percent annually . Ballmer had Windows Mobile on the market way back when, but it was never a great product, despite his repeated promises to make it better. He also struck a belated partnership with Nokia, and reviews suggest that their product has some neat advantages (such as the camera\u2019s ability to take pictures at night -- cool!), but it all smacks of too little, too late. 2. Music It\u2019s easy to forget that Apple was nearly dead in the late 1990s. Their computers were overpriced and were incompatible with most software. Apple was saved by iTunes and the iPod, which provided a legal and convenient way to download and share music. Apple ended up succeeding in smartphones because they took what they learned making music gadgets to revolutionize the smartphone market. While Microsoft had an early head start making software for the portable music market, the manufacturers it relied on to make devices weren't very good at making great music gadgets. Eventually, in 2006, Microsoft came up with its own product -- the Zune -- but despite some neat features like the ability to share music over wifi, it turned out to be\u2026wait for it, wait for it\u2026a flop. 3. Tablets Microsoft debuted e-book software back in 2000, long before rivals like Amazon and Apple had offerings, but it failed to take off because no one had invented a screen that was easy on the eyes for hours at a time until Amazon gave us the Kindle. (See the pattern? When Microsoft first dominated the arena, software trumped hardware. But as time went on, software divorced from great hardware came to be a liability and Microsoft, except for the Xbox, has never been a primo hardware company.) Microsoft Reader was embedded on the Windows Pocket PC platform for mobile devices, and later, on Windows. But it was discontinued in August 2012. As with music, it was another case of getting in early but botching the execution.  4. Search Microsoft knew that the Internet was big and was ruthless at fighting and winning the browser war. Internet Explorer was so successful that Microsoft had to spend years fighting off antitrust suits that now seem silly. Those clashes probably distracted the company from the Internet\u2019s real money-maker: search products. Microsoft later realized that Google\u2019s success was due to its monopoly in search-based ad sales and tried to compete with its own service, Bing. Too late. Google already had become the Microsoft of search, and went out to strengthen its grip with the help of its Chrome browser, which included an integrated search engine. That sounds a lot like Microsoft\u2019s old strategy of bundling Internet Explorer with Windows, doesn't it? The difference is that Google hasn\u2019t faced the kind of regulatory scrutiny and backlash that Microsoft endured.  5. Innovation at Scale Microsoft did launch one very successful new product during Ballmer\u2019s tenure: the Xbox game console. Unlike its tablets, phones and music players, the Xbox brand combines a fine piece of hardware with excellent software. I may be partial to Sony\u2019s PlayStation, but no one can deny the impact of games like Halo and Gears of War on the industry. The question is: Why was the Xbox the only successful venture Microsoft made into a new product line? Maybe the answer lies in the next point. 6. Corporate management Running companies well is hard. Running huge companies well is even harder. Thus it has been and thus it will always be. It takes dedication, hard work, foresight and -- one of the trickiest ingredients of all -- creativity. All of Microsoft's problems boil down, at some level, to a mixture of bad luck and bad management. Microsoft continues to make excellent office productivity software (I\u2019m writing this on Word, and I use Excel all the time), and I have no interest in trading in my Windows operating system for anything else. Yet these are successes engineered by a company that is, essentially, a very profitable utility, not a company that is a groundbreaking innovator. That explains why Microsoft's stock price hasn\u2019t budged for more than a decade even as management has distributed billions of dollars in dividends. The company has certainly been willing to invest lots of money and effort in competing in a range of markets, yet it keeps losing to nimbler, more creative rivals like Apple and Google. Microsoft has helped make up some of these losses by branching into business services, although it hasn\u2019t made that transition as well as IBM. Steve Ballmer certainly wasn\u2019t the only reason for these failures, but it was ultimately his responsibility, as Chief Executive, to fix them. His departure is long overdue, and his successor has a lot of work to do. (Matthew C. Klein is a writer for Bloomberg View. You\u2019re a patriotic American with a 17-year-old daughter,\nand you just won $102,000 in a lottery. One catch: The rules say\nthe money must be spent for the public good.  You could give  Uncle Sam  the cash to repair roads and\nbridges. It turns out, though, that $102,000 is the total\naverage cost of a four-year college degree, including tuition,\nfees and forgone earnings. Can you justify investing the money\nin your Goth child?  Absolutely, judging from \u201cThe New Geography of Jobs,\u201d\nEnrico Moretti\u2019s persuasive look at why some U.S. cities have\nprospered in recent decades while others have declined.  The short explanation for these diverging fortunes is that\ntowns such as Seattle are teeming with college-educated workers\nin high tech. So giving your daughter the right education could\nboost both the economy and her earnings.  Tune out, for a minute, the grim news about student-loan\ndebts reaching $1 trillion and graduates struggling to find\njobs. Investing in a four-year degree produces an inflation-\nadjusted annual return of more than 15 percent, according to\n research  from the  Brookings Institution  in  Washington .  \u2018Brain Hubs\u2019  Moretti is a professor specializing in labor and urban\neconomics at the  University of California , Berkeley. He has\ncombed through U.S. census data and teased out a secular trend.  Over the past three decades, education has become a great\ndivider, he says. Even as communities desegregated racially,\nthey became more segregated scholastically.  Conurbations with many college graduates, including  Boston ,\n San Jose  and the Raleigh-Durham research triangle in North\nCarolina, have become \u201cbrain hubs.\u201d They offer higher wages and\nlonger  life expectancy .  At the other extreme are traditional manufacturing centers\nsuch as Flint, Michigan. In between stand cities that could flip\neither way, he says.  This sounds blindingly obvious. Yet the winnowing has\nprofound implications for today\u2019s gnawing debate about why\ninequality has reached a level not seen since before the Great\nDepression.  Joseph Stiglitz  and others have framed today\u2019s income\ndisparity as a conflict between the top 1 percent of earners and\nthe remaining 99 percent. For Moretti, the more consequential\ndivide lies elsewhere -- between the 45 million workers who have\na college education and the 80 million who don\u2019t.  Driving Prosperity  Education has long been a driver of a productive economy.\nThat\u2019s one reason why the U.S. made such rapid gains after\npublic high schools became widely available early in the 20th\ncentury, Moretti says. Today, innovation is becoming what\nmanufacturing used to be, America\u2019s \u201cmain engine of prosperity,\u201d\nhe argues.  Without question, innovation is throwing off dream jobs.\nMoretti introduces us to a digital programmer who designed a\nstarship for \u201cAvatar\u201d and a mathematician who blended colors\nfor \u201cRatatouille\u201d and \u201cToy Story.\u201d  Not everyone can create video games or discover\nbreakthrough medications, of course. Yet the\npresence of these workers creates demand for local services,\nwhich provide the vast majority of today\u2019s jobs.  Yoga Teachers  Luring biotech scientists and software engineers to town\ncreates more work for plumbers and yoga instructors. Everyone in\ntown winds up earning more than they would elsewhere.  One drawback is that the cost of living also runs higher.\nNor is there an easy fix for the Flints of the world, contrary\nto what  Richard Florida  suggested in \u201cThe Rise of the Creative\nClass.\u201d  If all it took to ensure success were a flood of creative,\ncollege-educated kids, uber-cool Berlin wouldn\u2019t have such high\nunemployment, Moretti says. To get a Silicon Valley cooking, you\nneed an intellectual star like William Shockley to draw a bunch\nof \u201chot minds\u201d to your startup in the orchards. One thing\nleads to another and, sure as Moore\u2019s law,  California  ends up\nproducing more patents than any other state, with  New York  and\nits Silicon Alley a distant second, Moretti says. (PCAR)  Employers were scaling back and unemployment was\nhigh.  Then  Bill Gates  and  Paul Allen  decided to move their\nsoftware company to the city of their youth. So  Microsoft Corp. (MSFT) \nput down roots near Seattle.  Tech Magnet  As Microsoft grew, Seattle became a magnet for other high-\ntech companies, including  Amazon.com Inc. (AMZN)  What\u2019s more,\nmillionaire Microsoft alumni set up some 4,000 new companies, a\nmajority of them around Puget Sound, Moretti says. By his\nestimate, Microsoft can be credited with creating 120,000 jobs\nfor workers with limited education and 80,000 for those with\nadvanced degrees, including doctors and architects.  So how can we boost the number of innovation workers in\nAmerica and, by extension, create more jobs for everyone else?\nThe answer should be clear:  import them  or grow our own.  Giving work visas to more foreign engineers and scientists\nwould be a cheap solution. Educating more Americans would be\ncostly, yet good for the nation\u2019s future, assuming students can\nbe persuaded to major in computer science, chemical engineering\nand microbiology. In a 7-1 ruling, the court left intact a 2003 decision that reaffirmed the right of universities to use race as an admissions factor. The majority instead said a federal appeals court hadn\u2019t properly applied the standards laid out in the 2003 ruling.  Today\u2019s decision provides a limited victory to opponents of racial preferences, giving them new grounds to challenge university admission policies around the country. The majority said universities must prove that their means of attaining diversity meet a demanding constitutional test known as \u201cstrict scrutiny.\u201d  \u201cStrict scrutiny imposes on the university the ultimate burden of demonstrating, before turning to racial classifications, that available, workable race-neutral alternatives do not suffice,\u201d Justice Anthony Kennedy wrote for the majority.  Affirmative action has been a fixture on U.S. campuses since the 1960s, diversifying what had been many virtually all-white student bodies. Most of the nation\u2019s selective colleges and professional schools consider race as they seek to ensure a multiracial student body. Blacks and Hispanics now make up more than a quarter of U.S. college students.  10 Percent  At the core of the debate was whether universities can adequately diversify without resorting to racial preferences. Texas admits three-quarters of its freshman class each year on the basis of high school class rank -- the \u201ctop 10 percent\u201d rule. That system, while race-neutral on the surface, ensures a significant number of minorities because it guarantees slots to students at predominantly Hispanic and black schools.  The university considers race only in admitting the rest of the class. Opponents of preferences say that\u2019s unnecessary, given the success of the class-rank method. Texas counters that even with race-based admissions, a high percentage of its classes have few if any black and Hispanic students.  Kennedy said that while courts should defer to universities in determining whether diversity is essential to their educational mission, judges should closely scrutinize the means schools use to bolster minority enrollment.  \u201cThe university must prove that the means chosen by the university to attain diversity are narrowly tailored to that goal,\u201d Kennedy wrote. \u201cOn this point, the university receives no deference.\u201d  \u2018High Hurdles\u2019  Edward Blum, who organized the challenge to the University of Texas policy, said the court had established \u201cexceptionally high hurdles\u201d for colleges to meet.  \u201cIt is unlikely that most institutions will be able to overcome these hurdles,\u201d said Blum, the director of the Project on Fair Representation in Alexandria,  Virginia , in an e-mailed statement. \u201cThis opinion will compel the Fifth Circuit to strike down UT\u2019s current use of race and ethnicity.\u201d  Texas said the ruling won\u2019t force any immediate changes in its admissions policies. Bill Powers, the university\u2019s president, said in a statement that its system \u201cfully satisfies\u201d the standards laid out by the Supreme Court.  Current admissions practices at universities can continue for at least another year as the case works its way again through the courts, said Michael Olivas, a University of Houston law professor who helped draw up the University of Texas admissions plan. Proponents of affirmative action will be relieved by the ruling, he said.  Grutter Ruling  \u201cThis could have been so much worse and may yet be,\u201d Olivas said in a telephone interview. Affirmative action \u201clives on, but all of us believe it\u2019s under an impending death penalty.\u201d  The 2003 decision, Grutter v. Bollinger, said colleges and graduate schools could consider race as long as they do so through a broad review of a student\u2019s application and don\u2019t mechanistically award extra points to every minority. The author of that 5-4 ruling, Sandra Day O\u2019Connor, retired in 2006.  Joining Kennedy\u2019s opinion today were Chief Justice John Roberts and Justices Antonin Scalia, Samuel Alito, Clarence Thomas, Stephen Breyer and Sonia Sotomayor. Sotomayor, the court\u2019s first Latina justice, is a supporter of affirmative action who says she benefited from it during her career.  Writing in dissent, Justice Ruth Bader Ginsburg said Texas had followed the model the court approved in the 2003 case. She said government actors, including state universities, need not be blind to the lingering effects of \u201can overtly discriminatory past.\u201d  Thomas Opinion  In a concurring opinion, Thomas said he would have outlawed the use of race by university admissions offices.  \u201cIf the court were actually applying strict scrutiny, it would require Texas either to close the university or to stop discriminating against applicants based on their race,\u201d he wrote. \u201cThe court has put other schools to that choice, and there is no reason to treat the university differently.\u201d  Justice Elena Kagan didn\u2019t take part in the case. She was the Obama administration\u2019s top courtroom lawyer when the administration filed a brief at the appeals court level.  Columbia University President Lee Bollinger, who was involved in the 2003 case, said before today\u2019s ruling that a decision barring affirmative action would undermine the ability of universities to ensure integrated student bodies.  \u2018Serious Work\u2019  \u201cThe integration would not stop completely, but it would fall very significantly,\u201d Bollinger said on Bloomberg Radio\u2019s \u201cBloomberg Surveillance\u201d program. \u201cIf the Supreme Court were to overrule this, it would upset 50 years of very important and serious work to help realize Brown v. Board of Education,\u201d the landmark 1954 school integration case.  The Texas policy was challenged by Abigail Noel Fisher, who applied unsuccessfully to the school in 2008 and later enrolled at Louisiana State University. A graduate of a Houston-area public high school, she said she was passed over by UT in favor of minority classmates with lower grades and fewer extracurricular activities.  Texas had support in the case from some of the nation\u2019s most powerful institutions. Fifty-nine companies -- including  Microsoft Corp. (MSFT) ,  Wal-Mart Stores Inc. (WMT) , (WMT) Gap Inc.,  General Electric Co. (GE)  (GE), Pfizer Inc., Shell Oil Co. and  Viacom Inc. (VIAB)  (VIAB) --filed a  brief  saying they rely on universities to prepare a racially diverse workforce.  Those corporations were in the unusual position of arguing alongside the Obama administration, which  cast  affirmative action as a national security issue. The administration said race-conscious admissions, at the country\u2019s military academies and at universities with Reserve Officer Training Corps programs, help ensure a diverse officer corps.  Texas argued that its program is a model of the type of plan the high court approved in the Grutter ruling.  The case is Fisher v. University of Texas at Austin, 11-345. He takes the\nhelm of a company facing slowing revenue growth and accelerating\ncompetition in cloud computing, a fast-growing area of\ntechnology that delivers software and storage via the Internet. (AAPL) \u2019s legal battle with\n Samsung Electronics Co. (005930)  over smartphone inventions could\ndetermine if there are limits to the power of patents that cover\nmost widely-used technology for electronics.  The U.S. International Trade Commission in Washington is\nscheduled to announce June 4 whether Apple infringed Samsung\npatents for transmitting data and, if so, whether the Korean\nhandset maker can block such a fundamental function of a mobile\ndevice. The decision, postponed from today, would be the first\nfinal decision in any U.S. cases between the world\u2019s two largest\nsmartphone makers.  The commission, which can block imports into the U.S., in\nMarch asked for comments on how banning older models of the\niPhone and iPad tablet computer would affect the public. On a\nbroader scale, the commission must decide if it\u2019s appropriate to\nexclude a product for infringing a patent that\u2019s part of\ntechnical standards it must follow.  \u201cThis will be the most important decision from the ITC\ndealing with the standard-essential patents to date,\u201d said\nDavid Long, a patent lawyer with Dow Lohnes in Washington. \u201cIn\nother cases, they found ways out. Here, they seem to be\nindicating there\u2019s infringement, now what do we do.\u201d  Whether owners of standards patents should be able to block\nothers from using those ideas has been the topic of U.S.\ncongressional hearings, a policy paper from President  Barack\nObama \u2019s administration and regulatory investigations on three\ncontinents, including one that led to a settlement between the\nU.S. and Google Inc.  Widely-Used Patents  Samsung, based in Suwon,  South Korea , has been making\nmobile phones since the 1980s and participated in industry\ngroups that established ways phones communicate with each other,\nexchange data and perform other key functions. Companies that\nhelp develop standards have the advantage of ensuring their\ntechnology is widely used, so they are required to pledge to\nlicense any relevant patents on fair terms.  In the ITC case, Samsung contends Apple infringes four\npatents, including two standards patents that relate to how\nphones transmit data. A judge initially said Apple didn\u2019t\ninfringe any of the patents, and that one, for a way to detect\nmovement on a touch-screen, was invalid. The fourth patent is\nfor a way to detect phone numbers in e-mails so they can be\ndialed or stored in the phone\u2019s contact list.  The six-member commission, which is reviewing the judge\u2019s\nfindings, in March  asked  for additional information about\nlicensing negotiations.  Apple Pledge  Apple, based in Cupertino,  California , denies infringing\nany of the Samsung patents. Even if a violation is found,\nSamsung shouldn\u2019t be allowed to use patents on standard-essential technology to block competition, Apple has said. The\niPhone maker has pledged not to seek court bans on the use of\nany patents it owns on fundamental technology.  Apple won a $1.05 billion verdict against Samsung last year\nfor infringing patents that weren\u2019t part of standards, although\na new trial has been ordered for part of the case.  \u201cThe upcoming ITC ruling may have a greater significance\nthan the court\u2019s ruling because the latter is made based on the\njurors\u2019 decisions, while the ITC\u2019s is made by professionals,\u201d\nsaid Lee Sun Tae, a Seoul-based analyst at NH Investment &\nSecurities.  Standards Patents  The issue goes beyond the Apple-Samsung battle. Ericsson AB\nand Samsung have accused each other of failing to offer fair\nlicensing terms in cases before the ITC and federal courts.\nHuawei Technologies Co.,  China \u2019s largest phone-equipment maker,\nfiled an antitrust complaint with European regulators over\nInterDigital Inc.\u2019s royalty demands for patents on wireless\ntechnology.  Apple and Microsoft Corp. have each accused Google Inc.\u2019s\nMotorola Mobility unit of demanding unfair rates for its\nstandard-essential patents. A federal judge in  Seattle  last\nmonth said Google is entitled only to pennies per unit from\nMicrosoft, while a different judge threw out Apple\u2019s breach of\ncontract case.  House judiciary committee members, in a May 10 letter to\nthe commission on the Apple case, repeated a request made last\nyear that the ITC \u201ccarefully assess the substantial public\ninterest considerations that exist with regards to this and\nother cases.\u201d  The Apple case against Samsung is In the Matter of\nElectronic Digital Media Devices, 337-796, and Samsung\u2019s case is\nIn the Matter of Electronic Devices, Including Wireless\nCommunication Devices, Portable Music and Data Processing\nDevices, and Tablet Computers, 337-794, both U.S. International\nTrade Commission ( Washington ). The\nEuropean Union proposed yesterday raising about 57 billion euros\n($78 billion) a year by taxing trades of stocks, bonds and\nderivatives by financial institutions.  In addition to being politically unfeasible and poorly\ndesigned, the tax would undermine the one thing Europe needs\nmost to counter rising debt burdens: economic growth.  A transactions tax was first championed by John  Maynard Keynes  during\u00a0the Great Depression.\u00a0Another prominent economist,\n James Tobin , resurrected the idea in the 1970s -- the levy is\noften called a \u201c Tobin tax \u201d -- as a way to dampen  currency\nspeculation . In 2009, the tax idea rose again, this time\u00a0as a\nRobin Hood effort to reclaim money from the bailed-out financial\nsector to make U.S. and European taxpayers whole.  Bill Gates ,\nthe Microsoft founder, is said to be considering recommending a\ntransactions tax as a means for the Group of 20 bloc to\nreplenish development financing for poor nations.  The tax is doomed -- and for good reasons. Politically,\nit\u2019s a nonstarter because EU treaty rules require region-wide\ntax proposals to be adopted unanimously by the 27 member\nnations. With many British jobs dependent on the vibrancy of the\nCity of  London , Europe\u2019s busiest financial district, Britain\nwon\u2019t back it.  The British are being slyly hypocritical here. They already\nimpose a small duty -- a \u201cstamp tax\u201d dating from the 17th\ncentury -- on stock trades. The new proposal would raise that\ntax and divert the extra amount to Brussels. Seeking to soften\nBritish opposition, the EU has proposed exempting foreign\nexchange trades, which the City dominates. U.K. officials still\nfear the tax would drive financial jobs offshore and so insist\nthey will only support it if it\u2019s adopted globally.  Highly Unlikely  That\u2019s highly unlikely even without the opposition of U.S.\nTreasury Secretary  Tim Geithner , who appears dead-set against a\ntransactions tax.  The case against the tax includes more than political and\npractical arguments. The U.K.-based  Institute of Development\nStudies  has concluded that the tax, which the group supports,\nwouldn\u2019t increase market distortions but probably wouldn\u2019t\nstabilize volatile financial markets, either. At the same time,\nthe IDS study agreed with Geithner and others that the tax would\nultimately miss its intended targets.  Financial institutions would bear the initial cost, the\nstudy said, but in the long run a significant proportion could\nbe passed to retail investors and consumers. Although the EU\nwould try to insulate households and small businesses from the\nlevy -- a 10-euro fee on a 10,000-euro stock purchase would be\n\u201cnot excessive\u201d it said -- banks could bypass fee caps by\nembedding additional costs in commissions, markups or other\ntricks.  Among the many reasons to oppose the tax, however, one\nreigns supreme. The EU says the tax would slow economic growth\nby 0.5 percent of gross domestic product. At a time when  Europe \nwould swoon over a growth rate of 1 percent or more, a proposal\nthat entails a half-point decline in GDP represents bad policy,\nbadly timed. The second of five children of Mexican immigrants, Brindis has a father who works in a wine company warehouse and makes less than $40,000 a year. His mother is unemployed. Yet, financial-aid officials at  Boston College , where it costs about $60,000 to attend, told Brindis he needed to pay about $2,500 a year -- part of a mandated student contribution. Lacking the cash, he took out $5,000 in loans over two years, he said.  The aid officer \u201cwould tell me that I was contributing such a small percentage to what my education costs, but she didn\u2019t understand that small percentage was a much bigger percentage to my family,\u201d Brindis, 21, said.  Scholarship programs funded by some of the nation\u2019s biggest donors, including Gates, Coca-Cola Co. and  Michael Dell , are taking aim at practices used by wealthy colleges, such as Boston College, which has a $1.65 billion endowment, Amherst, with a $1.64 billion fund and  Barnard , with $216.4 million. They say the schools hurt poor and minority students by rescinding aid once they find out they have awards from outside sources or by banning use of the funds to cover some student contributions. Donors complain that, in some cases, their gifts are boosting a school\u2019s bottom line rather than the students they seek to help.  Boston College said its policy evens the playing field for financial-aid students, said Bernie Pekala, director of student financial strategies at the private institution.  A \u2018Conundrum\u2019  Any student receiving financial aid from the college must still fork over what is known as the summer contribution, though students can earn the amount during the school year or borrow.  Letting students like Brindis use outside grants to cover the contribution \u201cwould be unfair to all the other ones who didn\u2019t win the Gates,\u201d Pekala said.  Similarly at Amherst College, a wealthy liberal arts school in  Massachusetts , students can\u2019t use outside scholarships to pay their \u201c summer contribution ,\u201d which can run as high as $1,600, said Tom Parker, dean of admission and financial aid.  \u201cHere\u2019s the conundrum. You want to treat everybody as equally as you can,\u201d Parker said. \u201cMorally it\u2019s a difficult question.\u201d  Scholarships have become more valuable as tuition increases have outpaced the inflation rate for four decades, saddling student borrowers with $1 trillion in education loans. President  Barack Obama  and Congress are pressing colleges to control costs and ease the financial burden on students and their families.  Job Disadvantage  To require students to net several thousand dollars in a summer job adds to their financial strain, said  Harley Frankel , executive director of College Match, a nonprofit group in Los Angeles that helps low-income students get into top colleges.  \u201cA lot of times, low-income kids can\u2019t get summer jobs, especially in this economy,\u201d which forces them to borrow, said Frankel, who had run the national Head Start program. The savings requirement also prevents most students from taking unpaid summer internships, which puts them at a disadvantage later in the job market, he said.  Established in 1999 with an initial $1 billion from the Bill & Melinda Gates Foundation, the  Gates Millenium Scholars  program bestows 5,000 awards annually to low-income, minority students. It gave $86 million in the current academic year, and the average annual award was $11,593 in the decade through 2010.  Fee Waived  \u201cStudents end up with loan debt that is unnecessary because the institutions are forcing them to take out loans they should not have to,\u201d said  Larry Griffith , vice president at the United Negro College Fund, which administers the Gates program.  Griffith flew to  Boston  to argue on Brindis\u2019s behalf, though he was unable to reverse the school\u2019s decision about the summer expectation for his first two years. Boston College agreed to waive Brindis\u2019s contribution this year because he had an unpaid internship last summer with the Education Department that fit in with the school\u2019s service mission.  \u201cFor low-income students, the amount of money can sometimes be as much as 10 to 15 percent of the family\u2019s annual income,\u201d Griffith said, referring to the student contribution.  Brindis said he has received almost $96,000 in grants from Boston College that cover his first three years there.  College policies rescinding or cutting funding because of outside scholarships \u201ctakes away a reward that the student earned through hard work and concentrated effort,\u201d according to a report to be released this month or in April by the  National Scholarship Providers Association .  NSPA Recommendations  \u201cThere is no net financial gain to a student despite winning a private scholarship, and therefore no additional improvement to his or her ability to pay for college,\u201d the authors wrote in a draft version provided to Bloomberg.  The Boulder, Colorado-based group, whose 320 members include Gates, the  Coca-Cola Scholars Foundation , Michael & Susan Dell Foundation and Walmart Foundation, is recommending schools waive minimum contributions and summer work expectations for low-income students.  At Barnard, students must fill a summer savings requirement ahead of each school year, averaging about $2,200 annually, according to Nanette DiLauro, director of financial aid. Students can either earn the money through a job or take out a loan to cover the cost. As at Boston College, Barnard says it wants to be consistent in its aid policy and can\u2019t waive the requirement for some students, she said.  Aid \u2018Displacement\u2019  \u201cIt\u2019s not fair to do it for a Gates recipient,\u201d DiLauro said. \u201cWe do our best to really work with our students, especially our low-income students.\u201d  In some cases, students with outside scholarships find their colleges reducing the grant they had been awarded. The colleges say the practice, called displacement, lets them give financial aid to other needy students.  Amherst,  Cornell University  and Dartmouth College displace institutional aid, according to the schools.  At Amherst -- where the school\u2019s average aid package was about  $44,000  in 2011-2012 -- outside scholarships are applied to a student\u2019s $1,800 work expectation during the school year, and can be used to buy a computer. Leftover funds then replace the school\u2019s direct aid, said Parker, the admissions dean.  Amherst doesn\u2019t require students to take out loans, and in some cases can make exceptions on summer earnings expectations for needy students who get unpaid internships, Parker said.  \u2018Universities Profit\u2019  While displacement has been around for years, scholarship providers are concerned it may become a larger problem if colleges become more strapped for money, said Amy Weinstein, executive director of the NSPA, whose members collectively grant more than $1 billion each year.  The financial-aid money that schools save doesn\u2019t always go directly to other needy students, and can be used to fund other parts of a college\u2019s budget, said Griffith, of the Gates program.  \u201cUniversities profit from attracting talented kids who bring scholarships in tow,\u201d said Michael Mallory, executive director of the  Ron Brown Scholar Program , which funds high- achieving, low-income African-American students.  In the Dell Scholars\u2019 first two years, about 60 percent of recipients reported some form of displacement, said Oscar Sweeten-Lopez, director of the Austin, Texas-based program that began in 2004. If recipients have to take on loans, they can defer their scholarship and use it toward loan repayments, he said.  \u201cThat\u2019s a solution, but it still doesn\u2019t address the problem,\u201d Sweeten-Lopez said.  An \u2018Oversight\u2019  Winston-Salem State University  gave De\u2019Jana Parker, 19, of Harvey,  Louisiana , a scholarship covering all educational costs, including tuition, fees, room and board and a $250 book voucher each semester, according to a March 2011 letter to Parker, now a sophomore and biology major.  Once the university was notified Parker was a Gates recipient, it rescinded some of its own funding, Griffith said. Parker said she was dismayed by the North Carolina school\u2019s change in award, which was fully made up by Gates.  \u201cI couldn\u2019t believe the university would promise me a full scholarship and not come through,\u201d said Parker, who wants to pursue a medical degree and Ph.D. in microbiology or immunology.  After the Gates program inquired about Parker\u2019s case last month, Winston-Salem e-mailed the organization, indicating there had been an \u201coversight\u201d in monitoring her award. The school said it had made adjustments and would be returning $17,143 to Gates for the 2011-2012 year and $9,106 for the current year, according to Griffith.  The university\u2019s Chancellor Scholars Program insures that students don\u2019t incur loans and there is no federal work study required, Provost  Brenda Allen  said in an e-mailed statement last week. Winston-Salem is reviewing its process with regards to the Gates program, she said. Still Pricey  The trend toward cheaper handsets will help smartphone shipments grow 40 percent from last year to hit 1 billion units this year, researcher IDC said in a report this month. A proposed Australian law, being watched by governments\nglobally and challenged by companies including British American\nTobacco Plc, would require cigarettes to be sold in dark olive-\nbrown  packages , with corporate logos replaced by graphic images\nof diseases blamed on smoking, and a uniform font previously\nassociated with  Microsoft Corp.\u2019s (MSFT)  Windows software. The choice\nof color and font was based on  studies  by Australian health\nauthorities, who sought to minimize the packs\u2019 attractiveness.  That research dovetails with decades of polling and\nexperimentation by companies such as  BAT (BATS)  and  Imperial Tobacco\nGroup (IMT) , who have long viewed their packages as \u201csilent\nsalesmen.\u201d The Australians took all that knowledge and turned\nit on its head in a fit of anti-marketing. Logos on tobacco\npackaging are slated to be banned in the country from December,\ndealing a body blow to the $661 billion global industry.  \u201cMaking choices to dissuade, or prohibit the packages from\nstanding out or drawing attention, is not the norm, but the\ndesign process is really the same,\u201d Jeff Bellantoni, chair of\nthe package design program at the Pratt Institute\u2019s School of\nArt & Design in New York, said in an interview.  International Interest  New Zealand ,  Canada ,  Belgium ,  Iceland  and  France  have all\nshown an interest in implementing a plain-packaging law like\nAustralia, which accounts for 0.3 percent of global tobacco\nvolumes, according to Euromonitor International research. The\nU.K. government this month called for reactions to standardize\ntobacco packaging, which  tobacco companies   claim  would illegally\nseize their trademarks and increase sales of illicit smokes.  If Australia\u2019s  High Court  upholds the  law , brands such as\nDunhill, made by British American, and  Philip Morris\nInternational Inc.\u2019s (PM)  Marlboro would lose their iconic logos and\nrecognizable imagery overnight. All that would remain is the\nbrand name, written in a font known as Lucida Sans, on a pack\nwhose color is known in the design trade as  Pantone 448C .  Neither choice was random. The Australian health department\nhired Sydney-based research company GfK Blue Moon to come up\nwith the most repellent packaging possible. GfK selected both\nthe color and font to \u201cunplug the product\u201d from its marketing,\ncreating a gap between the tobacco in the pack and its\nassociation with anything elegant, masculine, or exciting,\naccording to Scott Morris, associate professor of food\nengineering and packaging at the University of  Illinois .  Legible Font  Known mostly for being legible, Lucida was designed by the\nBigelow & Holmes studio in 1985. Designers Charles Bigelow and\nKris Holmes wanted to create a font that transmitted well onto\nlaser printers. The Lucida family includes a sans-serif version,\nwithout small lines at the end of the characters. Microsoft has\n licensed  it for use on its Windows systems.  \u201cLucida Sans is one of the least graceful sans-serif\ntypefaces designed,\u201d Tom Delaney, a senior designer with  New\nYork  design and identity consultant  Muts & Joy , said in an e-\nmail. \u201cIt\u2019s clumsy in its line construction.\u201d  Pantone 448C, meanwhile, isn\u2019t a color found on most\nproduct packages, for good reason. Australia commissioned GfK to\nfind a color that was \u201cthe least appealing\u201d and contained\ncigarettes that were lowest quality, according to GfK\u2019s 2011\n report .  To aid its search, GfK could consult studies done by\ntobacco companies, who have come to rely on packaging more as\ntraditional avenues of advertising, such as television and\nprint, have been shut by regulators.  Social Visibility  Cigarette packages are different from other consumer\nproduct containers, in that smokers retain the pack until it\u2019s\nfinished, and frequently display it in public. Such social\nvisibility means cigarettes are known as \u201cbadge products,\u201d\nwhich associate the user with the brand\u2019s image.  Most importantly, perceptions of cigarettes can be changed\nby altering the color or shade of color on a pack, through a\nprocess called \u201csensation transfer.\u201d Lightening the tone is a\ncommon practice, as it reduces the perception of a cigarette\u2019s\nstrength. Red conveys a strong smoke, blue is associated with\nlower-tar, and white is usually the lightest smoke available.  \u201cConsumers use things like color as an indication of\nrisk,\u201d said David Hammond, an associate professor at the\nUniversity of Waterloo\u2019s School of  Public Health  who has studied\ntobacco packaging. \u201cIt\u2019s effective with tobacco as smokers are\nmotivated to believe their brand is less harmful.\u201d  Red or Blue?  Philip Morris , now called  Altria Group Inc. (MO)  in the U.S.,\nonce compared smokers\u2019 responses to identical cigarettes\npackaged in separate blue and red packs. Some smokers found the\ncigarettes in the blue pack to be too mild, while others felt\nthose in the red pack were too harsh.  GfK recommended eight colors for testing on smokers. Dark\ncolors were perceived as more harmful, and dark brown was the\nleast appealing, carrying connotations of uncleanliness. A\nlighter-brown color was rejected as it could be perceived by\nconsumers as gold. An olive tint prevents the brown from looking\nlike chocolate, which also has positive associations.  \u201cPantone 448C is discouragingly drab, both literally and\nfiguratively,\u201d Morris, the packaging professor, said in an e-\nmail. \u201cYou can see that there isn\u2019t much left that connects the\nbrand with any advertising, and it\u2019s certainly unappealing.\u201d  Yet by using Lucida Sans, a common font available to\nanyone, Australia may have provided tobacco makers with a window\nof opportunity, according to Jason Smith, founder of Fontsmith,\na London-based font design company that has worked with\ncompanies such as  Xerox Corp. (XRX)  and the British Broadcasting Corp.  \u201cThey probably should have gone for something less\nfamiliar,\u201d Smith said in an interview. \u201cThere is absolutely\nnothing to stop the cigarette companies from taking Lucida Sans\nand using it on the side of a Formula One car, in their own\nbrand colors.\u201d  To contact the reporter on this story:\nMatthew Boyle in London at \n mboyle20@bloomberg.net   To contact the editor responsible for this story:\nSara Marley at \n smarley1@bloomberg.net","path":".\/2008_2012_msft_bloomberg_news\/consumers-buy-death-in-australia-s-cigarette-package-law.txt"},{"id":99801899,"title":"Lilly, Ironwood, Mattel, Celgene: Intellectual Property","released_at":"<date>January 5 2012<\/date> <time>12:00:01<\/time>","content":"Eli Lilly & Co. No one had seen its like before. You hooked it up to your\nhome television, connected it to the Internet and -- presto! --\nyou could take your TV remotely with you everywhere.  Eventually, Sling was acquired by EchoStar -- controlled by\nsatellite mogul Charlie Ergen -- and its hardware business\nlanguished. The last new Slingbox was introduced in 2008, eons\nago in tech terms.  Now Sling at long last is back with two new devices, the\n$300 Slingbox 500 and the $180 Slingbox 350, and a few new\ntricks. After a week or two with the swoopy black 500, I\u2019ve\nconcluded that it\u2019s still the most comprehensive and\nstraightforward way to consume video content on the go, though\ncertainly not the most elegant.  Setting up an Apple TV required me to run a cable to the TV\nand plug in a power cord. Setting up the  Slingbox  500 required\nme to connect nine, count \u2019em, different cables. There would\nhave been 10, except that I opted to use Wi-Fi rather than run\nan Ethernet cable from the Slingbox to my router.  For the first time, the 500 incorporates the now-ubiquitous\nHDMI high-definition connector that\u2019s supposed to make\neverything simpler -- so why all these wires?  Belt and Suspenders  It\u2019s because of the way some cable channels are encrypted,\nleading Sling to recommend using both the HDMI and older\ncomponent audio-video cables at the same time. (At least all of\nthem were included with the Slingbox.)  It\u2019s a belt-and-suspenders approach that gets the job done\nbut adds to the chances something will go wrong during the\nsetup: My first attempt knocked out the sound from the TV. I\neventually got it back by disconnecting and reconnecting the\naudio cables.  Once everything was working right -- about a 40-minute\nprocess from start to finish -- the Slingbox did its thing. And\neven after all these years (the first Slingbox appeared in\n2005), its thing is still pretty cool.  From any computer\u2019s web browser, or using one of Sling\u2019s\nextra-cost SlingPlayer mobile-device apps, you can access\neverything on your home TV. You can turn your cable box on\nremotely and view your full channel lineup, as well as content\nyou\u2019ve saved to a DVR, on-demand programs and even pay-per-view\nchannels.  No Juggling  There are a lot of advantages to watching TV this way.\nYou\u2019ve already paid for the content through your cable or\nsatellite subscription, so you don\u2019t have to pay again. You\ndon\u2019t have to juggle multiple apps, like  Hulu Plus  and  HBO GO ,\ndepending on what you want to watch. And you don\u2019t get tripped\nup by blackout or other rules that prevent you from accessing\nsome content online.  In my case, for instance, I was able to log in to my home\nTV from the office and watch San Francisco Giants baseball\nplayoff games on my iPad, even though the games were unavailable\nthrough the MLB At Bat app.  There are some disadvantages to watching TV this way, too.\nFor one thing, the SlingPlayer apps cost $15 each (down from\n$30), and you\u2019ll need one for each mobile device you use. In\naddition to separate versions for Apple\u2019s iPad and iPhone\/iPod\ntouch, there are SlingPlayers for  Google (GOOG) \u2019s Android operating\nsystem;  Microsoft (MSFT) \u2019s Windows Phone; and  Amazon.com (AMZN) \u2019s Kindle Fire.  Limited Selection  You\u2019re also limited by the selection available through your\nhome TV provider. So you might be able to access last week\u2019s\nepisode of \u201cModern Family,\u201d but not necessarily ones from\nearlier seasons. And while the video streams are now full 1080p\nhi-def, picture quality can be affected by several factors,\nincluding the speed of your home network and the one over which\nyou\u2019re watching.  Sling says half of all Slingbox use occurs within the home,\nso the 500 is also beginning to incorporate features similar to\nApple\u2019s AirPlay, allowing photos and other content on mobile\ndevices to be displayed on the TV. That feature is missing from\nthe industrial-looking 350 model, which also lacks an HDMI\nconnector and must be hooked directly into a router, rather than\nusing Wi-Fi.  Still, remote viewing remains the core of the Slingbox\u2019s\nappeal. And granted, downloading and installing an app is a lot\nmore painless than spending $300 for a Slingbox, hooking up nine\ncables, then downloading and installing an app that may cost you\n$15 more.  But you can also look at it this way: With Slingbox, you\nget the pain out of the way up front. And that monthly cable or\nsatellite bill might be a little more bearable knowing your\nservice is now completely portable.  ( Rich Jaroslovsky  is a Bloomberg News columnist. The\nopinions expressed are his own.)  Muse highlights include Jason Harper on  cars  and Lance\nEsplund on  art . Allows \u2018Open Discussion\u2019  Keeping a portion of the fundraiser out of public view\nallows \u201cfor a freer form for having an exchange of ideas,\u201d\nsaid Jack Rosen, a real-estate developer who threw a Nov. 30\nfundraiser for Obama at his Upper East Side  New York  townhouse.\n\u201cI imagine as president of the  United States  you want to feel\nfree to have an open discussion without being dissected by the\npress.\u201d  Policies to limit coverage at a fundraiser help promote a\nfeeling of exclusivity for top donors, and insulate candidates\nfrom verbal gaffes that have the potential to overpower their\npublic messages.  \u201cIt\u2019s much more comfortable for the donors and for the\ncandidates to have these private conversations,\u201d said  Sheila Krumholz , executive director of the Center for Responsive\nPolitics, a Washington-based research group that tracks campaign\ncontributions. Yet \u201cit\u2019s a detriment to the public debate about\nthe campaign.\u201d  Bagging Mobile Phones  Obama and Romney have taken steps to ensure that glimpses\ninto their private world of fundraising remain a rarity. At a March 30 fundraiser, as the press was being ushered\nout of earshot at Maine\u2019s Portland Museum of Art, Obama asked\nhis 130 supporters in attendance not to post any video of their\nprivate discussion on YouTube. Because Obama is president, he has a group of journalists,\nincluding photographers, print reporters and television\nproducers who travel with him, even to campaign events at\nprivate homes such as Spike Lee\u2019s Upper East Side Manhattan\nbrownstone, where a 40-person dinner was held Jan. 19.  Public Pep Talks  Access is limited to brief introductory remarks, which\noften include familiar jokes, like a reference to dusting off\n\u201crolled-up \u2018Hope\u2019 posters\u201d from four years ago, and\npredictable calls to action.  \u201cI hope that you are game to work just as hard, if not\nharder, in the coming months to make sure we finish what we\nbegan,\u201d Obama told 40 high-dollar contributors, including  Oprah Winfrey , who were dining March 16 among red roses and white-\npillar candles in producer Tyler Perry\u2019s 30,000-square-foot\nFrench chateau-style Atlanta mansion. \u201cI\u2019ll be counting on it,\nand more importantly, the American people are counting on it.\u201d  As his 10-minute speech drew to a close, he told the\ndonors, \u201cI\u2019m going to let the press pool go.\u201d He turned to\nwatch them gather their notebooks and laptops before continuing. (GOOG) \u2019s Motorola Mobility\ndidn\u2019t act in good faith when it demanded patent royalties from\n Microsoft Corp. (MSFT)  for use of video-compression and Wi-Fi\ntechnology, a federal jury said yesterday.  The jury in  Seattle  acted in its first day of\ndeliberations. Microsoft was awarded about $14.5 million in\ndamages, the Seattle Times newspaper reported in a  blog  post.  \u201cThis is a landmark win for all who want products that are\naffordable and work well together,\u201d  David Howard , Microsoft\ndeputy general counsel, said in an e-mailed statement. \u201cThe\njury\u2019s verdict is the latest in a growing list of decisions by\nregulators and courts telling Google to stop abusing patents.\u201d  \u201cWe\u2019re disappointed in this outcome, but look forward to\nan appeal of the new legal issues raised in this case,\u201d William\nMoss, a Motorola Mobility spokesman, said in an e-mailed\nstatement.  The verdict could help the two companies resolve a dispute\nover patent royalties for both fundamental technologies in\nelectronic devices and features that make them easier to use.\nMore broadly, the case is one front in a global debate on how to\nhandle patents that relate to technology included in industry\nstandards used by all manufacturers.  Microsoft claimed that Motorola Mobility acted unreasonably\nby demanding royalties of 2.25 percent of the price of an Xbox\nvideo-gaming system or a computer that runs on the  Windows\noperating system , and then threatening to get a court order\nhalting sales of the products if the money wasn\u2019t paid.  Common Tactic  Motorola Mobility said the October 2010 letters sent to\nMicrosoft were a common opening offer that it used in\nnegotiating patent licensing with other companies for years.\nRather than sitting down to negotiate a licensing agreement as\nother companies do, Microsoft went to the courts, Motorola\nMobility said.  Microsoft, which reported $73.7 billion in 2012 revenue,\nhas said the royalty demand would equal more than $4 billion a\nyear, a figure Motorola Mobility disputed.  U.S. District Judge James Robart, who presided over the\ntrial, determined in April that the appropriate royalty rate was\nabout a half-cent per unit for video-decoding technology and 3\n1\/2 cents for wireless technology. Microsoft said that would\nequal about $1.8 million a year.  The issue for the jury was whether Motorola Mobility\u2019s\nactions were in keeping with the standards of good faith and\nfair dealing. Robart, in pre-trial rulings, said Motorola\nMobility\u2019s offers have to be made in good faith, though the\ninitial offer doesn\u2019t have to be on fair terms as long as the\nresult is fair.  Royalty Demand  Microsoft struck first in 2010, demanding royalties from\ncompanies using Google\u2019s Android operating system and filing a\ncomplaint with the U.S. International Trade Commission. Motorola\nMobility responded within weeks by sending a letter saying it\nwas owed royalties on the Xbox and Windows. The company then\nfiled its own infringement lawsuits.  Microsoft, based in Redmond,  Washington , won a ruling that\nlimits imports of Motorola Mobility phones that have a feature\nto synchronize calendars with computers. It sued  U.S. Customs \nand  Border Protection  for letting the phones continue to enter\nthe U.S., and both companies are appealing aspects of the case\nto the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Federal Circuit in\nWashington, D.C.  $293.9 Billion Market  The patent fights are part of a global war for an increased\nshare of the $293.9 billion smartphone market. They\u2019ve become a\ntesting ground to determine how to treat patents that cover\nbasic technology used by companies so that, for instance,\nchargers can plug into any device or  Apple Inc. (AAPL) \u2019s iPhone can\nsend and receive images from Samsung Electronics Co.\u2019s Galaxy S4\nhandset.  Companies that participate in groups to establish\nindustrywide standards pledge to license any relevant patents on\n\u201cfair, reasonable and non-discriminatory\u201d terms. In return,\nthey have the advantage of ensuring their technology is widely\nused, giving them a leg up on implementing the standard and\nestablishing a broad base of potential licensees.  A patent gives its owner the power to block others from\nusing the invention. Microsoft and Apple have both pledged not\nto exercise that power when it comes to patents on industry\nstandards, though they have used other patents in their legal\nfights with competitors.  Motorola Mobility and Samsung, two companies with long\nhistories with mobile phones, have lodged patent-infringement\nsuits using their patents on fundamental phone technology, such\nas how data is transmitted.  Obama Veto  President  Barack Obama \u2019s administration said limits should\nbe placed on such patents, and on Aug. 3 vetoed an import ban on\nsome of Apple\u2019s older phones that Samsung had won.  Samsung, which is under investigation by European\nregulators over its use of standard-essential patents, had\nagreed not to seek a sales ban on that continent against Apple\nfor use of any such technology. Google, of  Mountain View ,\n California , reached an agreement with the U.S. Federal Trade\nCommission that limits its activities regarding those patents.  Robart last year precluded Motorola Mobility from halting\nsales of any Microsoft products based on an infringement finding\nin  Germany . Part of Microsoft\u2019s request for damages was based on\nthe cost of relocating a logistics center warehouse to the\nNetherlands from Germany.  Sept. 11 Arguments  The  U.S. Court of Appeals  for the Federal Circuit, which\nspecializes in  patent law , is scheduled to hear arguments Sept.\n11 on whether there should be different rules for standard\nessential patents, and when companies can obtain court orders to\nblock the use of patented technology.  U.S. Circuit Judge  Richard Posner , who normally presides on\nthe 7th Circuit Court of Appeals in  Chicago , threw out cases\nApple and Motorola Mobility had filed against each other. Posner\nruled in June 2012 that Motorola Mobility wasn\u2019t entitled to any\nban on the use of standard-essential patents, while Apple wasn\u2019t\nentitled to halt sales of complicated electronics based on an\ninfringement claim over device features.  The case is Microsoft Corp. v. Motorola Mobility Inc.,\n10cv1823, U.S. District Court for the Western District of\nWashington (Seattle). From 2005 to 2007, the peak of the buyout boom, private-\nequity firms completed four technology deals of comparable scale\nto the Dell deal yesterday, according to data compiled by\nBloomberg. Two of the LBOs are mired in losses, while the\nothers, including the Silver Lake-led acquisition of SunGard\nData Systems Inc., have produced minimal gains for the buyers\nand their investors.  Dell, chairman and chief executive officer of the computer\nmaker he founded in 1984, has negotiated a lower price relative\nto cash flow and a lighter debt load than the buyers in the\nearlier megadeals. While that doesn\u2019t guarantee that the 47-\nyear-old billionaire can turn his company around in the fast-\nchanging computer market, it gives him the financial flexibility\nthe other LBOs lacked and a shot at a higher return.  \u201cThis is a very reasonably priced deal,\u201d said  Scott Sperling , co-president of Boston private-equity firm Thomas H.\nLee Partners LP.  Financing Details  Michael Dell and Silver Lake together will inject about\n$5.8 billion of equity into the deal, people familiar with the\nmatter said. Dell will have a controlling stake in the private\ncompany.  Microsoft Corp. , whose software powers many of Dell\u2019s\ncomputers, will provide a $2 billion loan, according to a\nstatement announcing the deal. The balance will be funded with\n$13 billion in additional borrowing and cash from  Dell\u2019s  balance\nsheet, said the people, who asked not to be identified because\nthe information is private. The deal\u2019s enterprise value -- or\nmarket capitalization and debt minus cash -- is about $22.2\nbillion.  The enterprise value works out to about 5.1 times a measure\nof cash flow known as earnings before interest, taxes,\ndepreciation and amortization, or Ebitda. The peak-era\ntechnology LBOs were priced at 9 times Ebitda or more.  \u201cTech buyouts valued at 7 times or less have often done\nwell,\u201d Sperling said.  Quarterly Grind  The buyout will add $8 billion to Dell\u2019s debt, bringing the\ntotal to $17 billion, the people said. Based on prevailing LBO\nloan rates and those on Dell\u2019s  existing bonds , annual servicing\ncosts could be as much as $1.2 billion, or about 28 percent of\nEbitda. That would leave  Dell  with $2.6 billion in cash flow\nafter capital expenses and interest, based on the company\u2019s\nfinancial performance in the 12 months ended Nov. 2.  The deal\u2019s valuation compares with an average multiple of\n9.2 times Ebitda for all LBOs announced or completed in the past\n12 months, according to data compiled by Bloomberg.  Michael Dell and Silver Lake aim to replicate the outcome\nof a much smaller deal they did: a $2 billion buyout of disk-\ndrive maker Seagate Technologies Inc. in 2000. It was the\nbiggest LBO of a technology company at the time. Silver Lake, in\nwhich Michael Dell was an investor, led a group that scored more\nthan 700 percent gain on the deal, according to a recent Silver\nLake private placement memorandum obtained by Bloomberg News.  Spending Freedom  Silver Lake paid 2.6 times Ebitda, according to a\nregulatory filing. Flush with  free cash flow , Seagate boosted\nresearch and development spending to $800 million in fiscal\n2001, from $660 million the year before, and to $700 million in\nfiscal 2002. The step-up was pivotal to Seagate\u2019s being first to\nmarket with the most advanced disks of the day.  \u201cThey invested and stayed on top of the product cycle, and\nthey emerged a winner,\u201d said  John Moore , a Standard & Poor\u2019s\ncredit analyst in New York.  Even paying a favorable price, Michael Dell faces\nsignificant obstacles in trying to make good on his ambitions to\nbreak into new businesses such as cloud computing and mobile\ndevices and lessen the company\u2019s reliance on its weakening\nflagship PC business.  About 70 percent of Dell\u2019s  business  is still tied to\npersonal computers, which are \u201cunder secular and structural\npressure,\u201d even after it has spent $13 billion on acquisitions\nsince 2008,  Shaw Wu , a San Francisco-based analyst at Sterne\nAgee & Leech Inc., wrote in a Jan. 22 report. As much as half\nthe company\u2019s revenue is from desktop and notebook computers,\nand an additional 20 percent from businesses tied to such\ncomputers, he wrote.  No Cushion  While the reliance on the personal computer business has\nweighed on Dell\u2019s growth prospects, it still helped the company\nproduce an estimated average of $4.4 billion in  Ebitda  annually\nover the past five years. The megadeals done during the boom era\nwere financed so aggressively that they were left without a\ncapital cushion when the financial crisis hit, said  Jamie Rizzo ,\nan analyst at credit-rating company Fitch Ratings in New York.  \u201cThe projections going into these deals were close to\nperfection,\u201d Rizzo said. \u201cThen you get hit by a substantial\ndownturn like we had and that no one was expecting, and it sets\nyou back multiple years.\u201d  A fast-evolving industry full of money-hungry startups,\ntechnology long was a magnet for venture capital that buyout\nsponsors shied from. Debt was seen posing too much risk in a\nfield where cash flows can be volatile. Prior to 2005, the\nbiggest technology LBOs had been valued at about $2 billion.  Freescale, SunGard  That changed when a Silver Lake-led group agreed to buy\nSunGard, a supplier of software to financial institutions and\ndata-backup services, for $10.6 billion in March 2005. At the\ntime, it was the largest LBO since KKR & Co.\u2019s iconic\nacquisition of RJR Nabisco for $31.3 billion in 1989. SunGard\nshouldered $7.4 billion of debt and an interest-to-Ebitda ratio\nof almost 60 percent.  The SunGard deal was topped by the $11.1 billion purchase\nof NXP Semiconductor NV by KKR four other firms, including\nSilver Lake, in August 2006. NXP\u2019s interest ratio rose to 55\npercent.  A month later  Blackstone Group LP  and two other private-\nequity firms agreed to buy Freescale Semiconductor Inc. for\n$17.6 billion, leaving interest-to-Ebitda at 45 percent.  The largest technology LBO is KKR\u2019s takeover of First Data\nCorp. for $29.7 billion in April 2007, about three months before\ncredit markets started to collapse under the weight of subprime-\nmortgage defaults. The credit-card payment processor\u2019s debt rose\nto almost $22 billion, with interest surpassing 70 percent of\nEbitda.  Unexpected Troubles  The deals\u2019 values ranged from 9.3 times trailing 12-month\nEbitda for SunGard to 10 for Freescale, 12 for First Data and\nalmost 15 for NXP, regulatory filings show.  Tailored to the companies\u2019 cash flows, the debt wasn\u2019t\ncrippling at first. Then the recession hit, sales fell and debt\nservice consumed an increasing portion of cash flows. Shifts in\ntechnology and customer tastes also took a toll.  NXP  lost market share in key products, and Freescale\u2019s\nresults took a turn for the worse when sales of Motorola\u2019s once-\npopular Razor cell phones tumbled and Freescale\u2019s second-biggest\nbusiness, selling chips to automakers, went into a free fall.  Several of SunGard\u2019s biggest customers switched to newer\nand cheaper technologies, while a shift to debit-card card\npurchases and consolidation among financial-services companies\ncost First Data revenue. Since 2009, the four companies\u2019 results\nhave improved, although the effects of paying steep prices and\nusing high leveraging linger.  Poor Returns  NXP, which went public in 2010, has given investors, who\nsank about $4.5 billion into the company, an unrealized profit\nof about 10 percent after six years, based on the company\u2019s\nrecent stock price. SunGard\u2019s backers, who in December extracted\na $718 million dividend that returned about 20 percent of their\nmoney, are barely breaking even, said a person with knowledge of\nthe matter.  With Freescale, whose IPO was in 2011, Blackstone and its\nco-investors have registered about a 60 percent loss on their\n$7.2 billion outlay, based on the  current share price  of $14.56\na share. KKR and other First Data shareholders have posted a 30\npercent mark-to-market loss on their $6.3 billion investment,\nKKR\u2019s third-quarter earnings statement shows.  Uphill Battle  Unlike Seagate, where the buyout helped the company\nsolidify its position in a market where it was already strong,\nMichael Dell has made no secret of his company\u2019s need to revamp\nits entire business. While a cash cushion will help, it may not\nbe enough.  Dell faces an uphill battle as it seeks to challenge\nestablished rivals like  Oracle Corp. , EMC Corp. and  Hewlett-\nPackard Co.  in lines like servers and tablet computers, where\nDell has little presence, Rizzo  said.  \u201cPeople are concerned about the business model,\u201d said\n Louis Meyer , a special situations analyst in New York for broker\nOscar Gruss & Son Inc. \u201cYou have a consumer business that is\nsort of dying on the vine. They may have products in development\nthat could arrest that. But even if they do, they\u2019ve still got\nto invest in that.\u201d  Should he succeed, the reward for Michael Dell and his co-\ninvestors could be significant.  \u201cThis has the potential to make Michael Dell a lot richer\nthan he already is,\u201d said Erik Gordon, a private-equity and law\nprofessor at the University of Michigan. Underwriters Paying to Pass Bond Issues Face Regulatory Scrutiny  Underwriters that fund bond-authorization campaigns and\nthen collect fees from approved debt sales are among the\nunresolved pay-to-play issues in the $3.7 trillion municipal\nbond market that will come under rulemaker scrutiny.  The Municipal Securities Rulemaking Board, after collecting\ndata on dealer contributions to bond campaigns for two years, is\nstarting to examine the need for restrictions based on such\ncontributions, said Ernesto Lanza, deputy executive director and\nchief legal officer.  Hiring an underwriter based on whether it supports a\ncampaign rather than its ability to market bonds can lead to\nissues from mispricing, which can hurt investors, to higher fees\nand borrowing costs for taxpayers. The rulemaking board\u2019s focus\nis on ensuring investors are protected, Lanza said by telephone.  The MSRB has banned would-be underwriters from giving to\nmost campaigns for elected officials who could influence the\naward of bond sales. Banks have been divided over whether they\nshould be allowed to support drives in favor of referendums\nauthorizing debt issues that they later underwrite. Some say it\ncreates the appearance of undue influence, while others say it\nmerely helps issuers win the votes and finance needed projects. The extra yield investors demand to own bonds issued by\ntop-rated companies versus Treasuries reached 0.81 percentage\npoint, the most since July 2010, after S&P cut the U.S. one\nlevel to AA+ on Aug. 5, according to Bank of America Merrill\nLynch index data. A wider spread indicates investors perceive\nthe higher-rated companies to be a greater credit risk.  S&P, which along with Moody\u2019s Investors Service and Fitch\nRatings was  blamed  by U.S. investigators for fueling the worst\nfinancial crisis since the Great Depression by assigning AAA\nratings to bonds backed by subprime mortgages, is again muddying\nthe waters for investors attempting to divine the relative\ncreditworthiness of fixed-income securities.  \u201cThe Treasury bond is still regarded as the ultimate risk-\nfree security,\u201d Edward Marrinan, the head of macro credit\nstrategy at RBS Securities in  Stamford ,  Connecticut , said in an\ne-mail. \u201cThe U.S. government has taxing and legislative\nauthority over corporations domiciled in this country. (GOOG)  is relying on its\nplanned $12.5 billion purchase of Motorola Mobility Holdings\nInc. to forestall patent litigation and force settlements with\n Apple Inc. (AAPL)  and  Microsoft Corp. (MSFT)  over smartphone technology.  Google cited patent disputes as key to its agreement to buy\nMotorola Mobility, announced yesterday. Apple, maker of the\niPhone, and Microsoft, developer of Windows Phone software, have\ntargeted phones that run on Google\u2019s best-selling Android\nsystem, including handsets built by Motorola Mobility, Samsung\nElectronics Co. and  HTC Corp. (2498) , in lawsuits worldwide.  Lacking its own trove of patents to vie with Apple,\nMicrosoft and other companies, Google and its hardware partners\nwere targeted by suits aimed at slowing the adoption of Android\nsmartphones. Adding the 17,000 patents of Motorola Mobility,\nwhich has been inventing mobile-phone technology since the\nindustry began, may help Google stanch the onslaught.  \u201cThe analogy to a nuclear arms race and mutually assured\ndestruction is compelling,\u201d said Ron Laurie, managing director\nof Inflexion Point Strategy LLC, which counsels companies on\npurchasing intellectual property. Patent Weaponry  Competition for dominance in the smartphone market has\nheated up since Google introduced Android in 2008. Patents,\nwhich grant exclusive rights to use a specific invention, have\nbecome a way to fight for market share and inhibit rivals from\nintroducing new features.  Apple stepped up the patent feud by suing Android\nmanufacturers, claiming Google-powered devices copy the iPhone\nand iPad. Oracle is seeking billions\nof dollars in damages for patent- and copyright-infringement,\nand Google\u2019s response has been limited to challenging the\nvalidity of Oracle\u2019s patents.  Heightening the dispute, a group led by Apple and Microsoft\nwon an auction of patents owned by Nortel Networks Corp. in June\nafter bidding up the price to $4.5 billion, beating out Google\nin the largest-ever patent auction.  Google Shops Around  Before agreeing to buy Motorola Mobility, Google had few\npatents on mobile-phone technology. The company\u2019s research had\nfocused largely on its main search-engine business.  Google, seeking to tilt the balance, has actively sought\npatents that it said could be used as a deterrent to litigation,\nculminating in the purchase of Motorola Mobility.
