(GS)  director and McKinsey & Co. managing director who rose to the pinnacle of  Wall Street , was sentenced to two years in prison for passing inside tips to his business partner.  Gupta, who ran McKinsey from 1994 to 2003, was sentenced yesterday by U.S. District Judge Jed Rakoff in  Manhattan  for leaking stock tips to Galleon Group LLC co-founder Raj Rajaratnam. Gupta, 63, was convicted by a jury in June of one count of conspiracy and three counts of  securities fraud .  Rakoff ordered Gupta to report to prison on Jan. 8 and fined him $5 million, rejecting a bid to allow him to remain free pending appeal. The judge said he would recommend to U.S. Bureau of Prisons officials that Gupta serve his term at the federal prison in Otisville,  New York .  The evidence that Gupta passed illegal information about New York-based Goldman Sachs to Rajaratnam, his friend and business partner, \u201cwas not only overwhelming, it was disgusting in its implications,\u201d Rakoff said in court.  Gupta leaked information about a $5 billion investment in Goldman Sachs by  Warren Buffett \u2019s  Berkshire Hathaway Inc. (BRK\/B)  on Sept. 23, 2008, and a tip on a quarterly loss. Rakoff said yesterday he was especially troubled by Gupta\u2019s actions during this tumultuous period.  \u2018Possible Ruin\u2019  \u201cWith  Goldman Sachs in  turmoil but on the verge of being rescued from possible ruin by an infusion of $5 billion, Gupta, within minutes of hearing of the transaction, tipped Rajaratnam, so that the latter could trade on this information in the last few minutes before the market closed,\u201d the judge said just before he imposed sentence. \u201cThis was the functional equivalent of stabbing Goldman in the back.\u201d  Prosecutors had sought a prison term for Gupta of as long as 10 years in prison. Assistant U.S. Attorney Richard Tarlowe yesterday argued that Gupta\u2019s crimes warranted a substantial prison time because of his prominence in the business world and the egregiousness of his crimes. Tarlowe said a sentence of probation would give the impression that there is \u201ca two-tier system of justice.\u201d  While Gupta didn\u2019t personally profit, his tips allowed Rajaratnam to earn millions of dollars, Tarlowe said.  \u201cThe crime is so serious because of the position that was held, and that is why the fall from grace is more steep,\u201d Tarlowe said.  Clear Message  \u201cIt is very important that the message be clear to that community, to that target audience, that this is insider trading,\u201d Tarlowe said. \u201cIf you are a senior executive, if you tip another professional, another prominent businessperson, a hedge fund manager, even if you do it using your regular phone from your executive suite, that is insider trading and that will be punished severely.\u201d  Gupta requested probation and community service. His lawyer,  Gary Naftalis , had proposed that he work with needy children in New York or the poor in  Rwanda . Citing Gupta\u2019s good works and saying he\u2019d suffered enough with his reputation destroyed, Naftalis argued yesterday that his client should be granted leniency.  \u201cThe fall from grace that Mr. Gupta has suffered or experienced as a result of this matter is as steep as I have ever seen anyone in any case that I have ever seen,\u201d Naftalis said. \u201cThis was an iconic figure, someone who had been a role model for people around the globe for his work.\u201d  Gupta served on the boards of  Procter & Gamble Co. (PG)  and  AMR Corp. (AAMRQ)  and won praise for his charity from  Microsoft Corp. (MSFT)  Chairman  Bill Gates  and former United Nations Secretary-General  Kofi Annan . As McKinsey\u2019s youngest managing director, he almost tripled the firm\u2019s revenue.  \u2018Extraordinary\u2019 Life  Gupta\u2019s life \u201chas been an extraordinary one,\u201d Naftalis said yesterday in court. The lawyer said his client has made \u201cextraordinary contributions that have tangibly helped many, many people on this planet.\u201d His crimes are a \u201ctotal aberration in an otherwise laudatory life,\u201d Naftalis said. \u201cThis is a man who has suffered punishment enough.\u201d  Rakoff said he agreed with the description of Gupta\u2019s good works.  \u201cI think the record, which the government really doesn\u2019t dispute, is that he\u2019s a good man, but the history of this country and the history of the world are filled with good men who do bad things, so I don\u2019t think that\u2019s the end of the subject,\u201d Rakoff said.  Rwanda Proposal  Rakoff yesterday called Naftalis\u2019s suggestion about community service in Rwanda \u201cvery innovative,\u201d adding that he believed some period of incarceration was necessary.  \u201cI thought, ah, this was the  Peace Corps  for insider traders,\u201d the judge told Naftalis. \u201cBut I think if everything you told me about Mr. Gupta\u2019s character is correct, and I think it is, he would be doing this regardless of a court order or not. So looking at it in a cynical kind of way, it is not punishment.\u201d  Rakoff, who has long criticized the federal sentencing guidelines, which are advisory, said he needed to consider the totality of Gupta\u2019s crimes in fashioning a sentence.  \u201cThe court can say without exaggeration that it has never encountered a defendant whose prior history suggests such an extraordinary devotion, not only to humanity writ large, but also to individual human beings in their time of need,\u201d Rakoff said.  Picture Darkens  \u201cBut when one looks at the nature and circumstances of the offense, the picture darkens considerably,\u201d Rakoff said. \u201cIn the court\u2019s view, the evidence established, to a virtual certainty, that Mr. Gupta, well knowing his fiduciary duties, brazenly disclosed material nonpublic information to Mr. Rajaratnam at the very time, September and October 2008, when our financial institutions were in immense distress.\u201d  Before he was sentenced, Gupta briefly addressed the court.  \u201cI lost my reputation that I built over a lifetime,\u201d he said. \u201cThe last 18 months have been the most challenging period of my life since my parents died when I was a teenager.\u201d  While Gupta didn\u2019t take responsibility for his conviction, he apologized to his family, friends and McKinsey & Co., as well as the institutions he helped create, such as the Indian School of Business, the Public Health Foundation of India and the America India Foundation.  \u201cYour Honor, as I come before you to be sentenced, the overwhelming feelings in my heart are of acceptance of what has happened, of gratitude to my family and friends, and of seeking forgiveness from them as well,\u201d Gupta said. \u201cIt is with these feelings that I hope to move forward and dedicate myself to the service of others.\u201d  400 Letters  In his bid for leniency, Naftalis said Gupta\u2019s crimes were limited to a two-month span in 2008 and presented some 400 letters to the judge chronicling Gupta\u2019s good works.  Naftalis also told Rakoff that he would file an appeal challenging the judge\u2019s decisions on evidence during the trial, including allowing the use of a recording of a wiretapped phone call.  Gupta declined to comment as he left the courthouse with his wife, Anita, and four daughters.  \u201c\u2018\u2018Mr. Gupta maintains his innocence and will vigorously pursue an appeal,\u2019\u2019 Naftalis said. \u2018\u2018We continue to believe that the facts of this case demonstrate that Mr. Gupta is innocent of all of these charges, and that he has always acted with honesty and integrity.\u2019\u2019  \u2018Sad Chapter\u2019  Goldman Sachs said yesterday in a statement that it was \u2018\u2018disappointed that Mr. Gupta breached his duties as a director and violated our shareholders\u2019 and the firm\u2019s trust.\u201d It said it hoped Gupta\u2019s sentencing \u201cbrings this sad chapter to a close.\u201d  Since August 2009, prosecutors in the office of Manhattan U.S. Attorney Preet Bharara have charged at least 72 people with insider trading. The Galleon case was part of a federal initiative by Bharara\u2019s office and the  Federal Bureau  of Investigation in New York, called \u201c Perfect Hedge ,\u201d that used techniques such as informants and wiretaps, commonly used to combat drug dealers and organized crime figures, against white-collar defendants.  \u201cRajat Gupta now must face the grave consequences of his crime -- a term of imprisonment,\u201d Bharara said in a statement. \u201cHis conduct has forever tarnished a once-sterling reputation that took years to cultivate.\u201d  The jury acquitted Gupta of charges that he leaked information that Cincinnati-based P&G\u2019s organic sales growth would fall below estimates and that he tipped Rajaratnam, 55, about Goldman Sachs\u2019s  earnings  in the first quarter of 2007.  Wiretaps  Rajaratnam is serving 11 years in prison for trading on tips from Gupta and others.  Unlike the Rajaratnam prosecution, which was based on dozens of wiretaps of his mobile-phone conversations, the case against Gupta was largely circumstantial and built on trading records, business relationships, telephone records and comments by Rajaratnam or others about Galleon\u2019s sources of information.  At the trial, Goldman Sachs Chief Executive Officer Lloyd Blankfein testified that on Sept. 23, 2008, he briefed his board over the phone on the Buffett investment beginning at 3:15 p.m.  Within a minute after the call with the directors concluded at 3:53 p.m., Rajaratnam answered a call on his private line from a McKinsey conference room being used by Gupta, according to phone records and testimony.  On a Sept. 24, 2008, wiretap played for the jury, Rajaratnam spoke to a Galleon trader describing why he had directed Galleon to buy Goldman Sachs shares the day before, just before the market closed.  \u2018Something Good\u2019  \u201cI got a call at 3:58, right?\u201d Rajaratnam could be heard telling another trader. \u201cSaying something good might happen to Goldman.\u201d  The jury also heard one wiretapped conversation between Gupta and Rajaratnam in which Gupta told him about board discussions about purchasing a commercial bank.  Rakoff said that during his 17 years as a judge, he had never encountered a defendant like Gupta. The judge added that Gupta\u2019s prominence meant he had to be sentenced to prison.  \u201c Insider trading  is an easy crime to commit but a difficult crime to catch,\u201d Rakoff told Gupta. \u201cOthers similarly situated to the defendant must therefore be made to understand that when you get caught, you will go to jail.\u201d  Rakoff has sentenced at least nine defendants other than Gupta for insider trading, including seven who pleaded guilty and two whom he jailed after they were found guilty by juries. Rakoff has a track record of imposing sentences that are half what the government recommends.  Average Sentences  From Jan. 1, 2011 to July of this year, federal judges in Manhattan sent the average insider-trading violator to prison for more than 22 months, according to an analysis of sentencing data by  Bloomberg News . That was a 20 percent increase from the average term of 18.4 months during the previous eight years.  Over the same 18-month period, the average sentence after trial was 58 months, compared with 22 months during the same time for 18 defendants who pleaded guilty. Of the dozen defendants who pleaded guilty and agreed to cooperate with the U.S. insider-trading probe during that time, 11 avoided prison altogether. One got six months.  The case is U.S. v. Gupta, 11-cr-00907, U.S. District Court, Southern District of New York (Manhattan). (GOOG)  is free to extend its dominance of the $50 billion Internet-search market after U.S. regulators ended an investigation into whether the company unfairly disadvantaged competing websites by favoring its own services in search results.  The Federal Trade Commission, after a 20-month antitrust probe, concluded Google was motivated more by wanting to improve its search results and the user\u2019s experience than by a desire to stifle competition, said Chairman  Jon Leibowitz , who drew a distinction between dominating a market and doing so unfairly.  The FTC\u2019s decision clears the way for Google to continue adding features that have helped it beat back Microsoft Corp. and  Yahoo! Inc. (YHOO)  to become the world\u2019s top search provider and most valuable  Internet company .  \u201cNothing in the decision is a serious blow to any of Google\u2019s ambitions,\u201d  Whit Andrews , an analyst for technology research firm Gartner Inc., said in an interview. The FTC didn\u2019t get into the question of \u201cwhere the boundaries are going to get drawn\u201d in the search business, he said.  Google, which makes money by selling advertising next to search results, should grab 76 percent of the U.S. search market this year, up from 75 percent last year. Microsoft should get 9 percent while Yahoo may land 6 percent, according to EMarketer Inc.  The global Internet search market is expected to grow to more than $50 billion this year, up 15 percent from the year-ago period, ZenithOptimedia, an advertising research unit of Paris based  Publicis Groupe SA (PUB) , said in a report last year.  Manipulating Searches  The FTC investigation looked into allegations that Google manipulated its search algorithms to promote its own products and services, harming competitors and consumers. While some evidence suggested Google was trying to eliminate competition, its \u201cprimary reason\u201d for changing the look and feel of search results was to improve user experience, Leibowitz said at a news conference in  Washington  yesterday.  The agency\u2019s decision to close its probe without enforcement action is a blow to competitors including Microsoft,  Yelp Inc. (YELP) , and  Expedia Inc.. (EXPE)  An alliance of e-commerce and Web- search companies pressed the agency to bring an antitrust lawsuit.  Google Concessions  Google made some concessions, agreeing in a letter to the FTC to let websites remove their content from focused search services like Google Shopping or Google Local without removing or demoting that content in the main Google search engine.  Advertisers will also be able to compare data from other  search engines  within third-party services that use Google\u2019s AdWords software, Google said in a blog  post  yesterday. The FTC said the commitments are enforceable.  The FTC\u2019s resolution of the matter is \u201cweak and -- frankly -- unusual,\u201d Dave Heiner, a  Microsoft (MSFT)  vice president and deputy general counsel, said in a blog post yesterday.  \u201cGoogle has long said that it merely aims to offer customers the most relevant answer to their query, and the FTC commissioners accepted that view,\u201d Heiner said. \u201cYet we know that Google routinely and systematically heavily promotes its own services in search results.\u201d  \u201cIs Google+ really more relevant than Facebook?\u201d he asked. \u201cAre Google\u2019s travel results better than those offered by Expedia, Kayak and others?\u201d  \u2018Hand-to-Hand Combat\u2019  Search-engine competitors made many of the same product- design choices Google did, \u201csuggesting that this practice benefits consumers,\u201d Leibowitz said yesterday.  Some companies or people may think the agency should do more \u201cbecause they are locked in hand-to-hand combat with Google around the world and have the mistaken belief that criticizing us will influence the outcome in other jurisdictions,\u201d Leibowitz said.  Google also agreed in a consent decree to limitations on when it can seek to bar sales of competitors\u2019 products that rely on so-called standard-essential patents. Industry-standard technology helps ensure products such as mobile phone antennas and global-positioning system software can operate together when made by different manufacturers.  Google paid $12.4 billion to buy Motorola Mobility, an early pioneer in the mobile-phone market, in part to get access to its standard-essential patents. Motorola Mobility has been locked in licensing disputes with Microsoft and Apple Inc. in courts and at the U.S. International Trade Commission over their use of those patents in smartphones, tablets and gaming systems.  \u2018Bad Precedent\u2019  FTC Commissioner Tom Rosch, a Republican, said that while he believed Google\u2019s conduct in search didn\u2019t warrant action, the agreement the agency accepted \u201ccreates very bad precedent and may lead to the impression that well-heeled firms such as Google will receive special treatment at the commission.\u201d  \u201cInstead of following standard commission procedure and entering into a binding consent agreement to resolve the majority\u2019s concerns, Google has instead made non-binding commitments with respect to its search practices,\u201d said Rosch, who steps down today. \u201cAfter promising an elephant more than a year ago, the commission instead has brought forth a couple of mice.\u201d  The FTC announcement is \u201cmaintaining the status quo,\u201d  Danny Sullivan , founder of the industry blog Search Engine Land, said in an interview. \u201cI doubt it will result in any significant change in how consumers interact with search engines or to the market share of respective competitors.\u201d  European Regulators  It\u2019s now up to European antitrust regulators to determine whether any restrictions should be placed on Google\u2019s search practices, said William Kovacic, a former FTC commissioner and chairman and a professor of law at George Washington University.  Google has agreed to offer the European Union detailed commitments on how it would resolve regulators\u2019 concerns, including how Google\u2019s own services are promoted above those of rivals and how it uses and displays other content on search services.  \u201cThe European framework is more amenable to enforcement than the U.S. one is,\u201d Kovacic said. \u201cThat gives the Europeans a bigger margin to demand concessions.\u201d  Consumer Watchdog , an advocacy group, pressed the U.S. Justice Department and state attorneys general to investigate Google\u2019s \u201cmonopolistic behavior in search results\u201d in the wake of the FTC announcement.  \u201cThe FTC rolled over for Google,\u201d  John Simpson , director of Consumer Watchdog\u2019s privacy project, said in an e-mail. EFF has\n accused  counsel for AF Holdings as both a \u201ccopyright troll\u201d\nand a \u201cporn troll.\u201d  In a separate AF Holdings case in California, a federal\njudge granted a defendant\u2019s motion to dismiss the case while\nrejecting AF\u2019s similar request. U.S. District Judge Edward Chen\nsaid that AF had an \u201capparent inability to prove standing to\nassert its claim of copyright infringement.\u201d  Chen said he was unpersuaded by AF\u2019s argument that it was\ndismissing the case because the defendant had allegedly damaged\nthe evidence or the company couldn\u2019t afford to post the $50,000\nbond required by the court.  He said there was no evidence to suggest that AF actually\ninvestigated whether the defendant deliberately damaged the\nevidence. He found AF\u2019s financial-hardship argument\n\u201cunconvincing,\u201d noting that \u201cas the plaintiff which initiated\nthe action, AF knew at the outset that a bond might be\nrequired.\u201d  AF had sought a dismissal under terms that would permit\nrefilling of the case at a future date. Instead, Judge Chen\ngranted a dismissal \u201cwith prejudice,\u201d which bars AF from\nfiling the claim a second time against the defendant. He said\nthat this order didn\u2019t preclude the defendant\u2019s filing a motion\nseeking attorney fees from AF.  The Georgia case is AF Holdings LLC v. Rajesh Patel, 2:12-\ncv-00262-WCO, U.S. District Court, Northern District of Georgia\n(Gainesville).  The California case is AF Holdings LLC v. Joe Navasca,\n3:12-cv-02396-EMC, U.D. District Court, Northern District of\nCalifornia (San Francisco).  A third AF case was dismissed April 9 because the defendant\nwas never served with the complaint. That case is AF Holdings\nLLC v. Christopher Heggum, 2:12-cv-02130-SRB, U.S. District\nCourt, District of  Arizona  (Phoenix).  For more copyright news, click here.  Trade Secrets\/Industrial Espionage  U.S. Making Cybertheft Focus of Talks With China, Donilon Says  The U.S. has taken a hard line and insisted cybersecurity\nbe central to any economic dialogue with China, given the scale\nof attacks waged against U.S. companies, White House National\nSecurity Adviser Thomas Donilon said.  \u201cThe only way to deal with this was to bring it to the\ncenter of the relationship and to present the proposition that\nany economic discussion with the United States -- given the\nthreat to the United States, the degree of theft that is going\non -- was going to involve cyber,\u201d Donilon said yesterday at\n Columbia University  in New York.  Ties between the U.S. and China have been strained by a\nreport from a U.S. security company, Mandiant Corp., saying\nChina\u2019s army may be behind cyberattacks on companies worldwide.\nChinese officials have rejected the findings.  General Martin Dempsey, chairman of the U.S. Joint Chiefs\nof Staff, met this week with Fang Fenghui, chairman of the\nPeople\u2019s Liberation Army General Staff, who compared the effects\nof an Internet attack to those of a nuclear bomb. Still, no\nspecifics measures on a code of conduct for cybersecurity were\ndiscussed.  Donilon said the U.S. asked the Chinese to recognize the\nscope of the problem, to begin an investigation of computer\ncrimes and to engage in a discussion on a set of rules.  \u201cWe are moving on all of them, they have agreed to open up\na dialogue,\u201d he said. \u201cThis is not general cybercrime or\nhacking, this is a direct theft of United States private and\ngovernment assets for use for advantage. That is the discussion\nwe are having with the Chinese.\u201d  In a speech last month, Donilon said that the widespread\ntheft of  intellectual property  and  trade secrets  through\n\u201ccyberintrusions emanating from China at a very large scale\u201d\nhas become a point of contention with the Chinese government.  Donilon has said the U.S. would do everything necessary to\nshield the nation\u2019s computer networks from attacks on vital\ninfrastructure, such as power grids and transportation links.  Mandiant, based in Alexandria, Virginia, said in a February\nreport that the Chinese army may be behind a hacking group that\nhas hit at least 141 companies worldwide since 2006. Sales Bans  Microsoft and Apple have pledged not to use standard-\nessential patents to block competitors\u2019 products and demanded\nthat other companies follow suit. The overhaul enacted two years ago includes a tax on\nunearned income to help pay for the expansion of insurance\ncoverage. It\u2019s set to start in 2013 and will apply to capital\ngains -- such as private-equity managers\u2019 profits on leveraged\nbuyouts -- as well as interest, dividends, annuities, royalties\nand rents for married couples who make more than $250,000 and\nindividuals who earn at least $200,000.  The impact will be even greater if tax cuts enacted during\nthe presidency of George W. Bush expire as scheduled at the end\nof this year. Unless Congress acts, the top rate on long-term\ncapital gains and dividends, now 15 percent, would go to 20\npercent and 39.6 percent. For high earners above the threshold,\nthe health-care tax would bring the levy on dividends to as much\nas 43.4 percent.  The Supreme Court heard arguments last week on the\nconstitutionality of parts of the health care law, and a ruling\nexpected by the end of June could determine whether the tax\ntakes effect.  The share of profits private-equity managers receive from\ninvestments is known as carried interest. It is often taxed as\ncapital gains, which carry a lower rate than ordinary income and\nfall under the new Medicare levy, said Elizabeth Kessenides, a\ntax attorney in  New York City  who represents people in financial\nservices including private-equity and hedge-fund managers.  The private-equity industry has argued that carried\ninterest should be taxed as investment income rather than wages\nbecause it encourages entrepreneurial risk-taking. Compliance Policy  U.S. Regulators to Move Closer to Designating Systemic Firms  The U.S.  Treasury Department  and regulators will move one\nstep closer today to designating some companies as posing a risk\nto the country\u2019s financial system in the event of their failure.  The Financial Stability Oversight Council will hold a\nmeeting at which it will finalize criteria for singling out non-\nbank financial companies as systemically important and thus\nsubject to greater supervision, the U.S. Treasury Department\nsaid.  The final rule is FSOC\u2019s second attempt to define metrics\nand a procedure for designating non-bank companies as systemic.\n Federal Reserve  Chairman Ben S. Bernanke said March 29 that\nFSOC\u2019s designation tool is a way regulators have become more\nprepared for a crisis.  The FSOC, headed by Treasury Secretary Timothy F. Geithner,\nproposed a rule in October that set standards for determining\nwhich non-bank firms require Federal Reserve scrutiny. Banks\nwith over $50 billion in assets were automatically deemed risky\nto the financial system in the event of their failure.  The final rule regulators will approve today will be\nlargely unchanged from that proposed in October, said officials\nfamiliar with the deliberations who spoke on condition of not\nbeing further identified. The wording, however, can be changed\nuntil the vote is taken.  Under the October proposal, regulators will evaluate non-\nbank financial companies with more than $50 billion in assets if\nthey meet any one or more of the following thresholds: A 15-to-1\nleverage ratio; $3.5 billion in liabilities on derivatives\ncontracts; $20 billion of outstanding loans borrowed and bonds\nissued; $30 billion in gross notional credit-default swaps\noutstanding; or a 10 percent ratio of short-term debt to assets. All over the\ncountry, venerable old dailies are shedding reporters, editors\nand other workers.  In my hometown, the Seattle  Post-Intelligencer  stopped its\npresses for good in 2009, as did the  Rocky Mountain News , in\nDenver. In the past few years, major papers have gone bankrupt\nin Philadelphia,  Minneapolis  and other cities, as circulation\nand advertising revenue have plummeted. Even the proud  New York\nTimes  recently needed a $250 million loan from  Carlos Slim , a\nMexican multibillionaire.  Just a decade ago, newspapers were still the primary\nconduit for local information. Where else could the neighborhood\nfurniture store advertise a sale; the local factory attract new\nworkers; or town residents sell their used cars or sofas? The\npaper used to be dropped daily on almost every stoop in town.  For much of the early 20th century, the newspaper business\nwas both profitable and competitive.  New York City  still had\n seven  dailies in 1960, spanning a full range of political\nphilosophy and journalistic style. Movies such as \u201c Citizen Kane \u201d\nand \u201c The Front Page \u201d portrayed an era when driven newspapermen\nwould do anything to get a story. The U.K.\u2019s rough-and-tumble\nFleet Street remains something of a throwback to that era, as\ndemonstrated by the recent phone-hacking scandal -- which led to\nthe demise of yet another century-old paper, the News of the\nWorld.  Selling the News  The great winnowing of the industry began slowly, as the\nrise of television siphoned off much of the national advertising\nbusiness. Even then, most cities retained one or two papers\noperating profitably as monopolies or duopolies. Newsrooms took\nthis privileged economic position for granted; they began\nthinking of themselves as selling news rather than ads.\nCompetition based on journalism, they rationalized, would drive\nreadership, and ad revenue would follow.  In market research I did at Microsoft Corp. in the early\n1990s, I estimated that the  Wall Street Journal  took in about 75\ncents per copy from subscribers, $1.25 at the newsstand and a\nwhopping $5 per copy from ads. The ad revenue let them run a far\nbigger newsroom than subscribers were paying for. It was a\nbargain for readers and a boon for journalists, who were able to\ntravel to distant assignments and do in-depth reporting.  The trouble was, the tie between excellent journalism and\nrevenue worked only so long as the ads did. New online formats\ngutted the newspaper-ad business.      Why pore over tiny print\nlooking for a job in the want ads when you can tap a few\nkeywords into monster.com, then click through and apply? Why pay\na steep per-character rate for a classified when you can hawk a\nwhole garage full of used stuff on EBay or Craigslist for free?\nIn so many ways, Match.com, OkCupid.com and hundreds of others\noffer a better experience than personal ads can.\nRottenTomatoes.com tells you what movies to watch, Fandango.com\nlets you book the tickets, and OpenTable.com gets you a dinner\nreservation.  Newspaper websites tried offering these services, too, but\nit wasn\u2019t their strength, and they failed to keep up. It didn\u2019t\nhelp that online sites such as Google News could serve up most\nof the news without ever hiring a reporter; they just aggregate\ninformation from many free news sites. Newspapers\u2019 trump card\nhad been the local information that they alone offered, but the\nInternet was simultaneously better at both local and global\ninformation distribution.  At least when television burst on the scene in the 1950s,\nit largely spared classified and truly local advertising. It\nalso created its own journalism; some of the revenue that\ntelevision diverted from newspapers was reinvested in TV news.\nIn contrast, the new forms of  Internet advertising  rarely\nsupport news gathering, or content creation of any sort.\nInstead, most of the ad money now goes to infrastructure\ntechnology that connects people with ads,  search engines  such as\nGoogle, or social networks such as Facebook.  Who Will Pay  The dilemma for early 21st century journalism is this: Who\nwill pay for the news? This column is part of an experiment in\none direction. Bloomberg makes its money providing proprietary\nfinancial information to subscribers, and this business has not\nbeen hurt by the Internet, so it can afford to offer a good old-\nfashioned op-ed page without ad subsidy. As the saying goes,\nit\u2019s nice work if you can get it. But this model won\u2019t extend\nvery far because there aren\u2019t a long list of similarly situated\ndata providers dying to support journalism.  Filmmakers and book publishers have never relied much on\nadvertising revenue; when we want to read \u201c The Girl With the\nDragon Tattoo ,\u201d or watch \u201c Avatar ,\u201d we know we need to pay\nwithout an ad subsidy. Would the public be willing to pay full\nprice for journalism, too?  A few newspapers -- the  Economist , the Wall Street Journal,\nthe New York Times -- have started selling digital-only\nsubscriptions. It\u2019s a first step, but they still plainly\nconsider their print editions to be the gold standard, so they\ngenerate little unique digital content and fail to tap the full\npotential of online news. Tellingly, their current web revenue\nfalls far short of what it would take to support their\nnewsrooms. Meanwhile, most online news sites are still free,\nwhich tends to undercut the business model of those who charge.  The situation reminds me of the early 1970s, when cable\narrived in our neighborhood, and the adults in my family were\narguing over why anybody would pay for something they could\nalready get free. After all, with a set of rabbit ears, you\ncould tune in three major networks and plenty of local\naffiliates, all supported entirely by ads.  Quality Cable TV  Initially, cable providers offered the same channels as\nconventional broadcasters did, so picture quality was the\nselling point. Cable cut down on ghosts and snow and having to\nfuss with an antenna. Once improved reception got cable-TV\noperators going, they shifted their selling proposition toward\nquality -- and quantity -- of programming.  Ted Turner  started\n CNN . Others started  HBO ,  MTV  and Discovery, betting that\nconsumers would pay for a kind of television they never had\nbefore.  It took 20 years, but the cable-TV industry prevailed. A\ngeneration grew up thinking \u201cI want my MTV.\u201d Today, 85 percent\nof American households subscribe to cable, satellite or\ntelephone-company TV, paying an average of $82 a month,\naccording to the research firm SNL Kagan. This revenue has been\na bonanza for TV production, financing some of the best\ntelevision shows ever made, all outside the original broadcast\nnetworks.  Could newspaper journalism likewise entice readers to pay\nfor online news? People like quality journalism, so I believe\nthat, ultimately, they can be persuaded to pay for it. But as\nwith cable, the price will have to start low; it can then inch\nupward as the public gradually accepts the new business model.  The question is whether paid-subscription news sites can\nmake the transition fast enough to make up for their plummeting\nad revenue. It takes time to persuade people to pay for\nsomething they expect to get free. Ultimately, the change will\nhappen, but maybe not fast enough to save some of the great\ninstitutions of newspaper journalism.  ( Nathan Myhrvold , the former chief strategist and chief\ntechnology officer at Microsoft Corp. and the founder and chief\nexecutive officer of\u00a0 Intellectual Ventures , is a Bloomberg View\ncolumnist. The opinions expressed are his own.)  Read more opinion online from  Bloomberg View . The new design will offer processing power three times\nfaster than currently available technology and will help data\ncenters use less energy, ARM said today. The company, whose chip\ndesigns can be found in  Apple Inc. (AAPL) \u2019s iPhone and devices that run\non Google Inc.\u2019s Android operating system, is now trying to\nprovide options for the powerful computers used by companies\nsuch as Google and  Facebook Inc. (FB)   Power Demand  \u201cWe\u2019re finding people building these huge data centers\nwith lots of racks empty because they can\u2019t get the power,\u201d\nEast said. \u201cIf we don\u2019t change the way in which we process the\ndata here, then a 10 times increase in the amount of data means\na 10 times increase in the amount of power used.\u201d  AMD will begin offering 64-bit processors based on ARM\u2019s\ndesigns in 2014, CEO Rory Read said at a company event in  San\nFrancisco  yesterday. Makers of servers are seeking a greater\nvariety of chip choices, Read said in an interview.  AMD, whose market share in servers has slipped to less than\n5 percent, is turning to ARM designs to differentiate itself\nfrom larger rival Intel and win customers for data center chips.\nAfter Intel, AMD is the biggest maker of PC chips on Intel\u2019s x86\ntechnology. A partial defection by AMD to ARM adds to backers of\nthat technology.  \u201cThe status quo isn\u2019t good for anyone, apart from one\ncompany,\u201d said Read. So John Chambers, Cisco System's chief executive officer, had to be disheartened when his company's stock tanked by more than 7 percent after he  announced  his plan to fire 4,000 people, or 5 percent of the work force, during a conference call with investors and analysts. This all suggests that Cisco, like so many other high-tech heartthrobs from the 1990s, is struggling to find purpose in a world that seems to be passing it by. Under Chambers, Cisco became dominant in the business of making routers and switches, forming the backbone of the Internet. That business now is shrinking thanks to competition and alternative technologies. Sound familiar? Microsoft still has a monopoly on PC operating systems and office software, but it's nowhere in smartphones and tablets. AOL, once the leading web service provider, earns most of its money from a dwindling base of subscribers to its Internet service, not from the ads it sells on its websites. Managers with the right combination of skill and luck can take the profits generated by the dwindling core business and invest them into new enterprises. IBM has done a solid job of this, transforming itself from a computer manufacturer into a provider of data-consulting services. Others have wasted the money in fruitless acquisitions (Hewlett-Packard's  purchase of Autonomy ) or doomed ventures (Microsoft's  Surface tablets ), while a few prefer to hoard their profits in cash (Apple). Cisco has managed to do all of those things over the past few years. Although its videoconferencing platform has become almost ubiquitous among big companies, Cisco has squandered billions on ill-fated efforts to diversify into products aimed at  regular people  (like the notorious  Flip  video camera) rather than corporate customers. And like Apple, it has accumulated a very large cash stockpile. Cash is a mixed blessing. It certainly provides security and flexibility. But if Cisco's leaders can't find good investments the money  should be handed back  to its shareholders. Chambers wants Cisco to shift from hardware to high-margin software and services, including security software and cloud computing data centers. The goal is \" to become an IT player .\" There is some evidence that this strategy is working. Earnings from services have increased 73 percent during the past five years even as profit from selling products has stagnated. Unfortunately for Chambers, his timing doesn\u2019t look so great, as Cisco confronts slowing sales in overseas markets, where it gets more than 40 percent of its revenue. From the look of things, that was more than enough to offset any good news investors might have taken away from the job cuts. (Matthew C. Klein is a writer for Bloomberg View. A decade later, Biggs says another bubble is beginning in\nemerging-market  shares . This time, he\u2019s bullish.  \u201cWe\u2019re only halfway along the way to a gigantic eventual\nbubble in the emerging markets,\u201d Biggs, the managing partner of\nNew York-based hedge-fund firm Traxis Partners LLC and former\nchairman of Morgan Stanley Asset Management, said in an Oct. 29\ninterview on Bloomberg Television. \u201cThe emerging markets,\nparticularly Asia, are a place where I want to have a really\nmajor representation.\u201d  Biggs\u2019s view is shared by  Jeremy Grantham , whose investment\nfirm had its assets under management shrink 45 percent in the\nlate 1990s as his pessimistic outlook for high-priced  technology \nstocks spurred clients to buy better-performing mutual funds.\nThe chief strategist at Grantham Mayo Van Otterloo & Co. wrote\non Oct. 26 that his forecast for an \u201cemerging emerging bubble\u201d\nwas in \u201csplendid shape\u201d after the  MSCI Emerging Markets Index \nsoared 146 percent in the past two years. Surging Growth  Investment strategists at Bank of America Corp., Credit\nSuisse Group AG and Societe Generale SA have all said in the\npast two weeks that emerging-market stocks may climb above\nlevels justified by companies\u2019  assets  and earnings because of\nsurging economic growth and the Fed\u2019s efforts to reduce yields\non debt securities. It\u2019s hard to imagine now that the first article for which I was paid money was a piece on the antitrust suits that were supposed to keep Microsoft from taking over the world. Ten years later, it has lost out on search, and again on mobile. The most prominent portent for the company\u2019s future is that it's coming out with  an awesome game console  this holiday season. Nokia, meanwhile, has been declining even faster, as Samsung Electronics Co. Ltd. and Apple Inc. have carved up the market between them. The company that used to account for 20 percent of Finland\u2019s gross domestic product  has seen its sales decline dramatically in the smartphone era  and is operating at a loss. That raises an interesting question: What does this mean for Finland? I\u2019m not exaggerating how dependent Finland\u2019s economy has been on Nokia. Here\u2019s  the Economist  last year, detailing the extent of the country\u2019s reliance: One way to answer this question is to look at what happened to the companies' respective stock: Nokia\u2019s went up and Microsoft\u2019s went down. Nokia\u2019s shareholders will get to cash out at a premium, and if the businesses that are left (maps and telecoms infrastructure) don\u2019t make that much money, at least they don\u2019t seem to be in a cash-vaporizing downward spiral. But that\u2019s a snapshot. What will the moving picture look like? On the plus side of the balance sheet, Microsoft is still a huge company with a big pile of cash that it can spend on making Nokia phones better. On the downside, it's a big company that hasn\u2019t had a lot of hit products recently; will it boost Nokia\u2019s efforts, or will the corporate culture stifle its research and development? Even if Microsoft does manage to make things work as an integrated manufacturer of devices and software (something it has done very well with the Xbox), that doesn\u2019t necessarily mean that Finland will prosper. R&D often shifts around inside large, multinational corporations that don\u2019t feel the same kind of loyalty that a homegrown firm does. Over the years, I\u2019d expect to see Nokia\u2019s center of gravity shift toward the U.S. -- which for Finland means fewer high-paying, satisfying jobs in R&D, or global strategy. Of course, those jobs were always relatively few -- but a global company run out of a small country can offer disproportionately rewarding jobs when times are good. The corollary is that when times aren\u2019t good, the whole local economy gets pretty bumpy. You don\u2019t need to go to Finland to see what this looks like; just take a peek at \u201ccompany towns\u201d like Detroit and Rochester, New York. Overall, I\u2019d expect that this merger signals leaner times to come for Finland -- not an economic contraction necessarily, but slower growth than it was probably expecting six years ago. Which is not to say that this is somehow the wrong thing to do. The whole reason that it's selling to Microsoft is that the company\u2019s in deep trouble. The breadth of the rebound can be seen in the S&P 500\u2019s  weightings , where none of the 10 industry measures represents more than 18 percent of the index. So we\u2019ve seen this significant but drawn-out recovery across the board in equities -- small, medium, large, defensive, dynamic, value, growth.\u201d  Record Surpassed  The S&P 500 climbed 0.7 percent to 1,558.71 yesterday to pull within 0.5 percent of the all-time high it reached on Oct. 9, 2007. The  S&P 500 Equal Weighted Index (SPX) , which gives each company the same contribution regardless of size, surpassed its record on April 28, 2011. That month, the number of S&P 500 companies trading above all-time highs climbed to more than half, Bloomberg data show.  The S&P 500 slid 0.8 percent to 1,545.8 in New York today.  Apple Inc. (AAPL)  (AAPL), the iPhone maker valued at $424.5 billion, gets the same credit in the equal-weighted measure as for-profit educator  Apollo Group Inc. (APOL)  (APOL), worth $1.9 billion. About 59 percent of S&P 500 stocks have exceeded their previous records set before the benchmark gauge peaked at 1,565.15 in 2007.  U.S. stocks are close to completing a recovery in the benchmark index following a 57 percent plunge between October 2007 and March 2009, triggered as the collapse of the subprime mortgage market caused the worst American economic contraction in seven decades.  Retailers, Restaurants  Shares of retailers, restaurant chains and other companies that depend on discretionary consumer spending jumped 231 percent since the bottom  to lead gains  in the S&P 500. Gauges of financial companies and industrial shares have almost tripled, while technology, commodity and health-care stocks are up more than 100 percent.  Wyndham Worldwide Corp., CBS Corp., Fifth Third Bancorp and Gannett Co. are among seven companies in the index that have surged more than 1,000 percent since March 9, 2009.  Stocks rebounded as the Federal Reserve pumped more than $2.3 trillion into the economy through monetary easing since 2008, sending Treasury rates to record lows last year. The S&P 500\u2019s dividend yield, currently at about 2.11 percent, has been above the payout on 10-year Treasuries for almost a year.  Corporate profits  have jumped to a record during the rebound, with earnings for S&P 500 companies surging to $100.75 a share last year from $61.83 in 2009.  \u2018Fundamental Improvement\u2019  \u201cThe market is reflecting fundamental improvement, earnings growth, revenue growth and dividend growth, more than it is price momentum,\u201d Richard Slinn, a San Francisco-based managing director and senior investor at JPMorgan Private Bank, which oversees $877 billion, said by phone. \u201cPeople are naturally kind of hesitant to jump into something they feel like has gone too far, but we disagree with that premise.\u201d  The S&P 500 Equal Weighted Index  underperformed  versus the S&P 500 during the 1990s bull market, which was dominated by rallies in larger U.S. companies and technology stocks. The  S&P 100 Index (OEX) , whose average company\u2019s market cap is $92.3 billion, increased 494 percent from October 1990 to March 2000. That compared with the 417 percent advance by the S&P 500, whose average stock\u2019s market cap is $29.4 billion.  Cisco (CSCO) , the world\u2019s largest maker of computer-networking gear, led gains in the S&P 500 during the 1990s rally, surging more than 111,000 percent. Microsoft increased 6,831 percent during the same period. From the bench, the Phoenix Suns assistant coach watched his basketball team easily give up 48 points to the Golden State Warriors halfway through a game last year. One play in particular was hurting them -- the \"pick and roll.\" It's when a player blocks for his teammate before slipping behind him to receive a pass and score.  But as it turns out, the Suns had a new weapon they were preparing to try out. Call it the swipe and scroll. Gillespie pulled out his Samsung Galaxy tablet and called up a video clip from the first quarter. He was able to immediately show his players what their opponents were doing so they could make quicker adjustments during the game. Meet the extreme mobile worker: the professional athlete, whose closest thing to an office is the airplane seat when traveling from arena to arena. As smartphones and tablets change the way companies do business, sports teams are also increasingly tapping mobile devices to get a technological leg-up on the competition. The Suns became the first NBA team this season to outfit both players and coaches with tablet computers for use on and off the court. The Suns coaches use an app that lets them draw plays, see them in action, review playbooks and pull up game videos. This replaces whiteboards, reams of paper, bulky laptops and \"a rack of DirecTV boxes recording other teams, and having a guy making DVDs all night long,\" said John Brandstetter, president of Flying Tiger Entertainment, whose company developed the software. Players and coaches said the tablets have had the biggest impact during travel. Kendall Marshall, the 21-year-old point guard who the Suns drafted last year, said he reviews video from his plane seat en route to the next game. Gillespie thinks up plays and inputs them into the tablet by swiping his finger along the screen. \"If I'm going on a road trip, instead of having six three-ring binders, I have all of that information on the tablet,\" said Gillespie, who recalls using VCRs to look at game footage when he entered the NBA 11 years ago. \"As technology has changed, the NBA is trying to change.\" Meanwhile, other professional sports leagues have been experimenting with tablets. Verizon Wireless, which helped bring Samsung's Android-based tablet to the Suns, arranged a similar deal with the Denver Broncos for use in the National Football League, said Tom Gainor, the wireless company's associate director of marketing and sales operations. Like any fast-moving business, sports teams rely heavily on having data at their fingertips. Some in the NBA have been using video technology from STATS LLC's SportVU to record player movements and collect statistical information. The data-driven, so-called Moneyball approach to gain a competitive edge is popular with some Major League Baseball teams.  When successful, such innovations can find their way to college, high-school and even little-league sports. Mobile apps such as GameChanger lets coaches and parents track every play of a game so they can monitor the progress of their kids over the season .  If Samsung's tablet or Apple's iPad passes muster in the NBA, the next generation of athletes could be prepping for after-school sports on their devices in between games of \"Angry Birds.\" In Flying Tiger's current app, the playbook and play-creation features give an animated, overhead view of how each formation might play out, with players represented by X's and O's. The next version will have 3-D players dribbling and passing to each other. It could end up looking like a game for Microsoft Corp.'s Xbox 360 console. \"This is basically bringing what you have in video games to professional sports,\" said Brandstetter, who had previously worked on a Sega basketball game called \"David Robinson's Supreme Court\" and a version of \"Madden NFL.\" \"At some point down the road, we may even put sensors in their shoes\" to monitor movement and speed, which could help coaches decide when to give a tired player some rest. The companies are mulling whether to make these tools available to other NBA teams. The Denver Nuggets, Houston Rockets and Los Angeles Clippers have expressed interest in using the technology, Gillespie said. While he's a fan of the technology, Gillespie said he's still not comfortable using the device during the game. \"It doesn't seem natural for an assistant coach to all of a sudden pull out a tablet and watch a video,\" he said. Time is better spent monitoring the game and coaching players rather than reviewing tape. Of course, there is the occasional instance when it's useful to have a tablet handy -- like during the game against the Warriors, who are now in the playoffs. After studying the pick-and-roll footage, Phoenix outscored Golden State in the second half. Still, the Suns lost by 2 points. A tablet can't solve everything. Hunt","released_at":"<date>July 25 2010<\/date> <time>15:00:57<\/time>","content":"This week is the 20th anniversary of\nthe  Americans with Disabilities Act , one of the country\u2019s\nlandmark civil rights measures and the signature domestic\nachievement of President  George H.W. Bush .  \n The ADA mandates equal opportunities for individuals with\ndisabilities in  employment , access to public facilities,\ntransportation and telecommunications.  \n Although problems persist, particularly in employment, it\nhas transformed America, improved the lives of the  50 million \npeople with disabilities (half of them severely disabled) and\nserved as a model for much of the rest of the world.  \n \u201cIn very fundamental ways, it has changed the basic\nsocietal perception and expectations of the role of people with\ndisabilities in America, and of the country\u2019s obligation to make\naccommodations to enable the fullest practicable participation\nof this segment of the population,\u201d says  Robert Burgdorf Jr. , a\nlaw professor at the University of the  District of Columbia  who\nwrote the first draft of the measure.  \n The gains have been most visible in accessibility, with\ncurb cuts, transportation and access to public facilities. \u201cThe\nADA has changed the way Americans get around and relate to their\ncommunities,\u201d says  Andy Imparato , the president of the  American\nAssociation  of People with Disabilities.  \n Citing the landmark 1954 civil rights school desegregation\ncase, Imparato says, \u201cThe ADA is our Brown v. Board of\nEducation.\u201d And like Brown, it\u2019s an evolving process that takes\nyears, decades.  \n UN Convention  \n A look around the globe and the ADA\u2019s impact is evident; it\nwas a catalyst for the 2006 United Nations Convention on the\nRights of Persons With Disabilities, an international  accord \nthat requires parties to promote equal rights for and full\nemployment of the disabled.  \n \u201cThe U.S. still leads the world in safeguarding the rights\nof its citizens with disabilities,\u201d says Tanya Gallagher, head\nof the  Disability Research Institute at the University of\nIllinois .  \n The Japanese are developing their own ADA-type law now, and\n China  proudly hosted the Special Olympics for the\ndevelopmentally disabled in 2008;  developing countries  are using\nthe ADA as a model to start to deal with the issue.  \n There remain daunting challenges in health care, technology\nand especially jobs. The jobless rate for disabled people in the\nU.S. is officially  14.3 percent , or almost double that of able-\nbodied workers; since this figure only counts those looking for\njobs, the real  unemployment rate  for the disabled, experts say,\nprobably exceeds 50 percent.  \n Company Hiring  \n There are companies that have adopted a more aggressive\npolicy for hiring employees with disabilities. Professor Peter Blanck, chairman of the  Burton Blatt Institute  at  Syracuse\nUniversity , recently surveyed 30,000 disabled employees at 14\ncompanies. He found that in firms labeled by employees as\n\u201cdisability friendly\u201d -- providing more accommodations,\nflexibility and less autocracy -- disparities in wages,\nretention and workplace issues disappeared.  \n In an interview, Blanck cited several examples of\ndisability-friendly companies: Redmond, Washington-based\n Microsoft Corp. (MSFT) ,  Hoffman Estates , Illinois-based Sears Roebuck &\nCo. and Cincinnati-based  Procter & Gamble Co. (PG)  among them.  \n The courts, especially conservative judges, and all the way\nto the Supreme Court, handed down a series of anti-ADA decisions\nlimiting these civil rights. Often, discrimination claims then\nwere summarily dismissed.  \n ADA Amendments  \n However, the last Congress passed the ADA Amendments Act of\n2008, which overturned a number of these unfortunate court\ndecisions, and has facilitated the legal process for people with\ndisabilities.  \n The political problems haven\u2019t disappeared. A few months\nago,  Rand Paul , the Republican candidate for senator in\n Kentucky , dismissed government efforts. \u201cI think if you have a\ntwo-story office, and you hire someone who\u2019s handicapped, it\nmight be reasonable to let him have an office on the first floor\nrather than the government saying you have to have a $100,000\nelevator,\u201d he said.  \n Much of the disabilities community considers the term\nhandicapped pejorative; it originated in Elizabethan England,\nwhen people with disabilities were forced to beg on the street\nand were given a cap for handouts. Contrary to Paul\u2019s\nassertions, accessibly costs for businesses and public\nfacilities have been comparatively low.  \n State Cuts  \n With pervasive fiscal travails, many states are cutting\nback on Medicaid, often disproportionately hitting those with\ndisabilities.  Arizona  this year is cutting mental  health\nservices  by more than one-third.  \n And despite the controversial court decisions,  Supreme\nCourt  nominee Elena Kagan wasn\u2019t asked one question about the\nADA during her confirmation hearings and there was only a single\nfleeting reference to disabilities. By contrast, four senators\ngrilled her on abortion, which was mentioned 38 times in the\nhearings.  \n Still the progress, in politics, business and social\nmindsets, is impressive. The health-care bill passed this year\nbanned insurance companies from denying coverage because of\npreexisting medical conditions, a major triumph for those with\ndisabilities.  \n Vehicle Production Group LLC, with a principal investment\nfrom the Washington-based private-equity fund Perseus LLC, is\nproducing the first passenger car specifically designed for\npeople with disabilities, with a ramp and enough space for\nwheelchairs and carts to easily maneuver. The $40,000 vehicle\nwill be available next year.  \n Telecommunications  \n Last week, House Energy and Commerce Committee Chairman\nHenry Waxman, a California Democrat, shepherded through the\npanel a measure that updates the telecommunications portion of\nthe ADA, reflecting changes in technology. It requires smart\nphones to be more accessible to the disabled and online videos\nto include captioning.  \n Like the great struggles over civil rights and race, the\nmost determinative issue is attitudinal. \u201cWithout the ADA,\nignorance about the abilities and potential of persons with\ndisabilities would be far more pervasive,\u201d Professor Gallagher\nsays.  \n The progress since Bush signed the measure in the summer of\n1990 has been notable. Moreover, auguring well for the future,\nthere\u2019s a generational divide, with younger people far more\ncomfortable and accepting of those with disabilities.  \n Yet the most remarkable change has been for those most\naffected.  \n \u201cThe ADA has helped disabled people think about their\nstatus as a measure of civil rights and equality, not simply as\na medical or social welfare policy,\u201d Imparato says. \u201cThe ADA\nhas given us the right to talk about our disabilities and not be\nashamed.\u201d  \n ( Albert R. Hunt  is the executive editor for  Washington  at\nBloomberg News. The opinions expressed are his own.)  \n To contact the writer of this column:\nAlbert R. (GOOG)  agreed to settle U.S.\nFederal Trade Commission claims that it used deceptive tactics\nand violated its own privacy policies when it introduced the\nBuzz social-networking service last year.  The proposed settlement bars Google from misrepresenting\nhow it handles information, obliges the company to follow\npolicies that protect consumer data in new products and requires\nperiodic reviews to ensure the policies are followed, the FTC\nsaid in a statement today.  \u201cWhen companies make privacy pledges, they need to honor\nthem,\u201d  Jon Leibowitz , the commission\u2019s chairman, said in the\nstatement. \u201cThis is a tough settlement that ensures that Google\nwill honor its commitments to consumers and build strong privacy\nprotections into all of its operations.\u201d  Google is grappling with increased government scrutiny from\nregulators around the world who say it doesn\u2019t do enough to\nsafeguard users\u2019 information. They also say the company may use\nits dominance of Web search to thwart competition. The proposed\nsettlement, which doesn\u2019t call for a fine, will be in effect for\n20 years, and covers future situations such as Google\u2019s\ncollection of Wi-Fi data, FTC deputy director Jessica Rich said\non a conference call.  Customer Harm  The settlement stems from a Feb. 16, 2010, complaint filed\nby the  Electronic Privacy Information Center , a Washington-based\nadvocacy group. The center asked the FTC to investigate whether\nconsumers were harmed when users of Google\u2019s Gmail service found\nprivate e-mail contact information automatically displayed to\nother users when they enrolled in Buzz. Ten lawmakers sent a\nletter to the FTC on March 25, 2010, urging the commission to\ncarefully look into the group\u2019s complaint.  \u201cThe FTC action is far-reaching,\u201d the center\u2019s Executive\nDirector  Marc Rotenberg  said by e-mail. \u201cThis is the most\nsignificant privacy decision by the commission to date. For\n Internet users , it should lead to higher privacy standards and\nbetter protection for personal data.\u201d  Google said it agreed to an independent review of privacy\nprocedures every two years and will ask users to give\n\u201caffirmative consent before we change how we share their\npersonal information.\u201d  \u201cWe don\u2019t always get everything right.\u201d Google said in a\nblog posting today. \u201cThe launch of Google Buzz fell short of\nour usual standards for transparency and user control.\u201d  Regulatory Issues  Colin Gillis , an analyst at BGC Partners LP in  New York \nsaid Google wants to avoid the regulatory issues that affected\nMicrosoft Corp. and slowed down that company\u2019s ability to be\ninnovative. Google introduced Buzz on Feb. 9, 2010. The service was\nlinked to a user\u2019s Gmail account \u201cso you don\u2019t have to peck out\nan entirely new set of friends from scratch -- it just works,\u201d\nGoogle wrote in an official blog post at the time.  Users weren\u2019t explicitly warned that their e-mail lists\nwould be automatically visible to the public, the privacy group\nwrote in its complaint.  \u2018Estranged Spouses\u2019  \u201cGmail contact lists routinely include deeply personal\ninformation, including the names and e-mail addresses of\nestranged spouses, current lovers, attorneys and doctors,\u201d the\ncenter said in its complaint.  Users could hide their lists only by clicking through\nseveral links to un-check a box labeled \u201cDisplay the list of\npeople I\u2019m following and people following me,\u201d the group said.\nIt called on the FTC to take action under Section 5 of the FTC\nact, which allows the agency to enforce against unfair and\ndeceptive trade practices.  Google\u2019s fix allows users to opt in and control how much\ninformation they share. Such a law\nwould immediately be found unconstitutional. Yet we all carry\nmobile phones.  If the National Security Agency required us to notify it\nwhenever we made a new friend, the nation would rebel. Yet we\nnotify  Facebook Inc. (FB)  If the Federal Bureau of Investigation\ndemanded copies of all our conversations and correspondence, it\nwould be laughed at. Yet we provide copies of our e-mail to\n Google Inc. (GOOG) ,  Microsoft Corp. (MSFT)  or whoever our mail host is; we\nprovide copies of our text messages to  Verizon Communications\nInc. (VZ) ,  AT&T Inc. (T)  and  Sprint Corp. (S) ; and we provide copies of other\nconversations to Twitter Inc., Facebook,  LinkedIn (LNKD)  Corp. or\nwhatever other site is hosting them.  The primary business model of the Internet is built on mass\nsurveillance, and our government\u2019s intelligence-gathering\nagencies have become addicted to that data. Understanding how we\ngot here is critical to understanding how we undo the damage.  Computers and networks inherently produce data, and our\nconstant interactions with them allow corporations to collect an\n enormous amount  of intensely personal data about us as we go\nabout our daily lives. Sometimes we produce this data\ninadvertently simply by using our phones, credit cards,\ncomputers and other devices. Sometimes we give corporations this\ndata directly on Google, Facebook, Apple Inc.\u2019s iCloud and so on\nin exchange for whatever free or cheap service we receive from\nthe Internet in return.  The NSA is also in the business of spying on everyone, and\nit has realized it\u2019s far easier to collect all the  data  from\nthese corporations rather than from us directly. In some cases,\nthe NSA asks for this data nicely. In other cases, it makes use\nof  subtle threats  or  overt pressure . If that doesn\u2019t work, it\nuses tools like  national security letters .  The Partnership  The result is a corporate-government surveillance\npartnership, one that allows both the government and\ncorporations to get away with things they  couldn\u2019t otherwise .  There are two types of laws in the U.S., each designed to\nconstrain a different type of power: constitutional law, which\nplaces limitations on government, and regulatory law, which\nconstrains corporations. Historically, these two areas have\nlargely remained separate, but today each group has learned how\nto use the other\u2019s laws to bypass their own restrictions. The\ngovernment uses corporations to get around its limits, and\ncorporations use the government to get around their limits.  This partnership  manifests  itself in various ways. The\ngovernment uses corporations to circumvent its prohibitions\nagainst  eavesdropping domestically  on its citizens. Corporations\nrely on the government to ensure that they have unfettered use\nof the data they collect.  Here\u2019s an example: It would be reasonable for our\ngovernment to debate the circumstances under which corporations\ncan collect and use our data, and to provide for protections\nagainst misuse. But if the government is using that very data\nfor its own surveillance purposes, it has an incentive to oppose\nany laws to limit data collection. And because corporations see\nno need to give consumers any choice in this matter -- because\nit would only reduce their profits -- the market isn\u2019t going to\nprotect consumers, either.  Our elected officials are often supported, endorsed and\nfunded by these corporations as well, setting up an incestuous\nrelationship between corporations, lawmakers and the\nintelligence community.  The losers are us, the people, who are left with no one to\nstand up for our interests. Our elected government, which is\nsupposed to be responsible to us,  is not . And corporations,\nwhich in a market economy are supposed to be responsive to our\nneeds, are not. What we have now is  death to privacy  -- and\nthat\u2019s very dangerous to democracy and liberty.  Challenging Power  The simple answer is to blame consumers, who shouldn\u2019t use\nmobile phones, credit cards, banks or the Internet if they don\u2019t\nwant to be tracked. But that argument deliberately ignores the\nreality of today\u2019s world. Everything we do involves computers,\neven if we\u2019re not using them directly. And by their nature,\ncomputers produce tracking data. We can\u2019t go back to a world\nwhere we don\u2019t use computers, the Internet or social networking.\nWe have no choice but to share our personal information with\nthese corporations, because that\u2019s how our world works today.  Curbing the  power  of the corporate-private surveillance\npartnership requires limitations on both what corporations can\ndo with the data we choose to give them and restrictions on how\nand when the government can demand access to that data. Because\nboth of these changes go against the interests of corporations\nand the government, we have to demand them as citizens and\nvoters. We can lobby our government to operate more\ntransparently -- disclosing the opinions of the Foreign\nIntelligence Surveillance Court would be a  good start  -- and\nhold our lawmakers accountable when it doesn\u2019t. But it\u2019s not\ngoing to be easy. There are strong interests doing their best to\nensure that the steady stream of data keeps flowing.  ( Bruce Schneier  is a computer security technologist. He is\nthe author of several books, including his  latest , \u201cLiars and\nOutliers: Enabling the Trust Society Needs to Thrive.\u201d)  To contact the writer of this article:\nBruce Schneier at  schneier@schneier.com . The next day, the stock jumped as much as 19 percent.  A month later, the proposed acquisition was dead. Severn Trent\u2019s management, which deemed the bid too low, benefited from new takeover rules, unique among major economies. It refused to enter into negotiations while a 28-day deadline for the acquirer to make a fully financed bid came and went. Since then, Severn Trent shares have dropped 12 percent.  The aborted deal shows how the rules, introduced by the U.K. Takeover Panel in 2011, are strengthening the hand of target companies and, critics say, holding back some U.K. transactions even as global deals rebound, helped by Verizon Communications Inc.\u2019s $130 billion buyout of Vodafone Group Plc\u2019s stake in their wireless venture. The most controversial provision of the directives requires companies to disclose talks at the slightest sign of a leak, triggering the 28-day timeline for a formal bid.  \u201cThe consequences of a leak are pretty significant under the new rules, which can make buyers more cautious and lead to a dampening effect on M&A,\u201d said Tim Gee, the London-based head of global mergers at law firm Baker & McKenzie. \u201cBuyers now have to do a lot more blind work before initiating contact to make sure they\u2019re ready to go.\u201d  Cadbury Law  The Takeover Panel, the world\u2019s oldest acquisition oversight body, introduced the tougher regulations a year after the hostile takeover of chocolate maker Cadbury Plc by  Kraft Foods Group Inc. (KRFT)  in 2010 sent Cadbury shares on a roller-coaster ride.  They come amid other changes to rein in the perceived excesses of  London \u2019s financial sector that have been encouraged by politicians including Business Secretary Vince Cable. After a series of scandals, U.K. regulators are making it more difficult for companies controlled by overseas billionaires to list on the London Stock Exchange and are taking a harder look at the foreign operations of natural resources firms.  The so-called Cadbury Law stipulates that any hint of a transaction involving a U.K.-listed target -- unusual stock movement, a news article based on anonymous sources, or even a tabloid market column that cites stock-trader chatter -- can force a company to issue a press release confirming or denying the existence of negotiations and identifying any potential bidder.  Virtual Bids  At that point, an acquirer has 28 days to \u201cput up or shut up\u201d -- either making a firm, fully financed bid or walking away for six months, unless the target requests an extension. M&A insiders call it the \u201cPUSU\u201d period.  Underscoring how practices have changed, earlier this month Vodafone twice issued press releases confirming media reports on its talks to sell its stake in  Verizon Wireless  -- even though bids for assets aren\u2019t the focus of the new rules.  The regulations are meant to discourage so-called virtual bids that send stocks on a speculative tear, putting target companies in a defensive position and harming shareholders and employees if the bid never materializes, the Takeover Panel has said.  The U.K. rules stand in sharp contrast to the U.S., where companies aren\u2019t subject to disclosure requirements and can simply refuse to comment on speculation or stock moves.  Swinging Balance  \u201cThe 2011 reforms have achieved the Takeover Panel\u2019s aim of swinging the balance of power in an offer situation away from the bidder in favor of the target,\u201d said Charles Jacobs, an M&A partner at Linklaters law firm in London.  For some bankers and lawyers, the directives have shifted too far in favor of targeted companies. Once talks are announced, the management of a stalked company holds most of the cards. Since a target company must consent to an extension of the 28-day deadline, executives can run out the clock if they choose.  A spokeswoman for Severn Trent declined to comment, referring only to earlier statements that the company gave \u201ccareful consideration\u201d to all proposals and the bidder wasn\u2019t able or willing to \u201cbridge the value gap.\u201d  Management at  Kentz Corp. (KENZ) , a U.K.-listed oil-engineering company that\u2019s fighting a takeover offer from rival  Amec Plc (AMEC)  it views as too low, may also end up benefiting from the rules. So far, it has refused to enter into talks or allow access to its books before a Sept. 16 deadline that kicked in after news Kentz was approached broke on Aug. 18. Amec\u2019s offer was at a 22 percent premium to Kentz\u2019s share price before the leak.  Too Far  \u201cIt\u2019s good to give management at the target company the tools to say no, but there are many practitioners who believe the pendulum has swung too far,\u201d said Selina S. Sagayam, a London-based partner at law firm Gibson, Dunn & Crutcher LLP, who has worked at the Takeover Panel.  The deadline played a role in the collapse of merger discussions between Airbus owner  European Aeronautic , Defence & Space Co. and BAE Systems Plc. After a story by  Bloomberg News  last Sept. 12, the two companies were forced to confirm the talks the same day, sparking a flurry of political controversy in  Germany , France and the U.K.  When the talks fell apart a few weeks later, some advisers blamed the leak and subsequent mandatory announcement for hurting the deal, as discussions had to be rushed with the German government to meet the timetable.  Especially Critical  \u201cThe likelihood of getting the deal would\u2019ve been higher if there had been more time to educate the capital markets and politicians,\u201d said Stefan Maichl, an analyst at Landesbank Baden-Wuerttemberg in Stuttgart, Germany. \u201cWhether the deal would\u2019ve gotten done in the end is impossible to say, but it would\u2019ve helped.\u201d  Private-equity firms are especially critical of the new regime. The time limit for conducting due diligence increases the risks of getting a deal done, making buyout firms more hesitant to pursue public companies, said one London-based private-equity executive, who asked not to be identified because he didn\u2019t want to be seen publicly criticizing the Takeover Panel. A ban on breakup fees, which can cover a firm\u2019s costs if a deal craters, has also upset private-equity firms.  \u201cOur anecdotal conversations suggest various aspects of the changes are proving difficult for our members,\u201d said Simon Horner, the director for policy and public affairs at the British Venture Capital and Private Equity Association.  Voicing Concern  Some U.S. companies have voiced concern about being identified if they pursue a U.K. target, said two lawyers who have worked on transatlantic deals and asked not to be identified discussing client issues.  \u201cThe takeover code can be off-putting to non-U.K. buyers looking at the U.K. for the first time,\u201d said Andrew Bell, head of European and Asian M&A at investment bank Jefferies Group LLC. \u201cThe timetable and real possibility of your name being disclosed before a deal is agreed can be intimidating. So, when advising non-U.K. clients, we work hard to ensure they take a well informed and balanced view of the code.\u201d  With many factors affecting the frequency of deals, it\u2019s difficult to prove the rules are directly to blame for discouraging takeovers, M&A experts said. In a  study released  in November 2012, the Takeover Panel said the number of firm bids was roughly the same as the year before, around 80.  There have, however, been fewer U.K. hostile offers this year and last -- 5 in 2013 and 4 in 2012 -- than in any year since 2002, when there were 3, according to data compiled by researcher Dealogic.  Leakiest Market  The Takeover Panel also rejected complaints from private-equity firms that 28 days isn\u2019t long enough to arrange and finance a transaction. Only 15 target companies requested an extension, and in all cases it granted them, relieving pressure on buyers to secure a deal quickly, the Panel report said. A spokesman for the Takeover Panel declined to comment.  The takeover rules, along with a crackdown by the U.K.\u2019s markets regulator on  insider trading , have been factors in keeping more deals secret in London, which a Cass Business School  study  showed is the world\u2019s leakiest M&A market.  The value of U.K. deals that showed significant pre-announcement  stock trading  fell to 13 percent of the total between 2010 and 2012 from 22 percent between 2004 and 2007, a steeper decline than in any other market, according to the study. The most recent global average was 9 percent.  In another study, the Financial Conduct Authority regulator found abnormal share-price movements before the announcement of 15 percent of deals in the year to March, down from as high as 31 percent in 2009.  Important Test  In a city once known for cozy relationships between dealmakers, public relations firms and journalists, \u201cthe stricter rules and enforcement have led to a cultural shift,\u201d said Scott Moeller, director of the M&A unit at Cass and a former investment banker at Deutsche Bank AG. \u201cLeaks have definitely gone down since the changes.\u201d  The most important test of the Panel\u2019s new approach will come as merger volume picks up. Although the first eight months of the year were on track to be the slowest in a decade, with about $82 billion in transactions, M&A volumes are rebounding thanks to the Verizon-Vodafone transaction and Microsoft Corp.\u2019s agreement to buy Nokia Oyj\u2019s handset business for $7.2 billion, both announced this week.  A more robust business environment may mean a higher proportion of leaks, as dealmakers get more bullish about their chances of completing transactions, said Philip Whitchelo, vice president of product marketing at IntraLinks, which operates electronic data rooms for M&A transactions.  \u201cIf markets start to recover and people feel more confident about getting deals done, then there may be a pick-up in leaks,\u201d he said in an interview. \u201cBut I don\u2019t think we\u2019ll return to the pre-2007 levels. What happened to the 48-year-old American had nothing to do with technology and everything to do with a turf war between backers of Prime Minister  Dmitry Medvedev , who made crafting a Russian version of Silicon Valley the cornerstone of his presidency, and allies of President  Vladimir Putin  who see the premier as a rival and want him out, said  Masha Lipman , an analyst at the Moscow Carnegie Center.  \u201cThis group of influential people are doing what they can to accelerate a decision to dismiss Medvedev because he has encroached on their interests,\u201d Lipman said. Microsoft to Siemens  Since announcing the creation of Skolkovo in 2010 as part of a drive to wean the economy off oil and gas, which account for half of state revenue, Medvedev has lured almost $500 million of investment pledges from companies including Intel,  Microsoft Corp. (MSFT) ,  Siemens AG (SIE)  and  Samsung Electronics (005930)  Co. He\u2019s also won a $1 billion commitment for Russian technology projects, much of it in Skolkovo, from  Cisco Systems Inc. Medvedev became the first Russian leader to visit Silicon Valley in June 2010. He toured the offices of  Apple Inc. (AAPL) , Twitter Inc. and Cisco, where he secured the $1 billion investment pledge. Medvedev was president from 2008 to 2012 while Putin, who was barred from serving a third-straight term, bided his time as prime minister.  Medvedev\u2019s plan for Skolkovo calls for the 400-hectare (1,000-acre) site to have 25,000 permanent residents, including employees and their families, by 2020, as well as schools and rail links to central Moscow.
