(AMZN) \u2019s Web Services division, whose server farms generate the processing power the retailer sells to heavy corporate data users on the cheap, has grown so large that the unit routinely finds itself with thousands of spare machines.  So the e-commerce giant created a supply-and-demand-driven market called Amazon EC2 Spot Instances that lets clients rent processors for as little as 10 percent of Amazon\u2019s standard cloud-services fees. To use Spot Instances, companies bid for the rights to a certain number of servers. Winning bidders are billed by the hour, as long as the market price hasn\u2019t risen above an upper bound they specify.  The marketplace gives Seattle-based Amazon and its 7-year- old cloud-computing division an added advantage over Microsoft Corp. and  Google Inc. (GOOG) , which are racing to catch up after a late start. Analysts at Macquarie Securities estimated in a Jan. 7 report that total Amazon Web Services revenue will almost double this year to $3.8 billion and will reach $8.8 billion by 2015. Web Services will kick in close to 5 percent of  sales  this year, up from 3.4 percent last year, and will rise to almost 8 percent by 2015, Macquarie projected.  Were AWS a standalone company, it would be worth $24 billion, according to a March 5 report by Carlos Kirjner, an analyst at Sanford C. Bernstein & Co. That\u2019s more valuable than two-thirds of the companies in Standard & Poor\u2019s 500 Index, and accounts for about a fifth of Amazon\u2019s stock market value.  Analyzing Terabytes  Amazon\u2019s lead in the public-cloud market, which Gartner Inc. estimates jumped 20 percent last year to $109 billion, poses a challenge for technology competitors. As an e-commerce company, Amazon\u2019s operating  margins  are already razor-thin - -1.11 percent in 2012 -- while Google and Microsoft generated margins last year of greater than 25 percent. That means Amazon can cut prices on cloud services without affecting its total profitability.  Investors aren\u2019t fazed by Amazon\u2019s low margins. The stock trades at 186 times estimated earnings for this year, compared with a ratio of 18 for Google and 10 for Microsoft.  Spot Instances was started in 2009, though the  spot market  has taken off only in the past year, Amazon EC2 Vice President Matt Garman said. Researchers in genomics and drug design as well as online advertising increasingly use Spot to analyze terabytes of data, while companies such as  Cycle Computing LLC , Princeton Consultants Inc., and  Numerate Inc.  have built businesses that track market prices for heavy data users. Princeton Consultants, a strategy and software firm, is among the companies that developed algorithms to monitor Spot Instances\u2019 pricing and availability for clients in need of server time. Otherwise, Amazon shuts their servers off in midstream. That\u2019s a deal-breaker for clients using it to host websites or stream video.  \u201cFor people running with hard deadlines, it\u2019s not an appropriate solution,\u201d said Michael Crandell, CEO of RightScale Inc., which helps companies manage cloud services. After all, any member of a \"tribe\" has markers to demonstrate their allegiance to the tribe. But Alex continued. \"Don't you think instead this room should be bursting with products made by competitors? Or other solutions consumers turn to instead of the company's products?\" \n\n It was a thought provoking point. At most companies, it is a mark of shame to use anything other than the company's product. I doubt that you would see many tubes of Crest at Colgate-Palmolive. Try bringing a Coke product into Pepsi. Steve Ballmer from Microsoft famously berated an employee last year for using an iPhone at a company event. I remember a few years ago when we were working for DHL and we committed a cardinal sin. Not only did we send the company something via FedEx. It was an invoice. (Fortunately a friendly client interceded and saved us from trouble).  \n\n It's kind of silly, isn't it? An innovation-focused company shouldn't have an avoid-the-competition-at-all-costs mindset. Instead, the company should always be wondering: What is the competition up to?  Why might people prefer their products to ours?  How does the customer think through purchase-and-use decisions? Some companies have people who focus solely on competitive intelligence, but the simplest form of competitive intelligence is to encourage employees to act like \"regular\" customers. Pick whatever solution gets the job done better than anyone else.  \n\n Intentionally try the competitor's products to see what works and what doesn't work. Don't consider it a mark of shame. Market researcher IBISWorld estimates that revenue in the U.S. security,\nburglar, and fire alarm industry fell 0.4 percent annually over the last five years, to $16.2\nbillion, 40 percent of which comes from the residential sector. Over the next five years, it\nexpects a 2.6 percent average annual increase in total revenue. The U.S. home\nautomation market is expected to grow much faster. ABI Research predicts that\nshipments of controllers -- the systems\u2019 hubs -- will soar to 2.8 million by 2016, from\n150,000 units last year.  At its inception, Pedersen\u2019s company (then named APX Alarm Security Solutions) sold\nand installed security systems, handing off customers to ADT, Protection One, and\nother home-monitoring providers. In 2006, APX became a provider, which meant it\ncould keep its customers. The bulk of the company\u2019s revenue has always come from\ndoor-to-door sales, mostly by college students, many of whom sell full-time during the\nsummer and part-time during the school year. Roughly half of Vivint\u2019s employees are in\nsales.  Selling door-to-door requires a strong personality, and the company\u2019s salespeople have\nbeen accused of being too aggressive. In 2009, the Better Business Bureau of Utah\ncollected 573 complaints from bureaus nationwide; the number decreased to 448 last\nyear, says Jane Driggs, president and chief executive of the accreditation group in  Salt\nLake City . [Otherwise] you\u2019re not going to sell\nanything,\u201d he says.  In 2008 and 2009, the company paid a total of $65,850 in  Arkansas  to settle allegations\nof improper licensing of employees. Pedersen says the company had expanded\ninto areas faster than it could keep track of differing state laws and now has procedures\nin place to ensure compliance.  Having tackled its growing pains, Vivint will have to hone its tactics as it faces a new set\nof competitors. New York has an uphill fight in trying to draw startups and\nengineers away from the San Francisco Bay area -- home to Apple,\nGoogle, Facebook and Twitter Inc. Silicon Valley attracted\nalmost  six  times more venture-capital investment dollars than\nNew York in the second quarter, according to a\nPricewaterhouseCoopers LLP  study . A $350\nmillion donation from Cornell graduate Charles Feeney helped\nseal the university\u2019s victory. President  Barack Obama  should have U.S. agencies identify\ntwice as much spectrum for shared use as he directed in a 2010\nmemorandum setting mobile-computing growth as a national\npriority, the President\u2019s Council of Advisors on Science and\nTechnology said in a letter and report issued today.  Carriers led by  Verizon Wireless , the largest U.S. wireless\nprovider, and No. 2  AT&T Inc. (T)  have pushed the government to\ndevote more airwaves to wireless high-speed Internet, or\nbroadband, as they seek to handle data traffic that has more\nthan doubled four years in a row.  Today\u2019s recommendation signals a U.S. shift from granting\ncompanies exclusive use of airwaves vacated by federal agencies,\nand toward having frequency bands accommodate demands from\nmultiple users.  Mobile carriers have said they prefer to have swaths of\nairwaves they control.  \u201cFull ownership of the spectrum has proven over time to be\nthe best model,\u201d AT&T Chief Executive Officer  Randall Stephenson  said at June 1 conference. \u201cSpectrum sharing models,\nit\u2019s really hard for somebody like us to control network\nquality.\u201d  Doubling Airwaves  Obama in 2010 pledged to almost double the airwaves\navailable for wireless devices such as smartphones and tablet\ncomputers by making another 500 megahertz available over 10\nyears.  U.S. mobile providers are assigned 409.5 megahertz for\ncommercial use, according to CTIA-The Wireless Association.\nMembers of the Washington-based trade group include AT&T,\nVerizon Wireless, No. 3 carrier  Sprint Nextel Corp. (S)  and the\nfourth-largest, T-Mobile USA Inc.  The 500-megahertz plan has been progressing slowly, and it\ncan be prohibitively expensive to move federal agencies aside as\nrelocation costs mount, the White House advisory council said in\ntoday\u2019s report. It recommended the federal government find 1,000\nmegahertz for shared use.  As an example of possible ways to share, the report said\nsome users could operate in airwaves and cease when primary,\nfederal users begin to emit signals. In another example, devices\ncan automatically switch to different airwaves when a higher\npriority use takes place, the report said. Or devices could use\nspectrum in one place that is reserved for government uses in\nother locations, the report said.  Defense Spectrum  Defense agencies are the largest users of federal spectrum,\nholding about 37 percent of airwaves assigned to U.S. users, the\nWhite House panel said in its report.  The advisory group issuing today\u2019s report was appointed by\nthe president to augment the science and technology advice\navailable to him from inside the White House. Members include\nGoogle Inc. Executive Chairman Eric Schmidt; Mark Gorenberg, a\nmanaging director of San Francisco-based investors Hummer\nWinblad Venture Partners; and Craig Mundie, chief research and\nstrategy officer at Microsoft Corp.  Congress in February approved auctions of unused television\nairwaves for use by wireless services, another step aimed at\nalleviating the spectrum shortage. The Federal Communications\nCommission is working to devise auction rules.  Blair Levin, a former FCC official who\u2019s now a fellow at\nthe Washington-based policy group  Aspen Institute , has said the\nauctions may reap 60-to-80 megahertz of airwaves, compared with\n120 anticipated by the agency. Broadcasters can choose whether\nto sell their airwaves in the voluntary auction. That was no empty threat. In the 18 months before Jobs died\non Oct. 5, Apple sued  HTC Corp. (2498) , Samsung Electronics Co. and\nMotorola Mobility Inc., the three largest Android users. It\nalleged that the phone makers stole Apple\u2019s technology and asked\ncourts to make them stop.  Now, as rulings start coming in, it might be time for a\nd\u00e9tente that helps Apple maximize the value of its patents, said\nKevin Rivette, a managing partner at  3LP Advisors LLC , a firm\nthat advises on intellectual property. When courts side with\nApple and impose bans on infringing products, competitors can\noften devise workarounds; in cases where Apple doesn\u2019t win\nimport restrictions, it would be better off striking settlements\nthat ensure access to a competitor\u2019s innovation, he said.  \u201cA scorched-earth strategy is bad news because it doesn\u2019t\noptimize the value of their patents -- because people will get\naround them,\u201d said Rivette, whose clients include Android\nlicensees. \u201cIt\u2019s like a dam. Using their patents to keep rivals\nout of the market is like putting rocks in a stream. The stream\nis going to find a way around. Wouldn\u2019t it be better to direct\nwhere the water goes?\u201d  Steve Dowling, a spokesman for Cupertino, California-based\nApple, declined to comment for this story.  Early Victories  For a time, Apple\u2019s strategy looked sound. In October, an\nAustralian court banned the sale of Samsung\u2019s Galaxy 10.1 tablet\nin that country, and the U.S. International Trade Commission\nagreed to consider an import ban on sales of certain HTC\ndevices.  Then the tide began to turn. Apple suffered a setback Nov.\n30 when a higher Australian court overturned the ruling against\nSamsung. On Dec. 22, a German judge said he was unlikely to\nuphold an import ban on a version of the Galaxy, which Samsung\nhad modified in response to a ban on the original design.  The ITC gave Apple only a partial victory on Dec. 19 by\nruling that HTC had violated only one of four patents Apple said\nit infringed. The patent covered so-called data detection, a\nfeature that helps users make a call, send an e-mail or find an\naddress on a map with a single keystroke.  Can\u2019t Last?  HTC decided to drop the feature. That\u2019s a significant loss\nfor HTC, since the capability has come to be an expected part of\nusing a smartphone. Still, the ruling reinforced predictions\nthat Apple won\u2019t succeed forever in preventing Android rivals\nfrom selling gadgets with the now-familiar hallmarks of Apple\u2019s\npioneering devices. These include touch screens and app stores.  Legal history isn\u2019t on Apple\u2019s side, said  Marshall Phelps ,\nformer head of intellectual property at  International Business\nMachines Corp. (IBM)  and Microsoft Corp.  \u201cNobody has ever kept competitors out of any market with\npatents,\u201d in part because software can usually be slightly\nchanged to find a non-infringing alternative, he said.  Exceptions, he said, include an IBM patent that\ncharacterized the basic architecture of a computer and Texas\nInstruments Inc.\u2019s original patent for the integrated circuit,\nor computer chip. IBM was ordered by the  U.S. Department of\nJustice  to license its patent, while Texas Instruments decided\nto do the same, which has resulted in billions of dollars in\nroyalties, Phelps said.  Many of Apple\u2019s patents, by contrast, relate to the look\nand feel of devices or particular ways of using a machine,\nrather than a basic technology breakthrough.  Shift Ahead  The question on the minds of many patent lawyers isn\u2019t\nwhether Apple should adapt its legal stance, but when. For now,\nthe company\u2019s approach is costing rivals millions of dollars in\nfees, distracting management and preventing them from emulating\nApple\u2019s products more boldly, said  Ron Epstein , a former\nattorney at  Intel Corp . who now runs patent licensing firm\nEpicenter IP Group.  Apple\u2019s patent portfolio remains strong compared with those\nof rivals, thanks both to the innovations that went into\ngroundbreaking products such as the iPhone and iPad, and to the\neffectiveness of Apple\u2019s legal department in obtaining patents\nfor those innovations, said Christopher Marlett, chairman and\nco-founder of MDB Capital Group, an investment bank that advises\ncompanies on buying and selling patents.  \u201cApple has the patents, the money and the expertise to go\nto war,\u201d Marlett said. \u201cI just don\u2019t see why Apple would seek\nd\u00e9tente, since they\u2019re the clear leader. Until they\u2019re hit with\nan injunction by  Google (GOOG)  or Samsung, they don\u2019t need to get\nserious about licensing.\u201d  Right Back at You  Still, as more companies pour resources into the booming\nmobile-devices market, Apple should eventually cut deals to\nensure access to rivals\u2019 innovations as well, Epstein said.  \u201cHow long can you beat everyone else over the head before\nthey can do the same to me?\u201d he said.  Tim Cook , who took over in August when Jobs announced he\nwould be unable to come back as CEO, has many other ways to take\nadvantage of the company\u2019s patent portfolio. The company could\nprobably collect as much as $10 in royalties for every device\nsold, more than the amount analysts speculate  Microsoft (MSFT)  receives\nfrom Samsung and HTC, which use its mobile technology, said\nRivette at 3LP.  Other Arrangements  With $81 billion in cash and investments, Apple has little\nneed for more. Instead, the company could pursue out-of-court\nsettlements that would help it take on Android in other ways,\nRivette said. The company could offer to drop its more than two\ndozen patent claims against Samsung in exchange for an agreement\nto hold off using Apple technology for six months or a year, he\nsaid. Cook could also try to get price breaks or guarantees that\nwould give it greater access to Samsung parts, Rivette said.  Apple and Samsung also could agree to focus on different\nparts of the market. For example, Apple might make iPad-sized\ndevices while agreeing to stay out of the market for smaller\ndevices with 7-inch displays that could compete with  Amazon (AMZN) .com\nInc.\u2019s new Android-based Fire tablet, Rivette said.  If Apple agreed to let Samsung include Apple\u2019s proprietary\niTunes software in such a device -- an unprecedented and\nunlikely step, he said -- Samsung\u2019s sales would probably\nincrease. That would help slow gains by Amazon, whose push into\nhardware makes it a threat to Apple. (AAPL)   Compared to the previous version of Apple\u2019s OS X software,\nLion -- which overhauled everything from how programs are\nlaunched to how you scroll through a web page -- Mountain Lion\nis an incremental improvement, bringing to the Mac several\nfunctions already familiar to users of the company\u2019s mobile\ndevices.  I\u2019ve been running the new software for a week, both on a\nlaptop borrowed from the company and on an iMac desktop where I\ninstalled it myself. The upgrade, which is available only as a\ndownload from the Mac App Store, costs $20 and allows you to\ninstall it on all your personally owned Macs.  Mountain Lion works on most models released since 2007,\nthough it requires that you already have either Lion or its\npredecessor, Snow Leopard.  The upgrade process took about an hour and a quarter using\na cable modem. It required little input from me and was\naggravation-free. The biggest issue I confronted was the\ntemporary disappearance of an icon for  Google (GOOG) \u2019s Chrome browser,\neasily fixed.  ICloud Integration  The most significant change in Mountain Lion is its\nintegration with iCloud, the free Apple service that\nautomatically stores your data online and lets you easily access\nit from any Apple device.  For instance, using the Documents in the Cloud feature, I\ncreated a file on the Mac using Apple\u2019s Pages word-processing\napplication, pulled it down on an iPad to make a few tweaks,\nthen saw them reflected the next time I came back to the Mac.  At the outset, Documents in the Cloud is limited to Apple\napplications such as Pages and the other components in the\ncompany\u2019s iWorks productivity suite. It will be up to third-\nparty developers, such as  Microsoft (MSFT) , whether they want to adopt\nit for their products too.  Mountain Lion also brings the Messages app, already used on\nthe iPhone, iPad and iPod touch, to the Mac. Messages, which\nreplaces the previous iChat program, allows you to send free,\nunlimited texts to fellow Apple users.  Even better, your conversations are duplicated and kept up\nto date on all your Apple devices, so that, in my case, I was\nable to start a conversation with an iPhone-wielding offspring\nusing the Mac, then seamlessly continue it on an iPad.  Mac Migration  Messages is just one of the applications hatched on the\niPad-iPhone operating system, called iOS, that have now migrated\nto the Mac. Others making the trek include the Game Center hub\nand social network, a new centralized Notification Center that\nslides in and out with a finger swipe, and new apps for notes\nand reminders -- all of them tied together so anything done on\none Apple device is reflected on all Apple devices.  For all the convenience, Apple\u2019s relentless drive to put\nitself at the center of your entire online experience can\nsometimes feel a little overweening.  A good example is the new Gatekeeper feature, designed to\nenhance security by throwing up obstacles to keep you from\nunknowingly installing malicious software.  Programs from the Mac  App Store  or from developers\ncertified by Apple glide through, but for anything else, you\nhave to manually override Gatekeeper and convince Mountain Lion\nyou really, really want to install that software.  Apple\u2019s Approval  Eventually, perhaps, every Mac program will have some sort\nof Apple stamp of approval. After all, the only official source\nfor iPad and iPhone apps is the company\u2019s carefully controlled\nApp Store.  Personal computers, though, have a long tradition of user\nchoice in software. And Gatekeeper\u2019s harping seemed a bit much\nto go through when all I wanted was to install software from\n Verizon (VZ)  to let me use my wireless modem. Even adding an \u201cInstall\nanyway\u201d button to the warning window would have reduced my\nannoyance.  Lest you start to feel completely imprisoned by the Apple-\ncentric ecosystem, though, Mountain Lion includes a few new nods\nin the direction of connecting with the wider world.  Twitter, for example, is now deeply integrated throughout\nthe operating system. Once you log in to your account through\nthe System Preferences setting, you can easily tweet through the\nNotifications Center, as well as a Share button built into many\napplications.  A similar tie with  Facebook (FB)  will be rolled out in an\nupdate, though I was able to check out a pre-release version.\nYou\u2019ll also be able to bring your Facebook friends into your\nContacts address book, and receive activity alerts through the\nNotification Center.  Then there\u2019s AirPlay Mirroring, which allows you to\nwirelessly toss anything from your Mac\u2019s screen onto a high-\ndefinition television equipped with the compact $99 Apple TV\nset-top box.  It sure beats fumbling with a projector and cables if\nyou\u2019re doing, say, a PowerPoint or Keynote presentation. But it\nmakes you dependent on yet another piece of Apple technology.  Which, of course, is precisely the idea.  (Rich Jaroslovsky is a Bloomberg News columnist. The\nopinions expressed are his own.)  Muse highlights include  car  and  book  reviews. They span the decades from millennial  Mark Zuckerberg  to 93-year-old  Karl Albrecht .  This diverse bunch enjoys a unifying characteristic: Most spent the year making more money. Their collective fortunes have soared $200 billion to $2.1 trillion since Bloomberg Markets published its inaugural list in December 2012.  Zuckerberg, the 29-year-old co-founder of Facebook Inc., is not only the youngest billionaire, he\u2019s the biggest gainer, Bloomberg Markets will report in its December Billionaires Issue. Zuckerberg doubled his fortune to $24.5 billion from Jan. 1 to Sept. 30, the day we took a snapshot of Bloomberg\u2019s exclusive daily wealth ranking, the Bloomberg Billionaires Index. (Or see  http:\/\/bloomberg.com\/billionaires .)  Veteran technology icon  Bill Gates , 58, claimed the top spot. Microsoft Corp.\u2019s chairman and co-founder bumped  Carlos Slim , last year\u2019s No. 1, to second richest. Gates\u2019s net worth surged $10.2 billion to $72.9 billion. Slim, who controls America Movil SAB, Latin America\u2019s biggest telecom company, saw his fortune crumble by 12.9 percent to $65.5 billion.  More from the December issue of  Bloomberg Markets : Denis O\u2019Brien , founder of Digicel Group Ltd., falls shy of the top 100 list -- so far. Ireland\u2019s richest native-born citizen, the subject of one of our five profiles of billionaires outside the top 100, has built his $5.4 billion telecom fortune chiefly by entering markets in the Caribbean.  Gambling Bet  Gambling proved a good bet for Asian billionaires. Philippine ports magnate  Enrique Razon  is taking on Galaxy Entertainment Group Ltd. founder  Lui Che Woo , Hong Kong\u2019s third-richest person, after  Li Ka-shing  and  Lee Shau Kee . Razon opened Solaire Resort & Casino in March, the first of four gaming resorts set to rise along Manila Bay.  Siblings J.B. and  Tony Pritzker , who got at least $2.7 billion following the acrimonious breakup of their family\u2019s empire, are investing in private-equity and venture deals.  South African-born  Kerr Neilson , who became rich managing other people\u2019s money, set up a foundation to fund his wife, Judith, in her passion: giving wider exposure to contemporary Chinese art at her gallery.  Some of the more than 80 hidden billionaires Bloomberg News unearthed in 2013 through Sept. 30 also have family ties. Brothers Sergio and  Pier Luigi Loro Piana , who head Italian cashmere clothier Loro Piana SpA, joined the billionaire ranks after agreeing in July to sell 80 percent of their company to No. 14  Bernard Arnault \u2019s LVMH Moet Hennessy Louis Vuitton SA.  Batista Falls  In Kazakhstan, meantime,  Bulat Utemuratov  is trying to avoid the taint of his nation\u2019s reputation as a dubious business destination. In his first lengthy interview with a news organization, Utemuratov tells Bloomberg Markets that he never used his government positions to amass one of Central Asia\u2019s greatest fortunes.  Not all of the superwealthy added to their billions. EBX Group Co. founder  Eike Batista  was once Brazil\u2019s wealthiest man and was No. 28 on Bloomberg\u2019s list last year. He not only fell from the top 100 -- he lost his fortune after his commodities companies imploded.  Crunching Numbers  In calculating a billionaire\u2019s net worth, we valued his or her stakes in publicly traded companies using closing prices of Sept. 30. Valuations of foreign assets were converted to U.S. dollars.  Closely held companies were valued in several ways. We compared the average enterprise value-to-sales; enterprise value-to-earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortization; price-to-book value; or price-to-earnings multiples of similar publicly traded companies. Comparable companies were chosen based on the closely held company\u2019s industry, size and location.  Estimates of company debt were based on the average net debt-to-Ebitda multiple of peers. A liquidity discount of 5 percent was applied to most closely held companies where assets might be hard to sell. Higher liquidity discounts were given to companies for which the structures were more complex. No liquidity discounts were used in calculating public stakes. In some instances, we also applied a country risk discount based on a person\u2019s concentration of assets.  We usually valued real estate by applying average regional occupancy and capitalization rates to the square footage of closely held commercial properties. For personal property, we used its appraisal value. Land was valued using the market price per acre.  Yachts, Planes  Estimates for art, furniture and jewelry were based on their insured value and expert assessments. Yachts, planes and other vehicles were assessed based on market value. Net worth estimates include dividends, proceeds from asset sales and real estate. In cases where most of a fortune comes from closely held companies, estimated dividends are calculated only if historical financial information is available.  We deducted taxes based on personal income, dividend and capital gains rates in a billionaire\u2019s country of residence. Taxes were applied at the highest rate unless there was evidence to support a lower percentage. For estimates of cash and other invested assets, we applied a hybrid market return based on holdings in cash, government bonds, equities and commodities. We attempted to identify and confirm all potential liabilities.  Personal Debt  No assumptions were made about personal debt. Family members often hold a portion of the billionaire\u2019s assets. Such transfers don\u2019t change the nature of who ultimately controls the fortune.  We operate under the rule that all billionaire fortunes are inherently family fortunes. Each billionaire or his or her representative has been given an opportunity to respond to questions regarding the calculation of his or her net worth.  Get your free issue of Bloomberg Markets! That gets depressing when the\nglobal economy is in a sorry state, as it is now.  Most economists gloomily advise us to just tough it out. No\nmagical solution can save us.  I submit that the situation is not as bleak as it seems.\nYes,  Virginia , there is a magical engine for economic growth. It\nis invention -- the process by which the human mind creates new\nideas with practical consequences. Invention is magical because\nthe magnitude of the output can exceed by almost infinite\nmeasure the magnitude of the inputs. A single great idea can\ngenerate enormous transformations, economic and otherwise.  Unlike almost all other forms of human economic activity,\ninventing is not limited by a law of diminishing returns. It\ncomes with no dismal trade-offs.  Invention and its weaker cousin, innovation, are ultimately\nthe source of all wealth and luxuries. In the age of Kindles and\nsmartphones, we are surrounded by obviously invented products.\nBut \u201ctraditional\u201d society, too, was built by the accumulation of\npast inventions. Earth now supports 7 billion humans only\nbecause our ancestors invented agriculture -- and subsequent\ninventors continually improved it century after century. We live\nfar longer and better lives than our great-grandparents did\nbecause clever doctors invented medicines, therapies and public-\nhealth measures. The invention of steel and concrete built our\nworld, and the invention of democracy governs it.  Economic Pulse  The economy of the world is not based on the simple\ninterplay of capital and labor. Sure, these are involved. But\nthey are secondary characteristics, not fundamental ones.\nMacroeconomists are often said to have their fingers on the\npulse of the economy, and that\u2019s an apt analogy. A pulse is a\ndecent secondary indicator of life because blood flow is one\nprerequisite for the body\u2019s survival. But the pulse is a weak\nand incomplete measure of life. A brain-dead patient, after all,\nmay have a pulse even though the person\u2019s life is over.\nConversely, a machine can drive a pulse without giving life.  So while it\u2019s all well and good to measure the flow of\ncapital and the markets for labor, don\u2019t mistake this data for\nthe forces that really drive growth, which are inventions (or,\nif you prefer, ideas) and the ways that they are made real. In\nresponse to these forces, capital is deployed and labor is\nexpended.  Physics is obsessed with conservation laws; mass and energy\ncan be neither created nor destroyed. Economics, on the other\nhand, obsesses about growth and recession, in which economic\nvalue is explicitly created and destroyed. Invention is,\ndirectly or indirectly, a primary source of the value we call\ngrowth.  Yet economists give invention short shrift. That is partly\nbecause they are still hazy about the origin of inventions. I\nfind talking to economists about invention\u2019s role in the economy\na bit like talking to fourth graders about where children come\nfrom. A smart fourth grader can tell you all about how kids\nprogress through elementary school. They can even tell you about\ninfants, and that mommy\u2019s belly gets big before one appears. But\nhow and why the spark of conception occurs may be a mystery.  Economists similarly expend great effort documenting the\ndevelopment of products. A few can tell you what inventions look\nlike in their infancy, but even these experts don\u2019t yet\nunderstand the spark of inventive conception.  Invention is also frequently overlooked where its role is\nsubtle. In some parts of the world, new ideas arrive slowly and\nmainly by importation, but they still have great impact.\nSubsistence farming in  Africa , for example, may not seem to be\nan invention-related activity, but it is. Three key inventions -\n- corn in Mesoamerica; the process of cultivating and\ndetoxifying cassava in  South America ; and pastoral cow herding\nin Central Asia -- feed much of Africa. Those inventions were\nimported and adapted long ago, and African subsistence farmers\ncouldn\u2019t survive today without them.  Power of Invention  Moreover, that the poorer parts of the world have adopted\nso few new ideas isn\u2019t just a symptom of the economic problems\nthere -- it is the root cause.  It\u2019s interesting to look back at 19th-century America to\nsee the transformative power of invention. Back then, the U.S.\nwas considered a lawless, developing country of subsistence\nfarmers. Early in the century, the country became embroiled in\nwar with the greatest power of the time, and half a century\nlater it got tangled up in a brutal civil war. American\ngovernment could be deeply corrupt (think of Tammany Hall in  New\nYork City ), and its state of development ranged crazily from\nEuropean-influenced  Manhattan  to the anarchic Wild West. Alexis de\nTocqueville, who toured America at the time, shook his head at\nhorrible urban slums, sweatshop child labor, slavery and\npersecution (or worse) of the indigenous population.  At its best, America in the 19th century was like  Brazil \ntoday, although in many ways Brazil is far more civil and\nsophisticated. At its worst, 19th-century America was the heart\nof darkness.  And yet it was during this time that the U.S. became the\nworld\u2019s greatest inventing nation. Samuel Morse helped create the\ntelegraph; Eli Whitney, the cotton gin; and Thomas Edison, the light\nbulb, phonograph and movies.  Europe  remained the center of\nlearning, culture, technology and industrial prowess, but within\nseveral generations, Europe found itself relying on the U.S. for\nhigh-tech inventions.  Talented inventors the world over flocked to the new hotbed\nof creativity -- Alexander Graham Bell from  Canada , Nikola Tesla and Charles\nSteinmetz from Europe, among many others. It was a stunning\ntransformation. Imagine Brazil suddenly becoming the world\u2019s\nleading source of new technology, and you get the idea.  If inventing is the driver of economic growth, then it\nfollows that those regions fostering the creation and\nexploitation of new inventions will enjoy prosperity. The poster\nchild for this phenomenon is Silicon Valley, where academic and\ncommercial inventors, assisted by venture capitalists and other\nsupporting players, nurture the most dynamic environment in the\nworld for generating businesses.  Silicon Valley  What we now call Silicon Valley had origins as inauspicious\nas those of the U.S. more broadly. A sleepy agricultural area\nwith no industrial or business base worth mentioning, its most\nnotable asset was a university set up by Leland Stanford, a 19th-\ncentury robber baron. And even that wasn\u2019t unique: public\nuniversities grace every state, and private universities dot the\nlandscape, yet none has fostered an invention engine like\nSilicon Valley.  So, why did this area, and America more broadly, succeed in\ncreating invention-friendly climates when others failed? The\nsecret remains maddeningly elusive. The track record of other\nplaces that have tried to set up their own versions of Silicon\nValley -- and there are many -- is poor. Policy makers have\npulled all the levers they have, from lower tax rates to\nfavorable zoning laws to research-and-development support, but\nnone of these really sparks invention. These incentives may\nattract big companies, startups and  venture capital , all of\nwhich are ingredients in an invention-based ecosystem, but\nthey\u2019re not sufficient to stimulate the magic.  I\u2019d like to report that someone has figured out a formula\nfor harnessing the power of invention. Alas, that is not the\ncase. If someone can, it would be, in many respects, one of the\nmost important inventions in history because it would allow us\nto craft the economy we want.  ( Nathan Myhrvold , the former chief strategist and chief\ntechnology officer at Microsoft Corp. and the founder and chief\nexecutive officer of\u00a0 Intellectual Ventures , is a Bloomberg View\ncolumnist. The opinions expressed are his own.) Today\u2019s newest and brightest example is a distributed philanthropic movement\ncalled  GivingTuesday . I\u2019ve seen the\nunderlying trend firsthand as an advisor to General Electric Co.\u2019s Innovation\nAccelerator, an initiative led by GE\u2019s Chief Marketing Officer Beth Comstock in\nwhich GE convenes partners in academia, venture capital, business\nentrepreneurship, social entrepreneurship, branding and social media. They're\ndiscussing megatrends, such as Big Data, the future of MRI imaging, or how to\nbuild out  ecoimagination  into to\nnew sustainability partnerships across sectors. Obama Administration officials describe a similar transition, manifested\nin their recent decision to preserve the social media arm from the 2012\ncampaign, as well as the recent national \u201clistening tour\u201d with potential\npartners and collaborators led by White House Chief Technology Officer\u00a0Todd Park. Increasingly,\nadministration officials\u00a0view the White House as a platform for convening power, rather than a monolith that hands down executive orders and speeches from upon high, including\u00a0Jonathan Greenblatt, special assistant to the\nPresident and director of the Office of Social Innovation and Civic\nParticipation in the Domestic Policy Council, and Alec Ross, senior advisor for innovation to Secretary of State Hillary Clinton. This is just the\nbeginning. The era of the command-and-control organization is over, at least\nfor now. Its replacement is still taking shape. Companies like Cisco Systems Inc., GE and Genentech Inc.\u00a0and are out in front, trying to restructure their\nlegacy hierarchies into more collaborative networked organizations. It\u2019s a messy\nand inefficient process. Also, witness\nthe U.S. Army\u2019s attempts to modernize its archaic structure, which, as Thomas\nRicks\u2019 has documented in his latest book,  The\nGenerals , has not gone well. Change is indeed hard -- but critical to\ncapitalize on pervasive change in technology and society. New kinds of\norganizations are emerging where effective social entrepreneurship meets the\nnetworked effects of technology. My favorite case study of the moment is\nGivingTuesday, which describes itself as a \u201cnational day of giving at the start\nof the annual holiday season.\u201d What started just a few months ago as a small\nsocial media campaign has blossomed into a networked philanthropy that claims  2,000 partners  across\nall 50 states. They include well-known social causes like  Kiva  and  DonorsChoose.org ; companies, such as JC Penney and\nMicrosoft; small nonprofits and charities, such as the Case Foundation and the\nOtsego County (New York) United Way; and local governments, including Atlanta.\n(Disclosure: I\u2019ve been advising and supporting the founding team personally for\nsome time now; my company,  the BLKSHP ,\nis a partner organization.) The idea is simple.\nInstead of starting the giving season with shopping on Black Friday or Cyber\nMonday, people are encouraged to start on GivingTuesday with philanthropy.\nCo-founder Henry Timms, deputy executive director of New York\u2019s 92nd Street\nYMHA ( 92Y ), contrasts Black Friday shopping\nand GivingTuesday philanthropy: \u201cWe have two days that are good for the\neconomy. Here's a new day good for the soul.\" American culture\nseems primed for this message, especially in the wake of superstorm Sandy. The\nway that GivingTuesday has proliferated has been quite remarkable to me. It\ncame to life at the 92Y, in partnership with the United Nations Foundation, and\nthen spread quickly across real and virtual social networks, attracting more\norganizations and people into its sway. I\u2019ve watched with great admiration and\nexcitement as the idea has developed into a movement. How did it happen?\nDistributed leadership. We\u2019re living in a tribal society. The Web\u2019s nimble,\nnetworked structure allows organizations to tap vast, hive-like relationship\nclusters. Once a novel idea emerges, like GivingTuesday, and large institutions\nidentify them and sign on to it, as JPMorgan Chase & Co.\u00a0or the Salvation Army has,\nthen a constellation of smaller non-profits or charities will follow suit.\nBefore you know it, a movement is born. This is not unlike the way traditional\nconsumer behavior often unfolds, as early adopters scale up toward mainstream\nadoption. The combination of\ntechnology savvy, such as  Mashable\u2019s  and  Facebook\u2019s , and\npublic-service organizations, like the 92Y and the U.N. Foundation, can open\nnew pathways for civic activity, allowing like-minded business leaders, social\nentrepreneurs, activists, technologists, opinion-makers and bloggers to follow\nsuit. GivingTuesday portends big things for the future of citizen-focused,\nempathic, bottom-up social change in the government sector and society at\nlarge. The movement is\nreinventing how a simple, good idea can reshape networks online and off. The\nrevolution will be improvised. Peter Sims  is founder & a\n\u2018sir\u2019 of the BLKSHP, cofounder of the social venture Fuse Corps, and his latest\nbook is  Little Bets: How\nBreakthrough Ideas Emerge from Small Discoveries. Nearly four decades after\n Microsoft  was founded, it has finally delivered its first full-\nfledged, honest-to-God personal computer.  And it\u2019s all right, with an innovative if occasionally\nimpractical design, solid construction and a bright, beautiful\nscreen that fulfills the company\u2019s stated goal of providing a\nshowcase for its Windows 8 operating system.  It\u2019s just that the Surface Pro, which goes on sale Feb. 9,\nwants to be more. With its tablet form factor, detachable\nkeyboard and touch screen, it wants to be an iPad too. And it\njust isn\u2019t.  Sure it has flash memory, like an iPad, and a store where\nyou can choose and download applications, like an iPad.  But it\u2019s heavier, slower -- it takes about three seconds to\nwake from sleep -- and doesn\u2019t have nearly the battery life.\nEven its mini-brick power adapter screams \u201cPC.\u201d  Both in design and use, the Pro resembles the Surface RT\ncomputer Microsoft released late last year: same size screen\n(10.6 inches) and same kickstand design so you can prop it up on\na desktop or airline tray (but not your lap).  The screen, though, is almost twice the resolution of the\nRT\u2019s. It\u2019s also ever so slightly thicker, and weighs about 2\npounds to the RT\u2019s 1.5 pounds.  Price, Storage  The biggest differences are price and the amount of\nsoftware available for it.  The Pro starts at $899 for a model with four gigabytes of\nmemory and 64 gigabytes of storage. That\u2019s $300 more than the\ncheapest 32-gigabyte RT and $200 more than a 64 GB iPad.  The RT, which uses the kind of microprocessor found in\nmobile devices, can\u2019t run any of the millions of programs\nwritten for previous versions of Windows. No Microsoft Outlook,\nno  Adobe  Photoshop, no  Intuit  TurboTax.  The Pro, by contrast, is built around an  Intel  Core i5\n\u201cIvy Bridge\u201d chip, the same sort found in more traditional PCs\n(and  Apple \u2019s Macs, for that matter). I installed fully-featured\nversions of the Microsoft Office productivity suite, including\nOutlook and the Access database, as well as the  Verizon  Wireless\nsoftware needed to run a Pantech 4G LTE wireless modem.  PC Performance  All performed exactly as they would on any other PC, as did\nthe modem itself when plugged into the Surface Pro\u2019s single USB\n3.0 port. (A second USB port, thoughtfully included on the power\nadapter, allows for recharging mobile devices.)  The biggest drawback is the limited amount of space\navailable for your programs and data, especially when you\nsubtract the amount used by Windows 8 itself. A more usable 128-\ngigabyte model costs $999, $200 more than Apple\u2019s just-\nintroduced 128 GB iPad.  As with little-brother RT, you\u2019ll almost certainly need one\nof Microsoft\u2019s combination cover-keyboards. They\u2019re sold\nseparately and aren\u2019t cheap: $120 for the Touch Cover, which has\npressure-sensitive keys, and $130 for the Type Cover, with\nphysical keys that actually move.  With a little practice, I could type faster on the Touch\nCover than I could straight onto the glass. But I vastly\npreferred the Type Cover, where I could pound away at much the\nsame speed as on a standard laptop.  Still, the keyboard is cramped, and there isn\u2019t a clear\nenough demarcation between the halves of the track pad, which\nmeant I was often left-clicking when I meant to right-click.  Jumpy Cursor  I noticed other quirks as well. Using the Type Cover, I\nfound that the cursor would sometimes inexplicably jump to\nanother spot. And the screen was often slow to reorient itself\nfrom portrait to landscape mode, even though I had snapped on\nthe keyboard and was ready to begin working.  Microsoft says I may have caused the jumpiness by\ninadvertently brushing the track pad, though I don\u2019t think I\ndid, and that the orientation problem is a known Windows 8\nissue.  As part of its I\u2019m-a-tablet-too effort, the Surface Pro\nincludes a pen, as do  Samsung \u2019s Galaxy Note products. But unlike\nSamsung, Microsoft doesn\u2019t give you a dedicated place to store\nit. When the Surface isn\u2019t charging, the pen magnetically snaps\ninto place where the power connector normally attaches. But when\nyou need to recharge the Surface, you\u2019ll have to find somewhere\nelse. (It does have a pocket clip; nerd pack not included.)  Microsoft says it has improved the magnetic connector from\nthe RT, but I still found myself frequently fumbling with it.\nAnd the battery life isn\u2019t great. I was sometimes able to coax\nas much as six hours on a charge -- long enough to survive a\ncross-country flight, but far short of the iPad\u2019s nine-to-10-\nhour life.  If there\u2019s any Apple product the Surface Pro could take on,\nperhaps it\u2019s the $999 MacBook Air. But an iPad? No way. At best,\nthe Surface Pro is a second Windows PC in an era where having\ntwo PCs is less and less common.  ( Rich Jaroslovsky  is a Bloomberg News columnist. The\nopinions expressed are his own.) He and Egon Durban, his financial partner at  Silver Lake  Management LLC, which co-sponsored the LBO, had agreed to increase their offer by 13 cents a share. Shareholders would get $24.9 billion, or $13.88 a share, for a stock that was trading lower than $9 before Dell announced his bid. The board would escape criticism that it had folded before the iconic CEO. And Dell would get to keep his company -- and a shot at redemption.  Failed Deal  \u201cMichael might have lost the board if the deal failed,\u201d said Jimmy Lee, the longtime chief of  investment banking  at  JPMorgan Chase & Co. (JPM)  who advised the special committee with Kurt Simon, head of technology, media and telecommunications. Lee had earlier warned Dell: \u201cPeople you thought were with you will be against you.\u201d  A representative of the board\u2019s special committee declined to comment.  With the deal\u2019s official closing yesterday, Dell will now embark on one of the most challenging buyouts in history as he tries to accelerate a four-year effort to turn the struggling Round Rock, Texas, PC maker into a supplier of all the hardware, software and services needed to run Internet data centers. With revenue of $57 billion, Dell is the largest company ever to be taken private based on sales, according to data compiled by Bloomberg. By size of the deal, the LBO is the 10th-biggest, data from market researcher Preqin show.  Revered Wunderkind  If he succeeds, Dell could complete one of the most unlikely personal makeovers in business history. A decade ago, he was gracing magazine covers, the revered wunderkind whose direct-sales model made Dell the best-performing stock of the roaring 1990s. Now, as the buyout unfolded over the past year, he had to overcome a frustrated  board  preparing to appoint a strong second-in-command over his objection, a bid by buyout firm  Blackstone Group LP (BX)  that may not have included him, and a potential proxy fight by billionaire investor  Carl Icahn  to install a new board that would have replaced him.  There were plenty of other obstacles. Dell\u2019s board demanded six price increases before even agreeing to put the proposal to a shareholder vote. To try to drum up a better deal, the board then hired another bank that talked to 72 potential bidders during a lengthy \u201cgo-shop\u201d period. Twice, the CEO had to accept a discount on his shares in the company to increase the offer while Silver Lake refused to budge, and once had to sit by as Durban got into a nose-to-nose screaming match with Jimmy Lee.  Unknown World  \u201cThis is a guy from Austin who founded his own technology company and now he is on  Wall Street  trying to buy it out and he is entering an unknown world,\u201d Lee, 61, said.  \u201cIt\u2019s like going into a haunted house,\u201d he said, \u201cand every time you go around a corner some ghost pops up, and then a witch flies down on a broom, and then you go into another room and some devil tries to stab you with a pitchfork.\u201d  Lee, who has worked for JPMorgan or its predecessors since around 1975, helped negotiate Comcast Corp.\u2019s acquisition of NBC from GE in 2009, the United-Continental airline merger in 2010 and General Motors Co.\u2019s $23 billion IPO later that year.  The transaction was \u201cmore challenging than I thought,\u201d Dell, who had read almost a dozen books on private equity as he embarked on the LBO, said in an interview. \u201cBut I am a believer that what doesn\u2019t kill you makes you stronger.\u201d  Tennis Match  He has no love lost for Icahn, from whom he received two congratulatory phone calls before and after the shareholder vote approving the deal on Sept. 12.  \u201cIt was like a tennis match where there\u2019s all kind of trash-talking, and then afterwards you\u2019re telling each other \u2018nice backhand\u2019 and \u2018great serve,\u2019\u201d Dell said of his chat with Icahn. \u201cFor Carl, it was all just a game. But it\u2019s not just a game.\u201d  Icahn said the game was rigged. \u201cHe is right this is not a game,\u201d Icahn said. \u201cMichael has set it up in a way that he can\u2019t lose -- and in a game you can lose. The board changed the rules in the middle of the game.\u201d  In all, Dell invested his 15.6 percent stake in the company, valued at about $3.4 billion, and about $500 million of his $15.3 billion fortune, which makes him the world\u2019s 60th-richest person, according to the Bloomberg Billionaires Index. Investors in MSD Capital Corp., Dell\u2019s family office, invested an extra $250 million. Silver Lake and its limited partners invested about $1.35 billion, the firm\u2019s biggest equity check ever.  Veto Power  While his stake in the private company will jump to 75 percent, he made concessions that give Silver Lake control over important management decisions, according to people familiar with the matter. The private equity fund, which will own the remaining 25 percent of the company, can veto any transaction or spending exceeding $500 million, the people said.  Dell\u2019s and Silver Lake\u2019s representatives declined to comment on the veto rule.  In addition, two Silver Lake partners -- Durban and Simon Patterson, who is based in the firm\u2019s London office -- will sit on the newly constituted three-member board.  Dell said he is content with the deal and regards Durban as a friend.  \u201cWe couldn\u2019t do this if we weren\u2019t happy to have dinner together with our wives or to take each other\u2019s calls on the weekend,\u201d Durban said.  Forgo Profits  Their plan is to forgo profits by pumping money into research and development and to expand the company\u2019s sales staff as they seek to become a broader-line supplier of cloud-computing gear to small and medium enterprises.  Rather than retreat from the rapidly shrinking PC business, Dell intends to go on the attack to regain the global market share lead by overtaking Hewlett-Packard Co. and Lenovo Group Ltd., including opening hundreds of retail stores in China, said two people familiar with his plans.  If all goes well, they would take the company public again in five to eight years, according to two advisers who requested anonymity because the time frame isn\u2019t public.  \u201cThe capital structure gives us enormous possibilities to grow in cloud, mobile, Big Data, without thinking about the next quarter,\u201d Dell said. He and Durban declined to comment on their exit plan.  Little Currency  After the LBO, the company will have little currency for acquisitions and other initiatives because the debt load will triple to about $18 billion, said people with direct knowledge of the company\u2019s finances. Dell said he and Silver Lake are ready to inject more equity if needed.  Dell had had his fill of trying to satisfy public shareholders\u2019 more short-term demands by mid-2012, said two advisers who requested anonymity because the information isn\u2019t public.  Two years earlier, he\u2019d succumbed to calls for Dell to focus on profitability over market share by backing away from cheaper PCs -- only to see its stock drop as  revenue faltered .  The first tangible taste of going private came on June 15, 2012, when Southeastern Asset Management Inc., which was Dell\u2019s second-largest shareholder with a stake of about 8 percent, proposed Dell undertake a buyout into which the firm would roll its shares, according to Dell\u2019s proxy filing.  Dell told Southeastern he wasn\u2019t interested after bankers at  Goldman Sachs Group Inc. (GS)  explained to him how complicated the deal would have been. A representative for Southeastern declined to comment, as did Michael Duvally, a spokesman at Goldman Sachs.  Golf Club  Just a few weeks later, on July 17, as Dell was leaving the stage at a Fortune magazine technology conference in Aspen, Colorado, Durban approached him. \u201cLet\u2019s get together in Hawaii,\u201d Durban whispered.  On Aug. 10, the two met at  Kukio , the massive golf club on the Big Island where Dell owns a house also known as the Raptor Residence. Worth about $50 million, it\u2019s one of the most expensive properties in Hawaii, said  Harold Clarke , a local real estate broker. Durban has a home in the neighborhood, too.  In some ways, they make an unlikely pair. Durban, 40, has the tanned, fit look of the runner and golfer that he is. He tends to wear the Silicon Valley uniform of khakis and no tie. People who know him describe him as \u201csmart as hell\u201d and aggressive.  Dell exudes a calmer confidence, still boyish-looking, if now a bit grayer and heftier. Even with his vast wealth, he is invariably described as a humble and unassuming -- many say boring -- family man. Dell and Susan, his wife of 24 years, have four children.  Beach Resort  Durban sketched out the LBO idea as they wandered for two hours through the grounds of the beach resort -- a practice Dell had picked up from walking meetings he\u2019d had with Apple CEO  Steve Jobs  in years past.  \u201cIf I were you, I would consider taking Dell private,\u201d Durban told Dell. \u201cAnd I don\u2019t think you need Silver Lake to do it.\u201d  Dell sought the advice of another Hawaiian neighbor, KKR & Co. co-founder  George Roberts . When Roberts confirmed that a deal might make sense, and that KKR might even make a bid, Dell decided to inform the board of his thinking. Roberts declined to comment for this story.  On the evening of Aug. 14, Dell phoned Alex Mandl, the lead director on Dell\u2019s board in charge of CEO-related issues, to tell him of the LBO plan. Mandl informed the board, and within a few days he was named to head a special committee that would consider the Dell-Silver Lake bid while also trying to drum up other offers.  Due Deference  Relations between Dell and the board weren\u2019t as they once were -- when directors had treated Dell with the deference due a manager once considered in a league with  Henry Ford  and  Jack Welch . For the past two years some directors had asked Dell to sharpen his strategy and to improve the quality of his management team, according to two people close to the board.  Since achieving No. 1 market share in PCs in 2002, Dell hadn\u2019t come up with a follow-up to his first big idea -- selling build-to-order PCs over the phone or online, rather than through retailers. Attempts to diversify beyond PCs, including such consumer devices as music players and smartphones, had foundered. By the time of Dell\u2019s call to Mandl, the management team had missed its own  revenue targets  seven quarters in a row.  Dell paid scant attention to the board\u2019s complaints, the people said, and the board never forced the issue -- until the buyout bid sparked a more aggressive approach.  Outside Firm  As the committee started evaluating Dell\u2019s LBO idea, it took the unusual step in November of hiring an outside firm, the  Boston Consulting Group , to provide a more realistic picture of the company\u2019s health. BCG lowered Dell management\u2019s forecast for PC industry profits by $10 billion over the next four years.  The special committee also became more assertive in demanding an upgrade of Dell\u2019s management team. On Jan. 17, Mandl told Dell that the board would want him to hire a chief operating officer if the buyout wasn\u2019t approved, according to people familiar with the board\u2019s thinking. As the board considered further contingencies, one of the most-discussed options was to fire most of the management team even if it retained Dell himself, those people said.  Dell said he disagreed with the naming of a COO because his management was strong enough.  Tough Stance  As the bidding to take Dell private began, the board took a tough stance. It had initially set $14 a share as its minimum demand, and it rejected lower offers from Dell-Silver Lake and from KKR, which dropped out in December, said people familiar with the matter.  When  Bloomberg News  broke the news on Jan. 14 that Dell was in talks with buyout firms, Dell\u2019s shares jumped 13 percent to $12.29, creating pressure on Dell and Silver Lake to raise the bid. They soon secured a $2 billion loan from  Microsoft Corp. (MSFT)  -- which had an interest in helping  Michael Dell , one of its closest business partners, keep control of his company -- and increased their offer to $12.90 a share.  Not good enough, came the response. As weeks passed, and another sweetened bid was rejected, some Dell board members grew exasperated at the CEO\u2019s refusal to ante up more money. They thought a few hundred million dollars were insignificant compared with his $15 billion fortune, according to people close to the board.  Share Cost  For Dell, it was a question of fairness, meaning he wanted Silver Lake to share the cost of any increase, Lee recalled. While driving in Florida on a weekend break in late January, the banker called Dell to persuade him to fund an increase by taking a discount on his shares.  \u201cI\u2019m not going to do that,\u201d the CEO told Lee.  \u201cI understand that, and I\u2019m sympathetic,\u201d said Lee. \u201cBut if this deal falls apart over 5 or 10 cents you\u2019ll feel good for probably less than a minute, and then you\u2019ll regret it for the rest of your life.\u201d  Dell confirmed Lee\u2019s account.  A few days later, Dell agreed to invest $500 million of his money to push the offer to $13.60. To get Silver Lake to go along with the 35-cent price boost, Dell agreed to let his shares be valued at $13.36, a discount that would increase Silver Lake\u2019s equity stake.  The board remained cool. Dell and Durban came through again with the extra 5 cents the board was demanding, for a $13.65 per-share bid. The board approved their bid unanimously at 11 p.m. on Feb. 4.  Carl Icahn  If Michael Dell thought the tough part was over -- enter Carl Icahn. One of the pre-eminent corporate raiders of the 1980s, the 77-year-old billionaire investor had amassed stakes in companies such as RJR Nabisco Holdings Corp., Texaco Inc. and Time Warner Inc. so as to pressure their boards into making stock-lifting cost-cutting and divestitures.  On March 5, 2013, Icahn notified the board that he had accumulated a large stake and, in the first of his five proposals, demanded that Dell issue debt to fund a $9 per share dividend, or face a proxy fight for control of the board. Later Icahn, who never made a full counterbid, would team up with Southeastern. In January, the Memphis, Tennessee-based asset manager had proposed that Dell take on debt to finance a large dividend rather than to buy the company\u2019s equity, leaving the company public.  They weren\u2019t Dell\u2019s only problem. T. Rowe Price Group Inc., Dell\u2019s third-largest shareholder, announced it would oppose the buyout, an unusual move for an institutional shareholder. And Blackstone Group LP, another large buyout firm, was emerging as by far the most serious bidder yet with a $14.25 a share buyout offer.  Austin Compound  Dell invited Dave Johnson, Dell\u2019s former chief strategy officer now at Blackstone, and Chinh Chu, the co-chairman of Blackstone\u2019s private equity practice, to his 30,000-square-foot Austin compound, where sculptures line the driveway and the grass grows so thick that one visitor compared it to walking on a mattress. Over dinner, Dell said he would prefer to stay on as CEO, yet didn\u2019t rule out supporting a superior proposal that didn\u2019t include him.  Dell had reason to worry that Blackstone wanted him out of the picture. He had been contacted by people who said they had been approached by Blackstone or its advisers about running the company after a buyout.  \u201cA number of guys called to say, \u2018I wanted you to know I wouldn\u2019t take the job,\u2019\u201d Dell recalled.  Issue Moot  The issue became moot on April 18, when Blackstone pulled out of the bidding after market-research firm IDC reported that PC sales had plummeted 14 percent in the first quarter, the steepest slump it had ever recorded.  Christine Anderson , a Blackstone spokeswoman, declined to comment.  The board set July 18 for the shareholder vote. Dell had won the endorsement of Institutional Shareholder Services, an influential voice for institutional investors. Yet big shareholders including BlackRock Inc. still opposed the deal.  At 7 a.m. shareholders began filing into a section of office space at Dell headquarters in Round Rock that had been spruced up with faux white curtains tacked to the walls. While attendees munched on breakfast burritos, tensions were high in an adjoining conference room.  Dell and Durban were unlikely to have enough votes to secure passage. The board had adopted voting rules months earlier that were now coming back to haunt Dell\u2019s bid. The shares of holders who failed to vote would be counted as no votes, and Michael Dell was barred from voting his stake, under the provision. The missing votes had ballooned to 27 percent, twice the amount in typical votes.  Stormed Out  At 8 a.m., Dell board member Mandl opened the meeting, then promptly adjourned it until a week later. When Durban stormed out of the meeting to go to the airport, JPMorgan\u2019s Lee pulled him and Dell into an adjacent conference room.  Lee told Durban that the board might change the voting rules if they offered $14 a share, a price at which he said he believed the deal would get done. That triggered the nose-to-nose faceoff between Lee and Durban, who demanded, among other things, that Lee fire the vote-counting firm that had been surprised by the high number of abstentions.  \u201cDo you think you are talking to a summer intern at Silver Lake?\u201d said Lee, who is vice chairman of JPMorgan Chase. \u201cLook, dude, these are the cards we were dealt, but at this stage that\u2019s not happening, so you better just calm down.\u201d  While Durban and Lee battled, Dell sat silently, head in his hands. Dell confirmed the account.  Price Increase  Durban declined to comment on the confrontation and said he called Lee the day after to start negotiating conditions for a price increase.  The second of the planned shareholder meetings, late on the afternoon of July 24, was also postponed as it was clear the LBO still lacked the necessary votes.  That same day, Dell and Durban agreed to raise the offer by 10 cents to $13.75, declaring it their \u201cbest and final\u201d -- and made it contingent on the board agreeing to change the voting rules.  On July 31, Dell and Duberstein had their phone conversation and the deal was clinched. In exchange for a price increase, Duberstein told him, abstentions would no longer be counted as no ballots, and the record date was changed so that investors holding the stock as of Aug. 13 would be eligible to vote. That was key to getting more yes votes from arbitrage investors.  Final Bid  Two days later, a deal was announced with a special dividend payment of 13 cents to Dell shareholders, bringing the final bid to $13.88. Dell financed the $300 million bump with company cash, people familiar with the matter said, while agreeing to roll his stake into the deal at $12.51. He took another discount from the original $13.36.  The fourth and final shareholder vote was held on Sept. 12 in Round Rock, its passage a foregone conclusion with the new voting rules.  That evening, 150 guests gathered at Michael Dell\u2019s home to celebrate, eating rib barbeque, drinking Lone Star beers and listening to the country-swing band Asleep at the Wheel. Advisers were wearing oversized blue metal pins, given them by Dell, depicting Road Runner, the cartoon character who always outwits his nemesis, Wile E. Coyote. Compliance Policy  Failing Banks\u2019 Derivative Trades May Face EU Write Downs  European Union regulators may write down the value of\noutstanding derivatives contracts issued by banks in crisis as\npart of broader plans to protect taxpayers from having to bail\nout failing lenders.  Bank supervisors should be given power to impose losses on\n\u201cas wide a range of the unsecured liabilities of a failing\ninstitution as possible,\u201d to help cover winding-up costs,\naccording to a draft EU document outlining the plans. This may\ninclude liabilities from \u201cderivatives that are not fully\nsecured by collateral,\u201d as well as unsecured senior bonds,\naccording to the document obtained by Bloomberg News.  Unsecured derivatives \u201cshould, in principle, be within the\nscope of the debt write down powers,\u201d the document said.\nExceptions could apply if imposing losses would have a negative\nimpact on the banking system, adversely affect counterparties or\nharm clearinghouses, according to the EU document.  The European Commission delayed publishing the plans this\nmonth because of concerns the measures may spook investors at a\ntime of market turbulence and that they need more work,\naccording to two people familiar with the situation. The final\nproposals may be released next month.  Derivatives are financial instruments derived from stocks,\nbonds, loans, currencies and commodities, or linked to specific\nevents like changes in  interest rates .  Chantal Hughes, a spokeswoman for  Michel Barnier , the EU\u2019s\nfinancial services chief, declined to immediately comment. IRS Lets Employers Come Clean on Contractor Payroll Taxes  The  Internal Revenue Service  is giving companies that have\nbeen misclassifying employees as independent contractors a\nchance to pay a fraction of back taxes to avoid interest,\npenalties and audits for previous years.  Under the program announced yesterday by IRS Commissioner\nDouglas Shulman, U.S. companies would have to agree to treat the\nworkers as employees going forward and pay 10 percent of the\nprevious year\u2019s payroll taxes. The program is open to employers\nof all sizes, though Shulman said he is trying to encourage\nsmaller businesses to participate.  Worker misclassification is a particularly complex area of\nthe  tax code  without clear rules to guide businesses, Shulman\nsaid. Since 1978, Congress has prohibited the IRS from issuing\ngeneral clarifying regulations.  Employers are responsible for paying part of the  payroll\ntax  as well as paying federal unemployment taxes for their\nworkers. Independent contractors pay both the employee and\nemployer shares of the payroll tax.  Shulman said he didn\u2019t have estimates of how many employers\nwould join the voluntary compliance program or how much money it\nwould generate. The program has no deadline. The encounter marks a shift for the 67-year-old Gruebel,\nbrought in 2 1\/2 years ago to rebuild Zurich-based UBS after\nrecord losses on U.S. subprime mortgage securities led to a\nstate rescue. Gruebel earned the moniker \u201cSaint Ossie\u201d in\nSwitzerland for helping to restore  Credit Suisse Group AG (CSGN) \u2019s\nprofits and reputation in his previous CEO role, and for a\ntrading acumen that included spotting the subprime debacle\nearly. Bank of America Corp. (BAC) ,  JPMorgan Chase & Co. (JPM)  and  Wells Fargo\n& Co. (WFC)  are adding staff, creating easier-to-use technology and\ncompeting on fees in an effort to win more of the  $2.9 trillion \nAmericans held in 401(k)s savings plans as of September from\ntraditional account managers such as  Fidelity Investments  and\nVanguard Group Inc. That number may reach $4 trillion by 2015,\naccording to  Cerulli Associates , a Boston-based research firm.  \u201cIt\u2019s one of the top priorities,\u201d at JPMorgan, said\nMichael Falcon, whose job as head of retirement in the U.S. and\n Canada  for the bank\u2019s asset management unit was created in\nJanuary. The New York-based company is the second-largest U.S.\nlender by assets behind Bank of America.  The competition may mean lower costs and more choices for\nemployers and savers, said Laura Pavlenko Lutton, an editorial\ndirector in the mutual-fund research group at Chicago-based\n Morningstar Inc. (MORN)  Greeting-card seller Hallmark Cards Inc.\nswitched its plan to JPMorgan last year to reduce costs and\nimprove services for employees, said Tresia Franklin, head of\nbenefits and compensation for the Kansas City, Missouri-based\ncompany.  Participants in the  most expensive plans  pay more than 6\npercent annually, while the lowest-cost ones charge less than 10\nbasis points, according to Ryan Alfred, co-founder of San Diego-\nbased  BrightScope , which rates plans. A basis point is 0.01\npercentage point.  Fast-Growing  Over the past two decades, 401(k)s have become the fastest-\ngrowing retirement-savings option for U.S. workers, according to\nthe Washington-based  Employee Benefit Research Institute .\nThey\u2019re the most common type of defined-contribution plan, which\nlets employees defer a portion of their salary into an\ninvestment account and generally not pay taxes on the money\nuntil it\u2019s withdrawn during retirement.  These assets tend to be \u201csticky money,\u201d said David Wray,\nhead of the  Profit Sharing\/401k Council of America , which is\nappealing to banks because of on-going fees and contributions to\nthe accounts. The banks also may get an opportunity to pitch\ntheir proprietary mutual funds as plan investments and sell\nproducts such as individual retirement accounts to workers who\nleave their jobs and want to roll over their money.  Banks may have to overcome the perception that mutual funds\naren\u2019t their expertise, said Morningstar\u2019s Lutton. \u201cTheir main\nbusiness is taking deposits and making loans, and many have\ngotten into the mutual-fund business as a way to grab wallet\nshare of their customers,\u201d she said.  Fund Returns  The average 15-year return of mutual funds including stock,\nbond, alternative and balanced investments from Wells Fargo and\nJPMorgan as of January was about 6 percent, Morningstar data\nshows. That compares with about 7 percent for mutual-fund\nmanagers Fidelity, Vanguard and Baltimore-based T. Rowe Price\nGroup Inc. Bank of America doesn\u2019t offer its own proprietary\nmutual funds, according to spokesman Matt Card.  Banks also will have to compete on investment management\nfees with firms including Vanguard, which pioneered low-cost\nindex investing for individuals. The  Valley Forge , Pennsylvania-\nbased mutual-fund manager charged an average 0.19 percent for\nits target-date funds, according to a 2010 report by\nMorningstar. Target-date funds are the most popular investment\nin 401(k) plans for workers who don\u2019t choose their own lineup.  The 0.62 percent average fee for Wells Fargo\u2019s target-date\nseries was more than three times Vanguard\u2019s cost. Fidelity\u2019s\nexpense ratio was 0.71 percent and JPMorgan\u2019s, 0.85 percent,\naccording to Morningstar.  Held Hostage  \u201cThere are a lot of individuals who are held hostage to a\nbunch of mediocre, or worse, funds,\u201d in their 401(k) plans,\nparticularly among plans that only offer investments from their\nrecordkeeper, said Adam Bold, founder of the Mutual Fund Store,\na registered investment adviser based in  Overland Park ,  Kansas ,\nwith $6.1 billion under management. \u201cOver the last few years\nthere\u2019s been a trend toward more plans giving open platforms,\nwhere investors have more choice,\u201d he said.  The banks\u2019 push for more of workers\u2019 savings may mean less\nrevenue for the top-three 401(k) administrators, Fidelity, Aon\nHewitt and Vanguard, which together had 43 percent of the market\nat the end of 2009, compared with a combined share of less than\n10 percent for Bank of America, JPMorgan and Wells Fargo,\naccording to Cerulli.  \u2018Upping the Ante\u2019  \u201cWe\u2019ve been upping the ante on retirement,\u201d Andy Sieg,\nhead of retirement services for Bank of America Merrill Lynch\nsaid in a January interview at Bloomberg headquarters in  New\nYork . The Charlotte, North Carolina-based bank added about $88\nbillion in 401(k) assets from its 2009 acquisition of Merrill\nLynch, according to Card, the bank spokesman. The bank has been\nbeefing up its retirement-services staff with executives brought\nover from Fidelity and other rivals, including Rich Linton, who\nhad overseen Fidelity\u2019s adviser retirement group and now has a\nsimilar role with Bank of America.  JPMorgan roughly doubled its sales force dedicated to\n retirement plans  in the last year, according to Falcon. Wells\nFargo has been adding new features that allow employers to more\nclosely track the savings and investing behaviors of their\nemployees, said Laurie Nordquist, director of Institutional\nRetirement and Trust for the San Francisco-based bank.  Banks are searching for new ways of making money as losses\non mortgages and regulation on fees have limited their revenue\nsources, said Terry Moore, managing director of the North\nAmerica banking practice for  Accenture Plc (ACN) , a consulting firm\nbased in Dublin.  Interest Income Declines  Interest income for the largest 25 U.S. banks was down 15\npercent in 2010 compared with 2007, Moore said. Regulation\nrequiring consumers to opt in for overdraft checking protection\nwill cost banks an estimated $5.6 billion annually, according to\nPleasanton, California-based Javelin Strategy & Research.  Administrators of 401(k)s are paid for their recordkeeping\nservice, which includes sending out account statements and other\ncommunications to participants. They also may make money from\ninvestment-management fees if their mutual funds are offered in\na plan and through an arrangement with third-party fund\nproviders known as revenue-sharing.  Revenue-sharing, where a mutual-fund company passes some of\nthe fee revenue it earns back to a plan\u2019s recordkeeper, \u201cis a\nwidespread practice,\u201d a January study by the U.S. Government\nAccountability Office found. Compensation can range from 5 basis\npoints to 125 basis points from those arrangements, the study\nfound.  Paying Attention  Employers are paying more attention to fees and investment\nchoices in their 401(k)s than ever before, said Wray of the\nProfit Sharing\/401k Council of America, a Chicago-based\nnonprofit representing employers that offer retirement plans.\nThat scrutiny may allow some banks to win new business if they\noffer lower fees, better investments or both, he said. Bank of\nAmerica, JPMorgan and Wells Fargo would not disclose the average\nfees for plans they serve. The company has\nabout 13,000 workers in its 401(k) plan with $2.4 billion in\nassets, she said.  Employers who sought bids on their 401(k)s in the last year\nwere able to realize average cost savings of 31 percent, said\n Institutional Investment Consulting  Managing Director Michael\nKozemchak, based on the plans his firm works with. Kozemchak,\nbased in Bloomfield Hills, Michigan, works with plan sponsors\nthat are choosing a 401(k) administrator.
