Copyright  GM Didn\u2019t Infringe Rights to Einstein Persona, Judge Says  The use of images of the late  Albert Einstein , \u201ceven in\ntasteless ads,\u201d can\u2019t be barred by invoking copyright law, a\nfederal judge in  Los Angeles  said.  U.S. District Judge A. Howard Matz ruled in a case brought\nby  Hebrew University of Jerusalem  against General Motors Co. The\nschool, which inherited the rights to all of the physicist\u2019s\npapers, copyrights, royalties, publication rights and literary\nproperty, objected to GM\u2019s use of an image of Einstein in an\nadvertisement.  According to court papers, that ad, which ran in one issue\nof \u201cPeople\u201d magazine, was used to promote GM\u2019s 2010 Terrain\nvehicle. The university said the ad, which featured Einstein\u2019s\nface over the body of \u201ca shirtless, muscle-bound underwear\nmodel\u201d and the text \u201cideas are sexy too\u201d infringed its IP\nrights.  The school also claimed that such a use of Einstein\u2019s image\ndenigrated and caused injury to its \u201ccarefully guarded rights\u201d\nto the image of the famous scientist.  The case was filed in California rather than New Jersey,\nwhere Einstein died in April 1955. A New Jersey court said that\na term of life plus 50 years would be appropriate. In\nCalifornia, that right extends for 70 years after the person\u2019s\ndeath.  The university had argued that California law prevails and\nthat, in any case, the term should be 70 years under federal\ncopyright law.  Matz noted that nothing in Einstein\u2019s will specifically\nmentioned any right of publicity and that during his lifetime,\nhe never claimed or received compensation for the use of his\npersonal image.  Matz said it \u201cassumes without deciding\u201d that the school\nhad succeeded in proving that Einstein had intended to transfer\nhis publicity rights along with the rest of his  intellectual\nproperty . California\u2019s 70-year term for publicity rights doesn\u2019t\napply to Einstein because the physicist died in Princeton, New\nJersey, and California\u2019s rights extend only to its residents, he\nsaid.  A maximum 50-year postmortem duration would be \u201clong\nenough for a deceased celebrity\u2019s heirs to take advantage of and\nreap the benefit,\u201d according to the court. The court noted that\nat the time the university acquired Einstein\u2019s rights, the term\nof copyright law was only 50 years postmortem.  Matz decided that 2005 was the last year in which the\nuniversity could sue to enforce any right of publicity related\nto Einstein. Because the case wasn\u2019t filed until 2012, the\nschool isn\u2019t entitled to pursue it further, Matz said, saying\nthere would be no trial.  GM has until Oct. 22 to file a proposed judgment in accord\nwith the court\u2019s ruling.  The case is Hebrew University of Jerusalem v. General\nMotors LLC, 10-cv-03790, U.S. District Court, Central District\nof California (Los Angeles).  Microsoft\u2019s Infringement Filter Targets \u201845\u2019 on Websites  For  Microsoft Corp. In 1990, when he was a Democratic congressman from\n Connecticut  and chairman of the House immigration subcommittee,\nunions complained that U.S. employers were using H-1 visas to\nexploit skilled foreign workers, paying them low wages that\nundercut American job seekers.  So Congress created a new visa, the H-1B, with tighter\nrules. Workers had to have a bachelor\u2019s degree, and employers\nhad to meet wage standards. At the same time, lawmakers roughly\ndoubled the number of green cards available for these desirable\nimmigrants to encourage companies to sponsor them for permanent\nresidency and citizenship.  The transition from guest worker to citizen didn\u2019t go as\nplanned. Paperwork and bureaucratic hurdles made the green cards\nhard to get; it sometimes took years for the government to\napprove applications.  Thousands of green cards went unissued even with a backlog\nof people seeking them. Many employers decided the hassle wasn\u2019t\nworth it.  \u201cWe were fools\u201d to believe that companies would move\ntheir workers from H-1Bs to green cards, says Morrison, now a\nlobbyist for a professional association representing engineers\nand programmers. \u201cThat\u2019s not how it worked out.\u201d  The bipartisan immigration bill the Senate is considering\nthis month is an attempt to fix the problem.  Citizenship Path  While the debate in  Washington  has focused on whether to\ncreate a path to citizenship for low-skilled, undocumented\nworkers, another provision in the legislation has gone largely\nunnoticed: It would make it easier and more desirable for\ncompanies to sponsor highly skilled foreign workers for green\ncards, creating a citizenship path for them, too.  The thinking is that knowledge workers with permanent\nresidency are valuable to the economy because they can more\nfreely switch employers to go where they\u2019re most needed, or\nstart a company of their own, creating jobs for Americans.  Workers brought to the U.S. on H-1Bs are beholden to the\nemployer who hired them. They risk deportation if they quit or\nare fired and can\u2019t find a new H-1B sponsor. This makes them\nsusceptible to exploitation.  The Senate bill adds to the number of employment-based\ngreen cards available and gives incentives to employers to help\ntheir H-1B workers obtain them.  Keeping \u2018Brightest\u2019  \u201cThe  United States  must do a better job of attracting and\nkeeping the world\u2019s best and brightest,\u201d the eight Senate co-sponsors said in a statement.  Yet the legislation -- the biggest attempted overhaul of\nimmigration law since 1986 -- may still leave many foreign\nworkers stranded in H-1B limbo. That\u2019s in large measure because\nof heavy lobbying from the tech industry, which asked for -- and\ngot -- many more H-1Bs.  Microsoft Corp. (MSFT) ,  Google Inc. (GOOG) , and  Facebook Inc. (FB)  each spent\nmore than $2\u00a0million on lobbying in the first three months of\nthe year during the run-up to the bill\u2019s consideration,\naccording to the Washington-based Center for Responsive\nPolitics.  The tech industry urged lawmakers to increase the number of\nH-1B visas. The Senate bill raises the annual cap to 115,000\nfrom 65,000. It can rise over time to 180,000 as long as the\njobless rate in management and professional occupations is below\n4.5\u00a0percent; currently it\u2019s 3.7\u00a0percent.  The tech executives argued that there aren\u2019t enough\nqualified Americans for all the jobs they want to fill.  Microsoft Jobs  Brad Smith , Microsoft\u2019s general counsel, said at a Senate\nhearing in April that the company had 3,300 openings for jobs in\nthe U.S. in core research, engineering, and development -- a 29\npercent increase from a year earlier.  What Smith and other tech lobbyists didn\u2019t say is that an\nincrease in the number of H-1B visas makes things easier for\nthem than an increase in the number of green cards.  More work visas means U.S. companies will be able to\nrecruit the workers they need from abroad, while avoiding having\nto go the extra lengths required to help foreign employees get\nresident status.  \u201cPeople come to this country for permanent jobs,\u201d says\nMorrison. \u201cI have regrets about how the tech industry has\nsteadfastly disdained green cards in favor of the H-1B\nprogram.\u201d  Labor unions have failed to persuade Congress that making\nmore visas available would just provide Silicon Valley with\ncheap bodies.  Salary Drop  Hal Salzman, a professor at  Rutgers University , says the\naverage salary of a programmer in the U.S. fell slightly, to\n$70,589 in 2012 from $71,762 in 1999. If the profitable tech\nindustry needs more workers, he argues, it should simply raise\npay instead of turning to foreign labor.  Unions and the Institute of Electrical and Electronics\nEngineers, for which Morrison lobbies, say that H-1Bs can be\nhired on the cheap, dragging down compensation for U.S. workers.  Studies that have tried to determine whether this is true\nhave produced conflicting results.  Many of the complaints involve foreign outsourcing\ncompanies that provide services for American customers. They\nincreasingly operate in the U.S. using workers from abroad.  In February,  Tata Consultancy Services Ltd. (TCS)  of  India , an\n information technology  outsourcing firm, agreed to pay $29\nmillion to settle a class-action lawsuit by Indian workers who\nsaid they were forced to give the company their U.S. tax\nrefunds.  Texas Inquiry  A grand jury in  Texas  is looking into charges that another\nIndian firm, Infosys, asked some of its U.S.-based employees to\nfalsify documents to evade the limit on the number of workers it\ncould bring from India on H-1Bs.  Tata spokesman Michael McCabe says the company settled to\nend costly litigation and \u201cbelieves that it always acted\nappropriately.\u201d  Infosys spokeswoman Danielle D\u2019Angelo says \u201cwe take our\nobligations seriously\u201d to ensure that employees obey the law.  The extra visas that tech companies got in the new bill\ncome at a price. To prevent exploitation of employees on H-1Bs -\n- and the undercutting of Americans who compete with them for\njobs -- current law requires that the foreign workers be paid\nthe \u201cprevailing wage\u201d -- that is, whatever the going rate is\nfor their job.  Seek Americans  The Senate legislation takes that a step further. It\nrequires all U.S. companies to show they tried to find Americans\nto fill  openings  before turning to foreigners.  The rules are tighter for companies designated as \u201cH-1B\ndependent,\u201d a group that includes not only the likes of Tata\nand Infosys but also Facebook.  They must pay at the top end of the prevailing wage range\nand offer jobs first to any equally qualified Americans, not\njust look for them. The intention is to make H-1Bs just\nunattractive enough that employers won\u2019t reflexively look\noverseas to fill jobs.  The Senate bill has one more coercive trick up its sleeve.\nIn what\u2019s called the \u201cFacebook loophole,\u201d companies with lots\nof H-1B employees can get around the rule requiring them to\nprove they tried to hire Americans -- if they sponsor at least\n90\u00a0percent of their H-1B workers for green cards.  The loophole has the twin effect of making it harder for\nforeign outsourcing companies in the U.S. to operate exclusively\nwith non-American workers, while nudging U.S. employers to help\nthe best minds from overseas make the U.S. their permanent home.  Of course, that was the idea in 1990, too.  \u201cOnce again,\u201d says Morrison, \u201cthe experiment is being\nrun.\u201d  To contact the reporters on this story:\nPeter Coy in  New York  at \n pcoy3@bloomberg.net ;\nElizabeth Dwoskin in Washington at \n edwoskin@bloomberg.net   To contact the editors responsible for this story:\nRobin Meszoly at \n rmeszoly@bloomberg.net ;\nWes Kosova at \n wkosova@bloomberg.net","path":".\/2008_2012_msft_bloomberg_news\/green-cards-for-best-brains-from-abroad-goal-of-senate-measure.txt"},{"id":29812021,"title":"Tango Video-Chat Service for Smartphones Said to Be Valued at $160 Million","released_at":"<date>June 17 2011<\/date> <time>04:01:00<\/time>","content":"Tango , a service that lets users\nmake video calls from their smartphones, received about $30\nmillion in a round of funding that values the startup at $160\nmillion, two people with knowledge of the matter said. That\u2019s a fair price.\u201d  Wang\u2019s attitude springs from a labor-market squeeze across the country after China\u2019s pool of young workers  shrank  by almost 33 million in five years at the same time as industry added 30 million jobs. The resulting wage pressure means Foxconn,  Apple Inc.\u2019s (AAPL)  biggest supplier, pays the same basic salary at the Zhengzhou plant it built in 2010 among the corn and peanut fields of  Henan province , as it does in Shenzhen, the southern city that spawned the nation\u2019s industrial boom.  \u201cChina\u2019s advantage in low-cost manufacturing will end much sooner than expected, I believe within five years,\u201d said Shen Jianguang, Hong Kong-based chief economist at Mizuho Securities Asia Ltd. \u201cWages are rising faster inland than on the coast. The number employed in  industry  rose to 147 million from 117 million in the five years through September.  Inland Wages  The labor squeeze means wage costs inland are fast catching up with the industrial belt in the south and east. Average  factory pay  in Henan, about 800 kilometers (500 miles) from the coast, rose 110 percent in the past five years and gained 84 percent in Chongqing, 1,700 kilometers up the  Yangtze River . In the same period, salaries rose 78 percent in  Shanghai  on the east coast and 77 percent in Shenzhen\u2019s province of  Guangdong (CHAWMAGD) .  \u201cThe wage differential between inland and coastal regions is down by more than half since 2006,\u201d said Jitendra Waral, a Bloomberg Industries analyst in  Hong Kong . In Wuhan, the capital of Hubei province, Japanese automakers Nissan Motor Co. and Honda Motor Co. pay a basic wage of $333 a month, compared to $352 in Guangzhou and $317 in Shenzhen, according to an April 2012 report by the Japan External Trade Organization.  \u2018Tipping Point\u2019  The gap between manufacturing costs in the U.S. and China has almost halved in the past eight years and will fall to 16 percent this year, according to  Hackett Group Inc. , a Miami- based consulting company. That\u2019s a \u201ctipping point\u201d that will prompt some companies to shift factories back to the U.S. or to destinations nearer consumers, says Hackett, which lists customers including Pfizer Inc., Microsoft Corp. and Boeing Co. on its website.  Nations including Vietnam,  Cambodia  and Bangladesh already are reaping gains. Vietnam\u2019s foreign  investment  increased more than threefold to $7.4 billion in 2011 from five years earlier, according to the United Nations Conference on Trade and Development. Compliance Policy  Basel Becomes Babel as Conflicting Rules Undermine Bank Safety  The  first Basel agreement  on global banking regulation,\nadopted in 1988, was 30 pages long and relied on simple\narithmetic. The latest update, known as Basel III, runs to 509\npages and includes 78 calculus equations.  The complexity is emblematic of what happened during the\npast four years as governments that injected $600 billion to\nrescue failing banks during the worst financial crisis since the\nGreat Depression devised ways to make the global banking system\nsafer. Those efforts have been stymied by conflicting laws,\ndivergent accounting standards and clashing rules adopted by\nnations to protect their interests, all of which have created\nnew risks.  While higher capital requirements, curbs on banks trading\nwith their own money and other rules have reduced risk, they\nhave magnified the complexity of supervision, according to two\ndozen regulators, bankers and analysts interviewed by Bloomberg\nNews.  Risk has been reduced by a complex web of rules. Twenty-\nseven nations represented on the  Basel Committee on Banking\nSupervision  agreed in 2010 to require banks to hold more\ncapital, or shareholders\u2019 money, to absorb losses. Dozens of\ncountries including the U.S. have issued other regulations or\npassed laws to curtail risk, and lenders on both continents have\nboosted capital and improved its quality since the crisis.  Trading of most derivatives, an opaque  $639 trillion\nmarket , is being forced onto central clearinghouses, where\ntransactions are backed by collateral. The Volcker rule, part of\nthe 2010 Dodd-Frank Act, the U.K.\u2019s proposed Vickers rule and a\nEuropean Union version named for Bank of Finland Governor Erkki\nLiikanen seek to separate riskier trading from other businesses.\nSeven nations have created resolution mechanisms for an orderly\nshutdown of their biggest lenders if they fail, according to the\nBasel, Switzerland-based Financial Stability Board.  Still, the global financial system remains vulnerable. Only\n11 of the more than 100 nations that vowed to adopt the latest\nBasel rules met a Jan. 1 deadline to start implementation. The\nU.S. and the EU, each of which drafted  700-page proposals , are\nstill debating them, while banks work within their nations on\ncapital standards.  For more, click here. The Commodity Futures Trading Commission and other\nregulators need to complete swap rules to allow \u201cfederal\ndepository institutions to make well-informed determinations\nconcerning business restructurings that may be necessary,\u201d the\nOCC said in the notice. The so-called push-out provision of\nDodd-Frank requires that equity, some commodity and non-cleared\ncredit derivatives be moved -- or pushed out -- into separate\naffiliates without federal assistance.  In February, the U.S. House Financial Services Committee\napproved with bipartisan support legislation that would let\nbanks keep commodity and equity derivatives in federally insured\nunits by removing part of the push-out rule.  The OCC is prepared to \u201cconsider favorably\u201d requests for\ntransition, the regulator said in the six-page notice. The\nagency said delays could be extended for a third year based on\nconsultations with other regulators.  For more, click here. Those words alone seem to tell the story: Newsweek was a phenomenally successful product designed for a world that no longer exists. It was an amazing world for journalists, to hear the great Clift describe it. But it couldn\u2019t survive the new financial realities. In the Washington Post last week, my friend Tim Lee argued that we shouldn\u2019t mourn the old world; we should celebrate a vibrantly competitive market. Newspapers made so much money in the late 20th century, he points out, because they effectively had a monopoly on most local markets (ironically, because competition for television and radio meant that most markets could support only one newspaper). That allowed them to charge a lot for ads and spend a lot on reporters. Those days are over,  he says , precisely because there are now so many ways to get news: I think Tim is right about one thing: The last 10 years have been an extremely exciting time to be a digital journalist, because we can do so much more. Policy journalism is better than ever, because reporters can easily access data and research that would have been difficult and time-consuming to track down even in the 1990s. Digital has also allowed us to develop narrow and deep niches, instead of pitching our writing to the proverbial old lady in Dubuque. Economics and finance blogs assume a level of background comfort with technical terms and concepts that would have been impossible in the days of print for anyone except trade publications -- something I am vividly reminded of every time I write a magazine feature. (\u201cNo one wants to read this,\u201d said the editor who excised 1,000 words on the intricacies of calculating confidence intervals for small samples. I protested. He responded with a raised eyebrow, which brought me to my senses. But I bet if I\u2019d put it on the Web, I would have gotten at least 50 comments, proving that some people -- however few and brave -- do want to read that sort of thing.) And Tim is right that this is all to the good, however much print journalists dislike the haste of digital journalism. But he is wrong to say that this flowering of competition is the reason that so many news media outlets are in trouble. Or rather, he\u2019s right about the competition, but wrong about the source. The competition does not come from other news producers; it comes from other people selling ads. And most of those companies are not in the business of producing news. The accompanying is a nice chart of ad spending in 2011, lifted from  this presentation  by Microsoft Advertising. Over the next few years, they expect newspaper ad spending to decline by 7.1 percent and spending on magazine ads to decline by 8.1 percent, while digital rises 27 percent. Yet who will be getting those dollars? According to  eMarketer.com , the answer is \u201cbig technology companies.\u201d Google Inc., Yahoo! Inc., Facebook Inc., AOL Inc. and Microsoft Inc. took in almost two-thirds of U.S. digital ad spending in 2012. And the New York Post  reports  that Google and Facebook account for basically all of the growth in digital ad revenue; without them, according to an analyst at Pivotal Research, web ad revenue grew just 1 percent last year, even slower than our slow economy. The problem for newspapers and magazines and websites is not that other people are in the news business. The problem is that in the days of print, a newspaper or a magazine controlled a valuable distribution channel -- its printing presses and delivery vans. People would pay a lot of money to use that distribution channel to spread news about their products and services. They owned \u201cthe pipes,\u201d as we used to call them, back in my brief summer internship as a technology investment banker. But now the cable company owns the pipes. All the media companies have is the news. And that was never a very good business to be in -- which is why it was getting subsidized by advertising copy about Chevrolets and GE stoves. In some sense, Facebook and Google are \u201cpipes\u201d -- at least as long as they\u2019re dominant, they can sell a lot of ads, because they are the mechanism by which we access information. And data services such as those provided by Bloomberg LP and Thomson Reuters Corp. are pipes, because they control proprietary software. But Bloomberg and Reuters are in a somewhat unusual position: They make money because they sell people information that they can use to make money. That information has a short half-life; you can copyright a story, but you cannot copyright facts, so once information has appeared on a market data service, it propagates pretty quickly. Given the speed at which the markets move today, that really doesn\u2019t matter for market data services. By the time you have rewritten their story and posted it online, the financial value of that information has already fallen to zero. But that\u2019s not the business that newspapers or magazines were in -- at least, not since the 1960s. They were in the business of giving ordinary people news. That worked as long as they could also sell those eyeballs to advertisers. That\u2019s getting harder and harder, because the Washington Post is no longer a pipe. Newsweek is no longer a pipe. They produce the stuff that travels down the pipes. And because the people who actually control the pipes are not willing to pay them for the content, that makes it pretty hard to monetize.  And it\u2019s getting harder all the time. Ten years ago, there was a plausible story where great news media brands transferred their advertising to the web and still got paid almost as much. That story is no longer believable, partly because of the ad inventory glut that Tim mentions, but mostly because people no longer access stories the way we thought they would. Instead of turning print Washington Post readers into digital Washington Post readers, we\u2019ve turned them into consumers of stories that they find via Google and Facebook and Twitter. Saturday night, I was at an event with a bunch of bloggers and Web journalists. We started talking about the demise of Google Reader, and I turned out to be one of the few people who still uses an RSS reader every day. They figure they\u2019ll get what they need off Twitter and Facebook. I defended the usefulness of RSS, but it felt a bit like the old doctor in the period movie arguing that horseless carriages will never catch on. So now two layers of pipes are between us and our readers. Each layer takes away some of our ability to get revenue. We can\u2019t get readers to pay us for the product, and we lose leverage with advertisers. So even as more people than ever are reading stories from the New York Times, less revenue exists to support reporting those stories. Fitful attempts to raise a paywall have stanched some of the bleeding, but they don\u2019t alter the underlying terrible economics. Question: Why does nytimes.com allow me to read stories for free if I come in via Google? Answer: Because search is too important a component of their traffic to cut off. And there you have the underlying paradox of the news business: Google is selling ads against content that the New York Times provides to it for free. Those ad sales hurt the New York Times's ad sales. But the Times cannot afford to cut off Google, because then it will lose the pitiful amount of ad revenue it collects from all the eyeballs that Google sends them. It\u2019s like the mordant old economist\u2019s joke: \u201cWe\u2019re losing money on every unit -- but we\u2019ll make it up in volume!\u201d If the problem was competition from other news providers, it would be self-correcting (as Tim notes): Eventually, the market would shake out, and the winners would have enough money to live on. Maybe the market wouldn\u2019t be ideal -- maybe it wouldn\u2019t be able to support the kind of deep, careful reporting that wins prizes, or have reporters spending months sitting around waiting for the president to do something. But that\u2019s not the problem. The problem is competition from people who are not in the news business. Microsoft completely overhauled its flagship operating system to make it more appealing to users amid a shift to mobile, touch-based computing. Still, Windows 8 has failed to reignite the ailing personal-computer market, where shipments plummeted by their largest margin on record in the latest quarter, according to market-research firm IDC. While Microsoft said it\u2019s planning to update Windows 8 to address customer feedback, updates won\u2019t quickly turn the PC industry around.  \u201cThe changes will help some but there are some serious challenges that the PC industry is facing that I\u2019m not sure can be easily fixed,\u201d said Bob O\u2019Donnell, an analyst at IDC who is based in San Mateo,  California . Larson-Green will begin talking about Blue\u2019s features in the next several weeks and offer more detail on what the company has decided to do in response to customer demands to restore design features such as the Windows Start button and Start menu, Reller said.  \u201cThe learning curve for Windows 8 is real and we need to address that,\u201d Reller said. While the Blue upgrade will restore the Start button, it won\u2019t restore the menu, Verge  reported  last month.  Design Overhaul  Microsoft heavily promoted Windows 8\u2019s design overhaul, which features a start screen with colored tiles that represent programs, websites and contacts, featuring automatically updated information. Some customers testing the new software before it was released in October did complain about the removal of the iconic Start button, Larson-Green said in an October interview. The design changes were aimed at consumers who are increasingly checking e-mail, browsing the Web and watching television and movies on tablets. Led by  Apple Inc. (AAPL)  and  Cisco Systems Inc. (CSCO) , technology companies in the Standard & Poor\u2019s 500 Index distributed $10.8 billion in dividends in the most recent quarter, up from $5.1 billion in the same period in 2010. They paid a record $11.9 billion in dividends in the previous quarter, according to data compiled by Bloomberg.  Their average dividend yield, a metric for measuring payments in the past 12 months as a percentage of market value, stands at 1.21 percent for technology companies, the first time it has exceeded 1 percent in at least 15 years, the data show.  Apple, Cisco,  Dell Inc. (DELL)  and their peers have a total of $590 billion of cash on hand, up from $508.5 billion a year ago and $436.5 billion two years ago, according to data compiled by Bloomberg. Dividend payouts are likely to keep rising as once-cash-strapped startups become larger, slower-growth companies -- a shift that may raise expectations that holdouts such as Google Inc. will follow suit, said  Jennifer Koski , a finance professor at the  University of Washington  in  Seattle .  \u201cThese companies are now grownups,\u201d Koski said. \u201cThey are more developed in their life cycle, they are profitable and they don\u2019t need as much in terms of capital.\u201d  The cash reserve numbers are likely to be even larger when technology companies start reporting quarterly earnings, with  Intel (INTC)  Corp., Microsoft Corp. and Google announcing results next week. Apple\u2019s report will follow on July 23.  Per Company  The average per-company payout for hardware and software makers has reached $154.9 million, compared with $151.1 million for all companies in the S&P 500, according to data compiled by Bloomberg. That\u2019s a shift from years past, when technology firms traditionally avoided dividends out of concern that they signaled a slowdown in innovation and growth, said  Barry James , president of James Investment Research Inc. The firm oversees about $3.5 billion, including shares of Microsoft, which initiated a dividend in 2003.  \u201cIt takes off some of the growth luster,\u201d James said.  Apple for years held its ground, with late co-founder  Steve Jobs  spurning investor requests for a dividend before he handed the reins to  Tim Cook , who became chief executive officer in August 2011. In March 2012, Apple unveiled its first dividend in 17 years, heeding investors who had been clamoring for a bigger slice of the company\u2019s cash pile, which at the time had swelled to almost $100 billion, bolstered by demand for iPhones and iPads.  Apple\u2019s Boost  That wasn\u2019t enough for some investors, as the Cupertino, California-based company continued to rake in money, boosting its cash hoard to $137.1 billion at the end of last year. Investors, led by hedge-fund manager  David Einhorn  of Greenlight Capital Inc., lobbied Cook to return more money as Apple\u2019s stock price languished.  In April, the company unveiled a plan to add $55 billion to its dividend and buyback plan, for a total of $100 billion. The announcements came the same day Apple reported its first profit drop in a decade, and were followed in May by a congressional hearing at which senators accused the company of using loopholes and offshore entities to avoid paying some U.S. taxes.  Investor Rewards  The industry\u2019s dividends are rewarding firms such as BlackRock Inc., Vanguard Group Inc. and State Street Corp., which are the largest  shareholders  in both Apple and Cisco.  The rising payouts also make technology firms more attractive to value investors, or those who are looking for stable and steady returns, a shift for an industry that has long been a favorite of hedge-fund managers and investors looking for fast gains, Koski said.  Still, technology companies\u2019 payouts remain a drop in the bucket compared with the cash they generate each quarter. The industry produced $57.4 billion in cash flows in the first quarter, excluding dividend payments, according to the data. There have only been three other quarters since 2001 where that cash figure was higher.  The new wave of payouts will increase pressure on those technology companies with big balance sheets that don\u2019t pay a dividend, James said. Of the 70 companies classified by the  S&P 500  as technology, 36 pay dividends, according to data compiled by Bloomberg.  Microsoft, Intel, International Business Machines Corp. and  Oracle Corp. (ORCL)  are among the technology companies that have paid dividends since before 2010 and have steadily increased the payments.  Google, owner of the world\u2019s largest Internet search engine, doesn\u2019t pay a dividend, even though it has $51.6 billion of cash and investments. (GOOG)  went public in\n2004,  its founders declared  that the search-engine leader wasn\u2019t\na conventional company and didn\u2019t intend to become one. This\nmaverick attitude has defined Google ever since, especially in\nits hot-and-cold relations with the world\u2019s governments.  Regulators constantly find some aspect of Google\u2019s business\nthat demands attention. There are bogus advertisers to be shut\ndown and offensive YouTube videos to be challenged. The Federal Trade Commission has embarked on a wide probe\nof Google, looking for antitrust violations. The agency is\nadopting the time-honored way of dealing with market dominators,\ngoing back to the meatpackers and steel companies of the 1920s.  The protracted rituals of antitrust, however, were built\nfor a world in which monopolists stymied innovation, jacked up\nprices, stifled competition and arm-twisted customers into\nbuying extra goods or services they didn\u2019t need. Antitrust Cudgel  Complaints about Google overstepping its right to treat\nothers\u2019 data as public-domain material may carry more weight.\nHere, though, the antitrust cudgel is an ill-suited fix. The\ndecade-long pace of many antitrust cases makes it impossible to\ncure problems as they unfold. What\u2019s more, the classic trust-\nbusters\u2019 remedies -- forcing divestitures or asking Google to\noperate under a consent decree -- seem more anticompetitive than\nthe supposed problems they might cure. Do we want the U.S.\ngovernment constantly fiddling with Google\u2019s algorithms?  Fortunately, better approaches are at hand. In highly\ntechnical fields, such as health care or engineering, regulators\nroutinely convene expert panels to help make specialized\njudgments or set industrywide standards. Google, its critics and\nthe FTC should sign on to a similar, binding approach. Doing so\nwould let them negotiate contentious issues calmly and\nefficiently. Other thorny matters, such as how to allocate\nInternet domain names, have been resolved by forming\n international, multiparty rule-setters .  Privacy Concerns  The ultimate answers on licensing, copyright and privacy\nmay require legislation some day. In the meantime, face-to-face\nnegotiation is bound to be more efficient than a drawn-out\nantitrust suit. An example: In March, the FTC announced a well-\ncrafted resolution of privacy concerns regarding Google\u2019s Buzz\nsocial-networking service, barely a year after lawmakers and\nadvocacy groups asked the agency to investigate.  The FTC\u2019s rightful role in watching Google may be more as a\nconvener of working groups on specific Internet business issues\nthan as an old-fashioned trust-buster. That\u2019s less exciting than\ntrying to gear up for a big antitrust case. But a tighter focus\navoids debacles like the  13-year government probe  of\nInternational Business Machines Corp., which ended in a big\n\u201cnever mind\u201d in 1982. That inquiry became a litigation time\ncapsule -- trapped in debating an outdated set of facts while\nthe information economy kept rolling forward.  Read more  Bloomberg View editorials . Three Mile Island, Chernobyl,\nFukushima. First the accident, then the predictable allegations\nin the postmortem: The design was flawed. Inspections were\ninadequate. Lines of defense crumbled, and reliable backups\nproved unreliable. Planners lacked the imagination or willpower\nto prepare for the worst.  There\u2019s a way to break out of this pattern. Nuclear power\nplants will never be completely safe, but they can be made far\nsafer than they are today.  The key is humility. The next generation of plants must be\nbuilt to work with nature, and human nature, rather than against\nthem, Bloomberg Businessweek reports in its March 28 edition.\nThey must be safe by design, so that even if everything goes\nwrong, the outcome won\u2019t be disaster.  In the language of the nuclear industry, they must be\n\u201cwalkaway safe,\u201d meaning that even if all power is lost and\nthe coolant leaks and the operators flee the scene, there will\nbe no meltdown of the core, no fire in the spent fuel rods, and\nno bursts of radioactive steam into the atmosphere.  For inspiration, consider the manhole. If manholes were\nsquare, a cover that got jounced around by a passing vehicle\ncould fall diagonally through the open hole. That\u2019s why manholes\naren\u2019t square--they\u2019re round, because no matter how you rotate a\nround cover, it can never fall through a round hole. The\nsolution is brilliant in its simplicity, and cheaper than hiring\narmies of inspectors to go around making sure square covers are\ncorrectly aligned on square holes.  Manhole Wisdom  The beginnings of manhole wisdom are incorporated into\nnuclear power plants under construction in China,  India , and\nprobably soon in the U.S.  The plants use \u201cpassive\u201d safety features, a label that\nsounds underwhelming until you consider its implications.\nPassive means that the reactor\u2019s safety doesn\u2019t depend on active\ninterventions, such as operators flipping the correct switches\nor sensors and actuators working properly. The safety depends,\nrather, on physics.  The new Westinghouse AP1000 (the AP stands for Advanced\nPassive), for example, has a huge emergency water reservoir\nabove the reactor vessel that\u2019s held back by valves.  If the cooling system fails, the valves open and a highly\nreliable force takes over: gravity. Water pours down to cool the\noutside of the containment vessel. Then another highly reliable\nforce, convection, kicks in. As the water turns to steam, it\nrises. Then it cools under the roof, turns back into a liquid,\nand pours down again.  Three Days  Westinghouse estimates that the pool contains enough water\nto last three days, after which pumps operated by diesel\ngenerators are supposed to kick in and add water from an on-site\nlake.  This isn\u2019t an idea on the drawing board. Westinghouse,\nowned by  Toshiba Corp. (6502) , is about halfway to completion of one of\nthe plants at Sanmen in China\u2019s Zhejiang province. It\u2019s supposed\nto go online in 2013.  At the Vogtle plant in Georgia, excavation and non-safety-\nrelated construction has begun for two AP1000 reactors. Southern\nCo., the largest utility in the U.S. by market capitalization,\nhas 1,400 workers on the site and is expecting a combined\nconstruction and operating license for them later this year.  France\u2019s  Areva SA (CEI)  and a venture between  General Electric\nCo. (GE)  and  Hitachi Ltd. (6501)  are among groups lined up behind\nWestinghouse in getting Nuclear Regulatory Commission\ncertification for their own safer designs.  Obama Call  Critics continue to argue that there will never be a truly\nsafe nuclear power plant, and it\u2019s true: Any time you split\natoms, there\u2019s risk. But nuclear plants have one thing going for\nthem that hasn\u2019t changed since the leak at Fukushima. They\ngenerate badly needed electricity without creating  greenhouse\ngases  that cause global warming.  In his State of the Union address in January, U.S.\nPresident  Barack Obama  called for \u201cbuilding a new generation of\nsafe, clean nuclear power plants in this country.\u201d  In his fiscal 2012 budget request in February, Obama asked\nfor $36 billion in government-backed loan guarantees for new\nnuclear reactors. Obama also asked for $125 million for what the\nEnergy Department calls Generation IV nuclear reactors that the\ndepartment said \u201cwill feature advances in safety and\nreliability to improve public confidence in nuclear energy while\nproviding enhanced investment protection for plant owners.\u201d  Nuclear power faces all sorts of challenges, including the\nmultibillion-dollar construction cost of each new plant.\nFukushima is a reminder that making the plants simpler and safer\nis the biggest challenge of all.  Ax Man  In late 1942, Enrico Fermi, the Italian physicist who was\none of the key figures in the development of the atomic bomb,\ncame up with nuclear power\u2019s first safety mechanism: a man with\nan ax. In case of a runaway reaction, he decided, the ax man\u2019s\njob was to cut a rope, dropping cadmium rods that would absorb\nneutrons and halt the reaction.  \u201cThe ax man received his hand-signaled instructions from\nFermi, who stressed the speed necessary by holding one hand flat\nand depicting a chopping motion with the other,\u201d recalled Edwin\nBlackburn, a millwright who was on the scene, in an Oak Ridge\nNational Laboratory publication.  The ax man\u2019s skills were never needed, but in the decades\nthat followed, nuclear energy suffered a series of stigmatizing\naccidents.  Light Water  One reason for that is the almost total reliance on one\nparticular design, the light water reactor, which has some\ninherent problems. The light water\u2019s prominence dates to a\nfateful 1950s choice by Admiral Hyman Rickover, father of the\nnuclear Navy.  Rickover decided that the first nuclear submarine, the USS\nNautilus, which was launched in 1955, would be powered by solid\nuranium oxide and would use water as both a coolant and a\nmoderator. (A coolant carries heat from the reactor to produce\npower; a moderator slows down the neutrons emitted by the fuel\nso they have a better chance of interacting with other fissile\nmaterials to keep the reaction going. There\u2019s no requirement\nthat water perform either of those functions, but that\u2019s the way\nlight water reactors work.)  Rickover went with the design because it was likely to be\nready soonest and because it produced plutonium-239, a bomb-\nmaking material, as a byproduct. It has some big drawbacks, as\nexplained by physicist Robert Hargraves and nuclear engineer\nRalph Moir in a 2010 article in the American Scientist.  Damaged Rods  The bundles of fuel rods are quickly damaged by heat and\nradiation. Short-lived byproducts such as xenon-135, which\npoisons the fission process, are tricky to manage--and\ncontributed to the instability that led to the Chernobyl\nexplosion. Long-lived byproducts are abundant and highly toxic.\nThe water is corrosive and radioactive. To raise its boiling\npoint, it must be pressurized to 150 times atmospheric pressure.\nThat necessitates a costly network of vessels, pipes, and\nvalves--and raises the risk of an explosive release of\nradioactive steam to the atmosphere. Overall, the design is the\nprecise opposite of passive safety.  Rickover\u2019s choice had lasting consequences. The first\ncommercial nuclear power plant in Shippingport, Pennslyvania,\nused a design similar to that of the Nautilus, setting a pattern\nthat endures to today.  Solid Fuel  \u201cMaddeningly,\u201d write Hargraves and Moir, \u201chistorical,\ntechnological, and regulatory reasons conspire to make it hugely\ndifficult to diverge from our current path of solid-fuel,\nuranium-based plants.\u201d  New reactors such as the Westinghouse AP1000 and Areva\u2019s\nEPR don\u2019t diverge from Rickover\u2019s path. They too have the solid-\nfuel cores and high-pressure water cooling systems. But they are\nsubstantially safer than older light water reactors.  Areva says its EPR has four redundant safety systems\ninstead of the two or three found on most current reactors.\nWestinghouse says the AP1000 is 100 times as safe as current\nplants.  Those claims, while subject to debate, are not mere\ncorporate puffery. They\u2019re based on engineering analyses that\nhave been reviewed by the  Nuclear Regulatory Commission  as part\nof the plant certification. The Energy Department is also\nsupporting development of small \u201cplug-and-play\u201d modular\nreactors such as the 125-megawatt mPower design from  Babcock &\nWilcox Co. (BWC)  and Bechtel Group.  The case for these new, safer plants doesn\u2019t come through\nclearly because their existence conflicts with the agendas of\nboth pro- and anti-nuclear organizations.  Older Designs  Utilities and manufacturers don\u2019t want to imply that the\nolder designs now in service are unsafe. In fact, Westinghouse\npoints out in its marketing materials for the AP1000 that even\nthe older reactors are twice as safe as the NRC requires.  \u201cThe plants we\u2019re operating now are extremely safe as\nwell,\u201d says Beth Thomas, spokeswoman for  Southern Co. (SO)   Nuclear opponents have even less reason to point out safety\nadvances.  \u201cMy shortest answer is that we shouldn\u2019t build more\nnuclear plants,\u201d says Charles Perrow, a retired Yale University\nsociology professor who wrote extensively about the partial\nmeltdown in 1979 at Three Mile Island nuclear power plant near\nHarrisburg, Pennsylvania. \u201cThere\u2019s no way to make any system\nfree of a disaster.\u201d  If worse comes to worst, as it so often seems to, the\nsafety systems that give the most confidence are the passive\nones.  The  International Atomic Energy Agency  has created an\nelegant hierarchy of these passive systems. The ones at the\nhighest level, Category A, require no signal inputs, no external\npower sources or forces, no moving mechanical parts, and no\nmoving working fluid. Example: really thick concrete walls.\nWestinghouse\u2019s reservoir above the AP1000\u2019s containment vessel,\nclever as it is, doesn\u2019t fit into Category A because it involves\nmoving fluids and valves.  Bigger Departure  Generation IV reactors will be a much bigger departure.\nMany will do away with water, using elements such as helium or\nliquid sodium as a coolant. Most also get rid of solid uranium-\n235 as a fuel, relying instead on different uranium isotopes, or\nliquid uranium mixtures, or even thorium as the primary fuel.  The profusion of creativity in nuclear design recalls the\nearly days of the automobile, when the Stanley Steam Car\ncoexisted with the Columbia electric buggy and internal\ncombustion engines running on gasoline and diesel.  The comparison with cars goes deeper. Just as electric\nvehicles are staging a minor comeback after their early demise,\nsome long-since-rejected concepts for nuclear energy are getting\na second look as the faults of the incumbent technology become\nclearer.  New Design  The only requirement is that somehow a nuclear chain\nreaction must occur: A fissile material absorbs a neutron and\nsplits, releasing energy and more neutrons that carry the\nprocess on. There are probably 1,000 conceivable combinations of\nthe basic choices, an Oak Ridge official once calculated.  The new design that\u2019s closest to commercial electricity\ngeneration is the pebble bed reactor, which has been under\ndevelopment for decades in Germany, then  South Africa , and now\n China  and the U.S.  Its uranium fuel is encased in more than 300,000 tennis-\nball-sized \u201cpebbles,\u201d each one containing thousands of tiny\ngraphite-coated fuel seeds, like a metal pomegranate. The\nradioactive fission products are absorbed in the coatings, and\nthe fuel doesn\u2019t get hot enough to melt down even if the plant\nloses all its cooling for days.  China Closest  China is closest to commercializing the pebble bed, pushing\nforward where the South Africans left off for financial reasons.\n Tsinghua University , working with Massachusetts Institute of\nTechnology, already has a 10-megawatt experimental reactor in\noperation. It is building a 200-megawatt plant in Shidaowan in\nShandong province with a unit of China Huaneng Group, the\nnation\u2019s largest power group.  The Energy Department is leading a U.S. initiative, based\nat Idaho National Laboratory in Idaho Falls, called the Next\nGeneration Nuclear Plant. It, too, may be a pebble bed design.  Energy Secretary Steven Chu has appointed a review\ncommittee to decide later this year whether to move on to the\nsecond phase of the project, which could lead to an operating\npebble bed plant in the U.S. by around 2025, says David A.\nPetti, director of the Very High Temperature Reactor Technology\nDevelopment Office at Idaho National Laboratory.  Scale Up  Pebble bed reactors don\u2019t scale up well. Above 600\nmegawatts they lose their safety advantage over reactors with\nordinary fuel rods, says Petti. At that scale the pebbles can\nget so hot that they can\u2019t shed heat fast enough and can melt\ndown just like any other uranium fuel, releasing radioactivity.  The sweet spot for pebble bed reactors is 250 to 600\nmegawatts, Petti says. He envisions them being located next to\nindustrial plants, where their excess energy could be used to\nheat facilities and produce petrochemicals.  Liquid fuels are getting another look, too. As early as\n1944, Fermi tested the world\u2019s first liquid-fuel reactor in\nChicago. It used uranium sulfate dissolved in water.  In 1965, Oak Ridge National Laboratory in Tennessee\nachieved criticality with a reactor using a more advanced liquid\nfuel: molten fluoride salt with uranium dissolved in it. The\nexperiment ran for five years, then stopped when the money ran\nout. Now, scientists in India, France, and the U.S. are\nexperimenting with another variety: liquid fluoride thorium\nreactors (known as \u201clifters\u201d).  Perhaps the farthest-out design comes from a spinoff of\n Intellectual Ventures , a company headed by former Microsoft\nCorp. chief scientist  Nathan Myhrvold  and funded in part by\nMicrosoft co-founder  Bill Gates .  \u2018Massive Power\u2019  TerraPower LLC, as the spinoff is known, used massive\ncomputing power to design a reactor that could run for decades\non an isotope of uranium that is today considered waste.  The concept, first proposed in the 1950s, is to set up a\nslow-moving wave in which neutrons transmute inert, nonfissile\nfuel such as uranium-238 into fissile isotopes such as\nplutonium-239 that can split and throw off energy.  TerraPower says its spent fuel would not be useful for\nmaking weapons. The company, chaired by Gates, has been seeking\na production partner and a host country. So far, no takers.  Wave Reactor  Technological breakthroughs such as the traveling wave\nreactor are part of the answer to nuclear safety, but not the\nanswer in its entirety. Better management is crucial as well.  For many people, the most disturbing thing about the\nFukushima disaster is that it occurred in a nation renowned for\nquality control.  Japan  invented poka-yoke, a design approach\nthat is supposed to remove the possibility of doing things the\nwrong way. (It means mistake-proof. Round manhole covers are\npoka-yoke in spirit.)  The trouble with poka-yoke is that it lends itself mainly\nto preventing day-to-day types of mistakes, not strategic\nerrors. On that score, Japanese regulators and officials of\nTokyo Electric Power Co. (known as Tepco) appear to have\nunderestimated the risk that a huge tsunami would overwhelm\nFukushima\u2019s defenses.  Katsuhiko Ishibashi, Japan\u2019s leading seismologist and an\nadviser to the government, warned in 2007 of what he called\ngenpatsu-shinsai -- meaning a quake-caused meltdown.  The oldest of the six reactors on the site was recently\ngiven a 10-year license extension in spite of regulators\u2019\nfindings of inadequate management maintenance and Tepco\u2019s spotty\nhistory of compliance with regulation. (In 2003, regulators\nforced it to suspend operations briefly at 10 reactors after\nevidence emerged that it had falsified inspection records.)  Made Safe  In fairness to Tepco, no system can be made safe against\nevery risk.  \u201cIt\u2019s a very difficult question,\u201d says Tepco spokesman\nHiro Hasegawa. \u201cMaybe we should have prepared for the worst,\nworst, worst, worst, worst. But we can\u2019t do anything if we\nconsider every risk.\u201d  Hasegawa says the utility did reinforce the Fukushima Dai-\nIchi reactors after the 2007 quakes. And he says the 2003 tussle\nwith regulators was caused in part by their overstrictness about\na hairline crack in one key part.  There\u2019s nothing particularly Japanese about what went wrong\nat Fukushima. It\u2019s natural to minimize the risk of catastrophic\nevents when you have no clear idea about how to deal with them,\nsays J. Edward Russo, a management professor at Cornell\nUniversity\u2019s Johnson Graduate School of Management.  \u201cIt\u2019s human nature to want to lower the probability of a\nparticular disaster. They say, \u2018We can\u2019t plan for and pay for\neverything, so let\u2019s knock that off the list.\u2019\u2009\u201d  Homer Simpson  Homer Simpson, the ultimate everyman-nuclear technician,\nwould approve.  To be truly safe, the reactors of the future will have to\nwithstand the worst that the Homer Simpsons of the world can\nthrow at them.  Remember the cynical adage: Whoever invented the term\n\u201cfoolproof\u201d underestimated the ingenuity of fools. Actually,\nit\u2019s worse than that. In a genuine emergency, even calm,\nseasoned pros can make terrible decisions.  At Three Mile Island, operators refused to believe a dial\nthat told them the reactor was boiling dry, preferring to trust\nanother dial that was giving a different (and incorrect)\ninterpretation, says Perrow, the Yale sociologist, who studied\nthe accident in a 1984 book called Normal Accidents.  That\u2019s where passive safety comes in.  The ideal system is one that\u2019s inherently stable, like a\nball at the bottom of a bowl. However it\u2019s shaken, the ball\ntends to roll back to the bottom.  An inherently unstable system is the opposite, like a ball\nbalanced on top of another ball. In some special cases, such as\nfighter aircraft, inherent instability is an asset.  Fighter Jets  Fighter jets are built to perform incredible dogfighting\nmaneuvers, but the price for achieving that airborne\nmaneuverability is radical instability: The onboard computer\nmust send adjustment signals as many as 40 times a second to the\nengines and various wing surfaces to keep the plane flying true.  A nuclear plant should be like a ball in a bowl, not a jet\nfighter. In other words, stable and safe.  For future plants, safety can be designed in as a basic\nfeature. Not so easy for existing plants, some of which may be\nwith us for decades to come. For them, the solution is\nretrofitting where possible, greater vigilance, and creative\nthinking about what might go wrong.  A \u201cpremortem\u201d might help. Gary Klein, a consultant to the\nAir Force Research Laboratory, advises institutions that deal\nwith risk to analyze a failure before it even occurs.  \u2018Clever Enough\u2019  Often, Klein says, planners will underestimate dangers by\nassuming they will be clever enough to surmount any difficulty\nthat arises. Klein, who is senior scientist of MacroCognition in\nYellow Springs, Ohio, removes that overconfidence bias in\nsessions with clients by asking participants to assume that a\nterrible accident, however unlikely, has already occurred. The\nchallenge is to explain how it happened.  \u201cYou show you\u2019re smart by trying to identify things that\nare plausible and worrisome,\u201d says Klein. \u201cIt almost gets into\na competition.\u201d  To say nuclear power can be made much safer is not to say\nit can be made safe enough. That\u2019s a political judgment, not a\nquestion for nuclear engineers.  If Japan\u2019s radiation nightmare continues to worsen, the\noutcry against nukes will be hard to ignore.  Some are already calling nuclear energy dead. Although\nthat\u2019s premature,  NRG Energy Inc. (NRG)  said on Mar. 21 that it was\nslowing work at its South Texas nuclear plant expansion because\nof possible regulatory changes stemming from the Fukushima\ndisaster. Those plants are based on evolutionary, Generation\nIII+ designs.  Generation 4  On the other hand, Chinese executives confirmed on Mar. 22\nthat they are going ahead with building their Generation 4\npebble bed reactor.  \u201cJapan\u2019s Fukushima plant was using old technology while\nChinese reactors are more advanced,\u201d Cui Shaozhang, deputy\ngeneral manager at Huaneng Nuclear Power Development, told\nBloomberg News.  Those are the two faces of the nuclear debate. Fukushima\ncould bring reactor development to a halt. Or it might stimulate\nthe demand for safer designs. The future of atomic energy is at\nstake. Shanker, a graduate of the Indian Institute of Technology, a top engineering school, is praying for an H-1B visa to enter the U.S. He needs all the divine intervention he can get, because he\u2019s not just vying with other software engineers for the high-skill work permits. His other rivals? Fashion models.  An oversight by Congress two decades ago led to the inclusion of models in the H-1B class. A 2007 bill to put them in another category -- and let their numbers soar -- failed. Its sponsor: then-Representative Anthony Weiner of  New York , who quit Congress in 2011 after engaging in lewd online behavior.  While models will get fewer than 1 percent of the non-immigration H-1Bs, the employer-sponsored temporary work permits are increasingly coveted. Demand was so high this year that the government\u2019s cap on applications was reached only five days after the filing period opened on April 1.  \u201cIt\u2019s the one exception that we all scratch our heads about,\u201d Neil Ruiz, an analyst at the  Brookings Institution \u2019s Metropolitan Policy Program, said of the addition of models as the only H-1B category that requires no bachelor\u2019s degree.  Immigration Debate  As Congress again debates a plan to steer more skilled foreign workers to the U.S., it\u2019s likely to leave intact the provision allowing fashion models to compete for permits. Revisions being considered in the Senate would raise the basic H-1B visa cap to 110,000 from 65,000 permits and increase fees on employers who depend heavily on the foreign workers. Senator  Charles Schumer , a New York Democrat co-sponsoring a bipartisan proposal, declined comment.  Fashion models are almost twice as likely to get their visas as computer programmers, by one rough measure. There were 478 initial applications made for fashion models in 2010, according to U.S. Labor Department data compiled by Bloomberg. The U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services  approved 250 visas  for models. More than 325,000 H-1B petitions were filed for computer-related occupations; about 90,800 visas were distributed to foreign information-technology workers, including immigrants whose visas were being renewed or changed, and those who worked for higher education or nonprofit institutions that weren\u2019t counted against the H-1B cap.  Higher Education  More than 99 percent of H-1B applicants had earned a bachelor\u2019s degree or higher. Slightly more than half the H-1B models had no high school diploma, Ruiz said. Still, the average salary for an H-1B model was $161,000, almost three times the U.S. median household income, he said.  The Washington-based research organization found that New York was the most commonly sought destination for H-1B models, with 68 percent of applications originating from potential employers in the city. More than one in four H-1B models came from Brazil, Brookings found.  The inclusion of fashion models into the visa category that allows at least 65,000 scientists, engineers and other highly skilled foreign workers to work in the U.S. has its roots in a 1990 revision of  immigration law  that created separate classes of visas for performers, athletes, Nobel Prize laureates and religious workers.  After Congress passed the revision, former Representative Bruce Morrison, a Connecticut Democrat who led the House immigration panel, said lawmakers realized they hadn\u2019t put fashion models in a separate category or moved them to a special class reserved for performers and athletes.  Weiner\u2019s Bill  \u201cIt just wasn\u2019t something anybody talked to us about,\u201d said Morrison, currently working as an immigration lawyer and lobbyist.  Fashion models were placed into the H-1B visa category under a 1991 technical amendment sponsored by the late Senator  Edward Kennedy . Sixteen years later, Weiner sponsored a bill to put models in the category for performers and athletes and allow as many as 1,000 to work in the U.S.  \u201cThe only question that we are trying to assess out here with this bill is whether or not people who come in for a day or two at a time to do a photo shoot and then want to go back, whether we should facilitate that type of commerce,\u201d Weiner said during a 2008 hearing on the bill.  U.S. Representative John Conyers Jr., a Michigan Democrat who led the panel that considered Weiner\u2019s bill, said the addition of fashion models in the same category as highly skilled technical workers had \u201cincreasingly caused real problems\u201d as demand for  H-1B visas  began outstripping supply. Even after a 20-3 committee vote in favor of the Weiner bill, the legislation stalled.  \u2018Ugly American\u2019  Representative Steve King, an Iowa Republican, derided the legislation as \u201cThe Ugly American Bill.\u201d  Weiner, who is considering a run for mayor of New York, didn\u2019t return calls left through an aide.  \u201cThey viewed it as frivolous, something about pretty girls,\u201d Morrison said of the bill. \u201cBut it\u2019s important, a big business.\u201d  Foreign models such as England\u2019s  Kate Moss  and Brazil\u2019s Gisele Bundchen are among the public faces of a global fashion industry that generated revenue exceeding $1.3 trillion in 2008, according to  a 2009 study  by the Datamonitor Group, a London-based market-research firm.  In New York,  an annual fashion week  event has an economic impact of $865 million, according to the city. More than 170,000 people, about one in 20 of New York\u2019s workforce, are employed in the fashion industry, according to the mayor\u2019s office.  Modest Pay  Even so, most U.S. models don\u2019t see many of the benefits. The typical model in 2009 earned $27,330, with the average magazine shoot paying about $100 daily, said Ashley Mears, a former model and Boston University sociologist.  The Ford Modeling Agency, owned by Altpoint Capital Partners LLC, a New York private equity firm, and  Wilhemina International Inc. (WHLM) , whose largest shareholder is Dallas-based hedge fund Newcastle Partners LP, have been responsible for 15 percent of the 11,751 H-1B model-related initial applications during the last decade, according to data compiled by Bloomberg.  Government data also show agencies including Trump Model Management, the New York-based company owned by  Donald Trump , and Playboy Enterprises Inc., the Beverly Hills, California-based company owned by founder  Hugh Hefner  and private-equity firm Rizvi Traverse Management LLC, have filed more than 200 H-1B applications.  Different Markets  Agencies use models from various countries to appeal to different market segments, said Harold Mindel, director of Click Model Management Inc., whose roster has included models such as Australian Elle MacPherson, Italian  Isabella Rossellini  and Jamaican  Grace Jones .  He said foreign fashion workers shouldn\u2019t have to compete with science, technology and engineering applicants.  \u201cAs a single man, would you prefer to look at a beautiful woman or a high-tech worker?\u201d he asked.  The expansion of H-1B visas is supported in Silicon Valley, where thousands of applications are made. A half-dozen firms --  Microsoft Corp. (ORCL) \u2019s defeat in a two-year-\nold lawsuit against  Google Inc. (GOOG)  will make it harder for the\n software company  to harness demand for mobile devices and\nbenefit from its $7.4 billion Sun Microsystems purchase.  A federal judge ruled on May 31 that Google didn\u2019t violate\nOracle\u2019s copyrights on programming interfaces related to the\nJava computer language, which came as part of the 2010 Sun\nacquisition.  That means Google doesn\u2019t have to pay Oracle to use\nelements of Java in its Android operating system, the software\nused in more than 300 million mobile devices. And since Apple\nInc. doesn\u2019t use Java in its iPhones, Oracle misses out on a\nchance to make money from the world\u2019s two biggest providers of\nsmartphone software just as Sun\u2019s hardware business  shrinks .  \u201cOne of the crown jewels of the Sun acquisition was\nJava,\u201d said  Brent Thill , an analyst at UBS AG in  San Francisco ,\nwho has a buy rating on Oracle. \u201cThey had grand aspirations of\nbeing able to take the ubiquitous platform of Java and monetize\nit at a potentially higher rate. There are some questions now\nabout what their ability to monetize this is.\u201d  Google and Oracle have jousted since August 2010 to resolve\nOracle\u2019s allegation that Google ripped off software code and\nprogramming tools to build Android. Java lets developers write\nprograms that work across a variety of operating systems and\ncomputers by translating their code into instructions various\nmachines can understand. Part of the reason Oracle sued was to\nprevent Google and other companies from coming up with software\nthat runs functions like Java without taking an official\nlicense. Oracle\u2019s database,\nmiddleware and business applications revenue may climb 9 percent\nthis year to $26.2 billion and account for 70 percent of the\ncompany\u2019s sales. Android Dominance  At issue in the court proceedings, which began on April 14,\nwas Google\u2019s use of instructions called application programming\ninterfaces, which help developers create a wide range of\nprograms -- from operating systems to smartphone applications. To be sure, Oracle gained much more than Java when buying\nSun, including the Solaris operating system and Sparc chips. The\nbusiness is \u201cenormously profitable\u201d and the deal has \u201calready\npaid for itself\u201d given Sun\u2019s cash, Ellison said at a\ntechnology-industry conference May 30.  Appeal Plans  \u201cJava is only one component of the Sun acquisition,\u201d said\nUBS\u2019s Thill. \u201cThey have had favorable legal battles in the past\n-- they can\u2019t win \u2019em all.
