The numbers don't lie. The Android operating system has been outselling Apple's iOS by nearly a 5:1 ratio. Android dominates \"device share.\" Yet by virtually every meaningful metric that matters, Apple's users are reliably, revealingly and remarkably more engaged in ecommerce, browsing and apps than their Android counterparts. Where Android jumped from 1.43% of Black Friday shopping traffic in 2010 to 4.92% this year, Apple's iOS pole-vaulted from 3.85% to 18.46%. Barely 3% of Adobe digital magazine downloads went to Androids, fully 97% were iOS.  Put harshly, Android sells disproportionately more devices that are used disproportionately less. What gives? Literally hundreds of billions of dollars rides on the answer(s). You can be sure Amazon and Microsoft are paying \u2014 and investing \u2014 disproportionate attention to the possibilities. The mystery shouldn't be a mystery: Designing a great device is not the same as designing a great user experience. Designing a great user experience is not the same as designing greater engagement. While it's completely understandable why designers, product managers and marketers might conflate them, reality suggests that a great user experience doesn't necessarily generate engagement any more than meaningful engagement inherently assures a great user experience. For example, Twitter (or LinkedIn) may represent a less enjoyable user experience than, say, Facebook but the nature of the engagement they facilitate might mean users spend more time, thought and care with them. In other words, user experience is not the same and must be measured\/assessed differently than \"utilization experience.\" To make a vulgar comparison, just because someone buys a lot of books doesn't mean those books are read. Just because someone has a lot of friends doesn't mean those friendships are nurtured, cultivated or honored.  No one would disagree that Apple has made great user experience an organizing principle for its design culture. But much of the firm's success arguably emerges from the experiential reality that its products, services and marketing efforts align around engagement behaviors \u2014 downloading music and apps, Siri, games, etc. Engagement is how people choose to get value from the user experiences their devices enable. Engagement represents the purposeful choices users make to get what they want.  Engagement is smack at the intersection of commanding attention and taking action.   I'd argue that driving such engagement is at the core of Apple's user experience design sensibility. By contrast, engagement is what Android's UX designs enable. The difference between \"driven\" and \"enabled\" goes a long way in explaining the \"utilization gaps\" the statistics identify. Put another way, Apple's UX metric seems to encourage ROE \u2014 Return on Engagement \u2014 where Android emphasizes ease-of-use and opportunity. More vulgarly, Apple is an \"active invitation\" where Android offers a more \"passive menu.\"  When engagement is treated like a UX feature or function instead of a defining sensibility, you get less of it. At risk of sounding \"meta,\" one of the great design challenges innovators increasingly confront in increasingly competitive markets is how to get their best people to engage around engagement.  You need to devote as much creativity and ingenuity around designing for engagement as you do for the entire user experience.  A decade ago, companies hurt themselves by treating \"interface design\" as what you slapped on to your finished product. Today, innovators hurt themselves by treating \"engagement\" as a subset of the total UX. Don't make that mistake. Re-engage with engagement.","path":".\/2008_2012_msft_bloomberg_news\/don-t-confuse-engagement-with-user-experience.txt"},{"id":70823391,"title":"Tax Holiday for $1 Trillion May Lure Back Profits Without Growth","released_at":"<date>March 17 2011<\/date> <time>21:09:34<\/time>","content":"Google Ireland is not a branch\noffice of the U.S.-based search giant  Google Inc. (GOOG)  It\u2019s a\nseparate corporation, and American tax collectors can\u2019t touch a\ndime that Google Ireland earns from its core business until it\nsends profits back home to the mother ship in Mountain View,\nCalifornia.  The term of art for bringing the money back is repatriation\n-- the same as for a soldier captured abroad. U.S.\nmultinationals have more than $1\u00a0trillion in profits stashed in\noverseas subsidiaries.  Some of the companies with the most money squirreled away\nsay they\u2019re prepared to bring a big chunk of it home. All they\nwant in return is a temporary tax break that wouldn\u2019t cost the\nU.S. Treasury anything, since it\u2019s money that would otherwise be\nkept abroad and not taxed at all. The tax break would actually\nraise billions of dollars from applying the reduced  tax rate  to\nthe money that\u2019s been repatriated.  What\u2019s not to like? John T. Chambers, the chief executive\nofficer of  Cisco Systems Inc. (CSCO) , told securities analysts in\nFebruary that \u201cyou\u2019re now seeing political leaders at all levels\nunderstand\u201d the case for a tax holiday on repatriated foreign\nprofits. \u201cI think this one has well over a 60\u00a0percent\nprobability of being resolved in a positive way,\u201d he said.  Although a lobbying campaign is just getting under way,\nRepresentative Brian P. Bilbray, a California Republican, has\nalready introduced a bill that would let companies bring home\nmoney tax-free if they used it for research and development or\nfacilities expansion.  Fundamental Changes  Aside from Cisco, the coalition for repatriation relief\nincludes  Adobe Systems Inc. (ADBE) , Apple Inc., CA Technologies,  Duke\nEnergy Corp. (DUK) , Google Inc.,  Microsoft Corp. (MSFT) ,  Oracle Corp. (ORCL) ,  Pfizer\nInc. (PFE)  and  Qualcomm Inc. (QCOM) , Bloomberg Businessweek reports in its\nMarch 21 issue.  The group is seeking fundamental changes in tax law. If it\ncan\u2019t get them right away, it still wants the tax holiday. Its\nopening position is that there should be no conditions on how\nthe money is used. Chambers  argued in the Wall Street Journal \nlast October that a repatriation might create as many as\n2\u00a0million jobs.  It\u2019s a seductive argument -- reap billions in tax revenue\nfrom money that\u2019s currently untaxed and generate economic growth\nto boot. On closer inspection, though, the coalition\u2019s argument\nhas some logical loopholes. An almost identical holiday passed\nby Congress in 2004 and taken mostly in 2005 did little to boost\njobs or investment, according to several independent economic\nstudies.  No Cash Shortage  Some economists say a holiday today might be even less\neffective because cash isn\u2019t a constraint in 2011 -- it\u2019s\nbountiful, thanks to the Federal Reserve\u2019s loose-money policy.\nU.S. nonfinancial corporations have $1.9\u00a0trillion in liquid\nassets, the Fed says. No more than half of that -- probably\nsignificantly less -- is offshore. An unknown portion of the\n$1\u00a0trillion-plus in foreign-held profits isn\u2019t cash. It\u2019s tied\nup in foreign factories, offices and the like and can\u2019t easily\nbe repatriated.  \u201cThe problem is lack of demand or lack of investment\nopportunities\u201d in the U.S., says  Dhammika Dharmapala , an\neconomist and law professor at the University of Illinois at\nUrbana-Champaign.  Granting another holiday so soon might induce companies to\nstash even more money abroad, convinced that if they wait long\nenough another holiday will arrive, says  Thomas J. Brennan , a\nprofessor at Northwestern University School of Law in Chicago.  Lawmakers Reluctant  Lawmakers have thus far been cool to the idea of a\nrepatriation holiday. Passing one without reform \u201cmakes a farce\nout of the whole system,\u201d says Kent Conrad, a North Dakota\nDemocrat on the Senate Finance Committee. Even corporate America\nisn\u2019t unanimous in its support.  \u201cA one-time repatriation of profits is a bad idea,\u201d says\nGregory J. Hayes, chief financial officer of  United Technologies\nCorp. (UTX)  \u201cMy fear is that we\u2019ll have a repeat of 2004. If companies\nrepatriate these profits and spend it on things like share\nbuybacks, that will create such negative connotations around  tax\nreform  with the public.\u201d  Still, the idea lingers. Congress and the Obama\nadministration are turning over trash cans in search of ways to\naccelerate growth and bring down the unemployment rate without\nstimulus measures that increase already-huge budget deficits.\nHence the appeal of what looks like a free lunch. For\ngovernment, the challenge is to choose emergency fixes that\nwon\u2019t end up causing long-term harm.  \u201cThe problem is, there\u2019s no lobby group for good\ngovernment,\u201d says John L. Buckley, former chief Democratic tax\ncounsel for the House Ways and Means Committee.  \u2018Mulcting the Treasury\u2019  Tax collectors have been struggling to get their hands on\nthe profit from international operations since the early days of\nthe corporate income tax, enacted in 1909. Each year brings\nanother strategy for legal  tax avoidance .  \u201cAll are alike,\u201d President Franklin D. Roosevelt wrote to\nCongress in 1937, \u201cin that failure to pay results in shifting\nthe tax load to the shoulders of others less able to pay and in\nmulcting the Treasury of the government\u2019s just due.\u201d  Legal avoidance is booming, according to data collected by\nBloomberg Businessweek from the footnotes of annual 10-K\nstatements of companies on file at the Securities and Exchange\nCommission. Congress says that companies don\u2019t have to pay tax\non actively earned profits from their foreign subsidiaries as\nlong as they keep the money permanently reinvested outside the\nU.S. in subsidiaries that are organized as foreign corporations.\nEach year the parent companies state in their 10-Ks how much\nmoney is stored in that category. For 30 big companies, the\nprofits kept abroad grew 560\u00a0percent, to $740 billion, from the\nend of 2000 to the end of 2010, SEC filings show.  2004 Holiday Results  The temporary holiday passed in 2004 was supposed to shrink\nthe pile. It allowed companies to repatriate profits attributed\nto their foreign operations at a 5.25\u00a0percent tax rate instead\nof the usual 35\u00a0percent. (Companies get a credit for foreign tax\nalready paid.)  According to the  Internal Revenue Service , $362\u00a0billion\ncame back to the U.S., of which $312\u00a0billion was eligible for\nthe reduced tax rate. The amount repatriated was 45\u00a0percent of\nthe total held abroad at the end of 2004. In one of the more\nextreme repatriations,  Hewlett-Packard Co. (HPQ)  brought back\n$14.5\u00a0billion, almost all of the $15\u00a0billion that it had abroad,\nSEC filings show.  Incentive to Wait  In the long run, though, the holiday was rife with\nunintended consequences.  Research  by Northwestern\u2019s Brennan\nindicates companies rationally concluded that if they were\ngranted one special one-time tax break, they might very well be\ngranted another. That gave them the incentive to attribute even\nmore of their profits to foreign operations, like a shopper\nwaiting for an end-of-season sale. By the end of 2006 the total\n\u201cpermanently\u201d reinvested abroad had exceeded the 2004 peak. It\nhas continued to grow since.  Business did indeed lobby for seconds soon after its first\nhelping of tax relief. In 2009, just five years after the 2004\nbreak, Congress debated giving another one as a stimulus-bill\namendment sponsored by Democratic Senator Barbara Boxer of\nCalifornia and Republican Senator John Ensign of Nevada. The\namendment was defeated 42-55 on the floor of the Senate as anti-\nbusiness sentiment swept the nation after the financial crisis.  Lobbying Campaign  Cutting taxes on big businesses that stow profits abroad is\nnever going to be an applause line for candidates on the\ncampaign trail. Then again, it doesn\u2019t have to be. All business\nhas to do is get a bill through Congress and signed by the\nPresident using carefully targeted contacts, not billboards and\nairtime. To that end, the pro-holiday coalition has quietly\nassembled an all-star lobbying and communications team heavy on\nDemocratic representation, as if to counter the impression that\ntax relief for big business is solely a Republican objective.  The team\u2019s chief communications strategist is Anita Dunn,\nthe Democratic media consultant who served as President Barack Obama\u2019s interim communications director during his first year in\noffice. Politico.com  first reported  her involvement on March\u00a04.\nDunn runs strategic communications and public relations for\nSKDKnickerbocker, a new firm created from the merger of\nWashington\u2019s Squier Knapp Dunn Communications and  New York \u2019s\nKnickerbocker Consulting.  The lead lobbyists are former Representative Jim McCrery of\nLouisiana, who was the ranking Republican on the House Ways and\nMeans committee, and Jeffrey A. Forbes, the former chief of\nstaff to Senate Finance Chairman  Max Baucus , the Montana\nDemocrat.  Obama Shift  The pro-holiday message has gained traction, at least a\nlittle. As Bloomberg News reported on Feb.\u00a011, Obama\u2019s\nconsistent pledge to \u201cend tax breaks for companies that ship\njobs overseas\u201d disappeared from his stump speech after\nRepublicans won the House in November and Obama began talking\nwith executives about a corporate tax code overhaul.  In his State of the Union address, Obama even proposed\ncutting the corporate tax rate while simultaneously closing\nloopholes. Treasury Secretary Timothy Geithner has expressed\nopenness to some kind of repatriation-tax holiday as long as\nit\u2019s linked to \u201ccomprehensive\u201d tax reform.  The economics of a holiday, however, are less pliable than\nthe politics. While many economists agree there\u2019s something\nwrong with a tax code that induces companies to keep profits\nabroad when they could be more efficiently deployed in the U.S.,\nfewer say that a one-time tax break is the right remedy.  Take Federal Reserve Chairman  Ben Bernanke . The coalition\u2019s\ntalking points include what sounds like a plug from him in\ncongressional testimony March\u00a02.  Bernanke, Zandi  \u201cAs you know,\u201d Bernanke said, \u201cI\u2019ve suggested looking at\nthe corporate tax code, and one aspect of it is the\nterritoriality provision. If you were to allow firms to bring\nback cash, you know, from abroad without additional taxation or\nlimited additional taxation, there might be more incentive for\nthem to bring it home and use it domestically.\u201d  On closer reading, it\u2019s apparent that Bernanke wasn\u2019t\ntalking about a one-time holiday but about changing the method\nof taxation to a territorial system, in which only profits\nearned in the U.S. are taxed. The same goes for a December quote\ncited in the talking points from  Mark Zandi , chief economist of\nMoody\u2019s Economy.com: \u201cThe (repatriation) proposal is a\nreasonable, albeit very modest, idea.\u201d Says Zandi now: \u201cAt this\npoint I don\u2019t think I would go down that path\u201d of a stand-alone\ntax holiday. \u201cIt makes much more sense to fold it into broader\ntax reform.\u201d  Economic Argument  Even on theoretical grounds the tax holiday is debatable.\nCutting taxes can stimulate the economy if it adds to companies\u2019\nincentives to invest and expand. But the holiday, as a break on\nprofits that have already been made, wouldn\u2019t improve\nincentives, says  Edward D. Kleinbard , former chief of staff of\nthe Joint Committee on Taxation, who is a professor at the\nUniversity of Southern California\u2019s Gould School of Law in Los\nAngeles.  To build the economic case for a holiday, the coalition\ncites several studies, including two from 2003 and 2008 by  Allen Sinai , president of the consulting firm Decision Economics,\nwhich predicted their impact based on an econometric model. The\nstudies -- sponsored by the American Council for Capital\nFormation, which favors lower corporate taxes -- didn\u2019t consider\nthe outcome of the 2005 repatriation.  Share Buybacks  Some analyses that did showed disappointing results. The\n2005 repatriation \u201cdid not increase domestic investment,\nemployment, or R&D,\u201d but did boost share buybacks, concludes a\nforthcoming Journal of Finance  article  by Illinois\u2019 Dharmapala,\nC. Fritz Foley at Harvard Business School and Kristin J. Forbes\nat the Massachusetts Institute of Technology Sloan School of\nManagement.  One anecdote makes the point acutely: Hewlett-Packard, even\nas it was pulling its $14.5\u00a0billion home from abroad, announced\nplans in 2005 to reduce its workforce by 14,500.  \u201cGiven that the last holiday did not result in repatriating\nfirms increasing investment levels, it seems the burden is on\nthe advocates of another holiday to explain why things would be\ndifferent this time,\u201d Dharmapala said in an interview.  Sinai, of Decision Economics, stands by his research: \u201cI\u2019m\nquite sure there were some jobs created,\u201d he said. Hewlett-\nPackard declined to comment.  Subpart F  Legal tax avoidance intensified after World War\u00a0II, as the\nU.S. dominated the world economy. Companies with newly\nestablished foreign operations had fresh opportunities to shift\nincome. The Kennedy Administration worried that the flow of\ndollars out of the country was jeopardizing U.S. adherence to\nthe gold standard. In 1962, Congress passed Subpart F of the\nInternal Revenue Code, which reduced companies\u2019 ability to keep\nforeign profits out of reach of the U.S. tax authorities by\n\u201cdeferring\u201d taxation in overseas vehicles. Subpart F didn\u2019t lock\nthe door.  As is often the case in Washington, the scandal isn\u2019t\nwhat\u2019s illegal -- it\u2019s what\u2019s legal, in this instance tax-\navoidance systems with names like the Double Irish and the Dutch\nSandwich. As detailed in a Bloomberg Businessweek  investigative\nstory last May ,  Forest Laboratories Inc. (FRX) , which makes the\nantidepressant Lexapro, sells almost 100\u00a0percent of its drugs in\nthe U.S. and cuts its U.S. taxes dramatically by attributing the\nbulk of profits to a law office in Bermuda.  Similarly, Google reduced its income taxes by $3.1\u00a0billion\nover three years by shifting income to Ireland, then the\nNetherlands, and ultimately to Bermuda. Microsoft has used a\nsimilar arrangement. Records in the Cayman Islands and Ireland\nshow that Facebook is setting up such a structure too.  Profits Rise Faster  The clearest evidence that companies are carefully managing\nwhere they report their taxable profits is that earnings\noverseas have grown faster than sales abroad. In 2008, large\nU.S. pharmaceutical companies reported about 80\u00a0percent of their\npretax profits overseas, up from about a third a decade earlier,\naccording to Martin A. Sullivan, a contributing editor to the\ntrade journal Tax Notes and a former U.S. Treasury tax\neconomist. Those companies\u2019 foreign sales grew more slowly\nduring that period: to 52\u00a0percent of revenue from 38\u00a0percent.  The very success of tax-avoidance strategies is what\nmotivates the push for a holiday. U.S. multinationals have an\nembarrassment of overseas riches, more than they can use. If\nthey bring profits home, they must pay the difference between\nthe U.S. tax rate and what they have already paid abroad. That\nwould sting: From 2007 through 2009, Google reported an average\ntax rate of 2.4\u00a0percent on the earnings it claims overseas. If\nGoogle and others can get the repatriation rate down to\n5.25\u00a0percent as in 2005, the pain will be more tolerable. (In\n2005, tax-planning strategies helped lower the average tax paid\non repatriated funds to just 3.7 percent, according to the Joint\nCommittee on Taxation.)  New Tax Code  Critics of a proposed repatriation break complain that it\nwould reward companies that have aggressively shifted profits\ninto tax havens. \u201cThis is the system they bought into,\u201d USC\u2019s\nKleinbard says. \u201cNow they present (paying tax on) the fruits of\ntheir success as some kind of a hideous punishment.\u201d  There\u2019s broad agreement that, if done right, corporations\nand the federal government would benefit far more from a new tax\ncode than a tax holiday. Many multinationals, including\ncompanies on both sides of the holiday debate -- such as Cisco\nand United Technologies -- want the U.S. to adopt a territorial\nsystem similar to that used by most of the rest of the world.\nUnder such a system, the U.S. would largely stop trying to go\nafter companies\u2019 worldwide income and instead mostly tax profits\nearned in the U.S., whether by U.S.-based or foreign-based\ncompanies. The only other sizable countries that still use a\nsystem like the one in the U.S. are Chile, Israel, Mexico,\nPoland and South Korea. Supporters of territorial taxation\ninclude the bipartisan National Commission on Fiscal\nResponsibility and Reform created last year by Obama.  Territorial System  A pure territorial system has its own disadvantages.\nBecause it doesn\u2019t tax companies\u2019 foreign income, it amps up the\ngains from shifting income to low-tax jurisdictions. So it works\nonly if accompanied by close supervision and rules against\ngaming the system. Most developed countries, including Germany\nand Australia, have regulations to curb this sort of gaming,\nmeaning that their systems, while opposite in concept to that of\nthe U.S., are not all that different in practice.  Lowering the U.S. tax rate on all earnings, foreign and\ndomestic, from 35\u00a0percent is a high priority of business groups.\nThanks to loopholes, what companies actually pay as a percentage\nof their income is around 30\u00a0percent. That\u2019s roughly the same as\nin several large industrialized countries in Europe and lower\nthan the effective rate reported by Japanese companies,\naccording to recent research by  Kevin S. Markle  of Dartmouth\u2019s\nTuck School of Business and  Douglas A. Shackelford  of the\nUniversity of North Carolina\u2019s Kenan-Flagler Business School.  More Generous  The American system works out to be more generous than that\nof other countries for some companies, says  David S. Miller , a\npartner at Cadwalader, Wickersham & Taft in New York. Consider\nthis: A U.S. company that pays a lot in high-tax Germany can\napply the resulting credits against profits repatriated from a\nzero-tax location like Bermuda.  One proposed change in the tax code would allocate profits\nbetween countries the way most U.S. states with a corporate\nincome tax do, using hard-to-fudge measures like employment or\nsales in each jurisdiction. If a company had 90\u00a0percent of its\nemployees in the U.S., the IRS would tax 90\u00a0percent of its\nprofits. Simple, but few multinationals are in support.  In Washington, framing the debate is everything. John\nChambers and others frame the repatriation-tax holiday as\nsomething for nothing -- jobs for the unemployed, dividends for\nshareholders, tax payments for the Treasury. But the free lunch\nisn\u2019t really free. If companies are once again given a big tax\nbreak on profits they\u2019ve kept abroad, they\u2019ll be induced to\nsteer even more of their income offshore. That\u2019s a frame that\nputs the repatriation holiday in a decidedly unflattering light. Credit Swaps  The measure typically falls as investor confidence improves\nand rises as it deteriorates. Credit-default swaps pay the buyer\nface value if a borrower fails to meet its obligations, less the\nvalue of the defaulted debt. A basis point equals $1,000\nannually on a contract protecting $10 million of debt.  In  London , the  Markit iTraxx Europe Index  of 125 companies\nwith investment-grade ratings fell 2 to 98.3. (AMD) , the\nlong-struggling competitor of giant rival Intel Corp., is facing\nyet another crisis amid a shifting technology landscape and\ndeclining demand for personal computers.  Chief Executive Officer Rory Read is firing workers to pare\nexpenses as the chipmaker\u2019s sales slide. Still, he can\u2019t cut\ncosts fast enough to head off his next looming challenge:\nshrinking cash reserves. Cash declined to $1.5 billion in the\nthird quarter, shedding $279 million from the previous period.  If the trend continues, cash levels may drop to $600\nmillion by this time next year, according to an estimate by\nSanford C. Bernstein & Co. That compares with the $1.1 billion\nin reserves the company said it requires, and a quarterly\noperating expense target of $450 million. AMD has $2.04 billion\nof debt.  \u201cI\u2019d never been worried about cash flow; I am now\nworried,\u201d said Stacy Rasgon, an analyst at Bernstein.  Read said the decline of the PC market -- which provides 85\npercent of AMD\u2019s sales -- happened faster than he expected and\nleft him with less time to remake the company. As AMD\nconcentrates on developing products for new markets, Rasgon,\nChris Caso at Susquehanna International Group and Craig Berger\nat FBR Capital Markets are among analysts who say they\u2019re\nconcerned AMD might run out of money before any transformation\ncan happen.  Rasgon, who cut his rating on the stock to market perform\nearlier this month, said a lack of compelling new products from\nAMD could leave the Sunnyvale, California-based company with as\nlittle as $300 million by the end of next year, he said.  Market Squeeze  Amid a squeeze by the weak economy and changing consumer\ntastes, the global PC market will contract by 1.2 percent to\n348.7 million units this year, according to  IHS ISuppli . That\nwould be the first annual decline since 2001.  As the market shrinks, AMD\u2019s spot as the alternative to\n Intel (INTC)  in PC processors is also being threatened by the entrance\nof companies such as  Qualcomm Inc. (QCOM)  and  Nvidia Corp. (NVDA)  At the same\ntime, computer makers looking to move into tablets -- responding\nto the success of Apple Inc.\u2019s iPad -- may turn away from AMD,\naccording to Pat Becker Jr., a fund manager at Becker Capital\nManagement in  Portland ,  Oregon .  \u201cYou have to wonder if this is it for AMD,\u201d Becker said.\n\u201cAre they done?\u201d  Chasing Sales  The company\u2019s cash flow became a focus for analysts during\nits third-quarter earnings call on Oct. 18, provoking analysts\nsuch as Longbow Research LLC\u2019s Joanne Feeney to ask how AMD\nwould simultaneously reduce expenses and speed up the\nintroduction of new products.  Read said he plans to get more sales from markets such as\nindustrial equipment, computer games and communications by\nadapting existing computer designs to fit in new devices with a\nminimum of research and design effort.  A failure to deliver that new revenue might leave AMD\nneeding to make further cuts, which in turn would damage its\nability to produce competitive designs, Susquehanna\u2019s Caso said.  AMD interim Chief Financial Officer Devinder Kumar, who\nstepped in last month after the resignation of Thomas Seifert,\nsaid that once AMD completes its operating-expense cuts, cash\nreserves of $700 million to $800 million will be sufficient. In\naddition, AMD is negotiating with a chip supplier,\nGlobalfoundries Inc., to reduce purchase commitments and\ntherefore expenses, he said.  \u201cThose negotiations are going well,\u201d Kumar said in an\ninterview. Much of the spending required to develop chips\ncapable of competing in new markets has already been done, he\nsaid.  Lower Forecast  AMD stock, the worst performer on the  Philadelphia\nSemiconductor Index (SOX)  this year with a decline of 61 percent,\nadvanced 1.9 percent to $2.12 at the close in New York.  The second-largest maker of PC processors, behind Intel,\nlast week forecast sales that will again miss analysts\u2019\nestimates and said it will cut 15 percent of its staff, or about\n1,770 jobs. It\u2019s reported a loss in three of the past four\nquarters.  \u201cThe fourth quarter will continue to be challenging and we\ndo not expect PC market conditions to improve for several\nquarters,\u201d Read, who took over in August 2011, told analysts on\nthe conference call.  Cash Burn  The company had already disclosed on Oct. 11 that third-\nquarter sales fell short of its earlier predictions, leading\nStandard & Poor\u2019s to place the company\u2019s BB- credit rating on\nwatch for a possible downgrade.  Credit default swaps on AMD debt, which rise as investor\nconfidence deteriorates, are trading at their highest level\nsince Nov. 11, 2009. Derivatives traders are now pricing in a\n62.5 percent chance of AMD defaulting within five years, up from\n51 percent on Oct. 17, according to a standard pricing model\nmaintained by data provider CMA. Contracts protecting the\ncompany\u2019s debt climbed to 18.5 percentage points upfront today,\nup from 9.3 percentage points on Oct. 17.  The company\u2019s  $500 million  of 7.75 percent notes due in\nAugust 2020 fell to 82.09 cents on the dollar, to yield 11.27\npercent, on Oct. 22, according to Trace, the bond-price\nreporting system of the Financial Industry Regulatory Authority.\nThat\u2019s the lowest level for the debt since it started trading in\nJanuary 2011.  New Technology  AMD is facing an even greater challenge than the one it has\nfought against Intel since they were both founded in the late\n1960s. Microsoft Corp. (MSFT)  Chief Executive Officer  Steve Ballmer  had read about her and wanted to meet.  Athey, 36 at the time, had just become the first woman to receive the  John Bates Clark Medal , joining a group that now includes 12 Nobel Prize winners and two White House chief economists. She flew to Redmond,  Washington , and was ushered into a windowless conference room with Ballmer and several of his vice presidents. The company was at a crossroads, struggling to gain ground with a search technology that had long trailed Google.  \u201cThe obvious question was, would this become a one-firm show or was it possible to have two competing search engines?\u201d recalled Athey, an authority on timber auctions who had just begun studying the market for digital advertising. \u201cI believed then, based on economic theory and some data, and I believe more strongly now that it\u2019s indeed possible to have two competing search engines and that it\u2019s also incredibly important for the Internet ecosystem.\u201d  The meeting with Ballmer would steer her from what was already an award-studded career into the nascent field of Internet economics. Taking on the role of consultant as chief economist for the world\u2019s largest software maker, she focused her research on the real-world puzzles she witnessed in Redmond.  Advising Engineers  With access to information on a scale so vast she says \u201cit takes hundreds of machines just to open up the dataset and take the first average,\u201d Athey started guiding Microsoft\u2019s executives and engineers with the latest theories and findings in economics, advising them on decisions that would affect millions of the world\u2019s Internet users.  \u201cThere are people who build on other people\u2019s research,\u201d but Athey \u201cdoes a single paper that moves the entire field along 10 years,\u201d said Joshua Gans, a professor of strategic management at the  University of Toronto  and a graduate-school classmate with whom she has co-authored several studies. \u201cNow she\u2019s running an economic movement\u201d and she\u2019s \u201cnearly starting from scratch. It\u2019s the kind of thing you would want someone like Susan to do.\u201d  Athey returned this year to  Stanford University  in the heart of Silicon Valley, where she got her Ph.D., to spearhead a vision that\u2019s emerged from her years with Microsoft, where she still consults.  Creating Opportunities  \u201cWe\u2019ve never had data on that scale before to study behavior,\u201d which \u201ccreates opportunities for new science,\u201d she said. \u201cI want to help the economics field embrace those opportunities.\u201d  In a profession that tends to encourage expertise in a single area, Athey\u2019s research is distinguished for its diversity. When she won the Clark medal as the most influential U.S. economist under 40 -- one of economics\u2019 most prestigious prizes -- the American Economic Association cited her work spanning fields from pure theory to the invention of new statistical tools and her analysis of real-world data.  \u201cShe\u2019s very motivated by applied problems, but she has all the tools, abilities and firepower to go at those problems in a general way with deep theory,\u201d said Robert Marshall, her undergraduate adviser at  Duke University  and now a professor of economics at Penn State University. \u201cThat combination is very rare.\u201d  Extra Math  Born in  Boston  to a physicist and an English teacher, Athey spent her childhood asking her parents for extra math problems and reading textbooks \u201cjust for fun.\u201d Taking the SAT college-admission test when she was 12, she scored so high in math that she was placed into a special cohort of gifted students tracked by the  Study of Mathematically Precocious Youth . She also had high verbal marks.  After a brief rebellion \u201cagainst all things academic\u201d as an early teen, she convinced her parents and guidance counselor to let her graduate high school a year early, when she was 16. To help pay for college, she took a summer job as a receptionist at a startup company that sold computers to the government through procurement auctions. At Duke, in Durham,  North Carolina , she wrote her economics thesis on this bidding process.  While she also majored in computer science and math, she chose to pursue economics for her graduate degree because of its potential to influence public policy. \u201cIt was incredibly powerful\u201d watching her adviser Marshall testify in Congress based on research she did under his direction, she said.  Lifting Weights  At Stanford\u2019s Graduate School of Business, where she got her doctorate at age 24, she lifted weights because she realized she was missing out on valuable networking conversations with her male classmates and professors who socialized at the gym, she said.  Her  dissertation  led to her first national media attention, with the  New York  Times profiling her as \u201cthe top draft pick in economics.\u201d Working with models that predict how, say, an investor or company makes a risky decision, she developed a tool now taught in graduate economics courses that simplified the assumptions researchers use to make forecasts, allowing them to focus on the essence of the problem and not complicated math.  After graduate school, she chose to join the  Massachusetts Institute of Technology  as an assistant professor; it had competed with about two dozen of the country\u2019s best economic departments to recruit her.  \u2018Crushing\u2019 Expectations  With early achievement also came pressure to live up to what she says were sometimes \u201ccrushing\u201d expectations. At MIT, Athey became known for pulling late nights and sleeping multiple times a week in her office -- equipped with a couch, refrigerator, freezer and microwave. To streamline a 40-page mathematical proof, she once spent three weeks secluded in her office, leaving only to shower, she said.  \u201cI had the feeling that everyone was watching me and I was basically set up to fail, that there was no way that I could achieve,\u201d said Athey during an interview at Stanford near  Palo Alto ,  California . \u201cMy success on the job market was more based on potential than the things that I had accomplished at that point.\u201d  She won the 2000  Elaine Bennett Research Prize , presented for \u201coutstanding contributions by young women in the economics profession,\u201d and then left MIT for Stanford in 2001. She joined Harvard\u2019s faculty five years later.  Timber Auctions  Examining the results of U.S. Forest Service auctions to sell off timber, she stumbled upon  results  that defied conventional thinking. Among them: The way the rules were designed was crucial in making sure small bidders participated, keeping the proceedings competitive. She used her findings to help the Canadian government deregulate its timber auctions.  The principles she gleaned from the economics of forestry would prove invaluable for her later work. Auctions were becoming ubiquitous on the Internet, from consumers selling bicycles on EBay to companies bidding to have their advertisements appear next to search results on  Google. (GOOG)   What Athey saw in these online marketplaces was a treasure trove of largely unexamined data. She had just started studying the auctions for ads when Microsoft contacted her. She quickly saw the bigger picture: a chance to inject more competition into the  then-$8.8 billion U.S. search business , which people used to find not only commercial information but also \u201cpolitical information and information that\u2019s relevant to a democracy,\u201d she said.  Strong No. 2  \u201cHaving a strong No. 2 is what drives a lot of the investment decisions, the prices for the advertisers and the quality of the search for the user.\u201d  The work for Microsoft meant Athey needed to study the company\u2019s proprietary computer-programming language, along with the details of running a search engine. She says she already was exhausted from juggling responsibilities on academic committees, teaching full-time and raising two young children. She took a year off from teaching at Harvard in 2008, shuttling between Microsoft\u2019s  research center  in Cambridge,  Massachusetts , and meetings at the Redmond headquarters.  She wrote her own computer code to extract information on advertiser bids, often submitting computing requests to the company\u2019s servers at 1 a.m. She also performed hundreds of Internet searches individually, checking the advertisements to see what was going right and wrong.  \u201cSusan is one of the most respected leaders in her field and we\u2019re fortunate to have the opportunity to work with her,\u201d Rik van der Kooi, chief operating officer of the company\u2019s Online Services Division, said in an e-mail. \u201cShe has provided valuable advice on search economics and helped us think through the dynamics of the  search market , as well as opportunities to re-imagine advertising.\u201d  Statistical Debates  Athey now has one boy and two girls with husband and fellow economist  Guido Imbens . They occasionally collaborate on research, she said, which sometimes leads to debates about statistical methodology as they change their youngest daughter\u2019s diapers.  While she no longer sleeps in her office, she works 75 hours a week, often starting at home in the morning to get her children ready for school, returning by 6 p.m. for dinner, then logging back online from 9 p.m. until midnight. She blocks off weekends to spend with her family, although she typically takes three hours each night on Saturday and Sunday to work after her children go to bed.  \u201cShe really cares about making sure you don\u2019t take short cuts and that everything is done incredibly carefully,\u201d said Jonathan Levin, an economics professor at Stanford who has written a number of papers with her. \u201cShe has a remarkable energy to get things done.\u201d  Delegate Meticulously  Athey has learned to decline some opportunities, delegate meticulously and accept that some nonessential tasks won\u2019t turn out \u201cperfect the way I want them to be\u201d -- all decisions she says she would like to see more women make. Halfway through a year in which her husband was preparing their children for school, she remembers asking him where the hairbrush was. He asked her if they had one.  \u201cBut you know what? That was fine. Who really cares if a five year-old\u2019s hair is brushed?\u201d she said. \u201cHis approach was different, not worse, and I had to let go.\u201d  That letting go ensures she has time to build out her new big-data-meets-economics vision. She uses advanced techniques such as  machine learning , developed by scientists using large sets of data that enable computers ultimately to program themselves. While such techniques have become commonplace at technology companies, they aren\u2019t widespread among her colleagues.  New Generation  She\u2019s helping to train a new generation of economists who can straddle the worlds of research and real-world market design. Just this month, Athey finished teaching her first class on the  economics of e-commerce and the Internet , a Ph.D.-level course drawing on much of her own research from the last six years.  \u201cThroughout her career, she tried to be where the action was,\u201d said Glenn Ellison, an MIT economics professor who also was at Athey\u2019s first meeting with Ballmer in 2007. \u201cThere are some people who have done the same thing for the past 20 years and you know they\u2019re going to keep doing that for the next 20 years. Download this podcast SARAH GREEN: Welcome to the HBR IdeaCast. I'm Sarah Green. I'm talking today with Bruce Nussbaum, professor of innovation and design at Parsons School of Design and author of the new book Creative Intelligence, Harnessing the Power to Create, Connect, and Inspire. Bruce, thanks for talking with us.  BRUCE NUSSBAUM: Oh, it's my pleasure.  SARAH GREEN: You say that only 9% of all US public and private companies are doing any kind of serious innovation, which is hard for me to believe that it's really that bad. So how did you get that number and tell me a little bit about the dire straits that we're in.  BRUCE NUSSBAUM: Well look, I was stunned when I heard about this. A good friend of mine, Mike Mandel, who is the Chief Economist at Business Week when I was there, did a great cover story in which he coined the term \"the innovation shortfall.\" And it was a stunning idea. We're all used to our iPads and iPhones and Facebook and we live, most of us, in a space that we think is very high tech in very innovative and so we think the whole world is like that.  But when he went back and did some very serious economic research he came upon these great-- and I'm going to be very specific with you, right. The National Science Foundation report released in September 2010-- called the 2008 because the research took place at that time. Business R&D and innovation survey, and it's known in economic circles as the BRDIS, that showed that only 9% of public and private companies engage in either product or service innovation between 2006 and 2008. And then they did a second survey which showed it continued into 2009 and 2010. And I'm sort of quoting from my book.  That's a stunner, and anecdotal, right? This is serious analysis, a huge survey of corporations. So it killed me, just stopped me dead. 9% of all corporations, private and public, do any sort of serious innovation. And I thought to myself, well, you know, let's stop, take a moment and think about the economy as a whole. And it could be true, right?  And I did further research and anecdotal stuff and there you go. Whether it's 9% or 10% whatever it is, a tiny, tiny percentage of our companies do any sort of innovation. And that's where it kind of all began there. And I said to myself, whoa, we ought to stop and think about what is really going on in corporate America, around the world, and that began part of my research into creative intelligence.  SARAH GREEN: I know there are things-- and you talk about a lot of these things in the book-- that individuals can do to try and overcome that. But I'd like to focus now a little bit on sort of the broader innovation ecosystem that we're talking about. Because it seems like if it's really that few companies who are really innovating there's got be something bigger going on.  I'd love to have your thoughts on America's innovation policies, should we be reallocating some of our investment dollars at a government level into something that might be more fruitful and help make a better innovation ecosystem? And we'll go through a lot of different facets of this. But let's just start there. What should we be investing in?  BRUCE NUSSBAUM: So let's start with what should be America's national innovation policy. I would start with we actually spend a huge amount of money, billions and billions of dollars on research every year. Most of that research for, I would say, the last 20 years has gone into bio science. We've made enormous bets on bio science.  And one of the reasons why that has happened is because there's an agreement on that. There's no big infighting among industries in this and that as to where to put money. It's about health, it's about safety, it's about longevity. We've put a fortune into bio science with very little return. We were expecting the world to move from a silicon based society to a bio based genome based-- it hasn't happened. We could go into those reasons at another time. But it hasn't happened.  We need to redistribute the amount of government money, your money, my money, taxpayer money, away from bio science. Keep some of it there, or a lot of it there, and put it into manufacturing. Put it much more into the making of things, the materiality of things, into 3D printers, robotics, digital fabrication. We simply need to get back to a more balanced investment portfolio coming out of the government.  I really am big into making culture. I think it was a disaster for us to move away from it. I think now we're really at the point-- we have a whole new series of technologies that can give us back our making culture. And people are taking it back.  SARAH GREEN: You mean like the manufacturing economy?  BRUCE NUSSBAUM: Yes. The manufacturing economy. I think we need to get back to the manufacturing economy. And we as individuals, we could talk about that a little bit later, we need to become makers again. It's very important for us to become makers again and to learn by doing, to learn by making.  Actually that's my second thing. In addition to redistributing government money away from bio science into making and materials manufacturing the materials, I think in education we need to augment our focus on math and science with a much bigger investment on creativity. And that means very simply you know, bring back shop. Art and shop should be central to education. These are the making tools that we need to learn. We need to go back to Dewey, John Dewey, whose whole educational philosophy was learning by doing. So we need to bring you doing and making back to our educational experience. And that is absolutely essential.  A part of that, I think, has to involve moving away from teaching to the test. Memorization in a time of search is just ludicrous. And teaching to the test is all about memorization and the assumption that you know what the major problems are and that you know what the solutions to them are. We live in an age where we don't even know what the problems are.  And we have enormous challenges and there are many ways to respond to these challenges. We need to be able to creatively deal with challenges and have the agility to offer up many options. That's the way we have to think. That's a creative way of thinking. Not problems and solutions. So that's another big thing.  I would also say that in terms of people in Washington, Washington is full of Wall Street people. Washington is full of people from big banks and big corporations. We need to have entrepreneurs in Washington. We have venture capitalists in Washington. We need to have people who know how to start up a company and what that means populating the regulatory agencies, in Congress. I wouldn't mind seeing one as a president. So I think we need to shift away from only focusing on the big and bring in the entrepreneurs, bring in the start up people, and bring in the people who are into creativity.  I would make, myself personally, David Kelley the head of the Department of Education. he's the co-founder of IDEO and the founder of the d.School at Stanford. He's got great ideas about education. Bring him in, or Katie Salen who has these great schools in New York and Chicago where all the lesson plans are gamed. They're in the form of a game. So she's gamified the public school curriculum in New York and Chicago. Bring in people like that and really shake it up.  So I think Washington needs to really shift its focus from big business to small start ups and from CEOs to entrepreneurs. Both in the economic policy and education policy. And of course tax policy has to be modified somewhat to the capital gains stuff. All of that really has to be shaped so that it promotes and encourages start ups and entrepreneurs. That's the easy part. So I'll stop there.  SARAH GREEN: Well, there's certainly a lot there to unpack. And it's a very ambitious agenda. I'd like to, actually, since you were talking about education, I'd like to talk a little bit more about college students. Because I think some of the splashiest companies have been started while students were still in college like Microsoft or Facebook.  But it's easy to see that if you were shackled with student debt you're not going to be spending your free time building Facebook. So do you think that the student loan crisis is part of a drag on our national creativity? And if so, what would you do about that?  BRUCE NUSSBAUM: That's a very good question. I think the fact that students are burdened with an average of $20,000 of debt these days that there's a trillion dollars of student debt overhanging basically the whole Gen Y population, right, it's really demographically specific to Gen Y, is a catastrophe and a shame. It's really shameful that a country like in the US says got to finance its higher education by putting such a burden on people.  I wrote a blog item a couple of years ago calling for renunciation of student debt. It was a little bit tongue in cheek and I said, look, you know, when we had a Latin American debt crisis the banks wrote off the debt. And they stuffed it in their portfolio, and they went on. And Latin America went on and started growing and we ought to start thinking about doing that here. Frankly, it's not a bad idea. OK? There are other ways of doing it. I think we need to structurally change the way we finance our education so that it doesn't land on students.  When I went to school in grad school in the '70s I had full fare through a National Defense Language Fellowship. The Cold War basically paid my way. Well, there are all kinds of major reasons why the US should be finding a way to finance students higher education in a way that doesn't land on them or their families. We need to be creative about this.  We also need to be creative about our education system. How do we really need four years in undergraduate? The Europeans take three. Most of our college year is really short. We have one of the shortest college years of any country around. We could probably do it in three for most people who then will, especially those who want to go on for a professional degree, want to go on for their masters in something. That would really cut the cost of education. And then of course we all this MOOC and online stuff. We really need to be more creative about structuring our education one, and two we need to be much more creative about reducing the personal debt of people.  SARAH GREEN: So it's interesting when you are talking more about different government policies and financing models there, because that goes back to something else you mentioned that I wanted to unpack, which is that one of your underlying points throughout the book is that creativity and innovation rarely moves in a perfectly straight efficient line. And if you try to make it into as efficient a process as possible, you end up squeezing out a lot of what is useful about it. At the federal level that can be a challenge because I think all of us want our tax dollars to be spent efficiently. So how do you see that shaking out in the real world?  BRUCE NUSSBAUM: It's a good question. Well, I'm going to rephrase it. Do we want our tax dollars to be spent efficiently or do we want our tax dollars to be spent credibly, or adequately? I worked at Business Week for a long time, right? Business works in a culture of efficiency. Business schools teach the culture and the analytical tools of efficiency. And it's a very important variable, and a very important value. But it's not the only one.  Creativity doesn't work on the principle of efficiency. It works on other principles and other variables. If you get right you can build a system that will probably deliver you some wonderful stuff that has great economic value over time. In the book I talk about the Hewlett Packard labs when David and his partner created Hewlett Packard and they set up a series of labs where you had two or three scientists and engineers, mostly engineers, just mucking around. Pretty much doing what they wanted to do. And the end result was Hewlett Packard created this innovation machine of enormous economic value that produced a whole series of things that weren't particularly related. You know, they had scientific instruments and then they had the HP printer.  They allowed this cauldron of creativity to bubble. And they knew how to scale it. OK? They knew how to connect people with resources who could do the scaling to the scientists and engineers who were doing the creating. That's a system that you can build. And HP was wildly successful decades before Apple in doing that and then it all went to hell when they stopped doing that.  I mean, on one level it's a very efficient system, on another level you're building in pockets, I would call them circles of creativity where efficiency isn't really the value. Originality adaptivity, agility those are other values that are, I think, quite important to creativity.  So let's take it to the national level. Over time if you invest properly you're going to get, I would say, you're going to get a lot of economic value from the dollars that go into the kind of R&D and creativity that lead to economic value. Looking at it in terms of efficiency over one year or three year time frame is not the way to go.  SARAH GREEN: Well I know we've spend most of the time today talking about some of the headwinds companies are facing and your book is actually full of solutions. I don't want people to get the wrong impression. But thank you so much for talking about some of those headwinds with us today.  BRUCE NUSSBAUM: Oh sure, it's my pleasure. And as you said the book is full of really interesting [INAUDIBLE] skills, both for individuals and for big business managers to make their organizations much more creative. And I argue that we can make creativity routine. It's not something special. It's something, you know, we all play sports. We're good at sports. Some of us are really good at a very particular sport. Creativity is really like sports. You can train for it, and you could make it routine and you could amplify your creativity.  SARAH GREEN: Well, I'm glad we were able to end on a hopeful note there. Thank you Bruce for talking with us today.  BRUCE NUSSBAUM: Sure. Thank you.  SARAH GREEN: That was Bruce Nussbaum, author of Creative Intelligence, Harnessing The Power to Create, Connect, and Inspire. Profit for the just-ended quarter fell 8.6 percent to $7.51 billion, or $8.26 a share, above the $7.92 projected by analysts on average and the third-consecutive period of declines.  Margin Pressure  In a conference call with analysts, CFO Oppenheimer said gross margins are being influenced by higher costs for new products, currency pressure from conversions in  Japan , and an accounting change related to revenue adjustments for software that the company is now giving away for free with new iPhone, iPads and Macs.  Without the deferred revenue, Apple\u2019s gross margin outlook would have been about 38 percent, Oppenheimer said.  \u201cWe\u2019re going to work hard to work down the cost curve,\u201d he said.  Apple investors are facing a new dynamic in which the company\u2019s growth has slowed, said  Jack Ablin , chief investment officer at BMO Private Bank, which has $66 billion under management and owns Apple shares.  \u201cThis is a company that has routinely blown the doors off their estimates so meeting or just exceeding is probably a disappointment,\u201d he said.  Product Lineup  Apple has been busy updating its product lineup ahead of the holiday season. The company has said its new iPhones will be available in about 100 countries by the end of the year. The higher-end iPhone 5s costs $199 with a two-year wireless contract and includes a more powerful processor, improved camera and fingerprint-reading technology.  The new iPhone 5c is mainly last year\u2019s model with colorful plastic cases. The handset is seen as Apple\u2019s bid to win more customers in  emerging markets  like China and  Russia . Without a contract, the handset costs about $800, leading analysts to say it\u2019s too expensive for those markets and that demand is light.  A new iPad Air also goes on sale on Nov. 1, followed later in the month by an updated iPad mini with a high-definition screen.  On the conference call, Cook hinted that new products are in the works. Apple is exploring entering new product categories with \u201csignificant opportunities,\u201d he said.  Changing Momentum  The holiday releases arrive as some of the momentum in the smartphone and tablet industries has shifted toward the lower-end of the market. Samsung has become the world\u2019s largest smartphone maker by offering customers handsets with different screen sizes and prices. The South Korean company also is Apple\u2019s closest competitor in tablets, along with devices from  Google Inc. (GOOG) ,  Amazon.com Inc. (AMZN)  and  Microsoft Corp. (MSFT)   Apple also is being pressured to return more money to shareholders. Billionaire activist investor  Carl Icahn  has been on a publicity campaign to get Apple to initiate a $150 billion buyback to boost the company\u2019s stock price.  Cook said on the conference call that Apple\u2019s board discusses what to do with cash on an \u201congoing basis.\u201d The company will seek input from shareholders and announce any change to the existing dividend and buyback plan in early 2014, he said. Apple paid out $36 billion in dividends and buybacks in the past five quarters, he said. Google, along with other technology companies, including\nApple Inc. and Facebook Inc., is seeking greater latitude to\ndisclose information about the government requests for user data\ncollected by intelligence agencies.  \u201cWe have long pushed for transparency so users can better\nunderstand the extent to which governments request their data --\nand Google was the first company to release numbers for National\nSecurity Letters,\u201d Niki Fenwick, a spokeswoman for Google in\n Washington , said in an e-mail. Google is seeking a declaration from the court that would\nallow it to release the statistics without violating the Foreign\nIntelligence Surveillance Act, or FISA, according to the filing,\nwhich was provided by Google.  Corporate Scrutiny  The role of private companies has come under scrutiny since\nEdward Snowden, a computer technician who did work for the\nNational Security Agency, disclosed this month that the agency\nis collecting millions of U.S. residents\u2019 telephone records and\nthe computer communications of foreigners from Google and other\nInternet companies under court order. The question concerns Turkey's government, which in the space of a few days has  ended a headscarf ban  for civil servants (except in the judiciary and security services), but also caused a female TV music-show presenter to be fired for showing too much cleavage. The headscarf ban was a piece of unabashed social engineering introduced in the 1920s to make Turkey, the rump of the former Ottoman Empire and Islamic Caliphate, secular. If you are liberal and not Islamophobic, ending the ban is a good thing: Women should not be excluded from the workplace just because they are devout and believe this requires covering their hair, period.  But what if the change -- which Prime Minister Recep Tayyip Erdogan introduced as part of a broad \"democratization\" package -- is part of a wider plan of social re-engineering, this time designed to impinge on the liberties of non-religious conservatives? If so, the numerous cases in which women were discriminated against, fired or passed over for promotion for wearing a headscarf even outside of work would now be repeated in reverse: Women who don't wear headscarves to work, and men whose wives don't cover their hair, will be discriminated against, fired and passed over for promotion. Turkey's secularists say this is already happening to men whose wives show their locks. That's hard to prove, but the real issue is trust -- secularists believe the worst of Erdogan's intentions. Are they right?  The  firing  of a TV presenter, Gozde Kansu, this week is indicative. Huseyin Celik, spokesman for the ruling Justice and Development Party attacked Kansu (without actually naming her) for wearing a dress with a plunging neckline while on the air. A few days later, she was fired. There are a few points to make. First, Celik should watch more Italian TV -- he would then understand that Kansu is a model of shy decorum. Second, Celik's words were as follows: \u201cWe don\u2019t intervene against anyone, but this is too much. It is unacceptable,\u201d according to Hurriyet Daily News. He later complained that it wasn't his fault that she was fired, and he had a right to express his opinions. None of this is credible. Celik knows what \"unacceptable\" means; he knew that Kansu was on ATV television, which belongs to a company called Calik Holding; and he knew that Calik's chief executive officer is Erdogan's son-in-law, Berat Albayrak. There is no coincidence or unintended consequence here. Celik wants to re-engineer Turkish TV.  There are plenty of other pointers about the depth of the government's commitment to \"democratization,\" such as the repeated tightening of restrictions on the sale of alcohol, frowned upon by devout Muslims; the routine prosecuting and jailing of journalists; and the crushing of dissent in the Gezi Park protests earlier this year. One last piece of evidence: A Turkish appeals court today upheld the convictions 237 Turkish military officers convicted of plotting a coup against the government in 2003. The case, called Sledgehammer, has been  thoroughly discredited . Forensic examination showed that the evidence on which the conviction rested was forged: The documents involved were on a CD-ROM date-stamped 2003, yet were written using a 2007 Microsoft program.  Again, a case first hailed abroad as good for democracy -- an effort to hold the country's generals accountable after decades of impunity -- turns out to be something else. The Sledgehammer case shows only continuity in Turkish governments' use of politicized courts against their enemies: In the old days the military and secularists abused the law to suppress Islamists; now the Islamists are returning the favor. Chief\nexecutive officers who repurchase their companies\u2019 shares follow\nthe dictates of Wall Street, lacking the imagination to use\ntheir cash more wisely.  Today\u2019s low stock prices, however, open a window for\nsensible buybacks.  Stocks comprising the benchmark  Standard & Poor\u2019s 500 Index \non average trade at 15 times earnings. That\u2019s about half of\ntheir price-earnings ratio in 2001 and compares with a P\/E of 23\nas recently as December.  The 30 companies that make up the  Dow Jones Industrial\nAverage  now have an average yield of 2.6 percent, about the same\nas the yield on the 10-year U.S. Treasury note, considered a\nsafer, more conservative investment.  Stocks such as Intel Corp.,  McDonald\u2019s Corp.  and Procter &\nGamble Co. now have a dividend yield that\u2019s even higher, making\nthem attractive to investors who think the run in Treasuries and\nother bonds is over.  CEOs, many serial repurchasers in the past, are already\nleaping back into the game. Share buybacks have increased for\nthe last four quarters, according to Standard & Poor\u2019s, which\ndoes stock research along with its bond-rating activities. S&P\nsaid it expects buybacks in 2010 to exceed $300 billion,\ncompared with $137.6 billion last year.  Easy Money  Many companies borrow at today\u2019s low interest rates to\nfinance share repurchases.  Microsoft Corp. , the world\u2019s biggest\nsoftware maker last week said it would borrow as much as $6\nbillion to finance buybacks and pay higher dividends. Though\nMicrosoft is cash-rich, it\u2019s borrowing because much of the money\nis tied up overseas.  ConocoPhillips , a Houston-based oil company with a market\nvalue of about $83 billion, just arranged the sale of $2.4\nbillion of shares in Russia\u2019s OAO Lukoil, earmarking the money\nto repay debt and repurchase its own stock, which now yields\nalmost 4 percent.  For a time, at least, CEOs can buy back shares for\nfundamentally sound reasons. Their shares look like bargains.\nBuybacks reduce the number of shares outstanding, increasing\nearnings per share. That\u2019s what Wall Street analysts like. In\ntheir minds, buybacks rank right up there with the firing of\nworkers to cut costs.  Options in Mind  Higher earnings per share tend to lift stock prices. CEOs\nwill tell you that this is what buybacks are all about. They\ntend not to mention that the process also keeps their stock\noptions in the money.  Companies hot to buy back shares also do it when their\nstocks are overvalued, though they can argue that by\nrepurchasing regularly, the average price they pay is\nreasonable.  Continual demand from ongoing buyback programs puts a floor\nunder a company\u2019s stock. Exxon Mobil Corp., the king of\nbuybacks, repurchased $142.8 billion of its stock since late\n2004, according to Standard & Poor\u2019s. That\u2019s a lot. The oil\ngiant\u2019s total stock market value is about $314 billion.  Similarly,  International Business Machines Corp. , with a\nmarket value of about $170 billion, bought back $61.7 billion of\nits shares in the same period, making it a ready buyer for\ninvestors who wanted to sell.  Buybacks, while rational now, will continue long after\nstock prices recover to a level where smart CEOs should put\ntheir money to better use.  We\u2019ll never know if cash spent on expansion or higher\ndividends would have done a better job of increasing share\nprices.  ( David Pauly  is a columnist for Bloomberg News. Opinions\nexpressed are his.) The company\u2019s guilty plea to criminal charges means it\ncan\u2019t assert attorney-client privilege to keep the information\nconfidential, prosecutors said yesterday in a filing in federal\ncourt in New Orleans. Since BP\u2019s lawyers were \u201cintimately\ninvolved\u201d in aiding the company\u2019s criminal conduct, the\ncustomary shield over their work is eliminated, the U.S. said.  BP Exploration & Production Inc. on Jan. 29 won final\napproval of its plea to 14 criminal counts related to the\nexplosion of the Deepwater Horizon drilling rig, which killed 11\nworkers and sparked the worst offshore  oil spill  in U.S.\nhistory. Among those charges was a count for obstructing justice\nby lying to the  U.S. Congress  about the size of the spill, which\nthe government said dumped more than 4.1 million barrels of\ncrude into the gulf.  \u201cBecause BP used its attorneys to aid in its wrongdoing,\nit can no longer claim privilege with respect to communications\nrelated to developing the flow-rate information and\ncommunications forming the basis of BP\u2019s false and misleading\nstatements,\u201d prosecutors said in the filing. This applies even\nif the lawyers were unaware they were aiding criminal conduct,\nthe government said.  BP previously admitted in court papers \u201cthat the\npreparation of the false and misleading documents in question\nwere attorney-directed efforts,\u201d according to the filing. BP\u2019s\nfraudulent statements were \u201cdrafted in a collaborative process\nled by  Wilmer Hale  and involving both in-house and external\nlawyers,\u201d government lawyers said.  Wilmer Hale Pickering Hale and Dorr LLP , a 1,000-lawyer\ncorporate defense firm based primarily in Boston and Washington\nD.C., had no immediate comment on the government filing, Molly\nNunes, a firm spokeswoman, said today.  BP initially told the government and the public that the\nflow rate was from 1,000 to 5,000 barrels a day, when internal\nestimates pegged the rate as high as 96,000 barrels a day,\nprosecutors said.  \u201cNothing in the plea deprives BP of the right to invoke\nthe core protections provided under federal law,\u201d  Scott Dean , a\nspokesman for London-based BP, said in an e-mailed statement.\n\u201cWe will respond to the government\u2019s motion on a schedule set\nby the court.\u201d  BP agreed to pay $4 billion in fines and penalties to\nresolve all criminal charges tied to the fatal explosion and\nspill. BP pleaded guilty to 11 counts of felony seaman\u2019s\nmanslaughter and two counts of violating federal environmental\nprotection laws.  Separately, BP entered a consent judgment with the U.S.\nSecurities and Exchange Commission to pay an additional $525\nmillion for lying about the size of the spill.
