He was 56.  Jobs, who resigned as  Apple Inc . chief executive officer on\nAug. 24, 2011, passed away yesterday, the Cupertino, California-\nbased company said. He was diagnosed in 2003 with a\nneuroendocrine tumor, a rare form of pancreatic cancer, and had\na liver transplant in 2009.  \u201cWe are deeply saddened to announce that  Steve Jobs  passed\naway,\u201d Apple said. \u201cSteve\u2019s brilliance, passion and energy\nwere the source of countless innovations that enrich and improve\nall of our lives. The world is immeasurably better because of\nSteve.\u201d  Jobs embodied the Silicon Valley entrepreneur. He was a\nlong-haired counterculture technophile who dropped out of\ncollege and started a computer company in his parents\u2019 garage on\nApril Fools\u2019 Day, 1976. He had no formal technical training and\nno real business experience.  What he had instead was an appreciation of technology\u2019s\nelegance and a notion that computers could be more than a\nhobbyist\u2019s toy or a corporation\u2019s workhorse. These machines\ncould be indispensable tools. A computer could be, he often\nsaid, \u201c a bicycle for our minds .\u201d He was right -- owing largely\nto a revolution he started.  Obama Statement  Jobs\u2019s passing was met with grief from consumers who laid\nflowers and posted tributes on the walls of Apple stores and\ntechnology executives who had partnered and competed with Jobs\nover the years. Flags flew at half-staff at Apple\u2019s\nheadquarters. Apple plans a celebration for employees. It \ndoesn\u2019t intend to hold a public ceremony, a person familiar with\nthe matter said.  Even U.S. President Barack Obama and first lady  Michelle Obama  lamented the loss.  \u201cMichelle and I are saddened to learn of the passing of\nSteve Jobs,\u201d Obama said. \u201cSteve was among the greatest of\nAmerican innovators -- brave enough to think differently, bold\nenough to believe he could change the world, and talented enough\nto do it.\u201d  On his watch, Apple came to dominate the digital age, first\nthrough the creation of the Macintosh computer and later through\nthe  iPod digital music player , the iPhone and the iPad tablet.  With each product, Jobs confronted new adversaries -- from\n International Business Machines Corp. (IBM)  in computers to Microsoft\nCorp. in operating systems, to  Sony Corp. (6758)  in music players and\nGoogle Inc. in mobile software.  Visionary to Virtuoso  And Jobs would prove himself not just a techie visionary,\nbut the virtuoso executive who built the world\u2019s second-most\nvaluable company after  Exxon Mobil Corp. (XOM)   The opening act of Jobs\u2019s professional ascent stretched\nfrom 1976 to 1984. He scored his first hit with the  Apple II \ncomputer, a device that resonated with schools and some\nconsumers and small businesses, and made Apple an alluring\nalternative to IBM, then the world\u2019s largest computer maker.\nApple had its initial public offering in 1980 and the graphical\nMacintosh was born just over three years later.  During his second act, from 1984 to 1997, Jobs\u2019s star\ndimmed. In 1985, he was fired after a power struggle with\nApple\u2019s board. He started another computer company, NeXT\nComputer Inc., and bought a digital animation studio from\nfilmmaker George Lucas. The firm later took the name Pixar.  String of Hits  Apple\u2019s purchase of NeXT in 1997 brought Jobs back to the\ncomputer maker he helped found and commenced his career\u2019s third\nact. The company was foundering. He ignited a flurry of\ninnovation and growth -- and achieved what may be the greatest\ncomeback in business history.  Whether he was working on the Mac or the iPhone or backing\nthe  computer animation  that yielded an unbroken string of Pixar\nhits, Jobs proved that complex technologies could be designed\ninto simple, beautiful products that people would find\nirresistible.  His meticulous attention to product detail carried over to\nhis public image, which grew inseparable from the Apple brand.\nIn public he wore beltless jeans and a black mock-turtleneck.  On the few occasions he granted interviews -- appearing on\nthe covers of Time, Fortune or BusinessWeek, for instance -- he\nfretted over such minutiae as which photographer would take his\npicture. The reclusiveness only added to his mystique.  \u2018Wonderful\u2019 Mystery  \u201cThe mystery is actually wonderful,\u201d said Regis McKenna,\na  computer-industry marketing consultant  who first worked with\nApple in the 1980s. \u201cYou want to know more about this company\nthe more mysterious it is.\u201d  Another way Jobs manufactured his aura was with product\nunveilings. He obsessively prepared for the choreographed\noccasions, often at Apple\u2019s Cupertino campus or  San Francisco \u2019s\n Moscone Center , rehearsing his delivery many times over. He\nwould scrap presentations wholesale, even at the last minute, if\nthey weren\u2019t up to snuff.  He captivated audiences, and the gadgets he introduced\nresonated with consumers the world over, adding billions of\ndollars in revenue. Sales surged 82 percent to a record $28.6\nbillion in the June 2011 period, the last full quarter before\nJobs resigned, and the stock closed at $376.18 on Aug. 24,\nbefore the move was announced. That gave Apple a market value of\n$348.8 billion.  All that success came with an ego to match. Jobs was a\nnotorious control-freak with authority issues, associates and\nformer employees say. He came close to breaking securities laws\nby backdating employee stock options. Even his worsening health\n-- or his non-disclosure of his illness to shareholders -- drew\nscrutiny from authorities.  \u2018Park Different\u2019  In Apple\u2019s parking lot,  people often noticed  Jobs\u2019 silver\nMercedes-Benz SL 55 AMG parked in the handicapped spaces. His\ncars were easy to spot because he refused to put license plates\non them. \u201cIt\u2019s a little game I play,\u201d he told Fortune in 2001.\nEmployees stuck notes under the car\u2019s windshield wipers,\nencouraging Jobs to \u201cPark Different,\u201d a play on the \u201cThink\nDifferent\u201d Apple advertising slogan.  Jobs was known to praise people one minute and belittle\nthem the next. According to  \u201cThe Second Coming of Steve Jobs\u201d \nby Alan Deutschman, this management style was known at Apple as\nthe \u201chero-shithead roller coaster.\u201d No one was immune from\nJobs\u2019s tirades, and he had strained relationships with\ncolleagues, friends, and family throughout his life.  \u2018Like a Campfire\u2019  \u201cSteve Jobs is a bit like a campfire,\u201d Neil Sims, a\nheadhunter who helped recruit executives for Jobs, said in an\ninterview in October 2008. \u201cEveryone wants to be close enough\nto stay warm. No one wants to get close enough to get burned.\u201d  Steven Paul Jobs  was born  Feb. 24, 1955, in San Francisco,\nto unwed college graduate students Joanne Carole Schieble and\nSyrian emigrant Abdulfattah \u201cJohn\u201d Jandali. He was adopted by\nClara and Paul Jobs, who raised Steve in the middle-class\nenclaves of Mountain View and Los Altos in  California .  \u201cThat was right in the heart of Silicon Valley, so there\nwere engineers all around,\u201d Jobs said in a 1995  interview \nconducted by the Smithsonian Institution. \u201cIt was really the\nmost wonderful place in the world to grow up.\u201d  Jobs took advantage of the local technological ferment. His\nfather had a workshop in the garage, and created a space for his\nson to tinker. A neighbor, who was a ham radio operator and\nHewlett-Packard employee, taught him about electronics. Young\nSteve loved figuring out how things worked.  \u201cIt gave a tremendous level of self-confidence,\u201d Jobs\nsaid in the  Smithsonian interview . \u201cThrough exploration and\nlearning one could understand seemingly very complex things.\u201d  Self-Confidence  That self-confidence was on full display before he hit high\nschool. As Jobs once told BusinessWeek, at age 12 he called\nWilliam Hewlett, the co-founder of  Hewlett-Packard Co. (HPQ) , about\nsome parts for a frequency counter he was trying to build.\nHewlett stayed on the phone 20 minutes; Jobs got the parts he\nneeded -- and eventually, a summer gig at Hewlett-Packard.  Catherine Lawler Jacobs, who lived around the block from\nthe Jobs family, said she remembers Steve as a teen. Jobs\nappeared in her driveway one day, asking for her help setting up\nan office in his parents\u2019 house. She\u2019d been earning money\nselling turquoise jewelry and a neighbor recommended her as\nsomeone who knew a little about business. Jobs had no money to\npay her but offered her shares in his new company.  \u201cI said, and I remember this exactly, \u2018I don\u2019t want any\nphony shares. I want to get paid,\u2019\u201d Jacobs recalled in an\ninterview. \u201cYou see, I wasn\u2019t going to be burned by some nerd\nwho was always hanging out in his garage.\u201d  5-Cent Cans  In 1972 Jobs graduated from  Homestead High School  in\nCupertino, also the alma mater of his future business partner,\nSteve Wozniak, Class of 1968. He then headed north to attend\n Reed College , a liberal arts school in Portland, Oregon, famous\nfor its Bohemian atmosphere. He dropped out after six months.  He didn\u2019t leave right away, though. He stuck around campus\nfor another year and a half, sleeping on friends\u2019 floors and\nliving off the money he raised by collecting bottles for 5-cent\ndeposits. He listened in on classes, too, including one that\nwould inspire a lifelong mission of elegant design -- a course\non calligraphy.  \u201cIt was beautiful, historical, artistically subtle in a\nway that science can\u2019t capture, and I found it fascinating,\u201d\nJobs said in a 2005  commencement address  at Stanford University.  As Jobs  told  those Stanford grads, he \u201cconnected the\ndots\u201d between this developing aesthetic sense and his technical\nunderstanding. He realized that technology and artistry could be\ncomplementary. More than that, the new world of computers\noffered a new medium for creativity.  Back in California  By late 1974, Jobs was back in California, immersed in the\ntechnology-tinged counterculture of Silicon Valley. He traveled\nto India, became a Buddhist, experimented with LSD. He also hung\nout with his friend Wozniak -- they\u2019d met a few years earlier\nthrough a fellow electronics enthusiast -- at the  Homebrew\nComputer Club , a group of engineers and hobbyists who would meet\nto swap parts and ideas.  \u201cHe was one of those cool guys,\u201d Wozniak said in an\ninterview with Bloomberg TV after Jobs\u2019s death. \u201cHe knew\ntechnology, he understood it. We talked about the philosophies\nof the day, the hippy movement, words in songs and went to\nconcerts together. It was a strong friendship.\u201d  The two started working together on projects, with Woz the\ntech genius and Jobs the brash idea man. An early effort was a\n\u201cblue box\u201d -- a hacker\u2019s term for a device that taps into the\nphone system to make free long-distance calls. It worked.  \u201cWhat we learned was that we could build something\nourselves that could control billions of dollars worth of\ninfrastructure in the world,\u201d Jobs said in the 1996 PBS\ndocumentary \u201c Triumph of the Nerds .\u201d \u201cThat was an incredible\nlesson. I don\u2019t think there would ever have been an Apple\ncomputer had there not been blue boxes.\u201d  Apple\u2019s Origins  Wozniak began putting together a contraption he and Jobs\ncould show off to their Homebrew buddies. The Apple I was little\nmore than a motherboard, the main circuit board in a personal\ncomputer. Whoever bought one -- Woz and Jobs sold 50 to a local\nhobby store -- had to supply their own case to hold the\ncircuitry, not to mention a keyboard and monitor. It may have\nbeen primitive, but it was the proof of concept they needed.\nThey knew they could build a better computer, and Jobs knew\npeople would buy it.  The pair officially began Apple Computer on April 1, 1976.\nTwelve months later the company introduced the Apple II. It was\na hit and became the first widely used home computer. The\ncompany\u2019s sales reached $117 million in fiscal 1980, the year\nthe company went public.  \u2018Welcome IBM. Seriously\u2019  The Apple II was hardly a technological great leap forward.\nYet unlike its predecessor, it did come with a keyboard and was\nhoused in a plastic case. Nor was it alone in the marketplace.\n Commodore  and  RadioShack Corp. (RSH)  also came out with early home-\ncomputer models around the same time; the Altair 8800 had been\nintroduced in 1975.  IBM entered the market in 1981 with its own PC, using\nsoftware from a tiny startup called Microsoft Corp. rather than\nbuilding its own operating system. Jobs professed to be\nunconcerned, even running a full-page ad in the Wall Street\nJournal, saying \u201cWelcome, IBM. Seriously.\u201d  The Mac\u2019s slow start gave IBM and other machines running\nMicrosoft software and  Intel Corp. (INTC)  chips a chance to win\nadherents and build an ecosystem.  Us Against Them  What set Apple apart was its charismatic frontman, Jobs,\nwho was rapidly turning into a business superstar. He hyped. He\ndated Joan Baez and Diane Keaton. He saw himself and his company\nas an anti-establishment force, waging a noble campaign to\nbattle the faceless power of IBM.  \u201cYou always need to have bad guys and good guys in\nAmerica,\u201d said McKenna, the technology marketing expert.\n\u201cApple was thumbing its nose at this big world of monolithic\nstandards. It became a rebel. It became a symbol of fast growth,\nyouth.\u201d  Us-versus-IBM was the guiding worldview behind the famous\nTV commercial that introduced Apple\u2019s next major product, the\nMacintosh. The  60-second spot , directed by Ridley Scott, ran\nonly once, during the 1984 Super Bowl. It depicted an Orwellian\nworld of grim conformity. A lone woman wearing a tank top\nsprints through the grayness and throws a hammer through a giant\nscreen, shattering the droning visage of  Big Brother .  The Mac, with its mouse and graphics, demonstrated Jobs\u2019s\nability to see the potential of new technologies and package\nthem in a way that would appeal to the most demanding aesthete\nhe could imagine: himself.  Matter of Taste  Jobs had first seen a graphical user interface prototype a\nfew years earlier on a visit to  Xerox Corp. (XRX) \u2019s  Palo Alto Research\nCenter , and immediately knew it was the future of computing. He\nhad no compunction about copying the idea.  \u201cUltimately it comes down to taste,\u201d Jobs said in\n\u201cTriumph of the Nerds.\u201d \u201cIt comes down to trying to expose\nyourself to the best things that humans have done and then\ntrying to bring those things in to what you\u2019re doing. I mean,\nPicasso had a saying. He said, \u2018Good artists copy. Great artists\nsteal.\u2019\u201d  The Mac project showed another side of Jobs: the\ninscrutable autocrat. He could be charming and rude almost in\nthe same sentence, leaving underlings scared or dazzled or both.\nPeople who worked for Jobs called his powers of persuasion the\n\u201creality distortion field.\u201d  \u2018Indomitable Will\u2019  Andy Hertzfeld, an early Apple engineer, described the\nphenomenon in \u201c Revolution in the Valley ,\u201d his 2005 book about\nthe development of the Macintosh computer.  \u201cThe reality distortion field was a confounding melange of\na charismatic rhetorical style, an indomitable will and an\neagerness to bend any fact to fit the purpose at hand,\u201d\nHertzfeld wrote. \u201cIf one line of argument failed to persuade,\nhe would deftly switch to another.\u201d  Andrea Cunningham, who worked with McKenna on marketing\nthe Mac in the 1980s, said that Jobs\u2019 intolerance of aesthetic\ninfractions never let up. Cunningham was with Jobs in his room\nat  The Carlyle  hotel in  New York  City for a magazine cover\nshoot. Jobs, who Cunningham said \u201calways had to have the\nenvironment exactly right,\u201d began yelling about a particular\nflower he wanted -- a calla lily.  \u201cHe was being such a pill,\u201d said Cunningham, who is now\n head of marketing  of Rearden Commerce in Foster City,\nCalifornia. \u201cWhere do you get a  calla lily  in New York in\nDecember at 11 at night? I found a florist. I found the calla\nlilies. And the next thing was a bowl of strawberries on the\npiano. And a separate bowl of whipped cream. We spent three or\nfour hours doing this.\u201d  Courting Sculley  Jobs could bewitch too, as he did when he hired PepsiCo\nInc. executive John Sculley to be Apple\u2019s CEO in 1983. Jobs\nfamously asked him, \u201cDo you want to sell sugar water for the\nrest of your life, or do you want to come with me and change the\nworld?\u201d  \u201cHe looked up at me and just stared at me with the stare\nthat only Steve Jobs has,\u201d  Sculley recalled  in \u201cTriumph of the\nNerds.\u201d \u201cI just gulped because I knew I would wonder for the\nrest of my life what I would have missed.\u201d  Not long after the launch of the Mac, Jobs\u2019 relationship\nwith Sculley and Apple\u2019s board soured. Arthur Rock, the Silicon\nValley venture capitalist and early Apple board member, said\nJobs\u2019s obsessions and unyielding personality got the best of\nhim.  Jobs Ousted  \u201cBack then he was uncontrollable,\u201d Rock said in a 2007\ninterview with Institutional Investor. \u201cHe got ideas in his\nhead, and the hell with what anybody else wanted to do. Being a\nfounder of the company, he went off and did them regardless of\nwhether it ended up being good for the company.\u201d  The Mac  didn\u2019t sell well  during the 1984 holiday shopping\nseason, and Sculley demanded in April 1985 that Jobs be relieved\nof day-to-day duties and serve as a non-executive chairman,\nplaying the role of outside spokesman. Jobs hated the idea and\ntried to get the backing of Apple\u2019s directors. The board sided\nwith Sculley and Jobs was out.  Jobs was 30 years old and devastated, but not for long.  \u201cI didn\u2019t see it then,\u201d Jobs said in his 2005 Stanford\nspeech, \u201cbut it turned out that getting fired from Apple was\nthe best thing that could have ever happened to me. The\nheaviness of being successful was replaced by the lightness of\nbeing a beginner again.\u201d  In 1985 he founded NeXT, which developed a powerful\ncomputer based on the Unix operating system. The sleek, black\nmachines earned a reputation for elegant design and high\nperformance; Tim Berners-Lee  created the World Wide Web  on a\nNeXT workstation.  Pixar  NeXT was hardly a success. The computers were too expensive\nto gain a wide following. Still, the software developed at NeXT\nwould later provide the technological underpinnings for Apple\nmachines.  The following year,  Jobs bought  George Lucas\u2019s computer-\ngraphics shop for $10 million and renamed it Pixar. The studio\u2019s\nfirst feature film, \u201cToy Story,\u201d was the  top-grossing film  of\n1995, and kicked off an unbroken string of hits.  Walt Disney Co. (DIS) \nbought Pixar in 2006 for $8.06 billion and gave Jobs a seat on\nthe company\u2019s board. He became Disney\u2019s largest shareholder.  In his personal life, Jobs settled down. He married Laurene\nPowell in 1991 in a Buddhist ceremony at the  Ahwahnee Hotel  in\nYosemite National Park, according to biographer Deutschman. The\ncouple have three children.  \u2018Glamorous World\u2019  He also reconciled with his daughter, Lisa Brennan-Jobs,\nwho was born in 1978 to his then girlfriend Chrisann Brennan.\nChrisann raised Lisa mainly on her own. By the time Lisa was a\nteenager and before she attended Harvard University, she moved\ninto her father\u2019s home.  \u201cIn California, my mother had raised me mostly alone,\u201d\nLisa  wrote  in an article for Vogue in 2008. \u201cWe didn\u2019t have\nmany things, but she is warm and we were happy. We moved a lot.\nWe rented. My father was rich and renowned, and later, as I got\nto know him, went on vacations with him, and then lived with him\nfor a few years, I saw another, more glamorous world.\u201d  Neither Lisa Brennan-Jobs nor Chrisann Brennan, now a\npainter in San Francisco, would comment when contacted recently.  Jobs didn\u2019t get in touch with his biological father, John\nJandali, a onetime academic who went on to run beverage services\nat the  Boomtown Casino  in Reno, Nevada. Jandali and Schieble had\nanother child after putting Steve up for adoption, a daughter\nnamed Mona Simpson, now a  novelist . Jandali left the mother of\nhis child. Schieble raised the girl alone.  Gates Ascends  \u201cI\u2019m proud of the fact that he\u2019s my biological son, even\nthough I cannot take credit for anything he\u2019s done,\u201d Jandali\nsaid in an interview at the Boomtown Casino in April 2009. He\nsaid he had never spoken to Steve.  Jobs\u2019s absence from Apple coincided with the ascendance of\n Bill Gates  and  Microsoft Corp. (MSFT) , developer of a graphics-driven\noperating system of its own called Windows. Apple filed, and\neventually lost, a lawsuit against Microsoft, arguing that\nWindows was a Mac knockoff.  When Jobs got wind of Microsoft\u2019s plans for what would\nbecome Windows, he screamed at Gates about ripping Apple off,\naccording to a  1983 essay  by Andy Hertzfeld, the Mac\u2019s chief\nsoftware designer.  Gates coolly replied, \u201cIt\u2019s more like we both had this\nrich neighbor named Xerox, and I broke into his house to steal\nthe TV set and found out that you had already stolen it,\u201d wrote\nHertzfeld, who witnessed the interchange.  \u2018Shut It Down\u2019  Meanwhile, Apple was dying. By late 1997, it had racked up\ntwo years of losses and the Mac\u2019s share of the PC market was in\nthe single digits and falling. On stage at a conference that\nyear, Michael Dell was asked how he would revive Apple if he\nwere CEO.  \u201cWhat would I do? I\u2019d shut it down and give the money back\nto the shareholders,\u201d he said. Jobs would later say the company\nwas 90 days from bankruptcy.  In desperation, Apple agreed to buy NeXT for $400 million\nin late 1996, and Jobs accepted a role as adviser to then-CEO\nGil Amelio. Within seven months, Amelio was gone and Jobs was\nonce again running the company.  One of the first things Jobs did upon retaking the reins\nwas fire all but two of Apple\u2019s board members. His handpicked\nreplacements were Bill Campbell, a former Apple executive and\nthen-CEO of Intuit; Jerome York, former IBM CFO and onetime\nadviser to Tracinda Corp. CEO Kirk Kerkorian; and Jobs\u2019 longtime\nfriend, Oracle CEO Larry Ellison. Ellison left the board in\n2002; York died in 2010. Campbell is still a director.  $1 a Year  Jobs also rebuilt the executive team, installing key\ntechnical managers from NeXT who would help him guide Apple\u2019s\nstrategy over the next decade. They included Jon Rubinstein, who\nhad run NeXT\u2019s hardware engineering, and Avie Tevanian, the\nyoung software engineer who  helped create  NeXT\u2019s operating\nsystem.  Rubinstein went on to lead Apple\u2019s iPod division before\ndeparting for smartphone maker Palm Inc., while Tevanian served\nas chief software technology officer. Jobs also found talent\nwithin Apple, singling out a British-born designer named\nJonathan Ive to lead industrial design.  As a show of Jobs\u2019s not-in-it-for-the-money drive to fix\nApple, he insisted on getting paid $1 a year, a salary package\nthat continued for the remainder of his career.  Jobs\u2019s remuneration instead came mainly from stock options,\nrestricted stock and an $84 million Gulfstream V jet, given to\nhim by the board in 2000.  Billionaire  Jobs\u2019s net worth was at least $6.7 billion as of Sept. 6,\naccording to Bloomberg estimates. His 7.4 percent Disney stake\nwas worth $4.4 billion, and his 5.5 million shares of Apple were\nworth $2.1 billion. Jobs\u2019s 138 million shares of Disney had paid\nhim at least $242 million in dividends before taxes since 2006,\naccording to Bloomberg data.  Stock options let holders buy shares later, usually at the\ntrading price on the day the options were granted. Like other\nSilicon Valley executives, Jobs viewed the securities as a\nnecessary incentive to keep valuable employees.  \u201cThat\u2019s the key asset Apple has -- is its talent,\u201d Jobs\nwould later say in a March 2008 deposition with the Securities\nand Exchange Commission.  \u201cI was very concerned that Apple\ncould really suffer some big losses on its executive team with\nthe business environment we were in, and the competitors coming\nafter our people.\u201d  And like hundreds of other technology companies, Apple\nengaged in \u201cbackdating,\u201d or retroactively changing grant dates\nto those with lower stock prices. The practice could\nartificially boost employee compensation and ran the risk of\nshielding compensation costs from investors. It came under\nscrutiny by the SEC.  Backdating Options  Jobs admitted in 2006 to recommending some favorable dates\non options other than his own. A special committee of Apple\u2019s\nboard exonerated him of any misconduct, and the SEC said in\nApril 2007 that Apple wouldn\u2019t be sanctioned.  \u201cJobs was one of these CEOs who ran the company like he\nwanted to -- he believed he knew more about it than anyone else,\nand he probably did,\u201d Arthur Levitt, a former chairman of the\nSEC, said in a February 2009 interview.  Levitt said that around the time of the two grants that got\nApple in trouble, Jobs invited him to join the company\u2019s board -\n- then disinvited him because his views on corporate governance\nwere \u201ctoo independent, too doctrinaire\u201d for Jobs.  Levitt also praised Jobs.  \u201cHe\u2019s among the best CEOs I\u2019ve ever known, in spite of his\nirreverence, irascibility and ego,\u201d Levitt said.  Back to Apple  When Jobs returned to Apple in 1997, he was still an\nexacting connoisseur of design. Only now, he demonstrated an\nunderstanding that he needed to place his bets carefully. He\nculled the company\u2019s product line, killing money-losing projects\nsuch as the Newton personal digital assistant. He ended the Mac\n\u201cclone\u201d program that let other computer makers install Apple\u2019s\noperating system on their machines; he called the welcoming of\nclones  an \u201cill-conceived\u201d move  that undercut Apple\u2019s own Mac\nhardware sales.  \u201cWe\u2019re always thinking about new markets we could enter,\u201d\n Jobs told  BusinessWeek magazine in 2004. \u201cBut it\u2019s only by\nsaying no that you can concentrate on the things that are really\nimportant.\u201d  \u201cHow he looked at things from a product perspective is\nvery rare,\u201d said Ed Zander, a CEO of Motorola Inc. before it\nsplit into two companies. \u201cYou don\u2019t find many CEOs who have\nthe attention to detail from the product experience point of\nview -- and understand the business side of the house.\u201d  Of Macs, IPods  The first tangible result of Jobs\u2019 return was the iMac,\nwhich he introduced at the Flint Center in Cupertino,\nCalifornia, in 1998. The iMac looked like no other computer: It\nwas a bulbous, sci-fi looking number encased in translucent\nplastic. The  unveiling  that day had all the usual language of a\nJobs keynote -- the iMac was \u201cbeautiful,\u201d \u201ccool,\u201d and \u201ca\nreally big deal.\u201d  The iMac would become Apple\u2019s best-selling desktop ever,\naccording to the company. The decision to offer the computer in\nfive colors flew in the face of the then-common industry\npractice of packaging machines in easy-to-manufacture -- if dull\n-- beige boxes.  \u201cI remember scratching my head at the time, when Apple\nfirst came out with those first little colored desktop Macs, the\niMacs,\u201d said Blake Johnson, an  assistant professor  in\nengineering at Stanford University. \u201cBut the message and splash\nof five different colors was a conscious decision -- okay, we\nhave some supply chain inefficiencies, but those are more than\noffset by the positive impact on customers.\u201d  Software Matters  Apple was profitable again by 1998, and over the next\ndecade released a series of blockbusters that went beyond\ntraditional computing. The iPod media player and the iPhone were\nbeautiful objects that ignited consumer lust in Apple\u2019s sparsely\nelegant -- and typically crowded -- retail stores. Jobs dropped\n\u201cComputer\u201d from the company name in 2007 at the time he\nunveiled the iPhone.  Beneath the contours of Ive\u2019s designs were two less obvious\nachievements. The first was the software that made all those\ndevices work together.  All of it was rooted in a single operating system, OS X,\nwhich had its beginnings in Tevanian\u2019s work at NeXT. Apple\u2019s\ngreat strength, Jobs would say repeatedly, was that it was a\nsoftware company.  \u201cAn iPod is really just software,\u201d Jobs said at the All\nThings D  technology conference  in 2007. \u201cIt\u2019s in a beautiful\nbox -- but it\u2019s software. If you look at what a Mac is, it\u2019s OS\nX. It\u2019s in a beautiful box, but it\u2019s OS X. And if you look at\nwhat an iPhone will hopefully be, it\u2019s software.\u201d  Cancer Diagnosis  The other big achievement was Jobs\u2019 ability to create hits\nby getting industry partners to do his bidding. For the iTunes\nmusic store, he not only demanded that the major music labels\nsell their product over the Internet, but do so at a single\nprice, 99 cents a song.  He convinced AT&T Inc. to modify its network to handle the\niPhone\u2019s many features in exchange for exclusive rights to sell\nthe iPhone to U.S. buyers.  Verizon Communications Inc. (VZ) \u2019s\nwireless division started selling the iPhone in February 2011.  \u201cThe AT&Ts and Verizons of the world want to control the\nsoftware, product, the brand, the colors, where the keyboard\ngoes, the pricing, the distribution,\u201d said Zander, the former\nMotorola CEO, who partnered with Jobs on an early music-playing\nphone. \u201cHere comes Steve and he says to AT&T, you get the\nproduct but I get the brand, I get the colors, I get the\nsoftware, I get the distribution pretty much, I get the\npricing.\u201d  \u2018Follow Your Heart\u2019  Apple\u2019s iPhone became the world\u2019s best-selling smartphone\nin the second quarter of 2011.  Jobs said in 2004 that he had been diagnosed and treated\nfor a neuroendocrine tumor in his pancreas. After surgery to\nremove an islet cell tumor, he took a month off to recuperate\nand declared himself healthy and cancer free.  For a few years he looked that way. He was thinner, which\nwas no surprise after what he\u2019d been through. One person who\nknew him well said that the cancer scare didn\u2019t slow him down,\nconvince him to spend more time with family or reconnect with\nfriends. If anything, Jobs seemed to get even more engaged with\nwork, said this person, who wished to remain anonymous because\nthe matter was private.  During the 2005 Stanford commencement address, Jobs\ndescribed how the inevitability of death was a motivating force\nin his life.  \u201cRemembering you are going to die is the best way I know\nto avoid the trap of thinking you have something to lose. You\nare already naked; there is no reason not to follow your\nheart,\u201d he said.  Reports of Death  Jobs\u2019s appearance changed noticeably by early 2008. He\nstarted looking gaunt. Tech blogs bubbled with discussion about\nwhat was going on. Typical headlines: \u201cThe Incredible Shrinking\nApple CEO,\u201d and \u201c Why Does Steve Jobs Look So Thin? \u201d  When he took the stage at Apple events, Jobs joked about\nhis health. In August of that year, Bloomberg News erroneously\npublished an obituary; at a product launch a month later he\nrecited the Mark Twain line that reports of his death were\ngreatly exaggerated. At another event that year, he projected a\nslide of his blood pressure.  In January 2009, Jobs said that his weight loss was caused\nby a \u201chormone imbalance\u201d; nine days later, he began a five-\nmonth medical leave, handing control of the company to his COO,\nTim Cook. Later that year, he underwent a liver transplant at\nMethodist University Hospital in Memphis.  Illness Disclosure  Apple\u2019s disclosures -- or lack thereof -- around Jobs\u2019s\nhealth became a matter of debate among investors and corporate\ngovernance experts. Some said that because his health was\ncritical to the company\u2019s success, Apple should have said more,\nsooner. The counterargument: privacy laws trump investors\u2019 right\nto know the details of his health.  U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission officials examined\nin 2009 whether the company violated disclosure rules regarding\nJobs\u2019s medical status, a person familiar with the matter said at\nthe time. No legal action was taken.  While Jobs was on leave that year, Apple came under\ncompetitive pressure from an unexpected source:  Google Inc. (GOOG)  The\nsearch giant, whose then-CEO Eric Schmidt was an Apple board\nmember, had gotten into the smartphone business with its Android\noperating system.  Unlike the iPhone, Android phones were made by multiple\nmanufacturers. The budding rivalry evoked the Mac vs. PC\nshowdowns of the 1980s. It pitted a company -- Apple -- that\nmade one kind of device against an array of manufacturers\norbiting around a software operating system -- in this case,\nGoogle\u2019s Android.  \u2018Global Footprint\u2019  By the time Jobs returned to work in June, several Android\ndevices were on the market. Google\u2019s Schmidt resigned from\nApple\u2019s board in August, acknowledging the escalating tension\nbetween the two companies.  \u201cThe economic engine that Steve built is an amazing one in\nterms of cash generation, global footprint distribution,\u201d\nSchmidt said in an interview with Charlie Rose after Jobs\u2019s\ndeath. \u201cIt is just one of the great American success stories.\u201d  Jobs the following year introduced his next epoch-making\nproduct: the iPad. The run-up was full of the buzz that greeted\npast products. What would it look like? What would it do? Only a\nselect handful of developers and media companies got access to\npre-release versions of the iPad, and then only under strict\nconditions. Recipients had to agree to keep the devices tethered\nto a fixed object in rooms that blacked-out windows.  \u2018Antennagate\u2019  At the product unveiling, Jobs said that the tablet\ncomputer would go on sale later that year, calling it\n\u201cmagical.\u201d The public agreed: Apple sold more than 300,000\niPads on day one, and within a few months the device had a near\nmonopoly share of the tablet market that companies led by\nMicrosoft had failed to crack for a decade.  Another momentous product was in store for 2010. The iPhone\n4 boasted a glass front and back and a brushed-steel band around\nthe edge. It also came with a front-facing camera that would\nallow mobile videoconferencing.  While the iPhone 4 was destined for success, this time\nthere was a glitch. Customers who held the phone a certain way\nexperienced dropped phone calls -- the \u201cdeath grip,\u201d it was\ncalled.  At first, Apple denied anything was wrong and suggested\nthat customers were holding the phone incorrectly. The flaw\nsnowballed into a public-relations crisis that came to be known\nas \u201cAntennagate,\u201d stoked by longtime grumbling over service\nquality on the network of AT&T, then the only U.S. iPhone\ncarrier.  Cook Comes to Fore  By July, Jobs had changed his tune. He apologized to\ncustomers and offered free \u201cbumpers,\u201d rubber cases that fit\naround the metal edge of the phone, so that fingertips wouldn\u2019t\ncause any antenna interference.  The imbroglio had little impact on iPhone demand. Apple\nsold 1.7 million iPhone 4 units during the first three days it\nwas on sale; by the end of the year, the iPhone would represent\nnearly 40 percent of revenue.  During the introduction of a new MacBook Air in October\n2010, Jobs appeared thinner than ever. Three months later, Jobs\nsaid he would be taking a new leave of absence to \u201cfocus on my\nhealth.\u201d \u201cI love Apple so much and hope to be back as soon as\nI can,\u201d he said.  For the third time since 2004, Cook took over day-to-day\noperations. He oversaw the introduction of the second version of\nthe iPad and introduced a music-storage service called iCloud.\nHe traveled to  China  to discuss the iPhone with  China Mobile\nLtd. (941) , the country\u2019s largest mobile-phone carrier.  Post-Jobs Era  Jobs announced his resignation Aug. 24. \u201cI have always\nsaid if there ever came a day when I could no longer meet my\nduties and expectations as Apple\u2019s CEO, I would be the first to\nlet you know,\u201d Jobs said in a statement. \u201cUnfortunately, that\nday has come.\u201d  In the weeks preceding his resignation, Jobs was largely\nhousebound, according to a person familiar with the matter.  \u201cUnder Steve\u2019s leadership Apple has not only\nrevolutionized the computer industry but also transformed how\nthe world communicates, plays, shops and works,\u201d Frank Quattrone, CEO of Qatalyst Partners LLP, a Silicon Valley\ninvestment bank, said at the time. \u201cIn the entrepreneur hall of\nfame, he is the charter member. He is, and will remain, an\ninspiration to the world.\u201d  Cook became CEO for good. While Cook had mastered an\nexpanding list of operational roles, including manufacturing,\ndistribution, sales and customer service, he hadn\u2019t demonstrated\nJobs\u2019s penchant for product vision.  Ive, Forstall, Schiller  In the post-Jobs era, that role would lie more squarely\nwith head product designer Ive, who oversaw the development of\ndevices including the iMac, iPod, iPhone and iPad.  Rounding out the executive team are Scott Forstall, who is\nin charge of the iOS software that powers the iPhone and iPad;\nPhilip Schiller, who leads product marketing; Bob Mansfield, who\nheads Mac hardware engineering; and Chief Financial Officer\nPeter Oppenheimer, who is tasked with overseeing Apple\u2019s more\nthan $75 billion in cash and long-term holdings.  Jobs left a company with a market value larger than that of\nMicrosoft and Dell combined. Apple\u2019s revenue reached a record\n$65 billion in fiscal 2010, with analysts predicting that they\nwill exceed $100 billion in 2011.  Besides relying on surging demand for the iPhone and iPad,\nApple is also counting on growth in China. \u201cWe\u2019re just\nscratching the surface right now,\u201d Cook said of the region in\nJuly. The company is also due to sell a new service called\niCloud that will let users access photos, videos and other\ncontent across an array of Apple products.  \u2018Magical\u2019 Thinking  The Apple Jobs left behind was well suited to confront the\nchallenges it then faced, including the Google threat, largely\nbecause of a product lineup Jobs set in motion, analysts and\ninvestors said at the time of his resignation. The concern is\nwhether the company can produce industry-disrupting devices long\nafter Jobs\u2019s influence recedes.  \u201cThe world rarely sees someone who has had the profound\nimpact Steve has had, the effects of which will be felt for many\ngenerations to come,\u201d Bill Gates said after his passing.\n\u201cSteve and I first met nearly 30 years ago, and have been\ncolleagues, competitors and friends over the course of more than\nhalf our lives.\u201d  At the AllThingsD conference in 2007, Gates had  said , \u201cI\u2019d\ngive a lot to have Steve\u2019s taste. The successors to the KGB\nclearly don\u2019t have a clue about how the modern economy works.  \n If they had picked  Apple Inc. , Moody\u2019s Investors Service or\nHarvard Business School, they might have had some real influence\nand gained access to useful information.  \n The story of how Russian agents burrowed into ordinary\ncommunities has kept the world enthralled for weeks. At least\ntwo had found their way into important businesses. It emerged\nlast week that a 12th member of the group worked as a software\ntester for Microsoft. Microsoft is a big\nlumbering beast of a company that seems to have forgotten why it\nexists. Barclays is a retail British bank that was lucky to\nsurvive the credit crunch, and while it may be expanding its\ninvestment banking, it isn\u2019t at the cutting edge of anything.  \n If you really want to go undercover in the global economy,\nand manipulate it to your own ends, here\u2019s where to go:  \n Goldman Sachs Group Inc.: The U.S. investment bank is on\nthe inside of every deal. It is ahead of most trends. And its\n alumni network  is the most powerful in the world. Infiltrate it\nsuccessfully, and within a couple of decades you should have one\nof your spies running at least one of the major central banks,\nand probably a finance ministry or two.  \n Harvard Business School : Get one of your agents installed\nat the world\u2019s most influential center of learning and you can\nwreak havoc for years. Teach a whole generation of bright and\nambitious students some crazy theory -- that options trading\nmakes markets safer by spreading risk, for example -- then sit\nback and watch the financial system collapse 20 years later when\nyour moles are running it.  \n A debt rater: As we saw during the Greek debt crisis,\nratings companies have the real power to make or break\neconomies. Even better, they can just make this stuff up. One\nminute Greece was investment grade, the next it was junk,\nalthough not much had changed about the country in the meantime.\nChoose a nation that you want to destroy, then get your agents\ninstalled as analysts at the three main assessors -- Fitch\nRatings, Standard & Poor\u2019s and Moody\u2019s. At the right moment,\npull the trigger, whack it with three downgrades, and watch the\nimplosion. (IBM) \u2019s Watson computer, which beat champions of the quiz show\n\u201cJeopardy!\u201d a year ago, will soon be advising Wall Street on\nrisks, portfolios and clients.  Citigroup Inc. (C) , the third-largest U.S. lender, is Watson\u2019s\nfirst financial services client, IBM said yesterday. It will\nhelp analyze customer needs and process financial, economic and\nclient data to advance and personalize digital banking. (WLP)  and Seton\nHealth Family analyze data to improve care. IBM executives say\nWatson\u2019s  skills  -- understanding and processing natural\nlanguage, consulting vast volumes of unstructured information,\nand accurately answering questions with humanlike cognition --\nare also well suited for the finance industry.  Financial services is the \u201cnext big one for us,\u201d said\nManoj Saxena, the man responsible for finding Watson work. IBM\nis confident that with a little training, the quiz-show star\nthat can read and understand 200 million pages in three seconds\ncan make money for IBM by helping financial firms identify\nrisks, rewards and customer wants mere human experts may\noverlook.  Banks spent about $400 billion on  information technology \nlast year, said  Michael Versace , head of risk research at\nInternational Data Corp.\u2019s Financial Insights, which has done\nresearch for IBM.  Cloud-Based Service  Watson the financial assistant will be delivered as a\ncloud-based service and earn a percentage of the additional\nrevenue and cost savings it is able to help financial\ninstitutions realize. Watson, including its work in the health-\ncare and finance industries, will contribute \u201ca portion\u201d of\nIBM\u2019s  target  of $16 billion of analytics revenues in 2015,\nSaxena said, and that portion will \u201chave a B next to it.\u201d  Watson may add $2.65 billion in revenue in 2015, adding 52\ncents of earnings per share,  Ed Maguire , an analyst at CLSA in\n New York , estimated in a November research note.  IBM, the world\u2019s biggest computer-services provider,\nreported  revenue  of $107 billion in 2011 and earnings of $13.06\na share. The company ended 2011 with $11.9 billion in cash.  IBM shares closed above $200 for the first time yesterday,\nfactoring in stock splits. The stock fell 1.7 percent to $197.26\nat the close in New York today.  Language of Wall Street  Watson \u201ccan give an edge\u201d in finance, said  Stephen Baker ,\n author  of books The Numerati and Final Jeopardy, a Watson\nbiography. \u201cIt can go through newspaper articles, documents,\nSEC filings, and try to make some sense out of them, put them\ninto a context banks are interested in, like risk.\u201d  In addition to Citigroup, Armonk, New York-based IBM has\nbeen working with financial institutions teaching Watson the\nlanguage of  Wall Street , and adding content including regulatory\nannouncements, news and social media feeds. IBM won\u2019t say which\nother institutions Watson is already working with.  \u201cIt\u2019s not selling them software, it\u2019s selling them\noutcomes,\u201d Saxena said in a phone interview. It can also\nmonitor trading, news sources and  Facebook (FB)  to help a treasurer\nmanage foreign exchange risk.  \u2018Huge Marketing Edge\u2019  Some of the biggest financial institutions have already\nbuilt big data centers. (MSFT)  to\nobtain intelligence for businesses by teaching machines to\nunderstand sentences and paragraphs rather than searching for\nsingle words or phrases, said author Baker.  Parts of Watson could already be combined with other IBM\ntechnologies to help banks with regulatory compliance by\nsurveying internal documents and flagging those that seem amiss,\nBaker said. Watson was designed to be loaded with information\nrather than grapple with a live streaming feed, making it likely\nIBM will partner it with other technologies.  Applications Beyond Banking  Beyond banks and other financial institutions, and\ninsurance companies, Watson may have applications for\ntelecommunications companies, and perhaps even call centers,\nsaid Saxena, who joined IBM when it acquired his company Webify\nSolutions Inc. in 2006.  IBM plans to use Watson in financial services \u201cmostly for\nportfolio risk management, they\u2019re not going to do stock\npicking,\u201d CLSA\u2019s Maguire said in a Feb. 17 phone interview.\n\u201cThey think that Watson can make a difference.\u201d Still, Watson\nisn\u2019t perfect. It is weak in languages other than English, and\nits processing of social media streams from platforms including\nFacebook and Twitter can be sluggish. The lag is \u201cgetting\nshorter\u201d, Saxena said. Now meet what makes it possible: the  Leap Motion Controller , an $80 device that\u2019s already responsible for at least 73,600 online references to the Steven Spielberg-Tom Cruise movie \u201c Minority Report .\u201d  The controller, which is about the size of a pack of gum, connects to your Windows PC or  Apple (AAPL)  Mac via a USB cable. Sensors on its top create an invisible bubble about two feet around, within which your hands\u2019 motions and gestures are sensed and translated into actions on the screen.  This being new technology, you shouldn\u2019t expect a polished user experience, and indeed I encountered a number of hiccups. But early adopters willing to put up with its quirks can have some fun.  Using the controller and special Leap Motion-enabled apps, I was able to virtually dissect a frog simply by moving my hands. I was also able to page through a selection of  New York Times (NYT)  stories, play drums and soar around the Earth at hyperspeed, all without touching the computer.  No Lag  It took me a while to get the hang of controlling the screen with my hands, but once I did I found the Leap Motion device swift and sensitive. There was no discernible lag time in interpreting my gestures, and it could distinguish not just my hands but individual fingers.  The Leap Motion unit is a cousin to  Microsoft (MSFT) \u2019s Kinect, the motion controller first introduced for the Xbox game console and now available for Windows PCs too. But the much-larger Kinect is designed for whole-body sensing, while the Leap Motion is intended for close-in work focusing solely on your hands.  Installation took about five minutes, and couldn\u2019t have been much simpler. Once I connected the unit -- Leap Motion thoughtfully provides two cables, one long and the other short -- I downloaded the software and was ready to go.  Or would have been, except that the 2009-vintage machines I installed it on, a Windows PC and MacBook Pro, proved insufficient. Only up-to-date hardware is powerful enough to make use of the controller: at a minimum, an  Intel (INTC)  Core i3 or  AMD (AMD)  Phenom II processor, Windows 7 or 8 for Microsoft-powered PCs and Snow Leopard for Macs.  Other Issues  I was able to install it successfully on two more recent Macs and a Windows PC, all with i5 processors. But I ran into other issues as well.  Sometimes, things on the screen would bounce around even when my hands were still; the company says that might have been caused by the amount or type of ambient lighting. (Among other things, halogen bulbs can cause interference, and a light located directly above the sensor can confuse it.)  In addition, Leap Motion\u2019s digital-rights management scheme made my  Symantec (SYMC)  Internet-security program go nuts; the company says it\u2019s working with antivirus companies to get their programs updated to recognize that its software poses no threat.  Initially, at least, most users will probably take advantage of the Leap Motion\u2019s capabilities through dedicated apps downloaded from its online marketplace, called Airspace. About 75 are available at launch, in categories ranging from games to productivity.  Showing Off  These early apps vary widely in quality as well as price, and many of them seem more designed to show off the sensor\u2019s capabilities than to perform useful functions. The Times app, for instance, displays only a handful of stories; you page through them with your hand, select one by hovering over it and scroll up and down by rotating your finger.  If the technology catches on, you can also expect to see motion control built into existing software. It\u2019s already, for instance, supported in the  Google (GOOG)  Earth satellite-imagery  virtual-globe  program.  The Leap Motion technology has stirred a great deal of interest in the tech community. At launch, the controller is being sold at  Best Buy (BBY)  stores in the U.S. and from  Amazon.com (AMZN) \u2019s  UK site , while PC makers  Hewlett-Packard (HPQ)  and  Asus (2357)  have also struck deals to bundle it with some of their models. (HP has plans to build the technology directly into some machines as well.)  For now, it\u2019s a work in progress, one whose transformative power is more theoretical than real. Still, it provides a fascinating glimpse into one potential future.  Come to think of it, wasn\u2019t that the plot of \u201cMinority Report?\u201d  ( Rich Jaroslovsky  is a Bloomberg News columnist. The opinions expressed are his own.)  Muse highlights include Jason Harper on  cars  and Philip Boroff on  theater . U.S. District Judge Kevin Castel in  Manhattan  yesterday\ndenied a request by Wireless Ink Corp. to depose  Facebook  co-\nfounder Zuckerberg.  \u201cIf the CEO of Facebook has relevant knowledge not readily\navailable from other sources, Wireless Ink ought to be able to\nestablish this from documents produced in discovery or the\ntestimony of other employees of Facebook,\u201d Castel said in his\norder.  Wireless Ink, which operates the Winksite social networking\nservice, said in a complaint filed in 2010 that Facebook Mobile\nand  Google Inc. (GOOG) \u2019s Google Buzz infringed a patent related to ways\nof offering content on mobile devices.  Facebook\u2019s lawyers said in a letter to the judge that\nWireless Ink \u201chas not identified any relevant knowledge that\nMr. Zuckerberg uniquely possesses that cannot be obtained from\nother witnesses.\u201d  Facebook, based in Menlo Park, California, is planning an\ninitial public offering of stock.  The case is Wireless Ink Corp. v. Facebook Inc., 10-01841,\nU.S. District Court, Southern District of  New York  (Manhattan).  USPTO\u2019s \u2018Patents for Humanity\u2019 Prize to Speed Up Office Process  The U.S. Patent and Trademark Office has set up a project\nthat will move some patent owners to the head of the line for\nproceedings within the office if their patented technology has\nbeen used for neglected humanitarian issues.  The  \u201cPatent for Humanity\u201d project , which will run for 12\nmonths, is aimed at public health  or quality-of-life issues\naffected the poor, the patent office said in a  statement \nyesterday.  Judges, drawn from academia in medicine, law science,\nengineering, public policy or a related field, will consider\napplications in four categories: medical, food and nutrition,\nclean technology and information technology.  Winners will receive an \u201cacceleration certificate\u201d which\ncan move several different kinds of patent-office procedures to\nthe head of the line, including patent appeals and re-\nexaminations. The certificate can be used for one item in the\nwinner\u2019s portfolio, regardless of whether it is related to the\nhumanitarian program.  The submission period for applications runs from March 1\nthrough Aug. 31.  Copyright  Lenovo, Computer Makers Settle Case Over Green Dam Software  Lenovo Group Ltd. The Chinese government made Green Dam\nmandatory on personal computers sold there in 2009. (GOOG) \u2019s requirement to make new\npatent-licensing offers to Apple Inc. and  Microsoft (MSFT)  Corp. under\nits settlement with the U.S. Federal Trade Commission probably\nwon\u2019t resolve lawsuits among the technology giants, according to\npatent lawyers.  Last week\u2019s agreement requires Google to offer competitors\n\u201cfair and reasonable\u201d terms for using its patents included in\nindustrywide standards for smartphones, tablet computers and\nother electronic devices, and to give them time to respond.  Microsoft and Apple rejected earlier royalty demands,\naccused Google\u2019s Motorola Mobility unit of misusing its patents,\ncomplained to U.S. and European regulators and filed breach-of-\ncontract suits in federal court.  \u201cIt\u2019s going to be a more reasonable offer than last time -\n- I\u2019m not sure it\u2019s going to be perfectly reasonable,\u201d said\npatent lawyer Robert Stoll of Drinker Biddle in Washington,\nwho\u2019s not involved in the disputes. \u201cYou might see further\nactivity by the FTC if they think Google is not acting in good\nfaith.\u201d  The global litigation has become central to shaping the\nworldwide market for mobile devices, which includes phones,\ntablets and e-readers, that reached $436 billion last year and\nis projected to almost double to $847 billion by 2016, according\nto  Carl Howe , an analyst with  Yankee Group .  Patent Abuse  The FTC agreement resolved claims that Motorola Mobility,\nwhich Google bought for $12.4 billion last year, abused patents\nessential to industry standards to extract higher royalties.\nIndustry-standard technology helps ensure products such as\nmobile phones can operate together when made by different\nmanufacturers, meaning companies making those products must\nconform with the standards.  Under the FTC settlement, Google can\u2019t try to block sales\nor imports of competitors\u2019 products during the license-offer\nprocess and must report to the FTC on steps it\u2019s taken to\ncomply.  In a filing with the U.S. International Trade Commission\ntoday, Microsoft said that means Google must drop two video-\ncoding patents from a case in which it seeks to block imports of\nthe Xbox gaming system. The third patent, for a way to establish\ncommunication between the Xbox and accessories, doesn\u2019t relate\nto any industry norm, so wouldn\u2019t be affected by the FTC\nagreement.  \u201cAs a result of the settlement Motorola and Google have\nentered with the FTC, Microsoft expects that Motorola will\nimmediately dismiss from this investigation its claims\u201d related\nto the two patents, Microsoft said in the filing.  Wireless Claims  The commission already has cleared  Apple (AAPL)  of claims it\ninfringed Motorola Mobility patents for wireless technology.  Making offers to appease the FTC, and European regulators\nwho are investigating Google\u2019s practices, may not be enough to\nstop the litigation among the companies, said James Kulbaski, a\npatent lawyer with Oblon Spivak in Alexandria,  Virginia , who\u2019s\nnot involved in the cases.  Microsoft, which said the FTC agreement does little to\nresolve issues it raised over Google\u2019s business practices,\nprobably will decide it would rather wait to hear from a federal\njudge in  Seattle  who is considering what the appropriate royalty\nshould be, he said. Apple, in a different case, has told a judge\nin  Wisconsin  that it won\u2019t pay Motorola Mobility more than $1\nper handset.  Apple also is trying to get Motorola Mobility and other\nmakers of phones that use Google\u2019s Android operating system to\nstop what it calls copying of the iPhone.  \u2018Clear Rules\u2019  \u201cIt takes two entities to reach a settlement and Apple has\nmade clear they are doing everything they can to seek every\npossible remedy,\u201d Kulbaski said. \u201cIf Apple\u2019s not willing to\nsettle, there can\u2019t be a global settlement.\u201d  Kristin Huguet, a spokeswoman for Apple, said the\nCupertino, California-based company had no comment.  The agreement doesn\u2019t require  Mountain View , California-\nbased Google to drop lawsuits where it is seeking cash damages.\nNor is it precluded from trying to block imports or sales of\ncompetitors\u2019 products after taking the steps required by the\nFTC, including an offer of binding arbitration on issues that\ncan\u2019t be resolved through negotiations.  The agreement \u201cestablishes clear rules of the road for\nstandards essential patents going forward,\u201d Google said in a\n statement .  Thwarting Competition  At issue are Motorola Mobility patents related to technical\nstandards on things like wireless transmissions and video\ndecoding, a legacy of the company\u2019s history as a mobile-phone\npioneer. As one of the companies that helped establish\nspecifications for how the phones operate, Motorola Mobility\npledged to license any relevant patents on fair terms to anyone\nwho asked.  It demanded royalties equal to 2.25 percent of the retail\nprices of products and devices including Microsoft\u2019s Xbox and\nApple\u2019s iPhone. Redmond, Washington-based Microsoft said that\nwould amount to $4 billion a year, a figure Motorola Mobility\ndisputed. Motorola Mobility lowered the offer in June, to what\nMicrosoft said was still unreasonable.  Because companies that participate in standard-setting\ngroups have an advantage in getting their technology adopted,\nthe FTC and European Commission have argued standard-setters\nshouldn\u2019t be allowed to use those patents to thwart competition.\nA patent gives its owner the right to exclude others from using\nthe invention.  Judges in Seattle and  Chicago  have said Motorola Mobility\nisn\u2019t entitled to orders halting U.S. sales of products based on\nthe use of standard-essential patents. The ITC, which has the\npower to block imports, is considering similar rules.  Court Bans  Microsoft and Apple pledged not to seek court bans based on\nstandard-essential patents to help gain Justice Department\nclearance to join a group that bought Nortel Networks Corp.\npatents in July 2011 for $4.5 billion. Apple, in a patent fight\nwith  Nokia Oyj (NOK1V)  that was settled in 2011, argued against the\nFinnish company\u2019s use of standard-essential patents in the\ndispute.  Google, while seeking regulatory approval to buy Motorola\nMobility, said it would continue the handset maker\u2019s policy of\nnot seeking sales bans as long as licensing negotiations were\nunder way. In Chapter 7, an impartial trustee is appointed to administer the case and sell assets such as automobiles.  Fresh Start  Chapter 7 is designed to give an individual a \u201crelatively fast\u201d fresh start and usually doesn\u2019t give creditors \u201cany significant dividends,\u201d said Harvey Miller, lead bankruptcy lawyer to defunct Lehman Brothers Holdings Inc. Inc.'s Chief Executive Officer Marissa Mayer gave for her  $1.1 billion acquisition  of Tumblr Inc. was the opportunity to target the elusive 18 to 34-year-old demographic with the company's endless web of online advertising. The financials of the deal are a little more difficult to grasp: Yahoo's revenue has stagnated over the last few years and Tumblr is still so new that it barely has any revenue at all, much less any profit. One difficulty is that Yahoo, which generates the majority of its income through banner ads, is taking over a blogging site whose founder loves to proclaim that he hates online advertising. The bigger problem is the way Yahoo is paying for the acquisition. The accompanying chart shows Yahoo's revenue over the last few years. As other technology companies such as Google Inc. and Microsoft Corp. introduced new products and branched out into new markets, Yahoo fell behind. The one bright spot was its 40 percent stake in China's  largest e-commerce  company, Alibaba Group Holdings Ltd. In 2012, however, Yahoo agreed to  sell back  half its stock in a company that dominates a high-growth market in the world's fastest-growing region. The deal, which Yahoo's board approved unanimously, was worth $7 billion, of which Yahoo netted $3.65 billion after taxes and buybacks. This week, Yahoo used a chunk of that cash to buy Tumblr.  Being a pessimist about the growth of social media won't make you popular but arguing against the growth of e-commerce in Asia is a good reason to get your head examined. According to the World Bank, only 38 percent of China's 1.3 billion people had access to the Internet in 2011 -- by contrast, 78 percent of the U.S. population was online.  Of the 512 million people who accessed the Internet in China,  about half  engaged in some form of e-commerce, accounting for 1.26 trillion yuan ($205 billion) in exchanges. Alibaba handled almost 90 percent of those transactions. According to  Morgan Stanley , the company's net income this year could surpass $2 billion -- double the total last year. Alibaba and its sites charge a fee for every transaction they process, much like a credit-card company. Though Alibaba's  dominance  is far from sustainable, even in China, as more Chinese begin using the Internet its revenue will inevitably increase even as its market share drops off.  Contrast that with Tumblr, a company that has never posted a profit and operates in a crowded market that isn't particularly favorable to its business model of corporate marketing.  The company's founder, David Karp, made his direction clear when he  told  the Los Angeles Times in 2010, \"We're pretty opposed to advertising.\" The problem advertisers have with social media platforms, besides the prickly high school drop-out geniuses who run them, is that these wunderkind typically have no idea how to profitably operate their creations.  Yahoo still brings in the majority of its income from those ads you see at the top, bottom or side of a webpage. Purchasing Tumblr gives Yahoo access to more eyes for its banner ads within the 18 to 34-year-old demographic -- and it gives Yahoo another platform to sell advertising on (even though Yahoo has promised not to \"screw up\" Tumblr with its eyesore ads).  In 2002, Yahoo could have  bought Google  for $5 billion. A decade later, it has sold off most of its shares in Alibaba. Ten years from now, both decisions may look equally bad. (Alex Bruns is on the staff of Bloomberg View. While some queries can\nbe answered quickly from Intel\u2019s annual sustainability\nreport, others require further research, so Fallender\nprioritizes a core list of about a dozen requests and responds\nto the rest when she can get to them. \u201cThere are many, many\nratings out there,\u201d she says. \u201cMore every year.\u201d  Investors and the public are demanding increasingly\ndetailed information on nonfinancial metrics that define\nsustainability. Companies that take the lead in the field, the\nthinking goes, are likely to continue churning out profits in\nan era of growing global competition, climate change, and\ndiminishing resources. In response, scores of data analysis\nand rating outfits have sprung up, vying to be the arbiter of\nwho\u2019s really green. That\u2019s \u201cconfusing, congested, chaotic,\u201d\nsays Allen White, a senior fellow at the Tellus Institute, a\nnonprofit research group. \u201cIf you are an investor trying to\nmove $1 billion, you\u2019re left throwing up your hands. In the\nworst case, you just ignore all of the ratings.\u201d  White is one of a small cadre of data junkies who have\nspent the past decade trying to get executives, investors, and\nnonprofit groups to agree on how to distinguish dirty, risky\ncompanies from cleaner, sustainable ones. As more companies\npublish annual sustainability reports, many are looking to the\nGlobal Reporting Initiative, a group White co-founded in\n1997, for guidance on the most important factors to disclose.\nToday, 80 percent of the world\u2019s 250 largest companies use\nGRI\u2019s framework for their sustainability reports, according to\nconsultancy KPMG.  Investment managers say many companies don\u2019t go far\nenough in their disclosures. Since GRI\u2019s guidelines are\nvoluntary and reports are rarely audited, few companies\nprovide information on all of the group\u2019s 100-plus metrics in\nareas such as  workplace safety , use of recycled materials, or\ntoxic waste spills. \u201cWe believe current corporate\nsustainability reports are insufficient to form a fully\nintegrated and long-term investment view,\u201d says Paul\nAbberley, CEO of Aviva Investors, an asset manager in  London .  Further complicating the issue: GRI doesn\u2019t judge\nperformance, leaving raters and analysts to evaluate companies\nin ways that are digestible for investors. These groups make\ntheir own determinations as to whether, say,\u00a0Ford\u00a0is more\nsustainable than Volkswagen or\u00a0Microsoft\u00a0is better\nthan\u00a0Apple.\u00a0 Newsweek \u2019s \u201cGreen Rankings\u201d rate companies on\ntheir commitment to the environment,\u00a0Dow Jones publishes\nindexes of companies it deems the most sustainable, and the\nEthisphere Institute ranks the \u201cWorld\u2019s Most Ethical\nCompanies.\u201d Others carve out niches such as evaluating\ntransparency, water usage, or the suitability of the workplace\nfor employees over 50.  Only a third of these groups rely solely on corporate\nsustainability reports; the rest seek extra stats, often\nasking companies to slice and dice numbers in ways that\nconform to the groups\u2019 metrics. Wayne Balta,\u00a0IBM\u2019s\nenvironmental affairs chief, says companies need a \u201crock\nsolid\u201d commitment to data analysis to ease the hassles of\nresponding to such queries. (Bloomberg LP, the owner\nof\u00a0Bloomberg Businessweek, compiles sustainability data and\nscores companies on how much information they disclose.)  In 2000, the consulting firm SustainAbility, which\nadvises clients on green business strategies, identified\n21\u00a0raters; by last year, that number had swelled to 108, both\nnonprofits and companies seeking to sell research to\ninvestors. IBM\u2019s Balta says the rankers\u2019 ranks will probably\ncontinue to grow. \u201cIt\u2019s in our collective American culture to\nrate,\u201d he says. \u201cLook at\u00a0Dancing with the Stars.\u201d  Many companies face further demands from corporate\ncustomers.\u00a0Wal-Mart, for instance, in 2009 brought together\nretailers, suppliers, and research groups to develop a\nsustainability index to track suppliers. The group, a\nnonprofit called the Sustainability Consortium, is creating\nstandards for cotton towels, TVs, yogurt, and nearly 50 other\nproduct categories. For laundry detergents, the biggest factor\nis customers using energy to heat water for washing, so the\nnew metrics favor products for cold-water use. For\nlaptops, the greatest greenhouse gas emissions come during\nmanufacturing, not use by consumers, so the standards largely\naddress production methods. \u201cWe want to make sure we are\nsending the right signals, measuring the right things,\u201d says\nJeff Rice, Wal-Mart\u2019s director of sustainability.  Some corporations grouse that the raters can lack\ntransparency, though few want to say so on the record. About a\nquarter of the ranking groups disclose no information on their\nmethods and a majority offer only partial\ndisclosures, according to \u201cRate the Raters,\u201d a report\nSustainAbility released last year. The upstart online service, which provides easy, low-cost\naccess to broadcast TV over the Internet, is more than just\nnirvana for would-be cable-cutters. It may also be a huge step\ntoward a future when programming options come a la carte,\ndivorced from the expensive packages assembled by cable and\nsatellite carriers.  If, that is, it\u2019s allowed to stay in business.  Aereo is currently available only in New York City, but the\ncompany has announced plans to expand the service to  22 more\ncities  this year, starting in the spring. San Francisco, where\nI\u2019m based, isn\u2019t one of them, but the company set me up with a\ntemporary account allowing me to use the service as if I were in\nNew York.  I found it both powerful and easy to use, turning my tablet\nand smartphone into go-anywhere TVs, complete with DVR features\nto record shows for later viewing -- and, of course, skip over\nthe commercials.  The key to the service -- whose backers include\n IAC\/Interactive Corp.  Chairman  Barry Diller  -- is a tiny, coin-\nsize antenna, deployed by the thousands at Aereo facilities.\nWhen you sign in, you\u2019re assigned two of them, which pull in\nlocal over-the-air broadcast signals, just like the full-sized\naerials that still dot many rooftops.  Streaming Signal  Aereo takes the signal received by \u201cyour\u201d antennas and\nstreams it over the Internet to you. The two antennas allow you\nto record one program for later viewing while you\u2019re watching\nanother live.  There\u2019s no app or special software to download. You log\ninto Aereo through a standard Web browser and can authorize up\nto five devices for viewing.  I tried it using  Apple \u2019s Safari browser on an iPhone and an\niPad;  Google \u2019s Chrome on the iPad,  Samsung \u2019s Galaxy S III phone\nand a Windows PC; and Internet Explorer 10 on a  Microsoft \nSurface Pro PC-tablet.  All were successful except for the Galaxy; the company says\nit\u2019s still working on support for Android devices. (On the\nSurface, I couldn\u2019t use the Windows 8 \u201ctile\u201d version of IE,\nbut the desktop version let me in.)  The service can also be used on a television that\u2019s\nequipped with  Roku \u2019s streaming-media player or by using an Apple\nTV box\u2019s AirPlay feature.  To view your Aereo programs, you can choose low, medium or\nhigh-quality streams, depending on the speed of your Internet\nconnection, or have Aereo automatically configure itself to your\nsignal.  Remarkably Good  The quality on both live and DVR\u2019d content was remarkably\ngood over both Wi-Fi and 4G LTE, with little of the buffering\nand stuttering that can sometimes make video over a wireless\nconnection a painful experience.  Video quality over 3G is lower; as with LTE, you also run\nthe risk of rapidly chewing through any data limits imposed by\nyour carrier.  As the service rolls out, customers will only be allowed to\nsubscribe to the channels available in their markets; you won\u2019t\nbe able to watch Providence stations in Tampa, for instance. But\nthe biggest weakness of the service is the programming that\u2019s\navailable -- or more precisely, the programming that isn\u2019t.  Once I logged in to the service, I had access -- via the\nover-the-air New York City stations -- to all four major\nbroadcast networks: NBC, CBS, ABC, and Fox. I could also get the\nPublic Broadcasting Service and its PBS Kids offshoot, the CW\nnetwork, retailer  HSN  and Spanish-language broadcasters\nTelemundo and Univision -- 31 channels in all.  But almost all the big cable networks were missing. No\nESPN, no CNN, no Fox News, no HBO or Showtime. Many of their\ncorporate parents, including  Walt Disney Co. ,  Comcast Corp. ,\n News Corp.  and  CBS Corp. , are among those driving so-far\nunsuccessful legal efforts to shut the service down.  Cable Names  The best-known cable network on the service may be\nBloomberg TV, which has signed an agreement with Aereo. (The\nchannel is owned by Bloomberg LP, parent of Bloomberg News.)  While the choices are limited, the cost is too: Aereo is a\nfraction of the typical cable or satellite bill.  For $8 a month, you get all the channels live, plus 20\nhours\u2019 worth of storage space for your recorded content; four\ndollars more doubles the storage to 40 hours. There are also\noptions for an annual subscription -- $80 with 40 hours of\nstorage -- and a $1 day pass.  At those prices, and given the disruptive potential of the\nservice, many established players are reacting as if it poses a\nmajor threat. CBS -- whose Chief Executive Officer  Les Moonves \nlast year said Aereo was \u201cnot something I lose sleep over\u201d --\nhas since gone to the  extraordinary length  of barring  CNET , the\ntechnology-news website it owns, from reviewing the service.  I can\u2019t speak to the legal issues involved. But in terms of\nAereo\u2019s power, flexibility and quality of service, it\u2019s a\nwinner.  ( Rich Jaroslovsky  is a Bloomberg News columnist. The European Commission, the EU\u2019s antitrust regulator,\nfailed to provide the required proof to uphold its 2009 decision\nand ignored \u201cpotentially exculpatory\u201d documents from a\ncompetitor and failed to record a meeting with a Dell Inc.\nexecutive, Intel lawyers said.  \u201cProsecutors cannot pick and choose what evidence to\nrecord and which to ignore and thereby prevent exculpatory\nevidence,\u201d Nicholas Green, a lawyer for Intel, told the EU\nGeneral Court in Luxembourg in its opening arguments of a\nhearing scheduled to last four days. \u201cIt represents a wider\nsystemic failure by the commission\u201d and \u201cmust lead to the\ndecision being set aside.\u201d  The EU probe found that Intel impeded competition by giving\nrebates to computer makers from 2002 until 2005 on the condition\nthat they buy at least 95 percent of chips for personal\ncomputers from Intel.
