(GOOG) \u2019s Motorola Mobility unit isn\u2019t entitled to the potentially billions of dollars it sought for its patents on technology used throughout the electronics community, a federal judge ruled in a victory for  Microsoft Corp. (MSFT)   Microsoft should pay about a half-cent per unit for video- decoding technology and 3 1\/2 cents for wireless technology, U.S. District Judge James Robart in  Seattle  said in a decision made public yesterday. That equals about $1.8 million a year, Microsoft said, far less than the 2.25 percent of the retail price on Microsoft products Motorola Mobility initially demanded.  The ruling marks a rare instance in which a U.S. court has set guidelines on how patent owners should value inventions on industrywide standards developed so devices running on different platforms can work together. Participants in these groups promise to license patents on \u201cfair, reasonable and non- discriminatory\u201d terms, an issue that has prompted inquiries by antitrust regulators on three continents involving companies such as Samsung Electronics Co. and  InterDigital Inc. (IDCC)   \u201cPeople are not going to stop participating in standardization because of this -- it\u2019s too important to the market,\u201d said Jorge Contreras, an associate law professor at American University in Washington. He said the ruling will help bring some \u201cdisputes to a speedier close, potentially.\u201d  Standards Patents  Companies meet to develop standards so, for instance, data can be sent to any smartphone no matter the manufacturer, or a video sent from one type of device can be watched on another. Companies that help establish the criteria gain an advantage in having their technology included in standards.  \u201cThis decision is good for consumers because it ensures patented technology committed to standards remains affordable for everyone,\u201d  David Howard , deputy general counsel for Microsoft, said in a statement.  The next step in the case is a trial in August to determine whether, based on the ranges set by Robart, Motorola Mobility met its contractual obligation to license its patents on fair terms.  \u201cMotorola has licensed its substantial patent portfolio on reasonable rates consistent with those set by others in the industry,\u201d Matt Kallman, a spokesman for Motorola Mobility, said in a statement after the ruling.  Among the factors that must be considered, Robart decided, is what would be the total rate charged to manufacturers when added to amounts paid to other patent owners on the standard, and whether that would meet the goal of ensuring a standard gets wide acceptance.  Public Interest  \u201cHe acknowledges the public interest aspect of these calculations,\u201d Contreras said. \u201cIt\u2019s not just two companies going to a back room and coming up with whatever they want to.\u201d  The judge also considered how valuable the patents are to the standard, and how valuable the standard is to the products involved in the dispute, the professor said.  Robart said the proper royalty range for the video-decoding technology, used in both the Xbox video-gaming system and  Windows operating system , should be no more than 16.4 cents per unit.  Motorola Mobility\u2019s portfolio \u201conly constitutes a sliver of the overall technology incorporated\u201d into the standard, Robart said in his 207-page opinion. For the Wi-Fi portfolio, applicable to the Xbox, the upper rate would be 19.5 cents per unit, he said.  Dispute\u2019s Origins  The dispute between Microsoft and Motorola Mobility, then a standalone company, began in 2010, when Redmond, Washington- based Microsoft demanded that Motorola Mobility pay patent royalties on its mobile phones that run on Google\u2019s Android operating system.  Motorola Mobility, which helped establish standards for technologies such as video decoding and Wi-Fi, responded by demanding that Microsoft pay royalties on the Windows operating system and Xbox. It sent letters in October 2010, demanding 2.25 percent on the retail price of the products. Microsoft, which reported $73.7 billion in 2012 revenue, has said the royalties would total more than $4 billion a year, a figure Motorola Mobility disputes.  At trial, Robart\u2019s decision says, Motorola Mobility\u2019s expert testified that, when possible cross-licensing deals were taken into account, Microsoft would pay $36 million to $54 million in fiscal 2011, or a per unit rate of as much as $4.50 for the Wi-Fi technology in each Xbox. For the video-decoding patent, Motorola Mobility\u2019s expert said the net payment would cap at no more than $125 million a year, or as much as 63 cents a unit, according to Robart\u2019s decision.  Patent Pools  While Motorola Mobility focused on the possible outcome of negotiations between the two companies, Microsoft urged the judge to compare the rate charged by patent pools, in which a large number of companies get together and establish a single licensing rate for everyone. Robart mostly sided with Microsoft on this issue.  Microsoft had argued that, based on the different pools for those two standards patents, the proper royalty rate would be pennies per product, with the royalties on the standard for video compression totaling no more than $521,000 a year. It also contended the rate for wireless technology should be based on what it calls the smallest salable unit, meaning the  Marvell Technology Group Ltd. (MRVL)  chips, which cost about $3.  Xbox Demand  Microsoft argued the games -- not wireless technology -- drive demand for the Xbox. Motorola Mobility contended sales of the device fell when Microsoft failed to include Wi-Fi before 2010.  Motorola Mobility said it had originally charged licensees a flat rate of $9 per unit, and converted that to the 2.25 percent royalty at the request of companies that said falling phone prices were pushing the rate up. It said Microsoft refused to make a counteroffer, instead filing the breach-of-contract suit on which Robart ruled.  Apple Inc. (AAPL)  made similar breach-of-contract allegations against Motorola Mobility in a case in federal court in  Wisconsin . U.S. District Judge Barbara Crabb threw out the case last year after Apple said it wouldn\u2019t abide by any royalty rate she set. Apple has filed an appeal.  Google, which bought Motorola Mobility last year, reached an agreement with the U.S. Federal Trade Commission that it wouldn\u2019t seek to block sales of products that comply with industry standards. Kraft, with a $69.3 billion market value that\u2019s ranked 20th\nin the 30-stock gauge, may be dropped because the spinoff of its\nU.S. grocery business will shrink the world\u2019s second-largest\nfood company, said  Keith Wirtz  at Fifth Third Asset Management.\nHewlett-Packard Co. and  Alcoa Inc. I wouldn\u2019t be surprised to see a\nswitch.\u201d  The Dow, which began in 1896 with General Electric Co.,\nAmerican Tobacco and 10 other companies, was taken over last\nweek by S&P Dow Jones Indices, a joint venture of McGraw-Hill\nCos. and CME Group Inc. About $28 billion in products such as\nexchanged-traded funds are linked to the index, and changes\nprompt money managers to buy or sell stocks to match the\nadjustments.  Rare Change  Changes in the composition of the average \u201care rare, and\ngenerally occur only after corporate acquisitions or other\ndramatic shifts in a component\u2019s core business,\u201d according to\nthe S&P Dow Jones Indices Web site. \u201cWhen such an event\nnecessitates that one component be replaced, the entire index is\nreviewed,\u201d and \u201cmultiple component changes are often\nimplemented simultaneously,\u201d it said.  Dave Guarino, a spokesman for S&P Dow Jones Indices,\ndeclined to comment on potential additions and deletions.  Kraft is separating its global snacks business, which will\nbe renamed Mondelez International Inc., from its grocery\nbusiness. Mondelez will retain about $35 billion in annual sales\nfrom brands including Cadbury chocolate and Oreo cookies, while\nthe grocery company will have about $19 billion in revenue,\nbased on 2011 results,  Michael Mitchell , a spokesman for Kraft,\nsaid in an e-mail today. Altria Group Inc. was\ndropped in February 2008, one month before the divestiture of\nits overseas tobacco unit and almost one year after its spinoff\nof Kraft. Westinghouse Electric Corp.\u2019s split into separate\nmanufacturing and media companies led to its removal in 1997.  \u201cIt\u2019s a reasonable expectation that  Kraft (KFT)  is a member\nchange in the Dow Jones,\u201d Wirtz, who oversees $15 billion as\nchief investment officer for Fifth Third in Cincinnati, said in\na July 9 phone interview. \u201cWhenever you have a strategic\nadjustment, a restructuring, it always elevates it to a\npossibility.\u201d  AIG Replaced  Kraft joined the Dow in September 2008, replacing American\nInternational Group Inc. when the insurer\u2019s 97 percent plunge\nthat year spurred a federal bailout amid the U.S. subprime-\nmortgage crisis. Apple, Google  Apple, the world\u2019s largest company by market value, may be\nincluded in the index if the selection committee changes its\nmethodology to include higher-priced stocks, according to\nMoroney at Horizon. Selection Committee  The selection committee for the Dow average may decide not\nto change the components because the gauge still reflects the\nbroad market and moves in line with the Standard & Poor\u2019s 500\nIndex, said Jeffrey Yale Rubin, an analyst at Birinyi Associates\nInc. in Westport,  Connecticut . (ADBE) \u2019s Flash, which is how most Web videos and\ngraphics are displayed today. The aircraft\nmaker plans to increase commercial-jet production by more than\n60 percent between 2010 and 2014.  The facility just north of  Seattle  is where Boeing builds\nwide-body jets. Erected in 1967, it remains the world\u2019s biggest\nbuilding by volume and houses the production lines for the 747\njumbo jet, 767, 777 and the new 787 Dreamliner, which was\nObama\u2019s backdrop. Air Force One, the presidential 747, was\nassembled there.  Boeing a Symbol  \u201cThe president has embraced U.S. manufacturing, and Boeing\nis an iconic symbol of U.S. success,\u201d said  Harley Shaiken , a\nlabor professor at the  University of California  at Berkeley.  The U.S. lost 1.9 million manufacturing jobs since December\n2007, the start of an 18-month recession that was the worst\nsince the Great Depression.  \u201cWe can\u2019t bring every job back,\u201d Obama said. \u201cBut right\nnow, it\u2019s getting more expensive to do business in places like\n China . Meanwhile American workers have never been more\nproductive, and companies like Boeing are finding out that even\nwhen we can\u2019t make things faster or cheaper than China we can\nmake them better.\u201d  Obama also named two new members to the President\u2019s Export\nCouncil today. Gary Loveman, chief executive officer of casino\noperator Caesars Entertainment Corp., and Denise Morrison, CEO\nof Campbell Soup Co., are joining the advisory committee.  Assembly Line  Obama spoke at the end of the 787 assembly line. He was\ngiven a tour of the factory and then appeared to a crowd of\nhundreds of Boeing workers, stepping down to a stage on the\nfactory floor from a red-carpeted staircase leading from a 787\nDreamliner in the livery of United Continental Holdings Inc.,\nwhich will be the first U.S. carrier to fly the plane.  David Eddines, 57, of Everett, a quality technician on the\n787 Dreamliner assembly line, met the president during his tour\nof the factory today with Boeing Chief Executive Officer Jim McNerney and commercial-jet President  Jim Albaugh .  \u201cI found it reassuring that he said America is going to\nrebound,\u201d Eddines said in an interview after Obama\u2019s speech.\n\u201cThere\u2019s a lot of fixing that needs to take place. There\u2019s a\nlot of loopholes for companies taking work abroad.\u201d  In his State of the Union speech, Obama called for a\nprogram to provide credit to companies competing against foreign\ncounterparts that benefit from preferential credit from their\ngovernments.  Foreign Competition  The administration will use existing authority \u201cso that\nthe Export-Import Bank can provide U.S. firms competing for\ndomestic or third-country sales with matching financing support\nto counter foreign non-competitive official financing that fails\nto observe international disciplines,\u201d the White House said in\na statement released in conjunction with Obama\u2019s Boeing visit.  The duopoly in jetliner production shared by Boeing and its\nlarger European rival,  Airbus SAS (EAD) , is being challenged by new\ncompetitors. Canada\u2019s Bombardier Inc. and China\u2019s Comac are\ndeveloping new single-aisle planes set to enter service this\ndecade that will compete with the 737 and the A320, the\nworkhorses of the airline industry.  John Kvasnosky, spokesman for Boeing Capital Corp., said\nObama\u2019s move to increase Ex-Im support was a new initiative.  \u201cWe\u2019re always encouraged about efforts to support U.S.\ncompetitiveness, but we need to understand more about how it\nwould apply in our circumstances,\u201d he said in an interview\nbefore the president spoke.  Plan Critic  Chris Chocola, head of the anti-tax advocacy group Club for\nGrowth, said the aid would just create a \u201ccorporate welfare\nslush fund\u201d for companies with lobbyists, such as Boeing.  \u201cCongress should end the federal bank of Boeing, and\ninstead promote more international trade through corporate  tax\nreform  and lower tariffs,\u201d Chocola said in a statement.  Obama also called for extending the lending authority of\nthe Ex-Im Bank, which may reach its $100 billion ceiling before\nApril. The bank, which is self-sustaining, provides financing to\nU.S. exporters through loans, loan guarantees and payment\ninsurance. About 3,600 companies benefited last year from its\ncredit. Over the last three years the bank supported the export\nof about 460 Boeing jets.  Boeing and the White House have numerous ties: McNerney is\nchairman of the President\u2019s Export Council;  William Daley  left\nBoeing\u2019s board to become Obama\u2019s chief of staff;  John Bryson ,\nalso a Boeing director, became Obama\u2019s Commerce secretary in\nOctober.  NLRB Complaint  Boeing was targeted in a 2011 National Labor Relations\nBoard complaint that Republicans said showed the\nadministration\u2019s hostility toward business. The case was dropped\nafter a new union accord helped pave the way for a planned\noutput boost at the biggest U.S. exporter.  \u201cIt is a love-hate relationship,\u201d with the company and\nthe White House wanting and needing rapport yet clashing over\nregulations, said  Gary Chaison , a labor professor at  Clark\nUniversity  in Worcester,  Massachusetts . \u201cBoeing becomes\nincredibly symbolic now after the troubles they\u2019ve been through\nwith the NLRB.\u201d  Obama is on the last day of a three-day trip in which he\nalso is raising money for his re-election campaign in California\nand Washington state. Not because you want to -- or maybe you do after this ordeal -- but because the doors are closing. Today, MIT is working with the Russians rather than against them.  Just 20 kilometers (12 miles) from the Kremlin, rising from a field once used for agricultural experiments, the  Skolkovo Institute of Science and Technology  will have a curriculum designed by MIT and financial backing from the Russian government, Bloomberg Markets will report in its June issue.  More from the June 2013 issue of Bloomberg Markets The school--nicknamed Skoltech--which will offer graduate degrees only and teach in English, will serve as the centerpiece of an 85 billion ruble ($2.7 billion) innovation hub funded by the Russian Ministry of Finance. Russian officials say they\u2019re aiming to create tech startups and lure corporate research laboratories with tax breaks and relaxed visas and customs regulations. International Business Machines Corp.,  Microsoft Corp. (MSFT)  and Siemens AG have already agreed to locate there.  \u2018Beautiful Ideas\u2019  \u201cRussia has beautiful ideas but very poor commercialization,\u201d says  Viktor Vekselberg , the billionaire who\u2019s president of the Skolkovo Foundation, which is developing Skoltech. Vekselberg, 56, earned a Ph.D. in mathematics from the USSR Academy of Sciences before amassing a fortune in the oil and energy sectors that the  Bloomberg Billionaires Index  valued at $14.6 billion on April 15. \u201cWe are very concerned that Russia today is not able to create a serious pipeline of innovative projects,\u201d he says.  The foundation says it has recruited 52 venture capital firms to the Skolkovo Innovation Centre, which was founded in 2010.  MIT, which already has programs in Abu Dhabi, China,  Portugal  and Singapore, sees advantages as well. Skolkovo will give it access to the most-promising scientists in a country where it has had little contact, says Leo Rafael Reif, MIT\u2019s president.  \u201cThere is a tremendous amount of talent there,\u201d Reif, 62, says. \u201cIt is really an incubator.\u201d  Expanding Abroad  MIT is one of scores of U.S. schools expanding around the globe. There were 83 international branch campuses of U.S. universities as of March, not including partnerships such as MIT and Skolkovo\u2019s, according to  GlobalHigherEd.org , a website run by researchers at the State University of New York at  Albany . That number has climbed from 10 in 1990, says Jason Lane, a SUNY Albany professor.  The result may be a higher education bubble--with too few qualified or interested students--in regions such as the Middle East and China, says Philip G. Altbach, director of the Center for International Higher Education at  Boston  College. He cited Michigan State University, which closed its undergraduate campus in Dubai in 2010 after failing to attract enough students. (It reopened with graduate programs in 2011.)  \u201cThe U.S. universities involved have come out with significant egg on their face,\u201d he says.  There can also be pitfalls to expanding into countries that have different concepts of political and academic freedom from those in the U.S., some elite schools have learned. Yale University\u2019s joint venture with the National University of  Singapore , where classes are scheduled to start in August, led angry Yale faculty to pass a resolution urging the school to respect civil liberties.  Silencing Criticism  Singapore\u2019s government censors the media and uses the courts to silence criticism of the regime, according to New York-based Human Rights Watch. Yale-NUS has adopted policies of non-discrimination consistent with Yale\u2019s and will protect freedom of expression, the college said in an e-mailed statement.  At Johns Hopkins University\u2019s 27-year-old venture with Nanjing University, police monitor Internet usage, according to Jan Kiely, a former co-director of the campus. Chinese law permits the government to monitor all Internet activity, and the campus isn\u2019t exempt, says Dennis O\u2019Shea, a university spokesman.  Under President Vladimir Putin,  Russia \u2019s government has cracked down on critics ranging from newspaper owner Alexander Lebedev to punk rock group Pussy Riot.  Scientists Arrested  Professors are also in jeopardy. Since 1998, more than a dozen Russian scientists have been arrested, most of them engaged in collaborations with foreign academics, according to Igor Sutyagin, a London-based defense analyst and former researcher at Moscow\u2019s Institute for the U.S.A. and Canada Studies who himself was jailed for 11 years. That should give MIT pause, he says.  \u201cThey should know they risk their own people and they put in danger the Russians who work with them,\u201d says Sutyagin, who says he was arrested for passing material about the Russian military that was in the public domain to a U.K. firm that was accused of being a cover for U.S. intelligence services.  He eventually signed a confession in order to be included in an exchange of spies with the U.S. and was released in 2010.  Vladimir Kara-Murza, a member of the Coordinating Council of the Russian Opposition and a Putin critic, says Skoltech merely serves as propaganda.  \u2018Lending Legitimacy\u2019  \u201cMIT is lending legitimacy and a cloud of respectability to an undemocratic regime,\u201d Kara-Murza, 31, says. \u201cThey should fully understand what they are supporting and what they are doing.\u201d  While Reif, a Venezuela native who holds a Ph.D. in electrical engineering from Stanford University, says he is troubled by some of what he reads about Russia, he adds, \u201cI don\u2019t get involved in the political issues.\u201d  Politics and science have historically been intertwined when it comes to Americans and Russians. The Soviets\u2019 1957 launch of Sputnik, the world\u2019s first man-made satellite, triggered U.S. anxiety about falling behind the rival superpower. Congress passed the  National Defense Education Act  in 1958, increasing funding for scholarships, research grants and the teaching of high school math, science and languages.  Since then, Soviet leaders have neglected their educational system, says Harley Balzer, a Georgetown University professor who writes about higher education in Russia.  \u201cThe Soviet system was inefficient and was riddled with corruption,\u201d he says. \u201cIn the 20 years since the end of the Soviet Union, it\u2019s just gotten worse.\u201d  Reputation Poor  While Russia still produces skilled graduates in math and science, its reputation for world-class research is poor. Until recently, faculty were rewarded for publishing in journals sponsored by their universities instead of international peer-reviewed publications, Balzer says.  In 1997, Russian scholars published roughly 32,000 journal articles--comparable to their Chinese peers, according to Scopus, a citation database owned by Reed Elsevier Plc. By 2012,  China  had increased its research output to 386,152 articles, making it second in the world behind the U.S., with 527,549, while Russia published only 38,102.  Russian international patent applications follow a similar pattern. After being roughly level with China in 2000, when it had 23,377 patent applications, Russia had just 26,879 in 2011, compared with China\u2019s 415,829, according to the Geneva-based  World Intellectual Property Organization .  Modernizing Economy  After the global economic crash in 2008 showed Russia\u2019s vulnerability to commodities price swings, then-President Dmitry Medvedev announced a plan to modernize the economy.  \u201cTwenty years of tumultuous change has not spared our country from its humiliating dependence on raw materials,\u201d Medvedev wrote in an  article  published on the president\u2019s website in 2009. \u201cOur current economy still reflects the major flaw of the Soviet system: It largely ignores individual needs.\u201d  Medvedev recruited Vekselberg, Russia\u2019s fourth-richest man, to head the Skolkovo Foundation. Russian officials approached a dozen or so top research institutions about setting up a university, including the  California  Institute of Technology, ETH Zurich, Imperial College  London  and Stanford, says Alexei Sitnikov, Skoltech\u2019s Stanford-educated vice president for institutional and resource development.  The association with MIT will tempt Russian students--many of whom head abroad for their graduate studies--to stay home, says Vekselberg, who used some of his fortune to buy and repatriate a collection of Czarist-era Faberge eggs from the estate of Malcolm Forbes.  Name \u2018Useful\u2019  \u201cThe name MIT is very useful,\u201d Vekselberg says in accented English, wearing a pink button-down shirt with a \u201cV.V.\u201d monogram embroidered near the waist. \u201cIf MIT is here, people feel comfortable.\u201d The degrees will be conferred by Skoltech, not MIT.  MIT\u2019s involvement helped convince  Yuri Shprits , a Russian-born geophysics researcher, to leave the University of California, Los Angeles for a job teaching and doing research at Skoltech.  \u201cThe fact that MIT was behind this, that I found MIT faculty actively involved, is what gave me confidence,\u201d says Shprits, a naturalized U.S. citizen who studies the effects of the earth\u2019s radiation belts on satellites. \u201cIt\u2019s clear that it will be a top-ranked graduate school in Russia and we will be able to select the best graduates from Russian universities.\u201d  Nobel Prizes  Since its founding in 1861, MIT claims its faculty, staff and alumni have won  78 Nobel Prizes . It\u2019s also one of the world\u2019s richest universities, with an endowment worth more than $10 billion as of June 30, 2012.  While MIT began forming international alliances decades ago, the process accelerated under Reif, who was the school\u2019s provost for seven years before becoming president last year. In 2007, MIT helped found the  Masdar Institute of Science and Technology  in Abu Dhabi, part of a $19 billion hub of research in renewable energy.  In Russia, the Skolkovo Foundation is paying MIT $300 million for its participation in the university, Vekselberg says. That involvement includes designing the university curriculum and research programs and providing visiting faculty. Skoltech\u2019s first president, rocket scientist Edward Crawley, 58, is an MIT professor on long-term leave.  Crawley, who signed a five-year contract, says Skoltech aims to have hired 30 to 35 professors by the end of this year and plans on adding about 30 more annually until the faculty reaches 200 at the end of the decade.  Setting Culture  \u201cThe first five or 10 or 15 people get to set the culture,\u201d says Crawley, who studied in Leningrad as an MIT undergraduate in 1975 and speaks Russian. \u201cIt\u2019s the thing that long endures.\u201d  When fully staffed, the school will teach more than 1,200 graduate students, he says. A dozen of Skoltech\u2019s first 20 students are spending a year at MIT in Cambridge, Massachusetts, while they wait for the Moscow campus to be completed.  Nikita Rodichenko, who is scheduled to graduate from Skolkovo in 2015 with a master\u2019s degree in information technology and computer science, says he\u2019s been impressed by the hands-on experience and industry focus in his courses at MIT. In a class teaching students to evaluate concepts in biomedicine, he did due diligence on real proposals being considered by venture capitalists, he says.  \u201cI am exploring the possibility of doing entrepreneurship in Russia,\u201d Rodichenko, 24, says. \u201cI have ideas of what I want to do, and I need ideas about how to do it. That\u2019s what I want from Skolkovo.\u201d  Stem Cells  Skoltech and MIT are creating up to 15  research centers  where scientists from Skoltech and international and Russian universities will collaborate. The centers will each receive as much as $60 million--out of a total research budget of $675 million--over five years.  In the first such hub, announced in April, Skoltech scientists will team up with researchers at the N.I. Vavilov Institute of General Genetics in Moscow and the University of Groningen in the Netherlands to study stem cells. Other centers will investigate infectious diseases and electrochemical energy storage.  Crawley says the focus on commercial research will protect faculty from running afoul of Russian regulations regarding espionage. Because the university won\u2019t be engaging in classified military research, its professors won\u2019t be in jeopardy, Crawley says.  \u2018Open Publication\u2019  \u201cWe\u2019re only going to do things that have open publication,\u201d he says. \u201cIt\u2019s not our intent to deliberately go into militarily sensitive or strategically sensitive fields.\u201d  Skolkovo\u2019s focus on research with commercial applications has drawn corporations such as  Microsoft (MSFT) , which will have 140 software engineers in Russia when it relocates to the Skolkovo research center in 2015.  Microsoft had been looking for ways to help spur enterprise in Russia, says Alexey Palladin, a Russian-American who relocated from the software company\u2019s headquarters in Redmond,  Washington , to head its efforts at Skolkovo.  \u201cWhat\u2019s missing in Russia is the angel community,\u201d Palladin says. \u201cWhen kids come up with a concept and need $10,000, $30,000, they don\u2019t know where to come up with the money.\u201d  Microsoft has given out more than $1 million in seed funding to 25 companies in Russia, he says.  As Crawley sees it, Skoltech, too, is just another fledgling enterprise.  \u201cThis is a startup like any other startup, and the most important thing is time to market,\u201d he says. \u201cWe can only sustain it if we\u2019re successful, and the real question is how quickly we can be viewed as successful.\u201d  Demonstrating Value  Skoltech is working on projects with immediate impact, such as improving undergraduate science education in Russia, in order to demonstrate its value to the government, he says.  Skolkovo\u2019s image may be tarnished by a probe into corruption by the State Investigative Committee. Two former foundation officials are accused of stealing 23.8 million rubles, and the foundation\u2019s offices were raided by police on April 18. The foundation is cooperating with the investigation, according to spokesman Roman Shcherbakov. Crawley says Skoltech\u2019s work won\u2019t be affected by the probe.  International prestige is one of Russia\u2019s goals for Skoltech, much like its hosting of the 2014 Winter Olympics, says  Vladimir Gel\u2019man , a political science professor at the European University at St. Petersburg. Unlike the Olympics, he says, the university will need support from politicians for decades before it can become a world-class educational institution.  Otherwise, Gel\u2019man says, \u201cwe will build some large buildings, but I doubt they will be very useful.\u201d  Although Medvedev is no longer president, Vekselberg says Putin remains behind the project, despite his December veto of a bill that would have expanded the special freedoms from regulation that Skolkovo enjoys. Vekselberg says he wants the hub to be self-sustaining within five to seven years through endowment funding, corporate research grants and venture capital.  Get your free issue of Bloomberg Markets! Nokia\u2019s devices and services unit, which accounted for half of the company\u2019s 2012 revenue, along with 32,000 employees, will transfer to Microsoft, the companies said. Nokia CEO Stephen Elop, 49, will return to Microsoft after a three-year stint running the Finnish manufacturer. Microsoft is deepening a push into hardware as dwindling computer sales sap demand for the programs that made it the world\u2019s largest software maker. Even combined, the companies have less than 4 percent of the smartphone market, leaving them far behind Apple and Google.  \u201cThe question is whether combining two weak companies will get you a strong new competitor -- it\u2019s doubtful,\u201d said Paul Budde, a telecommunications consultant in Sydney. \u201cBoth Nokia and Microsoft really missed the boat in terms of smartphones, and it is extremely difficult to claw your way back from that.\u201d  Market-Share Decline  Nokia, based in Espoo,  Finland , racked up losses of more than 5 billion euros over nine quarters as Elop\u2019s comeback efforts failed to eat into the dominance of  Apple (AAPL)  and Google\u2019s Android platform in the smartphone market. Ballmer declined to say whether Elop would become CEO, or had been a candidate to succeed him.  Microsoft Tie-Up  Ballmer called Nokia\u2019s Siilasmaa shortly after the new year to initiate discussions on an acquisition and the two met in February at the  Mobile World Congress  in Barcelona, according to Microsoft. Some shareholders said they\u2019d be satisfied with higher dividends and bigger buybacks. Directors have been working with Goldman Sachs Group Inc. to determine the best course, according to a person with knowledge of the plans, who asked not to be named because the talks are private. The rest of the balance is invested in long-term marketable securities.  \u2018Ongoing Dialogue\u2019  Einhorn is recommending that Apple issue $50 billion of preferred stock, to be traded alongside common shares and funded by operating cash flow. It would have a 4 percent annual cash dividend, paid quarterly, he said in a letter to shareholders. Preferred stock can have a higher yield and be issued without diluting the value of common shares.  Yesterday\u2019s statement suggests Apple is softening its stance on the preferred shares, after previously saying in its annual  proxy  that there aren\u2019t any plans to issue them. Apple also said it\u2019s already committed to returning $45 billion over three years.  David Wells , a spokesman for Goldman Sachs, declined to comment.  Apple rose 1.4 percent to $474.98 at the close in New York. The shares are down 33 percent from a record in September.  \u201cWe remain committed to having an ongoing dialogue with our shareholders to get perspectives around return of capital and driving shareholder value,\u201d Apple said in the statement.  Greenlight Sues  Preferred dividends entered the cash debate after Apple included a proposal to investors to do away with so-called blank check preferred stock offerings, which can be issued without shareholder approval, in a government filing in December. Apple said the company had no intention of issuing preferred shares and hasn\u2019t activated any since 1997, the year the late  Steve Jobs  returned to lead the company he co-founded.  Greenlight, which holds more than 1.3 million Apple shares, sued to block Apple management\u2019s proposal, asking a federal court in Manhattan to bar Apple from certifying votes cast in its favor at Apple\u2019s annual meeting on Feb. 27. Einhorn, who said he\u2019s been in discussions with Apple\u2019s management, said the cash hoard equates to about $145 a share.  \u201cSeveral hundred dollars per share would be unlocked if Apple were to follow through on this suggestion,\u201d Einhorn said in an interview on Bloomberg Television. People argue\nabout which version is authentic. Secret recipes are handed down\nin families through generations. Cook-offs are held to see whose\nrecipe is best. And perhaps most important, people invest so\nmuch pride in the dish, it is a fundamental part of their\nidentity.  Near Marseilles in the south of  France , bouillabaisse is a\ncult food. In Toulouse and Carcassonne, the bean-based stew\ncassoulet is a cult food.  Spain  has paella and a number of\nothers. Italy has so many, its cuisine is practically defined by\nthem.  Cult foods of the U.S., for the most part, have not been\naccorded the same attention, though we have plenty of them, from\nclam chowder to chili. Southern barbecue -- meat that is hot-\nsmoked for many hours over a hardwood fire -- is perhaps our\nmost extreme cult food. There are championships. (I\u2019ve competed\non John Willingham\u2019s team in one of the two \u201cworld\u201d\nchampionships that are held each year.) And there are huge\nvariations from one area to another. My book \u201cModernist\nCuisine\u201d identifies nine regional styles, with variations (a\nmap is included).  On a recent business trip to Austin,  Texas , I and a couple\nof friends took time out to visit four famous barbecue joints\nnot far from the city. I first went to Lockhart, Texas, about 35\nmiles south of Austin, for classic central Texas meat-market\nbarbecue. This area was settled in part by immigrants who\nbrought with them the great butcher traditions of  Germany  and\nthe  Czech Republic . In Texas, butchers set up shop in small\ntowns to sell fresh meat as well as sausages, hams and other\nprepared meats. Over time they started to offer barbecue --which\nwas sold, like all other meat, by the pound and wrapped in\nbutcher paper.  Tradition Continues  To this day, a typical barbecue joint in central Texas\nstill serves its fare on butcher paper. By now the rest of the\nmeat market has disappeared, so the place is a restaurant. But\nthis hasn\u2019t led people to start using plates. They\u2019ve always\nserved their barbecue on butcher paper, so they still do.  What\u2019s also surprising is that there is no sauce. A sign at\none place tells you not to even ask. And, although the meat\nitself has been slaved over for hours by the pit master and\nrefined to the nth degree, no one sees any contradiction in\nserving it with cheap saltines, industrial white bread or the\nworld\u2019s worst beans or corn bread. As in any cult, devotees will\ntell you that the butcher paper, the lack of sauce and the bad\nside dishes are part of the charm.  Our first stop in Lockhart was Smitty\u2019s Market, which has a\nbit of a twisted  history . The place opened in 1900 as Kreuz\nMarket (named for the owner, Charles Kreuz), but was sold in the\nlate \u201840s to Edgar (Smitty) Schmidt, an employee. Smitty died in\n1990, having sold the business to his sons, Rick and Don, but he\nleft the building to his daughter, Nina Sells. The siblings got\ninto a dispute over rent, and eventually  Kreuz Market  moved to a\nnew place down the road. The pit master dragged along a barrel\nof embers from the fire at the old location that had been\nburning continuously for a century. Then Sells opened Smitty\u2019s\nMarket in the original Kreuz building, supposedly with the same\nfamily recipes.  It was well over 100 degrees on the day we stopped for\nlunch, and as soon as you come inside  Smitty\u2019s  you are in the\npit room, with its roaring fire. The heat was oppressive, but we\nordered all three things you get in Texas barbecue -- beef\nbrisket, pork ribs and sausage. Brisket is the defining meat of\nTexas barbecue. The flat portion, known as the point, is lean,\nand thus very dry, while the thicker back portion, known as the\ndeckle, is fatter and juicier. Brisket is also tough, so it must\nbe cooked slowly, typically for 12 to 18 hours. These challenges\nlead most of the Southeastern barbecue world to avoid brisket\naltogether. You find it only in Texas, Oklahoma and  Missouri .  Cheap Cuts  Pork ribs are another cheap cut -- not \u201chigh on the hog\u201d\nlike chops, loin and tenderloin, but lower down on the chest --\nthough ribs are easier than brisket to cook well. Sausage is\nanother classic Texas barbecue item, not generally found in\nother parts of the country, and it\u2019s made of beef, pork and\nsometimes additions like cheese and jalapeno.  I had eaten at this place years ago when it was still Kreuz\nMarket, and everything looked the same. However, the food didn\u2019t\nmeasure up. The sausage was tasty, but its texture was terrible.\nGood sausage must hold together after cooking. The sausage at\nSmitty\u2019s did not. It \u201cgreased out,\u201d -- that is, the fat melted\nand separated so that the meat disintegrated with each bite into\ncrumbling pieces swimming in fat.  The brisket was OK, but a bit too dry, even though I had\nordered it from the deckle. The pork ribs were also OK, but it\u2019s\nhard to ruin pork ribs.  Next we headed to Kreuz Market, which is in an enormous new\nbuilding that\u2019s done up to look old. Here, the brisket was far\nbetter -- juicy and delicious. The ribs were great, too, well\nsmoked without being overcooked. The sausage was also far\nsuperior to Smitty\u2019s, though still a bit greasy for my taste. I\nsuspect that both Smitty\u2019s and Kreuz smoke their sausage in the\nsame pits as their ribs and brisket, and that is likely too hot.  What\u2019s funny is that Kreuz Market seems to be the\ninspiration for an entrepreneur who opened a virtual clone in,\nof all places,  Manhattan  -- Hill Country Barbecue Market on 26th\nStreet. (I\u2019ve eaten there, and it\u2019s pretty good.) How is it\npossible to transfer barbecue knowledge across the country, but\nnot across town?  Our third stop in Lockhart was  Black\u2019s Barbecue , which\ntouts itself as the \u201coldest and best major barbecue restaurant\ncontinuously owned by the same family.\u201d You can bet that every\none of those qualifiers is needed because, in Texas, tradition\nis important. There must be a really good place that is family-\nowned, but not continuously by the same family, and another\nplace that is older but not \u201cmajor.\u201d  With cult foods, there is an underlying assumption that the\nbest cooking ideas came generations ago. Yet culinary innovation\nis nothing to be ashamed of. When a chef tells me he is cooking\nwith his grandmother\u2019s recipe, I always wonder why. Did talent\nskip the past two generations?  Best Brisket  Black\u2019s is in many ways the least appreciated barbecue\nplace in Lockhart, not often included on \u201cbest of\u201d lists. But\nthe brisket there was the best I had in Lockhart: a thick set of\nslices from the deckle and fantastic -- all that brisket should\nbe. The ribs and sausage at Black\u2019s were also good, on a par\nwith or slightly behind those at Kreuz.  At that point my merry band had ordered and eaten, within a\nperiod of two hours, a pound of brisket, a pound of pork ribs\nand a couple of links of sausage at each of three places. So we\ncouldn\u2019t stop at the fourth place in Lockhart, Chisholm Trail.\nThe next day in Austin at a business meeting, some Texans told\nme, \u201cWell, that\u2019s where the locals all go.\u201d  Which brings up another assumption about cult foods -- that\nthe locals are great gastronomes. People who grow up in a region\ndoubtless have a better cultural awareness of their own cuisine,\nbut it\u2019s also true that a lot of locals go to McDonald\u2019s,\nApplebee\u2019s and the like. All I can report about Chisholm Trail\nis that to be able to survive in Lockhart with three strong\ncompetitors, it must be pretty decent.  My next barbecue pilgrimage was more unusual. I got up at\ndawn on a Saturday morning and went to  Snow\u2019s BBQ  in Lexington,\nabout 50 miles east of Austin. Lexington is a very small town,\npopulation about 1,200. There is almost nothing there but a\nwater tower bearing the town name and some rusty corrugated iron\nbuildings. \u201cNow this,\u201d my limousine driver said as he turned\naround at a stoplight, \u201cthis is Texas.\u201d  Snow\u2019s is open only on Saturday mornings, from 8 a.m. until\nthey sell out of meat, which is usually about 11. This unusual\npolicy reflects the original mission of Snow\u2019s, which was to\nserve the ranchers who come to town on Saturdays to sell their\ncattle at the local auction. Well before 8 o\u2019clock, I joined the\nline at the door. Pickups rolled down the streets, and the\ncattle mooed loudly in their trailers.  Cow Town  Yet many of the people in line with me weren\u2019t in town to\nsell cows; they had come for the barbecue. Snow\u2019s found itself\nin the limelight in 2008, when Texas Monthly proclaimed it the\nbest barbecue joint in Texas. You might think that would be\nenough to get the owners to open on other days, or at least cook\nenough meat to last all day Saturday. But then, you clearly\nwouldn\u2019t be thinking as they do.  At 8 a.m. sharp, the door opened, and we all went in and\nsoon had brisket, ribs and sausage. Strangely, they also had\nchicken and \u201croast pork,\u201d which was a slice of smoked pork\nshoulder. The chicken was pretty dry. (It\u2019s hard to get a decent\nresult from smoking a chicken.) But the brisket slices, even\nthough they were from the point, were very good. And the sausage\nwas great, as was the pork shoulder. Getting up ridiculously\nearly had paid off.  The Michelin guide in France rates restaurants in stars --\nthree stars are \u201cworth a journey,\u201d two are \u201cworth a detour.\u201d\nBy that standard, the barbecue I had in Lockhart and in\nLexington was three-star -- worth the journey. (DELL)  without retaining  Michael Dell  as chief executive officer, spurring debate over whether the personal-computer maker would be better off without the entrepreneur who founded it three decades ago.  Dell said yesterday that it has received proposals from Blackstone and Icahn that may be superior to a $24.4 billion buyout plan from Silver Lake Management LLC and Michael Dell.  As CEO, Dell oversaw the company\u2019s rise to the top of the PC industry, yet failed to prepare it for new challenges in mobile technology and high-margin business services. While Dell\u2019s 15.6 percent ownership stake gives him leverage to negotiate a key role, the company could benefit from new leadership that can accelerate efforts to add growth, said  Erik Gordon , a business professor at the  University of Michigan .  \u201cMichael is no longer essential to Dell,\u201d Gordon said. \u201cHis attractiveness as a partner to a buyer is the size of his ownership stake. If you are willing to take less than total control, you don\u2019t need him as much.\u201d  Blackstone invited the executive to use his equity to participate in the transaction, which it\u2019s pitching as a leveraged recapitalization that gives investors a chance to participate. Still, the firm\u2019s proposal doesn\u2019t include Michael Dell as CEO, people with knowledge of the matter said. Icahn also doesn\u2019t intend to keep Dell on as CEO, according to people familiar with his planning.  Dell fell less than 1 percent to $14.50 at the close in  New York , 6.2 percent more than the $13.65-a-share offer from Michael Dell and  Silver Lake , outlined Feb. 5.  Blackstone Proposal  Blackstone\u2019s plan values Dell at more than $14.25 a share, while Icahn would pay $15 a share in cash for as much as 58.1 percent of the stock, Dell said yesterday in a statement that included their offers. Under both plans, some shares may continue to be publicly traded.  Blackstone, which has teamed up with  Francisco Partners (PEF3393) , a San Francisco-based technology-oriented buyout shop, and New York-based venture firm Insight Venture Partners, said it plans to fund the transaction with a combination of equity and debt financing, in addition to using Dell\u2019s cash and equivalents.  The Blackstone plan also has envisioned a sale of certain assets, such as the Dell Financial Services business, people have said.  The proposal from Silver Lake and Michael Dell would give the founder majority control, letting him continue to pursue a plan to transform Dell into a provider of a broad range of business-computing services and products.  Dell\u2019s Views  Plans by software maker  Microsoft Corp. (MSFT)  to provide a $2 billion loan for the buyout lessen the likelihood that Dell would sell off its PC division, one of the biggest  users  of Microsoft\u2019s software.  Michael Dell has expressed different views on the Blackstone bid, people familiar with the matter said. President  Mark Hurd  about running the computer maker, a person said last week.  \u201cMichael could lose complete control of the company, and he doesn\u2019t want that,\u201d said  Abhey Lamba , an analyst at Mizuho Securities USA, who has a neutral rating on Dell. \u201cMichael knows the company the best and has not only a financial stake, but also a reputation stake.\u201d  Icahn Offer  Under the Silver Lake-led proposal, Michael Dell would contribute his stake, plus cash, and buyers would pay $13.65 a share. The deal precludes existing shareholders from participating in possible gains.  Icahn is offering investors the option to roll over their stakes or receive $15 a share in cash, with the amount of cash limited to $15.65 billion, according to the statement. Icahn has enlisted Jefferies LLC to conduct due diligence.  Icahn\u2019s offer assumes that Southeastern Asset Management Inc. and T. Rowe Price Group Inc., the largest investors after Michael Dell, would contribute their stakes and won\u2019t receive a cash payment.  Dell\u2019s founder pursued a buyout after failing to keep his company up with the times. About two-thirds of Dell\u2019s sales are tied to low-profit PCs, which businesses and consumers are slow to replace as they adopt tablets and smartphones for many tasks.  Cross-Selling Setbacks  In the lucrative data-center market, where companies are upgrading servers, networks and business software to power complex websites, Dell has cobbled together a patchwork of enterprise storage, networking and software products through about $13 billion of  acquisitions  the last four years. Yet he\u2019s added new products without always effectively cross-selling them, said  Jayson Noland , an analyst at Robert W. Baird & Co. in San Francisco, who has a  neutral  rating on the shares.  Case in point: Dell is No. 2 in Intel-based servers behind  Hewlett-Packard Co. (HPQ) , giving it an avenue for selling gear gained through acquisitions, including storage companies EqualLogic and Compellent Technologies, networking firm Force 10 Networks, and  Quest Software , which focuses on management.  Yet while Dell has effectively sold its standard-issue PowerVault storage devices with its servers, it\u2019s done a \u201cless good job\u201d selling server customers on higher-end EqualLogic and Compellent systems, Dell vice-president Forrest Norrod said in a recent interview.  Disruptive Departure  Even so, running Dell without the executive who founded it in a  University of Texas  dorm room in 1984 won\u2019t be easy. Dell might have a hard time retaining customers, attracting new ones and keeping in place a management team that\u2019s been handpicked by the CEO. And while Michael Dell shoulders much of the blame for his company\u2019s performance because he stuck with a low-cost PC model for too long, outsiders may be hard pressed to find someone with the founder\u2019s personal drive to remake his company as an enterprise computing powerhouse.  \u201cIt would be disruptive to have him leave,\u201d said  Shannon Cross , an analyst at Cross Research in Livingston,  New Jersey , who has a hold recommendation on the shares. \u201cYou\u2019d have to find a CEO to step in, and there are a lot of changes that need to be made. Dell definitely has made the determination that services and enterprise-type offerings are the future of the company, so he\u2019s going in the direction they want.\u201d  Sales at Dell, based in  Round Rock ,  Texas , will fall to $55.9 billion this year from $61.5 billion in 2011, according  estimates  compiled by Bloomberg.  Name, Legacy  The stock has plummeted from more than $30 a share in 2007 -- when its founder took back the reins as CEO from  Kevin Rollins  -- to $10.88 on Jan. 11, the last trading day before  Bloomberg News  first reported that the CEO was in talks to take back majority control of the company.  For the 48-year-old chief executive officer, once part of a technology-industry pantheon that includes Microsoft Corp. co- founder  Bill Gates  and Oracle Corp. CEO  Larry Ellison , prevailing in a surprise takeover fight could help in the effort to restore Dell\u2019s reputation and  performance .  Michael Dell has an incentive to use his stake to lobby for a leadership role long after any buyout goes through.  \u201cHe definitely wants to stay involved in the company and put it on a growth trajectory again to redeem his name and some of his legacy,\u201d Lamba said. The screen makes the new Kindle something of a tweener:\nlarger than  Apple (AAPL) \u2019s iPad mini and  Google (GOOG)  Nexus 7, but smaller\nthan the full-size iPad and Nexus 10. Its price tag is very\nattractive, starting at $299 for a model with 16 gigabytes of\nstorage, as long as you\u2019re willing to look at ads.  It is also seamlessly integrated with Amazon\u2019s enormous\nlibrary of e-books, movies and music -- and becomes even\nsweeter, with features like the Kindle Lending Library, if\nyou\u2019re already a member of the extra-cost Amazon Prime service.  The $499 and $599 models with built-in access to  AT&T (T) \u2019s\nfast 4G LTE network offer a minimalist, rock-bottom first-year\ndata plan: A one-time $50 payment buys you 250 megabytes a month\nfor 12 months.  The downside is that the device itself is, at best, ho-hum.\nThe display is nice enough, but the controls are hard to use,\nand the twin stereo speakers are located just where your hands\nnaturally rest when you\u2019re holding the tablet in landscape mode.  The software -- a heavily customized version of Google\u2019s\nAndroid operating system -- is sometimes sluggish. And there\naren\u2019t many applications for it, compared to the vast numbers of\niPad and off-the-shelf Android apps.  With its low cost and extensive parental controls, this is\na good tablet for families -- especially families with not-too-\ndemanding users.  Galaxy Camera  We\u2019re all used to smartphones with cameras built in. Now\n Samsung (005930)  has taken a camera -- and built in a smartphone.  It\u2019s the new Galaxy Camera point-and-shoot, and it\u2019s being\nsold by Verizon and AT&T.  Several manufacturers, including Samsung, already make Wi-\nFi-enabled models that let you upload your photos to Instagram,\nFacebook and the like once you come within range of a network.\nFor other cameras,  Eye-Fi  makes an SD card that both stores and\nsends pictures.  But the Galaxy Camera goes one better by untethering the\ncamera from Wi-Fi hotspots and allowing you to upload your\nphotos and videos on the spot.  It is, essentially, an Android smartphone, minus the voice\nbut including a 16-megapixel sensor, 21x optical zoom, and the\nability to play \u201cAngry Birds\u201d on the 4.8-inch touch screen\nthat also functions as the viewfinder.  The Galaxy Camera is hefty for a point-and-shoot, but\nproved pleasingly idiot-proof for this not-great photographer. A\nmore accomplished one to whom I lent it came back raving.  The big drawback is its cost: $500 from AT&T or $550 from\n Verizon (VZ) , plus a month-to-month $5 to $10 data charge, depending\non your wireless plan and carrier. It\u2019s a nice camera, though\nthat seems like a high price to pay for impatience.  Wii U  With its handheld Remote controller, Nintendo\u2019s original\nWii introduced something new to the world of console gaming: the\nability to get up and move around.  The new Wii U again brings innovation to the table: a\nwireless controller called the GamePad that has its own 6.2-inch\ncolor touch screen. The screen can mirror what\u2019s on the TV\nscreen, or display something else, such as a different\nperspective on the game being played. Games take a long time to load, battery life on the\nGamePad isn\u2019t great, and while the Wii U is the first  Nintendo (7974) \nwith full high-definition graphics, the benefit is lost on the\ntablet. Given the increasingly long periods between new gaming\nconsoles -- this is the first since 2006 -- Nintendo will have a\nwhile to work out the kinks. (MSFT)  Chief Executive Officer  Steve Ballmer  says Windows 8, the next version of his company\u2019s operating system, will be bigger than Windows 95, an early and much heralded upgrade unveiled almost two decades ago.  It had better be.  Bill Gates , then CEO of the largest software maker, introduced Windows 95 when the World Wide Web was still coming of age. While the program met with robust demand, it failed to catapult Microsoft to the forefront of the Internet industry.  On the eve of Windows 8\u2019s release, Microsoft is facing the risk of being left behind again by another technological wave -- the rise of mobile computing in the form of tablets and smartphones, led by  Apple Inc. (AAPL) \u2019s iPhone and iPad. To respond, the company has completely redesigned the software to include touch-screen capabilities. To showcase the new operating system, Microsoft has also broken with tradition by making its own tablet, becoming a competitor to longstanding hardware partners.  \u201cIt\u2019s starting to look like the biggest thing that Microsoft has ever done is going to be getting past the next few weeks,\u201d said  Michael Gartenberg , an analyst at Gartner Inc. who has covered the company since the release of Windows 95. \u201cThey have to match what it took competitors 10 years to do -- oh, and they have to bring partners along with them.\u201d  PC Slump  Windows 8, which will power desktops, laptops and handheld tablets, and the company\u2019s new device, called Surface, will go on sale Oct. 26 following a kickoff event in  New York  tomorrow. Redmond, Washington-based Microsoft is relying on the software, a product conceived in 2009, to revive interest in the personal computer. The PC market will contract by 1.2 percent to 348.7 million units this year, according to IHS ISuppli. That would be the first annual decline since 2001.  Yet the software may not be able to outweigh consumers\u2019 growing attraction to tablets and smartphones, which are getting faster and more powerful and doing more tasks people once needed PCs for. IDC, another researcher, is likely to cut its projection for fourth-quarter PC shipment growth, which had been estimated at 4.8 percent, analyst Loren Loverde said. Even that gain would have represented \u201climited\u201d growth for a quarter in which a major new Windows program goes on sale, he said. It\u2019s also slower than historical growth rates that averaged more than 10 percent a quarter from 2003 through 2010.  Casting a further shadow over the introduction,  Intel Corp. (INTC)  CEO  Paul Otellini  told staffers in  Taiwan  last month that Windows 8 is being released before it\u2019s fully ready, a person who attended the event said. Otellini told employees that releasing the operating system on schedule was the right move, and said Microsoft can make improvements after it ships, the person said.  Mobile Moves  While it\u2019s betting on a comeback in PC-market growth, Microsoft is also counting on Surface to make a mark in mobile computing. The product will thrust the company into a hardware market it has left to partners since Bill Gates and  Paul Allen  founded the company in 1975. In addition, Microsoft will unveil a new version of its Windows Phone software next week.  \u201cThe last three and a half years has been in some ways the most pivotal set of products that we have ever designed and launched,\u201d said  Jensen Harris , director of program management for Windows user experience. \u201cWe wanted to shake people loose, to be free to think about what would we do if we didn\u2019t feel constrained by the past. Taking that leap forward meant taking a risk.\u201d  Ballmer brought Steven Sinofsky, a veteran of Microsoft\u2019s Office software, into the Windows business to stabilize the flagship product ahead of the much-delayed release of Windows Vista, which shipped more than two years late in 2007 and was met with little customer enthusiasm. In 2009, Windows 7 brought the business back on course in part by appealing to corporate customers.  Tablet Threat  Still, Windows 7 hasn\u2019t kept consumers from shifting some computer purchases to tablets like Apple\u2019s iPad. Windows revenue has missed analysts\u2019 estimates in six of the past eight quarters. The company knew it needed to do something drastic to show Windows could go mobile.  \u201cWe started thinking about if we were to start Windows today, if we were starting fresh, what would it look like?\u201d said Julie Larson-Green, the vice president who oversaw the design and delivery of Windows 8.  Larson-Green\u2019s team got rid of Windows 95\u2019s iconic multicolored Start button, even though some product testers complained. The new Windows\u2019 home screen adopts the tile-like interface now used in Windows Phone, which can be personalized and automatically updates with weather or messages from friends and family.  In another departure for Microsoft, computers with chips based on  ARM Holdings Plc (ARM) \u2019s technology will be able to run a version of the new software called Windows RT.  \u2018Strong Opinions\u2019  \u201cSome people are going to see it and they\u2019re going to have strong opinions that are going to be negative, and some people are going to love it in a way that they\u2019ve never loved Windows before,\u201d Harris said.  Still, Larson-Green said she\u2019s never been concerned that the design and direction would be poorly received. By the time she and Sinofsky first unveiled it in June 2011, the team had done enough research to feel \u201cconfident but not cavalier,\u201d she said.  One thing Microsoft has sought to replicate from Apple is the company\u2019s famous attention to detail, Harris said. For Windows 8, that meant a lot of time spent perfecting things that previously might have been declared good enough.  Five Buttons  Swiping from the right edge of the screen brings up five buttons Microsoft calls charms. The Windows logo button exhibits a subtle animation that looks almost as if light is coming across it, Harris said. To get it right, a team of six or seven people spent an entire weekend holed up in an office in Microsoft\u2019s building 84. Every hour, they looked at 30 to 40 different versions until it was perfect.  \u201cThat level of detail has not existed in this product in that way before,\u201d he said.  The emphasis on tablets and on touch controls, which IDC estimates will only be available in 15 percent of notebook PCs next year, has some analysts concerned that the operating system is too consumer-focused.  \u201cAs far as enterprise is concerned, Windows 8 is Windows Vista version 2 -- it\u2019s the version they skip,\u201d said Bob O\u2019Donnell, an analyst at IDC.  Business Customization  Larson-Green disagrees. She said the customizable nature of Windows 8\u2019s start screen means businesses can tweak versions to show exactly what their employees require and to display the latest information in the automatically updating tiles.  With corporate use of the iPad rising, Apple is no longer just a consumer threat. Currently there\u2019s no version of Microsoft\u2019s Office productivity software for the iPad, which means the success of those devices with businesses also may imperil growth in Microsoft\u2019s biggest division.  \u201cOffice and Windows are bosom buddies,\u201d said Wes Miller, an analyst at Directions on Microsoft in Kirkland,  Washington . \u201cAs Office goes, so goes Windows, and vice versa.\u201d  If Microsoft\u2019s strategy fails, it won\u2019t be for lack of guts, said IDC\u2019s O\u2019Donnell.  \u201cIt\u2019s incredibly bold, it\u2019s incredibly hard to do,\u201d he said. \u201cI\u2019m not convinced it\u2019s all going to work out exactly as they hoped.\u201d  To contact the reporter on this story: Dina Bass in Seattle at   dbass2@bloomberg.net   To contact the editor responsible for this story: Tom Giles at   tgiles5@bloomberg.net","path":".\/2008_2012_msft_bloomberg_news\/icrosoft-windows-8-surfaces-as-challenge-to-apple-mobile-tec.txt"},{"id":72054802,"title":"Hulu Seen at 50 Times Earnings With Netflix Multiple: Real M&A","released_at":"<date>June 23 2011<\/date> <time>03:48:12<\/time>","content":"Hulu  LLC may cost potential buyers\nfrom Yahoo! (ORCL)  reported fiscal second- quarter sales and profit that topped analysts\u2019 estimates on growing demand for Internet-based software, which is now on track to bring in more than $1 billion in revenue this year.  Profit excluding some items was 64 cents a share on adjusted revenue of $9.11 billion, the  Redwood City , California- based company said yesterday in a statement. That compares with analysts\u2019 average projection for profit of 61 cents on sales of $9.02 billion, according to  data  compiled by Bloomberg. Adjusted revenue includes some subscription and support contracts, as well as other licensing revenue.  Chief Executive Officer  Larry Ellison  has been using acquisitions -- including RightNow Technologies Inc. and Taleo Corp. this year -- to add cloud-computing software that customers can access online instead of storing it on their own servers. That\u2019s bolstering profit margins as Oracle fends off smaller rivals such as  Salesforce.com Inc. (CRM)  and  Workday Inc. (WDAY) , which also offer Web-based business products.  \u201cBuyers are consolidating their purchases among fewer vendors in order to get better discounts\u201d in tough economic times, said Yun Kim, an analyst at Janney Montgomery Scott in New York. Applications Software  Sales of software that companies use to manage their operations and workforces increased more than 30 percent.  \u201cWe\u2019re seeing some smaller vendors getting squeezed out,\u201d said Kim, who recommends buying Oracle shares.  For the third quarter, which ends in February, adjusted revenue will increase 1 percent to 5 percent and profit excluding certain items will be 64 cents to 68 cents a share, the company said. Oracle\u2019s operating margin grew to 47 percent in the second quarter from 44.6 percent a year ago -- topping Kim\u2019s 45.9 percent estimate. The company is expanding margin by focusing on more profitable systems packaged with deals with its database and applications software, Catz said in a statement.  In addition, cloud-computing software is on track for $1 billion in revenue and \u201cwill become much bigger over time,\u201d co-President  Mark Hurd  said in the statement.  \u201cThese are new technologies that are certainly giving chief information officers more options,\u201d said  Josh Olson , an analyst at Edward Jones & Co. in  Des Peres ,  Missouri . \u201cIt\u2019s a sticky franchise that will help them weather the storm from these competitors.\u201d  Software Licenses  In an interview on Bloomberg Television\u2019s \u201cBloomberg West\u201d yesterday, Hurd said \u201cstrong M&A\u201d and the addition of 3,000 salespeople over the past year and a half helped lift software sales, and boosted new license sales in  Europe . Oracle\u2019s hardware business is also poised to reverse a series of sales declines, he said.  \u201cWe\u2019re in a position where we can now grow,\u201d he said.  Net income for the second quarter, which ended Nov. 30, rose 18 percent to $2.58 billion, or 53 cents a share, from $2.19 billion, or 43 cents, a year earlier.  New software license and subscription sales -- a closely watched metric because it\u2019s a predictor of future revenue -- gained 17 percent to $2.39 billion. Analysts on average had anticipated $2.24 billion, according to Olson. Applications sales grew more than 30 percent.  Hardware Turnaround?  Hardware revenue -- servers and storage gained in the 2010 acquisition of Sun Microsystems Inc. -- declined 23 percent to $734 million, while Olson said analysts were expecting $810 million. On the conference call, Ellison said the Sun deal has been \u201cthe most strategic and profitable acquisition Oracle has ever made.\u201d  Hardware sales -- which have declined in the past two years -- will increase in the fourth quarter, which ends in May, Ellison said.  The Java software Oracle gained from Sun for writing business programs and linking applications to  database software  \u201cis booming,\u201d the CEO also said.  Oracle also plans to ship a new version of its database called 12c for running cloud-computing applications next year.  In addition to Salesforce and Workday, Oracle is competing with SAP and Microsoft Corp. in the cloud-software market as customers replace aging software and servers with updated, Web- based products. Since the middle of the last decade, Oracle has spent more than $50 billion on more than 80 deals, fueling an expansion in sales and earnings.  Ellison has said Oracle will use cash to boost  dividends  gradually over time, rather than to make big acquisitions. The company will accelerate dividend payments for its next three quarters, making one payment on Dec. 21 and joining a list of businesses moving up payouts ahead of potential U.S. tax increases next year. His company,  Berkshire Hathaway Inc. (BRK\/B) , has spent more than $342 million on 80 newspapers -- including its hometown paper, the  Omaha World-Herald  -- and used them to build a new business unit. And Buffett isn\u2019t done. Though the division announced plans to close an underperforming newspaper in  Virginia  last month, he\u2019s said that more acquisitions may be in store.  Terry Kroeger, the newly installed chief of Buffett\u2019s newspaper empire, runs the operation from a 15th-floor office overlooking the expanse of wide streets that make up Omaha,  Nebraska . The goal, Kroeger says, is to reintroduce newspapers to what they do best: delivering urgent, local information that readers can\u2019t get elsewhere -- and coaxing people into paying for it. He\u2019s also creating offshoot websites with corporate sponsors and branching out into Internet video.  \u201cWe\u2019ve got to evolve with what people are looking for, and I think our industry has done kind of a crappy job with that,\u201d Kroeger, 50, said in an interview.  Kroeger, who started working at the World-Herald 27 years ago, once kept a pair of sneakers under his desk to mow the lawn whenever the grass around the office building got unsightly. Just like in those early days, it\u2019s essential to charge readers for the reporting that journalists provide, he said. The World-Herald erected a so-called pay wall last year, and Kroeger aims to roll out the same approach across his other newspapers.  No Giveaways  \u201cYou can\u2019t spend millions of dollars assembling something and then give it away,\u201d he said, endorsing a strategy adopted by the New York Times,  News Corp. (NWSA) \u2019s Wall Street Journal and most of Gannett Co.\u2019s papers.  The World-Herald, Buffett\u2019s flagship paper, will see its revenue decline this year as circulation shrinks, Kroeger said. It generates about $100 million annually and remains profitable, said Kroeger, who declined to elaborate on its finances.  Buffett\u2019s acquisition of 63 newspapers from  Media General Inc. (MEG)  earlier this year accounts for most of the newspaper unit. Based on Media General statements, those newspapers generated $299.6 million last year, a 50 percent decline from 2006.  Kroeger said that Buffett\u2019s total newspaper division is in the black and should remain so, despite the shrinking revenue.  Profitable Business  \u201cWe\u2019re profitable this year,\u201d he said. \u201cI have a high degree of confidence we will remain profitable next year as well. We\u2019re very high on the industry.\u201d  The paywall has helped support revenue, though the program is still in the early stages, he said. The World-Herald\u2019s circulation, meanwhile, has continued to shrink. It fell 3.2 percent in weekday readership to 130,932 from a year earlier, according to the most recent data from the  Alliance for Audited Media . The Sunday edition dropped 2.9 percent to 165,397.  Even if the paywall draws help boost subscriptions, the move is more of a palliative than a cure, Kroeger said.  \u201cWe have to get into new businesses,\u201d he said.  One such venture, already  under way , aggregates health-care articles from the World-Herald and other Berkshire-owned Nebraska newspapers into a website sponsored by Blue Cross and Blue Shield of Nebraska. The site, which is freely available to readers, has advertising in addition to the sponsorship.  Staying Objective  The risk is that sponsorships jeopardize a newspaper\u2019s objectivity, especially when it comes to medical information, said Todd Gitlin, a professor at the Columbia University Graduate School of Journalism.  \u201cMedical news is already rigged or bent toward breathless accounts of miracle cures,\u201d Gitlin said. \u201cIt\u2019s risky to indulge further in corporate sponsorship.\u201d  Kroeger said the arrangement with Blue Cross doesn\u2019t affect the content.  The broader question is whether newspapers can evolve quickly enough to revive a decaying business. They\u2019re confronting shrinking demand for print advertising, declining circulation, and encroachment from Internet companies such as  Google Inc. (GOOG)  and Facebook Inc. The industry\u2019s ad dollars dropped 6.6 percent in the first six months of 2012 from a year earlier, according to the  Newspaper Association of America .  While community papers have an edge over publications in crowded media markets, no one has found a way out of the slump, said  Ken Doctor , a media analyst with  Outsell Inc.  in Burlingame,  California .  \u2018Silver Bullet\u2019  \u201cThere\u2019s no silver bullet,\u201d he said. Newspapers in many places had enjoyed a near-monopoly pricing on print advertising, Doctor said. \u201cThat\u2019s not coming back -- for anybody.\u201d  Kroeger said last month the company will shutter the Virginia-based Manassas News & Messenger, one of Buffett\u2019s most recent acquisitions, and cut 105 jobs in the process. The newspaper faced too much direct competition from other papers in the area, which includes  Washington , and was continuing to lose money, Kroeger  said in the World-Herald .  \u201cWe didn\u2019t see any way to really turn it back into a profitable enterprise, reliably, so what made the most sense was to just cease publication,\u201d he said.  Other billionaires have tried and failed to turn around the newspaper business. Tribune Co., the owner of the Los Angeles Times and  Chicago Tribune , filed for bankruptcy in 2008, one year after a buyout led by real-estate magnate  Sam Zell .  Small Bet  Buffett\u2019s gamble is less ambitious. His recent spending spree on newspapers amounted to less than two-tenths of 1 percent of Berkshire\u2019s total market value.  He also may have more success than others, said Don Graham, chairman and chief executive officer of Washington Post Co. Part of Berkshire\u2019s strategy is focusing on smaller market papers that don\u2019t have to compete with other media, Graham said.  \u201cWhen you get larger, you get challenged by more forms of media competition for advertising delivery,\u201d he said last week at an investor conference. \u201cAnybody who really focuses on the newspaper business should be studying one company this year: Berkshire Hathaway.\u201d  At Buffett\u2019s Omaha paper, Kroeger is investing in high-definition video equipment, with an eye toward doing an online sports show featuring its reporters. Unlike those national publications, though, Buffett\u2019s newspapers embrace a simple tenet: All news is local.  \u201cThe community aspect of what we do is so important,\u201d Kroeger said. \u201cObituaries, for example, are huge. Copyright  \u2018Disturbia\u2019 Doesn\u2019t Copy Hitchcock\u2019s \u2018Rear Window,\u2019 Judge Rules  \u201cDisturbia,\u201d the 2007 film made by  Steven Spielberg \u2019s\nproduction company, didn\u2019t infringe the copyright of  Alfred Hitchcock \u2019s \u201cRear Window\u201d or the short story on which the\nolder movie was based, a judge in New York federal court ruled.  The Spielberg film isn\u2019t \u201csubstantially similar\u201d to the\nmurder mystery \u201cRear Window,\u201d U.S. District Judge  Laura Taylor Swain  said in a partial summary judgment ruling filed Sept. 21\nin federal court in Manhattan.  The Sheldon Abend Revocable Trust, the copyright holder for\nthe story on which \u201cRear Window\u201d is based, sued Spielberg,\nDreamworks LLC and  Viacom Inc. \u2019s Paramount studio, alleging\nsimilarities between the two works.  \u201cMurder From a Fixed Viewpoint\u201d was written in 1942 by\nCornell Woolrich and first appeared in \u201cDime Detective\nMagazine,\u201d according to court papers. Hitchcock\u2019s adaptation\ncame out in 1954.  Sheldon Abend, who died in 2003, was a literary agent who\nin 1990 won a U.S. Supreme Court case brought by actor James\nStewart over the copyright to the detective story on which\n\u201cRear Window\u201d is based.  According to the court opinion, Abend acquired the\ncopyright for $650 and 10 percent of the proceeds from the\nexploitation of the work from Chase Manhattan Bank, Woolrich\u2019s\nexecutor. Stewart and Hitchcock\u2019s production company had sought\nto show the film on television and otherwise exploit it.  Abend sued for copyright infringement, claiming he had the\nright to control derivative works.  Justice Sandra Day O\u2019Connor agreed, writing for the high\ncourt that because Woolrich didn\u2019t reassign the copyright to the\nfilm company, Abend\u2019s rights governed the use of the material.  That case was Stewart v. Abend, 88-2102, Supreme Court of\nthe United States.  In \u201cRear Window,\u201d  James Stewart  plays an injured\nphotographer convalescing at home who spies on neighbors in a\nNew York apartment building and comes to suspect one of them\nmurdered a woman. In \u201cDisturbia,\u201d a teenager under house\narrest spies on his neighbors and suspects one is responsible\nfor the disappearance of several women.  The case is The Sheldon Abend Revocable Trust v. Spielberg,\n08-7810, U.S. District Court, Southern District of New York\n(Manhattan). Last week Berkshire released an 18-page  report  by its audit\ncommittee, detailing the findings of the panel\u2019s investigation\ninto Sokol\u2019s trading in  Lubrizol Corp. (LZ)  Sokol, you may recall, is\nthe former chairman of several Berkshire units who resigned in\nMarch amid revelations he bought about $10 million of Lubrizol\nshares shortly before he recommended successfully to  Warren Buffett  that Berkshire buy the company.  The audit  committee , which consists of three\n\u201c independent \u201d directors, concluded Sokol had violated\nBerkshire\u2019s insider-trading policies and code of ethics, an\nallegation he denies.  The report itself, however, was anything but independent.  Rather than hire its own separate legal counsel, as the\ncompany\u2019s charter authorizes it to do, the  audit committee \nrelied on Berkshire\u2019s longtime law firm,  Munger, Tolles & Olson ,\nto help conduct its probe and prepare the report. Unexplored Issues  A truly independent, no-holds-barred report would have\ndelved into whether Buffett, Berkshire\u2019s chairman and chief\nexecutive, made any incorrect or misleading statements in his\nMarch 30  letter  to shareholders announcing Sokol\u2019s resignation.\nIt also would have addressed the advice Buffett received from\nOlson and any other Berkshire directors in drafting that letter,\nwhich Berkshire disclosed as part of a company press release.  As Berkshire\u2019s  code  of business conduct and ethics says,\nall officers and directors involved in preparing communications\nto the public \u201cshall make disclosures that are full, fair,\naccurate, timely and understandable.\u201d  The report by the audit committee, led by former Capital\nCities\/ABC Inc. chief Thomas Murphy, didn\u2019t address whether the\nstatements in Buffett\u2019s March letter lived up to that standard.\nThe main reason Buffett has received so much harsh criticism\nlately is that lots of people seem to believe they didn\u2019t.
