The panel\u2019s other member, former\nMicrosoft Corp. executive Charlotte Guyman, declined to comment.  \u2018No Conflict\u2019  Olson, in an interview, told me he saw no problem with\nserving as a Berkshire director at the same time he\u2019s an outside\nlawyer for both Berkshire and its audit committee. \u201cThere\u2019s no\nconflict in our operating on behalf of the audit committee as\ntheir lawyers, and we did it,\u201d he said. \u201cI don\u2019t see that\nbeing inconsistent with my role as a director in any way.\u201d  Yet Olson seemed stumped when I asked him how he keeps his\nactivities as a director and lawyer for the same company\nseparate; essentially Olson is his own client. \u201cI\u2019m not going\nto go into detail about all of this,\u201d he said.  If the owners of a closely held company want to put its\noutside attorney on the board, fine, that\u2019s their business.\nBerkshire, however, has public responsibilities. Olson and\nMunger Tolles should have told Berkshire\u2019s audit committee to\nhire its own independent counsel to assist with its inquiry into\nthe Sokol affair, says  James Cox , a securities-law professor at\nDuke University School of Law.  Failing Grade  \u201cIn these high-profile matters, communicating that you are\nindependent and that you are acting independently is the\nultimate message and not the report itself,\u201d Cox told me. The\naudit committee\u2019s members \u201cshould have managed that, and they\nfailed.\u201d  Buffett\u2019s March 30 letter, in which he praised Sokol\nprofusely, provided plenty of material for the committee to\nexamine. For example, Buffett opined that none of Sokol\u2019s\nLubrizol purchases \u201cwere in any way unlawful,\u201d a statement\nthat was incomplete at best.  Buffett\u2019s letter said nothing about whether Sokol\u2019s trades\nviolated Berkshire\u2019s internal  policies . Buffett later said they\ndid. Nor did it mention that, on that same day, Berkshire\nreported Sokol\u2019s trades to the Securities and Exchange\nCommission\u2019s enforcement division. Berkshire \u201cturned over some\nvery damning evidence,\u201d Buffett  said  at Berkshire\u2019s annual\nshareholder meeting last weekend.  In his March letter, Buffett also wrote that Sokol had said\nhis Lubrizol purchases \u201cwere not a factor in his decision to\nresign,\u201d a line that wasn\u2019t remotely credible. It wasn\u2019t until\na month later, at last weekend\u2019s annual meeting in Omaha,\n Nebraska , that Buffett said Sokol\u2019s trades were a firing\noffense.  Not So Clever  Buffett also said last week that he consulted with Olson\nand Berkshire Vice Chairman Charlie Munger after he wrote a\ndraft of the March letter. The audit committee\u2019s report didn\u2019t\naddress the advice they gave him. Instead the committee limited\nthe report\u2019s scope to Sokol\u2019s conduct alone.  Munger did tell shareholders over the weekend: \u201cI think we\ncan concede that that press release was not the cleverest press\nrelease in the history of the world.\u201d That\u2019s far too kind.  Berkshire\u2019s audit committee had the opportunity to provide\na full accounting of what went wrong. Instead its members lent\ntheir names to a whitewash that ignored the most important\nquestion: Whether Buffett or anyone else on Berkshire\u2019s board\nmay have violated the company\u2019s ethical standards. The fund, Silver Lake Partners IV LP, has a target of $7.5\nbillion, with the option of raising more, the firm told\nprospective investors this month in the private-placement\nmemorandum, a copy of which was obtained by Bloomberg News.\nSilver Lake\u2019s third flagship fund, which had the same initial\ntarget, ultimately raised about $9.4 billion in 2007. The discount the firm is offering grows as a client\u2019s\ninvestment increases. The management fee will be as high as 1.5\npercent for commitments of less than $250 million and as low as\n1.375 percent for those putting up at least $500 million,\naccording to the document.  Silver Lake charged all clients a flat 1.5 percent for the\nthird fund.  The firm also will collect the standard 20 percent of\nprofits as a performance fee, known as carried interest.  Key-Man Clause  The firm won\u2019t include co-founders David Roux and  Glenn Hutchins  as key men on the fund, according to the sales\ndocument. The change is part of a leadership transition that\nwill see the two men, as well as co-founder Jim Davidson, reduce\ntheir ownership stakes and play less active roles at the firm.  A key-man provision is a common feature in private-equity\ninvestment contracts that governs what happens when personnel\nconsidered essential leave a fund or change their role.  The clause names a newly formed five-member managing\ncommittee, comprised of Davidson and four younger managing\ndirectors: Egon Durban, Mike Bingle, Ken Hao and Greg Mondre.\nAll but Davidson are taking a bigger ownership stake in the\nfirm, two people familiar with the firm said in December.  A key-man event will occur if fewer than three of the five\nare devoting \u201csubstantially all\u201d of their work time to the\nfirm and making the funds under management their primary\nbusiness activity, according to the marketing memo. That would\ncause the firm to suspend investments until a majority of\nclients agree to resume commitments.  Fund Returns  Roux, a senior director, Hutchins, a managing director, and\nDavidson, a managing partner and managing director, were listed\non the key-man clause for the firm\u2019s last fund. The three men\nfounded Silver Lake in 1999.  The firm\u2019s best returns have come from its $2.3 billion\ndebut fund, Silver Lake Partners LP, raised 13 years ago. The\nfund produced a net multiple of 2.5 times invested capital and a\nnet internal rate of return of 25 percent as of Dec. 31,\naccording to the marketing memo.  Silver Lake Partners III LP generated a net multiple of 1.4\ntimes invested capital and a net internal rate of return of 19\npercent, according to the document. The third fund has\ndistributed about $5.4 billion in cash.  Skype Technologies SA has been the strongest investment\nfrom the fund, producing a more than threefold profit for\ninvestors when the video-chat company was sold to Microsoft\nCorp. last year.  Groupon, Go Daddy  The third fund deployed more than $1.2 billion across six\ncompanies in 2011. It invested $50 million in online coupon\nprovider  Groupon Inc. (GRPN) , $358 million in Web registration and\nhosting provider Go Daddy Group Inc. and $328 million in Chinese\nInternet company Alibaba Group Holding Ltd.  Big private-equity investors are turning to separately\nmanaged accounts to obtain cheaper fees and more control in\nexchange for locking up their money for a decade or more.  New\nJersey  said in December it would put as much as $1.5 billion\ninto four custom funds to be managed by New York-based\nBlackstone, which the state said will save about $120 million in\nfees. In the popular imagination, Apple Inc. is the leading maker of premium smartphones, Samsung Electronics Co. comes in at a respectable second place and all other contenders hardly register.  One of these also-rans is Nokia Oyj, the Finnish company that used to make half of the world\u2019s mobile phones but recently felt compelled  to sell  that money-losing unit to Microsoft Corp. Apple, meanwhile, is the world\u2019s most valuable company. Nokia\u2019s failure to compete is all the more remarkable because its latest smartphone is  technologically superior  to Apple\u2019s newest model.  Despite these radically different fates, savvy investors hold both companies in poor esteem when it comes to the management of financial resources. Bloomberg News  reports  that Third Point, the hedge fund run by Daniel Loeb, bought a large stake in Nokia shortly after it agreed to off-load its consumer business to Microsoft. While the firm's  investor letter  details several reasons for taking the stake, it notes that Third Point expects Nokia to pay out some of its cash hoard -- about 8 billion euros after netting out the company\u2019s debt -- to shareholders. That sounds very similar to Carl Icahn\u2019s  rationale  for buying a stake in Apple earlier in the year. In general, activist investors such as Loeb and Icahn often ask (and then demand) that companies dispose of their large cash piles by handing them back to shareholders. This is a perfectly reasonable request to make of companies that are doing a bad job of managing their resources. Businesses are supposed to invest in new products and sell them at a profit. Anything else is wasteful. If the managers can\u2019t come up with any constructive uses of their tens or even hundreds of billions of dollars of cash on hand, they should give it back to people who can allocate that capital more effectively, whether it\u2019s the widow and orphans fund or Loeb and Icahn. After all, if I want to accumulate low-yielding short-term assets I can do it myself with far less risk than buying shares of a tech company. Apple may have crushed Nokia in the business of selling consumer devices, but the two companies have something in common that neither would like to admit. (Matthew C. (MSFT)  filed a lawsuit\ntoday accusing  U.S. Customs  officials of refusing to follow a\ntrade agency\u2019s order to block imports of phones made by  Google\nInc. Trouble is, sometimes the things that we know to be true\nare dead wrong. For the larger part of human history, for\nexample, people were sure that the sun circles the Earth and\nthat we are at the center of the universe. It doesn\u2019t, and we\naren\u2019t. The conventional wisdom that the rich and businesses are\nour nation\u2019s \u201cjob creators\u201d is every bit as false.  I\u2019m a very rich person. As an entrepreneur and venture\ncapitalist, I\u2019ve started or helped get off the ground dozens of\ncompanies in industries including manufacturing, retail, medical\nservices, the Internet and software. I founded the Internet\nmedia company aQuantive Inc., which was acquired by  Microsoft\nCorp. (MSFT)  in 2007 for $6.4 billion. I was also the first non-family\ninvestor in  Amazon.com Inc. (AMZN)   Even so, I\u2019ve never been a \u201cjob creator.\u201d I can start a\nbusiness based on a great idea, and initially hire dozens or\nhundreds of people. But if no one can afford to buy what I have\nto sell, my business will soon fail and all those jobs will\nevaporate.  That\u2019s why I can say with confidence that rich people don\u2019t\ncreate jobs, nor do businesses, large or small. What does lead\nto more  employment  is the feedback loop between customers and\nbusinesses. And only consumers can set in motion a virtuous\ncycle that allows companies to survive and thrive and business\nowners to hire. An ordinary middle-class consumer is far more of\na job creator than I ever have been or ever will be.  Theory of Evolution  When businesspeople take credit for creating jobs, it is\nlike squirrels taking credit for creating evolution. In fact,\nit\u2019s the other way around.  It is unquestionably true that without entrepreneurs and\ninvestors, you can\u2019t have a dynamic and growing capitalist\neconomy. But it\u2019s equally true that without consumers, you can\u2019t\nhave entrepreneurs and investors. And the more we have happy\ncustomers with lots of disposable income, the better our\nbusinesses will do.  That\u2019s why our current policies are so upside down. When\nthe American middle class defends a tax system in which the\nlion\u2019s share of benefits accrues to the richest, all in the name\nof job creation, all that happens is that the rich get richer.  And that\u2019s what has been happening in the U.S. for the last\n30 years.  Since 1980, the share of the nation\u2019s  income  for fat cats\nlike me in the top 0.1 percent has increased a shocking 400\npercent, while the share for the bottom 50 percent of Americans\nhas declined 33 percent. At the same time, effective tax rates\non the superwealthy fell to 16.6 percent in 2007, from 42\npercent at the peak of U.S. productivity in the early 1960s, and\nabout 30 percent during the expansion of the 1990s. In my case,\nthat means that this year, I paid an 11 percent rate on an\neight-figure income.  One reason this policy is so wrong-headed is that there can\nnever be enough superrich Americans to power a great economy.\nThe annual earnings of people like me are hundreds, if not\nthousands, of times greater than those of the average American,\nbut we don\u2019t buy hundreds or thousands of times more stuff. My\nfamily owns three cars, not 3,000. I buy a few pairs of pants\nand a few shirts a year, just like most American men. Like\neveryone else, I go out to eat with friends and family only\noccasionally.  It\u2019s true that we do spend a lot more than the average\nfamily. Yet the one truly expensive line item in our budget is\nour airplane (which, by the way, was manufactured in  France  by\n Dassault Aviation SA (AM) ), and those annual costs are mostly for\nfuel (from the  Middle East ). It\u2019s just crazy to believe that any\nof this is more beneficial to our economy than hiring more\nteachers or police officers or investing in our infrastructure.  More Shoppers Needed  I can\u2019t buy enough of anything to make up for the fact that\nmillions of unemployed and  underemployed Americans  can\u2019t buy any\nnew clothes or enjoy any meals out. Or to make up for the\ndecreasing consumption of the tens of millions of middle-class\nfamilies that are barely squeaking by, buried by spiraling costs\nand trapped by stagnant or declining wages.  If the average American family still got the same share of\nincome they earned in 1980, they would have an astounding\n$13,000 more in their pockets a year. It\u2019s worth pausing to\nconsider what our economy would be like today if middle-class\nconsumers had that additional income to spend.  It is mathematically impossible to invest enough in our\neconomy and our country to sustain the middle class (our\ncustomers) without  taxing the top 1 percent  at reasonable levels\nagain. Shifting the burden from the 99 percent to the 1 percent\nis the surest and best way to get our consumer-based economy\nrolling again.  Significant tax increases on the about $1.5 trillion in\ncollective income of those of us in the top 1 percent could\ncreate hundreds of billions of dollars to invest in our economy,\nrather than letting it pile up in a few bank accounts like a\nhuge clot in our nation\u2019s economic circulatory system.  Consider, for example, that a puny 3 percent surtax on\nincomes above $1 million would be enough to maintain and expand\nthe current payroll tax cut beyond December, preventing a $1,000\nincrease on the average worker\u2019s taxes at the worst possible\ntime for the economy. With a few more pennies on the dollar, we\ncould invest in rebuilding schools and infrastructure. And even\nif we imposed a millionaires\u2019 surtax and rolled back the Bush-\nera tax cuts for those at the top, the taxes on the richest\nAmericans would still be historically low, and their incomes\nwould still be astronomically high.  We\u2019ve had it backward for the last 30 years. Rich\nbusinesspeople like me don\u2019t create jobs. Middle-class consumers\ndo, and when they thrive, U.S. businesses grow and profit.\nThat\u2019s why  taxing the rich  to pay for investments that benefit\nall is a great deal for both the middle class and the rich.  So let\u2019s give a break to the true job creators. Let\u2019s tax\nthe rich like we once did and use that money to spur growth by\nputting purchasing power back in the hands of the middle class.\nAnd let\u2019s remember that capitalists without customers are out of\nbusiness.  ( Nick Hanauer  is a founder of Second Avenue Partners, a\nventure capital company in  Seattle  specializing in early state\nstartups and emerging technology. He has helped launch more than\n20 companies, including aQuantive Inc. and Amazon.com, and is\nthe co-author of two books, \u201cThe True Patriot\u201d and \u201cThe\nGardens of Democracy.\u201d The opinions expressed are his own.)  To contact the writer of this article:\nNick Hanauer at  Nick@secondave.com .  To contact the editor responsible for this article:\nMax Berley at   mberley@bloomberg.net .","path":".\/2008_2012_msft_bloomberg_news\/raise-taxes-on-the-rich-to-reward-job-creators-commentary-by-nick-hanauer.txt"},{"id":96180485,"title":"Kindred, MEMC, Occidental, Pitney Bowes, VF: U.S. Equity Movers","released_at":"<date>April 29 2011<\/date> <time>20:39:47<\/time>","content":"Shares of the following companies\nhad unusual moves in U.S. trading. Electronic Arts Inc. (EA) , whose \u201cCommand & Conquer\u201d is ranked\nby researcher NPD among the top-five best-selling PC franchises\nof all time with more than 30 million copies sold since 1995,\nwill make the game free online next year. Free games with extras that cost often less than $1, a\nmodel pioneered by  Zynga Inc. (ZNGA) , are poised to push sales in\ncountries where disposable income is low and piracy has hurt\nrevenue. Latin America,  Africa  and the  Middle East  made up 6\npercent of the industry\u2019s almost $67 billion in revenue last\nyear, according to researcher Idate Digiworld.  \u201cWith the growing availability of mobile devices and PCs,\nthe number of potential customers is rapidly expanding,\nespecially in emerging markets,\u201d said Frank Gibeau, head of\nlabels at Electronic Arts, the world\u2019s second-largest game\ndeveloper by revenue. \u201cThe free-to-play model makes our games\naccessible to these audiences.\u201d  Eastern Europe  Gamers in emerging markets are more likely to use a handset\nthan a recent  Microsoft Corp. (MSFT)  Xbox or Nintendo Co. Wii games\nconsole. More than half of U.S. households own a current-\ngeneration console, according to research firm  Nielsen Co .\nOwnership in emerging markets is about 25 percent to 33 percent\nof the level of that in Western countries, said Peter Warman,\nchief executive officer of researcher Newzoo.  \u201cEmerging markets are where the growth is,\u201d said Jan Ten\nSythoff, a Brighton, England-based analyst at Pyramid Research. Overcoming Piracy  Those gamers may be willing to pay for in-game items or\nskills, new content and maps. Ubisoft fell 1.6 percent to 6.10 euros at 3:31 p.m. in\nParis trading, paring the advance this year to 18 percent.\nElectronic Arts rose 0.7 percent in  New York  and has fallen 37\npercent this year. Now it\u2019s dealing in something completely different: patents.  Two months ago, Spherix merged with North South Holdings Inc., owner of a portfolio of 224 patents. The new Spherix, which calls itself an \u201cintellectual property development company,\u201d is pursuing infringement cases against the likes of T-Mobile US Inc. and buying former Nortel Networks patents from a consortium set up by Microsoft Corp. and Apple Inc.  Spherix\u2019s overnight transformation from a struggling scientific research company into a patent collector is the latest step in the race to turn other people\u2019s ideas into dollars. In the past 16 months, at least five U.S. companies have used deals to become publicly traded patent owners, adding the firepower that comes with raising funds in the stock market to lure investors with the potential of a big payday as mobile and Internet technologies proliferate.  \u201cI may be either delusional or naive, but I\u2019m doing this because this is an asset class that is evolving,\u201d said  Anthony Hayes , the former chief executive officer of North South, who took the helm of Spherix after the deal. \u201cWe\u2019re at a tipping point. The guy who gets it right will have the chance to build something.\u201d  Investors betting on Hayes are not just backing a risky business model. They\u2019re also joining an escalating debate over the practice of buying up patents without making products or developing technology.  FTC\u2019s Plans  The U.S. Federal Trade Commission is planning to  examine  whether patent monetization helps or hinders innovation. Technology providers including Google Inc. and Adobe Systems Inc. say more needs to be done to curb so-called trolling, in which patent-focused entities send royalty demand letters to hundreds of companies at a time.  Hayes, who previously worked as a trial lawyer, says his model rewards inventors who may otherwise receive no compensation for their ideas. Reverse mergers, where private companies combine with listed entities, can also breathe life into ailing public companies.  Spherix had not generated as much as $2 million in  annual revenue  in seven years and was burning through cash in an attempt to develop and market drugs. North South was formed a year ago to acquire patents and \u201cmonetize those patents through sales, litigation or licensing,\u201d according to its website.  Raising Capital  Earlier this month, Spherix, based in Tysons Corner, Virginia, about 15 miles west of Washington, D.C., raised $2.24 million in a private placement to go after patents in areas like WiFi, cellular communication and antenna technology. The financing almost doubled the company\u2019s cash on hand, based on its reported figure at the end of September.  Patent-licensing firms have targeted companies such as Google, ZTE Corp. and  Apple , which have mobile and cloud products. The rationale is that if they can win, licensing firms can generate sustained royalty revenue on products that big companies sell.  It\u2019s an expensive proposition. Against such competitors, even a small case can require $650,000 in legal fees, with bigger cases costing more, according to a survey by the American Intellectual Property Law Association. Furthermore, a case could take years getting through trial and appeals.  Monetizing Patents  \u201cThere\u2019s no way to monetize a patent, no matter how brilliant an inventor you are, without access to capital,\u201d said  Ron Epstein , CEO of patent brokerage Epicenter IP Group LLC in Redwood City, California. \u201cTen years ago, contingency fee lawyers were your only source for capital. Now billions of dollars are looking to invest itself in patent enforcement.\u201d  Public-market investors have to be prepared for a bumpy ride.  Spherix , with a market value of $23.6 million, has dropped 11 percent since the merger closed.  Vringo Inc. , a provider of software for mobile and video applications, has tumbled 19 percent since merging with intellectual property company Innovate\/Protect Inc.  Vringo entered the patent market after struggling to build an ad-supported ringtone business. Eighteen months after its June 2010 initial public offering, the stock fell below $1.  Vringo acquired Innovate\/Protect in July 2012, and in November was awarded about $30 million from Google and some customers over patented ways to generate ad revenue. Vringo has sold about  $75 million  in stock to fund the new business and used part of the proceeds to buy telecommunications patents from Nokia Oyj.  Microsoft Deal  In May of this year, it got six telecommunications and data management patents from Microsoft as part of a settlement deal in which Microsoft agreed to pay $1 million plus 5 percent of whatever related royalties Google pays in the future. Vringo shares rose as much as 10 percent on May 30, after the announcement, and closed up 2.6 percent.  \u201cThe market reacted very positively and we realized that we could use that liquidity to acquire additional assets,\u201d  Andrew Perlman , CEO of the New York-based company, said in an interview. \u201cI\u2019m a big fan of the licensing model. When it works, there\u2019s no better business.\u201d  Vringo\u2019s stock-market value jumped to $235 million at the end of 2012, from $9.9 million a year earlier.  Dig a little deeper and a cautionary tale emerges. In the win against Google, Vringo had sought almost $500 million. When the jury announced a $30 million award, Vringo shares sank 9.6 percent.  Herd Investing  \u201cIf you don\u2019t know what you\u2019re doing and you\u2019re investing alongside the herd, that can be a problem,\u201d said  Kevin Rivette , a managing partner in the Silicon Valley office of 3LP Advisors LLC, which has advised companies on patent strategies. While there are good patents for investors to back, \u201cSome you look at and say, \u2018You\u2019ve got a better chance of finding gold in Palo Alto,\u2019\u201d Rivette said.  A bigger concern may be that businesses are fighting back. Companies like Google and Cisco Systems Inc., which get dozens of royalty demands a year, are pushing the courts and Congress to limit suits that involve common technology, such as wireless networking.  Of the past 12 trials in East Texas, the most popular venue for patent suits, 10 were unsuccessful, according to  Michael Smith  of law firm Siebman Burg Phillips & Smith LLP in Marshall, Texas.  Since July, Spherix has filed a complaint against T-Mobile for geolocation technology, and infringement lawsuits against VTech Holdings Ltd. and Uniden Corp. for patents related to cordless handsets.  Nortel Patents  The case against Uniden is tied to patents Spherix bought from Rockstar Consortium US LP, a joint venture that Apple and Microsoft created in 2011 to hold some of the Nortel patents acquired for $4.5 billion in 2011.  Document Security Systems Inc., based in Rochester, New York, is suing Facebook Inc. and LinkedIn Corp. for infringing technology covering online collaboration. The patents were acquired in a reverse merger with Lexington Technology Group Inc., an intellectual property company. The  shares  have fallen 33 percent since the deal closed on July 1.  Peter Hardigan , Document Security\u2019s chief operating officer, said investors looking for fast returns have turned away from his company.  \u201cIP investors tend to be very quick on the trigger,\u201d Hardigan said. \u201cWe\u2019re building a business and trying to manage it for the long term.\u201d  To contact the reporters on this story: Ian King in San Francisco at  ianking@bloomberg.net ; Susan Decker in Washington at  sdecker1@bloomberg.net   To contact the editors responsible for this story: Bernard Kohn at  bkohn2@bloomberg.net ; Pui-Wing Tam at  ptam13@bloomberg.net","path":".\/2008_2012_msft_bloomberg_news\/publicly-traded-patent-collectors-plaguing-google-apple.txt"},{"id":85191368,"title":"Alibaba Said to Seek Financing From Temasek to Buy Back Stake From Yahoo","released_at":"<date>October 10 2011<\/date> <time>18:48:09<\/time>","content":"Alibaba Group Holding Ltd. has\ntalked with  Singapore \u2019s Temasek Holdings Pte about providing\nfinancing to buy out Yahoo! The potential\nimpact involves amorphous predictions about how the leaks will\nalter the behavior of would-be plotters, friendly intelligence\nagencies and technology companies, according to former U.S.\nintelligence officials.  Clapper said in an interview with NBC News that the\ndisclosures about telephone and Internet data collection by\nEdward Snowden, a 29-year-old former security contractor and CIA\ntechnical analyst, will do \u201chuge, grave damage\u201d to \u201cour\nintelligence capabilities.\u201d  Already Revealed  Fingar, now a fellow at  Stanford University \u2019s Freeman\nSpogli Institute for International Studies, said news coverage\nof former President  George W. Bush \u2019s warrantless wiretapping\nprogram and political debate as intelligence surveillance laws\nwere reauthorized in recent years should have alerted terrorist\nnetworks and foreign spy services that the U.S. was engaging in\nthis kind of monitoring.  Still, Snowden\u2019s hand-off of classified material to the\n Washington Post (WPO)  and U.K.-based Guardian newspapers may motivate\nterrorists to shift more time and resources to concealing their\ncommunications, though that involves a trade-off of speed and\nefficiency. While al-Qaeda leaders such as  Osama bin Laden  used\nhuman couriers to evade detection by electronic eavesdropping,\ncommunication through intermediaries, even trusted ones, \u201ccan\nbe slow and clumsy,\u201d said  Paul Pillar , former deputy director\nof the Central Intelligence Agency\u2019s counterterrorism center.  \u201cIt\u2019s a mistake to assume that every communication of al-Qaeda or anyone else is done solely on the basis of maximum\nsecurity,\u201d he added.  Government Cooperation  Allied governments also may hesitate in sharing sensitive\ninformation if the leak generates broader concern about U.S.\nability to keep secrets within an intelligence community that\ninvolves a multitude of private contractors, including  Booz\nAllen Hamilton Holding Corp. (BAH) , where Snowden had worked for the\npast three months. McLean, Virginia-based  Booz Allen  fired\nSnowden on June 10, the day after he revealed his role.  The disclosures Snowden has made so far may not have much\nimpact on the trust allied intelligence agencies place in the\nU.S., Fingar said. \u201cWhat\u2019s there so far, I don\u2019t think would\ncause people to overreact.\u201d  Still, the latest disclosures of classified information\ncame as another self-described whistle-blower, Army Private\nFirst Class Bradley Manning, 25, is on trial for providing a\ntrove of classified State Department documents to the anti-secrecy WikiLeaks website.  \u201cAny time you have a leak, anybody who is a cooperator or\npotential cooperator with your own service is going to think\ntwice about cooperation,\u201d Pillar said. \u201cLeaks have hurt\ncooperation with a variety of foreign counterparts in the\npast.\u201d  Sharing Reluctance  A cooling of intelligence sharing can be subtle and still\nhave consequences, Pillar said. \u201cIt\u2019s not an on-off switch,\u201d\nhe said. \u201cIt\u2019s a question of how much, how often, how fast\nthings are shared. It\u2019s a matter of degree.\u201d  Technology companies also could become more resistant to\nsharing data with U.S. intelligence services if they lose\ncustomers or face sanctions from European authorities raising\nconcerns about surveillance on privacy grounds.  \u201cIt\u2019s a major public relations problem clearly for the\ncompanies that have been named in doing their duty and\ncooperating with the government on this,\u201d Pillar said. \u201cThat\ncannot help the trust and confidence of the business community\nin the future and certainly in these companies in particular.\u201d  Citing classified documents, the Washington Post and\nGuardian reported that the  Federal Bureau of Investigation  and\nNational Security Agency had accessed the central servers of\nnine U.S. Internet companies, extracting audio and video chats,\nphotographs, e-mails, documents and connection logs.  Companies Involved  Microsoft Corp. (MSFT) , Yahoo! Inc., Google Inc.,  Facebook Inc. (FB) ,\nand Apple Inc. are among the companies involved, the newspapers\nreported. They have issued statements either denying that they\nhad granted the government direct access to their servers or\nsaying they were unaware of the program.  Google and  Facebook  yesterday asked the  Justice Department \nfor more leeway to disclose information about national-security\nrequests for data, seeking to reassure users that the Web\ncompanies don\u2019t give authorities unfettered access.  The operator of the world\u2019s most popular Internet search\nengine sent a letter to Attorney General Eric Holder and FBI\nDirector  Robert Mueller , Google said in a  blog post  showing the\nletter. The  Mountain View , California-based company asked for\nthe ability to report aggregate numbers of national-security\nrequests.  \u2018Transparency Report\u2019  \u201cWe would welcome the opportunity to provide a\ntransparency report that allows us to share with those who use\nFacebook around the world a complete picture of the government\nrequests we receive, and how we respond,\u201d Ted Ullyot, general\ncounsel of  Menlo Park ,  California-based Facebook , wrote in an e-mailed statement.  Snowden fled to  Hong Kong  before revealing his role in the\nnewspaper reports of surveillance. General Keith Alexander, the\nNSA director, told members of the Senate Intelligence Committee\nin a briefing that he didn\u2019t know Snowden\u2019s whereabouts, said\nGeorgia Senator  Saxby Chambliss , the panel\u2019s top Republican.  Chambliss said in an interview that he expects Snowden to\nrelease more classified data.  \u201cApparently he\u2019s got a thumb drive,\u201d Chambliss said,\nwhile its contents are unknown. \u201cHe\u2019s already exposed part of\nit and I guess he\u2019s going to expose the rest of it.\u201d  Federal prosecutors have started preparing criminal charges\nagainst Snowden, which they may try to finish quickly in order\nto start talks about extradition, according to U.S. officials.\nThe FBI is conducting a broad investigation, according to the\nofficials, including interviews with family, examination of his\ncommunications and whether he had any assistance with his\nefforts to obtain the leaked material. Now the end may come a lot sooner than that.  The high court revisits race-based admissions today,\nhearing the case of a rejected white applicant to the University\nof  Texas . The court\u2019s reconstituted membership makes new limits\nprobable, even as dozens of the nation\u2019s largest companies, such\nas  Microsoft Corp. (MSFT)  and  Wal-Mart Stores Inc., (WMT)  call for continued\nuse of affirmative action to ensure a diverse workforce.  \u201cIt\u2019s just a matter of time before the use of race is\nrestricted, prohibited,\u201d said Ward Connerly, a former member of\nthe University of California Board of Regents who led a\nsuccessful fight to end preferences at public institutions in\nthat state.  Affirmative action has been a fixture on U.S. campuses\nsince the civil rights movement in the 1960s, helping integrate\nwhat had once been overwhelmingly white universities. All but a\nhandful of the nation\u2019s selective colleges and professional\nschools now use race as a consideration in admissions as they\nseek to ensure a diverse student body.  A ruling against Texas would raise new legal questions\nabout those programs -- and perhaps even wipe them out. Public\nand private universities alike may be forced to turn to race-\nneutral steps, such as class-based affirmative action and the\nabolition of legacy preferences, which disproportionately go to\nwhite students, to maintain the same level of campus diversity.\nA ruling by the court isn\u2019t expected until next year.  Corporate Allies  Proponents of affirmative action say those moves would be\nan inadequate substitute for traditional racial preferences.  Texas has support in the case from some of the nation\u2019s\nmost powerful institutions. Fifty-nine companies -- including\nGap Inc.,  General Electric Co. (GE) , Pfizer Inc., Shell Oil Co. and\n Viacom Inc. (VIAB)  -- filed a  brief  saying they rely on universities to\ntrain a racially diverse workforce.  For companies to succeed, \u201cthey must be able to hire\nhighly trained employees of all races, religions, cultures and\neconomic backgrounds,\u201d the companies argued.  Those corporations are in the unusual position of arguing\nalongside the Obama administration, which is  casting  affirmative\naction as a national security issue. The administration says\nrace-conscious admissions, both at the country\u2019s military\nacademies and at universities with Reserve Officer Training\nCorps programs, help ensure a diverse officer corps. A group of\n37 former military leaders is making similar arguments.  Harvard, Yale Support  In addition, Texas has the support of the nation\u2019s higher-\neducation establishment, including  Harvard University ,  Yale\nUniversity  and  Princeton University .  O\u2019Connor pointed to corporate and military support for\naffirmative action when she wrote the court\u2019s 2003 majority\nopinion in Grutter v. Bollinger.  That 5-4 decision, which reaffirmed the landmark 1978 Bakke\nruling, said colleges and graduate schools could consider race\nas long as they do so through a broad review of a student\u2019s\napplication and don\u2019t mechanistically award extra points to\nevery minority.  O\u2019Connor\u2019s 2006 retirement, and succession by Justice\n Samuel Alito , may prove to be affirmative action\u2019s turning\npoint. Alito gives the court five skeptics of racial\npreferences, joining Chief Justice  John Roberts  and Justices\nAntonin Scalia,  Anthony Kennedy  and  Clarence Thomas .  Kennedy now stands as the court\u2019s swing vote on the issue.\nHe dissented in 2003, saying the University of Michigan Law\nSchool policy at issue in that case was akin to a quota.  \u201810 Percent Rule\u2019  A central question in the Texas case is whether\nuniversities can adequately diversify without resorting to\nracial preferences. The University of Texas admits three-\nquarters of its freshman class each year on the basis of high\nschool class rank -- the \u201ctop 10 percent rule.\u201d That system,\nthe product of a 1997 state law, ensures a significant number of\nminorities because it guarantees slots to students at\npredominantly Hispanic and black schools.  The university considers race only in admitting the rest of\nthe class. Lawyers for  Abigail Noel Fisher , the rejected white\napplicant, say that\u2019s unnecessary, given the success of the\nclass-rank method.  Texas shouldn\u2019t use the \u201cextreme measure of racial\nclassifications to obtain trivial gains in minority enrollment,\nespecially in light of the meaningful impact of existing race-\nneutral measures on UT\u2019s student-body diversity,\u201d Fisher\u2019s\nlawyers argued in court papers.  \u2018Compelling Interest\u2019  Fisher applied unsuccessfully to Texas in 2008 and later\nenrolled at  Louisiana State University . A graduate of a Houston-\narea public high school, she says she was passed over by UT in\nfavor of minority classmates with lower grades and fewer\nactivities.  Texas says its affirmative action program is a model of the\ntype of plan the high court approved in the Grutter ruling.  \u201cThis court has recognized that universities have a\ncompelling interest in promoting student body diversity, and\nthat a university may consider the race of applicants in an\nindividualized and modest manner,\u201d the university argued.  A federal appeals court upheld the Texas admission system,\nsaying it squared with the admissions policy upheld in Grutter.  Justice Elena Kagan isn\u2019t taking part in the case. She was\nthe Obama administration\u2019s top courtroom lawyer when the\nadministration filed a brief at the appeals court level.  The case is Fisher v.  University of Texas  at Austin,\n11-345. The policy shift was announced today by the U.S. State and\nTreasury departments, which administer the sanctions imposed on\nsuch consumer electronics since 1992. The Treasury Department is\nissuing what\u2019s known as a general  license , permitting sales to\nnon-government consumers involving U.S. hardware such as mobile\ntelephones and  laptop computers , and software such as antivirus\nprograms.  The change is intended to help Iranians communicate through\nsocial media, text messaging and mobile-phone videos in order to\novercome some of the media and communications restrictions\nimposed by Iranian authorities. Due to U.S. sanctions, Iranians\nhave turned to black-market-supplied and non-U.S. technology.  The action \u201caims to empower the Iranian people as their\ngovernment intensifies its efforts to stifle their access to\ninformation,\u201d according to a Treasury Department statement.  The products covered by the general license issued today\ninclude mobile phones, satellite phones and broadband hardware,\nmodems, network interface cards, routers, WiFi access points,\nlaptop computers, tablets, disk drives, data storage devices,\nanti-virus and anti-tracking software, online store\napplications, virtual private networks, anti-censorship tools,\nand fee-based personal communications tools including voice,\ntext, video, voice-over-IP telephony, and video chat.  Countering Crackdown  \u201cThe U.S. is taking steps to ensure that, as Iran\u2019s\ngovernment cracks down on Internet access and SMS, sanctions\nwill no longer block cellphones, software and hardware,\u201d\naccording to Jamal Abdi, a spokesman for the National Iranian\nAmerican Council, a nonprofit group based in  Washington . SMS is\nan abbreviation for short message service text messaging.  Internet social-media sites such as  Facebook.com (FB) ,\nTwitter.com and YouTube.com have become vital for activists, as\nthe Arab Spring uprisings demonstrated.  \u201cProviding the democracy movement in Iran with access to\nthe latest social-media organizing tools will strengthen their\nefforts to bring about positive change to a government that\nfears information it can\u2019t control,\u201d Representative Jim Moran,\na Virginia Democrat who has sought such action, said in an e-mailed statement today.  \u2018Malign\u2019 Blocking  The U.S. has supported attempts to boost democratic\nmovements and stepped up efforts to stop regimes such as those\nin Iran and  Syria  from blocking social media through what Obama\nhas called the \u201cmalign use of technology.\u201d  In November, the administration imposed sanctions on\nIranian officials -- including the nation\u2019s communications\nminister -- and government agencies for blocking  Internet\naccess , mobile-phone lines and satellite-television channels to\nstifle free speech.  The Treasury named today additional individuals and\nentities who are \u201ccontributing to serious human rights abuses\ncommitted by the Iranian regime, including through the use of\ncommunications technology to silence and intimidate the Iranian\npeople.\u201d The State Department issued visa restrictions on about\n60 Iranian officials linked to human rights abuses.  New Sanctions  Those designated include the Committee to Determine\nInstances of Criminal Content, the government entity charged\nwith filtering the flow of information to the Iranian people, as\nwell as Asghar Mir-Hejazi, the deputy chief of staff to Supreme\nLeader Ali Khamenei, who \u201chas used his influence behind the\nscenes to empower elements from  Iran \u2019s intelligence services in\ncarrying out violent crackdowns against the Iranian people.\u201d  The decision to lift some sanctions runs counter to recent\nactions in which the U.S. has generally tightened financial and\ntrade restrictions on Iran as part of an international effort to\npersuade the regime in Tehran to give up activities that could\nlead to making nuclear weapons.  The National Iranian American Council has been urging the\nU.S. to aid ordinary Iranians and to assist the reform movement\nin the Persian Gulf country by ending the communications-equipment sanctions, making it easier and less costly to obtain\nsuch gear.  Green Movement  \u201cThe sanctions were felt most acutely four years ago, at\nthe height of Iran\u2019s green movement protests,\u201d the group said\nin a statement. \u201cThe world was galvanized by cell-phone videos\nand reports of abuses coming from inside of Iran, and SMS and\nother communications tools were being used to help organize\nmassive demonstrations. Under the Iran-Iraq Arms Non-Proliferation Act of 1992, the\npresident may waive the requirement to impose certain sanctions\nif it is \u201cessential to the national interest\u201d of the U.S. This\nwaiver authority has since been delegated to the under secretary\nof state for  arms control  and international security. (MSFT)  and  Google Inc. (GOOG) , based in\n Mountain View ,  California , to continue providing essential\ncommunications tools to ordinary Iranians. The change in methodology, approved by EU technical experts, was eagerly awaited in crisis-hit southern European countries, particularly in Spain. Currently, the EU sees two-thirds of Spain's six percent gross domestic product budget deficit as structural rather than cyclical, and Spain is pressured to collect more taxes and cut public spending. The calculation assumes that Spain's \u201cnatural\u201d unemployment level is 23 percent, just a little lower than the actual 27 percent. The Council of Economic Policy's refusal to cut countries like Spain any slack is natural after Angela Merkel's landslide victory in the German parliamentary election: The EU's most powerful nation is a tough proponent of austerity for the weaker countries. Spaniards, however, may wonder how they will ever restart growth if they are stuck with the current policy, which the European Commission's bureaucrats also consider too tough, especially since not all of the continents stronger economies hold to strict austerity. France, for one, is about to  approve  a budget with a deficit of $110 billion, or 4.1 percent GDP, up from 3.6 percent this year, driven by an ambitious investment program, which does not qualify as deficit spending under EU rules. Nokia chairman  admits  misleading public about CEO's payoff   Nokia chairman Risto Siilasmaa admitted he was wrong when he said the terms of outgoing chief executive Stephen Elop's $25.4 million payoff were \u201csubstantially similar to those of former Nokia CEOs.\u201d In fact, Elop's predecessor Olli-Pekka Kallasvuo was not entitled to anything like Elop's $19.7 million equity award. Siilasmaa is struggling to justify Elop's golden parachute, which was extremely unpopular in modest Finland. Prime Minister Jyrki Katainen has called it \u201cquite outrageous.\" Indeed, from many Finns' point of view, Elop helped destroy a former national champion: Nokia once provided 20 percent of Finland's corporate taxes and now a large part of the company has been sold to Microsoft, where Elop is headed to run the newly-acquired business. The public outrage, however, will change nothing: Microsoft is providing 70 percent of the payoff, and it is not bound by the constraints of Nordic egalitarian culture. France  investigates  Apple's relationship with dealers   The French government has ordered the country's competition authority to investigate Apple's relationship with dealers, including any obligations they take on to promote the iPhone over other devices, promises to buy a certain volume of Apple products. This is the second such investigation this year: The French authorities raided Apple's Paris office in July. Nothing happened in the aftermath, and one might conclude that French bureaucrats are merely harassing Apple, known among distributors as a tough negotiator, to warn it to stick to local rules. France deeply distrusts U.S. technology companies and envies them their market dominance. If it can make their life difficult on French soil, it will use every opportunity to do so. Chinese sovereign fund  buys  into Russian potash   The Chengdong Investment Corporation bought 12.5 percent of Russian potash producer Uralkali, worth at least $2 billion, from its major Russian shareholders, Suleiman Kerimov, Filaret Galchev and Anatoly Skurov. The CIC has had an option to buy the stake since last year if Uralkali's share price dropped below a certain threshold, and it has now exercised that right. Uralkali, which produces about 20 percent of the world's potash, broke up its cartel with Belarussian state-owned company Belaruskali, causing fears of a global price war and essentially forcing Belaruskali to halve output in August. In response, Belarus president Alexander Lukashenko had Uralkali's chief executive arrested. The Chinese deal is a step toward the conflict's resolution. Kerimov, the biggest Uralkali shareholder, is looking to sell his entire stake. A new investor would not have his acrimonious history with Lukashenko and could make a deal with him. In any case, China, one of the biggest potash importers, now has a ringside seat. Germany's Ifo index  hits  post-crisis high   The Ifo institute's index of German business executives' confidence rose from 107.5 in August to 108 in September, the highest since 2007. Germans are happy with their government, the relatively healthy export-driven economic growth and the lowest unemployment level in years. There are signs that domestic demand is finally picking up. It is now up to the victorious Chancellor Angela Merkel to form a governing coalition as quickly as she can, so as not to squander her advantage and start solving EU problems that accumulated during the German election campaign. Germany is doing well enough for her to concentrate on external matters. (Leonid Bershidsky, an editor and novelist, is a Bloomberg View contributor. Designing the gadget may prove easy compared with convincing media and cable companies to loosen their grip on the television industry.  This battle is nothing like Apple\u2019s previous forays into the music and mobile phone spheres, when the maker of iPods and iPhones negotiated with weakened record labels and a fractured wireless industry. Now the stakes are even higher and the competition tougher.  Apple is vying with the likes of  Google Inc. (GOOG) ,  Microsoft Corp. (MSFT)  and  Amazon.com Inc. (AMZN)  to make TVs the digital hub of people\u2019s lives in an industry  projected  to reach $200 billion worldwide by 2017. Whoever wins must first strike deals with media companies or cable providers who have little incentive to cede valuable revenue streams. The result: Apple won\u2019t be releasing a new TV product this year, as analysts had predicted, said a person familiar with the company\u2019s plans.  \u201cIt\u2019s not a nice, simple, easy story that Apple is going to come in and turn the world upside-down and we\u2019re all going to live happily ever after,\u201d said  Craig Moffett , an analyst with Sanford C. (TIVO)  has been offering for more than a decade with its hard drive-equipped set-top box that allows viewers to easily record broadcasts and, more recently, stream Internet fare. Unlike set-top devices from cable providers, it doesn\u2019t deliver live broadcasts or record shows. He also has an abiding faith in technology. And so it is that the former head of Microsoft Corp., now  co-chair  of the  Bill & Melinda Gates Foundation , has turned his attention to the  reinvention of the toilet . As Gates knows, two-thirds of the world's people have no access to that great leap in sanitation, credited with adding a decade to our longevity. Their communities can't afford the water and sewerage systems to which the toilet must be attached. So they make do with latrines or squat in the open, and consequently suffer diarrheal diseases that kill two million annually. Gates intends to change that. The Gates Foundation yesterday  announced  three  winners  from eight projects it funded to develop low-cost, water-less toilets. The  California Institute of Technology  won first prize for a device that includes a solar-powered electrochemical reactor that disinfects waste and generates hydrogen to be used as fuel. The model from the U.K.'s Loughborough University generates clean water from urine and feces and uses a hydrothermal carbonization reactor to turn solid waste into biological charcoal that can be used as fertilizer. The  University of Toronto  entry dries and smolders waste to sanitize it and uses a sand filter and ultra-violet light to recover clean water. The foundation will determine whether one, two or all three of these prototypes are viable and will field test them before initiating pilot studies in the developing world in about 2015. The goal is to develop a toilet that can be operated for no more than 5 cents per day per user. That's an ambitious goal, but it's the right one. If the new toilets aren't affordable, they won't be adopted. The foundation's model assumes that, rather than governments or donors buying the devices and imposing them on users, the private sector will deliver them to interested consumers and that commerce will flourish around the collection of waste-turned-to-resources. At the awards ceremony, Gates noted that the toilet has changed so little in 200 years, today's versions would be familiar to  Thomas Crapper , who popularized the flush variety in the late 1800s. With the innovations the foundation's grants are generating and a free-market model, Crapper's ghost may yet be surprised. ( Lisa Beyer  is a member of the Bloomberg View editorial board.) (AAPL)  and\n Microsoft Corp. (MSFT)   The sale marks a watershed in the maturity of intellectual\nproperty markets and a dramatic shift in strategy for technology\ncompanies. Suddenly these companies are acknowledging that\npatents are a strategic asset worth billions.  Here\u2019s an inside look at what happened -- and what\u2019s at\nstake -- and remember, as you read this, that my company buys\nand licenses high-tech patents.  Most big tech companies inhabit winner-take-most markets,\nin which any company that gets out in front can develop an\nenormous lead. This is how Microsoft came to dominate in\nsoftware,  Intel Corp . in processors,  Google Inc. (GOOG)  in web search,\nOracle Corp. in databases, Amazon.com Inc. in web retail, and so\non.  As a result, the tech world has seen a series of mad\nscrambles by companies wanting to be king of the hill. In the\nlate 1980s, the battle was for dominance of spreadsheet and\nword-processing software. In the late 1990s, it was about e-\ncommerce on the emerging Internet. The latest whatever-it-takes\nstruggle has been over social networks, with enough drama to\nscript  a Hollywood movie .  In each case, the recipe for success was to bring to\nmarket, at a furious pace, products that incorporate new\nfeatures. Along the way, inconvenient intellectual property\nrights were ignored.  Copyrights Are Easy  Yes, copyright was almost religiously enforced. Copyrights\nare trivial to obtain (just type the \u201cc\u201d in a circle symbol),\nand software companies see them as essential to restraining\npiracy, which hurts revenue. Patents are a different story,\nhowever. It takes time for engineers to apply for patents and\neven more time if they diligently respect other people\u2019s\npatents. So technology companies typically did neither.  In fact, many tech companies forbid their engineers from\nchecking whether their products incorporate others\u2019 patents. The\npractice amounts to an intellectual property version of \u201cdon\u2019t\nask, don\u2019t tell.\u201d  As tech giants commercialized ideas that had been pioneered\nby small companies and merged once-separate technologies into\nnew products, they infringed other people\u2019s patents. Personal\ncomputers took over publishing, photo processing, cash handling\nand a million other functions once performed by other companies\u2019\npatented products. Smart phones likewise displaced more\nspecialized devices, such as GPS units and bar-code readers.\nWhen the TV commercial says, \u201cThere\u2019s an app for that,\u201d the\n\u201cthat\u201d part is sometimes covered by patents the app creator\ndoesn\u2019t own.  Patent Vulnerability  Once tech giants got to the top, they realized that their\ncavalier treatment of patents had left them vulnerable. If you\nalready control 90 percent of the market, your own patent\nportfolio does little for you. But outside patent owners\nsometimes show up and ask to be paid. Last month, the U.S.\nSupreme Court decided that Microsoft, the company I used to work\nfor, must pay almost $300 million to a Toronto-based company\ncalled I4i LP, which claimed its patented technology was used in\nMicrosoft Word. All tech companies face this sort of claim, and\nthey\u2019re not happy about it.  The biggest companies, which have always touted their\nbrilliant innovations to justify the billions of dollars in\n stock options  they pay their executives, have been in the odd\nposition of attacking the patent system and publicly deprecating\nthe innovations of others. Patents attempt to create a level\nplaying field, but the last thing an 800-pound gorilla of a\ncompany wants is a fair fight. After succeeding in part by\nstealing other people\u2019s inventions, they decry any inventors who\nhave the temerity to ask for a share of the returns.  In Congress, lobbyists for every major semiconductor,\nsoftware and Internet-services company worked for seven years to\nundermine the much-needed patent reform bill and to delay its\npassage. (The House and Senate each recently passed a version of\nthe bill; they are now working to reconcile the two measures.)  Yet even as that was going on, a growing number of tech\ncompanies started to discover that patents might be useful after\nall. In 2009, Micron Technology, a major computer chipmaker,\ntransferred about 4,500 of its patents to a renowned patent\nlitigator in the hope that he could make some money on them. And\nin the past two years, Microsoft has sued companies that were\nusing the Linux computer operating system and Android, Google\u2019s\nmobile-phone platform, to collect on what it viewed as its share\nof the patent liability that is hidden in a lot of \u201cfree\u201d\nsoftware.  Attack by Apple  It isn\u2019t just about the money; these are also strategic\nmoves. Apple, flush with the iPhone\u2019s success but understandably\nworried that it might wind up becoming the R&D outfit that\nprototyped ideas that made others rich, has recently sued HTC\nCorp., Samsung and others. Just last week, the company won a\npreliminary ruling from the International Trade Commission,\nwhich if upheld will prevent HTC from importing smart phones\ninto the U.S., essentially wiping out its business here.  Microsoft and Apple could have sued Google; most of the\ndisputed features are in Android code. Instead, they elected to\nsue Google\u2019s customers as a way to avoid an all-out war with the\nsearch giant -- reminiscent of how, in the  Cold War , the U.S.\nand the  Soviet Union  used to battle by proxy in places such as\n Vietnam . Oracle, buoyed by patents it got in its acquisition of\nSun Microsystems, was less circumspect; it sued Google directly.  These tussles set the stage for Nortel to put on the block\nmore than 6,000 patents and patent applications, which cover\nmany features of current and future mobile phones, in an auction\norchestrated by Lazard Ltd. Analysts at my company and elsewhere\nin the industry found that the patents were good, but what made\nthem extraordinary wasn\u2019t their quality -- it was simply that\nthey were on the market and hadn\u2019t been widely licensed. Just\nsix months ago, the expected selling price had been $200 million\nto $400 million -- a lot of money, but still a pittance compared\nwith the prize of being the biggest winner in the smart-phone\nbusiness.  Google Bids  Google then made its move, tendering a public stalking-\nhorse offer of $900 million that sent shock waves through the\nindustry. Even stranger, its offer allowed Lazard to shop the\ndeal for several months.  Many people were surprised that Google stepped forward; it\nhas consistently been one of the most outspoken critics of the\npatent system, presumably because it faces enormous potential\npatent liability. Even its basic business model of advertising-\nsupported search was first invented and patented by a company\ncalled  GoTo.com , which sued Google for infringement in 2002.\nGoogle settled the lawsuit shortly before its initial public\noffering in 2004.  The amount of Google\u2019s offer was unexpected, but the high\nprice made perfect sense. Google has very few of its own\npatents; with Nortel\u2019s portfolio, it could change the balance of\npower in the smart-phone industry. It could threaten to\ncountersue any company that attacked Android, or it could even\ntake a page from Apple\u2019s book and go on the attack. Such potent\nammunition in the battle for smart-phone supremacy could be\nworth far more than $900 million.  A third shocker was how Google structured its public bid.\nNeither I nor anybody I have spoken with can explain what Google\nwas thinking. Had it simply waited for the auction, it easily\ncould have won. Other bidders had much lower expectations and\nwouldn\u2019t have had the time to get board approval for bids large\nenough to stay in the game.  Schemes and Counterschemes  Instead, the stalking-horse offer set in motion\nunprecedented scheming and counterscheming among strange\nbedfellows. Companies that normally fight one another, such as\ngame-console rivals Microsoft and Sony and smart-phone rivals\nApple and Research in Motion Ltd., pondered whether they hated\nthe prospect of a patent-powerful Google even more. Investment\ncompanies like mine, which had been interested in Nortel\u2019s\nportfolio for its potential financial return, decided the\nbidding was too rich for our blood, and dropped out. As the\nauction neared, rumors flew about who was teaming up with whom\nand how high the bids would soar.  Then, as the auction began, Google unveiled one more\nsurprise. Its bids were numbers like $1,902,160,540. That\u2019s a\nbillion times Brun\u2019s constant, which appears in the mathematics\nof prime numbers. And its successive bids were other\nmathematical constants, including one for pi billion dollars\n($3,141,592,653).  Math geekiness, it turns out, doesn\u2019t guarantee victory. A\nconsortium of six other companies -- Microsoft, Apple, RIM, Sony\nEricsson Mobile Communications AB and EMC Corp\/ Massachusetts  --\nwon with an astounding $4.5 billion bid.  Google\u2019s Strategy  The result effectively retains the status quo. Google still\nhas no strategic weapon to compensate for the patent liability\ninherent in Android, so the lawsuits will continue. Some in the\nindustry think Google acted brilliantly; the company is no worse\noff than it was before, and it cost its competitors $4.5\nbillion. Others argue that Google was somehow snookered by\nLazard into a disastrous strategy that has left its competitors\nbetter armed for the fight -- and more than a little angry. You\ndon\u2019t pay $4.5 billion for assets and then let them sit on the\nshelf.  More importantly, this sale validates the notion that\npatents will be a fundamental tool in the tech industry. They\nhad been moving toward that position for years, but the\nmagnitude of Nortel\u2019s sale shows that they have arrived. Patents\nvirtually define the pharmaceutical and biotech markets, and in\nthe future they could play the same role for tech.  What\u2019s next? The history of mergers and acquisitions\nsuggests one possibility. Once upon a time in the clubby\natmosphere of corporate America, hostile takeovers were rare;\ngentlemen just didn\u2019t do such things. Then, in the 1960s, the\nhostile takeovers came to be accepted as a legitimate business\ntool. Similarly, the strategic use of patents now appears to be\naccepted in the technology industry. If that\u2019s true, then Nortel\nis just the beginning. Instead, the program spurred infidelity.  Participants in the project texted questions on sexual health topics to a service set up by Google, Grameen and the local mobile-phone provider. Using its search technology, Google worked with Grameen to develop a way to pick up key words in the texts and reply with templated answers. Infidelity jumped to 27 percent from 12 percent of those involved in the project, one of the findings of a soon-to-be published Google-funded  study  by  Innovations for Poverty Action , a non-profit organization.  The unexpected result exposes kinks in the growing field of mobile health, which is bringing together technology companies, wireless carriers, drugmakers and non-profit organizations to explore applications ranging from diagnostics to disease tracking. They see the potential to improve the health of more people using mobile phones, with  subscriptions  at about 96 percent of the global population, more than twice the number of Internet users.  \u201cAlong with the successes, there have been some definite failures,\u201d John Tippett, who spent 18 years working on software development at Microsoft Corp. and is now director of mobile health innovation at the Washington, D.C.-based Grameen Foundation, said in an interview. \u201cAs an industry, we\u2019re not crawling anymore, but we\u2019re not quite running yet.\u201d  Withholding Sex  With the program in Uganda, which began in 2009, infidelity may have risen as women became more aware of the risks of cheating and insisted on going for testing with their husbands, said study author  Dean Karlan , an economics professor at Yale University in New Haven,  Connecticut . Some men resisted, leading women to deny them sex, which the men then sought from other women, Karlan said.  Mobile health still holds promise in the world\u2019s poorest nations, where it offers an inexpensive way to reach many people, even in rural areas. Cellular penetration in developing countries is at 89 percent, the International Telecommunication Union, a United Nations agency, said in a February  report .  Using mobile technology may also help health systems cut spending through remote patient monitoring, better adherence to drug regimens and lifestyle improvements that may prevent chronic diseases from developing. Such measures could help reduce costs by almost 100 billion euros ($130 million) in the European Union by 2017, according to a report yesterday by PricewaterhouseCoopers and GSMA, a mobile operators industry group based in  London .  Vodafone Partnership  Vodafone Group Plc , the second-largest wireless carrier, in December said it is working with U.K. drugmaker  GlaxoSmithKline Plc (GSK)  to develop a pilot program to increase vaccination coverage in  Mozambique  using mobile technology. Glaxo, based in London, sells vaccines including Rotarix for rotavirus and Pediatrix for childhood illnesses.  Vodafone, based in Newbury,  England , has also implemented a program in  Tanzania  using its M-PESA  text-based payment service  for treatment of  fistula , or chronic incontinence after giving birth, which affects more than 2 million women in Asia and  Africa . Since the program began, the number of surgical interventions to treat fistulas at a hospital in Tanzania has risen to 601 last year from 162 in 2009, according to Vodafone.  Turned Off  Results from various programs show phone technology is better suited for some initiatives than others.  The Google-funded study found that people\u2019s usage of the texting service from mobile-service provider  MTN Group Ltd. (MTN)  dropped by more than half the peak level after a three-month period of heavy advertising by a professional marketing firm. While some of them may have forgotten about the service, they may also have been turned off by the algorithm-based program that didn\u2019t always supply appropriate answers to their questions, especially in the local Luganda language, Yale\u2019s Karlan said.  Designed differently, other projects have seen success. A program in Uganda involving an  SMS-based quiz  on HIV and AIDS and reminders of free screening led to a doubling in test uptake.  \u201cUnlike before, there\u2019s now an almost zero-cost way of giving and receiving information,\u201d Karlan said. \u201cIt just requires the creativity and ingenuity of development and health experts to figure out how to use this technology and design better programs.\u201d  Google is no longer involved in sexual health projects, and current health efforts focus on tracking diseases such as flu and dengue using search technology, according to Kelly Mason, a spokeswoman for the Mountain View, California-based company.  Expectant Mothers  Mobile-health programs work best where the objectives of the users match those of the project organizers, Tippett said.  In the Uganda project, \u201cthe men didn\u2019t have the goal to have safer sex, even though the women did,\u201d he said.  Better suited to mobile technology are projects to improve maternal health, where pregnant women want to deliver a healthy baby, or with sick patients who want to be reminded to take their medication, according to Tippett.  Even in those areas, many details need to be worked out. Grameen\u2019s work in developing countries has shown that in most cases, users prefer voice messages over text messages, while other features such as preference for a man or woman\u2019s voice, whether they prefer that voice to sound like a doctor or a peer, how often they want those messages, and the length of each message, vary by population, Tippett said.  Those accumulated experiences have enabled Grameen to build template-based platforms that can be adapted for each new project. Because the software is open-source, they can be taken to any country.  There are discussions under way about bringing a program in  India  funded by  Johnson & Johnson (JNJ)  -- sending reminders to HIV patients about taking medication and tips on healthy living --to the developed world, he said.  \u201cOur hope is that by building these common pieces and letting others build on top of those, they can more quickly try out things and figure out what works and improve the overall industry,\u201d Tippett said. (AAPL) \u2019s iPhone and  Research in Motion Ltd. (RIM) \u2019s BlackBerry, an analysis of presumed samples of the software shows.  The program can secretly turn on a device\u2019s microphone, track its location and monitor e-mails, text messages and voice calls, according to the findings, being published today by the University of Toronto Munk School of Global Affairs\u2019  Citizen Lab . Researchers used newly discovered malicious software samples to further pull back the curtain on the elusive cyber weapon.  The hunt for clues to the software\u2019s deployment has gained speed since July, when research based on e-mails obtained by  Bloomberg News  identified what looked like a FinFisher product that infects personal computers. In that case, the malware targeted activists from the Persian Gulf kingdom of Bahrain.  The latest analysis, led by security researcher Morgan Marquis-Boire, may demonstrate how such spyware can reach a broader range of devices to follow their owners\u2019 every move.  \u201cPeople are walking around with tools for surveillance in their pockets,\u201d says John Scott-Railton, a doctoral student at the  University of California  Los Angeles\u2019  Luskin School of Public Affairs  who assisted with the research. \u201cThese are the tools that can be used to turn on your microphone and turn your phone into a tracking device.\u201d  Transforming Surveillance  The findings -- which are consistent with Gamma\u2019s own promotional materials for a FinFisher product called FinSpy  Mobile  -- illustrate how the largely unregulated trade in offensive hacking tools is transforming surveillance, making it more intrusive as it reaches across borders and peers into peoples\u2019 digital devices.  FinFisher products can secretly monitor computers, intercepting Skype calls, turning on Web cameras and recording keystrokes. They are marketed by Gamma for  law enforcement  and government use.  \u201cI can confirm that Gamma supplies a piece of mobile intrusion software -- FinSpy Mobile,\u201d Gamma International GmbH Managing Director Martin J. Muench said in an Aug. 28 e-mail. \u201cI certainly don\u2019t intend to discuss how or on what platforms it works. I do not wish to inform criminals of how any of our detection systems are used against them.\u201d  Muench, who is based in Munich, said his company didn\u2019t sell FinFisher spyware to Bahrain. \u201cI am still investigating how a piece of our software went astray,\u201d he said in his e- mail.  In a news release today, Gamma said that information from its sales demonstration server had been stolen at an unknown time by unknown methods.  FinSpy Marker  \u201cThe information that was stolen has been used to identify the software Gamma used for demonstration purposes,\u201d the release said. \u201cNo operations or clients were compromised by the theft.\u201d The Gamma statement said that while its demo products contain the word \u201cFinSpy\u201d -- a marker the researchers used to help identify samples -- its more sophisticated operational products don\u2019t.  Gamma International GmbH in  Germany  is part of U.K.-based Gamma Group. The group also markets FinFisher through Andover, England-based Gamma International UK Ltd. Muench leads the FinFisher product portfolio.  Muench says that Gamma only sells to governments and their agencies and complies with the export regulations of the U.K., U.S. and Germany.  More Samples  The July report on Bahrain led security professionals and activists to give Marquis-Boire\u2019s team additional samples of malware for testing.  Several of those samples became the basis of the new report, and include what appear to be a FinSpy Mobile demonstration copy and live versions sent to actual targets.  The report contains no information about any individuals who were targeted, or whether devices were infected.  In December, anti-secrecy website WikiLeaks  published  a promotional brochure and video for FinSpy Mobile. The video shows a BlackBerry user receiving a message to click on a link for a fake update -- and then making the mistake of doing so.  \u201cWhen FinSpy Mobile is installed on a mobile phone it can be remotely controlled and monitored no matter where in the world the Target is located,\u201d a FinSpy brochure published by WikiLeaks says.  Systems that can be targeted include  Microsoft Corp. (MSFT) \u2019s Windows Mobile, the Apple iPhone\u2019s iOS and BlackBerry and  Google Inc. (GOOG) \u2019s Android, according to the company\u2019s literature. Today\u2019s report says the malware can also infect phones running Symbian, an operating system made by  Nokia Oyj (NOK1V) , and that it appears the program targeting iOS will run on iPad tablets.  Simple Process  A mobile device\u2019s user can become infected by being tricked into going to a Web link and downloading the malware, which can be disguised as something other than FinSpy.  As Gamma\u2019s promotional video illustrates, the process can be as simple as sending someone a text message with a link that looks as if it comes from the phone maker, and asking the user to \u201cplease install this system update,\u201d Marquis-Boire says.  Otherwise, without the use of a previously undiscovered vulnerability, the person sneaking the program onto a phone must gain physical access to the device or know its passwords, the study says.  The spyware doesn\u2019t appear to take advantage of any vulnerability in the phones or their operating systems, the study says.  \u2019Avoid Clicking\u2019  FinSpy software written for Windows Mobile shouldn\u2019t be able to infect the newer Windows Phone system, which Microsoft introduced in 2010, said Claudio Guarnieri, a researcher for Boston-based security risk-assessment company  Rapid7 , who analyzed the Windows portion of the malware for the new report.  Redmond, Washington-based Microsoft said its anti-malware software blocks the FinSpy Trojan, and that Windows Phone doesn\u2019t allow for the installation of unknown, third-party software.  \u201cWe strongly encourage Windows Mobile owners to avoid clicking on or otherwise downloading software or links from unknown sources, including  text messages ,\u201d Microsoft said in a statement.  \u201cBlackBerry smartphones give customers control over what can be installed on the device in addition to prompting users to grant permissions to third-party applications,\u201d Waterloo, Ontario-based RIM said in a statement. \u201cWe recommend customers only download applications from trusted sources to help protect against potentially malicious software.\u201d  Espoo, Finland-based Nokia\u2019s press office issued a statement saying users would need to actively choose to install an application such as FinFisher.  Apple Certificate  \u201cThough we have seen claims made for similar products in the past, we have not had any reported incidents from customers as a result of such spyware,\u201d the statement said. Nokia decided last year to abandon Symbian in favor of Windows Phone.  Cupertino, California-based Apple and Mountain View, California-based Google declined to comment, spokeswomen for the companies said.  The researchers said it appeared an Apple developer\u2019s certificate in Muench\u2019s name was used in building the application that targets iOS, citing text found in the program. Muench said the certificate was used only for research purposes. An Apple spokeswoman didn\u2019t immediately respond to a request for comment on the certificate.  Global Reach  The new study also sheds light on FinFisher\u2019s global reach, bolstering separate findings by researchers who said on Aug. 8 that computers in at least 10 countries on five continents show signs of being command servers to which computers infected by FinFisher send their pilfered data. That study was led by Guarnieri of Rapid7.  The research published today used the original Bahraini samples to establish a unique pattern in which command computers communicate with infected machines -- and then scanned  computer networks  for such patterns.  More Clues  The scanning effort, led by Bill Marczak, a computer science doctoral candidate at the University of California Berkeley, turned up many of the same machines found by Guarnieri, who had used a different method. It also identified new countries, bringing the total number of nations with suspected command servers to at least 15.  The mobile-infecting samples obtained for the report, which transmit data via the Internet and text message, also provided clues to FinFisher\u2019s deployment.  In one case, a sample was found transmitting to the same Internet address in the  Czech Republic  that Guarnieri had identified in his study as a likely FinFisher command computer.  It\u2019s unclear whether any government agencies in the countries identified in the studies are Gamma clients or whether the users may be based in other countries.  A spokesman at the Czech Republic\u2019s interior ministry said he has no information of Gamma being used there, nor any knowledge of its use at other state institutions. A spokeswoman for the  Defense Ministry  said it has never used Gamma products. The Czech secret service didn\u2019t respond to an e-mailed request for comment.  FinFisher Oversight  Gamma\u2019s Muench said the focus on his product was unfair because there are other intrusion tools that lack the oversight provided by FinFisher, which is designed to gather evidence for use in court and is only sold to governments.  He pointed to Rapid7, which while investigating Gamma also distributes  Metasploit , a product downloadable for free that contains a database of exploits, which hackers can use to take advantage of vulnerabilities in systems or software. Rapid7 markets Metasploit as a defensive tool for testing whether computers can be penetrated.  \u201cWhy is no one making a fuss about the free malware available through their website which is completely unrestricted and could and does go anywhere?\u201d Muench said in his e-mail. \u201cCan Rapid7 claim that they have never directly or indirectly supplied malwares worldwide?\u201d  Rapid7 said in a statement that it provides the security industry with a way to test defenses against known exploits that are already being abused, and levels the playing field with malicious attackers. \u201cMetasploit is not malware,\u201d the statement said.
