To contact the editor responsible for this story:\nNick Baker at \n nbaker7@bloomberg.net","path":".\/2008_2012_msft_bloomberg_news\/u-s-stocks-advance-on-european-debt-optimism-economic-data.txt"},{"id":54482473,"title":"Descended From Apes, Acting Like Slime Molds: Nathan Myhrvold","released_at":"<date>August 18 2011<\/date> <time>00:00:51<\/time>","content":"As we lurch from one high-stakes\npolitical drama to another, it is natural to wonder why\nsocieties aren\u2019t better at avoiding self-inflicted crises. Here\nin the U.S. earlier this month, the government barely dodged\ndefault, even though economists reached consensus months ago on\nwhen the debt limit would need to be raised.  Meanwhile in  Europe , one inadequate government response\nafter another has all but assured that anxiety over the solvency\nof  Greece  and the creditworthiness of Italy and  Spain  will\ncontinue to fester, roiling global markets and pushing the\nEuropean Union to the brink of ruin.  Pundits have been referring to these spectacles as \u201ctrain\nwrecks,\u201d as if they happen at high speed. Hardly. These trains\nare moving at inches an hour; for years, we\u2019ve seen the\npotential accident ahead. So why do we end up with the tangled\nmess?  It\u2019s an important question because, looking down the track,\nit\u2019s easy to spot other big trains on collision courses. In the\nU.S., our deeply flawed health-care system long ago lost its\nbrakeman, and the  Affordable Care Act , enacted last year, failed\nto fix the major causes of runaway costs. To the contrary, many\nargue that it exacerbated some of them. The problem of providing\nhealth care in the U.S. is not solved; we\u2019re going to have to\nwait for some future crisis before it gets more attention.  The current funding structure for Social Security is going\nto run headlong into the demographic shift of aging baby\nboomers, bankrupting the program and perhaps the country along\nwith it. Economists know this, but the political reality is that\nwe cannot fix the system in advance; we have to wait for the\ncrisis to occur. Europe and  Japan  face even worse trouble with\ntheir state pensions.  Ignoring  Climate Change   We have yet to develop the technology that will be needed\nto meet the world\u2019s fast-growing demand for energy. And although\nclimate scientists are almost apoplectic about the economic and\necological risks created by global warming, no efforts to combat\nit have been even remotely commensurate to the challenge. Global\nlevels of carbon dioxide continue to climb unabated.  Politicians don\u2019t like to face unpleasant realities. In\ntruth, nobody does, but as individuals, we have no choice; if we\nneglect to plan ahead, we are held accountable. Fail to meet\nyour responsibilities at work, and you get fired. Ignore your\ncar\u2019s gas gauge, and you get stranded.  So why do we have trouble avoiding catastrophes as a\nsociety? The answer may lie in the biology of colonial\norganisms. Society, it turns out, behaves a lot like a slime\nmold.  A slime mold is a colony-forming creature that occupies the\nevolutionary middle ground between single-celled microorganisms\nsuch as bacteria, which generally fend for themselves, and truly\nmulticellular animals such as humans, in which trillions of\nhighly specialized cells organize themselves into the heart,\neyes, brain and so on. Heart cells aren\u2019t out for themselves --\nthey dutifully perform their very specific job of pumping blood\nto the rest of the cells in the body.  Colonial organisms, in contrast, are creatures that can\nlive by themselves, but instead frequently band together in\nmacroscopic collections. Sometimes -- as in ant hills and bee\nhives -- the members of the colony specialize to a modest\ndegree, but they are still full-fledged individuals. Yet the\ncolony as a whole acts like a larger organism. Certain slime\nmolds, for example, can move, reproduce and exhibit other simple\nanimal-like properties.  Brainless Organism  But a slime mold doesn\u2019t have eyes or a brain -- or any\nother organ, for that matter. Creating an organ requires a deep\nsubjugation of interests. The heart has to trust that the brain\nwill run things and that the reproductive system will look after\nits long-term interests.  Although it may be tempting to think of social institutions\nas functioning like organs, human societies behave, in practice,\nmuch more like slime molds. They don\u2019t have eyes or brains that\nare anything like human eyes and brains. So although any one of\nus can learn from our mistakes, foresee problems and act\nreasonably to solve them, collectively we don\u2019t do a very good\njob of this.  Granted, our species is very intelligent and has developed\nexquisite communication across the world and through the\ncenturies. But while people are smart enough to anticipate\nproblems, they are also smart enough to make counterarguments.\nEvery good idea in history has had to fight against many bad\nideas before winning broad acceptance.  Like the individual mold cells in a slime colony, most\npeople mainly pursue their self-interest, influenced only\npartially by a concern for the common good. And our individual\nagendas often conflict. You can\u2019t balance the federal budget,\nfor example, without goring somebody\u2019s ox. Do we raise taxes,\ncut spending, eliminate subsidies? Every option is resisted by\nsome people.  What\u2019s more, society as a whole isn\u2019t rational. In\npolitics, religion and other areas of culture, people disagree\non the worth of competing ideas. There is no equivalent to the\nscientific method that can determine in a robust way which ideas\nmatch the real world, and which ones can be ruled out.  So\nconflicting ideologies persist indefinitely.  Economics suffers from this problem, too. Economists want\ntheir discipline to be a science, and they have nailed down a\nfew precepts, but many of their debates are still clouded by\nideology.  Absent a political counterpart to the scientific method,\ndemocracies rely on an error-correction system that is based\npartly on checks and balances and partly on elections. Checks\nand balances slow decision-making by giving rise to horse\ntrading: Rather than block your tendency to overspend, I agree\nto fund your project, so long as you agree to fund mine.  Popular Policy Makers  Elections, for their part, are typically popularity\ncontests rather than measures of candidates\u2019 relative competency\nor effectiveness. Imagine if scientific truth were determined\naccording to which scientist was most popular. To be successful,\nscientists would have to be charismatic and attractive -- and\nhuman knowledge would suffer terribly. It\u2019s easy to blame\npoliticians for their many faults, but ultimately we have the\npoliticians we insist on having.  The net result of these limitations is that even advanced\ndemocracies are functionally blind, so they deal with problems\nonly when they bump into them and perceive a \u201csudden\u201d crisis.\nAmericans put up with increasing air pollution for decades\nbefore the situation got so intolerable that Congress passed the\n Clean Air Act . Hundreds of species went extinct before\nsystematic action was taken to save endangered plants and\nanimals.  Unfortunately, this way of responding to problems runs the\nrisk of being too little, too late. Not all problems can be\nfixed after they have become severe. If we wait until all the\ncheap oil is gone before developing alternatives, the resulting\neconomic disruption will be traumatic. And if we wait until\nglobal warming is intolerable before making serious cutbacks in\nemissions of long-lived  greenhouse gases , the physics of the\natmosphere virtually guarantees that all our efforts will then\nbe too late. To head off these problems, this slime mold needs\nto grow eyes and a brain.  ( Nathan Myhrvold , the former chief strategist and chief technology \nofficer at Microsoft and the founder and chief executive officer of \n Intellectual Ventures , is a Bloomberg View columnist. The opinions \nexpressed are his own.) (MSFT) \u2019s vow to negotiate\nwith competitors over industry-standard patents, instead of\ntrying to block their products, marks a change from the\ncompany\u2019s position less than a year ago.  The policy announced yesterday by Microsoft came the same\nday that  Google Inc. (GOOG)  made its own promise regarding standard-\nessential patents to appease regulators scrutinizing its $12.5\nbillion acquisition of Motorola Mobility Holdings Inc.  Microsoft, Google and  Apple Inc. (AAPL)  are staking out positions\non standard-setting patents amid global litigation over wireless\ndevices and tighter regulatory scrutiny. The Microsoft pledge,\nand an Apple policy made public Feb. 7, were timed to undermine\nGoogle, said Andrew Updegrove, a lawyer with Gesmer Updegrove in\n Boston .  \u201cYou already have Google increasingly under the\nspotlight,\u201d said Updegrove, who advises standard-setting boards\non intellectual property policies. \u201cThey\u2019re living in a tighter\nand tighter confinement just because their market power is\nincreasing.\u201d  By issuing policies that contrast with Google, Microsoft\nand Apple \u201care playing to the marketplace and they\u2019re playing\nto the regulators,\u201d he said.  Google sent letters to standard-setting boards yesterday\nsaying it would seek a royalty fee of no more than 2.25 percent\nof the net cost of devices using its patents, and would try to\nresolve any disputes through negotiation before asking courts to\nblock use of the Motorola Mobility technology. It didn\u2019t match\nMicrosoft\u2019s pledge to not pursue bans on technology that\u2019s\nessential to industry standards.  Microsoft Shift  Microsoft will also make its industry-essential patents\navailable without requiring companies to cross-license their own\nnon-essential technology, according to a  posting  yesterday on\nthe company\u2019s website.  \u201cPatent holders should not seek to block shipments of\ncompeting products just because they implement an industry\nstandard -- a license on reasonable terms is always available,\u201d\nDave Heiner, who heads Microsoft\u2019s corporate standards and\nantitrust groups, said in a blog  posting .  That\u2019s different from what Microsoft told the U.S. Federal\nTrade Commission in June. The company said the existence of a\npledge to offer patent licenses on fair terms \u201cshould not\npreclude a patent holder from seeking preliminary injunctive\nrelief or commencing an action in the International Trade\nCommission just because the patent holder has made a licensing\ncommitment.\u201d  A requirement to not seek any ban \u201cmay reduce any\nincentives that implementers might have to engage in good faith\nnegotiations with the patent holder,\u201d according to a written\n statement  submitted by Heiner in June and posted on the FTC\u2019s\nwebsite.  EU Scrutiny  Motorola Mobility has accused Microsoft and Apple of\ninfringing patents that are covered partly by standards in which\ncompanies agree to share technology that is common across their\nindustry. Google, which has drawn scrutiny over the acquisition,\nsent letters to standard-setting groups reassuring them it will\nmaintain Motorola Mobility\u2019s licensing program.  The European Union\u2019s antitrust regulators will rule on the\nacquisition by Feb 13, Antoine Colombani, a spokesman for the\ncommission in Brussels, said Feb. 7. The agency could clear the\ndeal or open an in-depth probe that would last about 90 working\ndays.  That same agency is investigating whether  Samsung\nElectronics Co.  broke a 1998 commitment to license standard-\nessential patents on fair terms. Samsung accused Apple of\ninfringing such patents, part of a global patent battle between\nthe two companies.  Apple Letter  In a November letter to the European  Telecommunications\nStandards Institute , Apple said the \u201cindustry suffers from a\nlack of consistent adherence\u201d to policies that require\ncompanies to license standard-essential patents on \u201cfair,\nreasonable and non-discriminatory\u201d terms.  In that letter, reported Feb. 7 by the Wall Street Journal,\nApple said companies that pledge to license their patents on\nfair terms can\u2019t seek to prevent use of the inventions without\nbeing in violation of their commitment.  Motorola Mobility has sought sales bans in  Germany  on Apple\nproducts using standard-essential patents, and is seeking to\nhalt U.S. imports of Microsoft\u2019s Xbox gaming system. Microsoft\nhas argued that the U.S. International Trade Commission\nshouldn\u2019t impose import bans when there is a violation of\nstandard-essential patents.  Microsoft\u2019s policy doesn\u2019t bar the company from seeking\nbans on the use of patented technology that isn\u2019t part of an\nindustry standard or from suing to demand compensation for the\nuse of the essential patents. The cash concerns underscore the depth of Nokia\u2019s crisis. The company has paid a dividend every year since at least 1989, which is as far back as its  electronic records  go. Even the breakup of the  Soviet Union , a major buyer of Nokia\u2019s networking gear whose demise spelled financial tumult for the company more than 20 years ago, didn\u2019t prevent it from returning cash to investors.  Paper Mill  Nokia, based in Espoo,  Finland , will probably omit the payout for 2012 after slashing it by more than half over the past four years to 20 cents a share, according to  data compiled  by Bloomberg. To maintain the dividend at its current level, Nokia would have to pay about 750 million euros ($964 million) annually out of its dwindling bank account.  Doug Dawson , a spokesman for Nokia, declined to comment on dividend plans. The phonemaker typically announces its annual payout when it  reports  fourth-quarter earnings in January.  Founded in 1865 as a pulp and paper mill on the Nokia River, the company expanded into mobile phones in the 1980s and became  Europe \u2019s most valuable corporation at the height of the technology boom. But Nokia was slow to adapt as touchscreen smartphones became the real drivers of the mobile handset market, and its stock has plunged about 90 percent since Apple introduced the iPhone in 2007.  The company has announced more than 20,000 job cuts, closed production and research facilities and sold patents and other assets in a bid to become profitable again.  Dwindling Cash  Nokia lost 2.34 billion euros in the first half and analysts estimate losses will continue at least  six more quarters , the average projections compiled by Bloomberg show. Its net cash has shrunk by half in the past five years to 4.2 billion euros at the of June and will drop below 3 billion euros by year-end,  Standard & Poor\u2019s  predicts. Gross cash at the end of June was 9.4 billion euros.  Nokia also has debt of 5.2 billion euros and some repayments are looming. A 1.25 billion-euro bond matures in February 2014, and the company faces repayments in 2016, 2017 and 2019, according to  data  compiled by Bloomberg. A 1.5 billion-euro revolving credit facility could help Nokia shore up its cash reserves.  The cost of insuring Nokia bonds using credit-default swaps has almost tripled this year and reached a record of 1,240 basis points on July 18. It added 18 basis points, or 1.9 percent, to 950.58 basis points as of 4:48 p.m. Helsinki time, the biggest intraday jump in three weeks, according to data compiled by Bloomberg.  Credit-Default Swaps  Credit-default swaps pay the buyer face value if a borrower fails to meet its obligations, less the value of the defaulted debt. A basis point equals $1,000 annually on a contract protecting $10 million of debt.  With Nokia\u2019s debt at  junk status  with the three main rating companies, it should already have suspended dividends, said Sami Sarkamies, a Nordea Bank AB analyst in Helsinki.  \u201cIt was a mistake not to stop the dividend payment given the weakened outlook,\u201d he said. \u201cThis may cost shareholders dearly if Nokia for example needs to pull the plug early on its smartphone revamp due to not being able to afford the costs.\u201d  Nokia controlled more than half of global smartphone sales before the first iPhone and Android devices were introduced. Today Nokia\u2019s share in smartphones is about 6.6 percent, according to research firm IDC. IPhone and Android combined make up 85 percent of the market.  IPhone Challenge  Nokia last year abandoned its home-grown operating system and began using the  Windows operating system  from  Microsoft Corp. (MSFT) , where CEO Elop used to work. On Sept. 5, Nokia introduced two new models that run Windows Phone 8, the newest version of the program that Nokia is betting on to lure customers away from Apple and Google. The phones will face off against the iPhone 5, which was unveiled on Sept. 12 and shattered the first-day sales of the previous version. The Lumia 920 will be priced at 599 euros and the Lumia 820 at 499 euros in the country.  TeliaSonera AB (TLSN)  in Sweden will sell the device from Nov. 12.  Shares of Nokia added 2.6 percent to 2.05 euros at 4:58 p.m. in Helsinki. They have slumped more than 70 percent since February 2011, when the company said its phones would run Windows. In fact, his boss raved about him. His manager gave him top ratings in his performance evaluations, space to do his work, and had never been controlling. He was, according to Chris, terribly, unswervingly nice. Picture perfect boss, right? Wrong. His manager had been in the company for 20 years. He had learned how to survive in the bureaucracy: don't make too many waves, don't cause problems. He played the political game well enough to still be there but not well enough to strengthen his reputation. He had slowly lost his political clout. As a result, his team had been winnowed away to a fraction of the size it used to be. His own reputation bled over onto the members of his team. For Chris it had a powerful effect on his career: he had been passed up three times for a promotion he was repeatedly promised. It was not what his boss was doing that caused the problem. It was what his boss was  not  doing. Over a twelve-month period I have gathered data from 1,000 managers about their experiences at over 100 companies including Apple, Cisco, HP, IBM, Intel, Microsoft, Novel, and Symantec. I wanted to understand the conditions under which people did the very best work of their careers. What I expected to find were examples of over managing, controlling, tyrannical managers. About half of the participants confirmed this assumption. The other half surprised me: what they described were managers who were nice but weak. I once spent two days running a strategy session with just such an executive. He spoke with a soft, quiet voice. He never interrupted anyone when they were speaking. When he walked into the meeting he had a \"nice\" word for everyone. Every time the team became \"positively frustrated\" and ready to make the change necessary to get to the next level he would stand up and say sweetly, \"Oh, I just wanted to remind you all of how far we have come.\" And after a few more sentences the spark of aspiration was gone from the room. He unintentionally signaled the status quo was plenty good enough. There was no need to try harder or change how things were going. He reminded me of what Jim Hacker (the fictional politician in the English cult classic \" Yes, Minister \") said to his bureaucratic colleague, \"You really are a wet blanket, Humphrey, you just go around stirring up apathy.\" Another executive I worked with had an almost voodoo ability to neutralize people's desire to take action. With an almost Jedi-like wave of the hand he seemed to say, \"These are not the things you care about changing.\" People would be kicking and cussing before he walked into the room but a little later they would wonder what they had been frustrated about. That is a useful party trick to be sure but the result was career limiting for each member of his team. Everyone on the team was branded as average and in a reorganization the entire team were \"let go.\" These nice but somewhat absentee managers can continue to survive, unchecked for decades. At least a controlling boss who yells all the time gets noticed: they create acute pain and people complain. In contrast, the pain these nice \"Neutralizers\" produce is chronic. The pain is inflicted slowly, drip by drip. On any given day an employee can say, \"Well, it's not so bad.\" They are, after all, nice. But the cumulative effect on your career can be dramatic. \nThis is a problem hidden in plain sight. The issue has been unintentionally camouflaged by leadership thinkers (I am guilty) who may have overemphasized overmanagement and underemphasized undermanagement. The majority of the leadership literature over the past 25 years has done this. But what happens if an undermanager reads an article, book or attends training of this kind? It may encourage them to continue in their hands-off, low control, absentee approach. They may say, \"Yes, I don't like to smother my people or control them.\" They may speak about empowerment and enablement. All the while they allow their people's career prospect to decline slowly. In the case of Chris, just naming the problem was liberating. Once he could see how toxic the situation was he took action. He met with his mentors. He visited with his connections. Within a few weeks he took a lateral move to get away from his \"nice\" manager. After another move a year later he is in a terrific position in a better company with far better prospects than he had before. Just developing a heightened awareness of the issue can be helpful. After all, we cannot solve a problem we do not see. (MSFT)  for failing to fulfill its antitrust obligations\nto the EU. The fine could be as high as 10 percent of\nMicrosoft\u2019s annual revenue, or about $7 billion.  That isn\u2019t a paper threat. The EU has levied huge fines\nagainst Microsoft before. Governments should wield that kind of\nimmense power against private parties only when they are certain\na real wrong is being corrected. Unfortunately, everything about\nthe EU\u2019s antitrust  history  with Microsoft should make us\nquestion whether that is the case here.  Microsoft\u2019s battle with the EU also offers a broader\ncautionary tale: Companies can create real risks for themselves\nand shareholders when they make product-design commitments to\nsettle government actions. We have seen this happen in recent\nsettlements between the U.S. Federal Trade Commission and Google\nInc., Facebook Inc. and MySpace Inc. In each case, the companies\nface an extra layer of regulation for the next 20 years for\nproducts that could change daily. Google may soon face new\nantitrust actions in the U.S. and the EU for its search engine\ndesign and patent licensing practices.  In a world dominated by Apple Inc., Amazon.com Inc., Google\nand Facebook, there is little doubt that Microsoft\u2019s market\npower has declined. U.S. antitrust officials have been finished\nwith Microsoft for some time, yet the EU continues to regulate\nthe company through its antitrust laws. (Disclosure: I have\nreceived research funding in the past from Microsoft, but have\nnot been involved in any of the EU matters. The  University of\nChicago Law School , my employer, continues to receive Microsoft\nfunding.)  Media Players  A little background is in order. The EU in 2004 found that\nMicrosoft had violated competition laws because of the way\nWindows worked with certain programs that run computer servers.\nIt also thought Microsoft was tilting competition in media\nplayers by distributing its player software with Windows, an\nactivity called tying in antitrust-speak.  When the EU decided in 2008 that it didn\u2019t like the way\nMicrosoft was complying with that decision, it fined the company\n899 million euros, or $1.1 billion in today\u2019s dollars. The EU\nhit the company again in 2009, this time claiming it was tying\nInternet Explorer to Windows.  With that history, and possibly facing a delayed\nintroduction of Windows 7, Microsoft chose to settle rather than\nfight -- hardly a surprising decision. The settlement gave birth\nto the \u201cbrowser ballot.\u201d When you first try to access the\nInternet on a Windows 7 machine in the EU, a choice of browsers\nto install -- 12 of them currently -- pops up.  Microsoft, however, admitted that it  violated  the browser\nagreement again when it released its first major upgrade of\nWindows 7. From February 2011 until July 2012, it rolled out\nmillions of new computers in the EU without the browser ballot.\nMicrosoft said it was a mistake, but how this could go on for 17\nmonths is hard to understand. You would think Microsoft and the\nEU would be monitoring the marketplace. Microsoft created the\nproblem by not quickly fixing its browser-ballot glitch; the EU\nwas seemingly asleep at the switch.  The lesson for companies is that they shouldn\u2019t violate\nsettlements with governments. Yet an even larger issue is at\nstake here: Companies also shouldn\u2019t face huge fines for\nmistakes that may well prove irrelevant in the marketplace.  I refer here to another EU antitrust remedy, which forced\nMicrosoft to release two versions of Windows, one with its media\nplayer and one without. But almost everyone bought the version\nwith the media player. While well-intentioned, the solution\naccomplished little beyond forcing Microsoft to spend money on\nversions of Windows no one wanted.  Hidden Tax  The upshot is that government-dictated product design has\nconsequences, especially in sectors where products change with\ngreat speed. Indeed, antitrust settlements can act as a hidden\ntax on innovation.  At any rate, the EU needn\u2019t have worried. Despite\nMicrosoft\u2019s dominance in personal computers, its Zune MP3 player\nwas a failure due to competition from what consumers decided was\na better product, Apple\u2019s iPod. The EU prescription had wrongly\nfocused on the PC rather than the emergent competition in music\ndevices.  What has happened in the marketplace because of the browser\nballot? We don\u2019t know; the EU doesn\u2019t make its data on this\npublic. That\u2019s too bad. We should expect antitrust regulation to\nbe subject to public scrutiny. There is an unfortunate tendency\nfor governments, in the U.S. and abroad, to want to act without\naccountability.  Not knowing browser market shares, it\u2019s impossible to say\nwhat sort of fine would make sense. It\u2019s clear that EU officials\nwould be overreaching if they sought the maximum penalty.\nInstead, the episode is a technology problem crying out for a\ntechnology remedy, such as taking  Internet Explorer  off the\nbrowser ballot for a period of time to restore competitors\u2019\nmarket shares.  When governments try to design products, the EU\u2019s record\nwith Microsoft suggests they will often fail. Companies\ncontemplating antitrust settlements should take into account the\npossible penalties from mistakes, as well as the risks from\ntying their hands on how rapidly they can innovate. A  report  released today by the  Brookings Institution  found\nthat while the  San Jose , California, metropolitan area still\nleads the nation in hiring skilled foreign workers on temporary\nvisas, places such as Columbus,  Indiana , and Bloomington,\nIllinois, are also becoming centers of activity for foreign-born\nemployees hired under the H-1B program.  The study highlights the nation\u2019s growing reliance upon\nworkers from overseas to fill positions in science, technology\nand engineering. Just 4 percent of the world\u2019s undergraduate\ndegrees in engineering are awarded in the U.S., it said.  \u201cThe heartland is really looking for engineers,\u201d Neil\nRuiz, the study\u2019s co-author and a senior policy analyst at the\nBrookings Metropolitan Policy Program, said in a telephone\ninterview.  The study by the nonprofit Washington-based research\norganization focused on hiring patterns in 106 metropolitan\nareas under the H-1B program, which was created in 1990 to allow\nU.S. companies to hire foreign workers for three to six years\nwhile they seek permanent residency.  It found that demand for foreign workers was intense in\nsmaller Midwestern metropolitan areas such as Fayetteville,\nArkansas, which includes the corporate headquarters for  Wal-Mart\nStores Inc. (WMT)   Driving Demand  In Columbus, a metro area of 76,794 people about 45 miles\nsouth of Indianapolis, the demand was driven largely by  Cummins\nInc. (CMI) , which designs, manufactures and services diesel and\nnatural gas engines. Revenue grew to more than $18 billion last\nyear from $5.7 billion in 2001, data compiled by Bloomberg show.  \u201cAbout half of engineering graduates from U.S. colleges\nare from outside the U.S., so that\u2019s really shaping our pool of\nemployees,\u201d said Janet Williams, a company spokeswoman. \u201cWe\nreally need a wide range -- mechanical engineers, chemical\nengineers, electrical engineers.\u201d  Demand for foreign-born workers has been strongest among\ntechnology companies.  Microsoft Corp. (MSFT)  led all employers in 2010-\n2011, requesting an annual average of 4,109 H-1B workers.  The Redmond, Washington-based company was trailed by  Tata\nConsultancy Services Ltd. (TCS) , a Mumbai-based division of Tata Sons\nLtd. that ranked No. 2 with an average of 3,179 requests a year.\nDeloitte Consulting LLP, a subsidiary of Arlington, Virginia-\nbased Deloitte Touche Tohmatsu ILA Group Ltd., was third with an\naverage 2,981 requests during the 10-year period.  Changing Cap  The number of H-1B visas available during the last decade\nhas varied, with a cap of 195,000 from 2001 to 2003. The maximum\nwas lowered in 2004 to 65,000, with another 20,000 positions\nallowed beginning in 2006 for foreign-born workers with graduate\ndegrees earned at U.S. schools. The limit doesn\u2019t apply to\nacademic or research institutions.  The study found science, technology, engineering and\nmathematics disciplines accounted for 64 percent of all H-1B\nrequests, even though they only made up 5.4 percent of U.S.\nemployment in 2010.  The top areas of demand for  H-1B visas  generally track\npopulation. Employers in the  New York  metro area, the nation\u2019s\nlargest, requested an average of 52,921 foreign-born workers in\n2010 and 2011, or 16.3 percent of the national average.  LA, DC  Companies in the Los Angeles area ranked second, with\n18,048 average requests per year, or 5.5 percent of the total.\nThe  Washington , D.C., metro area ranked No. 5, with 14,569\naverage visa requests, about 4.5 percent of the national total.  Nationwide, there has been an average of 2.4 H-1B requests\nper 1,000 U.S. workers, Ruiz said. In San Jose, employers\nrequested 17.1 H-1B workers for every 1,000 domestic employees.\nColumbus ranked No. 2, with 14.6 H-1B requests per 1,000 such\nworkers; Durham-Chapel Hill,  North Carolina , was third with\n9.79; and Trenton,  New Jersey , fourth with 8.46.  At Cummins, Williams said, H-1B workers total about 1,300,\nwith 900 working at the company\u2019s Columbus headquarters. The\ncompany has about 44,900 employees. She said a substantial\namount of the company\u2019s growth over the last decade has been\nfueled by environmental regulations that affect diesel engines.  The company prefers to hire workers directly from college\nto ensure they adopt its values, Williams said. The downside,\nshe said, is that the small city may be more attractive to\nadults with families than 22-year-old college graduates.  \u201cWe call it \u2018The Athens of the Prairie,\u201d\u2019 said Emily\nFoster, a Washington-based Cummins spokeswoman. This spring, Space\nExploration Technologies Corp., known as SpaceX, launched a\ncapsule that docked with the International Space Station --\nthe first commercial space vehicle to do so.  In the desert of  New Mexico , Virgin Galactic is\npreparing for the first suborbital space flights for paying\ncustomers, with actor  Ashton Kutcher  one of the latest to\nsign up for the privilege. In Huntsville,  Alabama ,\nStratolaunch Systems Inc. is busy dismantling Boeing 747s,\nhoping to use their engines and other systems to build the\nworld\u2019s largest plane, which will help propel a new\nspacecraft into flight.  All three projects have wealthy entrepreneurs backing\nthem: PayPal Inc. co-founder Elon Musk is the head of\nSpaceX, U.K. billionaire  Richard Branson  is the founder and\nchairman of Virgin Group Ltd., and Paul G. Allen, the co-\nfounder of Microsoft Corp., started Stratolaunch last year.  The three men might not know it, but they\u2019re following\nin a grand tradition of private wealth furthering advances\nin rocketry and space exploration.  Baron\u2019s Bounty  In the 19th and early 20th centuries, private citizens\nraised money to promote Earth-based exploration of the\nstars. Charles Tyson Yerkes, a robber baron who transformed\nurban transportation, gave $300,000 to  University of\nChicago  to establish an observatory. James Lick,\n California \u2019s richest man, left much of his  considerable\nfortune  to the  University of California  in 1876 to build an\nobservatory with the world\u2019s most powerful telescope.\nPhilanthropists from  Andrew Carnegie  to  John D. Rockefeller \nhelped fund ever more elaborate technology for scanning the\ncosmos.  But when it came to actually putting a vehicle into\nspace, Daniel Guggenheim stood alone. He and his family\nearned their millions in copper mining and other extractive\nendeavors. Taking over from their father, Guggenheim and\nhis brothers expanded the family business, sometimes\nseeking new technologies to reduce costs.  In 1924, Guggenheim and his wife, Florence, started a\nfoundation, hoping to use their fortune to promote \u201cthe\nwell-being of mankind throughout the world.\u201d  Seeing the effects of engineering breakthroughs and\nexperimentation in business, Guggenheim also wanted to\nsupport science -- in particular, heavier-than-air flight.\nIn 1925, he donated $250,000 to  New York  University to\nstart the first U.S. school of aeronautics. The next year,\nhe spent $2.5 million to start the Daniel Guggenheim Fund\nfor the Promotion of Aeronautics.  Guggenheim\u2019s son Harry, a former Navy pilot, became\nthe fund\u2019s first president. Harry had previously tried to\nget President  Calvin Coolidge  interested in supporting his\nfather\u2019s efforts. Coolidge, not uncharacteristically,\nreplied, \u201cWhat\u2019s the use of getting there quicker if you\nhaven\u2019t got something better to say when you\u2019ve arrived?\u201d  But Harry had a breakthrough when he met  Charles Lindbergh . The fund had provided support to Lindbergh, and\nthe two men became good friends. Lindbergh knew of\npioneering work being done by the physicist Robert Goddard\nat  Clark University  in Worcester,  Massachusetts .  Rocket Man  In 1926, Goddard had tested the world\u2019s first liquid-\nfueled rocket. Using his aunt\u2019s farm as a launch site,\nGoddard sent the rocket to a less-than-dizzying altitude of\n41 feet. Goddard was sure he could do better and was soon\ntalking publicly about the potential for space travel with\nrockets. By 1929, his work had caught Lindbergh\u2019s\nattention.  The next year, Harry introduced Lindbergh to his\nfather and the pilot stirred the elder Guggenheim\u2019s\ninterest in funding Goddard\u2019s work. In 1930, Daniel told\nthe  New York Times (NYT) , \u201cI am convinced the experiments deserve\nsupport.\u201d He backed that up with $100,000, and over the\nyears more than double that amount followed.  With Guggenheim\u2019s money (and some from other sources,\nincluding the Smithsonian Institution), Goddard carried out\nextensive research in Roswell, New Mexico -- about 200\nmiles, as the rocket flies, from where Virgin Galactic will\nlaunch its spacecraft. Through the 1930s, in a series of\nsuccessful launches, he broke the sound barrier and\nincreased the rockets\u2019 altitude to almost two miles.\nGoddard also earned dozens of patents for his work.  There were failures too, of course, including rockets\nthat exploded on the launch pad. Still, with private money\nbacking him, Goddard helped start the Rocket Age. As\nGoddard biographer David A. Clary noted, the Guggenheim\nfamily\u2019s contribution continued even after the scientist\u2019s\ndeath, as it helped his wife, Esther, transcribe his\nresearch notes and diaries.  Daniel and Harry Guggenheim were philanthropists who\nsaw the potential value in speeding the mail, or people,\naround the world on rockets. Yet years after Goddard died,\ntheir support of rocketry also led to a financial payback.\nIn 1960, the U.S. government agreed to pay the Guggenheim\nFoundation $1 million for infringing on patents Goddard had\nwon years before.  Today, Musk, Allen, Branson and others spending their\nway into space see their ventures as potential moneymakers\n-- why else do it? But at some level, they must share what\nGuggenheim family biographer John H. Davis wrote Daniel\n(and surely Harry) had as well: \u201cfaith in the wonders of\ntechnology.\u201d  (Michael Burgan is a freelance writer and the editor\nof \u201cThe Biographer\u2019s Craft,\u201d the official publication of\nBiographers International Organization. The opinions\nexpressed are his own.)  Read more Echoes columns  online . Developers said that while Nokia\u2019s handset business gives Microsoft a ready pipeline of Windows Phone devices, it isn\u2019t enough to overcome a lack of users, or the cost and confusion related to the technical specifications of writing for the company\u2019s phone and tablet devices.  Ultimately, it comes down to where developers can make money -- and that\u2019s not with Microsoft, said William Hurley, a co-founder of  Chaotic Moon , a maker of apps for companies including  Walt Disney Co. (DIS)  He said the company\u2019s most recent game, \u201cDragon Academy\u201d-- which is free to download, with consumers paying for upgrades -- generated more in one hour of sales on Apple devices than was made through all of Chaotic Moon\u2019s releases globally for Windows Phone in the past year.  \u201cWhat basket would you put your eggs?\u201d Hurley said, adding that Chaotic Moon chose not to make \u201cDragon Academy\u201d for Windows Phone.  Big Lag  Microsoft, based in Redmond,  Washington , currently has more than 175,000 applications for Windows Phone, compared with more than 900,000 for Apple iOS and more than 1 million for Google Android -- and even those apps that it does have typically come to its platform later than for rivals.  News-reading app Flipboard Inc., for one, debuted on Apple\u2019s iPad in 2010 and joined Android in 2012, yet has no immediate plans to release a version for Windows Phone. Other notable apps missing include Pinterest, Instagram and Uber.  The paucity of applications has impeded gains in Microsoft\u2019s smartphone market share. The company had  3.7 percent  of the global smartphone market in the second quarter, compared with 79 percent for Android and 13 percent for Apple, according to IDC.  Microsoft executives said they are well aware of the shortcomings and said that adding Nokia will help. Joe Belfiore, vice president and manager for Windows Phone, said owning Nokia will speed creation of handsets with its software and result in a more cohesive marketing strategy.  He said that the takeover will also let Microsoft utilize Nokia\u2019s sales team to educate more people about Windows Phone, especially the staff at retail outlets where people buy their devices.  Changing Perceptions  \u201cIf you\u2019re not paying attention as a retail sales person, a customer walks into your store and asks about phones, you\u2019re going to make your assumption about where Windows Phone is at based on the last time you paid close attention,\u201d Belfiore said.  Microsoft also continues to lighten the cost of building apps for Windows Phone by paying for development and marketing. An example is  Pandora Media Inc. (P) \u2019s music-streaming service, which debuted this year. Microsoft built the application and keeps the software updated.  Facebook Inc. (FB) \u2019s Windows Phone app, which came out in 2010, also was made by Microsoft.  \u201cWe help them with development, whether that\u2019s funding their own development or working with vendors,\u201d Belfiore said. \u201cIn some cases, we\u2019re doing development ourselves.\u201d  Swaying Skeptics  Belfiore said Microsoft will do more promotions for developers once it owns Nokia, including having apps pre-installed on phones.  Some developers still need more convincing. Take Greg Kostello, CEO of video-editing application Givit. Last year, Kostello created an app for Microsoft\u2019s Windows 8 operating system and Microsoft\u2019s Surface tablet. Given Microsoft\u2019s success in personal computers, Kostello expected Surface to be a hit.  Yet after several months and little market traction, San Diego-based  Givit  pulled the plug, choosing instead to focus on the iPhone and Android devices.  Now with Microsoft\u2019s purchase of Nokia\u2019s phones, Kostello wants to see the marketplace emerge before committing resources. \u201cWe tried it, made a bet and didn\u2019t see it take off,\u201d he said. \u201cWe\u2019re a little more gun shy.\u201d  Other Repercussions  Attitudes like Kostello\u2019s ripple beyond Microsoft\u2019s smartphone endeavors to the tablet market now dominated by Apple\u2019s iPad. Microsoft wrote off $900 million of unsold Surface tablets this year after lackluster sales. Microsoft won\u2019t disclose how much it makes from mobile devices and services.  \u201cThe lack of applications that exists for the Windows platform is a critical deterrent in customer adoption,\u201d said David Yoffie, a professor at  Harvard Business School .  Many developers still want Microsoft to succeed in adding another viable outlet for their apps outside of Apple and Google.  \u201cIt would be great to have a third horse in the race,\u201d said John Hayase, chief product officer for music service Slacker Inc. \u201cIf we see a third major mobile platform emerge, that would compel us to change organizationally how we do things.\u201d  Making it easier to create applications that work across Microsoft\u2019s smartphones and tablets will help developers, said Smith of Smule. Right now, the cost of developing for both isn\u2019t worth it, he said.  Another area where Microsoft can focus is business customers, said John Arrow, chairman of Mutual Mobile Inc., which makes apps for companies including Citigroup Inc. Since many businesses already use Microsoft technology, the company is well positioned to expand with phones in the enterprise arena, he said. Some  computer experts are saying  the only way to save the system is to scrap the current bloated code and start over.  Looking back, it seems crazy that neither the  Barack Obama  administration nor the public was prepared for the startup difficulties. There\u2019s no shortage of database experts willing to opine on the complexities of the problem. Plenty of companies have  nightmarish stories  to tell about much simpler software projects. And reporting by the  New York  Times finds that the people involved with the system knew months ago that it was in  serious trouble . \u201cWe foresee a train wreck,\u201d one said back in February.  So why didn\u2019t the administration realize that integrating a bunch of incompatible government databases into a seamless system with an interface just about anyone could understand was a really, really hard problem? Why was even the president seemingly taken by surprise when the system didn\u2019t work like it might in the movies?  We have become seduced by computer glamour.  Whether it\u2019s a television detective instantly checking a database of fingerprints or the ease of Amazon.com\u2019s \u201c1-Click\u201d button, we imagine that software is a kind of magic -- all the more so if it\u2019s software we\u2019ve never actually experienced. We expect it to be effortless. We don\u2019t think about how it got there or what its limitations might be. Instead of imagining future technologies as works in progress, improving over time, we picture them as perfect from day one.  Computer Magic  The most successful companies encourage that illusion. \u201cWe feel our job is to try to solve tough, difficult problems,\u201d Jony Ive, head of design for Apple Inc., said in a  recent interview , \u201cbut we don\u2019t make the complexity of the problem apparent in its resolution.\u201d His company regularly describes its products as  \u201cmagic,\u201d  and the illusion of ease is essential to their glamour. They promise a world in which, contrary to the frustrations of everyday experience, computers \u201cjust work.\u201d  Freed from real-world technical constraints, Hollywood amplifies that promise. \u201cThe police on the CBS show \u2019Hawaii Five-O\u2019 have these amazing computer databases at their disposal where images, maps and photographs can be digitally thrown from a digital table onto a giant wall screen with the flick of the officer\u2019s hand into space,\u201d says Tom Simon, a special agent with the  Federal Bureau  of Investigation in Honolulu. In real life, \u201cwe work in a Microsoft Windows environment with all its benefits and limitations.\u201d  Understanding Health Insurance Exchanges Glamorous Hollywood visions make us forget that effortlessly informative, endlessly flexible databases represent the world as we wish it were -- or fear it might be -- not as it actually is. \u201cTV computer hackers, especially those employed by the police, can instantly tap into any video feed, satellite imagery, internal database, or record ever created by man, even though the record exists only on paper and has never been digitized,\u201d retired police officer Tim Dees  wrote  on a Quora thread about ludicrous crime-show conventions.  Audiences know such portrayals are fiction, but unless viewers are themselves professionals, they can\u2019t be sure where the boundary between reality and imagination lies. The result is an alluringly unrealistic view of both what\u2019s possible and what efforts even the possible might require.  Artificial Grace  In the case of the health-care exchanges, advocates emphasized how simple they\u2019d be. \u201cGetting insurance through the marketplace is as easy as applying for a plan, finding out if you qualify for subsidies and then comparing competing health plans,\u201d  declared  ObamacareFacts.com. It was a seductive idea.  But, like other forms of glamour, it hid the tradeoffs and difficulties involved. Such artificial grace is what makes glamour so dangerous and so persuasive. By concealing anything that might break the spell, it leads us to feel that the life we dream of exists, and to desire it even more: \u201cTo provide affordable, quality health care for all Americans and reduce the growth in health care spending.\u201d That sounds wonderful. As Captain Picard of \u201c Star Trek : The Next Generation\u201d would say, \u201cMake it so.\u201d But turning hopes into reality requires more than a command.  The health care law, the White House  argues , \u201cisn\u2019t just a website.\u201d True enough. But the software problems are representative of a larger rhetorical choice. Rather than argue that the new health-care law would require adjustments and sacrifices, and that the costs would be worth it to give more people health insurance, the president and other supporters assured the public that if they liked their insurance, they could keep it. There might be costs for industry, this rhetoric suggested, but individuals would be better off. It was a glamorous vision of reform, with the trade-offs -- in higher costs and less choice for some people, and the hardships of implementation -- concealed.  Glamour is a powerfully persuasive tool. Taken as a guide rather than the literal truth, it can lead to positive, sometimes life-changing, action. But it is also an illusion. In the real world, the hidden details matter.  ( Virginia Postrel  is a Bloomberg View columnist. Her next book, \u201cThe Power of Glamour,\u201d will be published Nov. 5 by  Simon & Schuster . The role of technology companies has come under scrutiny since Edward Snowden, a computer technician who did work for the National Security Agency, disclosed this month that the NSA is collecting data under a U.S. government program code-named PRISM. Requests came from federal, state and local authorities and included both criminal and national security matters, it said. Police investigations into crimes such as robbery were the most-common form of request, it said.  E-mails, Videos  Apple sold 125 million iPhones and 58 million iPad tablet computers last financial year, according to  data  compiled by Bloomberg.  No government agency has direct access to Apple servers and it doesn\u2019t store data related to customers\u2019 location, map searches or Siri requests in any identifiable form, the company said.  Conversations over the iMessage and FaceTime functions are protected by end-to-end encryption, which means only the sender and receiver can see or read them, and Apple can\u2019t decrypt the data, the company said.  PRISM gathers e-mails, videos and other private data of foreign surveillance targets through arrangements that vary by company, overseen by a secret panel of judges, according to slides provided by Snowden to the Guardian and Washington Post newspapers. New Lawsuits  Business Groups Sue SEC Over Proxy-Access Rule  The U.S. Chamber of Commerce, the nation\u2019s biggest\nbusiness lobby, and the  Business Roundtable  sued the Securities\nand Exchange Commission to overturn a rule that makes it easier\nfor investors to oust corporate directors.  The two groups decided to sue after completing a legal\nanalysis of the regulation, they said yesterday at a news\nconference in Washington. The rule, which allows shareholders\nowning 3 percent of a company to nominate board members on\ncorporate ballots, was passed by a divided SEC last month.  \u201cThese rules are wholly unnecessary,\u201d said David\nHirschmann, president of the chamber\u2019s Center for Capital\nMarkets Competitiveness. \u201cThis special interest-driven rule\nwill give small groups of special-interest activist investors\nsignificant leverage over a business\u2019 activities.\u201d  SEC Chairman Mary Schapiro has said the 2008 credit crisis,\nwhich cost financial firms more than $1.82 trillion, shows\nshareholders need more clout in picking board members to oversee\ncompanies.  Before the SEC approved its rule, shareholders could\nnominate dissident directors only by mailing a separate ballot\nand persuading other investors to vote with them. Activist\ninvestors such as Carl Icahn and Nelson Peltz have waged proxy\nfights to get their candidates elected to boards of companies\nthey said were underperforming.  The SEC, in a 3-2 vote, stipulated that investors or groups\nof shareholders who have owned 3 percent of a company for three\nyears could have board candidates on proxy statements.  Under the regulation, shareholders would be able to\nnominate at least one director and as much as 25 percent of a\nboard. Investors couldn\u2019t use the rule if their intent is to\noust a majority of board members and take over a company.  The financial-regulation law signed by President Barack\nObama in July authorized the SEC to let investors place director\nnominees on corporate proxies. The law\u2019s language was meant to\nmake it easier for the SEC to withstand a legal challenge.  The chamber and Washington-based Business Roundtable, which\nrepresents chief executive officers of the biggest U.S.\ncompanies, have retained Gibson Dunn & Crutcher LLP lawyers\nEugene Scalia and Amy Goodman to handle the case, which was\nfiled in the U.S. Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia.  \u201cWe believe that the commission\u2019s proxy-access rules are\nboth lawful and in the best interests of the public and\nshareholders,\u201d SEC spokesman John Nester said in the agency\u2019s\nstatement. \u201cThe commission will, of course, carefully consider\nand timely respond to the motion for a stay.\u201d  For more, click here.  Ambac Sues Countrywide Over Mortgage-Backed Bonds  Ambac Assurance Corp. sued  Bank of America Corp.  over $16.7\nbillion of mortgage-backed securities, saying the bank\u2019s\nCountrywide Financial Corp. fraudulently induced Ambac to insure\nthe bonds.  Ambac  found that 97 percent of 6,533 home mortgage loans it\nreviewed across the 12 securitizations sponsored by Countrywide\ndidn\u2019t conform to the lender\u2019s underwriting guidelines,\naccording to the complaint filed in New York state Supreme\nCourt. Many of the loans were made to borrowers with limited or\nno ability to meet their payment obligations, Ambac said.  Ambac has paid hundreds of millions of dollars in claims\nconnected to defaults in the securities, according to the suit\nfiled yesterday. At the same time, Countrywide has refused to\ncomply in a timely fashion with its obligations to repurchase\nthe out-of-guideline loans or bring them into compliance, the\nlawsuit claims.  Ambac  is \u201centitled to redress for Countrywide\u2019s massive\nfraud and pervasive and material breaches, including damages\nsufficient to place Ambac in the same position it would have\nbeen in had it never insured the transactions,\u201d the suit says.  Shirley Norton, a spokeswoman for the Charlotte, North\nCarolina-based lender, said the bank has no comment.  The case arises out of 12  Countrywide-sponsored \ntransactions that closed between 2004 and 2006, nine of which\ninvolve home equity lines of credit secured by second-lien\nmortgages and three that involve fixed amount second-lien loans.  Over the last two years, the loans in the transactions have\n defaulted  at what Ambac calls \u201cextraordinary rates.\u201d To date,\nthe suit claims, more than 35,000 loans with a total principal\nbalance of more than $1.95 billion have defaulted or been\ncharged off. As a result, the suit says, Ambac has been forced\nto make more than $466 million in claim payments.  The case is Ambac Assurance Corp. v. Countrywide Home Loans\nInc., 651612\/2010, New York state Supreme Court (Manhattan).  Lehman, Nortel Challenge U.K. Regulator on Pension Debt  Lehman Brothers Holdings Inc. \u2019s European unit and  Nortel\nNetworks Corp.  are challenging the U.K. Pensions Regulator in\ncourt over whether they must pay as much as a combined 2.25\nbillion pounds ($3.55 billion).  The  Pensions Regulator  this month issued a so-called\nfinancial support direction against Lehman Brothers and its\naffiliates seeking funds to cover a deficit of more than 148\nmillion pounds in the former investment bank\u2019s retirement plan.\nThe panel  issued a similar order  against Toronto-based Nortel in\nJuly seeking as much as 2.1 billion pounds for the underfunding\nof its plan.  Lehman Brothers International Europe and Nortel are jointly\nchallenging the regulator\u2019s claims in a London court, saying\nthey shouldn\u2019t be required to pay the deficits while they are in\nadministration or bankruptcy protection. Judge Kim Lewison ruled\nat the hearing yesterday that the parent company and Lehman\nBrothers Asset Management (Europe) Ltd. can also join the\nchallenge to protect their specific interests.  Lehman doesn\u2019t want to have to pay the European unit\u2019s\ndebts, its lawyer, Barry Isaacs, said at the hearing.  David Hannant, a spokesman for the regulator, declined to\ncomment because the case is ongoing.  Lehman Brothers filed the largest bankruptcy in U.S.\nhistory in September 2008, and its European unit is liquidating\nin London. Nortel and affiliates filed for bankruptcy in the\nU.S., Canada and London in January 2009.  A bankruptcy judge in Delaware ruled last month that\nefforts by the U.K. regulator to force Nortel to contribute to\nits retirement plan violate the so-called automatic stay in the\ncase, and halted the request.  ABB Units Charged With Violating U.S. Bribery Law  The U.S. charged two units of  ABB Ltd. , the world\u2019s biggest\nelectricity-networks builder, with conspiracy and violating the\nForeign Corrupt Practices Act.  According to the complaint filed yesterday in federal court\nin Houston, ABB and its co-conspirators made \u201cconcealed,\ncorrupt payments\u201d to officials at Comision Federal de\nElectricidad, an electric utility owned by Mexico, \u201cin exchange\nfor improper business advantages to ABB Inc. and ABB NM,\nincluding the award of contracts.\u201d  The payments related to an upgrade for Mexico\u2019s electrical\nnetwork in a contract that generated $44 million in revenue for\nan ABB unit, prosecutors claim.  Laurence A. Urgenson, a lawyer representing Zurich-based\nABB, didn\u2019t immediately return a call seeking comment.  The case is U.S. v. ABB Inc., 10-664, U.S. District Court,\nSouthern District of Texas (Houston).  Boston Scientific Claims Rivals Infringe U.S. Stent Patents  Boston Scientific Corp.,  the world\u2019s second-biggest maker\nof heart devices, sued Cook Group Inc., TaeWoong Medical Co. and\nEndoChoice Inc. over mesh tubes used in minimally invasive\nsurgery.  Boston Scientific claims the tiny tubes that prop open\narteries and are used in endoscopies are infringing at least\nthree patents. The complaint, filed Sept. 27 in federal court in\nBoston, targets Evolution stents made by closely held Cook\nGroup; TaeWoong\u2019s Niti-S; and the Bonastent made by EndoChoice\nand South Korean partners Standard Sci-Tech Inc. and Sewoon\nMedical Co.  Boston Scientific makes the WallFlex stent and related\ndelivery system. The products are used in endoscopy products for\nthe treatment of diseases of the digestive system, according to\nthe complaint. The patents relate to types of stents that work\nbetter when inserted, for instance, in the food pipe.  The company\u2019s endoscopy unit generated $134 million in U.S.\nsales in the second quarter, driven largely by the U.S.\nintroduction of the WallFlex binary stent system and continued\nsales of the WallFlex esophageal stent, Boston Scientific  said \nin an Aug. 5 regulatory filing.  Boston Scientific, based in Natick, Massachusetts, is\nseeking unspecified cash compensation and an order that would\nprevent further use of its inventions. Three patents were\nasserted against all of the companies, and a fourth, for a self-\nexpanding esophageal stent, was asserted only against\nBloomington, Indiana-based Cook.  The Bonastent received U.S. Food and Drug Administration\nclearance earlier this year, Alpharetta, Georgia-based\nEndoChoice said April 29. Officials at Cook and EndoChoice\ndidn\u2019t immediately respond to messages seeking comment.\nOfficials at  TaeWoong  and Standard Sci-Tech couldn\u2019t be reached.  Closely held TaeWoong is based in Goyang-Si, South Korea,\nand Standard Sci-Tech is based in Seoul, according to the\ncomplaint.  The case is Boston Scientific Corp. v. Cook Inc.,\n10cv11646, U.S. District Court for the District of\nMassachusetts.  Eli Lilly Sues Celesio U.K. Units Over Generic Zyprexa Sales  Eli Lilly & Co. , the world\u2019s biggest maker of psychiatric\ndrugs, sued two U.K. units of drug distributer  Celesio AG  for\nallegedly infringing its patent for the schizophrenia drug\nZyprexa two years ago.  Celesio\u2019s  Lloyds Pharmacy  and Aah Pharmaceuticals\nbusinesses sold about 800,000 tablets of generic Zyprexa before\nagreeing in 2008 to halt sales, Eli Lilly said in a complaint\nfiled in the High Court in London on Aug. 18 and made public\nlast week.  Eli Lilly, based in Indianapolis, took legal action two\nyears ago against \u201ca number of companies\u201d to stop sales of the\ngeneric known as olanzapine, according to an e-mailed statement\nfrom Edward Sagebiel, an Eli Lilly spokesman. The sales ended\nafter Eli Lilly\u2019s patent expiration won an extension until Sept.\n26, 2011, according to the complaint.  The lawsuit \u201chas been undertaken by Lilly to obtain its\ndamages as a result of the sale of those products\u201d in 2008,\nSagebiel said.  Lloyds Pharmacy agreed to halt the sales \u201cand hold the\nremainder of the stock in quarantine,\u201d Sarah Stokes, a\nspokeswoman for Lloyds Pharmacy, said in an e-mail. The lawsuit\nrelates to a single batch of olanzapine that Lloyds Pharmacy\npurchased and the company is no longer selling it, she said.  Dean Enon, a spokesman for Coventry, England-based Aah\nPharmaceuticals, referred calls to Stokes.  The case is: Eli Lilly v. AAH Pharmaceuticals, Lloyds\nPharmacy, High Court of London, Chancery Division, No.\nHC10C02699.  For the latest lawsuits news, click here.  Court Rulings  Visteon Accord on Contract, Bankruptcy Debt Approved  Visteon Corp.  won court approval to settle a dispute with\n Ford Motor Co.  over the automaker\u2019s claim that Visteon owed it\n$160 million.  U.S. Bankruptcy Judge Christopher S. Sontchi in Wilmington,\nDelaware, approved the deal\u2019s terms yesterday. Under the\nsettlement, Ford will drop its demand for $160 million from\nVisteon and instead will pay the company $29 million, James\nMazza, a Visteon attorney, said in court.  The approval was the last Visteon needed to exit\nbankruptcy, Mazza said in an interview after the hearing. Visteon will continue supplying parts to Ford under a\ncontract valued at about $600 million, Mazza said in court.  The case is In re Visteon Corp., 09-11786, U.S. Bankruptcy\nCourt, District of Delaware (Wilmington). Functions controllable by touch and gestures.\nApplications that are better designed and better looking than\nyou\u2019ve ever seen before.  If Windows has a future, this is it.  Windows 8, the next version of the world\u2019s most widely used\noperating system, is probably still a year from release. But\n Microsoft Corp. (MSFT)  has begun to bang the drum for it, unveiling it\nto developers and the media at a conference last week in\n Southern California .  I\u2019ve been exploring the preview version for a week or so,\nand am both impressed and intrigued. It may change significantly\non its way to your office, home or briefcase, but even at this\nstage, it is the most radical overhaul of Windows ever.  Microsoft had little choice. The future belongs to mobile\ndevices: Sales of smartphones and tablets -- most of them\nrunning software from  Apple Inc. (AAPL)  and  Google Inc. (GOOG)  -- are\n projected to surpass  traditional personal computers this year\nfor the first time. Meanwhile, Microsoft continues to lean\nheavily on the Windows and Office franchises for the bulk of its\nprofits and can\u2019t afford to sit back and watch them wither away.  Two in One  Moreover, even if the PC market is no longer the engine of\ngrowth it once was, a huge number of people work on PCs and will\ncontinue to for years. So Microsoft is attempting something\nextraordinarily ambitious: combining a state-of-the-art\noperating system for tablets and other mobile devices with a\ntraditional desktop environment. Two for the price of one.  The most striking thing about Windows 8 is its new \u201cMetro\nstyle\u201d user interface. For a taste of it, try a device running\nWindows Phone 7. Applications are represented by large tiles\nthat can be resized and can update themselves dynamically -- the\nmail tile displaying the most recent incoming message, for\ninstance, or the calendar tile showing your next appointment.  One little irony of Windows 8 is that it de-emphasizes\nwindows. When you poke at or click on a tile, a Metro-style\nprogram launches full-screen, with nary a toolbar or pull-down\nmenu in sight. The traditional taskbar is replaced by what\nMicrosoft calls \u201ccharms,\u201d icons representing basic functions\ncommon to all programs that are summoned by a finger swipe from\nthe right-hand edge of the screen (on the prototype Samsung\ntablet PC handed out to developers last week, that is).  Apps Zapped  But what happens to the huge body of software written for\nearlier versions of Windows? Some may be rewritten for Metro --\nthe developer\u2019s preview includes a Metro-style version of the\nInternet Explorer 10 browser -- but many won\u2019t be.  Microsoft\u2019s answer is a tile on the new Start screen that\nlaunches a traditional desktop similar to what you get when you\nboot up Windows 7. At the developer conference, Steven Sinofsky,\nthe executive in charge of the operating system, denied that\nWindows 8 demotes the desktop to the status of a \u201cpenalty\nbox,\u201d the place you\u2019re exiled to if you can\u2019t get with the hip\nnew program.  Still, you can\u2019t help but wonder about the potential for\nconfusion. Let\u2019s see: Does my program use the Metro start\nscreen, or the desktop? If I need to look something up on the\nWeb, do I launch Metro-friendly IE 10, or desktop-style IE 10?  Another bunch of questions concern one of Windows 8\u2019s\nbiggest changes, one that will be invisible to the naked eye.  Hot Chips  Until now, Windows has always run only on \u201cx86\u201d\nmicroprocessors -- the type of electronic brains made by  Intel\nCorp. (INTC)  and  Advanced Micro Devices Inc.. (AMD)  Microsoft says that any\nmachine capable of running Windows 7 will also run Windows 8.\nBut the new operating system also promises to run on the\nprocessors being used in tablets, smartphones and other mobile\ndevices. These chips, utilizing technology licensed from  ARM\nHoldings PLC (ARM) , tend to be less potent than x86 chips -- but also\nuse less power, generate less heat and allow for longer battery\nlife.  While there was much talk at last week\u2019s session about ARM\ncompatibility, almost everything shown was running on Intel-\npowered machines. The demonstration tablet had an i5 chip -- the\nsame one that powers many desktop and laptop PCs today, and\ngenerates so much heat that the tablet had an internal fan.  An ARM-based Windows 8 device wouldn\u2019t have those issues.\nBut it also, according to Microsoft, will only run newly written\nMetro-style applications, not the more traditional and familiar\ndesktop software. So here\u2019s another potential layer of\ncomplexity and confusion. Will a given program run on a given\nWindows 8 device?  No one knows what the volatile digital marketplace will\nlook like when Windows 8 reaches consumers. And that must be a\nlittle scary for Microsoft. The operating system may provide an\nimportant transitional link between computing\u2019s past and future.\nOn the other hand, it could just end up being remembered as a\nlast-ditch effort to squeeze a little more milk from the\ngreatest cash-cow in the history of technology.  ( Rich Jaroslovsky  is a Bloomberg News columnist. The\nopinions expressed are his own.)
