(GS)  partner\n Dinakar Singh  discovered in 2001 that his 19-month-old daughter,\nArya, had a crippling genetic disease called spinal muscular\natrophy.  The malady makes the nerve cells that control muscles\ngradually deteriorate. There are no treatments, let alone a\ncure, Bloomberg Markets magazine reports in its October issue.\nWorse still, while the gene causing the ailment had recently\nbeen discovered, nobody in the drug industry was doing much\nabout it, he says.  \u201cI was fearful and anxious that treatments would be\ndeveloped, but far too late to save Arya,\u201d says Singh, 42, who\nfounded and runs New York hedge fund TPG-Axon Capital Management\nLP, which has $8.1 billion in assets. \u201cWe didn\u2019t want to find\nout 25 years later that the science was really there but there\nisn\u2019t a drug because nobody focused on it.\u201d  Singh, who left Goldman in 2004, has spent almost $100\nmillion of his own money to create and fund the Spinal Muscular\nAtrophy Foundation. He wants to discover and develop a drug that\nhe hopes will help his daughter, who is one of 25,000 SMA\npatients in the U.S. Children with severe forms often die within\na few years, while those with mild cases can live a normal life\nspan with supportive care. Arya, 11, and starting sixth grade,\nuses a wheelchair.  \u2018High-Speed Initiative\u2019  Singh\u2019s foundation is making progress. It\u2019s collaborating\nwith  Novartis AG (NOVN) , which may bring a drug into human tests as\nsoon as 2013, says Mark Fishman, research chief for the Basel,\nSwitzerland-based drugmaker.  The foundation has pumped $13 million into PTC Therapeutics\nInc. in South Plainfield,  New Jersey , which has produced a pill\nthat increases the life span of mice with SMA. It also has\nfunded a scientist whose research has led to an injectable drug\ndeveloped by  Isis Pharmaceuticals Inc. (ISIS)  of Carlsbad,  California .\nThat treatment may enter human trials before year\u2019s end. Singh\nsays he\u2019ll enroll Arya if that drug gets to the testing phase\nbefore others.  \u201cThe SMA Foundation has converted this from a slow-moving\nexercise to a high-speed initiative,\u201d says Darryl De Vivo, a\npediatric neurologist at  Columbia University Medical Center  in\n New York , who has overseen Arya\u2019s care since her diagnosis.  Frustrated with the sluggishness, or nonexistence, of\nmedical research, Singh and a small band of wealthy parents\nwhose children have serious illnesses are spending millions of\ndollars to fund drug development.  \u2018Change the System\u2019  These benefactors include hedge-fund managers, private-\nequity investors and entrepreneurs, many of whom have made their\nfortunes on  Wall Street . The principles they apply in their jobs\n-- managing complicated tasks, making investments and expecting\npositive results -- translate to their new endeavors, says Stacy Palmer, editor of the  Chronicle of Philanthropy .  \u201cBusiness executives have a better understanding of how\nmarkets work and have started to ask tougher questions,\u201d Palmer\nsays. Their goal: \u201cChange the system and whatever is slowing it\ndown.\u201d  The new philanthropists are building on a foundation laid\nby well-known predecessors. John D. Rockefeller in 1901 formed\nthe medical research institute that would become New York\u2019s\n Rockefeller University  after his grandson died of scarlet fever.\nBillionaire Michael Milken, who pioneered junk bonds, founded\nthe Prostate Cancer Foundation and FasterCures, a think tank to\nspeed progress toward cures in all medical fields.  \u2018Lots of Shovels\u2019  Microsoft Corp. co-founder  Bill Gates  and his Bill &\nMelinda Gates Foundation have focused on malaria, polio and\nother global health threats.  James Simons , founder of hedge fund\nRenaissance Technologies LLC, and his wife, Marilyn, started the\nSimons Foundation. It\u2019s the second-biggest funder of autism\nresearch, after the U.S. National Institutes of Health,\naccording to recent data.  Benefactors such as Singh are taking a direct role in early\ndrug research. They want to make it easier for companies to\nproduce a medicine or venture firms to fund it. They begin with\nbasic research discoveries, often in obscure illnesses, and\nadvance the work. Instead of handing money to scientists and\ngetting out of the way, they stay involved, hire experts and\npush researchers to work together rather than compete.  \u201cWe have focused on having lots of shovels ready and\nhaving the maps ready and having all the supplies ready, so\ncompanies are willing to prospect for SMA drugs,\u201d Singh says.\nHis idea: \u201cMake it easy for companies, take the risk down for\nthem so they can get a sense cheaply and easily whether there is\nsomething there.\u201d  Arya\u2019s Efforts  Even Arya is doing her bit. In her family\u2019s 11th-floor\ncondominium that looks north over New York\u2019s Central Park, she\nsays she\u2019s excited about holding a bake sale to raise money for\nSMA research. She has just returned from precautionary tests to\nmake sure a respiratory infection didn\u2019t become serious. Her\nmother pats her back when she coughs weakly. Then Arya scoots\noff in her wheelchair to play with her younger brother and\nsister.  James O\u2019Sullivan , director of foundation services for\n Rockefeller Philanthropy Advisors , says about half of his 25\nmedical philanthropy clients at any time are interested in the\nhands-on approach Singh\u2019s foundation is taking, up from a\nhandful 15 years ago.  \u201cThere is a world of difference between 10 years ago and\nnow,\u201d says O\u2019Sullivan, whose New York-based organization\nadvises wealthy patrons. \u201cToday\u2019s donors are much more\ninterested in seeing how their dollars make a difference in a\ndisease.\u201d  New Breed  Victoria Jackson, a cosmetics entrepreneur whose husband,\nBill Guthy, co-founded direct marketer  Guthy-Renker LLC , is\namong the new breed. Her daughter, Ali, came down with a central\nnervous system disorder at age 14 called neuromyelitis optica,\nwhich can cause blindness.  Since then, Jackson has spent more than $15 million on her\nfoundation to develop treatments. Ali, now 18, has avoided\nsevere complications by taking immunosuppressants.  Jackson says scientists often work independently with their\nown agendas, wasting money.  \u201cI manage where every dime goes and make sure there is\ncomplete disclosure and collaboration among the researchers,\u201d\nshe says.  Private Investors  Private investors may become crucial as drugmakers cut\nresearch and close labs, O\u2019Sullivan says.  Pfizer Inc. (PFE) , the\nworld\u2019s largest drugmaker, will spend $6.5 billion to $7 billion\non research in 2012, down from $9.4 billion in 2010. That makes\nworking with a foundation that already has done some of the\ngrunt work attractive.  \u201cDrug companies want to come in later in the R&D process\nand provide backing for potential therapies that have more\nevidence behind them than in the past,\u201d O\u2019Sullivan says.  Singh says his foundation can focus on the science because\nit doesn\u2019t have to invest huge amounts of time raising money.\nAnd with no need to impress donors, the organization can spend\non the business of developing lab tests and building the pieces\nthat make it easier for companies to discover SMA drugs.  The foundation\u2019s $16 million in research spending last year\nalmost equals the $19 million the NIH spent on spinal muscular\natrophy.  Novartis saved years by taking advantage of advances made\nby foundation-backed scientists and the laboratory techniques\nthey developed to test compounds for SMA. The company was able\nto focus on screening for drugs rather than diverting staff to\nbasic research, says Daniel Curtis, a research manager at\nNovartis.  Rich Donors  The SMA Foundation and its academic partners may reap a\nbenefit if a Novartis drug reaches the market and sells well.\nSingh\u2019s foundation could get back a multiple of its spending on\nthe collaboration, says Karen Chen, the organization\u2019s chief\nscientific officer, who declined to give specifics. Any money\nwould allow the foundation to reinvest in science, she says.  As an incentive for Novartis to work quickly, an agreement\nallows the company to repay nothing if it completes clinical\ntrials fast enough.  Rich donors with a personal stake in a disease, while well-\nmeaning, can divert resources from illnesses that may be closer\nto a cure or afflict more people, says Arthur Caplan, a\nbioethicist at the  University of Pennsylvania  in Philadelphia.  \u201cThere can be some kind of distortion of emphasis,\u201d he\nsays.  SMA affects 25,000 Americans versus 5.4 million for\nAlzheimer\u2019s disease, according to the SMA Foundation and the\nAlzheimer\u2019s Association.  Head Start  Singh says spinal muscular atrophy is more likely to be\ntreatable than common neurological diseases such as  Alzheimer\u2019s ,\nwhose origin is uncertain. He says he wouldn\u2019t have spent as\nmuch money if he thought an SMA treatment was a long shot.\nScientists already know what causes SMA, giving researchers a\nhead start, he says.  Garen Staglin, a senior adviser at San Francisco-based\nprivate-equity firm FTV Capital, is tackling diseases that are\nmore widespread, including schizophrenia. Staglin\u2019s\nInternational Mental Health Research Organization has raised\n$135 million for brain research during the past 17 years. It\nhosts an annual music concert at his Napa Valley, California,\nvineyard. Dionne Warwick was scheduled to headline a concert in\nSeptember.  Staglin\u2019s son, Brandon, now 39, was diagnosed with\nschizophrenia in 1990. Staglin was in  France  on business and got\na call that police had pulled Brandon over as he drove\nerratically.  \u201cHe told me he felt like he had lost half his brain,\u201d\nStaglin recalls. \u201cHe just lost his ability to think\ncoherently.\u201d  \u2018Run Toward It\u2019  Rather than hide Brandon\u2019s situation, Staglin acted.  \u201cWe decided we had two choices: We could either run away\nfrom the problem like too many families with these illnesses,\u201d\nhe says. \u201cWe wanted to run toward it.\u201d  Another effort, Staglin\u2019s  One Mind for Research , is working\nwith former Rhode Island Congressman Patrick Kennedy to get drug\ncompanies and brain researchers to collaborate on treatments for\nAlzheimer\u2019s, autism, schizophrenia and other conditions. This\neffort is based on the joint-research approach that has long\nbeen used in the semiconductor industry.  For Alexander Silver, the motivation is his 4-year-old son,\nJackson. Silver, a partner at New York-based private-investment\nfirm P2 Capital Partners, LLC, started the  Jackson Gabriel\nSilver Foundation  in 2010 to find a treatment for a rare genetic\ncondition called epidermolysis bullosa. In the disease, a\nprotein that holds skin layers together is missing, and the skin\nblisters and shears off with any friction. Half of Jackson\u2019s\nbody is covered in high-tech bandages that cost $6,000 a month.  Cutting Red Tape  Silver, 34, who has raised more than $400,000 since 2008\nand aims for $10 million or more, predicts a good treatment will\ncome if money flows without red tape to the right projects. His\nfoundation -- along with one run by Paul Joseph, a private-\nwealth broker at Morgan Stanley Smith Barney LLC whose 7-year-\nold son has the condition -- has backed work at the University\nof  Southern California  in  Los Angeles . The research has produced\na potential drug.  The approach has garnered $26 million in venture capital\nfrom Boston-based Third Rock Ventures to form a company and move\nthe therapy in human trials.  No Budget on Life  \u201cThe skills I developed professionally matter a lot for\nthis,\u201d Silver says. \u201cJust like investing, you are allocating\ncapital to the projects that have the highest probability of\nsuccess and the lowest probability of failure in the quickest\ntime frame.\u201d  For Singh, the effort to save Arya is a family affair, and\nhe promises to spend as much money as necessary. Singh\u2019s wife,\nLoren Eng, has a Master of Business Administration from  Stanford\nUniversity  and works fulltime leading the foundation.  The eight-member staff includes former researchers from\n Roche Holding AG (ROG)  and Pfizer.  While Arya has a mild form of SMA, she has gotten weaker.\nShe has trouble lifting her arms above her head and needs\nfulltime nursing. Every cold is a threat because her frail lung\nmuscles put her at risk for pneumonia.  \u201cI don\u2019t think there is a budget on your daughter\u2019s\nlife,\u201d Singh says. \u201cAs long as there is a chance of doing\nsomething and we have the ability to do it, we will do it.\u201d  \u2018In Tears\u2019  Singh, who won\u2019t disclose his compensation, says his fund\nreturned 60 percent in the six-and-a-half years since he started\nit on Feb. 1, 2005. That\u2019s more than double the Standard &\nPoor\u2019s 500 Index\u2019s 25 percent return during the period.  Arya, the oldest of Singh and Eng\u2019s three children, was\nborn in March 2000 and developed normally at first. She was slow\nto walk, however, taking her first wobbly steps at 15 months.\nWithin months, she began regressing. A doctor friend saw Arya\u2019s\nstiff gait at a party in August 2001 and told them to get it\nchecked out right away.  Eng had become pregnant again, and two days before her\ndelivery date, she got an abrupt call from the neurologist\nconfirming the worst about Arya.  \u201cLoren called me in tears,\u201d Singh remembers. \u201cI was\nsaying: \u2018What does it mean? What does it mean?\u2019 She said the\ndoctor didn\u2019t say anything. She has SMA. That\u2019s it.\u201d Singh and\nEng spent the next days in a frantic race to figure out the\nprognosis -- and to discover whether their second child, Kiran,\nalso had SMA. He didn\u2019t.  \u2018Untreatable, Incurable, Fatal\u2019  \u201cWhen we found out about it, we were told it was\nuntreatable, incurable and fatal,\u201d Singh says.  De Vivo, the Columbia University neurologist, met the\ncouple and explained that children like Arya have defects in or\nare missing a gene called SMN, discovered only in 1995. It\ndirects cells to make a protein necessary for neurons that\ncontrol muscles.  He introduced them to Columbia colleague Thomas Jessell, a\nmotor neuron biology expert. They also met Gerald Fischbach, a\nneuroscientist and then dean of Columbia\u2019s health sciences and\nmedicine faculty. All three became key advisers to the SMA\nFoundation.  \u201cI met them and decided that SMA was a perfect disorder to\nmount a major attack on,\u201d says Fischbach, who\u2019s now scientific\ndirector for the  Simons Foundation  Autism Research Initiative.\n\u201cThe science was ripe.\u201d  \u2018Truly Solve It\u2019  At first Singh and Eng had planned to back existing\ncharities, such as  Families of Spinal Muscular Atrophy . They\ngave $750,000 in May 2002 to fund a clinic at Columbia. In 2006,\nthey agreed to give as much as $15 million to help fund a motor\nneuron research center at the university.  The more they learned, the more they became convinced that,\nunlike most neurological diseases, SMA might be conquered.  \u201cWhat struck us as different about SMA was that there\nreally seemed to be a chance to truly solve it -- and perhaps\neven in a time frame that could really help Arya,\u201d Singh says.  A quirk in the genetics of SMA increased their hope. In\nmany inherited diseases, a crucial gene is missing or defective\nand the protein it makes is absent or doesn\u2019t work. In SMA, the\nbody has a backup gene that produces small amounts of the SMN\nprotein. That\u2019s why children with the disease live at all.  By the time Singh and Eng became involved, an idea with\npotential to help SMA sufferers was already being discussed in\nthe medical literature: If someone could find a chemical that\ncould safely boost the availability of the backup protein, that\ndiscovery could form the basis of a drug. Yet as far as they\ncould tell, no large drug or biotech company was focused on SMA.  \u2018Terrible Gap\u2019  \u201cYou had this terrible gap,\u201d Singh says. \u201cThere was no\none saying, let us take these interesting discoveries and come\nup with something that could be a drug.\u201d  The couple started the foundation in 2003. Equipped with\nPowerPoint presentations that showed why SMA was a lower\nresearch risk than most genetic diseases that could yield a drug\nwith $1 billion in annual sales, they approached more than a\ndozen companies. It was a hard sell.  At the  American Academy of Neurology  conference in 2004,\nonly three of seven biotech companies they invited showed up.  \u201cThere was never an outright no,\u201d Eng says. Instead,\n\u201cpolite conversations went nowhere or calls were not\nreturned.\u201d  To her, it seemed drugmakers were focused on heart disease,\ncancer or diabetes and their significant commercial markets. The\nNIH alone spends $5.8 billion a year on cancer research.  \u2018A Buzz\u2019  Singh and Eng started paying small biotech companies to\nscreen for chemicals that might increase the supply of the SMN\nprotein. They, along with other SMA charities, also funded\nAdrian Krainer, a researcher at  Cold Spring Harbor Laboratory  on\n Long Island  in New York. He was working on a technology that had\nshown some promise, even though the foundation\u2019s scientific\nadvisers said the approach was a long shot.  \u201cThere was a buzz; there was this new couple, they are\nvery wealthy, people thought they were in a position to make a\ndifference,\u201d says Krainer, who met Arya in 2002 when she could\nstill walk.  For the next few years, the foundation backed research\ntesting dozens of existing drugs to see if any of them increased\nthe SMN protein. The scientific advisers got together in 2008\nfor a meeting at the Ritz-Carlton hotel in Half Moon Bay,\nCalifornia.  \u201cIt was the most-depressing meeting ever,\u201d Eng recalls.\n\u201cIt was clear we had nothing.\u201d  \u2018Huge Implications\u2019  By then, Arya was in a wheelchair. At this point, the SMA\nFoundation had captivated Novartis. In 2002, the company had\nappointed Fishman, a scientist and former  Harvard Medical School \nprofessor, to direct research operations.  He says one idea was that success in treating rare genetic\ndiseases might pave the way for dealing with more-common ones.\nColumbia\u2019s Jessell and Fischbach pitched him on SMA in 2005.  \u201cIt seemed tractable from a scientific point of view, with\npotentially huge implications on health,\u201d Fishman says.\n\u201cOthers weren\u2019t working on it, which is another good reason to\ndo it.\u201d  Still, it wasn\u2019t until November 2007 that Novartis began\nits effort. It started with neurobiologist Rajeev Sivasankaran\nand a few assistants. Sivasankaran, 41, designed a quick way to\ntest the more than 1 million compounds in Novartis\u2019s collection\nof chemicals to see if any had potential for SMA. A compound\nwith some modest effect could become a starting point for a safe\nand effective medicine.  \u2018Full-Court Press\u2019  Novartis was lucky. By December 2009, the researchers had\nfound a drug that improved motor function in mice with SMA.  \u201cThat got the whole group excited,\u201d Sivasankaran says.\nThe SMA Foundation and Novartis scientists get together every\nthree months to review progress. At a June 1 meeting,\nresearchers from the foundation, Novartis, Columbia and Harvard\ncrowded into a conference room to hear the latest results.  \u201cIt is a full-court press,\u201d Fishman says. \u201cWe are\npushing as hard as we can.\u201d  Still, Novartis human trials are two years off at best,\nFishman says.  Meantime,  Repligen Corp. (RGEN) , a Waltham, Massachusetts-based\nbiotechnology company, in July began an initial safety test of\nits SMA drug on people. It licensed this drug from the charity\nFamilies of SMA, based in Elk Grove Village,  Illinois .  More Efforts  Singh\u2019s foundation is closing in with two more efforts. PTC\nTherapeutics last year found compounds that boost the life span\nof mice with the disease. The company could begin human trials\nin late 2012, Chief Executive Officer Stuart Peltz says.  \u201cIt is absolutely incredible,\u201d he says. Mice that would\notherwise barely be able to move look normal with PTC\u2019s drug, he\nsays.  Singh and Eng say they\u2019re particularly excited by Isis\nPharmaceuticals\u2019 progress, based on work by Krainer at Cold\nSpring Harbor. Isis published data in March showing that its\ndrug could boost motor neuron levels -- and survival -- in mice\nwith SMA. The medicine, which is injected into spaces around the\nspine, corrects the defect that causes the backup gene to\nproduce too little protein.  \u201cI have been doing drug development half of my life,\u201d\nsays Roy Vagelos, former Merck & Co. CEO, who has followed the\nSMA Foundation\u2019s research. \u201cThis will be the first time if it\nworks that a family had gotten behind a problem, a genetic\ndefect in their own family, and come up with a solution.\u201d  Arya is very aware of her illness and the battles to\nconquer it, even though she doesn\u2019t like to talk about it, Singh\nsays. She often asks her parents what her adult life will be\nlike and why she has to be sick.  \u201cTrying to understand what this all means is a big deal\nnow,\u201d Singh says.  Arya\u2019s Homework  For a homework assignment last year on Egyptian mythology,\nArya imagined a goddess of illness.  \u201cShe thinks of cures for sicknesses and puts hints for\nthese cures in people\u2019s minds,\u201d Arya wrote. \u201cShe has a puppy\nface, puppy paws, human body and is always thinking of cures.\u201d\nEng sent a copy of her daughter\u2019s essay to Novartis\u2019s Fishman.  \u201cIt hits you right where you live,\u201d he says. \u201cThat kind\nof innocent gratitude is the most wonderful reward you can\nget.\u201d  To contact the reporters responsible for this story:\nRobert Langreth in New York at \n rlangreth@bloomberg.net ;\nAlex Nussbaum in New York \n anussbaum1@bloomberg.net . The Standard & Poor\u2019s 500 Information Technology Index,\nwhich includes  International Business Machines Corp. (IBM)  and\n Microsoft Corp. (MSFT) , has fallen 3.4 percent since June 20, compared\nwith with a 12.1 decline in the  S&P 500 Index .  While it\u2019s unusual for a cyclical industry to outperform\nwhen economic growth decelerates, \u201cthere\u2019s probably a lot less\ndownside here than in any other cyclical sectors,\u201d said Doug Cliggott, a Boston-based U.S. equity strategist at Credit Suisse\nGroup AG.  Strong balance sheets for technology companies may be\n\u201ccounterbalancing\u201d the cyclical risk, according to Todd Coupland, an analyst at  CIBC World Markets  in Toronto. The\nindustry may top $700 billion in cash on hand this year,\ntrailing only financial services, he said.  \u201cHaving a big cash balance is defensive; it\u2019s a buffer,\u201d\nsaid Rick Campagna, chief executive officer of 300 North Capital\nLLC, who manages $500 million at the Pasadena, California-based\ninvestment firm.  U.S. gross domestic product climbed at a 1.3 percent annual\nrate in the second quarter, after almost stalling with a 0.4\npercent gain in January-March, Commerce Department data show.\nGDP will rise 1.6 percent this year, according to the median\nestimate of 66 economists surveyed by Bloomberg News, after\nexpanding 3 percent in 2010.  Mergers, Acquisitions  Some companies are using their cash for mergers and\nacquisitions as they try to \u201ccontinue growth in the face of a\nslowing economy,\u201d Coupland said.  Celestica Inc. completed its acquisition of the\nsemiconductor-equipment contract-manufacturing operations of\nChelmsford, Massachusetts-based Brooks Automation Inc. in June.\nThis allows Celestica to maintain operating targets amid\ndeclining customer forecasts, said Coupland, who maintains a\n\u201csector outperform\u201d rating on the Toronto-based electronics\ncompany.  In the absence of a potential takeover, the \u201cpreferred\nstrategy\u201d for companies with excess cash is to repurchase their\nstock rather than increase dividends, according to Coupland.\nArmonk, New York-based IBM bought back $4 billion worth of\nshares in the three months ended June 30, while Microsoft in\nRedmond,  Washington , repurchased $1.3 billion during the same\nquarter and is planning a $40 billion buyback program that runs\nuntil 2013, the companies said in July. Both also have boosted\ntheir dividends.  Earnings Projections  Beyond health balance sheets, low valuations and modest\nearnings expectations are attracting investors, Cliggott said.\nEarnings are projected to grow 10 percent in 2012, compared with\n16 percent for industrials and 14 percent for basic materials,\nsetting the bar \u201clow for tech stocks relative to other\ncyclicals,\u201d he said.  Technology companies are trading at a multiple of about 12\ntimes consensus earnings expectations for this year, similar to\nthe  S&P 500 , whereas they\u2019ve historically traded at a \u201cmodest\npremium,\u201d he said.  \u201cThis mitigates downside risk for investors if the economy\nwere to slow further,\u201d Cliggott said.  A change in the business composition of the tech index has\nmade it less economically sensitive, said Gina Martin Adams, an\nequity strategist in  New York  with  Wells Fargo Securities LLC .\nInformation-technology services are increasingly significant,\nrepresenting almost 30 percent of the total market\ncapitalization of the sector, compared with a five-year average\nof 10.8 percent, she said.  \u2018Stickier\u2019 Services  \u201cServices are just stickier,\u201d Martin Adams said. \u201cWhen\nthere\u2019s a cyclical correction, spending on tech services tends\nto decline less than hardware.\u201d  Still, \u201cthere\u2019s absolutely some downside risk\u201d if the\ncompanies miss expectations when they report their earnings in\nmid-October, particularly given the recent outperformance,\nCliggott said.  The earnings likely will be \u201cvery inconsistent,\u201d as\nwinners and losers emerge in the race to develop new, innovative\nproducts and services, Campagna said. He holds positions in\n Apple Inc. (AAPL)  and  Analog Devices Inc. (ADI) , which may be on \u201cthe\nwinning side.\u201d  The Cupertino, California-based maker of iPhones and iPads\nis up 18 percent since June 20; Analog Devices, the Norwood,\nMassachusetts, maker of chips used in cars, consumer electronics\nand telephone networks, is down 12 percent. The\ntechnology sector is his only \u201cneutral\u201d rating among cyclical\nindustries; he maintains \u201cunderweight\u201d recommendations on all\nthe others.  Campagna is buying tech stocks now because there may be\nsome \u201clight at the end of the tunnel\u201d in the economic\nslowdown. If growth stabilizes sooner than expected, these\ncompanies will continue to outperform the market, he said.  \u201cSome tech stocks don\u2019t look too risky because\nexpectations aren\u2019t that high and valuations are good,\u201d\nCliggott said.  -- Editors: Melinda Grenier, Daniel Moss  To contact the reporter on this story:\nAnna-Louise Jackson in New York at \n ajackson36@bloomberg.net   To contact the editor responsible for this story:\nAnthony Feld in New York at \n afeld2@bloomberg.net","path":".\/2008_2012_msft_bloomberg_news\/ech-outperforms-as-excess-cash-beats-u-s-cyclical-risk-on-low-valuations.txt"},{"id":70897314,"title":"Dimon\u2019s Dust-Up, Poor Fed Data, Hedge \u2018Mirage\u2019 Enliven Top Business Books","released_at":"<date>February 18 2012<\/date> <time>00:00:01<\/time>","content":"Bank analyst Mike Mayo describes a\ndust-up with  Jamie Dimon  of  JPMorgan Chase & Co. , while a former\nFederal Reserve Board staffer dissects the central bank\u2019s shoddy\nmonetary data in two of our favorite business books of late. (AAPL) \u2019s debut of its redesigned iPhone will test anew its high-stakes strategy of once-a-year upgrades for a product that accounts for about 70 percent of the company\u2019s profits.  The new phone, to be introduced tomorrow by Chief Executive Officer  Tim Cook , will probably have a new hardware design, including a bigger screen and thinner body, as well as new mapping software and compatibility with speedier next-generation  data networks . Analysts predict the iPhone may be among the biggest consumer-electronics releases in history. Still, Apple\u2019s reliance on the device leaves Cook little margin for error.  \u201cThe iPhone is the make-or-break product for Apple,\u201d said Sarah Rotman Epps, a mobile-phone industry analyst at  Forrester Research. (FORR)  \u201cApple has the undeniable lead, but to stay on top they need to keep innovating.\u201d  Related Stories: Apple could sell as many as 10 million iPhones by the end of September alone, according to  Gene Munster , an analyst at  Piper Jaffray Cos. (005930)  about 50 days to sell 10 million of its flagship Galaxy S III smartphone.  \u201cUntil they do something really unimpressive, which I don\u2019t see happening this time around, Apple has a serious hit on its hands,\u201d said  Ramon Llamas , senior research analyst at IDC.  Competing Army  Almost one year removed from the death of Apple co-founder  Steve Jobs , the newest iPhone faces a growing army of competitors looking to grab a piece of a smartphone market that Bloomberg Industries estimates was worth $219.1 billion last year. Samsung, Google Inc.\u2019s Motorola Mobility,  Nokia Oyj (NOK1V)  and  HTC Corp. (2498)  are among those taking aim at Apple by introducing dozens of new devices each year, instead of just one.  The new iPhone will be Apple\u2019s first change to the handset\u2019s hardware design since 2010, raising anticipation among customers who have been holding off on buying a new smartphone.  The company garnered 43 percent of its $108.2 billion in sales last year from the iPhone. And because wireless carriers such as  AT&T Inc. (T)  and  Verizon Wireless  subsidize the roughly $620 Apple gets for each iPhone sale, the device accounts for about 70 percent of its profits, according to Sanford C. Bernstein & Co. IPhone sales last quarter alone reached $16.2 billion, 33 percent higher than  Google Inc. (GOOG) \u2019s total sales and almost as much as  Microsoft Corp. (MSFT) \u2019s $18.1 billion.  Apple\u2019s new iPhone could contribute as much as a half a percentage point to U.S. economic growth in the fourth quarter, according to analysts at JPMorgan Chase & Co.  Closely Watched  IPhone sales also are what investors watch the most closely. Apple\u2019s shares fell in July after the company reported disappointing sales of the handset. Glyde Corp. and Gazelle Inc., two companies that facilitate the trade-in of older gadgets, said they\u2019ve seen a surge in business in recent weeks as people look ahead to upgrading to the newest iPhone.  Supply Challenge  One of the biggest challenges for Apple may be manufacturing enough devices to keep up with demand. Shortages from screen manufacturers  LG Display Co. (034220)  and Japan Display K.K. may limit how many iPhones Apple can ship, according to Barclays Plc. That may hinder Apple\u2019s ability to sell about 50 million iPhones by December, as many analysts have predicted.  Apple\u2019s event starts at 10 a.m. local time at the Yerba Buena Center for the Arts Theater in downtown San Francisco. It will be the company\u2019s first iPhone introduction since Jobs died last October on the day after the iPhone 4S was unveiled.  With the newest iPhone, Apple will attempt to balance giving existing customers a design different enough from previous models to inspire purchases, while also remaining true to the style that has made it a market leader among first-time buyers, said IDC\u2019s Llamas. Adding a bigger screen will be a critical new feature for consumers who want to use their phones for basic tasks that were once completed on laptops and personal computers, he said.  Data Demands  Data demands of new iPhone users could also put a strain on mobile data networks being introduced by wireless carriers including Verizon Wireless and AT&T. Known as long-term evolution, or LTE, the communications technology allows users to watch video, stream music or perform other data-intensive tasks at a faster speed than existing 3G networks.  \u201cApple is going to sell a lot of LTE phones. (FB)  so that members will be able to quickly post photos, comments and other content to the world\u2019s largest social network. Apple also has built its own mapping software that will replace Google\u2019s technology, as well as a new feature for consolidating all of a user\u2019s digital loyalty and gift cards. The region that was a darling of the 1990s, when companies\nincluding Starbucks and Microsoft Corp. hired workers by the\nthousands and influenced the popular culture, is still drawing\nmigrants like Gowen, according to 2010 Census data released\nyesterday. It\u2019s the jobs that are scarcer.  \u201cPeople move here because they really want to live\nhere,\u201d said  Charles Rynerson , senior demographic analyst for\nthe Population Research Center at Portland State University,\nreferring to the Northwest\u2019s scenic beauty and pace of life.\n\u201cTo some extent they may have to accept less opportunity.\u201d    Washington \u2019s population increased 14.1 percent to\n6,724,540 between 2000 and 2010, census data show. Oregon\u2019s population rose 12 percent to 3,831,074 since\n2000, the slowest pace since the 1980s, census figures show.  Northwest Remade  After decades in which lumber, fishing and airplane\nmanufacturing were mainstays of the regional economy, the\nNorthwest remade itself into a technology powerhouse through\nthe growth of companies such as Redmond, Washington-based\nMicrosoft and  Santa Clara , California-based  Intel Corp .  Hillsboro, a town west of Portland, expanded with lofts\nand brownstones for workers commuting to two Intel computer-\nchip plants. Microsoft\nundertook its first companywide layoffs in 2009 as the\nrecession sapped demand, and rivals including Google Inc. made\ninroads in the software market. The company\u2019s stock has\ndeclined 5.5 percent in the past decade as of Feb. 18. Collapse in Housing  Construction is one reason for higher unemployment.\nPortland and Seattle are both lagging the national recovery\nfrom the collapse in housing prices. U.S. Antitrust Plea Deals Won\u2019t Name Non-Culpable Employees  The U.S. Justice Department\u2019s antitrust division said it\nwill stop publicly naming individuals associated with corporate\nantitrust plea agreements who aren\u2019t believed to be culpable in\nany alleged wrongdoing, according to a statement.  The names of so-called carved-out employees, which included\nthose who refused to cooperate with a probe, are currently\nincluded in publicly filed corporate plea deals, Assistant U.S.\nAttorney General Bill Baer said April 12 in an e-mailed\nstatement.  Employees against whom the government is still developing\nevidence, or employees with \u201cpotentially relevant information\u201d\nwho can\u2019t be located, will be omitted from the publicly filed\nportion of plea agreements.  In the past, corporate plea agreements have included a\nprovision offering non-prosecution protection to those employees\nwho cooperate and whose conduct didn\u2019t warrant prosecution.\u00a0The\ndivision excluded, or carved out, employees who were believed to\nbe culpable from such receiving non-prosecution deals.  Baer said the division will continue to exclude from non-\nprosecution agreements any employees whose conduct may warrant\nprosecution.  Those decisions will be made on an \u201cemployee-by-employee\nbasis\u201d depending on the evidence, he said.  \u201cWe will continue to demand the full cooperation of anyone\nwho seeks to benefit from the non-prosecution protection of a\ncorporate plea agreement, and will revoke that protection for\nanyone who does not fully and truthfully cooperate with division\ninvestigations,\u201d Baer said. Inc. (YHOO)  will hinge on the success of a private-equity veteran named Jacqueline Reses who was largely unknown in Silicon Valley six months ago. Chief Executive Officer Mayer has put Reses in charge of talent management and mergers and acquisitions, as the biggest U.S. Web portal struggles to reinvent itself and stay relevant in the age of all things mobile. Reses\u2019s mandate has expanded to include partner and culture development, and this week she was given the new title of chief development officer, Mayer said in an interview.  Almost a year into her tenure, Mayer is racing to transform the company into a more robust competitor to Google Inc. and Facebook Inc. for users, advertisers and employees, and Reses is critical to that effort. Yahoo has cash and equivalents of about $6 billion. Reses\u2019s dealmaking challenge is finding targets specializing in cool technologies that can make its own pages and services more attractive.  \u201cMarissa Mayer is trying to bring back talent to Yahoo and make it a place which has vibrancy in Silicon Valley,\u201d Gene Sykes, co-head of global mergers and acquisitions at  Goldman Sachs Group Inc. (GS)  and a former colleague of Reses, said in an interview. \u201cOne way you do that is by buying startups and combining the people.\u201d  Talent Retention  The company must also persuade the smart, young software geeks who come with its M&A deals to stick with Yahoo. Entrusting human resources to the person in charge of landing deals may ease the difficulty of hanging onto entrepreneurs -- such as Nick D\u2019Aloisio, the 17-year-old founder of Yahoo target Summly -- who become rich after selling out.  Before Mayer\u2019s arrival, Yahoo lost hundreds of key executives and skilled engineers to faster-growing rivals offering more alluring equity and better workplace amenities.  \u201cIt\u2019s a land grab for talent, and it\u2019s a land grab for great innovative products,\u201d said Kevin Stadtler, president of Stadtler Capital Management, which has $16.4 million under management, including Yahoo shares. \u201cThey have billions of dollars at their disposal to acquire talented companies in digital media.\u201d  Six Startups  Yahoo has  purchased  six startups -- Stamped Inc., OntheAir, Snip.it, Alike, Jybe Inc. and Summly -- since July, when Mayer  took over  as the Web portal\u2019s fifth CEO in four years. So far, she\u2019s concentrated on talent acquisitions -- small teams bought at low prices -- an approach she advocated during her first conference call with analysts last year. Emin Gun Sirer , a Cornell University computer science professor,  said  he thinks Yahoo overpaid, given that Summly\u2019s core technology isn\u2019t impressive or complex.  Reses has also been quick to earn a reputation as a no- nonsense manager. The meeting didn\u2019t last long: Reses fired Katz, two weeks before he was due to receive a bonus related to Yahoo\u2019s 2011 acquisition of his startup, Interclick Inc., according to the complaint in a  lawsuit  filed by Katz.  Employee Memo  Yahoo didn\u2019t make Reses available for comment. Sara Gorman, a company spokeswoman, declined to comment on the executive or acquisitions.  Reses is also the author of a now-infamous February memo that restricted employees\u2019 ability to work from home. The policy switch revived a nationwide debate over flexible work schedules, pitting advocates who say it enhances productivity against critics who say coming into the office fosters collaboration and creativity.  While the company is focused on small groups of engineers and more modest deals, it might consider larger acquisitions, said  Brian Wieser , a New York-based analyst at Pivotal Research Group LLC. The law firm in March hired Jon Kyl of  Arizona , who last year was the second highest ranking Senate Republican, and Howard Berman, a  California  Democrat who had been chairman of the House Foreign Affairs Committee. The two serve as senior advisers, sharing their expertise and personal knowledge about lawmakers with clients and colleagues lobbying on legislation and regulations.  Since the November elections, at least 22 members of the last Congress took jobs with lobbying firms, running trade associations or handling government relations for organizations. That is an increase of 14 percent over 2012 in the number of former lawmakers now in the lobbying business, according to the Washington-based Center for Responsive Politics, which tracks ex-lawmakers\u2019 employment. Since 1998, a total of 338 former members of Congress have worked as lobbyists or joined such firms for at least some of their time since leaving office.  Covington\u2019s public policy group chairman, Dan Bryant, said he hired the former lawmakers because they \u201cunderstand the mindset of key members in the House and Senate.\u201d Covington was paid $2.5 million in this year\u2019s first quarter to lobby by  Chiquita Brands International Inc (CQB) .,  Eli Lilly & Co. Gaining an Edge  Lobbying and other advocacy groups seek out former members in order to gain an advantage over the opposition. A former lawmaker may know about a senator\u2019s family or a House member\u2019s parochial concerns, insights that help advocates make quick, personal connections while pressing a policy position. They also have better prospects for getting a private meeting with their former Senate or House colleagues.  \u201cThey know the process, the policy and the players well, so they often have a special inside connection with key policymakers,\u201d said James Thurber, director of the Center for Congressional and Presidential Studies at American University in  Washington . So Why Didn't Ballmer Build Any of It?","released_at":"<date>September 11 2013<\/date> <time>17:58:50<\/time>","content":"(Corrects spelling of Microsoft spokesman's name in 6th paragraph.) On June 22, 2000, a few months after Steve Ballmer took over as CEO of Microsoft, the company summoned several hundred reporters and analysts to a conference center at its headquarters in Redmond, Washington. Ballmer, under pressure from a U.S. antitrust case and super-hot dot-com rivals, was set to unveil his company's vision for the future of computing. I sat in a packed room as Microsoft held a daylong series of sessions during which the company announced what it called the .NET strategy. To regain its place within the vanguard of personal computing, Ballmer's Microsoft promised to deliver an interconnected set of Web services that could serve up relevant information to users across multiple devices and let them share with family, friends and co-workers. In a statement then, Ballmer said Microsoft would create a \"unified platform through which devices and services cooperate with each other.\" Microsoft filmed a bunch of concept videos to illustrate its product ideas. You can watch an edited version of the videos at the top of this post. Cheesiness aside, it's pretty spot-on, no? There's personalized content for each family member synchronized across PCs, televisions, tablets, mobile phones and cars; location-aware devices that tell you when friends are nearby; photo-sharing; voice controls -- all years before Facebook, Foursquare, or Apple's iCloud and Siri. More incredible than the foresight of these videos is how Microsoft failed to execute on nearly all of it. What went wrong? Well, lots of things. Some of the ideas were simply before their time. Others became bogged down in internecine squabbles between Microsoft fiefdoms, and philosophical debates about whether to keep Windows at the center of this new world or to build a separate platform. And then, the dot-com bubble burst. The Office group scrapped a planned Internet-based document service called NetDocs. Some of the Windows work in this area got derailed by the late-running train that was Longhorn (later renamed Vista). Microsoft's early tablet efforts failed, and the company didn't go back for more until Apple showed them the way. Peter Wootton, a spokesman for Microsoft, declined to comment. Business users did get some of the promised technology. SharePoint and Lync provide project sharing, Internet voice calls and teleconferencing. But as Microsoft slapped the .NET name on a variety of products, very few of them fulfilled the initial promise of that first day. Many of the people who worked on the effort left the company. Vic Gundotra and Mark Lucovsky wound up at Google. Paul Maritz, who led much of the planning for .NET, left just three months after Ballmer's big event in Redmond and eventually wound up as CEO of VMware. Now, industry watchers are suggesting Gundotra or Maritz as possible successors to Ballmer when he  retires sometime in the next 12 months . \"Had the company executed on even a fraction of its vision, Microsoft wouldn't be out looking for a new CEO,\" said Charles Fitzgerald, a former Microsoft executive who worked on .NET. Now, with Ballmer poised to step down after more than 13 years at the helm,  Microsoft's acquisition of Finland-based Nokia's handset unit  could help the company pull off its devices-and-services strategy. If that works, Microsoft may get another shot realizing what it promised in 2000. Ballmer's Microsoft wasn't lacking for ideas; it was lacking execution. The videos live on not as a celebration of how prescient Ballmer's Microsoft was but as a testament to what could have been.","path":".\/2008_2012_msft_bloomberg_news\/icrosoft-s-concept-videos-from-2000-were-spot-on-so-why-didn-t-ballmer-build-any-of-it-.txt"},{"id":67678679,"title":"Airbnb Said to Be Raising Money From Peter Thiel","released_at":"<date>October 19 2012<\/date> <time>23:21:49<\/time>","content":"Airbnb Inc. , operator of a website\nthat lets people rent out rooms and residences, is raising about\n$150 million in new funding that values the company at about\n$2.5 billion, said people familiar with the matter. Four Ways to Integrate Fiefdoms.","released_at":"<date>July 23 2013<\/date> <time>13:00:17<\/time>","content":"One Ford. One Apple. Now one Microsoft.  Last week, Microsoft CEO Steve Ballmer  unveiled a restructuring  designed to unite the organization behind a single strategy and create high-value experiences for their customers.   Many more organizational structure changes are likely to come. Why?  Because digitization has passed power to the consumer, pressing companies to pull together their old decentralized profit and loss fiefdoms to produce experiences consumers find compelling. As Ballmer wrote in  his memo  to Microsoft employees, \"We will see our product line holistically, not as a set of islands.\"  \nBut changes in organizational structure get you only part way there. Ballmer acknowledged as much when he went on to say, \"The final piece of the puzzle is how we work together.\"  Achieving speed and customer centricity depends on a crucial ingredient that's often missing: integration.  It's the job of a leader to create it.   Integration has two parts to it. The first is to get various functional silos and P&L centers sharply aligned with the specifics of customer requirements. The second applies to the multiple channels a consumer might use as part of that experience \u2014 for example, for a bank these would include a website, an ATM, and the lobby of the local branch.  The person in charge of online banking might want a different offering than the person leading the branch offices, just as an engineering head might want a different set of product features than a manufacturing VP. Integration means taking into account all of those points of view and making the right trade-offs to give consumers a total end-to-end experience better than the competition.   Structure divides; leaders integrate.  Transforming an organization into a synchronized high speed decision-making body is no picnic.  In my experience, only a few leaders, such as Ford's Alan Mulally and Apple's Steve Jobs, have succeeded in making this crucial transformation.    Leaders who want to adapt should consider the following lessons:  \t1.  Understand that 2% of the people in your organization have tremendous impact on the other 98%.  I call this the rule of 98\/2.  Silos have nurtured people with narrow expertise and perspective; so, in many companies, the 2% is ill-equipped for integration.  Make sure the 2% have the distinctive skills and personality constructs required.  These include the attitude and drive to deliver a winning customer proposition and the ability to synchronize different viewpoints and make the right trade-offs. Pay particular attention to the values of the decision makers. Collaboration must be in their blood. This is a difficult if not impossible shift for those who have been running their own show.    \t2.  Design \"integration mechanisms\" and operate them with rigor. You as a leader must be hands-on in creating a rhythm for integration. In creating One Ford, Mulally brought his top team together every Thursday.  Attendance was mandatory.  Most of the team he inherited is intact, yet the divisiveness of fiefdoms that originated with Henry Ford has now disappeared.  The weekly discussions have kept the team on the same page strategically and operationally.  COO Mark Fields now runs this mechanism. Apple's consumer-friendly innovation and Wal-Mart's quick inventory and price adjustments were the result of similar mechanisms masterfully run by Steve Jobs and Sam Walton respectively.   \t3.  Be sure key performance indicators and incentives reinforce synchronization and integration. Basing a portion of compensation on common goals fosters collaboration.  \n\t4.  Cultures change when leaders repeatedly and consistently intervene to correct deviant behaviors.  It requires discipline and skill to continually demonstrate the behaviors and values conducive to integration and to promptly resolve any underlying conflicts.  Through joint work, attitudes get reshaped and energy gets created. Those who cannot adapt begin to opt out. Companies that lack speed and fail to deliver the right consumer experience on a timely basis can go over the cliff very quickly, as some have already done. It is essential to build the new core capability of integration, starting from the CEO throughout the organization.","path":".\/2008_2012_msft_bloomberg_news\/one-microsoft-four-ways-to-integrate-fiefdoms-.txt"},{"id":78752773,"title":"GameStop Members May Snub Next-Gen Console Restrictions","released_at":"<date>February 7 2013<\/date> <time>05:07:11<\/time>","content":"GameStop Corp. , responding to a\nreport about features on  Microsoft Corp. \u2019s next Xbox video-game\nconsole, said customers would snub any new machine that\nrestricts play of pre-owned titles. U.S. Patents Held Hostage by Lawmakers in Budget Fight  Efforts to make the U.S. Patent and Trademark Office more\nefficient for businesses may be derailed by the inability of\nCongress to agree on a federal budget.  The office, one of the few self-funded federal agencies,\nmay not be able to use an estimated $200 million in fees to be\ncollected from patent and trademark owners in fiscal 2011\nbecause of a budget impasse in Congress. Instead, a\nbudget is set for the agency based on estimates of what it will\ncollect. Any money above that figure is put into the U.S.\ngeneral treasury, where Congress can use it for other purposes.  \u201cI don\u2019t see why Congress treats user fees specifically\ndesigned to fund the patent office as if they were taxpayer\u2019s\nfunds,\u201d Paul Michel, the former chief judge of the U.S. Court\nof Appeals for the Federal Circuit who retired last year, said\nin an interview. \u201cNot a single dollar of tax money is involved.\nThe funding is private money from private corporations.\u201d  More than $800 million has been kept by Congress since a\n1990 law mandated the office pay for itself through fees,\naccording to the agency\u2019s 2010 performance report. The  National Merit Scholarship Corp.  distributed more than\n$50 million to students in the 2009-2010 year based on the PSAT\ncollege entry practice exam. Most of the money comes from almost\n200 colleges, including  Northwestern University  and  University\nof Chicago , to fund awards of as much as $8,000 over four years.\nCompanies such as  Boeing Co.  and  Pfizer Inc. (PFE)  also sponsor the\nprogram, primarily to benefit their employees\u2019 children.  NYU\u2019s withdrawal is another blow to National Merit, already\nignored by many elite colleges and a subject of a critical\nreport by a Harvard College-chaired commission. Schools are\ndebating how to allocate scarce financial-aid dollars as tuition\ncosts rise and the economy remains sluggish. While high schools\ntrumpet National Merit winners, relying heavily on a\nstandardized test is a flawed way to evaluate students, said\nShawn Abbott, assistant vice president of admissions at NYU.  \u201cWe simply do not feel that enrolling a larger number of\nNational Merit finalists is a necessary way for us to attract\nthe most academically qualified freshman class,\u201d Abbott said in\nan interview.  NYU stopped funding grants to finalists with the freshman\nclass that started school in September, Abbott said. Students\nfrom earlier classes that were named National Merit scholars\nwill continue to receive their annual grants. Lack of Transparency  \u201cNational Merit has never been transparent about, for\nexample, the ethnic diversity of the people who receive National\nMerit scholarships, nor do we get any information about whether\nor not this very large amount of money is used by, for example,\nlarge numbers of people who have great financial need,\u201d\nFitzsimmons said in an interview. The patents\ncover Ludwigshafen, Germany-based BASF\u2019s  Termidor , which has\nbeen sold for more than a decade and is the top-selling termite\nproduct in the U.S. BASF sued Makhteshim-Agan in 2010, after it\nbegan selling its own version of the insecticide under the name\nTaurus SC.  U.S. District Judge William Osteen in Greensboro,  North\nCarolina , was correct in finding the BASF patents covered a\nspecific way of applying fipronil, while Makhteshim-Agan used a\ndifferent application method, the three-judge Federal Circuit\npanel ruled.  Anne Burt, a spokeswoman for BASF, said the company is\nreviewing yesterday\u2019s decision.  BASF filed a new patent-infringement suit March 19 against\nMakhteshim-Agan in federal court in  Georgia . It claims Taurus SC\nis made using a manufacturing process covered by another patent.  \u201cIntellectual property is the cornerstone of our\ninnovation-based marketplace,\u201d Jan Buberl, director of\nspecialty products for BASF North American Crop Protection, said\nin a statement. \u201cImproper activity that undermines patent\nprotection laws is unfair to those who act properly and\nlawfully.\u201d  Fipronil is an insecticide also used in flea and tick\ncontrol products for pets. Makhteshim-Agan, based in Tel Aviv,\nwas bought in 2011 by China National Chemical Corp. and taken\nprivate.  The case is BASF Agro BV Arnhem v. Makhteshim Agan of North\nAmerica, 12-01206,  U.S. Court of Appeals  for the Federal Circuit\n(Washington). The lower court case is BASF Agro B.V. Arnhem v.\nMakhteshim Agan of North America, 10-cv-00276, U.S. District\nCourt, Middle District of North Carolina (Greensboro).  The new case is BASF Agro B.V. Arnhem v. Makhteshim Agan of\nNorth America, 13-cv-00867, U.S. District Court, Northern\nDistrict of Georgia (Atlanta). He contrasts the performance of the Obamacare websites with what\u2019s going on at one particular agency: I think this is absolutely right, but it\u2019s for exactly that reason that I think the quest to create an \"iPod presidency\u201d was always doomed. The process that Ezra describes -- the sclerotic process by which bureaucracy and encroaching risk aversion come to block off the arteries of innovation -- is the natural aging process of an organization. It\u2019s why companies like Hewlett-Packard Co. and Xerox Corp. and International Business Machines Corp., which were once radical disruptors, now seem like slow-moving supertankers: hard to capsize but not exactly nimble. You can see the process happening now at firms like Microsoft Corp., and even Apple Inc. And in a decade or so, you\u2019ll see it happening at Google Inc. and Facebook Inc. It\u2019s an inevitable part of the process of aging.  Old organizations definitionally have a lot of longtime stakeholders. And in a sort of ecological process, those stakeholders have been selected for a certain amount of fitness for their environment, which is to say that they are good at doing things the way they have always been done, and they like things the way they are. They are averse to any sort of big change, and they will fight you with every tool at their disposal, from open warfare to passive-aggressively going through the motions on everything you ask them to do. That\u2019s why organizations in crisis frequently need to fire the majority of their staffs to turn things around -- and, more than once, an organization that has done so has found that it\u2019s still stuck with the same corporate culture that wasn\u2019t working before. As sociologist Gabriel Rossman  told me : The CFPB is doing a good thing by taking a radical approach. But it can only do that because it\u2019s a brand-new agency. In 25 years, if the CFPB is still around, I can virtually guarantee that it will have all the turf wars, bureaucratic inertia and so forth that has hobbled the Department of Health and Human Services. Not because government agencies are somehow especially awful, but because every organization calcifies over time. Of course, there is one key difference with government: It doesn\u2019t go away. When a Polaroid Corp. or an Eastman Kodak Co. runs out of creative steam, it fails, and downsizes, and gets replaced by a different company. HHS, on the other hand, is not going to get its job taken over by a lean upstart. Government structure is not quite written in stone -- over the last 10 years, we\u2019ve gotten the Department of Homeland Security and the CFPB. But note that it took the worst terrorist attack on U.S. soil, and the worst financial crisis since the Great Depression, to make these things happen. And at that, Homeland Security simply replicates much of the old bureaucratic structure of the agencies that were put together under its umbrella. America thinks of itself as being one of the youngest nations in the world. But as far as governments go, we\u2019re one of the oldest: We\u2019ve been operating continuously under the same constitution for more than 200 years now. A certain amount of what  Jonathan Rauch  has dubbed \u201cdemosclerosis\u201d was inevitable. In recent years, one of the few things Republicans and Democrats could agree upon was that an artificially cheap yuan damaged U.S. exports and stole U.S. jobs. The currency\u2019s climb thus seemed like a nod from China\u2019s president to America\u2019s, a quiet signal that Xi understands how sensitive the issue is. During Obama\u2019s time in office, in fact, the yuan has risen more than 10 percent in value. Talk of a currency war has faded.  Of course, a stronger  yuan  means a different kind of problem for corporate America. This will dawn on executives as they begin to see the prefix \"+86\u201d --  China (CNGDPYOY) \u2019s country code -- on more and more incoming phone calls. Just as Chinese consumers now have more money in their wallets to spend, so do Chinese companies. They could well embark on a shopping spree far more earthshaking than the Obama-Xi summit.  The recent bid by Shuanghui International Holdings Ltd. to buy  Smithfield Foods Inc. (SFD)  has brought this possibility into sharp relief. The deal, which at $7.1 billion including debt would be the biggest Chinese acquisition of a U.S. company, has prompted frantic machinations on  Capitol Hill . Politicians have managed to turn the proposed buyout of a hog producer into a threat to national security.  Just imagine the reaction if cash-rich Chinese companies start to go after banks such as Goldman Sachs Group Inc., or iconic U.S. manufacturers such as Boeing Co. and  General Electric (GE)  Co. China can surely do better than provide sweatshops for Apple Inc. and Wal-Mart Stores Inc. Why not own them outright?  Attractive Deals  There are several reasons such bids are becoming increasingly attractive to Chinese leaders. As the all-important manufacturing engine burns out, officials in Beijing are desperate to diversify sources of growth.  China (CNFRBAL$)  needs to modernize its economy, boost innovation and create well-paying jobs. It has to feed 1.3 billion people and gain access to energy and raw materials.  What a strengthening yuan takes away from exports, it adds in global purchasing power: A struggling American company such as Smithfield is now 12 percent cheaper for a Chinese executive than it would have been five years ago.  Xi and Premier  Li Keqiang  could spend the next 10 years working to create a stable of globally competitive names -- a Chinese Microsoft or Toyota. Or they could put that stronger yuan to work and bypass the tedious process of indigenous-brand making. Don\u2019t forget that China has $3.4 trillion in currency reserves to use as a war chest. Chinese savers face a dearth of investment options, so their money is the state\u2019s to invest.  Tough Spot  Such a buying binge would put the U.S. in a difficult position. Obama can\u2019t preach the gospel of openness and transparency, while rejecting deal after deal on national-security grounds. In China, cries of hypocrisy would surge along with anti-American sentiment. The acrimony could easily scuttle hopes created over the weekend in  California  that Obama and Xi can put the Cold War mentality aside and work together.  The greatest victim of a global mergers-and-acquisitions assault, however, would be China itself. The country\u2019s more than 100,000 state-owned enterprises continue to dominate the economy, generating as much as half of gross domestic product in recent years. They enjoy generous subsidies and cheap financing -- both of which would greatly aid any buyout attempts.  While there is nothing to stop private Chinese companies from also seeking to take over foreign brands, in reality they would be outgunned. For the most important deals -- where the target controls critical technology, a powerful global  brand , or both -- China is almost certain to favor a state buyer over a private one.  This is the last thing the Chinese economy needs. State-directed businesses tend to misallocate credit and restrain entrepreneurship. Communist Party bigwigs and executives at state-owned companies happily skim profits into their own bank accounts. State companies rack up piles of unhealthy debt, knowing the government will ultimately be forced to bail them out.  Instead of trying to build up national  champions , Chinese leaders should be focused on creating a more dynamic economy. They should start by reducing barriers and red tape so that private companies can better compete in industries where the state currently enjoys a monopoly. A more transparent bidding process would lead to more efficient growth. Rather than reviving inefficient enterprises by slapping a global brand on them, the government should be looking for ways to stimulate homegrown innovation.  Real Retooling  Until now, resistance to Chinese business abroad has largely revolved around issues of governance. In its global quest for customers and especially natural resources, China has blithely supported unsavory regimes, altered the rules of trade, and run roughshod over ecosystems from  Asia  to  Africa . Chinese businesses have alienated more than just Americans: In late 2011, Myanmar President  Thein Sein  underscored his country\u2019s dramatic turn toward the West by scrapping a huge Chinese hydroelectric-dam project that had spurred local protests.  However tempting a shopping spree might be, Beijing officials must discourage one. Xi has pledged to retool an economy out of step with the tenets of modern capitalism. If he is sincere, he needs to reduce the state\u2019s role, instead of using a stronger yuan to expand and export it.  (William Pesek is a Bloomberg View columnist.) Paper money tends to\ncirculate more freely than silver, and silver more freely than\ngold, because people hoard whatever type of money is seen as\nbest. It\u2019s why we spend those torn dollar bills first.  I have no problem with this. It might even be a good thing,\nbecause it expands the money supply and credit. But I do have a\nproblem when a similar dynamic takes over language, as bad,\nbureaucratic, bulky and bothersome words drive out simple,\nshort, clear and good ones.  Examples would fill a dictionary. There is corporate speak\nsuch as actualize, differentiate, facilitate, repurpose and\nsynthesize. But this is mere detritus, easily swept away. What\nbothers me more is when a fluffy, pretentious and bureaucratic\nword replaces a simpler one, often with a history.  With the advent of the personal computer, \u201cword\nprocessing\u201d began to replace \u201ctyping\u201d as the preferred term.\nThis was an unnecessary change: Fingers were still placed on\nletters on a keyboard, and sentences still transmitted to a page\nor screen.  Similarly, I noticed a few years ago that a public\nelementary school had renamed its library \u201cthe media center,\u201d\nas if an old and distinguished word such as \u201clibrary\u201d was\nunable to encompass information-delivery devices such as\nmicrofilm or the Internet. Simply updating or expanding a\ntechnology doesn\u2019t require a new word.  Continuity Helps  There is value in what came before.  Apple Inc. (AAPL) \u2019s Steve Jobs\nwon converts to his Macintosh computers by having users\n\u201cpaste\u201d and \u201ccut,\u201d rather than \u201cinsert\u201d and \u201cdelete,\u201d as\nin the Microsoft world. He wasn\u2019t dumbing down. That continuity\nof language helped this new tool, the computer, establish\nitself.  The allure of most bad words is that we think they make us\nsound smarter. Because we associate complexity with smartness,\ncomplicated words tend to replace simpler ones. Once\n\u201cshipping\u201d was the term to move any sort of package or cargo,\nwhether by boat, train or air. This is still true in some\nsectors. The U.S. Postal Service, bless its heart, still has a\ndepartment of \u201cshipping.\u201d But many people and companies prefer\nthe term \u201clogistics,\u201d which essentially means just moving\nthings around on a schedule. I\u2019m sure this justifies several\ndollars more per hour or pound.  Another offender is \u201cinfrastructure.\u201d Once unknown in\npublic discourse and used only by the military, it now pops up\nin headlines. It has replaced simpler, more descriptive terms,\nparticularly \u201cpublic works\u201d and the even older \u201cinternal\nimprovements.\u201d  Another fancy term in management circles is \u201cmetrics.\u201d We\nnow ask about the metrics of a project, rather than its\nmeasurements, statistics or, simply, numbers.  Fellow lovers of simple language probably have their own\ncandidates for worst words. My own is \u201cbrand.\u201d I\u2019d like to\nblast it out of the air whenever it floats across a conference\nroom table.  It once had a specific and legitimate use: the name of a\ncompany or a product. It was McDonald\u2019s hamburgers, Campbell\u2019s\nsoup, Clorox bleach and Kleenex tissues. But about two decades\nago it oozed into other fields. It became a verb -- always a bad\nsign -- and eventually even an occupation.  Branding as a concept is bad because it advances a notion\nboth seductive and appalling, which is that we can change our\nimage or public face as easily as letters on a movie marquee. It\nsuggests falsity, a con, sleight of hand.  Context Matters  The better, simpler and more sober term is \u201creputation.\u201d\nIt doesn\u2019t mean exactly the same thing, but it\u2019s better for what\nit is lacking. Our parents taught us that reputations are made\nslowly, and can be lost quickly. A reputation is not a\nprojection. In 1982, when  Johnson & Johnson (JNJ)  famously recalled\nall its Tylenol products after several deaths from intentionally\ntainted products, the company wasn\u2019t building its brand. It was\nbuilding its reputation.  I may sound like a linguistic Luddite. I will concede that\nmost disciplines have and need their own specialized language.\nArchitects, for example, talk about \u201cthe program\u201d of a\nbuilding -- meaning what it will be used for. It confuses\neveryone else, but it helps determine the design of the\nbuilding.  But let us leave specialized language to those specialized\nplaces. We may actually understand one another better, which is\nusually a good thing. Although  Gresham\u2019s law  may still rule in\nmoney matters, we can seek to repeal it in matters of words.  (Alex Marshall\u00a0is the  author  of\u00a0\u201c The Surprising Design of\nMarket Economies ,\u201d and a senior fellow at Regional Plan\nAssociation in  New York  City.)
