Investors\nmust risk capital to fund failures. The potential payoffs\nprovide the incentive to suffer the losses.  Those who favor income redistribution point to the\nsteadiness of long-term  economic growth  as evidence that\ninnovation bubbles up randomly in the normal course of business.\nThey emphasize culture, claiming that Americans are eager to\ntake risks regardless of the incentives, while Europeans and the\nJapanese are reluctant. Economists with these views see minimal\ncosts from redistributing income from wealthy investors to\npoorer consumers.  Opponents of income redistribution worry that  higher taxes \nwater down incentives and that redistribution slows the\naccumulation of capital, especially risk-bearing equity.  -- Investment produces innovation: The more time and\nresources investors and entrepreneurs devote to searching\nrandomly for innovation, the more likely they will be to find\nit. This requires time that the economy could devote to other\nendeavors. An increase in investment by one economy relative to\nanother will likely affect their relative rates of discovery and\nimplementation. When successful, risky investments in innovation\nwill grow the economy faster than less risky investments that\nenlarge existing capacities.  Successfully commercializing good ideas is as important as\ndiscovering them and requires similarly risky investments. Even\nif  Facebook Inc. (FB)  and  Google Inc. (GOOG)  had randomly stumbled upon\ngreat ideas, they still had to invest inordinate amounts of\nmoney and overcome high levels of risk to commercialize them.  In \u201cThe Age of Turbulence,\u201d former Federal Reserve Board\nChairman  Alan Greenspan  reminds us that the U.S. economy has\ngrown sevenfold in real terms since World War II, while physical\ninputs, such as steel and oil, have risen only twofold. Most of\nthe growth came from intellectual capital. Cutting-edge\neconomies like that of the U.S. invest largely by paying the\nsalaries of talented thinkers who invent and design new products\nand processes.  -- Innovation expands the economy: Innovation benefits\nconsumers through lower prices. Yet these can be hard to\nquantify, particularly when they show up in the form of higher-\nquality goods, which may sell at the same price but offer\ngreater benefits than the products they replaced. Because of the\ndifficulties of measuring such \u201cquality-adjusted\u201d prices,\neconomists generally disregard the ebb and flow in the rate of\nthese improvements.  Sometimes, workers capture the value of innovation and\nproductivity gains through higher wages. Ultimately, higher\nwages and lower prices are the same because workers are both\nwage earners and consumers. With increased productivity, prices\nfall and real wages rise.  As tangible or intangible investment per worker increases,\none might expect capital to capture an increasingly greater\nshare of the output. But that hasn\u2019t happened. Figure 1,\nattached, shows that as the  U.S. economy  has grown more capital-\nintensive, labor has continued to capture about 70 percent of\ngross domestic product as wages.  Consumers also capture the value of products over and above\ntheir cost. A car, for example, is worth much more than its\nprice. Economists call this \u201cbuyers\u2019 surplus.\u201d GDP measures the\nvalue of goods at their prices, not at their value to\npurchasers. If consumers capture 70 percent of GDP as wages and\n100 percent of the buyers\u2019 surplus, they are capturing a very\nlarge share of the value created by investment -- perhaps 90\npercent or more.  We see these dynamics in agriculture. As agricultural\nproductivity has doubled since the 1940s, expenditures on food\nas a percent of GDP have fallen proportionately from more than\n20 percent of disposable income to less than 10 percent today,\nsee Figure 2, attached. In the U.S., these savings provided much\nof the resources needed to increase demand for manufactured\ngoods. Today, similar  productivity gains  in manufacturing are\ndriving growth in services.  The reduction in food expenditures displayed in Figure 2,\nattached, allows us to approximate the magnitude of the value\ncaptured by consumers relative to producers. Consumers captured\nthe difference between 24 percent and 10 percent of  disposable\nincome  -- income that is approximately seven times larger today\nthan it was in 1950. Producers, on the other hand, benefited\nless. Their profits, after depreciation and before interest and\ntaxes, remained stable at about 10 percent of revenues, or 10\npercent of what consumers spent. The split of value (before\ncorporate taxes) between consumers and producers created by\nagricultural innovation and investment is in the range of 20-to-\n1 in favor of consumers.  This one-sided split of the returns from capital between\ninvestors and labor is the reason radical proponents of income\nredistribution, such as  Paul Krugman , seek to regulate the\nallocation of capital through the political process rather than\nthrough free markets. They argue that many investments may be\nvaluable to society but not to investors, so why let the small\nreturns to private investors determine the allocation of capital\ncritical to the welfare of mankind?  Proponents of free markets are concerned that regulations\nwill reduce profitability and return on investment. Small\nreductions in profits and subsequent investment can have a big\nimpact on wages, employment and the price of goods. This can\nunwittingly destroy more value than well-intended regulations\ncreate.  -- What is too much?: A broad range of investment continues\nto drive productivity because investment and risk taking, as a\nwhole, are far below the optimal level. The work of Nobel Prize-\nwinning economist  Edmund Phelps  presents empirical evidence that\nunder optimal conditions capital would earn a real return equal\nto the growth rate of the workforce -- in highly developed\neconomies, 1 percent to 2 percent per year.  Today, the U.S. has a surplus of  debt . We are flooded with\nrisk-averse savings. We face a shortage of risk-bearing equity\nto underwrite risk, rather than a shortage of capital more\nbroadly. Equity in the U.S. and worldwide earns about 7.5\npercent per year, indicating that equity and the risk taking it\nunderwrites are well below the optimal level.  Investors can make poor choices and take imprudent risks in\none sector -- housing and mortgage risks, for example -- without\nthe economy as a whole extending beyond the point of optimality.  Government subsidies can also drive risk taking beyond the\npoint of optimality by over-allocating investment to one sector\n--  subprime housing , for example -- at the cost of\nunderinvestment in other sectors.  --  Monetary policy : Printing money doesn\u2019t magically\nstimulate the economy. Instead, monetary policy allows risk\ntaking to grow when it is hampered by a lack of credit, and the\neconomy has excess capacity available to produce the increased\ngrowth. An owner of future cash flows (assets) may seek to\nincrease the amount of risk he is taking by splitting his future\ncash flows into tranches so that he can exchange the low-risk\nfirst-to-be-repaid tranche (debt) for a risk-averse saver\u2019s\nincome. Putting that hoarded capital to use expands the economy.  If credit is restricted, risk takers may be unable to tap\nthose savings. Constraints on credit may occur if banks have\nalready loaned all the available deposits, or if they have used\nall their equity to meet capital-adequacy requirements for\nexisting loans. Lower short-term  interest rates  increase the\nspread that banks earn by borrowing short-term savings and\nmaking long-term loans. This increases bank profits and grows\ntheir equity, which reduces constraints. Relieving credit\nconstraints will grow the economy, but only if the economy has\nthe capacity to produce the increase in demand and an appetite\nfor risk.  Increases or decreases in optimism tend to create self-\nreinforcing feedback loops that monetary policy can either allow\nor restrict. As risk takers grow increasingly optimistic, asset\nvalues rise. This makes investors and consumers grow\nincreasingly willing to take risks. As risk taking grows, the\neconomy expands, increasing the amount of investment and the\nvalue of assets relative to the economy.  -- Investment is understated: Our antiquated 1940s\nmanufacturing-based accounting rules expense the salaries of\ncreative thinkers and leaders as intermediate costs of\nproduction, rather than capitalizing them as investments. Only\nrecently have accounting rules allowed the capitalization of\nsoftware-development costs, for example. Accounting rules demand\nhighly restrictive measures of investment to ensure\ncomparability between results. A fast-growing company with\nhigher profit margins that is pouring more money into investment\nthan its competitors looks more attractive to investors and\ngarners a higher stock price. Accounting rules prevent this lack\nof comparability by erring on the side of expensing rather than\ncapitalizing costs, especially employee-related costs.  Survivor bias exacerbates this masking effect and further\nobscures the link between investment in risky innovation and its\nreturn. One breakthrough may require hundreds of failures.\nFailed investments in intellectual capital are expensed and\nforgotten, decoupled from the cost of the resulting success.\nWithout clear linkages between the value of success and the\nhidden cost of failure, investment appears dramatically\nunderstated.  Conservative measurements such as those employed in a 2006\nFederal Reserve study, \u201c Intangible Capital and Economic Growth ,\u201d\nshow significant increases in intangible investments. According\nto the Fed, intangible investments rose from about 7 percent of\nnon-farm business output in the late 1970s to 10 percent in the\nearly 1990s to about 14 percent today, see Figure 3, attached.\nThese investments rose dramatically in the 1990s when\nproductivity accelerated.  Over the same period, traditional business investments in\nfactories and machinery grew from about 5.5 percent of GDP after\nWorld War II to about 8 percent today. Adding both tangible and\nintangible investments shows that business investment grew from\n15 percent of GDP after the war to a level approaching 25\npercent today.  It is likely that these simple estimates understate\ninvestment, and that the expenditures that increase the\nproductivity of the most talented employees are much broader.\nAlmost everyone engaged in finance, for example, thinks about\nthe value of future cash flows and how to maximize them. They\nmake decisions about the allocation of assets that set the\nprices for various risks. These prices influence the allocation\nof investment. Again, economic statistics expense all these\ncosts.  There are other forms of overlooked investment. The most\ntalented U.S. workers now spend more time working while the\nhours of their European peers have declined.  The productivity of the most talented workers is also\ngrowing faster than the U.S. economy as a whole. With 5 percent\nof the workforce producing more than a third of the output,\nincreases in this group\u2019s productivity have a big impact on the\neconomy overall.  Pundits often wonder why median wages have failed to rise\nin proportion to increased levels of productivity, as they have\nin the past. The answer is obvious: The median wage is the\nhighest wage of the lowest 50 percent of workers, and\nproductivity growth has occurred predominantly at the  top of the\nwage scale . Above the median, the wage premium for the most\ntalented workers grew, despite a surge in the productivity-\nenhanced supply of knowledge workers, see Figure 4, attached. An\nincrease in supply should drive down wages, but pay rose because\nthe value from deploying this talent was greater than their pay.  We can also see the increase in intangible investment in\nthe changing composition of U.S. jobs since the mid-1980s.\nAgain, half of all the new jobs created over the last 25 years\nhave been in thought-oriented professions. Such jobs made up\nonly a quarter of total employment in the 1980s.  It\u2019s also clear why the income of the top 1 percent is\ngrowing faster in the U.S. than in Europe and  Japan . U.S.\ninnovators produced  Intel Corp. (INTC) ,  Microsoft Corp. (MSFT) , Google and\nFacebook. The rest of the world contributed next to nothing. He used the tool favored by traders for more than a century: a telephone. Corpina, senior managing partner with Meridian Equity Partners Inc. who works on the floor of the  New York  Stock Exchange, called a client two blocks from the president\u2019s house.  \u201cHe did not know what I was talking about,\u201d Corpina told  Bloomberg Radio  yesterday. \u201cHe said \u2018I\u2019m staring at the White House and there\u2019s nothing going on here right now.\u2019\u201d  There was something going on in the market, with the Standard & Poor\u2019s 500 Index reversing a 1 percent rally after a hacker got hold of an Associated Press Twitter account and sent a post claiming explosions had injured President  Barack Obama . The plunge has drawn scrutiny to the computerized systems that dominate the  $18 trillion  U.S. market, including programs that base trading decisions on news headlines, and the role of humans in managing them.  The incident is also raising concerns over trustworthiness of information spread on Twitter less than a month after social media received the blessing of regulators to be a conduit for market-moving news.  Luis Aguilar , a commissioner with the Securities and Exchange Commission, said he asked staff to look at whether the hacking was an attempt to manipulate the market. Jenny Shearer, a spokeswoman with the  Federal Bureau  of Investigation, said the agency was investigating the matter with the AP and Twitter Inc.  Security Review  The AP restored its Twitter account this morning after suspending it yesterday for a security review. Hackers have made repeated attempts to gain access to AP reporters\u2019 passwords, the AP said, adding it was working to fix any vulnerabilities.  The  S&P 500  was up 1 percent at about 1,578 at 1:08 p.m. New York time yesterday before the post on the AP Twitter account sent stocks lower. The benchmark gauge for American stocks erased almost the entire gain, falling  as low as  1,563.03 by 1:10 p.m. and wiping out about $136 billion in market value from companies in the index.  The index recovered from the plunge within three minutes as investors determined the post was incorrect and the news service confirmed that its Twitter account had been hacked and there were no explosions. The  S&P 500 (SPX)  ended the session up 1 percent at 1,578.78 as better-than-estimated earnings and growth in home sales lifted stocks.  \u2018Humans Win\u2019  Corpina and other traders said the dip in stocks may have started when program-trading systems ingested the fake news and canceled buy orders while automated sell orders looked to dump shares.  \u201cNo human believed the story,\u201d Rick Fier, director of equity trading at Conifer Securities LLC in New York, said in an interview. Washington Post Co. was unchanged for the two minutes, while Gilead Sciences Inc. dropped 2.1 percent for the biggest loss among the 500 members.  \u2018Efficient Selloff\u2019  Exxon Mobil Corp., Apple Inc., Johnson & Johnson and Microsoft Corp. briefly lost about 1 percent in two minutes before rebounding. The plunge didn\u2019t trigger circuit breakers for individual stocks. Shares for most companies pause for five minutes if they lose 10 percent in five minutes.  \u201cIt was a very efficient selloff that was met with an equally efficient rebound,\u201d  Peter Kenny , managing director for institutional sales at Knight Capital Group Inc., a financial services company in  Jersey City ,  New Jersey , said in a phone interview. \u201cIt gave everyone on the desk a very brief moment to consider the news, the likelihood of the news and to not overreact. The default was pause and assess, not react.\u201d  The  Dow Jones Industrial Average (INDU)  lost about 145 points from its level at 1:08 p.m. before recovering and ending the session 152.29 points higher on the day at 14,719.46. VIX Jumps  The Chicago Board Options Exchange Volatility Index, or VIX, surged more than 9 percent from 13.6 at 1:08 p.m. to as high as 14.87 at 1:10 p.m. before reversing the gain in the following three minutes. The VIX, which moves in the opposite direction as the S&P 500 about 80 percent of the time, ended the session 6.3 percent lower at 13.48 and is down 25 percent for the year.  Stock markets have become predominantly electronic over the last 15 years as technology costs fell, rules changed and computers that match orders replaced human traders. Algorithms, which buy or sell larger orders in smaller pieces across venues, automated a process previously handled by individuals as the complexity and speed of markets increased.  Some trading firms incorporate data feeds designed to identify market-making news into algorithms so they can try to buy or sell before the information is widely disseminated. Bloomberg LP, the parent of  Bloomberg News , provides news feeds for use by algorithmic and computerized trading systems. News Corp.\u2019s Dow Jones unit, Thomson Reuters Corp. and other vendors supply similar feeds.  \u2018Algos Evolve\u2019  \u201cThis is early in the game for algos integrating news feeds,\u201d  Robert Stowsky , senior analyst at Boston-based research firm Aite Group LLC, said in an e-mail. \u201cInclusion of verification from a second trusted source is inevitable as news-based algos evolve. It\u2019s unnerving.\u201d  Traders said the selloff may have been exacerbated by so-called stop-loss orders, which are placed by investors to automatically sell stocks when declines of a specified threshold are reached.  \u201cThe whole lesson is never do stop-losses,\u201d said  Barry Schwartz ,  fund manager  with Baskin Financial Services Inc. in Toronto. He helps manage about C$500 million ($487 million). \u201cThat\u2019s what I took from this.\u201d  Flash-Crash Flashback  Yesterday\u2019s plunge reminded many traders of the May 2010 flash crash that briefly erased $862 billion in market value in less than 20 minutes. Regulators and exchanges are altering the speed bumps adopted after that incident in an effort to boost confidence in a market that has become faster and more complex.  Under the limit-up\/limit-down system, which is going into effect gradually for stocks, trades aren\u2019t allowed to occur at more-than specified percentages above or below a stock\u2019s rolling five-minute average price.  The changes are intended to prevent a repeat of the flash crash, which was caused partly by one firm\u2019s trade in stock-index futures, according to a study released Oct. 1 that year by the Securities and Exchange Commission and the U.S. Commodity Futures Trading Commission.  The trading algorithm employed by the firm, identified by two people with knowledge of the findings as Waddell & Reed Financial Inc., sparked the rapid selling of  stock futures  because it took into account volume but not price or time, the report said. Earlier this week I spent a few hours at the federal\ncourthouse in downtown  Manhattan  reading through the  hundreds of\nletters  sent on Rajat Gupta\u2019s behalf to U.S. District Judge Jed Rakoff. Gupta is the former Goldman Sachs board member and\nMcKinsey & Co. managing partner who is scheduled  to be sentenced \nfor  securities fraud  next week. Prosecutors have said they\nbelieve Gupta should receive about eight to 10 years in prison.  The letters that most interested me were from people with\nties to Berkshire Hathaway, the conglomerate run by  Warren Buffett . One person  who wrote  was Microsoft founder  Bill Gates ,\nwho is a member of Berkshire\u2019s board of directors.  Another was \nAjit Jain, Berkshire\u2019s reinsurance chief.  A third  was Manoj Singh, chief operating officer of  Deloitte Touche Tohmatsu .\nDeloitte\u2019s U.S. arm, Deloitte & Touche LLP, is Berkshire\u2019s\nindependent audit firm.  Here\u2019s the rub. Gupta was convicted of illegally tipping\nhis friend and business partner, hedge-fund manager  Raj Rajaratnam , about Berkshire\u2019s $5 billion investment in Goldman\nin September 2008. Rajaratnam, who got an 11-year prison\nsentence, used that information to trade illegally in Goldman\u2019s\nstock. This is why it seems awkward, and perhaps even\ninappropriate, for Gates, Jain and Singh to have written to the\njudge seeking leniency for Gupta.  Their letters were of a personal nature. None identified\nhis business relationship with Berkshire. Nonetheless, it would\nhave been better for the three of them to have kept their views\nto themselves on this occasion.  When Gupta passed along the illicit tip, he wasn\u2019t only\nmisappropriating information from Goldman. He was stealing from\nBerkshire, too. By sending their own personal appeals for\nleniency, Gates, Jain and Singh chose a side and put themselves\nat odds with those Berkshire stakeholders who disagree with them\n-- and surely there are plenty who do.  My own view is this isn\u2019t something a corporate director, a\nhigh-ranking executive or a professional at an ostensibly\nindependent audit firm should have done. ( Singh  identified\nhimself in his letter as Deloitte\u2019s chief operating officer.)  One final note: Gupta also was convicted of providing\nRajaratnam with inside information he learned as a board member\nat Procter & Gamble, which is another Deloitte audit client.\nIronically, Deloitte\u2019s own former vice chairman, Thomas Flanagan,  pleaded guilty  to  insider trading  in August;  the\ngovernment said  he made $420,000 of illegal trading profits\nusing inside information he obtained about several Deloitte\naudit clients. Separately, Flanagan in 2010 settled  a complaint \nby the Securities and Exchange Commission that accused him of\nviolating auditor-independence rules by trading in shares of\nseveral Deloitte audit clients -- including Berkshire.  Flanagan is scheduled to be sentenced Oct. 26, two days\nafter Gupta. The docket in Flanagan\u2019s case says the character\nreference letters written on his behalf have been sealed. (BBRY) \u2019s fate seemed to be decided two years ago after its market value plummeted by $65 billion. It took losing another $13 billion since then for the board to hang a for-sale sign.  The smartphone maker yesterday said for the first time it\u2019s considering a sale, after a string of quarterly revenue  declines  in the past two years pushed its market value down to $5.1 billion as of last week.  That\u2019s left the company as the cheapest among communications-equipment rivals in North America, according to data compiled by Bloomberg. Even at that valuation, the latest setback with its new BlackBerry 10 may rule out interest from most strategic buyers, making a buyout in conjunction with Canadian investors or a breakup the likeliest outcome.  \u201cIt makes sense that they might look at throwing in the towel as a public company,\u201d said  Malcolm Polley , who manages $1.1 billion as chief investment officer at Stewart Capital Advisors LLC in  Indiana ,  Pennsylvania . \u201cThey\u2019re trying to turn themselves around and make themselves relevant again.\u201d  BlackBerry has no  debt  and $2.8 billion of  cash  and marketable securities that could help finance a buyout, data compiled by Bloomberg show.  Canada Pension Plan Investment Board said last week it would weigh an investment if the company decided to go private, and Alberta Investment Management Corp. echoed that sentiment yesterday.  Sale Indication  BlackBerry, whose market value peaked at $83 billion in 2008, said yesterday that a special committee of the board has been tasked with finding ways to enhance its value and scale, including an outright sale, joint ventures or partnerships. It\u2019s the strongest indication yet that the company won\u2019t remain independent.  Last year, BlackBerry hired two banks to help evaluate options, none of which explicitly included a sale. Chief Executive Officer Thorsten Heins had said that it wasn\u2019t the \u201cmain direction\u201d he was considering at the time.  \u201cThis has certainly been a long time coming,\u201d Walter Todd, who helps oversee $950 million as chief investment officer of Greenwood Capital Associates LLC in Greenwood, South Carolina, said in a phone interview. \u201cThey need to do something, whether that\u2019s taking themselves private or selling out to another company. That said, there\u2019s not a ton of strategic buyers left that would be interested.\u201d  Cheap Valuation  The stock rose 10 percent to $10.78 yesterday, giving the company a market value of $5.65 billion. At a 50 percent discount to its revenue, BlackBerry has the cheapest price-sales ratio among North American communications-equipment makers with market capitalizations exceeding $500 million, data compiled by Bloomberg show.  Today, BlackBerry climbed 1.4 percent to $10.93.  BlackBerry\u2019s board may be realizing what others have seen coming for at least two years. In 2011, investors and analysts told Bloomberg News that BlackBerry was a takeover candidate and that  Microsoft Corp. (MSFT) ,  Dell Inc. (DELL)  and Samsung Electronics Co. were among likely suitors at the time. While Microsoft is still a possible buyer, Todd of Greenwood Capital, a Microsoft  shareholder , said he hopes it doesn\u2019t bid for BlackBerry.  Samsung said in an e-mailed statement that the company \u201cis not considering the acquisition of BlackBerry.\u201d Dell declined to comment, and a representative for Microsoft didn\u2019t immediately return a phone call seeking comment.  Canada Participation  In April 2012, UBS AG analyst Phillip Huang said BlackBerry\u2019s fate and any potential takeover rested on the success of its Z10 and Q10 devices. So far, the lineup\u2019s debut has been lackluster, missing analysts\u2019 shipment estimates and failing to stem customer losses. The company posted a net loss last quarter.  A leveraged buyout is a feasible option, according to  Peter Misek , a New York-based analyst at Jefferies Group LLC. BlackBerry\u2019s  largest shareholder ,  Fairfax Financial Holdings Ltd. (FFH) , and some of Canada\u2019s pension plans are probably considering taking the smartphone maker private, he said in a research note yesterday.  Prem Watsa, CEO of Fairfax Financial, is stepping down from BlackBerry\u2019s board, raising the possibility he may play a role in the outcome of the strategic review. Watsa said his firm has no intention of selling its BlackBerry stake, which was 9.9 percent as of March 31, data compiled by Bloomberg show.  Pension Interest  If holders of 15 percent of BlackBerry\u2019s equity were to participate in a buyout, the remaining shareholders could be bought out for $15 a share, Misek estimates. Joseph Woodland, a co-inventor of\nthe system of thick and thin lines that today is the ubiquitous\nbar code, has died. He was 91.  He died on Dec. 9 at his home in Edgewater,  New Jersey , the\n New York  Times reported, citing his daughter, Susan Woodland. No\ncause was given.  Woodland and Bernard Silver developed the bar code as\ngraduate students at  Drexel University  in Philadelphia -- then\ncalled Drexel Institute of Technology -- in the late 1940s.  According to  Drexel, the head of a local grocery-store\nchain had sought the university\u2019s engineering help in 1948 to\nadvance the checkout process. Woodland, in an article in Wonders\nof Modern Technology, recalled that he took his inspiration from\nthe dots and dashes of Morse code.  \u201cI just extended the dots and dashes downwards and made\nnarrow lines and wide lines out of them,\u201d Woodland said in the\narticle, according to Drexel.  The system created by Woodland and  Silver  relied on the\nvarying brightness of light shone through the lines -- the\nthicker the line, the more light it blocked. The engineers filed\nfor a patent on Oct. 20, 1949.  Woodland went to work for  International Business Machines\nCorp. (IBM)  in 1951 with hopes that the idea would be further\ndeveloped. He received the patent, No. 2,612,994, on Oct. 7,\n1952,  according  to IBM.  Manhattan Project  In 1973, a rectangular bar code promoted by IBM, after\nsubstantial design input by Woodland, was formally adopted as\nthe Universal Product Code, according to the National Inventors\nHall of Fame, which inducted  Woodland  and Silver in 2011. Silver\ndied in 1963, according to the Times.  Norman Joseph Woodland was born on Sept. 6, 1921, and grew\nup in  Atlantic City , New Jersey, according to the Hall of Fame.  During World War II, he was a technical assistant on the\nManhattan Project to develop the world\u2019s first atom bomb,\naccording to an IBM  profile .  After the war, Woodland earned his bachelor of science in\nmechanical engineering from Drexel and a master of science at\n Syracuse University  in Syracuse, New York.  He retired from IBM in 1987. In 1992, he received the\nNational Medal of Technology from the U.S. Patent and Trademark\nOffice, along with Microsoft Corp. founder  Bill Gates  and six\nother recipients.  In addition to his daughter, Susan, Woodland is survived by\nhis wife, the former Jacqueline Blumberg, whom he married in\n1951; a second daughter, Betsy Karpenkopf; a brother, David; and\na granddaughter, according to the Times. Offices at nearby Soho Square, a favorite of technology and\nmedia companies like  Twenty-First Century Fox Inc. (FOXA) , go for 65\npounds a square foot, according to Lock. Workplaces on the\nStrand \u201ccan now accommodate those sort of rents,\u201d he said.  Tenants occupying 26 million square feet of central London\noffices have the option to move by the end of 2016, according to\nLock. Meanwhile, demand for central-London office space has\nrisen 13 percent from a year earlier, broker  Jones Lang LaSalle\nInc. (JLL)  said in a July report.  Limited Options  As leases expire, companies looking for new space will have\nto consider districts on the edges of the best West End\nneighborhoods. Options are limited because vacancy levels in\nMayfair, Soho and St. James\u2019s were about a quarter below the\nlong-term average at the end of June, broker  Knight Frank  said\nin an Aug. 1 report.  Kings Cross and Paddington are among areas on the edge of\nthe West End set to benefit from better transport links such as\nCrossrail, a high-speed train line that will link  Heathrow\nAirport  to the Canary Wharf financial district, Deutsche Bank AG\nresearchers including Simon Durkin wrote in a Sept. 3 report.  British Land Co. (BLND)  bought offices, stores and land near\nPaddington Station, the terminus of Heathrow Express trains, in\nJuly for 470 million pounds. The site, about 1.5 miles from\nMayfair, will give the developer an annual yield of 6.2 percent\nwhen fully leased, Chief Executive Officer Chris Grigg said on\nan investor call in July. That compares with a 3.5 percent yield\nfor offices in prime West End areas, broker  Savills Plc (SVS)  said\nlast month. Yields for the best U.K. property nationwide fell to\n5.66 percent on average in August, the lowest in more than five\nyears, Cushman & Wakefield said in a report yesterday.  Larger Floors  \u201cIt\u2019s those larger floor-prints which really make a\ndifference,\u201d Grigg said in a July 24 interview.  British Land, the U.K.\u2019s second-largest REIT, also owns\nRegent\u2019s Place, a development less than a mile from Oxford\nStreet, where rents are more than 60 pounds a square foot, Grigg\nsaid. That\u2019s an increase of more than 20 percent in less than\ntwo years.  Developers betting on the expanded West End will face\nmounting competition from new projects in the City of London,\nmany offering cheaper rents and targeting the same technology,\nmedia and telecommunications companies. Amazon.com Inc. chose to\nlocate south of Farringdon, on the City\u2019s western edge, where\nrents are about 48 pounds a square foot.  Farther east is London\u2019s emerging technology hub nicknamed\n\u201cSilicon Roundabout\u201d on Old Street.  Derwent London Plc (DLN) , a REIT\nfocused on central London, is tailoring a 290,000-square-foot\noffice complex to tech firms with construction set to begin next\nyear.  Google\u2019s Gain  Google opted for the West End\u2019s northern edge in King\u2019s\nCross, buying 2.4 acres (1 hectare) of land that\u2019s part of a\nlarger development by King\u2019s Cross Central LP near the Eurostar\nrail link to mainland Europe. The owner of the world\u2019s largest\nsearch engine is building its new U.K. headquarters on the site\nabout 1.5 miles northeast of Oxford Street.  Tenants \u201care drifting east from the West End,\u201d enticed by\ncheaper office space neighboring companies with global brands\nlike Google, said Guy Grantham, a  Colliers International \ndirector in London. \u201cWe were expecting mostly media and\ntechnology tenants, but we\u2019re seeing occupiers from the legal\nsectors and beyond\u201d consider King\u2019s Cross, he said.  Rents for the best buildings in Kings Cross are forecast to\nrise more than 20 percent to about 65 pounds a square foot by\n2016, according to Colliers.  \u201cThese peripheral locations people talk about will no\nlonger be peripheral,\u201d said  Mike Prew , a Jefferies Group LLC\nanalyst in London. They\nshould also do fine if the economy improves, as I expect.  \n Only 8 percent of U.S. companies with a market value of\n$250 million or more achieved a return of 25 percent or more on\nstockholders\u2019 equity last year. And only 23 percent of companies\nhave debt less than 10 percent of stockholders\u2019 equity.  \n The real trick is meeting both criteria at once. A paltry 2\npercent of companies managed the feat last year.  \n The three largest companies that qualify are  Apple Inc. ,\n Mastercard Inc.  and  Gap Inc.  Of those three, I prefer Gap\nbecause it sells for 12 times earnings compared with 23 for\nApple and 18 for Mastercard. However, there are smaller stocks I\nlike better.  \n Let\u2019s begin with  Western Digital Corp . Based in Lake\nForest, California, Western Digital is the world\u2019s No. 2\nmanufacturer of hard disk drives for personal computers.  Seagate\nTechnology , based in the Cayman Islands and run from Scotts\nValley, California, is No. 1. The two rivals hold more than half\nthe market.  \n Technological obsolescence might threaten the big two some\nday. Solid state drives or other innovations could someday\nreplace the spinning disks in common use now. For the moment,\nthough, the threat seems distant. Western Digital has been\nprofitable in its past eight fiscal years.  \n Rising Computer Sales  \n Disk makers should benefit from the transition to Microsoft\nCorp.\u2019s Windows 7 as the standard operating system for PCs. Many\nbusinesses that normally replace their computers every three\nyears delayed purchases during the recession.  \n Now that the recession seems to be over and Windows 7 is\navailable, I foresee robust spending on new personal computers\nby both corporations and individuals in 2010 and 2011. Western\nDigital sells for six times earnings.  \n Next let\u2019s look at  Wet Seal Inc. , an apparel retailer\nlocated in Foothill Ranch, California. It sells clothing to\nteenage girls and young women at its Wet Seal stores, and offers\nwomen\u2019s fashions at its Arden B. line.  \n Wet Seal is debt free, a quality I find alluring. Its\ncurrent ratio (assets divided by liabilities) is a healthy 3.9.  \n Unlike Western Digital, which has been consistently\nprofitable in recent years, Wet Seal\u2019s performance has been\nerratic. It posted losses every year from 2004 through 2007.\nUnder Chief Executive Officer  Edmond Thomas , it seems to have\nturned around and gotten back onto profitable footing.  \n Financially Sound  \n Never will I rest easy owning shares in a clothing\nretailer: Fashion is too fickle. But I like Wet Seal\u2019s financial\nstrength and its low valuations. The stock sells for four times\nearnings.  \n Another comeback story is New York-based  Loral Space &\nCommunications Inc. , which operates a fleet of communications\nsatellites. A predecessor company went bankrupt in 2003, but the\ncurrent Loral, which emerged from Chapter 11 bankruptcy in 2005,\nis debt free and earned a $232 million profit last year on sales\nof $993 million.  \n Loral lost money in four of the past six years.\nDisenchanted investors value the stock at less than five times\nearnings. Disgruntled analysts don\u2019t bother to cover it. The\nstock is covered by one small brokerage firm, which rates it\n\u201chold.\u201d  \n I think Loral is an interesting speculation for a risk-\ntolerant investor.  \n Controversial Pick  \n Also worth considering, though highly controversial, is\ngunmaker  Sturm Ruger & Co. , located in Southport, Connecticut.  \n Last year the company earned $27 million on sales of $271\nmillion. It has been profitable every year for at least two\ndecades though earnings have bounced up and down. Only three\nanalysts follow the stock, and all suggest buying it.  \n There is, of course, a moral aspect to this investment. The\ncities of New York and Washington unsuccessfully sued Sturm\nRuger and other gunmakers, alleging that they sell weapons to\ncareless or greedy dealers who allow them to fall into the hands\nof criminals. The company\u2019s defenders say the weapons are used\nmainly by law-enforcement officers, the military and hunters.  \n Sturm Ruger is debt free and earned a 34 percent return on\nequity last year. The stock sells for 10 times earnings.  \n Disclosure note: I own Western Digital personally and for\nclients. I have no long or short positions in the other stocks\ndiscussed in this week\u2019s column.  \n ( John Dorfman , chairman of Thunderstorm Capital in Boston,\nis a columnist for Bloomberg News.
